## Series title page

**THE COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, AND ECONOMICAL LIBRARY OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINT OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THAT HAVE SURVIVED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, CAREFULLY COLLATED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH VARIOUS MANUSCRIPTS, AND MOST DILIGENTLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED BY DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE EXTENSIVE EDITIONS PRODUCED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES HAD BEEN COMPLETED; PROVIDED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING EACH VOLUME OR EACH AUTHOR OF ANY IMPORTANCE; ADORNED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY SET OUT WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AS WELL AS WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; AUGMENTED BY WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDICES: THE FIRST, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH EVERYTHING WRITTEN BY EACH OF THE FATHERS ON ANY THEME MAY BE SEEN AT A GLANCE; THE SECOND, OF SACRED SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY EASILY DISCOVER WHICH FATHERS, AND IN WHICH PLACES OF THEIR WORKS, COMMENTED ON THE INDIVIDUAL TEXTS OF THE INDIVIDUAL BOOKS OF SCRIPTURE. AN EDITION MOST ACCURATE AND EASILY PREFERABLE TO ALL OTHERS, IF ONE CONSIDERS THE CLARITY OF THE TYPE, THE QUALITY OF THE PAPER, THE INTEGRITY OF THE TEXT, THE PERFECTION OF THE CORRECTIONS, THE VARIETY AND NUMBER OF THE WORKS REPRINTED, THE EXTREMELY CONVENIENT FORMAT OF THE VOLUMES, CONSTANTLY SIMILAR THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE WORK, THE LOW PRICE, AND ABOVE ALL THIS COLLECTION, SINGLE, METHODICAL, AND CHRONOLOGICAL, OF SIX HUNDRED FRAGMENTS AND SHORT WORKS HITHERTO SCATTERED HERE AND THERE, BUT NOW FOR THE FIRST TIME BROUGHT TOGETHER IN OUR LIBRARY FROM WORKS RELATING TO EVERY AGE, PLACE, LANGUAGE, AND FORM.**

**SECOND SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical science.

# [The Complete Works of Venantius Fortunatus]

[Col. 0009]

# Dedication

To the most illustrious and most reverend lord, Don Nicolaus Antonius Justinianus, formerly a Benedictine Cassinese monk and bishop of Padua, Michael Angelus Luchi, monk of the same congregation, offers respectful greetings.

This work was owed entirely to you and to your name, most illustrious and most reverend bishop; and if it now emerges into public view, the credit must be referred wholly to you. For you were at once the one who encouraged me to undertake and begin it, and throughout you remained my helper and overseer in bringing it to completion and perfection—not merely devoting care and concern to it, but also supplying the necessary expenses.

Accordingly, even if there were no other reason why this work of mine should now be dedicated to your name, that one reason alone would seem sufficient and just to all, or at least to fair-minded judges of affairs. But since this is joined by the circumstance that so many distinguished and illustrious adornments—whether of family and lineage, rank and dignity, or character and intellect—have combined with wonderful harmony to honor and exalt you, such as one might scarcely find in any other man, I earnestly wished that this work of mine, whatever its worth, might be dignified by your auspices and patronage.

If I consider your lineage and the family from which you descend, it is reckoned among the oldest and noblest of the Venetian patrician houses. From it, throughout the ages, the republic has received its gravest and wisest governors; the churches, capable and industrious bishops; and heaven, many heroes distinguished by outstanding piety and religion.

If instead I consider your dignity and position, you preside over a Church that rightly outshines and surpasses so many others in splendor, antiquity, succession of pastors, virtue, number, and privileges, that the greatness of the see which you occupy makes that dignity which you share with other princes or pastors of the Church in you somehow more splendid and august.

Finally, the adornments of your character and intellect are sufficiently proved and displayed both by the books you have published, filled with every liberal discipline and refined by industry, and especially by your concern and diligence in governing your Church and feeding your flock, your generosity toward the poor, and your zeal and munificence in building the great hospice at Padua.

Each of these qualities is of such a kind that, by itself, it both wins true and solid praise for you and can bring great light and benefit toward recommending the labor and intellect of another who enjoys your patronage.

To these considerations is added the fact that Venantius Fortunatus—whose poems and other writings, contained in these two volumes, we are publishing—was born at Duplavilis [a place belonging to your diocese] and seems in a certain sense to desire you as his patron and protector. While he lived in Gaul, he dedicated and inscribed his poems to Gregory of Tours, a most learned man and his dear friend, then bishop of the principal see. Now, after his death, as though coming to life again through a new edition of his works, he rightly calls for and demands you as his patron. His native soil is subject to your jurisdiction and authority because of the greatness of the see which you occupy.

Since matters stand thus, I ask that you receive this work, which appears in public marked with your name, in such a way that you regard it as a gift owed to you and at the same time embrace the spirit of the giver. I am bound to you by many ties of respect, service, and devoted affection; and an even greater reason for service is added by the fact that the Cassinese congregation educated, formed, and nurtured me—an order to which you also once belonged, although later, in recognition of your blameless life and merit, and for the greater good of the Christian commonwealth, you were called first to govern the Churches of Torcello, then Verona, and finally Padua. Thus you exchanged the silence and solitude of the monastery for the splendor and renown of the most populous Churches and sees.

For a long time I had wished to bear witness, by some testimonial, to the respect and connection I feel toward you, arising from the reasons I have mentioned. This seemed the most suitable opportunity, since, expressed in a literary monument and published for the public, it could not remain unknown to anyone and might survive into our own times and reach even a distant posterity.

Meanwhile, although I am bodily far away and separated by long distances of land, I am present in spirit and most obediently kiss your sacred hands.

Rome, on the Nones of July, 1786.

[Col. 0009]

# Preface

Since we have undertaken this new edition of the works of Venantius Fortunatus at the command and recommendation of the most illustrious and most reverend lord Nicolaus Antonius Justinianus, formerly a Benedictine Cassinese monk and now bishop of Padua, it will not be out of place to state briefly here what moved that distinguished and learned man to arrange a new edition of Fortunatus’s works.

First, no one who has even a slight acquaintance with the study of antiquity is unaware how much assistance and light everyone customarily draws from the writings of Fortunatus for illuminating the history of the sixth century, and especially the Church and kingdom of Gaul. That man, most renowned in his age for learning and piety, was bound in the closest friendship with the leading bishops of Gaul, who excelled either in holiness or learning [Col. 0011], and with many other nobles and eminent men of that kingdom. He was also welcome and acceptable to the very kings who then ruled in Gaul and to their royal families, and wrote much about them and to them, both in prose and in verse, concerning matters that served to illuminate their private affairs and fortunes, public business, and the condition of the kingdom as a whole.

I can therefore safely affirm that the names and deeds of many bishops of that age and many nobles of the kingdom of Gaul would already have lain in perpetual oblivion had Fortunatus not handed them down to later posterity in his writings. His poems have rescued their names and sees from oblivion, and they provide much light and assistance for marking and dating the periods in which those men lived or in which something worthy of remembrance occurred in their cities and provinces.

It should therefore not be surprising that almost all who subsequently wrote about Gallic affairs in any age drew from this source.

Nor are the materials that can be drawn from Fortunatus’s works for confirming the doctrines of religion itself and defending them against the ingenuity and new inventions of heterodox writers few, insignificant, or obscure. Since they are supported by the testimony and authority of a respectable antiquity, they ought to be of great value in refuting the slanders of those same opponents.

Add to this the charm of cultivated elegance, which is found expressed throughout the writings of Fortunatus. Thus, for more than one reason, it is of no small importance that the works—whether of another author or, certainly, of Fortunatus himself—should be brought into public view as fully illuminated, corrected, and enlarged as possible.

Although several men have labored in this matter, and the works have often been published and enlarged by new additions, I do not know how it happened that, according to almost everyone’s wishes and judgment, they still seemed to need greater light.

The first edition of Fortunatus’s works, completed at Cagliari in Sardinia in 1573, contains nothing other than his hymns, corrected by Cassander and, as Cassander himself declares, restored to their original integrity.

A copy of his works, likewise produced at Cagliari in the following year through the work and care of Jacobus Salvator Solanus and printed by Nicolaus Canyelles, was divided into eight books. In the judgment of the most learned men, however, it was defective and mutilated, and corrupted and deformed by almost innumerable errors.

When it was transferred to the Venetian edition, published by the heirs of Jacobus Simbenius in 1578, it appeared infected and disfigured by the same errors and by still more. Reprinted once again at Cagliari in 1584 and at Cologne in 1600, with Expositions on the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer also added, it was no more cleansed or purified.

Among these editions, the Parisian copy, which was inserted into volume 8 of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers of the Church* and published at Paris, surpassed all the others in the number of books. Yet even this copy, torn and mutilated by the loss of many poems and corrupted in many places by an altered and faulty reading, seemed to call for a more careful and fuller edition.

The distinguished Father Christopher Browerus of the Society of Jesus undertook this task and completed and published it at Mainz in 1603, printed by Balthasar Lippius. He renewed and corrected it in 1617, likewise published at Mainz at the expense of Bernard Gualther, a Cologne bookseller, and printed by Johannes Volmarius.

This edition of Fortunatus’s works certainly appeared fuller, more careful, and more elegantly presented than all those previously prepared. With the help of manuscript codices, Browerus added to his copy much that had not previously been published and carefully corrected material that bristled with almost innumerable errors.

He states that he used chiefly three highly trustworthy manuscripts: one from Trier, another—from which he claimed more value than from the others—from the abbey of Saint Gall, and a third from the abbey of Siegburg. He also reports that he had in his possession a manuscript fragment from the Church of Trier and another manuscript fragment from Cusa.

Furthermore, he collated his copy with the published editions from Cagliari, Venice, and Paris in the *Library of the Fathers*, as well as with Georg Fabricius’s *Sacred Poets*. He added an old manuscript of unusual quality belonging to Friedrich Tiliobroga and a manuscript book of Theodorus Pulmann of Craneburg, which Theodorus himself had carefully collated with ancient books and copied in 1570; he also set out various readings in the margin.

Browerus adorned and enlarged this edition with both a Life of Fortunatus composed by himself and extensive notes. He may therefore truly be said to have deserved well of our Fortunatus.

Browerus’s copy, together with the Life of Fortunatus, was later reprinted at Lyons in 1677 in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*. It was, however, sprinkled here and there with several errors through the carelessness of the printers, as I was able to establish by collating it with Browerus’s copy published at Mainz in 1617.

Although Brower’s edition was more successful and complete than all those that had appeared up to that time, there still seemed to be certain things that should be added to it, corrected, or more accurately noted.

Some poems that were unknown in Brower’s time, or at least had not come into his hands, later came to light. These, scattered here and there among the works of other authors, had to be collected and attached to Brower’s edition. Moreover, many prose writings, which Browerus did not think should be joined to his edition, seemed properly to belong among the other works of Fortunatus, so that all the writings we have received from him, whether in verse or prose, might be contained together in one work.

The notes with which Browerus thought the writings of Venantius Fortunatus should be adorned and illuminated, although generally learned and scholarly, were nevertheless sometimes excessively long, sometimes incomplete and barren, and occasionally false and erroneous through mistakes and confusion in dating events. They therefore called for another hand and greater diligence.

For these reasons, the most illustrious and most reverend Nicolaus Antonius [Col. 0013] Justinianus, whom I mentioned above, judged that a new edition of Fortunatus’s works should be prepared and entrusted this task to me, whatever strength I might be able to bring to its completion.

He believed that it would produce great usefulness and benefit—as I indicated above—for confirming religion, illuminating the memory of that age, and adorning letters themselves. He also judged that it would bring no small distinction and light to the Church of Padua, which he governs and feeds with exceptional care and diligence, since Duplavilis belongs to its diocese and the most certain and weighty evidence confirms that it was Fortunatus’s native land, as we shall show in his Life.

Now, to give some account of the labor and work I devoted to collating, illuminating, and enlarging the writings of Venantius, and to place before the reader some view or form of the entire edition I have undertaken, I retained and preserved whatever in Brower’s copy deserved to be retained and preserved.

Let this, as it always will, be counted as no ordinary praise of that distinguished man: he searched out in the hidden recesses and secret places of ancient libraries so many poems of Fortunatus that had previously been unknown to everyone; he corrected and brought them forth; and he tested, chastened, and revised those already published according to the authority and testimony of manuscript codices.

Accordingly, we transferred Brower’s copy intact into this edition of ours. He had prepared it according to manuscripts of the best quality, and we judged that the readings of those codices—which we ourselves were unable to consult—were sufficiently indicated and expressed in his text. If anything seemed less satisfactory and could be better supplied from elsewhere, we preferred to note it rather than alter Brower’s text contrary to the form in which he had published it.

Thus our edition contains, as it were, two copies: the one first published by Browerus, and the one which we ourselves have supplied by indicating better readings.

We collated all the works of Fortunatus contained in the first volume with three complete Vatican manuscript codices, formerly belonging to the Palatine Library, as carefully as we could. We conjectured that they had been written around the ninth or perhaps the tenth century.

Moreover, whenever torn and worn parchment leaves appeared to contain some poem or other work of Fortunatus, we extracted whatever variation they offered in the reading and carefully entered it in its proper place.

Since the three manuscripts just mentioned all lacked poem 6 of book VIII and the four books *On the Life of Saint Martin*, these materials were supplied by another codex of no lower antiquity, likewise belonging to the Vatican Library, which we were able to collate with them.

We also collated once again with Brower’s copy the copy of the Cagliari edition published at Venice in 1578 by the heirs of Jacobus Simbenius. Whatever Brower had noticed and recorded less fully, but which nevertheless seemed worthy of notice to us, we recorded, after carefully separating it from the almost innumerable errors with which that edition abounds.

Nor, if we found some variation in any other edition, did we think it should be neglected.

We have added to this edition the poems of Fortunatus that came to our knowledge and were lacking from Brower’s edition.

Thus, in book II, chapter 10, we appended a hymn written by our Fortunatus to Saint Dionysius the martyr, the first bishop of Paris, published by the distinguished Dubletus in his *Antiquities of Saint-Denis*.

To the same book II were added poem 8, on sacred baptism, and poem 9, in praise of chrism, likewise written by Fortunatus, as we have noted in their proper places.

We also added poem 21, written in praise of Saint Martial, the first bishop of Limoges. Until this time it had remained hidden at Florence in the Laurentian Library, written in a codex of the early twelfth century. It was first published at Rome in 1783 in *Literary Anecdotes*, volume IV, printed by Antonius Fulgonius.

Furthermore, we transcribed from the hymnary of the distinguished Cardinal Tomasi two hymns used by the Church on feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mary. One begins, “Whom earth, sea, and sky”; the other, “Hail, Star of the Sea.” They are read there under the name of Venantius Fortunatus, and we inserted them in book VIII, chapters 4 and 5.

We added to the same book poem 8, which appeared in a Vatican codex at the end of Fortunatus’s works. Since it seemed to possess the style and character of Fortunatus himself in writing, we judged that it should be transferred into this edition.

It seemed scarcely possible to correct it, however, because it was sprinkled with numerous errors arising from the ignorance of the copyists. In fact, although I have restored much of it to its integrity, certain passages remain for which no probable conjecture could be offered.

Likewise, in chapter 9 of book X, we added a poem written in praise of King Childebert, which the distinguished Mabillon had published in the first volume of the *Ancient Analecta*, page 360.

At the end of book XI we appended a poem apparently recited by Fortunatus at a gathering of the nuns of the monastery of Poitiers, perhaps on the day on which he was consecrated bishop. It was supplied to us by a worn sheet attached to one of the Vatican codices, as we have indicated in its proper place.

The second part of our edition contains the Lives of the saints which ancient testimony and similarity of style have identified as works composed by Fortunatus. They had hitherto been scattered among various writers, but now, for the first time—as far as I know—are brought together and published with the other works of Fortunatus.

Some of these we took from the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*; others were supplied to us by the Bollandists or by other authors, as we have carefully indicated in their proper places.

We also thought it appropriate to append the learned notes with which we found them enlarged and adorned by distinguished editors, adding some of our own wherever it seemed useful.

We further added the *Acts of the Passion of Saint Dionysius, Bishop of Paris*, published by the distinguished Bosquetus in the second part of the *Ecclesiastical History of Gaul*. At the same time we presented the arguments by which Adrian Valesius attempts to show, against Launoy, that this work was composed by Fortunatus.

Finally, we placed here the Creed commonly called the Athanasian Creed, together with an exposition written on it which the distinguished [Col. 0015] Muratorius published in the second volume of his *Anecdotes*, page 212. He extracted it from a parchment codex of the Ambrosian Library.

Muratorius thinks that one or the other of these works may perhaps be attributed to our Fortunatus. We have presented the considerations by which he supports his opinion and have also indicated our own judgment.

As for Brower’s notes on the poems of Fortunatus, it had indeed been my intention to add them in their entirety to this edition. Their excessive and often useless length, however, as well as the errors into which he is occasionally found to have fallen, entirely dissuaded us from that plan.

We therefore thought it better to select from Browerus those observations that were free from error and seemed useful for shedding light on the subject, and to present them as products of that distinguished man’s learning, rather than to append everything indiscriminately.

Where Browerus himself or someone else seemed to have been mistaken, we have declared our judgment as best we could, while awaiting in good faith the same service from others if we ourselves, as human beings, should have been mistaken in anything.

Whatever could contribute to illuminating Fortunatus’s own works and came to our knowledge, we gathered and excerpted from every source, faithfully and without envy assigning the names of those from whom we borrowed anything.

Gregory of Tours, Fortunatus’s contemporary, gave us especially great assistance, as did other writers on Gallic affairs.

Browerus also contributed much help in identifying and marking the places in Germany mentioned by Fortunatus. Since he had lived in those very places when writing about them, we attributed great authority to him and therefore did not hesitate sometimes to transcribe his testimony in full.

This would perhaps be the place to examine those matters that are occasionally doubtful and obscure in the works of Fortunatus. We preferred, however, to bring each matter back for examination in its proper place and state what we thought about it, rather than distract readers from the subject and send them elsewhere.

It seems more appropriate now to investigate which of the works we have received as composed by Fortunatus may have been lost through the injury of time, or which, although adorned by the ancients with different titles, may appear to be other works than those now in our hands, even though they were not inscribed with the same titles.

Paul the Deacon, in *History of the Lombards*, book II, section 13, relates that Fortunatus composed hymns for individual feasts. Trithemius, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, while listing Fortunatus’s works, counts seventy-seven hymns collected into a single volume and states that they were written by Fortunatus himself.

He places first the hymn that appears in our edition in book VIII, chapter 3, beginning, “Let every age acknowledge,” and so forth.

We, however, possess only a very small number of hymns that we know to have been composed by Venantius; and these are scattered among Fortunatus’s other works, so that they should certainly not be judged to be the hymns of which Paul the Deacon and Trithemius speak.

It must therefore be concluded either that those hymns were destroyed by age, that they still lie somewhere unknown, or that they are circulated under the names of others.

Browerus, however, by no means agrees that as many hymns were composed by Venantius as Trithemius records. The total number of hymns, he says, which the Church recites throughout the year is ninety-two, or not many more; most of these can safely be assigned to their authors, and only very few to Fortunatus.

Yet it is entirely possible that, in the time of Paul the Deacon, more hymns composed by our Venantius were being used throughout Gaul to celebrate the feasts of the saints, and that later others were substituted in their place, as frequently happens; or that, after being corrected and restored by others, they ceased to be called Fortunatus’s by most people, even though, collected into a single volume by someone, they survived until the age of Trithemius.

Certainly the hymn written by Fortunatus to Saint Dionysius the martyr, of which we spoke above and which seems to have been composed for the use of the Church of Paris, later became obsolete and was removed from the catalogue of hymns. Unknown to everyone, it lay for a long time in dust and darkness until the distinguished Dubletus unearthed it and published it in the *Antiquities of Saint-Denis*.

Likewise, the ancient codex of the distinguished Cardinal Tomasi shows that two hymns written in praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary, continually used and retained by the Church, are Fortunatus’s, as we stated above.

Sigibertus also, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45, mentions a *Hodoeporicon* of Fortunatus. It is uncertain whether this short work has perished or whether it is one of the works that survive, in which Fortunatus describes some journey of his own—either from Italy to Gaul or through Gaul to some place in Gaul or Germany.

Paul the Deacon seems to indicate this same *Hodoeporicon* when he says, in the passage cited above, that Venantius recounts in his poems the journey by which he went to Gaul.

Unless perhaps he meant that part of a poem in which Fortunatus, in book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, addresses in poetic fashion the little book he is sending from Gaul to Italy and shows it the route it must take, indicating in reverse order the very places through which he himself had passed while traveling from Italy to Gaul.

Indeed, the names of the cities and regions mentioned there correspond closely to those listed by Paul.

Or perhaps Trithemius mentions Fortunatus’s *Hodoeporicon* under this title: *Hodoeporicon of his journey, book I*. This seems to separate it from book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*.

Someone might conjecture that the *Hodoeporicon* of which Trithemius and Sigibertus speak is poem 10 of book X. In it Fortunatus gives an extended account of the journey by which he reached Metz, to King Childebert, and then, after departing with the royal family and its entourage, entered the Moselle and other rivers and traveled through the surrounding cities and towns.

This conjecture does not seem implausible.

Browerus thinks that Trithemius means poem 27 of book XI, which is written to Agnes and Radegund and is entitled *On His Journey*. It may seem strange, however, that so short a poem should be counted as a book.

Giraldus, in his *History of Poets*, dialogue 5, appears to confuse Fortunatus’s *Hodoeporicon* with the poem he himself wrote to the emperor Justin and the empress Sophia under the name of Radegund.

For after listing among Fortunatus’s works a poem *On the Destruction of Thuringia*, he adds that Fortunatus wrote a *Hodoeporicon of his* [Col. 0017] *journey* to the younger emperor Justin and to the empress Sophia.

Moreover, Vossius, in *On Latin Historians*, book II, and J. Albert Fabricius, in the *Latin Library of the Middle and Lower Ages*, cite the same poem under the same title. It is therefore possible that it was found in certain manuscripts with the title *Hodoeporicon*.

Or might it be that this poem was given to those whom Radegund sent to Constantinople as a companion for their journey, so that they might offer thanks to Justin and the empress Sophia for the wood of the Holy Cross sent from Radegund’s house, and carry small gifts, as Baudonivia relates in the *Life of Saint Radegund*, section 20?

The same Giraldus, in his *History of Poets*, dialogue 5, and Platina, in his *Book of the Lives of the Pontiffs*, in the Life of John III, mention a book *On Governing the Kingdom*, which they say Venantius wrote to King Sigibert.

Here are Platina’s words:

“Fortunatus, a man of singular learning and eloquence, brought the Gauls back to a gentler culture by his writings and example. For he wrote to Sigibert, their king, a little book on governing the kingdom.”

Could this book be poem 2 of book VI, in which Fortunatus, praising Sigibert’s virtues, shows what sort of man he ought to be who presides over others with sovereign authority?

If it is another little book, as seems more likely, it must either still lie hidden or be considered to have perished through age.

The same Gregory is witness that the Life of Saint Severinus, bishop of Bordeaux—of whom Gregory of Tours speaks in book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 45—was written by Fortunatus. He says:

“After we had written these things, we learned that the Life of this holy Severinus was written by Fortunatus the presbyter.”

Browerus and others affirm that this Life has been lost, in chapter 5 of the *Life of Fortunatus*. Nor have I been able to discover that anyone has found or published it.

I would not doubt that Fortunatus wrote many other works, whether in verse or prose, which have either entirely perished through age or perhaps lie hidden somewhere, covered by darkness and neglect, and which another person’s diligence and care will someday bring to light.

I infer this from the man’s talent and eloquence.

Would that the distinguished and learned Philippus Labbaeus of the Society of Jesus had completed or published the edition of Fortunatus’s works which he had promised! There is no doubt that it would have been fuller and more splendid than all the others.

For he himself testifies in his dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume II, after mentioning Christopher Brower’s edition:

“We have all the same short works of Fortunatus ready for the press, corrected in countless places, partly from manuscripts of the highest quality and partly from certain conjectures, and enlarged with additions to the published texts, awaiting only an opportunity for publication.”

It is not easy to guess what prevented the completion of his undertaking. Nor, although we have employed every diligence, have we been able to discover into whose hands, after his death, the materials he declared ready for the press came.

We had hoped that they might perhaps be found in the place where he died. He died at Paris in 1667.

When we had inquired by letter and had sought the assistance of the most reverend Father Patertius, librarian of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, he replied in these words:

“As for the promise made more than a century ago by Father Labbe to publish an edition of Fortunatus, I know of no trace of his work. For two years, during the destruction of the three Jesuit houses in Paris and the sale of their property and movable goods in 1762, I was the custodian of their manuscripts, and I found nothing there belonging to any of Father Labbe’s literary works. I do not know where all his papers went after his death in 1667.”

These, then, are the things concerning Fortunatus’s writings whose loss we have every right and reason to lament. As for his learning, talent, and ability in composition, however, this ought not altogether to be passed over here, although mention of it will occur elsewhere. Fortunatus appears to have been suitably well versed and learned in theological matters—as his *Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer* demonstrates above all—and he also shows himself to have been thoroughly conversant with the works of Greek and Latin poets and other writers. He explicitly cites Homer, Menander, Aratus, Sappho, Pindar, and Cato, Pythagoras, Chrysippus, Plato, and Cleanthes; among the Latins, Virgil, Horace, Ovid, and Cicero. He also mentions the more celebrated Latin and Greek Fathers, and one can repeatedly detect that he followed and reproduced something of the wit and learning of all of them in his own writing.

Some people, however, are offended that he did not hesitate occasionally to use the names of the false gods whom blind antiquity once worshiped. Among his other poems, one notable example of this kind is found in Book VI, chapter 2, where, singing an epithalamium for the marriage of Sigibert, king of Austrasia, and Brunichild, he introduces Cupid and Venus in the poetic manner, celebrating the praises proper to each. Yet Fortunatus was writing at a time when there was less danger that people would be deceived by an error concerning such gods: throughout Gaul the Christian religion was flourishing under the most devout care and diligence of the rulers and the teaching and virtues of distinguished bishops. It should therefore hardly seem strange that Fortunatus, still a young man, should have indulged his poetic temperament somewhat more freely, especially in a subject that seemed to call for a more playful style of expression, and should, for the sake of ornament and wit, have introduced the conversations of gods that had once been familiar to pagan poets. With greater maturity of age and judgment, however, he not only abstained from such trifles but devoted himself entirely to more serious studies, and wrote verse only rarely and when provoked to do so by his friends—as he himself states concerning himself in Book II, chapter 13.

He also displays no ordinary knowledge of history and geography, not only with regard to the regions through which he himself traveled and which he could know by personal observation, but also with regard to those he had never visited, such as Spain and the whole of the East. Hence the many descriptions of rivers, the names of cities and barbarian peoples, [Col. 0019] their settlements and deeds, and other matters of this kind, all of which show that in history, as in geography, he was not merely unskilled but learned and well informed.

What shall I say, moreover, of his studies in natural philosophy? He clearly had considerable training in them, as is shown by the many kinds and names of herbs, trees, stones, gems, and spices that he frequently uses; and he repeatedly investigates and seeks the causes of natural phenomena. Thus, to mention no other passage, in Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, when he inquires, in the manner of the poets, how Martin, shut up in his cell, could have seen and rebuked a monk sitting by the fire with his groin exposed, [Col. 0019] he writes:

> What was this? Tell me, learned sophists, I pray you.  
> Was a wall before Martin’s eyes, like linen spread into the light,  
> or like a spider weaving its agile webs from thread,  
> or nets made of threads interlaced through wide-spaced openings?  
> Whence does this structure, so thin and gaping, become visible?  
> Do the stones rise up and return a window split open,  
> or do the hard rocks dissolve in a slow-flowing bond?  
> Does the house open its material with a glasslike edge?  
> Or did it provide a transparent surface through which the holy man’s light could pass?  
> Or did the lighter wall yield, curving backward in an arch,  
> [Col. 0020] and remain unharmed, suspended in the swift instant?  
> Or was the noble power of the eyes such that it passed through marble,  
> and a clearer sight proceeded through every obstacle?  
> Or did a winged attendant fly to the face of the one enclosed,  
> and open a way through what was covered, entering as a messenger where no path existed?  
> Or, because it was light, did he possess the whole of it outside and within?  
> Or, while the body remained seated in its place, did a swift spirit pass through?  
> Reveal these closed things, eloquent speakers, learned in speech,  
> who by numbers, atoms, reason, and utterance can comprehend them.

Although Fortunatus possessed the talent and learning I have described, it must nevertheless be admitted that he sometimes suffered from certain faults in writing. To pass over the barbarous and scarcely Latin words that he occasionally uses—for which Browerus has compiled a catalogue to be added by us at the end of this edition—he is often obscure and involved, especially when writing in prose. He reflects the faults of his age by drawing out long periods in a manner that is not natural but excessively artificial in its construction and ornament. His style consists almost entirely in an abundant and redundant profusion of words, linked together to create the appearance of grandiloquent eloquence, and sometimes answering one another in equal syllables. From this arise both obscurity in his prose and, in its ornamentation, a fastidiousness and painstaking elaboration scarcely tolerable to more refined ears. Yet this, as I have said, is almost a common fault of that period, as can be seen from the writings of others who flourished in the same age as Fortunatus.

In the expositions that he wrote on the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer—which, after he had been made bishop, he appears to have recited to the people—he is nevertheless clearer and more accessible. Likewise, in the *Lives of the Saints* he does not habitually pursue the same artificiality and fastidiousness in weaving his prose that he is found deliberately to employ in his letters, perhaps indulging the taste of those to whom he wrote.

In his poems, too, he is at times more polished and elegant than seems appropriate to the age into which he fell, and at other times rougher and less finished. This is especially true of poems that he either poured out almost extemporaneously while distracted by other business—as will be said in his Life—or that he neglected to polish because he was writing carelessly to his closest friends, such as Gregory of Tours. In individual passages, however, his remarkable poetic ability and fluency are everywhere apparent; and they are most apparent when he describes the position and character of some region, field, or river. How inventive, elegant, and pleasing he is then! In his poems one often seems not merely to read descriptions of rows of vines, fields blooming with flowers, crops yellowing with grain, grasses waving their tresses, and springs of perennial water, but actually to see them with one’s eyes.

If, carried away by the heat of his inspiration—or rather by the grandeur of the subjects embraced in his verse—he sometimes forgets meter and the common laws of poetry, this he shares with nearly all Christian poets, such as Arator and Sedulius. They considered themselves obliged to serve the subject matter and the dignity of the persons of whom they were speaking more than meter, in the manner of pagan poets. I believe that this is enough to say about the purpose of our work, and about Fortunatus’s writings, talent, and learning.

To mention at least briefly those who have deserved well of this edition and contributed some assistance and support toward beginning or completing it, first place certainly belongs to the man whom I mentioned above, the most illustrious and most reverend Nicolaus Antonius Justiniani, bishop of Padua, the originator and supporter of the preparation of this edition, as we have said. Likewise, the most illustrious and most reverend Stephanus Borgia, secretary of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, a man of great distinction and learning, often helped me with his advice and also pointed out two poems that I added to Browerus’s edition, in Book II, chapters 8 and 9. Finally, the most distinguished and learned man Rambaldus de Azzoniis, advocate and canon of the Church of Treviso, most generously communicated certain documents to me, as we shall indicate in their proper place. The monks of our community, too, have frequently offered me their devoted assistance, labor, and diligence as I prepared this edition.

[Col. 0019]

# LIFE OF VENANTIUS HONORIUS CLEMENTIANUS FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF POITIERS

[Col. 0019] 1. Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, was Italian by origin and nationality. Besides these four names, by which he is generally better known, he appears to have assigned himself a fifth, as the most learned man Joan Josephus Liruti observed in his work entitled *Notizie delle Vite ed opere scritte da Letterati del Friuli* [Notices of the Lives and Works Written by Men of Letters of Friuli], vol. I, chapter 12. For, when writing the epitaph of Leontius, a former bishop of Bordeaux, in Book IV, chapter 9, he addresses him at the end as follows:

> These little verses, far too small for you, since you deserve rich ones,  
> are offered by Theodosius, your devoted friend.

Unless, perhaps, one should say that Fortunatus wrote that poem under another person’s identity and name, especially since there is no independent evidence that he possessed this name in addition to those by which he is known. Certainly, we can understand from several of Fortunatus’s poems that he sometimes lent his poems to another person’s identity. To go no farther, the poem that immediately follows the one just cited, in Book IV, chapter 9, written for the funeral of the younger Leontius, likewise a bishop of Bordeaux, concludes in much the same way, with Placidina, the former wife of Leontius, introduced as speaker under her own name:

> As a duty owed at the funeral, a solace for great love,  
> Placidina still sweetly gives you this to your ashes.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] See what we said in the notes on Poem 9, Book IV.]

2. P. Christophorus Browerus, in chapter 1 of his *Life of Fortunatus*, judges that Fortunatus borrowed the name Venantius from Saint Venantius of Bourges, who once flourished in Gaul with a great reputation for holiness. He likewise thinks that Fortunatus took the name Fortunatus from Saint Fortunatus, a martyr of the Church of Aquileia, whom he always followed with particular piety and devotion. But there is no time to investigate these and similar matters at greater length, although Browerus examines them with considerable curiosity.

3. From the number of names with which Fortunatus was endowed, some have inferred—Liruti, in the work cited—that he was descended from an ancient Roman people and lineage, since it was customary among the ancient Romans to assume several names, both as a mark of family and to signify some virtue or personal characteristic. Appian of Alexandria writes the following in the Preface to the *Roman Wars*:

> Formerly each Roman had one name, like other men; later a second was added, and not long afterward some began to add a third as well, so that they might be more readily recognized by some bodily mark or quality of character, just as the Greeks also had surnames attached to several names.

4. While the Roman republic still stood, when individuals assumed several names, the first in order—as Browerus also observes—was called the *praenomen*; the second, which designated the clan or family, was the *nomen*; the third was the *cognomen*; and a fourth, the *agnomen*, was sometimes added after the latter. In a later age, however, these names began to be used indiscriminately, and generally the name placed last had the force of a *praenomen*, serving to distinguish individuals from the other members of the same household and clan. On this subject it is preferable to read the distinguished Sirmond, in the dissertation prefixed to his edition of the works of Sidonius Apollinaris, where he discusses at greater length the custom of people in the later period of assuming several names.

It was this very custom that caused our Fortunatus, although distinguished by many names, to be generally better known in his own age and afterward by the name Fortunatus.

5. He had a sister named Titiana, whom he mentions in Book XI, chapter 6, writing to the abbess Agnes in these words:

> You were to me in eye and heart no other than  
> you would have been, Titiana, my sister from the womb.

From this the distinguished Liruti infers that Fortunatus’s father was named Titius or Titianus, in accordance with the ancient Roman custom by which daughters were commonly named from their fathers. He adds that this must have been the proper name of the clan or family from which Fortunatus was descended.

But I am surprised that, if this was the family surname proper to them, the sister rather than Fortunatus should have been called by it, or that it was not at least common to both. For this reason I agree with Sirmond, who, in the passage cited above, demonstrates from the testimony of ancient monuments that in later centuries the custom of assigning names prevailed as follows:

> Both the names proper to each individual and the names attached to them—whether surnames or additional names, for all of these varied in almost every individual—were for the most part borrowed from parents, relatives, fathers, uncles, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and other persons held dear . . . For the fixed and established designations of clan and family that had existed in former times were no longer in use—names that were common to mothers as well and passed on to their descendants, as when all those born from the Cornelian or Julian clan were called Cornelii or Julii, and likewise Scipios or Ciceros, those belonging to the household and family of the Scipios or Ciceros. But after the decline of the republic all these things gradually began to change and disappear. Although at first some traces of the ancient custom remained in hereditary names retained by certain families . . . later even this practice was neglected, to such an extent that no fixed family name and no fixed clan name remained. Sons also often differed from their fathers and brothers in every name, or nearly every name.

6. As for Fortunatus’s homeland, he was born in the territory of Treviso, in a place called Duplavilis, or Duplabilis or Duplavenis. This is established by clear testimony both from Fortunatus himself and from others. In Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, addressing in poetic fashion his book, which he was sending from Gaul to Italy, he testifies that he was born at Duplavilis in these words:

> Where my Treviso lies, if you enter gently,  
> seek, I pray, my illustrious companion Felix.  
> Passing through Ceneta, and [among] the friends of Duplavilis,  
> where my native soil is, by blood and by my parents’ dwelling,  
> the origin of my offspring and fathers, my mother, sister, and line of descendants—  
> all whom I honor in heart and faith—briefly, I ask you, convey my greeting to them.

Paul the Deacon likewise explicitly states in Book II, chapter 13 of his *History of the Lombards* that Fortunatus was born at Duplavilis, saying:

> Fortunatus was indeed born in a place called Duplavilis, which lies not far from the fortress of Ceneta or from the city of Treviso.

7. Fortunatus, then, was born in the territory of Treviso, at Duplavilis, whether this was a village or town, or some tract of country extending along the river Piave, from which it also seems to have taken its name. Even today there is a village or town in those places called in the vernacular Valdebiadena. This place, the home of many highly respectable men, claims our Fortunatus as its citizen and native son.

8. Cluverius, in volume I of *Italia Antiqua*, chapter 18, thinks that Duplavilis was located where, he says, a town can now be seen on elevated ground on the left bank of the river, commonly called San Salvatore. But the most learned and distinguished Count Rambaldus de Azzoniis, canon of the Church of Treviso—whom I have praised elsewhere—in his dissertation demonstrating that Venantius Fortunatus was from the territory of Treviso, which he most generously lent me along with other materials, proves by very weighty arguments that Duplavilis could not have been the same as the town described by Cluverius.

For when Fortunatus indicates in his account of his journey from Gaul to Italy that one must travel from Aquileia to Concordia, and from there to Treviso, then to Ceneta and Duplavilis, on the route toward Padua, Duplavilis, the homeland of Fortunatus, would therefore not lie between Treviso and Ceneta but beyond Ceneta, for someone traveling toward Padua. Yet the town of San Salvatore does not have this position, since it lies between Treviso and Ceneta. Moreover, this town did not exist in the sixth century; indeed, until the year 1245 the site remained merely an isolated and deserted slope of a mountain.

For this reason he has no doubt that Duplavilis, where Fortunatus’s native soil lay, is the same place now commonly called Valdebiadena, situated in the territory of Treviso. The similarity of the name—which is shown even more clearly by the ancient documents he produces—also strongly supports this opinion.

9. Joan Josephus Liruti, while agreeing with Cluverius on this point, adds an opinion of his own: Duplavilis was nothing more than Fortunatus’s ancestral or paternal estate. His parents or grandparents, citizens of Aquileia, as Liruti supposes, had withdrawn there to escape the savagery and violence of the arms of Attila and the other barbarians who had often attacked Aquileia with their armies.

10. But I do not know how much weight should be given to this singular opinion of an otherwise most learned man. In the poem quoted above, Fortunatus says so plainly not only that Treviso is his own city, and that among the people of Duplavilis his native soil is his by blood and by his parents’ dwelling, but also that it is the origin of his fathers’ descendants, that I do not know what clearer evidence could be offered for identifying a person’s homeland.

11. I will nevertheless readily grant that he did not remain long in his paternal home and region. From his earliest years he appears to have lived for some time at Aquileia, once a most powerful city, as he himself states in Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, addressing his book in the same way:

> Or, if you should happen to approach the city of Aquileia,  
> greatly venerate the Cassians, friends of the Lord;  
> and eagerly worship the blessed martyr Fortunatus’s urn,  
> and the holy bishop Paul,  
> who desired to convert me from my earliest years.

12. From these final words Joan Josephus Liruti infers that Fortunatus received baptism at Aquileia from Paul, the bishop of that city. He considers this especially supportive of his opinion that Fortunatus was a citizen of Aquileia.

13. But, setting aside the fact that one cannot conclude from Paul’s desire that Fortunatus should be converted from his earliest years that he had actually been converted, it seems to me much more likely that Paul, the bishop of Aquileia, wished Fortunatus—while still a boy or adolescent—to embrace the monastic life at Aquileia after laying aside all other concerns. Fortunatus, however, perhaps because he was planning to go to Ravenna to devote himself there to literary studies, in a city that was a kind of Lyceum of every science, judged that he should not comply with the bishop’s wishes.

It was certainly customary in those times for someone who embraced the monastic life to be said to have been “converted.” To pass over the testimony of Saint Benedict, chapter 58 of the *Rule*, and of Saint Gregory the Great, Book II, letters 4 and 66 of the Paris edition, Baudonivia, a contemporary of Fortunatus and a nun of the monastery at Poitiers, speaks of Radegund in her *Life of Blessed Radegund*, section 3, as follows:

> After, through the working of divine power, she had departed from the earthly king, as her vows required, while she was residing at Suaedas, an estate that the king had given her, in the first year of her conversion, and so forth.

It is certain that Radegund had been raised in Christian devotion from earliest childhood. After she had left Clotaire, her husband, as will be related below—Fortunatus, *Life of Saint Radegund*, section 12—she immediately received the monastic veil at Noviomagus from Saint Medardus, the bishop. Baudonivia therefore calls this the first year of her conversion.

Likewise, Fortunatus, speaking in Book IV, chapter 23, of a certain Julian who had previously practiced commerce but then abandoned it and consecrated himself wholly to God, distributing what he possessed to the poor, writes:

> Once a merchant, converted with a blessed end,  
> he was snatched from this world, a man freed from sin.  
> He had gathered much gold, but scattered it among the needy;  
> he sent ahead all the wealth that he would later follow.

14. There was a very celebrated monastery at Aquileia even in the time of Rufinus, who had lived there as a monk, when, apart from the one at Vercelli, there was scarcely another monastery in Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0023D] See the *Life of Rufinus* prefixed to the edition of his works, Verona, 1745, Book I, section 5.]

It is therefore credible that Paul invited Fortunatus at that time to this Aquileian monastery, and that Fortunatus, perhaps also admitted to the clergy—for at that time the clerical profession almost always included a monastic way of life—might subsequently render greater services to the Church of Aquileia, in keeping with the innocence of his life and the sharpness of his intellect.

[Note: [Col. 0024D] See Ruinart, in the preface to the works of Saint Gregory of Tours, section 35.]

15. When I observe, however, that Paul, or Paulinus—for Ughellus discusses him more fully in *Italia Sacra*—did not begin to occupy the see of the Church of Aquileia until the year 558 or 559, I am readily led to believe that Fortunatus did not reside at Aquileia at a very early age.

[Note: [Col. 0025D] Read Pagi, on the year 559, no. 9; and Muratori, on the years 550 and 570; Paul the Deacon, Book II, *On the Lombard War*, chapter 25.]

For if he is believed to have been born around the year 530 and died as an old man at Poitiers near the beginning of the seventh century, he was twenty-eight or twenty-nine years old when he lived at Aquileia under Bishop Paulinus.

[Note: [Col. 0026D] Author of the *Literary History of the Franks*.]

If he says that Paul had invited him to conversion from his earliest years, then either the poet must be understood to have written this with reference to the time when he was composing those books of the *Life of Saint Martin*—that is, before the year 576—

[Note: [Col. 0026D] See what we noted on Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, p. 470.]

—or else Paul must be said to have invited Fortunatus, while the former was not yet bishop of Aquileia but perhaps already a cleric or monk of that Church, to embrace the same manner of life while Fortunatus was still a boy or adolescent.

16. I would not, however, dispute that Fortunatus could have advanced at Aquileia in piety and in knowledge of matters relating to the practice of religion, and that he may perhaps have used Paulinus’s assistance for this purpose. As for the evidence that the distinguished Liruti adduces for this claim—namely, that the *Exposition of the Creed* published by Fortunatus agrees exactly in its formulations with the exposition previously published by Rufinus, a presbyter and monk of the Church of Aquileia—it seems to me to indicate rather, as I shall say in its proper place, that when Fortunatus obtained Rufinus’s *Exposition of the Creed*, he adapted it for the instruction of the people of the Church of Poitiers. It does not prove that both men received the first rudiments of the Christian religion in the same Church.

This is especially so because, as Rufinus testifies in Book I of his *Invective against Saint Jerome*, the Aquileian Creed, by the tradition and custom of that Church, included the resurrection of this flesh—a phrase for which there is no corresponding indication in the Creed expounded by Fortunatus.

17. He therefore—as I return to the point from which I digressed—did not comply with Paul’s wishes and desires, probably for the reason I mentioned: he was planning for himself another home and place of residence where he could devote himself to literary studies more freely and conveniently. At that time Ravenna was especially suited to this purpose. It was a most celebrated city in which Honorius, emperor of the West, had long before established his royal residence; afterward, when the Romans had been defeated and driven out, Odoacer, king of the Goths, and then, after Odoacer had been overthrown, Theodoric, king of both Goths and Romans, and later rulers had their residences there.

Royal cities generally abound not only in the resources needed for other purposes but also in numbers of learned men and in the cultivation of the sciences, and they often surpass other places in these respects. The generosity of kings, their desire for distinction, and other advantages commonly drew such men from nearly every land, especially when the ruler who held supreme power appeared to be favorably disposed toward learning.

Among such rulers, Theodoric certainly was one. Though at times harsh and forceful, he favored learned men and was himself extremely devoted to literary studies. Writing to Cassiodorus, he says of himself:

> We are always pleased by the sight of those who have settled in our minds through glorious actions, since they have given us a perpetual pledge of their affection—those who have proved among us that they practice virtue.

(*Letters*, Book III, letter 28.)

Athalaric, who succeeded him in the kingdom, commends Theodoric’s diligence and constancy in cultivating literary studies in these words, writing to Cassiodorus:

> When he had been freed from public cares, he demanded the judgments of the wise from your conversations, so that by his own deeds he might equal the men of ancient times. He investigated the courses of the stars, the inlets of the sea, and the marvels of springs with the keenest scrutiny, so that, after examining more carefully the natures of things, he might appear to be a philosopher wearing the purple.

It is therefore hardly surprising that under such kings the study of the sciences flourished especially at Ravenna, and that, having been splendidly established in public schools, it was able to continue into later times, when people eager for learning gathered there from every direction to study.

18. Fortunatus therefore went there and remained there until he had carried away a rich and precious store of the liberal arts. Paul the Deacon writes of him in Book II, chapter 13 of his *History of the Lombards*:

> At Ravenna he was raised and educated in grammar, rhetoric, and also meter, and became highly distinguished.

Fortunatus himself, speaking with great modesty of his own abilities, tells us in Book I of the *Life of Saint Martin* what arts he chiefly studied at Ravenna:

> But I am poor in understanding; how small a part of the Italian tongue am I?  
> Heavy with dregs, weak in speech, sluggish in reasoning,  
> dull in mind, lacking in art, inexperienced in practice, yet not without utterance;  
> barely tasting a drop from the streams of grammar,  
> taking only a small sip from the whirlpool of rhetoric,  
> from the legal whetstone, whose rust has scarcely been removed—  
> forgetting what I first learned, and possessing only  
> the scent of those arts in these nostrils of mine.  
> No shining bordered toga gleams upon me, no *pennula* (teacher’s mantle);  
> now only my naked hunger remains from my impoverished tongue.

19. From this Browerus, in chapter 2 of the *Life of Fortunatus*, thinks that Fortunatus had only a light education: he never attained the bordered toga, the mark of public office, nor ever took up the *pennula*, a teacher’s mantle, for teaching. It is much more plausible, however, that Fortunatus, out of modesty and in accordance with the way of life he had chosen, voluntarily abstained from such honors—if they were available—than that a man of no ordinary talent and of no mean learning was unable, because of the weakness of his knowledge and lack of education, to obtain insignia of honor that were open to many.

This is especially likely since it is otherwise clear that he was always extremely eager to diminish his own praises. It should therefore cause no surprise that he transferred to the task of diminishing the reputation for talent and learning that he possessed something he had neglected to pursue because of a particular personal choice and conviction.

20. At Ravenna, then, he diligently devoted himself to grammar, rhetoric, and meter. With the help of these arts he subsequently wrote many excellent works, both in prose and in verse. Nor was he ignorant of legal knowledge, although, because of his singular devotion to modesty, he admits that he had only lightly touched and, as it were, sampled it.

21. In these studies Fortunatus had companions—as was almost inevitable in that home of learning—men distinguished for both knowledge and talent. Inviting all of them to join in celebrating the praises of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, he addresses them through his little book as follows:

> More readily, I pray, seek out companions from there;  
> if you speak with companions, your devotion will win forgiveness.  
> I offer material to those who, with rounded speech,  
> may compose flourishing verses on Martin’s deeds  
> and weave them with bright talent, to be scattered throughout the world.

22. While he was still at Ravenna, Fortunatus began to suffer severely from his eyes, so that he nearly lost their light altogether. In that city there was a basilica of the holy martyrs John and Paul. In it stood an altar dedicated to the memory of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, who was already famous throughout the world for the glory of his sanctity and miracles; an image of him was painted on the wall.

Fortunatus hurried to this basilica to seek help. A lamp happened to be burning beneath a certain window near the altar, and when the oil from the lamp touched his eyes, he was immediately freed from his illness. It is better, however, to hear Fortunatus himself recount the whole event as it occurred, in the verses cited above from Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*:

> From there seek the pleasant city of Ravenna, made still sweeter;  
> and seek the tomb of Martin, where, by the right of the shrine,  
> the power of the saint restored to me my light, already despaired of.  
> To him who grants gifts, repay at least words, I ask you.  
> There stands the basilica whose roof belongs to Paul and John;  
> here the wall holds the form of the saint beneath his image,  
> to be embraced in the sweetness of its painted color.  
> Beneath the feet of the righteous, the wall has a window fashioned by art;  
> a lamp is there, whose fire floats in a glass vessel.  
> As I hasten there, while fierce pain twists me,  
> and the light of my eyes flees through the windows, groaning,  
> as soon as from afar I touched the light with the blessed olive oil,  
> that fiery vapor withdrew from my failing brow,  
> and the present medicine drove away my diseases with its gentle ointment.

23. Felix, Fortunatus’s intimate friend and companion in literary studies, was suffering from a similar eye ailment. He too was cured through the patronage of Saint Martin and the power of his oil. Paul the Deacon recounts the story of both men in Book II, chapter 13 of his *History of the Lombards*:

> When he—Fortunatus—was suffering from the most severe pain in his eyes, and Felix, his companion, was likewise afflicted with pain in his eyes, they both went to the basilica of the blessed Paul and John, which stands within the same city. There an altar had been constructed in honor of the blessed confessor Martin, and near it was a window in which a lamp had been placed to provide light. As soon as Fortunatus and Felix touched their suffering eyes with the oil from it, the pain immediately fled, and they obtained the health they desired.

Gregory of Tours tells the same story in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 15.

24. This Felix was not long afterward made bishop of Treviso. When Alboin, king of the Lombards, invaded Italy with a large army, Felix went out to meet him at the river Piave. As Paul the Deacon relates in the passage cited, Alboin, being extremely generous, granted him all the resources of his Church when Felix requested them, and confirmed what had been requested by a royal decree.

Fortunatus mentions this Felix in Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin* in these words:

> Where my Treviso lies, if you enter gently,  
> seek, I pray, my illustrious companion Felix,  
> to whom Martin once restored the light along with me.

25. In consequence of the magnitude and grace of the benefit he had obtained, Fortunatus began to burn with greater piety and devotion than before toward blessed Martin. He began to plan a journey to Gaul, so that he might visit the tomb of Saint Martin himself, venerate it in person, and fulfill his vows.

Paul relates the matter in the frequently cited passage:

> For this reason Fortunatus venerated blessed Martin so greatly that, having left his homeland, he hurried to Tours, to the tomb of that blessed man, shortly before the Lombards invaded Italy.

Fortunatus himself gives the same reason for his journey near the beginning of Book I of the *Life of Saint Martin*. Meanwhile, he may also have hoped that the military disturbances that were already threatening wretched Italy from every side through the arms of the barbarians—or with which it had long been afflicted—would eventually come to an end, so that, once tranquility had been restored and affairs pacified, he could return to his homeland and his own people.

26. There is no unanimous agreement as to the year in which Fortunatus left Italy and departed for Gaul. Browerus states that he reached Gaul in the year 565. Pagi holds the same opinion in his notes on Baronius, under the year 564. Certainly, as Paul the Deacon testifies in the passage cited so often, Fortunatus departed for Gaul not long before the Lombards invaded Italy. But the Lombards invaded Italy in the year 568, as the same Paul the Deacon records in Book II, chapter 33 of his *History of the Lombards*.

27. The following considerations seem to confirm the opinion of Browerus and Pagi. Fortunatus was already in Gaul when Sigibert, king of Austrasia, married Brunichild, the daughter of Athanagild, king of the Goths in Spain; for Fortunatus composed an epithalamium for the marriage, which can be read in Book VI, chapter 2.

Sigibert entered into this marriage in the fifth year of his reign, having begun to reign in the year 561, when his father Clotaire died in that same year, as Gregory of Tours testifies in Book IV, chapter 21 of his *History of the Franks*. Thus, by the year 566, Fortunatus was already in Gaul and enjoying the patronage and favor of King Sigibert.

[Note: [Col. 0027] See Pagi, under the years 564 and 567, no. 9. Read also the *Frankish Annals* prefixed to the works of Gregory of Tours.]

28. Moreover, Fortunatus was already living at Poitiers when Gelesuintha, Brunichild’s sister, passed through the city on her way to marry Chilperic, Sigibert’s brother. Fortunatus writes of her in Book VI, chapter 7:

> After passing through several cities, she reached the citadels of Poitiers,  
> as royal pomp proceeded along the road.  
> I, newly arrived, saw her passing by,  
> gently carried in a revolving tower of silver.

This marriage is assigned to the year following Sigibert’s marriage to Brunichild. Fortunatus, therefore, had not arrived at Poitiers until after he had spent some time with Sigibert and had fulfilled his vow at Tours, at the tomb of Saint Martin, as Paul relates in the passage cited so often.

29. Browerus adds that Fortunatus praises Sigibert in Book II, chapter 17, because he completed with the greatest zeal the basilica of Saint Medard, begun by Chlothar, and had already placed its roof upon it. For at the end of the poem the poet addresses Saint Medard himself in these words:

> Behold, Sigibert worships your temples with excessive love,  
> Zealously devoted to the work out of love for you.  
> Guard the roof, you who raised the temple to its summit;  
> Protect him who, in accordance with his merits, gave you the temple.

“But,” he says, “it is believable that Sigibert undertook this work not long after Chlothar’s death, since he knew how concerned his father had been about it and how eager he had been to complete it, and since he had wished to be buried in that place.”

[Col. 0029B] 30. The distinguished Joannes Josephus Liruti, however, differs somewhat from Browerus and Pagius, since he wishes Fortunatus’s arrival in Gaul to be assigned to the year 567, or at the earliest to 566. It is not irrelevant briefly to examine his view—which I see is shared by others as well—since it may shed some light on the matter under discussion.

He first doubts whether Fortunatus could have set out for Gaul shortly before the Lombards invaded Italy. For, according to Paul the Deacon, Felix, Fortunatus’s companion—and indeed, as Liruti thinks, his traveling companion—had already been made bishop of Tarvisium and met Alboin, king of the Lombards, at the Plavis, as we said above. It would scarcely have been possible for Felix, within so short an interval, to go to Gaul, return from there to Italy, [Col. 0029C] and then, after being made bishop of Tarvisium, go out to meet Alboin. Liruti therefore thinks that Paul, who was often less careful when recounting events distant from his own age, may in this matter also have departed from the true chronology.

31. But, without attempting here to excuse or defend Paul the Deacon, there was certainly no reason for the distinguished writer to doubt his diligence or reliability on the basis he adduces. For, as far as I have been able to ascertain, no testimony or written record establishes that Felix traveled to Gaul together with Fortunatus. Paul the Deacon does not assert this, although he relates that both Felix and Fortunatus suffered from the same eye disease and were delivered from it in a similar manner through the patronage of Saint Martin. Rather, when speaking of Fortunatus and his vow to set out for Gaul, he seems clearly to separate Felix from him.

Nor does Gregory of Tours establish it, although he recounts the same event as Paul the Deacon in Book I, chapter 15, of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*. Finally, Fortunatus himself nowhere indicates it, although his writings often provide both the occasion and the chronological setting for him to have mentioned it, had it in fact occurred.

Indeed, in his letter to Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 1, he makes it sufficiently clear that he had no companion on his journey from Italy to Gaul, in these words:

> In the midst of all this, you yourself, as judge, may measure what “extended provisions” could prudently mean, when neither fear of a judge was pressing . . . nor favor from a companion inviting me, and so forth.

32. As for Liruti’s further addition—that it is scarcely credible that Felix, who was Fortunatus’s contemporary and therefore still a young man, was made bishop of Tarvisium at a time when access to that highest honor was opened only gradually, after mature age and through all the ranks of honor—I shall say nothing of the discipline of those times, when merit was often considered more than age, although I could demonstrate this with many examples. Even granting that Felix was exactly Fortunatus’s contemporary, it follows rather that Fortunatus did not migrate to Gaul at a very youthful age: if, as is believed, he was born around the year 530, he would have been thirty-five or thirty-six when he set out for Gaul.

33. The principal reason why the journey of Fortunatus to Gaul should be assigned to the year 567 is, according to the distinguished author, that Fortunatus says he was then a newcomer at Poitiers when Gelesuintha passed through on her way to marry Chilperic. This occurred in the year 567, as we indicated above.

But as soon as Fortunatus arrived in Gaul, he must be thought to have gone to the tomb of Saint Martin, and from there immediately to have come to Poitiers. For Paul the Deacon writes of him that, after arriving at Tours in accordance with his vow, he passed through Poitiers and settled there. Fortunatus therefore reached Gaul no earlier than 567, or at the very least in 566. So much for Liruti.

34. Yet I do not see why the distinguished author should be influenced by this authority of Paul, who, by his own testimony, sometimes falls into error when reporting events remote from his own age. If he could have erred in determining approximately the time when Fortunatus set out for Gaul, he could much more easily have erred in establishing when Fortunatus went to Poitiers to live there.

But let us set this aside. It is believable that Fortunatus did not go to Tours immediately after his arrival in Gaul, but spent some time with King Sigibert at Metz or Rheims, cities in which the kings of Austrasia resided. For Fortunatus composed an epithalamium for Sigibert, and received from him a companion and guide for the journey he was to undertake through Gaul, as will be said below.

Nor does Paul’s testimony seem sufficient to demonstrate clearly that Fortunatus came to Poitiers immediately after leaving Tours. Paul asserts only that, after he had fulfilled his vow at Tours, Fortunatus went to Poitiers for the sake of travel and lived there, without establishing how much time intervened between the two events.

It is also uncertain how long he remained at Tours, both out of piety and religious devotion toward the ashes of Saint Martin, and because he was detained by the attentions and kindness of Euphronius, bishop of Tours, to whom he was very closely attached.

Moreover, what prevents us from supposing that Fortunatus wrote that he was then a newcomer when Gelesuintha passed through, referring to the time when he was composing the funeral poem on her death—a death that occurred considerably later?

What adds considerable weight to these considerations is that Fortunatus was necessarily already in Gaul before the year 567: he celebrated in verse the marriage of Sigibert and Brunichild, contracted in 566, as we have often said, [Col. 0031A] and he was bound by friendship to Nicetius, bishop of Trier, to whom he wrote Poem 11 of Book III while Nicetius was still alive. Nicetius, however, died around the end of the year 566, as Cointius conjectures under that year, no. 60.

35. From all this, then, it seems that Fortunatus’s journey to Gaul must be placed in the year 565; certainly it should be assigned neither before 564 nor after 566.

As for the route he followed in setting out for Gaul and the places he visited, he himself recounts them sufficiently in his letter to Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 1, in these words:

> Especially since I, inexperienced as I was, setting out from Ravenna, crossed the Po, the Adige, the Brenta, the Piave, the Livenza, and the Tagliamento; then, hanging among the mountain bends of the Julian Alps, I crossed the Drava of Noricum, the Inn of the Breones, the Lech of Bavaria, the Danube of Alemannia, and the Rhine of Germany; afterward, crossing the Moselle, the Meuse, the Aisne, and the Seine, and then the Loire and the Garonne, the greatest rivers of Aquitaine, I came upon the Pyrenees in the month of July, having passed almost the whole journey either on horseback or half asleep.

Paul the Deacon embraces this journey of Fortunatus more briefly, saying:

> He describes the journey he made, as Fortunatus himself reports in his poems, when hastening there: across the waters of the Tagliamento [perhaps; printed: *fluentilia menti*] and Reunia [printed: *Rounam*], and through the Osoppo, across the Julian Alps, through Aguntum, and across the rivers Drava and Birrus, and through the Breones and the city of Augusta, watered by the Virdo and the Lech—that is, the Vindo and the Lychus.

36. From this it is therefore clear that, after departing from Ravenna, he came by a continuous journey to Padua and from there to Tarvisium, although, as is likely, he turned aside to Duplavilis to visit his relatives. Then, after crossing the Noric Alps and entering Germany, he proceeded from there into Gaul, by the route that was then well known and customary for reaching that kingdom.

Accordingly, in Book IV of *The Life of Saint Martin*, he indicates the same route to someone traveling from Gaul to Italy, in these verses:

> If you are permitted to travel through barbarian rivers,  
> So that you may calmly cross the Rhine and the Hister,  
> Proceed to Augusta, which the Vindo and Lycus water.  
> If you have time to travel, and no Bavarian obstructs you,  
> Where the neighboring lands of the Breones lie, go across the Alps,  
> Entering where the Inn rolls along in its swift current.  
>   
> From there seek the shrines of Valentine and Benedict,  
> Making for the Noric countryside, where the Birrus turns in its waters.  
> The road runs across the Drava, where the fortresses rise on the heights.  
> Here Aguntum, seated on a mountain ridge, proudly dominates.  
>   
> From there seek the rapid roads where the Julian Alps unfold,  
> Rising higher, while the mountain reaches into the clouds.  
> From there depart from Forum Julii, named after its ruler,  
> Through your crags, O Osoppo, where the river flows,  
> And Reunia rises above the waters of the Tagliamento.  
>   
> From there proceed through the Venetian passes and across the level fields, etc.  
> Or, if by chance you come to the city of Aquileia, etc.,  
> Where my Tarvisium lies, if you enter gently,  
> Proceeding through Ceneta, and to your friends at Duplavilis, etc.  
> If the road to Padua lies open to you, proceed to the city, etc.;  
> From there seek the pleasant city of Ravenna, more sweetly beloved, etc.

37. Fortunatus relieved this journey, which he made mostly through solitary and deserted regions, by composing poems, as though with a seasoning and tempering supplied by the Muses. He declares this about himself in his letter to Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 1, saying:

> As I walked among barbarians over a long stretch of road, weary from the journey or overcome by drunkenness beneath the winter’s cold, with the Muse urging me on—whether I was more frozen or more drunk I do not know—I, a new Orpheus, gave the voices of the forest to the lyre; the forest gave them back.

He was also invited and received as a guest by the barbarians and country people through whose lands he traveled, and he often poured out poems at their banquets. There, he says, his harp alone, buzzing and rattling, often resounded with barbarian songs.

He refers to this as the reason why some of his poems were written less elegantly and were less polished and refined. “For,” he says, “what can be finely expressed where no one is thought sane unless one goes mad along with him, so that it is all the more cause for rejoicing if one is permitted to remain alive after drinking?”

38.
