On this same journey through Germany and Gaul he could easily enter into friendship with men of the highest rank and distinguished for virtue and honor, and win their favor—both because of the innocence of his life and the gentleness of his character, and because of the reputation of his learning and talent, but especially because of a certain recommendation from the Muses, which has always been accustomed to make even foreign and unknown men acceptable among foreign peoples.

Certainly many men are mentioned by Fortunatus in his poems who seem to have received him as a guest in Germany, judged him worthy of their friendship, and shown him other services. Among them were Lupus and Gogo, men of princely rank at the court of the king of Austrasia; Magnulphus, the brother of Lupus; Jovinus the prefect; Bodigisilus the duke; and others whom he sometimes testifies that he saw in Germany and with whom he stayed.

Thus, writing to Lupus in Book VII, chapter 8, he says:

> When Germany, foreign land, held my eyes,  
> You, father, were ready to care for the welfare of your country.  
> Whenever I joined conversation to your speech,  
> I thought I was reclining among ambrosial roses.

Likewise, writing to Jovinus in chapter 12, he says:

> I did not expect that, after Germany  
> Had brought our eyes together, love would spring back so strongly.

39. He also testifies that the brothers Sigismund and Aregisilus were generous and beneficent toward him in those regions, and for that reason he does not hesitate to equal them with his parents in affection and kindness. Thus he writes to them in Book VII, chapter 21:

> A sweet letter reveals to me the names of my friends:  
> From here, shining Sigismund; from here, gracious Aregisilus.  
> After the Italian lands, Rhine, you send me parents;  
> With the arrival of my brothers, I shall no longer be a stranger.

40. From this it is easy to conjecture that he spent some length of time in Germany and the neighboring regions—long enough, that is, to visit and conveniently approach the distinguished men whom he so often celebrates in his poems, to win their friendship through frequent services, and also to become acquainted with and travel through so many cities and regions, whose careful and accurate descriptions occur in his poems.

41. When Fortunatus came into Gaul, he was received by the man whom we have often mentioned, Sigibert, king of Austrasia, who treated him with every generosity and courtesy. He had likely been recommended by letters and testimonials from many distinguished men of rank whom he had won over in Germany, and he was already sufficiently distinguished and well known through the reputation of his talent and learning.

42. The distinguished Joannes Josephus Liruti, wondering how it could have happened that Fortunatus was able to enter into friendship with so many kings and princes and win their hearts, thinks that the nobility of his family and lineage was responsible, since it would have given him easy access to the friendship of princes and kings.

To state openly what I think about this matter, it seems quite difficult to me that a man whose paternal seat and home lay in a humble and insufficiently celebrated place—I mean Duplavilis—and who, as he himself declares, possessed an ancestral origin but had held no public office and acquired no recognized mark of honor or dignity [Col. 0033B] (as we have explained above), could have obtained such a distinguished and glorious nobility of descent that he would become renowned not only in Italy but also in Germany and the farthest reaches of Gaul.

This is especially so in such turbulent times, when everything was being thrown into confusion by wars and rebellions, and when even the lineage of more distinguished men could easily have been obscured unless they had rendered service in conducting wars or administering the commonwealth at home.

I therefore prefer to agree with Hincmar, who writes in the preface to *The Life of Saint Remigius* concerning Fortunatus that, throughout various places in the Gallic and Belgic regions, he was then invited by many powerful and honorable men, on account of the merit of his life and learning.

43. Since Sigibert performed great and exceptional acts of kindness and generosity toward Fortunatus, and since there has been and will often be occasion to speak of him, it will not be out of place to say something here about him and his kingdom, as well as about his royal lineage and relations.

He was the son of Chlothar I, king of the Franks, the most powerful man of his age. After the death of his father Clovis, Chlothar had begun to reign, when the paternal kingdom was divided into equal parts among himself and his three brothers (Gregory of Tours, Book III of *The History of the Franks*, chapter 1). When they had died, he claimed the entire Frankish empire for himself, partly by inheritance and partly by arms and power.

When Chlothar himself died, he left behind four sons: Charibert, Guntram, Chilperic, and Sigibert. They divided the kingdom among themselves by lot. To Sigibert, to use Gregory’s words in Book IV of *The History of the Franks*, chapter 22, fell the kingdom of Theuderic, the brother of Chlothar, and he was to have Rheims as his seat.

The rule of the kings of Austrasia who resided at Rheims extended far into Germany. On this subject, see Fortunatus, Book VI, chapter 2, and Ruinart’s notes on Gregory of Tours, Book IV of *The History of the Franks*, chapter 22.

44. Meanwhile, when Sigibert saw that his brothers had married women of the lowest and most servile condition, forgetful of their lineage and dignity, he himself, with royal mind and judgment, decided that he should take a wife from a royal family.

For this purpose he sent envoys to Spain to ask Athanagild, king in Spain, for his daughter Brunichild in marriage. She was distinguished not only by her physical beauty but also by her intelligence, moral integrity, prudence of judgment, and pleasantness of speech.

When he had obtained her, he married her with royal pomp and ceremony, amid the greatest joy and congratulations of the whole kingdom (Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 27). Fortunatus composed an epithalamium for this marriage, as we discussed above, no. 34. In a letter to Gogo he likewise describes the recently completed event in these words:

> Recently, from the lands of Spain, through many dangers,  
> You bring the greatest joys to an outstanding king.

45. Chilperic, Sigibert’s brother, imitating his marriage, likewise sent to Spain to ask for Gelesuintha, Brunichild’s sister, to marry her. About a year after Sigibert had married Brunichild, he took Gelesuintha as his wife, rejecting Fredegund, a woman of the lowest and most servile condition, whose love had captivated him.

Not long afterward, however, when Gelesuintha, offended by Chilperic’s treachery, was preparing to return to Spain, she was killed at his command while lying in bed. A few days later Chilperic took Fredegund back, through whose deceit and plots both Sigibert and Chilperic himself were later killed.

Fortunatus saw Gelesuintha as she passed through Poitiers, when he was still a newcomer in that city, and expressed his bitter grief at her death in a mournful poem, which may be read in Book VI, chapter 7.

46. Sigibert, then—to return to the point from which we digressed—was a very noble and wise king in those times, whose virtues are celebrated everywhere by Fortunatus, Gregory of Tours, and many others. When Fortunatus came into Gaul, Sigibert received him with the greatest honor and gave him Count Sigoald as a companion and guide for the journeys he had to undertake through Gaul, so that Sigoald might provide him with assistance, constant attendance, and protection, whether he was going to Tours or traveling through other cities and regions of Gaul.

We know this from Fortunatus himself, who writes to Sigoald in Book X, chapter 20, in these words:

> When I first came from the borders of Italy to the kingdoms,  
> King Sigibert appointed you as my support,  
> So that I might travel more safely with you as my companion,  
> And that a horse might be prepared here, food there.  
> You fulfilled your duty, etc. . . .

47. It should be believed that, as soon as Sigibert permitted it, Fortunatus went directly to Tours to venerate the tomb of Saint Martin. He knew how greatly Martin had benefited him at Ravenna, and since Martin’s sake had brought him to Gaul, Fortunatus wished, in person, to honor his ashes and fulfill his vow.

At that time the Church of Tours was governed by Euphronius, nephew of Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres—a man most noble in lineage and most distinguished in holiness. [Note: Browerus wrongly states in his *Life of Fortunatus* that Gregory was then seated at Tours; Gregory did not obtain that see until 573.] Fortunatus was afterward joined to him by singular goodwill and a close bond of friendship, as is shown by the letters he wrote to him in Book III, chapters 1 and 2.

Fortunatus must therefore be said to have met him at that time and laid the foundations of a friendship which, cultivated and strengthened thereafter by mutual services, eventually reached the point that Fortunatus regarded him in the place of a father.

48. After leaving Tours, Fortunatus came to Poitiers for the sake of his journey and established his home and residence in that city. We learn this from the testimony of Paul the Deacon, and Fortunatus himself declares it in Book VIII, chapter 1, writing as follows:

> I, Fortunatus, greet you from here with humble prayer and voice:  
> The Gallic countryside holds me, born in Italy.  
> I reside at Poitiers, where Saint Hilary,  
> A Father known throughout the world, was once born.

He thereafter also deserved to be enrolled in the clergy of that city, although he was an immigrant, and to be ordained to the priesthood. This is certainly a strong indication of his virtue and the integrity and innocence of his life.

It is not, however, so easy to determine in what year he became a priest of the Church of Poitiers. When Paul the Deacon relates that he was eventually ordained in that same city—that is, first a priest and afterward a bishop—he seems to place the event at the very end of Fortunatus’s life.

But since Gregory of Tours repeatedly calls Fortunatus a priest in his writings, the matter must apparently be judged otherwise. For in Book I, chapter 13, of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, he expressly calls him “his fellow servant, Fortunatus the priest.”

Gregory of Tours had composed his books on *The Miracles of Saint Martin* before Fortunatus wrote his four books in verse on *The Life of Saint Martin*. In the letter prefixed to those books, Fortunatus writes to Gregory that, when Gregory had ordered the work he had composed concerning the miracles of Saint Martin to be rendered in verse, he should send it to Fortunatus so that he might encompass it in poetry.

Fortunatus, moreover, completed the four books of *The Life of Saint Martin* while Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, was still alive; Germanus died in the year 576, as we noted in the annotation to Book IV of *The Life of Saint Martin*, p. 470. It follows that Fortunatus was already a priest by that time.

To state my own view on this matter, it seems to me that Fortunatus was already a cleric when he left Italy. I infer this from the fact that his contemporary Gregory of Tours repeatedly calls him “the Italian priest,” a title that his own works also seem to bear out.

49. It is much more difficult to determine when Fortunatus stayed as a guest with Agricola, or Agroecula, bishop of Chalon, or, as seems more probable, bishop of Nevers, as we noted under chapter 24 of Book III of Fortunatus’s works.

For, in writing to him, Fortunatus not only indicates that he lived with him but also testifies that he was taught, instructed, and nourished by that excellent man’s father, in these verses:

> When my land deserved to be plowed by the hand of its father,  
> Let it be cultivated again by the plow of his son.  
> For the father, with sweet affection, memorable throughout the world,  
> Cherished me together with you both with a single love.  
>   
> A father in heart, a nurse in nourishment, a good teacher in speech,  
> He loved me, honored me, guided me, and gave me what was honorable.  
> With pious zeal he sowed the newly broken fields;  
> What the Father poured out, let that seed nourish me.

I therefore believe that Fortunatus stayed with him before giving himself entirely to Radegund—of whom we shall speak shortly—and to the completion of her affairs. Thereafter he seems not to have been separated from her for long.

50. It is often asked here for what reasons Fortunatus, after fulfilling his vow at Tours—which had been the principal reason for coming from Italy to Gaul—continued to remain in Gaul and did not return to his own people.

P. Browerus, in chapter 2 of *The Life of Fortunatus*, attributes this to the military disturbances by which Italy was then being especially afflicted by the arms of the Lombards. At that time Tarvisium, Fortunatus’s homeland, and the neighboring regions, situated at the very entrance and throat of Germany, were particularly exposed to enemy raids and assaults.

Fortunatus therefore decided to remain in Gaul until peace and tranquility had been restored to Italy, so that he could safely return to his ancestral region and home.

Certainly he did not remain in Gaul with an easy heart, nor does it seem that he preferred a foreign land to his homeland and his own people by deliberate choice. Writing to Lupus in Book VII, chapter 9, he says of himself:

> An exile from Italy, I have now, I think, been wandering for nine years,  
> Along the shore touched by the waters of the Ocean.  
> So many seasons pass, and still, through letters from my parents,  
> No message from beyond their closed doors has refreshed me.

He laments his departure from Italy even more grievously in Book VI, chapter 10, in these words:

> Too sadly I wander, an exile roaming far from my native shores,  
> More sadly than a shipwrecked guest upon Apollonian waters.

51. Nor should another reason be passed over, because of which he remained in Gaul and never again returned to his own people. He himself explains it in Book VIII, chapter 1, saying:

> Desiring Martin, I clung to Radegund’s vow,  
> She whom the Thuringian land gave to holy heaven.

That is, he had come to Gaul with the intention of visiting the tomb of Saint Martin and satisfying his devotion toward him; but he was detained by the prayers and vows of Radegund, a most devout woman, from returning to Italy. It therefore came about that he spent the remainder of his life in Gaul.

52. Since mention has been made of Radegund, through whose efforts Fortunatus chiefly remained in Gaul, and whom he always honored and attended with every service of generosity and goodwill, it will not be out of place to say something about her royal lineage and circumstances, as well as her outstanding virtue and holiness. This may add much light to the interpretation of the *Life of Fortunatus* and many of his poems.

Radegund was the daughter of Berthacharius, king of the Thuringians. When Hermenefridus, Berthacharius’s own brother, had overthrown him, Radegund, still a girl and deprived of her father, was left under the guardianship of her uncle (Gregory of Tours, Book III of *The History of the Franks*, chapter 4).

Later, after Hermenefridus himself had been defeated and conquered by the Frankish kings Chlothar and Theuderic, she was brought into Gaul as a captive. A dispute then arose between Theuderic and Chlothar as to which of them should receive her as wife. Chlothar prevailed, and he married her as soon as her age permitted, having meanwhile entrusted her to guardians to be raised and cared for in a royal estate (Fortunatus, no. 2 of *The Life of Radegund*).

Royal marriage and the pleasures of the most powerful court did not diminish the devotion to piety and religion that had already shone out in the young girl—she was accustomed to clean the lower part of the altars with her own hands and lead the choirs of boys singing divine praises—but rather made it more conspicuous. Her courtiers were already saying to Chlothar that he had a nun for a wife rather than a queen, and for this reason he was sometimes harsher toward her.

Meanwhile, Radegund’s brother was unjustly killed by Chlothar through the deceit and treachery of his courtiers. Taking this time and opportunity, she decided that she must withdraw from Chlothar and began to consider embracing the monastic life, to which she was especially devoted.

Accordingly, when she had been sent by her royal husband to Saint Medard, bishop of Noyon, she began to insist that he consecrate her to the Lord after changing her clothing. At first he refused, fearing that he would arouse Chlothar’s anger against himself. At last, however, he yielded to her prayers and placed a veil upon her head, thereby declaring her a nun.

After departing from there, she came to Tours, to the basilica of Saint Martin. Then she went to Saix, an estate in the territory of Poitiers, and there, after building a monastery, lived in the greatest holiness until the end of her life (Fortunatus, ibid., chapter 12).

Gregory of Tours writes of her in Book III of *The History of the Franks*, chapter 7:

> After changing her clothing, she built a monastery for herself within the city of Poitiers. Endowed with prayers, fasts, vigils, and almsgiving, she shone forth to such an extent that she was held in great esteem among the people.

53. In this monastery at Poitiers she appointed as abbess Agnes, a virgin distinguished by singular piety and virtue. Radegund had formerly kept Agnes as a servant, but from her earliest age had honored and raised her as a daughter, to use Radegund’s own words. Radegund entrusted herself, after God, to obey Agnes’s direction according to the rule.

She admits this about herself in Gregory of Tours, Book IX, chapter 42. Accordingly, Fortunatus sings of her in Book VIII, chapter 1:

> Exchanging royal robes for a milk-white habit,  
> She is covered by the beloved, humbler garment of a servant.  
> Once borne aloft in a splendid, proud carriage,  
> Now her modest foot strikes the ground in obedience.  
>   
> Her right hand, once laden with inlaid emeralds,  
> Now, poor, serves her attendants with diligent care.  
> Once governing the lofty court, now she ministers at command;  
> She who formerly pleased by ruling now pleases by serving.

Writing to Agnes in Book VIII, chapter 4, he addresses her as follows:

> But before all others the pious Mother stands dearer to you,  
> Choosing to join you to the exalted choir.  
> The matter itself proves it, since, though you remain her daughter,  
> She desires in her prayers to have you as her mother.  
>   
> Behold, she places in her own position the beloved foster-child  
> Whom she cherished at her knees and raised for herself.  
> And she who always guided you with the authority of her staff  
> Is now eager to be more fully under your command.

54. Because of her royal kinship and lineage, Radegund had great means and opportunity to enrich her monastery at Poitiers with precious gifts. Among these, the most notable were those that she obtained from the emperor Justin through an embassy sent to him around the year 569, with the efforts and favor of Sigibert contributing greatly to the matter.

As Baudonivia writes of her in *The Life of Radegund*, no. 8:

> She obtained what her vows requested: she gloried in possessing, gathered in one place, the blessed wood of the Lord’s cross, adorned with gold and gems, and many relics of the saints that the East preserved. At the request of the holy woman, the emperor sent envoys with Gospels adorned with gold and gems.

55. This provided Fortunatus with the occasion to compose several hymns and other poems in honor of the holy cross. Among them is the very famous hymn that begins, *Vexilla Regis prodeunt*—“The banners of the King advance”—which has long been consecrated by the use of the Church itself.

He also wrote an extensive poem in which, in Radegund’s name, he gives thanks to the Augusti Justin and Sophia for the most precious gifts sent to her, gifts by which he asserts that the entire West had been illuminated and adorned.

56. Fortunatus himself bears witness to the nature and extent of the bond of supreme piety, goodwill, charity, and affection that existed between him and Radegund and Agnes—a bond entirely free from every suspicion or danger of improper familiarity. In Book XI, chapter 6, he writes to Agnes in these verses:

> A mother to me in honor, but a sweet sister in affection,  
> I honor you in piety, faith, breast, and heart;  
> With heavenly affection, with no bodily passion,  
> I love not the flesh, but what the Spirit desires.  
>   
> Christ is witness, with Peter and Paul as his ministers,  
> And holy Mary with the pious companions sees it:  
> You have been to me in mind and eyes no otherwise  
> Than if you, Titiana, were my sister born from the same womb;  
> And as though Mother Radegund, in one birth,  
> Had brought us both forth from her chaste womb, I was your brother.

57. He declares his particular affection for Radegund in Book XI, chapter 2, in these verses, in which he expresses his longing for her when she shut herself away, as will be explained below:

> Where does my light hide herself from me,  
> Without permitting herself to be revealed to my sight?  
> I see all things at once—the heavens, the rivers, the earth;  
> When I do not see you, everything is insufficient for me.  
>   
> Though the sky is clear, with the clouds fled away,  
> When you conceal yourself from me, day stands without the sun.

58. He often celebrates their generosity and munificence toward him in his poems, in which he gives them thanks for the little gifts they sent. How frequently this occurred is sufficiently indicated by these words, which he writes to Agnes in Book XI, chapter 9:

> One carrier is not enough when sent to such great women;  
> So often have the feet of those returning become exhausted.  
> I do not recount each gift, because your gifts overwhelm me, etc.

He also indicates that he was repeatedly received at table by them and generously fed. Among other examples, in Book XI, chapter 11, he recalls and describes a meal prepared for him by Agnes, decorated and arranged with various flowers and leaves so as to resemble a flourishing garden. From this their diligence and attentiveness toward Fortunatus can be discerned.

59. Their mutual affection and close relationship therefore prompt us to ask what principal service or office Fortunatus performed for these most religious women. But certain matters must first be noted.

First, I observe that Radegund always displayed a singular eagerness to honor and listen to those from whom she could receive instruction in piety and religion. As Fortunatus writes in *The Life of Radegund*, no. 8:

> If any servant of God, whether of his own accord or summoned, was seen approaching her, you would see her filled with heavenly joy . . . On the following day, entrusting the care of the household to her stewards, she devoted herself entirely, in accordance with the words of the just man, to the principles of salvation and to the commerce by which heavenly life is attained, and she remained occupied with these matters for days.

This concerns Radegund while she was still living at the royal court.

60. In addition, there were already many matters for the nuns of the monastery at Poitiers to manage, whether they concerned their private responsibilities and duties or the affairs and condition of the monastery as a whole. In administering these matters, the diligence and fidelity of someone living outside the monastery enclosure were required.

To give one or two examples, Gregory of Tours, Book IX of *The History of the Franks*, chapter 42, preserves a copy of a letter that Radegund sent to the bishops of Gaul, seeking some assistance from their patronage and authority against those who might wish to violate the rights or property of the monastery at Poitiers.

Likewise, in chapter 39, there is a rescript from the bishops to Radegund, in which those nuns who had ever wished to leave the monastery or marry were struck with anathema.

Such matters, and others of the same kind, often had to be communicated to bishops, kings, or other men of rank, and sometimes settled through them. They therefore required a man distinguished for judgment and skill, who could manage and arrange these affairs.

61. Since this is so, I think I may first affirm that Radegund and Agnes had Fortunatus as the director and teacher of their entire life, and that they employed his judgment and counsel both in directing their private affairs and in regulating the discipline of the whole monastery. This is plainly consistent both with the close relationship which, as we have shown, existed between him and them, and with Fortunatus’s religion, learning, and prudence. I would readily say that these were Radegund’s entreaties, to which Venantius himself confesses that he clung, so that he did not return to his own people in Italy. There are also several indications in Fortunatus’s writings that confirm this very point.

Thus, in Book XI, chapter 4, he advises Radegund to take some wine to strengthen and refresh her stomach, producing the Apostle’s example and authority, since he recommends this to Timothy. Likewise, in chapter 7, writing to Agnes, he asks her to provide, on his behalf, the service or attendance which he himself, while absent, could not render to Radegund. In chapter 8, he thanks Agnes for having, at his request, granted the nuns a feast, and finally expresses the wish that Agnes and Radegund might long survive, so that under their restraint—or authority—the condition and discipline of the Pictavian monastery might long flourish and remain secure.

Finally, in Book VIII, chapter 17, writing to Gregory of Tours, when a serious scandal leading to dissension had arisen in the same Pictavian monastery after the death of Saint Radegund, he commends the abbess’s cause to him in these words:

“Remember the recommendation of my blessed lady, daughter—or now already your mother—Lady Radegund. For the stability of her place, her person, and the whole Rule, she asked and entrusted this to you with the supplication of her words and of her heart: command that you labor tirelessly, so that he who provides help to the needy may repay you in everlasting recompense.”

From these words it may be understood what position Fortunatus held with Radegund and Agnes, and what services he rendered to them.

62. From the very frequent journeys which we learn that Fortunatus undertook through Gaul and Germany, it may also be inferred that he was accustomed to transact many affairs concerning the Pictavian monastery. Thus, in Book XI, chapters 27 and 28, writing to Agnes and Radegund, he recounts some of his journeys. On one of them he had long been tossed by a storm and had consequently come into grave danger of losing his life; on another he describes having endured winter cold and frost, while everything far and wide was held fast by snow and ice. He himself indicates that he had certain matters to discuss with them in person rather than commit to a letter, in these words:

“I keep the complaints to be recounted together concealed in my heart.”

Likewise, in Book VI, chapter 10, when he had reached Metz, he relates that the boat on which he was traveling was taken away from him by a royal cook. When he arrived at Nauciacum, or Nasium, he says that he was received with great generosity by King Sigibert and also by his ministers Papulus and Gogo, and that he received from them both the boat and all the other supplies necessary for continuing his journey.

Again, in Book X, chapter 10, he describes another journey which he made around the Rhine and Moselle. On that occasion he encountered the royal household—that is, Childebert and his mother Brunichild—and was most courteously detained and received by them. He then accompanied them as they traveled with royal pomp and equipment.

It is therefore highly probable that Fortunatus visited these places not so much for his own pleasure or private business as to satisfy the wishes and concerns of those to whom he had devoted himself and his service.

63. From these journeys, whatever their ultimate purpose and rationale may have been, he gained a great opportunity to visit the celebrated bishops of Gaul and Germany, and to become acquainted with those with whom he was joined by the most friendly affection, as is repeatedly evident from his poems. To mention some of them, from whose friendship and companionship an exceptional commendation of Fortunatus’s innocence and virtue may be drawn, Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, displayed the greatest goodwill and affection toward him. This is clear, among other evidence, from Book VIII, chapter 2 of Fortunatus’s Works. When Fortunatus wished to go to him but was detained by Radegund, he says:

“From there my father calls me, Germanus, radiant throughout the world;

“Here my mother holds me back; from there my father calls me.

“Both are sweet to me, joined together as my desire embraces them;

“Both are sweet to me, filled with the love of God.”

This was the Germanus by whom Agnes, abbess of the Pictavian monastery, was consecrated, as is clear from Radegund’s testimony in Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the History of the Franks, chapter 42. From this it may be understood that there was a great basis for a relationship and goodwill between Germanus and Fortunatus as well.

64. Fortunatus was especially welcome and pleasing to Felix, bishop of Nantes, a man distinguished both by the nobility of his birth and by the virtue of his character. This is indicated by the poems of Fortunatus addressed to him and by Felix’s letters to Fortunatus, which may be read in Book III, chapters 4, 5, and following.

He also held a prominent place in the goodwill and favor of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, and of Placidina, formerly his wife, a woman of imperial family and especially distinguished for her outstanding reputation for piety. Poems 15, 16, and 17 of Book I plainly testify to this. In Book IV, chapter 10, there is a poem which he himself wrote for the funeral of Leontius. In it he gives an excellent testimony to Leontius’s nobility of descent, his virtue, his diligence toward his flock, and his authority and favor among kings.

65. What, then, shall I say of Euphronius, bishop of Tours? What of Nicetius, bishop of Trier, or of Magnericus, who succeeded him? To each of these men Fortunatus wrote letters or poems, found in Book III, chapters 1, 2, 3, 11, 12, and 13.

Nor must Saint Martin be passed over, the bishop of Galicia who converted the Suebi, the inhabitants of Galicia, from their ancestral superstition to the embrace of the Christian religion. Fortunatus also wrote a letter to him, filled with the longing of the warmest friendship, as well as a poem in which he commends his virtues and his merits toward his flock. These may be found in Book V, chapters 1 and 2.

66. Avitus, bishop of Auvergne, must be added to these men. Gregory of Tours records in the Book of the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 2, that Avitus roused and encouraged him to study divine matters. Avitus therefore held Fortunatus in particular affection, as the close relationship which both men had with Gregory already seemed to require. Moreover, when Avitus had converted more than five hundred Jews to Christ on the holy day of Pentecost, Fortunatus, at Gregory’s urging, celebrated this deed in an extended poem.

67. But, not to enumerate individually all those who are found to have embraced Fortunatus with goodwill and acts of kindness, let Gregory of Tours, the bishop of Tours, whom we mentioned above, stand for all the rest: a man distinguished both by his see and position and by his piety and learning.

How deeply Gregory loved Fortunatus, and how great a friendship and intimacy existed between them, is shown by the many and frequent letters or poems which Fortunatus wrote to him. In them he shows that he was attached to Gregory as to a father, and in turn bears witness to Gregory’s exceptional devotion and goodwill toward himself.

Since distance separated them and he could not be with Gregory or enjoy his presence as much as he wished, he compensated for his longing by writing frequently. For, as he himself declares about himself in Book V, chapter 14, writing to Gregory:

“Constantly I desire, holy Gregory, whom I long to embrace,

“To behold you with my eyes, to seek you through little letters.

“It is sweet for me to see you; and if the chance to see you is lacking,

“My hope as I pray will be at least to address words to the Father.”

68. At Gregory’s urging Fortunatus wrote or published many works which, had Gregory’s encouragement and impulse not intervened, might perhaps have lain forever in the darkness and oblivion of posterity. How highly Gregory valued Fortunatus’s writings, and how greatly he thought it mattered that they should be brought into public view, may be understood from the fact that he did not merely deal lightly with Fortunatus but pressed him with entreaties and solemn adjurations to publish his poems and other little works collected into a single volume.

We learn this from Fortunatus’s own testimony, as he writes to Gregory in Book I, chapter 1:

“Therefore, apostolic man, illustrious Pope Gregory, since you vigorously demand that I bring forth for you certain pieces from the little works of my incompetence to be transferred, I marvel that you are led astray by your love of my trifles.”

And again:

“But since, having been driven on while humbly and eagerly resisting, you adjure me under the testimony of the divine mystery and by the glory of the virtues of the most blessed Martin, you diligently urge me to be brought into public view against my modesty, etc.”

In Book V, chapter 5, he likewise writes that Gregory had stirred him to write, in these words:

“You urge me, excellent Father, with serious concern yet sincere sweetness, to make the tongue-less man speak in poetry and to make the sluggish man run in pedestrian verse.”

He writes much the same in Book IX, chapter 6.

69. Among the poems which Fortunatus then published were many written to Gregory himself, containing praise and commendation of his virtues. Among them, the poem found in Book V, chapter 3, stands out in particular. It was written to the citizens of Tours, to whom Venantius congratulates them because Gregory had been made bishop of that church, and wishes them every blessing from the arrival and presence of their pontiff.

70. Gregory’s generosity and liberality toward Fortunatus are repeatedly declared by Fortunatus in his poems. To say nothing of other passages, in Book VIII, chapter 25, he records that Gregory had provided him with a small estate for his food and other expenses. He compares Gregory’s generosity with that of Saint Martin, who covered a naked and needy man with part of his cloak, in these verses:

“Restoring the deeds of generous Martin, Gregory,

“As he covered that man with clothing, so you cover us with food.

“As he once divided his cloak, so you divide a little estate;

“He was powerful in covering, and you are gracious in sustaining.”

Describing the location and beauty of this small estate in chapter 24 of the same book, he says:

“On that tract of land the gift was bestowed,

“Where the impetuous Vienne breaks its waters against the shore.

“While the sailor is borne along in plunging, swollen-hulled craft,

“He sees cultivated acres as he sings the boating-song.”

71. Summarizing the gifts and benefits which Gregory had bestowed upon him, Fortunatus expresses their magnitude and number in Book VIII, chapter 23, saying:

“If my tongue watered its streams after the manner of a flood,

“Or were swept away by the waters in the whirl of a torrent,

“Even then, Gregory, in praising your supreme generosity,

“If I could not fill the river, I would be but a drop.

“Nor could even the Muse of Maro equal the generous Father:

“Who can speak with his mouth of how many blessings you bring me?”

72. Why should I enumerate the others whom Fortunatus had as friends and patrons among the Gauls? I mean kings and princes, to whom he was so welcome and at all times so pleasing and dear that, in my judgment, this provides very great testimony both to his talent and learning, to the integrity of his life, and also to a certain urbanity and cheerfulness in familiar intercourse.

We have already said how welcome and pleasing he was to Sigibert, king of Austrasia. To him must be added Sigibert’s brothers, Charibert, Guntram, and Chilperic, as well as Sigibert’s son Childebert, who later held the kingdom of Austrasia, together with their queens Brunichild, Gelesuintha, and Fredegund, and with the royal households. The many poems written about them and to them repeatedly testify that Fortunatus was held in honor and esteem by all of them.

73. In addition to Gogo, Lupus, Magnulfus, Jovinus, and the others whom I mentioned above, Mummulenus, a man distinguished by rank in those times and the most noble among his peers, was also a close friend of Fortunatus. Fortunatus praises him magnificently in Book VII, chapter 14, and in Book IX, chapter 2, writes him a consolatory letter on the death of his daughter.

Likewise, Papulus, a man of great power under Sigibert; Berulfus, Condo, Gundoarius, Boso, Galactorius, Chrodinus, Mummolus, and other men distinguished both by virtue and rank and honored and favored by their kings are found to have shown Fortunatus exceptional goodwill.

What, in my judgment, ought to contribute greatly to his commendation is this: although most of those whom I have named experienced changing fortunes, and some even conspired against the kings themselves or defected from them, while others, suspected and offended for serious reasons, lost their positions and rank and miserably perished in exile or death, Fortunatus alone, or almost alone, is never recorded as having been summoned or suspected for any reason. Nor did the misfortunes of those whom he held as his closest and dearest friends ever diminish the favor which he enjoyed with the kings.

This is a powerful indication that he cultivated the friendships of the most noble men in such a way that he did not involve himself in affairs alien to his own person and rank. Free from every partisan attachment, he pursued his own work and was a lover of peace and leisure.

74. For some period Fortunatus lived in that part of Lesser Brittany which lies along the Ocean and is washed and encircled by its waves. Thus he writes to Felix of Nantes in Book III, chapter 4:

“While I lay in bed, yawning amid the gentle influence of the nearby sea and remaining for a long while stretched out upon the shore, suddenly, through the wave-breaking floods of your eloquence, as though shattered against the rocks, I was touched and sprinkled by a shower of salt.”

Likewise, writing to the Deacon Druco in Book III, chapter 33, he says:

“The swollen surface of the Ocean sea flows around us;

“And Paris, dear companion, holds you.

“The Seine retains you; the Breton wave encircles us.

“Though separated by lands, one love binds us together.

“Here no fury of the sea removes your face from me,

“Nor does the North Wind take away your name, my friend.”

75. It seems necessary to ask for what principal reason Fortunatus withdrew to those shores and coasts. If we may make some conjecture on the matter, I first observe that it was customary at that time for most deeply religious men to withdraw during the year, and especially during the sacred season of Lent, to some place removed from the crowds of human beings, where they might devote themselves alone to prayers and fasts.

Thus Gregory of Tours relates concerning Saint Senoch in the Book of the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 15, that from the day of Saint Martin until Christmas, and again for the forty days before Easter, he lived shut up in a cell. Likewise, concerning Berecundus, bishop of Amiens, an author contemporary with Gregory relates that he withdrew to a secluded place so that during the sacred Lenten season he might devote himself more earnestly to the contemplation of divine things.

[Note: Read the preface to the first century, no. 111.]

76. Islands were especially suitable for this purpose, since, surrounded on every side by the sea, they kept away the more frequent approaches of human beings. Hence Gregory relates concerning Palladius, bishop of Saintes, in Book VIII of the History of the Franks, chapter 43, that he withdrew to a sea island during Lent for the sake of prayer.

Saint Marculf, abbot of Nantes, likewise fled every year to a certain island so that there, during that sacred period of forty days, he might mortify his body more rigorously than usual. The farther he was removed from human sight, the more suitable and free he was for performing vigils, prayer, and fasting, as is read in his Life, no. 12, reproduced in the Benedictine first century, p. 128.

Already in the age of Saint Ambrose, islands were commonly frequented by those who, for the sake of piety, wished to withdraw to solitary and secluded places. Ambrose himself indicates this in the Hexameron, Book III, chapter 5, in these words:

“Why should I enumerate the islands . . . in which those who renounce the enticements of worldly excess, committed to the purpose of continence, choose to hide from the world and avoid the uncertain winding paths of this life? The sea is therefore the solitude of temperance, the exercise of continence, the retreat of gravity, the harbor of security, the tranquility of the age, the sobriety of this world, and for faithful and devoted men an incentive to devotion, so that, while the waves gently wash the shores, the songs of those singing psalms may contend with their sound, and the islands may applaud the tranquil chorus of the holy waves and resound with the hymns of the saints.”

77. Since this is so, I am led to believe that Fortunatus may at times have been accustomed to withdraw to some island, perhaps during the sacred season of Lent, where, removed from the crowd of human beings and free from every other business, he might devote himself more earnestly to fasting and prayer.

That he lived on some island may be understood from the words with which he writes to Placidina in Book I, chapter 17:

“Receive, I beg you, these very small gifts with kindness,

“Although the island itself, more becomingly, shines as a gift in the world.

“From the midst of the waves it offers these gifts to you,

“And the Ocean presents them amid the murmur of its swelling waters.”

78. Yet perhaps Fortunatus sought islands or other maritime places for another reason: he may have been searching for memorials of the most holy men who had lived in those regions and of the deeds which they had performed. These would both kindle his devotion and sharpen his desire for imitation through the likeness of their examples, and would lead him to compose their Lives.

That this was especially customary for him is testified by so many Lives of the saints which he labored over, and is also confirmed by these words in which he speaks of himself in Book II, chapter 12:

“Let other hearts resound with human praises;

“For me, it is pleasing to commemorate the just.

“For my mind is urged by a twofold reason

“To weave the deeds of victors into books as a work of piety.

“First, it is fitting to proclaim great things about the great,

“For whoever keeps silent about good deeds will be guilty of a crime.

“Another reason urges me: success is loved,

“And whoever reads his own deeds desires better things.”

79. Fortunatus himself provides us with a clear indication of this matter when, writing to Placidina in Book I, chapter 17, he says:

“While I hastened to explore those places of the sea,

“A raging wave coming from the North Wind drove me back.

“Yet, so that your prosperity might prove itself complete,

“On land it offered what was sought upon the waters.”

By the final verses he seems chiefly to indicate this: while he was sailing with the intention of discovering in certain maritime places traces of piety and holiness left by devout men, he was driven back by a storm and carried to Placidina. In her person and manner of life he found expressed what he had been seeking elsewhere by sea.

80. P. Brower, to whom the distinguished Joseph Liruti also assents, holds that Radegund followed Fortunatus and lived with him, or at least on a nearby island, during that period. He is led to this view because, when Fortunatus writes to Felix, bishop of Nantes, in the same letter in which he says that he was yawning near the sea, he reports words of Felix which Felix had earlier written to him:

“Radegund lives enclosed by the wall of charity.”

81. But this does not seem to me sufficient reason for believing that Radegund, forgetful of the Rule to which she had conformed her conduct and of her own vocation, ever left the monastery to go elsewhere.

For she followed the Rule of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, in which it was expressly decreed, in the fifth recapitulated article:

“That none of you [the nuns] shall be permitted to leave the monastery until her death, nor presume to go out by herself.”

Hence Baudonivia writes concerning Radegund in her Life, no. 28, that, while she lived, she had established that none should go outside the monastery gate. Indeed, Radegund herself, in her letter to the bishops of Gaul—which may be read in Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the History of the Franks, chapter 42—invokes their authority against those nuns who had attempted thereafter to leave the monastery contrary to the Rule.

Finally, in the Book on the Destruction of Thuringia, Fortunatus is made to address Hamalafredus, his paternal cousin, in these words:

“If the sacred walls of the monastery did not hold me,

“I would suddenly be present in whatever region you dwell.”

It is therefore in no way credible that Radegund ever withdrew from the monastery in order to follow Fortunatus, whether he was seeking maritime places for religious and pious purposes or for any other reason.

82. From the relationship which existed between Radegund and Fortunatus, Brower further conjectures that Fortunatus embraced the monastic life and perhaps followed the Rule of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, for which Radegund’s devotion was especially notable. Fortunatus testifies to this in his account of her in Book VIII, chapter 6:

“Radegund, conceiving the love of Christ through faith,

“Touches with her lips whatever the Rule of Caesarius contains.

“She gathers the honey flowing from that bishop’s heart,

“And, never satisfied, drinks in its streams.”

83. Brower adds that Fortunatus was accustomed, after the manner of the ancient anchorites, to weave little baskets. Sending one of them to Radegund and Agnes, he addresses them in Book XI, chapter 13:

“This little basket was woven with my own hands from willow,

“Believe me, my dear mother and nourishing sister.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 17, he sends them another work made by his own hands, in these words:

“With my own hands I fashioned this gift of affection,

“But I ask that it be pleasing either to you or to my lady.”

Who does not know that it was especially characteristic of monks to devote themselves daily to manual labor, and to make and weave baskets and other such objects?

84. To these conjectures of Brower I am pleased to add what the distinguished Ruinart observed in the preface to the Works of Gregory of Tours, no. 35, where he says:

“In Gregory’s time the monastic order was already so closely joined to the clergy that being a monk and being a cleric were the same thing.”

We may also derive some conjecture from the fact that, when Fortunatus writes in Book IV of the Life of Saint Martin concerning Paul, bishop of Aquileia:

“He who wished to convert me from my earliest years,”

he seems to imply that, although not converted from his earliest years, he was converted later—that is, that he embraced the monastic life, as we showed above, no. 13.

85. Besides the monastery of women which Radegund had entrusted to Agnes to govern, and in which she herself lived, Radegund had also built a monastery for men at Tours. Moreover, it is clear from Baudonivia, Book of the Life of Saint Radegund, nos. 19 and 31, that another monastery for men was attached to the Basilica of Saint Radegund at Poitiers.

It is credible that Fortunatus also lived as a monk there, either by Radegund’s example and imitation or through her encouragement and urging, both so that he might be at hand if she needed any counsel or assistance from him, and so that through his manner and practice of life he might draw nearer to a likeness of hers.

86. Although Fortunatus performed very many services for Agnes and Radegund, and his diligence and concern never seem to have been lacking, he must nevertheless be said to have rendered no lesser services of piety and devotion to the Church of Poitiers, to whose clergy, as we said earlier, he had been attached.

Nor could a man, especially a newcomer, have eventually attained the highest see of that Church without outstanding merits toward it.

87. It is astonishing that some have denied that Venantius Fortunatus was ever a bishop, or have imagined another Fortunatus, claiming that the episcopal office was conferred upon him and that he was entirely different from our Fortunatus. They are chiefly led to this view because Gregory of Tours, whenever he mentions him, calls him only a presbyter.

But two exceedingly weighty and certain testimonies prove that our Fortunatus was a bishop, and indeed bishop of Poitiers.

First, Baudonivia, a nun of the Pictavian monastery and a contemporary of Fortunatus, writes of him in the prologue to the Life of Saint Radegund:

“We do not repeat what the apostolic man, Fortunatus the bishop, composed concerning the life of the blessed woman.”

Who, then, could claim that the Life of the blessed Radegund, which is customarily prefixed to the Life written by Baudonivia, was not composed by our Venantius Fortunatus?

Next, Paul the Deacon writes of him in Book II of the History of the Lombards, chapter 13:

“Finally, in that same city [Poitiers], he was first ordained a presbyter and afterward a bishop.”

Paul the Deacon was brought into Gaul by Charlemagne after Charlemagne had destroyed the Lombard kingdom in Italy. Since Paul also came to Poitiers to visit Fortunatus’s tomb, he could learn the whole matter from reliable records.

88. The fact that Gregory of Tours calls him only a presbyter causes no difficulty, since Fortunatus was made bishop of Poitiers only at the very end of his life, as we shall say below. By that time Gregory had not only published his books but had also died, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place.

This, then, was why his works, dedicated to Gregory of Tours, bear the name of an Italian presbyter rather than that of the bishop of Poitiers.

89. It is difficult to determine in what year Fortunatus ascended the see of Poitiers. At the time of Radegund’s death—which occurred in 587, according to Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the History of the Franks, chapter 2—the Church of Poitiers was still governed by Mauroveus, according to Gregory himself, who in chapter 106 of the Book on the Glory of the Confessors testifies that, in Mauroveus’s absence, he arranged the funeral and burial of the blessed Radegund.

Mauroveus was succeeded by Plato in 592. Plato was raised to that see while Gregory was still alive, and had been his disciple. Thus, on the day when Plato was appointed bishop of Poitiers, Fortunatus sang of him in Book X, chapter 18:

“May holy Gregory’s presence bring forth joyful gladness,

“And may one faith aid the twin cities.

“He who now, with Plato as supreme bishop, his disciple,

“Has made this a solemn day for the Church.”

Some claim that Placidus succeeded this Plato in the see of Poitiers. But Placidus was none other than Plato himself, as the distinguished Ruinart notes in his remarks on Gregory of Tours, Book IV of the Miracles of Saint Martin, chapter 32.

After Plato’s death, no one other than Fortunatus succeeded him. Since Plato’s death is assigned to approximately the year 599, Fortunatus must be regarded as having been made bishop of Poitiers at about the same time, since Gregory of Tours had already died by 595.

[Note: See Pagi, under the year 590. Read Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 96, and Book IV of the Miracles of Saint Martin, chapter 32; also Cointius, under the year 592, no. 3; and Ruinart, in the notes to Gregory of Tours, at the cited passage.]

90. In Book IV of Fortunatus’s Works, chapter 25, there is a poem which he wrote for the funeral of Queen Theodechild, who died in 598, as the distinguished Pagius demonstrates under that year, no. 4.

Not long after he wrote that epitaph, Fortunatus was proclaimed bishop of Poitiers, when he was already advancing into old age. For since he came to Gaul at approximately thirty-six years of age and spent another thirty-four years in that kingdom before becoming a bishop, it is clear that he reached this degree of dignity when he had already descended into old age.

91. Once he had obtained that position, Fortunatus benefited his flock greatly through the innocence of his life, the example of his virtues, and especially his learning.

His Expositions of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer are extant in Book X, chapters 1 and 2. He seems to have composed them for the purpose of reciting them to his people. In the latter work, among other things, he says:

“Retaining from it [the Lord’s Prayer] its mysteries, and learning to explain briefly how many things have been joined together in its brevity, for the edification of the Church, we are taught to set them out in a few words, because they will then please us more when heard, once they have become clear through understanding. Let us therefore come to the discourse of the holy Prayer, etc.”

In these words the person of a pastor instructing his flock is sufficiently apparent.

92. Fortunatus did not preside over the Church of Poitiers for many years. After his death, Caregisilus succeeded him, and Ennoaldus succeeded Caregisilus. Ennoaldus governed the Church of Poitiers in 615; concerning him, Cointius should be consulted under that year, no. 27.

Fortunatus must therefore be regarded as having departed this life at the beginning of the seventh century. He rests buried at Poitiers in the Basilica of Saint Hilary with fitting honor, as Paul the Deacon relates in the passage so often cited.

When Paul came to his tomb out of reverence and devotion, he composed the following epitaph at the request of Aprus, the abbot of that place, as he himself relates:

“Renowned in talent, swift in understanding, sweet in speech,

“Whose many pages sing a melody of sweetness,

“Fortunatus, the summit of poets, venerable in conduct,

“Born in Ausonia, lies buried in this earth.

“From his sacred mouth we learn the deeds

“Of the saints of old; these show us the path by which to seek the light.

“Happy Gaul, adorned with such great jewels,

“By whose radiance the dreadful night flees from you.

“These modest verses I have brought forth in plebeian song,

“So that your holy honor might not lie hidden among the peoples.

“Return the favor to the wretched man, lest I be rejected by a just judge;

“By your exceptional merits, blessed one, I beg you, plead for me.”

93. Fortunatus has accordingly been highly commended both for his piety and holiness and for the gifts of his talent and learning. He has had almost as many heralds and witnesses of his virtue as there have been writers about him.

Certainly, the many men renowned for holiness in Gaul and Germany, among them the most celebrated bishops of that age, who were joined to Fortunatus by intimate friendship and familiarity, and especially Radegund and Agnes, who flourished in those times with such an exceptional reputation for piety, sufficiently declare both the esteem in which he was held in Gaul and the general opinion concerning his virtue.

94. It is therefore unsurprising that Baudonivia called him an apostolic man; that, when Paul the Deacon came to Gaul, he visited Fortunatus’s tomb for the sake of prayer, as he himself declares; and that in the poem which he composed at Fortunatus’s sepulcher he called him holy and blessed and implored him to become his advocate before the just Judge on account of his exceptional merits.

From these facts it may be understood that the opinion then held in Gaul concerning Fortunatus’s holiness continued into later ages through the enduring agreement of the people.

95. We next read that Fortunatus himself was included among the images of the saints of Augsburg, in these words:

“Saint Fortunatus, formerly an Italian presbyter, bishop of Poitiers.”

Some think that this honor was bestowed upon him because, on his journey through Germany, he visited that city to venerate the ashes of Saint Afra buried there; and perhaps, after spending some time in that city, he gave some example of outstanding virtue. (Book IV of the Life of Saint Martin.)

He is likewise invoked in the litanies of Saint Cyprian outside the walls of Poitiers, as Andreas Suassaius demonstrates from the sacred records of that Church at the end of the Gallican Martyrology.

On this matter, Cointius under the year 599, no. 28, and Pagius under the year 568, no. 4, should be consulted.

In the most ancient prayers, or litanies, customarily recited by Charles the Bald, the name of Fortunatus is also found among the other holy bishops, in these words:

“Saint Fortunatus, pray for us.”

This appears in a most ancient manuscript published by Stephanus Balutius in the appendix to the Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks, chapter 94.

Finally, his feast is celebrated in the Church of Poitiers under the double rite on December 14, as the Sammarthani report in Gallia Christiana, volume II, p. 1151. Suassaius should also be consulted in the Gallican Martyrology, volume II, p. 13, under the Kalends of January.

96. These, then, are the external testimonies concerning Fortunatus’s piety and religion. If his writings, whether composed in prose or verse, are read, they display almost nothing other than an outstanding piety and reverence toward God, blessed Mary, and all the saints, together with an exceptional zeal and diligence, free from every trace of envy, in celebrating human virtues and illustrious merits.

Throughout them there appears a candor and simplicity of character worthy of a Christian; in the cultivation of friendships, an exceptional innocence and fidelity; and everywhere a marked love of justice and honesty.

Whenever he speaks of himself, he not only refrains from displaying in words the gifts which others admired in him, but is entirely occupied in concealing or diminishing them. At the same time, he shows himself ready and generous in adorning others whom he recognized as excelling in any praise of virtue.

97. The Church confirmed Fortunatus’s piety in his writing both by its testimony and by its practice, since it employed many hymns composed by him in the divine offices and in the celebration of the feasts of the saints, and consecrated them through its use.

That these hymns were very numerous—although some may later have ceased to be used and others may through human negligence and forgetfulness have lost the name of their author—we may learn from Paul the Deacon and Johannes Trithemius. The former reports that Fortunatus composed hymns for the individual feasts; the latter enumerates seventy-seven hymns produced by him.

The first of these is held to be the hymn beginning, “Let every age acknowledge,” and it is found in Book VIII, chapter 3 of Fortunatus’s Works.

[Col. 0050A] **98.** As for Fortunatus’s talent and learning, although I grant that his poems are not always steeped in those charms and graces which certain over-refined readers habitually pursue and desire—and that they sometimes even display a certain barbarism, in keeping with the character of the age—I nevertheless affirm that almost the whole of them is woven from apt and well-formed thoughts (a quality to be prized above all, not only in prose but also in poetry), and that he employs no crude or unpolished manner of expression, at least in most passages; indeed, he uses one which at times may delight even more delicate ears. In expressing the emotions of the soul according to the nature of the times and persons—a matter that above all displays the power of art and talent—he is especially outstanding; nor is he found lacking in wit and charm when the occasion calls for them.

**99.** If anyone should perhaps desire him to have been at times more elegant and more painstaking, that person ought to remember that he lived in an age when, through prolonged wars and frequent barbarian incursions, not only Italy, in which he had been educated and brought up, but also Gaul, where he subsequently lived, was repeatedly harassed and afflicted. It is therefore rather astonishing if, in that age, he did not give off some odor of barbarism and savagery both in other matters and in the Muses and literature. Moreover, if anything else is needed, the Muses certainly require peace and leisure, and a certain freedom from anguish. How, then, could one who, anxious and troubled, often asked:

> If a foreigner, bearing heavy arms, tramples the Italian sands?

and who, long an exile from Italy, lamented this both to himself and to others:

> Why do you bind such powerful laments of care upon me?  
> I wander too sadly, an exile, homeless from my native shores,  
> More than a shipwrecked stranger upon the waters of Apollo.

have sung anything festive and joyful, perfected according to its own measures?

**100.** Add to this that he wrote most of his poems not leisurely at home, so that he could work them out with the same serious care and diligence and, if anything had fallen out less suitably, reshape and polish it more finely, but that he poured them forth while traveling, sailing, or riding, or improvised them among barbarian peoples when invited to banquets. For, as he himself writes about himself to Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 1:

> “Especially since, inexperienced as I was, setting out from Ravenna and crossing the Po, the Adige, etc., hanging among mountain turns and coming upon the Pyrenees in snowy July, I composed almost everything either while riding or dozing. While proceeding for a long stretch among barbarians, weary from the road, or overcome by winter revelry, or by the cold, with the Muse urging me on—I do not know whether more frozen or more drunk—I, a new Orpheus of lyric song, gave my voice to the forests, and the forest gave it back.”

For this reason he apologizes to Gregory for not publishing his poems. Likewise, in another letter to the same Gregory, prefixed to the four books *On the Life of Saint Martin*, he says that he is sending him a certain poem of his, which, he says, “in the work of the harvest,” that is, during the harvest itself—as the courier present will be able to explain—“it was neither possible to complete nor to attempt in detail.” He adds:

> “I plowed through that entire work”—namely, the four books *On the Life of Saint Martin*—“in verse within the space of this two-month period, more bold than eloquent, neither effective nor accomplished, hastily and without polish, amid trivial occupations.”

At the end he asks pardon because, while writing at harvest time, rain had poured over a large erasure. Likewise, he writes that he completed within two days—not even two full days—the lengthy poem found in book V, chapter 5, composed at the request of the same Gregory in praise of Avitus, bishop of Clermont, since, as he himself says, the courier’s departure was imminent and, “through words falling one by one from my gaping mouth, like a stern creditor, he compelled me not so much to pay interest as to weigh it.”

**101.** From these facts it can easily be seen that Fortunatus poured forth his poems while occupied with almost every other kind of business or when pressed by lack of time. Hence everyone ought readily to infer what kind and how great a poet he would have been had he been born in better times and, free from business, been able to cultivate the Muses leisurely at home—since, amid such barbarism and so occupied a life, he became not merely an ordinary or mediocre poet, but plainly a good poet and easily the foremost of his age.

**102.** What the ancients thought of Fortunatus’s talent and learning can be understood from the testimonies which we shall present in their proper place. Here, however, it may be permitted to cite only the testimony of his closest friend and contemporary, Gregory of Tours. In the letter that he prefixed to the four books *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, after declaring himself unequal to completing so great a work as he had undertaken, he says:

> “Would that Severus or Paulinus were alive, or at least that Fortunatus were present, to describe these things.”

The same Gregory adjured Fortunatus, under witness of the divine mystery and by the splendor of the virtues of the most blessed Martin, to publish his poems collected into a single volume, considering it of the greatest importance that they should no longer lie hidden in silence and darkness but be brought forth for the common benefit. We must add Felix, bishop of Nantes, who wrote to Fortunatus that his voice, unsurpassed by any acclamation of praise, had resounded in the remotest corner of the world. From these words it can be understood what common reputation and estimation of his talent and learning prevailed throughout Gaul.

**103.** Nor did he excel only in composing poems and writing the Lives of the saints; he was not even a stranger to theological studies. His exposition of the Lord’s Prayer plainly shows, above all else, with what understanding and judgment he approached theological matters. Likewise, poem 7 of book VIII, which was written [lacuna] in praise of the holy Virgin Mary and Mother of the Lord, sufficiently shows how familiar he was with theological disciplines.

Nevertheless, he seems to remove from himself the praise of such knowledge when he writes to Martin, bishop of Gaul, book V, chapter 1, in these words:

> “Plato, Aristotle, Chrysippus, and Pittacus are scarcely known to me even by reputation; nor, as I read, are Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and Augustine known to me—though, even if they were made known to me in a vision while I was half asleep, I would not truly recognize them.”

But what is surprising if a man so skilled at concealing his own praises wrote this to Martin, when Martin himself, in one of his letters to Fortunatus, had written that Fortunatus, after Stoic and Peripatetic criticism, had devoted himself to the study of theology and contemplation? Certainly, after first being a presbyter and then being appointed—or even consecrated—a bishop, he could not long remain without that knowledge. He could have been inspired to acquire it even by the example of Radegund, of whom Baudonivia reports in her *Life*, no. 9, that she spent day and night for a long time in constant meditation upon divine matters and constant reading.

**104.** Nor, as John Joseph Liruti judges, was he without knowledge of Greek letters, which he may perhaps have learned at Ravenna, that Lyceum of every branch of learning, and brought with him to Gaul. He himself offers evidence of this when, writing to Felix, bishop of Nantes, whose eloquence he says had struck him with admiration, he says:

> “I believed them to be tetrastrophic verses compacted with Pindaric sound and smeared with pedestrian glue.”

(*Letter prefixed to book I of the* Life of Saint Martin*.)

Indeed, a man who, writing to Gregory of Tours, begins his letter as follows:

> “In a heart devoted to piety, what is less inscribed by deed is enlarged by the regard of affection. For arguments, diction, divisions, exhortations, and the rest may be left to orators and dialecticians,”

hardly appears to have been ignorant of Greek letters. Finally—and in my judgment this bears most strongly upon the matter—many features of his writings repeatedly reflect Greek elegance and manner of expression.

Hilduin the abbot therefore deserves censure when, in his letter to Louis the Pious, he says that Fortunatus did not mention the nation of Dionysius the Areopagite, concerning whom he had written a most beautiful hymn, or the manner of his episcopal ordination, because he was entirely ignorant of the Greek language. I believe that I have said enough concerning Fortunatus’s piety, learning, and talent.

[Col. 0052D] In order that the matters reported in his *Life* may be confirmed by the authority and testimonies of the most learned men who, throughout nearly every age, have written something about Fortunatus, I shall append here a catalogue of them.

[Col. 0051]

# TESTIMONIES OF ILLUSTRIOUS MEN CONCERNING VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS

**Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 8.**

[Col. 0051D]

> “If anyone earnestly wishes to investigate the virtues that he [Saint Germanus of Paris] performed in the body, he will find everything by reading the book of his life, composed by Fortunatus the presbyter.”

The same author, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 42, speaking of the church of Saint Lawrence at Brionas and of the beam that had grown miraculously, from which pieces were cut off for the curing of diseases, writes:

[Col. 0051D]

[Col. 0052D]

> “Fortunatus the presbyter,” he says, “treated this in the following verses: ‘By the merit of Lawrence,’ etc. He wrote many more verses about it, which I have omitted, writing only these as a testimony to the truth,” etc.

The same author, in the letter prefixed to the four books *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*:

[Col. 0053A]

> “Would that Severus or Paulinus were alive, or at least that Fortunatus were present, to describe these things,” etc.

He mentions the same Fortunatus in other places as well.

**Baudonivia the nun, in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Radegund*.**

> “We do not repeat what the apostolic man Fortunatus, bishop, composed concerning the life of the blessed woman,” etc.

**Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 13.**

> “Since we have made mention of this Felix, it is also fitting that we relate a few things about the venerable and most learned man Fortunatus, who asserts that this Felix was his companion. Fortunatus, the man of whom we speak, was born in a place called Duplavilis, which lies not far from the fortress of Ceneta or the city of Treviso; nevertheless, he was brought up and educated at Ravenna and became highly distinguished in grammar, rhetoric, and even meter. When he was suffering from an extremely severe pain in his eyes, and this same Felix, his companion, was likewise suffering from pain in his eyes, both proceeded to the basilica of the blessed Paul and John, which is situated within that same city. Near it is an altar constructed in honor of the blessed confessor Martin, with a window in which a lamp had been placed to provide light. Fortunatus and Felix immediately touched their afflicted eyes with its oil; the pain at once departed, and they obtained the health they desired.

> “For this reason Fortunatus venerated Saint Martin to such an extent that, abandoning his homeland shortly before the Lombards invaded Italy, he hastened to Tours to the tomb of that blessed man. As he himself relates in his poems, he describes the journey of one hastening there: through the waters of Menti [uncertain] and Rouna [uncertain], through Osopus, across the Julian Alps, through the fortress of Aguntum and the rivers Dravus and Birrus, and through Briones and the city of Augusta, through which the Virdo and Lech flow. After he reached Tours according to his desire, he passed through Poitiers, settled there, and wrote the deeds of many saints, partly in prose and partly in metrical discourse. Finally, in that same city he was first ordained presbyter and then bishop, and there he rests, buried with fitting honor.

> “In four books, in heroic verse, he composed the life of Saint Martin; and he composed many other works, especially hymns for individual feast days and, above all, little poems for individual friends, in sweet and eloquent language, second to none of the poets. When I had come to his tomb for the sake of prayer, I composed this epitaph at the request of Aper, abbot of that place,” etc. (See this poem in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 92.)

**Hilduin the abbot, in his letter to Louis the Pious, in Surius, 9 October.**

> “For the rest, one must spare the simplicity of Gregory, bishop of Tours, a religious man who, judging many matters otherwise than the truth required, commended them to writing not through crafty deceit but from a disposition of kindness and simplicity. We can plainly recognize that he did not investigate certain matters very carefully, since his contemporary, the prudent and most learned Fortunatus, who had often written many things to him, composed a most beautiful hymn in rhythmic form concerning this glorious martyr. In it he mentions that he had been sent by Saint Clement, as he had learned from the pages of the Latins. But he makes no mention of his nation or episcopal ordination because he was entirely ignorant of the Greek language.”

**Hincmar, in the preface to the *Life of Saint Remigius, Bishop of Rheims*, no. 2.**

> “Egidius, the fourth bishop of this city after Saint Remigius, requested a certain religious man named Fortunatus, distinguished in metrical verse, because at that time he was invited in various places by many powerful and honorable men in these Gallic and Belgic regions on account of the merit of his life and learning, to extract from the same book, dictated in the Gallic buskin, certain miracles in plain speech that might be recited to the people,” etc.

**Among the inscriptions of Blessed Flaccus Alcuin in a certain monastery (perhaps Nobiliacum), the following poem is found:**

## EPITAPH OF FORTUNATUS, CHRISTIAN POET

> Here too, in this present hall, the bishop rests,  
> Fortunatus, a man, the Church’s glory;  
> He composed very many songs of the saints in meter,  
> Celebrating the saints with hymnic praises.  
> His speech was polished, and faithful was his understanding,  
> His talent ardent, and his utterance ready.

[Col. 0054C] Thus the poem is transmitted in the Ratisbon edition of 1777, prepared by the most illustrious and reverend Frobenius, prince of the Holy Roman Empire and abbot of Saint Emmeram.

**Flodoard, *History of the Church of Rheims*, book II, chapter 2.**

> “The Italian Fortunatus was considered distinguished in metrical composition among the Gauls.”

**Aimoins, *History of the Franks*, book III, chapter 13.**

> “Fortunatus, who was considered famous in the arts of rhetoric and meter, crossed from the West into Gaul and was ordained bishop of Poitiers. He composed the Lives and Passions of many saints, partly in prose and partly in verse, and also wrote elegant couplets for individual friends as an accomplished orator. Hence he sent an elegiac poem to King Sigibert, congratulating him on his marriage to Brunichild. When fortune brought into my hands a book that he had written to various friends, I greatly admired in it the man’s fertility and his sweet affability.”

**Regino, *Chronicle*, book I.**

> “The poet Fortunatus is considered distinguished in Gaul.”

**Sigibert, *Chronicle*, under the year 575.**

> “The poet Fortunatus, coming from Italy, shines in Gaul.”

**The same author, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 45.**

> “Fortunatus, an Italian by nation and trained in the liberal arts, was cured of an eye ailment by the power of Martin, bishop of Tours, and for this reason came to Tours. Proceeding to Poitiers, he was first made presbyter there and then consecrated bishop. He wrote his *Hodoeporicon* in meter; he wrote four metrical books on the life of Saint Martin, and many other works, especially hymns for individual feast days. For individual friends he composed verses in sweet and eloquent language.”

**Vincent, *Speculum*, book XXII, chapter 126, from Hugh of Fleury.**

> “Fortunatus, an excellent man,  
> Famous for talent, quick in understanding, sweet in speech,  
> Coming from Italy to Tours, composed in four books,  
> In heroic meter, the deeds of blessed Martin.  
> He was then taken from there and ordained bishop of Poitiers.  
> He also wrote the life of blessed Hilary of Poitiers  
> And the life of blessed Maurilius of Angers.  
> This concise and useful saying is his:
>
> > The poor man reigns when he possesses God.”

(Found in book VIII, chapter 6, verse 396.)

**Peter de Natalibus, *Catalogue of the Saints*, book IX, chapter 65.**

[Col. 0055B]

> “Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, flourished during the reign of the younger Emperor Justin. An Italian by nation, he was first a poet and thereafter elevated to the episcopate of the aforementioned city: an excellent man, famous for talent, quick in understanding, and sweet in speech.”

**Platina, *Life of Pope John III*.**

> “Fortunatus, a man of singular learning and eloquence, brought the Gauls back to a gentler culture through his writings and example. For he wrote a little book to Sigibert, their king, on governing the kingdom, and elegantly composed the life of Saint Martin.”

**Johannes Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.**

> “Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, an Italian by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly educated in secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent and polished in speech, excellent in verse and prose, shone among all the teachers of his age no less by the holiness of his conduct than by the knowledge of his learning. Freed from an eye ailment by the power of Saint Martin, he came to Tours to give thanks at his tomb; proceeding to Poitiers, he was first ordained presbyter and then bishop there, and became renowned for great learning and religion. He wrote many useful and devout little works in elegant verse, of which I have seen only those listed below.

> “To Saint Radegund, daughter of the last king of the Thuringians and captive of the king of the Franks, later abbess of the monastery at Poitiers, in hexameter verse:

> “*The Destruction of the Kingdom of the Thuringians*, book I: ‘The sorrowful condition of war.’

> “*To Jovinus concerning Radegund*, book I: ‘The Aonian [Muses], whom he eagerly...’

> “*To Justin the Younger*, book I: ‘The supreme glory of the Father and the Son.’

> “*To the Empress Sophia*, book I: ‘To whom in merits comparable...’

> “*In the person of Radegund*, book I: ‘After the ashes of my homeland.’

> “*In praise of Bishop Martin*, book I: ‘The apostolic light.’

> “*On the venerable Bishop Leontius*, book I: ‘Among whom he begot.’

> “*Another poem of praise for the same*, book I: ‘Let every age acknowledge.’

> “*Seventy-seven hymns*, book I: ‘Let every age acknowledge.’

> “*On the miracles of Saint Martin*, book IV.

> “*Life of Saint Hilary of Poitiers*, book I.

> “*Hodoeporicon of his journey*, book I.
