> “*Life of Saint Maurilius, bishop*, book I.

> “*Letters to various persons*, book I.

> “*Poems to friends*, book I: ‘King, summit of the realm,’ etc.

> “He also composed many other works, which, since they are brief, I did not record under the name of books. For he wrote many epitaphs and short verses, which I have seen. He flourished under the Emperor Justin the Younger, in the year of the Lord 570.”

**Peter Crinitus, book V, *On Latin Poets*.**

> “Venantius Honorius Fortunatus is numbered among the Christian poets. Since he greatly excelled both in talent and in character, he is said to have been educated at Ravenna and trained with great diligence in Latin literature. Much is reported about this Fortunatus by those authors who composed annals concerning the deeds of the Gauls. Nor are there lacking those who write that he spent a long time in Gaul and, on account of his outstanding learning and excellent talent, was made bishop of Poitiers. He published numerous and varied works, demonstrating the ease of his talent and a learning by no means inferior. His poems and many hymns are still read, and have been highly commended by our grammarians. He also composed four books in hexameter verse on the deeds of Saint Martin, declaring beforehand that in such a work he was imitating the Christian poets Alcimus, Prudentius, Juvencus, Paulinus, and many others. Fortunatus also pursued with the greatest affection and singular benevolence Gregory the bishop, Euphronius, and Felix, to omit others. In very ancient copies the name Clementianus has been added; this may be approved by those who wish to investigate antiquity somewhat more carefully.”

**Hieronymus Bologni, *Selected Elegiacs*, from book XII of the *Miscellanies*, no. 23.**

> Fortunatus, the valley of Duplavilis gave you birth,  
> In the region of Treviso where it lies.  
> At your birth the Muses smiled, Apollo smiled,  
> Adding gifts worthy of your talent.  
> Without delay you wrote Pindaric hymns  
> To the heavenly gods, and sacred mysteries in varied forms.  
> You also wrote in verse the life of blessed Martin  
> When you undertook to visit Tours.  
> Under your episcopate, the people of Poitiers learned pious ways,  
> And there at last, properly laid in earth, you rest.  
> Let not the city of Aponus boast of a star or of Flaccus’s pupils,  
> With the pride in which Padua so swells.  
> You sing neither of plunderers raging  
> With audacious fleet, nor of Venus’s foul and shameful outrages.  
> Through you—but how much greater are divine things than profane!—  
> A greater glory has been won for Treviso through your work.

**Orlendius, *The Sacred and Profane World Illuminated*, part II, volume I.**

[Col. 0056D]

> “Treviso produced very distinguished men, and among them the most outstanding were ... Venantius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, a noble ornament of Christian poetry, who identifies himself as originating from Treviso in these verses:
>
> > ‘Where my Zarvisus [Treviso] rests, if you enter gently,’ etc.”

**Joannes Antonius Oliva, native of Treviso and rector of the artists at Bologna, in an oration on the praises of his homeland delivered in 1537, from a manuscript used by the most learned and erudite Rambaldus de Azzoniis, canon of the Church of Treviso, from whom we received this testimony.**

> “Fortunatus of Treviso, companion of Felix, must not be wrapped in silence; and we rightly consider him fortunate. For Pythagoras, the first to be called a philosopher, among the many salutary teachings he prescribed for the human race, especially warns that God must be honored through religion and that the soul must be cultivated by disciplines. These two things, joined by a social bond, will undoubtedly produce happiness: religion, which drives out vices, reconciles us to God, and binds us to him with the most beautiful bond; learning, meanwhile, the investigator of virtue—or rather virtue itself—adorns, nourishes, beautifies, cherishes, and governs our minds.

> “This remarkable cultivator of both was so devoted to religion that the people of Poitiers in Gaul rightly glory in him as their bishop; and he was so adorned with learning that he is considered not least among the most eloquent orators and sweetest poets.”

**Cardinal Baronius, under the year 825.**

[Col. 0057B]

> “But how poorly those who oppose sacred images boast of the custom of their ancestors—it will be enough if we clearly demonstrate, by the testimony of the most holy man Martin and the assertion of Venantius Fortunatus, a holy man and learned bishop of Poitiers, both of whom illuminated the Gallican Church, that the veneration of holy images was accepted in antiquity and pleasing to God,” etc.

**Gaspar Barthius, *Commentaries in the Adversaria*, book V, chapter 12.**

> “That poet—I mean Venantius—possessed a wondrous and admirable talent, born in times and among peoples most hostile to eloquence. As almost always happens, by the greatness of his talent he corrupted his language even more severely than one or another person born with less fortunate natural gifts. Nevertheless, he contains much that demonstrates varied reading and no ordinary learning, and for that reason he does not seem entirely unworthy of our attention ... His learning is easily proved by the authors whom he expressly cites: Homer, Menander, Aratus, Cato, Pythagoras, Chrysippus, Plato, Cleanthes, Ovid, Virgil, Horace, Cicero, Pindar, Sappho; finally, all the more celebrated Greek and Latin Fathers. He not only gives the names of both pagan and Christian authors, but often reproduces their phrasing and encloses their teaching within his meters. Add to this a knowledge of history and geography uncommon for that time; add a not unsuccessful study of natural philosophy, as is clear from the kinds of herbs, gems, trees, and spices about which he speaks suitably and learnedly,” etc.

**The same author, book XLVI, chapter 3.**

[Col. 0057D]

> “Those who published Venantius Fortunatus have deserved great gratitude from readers of every Christian age. For in that poet of immense talent there is an infinite amount that is extremely useful for illuminating famous men, cities, peoples, customs, and history; much of it has not unsuccessfully been related and explained by those same editors. Yet, apart from the blemish of an excessively hurried work, the passages that concern his understanding of literary genres and style itself, as well as places polluted by errors, have contributed little to the work. Whoever undertakes notes on this poet will assist not only Fortunatus himself but also his entire age and all succeeding ages. For the whole chorus of later poets looked to this Fortunatus as to a certain Calliopean master and leader of musical melodies.”

**Cardinal Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 570.**

> “Venantius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, flourished in learning and holiness during the reign of Justin the Younger,” etc.

**Antoine Godeau, *Ecclesiastical History*, volume IV, book II.** After relating Fortunatus’s homeland and his journey into Gaul, he adds:

> “His principal occupation during the first years of his life was Latin poetry, and if one considers the barbarism of his age, he deserves some praise. It is true that he is accused of having praised Fredegund, Brunhild, and other princes who deserved censure rather than praise. But he must be excused, since he was living at their court, where he survived only by his pen.”

**Vossius, *On Latin History*, book XI, chapter 22.**

> “The poet Fortunatus was distinguished, considering what those times were.”

**Andreas de Saussay, *Gallican Martyrology*, part II, 13 Kalends of January.**

> “Blessed Venantius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, a man in whom it is uncertain whether the excellence of learning and beauty of talent surpassed the holiness of life; one who was the foremost encomiast of the saints in his age, their devoted imitator, an exceedingly graceful herald of the majesty of omnipotent heaven, and a most weighty narrator of God’s wondrous works in the saints. Having completed a life exact in every exercise and action of piety, and having been broken by old age not so much as by holy practices—since he had devoted himself both to the continual performance of the sacred ministry and to the cultivation of Christian wisdom and the inscription of excellent works—he was brought to a blessed end and advanced to the heavenly crown, destined to be received by those friends into eternal dwellings whom he had acquired not from the mammon of iniquity but from the storehouse of the gift of knowledge and by the most righteous interest of grace and piety ... By this title, although he is not listed in the martyrology of the Roman Church, the most diligent investigators of the saints testify that he was nevertheless rightly numbered among the saints long ago. Indeed, he was formerly honored in Aquitania with the sacred honors paid to the blessed.”

**Cointius, under the year 599.**

[Col. 0058D]

> “Fortunatus shone in piety no less than in learning, and he is invoked in the litanies of the monastery of Saint Cyprian outside the walls of Poitiers, as Andreas Saussayus reports from the sacred records of the Church of Poitiers at the end of the *Gallican Martyrology*.”

**Dupin, *New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, volume V.**

> “In his own time Fortunatus was regarded as an excellent Orator and a good Poet; and not without reason. For he not only surpasses all the other Poets of his century, but approaches those of a better age—not, in truth, in purity of expression or beauty of verse, but in poetic construction and the marvelous ease with which he writes in verse.”

**Muratori, *Latin Anecdotes*, volume II.**

[Col. 0059A]

> “The Fortunatus mentioned here is none other than the Fortunatus whom the mitre of the Church of Poitiers and the ornaments of Christian poetry have given to eternity. Many monuments of his talent and learning, produced by him, have been preserved down to our own age, not without great commendation of him, since he surpassed all other contemporary writers in a completely barbarous age.”

**William Cave, *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, Cologne of the Allobroges, in the Eutychian age.**

> “He composed many works, partly poetic and partly historical. Barthius praises his poetic power as follows, *Adversaria*, book IV, chapter 3: ‘A poet of immense talent,’ etc.”

# THE FIRST PART OF THE COMPLETE WORKS OF VENANTIUS HONORIUS CLEMENTIANUS FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF POITIERS, CONTAINING THE BROWER EDITION

[Col. 0059]

# MISCELLANIES (C, S)*

## Prologue

**TO THE LORD, HOLY GREGORY THE POPE, SIMULTANEOUSLY ADMITTED TO AND RAISED UP BY THE SACRED ALTARS, AND ENDOWED WITH THE GIFTS OF MERITS**

[Note: [Col. 0059B] In the Calarian copy this title reads as follows: “To the apostolic man and venerable pope”; from Brower.]

[Note: [Col. 0059B] This letter, which is prefixed to Fortunatus’s works, serves as a dedication. It is addressed to Gregory, bishop of Tours, Fortunatus’s closest friend, as we stated in his *Life*, no. 67 and following. Some, misled by the title, have thought that this was Gregory the Great, bishop of Rome, thereby departing considerably from the truth. For, to pass over the fact that no relationship of friendship or exchange of letters between Fortunatus and Gregory the Great is otherwise established, whereas it is entirely certain that Fortunatus shared such a close friendship and lifelong association with Gregory of Tours, by whom he says he was repeatedly urged—or rather invited, by right and in the name of their friendship—to write, let us also pass over the fact that Gregory the Great ascended to and occupied the Roman see at almost the very end of Fortunatus’s life. Certainly, the adjuration by which Gregory urges Fortunatus, under witness of the divine mystery and by the splendor of the virtues of the most blessed Martin, to publish the poems he had written makes it sufficiently clear that the man who thus adjured him was not the Roman pontiff but the bishop of Tours.

Nor was it unusual in those times for the bishops of other churches, apart from the supreme pontiff, to be honored with the name “pope”; they were even called “apostolic,” as Fortunatus’s own letter shows. Writing to Euphronius, likewise bishop of Tours, he begins as follows: “To the holy lord, the apostolic lord according to his merits, and the twice-father Euphronius, Pope Fortunatus.”

Although all episcopal sees were called apostolic, when the term was stated simply and absolutely, without adding the name of a particular church, see, or bishop, it was customary to indicate the Roman pontiff. Thus, when the presbyter Nuncupatus came to King Charibert on behalf of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, and his fellow provincials, and greeted him in these words—“The apostolic see sends abundant greetings to your eminence”—the king replied: “Have you visited the city of Rome, then, to bring us greetings from its pope?” So Gregory of Tours reports, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 26.

And just as the Roman see was called “the apostolic see” by excellence, according to the usage established among the Franks, so the name “pope” was attributed by antonomasia to the Roman pontiff. On these matters Cointius says more, under the year 562, nos. 10 and 11. This letter to Gregory of Tours is missing from the Venetian edition.]

**FORTUNATUS**

[Note: [Col. 0059] Fortunatus excuses himself in this letter to Gregory, bishop of Tours, who had strongly urged and adjured him to publish his poems collected into a single volume. He pleads his lack of skill and the business that had prevented him from polishing them more carefully. At last he yields to the petitioner and declares that Gregory’s goodwill and desire toward him had proved stronger than his own fear and embarrassment. Taking the opportunity, he describes the journey that he had undertaken from Italy to Gaul.]

[Col. 0059B] The illustrious talents of those men [Note: [Col. 0060D] *Eorum* (“of them”) is absent in two Vatican manuscripts.] of former times, whose natural disposition was ardent, whose cultivation was brilliant [Note: [Col. 0060D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “worn by practice, relying on bolder daring—or rather, relying on secure daring and fluent speech.”], whose practice was polished, whose confidence rested on bold undertaking, whose speech was fluent, whose manner was festive, and whose [Col. 0060B] splendid works were destined to be celebrated and praised with wonder by posterity [Note: [Col. 0060D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “celebrated by works.”], left behind these traces of themselves. Certainly, they were provident in invention, serious in division, balanced in arrangement, delightful in the close of their epilogues [Col. 0061A], flowing from the fountain of cola [Note: In the Caralitanus manuscript, *scholae*, as Browerus reports. A *colon* is formed when a sentence conveys its meaning but something still remains of the sentence’s fullness; we call it a middle division because we place the point at the middle of the letter. Papias, Biturican manuscript, cited by Dufresne.], graceful in the sharply cut comma, crowned and at once elevated by tropes, paradigms, periods [Note: This word, *periodis*, is absent from one Vatican manuscript.], and epicheremata [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *pariter et cothurni*—“and also cothurni.”], they gave such an example of themselves in song that even in our own time they are thought to live as though posthumous to themselves—if not in the flesh, at least in song.

Although fate [the reading may be *mors*, “death”] brought them to an end, nevertheless, since their sayings remain [Note: [Col. 0061C] The Paris edition reads: “their sayings.”], death left something of the dead to living memory and did not bury everything entirely in the tomb. It remains free for them to live in the world by their language, something greedy death does not know how to take away with the funeral: what it sees the deceased running through the mouths of the living, if not on foot, at least in poetry. In this respect envious death has been conquered all the more successfully, if it recognizes through speech that it has been defeated twice, and at a price.

But just as those whom the clear light of language proclaims illustrious, whose words it was plainly a loss to conceal [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “whose words it was a loss to suffer concealed”; another: “whose words were plainly a loss”; a third: “whose deeds were concealed.”], and who, unless they had sent into public view the flowering shoots of their splendid eloquence, would have made a hidden treasure of them [Note: The Paris edition reads: “they had made a hidden treasure”], rightly drew the rays of fame in every direction, so that, as they traveled everywhere, their praise might increase wherever places became better known through their poetry [Note: [Col. 0061C] Two Vatican manuscripts read, in effect, “whatever places became better known by poems”; a third reads “whatever places became better known by a poem.”]; so it is more prudent for those persons to remain silently hidden which, once revealed, might become wearisome [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “which, once revealed, might have become wearisome.”].

It is not so disgraceful to be unknown in what is repellent as it is to expose what causes pain [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read: “as it is to become exposed.”]. Ignorance kept concealed seems to entail a lesser loss than ignorance brought forth: in the former case shame prevents knowledge from being disclosed; in the latter, boldness betrays it and imposes disgrace.

Therefore, O apostolic man, worthy of proclamation, Pope Gregory, since you vigorously demand [Note: [Col. 0061C] Three Vatican manuscripts read *viritim* (“individually” or “man by man”).] that I bring forth for you certain pieces from the little works of my ignorance, I marvel that you are led astray by love for my trifles. Once they have been brought forth, they will be able neither to astonish nor to be loved. Especially since I, an unlearned man [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read *impos*, “unskilled”], traveling from Ravenna across the Padus, the Athesis [Note: The Athesis and Brinta, also called the lesser Medoacus, rise in the Rhaetian Alps and flow through different mouths into the Adriatic gulf.], the Brinta, the Plavis [Note: The Plavis, beyond Altinum and Tarvisium, descends in a precipitous course from the neighboring mountains, then, its current having become level, spreads into the Venetian gulf.], the Liquentia [Note: The Liquentia is a river beyond Opitergium, separating the territory of Tarvisium from the province of Forum Julii.], and the Tiliamentum [Note: The Tiliamentum is a river on the borders of the Veneti and Carni; see Cluverius, *Italia Antiqua*.], crossed the Julian Alps [Note: Cluverius, *Italia Antiqua*, book I, chapter 20, observes that Fortunatus and Paul the Deacon incorrectly call the Noric Alps the Julian Alps. The latter, he says, were near the sources of the Frigidus and Nauportus, between the Carni and Pannonia. He therefore believes that this name was given to the Noric Alps by people of a later age, either from the nearby town called Julium Carnicum or from an ancient inscription at the very passes of the Noric Alps, bearing the name of C. Caesar.], hanging over mountain ravines, then crossed the Dravus [Note: The Dravus rises in Noricum, or the Noric Alps, and flows into the Danube.], the Oenus [Note: Oenus—or, as Cluverius believes it should be read, Aenus—separated the Vindelici from the Norici on the east. “Breonis” is added because of the Breoni, the peoples who lived along that river; see Pliny, book III, chapter 20. They are also mentioned by Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 9, and Horace, book IV, ode 14. Fortunatus himself likewise says in *The Life of Saint Martin*, book IV:

> If you have leisure to travel, and no Bavarian obstructs you,  
> Proceed through the Alps, where the neighboring lands of the Breoni lie,  
> Entering where the Oenus rolls in its rapid torrent.

], the Breonian river, the Licca [Note: The Licca is the Bavarian Lech; see Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*: “The Lech River,” he says, “divides the Bavarians from the Alemanni.” One Vatican manuscript reads: “the Licca of Bavaria.”], Bavaria, the Danube, Alemannia, Germany, and the Rhine; afterward, crossing the Mosella [Note: The Moselle rises from Mount Vosegus in Gaul and flows, not far from the sources of the Arar, through the Mediomatrici, the royal estate of Theodoric, Augusta Treverorum, and Confluentes into the Rhine, as is read in the notes to Ausonius, *Eclogue* 10, edited by Julianus Floridus, canon of Chartres.], the Mosa [Note: The Mosa flows between the cities of the Remi and the Treveri, separating the two dioceses. It also discharges into the German Ocean.], the Axona [Note: The Axona is a river of the Campania of the Catalauni; after watering the territory of the Suessiones, it joins the Isara near the town of Compendium.], the Sequana [Note: The Liger, commonly called the Loire, is the best-known river of Gaul; likewise the Sequana and Garumna, concerning which Fortunatus will speak elsewhere.], the Liger, and the Garumna, the greatest rivers of Aquitaine, I came to the Pyrenees, still snowy in July, and composed almost either on horseback or while dozing.

There, walking for a long stretch among barbarians, whether weary from the road or drunk beneath the winter cold, with the Muse urging me on—I do not know whether I was more frozen or more intoxicated—I, a new Orpheus in lyric song, gave my voice to the forest, and the forest returned it [Note: The Paris edition reads: “the forest returned it through Echo.”]. You yourself must judge what could prudently be said amid such extended journeys, where neither fear of a judge compelled me, nor practice approved me according to any rule, nor favor encouraged me as a companion, nor a reader corrected me by art. There, a hoarse groan was worth as much to me as singing; among those people there was no distinction between the honking of a goose and the song of a swan. My harp alone, often humming, struck back barbarian *leudes* [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read *harpa relidens* (“the harp striking back”). *Relidere* means “to strike back” or “to reverberate”; Fortunatus uses the word elsewhere. Note:

A *leudus* is a song, from the Germanic *lied*. Fortunatus uses the same word in book VII, chapter 8:

> May they give you little verses, and barbarian songs, *leudes*.

See also Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans*, and Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book I, chapter 27.
] so that among them I myself, no musician-poet but a “murician,” with the flower of my song gnawed away [Note: *Deroso flore*—“with the flower gnawed away”—has been restored from an old Gallic manuscript, which read *de roseo flore* (“from the rosy flower”), a reading deleted by Browerus. The Vatican manuscripts support the present reading.], would not sing a poem but chatter one; and the seated listeners, drinking frenzied toasts among maple cups, would revel under the judgment of Bacchus.

What could be artfully said there [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “What could be said there skillfully?”], where scarcely anyone is believed to be sane unless he goes mad along with the rest [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “unless one goes mad along with oneself.”]. There it is more fitting to rejoice if one is allowed to live after drinking; and from such a feast a man may indeed emerge as a thyrsus-bearing reveler, though not as a prophet, but as a fool. For, as far as my understanding can reach, since the brutish soul does not unfold itself, its very fasts are drunk.

This is why a hidden little work, even if it seems less famous [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “even if it seems to be famous”], is freer [Note: The Paris edition reads: “even if it seems handsome”], because in being examined it has no reason to fear equally when private and when public [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “because in examination another will not give it…”]. Hence an intellect of narrow powers must measure itself by a judge before whom it is to be sent.

But since you earnestly urge me—calling upon the testimony of the divine mystery and the splendor of the virtues of the most blessed Martin—to be led into public view, you who eagerly retain even the humble impulse that I hold back with some vigor, I, judging myself in my own trifles [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “judging, while confessing the same thing”], and confessing my ignorance of a rough work [Note: The Paris edition reads: “I shall lead myself into public view; judging myself … and confessing…”], which I delayed revealing to others who demanded it, yield in obedience to your virtue. I shall at least repay this exchange of obedience, so that, since these pieces are entrusted more to favor than to judgment, you may either read them as becoming known only to you [Note: One manuscript reads: “only to you and no other”], or, in a friendly way, commit them to the ears of your intimates [Note: The same manuscript reads: “share them amicably with yourself”], I ask, as something to be contributed [Note: One manuscript reads: “I ask, as something that may console you.” *Collatura* is used for *conferenda*, “to be contributed,” just as above *curatura* is used for *curanda*, “to be cared for.” This is characteristic of Fortunatus, as Father Brow notes.] [Note: The Paris edition reads: “repay them.”].

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0063]

## CHAPTER I. To Vitalis, Bishop of Ravenna

[Note: Vitalis, although he does not appear at all in the catalogues of the bishops of Ravenna—as Father Browerus long ago observed—must certainly have presided over the Church of Ravenna at approximately the time when Fortunatus lived there. We stated in his Life, section 17 and following, that Fortunatus lived there for some time; perhaps at the urging and with the advice of this Vitalis he celebrated in this poem the dedication of a basilica built by him. Browerus, however, believes that Vitalis should be identified with Peter the Elder, who was not made bishop of Ravenna until 568—by which time, according to Browerus himself, Fortunatus had already reached Gaul. I shall explain below what I myself think concerning this Vitalis.]

[Col. 0063B] [Note: He reports in this poem that the Basilica of Saint Andrew, built and dedicated by Vitalis, bishop of Ravenna, was celebrated. He commemorates the solemnity of the dedication and the people’s exceptional zeal and goodwill toward Vitalis.]

Bishop of the Lord, living through your merits forever,

You, a shepherd who possess the joys of Christ’s flock,

When antiquity chose to call you Vitalis,

It knew that you had deserved eternal day.

A priest worthy and radiant with an apostolic mind,

You establish such holy temples for Andrew.

How fittingly, according to your merits, he has taken his seat in the Lord’s palace,

Through whom a house worthy of God has been built.

[Col. 0064B] You received your exalted office from the Lord, for whom you build the heights;

He who gave you worthy gifts, you repay in honor.

[Col. 0064C] The splendid palace shines, completed in solid metal,

Where day remains continuous, without night.

The place itself invites God, beneath perpetual light,

To enter the dwelling lovingly with peaceful steps.

You provide places where peoples may always adore the Lord;

So that they may receive pardon, you yourself make the way [Note: Another Vatican manuscript reads: “you yourself make the road.”].

Grace, mind, spirit, goodness, love of the people,

Rank and piety have made you a father.

Your secure prosperity proves itself: supplying joys,

It brought distinguished men to your vows [Note: Another Vatican manuscript reads: “secure prosperity proves itself.”].

The commander [Note: Father Browerus thinks that these words indicate the exarch, who attended the dedication of the basilica with the *nomophylax*. But since exarchs did not begin to sit at Ravenna until 568, and the first was Longinus, an exarch certainly could not have attended the dedication while Fortunatus was still at Ravenna; he had departed for Gaul in 565, or at the latest in 566, as Browerus himself acknowledges. (Note from the first revision.)—The commander whom Fortunatus mentions in this poem as having attended the dedication of the Basilica of Saint Andrew, built or restored by Vitalis of Ravenna, I believe to have been Count Narses. Justinian sent him to Italy in 551, as is well known, to defeat the Ostrogoths; he could conveniently have remained at Ravenna and attended the dedication of the basilica mentioned here. Narses was recalled to Constantinople in 567 or 568, as Pagius believes for the latter year. Longinus succeeded him; he was the first to be sent to Italy with the title and rank of exarch and settled at Ravenna, apparently in 568, when the Lombards invaded Italy. From this it is clear that the period during which Narses lived in Italy agrees very well with the period when Fortunatus lived at Ravenna; we therefore believe that, while Fortunatus was present, the Ravenna basilica was dedicated. Gregory of Tours calls Narses “Duke of Italy,” *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 20. The words Fortunatus uses here therefore suit Narses’ person and rank: “The commander shines here in arms,” and so forth. (Note from the second revision.)] shines here in arms, the prefect there in laws;

Those through whom festivals generally grow have come.

[Col. 0065A] May honor not be lacking to you: God has increased the wealthy people,

Who saw that you intended this.

The mystery of faith has fulfilled the prayers of those who asked;

Happy the man for whom the Lord brings precisely what he desires.

Celebrate many solemnities through the divine gift,

And, by establishing flourishing temples of God, cultivate them [Note: The Paris edition reads:

> And, by establishing temples to be cultivated, place the praises of God.

].

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the Temple of the Lord Andrew, which Vitalis, Bishop of Ravenna, Built

[Note: One Vatican manuscript gives the title as follows: “Verses concerning the Temple of Saint Andrew; Vitalis, Bishop of Ravenna, built it.”]

[Note: He relates that the same Basilica of Saint Andrew was built and completed in a short time through Vitalis’s extraordinary zeal and generosity. He lists the sacred relics by which it was distinguished.]

Whoever comes to these thresholds of the holy temple,

If you come as a suppliant, here you receive help through prayer.

[Col. 0065B] The holy bishop Vitalis founded this citadel,

Which, with its roof, was raised toward heaven in a short time [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “whose roof was raised toward the Most High.”].

He laid its foundation, built it, endowed it, and then dedicated it,

And deserved to fulfill the vows of his temple.

[Col. 0066A] Here rest the venerable remains of pious Peter,

Who alone deserved to bind the heavens with the key.

Paul likewise is held in this apostolic palace,

Once a deceiver, but now triumphant as a teacher.

Holy Andrew claims this citadel as his own,

And governs it jointly with his pious brother.

Laurence fills this roof of his with a serene fire,

For whom a holy flame granted everlasting day with its light.

This house pleases Vitalis, who, buried alive in sand,

Deserved to lose the path of death.

Here are the places of Martin, who covered the Thunderer with his garment;

To keep Him from growing colder, he gave himself to be stripped.

Behold the citadel of Vigilius, whom the rustic crowd killed:

From the place where he wished to die, death itself fled all the more.

Maturius and Sisennus likewise inhabit this place [Note: Maturius and Sisennus were martyrs of the Felix Legion, called the Agaunian martyrs; more will be said of them below, book II, chapter 15]:

[Col. 0066B] Whom common lineage, faith, and one salvation hold together.

Holy Alexander and blessed Cecilia prevail;

One crown awaits all of them for their merits.

[Note: The distinguished Bacchinius, in his *Ravenna of Agnellus*, in the observations on the Life of Saint Maximian, believes that John, whom Fortunatus mentions here, was a bishop of Ravenna—the John who occupied the see immediately after Peter the Elder. Bacchinius further believes that Vitalis, whom Fortunatus reports as having built the Basilica of Saint Andrew, was not a bishop of Ravenna, but merely a native of Ravenna and bishop of one of the dioceses subject to the metropolitan of Ravenna. This Vitalis himself, he thinks, built and dedicated a splendid church to Saint Andrew and obtained from the metropolitan the relics recounted here, together with permission for their solemn translation into their own shrines, in the presence of the nobles of the Ravenna people and amid a great gathering of neighboring inhabitants. The metropolitan from whom Vitalis obtained the relics mentioned in this poem, Bacchinius believes, was John himself, who is said to have occupied the see of Ravenna after Peter the Elder.

Yet I myself would perhaps not refuse to follow the judgment of this most learned man if it either seemed plausible that Fortunatus called Vitalis a bishop of Ravenna from the name of his native place rather than from the name of the see he held—contrary to the custom of all antiquity, so far as I have been able to ascertain it—or if it could be shown that Fortunatus wrote this poem after he was already living in Gaul, where he arrived in 565, or at the latest in 566, as I have shown in his Life, section 26 and following. John, however, who occupied the see after Peter the Elder, did not govern the Church of Ravenna before 575, according to Bacchinius himself.

It is certainly not credible, especially in such stormy and troubled times, that any friend living in Italy addressed Fortunatus in order that he might compose a poem for the dedication of that basilica, particularly since Fortunatus himself, after a long exile from Italy, complained that he had taken it with him, in book VII, chapter 11:

> I think I have been rolling in exile from Italy for nine years,  
> With the sea of the Ocean bordering the shore.  
> So many years flee, and still, through the writings of my parents,  
> No message from those excluded has refreshed me.

If anyone ought to have greeted Fortunatus by letter in his absence, it would have been one of his relatives—especially since, as he himself relates elsewhere, his mother and sister were still alive, and a long line of nephews existed, although, shut out by the turmoil of war, they had sent him no letter for the space of nine years.

Furthermore, in this poem Fortunatus does not indicate that he is absent, as he often customarily did; nor does he address absent persons. He says that those who attended the dedication were present—something he could scarcely have known if he had been absent. Finally, the poem does not seem important enough to have caused him to send it from Gaul to Italy, whether deliberately or at the invitation of one of his friends.

For these reasons I incline to the opinion that this Vitalis, bishop of Ravenna, was none other than Maximianus. Maximianus was made bishop of Ravenna in 546 and occupied the see until 553; Agnellus of Ravenna is said to report that he restored the Basilica of Saint Andrew, as will be said below. When Maximianus came to Constantinople to obtain the body of Saint Andrew and bring it to Ravenna, he could not obtain it from the emperor of Constantinople; he therefore cut off the saint’s beard from his body and brought it to Ravenna together with several other relics of the saints.

Nor is it unusual that the same man should have been called both Vitalis and Maximianus, especially in an age when individuals commonly adopted several names, as we observed in the Life of Fortunatus, sections 3 and 4. The principal reason leading me to this opinion is Agnellus’s own testimony. He adds that Maximianus supported the church of the blessed apostle Andrew with marble columns throughout and adorned it, after removing the old wooden ones, with proconnesian marble. It is therefore plausible that the dedication of the Basilica of Saint Andrew mentioned here by Fortunatus was celebrated by him.

As for John, who is mentioned in this passage, I believe that he was not a bishop of Ravenna but a Roman—perhaps the third of that name—from whom Vitalis, already bishop of Ravenna, obtained those sacred relics to be placed in the Basilica of Saint Andrew. It was customary enough for relics of the saints to be requested from Roman pontiffs to enrich churches. This is clearly shown by an old poem reported by Agnellus in the Life of John, bishop of Ravenna, who built the monastery of Saints Mark, Marcellus, and Felicula. The poem, inscribed above the gates of that monastery, contains among other lines:

> The illustrious thresholds of the saints’ temple shine forth,  
> Of Mark, Marcellus, and Felicula together.  
> Rome received these pontiffs; this martyr is honored here;  
> Pope Gregory gives their relics.  
> John, the bishop, asks for them in merit and in spirit;  
> He prepares to return small gifts in exchange for great ones.

]

These things John, the good bishop, at the urging of Vitalis [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “At the urging of Vitalis, and with the superscription ‘requesting’”],

[Col. 0067A] placed—the sacred remains in an excellent place.

O exceedingly happy man, destined to enter eternal light,

Whose life advances this work for its God [Note: One manuscript reads: “in devotion to God.”].

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the Basilica of the Lord Stephen

[Note: He describes the triumph and glory of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr, in undergoing death for Christ; Palladius had dedicated a basilica in his memory.]

The lofty glory of the Lord surrounds His pious friends,

Whose honor, spread abroad, lives throughout the world.

Here the martyr endured for Christ in the eastern quarter of the world;

Behold, blessed, he possesses temples beneath the setting sun.

Founded upon the power of God, triumphing over death,

He received the stones, for Christ was his rock.

[Col. 0067B] The fierce Jewish people, O Stephen, whom you think you are destroying:

Even though he dies in the flesh, he does not know how to die in glory.

He holds the palm because of his merits; you hold punishment because of your crime.

He possesses the heavens; you seek the depths all the more.

This holy Palladius [Note: Palladius, bishop of Saintes, flourished in the age of Fortunatus, who often mentions him. He had brought the ashes of Saint Eutropius into a basilica that had collapsed through age and had been restored to its former beauty, depositing them in a place he had prepared for that purpose, as Gregory of Tours relates, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 56. Was this the same Palladius whom Fortunatus reports in this poem as having built the Basilica of Saint Stephen?

Browerus, however, prefers to identify this Palladius with the bishop of Bourges, since two Palladii are listed in the catalogue of the bishops of Bourges: one is said by Dionysius Sammarthanus, in *Gallia Christiana*, to have flourished in the fourth century, the other in the fifth. Certainly there was at Bourges, already in the age of Gregory of Tours, a church consecrated to the memory of Saint Stephen, distinguished for its religious devotion and magnificence; Gregory describes its beginnings in *History of the Franks*, book I, chapter 29.] established the temples of the Levite,

From which he may know that a house imperishable for himself [Note: A later hand had inserted, as Browerus reports: “that there may be for him a house from which he may exist.” He restored the reading found in reliable books: “from which he may know.” The Venetian edition reads: “from which he preserves for you”; the Paris edition: “from which it may come to him.”].

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Basilica of Saint Martin

[Note: He honors in this poem the basilica erected in honor of Saint Martin by Bishop Faustus, celebrated for its religious devotion.]

A dignified palace shines forth, raised upon a venerable height,

Sanctified to God by the name of Martin.

For the merit of his life shines with such great confidence

That he grants to peoples what their pious prayers ask.

The priest Faustus raised this structure with devoted heart [Note: Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book VIII, chapter 22, mentions Faustus, bishop of Auch, who attended the Second Synod of Mâcon in 585. He appears to be the same man whom Fortunatus mentions here.];

[Col. 0067C] And restored prosperous gifts to his own Lord [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “and restored his prosperous gifts.”].

## CHAPTER V. To the Cell of Saint Martin, Where He Clothed a Poor Man, at the Request of Bishop Gregory

[Note: In this poem he celebrates the generosity of Martin of Tours in removing his own tunic and using it to clothe a needy man; he also commends the religious importance of the place where this occurred.]

You who prepare to hasten onward, traveler, turn your path here;

This place teaches the person who prays to proceed more carefully.

[Col. 0068A] For, an exile on earth and often an inhabitant of heaven,

Martin, shut away here, used to open the heavens.

Living beneath this roof, he kept the solitude of the desert,

A powerful anchorite in the midst of the people.

Here [Note: Sulpicius, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 1, relates that this happened in the church’s *secretarium*, the place to which Martin customarily withdrew until he was to go out among the people to perform the sacred rite. We have said more in the notes to *The Life of Saint Martin*, book III.], after stripping himself, he clothed a poor man with his tunic;

While covering the man who was cold, he himself grew warmer in faith.

Then the priest himself was clothed in a cheap tunic;

And supreme honor went forth beneath a poor covering.

Yet while he handled the sacred mysteries of the altar,

Giving signs over the chalice, he gave blessed signs.

For a flame shone forth from the sacred head of the man;

And a globe of harmless fire rose toward the stars.

And, lest injury be done to his right hand by the short sleeves,

Gems covered the place where his flesh was bare.

The arms of noble stones flashed with radiance,

And in place of the tunic there was a beautiful emerald.

How well he makes a bargain who, while he clothed a poor man,

Covers his own arms with gems instead of a tunic.

You also, Martin, who dwell in heaven, intercede,

And bear holy words to God on behalf of Fortunatus.

To obey your commands, pious and beloved priest,

As much as ability permits, I prefer that my willingness be greater.

[Note: Some manuscripts separate the final couplet from what precedes it under the title “Likewise, to the same man,” or “To Gregory.” One Vatican manuscript gives the title: “These two verses are addressed to Gregory.”]

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Basilica of Saint Martin

[Note: He commends the generosity and religious devotion of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, in constructing the Basilica of Saint Martin, and of Placidina, formerly his wife, in adorning it. He then describes the pleasant setting in which it had been built.]

Whoever desires to be joined to the blessed in an eternal dwelling [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “to join himself to the blessed in their dwelling,” corruptly],

[Col. 0068C] Makes them his companions through pious prayers.

Nor does he suffer to be delayed what must be done,

When he considers the good things he has given to be his own profits.

Therefore Leontius built a gracious sanctuary in the fields [Note: Leontius, whom Fortunatus mentions here, was bishop of Bordeaux, a man distinguished both for piety and strength of character and for noble birth. He is well known from the poems of Fortunatus and from the testimony of Gregory of Tours, which can be read throughout the *History of the Franks*. He died around 567 and therefore did not long survive Fortunatus’s arrival in Gaul.],

So that he himself might enter heaven through such services.

Supported by the merits and name of Martin, they shine forth;

It is certain that he gave signs of heaven on earth.

He cleansed the spots of leprosy [Note: Sulpicius, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 19, relates that when Martin was entering the gate of Paris, he encountered a leper horribly disfigured and healed him with a kiss. I readily believe that this deed of Martin was represented in some painting in Leontius’s basilica. Certainly it was customary to adorn churches with sacred paintings, as Fortunatus himself makes sufficiently clear—among many others, in book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, where he says that he was healed of an eye ailment by the oil of a lamp burning before a painted image of Saint Martin in the Basilica of Saints John and Paul at Ravenna.] by medicinal kisses,

And took away the wars of sickness through an embrace of peace.

Nevertheless, these things were built by skilled workmanship,

So that no exceptional glory of praise should lack anything [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “so that nothing more splendid might produce the glory of praise that pleases.”].

The place itself is added as an ornament [Note: Fortunatus himself, in chapters 19 and 20 of this first book, describes the estates of Vereginis and Proemiacum in the territory of Bordeaux, which Leontius had adorned with most magnificent buildings. It is therefore probable that this church, built under the patronage and name of Martin, bishop of Tours, stood on one or the other estate, especially since their site—on a gently sloping hill overlooking most pleasant fields—corresponds to the place where Fortunatus here describes the Basilica of Saint Martin. That the most devout bishops of that age customarily adorned their estates with sanctuaries and in some measure endowed them with religious character is sufficiently shown by the example of Nicetius, bishop of Trier. Describing his estate, Fortunatus expressly identifies a chapel there in these verses, book III, chapter 12:

> The tower which stands opposite upon the slope,  
> Is the place of the saints, arms to be grasped by men.

]: it rises above the fields,

And, set upon a lofty ridge, opens out from a swelling hill:

Its higher back, raised aloft, holds everything beneath it,

And wherever one looks, it sees delightful things.

Coming from far away [Note: A Vatican manuscript reads: “coming from far off”], one is regarded as near by the eye;

The gaze joins what distance separates.

The traveler, weary, is drawn there by the inviting view;

If his feet fail, he approaches, carried onward by the sight [Note: The Paris edition reads *defuerit*, “if it is lacking”; in the margin, *defecit*, “if it has failed.”].

Placidina adorned its heights with sacred hangings [Note: Placidina was the wife of Leontius, a highly religious and devout woman. She was of imperial lineage, as will be said below, chapter 15 of this book.],

And the two compete together: he builds, she tends and adorns [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read: “and, competing together, the one builds, the other venerates.”].

## CHAPTER VII. In Honor of the Basilica of Saint Martin, Which Basil and Baudegundis Built

[Note: He commemorates the temple in honor of Saint Martin, renovated and restored by Basil and Baudegundis, his wife; they diverted elsewhere the waters that had covered the site of the building.]

Learn, mortals: nothing on earth can stand in the way of love [Note: The Venetian edition reads:

> Learn, mortals: nothing can obstruct one who loves.

].

[Col. 0070A] When the sacred temples of God remain fixed in the river.

So that a beautiful palace might rise through narrow passages,

And although the mountain forbade it, the water provided a place.

So that the wandering water might serve the house above,

New skill subjected the ancient waters to channels;

When Basil, of one mind with Baudegundis, [Note: Fortunatus wrote an epitaph for this Basil, preserved in book IV, chapter 18. Among his other virtues, he commends his religious devotion and generosity in enriching sacred buildings in these verses:

> Enriching churches and suitably honoring holy places,  
> Giving to the poor, he ascends rich to the stars.

Whether this was the same Basil who was a citizen of Poitiers, whom Gregory of Tours mentions in *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 46, is entirely uncertain. Basil, who supported Chilperic’s party, wished to prevent Mummolus, who had come with an army on behalf of Sigibert, from entering the city, but was defeated by him.

We may perhaps form some conjecture that he was the same man from the fact that Fortunatus says in book IV, chapter 18, that he was sent to Spain in the king’s name, in these words:

> When ambassadors often consulted this man,  
> Gallic concern sent him to the Spaniards.

From this it is clear that he was accustomed to conduct public affairs and held an eminent position among his people. Now, if anyone had reason to send ambassadors to Spain, it was certainly Chilperic, who had married Athanagild’s daughter, the daughter of the Gothic king in Spain—although the marriage ended unhappily, as we related in the Life of Fortunatus, section 45—and had betrothed his own daughter Rigunth to Reccared, likewise king of Spain and grandson of Athanagild, although she had already begun the journey to Spain and was unable to reach that marriage.

It is therefore not improbable that Chilperic made use of Basil’s service and diligence in conducting an embassy on his behalf among the Spaniards, and that Basil likewise stood on Chilperic’s side against Mummolus. Certainly Fortunatus calls this the king’s love in the cited poem, book IV, poem 18. (Note from the first revision.)—As we have noted elsewhere, Reccared was the son of Leuvichildus, or Leuvigildus, who, after the death of his father Athanagild, obtained the kingdom jointly with his brother Leuva. When Leuva died, he held the entire kingdom alone, as is read in the epitome of the *History of the Franks*, section 63. Leuvigild therefore fathered Hermenegild, who died a martyr for the Catholic faith after being killed by his father, and Reccared, who inherited his father’s kingdom and, after renouncing Arian impiety, converted the Visigothic people in Spain to embrace the Catholic doctrine concerning the divinity of the Son. He is the Reccared mentioned here. (Note from the second revision.)]

together with her,

Renewing this, restores and enlarges the ancient work.

Thus, Martin, your honor deserves to be great everywhere,

So that no places refuse the festivals that sound for you [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “the festivals that sound for you.”].

Pacified by such services, generous priest,

Since you see their vows, kindly return the favor [Note: In the same manuscript, the final line is absent.].

# CHAPTER VIII. On the Basilica of Saint Vincent on the Garonne

[Note: [Col. 0070D] Saint Vincent was a martyr of the city of Aginnum, from the order of Levites, as Gregory of Tours reports in Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 105. Browerus, in his notes on Fortunatus, criticizes Baronius because he confused Vincent of Aginnum with Vincent of Saragossa under the year 561, despite the clear testimony both of Gregory of Tours and of Fortunatus himself. This error of Baronius was also shared by several others, [Col. 0071C] who, deceived by the similarity of the names, honored Vincent of Saragossa in place of Vincent of Aginnum; and, as the error spread more widely, basilicas once dedicated under the title of Saint Vincent of Aginnum gradually acquired Vincent of Saragossa as their patron, as learned men believe. See the distinguished Ruinart, in his notes on Gregory of Tours, Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 105. See also Scaliger, Book VI, *On the Emendation of Time*.]

[Note: [Col. 0070D] Three Vatican manuscripts read *ultra Garonna* or *Garomnam*. In the Venetian edition: “On the basilica of Saint Vincent by the Garonne.”]

[Note: [Col. 0070A] [He describes the contest and glory of Saint Vincent, martyr of Aginnum. He commends the generosity of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, in adorning and strengthening his basilica, situated near Aginnum, with a tin roof. [Col. 0070B]]]

While life is brief, faith makes it longer through blessed merits,  
and extends narrow days through honor.

[Col. 0071A] After the end, without end, the mind devoted [Note: [Col. 0071C] In the Venetian edition: “the mind restored to Christ.”] to Christ remains,  
leaving the human throng, it stands joined to God.

Supported by this help, Vincent lives throughout the ages;  
the abundant glory of his martyrdom flourishes.

With his head cut off, he seized triumph from death,  
and a new offspring from earth flies toward the stars.

The enemy, from the place where he believed he had brought death,  
gave honor to the saint;  
and the executioner, struck down more enduringly by death, lies fallen.

That wretched man would have prevailed [Note: [Col. 0071C] One Vatican manuscript reads *vinceret ille miser* (“that wretched man would prevail”). A Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition likewise read *stagnea tecta* (“tin roofs”).], had he been able to slaughter him;  
for from the place where he took away his head,  
from there he bestowed heaven.

Fulfilling pious vows in his new love, Leontius gave a tin roof [Note: [Col. 0071D] This basilica of Saint Vincent was near Aginnum, at a place called Pompeiacus, where Vincent, after confessing Christ, had been beheaded. Gregory of Tours relates, in Book VII of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 35, and Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 105, that this basilica was violated by Guntram’s soldiers in order to plunder treasures deposited there by the local people, and that divine power immediately avenged their crime. Scaliger, Book VI of *On the Emendation of Time*, thinks Gregory of Tours mistaken in believing that the basilica was near Aginnum, since it was near Lugdunum Convenarum, four days’ journey from Aginnum. But Gregory is excellently defended by the distinguished Ruinart in his notes on Book VII, chapter 35, of the *History of the Franks*.]  
where the sacred limbs lie.

And although the venerable temple shines with merits,  
he nevertheless supplied his own adornment.

May long rewards of salvation follow the one who works,  
[Col. 0071B] so that the holy heights may gleam through his services.

# CHAPTER IX. On the Basilica of Saint Vincent at Vernemetis [Virnimetis]

[Note: [Col. 0071D] Although we do not know where this place, commonly called Vernemetis, truly was, we readily believe that it was situated somewhere in the territory of Bordeaux, conspicuous both for the pleasantness of its location and for its religious significance, as we can infer from this very poem. It appears to have belonged to the diocese of Leontius, who had shown such generosity in constructing and adorning the basilica of Saint Vincent. [Col. 0072C]]

[Note: [Col. 0071B] [He celebrates the basilica erected in memory of Saint Vincent of Aginnum at a place commonly called Vernemetis, and relates that an evil spirit was expelled from a possessed man at the dedication of the same basilica.]]

The fame of the Lord’s servant has gone out through the whole world,  
and there is no place where his lofty glory is absent.

But since we know that his merit traverses the world,  
everywhere it is fitting that temples to this man should rise.

Behold, the blessed heights of the supreme Vincent shine,  
of him who, through the gift of martyrdom, inhabits the stars of heaven.

Prompted by pious love, Pope Leontius founded it long ago,  
and made it secure in an illustrious place.

Ancient times wished to call it by the name Vernemetis,  
which in the Gallic language signifies something like “a great shrine” [Note: [Col. 0072C] The common editions read *favum ingens* (“a great honeycomb”), a reading corrected by Browerus.].

Faith had been sent beforehand as the pledge of what was to come [Note: [Col. 0072C] Three Vatican manuscripts read *arce futura*. The Venetian edition reads in full: “Faith, sent beforehand under auspices, was for the citadel to come.”],  
so that now the lofty house might stand in the honor of God.

Here too the saint, supported by love of the Lord,  
gave terrifying signs of supreme virtue.

For when the bishop, as customary, dedicated God’s temple,  
the demon’s rage fled at the martyr’s arrival.

A certain man was restored unharmed from evil possession [Note: [Col. 0072C] Two Vatican manuscripts read “from malignant disease.”];  
for him, seeing the temple of the holy man, was the remedy.

The mighty hall gleams, filled with divine serenity,  
so that God may rightly be pleased to dwell here.

Now the beauty of the place, together with the honor of virtue,  
draws the peoples here: on one side splendor, on the other salvation.

The founder of the revered shrine kindles the people;  
for such services he reaps fitting rewards [Note: [Col. 0072D] One Vatican manuscript reads *metet*, “will reap.”].

# CHAPTER X. On Lord Nazarius

[Note: [Col. 0072D] It is uncertain who this Nazarius was, since three persons are celebrated under this name on 12 June. The first suffered at Milan with the boy Celsus; their bodies were discovered by Saint Ambrose. The second suffered at Eburodunum; the third at Rome, whose body was brought to Gaul through the agency of Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, in the year 765. See Ruinart, in his notes on Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Book I, chapter 61, from which we have drawn this information.

The relics of Saint Nazarius were venerated in the territory of Nantes in the time of Gregory of Tours, as may be seen in the passage cited above.]

a martyr of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0072A] [He commemorates the basilica erected from its foundations, likewise by Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, in memory of Saint Nazarius the martyr, after the older and narrower structure had been demolished. He describes the triumph and glory of the martyr himself. [Col. 0072B]]]

[Col. 0072B] The venerable heights of the illustrious Nazarius shine,  
whose limbs possess heaven and whose spirit holds the stars.

Born from earthly seed, yet estranged from earthly uses,  
an immortal good, a man born from dust,

he desired nothing carnal, but sought Christ’s rewards,  
a worthy victim to God through his own blood.

This temple, consecrated to you, holy Leontius offers,  
and from this place he wishes his house to be made greater.

Previously this structure had been built within a narrow circuit,  
so that then the venerable people could not fit there.

Having demolished it to the ground, he founded it anew from the bottom,  
and gave this building, which now pleases us enlarged.

# CHAPTER XI. On the Basilica of Lord Dionysius

[Note: [Col. 0072D] Saint Dionysius, bishop of Paris, is reported by Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 28 of the *History of the Franks*, to have suffered in the year 250 or even later; but other records show that he was sent to Gaul by blessed Clement, so that his martyrdom should be assigned to the second century. See Ruinart, in his notes [Col. 0073B] on Gregory of Tours, Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 72. See also what we have noted concerning the *Acts of Saint Dionysius*, Part II of Fortunatus’s works. The basilica of Saint Dionysius near Paris was exceedingly famous; Gregory of Tours often mentions it, and Adrian Valesius discusses it at length in Part II of his defense against Launoy. But the one of which Fortunatus speaks here appears to have been situated at Bordeaux or in the territory of Bordeaux, and to have been originally erected by Amelius, the predecessor of Leontius.]

[Note: [Col. 0072C] [He commemorates the basilica of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Paris and martyr, likewise enlarged by Leontius, who did not demolish the old structure until the new one had been built. He celebrates the praises of the martyr himself.]]

[Col. 0072C] If you wish to know the builder of this excellent temple,  
I shall not allow such pious vows to remain hidden from you.

[Col. 0073A] Since once the sacred shrines were farther away,  
and the people often feared the journey because of the distance,

the bishop Amelius had provided here a small [Note: [Col. 0073B]

This Amelius preceded Leontius I in the see of Bordeaux, and was the predecessor of our Leontius. (First note of the first revision.)—We have placed Amelius immediately before the elder Leontius in the see of Bordeaux because too much time would otherwise intervene between Cyprian, who took part in the Council of Agde in 508 [Col. 0073C] and the First Council of Orléans, and Leontius, who took part in the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541, as Cointius shows under the year 541, number 65. For this reason we assign Leontius immediately after Cyprian. Oihenartus, however, as Cointius reports, places both Leontii after Cyprian in Book III, chapter 7 of the *Notice of Both Gasconies*. Robert, on the other hand, reports that Callicinus succeeded the first Leontius in the see of Bordeaux, that Amelius succeeded Callicinus, and then Cyprian, followed by the younger Leontius. We have not thought that the two Leontii should be separated, because Leontius I signed the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541, while the younger Leontius began to occupy the see before 549, when he signed the Fifth Council of Orléans through a legate; they therefore do not appear to be separable.

The Sammarthani, in *Gallia Christiana*, place Leontius I after Amelius; between him and the younger Leontius they place Cyprian. Nor does their reason seem convincing: they wish to establish that Leontius I sat after Amelius because Fortunatus, Book I, chapter 11, reports:

“Here the bishop Amelius had provided a small fortress,  
a place unable to contain the Christian people;  
when he had closed the day of his life, thereafter, by succession and rank,  
this work and place came to his heir.  
And Pope Leontius founded this pious hall,” etc.

Fortunatus does not say that the work, left narrow and inconvenient by Amelius, came to the man who was immediately his heir in place and rank, to be enlarged and renewed. On the contrary, all these words can very well be understood of Leontius II, who, although not Amelius’s immediate successor, was nevertheless his heir in the see of Bordeaux. Accordingly Robert, whom Cointius cites, interpreted Fortunatus’s words as referring to the younger Leontius. This is especially so because Fortunatus, who devoted himself entirely to exalting the praises of the younger Leontius, frequently displayed his zeal in either repairing or building basilicas; yet he narrated nothing of this kind about Leontius I, whose epitaph he wrote, preserved in Book IV, chapter 9.

[Col. 0074B] Launoy, however, in his *Dissertation on the Two Dionysiuses*, chapter 6, observation 6, believes that the basilica of which Fortunatus speaks here was not in the diocese of Bordeaux but at Paris: that Amelius, bishop of Paris, first erected it around the year 530, when Amelius governed the Parisian Church, and that Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, enlarged and restored it out of zeal and religious devotion toward Saint Dionysius. But, apart from the fact that Fortunatus nowhere mentions that this basilica was at Paris or that it was restored by the bishop of Bordeaux, it is certainly clear from the following that Amelius was not bishop of Paris but bishop of Bordeaux: Fortunatus reports that Leontius, plainly bishop of Bordeaux, succeeded Amelius in that see in Book I, chapter 11, in these words:

[Col. 0074C] “When he [Amelius] had closed the day of his life, thereafter, by succession and rank,  
this work and place came to his heir.  
And Pope Leontius founded this pious hall,” etc. (Second note of the second revision.)]

fortress,

a place unable to contain the Christian people;

when he had closed the day of his life, thereafter, by succession and rank,  
this work and place came to his heir.

And Pope Leontius founded this pious hall [Note: [Col. 0074C] In *Gallia Christiana*, edited by the Sammarthani, this work is attributed not to Leontius II, who in Fortunatus’s time was bishop of Bordeaux in Gaul, but to his predecessor Leontius I—a surprising attribution.],

and offered splendid gifts to his own Lord.

The venerable Dionysius possesses this temple as his own,  
consecrated under the name by which it shines.

He, strengthened by fervent faith and the love of Christ,  
placed his neck beneath the sword that was to cut it.

He despised his limbs, longing for the crown,  
regarding as worthless whatever love of God might bring.

So that dying flesh might prepare an immortal gift,  
he loved the wounds that would not end in death.

Meeting the hostile sword, he sent himself to Olympus;  
from the place where he wished to die, he possesses the vows of salvation.

[Col. 0074A] The bishop did not first remove the cramped shrines [Note: [Col. 0074C] The Venetian and Parisian editions, and one Vatican manuscript, read “nor the shrines previously gathered together.”],

until he had completed these things, which now, adorned [variant: *facta*, “made”], please us,

continually carrying out the rites in the ancient temple,  
until, in due order, the succeeding work had been consolidated.

# CHAPTER XII. On the Basilica of Saint Bibianus

[Note: [Col. 0074C] It appears from the testimony of Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 58, that this basilica of Saint Bibianus was in the suburb of Saintes.]

[Note: [Col. 0074A] [He reports that the basilica of Saint Bibianus, bishop of Saintes, had been begun by Eusebius but left unfinished; Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, completed it at the request of Emerius, bishop of Saintes, with no small contribution also made for this purpose by Placidina, formerly Leontius’s wife. Fortunatus therefore commends their piety and generosity.]]

The temples of the priest Bibianus worthy of praise gleam,  
where faith, if you seek what is right, grants pious vows.

The temples which the joyful bishop Eusebius once founded [Note: [Col. 0074C] This Eusebius was Emerius’s predecessor in the see of Saintes. [Col. 0074D] He took part in the Second Council of Orléans in 533 and the Fifth in 549.];

yet, before he could complete them, he was snatched from the world.

The priest Emerius [Note: [Col. 0074D] This Emerius, called Aemulus from childhood, was the man whom Leontius, together with the bishops of the province assembled in synod, removed from the episcopate. He had obtained from King Chlothar that he be consecrated without the metropolitan’s advice, as Gregory of Tours relates in Book IV, chapter 25 of the *History of the Franks*. It therefore appears that Leontius undertook to complete the basilica of Saint Bibianus before deposing him in the synod, or at least after they had been reconciled. Charibert, Chlothar’s son, had become violently enraged against Leontius and his fellow bishops because they had rescinded his father’s action without consulting him; he then sent the cleric who brought news of that judgment into exile, having placed him on a cart spread with thorns. Leontius himself escaped the calamity suffered by the other bishops who had assembled for that synod only after paying a certain sum of gold.] succeeded him in the sacred office,

but refuses to bear the burden of building what had been begun [Note: [Col. 0074D] The Paris edition reads “what had been adorned.”].

[Col. 0075A] He entrusted the work to you through his prayers, Pope Leontius,  
whose love persistently presses toward this vow.

Of its own accord, such honor reserved itself for you to accomplish;  
none but you could give these places their sacred character.

O merit of the just man, destined to remain in everlasting light,  
through whom the venerable temples desire to be worshiped.

Silver roofs cover the sacred tombs of Bibianus,  
which Placidina, united with you, gave.

Above the poured-out surface, shining gold glitters,  
and pure metals scatter their rays.

The ceilings, perfected with a new design, gleam,  
and you would think that the artist had given life to beasts [Note: [Col. 0075B] It may be inferred that it was customary from ancient times to adorn the vaults and walls of temples with figures of beasts and other living creatures, whether painted or sculpted, both from other monuments and from Oration 19 of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus. Praising his dead father and describing a temple built by him, he says among other things that it was “Κιόνων, καὶ ζώων κάλλεσι· δι` ὀρόφων εἰς ὕψος αἰρόμενον, καὶ τοῖς ὑπὲρ ἀυτῶν πλάσμασιν οὐ λειπομένοις τῆς φύσεως”—that is, “made most beautiful and magnificent by the beauty of columns and living creatures, rising aloft through vaulted ceilings, with the figures above them not falling short of nature.” Fortunatus relates the same thing in the next poem about the Basilica of Saint Eutropius, in these verses:

[Col. 0075C] “Here the beauty of sculpted ceilings, finely carved, hangs;  
wood has supplied the playful forms that painting usually provides.

The wall has assumed imagined figures by imitation;  
what was not previously covered now gleams painted.”

I believe that this custom of adorning the walls and vaults of temples with painted or sculpted images arose from the very decoration of Solomon’s Temple, which we read of in Book III of Kings, chapter 6, in these words: “And he carved all the walls of the temple round about with various engravings and with the lathe; and he made in them cherubim, and palms, and various figures, as if projecting from the wall and emerging.”]

[Note: [Col. 0075C] Two Vatican manuscripts read “and you think that the artist…”]

But to whom you have given such great gifts with willing hearts,  
may he act so that lasting salvation may remain for you.

And let those who offer worthy gifts not doubt  
that great things will be repaid to them.

[Col. 0075B] While God returns abundant rewards [Note: [Col. 0075C] The same manuscripts read, “while he also returns for small things.”]  
for the gifts they have given [Note: [Col. 0075C] The Venetian edition reads:

“While God himself returns abundance in return.”]

# CHAPTER XIII. On the Basilica of Saint Eutropius

[Note: [Col. 0075C] Saint Eutropius, as Gregory of Tours relates in Book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 56, was sent to Gaul by Saint Clement and consecrated bishop by him; there he was attacked by pagans and died when his head was crushed. However, Gregory’s statement that Eutropius was sent to Gaul by Saint Clement derives more from popular opinion than from historical fact, as the distinguished Ruinart observes in his notes on the cited passage of Gregory. Moreover, Palladius, bishop of Saintes, restored the memory of Saint Eutropius, which had partly faded in Gaul, after discovering his body, whose head still bore a visible scar left by the burning, and carrying it into a new basilica dedicated under his name. See Gregory in the passage cited above.]

[Col. 0076A] [Note: [Col. 0076A] [He reports that the basilica of Saint Eutropius, bishop of Saintes, already collapsing, was restored and adorned by Leontius, not without divine admonition and direction.]]

How great is the love of the Lord that remains in you, Pope Leontius,  
whom the temples of the saints now urge to renew them [Note: [Col. 0075D]

I believe this to be the same basilica restored and adorned by Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, into which Palladius, bishop of Saintes, later brought the body of Saint Eutropius after discovering it, as I have said. Certainly Gregory of Tours, Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 56, mentions the basilica in which the sacred relics of Eutropius were buried [Col. 0076B], as one already completed and finished, and he records no work performed there by Palladius. Fortunatus himself sufficiently testifies that Leontius left several such monuments of his piety and generosity at Saintes—which was subject, as a provincial metropolitan church, to the Church of Bordeaux—in chapter 15 of this book, where, speaking of Leontius, he says:

“Not only here at Bordeaux, but everywhere your temples gleam, O priest;  
among them, Saintes applauds and points out that one.”

Browerus therefore is not correct in thinking that this basilica was founded by Palladius and repaired and restored by Leontius with new work. Leontius preceded Palladius in age, so that I am surprised whether he could ever even have seen the bishop of Saintes. [Col. 0076C] Leontius, in early youth—as Fortunatus reports in chapter 15 of this book—followed King Childebert’s army into Spain. That expedition took place around the year 531. He lived about fifty-four years, as the same Fortunatus states in the poem he wrote for Leontius’s funeral, Book IV, chapter 10, so I do not know whether he could have lived as late as 570. Palladius was the third bishop in the see of Saintes after Emerius, whom Leontius, as we said above, deposed in a synod around 563 or 564. Palladius was still governing the Church of Saintes around 597, at which time he obtained sacred relics from Gregory the Great, Roman pontiff, through his priest Leuparicus. But see Cointius under the year 567, number 26.

Since this is so, how could Leontius restore a basilica built by Palladius, collapsing from age and almost destroyed, as Fortunatus reports here? Before Palladius—and before Leontius himself—therefore, an old temple dedicated in honor of Saint Eutropius already stood. Gregory of Tours should consequently be understood to mean only that Palladius renewed its memory in part, since before Palladius discovered the body, distinguished by its clear scar, it was unknown that Eutropius had been a martyr. Fortunatus’s silence also lends some weight to this point: nowhere in this poem does he mention that Eutropius was a martyr, although otherwise he would never have silently omitted that fact, especially since Gregory of Tours relates that it had been confirmed by divine intervention.]

for it is the hall of the venerable bishop Eutropius [Eutropis] [Note: [Col. 0076D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “For it is the hall of the venerable bishop Etropitis.”—that venerable bishop’s hall—

which was collapsing, torn apart by its own old age [Note: [Col. 0076D] Two Vatican manuscripts read *corruerat senio* (“had collapsed through old age”); the remaining words of the supplied apparatus are uncertain.].

The walls stood stripped of their beams,  
pressed down not by the weight of the roof but by water’s destructive force.

When light sleep came upon a certain minister at night,  
it showed him that you were to be its restorer [Note: [Col. 0076D] Browerus says in his notes on this poem that Leontius was admonished in sleep to restore the temple of Saint Eutropius, although Fortunatus so plainly says that the divine message came to one of his ministers, who afterward admonished Leontius.].

[Col. 0076B] In exchange for your reward, he deserved even more to be warned;  
O happy man, for whom God takes pious care.

[Col. 0077A] Now the old structure, renewed by a better way, has grown green again,  
and reborn splendor has entered the weary building.

Age has been added, yet it grows youthful in honor;  
from the place where it would have grown old, it returns younger.

Here the beauty of carved [manuscript: sculpted] ceilings, finely worked, hangs;  
wood has supplied the playful forms that painting usually provides.

The wall has assumed imagined figures by imitation;  
what was not previously covered now gleams painted.

He was the first priest of the city of Saintes,  
and rightly gave the first honors to you who restore him [Note: [Col. 0077C] By these words, “rightly gave the first honors,” it is declared that Leontius was the metropolitan whose diocese included the neighboring Church of Saintes. [Col. 0077D]].

Since the saint now possesses his temples and dwells there in peace,  
he returns honor in exchange to the restorer [Note: [Col. 0077D] Three Vatican manuscripts read, “he returns love in exchange.”].

# CHAPTER XIV. On the Chalice of Bishop Leontius

[Note: [Col. 0077D] Fortunatus appears to mention this chalice again in the following poem, in these lines:

“With pious gifts you endowed Christ’s altars,  
when your vessels bear the holy entrails of God.”]

[Col. 0077B] [Note: [Col. 0077B] [He commemorates the chalice offered by Leontius and Placidina to the sacred church.]]

Leontius offers pious gifts at the highest citadel of God,  
and Placidina likewise, joined with him in sacred vows.

Happy are those whose work is suited to the altars [Note: [Col. 0077D] The printed editions read, “whose every vessel is suited to the altars”; Browerus restored the present reading from an old manuscript.],

who in a short time bring forth things that will not perish.

# CHAPTER XV. On Leontius

[Note: [Col. 0077D] This Leontius succeeded another Leontius in the see of Bordeaux and appears to have been related to him by family connection. Browerus traces their lineage and origin to the family of the Paulini, conjecturing this from a passage of Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, Letter 12. Certainly that Leontius, whom Sidonius readily calls the foremost of the Aquitanians, appears to have been related by origin and family to the Leontius of whom Fortunatus speaks here, just as the similarity of the villas mentioned by Sidonius and Fortunatus shows that they belonged to their households and families, as we shall indicate in its proper place.]

bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0077B] [In this poem he celebrates Leontius’s noble birth, episcopal rank, and generosity toward temples, and adds praises of Placidina, formerly Leontius’s wife.]]

[Col. 0077C] Among whom the radiant Aquitanian [Note: [Col. 0078D] One Vatican manuscript reads “Aquitanian axis.”] region produced you,  
you hold the foremost heights through your excellent merits.

Your lofty power rises above citizens from Gaul [variant: *et Gallis*, “and the Gauls”];  
you are superior to the rest, and no one is before you.

You surpass many; you are inferior and second to no one,  
nor is there any honor left that could be added to you.

When youth first clothed itself in bloom,  
you were young in years but old in gravity [Note: [Col. 0078D] One Vatican manuscript reads “old in the gravity of an old man.” In this manuscript *senis* is almost always written for *senex*, which need only be noted once.].

When you turned toward the Spanish battle-lines with the serene king [Note: [Col. 0078D] Gregory of Tours reports in Book III, chapter 10 of the *History of the Franks*, that King Childebert entered Spain with an army and, after its king had been killed, gained possession of the country. Leontius should therefore be understood to have followed this army, already then reaching manhood. The expedition occurred around the year 531, as we said above in the notes on Poem 13 of this book. I have no doubt that Childebert is indicated under the name “serene king”; Fortunatus often praises his religion and piety, but especially in Book VI, chapter 4.],

the second palm of victory grew in your military service.

The first fruits of that service pleased so greatly when reported  
that this rank was owed to your merits.
