[Col. 0078A] Your lofty honors could not suddenly have been prepared for you  
unless your worthy work had earned them.

Powerful in nobility, you excel, Pope Leontius,  
renowned from ancient times, if your ancestors are counted.

For your lineage, your forefathers, and whatever I may name in order,  
run as an ancient origin through lofty nobles.

The times flee, yet the hall of your parents remains;  
with you restoring it, the house does not suffer decline.

Nobility has not bowed through the long years;  
rather, a noble offspring gave it a greater ascent.

An illustrious line adorned those who came before with light;  
the origin of your fathers shines through the radiance of its heir.

Antiquity has clothed itself in flowers from its own root;  
the honor of your praise rightly overshadows it.

Although no one may now be regarded as superior,  
you surpass yourself by magnifying your fathers.

A lofty summit shines forth, displaying noble lineage,  
whose unique palm is evident before kings.

Now you govern the rights of the Church, venerable priest;  
from this another nobility has been added to you.

Although the pontifical summit is lofty in the city [or world],  
once it received you, the honor it had gained increased.

The house of God and the shepherd return rewards to one another:  
you gave it adornment; it gave you hope.

By divine gift you both flourish equally;  
you please through your reward, and it gleams through your beauty.

You are reckoned the thirteenth bishop of this city,  
but in merits you will be counted as the first.

You restored God’s ancient temples to their former height,  
and after their fall they now please us in better form.

[Col. 0078C] They shine with the flower of youth, while old age flees,  
and they happily favor you, flourishing through your renewal.

So that you might do more, fires burned the roofs,  
and now those same buildings gleam more beautifully through your praise.

The fire-born ruins suffered no loss,  
which now, after the flames [Note: [Col. 0078D] One Vatican manuscript reads “through the flames.”], shine full of light.

I believe that they themselves wished to be burned,  
so that your labor might make them better.

After being consumed by their own ashes and thin embers,  
the old Phoenix likewise renews itself [Note: [Col. 0078D] One Vatican manuscript reads corruptly, “thus the Phoenix also flourishes.”].

The sacred baptistery too was restored [Note: [Col. 0078D] Browerus shows in his notes on this passage [Col. 0079C] that baptisteries, according to the practice and custom of the ancient Church, were generally built separately from basilicas; this is also confirmed by Fortunatus’s testimony here. Saint Gregory of Tours likewise, in Book X, chapter 31 of the *History of the Franks*, lists a baptistery among the works with which he had adorned the Church of Tours, saying that he had ordered it built near the basilica: “I ordered a baptistery to be built beside that basilica.” It may likewise be inferred from Fortunatus, Book II, chapter 12, that the baptistery at Mainz, built by Sidonius, bishop of that city, had its own hall, separate from the basilica’s building. Finally, even in our own age, baptisteries of ancient basilicas, generally set apart from the basilicas themselves, sufficiently reveal that ancient custom and practice.],

where a single fountain washes away old stains with its waters.

[Col. 0079A] Behold, you founded blessed temples of holy Mary,  
where night, defeated, flees, since it always possesses day.

The hall, full of light and gleaming, imitated Mary:  
she enclosed the light in her womb, and this hall encloses the day [Note: [Col. 0079D] Fortunatus appears here to indicate that the basilica of Saint Mary built by Leontius was fitted with glass windows, just as he said in a similar way when speaking of the church at Paris, Book II, chapter 11:

“It first receives the rays, eyed with glass windows,  
and by the craftsman’s hand has enclosed the day within its heights.”].

And not only here but everywhere your temples gleam, priest;  
among them, Saintes applauds and points out that one [Note: [Col. 0079D] The Paris edition reads “announces.”].

You give the peoples places where they may continually pray to Christ;  
you make yourself the road by which salvation may come.

The house of the Church flourishes as its summit rises,  
and proves that what now pleases, adorned, belongs to you.

You have made all the citizens eager to hasten here,  
and one house calls together whatever remains in the city.

You adorned your homeland, to which you grant enduring gifts;  
you too must be called the glory of Bordeaux.

[Col. 0079B] As far as this city has raised its head above the other cities [Note: [Col. 0079D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “has raised its head exceedingly high.”],

so far you surpass the bishops in the honor of your rank.

The Rhine, flowing from the Alps, does not foam with such sands,  
nor does the stronger Po enter the Adriatic waters;

the Danube is its equal, though it drives its waters farther [Note: [Col. 0079D] The Paris edition reads “though it will drive its waters.”].

I have crossed these; I judge them known to me.

With pious gifts you endowed Christ’s altars,  
when your vessels bear the holy entrails of God.

For the blood and body of the supreme Lord  
come by the proper ministry (*ministerio* [variant: *ministerium*]), as you provide it.

O happy man, whose wealth enriches pious temples,  
for whom this possession remains even more imperishable.

Rust will not wear away the talent with its biting tooth [Note: [Col. 0079D] The Venetian edition reads “rust will not hold it.”],

nor do thieves bring deceitful weapons against these things.

The gift lives, and makes the giver live well,  
when he dies on earth, he is carried from there to heaven.

[Col. 0080A] The possessor retains whatever he has sent on beforehand;  
only that which he causes to go ahead remains with him [Note: [Col. 0079D] These two verses are absent from the Venetian edition: “only that which it holds with itself,” and the following verse.].

These temples and consecrated vessels—and whatever else I cannot count—will grant this to you, priest:  
may you, the Church’s pillar [variant: *culmen*, “summit”], govern through long ages  
and shine everywhere in the fruit of your pious reward.

I am compelled by love to say a little about Placidina,  
who was then your wife and is now your dear sister [Note: [Col. 0080C] Those who had been wives before their husbands entered the episcopate were regarded as sisters after their husbands had been elevated to this dignity. For they lived with them no differently than with sisters, completely separated from the marriage bed, in accordance with the decrees of the canons and the ancient custom of the Church. Thus Constantius, priest, says in the *Life of Germanus of Auxerre*, chapter 2: “A wife is changed from spouse into sister.” But see Sirmond, in his notes on Sidonius, Book V, Letter 16, where he explains this at greater length.].

The light coming from her father Arcadius shines forth,  
in her, Avitus, your august offspring endures:

he who ruled the grandeur [manuscript: *fasces*] of empire [Note: [Col. 0080C] One Vatican manuscript reads corruptly, “made through empires”;] throughout the whole world,  
whose laws the still-powerful senate continues to possess.

If you seek the highest heights of the human race,  
nothing can remain beyond Caesar’s seed [Note: [Col. 0080C] Avitus, through the dignity of the imperial office, had made his otherwise most noble family much more august and illustrious. Born among the Arverni from the Anician family, he could enumerate a long line of grandfathers and great-grandfathers distinguished by honors and by the patrician order. Concerning him, Sidonius Apollinaris sings in the panegyric he recited at Rome to Avitus—whose daughter Sidonius himself had married:

“...for whom long ago the greatest radiant  
lineage embraced an offspring; through forefathers  
the palm-bearing patrician summit ran,  
and, with you as witness, Philagrius, the glory of his race shines.”

Avitus himself, however, was less fortunate in governing after he had obtained the Empire. For, having incurred the hatred of the senate, he was forced into exile; during that time he was made bishop of Piacenza. But fleeing from there as well, because he perceived that he was being sought everywhere for execution, he died on the journey while making for Gaul. See Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 11 of the *History of the Franks*.].

[Col. 0080B] But by the moderation of her understanding she surpassed her own lineage,  
from whose speech sweet honey flows.

Dear, serene, graceful, skillful, pious, gentle, generous—  
she possesses every good quality, whatever is pleasing in honor.

Gleaming in character, talent, and the radiance of her merits,  
her precious mind adorned her sex.

Why should I recount the many qualities with which she is endowed,  
since she was able, as your wife, to please your vows?

May she increase your life—you to whom you gave temples—  
and may she cover your summits with her own heights.

# CHAPTER XVI. Hymn on Bishop Leontius.

[Note: [Col. 0080B] When someone seeking the position of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, spread the false report that he—already absent—had died, so that he might be appointed in the dead man’s place, and when Leontius unexpectedly returned from his journey and showed himself alive to his flock, Fortunatus congratulates him in the following poem on his most welcome return. He declares that it was all the more joyful because it occurred on the very day on which Leontius had first taken possession of the see of Bordeaux. Taking this opportunity, he says much against those who seek episcopal honor and rank.]

[Col. 0081A] Let the whole age acknowledge

Leontius the prelate,

the prize of Bordeaux,

restored by a heavenly gift.

With his clever, two-tongued speech,

he nourished envious crime,

bringing the bitter report

that this man was already buried.

He did not endure concealing himself,

the man who announced the mournful death.

Although he ceased to do harm,

he revealed his insane desires.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] The first verses, arranged in cola, are acrostics, set out in order according to the letters of the alphabet, as Browerus observed long ago.]

[Col. 0081B] Deceived by his wicked scheme,

he laments his frustrated crimes,

while what he had thought grievous

has been turned into joy.

He produced savage precedents,

to be trampled upon for all time,

so that he might already draw up

decrees while the prelate was alive.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] One Vatican manuscript reads *cassa deflet* (“he laments what has been made void”); the Paris edition has *causata* in the margin.]

This deceptive affair occurred,

to be avoided by a chaste heart:

while the bishop survived, he presumed

what he could scarcely have done after his death.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] The Paris edition reads *fugata* (“driven away”).]

The priest burdens the order

who seeks the episcopate in this way;

he who embraces the commandments

flees the ambition for honor.

If this office is owed to anyone,

let him ascend the rank under compulsion,

not by cunningly seeking it himself,

but by the gift that Christ bestows.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] The Venetian edition reads *hoc si qui jussit, debitum* (“if someone has ordered this, [it is] due”).]

He is foolish who wishes

to put himself before the Church;

for to receive a sacred office

must be a divine election.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] One Vatican manuscript reads *qui ipse se* (“who himself”).]

The wise priest Hilary

did not seek the rank;

Martin avoided it;

Gregory scarcely endured it.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] The Venetian and Paris editions read *Charus sacerdos* (“the dear priest”).]

The laws reject ambition;

every usurper is driven away.

What civil tribunals reject,

let the Church avoid as sacrilege.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] One Vatican manuscript reads *vitat nefas* (“avoids sacrilege”).]

[Col. 0081D] These contests were wicked,

although not over his own see;

an evil mind neither desires to endure it

nor imposes it.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] One Vatican manuscript reads *maligna erunt* (“the contests will be wicked”).]

Nor do they remain longer

in this murmuring dispute:

while they are thinking of succeeding,

the priest who had been there returns.

[Col. 0082A] At the prayer of the people,

while no one believes it,

he is suddenly restored.

The joys that follow

the sorrows are all the greater.

[Note: [Col. 0082D] One Vatican manuscript reads *post tristia* (“after the sorrows”).]

[Col. 0082B] The city applauded,

for which happiness had returned.

In anxious grief, deprived of him

and mourning the one it had lost,

it received its father back.

The man whom it scarcely thought restored,

his wish forestalled by favorable success—

when the extraordinary event is seen,

sight itself is accustomed to be astonished.

The rector gathers the flock;

he receives it, caught by error;

once the shepherd’s stronghold is recognized,

the sheepfolds rejoice.

[Note: [Col. 0082D] In the Venetian edition the following stanza is read:

“The rector gathers the flock,

the path having been led astray by error.

Recognizing the shepherd’s voice,

the sheepfolds rejoiced.”]

[Note: [Col. 0082D] In one Vatican manuscript and in the Paris edition, the second line of the stanza reads: “Captivated by the error of the path”; in the margin of the same Paris edition: “He drives error from the path.”]

At the time when he had taken his rank,

on that very day he returned.

Who would not declare that this

had happened by a heavenly gift?

Never before had the people received

so great a benefit, when he was appointed;

[Col. 0082C] nor did it rejoice so greatly then

as when it received its bishop.

Come, citizens, applaud,

and add vows to vows,

so that the things wrought as miracles

may endure together with heavenly things.

May Christ, with serene light,

hover around the man whom he restored,

so that grace may increase threefold

in reward, life, and glory.

Let everyone who does not begrudge God

resound with a hymn as he sings:

his praise belongs to the one who

draws the bishop back from death’s jaws.

[Col. 0082D] With a faithful heart aflame,

I am not ashamed to speak such truths:

these small verses we offer

to Leontius, the most noble pope.

## CHAPTER XVII. To Placidina, mother of Leontius, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0083C] Was she formerly the wife of Leontius, and is she here called his mother because of her outstanding affection and exceptional virtue toward Leontius? Or, more probably, has the name “mother” intruded in place of “sister”? Certainly Browerus denies that the word “mother” appears in the manuscript of Saint Gall. It is also absent from the Vatican manuscripts.]

[Col. 0083A] [Note: [Col. 0083A] Fortunatus sends Placidina some small gifts from the island where he lived, and relates that, while sailing against the north wind, he was driven back to the shore and landed at Placidina’s own place.]

Kindly accept these very small gifts, I pray,

for you yourself shine more fittingly as a gift in the world.

That the island might give these things to you

from the midst of the waves,

the Ocean, with swollen murmuring,

offers its waters.

[Note: [Col. 0083C] One Vatican manuscript reads *ut haec daret* (“so that it might give these things”).]

[Note: [Col. 0083C] The Venetian edition reads:

“The Ocean then offers its swelling waters with a murmur.”

Two Vatican manuscripts read: “offers its swelling waters.” The Paris edition reads: “The Ocean, swollen with murmuring, pressed the waters,” with *tumidas* (“swelling”) in the margin.]

While I hurried to visit those places of the sea,

a raging wave drove me back,

coming from the north wind.

Yet, so that your prosperity might prove itself complete,

it offered on land

what had been sought in the waters.

[Note: [Col. 0083C] See what I said in the *Life of Fortunatus*, section 79.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Bissonum [Bissonnum], a villa near Bordeaux.

[Col. 0083B] [Note: [Col. 0083B] He describes the pleasantness of Bissonum, a villa situated in the Bordeaux countryside, and also mentions the buildings that had collapsed through age and that Leontius had restored and embellished.]

There is a place, although the heat is burning

in the summer season,

where the renewed field remains continually green

with flowers.

The meadows, painted in saffron colors,

breathe out their fragrance,

and the sweeter grass is scented

with its fragrant tresses.

The inhabitant calls this place Bissonum

after its ancient name;

the city of Bordeaux is seven miles distant.

There the loving owner established

a pleasing country residence,

and a portico equal in length

extends on three sides.

[Note: [Col. 0083C] Sidonius Apollinaris, poem 22, describes the villa of Pontius Leontius, called Burgus, situated on the Garonne on the bank of the Dronne, or Dordogne. This villa, judging from its situation and description, as well as from the elegance of its buildings and the convenience of its baths, seems certainly to be one of those which Fortunatus records in this poem and the two following ones, although under a different name. Read that entire poem.]

[Note: [Col. 0083D] The name *praetoria* was given to costly and magnificent houses built in the countryside, perhaps because their size and construction seemed to equal public buildings or palaces. Suetonius, in *The Life of Caligula*, chapter 37, says: “In constructing praetoria and villas, setting every other consideration aside, he desired nothing so much as what was said to be impossible to accomplish.”]

Age had itself laid it upon the ground,

and its graceful form had lost its appearance.

Leontius’ work restores it by a better method,

so that, while he is present,

no ruin oppresses the house.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *haec meliore* (“this by a better [method]”).]

[Note: [Col. 0083D] The Paris edition reads *domos* (“houses”).]

[Col. 0083C] Now too it rises again more prosperously,

like a buried palace,

and, brought back to life,

it favors its restorer.

[Col. 0084A] Meanwhile he restored the baths

to their ancient elegance,

so that the gentle baths

refresh weary men.

Here, they say, wolves had been nourished,

occupying the deserted place;

here he brought in men

and drove out the wild beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0084C] The Venetian edition reads *intulit huc* (“brought here”); *huc* is absent from one Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0084C] The Paris edition reads *inde* (“from there”).]

[Note: [Col. 0083D] In one Vatican manuscript this poem is found mutilated, as is poem 20; the entire following poem is missing.]

## CHAPTER XIX. On Vereginis, a villa near Bordeaux.

[Note: [Col. 0084A] He celebrates the situation and description of Vereginis, also located in the Bordeaux countryside, and the buildings restored by Leontius.]

Amid the fertile abundance

through which the Garonne’s waters flow,

a pleasant field blossoms

on the banks of Vereginis.

Here a short ascent rises gently

upon a slight embankment,

and the traveler follows a winding road

along the sloping mass.

It rises higher than the level plains,

but is lower than the lofty heights;

neither excessively humble

nor boastfully elevated is its summit.

[Note: [Col. 0084C] One Vatican manuscript reads *nec humilis* (“not humble”).]

[Col. 0084B] A house is agreeably seated

in the middle of the hill;

one side of it lies downward here,

while the other swells upward there.

A lofty structure of the house

is suspended on a triple arch,

where you would think the painted waters

of the sea were running.

A hidden stream leaps forth,

born from living metal,

and sweet, perpetual water

flows from the irrigating spring.

Sitting above it, the master celebrates banquets,

and, with fish swimming

in the enclosed pool,

he drinks.

[Note: [Col. 0084C] It was customary among the ancients to build country houses near rivers, so that they might enjoy both the pleasantness of the countryside and the broad view over the fields, as well as fishing. Among many other examples, this may be understood from Sidonius, who, in poem 22, describing the villa called Burgus, says:

“Do you turn to the left? A spacious portico receives you,

curved along straight paths, where at the upper edge

it hangs out, and a forest of stone stands

between compressed columns.

Here a lofty dining room opens through revolving doors;

nearby an artificial channel, and water falls from above.

Before the doors, with a pool hanging there,

and following the spring, swimming fish

find their watery dining rooms.”

Fortunatus likewise, in book 10, poem 9, describing the villa of King Childebert, son of Sigibert, says among other things:

“Finally, while kings preside in the seats of the palace

and honor festive banquets with the service of the table,

the salmon is seen being lifted from the net by the wickerwork.

And, sitting in the citadel, he counts the fish.

The king rejoices while the immense fish leaps from the water,

and refreshes his spirit because his own prey has arrived.”]

Now it has come to be renewed

at the expense of Pope Leontius,

whom the house, cultivated for so long,

desires as its master.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] One Vatican manuscript reads *nunc removenda* (“now to be removed”).]

[Note: [Col. 0084D] The Paris edition reads: “Which the master desires, cultivated for a long time.”]

## CHAPTER XX. On Praemiacum, a villa near Bordeaux.

[Note: [Col. 0084B] As Fortunatus passes Praemiacum, the villa of Leontius, on his journey, he celebrates its situation and beauty in a poem and declares that Leontius enlarged and embellished it with buildings.]

[Col. 0084C] Although the journey presses on,

and cares draw me back by their weight,

as I bring a few verses to you,

I bend my course toward you.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Browerus first published: “and may the volume turn back my cares”; later he published: “and may I be drawn back by the turning volume of care.” Either reading may be preferred; the sense is complete. The Vatican manuscripts favor the first reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0084D] One Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition read: “With a poem I bend the road.”]

[Col. 0085A] Captivated by love of you,

I shall never be silent about what deserves remembrance;

nor shall I pass you by

while passing through the place.

When I speak fitting things of it, if the fourth syllable is elided,

mighty Praemiacum,

you bear a name rich in rewards.

The countryside is filled with delights

in its green fields,

and natural grace belongs

to the rural landscape.

Where the house has been established,

a level swelling rises upward,

nor does the summit command

with an excessively raised crest.

Above it lies a place sloping down

toward the river.

The flowering meadows shine

with jeweled grass.

Whenever the East Wind gently blows upon them,

the bending grass ripples

with its upturned tresses.

On the other side, grain grows yellow

with ears of corn,

and the heavy vine shades

the nourishing soil.

The water of the Garonne

does not lack countless fish;

though the fields may lack produce,

it abounds in waters.

[Note: [Col. 0085C] One Vatican manuscript reads *Garonnae* (“of the Garonne”).]

But these great gifts were seeking you, Leontius:

you alone were absent,

the one who could make the blessings complete.

For because the beautiful house

and pleasing baths shine,

they have sung of you

as their restorer.

Yet, so that they may still acquire

the beauty of what must be built,

may you govern these gifts of yours

for many years.

[Note: [Col. 0085C] In one Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition, the preceding line reads: “Yet, nevertheless, may they acquire.”]

## CHAPTER XXI. On the river Egircius.

[Note: [Col. 0085B] He describes the character and changing conditions of the river Egircius.]

Perhaps your praise, noble Garonne,

would have been less

if another did not possess

such scanty waters.

For Egircius slips along here

in a thinned-out stream,

and displays your riches

from its impoverished spring.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] The Paris edition reads *generosa* (“noble” in the feminine form).]

[Note: [Col. 0085D] The Venetian edition reads *profert* (“brings forth”) rather than *praefert* (“displays”). Egircius, Browerus says, washes the city of the Ausci, the most distinguished people of Aquitania, now the metropolis of Novempopulania, or Gascony.]

[Col. 0085C] Finally, if anyone compares

the two with one another,

here, where it becomes a stream,

you, I think, will be the Nile.

It enters you as your servant,

but your realm restrains it here;

you flow as the Gallic Euphrates,

while this one lies hidden.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Browerus observes that it was almost invariably Fortunatus’ practice to treat the letter *h* as a strong consonant, so that it did not disappear and also prevented elision. Bede, he says, noticed this in his discussion of elision in poetry, when he writes that it lies within the poet’s discretion whether *h* serves as the sign of a consonant or of aspiration, especially when the following word begins with that letter. Similar examples occur frequently in other poets, but it would be superfluous to include them here. I will merely note that in the couplet inscribed on the Vatican cross, which Justin the Younger and the empress Sophia sent as a gift to the city of Rome, and which the learned Stephen Borgia, secretary of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, illuminated, the letter *h* is likewise treated as a consonant:

“The wood by which Christ subjected the human enemy …”]

For as much as you, swollen in your courses,

increase the Ocean,

so much does this river enable your waters

to grow.

[Note: [Col. 0086C] The Paris edition reads: “This one lifts you up with its own waters.”]

Especially when burning summer

lies upon the lands,

and the sad field gasps

with thirsty soil,

when the sun, with burning rays,

scorches the fields,

and heat splits the earth

with a fiery plow.

[Col. 0086A] Fleeing languidly,

it scarcely unfolds its dry waters,

and, with its fish,

it itself struggles at the same time.

With the river withdrawn,

it licks the empty sands,

and, an exile in its own bed,

wanders in its proper waters.

As the lake migrates,

the river is consumed in the mud,

and the land becomes sterile

where the water had raged.

All relief fails

under the parching heat;

sad and sick,

it lacks even its own name.

Perhaps the traveler, walking along the road,

finds no draught

with which to refresh himself,

for he himself is thirsty.

The river longs to be poured into itself,

if you offer waters—

if indeed it is a river

that a man makes wet.

As it rolls or rubs along, a wheel traces marks on the sand impressed by the stream,

and its track stops the waters that seep out.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The manuscript reads *lambens* (“licking/rubbing”) for *labens* (“gliding”); the Paris edition reads *habenas* (“reins”) rather than *arenas* (“sands”).]

[Col. 0086B] If you come riding along the road

during the season of Cancer,

the horse’s hoof scarcely sinks,

though the stream lies in wait.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The Paris edition reads *diem* (“day”); in the margin, *viam* (“road”).]

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The Venetian edition reads “although the hoof lies in wait.” One Vatican manuscript reads “although the hoof sits down.”]

We saw a tiny fish rise

from the mud,

and, held fast by the mire,

wander shipwrecked over the earth.

There is neither river nor field,

neither land nor water;

no one can plow

land unfit for fish.

Only a frog, swimming in the marsh,

utters complaining murmurs;

with the fish excluded,

a foreigner reigns in the waters.

But if by chance a thin rain

should flow from the clouds,

scarcely has it rained on the earth

when this river already swells menacingly.

It recovers immense strength

from a small cloud:

the lake that it had been before

suddenly becomes a sea.

Advancing turbidly,

it itself needs to be washed

by its own waters;

always unequal,

it has either nothing or too much.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The Venetian edition reads *qui nihil* (“which has nothing”).]

[Col. 0086C] Not content with its banks,

it hastens along shortened courses,

and vomits over the full fields

what it drank from the mountain.

It is swept away in a rushing whirlpool,

as though at the death of a tyrant;

angry at the route,

it ravages the gifts of the fields.

The crop runs into the river,

but the fish stands in the field;

in reversed order,

the harvest lies swimming.

[Note: [Col. 0086C] The manuscript reads *sed* (“but”) for *stat* (“stands”).]

[Note: [Col. 0086D] Browerus later corrected the reading, which he had printed twice as “in the field,” to *sufficiens in arvo* (“sufficient in the field”), as it appears in the Venetian edition. I have found no similar correction in the Vatican manuscripts.]

The pastures that had belonged to sheep

are given to frogs;

fish occupy the meadows,

and the water drags along the flock.

The expelled catfish occupies

the country stable,

and more fish are caught on land

than just now in the water.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The Venetian edition reads: “The country stable contains the expelled catfish.” The Paris edition reads *silvestre silurus* (“the wild catfish”).]

[Note: [Col. 0086D] One Vatican manuscript reads “the pasture for oars.”]

[Col. 0087A] Unlucky nets disturb

the fields that hoes would dig;

the branch is fixed here

where the marsh had previously stood.

[Note: [Col. 0087A] One Vatican manuscript reads *male retia* (“bad nets”).]

[Note: [Col. 0087A] The Venetian edition reads “the hook is fixed here.” One Vatican manuscript has *banus*, corruptly; perhaps *hamus* (“hook”) should be read.]

The fish has one fate,

whether the rivers dry up

or grow:

now it sits in the mud,

now it lies exiled in the field.

But why do we speak so long

of the sad little whirlpool?

It burns from words

and is not refreshed by waters.

[Col. 0088A] Let it be enough for itself to burn;

why do I add vapors?

And why do I make the summer season

grow twice as long?

But at last we offer this single consolation of praise:

that the river, emptied of its waters,

has bestowed fish.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0087]

## CHAPTER I. On the cross of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0087C] We have already indicated in the *Life of Fortunatus*, section 55, what cause and occasion led him to compose these hymns and other poems in honor of the holy cross. Nevertheless, it is useful to touch briefly upon the matter here as well. Radegund, a religious woman born of the royal family of the Thuringians and formerly the wife of Clotaire, king of the Franks—a woman who had rendered the greatest services to our Fortunatus—had obtained from the emperor Justin and the empress Sophia a fragment of the wood of the holy cross, with which she enriched her monastery at Poitiers, later famous for its miracles. This, then, was the reason why Fortunatus, devoted above all to Radegund and to Abbess Agnes, often composed poems celebrating the excellence and power of the holy cross.]

[Col. 0087A] [Note: [Col. 0087B] He praises the dignity and power of the Lord’s cross.]

[Col. 0087B] The blessed cross shines,

on which the Lord hung in the flesh,

and with his own blood

washes away our wounds.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] This hymn is also found in Cardinal Tommasi’s hymnary under Fortunatus’ name. One Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition read “washed away our wounds.” The same reading occurs in Tommasi’s hymnary.]

Gentle in devoted love,

he became a victim for us;

the sacred Lamb drew the sheep

from the wolf’s mouth.

When, with his palms pierced through,

he redeemed the world from destruction

and closed the path of death

with his own death,

[Note: [Col. 0087D] The Venetian edition reads *transfixus palmis* (“pierced through in the palms”); Tommasi’s hymnary omits *a* (“from”) in *a clade* (“from destruction”).]

this was the hand fixed

by bloody nails:

the hand that rescued Paul

from sin and Peter from death.

Powerful in fruitfulness,

O sweet and noble wood,

what new fruits you bear

upon your branches!

By your new fragrance

dead corpses rise,

and those who lacked the light

return to life.

[Col. 0087C] No heat will burn anyone

beneath the foliage of this tree;

neither moon by night

nor sun at midday.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Tommasi’s hymnary reads “neither moon by night.”]

You shine, planted beside

the course of the waters,

and you scatter your adorned tresses

with fresh blossom.

A vine hangs between your arms,

from which sweet wines

flow with a blood-red hue.

## CHAPTER II. Hymn in honor of the holy cross.

[Col. 0088A]

[Note: [Col. 0087D] It is pleasant to append here the judgment of the most learned Jacob Sirmond on this hymn, which he gives in his notes on book 4, letter 3, of the letters of Sidonius: “A certain scholiast had noted at this place that the hymn mentioned there—namely, the one Sidonius mentions in his letter to Claudian—was the hymn whose opening is: ‘Sing, tongue, the battle of the glorious struggle.’ Indeed, it has a more polished style than is usually found in Fortunatus, to whom, nevertheless, ancient writers and manuscripts also attribute it. Moreover, everything praised by Sidonius fits it admirably. It is written in trochaic verses, with occasional pyrrhic feet inserted; it is commatic, cut into frequent and well-suited cola, with its sentences not broken off but falling smoothly with the verse. Finally, this poem is claimed for Claudian not only by the old scholiast whom I have mentioned, but also by Gennadius—not as it is printed, but as it is read in the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Michael at Tumba, where the account of Claudian is fuller than in the published text, in these words: ‘He also wrote several other works, among them a hymn on the Passion of the Lord, whose beginning is: “Sing, tongue, the battle of the glorious.” He was the brother of Mamertus, bishop of Vienne.’”

This is the judgment of the distinguished Sirmond. The authors of the *Histoire littéraire de la France* likewise take this poem away from Fortunatus and attribute it to the same Claudian. Yet nearly all earlier antiquity favors Fortunatus, as does the authority of almost all the manuscripts and of very many learned men. In the hymnary of the distinguished Tommasi it is found under this title: “Of Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers.” Likewise, in the Vatican manuscripts it is attributed to Venantius.]

Sing, tongue, the battle

of the glorious struggle,

and tell upon the trophy of the cross

the noble triumph:

how the world’s Redeemer,

sacrificed, conquered.

Grieving over the deception

of the first-created parent,

when by the bite of the poisonous fruit

he fell into death,

he himself then marked the wood,

so that he might undo

the damage caused by the wood.

[Note: [Col. 0088D] Tommasi’s hymnary and one Vatican manuscript read “grieving over the fraud by which he was made.” Tommasi’s hymnary reads *tunc* (“then”) for *tum* (“then/at that point”).]

The order of our salvation

demanded this work:

that by the art of the many-shaped betrayer

he might outwit his art,

and bring healing from the place

from which the enemy had wounded us.

[Note: [Col. 0088D] One Vatican manuscript reads “the art of the many-shaped destroyer.”]

When, therefore, the fullness

of the sacred time arrived,

the Creator of the world,

born from the Father’s citadel,

was sent forth and appeared,

made flesh in the Virgin’s womb.

The infant cries,

enclosed in the narrow manger;

the virgin mother binds

his limbs in swaddling cloths,

and a band tightly wraps

his feet, hands, and legs.

[Note: [Col. 0088D] Tommasi’s hymnary reads “and hands, feet, and legs.” Two Vatican manuscripts read “and the band paints his feet and hands.”]

[Col. 0088C] When six lustrums had already passed,

and the time appointed for the body was fulfilled,

born for this purpose by his own will,

he gave himself to suffering:

the Lamb is lifted up

to be sacrificed on the cross.

Here vinegar, gall, reed, spittle,

nails, and spear

pierce his gentle body;

blood and water flow forth.

By that stream the earth, sea, stars,

and world are washed.

[Col. 0089A] Faithful cross, among all trees

the one noble tree,

no forest produces one like you

in flower, foliage, or bud.

[Note: [Col. 0089B] One Vatican manuscript reads *germinat* (“it buds”).]

Sweet wood, bearing sweet nails

and sustaining the sweet weight.

[Note: [Col. 0089B] One Vatican manuscript reads “sweet nail”; another reads “bearing the sweet nail.”]

Bend your branches, lofty tree;

relax your stretched limbs,

and let that stiffness soften

which your nature gave you,

so that upon your gentle trunk

you may extend the limbs

of the heavenly King.

You alone were worthy

to bear the price of the age [manuscript: *saecli pretium*]

and to prepare a harbor

for the shipwrecked world,

which the sacred blood poured out

from the Lamb’s body anointed.

## CHAPTER III. In honor of the holy cross and the church building of the oratory at Tours.

[Note: [Col. 0089B] The title of this poem in the Venetian edition reads: “In honor of the holy cross, or of the oratory,” and likewise in two Vatican manuscripts. Gregory of Tours mentions this oratory in book 1 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 15, saying: “At the city of Tours, while we were placing the relics of the forerunner himself in the oratory of the court of blessed Martin … they say that oil boils forth from a lamp in this oratory.” Relics of the holy cross are also kept there.]

[Note: [Col. 0089A] He celebrates the power and worth of the Lord’s cross, and commends Gregory of Tours’ devotion to that same cross, as well as his generosity and liberality in adorning the oratory at Tours.]

The lofty power of the cross

rightly occupies the whole world,

for it restores all things

that the world had lost.

[Note: [Col. 0089C] The Venetian edition reads “and now the things of the world”; the Paris edition reads “when these things,” with “because” in the margin.]

Whatever the savage serpent infected

with the gall of poison,

Christ’s blood washes clean

with sweet fluid upon this cross.

The sheep that had been prey

for the fierce, ravaging wolf

the Virgin’s Lamb restores

upon the cross.

Stretched upon these branches,

with arms outspread, hanging there,

he himself, hanging upon the cross,

establishes the Church.

In this wood the devout one restores

what had long been lost—

what the fruit of the forbidden, good tree

had taken away.

Moreover, a flame of virtues

shines forth in addition:

the cross itself prepares gifts

through its acts of devotion.

Finally, Gregory offers these temples

to the holy cross,

while he covers the palls,

bearing the signs of the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0089C] The Paris edition reads “this work.” The Venetian edition reads “while he covers the palls.” One Vatican manuscript reads “while the pall covers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0089C–0090B] Browerus struggles greatly to explain this extremely obscure passage. Nevertheless, he tends to believe that by the verse “while he covers the palls, bearing the signs of the cross,” the poem indicates either the cloths with which the miraculous cloth brought from Jerusalem had been covered, or the temple itself which Gregory had erected in its honor and memory, in which it had been deposited and, as it were, covered and enclosed. He thinks that this temple, or oratory, was dedicated by Gregory before he was made bishop of Tours. Thus God, he believes, adorned Gregory’s piety and devotion in decorating the cross through the construction of this new work, with an episcopal pallium into which purple crosses had been woven. The following verses would explain this:

“Christ’s divine power suddenly gave gifts;

and soon the fulfillment of the pious wish followed.

For he deserved the palls, beautiful cloths

woven with the cross,

and the gracious cross has crosses

for its acts of devotion;

silks that are *agnava* among snowy

purple-colored fabrics,

and the work is magnified

with woven crosses.”

But, if I may offer a conjecture about this extremely obscure matter—though I submit the whole question entirely to the judgment of learned men and leave it to them to decide—it seems that Gregory of Tours offered and dedicated his oratory at Tours in honor of the holy cross, or, if it had already been dedicated, enlarged and adorned it with new gifts. Accordingly, I would understand the verse “while he covers the palls, bearing the signs of the cross” as follows: by *pallae* are meant the cloth hangings with which the walls of churches were customarily decorated and covered. Gregory of Tours mentions such cloths in book 1 of *The Miracles of Saint Julian*, chapter 20, where he relates that a thief entered the basilica of Saint Julian at night and plundered it. “He tore down,” he says, “from the height a cross flashing with gems and threw it to the ground; then, gathering the little veils and small cloths hanging around the walls, he made one bundle of them.” It therefore seems that Gregory adorned the walls of that oratory at Tours with such veils and small cloths, painted and interwoven with textile crosses and other designs for appearance and decoration. I believe this is indicated, though somewhat obscurely, by the verse cited above.]

while he covers the palls,

bearing the signs of the cross.

[Col. 0090B] Christ’s divine power suddenly gave gifts,

and soon the fulfillment of the pious wish followed.

For he deserved the palls,

beautiful cloths woven with the cross,

and the gracious cross has crosses

for its acts of devotion.

[Col. 0090C] As for what follows:

“Christ’s divine power suddenly gave gifts,”

I prefer to refer it not to the archiepiscopal pallium, as Browerus and others with him think, but to the silken cloth which Gregory testifies, in book 1 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 6, that he received from a certain stranger. The stranger claimed that this cloth had wrapped the Lord’s cross at Jerusalem. Since it had shone with so many miracles, it was certainly worthy of answering Gregory’s pious wishes in adorning the oratory at Tours in honor of the holy cross; and these would be the gifts which Christ’s divine power gave. Indeed, the following verses seem to confirm the same point, where Fortunatus says:

“Thus quickly devoted goodwill gave this to the bishop,

and the consecrated coverings dedicated to the cross are pleasing.

Therefore, by this saving sign, illustrious priest,

he to whom this was pleasing is able to return great gifts to you.”

I do not see how these words can suitably be referred or adapted to an archiepiscopal pallium. Nothing seems more likely than that this silken cloth was decorated and interwoven with textile crosses for the purpose for which it had served, and that those crosses were mingled in both purple and white. This appears to be indicated by the following verse:

“Silks that are *agnava* among snowy purple fabrics.”

Although this verse is extremely obscure, chiefly because the true meaning of the word *agnava* is unknown, I do not approve Browerus’ view that *agnava* is used for the Greek word ἄγναφα. That word is plainly Greek and, so far as I know, is not customary among Latin writers; nor does the sense attached to it suit this passage at all. For ἄγναφα means “not cleansed at all by the fuller.” I would therefore prefer to read *addita* (“added”), unless I feared imposing too much force upon the word.]

[Col. 0091A] Silks, *agnava* [*agnina*], purple cloths

with snow-white threads,

[Note: [Col. 0091D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “Silks adorned with purple-colored fabrics.”]

[Note: [Col. 0091D] *Blattea* is derived from *blatta*, the name of the worm with which purple was dyed; later it came to be used for purple itself or for the color purple.]

and the work is magnified

with woven crosses.

Thus quickly this devoted goodwill

gave these things to the bishop,

and the consecrated coverings dedicated

to the cross are pleasing.

[Note: [Col. 0092D] Three Vatican manuscripts and both the Venetian and Paris editions read “the conscious cloths.”]

Therefore, by this saving sign,

illustrious priest,

he to whom this was pleasing

is able to return great gifts to you.

## CHAPTER IV. Likewise on the sign of the holy cross.

[Col. 0091]

[Note: [Col. 0091D] For the sake of easing the reader’s labor, it seemed worthwhile to set out here the solution of this acrostic, in case anyone should wish to read it quickly without stumbling over the individual letters, although from the structure above one may admire the poet’s industry and skill in beginning this poem, weaving its parts together suitably like the threads of a loom, and coloring it, as it were, into the arrangement and structure of a single fabric. Here, then, is the acrostic resolved:]

[Col. 0091D] The divine summit, fashioning the generative organs

from the flesh of moist earth,

joins the clay with life-giving blood.

There the light-bringer flows over the living airs;

Adam is formed, laboring in the likeness of his Maker.

The first-created man sprang forth,

a noble being whose use was confined to the soil,

rich in free choice and radiant with light;

then from Adam’s limbs

a vessel is made of the virgin Eve.

[Col. 0092D] Created from the man’s flesh,

she is then joined to him,

so that they might rejoice well

in the paradisal garden.

But a rash throat drove him

from the holy seat,

when, at the serpent’s persuasion,

he offered the dark juice of the fruit.

From there hunger came upon

death that could not be satisfied.

For this reason, “*Gavisurus ob hoc coeli fluis arce locator*”:
“about to rejoice because of this, you flow, O dweller in heaven’s citadel”
[the compressed syntax and relation of *fluis* are uncertain; the source does not say that he “comes down”].

You pity us by being born for us,

and by the wound of the nail

you are fastened to the cross.

With such a remedy applied,

one salvation comes to us

through the wood and the Lamb’s blood.

Joyful is the sight:

upon you the devout arms of Christ

stood fastened,

and upon this saving cross

dear flesh bore merciless punishments

by its draught.

Sweet tree of the field,

with you new life is prepared.

Chosen in appearance,

and beautiful in the order of the cross,

you are carried as light, hope,

and shield against the blow of malice.

Immortal glory,

by the death of the righteous

you prepared joy.

Thus your single cross

watered all life,

with a devout bloody rain;

to sailors you give a harbor;

you cleansed the sad wounds

with the submerged nail.

Sweet tree of the field,

dripping nectar from your bark,

from whose branches life-giving ointments

give off their fragrance;

excellent in cultivation,

divine in origin,

shining in fruit,

delightful as food,

and sweet in the shade of your fruits.

Behold, you gleam as the noble sign

of the great King;

a wall and weapon for men,

strength, light, and altar in prayer.

Open, kind and life-giving,

the way and fertile light;

then, mindful of us,

bring aid from David’s offspring,

when the judge fixed upon the cross

shall rule the world.

The verse formed from the first letters of the individual lines is:

[Col. 0094A] “Sweet glory of the sign, way of heaven, life of the redeemed.”

The verse formed from the final letters of the individual lines is:

“On the cross Christ’s death healed the dead things of the world.”

The verses that describe a cross in the middle are:

“Pious cross, cover devoted Agnes together with Radegund;

you, holy cross, protect fragile Fortunatus;

true hope for us in the wood, in the Lamb’s blood, in the nail,

sweet tree of the field, with you new life is prepared.”

[Note: [Col. 0094A] Observe that each line consists of thirty-five letters, which is also the number of verses composing the entire poem. This acrostic, like those that follow, was absent from the common editions and is also absent from the Vatican manuscripts. Father Browerus copied it and first published it from the manuscript codices of Saint Gall and Trier.]

## CHAPTER V. On the holy cross.

[Col. 0093]

[Col. 0093D] Browerus likewise first published this acrostic from the manuscript codices of Saint Gall and Trier. Here, too, is its solution:

This pardon-granting sign,

by God’s lot or ordinance (*sorte Dei*),

draws rustic praises to be rendered

with living breath.

“In me, who governs the going of pliable clay, O Divinity—

portion of living beings, blessed care of healing,

remover of guilt, outpoured Trinity, Creator,

whose honor, light, law, glory, and kingdoms are coeternal—

by the merit of faith you piously make Abraham great.”

[The printed sequence *In me, qui regit ire lutum plasmabile …* is syntactically compressed and its exact attachment is uncertain; this literal rendering retains its terms rather than reconstructing a smoother prose sentence.]

[Col. 0094D] Thus [are] the Father and the Begotten;

thus the one Holy Spirit.

The verses placed along the sides are:

“Rescue believers, glory of faith,

weapons of salvation;

through your gift, Christ,

the cause of guilt is removed.”

The verses that describe a cross in the middle are:

Sweet to me, O pious one, is the wood, greater in fragrance than rosebushes;

wooded hills, you have produced the wood of honor,

the cross enriching God’s temples and adorning the veil.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Holy Cross

[Col. 0095A]

## CHAPTER VII. Hymn in Honor of the Holy Cross

[Col. 0095C]

The banners of the King advance;

the mystery of the cross shines forth,

on which the creator of flesh,

having taken flesh, was suspended on the gallows.

His flesh pierced by nails,

stretching out his hands and feet,

for the sake of redemption:

here the victim was sacrificed.

[Note: One Vatican codex has *confixus clavis*, “fastened with nails.”]

[Note: One Vatican codex reads *et sanguine*, “and with blood,” in place of *unda sanguine*, “a stream with blood.”]

Upon it he was wounded,

moreover, by the cruel point

of the lance,

so that he might wash us from guilt;

a stream flowed with blood.

[Note: The same codex has *quod vulneratus*, “because he was wounded.”]

[Note: The same codex has *dire lanceae*, “of the cruel lance.”]

What David sang

in his faithful song

has been fulfilled,

when he said: “Among the nations

God reigned

from the wood.”

[Note: The hymn of the distinguished Thomas has *David fidelis carmine*, “David, in faithful song”; two Vatican codices read *dicendo nationibus*, “saying to the nations.”]

[Note: These words, “God reigned from the wood,” are read in Psalm 95 according to the Septuagint version, a reading followed by most Latin Fathers. In the Vatican and Alexandrian codices, however, they are absent, and only *ὅτι Κύριος ἐβασίλευσε*—“for the Lord reigned”—is read.]

A beautiful and radiant tree,

adorned with the King’s purple,

chosen with worthy trunk

to touch such holy limbs.

Blessed is the tree whose arms

held the ransom of the world;

it was made the balance of the body

and carried off the spoil of Tartarus.

[Note: One codex has “and carried off the spoil.”]

From your bark you pour forth fragrance;

you surpass nectar in savor;

delightful in fruitful yield,

you rejoice in noble triumph.

[Note: The Venetian edition has “you rejoice in noble triumph.” One Vatican codex, incorrectly, has “you rejoice in noble triumph.”]

[Note: One Vatican codex has “you pour forth fragrance from the bark.”]

[Note: One Vatican codex has “you surpass the savor of nectar.” The same reading occurs in the hymn of the distinguished Thomas Browerus. Browerus nevertheless states that this reading is rejected by the manuscript codices, while the reading followed here is approved. “There is no doubt,” he says, “that Fortunatus wrote *vincis sapore nectare*, so that *membra in cortice* and *nectare* may correspond.” One Vatican manuscript likewise reads: “you surpass nectar in savor.”]

Hail, altar; hail, victim,

glory of the Passion,

through which life endured death

and by death restored life.

[Note: One Vatican codex reads *quia vita*, “because life,” in place of *qua vita*, “through which life.”]

[Note: The hymn cited above has “of the victim of the Passion.” At the end is added “O hail, cross, our only hope,” as it appears in the commonly used hymn of the cross.]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Holy Baptism

[Note: This hymn, or rhythmical poem, was published by the distinguished Edmund Martene in *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book I, chapter 1, article 18, section 9, taken from the pontifical of the Church of Poitiers, from the year 800. He considers it to be by Fortunatus; anyone who has observed its affinity and similarity to Fortunatus’ style will readily agree. It is now published for the first time together with the other works of Fortunatus.]

To you be perpetual praise, author

and consecrator of baptism,

who by the lot of the Passion

give the reward of salvation.

The bright and nourishing night,

more than the moon, sun, and stars,

you who are the crown of lights,

restore the day through shadow. To you.

Sweet, consecrated, gentle,

chosen, pure, beautiful,

dripping with the honey of honor,

watering with fragrant chrism. To you.

In it the Redeemer of the world

comes forth alive from death,

and those whom the chain had bound,

once buried, he releases. To you.

Christ opened it

for the salvation of the nations;

through its health-giving care,

the renewed creature returns. To you.

Come, therefore, worthy ones,

to the grace of the washing,

so that, refreshed by the fountain,

you may shine like lambs. To you.

This is the pool that cleanses faithful minds with its liquid.

While the body sweats with dew,

the water wipes away sins. To you.

Rejoice, candidates for baptism,

chosen vessels of the kingdom,

buried together in death,

reborn through the faith of Christ. To you.

## CHAPTER IX. In Praise of Chrism

[Col. 0097C]

[Note: The fact that the hymn given above, which the Church uses in the preparation of sacred chrism, is a product of Fortunatus is indicated by a ritual codex of the Church of Besançon, written in the eleventh century and preserved in the archive of the cathedral church of Velletri. It is found there under this title: “Verses of Fortunatus in praise of chrism”; its style, moreover, is very closely related to Fortunatus’ style. The distinguished Joan Chrysostomus Trombellius published it in volume II of his treatise *On the Sacraments*, p. 235, in the Appendix, together with the following notes.]

[Col. 0097D]

Verse 1. In some codices and printed books this hymn, or rhythmical poem, begins with the verse: “Hear, judge of the dead, who sing together.” Ritual of Besançon, Bologna Codex, Pontifical of Brother Alberto Castellani, and others.

Verse 2. “The one hope of believers.” Pontifical of Innocent VIII.

Verse 3. “Of those bringing forth.” Ritual of Besançon, Bologna Codex, Pontifical of Castellani, edition of 1743.

Verse 4. “The gift, the reward of peace.” Besançon Ritual, Bologna Codex, Pontifical of Innocent VIII. But the Bologna Codex has “the reward of the Lord of peace.” I think it refers to the olive branches with which the crowd famously met Christ the Lord as he entered Jerusalem before his Passion. Consult the prayers that the priest sings on Palm Sunday, at the blessing of the palms and olive branches—that is, the prayers beginning with these words: “We ask, Lord”; “O God, who scattered”; “O God, who by a wonderful ordering”; “O God, who through the olive branch announced to the earth, by the dove, peace,” and so forth.

Verse 11. “Standing humbly on the ground before the altar.” Pontifical of Innocent VIII. But the Bologna Codex has “humbly upon the ground.” I prefer this reading to the others, and suspect that the common reading, “humbly below,” derives from it. “He stands at the altar” occurs in the Besançon Ritual. On *infulatus*, “wearing the mitre,” consult what Ducange reports under *infula* and *infulatus* in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*.

Verse 13. “May he complete.” Brixen Pontifical, thirteenth or fourteenth century.

Verse 15. “To preserve.” Pontifical of 1572. “This living sign of the olive.” Bologna Codex and Pontifical of Innocent VIII. I prefer the common reading. The Brixen Pontifical has: “This living sign of the olive.”

Verse 18. “Against the rights of demons.” Pontifical of Innocent VIII.

Verse 20. “And may the wounded woman be healed,” Bologna Codex; “may she be cured,” Brixen Pontifical.

Verse 23. These verses are absent from the Bologna Codex: “Washed in mind . . . they flee . . . Anointed . . . flow in.”]

Take up, O Redeemer,

the song of those singing together on high.

Hear, judge of the dead, the one hope of mortals;

hear the voices of those bringing forth

the gift that goes before peace. O Redeemer.

A tree, fruitful with nourishing light,

produced this thing to be consecrated;

this present prostrate crowd offers it,

O Savior of the world. O Redeemer.

Standing humbly at the altar,

the mitred bishop

fulfills every obligation

with consecrated chrism. O Redeemer.

Deign to consecrate,

eternal King of your homeland,

this olive oil, a living sign

against the powers of demons. O Redeemer.

So that every sex may be renewed

by the anointing of chrism,

so that the wounded glory

of dignity may be healed. O Redeemer.

Washed in mind by the sacred font,

sins are driven away;

anointed at the font, the holy

chrism flows in. O Redeemer.

Born from the Father’s heart,

filling the Virgin’s womb,

grant light, close death

to those who share in chrism. O Redeemer.

May this day be festive for us

through age after age;

may it be consecrated and worthy of praise,

and never grow old with time. O Redeemer.

## CHAPTER X. Hymn on Saint Dionysius

[Note: The abbot Hilduin had mentioned this hymn in his letter to Emperor Louis the Pious, preserved by Surius under October 9, in these words: “A contemporary of Gregory of Tours, and a most learned man, Fortunatus, who had often written much to him, composed for this most glorious martyr a most beautiful hymn in rhythmical composition, in which he recalls that he was sent by Saint Clement, as he learned from the pages of the Latins,” and so forth. Jacobus Dubletius first published this hymn in book I of his *Antiquities*, from which others took it, including the editors of the works of Saint Denis, Venetian edition of 1756. It is also found in P. Lorenzo Cozza’s *Apologetic Vindications*, published at Rome in 1702. Joan Launoy, however, in his dissertation *On the Two Dionysiuses*, chapter 18, denies that this hymn is by Fortunatus, but does not establish the point. I have therefore not hesitated to publish it under Fortunatus’ name, especially since its style, the best witness, supports this attribution.]

Let the people resound in heart and voice

the strong and faithful soldier,

Dionysius the martyr,

who followed the Prince of heaven.

Sent from Rome

by Bishop Clement,

he came

to be the fruit of the seed

of the heavenly Word

for Gaul.

He builds a sacred work

and teaches the faith of baptism;

but the blindness of his hearers

rejects the gift of the seed.

When the holy bishop pressed on

to free the people from error,

while offering the hope of salvation,

he fell into the torments of death.

He is seized by the pagans,

pleasing to Christ’s altars;

for love of such great glory

he willingly undergoes punishment.

The one thing that was lacking to him:

he surrendered his neck for the King;

he revealed the love of his heart

when his head was cut off.

A great priest, who used to give

the sacred gifts of the temple,

with blessed blood poured out,

he himself became the victim.

Happy is the punishment

that offered the palm through a pious wound!

You who crush death by death,

now you possess the kingdoms of heaven.

Glory to God the Father,

glory to the Only-Begotten,

together with the Holy Spirit,

through everlasting ages.

## CHAPTER XI. On Lord Saturninus

[Note: Gregory of Tours says that Saint Saturninus was established as bishop of Toulouse in the consulship of Decius and Gratus, that is, in the year 250; the distinguished Ruinart also confirms this with his own support, on the basis of the Acts of Saturninus themselves, which he considers genuine. The same Gregory of Tours, in book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 48, contradicting himself, reports that the martyr Saturninus, ordained by disciples of the apostles, was sent to the city of Toulouse; yet he plainly shows that he is following popular opinion by inserting the words “as it is said.”]

[Col. 0099B]

[Note: He describes the martyrdom of Saint Saturninus, the first bishop of Toulouse, and the miraculous power of his tomb.]

The lofty gate of heaven opens,

while the earth knocks,

and receives its children,

whom the soil brought forth.

This is a wondrous occasion of salvation:

that from his own death

they may purchase the rewards of light.

For Saturninus, desiring to bind himself to Christ,

did not wish to remain long

in bodily form.

Longing to dissolve [variant: *dissolvi*, “to be dissolved”] the bonds

of the bodily prison,

so that the human being might join himself

more fully to the Lord,

when the mature time had come

and hope was already grown,

his blessed vows received

their promised reward.

While he enjoyed the priesthood

in the city of Toulouse,

and proclaimed to the people

that Christ is God,

demonstrating it in words

and adding miracles in deeds,

so that the work might fulfill

what speech had given,

he snatched pagan souls

from the tyrant’s jaws

and subjected them to the King

who had given him his weapons.

But the people, corrupted by evils

and infected with poisons,

fleeing healing

and wishing to lie sick,

the sick-minded crowd seized the man,

led him to the Capitol,

and gave his physician

many wounds in return.

[Note: One Vatican codex has *comprehendit*, “seized.”]

Returning treachery for piety,

poisons for honey,

it wages wicked war

against its protector.

[Note: In the Venetian edition, the four verses following this line are missing.]

It binds the holy man

to the feet and tracks of an untamed bull

[Note: The Paris edition reads *ad*, “to,” in place of *et*, “and.”],

and goads it,

lest the beast’s flight become slow.

[Note: Gregory of Tours describes the martyrdom of Saint Saturninus in book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 48: “He was bound, at the instigation of the pagans, to the feet of a maddened bull, hurled down the steps of the Capitol, and ended his present life with the structure of his skull scattered.” Sidonius sings of him as follows in book IX, letter 16:

“Among these, let the first hymn sing to me

of him who held the see of Toulouse,

hurled down from the highest steps

of the Capitol.

The raging crowd bound him

because he denied Jupiter and Minerva

and confessed the good of Christ’s cross,

to the side of an unyoked bull,

so that, driven through the steep places

by the maddened ox,

it might scatter the mangled corpse,

the warm brain-pulp loosening

and staining the rocks.”]

O most evil mind of men,

new beast of a dreadful monster!

You know how to add

the savagery of raging nature;

what it does not know by itself

it rages to do when you goad it.

[Note: One Vatican codex has “what it does not know by itself, when you goad it, it does.”]

Bloody, guilty crowd,

you destroy yourself by wounding him;

and if you will not spare him,

learn to spare yourself.

[Note: The Paris edition has “you reveal yourself”; its margin has “you destroy yourself.”]

This savage beast, unrestrained,

soon dragged him through winding byways

and scattered throughout the city

the limbs of the holy man.

[Note: Vatican codices and the Venetian edition have “from there the savage beast.”]

Then a woman, rejoicing,

gathered up and buried his remains,

with one maidservant alone

sharing the task with her.

[Note: Two Vatican codices have “one, but a maidservant.” One manuscript has *miracula*, “miracles,” rather than *participante sibi*, “sharing the task with her.”]

This was the reason

for snatching the distinguished crown;

thus celebrated, the glory

of martyrdom shines.

[Note: The Paris edition has “thus to be celebrated.”]

Before the holy man’s tomb

gifts of salvation are now given,

and the lacerated body

restores many bodies.

Tell me, where do you lie,

hostile death? Where do you rest,

vanquished,

when you see vows being offered

at the death of the saint?

[Note: The Paris edition has “which,” rather than “who.”]

The one whose salvation you wrongly thought

to end by death

gives life to many

and keeps his own life.

Here you lie captive,

you who thought you would reign;

you perish by attacking

and kill yourself in your fury.

Your own punishment weighs upon you;

your own savage bonds torment you.

The groans you wish to inflict,

you groan yourself as you endure them.

The martyr, rejoicing,

holds the heavens;

but you, livid and sorrowful death,

hostile to yourself,

inhabit the black Tartarus.

Now the blessed one remains forever

in a flower-bearing seat,

among fragrant choirs

where burning incense is offered.

[Note: The supplied variant reads *thura adoletque*, “and he burns incense.”]

[Note: The Paris edition has “among adored choirs”; its margin has “among fragrant choirs.”]

He fears no charges

before the judge now reconciled;

as a victorious soldier,

he seeks the rewards he must receive.

The worthy palm that awaits him

will follow the triumphant man:

to die for you, Christ,

is glory, life, and rest.

## CHAPTER XII. On Launebode, Who Built the Church of Saint Saturninus

[Note: He declares his zeal for adorning and celebrating the deeds of the holy martyrs. He describes the martyrdom of Saint Saturninus. He commends Launebodes, the duke who built a basilica in his memory at the place where he had been bound by the barbarians, as well as Launebodes’ wife Berethrud, who was generous toward the same basilica. He also commemorates the other virtues of this most devout woman.]

Let the hearts of others resound

with human praises;

but let it be my task

to commemorate the just.

[Note: The Paris edition reads *licet*, “may it be permitted,” in place of *vacet*, “may it be my task.”]

For the work of piety—

to weave the deeds of victors into books—

my mind urges me to undertake,

and the matter is doubly justified.

First, because it is fitting

to acknowledge great things as great;

for whoever conceals good deeds

will be guilty of wrongdoing.

The second reason urges me

because success is loved,

and whoever reads of his own deeds

desires better things.

For the martyr Saturninus

is revered throughout the world,

and the blessed palm

of the excellent man is not hidden.

When he had hastened

from the city of Rome to Toulouse,

carrying the pious seeds

of the Christian field,

then the mad throng seized

the friend of the Lord,

and arranged for the limbs

of the holy man to be dragged

and worn away.

He hung entangled

by the hind foot of a bull;

dragged sideways,

he died torn apart.

By this means

he sent his soul from earth

to Olympus.

O happy man,

by whose funeral death itself dies!

But that place where the saint

had taken on his bonds

had not been supported

by the honor of any temple.

For after many ages,

while Launebodes was exercising

the office of duke,

he built a sacred roof

over the place.

What no one coming

from the Roman people had built,

this man accomplished

with barbarian offspring.

[Note: From this, Browerus conjectures that Launebodes was of Gothic origin, since it was not customary for Fortunatus to call the Gauls, who at that time were masters, barbarians; rather, he calls them Romans.]

Together with his own wife Berethrud,

illustrious in beauty,

whose gentle heart

shines even more brightly,

he added adornment

to his noble lineage

from the stock of powerful men,

by honoring God.

[Note: Perhaps the reading is *proprio Berethrudes*, “with his own Berethrud.” Gregory of Tours mentions this Berethrud in book IX of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 35; her death seems to belong to the fourteenth year of Childebert’s reign, or the year 589. Gregory reports there that, when she was dying, “she appointed her daughter as heir, leaving something either to the convents of women which she herself had founded, or to the churches and basilicas of the holy confessors”—matters that agree very well with Fortunatus’ praises of her.]

With her own hands

she provides fitting nourishment,

giving to the poor

and desiring to satisfy them.

Untiring, she seeks

the hope [variant: faith] of Christ at the churches,

constantly hastening

to the work of piety.

The Paris edition has “untiring among the needy.”

She clothes the naked,

offers cups to the thirsty,

and, as a woman,

fills herself more fully

from the eternal fountain.

Whatever she does

also benefits her husband,

for whose salvation

she anxiously offers prayers.

The duke, who excels

among his people in abundant merits,

is lofty everywhere,

shining through the power of his nobility.

But although he holds

a high summit of lineage,

he himself enlarged

the greatness of his ancestors

through his character.

Therefore, may they remain joined

through the ages by equal devotion,

and may a strengthened love

shine for them both.

## CHAPTER XIII. To the Clergy of Paris

[Col. 0102A]

[Note: He declares that he has long since grown unaccustomed to writing poems. Nevertheless, challenged to do so, he composes this poem in praise of the clergy of Paris, commending their orderliness and skill in continual psalmody. Above all, he praises the faith and piety of Germanus, bishop of Paris, as well as his pastoral diligence and concern in governing the Church.]

Honor and dignity of the illustrious order,

fathers whom I revere in heart,

faith, and religion,

you who long ago caused me,

forgetful and unused to the plectrum of poetry,

to renew my ancient lyre.

You spur [variant: *simulastis*, “you prompted”] my dull fingers

to touch the strings [the supplied text has a damaged opening bracket before *chordas*],

although my hand no longer runs

in its accustomed art.

Now my tongue, rough with rust,

makes words resound,

and a hoarse crash emerges

from my unpolished mouth.

The whetstone will scarcely give sharpness

to old rust,

nor will color shine

in bronze stained by smoke.

But because sweetness,

striking like a hammer,

presses upon me,

and like care rubbed against an anvil

wears me down,

you kindle the furnace

of my heart and breast,

from which heat is supplied

in the citadel of my heart.

Therefore I obey,

since your love, as though I had been

reforged in a furnace,

has compelled me to the work of art.

The lofty reverence

of the powerful clergy of Paris,

the glory, gift, and honor

of the Church’s genius.

[Note: *Ecclesiae genium* means “the genius of the Church”; the printed editions wrongly use *genium* for *ingenium*, “talent” or “genius,” as Browerus observes in his note on this passage.]

Singing divine poems

in David’s song,

it continually turns over

the sweet work in its courses.

[Note: The Paris edition has “you turn over.”]

From this side are priests;

from that, the Levitical order shines.

Canities covers the former,

a beautiful stole the latter.

Pallor belongs to the former;

on the faces of the latter

a blush wanders.

And lilies gleam,

mingled with radiant roses.

The former are already white with age,

and the latter too are well whitened

by their garments,

so that the painted crown

may please the supreme God.

In the midst stands Germanus,

the bishop in his honor,

who rules the young on one side

and raises up the old on the other.

[Note: Saint Germanus died in 576, as Gregory of Tours establishes in book V, chapter 8; this poem was therefore written before that year.]

[Note: One Vatican codex and the Paris edition have “subdues the old on the other.”]

The Levites go before;

the solemn order of singers [the supplied alternate is *canentum*] follows.

As they walk, he moves some;

as he directs, he leads others.

Yet he himself advances gently,

like another Aaron,

shining not through clothing

but pleasing through piety.

No gems, scarlet, tiara (*cidaris*),

gold, purple, or fine linen

adorn his shoulders;

holy faith shines instead.

[Note: Hugo Menardus, in his notes on the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Pope*, emends this verse as follows: “No gems, saffron, bright gold, purple, or fine linen,” from an ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. In that manuscript *cidar.* is written, but *clar.* is superimposed over it, with *cidar* struck through as an error. From *clar.* he reports that he formed *clarum*. The Paris edition has *cidarion*.]

This priest is far better

than the priest of the ancient law,

because he practices what was true

and what was previously only shadow.

Thinking of all future things as great,

he rejects all present things,

already lacking in flesh

before the flesh collapses at the end.

Concerned lest the anger of wolves

devour anyone,

the excellent shepherd gathers

the sheep into the folds.

Called by continual warnings

to the salty pastures,

the flock recognizes the voice

and runs after it lovingly.

[Note: The common reading is “safe pastures,” as also in the Venetian edition and one Vatican codex. Browerus says, however, that the Treves manuscript showed the genuine reading, adding the gloss: “You are the salt of the earth.”]

Swift as a soldier to arms,

as soon as the signal rings in its ears,

it raises its limbs

from its shaken bed of sleep.

[Note: Fortunatus relates in the *Life of Saint Germanus*, chapter 12, that Germanus continually exercised himself in vigils and consequently weakened himself through prolonged fasting. His old age spent whole nights in the cold, enduring a double winter: the cold of age and of the season, which even well-fed young men could scarcely endure.]

He flies before the others,

seeking the sacred mysteries;

each person hastens from every side

to the churches assigned to him.

With burning zeal

he waters the whole people of the household,

and they urge one another,

each asking who can be first to go.

[Note: The Paris edition has “the whole household.”]

Joining sleepless nights

to the first dawn,

the reverent crowd builds

angelic choirs.

Steadfast, with vigorous steps,

in the venerable work,

it moves its weapons in song,

as though it would force heaven.

Weaving the threads of the psalter

with lyric melody,

it draws out with love

the song begun in verses.

[Note: Here Fortunatus beautifully compares the thin voices of boys to small organ pipes, and the deeper voices of old men to trumpets; when these were mingled, the sweetest harmony sounded in the ears. Expressing this same harmony, which used to be employed in psalmody, Fortunatus says elsewhere, in book III, chapter 6:

“Behold, the clergy resounds in choirs, and the people in chorus;

each sings your vow with whatever art he knows.”

Browerus observes in his notes on this passage that boys were customarily trained for this purpose, singing according to the ancient practice of the Church. He gathers this from many sources, namely the Fourth Council of Toledo, the Council of Aachen under Louis the Pious, and the *Life of Gregory the Great* by John the Deacon, book II, chapter 6. He adds that Victor, in book III of *The Vandal Persecution*, seems to have called such boys *infantuli*, “little children”; he celebrates them, together with the readers, among those confessors who, after being exiled at Carthage with the rest of the clergy, later gained the palm of martyrdom.]

Here a boy adjusts

the instruments to small pipes;

then an old man

bursts from his mouth

with a broad trumpet.

[Note: One Vatican codex has “from the mouth of an old man.”]

Cymbal-like voices mingle

with the sharp reeds,

and the pipe sounds sweetly

with unequal melodies.

The boy’s flute soothes

the hoarse drums of the old men,

and the melodious words of the people

restore the lyre.

One melody draws gently;

another carries eagerly;

thus the work varies

according to sex and age.

Christ’s burning threshing floor

grinds wheat-like grains,

when indeed it builds

the storehouses of God.

Recalling the Creator’s voice—

that those whom the Lord sees watching

when he himself returns

are blessed—

what great lights lie hidden

under the covering of the body

in their merits, mind,

virtue, and faith!

At the bishop’s admonitions

the clergy, people, and child sing psalms,

so that from this brief labor

a harvest may be gathered.

Under Germanus as leader

this is a happy army:

Moses, stretch out your hands

and help your camp.

[Note: One Vatican codex and the Paris edition have *Moyses*, “Moses.” Fortunatus relates in the *Life of Saint Germanus*, chapter 7, that when Germanus entered the house of a man named Ebro, Anna, the wife of that man, exclaimed that she saw something marvelous. When her husband asked what she saw, she replied: “Behold, blessed Germanus seems to me to be walking with a horned face. I can scarcely bear either to look upon the holy man with my eyes or to speak of him, radiant in a new manner with horns.” Fortunatus adds that the woman, terrified, wondered whether she had been able to see a man of her own time in the form of Moses. Fortunatus appears to allude to this event here, as Browerus also observed, concluding the poem as follows: “Moses, stretch out your hands and help your camp.” The Paris edition has “help your camp” in the subjunctive; its margin has the imperative reading.]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Church of Paris

[Note: He celebrates the Parisian basilica dedicated in honor of the holy cross and elevates its praises above the Temple of Solomon. He commends King Childebert’s generosity and zeal toward this basilica.]

If the structure of Solomon’s temple

is recalled,

although this one may equal it in workmanship,

it surpasses it in faith.

For whatever was once enclosed there

under the veil of the old law

is here opened and visible.

[Note: One Vatican codex has “here opened things please.”]

That temple flourished,

interwoven with varied metal;

this one shines more brightly,

dyed with Christ’s blood.

[Note: In the *Life of Saint Droctoveus*, where this verse is preserved, it reads: “This one shines, dyed and radiant with Christ’s blood.” One Vatican codex has “this one shines more brightly with Christ’s blood”; the Paris edition has “dyed with blood.”]

Gold, stones, and cedar woods

adorned the former;

in this one the more venerable honor

of the cross shines forth.

The old one stood,

built upon a wealth destined to fall;

this house stands firm,

solidified by the price of the world.

A splendid hall rises

on marble columns,

and because it remains pure,

greater grace is present in it.

[Note: An anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Droctoveus*, apparently flourishing in the ninth century, describes the beginnings and structure of this basilica in sections 8–10.
