When King Childebert, together with Chlothar, had led an army into Spain and besieged Zaragoza, the city’s inhabitants, distrusting human resources and wishing to drive calamity from themselves and their homes through religion, began to carry the tunic of Saint Vincent, martyr of Zaragoza, around the walls, imploring his protection against the enemy in a public procession. Struck by this spectacle, and learning what was happening, the enemy reported the matter to Childebert. He immediately judged that the army should withdraw, lest he be forced to fight against the powers above. He therefore departed, accepting from the citizens the tunic of Saint Vincent as a gift. When he had brought it to Paris, he arranged for a basilica to be built as quickly as possible in the saint’s honor. Later, after defeating Amalaric, king of the Goths in Spain, he carried from Toledo a golden cross encircled with precious gems and brought it into Saint Vincent’s basilica. From that time the title “basilica of the Holy Cross” adhered to it. It is now called Saint-Germain, in the Paris suburb, because the ashes of Saint Germanus were buried there.

The same author gives us the following description of the basilica in section 10. Since it can contribute considerable light toward explaining Fortunatus’ poem, his words are transcribed here:

“Therefore, by the grace of the life-giving cross, he decided to build in the form of a cross the church of the most holy martyr, where Childebert had deposited the cross together with other most precious ornaments. It seems superfluous to describe the marvelous work of this basilica: how it was distinguished by windows, supported by columns of the most precious marble, adorned with a vaulted ceiling and gilded coffers, and how the walls, as befitted Christ’s hall, shone with paintings of golden color, while the floor below was laid with a beautiful mosaic. The roof of the basilica itself, splendidly covered with gilded copper and bronze, reflected the sun’s rays and glittered with such fiery brilliance that it struck back the eyes of those who looked upon it with excessive brightness. Thus, because of its extraordinary beauty, the house was not unjustly called by the people, metaphorically, the gilded hall of Germanus.” The same author then produces Fortunatus’ poem as further confirmation of what he has related.

Adrian Valesius, however, in his treatise against Launoy on the basilicas of Gaul, argues that the Parisian basilica discussed here by Fortunatus was not the basilica of Saint Vincent. He maintains that the latter is always designated by the name of Saint Vincent or of the Holy Cross, rather than simply by the name “Parisian church.” “What is said here about the Holy Cross,” he says, “can suitably apply to any other basilica in which the honor and worship of the cross flourish and which can truly be said to shine with the price of redemption, Christ’s blood, distinguishing it from Solomon’s temple.” Fortunatus, he continues, speaks of a church built by Childebert and given to the people of Paris, whereas Saint Vincent’s basilica, situated outside Paris in the suburbs, was given not so much to the people as to monks, who performed the divine service there. Childebert, although he built and enriched Saint Vincent’s basilica, nevertheless, in the seventeenth year of his reign—if the royal charter may be trusted—granted certain properties to the Parisian church to increase its resources. Thus Fortunatus could truthfully be said to have increased that basilica’s wealth. Finally, Valesius cites as supporters of his opinion Jacobus Brolus and Joannes Tilius, who believe that Childebert built the Parisian church.

Yet I do not see how we can easily deny that this basilica was dedicated to the Holy Cross under that title and with that worship, since Fortunatus here repeatedly derives its honor and value from the cross. It is especially uncertain that Childebert built the greater Parisian church, whereas the basilica later called the Holy Cross certainly was built by him. I would therefore rather say either that this basilica of Saint Vincent was at least designated by Fortunatus under the name “Parisian church,” because of its fame and size, or that it was so designated to distinguish it from the basilica of the Holy Cross at Poitiers. The fact that it is called by that title does not prove that it was not Saint Vincent’s basilica. Nor does it matter that Childebert handed it over to monks so that they might perform the divine service there, since the people were not thereby excluded from entering or using it.]

At the front, with glass-eyed windows,

it receives the rays

and, by the craftsman’s hand [variant: *manus*, “hands”],

shuts the day within its citadel.

The wandering light

of dawn fills the ceilings,

and with its own rays

it shines even without the sun.

[Note: One Vatican codex has “with the chariots of Aurora.” The Paris edition has “and here, without the sun, it shines.”]

This church King Childebert first,

with exceptional love,

gave imperishable gifts

to his people.

[Note: One Vatican codex has: “Here the pious and excellent King Childebert”; another has “here, pious.” Childebert was the brother of Chlothar and son of Clovis. Fortunatus praises him highly in the *Life of Saint Germanus*, bishop of Paris, chapter 13, commending his piety, his ardent concern for relieving the poverty of the poor, and his care for ecclesiastical discipline. Numerous monuments testify to his zeal and generosity in building, adorning, and enriching churches and to his reverence for priests. Valesius says in book VIII of his *History of the Franks* that it would be difficult to find anyone whose piety and concern for the highest affairs of the Church had been demonstrated by more numerous and greater proofs than Childebert’s. It should therefore not seem strange that Fortunatus calls him Melchizedek, that is, both king and priest, since he combined royal dignity with priestly vigilance and zeal for sacred matters. Childebert was buried in the same basilica of Saint Vincent, as Gregory of Tours reports in book IV of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 20. See further concerning his tomb in the appendix to Gregory of Tours’ works, where the rule of the abbots of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris is discussed.]

Entirely devoted

to divine worship,

he continually increased

the resources of the Church.

[Note: In the *Life of Saint Droctoveus*, at whose conclusion this poem is preserved, the verse reads: “Entirely clinging to divine worship.”]

Our Melchizedek,

rightly both king and priest,

as a layman fulfilled

the work of religion.

Ruling public laws

and guarding lofty palaces,

he was a unique glory

and a model for bishops.

Departing from here,

he lives there in the honor of his merits;

here too he will remain eternal

through the praise of his deeds.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Baptistery of Mainz

[Note: He celebrates the baptistery built by Sidonius, bishop of Mainz, with Berthoara, daughter of King Theodebert, contributing greatly to the undertaking. On this occasion he sings several things about Adam’s sin and the power of baptism in accordance with the teaching of the Church. Finally, he adds praises of Berthoara herself and of her father Theodebert.]

[Col. 0106A]

The lofty hall of sacred baptism shines,

where Christ washes Adam’s sins

in the stream.

Here, with God as shepherd,

the flock is immersed in pure waters,

lest the sheep bear stained fleeces for long.

The source derived death from the seed, but the Father of the world

cleansed the crimes of death with healing waters.

Nevertheless, Bishop Sidonius [Note: [Col. 0106D] There survives in book IX, chapter 9, a poem of Fortunatus addressed to this Sidonius, bishop of Mainz, in which his piety and generosity toward the poor are highly praised. His zeal in restoring churches lying ruined amid the wreckage of Mainz is shown by these verses: “Renewing ancient churches, upheld by splendid adornment.”] raised this fortress,

who, by renewing the churches, fosters the worship of the Lord.

The priest built it, fulfilling Berthoara’s vow [Note: [Col. 0106D] Theodebert had two wives, Deuteria and Wisigard. Deuteria threw her own daughter—whom she had probably borne by another man before marrying Theodebert—into a torrent from a bridge, lest the king, attracted by the girl’s beauty, should someday seek her in marriage. Having repudiated Deuteria, Theodebert married Wisigard, to whom he had previously been betrothed; Berthoara, of whom this passage speaks, seems to have been born to him by her.],

she who pleases as the Church’s adornment through the love of her heart.

**[Col. 0106B]** The splendor of the Catholic faith, flashing with devotion,

she is a worshiper of temples and lavish toward the poor.

**[Col. 0107A]** She sows, so that she may reap harvests, storing them by scattering them [the Paris edition: “by restraining herself”].

She prepares, through earthly riches, what will not die.

A daughter worthy of her father, reforming you, Theodebert,

you who ruled your country with a father’s devotion [Note: [Col. 0107C] Gregory of Tours splendidly praises Theodebert, *History of the Franks*, book III, chapter 25: “He governed the kingdom with justice, honored priests, endowed churches, relieved the poor, and generously bestowed many pious and most gracious benefits upon many. He mercifully remitted all the tribute which churches situated in Auvergne paid to his treasury.” Yet in *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17, Gregory does not conceal his faults.].

And, with faith accompanying you, you brought back triumphs from the enemy [Note: The same Theodebert was ennobled by numerous victories and was exceptionally fortunate in conducting wars. Perhaps Venantius refers here to the campaign in which Theodebert himself was sent by his father Theoderic against the Goths. After the death of Clovis, the Goths reclaimed many things they had lost during his reign; defeated and overcome by Theodebert, and threatened with an even greater disaster unless they yielded, they voluntarily submitted to his authority, as Gregory of Tours relates, *History of the Franks*, book III, chapter 21],

but soon the captives returned after paying your price.

Supporter of the Church, glory of the kingdom [Note: In the Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition, “glory of kings.” In one Vatican manuscript, “glory of kingdoms,” evidently for “of kings”],

shepherd of the needy,

care of priests, ready for every good deed.

No one says that he has groaned beneath his gentle yoke;

you still live, O king, in the love earned by your merits.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Basilica of Saint George

[Note: [Col. 0107A] This poem mentions the basilica of the martyr Saint George, likewise built by Bishop Sidonius, and commends the martyr’s glory and his celebrated memory in the West.]

**[Col. 0107B]** The shining hall of the outstanding martyr George glitters in its strength [Note: [Col. 0107D] Saint George is said to have suffered in the year 284, in which year the Alexandrian, or Paschal, Chronicle says that he suffered under the consuls Carinus II and Numerianus. Others prefer the reign of Decius. See Ruinart’s notes to Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 101],

whose lofty honor is spread throughout this world.

In prison, slaughter, hunger, chains, thirst, cold, and flames,

having confessed Christ, he led his head to the stars.

He who, powerful in virtue, was buried in the eastern quarter,

behold, beneath the western sky, he offers aid.

Therefore remember to pray and to return gifts, traveler [one Vatican manuscript: “vows, traveler”];

here devout faith obtains by his merits what it seeks.

Bishop Sidonius decently founded these works;

may the new temples benefit his soul.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Oratory of Trasaricus [Trisaricus, Trasericus]

[Note: [Col. 0107B] This poem treats of a church, or oratory, dedicated by Trasaricus in honor of Saints Peter and Paul, Saint Martin of Tours, and Saint Remedius.]

The gleaming thresholds of the transparent temple shone,

where venerable faith embraces an unquestionable hope [one Vatican manuscript: “which receives”].

This is Peter’s hall, he who chains the heavens with a key;

and the sea stood firm like stone where he walked [the Venetian edition: “Pelagius”; one Vatican manuscript: “the lakes where he walked over the sea”].

Paul dwells in these seats, the one trumpet for the nations;

he who was formerly a persecutor remains here now a herald.

It is Martin’s house, who clothes Christ in the needy,

covering the King as a recruit, and, as a man, God by right.

Behold, the hall of the holy priest Remedius shines [Note: [Col. 0107D] Saint Remedius is the same as Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims. Among others, Hincmar, his successor in the see of Rheims in the ninth century, wrote his Life. Saint Remigius died in 533, after occupying the see for about seventy years. See below his Life, written by Fortunatus.],

he who abandoned the world’s darkness and possesses the stars.

Excellent worshiper of God, Trasaricus [Note: [Col. 0107D] Ennodius, in his *Panegyric of King Theoderic*, mentions a Trasaricus who was king of the Gepids and held Sirmium, capital of Pannonia, before being defeated by Theoderic, king of Italy. From this one may conjecture the nation of the Trasaricus mentioned here by Fortunatus. The Paris edition always reads *Trasaicus*.], you dedicated this temple;

the one to whom you pay these offerings returns riches to his lover [one Vatican manuscript: “will return”].

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Saints of Agaunum

[Note: [Col. 0108C]

Saint Maurice and his companions, called soldiers of the Felix, or Theban, Legion, suffered martyrdom in the year 286 under Maximian. Their martyrdom, described by Saint Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, was published by the distinguished Ruinart among the *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 274, Amsterdam edition, 1713, from the Wetstein press. They were called Agaunenses from the place where they suffered. At Agaunum, a town in the Alps near the banks of the Rhône, they confessed Christ and were crowned with martyrdom, when Maximian, having summoned that legion there in order to suppress the revolt and efforts of the Bagaudae in Gaul, was campaigning in the region. Sigismund, king of Burgundy, arranged for a basilica to be built at Agaunum in memory of the martyrs and established a monastery of monks who sang psalms continually, around the year 516, as may be read in Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book III, chapter 5. He confirms the same in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 75.

Saint Eucherius describes the situation of Agaunum as follows: “Acaunus is situated about sixty miles from the city of Geneva, and is fourteen miles distant from the head of Lake Geneva, into which the Rhône flows. The place itself is now situated in a valley among the Alpine ridges; for those traveling toward it, a rough and narrow road opens through a difficult passage . . . Once the defiles have been conquered and crossed, suddenly a broad, though not extensive, plain opens among the mountain crags, in which the holy legion had taken its position.”]

[lacuna]

**[Col. 0108B]** [Note: [Col. 0108B] In this poem Fortunatus sings of the triumph of Saint Maurice and his companions.]

When the wicked persecuted [one Vatican manuscript: “were persecuting”] the Christians

amid the world’s storm, and savage turmoil delivered Christ’s worshipers to death,

after driving away the cold and setting hearts aflame,

fervent faith waged war upon the icy crags.

There, pious Maurice, commander of the mighty legion [one Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition: “with the teacher of the legion”],

you led brave men to submit their necks.

They laid down their swords and armed themselves with Paul’s doctrines [one Vatican manuscript: “had armed themselves”; the Paris edition reads: “With their swords laid down, their weapons were the teaching of Paul”],

for it was sweeter to die in Christ’s name.

Those who, with warlike hearts, could conquer by the sword

offered their beloved throats to wounds.

Urging one another onward through their own slaughter [the Paris edition: “through their own killing”] to go to the stars,

one hero swam in the blood of another [the Paris edition: “of his lord”].

**[Col. 0109A]** A fountain of blood aided the rushing waters of the Rhône [the Venetian edition reads, with correction, “heard”],

and bloody wrath stained the Alpine snows [the Venetian edition: “dragged along”].

With such an end the blessed army entered the heavens

and, joined to the apostolic choirs, rejoices in honor.

The holy army is surrounded above the blessed stars

by an angelic senate [one Vatican manuscript has the corrupt reading: “The holy army is surrounded by an angelic senate of blessed stars”; the Paris edition is also corrupt: “Virtue, clothed in a robe, is surrounded by a senate”].

Where death once was, light now cherishes the men.

Behold, most mighty commander [the same edition: “most mighty teacher”], with you

four holy pledges of leaders lie here [Note: [Col. 0109C] Three principal commanders, or prefects, of this most holy legion are counted: Maurice, Exuperius, and Candidus. Maurice was *primicerius* of the same legion, a rank next to that of military tribune. Exuperius was its standard-bearer; and Candidus was a military senator, as Eucherius relates in the same place. Victor, who is commonly counted fourth, was neither prefect nor soldier of that legion, but a veteran soldier of another legion. When he happened to pass by the place where Maximian’s soldiers were joyfully feasting on the martyrs’ spoils, he refused their invitation to eat with them. Recognized as a Christian, he was killed there] [Note: [Col. 0109C] Sacred relics of the Agaunensian saints were also preserved in the basilica at Tours, which Gregory of Tours says had been restored in the apse, *History of the Franks*, book X, chapter 31. Fortunatus may perhaps be thought to have celebrated them in this poem because of the close relationship between himself and Gregory of Tours.]

Beneath a yellow mound a heavenly treasure lies hidden,

and common sand covers God’s riches.

They cause the sacred treasury of paradise to increase;

they have been given as the Lord’s heirs in everlasting light.

That choir, with flesh, is to be placed upon the starry throne;

when the Judge comes, it will be the arbiter of the world.

Thus the devout multitude together, hastening to behold Christ,

made a road to heaven from death.

Therefore, through the radiant gifts of the Thunderer,

I, Fortunatus, beg you to bring aid, lest I be tormented in darkness.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Saint Hilary

[Note: [Col. 0109B] In this poem he praises Saint Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, for his steadfast defense against the Arians of the Catholic doctrine concerning the divinity of the Son, and for enduring exile on its behalf.]

If you seek to know who Hilary is [one Vatican manuscript: “who he is”], reader,

the Allobroges [Note: [Col. 0109D] The Allobroges were peoples who lived on this side of the Rhône, toward Mount Lure and Lake Geneva, as Browerus reports. They are often used as a name for the Gauls] declare that he was born at Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0109D] Fortunatus also says elsewhere in his poems that Saint Hilary was born at Poitiers. Thus, in book VIII, chapter 1, speaking of himself, he says:

“Dwelling at Poitiers, where Saint Hilary once

was born in the city, the Father known throughout the world.”

See also Jerome, in the preface to *Paula and Eustochium*, and book II of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians].”

When the priest governed the people with divine understanding,

he carefully kept the covenant of the law.

When the wicked man saw the peoples being divided by error,

he brought the poison of the Greeks into the midst [two Vatican manuscripts: “and the men of the Greeks”].

Those who always bring forth poisons from a viperous heart

say that the Son of God is a creature [one Vatican manuscript: “so that they say: He is a creature.” Fortunatus, in order to express the Arians’ perverse doctrine concerning the Son of God, disregards metrical rules and shortens the first *a* in *creatura*. Browerus rightly observes that Fabricius wrongly substitutes *genitura* for *creatura* so that the meter may stand, although that word reflects the opinion of the Arians no more than that of the Catholics. Indeed, Fortunatus himself shortly afterward says:

“The worldly wisdom gives them [the Arians] greater aid,

which denies that God, begotten from the Unbegotten, is God.”

The Arians wished, as Sulpicius Severus says, *History*, book II, that the new and other Lord had been made from nothing into a new and separate substance, and that there had been a time when the Son did not exist].

For them worldly wisdom provides greater aid,

which denies that God, begotten from the Unbegotten, is God.

When the unhappy Arius rashly embraced this doctrine, wishing to trample upon the prophets,

he burst apart while holding it [Note: Evidently with his entrails spilling out as he evacuated himself, as is well known].

An outstanding teacher, following the records of the ancients,

whom Stephen saw, proves that he is God.

Bound by love of God, despising the prince of the world [Note: This was Constantius, son of Constantine the Great and supporter of the Arians. Under him Saint Hilary was driven into exile and banished to Phrygia, as Sulpicius relates, *History*, book II],

his undefiled faith endured exile.

In the Father, who is almighty God, he teaches us to recognize the Son,

and expresses this only in divine words [one Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition: “in the Father, who is powerful”; another Vatican manuscript, corrected: “in the Father, each God mighty”].

He teaches in twelve books that Christ is everlasting light,

and Lord and God [Note: Saint Jerome, in letter 83, addressed to Magnus, an orator of the city of Rome, writes of Hilary: “Hilary, confessor of my times and bishop, imitated the twelve books of Quintilian both in style and in number”].

## CHAPTER XX. On Saint Medard, Bishop

[Note: [Col. 0110D] Saint Medard was made Bishop of Vermandois, as Fortunatus expressly teaches in his *Life*, section 9. Later he transferred the episcopal see to Noyon, as related in his *Life*, written by Radbod, Bishop of Noyon and Tournai, which appears third among the materials published by the Bollandists for 8 June; the reason for the transfer is described there at length.]

[Note: [Col. 0110B] In this poem he celebrates the holiness of the life of Saint Medard, Bishop of Noyon, and his flight from the world. He also recounts the miracles by which his piety had become renowned. Finally, he commemorates the basilica begun in his memory by Chlothar and completed by Sigibert.]

Among the worshipers of Christ whom their deeds have carried to the stars [three Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition: “among the stars”; the Bollandists: “into the breezes”],

a great portion, Medard, is open to you according to your merits.

You lived as a stranger upon earthly shores

so that heaven might be believed to be your homeland [one Vatican manuscript: “so that you might make the heavens your homeland”; the Venetian edition: “so that heaven is believed to be your homeland”; another Vatican manuscript: “you are shown to be”].

**[Col. 0111A]** The world was exile to you, as you avoided its muddy places,

and now heaven rejoices that you remain its citizen.

Stripped of darkness and clothed in a covering of light,

after death you enjoy a freer day [Note: Cointius assigns Saint Medard’s death to the year 545; Valesius to 560. See Cointius under the year 545, section 9, where he gives the reason for this disagreement and confirms his own view].

Born from the earth, made possessor of Olympus,

you hold joyful things with the Father, leaving your mother [Note: I have no doubt that punctuation should be placed after “leaving your mother,” so that the meaning is: Medard, leaving the earth from which he had been born, holds joyful things with God the Father. Fortunatus is speaking of his condition after death].

Victor over human vice, you triumph above the stars,

and, burning the flesh, grant rest to the soul.

As you walked amid the world’s thorns, we confess

that, having trampled the thorns, you earned roses.

The field, refreshed with blossom [the Bollandists: “filled with blossom”], pours sweet fragrances for you [one manuscript: “pours in”];

the balsams and frankincense that paradise possesses fill it.

Carefully setting your steps along the narrow path,

thus the constricted way gave you a road to the light.

The broad road of pleasures, which plunges into Avernus,

nourishing the sweetnesses of the flesh, prepares the bitterness of death.

You never turned your holy steps onto this path,

nor could wicked things hold your feet.

The hard road leads upward to praise, the more arduous path [the Venetian edition: “the grave path leads you upward”];

where the labor is greater, the glory will be greater.

What miracles of a sacred deed shall I begin with,

when, whatever you do, everything shines as the first?

While life was [or, according to the corrected reading, “fled”] heavenward in a human body,

as it fled from his eyes, it was light to your heart.

If a blind man came, he seized salvation by feeling his way;

in the midst of darkness, open day shone forth.

The one who wished to penetrate the hidden causes of the theft [the Bollandists: “to penetrate the cause of the theft secretly”],

while you bound him, sits; while you release him, he flees.

The thief, deceived without completing his vow [the Bollandists and one Vatican manuscript: “without success”],

restoring everything, bears all the charges of fraud.

**[Col. 0111C]** For once they had plucked the grapes from the tender vine,

they could not carry their steps back outside [or: “outdoors”].

Nor could the robber withdraw his booty with his feet;

rather, his booty took the robber’s feet away.

Thus the wretched man began to be bound by his own snares [the Paris edition: “behold”]:

he had come to seize, but he himself was seized [the Venetian edition: “he himself was captured”].

He did not touch the must, but was whirled about by an evil mind;

before he could drink, the drunken crowd lay there [Note: In Saint Medard’s *Life*, Fortunatus says that only one thief entered his vineyard. What he later relates—“the drunken crowd lies there”—should therefore be understood as poetic language].

He began to guard the grapes rather than carry them [one Vatican manuscript: “rather than carry away the clusters”],

and was made a watchman who had wished to be a robber.

Until, holy one, you ordered him by your words to depart,

so that he might make restitution for the theft; taught by his foe, he returned.

**[Col. 0112A]** What piety of heart is this, most holy bishop,

that you make the one who harms you go away with your help?

Another needy man, more wicked still, steals a bell [Note: [Col. 0112C–D] Radbod, in his *Life of Saint Medard*, chapter 2, relates that the thief stole not only a little bell but also livestock, or an ox, and was divinely exposed by its ringing. The Bollandists correct: “more wicked, that man”],

he who is accustomed to hold the necks of beasts.

He hides it in his bosom and blocks the opening with hay,

and holds it in his own hand so that it may not reveal his deed.

When you came, holy one, it disclosed the hidden causes,

beginning by its ringing, as though already speaking of the thefts.

Nothing can be hidden, nothing shut, nothing held;

with eloquent clamor it betrayed the whole crime.

It laid out its own case as though before a judge,

fearing nothing from the thief, with a freer sound.

It points out, accuses, convicts, condemns, and aggravates;

yet, in your presence, the guilty man is not permitted to remain guilty.

You absolve the thief, out of your customary love of mercy [one Vatican manuscript: “out of love of such great mercy”],

**[Col. 0112B]** adding a warning: let him enter the road cautiously.

You order him to carry the stolen, complaining object with him,

so that the needy man might not return sadly and empty of hope.

From this point, however, as I am able, after you have been taken from the city [the Venetian edition: “from the world”],

I shall tell what reverent signs you gave to the people.

When your pious limbs were carried in an arranged bier,

the blind man deserved to receive the day that had been taken away.

Anxiously, he received light from the sacred shadow,

and your death became the source of light for him.

While they were giving you burial, the buried man’s eyes returned,

and your sleep caused him to keep watch.

As you fled from the world, the world of light was given to him;

when you left the day, darkness fled from him.

Ancient faces marveled at a new light,

and the first window came to an old structure.

**[Col. 0112C]** Another man, bound with strong fetters and handcuffs,

as soon as he touched the temple [one Vatican manuscript, corrected: “as soon as he touched the garment”; the Paris edition: “together, as he touched”], the iron bonds fell [Note: Saint Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 19, reports that chains and fetters lay broken at Saint Medard’s tomb and were preserved there to this day as testimony to his power. In book V, chapter 5, he tells of a certain Modestus, a smith who was held innocently in prison between two guards, bound with chains and fetters. Having implored Saint Medard’s patronage, he suddenly escaped free and unbound when his bonds were broken and the door opened].

To see such a great fragment is itself painful—a punishment—

that so many weights should have been borne by wretched feet.

If they had been joined together, they could have released an elephant [the Bollandists correct: “an elephant could not release itself”; one Vatican manuscript: “they could not release an elephant”; perhaps, “an elephant could not release itself”],

nor could he himself move his rigid steps.

It is no less for him than for an anchor lying broken

on Libyan shores after a storm has overturned it.

A heavier punishment fell as the triumph increased;

to conquer a savage thing was the greater glory.

The wretched man did not have to endure so many bonds while bound,

but your deed deserved more because of your power.

When they were joined, the chains did not rattle so loudly

as when the wild beasts crashed apart [the Venetian edition: “when the doors burst”; the Bollandists: “wild beasts”].

What had previously been badly bound by excessive chains,

now, once you released it, favors you with a free hand.

Another man carrying wooden bonds fled to the hall;

they suddenly fell apart with a similar miracle.

No delay: scarcely had he touched the sacred threshold of the temple

when thunder arose in the heavens, bearing arms in your service [Note: The author of the *Life of Saint Medard* published second by the Bollandists, a man of Soissons of the ninth century, relates this event, chapter 2, section 17: “As soon as he, bound with wooden bonds and inspired by faith, touched the threshold of the sacred building, in a sudden crash, at one and the same moment, the heavens thundered and the massive fetters burst apart and flew far away. Restored to the freedom he had so greatly desired, the man, stunned with amazement, fell prostrate upon the ground.” The Bollandists read: “Thunder arose in the heavens”].

The great divided weights of the wood fell,

and he who had carried the burden fell down together with it.

He suddenly trembled at the freedom he had received,

and feared all the more when he had been released.

Why he fell headlong upon the ground became clear:

great joys often cause fear.

While he marveled at the source of salvation restored to his wounded feet [one Vatican manuscript: “while he marvels”],

with astonished spirit his loosened limbs relaxed.

Then an old woman, with the affliction likewise present from birth,

bore limbs made lifeless by a congenital defect.

She held her enclosed fingers, with disease counting them [the Bollandists restore: “She held diseases enclosed in her finger, counting them”; the “counting finger” evidently means the index finger],

and could not draw the threads with her extended thumb [one Vatican manuscript: “with her trained thumb”].

Born with her, indeed, but not her own, her right hand hung;

joined to her body, it was something alien.

But it was late, when hope already lay broken:

before your tombs, the hand was restored to life [the Paris edition: “before your tomb”].

Thus grace recommends an unexpected vow;

salvation that had been despaired of is usually sweeter.

Therefore mobile fluid came to her stiff fingers,

and strength, distributed through them, flowed into the nail.

**[Col. 0113C]** The dry connection of the nerves stretched itself,

and the loosened vein recognized its own place.

The palm, made fit for service, began to move;

learning its task, the right hand became free.

Nor did your mercy merely restore the fleeing limbs;

it restored livelihood as well, with the hand drawing out the allotted work.

You rescued another girl from a similar affliction

and, restoring her limbs, gave more to her soul.

**[Col. 0114A]** Betrothed to a man according to mortal law, she had lain there;

now, as a virgin dedicated to Christ, she shines in the bridal chambers [Note: This girl, who had been destined for marriage, evidently became a religious woman and later seems to have attained the rank of abbess. The sterility of her womb was compensated by a more fruitful and happier offspring: the virgins she bore to Christ. The Bollandists read “in the bridal chambers of Christ”; the Paris edition, “in the bridal chamber”].

The bride shines indeed with modest virginity,

enjoying a better hope, destined to be held by heaven.

Nor does she lose the honorable fruit of a barren womb [the Bollandists: “of a burdened womb”];

she is pleasing as a mother to the flower of chastity.

She acquires everyone, and also a child—one whom she does not have [one Vatican manuscript: “a child whom she did not have”; the Paris edition: “likewise, whom she did not have”],

and, through the love of God, generates offspring for herself.

Then, from the same disease, a small infant, deserving lamentation,

coming into the light, carried limbs that were dead.

Death and origin alike proceeded from the unhappy womb [the Bollandists: “from the unhappy woman’s womb”],

the exhausted mother giving birth to a lifeless hand.

Entrusted to your tomb, she returned healed;

what was lost from the mother she received back from the tomb.

While another needy man lay there, shut in by the darkness of sight,

blind, and with no light in his wretched eyes,

a long night pressed upon his eyes for four months already;

dark in the light, alive as an image of death.

You instructed him through healing words during sleep [one Vatican manuscript: “through the physician’s words”]

to hasten his step toward your temples.

Then, when day came, but without a razor having cut it for him,

Christ’s sheep shone, shorn at the crown [Note: This verse was formerly read:

“Christ shone at the crown, his hair having been cut.”

Browerus restored it with the aid of the oldest Antwerp manuscript, which read:

“Christ’s sheep shone at the crown, shorn.”

The Vatican manuscripts also have this reading. *Oves* is used for *ovis*, just as *apes* is used for *apis*. The Bollandists read: “a shorn man.”

Fortunatus seems here to indicate that, in sleep, the blind man’s hair was cut not by human hand but by divine agency; by this act he was divinely designated as a monk or cleric, and he received it as a pledge that he would later recover his sight.]

Here he removes [one Vatican manuscript: “from here he removes”] his hair so that he may have shining little eyes,

and, selling his hair, buys the gifts of light.

He who, with faltering step, was dragged to the hall

lay for two days before the tombs.

On the third day returning, the light dissolved the nocturnal shadows,

and thus the restored day met the blind man.

From every side, darkness smeared upon his forehead fell away [the Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript: “polished”; the Bollandists: “polished,” singular],

and a stream of blood moistened it, washing away the blackness of blindness.

**[Col. 0114C]** A dry lamp, blazing with fresh oil, shone again,

and the foreign light recovered its proper place.

What more shall I say [one Vatican manuscript: “What shall I say of many things?”] of how you gave speech to the mute through a word?

By removing what burdens and assigning everything that helps [one Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition: “assigning everything”].

I do not enumerate everything; your praises overwhelm me.

Even if I have not been able, regard me as having wished to be able.

Behold, Sigibert reverently honors your temples

with exceedingly great love [the Bollandists think “with honor” should be read, lest “love” be repeated too often and so that the temple’s splendor may be expressed] [Note: When Chlothar heard that Saint Medard was lying ill at Noyon, he went there to visit him and asked permission to transport his body after death to Soissons and bury it in that city. Having obtained permission, Chlothar transferred the dead man’s body to Soissons with great pomp and ceremony. Meanwhile, after a wicker hut had been built over the tomb, he began, with royal magnificence and generosity, to construct a notable basilica. Since Chlothar could not complete it because death overtook him, Sigibert completed it with equal zeal and devotion. This seems not to have occurred before Sigibert, moving against his brother Chilperic, captured Soissons, the seat of Chilperic’s kingdom, and brought it under his own authority; this happened around the year 564. See the *Lives of Saint Medard* published by the Bollandists, where the translation of Saint Medard to Soissons is described at length.

Soissons was a city on the river Aisne, formerly in Belgica Secunda. Chlothar held his royal residence there, as did Chilperic after Chlothar’s death.]

devoting himself to the work, ready with love for you.

Guard him who brought the church to its summit [the Venetian edition and the Bollandists: “guard at the summit.” They criticize Velserus, who thinks one should read “grant him rest,” since rest should not yet be requested for the living];

according to his merits protect him who gave you this roof.

I, Fortunatus, bringing these few offerings with devotion [the Bollandists: “these very few offerings”],

ask your aid; grant my prayers, I beg.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Saint Martial, Bishop of Limoges

[Note: [Col. 0115C] We present this poem of Fortunatus on Saint Martial from manuscript 3 of Pluteus XX in the Laurentian Library, a parchment manuscript from the beginning of the twelfth century containing a Passional of the saints. It gives this title: “Verses of Fortunatus on the life of the most holy Martial, apostle of Christ.” The same poem was published before us in Rome, *Auctores Anecdoti*, 1783, vol. IV, p. 433.]

[Note: [Col. 0115A] In this poem he sings of the outstanding merits of Saint Martial, the first bishop of Limoges, and declares that no tongue or pen is equal to celebrating them.]

Christ, the beginning, the end, and the light, is Christ the way;

in whose life-giving and ever-blessed name

the most holy deeds of Martial resound here [F. *Christus* for *Christe*].

**[Col. 0116A]** Who among men, however learned, could ever worthily say

how great is the merit of this illustrious apostle,

in prose or in the beautiful song of meter,

so that the page might at least be adorned with modest words?

Let Cicero and Virgil come; let the tongue be eloquent [Note: [Col. 0116B] We added the word *facunda*, guided by the initial letters found in the manuscript, although we would have preferred *diserta*, since the first syllable of *facunda* is long, whereas it ought to be short for the meter to stand. We have judged this less strictly in the case of this poet, who, as we have noted elsewhere, often shortened syllables that should have been long and lengthened those that should have been short. In this same poem, verse 15, we printed *sic*; nevertheless, the other reading, *hic*, is preferable, especially since Fortunatus often treats the letter *h* as a strong consonant, as we noted at book I, chapter 21].

Whether running in verse or weaving the fabric of prose [the manuscript: “reweaving nothing”],

it will not be able to bring forth your deeds, holy Father.

The Roman land remembers you, and the Gallic land remembers you,

as a younger Peter in the second portion [Note: Younger than Peter in age and in the prerogative of apostleship; perhaps equal to the first Peter in that he shared the same glory],

and perhaps remembers you as equal to the first Peter.

The tribe of Benjamin carried you in illustrious blood.

The city of Limoges now holds you in a holy body.

Therefore to you, great King God, be praise and glory, O Christ;

Christ, renowned head and end, peace, light, and way, O Christ.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER I. To Euphronius, Bishop of Tours

[Note: [Col. 0115D] Saint Euphronius was Gregory’s predecessor in the see of Tours, a man of senatorial origin but especially renowned for outstanding devotion and religion. He was the grandson of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Langres, concerning whom Gregory of Tours speaks in *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7. Saint Euphronius died in the twelfth year of King Sigibert, that is, in the year 573, as Gregory relates in *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, book II, chapter 1. Gregory himself counts him as the eighteenth bishop of the Church of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book X, chapter 31. He died at the age of seventy, after occupying the see for seventeen years.]

[Note: [Col. 0115C] Having received a letter from Euphronius, Fortunatus shows how greatly he rejoiced, declares his reverence and gratitude toward him, extols his remarkable virtue in thinking humbly of himself and his own affairs, and finally commends himself to his prayers.]

To the holy lord, apostolic in merits, lord and twice a father, Euphronius the pope, Fortunatus.

Ante the passage of a few days’ revolving course [Note: [Col. 0116D] The Venetian edition: “bearing the elapsed passage of time.”], when the bearer of the present letters [Note: [Col. 0116D] The Paris edition: “of these present letters.”] delivered the salutary greeting of your venerable countenance [Note: [Col. 0116D] One Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition: *portitorem*, “the bearer.”], I signify that I was instructed to regard it as a heavenly gift [Note: [Col. 0116D] One Vatican manuscript: “a human gift for a heavenly one.”]; and, with God the Creator as witness, I embraced it with the same eagerness with which I have continually approved your most devout spirit, lavish toward my humility, and acknowledge myself, your suppliant, devoted, filled with many benefits [Note: [Col. 0116D] One Vatican manuscript: “filled abundantly with many benefits”; perhaps, “abundantly.” [Col. 0117C] When Fortunatus first came to Tours, to the tomb of Saint Martin, Euphronius, bishop of that city, was seated there. From these words of Fortunatus we may infer that Euphronius received Fortunatus with great kindness, since he testifies that he had been filled with many benefits by Euphronius; the following letter shows this still more clearly. Fortunatus then went to Poitiers and lived in that city. I agree with Browerus that this is indicated here by the words “although I dwell in another city.” See what we said in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 47.].

Although I dwell in another city, God knows that I am absent from you only in place, not in spirit; and wherever I may be, I shall have you enclosed within me [Col. 0117A] [Note: [Col. 0117D] The Venetian edition: “I have you enclosed.”].

I speak truly: that is not a heart of flesh in which the wondrous sweetness of your soul is not received, but it is harder than marble [Note: [Col. 0117D] One Vatican manuscript: “harder than marble,” neuter] if it does not embrace the caress [Note: [Col. 0117D] The Venetian edition: “the caress,” accusative] of such great charity.

For who could praise you so appropriately as a truly holy mind demands? Or who could satisfy his own heart so fully as to reveal worthily the affection that befits you—since on earth you are so humble that you dwell upright in heaven, and by bending toward the lowly you cause yourself to be raised to the heights, so that you are now recognized [Note: [Col. 0117D] One Vatican manuscript: “so that you might then recognize.” The Venetian and Paris editions: “so that you may recognize.”] as one who gladly embraces Christ’s humility: what will you possess from the gift of his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0117D] One Vatican manuscript omits “of his kingdom”; another also omits it.]? Since, according to the commandments of the One who wishes to appear little among human beings, each person should desire and explain how he may be regarded as exalted in heaven [Note: [Col. 0117D] One Vatican manuscript: “and may be explained.”].

I rejoice that the love of my Lord Martin has taken its seat [Note: [Col. 0117D] One Vatican manuscript: “has felt.”] in the heart of Lord Euphronius.

Therefore, commending myself with repeated prayer to your apostolate and holy charity, I ask by that same Lord Martin, whose fellowship you enjoy as a participant, that you order me to be remembered before him as his servant and devotee, so that you may continually show what influence you possess with him, by your merits, in protecting my humility [Note: [Col. 0117D] One Vatican manuscript: “what influence you possess with him.”].

Pray for me, holy and apostolic lord, my particular lord and father.

## CHAPTER II. To the same

[Note: [Col. 0117B] He praises Euphronius’s exceptional benefits and merits toward himself and declares his remembrance and affection for him. He then elaborates at length on Euphronius’s virtues, by which he was an example to the rest; finally he earnestly begs that Euphronius himself act as an intercessor with the Father for his offenses. [Col. 0117C]]

To Euphronius, my holy lord and my special patron in God [Note: [Col. 0117D] One Vatican manuscript: “in the Lord.”], Pope Fortunatus.

Who could, as is fitting [Note: [Col. 0117D] One Vatican manuscript omits “is” after “as is fitting.”], conceive in his heart or express in words the abundant and overflowing sweetness of your true heart, which, most loving Father, I confess that your blessedness has lavished upon my devotion?

That sweetness has bound me to itself with so great a bond of wondrous charity that I seem not to be separated for even the space of one hour from the sight of the one whom, though I do not see him present, I nevertheless retain stored and shut away within the dwelling of my heart [Col. 0118A] [Note: [Col. 0117D] The Venetian edition: “closed up.” Two Vatican manuscripts have the same reading.].

For who is not rendered special (*peculiaris*) to your piety [or: charity], in which the benefits of such great goodness are contained [Note: [Col. 0118C] The Venetian edition: “in whom such benefits are contained by your piety.”]? Or whom would you not lead, even unwillingly, toward your sweetness, since we have proved your heart to be poured out [or: steeped] in ineffable charity?

How could I not embrace this with wonder, when I see you love everyone as though you had seemed to beget each one from your own side?

Who among sons would proudly desire to be elsewhere, when he recognizes in you a father and teacher of such humility? Or who, descending from the summit of the highest nobility [Note: [Col. 0118D] The Venetian edition: “descending from the summit.”], when he sees you so suppliant, would not, prostrate upon the ground at your feet, extend himself [or: show himself] [Note: [Col. 0118D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition: “he extends himself.”]?

I speak truly. If pride casts down the swollen, great indeed is the humility that raises you [Note: [Col. 0118D] Two Vatican manuscripts have a corrupt reading approximately meaning: “you, who are greatly praiseworthy, have raised.”].

Finally, who could be angry or turbulent there where a priest and bishop has been found to be so tranquil?

For the whole flock knows how to live without rapacity where it learns tranquility of life from its shepherd.

What should I say of the rest of your conduct, in which you expend yourself upon each individual so completely that you are praised by all [Note: [Col. 0118D] The Venetian edition: “praised in all things.” Two Vatican manuscripts have the same reading.]? Even if we cannot imitate these things, we rejoice at least to have seen what we ought to imitate.

Therefore, commending myself especially to your lordship and holiness, I ask and implore that my lord Martin, through his intercession, obtain this: that divine mercy place you, according to your merits, with him in perpetual light, and that you deign to pray at his blessed tomb for me, your humble son and servant, so that you may approach as a merciful intercessor for the remission of my sins [Col. 0118C] [Note: [Col. 0118D] One Vatican manuscript: “so that he may approach.”].

I respectfully greet all those who belong to you, all my lords and beloved [or: leaders]. I especially beg that my lord Eventius [Note: [Col. 0118D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “Aventius.” Browerus thinks this was Eventius, or Evantius, of whom Gregory of Tours speaks in Book VIII, chapter 39, of the *History of the Franks*: he was made bishop of Vienne and died in the eleventh year of Childebert’s reign, that is, in 586. Another Eventius is mentioned by Gregory in Book X, chapter 2: sent as an envoy to Constantinople by Chilperic, he was carried to Carthage and killed there during a popular uprising, as Gregory relates in the cited passage. It is uncertain which of these men—or whether either of them—is Fortunatus’s subject here.], your son, whom I love above all things, be greeted many times on my behalf.

If my lord Felix the bishop has come to you, I ask that I be commended to him with a kindly spirit [Note: [Col. 0118D] This Felix seems to have been none other than the bishop of Nantes, of whom more is said below.].

Pray for me.

## CHAPTER III. To the same

[Note: [Col. 0118C] He celebrates Saint Euphronius’s virtues and especially commends his pastoral care and diligence.]

Although my sluggish tongue lies inactive without a spark,

and I cannot render worthy things to worthy men [Note: [Col. 0119C] The Paris edition: “to worthy fingers,” that is, “with worthy fingers”],

nevertheless, holy Father, venerable priest of Christ,

Euphronius, I desire to offer you a small gift.

I owe you much indeed, but gladly receive the little;

I beg that what your affection produces may be forgiven.

Under you, the lamp of the Church flashes forth in radiant light;

the faith of the bishop shines everywhere.

Outstanding grace blooms in a sincere heart,

in which there is no deceit: you are an Israelite man (*vir es*; variant *virens*, “flourishing”).

Your blameless conduct runs prosperously,

and this path opens the way for you to enter heaven.

You pour forth the sweet words of conversation without deceit;

your words please me more than honey.

Whatever the mind contains, your tranquil tongue releases,

and no fraud occupies a place within your breast.

You remain without gall in the simplicity of a dove,

nor does the serpent nourish dreadful poisons within you.

If a stranger comes, you make his homeland beloved again,

and through you the guest possesses his own resources here [Note: [Col. 0119C] Three Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition: “the exile.”].

If anyone groans beneath injustice, no one leaves here sorrowful;

removing his tears, you make him glad.

Martin placed you in this seat because of your merits;

you were worthy to be his heir, since you observe his commands.

He holds heaven, giving all things with generous favor;

you will be joined to Christ by imitating this man [Note: [Col. 0119C] Three Vatican manuscripts: “you will be joined to Christ.”].

The flock of yours that returns to the fold does not perish here,

nor does the sheep lose its white fleece among thorns.

When the shepherd is vigilant, the wolf does not seize prey with its jaws,

but, shut out, flees without tearing the flocks.

May this light remain for you, venerable one, through long years,

and may the coming day bring brighter things.

## CHAPTER IV. To Felix, bishop of Nantes

[Note: [Col. 0119C] This Felix was bishop of Nantes. He died in the seventh year of King Childebert, that is, in 582, after having held his seat for thirty-three years, according to Gregory of Tours, Book VI, chapter 15, of the *History of the Franks*. Gregory relates that serious disagreements existed between Felix and himself; indeed, in several places he casts a shadow over Felix’s name. This nevertheless did not prevent Felix from being venerated as a saint among the people of Nantes, nor did it prevent his memory from remaining there clear and distinguished. [Col. 0119D]]

[Note: [Col. 0119C] After receiving a letter from Felix, Fortunatus says that he was struck by its eloquence and grand style. He writes much in Felix’s praise and tries, out of modesty, to diminish the very affectionate and honorable things Felix had written about him. Finally he returns the same praises to Felix himself. At the end he shows how eager he is for Felix’s presence and companionship. [Col. 0120A]]

To Felix, my holy lord, most worthy of the apostolic see, my lord and father, Pope Felix,

Fortunatus.

As I lay on my bed, drowsily near the neighboring shore of the sea [Note: [Col. 0119D] See what we said in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 74.], overcome by the blandishment of natural sluggishness,

and as I had lain for a long while upon the coastal margin [Note: [Col. 0119D] One Vatican manuscript: “on a bed prepared.” The Paris edition: “lying down.”],

suddenly, amid the wave-breaking surges of your eloquence, as though the waves had dashed against rocks and splashed me with scattered brine, I happened to be sprinkled by them. At the first goads of awakening [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Paris edition: “awakening.”] I could be drenched, but not aroused; still sleeping heavily in my customary fashion, at last I scarcely rose amid the crashing thunder of your words [Note: [Col. 0119D] One Vatican manuscript omits “your.”].

When I considered each of your sayings, uttered in the trumpet-like blare of speech and suffused with a kind of starry brilliance, it seemed to me that you had struck my eyes with the visible light of flashing rays: you opened my drowsing eyes with thunder, yet closed them again with lightning.

For such was the radiance of your tongue’s practiced conversation [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Venetian edition: “radiance.”], such the light that flashed from your smiling eloquence [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Venetian edition: “of your radiant eloquence.”], that, with the order reversed, it seemed to me that while you spoke the sun was rising from the west [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript: “the sun is born from the west while you speak.”].

I thought that, in a sound almost Pindaric [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Venetian and Paris editions: “as though Pindar were speaking.”], an eloquent discourse had flowed forth, made of fourfold strophes [Note: [Col. 0119D] One Vatican manuscript: “compacted”; another: “fourfold strophes.”], its words fastened together by pedestrian glue [Note: [Col. 0119D] The Venetian edition: “earthly glue.”], as though giving birth to a chained sequence of enthymemes, woven with coils and foreign sophistry.

Finally, so far as the depth of your diction is concerned, you had made me ignorant, wandering along the crossroads of speech [Note: [Col. 0120C] The Venetian edition: “through the crossroads of speeches.” One Vatican manuscript; another corrects it to “through completed speeches.” The Paris edition: “through the winding paths of speeches.”] as though among the rocks of the Echinades [Note: [Col. 0120C] The common reading was formerly corrupt. Browerus restored the present text from a manuscript of Trier, and it is supported by the Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition, except that the latter has “Echinadas”; two Vatican manuscripts have “Echinades.” The Echinades are islands in Epirus opposite the Ambracian Gulf, formed when the force of the Achelous carried sand and mud to that place. They are mentioned by Pliny, Book II; Thucydides, Book II, near the end; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII; and Dionysius in his description of the world, verses 430 ff.:

> Above Dodona, toward the south, beneath the height of Aracynthus,  
> lies the great plain of the Aetolian people; through its midst  
> the silver-eddying Achelous drags his winding course,  
> turning toward the sea of Trinacria through the middle  
> of islands called the Echinades, beside which  
> the cities of the Cephallenians follow one another in scattered succession.]

unless a guiding lamp from your own self had come to meet me on my journey [Col. 0120C].

As for what you inserted into your letter—that my voice, not surpassed even by acclamations of praise, had resounded in the farthest corner of the world—when I read this over, I began to marvel that I had suddenly grown through your conversation. I had not deserved such favor through any adornment of my own, yet I rejoiced to be raised so high by the affection of my supporter, while I recognized that I was being placed beneath him by the quality of my talent.

O how powerful charity is, when the tongue of the one who praises adds what the vein of the one praised takes away [Note: [Col. 0120D] One Vatican manuscript: “of the praised man” or, perhaps, “of the polished man.”]!

It is indeed to be desired that, concerning me, a person so humble should be believed rather than the author himself.

For Polydeuces would not have commended himself through the abundance of his leaping spring, unless he had been touched by the prophetic liquid of the Smyrnaean fountain [Note: [Col. 0121B] Two manuscripts and the Venetian edition have variant forms of the name, including “Polydiochen” and the common “Polydeachen.” Browerus adds that a Trier manuscript had “Pollux” in the margin. Fortunatus seems to imply here that Polydeuces, or Pollux, was not so much illustrious in himself as made illustrious by the testimony Homer gave concerning him—whether elsewhere or in the hymn entitled “To the Dioscuri,” which begins:

> Sing, Muse of the bright eyes, of the Dioscuri,  
> the Tyndarids, glorious sons of fair-ankled Leda,  
> Castor, breaker of horses, and blameless Polydeuces.

Theocritus likewise writes in *Idyll* 22, entitled “The Dioscuri”:

> For you, lords, the Chian singer fashioned glory  
> when he sang of Priam’s city and the ships of the Achaeans,  
> the battles of the Iliad, and Achilles, tower of war-cry.]

Thus, what you said—that I seem to inhabit your presence in the farthest corner of the world—should rightly be understood in this way: you ought to believe me about yourselves, since you so sweetly urge me to be believed by you concerning myself.

Although the regions are remote, they are first because you are their citizen; for if cities claim precedence through the merit of their persons, no place through you is inferior where Felix the bishop is asserted to be the champion of whatever praise is sought [Note: [Col. 0121C] The Venetian edition: “where the bishop Felix asserts it.” One Vatican manuscript: “where the bishop is the champion.”].

In the end, it is not the snow of Caucasus, nor the constellation of the raging Bear [Note: [Col. 0121C] The old reading, according to Browerus, was: “Finally, neither blind winter nor raging wind breathes.” The Venetian edition: “Finally, neither the position of the raging Bear, woven with cold, breathes.” The Paris edition: “Finally, neither beneath the raging Lion does the heat of the Titan burn for you, nor the position of the Bear …”], interwoven with frost, that breathes here; rather, through you, with the dwellings changed, springtime blooms while the continual whisper of the west wind plays its music [Note: [Col. 0121C] The Paris edition: “while the west wind plays.” The Venetian edition: “spring is made.” One Vatican manuscript has the same reading.].

Your holiness also complains that, when I was at Tours, you had enjoyed my conversation only briefly [Note: [Col. 0121C] The Paris edition: “had taken part in conversation for a brief time.”], whereas I am ashamed that in so short a time I revealed my ignorance and concealed the grace I had acquired from so great a bishop.

Yet, if you are willing to consider the relation between our friendship [Note: [Col. 0121C] Two Vatican manuscripts: “if you consider our friendship.” The Venetian and Paris editions: “if you consider our friendship in its parts.”], although I enjoyed your sight for an extended time, I could be stimulated but not satisfied.

For who, once filled with the fragrance of roses, would ever judge himself satisfied, or allow himself to become weary of it [Note: [Col. 0121C] The Venetian edition: “For who, once filled with the fragrance of sweet roses, would ever judge himself satisfied, or allow himself to become weary?”]?

The longer we had been face to face [Note: [Col. 0121D] Two Vatican manuscripts: “for a longer time.” The Paris edition: “for a longer time.”], the more deeply I would have been inflamed with affection, the more I would have recognized whom I loved.

What you wrote was:

> “If I had ascended the Loire with you on favorable currents and had met you at Nantes, …” [Note: [Col. 0121D] The common reading had “if I lived with you,” corrupting the name of the well-known river, near whose mouth the city of Nantes lies. The Venetian edition likewise has “if I read with you,” which comes closer to the river’s name. The Paris edition: “if I had ascended the Loire with you on favorable winds and had met you at Nantes.” The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript preserve the remainder in a thoroughly corrupt form: “I know indeed, with the Canopus of the Cherusci summoning the swift myoparon, caught by harmonic art, safe amid biting symphonies, I would have gone out, and if necessity required, I, shut in and creaking, would have struck the Tirynthian poet, with Pindar breathing.” Other Vatican manuscripts are likewise corrupt. The Paris edition has: “with the Tirynthian, with Pindar in Pindar.”]

I knew that, with you as my Canopus, when the Cherusci summoned a swift myoparon, I would have escaped safely amid the biting Symplegades, guided and protected by harmonic art; and, if the matter required, with Pindar breathing through me, I would have struck Oeta of Tiryns with resounding applause [Note: [Col. 0123C] This passage is corrupt in the Vatican manuscripts.].

[Note: [Col. 0122B] Browerus both restored the complete reading and attempted to explain the meaning of this exceedingly obscure passage. He says that the Cherusci were a German people living around the Elbe in Saxony, surviving by plunder and brigandage in the manner of pirates. Hence the name was used indiscriminately for the Saxons, who often invaded Gaul and harassed it with their weapons and raids. Sidonius Apollinaris speaks of them in a letter to Namatius, Book VIII, letter 6:

> But behold, while I was already wishing to close the letter, which has been chattering for a long time, a sudden messenger from Saintes … firmly asserted that recently you had sounded the trumpet on your fleet, and that now as sailors, now as soldiers, you were roaming along the curving shores of the Ocean against the crooked myoparons of the Saxons; and that, however many oarsmen you saw, you thought you saw just as many pirate commanders.

Browerus shows from several records that the Saxons excelled especially in the speed of their myoparons and in nautical skill. Hegesippus likewise writes of them in Book V concerning the Saxons: “A strong race of men, outstanding above the rest, relying not on strength but only on pirate myoparons.” This is quoted by Sirmond in his notes on Sidonius, Book VIII, letter 6.

Browerus also observes that Canobus, or Canopus, was the pilot of Menelaus, from whom the Mediterranean island at the mouth of the Nile—the mouth called Canopic—received its name.

The Symplegades, which Browerus conjecturally reads where the manuscripts had “Sympheras” and the Calar. edition “Symphonias,” were islands opposite the Thracian Bosporus. They are mentioned by Pliny, Book VI, chapter 13, by Pomponius Mela, Book XI, and frequently by other authors. The poets famously imagined that these islands, also called the Cyaneae or Cyanitae because of their dark or blue color, collided with one another, intercepting and crushing passing ships. The ship of the Argonauts, guided by Minerva or Juno, first passed safely between them; thereafter they ceased their collisions. See Homer, *Odyssey* XII, where he describes them, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV, chapter 7.

The sense of Fortunatus’s words is therefore this: under Felix, as under another Canopus, he promises that, having boarded some swift myoparon of the Saxons or Cherusci, he will sail successfully through the straits of the Symplegades. Having escaped safely from this voyage, he would then sing, with applause, some Pindaric song of deliverance, just as Pindar, the foremost of lyric poets, exalted Oeta, the Herculean or Tirynthian mountain—between Thessaly and Macedonia, celebrated in song as Hercules’ tomb—even more through his lyric poems.

Oeta is called “Tirynthian” because Hercules was buried there; he had been raised in the city of Tiryns near Argos. Concerning him Pylades writes in *Theog.*, Book V:

> The same man was called Tirynthian from the city that raised him,  
> where the Tyrian land lay closest to Argos.

For a clearer explanation of this obscure passage, it may also be added, by way of conjecture, what Gregory of Tours relates in Book II, chapter 19: that the Saxons occupied certain islands which were later captured and destroyed by the Franks. Cointius thinks these islands were situated on the Loire, in the year 477. The Saxons had fortified them, so that, if matters turned out badly, they would have free opportunity to sail out into the Ocean. I could therefore readily believe that Fortunatus refers here to those Saxons who had survived that slaughter and disaster and either lived by robbery or offered their services in piloting vessels down the Loire. One of these possibilities is perhaps indicated by Fortunatus’s words: “with the Cherusci summoning a swift myoparon.”]

With what eagerness do you think I read what pure affection compelled you to insert—that is, your words:

> “Even if they had come to take vengeance, they would not have been able to carry me off as your consolation” [Note: [Col. 0123D] The Paris edition: “for if the Volscians had come.” The Venetian edition: “carry me away.”]?

Believe me: as far as my mind can perceive, Rome itself could scarcely have given me as much assistance as you supplied in a word [or: words]. In my view, to expend more in deeds is no greater thing than to offer the wishes of one’s goodwill; for, with the sweetness of your conversation flowing back to me, I need nothing more [Note: [Col. 0123D] The Venetian edition: “there is no need to do more.”].

As for the jest you added—“Unless stirred by praise, the rustic pen would not have turned” [Note: [Col. 0123D] The Paris edition: “would not have spent the night.”]—although such a cultivator, a most fruitful worshiper of Christ, has often plowed rich acres, nevertheless I confess that recently he made your Ithyphallic games resound on Amphion’s lyre [Note: [Col. 0123D] Browerus reports from the Tiliobrogan manuscript, which he greatly trusted, the reading “Ithyphallic games.” The Venetian edition also supports this: “Nevertheless, recently I confess that he made your Ithyphallic games resound on Amphion’s lyre,” perhaps *barbilo* for *barbito*. Browerus thinks that Fortunatus used the expression “Ithyphallic games,” which by origin and institution was associated with every kind of licentiousness and wantonness, only verbally, without intending its meaning, or rather to designate the meter called Ithyphallic. Terentianus Maurus writes in his *Book on Meters*:

> The musical poets  
> called these verses Ithyphallic;  
> they gave Bacchus playful songs  
> in wanton verses,  
> with the Greek-barked Phallus,  
> three trochees,  
> so that the very name creates the sound:  
> Bacchus, Bacchus, Bacchus.]

I know, too, what you pleasantly added:

> “Enclosed within the wall of charity belonging to my lady Rhadigunda.”

I know that you infer this not from my merits, but from the kindness which she is known to extend toward everyone [Note: [Col. 0124C] One Vatican manuscript: “I know what it is, because …”].

And just as poetically you touched upon a panegyric in my own person, so you referred it to the history of her praise.

Yet in your words I deserved to read again what I have already received through her favor; but since you paint great things from me, a little man, I beg you to proclaim the greatest things about the great [Note: [Col. 0124C] One Vatican manuscript: “in your words your …”].

Therefore, commending myself with humble supplication to your lordship and holiness, I beseech you by the Lord, Redeemer of our souls, who will make you, his predestined ones [Note: [Col. 0124C] The Venetian edition: “who will make you, the predestined, …”], sharers in his light, that you deign to remember me, out of regard for your piety, in your holy prayers.

For it will be a great help to my hope to obtain from you what I ask.

If tongues should come together, Greek and Latin alike,

they could not render all things according to your merits.

Surrounded by praises, you are held venerable for your prayers,

Felix, you will be the light of everlasting understanding [Note: [Col. 0124C] One Vatican manuscript: “Felix, he will be everlasting light.”].

## CHAPTER V. To the same, from his name

[Note: [Col. 0124A] He praises Felix fervently and relates that by his action and faith the Breton forces were driven away and the rights of the kingdom defended and preserved.]

Faithful salvation of the fatherland, Felix in hope, name, and heart,

through whom the order of priests shines radiant.

You restore to the lands what the public laws demanded,

bringing back the ancient joys in our times.

Voice of the nobles, light of your race, defense of the people,

you prevent shipwreck where you are present as a harbor.

An apostolic champion, overcoming the Bretons’ claims,

safe amid adversity, through hope in the cross you put their arms to flight [Note: [Col. 0124C] Gregory of Tours relates in Book V, chapter 32, of the *History of the Franks*, that in 579 the Bretons especially ravaged the territory of Nantes and Rennes. Felix, bishop of Nantes, sent an embassy to them; moved by it, they promised to repair whatever loss and harm they had caused by their arms, although they did not keep their promises. Fortunatus plainly seems to refer to this deed of Felix, and I therefore readily believe that this poem was written around the aforementioned year, 579. Fortunatus also sings of Felix in chapter 8 of this book:

> You remove the Breton conspirators by your watchful skill.  
> No one’s weapons can accomplish what your tongue accomplishes.]

Live, glory of the fatherland, light of faith, source of honor,

splendor of bishops, our love and the love of the world.

## CHAPTER VI. To Felix the bishop, on the dedication of his church

[Note: [Col. 0124D] Cointius dates the dedication of this church to the year 568, and says that the Nantes Breviary records it as having taken place on the day before the Kalends of October. He likewise maintains that it could scarcely have been delayed longer, since Euphronius completed the course of his life five years later; it is certain that Euphronius outlived Domitian, bishop of Angers. Domitian appears to have attended this dedication, as is evident from Fortunatus’s poem, and so did Baudegisius, Domitian’s successor.]

[Note: [Col. 0124B] In this poem he sings of Felix’s zeal and care in constructing and dedicating a basilica in honor of Saints Peter and Paul, and of the solemnity and rite of the dedication itself.]

When Solomon celebrated the dedication of the noble temple,

he summoned the Israelite men to be present [Note: [Col. 0124D] The Venetian edition: “he made the chosen Israel present.” One Vatican manuscript: “he made the Israelites present to you,” corruptly.].

Levites, nobles, boys, young men, and old men—

royal pomp drew them eagerly from every direction.

Calves were slaughtered, bulls were sacrificed at the altars,

and the joy of the people in their vows was found in slaughter.

But now a more righteous altar rises,

destined to please God through a blessed rite after the passage of time.

The prosperous festivals that Felix now provides for the peoples [Note: [Col. 0125C] One Vatican manuscript: “providing.” The Venetian edition has the same reading],

surpass the earlier events through these new achievements [Note: [Col. 0125C] One Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition: “surpasses.”].

He summons distinguished fathers to the sacred solemnities,

where true salvation stands and the ancient shadow flees.

Learned in Peter’s key, seeking to open the heavens [Note: [Col. 0125C] The Paris edition: “powerful.”],

and in Paul’s teachings, through which we recognize the secrets of heaven.

So that the wolf may not enter among the sheep, nor sickness wound the lambs [Note: [Col. 0125C] One Vatican manuscript: “may not make them invulnerable”; perhaps “may not ulcerate them.”],

these men are guardians here and there the medicine of the flock.

Their voice, flowing back from the fountain of salvation,

extends faith to the people for drinking by the ear,

and offers salt through the mouth [Col. 0125B].

Among them, seated in Martin’s priestly see,

the holy metropolitan Euphronius shines [Note: [Col. 0125C] Concerning Euphronius, bishop of Tours, see what we said above, Chapter I of this book.].

Rejoicing as the sacred crown of brothers gathers,

and seeing his own members, the summit stands stronger.

His head is happier because his own limbs are with him;

the honor of the Church grows as its body is joined together.

Domitian and Victorius also, both pillars,

remain hope in the two of them for the aid of the region [Note: [Col. 0125D] One Vatican manuscript: “both doves.” Domitian is thought by Browerus to have been bishop of Châlons, and by Cointius bishop of Angers; we follow the latter. He attended the Second Council of Tours, held in 566 or 567. Domitian does not even appear in the catalogue of the bishops of Châlons in a way that would allow him to belong to Fortunatus’s period. [Note: [Col. 0125D] Victorius seems to have been Victorius, or Victurius, bishop of Rennes, whom Gregory of Tours mentions in Book VIII, chapter 32, of the *History of the Franks*, and who attended and signed the same Second Council of Tours. I do not see why Browerus wishes him to be Victor, bishop of Troyes, thereby doing such violence to the name. Browerus himself, following Baronius, admits that nearly all the bishops whom Fortunatus names here attended the Second Council of Tours, although he incorrectly dates that council to around 570; yet Victor of Troyes appears nowhere among those who signed it.].

Here Domnulus shines in merits; there Maracharius,

each, by right of priesthood, a worshiper of God [Note: [Col. 0126C] The Paris edition: “by the light of priesthood.” Domnulus was bishop of Le Mans; his name also appears among the bishops who attended the council mentioned above. Gregory of Tours discusses him in Book VI, chapter 9, of the *History of the Franks*. [Note: [Col. 0125D] Maracharius was bishop of Angoulême, concerning whom Gregory writes in Book V, chapter 37, of the *History of the Franks*. Cointius reads “Romacharius, bishop of Coutances.” The Venetian and Paris editions likewise have “Romacharius”; one Vatican manuscript has the corrupt “Riomacharius,” another “Romacharius.”]].

Behold, the day that has now come is destined to be remembered through the ages [Note: [Col. 0126C] The Venetian edition: “Behold, assisted, it comes, destined to be remembered through a new age.” One Vatican manuscript, corruptly: “Behold, long regarded, now made memorable”; another: “gifts have been given, memorable through the ages.” The Paris edition: “Behold, long awaited, it comes now to be remembered,” and so forth.],

filled with holy vows, it shines throughout the world [Note: [Col. 0126C] The Venetian edition: “throughout the city.” Three Vatican manuscripts have the reading translated here.].

On this day the shepherd deserved to see his own joys

and to fulfill his vows to God through sacred duty [Col. 0125C].

For a long time he had awaited its coming;

despising everything else, this was his entire love:

fearing every danger along the uncertain path of life,

lest he should depart before giving this gift to God.

Often concealing his sighs, he drew out his weary breath,

so that the Lord might permit this honor to hasten.

Anxious, laboring beneath the uncertain burden of cares,

while he watched for the fulfillment of his vow, time itself was a weight.

But now the festival is here: let the burden of care be released;

let an abundance of joy drive away the sorrowful load.

As you grant prosperity to the peoples and lavish joys throughout the city,

celebrate, Felix, as a happy shepherd with a happy flock.

Here bishops surround you, there ministers;

on one side honor, on the other favor, encircle you completely.

Behold, the clergy resounds in choirs; the people, on the other hand, with choraules (choir-leaders or instrumental accompanists) [Note: [Col. 0126D] *Choraules* is sometimes used for the head of a school and sometimes for a musician or instrumental accompanist. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*. Fortunatus, in the *Life of Saint Radegunda*, no. 36, says that although secular people sang loudly around the monastery at night amid choraules and lyres, she, intent on prayer, heard nothing. See also what Fortunatus said above, Book II, chapter 11, in describing the psalmody of the church of Paris.];

each sings your vow with whatever art he possesses.

The delay seemed long to you, because delay is always long to one who loves;

a sublime work comes slowly, but it comes abundantly.

Now sing the praises of the Lord amid your trumpets [Note: [Col. 0126D] One Vatican manuscript: “he sings.”],

and let the threefold mechanism resound with the aid of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0126D] The Paris edition: “with the aid of the Godhead.” Browerus thinks that “the threefold mechanism” refers figuratively to the basilica, whose structure and description are given in the form of a cross. This is made clearer in the following poem.].

As priest, add the marrow-filled holocausts in the temples,

so that, as a pure victim to God, you may shine through enduring time.

## CHAPTER VII. In honor of those whose relics are contained there
