[Note: [Col. 0126B] He celebrates the merits and names of those whose sacred relics had been deposited in the basilica at Nantes. He describes the remarkable structure and adornment of that same basilica.]

Starry mountains, beautiful peaks of Zion,

Twin cedars from Lebanon, luxuriant with flowering foliage.

Gates of heaven, two broad lights of the world;

Paul thunders with his voice; Peter flashes from his citadel.

Among the apostolic crowns shining with radiant light,

The one is more learned in instruction, the other loftier in rank.

[Col. 0126C] Through the one human hearts are opened, and through the other the heavens;

What the former teaches with his pen, the latter receives into heaven.

Here one opens the way to heaven by his teaching; the other by his keys.

Paul is the way, Peter the trustworthy gate.

[Col. 0127A] The one is regarded as the firm rock, the other as the architect;

Upon these two the temple rises, in which the altar is pleasing to God.

Equal from one spring, watering the world with healing streams,

They quench thirsty longing with a sweet liquid.

Whoever desires to hold the stars, waging vigorous battles,

The King appointed these leaders to be commanders of his army.

Gaul, gladly rejoice: Rome sends you her greeting;

The apostolic splendor visits the Allobroges.

Two fortifications stand guard against the hostile face,

Whom the city—the head of the world—possesses as towers of the faith.

These are the radiant eyes in Christ’s precious body,

Who by their own light govern the other members.

Receive, Gaul, the fruits of Felix’s heavenly gift,

And honor the blessed prayers of your bishop,

Whose chaste love gave this house, in heavenly honor,

As an everlasting dowry to the Church, his bride.

[Note: [Col. 0126D] The Paris edition reads *montis*, “of the mountain”; in the margin, *montes*, “mountains.”]

[Note: [Col. 0126D] The Paris edition reads *monitis*, “instructions”; in the margin, *monitu*, “instruction.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] One Vatican manuscript reads *quod*, “which”; this reading is preferable.]

[Col. 0127B] At its lofty summit the form of the hall, threefold,

Is visible, consecrated to God by the apostolic name.

How much their merit rises above that of the other saints—

So much higher does this summit possess its crown.

A towered apex rises in the center above the lofty structure,

And, lifting a square, rounds the building with a circular crest.

So that you may marvel at the height as the citadel rises through arches,

It has the sharpness of a building acting like a mountain.

There, among painted living figures, with their limbs displayed,

You might think the paintings alive, as art breathes upon them.

As the wandering sun has given color through the tin-covered roofs,

A milky light flashes back when red strikes it.

[Note: [Col. 0127C] One Vatican manuscript reads *quod*, “which”; this reading is preferable.]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] The Venetian edition reads *bella gerit*, “he wages battles.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] One Vatican manuscript reads *membra tegunt*, “cover the members.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] The manuscript reads *munera Felicis*, “the gifts of Felix”; the Paris edition has *felices*, “happy,” while the margin has *Felicis*, “of Felix.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] The Venetian edition reads *in honore supremo*, “in supreme honor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] Here he expresses more clearly what the poet had said above:

“And let the threefold structure resound with the aid of the Trinity.”]

[Col. 0128A] You see the figures move back and forth as the ray ripples,

And the ceiling produces the effect that a wave of the sea does in the sun;

The roofs meditate the radiance of the stars in metal,

And the summit possesses a star in its own brilliance.

Whenever the moon has shone with its crowned rising,

Another beam rises from the sacred building toward the stars.

If a traveler, passing by at night, should look upon it,

He will believe that the earth possesses its own stars.

The whole structure captures the rays with its broad-eyed windows,

And what you would marvel at outside, you find within.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] One Vatican manuscript reads *tota rapit*, “the whole structure carries off [the rays].”]

When the darkness returns, let me say what is permitted:

The world has night; the hall retains the day.

The right side of the temple shines with the merits of Hilary,

With Martin, his companion, sharing the rank.

[Note: [Col. 0127C] In one Vatican manuscript: *illic expositis suis animantibus*, “there, with its living figures exposed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] In the same manuscript: *arce reflante*, “as the citadel blows back.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] One Vatican manuscript reads *stagnea*, “tin-like”; the Venetian edition likewise.]

[Note: [Col. 0127C] The same ornamentation belonged to the basilica that Leontius had built in honor of Saint Bibianus of Saintes, as we saw in chapter 12 of Book I, where one should read what we noted at that passage. Sidonius, also praised by Browerus, describes in Book II, Letter 10, the basilica at Lyon built and adorned by Bishop Patiens:

[Col. 0127D]

“The lofty building shines, and is drawn neither to the left

Nor to the right, but from the front of its summit

Looks toward the rising of the equinoctial sun.

Inside, the light sparkles, and the gilded

Sun is so drawn toward the coffered ceiling

That, matching the golden metal, it wanders through it.

Marble marked with varied brilliance

Runs through the vault, the floor, and the windows,

And beneath multicolored figures

The fresh green crust bends sapphire-colored

Stones through emerald glass.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The Paris edition reads *alterum*, “another [beam].”]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The Venetian edition reads *credit habere*, “believes it has.”]

[Col. 0127D] The right side of the temple shines with Hilary’s merits,

With Martin, his companion, sharing the rank.

Thus Gaul, while everywhere pouring forth her own patrons,

Possesses lights for the world in those whom this earth covers.

The other side belongs to Ferreolus, who, by the wound of the sword,

Shines as a jewel made splendid by martyrdom.

Felix offered these things so that he himself might be more truly a priest,

O Christ, your temple, who gave temples to you.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The Venetian edition reads *monitis praefulget*, “shines with admonitions.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The same edition has *cum patre Martino*, “with Father Martin”; likewise one Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The same edition reads *fudit*, “poured forth”; one Vatican manuscript likewise. The Paris edition has *propriis diffundit*, “diffuses with its own.”]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The Venetian edition reads *gemma superna*, “a heavenly jewel.”]

## CHAPTER VIII. To the same man, in praise of him and of the Armorican region

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The Armorican region was a district in Gaul situated along the western Ocean. It was also called Lesser Britain, because Britons once inhabited that part of Gaul; it was called Letavia, or “the littoral,” as the author of the Life of Saint Gildas, abbot of Rhuys, reports, no. 16. It was likewise called Aremorica, as though situated beside the sea, the word supposedly being derived from *ar*, meaning “above,” and *mor*, “sea,” as Mabillon explains in his notes on the aforesaid Life of Saint Gildas, Benedictine century I. The ancients also called it the world’s outermost shore and region, because the Ocean bounded it; according to ancient opinion, that Ocean separated Greater Britain, lying beyond our world, from Gaul. Browerus provides more concerning the expansion and decline of the Armorican dominion and the various changes experienced by that people; since these matters do not bear upon our purpose, we have thought it best to omit them.]

[Note: [Col. 0128B] He praises Felix both for the antiquity and nobility of his family and for his virtue and care and solicitude in protecting his flock.]

A festive day has dawned; joy compels me,

So that, although the people could speak, I alone may speak out of love.

Although the Armorican region is the world’s farthest land,

It is seen to be foremost through Felix’s merits.

[Note: [Col. 0128C] It is credible that this Felix, whose illustrious lineage Fortunatus celebrates, belonged to the family of the Felixes, who are recorded to have once flourished in Aquitania as men of the greatest nobility and power. There survives a poem of Sidonius Apollinaris addressed to Felix Magnus, who was praetorian prefect and patrician, the son of Felix Magnus the consul. In it, when Felix had already pressed Sidonius to publish his poems, Sidonius addresses him as follows:

“Tell me, tell me what I ask, Magnus—please tell me—

Felix in name, in mind, in honor, and in fame,

In children, wife, brothers, and father,

In the kinsmen of your father and mother,

And in the great Camillus among your cousins:

Why do you order the reckless trifles of a friend,

The jokes scattered by the playfulness of tender youth,

To be reduced to the form of a little book?”]

There also survives a letter of the Emperor Constantine Augustus to Felix, the praetorian prefect, which Sirmondus reports in the appendix to the Theodosian Code; see it there. Theodoric, king of Italy, writing to the Emperor Anastasius in Cassiodorus, Letter 1 of Book II, and speaking of Felix’s consulship, says:

“Let the year take its beginning from the consul Felix; let the year dedicated by such a name enter the gate of days, and let fortune favor the rest of the prince’s portion. For what could be more desirable for us than that Rome should gather her own foster-children again to her breast and number a Gallic senator among the venerable assembly of her name? Let the senate recognize the glory of transalpine blood, a senate that has more than once clothed the crown of its nobility in the flower of this man. It knows how, among the other fasces, to choose consular men from that stock, men whose long pedigree, traced through the trabeae, is by the law of the ages native to honor.”

In Letter II, addressed to Felix himself, by which he declares him consul, he says:

“We do not permit those who are celebrated for the splendor of their lineage to remain without glory: indeed, let the grace of honors run through their ancestors … Through you the consulship of the transalpine family returns, and you have renewed its withered laurels with green growth.”]

He is seen to be foremost in merit.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] One Vatican manuscript reads *Felicis merito*, “by Felix’s merit.”]

[Col. 0129A] The East and Gaul sent forth similar destinies;

The former shines with the sun’s rays, the latter with yours.

For each supplies his gifts with a new splendor:

You bring light to the Ocean, and he to the Red Sea.

Finally, if understanding shines brightly like a lamp,

Your intellect has the likeness of light.

A most illustrious lineage, adorned with ancient titles,

Whose lofty glory thunders from its forefathers.

For whoever conquered the powerful fields of Aquitania,

That man was your kinsman by blood, by light, and by ancestry.

A venerable summit of ancient stock throughout the world,

In whose praise every distinction serves.

The flower of your family, protector of your homeland, reformer of the people,

A river of eloquence, a fountain of wit, a talkative stream.

A path of instruction, a defense in legal causes, a limit to anger,

To whose intellect the new Rome has come.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] The Paris edition reads *semina*, “seeds,” rather than *semita*, “path.”]

[Note: [Col. 0129D] One Vatican manuscript reads *hic nova Roma*, “here [is] the new Rome.”]

[Note: [Col. 0129D] Gregory of Tours relates, in Book IV of the History of the Franks, chapter 4, that Chanao, count of the Britons, after killing his brothers and wishing likewise to remove a fourth, named Macliavus, from his way, was restrained from that murder by Felix of Nantes. I think Fortunatus refers here to that deed.]

[Col. 0129B] What that city could teach through many teachers,

Gaul, content with her own citizen, is pleased to possess in you.

You bear ornaments shining with a double gift,

And here your work, there your lineage, celebrate you together.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] Fortunatus commended Felix’s intelligence and eloquence still more highly in the letter addressed to him, chapter 4 of this book.]

But you who once shone with earthly nobility,

Now rule the Church with a nobility of greater hope.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] One Vatican manuscript reads *nobilitate regis*, “with a king’s nobility.”]

At her plow [*odoratum*, “fragrant”], as a good cultivator, you continually stand,

So that you may now give many splendid gifts to God.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] One Vatican manuscript reads *cujus ad ornatum bene cultor*, “as a good cultivator for her adornment.” The Venetian edition reads *cujus ad ornatum*; two other Vatican manuscripts agree.]

You married the Church and joined happy vows,

Filling this matron with a powerful dowry.

In whose embrace you lead a life without guilt;

No other woman has been received into your heart.

You retain her in your eyes, in your mind, and with a chaste heart;

From the very place where she married you, she remains the more chaste.

She bore children for you, yet remained a virgin in body,

And, loved by you, pours forth [*fudit*, “poured forth”] a people into your embrace.

Behold your children, taken from a divine spouse,

And now they rejoice in you, whom the father’s shadow protects.

For the flock’s salvation you run through the crossroads,

And, once the wolf has been driven away, the whole sheepfold is kept safe.

With vigilant skill you drive off the ambushing Britons;

No weapons avail as much as what your tongue accomplishes.

[Note: [Col. 0130C] Browerus refers here to what we said about Felix at chapter 3 of this book. Browerus thinks Fortunatus may indicate Felix’s outstanding work in removing Pelagians from his flock, whose leader Pelagius was a Briton by nationality. I rather believe this passage refers to Felix’s virtue and shrewdness in restraining the arms and license of the Britons, lest they ravage the territory of Nantes; the following verse makes this clearer:

“No weapons are as effective as what your tongue accomplishes.”]

You are also food to the fasting, bread to the hungry;

Whatever each person desires, he sees his wishes fulfilled here.

[Note: [Col. 0130C] The Paris edition reads *ac*, “and.”]

You store your own riches in the poor man’s mouth;

You place abundant wealth in the beggar’s belly.

When Christ comes, this little purse will then present everything for you

Before the Judge’s face.

[Note: [Col. 0130C] One Vatican manuscript reads *quae si quisque*, “whatever each person [desires].”]

May salvation remain fixed for you through abundant years,

Ever fortunate in name, mind, and faith.

[Col. 0130B] [Note: [Col. 0130C] Browerus indicates in the margin that this alternative reading should be noted throughout for the final verse.]

## CHAPTER IX. To Bishop Felix, on the Easter of the Lord’s resurrection

[Note: [Col. 0130B] He celebrates the Easter festivals and joys; taking the beauty of spring as his opportunity, he describes more fully the happiness of that season and the divine mysteries being celebrated. Finally, in the poem he consecrates the diligence and labor of Felix of Nantes in winning the Saxon people and converting them to Christ.]

The seasons shine, distinguished by flower-bearing serenity,

And the gate of heaven opens with a greater light.

The orbit of heaven drives the fire-bearing sun higher,

By which the wandering Ocean emerges and enters the waters.

[Note: [Col. 0130C] In the Paris edition of 1644 and in the Lyon edition printed by Jean de Tournes and Guillaume Gazeius in 1561, where this poem is appended to Lactantius’s works, the poem begins with the two verses numbered 39 and 40 in Browerus’s edition: “Hail, festive day,” etc.; immediately afterward the two verses numbered 31 and 32 are added: “Behold, the renewal,” etc. The same arrangement occurs in the hymnary of the distinguished Tommaseo. In that book, however, the poem is mutilated: after those two couplets the poem continues, “For after the bitter depths,” etc., omitting the preceding material and also omitting the two couplets that follow—“From here the forest with its foliage,” etc., and “If the thickets now resound,” etc.—and then ends before the verses “And Felix is added,” etc. Augustus Buchnerus, in his notes on this poem, believes that the couplet “Hail, festive day,” etc., should be read where Browerus placed it. The sequence of the subject also appears to require this.]

Armed with rays and surveying the liquid elements,

It still stretches the day through the brief night in its course.

The bright heavens display a pure countenance,

And the clear stars prove their own joy.

[Col. 0131A] The kindly earth pours forth little gifts in varied birth,

When the year has restored its springtime wealth.

[Note: [Col. 0131C] The Lyon preface reads:

“When spring has flourished well, the year returns its riches.”]

Soft violet beds paint the purple field,

The meadows grow green with grasses, and the grass gleams with foliage.

Little by little the dripping lights of flowers arise,

And the grasses, colored in their own hues, smile upon the eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0131C] The same edition reads *stellantia lumina florum*, “star-like lights of flowers.”]

[Note: [Col. 0131C] The same preface reads:

“All the grasses smile with their own flowers.”]

Once the seed has been planted, the milk-bearing crop leaps up from the fields,

Promising the farmer that it can overcome hunger.

[Note: [Col. 0131C] The Venetian edition reads *late seges*, “the crop spreads widely.” The Lyon edition likewise.]

The vine-shoot weeps its joys after the trunk has been cut,

From which it may give wine, while now the vine gives water.

[Note: [Col. 0131C] The same edition reads *caudice deserto*, “after the trunk has been abandoned.”]

Rising from its mother’s bark with tender down,

The swollen bud prepares its womb for birth.

[Col. 0131B] In wintertime, when its crown of leaves has been stripped away,

The grove, growing green again, now restores its leafy roofs.

[Note: [Col. 0131C] One Vatican manuscript corrects the reading to *corpore sub hiemis*, “beneath winter’s body.”]

[Note: [Col. 0131C] The Lyon edition reads *crine refuso*, “with its foliage poured back.”]

Myrtle, willow, fir, hazel, osier, elm, maple, and walnut—

Each lovely tree applauds with its own foliage.

[Note: [Col. 0131C] The same edition reads *mista salix*, “the mingled willow,” as a correction.]

[Note: [Col. 0131C] One Vatican manuscript reads *ulmus, acernus*, “elm, maple.”]

The bee, intent on constructing honeycombs, leaving its hives,

Buzzing on its knees, snatches honey from the flowers.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] One Vatican manuscript reads *construitura favos*, “about to construct honeycombs.”]

[Note: [Col. 0131D] One Vatican manuscript reads *apes*, “bees.”]

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The Paris edition reads *increpitans*, “rushing noisily.”]

The birds are summoned back to their songs, although their music had been silenced

And they had been sluggish and mute in the winter cold.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The Venetian edition reads *avis*, “the bird.”]

Here the nightingale tunes its instruments to its own reeds,

And the breeze becomes sweeter with its echoed melody.

Behold, the renewal of the world bears witness to the grace

That all gifts have returned with their Lord.

For after the bitter depths, to Christ victorious

The grove everywhere offers its foliage and the grass its flowers.

[Col. 0131C] When the laws of hell have been crushed, and he travels above the stars,

Light, heaven, fields, and sea duly praise God.

Behold, the God who had been crucified reigns everywhere,

And all created things offer prayer to the Creator.

[Col. 0132A] Hail, festive day, venerable through every age,

On which God conquered hell and holds the stars.

The year’s nobility, the months’ distinction, the nourishing days,

The splendor of the hours, fostering the smallest points of time.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The Lyon edition reads *mobilitas anni, mensum decus*, “the mobility of the year, the distinction of the months.” The Venetian edition likewise has *mensum*. One Vatican manuscript reads *mensum decus, arma dierum*, “the distinction of the months, the weapons of the days.” Another has *mensum decus*, with *mensum* evidently used for *mensium*, “of the months,” through synaloepha. Thus Ovid, *Fasti* V.187:

“Though they do not exist, let the boundaries of the months yield to you.”]

The splendor of the hours, fostering the smallest points of time.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The Lyon edition and the hymnary of the distinguished Tommaseo read *stridula cuncta favent*, “all shrill things favor”; the Venetian edition, *stridula puncta fovens*, “cherishing the shrill points.” Two Vatican manuscripts have *scripula*. As printed in Browerus’s edition, *scrupulum* or *scriptulum* is a twentieth part of an ounce, but the word is also used for any small thing. Buchnerus notes that Fortunatus here says *scriptula puncta*, “little points,” just as Virgil uses *metra* for “words” and Phaedrus *verba* for “sayings.”]

[Col. 0132C] Priscianus Fannius, in his book on coins and weights, says: “The obolus, as Dardanus teaches, is called a *scripulus*, that is, six siliquae.” Elias Vinetus adds many notes to this passage of Fannius and says that the *scripulum* was called by the Greeks γράμμα (*gramma*), according to this couplet:

“The obolus is twice the half-obolus, which, with double weight,

The Greeks call γράμμα; our ancestors called it *scriplum*.”]

From here the forest with its foliage, from here the field with its ears of grain, applaud you;

From here the vine gives thanks with its silent shoot.

[Note: [Col. 0132C] The Lyon edition reads:

“From here the forest with its foliage, and the field with its ears, applaud you.” One Vatican manuscript reads *plaudit hio*, an uncertain form.]

If the thickets now resound for you with the whispering of birds,

Among them the smallest sparrow sings out of love.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The same edition reads:

“From here now the thickets of birds …”

“Among these the sparrow sings from excessive love.”]

Christ, salvation of the world, good creator and redeemer,

Only offspring from the Father’s divinity.

Inexpressibly flowing from the Parent’s heart,

The subsistent Word, and mighty to penetrate.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The same edition reads *et patris ore potens*, “and powerful from the Father’s mouth.”]

Equal, harmonious, sharing the same nature, coeternal with the Father,

Through whom the world received its beginning from its ruler.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] One Vatican manuscript reads *aequalis consors*, “equal companion.”]

[Col. 0132B] You suspend the heavens, heap up the lands, and spread out the seas,

And the things dwelling in their places flourish under your governance.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The same edition reads *quae moderata vigent*, “which flourish when governed.”]

When you saw the human race sunk in the abyss,

To rescue humanity you also became human;

[Note: [Col. 0132D] Three Vatican manuscripts read *mersisse*, “to have sunk”; the Venetian edition likewise.]

Nor did you merely will to be born in the body,

But in flesh that endured both birth and death.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The hymnary and the Lyon edition read:

“Nor did you merely will to be born from our body.”

The Venetian edition reads:

“For you did not merely will to be born from the body.”]

You, author of life and of the world, suffer the funeral rites,

Entering the path of death while granting the help of salvation.

The sad bonds of the infernal law gave way,

And chaos was terrified to be pressed by the face of light.

The darknesses perish, driven away by Christ’s radiance,

And the thick coverings of the earth’s night fall away.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] One manuscript reads *aeternae noctis*, “of eternal night.” The Paris edition has *tetris noctis*, “of gloomy night”; perhaps *terris* is intended, “of the earth.”]

But fulfil the promise, I pray, kindly Power:

The third light has returned; rise, my buried one.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The same edition reads *sollicitam*, “anxious,” rather than *pollicitam*, “promised.”]

[Col. 0132C] It is not fitting that your limbs be covered in a humble tomb,

Nor that worthless stones press down the price of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The Lyon edition reads *non decet ut vili*, “it is not fitting that in a worthless [tomb].”]

It is unworthy that a stone, which all things are enclosed by your fist,

Should cover you enclosed within, with the rock barring the way.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The same edition reads *non pretium*, “not the price.”]

[Col. 0133A] Take away the linen cloths, I pray, and leave the napkin in the tomb;

You are enough for us, and without you nothing exists.

Release the chained shades of hell’s prison,

And summon upward whatever has fallen to the depths.

Restore your face, so that the ages may see the light;

Restore the day that fled from us when you died.

But plainly you fulfilled everything by returning to the world,

Pious victor; the depths of hell lie crushed and do not retain their rights.

[Note: [Col. 0133C] The Lyon and Venetian editions read *pie victor Olympum*, “pious victor, [returning to] Olympus.”]

Hell, opening its hollow throat insatiably,

Which had always seized its prey, becomes your prey, O God.

[Note: [Col. 0133C] The same edition reads *qui raperet semper*, “which would always seize.”]

You rescue an innumerable people from the prison of death,

And the freed man follows wherever his author goes.

[Note: [Col. 0133C] The same edition reads *quo suus auctor abis*, “wherever you, its author, go.”]

The savage beast fearfully vomits up the people it had swallowed,

And the lamb draws the sheep away from the wolf’s jaws.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The Paris edition reads:

“The savage beast vomited out its swallowed, trembling prey.”]

[Col. 0133B] Then, returning to the tomb and taking up your flesh after the depths of hell,

As a warrior you carry magnificent trophies to the heavens.

The condemned souls whom chaos possessed it has now restored to you,

And those whom death sought are held by new life.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The Lyon edition reads *reddidit iste*, “this one restored.”]

Sacred King, behold, a great part of your triumph shines forth,

When sacred baths bless pure souls.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The same edition reads *pars magna tropaei*, “a great part of the trophy.”]

A shining army emerges from gleaming waters,

And washes away the old sin in a new stream.

A white garment also marks the radiant souls,

And the shepherd rejoices in his flock of snow.

And Felix [*hac*, “here”], the priest who shares in the reward, is added—

He who wishes to give double talents to his own Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] We can scarcely suspect that this Felix, of whom Fortunatus speaks here, was anyone other than the bishop of Nantes. It is therefore evident how mistaken were those who attributed this poem to Lactantius.]

Drawing toward better things those who wander in pagan error,

He guards God’s sheepfold so that the beast may not seize it [*raperet*, “might seize it”].

Those whom harmful Eve [*Heva*] had previously infected, he now restores

To the Church, nourished at her breast, with her milk and in her embrace.

By cultivating rugged hearts with gentle words,

Through Felix’s gift a harvest has grown from the thornbush.

The harsh Saxon people, living almost like wild beasts,

By your healing, O holy man, the beast restores a sheep.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Browerus observes that the line was formerly written most corruptly as *asper agens Saxo*, “the harsh Saxon driving.” He asks how Felix of Nantes could have exercised his piety among the Saxons, who lived so many regions away from his diocese. He thinks that a large number of them, worn down by frequent defeats at the hands of the Franks, were carried captive into Gaul, and that Felix devoted his work and generosity to purchasing them—as was then customary among deeply religious men—and winning them for Christ. See, however, what we noted at chapter 4 of this book.]

With a hundredfold return, destined to remain with you forever,

You fill the barns with the grain of an abundant harvest.

May this immaculate people grow strong in your arms,

And may you carry a pure pledge to God among the stars.

May one crown be granted you from above, through yourself,

And may another spring forth from the people you have won.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Lord Felix of Nantes, when he diverted a river elsewhere

[Note: [Col. 0134D] Browerus thinks these words of Fortunatus should be understood of the bed of the Loire, transferred elsewhere; if not, of the less celebrated and renowned Cariac River, which is not far from the city of Nantes. Concerning it the same Fortunatus sings in Book V, chapter 8, also writing to Felix:

“Where the cold Loire washes your fields with glassy water,

The beautiful land of Cariac slopes down toward the river.”]

[Col. 0134A] [Note: [Col. 0134A] He celebrates the very costly work of Felix of Nantes in diverting the course of the river—partly by constructing a new embankment, partly by lowering and excavating the old one—and describes, with no small praise of Felix, the abundance that would thereby come to neighboring peoples.]

Let the ancients yield, whatever poets remember;

Ancient achievements are conquered by new deeds.

If Homer had then witnessed rivers being enclosed,

He would rather have filled his sweet poem with that subject.

Everyone would now read Felix, and no one Achilles,

Under whose name the honor of skill would increase.

You, upright in intelligence, changing the course for the better,

Make ancient rivers run according to a new law.

[Col. 0134B] With an embankment constructed, removing the river’s course from its whirlpool,

You compel it to have a path where nature denies one.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The Venetian edition reads *erigis hinc*, “you raise from here.”]

Here you raise a valley, placing a mountain beneath its hollows;

With their positions reversed, the one swells while the other lies low.

Each has migrated into the other’s form:

The mountain sits in the valley, and the valley rises to the heights.

Where the fleeing water had been, earth grew through the sluggish barrier;

Where the prow once passed, carts now travel.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript read *hic modo plaustra*, “now carts [travel] here.” This verse was formerly read corruptly, according to Browerus, as follows: “Where the raging waters were, carts now travel here.”]

Over opposing hills you convey the winding waters,

And, with the mountain barring it, draw the obedient river along.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The Paris edition reads *collis in*, “upon the hill.”]

Where the rapid [river] would have flowed, the swift stream came and adhered,

And, when a hill had suddenly arisen, turned back its course.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] One Vatican manuscript reads *qua rapidus*, “where swiftly.”]

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The Venetian edition reads *amnis obhaesit*, “the stream adhered.”]

The waters that had previously irrigated the slopes headlong, as if without yield,

Now serve the nourishment of the people.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The same edition reads *sine fruge rigebant*, “had stood rigid without fruit.”]

[Col. 0134C] From the river another harvest arises for humankind,

When through you the water gives birth to food for the people.

How well you know how to bend the uncertain movements of men,

You who govern swift springs with your reins!

May your life, Felix, remain devout and unstained forever,

You whose command has transferred the river to another place.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Nicetius, bishop of Trier

[Note: [Col. 0134D] Gregory of Tours describes the holiness, miracles, and course of Saint Nicetius’s life in his book *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17. He also praises him in Book X of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 29, and in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 94. Chlothar drove him into exile because he had freely rebuked that king’s vices; but as soon as Sigibert had obtained the kingdom after his father’s death, Nicetius was recalled and restored to his see. He died about the year 566, on 5 December; accordingly, these poems addressed to Nicetius must be considered to have been composed not long after Fortunatus’s arrival in Gaul.

Browerus, however, dates Nicetius’s death to the year 564, but is otherwise mistaken: how could Fortunatus have known him and spoken with him, if, by Browerus’s own admission, Fortunatus came to Gaul only in 565? Moreover, Nicetius had written a letter to the Emperor Justinian, in which he attempted to recall him from heresy; Cointius assigns this to the year 566. Nicetius, however, should not be thought to have survived long after writing that letter.]

Bishop of Trier.

[Note: [Col. 0134C] He praises Nicetius, bishop of Trier, for his innocence, mercy, and generosity toward the needy and strangers; and for his pastoral care and zeal in restoring sacred buildings.]

[Col. 0135A] Splendor, summit of faith, venerable in mind, Nicetius,

Love of the whole world and head of bishops.

Supreme shepherd, surpassing in the apostolic fold,

You have increased by your merits whatever honor you possess.

Devoted to divine work, you leave earthly things behind;

For the world dies, but you, who do not die, remain.

Life is brief for all, but not that life which belongs to the blessed;

Since good things do not perish, you will rightly be everlasting.

[Note: [Col. 0135C] In Benedictine century I, where this poem is transmitted, the reading is *veneranda mente*, “venerable in mind.”]

[Note: [Col. 0135D] The same source reads *perennis erit*, “will be everlasting.”]

While you remain restrained toward yourself and generous to the needy,

Believe that, whatever you do for the least, you give to God.

Whenever a captive returns and sees his own threshold,

He receives his ancestral home; from that place you receive the heavens.

Here the exile finds help; the fasting man finds food;

He who comes hungry departs satisfied.

You place care upon the sorrowful by cleansing away their complaints,

And one remedy heals all men.

Here you dry the poor man’s tears, granting joy;

He who had previously groaned now possesses the hope of salvation.

While you feed the flocks, the wolf never snatches the lambs;

Those whom your sheepfold shelters are wholly secure.

You restored God’s ancient temples to their former height,

And, as you repair it, the old house flourishes.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] The same source reads *in lumine prisco*, “in the ancient light.”]

Here grant the peoples devout prayers for many years,

And remain a shepherd, lest the sheep be torn apart.

[Note: [Col. 0135B] The source has *hic*, “here,” rather than *hinc*, “hence.”]

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the castle of the same man above the Moselle

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Browerus places this castle of Nicetius, about which Fortunatus speaks, within Catadunum, not far from the confluence of the rivers, in the territory of the archdeaconry of Trier; even today the inhabitants call the bishop’s rock or crag by its local name. Browerus asserts this not merely as a conjecture, but also on the testimony of an old, partially damaged sheet that bore this poem under that name. In this matter we defer greatly to Browerus’s judgment, since he had personal knowledge of these places.]

[Note: [Col. 0135B] He celebrates Nicetius’s castle, situated above the Moselle, its beauty, and Nicetius’s zeal and refinement in adorning and fortifying it.]

A mountain swells on a steep slope, suspended in a massive bulk,

And the rocky cliff raises its lofty head.

[Col. 0136A] With exposed rocks, it lifts its unshorn summits;

The secure apex reigns with its raised crown.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] One Vatican manuscript reads *totus elevato*, “wholly with raised [crown].”]

The fields that recede into the valleys benefit the hills,

The earth slopes downward everywhere, while this height rises.

The swelling Moselle surrounds it, as does the little Rhone,

And the two vie in feeding the place with their fish.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Browerus observes that not far from the site where he believes Nicetius’s castle should be placed, a stream flows still called the Rhon, its name abbreviated. He thinks it is the same stream that Fortunatus calls the little Rhone.]

Elsewhere wandering rivers tear away sweet crops;

These waters bring you, Mediolanus, food.

[Note: [Col. 0136C] Browerus also attempts to associate the name *Mediolanum* with the land lying between this castle of Nicetius and the Moselle, on account of the similarity of the names. Yet after so many centuries, during which even more famous cities and kingdoms have undergone such great changes, it is not surprising that the names of one or another castle or district have disappeared and changed together with their former inhabitants and rulers. Gregory of Tours mentions the castle of Mediolanum in Book VI of his *History*, chapter 31, near which the Bituriges fought a battle after taking up arms against Duke Desiderius. Cointius places it by the River Avara in the territory of the Bituriges, under the name Magdunum, now so called. I would not dare determine whether it was the same place as the one Fortunatus mentions here.]

As the water rises, it offers fish in greater abundance nearby;

From the place where plunder comes, it provides feasts.

The inhabitant rejoices as he looks upon the fruitful furrows,

Carrying hopes for the crop under its heavy fertility.

The farmers feed their eyes on the future harvest;

By sight they reap before the year supplies its bounty.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] One Vatican manuscript reads *crescit aqua*, “the water rises.”]

[Col. 0136B] The pleasant field smiles, covered with greening grasses;

The soft meadows delight wandering minds.

This apostolic man, Nicetius, traversing these fields,

The shepherd established a desired sheepfold for the flock.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] Two Vatican manuscripts read *hoc vir*, “this man.”]

[Note: [Col. 0136D] The reading *arva peragrans*, “traversing the fields,” occurs in both Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition.]

He encircled the hill on every side with thirty towers,

And provided this construction where formerly there had been a grove.

From the highest summit the arms of the wall descend,

While the Moselle remains its boundary with its waters.

Yet a hall gleamed, constructed on the crest of the cliff,

And the house itself was a mountain placed upon a mountain.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] One Vatican manuscript reads *tuta tamen nituit*, “yet it gleamed securely.”]

He wished to enclose a broad field with a wall,

And this single house itself makes a castle nearby.

The lofty hall hangs upon marble columns,

From which the summer season looks upon boats in the river.

The structure, stretched across three levels, grew,

So that, after climbing, you might think the roofs contained acres.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] Fortunatus is expressing the size of the building: one might think broad fields were enclosed by walls and measured from the roof. We have therefore removed the comma after *jugera* and placed it before that word. He expressed the same idea above:

“He wished to enclose a broad field with a wall;

And this single house makes it lie beside the castle.”]

The tower that stands opposite, confronting the slope,

Is a place for the saints and a place where men must keep arms.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] See what we noted concerning a nearly similar description of a building at chapter 19 of Book I.]

[Note: [Col. 0136D] The Venetian edition reads *arma tuenda viris*, “arms to be guarded by men.”]

[Col. 0137A] There also is a ballista with a double flight,

Which leaves death behind it and itself flees.

[Note: [Col. 0137C] “With double flight” means, according to Browerus, a double ballista: one for throwing spears, another for throwing stones. He adds that “double flight” may perhaps refer to the wings with which a projectile, like an arrow, was equipped so that it might cut through the air more easily.]

Water is led through rigid, winding channels;

From it the driven mill carries food for the people.

He introduced smoothly flowing vines onto the barren hills;

The cultivated vineyard grows green where once there was only brush.

Orchards of grafted fruit trees rise everywhere,

And feed the place with the varied fragrance of flowers.

All these things flourish for you—whatever we praise in them—

Because you, shepherd, bestow so many rich blessings upon the flock.

[Note: [Col. 0137C] One Vatican manuscript reads *pastor opime gregis*, “excellent shepherd of the flock.”]

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Magnericus, bishop of Trier

[Note: [Col. 0137A] He praises Magnericus, bishop of Trier, for his virtue and diligence in governing his Church, for his kindness toward everyone, and for his generosity toward the needy and guests.]

The summit of honor, Father of Fathers, high priest,

The pontifical dignity advances by an upward step.

[Note: Col. 0137C: This poem is absent from three Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition.]

He whom the title of faith raised aloft through his merits,

And whom God’s dispensation made head of the Church.

Excellent disciple of good Nicetius, Magnericus,

Magnericus, to be sung under the auspices of your great name.

[Note: Col. 0137C–D: Magnericus succeeded Nicetius in the see of Trier about 566 and lived until 597. Eberwinus, abbot of Saint Martin’s monastery at Trier, wrote his Life in the tenth century; Browerus attests that he was the first to publish this poem from it.]

Illustrious through sacred merit, instructed by so great a teacher,

[Note: Col. 0137D: See what we have said on chapter 11 of this book.]

Whom you restore in a place made fruitful by good works.

As his excellent follower, preserving his holy footsteps,

Acting rightly as a minister, behold, you have become the teacher.

You are regarded as a worthy successor of the devout author,

And you remain the heir and fruit-bearing father of his inheritance.

The father grew after death, and caused you to grow,

While he takes possession of heaven, you take your place in the citadel.

For your sake, in the place of your predecessor, the nurseling flock is fed;

Nor does it mourn its own losses while it holds your gains.

Desired by the brethren, agreeable in honor to your ministers,

You please the peoples still more dearly as a pastor loved by them.

The hungry has you as bread, the stranger as shelter, the naked as clothing,

The weary as rest, and the exile as hope.

In doing these things, strive still more, venerable priest,

That you may bring back the talents entrusted to you doubled.

Also pleading for Fortunatus, your sweet lover,

You become a palm of victory for me by giving me hope of forgiveness, Father.

## CHAPTER XIV. To Villicus, Bishop of Metz

[Note: Col. 0137D–0138C: Villicus succeeded Hesperius in the see of Metz; Hesperius had attended the First Council of Clermont in 535. Villicus held the see of Metz for twenty-five years and two months, according to Cointius under the year 566, on the basis of the manuscript of Saint Symphorianus of Metz. In the manuscript copy mentioned by Browerus in his notes on this passage, however, Villicus was said to have lived under the apostolic pontificates of Pelagius I, John III, and Benedict I, and under the emperors Justin and Tiberius Constantine. Benedict I became pope in 573; Tiberius was declared Caesar by Justin in 574 and Augustus in 578. But see Cointius at the passage cited above: from the said manuscript of Saint Symphorianus he transcribes the catalogue of the bishops of Metz and the years during which they held office, and concludes that the death of the Villicus spoken of here must be placed neither before 562—the approximate year in which Fortunatus is likewise thought to have come to Gaul—nor after 566.]

[Note: Col. 0138A: He describes the situation and pleasantness of the city of Metz, then praises Bishop Villicus for his devotion and perseverance in offering prayers to God, his pastoral vigilance, his graciousness, his mercy toward strangers, and his generosity toward the poor.]

In its blue depths the Moselle loosens the sea,

And the river gently stirs its immense waters.

It laps the fragrant banks with springtime grass,

And the wave softly washes the tresses of the herbs.

From here, on the right-hand side, flows the stream where the Salia is borne,

[Note: Col. 0138C: Two Vatican manuscripts, the Venetian edition, and the Paris edition read *Salia*. The common reading is *Sallia*, as also in the Venetian edition.]

But it draws along a poorer current of water.

[Note: Col. 0138C–D: This river, Browerus observes, wonderfully both fortifies and adorns the city of the Mediomatrici. It flows in very gently from the west, descending from above. Before slipping within the city walls, it offers a remarkable play of nature to those viewing it from afar or from a height: proceeding almost parallel with the Moselle, it forms, by a circuitous course, a rather diffuse image of a heart; then, reuniting, it makes for the citadel and soon, more broadly divided into several channels, partly passes through the city and partly washes the outer walls, until at last it empties into the Moselle. Fortunatus speaks of the river Salia in book VII, chapter 4: “Or he who approaches Metz, taking his name from the Sale.”]

Here, where it enters the Moselle in clear-running channels,

It fills the other river’s strength, and itself disappears.

Here stands beautiful, gleaming Metz, founded in this place,

[Note: Col. 0138D: Metz, a most famous city in Gaul, was a seat of the kings of Austrasia, although they also resided at Rheims, because, I suppose, of the extent of their dominion and the diversity of their affairs, since their kingdom stretched even into Germany. For Metz as the royal seat of Austrasia and for the city’s site, see Fortunatus himself, book X, chapter 9. This city was first burned by the Huns under Attila, and later captured and devastated by the Vandals. See Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 6, and Fredegar the Scholiast, *Fragments*, no. 5.]

Glad that fish surround both its sides.

A delightful countryside smiles in its green fields;

Here you see cultivated crops, and there you behold roses.

You look upon hills clothed with shady vines;

The region vies with itself in varied fertility.

A very well-fortified city, which wall and river enclose,

You stand more securely still through the merits of your bishop.

[Note: Col. 0138D: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *pontificis merito* (“through the bishop’s merit”).]

Villicus, who thus serves well with heavenly weapons,

Lying on the ground upon his knees, raises you through his prayers.

From there, holy priest, you cast yourself humbly upon the earth;

By praying here, you lift your country’s head to the stars.

By constant tears you acquire joys for the people.

The shepherd’s tears make the sheep rejoice.

Although the wicked man threatens with ineffective blows,

You, being their wall, make them fear no wounds.

[Note: Col. 0138D: The Venetian edition reads *in quibus es* (“among whom you are”).]

And even though the wolf lies in wait for the enclosed sheepfold,

With you as guardian of the flock, no robber harms you.

[Note: Col. 0138D: The Venetian edition reads *nil sibi* (“harms itself/himself”), rather than *nil tibi* (“harms you”).]

You delight the peoples with a serene face free of cloud,

And gentle grace cherishes the hearts of all.

If a new guest asks for aid, you extend provisions;

Under your roof he finds a home of his own.

While you satisfy the complaining stranger, he more readily forgets

The wealth he possesses in his native land as an exile.

From him who recounts his losses you draw his groans from his mouth;

[Note: Col. 0139C: The Venetian edition reads *subducit ab ore* (“draws away from the mouth”).]

Restoring joy, you drive away every sorrow.

Here you protect the naked; there you feed the needy.

The poor man gives you nothing in return; God returns love.

You send provisions ahead, preserving your stored goods more wisely;

The riches which you thus distribute are given by paradise.

You have renewed the heights of the temples, Villicus, their devoted guardian;

When the Lord comes, behold, your labor will remain.

I see that you have not buried the talent entrusted to you,

But that the work you desired is multiplied still more.

May you carry out such worthy deeds through many extended years,

[Note: Col. 0139C: The Venetian edition reads *longius extensos*; one Vatican manuscript reads *longius extensus*.]

And may your name, excellent man, remain forever.

## CHAPTER XV. To the Same

[Note: Col. 0139C–D: This poem, like the following one, seems to have been recited by Fortunatus after he had been received at Villicus’s table. During his journey through Germany into Gaul, I would suppose that Fortunatus formed his friendship with Villicus and was treated by him with many acts of kindness and gracious hospitality.]

Excellent shepherd of the flock, your pastures benefit everyone;

[Note: Col. 0139D: One Vatican manuscript reads *pabula praesunt* (“the pastures preside”), corrected here.]

You satisfy souls; how well you cherish their bodies!

Thus you return greedy guests filled with the nectar of milk,

So that the bowl lifts up what the spoon is accustomed to hold.

## CHAPTER XVI. To the Same

The sheep runs back to you, pastor, seeking its pastures from you;

You who are accustomed to be its food, give me the help of bread.

## CHAPTER XVII. On a Painting of a Vine, Spoken at His Table

[Note: Col. 0139C: On the occasion of a painting in which a bird was picking grapes with its beak, he praises Villicus’s generosity toward his guests.]

On a vine woven beneath its shade, a bird flourishes,

And lightly plucks the painted delicacies with its beak.

The guest deserved to possess abundant dishes:

Here he gazes upon grapes, there he drinks Falernian wine.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Fish at His Table

[Note: Col. 0140A: On the occasion of the fish abundantly served at Villicus’s table, he commends Villicus’s heavenly calling to pastoral office.]

Your nets, Father, overflow with burdensome fish;

[Note: Col. 0139D: The Venetian edition reads *retia vestra patent* (“your nets are open”).]

It is clear that you have deserved to take Peter’s place.

[Note: Col. 0139D: The same edition reads *apparet et Petri* (“and Peter’s [place] appears”).]

## CHAPTER XIX. To Charentinus, Bishop of Cologne

[Note: Col. 0140A: He praises Charentinus, Bishop of Cologne, for his hospitality and singular charity toward his neighbors, for his calm and peaceful character, his mercy toward the poor, and his generosity toward the churches.]

Charentinus, glory of faith and friend of the Godhead,

Your name itself proclaims an enduring love.

[Note: Col. 0139D–0140A: Charentinus succeeded Somoenus in the see of Cologne and preceded Ebregisilus, who in 590 was sent by King Childebert as envoy to settle dissensions and disturbances in the monastery of Poitiers, as Gregory of Tours reports, *History of the Franks*, book X, chapter 15. Charentinus is therefore wrongly placed after Ebregisilus in the catalogues of the bishops of Cologne, as Cointius observes under the year 562; there he reports, following the judgment of Henry Pantaleon in part I of *On Illustrious Men of Germany*, that Charentinus held the see until 560. I would add that he held it beyond 564, so that he could have been known to Fortunatus, who did not arrive in Gaul until about 565, as we have shown in his Life, no. 27 and following.]

Powerful Cologne, the city of Agrippina, presents you as its bishop,

A worthy cultivator of God’s fruit-bearing fields.

[Note: Col. 0139D–0140C: Cologne Agrippina, or Agrippinensis, was founded by Agrippina, the wife of Germanicus, as Tacitus relates in the *Annals*, book XII, chapter 27: “To display her influence even among allied nations, Agrippina ordered veterans and a colony to be settled in the town of the Ubii, where she had been born; the colony was given a name derived from her own.”]

If you see people born of any nation whatsoever,

Though unknown, you immediately make them your own.

Those whom once you bind to yourself with affection and fatherly devotion,

You can never afterward separate from yourself.

Nor does your love suddenly withdraw like a fugitive,

But the grace once granted quickly remains fixed,

Fulfilling God’s command, just as you love yourself.

So every human being near you is loved.

You are rightly regarded as a worthy follower of the apostolic utterance,

Which set loving hearts before faith.

[Note: Col. 0140D: The Venetian edition reads *proposuit fidei* (“proposed to faith”) instead of *praeposuit fidei* (“placed before faith”).]

Calm, peaceful, gentle, serene and free of cloud,

[Note: Col. 0140D: One Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition read *placidusque mihi* (“and peaceful to me”).]

You whom the world’s fury cannot dominate.

You refresh everyone’s hearts with the sweetness of your word,

And with your face you gladden sorrowful hearts.

You are food for the poor, and nourishment for the hungry,

A true father of the people, giving the help of salvation.

You renew golden temples, supported by precious [variant: splendid] beauty;

[Note: Col. 0140D: Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 62, relates that near Cologne Agrippina there was a basilica built in memory of fifty martyrs of the Theban Legion. Because it shone with marvelous workmanship, being almost gilded with mosaic, the inhabitants called it the Basilica of the Golden Saints. Fortunatus seems to indicate that Charentinus renewed or restored this basilica with the verse: “You renew golden temples, supported by precious beauty.”]

You shine, and from you the house of God gleams with honor.

So that the temples may be capacious enough for a greater number,

A second suspended row is provided above.

The devout care of the flock occupies you, excellent shepherd;

While you keep watch, the wolf snatches nothing from the folds.

May you hold happy seasons through a long span of years,

And through you may the Lord’s sheep be multiplied.

## CHAPTER XX. On Igidius [manuscript: Egidius], Bishop of Reims [manuscript: of the Remi]

[Note: Col. 0141A: He warmly praises Aegidius, Bishop of Reims, for his diligence in caring for the flock entrusted to him, for the force of his eloquence and his learning in instructing the people, and for his beneficence toward the wretched and afflicted.]

[Note: Col. 0141C–D: This Aegidius was a very powerful man with King Childebert, who sent him as envoy to Chilperic to transact, in his name, matters of the greatest importance and to settle the dissensions that had arisen between them. Later, convicted of conspiracy and treachery against that same Childebert, he was deposed from the priestly rank by a synod of bishops and exiled to Strasbourg. This happened in 590; before then Aegidius, still flourishing in the reputation of integrity and in great influence and favor with kings, is praised by Fortunatus in this poem. Read Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 19.]

Venerable summit of office, Igidius, through your excellent deeds,

Your merits have caused your rank to grow in honor.

I am restrained by my own ability, yet compelled by ready love,

Gladly to reveal a few words in praise of you.

For I seem guilty of so great a charge

If I alone remain silent about what resounds everywhere.

But although I cannot acknowledge it in worthy speech,

Forgive me for having wished to speak according to my desire.

The fame of your deeds has gone out into the world,

[Note: Col. 0141D: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *exiit in mundo* (“has gone out in the world”).]

And through your own merits you shine like a star in the world.

You shine more brightly than the morning star with your serene face;

It gleams through its rays, but you shine through devotion.

The wolf snatches nothing by stealth from the guarded fold,

While you, holy shepherd, keep vigilant watch over the flock.

With eloquent speech you pour forth heavenly doctrines,

And under your instruction the house of the Church has grown.

[Note: Col. 0141D: Flodoard, *History of the Church of Reims*, book II, chapter 2, relates that Aegidius increased the patrimony of the Church of Reims with many possessions, especially through King Childebert’s generosity.]

Through the bishop’s devotion you are regarded as the people’s correction,

[Note: Col. 0141D: One Vatican manuscript reads *correctio plebis alumnae* (“correction of the fostered people”).]

Lest darkness cause harm; you are a path of light.

You revive everyone’s hearts with the sweetness of your word;

You satisfy them with feasts and feed the flocks with your mouth.

The commandments are fulfilled; we are not nourished by bread alone.

We receive the delights conveyed by your words.

As the body rejoices when gentler food is prepared for it,

So souls rejoice when your tongue sounds forth.

Heresy and anger fall before you, Christ’s mighty soldier;

You win subjects for the King who gave you your weapons.

You clear the fields of thorns with your cultivated speech,

And everywhere a harvest cleansed for God rises up.

Whoever comes here exiled, sad, weary, and poor

Receives his own homeland here, because you restore his strength.

You remove the groans of the one who has suffered, turning them into joys;

You take away exile and restore a home through love.

[Note: Col. 0141D: The Venetian edition reads *quae doluit* (“the things that suffered”), rather than *qui doluit* (“the one who suffered”); one Vatican manuscript reads *reddis amore dapes* (“through love you restore provisions”), rather than *Lares* (“a home”).]

The poor man gains food, and the naked also deserves clothing;

Here everyone finds whatever good he desires.

You provide one common remedy for all,

For you are the father of the people and rightly govern so many things.

[Note: Col. 0141D: The printed reading is *regis* (“you govern”); the bracketed alternative is *geris* (“you carry out/manage”).]

May this life of yours endure long, with the Lord granting it,

And may the life to come shine with a brighter day.

## CHAPTER XXI. To Hilary, Bishop

[Note: Col. 0141D–0142D: Browerus thinks that this was Hilary, Bishop of Gévaudan; but since he attended the Council of Clermont in 535, I am surprised that he lived down to Fortunatus’s time. Indeed, Evanthius is reported to have succeeded Hilary of Gévaudan; Evanthius attended the Fourth Council of Orléans, held in 541. See the learned Ruinart’s notes on the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6, numbers 4 and 5. Another Hilary was Bishop of Digne, who was already seated in office by 554. Perhaps this was the man to whom Fortunatus wrote this poem?]

[Note: Col. 0142A: He sends a letter of greeting to Bishop Hilary and declares his remembrance and goodwill toward him in his absence.]

Sincere light of my spirit, always sweet Hilary,

Although absent, whom my care beholds.

[Note: Col. 0142D: The Venetian edition reads *semper mihi dulcis* (“always sweet to me”).]

Your honorable love has so filled my heart

That without you I never speak with an empty mind.

In brief verses I entrust my prayers for your health;

May what affection has given be dear to you, I pray.

[Note: Col. 0142D: The bracketed reading is *grata* (“pleasing/dear”), rather than *chara* (“dear”).]

## CHAPTER XXII. To Bertechramnus, Bishop, When He Was Raised into the Carriage

[Note: Col. 0142D: Bertechramnus was Bishop of Bordeaux and related by marriage to the mother of King Guntram, as Gregory of Tours reports, *History*, book VIII, chapter 2. He attended the Second Synod of Mâcon, held in 585, and died that same year after returning from the synod, as Gregory of Tours relates, *History of the Franks*, book VIII, chapter 22.

There was also another Bertchramnus, Bishop of Le Mans, who succeeded Badegisilus around 586; Gregory of Tours speaks of him in book VIII, chapter 39. He was one of the bishops who contributed their efforts and authority toward suppressing the disturbances at the monastery of Poitiers, of whom Gregory speaks in book IX, chapter 41. I would not venture to determine to which of these Fortunatus is writing here, since the dates of both coincide with Fortunatus’s lifetime.]

[Note: Col. 0142B: Fortunatus, having been received into the carriage by Bishop Bertechramnus as an honor, dedicates this poem to Bertechramnus’s graciousness toward himself and his humanity and goodwill toward everyone else.]

This is the kind of carriage that Gaul calls a *rheda*;

Its smoothly moving wheel cuts across the ground.

Springing forward on its double yoke, it flies upon its swift axle,

And the joined four-horse team sets the rapid wheels in motion.

While I, serving, am joined to the same retinue,

And while my limbs were soon to be carried by the horses,

I was snatched up and raised onto the axle by the hand

Of the holy bishop Bertechramnus, in honor of his office.

As a mother swallow tenderly warms her featherless young,

And gently covers them with outstretched wings,

So, powerful in goodness and rich in excellent affection,

The pastor places me in his soft seat as one of his own.

Nor does his devout mind embrace only me, but it loves everyone,

So that a unique love may shine more greatly among the peoples.

[Note: Col. 0142D: One Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition read *unus* (“one”) instead of *unicus* (“unique”).]

## CHAPTER XXIII. To the Same, on His Little Works [His Works]

[Note: Col. 0143A: He says that he received Bertechramnus’s poems, composed in grand and inflated language, and praises them in part, while in part he notes and criticizes them.]

I undertook lofty epigrams on sheets that had been sent,

And words revolved in the buskined style of a *sophus*.

[Note: Col. 0143B–C: *Sophus*, used for popular applause and the acclamation of people approving some wise saying or written work, derives from the Greek *sophōs* (σοφῶς, “wisely”). It is used in this way by Martial in several places and by Sidonius Apollinaris, *Letters*, book I, letter 9; book VIII, letter 6; book IX, letter 13; *Poems*, poem 8; and elsewhere, as Browerus also observes. Here, however, Fortunatus plainly uses *sophus* for elegance and dignity of diction, in which sense he often uses it elsewhere.]

Running through poems foaming with an inflated rhythm,

I thought that I was setting sail upon a billowing sea.

The level page belched forth stormy waves,

And, like Ocean, poured back waters from its source.

Only with difficulty does venerable Rome hear poems

So splendidly adorned and polished in such a bright style

In Trajan’s Forum.

[Note: Col. 0143C: One Vatican manuscript reads *Trojano*, corrected to *Trajano*; two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *Oceanas* (“Ocean’s waters”), rather than *Oceanus* (“Ocean”).]

[Note: Col. 0143C–D: Sirmondus, in his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris, *Letters*, book III, letter 8, and on Dict. VII of Magnus Felix Ennodius, indicates that rhetors used to declaim not in only one Roman forum but in several. Lampridius gives similar evidence concerning the Athenaeum, saying in his Life of Alexander that the emperor frequently went to the Athenaeum to hear Greek and Latin rhetors or poets. An old annotation in the Apuleian manuscript of the Vatican Library concerns the Forum of Mars, as Sirmondus reports in his notes on Sidonius’s third book, letter 8. Finally, Fortunatus refers here and in book VII, chapter 8, to Trajan’s Forum.

Browerus observes in his notes on this passage that statues used to be erected in Trajan’s Forum to men distinguished by some excellence of intellect and letters; he confirms this from the testimony of Volaterranus and Sidonius, since such examples sharpened human talents and studies toward imitation of the same glory. Thus Ennodius, Dict. VII, entitled “At the Dedication of the Auditorium,” when the transfer to the forum had taken place, writes: “As the field rouses the soldier, the sea the sailor, the forums the advocate, and secluded places the robber, so auditoria exercise tongues. For what reason would persuade silence in a place where rewards for words have been established? Where is the palm of eloquence, if here the favor belongs to silence? The price of labor is well paid where there are temples of victory,” and so forth. But see Sirmondus’s notes on Sidonius, poem 9.]

What if the Senate had heard such a distinction recited into its ears?

They would have spread golden threads beneath your feet.

[Note: Col. 0143D: We have corrected *plantis* (“beneath the feet”) from the Venetian edition, in place of *blandis*.]

Through places, through peoples, through every crossroads you would have seen

Your little verses running, with the common people applauding.

Yet I noticed certain things in your speech:

That you speak of new thefts from an old poem.

In a few places an added syllable has broken the meter,

And the music, wounded in its own foot, lies limping and groaning.

[Note: Col. 0143D: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read *cloda gemit* (“limps and groans”) rather than *clauda jacet* (“lies lame”).]

Now, venerable Father, I greet you with prayer, vow, and voice,

Commending my spirit with a suppliant heart.

May your life be long, for through your tuneful Muse

We are compelled to return words to the games we desire.

## CHAPTER XXIV. To Agricola, Bishop

[Note: Col. 0143D–0144C: Browerus thinks that this Agricola, or Agraecula, was the Bishop of Chalon, whose father, a man of senatorial rank, had shown Fortunatus such munificence and generosity. I agree more with Cointius, who prefers to identify him as Agricola, Bishop of Nevers, who obtained that see around 580; attended the First Council of Mâcon in 583; and, together with the other bishops, exercised his authority in suppressing the disturbances at the monastery of Poitiers, as is clear from Gregory of Tours, book IX, chapter 41. He died in 594, from which it may be understood that he was approximately Fortunatus’s contemporary.

Agricola, Bishop of Chalon, whom Gregory of Tours praises in book V of his *History*, chapter 46, died in 580 at the age of eighty-three, after having held office for fifty-eight years. It therefore scarcely seems likely that his father was still alive when Fortunatus came to Gaul, much less that he could have instructed and raised his son Agricola.]

.

[Note: Col. 0144A: Writing to Agricola, he recalls the benefits his father had bestowed upon him and asks that the son nourish and bring to completion what his father’s diligence and labor had planted in him.]

Bishop, summit of honor, pinnacle of lineage and faith,

Powerful cultivator of the field, excellent shepherd of the flock,

Since my soil deserved to be plowed by the hand of your father,

Let it be cultivated again by the plowshare of his son.

For by his deed, a father memorable to the sweet world,

He cherished two of us with a single love, you and me.

A parent in heart, a nurse in nourishment, a good teacher in speech,

He loved, honored, directed, and gave honorable things.

He sowed the fallow ground broken up by devout effort;

What your father poured out, let this seed nourish me.

## CHAPTER XXV. To Felix, Bishop of Bourges, Written on His Tower

[Note: Col. 0144C: This Felix was made Bishop of Bourges in 568; he attended the Fourth Council of Paris in 573 and died not long afterward. Gregory of Tours praises his holiness in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 102.]

[Note: Col. 0144B: He celebrates in verse the tower that Bishop Felix had arranged to be built for containing the most holy body of Christ.]

How well joined things are made beautiful, as when the Lamb’s sacred body

Is borne within a great golden *margaritum*.

[Note: Col. 0144C–0145D: Among Greek writers, *margarita* denotes particles of the sacred Eucharist, cut into small pieces from the host—of which the priest took one quarter—and preserved for the sick. The vessel in which they were kept was called Μαργαρίτις (*Margaritis*) by later Greeks, as Franciscus Richardus teaches in his *Relation of the Island of Saint Irene*, p. 221, as cited in Du Cange’s *Glossary*. Prudentius also mentions a great *margaritum* in the poem entitled *Psychomachia*, where, describing the hall of Wisdom, he writes:

“Within, the house is built, resting upon seven columns,

Of cold crystal, cut from a glassy rock;

Their raised summit a shining white stone covers,

Cut into a cone, and beneath, with a hollow

Withdrawn in the shape of a shell, which the great

*Margaritum*, purchased for a thousand talents,

With wealth and revenues, by courageous faith had secured.”

From these verses its appearance and form can easily be inferred. It may also be gathered that such a *margarita* took the shape of a cross and was therefore called a little cross, from a book *On the Blood of Christ* preserved at Anchin and printed by Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. III, p. 699.

Browerus aptly observes concerning this passage that Felix’s care in constructing a *margaritum* to carry and contain Christ’s sacred body corresponds to canon 3 of the Second Council of Tours, which Germanus of Paris is found to have attended and subscribed. That canon decreed that the Lord’s body should be placed upon the altar not in an imaginary arrangement but under the sign of the cross; or, as Cointius explains, not among the sacred images customarily placed above the altar, but beneath the cross itself, which was customarily placed in the middle of the altar as the more distinguished and elevated location. Browerus is mistaken, however, in reporting that Felix attended the Second Council of Tours with Germanus of Paris, by whom he had formerly been ordained bishop: the council was held in the sixth year of Charibert’s reign, that is, in 566, whereas Felix became bishop only in 568; nor is Felix’s name found anywhere among the other bishops who attended the synod. See Cointius under the years 566 and 568.

Cointius, under the year 566, no. 19, proves through many examples and testimonies this ancient custom of the Church of preserving fragments of the holy Eucharist, which Fortunatus here admirably displays. See that passage.]

Let Solomon’s vessels of metal yield to chrysolite;

This workmanship makes these things more pleasing, and so does faith.

[Note: The printed reading is *ars* (“art/workmanship”); *arx* (“citadel”) is the bracketed variant.]

May the gifts Felix has given to you, Christ, be such

As those which the shepherd Abel once offered from his flock.

And you, who see his heart, make it equal in piety to the merit of Sarepta,

Who gave her two small coins.

[Note: Col. 0145D–0146C: The common reading is *ut raptae merito* (“as deservedly seized”), while Baron, in the appendix to volume VII, restored *par viduae merito* (“equal in merit to the widow”) from the Trier and Saint Gall manuscripts. Browerus restored *Saraptae merito* (“of Sarepta”), supported by the Vatican manuscripts and Venetian edition, which read *Siraptae merito*; one Vatican manuscript reads *Syraptae*. Browerus then attempts to explain why Fortunatus called the Gospel woman praised by Christ in Luke 21:1 and following—because she put two small coins into the treasury—“of Sarepta,” confusing her with the widow of Sarepta who received Elijah as a guest. He attributes this to the similarity of their circumstances and generosity, and to the fact that both represented the Church.]

## CHAPTER XXVI. To the Holy Lord, a Lord Worthy of Praise for Apostolic Deeds, the Devout and Especially Beloved Father in Christ, Avitus, Pope

[Note: Col. 0146C: The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript add: “Fortunatus, the humble.”]

[Note: Col. 0145A: He celebrates the hospitality of Avitus, Bishop of Clermont, and his diligence in feeding and protecting his flock; he also recalls certain gifts that Avitus sent to him, Agnes, and Radegund.]

Avitus, devoted to pious duties, Father of the world,

Glory of bishops and our lofty love.

[Note: Col. 0146C–D: Avitus succeeded Cautinus in the see of Clermont. Cautinus died in 571, carried off by the pestilence that raged that year in Italy and Gaul, concerning which Gregory of Tours speaks in book IV of his *History*, chapter 31. Saint Avitus’s death is assigned to 594, according to Cointius, following John Savaro in his *Origins of Clermont*. Gregory of Tours praises this Avitus warmly in book IV of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 35. The same Gregory relates in *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 2, that this holy bishop’s zeal prompted him to devote himself to ecclesiastical writings.]

Through whom people, countrymen, foreigners, and guests are nourished,

And in whom everyone finds whatever he desires.

[Note: Col. 0146D: Gregory of Tours, book IV, chapter 35, praises Avitus’s hospitality thus: “If a stranger came to him, he was loved in such a way that he recognized in him both a father and a homeland.”]

Though undeserving because of my work, I have received the pious gifts of my patron,

So that you would not be forgetful even of the smallest sheep you feed.

You lead flocks by your voice toward Christ’s eternal pastures;

You also care how they may live from this place.

[Note: Col. 0146D: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *cura tui* (“care of you”) rather than *cura tua* (“your care”).]

Your wing always protects those who are absent as though present;

Where your foot does not run, you are wholly present through your gift.

[Note: Col. 0146D: The Venetian edition reads *munere totus adis* (“by your gift you wholly approach”) rather than *munere totus ades* (“by your gift you are wholly present”).]

By reason of your gifts, Agnes and Radegund,

Praying, render thanks with the manifold warmth of their speech.

O lofty Father, sow talents that are to penetrate the heavens,

Which, cultivated in their season, you may reap a hundredfold.

[Note: Col. 0146D: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *ad coelos* (“to the heavens”); the Venetian edition reads *seris* (“you sow”), rather than *seras* (“that you may sow”).]

Through the good Lord and King, I beg you, bishop honored at court—

[Note: Col. 0146D: Fortunatus seems here to indicate Avitus’s favor with his king, about which Gregory of Tours gives further information in book IV of his *History*, chapter 35.]

May you, gracious one, remember your Fortunatus.

## CHAPTER XXVII. By the Same to the Same

[Note: Col. 0145C–0146A: Avitus had insisted that Fortunatus write some verses; Fortunatus says that he has complied, excusing the weakness of his talent and the poverty of his language, which he says are compensated by his good wishes.]

We have obeyed your commands, holy and venerable priest,

And, Father, your orders, sweet Avitus.

Rather with the light, shrill sound of a hemlock pipe

Than with a clear melody does my Muse give pleasure.

Yet, lover of devotion, grant forgiveness;

Attend to my obedience, and do not weigh the *sophus* too strictly.

[Note: Col. 0146D: The Venetian edition reads *intende obsequium* (“attend to the obedience”) rather than *intende obsequio* (“attend to my obedience”).]

For a great gift I offer these small, modest things;

Let them be measured by my prayers, since my tongue is unskilled.

[Note: Col. 0146D: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *est cui lingua* (“whose tongue it is”) rather than *est quia lingua* (“since the tongue is”).]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. To the Same

[Note: Col. 0146A–B: He commends Avitus’s remarkable ability to win people’s hearts and bind them to himself through affection, especially his generosity toward foreigners and guests, as well as his other virtues; he also declares his own particular devotion and goodwill toward him.]

You prove, highest of priests, sweet Avitus,

What honor the exalted faith of virtues deserves.

You bind everyone’s hearts in blessed love,

And, dear Father, draw captive hearts behind you.

Yet among those whom your sweetness has filled,

I am driven forward as the greater portion in affection.

My sweet light, strength of my homeland, nourisher of the needy,

Hope of foreigners, guide and honor of fathers.

If my voice resounded with unbroken sharpness in song,

I would speak less in praise, but more in love, Father.

Yet this greatest opportunity for my prayer is granted me:

To recall your sacred name, excellent man.

Agnes and Radegund likewise commend themselves

To the love of your devotion, with humble and equal voice.

May your life flourish through long years that bring salvation;

For whatever your well-being is, dear one, becomes my own.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Lord Agericus [to Agericus], Bishop of Verdun

[Note: Col. 0147D: Agericus succeeded Desideratus in the see of Verdun in 550, while still a citizen of Verdun. He was highly favored by King Childebert, whom he himself had received from the sacred font. He was a man distinguished by exceptional devotion and illustrious merits of life. He died around 588 from profound grief and mental anguish, which he had conceived because of the killing of Guntram Boso, for whom he had given surety, and of Berthefred, whom he had been unable to defend from Childebert’s attendants when Berthefred had taken refuge in Agericus’s oratory, as well as because of the violation of the sacred place. Read Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IX, chapter 23.]

[Note: Col. 0147D: One Vatican manuscript reads “to the bishop of Verdun.”]

[Note: Col. 0147A: He praises Agericus, Bishop of Verdun—also called *de Veroduna* or *Virodunum*—for his beneficence toward the poor, his diligence and learning in feeding the flock, and his generosity toward the temples.]

Although the city of Verdun is enclosed within a small circuit,

You please, enlarged by the merits of your bishop.

[Note: Col. 0147D: Verdun is a city of Belgica I, situated very pleasantly on the Meuse and well supplied with basilicas, monasteries, and churches. It belonged to the province of the metropolitan see of Trier; formerly it was renowned in the kingdom of Lothar and more recently in the German Empire, where its county, held by the local bishop, was not obscure. Browerus, in his notes on this passage.]

A greater grace shines within your narrow bounds;

Agericus, your honor has increased it still more.

You have poured forth very many seeds of great praises,

Which you reap when they have ripened through the fertility of your deeds.

[Note: Col. 0147D: One Vatican manuscript reads *fertilitate metes* (“you will reap through fertility”).]

In the present age you generously give sustenance to the needy;

For this the future day will multiply your riches a hundredfold.

Pastor, you unlock the inner chambers of hidden doctrine,

And you feed the flocks not only with food but also with your mouth.

You build new temples upon old ones, and new ones with greater splendor;

[Note: Col. 0148D: Agericus built or restored several basilicas at Verdun; see Cointius under the year 562, no. 47.]

While you serve, the Lord’s house becomes more refined.
