You fill the sacred baptismal fonts with excellent waters;

[Note: Col. 0148D: The Venetian edition reads *egregius fontes* (“excellent fonts”) rather than *egregios fontes* (“excellent waters”).]

Filled with such devotion at the divine font, you act with holiness.

This hall shines white with sincere serenity,

And, even if the sun should flee, daylight remains here through art.

From every side eager peoples hurry toward the new temples.

And you grant the peoples more of God through love.

The needy has deserved you as comfort, the naked as clothing,

And you alone remain drink and food for all.

Happy is the one who, a lover of eternal light through his merits,

Prepares things that will not perish within so short a time.

# CHAPTER XXX. On Ageric, Bishop of Verdun

[Col. 0147C] [Note: [Col. 0147C] [He likewise praises Ageric for excellence in learning, contempt for human affairs, innocence of life, sincerity, knowledge of divine matters, and generosity toward the poor.]]

When Phoebus raised his lofty chariot into the ether,

he scattered his pure, fiery radiance everywhere;

with his outpoured rays he claims the whole world for himself,

filling mountains and plains, and possessing the low places and the heights.

So you, bishop, shine with the sun through the splendor of your soul.

The sun gleams with his own rays, and he with yours.

Sacred Ageric, by whose cultivated speech

the harvests of the Church delight in their fertility.

Barren of earthly things, fruitful in things above,

scorning human affairs, you go forth rich toward the heavens [polos].

[Col. 0148A] Pure amid the world’s allurements, rejecting its wantonness:

the bitter love of the flesh has stolen nothing from you.

Slippery guilt perishes; nor does death rejoice in crime.

When you see your members free from sins,

by dwelling in holy temples you are regarded as pure,

so that your heart, Father, may be a holy temple of God.

Christ chooses to hide himself in such a vessel;

he himself possesses the house that he purified for himself.

There is no deceit upon your lips, nor savage clouds in your mind;

in sincere souls, daylight blooms upon your lips.

You pour forth a river eloquent in speech from a leaping spring,

and you nourish barren understanding by watering it with your voice.

You open to the earth the lofty mysteries of heaven:

through you one knows, fears, prays to, and loves the Lord more.

By divine doctrine, eloquent bishop, you triumph,

[Col. 0148B] giving admonitions as a shepherd [Note: [Col. 0148D] The same edition: “giving admonitions as a shepherd”],

lest error oppress the sheep.

You refresh them with the delights supplied by heaven, earth, and water,

and food satisfies the peoples from one side, faith from the other.

The poor receives help, the sorrowful hope, the naked clothing;

whatever you have, you make available to everyone.

May lasting salvation remain with you here, although [Note: [Col. 0148D] Paris edition: “light”] the future lies beyond,

and for a long time, shepherd, may you offer prayers for your flock.

# CHAPTER XXXI. To Amphion, a Venerable Presbyter

[Note: [Col. 0148B] [He praises the presbyter Amphion for piety, sweetness of character and speech, prudence and firmness both of spirit and judgment, moderation in exercising authority, and hospitality.]]

A man glowing with piety, blossoming with gentle sweetness,

in whose countenance a precious mind shines.

Amphion, dear Father to me, venerable priest,

and love whom my heart must always hold.

[Col. 0148C] [Note: [Col. 0148D] In one Vatican manuscript the couplet “When first, etc., I perceived, etc.” is placed before the preceding one: “Amphion, dear to me, etc., and always, etc.”]

When, as I deserved, I first came to know you by the light of your face,

I perceived that the light of understanding was within you.

Whoever new person you see, you make a close acquaintance;

if you do not know his lineage, he becomes your kinsman in spirit.

Joyful pleasure invites everyone to conversation [Note: [Col. 0148D] One Vatican manuscript: “invites everyone by conversation”],

and you continually compel them all to be yours in one accord.

Lively in intelligence, firm through disciplined understanding,

fixed everywhere, remaining steadfast by the weight of your counsel.

You wisely guide the reins of mature old age [Note: [Col. 0148D] In two Vatican manuscripts: “you rule skillfully”],

and you know how to regulate the step of one to whom honor is due [Note: [Col. 0148D] Venetian edition: “whom he honors”].

Ready for every distinction, you overflow with generous goodness,

and whoever comes into the world joins himself to you.

[Col. 0149A] Flowing with human kindness [Note: [Col. 0149C] One Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition: “flowing, humane”; Venetian edition: “flowing with human things”], you offer nourishment to those who come,

and your house becomes one house for all peoples.

For Pope Leontius extols you in his own words [Note: [Col. 0149C] One Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition: “Leontius offers”];

we believe these things on the judgment of so great a man.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] It is likely that this Amphion belonged to the clergy of Bordeaux, since Fortunatus says here that he was commended by the testimony of Leontius of Bordeaux.]

# CHAPTER XXXII. To Paternus the Abbot, on the Correction of a Manuscript

[Note: [Col. 0149D] P. Browerus thinks that this was Paternus the abbot, who later became bishop of Avranches, a man conspicuous for outstanding piety. But since he died in 563, as Cointius believes, or at the latest in 565, as the distinguished Mabillon judges in his notes on the Life of Saint Paternus in the first century of the Benedictine collection—and thus several years after he had attended the Council of Paris held in 557—it is difficult to suppose that Fortunatus could have known him and been familiar with him. For what shall I say of Paternus still being an abbot at the time Fortunatus lived in Gaul, when Paternus had already spent thirteen years in the episcopate? Read his Life in the first century of the Benedictine collection, p. 152 of the Paris edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0149A] He praises the abbot Paternus for piety and holiness; then he asks pardon if some error had slipped into the manuscript which, at Paternus’s command, he had undertaken to correct or copy.]

At last we have obeyed your commands, venerable priest;

you rightly bear the office of your name, Paternus [Note: [Col. 0150C] In two Vatican manuscripts: “Paternus, you rule”].

You who adorn the altars of Christ by your own merits

give what is pleasing to God both by prayer and by vow.

Yet I beg you, forgive me if I have perhaps been mistaken;

for this hand of mine is accustomed to harbor error.

May the page now sent in supplication obtain your greeting [Note: [Col. 0150C] Venetian edition: “sent forth greeting”];

when you read it again, may you remember me.

# CHAPTER XXXIII. To Druco the Deacon

[Note: [Col. 0150C] The title in the Venetian edition reads: “To Druco the deacon, now a presbyter.”]

[Note: [Col. 0149B] [Fortunatus sends greetings from the maritime region where he was living to Druco the deacon, and expresses most affectionately his goodwill and remembrance of him.]]

Good Druco, powerful minister of the Lord’s altar,

from here I hasten to send you this work of greeting.

The swelling sea of Ocean flows around us,

while Paris holds you too, dear companion.

The Seine [Note: [Col. 0150D] The Seine is a river near Paris] keeps you; the British tide surrounds us;

one love binds us together though separated by land.

[Col. 0149C] Here the sea’s fury does not remove your face from my sight,

nor does the north wind carry away your name, my friend.

You so often return within my loving heart

as the sea’s wave returns in winter.

As the sea is shaken whenever the east wind has blown,

so my spirit does not stand without you, dear friend.

Gentle weather burns within my calmed breast,

and with varied movement draws me toward you.

But remember me, and return the prayer of one who asks,

that God may give his gifts equally to us both.

May grace enrich the human mind through Christ,

and may our minds and lips be free for our Lord [Note: [Col. 0150D] In two Vatican manuscripts: “for our holy Lord”].

# CHAPTER XXXIV. To the Archdeacon of Meaux

[Note: [Col. 0150D] Meaux lies in Lugdunensis Quarta, under the archbishop of Sens; today its see, according to Orontius Fineus, is the celebrated city of Meaux on the Marne, known for the Council of Meaux held there sometime around the year of Christ 840 under Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims. Browerus, in his notes on this passage.]

[Col. 0150A] [Note: [Col. 0150A] [He thanks the archdeacon of Meaux in this poem because, although he had not yet met him face to face, the archdeacon had sent him new wine as a gift.]]

If it had been granted me to see your face,

I would have offered many words in return for so great a gift.

Your dear goodwill sent us new wine,

and sweet gifts prove a sweet disposition.

You prepared to satisfy one whom you had not seen:

what will you do for one who is known to you?

May God give you abundance, since with faithful mind,

great minister, you care for the bishop’s flock.

# CHAPTER XXXV. To John the Deacon

[Note: [Col. 0150B] About to undertake a journey, Fortunatus left this poem with John the Deacon as a lasting pledge of friendship, and through him sends greetings to their common friends.]

Always memorable pledge of our friendship,

receive these little verses, dear John [Note: [Col. 0150D] Is this the same John the Deacon of whom Gregory of Tours speaks in Book I of On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapters 19 and 88? When he had departed from Gaul as a leper and gone to Palestine, he was washed in the waters of the Jordan and cured of leprosy; then he returned to Gaul, bringing with him relics of blessed Mary?].

So that, when places perhaps unknown to me carry me away,

I may not seem, in your heart, to be absent from your affection.

Through you I greet Father Anthemion, venerable man,

whose affection strengthens and impels me.

I likewise insert into my verses Hilary,

steadfast with us in love, whom my heart cherishes [Note: [Col. 0150D] Paris edition: “partly”].

May you remain forever in a blessed age through your merits;

when you read these things too, may you remember me.

# CHAPTER XXXVI. To Anthemion the Deacon

[Note: [Col. 0150C] He excuses himself to Anthemion because, unwilling to wake him from sleep, he departed without greeting him.]

Receive these little verses, Anthemion, a pledge from one who loves,

which love has poured forth for you from a sincere heart [Note: [Col. 0150D] Paris edition: “which your love pours forth from a sincere heart”; in the margin, as in Browerus].

While sleep held your gentle eyes,

and made your weary limbs lie upon the bed,

while I hesitated, I did wrong, unwilling to disturb your rest;

thus my fault will be the cause of your sleep.

I departed silently, like a thief, without any sign;

nor, embracing you [Note: [Col. 0150D] Paris edition: “embracing”], did I say: “Beloved brother, farewell.”

I could not entrust my message to your loving heart,

nor did even a single hour remain for your words.

[Col. 0151A] I call the Lord to witness that I am deeply troubled

because I depart in this way [Note: [Col. 0151B] Three Vatican manuscripts: “because I depart in this way”] and carry away none of your words.

But what I could have said to you in person, had I wished to say more,

let this page sent forth now speak in a few words.

Yet I ask you to grant me these gifts before God:

may you always shine everywhere, dear to all.

Let no one provide me with clothing or gifts [Note: [Col. 0151B] In two Vatican manuscripts and the Paris edition: “let no one provide money”];

whatever sweetness counsels, let no one deny me this.

# CHAPTER XXXVII. To Sindulphus the Deacon

[Note: [Col. 0151A] [He encourages the deacon Sindulphus to endure labor under Christ’s yoke, in hope of the promised fruit and reward, affirming that nothing is burdensome to one who loves.]]

Brother [Note: [Col. 0151B] This poem is absent from the Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript], memorable for a worthy deed through the love of God,

fixed in my heart [fote], brother [Note: [Col. 0151B] This type of poem, in which the following pentameter closes with the half-line of the preceding hexameter, is called “Ophite,” or “serpentine,” because it advances like a serpent through various turns and recurrences. This kind of poem was uncommon among the ancients, as Browerus observes. Fortunatus uses it elsewhere as well, namely in Book VIII, chapter 2. Paul the Deacon likewise wrote a poem of the same form and meter in praise of Saint Benedict; it appears in Book I, chapter 16, of his works. Apollinaris Sidonius, writing in Book VIII, Letter 11 about the poet and orator Lampridius, also mentions this type of poem, calling them “echoic elegies,” and reports that Lampridius practiced this kind of composition. He seems to call them “echoic” because the half-line that has already sounded is returned again to the ears of the listeners like an echo. Sirmondus (see him), in his notes on Sidonius, cites for this purpose a distich about Echo from an epigram by Pentadius, composed on the coming of spring in echoic elegies. Here it is:

> Through hollow rocks Echo resounds to the lowing of cattle,  
> and the voice, rebuffed by the hills, resounds through hollow rocks.

The rhetor Cestius, in Seneca the Elder, Book VII, *Controversies* 7, called repetitions of this sort even in prose “ἠχώ, echo,” and would immediately shout to a student reciting: “μὴ τὴν ἠχώ” (“not the echo”). Read Sirmondus, in the preface to the cited passage.]

Go gladly along the road that leads to the hall of heaven;

so that you may rise higher, go gladly along the road.

Bear patiently the burden, lest the holy load weary you;

whence rest awaits; bear patiently the burden.

It is fitting to submit your neck, for Christ’s yokes are sweet;

that we may deserve help, it is fitting to submit your neck.

Whoever cultivates his own fields ordinarily keeps full granaries;

and the man who cultivates his own fields will not be hungry.

The sailor flies across the sea, seeking to increase his wealth;

so that he may prosper through his merchandise, the sailor flies across the sea.

He does not fear death when the storm rages furiously,

so that he may win riches; he does not fear death.

The soldier comes to arms, seeking the palm through wounds;

so that he may return victorious, the soldier comes to arms.

[Note: [Col. 0152B] Although Browerus’s edition reads “rewards,” as printed here [Col. 0152C], we have no doubt that “battles,” not “rewards,” should be read, so that the beginning of this verse corresponds to the final part of the following one. Fabricius certainly printed “rewards” in his *Collection of Ancient Christian Poets*, not “battles,” as did the Paris edition.]

Take your rewards gladly, dear companion, as I do too;

from which triumph will arise, take your battles gladly.

Whoever comes through love does not know that he bears labor;

no one is laid low by labor who comes through love.

As I bring little songs, I return to you the greeting owed to you;

grant better things, I pray, as I bring these little songs.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0151]

## CHAPTER I. Epitaph of Evemerus [Eumerius, Eumerus], Bishop of the City of Nantes

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Eumerus, or Evemerus, was the predecessor of Felix of Nantes, of whom we have often spoken. He attended the Second Council of Orléans in 533 and the Fourth, held in 541. He died in 549 or 550, having obtained the see of Nantes in 531, according to Cointius.]

[Note: [Col. 0151D] [He praises Evemerus, bishop of Nantes, after his death, for nobility of birth, gentleness and mildness of spirit, hospitality, mercy, beneficence toward the poor, care and diligence toward the sick, and generosity toward churches.]]

Although all things are snatched away from the world by eager, rapid flight,

nevertheless blessed life prolongs the day.

He suffers no loss from his end whose glory lives,

and, sent to the stars, he holds an eternal place.

Thus Evemerus rests in this gracious tomb,

through whom the honor of bishops rises richly.

[Col. 0152C] A summit descended from a noble line shines

from its origin [Note: [Col. 0152D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Paris edition: “he traces his ancestry, he shines,” etc.]; [Note: [Col. 0152D] Venetian and Paris editions: “shining from his origin”]

and by his merits he caused his ancient ancestors to grow.

A memorable double gift shone forth among the peoples:

in one respect a judge by office, in another a father by piety.

[Col. 0152D] Sweet in speech, tranquil in sacred governance,

in whose understanding anger found no place.

He conquered another’s passion with a patient heart;

when levity wounded him, he bore it with gravity.

If some guest hurried from foreign dwellings,

he soon felt that he had his own household with this man.

Here the rough exile wished to dwell, away from his native shores,

forgetting his former father through love of this one [Note: [Col. 0152D] Venetian edition: “here, wishing to have dwelt”].

He rejoiced and smiled; seeing the other weep, he approved,

and soon made the other’s tears his own.

[Col. 0153A] He shared his lot with the hungry, guided by piety [Note: [Col. 0153C] One Vatican manuscript: “he shared his portion with the hungry”];

where grief arose, there he immediately offered prayers.

Rich toward the poor, he transferred his wealth to the needy;

he gave in advance, before they suffered need [Note: [Col. 0153C] Three Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition: “before help was sought”; I think this reading should be followed].

He scattered rich seeds with a hundredfold harvest,

and now delights in the mature harvest of their return.

His one concern was to visit all the sick;

he himself was their physician, and he himself lived as their food.

He raised the summit of the church, which he handed on entire [Note: [Col. 0153C] The same source: “which alone resisted”];

it came to an heir who would enlarge the work [Note: [Col. 0153C] On the dedication of this church, see Book III, chapter 6].

That blessed man departed, leaving Felix in his place;

the Father lives in the world through the merits of his heir.

## CHAPTER II. Epitaph of Lord Gregory, Bishop of the City of Langres

[Note: [Col. 0153C] Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres, died in 539, as Cointius demonstrates under that year. He had attended the Council of Épaone in 517, the First Council of Clermont held in 535, according to the same Cointius, and the Third Council of Orléans, celebrated in 538 through the presbyter Evantius. Gregory belonged to a senatorial family. When he had sought and obtained the office of count at Autun, as Gregory of Tours relates in chapter 7 of *The Lives of the Fathers*, he exercised justice with such religious seriousness that none of the guilty escaped his deserved penalties. Later made bishop of Langres, he governed that Church with outstanding piety and diligence, and died renowned for miracles. Fortunatus confirms what we have related about Gregory of Langres in these two verses:

> Before, a fierce judge; afterward, himself a devout priest.  
> Those whom he subdued as judge, he cherished with a father’s love.]

[Note: [Col. 0153B] [He praises Gregory, bishop of Langres, for the antiquity of his family and lineage, for charity and piety in exercising his pastoral office, and by this poem consecrates his memory, already renowned for miracles.]]

After the heavenly Prince broke open Tartarus,

you lie beneath the feet of the just, hostile death.

The venerable life of holy Gregory bears witness to this,

for now, after the tomb, he enters the heavens in honor.

Noble, descended through an ancient line of parents,

now more noble in deeds, he remains above the stars.

Before, a fierce judge; afterward [Note: [Col. 0153D] Paris edition: “and afterward”], himself a devout priest;

those whom he subdued as judge, he cherished with a father’s love [Note: [Col. 0153D] One Vatican manuscript: “those whom he diminished as judge”; three Vatican manuscripts: “he cherishes with a father’s love”].

He piously ruled the flock for thirty-two years,

and as shepherd he possesses the joys of Christ’s flock.

If you ask about his merit, miracles of events proclaim it;

through him, it is said, friendly salvation comes to the weak.

## CHAPTER III. Epitaph of Lord Tetricus, Bishop of the City of Langres

[Note: [Col. 0154C] Saint Tetricus was the son and successor in the same see of Gregory of Langres, mentioned in the preceding chapter. For Gregory of Tours relates of him in *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7: “He had a wife named Armentaria, whom he is said to have known only for the sake of propagating offspring; by her, with the Lord’s generosity, he had sons . . . after his wife’s death he turned to the Lord, and, elected by the people of the city of Langres, was ordained bishop.” Tetricus is mentioned there as the son and successor of Gregory of Langres. He enlarged and adorned the basilica in which Saint Gregory, his father, had been buried, and Gregory of Tours reports that he also transferred the tomb to a newly erected apse of marvelous workmanship. Tetricus himself was later buried in the same basilica near his father, as the distinguished Ruinart records in his notes on Gregory of Tours, *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7, and Cointius under the year 539.]

[Col. 0154A] [Note: [Col. 0154A] [He commends Tetricus, bishop of Langres, already dead, for diligence in guarding his flock, for learning, and for mercy toward the needy and weak; then he recalls the goodwill of kings and people toward him.]]

Palm of the priesthood, Tetricus, in venerable worship [Note: [Col. 0154D] One Vatican manuscript: “Tetricus, in countenance”],

your native see holds you, while we are held by exile [ten/holds].

With you as a pious guardian, the wolf never carried off the lamb,

nor did the sheep, fearing the thief, nibble at its pasture.

Bearing nearly six lustra [Note: [Col. 0154D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Paris edition: “six times five years”] and, in addition, three years,

you ruled the flock with a peaceful shepherd’s love.

For, so that hearts might be seasoned with divine flavor,

you continually poured sweet salt from your mouth.

Highest love of kings, glory of the people, arms of parents [manuscript: “of the powerful”],

cultivator of the Church, honor of the nobility,

food of the poor, protector of widows, guardian of children—

you were a shepherd, everything to all in every duty.

But for those to whom your care offered varied healing,

the people now grieve sadly at the death of their ruler.

Yet this we hope, gracious Father: worthy in the stars,

as you shine there in honor, may you prove yourself here in piety [Note: [Col. 0154D] Two Vatican manuscripts: “may you prove yourself here in piety”].

## CHAPTER IV. Epitaph of Lord Gallus, Bishop of the City of Clermont

[Note: [Col. 0154D] Saint Gallus was made bishop of Clermont around 527 and died in 554, as Cointius demonstrates under that year, no. 3. Gregory of Tours commemorates his most noble lineage in *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6, in these words: “His father was named George, and his mother Leocadia, descended from the line of Vettius Epagathus, whom the history of Eusebius testifies was martyred at Lyon; they were so distinguished among the leading senators that nothing more generous or noble is found in Gaul.” Saint Gallus was the uncle of Saint Gregory of Tours, since Florentius, a senator and father of Gregory of Tours, was the full brother of Saint Gallus. See Gregory of Tours, *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 14, no. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0154B] [He commends the vigor of Saint Gallus, bishop of Clermont, from childhood onward, in leaving his household and relatives in order to follow Christ; his favor with King Theuderic; and his gentleness, learning, and vigilance in carrying out his pastoral office.]]

Unjust enemy, by fraud you drive Adam from paradise;

behold, God grants his servants access to the heavens.

Envious one, thus your death prepared better things for humanity:

you expel them from the earth, but he gives his own the stars.

This blessed bishop Gallus bears witness and proves it,

noble on earth, rich as he goes to the heavens [Note: [Col. 0155C] Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts: “as he goes to the heavens”].

Supported by Christ’s help, while not yet advanced in years,

he came to hate his home, seeking greater things [Note: [Col. 0155C] One Vatican manuscript: “with love”; Paris edition: “through the love of hatred”].

He escaped his father’s embraces [Note: [Col. 0155C] Gregory of Tours relates in *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6, that when Saint Gallus’s father sought a girl from a senatorial family as a marriage partner for him while he was still a boy, Gallus fled to the monastery called Cournon, six miles from Clermont; there the abbot received him, and he became a monk and cleric, with his father’s consent] and left his mother [Note: [Col. 0155C] One Vatican manuscript: “and left his mother”].

An abbot and father was sought there to govern the monk.

There the inexperienced novice began, from his noble youth,

to endure the weapons of the Lord’s warfare.

At last, with the holy bishop Quintianus as his learned teacher,

a man proved in heart is more beautiful than gold [Note: [Col. 0155D] Venetian edition: “a man proved in heart is more beautiful than gold”].

From there he was transferred to the king’s palace,

and lived, Theuderic, through your devoted affection.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] When reports reached King Theuderic that Saint Gallus excelled in the wondrous sweetness of his voice and the delight of his singing, he summoned him to the royal household and loved him so much that, as Gregory of Tours relates, he loved him more than his own son. The queen, Theuderic’s wife, also loved him greatly—not only for his exceptional sweetness and skill in singing, but also for the integrity and chastity of his character, by which he surpassed others.]

When his teacher soon left the earth and sought the stars,

the care of the flock was handed over to the disciple [Note: [Col. 0155D] Gregory of Tours, in the passage cited repeatedly above, relates how Saint Gallus was substituted in the place of the deceased Quintianus] [Note: [Col. 0155D] One Vatican manuscript: “to guard the flock”; Venetian edition: “to hold the flock”].

For, guiding the reins of the episcopate, he governed it in such a way

that as shepherd he was a father in his duties through love.

Gentle, patient, good, fair, loving and lovable,

this was no place for offense, but for pardon.

If some offense came upon him, it became a virtue;

from where anger could arise, from there came triumph.

Nourishing the people with his voice, like a nurse her children at the breast,

he sprinkled them with sweet honey seasoned with salt [Note: [Col. 0156A] “giving”].

In carrying out this work, he foresaw the gifts of the future:

under such a shepherd, he knew that nothing could perish from the flock.

Thus as Father he governed the Church for five five-year periods [Note: [Col. 0156C] Gregory of Tours relates that Gallus died in the sixty-fifth year of his life and the twenty-seventh of his episcopate. Fortunatus perhaps reduced the number of years to conform to the demands of meter, using *lustra* for years—a usage that can also, though rarely, be found in the Glossary of Du Cange’s new edition. Saint Gallus attended the Council of Clermont in 535, the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541, and the Fifth in 549. Cointius assigns his death to 554. Certainly he died after the Fifth Council of Orléans, which he attended, as stated above, and before the death of King Theudebald, who survived Saint Gallus for some time, as appears from Gregory of Tours, Book IV of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 6. His death must therefore be placed between 549, the year of the Council of Orléans, and 555, the year Theudebald died. See Ruinart’s notes on chapter 6 of *The Lives of the Fathers*. Browerus, in his notes on this poem, says that the sixty-fifth year of Saint Gallus’s life was the year 573 of Christ, although King Theudebald had died long before; Saint Gallus nevertheless died while Theudebald was still alive, as Gregory of Tours explicitly asserts in the cited passage.]

while nonetheless living beyond twice thirty lustra.

Hence, carried by a better road to the holy realms above,

he is not pressed by the urn of the funeral pyre, but is held in God’s arm [variant: hall] [Note: [Col. 0156D] Paris edition: “the urn”; in the margin, “the arm”].

## CHAPTER V. Epitaph of the Two Ruricii, Bishops of the City of Limoges

[Note: [Col. 0156D] Limoges, today Limoges, is a provincial city in the archbishopric of Bourges, in Aquitania Prima, not far from the sources of the Vienne, according to Browerus on this passage.]

[Note: [Col. 0156A] [He praises Ruricius the grandfather and Ruricius the grandson, both bishops of Limoges, men of extremely noble birth who have died, for their generosity toward churches and beneficence toward the poor; because of their outstanding merits he does not hesitate to number them among the saints.]]

Although, envious death, you threaten with rapid jaws,

you cannot claim authority over the saints.

For after Christ, returning, conquered savage Tartarus,

you lie defeated beneath the feet of the just.

Here the tombs cover the sacred limbs of bishops

shining throughout the whole world; their spirit inhabits the stars.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] The elder Ruricius was bishop of Limoges at the time when Clovis waged war against the Visigoths, as Cointius relates under the year 508. He was a contemporary of Sidonius Apollinaris and was bound to him by the closest friendship and goodwill, as the letters written by Ruricius to Sidonius sufficiently demonstrate—Book I, letters 8, 9, and 16, as they appear in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers of the Church*, Lyon edition, vol. VIII, p. 559. Sidonius himself, in poem 2, celebrates Ruricius’s marriage to Iberia, daughter of Ommatius; from this marriage came Ommatius, who later presided over the Church of Tours, of whom Gregory of Tours speaks in Book X of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 31.

The other Ruricius, called the younger and the nephew of the elder, was made bishop of Limoges. He attended the First Council of Clermont in 535 and the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541, and sent Bantaridus, his archdeacon, to preside in his name at the Fifth Council of Orléans. The author of the *Life of Saint Junianus the Hermit*, which appears in Book IV of the *Lives of the Western Fathers*, relates that this Ruricius, afflicted by an evil spirit, was freed through the prayers and fasts of Saint Junianus. Subsequently, mindful of the benefit he had received, after being made bishop of Limoges he built a basilica in memory of Saint Junianus, into which the saint’s body was brought.]

The twin flowers through whom Rome was joined

to the ancestral summit of the Anician family [Note: [Col. 0156D] The most noble family of the Anicii has been made illustrious by so many people that it needs no commendation from our writings. Let Saint Jerome alone stand for all the others; in Letter 97 of the Paris edition, writing to Demetrias, he says: “Now I must recall the famous names of the Probi and the Olibrii, and the illustrious lineage of Anicius, in which scarcely anyone, or no one at all, failed to deserve the consulship.”].

[Col. 0157A] Joined in deed, mind, rank, name [Note: [Col. 0157C] One Vatican manuscript: “in rank, hope, and name”; Venetian edition: “with rank accumulating from the name”], and blood,

they rejoice together, the grandfather on one side and the grandson on the other.

Each in his own time founded holy temples for a patron:

the one built Augustine’s, the other Peter’s.

This one was upright, that one devout; this one serious, that one serene,

each striving equally to see which would be greater than the other.

Giving very much to the poor from their abundant wealth,

they sent to heaven riches that would follow them.

With hands scattering wealth, redeeming the sins of the world,

we believe them to be among the apostolic choirs.

Blessed are those who, from fleeting nobility [Note: [Col. 0157C] The same manuscript: “from fleeting weakness”],

have purchased and possess in heaven the rights of the senate.

## CHAPTER VI. Epitaph of Exotius [Manuscript: Esocius], Bishop of the City of Limoges

[Col. 0157B] [Note: [Col. 0157B] [He praises Exotius, also bishop of Limoges, for outstanding chastity, patience, gentleness, devotion toward churches, and beneficence toward the citizens. He recalls the people’s longing for him and remembrance of him.]]

[Col. 0158A] Although trembling old age weighed upon the bishop,

nevertheless the people wished this father to survive them.

Or if the things owed to nature could be changed,

the flock would have hastened along its way in place of its shepherd.

But since that was not permitted, let that hope console the people [Note: [Col. 0157C] *Consulat* is used for *consoletur*, “may console,” although this is a rare usage, as Browerus notes. The same word in the epitaph of Vuilithuta is understood as “may be a consolation”];

faith has carried this man to the stars in accordance with his merits [Note: [Col. 0157C] Two Vatican manuscripts: “because of this man’s merits”].

By preserving his spotless limbs for God through chastity,

Exotius earned a day without end [Note: [Col. 0157D] Paris edition: “Ocius here earned”; in the margin, “Exotius”].

Within his breast patience reigned victorious,

his understanding an anchor amid such great waves.

[Note: [Col. 0157D] One Vatican manuscript, explaining *felle carens* as “free from gall,” that is, from anger. Paris edition:

> He bore a spirit nourished by peaceful sweetness,  
> and did not know how, in offenses, to return anger in kind.]

Free from gall, peaceful in spirit, nourished by sweetness,

he did not know how to return anger for offenses.

Cultivator of temples, reviving the citizens by his song [Note: [Col. 0157D] Paris edition: “by his governance”; in the margin, “by his song”],

Wounds—

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Fortunatus here seems clearly to allude to certain calamities and disturbances of the city of Limoges, in enduring which Exotius displayed remarkable patience. Since the city was often harassed and afflicted, it is useful to explain which of those disturbances and misfortunes corresponds to Exotius’s time. Gregory of Tours relates, in Book IV of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 48, that King Chilperic, after invading and devastating the cities of Sigibert, “among the rest,” he says, “having raised an army, invaded Limoges, Cahors, and the other provinces belonging to them, ravaged and overthrew them. He burned churches, stripped them of their sacred vessels, killed clerics, demolished men’s monasteries, dishonored those of maidens, and devastated everything; and at that time there was worse lamentation in the Churches than during the persecution of Diocletian.” These events took place around the year 573, at which time King Guntram had summoned the bishops of his domain to Paris to settle these disputes. See the notes of the distinguished Ruinart on Book IV of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 48, and the annals prefixed to Gregory of Tours’s works, under the year 573.]

Moreover, a great revolt took place at Limoges in the year 579, when Chilperic imposed new and burdensome assessments [Col. 0158C] throughout his kingdom, so that the people of Limoges, oppressed by taxes, rose in revolt and overpowered the royal official. As a result of this crime, the most grievous disasters overtook the wretched city. Gregory of Tours speaks of this revolt in Book V, chapter 29.

Finally, this city also seems to have suffered some calamity at that time, when Chilperic, after occupying the cities of his brother Guntram, appointed new counts over them and imposed new taxes upon them; among these cities Limoges may perhaps be reckoned by Gregory of Tours, Book VI of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 22. This occurred in 582.

P. Browerus expressly asserts in his notes that in this poem Fortunatus is speaking of the disturbances that arose between King Chilperic and King Guntram, which we placed third, since Nonnichius, count of Limoges, appointed by Chilperic, had proved unjust [Col. 0158D] and wicked toward Charterius, bishop of Périgueux.

But Browerus failed to notice that these events, which he himself thinks fell within Exotius’s lifetime, occurred around 582, as is clear from Gregory of Tours, whereas Ferreolus was then in charge of the city of Limoges. Ferreolus took part in the Second Council of Mâcon in 585, and he was the very man who saved the city of Limoges from utter calamity and destruction in 579, coming to Chilperic as an intercessor after the revolt had broken out—the revolt we placed second, as may be read in Gregory of Tours, Book V of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 29.

It therefore remains that Fortunatus is speaking of the calamity we reported first, which better fits the times of Exotius, since Browerus himself openly admits that Exotius succeeded Ruricius in the see of Limoges.]

was a faithful remedy for his native city.

[Col. 0158B] Having completed three lustrums in the honor of the episcopate,

he proceeds to the ancient fathers, while the people mourn.

It is therefore not fitting to lament him with empty complaints,

for, after the world’s darkness, the court of heaven now holds him [Note: [Col. 0158D] The edition adds in the margin:

“Whom the court of the Most High now holds in joy.”].

## CHAPTER VII. Epitaph of Calactericus [Note: [Col. 0159B] Calactericus, or Caletricus, succeeded Saint Leobinus in the see of Chartres around the year 556, as Cointius shows under that year. He took part in the Third Council of Paris in 557 and subscribed to its acts, and then in the Council of Tours in 566. Concerning this Caletricus, certain things are related in the *Life of Saint Leobinus*—which appears in the first century of the Benedictine edition, p. 123, and which we have appended to Fortunatus’s works, and which also appears in the second part of this edition—that it will not be out of place to report here, in order to shed further light on the memory of this man. The following is therefore read in section 23:

“A certain blessed man named Caletricus, noble by birth but nobler in merits, was appointed bishop at Chartres after the death of blessed Leobinus. While still in the rank of presbyter, he made himself pleasing both in the sight of God and in the eyes of men by his holy way of life. He was then seized by such severe illness that he scarcely breathed his last breath. His venerable sister, named Mallegundis, quickly sent messengers to the holy bishop, asking him to send blessed oil for the relief of her brother’s illness. He himself came immediately with the oil and requested silence from everyone, saying: ‘Lord, who know all things, if you judge this servant of yours necessary to your Church or to your people, restore him to health by your assisting power.’ Then, as soon as the sick man had been anointed with the oil of sacred unction, he was restored to such a degree of health that no affliction of illness ever again touched his limbs. To demonstrate the holy man’s power, the remaining portion [of the oil] was changed into such radiant beauty that to all who were present it seemed that not the sheen of oil but the brilliance of crystal was shining. This clearly foreshadowed that he who was to become a bishop would, through episcopal ministry, sanctify the oil of consecration and shine with divine virtues through heavenly grace.” Mallegundis, who is named in the testimony just cited as Caletricus’s sister, is thought by some scholars to be the same person as Monegundis, of whom Gregory of Tours speaks in the *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 19. But we discuss these matters more fully in the notes to the *Life of Saint Leobinus*.] bishop of the city of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0159D] Chartres—commonly called CHARTRES—lies between the Loire and the Seine. It is a renowned town on the Eure, subject to the metropolitan see of Sens. Its territory was formerly called the pagus of Chartres, as is read in the example of the treaty between Kings Childebert and Guntram in Gregory, Book IX, chapter 20. —Browerus].

[Col. 0159A] [Note: [Col. 0159A] [In this poem he mourns Calactericus, bishop of Chartres and his friend, who died prematurely. He celebrates the man’s eloquence, kindness of spirit, mercy toward the needy, the sweetness of his voice and singing in psalmody, his diligence in governing his church, and his care in tending his flock.]]

My eyes weep tears; my inmost being is shaken by grief,

and my trembling fingers cannot write what is harsh.

Since I now give the buried man the words

I wished to give him while alive, I am forced to speak bitterly in sweet verse.

Worthy of your merits, Calactericus, priest,

late known to me, how quickly, dear friend, you depart!

You return to your homeland; you leave us sadly beneath the city [Note: [Col. 0160C] The Venetian edition reads “beneath the world.”],

while the shining court holds you and a tearful [dark] day holds us.

[Col. 0159B] Behold, beneath this tomb the limbs of a pious man rest;

his tongue, sweeter than honey [and sweeter from the tomb, according to the edition],

lies buried.

A handsome form, a fitting spirit, endlessly kind,

a sweet voice, mindful beforehand of God’s law.

The clergy’s hope, protector of widows, bread of the needy,

the care of his relatives, ready for every good deed [Note: [Col. 0160C] The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts read: “wholly devoted to every good deed.”].

He sang the instruments of the psaltery with sweet melody,

and, praising, touched God’s blessed plectra [Note: [Col. 0160C] The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read *et tetigit laudi* (“and touched [them] for praise”); the reported reading *laudis* means “of praise.”].

Skillfully purging the wounds of illness with the cautery of his speech [Note: [Col. 0160C] One Vatican manuscript reads *clautere* instead of *cautere*, with a correction; the Venetian edition reads “purging the wounds” (*purgando vulnera*)],

he was a faithful healer to the flock as he tended it.

Having lived six lustrums and eight additional years [Note: [Col. 0160C] Browerus prefers to understand Fortunatus here as indicating the number of years during which Calactericus sat as bishop, rather than the number of years he lived. But this is wholly impossible. Since Leobinus, bishop of Chartres, died around 556, having taken part in the Council of Paris in 551—as the learned Mabillon shows in his notes to the *Life of Saint Leobinus*, first century of the Benedictine edition, p. 128, Paris edition—Caletricus cannot be said to have become bishop of Chartres before that year. Moreover, since Pappolus, Caletricus’s successor in that see, complained gravely to the Fathers of the Council of Paris in 573 against Promotus, who had invaded a place in his diocese [Col. 0160D], there certainly were not thirty-eight years between Leobinus’s death and Pappolus, the total which Fortunatus gives here. It follows, therefore, that these must be the years of Calactericus’s age; he was accordingly made bishop while still young and died while still young.],

he was taken justly from earth and returned to the stars.

[Col. 0160A] With you restored as a citizen to the feasts of paradise,

the world groans, while heaven rejoices in its honor.

And because I do not doubt how great your glory of praise is,

you, a friend of God, ought not to be mourned.

These small words, holy Father, I whisper in place of great things;

I beg you, pray for your Fortunatus.

## CHAPTER VIII. Epitaph of Chronopius [Note: [Col. 0160D] Chronopius occupied the episcopal see of Périgueux in 511, when he took part in the First Council of Orléans; he was still alive in 533, when he took part in and subscribed to the Second Council of Orléans.] bishop of Périgueux.

[Note: [Col. 0160A] [He praises Chronopius, bishop of Périgueux, after his death, for his innocence, noble birth, courtesy, sincerity, eloquence, and pleasant speech; for his mercy toward the poor, generosity toward the townspeople, diligence in protecting his flock, and liberality toward churches.]]

If, sacred man, earthly care had once been yours,

I would now give more tears than words in verse.

But because you are pure and the world’s crimes are not yours,

you urge us to rejoice, since you remain without death.

Bishop burning with piety, venerable Chronopius,

the tomb covers your limbs, but your spirit holds the stars.

The succession of priests, which flowed from both parents [Note: [Col. 0160D] From this passage Browerus conjectures that Pegasus, that bishop of Périgueux praised by Paulinus in Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 13 of the *History of the Franks*, may have been the father or grandfather of this Chronopius. But in so obscure a matter I do not wish to decide anything unless further light comes from elsewhere, since Fortunatus could have designated here as Chronopius’s relative no more readily Pegasus than another bishop, whether of Périgueux or of another see.],

brought the episcopal crown to its heir.

Holy succession rightly prepared this rank for you,

so that the honor might already seem due to you by merit.

Noble, coming from the ancient line of fathers,

but nobler still in Christ through merit.

His face was always calm, his mind serene;

his heart was sincere, his brow without a cloud.

[Col. 0161A] Nectar flowed through his words from his eloquence,

so that you would surpass sweet honeycombs with your moistening mouth.

You were clothing for the naked, a covering for the shivering;

whoever fled to your roof returned himself protected [Note: [Col. 0161C] One Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition read: “whoever was at your roof.”].

You placed all your wealth in the bellies of the poor.

Thus living talents always remain for you.

The hungry deserved to receive you as food, the thirsty as drink,

the afflicted and exile as help.

You filled with their own citizens the city that had been widowed,

and, by redeeming them, they saw their native homes again.

The sheep, which the wolf had carried away from the fold in snarling plunder,

rejoices, restored to the flock by you, its shepherd [Note: [Col. 0161C–D] The Venetian edition has masculine *quem lupus* rather than feminine *quam lupus*, and reads *pendente rapina* (“with the plunder hanging”) for *frendente rapina* (“in snarling plunder”); it also reads “with you as shepherd of the flock.”].

Swiftly you restored the burned churches to their ancient height [Note: [Col. 0161D] As Cointius records under the year 530, Chronopius completed the basilica of Saint Front and transferred the saint’s body from an old shrine to a more splendid place. This translation is celebrated on the day before the Ides of October. The burned churches which Fortunatus says Chronopius restored, however, seem to indicate hostile fire, perhaps set to the sacred shrines by the Goths.],

and hence your house stands undefiled in heaven.

You yourself lived eight lustrums in the body,

but now, in accordance with your merits, may your day endure without end [Note: [Col. 0161D] The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read: “may there be a day without end.”].

## CHAPTER IX. Epitaph of Leontius, an earlier bishop of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 0161D] The Leontius whom Fortunatus discusses here was the predecessor of the younger Leontius, of whom there has often been mention above and who will be discussed in the following poem, as Cointius shows under the year 541, no. 58 and following. Cointius demonstrates in the same place that he took part in and subscribed to the Fourth Council of Orléans, held in 541. Browerus asserts that this was the Leontius to whom Sidonius writes in Letter 3 of Book VI and about whom he speaks in Letter 6 of Book VII; but he is mistaken, since the man to whom Sidonius writes was bishop of Arles, not Bordeaux, as Cointius shows under the year 541 and Sirmondus in his notes to Sidonius’s Letter 3 of Book VI.]

[Note: [Col. 0161B] [In this poem he praises the elder Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, already dead. He also commends the people’s love, longing, and memory for Leontius, together with Leontius’s outstanding virtues.]]

The final fate hastened heavily with greedy jaws,

snatching away the shepherd who had been the flock’s defense [Note: [Col. 0162C] One Vatican manuscript reads: “the ark of the flock.”].

These are the limbs of the venerable Leontius resting in this tomb,

where his distinguished episcopal head once stood.

The whole people, groaning, seeks him with confused voices:

here a boy, here a young man, and there old men mourn him.

Every age has lost here the aid of its protector,

and now teaches by its tears how much it loved him.

No one can recall the buried man with dry eyes,

though he still lives among the people through devoted love.

Outstanding, second to no one in nobility,

he excelled in character and was first in rank.

[Col. 0162A] Here, through a new kind of piety, he wished to be lesser than everyone,

but through these merits he was greater, even in his own eyes.

In this man’s presence discord earned peace;

when fury was driven out, love bound hearts together.

He granted the Church the whole of his wealth,

and gave to Christ what had previously been his own.

To him the poor had aid and the captive a ransom,

considering as his own property whatever the needy received.

His wealth migrated from earth to the stars,

and this man lived more for God than for himself.

Holding the people in the embrace of his heart and in his breast,

he seemed to say that he had fathered the people.

For he used to admonish his fellow citizens in such a gentle voice

that you would have confessed him to be speaking to his own limbs [Note: [Col. 0162C] The Paris edition reads: “you would have testified.”].

Alert in intellect and rich in the teaching of Christ,

he deserved through his zeal to multiply his rank.

More generous in gifts, even while absent he drew lovers to himself,

and though he had not been present, he was known by his beneficence.

Dear to princes, and this city’s unique beloved,

he hastened in spirit to be a father to everyone.

He lived ten lustrums and seven additional years [Note: [Col. 0162C] One Vatican manuscript reads: “he lived through seven years.”];

then, as the day pressed on, he was snatched from the world.

But who could sing all his virtues, when he alone possessed so many?

Now countless prayers lie in a single tomb.

These poems are far too small for you, since you deserved rich offerings;

your Theodosius presents them to you in love [Note: [Col. 0162C] Fortunatus seems not to have written this poem under his own name, but rather on behalf of another person named Theodosius, since it is not otherwise established that Fortunatus bore this name. This is especially so because Fortunatus could not even have known Leontius by sight, as Leontius had died before Fortunatus came to Gaul, whereas this verse suggests that Leontius was known to this Theodosius:

“Your Theodosius presents the poems, your beloved.”

See what we have said in section 1 of the *Life of Fortunatus*. Moreover, Leontius’s feast is celebrated among the people of Bordeaux on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September.].

## CHAPTER X. Epitaph of the subsequent Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 0162D] We have said more about this Leontius in Book I, chapter 15; see there. Cointius assigns Leontius’s death to the year 567, on the grounds that he set out for the Spanish war at approximately eighteen years of age. He was therefore still young and had not yet married. That war must be assigned to the year 531. Since, according to Fortunatus’s testimony, he lived fifty-four years, his death falls in 567. Thus Cointius. Leontius presided over the Church of Bordeaux in 549, when he subscribed through a legate to the Fifth Synod of Orléans, and he presided over the Synod of Saintes under King Charibert in 562, as Cointius thinks. This Leontius is commemorated among the people of Bordeaux on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December.]

[Note: [Col. 0162C] [This poem follows the funeral of the younger Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, and extols both his noble birth, his virtues of spirit, and his generosity toward the poor.]]

Every good thing is swift, and the world’s joys are fleeting;

how quickly human prosperity, once seized, flies away!

I would rather have brought poems of well-being to him [Note: [Col. 0163C] The Paris edition reads: “I would rather bring them to one to whom.”]

but, contrary to my wish, I am summoned to weep at his tomb.

These are the limbs of the venerable Leontius resting in this tomb,

whom his own fame lifts as bishop to the stars.

His noble name drew its height from an ancient origin,

such as perhaps the Roman Senate possesses.

And although he flowed from the lofty blood of fathers,

he made his ancestors grow through his own merits.

The supreme love of kings, the head of his country, the strength of his forebears,

the protector of friends, the honor of the people and the city.

A worshiper of churches, a silent giver to the needy,

a host to strangers, distributing food.

If anyone had hastened from the farthest edge of the world,

the newcomer soon saw him and said: “This is a father.”

Alive in intellect, upright in spirit, serene in countenance,

I speak of what he was to me with a grieving heart.

He was the city’s illustrious man, such as Gaul now has none;

now his lofty eminence lies in a humble tomb.

He calmed kings and restored the citizens through moderation;

alas, a single day carried away so many joys from the people.

He lived happily for ten lustrums and four additional years,

and died, snatched away from the light of dawn [Note: [Col. 0163D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “and from our light.” The Paris edition has the same reading, but adds *aurorae*—“of dawn”—in the margin.].

The funeral service is a great solace for love;

Placidina, still sweet to the ashes, gives this to you.

## CHAPTER XI. Epitaph of Victorianus, abbot of the monastery of Agaunum [Note: [Col. 0163D] The monastery of Agaunum was built, or restored, by King Sigismund, son of Gundobad, as Gregory of Tours records in Book III of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 5. It stood in the diocese of Sion, at the foot of Mount Saint Bernard, as Ruinart states in his notes to the cited preface.

But the learned Mabillon, first century of the Benedictine edition, p. 189, demonstrates that this poem was written not about Victorianus, abbot of Agaunum—as almost everyone had believed, on the evidence of the title—but about Victorianus, abbot of Asana. For, he says, in the manuscript codices we read “Victorianus, abbot of Asana,” with the heading: “Epitaph of the abbot of the monastery of Asana.” Asana, or Asanio, is a village of Aragon near the river Cinca, which, descending through mountain gorges and swollen by streams, flows swiftly into the Ebro. Second, no mention of an abbot Victorianus occurs in the list of the abbots of Agaunum, [Col. 0164C] which the Sammarthani copied from the Agaunum records. [Col. 0164D] Thus Mabillon, who consequently insists that, beyond doubt, Victorianus of Asana should be substituted for the abbot of Agaunum. He could at least have been known to Fortunatus by reputation and name, just as Fortunatus himself was able, through a letter and eulogy, to address Saint Martin of Dumio in Galicia, a bishop living still farther away.].

[Note: [Col. 0164D] One Vatican manuscript reads “of the monastery of Asana”; another has the corrupt form “Agahenens.”].

[Note: [Col. 0163B] [He praises Victorianus, abbot, for his devotion and for his diligence in increasing the number of monks. He indicates that he was distinguished by learning and perseverance in offering prayers to God, and that his virtue became renowned through the brilliance and multitude of his miracles.]]

Whoever hastens here from the setting sun, whoever from the rising sun,

you have a gift in this tomb worthy of your reverence.

Look upon the talent enriched by a heavenly endowment,

whose heart’s treasury always possesses God.

The summit of religion, the adornment of life, the weapons of salvation,

the outstanding Victorianus stands here in merit.

He performed worthy work; through labor that bore fruit,

he lived for everyone in the world, not for himself alone.

Pouring throughout the fatherland great swarms of monks,

he made the bees produce honey from eternal flowers.

Powerful in speech, constant in piety, unceasing in prayer—

such was he that even then he seemed wholly to belong to the stars.

Dispensing many salutary oracles in response to needs,

his blessed life often gave credence to miracles.

For twelve lustrums he ruled with ancestral authority

the sheep rightly pleasing to God, an excellent shepherd.

Following Christ along the straight path through sacred footsteps,

he now enjoys the face he longed for in love.

## CHAPTER XII. Epitaph of Hilarius [Note: [Col. 0164D] Is this the Hilarius about whom Fortunatus himself writes in Book III, chapter 35?

“Hilarius also, steadfast in love for us,

I insert into my poems, the man my heart cherishes?”] presbyter.

[Note: [Col. 0164A] [He praises the deceased presbyter Hilarius for his noble birth, chastity, knowledge, careful diligence in judgment, and faith. He commemorates the services performed by his mother-in-law Evantia in memory of the dead man.]]

The same unavoidable fate awaits everyone at the hour

when, under the law’s compulsion, the final day arrives.

So rages the anger of death, and the orbit of death does not elude us;

flesh made from dust will be nothing but dust.

Nevertheless, the best hope nourishes distinguished souls [Note: [Col. 0164D] Three Vatican manuscripts read: “an unempty hope nourishes them.” The Paris edition reads: “a hope that does not wander.”],

because whoever does what is worthy fears nothing from death.

Here lies the venerable Hilarius, distinguished in character,

who by his body holds the earth and by his faith the stars.

A good man, radiant with outstanding noble birth,

a high eminence among honored descendants.

Joined in a fitting marriage, but after his wife was taken away,

he stood firm in the love of God; there was no other love.

Useful in his own affairs, learned in the governance of the law,

his judgment was balanced like a scale.

He administered justice to the people with upright scrutiny;

no case was ever sold for a price [i.e. no verdict was corrupted by bribery].

Weeping in the duty of burial, Evantia, for her beloved,

committed these buried limbs to her son-in-law [Note: [Col. 0164D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “his tomb.”].

## CHAPTER XIII. Epitaph of Servilion [Note: [Col. 0164D] This poem is absent from the Venetian edition and from one Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0164C] [In this mournful poem he celebrates Servilion, who had been a court official and had properly administered the royal revenues. Later, after becoming a presbyter, he proved especially attentive and generous toward widows and orphans.]]

Although time is long, this life is short and a lodging only;

yet blessed life alone does not know how to die.

Thus Servilion lies enclosed in this tomb,

noble, and powerful through a nobility more deserving still.

[Col. 0165A] He himself governed the Palatine court with moderation

and made the wealth of the household entrusted to him increase.

From there, as a holy presbyter, he remained venerable to the world [Note: [Col. 0165D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “venerable in the world.”],

and his life was free in the service of God.

The orphan mourns him as a father; widows mourn him as their consolation;

therefore he possesses even greater true joys in heaven.

Here he sees a bishop born through Christ’s gift [Note: [Col. 0165D] From this one may infer that the poem was written at the urging or on the occasion of some bishop recently appointed to govern the Church, to whose clergy Servilion had perhaps once belonged.],

and, snatched from the world, he returns joyfully to the stars.

## CHAPTER XIV. Epitaph of Praesidius [Note: [Col. 0165D] This poem is absent from the Venetian edition and from one Vatican manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0165D] One Vatican manuscript gives the heading: “Epitaph of the household of Praesidius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0165A] [He commends the deceased abbot Praesidius for the holiness of his teaching and for his diligence and care in tending his flock.]]

Human life is brief, but the life of the righteous is not brief,

while, as the day departs, they possess more prosperous things.

Those who have deserved better, departing from the prison of the flesh,

enjoy perpetual light after the world’s darkness.

Among these, Praesidius lies here, possessing blessed merits;

his flesh holds the tomb, his spirit the heavens in fire [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Paris edition reads “the heavens of the river”; in the margin, “his spirit.”].

Pouring forth Christ’s responses from his own heart,

he extinguished the thirst of many with a flowing spring.

Urgently inviting the sheep to the King’s pastures,

he distributed sweet salt to his brothers from his mouth.

For whenever a monk was pierced by the wound of sin,

he was sent to the craftsman, who was a sure remedy [Note: [Col. 0165D] From this it is understood that Praesidius was an abbot. To which monastery he was superior is uncertain, since this name does not appear at all in the catalogues of the abbots of the kingdom of Gaul, at least so far as I have been able to determine.].

He went to the abbot in service to him, and to the holy master,

a humble disciple, though previously he had been proud.

Devoted to such duties through love of the Thunderer,

he shines in honor among the angelic choirs [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Paris edition reads: “among the angels.”].

## CHAPTER XV. Epitaph of Bobolenus the deacon

[Col. 0165C] [Note: [Col. 0165C] [In this poem he mourns Bobolenus the deacon, who, while indulging in sleep, was killed by an assassin’s ax-blow.]]

Human life is subject to countless dangers,

and hostile fate presses upon it with varied accidents.

For Bobolenus, lying on his bed in the honor of the diaconate,

while enjoying sleep, was seized by black death.

The enemy, lying in wait, struck him in unsuspecting safety;

with the slaughtering ax he struck his brain and deceitfully brought him to death.

Tell me: what benefit comes to you from committing this wicked crime?

He lives for God; you, who will die, perish.

He earned a martyr’s honor, while you bear a robber’s penalties;

he is pleased by the palm of victory, but punishment awaits you [Note: [Col. 0165D] From this it may be suspected that Bobolenus was struck down because he was defending justice.].

## CHAPTER XVI. Epitaph of Atticus

[Col. 0166A] [Note: [Col. 0166A] [This poem follows the funeral of Atticus, who died worn out by old age. It extols his eloquence and wisdom, renowned throughout all Gaul, as well as his noble birth, learning, wisdom, piety, and generosity toward sacred buildings and the poor.]]

Although a long life is extended to an old man in its course,

when the end arrives, length of time is of no avail.

But since no one escapes unless earth conceals earth,

under this law one fate carries off all men.

That Atticus, lofty in this humble tomb, lies here,

the man who gave sweet honey through his eloquence.

Bestowing a peaceful tongue with sweet melody,

his pacifying speech was itself a remedy.

Gaul revered his abundant understanding

and always honored the old man as a father.

Renowned through his ancestors, a splendid hope of noble birth,

sufficient through his own resources, he was no plunderer.

Holding teachings in his heart, full like a treasury of books,

anyone could drink from his flowing spring whatever he desired.

Wise in counsel, pious in spirit, serene in countenance,

he was a father loved by every people.

Thus he favored venerable temples, thus he favored the needy [Note: [Col. 0166D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “thus he poured out [his gifts].” The Venetian edition reads: “thus he shines for the needy.”],

so that he might send to heaven the wealth that would follow him.

## CHAPTER XVII. Epitaph of Arcadius [Note: [Col. 0166D] Browerus thinks that this Arcadius was the son of the senator Arcadius of Auvergne, of whom Gregory of Tours often speaks in the *History of the Franks*. But since that father Arcadius was the father of Placidina, formerly the wife of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, from whom she was divorced in 549, it seems less likely that Fortunatus could have mourned the funeral of his brother, who would still have been a child. Fortunatus had come to Gaul by 565, as we have often said, unless one must suppose that this poem was composed much later for Placidina’s sake. I would therefore rather say that he belonged to the family of Arcadius than that he was his son.] a young man.

[Note: [Col. 0166B] [In a funeral poem he honors Arcadius, who was still young when premature death overtook him.]]

Every good thing passes swiftly in fleeing time;

whatever death sees as pleasing, death snatches away all the more [Note: [Col. 0166D] This poem is absent from the Venetian edition and from one Vatican manuscript.].

Here lies the boy Arcadius, descended from a senatorial line,

snatched from the world as the day hastened on.

His little age had scarcely yet been bound by the bridle,

so that, tender even in years, he might himself have risen to old age [Note: [Col. 0166D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “tender in years.”].

A torrent in eloquence, handsome with radiant appearance,

surpassing craftsmen, though still an untrained boy in art.

Why, beauty, do you compel me to recall the praises of the buried man?

If you recall each one, you prompt still greater tears.

But since he departed unstained by any impurity,

no one need mourn him whom paradise possesses [Note: [Col. 0166D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “he will be mourned by no one.”].

## CHAPTER XVIII. Epitaph of Basilius

[Col. 0167A] [Note: [Col. 0167A] [He praises the deceased Basilius in a funeral poem for his eloquence and learning, wisdom and devotion to peace, generosity toward the poor and churches. He recalls the embassies he undertook to Spain and his innocence in the administration of public offices, and shows how dear he was to the people and to kings.]]

I am hindered by tears from uttering the name of the man I love,

and my hand can scarcely write words that must be mournful.

By a wife’s affection, I am compelled to offer a few words to the buried man;

if I speak, I am afflicted; if I remain silent, I shall be hard-hearted.

Reader, if you wish to know whom this tomb covers,

sad graves conceal the illustrious Basilius [Note: [Col. 0167C] See what we have said about Basilius and Baudegundis, his wife, in the notes to Poem 7 of Book I.].

His gentle tongue refreshed people with pious speech,

and his eloquence offered kind words from his mouth.

On one side learning watered him, on the other sweetness overflowed;

a double light adorned the man with its radiance.

The king’s beloved, dear to the peoples, so sweet in heart

that he became a father to all through his goodness.

Calm, wise, pleasant, a friend of peace,

there were no seeds of strife wherever he stood [Note: [Col. 0167C] One Vatican manuscript reads: “and many seeds of milk were wherever he stood.”].

Gallic concern frequently sent him to the people of Spain,

acting in the capacity of an envoy and taking counsel.

Having sufficient resources, he was never an instrument of plunder;

he did not lack his own possessions, nor did he take what belonged to others.

Enriching churches, honoring holy places appropriately,

giving to the poor, he ascends to the stars as a rich man.

For twice ten years he was joined in one marriage-bed

with Baudegundis, his wife [Note: [Col. 0167D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “he joined two people in one marriage-bed in the city.”].

Yet, snatched away in the eleventh lustrum [Note: [Col. 0167D] Browerus doubts whether this is the same Basilius about whom Gregory of Tours speaks in Book IV of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 46, since the deaths of the two appear different. The man about whom Gregory speaks seems to have died overwhelmed by Mummolenus; the one about whom Fortunatus speaks died without any such accident or calamity. Yet Gregory’s passage does not establish clearly that Basilius, rather than the multitude gathered by him and Sigarius, was overcome by Mummolus’s forces. Nor does Fortunatus state by what kind of death Basilius died; he merely indicates that he was taken away while not yet very old. (Note from the first recension.) —Mommolus Eunius was the man who was granted the rank and dignity of patrician by King Guntram and who later repaid that honor many times over by brilliant victories, making the distinction with which he had been advanced far more illustrious than when he received it. He routed the Lombards and Saxons, who were invading Gaul, in great battles. Later, after defecting from Guntram and following Gundevald—whom he subsequently abandoned and betrayed—he was killed on Guntram’s orders, as Gregory of Tours relates in Book VII of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 39.],

he departed from life.

After the end of earth he seeks the heavenly kingdoms above.

You will no longer be mourned, departing from the human condition,

while, dear friend, you possess heaven as your homeland.

## CHAPTER XIX. Epitaph of Aracharius

[Note: [Col. 0167C] [In this poem he mourns Aracharius, who had been distinguished in the royal court and dear and agreeable to the king, but was taken by death while still in the flower of his age.]]

The earth suffers no loss from its own offspring [Note: [Col. 0168D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “the earth by its own nourishment.”],

but receives the limbs it gave, owed to the soil.

[Col. 0168A] Here lies Aracharius, his life now declining,

who, having completed six lustrums, was snatched from the world.

He himself shone brilliantly in the Palatine court,

and deserved to be honored by the king’s gracious affection [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Venetian edition reads: “he shone illustriously in the court.” Another variant reads: “and deserved to be honored by the king’s kindly love.”].

He returned to the world everything he had taken from it;

for himself alone he retains the good deeds he performed.

## CHAPTER XX. Epitaph of Brumachius

[Note: [Col. 0168A] [This mournful poem concerns Brumachius, a powerful man who, while returning to Gaul from an embassy he had completed, was overtaken by death on the journey. It praises his eloquence and prudence and commends the diligence of his wife Phrygia in arranging her husband’s funeral.]]

Whoever wishes to know whose ashes lie buried in this tomb,

Brumachius once shone as a powerful man in the world.

Having served as an envoy through his understanding and eloquence,

he was carried off by hostile fate while returning to his homeland.

Snatched away in the territory of Italy, his wife Phrygia [Fragia, Phrygia] [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Venetian edition reads: “Frisia, his wife.”]

brought her beloved husband’s funeral here out of love [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read: “brought here the funeral of her beloved husband through her loving care.”].

As though he were alive, she honored him; the husband’s shade is dear to her,

and for chaste spouses even the ashes themselves are pleasing.

He himself remained in the world for forty years,

then died, and a small tomb covers the great man.

## CHAPTER XXI. Epitaph of Avolus [Note: [Col. 0168D] Browerus thinks this was Avolus the presbyter, who took part in and subscribed to the Third Council of Orléans in the name of Agricola, bishop of Chalon. But if Avolus, the man now under discussion, was a presbyter, it is surprising that Fortunatus says nothing here of that rank of honor, and instead commends qualities more appropriate to a layman—namely, that he was generous and opposed to exacting interest.].

[Note: [Col. 0168B] [He praises Avolus for piety and devotion toward sacred buildings, generosity toward the poor, and munificence toward his fellow citizens.]]

Do not weep for buried Avolus with streaming tears,

for by his own merits he possesses the joys of light.

For if his virtuous deeds are weighed,

he possesses the blessed heavens after the tomb.

He honored the temples of God and, concealed from view, satisfied the needy;

he reaps more fully what he gave without a witness.

Powerful in nobility, upright in spirit, serene in countenance,

pleasing through the people’s love, ready to pour out his wealth [Note: [Col. 0168D] The edition adds in the margin:

“Ready to give his wealth, he gave enough by distributing it to the wretched.”].

He was not greedy for interest, although generous in his gifts;

he sought nothing more than he gave by counting it out.

Needing no payment, his one payment was salvation;

what is less in price advances him in merit.

Enjoying perpetual light, blessed is he for whom death is dead,

whom no punishment presses, while eternal life remains.

## CHAPTER XXII. Epitaph of the Innocent Ones

[Note: [Col. 0169C] In the Venetian edition this title appears here: “Epitaph of the Orientians.” By this word the proper name of the family and lineage from which the infant boys lamented here by Fortunatus came seems to be indicated. Nor was the name Orientians unknown in Gaul. See below, ch. 24.]

[Note: [Col. 0169A] He honors in a funeral poem the tomb of infant boys who, apparently born in a single birth, died—one earlier, the other at five years of age—and had been brought into the same grave as their mother.]

Here in this tomb lies the unwept infancy of brothers,

whom blessed life carried away as innocent men.

Born from one womb, they were buried by a like destiny,

and one light holds two who were born together.

The first departed first, washed in the sacred font and clad in white [garments] [Note: [Col. 0169C] Previously the reading was *prior ille recessit in alvo* (“the first departed in the womb”); Brower restored the present reading from ancient manuscripts. The Vatican manuscripts also support it; one has *Pius ille recessit* (“the pious one departed”).],

while this one, bearing five years, is led before God.

But the first was rightly called John by name [Note: [Col. 0169C] One Vatican manuscript has *vocitatur* (“is called”).],

while the other, Patrick, was greater in dignity.

[Col. 0169B] Concerning whose merit so many signs gave evidence [Note: [Col. 0169C] The same manuscript has *se plurima* (“very many”).]:

blessed are the souls that cultivate holy vows.

Here too their blessed mother rests,

who deserved to bring forth lights through her childbirth.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Epitaph of Julian

[Note: [Col. 0169B] He praises in this poem Julian, who had once practiced commerce and afterward poured out the wealth he had acquired upon guests and the needy, now that he is dead. He commends the love and care of John, Julian’s son, toward his deceased father.]

The limbs of Julian have been placed in this tomb,

whose honor knows how to live forever.

Once a merchant, transformed by a blessed end,

he was snatched from this world a man freed from sin.

[Col. 0169C] He amassed too much, but scattered gold among the needy;

he sent ahead all the wealth that he would later follow.

Attentive to anyone new whom he saw [Note: [Col. 0169D] Two Vatican manuscripts have *prospexit in urbe* (“whom he noticed in the city”).] in the city,

he deserved, when he came as an exile, to find in him a father.

Believing that he was feeding Christ beneath a poor man’s form,

before all others he, as a needy man, received help from him.

[Col. 0170A] And not merely by restoring him, but by secretly bestowing gifts,

he is the more pleasing because he gave without a witness.

Blessed the mind that passes into a brother’s womb [*alvo*],

and can build living stones.

John raised this tomb in honor of his father [Note: [Col. 0169D] Gregory of Tours, in the *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, ch. 8, no. 6, mentions a certain John, a priest of Tours, who had once practiced commerce, as he relates there, saying that the same man had formerly returned from the city of Massilia with the merchandise of his trade. It is highly credible that he is the same man about whom Fortunatus writes here: namely, that he followed the discipline of his father Julian from childhood, and afterward, having converted along with his father, was enrolled in the clergy of Tours.],

who now performs divine offices.

How lovingly he served his living parent,

since the devotion of a son itself honors the tombs?

## CHAPTER XXIV. Epitaph of Orientius

[Note: [Col. 0169D] One Vatican manuscript has: “Epitaph of Morientius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0170A] He praises Orientius, who had held a distinguished position of honor and favor in the royal court, now dead, for his prudence, justice, and moderation. He also displays the care of his wife Nicasia in tending her husband’s funeral and honoring his memory.]

[Col. 0170B] Our life here does not remain long while time flees;

it scarcely arrives beneath a brief ending, and then departs.

Behold, the fleeting ages of the world fly away and quickly collapse;

only the faith of merit does not know how to die with honor.

Here lies buried that powerful Orientius,

for whom the Palatine palace had formerly remained open.

Skilled in counsels and intimate with the royal court,

he deservedly held a lofty position in the citadel.

A wise, just, temperate, honorable, beloved man:

what he had done well as a man, that he took away from the world [Note: [Col. 0169D] The Venetian edition has: “what he had done well upon earth.”].

Scarcely completing the span of sixty years of light,

he lies here, with his wife Nicasia burying him.

Her chaste love honors the very tombs of her husband,

not seeking to please a human being, but giving herself to God.

## CHAPTER XXV. Epitaph of Theodechildis

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The Venetian edition has *Theodechildae*.—The Theodechildis of whom Fortunatus speaks here must by no means be confused with Theudechild, wife of King Charibert, concerning whom Gregory of Tours writes in Book IV of the *History of the Franks*, ch. 26. He says: “Charibert also had another girl, the daughter of a shepherd, that is, a herdsman of sheep, named Theudechild”; consequently, none of what Fortunatus praises here concerning Theodechildis’s lineage and nobility applies to her.

Cointius, under the year 504, nos. 5 and following, holds that two Theodechilds of royal stock must be distinguished: the elder was the daughter of King Clovis, while the younger was the daughter of Theoderic and therefore the granddaughter of Clovis. Fortunatus composed this funeral poem for the first.
