It will not be irrelevant to our purpose to examine briefly the arguments used by Cointius. He first tries to undermine the authority of Procopius, who, in Book IV of the *Gothic War*, ch. 20, wrote that Theodebert’s sister, and therefore Theoderic’s daughter, married Hermigisclus, king of the Varni. Procopius, he says, incorporated many things alien to the truth into his history, including the claim that Clotilde, daughter of the great Clovis—whom Saint Gregory of Tours explicitly reports, in Book III of the *History of the Franks*, ch. 1, to have married Amalaric, king of the Visigoths—was likewise called Theodebert’s sister, in Book I, ch. 13. It is therefore unsurprising if he was deceived by the same error and called Theodechild, who was actually Theodebert’s aunt, his sister.

Cointius next attempts to confirm his opinion on the grounds that, if Theodechildis was Theodebert’s sister and Theoderic’s daughter, she must be considered to have survived Gregory of Tours. But how could that be, when Fortunatus, born later, wrote her epitaph and inserted it into a work that he dedicated to Gregory of Tours while Gregory was still alive?

Yet this argument advanced by Cointius is of little weight. Fortunatus could have attached to his work, after Gregory’s death, the poem he had written for Theodechildis’s funeral; and others could likewise have gathered Fortunatus’s scattered poems into a single volume.

As for Theodechildis having been not Clovis’s daughter but Theoderic’s, and therefore Theodebert’s sister, setting aside the consistent silence of the writers who mention no daughter of King Clovis named Theodechildis but only one Clotilde, who married Amalaric, Fortunatus certainly recalls in this very poem things about Theodechildis that fit Theodebert’s sister, not Clovis’s daughter. In reviewing her royal lineage, he says:

“Her brother, father, husband, grandfather, and ancestors—

a royal line was hers in unbroken succession.”

These words, I say, fit better one who was Theoderic’s daughter than one who was Clovis’s daughter. For under Clovis the succession of royal name and blood was first established among the Gauls, and from him the kingdom was to remain perpetually with his descendants, as Gregory of Tours relates in Book II of the *History of the Franks*, ch. 9. Again, why would Fortunatus have named Theodechildis’s royal brother rather than brothers, if she had been Clovis’s daughter and therefore the sister of his four sons, all of them kings, rather than Theoderic’s daughter and Theodebert’s sister? This agrees admirably with another testimony of Fortunatus, written about Theodechildis, Theodebert’s sister, as Cointius himself admits. Here it is, from Book VI, ch. 5:

“An illustrious offspring, radiant with royal stock,

to whom ancestry gave a lofty name from forefathers.

The new glory of your lineage runs, flying, throughout the world,

and from one side your brother resounds, from the other your father.”

As for Cointius’s answer—that Fortunatus mentions only one of her brothers, although she had four, in order to indicate that Theoderic alone among them had been born from the same marriage-bed as Theodechildis—this is asserted without any certain evidence; moreover, for that very reason the poet would by no means have omitted it, especially since the meter did not prevent him from stating what contributed so greatly to Theodechildis’s praise: namely, that she had four royal brothers, who, although born from different marriages, were nevertheless truly her brothers. If that were the reason for the silence alleged by Cointius, there would have been no reason for Fortunatus, in Book VI, ch. 5, to mention the royal brother of the other Theodechildis, as he supposes, since Theodebert had not been born to Theoderic from the same marriage-bed as Theodechildis; for Theoderic had her by Suavegotta, whom he married long after Theodebert had been born. Yet Cointius himself admits that in that poem Theodebert is mentioned in praise of Theodechildis. See Pagius, under the year 572, no. 4, where he examines this question and refutes Cointius.]

of the queen.

[Col. 0170C] [Note: [Col. 0170C] He praises Queen Theodechildis, now dead, magnificently for her royal lineage and connections, for her generosity toward the poor, and for her munificence toward churches.]

Although old age was already bending the years of her life [Note: [Col. 0170D] One Vatican manuscript has *aetatis senium* (“old age of life”).],

she was nevertheless quickly snatched from the hopes of many.

[Col. 0171A] If what nature owes could be bent by prayers,

the people would by their tears have made her remain for them [Note: [Col. 0172B] The same manuscript has *sic precibus* (“thus by prayers”); another Vatican manuscript has *possint* (“might be able”); the Venetian edition has *huc superesse* (“survive here”).].

How many joys of the poor are enclosed beneath this tomb [Note: [Col. 0172B] One Vatican manuscript has *cumulo sunt clausa* (“are enclosed in a mound”); the Paris edition has *clausa sub uno* (“enclosed beneath one [tomb]”).]?

And how many vows did a single day take away from the peoples?

Illustrious nobility, radiant in the light of her birth,

here lies Theodechildis, hastened by the day.

Her brother, father, husband, grandfather, and ancestors—

a royal line was hers in unbroken succession.

Orphans, exiles, the needy, widows, and the naked lying in misery

grieve that they have buried their mother, food, and covering here [Note: [Col. 0172B] The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts have: “and the naked women lying in misery.”].

One thing alone pleased her: the abundance of a rich reward;

she gave everything beforehand, before help was requested.

Concealing her gifts from her own people, lest they perhaps prevent her,

she shows what she gave secretly, with God as witness [Note: [Col. 0172B] Flodoard wrote of Theodechildis: “In the time of this Mapinus, bishop of Reims, Queen Suavegotta is found to have assigned by testamentary document a third part of the estate of Virisiac to the Church of Reims. The bishop himself also granted that part of the estate, by precarious tenure and with the rights of the Church preserved, to Theudechild, daughter of the aforesaid queen, for her usufruct, on the sole condition that after her death it should be restored to the control of the Church of Reims without any prejudice, just as it had been improved by her. Thus Queen Theodechildis afterward transferred certain estates to the Church of Reims by the authority of her testament, in the time of Lord Egidius.

Cointius, however, believes that when Fortunatus celebrates Theodechildis’s munificence toward churches, he has in mind the monastery that she had arranged to build before the city of Sens through royal generosity, after the model of the one Clovis had built near Paris. To that monastery she had bequeathed the estates that she could possess, whether this side of the Loire in Francia or beyond the Loire in Aquitaine, whether inherited or acquired, so that monks might continually serve God there; she had also ordered that her own body be buried there after her death. See Cointius, under the year 564, no. 36 and following.].]

a devotee of the Lord’s churches, bestowing pious gifts,

[Col. 0171B] considering whatever she possessed to belong to the needy.

[Col. 0172A] It is one lot to die and to return earth to earth:

happy is the one for whom day stands without end through merits.

Devoting herself to these deeds, restored to the light of eternity [Note: [Col. 0172C] The Venetian edition has: “in eternal light.” One Vatican manuscript has: “reborn into the light.” The Paris edition has: “restored into the light”; in the margin, “returned.”],

she lived fifteen lustrums [seventy-five years] as an ornament in the world [Note: [Col. 0172D] Theodechildis was not born before the year 522, approximately when Theoderic married Suavegotta, daughter of King Sigismund, by whom he had Theodechildis, as we indicated above. If, therefore, one adds the seventy-five years that Fortunatus here says she lived, one will find that she died almost at the end of Fortunatus’s life. See what we said in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 90. One Vatican manuscript has: “as an ornament in the city.”].

## CHAPTER XXVI. Epitaph of Vilithuta [Vilitruta]

[Note: [Col. 0172D] One Vatican manuscript has *Vilithylae*. The Venetian edition has *Uttrogothae*; it then omits the two verses beginning “Vilithuta, distinguished …” and the following verse. The same is true of one Vatican manuscript.

Brower thinks that Vilithuta belonged to the Gothic people; Fortunatus calls her fierce, referring to the warlike temper and spirit of that people, or to signify their savage character and barbarous way of life. Sidonius Apollinaris asserts in the *Anthology* that this ferocity was common and almost innate among all Hyperboreans, saying:

“. . . A people lies beneath the Bear’s pole,

threatening in spirit and limb; such horror

is present even in the faces of their infants.”

That Vilithuta, although born in Paris, was not of the Frankish people is sufficiently shown by the verse that follows shortly afterward in this poem:

“Although she had no relative in this region,

by her service she became one mother to all.”]

[Note: [Col. 0172A] He laments Vilithuta, a noble woman but nevertheless of barbarian people and lineage, who died in childbirth together with her offspring. He praises both her excellent bodily beauty and the adornments of her mind and character. Taking the occasion, he discusses at length the Last Judgment and the differing future destinies of the good and the wicked; then, by describing Vilithuta’s present happiness, he tries to draw her surviving husband away from the grief that he had conceived at the death of his most beloved wife.]

Every good is swift, and the joys of the world are fleeting;

they are displayed to the earth and quickly fall and collapse.

[Col. 0173A] So that grief may gain strength when one loses the beloved,

it first makes her pleasing, and afterward presses all the harder.

Alas for the tears of human affairs, alas for the hostile lot of men!

Why do you make pleasing what, when you snatch it away, you make painful?

Vilithuta, distinguished, beloved wife of Dagaulf,

lies separated from her husband’s embrace.

Joined to him in body upon the marriage-bed, more closely bound to her husband in heart,

at the setting of her life she broke the bonds of love.

Her years could still have remained in bloom [Note: [Col. 0173D] The Venetian edition reads *poterant et adhuc* (“could still”), a reading that should be followed.],

but a bitter end possesses the beginning of her life [Note: [Col. 0173D] One Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition have: “the beginning of life.”].

Born of noble blood in the city of Paris [Note: [Col. 0173D] The Venetian edition has: “in the city of Paris.”],

she was Roman in cultivation, barbarian in descent.

She drew a gentle character from a fierce people [Note: [Col. 0173D] One Vatican manuscript has: “a fierce character from a fierce people.”];

it was a greater glory to conquer nature.

Never remaining sad, she carried new joys in her face,

driving away clouds from her brow, serene in heart.

She poured radiance from her mouth, her features crowned with beauty,

and her lovely form brought forth its own rays.

Beautiful, she surpassed the other maidens of her lineage,

and she bore a saffron-colored face and milk-white neck [Note: [Col. 0174D] One Vatican manuscript has: “a rosy face.”].

Brilliant to behold, she shone with a nobler heart,

worthy of shining in spirit, and no less in devotion.

Although she had no relative in this region,

by her service she became one mother to all.

Intent upon divine goods and supplying nourishment,

by what reward she sees herself most fully satisfied.

These gifts bestowed after death also make the dead woman live;

human beauty perishes, for good deeds remain.

Bodies will be dust, but a pious mind flourishes through the ages;

everything passes away except loving God.

At that time an orphan, she grew rich through the care of her excellent grandmother [Note: [Col. 0174D] The Venetian edition has, incorrectly: “Then the grandmother is an orphan.”],

and, in place of her daughter, she grew to adulthood as a granddaughter.

When she had first received him at the age of thirteen [Note: [Col. 0174D] The same manuscript has: “when she first received him.”],

she was given in marriage to the husband she desired.

Nobility shone loftily in her own lineage,

and another honor was added to her own merits.

Sweet, rejoicing, her youth was adorned with eager pursuits;

what nature could not provide, learning readily gave.

Yet, joined together, they deserved to survive for three years

and to enjoy their marriage, their hearts bound together.

Equal in spirit, desire, hope, character, and conduct,

competing with one another in mind, beauty, and faith,

at the appointed time the wife brought forth a child,

pregnant with her own loss, for she perished in childbirth.

[Col. 0174A] Envious death suddenly snatched away her tender beauty,

for she had completed two years and three lustrums [seventeen years] [Note: [Col. 0174D] Since Fortunatus said above that Vilithuta married at thirteen and lived three years with her surviving husband, it would follow that she completed her sixteenth year. Why, then, does he say here that she lived seventeen years? Perhaps he is here including the months omitted from the earlier reckoning.].

Thus, while generating life, she herself was deprived of life;

she gave birth to hope for the light, while the light denied itself to her.

But she gave a sad example to her unsuspecting parent [Note: [Col. 0174D] The same manuscript has: “she gave a sad example to her offspring.”]:

from where the race usually returns, from there it fails.

Wishing to become a father for the third time—alas!—he is found alone;

where the number ought to have increased, he himself falls [Note: [Col. 0174D] The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts have: “he himself becomes a corpse.”].

For the child [*partus*, “birth”; perhaps *parvus*, “the little one”] perished with its mother, buried at birth,

drawing nothing of life, born upon the threshold of death.

They would have been more fortunate alone, had they then been without offspring;

the added posterity took away what they possessed.

Born amid ill-fated vows from the mother’s funeral,

the mother was the source of death for her child.

[Col. 0174B] Each depended upon the other’s lethal fate;

and soon both gave death to one another.

But the grieving father and husband felt the heavier blows,

who mourns that by one death he buried two.

For the one scarcely born, already buried, he pours out tears,

and love saw what he should mourn, not what he possessed.

She who had been taken away from him, his wife, added a heap to his sorrow,

giving long tears to a marriage of brief duration.

Yet the husband has this consolation concerning his wife,

because her work of reward is not brought to nothing.

For whatever might have seemed suitable for a woman’s adornment,

she promptly gave to churches and to the poor.

She left none of those things to perish,

so that she might now possess the wealth previously sent ahead.

Distributing her possessions well, she did not wish them to exist without her;

for what she gave generously, that she now reaps in fullness [Note: [Col. 0174D] One Vatican manuscript has: “for what her tongue gave.”].

Whatever she extended to the needy, she stored up for herself,

and the nourishment she took as a needy person, she now possesses.

Blessed are those whom nothing concerning the second death burdens,

who do not make their limbs, subjected to punishments, food for savage beasts.

The one who does not build an Avernal realm for himself through sweet enticements [Note: [Col. 0174D] The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts have: “who does not build a bitter realm.”],

nor wish to bury his soul through the flesh,

but remains chaste in devotion, with a blameless life,

purchases in this life the rewards of that light [Note: [Col. 0174D] The Venetian edition has: “the rewards of this light in that light.”].

In how brief a time one gathers abundant tears,

or he whose life shines attains enduring joys [Note: [Col. 0174D] One Vatican manuscript has: “or for whom life endures.”].

Here the grief of death is light; for more severe is the fate of the one

whom black Tartarus holds while he is still living [Note: [Col. 0174D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition have: “this grief from death.”].

Unhappy is anyone who, having practiced deeds stained with sin,

sees that he has ensnared himself before the Redeemer [Note: [Col. 0174D] The printed text reads *ante* (“before”); *arte* (“by artifice”) is an alternative reading.].

[Col. 0175A] When the Judge of the world comes, borne upon the clouds,

and the terrible trumpet has stirred the weapons in the heavens [Note: [Col. 0175D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition have: “has stirred the armies.”],

Elijah comes to these, Enoch to those in his chariots,

going before his own; on this side Peter, on that side Stephen.

With a rosy company of maidens surrounding her,

Mary stands first among the virgin choirs.

Here Martha, there the bride Agnes, gentle Thecla, Agatha [Note: [Col. 0175D] One Vatican manuscript has *Agathe*.],

and every woman who pleases God by virginity.

What terror will there be then, when the senate of heaven is present?

What will the souls say before the face of the Judge?

Soon either punishment awaits the wretched or the palm awaits the blessed.

Each reaps the seeds sown by his own life.

Some will say: “Fall, mountain, and crush the body”;

but the hills, commanded to bear the tombs, will refuse.

[Col. 0175B] The least will be compelled to pay a quarter of a coin;

no one withdraws his foot where his guilt draws him.

Empty of hope, they will be sent like straw into the fires;

our flesh becomes food for the flames that feed upon it [Note: [Col. 0175D] One Vatican manuscript has: “thus the flesh.”].

They live for punishments in an eternally burning furnace;

so that death may torment more severely, evil death does not die.

Alas, the fiery river will offer no waters

to refresh souls exhausted and burned by the long fire [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Venetian edition has: “will offer.”].

On the other side, those who have been led forth by their happy merits [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts have: “holding the heights.”]

will shine, like the sun at the summit of heaven.

The worthy possess light; the condemned lament their fires;

splendor nourishes the former, vapor from fire cooks the latter.

It is indeed one substance, but it is divided in its operation:

it burns the unworthy with the very fire by which it tests the pious.

The blessed shine in the eternal light of paradise,

holding the kingdoms of their own Christ face to face.

How great the grace that remains for the one who will have looked upon those faces!

What honor for human beings: to be able to see God!

If one who sees a frail friend is lifted up too greatly,

how will the one who sees the face of God exult?

Lilies, narcissus, violets, roses, nard, amomum [Note: [Col. 0175D] The same source has *amomus*.],

whatever Arabia produces from fragrant shoots—

the flowering lights flourish in the Judge’s face,

but above all these the Lord breathes forth a sweeter fragrance.

As much as golden light is better than foul lead,

so all incense yields to God, and every fragrance.

As far as day differs from night, the sun from the moon’s lamp,

so his works yield to their Maker.

But when the righteous enjoy such great splendor,

they rejoice exceedingly that they have escaped death.

[Col. 0175D] They are glad to have migrated from darkness into perpetual light,

and they grieve that they came so late to so many blessings.

[Col. 0176A] You too, do not burn your wife’s pious deeds with tears,

for she is now believed to have received better things here [Note: [Col. 0175D] Two Vatican manuscripts have: “better things there.” The Venetian edition has: “these better things.”].

For if you mourn her who lives through her excellent merits,

you yourself will be envious of your wife’s blessings.

Especially since you report that she, joined to you in sense, spirit, and body [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript have: “joined.”],

was always joined in heart with Christ.

If, after seeing the Lord’s face, she were ordered to return to you,

she would weep that she had brought herself back to this world [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts have: “to bring back her step.”].

She holds more dearly the day that she knows she cannot lose

than this day, which she feared would be hers with its approaching end.

Do not make a heavy funeral of what nature offers to all,

what the poor share with princes.

Neither poverty nor abundant wealth deprives anyone of this;

rich and needy alike possess it in common.

[Col. 0176B] For child and old man, black and white, base and honorable,

weak and strong, gentle and harsh, all die.

[Note: [Col. 0175D] In a fifteenth-century manuscript used by the distinguished Jacobus Morellius, custodian of the library of Saint Mark in Venice [Col. 0176D], this verse—which is found incomplete in Brower’s edition and in the manuscripts used by us—is supplemented as follows:

“Here the wise, the foolish, the good, the wicked, and the proud”; and below:

“Thus death draws together those united by unequal merit.”

(From the notes of the second revision.)]

Here the wise, the foolish, the good, … the wicked, all,

the full, the small, the short, and the tall, approach.

Sooner or later this lot runs through everyone;

with unequal merit, one death draws all men along.

It is therefore not fitting to pour heavy tears for a wife

whose merits you do not deny.

Exceedingly blessed are those who rule here without sin,

who learn better how to live after death.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Epitaph of Euphrasia

[Note: [Col. 0176B] He rejoices that Euphrasia, a woman of the highest nobility, enriched by good deeds and distinguished by virtues, exchanged this mortal life for immortality. He praises her generosity toward the poor, her chastity, and also the nobility of her lineage.]

If the work of devotion will never die through the ages [Note: [Col. 0176D] The variant is *aevum* (“age”); this poem and the following one are absent from one Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition.],

you live according to your merit, holy woman.

Illustrious Euphrasia, radiant in the starry kingdom,

I do not have to mourn you, since you are happily pleasing there [Note: [Col. 0176D] One Vatican manuscript has: “nor do I, remaining, have to mourn you.”],

earth gave you to earth, but the spirit received you into the stars;

one part of you lies in the tomb, the other holds heaven.

Having laid aside the body and borne aloft on lighter flight,

you stand better in heaven than you formerly were upon earth.

Subduing the injustice of the flesh, triumphing in sacred deeds [Note: [Col. 0176D] Two Vatican manuscripts have: “triumphing in sacred works.”],

you return as a richly endowed citizen to your native dwelling.

The lofty nobility of your forefathers shines with ancestral light,

yet you must be glorified still more for your own merits.

[Col. 0176D] Your husband Namatius [Note: [Col. 0176D] Namatius was bishop of Vienne and succeeded Esychius, or Isicius, in the see of Vienne, around the year 558. He is called in the *Chronicle of Ado*, under the sixth age, a man noble in lineage but nobler in life and speech. It is uncertain whether this was the same Namatius to whom a letter of Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, letter 6, is extant, since there was also another Namatius, the father-in-law of Ruricius, to whom and to whose wife Ceraunia several letters of Ruricius are extant.

Brower, in his notes on this passage, says that Euphrasia left Namatius surviving her, destined eventually to become bishop of Vienne, since Fortunatus so plainly states here that, after her husband’s death, Euphrasia devoted herself entirely to the practice of religion and piety.

Brower is also mistaken in thinking that Namatius succeeded Pantagathus in the see of Vienne. Pantagathus attended and subscribed to the Third Council of Orléans, held in 538, whereas he was succeeded by Esychius, who likewise attended and subscribed to several councils, including some held between the Second Council of Paris, celebrated in 551, and the time in question, as can be seen in Cointius. Namatius therefore succeeded Esychius and died in 558, after occupying the see for seven years and living seventy-three years, as is clear from his epitaph, which is read in the *Antiquities of Vienne*. See Cointius, under the year 558.],

was thereafter appointed priest at Vienne:

when your husband died, you were joined to God,

pouring out everything for exiles, widows, and captives;

rich in holy poverty, you ascend to the stars.

Having purchased an eternal day in a brief [perhaps corrupt: *pravo*, “wrongful”] span of time,

you sent to heaven the riches that you would follow.

But I ask you, by the King who grants the joys of paradise,

pour out a prayer for Fortunatus, your suppliant.

May you obtain by your prayers for the one who sent you these verses

that I may someday deserve to be shut in with Peter’s key.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Epitaph of Eusebia

[Note: [Col. 0177A] He laments in this mournful poem Eusebia, who, at the age of ten and already betrothed to a husband, died prematurely.]

If parents could write hard words through their tears,

here the inscription would be weeping in place of painting.

[Col. 0178A] But since water does not mark a beloved name [Note: [Col. 0178B] That is, the eye cannot inscribe the beloved’s name through its tears.],

the moving hand follows wherever grief commands it to go.

Eusebia was noble; by the fate of the raging grave,

here, dark stone, you cover her shining limbs.

In whose intellect, or in the beautiful body of her form,

Minerva was present in skill, and Venus was overcome in beauty.

Skilled in holding pens and also in tracing letters with a thread,

what the page was for you, that the loom was for you.

Sweet Eusebia, already betrothed to Eusebius’s marriage-bed,

you were scarcely permitted to live two lustrums [ten years].

Though young, she surpassed an old person in understanding;

she even surpassed herself, though she was not destined to live long.

The father-in-law is crushed, from whom daughter and son-in-law depart;

she dies a deadly death, while he departs as the survivor [Note: [Col. 0178B] One Vatican manuscript has: “while he, the survivor, remains.”].

Yet let there be consolation: you are not dead to Christ;

you will live beyond the tomb, a virgin received by God.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0177]

## CHAPTER I. To Martin, Bishop of Galicia

[Note: [Col. 0177C] Saint Martin, bishop of Galicia, died around the year 580. Gregory of Tours writes of him in Book V of the *History of the Franks*, ch. 38: “At this time the blessed Martin, bishop of Galicia, also died, causing great mourning among that people. For he was born in Pannonia, and from there he hastened eastward to visit the holy places; he so thoroughly immersed himself in letters that he was considered second to none of his contemporaries. From there he came to Galicia, where, while the relics of the blessed Martin were being carried, he was ordained bishop. After fulfilling approximately thirty years in that priesthood, full of virtues, he departed to the Lord.” He himself composed the verses that are above the southern entrance of the basilica of Saint Martin. An account of Saint Martin, bishop of Galicia, is found in Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 22, in these words: “Martin, the most holy bishop of the monastery of Dumio, sailed from the eastern regions and came to Gaul; there, having converted the Suevian peoples from Arian impiety to the Catholic faith, he established the rule of faith and holy religion, instructed the clergy, founded monasteries, and composed abundant precepts of pious discipline.” Isidore also reports that Martin flourished under Theodemir, king of the Suevi, at the time when Justinian held imperial power in the Roman Republic and Athanagild in Spain [Col. 0178C]. This must be understood of the beginnings of Martin’s activity in Spain [Col. 0178D].

Fortunatus, however, as Brower observes, follows the opinion accepted in his time by many, namely, that the Apostle Paul brought the light of the Gospel to Spain; Baronius examines this opinion under the year 61 but decides nothing. Since Saint Martin had contributed greatly by his work and diligence to the conversion of the Suevi—who had held Galicia from the beginning of the fifth century—from the Arian heresy, as can be seen in Gregory of Tours, Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, ch. 11, Fortunatus therefore calls him, after Paul, the “first spear-bearer.” Among the Romans, a *primipilus* was the commander of the first cohort; in the legion he ranked immediately below the tribune.]

[Col. 0177C] [Note: [Col. 0177C] He compares the virtues of Martin, bishop of Galicia, with the delights of paradise. He declares with what joy he felt himself suffused when he received Martin’s letter, and on the occasion praises at length his eloquence and learning; then he most humbly commends himself, as well as Agnes and Radegund, to Martin’s prayers.]

To the holy and apostolic lord in the army of Christ the King, the first spear-bearer after the commander Paul, Martin, bishop, Fortunatus.

Felici [Note: This letter is absent from the Venetian edition and from one Vatican manuscript.] The breeze of your happy reputation, restored by a breath that drives away sadness, has caressed our ears; flattering them with its gentle passage and crackling whisper, it has, while bearing the fragrances of the paradise garden, filled our very nostrils with the spice of delightful flowers [Note: A manuscript gloss says: “that is, breathing, smelling.”], exhaling its perfume [Note: In one Vatican manuscript: “breathing out perfumes.”] in measured harmony. It made clear that, just as God had planted Eden in the East from the beginning, so, when the age had run its course, he had planted another Elysium in the West, in which a stronger Adam—that is, martial Martin, an unconquerable inhabitant of Christ—might live, richer in faith and perpetually observing the commandment [Note: In some manuscripts *ad* is absent]. The Lord would go to visit him there in the afternoon, not so much in the breeze as he himself, a man made paradise, would retain by faith the beloved Redeemer’s footsteps as he walked within him among the emerald streets of his transparent heart and the shaded clusters of his flourishing work [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “overshadowing clusters”], not because the fig tree covered him, but because its fruit adorned him. Thus the presence of the pious Creator would not slip away even for a moment, since no fault would mark the creature even in the smallest particle. Through those blessings, then, as though enticed by the delights of a fragrant grove, the Lord would possess Vernula, and the servant (*verna*) would possess the Lord—since, joined to one another by alternating sweetness, neither would be driven away by admission [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “would be driven away by admittance”], nor would the other be deprived of the embrace.

From here, with my spirit longing, my inmost being burning, my eyes watchful, and my hands outstretched, I awaited your great letter, more fervently than a thirsty man, if only I might be moistened by a small cloud saturating a soaked fleece. Conscious of my desire, I anticipated wish with wish, if some fixed letter from you, borne across the shifting waves, would most certainly announce something about you to me; so that the rain of your conversation, tempering my dryness, might water me so deeply that the page would not be erased [Note: The same manuscript reads “nor erase the page”]. Yet, by divine providence, deliberately through your son, my venerable lord, I received the holy charity refreshed, when I saw the letter which, as you know, was artfully composed and, as I felt, filled with flowers [Note: Another Vatican manuscript reads “made with flowers”], so that it seemed to carry one drinking rather than reading it, intoxicating him with a perfumed expression at every letter.

The rich poured a drink for the poor and, so to speak, like noble Falernian wine, first acting as my cupbearer through its very fragrance, replenished me. A double harvest of eloquence had been heaped together, seasoned with salt, steeped in honey, and mingled with charm. It came with the strength of a foreign drink—so much the more avid because I was unaccustomed to it—while one part enticed and another deterred me. As a guest placed in uncertainty on a narrow balance [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “a rustic guest”], and unable to endure drinking so much [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “willingly I consent,” with another reading “drinking”], I consent to the sweetness, for I yield to its power with certainty [Note: Another Vatican manuscript reads “for I yield to virtue”].

As this gift flowed forth, I confess that it came to me like a spring of drink across the gray hairs of the sea; it came, excellent father, across the salt sea, to quench my thirst. Pure sweetness came, mingling with the ocean’s wave [Note: The same manuscript reads “the sea, mingling its wave, sweetness”]. Its liquid would not merely taste upon the throat, though it soothed the hidden parts, since by such a drink you nourished not the flesh but the spirit. Therefore, to continue truly, the grape of this vine prolongs our thirst while it offers us drink.

With this unexpected fruit falling through the deep [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “unexpectedly here”], this first fruit from the waves came to me. That ship perhaps brought alum to the others; to me it certainly brought the light of your conversation. What a commerce, with such unequal trade: what for others was bought at a price, for us was unbought [inept]. There the thirst is quenched; here it is purified. The former stains; the latter makes white as snow.

What shall I say of periods, epicheiremata, enthymemes [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *enthymemata*], and intricate syllogisms, in which the square Maro labors and the rounded Cicero? What is profound in them is fluent here; what is exceedingly difficult there is readily available here. I have discovered that, with only a few punctuation marks, you spread out leafy branches wherever you wish [Note: Another Vatican manuscript reads: “how you wish, you spread the shoots of the branches.” Browerus adds that a Trier gloss has *colae*, that is, “of the growing [thing].” Varro also uses *colis* in *On Agriculture*, book I, chapter 31, for a tender shoot on a vine. Browerus’s note. Here Fortunatus uses *cola* for an intermediate division in writing, in which sense he employs it in book I, chapter 1. This sense is confirmed by what he adds shortly afterward: “whatever you wish, you cut down with the sickle of a sharp comma”; that is, “as you spread your speech more broadly, after the manner of a luxuriant vine, so you contract and cut it down.”], and you cut down whatever you please with the sickle of a sharp comma, so that, under the discipline of a careful vintner, luxuriant shade may not grow here into weariness, while the branch stretched there may please with its fruit.

For what you report in your letter—that, after Stoic and Peripatetic judgment, I have been devoted to the apprenticeship of theology and contemplation—I acknowledge what love can do when it adorns even the undeserving [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “adorns those who are not deserving”]. Why, good Father, do you reflect back upon me what is yours, and publicly proclaim about me what is private to you? The first things are known to you, and the second are familiar to you. For although Plato, Aristotle, Chrysippus, and Pittacus are scarcely known to me even by reputation, and although I have not read Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, or Augustine—if they became known to me even in a vision while I was half-asleep, I would not truly perceive them [Note: “I would have truly perceived them”]—nevertheless, because the resources of the arts have gathered in your house as in a common lodging, those things which are closer to heaven cling to you more tenaciously. You are not so much delighted by the display of doctrines as by the rule of virtues. Hence, without doubt, you have become a client of heavenly clients [Note: *Clientela* is also transmitted as *clienta* or *cliens*; one Vatican manuscript reads “you have become the client of clients.”].

But why do I say these things to you, sweetest Father and true disciple of Christ? In the likeness of the Samaritan, mixing wine and oil, you offered me a soothing salve while I lay sick. You will receive the reward of your pious work when he comes who promised that he owed the innkeeper payment, preserving in you, supreme bishop, what he himself bestowed, knowing that what most pleasingly conquers dignity itself is precisely what is most worthy to please his eyes.

Therefore, lying prostrate upon my breast, I place the feet of your most sacred, sincere, most loving apostolic crown; and, last of all, I make my submissive limbs a resting place for your feet. In this way, with eager desire, I commend myself to your piety, and I ask you in the Lord that, approaching as a kind of mediator between the sinner and the Redeemer of the world, you may smooth away the offense and, good Father, reconcile the rejected man after his guilt.

And because I have received the pledge of your confidence, I devoutly commend to your piety, together with myself, its daughters and servants, Agnes and Radegund, at their request and command. We jointly beseech you that, speaking for us to the Lord Martin, you may come as a faithful intercessor, just as he himself once showed himself ready before the Lord, when he would not leave an inanimate corpse until death had released the dead man. For it follows reasonably that hope of patronage should return to us through you, because a share of the patron has gone forth from here to you.

I beg you before the Lord, pious Father, that, received into your favor [Note: “that your favor may receive me”], I may feel, among those commended to you, that under your instruction I am guided by prayer as well as by song, loved as a son by a parent, advanced under a leader, and protected under a guardian.

As for the bearer of this letter, your servant, truly good Bonosus, I approach your piety as a suppliant and, by whatever prayer I can offer, commend him to you; nor will I release your feet until you have promised, sweet Father. When, through the intervention of the saints, he returns safely to you, fulfilling in person the wishes of one absent, may I first obtain this: that whenever anyone comes here, the joys of your celebrated word may quickly sprinkle me.

Noble by merit and by the name of Martin, heir, I beg you: pray to God for Fortunatus.

## CHAPTER II. Likewise to the same man

[Note: Just as he relates that various regions of the world were assigned and distributed to the apostles, so that they might bring the light of the Gospel to them, he says that Galicia was divinely given to Martin, so that he might sow and disseminate there the truth of Catholic doctrine. At the end he commends himself to him, as well as Radegund and Agnes.]

When the one Trinity [Note: It was formerly read *Triados*, as it is also read in the Venetian edition. Browerus states that he corrected the word and restored *Triades* as more suited to Fortunatus’s customary declension of such words. *Triades* is also found in each Vatican manuscript.] spread its light,

And the world welcomed a new day with honor,

So that the seed-bearing light might drive away the darkness of the soul,

And the enlightened mind might drink in the clear faith,

Rome, the chief city, is restored when the thorns have been torn away,

Cultivated by the plowshare of the distinguished prince Peter.

Paul, penetrating the Illyrians and the Scythian frosts,

Dissolved the cold of the earth with his fervent teaching.

Matthew tempered the heat of the Ethiopians with his speech,

And poured living streams upon the scorched land.

The warfare of Persia was subjected to Thomas’s strength [Note: Browerus observes that Fortunatus always lengthens the final syllable of *Persidis*. It is enough to mention once that he uses this and similar forms, perhaps rather freely, in the manner of poets.],

And the conquered tiara became stronger through God [Note: The Venetian edition reads: “the joined tiara [is] to God.”].

Livid India was given to clear-sighted Bartholomew,

And Achaea stands as a harvest through Andrew’s teaching.

But, hastening on lest I delay, ancient Gaul of Martin,

With its excellent faith, takes up the weapons of light [Note: Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, book I, chapter 11, relates that when the son of Charraric, or Theodemir—also called Ariamir—king of Galicia, was suffering from a serious illness, and the king heard that Saint Martin’s tomb in Gaul shone with miracles, he sent men to bring some of the saint’s sacred relics to Galicia. When they were carrying them into the harbor of Galicia, divine providence caused Martin himself—the Martin about whom this poem was written—to arrive from a distant region at the same shore and to be made bishop of that see. Thus the Suevi who inhabited Galicia, after renouncing the Arian heresy, embraced Catholic doctrine under Theodemir, with Martin contributing greatly to that cause, as Fortunatus relates here.].

Rejoice, Galicia, preserved by the new Martin;

This man of yours was of apostolic destiny.

By Peter’s power he gives you Paul in doctrine,

Granting you Jacob’s help on one side and John’s on the other.

Coming, as they say, from the region of Pannonia belonging to the Roman people [Note: Browerus observes that although most of Pannonia was held down by the barbarians, some considerable places in that region still remained under Roman rule. For this reason he thinks Fortunatus calls Pannonia, Martin’s birthplace, a Roman region.],

He became a still greater salvation for the Gallic Suevi [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “a true salvation for the Gauls.” The Venetian edition reads “true Gallic salvation.” The Trier manuscript has *Gallisuaeba*, as Browerus reports; the word appears to have been fashioned by Fortunatus to indicate how salutary Martin was to the Suevi inhabiting Galicia.].

He sowed plants of life in barren furrows,

Where nature delights in a harvest of fertility.

Another rain, through the merits of Elijah, returns to the ears of grain,

Bearing gifts of dew so that thirst may not oppress the fields.

Lest the dry acres lie idle in their senseless furrows,

A perennial spring pours into them from a source of flowing water.

He fixed the pious shoots of faith upon the branches of heresy;

What was a wild olive now flourishes as a rich olive.

The tree that stood thin, stripped of its leaves,

Now about to produce food, blooms with new honor.

The sad fig tree, destined for the hearths and without hope,

Cultivated with manure, prepares its bosom for fruit.

The swelling grape of the vine, to be torn apart by the raids of birds,

Under this good guardian the grape does not perish in the vineyard [*lacu*].

The vintner set the vine-rows [*antes*] in order by apostolic deeds [Note: Browerus reports that the line was formerly corruptly read: “He shows those praying to live through apostolic affairs.” The Venetian edition reads most corruptly: “He helped those praying through apostolic affairs,” with the remainder of the verse missing. One Vatican manuscript reads *escas* instead of *antes*. *Antes* are rows of vines, as in Virgil, *Georgics* II: “Now the vines are bound, now the vineyards put away the sickle, / Now the vintner sings of the last shoots.” In the preceding verse, where it was corruptly read *non peritura latet* or *patet*, Browerus restored *non perit uva lacu*—“the grape does not perish in the vineyard.” I consider the Venetian reading preferable: *non peritura lacu*, “the grape not destined to perish in the vineyard,” lest the word *uva*, “grape,” be repeated without reason.];

Moving the fields with the mattock and pressing the tendrils with the sickle.

From the Lord’s field he cut away the useless wild vine,

And the cluster appears where formerly there was only a shrub.

From God’s sowing he pulled up the bitter weeds,

And an even, rejoicing crop rises.

Rejoice, Galicia, preserved by the new Martin [Note: This distich was found in both kinds of manuscripts.],

This man of yours was of apostolic destiny.

Returning around his fold, through the shepherd’s devoted care,

He protects the sheep with love of the flock, lest the wolf enter.

Supporting it with his hand, he himself leads the unstable sheep

To Christ’s pastures, lest error devour it on the mountains.

His voice flowing back from a wholesome spring to the people

Offers faith to drink through the ear and salt through the mouth.

He prepared losses for the enemy but pious vows for the Lord,

And returns the entrusted talents doubled.

Awaiting the Gospel voice, the blessed laborer,

So that he may hear: “Good servant, go forward,”

Since you were faithful to me over a few things,

You will be placed over very many [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “you will be guarded by the Lord,” which is corrupt].

Behold, now enter more joyfully into the joys of your Lord,

And great things are prepared for you in exchange for brief labor.

You will hear, Martin, the blessed voice—

But remember Fortunatus himself.

I beg you, pray, Father, that I may see your joys with you,

So that you may please the King, with Peter’s gate standing open [Note: The manuscripts of Cologne and Trier read this way; the common text has “May Peter petition before you.” The Venetian edition is still more corrupt: “With Peter preparing beforehand.”].

Agnes, humble and suppliant, together with Radegund, piously asks

That they, commended to you, may be entrusted to you, holy Father;

And that, as the choir of sisters grows through sacred songs,

They may please their gentle Lord, with you as their guide,

And that Caesarius’s rule may be observed by the city of Genesius [Genesii], having adopted it for itself [Note: Saint Caesarius was born in the territory of Cabillonum and, as a boy, entered the monastery of Lérins, already renowned for its learning and holiness. There he lived for some time as a monk under the discipline of Abbot Porcarius. He then undertook the governance of a suburban monastery in the territory of Arles. Finally, after Eonius, bishop of Arles, died, Caesarius was appointed in his place, although unwillingly. He afterward took care to build a monastery for women and appointed as abbess Caesaria, his sister, whom he had arranged to be educated and trained in the monastery at Marseille. He composed the rule they were to follow. This rule was later adopted in other monasteries of Gaul, especially by blessed Radegund in her monastery at Poitiers. To obtain it, she had deliberately sent a delegation to Arles to Caesaria the abbess, who had succeeded Saint Caesaria, sister of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles. The city of Genesius mentioned here by Fortunatus is therefore the city of Arles, in which the memory of Saint Genesius was famous and distinguished. See his passion among the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 603 of the Paris edition.],

The nourishing rule of the pious prelate

Who was bishop of Arles, from the community of Lérins [Note: *Lerini*],

And remained a monk while possessing pontifical dignity [Note: Saint Caesarius, although he had attained episcopal rank, did not cease to undertake the duties and offices of monks, insofar as the care and responsibility of his dignity allowed. As written in his Life, part I, no. 8, he was ordained first deacon and then priest, yet never abandoned the canonical chanting of a monk or even slightly departed from the institutions of Lérins. In order and office he was a cleric; in humility, charity, service, and the cross he remained a monk. See his Life in the first volume of the Benedictine edition, p. 659.].

With a father’s diligence, protect your own foster daughters,

So that these good works they perform may benefit you.

Thus may you gird your illustrious head with a beautiful diadem,

And, as shepherd, give worthy thanks for the flock.

## CHAPTER III. To the citizens of Tours concerning Gregory, bishop of Tours

[Note: In this poem he celebrates the arrival in his own church of Gregory, newly made bishop of Tours, and from his presence, teaching, and vigilance he foretells every blessing for the people of Tours.]

Rejoice, fortunate peoples, holding new vows [Note: The Paris edition reads “fortunate ... holding.”],

And, at the arrival of the bishop [Note: Gregory himself reports the year in which he was inaugurated bishop of Tours in book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 1, saying: “In the one hundred and seventy-second year after the passing of blessed Bishop Martin, in the twelfth year of the reign of Sigibert, the most glorious king, after the death of Saint Euphronius, bishop ... I, unworthy, received the burden of the episcopate.” The twelfth year of Sigibert’s reign corresponds to the common era year 573, in which year Fortunatus therefore wrote this poem.

Browerus, who dates Gregory’s creation as bishop of Tours to the twelfth year of Sigibert’s reign, nevertheless assigns it to the common-era year 575. He can easily be refuted on this point, since Clotaire died in 561, after which Sigibert, having divided his father’s empire with his brothers, obtained the kingdom. See Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 22.],

Return your vows to God.

Let boyhood celebrate this, let bent old age celebrate this,

Let every person proclaim this common blessing.

Behold, the hope of the flock has come, father of the people, lover of the city;

Let the sheep rejoice in the office of their shepherd.

With watchful eyes, let those who sought him with prosperous prayers

See that he has come and keep festival joys.

Gregory by name, having rightly received the honors of the priesthood,

He is shepherd of the flock in the city.

Julian sends his own foster son to Martin,

And offers to his brother what was dear to himself [Note: This Julian is Saint Julian, martyr of Auvergne, who suffered at Brioude. His head was taken to Vienne, while the rest of his body was buried at Brioude; it is still preserved and venerated at Brioude in the distinguished basilica of the canons called Counts, as the learned Ruinart relates in his notes to Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book II, chapter 1. Because of the singular devotion with which Gregory honored the martyr, who had once deserved well of Gregory and his brother—as related in chapters 24 and 25 of the same book—Gregory does not hesitate to call himself Julian’s foster son, saying: “Because of their ancient affection, the thought had settled in my mind that I was his foster son, as I was Julian’s.”],

Whom the benevolent hand of Father Aegidius [Note: This was Aegidius, bishop of Reims, about whom we have already said more in the notes to book III, chapter 20. Why Gregory was consecrated by Aegidius, who was in Belgica Secunda, far from the diocese of Tours, we learn from Gregory’s Life, where the following is written in chapter 11: “A delegation was sent to the king” by the city of Tours after the death of Saint Euphronius, “and by God’s providence Gregory happened to be present. When summoned concerning this matter, with what humility did he try to excuse himself, and in what ways did he strive to withdraw? But because the Lord’s will prevails, everything else yielded. The king compelled him by authority; Queen Brunichildis pressed him insistently. But since disciplined humility does not refuse obedience, at last he consented. And so that, as I believe, he might not flee after being delayed on some pretext, Aegidius, archbishop of Reims, immediately ordained him.”],

Consecrated to the Lord with a father’s gracious hand,

So that he might refresh the people whom Radegund loves [Note: After Saint Radegund withdrew from Clotaire’s bed, she stayed for some time at Tours in order to venerate Saint Martin’s tomb in person. She had also already arranged for a monastery of men to be built at Tours, as we stated in the Life of Fortunatus, no. 85.].

Sigibert rejoices and favors him, and Brunichildis favors his honor;

By the king’s judgment, a noble dignity is present.

Under his feeding, may the flocks be guided through holy pastures,

And gather gifts from the seed of Paradise.

May he preserve the spotless sheepfold of pious Christ,

Lest it lie open to be torn apart by ravening wolves.

With ever-watchful care, may he govern the spotless stable,

And let no plunder burden the flock entrusted to him.

May he fortify the lambs enclosed within precious wool,

And, himself watchful, protect those whom he has saved [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “and those sleeping” or “and those put to sleep.” The Venetian edition reads “and those whom he protects through his favor.”].

May the flower-filled vineyard grow rich under divine cultivation,

And, ripe, be beautiful with its own cluster.

May it fill the barns of heaven with eternal fruits,

From which souls may drink streams from the living spring [Note: The Venetian edition reads “drinking from a living spring.”].

May the thirst for which Lazarus then sought relief with his wet finger, to soothe the fire, not torment them [Note: Here Fortunatus shortens the naturally long vowel in *petebatur* for metrical reasons. This is nevertheless the reading found in the Trier manuscript and ancient copies, according to Browerus. The common text reads: “Did he not seek help?” The Venetian edition reads: “He sought help.” The Paris edition has:

“By the wet finger of Lazarus,

That he might be asked to bring help to lessen the flame.”],

But may the shepherd lead the sheep into the flowering bosom of Abraham,

And with peaceful embrace guide them to the stars,

So that, with the entrusted talent doubled,

They may enter the true joys of their own Lord [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “may the Lord enter.”].

Let him rejoice beneath Peter’s key, through Paul’s doctrines,

Among the starry choirs shining with light.

Let mighty Athanasius stand there, and renowned Hilary,

Rich Martin, and gentle Ambrose.

Let Gregory shine, holy Augustine overflow,

Let Basil glow [Note: Another Vatican manuscript reads “let Blaise glow”], and let Caesarius sparkle.

Following their deeds and faithfully fulfilling their sayings,

May he rejoice as one sharing in perpetual life.

And, crowned with a worthy reward for his labors,

May the king’s soldier obtain a place in the citadel.

## CHAPTER IV. At the birthday [Note: It was an ancient custom to celebrate solemnly the anniversary of bishops, as may be understood from old sacramentaries and the homilies of the supreme pontiffs. The “birthday” was the day on which the bishop of a see and of a church had been consecrated, just as the anniversary of the Roman pontiff’s consecration is celebrated today.] of Bishop Gregory, when he was asked to recite an antiphon [Note: In his notes on this passage, Browerus commends the ancient custom in the Church of singing antiphons and illustrates it with several monuments of antiquity, showing that Ambrose first introduced into the Latin Church the practice that had long existed among Eastern Christians.]. Spoken at Mass.

Through the merits of Martin, Gregory,

May you cherish the flock of Tours for long ages as shepherd in the city.

May you be a standard in sacred councils and in the lives of the devout [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read “in the lives of those who came before.”],

And may the honor you have attained grow through your example.

May your tongue minister apostolic light to the peoples,

And, as you shine, may heaven’s gift gleam.

## CHAPTER V. To the same man, concerning the Jews converted through Avitus, bishop of Auvergne

[Note: This responds to Gregory of Tours, who had strongly urged him to celebrate in verse the distinguished deed of Avitus, bishop of Auvergne, in converting more than five hundred Jews to Christ Jesus. Fortunatus writes that he has satisfied him by sending the poem appended to this letter, which he says he poured forth without care or study because of the bearer’s insistence.]

To the holy lord, a lord to be proclaimed for his apostolic merits [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “to be proclaimed”; the Venetian edition reads “to be preached.”], and in Christ a father, Pope Gregory, Fortunatus.

You urge me, excellent Father, with serious insistence yet sincere sweetness, to make a speech in verse although I am tongue-tied, and to make the sluggish run in pedestrian meter; and, taking advantage of the occasion offered, at least to touch courteously, if not elegantly, upon the praise of the praiseworthy apostolic man, Lord Bishop Avitus [Note: On Saint Avitus, see what we noted on poem 26 of book III.]. You have found in me something that you would not love for the brilliance of its diction but would delete [Note: The Paris edition reads “you would love, but love.”], and, as I myself am conscious, you know that among us there is not so much what you may approve as what you may reject—especially since the importunate bearer, with words falling one by one from his gaping mouth like a stern collector, forced me not so much to pay interest [Note: Browerus here warns that *in* should be deleted, contrary to his own two editions. There is, however, no trace of this alteration in the Vatican manuscripts.] as to pay it [Note: The same source reads “as to spend it.”].

Although his headlong journey drove him on, so that, panting meanwhile, I could scarcely catch my breath [Note: The Paris edition reads “meanwhile”], nevertheless I obey your commands, though they were carried out in a tangled fashion [Note: The Venetian edition reads “though they were simply carried out”], preferring to serve rather than to please [Note: The Venetian edition reads “rather than that we may please you”]. I do not know whether I should attribute this more to you or to the pressure of time, since the task has been imposed on one who had neither means nor time available. Yet, devoted in obedient service, I shall sing with honor what your love commands concerning the praise of the aforesaid bishop.

In your venerable servants, excellent Creator,

It is fitting that your praise, Christ, should always sound.

Inspiring the mind, supplying desire and accomplishment,

You are the one without whom no good can prevail.

With clear light making the hearts of poets fruitful,

So that their holy inmost parts may generate faith for the peoples.

Set above the lampstand, their shining mouths

Make the gracious house gleam with the fire of doctrine.

And just as the eye directs the limbs of the head [Note: The Paris edition reads “of the arch,” but the margin has “limbs.”],

So may the pious care of the shepherd govern the sheep.

Enriching the hearts of bishops with heavenly virtue,

You, almighty God, supreme and everlasting summit.

Nourishing Spirit, poured into the lips of holy Avitus,

You speak through your servant, so that the order of the flock may grow.

He was not content with the number that he received from him,

But, as the Lord’s steward, returns the doubled talents [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “the steward in the Lord.”].

For the people of Auvergne, divided by a twofold uproar,

While dwelling in one city, were not one in faith.

To Christians the Jewish odor rebounded bitterly [Note: The Venetian edition reads “rebounded.” The Paris edition reads “remained.”],

And an impious crowd obstructed the holy rites.

Lifting its neck and refusing to bear the Lord’s yoke [Note: The same source reads “refusing to bear the Lord’s laws.”],

Thus an empty skin swells with proud spirits.

The priest often admonished them in the love of God,

So that a harvest of converts might rise to the stars.

But the shadow of a dark covering lay upon them,

Pressing their foul hearts and preventing them from seeing clearly [Note: The Paris edition reads “of darkness.”].

Therefore the day had come when the Lord was restored to the stars,

And the hanging man traveled the heavenly path [Note: The reading *pendulus ibat*, “went hanging,” is found in another witness.].

The people, animated by faith [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “the people, armed by faith”; the Venetian edition reads “armed”], tore down the Jewish temples,

And the field lay open where the synagogue had been.

At the time when Christ’s power returned to the heights,

As he ascended, the hostile nation fell [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “the hostile thing fell.”].

Yet this bishop gently addresses those rebellious against the law of Moses,

Whom anger had made fierce.

“What are you doing, Jewish band, ancient yet unlearned?

To renew life, learn to believe, old man [Note: The Venetian edition reads “learn, old man.”].

Let your milk-white hair understand things greater than youth;

Lay aside the grave understanding that belonged to childhood.

Let it not shame you, slow and aged,

To follow better things. Though failing in body,

Let old age increase in honor.

There is God—this is a lofty faith—one and three, and three and one [Note: The Paris edition reads “one, three things, and three, one.”];

One summit stands in three distinct persons.

For the Father, and the one begotten, and likewise the Holy Spirit,

Have one law, work, order, and throne in three.

The Lawgiver proclaims this; the patriarch Abraham confirms it [Manuscript: “believes it”].

Hence he is our father, because he is of our faith.

He sees three equals and venerates one in worship;

He asks one with his voice and washes three in the basin.

Thus, like his uncle, Lot receives the travelers as guests;

He feeds them in Sodom, and they rescued Segor [Note: Segor is the well-known city to which Lot fled, when the angels granted him reprieve.].

When the Lord rained grievous fire from the Lord upon Gomorrah,

The Son and the Father are the Lord from the Lord.

He who is your creator and maker is himself mine;

We are the creature of him who is God in the Trinity.

You are sheep of one shepherd—alas, why do you not go as one?

I beg that there be one flock; one shepherd is present.

Do you refuse? Or do you recall what David’s reed sings,

And what the prophetic virgin’s offspring accomplished?

He hung transfixed on the cross by his hands and feet,

But his flesh was not corrupted when he rose from the tomb [Note: The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript read “did not fall from the tomb.”].

Returning after three days, he heals us through a lasting wound;

That he returned to heaven, this day also bears witness.

Believe my words—or believe your own, convicted old age.

If you flee and tremble, you neglect [Manuscript: “nor do you read these things while reading.”]

We prolong a long word in a time meant for brevity:

Either admit the prayers, or, I beg you, yield your place.

No force presses here; gather yourself wherever you wish, free:

Either be my follower, or go away as your own fugitive [Note: The same source reads “or go away as your own fugitive.”].

Give back the place, settler, and take your contagion with you,

Or let that be the dwelling, if one faith possesses it.

The priest gave these pious words to the men in a gentle voice,

So that the path of the heart might go wherever it pleased.

But the Jewish band, rebellious and goaded by fury, [Source breaks off here]

Gathered, snatched away, and then shut up in the house.

When the Christ-worshippers then see the ranks of Manzara [Note: [Col. 0189C] The Venetian edition reads, “then the empty ranks join.” The Vatican manuscripts retain *Manzara*. This word seems to have arisen from the Hebrew term [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], which means “spurious,” “illegitimate,” and so forth, and from which the Greek *ἐκ πόρνης* (“from a prostitute”) is rendered. Hence Sedulius too, cited by Browerus, has in Book V:

[Col. 0189D] “With the Manserian peoples rolling toward worse things . . .”] joining,

At once they leap upon the place where that deceit lies hidden.

If they raged with swords, they would feel justice as they fell,

So that they might be able to live—or gracious faith would grant it [Note: [Col. 0189D] The Paris edition reads, “that they might conquer.”].

Envoys hasten to the prophet, bearing these messages:

“We, the Jewish people, are now your sheepfold.

Acquire for God those who can live, lest they perish;

If there is delay, we die, and your gains fall away.

Hasten your step; unless you hurry with swift course,

You, Father, will have to mourn the deaths of your children.”

Overcome by these tears [Note: [Col. 0189D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “overcome by these tears,”], the pitiable priest is carried away,

So that he may rightly bring the help of salvation to the afflicted.

They reach the place where the savage crowd lay shut in;

When it comes out to meet him, it pours prayers from its tearful mouth [Note: [Col. 0189D] The Paris edition reads, “groans.”].

A mind that holds to Jewish laws is slow toward the good [Note: [Col. 0189D] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “the mind is slow toward good things.” The Venetian edition reads, “the mind is slow for a man.”];

It sees the light late, when the day is passing.

Thus, from the beginning, a veil has been stretched over the eyes of the heart,

So that the blind person does not know where the straight road calls [Note: [Col. 0189D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “where the straight road leads.” The Paris edition reads, “where the straight road goes.”].

But at last we follow, Shepherd, where you often admonished us,

You who compel the sheep to run with such sweet salt.

Now believe your believers [Note: [Col. 0189D] The Venetian edition reads, “believers now to believe you, and not to deceive you with falsehoods.”], and do not deceive them with falsehoods [Note: [Col. 0189D] The Paris edition reads, “believe”; in the margin, “false.”];

We seek the bath; let the pool be ready for you [Note: [Col. 0189D] The Venetian edition reads, “let it be ready for you; wash.” The Paris edition reads, “let the place be ready.”].

We have perceived by the result [Note: [Col. 0189D] The Paris edition reads, “by sight.”] what you were rightly accomplishing by prayer,

What God himself, through you, urges us human beings to do.

Here he draws into the light those whom the shadow had covered while they denied.

The king opened a road for the new army [Note: [Col. 0189D] The Paris edition reads, “night opened a road.”].

The ranks, once divided, come together under one [Note: [Col. 0189D] One Vatican manuscript and the Venetian edition read, “divided under one”; the Paris edition reads, “under one,” with “under one” in the margin],

And God becomes one love among the two peoples.

[Col. 0189C] From this point the fleece of the sheep is drenched with olive oil,

And, sprinkled with the sacred substance, becomes another fragrance for the flock [Note: [Col. 0189D] Browerus inquires into and explains at length the fragrance of the Hebrews. Since these matters do not bear on our present purpose, we have willingly omitted them [Col. 0190C]. Fortunatus may here have meant not bodily fragrance but that of the soul, in the sense in which the Apostle said, “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place,” and so forth.].

Behold, the day had come when the gracious Spirit, from on high

Sent forth, flowed into the mouths of the apostolic men.

The sacred event awakens country people and townspeople alike,

And eagerly they wear a path to the holy celebrations [Note: [Col. 0190C] Three Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition read, “wear a path to the holy celebrations.”].

The Jewish odor is washed away by divine baptism,

And a new offspring, restored, rises from the waters.

Outdoing the Ambrosian dews [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Paris edition reads, “Ambrosius.”] with sweet breath,

The fragrance exhales from the head anointed with chrism.

[Col. 0190A] A new Passover is celebrated in immense numbers,

And sheep are born from the stock of the wolf.

One people received another people, one common folk another;

One who is not a parent by natural descent becomes your parent through the font.

From every side, a waxen light snatched up by hand summons the stars,

So that you might think the stars were moving along, dragging their hair.

Here there is the color of milk-white clothing [Note: [Col. 0190D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “here there is a milk-white garment.”], there the gleam of the lamp;

Day is drawn forth and painted with varied light.

Nor was that festive day less radiant than the one in which

One Spirit granted people to speak in different languages.

What, I ask, was the mind of Bishop Avitus there?

How powerful was his fervor when he offered these things to God?

The priest himself shone among the lampstands,

Gleaming within, illuminated by the Spirit’s diffused fire.

While he bore such true holocausts for himself [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Venetian and Paris editions read, “then for himself.”],

[Col. 0190B] When he offers the living victim to the living God [Note: [Col. 0190D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “when the living victim gladly makes God a sacrifice with wine.” The Paris edition reads, “while he offers the living victim to God with wine,” with “to God” in the margin.].

If the patriarch pleases God because he offered his only-begotten son,

How pleasing will the man be who offers so many?

Moses could not bring those people under our faith;

Who acquires for Christ what will be his own offering?

He poured the Lord’s aromatic libation upon the altar,

And sent new incense upward to God among the stars.

He obtained his vow, because he joined the sheepfold under one [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Paris edition reads, “He obtained his vow, because he joined the true olive.”],

And the Shepherd has joy in the snowy flock.

Consider these unpolished things as offered to you, gracious Father Gregory,

Which you command Fortunatus, though they will not suffice.

Add that an urgent bearer compelled me to carry this small work,

And in the time available scarcely a doubled day was granted.

We know from your affection that you love him especially [Note: [Col. 0190D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “rather, whom you love through affection.”],

This man whom you see in your heart and always hold upon your lips.

Nor is this enough for you, that you yourself are his reporter [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Venetian edition reads, “that he himself is the reporter.”];

You compel the others to applaud him with their voices.

It was not without purpose that you advanced him as your fosterling,

If, in mind and faith, he repays with love the one to whom he owes it [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Venetian edition reads, “thus to him to whom you give faith in your mind”; the Paris edition likewise has “faith in your mind.”].

May the Almighty approve this, memorably through a long age [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Venetian edition reads, “so that he may be remembered through a long age,”],

So that you may be his praise, and he yours.

May you also remember me, humble as I am, equally on both sides [Note: [Col. 0190D] The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript read, “may you both remember me together.”],

And in hope of forgiveness bring help with your voice.

## CHAPTER VI. To Syagrius, bishop of Augustodunum [Note: [Col. 0191C] Syagrius was made bishop of Augustodunum near the end of Chlothar’s reign and succeeded Remigius in that see—or, as others call him, Benignus, who had followed Eupardus. Browerus traces Syagrius’s very noble lineage and family to that Syagrian house in which Sidonius, in Letter 8 of Book VIII, recognizes a name descended from military cloaks, ivory curule chairs, ornamented litters, and purple-dyed official registers. In that same letter Sidonius tries to recall the younger Syagrius—whom he calls “the flower of Gallic youth”—from rural leisure and attention to household affairs to the course of domestic honor and glory. In Letter 5 of Book V he calls the same man the great-grandson, through the male line, of Afranius Syagrius, once consul. Let these remarks suffice for illustrating Syagrius’s family and lineage. Some wrongly believed that he was the brother of Queen Brunhild; Cointius refutes their error at the year 560, no. 5, and points out its cause and origin. Syagrius took part in the Second Council of Lyon in 567, the Fourth Council of Paris in 573, the First Council of Mâcon, held in 583, as Cointius shows, and the Second in 585. The same Syagrius—who, as Cointius teaches, lived until 600—was honored with the pallium by Pope Gregory, through the agency of Brunhild, to whom Syagrius was especially dear, as is clear from the letter of Saint Gregory the Great to Brunhild, Letter 11 of Book IX, or alternatively Book VII, Letter 5, indiction 1.].

[Col. 0191A] [Note: [Col. 0191A] Fortunatus recounts that, after he had long ceased composing poems and was living distracted by other cares and affairs, a father suddenly appeared before him, deeply distressed on account of his captive son. The father’s arrival shook Fortunatus out of his inactivity and laziness. He describes pitifully the man’s coming to him and the bitterest grief he had conceived over his son’s misfortune, and, at the father’s request, commends the matter to Syagrius. Taking advantage of the occasion, he sends him, as payment, an acrostic poem carefully composed by him about the Redeemer of the human race, and explains at length its elaborate structure and arrangement.]

To the holy lord, most worthy lord Syagrius, pope by apostolic authority: Fortunatus.

From the torpor of foolish leisure, by which a drunken mind, growing brutish as it sickens through long decay [Col. 0191B], is dulled and weighed down as though by the lethargy of an idle sleep, drowsing without any biting concern for the business that leisure indulges; when it seemed that reading was being neglected as much as practice was being abused, and I found no occasion arising from a subject that could be shaped [Note: [Col. 0191D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “from a subject that could be honored in poetry.” The Paris edition reads, “from a pattern that could be chosen.”] into poetry—and, so to speak, nothing was being shorn from the fleece that could be carded into verse—burying myself within myself in a kind of silence that served as a sarcophagus, and, singing nothing, having grown rusty through the worn-out plectrum of my tongue [Note: [Col. 0191D] The Paris edition reads, “though I sang nothing”], at last, unexpectedly—or not unexpectedly [Note: [Col. 0192C] Another Vatican manuscript reads, “not unexpectedly,” which is the reading accepted here.]—my fellow captive, delivered to me, as I think, by the lot of your good fortune, asks: “Who? From where? What does he report [Note: [Col. 0192C] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “what does he bring?” The Paris edition reads, “What does he bring?,” continuing in the margin, “while he consults, through the son’s shared misfortune,” and so forth.”]?” While I question him, he bursts forth, scarcely releasing his sobs, and declares the causes of his son’s misfortune, his own need, my compassion, and your reward [Col. 0191C]. His voice being interrupted, while he was not permitted to speak by the grief of his inmost being and the flood of his eyes, his tears confessed the father through silence itself: while the anxious father hung upon his words and did not utter them, since his throat’s instrument was silent, his eyes spoke through tears [Col. 0192A].

Such is the power of nature in love, that a parent is more able to reveal his affection before himself through feeling than through speech [Note: [Col. 0192C] The Paris edition reads, “to prove it.”]. His eyes therefore flowed, and his tears watered both the seed of misery and the fruit of mercy, staining his entreaty with a soothing lament so that even the cruel might be made compassionate. From one spring flowed the resin of dew [or, “the things of sorrow”] and of recompense: one watered with his eyes, the other drank with his ears, what the former pressed out in tears, while the latter stored it up as fruit.

Thus the mind of the captive made itself understood by a sign of sobbing; and grief, as though in a mirror, drew upon the face what anguish was seen to hold in the heart. Therefore, among those who were silent, when the cause of events was understood, while he wished to tell me what he wanted done [Note: [Col. 0192C] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “when he was able to say this.”], the emotion appeared wonderfully to speak without a tongue, so that he seemed to say what had to be done [Note: [Col. 0192C] One Vatican manuscript reads, “what had to be done,” with a variant spelling.].

Since this lamentable fellow citizen [Note: [Col. 0192C] From this it may be inferred that the man whom Fortunatus calls his fellow citizen was a native of Poitiers, since Fortunatus had by then established his home at Poitiers and had been enrolled in that city’s clergy. A homeland is not only the place where we were born, but also a place where someone has maintained a definite and stable residence for a long time, intending to remain there to the end. Poitiers was often troubled by wars, killings, and raids; consequently, after many captives had been carried away, Fortunatus may have been able, through the favor he enjoyed with kings and leading men, to interpose his services for liberating his fellow citizens.] moved me, suffering both loss and exile, and when I saw the father’s face drenched in the rain of affection, so that I myself almost passed wholly into another’s feeling, his tearful eyes fashioned complaints for me [Note: [Col. 0192D] The Paris edition reads, “fixed complaints for me.”] in place of encaustic painting; and, in an admirable manner [Note: [Col. 0192D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “and in an equally admirable manner,”], water, which normally erases, wrote through tears. Who would not believe one who weeps, one whom a wolf did not beget [Note: [Col. 0192D] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “whom a stone did not beget.”]? What humanity would not soften, one whom the offspring of a tigress did not produce? For the leopard’s course, the boar’s strength, the lion’s tooth, and the elephant’s bulk grow gentle under caresses [Note: [Col. 0192D] The Paris edition reads, “under caresses . . . and the tusks.”].

At last, when the clamor of his complaints had subsided, he pointed you out as the swift remedy for his pain [Note: [Col. 0192D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “he points you out as a prosperous remedy”; another, “he points out a prosperous remedy from you.”], since a mind sick within itself seeks healing.
