If you deigned to provide it, your tongue becomes a poultice [Note: [Col. 0192D] The Paris edition reads, “deigning . . . a healing remedy.”]. While you speak, mingling myself with myself through your words [Col. 0192C], I convinced the man, who trusted you, that through me you were being consulted [Note: [Col. 0192D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “trusting in you,” which the Paris edition also gives as “trusting in you.”].

It remained only not to weep, yet I had to consider whether I should send something for the ransom, by which the son might benefit, or something by which both might benefit [Col. 0193A]. Thinking of economy, lest the captive’s reward be cheapened for you by the low price [Note: [Col. 0193C] One Vatican manuscript reads, “by which the offspring might benefit . . . or by which you might benefit.” The Paris edition reads, “by which you might benefit . . . lest the usefulness of the price.”], I feared this above all: if it were received in a coin, it might look to a talent [Note: [Col. 0193C] One Vatican manuscript reads, “might breathe again.” The Paris edition reads, “to breathe again for you in a talent.”], especially since I desire you to enjoy treasures equally with your martyr [Note: [Col. 0193C] The reference seems to be to Saint Symphorianus, who was crowned with martyrdom at Augustodunum and whose memory was honored there with great devotion, as Gregory of Tours reports in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 52.].

But what could a small gift produce, and while I hesitated in my choice, I recalled the lethargic saying of Flaccus, the Pindaric poet:

“To painters and poets

There has always been equal license to dare anything.”

Considering this verse—if each artist mingles whatever he wishes, why should it not be possible, even without an artist’s intervention, to mingle both things, so that poetry and painting might be begun together as one fabric? Then, since I wished to offer a verse for the captive [Note: [Col. 0193C] One Vatican manuscript reads, “I wished to offer verses.”], considering the years of the Redeemer, so that Christ might complete the tones of his age [Note: [Col. 0193B] The supplied text gives variant readings “quotenos . . . annos,” apparently “equal numbers . . . years”; the wording is uncertain.], I would weave a poem with as many verses as there are letters.

Immediately repelled by the difficulty of the work—or rather enclosed by it through the necessity both of meter and of a summary of letters—what was I to do? There the traitor, by a new reckoning, made my cramped number expand yet more narrowly [Note: [Col. 0193C] One Vatican manuscript reads, “where the traitor expanded the narrowness.” The Paris edition reads, “What was I to do with the summary of letters, since the traitor expanded the narrowness of the number for me?”], there was no fixed endpoint, nor any place where length could shake itself free or brevity be confined; nor did the structure permit me to wander, since a barrier restrained the descending verses. In that beginning, as the summit continued to grow, I was permitted neither to loosen nor to slacken the threads, lest the wandering fabric, leaping beyond the number, disrupt itself.

Thus I was troubled by the task of making two complete verses descend through the heads, two diagonally, and one through the middle. One part remained: among all the letters, where could I place it at the center, so that it might receive everything without offending anyone? When I had gathered the threads of this fabric according to their number and begun to weave [Note: [Col. 0193D] Another Vatican manuscript reads, “gathered them so that I might hold them”; the Paris edition reads, “so that I might weave them among themselves.”], the threads tore both themselves and me [Col. 0194A]. I began, with the work nearly completed, to be bound; and, by a changed turn, while I wished to loosen the captive’s cords, I bound myself with a chain.

From this it may be inferred how difficult this little work is: whenever you wish, if you add something, the line grows; if you subtract, its grace perishes; if you change it, the beginnings no longer correspond; if you fix a letter, you cannot escape it [Note: [Col. 0193D] The Paris edition reads, “nor can you withdraw.”]. Thus, while this fabric hung, knotted together by verses, so that even if I passed over two I would still not escape three, I, an unwary sparrow, as though through deceptive clouds, ran into a panther [Note: [Col. 0193D] When Fortunatus says, “I, an unwary sparrow, as though through deceptive clouds, ran into a panther,” I do not think he is referring to the familiar beast, but to some kind of bird-catching device called *panthera* by a Greek word, because of the abundance of its prey. I heard not long ago that this type of bird-catching is still used among people of our own time and is called *panthera*.], because here my feather became bound by what I wished to avoid—or rather, to put it as it was said, it stretched out like fivefold split, sticky feathers smeared with birdlime [Note: [Col. 0194C] “Fivefold split and sticky” refers to the form of the following acrostic, divided and apparently split into five parts for readers, in whose composition Fortunatus nearly stuck fast from annoyance and labor. The Paris edition reads, “I stretched it out while turning it.”].

In all this, what troubles me is that I not only had made such a thing, but was not being drawn on by any similar example [Note: [Col. 0194C]

The Paris edition reads: “That I should not only make such a thing, but that I was not drawn on by a similar example.”

Browerus adds another reading to be placed in the margin: “that I might vindicate myself,” referring to “lest I be conquered in the work.” This is marked as a second revision.

Father Browerus observes that such acrostics were not unknown even before Fortunatus, and that Publius Optatianus Porphyrius offered Constantine Augustus certain poems constructed and interwoven with letters in the same fashion. Browerus reports in his notes on chapter 3 of Book II of Fortunatus’s works that these poems had been printed at Augsburg in his own time. It must therefore be said either that such examples, if they existed then, were unknown to Fortunatus, or at least that he could not have had them before his eyes.

As for Browerus’s further claim that Lampridius is also praised by Sidonius in Letter 11 of Book VIII for having made a *staechos*, I prefer, with the distinguished Sirmond, to read *elegi echoici* (“echoing elegiacs”) there rather than *staechos*. We have already discussed these echoing elegiacs in the notes on chapter 37 of Book III.

From this it is likewise understood that Fortunatus was the first to compose an acrostic of this form and workmanship, and that it therefore predates those poems about the holy cross by the same author which we cited above in Book II.]

I was being led.

Uncertain and trembling at this, suspended by the novelty itself, I wondered whether I should attempt what I had never undertaken, or reject more cautiously than I might rashly put it forth. At last, though unwilling, I speak almost what I do not know; and you conquer me by love, lest I be conquered by the work.

Behold, you demand from me what you scarcely find in me, and you use force against one who is yours, not rebellious [Note: [Col. 0194D] The Paris edition reads, “who am not rebellious.”]. You extort it, and you cannot be repelled. Love is a gentle tyrant.

To prepare this exchange, seized by affection, I, an inexperienced sailor, hung out my sails upon an uncertain sea [Note: [Col. 0194D] The Paris edition reads, “upon an uncertain journey.”]. I am carried through waves and rocks; you urge me headlong to cross unknown places. What is there that you cannot obtain? As you love, so you command.

You therefore have the work squared into a single fabric, yet divided into five parts for reading; and since there are thirty-three verses as well as letters, in imitation of the bodily age of Christ, through which the one who rose again completed our salvation, two letters are still read descending through the heads, two diagonally, and one through the middle. Thus, when the verse has ended, the letter does not end, because even if it reaches the endpoint by a slanting route [Note: [Col. 0194D] The Paris edition reads, “by a direct curve”], it still has a course remaining in descent, since it is joined again in the final verse.

In the center of this little work we fixed the letter that is counted as the middle among the twenty-three. It looks back upon as many letters before it as it leaps over after it, because, when the verses converge, the whole is both divided and remains intact as a divided thing. The letter marked in the descending verse is held in one verse and runs in another; and, so to speak, it stands for the warp and runs for the weft along the path, so that there may be, on the page, lettered threads.

Nor—rather, in the variant, “Lest”—should the fact burden us that we seem to mingle painted threads by a spider’s art [Note: [Col. 0195A] The same edition reads, “by a spider’s craft.”], since it is known to you that, in the books of the prophet Moses, an embroiderer wove the garments of the priests. Since crimson is absent here, the fabric is made of red pigment.

The verses descending diagonally from the corners stand according to a principle, even though in their placement they lean downward. As for how each is connected or what each contains, it is enough for the prudent to test the matter without an index.

In conclusion, commend me to your holy blessedness and, granting what is requested to your overflowing sweetness, with confident reciprocity [Note: [Col. 0195A] Another Vatican manuscript reads, “with confident reciprocal age.” Th. Pul. adds in the margin, “reciprocity.”] of service: if it pleases you, once this work has been written upon the wall, let the painted image keep watch over the vestibule as doorkeeper for me. Pray for me.

## CHAPTER VII.

[Col. 0195] [Note: [Col. 0195C] This acrostic poem, which was absent from nearly all copies—and indeed occurs nowhere in the Vatican manuscripts—and which the distinguished Baronius, under the year 587, no. 28, declared to have perished, was recovered by Father Browerus from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Gall and first published by him. Here it is laid out in deciphered form:]

[Col. 0195C]

The divine summit made Adam as he was, and gives dreams until

The rib, torn away, was formed into Eve, not unequal:

Happy together, covered with the doubled light,

Shining from their mouths, the married pair lived among holy fields.

The pleasant air returned to their nostrils from the joyful bank.

The delights of incense filled them with abundant breath:

One pleasure, fostering them both in a flowering place,

[Col. 0195D] A region famous for good things fed the blessed.

[Col. 0196C]

But when they possessed such great and still greater honor,

The whole earth of humankind wonderfully obeyed the two.

Soon the hidden liar draws out the weapons of poison,

The uplifted serpent, the jealous, masked enemy,

Savage, overcoming the innocent with harmful gall,

By persuasion he struck down those whom divine grace had blessed.

And the man, from the earth, then fell again into it,

And by the creeping one’s deceit was shut out from the eastern rising.

By this law of our parents, born under condemnation, we die.

But God, exalted, *aie*, and light from light,

While from the throne of heaven he freely provides his gifts,

The living Lamb entered the raw flesh of the chaste woman.

[Col. 0196D] From there salvation came forth, and the lamp of the Morning Star,

[Col. 0197A] The light of the untouched birth, awakened, drew the world out:

Rightly God from the Father, then human, fleshly, from the womb,

The Creator lowered himself into lowliness to rescue us,

O king’s head for sale, whom the cross fastened.

By spear, voice, hands, the blow of smell, and gall.

By this deed, Creator, you release captives from their lot:

Only late, through death, was the true purchase of life given;

Therefore I speak hymns to God, who releases us from guilt.

But you, supported by the praise of an eternal crown,

Rays of the Gauls, for whom even night may shine,

Break the cords from your necks and take up the weapons of day;

Freedom itself frees you and will make you blessed.

### Verses placed at the sides

Holy Syagrius, grant Fortunatus these devout prayers:

Christ sent himself when he brought us back from death.

### The middle verses, which describe the cross

Releasing captives, you will become the meditation of the Lord:

Sweet gift of God, by which the price may crown you, dear one:

Devotion dear to God gives the soul release from death.

The word placed near the center of the acrostic, “Aie,” I plainly cannot determine what meaning it conveys; nevertheless, the sequence and sense of the verses clearly show that it must be retained.

## CHAPTER VIII. To Felix, bishop of Namnetum [Note: [Col. 0197D] On Felix of Nantes and the magnificence of his estates, see chapters 8 and 10 of Book III, and compare them with what is reported here.] 

[Note: [Col. 0197B] He replies to Felix, who had invited him to the countryside. He describes the location and pleasantness of Felix’s estate, yet places Felix’s own presence and appearance far above them.]

[Col. 0197C]

I perceive, supreme Father, a light venerable to all,

Sweet head of the world, a name dear to me: Felix,

Whom I embrace in my heart and carry in the arms of affection.

You are my sweet burden, and this load does not weigh upon one who loves.

Why, supreme one, do you call me humble to visit the pleasant places [Note: [Col. 0197D] The common text reads, “to enter the lofty places.” Browerus.] 

That hold you, dear one, where I might sing with you,

Where the glassy Loire washes your lands with its chilly stream,

And the beautiful field of Cariacum slopes down toward the river [Note: [Col. 0197D] Cariacum seems to be the same as the river Carus or Caris, which flows into the Loire somewhat below Tours, or the field may have been named from that river.],

Where the river refreshes the land with its waters, and the vine with its shade,

And the crackling north wind lashes all the meadow’s leafy growth [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Venetian edition reads, “the north wind lashes the depicted, leafy growth.” Three Vatican manuscripts read, “all the painted growth.”].

The fertile soil is indeed beautiful beside its fish-filled shore [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Venetian edition reads, “beautiful beside its precious shore.” Some had supplied “beautiful, with the settler leaping,” as Browerus reports.],

But your face makes Fortunatus’s surroundings pleasant.

## CHAPTER IX. To Gregory, bishop of Tours, concerning a journey [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Venetian edition reads, “after the journeys.”]

[Col. 0198A] [Note: [Col. 0198A] He congratulates Gregory in this poem on his return to Tours and finally commends himself and the bearer of the letter to him.]

Honored summit, gracious glory, abundant light,

Shepherd, pleasing through love for the apostolic see,

Always to be embraced by me, holy and revered Gregory,

Never torn from my heart, venerable man.

I rejoice that the bishop has returned to Tours with honor,

And I rejoice for myself that you, Father, have come back.

We eagerly applaud, holding our common prayers,

Because you have restored the day to citizens and homeland.

I commend to you, priest, the servant who is present with me,

Wishing that you may long govern the flock [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read, “wishing you to govern the flock from afar.”].

## CHAPTER X. To the same.

[Col. 0198B] [Note: [Col. 0198B] He greets Gregory by sending a poem and praises his virtue and teaching. He excuses the letter’s brevity and says that the magnitude of his love makes up for it.]

In generous, devout duties, gracious Father Gregory,

You who seek the stars openly with a mind bringing salvation,

And whoever, unarmed, is animated by your counsels

Will possess the aid of a victor in the sacred warfare.

Commending your humble servant, I offer a greeting [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Venetian edition reads, “greet me with a greeting,” which is preferable.],

Always with devout love, blessed man, to God.

If the page is brief, the lover’s ardor is not brief,

For hearts cherish more than my words can sing.

## CHAPTER XI. To the same, concerning a book lent.

[Col. 0198C] [Note: [Col. 0198C] He gives thanks for certain poems apparently written by Gregory and lent to him; at the end he commends the bearer of the letter.]

Reading divine poems and composing them from your own breast,

Sharing them with others, you become the parent of a palm of victory.

These works also, which you once gave to the flock as shepherd,

I willingly praise with due thanks [Note: [Col. 0198D] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “I praise them duly.”].

Yet may lofty gifts from the Thunderer remain for you,

Because you distributed sacred riches to the poor [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Paris edition reads, “because, generous, you give riches well.”].

Since I can inquire into them [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Venetian edition reads, corruptly, “which I cannot through all things, I sing as a gift.” Two Vatican manuscripts read, “since I cannot inquire.” The Paris edition reads, “when he who,” with “as a gift for all” in the margin.], for so great a gift

May your grace sound all the more through my own mouth [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Venetian edition reads, “here may your grace sound more through his own mouth.”].

I humbly commend to you, supreme priest,

The servant who is present as the gift-bearer [Note: [Col. 0198D] One Vatican manuscript reads “the present servant Prodomerus”; another, “Prodemerus”; a third, “probomore.”].

To whom may you grant the management of a just balance [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read, “granting him the management of a just balance.” The Paris edition reads, “with the management of a just balance.”],

So that your future palm may grow in God’s honor.

## CHAPTER XII. To the same, concerning an invitation [Note: [Col. 0199C] In the Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript, *mulierum* (“of women”) is absent; nor does this word seem to have any connection with the poem.]

[Col. 0199A] [Note: [Col. 0199A] To Gregory, who had invited him to Tours, he offers the excuse that he was being detained from going by another bishop, also a bishop; then he asks that, for the sake of peace, Gregory forgive him for not coming.]

You invite me, holy Gregory, with the affection of a father to go

Where at Tours you feed the flocks with the honor of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0199C] The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts read, “with the love of the Lord.”].

Where the holy bishop Martin, with his excellent merits,

Entrusted to you the sheep he had previously possessed [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts read, “yielded these sheep to you.”].

Now also, through the sheepfolds and Christ’s flowering pastures,

You both rightly guide the flocks.

But your brotherly authority, exerting force upon me [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Venetian edition reads, “in the old manner.” I scarcely doubt that the bishop by whom Fortunatus says he was detained from traveling to Gregory at Tours was Maroveus, bishop of Poitiers, on whose will Fortunatus depended, since he was enrolled in the clergy of the church of Poitiers. Fortunatus seems certainly to have been at Poitiers when he wrote this, since he greets Gregory in the names of Agnes and Radegund, whom he calls Gregory’s own daughters, just as below, writing to Aredius in chapter 22, he designates them by the same name. He asks, for the sake of peace, that Gregory forgive him for not coming; perhaps some disagreement existed between Gregory and Maroveus, just as Gregory of Tours reports that there had been between Saint Euphronius, Gregory’s predecessor, and Maroveus himself, in Book IX, chapter 40, of the *History of the Franks*.],

Has turned my journey back, preventing me from hastening to you.

Often I have asked by vow, command, and a missile-like word,

And I have pledged myself to you [Note: [Col. 0199D] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “or promised.” Fortunatus seems to imply here that he did not obtain permission from his own bishop to travel to Gregory, although he had often requested it and claimed that he was bound by a promise to do so.].

You are a man pleasing through goodness, a shepherd who loves peace;

For the sake of the treaty, I pray that it may be forgiven [Note: [Col. 0200C] The Venetian edition reads, “thus, venerable one, I pray.” One Vatican manuscript reads, “may it be venerably forgiven.”].

Your own daughters also greet you with reverence [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript read, “greet you, venerable one.”];

But I, blessed Father, ask you to commend me.

## CHAPTER XIII. To the same, concerning the commendation of a woman.

[Note: [Col. 0199B] He praises Gregory’s virtue and likewise commends to him a woman whom he had received under Gregory’s recommendation and who was returning to him.]

Supreme Father of your homeland, outstanding model of devotion,

Sweet head of Tours, summit of religion,

Always following lofty things, Gregory, with a merciful heart,

Seeking from here the glory of the soul by this course [Note: [Col. 0200D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “seeking this by such reasoning.” The Paris edition reads, “in this way.”].

The woman whom you commended when she came, exalted priest—

Receive her, now returning to you, as a father would.

May you also, dear one, be the long-lived return of all,

And may your life be a harvest for me and for the others [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Venetian edition reads, corruptly, “may your life be a hedge.”].

## CHAPTER XIV. To the same, concerning his journey.

[Note: [Col. 0199C] He declares his affection and exceptional longing for Gregory and announces to him that he reached Poitiers safely, although, after departing from Tours, he had made a difficult and dangerous journey along roads covered with ice.]

I always gladly desire, holy Gregory, worthy of embrace,

To see you with my eyes and seek you through little letters.

It is sweet for me to see you [Note: [Col. 0200D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “but if there is no opportunity to see you.”]; and if the chance to see you is absent,

There will still be hope for one praying to speak words to the Father.

Recently, hurrying away from your presence,

I say that I traveled across glassy roads of ice.

But with the help of the cross, while Martin acted as patron,

I reached the mothers safely, gracious Father.

They greet you reverently with manifold honor [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript read, “they greet you with reverent honor.”];

But I offer prayers of well-being for your return.

## CHAPTER XV. To the same, a greeting.

[Note: [Col. 0200A] He extols Gregory’s virtue and recalls his devotion and teaching, while also testifying to his own goodwill toward him.]

Supreme of priests, abundant power of goodness [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Paris edition reads, “goodness and.”],

Summit through your honor, light through my love,

Venerable in sacred duties, nursling of devotion,

To be held in my heart as the pledge of my friendship,

Flourishing in studies and faithful to the sacred law,

Always bringing forth future gifts for your soul.

Therefore, Father, while I pray to you, I call earth, sea, and stars to witness,
So that you may wish to remember me with your sacred lips [Note: Venetian edition: “that I may be your remembrancer.” One Vatican manuscript: “that I may remember.”]

## CHAPTER XVI. To the same, concerning apples and grafts [graphiolis]

[Note: “Graffiola: a shoot, little twig, branch of a tree; a shoot grafted or inserted into another; whence our people say *greffe*, and the Occitans *grafion*.” Dufresne, *Glossary*, under this word. Browerus adds that *fercula* is found written instead of *graffiolis* in the *Calar* [reading uncertain], apparently corruptly, for *surcula*, “shoot.”]

[Note: He thanks Gregory because he had sent him as a gift apples together with their shoots.]

Generous in pious offices, holy Gregory, refuge,

Though absent, be present through your gift, supreme Father.

You send me parents together with their offspring,

Grafts inserted with fruit, apples as well.

May almighty God grant that, filled with the fruit of merits,

You may eagerly gather the apples that paradise possesses.

## CHAPTER XVII. To the same, concerning the commendation of a girl

[Note: When Fortunatus had come to the place where stood that tree which, once torn up by the roots, had blossomed again through the prayers and power of Saint Martin, and from which healing was sought for the sick, he stopped, moved by the tears of certain parents who were lamenting miserably that their daughter had been abducted. He therefore tells Gregory the story and implores his assistance and authority so that the daughter who had been carried away may be restored to her parents.]

As I hastened along my journey, gracious Father Gregory,

Toward the place where the holy signs of your predecessor are found—

Where, it is said, the tree, lying uprooted,

Put forth leaves before Martin’s prayers.

Now, through the merit of faith, it stands dispensing cures,

Healing many bodies while remaining bare of bark.

The girl’s father and mother were present here in tears,

Filling the air with their voices and wetting their cheeks.

I plant my foot, I prick up my ears; from their mouths

Their sold daughter is scarcely made known to me through sobs.

I ask further; the complaint declares that, with no proof of theft,

The father [*patet*, uncertain] bids her go beneath the yoke on a charge of theft.

Witnesses swore in due order that he had wished to give her away,

Each naming his own witness, although he had been unable to do so in his need.

There was no judge; an accuser was pressing the charge.

What could I do here, when sacred authority forbade action? [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read *vetante, sacer*, “when the holy one forbade,” a reading that should be retained.]

“If pious Martin were present here,” I said,

“The shepherd would not have allowed the sheep to be lost.” [Note: Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts: “would have permitted nothing.”]

Yet I gained strength by remembering you, supreme priest,

Who reproduce the predecessor’s hope through your compassion.

Investigate, constrain him; and, if the matter is otherwise, rescue her, beloved one,

And, as a father, add this girl to the flock and return her to her father.

Me also, your servant, dear one, subdued to your service,

Protect in your pious refuge, excellent shepherd.

## CHAPTER XVIII. To the same, concerning the commendation of a traveler

[Note: He praises Gregory’s compassion and commends both himself and a traveling man to him.]

Good man, attaining the summit of honor through your merits,

Noble protection, pontifical head,

Whom rank and character, through the rich fruit of compassion,

Raise more worthily, as God magnifies you.

The humble salutation of Fortunatus, mindful in kindly affection,

Prays you, Father, that it may serve you.

May this traveler likewise rejoice, supreme priest,

That he has merited you as his shepherd and his homeland.

## CHAPTER XIX. To the same, a greeting

[Note: He praises Gregory’s gifts and commends himself to his prayers.]

Shepherd, summit of honor, venerable holy priest,

Gracious glory of the Fathers, love of religion,

Glory of bishops, pious palm of merit, Gregory,

A noble head rightly rising with your rank.

Fortunatus asks you for aid from Olympus:

Through you, dear Father, act so that he may be found worthy.

## CHAPTER XX. To the same, a greeting

[Note: Having received a letter from Gregory announcing that he was enjoying good health, he shows how greatly he rejoiced at this and asks him to be more expansive in writing.]

A letter hastening from you visits me graciously,

Holy bishop, man of compassion, Father.

Eagerly receiving it with my eyes, I return to it in spirit,

Rejoicing that you are safe, as the letter reported.

May a page sent under your name, Pope Gregory,

Refresh me here at greater length with its message of health. [The transmitted text has *hinc*; *huc*, “here,” is also possible.]

## CHAPTER XXI. To the holy lords and apostolic fathers, the bishops of Christ’s Church, concerning the commendation of a traveler: Fortunatus

[Note: Browerus believes that this poem is addressed to bishops summoned to a synod, and that Fortunatus commends to them a traveler going to Italy. It seems much more likely to me, however, that the same text was written to those bishops whose sees lay along the road by which the well-traveled route to Italy was open, and whom Fortunatus, coming from Italy into Gaul, could have visited and come to know, thereby joining himself to them by some bond of affection and respect. Certainly, since he asks them to provide the man hastening to his homeland with necessary support, they seem to have been in a place from which they could conveniently supply suitable resources according to the needs and circumstances of the person commended. It would have been difficult for men who were away from their own homes and sitting in a synod to do this. The following statement also confirms this interpretation: “You who look upon the places … by coming to the aid of men”—that is, you who preside over cities and lands, exercising hospitality together.]

[Note: He commends to the bishops a traveler, an Italian by nationality, returning to Italy, so that they may supply him with the necessary provisions and other assistance suitable for completing the journey.]

Glory of bishops, reverence of those who worship Christ,

Rule of priests, summit and honor of the world,

You who survey the regions, in the honor [or love] of your own reward,

Coming to the aid of men so that your summit may stand:

Look: here comes an Italian, a traveler and a guest,

Seeing the shepherds, lest, I pray, the sheep go astray.

As he hastens toward his homeland, he asks for comfort:

Let the wandering exile, destitute, find a gift from you.

Make me, Fortunatus, your own through the compassion of fathers;

I ask you to reconcile me to heaven by praying to God.

## CHAPTER XXII. To Aredius, abbot

[Note: Saint Aredius was born of a most noble family of Limoges. As a young man he lived at the court of King Theudebert, honored with the office of his first chancellor. Then, at the urging and under the instruction of Nicetius, bishop of Trier, who had admired the young man’s outstanding character, he withdrew from the court and became a monk. Not long afterward he built a monastery near Limoges, where he lived most devoutly until the end of his life and died renowned for miracles in the year 591, as Gregory of Tours relates in Book X, chapter 29, of his *History of the Franks*. His life, written by Gregory, appears at the end of Gregory of Tours’ works.]

[Note: He says that, since he cannot meet Abbot Aredius in person, he meets him through letters and earnestly commends himself to his prayers.]

Kind Father, I wish to offer you greetings in words,

Since here I cannot see you with my eyes.

For such is the honor of your worship to me

That the summit sent from here may stand in your place before you.

Yet I ask you, blessed one, through Christ’s sweet pastures,

To remember me also when you offer prayers with your lips.

I believe that God’s gifts are granted to me, shepherd Aredius,

If, gracious one, you remember your Fortunatus.

Also greet the holy mother on my behalf, dear one [Note: Paris edition: “greet her.”]

And, when this boy returns, give him the power to speak for me.

Your own daughters likewise greet you, gracious Father:

Agnes, with devoted affection, and Radegunde together.

# BOOK SIX

## CHAPTER I. Concerning Lord King Sigibert

[Note: See what we said concerning the beginning of Sigibert’s marriage to Brunichilde in the *Life of Fortunatus*, section 44. Since that marriage is assigned to the year 566, this poem too should be considered to have been composed by Fortunatus in the same year, as was the following poem, written on the same subject.]

[Note: In this poem he celebrates the marriage of King Sigibert to Brunichilde, daughter of Athanagild, king of the Goths in Spain. He begins with the beauty of spring and a kind of renewal of nature. He declares the joy that arose throughout the kingdom from this marriage and the royal magnificence with which it was celebrated.]

When the earth has been stripped of frost in renewed spring,

The field clothes itself in painted grass.

The mountains extend their leafy summits farther,

And the shady tree renews its green tresses.

Promising grapes heavy upon its life-giving branches,

The lovely vine swells with budding tendrils.

Sending forth flowers and caressed by a delicate murmur,

The delicious bee stores honey in its cells.

Fertile in a chaste marriage-bed and renewing its offspring,

It desires to produce children through the flowering of its maker [or, according to the Paris edition, “of the cautious one”].

Bound together in its own ties through love of posterity,

The chattering bird hastens toward its offspring.

Each thing grows young again in its own seed despite old age;

While all things return, the world possesses every joy.

Thus now everything favors the matter, while through heavenly prosperity

The royal palace advances under the imperial yoke.

[Note: From this Browerus conjectures that envoys sent by the emperor Justinian, or Justin, into Austrasia to offer congratulations are indicated here—unless, he says, someone should seek Caesarean stock in Athanagild’s family, like a laurel in a cake. But I do not see why the poet, after the description of spring, whose gladness he takes as a favorable omen for celebrating Sigibert’s marriage, should immediately append this couplet: “Thus now everything favors the matter, while through heavenly prosperity / the royal palace advances under the imperial yoke,” if the phrase “imperial yoke” indicated an embassy sent by the emperor rather than the union of Sigibert and Brunichilde. Certainly the subject (*hypothesis*, ὑπόθεσις) of the poem seems to be royal nuptials, not the arrival and presence of Caesar’s envoys. Nor is there anything absurd in using “imperial yoke” for a royal one, especially in a Latin writer for whom, by native idiom and usage, “royal” and “imperial” meant the same thing. Indeed, no more august name could have been employed to express the royal magnificence and dignity amid the congratulations of the whole kingdom, by which Fortunatus, a newcomer to Gaul, might win some favor from the kings—particularly since Browerus himself admits that Fortunatus always calls the Franks Romans, never barbarians, as we have noted elsewhere.]

With manifold ceremony, great lights of leaders

Have surrounded the fortunate king for all ages.

So many summits of nobles converge upon a single summit;

Behold, Mars has its commanders, and peace has its glory.

The festive palaces seethe at the arrival of all,

And the people see their prayers fulfilled in the king’s marriage.

You whose stream flows from irrigating springs [Note: Venetian edition: “you whose irrigating spring flows,” which should be retained; Paris edition: “may reap from the irrigating spring”], favor the occasion:

By your judgment, small things customarily grow.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the marriage of King Sigibert and Queen Brunichilde

[Note: He likewise sings an epithalamium on the marriage of Sigibert and Brunichilde. First praising Sigibert’s chastity, he then introduces Cupid and Venus, who compete with one another in praising Sigibert and Brunichilde respectively. Finally he offers auspicious and joyful wishes for both.]

Sun, reveal a fortunate day and, with serene rays,

Scatter your hair, filling the bridal chamber with unclouded light.

Sigibert, exultant and born for our joys,

Makes his vows; now free from another’s love,

He undertakes dear bonds. With youth under control,

His chaste mind seeks marriage, restraining wantonness.

He flees to the yoke, from which his age takes nothing away.

Chaste in heart, ruling so many peoples as their single lord,

He has imposed reins upon himself; yet, in accordance with nature’s demand,

He is content with one embrace under the law of marriage.

Here love does not sin; rather, by preserving chaste bridal chambers,

It renews the household through offspring, when the heir shall have played there [Note: Venetian edition: “when the heir shall be light.”]

Perhaps winged Cupid, with his shrieking bow,

Bent his love-bearing arrows; flying, he burns every race upon earth.

Nor does the sea defend its waters [Note: The Venetian edition, one Vatican manuscript, and the Paris edition read “defend with waters,” which is preferable.]; soon he subdues

The worthless hearts, the sluggish crowd; at last thereafter

He drinks the rich senses’ breathless fire into the king’s peaceful bones,

Leaning softly upon him, and the flame clung to his marrow.

The royal summit was burning; no sleep-giving night

Brought rest to his heart, as he returned in eyes and mind

To the faces that love had painted [*finxit*, “formed”], exhausting his mind;

Often, under a false image, he played through an embrace.

As soon as Cupid saw the king being scorched

By the overpowering dart [one Vatican manuscript: “by the overpowering heaven”],

By the virginal lamp, he joyfully said to Venus:

“Mother, I have accomplished my wars.

In my burning breast another Achilles is overcome:

Loving Sigibert is seized by the fire of Brunichilde.

She pleases, suited to the marriage-bed, marriageable in mature years;

Her virginity, swelling in its flower, embraces her husband,

Destined to please him with its first offerings, and suffers no loss of modesty;

Hence she is called a queen, all the more powerful.

The virgin too desires this, although the modesty of her sex

Resists; loved by the man, she repels him with a gentler hand,

And forgives herself the faults that the fire has inflicted.

But now come joyfully, since your vows summon you.”

Soon Venus mixes violets with ambrosial amomum;

She cuts roses with her fingernail and hides them in her greedy lap.

Together they broke through the clouds on light wings [Venetian edition: “with wings”],

And together they came to adorn the splendid bridal chambers.

From that point Venus began to place her noble fosterling first;

Cupid, in turn, placed the man, both favoring the marrying pair,

And they engaged in a pious dispute. Then Cupid said a few words

To his mother: “Here is the man whom we promised you.

Sigibert, love of the people, light born to his parents,

Who traces his lineage from forefathers through a long succession of kings,

And will beget kings, the great hope of the people,

A noble offspring in whom ancestral honor has grown.

A better man returns from his stock [Paris edition: “here a better man … and the form of his ancestors”; marginal reading: “the fame of his ancestors”],

And an exalted posterity cherishes the fame of those before him.

He extends the name of his grandfathers with a warrior’s hand;

A courage inherited from his father [Note: After this verse the Paris edition inserts: “Although small, no greater age hinders anyone.”]

Which, as Nabis [one Vatican manuscript: *Nablis*, another *Nabilis*] proves, he displayed: he conquered Thuringia,

Completing a single triumph over two peoples.

Nor does compassion, in Dietheubert’s case, exact penalties for pardonable offenses [Note: The Venetian edition gives these two verses as:

“Alas, the piety of Bertholinus, restraining pardonable things,

Lost these two; one is sufficient in place of both.”]

This man lost two; one is sufficient for both.”

[Note: The Paris edition reads: “He restores these two; one in place of both”; marginally, “this one restored two.” Another marginal reading is, “but this one gave two in place of both.” One Vatican manuscript reads most corruptly: “Piety loses the Lord through Heuberto’s pardonable act; this one restores two in place of both.” Another reads: “He loses the house of three peoples; Heuberto’s piety restores what is pardonable, and this one restores two in place of both, one being sufficient.” A third reads: “He loses the Lord through Heuberto’s pardonable act, but this one gave two in place of both; one is sufficient.” Browerus had decided that these two verses should be deleted as spurious or marked with an obelus, since they were not found in the Trier manuscript and presented an obscure and corrupt meaning. Nevertheless, moved by the authority of three books, as he says, he retained them. He asserts that in the better manuscripts *Theubertum* is read instead of *Dietheubertum*, and traces of this name appear in the Vatican manuscripts just cited. He therefore believes that Theudebert, son of King Theuderic, is indicated here. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book III, chapter 7, reports that Theudebert took part with his father in the battle in Thuringia. The sense would then be that, through his piety, Thuringia was induced to lose two kings, Baderic and Hermenefred, and that Theudebert, eventually succeeding his father Theuderic, alone became king after their defeat. Browerus also notes that in other copies, instead of the published reading “this one lost two,” there is “this one gave two,” and he prefers to understand the passage as referring to the triumph by which both kings yielded to the victorious Frank.

A clearer meaning, and one more consistent with what follows, seems to me possible if we say that Fortunatus, after praising Clotarius for his military valor and, in the preceding verse, Theudebert for his piety—also commended by Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book III, chapter 25—then adds that Sigibert alone expressed in himself both Clotarius’ military valor and Theudebert’s piety. He thus represented in his own person the two most illustrious kings of his time: one of whom he had received as his father, while he had succeeded the other in the kingdom—for Theudebert had been king of Austrasia and had inherited the kingdom of his father, Theuderic. Accordingly, the verse may be read either as “but this one gave two,” that is, “expressed and surpassed them in himself,” or as “this one lost two,” that is, “lost them in death, so that one might suffice in place of both.” The other statements that follow concerning Sigibert’s person agree admirably with what precedes.]

Ruling the western quarter, in the flower of youth,

He has already surpassed old men in gravity, though tender in years [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “He has already, with the gravity of six years, surpassed tender years”; another: “of three years.” The Venetian edition reads: “So gravely he has surpassed six tender years.” The Paris edition: “With the gravity of elders he has surpassed tender years.”]

By his deeds he has deserved to precede nature’s law.

Although his age is small, no lesser age hinders anyone [Note: Venetian edition: “no one’s lesser age seeks”; one Vatican manuscript: “no greater age hinders anyone”; the manuscript is often extremely corrupt],

Whoever maturely governs his judgment is the nobler one here,

Whoever is more self-controlled within a narrow span of life.

Thus he cherishes these peoples from his earliest years,

So that he is both father and king, ruling no one harshly.

No day comes without fruit unless a suitable provision is made [Note: Venetian edition: “unless an appropriate leader presides; he considers it a loss to waste his profits.”]

He thinks he has lost much if he has not granted abundance.

He spreads joys from his radiant countenance;

No clouds weigh upon the people under a serene king.

With mature heart he forgives grievous faults.

Where others sin, he triumphs by forgiving.

For he is learned: since the first virtue in a ruler

Is to be compassionate, because one who knows how to spare always has someone to spare.

He first corrects himself in what he demands that another correct [Note: Venetian edition: “He first corrects himself in what he wishes another to amend.”]

Whoever is his own censor restrains the rest well by law.

In him remain all the qualities you could rightly seek in a king.

He alone loves everyone, and is loved by everyone.

Then Venus began to recount the girl’s praises:

“O virgin, wondrous to me [Venetian edition: “wondrous in my eyes”], destined to please your husband,

Brunichilde, shining brighter than the heavenly lamp,

You have surpassed the lights of gems with the light of your face.

A second Venus, endowed with the beauty of sovereignty,

No such Nereid swims from the depths of Iberian

Ocean, nor is any Nymph more beautiful;

The rivers themselves subject their nymphs to you.

Your milky face flashes with unbaked [natural] redness.

Lilies mixed with roses, if gold were to gleam among purple,

Would never equal themselves to your features.

Sapphire, white diamond, crystals, emerald, jasper—

Let them all yield: Spain has produced a new jewel.

Her beauty was worthy, and it could also bend a king.

Through harsh winters and deep snows, across the Alps and Pyrenees [Note: The Venetian edition has:

“Traveling through fierce winters and deep snows, across the Alps and Pyrenees.”

Whether Brunichilde made this journey into Gaul in late winter or at the beginning of spring cannot easily be determined, since Fortunatus elsewhere calls the Pyrenees snowy in July. Yet when I consider that the beauty of spring is introduced in the preceding poem as an argument for celebrating that royal marriage, and that here harsh winters and snows are mentioned through which Brunichilde is said to have traveled from Spain into Gaul, I am readily led to believe that the marriage fell at the beginning of spring. Sigibert married Brunichilde in the year 566, as we noted in the *Life of Fortunatus*, section 27; Fortunatus’ arrival in Gaul should therefore be assigned to that year, or more probably to the preceding one.]

And carried through savage peoples under the leadership of a serene king,

The queen passes across lofty mountains toward earthly marriage-beds [Note: Venetian edition: “toward an everlasting queenly marriage-bed.”]

You travel over a level road; nothing ever obstructs lovers

Whom divine powers wish to unite. Yet who would have believed

That a Spanish lady would be born for you in Germany,

One who joined two kingdoms under a single yoke [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts: “with a precious bond”; Venetian edition: “joined with a precious bond”; Paris edition: “attached with precious ties.”]?

Human effort could not accomplish so marvelous a thing;

For a difficult undertaking employs divine arms.

A long succession of the past scarcely produced such a king.

The greatest of achievements are accomplished with difficult exertion [Paris edition: “Difficult things are overcome”].

The exalted nobility of Athanagild shines,

He who extends his kingdom from the farthest realm across the world [Note: Venetian edition: “he who orders the world aright.”]

Rich in the wealth that the world possesses, he governs the Spanish people

Under his own authority, in a piety worthy of praise.

Why should I recount the kingdoms of your distinguished father,

When I see your parents increased through your merits?

You, radiant virgin, seem to surpass the throngs of women

As much as you, Sigibert, surpass husbands.

Go, you two, joined in limbs and yoked together in heart,

Both equal in character, both equal in merits and conduct,

Each adorning your own sex with noble deeds.

May your necks be joined in one embrace [Note: Venetian edition: “with your necks joined in one embrace”; Paris edition: “whose necks are bound together in one embrace”],

And may you pass all your years in gentle pleasures [Paris edition: “and many years in gentle pleasures.”]

May each of you desire whatever the other has loved.

May equal health attend you both and preserve two hearts;

May one love, joined in enduring support, grow strong [Venetian edition: “may it grow strong, bound together”].

May the joys of all rise under your auspices.

May the world love peace, and victorious concord reign.

Thus, parents, may you again celebrate the vows of your children [Venetian edition: “the vows of the parents”],

And may you hold grandchildren from the offspring of your children.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning King Sigibert and Queen Brunichilde

[Note: He extols Sigibert’s virtues and military praises at length, and rejoices that his wife Brunichilde has been converted from the Arian error to the truth of Catholic doctrine.]

Victorious from the setting sun, whose praise extends into the east,

And makes the head of the prince illustrious,

Who could offer you anything worthy? For even to say a few words

My talent does not draw forth, but your love compels me.

If Virgil were now here, or perhaps Homer,

A work bearing your name would already be read.

Powerful Sigibert, renowned for noble triumphs,

Your new valor is proclaimed by this side, your lineage by that.

Once Victory had taken wings after being seized by you,

And, spreading your prosperous deeds abroad, she flies.

The Thuringians, with the Saxons, resound [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts: “Saxon and Thuringian.” A marginal reading in the edition: “resounds with Thuringian.” No indication of this victory, which Fortunatus here says Sigibert won over the Saxons and Thuringians, appears among the ancient writers, so far as I have been able to investigate. I am therefore readily led to the view that this is the very victory which Sigibert’s father Clotarius is reported by Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book IV, chapter 10, to have won over the Saxons and Thuringians in the year 555. It is highly likely that Sigibert took part in that battle and performed brilliantly. That the Saxons obeyed Sigibert may also be understood from the fact that a Saxon force returning from Italy came to Sigibert, from whom they were restored to their own place and seat, as Gregory of Tours reports, *History of the Franks*, Book IV, chapter 43.]

lamenting their own losses;

So many men fell for the praise of one man.

Because then he was first of all of them on foot before the battle-line [Note: Venetian edition: “Because now this man outstrips all others on foot”; one Vatican manuscript retains *iste*, “this man”],

From this they now have kings who follow you [Note: The same edition and three Vatican manuscripts: “from which you have kings who follow you.”]

Your wars have given peace through new prosperity,

And your sword has produced assured joys.

Yet, though victory makes you boastful, you please all the more

Because the higher you rise, the gentler you remain.

You possess the highest honor, but your mind preceded your honor,

And your due summit stands forth in your conduct [Note: Venetian edition: “as your conduct ought to be.”]

A cultivator of justice, you shine with love of compassion;

The two virtues compete as to which will possess more of you [Note: The same edition: “so that you may have more of both.”]

Your speech, dignity, valor, goodness, mind, and grace are strong;

Your individual qualities would adorn all men.

You conceal the causes of all within your heart;

A pious concern for the people keeps you occupied.

You are given as one salvation to all, in sacred order;

In the present time you restore the joys of the past [Note: Paris edition: “a salvation of the kind assigned in due order.”]

Your excellent wife is adorned with Catholic worship.

Through you, the house of the Church has grown.

Christ joined Brunichilde to himself in love because of her merits

When he gave her to you.

You will keep these second vows better because, through Christ’s gift,

Hearts once joined now please more through the law [Note: Venetian edition:

“Once defeated in heart, she now pleases more through the law.”]

Pious king, rejoice in your queen’s great light:

She has been acquired twice, though married to you once.

Beautiful, modest, fitting, skillful, gracious, and kind,

Powerful in intelligence, appearance, and nobility.

Although she alone would have deserved such beauty,

She pleased a man before; now, behold, she pleases God.

May you pass long ages, radiant with your beloved wife,

Whom divine love has joined to you.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning King Charibert

[Note: Charibert was the son of Clotarius and the full brother of Sigibert. Gregory of Tours often speaks of him and repeatedly notes and criticizes his vices. After he had taken Marcovefa, a religious woman, as his wife—as Gregory himself relates, *History of the Franks*, Book IV, chapter 26—he was excommunicated by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, and died shortly afterward, in the year 567 or 570. This poem was therefore composed not long after Fortunatus had come to Gaul.]

[Note: He praises Charibert for the renown of his name, the nobility of his lineage, his virtues in administering the kingdom, his devotion to peace, his compassion, intelligence, tranquility and firmness of mind, prudence in conducting affairs, fairness, ease in settling private disputes, faithfulness in keeping promises, learning, and generosity toward his fellow citizens.]

The illustrious glory of great deeds has advanced,

And from the pious king scatters honor everywhere.

The setting sun and the rising sun proclaim the man,

Whom gravity, courage, judgment, and mastery of laws distinguish.

Under the four expanded regions of the world,

Through fruitful faith he possesses seeds of praise [or light; one Vatican manuscript reads “through fruitful day”].

On this side barbarism, on that side Roman civilization [Note: Venetian edition: “on that side Germany”] applauds him;

In different languages one praise of the man resounds.

Love the ruler, lofty Paris, in your citadel,

And honor the protector who gives you aid.

Now, rejoicing and favoring him, embrace him with eager hands—

He who by right is lord, but by compassion a father.

Restrain your former grief over Childebert:

The peaceful king has returned, who cherishes your prayers.

He was gentle, wise, good, and fair to all [Note: Gregory of Tours repeatedly and splendidly commended King Childebert’s piety and generosity toward temples in his *History of the Franks*, and we have mentioned him elsewhere in the notes to Book II, chapter 14.];

The uncle has not fallen while the nephew stands in the city.

He was worthy to take up his inheritance, the kingdom belonging to him,

For he is not inferior to him when praise speaks.

Charibert is here, governing the public laws;

In the present time he restores the joys of the past.

He has shown himself so faithful a follower of his uncle

That now this nephew is protector of his uncle’s wife [Note: This was Ultrogotha, and her daughters Chroteberga and Chrotesinda, whom Clotarius, after Childebert’s death and the seizure of his kingdom, had sent into exile. Charibert therefore took them under his protection.]

Retaining the sweetness of Childebert’s name,

He is brother to his daughters and himself their father.

They, well defended under the king’s peaceful rule,

Place in their cousin the hope of a father.

A great offspring, shining with noble light,

Whose glory runs from exalted ancestors.

For whichever ancient parents I might wish to recall,

Their royal order was the honor of an illustrious stock [Note: Venetian and Paris editions: “their royal order flows.”]

Whose lofty faith raised its summit to the stars  
and brought it to stand above the nations.

He trampled the swollen [enemies] [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read, “he trampled the swollen enemies.” The Venetian edition reads, “he trampled the enemies, swollen [with pride].”], raised up his friends,  
cherished his subjects, and terrified the fierce [Note: The Venetian and Paris editions read, “and terrified the savage.”].

Why, however, should I repeat here the lofty praises of earlier men,  
when rather your praise adorns your lineage with honor?

They enlarged their country by arms, but with bloodshed;  
you acquire more, since you rule without disaster.

Those whom wars previously exhausted with hostile dangers,  
you now cherish, secure, through your love of peace.

Everything sings of the king’s happy and prosperous times,  
under whose auspices rich repose flourishes.

Through you the earth’s peaceful harvest abounds;  
for devoted peoples, your life is a harvest [Note: The same edition reads, “for all peoples.”].

When the ages gained you as their king at your birth,  
day shone upon the world with greater light.

At last, seeing his joys increase through a new generation,  
your father said that he himself was growing through the honor of his offspring.

Although he was a ruler with a lofty crown,  
at your coming he raised his head higher.

Joyfully resting his hopes in the bosom of his heir,  
the old man thereafter flourished more greatly, in better hope [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read, “in the better hope of old age.”],

born before the other brothers from royal stock,  
senior in rank [Note: Charibert, whom Chlothar had fathered by Ingundis, is counted as third in age by Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 3. Yet he is called the first of the brothers because Gunthar and Childeric, born before Charibert, had died while Chlothar was still alive.], and thus first in devotion.

[Col. 0211C] On one side goodness praises you; on the other wisdom applauds;  
between the two, each excellence claims you for itself.

Your devotion shines forth from your uncle [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “while the devotion of your forefathers…”], and your intelligence from your father;  
in one face both parents live.

All the praises they possessed you gather together,  
and alone, with the law’s favor, restore the two of them.

You shine as the path of justice and the standard of gravity,  
and your precious faith provides a mirror of life.

[Col. 0212A] Firm moderation is maintained in tranquil minds,  
you who always possess a harbor in your own breast [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “a harbor…”].

No storm enters your heart with any tumult;  
lest you waver in judgment, the mind’s anchor is present.

A whispering breeze does not toss steadfast spirits,  
nor does fickle instability easily carry them away.

Hence glory accompanies its well-ordered course,  
because a disciplined mind conducts itself with maturity [Note: The Paris edition reads, “rules itself.”].

You draw wise counsel back from a deep root [Note: The same edition reads:

“You deal continually in the utterance of wise counsel.”],

and what is closed to others is clear to you.

If public concern should bring all the nobles together [Note: The Paris edition reads, “if you rule all the nobles with you,”],  
there is hope of following counsel under your guidance.

Hence, whenever a successful embassy finally proceeds,  
it enters cautiously, directed by your tongue.

Because patience flourishes with such marvelous cultivation,  
you possess the gentleness of David’s lyre [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read, “the gentleness of life.” The Venetian edition reads, “of the way.” The Paris edition gives this verse as:

“Great tranquility: the riches of life are yours.”].

Ruler of justice, lover of venerable law,  
you draw wise judgment from Solomon.

You are superior in the merit of faith; for, as a great prince,  
you display Trajan’s character in piety.

Why should I repeat the mature mind which, in our time,  
makes the ancient Fabius [Favius] pleasing through its gravity [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “you please by the gravity of ancient deeds.” The Paris edition:

“To the ancients, eagerly, gracious life is pleasing.”]?

If some cases come forward with discordant murmuring,  
the weight of the laws immediately flows from the king’s mouth.

Although they report confused voices of conflict [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “voices in the conflict,”],  
you can loosen the threads of a knotty lawsuit.

When he arrives, he who asks for justice obtains its fruit;  
the man whose case your favor supports receives the victor’s reward.

Your clear faith is held by a strong root;  
before your words fall, a mountain will move.

[Col. 0212C] Promised hope stands firm, unaltered in any action [Note: The same edition reads, “the promised matter stands near.”];  
what has once been promised remains perpetuated [Note: The same edition reads, “and once promised.” The Paris edition reads:

“For him to whom it has once been pledged, it remains perpetuated.”].

That house is kept safe by its own weight [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “That house, protected by its own weight, is kept safe”; the Paris edition, “under its own weight.”],  
which stands firmly fixed upon its foundation.

Since you were born from the illustrious race of the Sicamber [Note: “From the illustrious stock of the Sicambri, a people of Germany, arose Chlodovech, son of Childeric and father of Chlothar. When he entered baptism, as Gregory of Tours relates, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 31, the holy man of God—Blessed Remigius, bishop of Rheims—addressed him in eloquent speech: “Lower your gentle neck, Sicamber.” Browerus has more concerning the origin, location, and vicissitudes of the Sicambri; consult him if you wish. Here it is enough for us to report what Gregory of Tours says concerning the origin of the Franks, book II, chapter 9, from which one may also infer the location of the Sicambri in Germany. “Many,” he says, “maintain that these same people—namely, the Franks—had departed from Pannonia; that at first they inhabited all the banks of the Rhine, then, after crossing the Rhine, passed into Thuringia; and there, according to their districts or cities, created long-haired kings over themselves from the first, and, so to speak, the nobler family among their own people. This was later confirmed by the victory of Chlodovech: either because, on account of his proven valor in warfare, they granted Chlodovech that royal authority and rank should remain in him and in his family forever,” as the same Gregory of Tours relates, and as we have elsewhere noted.],

your Latin tongue flourishes in eloquence.

What are you like in your own speech, with learned language,  
when you surpass us Romans in eloquence?

[Col. 0213A] Day shines from your mouth, with serene brightness on a cleansed brow;  
no cloud weighs upon your sincere spirits.

Gentle grace surrounds your face made serene;  
the people receive joy from the king’s countenance.

Your grace fills everyone with generous gifts;  
the common people stand witness to me, proving that my words are true.

O immeasurable goodness of God, who, from his rich treasury,  
regards as his own whatever he grants to his servants,

you raise up the fallen and protect the upright by the law;  
you have become, altogether, every good thing for everyone.

May the Almighty protect the king through the gift of piety,  
and preserve as lord the man whom he has given to be a father.

May the citizens desire you, and may you add joys to the citizens;  
may the people please you in their service, and may the king rule with devotion.

## Chapter V. Concerning Queen Theodechild [Note: This was the same Theodechild whose epitaph he later wrote; see it reproduced above, book IV, chapter 25. Read what we noted concerning that poem.]

[Col. 0213B] [Note: He praises Queen Theodechild notably for the nobility of her royal lineage, her courtesy and generosity toward the needy, and her munificence toward sacred buildings.]

Illustrious offspring, shining with royal stock,  
to whom ancestry gave a lofty name from your forefathers.

The new glory of your lineage flies throughout the world [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “flies throughout the city.” The Venetian edition reads, “the new grace of your lineage.”],  
and at once your brother resounds on one side, your father on the other.

Yet although the noble line of your parents shines,  
honor is multiplied through your character.

We see in you whatever is praised in them;  
you adorn the ancient lineage [Note: The same edition reads, “and he adorns the ancient…”], Theodechild [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “Theudechild’s lineage”; another, “or Theudechild.”].

A venerable, seemly, skillful, devout, dear, and kindly mind,  
since you are powerful through offspring, possesses still greater grace.

Avoiding the causes of hatred [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “and avoiding hatred.” Fortunatus seems here to indicate, not obscurely, the reason why Theodechild withdrew from Radiger, son of King Hermigisclus, whom she had married. Procopius reports the reason in book IV of *The Gothic War*, chapter 20; it may be touched on briefly here to shed light on this passage. Hermigisclus, king of the Varni beyond the Rhine, had married Theodechild, daughter of Theodoric, in order to strengthen his kingdom through the alliance formed with the Franks. Since he had no son by her, as he was dying he ordered that Radiger, his son by a former wife, should marry the Theodechild whom he left behind, after sending a messenger to the virgin daughter of the king of Britain, an Englishwoman, to whom Radiger had been betrothed. The king’s will was also confirmed by the nobles of the kingdom. But the betrothed virgin, unable to endure such an insult, gathered a great fleet against the Varni; after defeating and capturing Radiger, she reproached him for his treachery and for plotting to abandon her contrary to his pledged faith. When he said that necessity had compelled him to act thus, and otherwise declared himself ready to repudiate Theodechild and marry her as he had promised, making amends for the earlier insult by later services, the girl received him back into her favor. This, therefore, was the reason why Theodechild left Radiger her husband and returned to her own people in Gaul; I have no doubt that Fortunatus indicates this reason here.], your extensive power shines forth,  
by which you approach less through terror and more through love.

[Col. 0214A] Gentle sound issues from your mouth in words of the greatest sweetness,  
and the words of your conversation are like honey from the comb.

As far as you surpass the female sex in honor,  
so far do you surpass other women in the power of your piety.

If a newcomer arrives, you receive him with such a kindly mind  
as though his ancestors had already pleased you by their service.

Your right hand scatters food among weary paupers,  
so that you may reap harvests with more fertile fruit.

By nourishing the needy, you will always remain satisfied,  
and the food the starving person receives becomes your own.

Whatever you bestow upon the needy reaches Christ;  
although no one sees it, it remains and will not perish.

When the final end comes to close the world,  
while everything else perishes, you seek better things.

With you as dispenser, sacred churches are renewed;  
you build Christ’s house, and he builds yours [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “you extend it, and he extends yours.”].

You build his on earth; he will give you one in heaven.  
You make the better exchange, thus destined to possess the heavens.

Your talent, which you send to the stars, stands there without deceit;  
the riches you distribute well, you store up for yourself.

Living for the Lord, you do not lose the highest honors [Note: The Paris edition reads, “the supreme honor of your husband.”];  
you hold kingdoms on earth, and hold kingdoms in heaven [Note: The Paris edition reads, “kingdoms destined for the heavens.”].

May your health now be long-lasting, as the people’s gift in the city;  
happy are you, who through your merits will be an everlasting light.

## Chapter VI. Concerning Berthechild [Manuscript: Berthide]

[Note: I scarcely doubt that this was Berthechild, apparently born of illustrious stock, who lived in the monastery at Poitiers under the blessed Radegund, together with the other consecrated women. Gregory of Tours relates concerning them, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 105, that “an immense multitude of consecrated women, numbering about two hundred, stood around the bier” of the dead Radegund; “converted by her preaching, they led holy lives,” and, according to the rank of the world, “not only women from senatorial families but also some from the royal stock flourished in this form of religious life.”]

[Col. 0214B] [Note: He commends Berthechild, or Berthild, a consecrated woman, for chastity, for generosity toward the needy and captives, and for contempt of perishable things.]

A mind devoted to God, Berthechild, shining in heart,  
within whose breast Christ dwells through love.

[Col. 0215A] Despising mortal evil and preserving what gives life,  
you flee the earth and seek the stars all the more.

Shining immaculate, you know nothing of the world’s contamination;  
your limbs are free from human filth.

The rewards of sacred chastity are owed to you,  
a virgin dedicated to God, hence to be snatched away to heaven [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “hence, when heaven snatches you away.”].

He holds the heavens whom you are seen to embrace;  
where your bridegroom is, there you yourself will be also [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “you will be here.”].

You do not desire to adorn your shoulders with gold or your neck with gems,  
but you shine more nobly through your chaste heart, hard though it be.

You changed your clothing and changed the honor of your race  
when, as the bride of the Lord, you came to be joined to his marriage chamber.

By how much better a way you have deserved to keep your vows,  
when the created form pleases the Creator.

You give generous food to the poor who hunger;  
the one who seeks your dwelling knows nothing of hunger.

To one who lies without clothing, you provide covering through your piety;  
the naked person is warm and fears no cold [Note: The Paris edition reads, “fears [the cold].”].

With you as his pious redeemer, the captive’s bonds are loosened;  
because you free the bound, you will always be free.

You distribute your wealth, denying no one his hopes,  
and make your riches belong to everyone.

Whatever you scatter in the fields, you gather in heaven;  
now sowing seeds, later you will reap better things.

Whatever the world possesses passes by on a fleeting path;  
you make what is to be possessed forever out of the brief span of time.

May life remain with you here for many long years;  
and may true salvation be yours again for eternity.

## Chapter VII. Concerning Gelesuintha [Note: We have said something about Gelesuintha—called Galsonta and Galasuentha by others—and her death in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 45. It will not be out of place to recount briefly here the cause of her death from Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 28. She had been requested and obtained by Chilperic for marriage through great entreaties and vows, but was not loved at all by her husband—perhaps not so much from conjugal affection and attachment as because she had brought great treasures with her from Spain. Before long they fell into serious discord. For while the king was entangled in an illicit passion for Fredegund, whom he had promised to dismiss, and while she, indignant at this, wished to return to Spain, Chilperic secretly laid an ambush and had her strangled in her bed. Shortly afterward he took Fredegund back, and she later became the cause of his own death, as Aimoinus relates, *History of the Franks*, chapter 57, and Ado in his *Chronicle*, in the sixth age.]

[Col. 0215C] [Note: He mourns in this sorrowful poem the bitter death of Gelesuintha, daughter of Athanagild, king of the Goths in Spain, who had married Chilperic. He also describes the tears of her mother Goisuintha and the grief and most bitter lamentations of others at Gelesuintha’s funeral.]

Fortune turns upon uncertain accidents,  
and wavering life fixes no steadfast foot.

The slippery wheel always rolls the world amid uncertainty [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “the age rolls along with uncertainty”; the Venetian edition likewise.],  
and the journey proceeds over fragile ice, with slipping steps.

No day is certain for anyone; no hour is more certain for anyone [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “no one has his own [hour] more certain.”];  
so weak is the condition in which we stand, like glass.

While deceptive ignorance drags us along an uncertain path,  
the art of the pit lies hidden where a person thinks there is a road [Note: The Venetian and Paris editions read, “where he thinks there is a way.”].

The human mind, unaware of what death and salvation may be,  
does not know whether light or life will have death as its evening [Note: The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript read, “whether death is life,” which is preferable. The Paris edition reads, “whether it is life.” The prologue of this poem suits Gelesuintha’s fortune exceptionally well: she was brought to Gaul for a royal marriage with great honor, but there was ordered to be killed by her husband.].

We are oppressed by these darknesses, ignorant of the future’s lot,  
and these times, so fleeting, possess a time that wanders.

[Col. 0216B] Toledo sent you two towers, Gaul [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “Toledo, doubling [its towers].” The two towers signify Brunichildis and Gelesuintha herself, sisters and daughters of Athanagild, king of the Goths in Spain. The former had married Sigibert the preceding year, before Chilperic married Gelesuintha, as we noted in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 45. The Gothic kings in Spain had their royal seat at Toledo.].

With the first still standing, the second lies broken.

High above the hills, beautiful with a fair summit,  
she has fallen headlong from her peak under hostile winds.

Leaving her foundations in the soil of her homeland,  
shaken from her own hinge, she did not stand long.

Having left her native ground, she was swallowed by strange sand [mors sit: “let death be”],  
and, an exile in these lands—alas!—lies as a stranger.

Who can begin the omens of such great grief,  
with the thread of sorrow on which the lament began to be woven?

When royal Gelesuintha was first sought in marriage,  
to be joined in a royal bridal bed to the cold north [Note: Gaul is indicated as lying toward the north, if one looks from Spain, from which Gelesuintha had departed.],

so that she might overcome its cold with Cupid’s flames [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read, “though fixed, she might desire the cold here”; the Paris edition, “fixed, desire might here seek the cold.”],  
and live warmly beneath a cold region.

[Col. 0216C] When the maiden perceived this, terrified by fear and by what she heard,  
Goisuintha ran to embrace her own child [Note: Goisuintha, or, as others write, Gunthesuentha, was first the wife of Athanagild and the mother of Brunichildis and Gelesuintha. After Athanagild’s death she married Leuvichild, who had succeeded Athanagild as king. When he too died, Recchared, Leuvichild’s son, received and treated her as a mother, although she was his stepmother. Later she conspired with Uldila, an Arian bishop, against Recchared, as John of Biclar relates under the third year of Recchared. This woman was an ardent supporter of the Arian party and often stirred up disturbances in Spain against Catholics. Read Gregory of Tours, book V, chapter 39, and also book IV, chapter 38, and book IX, chapter 1 of the *History of the Franks*.].

Then, gathered into her mother’s bosom and leaning there in troubled distress,  
she clung with nail and hand lest she be torn away [Note: The Paris edition reads, “with the nail of her hand.”].

Tightening her arms, she formed a chain without a rope [Note: The Venetian and Paris editions read, “a chain without end,”]  
and bound her mother’s limbs with her embrace.

The daughter begged to be held by those entrails  
from which the origin of light had earlier come to her.

Confidently entrusting herself to be borne by her whose closed womb  
had kept her safe as its pledge.

Then the house became sorrowful with groaning, the palace resounded with tumult,  
and everyone wept at the queen’s lament [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read, “all the honor.”].

On the people’s faces, streams of tears flowed miserably;  
even the infant, who knows nothing of grief, himself wept.

The envoys pressed that the Germanic kingdoms be sought [Note: The kingdom of the Franks, as we have already noted elsewhere, extended into Germany.],  
recounting the slow duration of the long journey.

But, moved by the mother’s groaning, their own hearts softened,  
and those who were urging her wished to pretend otherwise.

While the mother remained entwined in her daughter’s embrace,  
the second, third, and fourth days passed [Note: The Paris edition reads, “a double day.”].

The envoys pressed to return to the familiar region;  
[Col. 0217B] Goisuintha addressed them thus, groaning:

“If I were oppressed as a captive by the savagery of a fierce Gelonian [Note: The Geloni were fierce and barbarous peoples of Scythia, the same as the Getae, who fought armed with sickles. Sidonius mentions them in letter 1 of book IV, saying that if someone carried a message—having been trained from youth under Eusebius—to the swamp-dwelling Sicambri, the Caucasian Alans, or the horse-milking Geloni, ‘the hornlike hearts and icy sinews of those bestial and rigid nations would surely be softened and thawed.’],

perhaps even a compassionate enemy would yield to these tears.

If the enemy were not compassionate at heart, yet greedy would yield to me [Note: The Paris edition reads, “if he would believe me,”],

let him at least sell my daughter as barbarian booty [Note: The Paris edition reads, “so that even then I might not be given…”].

If he would not thus incline his bloodstained mind,  
let him grant this to the mother, so that she might travel with her.

Now no delay is allowed, nor can we bend him by any price.  
He who grants nothing is more savage in harm than an enemy.

After the groaning of the womb, after the many dangers of childbirth,  
after the burden of labor which I, pregnant, endured—

may I not be the mother of the daughter whom I bore?  
And does the whole law of nature perish for me?

Starved of my affection, I am driven away in tears;  
neither piety nor birth grants me access?

[Col. 0217C] Why do you tear her away? Put off the days while I learn my sorrows [Note: The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript read, “while I learn the labors.”],  
and let delay alone be the solace of my grief.

When will I see her again? When will these eyes play with her [Note: The Paris edition reads, “close”?],  
when will I again fall upon my daughter’s beloved neck?

From where, I ask, shall I watch the steps of my tender girl,  
or shall the very sight of her amuse her mother’s heart?

After the affairs that kingdoms pursue, where shall I rest in sorrow?  
Who will cherish her with affection, and kiss her head with lips [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “kiss her with his mouth”]?

[Col. 0218A] With outstretched hands, who will run to kisses, or what limbs  
will leap hanging upon my neck?
