Whom shall I hold in my lap, laboring beneath a gentle burden,  
or be struck by her with a light hand in playful jest?

Nor would I be burdened to carry you in my bosom, although you are grown,  
you who were once so sweet and such a light weight to me.

Why should you seek new fields, where I shall not be your mother?  
Or perhaps one region cannot contain two?

Then let the entrails that gave birth to her be torn by grief;  
the one whose joys are lost will possess seasons of tears.

Weeping, I shall lose my eyes, carrying my gaze with you;  
if I am forbidden to go wholly, a part of me follows you.

Then the nobles, servants, household, city, and king himself roar with lament;  
wherever you sought to travel, one heavy voice groans.

At last you will go outside, but the lingering crowd,  
while hastening to release you, binds itself by its haste.

Here affection holds them back; there tumult snatches those who depart;  
thus the sorrowful task seethes through alternating impulses.

One advises departure; another, out of love, asks for a return;  
with faith wavering thus, one draws while the other holds.

The ancient people is divided among the kingdoms of a new realm [Note: This seems to refer to the kingdom of the Goths in Spain, which had been established in those regions in the preceding century under Ataulphus, king of the Goths. See the distinguished Muratori, *Annals of Italy*, under the year 414 of the common era.].

The father stands; the son goes; the father-in-law stands; the son-in-law goes [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “the father stands, and the ancestor; the father-in-law stands, and the son-in-law goes.”].

Anyone who saw the commotion might have thought that the homeland was departing,  
and might have believed that captive soil was being borne away [Note: The Paris edition reads, “the one who stood trembling.”].

They proceed through the gates, with the serracum held upon the bridge [Note: The Paris edition reads, “held in the serracum…” A *serracum* was a kind of vehicle in Gaul. Fortunatus uses the same word in book VIII, chapter 1, speaking of Radegund:

“Once carried aloft in a splendid, proud serracum,  
now her modest foot wears down the ground in service.”

The vehicle is also mentioned by pagan authors, though such vehicles seem to have been used for more ordinary purposes. Juvenal uses the word in satire 5:

“The sluggish Bootes turns the cold wagons.”

In the Vulgate, “the earth retained with a bridge” had been read, contrary to all the manuscripts, as Brower relates.],

and Gelesuintha raised her head amid this weeping:

“Thus was I nourished in your bosom, Toledo, only to be driven from your gates—  
I, your sorrowful foster-child?

And, to torment myself more, revealing my wounds through grief,  
you stand happy, my country; why am I dragged away as booty?

Previously shut away, now I look upon all of you;  
formerly unknown to me, you become known when I depart.

From here I count you as I run my eyes over your roofs;  
behold, I alone shall no longer belong to your number.

Cruel gates, which opened for me as I departed,  
and, with your bolts placed against me, did not forbid my journey—

before a single open door gave any path here,  
one stone should have bound you both with adamant.

[Col. 0219A] You would have been a more dutiful city if, with a high wall of stone,  
you had enclosed me so as not to let me go [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “so as not to let me go away.”].

I go through places unknown, trembling at what I shall first learn:  
the people, spirits, customs, towns, fields, and groves [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “customs, people, spirits”; three Vatican manuscripts, “people, customs, spirits,” contrary to the meter; the manuscript reads, “peoples.”].

Whom, a stranger in foreign lands, shall I find, I ask—  
where no citizen, friend, or parent is mine [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “dear one, friend, parent.”]?

Tell me: if a kindly foreign nurse can please me,  
who will wash my face with her hand or arrange my hair with a comb?

No girl in the chorus, no foster-sister, will play;  
here my affection lies, here my care.

If I cannot be held here otherwise, at least bare graves might hold me;  
I may not live here; here it is sweet for me to die [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “it is not permitted that you live here.” One Vatican manuscript reads, “to live”; the Paris edition, “it is not permitted to live here.”].

I do not enjoy your embrace, nor do I depart fully with your face before my eyes;  
you who dismiss me, harsh Toledo, farewell.

Thus kindled spirits burst forth in streams of tears,  
and fixed fire gives birth to waters overflowing with moisture.

[Col. 0219B] From there the mother, daughter, and weeping crowds take up the journey,  
and the breathless mother does not begrudge her attendance [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read, “does not begrudge the attendance”; the Venetian edition, “does not desire the attendance”; the Paris edition, “does not blush at the attendance.”].

The mother escorts her sweet daughter through bitter travel;  
the valleys are filled with weeping, and the heights tremble.

The dense air is broken by empty wailings,  
and the forest itself groans with repeated murmuring.

The mother gives reasons for lengthening the journey,  
but the time and road were short for her desire.

They reached the place where the mother said she would turn back,  
but what she had earlier wished, afterward she did not wish.

She longs to return by the path that carries her mother,  
but the nobles hold her back lest the journey be prolonged [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “the path that leads the mother.”].

They clung to one another in embraces and were entwined together [Note: The manuscript reads, “turned back together”].

[Col. 0219C] Here Goisuintha begins in fierce lament:

“Hispania, broad for your own citizens, narrow for the mother,  
and a region of the sun, closed to me so soon [Note: The Venetian edition, one Vatican manuscript, and the Paris edition read, “and a region of the sun, closed to me so quickly,” which is preferable.].

Although you stretch from the warm Zephyr to the East Wind,  
and from the Tyrrhenian [Sea] extend to Ocean [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “and from the stock of the bastard you extend.”],

and are sufficient for peoples and broad regions,  
you are a narrow land to me while my daughter is absent.

Nor shall I be less lost and a stranger here without you;  
in my own place I shall be a citizen—and an exile.

I ask: what will my eyes look upon, whom will they seek, my daughter,  
those eyes which now carry their love away with you?

You alone will be grief to me: whatever infant plays for me,  
you will be a burden to me in another’s embrace.

Let another run, stand, sit, weep, enter, and depart;  
you alone return as the sweet image of my eyes.

[Col. 0220A] Wandering because you have fled, I shall run among foreign kisses,  
and groaning over mouths, press dry breasts.

I shall kiss the weeping eyes of infants;  
unsatisfied, I shall drink their tender tears.

Would that by such a drink I might be refreshed in some part,  
or that the eagerly wept-for stream might soothe my thirst [Note: The manuscript reads, “even [by this drink].” The edition reads, “or that the avidly wept-for [stream] might soothe the thirst.”].

Whatever happens, I suffer; no remedies help here.  
I drip with a wound, Gelesuintha, yours.

My dear daughter, on whose hand, I ask, will this hair be combed and shine?  
Who, without me, will kiss your peaceful cheeks with her mouth [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “who will kiss your cheeks with mouth and face”?]?

Who will cherish you in her lap, carry you on her knees, and encircle you with her arm?  
But you will have no mother there except me.

What remains, my groaning love commands you as you depart:  
‘Be happy, I beg you—but take great care; farewell’ [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read, “go, farewell.”].

Send greetings to your eager mother, even through wandering breezes;  
if the breeze comes, let it itself report to me some good news [bonum: “good”].

[Col. 0220B] Then the daughter, burdened by her mother’s powerful complaints,  
sad, helpless in spirit, and unable to speak,

her voice long closed, with speech barely loosened in her throat,  
utters a few words, her tongue heavy with the wound in her heart:

‘If the lofty majesty of God wished to grant me more time of life [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “if the majesty of God wishes to grant me time”],  
it would not grant me this road now.

But since the final, irrevocable fate presses upon me,  
if no one now forbids me, I shall follow the path which anger draws.

Yet these final words I shall speak, memorable to grief [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “these final words, nevertheless”; the Venetian edition, “these final words at last.”]:

‘What is yours is not yours, Goisuintha [Note: The Paris edition reads, “I am not yours.”], farewell.’

Thus kisses break off, and mouths fixed upon mouths repel one another [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “and fixed earlier mouths repel,” corruptly],  
while, unable to cling to one another, love licks the air.

Then, seeking the Gallic lands in a *pilentum* [Note: A *pilens*, or *pilentum*, was a kind of vehicle customarily used by matrons. It was invented by the Spaniards, just as the *petoritum* was invented by the Gauls. The former had two wheels, the latter four. Horace, book II, letter 1:

“Chariots, *pilenta*, *petorrita*, ships hurry onward.”], Gelesuintha  
stood fixed before her mother’s eyes, sorrowful as the wheel moved [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “Gelesuintha, seeking the places of Gaul.”].

[Col. 0220C] And in turn the mother, stretching her eyes after her daughter,  
continues herself also, remaining in one place.

Trembling all over lest the agile mule speed away with the four-horse carriage,  
or the impatient horse turn the wheels on the axle,

she flew around her beloved with anxious eyes,  
following in her mind the place where the road curved.

Often she spoke as though her daughter sat beside her,  
and seemed to hold the absent girl in her hand and bosom [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “and the absent hand.”].

Believing she could grasp her, she flings her arms into the wind [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read, “her arms into the winds”; so too the Venetian edition],  
but receives no daughter and strikes only the wandering breezes.

Among so many companions she watched one departing;  
she alone seemed to be going where her love traveled.

The mother, suspended in spirit, was more agitated than the daughter in the carriage;  
the one went faltering in her hopes, the other in her wheels.

[Col. 0221A] Until she vanished far from sight and across a great distance,  
and did not reach the eye while shadow covered the day.

The mother thinks she sees the daughter’s uncertain features,  
and when the form disappears, the sweet image returns.

O name glowing with devotion, O faithful care—  
although she was absent, what were you but a mother?

With her face stiff from tears, striking the stars with lament,  
she recalled each sweet, harsh, and dutiful thing.

A fickle, impatient, fearful, weeping, anxious mother—  
the lofty love that you follow in tears foretells [Note: The same edition reads, “what do you follow?”; the Paris edition, “another.”].

Yet the daughter proceeds along the path cut by the well-worn wheel,  
and each person fills the empty fields with his own tears.

From there she leaps through the clouds over the Pyrenean Alps,  
and where July [Note: I am surprised that Browerus thought Fortunatus had mistakenly given the name of the Julii to the extreme Pyrenean ridges toward the Mediterranean shore of Gaul, since Fortunatus so plainly indicates the month of July here, during which, although the heat of midsummer prevails elsewhere, hoarfrost and snow customarily form in the Pyrenean Alps. Thus, in book I, chapter 1, speaking of his own journey, he says that he encountered the Pyrenees “snowy in the month of July”; and above, writing of Brunichildis’s journey from Spain into Gaul, book VI, chapter 1, he clearly indicates the perpetual snows of the Pyrenean Alps in these words:

“Through strong winters of snow, and across the Pyrenean Alps,  
and through savage peoples she was carried.”

Browerus therefore wrongly thinks that Fortunatus transferred the name of July—which, he says, belongs to the Alps in Italy—to the Pyrenean ridges.] grows cold with icy waters.

By whose snow the singing mountains soar to the stars [Note: The Paris edition reads, “by whose gleaming snow”],  
and the sharp summit rises above the rains.

From here Narbo follows, gnawing at the level shores;

the gentle Atax softly enters the waters of the Rhône.

> [Note: The Atax is the river commonly called the Aude. It flows by Narbo and subsequently mingles its waters with those through which the Rhône flows, as Sirmondus observed from this passage of Fortunatus in his notes on Sidonius, book IX, epistle 15. See also Fredegar Scholasticus, *Chronicle, Continuation*, p. 3, ch. 109. Browerus reports that, following Sidonius, he restored *Atacem* in place of *Arari*. This reading is supported by the Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts, which read: “Gentle Atax, Rhône, etc.”]

> [Note: Narbo is the city from which Gallia Narbonensis took its name. It was formerly called Bracata, later Narbonensis and Viennensis, and comprised the southern region of Gaul along the Mediterranean, as Tillemont reports. The Goths, under Ataulf, entered Gaul, occupied and held this city, but were expelled from it by Count Constantius and withdrew into Spain in 414. Theodoric the Younger, king of the Goths and Visigoths and son of the great Theodoric, subsequently gained possession of the city in 462. See Sirmond, notes on poem 23 of Sidonius Apollinaris, and Muratori, *Annals of Italy*, under 463. Sidonius praises Narbo and calls it “Martian,” thereby, as Sirmondus thinks, indicating the city’s strength and power against the assaults of the Goths. (First editorial note.)  
>
> Observe that Narbo is called “Martian” not only by Sidonius but also by earlier writers, among them Marcus Tullius Cicero in the speech *For Marcus Fonteius*. Some attribute this name to the fact that Gaius Caesar led colonists there from the Martian legion; others—including Velleius Paterculus—believe that the colony was established under the consuls Porcius and Martius, and that Narbo was consequently called Martian because of the latter’s role in founding it. Sidonius therefore adapted its ancient designation to the circumstances and fortunes of his own age, as these words show: “While I linger at Narbo, once called Martian, but recently made a delay …,” etc. (Second editorial note.)]

After passing several cities, she reached the towers of the Pictavians,

moving along the road in royal procession.

That illustrious Hilary—truly great in the lands where

he was both born and set—was eloquent with thunderous voice.

> [Note: The Venetian edition corruptly reads:  
> “He drew along the straight road the Indian, Getan, Persian, and Briton.”]

Thracian, Italian, Scythian, Persian, Indian, Getan, Dacian, Briton—

from his eloquence each drank hope and took up arms.

The sun poured forth life-giving lights by its radiance; he, by his word:

the one gave day to the mountains, the other faith to minds.

> [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts, as also the Venetian edition, read *generalia lumina fundunt*, “pour forth universal lights.”]

I myself, a newcomer, saw this city as I passed by,

carried gently in a revolving silver tower.

Pious Radegund wished, with a mother’s love,

to see her fervently, if anyone would grant aid.

> [Note: The Paris edition reads *ferventem*, “burning” or “fervent.”]

Yet she often clung sweetly to her with letters sent,

and peacefully cherished what now mourns in sadness.

> [Note: The manuscripts and editions vary between *missis* and *mitis*. *Missa* is used by Fortunatus for letters or messages. Thus, writing to Artachis under the name and persona of Radegund, he says: “And when I have sent you letters, I ask you often to inquire after me in the monastery.”]

She then sought the lands of Tours, of Martin renowned to the stars,

moving onward with a slowly advancing step.

She crossed the swift channel of the Vienne in an alder-boat,

and a gracious throng emerged from the swift waters.

> [Note: *Alnus* means a ship or ferry, so called because it was made from alder trees. Fridegodus, in the *Life of Saint Wilfrid, Bishop*, printed in the first part of the third Benedictine century, p. 188, uses the word in the same sense: “Fearing nothing, therefore, he safely crosses the grasses, / and securely swiftly enters the hollow alder-boats.”]

> [Note: Browerus retained the word *Vigenna*, which Aimoinus also uses in book I, chapter 21, relating that Clovis crossed this river during his expedition against Alaric, not far from Tours and Poitiers. The word is absent from the Venetian edition, leaving the verse defective. The Vienne, or Vienna, as Browerus notes there, is a stream rising not far from Limoges which, after receiving other waters, soon enters the Loire.]

> [Note: The Paris edition reads *comes*, “the companion.”]

> [Note: The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts read *alacris exit aquis*, “comes forth lively from the waters.”]

From there the sudden, cold Loire received her in its glassy current,

where the light sand does not even conceal a fish.

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads *lenis arena*, “gentle sand.”]

She reached the place where the fish-filled Seine,

joined to the Rouen inlet, carries itself into the sea.

> [Note: From this passage Browerus conjectures that the marriage of Galswintha and Chilperic was celebrated at Rouen.]

Thus the maiden was joined to a royal marriage,

and deserved to be honored with the great love of the people.

Caressing these people also with gifts and with words,

she made even strangers her own.

And so that the armed people might be faithful to her,

each swore allegiance and bound himself by his own law.

She ruled, ordering her life along a peaceful path;

she gave to the poor and was a mother to strangers.

> [Note: The manuscript reads *quaque*.]

That she might remain all the more in the everlasting kingdom,

she is pleasing because she was reconciled to the Catholic faith.

O grief, why do you delay the seasons of mourning,

and, by saying more, fall silent about the turns of sorrow?

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads *plura loquenda taces*, “you are silent about more things to be said.”]

Wicked fortune of human beings, brought forth by an unforeseen fall,

you devour so many blessings when fortune suddenly takes flight.

> [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read *quae improviso abdita lapsu*, “which, hidden by an unforeseen fall.”]

For, having had only a brief time, bound in marriage to her consort,

she was carried away by death at the beginning of life.

> [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read *consortia nexa jugalis*, “joined to marital companionship.”]

Overtaken by a precipitous fall, struck by a swift blow,

she failed, and with the turning of her light her own light passed away.

The unhappy nurse, hearing of the death of her foster-child,

flew scarcely alive to the lifeless body.

She herself, the first and faithful among the handmaids, leaning over it,

was at last able, shut in by grief, to speak:

“Thus I, a most wretched nurse, promised your gentle mother

that you, Gelesuintha, would remain safe far away.

Thus my own eyes behold my own light extinguished;

thus your face is pale, where before there was a blush?

Say something in pity; give words back to me, wretched woman.

What shall I report to your mother, if I am permitted to return?

After I, a stranger, followed you through such great labors,

is this the recompense that you, my foster-child, return to me?

Did you desire life and graves alike for us,

you with whom I lived, yet allow me to die without you?

Would that the order of life had been reversed for young and old:

with you standing safe, would that I had gone first to death.

Scarcely does she utter a few words; another snatches the voice from her mouth,

and the whole palace, which sees this, groans, unable to speak with one voice.”

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads *vix paucis profert vocem*, “she scarcely brings forth her voice in a few words.”]

> [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read *aula gemi*, “the palace groans.”]

Meanwhile she is borne, tearful upon the bier (*lacrymosa feretro*),

and dutiful love performs the funeral rites.

> [Note: The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts read *lachrymata feretro*, “tearful on the bier,” not “tears for the bier.”]

> [Note: After this verse—“She is led forth, adorned, laid down, and mourned everywhere”—the Venetian edition inserts verses belonging to book VII, chapter 5, while the verses that conclude the present poem are transferred to book VIII, chapter 4. The same arrangement occurs in one Vatican manuscript. Browerus himself admits that he reconstructed this poem from several portions dispersed among Fortunatus’s other poems.]

She is led forth, adorned, laid down, and mourned everywhere,

and, a foreigner, is thus placed in her own tomb.

Here a wondrous sign suddenly arose:

while hanging above, a lamp shone for the funeral service (*lucet ad obsequium*).

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “the lamp came to the funeral service.” Saint Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 28, relates the portent here mentioned by Fortunatus. He adds that the lamp, falling from above, was not only unbroken but was caught by the pavement in such a way that, as the pavement yielded, it became half-buried in it.]

It fell upon a stone, did not tilt, and burned intact.

Neither did the glass perish against the rocks, nor the fire perish in the waters.

Fresh report struck the ears of her sister who remained behind.

Moved by pious affection, the sister thus opened her lips:

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads *ora sono*, “with sound from her mouth.”]

“Dear one, I ask: did you entrust this greeting to your sister?

Does this dear writing in your own hand tell this to me?

With anxious eyes I awaited where you would come from;

you do not make the journey that I prayed for.

I wished Spain to bring you here to the Gauls;

now neither your dear sister has you here, nor your mother there.

I, Brunichildis, did not come here for your final rites,

so that, having given you nothing while you lived, I might render you the honour of death.

Why, a stranger, did I not close your sweet eyes?

Why did I not drink your final words with eager ears?

I myself performed no service for my grieving sister;

this hand covers neither your limbs, nor your hands, nor your face.

I was not permitted to shed tears and wipe them from my face,

nor to wash your cold entrails in warm water.

Nurtured together and joined in the same lands,

why does deep grief divide us on the road to death?

And so the abandoned sister is torn apart by the misfortune of the one taken away:

this one calls, that one lies there, and does not return when called.

Germania hears the mighty laments of her sister,

and wherever the road turns back, she strikes the stars with her complaints.

Often calling you by name, Gelesuintha, her sister,

she makes the springs, forests, rivers, and fields resound.

Gelesuintha, are you silent? Answer your mute sister:

the stones, mountain, grove, wave, and sky answer.

Anxious and pleading, she questions the very breezes,

but all are silent about her sister’s welfare.”

The message suddenly crossed rivers and Alps,

and the heavy wing of grief flew so swiftly.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *pinna volat*, “the wing flies.”]

It would have been better, once it had filled every place,

if this grief had traveled more slowly to the mother.

But what rumor reports, the one who loves most hears first,

and, because fear gives credibility, believes even what is uncertain.

Soon, therefore, the mother’s darting grief reached her ears,

and, anxious, she fell when her knee gave way [or: collapsed].

One death heard of strikes another death,

and, though her body was nearly unharmed, she was a corpse.

> [Note: The Venetian edition corruptly reads: “though the funeral was unharmed, it was a funeral.”]

Then Goisuintha, pale with blush suffused over her pallor (*pallida suffuso rubore*),

with her spirit scarcely returning, said softly:

“Did I console myself in tender love for my daughter

only that now this wound might parch my entrails more grievously?

If our light has already gone out, if my daughter has departed,

why, jealous life, do you keep me for these tears?

> [Note: Paris reads *Has ad quid lacrymas invida me vocitas*: “Why, jealous [life], do you call me to these tears?”]

You erred, too-hard death, when you should have taken the mother:

fate gave you my daughter instead.

Would that the rivers had swollen with their banks submerged,

or that the shipwrecked land had floated upon spread-out waters;

would that the high mountains of the Pyrenees had touched the stars,

or that the road had solidified in glassy ice,

when I released you, Gelesuintha, beneath the northern sky,

so that neither chariot on wheels nor horse could travel through the waters!

Was this, then, what my foreknowing mind feared—

that I could not tear you, daughter, from my embrace?

We obeyed the wishes of others, following their commands;

you went forth as one promised in marriage, never to return to me.

This was the depth of my love, my daughter’s peaceful sweetness:

I gave my breast to your tender lips.

Why did the channel of my breast produce an abundance of milk?

Why did I give nourishment to one whom I was not to keep?

Often, while you slept, I suckled you with stolen kisses,

and placed my breast beneath you so that you might sleep lightly.

What did it profit me to wish this final thing for you—

that my little granddaughter might play in her grandfather’s lap—

when I saw neither happy hopes nor unhappy funerals?

Alas, excessive labor destroyed the one, and excessive love the other.”

With their tears divided, the sister here and the anxious mother there,

the one strikes the Rhine with her cries, the other the Tagus.

> [Note: The Tagus is a river of Lusitania, just as the Rhine is a river of Gaul along the border of Germania. The Tagus correctly indicates the region in which Goisuintha was located: Toledo, the seat of the Gothic kings, lies on that river, as Browerus observes.]

Here the Batavian people grieve, there the Baetician land groans.

> [Note: The Batavians were a people of Germania, just as the Baeticians were of Spain. Baetica was a province of Spain, named by its inhabitants after the river Baetis; indeed, the name can signify all Spain because the Baetis flows through its middle. The Batavians obeyed Sigibert, the Baeticians Athanagild.]

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads *Rheticus axis*, “the Rhaetian region groans.”]

The Waal roars here with its waters, the Ebro there.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *Vachalus*. The Waal is a river of Germania, concerning which Sidonius writes in poem 13:  
>
> “Thus, when the swelling of the double bank has broken,  
> may the shorn Sicamber drink the Waal.”  
>
> The Waal, Browerus adds in his note on this passage, is another branch of the Rhine, separated by a different channel near the head of Batavia. It flows westward toward Belgic Gaul as far as Nijmegen, a city once famous for the palace of the Frankish kings, which the river washes with a broader and calmer stream; then, after leaving it, it finally joins the Meuse, adding its waters to that river.]

It is enough that so many tears have dripped here and there;

from the rain of vapor, a drop offers help that cannot relieve thirst.

If affection can perhaps be softened, I shall say this:

she does not lie in a place that deserves mourning; she occupies joyful realms.

Tell me whether anything harmed her, whom, after time had passed,

death carried away along its road, while everlasting life sustains her.

Now she journeys with Stephen, the heavenly consul,

and shines gloriously with the apostolic prince Peter.

With Mary, the radiant mother of the Lord, she rejoices,

and serves God beneath the eternal King.

Reconciled, she is pleasing; she shines in a precious death:

having laid aside the old garment, she is now clothed in a beautiful robe.

And would that God, moved by love, might grant us to approach those faces

across the sea and through the swords.

She bears the signs of life: when the glass vessel fell,

neither water extinguished it nor the stone broke it upon the ground.

You too, mother, possess an oracle from the voice of the Thunderer,

concerning your daughter, son-in-law, granddaughter, grandson, and husband.

Believe, worshipers of Christ: she lives, because she believed;

it is not fitting to mourn one whom paradise possesses.

## Chapter VIII. On the Garden of Queen Ultrogotha

> [Note: Concerning Ultrogotha, see what we said above at chapter 4 of this book. Her outstanding piety is praised by Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, book I, chapter 12. The author—or rather interpolator—of the *Life of Saint Balthild*, preserved in volume II of the Benedictine collection, page 775, writes of her: “It is said of Queen Ultrogotha, wife of Childebert, the most Christian king, that she was the nurse of orphans, the consoler of the fatherless, the supporter of the poor and of God’s servants, and the helper of faithful monks.”]

> [Note: He describes the beauty of the garden once planted by King Childebert and then held by Ultrogotha, his wife; from this he takes occasion to celebrate Childebert’s praises.]

Here purple spring brings forth green grasses,

and scatters roses fragrant as those of paradise.

Here tender vine-shoots protect the summer shade,

and leafy coverings provide shelter beneath fruit-bearing clusters.

Flowers paint the place with varied growth,

and whiteness, followed by redness, clothes the fruit.

Here summer is gentler, where, with a soft and soothing murmur,

the light breeze continually shakes the hanging apples.

King Childebert planted these with great love;

the things that hand bestowed are dearer still.

The plant draws its honeyed flavor from its cultivator;

perhaps he also mingled silent honeycombs here.

Through the honor of the king, the fruit’s grace is doubled:

a sweet fragrance rises, and a pleasant taste is in the mouth.

How much good could that man have done for the salvation of human beings,

whose touch pleases even in the fragrance of his fruit?

May fruit be born from the tree forever,

so that every person may remember the pious king.

This was his route when he sought the holy thresholds,

which he now inhabits all the more because of his merits.

Previously, in turn, he lovingly visited the sacred places;

now he continually dwells in blessed temples.

May you possess these things happily throughout the ages, Ultrogotha,

as a rejoicing mother, a third together with your two daughters.

> [Note: Childebert left two daughters after his death, Chrotberga and Chrotesinda, whom he had by Ultrogotha.]

## Chapter IX. To the Pleasant Villa of Cantus: A Poem on Apples

> [Note: The title of this poem varies, as Browerus reports. The Vulgate manuscripts presented it as “spoken of Rome.” The Cologne manuscript has “of good things”; the Saint Gall manuscript, “of fruit,” with which the Venetian edition agrees.]

> [Note: When Fortunatus came to the villa of Cantus, he humorously describes his own greediness in eating apples.]

We came by a fortunate road to pleasant Cantus,

where I rejoice to have found Aredius, my father.

Whatever our greedy appetite seeks from its craving abyss,

golden apples meet my eyes.

From every side apples of varied color rush together,

so that you might think I had touched painted delicacies.

> [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read *me meruisse dapes*: “so that you might think I had earned painted delicacies.”]

Hardly had I touched them with my fingers before I drained them with my throat,

rolled them beneath my teeth, and the hastened prize moved elsewhere.

> [Note: Browerus preferred this reading to the one he had previously printed: “I devoured them with my throat rising.” The Venetian edition reads, “with my throat resting”; three Vatican manuscripts have the reading printed here.]

For taste pleases before the nose has drawn in its scent;

with appetite thus prevailing, the nose loses its honor.

## Chapter X. On the Cook Who Took the Boat Itself and Committed an Injustice

> [Note: When Fortunatus came to Metz, he says that the small boat in which he was traveling was unjustly taken from him there by a royal cook. He amusingly describes the cook’s appearance and office. He then recalls the kindness and generosity shown him by Sigibert and his servants Gogo and Papulus.]

Why do you weave such powerful complaints for me, anxiety?

Alas, pain, leave my heart at last!

Why do you recall misfortunes? My burden already wearies me.

Why, when I think I am casting it off, is the load doubled?

I wander too sadly, an exile roaming far from my native shores,

more shipwrecked than the guest of Apollonius upon the waters.

> [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read *Apollonius* and *Apollonia*, which, as Browerus notes, are found among the islands of Epirus. The Trier manuscript had *APOLLONIUS*, so that the reference might fit the Tyanaean, who was by far the foremost among the Bithynians, or the Rhodian, who described the wanderings of the Argonauts. Unless perhaps—as I too may venture a conjecture—the poet alluded to the wandering of Ulysses: after sailing from an island sacred to Apollo, where his companions had slaughtered the cattle of the Sun, Ulysses was driven by a violent storm and barely escaped shipwreck, as Homer relates in *Odyssey* XII.]

We came to Metz, where a royal cook, pressing forward,

stole from the absent man both the small boat and the raft.

He who with burning hand snatches food from the flames

does not know how to spare a raft, though safe upon the waters.

Black at heart, fed on smoke and stained with soot,

his face itself is another cooking-pot.

His arms had painted the same dirty color upon him:

the frying-pan, the dish, the pan, and the tripod.

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads *Frixurae*; the Vulgate had *Luxuriae cucumen*.]

Unworthy of verse, he should rather be marked in charcoal,

and his ugly likeness represent a man of pitch.

An outrage far too great—the injustice of the deed is grievous:

the cook’s stew-pot counts for more than my rights.

A cooking-pot makes more display of itself than a book,

so that my raft is not even shared with me.

Yet Villicus, who feeds the Lord’s sheep, extended help with his customary kindness.

> [Note: Villicus was bishop of Metz, the same man to whom poem 14 of book III is addressed. See what we said in the notes to that poem. Cointius dates Villicus’s death to 566 or 568; Fortunatus therefore wrote this poem before that time.]

He provided assistance and, fearful, hastened with the slender boat.

> [Note: The manuscript reads *placidus*, “calm,” instead of *pavidus*, “fearful.”]

I was drenched by rain, the Eurus, and the river.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *si madefactus*, “if I had been wet.”]

I threw out the others so that they might continue on foot from there,

for if no one had gone outside, no one would have remained inside.

> [Note: That is, if the others had not left the slender boat which Villicus had brought, it would have been overwhelmed by the weight and sunk beneath the waves, and no one would have escaped.]

Soon the danger, sweeping everything away, would have submerged us all;

no survivor would have remained to bear witness to the shipwreck.

Thus I was so near, after we had all been cast out,

that the water licked my feet with repeated blows.

“Remove this service,” I said; “for now I do not wish to bathe,”

but the water nevertheless persisted in wetting my feet.

> [Note: The Paris edition reads *ligare*, “to bind,” instead of *rigare*, “to wet.”]

Coming to Nauciacum [perhaps Nantiacum; the place-name is uncertain], I reported my sad circumstances to the king:

> [Note: In the old copies it read “the sailor, when he came,” as also in the Venetian edition. Browerus restored *Nauciacum*; indeed, he suspects that *Nantiacum* should be read, since King Sigibert and his court had withdrawn there, to a nearby place. He reports that Nanceium, or Nantiacum, a town still flourishing today and the perpetual seat of the dukes of Lorraine, bore the name *Nasium* under Roman rule. Browerus gives this explanation. But the learned Ruinart, in his notes on Fredegar Scholasticus, chapter 38, says that Nasium was a fortress in the duchy of Bar, situated on the river Ornain, commonly called the Naz, and that some incorrectly identify it with Nancey, the capital of Lorraine. In three Vatican manuscripts *Nauriacum* is read twice.]

he smiled and, with kindly lips, ordered a boat to be brought.

They searched, but could not find any vessel,

until the entire royal company had dispersed upon the waters.

Only Gogo remained, offering his support;

what he grants to everyone, he does not deny to his own.

He addresses more sweetly the companion Papulus who stands there,

so that he himself might return some boat to me.

Searching everywhere, he saw a small boat beneath the shore,

but even there our baggage could not fit.

Meanwhile the sailor made me wait a little,

and arranged the provisions that the place itself supplied.

Though the gift is small, the willingness alone is enough;

indeed, the help that a lover gives is not small.

The companion also added cups for me, a grateful friend,

as much unmixed wine as the countryside could provide.

Thus, Papulus, you directed my joyful prow.

Live happily; farewell, sweet friend and companion.

> [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts read “sweet friend, handsome.”]

## Chapter XI. To Dynamius of Massilia

> [Note: Dynamius governed the province of Massilia. More concerning him may be found in Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book VI, chapter 11.]

> [Note: He declares his affection and longing for the absent Dynamius and, in the name and right of friendship, earnestly asks for an equal remembrance from him; finally, he urges him to return to him.]

I await you, my love, venerable Dynamius,

although absent, for my concern sees you.

I ask the breezes as they come what places hold you;

if you flee my eyes, you do not flee my heart.

You are pleased with the realm of Massilia, while Germania is ours;

torn from my sight, you remain joined to my heart.

What part of you has remained here, forgetful of you,

and do you not recall the limbs left behind in your own mind?

If sleep has stolen over you, let even your dreams tell you of me,

for rest itself is accustomed to see those who are of one mind.

If you are awake, I confess that forgiveness will deny you your fault;

as a negligent man, you have nothing with which to excuse yourself.

When the second year of the sun-bearing year has revolved through its months,

the sun’s orbit tires its panting horses,

for, when you departed, you carried away my eyes with you,

and now, though day lies open, I see nothing without you.

Would that you would give me words poured forth from your eloquent spring,

so that the page sent might make you speak with it.

But finally, I urge you more dearly: come here,

and restore light to my eyes, my friend.

## Chapter XII. To Dynamius

> [Note: The manuscript reads “To the same.”]

> [Note: In the heat of midsummer, Fortunatus had arranged to have a vein opened. His hand was therefore hindered from composing poems, and he complains to Dynamius about this. He testifies at length to his affection and longing for the same man.]

O seasons, which have begrudged the love that hastens forward,

which have forbidden the service owed to my vow to be performed,

through lyric measures and eloquent strings played by plectrums,

where Erato is sweetly *reliditebur* upon the lyres [printed form corrupt or uncertain; exact construction is not normalized].

Look: the thirsty dog (*canis*) puts forth the heat-bearing star,

and the heat pants across the cracked fields.

> [Note: Venetian: *egerit astrum*, “may put forth the star.”]

Fearing, therefore, that I might be struck by some flame of infection,

I bear my arm bound after letting blood.

From there the blood flows; from there the hand is held by a knot,

and the opened vein binds my right hand, now harmless.

So that the love of powerful thirst might burn without restraint,

this grave cause has obstructed my prayers.

I do not know how useful the treatment may be when completed,

but what harms me is that it makes me keep silent.

If I were allowed to write with my fingers, that alone would be enough;

now my first concern is you, my second is myself.

Withdrawn from my studies by my devotion to you,

the stream of the Muse is silent.

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “and I withdraw study from studies.”]

Ichor flows from the flesh, lest liquid stiffen in the mouth (*Carne fluit sanies, ne riget ore latex*); the medical syntax is uncertain.

The musical fire is absent; the sisters grow cold at the spring,

for the blood freezes the waters whence it irrigates [variant: *latices hinc agit*, “drives the waters from here”].

If, with my spirit heated, I should compose poems to be recited,

you yourself know how severely this labor weighs upon such an undertaking.

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads, “how greatly this labor weighs.”]

For blood removed requires more extended rest,

where neither cold gapes open nor burning heat enters.

> [Note: The Paris edition reads: “where the cold penetrates, and burning heat is absent.”]

It seeks a secluded place, lest a blowing breeze lash it,

where greenery stands refreshing the spirit and fragrance exhales.

Yet, out of affection for you, I set my serious concerns aside;

care for you occupies my face, for my own concerns hold my back.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *terga tenet*, “holds my back.” The editor believes the whole verse should be read: “Care for you occupies my face; it does not hold my back,” meaning that he keeps the concern for Dynamius before his face and does not cast it behind him. He nevertheless leaves the transmitted reading unchanged, since the manuscripts do not provide sufficiently clear evidence for the alteration.]

For after my exertion I had only just begun to give my limbs rest,

when love, setting order aside, breaks through the appointed times.

I say little while I wish to bring you a greeting of my own,

but I look after myself while I honor your wishes.

Now accept these small things, wise Dynamius, powerful in resonant renown,

> [Note: The Venetian edition reads:  
> “Now accept these small things in your hand, you powerful in praise, Dynamius.”  
> One Vatican manuscript has *clue lance*; another, *et pollens clave, lance Dynami*. The edition adds in the margin: “with key and lance, say *clance*.” The Paris edition reads *pollens in lance*. According to the gloss of the Trier copy, as Browerus reports, *clue clance* is explained as a compound of *cluo*, “to be powerful, to excel,” and the German word *klang*, meaning sound or clangor. I prefer reading it as in the second Vatican manuscript: *pollens clave, lance Dynami*, by which phrases both authority in governing and fairness in judging are indicated.]

powerful in key and lance, Dynamius,

bright in your own beauty, dear through my favor.

When I had been brought from the regions of Italy, the Rhine and the Ister

had sung of you before the place itself granted that I should know you.

> [Note: Appian of Alexandria testifies that the Ister is the same river as the Danube in his book *On the Illyrian War*. He writes that Caesar, laying waste everywhere, advanced into the territory of the Segestani and Paeonians as far as the river Savus and attacked there a very strongly fortified city, because he intended to use it “as a granary of war against the Dacians and Bastarnae, who dwell beyond the Ister.” He then adds: “The same river is called the Danube; and not far below, after descending with richer waters, it takes the name Ister instead of Danube.” Hence everyone can see that Fortunatus uses the Ister for Germania and the Rhine for Gaul, regions in which Dynamius’s name was renowned.]

Renowned in appearance, exalted in dwelling,

wise in law, equal to all in hope, wit, peace, and faith.

It happened, I confess, by chance, that I came to see you

beneath the cold warmth of the northern region.

> [Note: Browerus correctly observes that this poem was written earlier than the preceding one. In the preceding poem Fortunatus writes to Dynamius as someone already known to him, whom he wishes to return to him; here he expresses his desire to become acquainted with him. He makes sufficiently clear that he had not even known him by sight in the following verse:  
>
> “Previously known to my heart than seen by my eyes.”  
>
> I therefore believe that Fortunatus wrote this poem while he was still in Germania, or had not yet penetrated far into Gaul. This may be indicated by the following verses:  
>
> “From there, I confess, the chance of seeing you came to me  
> beneath the cold warmth of the northern region.”]

My whole face burns with greater eagerness toward your features

than toward a company of foreigners returning to their homeland.

I would have gone to your sight more swiftly, even as

the son born of Telamon went to his father’s embrace.

> [Note: Ajax, son of Telamon, was the bravest of the Greeks, as everyone knows. Fortunatus seems here to signify the longing of Greeks who were long absent from their homeland to return to their own people, and he declares that his desire to see Dynamius surpasses that longing.]

Not even the countryman cuts the soil with such eager winding,

nor the sailor the sea with such eagerness in his ship.

From that moment, renowned friend, a part of me remains with you;

and you come here as the half-part of my soul.

Previously known to my heart before seen by my eyes,

I hold you fast in my mind, though I do not touch you with my hand.

Although I have not yet fastened my arms around your neck,

love binds what my fingers cannot.

Though absent far away, I reach what I desire there;

where my feet do not come, I go there wholly in my heart.

> [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “where my foot does not come.” Another has “I go there securely in my whole heart.”]

Though the Arar and the Rhône stand in our way,

we swim through love,

nor does he prevent the mind from going who prevents the step from going.

I have also read verses sent under another person’s name,

in which, as though in a mirror, the image returns the man.

You are scattered through the square world from the spring of the Muses,

and carried by the waters of your song to shores you do not know.

> [Note: The Vulgate reads “having crossed some spring.” The world is called “square” from the four most famous regions of the world, as Browerus notes here; the Venetian edition and the Vatican manuscripts support his reading. Dynamius wrote the *Life of Saint Marius*, abbot of Bodon, and also the *Life of Saint Maximus*, bishop of Riez; he was therefore a man distinguished by talent and learning. He was also known to Gregory the Great, from whom he received letters with small gifts. See the notes of the learned Ruinart on Gregory of Tours, book VI, chapter 7.]

From here, though not in any way to be erased from us, you depart,

yet through your writings you are known to remain fixed among us.

Penetrating into the innermost parts of me as possessor of my little estate,

happy always, sweet friend, farewell.

Looking toward the help of your face and hoping for better than the stars,

may affection run on, and may long-lasting health stand by you.

I applaud at the first sacred hearth of Theodore’s see (*Sacris Theodori primo lare sedis aplaudo*),

and [at] outstanding Felix, whom the world’s honor bestowed (*Felici egregio, quem dedit orbis honor*).

> [Note: Theodore was bishop of Massilia and later badly treated by Dynamius (Gregory of Tours VI.11); the closing ellipsis and referents remain uncertain.]

## Additional source apparatus and editorial notes

* **Cols. 0221C–0222D.** Narbo was Narbo Martius; Paris `urbem` (“city”) stands for `hanc` (“this”), and `novus` (“newcomer”) is discussed in the *Life of Fortunatus* §34. `alit` (“nourishes”), `lumen abit` (“the light departs”), and `tot lacrymas` (“so many tears”) are retained variants.
* **Cols. 0223D–0225C.** The source records Brunichild’s proposed journey and return to Spain; `ad obsequium` means “for the funeral service.” `Vitrea vel glacies consolidasset iter` means “glass or ice would have made the road firm.” The manuscript has `gremiis … avis`; Versailles `neptis avae` (“granddaughter [of] grandmother”).
* **Cols. 0225D–0226D.** Arar is the Saône; `consultum dote tonantis` is “assurance by the Thunderer’s gift.” The Tagus marks Goisuintha’s Spanish setting; `Vachalus` is the Waal. `mitior hic aestu sub molli`, `amore cibus`, and `tere bat amatus` are source readings. Childebert left two daughters by Ultrogotha, hence “a third with your two daughters.”
* **Cols. 0227A–0228D.** `me meruisse dapes`, `fauce assidente`, `rates`, `placidus`, `si madefactus`, `lactavi reliquos`, `ligare`, `Pappulus exstat`, `mihi sola voluntas`, and `rure` are all retained with their literal senses: earned feasts; throat close by; boats; calm; if soaked; enticed the rest; bind; Pappulus stands forth; my will alone; countryside. Nauciacum/Nantiacum/Nauriacum is explicitly uncertain.
* **Cols. 0229A–0230C.** Retained readings: `quos inter tua pars`, `si sopor oppressit`, `invidistis amore`, `ne me jacularer`, `lavitur unde cruor, modo`, `inde vocat, quo retinere`, Paris `ne` after `scribere`, `latices hinc agit`, `neu flabilis`, `non` after `modo`, and `si mea`; their broken syntax is not smoothed.
* **Cols. 0230D–0232B.** The `clue clance` note retains its `cluo`/German *klang* gloss and the Vatican `pollens clave, lance Dynami`; also retained are `viandi`, `effervet totus in illis`, `classe fretum`, and the note that Dynamius wrote lives of Saints Marius and Maximus.

To the distinguished Albinus, Helias, and the celebrated Jovinus,

[Note: Albinus was the man whom Dynamius, without consulting the king, caused to be made bishop of Uzès after he had been prefect. He died shortly afterward, just when arrangements were being made to remove him from the episcopate. See Gregory of Tours, Book VI, chapter 7.]

[Note: Likewise Jovinus, formerly governor of the Province, was declared bishop by royal command; but Marcellus, son of the senator Felix, was installed in his place through Dynamius’s agency. These events occurred in the year 581.]

[Col. 0232B] For Fortunatus, repay the work of salvation.

I have sung these for you in simple song;

But the barbitos thunders forth in learned grandeur.

[Note: Here *elisi* is understood by Browerus as *leusa*, or *lisa*, a kind of rhythm or song among the Franks and Alemanni, like *leudi*, or *lïedi*—names elsewhere used by Fortunatus. Yet, apart from the great violence done to the word, if *elisi* is taken as *leusa*, the whole sense of the verse becomes lame. I therefore do not hesitate to believe that *elisi* is the first person of the perfect verb *elido*, meaning “I have driven out” or “I have brought forth.” The Venetian edition has:

> This lyre of ours modulates for you in simple song,
>
> But from it the archetypal barbiton thunders learnedly.

Moreover, Browerus thinks that *archetypum* is used here for something inflated and grandiloquent.]

[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *si tonat*, “if it thunders.”]

[Note: Another has *barbitus*.]

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0231]

## CHAPTER ONE. To Gogo

[Note: This Gogo is called the fosterer of King Sigibert by Gregory of Tours, Book V, chapter 47. He had also brought Brunhild from Spain, as is stated in the *Epitome of Frankish History*, chapter 59; Fortunatus’s words here show this:

> Recently from the Spanish lands, through many dangers,
>
> You bring the greatest joys to the distinguished king.

In the same *Epitome* it is related that Gogo was brought into Sigibert’s hatred by Brunhild, and was killed by him. Aimoinus confirms this in Book III of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 4; but Gregory of Tours seems to disagree, assigning Gogo’s death to the year 581, whereas Sigibert, through Fredegund’s agency, had already been killed in 575.]

[Col. 0231D] [Note: He praises Gogo for his eloquence, generosity toward strangers, prudence, evenness of temper, piety, and handsome appearance. He commends King Sigibert’s judgment in choosing him as his minister.]

While Orpheus moved the woven strings with his thumb,

And the struck plectrum was giving words to the threads,

Soon, when the lyre resounded, he touched the forests with sweetness,

And drew wild beasts by love toward the songs of the cithara.

[Col. 0233A] From every side the deer left their emptied lairs,

And even the tiger, laying aside its rage, came.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *et ipse venit*, “and he himself came.”]

As the nightingale, stirred by the overwhelming melody, flew,

The bird, forgetting her young, hurried exhausted to him.

But although she had wearied her wings over a long distance,

On arriving as she wished, the bird recovered her strength.

So, Gogo, captivated and spurred by your sweetness,

The traveler, a stranger in distant realms, approaches.

From every side they hasten to come more readily,

For your tongue draws them as that lyre did.

After the exile himself, worn out, has come here,

What he previously suffered disappears when you heal him.  
[Note: The Paris edition has *mediante*, “when you intervene.”]

You draw groans from the afflicted and plant joys;

Lest they wither, you refresh them with the rain of your mouth.

You build honeycombs with speech and supply new honey,  
[Note: The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts have *nova mella ministrans*, “supplying new honey.”]

[Col. 0233B] And by the nectar of your sweet eloquence you surpass the bees.

The potent grace of your lips waters abundantly from a fertile fountain,

And from its hidden source flows a voice fit to be savored.

Rich prudence reigns in your wakeful mind,

In which, once the tinder is laid, the wave of wit swims.

You flash rays from your breast with the splendor of your spirit,

And an inward light shines, imitating day.

But in turn the sun and clouds fill the world,

Whereas your hearts always possess a clear day.

With ready affections you are held to be a temple of piety,

And by sacred gifts you are a house constructed for generosity.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *est fabricata*, “has been built.”]

A beautiful form flashes with its own radiance in you,

So that your face itself confirms the disposition of your mind.

You gather every kind of praise into a single beauty,

Nor is there anything greater than what your beauty possesses.

[Col. 0233C] By the judgment of King Sigibert you are held in high esteem,

And no one can deceive the king’s judgment.

The wise man chose the wise, the lover the loving,

Just as the learned bee selects flowers.

From his merit you have learned to be regarded as such,  
[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *Illius et merito*, “and by his merit.”]

And, kindly servant, you reproduce the character of your master.

Recently from the Spanish lands, through many dangers,

You bring the greatest joys to the distinguished king.

You love him as much as you have acquired what is better;

No one could give by arms what your tongue has given.

[Col. 0234A] If I were silent about these good qualities, our silence would praise you,

Nor should you look for words, since you possess my heart.  
[Note: The pentameter beginning *Nec voces spectes* and the following hexameter were supplied by Browerus from a Trier manuscript, since they were absent from the Vulgate and the manuscripts. They are also absent from the Venetian edition.]

I sing what is true in praising you, and no deceit condemns me;

I speak with the people as witness, and shall be free of blame.

May this lofty praise for you rise through distant ages;

May this life preserve you long, and may that other life honor you.

## CHAPTER TWO. To the Same, When He Was Invited to Dinner

[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *cum erogaret*, “when he was distributing.”]

[Col. 0234A] [Note: He recalls Gogo’s benefactions toward him and excuses himself to him for not attending when invited to dinner.]

Nectar, wine, food, clothing, learning, ability—

By your lavish gifts, Gogo, you are enough for me.

You are my overflowing Cicero, you are our Apicius;  
[Note: Apicius was the foremost leader of gluttons and wastrels. Since it was not enough for him to have consumed the largesses of princes and the public revenues in banquets, he wished to make his greed known to later generations through several books written about stimulants to the appetite. Seneca mentions him in *On Consolation to Helvia*, in these words: “Apicius lived in our time; in that city from which philosophers had once been ordered to depart as corrupters of youth, he professed the science of the cookshop and infected the age with his discipline. It is worth knowing how he ended. After he had poured ten million sesterces into his kitchen and swallowed so many princely gifts and the immense revenue of the Capitol in individual banquets, crushed by debt he was forced for the first time to examine his accounts. He calculated that one million sesterces would remain to him and, as though he were going to live in the extremity of hunger, if he lived on one million, he ended his life by poison.” Sidonius, *Letters*, Book III, letter 7, calls feasters “Apicii.”]

[Col. 0234B] Here you satisfy me with words, and there you feed me with food.  
[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *nec tua ruma cibus*, “nor is your rumination food.”]

But for now, with my belly swollen from beef, I rest;  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *bulla turgente*, “with the bubble swollen.”]

For there is strife in the womb if mixed meat begins to rage.

Where the ox lies down, there, I think, the chicken and goose will flee,

And between horns and feathers the contest will not be equal.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *pennis*, “feathers”; one Vatican manuscript has *aequus erat*, “was equal.”]

And now I close my eyes, languid with sleep,

For happy songs approve of my sleeping.

## CHAPTER THREE. Also to the Same

[Note: He clears himself before Gogo and casts back upon him the fault that Gogo had attributed to him, while nevertheless showing that the affection of their friendship remains safe and undiminished.]

The page just sent to me has held out complaints,

Yet I declare that I am free of blame toward you.

[Col. 0234C] For we think the reason is that your presence harmed us more;

For the crime in which you sinned, I am blamed.  
[Note: The Paris edition has *cur causaremus*, “why we should complain.”]

Yet affection will not perish because of such a charge;

The fruit of friendship remains, cherished in the heart.  
[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *corde colende*, “to be cherished in the heart.”]

## CHAPTER FOUR. To the Same

[Note: The poet asks the clouds and winds what Gogo is doing and where he is staying. Through them he sends him greetings.]

Clouds, which come when the swift North Wind blows,

Which the revolving starry axis moves along its hanging wheel,  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *axe rota*, “on the axis, the wheel”; one Vatican manuscript has *quae movet axe rotae*, “which moves the wheel on the axis.”]

Tell me where my dear Gogo enjoys health;

What does he do, serene in mind amid peaceful affairs?  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *quam vegetet*, “how he may thrive”; one Vatican manuscript has *salute*, “in health”; the Venetian edition has *mente serenus agit*, “he acts serenely in mind,” and two Vatican manuscripts agree, while another has the corrupt reading *serenus ait*, “the serene one says.”]

If he lingers near the wave-roaming shores of the Rhine,

So that the fat of salmon may be dragged from the waters by a net,  
[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *moratur littora*, “he dwells by the shores”; another has *reste trahatur*, “may be dragged by a rope.” The edition has in the margin *hinc retrahatur*, “may be drawn back from here.”]

Or strolls above the vine-bearing river Musella,

Where a light breeze tempers the burning day.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *et super uviferi Alus elle*, corruptly; the manuscripts have *Musellae*. For a description of this river and the beauty and fertility of its banks, see below, Book X, chapter 9.]

Where vine-leaf and river alike temper the heat;

Cool shade lies among the vines, and fresh water amid the waves.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has corruptly:

> A wave rigid among the vines, a wave ruling the waves.]

[Col. 0236A] Or where the sweet-sounding Mosa flows, where crane, wild goose, and swan are found,

Rich in threefold commerce—bird, fish, and boat.  
[Note: Other manuscripts have *dulcisonans*, “sweet-sounding.” The Venetian edition has *quo grus juncta anser*, “where the crane is joined by the goose”; the Vulgate has *grus tanta*, “so great a crane.” The Vatican manuscripts report Browerus’s reading. A *ganta* is a wild goose; Adso, in the *Life of Saint Walbert*, chapter 5, says: “Wild geese, which because of their whiteness or the sound of their voice country people call *gantas*.” Dufresne, in his *Glossary*, notes that the word is old French and is still retained by the Germans, who call these birds *Gänse*.]

Or does he remain where the Axona is broken by grassy banks,

Whose waters nourish pasture, meadow, and grain?  
[Note: The Venetian edition has “meadow and flocks.” The Axona, according to Marlianus’s description, is this river at the farthest limits of the Rhemi; it separates their diocese from that of Laon and is now called the Avaix by the French. Lucan refers to its inhabitants:

> And the light Axones in long warfare.

Gregory of Tours speaks of the Axona as a well-known river in Book VI, chapter 37, and elsewhere.]

Isara, Sara, Chares, Schaldis, Saba, Somena, Sura,

Or the river that reaches Metz, bearing its name from salt?  
[Note: In the Vulgate this verse formerly appeared as follows, according to Browerus:

> Esara, or Rachares, Scaldes, Sates, Ormena, Sura.

The Venetian edition reads:

> Esara, or Oscarus, Scaldis, Satis, Ormena, Sura.

Two Vatican manuscripts have *Sate* and *Somena*; one has *Sata*. Isara is a river of Narbonese Gaul, now commonly called the Oise. Browerus says that it rises in Savoy, on the mountain of the Salassi called Senis, or Cemenus according to Strabo and Pliny, Book III, chapter 4, and eventually joins the Rhône.]

[Note: Sara is likewise a river. According to the same Browerus, its source is shown on a ridge of the Vosges, on the border of Alsace and Lorraine. In Julius Caesar’s inscription it is called *Sarra*, and by Ausonius *Saravus*. Four miles from Trier it joins the Moselle: a genuinely fish-filled stream, once frequented by the highest nobility and inhabited by families of ancient lineage.]

[Note: Chares, or Caris, commonly called the Cher, cuts through the middle of the province of the Bituriges and, swollen by other little streams, flows into the Loire somewhat below Tours, as stated in Ruinart’s notes to the *Scholastic Chronicle of Fredegar*, p. 4, chapter 129. Browerus, however, prefers to understand Fortunatus’s Chares as the river Cheir in the region of the Meuse, which passes beneath the prominent town of Ivois and joins the Meuse. “No extraordinary fate,” he says, “befell the kings of the Mediomatrici except in Provence and among the Arverni,” so that Gogo could not have wandered beyond the boundaries of Sigibert’s kingdom. But I do not see why he could not have gone farther for the sake of hunting than Sigibert’s dominion extended. Nevertheless, I readily agree with Browerus’s view, because the Cheir of which he speaks agrees in location and proximity with the other rivers likewise mentioned here by Fortunatus.]

[Note: Schaldis, a river well known to Caesar, Pliny, and other reliable authorities, has its sources among the Veromandui above Chastelet, near the abbey of Martiniana. It flows through Crevecœur, Cambrai, Bouchain, and Valenciennes; enlarged by the Trouille at Condé and receiving the Scarpe at Mortagne through Antoing, it enters Tournai. From there, flowing past Oudenaarde, it rushes into Ghent with such force and greed that it swallows the Lys and the Lieve there; at Dendermonde it takes possession of the Dender, at Rupelmonde of the Rupel, and, swollen, absorbs the Nete and Dyle, finally displaying itself at Antwerp, broad and spread between its banks, as it enters the Ocean. This is Browerus’s account, drawn from Jacobus Marchantius, the historian of Flanders.]

[Note: Browerus reports that he restored *Saba* from an old manuscript, although the Calarensis manuscript and several others had *Satam* instead. Saba is the river which, according to him, the people of the Ardennes now call the Sambre. Rising in the former wilderness of that forest, not far from the borders of Hainaut and the Veromandui, it is eventually received first by the walls of the notable city of Namur and then by the Meuse.]

[Note: Somena, also called Sumina and Sumena, rises among the Veromandui not far from the source of the Scheldt. From there it visits Saint-Quentin, Péronne, and the Ambiani themselves; passing the village of the abbey and the town of Saint-Valery, it finally rushes into the Ocean. It is commonly called the Somme and is better known to Frankish than to Roman writers. Browerus.]

[Note: Sura rises in the Ardennes, in the territory of Luxembourg, carrying with it the streams Alisontia, Atartus, and Ura. It winds widely through their lands until, enriched by the Pronaea and Nemesis known to Ausonius, it becomes abundant in salmon and suitable for small boats. It then seeks Echternach, once the celebrated home of Saint Willibrord, and opens its mouths at Wasserbillig, where it disappears into the Moselle, about eight miles from Trier. Browerus.]

[Note: The Venetian edition has *seu qui mitis adit*, “or which approaches gently”; three Vatican manuscripts have *seu qui Mettis adit*, “or which approaches Metz.” For the river Salia, see what we noted at Book III, chapter 14.]

Or, wandering through the summer woods and forest glades,

Does he bind wild beasts here with the spear and kill them there with the net?  
[Note: The Paris edition has *hinc capit*, “captures them here.”]

[Col. 0237A] In the Ardennes—or Vosges—are there deer, goats, and Helicean bears?  
[Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts have *Ardenna, an Vosagus*, “the Ardennes, or the Vosges.” No ancient writer of any standing leaves the Ardennes forest and its immense wildernesses unmentioned. Much of it is now pierced by numerous towns, villages, and monasteries, extending from Trier to the Meuse and thence from the lands of the Condrusi, Liège, and Namur into the territories of the Nervii, Atrebates, and Veromandui, reaching the Scheldt, with scattered traces still remaining here and there of the branches of the ancient Ardennes. Just as *Ardenna* here has lost a letter, so *Vosagus* is read with a reversal of letters in several witnesses; both are characteristic of the usage of that age. The Vosges, or Vosegus, is the mountain range between Alsace and Lorraine, extending in a broad sweep from Trier toward the Lingones and Sequani. It is beautiful with extensive valleys and perennial waters, and with wooded, shaded ridges; in some places it rises so high that it seems to touch the clouds at its summit and even to challenge the Alps. Browerus adds that these forests were once famous for the hunting and fowling of the Frankish kings. See Cluverius, *Germania Antiqua*, Book II, chapters 38–39, for their ancient description and location.]

[Note: Browerus criticizes this passage and does not doubt that Fortunatus mistakenly uses *Helicis*, the constellation of the north pole, or the star which the ancients called Helice, and that he is greatly deceived both in gender and in prosody. I do not know whether Fortunatus might instead have used *Helicis* in the manner of the Greeks, who call oxen “ἕλικας” (*helikas*), either because they are dark-colored or because their legs are flexible. The Paris edition has *ilicis*, “of the holm oak.” (Note from the first revision.)

I should add what I learned from the advice of the most distinguished and learned Jacob Morelli, keeper of the library of Saint Mark in Venice. In the *Miscellaneous Critical Observations on Ancient and Recent Authors*, published at Amsterdam in 1732 and 1751, vol. V, part I, p. 246, an anonymous author thinks that Fortunatus’s verse should be read thus:

> Ardennes or Vosges: deer, roe deer, elks, and aurochs.

For he thinks that *elicis* was written by Fortunatus for *alicis*—the animal which others call the elk, *elech* among the Germans—and that *urus* was added as well, so that the two beasts found in the forests of Germany, and mentioned together by Caesar and certain old charters, might be named together here. It is useful to quote the Anonymous’s own words:

> You see, he says, elk and aurochs joined together here; Caesar also joined them, as did the charters. Indeed, the very same wild beasts mentioned by the charters are said by Venantius to have existed in Drenthe, in the Vosges, the Gallic mountain.

One charter names these animals as deer, bears—or rather, I should say, aurochs—roe deer, boars, and also beasts which in the Teutonic language are called *elo* or *schelo*. (Note from the second revision.)]

And bears—

Does the forest thunder with the crash of arrow-bearing slaughter?

Or does he strike the plain between the horns of mighty buffaloes,

While the bear, the wild ass, and the boar do not postpone death?

Or, tending his own fields, does he furrow the scorched fallow,

While the rough-necked bull groans beneath the plow?  
[Note: The Paris edition has *taurus ad arva*, “the bull toward the fields.”]

Or does he now sit happily in the palace hall,

Where the school, gathering together, applauds him with devoted affection?  
[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *Cui schola egrediens*, “where the school goes forth.” *Scholae* were called bands or groups; Gregory of Tours uses the word in this sense in Book X of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 15. Hence the *Palatine Schools* were various cohorts assigned to guard the palace and the ruler; each kept watch in its own school. Their rank varied according to the pay they received and the position they held, as Dufresne states in his *Glossary*. Thus Procopius, *Gothic War*, Book IV, chapter 27, speaking of the Lombard Ildigis, whom the emperor Justinian had placed over one band of soldiers, says: “He appointed him commander of one of the companies assigned to guard the palace, which they call *scholae*.”]

Or, when he discusses the laws of kindly devotion with Lupus,

Do they create gentle honey with equal counsel?

May they provide nourishment for the needy and comfort for the widow;

May the child receive a guardian and the destitute assistance.

Whatever they do together, may fortunate prayers support;

And may they be worthy to enjoy the love of Christ the King.

I ask you, winds that run forth and return,

Carry news of your Fortunatus to him.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On Duke Bodegisilus

[Note: Gregory of Tours mentions Bodegisilus in Book VIII of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 22, in these words: “In those days Duke Bodegisilus died, full of days, but none of his property was diminished for his sons.” These final words reveal his exceptional integrity in governing the provinces, since the fisc claimed nothing from the dead man’s property as ill-gotten from the public offices he had administered. This Bodegisilus must certainly be distinguished from the man whom Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 2, calls the son of Mummolenus of Soissons; when he had been sent as an ambassador to the emperor Maurice, that man was overwhelmed by a popular revolt at Carthage, as Gregory relates there. The Venetian edition has the title “On Godegisilus.”]

[Col. 0237B] [Note: He praises Duke Bodegisilus for the sweetness and grace of his eloquence, the gentleness of his character and disposition, the provinces he administered with faith, justice, and innocence, and then commends other virtues of his.]

If from a barren breast I poured forth abundant rivers,

I still would not be sufficient to speak of you, Duke Bodegisilus.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *Godegisle loqui*, “to speak of Godegisilus.” Gregory of Tours mentions Duke Bodegisilus several times in his *History of the Franks*.]

[Col. 0238A] Your grace suddenly seized our mind,

So that now I wish to be more yours than my own.

From the first moment I was worthy to know your peaceful countenance,

I carry limbs restored by the ointment of your mouth.

You satisfied the breast of one who loves with sweet conversation,

For your words give food to me, your devoted servant.

Others distribute feasts that sustain the body;

You yourself give richer banquets, by which you satisfy the mind.

The mildest honeys do not so flavor Falernian wine

As your taste sweetens our hearts.

How delightfully you charm those whom you always seem to love,

Making me yours within the space of an hour!

If I could, I would reveal what virtue is yours,

But my small talent is forbidden to report what is great.

I stumble, a little man beneath the weight of so many praises,

But I walk better when guided by your deeds.

To Massilia you gave fortunate hopes,

And she reports her governor with enduring praise.

Here Germany likewise applauds you with equal merit,

And each region competes in praising you.

There is a dispute between the two regions over your goodness;

That one claims you for itself, while this one wishes to retain you.  
[Note: *Utraeque*, as also *utrique*, was customarily used by ancient writers for *utriusque*, “of both.” Browerus notes this in relation to the passage.]

Justice never loses its case when you are judge,

Nor can a powerful man overturn the truth by payment.

[Col. 0239A] You do not bind the innocent, nor release the guilty from punishment;

Personal standing counts for nothing when one’s own case denies it.

You possess the eyes of the heart, with a lamp of the spirit shining,

And your summit gleams with everlasting light.

Eloquent with a rushing intellect from a health-giving spring,

You water pious riches with your flowing mouth.

If you happen to see someone failing through hardship,  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *forte labare*, “perhaps faltering.”]

As the Nile nourishes Egypt, so your tongue refreshes him.

You who store the laws of your country within your breast,

Can untangle the threads of a complicated case.  
[Note: The Paris edition has *simpliciter*, “simply.”]

By constant banquets you fill the companies, venerable man,

And whoever visits your house departs filled.

If you come into the fields, the people who must be fed hurry there,

And, accompanying you, each obtains his own banquet.

May you bear the prayers of all, surviving through long ages;

[Col. 0239B] And may you, powerful, always remain in the people’s mouth.

## CHAPTER SIX. On Palatina

[Note: In the Venetian edition the title of this poem is “On Palatina, daughter of Bishop Gallus Magnus and wife of Boso.” Three Vatican manuscripts likewise read “daughter of Bishop Gallus Magnus.” Browerus thinks that the word “bishop,” as an added gloss, should be rejected, since no offspring is recorded for Gallus, the bishop of the Arverni, who could be designated by that title. It may also be added that the death of Gallus, bishop of the Arverni, is assigned to the year 554, when Fortunatus had not yet come to Gaul, whereas here he seems to speak of Gallus Magnus as still living.

There was, however, another Gallomagnus, bishop of Troyes, whom Gregory of Tours mentions in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8, section 8. He is found subscribing to the Fourth Council of Paris in 573 and to the First Council of Mâcon in 581 or 583, as Cointius thinks. Whether this was the man about whom Fortunatus speaks here, I do not dare decide. Browerus thinks it more likely that this was Gallomagnus the referendary, whom Gregory of Tours mentions in Book IX of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 38. He possessed great power under King Childebert and afterward experienced varying fortunes, as Gregory relates there.

The claim that Godegisilus had Palatina, the daughter of Gallomagnus, as his wife also presents considerable difficulty, since the same Godegisilus is called the son-in-law of Lupus by Gregory of Tours, Book IX, chapter 12. Either Godegisilus must therefore be said to have contracted a second marriage, or this must have been another Godegisilus to whom Palatina was married. Whether it was Godegisilus himself, rather than Duke Boso, as the Venetian edition reports, cannot be established, since the matter admits only of conjecture. No one, however, will deny that what is said here of Godegisilus could equally be said of Boso, once a very powerful man in Gaul.]

[Col. 0239C] Daughter of Gallomagnus, wife of Duke Godegisilus.

[Note: Fortunatus praises Palatina, daughter of Gallomagnus and wife of Godegisilus, in this poem, commending her outstanding beauty together with an equal brilliance of intellect and eloquence.]

As Lucifer brings forth a shining face in the heavens,

And announces the day with a radiant and joyful countenance,

As he advances, he adorns the sky and sends his lamp to the earth,

And among the stars holds his kingdom by his light,

So you, diffusing radiant lights from your face,

Surpass the feminine choirs, more beautiful in countenance.  
[Note: The Paris edition reads this verse:

> Thus, spreading your own lights from your beautiful face.]

[Col. 0239C] And thus the multitude of women yields to you in beauty,

As the moon is inferior to the sun’s rays in light.  
[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts have *aut tibi*, “or to you.”]

Your bright beauty transforms clear hues,

Now restoring lilies, now modest roses.

Believe me: if anyone should behold that face,

He reads again the flowers that springtime is accustomed to give.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *hic retegit flores*, “here he uncovers the flowers.”]

[Col. 0240A] Words cannot paint your precious form,

Nor is eloquence able to recount my wonder.

More gracious in movement, venerable in modest feeling,

You possess in your character the same radiance as in your face.  
[Note: The Paris edition has *mitis, reverenda, pudica*, “gentle, venerable, modest.”]

More charming in conversation, sweetest in peaceful words,

I would despise the lyre if your tongue were sounding.

Prudent wisdom shines from your transparent breast,

And, as you radiate, your sex is adorned.

The hall of your husband shone more brightly with a watchful wife,
