And the household flourished under its excellent arranger.  
[Note: The Paris edition has *disposita arce domus*, “the house with its well-ordered citadel.”]

Rightly, indeed, she is great who is the daughter of great Gallus,

But the father grew in honor through the merit of his daughter.

She could not but be more illustrious through her endowment,

She who deserved, as worthy herself, to please a lofty man.

From many, he chose the beloved woman to love as his beloved.

[Col. 0240B] And, himself the judge of his country, he judges for himself.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has “He himself gives you the law of your country”; one Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition have “He himself vindicates it for himself.”]

May the two of you, joined as equals, remain for long years,

And may your every desired joy come to you.  
[Note: One Vatican manuscript has “May you remain through long years.”]

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On Duke Lupus

[Note: Lupus, to whom this poem was written, possessed great authority and influence with King Sigibert and governed the province of Champagne around Rheims. After Sigibert was killed, he fell into grave danger both in life and fortune because of the hostility of powerful men. He was rescued through the favor and efforts of Queen Brunhild and kindly received by King Guntram, Sigibert’s brother. He lived with him until Childebert, Sigibert’s son, had reached maturity, as may be read in Gregory of Tours, Book VI, chapter 4.]

[Note: He praises Duke Lupus for the dignity of his spirit, his eloquence, his endurance in bearing public offices and responsibilities, the courage of his spirit and eloquence in giving answers, the gravity with which he conducted embassies, his justice in weighing cases, the honors he attained and the happiness and virtue with which he exercised them, the victories he won, his military labor and diligence, his outstanding services to King Sigibert, and the sweetness of his character and speech. Finally, he declares the king’s singular devotion and benevolence toward him.]

Let all the ancient nobles and the lofty names of former times

Yield, conquered by the merit of Duke Lupus.

What wise Scipio, mature Cato,  
[Note: The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts have *maturus agebat*, “what mature Cato did.”]

And fortunate Pompey possessed—you alone possess it all.

Under those consuls Roman power shone;

Under your leadership, Rome has now returned to us here.

When you grant access, confidence rises in everyone;

A free tongue gives the aid of liberty.

If anyone carried sadness in a troubled heart,

After seeing you, he remains in better hope.

Established in gravity of spirit and deep in heart,  
[Note: One Vatican manuscript has *quoque corde profundens*, “pouring forth from every heart.”]

You pour from your mouth the salt of a tranquil sea.

But your eloquent gifts benefit the people still more;  
[Note: The Paris edition has *faciendo*, “by doing.”]

You compose thoughts, for the wave of wit seasons food.

You are the root of counsel, the vein of fruitful flavor,

Quick in intellect, loquacious with a rolling tongue.

You shine in two things, prepared in each;

Whatever you conceive in your heart, your tongue can reveal.

In whose breast the burdens of the king are made firm,

The public concern also flourishes through your aid.

You submit your limbs to great labors with renewed devotion;

For the king’s repose, the burden is thought sweet.

O happy spirit, which directs the affairs of its country,  
[Note: The Venetian edition has “which directs affairs.”]

And a noble mind lives for all its fellow citizens.

Envoys arrive and, when you answer, are bound fast,

And soon they lie pierced by the spear of your words.

Speech was a lance, and the speaker’s voice was armed;

Sigibert possesses an omen of victory in you.

In his reply he gives voice to the mind of the people,

And a single voice has the power to speak the people’s wish.

Through your intellect the case has gained its triumph;

With the aid of its advocate, it became the more just.

No one can set forth his own case in such a way

As your renowned tongue resounds on behalf of all.

As the Nile revives Egypt when it overflows,

So you nourish everything with the rivers of conversation.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has “with the river of conversation, which is pleasing.”]

With justice flourishing, the laws favor you as judge;  
[Note: The same edition has “with you fostering and judging, the laws…”]

And you remain the balanced scale of cases.

People flee to you; lofty belts of office seek you;

You do not seek honor in order to possess it—every honor seeks you.

[Col. 0242A] In whose lap the power he has attained is nourished,

Under whose governance the summit, once bestowed, knows how to grow.

How deservedly he always retains the honors granted to him,

Through whom worthy heights possess a still worthier summit.

Having acquired the ancient spirit of the Roman stock,

You wage wars with arms and govern laws in peace.  
[Note: The Paris edition has *animis*, “with spirits.”]

Supported by both goods—here by arms, there by laws—

How well he becomes first, to whom every distinction gives its favor.  
[Note: One Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition have “how well he becomes firm.”]

What your virtue is together with heavenly prosperity,

The Saxon and Danish peoples quickly prove, conquered.  
[Note: “The Saxons and Danes.” The Vulgate reads “of the Saxon and Rhône,” a reading also retained by the Venetian edition. A gloss in the Saint Gall manuscript, as Browerus reports, interprets the Danes as the Bavarians, so called from the Danube, beside which part of that people lived. The Franks often waged war against these neighboring peoples, who threatened the Frankish kingdom, as may be seen throughout Gregory of Tours’ history.]

By the river Borda, where the stream runs in a winding channel,

The opposing army, under your command, was cut down and fell.

[Note: The Venetian edition has *Borda*. One Vatican manuscript has *Bordaa quo fluvius*. Browerus is uncertain and doubtful in determining the location of this river, especially since the Oder, flowing from the frontier of Silesia, which he suspects Fortunatus designates by the name Bordaa, lies at too great a distance from Laugona, and it is not likely that Lupus’s victory extended from the Oder as far as Laugona. Yet it is not surprising that, over so long an age, the names of one or another river may have changed or their channels, diverted in another direction, have been transferred elsewhere, thereby causing error and difficulty for posterity.]

Then half the army obeyed your commands;

How deservedly he conquers who carries out your orders.

Victorious, you sweated beneath the weight of your iron tunic [variant: “you sweat beneath”],  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *ferrato tunicae*, “of the iron tunic.”]

[Col. 0242B] And you shone beneath a cloud of dust.

For so long you fought, pursuing the fleeing line,  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *tanta diu pugnax*, “so long, so warlike.”]

Until Langona was the boundary with its glassy waters.  
[Note: The Venetian edition has *Lingona dum vitreis*. Laugona, or Logana, as it appears in old books and charters, is a river which, according to Browerus, rises in the territory of the counts of Wittgenstein, not far from Mount Hario. From there it flows past Wittgenstein—said to derive its name from Wittekind, the famous Saxon leader—and reaches Marburg, then waters the town of Wetzlar. From there it flows more beautifully into the territory of Trier, where, turbulent and broken by abundant rocks, it displays on either bank the former residences of noble dukes, counts, and dynasts who once lived densely beyond the Rhine. A little above its confluence, near the town whose name was given by the river and the rock—Lonstein—it joins the Rhine. The local inhabitants call this river the Lahn.]

The man who fled sluggishly found in that river a tomb;

For a fortunate commander the rivers themselves wage war.

Among fellow citizens, Gaul deserved you as its light,

And everywhere you shine like the splendor of a lamp in the heart.

Some are preferred by powerful beauty, some by wisdom [Note: Venetian edition, “some are brought forth by wisdom.”],

Each has one particular gift, but you have many virtues.

As you approach the lords, you fill the venerable palaces [Note: Same edition, “filling them.” How greatly Lupus deserved well of the kingdom of Sigibert and of the entire royal household and court, Brunhild’s zeal and diligence in preserving him sufficiently demonstrated. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book VI, chapter 4, relates it thus: “Brunhild, grieving over the unjust persecutions of her faithful man Lupus, girded herself manfully, broke through the enemy’s ranks, and said: ‘Do not, men, do not persecute the innocent; do not engage in battle for one man, lest the region lose its support.’”],

And honor multiplies as it enters with you.

When you come, the gracious house shines with a new serenity,

And the royal halls recover their own spirit.

Indeed, the court regains its eyes when it sees you return,

You whom the common light of the leaders possesses as their light.

[Col. 0242C] The prince’s support, the country’s glory, the weapons of our ancestors,

A source of counsel to the rest, beloved by all as one.

What more should I say even of your admirable sweetness?

You, full of nectar, build honeycombs with your mouth.

Dear grace accompanies your serene face,

And an enduring day shines within.

[Col. 0243A] You satisfy with food and, kindly, restore with conversation [Note: Venetian edition, “you warm with kindly speech.”];

Once the feasts are removed, your words are banquets.

Who could speak words worthy of you, whom with open voice [Note: Same edition and three Vatican manuscripts, “with powerful voice.”]

The pious king proclaims to be his ornament?

May the highest summit belong to you while he reigns forever,

And may the present life be yours, and may the future honor it.

## CHAPTER VIII. To the same man.

[Note: Fortunatus declares in this poem the joy he had received from the report brought to him of Lupus’s complete recovery; then, finally, he gathers together the virtues and outstanding praises of that same Lupus.]

When scorching July burns the fiery sands,

And the dry earth thirsts along its dusty margin,

The languishing vine scarcely unfolds its peaceful shades,

[Col. 0243B] And the tender grass draws together its bluish locks.

With its leaves lowered beneath Phoebus’s ruling heat,

The grove scarcely defends its cool shelter.

The heifer, disdaining pasture, flees the glades in the heat,

And the horse himself does not feed on the afflicted grasses [Note: The Paris edition reads, “the horse takes grass.” In the Vulgate, “the world is fed by waters.” The Venetian edition is still more corrupt: “the hermus is fed by waters.” One Vatican manuscript has “herbus equis”; Browerus reports that he restored the reading as it now stands from manuscripts, but the verse has a metrical defect.].

The dog lashes its extended tongue from its mouth,

And the weary sheep, dragging its flanks, pants sadly.

Perhaps a traveler, walking on his journey during the blazing hours,

Is scorched, set on fire by the sun pressing upon his hair.

So that he may refresh himself, though the ground is parched, with a modest draught,

He anxiously longs again and again for running waters.

Or, beneath the green summit of a trembling tree, spread out,

The shade, interposed by its leaves, tempers thirst [Note: The Paris edition, “the mouth of the thirsty one.”].

If, for some new [uncertain reading] reason, a nearby grove now gives shade,

And a fresh wave of a glass-clear spring murmurs:

[Col. 0243C] Hurrying there, the joyful man lies down on the peaceful fields.

He rolls his limbs upon the grassy couches.

Holding favorable hopes, he is refreshed by a double delight [Note: One Vatican manuscript, “having followed favorable hopes.”]:

Here the shade lifts the day, there the water drives away thirst.

If he knows any songs, he returns to them with measured singing,

And the caressing breeze calls forth peaceful sounds.

[Note: The Paris edition reads this verse:

“If Homer happened to be well known to him as a wise man.”]

If Homer happened to be well known to him at Athens,

Or Maro, read in Trajan’s forum [Note: The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript have “the Trojan forum,” corruptly. See what we said in the notes to poem 23 of book III.],

[Col. 0244A] Or if he learned sacred doctrines from David’s plectrum,

He sings a hymn of honor with his turning throat.

Or if a lyre is touched by a finger, or a flute, pipe, or reed,

Each delights the birds with song, each according to his own Muse.

So I, exhausted by the powerful heat of cares [Note: Fortunatus, who says that he had been worn out on Lupus’s behalf by the heavy burden of cares and had laid them down at the joyful news of his recovery, seems to indicate the grave dangers into which Lupus had been summoned by hostile persons. Through Brunhild’s intervention and prayers he had been rescued from them and had taken refuge with King Guntram, as we said above; there he could easily preserve his position and honor, safe from the plots of his enemies. If this is so, the letter was written around the year 581. Certainly it does not seem to have been written while Sigibert was still alive, [Col. 0244C] under whom Lupus appears always to have flourished in wealth and favor, so that there would have been no reason for Fortunatus to show himself anxious on his behalf.],

On learning that you were safe, am restored as though by a spring.

O Lupus, a name sweet to me, ever to be repeated,

And one that the page of my heart bears written.

Once enclosed within the tablets of sweetness,

An unfading chest of the heart holds the man.

Possessing treasures of devotion, a precious will,

Bringing forth pure talents from its own spirit [Note: The Paris edition, “more.”].

The golden mind surpasses the riches possessed by the world,

And reflects the splendor of gems with its shining heart.

A fragrant understanding spreads sweet odors,

Granting the soul what incense customarily grants.

A word flavored with honey flows back from your heart,

And, seasoned with salt, you return wisdom from your mouth.

After the darkness of night, setting beneath it the lights of the stars,

You shine for me in mind as Lucifer shines with his rays.

As the light of the sun, coming from the east, renews the world,

So your words illuminate my mind.

When foreign Germany held my gaze,

You were a father and were about to be a guardian of my homeland.

When I deserved, exultant, to direct peaceful faces toward you,

At once a doubled day shone upon my world.

As often as I wove conversations together in your speech,

I believed myself to be reclining among Ambrosian roses.

Although you remained one for everyone, your grace bound me more closely,

In affection, as I hastened toward you.

[Col. 0244C] Now also, for such great honors, who could return anything worthy?

I am overcome by the subject, for my tongue is too small.

And so, as the lofty summit rises higher through ascent [Note: Venetian edition, “so, through an inaccessible summit.”],

My love presses from below, while your honor stands in the way.

But let the others, on my behalf, strive to return your praises,

And let each one, according to his ability, sound you forth in prayer and voice.

Let the Roman applaud you with the lyre, the barbarian with the harp [Note: Fortunatus elsewhere mentions the harp, a musical instrument especially customarily used by barbarians in Germany at banquets, namely in book I, chapter 1: “Often the harp alone, booming, struck back the barbarians’ songs.” Browerus, in his notes on this passage, thinks that the etymology of *harpa* derives from the Greek words *chordas harpazein*, “to pluck strings.” But why should someone not derive its origin from the Greek word *harpē*, which means a sickle or curved sword? The harp bears a certain resemblance to it, narrowing and tapering toward its end?],

Let the Greek sing on the Achillean lyre, and let the Briton sing on the *chrotta* [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “the British rotta canal.” The Calar manuscript, according to Browerus, reads: “Let the Greek and all Britain be pleased with the Iliad.” The Venetian edition and the remaining Vatican manuscripts agree with Browerus’s reading. The *Achillean* instrument, if we follow Browerus, is Achilles’ lyre, celebrated by the ancients and used among the Greeks—specifically the one with which Homer, in book X of the *Iliad*, represents Achilles consoling his grief, which he had conceived against Agamemnon because of the latter’s injury. Fortunatus appropriately summons it here to celebrate Lupus, since Achilles also employed it to sing the deeds of the bravest men, as Homer expresses in these lines:

“I found him delighting his spirit with the clear-sounding *phorminx*,

Which he had taken from the spoils when he destroyed the city of Eetion.

With it he delighted his heart, and he sang the glorious deeds of men.”

The *chrotta*, however, is a kind of flute, called *crowde* by the Welsh and English. Dufresne, in his *Glossary*, prefers to derive the name from a tortoise-shell, which he says is called *crotte* in Frankish and German. What he adds afterward about the Greek word *kryptē* or *krypta*, from which he claims that the name *crotte* arose according to another’s opinion, does not satisfy me, since those explanations are too twisted and forced to illuminate the word *crotte*. I would rather derive the word from *kroteō*, if indeed it means a tortoise-shell, since we read that *krotein kitharan*, “to strike the lyre,” is used by good writers.],



[Col. 0245A] Let some report you as brave, others rightly as powerful,

One praise you as swift with weapons, another in books.

And because you properly govern what peace is, wars demand,

Let one sing the glory of the judge, another that of the commander.

Let us offer you verses; let the *leudi*—barbarian songs—be given [Note: For *leudi*, the Vulgate and Paris edition give *ludi*, according to Browerus. The Venetian edition has *laedos*, corruptly, in one Vatican manuscript. Browerus splendidly restored *leudos*, or *liedos*.],

So that, with changing figures, one praise may resound for the man.

Let these commemorate you as famous, those as wise in law,

But I shall always hold you as gracious, Lupus.

## CHAPTER IX. To the duke Lupus.

[Note: He gives thanks to Lupus for letters and gifts sent to him. He recalls his departure from Italy and complains that meanwhile no letters from his relatives had reached him; he says that Lupus had taken their place in his affection.]

[Col. 0245B] Intent upon pious services, mindful of your loving friend [Note: The Venetian edition, “may you remember the lover.”],

You promptly provide for your client through your affection,

Having pitied the absent friend, who was too dear,

When love, though its place is hidden, seeks signs.

From what merit of mine is this granted to me, that at once

Fortunatus should be the object of Lupus’s kindly concern? [Note: The Paris edition, “from which this is given to my merits.”]

Exiled from Italy, I think I have been wandering for nine years [Note: Since Fortunatus came into Gaul around the year 565, as is shown in his Life, it is clear that this poem was written around the year 574 and therefore seems to have been composed before the preceding poem.],

Where the sea of the Ocean joins the shores together [Note: Venetian and Paris editions, “where the salt sea continues.”].

So many seasons flee, and still, through the writings of my relatives,

No one from the closed-off heights has refreshed me [Note: From this one may infer that Fortunatus was not lacking relatives’ remembrance and affection; rather, they were probably cut off by the disturbances of war then being waged in Italy by the Lombards, so that they sent no letters to Fortunatus, or letters sent were lost or intercepted.].

[Col. 0246A] What father, mother, brother, sister, or whole company of nephews [Note: This was Titiana, about whom see below, chapter 6 of book XI. The expression “order of nephews” has led some to conjecture that Fortunatus came from a very noble family, and that he obscurely indicates this himself by mentioning the succession of nephews. Although he seems to me not to have been wholly obscure or of common origin—and I infer this from the fact that he went to Ravenna for the sake of study, lived there for some time, formed a very close friendship with Felix, later bishop of Treviso, and then undertook the journey to Gaul to venerate the tomb of Saint Martin, things that are hardly common among ordinary people—I nevertheless think that he uses “order of nephews” here not to indicate any family privilege, but to signify their number and their degree of age.],

Whatever father, mother, brother, sister, and the whole company of nephews and homeland could do, you have supplied through devoted love.

The gracious page sent under your kindly name,

Refreshed me with waters of a nectarous spring [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts, “renewed me with waters.”].

Nor did the sweet letter from you alone nourish me;

A messenger sent from there also came to serve my needs.

Who, I ask, could recount so many gifts with a grateful voice?

The tongue cannot disclose the sweetness of your affection.

But may the heavenly King from above restore to you all things,

Even the smallest things that he teaches to be his own [Note: The Venetian edition reads:

“Who teaches that the smallest things are his own”; one Vatican manuscript has, corruptly, “whom the smallest things make.” The Paris edition has, “who makes the smallest thing.”].

## CHAPTER X. To Magnulfus [Note: Browerus doubts whether this Magnulfus is the same man who was bishop of Toulouse and who sent someone to represent and subscribe for him at the Second Council of Mâcon, held in 585—namely, the man who, the previous year, had been beaten by Mummolus and Desiderius, suffered a grave injury, and was driven into exile, as Gregory of Tours relates in book VII of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 27. But it is difficult to settle the matter by conjecture. Certainly Magnullus, bishop of Toulouse, is not recorded as having ever governed a province or as having been Lupus’s brother; nor, again, is Magnulfus, Lupus’s brother, found to have ever been made bishop of Toulouse, as far as I know, so that the two could be identified. They agree only in names and periods.] brother of Lupus.

[Note: He praises Magnulfus, Lupus’s brother, for his knowledge of law and his fairness in governing peoples. Finally, he excuses the brevity of the letter.]

How swiftly fame, stirred by swift wings, flies,

And fills all places, enlarged by its deeds!

For while the Rhine is near you and the Loire is near me,

Here, handsome Magnulfus, you appear great in honor.

Thus the trumpet sent by the herald Sigimundus [Note: This Sigismundus seems to be no other than the man to whom poems 20 and 21 of this book survive, whom this verse indicates, like Magnulfus, to have lived by the Rhine, in poem 21:

“After the Italian lands, O Rhine, you send me my relatives,

Namely Sigismundus and his brother Aregisilus.”]

Has run abroad, so that your virtues might be known throughout the region.

Yet because the letter marks them only in brief words,

Not because it sings everything, nor because it wishes to conceal anything [Note: Venetian edition, “nor because it can retain anything.”].

You are especially powerful in the torrent of legal discourse,

And so you govern that you renew ancient deeds anew [Note: The Venetian and Paris editions, “ancient deeds.”].

[Col. 0247A] Under your administration, the plow of the equitable cultivator

Makes your people reap their hopes from the seed of justice.

No one lacks what belongs to him; no one reclines upon another’s possessions.

You act so that the people have no opportunity to be guilty.

Your concern brings gifts of salvation to the rest,

And the labor of one becomes the peaceful rest of the people.

Equal and harmonious, so that all may call you gracious,

A judge here through laws, a father there through kindness.

Pardon my few words, since the messenger presses me,

For the matter of Lupus’s brother urges me to speak at length [Note: One Vatican manuscript, “the great matter moves me.”].

Thus may the Lord grant that you repay Him with your merits,

Him whom, together with you, I cherish with the love of my heart.

## CHAPTER XI. To Jovinus, governor of the province.

[Note: See what we said about Jovinus in the notes to chapter 12 of book VII.]

[Note: He rebukes Jovinus, the governor of the province, for prolonged silence and for delay in writing back. He asks that, since he is less able to enjoy his presence and sight, Jovinus should at least relieve and console this longing by sending letters.]

Whenever I have sent writings in prose,

And drink no cups from your spring,

Though previously you had refreshed me with a richer, flowing stream [Note: Venetian edition, “you, who had earlier refreshed me with a watery stream.”],

Nor is a draught now returned from Castalian waters.

If a lesser concern for your love had held me,

It would already have been a gain to clasp your neck with my hand [Note: The Venetian edition, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Paris edition, “it would already have been permitted.”].

Now I receive less from you precisely because I love you more [Note: One Vatican manuscript, “because I love more.”],

And although I desire more, I bear rejected hopes [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts, “I shall bear rejected hopes.”].

You who poured my heart into your faithful heart [Note: The Venetian edition, “who poured himself into his own heart”; one Vatican manuscript, “who poured himself into his own heart,” followed by the same words],

Why, I ask, do our eyes not possess a light equal to their light?

Or, my friend, since through writings I bear you greetings, dear one,

Let a page return me some aid by which I may be relieved.

## CHAPTER XII. To the same man.

[Note: Part of this poem is cited by George Fabricius in his collection of ancient Christian Latin poets under the title “On the uncertainty of life and the glory of man.”]

[Note: He describes the brevity and emptiness of human life, affirming that only piety survives all mortal things and is worth far more than they. Then he reproaches and gently rebukes Jovinus because, in so brief a life, he sends him no letters, although he indicates that he eagerly awaits them.]

Time passed flies away; we are deceived by fugitive hours,

And slippery life leads men into old age.

The rolling axis draws them swiftly to its end without a cord [Note: The Paris edition, “without an end.”],

Nor does it hold back its rapid wheels with reins.

Moving all moments and the weights of things with itself,

Until the goal compels the eager horses to halt.

Thus, too, all of us, though unlike, move toward the end;

No one withdraws his step from the place where his boundary will be.

It carries away the imperial head, the kingdom, and the senate alike [Note: One Vatican manuscript, “it carries away equally the senate,” and so forth],

And, when the hour comes, it snatches them away without waiting for daylight.

What are weapons to men? Hector falls, and avenging Achilles;

Ajax dies with his shield, the wall of the Achaeans [Note: The manuscript reads, “with the shield of Ajax.” The Venetian edition has “the bronze wall dies”; the Paris edition, “the Agivus wall.”].

What is enough for the greedy man, who stores it in his avaricious bosom [Note: The Venetian edition, “which the greedy man stores”?]

Attalus, swollen with delights, is gone [Note: The Venetian edition, “flowing back with delights”; the Paris edition, “with customary delights.”].

Who, however cunning, does not lie down at the final end,

When the art once powerful against Palamedes perishes in Ulysses? [Note: Fortunatus here indicates that no art can drive away the final destinies of human beings, and that even Ulysses’ cunning—otherwise powerful against Palamedes and victorious for a long time—was of no use in averting death from himself; he too must have departed this life. When Palamedes urged Ulysses to cross into Asia with the other leaders of Greece to wage the Trojan war, Ulysses pretended to be insane. To prove it, he began sowing salt after yoking animals of different kinds together and undertaking other actions that no sane and rational person would perform. In the end, however, Palamedes was more fortunate. For he placed Telemachus, Ulysses’ son, directly in front of the plow, whereupon Ulysses immediately stopped the plow so as not to harm his son. From this it became clear that he was not genuinely insane but was deliberately pretending.],

Graceful beauty flows away; the fairest Astur has fallen among the stars [Note: One Vatican manuscript, “the fairest Astus.”],

Hippolytus lies dead, and Adonis does not survive.

The swift do not escape the place where the appointed end commands them to go [Note: One Vatican manuscript, “where the end appears.”],

For Quirinus departs swiftly by fate, together with his brother.

What does song accomplish, I ask? Orpheus, who charmed with his sharp melodies,

Lies dead, and the voice animated by the lyre is silent [Note: The Vatican manuscript, “is charming with sharp melodies.”].

What does a learned tongue profit departing sophists,

Who wished to speak about the curved and rounded heavens? [Note: The same edition and the Paris edition, “what they wished to say.”]

Archytas, Pythagoras, Aratus, Cato, Plato, Chrysippus,

The foolish crowd of Cleantheses lies as worthless ash [Note: Cleanthes was the most distinguished pupil of Zeno of Citium and later became an author and teacher of the school.].

Or what can the poet accomplish—Maro, Lysias [Note: *Lysa* seems to stand for *Lysis*, who was a disciple of Pythagoras, mentioned by Cicero in book I of *On Duties* and book III of *On the Orator*. Lysias was also an eloquent and extremely acute orator at Athens, whom Cicero mentions in the *Brutus*.], Menander, Homer—

Whose limbs the tombs cover, stripped bare by decay? [Note: The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript, “whose stripped limbs”; Caspar Barth thinks one should read “whose naked limbs the tomb covers,” since otherwise, he says, there would be no sense.]

When the end comes, neither songs help the Muses,

Nor does it help that one has held melody in eloquence.

[Col. 0249A] Thus, while the moments fall, the present things flee away,

And a die snatched away carries off the tablet of life.

Yet there is one salvation, pious, greatest, sweet, and broad:

To be able forever to please the triune God.

This has power, flourishes, and remains, and will not perish with the end;

From it, too, after the tomb, blessed honor is born.

What remains, in the form of merits, with blessed flowering,

The sweet fragrance of the righteous exhales from the tomb [Note: The manuscript has *fragat*, “may it break”; the intended reading is evidently *fragrant*, “it exhales.”].

A flowing breeze is more pleasing than one that breathes Arabian perfume [Note: The Venetian edition, “a more pleasing flowing breeze.” The Paris edition, “than Sabaean aroma.”],

Surpassing the incense with which the rich balsam-bearing forest breathes [Note: The Paris edition, “and surpassing incense and the balsams.”].

Cinnamon, marigold, saffron, violets, roses, and lilies yield,

So that no similar fragrance is inhaled [Note: The Venetian edition, “so that no similar fragrance is inhaled,” feminine in agreement with *odor* as corruptly printed.].

What then? Virtue is generated more greatly in those who die,

And, while they occupy the tombs, they cherish their languishing limbs [Note: The Paris edition, “their limbs lie.”].

Pious funerals strengthen the uncertain life of many,

And the human being returns from the tomb, made alive again.

A noble urn covers the precious talents of the Thunderer,

And what reclines upon earth flies above the stars.

He who lives beneath the love of God, under sacred discipline,

Becomes a pilgrim on earth and, while journeying, a citizen of heaven.

Finally, after those whose foundations shine,

And after the thresholds of Peter and Paul, first in faith [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, “the lights, first in faith.”],

What number of saints, scattered throughout the world, shines forth?

How great is the grace of the columns poured out and flourishing?

Throughout places and peoples, their stars rule the world,

Whatever the circle of the Ocean encompasses with its waters.

North, south, east, and west honor

The thresholds [variant: lights], made bright by their gifts [Note: The Venetian edition, “the setting sun honors”; the variant *lumina* means “lights,” whereas *limina* means “thresholds.”].

As for the rest, there is nothing that is seen in the world:

We are entirely swelling, smoke, and shadow.

[Col. 0249C] Why, then, is the life granted to us dragged along by fear at a whisper,

And why, Jovinus, do you not send a few words to Fortunatus?

You see the passing seasons, yet you do not break your long silence,

Nor do you speak to restore me, though your silence is my loss.

I did not expect this, exultant, after Germany

Had brought our faces together, so that love would rebound.

Rather, I had believed that, as long as life extended itself,

The work of your affection would be doubled.

Alas, as I see, my hopes run in the opposite direction:

Time is lengthened, but love is shortened.

Or do I withdraw from your heart as much as I am distant from your eyes?

And are we as far apart in spirit as we are both distant in place?

I do not report it thus, for I am bound to you in my heart;

Your mind, where sweetness sounds, declares otherwise [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, “where sweetness nourishes”; the Venetian edition, “where sweet affection dwells.”].

For one whose dear fidelity has joined his heart to a friend [Note: The Venetian edition, “whose dear fidelity joined the heart of a friend”; one Vatican manuscript, “joined it as a friend”; the Paris edition, “for when dear fidelity … satisfied.”],

What is less in the eyes burns more greatly with love.

And although wall, place, and court keep you absent,

He is there in his own heart, wherever the pleasing image is.

[Col. 0250A] Through affection he sees the one whom he does not see with his actual face,

And a distant voice sounds from another region.

He seems to speak silently about what you are doing or where you are;

Love, shut within itself, speaks within the heart.

If a light breeze flies past, he thinks that greetings come from it;

The sound carried to his ear reports what the man holds in his mind [Note: The Paris edition, “the crash of the breeze carries this to the ear.”].

Therefore I, your client, dear and honored friend, seek you,

Whom places make absent, not the spirit.

You, who are always remembered by us [Note: The Paris edition, “to be remembered,”],

Are held upon my lips,

And while I write these things, I do not speak without you [Note: The Venetian edition, “and while we write these things.”].

With affection, zeal, and desire, I embrace your arms,

And in an embrace I bind your breast and neck.

You enter with me and move together with me as a lover,

And, as though speaking sweetly, I sip kisses from your lips.

I have you before my eyes, but the dear image flees;

Even the one whom I have here I cannot hold [Note: The Venetian edition, “even when I have you here”; the Paris edition, “whom I see.”].

Now you depart, now you return by alternating turns;

You scarcely flee from my eyes, and behold, your form returns.

And when you turn your back, your innocent face appears to me;

If you turn your foot, you are present again with your face.

Often I even seem to offer you pious words in speech;

Perhaps you are silent there, while here you return words to me.

This is the lesser part of you, because you cannot be grasped when absent;

For you are wholly there, as it were, and here you are mine.

How both of us breathed together for a few hours

Has not escaped my eyes while this day remains.

How often, O, we sent epigrams on anxious pages,

And your silent page remains quiet, so that I may not be refreshed [Note: One Vatican manuscript, “so that your page may not refresh me.”]?

Who, I ask, will restore those hours that we lose in silence?

The gentle and fleeting light does not recall past times.

[Col. 0250C] Tell me, my familiar friend: what are you doing? What reply do you make, my friend?

If you cultivate your fields, why do you deny my prayers?

Write when your mind is free; send lofty poems in verse,

And, as though cultivating a field of earth, cultivate me with your voice and melody.

Lead your plow, I beg, through my breast, with your mouth [Note: The Venetian edition, “I beg, lead that plow.”];

May our sowing be the furrow of your tongue [Note: The same edition and one Vatican manuscript, “may our fate be your own.”].

From it may the harvest of the heart be animated with pregnant ears of grain,

And may a fertile fallow field sprout in our wheat.

For if you speak to me, good man, rich in piety,

You surpass sweet honeycombs with your lips.

And you please me more than the liquid that the olive tree yields in its juice,

And refresh me more sweetly than what perfume exhales.

With Aspasius, together with your dear father, brother, and Leo,

While the long day stands, farewell, sweet friend.

## CHAPTER XIII. To Felix, his father-in-law [Note: Although the Venetian edition and the manuscripts all give this title as “To Felix, his father-in-law,” and one Vatican manuscript has “Jovinus’s father-in-law,” I nevertheless think the title has been corrupted and should be read “to Felix, his companion,” or “his own.” For this seems to be that Felix who was Fortunatus’s companion and associate in studies at Ravenna, and who was later made bishop of Treviso, as we said in the Life of Fortunatus, numbers 23 and 24. This verse also suits him well:

“Since the court of our homeland was one for companions,”

which could hardly apply in any way to Felix, Jovinus’s father-in-law. But Treviso was indeed a common homeland for Felix and Fortunatus, as we showed in the same Life of Fortunatus, number 10.].

[Col. 0250D] [Note: He says that he approaches Felix, outstanding in the praise of poetry, timidly and reluctantly. Nevertheless, relying on the bond of their former companionship [Col. 0251A] and on the connection of their common homeland, he addresses him in the following poem.]

The lofty heights of Pierian pride belong to one whose summit is firm;

I can scarcely touch its threshold with my humble hand.

But since the court of our homeland was one for companions,

Trusting in affection, I knock, kindly, at the door.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Mummulenus [Note: He appears to be the Mummulenus whom Gregory of Tours calls Suessionian, in book X of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 2. His son Bobo escorted Rigunth, daughter of Chilperic, into Spain to marry Reccared, as Gregory relates in book VI, chapter 45. Another son, Bodegisilus, when he had gone to the emperor Maurice as King Childebert’s ambassador, was unjustly killed at Carthage during a popular uprising.]

[Note: He relates that Mummulenus received him as a guest during his journey and treated him generously. He elegantly and humorously describes the indigestion he contracted from the abundance of food, especially from eating peaches. He praises Mummulenus himself highly.]

While, weary, I walked on my journey near the shadow of night,

At sunset, with the day already fleeing,

[Col. 0251B] When I saw pastures over the green grassy banks of the waters [Note: The Paris edition, “over the verdant banks”],

I myself was fed when I saw the pasture.

Captivated by the sight, drawn on by desire, I was pulled there;

Turning from the road, I sought better things.

For Mummulenus, who properly causes the king’s lofty palaces

To grow through his profound counsels,

Who deservedly stands more illustrious among his fellow citizens,

And whom a single palm raises above the nobles,

Powerful in nobility [Note: From this we can understand that Mummulenus’s lineage was very noble and distinguished in Gaul, since Gregory of Tours, speaking of Bobo, Mummulenus’s son, who had been appointed as Rigunth’s escort, says: “There were with her distinguished men, Bobo the duke, son of Mummulenus, with his wife, as a bridesman,” and so forth.],

Good in spirit, serene in face,

Skilled in talent and shrewd in integrity,

Whose lineage flashes with radiant light from his ancestors,

Yet whose own character surpassed his fathers in honor.

Thus, when I arrived there and was filled with splendid banquets,

Having seen him, I found that this itself was food for me.

[Col. 0251C] Great dishes indeed, heaped with generous delicacies,

As though a swelling hill, the loaded platter stood.

It had, as it were, a valley through the middle, the work of a mountain on every side,

Through which the fish made its way by the better route.

The fish occupied oil instead of waters, and the platter instead of turf;

The table was its whirlpool.

Yet before anything else, tender fruits were given to me,

Peaches, as they are called by the common name.

He grew weary from giving them, but I did not grow weary from eating;

On the one hand urging me with words, on the other providing dishes.

Soon, as though giving birth, I suddenly stretched out my belly,

Wondering that my abdomen had swelled so greatly.

For thunder was roaring within, with varied noise [Note: The Paris edition of the Library of the Fathers, 1644, reads this verse:

“For within it roared in various ways, like the winds.”],

And Eurus and Auster were disturbing my entrails.

The sandy shore is not so troubled by Aeolian storms,

Nor does a ship driven across the sea tremble so much.

Nor are bellows so inflated by the whirlwind of winds,

Those which the heated smith keeps for his apprentices.

[Col. 0252B] One rumble belched against another [Note: The same edition, “one mass exchanged murmurs with another.”],

And without me there was a proud battle within me [Note: “And without you.”].

May you enjoy long health, ruler, with your noble wife,

And may you be called grandfather through the offspring of your children.

Powerful in the honor of praise, may you see happy times,

And may you be strong enough to celebrate sweet amusements.

## CHAPTER XV. On Berulfus [Note: Berulfus was duke of the Touraine and Poitiers, as Gregory of Tours reports in book VIII of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 26. After Sigibert’s death, when he had secretly carried away the latter’s treasures, he was captured by King Childebert and thrown into prison together with Arnegisil, his accomplice in the same crime; unless the bishops had intervened, he would have lost his life by the sword. This occurred around the year 585.

Browerus observes in this passage, together with Sirmond in his notes on Sidonius, that in this age, when Fortunatus flourished, and in the preceding period, it was customary to rise from the rank and office of count to the higher rank of palatine duke. The distinction between the two ranks was that a count presided over only one city, whereas a duke governed several cities or an entire province, in which there were several cities, each with its own county. See Sirmond in his notes on letter 17 of book VII of Sidonius Apollinaris, where he illustrates the matter with several examples.]

count [Note: From this it may be understood that Fortunatus wrote this poem while Berulfus was still a count and had not yet obtained the dukedom of Poitiers and Tours. Yet Gregory of Tours already calls him duke in his *History of the Franks* under the year 580, when Gregory experienced Berulfus as hostile to him, as he relates in book V, chapter 50. Indeed, it is probable that Berulfus had obtained that dukedom under Sigibert, with whom he possessed authority and favor. Sigibert was killed in the year 575, and therefore this poem should be believed to have been composed before that year.].

[Note: Since Fortunatus expected Berulfus to invite him to lunch, he says that in the meantime he suffered from a double hunger. Finally, he offers him auspicious and joyful omens.]

Berulfus, as I gladly watched your delicacies [Note: The Venetian edition, “I gladly await”],

I confess that I endured a double hunger.

Thus I believed that I would be satisfied at the fourth hour [Note: The Paris edition, “that I would be satisfied at the fourth hour.”],

But your kindly table does not call me even at the eighth.

Through your banquets I learned to carry fasting;

Your lunches were more a litany [Note: One Vatican manuscript, *letania*. Browerus thinks that fasting itself is indicated here under the term *litanies*, since according to the ancient custom of the Church they always included fasting.].

[Col. 0253A] May God grant you your desires, through whom we now note joyful things [Note: One Vatican manuscript, “through whom joy is marked”];

While I write these things, I am made still more satisfied.

## CHAPTER XVI. To Condon the domesticus

[Note: The Venetian edition has *Condane*. The *domestici* were those who kept watch in the royal court and managed matters relating to the necessary expenses for the royal household and table, as may be read in Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book X, chapter 28. They were counted among the kingdom’s nobles and, together with the other dignitaries of the palace, sat beside the king in assemblies. See the distinguished Ruinart’s notes on book VI, chapter 11, and book VII, chapter 21, of the *History of the Franks*, where he reports that they were also called chamberlains. Dufresne gives further information in his *Glossary*, where he discusses at greater length the office and ranks of the *domestici*.]

[Note: Fortunatus praises Condon for the honors he had earned through his virtue and for his exceptional loyalty in administering the royal household, honors that he had successively attained under different kings of Austrasia.]

For many years, rich in the royal court,  
Your glory, Condon, shone through your merits.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “royal,” which follows; the Venetian edition reads “glory, Conda, through your merits.”]

For as soon as he saw you as a young man, vigilant in spirit,  
He chose to keep you with him always, even when old.

What was that spirit of yours? What self-command,  
Since you were the one beloved by so many kings?

Your noble mind shines with precious light,  
And by its own merits has enlarged the honor of your ancestors.

Your posterity flourishes, through which its origin grows,  
And makes your ancient fathers rise again through praise.

For if the man who preserves his family’s honor is preferred,  
How much greater the praise of ennobling one’s family?

Whoever, then, desires to raise his name through his deeds  
Should swiftly make your example his model.

Beginning from a lowly station, you always rose upward,  
And, passing through every rank, you hold the highest summits.

Theodoric, exulting, adorned you with the honor of tribune.

[Note: Theodoric is also written *Theuderic* in the Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts. He was the brother of Chlothar and the son of Clovis. A tribune was a collector of taxes. That tribunes also had charge of prisons and fortresses appears from Fortunatus’s *Life of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris*, chapters 62 and 68, and from his *Life of Saint Radegund*, chapter 38, where tribunes of the treasury are also named.]

From that point your ascent had already begun.

For Theudebert [Note: Theudebert was the son of Theodoric and succeeded him in the kingdom.] bestowed on you the rewards of the *comitiva* [Note: *Comitiva* was the name for the dignity of a count; it seems to have been a rank and position above the honor of tribune. See what we have noted concerning counts in the preceding poem.],  
And increased the honors appropriate to your service.

When he saw that distinguished spirits deserved greater things,  
He immediately wished to enlarge your well-earned rank [Note: The Venetian edition reads “he immediately wished to enlarge ranks through merits.”].

Desiring that you should thereafter be a *domesticus*, he appointed you;  
You suddenly grew, and the court grew with you.

The venerable palaces flourished together with you;  
The household applauded its vigilant administrator.

You lived even through the childhood of Theudebald [Note: The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts have *Theudebaldus*. Theude­bald was the son of Theudebert; when his father died, he succeeded him in the kingdom while still of immature age, in 548. After Theudebald’s death in 555, Chlothar added the kingdom left by him to his own, as Gregory of Tours relates in book IV, chapter 9, of the *History of the Franks. Under Chlothar, Condon— as Fortunatus reports here—retained his honor and position, just as he did under Sigibert, the son of Chlothar, to whom Theodoric’s kingdom fell, as we related in the *Life of Fortunatus*.],  
And your greatest care was devoted to his support.

By your outstanding actions you so upheld the public order [Note: The Venetian edition reads “you upheld the public order”; one Vatican manuscript, “he upheld the public care”; two read “you upheld,” a reading approved by the editor]  
That you made the young king an old man in wisdom.

You yourself governed, as though you were his guardian,  
And the task entrusted to you advanced under your direction.

Then came again the great rule of Chlothar in the court,  
Who ordered the household to be governed with the same devotion.

The kings changed, but you did not change your honors;  
And your successor was worthy of you.

Such was the people’s love, such your skill in governing,  
That no one would willingly have taken this burden away.

Even now, through the favor of tranquil King Sigibert [Note: The Paris edition has “of great Sigibert.”],  
Free gifts have been granted to your services.

He ordered you to sit among the distinguished powerful,  
Making you a fellow banqueter [Note: From this it is easy to understand that the king’s table-companions were ranked among those who were called *domestici*. In the twelfth Council of Toledo, canon 3, “the king’s companions” are those whom royal power makes participants in its table.] as your rank advanced.

The stronger king rightly prepared better things than the rest,  
And what he possesses that is greater, this he shows to be owing to you.

Such was your rank: always to deserve greater things;  
And the older you grew, the more your honor grew with you.

What your valor was, sorrowing Saxony proclaims [Note: That Sigibert took up arms against the Saxons is established by poem 3 of book VI.];  
It is praise that you did not fear arms in your old age.

For your country’s hopes and for great love of the king,  
For whom the beloved bodies of his two sons lie dead [Note: The Venetian edition reads: “because concern for the death of his sons lies …”].

Do not grieve too deeply that both fell manfully,  
For to die for glory is always to live.

He spreads gladness from his cheerful face,  
And carries faithful joys in a spirit without cloud [Note: The Paris edition reads “you carry.”].

Generous to all, you give abundantly with kindness,  
And through your gifts you make men devoted to you.

May a long life be more fortunate for you through peaceful years [Note: The Venetian edition, one Vatican manuscript, and the Paris edition have “more happily through the years.”],  
And may your flourishing offspring restore their father [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “rich offspring.”].

## CHAPTER XVII. To Gundoarius [M., Guntharius]

[Note: The Venetian edition has “to Guanduarius.”]

[Note: Fortunatus excuses the brevity of his letter and declares that scarcely any page is equal to his goodwill toward Gundoarius. He then praises Gundoarius for the sweetness of his character and speech and his other virtues, especially commending his loyalty and diligence in administering the royal patrimony.]

If the feelings of a loving heart could be revealed in words,  
Our page would give you more poems.

But since I cannot speak from my mouth what I carry in my heart,  
Let it be enough that a little of much is now given.

For if you consider the wish of the singer through his words,  
I would have preferred to bring you something greater, since I bring you little.

We behold a whole mind poured out in sweetness,  
In which serene hearts shine without a cloud of deceit [Note: The Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript read: “and serene hearts shine,” which is preferable].

Watering with a pure spring, nectar overflows from his throat;  
I willingly drink his words into my breast and heart.

Prudent, energetic, watchful, temperate, honorable—  
Your mind always possesses the seasoning of the soul.

You govern the lofty estates of the excellent queen,  
And everywhere she has entrusted them to you, she has found loyalty.

No one could be dearer to the pious queen [Note: It may be asked whether this was Queen Theodechild, whose piety Fortunatus praises splendidly in book VI, chapter 5, and whose affairs Gundoarius may perhaps have administered]  
Than one who himself was such in accordance with his merits.

Gundarius, may you flourish, destined to please through a long age,  
Remaining with your own wife as an enduring light.

## CHAPTER XVIII. To Flavus

[Note: He recalls his attentiveness toward Flavus and his diligence in sending him letters. He then reproaches him in a friendly way because he sends nothing back, and asks him to write in whatever manner he pleases.]

My letter so often goes to dear Flavus,  
Thus dutiful care urges it to speak through its services.

Now too, sending poems in prose-like verse,  
I flatter him and discharge the obligations of love through affection [Note: The Venetian edition has “I flatter him through effect”; perhaps “through affection.” One Vatican manuscript has “I flatter him through address.”].

No traveler who wishes to set out goes without bringing you a few words;  
No one may pass me by in silence.

As a child of friendship, the page often asks for you [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts have “nurtured by friendship.”],  
And if a carrier is lacking [Note: The Venetian edition places punctuation before “carrier.”], the breeze is welcome [Note: One Vatican manuscript has “the better breeze is pleasing.”].

In anxious spirit I reach out through wandering clouds [Note: The Venetian edition has “I weigh the clouds,”],  
Yet receive no messages brought back by any hand.

Is paper too seldom conveyed to you by foreign trade?  
Does love not compel what time itself does not allow?

So that you may write, cut a strip from a beech tree [Note: The meaning of this obscure passage seems to be: Are you failing to write because you lack paper? Paper used to be rolled, and hence it seems also to have been called a roll, being folded into the shape of a circle or wheel. But if this is the situation, he says, cut a piece of beech bark, encircling the tree like a band, and write on the bark as on paper. The Paris edition has “a strip of cloth.”],

And it will be sweet for me to read your words written on bark.

Does your Roman tongue disdain a whispered message?  
I ask you: return words even in Hebrew letters.

Write everything out in learned Achaemenian signs [Note: Browerus has *Achaemeniis*, as do the older books and the Trier manuscript. The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts support this reading. Browerus says that Achaemenian signs are Persian or Parthian. One Cologne manuscript reports “Ammonian,” so that, in Browerus’s opinion, the phrase would mean obscure and convoluted. The Saint Gall manuscript glosses it: “Achaemenian, that is, Chaldean.” Browerus adds that if Achaemenian signs are taken as Persian signs, no doubt remains, since Sidonius, in the panegyric he recited before Anthemius, says:

“Meanwhile you, Susa, tremble, and with suppliant worship  
The Achaemenian Persian bends the crescent-shaped tiara.”

Since we have so clear a testimony from Sidonius, what need is there to pursue conjectures? Certainly Herodotus, in book III, calls Cyrus’s ancestor Achaemenes and the Persians Achaemenids; hence Achaemenian letters may reasonably be understood as Persian letters.],  
Or, better still, compose something melodious in learned Argolic speech.

Let a barbarian rune be written on ashwood tablets [Note: The Danes called their letters *runes*. They used some of them to record events in writing and others in magical tricks. They customarily inscribed them on elongated staffs. Brynolphus, in his notes on the Saxon manuscripts, says: “The ancients entrusted their runes—that is, their letters—to wooden tablets,” and so forth. Browerus gives more on this word, which may be consulted if desired. The distinguished Scipio Maffei, however, in a work entitled *Verona Illustrated*, argues, following Salmasius, *On Hellenism*, and Johann Peter Ludewig, in his introduction to Greek coins, that runic letters were the same as Greek and Latin letters. Here Fortunatus clearly distinguishes them from those letters, since he calls them barbarian runes, especially as he wishes them to have been used first by the barbarians. One Vatican manuscript has *rhuna*, with aspiration. The same is found in a manuscript of Saint-Germain of Paris. Browerus observes that this word is also read with aspiration in other old books. In the Cologne manuscript, as in the Venetian edition, *rana* is mistakenly read for *runa*.],

And let a flat little rod serve for what papyrus does.

Let the written page return, a tablet hewn for writing [Note: By the name “hewn paper,” nothing other than a tablet shaped by cutting for the use of writing seems to be meant];  
What can be read again will be the fruit of a lover.

## CHAPTER XIX. To Flavus and Evodius

[Note: He commends the brothers Flavus and Evodius for their affection and harmony, which correspond to their bodily likeness. He declares that he has joined himself to them as a third person and asks that conversations by letter be added to bind their love more closely.]

How well they agree whom one father raised,  
If one heart holds them both together!

Flavus and Evodius, born from the same womb [Note: The Venetian edition reads “born from the same entrails”],  
Wholly envelop our hearts with a single love.

Each appears to me in the sight of the other,  
And one brother’s image gives me the appearance of the other.

From the face of one, the face of the second is known to me;  
Thus a reflected form returns an image like itself in a mirror.

Therefore, giving equal wishes of health to equals in equal affection,  
I shall be the third between you both.

Desiring that one love should hold us three together,  
Whom the same love embraces in dear affection, let the page bind us also.

## CHAPTER XX. Fortunatus to the most beloved and in every grace praiseworthy Sigismund

[Note: He declares his concern and diligence toward Sigismund and asks him to inform him about affairs in Italy and Germany, whatever they may then be.]

Fixed in your love, standing with eager wishes,  
I often ask travelers, dear friend, how you are.

Whenever a traveler arrives, hastening from the northern region [Note: Sigismund, to whom he is writing, seems to have lived in Germany, as appears more clearly from the following poem],  
Although I delay him by questioning him too eagerly [Note: The Venetian edition has: “Although perhaps I delay by troubling him too much.”],

Whether private or public concern has summoned the man,  
He shall not depart until I have questioned him.

How vigorous are your limbs? What places, dear friend, contain you? [Note: The Paris edition has “which rightly confine you.”]  
Love asks everything in orderly arrangement.

If some grim armed invader is wearing down Italian sands,  
Or whatever the Frank possesses, pray let your letter reveal it [Note: The Paris edition reads “or what the Franks possess.”].

Tell me, I beg, what you are doing; nevertheless, as far as I can, I desire it to be prolonged:  
Live, half of my soul.

## CHAPTER XXI. To Sigismund and Aregisil [M., Alagisus]

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have *Alagislum*, and likewise below.]

[Note: On receiving a letter from the brothers Sigismund and Aregisil, he declares how happy he was and foretells every good and tranquil thing for himself from their arrival in Gaul.]

A sweet letter reveals to me the names of my friends:  
From one side, shining Sigismund; from the other, graceful Aregisil.

Happy prosperity has poured forth the winds’ breezes,  
When the air announces beloved men to me.

I call both heads to witness: my hopes are helped  
As much as a flourishing field rejoices beneath the rain.

Lest I thirst amid the swift flames of summer,  
You have refreshed me with waters from a nectarous spring.

After the Italian lands, Rhine, you send me relatives [Note: The Paris edition has “parents,”];  
With the arrival of my brothers I shall no longer be a stranger.

In a time of war, new joys of peace arise,  
Because those whom my love desires have arrived here.

You double the honor of this festive day for me [Note: The Venetian edition has: “You double me in the honor of the festive day.” The Paris edition has: “who make the festive day twice as honorable for me.”];  
May your honor likewise increase through the king’s gift [Note: From this it may be understood that Sigismund and Aregisil held some public office in the kingdom of Sigibert, which, as we have said elsewhere, extended into Germany].

## CHAPTER XXII. To Boso the referendarius

[Note: Among the Frankish kings, *referendarii* were those entrusted with custody of the royal ring; they sealed the royal documents, as is evident from Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 3. The distinguished Mabillon discusses the office and privileges of the *referendarius* more fully in *On Diplomatics*, book II, chapter 11. Whether this Boso was the same man whom Gregory of Tours often calls the duke Guntram Boso in the *History of the Franks*, when he led the forces of King Guntram, we do not wish to determine. If he was the same, he must first have been a *referendarius* and afterward have been created duke.]

[Note: He prays to the divine power for the safety and prosperity of the king and his ministers, among whom Boso was one, drawing an omen from the prosperity of the kingdom and the king that Boso himself also would long remain happy and safe. Finally, he shows that he is anxiously awaiting someone.]

May the Almighty thus govern the radiant heights of the king [Note: The Venetian edition reads “thus protect,”],  
And may heavenly arms govern his affairs.

May divine power thus preserve the lord and his servants,  
And may the safety of the fatherland endure while he rules.

May the supreme and holy Author from above, for the peaceful king,  
Who once gave his hand to Peter, extend that hand himself.

May the favor of the long-lived king accompany you,  
And, while he flourishes, may your joys reach their settled goal.

I ask that whoever is commanded should come as quickly as possible,  
Lest this lingering delay burden my spirits any longer.

For one who hastens carries out what firm purpose has determined [Note: The Venetian edition reads “for if he hastens”];  
If he speeds the fulfillment of a wish, it is usually sweeter.

For this above all I ask in my pleading words:  
Mention me to my lord, remembering me.

May you remain outstanding in deeds and happy through the ages;  
And, remembering me yourself, farewell, dear friend.

## CHAPTER XXIII. To Paternus

[Note: He praises Paternus on the basis of the etymology of his name and recalls his generosity toward him.]

Your deeds shine with the omen of your name, Paternus [Note: This seems to be the same Paternus to whom poem 32 of book III was written above],  
For by your own generosity you make yourself a father.

Not forgetful of our service, you provide everything,  
And willingly offer pious gifts to those devoted to you.

Since you are now so ready to distribute good things,  
May your resources be enlarged, so that you may give even more.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Verses on *gavatae* (dishes)

[Note: *Gavatae* were plates or dishes suitable for holding food, as though “hollowed out.” Hence Isidore, book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4: “A *gavata* is a dish, as if *cavata*, with the letter *g* put for *c*.” Hence also the word *concha*: the former is hollowed, the latter concave. In Dufresne’s glossary, *paropsis gavata* means “a dish” or “bowl.” Fortunatus uses the same word in writing to Agnes, book XI, chapter 10: “The swollen silver dish bears the heaped-up gifts of flesh.” Browerus believes the name came from a shell whose shape a *gavata* or *gabata* represented; he says the Gauls call it a *cavette*. The name is also used by pagan writers, as Browerus notes.]

[Note: The Venetian edition has “on hollowed dishes.”]

Whoever reads the words encircled on beautiful metal,  
If you come pure, you will imitate this work.

For just as silver is tested in a hot furnace,  
So a person reveals himself when his heart has been purified.

## CHAPTER XXV. To a guest

[Note: He shows that a guest invited to an ordinary and homely meal was received generously out of affection.]

You who come as a faithful guest to dear friends,  
Whatever is lacking in the food, you receive in greater measure in love.

A foreign guest has not brought these things across the sea [Note: The Venetian edition has “not across the sea, guest”;];  
Freely accept what the household of your homeland has produced.

## CHAPTER XXVI. To the same person

[Note: He invites a certain poet from serious cares to the cheerfulness of a banquet, yet mixes in jokes in such a way as to preserve propriety.]

Although serious care, learned in speech, may weary you [Note: The Venetian edition has “although care always wearies you,”],  
Come here, poet, and mingle festive jokes with it.

Yet let propriety preserve its proper measure [Note: One Vatican manuscript has “let him preserve propriety”; the Venetian edition has “of propriety,”],  
For unwary speech is accustomed to provoke blows.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the brevity of life

[Note: From the brevity and frailty of life he commends virtues of the spirit and heavenly delights.]

Human life is brief; the things of the present flee.  
Cultivate instead what remains without dying.

Raise up justice, cultivate peace [Note: The Venetian edition has “hold fast to peace”], love Christ.  
Seek the delights that you may possess without end.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. To the same person

[Note: He invites someone from the noise and business of the courts to the pleasure and security of a banquet.]

Drive away the quarrels of the palace after so many affairs;  
A kindly table urges us to live joyfully.

Let lawsuits, anger, noise, the courts, quarrels, and laws fall silent [Note: The Paris edition has “let them fill the courts”];  
Here let the restfulness granted by a friendly day be pleasing.

## CHAPTER XXIX. To a guest

[Note: He asks the guest, having laid aside the pursuits of lawsuits and quarrels, to bring a free and tranquil spirit to the banquet.]

I ask you: bring peaceful spirits to the meal [Note: The Venetian edition has “I ask this of you”; two Vatican manuscripts have “whom I ask”; the Venetian edition and one Vatican manuscript have “bring back to the meal”].

Seek an enemy elsewhere, if battle pleases you.

Do not undertake quarrels amid delights;  
Let the field supply your weapons, and the table provide vegetables.

## CHAPTER XXX. To the same person

[Note: He invites someone and demands that he bring to the cups the same courage he possesses in warfare. He commends his banquet not so much for its food as for its goodwill.]

If you appear magnanimous through your stern courage [Note: The Venetian edition has: “He who comes here to learn the dishes of our table,”],  
Bring bold wars safely to the cups.

He who comes here to learn the dishes of our table [Note: The Paris edition has “to be reduced by virtue,”]—  
Let goodwill alone commend the food set before him.

## CHAPTER XXXI. To Galactorius the count

[Note: Fortunatus writes again to this same Galactorius in book X, chapter 22. In that poem he congratulates him on having been appointed judge after serving as defender and foretells for him an advancement to greater dignity. There he indicates that he was already count of Bordeaux, in these verses:

“You have finally come, friend, as you were bound to do,  
Previously a count in merit before the honor was bestowed;  
You were a Bordelais, and, while a defender, a friend.”]

[Note: Fortunatus says that he often wished to become a sailor, so that with favorable winds and waves he might reach Bordeaux as quickly as possible and visit Count Galactorius. But he says that he was deterred by fear of the dangers of navigation. What he would have done in person, however, he says he accomplishes by letter. Finally, he prays for all good and favorable things for Galactorius’s household and asks him to commend him to the bishop of Bordeaux.]

I had often wished to become a sailor at the oar,  
So that my vessel might travel the waters on wave-broken courses.

Or that swift breezes might carry me across the back of the Garonne [Note: The Paris edition has “the Garonne,”],  
As I sought Bordeaux, driven quickly along the route,

And that sails might draw me over the wandering waves, with the north wind favorable,  
While the breeze might return me to the shore’s embrace,

Where the holy bishop Gundegisilus [Note: Gundegisilus succeeded Bertchramnus in the see of Bordeaux in 585. He had previously been count of Saintes, with the surname Dodo, as Gregory of Tours reports, *History of the Franks*, book VIII, chapter 22. He later intervened to help settle the serious disturbances and disputes that arose in the monastery at Poitiers after the death of Saint Radegund.] offers sacred things,  
Where the altar of God shines from the height for the people [Note: The Venetian edition has “where the court of God shines”; two Vatican manuscripts have “which shines”],

And where you too reside, generous Count Galactorius,  
Dear friend, are the object of my earnest care [Note: The Venetian edition has “you too, who reside”].

To you, whom excellent King Guntram rightly grants honors,  
He still owes more, since he has given you great things.

Yet although I wished for this, fear opposed me, and that Hunus [Note: The Venetian edition has “that final one opposed me”; the Paris edition “that outermost one.” Most manuscripts, however, have “that Hunus,” as do the Vatican manuscripts. In the Trier and Cologne manuscripts it is *Ethimus*, as Browerus reports. Hunus seems to be a mountain or cliff situated on the Garonne River that endangered those navigating it.]  
—A white mountain roaring in the heap of the rushing water—

Civil sweetness invites, while the wave resists;  
Thus love calls on one side, fear forbids on the other.

Let the swiftly travelling letter fully discharge  
What remains; let the written word return in love what I would have done [Note: The Venetian edition has “what makes me easily return.”].

So now, dearest friend, I greet you above all,  
Hoping that, by the Lord’s will, you may live long.

And with your household, companions, bishop, wife, and children,  
Live as a count whose duty it is to govern the rights of a duke.

Commend me, noble friend, to the supreme bishop in your prayers;  
Thus may your right hand be allotted a share of merit in heaven.

If anything remains, perhaps, from the tribute that overflows [Note: The Venetian edition has “which perhaps”; one Vatican manuscript has “may overflow”],  
I ask you: I am now sending these little lines—send me some *pices* [Note: Fortunatus seems to be joking here and asking Galactorius for some gift in return for the poem he has written. Browerus is uncertain whether *pices* means pitch or resin collected from pine trees, or a kind of coin; he is more inclined to think that the latter is meant.].

# BOOK EIGHT

## CHAPTER I. On his own name, to various persons

[Note: One Vatican manuscript has “from his own name.”]

[Note: Fortunatus writes generally to poets and orators, and specifically to Christians, about his fortune and circumstances. On this occasion he also praises Radegund splendidly, saying that he remained in Gaul at her request and through her prayers. Finally, he invites each of them to send pious poems and letters to Radegund.]

You who eagerly lap up the Aonian Muses, I beg you,  
And those from whom the Castalian stream is drawn by art,

You whom the granaries of Demosthenes enrich with their fine harvest [Note: The Paris edition has “with his own grain,”],  
And whom generous Homer fills with irrigating waters,

Whether you are supplied with rich dishes [Note: One Vatican manuscript has “with which each is almost rich,”],  
Tullius gives food from his mouth, Maro cups from his spring—

You too, who gather foods that never die,  
Which Christ possesses from the seed of paradise [Note: The Venetian edition has “which Christ nourishes”; three Vatican manuscripts have “which Christ approaches”],

You who have been pierced by eloquent thunder, who are held now  
By the instructions of Paul and afterward by Peter’s key,

I, Fortunatus, greet you from here with humble prayer and voice.

Born in Italy, I am held by the fields of Gaul.

I reside at Poitiers, where the holy Hilary once,  
Born in the city, became a father known throughout the world.

With the wheel of eloquence in motion, he penetrated as far as India,  
And his powerful intellect is honored in the farthest Thule [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts have *Thyle*.].

Pouring light, in the manner of the sun, over all the lands,  
His gifts are possessed by the Sacae, the Persians, and the Briton [Note: The Venetian edition and three Vatican manuscripts have “whose gifts he favorably …” Browerus says he restored *Sacae* from the manuscripts and adds that the Sacae were called Scythians by the Persians, as is established by Pliny, book VII, chapter 17, and Strabo, book XI.].

The worshiper of Christ has loosened the Scythian frosts through love [Note: One Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition have “has loosened the Scythian frosts through honor.” Browerus observes that Fortunatus here imitated Prudentius, who says in the *Apotheosis*:

“The Gospel voice, penetrating through the word,  
Loosened the Scythian frosts.”],

And cold hearts grow warm through his fervent teaching.

Desiring Saint Martin, I attached myself to Radegund’s wish,  
Whom Thuringian earth brought forth for a sacred heaven.

She is the royal-born, pious granddaughter of Hermenefred [Note: Hermenefred was Radegund’s uncle—the man who arranged for Radegund’s father to be killed. Later, defeated in a great battle by the Frankish kings Theodoric and Chlothar, he was thrown from a wall and died, at Theodoric’s command, as was believed. Read Gregory of Tours, book III, chapter 8.],

To whom Hamalafredus, the son of her father’s brother, is joined [Note: Concerning Hamalefredus, Radegund’s cousin, and her exceptional affection for him, see the poem entitled “On the Destruction of Thuringia,” found below in the supplement to Fortunatus’s works.].

Adorned with virtues of mind, she scorns fugitive honors [Note: The Venetian edition, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Paris edition have “she scorned honors,”],  
Knowing that only in God does anything remain firm [Note: The Venetian edition has “preferring in the one”; the Paris edition “knowing in the one.”].

Exchanging royal robes for a milk-white garment [Note: This may be compared with what is read in Saint Caesarius’s Rule, which Radegund followed, section 42: “No other dye shall be made in the monastery except the gray and the milk-white, because anything else is not appropriate to the humility of virgins.” In the same observations, concerning which see also Peter Scriverius’s letter to Rosweyde, the name of the garment *Cataclista*, of which Fortunatus speaks in book III of the *Life of Saint Martin*, page 447, is held to indicate a kind of snow-white, washed, patterned garment: “*Catacliton* is a kind of patterned garment,” as learned men once noted concerning that African term. The use of the word is supported by Apuleius, who says in the *Milesian Tales*: “A chorus followed in a snow-white and brilliantly shining *Cataclista*.” The same writer interprets the word *effora*, which Fortunatus uses in the same passage, as “projecting” or “prominent,” saying: “*Ecphora*”—Ἔκφορα—among architects properly means the projection of the moldings which modern architects call corbels. Compare these remarks with what we noted on the same passage of Fortunatus, and let the reader choose which seems better. The Venetian edition has “royal, in a mournful garment.” The Paris edition has “royal, in a cleansing garment,” perhaps “woolen.”],

She covers herself in the beloved clothing of a lowly handmaid.

Once borne aloft upon a splendid, proud *serracum* [Note: See above, the notes on poem 7 of book VI. The Paris edition has “splendid in ironwork”],  
Now her modest foot treads the mud in service.

Her right hand, once burdened with set emeralds,  
Now, poor in worldly things, serves her attendants diligently.

Once governing the lofty court, now she ministers at commands;  
She who formerly pleased by ruling now pleases by serving.

Powerful in poverty and free through her single desire,  
She shines more brightly in the lowly place she has chosen.

Once holding golden supports, now regarding honor as nothing [Note: The Paris edition has “holding only for herself”],  
She escaped the bed that had been built up, scattering herself in dust.

If she is despised, then she confesses herself noble,  
And thinks herself lesser if any honor is bestowed.

Spare in food, surpassing Eustochium, abstinent like Paula,  
The leader Fabiola teaches her how to heal wounds [Note: Radegund is here compared with Fabiola, the Roman matron, in praise of repentance. After repudiating her husband and entering a new marriage while he was still alive, Fabiola used the indulgence of civil law, but underwent a severe and prolonged penance to expiate this offense. Jerome composed a eulogy of her in letter 84.].

Emulating Melania in zeal and Blesilla in piety,  
Able through her vows to equal Marcella [Note: One Vatican manuscript has “wishing to equal you”; the Paris edition “able to equal [her] in vows,”],

Through service renewing Martha, and through tears Mary,  
Vigilant like Eugenia, she seeks to resemble Thecla through suffering.

She carries within her whatever is praised in those women;  
I recognize the signs that I read were formerly enacted.

Despising everything, and still steadfast in the body,  
Her spirit lives here, but her flesh lies as though dead.

Living on earth, she enters heaven; rightly free in spirit,  
Even among human beings she already makes for the stars.

Whatever the pious Rule prescribes is her feast,  
Whatever Gregory and Basil teach,
