Whatever keen Athanasius and gentle Hilary bring forth,  
Both held by one light, which preserves them as partners in their causes,

Whatever Ambrose thunders and Jerome flashes,  
Or Augustine waters from his flowing spring,

Whatever sweet Sedulius and keen Orosius produce,  
Caesarius’s Rule is a rule laid down for her [Note: See what we said in the *Life of Fortunatus*, section 82. One manuscript reads “the broad line is hers.”].

With these foods the fasting woman nourishes herself; her flesh is never pampered,  
Unless the spirit has first already been satisfied.

Let me now be silent about the rest, which, better attested by the Thunderer [Note: The Venetian edition has “better, because witnessed”],  
Remain glorified in the judgment of God.

Let each person send her, as he can, the poems of holy poets,  
Rich gifts in little books.

Whoever brings her blessed writings in his prayers  
May think that he is furnishing God’s enduring temples [Note: The Paris edition has “building”].

And you who read these things, I ask you to return words of greeting;  
For to me a light page will be a weight of love.

## CHAPTER II. On his journey, when he was about to go to Lord Germanus and was detained by Lady Radegund

[Note: The title in the Venetian edition reads: “When he was returning to Lord Germanus.” Saint Germanus of Paris died in 576; this poem was therefore composed before that date.]

[Note: As the day approached on which he was to depart for Germanus, bishop of Paris, Fortunatus says that he was detained by Radegund’s affection. Each was exceedingly dear to him: one surpassed the other in episcopal position and rank, but the other was closer to him because of her greater affection. Although he was therefore to be absent from Radegund in body, he affirms that in spirit he would always remain present.]

Look—the day shines forth; the journey we must make is at hand;  
Paying what is owed, look—the day shines forth.

From there Father Germanus, radiant throughout the world, calls me;  
Here Mother detains me; from there Father calls me.

Both are sweet to me, joined together by embracing affection;  
Full of the love of God, both are sweet to me.

Although this one is dearer to my heart and that one dearer in his holy rank [Note: The Paris edition reads:

“This one dearer to the spirit, that holy one dearer in blessed honor.”],

That one is dearer in rank, this one dearer to my heart [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have “that one is brighter.”].

One mind holds the two traveling with equal steps,  
One mind holds the two as they journey toward holy things.

Whatever either one has done well benefits the other;

All the good of one benefits the other.

Since they are equal in heart, I do not refuse the command to go,

I shall obey them both, since they are equal in heart.

Yet I do not depart from here, although I shall see new dwellings;

I depart in body, yet I do not depart from here.

Here I shall be wholly [Note: In one Vatican manuscript: “Here I shall be safe,” and this twice.], nor am I torn away in heart and mind;

Thus also, while I return [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “Thus also, while I remain,” corruptly.], I shall be wholly here.

May the heavenly Mother extend her weapons to me as I depart,

So that she may possess me the more fully; may she extend her weapons to me.

## CHAPTER III. Hymn on the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: This hymn is absent from the Venetian edition and from three Vatican manuscript codices. It was likewise absent from the manuscripts available to Browerus. The Morbach manuscript, however, which Fabricius used, contained it; from it Browerus states that he extracted the two cola beginning “The manger to be placed...” and “He who gave the law...,” each consisting of four iambic feet. It is also read under this title in the distinguished Hymnary of Tomasi: “By Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers.”]

[Col. 0264B]

Let every age acknowledge

That the reward of life has come:

After the yoke of the harsh enemy,

Redemption has appeared.

The things Isaiah sang

Have been fulfilled in the Virgin;

The angel announced it,

The Holy Spirit has filled her.

Mary conceives in her womb

By the faithful seed of the Word [Note: In the hymn cited above, “of the faithful Word.” Fabricius likewise.],

And what the whole world [Note: In the hymn cited above, “what the whole universe.” Fabricius likewise.] cannot contain,

The maiden’s womb bears.

The root of Jesse has blossomed,

And the branch [Note: In the hymn cited above, “and the virgin bears fruit.” Fabricius: “fruit.”] has produced fruit.

[Col. 0264C]

The fruitful woman has brought forth a child,

And the virgin remains a mother.

He who established the source of light

Allowed himself to be laid in a manger;

With the Father he fashioned the heavens,

Under his mother he put on swaddling clothes.

He who gave the law to the world,

Whose ten commandments are,

Deigning to become human,

Became subject to the bond of the law.

What the old Adam polluted,

The new Adam cleanses;

What that proud one cast down,

This most humble one raises.

[Col. 0265A]

Now light and salvation have been born,

Night has been driven away, and death [Note: Fabricius: “death has been conquered,” which is preferable.]

Come, nations, believe:

Mary has brought forth God.

## CHAPTER IV. On Holy Mary

[Note: This hymn, like the following one, was written in honor of the most holy Mother of God. The Church has already consecrated them through its use; they are found under this heading in the aforementioned Hymnary of the distinguished Tomasi: “By Venantius Honorius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers.” It therefore seemed appropriate to append these hymns here.]

Whom earth, sea, and heaven

Worship, adore, and proclaim,

The ruler of the threefold universe—

Mary bears him within her enclosure.

For whom moon, sun, and all things

Serve throughout the ages,

The maiden’s womb,

Flooded with heaven’s grace, bears him.

The ages therefore marvel

That the angel bears the seed,

[Col. 0265B]

That the Virgin conceives

And receives it in believing heart.

Blessed is the Mother by this gift:

The heavenly Maker,

Who holds the world in his little hand,

Has been enclosed beneath the vessel of her womb.

Blessed by the heavenly messenger,

Made fruitful by the Holy Spirit,

He whom the nations desired

Has been poured forth through her womb.

### Division

O glorious Lady,

Exalted above the stars,

He who providentially created you,

[Col. 0265C]

You nursed at your sacred breast.

What grieving Eve took away,

You restore through your life-giving offspring;

That the sorrowful may enter the stars,

You have become the window of heaven.

You are the gate of the high King,

And the shining portal of light:

Nations redeemed through the life

Given by the Virgin, applaud.

Glory to you, O Lord, etc.

## CHAPTER V. On Holy Mary

Hail, star of the sea,

Nourishing Mother of God,

And ever-virgin,

[Col. 0265D]

Happy gate of heaven.

Receiving that “Hail”

From Gabriel’s mouth,

Establish us in peace,

Changing Eve’s name.

[Col. 0266A]

Release the bonds of the guilty,

Bring forth light for the blind,

Drive away our evils,

Ask for every good.

Show yourself to be a mother.

Through you may he receive prayers

Who, born for us,

Deigned to be yours.

Singular Virgin,

Gentle among all,

Having freed us from sins,

Make us gentle and chaste;

Grant us a pure life.

Prepare a safe path,

So that, when we see Jesus,

[Col. 0266B]

We may rejoice together forever.

Let there be praise, etc.

## CHAPTER VI. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of my lady Mary, his mother. On virginity

[Note: This poem, which was found mutilated and dismembered in the printed editions, was restored by Browerus with the help of manuscripts. In the Venetian edition and in the Vatican manuscripts also, this poem is found scattered, its torn parts dispersed partly in the poem inscribed “On Gelesuintha,” Book VI, poem 7, and partly in the poem “On Duke Godegisil,” Book V, chapter 7. Georgius Fabricius likewise mangled and dismembered this poem—already, as Browerus notes, assigning it a title of his own invention, “On the joys and hope of eternal life,” which perhaps pleased him less, as an unorthodox man, than the title “On virginity.”]

[Note: In this poem on virginity, written for Abbess Agnes, the choirs of heavenly spirits and the assemblies and festivals of other saints are described. Radegundis is also splendidly praised, and her example is proposed to Agnes for the pursuit and imitation of virtue. Finally, the heavenly triumph is presented, with Christ in the assembly of the saints proclaiming the arduous labors of virginity, its praises and fruits, and showing how greatly it surpasses marriage, both through its own praises and through the hardships and labors of marriage.]

Many summits fill the heavens with radiant light [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “They fill the summit with light.”].

[Col. 0266C]

And holy bands rejoice in pious choirs.

With Davidic song they weave applauding arms,

And are believed to dance in sacred procession [Note: The manuscript: “and are believed to dance.”].

The human race, joined to angelic assemblies,

Returns an honorific sound in love of praise;

They sing divine poems in alternating turns [Note: The manuscript: “with alternating voices.” The Paris edition: “with voices alternating,”]

And sing mystical words to the Creator.

The shining court of heaven resounds with sidereal tumult,

And the crash of praise shakes the stars of the Lord.

From here the melodies of the patriarchs’ voices resound,

Among whom Abraham has the greatest concern for faith [Note: One Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition: “the palm of faith.”].

From him they received the prophets’ words and now return them;

Moses, leader above all others, with the sea as witness to his men.

Then the brothers applaud, and the lofty company of the devout,

The apostolic light, with Peter meditating beforehand.

He who by his merits can animate buried ashes

And recall the day at a commanding voice.

From here the earlier order of the senate follows with equal reward,

Among whom Stephen is first, victorious in honor.

[Col. 0267A]

Those whom faith, rescued from the earth by stones and swords,

Hunger, thirst [Note: The manuscript: “thirst.”], cold, and flames, joins to the stars.

Alas, by various calamities, whom the rage of the furious persecutor carried off—

Although their deaths differed, one light nevertheless holds them.

Then the Mother of God, from whom the Virgin Mary shines forth,

Leads the sheep of the Lamb from the virgin flock [Note: The Venetian edition: “and of the Virgin Lamb”; two Vatican manuscripts and the manuscript: “and of the Virgin Lamb.”].

[Note: One Vatican manuscript: “this maidenly.”] She herself, surrounded by a maidenly company,

Leads a camp brilliant with the light of chastity.

Singing their vows amid the feasts of paradise,

This one gathers violets, and that one plucks roses [Note: The manuscript and the Paris edition: “this one gave violets.”].

They break the gems of the meadows and lilies with their fingers,

And gather whatever is fragrant, with its flower-topped bloom.

[Col. 0267C]

There Euphemia, and likewise Agatha, applaud,

And Justina together, with Thecla joining them [Note: The Venetian edition: “Euphemia, and likewise Agatha.” The Paris edition: “Christina, Euphemia, likewise.”].

Here Paulina, Agnes, Basilissa, and Eugenia reign [Note: Some, Browerus says, read “Blesilla” instead of “Basilissa.” But the Venetian Bede supports the manuscripts, having cited this whole verse in the *Art of Metre*. The Venetian edition and the Vatican manuscript codices likewise read “Basilissa.”],

[Col. 0267B]

And all whom sacred modesty has carried to the stars.

Happy are those whose fixed names in the book

Live forever through the love of Christ.

Among these, joined to her companions, Caesaria shines [Note: Caesaria, mentioned here by Fortunatus, was the woman who, after Caesaria—the sister of St Caesarius, bishop of Arles—headed the convent of nuns built at Arles by that same St Caesarius. For Caesaria’s benefit St Caesarius wrote the Rule which was afterwards made common to other monasteries, including the monastery of St Radegund at Poitiers, as noted elsewhere. Caesaria’s death is recorded in the year 559; Liliola, mentioned in the following verse, succeeded her. See *Histoire Littéraire de la France*, vol. III, p. 274. In the Cologne manuscript, one Vatican manuscript, and the Venetian edition, “Casaria” is read for “Caesaria,” with the diphthong resolved and one letter omitted for the metre.],

The glory of Arles in our own times.

Joined to the everlasting light through the teachings of Caesarius,

If not by martyrdom, then by the power of virginity.

Liliola [Note: The Venetian edition gives “Favillola,” perhaps for “Fabiola.” But the manuscript codices give “Liliola.” Cointius dates Liliola’s death to the year 574; this poem on virginity by Fortunatus must therefore have been composed before that time, since he speaks here of Liliola as still living.] reports both with equal conduct,

And the next palm awaits a distinguished heir.

And whoever, keeping watch, shall meditate on her own actions,

Will share in these things at an excellent rank.

With faith conceiving through love of Christ Radegundis,

She sips whatever Caesarius’ rule contains.

From the bishop’s breast she gathers honey flowing forth,

And drinks its streams without being satisfied.

The more she draws from the spring, the more thirst added to it grows [Note: The Paris edition: “which, while they draw from the spring...”],

And, more thoroughly moistened by God’s dew, she burns more ardently.

Not living for herself but uniquely for all,

She, blessed, opens a narrow way to the stars [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “Not for you, but for all.”].

But, above all others, she attends more lovingly to you, pious mother,

And chooses to join you to the exalted choir.

The fact itself proves it: since you stand as her daughter,

She desires by her vows to have you as her mother.

[Col. 0268A]

And the foster daughter whom she nourished as dear upon her knees [Note: The Paris edition: “whom she nourished with care”; and in the following verse, “She completes it.”],

Behold, she appoints to be established in her own place;

And she who always governed you with the authority of her staff,

Ready under command, wishes rather to be under yours.

She benefits herself when you are placed over her,

And she undertakes the vow when you possess the rank [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts: “She undertakes the vow by her wish.”].

Behold, at last she has the festal day, through the piety of the Thunderer [Note: It is not easy to determine which feast-day Fortunatus indicates here. Yet from the subject of the poem, wholly written in praise of virginity, and from its fuller discussion of Radegund and Agnes, I conjecture that it signifies Agnes’s birthday, or rather the day on which Agnes was appointed superior and made abbess of Blessed Radegund’s monastery at Poitiers. That day was customarily celebrated with a solemn annual observance, as may be understood both from other ancient monuments and from Fortunatus’s other poems written on the same subject. See, among other passages, Book XI, chapters 3 and 5.],

Whom the mother often entreated with prayers [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the manuscript: “whom the mother often entreated with prayers.”].

Her inmost heart breathes with a quiet pulse,

And abundant joys fill her constricted spirit [Note: The Venetian edition: “and abundant joys fill noble spirits.”].

Stretching her eyes toward the long-awaited moment,

She gathers the seeds of joy, heavenly gifts.

Still she humbly asks for the one remaining honor:

That you may please Christ, to be joined to heaven.

How you may obtain this seems to be a task for one who acts.

[Col. 0268B]

But this task will be repaid with brief labor and fruit.

Your neck must be subjected to the yoke of the Lord’s service,

And whatever you bear for love must be not grievous but light.

Do not seek examples elsewhere; look for them in your mother.

You see before your eyes the work you should contemplate.

Since you hasten to be with her together in everlasting light,

It is fitting that you run the road by a similar rule.

Let venerable Caesaria, present with you,

Be your sweet glory, while you will not lack your bishop Caesarius.

Following them in your heart, and fulfilling their commands in your body [Note: In the same place: “fulfilling them in your body,”],

So that you may hold flowers, imitate these bees.

Look upon him who wished to be born from a maiden’s womb [Note: In the same place: “who wished to be born from the womb,”],

And through whom the flesh of the supreme Lord came from flesh.

The venerable Spirit touched the untouched womb,

Desiring to inhabit a virginal dwelling.

As God entered her, who had known no man,

The virgin alone, conscious of her own child and husband.

Conceiving through faith, she did not sport with any seed [Note: The Paris edition and the manuscript: “she was not harmed by any seed.”],

And the one through whom he became human was not another human.

Blessed virginity, which was worthy of the Thunderer’s birth,

Which deserved to beget its own Lord.

The maiden’s chaste limbs are the Creator’s temple,

And God himself inhabits such a dwelling.

[Col. 0269A]

However pleasing a bride may be through virginity,

The Mother of God herself pleases only as a virgin [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts, as does ours: “she to whom the Mother gave birth.”].

Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Esther, Judith, Anna, Naomi,

Although they especially raise their summit to the stars,

None deserved to give birth to the parent of the world;

She who bore the Lord remains closed, Mary.

The undefiled woman hung God, born, from her breast [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts: “the one born at the breast.” The Paris edition likewise],

And nourished the bread of heaven with the gift of milk.

Therefore he now loves in the bride this womb,

Which he first chose in the mother as a sacred honor [Note: The Venetian edition: “which he first chose in the mother.”].

He penetrates more freely breasts known only to him,

And enters a path where no one else has been, with greater joy.

Thinking these limbs his own, which no injury defiles,

Which have not been shared with any other man,

Gentle in affection, he embraces that breast,

Ready in love to honor it, where another lover is absent [Note: The manuscript: “honoring my breast, where another lover is absent,”].

Although God wishes his kingdoms likewise to belong to all,

Christ nevertheless avoids having this common possession.

He desires to be co-heir in the feasts of paradise,

And alone wishes to inhabit a virgin dwelling.

The king himself better guards the camp of chastity

If the company dedicated to him does not violate its fidelity.

If he sees that the will is faithful,

God himself also holds weapons on behalf of his servants.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts: “A breastplate, shield, helmet.” (Note of the first recension.)—Browerus emends this, as I noted, to the reading found in two Vatican manuscripts: “A breastplate, shield, helmet,” differently from what he had printed in either edition. (Note of the second recension.)]

He fortifies the lover beforehand with breastplate, helmet, and shield,

And establishes a firm step in the citadel of the mind [Note: The Venetian edition: “and makes firm the solid step of the mind.”].

[Note: One Vatican manuscript: “Shooting a ballista.” The Paris edition likewise.] A ballista shooting for you soon goes out against the enemy,

To destroy those adversaries who wage war against you.

After the battles have been fought, he runs triumphantly to embrace you,

And fixes chaste kisses upon your sacred lips.

[Col. 0269C]

He caresses, refreshes, venerates, honors, overshadows,

And places your chaste limbs in his own bridal chamber.

The heavenly princes, frequenting the royal vows,

Come eagerly, gathering into a choir.

[Col. 0270A]

Besides cherubim, seraphim, and the other blessed,

Winged companions whom God’s shadow covers [Note: The manuscript: “angelic.”],

The glory of the twice twelve elder prophets hastens together,

Applauding in astonishment with mind, voice, and hand.

With these comes Elijah; with those, Enoch in his chariots;

And, by the gift of her Son, the Virgin Mary comes first.

With the flight of the jurist Paul accompanying him,

Peter, prince, runs from the Roman citadel.

They assemble together for the festivals, bringing their own gifts—

Those whose ashes the City, head of the world, possesses.

The apostolic summit, glittering with radiant light,

Sends noble Andrew from Achaea.

Venerable Ephesus sends its distinguished John for his merits,

And the blessed land sends the sacred Jameses.

Benevolent Hierapolis, rejoicing in its vows,

Brings forth Philip;

Edessa offers pious Thomas as a gift.

Then India brings Bartholomew in triumph,

And lofty Naddaver brings the exceptional man Matthew [Note: Some read “Naddaver attha,” as Browerus reports. The Venetian edition has “Naddaver apta.” Naddaver is a royal city of Ethiopia, into which Matthew first brought the light of the Gospel. Fortunatus repeats the same in the following poem: “Whom Patras, Ephesus, and Naddaver’s citadel possess”; and shortly afterward: “Matthew the Ethiopians, John’s gate the Ephesians, and each gate asks for the one whom it loves.” Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 41, prefers the city in which Matthew suffered to have been Myrmena, in the land of cannibals; Dorotheus, in the Synopsis, places it in Hierapolis of Parthia. In that case, Browerus says, it must be supposed that some portion of his body was formerly transferred to those cities.].

From here Persia, happy and with her bosom opened wide,

Sends the twin light of Simon and Jude to the stars [Note: The Venetian edition: “And, happy, sends him to the stars with her bosom opened.”].

And arid Egypt, fruitful without dew, sends Mark,

With Luke’s evangelical trumpet taking part.

Africa gives Cyprian;

Clear Siscia gives Quirinus [Note: Commonly, corruptly, “Sistia.” The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts support Browerus’ reading. One has “Scytia.” Siscia was a city in Upper Pannonia, where Saint Quirinus suffered, of whom Prudentius speaks in Hymn 7 of the Crowns. His acts are found among the Authentic Acts of the Martyrs, p. 552, under the year 309. On the martyrdom of Saint Quirinus, see also Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book I, chapter 33.].

From the Spanish citadel rises the glory of Vincent.

Fruitful Britain produces the distinguished Alban,

Victor the martyr comes from the city of Massilia.

Fair Arles herself offers pious gifts to Genesius,

With her own Caesarius accompanying him to the stars.

Dionysius himself hastens from the city of Paris;

From Augustodunum, Symphorianus, you come.

[Col. 0270C]

Gabalus sends Privatus, and overflowing Arvernia sends Julian [Note: Privatus is reported to have suffered in the territory of Gabalum or Gabalitanum under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus; he is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on August 21. Others prefer to assign his death to the beginning of the fifth century; on this see Tillemont, Ecclesiastical History, vol. IV. Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book I, chapter 32, says that he suffered when the Alemanni were invading Gaul. This reading, says Browerus, is supported by the authority of the ancient copies, to which all the Vatican manuscripts also agree. Joan. Savaro corrects it to “Arvernia abounds in Julian,” seeking support for his emendation in a passage of Claudian Mamertus: “He abounds in many talents of learning,” as Browerus reports in his notes on this passage. The Venetian edition has, corruptly, “Julianum Arvernus Abundum.” On Saints Julian and Ferreolus, see Gregory of Tours, Book II, On the Glory of the Martyrs.],

And beautiful Vienna likewise bears Ferreolus.

From here Gaul sends Hilary and Martin,

And you also, blessed Laurence, Rome has brought [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “Rome, blessed, has brought me.” The Venetian edition: “Blessed Rome has brought me.” Likewise one Vatican manuscript. The Paris edition: “Blessed Rome has brought you.”].

[Col. 0271A]

Joyful Vicetia pours forth Felix, distinguished in merits [Note: Vicetia. Others, Vincentia, as also the Venetian edition. Yet, as Browerus observes, the former reading is more common in antiquity. Aetianus has Βικητία; Pliny, Vicetia; and, according to Manutius, Veicetia, an inland city of the Veneti. Notable portions of the bodies of Saints Felix and Fortunatus are preserved at Vicenza in the monastery of Our Lady, which bears the name of Saint Felix.],

And Aquileia bears its own Fortunatus.

Vitalis, and the others whom beloved Ravenna entombs;

Gervasius and Ambrose, Milan, are mine.

Justina of Padua [Note: “Calar., Justina Patavum,” as Browerus reports. Two Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition have “Justinam Patavi.” “Patavum” is used for “Patavium” for metrical reasons. Saint Justina’s sacred ashes are preserved in the magnificent basilica of Padua, beneath the high altar, beside the monastery of Our Lady, already famous throughout Europe. The Paris edition: “Justinam Patavi.”], and Chalcedon offers Euphemia here;

Emerita lifts up Eulalia’s head from its city [Note: Emerita was formerly the capital of Lusitania; after its destruction, the episcopal see was transferred to Compostela. On Saint Eulalia and the miracle that occurred annually on her feast day at the basilica consecrated to her memory, see Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, Book II, chapter 91.].

[Note: Perhaps in Fortunatus’ time the memory of Saint Cecilia was honored especially in Sicily, although tradition records her as a Roman matron. Browerus aptly observes that Fortunatus, when speaking of the church at Ravenna and the relics of the saints buried there, counts Saint Cecilia among the saints of that church in these verses: “Holy Alexander and blessed Cecilia are powerful; one crown unites them all in merit.”]

Sicily produces Cecilia, Seleucia Thecla,

[Note: On the Agaunian Legion, see what was said in the notes to Book II, chapter 18. This verse is read most corruptly in the common editions: “Feliciam regio ... Cauninensis.” The Venetian edition is likewise corrupt: “And Felix of Agaunum has come.”]

And the blessed legion of Agaunum is present.

Who could recount such great lights of Europe and Asia?

Or who could speak of your children, Rome?

Gathered from every region of the world,

The royal procession leads them in joined ranks.

They enter the gates, blooming with sidereal light;

The opened city of heaven receives these princes.

[Col. 0271B]

Then the robed authority advances slowly,

Thus destined to occupy the patrician rank.

The nobility of heaven, rich in the cross and the blood of Christ,

Hastens to celebrate the festal choirs [Note: The Venetian edition and two Vatican manuscripts: “to celebrate the bridal chambers.” The manuscript: “thrones.”].

The poverty of earth, overflowing with heavenly wealth,

Honors royal vows before such great consuls.

Numerous, distinguished seats are filled on every side [Note: The manuscript: “wooded.”],

And the Fathers sit silent in astonishment while the King speaks.

Then the hidden majesty of God, fixed in solemn authority,

Addresses the princes whom his right hand governs.

“This virgin preserved for me the chastity she had promised,

And did not wish to tear apart the fidelity that pleased me.

With anxious hearts, following the footsteps of her bridegroom

And seeking my vows, she came undefiled.

[Note: The Paris edition: “Walking through many brambles, she becomes cautious.”]

Walking through thorns, she blunted the sharpness of the briar,

[Col. 0271C]

Unaware, amid the brambles, of carrying thickets.

The viper, the adder, the dart-snake, the basilisk, the haemorrhois [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “the viper, the serpent.” Another Vatican manuscript: “the serpent with darts.”], the asp,

With terrifying jaws, sluggishly twisted their hissing.

From there a flying arrow, from here a bow, terrified the traveler;

But, trained by their ambushes, she learned to proceed more cautiously.

Innocent among so many enemies, she submitted to none;

She received wounds, but escaped by enduring them.

[Col. 0272A]

Through darts and swords no delay held back the one who followed,

But love alone could endure such extreme hardships.

She stretched her ears, eyes, and spirit attentively toward me;

When she lay upon the earth, she was already above the stars.

Sobs, groans, cares, sighs, and tears

I often heard, not to be erased from my memory.

Hiding her pains from others, confessing them to no one,

She gave me, and only me, murmurs enclosed within herself.

Whenever she happened to see my face in an image,

Giving kisses with her lips, she poured out water from her eyes.

She kept watch, lying there in case I should come from somewhere else,

Pressing her cold limbs against the marble already warmed.

Though frozen, she preserved my fire in her bones;

In her stiffened entrails her breast burns with love.

Despising her body, she lay upon a bare mound,

And, lying there, forgot herself [Note: The Venetian edition: “herself, remembering me.” One Vatican manuscript likewise. The Paris edition likewise.].

[Col. 0272B]

With continual tears, the moisture drained from her cheeks,

Her eyes dried, and the earth swam with waters.

And because, while living, she had once been unable

To see me with bodily eyes, she sent a prayer to the one she loved.

For me, troubled, during the night hours,

A page written with her tears was often read.

It was indeed full of various laments in trembling speech,

Because she alone, without me [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “sad without me alone.”], lay mournfully upon the ground.

From her mouth, flowing with its natural liquid,

These signs were conveyed in trembling letters:

“I lie stretched upon the ground, weeping, and do not see what I desire;

Sad in my embrace, I press stones against my breast.

While my bridegroom is absent, I remain and keep such harsh beds;

And my limbs cannot hold the one whom they desire [Note: In the Venetian edition the poem ends at this verse; everything that follows is absent until Book X, chapter 18. In one Vatican manuscript also the present poem ends with this verse, inclusively.].

[Col. 0272C]

Tell me where you are, whom I seek in groaning— in what city shall I look for you?

Or by what path shall I follow, when no track is known in those places [Note: The Paris edition: “with no woman’s mark.”]?

I myself would wish to come, hastening, if I could somehow with my feet

Hold to the starry path, suspended among the stars.

Now without you night heavily occupies everything with dark wings,

And the day itself, shining with the sun, is blind to me.

[Col. 0273A]

Lilies, narcissus, violets, rose, nard, and amomum—

No flowers delight my spirit.

To see you, I seize each cloud [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the Paris edition: “I hang upon the clouds one by one.”],

And love leads my wandering eyes through the mists.

Behold, suspicious, I question the stormy winds:

What breeze may announce to me concerning my Lord?

For your feet I long to wash the pavement,

And I desire to wipe your temples with my hair.

[Note: The Paris edition: “What do I endure through you?”]

Whatever it may be, I shall endure it; all harsh things are sweet,

Until I see you; this punishment pleases me.

Yet remember, since I seek your vows [Note: The manuscript: “when I seek your vows.”];

I care for you—may you care for me.

Saying these things, she tossed her arms toward eager hands,

If perhaps she could somehow hold my feet [Note: The manuscript: “could.”].

But when, deceived, her right hand returned to her

Without me,

[Col. 0273B]

She washed her face, sprinkling it with waters from her eyes.

When she lay upon the ground, she did not rest, overcome by sleep;

I often lay beside her, about to comfort her.

I grieved with her, wiped away rivers of tears,

Giving kisses made sweet with bright honeycombs [Note: The manuscript: “watered with honey.”].

Now therefore let her reign and enjoy peaceful love [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “and enjoy love according to her desire,”],

She who long ago was joined to me in her heart.

At her ascent the court of heaven resounds as the senate takes its seat;

Her name is written there in the everlasting book.

An eternal inheritance, destined to remain through the ages,

Is bestowed; Olympus pours forth riches into the virgin’s bridal chamber.

A radiant diadem of beryl is inserted upon her head,

And white emerald is set among varied ornaments.

An amethyst band binds her shining hair,

Folding around it with pearl-studded artistry.

A necklace impressed with sardonyx flashes around her neck,

And purple sardian gems gleam [Note: The manuscript: “sardian.”].

An armlet of chalcedony mixed with jasper is given to her right hand,

Or her hand glistens with the honor of hyacinth.

[Col. 0273C]

Threads fasten the gem-studded cyclas [Note: According to Dufresne in the Glossary, a cyclas was a garment closed all around at its outer edge, with a curved form; as it swept the ground, it formed a kind of circle, hence it seems to have been called cyclas from the Greek word κύκλος, “circle.” Papias, cited there by Dufresne, says: “Cyclas, a kind of garment, named from its roundness, narrow above and broad below.” It was a garment proper to women, especially common among brides and newlyweds. Thus Sidonius, Book I, Letter 5: “The bridegroom is honored by a crown, now as a consul with the palm-embroidered robe, now with the bridal cyclas, now as a senator with the toga.”].

With heavenly gifts, closely set seals swell [Note: Seals were figures with which garments were embroidered, and garments of this kind were therefore called “sealed.” A law of Theodosius survives forbidding actresses to use such garments, in these words: “No actress shall use gems, sealed silks, or woven gold”; title 7, On Stage Performers. Pollux, Book XIII, chapter 7, describes sealed garments as follows: Κατάστικτος χιτὼν, ὁ ἔχων ζῶα, ἤ ἄνθη ἐνυφασμένα, καὶ ζωωτὸς δὲ χιτὼν ἐκαλεῖτο, ἢ ζωδιωτὸς—“A patterned tunic, one having animals or flowers woven into it; it was also called an animal-figured or zodiacal tunic.” See Dufresne in the Glossary. The manuscript has “with artistry.”].

A beautiful belt is weighed down with topaz stones,

And a golden fibula closes the pin [Note: Properly, the pin was the part of a brooch by which it was closed and fastened. Thus Trebellius Pollio, in The Divine Claudius, speaks of “a golden brooch with a single Cyprian pin,” etc. It was properly used to join and fasten garments.].

Over the garment, purple twice twisted over byssus [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “purple twice eightfold,” perhaps “twisted.” The Paris edition: “twice dyed.”],

Such as a maiden, bride of God, may wear,

She, heaped with these riches, will sit as queen in the bridal chamber,

And, a virgin, will press offspring beneath her feet in heaven.

[Col. 0274A]

Yet what need has she of this adornment along with virginity’s honor,

Save that a disciplined mind may please its own bridegroom?

Let steadfast patience hold a grave expression,

And move forward by its own strength, lest, shaken, it fall.

And let no fickle spirit be wearied by a windy storm;

Let the anchor of the heart hold fast amid the waves.

Patience shines as the special glory of the virtues;

Job will give you signs by which to walk the path.

Or why should I speak of the humble man whom lofty grace adorns?

The more he seeks the lowest places, the more he rises to the heights.

How utterly different is the condition divided between two men:

The one who lies low rises; the one who swells with pride falls.

Joseph and Pharaoh gave these examples:

The one is lifted from the pit, the other plunged into the sea.

It is also a mark of praise to ask only for the means of living,

So that greedy pestilence does not oppress its own breast.

Content with the least, if she does not seek greater things,

The poor woman reigns in narrow circumstances, possessing God.

[Note: Sapphira, elsewhere Sappyra and Sapira. Read Acts, chapter 5.]

Sapphira, or the woman who gave two small coins:

The former perishes by holding on; the latter endures by giving what is hers.

O exceedingly happy is the one whom soft things do not break,

Who, judging herself, wears out her limbs through labor!

She despises the snares of wealth, perfumes, and flowing works of art [Note: The Paris edition: “luxuries,”],

So that rigor itself may be guardian of her soul.

Remembering also what frugal use can accomplish,

Only sobriety makes Judith victorious.

Or why should I fail to remember the gentle spirit whom grace nourishes?

When dear inward parts bear peoples within themselves.

Peaceful and rejoicing, she embraces everyone as one,

And draws all hearts together in her affection.

[Col. 0274C]

O exceedingly happy will, flourishing in goodness,

Without which nothing pleases the people or the altar of God!

This is the work: whenever the mind is carried toward something bitter,

Let hope, accompanied by faith, strengthen it amid adversity [Note: The Paris edition: “imitating.”].

Let harsh things not break you, nor prosperous things make you arrogant;

Holding to moderation in this way, the path is traveled more safely.

A person receives these good things if the grace of Christ grants them,

As he inspires the will or guides the step.

Adorned with these good things, you pour forth radiant lights;

Holding these gems, you too shine like a gem.

Blessed virginity, to be matched by no words,

Not even if the mouth supplied a hundred sounds [Note: The Paris edition: “a hundredfold sound.”].

[Col. 0275A]

What came first shines without stain, venerable to the world,

Without corrupting the good proper to nature.

Preserving the body’s precious talent unharmed,

It retains everlasting wealth, knowing no thief.

It is not weighed down by enclosed, inert entrails through pregnancy [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “inert entrails through weeping.”],

Nor does it lie sorrowful, made heavy by its own pledge,

Amid the panting heats of soul and body,

With exhausted safety hanging upon an uncertain thread.

When the womb, about to be wounded by its own darts, swells,

And the diseased Hydra of pleasure grows.

The savage skin swells beyond human form [Note: The Paris edition: “through the skin’s deformity,”],

So that the mother is ashamed of what she carries through love.

She flees from herself, and, ashamed, withdraws from her own parents,

Until the burden releases its entrusted load.

Who could equal the groaning of childbirth in words?

Or who would have leisure to weep so many tears in verse?

[Col. 0275B]

When her secret honorable structure relaxes [Note: The Paris edition: “its burdened structure”],

And her entrails struggle under the heavy burden,

Overcome by childbirth, the gate of her limbs opens [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “the gate grows weary.” The Paris edition: “grows weak.”],

And the child emerges into the light, perhaps without light.

But if the child born lives, the mother, forgetting herself, seeks it,

And sadly directs weary eyes toward her newborn.

She looks upon the exposed child, the nursling, while she is no longer a mother—

She who has scarcely given birth now has a corpse.

Nor has this woman deserved to be called either mother [Note: The same edition: “nor has she ultimately deserved...”] or virgin;

Grieving these two losses, she laments herself as an unfortunate wife.

[Note: This verse was defective in all the manuscripts first used by Browerus. In them it stood thus: “Not strong, hope snatched away by pain.” In one Vatican manuscript it reads: “Weak, hope snatched away, pains.” Browerus reports that, through the assistance of later witnesses, he restored it to its integrity.]

For the mother’s hope had been snatched away by powerful grief.

Nor does she comfort herself with the weeping of her own child.

She does not drink back the dear tears from the infant’s mouth,

Nor seize its tender cries while milk flows.

[Col. 0275C]

Sad in her aged grief, she condemns her own entrails [Note: The Paris edition: “by a blow.”],

Because the womb in which the child lay, alas, suffers [Note: The manuscript: “by which.”].

But if the child’s life remains, though it is not always to be preserved,

And it begins to utter tender sounds,

With its unfinished, unformed tongue striking together murmurs,

As the whisper nourishes its mother with a sweet voice,

And if an outrage should occur, and it be snatched from its mother’s breast,
Mature age grew to its own ruin.

The grieving mother, bereft and her hair torn out,

presses her dry breasts upon the lips of the dead.

Pouring out tears, burning with grief, she revives her laments,

and washes the cold body with a warm spring.

She tears her face, pulls out her hair, beats her breast—

alas, grief armed, thus she strikes her own limbs!

If she sees another’s child, she mourns her own pledges,

and sadly laments that her equal has died.

[Col. 0275D]

[Col. 0276A] If another child weeps, runs, stands, or rejoices,

the image of her own child plays before her eyes.

The one whom she once brought forth, she seeks at every moment,

and the child no longer looks into the unhappy mother’s face.

What if something still more grievous occurs, and her husband himself dies?

She who was a new bride now lies widowed.

From bridal chamber to tomb, just now white, so quickly black;

she holds the cold limbs before which her own had been warm.

She prepares the funeral rites, and, celebrating perverse vows,

alas, adorns the tomb by stripping the marriage-bed.

Often, with grief, she revisits the marital grave;

despising her household, she tends the bitter funeral.

She leans upon the tomb, seeking empty consolations,

and presses upon the bones the limbs she once pressed upon him.

[Col. 0276B] With streaming tears and a song doomed to perish, she mourns:

in performing the funeral service, love loses its eyes.

Who could unfold how many evils come upon the common woman?

The widowed woman scarcely fares well even as a queen.

I do not forbid marriage, but I prefer the virgin’s womb,

as Paul proclaims from the apostolic trumpet.

Illustrious virginity, by whose dowry you deserve the heavens,

you please, destined to be joined to Christ’s bridal chambers.

You mourn no funerals and receive joys without limit:

love lives forever, and Christ does not die for you.

There you hold kingdoms; here you conquer and shine undefiled,

safe in every place, sanctified to God.

These verses I offer to you, Agnes, dear to God and venerable for your merits.

May you cultivate them by doing what makes them pleasing.

That a gift may be granted to both by the Judge’s command:

[Col. 0276C] when a crown is given to you, then may pardon be given to me.

I pray that through these waves you, Christ, may guide our souls,

by the tree and the mast made to billow by the cross,

so that, after we have crossed the storms of the world’s whirlpool,

your right hand may set us in the harbor of life.

## CHAPTER VII

[Note: G. Fabricius first published this poem as a book under the title *On the Virgin’s Childbearing*, having obtained at Basel a celebrated manuscript of the Morbach Abbey. Although this poem was absent from all the old books that Browerus had possessed, he nevertheless did not hesitate, on the evidence of a manuscript from the monastery of Saint Gall and because of its similarity of style and expression, to place this poem also among the works of Fortunatus. We found it complete in one—and a very ancient—Vatican manuscript, formerly belonging to the Palatine Library. In it, after the *Life of Saint Martin* composed by Fortunatus in verse, this poem, in praise of the holy Virgin Mary, is written immediately afterward. It is absent, however, from the other three manuscripts that we have used up to this point. We have recorded variant readings taken both from the Vatican manuscript and from Fabricius’s Basel edition, prepared by Johann Oporinus in 1564.]

### In Praise of Saint Mary the Virgin and Mother of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0276C] He reviews the prophecies concerning the Virgin’s childbirth and also reports other oracles relating to Christ, the fruit of her womb. He then pursues at greater length the praises of that same Virgin and Mother of God, and describes the service rendered to her by the heavenly host and by all nature. Finally, he embraces her triumph and glory in heaven.]

The tongue of the prophets sang of childbirth from a virgin;

[Col. 0276D] an angel from heaven bears this announcement to the earth.

[Col. 0277A] The harmonious voice of men recalls that a girl would bear this:

that a virgin, without a man’s seed, would give birth to a man.

Isaiah, agreeing with the Gospel, proclaims this;

[Note: [Col. 0277D] In the Vatican manuscript, “Isaiah.” Fabricius likewise.]

he himself sings what God inspires through him:

a torrent in speech, speaking profound things with due order,

singing of Emmanuel, given by a virgin,

foretelling long ago that, in honor of the Mother of the Thunderer,

a virgin would give the flower of Jesse’s root.

[Note: [Col. 0277D] Fabricius reads: “a virgin would give a branch.”]

This virgin was that branch from which Christ, the flower, sprang,

[Note: [Col. 0277D] In the Vatican manuscript: “from which Christ the flower [sprang].”]

whose life-giving fragrance raises buried limbs.

Lazarus, lying loosened in death, touched by its perfume,

breathed again through his mouth after the fourth day.

Jeremiah, himself sanctified from the womb,

pointing her out in a like utterance, likewise says as a prophet:

“Behold, days will come, and I will raise up a shoot for David,

and he shall reign as King, and he shall be wise.”

[Col. 0277B] This righteous shoot is the virgin, and her King is the infant,

making judgment, the arbiter and lord of the world.

This woman was sung by the psalmist’s plectrum,

when voice, lyre, string, and chorus produced their melody by art.

“Mother Zion,” he says, “a man—and a man was made in her.”

He himself founded her, made in her, and is man.

[Note: [Col. 0277D] The same place has: “in her this man.”]

Thus, too, the one who founded her is himself the Most High:

this mother Zion was the Virgin Mary.

[Note: [Col. 0277D] Fabricius reads “here as though”; afterward the manuscript has “in the womb of the bridal chamber.”]

He who, like a bridegroom, comes forth from the high bridal chamber,

and Christ, like a giant, rejoices as he travels his way—

O bridal chamber of the womb, new conjunction of salvation,

by which God and flesh were joined in a new honor!

In it God embraced flesh, and joined flesh adhered;

God stands, and becomes man: Christ is both kinds.

[Col. 0277C] God was not changed into flesh; God assumes limbs;

he does not change himself, but raises limbs for himself.

Since his divinity could not be seen through open revelation,

he took on a veil, so that as flesh he might be seen as man.

One in both natures, true in both,

in one respect equal to his mother, in divinity equal to the Father.

He does not confuse his own nature, but joins all that is ours to himself,

the man whom both natures bring forth without sin.

Born from the Father, possessing what is divine, and from his mother what is human;

from the Father exalted, from his mother humble.

When, in pious fashion, the incorporeal being clothed himself with bodily limbs,

[Note: [Col. 0277D] The same place has: “the incorporeal one clothed himself with bodily limbs.”]

he became equal to his mother and thereby lower than the Father.

Flesh, soul, bones, skin, sinews, veins, thigh, and nails—

[Note: [Col. 0277D] The same place reads: “sinews, belly, thigh.”]

assuming the form of a servant, thereby lower than the Father.

But I return to the praises by which the virgin draws me to be sung:

[Col. 0277D] there was none like her, nor has any like her appeared.

The one whom the clouds rain down as righteous from heavenly dew,

this earth gave as Savior from its own seed.

This is the closed gate into which a man enters, and no one exits;

except the Lord alone, for whom even closed things are open.

At whose coming John leapt from the womb,

[Note: [Col. 0277D] In the Vatican manuscript: “the infant, not yet healed by the gift, sounded forth as a new herald.”]

and the infant sounded forth as a new herald in his office.

[Col. 0278A] Across his mother’s womb, as though seeing through a window,

the mother’s limbs became a window for the child.

When he leapt, greeting the womb from within the womb,

he traveled by movement, though his foot could not yet make a path.

[Note: [Col. 0278D] Fabricius reads: “he goes forth on the journey.”]

I believe he lay prostrate and stretched out his palms,

moving his little limbs before the Redeemer,

and, because he was not worthy to loosen the strap of his feet,

he worshiped prone, I believe, with trembling knee.

Noble Elizabeth, of whom the lofty prophet sings,

through God’s working brings forth these joyful shoots:

“O blessed among women, how has this happened to me,

that the gracious mother of my Lord should visit me?”

Gabriel calls this girl blessed with praise,

and rightly exalts her, since she bears new gifts.

She was destined to give birth to blessed fruit from her seed,

[Col. 0278B] of whom Jeremiah speaks with a thundering voice:

“This is our God; no other is counted beside him.

Afterward he appeared on earth and lived as a man.”

Daniel proclaims him the one Holy of Holies,

cut from the mountain, who is both angel and stone.

Of him Moses says: “Behold, God raises up a prophet,

[Note: [Col. 0278D] The same place has: “of whom Moses says, ‘God.’”]

for you, from among your brothers, the salvation of the world.

If any soul does not hear him, that prophet himself,

as avenger, will destroy him from his people.”

David said: “Kings will worship him with gifts,

the nations will serve, and Sheba will bring offerings.”

The righteous Simeon, receiving him in both hands,

[Note: [Col. 0278D] The same place has: “Old in years, he gave these pious words.”]

worn out with old age, spoke these pious words:

[Col. 0278C] “Now release your servant in peace, O author from on high,

for my eyes have now seen the fulfillment of my vows.

Since I have been worthy to receive this salvation,

according to your word, to bear God in my hands

and rightly behold him with my eyes.”

O sacred virgin of God, Mary, by giving birth to such a one,

through whom the people once sunk in darkness receive light,

in the region of the shadow of death light arose and shone:

[Note: [Col. 0278D] The same place has: “the light itself.”]

“Wonderful is this counselor.”

[Note: [Col. 0278D] In the Vatican manuscript: “This is Wonderful, Counselor”; the *est* (“is”) has been wrongly transposed from the Greek τῷ.]

He is God the Strong, the Father, and prince forever,

whose empire’s peace remains without end.

The heavens rained down clouds and poured forth the righteous one,

whom the virgin gave as Savior from her own seed.

[Note: [Col. 0278D] The same place has: “Egypt, the labor of the Ethiopians.”]

Egypt, the labor of the Ethiopians, and lofty Sabaeans

[Note: [Col. 0278D] Fabricius reads: “and the wealthy Sabaeans”; our manuscript likewise.]

will pass over to him, following God in their minds.

In him alone there is God, and there is no God apart from him:

this is the hidden God, who is the God of Israel.

His righteousness is the belt around his loins,

[Col. 0278D] and faith is the girdle around his kidneys.

The hand dares to enter the hole of the basilisk and the asp;

the weaned child plays there, and none of them harms him.

Standing as a sign for the peoples—and his tomb,

how great a glory covers it, noble and worthy of worship!

He whom he sent as ruler of the earth to the Moabites,

the rock from the desert, who is present as a pious lamb.

[Col. 0279A] Of him Zechariah says: “Rejoice, daughter of Zion:

behold, your righteous one, your Savior, your King is coming.”

Riding upon an ass, and also upon the foal of an ass,

[Note: [Col. 0279D] Fabricius reads: “destroying the chariots of Ephraim”; another reading is: “and destroying the chariot from Ephraim.”]

destroying the chariots of Ephraim and the horse.

Hence Micah also says: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrata,

though little among the thousands of Judah, you remain.”

From you will go forth the one who rules Israel,

whose going forth has been powerful from the beginning.

The light of the holy ones in splendors, whom the Father

begot from the womb before Lucifer.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] In the Vatican manuscript: “healing our bruises with blessed bruising.”]

He heals our bruises with a blessed bruise,

and washes away the old stains of blood with a stream.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] The same place reads: “washing [them] in a stream.”]

O distinguished virgin, our remedy, Monad (*monas*),

[Note: [Col. 0279D] Writers of this period commonly called Eve *Monas*, as Browerus observes, because she was the mother of all living. *Monas*, or unity, is the simple and primary element used as the principal cause, since it generates every number and is generated by no number. Thus Hermes Trismegistus says in the *Pimander*: “The Monad is the beginning, root, and origin of all things,” and so forth. Fortunatus applies *monas* here to Saint Mary in this sense: life somehow began for human beings through her, from whom Christ arose like a flower from Jesse’s branch. Georg Fabricius reads the verse as: “O distinguished virgin, gracious mother, noble seed.”]

whom God filled with the resources of the whole world.

You who were worthy to hold the Creator in your womb,

[Col. 0279B] and, conceiving through faith, to give birth to God.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Fabricius reads: “and to generate the day.” Browerus likewise, although the Lyon edition of the Fathers reads “and to generate God,” which is not displeasing.]

By a new birth cleansing the world from guilt,

and by sacred offspring destined to bring forth God.

The pains which Eve bore for the human race,

your offspring, O Virgin Mary, healed.

The scar driven into the stock by sin’s arrow

bears no ulcers, and its marks are no longer visible.

For the bitter sap of the forbidden tree’s bark

tastes sweet because of the Redeemer standing upon the cross.

Then death hung from the foliage under the appearance of an apple;

now your womb is the fruit—here food, there salvation.

With holy and pious fruit you renewed the ages of the world,

and, as you give birth, the day shines more brightly.

After darkness, your womb recalls the sun to the world,

[Note: [Col. 0280D] The same place reads: “your womb recalls it.”]

when the crown of the Lord has radiated its splendor.

[Col. 0279C] The light of the world dwells in you in a shining station;

God flowered inwardly through your limbs.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] In the Vatican manuscript: “Then a living [radiance].”]

Now a living radiance penetrates to the depths of the abyss,

nourishes the world, rules the stars, and fills Tartarus with light.

The whole fabric of this world is covered by his single fist,

yet, chaste girl, he is enclosed within your womb.

The thing made bears its Maker, and humanity bears the Thunderer;

the little rod bears the root, made the Creator’s help.

How did those limbs contain the new light?

What beauty was within, and what honor came forth from it?

How great were the joys that your happy womb carried,

when, pressing upon your limbs, it made the greater burden lighter?

Then the mother, lightened of her burden and made whole by her offspring,

bearing the thing of splendor, had light that was no burden.

[Col. 0280A] Bearing help from the flower and relief from the fruit,

bearing the hope and bread of heaven as a fresh ear of grain.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] The same place has: “bearing a new harvest.” Fabricius likewise.]

The morning star and the sun were in her womb,

while beneath the ark she concealed the radiance of the shining moon.

Carrying the year-old lamb and the ancient giant,

and the strong lion who was from the tribe of Judah.

Producing horns like a rhinoceros,

lofty, snorting high with raised nostrils.

The young serpent and the asp yield to him, and all poisons—

the viper, the dipsas, the seps, the dragon, the *cenchris*, and the hydra.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Fabricius reads *chesydros*, *seps*.]

[Note: [Col. 0280D] The same place has *hybris*, perhaps *hydris*.]

The child himself is little, yet an ancient person of days,

whose coming forth stands without beginning.

Grace blooms, spread upon his lips:

[Note: [Col. 0280D] In the Vatican manuscript: “beautiful in form”; Fabricius reads: “O form radiant.”]

distinguished in form above those born of men.

His name of honor is the rising from on high,

[Col. 0280B] who visits us, bringing light, in the darkness.

He comes from Edom, from Bozrah with bloodied garments,

beautiful, bloodstained, white, and red.

He was to tread the lofty winepress alone,

to be weighed upon the cross, bathing his limbs in blood.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Fabricius reads: “who alone was to tread the winepress.”]

[Note: [Col. 0280D] The same place has: “to be hung upon the cross.”]

Hence his white robe, mingled with and dyed by red,

belongs to him before or after whom there is no other God.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] In the Vatican manuscript: “whom no other God will precede, nor will there be any after him.”]

His sacred magnificence surpasses heaven,

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Fabricius reads: “the heavens.”]

ruling all things with his palm—stars, fields, and seas.

What awareness did you then possess, holy mother of the Lord,

when such an offspring, new in honor, was yours?

How many rewards filled your womb, and joys your breast,

when your earth bore the Maker of the heavens?

O radiant in merits, tell me, virgin: do you think you saw

the angelic courses going and returning anew?

[Note: [Col. 0280D] The same place has: “O form radiant.”]

[Col. 0280C] Did you feel the army of heaven taking turns to serve you,

often raising its hands in attendance?

What host surrounded you, or, whenever you prepared to travel,

how many thousands accompanied your steps in advance?

What would Michael the leader do beneath the highest prince?

What would Gabriel, that sacred messenger, undertake?

How would Raphael graciously prepare to meet you,

while you carried God and he thought you were his throne?

I believe one wished to spread his palms beneath your feet;

another, shaking out his wing, would make the road gleam beneath you.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] The same place reads: “he himself would loosen the day.”]

One would drive away the breezes so that the oppressive heat would not burn you;

another, lifting his wings, would turn the rainwater aside.

One would hold his hand to the reins, lest the burden slip,

and would forbid the fluttering crowd to trip your foot.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] The Vatican manuscript and Fabricius both read: “the flying crowd.”]

[Col. 0281A] How many watchful troops, when deep sleep possessed you,

would you alone, sleeping, cause to keep watch?

With stellar service, O virgin most worthy of your merits,

while the wing of divine choirs encircled you.

At whose pure honor the sun itself would tremble at its rising,

[Note: [Col. 0281D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “at whose sacred honor.”]

and the moon would seek to be beneath your feet.

The structure of the world would submit to its own Maker,

and marvel at God through your limbs.

O excellent virgin, surpassing all mothers,

whom your race exalted, to whom God gave lofty things!

Your fruit is present, and the flower does not lose its honors:

you are mother through your child, and remain a virgin.

Blessed are you, who for the human race fallen beneath Tartarus

were made a lot, a way, a gate, and a wheel to the heavens.

Hall of God, adornment of paradise, glory of the kingdom,

[Col. 0281B] dwelling of life, bridge by which the heavens are entered.

You shine as the ark and mighty sheath of the two-edged sword,

the rising altar of God, the lofty beacon of light.

High above cedars and the broad summits of the mountain,

and beneath your feet stands even the wheel of the sun.

Leader of the virginal company, first among the second sex,

you alone, a girl, are preferred to the star-bearing choirs.

The potter’s creation, more beautiful than all vessels,

and the shining substance of the new creation.

Beautiful lampstand, receiving the lamp of the Word,

whose form the Craftsman sculpted so high above the stars.

Adornment of holy Jerusalem, beautiful loveliness,

a vessel of honor to God before the temple’s face.

Surpassing the gates of Zion with flashing radiance,

standing by the merit of faith, a proud jewel of the throne.

[Col. 0281C] With your mouth hurling day, shooting rays from your brow,

[Note: [Col. 0281D] Fabricius reads: “shooting arrows.”]

with ruddy eyes, turning light in honor.

Starry mirror, illustrious house of the Almighty,

bearing bright flashes from those faces.

Honored name, blessed Mary throughout the ages,

noble work of the Maker’s noble art.

Sweet girl, precious in angelic report,

possessing gifts of beauty beyond all human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] So too Fabricius; others incorrectly read “beyond man.”]

Here surpassing roses in redness, there lilies in whiteness,

a new flower from the earth, which heaven may worship in its citadel.

Crystal, electrum, gold, purple dye, white shell, emerald—

all metals lie defeated by the radiance of your beauty.

Snow is oppressed by your whiteness, the sun by your hair’s splendor.

The rays grow pale before your beauty, O virgin.

[Col. 0281D] The lamp-bearing stone is dim; blazing Lucifer yields to you.

In every office you surpass the lamp.

Aware on earth of the highest hidden sacrament,

the secrets of heaven have been disclosed to you.

Worthy field of the Lord, generating fruit without seed,

and pleasing, lest the crop be fruitless, when filled with harvest.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] In the Vatican manuscript: “and lest the crop be narrow.” Fabricius likewise.]

Alone fertile without example and free from bondage,

a rich mother in your womb, ignorant of embraces.

[Col. 0282A] A virgin remaining untouched, married through the abundance of faith,

unacquainted with marriage, pregnant while a man denied it.

You receive without knowing; thus you give back while remaining whole.

You neither bear violated nor suffer in bearing.

And yet God and man has been born, true and one:

Christ, spirit and flesh, both kinds.

Equal to the Father in divinity, and to his mother in bodily form,

[Note: [Col. 0281D] Fabricius reads “but”; the manuscript likewise.]

and flesh from his mother without sin.

The Maker, giving the law, made a servant under the law:

he himself is the world’s father, and he himself is your son.

Thus, mother, you give birth to your son and parent:

here a son, there a father; this is God, that is earth.

By his sacred honor, O mother, you surpass Olympus,

and raise your face above the star-bearing heavens.

[Col. 0282B] You are established upon a proud throne, a blessed queen,

and are encircled, a milk-white virgin, by snowy choirs.

More noble than the noble senate surrounding you,

you yourself sit higher than lofty consuls.

Thus, beside the king begotten from you, an eternal queen,

adorned by your childbirth, a bountiful mother.

The nobles approach, and John, great in glory,

known to God before he suffered as man.

[Note: [Col. 0282D] The same place has: “before man was made to suffer.”]

With the ascended brothers and the rest of the blessed,

[Note: [Col. 0282D] The same place has: “Paul.”]

Paul, the apostolic teacher, and Peter, the shining palm.

Jacob loves these gates of Zion above all,

those whom God brought forth in love for the patriarchs.

All of them, adorned by their own mouths, flash above the stars,

[Note: [Col. 0282D] “Adorned with gold”; the manuscript.]

If such are the disciples, what will the holy mother be?

Then, with the company of the patriarchs,

[Col. 0282C] the prophets assemble to bring gifts to the lofty throne.

Here and there a cohort of martyrs, crowned with wreaths,

[Note: [Col. 0282D] “Here and there a cohort”; the manuscript has *choros*, “choirs.”]

with Stephen as their leader, the citizen host of heaven.

The firstfruits of the flowers, the Bethlehem passion nursing at the breast,

which, born, deserved to live more through death.

Those whom Rome, the head of Italy and of the world, holds,

or the city of Alexandria, or the Antiochene land;

those whom Jerusalem or Byzantium holds in its regions;

those whom Patras holds, those whom Ephesus, those whom Naddaver holds in its citadel.

Those whom East and West possess, whom Africa and the North possess,

and those whom earth buries and the Ocean encircles—

nation, race, people, regions, armies, kings,

running from every side toward the Father’s new gifts.

Ethiopians, Thracians, Arabs, Dacians, Indians, Alans,

the dawn and the evening, Persians and Britons are present.

[Col. 0282D] Entering the kingdoms of God, redeemed through piety,

to see the king’s joys in the citadel of heaven.

Those whom Peter’s sacred gate receives, those whom Paul’s door receives,

Achaea seeks at Andrew’s threshold.

[Note: [Col. 0282D] The manuscript reads: “it lies open.”]

Matthew has the Ethiopians; John’s door, the Ephesians;

and whoever loves someone, that person’s own gate invites him.

Before their arrival, how does the lover adorn you,

blessed virgin, whose womb carried him?

[Col. 0283A] Giving you the abundance of heaven, for whom you were a narrow house,

he restores a throne in exchange for the hospitality of your womb.

He arranges your white head with a golden diadem,

and adorns your shining hair with the honor of jewels;

fastening precious necklaces around your white neck,

[Note: [Col. 0283D] In the Vatican manuscript: “covering your pure breast with varied splendors.”]

and covering your pure breast with varied brilliance.

How beautiful a mantle of honor he places upon your shoulders—

purple dyed and glowing with splendor!

O how often the molten gold flashes on the belt,

and the pale fringe of the cloak shines with light!

Who could sing what is worthy of you, how much beauty comes from your mouth,

or what jewel gleams green from your garment?

When a precious emerald lies spread beneath your feet,

when a white topaz is present upon the pavement.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] The same place has: “a topaz is present.” Fabricius likewise.]

[Col. 0283B] What the eye has not seen in its activity, nor the ear heard,

these ornaments, holy virgin, shine for you.

When the kingdom of heaven, therefore, and the whole army of the stars

shall behold you adorned, they move their mouths in praise.

Michael begins to proclaim the praises of the blessed one,

and with his troops reports this to you, O virgin:

“O excellent glory, O woman, beauty of salvation,

[Note: [Col. 0283D] Fabricius reads: “O woman, fame of salvation.”]

powerful in the fruit of childbirth, pleasing in virginity!

Through whom the world’s redemption deigned to be born,

and to restore the race that savage Eve destroyed.

To you, mother, a thousand thousand legions offer this aid;

their companies resound in song, voice, and lyre.”

Then the angel, your attendant, repeats your honors,

who brings you holy announcements from heaven.

He says: “O blessed virgin, incapable of imitation,

whose lamb crushes the mouths of the wolf.

[Col. 0283C] Breaking open Tartarus, bringing back the captives of their homeland,

you restore to liberty those who had been pressed beneath the yoke.”

Another part receives these praises and repeats them,

and the echoed voice resounds through all the choirs.

Then the earth begins to bring forth other favors:

the voice, trumpet, herald, and sound born of Zechariah,

with Peter and Stephen, and leaders amid great thousands

of assembled troops, sings loudly with mingled applause:

“O distinguished virgin, born for blessed joys,

help of earth, radiance and honor of heaven.

Behold what your flowering womb has bestowed upon the world:

because you give birth in faith, paradise possesses us.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] The same place has: “when you give birth.”]

What are we, or what were we? Those whom Eve had plunged into the depths—

your womb makes us go from clay to heaven.”

[Col. 0283D] At these praises, O mother of the Lord, thunder crashes among the stars,

and the army of heaven sounds this trumpet for you.

But although I wish to bear them, I seem to diminish your praises,

for each person longs to favor you with sacred voice.

Let the mind pray to the one begotten, and speak words worthy of his mother,

through whose pious love you live in new honor.

[Col. 0284A] Beautiful above jewels, overshadowing the sun’s splendor,

lofty above the heavens and shining above the stars;

whiter than snowy fleece, more radiant than gold,

brighter than a ray, sweeter than honey to the mouth,

more pleasing, and far redder than rose-colored purple,

you surpass fragrant hair in the scent of your mind.

Dear, kind, shining, pious, holy, reverend, beautiful—

flower, honor, altar, radiance, palm, crown, modesty.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] The same author alters the final verses as follows:

“All the ends of the earth have now earned salvation,

through Christ, your son, Virgin Mary,

born from the eternal Father for you at the appointed time,

who is my hope of pardon and cause of salvation. Amen.”]

Through him all the ends of the earth have earned salvation,

and the whole world rejoices: sea, shore, and heaven.

These praises I whisper to you, although unworthy in heart and mouth:

may you be my hope of pardon, you who bear the world’s salvation.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Note: [Col. 0283D] This poem seems to me to have been written by Fortunatus under the names of Agnes and Radegund, to exhort and invite virgins to the monastery at Poitiers and to profess there the discipline of monastic life under the rule of Saint Caesarius; this seems clearly shown by the following couplet:

“Poverty, though small, asks you, together with the wealthy Christ,

to come into our embrace, sweet foster-child.”]

### To the Virgins

[Col. 0284B] [Note: He praises virginity and describes the happiness and glory of virgins in heaven. From this he exhorts virgins to preserve chastity, both of soul and of body.]

Among the apostolic ranks and sacred prophets,

the virgin holds rewards next to the martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0284D] This poem, like the others that follow, is absent from one Vatican manuscript.]

Shining, surrounded by starry light, she advances;

the chaste girl is joined to the angelic choirs.

With the fruit of chastity, destined to be endowed with heaven’s talent,

she is led into the bridal chambers of the eternal King.

A beautiful crown encircles her head with a triple diadem,

[Note: [Col. 0284D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “and a jewel adorns.”]

and jewels adorn her breasts, neck, and hair.

Purple is added to her tender limbs,

and a mantle shining with the whiteness of snow covers her.

[Col. 0284C] Roses among eternal flowers feed her eyes, lilies feed them too,

and a paradisiacal fragrance enters her nostrils.

Therefore, dear one, we urge you all the more to seek these things,

which Christ gave to Eugenia and gracious Thecla.

Virgin of God, fruit of heaven, victory of the world,

seek these royal riches, that you may reign forever.

There are palaces built of gems of chrysolite,

and a doorway shines green upon an emerald post.

[Note: [Col. 0284D] Another manuscript reads: “sardonyx thresholds.”]

Sardonyx thresholds bloom with varied light,

and a hyacinth-colored row encircles the house.

Golden roofs glitter, a golden people shines in the hall,

and a radiant crowd gleams with the gracious king.

That is the place of girls who, from love of the light,

preserve faith in the Lord here, in body and mind.

Despise what belongs to earth, and you will sit brightly among the stars,

so that, pleasing as Christ’s bride, you may cultivate the heavenly kingdoms.

The present life passes in a time far too fleeting;

the integrity of the virgin remains to be glorified.

Poverty, though small, asks you, together with the wealthy Christ,

to come into our embrace, sweet foster-child,

[Col. 0285A] where you will pray to obtain the Father’s help from the Lord,

and acquire blessed kingdoms for yourself.

[Note: [Col. 0285C] The Paris edition reads: “and seek blessed kingdoms.”]

So that, joined to holy Mary, you may deserve equally

to celebrate perpetual joys in the choir.

Whatever pledges you receive with pious hands,

do not marry a man, but be loved by God.

## CHAPTER IX

[Note: [Col. 0285A] He commemorates the glory of the saints in heaven and prays for their intercession—and especially that of the most holy Mother of God—against the snares of the common enemy. Finally, he commends the majesty and greatness of the Godhead.]

### Metrica

[Note: [Col. 0285C] This poem is found in one Vatican manuscript, among the three that we have used up to this point, at the end of Fortunatus’s works. It seemed worthwhile to transcribe it, since it does not appear alien to Fortunatus’s style. It is an acrostic and consists of as many verses as there are letters in the first verse; this kind of poem was, as we have seen elsewhere, familiar to Fortunatus. This, however, is why the thoughts of the poem, constrained by the letters, do not always seem to be accurately connected with one another. It is found in the manuscript in a very corrupt state, apparently through the copyist’s ignorance. We have corrected some passages, relegating faulty readings to the notes; elsewhere we have conjectured how they should be read and have indicated our conjectures in the same place; elsewhere, since nothing worthy of Fortunatus came to mind, we have altered nothing and have left them corrupt as they are read in the manuscript.]

Let the novices now bring forth chaste songs,

and let the virgin receive praise in a square poem.

[Note: [Col. 0285D] I suppose that poem was called “square” because it contained as many verses as there were letters in the first verse, and each verse consisted of the same number of letters. Here we see the first, but not the latter, feature preserved in this poem.]

The triune God who rules in the citadel created the ages,

[Note: [Col. 0286C] Perhaps: “pale” (*pallens*).]

the ruler of the world reigning in lofty seats,

[Col. 0285B] may deign to grant me, unworthy as I am, for eternity,

rest with the saints whom I praise in these verses.

The high-throned Judge, who preserves the heavenly scepters,

gave these men to climb the threshold of heaven through fair weather,

so that among the ranks of the saints, with perpetual praise,

they might duly glorify the Thunderer who governs the kingdoms.

Almighty Lord, creator and maker of the world,

grant us poor ones sure intercession,

and do not permit us to be handed over to enemies there;

but, defending the insignificant, may your right hand touch us,

lest the deceitful robber close the threshold of heaven,

or the spectacle of sins deceive the saints,

lest the twisting thief (*strophosus*) thrust us into the black pit,

[Note: [Col. 0286C–D] *Strophosus* appears to stand for “tortuous”; Greek στροφή means “a turning.” The manuscript reads *strofosus*; it subsequently reads *detrudet* (“will thrust down”).]

which Christ, the Creator, guards from the highest Olympus,

the shepherd watching over the fold; nor may the robber snatch those perhaps “taken from the breast,”

[Note: [Col. 0286D] Perhaps: “those snatched from the breast” (*ab ubere raptos*).]

while devastating the royal pens—an exceedingly corrupt passage, perhaps “to carry off [them], the wolf” (*abducere lupus*).

[Note: [Col. 0286D] This passage is most corrupt; the editor could scarcely offer even a conjecture for its emendation. Perhaps: *abducere lupus*.]

[Col. 0285C] But may the guardian now defend every fold,

the greatest, which bears the foremost name.

Mother, deign to add protection through prayer;

for you have brought forth eternal light from light,

[Note: [Col. 0286D] Perhaps: “They praise you.”]

*Inantque*, going forth as the sacred breath cries—

[Note: [Col. 0286D] Perhaps: “They praise you” (*Te laudant*).]

whose great radiance shines from the lofty axis,

and whose stream fills peoples equally with its vibration.

The King of kings and prince of peoples, named from eternity,

great ruler from great rule over all things.

The heavens cannot bind or gird him,

[Note: [Col. 0286D] “Not” was not added by the editor.]

[Note: [Col. 0286D] *De superabat* (“he surpassed”) is against the meter.]

[Col. 0286A] nor does the sea, navigable with its foaming flood, enclose him,

nor the zones of the world that hem in the lofty ether.

I, a poor man, will undertake through holy efforts

to proclaim the life of the illustrious, who there,

with God’s help, flourished with everlasting bloom

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The manuscript reads *vernebat*, “was flourishing.”]

in chaste conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0286D] Perhaps: “So great and worthy.”]

If such a poor man loses rewards so great and worthy,

when no one explains everything in words, and suitably

[Note: [Col. 0286D] “And” was added by the editor.]

Enough [lacuna].

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The final verse is found thus in the manuscript: “Sot sac anim nec lux mor ponum se noririta cirtem”; from these words I could extract nothing.]

## CHAPTER X

### To the Lady Radegund

[Note: [Col. 0286A] He praises Radegund for despising the world and royal power, and foretells that an equal reward for her piety and labors will await her in heaven.]

Powerful Radegund, of royal stock in the world,

for whom another kingdom remains to be held in heaven,

[Col. 0286B] despising the world, you deserved to acquire Christ,

and, while you lie hidden behind closed doors, from here you see beyond the stars.

You trample underfoot the guilty joys of earthly rule,

so that you may please the joyful king, with heaven favoring you.

Now you dwell in narrow quarters, so that you may enter more spacious heavens;

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The Paris edition reads: “shedding tears.”]

shedding tears, you will reap true joys.

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The Paris edition reads: “while the body”; and near the end of the verse, one Vatican manuscript reads: “fasts nourish.”]

And you torment your body, while fasts nourish your soul.

Hail, you whom your Lord preserves in love.

## CHAPTER XI

### To the Same, on Violets

[Note: [Col. 0286B] He excuses himself to Radegund for sending violets rather than lilies and roses as a gift. He praises the violets themselves for the excellence of their color and fragrance, and from this exhorts her, as well as Agnes, to cultivate virtue.]

If the usual season brought me shining lilies,

[Col. 0286C] or if a beautiful rose had been available with its sweet redness,

I, gathering these from the countryside or from the turf of a poor garden,
