[Note: [Col. 0286D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “I would rather have sent.”]

would gladly have sent small gifts as great ones.

But since the first are lacking to me, I offer what is second-best:

he who brings violets also brings roses with love.

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The same place reads: “would bring them with love.”]

Among the fragrant herbs, however, these that we have sent

bear the noble offspring of purple violets.

They breathe forth fragrance alike, dyed with royal purple,

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The Paris edition reads: “shining in royal fashion.”]

and from their leaves one side is filled with scent, the other with color.

Since it bears both alike, may you two possess both,

and may the fragrance be the gift, the flower its enduring beauty.

## CHAPTER XII

### To the Same, on Flowers for the Altar

[Col. 0287A] [Note: [Col. 0287A] After the winter cold and frosts, he says that flower-bearing spring has arrived, and consequently praises the zeal and diligence of Radegund and Agnes in adorning the altars with wreaths and flowers. He describes their appearance and manifold variety in a lively and elegant manner.]

The world is bound by the ice of winter’s cold,

and all the light of the fields perishes when the flowers fall.

[Note: [Col. 0287D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “with the flower absent.”]

In springtime, when the Lord conquered Tartarus,

the grass rises more joyfully with perfect crowns.

[Note: [Col. 0287D] The same place reads: “the perfect grass rises.”]

Then men adorn doorposts and platforms with flowers,

while women fill their bosoms with a rose-colored fragrance.

But you bring fragrances not for yourselves, but for Christ,

and offer these firstfruits to the pious temples.

[Col. 0287B] You weave festive altars with varied wreaths;

the altar is painted with new flowers as though with threads.

A golden row of crocuses; here, a purple row of violets—
he/she/it goes out,
Crimson reddens here; there, milky white, it gleams like snow.

Blue-green stands firm, and the colors contend in their flowers;

in a peaceful place you might think that grassy wars were being fought.

This one pleases by its whiteness; that one flashes with ruddy beauty;

this one smells more sweetly; that one reddens more beautifully.

Thus, in varied appearance, the flowers’ shoots contend with one another,

so that one surpasses gems in color, another incense in fragrance.

May your fragrance also, Agnes and Radegund, who arrange these things,

breathe forth amid everlasting flowers.

## CHAPTER XIII. To the same woman, concerning flowers sent to her

[Note: [Col. 0287C] He sends flowers to Radegund, excusing the smallness of the gift; and, taking occasion from them, raises her toward hope and contemplation of heavenly things.]

O powerful queen, for whom gold and purple are worthless,

a loving man pays you homage with small flowers.

And although color is not itself a possession, nevertheless it is present in the grasses:

purple in violets, golden form in saffron.

Rich in the love of God, you have avoided the rewards of the world;

despising those things, you will retain these riches.

Receive the gift of flowers of many kinds sent to you,

to which blessed life rather calls you.

You who now afflict yourself, to be renewed in the light to come,

behold here what kind of field will receive you.

Through the fragile branches that we now offer, fragrant with scent,

consider how great a fragrance will refresh you there.

[Col. 0287D] To whom these things are owed, I pray that, when you have gone there,

a gentle right hand may draw me there also through your merits.

Although the grace of the flowers of paradise awaits you,

these flowers already desire to see you again at their doors.

And although they seem pleasing through their excellent fragrance,

they adorn their own crowns more richly when you return.

[Note: [Col. 0287D] One Vatican manuscript has *est tamen ipse* (“nevertheless it is itself”).]

[Note: [Col. 0287D] The Paris edition reads *gloria florum* (“the glory of the flowers”).]

[Note: [Col. 0287D] From this it is clear that the poem was written at the time when Radegund was already keeping herself enclosed; this was her custom every year during the sacred season of Lent, as we noted in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 82, and as the following poems show.]

## CHAPTER XIV. To the same woman, when she withdrew into seclusion

[Col. 0288A]

[Note: [Col. 0288A] Fortunatus follows Radegund in this poem when she was about to shut herself away, and declares his longing for her.]

Radegund, mind fruitful in God, life of the sisters,

who, to nourish your soul, wear down your limbs by subduing them,

observing your yearly vows, you return today to be enclosed;

my thoughts will wander, seeking you again.

How quickly you hide your eyes from our eyes,

for without you I am oppressed when night weighs heavily.

With everyone shut out, you will be confined in a single cave;

you enclose us even more, whom you make to be outside.

And although you hide here, a fugitive for a few brief days,

this month here will be longer than a swiftly passing year;

you withdraw the seasons, as though you were not seen by one who loves you,

although, while I behold you, I believe this is too little for me.

[Col. 0288B] Nevertheless, in accordance with my vow, we shall come together with you,

and in spirit I follow here, where the place forbids me to go.

This I pray: may the joys of Easter bring you back safe and sound,

and may doubled light return equally to us.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] One Vatican manuscript reads *largior hic mensis* (“this month is more abundant”).]

[Note: [Col. 0288D] The Paris edition reads *domando premis* (“you press down by subduing”).]

[Note: [Col. 0288D] Read *Fortunatus*, in the *Life of Saint Radegund*, no. 11.]

## CHAPTER XV. To the same woman, when she returned

[Note: [Col. 0288B] Fortunatus congratulates Radegund after she has returned from her withdrawal. With her return, he declares that everything has blossomed again for him, and that the abundance of the whole year has been represented to him in her return.]

Whence has the radiant face returned to me with shining light?

What delays held you away for so long?

You took my joys away with you and bring them back with you;

you make me celebrate Easter Day twice.

[Col. 0288C] Although the seeds are only now beginning to rise from the furrows,

here I myself reap today, as I see you again.

I already gather the crops and arrange peaceful sheaves;

what the month of August usually does, April is now doing.

And although at first only the bud and the tendril emerge,

my autumn has already come, and the grape with it.

The apple tree and the lofty pear tree are only now pouring forth pleasant fragrances,

but already they bear new fruit for me with their blossom.

Although the naked field is adorned with no ears of grain,

nevertheless, with your return, everything shines full.

## CHAPTER XVI. To Bishop Gregory, concerning his illness

[Note: [Col. 0288C] When Fortunatus was suffering from fever in the countryside, he relates that Gregory of Tours sent the presbyter Leo to him, inviting him to come and celebrate the sacred festivals of Martin. He describes the condition of his health and the character of his illness, and reports that it subsided when sweat appeared.]

The holy voice of the physician Gregory came to the sick man,

from the city of Tours, while I lay on a rural bed,

when the serene presbyter Leo urgently recited

that I should go where the festivals of holy Martin were being celebrated.

[Col. 0289A] Then, I confess, suffering from the grave weakness of disease,

burning with the highest fever, I was already inwardly rigid.

Reduced from excessive frailty to powerful languor,

I raised my weary flank; my breath was diseased.

A dry vapor passed through my panting mouth, scorching it;

a fiery breath came from my hidden depths, seething.

I was wholly fever, a mournful pyre, a burning furnace,

and fever stood openly revealed in my very fibers.

Until Christ poured forth help with streaming sweat,

and the burning fire drove away the icy waters.

Health itself is restored, gracious Father; I salute salvation;

I beg you, shepherd, to be an aid to your exiled sheep.

[Note: [Col. 0288D] Leo here seems to be no one other than the man whom Gregory of Tours mentions in Book IV of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 25, in these words: “Leo, our presbyter, in the vernacular …”; through his prayers and the patronage of Saint Martin, Gregory relates that a girl was delivered from fever and the danger of imminent death.]

[Note: [Col. 0289C] One Vatican manuscript reads *febre calens summa* (“burning with the highest fever”). The Trier manuscript and other books have:

“Burning with the highest fever, I was already inwardly rigid.”

The Cologne manuscript has *non rigor imus eram* (“I was not inwardly rigid”). Pulmann corrected it to *jam rigor unus eram* (“I was already wholly rigidity”). These readings are from Browerus. The Paris edition has *imus erant*.]

[Note: [Col. 0289C] The Paris edition reads *flatibus aura* (“a breath from the blasts”).]

[Note: [Col. 0289C] One Vatican manuscript reads *operta patens* (“covered, yet open”). The Paris edition has the same reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0289D] Browerus corrected this verse, which was corruptly read in the books as follows:

“Restore this, gracious Father; I salute salvation with a greeting.”

Or:

“May health be present, gracious Father, for salvation.”

One Vatican manuscript corruptly reads:

“Health is restored to him, gracious Father; I salute salvation.”

The Paris edition gives it as: “And thus health was restored.”]

## CHAPTER XVII. To the same man, concerning the affair of the abbess

[Note: [Col. 0289A] Fortunatus implores Gregory’s help against a grave disorder which, apparently, had crept into the monastery at Poitiers.]

[Note: [Col. 0289D] In this poem Fortunatus seems clearly to be speaking of the serious disturbances and dissensions that invaded the monastery at Poitiers after the death of blessed Radegund. Chrodieldis, a religious woman and, as she herself claimed, daughter of King Charibert, kindled their flame; and the dissension, fed by her fury, proceeded so far that matters reached sacrilegious and savage killings, along with other crimes. On these events, see Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book IX, chapter 39 and following. The Paris edition reads *repsit tale nefas* (“such an outrage crept in”); in the following verse it reads *verba putas* (“you think the words”).]

What sort of outrage has crept within the holy enclosure of the community?

Unconsidered grief, you forbid me to break into speech.

Such an outrage as previously neither polluted open ears before your eyes,

nor would those who honor their own shrines commit through vice.

Nevertheless, holy Father, labor out of love for piety,

as the sacred bishop whose heights you possess,

whence you represent Martin in sacred time,

giving aid for salvation through your journeys and faith.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Letter concerning the same matter

[Note: [Col. 0289B] He entrusts the same matter that he commends to Gregory in the preceding poem, sending his fellow presbyter to him, and asks, through the vows and memory of blessed Radegund, that he come to the aid of her monastery in its afflicted condition.]

Commending my humility to your most abundant sweetness and gentlest lordship, I suggest that, since the cause of the universal Church has you as its foundation, no leaning blast of wind and no mass of driving storms may there find anything that it can shake or overthrow. In this matter my fellow presbyter, bearer of this letter, comes confidently to you for singular protection, as he himself will be able to explain each detail.

Remember the commendation of my blessed lady, your daughter—or now already your mother—Lady Radegund, concerning the stability of her place, her person, and the whole rule. Since she requested this and entrusted it to you with the supplication of her words and inward feelings, order that tireless labour be undertaken, so that he who provides aid to those in need may himself recompense you in eternity.

[Col. 0290A] In the affair of Justina, may your apostolate labor pastorally.

[Note: [Col. 0290C] The Paris edition reads *habeat basidem* (“may it have a foundation”), followed immediately by *turbo vacillans* (“a wavering storm”).]

[Note: [Col. 0290C] One Vatican manuscript reads *quod labefactet, reperiat* (“may it find something to weaken”); the Paris edition has *aut quod lubefactatum* (“or something already weakened”).]

[Note: [Col. 0290C] The Paris edition reads *supplicatio* (“supplication”).]

[Note: [Col. 0290C] One Vatican manuscript reads *in causa justitiae* (“in the affair of justice”). The same occurs in another Vatican manuscript. This Justina—for whom *justitia* (“justice”) mistakenly entered the manuscripts cited above—was superior of the monastery at Poitiers when the serious seditions mentioned earlier arose. When assassins sought the abbess’s life, she covered her with the altar cloth; afterward she allowed herself to be led away in the abbess’s place, without revealing who she was. Later, when recognized, she was released and returned to the monastery. These events occurred around the year 589; see Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 15.]

[Note: [Col. 0290D] One Vatican manuscript reads *pastoraliter quod desudet* (“may it sweat pastorally”); another has *quod se subdat* (“may it submit itself”); the Paris edition reads *desudet* (“may it sweat”).]

## CHAPTER XIX. To the same man in the name of Justina

[Note: [Col. 0290D] The learned Ruinart supposes, in his additions and corrections to the notes on Saint Gregory of Tours, that this Justina was the daughter of Justin, who is called the husband of Gregory’s sister in Book II of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 2. Certainly, in Book IX, chapter 7, Fortunatus, addressing his little book and instructing it to greet Gregory in Justina’s name, speaks of her as follows:

“Add Justina, likewise praying,

that is, commending the servant, his kinswoman,

and report how greatly she brings forth

the honor of a granddaughter.”]

[Note: [Col. 0290A] Fortunatus writes this poem in the person and name of Justina. She asks Gregory to commend her through him to her father, and to convey her thanks to her grandmother because the latter had come to her.]

Bishop of the Lord, good shepherd and author of honor,

blessed adornment of your lineage, in whom noble faith resides,

remember Justina, your pious servant, blessed man;

through you may I be commended to my father by family and rank.

Then, conveying thanks to my grandmother, because at last

the sweet image of her granddaughter has come before her eyes,

you, ruler, who have long given joy to our hopes,

act as mediator between grandmother and granddaughter.

[Note: [Col. 0290D] The Paris edition reads *Justinae famulae* (“Justina’s servant”).]

## CHAPTER XX. A greeting to the same man

[Note: [Col. 0290B] Having received a letter from Gregory and learned of his good health, Fortunatus declares that he was especially delighted; finally he commends himself to him.]

Kind and blessed Father, Gregory, universal light,

head set in the high citadel of the priesthood by right.

I give thanks to God, having learned good news about you,

and now, made joyful by your letters, I give thanks.

Commending myself as well, I greet you with humble prayer and voice—

you whom my heart continually honors in service.

## CHAPTER XXI. A greeting to the same man

[Note: [Col. 0291A] He praises Gregory’s virtue, renown, and pastoral concern in guarding his flock.]

Supreme Father of your country, lofty and universal summit,

strong glory and pinnacle of the Turonian race.

A light coming happily from the fields of Auvergne:

illuminating peoples, you are scattered abroad as a beacon from your mouth.

Hastening from those Alps, your mind is higher than the mountains themselves,

a man seated amid the plains, who protects the sacred camp.

Lest enemies harm those who are faithful within the sheepfold,

you alone stand in the fields as a public tower.

O man given to the region, sweet head, dear Gregory,

whom the sacred seat of Martin retains as Father,

I, humble Fortunatus, commend myself to your patronage;

may your life thus long remain in this world before God.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] Concerning Gregory of Tours’s homeland and lineage, see his life written by Odo, abbot, prefixed to the works of Gregory edited by the learned Ruinart in the Paris edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0291D] The Paris edition reads *mons altior* (“a higher mountain”).]

## CHAPTER XXII. A greeting to the same man

[Note: [Col. 0291B] He declares his diligence and devotion toward Gregory, and finally commends himself to his prayers.]

Whenever some pleasant opportunity comes to me,

I wish, holy man, to discharge my vows with my pen.

Supreme Father of your country, venerable throughout the world,

dear to me everywhere, a radiant care of God,

I commend humble me to you, holy Gregory, enthroned on high.

Pray, I beg you, to God for your own servant.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] The Paris edition reads *fulgide, chare Dei* (“radiant, dear one of God”).]

## CHAPTER XXIII. To the same man

[Col. 0291C]

If men cease to travel swiftly through the southern regions,

I would wish my poems to be sent to you, dear Father.

But now, since I have a carrier, I offer you my word,

though it is less eloquent than the love with which I honor you.

Sweet and generous, our glory, holy bishop Gregory,

in brief little verses I discharge the duty of greeting.

But remember me yourself and commend me, I beg you, to the Thunderer;

may he make you my companion in honor at the throne.

## CHAPTER XXIV. To the same man

[Note: [Col. 0291C] He says that no eloquence is so great that he could adequately thank Gregory for his generosity toward him.]

If my tongue flowed with streams like a whirlpool,

or were swept away by the torrent’s force through the waters,

especially while I proclaimed your highest praises, Gregory,

I would still be a drop in the stream, unable to fill it.

Not even the Muse of Maro could equal the generous Father.

Kind one, who can express in speech how great are the gifts you bear to me?

[Col. 0292A] And in brevity, holy man, I commend to you your humbled servant,

me, Fortunatus; I beg that this may be forgiven.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] One Vatican manuscript reads *cujus in orbe prono* (“whose [praise] is in the bowed world”).]

## CHAPTER XXV. To the same man, concerning the estate granted

[Note: [Col. 0292A] He gives Gregory thanks for a field most generously bestowed upon him for his private expenses and use; then describes the site and pleasantness of the land.]

A page has completed its course along a generous way,

in sweet-flowing song, which your love sent forth.

In it, a grant of a place was made as the gift’s allotment,

where impetuous Vienne breaks its waters against the bank.

As the sailor proceeds in his swelling vessel,

he sees cultivated acres while he sings the sea-chant.

I return thanks, dear friend, for the bounty of kindness received,

you who make worthy distinction increase.

And, apart from these things, whatever is held from you is mine;

every flock has in its fields what you, good shepherd, possess.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] Vigenna, or Vingenna, is a river of Gaul, now the Vienne; it rises in Limousin and flows into the Loire.]

[Note: [Col. 0291D] One Vatican manuscript reads *fruge repleto* (“filled with the fruit”).]

[Note: [Col. 0291D] The manuscript reads *abit et quem* (“and whom he leaves”) instead of *quod* (“what”).]

## CHAPTER XXVI. To the same man, a petition concerning that same estate

[Note: [Col. 0292B] He likewise gives thanks for the portion of a small estate bestowed upon him, equating Gregory’s generosity toward him with Saint Martin’s liberality toward the poor. He declares that the field granted him will return to its owner at every command.]

Gregory, renewing the deeds of generous Martin:

as he clothed with a garment, you yourself nourish us with food.

The wise disciple imitates his gentle master;

where the leader sits, you will have help as a soldier.

As he once shared his cloak, so you divide a small estate;

he was mighty in clothing, and you are gracious in sustaining.

He, helping me formerly, raised me up; you, dear friend, do so anew:

each man becomes rich through the merit of his poor man.

When it is reclaimed, the field returns to your use,

and we shall restore the estate to its rightful lord.

Therefore I return ample thanks, sweetest ruler,

and, as your sheep, I repeat these things, declaring them, O shepherd.

Yet I do not give back as much as I owe you, bishop:

but for Fortunatus, I beg, bend God’s will.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] The Paris edition reads *decus* (“glory”) instead of *fovendo* (“sustaining”).]

[Note: [Col. 0292D] Fortunatus seems here to indicate Saint Martin’s beneficence toward him when, while suffering severely in his eyes at Ravenna, he was freed from that illness through the saint’s patronage. Thus he should be understood to call himself “former,” looking to the past time in which he experienced blessed Martin as beneficent toward him; “new” signifies Gregory’s present generosity toward him.]

[Note: [Col. 0292D] The manuscript reads *proprium* (“proper”) instead of *Domino* (“lord”).]

[Note: [Col. 0292D] One manuscript reads *pangens haec* (“composing these things”).]

## CHAPTER XXVII. To the same man, concerning skins sent to him

[Note: [Col. 0292C] He declares his delight upon receiving Gregory’s letter. He also includes praises of Gregory and commends himself to him. Finally, he mentions the snow-white skins sent to him for use as leggings and gives thanks.]

A page, composed with distinguished arrangement and adorned in its movement,

supported by Sophoclean wisdom,

moistened me, parched, with your rich watering,

and made the speech that I utter to be yours.

Sweet, dear, gracious, eloquent, kindly Gregory,

holy father of your country on the one hand, wise on the other,

equal in gifts, merits, spirit, and character,

possessing every quality for which you are revered,

I, little Fortunatus, prostrate myself before your lofty height,

and duly commend myself to you as yours with a suppliant vow.

[Col. 0294A] You give the means by which the footwear sent to me may be fastened,

and snowy skins may cover the soles of my feet.

For these may a white robe be granted you by the Lord,

you who give the least such things, whereby they may bear riches.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] The Paris edition reads *caligis* (“leggings”) in place of the more general footwear.]

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 0293]

## CHAPTER I. To King Chilperic, when the synod was held at Brinnacum

[Note: [Col. 0293C] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book V, chapter 50, explains at length why this synod at Brinnacum was convened; the matter may be touched on briefly. A cleric named Riculfus had fabricated a serious accusation against Queen Fredegund, Chilperic’s wife, and had falsely made Gregory of Tours the author of its denunciation and dissemination, inventing many things against him so that he might be brought into disfavor with the kings. His aim was that, once Gregory had been removed from the see of Tours and another, favorable to himself, substituted in his place, he might then be made archdeacon of the Church of Tours. Accordingly, so that the accusation might be investigated, Chilperic convened a synod of bishops at Brinnacum, where Riculfus’s fraud was exposed and Gregory’s innocence established. This synod was held in the year 580, and Fortunatus therefore wrote this poem in that year. Brennacum, or Brinnacum, commonly Braine, was apparently a royal estate at which Chilperic’s sons Dagobert and Chlodobert are reported by Gregory of Tours, Book V, chapter 35, to have suffered serious illness. Dagobert died there under the disease, while Chlodobert was carried on a bier to the basilica of Saint Medard at Soissons, where he breathed his last. Brennacum was only three leagues from Augusta Suessionum, toward Rheims, as the learned Ruinart states in his notes to Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 22. The treasures of Chlothar were also kept at the same estate of Brinnacum, as Gregory of Tours reports in the passage just cited.]

[Col. 0293A]

[Note: [Col. 0293A] Fortunatus addresses the fathers of the synod at Brinnacum in this poem and asks their permission to speak of Chilperic’s praises. He commends him for the nobility of his lineage and the fame of his reputation, as well as for his courage in battle and the glory of his achievements. After various reversals of fortune, he says that Chilperic recovered his former, indeed even greater, dignity through adverse circumstances. He proclaims him the protection of his country against barbarian nations and praises his justice and learning, by which he says Chilperic surpassed his ancestors. Finally, he adds an encomium of Queen Fredegund.]

Order of priests and venerable heights of Christ,

fathers whom holy faith has given to religion,

I, a little man, wish to speak the praises of the lofty king;

may your love raise up the verses of the insignificant.

Illustrious king in arms, born of lofty kings,

first among the ancients, ruling the highest heights.

By birth you possess dignity, but by governance you increase it;

a powerful flower, born from your father’s root.

As you ennoble one another in equal succession,

you adorned your lineage, and your lineage adorns you.

For you received the splendor of your people from its origin,

but through you the glory of your ancestors returns with honor.

When you were born to your father, another light was born for the world,

and you scatter everywhere the new rays of your name.

The East, Libya, the West, and the North prefer you;

wherever your foot does not tread, you arrive known through honor.

Whatever the world possesses, you have traversed in name, O prince,

and you travel that road as well which the sun’s wheel follows.

Known already to the sea and the Red Sea, and to the ocean beneath India,

your radiant fame crosses the Ocean.

[Col. 0294A] So that this name may resound, neither air nor wave impedes it;

thus all things at once, earth and stars alike, favor you.

A king pleasing through goodness, lofty glory, noble offspring,

in whom so many summits of great men find their summit.

Aid of your country, and yet its hope in arms,

a faithful strength to your people, renowned for vigor.

Powerful Chilperic, if the barbarian interpreter is right,

you are also called “strong helper.”

Your parents did not call you so in vain;

the whole name was a prophecy and an omen of praise.

Even then, the times offered judgment concerning the child,

and later gifts proved the earlier words true.

In you, sweet head, rested all your father’s care;

among so many brothers, you alone were his love.

For he recognized that you already deserved better things;

therefore your father honored you more and preferred you.

Your father placed you first, since he loved his child more;

no one can break a king’s judgment.

You grew under great auspices, greatest of princes,

remaining on the one hand in the love of the people, and on the other in that of your father.

But then the envious fortune of events, with such great merits,

prepared to disturb your tranquil kingdoms,

shaking the minds of peoples and the treaties of brothers;

although it wished to harm you, it favored your prosperity.

[Col. 0294C] Finally, when grave danger hung over your powerful head,

at the moment when death was about to strike, the hour drove death away.

When you were held surrounded by the weapons of death,

fortune, with God at work, snatched you from the swords.

Led to the very end, you returned from death to life;

the day that had been your last became your first.

While hostile wars desired to prepare an enemy for you,

faith, strong in battle, fought in arms on your behalf.

Prosperity accomplished its judgment without you, for your cause,

and the lofty seat returned to its proper place.

[Col. 0295A] Good king, do not grieve, for fortune gives you better things

where it wearied you with complaints.

After enduring so many harsh things for so long, joyful things now follow,

and you reap joys born from sorrows.

Sowing your kingdoms through manifold riches,

you recover them; great things commonly grow through hard labor.

Hardship did not harm you, but harsh fortune tested you;

from the place where you were burdened, you return the higher.

You grow taller through continual wars; you are not broken by arms,

and labor itself makes you skilled in war.

Through many dangers, prince, you become stronger,

and through your exertions you receive the gifts of repose.

Nothing is lost while you, the king, survive in the world,

which has preserved the kingdoms due to itself in their proper order.

[Col. 0295B] The Creator took thought for your household, your country, and your people;

the nations fear that you survive as a man.

Lest a rebel, armed, rush through the Gallic fields,

you are called by the name of victor, and you rule a broad realm.

The Getae, the Vascones, the Danes, the Estiones, the Saxons, and the Britons tremble,

whom it is clear that you and your father conquered in battle.

You are also a terror to the distant Frisians and Suebians,

who do not prepare wars but ask for your reins.

You were made a fear to all these peoples on that judgment-field,

and through new terror you became a lofty love.

In you, ruler, the region surrounded by you possesses a wall,

and an iron gate raises its lofty head.

You shine upon your country from the south as an adamantine tower,

and with an unshaken shield you protect the vows of the people.

[Col. 0296A] Nor does anyone find this oppressive: you extend pious defenses,

and with a strong boundary you protect the wealth of the region.

What should I say, prince, of your administration of justice?

By which no one returns harmed if he seeks what is rightly just;

in the mouth of the upright, whose measure is held on the scales,

the straight line of causes runs its course.

There is no delay; false error explains nothing before truth,

and fraud flees your judgments; order returns.

What? Even those whom you govern under the authority of your kingdom—

you surpass them all in learning and eloquent speech.

Discerning various voices without any interpreter,

you make the languages of different peoples one through your own tongue.

Your generosity raises up all the lowly,

and what you give to a servant, you believe to be your own.

Thus your praises extend themselves even farther,

and the crash of this accumulation of glory strikes the stars.

With arms also favoring you, and with letters established through love,

you are powerful in virtue here and pleasing through learning.

Wise in both, approved in arms and in law,

you shine as a warrior on one side and sparkle as a lawgiver on the other.

In virtue you are your father; in speech you restore your uncle;

by devotion to learning you surpass every kind of lineage.

You are judged equal to kings, but greater in poetry,

and in doctrine there had been no ancestor such as you.

Your arms make you resemble your lineage, but learning gives you precedence;

thus you surpass both the ancient kings and the one before you.

A king greatly admired by me, whose abundant skill

directs battles with strength and polishes poems with the file.

You arm the laws with weapons, and direct weapons with laws;

thus the road proceeds through arts of different kinds joined together.

[Col. 0297A] If everyone, ruler, could learn each of your achievements,

more people would adorn the good things that you alone accomplish.

But may these things remain and prosper for you,

and may you be permitted to enjoy an ever-increasing throne,

together with your lawful wife, who adorns the kingdom with her character

and, sharing the prince’s height, governs with him.

Prudent in counsel, skillful, cautious, useful to the court,

strong in intelligence, pleasing in generosity,

Fredegund, outstanding in every merit,

shines from her serene face with a radiance of her own.

A great queen indeed, bearing the weight of cares,

she honors you with goodness and assists you with usefulness.

With her ruling the palace together with you,

the house flourishes in honor through her aid.

Seeking how your vows of salvation might be doubled,

she obtains for you a reward from Radegund.

[Col. 0297B] She whose glory shines forth through her own merits,

and who has become a queen, the crown of her husband,

may honor you for a long time through the fruit of offspring,

and may a grandson arise from her, so that you may be renewed as a grandfather.

Therefore let fitting gratitude be returned to the Creator,

and honor, O king, the King who gives you aid,

that he may preserve and increase your prosperity; for the ruler from on high

alone possesses all things, who has given you so much.

[Note: [Col. 0294D] One manuscript reads *primus ab antiquis* (“first from among the ancients”).]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] Perhaps *arctos* (“the North”).]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] The Paris edition reads *tui* (“of you”).]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] The same edition reads *sit tibi et unda simul* (“let wave also be yours at once”).]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] Browerus discusses the etymology of Chilperic’s name, deriving it from the Germanic language, in his notes on this passage.]

[Note: [Col. 0294D] Two Vatican manuscripts read *eripuit gladio* (“snatched [him] from the sword”). Chilperic often waged war with his brothers and, though frequently broken by defeats, always emerged again. Finally, he would have been utterly conquered and overthrown by Sigibert, had the latter, already victorious, not suddenly been removed through the fraud and treachery of Queen Fredegund. See Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 52. Fortunatus appears here to have had in mind the outcome of that final war and Chilperic’s good fortune.]

[Note: [Col. 0295C] It seems that Fortunatus is here absolving Chilperic, suggesting that no plan or action of Chilperic was involved in Sigibert’s murder.]

[Note: [Col. 0295C] One Vatican manuscript reads *cathedra suo* (“to his own seat”).]

[Note: [Col. 0295C] The same manuscript reads *si sors te dura* (“if harsh fortune [had harmed] you”).]

[Note: [Col. 0295C] Concerning the Getae, the Vascones, and the other peoples named here: the Vascones were peoples living in the Pyrenean ranges who often harassed Gaul by their incursions. They are said to have been conquered and subdued by Theuderic and Theudebert, as reported in the chronicle of Fredegar the Scholastic.]

[Note: [Col. 0295C] The Paris edition reads *Danus Scythae* (“the Scythian Dane”).]

[Note: [Col. 0295C] One Vatican manuscript has *Euthio*. Browerus suggested that *Estio* might be read, yielding “the Estiones overcome,” if there was a people of that name. The Estones, or Estiones, are still counted among the remnants of the Saxons near the borders of Livonia, not far from the Swedes, Muscovites, and Danes.]

[Note: [Col. 0295D] The Paris edition reads *quos pridem te* (“whom formerly you”).]

[Note: [Col. 0295D] Two Vatican manuscripts read *cujus in orbe prono* (“whose [measure] in the bowed world”). The praises that Fortunatus surveys here do not seem to fit Chilperic, a man long immersed in his impure love for Fredegund, whose desire led him to have Galswintha, his lawful wife, murdered in his own bed, and who was always unjust and hostile toward his royal brothers. Although, after losing two sons to premature death, he seems to have been moved somewhat toward repentance, he nevertheless returned to his former mind and way of life and was finally murdered through the action and counsel of Fredegund, whom he loved most wickedly and at whose urging he had committed so many crimes, as Aimoinus relates in his *History of the Franks*, Book III, chapter 57. Gregory of Tours does not hesitate to call him the Nero and Herod of his time, and describes his vices and crimes at length in Book VI of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 46. Fortunatus must therefore be understood to have praised this king in the manner of poets, concealing his vices and magnifying whatever praise there might be in him. Even in a shameful man, some virtue difficult to suppress may shine forth and be praised.]

[Note: [Col. 0296C] Although Chilperic was less accomplished in learning, he nevertheless aspired to it. Gregory of Tours, Book V, chapter 45, reports that he even improperly claimed knowledge in theological matters, asserting that the Father himself was the Son, and that the Holy Spirit was himself the Father and the Son. He wanted Gregory of Tours and the other learned men of the churches to think and believe what he himself thought. He later abandoned this madness. Gregory also reports that he wrote other books in verse, as though following Sedulius, although the verses did not conform at all to metrical rules. He also added letters to our alphabet, namely ω, as the Greeks have it, together with *ae*, *the*, and *uvi*, whose characters we have included: ω ψ Ζ Δ. He sent letters to all the cities of his kingdom so that children might be taught by them and ancient books, smoothed with pumice, might be rewritten. Aimoinus reports the same matter in Book III of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 41. Aimoinus says that the letters added by Chilperic to the alphabet were χ, *ch*, θ, *th*, and φ, *ph*. For those letters and their variations, see the notes of the learned Ruinart on Gregory of Tours, Book V, chapter 45 of the *History of the Franks*.]

[Note: [Col. 0296D] The Paris edition reads *sed* (“but”) instead of *sub* (“under”).]

[Note: [Col. 0296D] One Vatican manuscript reads *generis similem* (“like in lineage”).]

[Note: [Col. 0296D] Aimoinus, Book III of *Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 16, reports the following epigram as composed by King Chilperic in praise of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris:

“Mirror of the Church, strength of the fatherland, altar of the guilty,

both father and physician, shepherd and love of the flock.

Germanus, blessed in virtue, faith, heart, and speech,

in the flesh he holds the tomb, in the honor of his mind the sky.

A man whom the harsh fates of the grave harmed in nothing:

he lived, for death itself fears the man whom it has taken.

Even after death the just man grew greater, for he who

had been an earthen vessel flashes as a splendid jewel.

His aid and merit are spoken by words given to the mute,

and restored daylight proclaims him with its voice to the blind.

Now the apostolic man, carrying a trophy from the flesh,

sits by triumphal right in the citadel of heaven.”

The learned Mabillon, in his notes on the *Life of Saint Germanus* in the first century of the Benedictine collection, observing that the verses of this poem are more elegant and ornate than could have been produced by Chilperic, thinks that Aimoinus polished them. Browerus, however, does not hesitate to deny them to Chilperic and attribute them to Fortunatus, considering their style and talent characteristic of him. I readily agree with Browerus, especially since Fortunatus also wrote other poems in another person’s name and at another’s request, as we have noted elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0297D] It is for those who know Fredegund’s life and crimes to judge whether these praises suit her. We have often indicated what sort of things they were, and they may be seen throughout Gregory of Tours’s *History of the Franks*, as well as in Aimoinus and other writers of Frankish history. Fortunatus therefore seems to have written these words for the immediate occasion rather than in accordance with the truth, perhaps praising Fredegund more lavishly than he wished in order to soften and calm her anger, which was fiercely directed against Gregory of Tours.]

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Fortunatus seems here to indicate that Fredegund commended the welfare and salvation of her husband to Radegund’s prayers.]

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Chilperic already had two surviving children by Fredegund, Dagobert and Chlodobert. Shortly after the synod at Brinnacum he lost them, not without divine vengeance, as may be read in Gregory of Tours, Book V, chapter 51, and will become clear from the following poem.]

[Note: [Col. 0298C] The Paris edition reads *hoc* (“this”).]

[Note: [Col. 0298C] Browerus corrects the line to *pia vota secundent* (“may they fulfill the pious vows”), but this correction is not found in the Vatican manuscripts.]

[Col. 0297C] Forgive me, victor: your praises surpass me,

and the fact that I am overcome becomes an even greater honor to you.

Yet, though I am small, I pray that your prosperous vows may be fulfilled,

so that these pious gifts may come from heaven to earth.

May the air favor you with temperate weather, and the seasons with peace;

may the fields shine with crops, and treaties bind the kingdoms.

May you subdue all Edomites, and protect the faithful with love,

and also be the pinnacle of Catholic religion.

The highest honor of a king, through whom honors are bestowed,

to whom long life and holy faith may be assured.

Let others pay kings gold or gifts of gems;

accept words from the poor Fortunatus.

[Note: [Col. 0298C] One Vatican manuscript reads *et domites omnes* (“and may you subdue all”).]

## CHAPTER II. To King Chilperic and Queen Fredegund

[Note: [Col. 0298C] Fabricius gave this poem the title “Concerning the Common Mortality of All Mortals.” It is found in the two Vatican manuscripts used up to this point, and in another very ancient manuscript, separate from the other works of Fortunatus, with this heading: “Here begin the verses of Fortunatus, bishop, in consolation of the dead.” Even there the poem is incomplete, ending with the verse “White as though red …”]

[Col. 0298A] [Note: He recalls the punishment inflicted on Adam and Eve, from whom the origin of sin arose, and says that from them death was propagated to their wretched offspring. He then confirms the necessity of death by the example of the fathers who died before them. From this he consoles Chilperic for the grief he had conceived from the bitter burial of his sons, affirming that tears accomplish nothing toward recalling dear ones from the underworld. He adds that the limits of every life were rightly established by God, and that God breaks human beings, like vessels, whenever he pleases. He urges him to bear this grief bravely and to console Queen Fredegund, who bitterly mourned the death of her sons. By the examples of Job, David, and the mother of the Maccabees, he advises that thanks should rather be given to the supreme God, because he took the innocent children away by premature death; and from this he also derives an occasion for consoling the parents, since the children migrated to God pure from the sacred washing of baptism, destined for a place in heaven. Finally, he predicts for the same parents new offspring in place of the dead.]

The harsh condition and irrevocable decree of the hour,

Which gave the human race [Note: The third Vatican manuscript omits “the origin of death.”] its sorrowful beginning:

When the serpent, persuading, cast venom from its mouth,

And by the serpent’s bite death came through guilty Eve.

From that time Adam, the father, took grief from the earth,

And the world, groaning from the mother, receives bitterness.

By transgression the two are condemned to shameful punishment:

He suffers through labor; she groans in childbirth.

[Col. 0298C] From there devouring death came, transmitted to their descendants,

And the guilty origin destroys its own heirs.

Behold, our parents produced this grievous evil for us:

From where it first began, from there the whole race falls.

First Abel fell, struck down by a pitiable wound,

And his brother’s hoes [Note: “They dig the limbs.” Thus the Trier and Cologne manuscripts, joined by the Vatican manuscripts, except that the last has “he digs the limbs.” Fabricius corrected the passage:

“And his brother’s hoes drag those limbs for him.”

Brower rightly judges that the reading *fodent* (“they dig”) should be retained, both because in that age people were already using many Latin words corrupted in common speech—as is especially clear from the testimony of Saint Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* II.13, and Cassiodorus, *Institutions* I.15—and because Fortunatus is often found to have distorted and corrupted words for things in order to bring them within metrical rules. It is therefore not at all surprising that he did so here as well.

Brower also explains the sense of the passage so that Cain is said to have dug through or pierced Abel’s body with a hoe, or afterward to have buried it in the earth in order to conceal it. But he first gives greater support to the former interpretation: “After I had examined somewhat more closely Aurelius Prudentius’s *Hamartigenia*, whose imitator Fortunatus seems especially to have been, I found that Prudentius writes of Cain as follows:

‘Then the brother arms his parricidal hand,

[Col. 0299D] rival of proven holiness,

and breaks his brother’s neck with a curved hoe.’

There the poet uses the name ‘hoe’ for whatever instrument Cain used in killing his brother. The hoe was especially so called because Cain was a farmer; hence it is likely that he used for his crime the instruments he had readily at hand—that is, agricultural ones, whatever their precise form may have been.

It should also be noted that Fortunatus seems to use *fodent* not for *fodient* (“they will dig”), as Brower thinks; otherwise the sense would be impaired, but for *fodiunt* (“they dig”), so that the sentence remains complete. The Paris edition reads: ‘and fraternal hoes … dig.’] dig the limbs.

[Col. 0299A] Afterwards Seth too died, restored in Abel’s place [Note: One Vatican manuscript has “it seems, to the same parents.” A third has “restored to the same parents.” Fabricius has the same reading. The Paris edition: “to the same.”],

And although he returned [Note: Seth is said to have “returned,” that is, to have been restored to his parents in place of the murdered Abel; although he succeeded the dead man in his place, he too nevertheless did not cease to die. Fortunatus speaks similarly of Solomon, saying:

“When he returns to his father in place of his brother.”], it was not without an end.

Why should I mention Noah, praised by the voice of the Thunderer,

Whom a light ark carried, and now a heavy ark presses?

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads this verse:

“So too Shem and Japheth, these most righteous offspring.”]

So too Shem and Japheth, the most righteous offspring of their fathers.

Holy progeny also traveled such a path.

Why mention the patriarchs Abraham, or Isaac, and Jacob too, who were worthy [Note: Fabricius: “the patriarch worthy …”],

Since no one is found released from the law of death?

Melchizedek too, the holy priest by the Lord’s own word,

And Job as well, just as his children did, departed.

The lawgiver Moses himself lies dead, and Aaron the priest,

Worthy of God’s conversations, dies as a friend.

[Col. 0299B] His successor, the renowned leader of the people, Joshua,

And the fathers whom you read of in the books of the Law, died [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “whom you read in the books,” and Fabricius follows that reading. The Paris edition: “whom you know.”].

Why mention Gideon, Samson, or any judge in succession?

No one escapes death under the Lord, the judge.

The mighty Israelite, King David and prophet,

Lies buried in the tomb with his Solomon.

Isaiah, Daniel, blessed Samuel, and Jonah,

Living beneath the sea, now lie pressed beneath the earth.

Peter, the prince with the key, and Paul, first in doctrine,

Although their souls were exalted, the earth covers their bodies.

Of human seed, for whom no greater one is regarded [Note: The third Vatican manuscript has “than whom no one.” The other manuscript has “with whom no one,” corruptly.],

The powerful Baptist himself, John, also died.

Enoch and Elijah still await this,

Both of whom were born from human stock and will die.

[Col. 0299C] The Creator himself, exultant, Christ, rising swiftly from the shades,

Because he was born a man, was buried in the flesh beneath the earth.

Who, I ask, does not die, when salvation itself tasted death,

When he wished my life to die for me?

Tell me, what can emperors accomplish [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have “or the summits of kings,” as does Fabricius],

And what can the heights of kings, when the Creator’s limbs have lain among the rocks?

[Col. 0300A] The strong do not withdraw their arms, nor purple robes their kings,

Whoever comes from dust will be dust.

We are born equal, and all die equally;

From Adam comes one death, and from Christ one salvation.

The reward is different, but the funeral is one for all:

Infants, young men, and thus the old died [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts: “thus the old died.” The Paris edition: “the old departed.”].

[Note: Fabricius presents this verse as follows:

“Therefore, what are we doing here beneath the doubtful funeral of life?”]

Therefore, what are we to do here, I now ask you, exalted power,

When can we be of help in this matter?

We weep and groan, but are unable to help;

There is mourning in our eyes, yet our grief brings no benefit.

Our entrails are twisted, our hearts are torn by turmoil;

Our dear ones are dead, and our eyes fall through weeping.

Behold, love calls, but the beloved is no longer recalled,

[Col. 0300B] Nor does he whom the sunken stone covers return to us.

Although we cry out, deaf death flees and does not hear;

The hard one does not know how to return to tender affection.

But I do not wish it, and yet I do: I shall migrate there with everyone;

We shall all go from here, and no one returns from there [Note: Fabricius: “there … no one, but from there.”].

Until, at the Lord’s coming, dead flesh lives,

And man rises again from his own dust,

When the wet skin has begun to cover the dry ashes [Note: Fabricius: “burning ashes.”],

And living ashes leap from the tombs.

Therefore we shall all go, to be settled in another region;

We shall go to our homeland, we whom foreign lands now hold.

[Note: This verse, “Therefore do not grieve,” together with what follows, is absent from the third Vatican manuscript. It contains several other lacunae of this kind.]

Therefore do not grieve, pious king, most valiant prince,

That those who were born go where every human being seeks to go.

As the potter wishes, so a clay vessel is fashioned;

When the potter wishes, the vessels fall apart.

[Col. 0300C] What the Almighty commands, we cannot resist,

At whose glance the stars and the earth tremble.

He himself creates man; what can we say to him? The same one

Who gave also takes back; he commits no crime.

Behold, we are his creation, and our spirit comes from him;

When he commands, we go from here—we who are his work.

[Col. 0301A] [Note: In the third Vatican manuscript: “if he wishes, in one hour, mountains.” Fabricius: “in one hour.” Fabricius presents this poem mutilated, omitting the couplet “Therefore do not grieve,” and ending with the following couplet: “King, I beg you.” The Paris edition has this verse as follows:

“If he wishes, he changes mountains, seas, and stars in an hour.”]

If he wishes, in an hour he changes mountains, seas, and stars.

When his works favor him, what does man, mere smoke, accomplish?

Therefore, powerful king, I beg you, do what benefits you most,

What benefits the soul with the help of the Godhead.

Be manly in honor; patiently conquer your grief;

Bear what cannot be avoided, or at least endure the burden.

What we drag with us from birth—without it no one passes through life [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts: “without which no one passes through life.” The Paris edition: “without this no one passes through life.”],

What no one changes, let him bear even by reason.

Care for the lady queen, your beloved beloved,

Who receives every good thing with you as her companion.

Command that the grieving woman be appeased with maternal affection.

Do not weep yourself at the same time, nor allow her to weep.

While you, a man, reign, it is not fitting that she be sad,

But rather let her rejoice greatly in your royal marriage-bed [Note: One Vatican manuscript and the Paris edition: “let her rejoice greatly on the throne.”].

I also beg this, wishing your wife a long life:

[Col. 0301B] Care for your daughter [Note: This was evidently Rigunthis, whom Chilperic had by Fredegund. She was later betrothed to Reccared, son of Leovigild, king of Spain, and sent to Spain with immense treasures and forces, but with an unhappy outcome. When news of her father’s murder arrived, those escorting her abandoned and betrayed her before she married Reccared, who was already seeking another marriage. She then returned to Gaul in great disgrace and humiliation, and shortly afterward, after quarreling with her mother, came very close to being killed by her. See Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* IX.34 and VII.9.]—care for your child; care for your country.

Such will the people be as everyone sees you;

From your countenance the people reap their own hopes [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “your hopes.”].

Finally, when Job lost seven children in one grievous stroke,

He returned praises to God with his mouth.

David the psalmist, when he lost his beloved son,

Soon placed him in the tomb and gave a festive meal.

[Note: The third Vatican manuscript: “twice-blessed offspring.”]

The woman twice blessed, the pious mother of the Maccabees,

Joyfully endured seven sons in a single funeral.

Coming readily before the Lord, glory always be yours, Ruler,

When you will, supreme Father, a mother has children.

[Col. 0302A] Therefore thanks are returned to God rather than to our own [Note: The last Vatican manuscript: “thanks may be returned to our own.” The Paris edition has the same reading.

Chilperic’s sons Dagobert and Clodobert died, as we have said, shortly after the Synod of Berny, in the year 580, in which year a dreadful plague raged in Gaul. Gregory of Tours describes it in *History of the Franks* V.35 in these words: “A dysenteric disease seized almost the whole of Gaul. Those suffering from it had a violent fever with vomiting, excessive pain in the kidneys, and heaviness in the head or neck. What they cast up from the mouth was saffron-coloured or at least green; many maintained that it was a hidden poison. … Therefore, in these days King Chilperic fell gravely ill. When he recovered, his younger son, not yet reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, began to fall ill; seeing him at the point of death, they washed him in baptism. When he had improved a little, his elder brother, named Clodobert, was seized by the same disease, and Fredegund his mother, seeing him likewise in danger of death, etc. … Afterwards the younger infant, wasting away through extreme illness, died. … They placed Clodobert on a bier and brought him to Soissons, to the basilica of Saint Medard; throwing him down before the saint’s tomb, they made vows for him. But at midnight, already pale and emaciated, he breathed out his spirit.”

Gregory of Tours does not hesitate to say that this death of Chilperic’s sons occurred by divine judgment, so that punishment might be exacted from Chilperic and his house. Indeed, in chapter 54 of the same book he relates that, while he was still at Berny after the Synod of Berny and was conversing privately with blessed Salvius, bishop of Albi, the latter suddenly said to him: “Do you see what I see above this roof?” “I see,” Gregory says, “the tiles which the king ordered placed on the roof.” Salvius said, “Do you see nothing else?” I replied, “I see nothing else.” For I thought he was speaking jokingly. And I added: “If you see anything more, tell it.” Then he drew a deep sigh and said: “I see the drawn sword of divine wrath hanging over this house.” Nor did the priest’s prediction fail: for twenty days later the king’s two sons, whose deaths we have recorded above, died.

Aimoinus adds, in *History of the Franks* III.24, that Archbishop Gregory himself, one night after the morning hymns, while lying on his bed, saw an angel of God flying above the church and saying in a clear voice: “Alas, alas! God has struck Chilperic and all his sons, and none of those now living shall be his successor in his kingdom.”],

Who causes offspring from your stock to proceed to heaven.

He chooses beautiful jewels from the world’s filth,

And from the midst of mud leads them to the stars’ throne [Note: The last Vatican manuscript: “leads them to the stars of heaven.” In that manuscript the poem ends with this verse, including “White as lilies mingled with red roses,” below.].

Your harvest pleased God, and he stores it in his granaries,

While he gathers sweet grains from tender ears.

You do not produce chaff, but bear sound wheat;

Not to be burned outside, but to be restored in heaven [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “not to be burned in the fires.” The Paris edition: “not to be lost in the fires.”].

Especially since, purified in holy baptism,

They deserved to be snatched from here, made new by the washing fountain.

Standing before God like golden vessels of beauty,

Or like a beautiful lamp shining on a candelabrum,

Immaculate souls, always radiant with honor,

They retain a place in the region of the living.

Planted in the house of the Lord, they flourish in light,

[Col. 0302B] White as lilies mingled with red roses [Note: The same manuscript: “white as lilies mingled with blue flowers.”].

And when the Lord commands the buried limbs to return,

He will then clothe your children in a beautiful robe.

[Note: The Paris edition: “Or a shining palm woven beneath gleaming gold.”]

Or a palm-embroidered cloak, woven beneath gleaming gold,

And a diadem of various jewels will crown their brows.

Wearing a snowy mantle across their shining breasts,

A bright belt binds their purple robe [Note: The Paris edition: “luminous.”].

Then you, father and mother, will rejoice among them,

When you see them dwelling among the stars.

Yet the Almighty exists, who increased Abraham’s seed;

He will give you as well what he gave Job in his love.

[Col. 0303A] [Note: These prayers of Fortunatus were not empty or ineffectual. For in fact, after the death of Clodobert and Dagobert, Chilperic had another son by Fredegund, who was called Theodoric; and when he did not long survive—he died the following year, as Gregory of Tours relates, VI.34—Chilperic again had another son by Fredegund and named him Chlothar. He inherited his father’s kingdom after the death of his father Chilperic.]

Restoring the number of children with worthy offspring,

And bringing back a line ennobled by faith.

He who brought forth Solomon in David’s royal line,

Returning to his father in place of his brother [Note: The manuscript has “in place of death.”].

He will be able to restore a son to you through your wife,

One whom the father may fondly embrace and the mother nourish at her breast.

Crawling between the necks of both parents,

He will provide long-lasting joys for kings and country.

CHAPTER III. To the same persons.

[Note: This poem must have been written in the same year as the preceding one, and not long after the death of Chilperic’s sons. It concerns the consolation of Chilperic himself and Fredegund, whose grief and sorrow at the death of their sons we can learn were especially bitter from Gregory of Tours V.40, who says: “Thus, after the death of Chilperic’s sons, the king, in the month of October, sat with his wife in the forest of Cotia, filled with mourning,” etc.]

[Note: By presenting the appearance of returning spring and the joys of the Easter festivals, he urges Chilperic and Fredegund, after setting aside all mourning and sadness, to return with the entire royal household to joy and liveliness.]

After storms and the troubled clouds of heaven,

When the earth is accustomed to stiffen under hostile frost,

After the harsh winters and the bitter cold of winter,

Or when the breath of swift Notus weighs upon the fields,

Springtime again succeeds in the world,

And after the ice the welcome breeze summons the day.

The fields are renewed again with fragrant flowers,

And every grove grows green with leafy trees.

The oaks bend beneath their sweet-tasting fruits,

And the field smiles as the grass returns to it.

So now, grieving over the Lord’s sorrowful losses,

I beg you also to make yourselves joyful with a better spirit.

Behold, peaceful days recall Christ’s Easter;

The whole world too resounds with renewed prayers [Note: The manuscripts, including the Vatican ones, have “The world too,” and so the reading is ancient; for, as Brower says, *urbs* and *orbs* are homonymous.].

Let joys be especially favorable throughout the lofty palaces of kings,

And through you let the servants celebrate blessed festivals.

May the Almighty add to your safety through our death [Note: Brower observes that this is expressed in the manner of the ancient formula:

“May Jupiter add years to your years.”

To the same expression may be referred the couplet in which a wife, extinguished by untimely death, speaks thus to her surviving husband, praying for his long life:

“I died before my time; but may you, happier, live your years;

Live, best of husbands, my years as well.”

But one Vatican manuscript reads:

“May the Almighty add your safety to us throughout the world,” which I judge to be the reading to retain; the Paris edition has the same reading.],

And may your lofty power rule the country for a long time.

CHAPTER IV. Epitaph of Clodobert.

[Note: See above what we said in the notes to poem 2 of this book.]

[Note: Fortunatus writes Clodobert’s epitaph. Clodobert was the son of King Chilperic and Fredegund. He reports that he died at fifteen years of age. He praises his royal lineage and recalls the hope he had offered the whole kingdom if he had lived. Yet he says that his death should not be mourned, since he departed this world young and innocent.]

Cruel funerals of kings teach the people to weep,

When sorrowful tombs cover the head of the world with earth.

Thus Clodobert lies resting in this tomb [Note: Gregory of Tours V.35 and Aimoinus, *Deeds of the Franks* III.32, relate that Clodobert was buried at Soissons in the basilica of the martyrs Crispin and Crispinianus.],

He who, having completed three lustral periods, was snatched from the world.

A lofty descendant coming from his great-grandfather Clovis,

Grandson of Chlothar and offspring of Chilperic,

Whom Fredegund took from her royal marriage [Note: The Paris edition: “beautiful royal marriage”],

And whose birth, as a boy, increased Frankish hopes.

But while his great hope for his father and country was growing [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “whose father’s … hope”],

Hostile fate took him away before his day.

But since no complaining contagions of the world harm him,

Let no beloved one weep for him whom honor now surrounds,

[Col. 0304B] For the innocent boy, passing through life without crime,

Is confident that he enjoys the citadel of the everlasting kingdom.

CHAPTER V. Epitaph of Dagobert.

[Note: To the preceding poem he adds the epitaph of Dagobert, likewise the son of Chilperic and Fredegund, who died at approximately the same time and by the same kind of death as his brother Clodobert. He recalls his royal ancestry and lineage. He proclaims him happy and blessed because he died scarcely washed in the sacred baptismal bath.]

Sweet head of the people, Dagobert, everlasting in love [Note: Gregory of Tours V.35 says that Dagobert was escorted with the greatest mourning from the estate of Brennacum to Paris and ordered to be buried in the basilica of Saint Denis.],

Support of your country, hope of the youthful world.

Born from royal stock, noble even as an infant,

Shown to the earth, soon snatched away to heaven.

[Col. 0304C] Coming from the powerful race of warlike Clovis,

The offspring of an excellent great-grandfather, equal in honor.

A noble infant, answering to ancient kings [Note: The Paris edition: “to ancient laws,”],

The son of Chilperic his father and of Fredegund.

Yet soon the venerable wave of baptism washed you;

Although snatched away from here, a blessed light now holds you on its throne [Note: The same edition: “a lofty throne.”].

Therefore you live in honor, and when the Judge of the world comes,

You will rise again, radiant, shining in your face.

CHAPTER VI. To Bishop Gregory, concerning Sapphic meters.

[Col. 0305A] [Note: He says that he has received Gregory’s letter, though it arrived late, and declares his own devotion and goodwill toward him. He says that he is sending the poems that had been requested. But he asks for time to compose the Sapphic verses he was asked for, since the harvest was then approaching; if it proceeded abundantly, he says he would be more ready to fashion verses.]

A letter of powerful eloquence arrived in haste [Note: The Paris edition: “with swifter course,”],

But it wished to come late in fulfillment of my desire.

Nor did it offend me, although delayed, when it asked this of one

Whom a mind-binding bond holds fast.

Since I wish a Gregory such as that Nazianzen was,

That you may restore him in doctrine, preserving his see [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “preparing the see,”],

Father, behold, I have sent the poems you assigned,

And they will prosper for me if they please you, dear one.

[Col. 0305B] You also command me to send back Sapphic meters;

Forgive me while the harvest of my small field presses upon me.

While I reap, grant me time; soon I shall prepare to obey you;

If I am filled with fruit, perhaps I shall sing better.

If I am able to compose it, I shall send the little book with its meter,

Which you will receive according to your desire, in the manner love dictates to you [Note: The manuscript has “which.” The Paris edition: “what love tells you.”].

CHAPTER VII. To the same, in the same meter.

[Note: Fortunatus sends Gregory the poem, composed in Sapphic meter, which Gregory had requested, as the preceding poem indicates. He first excuses himself and says that a task unequal to his shoulders has been imposed upon him; nevertheless, love for Gregory leads him not to refuse it. He recalls the little book Gregory sent him, filled with grandiloquent style, which, because of the weakness of his talent, he says he scarcely touched, especially since he was occupied with other cares and duties. Finally he addresses his own little book and orders it to go to Gregory and greet him in his own name and in the names of Radegund, Agnes, and Justina.]

With joyful heart and graceful pen,

You send a letter, your desire eager,

Writing words of gentle and serious greeting,

Dear Gregory.

Recently you demanded that I stir myself to compose new

Meters, which Sappho sang with elegance,

Thus recalling the Dionean [Note: “Dionean,” that is, Venus-like loves. Dione is traditionally said to have been Venus’s mother.] loves

Of the learned girl.

The Greek Pindar, and my own Flaccus after him,

With Sapphic meter, while the plectrum played,

The cithara-player gently composing, with a pleasing

Song, played.

[Col. 0306A] Why do you impose lyric melodies upon me,

Who now scarcely whisper in a hoarse voice,

Whose right hand does not know how to speak upon the strings

With a sweet thumb?

[Note: The same manuscript omits *qui*, beginning the verse: “or these.”]

If these things had once been known to me,

Through the teachable Muse of the wise,

I had forgotten the kindly Muse

For so many years.

Since it is labor for the learned to compose such things,

And no one enters the doctrine wisely [Note: In two Vatican manuscripts: *rapienter*, a word retained by other manuscripts, according to Brower.],

And since it is sufficiently clear that meters

Resound in only a few poets [Note: The Paris edition: “and that they are sufficiently established.”].

It is no light task for a sailor to cross the sea in a ship,

Or to conquer the vast deep by swimming;

Scarcely do they bring back their sails to harbor

Under the stormy South Wind.

The journey to which you order me to go is difficult and deep,

Yet I shall go, by desire;

If I cannot travel the road on foot,

I am led by love.

The will of the shepherd, your will, has given me

A book stuffed with grandiloquent style,

Which my poverty could scarcely

Touch with understanding.

It resists humility with royal words,

Refusing rich verses to the poor,

And unwilling to open itself to me, a Moschus [Note: The person of Moschus is famous in Virgil’s *Eclogues*.],

Although learned for sophists.

Arguing at length with varied red [Note: A gloss in a Trier manuscript explains this passage as “appearance or clothing of that kind,” following Brower. Brower nevertheless prefers to understand *milthum* here as the rubric, called μέλτος by the Greeks; I also accept Brower’s view, since it can be understood from book V, chapter 6, that Fortunatus sometimes used *minium* for marking verses: “Since there is no scarlet here, the work is woven with red.” One Vatican manuscript corruptly has “with varied mute.” The Paris edition: “with melody.”],

And whatever things are rhythmic or friendly to meter,

However much your Sapphic verses adorn my fields,

Sweet Epode.

There is a great number of authors,

Saying more things in melodious measure;

Wishing to recall their names in this meter,

I break the names [Note: The Paris edition: “I fashion names.”].

Especially now that I have been released by you,

And after twice ten years I speak

Of what the Lesbian maiden wrote,

Striking the clear-sounding lyre.

Whoever wishes to know these things should first try

To count the Libyan sands along the shore,

Before enclosing every matter with cautious

Reason in song and meter.

[Col. 0307A] For I myself have delayed, held back

By many causes, now here and now there,

And, not having leisure, I read the sweet work

Of the sophist in peaceful quiet.

For know, shepherd, that I have not yet run through

The whole arrangement by rereading the little book;

But believe me, it is enough—enough for a lover—

That desire alone exists.

Therefore, released, fly swiftly

To the holy father, accompanied by desire,

Renewing our love for him and his,

Go, little book.

Perhaps, sluggish, I cannot go with my steps

Where that beloved face of mine calls;

Give our mutual greeting, I beg you, little book,

[Col. 0307B] Return it.

If the Father remembers his son, with sweet speech,

Entreat him who made sea and stars

To preserve in his heart one who worships him

With pious prayers.

To the dear women joined to him in spirit,

Agnes and Radegund, whom he likewise honors,

As they request, in place of daughters,

Deliver my greeting.

Add also the greeting of Justina, who entreats him,

Commending, to be sure, the nearby servant [Note: Concerning Justina, see what we said at chapter 16 of the preceding book.].

And report how much honor a niece

Who is dear to her offers.

With prayer, voice, and mind ready for this,

Hardly fulfilling it in full, I, poor in art [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “I, poor in skill.” The Paris edition has the same reading],

Yet overflowing with abundant love,

Dear Gregory.

CHAPTER VIII.

[Note: Brower judges that Baudowald was bishop of Meaux, since he is found under that name in the catalogue of the bishops of Meaux by Antonius Monchiacenus and is reported to have held the see around this time; bishops of that name are scarcely found in other churches.

Cointius reports that Gundoald, or Gundobald, succeeded Baudowald in the see of Meaux; he was seated there in 614, while Baudowald had succeeded Edenus in the same see. Edenus had succeeded Medovechus, who took part in the Second Council of Paris in 551. Thus Baudowald’s time agrees with the period of Fortunatus. One Vatican manuscript lacks the title of this poem.]

To Bishop Baudowald.

[Note: He greets Bishop Baudowald in this poem, illustrious in rank, cultivated learning, knowledge, and piety, and commends himself to his prayers.]

Highest of priests, abundant power of goodness,

Summit through your honor, light through my love,

Venerable in sacred offices, fosterling of piety,

Kept in my heart as a pledge of friendship.

Flourishing in studies and faithful to the sacred law,

Always bringing forth future gifts for your soul,

Therefore, father, I beg you, calling earth, sea, and stars to witness,

That you may wish to remember me, your servant, with your sacred voice [Note: The Paris edition: “to have remembered me.”].

CHAPTER IX.

[Note: Sidonius, as may be read in Cointius, succeeded Ruthard in the see of Mainz. Sidonius was succeeded by Willebertus, whose successor, Leonisius or Ludegastus, held the same see until 612, as the same Cointius reports under that year, no. 5. From this one can infer approximately when Sulonius presided over the Church of Mainz; beyond this, at least as far as I know, nothing certain can be offered.

For this reason I am surprised that Brower says that he was close in age to Theodoric and Theudebert, kings of the Franks, and to Clovis: “When his new empire was rising among the Belgians,” he says, “a notable devastation was inflicted upon Germany I and II by those cities, and upon Mainz with even greater severity because it was repeatedly attacked.” Certainly, by the time Fortunatus came to Gaul, not only Clovis but also his son Chlothar, after a long and prosperous reign, had already ceased to live.]

To Sidonius, Bishop of Mainz.

[Note: He congratulates Sidonius, appointed over the Church of Mainz, which had already been deprived of its shepherd. He praises Sidonius for his pastoral rank and office, his care and diligence in exercising it, his generosity toward the poor, his kindness to exiles and prisoners, and his learning and sweetness of eloquence. He also recalls his munificence and generosity in restoring churches.]

Do not grieve, fortunate Mainz, at the misfortune restored [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “do not grieve at the misfortune restored.”];

The bishop has returned, one who would bring you help.

Lest you, deprived of him, lie weeping in heavy sorrow,

That you deserved to gain him through hunger [Note: Part of this pentameter is missing, with astonishing agreement, in all manuscripts, both Vatican and those used by Brower. The Paris edition of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* supplies it as:

“Rejoice that, with famine driven away, you deserved him.”

In that edition the following pentameter reads:

“Whom ancient ruin seeks to restore this place.”

].

[lacuna]

Behold, the father Sidonius extends his hand to the city:

As he renews the place, ancient ruin perishes.

He administers the rights of the priesthood with sacred governance,

And through his diligence the rank itself has grown.

The Church continually brings forth abundant fruits,

Although bound by apostolic love to the king [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “bound by the love of kings”; another: “joined by love to the kingdom”; a fragment: “of kings.” The Paris edition: “joined by love.”].

[Col. 0308C] He receives heirs, born from heavenly stock [Note: The Paris edition: “heir … born.” Perhaps *natos* (“children”) should be read],

Like a wife joined to such a husband when marriage pleases.

With you as vigilant guardian, the wolf does not tear the lambs;

With you feeding the flock, no sheep perishes.

More carefully you lead them through all the gentle pastures;

You prepare flowering fields, so that poisons may not harm [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “preparing fields.”].

Be food for the people, while you peacefully preserve fasts [Note: The same manuscript: “preserving fasts”],

And satisfy others by taking away from yourself.

[Col. 0309A] You clothe the naked, releasing captives from their bonds [Note: The same manuscript, corruptly: “the bonds of captives.” The fragment: “of the captured.”],

Restoring free necks once the yoke has been laid aside.

You are a home for exiles and food for the hungry;

Happy is he for whom Christ remains a debtor because of this.

Doctrine made you virtuous, sacred foresight modest,

And it made you prevail in eloquence, sweeter than honey [Note: The Paris edition: “And it makes you prevail in eloquence.”].

Renewing ancient temples, supported by splendid beauty [Note: The same edition: “supported by spacious beauty,”],

You thereby implant God more deeply in the people’s love.

So that you may dig up the people [Note: The Paris edition: “and may you be in harmony with the Rhine River.” The Trier manuscript has the reading printed by Brower. It seems that Sidonius, as Brower observes, fortified the banks and restrained the violence of the two rivers, the Rhine and the Main, which, swollen by snow and rain and joined together with greater force, usually rushed against the banks near Mainz; he did so by works or the construction of embankments. The Paris edition: “that you may dig trenches; the Rhine suits you.”], and the rivers corresponding to the Rhine,

What does he who provides good things through the waters accomplish for the lands?

[Note: [Col. 0309D] Previously it was commonly read: “Here, whom fame makes shine”; Brow corrected it to: “Here, because the shrines shine.” The Paris edition reads:]

Here, because the shrines shine, and because what exists has been restored,

You live in eternity, with praise flowing to you.

[Note: [Col. 0309D] The manuscript reads “Here.” The Paris edition reads “May you live long in this.”]

By this, may you grow through long years by the fruit of your merits,

And, as your flock long increases, may you bear vows from the flock.

## CHAPTER X. To Bishop Rhagnemundus

[Note: [Col. 0309D] Rhagnemundus was bishop of Paris. He succeeded Saint Germanus in that see after Germanus’s death in 576. In 585 he took part in the Second Council of Mâcon and died in 591. Gregory of Tours frequently speaks of him; in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 12, he relates that, while Rhagnemundus was still a deacon and had followed Bishop Germanus to Tours, he received a portion of dust from Saint Martin’s tomb and recovered from the severe dysentery from which he was suffering. He likewise reports in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 89, that Rhagnemundus, already a priest and afflicted with quartan fever, fell asleep beside the tomb of Saint Marcellus, formerly bishop of Paris, and rose from there healthy and unharmed.]

[Note: [Col. 0309D] One Vatican manuscript lacks the title of this poem.]

[Col. 0309B] [Note: [Col. 0309B] [He expresses his affection for Rhagnemundus, or Ragnemodus, bishop, and declares that it cannot be erased by any oblivion. He prays for a long life for him and, in the names of Radegund and Agnes, gives thanks for the dish of Parian marble and for the gems which Rhagnemundus had sent as a gift to adorn the holy cross of the monastery at Poitiers.]]

Most exalted father of your country, Rucco, who shine for me with a sweet light,

Holding the inmost recesses of my heart with love,

Whatever of our longstanding friendship we have gathered together,

That, excellent one, continually grows into my affection.

For no forgetfulness takes away from me those whom I love;
