May the end come before love for you fails me.

Therefore, blessed father, as I hasten, I offer you a greeting,

Wishing you to survive into distant old age.

[Col. 0309C] Hence the daughters also render thanks to you from their hearts,

For the gift of the snow-white Parian marble:

Whenever a feast is placed upon that dish,

They see you in the form of the gift, with devotion.

For the sequence of gems, may the venerable cross render you honor—

The cross to whose throne the gifts contribute.

## CHAPTER XI. To Droctoveus the Abbot

[Note: [Col. 0310C] Droctoveus was a disciple of Saint Germanus at the monastery of Saint Symphorianus at Autun, which Germanus himself governed before he was made bishop of Paris. Droctoveus was later appointed by Saint Germanus, after Germanus had become bishop of Paris, as abbot over that community of monks. King Childebert arranged for him to be installed in the church of Saint Vincent, which he had built; this monastery was later called Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Saint Droctoveus died around 580. His life was written by an anonymous ninth-century monk; see the first volume of the Benedictine edition, p. 252, at whose end this poem about Droctoveus the abbot, written by Fortunatus, is appended.]

[Note: [Col. 0310A] [In this poem he praises Droctoveus the abbot, a disciple of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, and his most devoted imitator, and commends himself to him.]]

Venerable man, sacred in merits and worthy of honor,

Droctoveus, always a father to me in love,

You who rightly belong among the blessed disciples of Germanus,

You yourself have become the model of his teaching.

Running along the sacred tracks of that bishop,

You despise this world while desiring to go to heaven.

Proceed willingly along the road of heaven, destined to remain in the world,

And, I beg you, pray to God for me, his servant.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “Here you despise the world.”]

[Note: [Col. 0310D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “Pray to God.”]

## CHAPTER XII. To Faramundus the Referendary

[Note: [Col. 0310D] The manuscript reads “Pharamundum.”]

[Note: [Col. 0310B] [Writing to Faramundus, he says that he is visiting him by letter, since he could not do so in person. He asks him to commend him to the kings and then to reply by letter.]]

Sweet friend to me, memorable name of one who loves,

Faramundus, ready in acts of service, a man of good character,

If I have not myself come to you, let the page I send greet you,

And discharge the service which I render less fully in person.

And, I beg you, willingly commend me to our royal lords,

And convey my thanks for the help of your devotion.

May your letter seek me with devoted affection;

When this letter returns, kindly return the favor.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “Faramode, in good things.”]

## CHAPTER XIII. To Lupus and Waldo the Deacons

[Note: [Col. 0310D] Waldo seems to be the same man of whom Gregory of Tours speaks in Book VIII, chapter 22, of his *History of the Franks*. Gregory writes that Waldo, already a deacon, had been designated by Bertram, bishop of Bordeaux, shortly before Bertram’s death, as his successor in the see of Bordeaux; but that Waldo could obtain nothing from the king, who conferred that rank upon Gundegisil, surnamed Dodo, count of Saintes. Waldo had been called Bertchramnus at baptism.]

[Note: [Col. 0310C] [He expresses his affection for the deacons Lupus and Waldo and says that he visits them by letter—the one consolation he says remains to him in their absence—since he cannot hold them before his eyes. He asks them to commend him to the bishop, the kings, and others.]]

Honored with fatherly affection and constant devotion,

Here is Lupus, gentle toward me, and Waldo, sacred in that respect.

As you are alike ministers in goodness and honor,

So may you be alike to me in constant love.

I do what I can: absent, I offer you a greeting;

If I cannot see you with my eyes, I seek you through little letters.

We ask you to commend us to the supreme bishop,

And to the kings and lords, perhaps as a means of salvation.

I beg you also to commend me to Droctoveus, the beloved clergy, and my fellow citizens.

What I would do in person, do in my place.

[Col. 0311A] May the excellent Mummulus and Caesareus be honored,

And remember me to my Constantine.

[Note: [Col. 0311C] The Paris edition reads: “I always offer an equal love.”]

[Note: [Col. 0311C] The same edition reads: “Absent, I offer a greeting,” which is required for the meter. The Paris edition likewise reads this.]

[Note: [Col. 0311C] Brower thinks that this was Mummulus the abbot, surnamed Bonus, later made bishop of Langres. Gregory of Tours speaks of him in Book V, chapter 5, of his *History*, and adds: “If there is room for conjecture.” But since Mummulus, surnamed Bonus, was first abbot of Saint John of Réomay in the territory of Tonnerre and was afterward made bishop of Langres, it is less likely that Fortunatus would number him among those living at Paris. On the other hand, Eunius Mummulus, also called Mummulenus—or certainly the Mummulus whom Gregory of Tours names as prefect in Book VII, chapter 15, and whom Gregory frequently indicates lived at Paris—could already have been at Paris while King Guntram was alive. From Guntram he also earned the rank of patrician, as Gregory of Tours relates in Book IV, chapter 42, of his *History of the Franks*.]

[Note: [Col. 0311D] We read in the *Life of Saint Aredius the Abbot*, chapter 26, appended to the works of Saint Gregory of Tours, about a certain Constantine who was at Paris, a companion of Saint Aredius the abbot. When Aredius visited him while he was suffering from a very severe and terminal illness, Constantine had subsequently died, but Aredius restored him to life. Is this the same man of whom Fortunatus speaks?]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Basilica of Saint Lawrence

[Note: [Col. 0311D] The manuscript reads: “On the beam of the basilica of Saint Lawrence.”]

[Note: [Col. 0311A] [He relates that the martyr Lawrence, who had become famous while alive through miracles and virtues, continued after death, by the presence of his power, to help the people. He says that, during the construction of his basilica, a beam that had already been cut grew again, and that pieces removed from it restored sight to the blind.]]

Lawrence, rightly burned by living flames,

Who, with faith burning, return victorious from the fire,

Man beloved by God, once in an earthly body,

Even then your mind was already star-like.

You were able by your touch to restore buried eyes,

And again to bring daylight to an empty brow.

We believe that you rekindled extinguished lamps of light

By the sign of the cross which you made.

Now you also grant miracles to the people,

And undoubtedly bestow help upon faith.

While the people renew your temples with a shorter timber,

The beams grew, and nourishing faith also grew.

[Col. 0311C] When the trunk was shortened, it extended itself through your reward,

As much as it had first been small and afterward cut.

The tree, cut down by axes, deserved to grow still more,

And learned, though dry, to have a longer crown.

[Col. 0312A] From the place where it was cut it brings salvation to the people:

If a blind man comes without fear, he receives eyes.

You, sacred Levite, purified by punishment for the faithful,

From the place where you once had flames, now you have light.

[Note: [Col. 0312C] In one Vatican manuscript: “Visit in the times,” incorrectly. The Paris edition reads: “In these circumstances.” The manuscript reads: “Seen.”]

Thus were the deeds of the venerable bishop seen in those circumstances,

Yet they are destined to be remembered on the eternal day.

[Note: [Col. 0312C] One Vatican manuscript reads: “He extended himself by his own cutting.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312C] Gregory of Tours relates in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 42, that when a basilica was being built in memory of Saint Lawrence near Briona, a fortress in Italy, and a beam had been cut shorter than necessary, the people invoked Saint Lawrence’s aid, and the beam grew so much that some of it could even be cut away to make it suitable for the work at hand. He reports that pieces of that wood were afterward used to seek cures for illnesses. Gregory appended to his History several verses taken from this poem of Fortunatus.]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Wooden House

[Note: [Col. 0312A] [He says that a certain wooden building, because of the excellence of the craftsman who constructed it, far surpasses many bronze and stone buildings. He mentions the ornamentation and description of the same building.]]

Give way a little, wall constructed of stony material [Note: [Col. 0312C] The Paris edition reads: “constructed of stone.”];

Because of the craftsman’s merit, I prefer wood to you.

With its mass, the paneled palace strikes the heavens,

Where no crack appears, since a firm hand has joined it together.

[Col. 0312B] Whatever stones, sand, lime, and clay protect,

The kindly forest built piece by piece.

It rises higher, and a square colonnade surrounds it,

And the craftsman played in sculptured artistry.

[Note: [Col. 0312C] The Paris edition reads: “Constructed of sand and lime.”]

[Note: [Col. 0312C] One Vatican manuscript reads “broader”; another, “more severe”; another, “higher, more severe.” Brower says he found in Th. Pulmannus’s manuscript the reading “it rests upon,” although he himself admits that various manuscripts read *immitior*, a word which Fortunatus seems here to use for “vast” or “immense.” The Paris edition reads: “Higher and gentle.”]

## CHAPTER XVI. To Chrodinus the Duke

[Note: [Col. 0312D] Read about Chrodinus in Gregory of Tours, Book VI of the *History*, chapter 20, where he recounts his piety, generosity toward the poor, munificence toward churches, and other outstanding merits of this most pious and religious man. Gregory says that he died at the age of seventy in 582. I think that he is the same man whom Aimoinus, in Book III, chapter 40, of his *History of the Franks*, calls the duke Rodinus and reports to have been a true giver of alms, full of goodness, acting justly in all things, and loving Christ’s poor. Aimoinus likewise relates that when Chrodinus himself had ordered his servants to open a certain monument in which he intended to bury a dead man, they opened it and found a treasure of immense weight, including a considerable number of solidi. They carried it to their lord, who immediately distributed it among the poor.]

[Note: [Col. 0312B] [He recalls the fame of Duke Chrodinus, celebrated throughout all Italy and Germany; then he extols his nobility and generosity and beneficence toward everyone. He further praises his justice, modesty, and affability, on account of which he declares him dear and admirable to all.]]

Illustrious duke, proclaimed throughout the whole world for your merits,

Whom splendid fame reports to be exceedingly excellent,

I will not pass over your lofty praises, Chrodinus,

Lest I alone seem to be silent about great goodness.

[Col. 0312C] The Italian land applauds you, and Germany likewise;

Your praise always sounds upon everyone’s lips.

Illustrious from ancient times, nobler than your worthy birth,

You were destined to please kings and your native land.

[Col. 0313A] Others acknowledge you as guardian and fosterer,

And there is rivalry over your devotion.

You refuse your gifts to no one who may receive them;

You increase for yourself the wealth that you generously distribute.

You gladly seek out and desire someone to whom you can give,

And by doing this you make him your own among all people.

[Col. 0314A] You are a universal blessing, burdensome to no one, impartial toward all;

No rapacity possesses you, companion of justice.

Gentle in speech, calm, gracious, and modest,

You have been given everything so that you may bear every distinction.

You are held in esteem by the nations and dear to the Romans;

Fortunate are you, who always remain upon the lips of the people.

[Note: [Col. 0313A] One Vatican manuscript reads: “You make these men your own.”]

[Note: [Col. 0313] The same manuscript reads: “Your gait, and…” corruptly. The Paris edition reads: “And gracious and modest.”]

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 0313]

## CHAPTER ONE. Explanation of the Lord’s Prayer

[Note: [Col. 0313D] The manuscript reads: “The Lord’s.” The *Exposition by Fortunatus of the Lord’s Prayer* is found in two Vatican manuscripts, written in an extremely corrupt form because of the copyists’ faults. We have therefore set aside and omitted passages that were either of little importance or openly displayed error and corruption, selecting what was most important and indicated differences in the readings.]

[Col. 0313B]

So great was the profound mercy of our Savior’s compassion toward the human race, beloved children, by which he carried us, rescued from the linked shipwrecks of the world, to the harbor of everlasting freedom, that it cannot be expressed in words, revealed by the tongue, or even touched by thought. Yet it seemed too little that he created us from the clay [Note: [Col. 0313D] In two Vatican manuscripts: “which he created”; accordingly, *quod* is subsequently used for *quem*, a reading to be retained.], redeemed us with blood, and renewed us through baptism, unless, for the increase of our salvation, our mind were also instructed in how to pray, lest it unknowingly fall [Note: [Col. 0314D] The manuscript reads: “might be instructed.”].

For if he had not taught us how we ought to offer the just petitions of our prayer, we would either be presumptuous or confused beneath a cloud of error; and, not knowing what we ought to ask, we would commit sin rather than cleanse away what had been committed [Note: [Col. 0314D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “than we ought to cleanse.”]. From the place where we hoped assistance could come [Note: [Col. 0314D] Another manuscript reads: “and whence we hoped it could come.”], we might seem to incur harm, since an ill-formed prayer would become a greater cause of danger than of petition.

Therefore, retaining his mysteries and the many things contained in their brevity, we are taught to explain them briefly for the building up of the Church, because they will please us better in hearing once they have become clear in understanding. Let us therefore come to the very words of the holy prayer.

“Our Father, who are in heaven.”

Behold the voice of the Lord preaching, of whom the prophet says: “Let the clouds rain down the Just One” (Isaiah 45:8). He poured forth the light of hidden knowledge; and, to refresh our dryness with a rain of speech, he burst forth like a spring of leaping water.

For who else would reveal so great a secret of heavenly mystery to human beings, or teach it, or presume to do so, or know it? Abraham? Moses? A prophet? Or an angel [Note: [Col. 0314D] Another manuscript reads: “an angel, except the Only-Begotten”; in some manuscripts the word “indeed” is absent.]? No—no one except the Only-Begotten, to whom alone the Father is known in the fullness of his majesty. The others merited knowing as much of God on earth as he willed to disclose from heaven.

For the Son, in whom the Father is wholly present through unity of substance, not confusion of persons, possessed this knowledge not through another’s gift but by the power of his nature.

[Col. 0314A] Therefore, by saying that our Father is in heaven, he signifies our exile while we are on earth, according to the saying: “I am a sojourner upon the earth” (Psalm 118). Hence he seems to instruct us that, continually raising our minds to things above, we should hasten, with God’s help, to accomplish those things which, once the Father is appeased and Christ is our guide, will make us enter the blessedness of eternal life, so that, as sons, we may obtain the promised rewards.

[Note: [Col. 0314D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “When God the Father has been heard.”]

Nevertheless, when God the Father has been heard of, let no son be so cruel that he does not hasten to the embrace of his true parent.

Likewise, “our Father” is fitting because, by being reborn through baptism, a human being has become a son of God—one who through transgression had become an enemy and lost. Therefore, the person who now enjoys his grace freely acknowledges him as Father.

But although we are not sons of that Father in the same manner as the person of our Lord Jesus Christ—for he was born from the Father’s own substance, whereas he graciously created us from the earth—we have nevertheless merited becoming adopted sons through the grace of the Only-Begotten. Therefore, whoever in the Catholic Church is born of water and the Holy Spirit is counted among the sons of God.

Likewise, “Our Father who is in heaven”: in this confession we both honor God and follow his commandments, set forth our faith, and reject those who deny the Father in heaven.

Likewise, by saying “Our Father,” we have someone whom we ought to love in him; and, by acknowledging God, we likewise have someone whom we ought to fear.

[Note: [Col. 0314D] One manuscript reads: “Whom we ought to fear.”]

Let us therefore fear him, because he is just; let us love him, because he is compassionate, lest we carelessly wish to lose what he has carefully bestowed, and lest divine gifts be trampled underfoot by our transgression.

Therefore, whoever calls him Father should, as befits a son, conduct his life without stain. For he is a son who does not grieve his parent, does not exasperate his fellow heir, does not violate the love of his brother, does not squander the testament of his creator, follows admonitions, and hastens to fulfill commandments. But if he rebels, he is cast out and defiantly departs from the inheritance; nor does he any longer reclaim the inheritance with any confidence, since the crime he has committed has condemned him.

[Col. 0315A] Hence, when we come to God the Father, we are called brothers in Christ if we do not remain involved in the crime of sin; for the one who becomes a slave of sin loses the name of son.

But the fact that we say not “my Father” individually, but “our Father,” is understood to mean that no one should pray for himself alone, but that all should universally entreat the merciful Lord, so that all together may be delivered from the treacherous enemy.

For all who assemble in the Church enclose themselves within the same wall. Although they are many members, they are nevertheless contained in one body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:21). Therefore those who are joined together in the church ought not to be separated, not even in their prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0315D] The same manuscript reads: “For just as…”]

For just as in our own members we see how shoulder helps shoulder, hand helps hand, and foot helps feet, so it is considered fitting that we assist one another through admonitions, prayers, and tears, because of the saying: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2).

[Note: [Col. 0315D] Two manuscripts read: “Bearing one another’s burdens.”]

Finally, one person frequently obtains confidently on behalf of another what he is ashamed, out of embarrassment, to ask for himself, because in his own crime shame dares nothing.

Therefore, let each person pray for everyone together, since, just as a divided house will not stand, so a united house is not subject to ruin. And rightly did the Lord, the author of peace, teach in such a way that whatever one person asked would seem to benefit everyone.

Likewise, “our Father” is rightly added because, unless someone rightly believes in Christ, he cannot have a Father in heaven. He is not the Father of Arians, Jews, Photinians, Manichaeans, Sabellians, or the other plagues infected with the poison of a corrupt heart and cut down by the sickle of a wicked confession. Blinded, they have withdrawn because they wickedly attempted to make the Son unequal to God our Father; they receive the fruit of the flesh from their father, the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0315D] The sentence is obscure in the manuscripts. In the Paris edition it is boldly clarified as follows: “Those who think wrongly about the Son are so cut off from God our Father that they receive the fruit of the flesh from their own father, the devil.” Since the final clause of the period had been placed in the Pulmannus manuscript, we have now restored it and relegated the older reading to the margin. BROW.]

[Note: [Col. 0315D] The manuscript reads: “The fruit of carnal fury.”]

And therefore God is our Father in heaven because we rightly confess the Son on earth.

## “Hallowed be your name.”

We must attentively consider what divine admonition signifies in this expression when it says, “Hallowed be your name.” It does not mean [Note: [Col. 0315D] The manuscript reads: “whether anything higher is found.”] that anything higher can be found by which God the Father could be sanctified, or that we seem to confer something upon him by praying, since he himself rather sanctifies all things.

[Note: [Col. 0315D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “Since he himself rather sanctifies all things.”]

Rather, “hallowed” means: “May your name be blessed without ceasing by every tongue and in every place,” since this very fact—that we breathe and live—is among his gifts.

“Hallowed be your name.” Since God must be praised and called holy by the harmony of all the elements, we desire that his name be sanctified in us, that is, firmly held, and that we live in the holiness of baptism with which he washed us.

[Col. 0316A] Therefore, at this time we do not seek a new sanctification, but ask that we preserve, without the stain of vice, the sanctification we received undefiled.

[Note: [Col. 0316D] The same manuscript reads: “We seek sanctification.”]

For in a human being, the fruit of good conduct is the sanctification of God.

In this way too we rightly say that his name is sanctified: if someone sees that, by divine gift, our life is sincere, let him return thanks to the giver and exalt his holy name in our works, since all praise is rightly rendered to the one by whom prayers are fulfilled.

Likewise, “Hallowed be your name,” because the prayer itself does not explicitly contain the words “in us.” By saying “Hallowed be your name,” we seem to desire not only for ourselves that his name be sanctified, but also for those who have not yet merited reaching the grace of baptism. For in the fullness of Christ’s love we are taught to pray even for our enemies, because he freed from the prison of death not only his friends and faithful followers but also his adversaries and the guilty.

## “Your kingdom come.”

There can be no doubt that the Lord God always reigns, both here and everywhere. The Holy Trinity did not at some time take its beginning from the allotment of a kingdom, nor does it have an end with which it must be closed, since with God the times do not change in his stability: neither does the sun set for him, nor does night succeed day in turn.

But when we say, “Your kingdom come,” we do not mean that it should come to him from elsewhere—that is, that a higher person should bestow a kingdom upon him—but we ask [Note: [Col. 0316D] One manuscript reads: “but, of course, that it may come to us.”] that the kingdom promised to us should come to us through Christ the mediator, so that we may reign freely with him, who now live continually under the law of sin in the world [Note: [Col. 0316D] The manuscript reads: “who have been slaves in the world.”].

[Note: [Col. 0316D] The manuscript reads: “That it should be possessed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0316D] The same manuscript reads: “Since, in truth, with God…”]

He himself asked this of the Father, saying [Note: [Col. 0316D] The manuscript reads: “Father, where I am, may they also be with me”; another reads: “Father, may they also be with me.”]: “Father, those whom you gave me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). And elsewhere: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

Finally, for this reason he emptied Tartarus, so that he might fill the heavens.

Therefore we pray for this reason that his kingdom may come—not so that he may acquire what he possesses, but so that he may fulfill what he promised us.

It can also be understood in this way: “Your kingdom come,” that is, may the sincere desire for your kingdom come into our hearts, so that we may be able to overcome the devil’s blandishments. For then the deceitful enemy does not prevail over us with serpentine falsehood, when he continually sees that we have conceived desires for the divine kingdom.

Likewise, while Christ reigns, sin cannot reign in our bodies.

[Note: [Col. 0316D] Another manuscript reads: “Sin may not be able to reign in our bodies.”]

Likewise, when we say, “Your kingdom come,” we are admonished [Note: [Col. 0316D] One manuscript reads: “it is recognized, that.”] not to expect anything from the riches of an earthly kingdom, since we plant all our hope in the resources of the kingdom to come.

Likewise, “Your kingdom come”: these words are understood to rebuke those persons who wish to prolong this life of the world for a longer time,

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “Since all the righteous seem to desire that kingdom to come quickly.”]

although all the righteous ask that it come quickly.

Or certainly, “Your kingdom come,” that is, may Christ the Lord come to us, whom the choir of the saints daily awaits with reverence. In his promise the righteous trust that they will reign. Concerning his coming the Apostle says: “Then we shall be caught up together in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

But let us see who will be caught up with blessed Paul in the clouds. Will it be murderers, immoral persons, deceivers, drunkards, adulterers, robbers, and slanderers?

[Note: [Col. 0317D] One Vatican manuscript adds: “Accursed robbers.”]

Unless such people have been corrected, they cannot share with the holy Apostle in that company, since they do not now follow his admonitions; nor can they meet Christ, whose paternal instructions they presume to claim.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Another manuscript reads: “Or presume upon his fatherly [instructions].”]

Indeed, if they were able to hide themselves from the face of God in the fissures of the rocks, they would rather wish the mountains to fall upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Another manuscript reads: “Then the mountains to fall.”]

Therefore, let us consider to whom that kingdom is promised: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

At the beginning of the beatitudes he placed the humble in heart first, and thereby excluded the proud and swollen, when he said that the poor in spirit would reign.

Then follow: blessed are the meek; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; blessed are the merciful; blessed are the peacemakers; blessed are the pure in heart; and the rest.

Behold, they are invited to such rest who have labored in such a manner amid temporal toil.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] The same manuscript reads: “They are invited to eternal rest.”]

Truly, this is to reign without end: to possess the crown of blessedness adorned with these flowers, to be found worthy to behold God without shame, and, in his presence, for the soul to find what it has loved.

For if in this world human frailty and a certain poverty are said to reign, at least for the present, if fleeting prosperity and false happiness flatter them, how much more must that kingdom be sought where the gentler light of lilies and roses always smiles; where the painted beauty of fragrant flowers does not wither; where the fruitfulness of the place is neither oppressed by cloud nor dried by sun; where possession does not end with its possessor; where the sight grants whatever the mind desires; where the righteous will tread upon gems in the streets—gems that kings now lack in their crowns; where mortality, transformed into immortality, rejoices with the angels in a like portion; where there is one possession for human beings and God!

[Note: [Col. 0317D] The manuscript reads: “The splendor of luxury.”]

There let us desire fellowship, where the grace of such great happiness is possessed.

## “Let your will be done, as in heaven so on earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Brow reports that in certain books the beginning of this petition is presented as follows: “What is it that is thus asked?” and so on; “could anyone ever …?” The same reading is found in two Vatican manuscripts. [Col. 0318D] The manuscript reads, “could anyone?”]

This is asked so that God’s will may be done—not because anyone has been able to resist his will, so that the omnipotent God could not at some time do what he wished, [Note: [Col. 0318D] The manuscript reads, “lest anyone be able to hinder him.”] nor because anyone can hinder him in anything, [Note: [Col. 0318D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “The Omnipotent, therefore, cannot have anything hindered by him”; this is corrupt.] but so that his will may be fulfilled and active in us; for, when the adversary resists, we cannot fulfill his will unless we are fortified by his protection. [Note: [Col. 0318D] The manuscript reads, “by his own protection.”]

If it is asked what God’s will is, you have the Ten Commandments, which were promulgated by Moses according to God’s will. You have the Son of God, who knew the Father’s will, disclosed what had been hidden and brought into the light what had been obscured. Therefore God’s will has been made known, and there will be no excuse to come to our aid. For he who descended from heaven to earth—what else did he wish to be understood as his will, except that he would save us? [Note: [Col. 0318D] The same manuscript reads, “wishes it to be believed, except that by his redemption he would …”] Through his redemption he taught us to follow the ornaments of charity and humility, since he himself deigned to do this with such charity and profound humility. [Textual reading: the printed *sincere* means “sincerely”; the manuscript has *sincera* (“sincere,” feminine), whose grammatical attachment is uncertain.] [Note: [Col. 0318D] Another Vatican manuscript reads, “but when the Redeemer deigned …”]

Then, having chosen a temple for himself in a virgin, what does he teach except that we should guard the gifts of chastity? He cultivated justice, had no deceit in his mouth, showed mercy, released guilt through pardon, and always walked with a pure heart. What else did he do except draw us after his footsteps by words and examples? Therefore we must pray that, if we do not wish to perish, his will may operate in us, [Textual reading: for *orandum* (“we must pray”), one Vatican manuscript has *prandum est* (“one must dine” or “a meal must be taken”).] according to the Apostle’s words: “He is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Philippians 2:13). [Col. 0318B] As our Lord said elsewhere: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16); otherwise, a human being would find Christ by his own power.

Blessed Paul had a will, but not truly directed toward Christ, whose people he was devastating throughout the churches. [Col. 0318C] But because the Redeemer deigned to be more merciful than just toward his persecutor, so that he might turn to better things, he chastised him through the bitterness of blindness and took away his bodily light in order to open his spiritual eyes. Of him he said: “I will show him how much he must suffer for me” (Acts 9:16). Thus Christ’s mercy bestowed that good will; human frailty did not possess it. [Note: [Col. 0318D] The manuscript reads, “did not possess it,” rather than “possessed it.”]

Let us hear what the Lord Jesus Christ himself said while placed in the weakness of the flesh: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26). [Note: [Col. 0318D] The same manuscript reads, “The Son of God says: ‘But not …’” Another Vatican manuscript reads, “The Son of God truly says, ‘Nevertheless, not …’” and so forth.] The Son of God says, “Not as I will, but as you will, Father.” Why, then, is a human being so proud as to say that the will toward good comes from himself, rather than testify that it is God’s gift?

If good will comes from a human being without God’s inspiration, then let a Christian say in prayer: “Let my will be done, because it is good.” But may it be far from anyone to dare confess this; rather, let him pray that God’s will may be done in the human being—not the human will, which cannot will what is good unless the Lord inspires it, according to the words: “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Psalm 58). Therefore it is not the human will that precedes God, but God’s mercy that precedes the human being who does not will; for, as it is written: “God is the one who justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). Again: “The Spirit blows where he wills” (John 3:8).

Why, then, does not everyone acknowledge his own darkness, lest, once enlightened like a lamp kindled from elsewhere, he be extinguished by the wind of his pride and, when his brightness has been withdrawn, remain in the gloom of blindness—while, if he has any desire to will what is good, he thinks it belongs to his own free choice, and does not give thanks to the one who bestowed it? [Note: [Col. 0319D] The manuscript reads, “thereafter.” Soon afterward, one Vatican manuscript reads, “attribute it to the one who bestowed it.”] Let him not finally hear the saying: “From him who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Mark 4:25). That is, what he has received in advance through grace—unless he ascribes it to God, he will lose through pride.

For, according to Scripture, the will itself is prepared by the Lord. Let us hear the Teacher on this point, when he said: “He who speaks falsehood speaks from his own” (John 8). Why did he not add, “and he who speaks the truth speaks from his own,” unless this example makes it clear that, when someone speaks the truth, it must be recognized especially that he has this good from God’s grace, not from himself? For from ourselves we possess only falsehood. Since Truth itself is God, when someone speaks from God, from where does the cause of truth arise in a lying human being unless Truth itself supplies it—that is, unless the God of truth inspires in the human being that good will which both grants the will and brings its ability to completion?

But if someone objects that the Apostle says, “To will is present with me” (Romans 7:18), while he himself says, “God is the one who works in you both to will” [Note: [Col. 0319D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “both to will and to work.”] “and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Philippians 2:13), then, if someone says that God does not inspire that very will, blessed Paul does not, in this interpretation, contradict himself by expressing different opinions. [Note: [Col. 0319D] In the same manuscript, “does not differ” is absent, as though the sentence were expressed as a question. It then adds: “But far be it …”] For far be it that this peaceful man, who spoke by one and the same Spirit, should have generated scandal in the Church by these statements.

Thus the Teacher of the Gentiles said that willing was present with him, because he was not only inspired but also shone as a vessel of election; and he taught, saying: “God is the one who works in you both to will.” Furthermore, what do you have that you did not receive? As though he were saying: What good is there in you except what the one who made you has given? For if God does not bestow good will, but what you have comes from yourself, then he lied who said: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). [Col. 0319D] The printed reference reads “I Corinthians LXIV, 7,” evidently an error.

Take away God’s will, and I shall immediately see whether you have any will toward good by yourself, since, unless you are illuminated by Christ like a lamp, each day you go astray, not knowing what divine power chooses. Let us humbly say that we have no will toward anything good unless, with the Lord’s generosity, we receive it each day, according to what is written: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17). [Note: [Col. 0319D] The same manuscript adds, “according to what is read.”] Thus Paul’s statements remain harmonious, and, if we refer every good thing to God’s grace, we attain faithful teaching. [Note: [Col. 0320D] Another Vatican manuscript reads, “we attain the teaching.”]

Whoever agrees with the Apostle Paul—that is, with the eye of the Church—and with blessed Augustine, his follower, does not remain under the darkness of ignorance. As for what is said about the two ways, the broad and the narrow, so that each person walks along whichever he has chosen: on the broad way, with the reins loosened, you proceed freely by serving sins. [Note: [Col. 0320D] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “you proceed with a free rein.”] But on the narrow way, let us consider the Apostle’s words: “That you may walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, through the Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 4:1). Therefore no one chooses or reaches the way unless he has been called by him who is the way, the life, and the truth. [Note: [Col. 0320D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “unless he has been called by him.”]

But let us run along this way with the words of the Apostle and the commands of the Gospel, saying to those who had already been converted from the Jews to faith in Christ: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). And consider what this means, as the Lord himself proclaims: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth has set you free” (ibid. 8:31–32). [Note: [Col. 0320D] One Vatican manuscript adds, “and consider when this is just”; another, “and consider when this is so.”] Thus he urges us, by following what he has given through grace, to lead us to true liberation.

Therefore a human being will possess free choice perfectly toward the good when he will be wholly unable to serve sin. Again: “Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth”—that is, as the angels honor you in heaven, so may human beings honor you on earth. [Note: [Col. 0320D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “may they worship you on earth.”] And just as they appear continually to cling to God’s praise in blameless harmony and devoted charity, so may he command us to purify ourselves without stain in his fear and love.

Again: “Your will be done”—that is, just as the spirit, which comes from heaven and contemplates heavenly things, does so, so also may the flesh, which is from the earth, not desire earthly things but attend to the things of the spirit; and, as though harmony had been established, may it ascend together to heaven. Therefore, as in heaven—that is, in the spirit—so also on earth—that is, in the flesh—may God’s will be done, so that after Christ’s coming the flesh, which is the mother of sin, may no longer hasten to deceive the spirit, as Eve did; rather, may Adam, who typologically represents the spirit, have the flesh serving him. Let not the master serve the maidservant, but let the maidservant serve her master.

“As in heaven and on earth.” Before baptism, a human being is described as carnal; after baptism, he becomes spiritual. Therefore we pray for those who have not yet been washed in the laver, that just as we appear to have become heavenly through baptism, so those who are still strangers to the Church may not be deprived of so great a benefit but may, through the Lord’s generosity, receive gifts like ours. For when they become our companions, we shall not lose our privilege but increase it. What sort of envy would it be for one human being not to pray for another, [Textual reading: manuscript *quare* means “why,” in place of printed *qualis* (“what sort of”).] when Christ did not spare his own blood in order to acquire us? [Note: [Col. 0320D] The same manuscript reads, “when Christ did not spare himself for us.”]

Again: “Your will be done.” The Father’s will was what the Son preached, did, suffered, died, and rose again, as he said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6:38). Therefore we must pray that we may likewise deserve to conduct ourselves, to act, to endure, and to rise again in him, so that we may be able to reign with him. [Note: [Col. 0321D] The same manuscript reads, “that we may deserve to say and to do likewise.”]

Again: “Your will be done.” God is unchangeably good, and wills nothing other than what is always good, although the mass of our sins obstructs us. Therefore we rightly seem to desire that those things happen to us which God wills, since we know that he possesses the perfection of good will, and so forth. [Col. 0321A]

## Give us our daily bread today.

[Col. 0321B] We must consider how wonderfully the text of this prayer is arranged: after eternal things have been named, temporal things are requested. For these three petitions—“Hallowed be your name,” “Your kingdom come,” and “Your will be done”—are necessary here in order to obtain eternal things. They begin here, but must be believed to be possessed perfectly in the life to come, where they will remain forever.

Therefore, “Give us our bread”—as much as is necessary for soul and body, spiritually or bodily. “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil”: these petitions appear to concern the necessities of the present life. Finally, the sanctification of his name and his kingdom will remain perfect in our spirit and body after the resurrection. [Col. 0321C]

Again, whoever has deserved to reach true salvation must not fail to recognize that our daily bread is Christ, the bread of everlasting life, because he said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). Therefore this bread is not common like the other: the one protects bodies, while this one knows how to nourish souls. Whoever eats the former becomes hungry, but whoever enjoys this one is tormented by no hunger. Thus this food must be sought all the more eagerly because the more one feasts upon it, the more it refreshes.

That we ask for daily bread seems to signify that, if possible, we should reverently receive communion of his body every day. Since he himself is our life, we make ourselves strangers to our nourishment if we approach the Eucharist slowly or reluctantly. [Col. 0321D] Again, when we say, “Give us our bread today,” we recognize that it is not enough for us to have asked God on the previous day unless we also devote ourselves to him in the present prayer, in accordance with the command: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17).

Here too we must observe that, after we have come to Christ and rejected the world with its pomp, we no longer need to seek food beyond what daily use requires. [Col. 0322A] We must truly seek him and continually await the Lord’s coming, for the world’s impediments make human beings wretched. Let us know that bread is sufficient for the one to whom God is not lacking—bread such as he supplied to Elijah living in the wilderness.

## And forgive us our debts.

Forgiveness of sins is rightly requested after the food has been sought, so that the one who is nourished by God’s food may live for God, provided that his sins are forgiven. This is also fitting, lest human pride exalt itself: by asking forgiveness, it appears to confess its offenses, while, if it desires to be cleansed, it should return to prayer more frequently.

Sins are appropriately called debts, because they are owed and must be demanded. For just as a debt is demanded by a creditor, so sin is necessarily demanded by God on the day of judgment, [Note: [Col. 0321D] The manuscript here reads, “must necessarily be exacted.”] [Col. 0322B] unless, while we live here, that exaction is forgiven us through his mercy and pardon. We rightly ask that everything be remitted here, where we commit our offenses, because in the future, just as it will not be permitted to pray, so there will be no opportunity to repent.

But he adds:

## As we also forgive our debtors.

He showed himself merciful and imposed the law that, unless someone forgives the offenses of the one who sins against him, he should not expect forgiveness from God, according to the saying: “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew 7:2). [Col. 0322C] Again: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you” (Psalm 100), because the one who is merciful toward us wishes us to be merciful toward others. Therefore the person who rejects his teacher’s words is rightly punished for his fault. The highest almsgiving is to forgive another for what he appears to have sinned against you. [Note: [Col. 0321D] The same manuscript reads, “for what he seems to have sinned against you.”]

Again: “Forgive us our debts.” Why, then, do we ask immediately after rising from the baptismal font and sharing in the body of Christ that our sins be forgiven? Because our frailty cannot preserve the purity of the washing it received from the font unless God’s grace deigns to guard it. [Note: [Col. 0321D] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “cannot preserve it.”] And it is fitting that he says, “As we forgive our debtors,” so that it might be shown that the God of peace wishes us to be in harmony with everyone.

## Do not lead us into temptation.

Does God lead anyone into the snare of temptation? Or would he desire that anyone be overthrown by the enemy, when he warns us not to fall? [Note: [Col. 0321D] One manuscript reads, “who warns us lest we fall.”]

## CHAPTER II. To the illustrious and salutary man Mummulenus: a consolation on the death of his ten-year-old daughter.

[Note: [Col. 0321D] The third letter that follows seemed to indicate that this letter was addressed to Mummulenus, a most distinguished man, and the Vatican index confirmed this by giving that name. But since it is omitted from manuscript copies, and since in the manuscript of Saint Gall I found written, “To the illustrious and salutary man,” I would not dare assert the name with complete confidence. Brow. In the two Palatine manuscripts of the Vatican Library that we have consulted, and in which alone this letter is found, the same heading appears as in the manuscript of Saint Gall: “To the illustrious and salutary man.” [Col. 0322D]]

[Note: [Col. 0322D] See what we said about Mummulenus in the notes to poem 14 of Book VII.]

[Note: [Col. 0322D] Fortunatus consoles Mummulenus for the death of his ten-year-old daughter. First he says that this punishment has flowed over the whole human race from the sin of Adam and Eve, and that no one is outside the law or exempt from it, so that no one should grieve less because someone has died. He recounts that many women, after entering marriage, were torn away by death from their bridegrooms’ first embraces; in their case there was a double loss, both of life and of chastity. Finally, by the examples of Job and David, he teaches that this event must be endured bravely and patiently, especially since the girl may have been snatched and taken from earthly marriage to heavenly marriage, for which she perhaps longed, to reign with Christ in the resurrection of the dead. [Col. 0323A]]

Among the wounds that creep into the human condition—wounds that always make the hopes of wavering minds and slipping times uncertain— [Textual readings: printed *subrepentia* means “creeping in”; manuscript *subripientia* means “stealing in” or “surreptitious.” Printed *Nam* (“for”) is replaced by *Cum* (“when” or “since”) in the manuscript.] nothing causes greater anguish than either not seeing what one desires or seeing what one must lose. For in both circumstances the trembling spirit succumbs beneath no small burden: it anxiously watches for a long time what it may possess, and, as soon as it begins to possess it, immediately loses it. [Col. 0323B] It is afflicted until it obtains the thing; it is crushed when it loses it. But the matter is struck by a heavier blow when one must lose what one hopes for while it still lies between hope and fulfillment. [Textual reading: another witness has *quod inter spectare vel spectata amittere*, “that between looking upon things and losing the things seen.”] [Note: [Col. 0323D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “and so that he may have, and so that he may possess.”] Thus, in the one case hope is stretched out; in the other it is condemned. [Textual reading: manuscript *tenetur* (“is held”) for printed *tenditur* (“is stretched”).] There uncertainty grieves over whether one possesses; here the pain is certain if one must surrender.

Nature has implanted this in us. Through the transgression of our first parent, nature was punished by death, which descended to us; thus what is scarcely acquired is often quickly abandoned. The tooth of the aged serpent struck the root so deeply that the tree could not stand unless, fixed in the stock of death, it continued to live. An inheritance from our parents handed this on to their descendants: subject to death, we seek to live though we are destined to die. The possession acquired from the unhappy tree wounded everyone; with its alluring fruits, it harmed its offspring before it nourished them.

Certainly death entered under the appearance of a feast, wounded the parents by its deadly touch, and afterward wounded their descendants. [Textual readings: alongside printed *Quod certe* (“This certainly”), witnesses have *Quo certe* (“whereby certainly”) and *Qua* (“by which”).] The taste afflicted them; the juice afflicts us, [Textual reading: manuscript *gustu … succo* puts both nouns in the ablative, “by the taste … by the juice,” rather than printed nominatives *gustus … succus*.] because the cup of poisonous persuasion that the father wickedly swallowed he poured into his offspring. [Col. 0323C] Thus, to put it so, what flowed from the fountain ran down into the stream. [Note: [Col. 0323D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “what flowed from the irrigated fountain flowed down”; the manuscript reads, “in the stream.”]

That mother therefore brought this into the race—yet, because of her crime, she became a stepmother to it: unhappy Eve, the solitary one (*monades*), to all her descendants. [The force of *monades* is somewhat uncertain.] She alone constructed it in such a way that she destroyed everything, using an ancient scheme of deception to ruin the inexperienced man and perish herself.

But what good will her offspring accomplish if they extend themselves into accusation of their parent’s evil? Or if, by reviling, they bite again the one who once perished by a bite, [Textual reading: *detrahendo demordeat* has “by disparaging, bite down upon” in place of printed *detrahendo remordeat*, “by disparaging, bite again.”] when his own fall was sufficient for him, and our downfall followed from it? Therefore I think it improper to bite him again, through whom grace was freely found, and through whose fall death began to consume the nourishment of life. [Note: [Col. 0324D] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “if I bite back”; afterward they read “he found grace” instead of “he found thanks.” The manuscript has “thanks came, ungrateful.”] When the opening of his eyes was promised him, light was taken away; and, though divinity had been promised, the fallen human being returned to earth. Thus the harmful food dragged the offspring born from him into captivity as prey.

That captivity made us exiles from prosperity and companions in adversity; and our wandering is all the more grievous the more familiar hard death becomes. From old Adam to the new human being, our life is born together with death. Abel did not escape it; Enoch did not evade it; Noah did not withdraw from it—he postponed death through the flood but did not change it. The patriarch did not reject this law; the lawgiver did not avert it; the prophet endured it, and one greater than a prophet succumbed to it. [Col. 0324A]

Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Hannah, and Elizabeth, although of the weaker sex, nevertheless drank this bitterness together with the rest. Who could complain about the others, when the conqueror of death himself, in that part by which he became flesh, was also subjected to death? He would not have been fully human if he had not experienced the tomb; nor would he be believed to be God unless he had risen from the grave.

This is why I speak, dearest friend, bound to you by the faithful pledge of my affection: [Textual reading: manuscript *fide* (“faith”) for printed *fideli* (“faithful”).] you lament the passing of your holy daughter, barely indicating it in broken sobs through a sorrowful pen, as the funeral of her ten years overtook her and the flower of tender youth withered. [Note: [Col. 0324D] Another manuscript reads, “the little flower withered.”] Though she had almost been drawn back from the threshold of marriage, she was given not to the bridal chamber at her father’s desire but to the tomb; and, to a different song, she was delivered not to the marriage bed but to the grave. [Col. 0324B] Perhaps the household was already eagerly hastening toward her wishes; her relatives and her homeland were being carefully stirred up. Her mother was suspended in expectation, the care of a nurse was already rising, and rosy modesty was joined to puberty, adorned by the festive art appropriate to her sex.

But why does the beauty of her appearance carry me away, betraying itself so quickly—fleeting as the flesh is deceptive? When glory is proclaimed for the dead, lamentation increases. You had her, then, as a father, but she was not your possession; [Note: [Col. 0324D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “you considered her entrusted to you instead.”] rather, you returned what had been lent to you. She is mourned as though lost, but let it be considered not lost, since she has returned to Christ undefiled.

Or do you complain as though you alone had suffered this, when such a calamity has overcome kings as well? Were you happier than Augustus, braver than Alexander, more favored than Trajan, holier than Theodosius, when both soldier and prince share equally in this kind of death? You must patiently grieve over what you share with the world. [Col. 0324C]

How many women has death drawn away to the tomb from their very first embrace? They suffered loss after recognizing what they did not possess; they must be mourned twice over, first for having lost their chastity and afterward for having perished in this way. Therefore, although you may complain that you have lost such offspring through such an event, this is not new to anyone. The girl could not have avoided what came through a woman.

Rather, consider this: let the event of her death be an event of virtue, and make yourself equal to the examples of those who, having conquered grief, rise to the crown. You have, among the heights of patience, Job as a first example and standard, as though in a mirror. [Col. 0324D] He gave thanks to the Lord for his children as though he had received them at the very moment when he lost them. That man of experience entrusted everything to the divine will, lest he fall.

And what of David? Though he had conquered Goliath, did he not submit himself like grass to the heavenly command when he lost his son? He washed and ate, lest he resist, understanding that he must yield to the one who formed all things. The faithful servant feared provoking the displeasure of his good Lord even by murmuring; the pious father continually poured himself out in tears so that she might be joined in the divine marriage. [Note: [Col. 0324D] The manuscript reads, “to whom he continually poured himself out in pious tears so that he might be joined to him.”]

Can you not infer that he would not have taken her away unless she had pleased him for his own bridal chambers? How do you know the depth of the divine counsel, or what longing for your daughter lay hidden in her heart? Perhaps she chose beforehand what she deserved, and what she desired came to light.

Therefore, excellent man, be your own judge and endure. For if you restrain yourself through charity and judge yourself, you do no offense—especially since the Redeemer’s promise and the voice of the herald Paul soften you. Like thunder, that voice declares that, in the twinkling of an eye, the buried will hasten to rise again and will live beneath Christ’s shadow, secure in their virginity. [Col. 0325A]

## CHAPTER III. Another letter.

[Note: [Col. 0325B] Fortunatus excuses himself for daring to offend the taste or judgment of those to whom he writes, accustomed as they are to refined and delicate fare, or to the delights of every kind of eloquence and learning, with his unpolished letters and rustic, rough style of writing. Nevertheless, he asserts that even rustic and ordinary foods sometimes please the most elegant person. Then he offers them greetings in whatever words he can, full of most loving longing, and at the same time prays for long life and immortal happiness after death for the entire royal household. Finally, he asks them to commend him to the kings and royal officials, and especially to receive favorably, in his own name and in that of Radegund, the bearer of this letter, sent by Radegund, and the matters concerning Radegund that he is to transact.]

[Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscripts do not indicate precisely who these people are to whom Fortunatus writes. If Mummulenus was from Soissons, and these were his wife and household, the kings mentioned later were perhaps Chilperic or Childebert, together with his royal household, under whom Mummulenus evidently lived, as can be inferred from Gregory of Tours in his History of the Franks.]

To the illustrious lords and all the magnificent servants of the lords, embraced with every longing. [Col. 0325C]

If this custom of human society extends generally among all people as a single practice, and has reached us by a kind of natural law from our ancient ancestors, since we pass from the pleasing whiteness of wheat bread and the sweetness that nourishes us to the bristling food of barley grain with a tooth, nose, and throat that are exceedingly reluctant to accept it; since the austerity of a meal does not invite us to proceed to the banquet when the sweetness of pleasing food has been exchanged, unless hunger presses us—[Note: [Col. 0326D] In the same manuscript, “after” is absent.]—this is why, after your illustrious and magnificent highness has been abundantly refreshed by the overflowing instruction of daily discipline and polished by the nightly labor of a fervent intellect, after, so to speak, that refined brilliance of your eloquence has been wiped clean and made transparently bright by exercise, [Col. 0325D] [Note: The manuscript reads the feminine form, “bright.”] the radiant light of your understanding turns with disdain toward the rusty eloquence of my tongue, when you hear the wavering sounds of my speech, as though after the banquets of the quail or the Phasis pheasant I were placing the food of cattle before the most delicate diners.

Yet amid all this I seem to be encouraged by one hope: that after royal delicacies a rustic dish may to some extent be desired, and that a rustic often offers something that delights the mind of the powerful. For although at royal banquets a purple robe glitters with flashes of gold, a table often pleases more through its charm when it is shaded by leaves arranged from the vine or covered by a curling cluster of ivy. [Note: [Col. 0326D] The same manuscript reads, “therefore he has …”]

Thus even the shepherd brought back from the forest has something that he can offer; and if the other things are lacking, his wealth of milk nevertheless invites the gracious guest.

Therefore, speaking before the Lord, we reverently and most eagerly offer greetings to your lordship and highness, to your lavish sweetness. We beseech the mercy of the eternal King that, while the most excellent lords reign happily and the offices of your authority and of all authority increase, the span of this fleeting life may be prolonged in such a way that, with him guiding you along the most merciful path and with you serving him most faithfully without stain, you may together enter the desired kingdom of our Creator and Redeemer. [Note: [Col. 0326D] The manuscript reads, “in the kingdom desired.”]

Trusting in Christ in the affection of your charity, commend our humility with overflowing sweetness to all the saints and servants of the Lord, and also to the reigning lords and their faithful servants. We confidently ask this of you: that you deign to regard the bearer of this letter, your venerable servant, a man of the lady Radegund, your mother, a holy soul, and the matters that he presents on behalf of that lady’s usefulness and necessity, before Christ and his angels, as your own concern—both out of reverence for her and in response to our prayer. [Note: [Col. 0326D] Another Vatican manuscript reads, “for the necessary matter on his behalf, as well as at my request.”] We make this known without any doubt, so that what you expend on her cause before the present lords, the kings, you may acquire from the eternal King with a hundredfold reward, according to his accounting. [Col. 0326C]

## CHAPTER IV. Another letter.

[Note: [Col. 0326C] He again consoles the same man, perhaps Mummulenus, or rather his wife, for the death of their daughter. He shows that he too shared in their grief and sorrow at losing her. He adds that what cannot be remedied by grief should be endured more gently, especially since the dead girl had been adorned with virtues that death could not extinguish along with her body—virtues by which she was esteemed among human beings, pleasing to God, and beloved by him.]

When your ambassadors passed through, we rejoiced that we had received your letters, filled with every kind of affection and with insatiable longing. [Note: Brow emends “revelationis” to “relevationis” (“relief”), which is to be followed.] In them we reread what concerned our consolation: the report concerning the safety of your highness; and, by including a remembrance of your sweetest daughter, we share in your grief. Indeed, those with whom joy was shared while she lived must necessarily share tears over her now that she is dead.

Reason does not permit you alone to claim the privilege of weeping for her, since you possessed her in an affection in which we too were bound, though not equally. For although she had come forth, fashioned from your very entrails, she lived no less fully in our hearts, since, having brought forth your child from the womb, you sent her, as it were, into our embrace to be received. [Textual reading: manuscript *nostro gremio* means “in our embrace,” in place of printed *nostrum gremium*, “into our embrace.”] Thus, though she was to depart from you in body, if not in heart, she became for us, through your charity, someone whom we might embrace. Hence what her mother had contributed through the natural cause of birth was completed in me by an adoptive affection, [Textual reading: one Vatican manuscript has *quod matri* (“what [belonged] to the mother”) in place of printed *quod mater* (“what the mother [had contributed]”).] since, though born to you, she was nevertheless reborn for us.

I had certainly hoped, in view of her merits, [Textual reading: the same manuscript explicitly has *pro meritis ejus*, “in view of her merits.”] to speak with you while she lived for a longer time about joy rather than to produce sorrowful consolation from tears. [Note: [Col. 0327C] The same manuscript reads, “rather than sorrowful consolation should arise.”] But the hostile sequence of events, which more quickly snatches away what it has recognized as most pleasing, [Textual reading: manuscript *quia* (“because”) for printed *quae* (“which”).] wished almost in a single moment both to offer me what I desired and to take it away. [Col. 0327B]

Why, then, did it bring us what it hurried to remove? Nothing in the human condition is more cruel than either not seeing what one possesses or seeing what one must lose. But how long will unwelcome grief intensify its own sorrow and rush headlong without the restraint of measured consolation? [Note: [Col. 0327C] Another manuscript reads, “How long will importunate grief sharpen his sorrow, or rashly …”] It should understand that what it could not change must be moderated, and should bear calmly what it cannot make undone. [Note: [Col. 0327C] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “what it will not be able to make happen.”] This is especially so because so many admirable qualities shone in her that she did not lack praise among human beings and, in God’s sight, may expect the rewards of one who is alive for her deeds.

For, apart from the other good qualities that must be praised in her—qualities that do not lie sealed in the tomb [Note: [Col. 0327C] One Vatican manuscript reads, “while they are spoken of.”] but circulate on everyone’s lips—let me say briefly this one thing: if faith and persecution for Christ make a martyr, then you have nothing in such a daughter that you should mourn. She was fortunate both to believe rightly and to endure; and although her lot was hastened in youth, innocence secure in the crown must nevertheless remain confident. [Note: [Col. 0327C] Another manuscript reads, “Although her lot was early, innocence, secure in the crown, is nevertheless owed.”]

## CHAPTER V. Here begin verses on the Oratory at Artanensis.

[Note: [Col. 0327C] Arthona, or Archtona, was a village in Auvergne, mentioned by Gregory of Tours in his book On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 5. At that time it was already a village renowned for the memory and miracles of Saint Martin of Tours. The distinguished Ruinart observes in his notes to chapter 4 of the same book that Artanensi is used here for Artonensi. [Col. 0327D]]

[Col. 0328A] [Note: The temple built at Arthona by Gregory of Tours in honor of the holy archangel Gabriel is mentioned, and praises of that same holy Gabriel are included.]

Whoever hastens to these thresholds of the venerable temple, [Note: [Col. 0327D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “the lights of the temple,”]

to pray for the gifts that God gives in his love,

all these things shine in honor of the holy Gabriel,

who rightly carries out God’s gracious commands as his minister.

He came to Zachariah, bringing news from heaven,

when a mighty prophet was given to Elizabeth.

And when he later proclaimed the Redeemer, the almighty King, from heaven,

so that Mary might give him to the earth from her womb. [Note: [Col. 0327D] Another manuscript reads, “which she brings about, so that she might give him to the earth.”]

For this the holy bishop Gregory raises new buildings,

so that the heavenly riches may be restored to him.

## CHAPTER VI. To the Church of Tours, which was renovated by Bishop Gregory

[Note: It commemorates the new church built by Gregory of Tours in honor of Saint Martin, in place of the old one, which was collapsing from age. Taking the occasion, it recounts at greater length Saint Martin’s power and deeds.]

[Note: This church, built by Briccius, successor of Saint Martin in the see of Tours, and then magnificently restored by Perpetuus, likewise bishop of Tours, after the old structure built by Briccius had been demolished, was finally restored again by Gregory himself. Gregory of Tours relates this in these words (Book X of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 31, §19): “I, Gregory, unworthy, the nineteenth, found the church of the city of Tours, in which blessed Martin and the other priests of the Lord had been consecrated to the office of bishop, dissolved and broken apart by fire; having rebuilt it with a broader and loftier elevation, I dedicated it in the seventeenth year of my ordination.” This was in the year 590, in which year Fortunatus’ poem appears to have been written. [Col. 0328C] The description of this church is given as follows by Gregory of Tours (*History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 14): “The basilica of Saint Martin is five hundred and fifty paces from the city; it is one hundred and sixty feet long and sixty feet wide; it is forty-five feet high up to the ceiling; it has thirty-two windows in the sanctuary, twenty in the nave, forty-one columns, sixty-two windows throughout the entire building, one hundred and twenty columns, and eight doors—three in the sanctuary and five in the nave.” Victor Giselinus, in his notes on Sulpicius Severus, refers this description of the basilica of Saint Martin to the work of Briccius or Perpetuus, bishops of Tours. Browerus prefers to refer it to Gregory’s work. But it seems impossible to doubt that the structure and description of the Tours basilica just mentioned cannot belong to the work of Briccius, since Gregory, in the passage cited above, says that the church built by Briccius was quite small and narrow, and that Perpetuus had it removed in order to build his own. Accordingly, that description must be understood to fit the basilica which Perpetuus first built and Gregory later restored. Although Gregory says that he restored it with a broader and loftier elevation, anyone can understand that its form and size did not greatly differ from that of Perpetuus, since, speaking of the same basilica which Perpetuus had erected, he adds in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 6: “There would be much to say about this building, but since it is still present, we thought it better to be silent about it.” In the *History of the Franks* also he often speaks of it as still standing. See the appendix to the notes on the works of Saint Gregory of Tours, where the basilica of Saint Martin is discussed at greater length, p. 1390, Paris edition, 1699.]

The venerable temple shines with the worship of the Most High,

A noble summit of a distinguished citadel.

When Martin covered a needy man with his own tunic,

He gave splendid signs in an ordered succession of deeds.

For while that same bishop was performing the sacred mysteries,

He was seen to have the light of gems in his hand.

And as much of the garment as his right hand left uncovered,

So much did a flashing gem cover his limbs.

[Col. 0328C] Saint Martin also, while blessing the gracious altar of the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0328D] Paris edition: “while he was blessing the nourishing altar.”]

Was seen to send from his head a fiery globe.

These temples, now renewed, holy Gregory brings forth,

And the ancient worship and honor have returned.

[Col. 0329A] Above all, the gleaming summits of the temple shone,

And, after its former uses, the new hall shines forth.

[Note: [Col. 0329C] Two Vatican manuscripts: “falling into old age.” Manuscript: “and falling into old age.” Paris edition: “turning toward old age.”]

Coming into old age, it learned to grow green again more beautifully;

Ruined after its collapse, it was built more firmly in its place.

The same Gregory, working with the aid of Martin,

Restored this new structure to what the old one had been.

[Note: In one Vatican manuscript: “where that old one flows”; another reading has *illa* (“that one”).]

The bright sanctuaries of the Lord gleam beneath their brow;

Though gracious in merit, they are also lofty in elevation.

Old age itself had ruinously overthrown them,

As a wall perhaps dissolved by flowing waters.

But Bishop Gregory took care to renew the building,

And he does not grieve that it fell, since it now gives greater support.

Martin saw the trembling beggar at Amiens

And immediately covered his limbs with half his cloak.

But before the angelic hosts, in the silent night,

[Note: [Col. 0329D] In the other Vatican manuscript: “he himself, in this silent night.”]

[Col. 0329B] Christ declares that he possessed it in the beggar’s form.

O holy bishop, worthy to be celebrated beneath the stars for your merits,

From where you cover the naked, from there you clothe your God.

Among the excellent vessels which God the Potter made,

Martin shines as a vessel honored for his merits.

Cleansing the leper’s spots with precious kisses—

For him, what he gave from his mouth was peace and healing.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] The same passage: “the diseased man’s entrails.”]

Thus, blessed one, healing the sick man’s ulcers with your mouth,

What the Jordan does, you accomplish by touching him with saliva.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] The same passage, and likewise the Paris edition: “drawn out by saliva.”]

How great was Martin’s generous faith, a citizen throughout the ages,

That wherever he was, death there lost its way!

[Note: One Vatican manuscript: “at last, having stretched himself out.”]

Finally, when a catechumen lay there with life extinguished,

He stretched himself over him and drove away the weapons of death.

Thus, for the widow’s son, hanged and then brought down,

Where this man of God is, there death is not permitted to come.

[Note: Gregory of Tours relates in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 21, that a man caught in theft and hanged by a noose, after invoking Saint Martin’s protection, did not die but hung from a tree for two days. At last he was lowered by a religious woman who had been warned in a dream by blessed Martin, and he lived until his own time, as a witness of so great a miracle. Fortunatus seems to have had this event in mind here.]

[Col. 0329C] When the saint compelled the pagan pine to be cut down,

The rustic crowd placed a just man beneath it to crush him.

Once the tree had been cut with an axe and was already bringing down its lofty mass,

At the command of the cross it was forced to move backward.

What power of faith is this? While the weight of the mighty pine

Was falling where nature directed, the cross makes it go where nature forbids.

When he placed his finger upon the man swollen from the serpent’s bite,

Who was approaching his final hour, the evil poison flowed away.

The disease gathered there, and, drawn from the ulcer through his thumb,

As the poisons fell, he raised his head.

As though he had drawn the venom out with a new ointment through his fingers,

So, by the craftsman’s touch, he overcame death.

[Col. 0330A] While a dead thief was being falsely honored,

[Note: [Col. 0329D] One Vatican manuscript: “by this voice”; manuscript: “by this.”]

At this word of Martin the shadow was compelled to speak.

Declaring publicly that he had been slain for his crimes,

He also confessed that he was not just but rather guilty.

O holy voice, compelling dead corpses to speak,

When the ashes lie dead after death, you give them their words!

While a viper was swimming down the river

And was about to touch the shore of the bank,

At Martin’s command it was called back into the flowing waters,

And, weary from the journey it had completed, retraced its course.

How great was the love of the Lord that burned in such a heart,

When he has power to turn back poisons through the very waters!

By Martin’s merits, for others also burning with fever,

The dry page gave back flowing sweat.

The paper, warmed by healing medicine,

Would moisten the severe fires with its letters.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] Paris edition: “The plague is absent from all who are moistened by this utterance.”]

How great was God’s grace that watered them through this utterance,

When its spring flowed upon those scorched by fever?

Nourishing God, creator of all things, gracious and supreme—

Gregory, for whom you provide a seat in the citadel,

Gives you temples in return.

For these had been utterly torn down by the ancient collapse;

Now, roofed by new labor, they shine in cultivated splendor.

By the right of your power, good creator of the world,

Return these heights to heaven, since he gives them to you on earth.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] One Vatican manuscript: “the narrowness of the summit, accomplished.”]

The narrow summit, overcome by the passage of age,

[Note: [Col. 0329D] Manuscript: “breeze.”]

Was torn down so that a better hall might rise from the ground.

There, while Martin performed the sacred mysteries of the Lord,

He sent a fiery globe from his head into the stars.

Yet, lest it should collapse and lie in a pitiable end,

It deserved a bishop who would bring it aid.

[Col. 0330C] Now revived and gleaming through Gregory’s urgent labor,

[Note: [Col. 0329D] Paris edition: “Fallen into old age.”]

Though fallen through age, it blooms with renewed honor.

Thus this priest, repairing the ancient foundations,

Raised up the distinguished structure that had once shone so brightly.

[Note: Odo, in the sermon he wrote about the burning of this basilica and its restored ornamentation, says: “Inside it was covered with marble plates. For sometimes a reddish wall of Proconnesian marble, sometimes white Parian marble, and sometimes green Laconian marble, displayed a varied and sufficiently beautiful pattern; outside it gleamed with little golden, sapphire-colored, and mosaic stones. The roof too was covered with sheets of tin.”]

Now the graceful hall is pleasing, pierced with broad-eyed windows,

Through which day is shut in by the fortress of night.

Painting adorns the structure more brightly with the pomp of its colors,

And you would think that the limbs drawn with pigments were alive.

[Note: Browerus correctly observes that the following seven epigrams express the subjects of the paintings with which Gregory had adorned the basilica of Saint Martin. Gregory himself says of this, in Book X, chapter 31, §19: “I found the basilicas of Saint Perpetuus burned by fire, and I ordered them to be painted or adorned by the work of our craftsmen so that they might be as splendid as they had been before.”]

He cleansed the leper.

The region of Pannonia sent you, Gaul, a fruit,

A hostile land producing a heavenly nourishment.

[Note: [Col. 0330D] Martin, of course, had been born at Sabaria in Pannonia. From Pannonia arose the Huns and many other barbarians, by whom Italy and other regions had been grievously harassed and ruined.]

[Note: [Col. 0330D] One Vatican manuscript: “the seed of Pannonia,” perhaps “the sowing.” Paris edition: “Pannonia sent its summer produce.”]

[Col. 0331A] Martin, illustrious in merits, who as a divine gift

Holds the summit of a senator in the heavenly seat.

He cleanses the spots of leprosy with healing kisses

And cures the infected man with pure saliva.

At the river of the Lord, where this man was not obliged to labor,

The saint gave from his mouth what the Jordan possesses.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] One Vatican manuscript: “to whom it was not labor to go”; this reading should be retained.]

And there, while you yourself, shepherd Gregory, act,

May he remove from Fortunatus, the guilty man, so many stains.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] The same manuscript: “he himself to me.” The Paris edition has the same reading.]

### The Divided Cloak

While Martin, poor himself, divided his cloak with the needy man,

Christ declares that he was well covered by that garment.

Rich poverty, which clothed the Lord with a covering—

He whom God the maker, who gave the stars, encountered!

### He Gave the Tunic

If you wish to know the deeds of blessed Martin,

Here you can briefly learn the man’s miracles.

Finally, when the holy man himself had given his tunic to the needy,
