And a small part of the tunic had been returned to him,

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Paris edition: “the sleeves’ fabric over.”]

What the short sleeves did not cover upon his arms,

That man’s hand was seen covered with gems.

O exceedingly happy man, for whom it came to pass that, in place of wool,

His limbs were covered with the radiance of noble stones,

So that, while he was still sprinkled with ash and embers,

The man might go forth gem-covered through angelic craftsmanship!

### He Raised Three Dead Men

What the loving and supremely good God accomplishes in his servants,

You can prove abundantly from Martin’s deeds:

He deserved to lead corpses from death to life,

And to restore daylight where he had driven death away.

### The Cut-Down Pine

[Col. 0331C] As the tree was falling and about to crush blessed Martin,

He immediately makes the cross, and the driven-back pine returns.

Who would not lend an ear to divine power,

When, with the trunk turned aside, the wood too gives way?

### The Idols Overthrown

While Martin wished to overthrow the firmly supported idols,

A great column, falling from heaven, crushes them.

The heavens deign to serve the just man’s aid;

What faith is this, whose weapons heaven itself hastens to provide?

### The False Martyr

While a thief was perhaps being worshiped as a martyr,

At Martin’s arrival he proves himself guilty.

By the merit of his virtue, with faith’s radiant flash,

The shadow of the dead man neither remains silent nor stays hidden.

## CHAPTER VII. To King Childebert and Queen Brunhild, on the birthday feast of Saint Martin of Tours

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Childebert was the son of King Sigibert. After his father was killed in 575, he was left as a child and succeeded to his kingdom, while Brunhild, his mother, administered the realm, as can be read in Gregory of Tours, Book VIII of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 22.]

[Col. 0331D] [Note: [Col. 0331D] As Fortunatus was traveling to King Childebert and his mother Brunhild, he relates that the feast day of Saint Martin occurred for him on the journey. From this occasion he describes the saint’s fame, spread throughout the whole world, and the glory he enjoyed in heaven. Finally, he offers prayers for Childebert’s entire royal household.]

While a servant small of heart approaches exalted lords,

I travel by boat through the shifting waters and shallows,

Behold, there arrives the day of the venerable citizen throughout the ages,

The day everlasting in light through Martin’s merits.

He now wondrously occupies the whole world from Gaul,

[Note: [Col. 0331D] One Vatican manuscript: “and the just man proceeds.”]

And his virtue proceeds where no one can walk.

Like a lofty beacon he extends his light as far as the Indians;

The Spaniard, the Moor, the Persian, and the Briton love him.

The East possesses him, and the West; Africa and the North possess him;

Martin’s glory is wherever the world has lands.

[Col. 0332B] He who travels across the waves along the ocean’s shore,

Circles the course of the world so that he may benefit all.

Ascending through ashes and harsh haircloth to heaven,

He now stands adorned with gems, once poor in the world,

Where the glory of the patriarchs is found and the prophets shine,

Where stands the sacred twice-twelve company of the fathers.

Among the apostolic number, amid the senate shining red,

[Note: [Col. 0331D] The same manuscript: “where he himself sits.”]

Where Christ the king of love sits upon his throne,

Where Peter excels with the key and Paul with doctrine,

Among the others too the palm, crown, and faith shine.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Two Vatican manuscripts: “with flourishing light,” which follows.]

Where the martyrs’ places bloom with reverent light,

And their blood is inscribed with honor in the book of life.

Where confessors fill gem-studded palaces

And possess golden dwellings in eternal day,

He too stands after the tears, where now the noble Radegund is,

[Note: [Col. 0331D] This shows that the poem was written after the death of blessed Radegund. She died around the year 587.]

[Col. 0332C] And perhaps that Eugenia holds this hand.

[Note: [Col. 0332D] Manuscript: “with her hand.”]

[Note: [Col. 0332D] One Vatican manuscript: “among you.”]

Among these Martin, beautiful, wears his diadems,

And a shining belt glows about his sacred loins.

[Note: [Col. 0332D] Paris edition: “And Gregory sings the glorious.”]

Gregory sings Christ’s triumph over death

And applauds the God who rose again with love.

You also honor this Martin, whom kingdoms choose as patron;

You honor him on earth, and he remembers you in heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0332D] Manuscript: “among.” Paris edition: “within.”]

May he sing of you beneath the stars among the angelic hosts,

You who honor him before human beings in this world.

May he read your names to patriarchs and prophets—

He whose name an ivory diptych proclaims today in the church.

[Note: This verse seems to indicate that a diptych, constructed or ornamented in ivory and preserved in the church at Tours, had once been inscribed with the name of blessed Martin, formerly bishop of the Church of Tours. Browerus says more about diptychs in his notes on this passage.]

May he render to you the apostolic princes and the other patrons

Whom you honor here and to whom you offer pious festivals.

[Col. 0332D] May that intercessor also go to Christ on your behalf,

[Note: [Col. 0332D] One Vatican manuscript: “he prays.”]

To whom you offer vows by praying in the temples.

May he present these solemn rites before the king of heaven,

So that from here kingdoms and the riches of salvation may be granted to you.

[Col. 0333A] May the Lord appoint this man as your patron,

So that he who is now honored may protect you by this aid.

He who, dwelling on earth, gave it many miracles,

May he, powerful, distribute miracles to you also.

May his jeweled right hand, then seen as blessed,

Protect both you and your hands.

He who then deserved to call corpses back to life,

May he here also bring gifts for your salvation.

He who drew poison from the flesh of the stricken man,

May he himself prevent harmful poisons from reaching you.

He who made the serpent’s course turn backward,

May he drive grave misfortunes backward from here.

[Note: [Col. 0333C] Paris edition: “may he drive them from here to go backward.”]

He who made Licontius’ house safe from plague,

May this house flourish unharmed through his aid.

[Note: [Col. 0333C] The same edition: “who by his virtue made the house safe … so that it might be secure.”]

His rich cloak covered the trembling needy man [the printed “rom.” is uncertain];

May the wing of that apostolic man cover you.

He who restored the widow’s son to his mother’s breast,

May he himself grant you, mother, these pledges,

[Note: [Col. 0333C] Here Fortunatus is referring to Brunhild, Childebert’s mother and therefore the grandmother of her sons. In the following poem:

“So that from her son and from her numerous descendants

Another illustrious generation may be given to the grandmother.”]

As Childebert may remain with his new offspring,

A king holding his own kingdoms and acquiring new ones.

[Note: [Col. 0333D] Childebert’s sons were Theudebert and Theuderic, as can be read in Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 20. His sister, likewise Brunhild’s daughter, was Chlodosinda; his wife was Faileuba. Fortunatus mentions them here. Browerus is especially mistaken in claiming in his notes on this poem that Childebert’s wife was Ultrogotho, erring both in fact and in chronology. Ultrogotho, whom we mentioned in the notes on Book VI, chapter 8, was the wife of Childebert I, son of Chlothar, not of the Childebert whom Fortunatus is now discussing, who was the son of Sigibert and Brunhild. In the time of the Childebert now under discussion, Ultrogotho could have been only an old woman, if she was still alive.]

May you, mother, see from your daughter what you most sweetly desire,

And, concerning your dear daughter-in-law, what your prayers request.

From her may the faithful here have happy celebrations,

And may you be the summit of honor among the servants of the Lord.

So that you may be more pleased, Brunhild, to have this patron,

[Note: [Col. 0334C] One Vatican manuscript: “when the Lord protects the house”; and “the Lord,” with another reading: “lords.”]

When the gracious Lord protects your house in the world.

May he thus instruct you, guide you, and lead you along the path,

So that, joined to him by pious deeds, you may shine.

## CHAPTER VIII. To the same persons, in praise

[Col. 0333C] [Note: [Col. 0333C] This poem too was written in praise of Brunhild and the entire royal family. After Fortunatus has reported the people’s love and devoted affection for their kings, he offers prayers for them, that they may remain safe and flourish in every respect for a long time.]

If one were to set forth the praises of kings,

I would not have enough to speak night and day.

How this people hangs upon the love of its lords,

And keeps its eyes fixed upon your faces.

[Col. 0334A] You who remain both mirror, light, and sweetness,

Are their dear ornament and, together, their honor.

A supreme gift, a tranquil and peaceable kingdom,

And in your condition a pious summit in the world.

In you kinship, fatherland, and protection shine;

Here are honor and rank, here the work of devotion.

Here is tranquil day, here the faithful man’s joyful hope;

After God, in you they possess the gifts of salvation.

Here I join my prayers and joys with those of the people;

May Christ, in his goodness, increase and bring them to growth.

May God’s care preserve you for a long time in your position,

And may you hold your kingdoms long through a heavenly gift.

May you acquire new possessions and rule those already possessed,

And in piety cherish these riches as participants in them.

May you, mother, radiant with honor,

See the harvest ripen from your son and offspring.

So that from your son and from your numerous descendants

Another illustrious generation may be given to the grandmother.

May you, mother, have fruit from Childebert’s sweetness, flourishing, and safety,

While his people behold their prayers fulfilled.

From your daughter and daughter-in-law may the Creator heap gifts upon you,

And may you stand pleasing to God through your pious merit.

[Note: [Col. 0334D] Paris edition: “Here, returning, may I deserve [to speak] to you.”]

Here too, on my return, may I deserve to offer words of greeting,

Rejoicing together with my pious little lords.

May the prosperity of the kings be secure and the joys of the peoples increase;

May the kingdom rejoice, and may this honor stand for a long time.

## CHAPTER IX. Also to King Childebert

[Note: [Col. 0334D] We have excerpted this poem from Volume I of Jean Mabillon’s *Ancient Analecta*, Paris edition, 1675, p. 366. These verses, as Mabillon notes there, are, unless I am mistaken, absent from the printed editions. I took them from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Viton at Verdun, written nearly eight hundred years ago, containing the poems of Theodulf. There they are read under this title: “Verses of Venantius Fortunatus to King Childebert, son of King Sigibert.”]

[Col. 0334B] [Note: [Col. 0334B] He extols Childebert’s dignity and virtue at length and finally commends Audulf to him. [Col. 0334C]]

King, summit of the region and ruler above kingdoms,

You who are the head of heads, a man of supreme excellence.

[Note: [Col. 0334D] Fortunatus sometimes seems to have delighted in playing with words of equal form and beginning with the same letters, as in this poem. Thus, near the end of Book I of *The Life of Saint Martin*, he writes:

“Martin’s illustrious religion, in whose honor

Faithful covenants make the foul beautiful, faith adorns the faithful.”]

Ornament of ornaments, more ornate and adorning,

You who are honor and seemly, doing everything seemly.

First, and from the first, prior even to the foremost,

You who are yourself powerful, whom the Omnipotent delights.

Delighting in sweet things, sweet, beloved power,

Good hope, or goodness, good through goodness.

[Col. 0335A] Worthy and not disdainful, worthy, with worthy dignity,

Flower of flowers, flowering, flowing with floral bloom.

[Note: [Col. 0335C] *Cluens* has the same sense as “powerful.” See what we noted on poem 12 of Book VI.]

O renowned Childebert, I, Fortunatus, bring these verses in affection,

Though poor myself, from poor resources.

[Note: [Col. 0335C] In the chronicle of Fredegar the Scholastic, §36, mention is made of a certain Baudulf—or, as other manuscripts report, Audulf or Adulf—a tall and prominent man whom Theuderic, Childebert’s son, chiefly at the urging and prompting of Brunhild his grandmother, left to drive Saint Columbanus from the monastery. Is this the same man to whom Fortunatus refers here?]

I commend Count Audulf with a suppliant prayer,

And myself as well; thus may you rule over us here, O summit.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning his voyage

[Note: [Col. 0335A] When Fortunatus had arrived at Metz, he relates that he was most courteously detained by the royal family and ordered to cross the Moselle. He says that he was in great danger of his life, having almost been swept away by the current. He then recounts the remainder of his journey through various regions and rivers, describing their situation and beauty. He also relates the location of the royal residence and the fishing carried out before the eyes of the kings.]

[Col. 0335B] Meeting the kings, where the walls of Metz stand in strength,

[Note: [Col. 0335C] On Metz, see what we noted on Chapter 10 of Book VI.]

I was seen by the lords themselves and retained on horseback.

[Note: [Col. 0335C] Paris edition: “May prosperity be yours, as I desire from my heart.”]

From here I am ordered, as a sailor, to travel the Moselle by oar,

Hastening to proceed over the trembling, gliding waters.

And as I climbed aboard, the sailor ran along the slender timber;

Even without being driven by the south winds, the prow flew over the waters.

Meanwhile there is a place among rocks hidden along the banks,

Where the narrowed shore makes the wave raise its head higher.

Here the swift force seized the entangled prow and drove it on,

[Note: [Col. 0335C] One Vatican manuscript: “it was then drinking the swollen waters with its belly.”]

For soon it was drinking the swollen waters with its belly.

It was pleasant to see me snatched away into the open fields,

And, fleeing the deep, I sought the pleasant countryside.

I am received by the current, beneath which the river Orne too—

[Note: The Orne, although not powerful or suitable for ships, is raised by this addition to the honor of the river. It receives the Moselle roughly five miles above Thionville. For, descending from rugged country near Rischberg into fertile soil, it spreads out briefly over level ground and is soon swallowed up. Browerus.]

Where the doubled current flows and speeds the journey.

From there, in a cautious boat, we proceed through waters shut off,

Lest the net should lift me as though I too were a fish.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] One Vatican manuscript: *nossa luet*, corruptly. A *nassa* is a fishing net, or a vessel woven from twigs for catching fish.]

[Col. 0336A] Among the smoking roofs of farms along the banks,

I arrive where the Sura is able to roll itself onward.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] On the river Sura, see what we reported from Browerus on Chapter 4 of Book VII. He likewise says that the Sura joins the Moselle two miles above Trier, toward the south.]

From there, through projecting hills and hollow valleys,

We glide down toward the Sura on the river’s descending waters.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Paris edition: “the river flows.”]

I am carried to where the lofty walls of Trier open out,

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Fortunatus uses the word “opens out” most appropriately. The sloping Moselle, after flowing from the region of the Mediomatrici and Luxembourgers and making winding turns in the river, opens into a valley in which Trier once stood out through the breadth of its walls. Browerus.]

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Browerus gathers many additional testimonies in his notes on this passage from ancient authors to demonstrate the former nobility of the city of Trier and its citizens. They may be read there if desired.]

A city noble among the noble, and likewise a capital.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Paris edition: “and a capital.”]

From here we are carried by the river past the ancient heights of the senate,

Where the very ruin itself reveals its former power.

[Note: [Col. 0335D] Salvian, Book VI of *On Providence*: “Trier, the richest city of Gaul, was conquered four times.” And lest you think that it was overthrown by light incursions or plunderings, he says that it suffered four destructions—Hunnic, Vandalic, Gothic, and repeated Frankish devastation. Browerus. On the destruction of Trier under the Franks, see Gregory of Tours, Book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 9, and Fredegar the Scholastic, epitome of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 7.]

Everywhere we look upon mountains threatening with their summits,

Where a sharp flint rises, piercing the clouds.

Where steep peaks stretch toward lofty crags,

Rugged stone grows toward the stars upon the hills.

Nor are these harsh stones without fruits;

In the end they give birth, and the rocks pour forth wine.

Here you see hills clothed everywhere with vine shoots,

And the wandering breeze fans their leafy hair.

Vines, embedded among the rocks, grow thickly in rows

And seek the brow marked out like a painted rule.

[Note: [Col. 0336C] Fortunatus seems here to indicate that the rows of vines, straight as if by a rule and painted with reddening grapes, stretched from the foot of the hills to their highest ridges. Ausonius, in poem 334, describing the Moselle, writes:

“Where the lofty summit rises over the steep length,

And cliffs, sunny ridges, bends, and hollows

Rise with vines, like a natural theatre:

[lacuna]

The happy throng of workers and hastening farmers

Now hurry at the very summit, now down the sloping ridge,

Competing with foolish cries [lacuna].”]

[Col. 0336B] Cultivated places gleam among the rugged rocks through the farmers’ work;

Against the pale stone, the lovely vine glows red.

Where rough rocks produce honey-sweet clusters,

And sterile grapes please upon fertile stone.

Along the ridge, beneath the bare mountain, the vineyards are adorned,

And green shade covers the dry veins of ore.

From there the vintner picks the colored grapes,

And, hanging from the cliffs, he himself hangs while gathering them.

I feasted my eyes and was nourished by food,

Holding these pleasant realms as a sailor and following onward.

From here too I am carried by the waters, where the river Contrua

[Note: [Col. 0336D] One Vatican manuscript has *Construa*. Browerus says that the form *Contrua*, supported by the authority and agreement of nearly all the manuscripts he had in hand—with the exception of F. Tiliobroge, where *Construa* is read—had long seemed suspicious to him because no trace or indication of it appeared in ancient books or other monuments. Nevertheless, he is led to believe that Contrua, of which Fortunatus speaks here, was the name of a small stream which, two or three miles above the confluence, flows down from the region of Trichonia and plunges into the Moselle, retaining the name Condta. He reports that traces of this stream remain, showing that formerly, with a wider mouth and larger bed, it flowed into the Moselle. He adds that a gloss in the manuscript of Saint Gall interprets *Contrua* as the proper name of a river.]

Fills the course.

[Col. 0336C] Where there once was a famous headland of noble birth.

[Col. 0337A] Then I come to where two confluent rivers join,

[Note: [Col. 0337C] At the place where the Rhine and Moselle meet stood a celebrated fortress called Confluentes, mentioned by Gregory of Tours, Book VIII, chapter 13. It still exists as a celebrated and strongly fortified town, called Koblenz, in the diocese of Trier, as Ruinart says in his notes on the cited passage of Gregory of Tours.]

Here the foaming Rhine, there the fertile Moselle.

Throughout that whole journey the waters served the fish,

[Note: [Col. 0337C] One Vatican manuscript: “the waters served the fish.”]

And for kings and lords abundance seethed in the waters.

[Note: [Col. 0337C] By the kings whom Fortunatus mentions here we understand Childebert and his royal household.]

Yet, lest any pleasure should be lacking for me as I traveled,

I was nourished by the Muses, with melody entering my ears.

When voices were released, the organs made the mountains resound,

And the hanging rocks returned their own melodies.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] One Vatican manuscript: “their tropes,” and shortly afterward the same reading.]

The bronze pipes then loosened their gentle murmurs,

And the thicket on the mountain answered again with its reeds.

Now with trembling roar, now with smooth musical song,

The rock resounds with whatever comes from the bronze.

Songs join the separated banks in sweetness,

And among the hills and rivers there was one voice of melody.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Paris edition: “By which he rightly refreshes the foremost people and the good law of kings.”]

To refresh the people, the favor of kings seeks this,

And always finds what its care commands.

[Col. 0337B] The castle of Antonnacum, ready with its heights,

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Antonnacum, commonly Andernach, is a town between Bonn and Confluentes. It is situated and cultivated—as Browerus adds in his notes on this passage—in an agreeable and even today beautiful location, although its name has been altered to Andernacum. It lies about eight miles below Confluentes on the bank of the Rhine and has an anciently built church, a monument of the emperor Valentinian, and other elegant sights. In ecclesiastical matters it is subject to the bishop of Trier and in civil matters to the people of Cologne.]

From there, drawing near, I proceed with the burden of my boat.

Although here vineyards may extend across broad hills,

The other part consists of a fertile stretch of level land.

Yet the abundance of that beautiful place has greater power,

Because the other part is regarded by the peoples as fruitful water.

Finally, while the kings preside in the seats of the hall

And festive banquets honor the service of the table,

One watches through nets the salmon being lifted in its bundle,

And counts the fish while seated in the citadel.

The king rejoices when the great fish leaps back from the water,

And refreshes his spirits by the arrival of his catch.

Seeing the favorable spectacle there and bringing the joyful palace back here,

[Col. 0337C] He first feeds his eyes and afterward nourishes himself with food.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Paris edition: “before his eyes.”]

A fish, a citizen newly arrived from the Rhine, is likewise presented at the table,

[Note: [Col. 0337D] “A citizen newly arrived from the Rhine,” namely, fish native to the Rhine. Paris edition: “also a newly arrived citizen of the Rhine.”]

And the company seated there takes pleasure in eating.

May the lord long provide these spectacles to his lords,

And may you grant the peoples sweet days to enjoy.

May you bestow joys upon all from your peaceful faces,

And may your summit rejoice through your own people.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the oratory at Arthona

[Note: [Col. 0337D] See what we noted on Chapter 5 of this book.]

[Col. 0338A] [Note: [Col. 0338A] He enumerates and reviews the sacred pledges, or relics, which were preserved in the oratory at Arthona and which made it distinguished through their veneration.]

This land holds great treasures of the blessed;

The soil is considered rich in divine riches.

On the right, peace flashes with the honor of the angel Gabriel,

Who brought joys to the world with his sacred mouth,

When the virgin conceived eternal salvation,

As that messenger carried the gifts of the Redeemer.

On the left is the stone of the tomb which Christ, with his body,

Pressed in brief death as he went victorious to the Father.

Here too that George gleams with holy relics,

[Note: [Col. 0337D] One Vatican manuscript: “Gregory with abundant [relics].”]

[Col. 0338B] Who returned unharmed from the fire and did not die submerged in pitch.

[Note: [Col. 0338C] Another Vatican manuscript: “Cosmas also.”]

There are also Cosmas and Damian themselves, healers,

Not craftsmen with iron, but through faith that brings healing.

Julianus too is present, slain by a friendly sword;

The Auvergne people, who honor him, possess weapons of salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0338C] See Book V, chapter 3, and the notes on that passage.]

And holy Martin, whom the Gallic world retains,

Whose half-cloak covers Christ.

Stripping himself of his tunic, he clothes the naked needy man;

From this you received the white stones, topaz and onyx,

Which certain holy men deserved to see upon this body,

When the sound of the gems revealed what had happened.

Victor too is added here with distinguished merits,

[Note: [Col. 0338C] This appears to be Victor of Marseille, whom Gregory of Tours mentions in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 77. He suffered at Marseille under Diocletian and Maximian; his acts are found among the authentic martyrs, Book I, p. 292.]

The one who, by the gift of martyrdom, holds the heights of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0338C] One Vatican manuscript: “by which he holds.”]

Here, through the power of the ancient hero, a new palm of victory: Nicetius,

[Note: Saint Nicetius was bishop of Lyons, renowned for holiness and miracles. Gregory of Tours says in *History*, book V, chapter 5, that he was his mother’s uncle. His Life, written by Gregory, survives in the *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8. He died in 573. Moreover, Gregory, speaking in that Life, chapter 8, of Saint Nicetius’s relics, says: “There has also been brought to us a towel woven with hanging shag or tassels, which the saint had over his head on the day of his death; we received it as something heavenly.” Gregory says that he placed threads taken from this linen in a certain basilica in Tours, where they immediately became illustrious through a miracle; he then adds: “I confess that I placed some of these pledges also upon the altars of other basilicas, in which both the possessed acknowledge the saint and faithful prayer more often obtains its effect.” It is therefore credible that relics of this kind belonging to Saint Nicetius had also been placed by Gregory in the oratory at Arthonne.]

who cherishes the city of Lyons with voice and bosom.

Their shepherd Gregory prays with heart and voice,

that the man may live without end for God enthroned on high.

[Textual note: The Paris edition reads “Gregory adorns” for “Gregory prays.”]

## CHAPTER XII. Verses composed upon the table at the villa of Saint Martin, before the census-takers

[Note: Gregory of Tours relates, *History*, book IX, chapter 30, that King Childebert sent Florentianus, master of the royal household, and Romulfus, count of the palace, to Poitiers to register the people and renew the old census; from there they came to Tours, but nothing was changed among the people of Tours, out of honor and reverence for Saint Martin, chiefly through the agency of Gregory of Tours himself. These events belong to the year 589, at which time this poem by Fortunatus seems to have been composed.]

[Note: Fortunatus, having been received at a banquet in Saint Martin’s villa on Easter Day, was challenged by musical instruments and songs. He then improvised the following poem, in which he celebrates at length Saint Martin and Gregory, his successor in the see of Tours. Finally he urges those who had gathered for the banquet to spend that day joyfully and pleasantly, and to offer prayers for the kings.]

When I see the eloquent wood of the lyre singing,

and the lyre modulating with its sweet strings;

when the bronze seems to resound with pleasing song,

and the gentle flute charms the ears with its melodies—

although here I am regarded as a dull guest, received among you,

even my mute flute wishes to say something.

Behold the day on which Christ rose from the depths,

powerful to break the bonds of the infernal law,

when he also released the weeping thousands of the imprisoned,

and shattered Tartarus vomited forth many men.

Here another distinction is added: this is the hall of blessed Martin,

where festive banquets now flow.

He who by his deeds was able to strike the ears of the Thunderer

obtains by his merits whatever faith seeks on high.

He who piously restored dead bodies to life,

and promptly offers the aid of God as his friend—

his successor, the exultant Gregory, now duly established—

what the former acquires, the latter governs by voice and faith.

He who asks here is present, though elsewhere he may sit absent;

and, a good shepherd throughout the world, he provides food.

Now therefore, all of you whom almighty God has granted to be here together,

celebrate the day solemnly,

you whom Martin has gathered to himself in kindly love,

and behold, here he makes his own food a banquet.

Therefore, under the safe rule of Childebert and Brunichild,

whom the Most High God has granted kingdoms to protect,

you whom they have sent to govern the faithful people

and to relieve the poor, if anyone is in want—

and may your kindly deeds, in knowing and serving your lords,

likewise be nourishment for joy in faith.

You whom the table of blessed Martin has invited,

take joyfully what the day gives in love.

May the good bishop Gregory, though personally unacquainted with these things,

applaud and sing your glory to the peoples.

Since this house is also his, may he, Christ’s devoted lover, entreat him

that God may protect kings and peoples with a stronghold.

[Textual notes: Paris edition, “Therefore celebrate this day”; one Vatican manuscript, “in kindly love”; manuscript, “moderate,” and in the following verse “relieve”; two Vatican manuscripts, “by recognizing and acting kindly toward lords,” which is the reading followed above; one Vatican manuscript, “may sing your joys”; another, “the king [protect] his peoples”; Paris edition, “with the king and.”]

## CHAPTER XIII. For a girl seized by judges, addressed to Bishop Gregory

[Note: He implores Gregory’s help, asking him to see that the girl, taken from her father and held captive, is restored to her father.]

Following the example of the Lord, venerable to the world,

you who, as shepherd, do not wish to lose even the smallest sheep,

extending your care through the pastures with anxious hearts,

you surround the flock with your voice, so that the sheep may not be absent from the folds.

Here is a messenger, weeping because his daughter has been wickedly taken away,

holding his offspring captive in a time of peace.

Gregory, successor of pious Martin in honor,

you who are the father of the people: I beg you, restore this girl to her father.

He continually illumines the bereaved by his sacred merits;

restore this bereft girl to her father, granting him the light of seeing her.

[Textual notes: One Vatican manuscript reads “that they may not be absent from the folds”; the reading “weeping” (*flens*) may perhaps be “lamenting” (*flet*); another manuscript, “he illumines the blind”; another has, corruptly, “restore the day by living.”]

## CHAPTER XIV. Likewise for the same matter, addressed to Romulfus, or Rainulfus

[Note: This Romulfus, like Florentinus, or Florentianus—the recipient of poem 16 of this book—seems to be none other than the men mentioned above in connection with poem 12, who came to Poitiers and Tours to register the people and collect the old taxes. It may therefore be conjectured that the girl of whom Fortunatus speaks here was perhaps the same girl as in the preceding poem, taken from her father by the census-takers, or by their attendants and officials, because he was unable to pay. I can therefore readily believe that Fortunatus, returning from Tours—where he had also attended the banquet—to Poitiers, had the girl’s father plead his case before him, and that he sent this man to Tours to Gregory and the census-takers, who, as it seems, were still staying at Tours awaiting King Childebert’s orders and letters, by which he would indicate whether or not the city of Tours was to be registered. All this is clear from the passage cited above in Gregory’s *History*.]

[Note: Fortunatus testifies to his goodwill toward Romulfus. Since he could not fulfill it in person, he says that he compensates for it by writing; then he commends to him the case of the father whose daughter has been taken away.]

[Note: In one Vatican manuscript this poem is joined to the preceding one, with no intervening title.]

If I could always see you with eager eyes, my friend,

even then love’s desire would scarcely be satisfied.

But if I cannot behold your face in person,

I gladly greet you, dear friend, at least through writing.

I commend this servant to you also; kindly and reverently

may your speech assist him, if he asks what is just.

He, grievously tortured, laments that his daughter has been taken from him;

he begs through you that his daughter may return.

When the poor man is heard, since you are medicine for the afflicted,

may God make your care a pious concern.

[Textual notes: Another manuscript reads, incorrectly, “and I gladly greet you”; the first Vatican manuscript, “kindly, to be revered”; Paris edition, “seized” for “taken.”]

## CHAPTER XV. Likewise for the same matter, addressed to Gallienus

[Note: Gregory of Tours mentions Gallienus in book V of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 50, and calls him his friend. He seems to be the same man to whom Fortunatus is now writing. Nor does the man whom Gregory mentions seem to have been an archdeacon, as Browerus maintains. See the notes of the learned Ruinart on the cited passage of Gregory of Tours.]

[Note: He praises Gallienus and declares his goodwill toward him; then he recounts the father’s grievous misfortune in losing his daughter and begs him to assist the man.]

Experienced in your duties and skillful in administration,

attentive in your endeavors, a companion in usefulness,

as is my custom, I discharge to you the service owed by affection;

I honor you, and, bound to you, repay the work of your goodwill.

Let the man whom injustice has cruelly afflicted be commended to you;

alas, this wretched man has lost his daughter.

Grant him the justice he has purchased through the wound inflicted on his body,

and piously make his captive daughter return to him.

Between the two deaths—when both law and daughter are absent—

be a single salvation present in both matters.

[Textual note: One Vatican manuscript reads “Exercise your offices”; the Paris edition, “Exercise the administrations of your offices.” The poet seems here to indicate that the same man ought not to be punished twice under the same heading: thus the man commended to Gallienus, though tortured and bodily injured, had been deprived of his daughter only through injustice.]

## CHAPTER XVI. Likewise for the same matter, addressed to Florentinus

[Note: He sends greetings to Florentinus and declares that he owes them to him in the name of affection; then he commends to him the case of the unfortunate father, mentioned above.]

As each person proceeds along his way, let my page hasten onward,

so that in speech it may reveal what love owes him.

Now also, dear to me, always good, faithful friend,

devoted in heart, I repay the service of goodwill.

I commend this servant also, previously harshly imprisoned,

who laments that he has not deserved such treatment under the law.

He grieves more heavily than over wounds fixed in his body

because his little, tender daughter has been taken from him.

Let compassionate kindness hear this voice,

for when you grant him what he asks, you will give yourself a great gift.

[Textual notes: See the note above on chapter 14. One Vatican manuscript reads “before being brought back.”]

## CHAPTER XVII. To bishops, commending a traveler

[Note: He commends to the bishops a man traveling toward Italy, ignorant of the route, asking them to help and console him. I judge that this poem, or letter, was not sent to bishops gathered in some synod, as Browerus supposes, but addressed to bishops living along the route from Gaul into Italy, by whom the traveler could be helped and conducted. A similar example of such a letter appears above, book V, chapter 21; see our notes there.]

Most exalted bishops, road of faith and path of life,

whom the Almighty has appointed to be guides of the light,

and whom the Lamb has entrusted as guardians of the heavenly flock,

be good shepherds, so that the sheep may be cared for.

Behold, a traveler is here, undertaking a journey of which he is ignorant,

alas, a foreigner lamenting within the borders of Italy.

Be helpers to the exile, a road to the wanderer, a rule of salvation;

as fathers, honorably guide him on his return to his homeland.

Sowing seeds of present reward, so that you may reap abundant harvest,

and so that the crop may return to you a hundredfold.

For I, humble Fortunatus, commend him to the excellent,

and through you, to the Lord, sacred heights [lacuna].

[Textual notes: One Vatican manuscript reads “guardians also of the flock”; the Paris edition, “Sowing seeds of present reward.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Bishop Plato

[Note: This Plato, whom Gregory of Tours calls his archdeacon in book V of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 50, succeeded Maroveus in the see of Poitiers in the year 592. See what we have said about him in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 89. See also Cointius, under the year 592, no. 3.]

[Note: He congratulates Plato on having been made bishop of Poitiers in this poem and offers prayers for the kings who had declared him bishop.]

The kings thoughtfully arrange comforts for the people,

appointing as bishop one whom pious faith approves.

So that he, the pupil whom Martin gives, may honor Hilary,

and so that the powerful wing of the confessor may protect him.

[Note: Gregory of Tours relates in book IV of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 32, that when Plato obtained the episcopate of the city of Poitiers, the power of Saint Martin was revealed. A house adjoining the church was consumed in a great fire, and sparks with burning coals were falling upon the church building, driven by the wind. But Plato, carrying with him dust from the blessed tomb, raised the reliquary containing the chrism toward the fire. Suddenly a contrary wind arose, defending the church roof from the flames and driving them in another direction; thus the church building was saved.]

As successor, may he direct the people here with blessed honor,

and govern the clergy of the Church with his support.

May Childebert, splendid in his fitting fortress, flourish throughout the world,

together with his children, his people, his mother, and his sister under his yoke.

May the holy presence of Gregory prepare joyful happiness,

and may one faith assist the twin cities.

He has now, with Plato the disciple as supreme bishop,

granted this solemn day to the Church.

[Textual notes: That is, Plato—who had been Gregory of Tours’s disciple, archdeacon of the Church of Tours, and servant of Saint Martin’s successor in that see—was chosen to govern the Church of Poitiers. Paris edition, “Here may he rule the peoples”; one Vatican manuscript, “may he flourish while holding the stronghold.”]

## CHAPTER XIX. To Armentaria, mother of Lord Bishop Gregory

[Note: This Armentaria was the daughter of a daughter of Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres; see Gregory of Tours, *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7, section 1. Browerus writes that she was Burgundian by birth and married an Aeduan, citing John Savaro’s commentary on Sidonius. Abbot Oddo, in the *Life of Gregory of Tours*, chapter 1, writes: “Gregory arose in the Celtic region of Gaul, a native of the territory of Auvergne, born of Florentius as father and Armentaria as mother . . . Thus Georgius, once a senator, took Leocadia as his wife . . . Leocadia gave birth to Saint Gall, bishop of the see of Auvergne, and to Florentius, the father of this boy,” and so forth.]

[Note: He praises Armentaria, mother of Gregory, bishop of Tours, and compares her with the mother of the Maccabees because of the virtue and happiness of her offspring. Finally, he commends himself to her prayers.]

Twice blessed in merit, to herself and to the world, is the Maccabean mother:

noble in lineage, nobler in her children.

She sent seven palms from her womb to heaven,

and that womb produced the glory of martyrdom.

You too, Armentaria, rightly blessed, powerful in your offspring,

are no less blessed in childbirth than that earlier mother in her womb.

The former was greater in number; you are greatest in heaven:

what many could accomplish, this one son of yours has accomplished.

Famous through your child, surrounded by the fruit of your offspring,

you have Gregory as a new palm, a crown.

[Textual notes: In the Venetian edition, and in two Vatican manuscripts: “who sends seven palms to heaven”; in the same source, “you greatest in rank”; in the same source, “this one of yours.”]

I, humble Fortunatus, reverently commend myself to you,

and ask that you pray heavenly assistance for me.

[Textual note: The Venetian edition lacks these two final verses.]

## CHAPTER XX. To Sigoaldus, concerning his escort

[Note: In one Vatican manuscript: “for accompanying him, Sigoaldus.”]

[Note: Fortunatus addresses in this poem Sigoaldus, whom King Sigibert once appointed as his count and traveling companion. He says that Sigoaldus had long been absent, and congratulates him on his return; he wishes that the rank of his comitatus, to which Childebert had raised him, may be increased by a new honor.]

When I first came from the borders of Italy to the kingdoms,

King Sigibert appointed you as my support,

so that I might travel more safely with you as my companion,

with a horse provided on one side and food on the other.

You fulfilled your duty; as a guardian, you are recalled by your friend.

At last my concern for you now returns to me.

Tell me, dear friend, from where you have come after so long a time,

great in your honor, greater still in my affection.

Ready in feeling toward your clients, kind Sigoaldus,

and, my friend, affectionate toward Fortunatus.

May King Childebert, growing in power, cause you to grow as well;

he who now grants you the rank of count, may he grant you the gifts of a duke.

May the faithful see their prayers fulfilled under such a lord,

and may life and its journey become prosperous.

## CHAPTER XXI. To Count Sigoaldus, because he fed the poor at the king’s expense

[Note: He praises divine providence and administration in distributing wealth, and reviews the advantages that arise from the unequal fortunes and conditions of human beings. He then declares Sigoaldus’s generosity in distributing royal wealth to the needy, and offers favorable omens and prayers for Childebert and for the prosperity and happiness of his kingdom. Finally he recalls the reason why Sigoaldus distributed those alms among the poor and shows that a multitude of poor people were fed at the king’s expense.]

May your resounding praise, Christ, shine forth in glorious deeds,

while each person performs good works.

You, Most High, provide the means by which the human race may please you,

for unless you give, no one accomplishes anything prosperous.

You are generous to the rich, and perhaps thereby sparing toward the poor,

so that the rich may be redeemed when the needy is cared for.

These are sweet and pious exchanges of your kingdom:

while the poor receives food, the wealth of the rich increases.

The poor, satisfied in body, satisfies the powerful man through his reward;

he receives little on earth and prepares great things in heaven.

The needy gives more to the rich than the rich gives to the needy:

he gives perishable food and receives the abundant things of God.

Giving a coin to the earth, he is destined to send a talent to the stars;

and from modest grains may a lofty harvest arise.

Let them give, scatter, sow, and commend their seeds to Christ;

here let them not hesitate to give what will remain when it returns.

Give, if Christ is to be your treasurer thence;

bestow upon the needy whatever Christ has to repay.

Encouraged by this aid, seeking better things from the Thunderer,

with unwavering faith that God will grant these things.

[Textual notes: Paris edition, “shining with brilliant praise”; the same edition, “therefore not sparing [the poor]”; one Vatican manuscript, “that the rich man may redeem himself”; Paris edition, “Give thus, Christ.”]

For the flourishing welfare of King Childebert,

may he rise upon the throne, who was already exalted through his grandfather.

May the young man from this time grow stronger in vigorous years,

and, as his great-grandfather flourished, so may the grandson flourish in the world.

[Textual notes: The manuscript reads “may he grow”; one Vatican manuscript, “May the young man become here.”]

Therefore his servant Sigoaldus, faithful in love,

gives to the poor, so that the king’s glory may endure.

Thus he proceeds to the thresholds of venerable Martin,

while he himself asks for the aid of his own Lord.

And while the king labors there for the realm,

he performs this work so that the saint may help him through his prayers.

Finally, proceeding eagerly to celebrate the sacred feasts,

he himself offered food to Christ’s poor.

The provisions distributed among Christ’s ranks are pleasing;

the people whom God protects in his fortress are fed.

A great crowd of blind men is refreshed,

among whom God is inward light and way.

Here a lame man is fed, whom Christ directs in due order,

and who, dependent upon his own lord, fulfills his work.

Who could recount in order so many kinds of illness,

which his care meets and cherishes alike?

Therefore, feeding the thousands who gather in crowds,

he distributes so that he may possess, and so that the king may also govern all things.

I, Fortunatus, your companion, greet you from here, Sigoaldus,

and pray that you give better things in aid of the king.

[Textual notes: One Vatican manuscript, “proceeding to the thresholds”; Paris edition, “while the king and his offspring labor”; another Vatican manuscript, “he provided a meal”; Paris edition reads: “For them may you be peace, light, and way, O God”; the manuscript reads “in” for “for.”]

## CHAPTER XXII. On the defensor’s banquet

[Note: Defensores were those entrusted with the protection and defense of the Church’s property. On this subject see Thomassinus, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 98. Their office is described in the Council of Carthage held in 407, where chapter 64 decrees: “Scholastic defensores are to be appointed, men active in the office or duty of defending cases . . . so that, following the custom of the priests of the province, those who undertake the defense of the churches may have authority in the churches’ affairs whenever necessity demands it, whether to resist encroaching wrongs or to provide what is necessary, and may enter the judges’ secretariats.” There were also defensores of cities, called so after the manner of the tribunes of the plebs, who—as Du Fresne says in the *Glossary*—watched over discipline, restrained the people and decurions from every insolence, protected sailors and merchants, collected taxes, and so forth. See Du Fresne under this word.]

[Note: He commemorates in this poem a banquet organized by a defensor at Easter, which Sigoaldus also attended, offering prayers for the happiness of King Childebert and for Sigoaldus’s own honor and welfare.]

Today this memorable Easter gift shines forth:

the defensor provides a feast which the count himself favors.

The Lord’s delights, which the seasons and prayers provide,

come together from every direction—in stream, in harvest, and in heaven.

May the long and resplendent rule of Childebert

raise you, Sigoaldus, for a long time in the fortress of your rank.

May the realm be happy through the love of its happy king,

and may faith in the good count increase with his honor.

[Textual notes: Paris edition, “whom he himself cherishes”; one Vatican manuscript, “whom the count himself [cherishes]”; the same edition, “which the times [provide].”]

## CHAPTER XXIII. To Count Galactorius

[Note: Paris edition: “to whom you were owed.”]

[Note: He congratulates Galactorius, who was made count by the king from the offices of defensor and judge; he wishes that he may henceforth be advanced to the rank of duke, teaching that this is to be expected from God, whose customary work is to raise the small and humble. Finally he commands him to hope well and urges him to cultivate the virtues and to have them as the omens and guides of his whole life.]

At last you have come, my friend, to the honor that was owed you,

having first been a count by merit before the dignity was conferred.

You were a Burdigalan, and, as a devoted defensor,

you were considered worthy, governing these two worthy offices.

By the king’s judgment you were able to rise as a judge,

and the royal voice gave you what your reputation had earned.

The powerful king himself owes it to you, so that you may continue to advance honorably,

to provide the arms of a duke, the summit still remaining for you.

So that wisely you may protect the borders and cities of your homeland,

and acquire for him who gives you wealth.

May the Cantabrian fear, may the wandering Basque dread arms,

and may he abandon the support of the Pyrenean Alps.

Or do I speak as though this were something great? The one sacred author accomplishes it:

from the Lord the small man is raised, and becomes great.

From a recruit come dukes, and from a soldier comes a prince.

To say nothing of others, Justinian was such a man.

This is also found in the Church, through Christ’s gift:

from some exorcist comes episcopal honor.

The distinguished Martin is rightly considered a witness,

who was already holy before he bestowed sacred offices.

This is the work of the Almighty, who created the whole world;

you may think great only those things which he himself, in his power, accomplishes.

Therefore, happier, I pray that you remain a ruler at the summit,

hoping for greater things, a man wise in understanding.

Flourishing under this king and seeking eternal kingdoms,

[lacuna]

May justice and piety shine forth beside you,

the former protecting your breast, the latter your side.

May lofty faith also and faithful love shine forth,

and may you be, for Fortunatus, a companion of abundant affection.

[Notes: Fortunatus addresses this Galactorius, already a count, in poem 31 of book VII. That he lived under King Guntram is shown by the distich: “To whom the excellent King Guntram rightly owes still greater honors, he who has given you great things.” Palatine judges, says Du Fresne in his *Glossary*, were those who judged with the count; the office and position of judge was therefore a step toward the dignity of count. Cantabria was a region of Tarraconensian Spain subject to the Goths; hence “Cantabrians” here means Goths. One Vatican manuscript reads, corruptly, “a prince from the frontier.” Justinian was the nephew of the emperor Justin through his sister. Justin, as is well known, was of very low and obscure birth and rose through every military rank to the summit of imperial power; this in part also applies to his nephew Justinian. Justin associated him with the empire in 527, after he had previously held many civil and military offices in the Roman empire. The pentameter of the preceding distich was absent from all the manuscripts, Vatican as well as those used by Browerus. The 1644 Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* supplies it: “Increase immortal glory by pious deeds.”]

# BOOK ELEVEN

## CHAPTER I. Exposition of the Creed

[Note: Whoever wishes to compare this exposition of the Creed with the one preserved among the works of Rufinus will easily see—as Browerus also observed—that this is rather an epitome of Rufinus, born from Rufinus’s thought, than a work of Fortunatus. What Rufinus had written, Fortunatus, apparently after becoming bishop of Poitiers, should therefore be regarded as having abridged in order to instruct his own people.]

In setting forth the summary of the whole Catholic faith, in which the integrity of belief is displayed,

[Textual note: Some manuscripts read “in setting forth,” producing an anacoluthon in the sentence.]

and the equality of the one almighty God—that is, of the holy Trinity—is declared, and the mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God is explained—how, for the salvation of the human race, he deigned to descend from heaven from the Father and to be born of a virgin; in what order and at what time he suffered; how, after being buried, he rose again; how, ascending in that very flesh into heaven, he sat at the right hand of the Father and will come as judge; how he granted remission of sins to those reborn through holy baptism; and how at last the resurrection of the human race in the same flesh will take place for eternal life—since so many things are contained in the Creed in a few words, our discourse must be moderated, lest brevity fail to disclose the meaning or excessive length produce weariness.

Therefore, when Christ had risen and ascended into heaven and the Holy Spirit had been sent, knowledge of languages was granted to the apostles. While they were still together in one place, they composed this Creed among themselves, each stating what he understood, so that when they departed from one another they might preach this rule equally throughout all nations.

Finally, *symbolum* in Greek means “collation” or “bringing together,” because they themselves wisely composed it together through the Holy Spirit. It is also called an “indication,” because by it the person who believes rightly is identified. Therefore, for all believers, salvation of souls and everlasting life are prepared through good works.

[Textual notes: One Vatican manuscript omits “is” in the preceding sentence; the same manuscript reads “may be prepared.”]

### I believe in God the Father almighty.

At the beginning there is placed the illustrious foundation of heavenly testimony, because no one can be saved who does not rightly believe concerning salvation, as the Apostle proclaims: “The one who approaches God must believe” (Hebrews I, 6). Likewise: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Romans X, 10); and: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Psalm CXV); or that other passage: “The righteous lives by faith” (Romans I, 17); and: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah VII, 9, according to the Septuagint).

Indeed, even in human affairs no undertaking is begun unless it is believed that all the labor will reach its completion. Therefore we must believe in God, from whom both the present life and the future life are bestowed.

The designation “God” refers to an eternal substance, or to reverence toward God. God, therefore, is without beginning and without end, simple, incorporeal, and incomprehensible.

When you hear “Father,” recognize that he truly has a Son begotten from him, just as one is called a possessor because he possesses something, and a lord because he rules over someone. “God the Father,” therefore, is a name belonging to the hidden sacrament, whose true Son is the Word, the Mirror, and the Character; the living image of the living Father, in all things like the Father, of the same nature, begotten in divinity, and in every respect coequal with the Begetter.

Nor should one ask how he begot the Son; even the angels do not know this, and it is unknown to the prophets. Hence it was said: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah LIII, 8). He alone who begot him knows that hidden origin together with his own Son.

God is not to be investigated by us but believed in; for even within ourselves we do not know how we possess what we know, or how our wisdom, intelligence, understanding, or mind generates the word.

But, to speak briefly, it is enough for us to know that light begot radiance, as the prophet testifies: “Amid the splendors of the holy ones, from the womb before the morning star I begot you” (Psalm CIX). And also: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him”; and afterward: “He appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 36, 38).

He is called almighty because he can do all things and possesses power over all things, since the Father created everything through the Son.

### And in Jesus Christ.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “But Jesus is called Savior in Hebrew.”]

“Jesus” is called *Savior* in Hebrew. This name rightly belongs to a leader who is able to grant salvation to the people following him. Jesus son of Nave, who bore his figure, is known to have led the people from the desert into their homeland,

[Textual note: In some manuscripts the words “into their homeland” are absent.]

and into the promised land.

[Textual note: Another Vatican manuscript reads “and into the land of promise.”]

This Jesus leads those who follow him from darkness and the land of ignorance into heaven.

He is called “Christ” from the anointing of chrism, and this name is either priestly or royal, since kings were anointed with oil subject to corruption. But he was divinely anointed by the Holy Spirit with the oil of exultation, as the prophet says: “The Holy Spirit is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isaiah LXI, 1).

Jesus, therefore, is so called because he saves the people; Christ, because he is the anointed High Priest forever.

### His only Son

This is said so that you may understand nothing earthly or bodily in the expression: from one comes one, from light radiance, from the heart the word, from the mind understanding, from strength power, from wisdom the wise one; from the eternal one is born the coeternal one, in every respect the same as the Father—the Son.

[Textual note: The same Vatican manuscript reads “the coeternal one is born.”]

He is called “only” because he admits neither comparison nor likeness with the other creatures, since he himself is the supreme Creator of all things. Human beings are called sons of God by grace; he alone is the Son begotten by nature.

Thus far the order of the text has followed the divinity of the Father and the Son.

### Who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary

[Note: In the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume VII, it reads: “Who was conceived of the Holy Spirit.” The manuscripts and Rufinus’s text read: “Who was born,” and so forth. Browerus.]

He who was born from the Father before the ages is afterward to be understood as born of the Holy Spirit, whose temple was fashioned in the Virgin. For just as there was no fragility in the sanctification of the Spirit, so no cause of corruption appeared in his birth.

He who is one in heaven and unique on earth deigned to enter the world through the Virgin’s gate. Hence the prophets spoke at length about the Virgin’s conception and childbirth. For the sake of brevity, however, we shall offer one example, concerning which Ezekiel said: “The gate that faces east shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel himself shall pass through it, and it shall be shut” (Ezekiel XLIV, 2).

This must nevertheless be noted: the Holy Spirit is the Creator of the Lord’s flesh. From this the majesty of the Holy Spirit is displayed. But that the God of majesty was born in the flesh from Mary does not mean that he was defiled by being born of a Virgin, any more than he was polluted when, from dust, he formed a human being.

Indeed, if the sun or fire looks upon mud, it purifies what it touches and yet does not defile itself. Nor was mercy a cause of insult to God, nor is it unbelievable that he himself was born of a Virgin—the one who was able to form Adam from dust and the first woman from a rib.

### Crucified under Pontius Pilate
From this point many prophets foretold [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “how he was crucified on the cross”] how he would be fastened to the cross, with his feet pierced, given vinegar, gall, or myrrhed wine to drink, crowned with thorns, struck with a spear, lots cast over his garment, and hanging during the day with outstretched hands in the sight of the wicked people; the diligent reader will find these passages. Yet, to state it briefly, he was hung on the cross so that he might release us from the condemnation of the ancient tree. He was given gall to drink so that he might cut away the bitterness of the transgressed fruit, which was exceedingly sour. He was crowned with thorns so that he might uproot the ancient guilt of the accursed earth. He was struck with a spear so that, through the wound in his side, from which water or blood flowed, he might proclaim baptism or the mystery of martyrdom. Or, to say something deeper: Christ was struck in the rib so that he might cut away the wound inflicted upon us through Eve, who had been formed from the rib of the man.

To extend this explanation somewhat for the sake of understanding it, as Scripture says, “The eyes of the heart have been opened to understand what is the height, breadth, and depth” (Ephesians III, 18)—which signifies the cross. But why did the Lord choose to suffer on the gallows? The explanation is this: the cross is the form of a trophy, which is customarily erected for a triumphant victor after the enemies have been defeated. Because the Lord subjected three kingdoms to himself, hanging in the air [Manuscripts: “in the air” with a different grammatical form], he gained victory over the heavenly and spiritual wickednesses; and, stretching out his hands toward the people [Manuscripts: “peoples”], he gained the palm of victory over earthly things. The fact that the cross was fixed beneath the earth shows that he also triumphed over Tartarus. Since, for the sake of brevity, we pass over many other matters lest we cause weariness, this discourse is extended here in honor of the holy cross, so that it may bring you edification and increase its praise.

Therefore, because not even the stars themselves were pure in God’s sight on account of human sin, and the whole earth was polluted, Christ was hung in the air [Manuscripts: “in the air” with a different grammatical form] so that he might cleanse both earth and stars at once. Or because he himself had said, “As Moses lifted up the serpent” (John III, 14), he was hung upon the cross so that the words foretold by the Creator might be fulfilled. Or because there was great discord between heaven and earth, he was raised up as reconciler, taking away the offense by placing himself between them. He was hung in the air [Manuscripts: “in the air” with a different grammatical form; one Vatican manuscript: “therefore he is hung upon the cross”] so that, placed in the midst between heaven and earth, and between humanity and God, peace might return after hatred.

Or for this reason: formerly a grievous robber was fastened to the cross. Therefore Christ chose this principal punishment so that he might absolve humanity from original sin [Manuscripts: “the original sin”], which was the principal torment. Or God was hung upon the cross so that, in exchange for our captivity, the merchant might weigh the price of his body on the scales. Or he was crucified because we had died through the fruit and the tree, so that once again the cross and Christ—that is, the tree and the fruit—might, through this very likeness, free us from death.

A sweet fruit with its tree!

## Under Pontius Pilate

This has rightly been added, so that, with the judge designated together with the time, the matter might not appear uncertain. It was under King Herod, who at that time was tetrarch, that Pilate sent the Lord bound to him; and through this peace arose between the judges after hatred. And with the Lord sent as an envoy—more properly, as a legate—peace came between the parties, and he freed the judges from spite [Manuscripts: “bound”].

## He descended into hell

The prophets said many things about this, including the statement: “My life drew near to hell, and I became free among the dead” (Psalm LXXXIV). And also: “Are you the one who is to come?” (Matthew XI, 3)—as the reader will find when searching the passage.

[Note: Some of the ancient Fathers, as Browerus observes, understood that, although John did not doubt that Christ was the true Messiah, by that embassy he had asked whether Christ would die in the same work and descend to hell. John, therefore—who, after his head had soon been cut off, was himself going to descend to hell—would have awaited his liberator. See Saint Jerome’s commentary on Matthew at this passage concerning John.]

But when he descended into hell, he suffered no injury, since he did so out of mercy, like a king entering a prison—not so that he himself might be held, but so that the guilty might be released.

## On the third day he rose again

The same prophets spoke many things about his resurrection, which Jonah also prefigured by remaining three days in the belly of the sea-monster [One Vatican manuscript: “during those three days in the belly”].

## He ascended into heaven

The Psalmist, prophet, and Apostle mention this; hence the statement: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ephesians IV, 8) [The same manuscript: “the Psalmist, prophet”; and “the Apostle” is absent].

Therefore, after the Passion, Christ ascended into heaven—not to a place where he had not been, for the Word, God, is always in heaven, but to a place where the Word made flesh had not yet sat. Hence the angels, seeing the nature of flesh enter heaven, were astonished and said: “Who is this King of glory?” (Psalm VIII).

[Note: In some manuscripts the following is joined to what precedes without a title.]

## He sits at the right hand of the Father

His very sitting is a mystery of the flesh assumed, and the advancement implied by sitting is required not by the divine nature but by the human nature. Hence this too was said: “Your throne is prepared, O Lord” (Psalm XCII). And: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Psalm CX). And also: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God, judging the living and the dead” (Matthew XXVI, 64).

Some say that “the living” means the righteous, and “the dead” the unrighteous. Or certainly “the living” means those whom the Lord’s coming will find in the body [One Vatican manuscript: “the Lord, and the dead already buried. Let us nevertheless understand the living”], and “the dead” means those already buried [Some manuscripts omit “let us understand”]. Nevertheless, let us understand “the living and the dead” as souls and bodies alike, both of which will be judged.

Malachi also speaks of the Lord’s coming: “Behold, the almighty Lord comes” (Malachi III, 1). And Daniel: “Behold, upon the clouds of heaven, one like a Son of Man” (Daniel VII, 13) [One Vatican manuscript: “the Son of Man”]. And also: “As lightning comes from the east, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

## I believe in the Holy Spirit

In this commemoration the mystery of the Trinity is fulfilled. There is one Father, one Son, and one Holy Spirit; but, so that a distinction of persons may be made, the names are separated: the Father, from whom all things come and who has no father; the Son, begotten from the Father; and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the mouth of God and sanctifying all things.

[Note: Venantius Fortunatus seems here to have referred to Psalm XXXII: “And by the Spirit of his mouth all their power was established,” and to John XX: “When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’” and so forth. Through these testimonies the divinity of the Holy Spirit, who is worshiped with the Father and the Son, and his procession from the Father and the Son are shown.]

Therefore there is one divinity in the Trinity, because the Creed says: “I believe in God the Father” [One manuscript: “and in the Lord Christ,” and so forth], “and in Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit.” Therefore, wherever the preposition “in” is placed, divinity is acknowledged, as in: “I believe in the Father, in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit.” For one does not say, “in the holy Church”; one does not say, “in the remission of sins” [Manuscripts: “the holy Church and”], but rather, “you believe the remission of sins.”

## The holy Church

Holy, because the Church is one and without wrinkle. Just as there is one faith and one baptism, in which one God, one Lord, and one Holy Spirit are believed. Of it we read in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one.” For heretics gather a church in which wrinkle and the stain of faithlessness are evident.

## The remission of sins

For us, in this statement, faith alone is sufficient; reason is not required where supreme mercy is acknowledged. No one questions the eternal King when he gives whatever he gives [One manuscript: “No one calls the earthly king to account”; corruptly]. For he who was able to make a human being from mud is likewise powerful enough to cleanse every muddy thing [One manuscript adds “even every muddy thing”]; and he who restores the buried and lost limbs to salvation can restore lost innocence.

## The resurrection of the flesh

The culmination of perfection is concluded, and the flesh itself, which falls, will rise immortal so that it may endure. Although pagans and certain heretics do not believe in the resurrection, Isaiah says: “The dead will rise and be raised,” and Daniel says: “Then those who are in the dust of the earth will rise.” Christ says: “But concerning the dead being raised, have you not read?” And: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” The Apostle likewise says: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.” Scripture also says: “After the resurrection they will be like the angels of God.”

Therefore this should not be judged impossible even by those who believe [One manuscript: “Therefore, lest this be impossible to believers”], because he who was able to form a human being from earth will be able to transform this human being into an angel and, after this temporal life, grant eternal life. Thus a human being dies like a grain in the furrow, so that he may rise with a spike and multiply with fruit, becoming like an angel. May the author of salvation himself deign to grant this to us: having triumphed over Tartarus, he reigns victoriously in heaven with the glorious Father and Holy Spirit, entering upon his dominion [or: “in his dominion”]. Amen.

# CHAPTER II. Verses to Lady Radegund

[Note: He declares his longing for Radegund, who at that time had withdrawn into seclusion, and wishes to see her return from her retreat as quickly as possible.]

Without me, my light, why do you hide from my wandering eyes,

Nor allow yourself to be revealed to my sight?

I see everything at once—the heavens, the rivers, the earth;

But when I do not see you, everything seems little to me.

Although the sky is clear when the mist has fled,

With you concealing yourself from me, the day stands without the sun.

But I pray that the wheel of the hours may hasten its course,

And that the days may wish to speed themselves along in brevity.

May this be advantageous to us and to the holy sisters [One Vatican manuscript: “may this be for the sisters”; Paris edition: “may this be so”],

So that, by your face, you may refresh those whom you hold in love.

# CHAPTER III. To the same, on the birthday of the abbess

[Note: This was the birthday on which Agnes had first been appointed abbess of the monastery of the Holy Cross at Poitiers by Radegund; the day was celebrated annually, as were the birthdays of bishops.]

[Note: In this poem he celebrates the birthday of Agnes the abbess, congratulates Radegund on the birthday of the daughter whom she had borne for Christ, and finally offers prayers for them both.]

Excellent and gracious mother, rejoice in your blessed vow;

Rejoice: your sweet daughter has her birthday.

The womb did not make her born to you, but grace did;

Not flesh, but Christ gave her to you in love.

The Author granted her to be with you eternally;

The Father gives an everlasting offspring without end.

Blessed is the posterity that fails in no age,

That remains together with its mother and will not die.

Let this day be festive in holy honor of Radegund;

The Lamb gave this Agnes to you in the world.

May you celebrate equal joys through expanding years,

And through you may the people worship heavenly vows.

Teaching the virgin choirs holy discipline,

May you distribute the riches of eternal life [Manuscripts: “work”].

May lasting salvation hold you bound together in the body [One Vatican manuscript: “you joined together in body”];

May love join you again in eternal light.

# CHAPTER IV. To the same, that she should drink wine

[Note: In his own name and Agnes’s, he asks Radegund to use wine and to care for her health by taking it in moderation.]

If piety and holy love grant the requests of one who asks,

Hear your servants and lavish your gift upon them.

Fortunatus and Agnes likewise entreat you in verse,

That, excessively wearied, you may kindly drink wine.

May the Lord grant you whatever you ask of him,

And, as you love, may each of us who asks live for you.

We both humbly ask, if we have not offended,

That you refresh your two children, excellent mother.

Let no appetite, but necessity, move you now to drink wine;

For such a beverage benefits wearied innards.

Thus Paul also commands Timothy, the one trumpet to the nations,

To drink wine so that he does not weaken his stomach.

# CHAPTER V. To the abbess on her birthday

[Note: Fortunatus declares the long-lasting and inexhaustible assistance Agnes has given him. While providing it, he reports that she abstained from conversation with Radegund and from food, although she was hungry. He tries to rouse Agnes, perhaps overcome by sleep, from sleep on account of the shortness of winter days and the length of the nights, and signifies that her joy also brings him tranquility.]

Our sweet glory, most holy virgin of Christ,

Agnes, who remain unstained in merit.

Today you were pleased to pass the time in such a way

That you distributed inexhaustible help to me,

Nor now give the mistress’s tongue its sweet melodies [Paris edition: “sweet disciplines”],

While she feeds on your mouth as you answer her.

I myself have observed that you abstained from food,

And hunger was made, as it were, on your behalf.

I hear that sluggish sleep has pressed upon your shining eyes;

Or do you wish to anticipate the excessively long nights? [Paris edition: “Ah, wishing to anticipate the excessive nights”; one Vatican manuscript: “to anticipate them for you”]

For whom are these long periods of rest not enough,

When night almost holds what the doubled day has held?

Clouds cover everything; neither moon nor stars are seen.

If you are joyful in spirit, the mists flee from me.

May she cultivate true joys, she who commanded us to write this [Note: This seems to have been none other than Radegund, who ordered Fortunatus to write this poem to Agnes. One Vatican manuscript reads, corruptly, “they join in writing”],

And, led beneath the vault of heaven, may she favor you.

# CHAPTER VI. Another poem to the same

[Note: He declares his goodwill toward Agnes, testifying that it arose not from any stimulus or motive of lust but from charity, and from a relationship full of devotion with Radegund.]

A mother to me in honor, but a sweet sister in love,

Whom I honor for piety, faith, breast, and heart:

I love you with heavenly affection, without any bodily offense;

Not the flesh, but that which the spirit desires, is what I love.

Christ is present as witness, with Peter and Paul as ministers,

And holy Mary sees it together with the pious companions:

I regarded you with no other eyes or disposition

Than I would if you, Titiana, were my sister from the womb.

As though Mother Radegund had borne us both in one birth [One Vatican manuscript: “Radegund in both respects,” which should be followed]

From a chaste womb, I would have been so.

And as though together the blessed mother’s dear breasts

Had nourished us both with one flowing milk.

Alas! I lament my losses, lest perhaps through a slight whisper

Harmful words impede my understanding [Paris edition: “soft words”].

Yet my spirit desires to live by the same resolve,

If you wish to be honored by me with sweet love.

# CHAPTER VII. To the same

[Note: Absent, Fortunatus expresses his longing and devotion toward Radegund, and asks Agnes to perform on his behalf certain duties toward Radegund that he has neglected. Finally he prays for long life for both and wishes that one day might take all three together, and that the condition of the future life might not divide those who lived in such close union in this mortal life.]

To the dear mother, to the sister, what sweet words

Shall I alone speak in the love of my heart while absent?

The place excludes them; my anxious mind will seek them by voice,

And at the same time, through pious prayers, asks to see them.

I ask you, dear sister, kindly mother in devotion [Paris edition: “mother in piety”],

That you be willing to serve her for what I have failed to give.

May she live with you, graceful one, for a long age,

And may there be, I pray, one salvation for the three in Christ.

May neither our present state nor the future life separate us,

But may one salvation shelter us, and one day carry us away.

Yet here, as I desire, may long years preserve you,

So that sister and mother may be an assured rest to me.

# CHAPTER VIII. To the same

[Note: Fortunatus declares his joy, which he received because, at his request, Agnes had granted a meal to the nuns. He then offers prayers for Agnes herself, for Radegund, and for the order and happiness of the entire monastery at Poitiers.]

The most delightful fortune has come to our prayers,

While my prayers have deserved to receive gifts.

That food of the sisters benefited me all the more [Paris edition: “The food of the nourishing women benefits me”];

You satisfy them with banquets and cherish me with devotion.

Shining in such goodness, you arrange both sides;

You restore me in spirit by satisfying them with food.

Banquets nourish the limbs; affection nourishes the soul

And comes as sweeter food to the one who needs you more.

May the Almighty hear you as you make your pious requests,

So that he may pour perpetual food into your mouth.

May you flourish together through long ages, with your mother surviving,

And may that choir stand for God beneath your guidance.

# CHAPTER IX. To the same, concerning gifts sent

[Note: In the ancient usage and language of the Church, *eulogiae* were taken to mean the loaves offered and blessed in church for the sacrifice, a portion of which was used to prepare the Holy Eucharist.
