The term was also customarily used for loaves or other foods that bishops and priests privately sent to one another with letters of greeting, having first blessed them themselves. It also denoted the foods placed on the tables of bishops and abbots and afterward distributed after receiving their blessing. Later *eulogiae* came to be used more broadly for any gift sent or received, as here and elsewhere by Fortunatus. In this sense the term is used in chapter 54 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, which asks whether a monk should receive letters or *eulogiae* and establishes that a monk may in no way receive or give letters, *eulogiae*, or any little gifts, whether to his parents, from anyone, or to one another, without the abbot’s command. The testimony of Saint Basil in the *Penitential Regulations*, no. 60, may be added: “If anyone sends a blessing to someone, or receives anything apart from the archimandrite, let it be without blessing.”]

[Note: He gives thanks for the banquet Agnes had sent him as a gift and recalls her generosity toward him, repeatedly demonstrated by gifts. Finally he humorously describes a platter laden with various foods, swelling like a hill and adorned.]

With solicitous devotion you always command me to know

How I am nourished here by banquets you provide.

This too was the first abundance of today’s dinner:

You gave me a vegetable drenched in honey [Paris edition: “drenched with honey”].

Not once or twice, but three and four times it came,

The mere odor of which could nourish me alone.

One porter is not enough when so many are sent;

The feet that returned so often have been wearied.

Moreover, a messenger arrived with lofty hills,

A summit proudly swollen with a fleshy mountain.

With all the delights that earth or water supplies

Set together as food, there was a single little garden [One Vatican manuscript: “inside there was a little garden”].

Hungry and gluttonous, I have now conquered all these things.

Both mountain and garden are held in my sluggish belly.

I do not recount each item, because your gifts overcome me.

May you, victorious, fly to the heavens and above the stars.

# CHAPTER X. On the same subject

[Note: He likewise describes the various foods Agnes had sent him, which he reports as having received from Radegund, whose generosity Agnes had administered.]

Many foods come together, poured out from every side;

A pleasant confusion holds me: what should I receive first?

A swelling meat-gift is carried in a silver bowl,

In which vegetables floated in excessively rich sauce.

A marble dish carries what the gardens produce,

From which a honeyed flavor flowed into my mouth.

A glass bowl swelled with chickens arranged in a circle;

Their feathers removed, what a heavy burden it held!

Many fruits come together from painted baskets,

Whose sweetly flowing fragrance has filled me.

A very black pot gives white cups of milk,

And it arrives splendidly, pleasing to the taste.

These things serve the lady mother; these gifts serve the daughter;

Joined to them in devoted love, I myself speak more truly [One Vatican manuscript: “I myself speak as a third”; Paris edition likewise].

# CHAPTER XI. Another poem on flowers

[Note: He attractively and elegantly describes the banquet Agnes had arranged for him, painted and decorated with flowers and leaves artfully interwoven so as to resemble a verdant garden.]

Look upon the blessed delights, fortunate guest,

Which fragrance adorns before taste itself approves them.

The abundance of crimson flowers smiles softly;

The field scarcely contains as many roses as the table now has.

Where milk-white lilies gleam amid purple petals,

The place exhales a new fragrance in rivalry.

The dishes, supported by dripping shoots, make a display;

Why, lovely rose, do you cover what a tablecloth customarily covers?

The table pleased better without a woven covering,

While a sweet fragrance, varied in its gifts, casts shade over it.

The wall shone with a green hanging cluster;

Wherever you tread, pressed roses redden.

Such is the abundance of things that, beneath a tranquil flower,

You might think soft meadows were green beneath the roof.

If fleeting things please, which depart so quickly after slipping away,

Let your banquets, paradise, invite us.

The woven work shone through the Daedalian hands of the sister;

Only a mother was worthy to possess such an ornament.

# CHAPTER XII. Another poem concerning gifts sent

[Note: Although he says that he sent gifts to Agnes, he says that they were not so much his own gifts as a return. He praises the generosity of Agnes and Radegund toward him and asks pardon for having sent those gifts. Finally he begs for the common prayers of the monastery at Poitiers on his behalf.]

I sent gifts, but they are not mine—believe one who confesses—

What comes to you is rather your own gift.

You offer everyone’s food, covered with honey,

From whose pious mouth sweet honey first flows [One Vatican manuscript: “from whose pious mouth”].

Believe how much of your gift remains for me,

While my defeated appetite now scatters the food.

But kindly forgive me, with your reverent heart,

For what love presumed to do; may it be forgiven me.

Now let that venerable choir adore Christ on my behalf,

And may my guilt not weigh down upon me as a sinner.

# CHAPTER XIII. For chestnuts

[Note: Fortunatus sends Agnes and Radegund, as a gift, a little wicker basket woven by his own hands, together with chestnuts.]

This basket was woven of wicker by my own hands;

Believe me, dear mother and gracious sister.

I offer these rustic gifts that the countryside produces:

Soft chestnuts, which the tree gave to the fields.

# CHAPTER XIV. For milk

[Note: Fortunatus thanks Agnes and Radegund for the milk porridge sent to him and describes its form and preparation. Finally he wishes that they may long survive.]

I saw fingers pressed into the milky gift,

And the painted hand stands here where you draw off the cream [One Vatican manuscript: “fingers fixed into the milky gift”].

Tell me, I ask, who compelled you to sculpt such tender skins—

Was it Daedalus, or was he your teacher in the art?

O venerable love, by whose theft at work [Paris edition: “with the theft fleeing”],

when the outward form was removed, its image came to me.

This was hope, since it broke through its slender covering;

For not even a small portion of it had been given to me in this way.

May you do such things, while the Lord grants long years,

And may you both remain together in this light for a long time, with your mother.

# CHAPTER XV. Another poem for milk

[Note: He likewise recalls the milk-gift Agnes and Radegund sent him and jokes that this kind of nourishment is suitable for him as an invalid.]

What could mother and sister give me so sweet

As the help of milk that they now suitably provide?

As Paul commanded in apostolic teaching:

He himself orders milk to be given to weak spirits.

You carry a solicitous concern for our name [Paris edition: “Solicitous sister and mother concerning”];

May God’s pious care always be for you.

# CHAPTER XVI. For a meal

[Note: He complains that through another person’s deception and action he was prevented from attending a meal to which the woman addressed in the poem was going. Since he lacked her speech and presence amid the banquet, he asserts that he fasted while dining, declaring that her words would have been more valuable to him than exquisite dishes.]

I confess that I did not know that refreshing meals were being prepared for me—

May I thereby deserve to be able to please your heart.

No one could have torn me away from your face

If the helpless trick of an artificer had not been concealed.

Who will give me the remaining dishes, when with faithful voice

I tell you that you are the delights of my soul?

Absent from you, I honored fasts while dining,

And without you food could not satisfy me [Paris edition: “I could not satisfy myself with food”].

Your tongue would have been the highest banquet for my hungry self;

Sweet words would have filled my spirit.

But with the order reversed, the physician creates fierce wounds,

And the deceiver tests his art by misleading.

He thought that he alone could satisfy me, though nothing that sea or earth provides ever satisfies me.

But now, please forgive me, with ready devotion;

May another’s crime not become a burden to me.

# CHAPTER XVII. Concerning his gift

[Note: Fortunatus sends Agnes and Radegund a little gift made by his own hands. Although it is small and slight, he asserts that it should not be despised because of the giver’s affection.]

I have fashioned this gift of love with my own hands,

But I ask that it be sweet to you or to my lady.

Although the workmanship may seem worthless because of its smallness,

May what I now offer, small as it is, grow through affection.

If you weigh the matter carefully, among all lovers

Gratitude is always greater for small gifts.

# CHAPTER XVIII. For little plums

[Note: He sends little plums to Agnes and Radegund, asking them not to despise them although the gift is small. He asserts that God will provide what would please them more by giving better things. Finally he encourages them to eat them confidently: no suspicion of poison lies hidden in them, as it may in mushrooms.]

Do not, I ask, despise the food sent to you,

Called little black plums, which the forest gave me.

If you deign to take wild fruits [One Vatican manuscript: “if I should deign”; Paris edition: “if it is your will to take woodland fruits”],

God gives better things by which I may be able to please.

Nor should you fear that what hung beneath a shading branch

Was given by the earth as mushrooms rather than by a tree as riches.

I am not cruel enough to offer a mother something unsuitable,

And do not hesitate to take the pure food into your mouths.

# CHAPTER XIX. For other delicacies and milk

[Note: When various delicacies had been sent to him by Agnes, he jokingly says that fasts had been sent to him, since the physician had forbidden him to eat. Nevertheless, he says that he will use the milk that had been sent along with the other things.]

Amid many foods you send me fasts,

And, seeing so many things, you burn my spirit.

My eyes look upon what the physician forbids me to use,

And that which my appetite requests is forbidden by his hand.

Yet, before anything else, when you provide rich milk,

You surpass royal gifts with your presents.

Now, rejoicing with the pious mother, be a sister, we pray,

For a kindly table of joy holds us.

# CHAPTER XX. For eggs and plums

[Note: Having received plums and eggs from Agnes and Radegund, he gives thanks and says that he obeyed their orders: they had prescribed that he take two eggs in the evening.]

From one side you feed me with delicacies, from the other with vegetables [One Vatican manuscript: “from here you feed me”; corruptly];

From this side eggs appear, from that side a plum is given to me [The same manuscript: “here eggs”].

White gifts and black are offered together;

If only my stomach may have peace amid such varied food!

You ordered me to be fed late with two eggs;

I tell you the truth: I myself drank four.

And would that I might deserve to obey you every day;

Thus the appetite obeys the command, as it does now.

# CHAPTER XXI. Concerning his absence

[Note: He says that rainy weather prevented him from coming to Agnes and Radegund, although otherwise he would not have been absent from them for even an hour.]

If excessively rainy weather did not prevent me,

While you were unaware, your lover would have returned to you.

Nor do I now wish, absent, to be detained even for one hour,

Since my light is present whenever the beloved is seen.

# CHAPTER XXII. Concerning a banquet

[Note: He adjures Radegund herself to take some food at the banquet.]

By the work of piety, by him who, pious, commands the stars,

By that which the mother loves and the brother himself desires:

While we take food, whatever you may eat,

If you do this, I shall be satisfied twice over [Paris edition: “whatever you may eat”].

# CHAPTER XXIII. On the same subject

[Note: He describes the banquet prepared for him, varied with many foods.]

I stretched out my swollen belly with varied delicacies,

Taking everything: milk, vegetables, eggs, and butter.

Now dishes furnished with new foods are given to me,

And the mixed food pleases more sweetly all together.

For with the milk they placed butter beside me;

The fat, which had first come from the milk, is recalled here [The butter is understood: extracted from the milk and mixed back into the milk].

# CHAPTER XXIV. Verses composed at a banquet

[Note: Fortunatus excuses himself to Agnes and Radegund because, overcome by sleep, he had been unable to pour out verses at the banquet. Having found an opportunity, he says that he is sending these verses to them, since love conquered sleep.]

Amid varied delicacies and mingled flavor,

While I was dozing and while I was being fed,

I opened my mouth and again closed my eyes,

And ate while looking upon every dish [Paris edition: “I opened my mouth and then closed my eyes again”].

Believe me, dear ones, I had confused thoughts,

Nor was I able easily to speak free words.

I could not paint verses with my fingers or pen [One Vatican manuscript: “not with my fingers”];

The wine-intoxicated Muse had made my hands uncertain.

For to me, as to the others drinking wine in this way,

The table itself seemed to swim in unmixed wine.

Yet now, as I was able, I gave small poems

To the mother and likewise to the sister in sweet address.

And although sleep assails me with many reins,

Love has drawn me to write these with a hesitant hand [The following poem is joined to this one in the same manuscript].

# CHAPTER XXV. On the same subject

The gracious mistress refreshed her servant with words and food,

And satisfied him with varied, delighting humor.

# CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning his gift

[Note: He writes that he is sending the same women a small gift, but one made great by love. Therefore he asks them not to despise it.]

[Note: After Compline had been completed, or after the service called Compline, monks and nuns were not permitted to speak with anyone and consequently could not receive gifts. See the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 42, and the related rule of Saint Caesarius, which the nuns of the monastery at Poitiers followed. In chapter 20 of the Life of Saint Agile, abbot of Rebais, it is written that, when the signal for Compline had been given, the porter closed the door and carried the keys to the abbot. Paris edition:]

If you have not yet completed what is here called “completa” [Compline],

receive this, I ask you humbly, most gladly [Paris edition: “receive the gifts gladly”].

Do not despise what is small [One Vatican manuscript: “for you are my prayers”; other manuscripts: “nor great gifts”; Paris edition: “Do not despise the small, nor do you”];

In a small gift, great love is seen [Another manuscript: “A gift in a narrow compass”; Paris edition: “A gift in a narrow compass”].

# CHAPTER XXVII. To the same, concerning his journey

[Note: Browerus restored this title on the authority of the Trier manuscript, and one Vatican manuscript also has it. He adds, however, that it cannot be denied that some books preferred the title “Concerning the oratory of Illacum” or “Tincillacum”; and the lacuna in the Vatican index indicated “Concerning the oratory of Piliacum.” This reading greatly troubled Pulmannus, who, having found the title “Concerning the oratory of Apiliacum” in his index, says that he found no poem by himself in the manuscripts of Metellus and Walter. It is an *Odoeporicon*, a name by which, as we suppose, Trithemius listed it as a distinct little work.]

[Note: He begins the poem with the fragility of common life and the uncertain accidents of fortune. He then describes the journey he had undertaken and the severe storm by which he had been tossed, asserting that he had barely escaped being overwhelmed by it. Finally he declares his longing for Agnes and Radegund.]

The moments of human beings are whirled through countless accidents [One Vatican manuscript: “moments are marked”],

And life moves on with an unstable, wavering step.

The anxious mind itself, staggering over future things,

Does not know what the coming light will bring for it.

For when I had departed from you, Eomundus the lover [In some copies, as Browerus notes, “Egomundus” was read; he says this is the form found in “Edmundus” and “Egmundus”]

received me with the kindness he customarily shows.

From there I hasten forth and am carried down to the hall of Cariacus.

Then I am borne from there to the place of Illacum. [Note: The reading of this passage has received remarkable variation, as Browerus observes. Three old books—G. S. and Fridericus Tiliobardus—read *Tincillacensi*; others retain the reading indicated. Yet the traces of the Vatican and Pulmannian manuscripts suggest that something belonging to *Illacum* should be added; from their writing one can readily derive *Apiliacum* and *Piliacum*. Until the matter becomes clearer in one direction or the other, I have restored *Dullacum*, formerly brought to light, where there must also have been an oratory, as several books remember. Browerus notes in the same place that the villa of Dullacum was not far from the city of Angers, since it is mentioned in the Life of Saint Albinus written by Fortunatus, no. 12. Others, however—and I agree with them—prefer to understand by the place called Illacum the monastery of Cincillacum or Tincillacum. Fortunatus states in the Life of Saint Albinus, no. 5, that Saint Albinus was abbot there before he was made bishop of Angers. I therefore believe that Fortunatus turned aside to this same monastery and was summoned from there by Domitianus to Angers for the celebration of Saint Albinus’s feast. Accordingly, it must be judged that *Tunc Illacensi* entered this poem through the error of copyists, produced by the slight alteration of a single letter.]

[Col. 0360B] From there the holy bishop Domitianus [Note: This Domitianus succeeded Eutropius in the see of Angers. He attended the Third Council of Paris, held in 557, as Cointius shows under that year, and later the Second Council of Tours in 566. He is the same man whom Fortunatus records as having attended the dedication of the church of Nantes, book III, chapter 6—and this in 568, as Cointius believes. He did not live long after that year, since his successor Baudigisius did not survive until 572, when Audoveus occupied the see of Angers, as Cointius shows in the same place. I do not see why Browerus calls Domitianus a bishop of Châlons, since I cannot find that a bishop of this name even occupied the see of Châlons in Fortunatus’s time, as I have said elsewhere. Saint Domitianus, indeed, a disciple of Saint Memmius, was bishop of Châlons, but lived long before Fortunatus.] snatched me away,

Taking me to the festive joys of Saint Albinus. [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “to the joy of Saint Elentius”; another, “to the holy Alennus.” Browerus restored “to Saint Albinus” from the manuscripts. Fortunatus wrote the Life of Saint Albinus, bishop of Angers, as Gregory of Tours testifies in chapter 96 of *On the Glory of the Confessors*; it may be seen below in the second part of Fortunatus’s works. In the prologue to that Life Fortunatus addresses the man at whose urging he undertook its composition: “I remember,” he says, “apostolic man, when I had come to the city over which you rule as Christ’s bishop, to present myself before your eyes, that among the other counsels of maturity which you seemed, with rich understanding, to pour forth like a torrent, you also made a slight mention of the most holy man, Lord Bishop Albinus,” and so forth. Or was this Domitianus perhaps the very man who, when Fortunatus had come to him—as this poem relates—modestly asked him to compose the Life of Saint Albinus?]

Released from there, after many dangers, weary,

I am driven in a small boat by waves and rain.

The fierce north wind pressed heavily upon the waters,

And the wave raised its badly curved hollows;

Nor could the shores contain the agitated waves,

As the waters poured forth and invaded new lands.

[Col. 0361A] Pastures, fields, groves, crops, viburnum, and willow thickets—

All were seized in one devastation by the enraged force.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “Here, entrusted to me”; the Paris edition reads, “Then, entrusted to me.”]

Here, entrusted amid the broken roar of the sea,

Winter raged with dreadful blasts. [Note: Another manuscript reads *flantibus horriferis* (“with horrible blowing”), incorrectly. The Paris edition has *flatibus horrificis* (“with terrifying blasts”).]

The boat rose and fell over the watery peaks,

Climbing the liquid paths where the mountain hollowed them. [Note: The Paris edition reads “with the mountain left empty.”]

In what manner could the sailor hold the clouds while the boat hung suspended,

When, the depths withdrawing, he returned again to the fields?

Amid hostile waves, while the sea foamed in the storm,

The prow continually drank the rushing waters.

The hostile waters lapped the hull in deadly peace,

More grimly embracing us in their harmful clasp.

But no delay prevents me from recalling various complaints;

I keep the murmurs in my heart, to be related all together later.

May divine power grant me this especially:

[Col. 0361B] That I may soon be able to see you happy once again.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Another Poem about His Journey

[Note: He describes the severity of winter, with frost and snow covering everything far and wide, and hints somewhat obscurely that it caused delay in his journey.]

Everywhere the ice lies rigid, congealed by hoarfrost,

Nor does the pliant grass lift its afflicted leaves.

The earth lies crusted with frost beneath a hard shell,

And deep snow covers the soft branches of the trees.

The flowing rivers have built a wall over their frozen surfaces,

And the compacted water has clothed itself in a heavy skin.

[Col. 0362A] The waters are restrained by their own mass; the liquid has bound itself,

And beneath its own barrier can scarcely open a path for itself.

In the midst of the rivers a crystalline bank has arisen,

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read, “Nor do we wish to go below.”]

Nor can we pass beneath it, nor is there a way over it.

The ice swelled more harshly while the north wind roared:

What water will give passage to that which fights against itself? [Note: In one Vatican manuscript the following poem is appended to Fortunatus’s poems. I place it here, although no indication appears that it is Fortunatus’s own composition. It is as follows:

“The tropic Capricorn now establishes the beginning of the year.

In the middle of Numa’s month the star of the waters stands by the Sun” [manuscript: “stands apart from the Sun”].

“The twin Fish advance toward the season of March.

The Ram looks back toward April with fixed face” [manuscript: “with face fixed upon”] “at the Kalends.

May marvels at the horns of Agenor’s Bull.

June sees the paired Laconians proceed evenly through the sky.”

At the solstice July bears the star of blazing Cancer.

In August the fervent Lion consumes the month with fire.

September, Virgin, fattens Bacchus under your star” [manuscript: “Bacchius”].

“October also balances the Scales at the season of sowing.

The headlong Scorpion commands November to proceed into winter” [perhaps “the winter Scorpion” or “Scorpius the Winter”].

“The Archer brings his signs to an end in the middle of December.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Note: Fortunatus offers prayers for the one who had consecrated himself, and also for the king; at the same time he invites the sisters present to make the same prayers.]

[Note: We present this poem transcribed from an old parchment attached to one of the Vatican Library manuscripts. On it are also found the poem on the Holy Cross beginning “The banners of the King,” and several other poems of Fortunatus—or rather, damaged portions of them. Although the title is absent, as it is likewise absent from all the poems contained in that parchment, both Fortunatus’s distinctive style and the mention of sisters, that is, nuns, to whom the entire speech is directed, sufficiently show that it is his; so too do the prayers for the king, something Fortunatus often did. The subject of this poem, however, is obscure and uncertain. If one may venture a conjecture, it seems to me to have been spoken extemporaneously in the assembly of the nuns of the monastery of the Holy Cross at Poitiers, perhaps on the day when he himself was ordained priest or even inaugurated bishop of Poitiers. Hence he offers prayers for the one who had consecrated himself and dedicated himself to God, as well as for the king, through whose agency he had perhaps attained that degree of honor. It is certainly regrettable that the opening words of the poem have been so worn away in the manuscript by age and long use that no trace of them remains; they might perhaps have shed light upon the whole poem. [Col. 0362D] They seem, indeed, to have expressed the name of the man of whom Fortunatus says that he had given himself to be consecrated. Let this conjecture suffice.]

[The opening is lost.] … us, whom he made consecrated,

May the consecrated man himself live; and speak, sister on the left.

May your light, Savior, surround him with such a gift—

He who appointed us for you; fifth, why are you silent?

May you be an unquenchable light, good king, forever, as I pray;

May these small prayers be able to remind you of this.

Receive, conqueror, an honor worthy of the luminous order;

I am the one who [Note: Perhaps “the middle one.”]: let the second follow beneath.

May this generous giver claim for himself an honored name

Among all peoples; why are you now silent, fourth?

May this worshiper of God be protected in the perpetual love of Christ;

Answer, final one, with your right hand.

For by your power, exalted God, crown the magnificent king—

I beseech you; and thus you seek the seventh.

When the darknesses have been driven from our hearts,

May we always shine with unquenchable splendor.

# FOUR BOOKS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MARTIN (C)

## PROLOGUE OF THE PRIEST FORTUNATUS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MARTIN

[Note: In this letter Fortunatus excuses himself to Gregory because he has worked out and polished the books on the Miracles of Saint Martin less elegantly and appropriately than he should have done. He gives as the reason the season of harvest and rural business, by which he had been occupied. He also declares himself ready to put into verse the work on the powers of Saint Martin that Gregory had composed. Finally, he explains the plan of his work and asserts that in four books he has included everything Sulpicius had written about Saint Martin, doing so within the space of two months. He promises to send these books as quickly as possible to be dedicated and consecrated to Saint Martin himself through Gregory of Tours.]

[Col. 0363A] [Note: This letter is absent from the Venetian edition, in which the following four books on the Miracles of Saint Martin are found. In the three Vatican manuscripts used up to this point, the books on the Miracles of Saint Martin are absent, and consequently this letter may also be absent. In one Vatican Library manuscript only these materials are found—the same manuscript from which we extracted the sixth poem of Book VIII, discussed in the notes to that poem. The letter is found there, but is mutilated in several places.]

To the holy, apostolic, most devout lord in Christ and special father, Pope Gregory, Fortunatus.

In a devout heart, what is less expressed by a work is enlarged through the regard of affection. For *epicheiremata* (arguments), *lexis* (diction), *diairesis* (division), *parainesis* (exhortation), and the other devices may be left to orators and dialecticians, among whom the other arts flourish through intricate techniques. These men are accustomed to adorn or extend such matters with long trains of speech [Note: *Syrma* is a kind of tragic garment, or the train or trailing part of a woman’s dress. The word is derived from the Greek verb *syrō*, meaning “to drag,” as is well known. Martial writes of it in Book XII, epigram 74:

“You too have fitted yourself with a long train.”

And again, in Book IV, epigram 37:

“May my Muse not help with her mad train.”

*​​Syrma* is used for the long sequence of tragic discourse, drawn out to the very end of its course.]

But you, in a spirit of piety and charity, grant forgiveness, setting aside for the moment the judgment of one skilled in meter. Whatever in these matters the trick of the ancients or the sophistry of the present generally elaborates, you will supply entirely for us, since we know less. In the work of the harvest—that is, during the harvest itself—as the messenger presently arriving will be able to explain, I had neither the opportunity nor the ability to work through or attempt each detail.

Therefore, commending myself especially and earnestly to your holy dignity and sweetness, and awaiting your continued willingness to pray for your humble servant, I make my request. When, however, you command that the work which, by Christ’s favor and through the intercession of Lord Martin, you have composed concerning his powers should be arranged in verse, see to it that you order it to be sent back to me. For, by the Lord’s kindness, what the eloquent man, my lord Sulpicius, wrote in prose in a single little book concerning Martin’s life, together with the remainder that he appended in the manner of a dialogue, I have embraced in two little books for the first work and two more for the subsequent dialogue. Thus, very briefly and according to the measure of our poverty, in four little books I have plowed through the whole work in verse during this two-month period, more daring than talkative, neither effective nor polished, rushing through it amid trivial occupations.

I shall arrange for these little books to be transcribed jointly and immediately for my lord and pious lord Martin, if he obtains permission to come, in the notebooks that you sent; through you I shall offer them to him. I ask only this: may his kindness, renewed by you, never cease to intercede for us humble and specially favored servants.

Grant forgiveness, sweet father, because rain poured over the writer during the harvest and soaked so great a blot. Pray for me, holy lord and sweet father.

## PREFACE TO THE SAME BOOKS

An unskilled sailor, when he wishes to spread his sails over the swelling deep,

And enters the stormy waters in ignorance,

While the sea barks hoarsely and the ocean roars,

And the wandering wave murmurs through the terrifying strait—

[5] When the sea leaps up and rolls watery hills,

And fears the level backs of the sea upon the shifting rock;

When the Ocean, gathering the heaps of shipwreck amid the breakers,

Crackles where the swift water rolls, a mountain floating upon it;

[Col. 0364C] When the blue shallows shake the entangled boat in rivalry,

As it crosses the hanging path of the liquid plain;

If the fierce winter rises so that it lashes the air with foam,

And lifts its blue head to the stars,

The sailor, hurled among the clouds by the waves, rushes on,

And the hanging prow enters the paths of the air.

[15] One part of the boat rises, another sinks toward the sands;

The slippery balance wavers in the doubtful strait.

[Note: In this note, the numbers refer to lines.]

25. Venetian edition: “with the method by which it must be handled”; this reading is preferable.

32. Venetian edition: “whose lake does not water the Muses’ mouth.”

36. Vatican manuscript: “So that my sails…”

38. The Vatican manuscript and Venetian edition: “and if its blasts”; this reading should be retained.]

[Col. 0365A] Now the raging ruin of the sea is seen above,

And from above the Ocean arms its angry waters.

Now, too, the boat, springing forward through the repulsion of the west wind and sea,

[20] Flies forth, driven by enormous waves.

The rash pilot is battered by trembling waters

And is amazed at which paths, entangled as they are, he should seek by skill.

Stunned, trembling, dull, wandering, anxious, uncertain,

With confused mind the sailor soon lacks assistance.

[25] And now, losing the rudder and the means of steering,

Overcome by the weight of the water, he lies helpless, ignorant of his art.

So I, least of the modest, venerable Agnes,

Together with holy Radegund, whom I honor with devout devotion,

[Col. 0366A] Am compelled to stretch the promised step toward difficult heights,

And am driven, unequal in strength, by such great commands.

My mind is tossed about, for the wave of the Muses does not float upon it;

My sandy understanding does not water the lakes with speech.

For Martin, renowned to the stars for his lofty merits,

Though I have prayers, my breast cannot speak of him.

[35] You must be asked that the shipwrecked prow not labor,

But that he assist my sails with his own blasts.

Then I shall be able to trust that my canvas can be carried to port,

If faith lends its breath and his lips favor me.

Pray bring aid, and ask words from the Word,

If that fountain waters, so may this little stream flow.

[40] Give what your pupil may return to you with interest,

So that I may add my small talents to his treasures.

17. Orontius. The manuscript reads *Orentius*.

20. Paulinus. This was not that Paulinus of Aquitaine, later bishop of Nola, who lived in Martin’s time, but a certain Paulinus of Périgueux. For Périgueux is the city of the Petrocorii, and is called *Vesunna* in the ancient designation. The learned Ruinart demonstrates this among other points in his notes on Gregory of Tours, chapter 2, Book I, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*. He gives the following arguments. First, the author who wrote six books on the powers of Saint Martin presents himself as having received an index of the miracles from Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, and praises him at the beginning and end of Book VI because he had related to him certain miracles worthy of all faith. Perpetuus was the sixth bishop of Tours and the third after Saint Martin, since Briccius and Eustochius sat between them and Saint Martin; one held the see for forty-seven years, the other for seventeen, as Gregory of Tours reports in Book X, chapter 31, of the *History of the Franks*. Second, the same author often praises Paulinus of Nola and speaks of him as of someone else. Third, the manuscript codices read “Paulinus of Périgueux.” Yet Gregory of Tours, in the cited passage, expressly asserts that this was Paulinus, bishop of Nola. The learned Ruinart says that Gregory was deceived by a passage in Sulpicius Severus’s *Dialogues*, Book III, where Posthumianus is instructed to visit Paulinus of Nola and communicate to him what he had heard, so that, as he had already done with the earlier little book, he might publish other accounts throughout Italy and Illyricum. Fortunatus seems to share this error of Gregory, judging from the notes and characteristics with which he describes the same Paulinus. Nevertheless, as Ruinart adds, since Saint Paulinus wrote many things in various places in praise of Saint Martin, Fortunatus’s words may be referred to him. See also Sirmond’s notes on Letter 11 of Book VIII of Sidonius Apollinaris.

After Christ, enthroned on high, returned to the heavens,

Bringing back the victorious standards in his triumphant flesh,

Illustrious, rich from the plundered prison of hell,

Suppressing the deadly laws of the tyrant of Tartarus,

[5] [Col. 0365C] And, almighty, tearing open the adamantine gates of Styx,

From the savage seat of a people covered in long darkness,

Drawing back the captive host through the gates opened wide,

After thousands had been rescued—therefore he was restored to the stars,

And sat upon the Father’s throne, at the right hand of the Right Hand,

[10] Through which, while he dwelt among us, he gave miracles to the earth.

The Hebrew, Greek, and Latin styles sang many things,

Opening the Gospel book,

Arranged in the manner of prose, in a common rhythmic movement.

For Juvencus was the first to distinguish the flesh in teachable order

[15] And sing the work of majesty by the art of meter.

[Col. 0366B] From there the conspicuous tongue of Sedulius also shone,

And Orontius touched upon a few things with flowering speech;

Sending these sacred gifts to the holy martyrs,

Prudentius prudently sacrificed his deeds.

[20] Paulinus, strong in lineage, heart, faith, and art,

[Col. 0366C] Set forth in verse the teaching of the master Martin.

The deeds and actions called “apostolic acts,”

The poet Arator plowed with eloquent speech.

What the genealogist once explained in a sacred sequence,

But I, lacking in understanding, a very small portion of the Italian tongue,

Heavy with dregs, light in speech, sluggish in reasoning,

Dull in mind, lacking in art, inexperienced in practice, yet not without a voice,

Licking only a tiny drop from the streams of grammar,

[30] Tasting a small draught from the gulf of rhetoric,

46. Sozomen, writing about Saint Martin in Book III, chapter 14, says: “Martin was distinguished by his lineage from Sabaria of Pannonia” (*Martinos apo Saborias tēs Pannonias episēmos ēn to genos*). Sabaria is today thought to be the Hungarian town of Szombathely, also formerly called Stain am Angern, in the county of Vas. Cluverus, however, thinks that ancient Sabaria once stood where the castle of Sarvar is now, which the Germans call Rothenturn, three leagues below the aforementioned town, at the confluence of the river Sabaria with the Raab. The learned Ruinart gives this information in his notes on Gregory of Tours, Book I of the *History*, chapter 34.

52. Venetian edition: “When the brave man had bound the waves with bit and ice.”

69. The Vangiones were a people of Germany, mentioned by Caesar and by Tacitus in *Annals* XII, chapter 27. Constantius had joined their barbarian auxiliaries to himself against Magnentius, though he was not helped by them. They later ravaged cities and regions subject to Roman rule and, invading Gaul, brought Strasbourg, Rouen, Tabernae, Saletio, Speyer, Worms, and Mainz under their control. Julian, proclaimed Caesar by Constantius and later emperor, defeated and routed them. See Socrates, Book III, chapter 1, of the *Ecclesiastical History*, and Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVI.

70. Vatican manuscript: “he refuses all pay and profits.”

Martin believed that after he had been initiated by baptism he was forbidden to take up arms and fight. When Julian reproached him with fear of the battle on the following day, Martin declared that he would stand unarmed before the front line. Julian therefore ordered the man to be bound lest he flee and to be placed on the following day in the very position in battle that he had named. But by divine intervention it happened that on the next day the enemy sent ambassadors to request peace.

Martin was then handed over to one of them to be stripped; Martin more successfully won this man, converting him to Christ, as Sulpicius relates in the Life of Saint Martin, chapter 4.

[Col. 0367A] I gather from legal writings, from which scarcely any rust has been removed,

Unlearning what I once learned, and from those arts

Retaining only a scent in these nostrils.

No shining bordered toga glows upon me, no little feather adorns me.

[35] Now my only possession is naked hunger from my poor tongue,

Certainly amid so many summits of holy poets,

The thunderbolts of learned men and the jeweled meadows of speakers,

I, green with no flower, shall attempt to weave a garland,

And mix these bitter wormwoods with honey from the flowing stream.

[40] Yet the matter itself compelled me to do this,

So that I should not be judged guilty and punished for a serious offense.

For reason rightly demanded that I speak forth

The praises of this bishop in words,

For whose sake it was that I came to this region.

[45] [Col. 0367B] Will I therefore be worthy to touch with my hand

Or compose with trembling tongue the deeds of blessed Martin,

Born in Pannonia, where illustrious Sabaria flourishes?

He does not need my darkness, since, shining with light,

A lofty Gallic beacon extends its radiance to the Indians.

[50] When, still a boy scarcely entering the years of puberty,

Under freezing cold, with hoarfrost curling the earth,

When grim winter had bound the waves with icy restraint,

And the wandering freedom of the rivers lay hidden, enclosed,

Weaving harsher frost into bonds for itself,

[55] Water colder than water, clothed in a garment of rigor—

A beggar came before the gate of Amiens.

To this man, who had stood in his way, Martin divided his cloak,

And, with fervent faith, offered it to his freezing limbs.

The beggar receives a share of the cold; Martin receives a share of the warmth;

[60] [Col. 0367C] Between the two needy men warmth and cold are divided,

And a new marketplace of exchange is created: cold and heat,

Together with poverty, are sufficiently divided between two.

Yet the Creator himself appeared clothed in this garment,

And Christ was covered by Martin’s cloak.

[65] No garment of the emperors deserved this honor;

A soldier’s white cloak is worth more than a king’s purple.

[Col. 0368A] This was the first earnest of virtue and pledge of love.

When savage barbarism later attacked the Gallic fortresses,

And the fiery enemy pressed upon the territory near the Vangiones,

[70] The saint refused all the profits of military service.

When Julian raged in imperial anger,

He ordered guards to keep the righteous man confined

And, when day came, to hurry him first into the battle line.

Yet before the front he declared that the holy man would go unarmed.

[75] The day of battle had therefore come; the enemy sought peace,

And while one man prayed, fury fell away from all their weapons.

Alone and without bloodshed he conquered innumerable battle lines.

From there, traveling through the places of robbers, thinking he was going across the Alps,

With his hands bound behind his back, led by one man,

[80] At the hour of death, reckoning the advantage of his enemy,

The robber believes in the God whom this man preaches as worthy of worship.

He who wished to give death receives salvation from his mouth.

The fierce man is led away, bound by religion,

And his own robber willingly becomes the prey of Martin.

[85] How good he was to that man! Yet this man was more devout toward him.

Both are preserved: the robber lives through faith, Martin in body;

Both are safe, since no one falls—thus each lives.

From there, passing through the beautiful places of Milan,

The traveler treads flowering fields and pleasant green spaces.

[90] An old and reckless enemy comes to meet him face to face,

Assuming a human appearance beneath the guise of a man,

A liar, with faith perishing, badly trained in deception.

He asks what road is being sought; and the saint replies

That he is hastening this way, wherever God should call him to go.

[95] The savage enemy says to him: “Whichever way you attempt to proceed,

[Col. 0368C] I shall go with you, working harm and running against your prayers.”

The saint immediately answers him with prophetic voice:

“​​The Lord is my helper; I shall fear no evil.

Why should I fear the cowardly one? God is the fear of those who fear weapons.

[100] I walk safely amid adversities, under a heavenly guide;

No road is open to ambush beneath the divine protection.”

147. Martin, returning from his homeland, found that Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, had been driven into exile by the faction of the Arians. He went to Milan and there built a monastery. But he was driven out from there by Auxentius, the Arian bishop. Sozomen writes of him in Book III, chapter 14: “Having come to Milan, he lived privately. He withdrew from there after being plotted against by Auxentius, the bishop, who himself was not sound concerning the faith of those who had assembled at Nicaea” (*Eis Mediolanon elthōn kath’ heauton diet­riben. Hypechōrēse te enthende epibouleuomenos para Auxentiou tou episkopou, oude autou hygiōs echontos peri tēn pistin tōn en Nikaia synelthontōn*).

149. *Gallinaria*. You will find the location and description of the Gallinarian Islands in the same Sozomen, Book III, chapter 14. In relating the same matter about Martin as Fortunatus does here, he says: “For a certain time, living on the roots of plants, he inhabited an island called Gallinaria; it is small and uninhabited, lying in the Tyrrhenian Sea” (*Kai epi tina chronon, rhizais botanōn arkoumenos, nēson ōikēsen hēn Gallinarian kalousin; mikra de hautē kai anoikētos en tō Tyrrhēnikō pelagei keimenē*). Varro, Book III of *On Agriculture*, chapter 9, and Columella, Book VIII, chapter 2, state that it was named from the abundance of domestic or wild hens. Varro writes of the island: “From these hens [the wild ones] the island is said to have been called Gallinaria; it lies in the Tuscan Sea, along Italy opposite the Ligurian mountains, and so forth.”

155. Hilary was again ordered to return from the East, where he was living in exile, not because he was recalled as though formally released from exile, but because he was found to be much more troublesome to the Arian faction in the East than in Gaul, as Sulpicius relates in Book II of his *History*. When Martin therefore came to Rome to meet Hilary on his return from the East, and found that he had already departed, he carefully followed his route and caught up with him not long afterward. Sulpicius likewise relates this in chapter 51 of the Life of Saint Martin.

156. Vatican manuscript: “his own footsteps behind him.”

This monastery, which Saint Martin built near Poitiers, was already famous for miracles in the time of Gregory of Tours, who testifies to this in Book IV of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 30. It was about forty stadia from the city of Poitiers, as Gregory of Tours reports in the same place.

[Col. 0369A] He said this, and the demon, pierced by the point of his powerful word,

Departs; thus a shadow flees when Christ overshadows it.

Meanwhile, freeing his mother from pagan error,

[105] She gives him birth for the world, and he gives her birth for heaven;

He makes the decrepit old woman be reborn in the holy stream,

And her own entrails generate their mother in a better womb.

The doctrine that Arius had poured forth with sacrilegious mouth

Had devastated the whole world in a grievous storm,

[110] And his disastrously shipwrecked tongue floated across Illyricum.

From this too new battles began to arise for the righteous man,

So that the warrior might become stronger, his weapons restored;

Growing through many dangers for the work of virtue.

Thus the devout man, wise and faithful athlete of faith,

[115] [Col. 0369B] Suppressed the scattered poisons of heresy while fighting the enemy,

Torn by punishments, given over to scourges, driven from the city.

For he confessed, through his own sufferings, that the Father and the Begotten Son,

And the power, nature, likeness, virtue, light, and honor of the gracious Spirit,

Were of one will, one of three.

[120] The sweet limbs of the man are carved by bitter lashes,

And ancient sins torment the young man of Christ;

Yet a light punishment becomes more severe through the name of the one he loves.

And because Hilary, the highest summit of faith, virtue, and honor,

Cast the rays of his fame throughout the world,

[125] Governing duly the inner laws of the priesthood,

A terrible trumpet, the trumpet of the law, the herald of the Thunderer,

More beautiful than electrum, more ardent than gold thrice refined,

[Col. 0369C] More generous than the Eridanus, more torrential than the broad Rhône,

Richer than the Nile, more abundantly scattered than the noble Danube,

[130] Skilled at pouring forth the streams of an overflowing heart,

Sprinkling thirsty breasts with the fountains of his understanding,

His mind full of the Gospel’s two-by-two books,

[Col. 0370A] Pouring four new rivers from his mouth upon the world,

The Church’s ornament, a powerful, shining diadem,

[135] Gleaming like a fillet upon the limbs of Christ the head,

Fighting in his breast, adamantine in skill, a topaz,

A mind unshaken in the arenas of virtue,

Gem-bearing in speech, more radiant in utterance than precious stones—

An apostolic teacher, refuting sophists by reason,

[140] Instructing his followers in doctrine, light, faith, and virtue.

Because he was grievous and unconquerable to his enemies,

He is led into exile, where he extends long silences,

And there the soldier seeks his rewards with the king’s assistance.

In his absence, wandering Gaul yields to error,

[145] And the region trembles when so great a tower is moved.

When Martin learned this too hastily from there,

He established a cell beneath the heights of Milan,

[Col. 0370B] From which Auxentius, the unjust author, then expelled the man.

From there, first an exile, he goes to the island of Gallinaria,

[150] Lacking grain and feeding on the roots of grass.

Then he immediately took poisonous hellebore into his mouth;

He began to die from the food by which he had believed he could live.

But prayer alone drove away the poison working its evil,

And, while the man lived, death itself died within him.

[155] When Hilary was again granted the opportunity to return,

The righteous man hastens forth along his footsteps.

The one who longs for him receives the one who longs for him; the lover receives the loving man,

And a monastery is established close to the city of Poitiers.

There the catechumen is joined to the sacred mouth, to be instructed;

[160] [Col. 0370C] Yet, while the man was absent, a grievous death carried off his friend.

Suddenly Martin is present, though he had been absent.

Behold, devotion returns, and with it the vessel of salvation.

When he saw the corpse cold with fever,

He weeps, groans, runs forward, grieves, howls, burns, and agonizes.
