165. Venetian edition: “and, conceiving faith”; this reading is preferable.

175. “Body,” namely, and “his guest,” namely, the soul. Hence “the same author and heir,” because, having returned to life, he reclaimed what he had left by testament to others.

179. *Lupicini*. Lupicinus is here called a distinguished man according to the secular age by Sulpicius. Cuspinianus, in his commentary on the Chronicle of Cassiodorus, thinks that he was the same man who was consul with Jovinus under the emperor Valentinian in 370. He says: “Lupicinus was formerly master of the cavalry, and Jovinus master of the soldiers, as Marcellinus reports; they were joined to Valens when he was setting out for the East, and so forth.”

183. The manuscript reads *hic* (“here”) instead of *hinc* (“from here”).

194. “With a sustaining hand,” that is, after Martin had grasped his right hand, as Sulpicius relates; he stood upon his feet.

198. Vatican manuscript: “as far as the vestibule of the house.”

204. *Ruritius*. The Vatican manuscript reads “a certain Rusticius.”

206. “From the remaining cities,” and so forth. This means that when Martin was to be made bishop of Tours, the clergy and bishops who governed their own parishes assembled in the principal and mother city so that they might take part in and subscribe to the election.

214. Sulpicius relates that when the lector whose duty it was to read on that day had been prevented by the crowd from being present, and confusion and tumult had consequently arisen, one of those present seized a Psalter. When he opened it, he happened by chance upon the verse of the psalm: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise, because of your enemies, that you may destroy the enemy and defender.” The people accepted this as a favorable omen, by which a certain bishop named Defensor, who opposed Martin’s election as bishop of Tours, might be driven away.

220. This monastery was later called Maius, as Gregory of Tours reports in Book X of the *History*, chapter 31, no. 3. In it Martin built a basilica in honor of Saints Peter and Paul. It was situated nearly two thousand paces from the city of Tours, in a vast and deserted place beneath a steep, overhanging cliff.

221. As Sulpicius writes concerning the same matter, after he had been made bishop Martin relaxed nothing of the custom or severity of his former life. The Venetian edition reads: “an outstanding monk.”

222. Eighty disciples had gathered there to Saint Martin, among them many distinguished by nobility; several of these later became bishops, as Sulpicius records in Book I, chapter 7.

226. Vatican manuscript: “the shadow of the tomb.”

230. Vatican manuscript: “to share with him.”

234. Vatican Codex: Sic altar pariter removetur, “Thus the altar likewise is removed” (altar rather than the main text’s altare).

**[Col. 0371A]**

And, seeing the faith, he ordered everyone to leave the cell.

He shut them out through the doors, left alone without a witness;

then the fervent petitioner before the Judge prostrates himself over the cold body,

that the underworld might vomit up the dead man.

Meanwhile, while the interval of two hours delayed him,

[170] Behold, the face returns; vapors leap through the limbs,

then redness stands upon the cheeks, and the pupil repaints the eyes;

again, sight inserted within restores the windows of the eyes,

and the vein swells with streams of blood from its enlivened source.

Gradually the column rises, though its structure trembles;

[175] the fallen house and its inhabitant rise together,

and he himself, living again, once more becomes his own originator and heir;

restored to life, he says that he had been led before the judge’s tribunal

to be condemned, but, through Martin’s prayer, had been brought back.

**[Col. 0371B]**

At last, hurrying past Lupicinus’ estate,

[180] he discovered—alas!—that the servant had been carried off by a cruel death,

his neck broken by the savage hanging;

he approached where the evil hanging prey lay,

drove everyone away, and alone sought his accustomed weapons,

then bent over the pale limbs of the lifeless man,

[185] and the holy man’s chest presses upon him, lest the coffin of the tomb press him down.

Soon, however, he sent a prayer from his mouth into the ear of the Living One;

with death’s foot turned backward, the fugitive abandoned its prey,

and the greedy devourer vomited its booty from its ravenous throat.

**[Col. 0371C]**

At once the dead man sprang up with slow effort,

[190] now lighter, the clay moves itself, animated by warmth;

raising his languid neck and scarcely opening his eyes, drowsy with death,

his waking eyes heavy with vision,

while the smell of death still lingered in his nostrils.

But, by his enabling hand, he raises all the limbs together;

[195] and the structure of the body stood upon its fearless feet.

For, brought back to life and relearning his steps by practice,

he rendered obedience to life as the reward of the holy gift,

while the man who had suddenly snatched the dead from the threshold of death

was intent on leading him home as far as the entrance,

[200] remaining there as his reward: such was the just compensation.

Glory to you, Christ, who perform these wonders throughout the world.

It happened that the bishop of Tours was being summoned to the city,

yet he could not be brought out from the threshold of his cell.

A certain Ruricius, pretending that his wife was ill,

[205] obtained the saint’s departure by entreating him at his feet.

New gatherings came running from the various cities,

all rejoicing together that they were carrying off a holy prize.

Yet, lest he escape, a proper guard surrounded him.

Meanwhile, while only a few were resisting, the innocent man

[210] **[Col. 0372B]** was chosen, dragged away, consecrated, and placed in the citadel.

There was one rival, the bishop Defensor, who opposed him,

lest Martin should care for the sheep entrusted to the shepherd.

Nor was there delay: by the judgment of the Lord, as the reader sang,

Defensor was marked out by a verse of the Psalm:

[215] “From the mouths of infants and nursing children perfect praise,”

“you who thus well destroy the defender,” he said.

Soon the crash reaches the stars, and a wandering shout fills the halls;

that favor reveals Defensor’s guilt,

and the man is handed over for judgment, with the prophet as witness.

[220] From there he founded a monastery for himself beneath a lofty cliff,

a monk steadfast in the dignity of the episcopate.

There a great number of holy companies of brothers gathered.

Thus there was a particular place, once most renowned,

after the long ages of antiquity had passed:

[225] **[Col. 0372C]** opinion spread that it was the pious cult-place of a martyr.

From the sacred tomb, as he prayed, a shadow sprang up,

speaking from the left side; by the ominous circumstances

the thing itself compelled the apparition to confess its name or deed.

In a voice it declared itself a robber, executed for its crime,

[230] and said that it had no share with the blessed martyrs.

Since the martyrs retain the crown, but evil punishment held this one,

this superstition was heard by all but seen by Martin alone,

and was forbidden under such a fate:

thus the altar too was removed, and the ghost driven away.

[235]

**[Note: [Col. 0373D]**

*In this note, the numbers refer to lines.*

236. Martin, traveling along the road, saw a funeral procession from a distance. The linen cloths placed over the corpse, inflated and flying in the wind, suggested to him that a pagan sacrifice was being performed, in which images covered with white linens were customarily carried about. After making the sign of the cross, he ordered the crowd to stop; immediately dizziness and stiffness of the limbs seized them. When he learned that it was a funeral, he again made the sign of the cross, thereby freeing and dismissing them.

240. Venetian edition: gressuque extorpuit aegra, “and the ailing crowd grew numb in its step” (aegra describes the crowd; the main text’s aegro describes its step).

249. Sulpicius relates that this shrine was demolished, not burned, by Martin.

271. “Country dwellers,” namely pagans who had stationed themselves on the opposite side, on elevated ground as though in a safe place, to watch the outcome. The tree, as if seized by a whirlwind, turned its ruin and fall upon them.

273. Vatican Codex: “vengeance was made into salvation.”

276. Judicio, “by judgment.” The manuscript reads indicio, “by indication.”

277. Vatican Codex: “with error driven away.”

283. Vatican Codex: Quantum globus igneus, “as much as the fiery mass—” (a compressed variant fragment).

284. Venetian edition: “to him words of prayer.”

290. Vatican Codex: in aera pinnas, “wings into the air”; pinnas rather than the main text’s pennas, both “wings.”

319. Vatican Codex: “He crushed the idols and uprooted the shrines.” The Venetian edition likewise reads: “he uprooted the shrines.”

323. Vatican Codex: “casting down the idols.”

325. Heduorum. The manuscript reads Eduorum; both mean “of the Aedui,” with different spelling.

*Ibid.* Sulpicius calls it the district of the Edui, or Aedui (Eduorum, sive Aeduorum).

*Ibid.* “He attempts.” The manuscript reads “he wished.”

*Ibid.* Vatican Codex: “while he wished to tear down the temple.”

**[Col. 0373A]**

After setting out again, with his religious company,

he suddenly came upon a pagan funeral,

while he thought that images were being carried there in profane ceremony.

He traced the sign of the cross against them; the procession ran

before the man, waging its own battle, friendly to piety.

[240] The opposing crowd stiffened in its steps and was numbed by painful torpor;

held motionless in its movement, it spun about, seized by dizziness.

The burden was added: they lowered the corpse from their shoulders,

for they could no longer carry it, and death grew heavier under the weight.

Then the holy man, recognizing that this was a funeral,

[245] ordered them to go away, again tracing the weapons of the cross with his fingers.

Thus he bound their path, and then, moved by pity, released it;

with one and the same hand he sent commands through the air,

performing this wonder as a priest who had suspected otherwise.

Immediately, wishing to burn down an ancient shrine,

[250] **[Col. 0373B]** he ordered a sloping pine nearby to be cut down.

A rustic, combative crowd came to oppose him,

lest the thing born for, and due to, the flames be cut down.

Accordingly they made this agreement: the pine would be felled

[255] if Martin could hold it back as it fell.

The people agreed, and the priest willingly gave his pledge.

He placed his tender body beneath the rigid trunk,

and the doomed fall of the pine was anxiously anticipated.

Meanwhile the tree, struck by swift double axes, resounds,

and, creaking beneath the blows, nods at its crown, about to fall.

[260] Gradually bending, now conquered by the axe, it rushed down.

The frightened monks watched their master’s final moment,

believing that its branches would pierce the righteous man’s entrails.

But the man stood fearless and offered the weapons of the cross

to the falling pine, adding his own battles to his triumphs.

[265] **[Col. 0373C]** The retreating tree feared the man and drew backward;

about to fall, it suspended its descent in the air at a distance,

shaking back its foliage, turned around, and, contrary to its nature,

held its falling leap, balancing itself through the emptiness.

Cut down against nature and bent back in resistance,

[270] it soon sought the path along which its own weight did not drive it.

From there a hostile dizziness whirled toward the country people,

springing toward the hill to punish the enemies.

The thing prepared for death was unexpectedly turned into salvation.

A crash rang out in every direction; the monks wept for joy,

the stupefied pagans grew pale at the new miracles,

and the judgment of the tree softened the human will.

It seeks the weapons of the cross, having abandoned its error,

and this fear of the pine made Martin beloved,

**[Col. 0373D]** producing greater fruit when the tree fell.

[280] From there he ordered the roof of another shrine to be set on fire.

While the neighboring building was being devoured by a fiery tongue,

**[Col. 0374A]** and the blaze, released with all its strength, drove forward,

he himself flew to confront it where the fiery globe was making its way,

climbing onto the roof of the building;

here he uttered words of prayer.

[285] Soon the whole fire, rolled back upon the winds, burned fiercely,

and the Vulcanian flame breathed against the north wind.

The domestic elements stir up quarrels in rebellion;

you could see the embers fighting against the opposing Zephyrs.

From one side the southern fury presses; from the other, with swift wings,

[290] the flying flame bit the northern wings through the air.

After struggling for a long time, at last overcome through the air,

the winds that usually arm the flames fled from the flames.

This was a sufficiently remarkable new condition for the world:

the blasts fear the fire, and the fire fears to devour the wood;

[295] the greedy flames dread their own nourishment,

and gradually the languid tongue of the hearth withdraws into itself.

The fire that is accustomed to burn is consumed by itself;

and Martin’s faith brought down rain from a cloudless sky.

Again, when he wished to overturn another temple,

[300] a rustic crowd prevented the profane shrines from being torn down.

Driven back from there, he went to nearby places, but, for two days,

covered with ashes and haircloth, observing fasts,

he prayed for divine aid to bring down the temples.

Immediately two men of the angelic army appeared before him,

[305] celestial leaders holding spears and shields.

They approached the holy man and addressed him freely:

“Martin, we descend from the stars to serve as your defenses.

You sit here filthy and squalid, but your concern is for the Thunderer.

By your intercessions the lofty axis of heaven thunders;

[310] warlike Olympus joins together in arms throughout its whole extent,

**[Col. 0374C]** so that you may accomplish what you have begun; through us the ether serves you.

We have been sent by the Lord, two of us, to guard your camp;

on this side we are leaders, where the better cause is laboring.

Now, come, break the delays, lest the rustic crowd rebel.

[315] You see that we supply the weapons: it is ours to overcome the proud.

Rush forward; do not fear, with our help, to demolish the temples.

You ought not to falter: the favor of the gracious God is with you.”

Then the holy man, hastening to attack and dissolve the temple,

destroyed the idols, stripped the shrines, and buried the altars.

[320] The entire lofty mass lay beneath the dust.

The rustic population, previously hostile, itself favored the ruin

and pressed on toward the destruction of what it had defended unjustly,

casting out the idols and confessing the divinity of the Thunderer.

With one and the same blow it rejected this and chose that.

[325]

**[Note: [Col. 0375D]**

*In this note, the numbers refer to lines.*

328. Vatican Codex: “with daring effort.”

329. Dum cuperet gladio, “while he wished, with a sword—.”

341. Vatican Codex: “and throws him backward upon the ground.”

348. Vatican Codex: Excussumque fuit, “and it was shaken loose.”

361. Vatican Codex: “indeed also.”

365. Vatican Codex: “a noble witness and author.”

368. Venetian edition: “wasting paralysis.”

**[Col. 0376D]** 383. Pontificum, “of bishops” (genitive plural). Perhaps pontificem, “the bishop” (accusative singular).

*Ibid.* Vatican Codex: “with the people roaring.”

391. Venetian edition: “friendly to piety.”

398. Vatican Codex: “this sweet life was mine,” etc.

400. Venetian edition: “of the pitiable father.”

408. Vatican Codex: “with the order arranged.”

423. In the Vatican Codex: “he saw the face of the foster-daughter.”

**[Col. 0375A]**

After he attempted to tear down the temple of the Haedui,

the uncultivated country worshipers opposed him,

lest they worship more effectively if their own worship were destroyed.

Among them, one, emboldened by a daring effort and wickedly stronger,

attacked the sacred head with a sword,

[330] while the father willingly offered himself with bare neck.

But when, savage in mind, he had gathered all his anger,

sharpening his rage but shorn of the sharpness of his heart,

he leapt more fiercely and suspended his whole body.

Twice the armed fury rushed to strike the throat,

[335] striking all the more heavily the higher the sword was raised,

his fingers tightly gripping the hilt while he restrained his nails.

Guilty, meditating dreadful wounds with his right hand,

a friend of death, loving the crime, he dared it cruelly.

Now leaning upon the blade, with the point drawn back toward the head,

[340] **[Col. 0375B]** he himself, who had been hanging poised for the blow, was thrown to the ground.

Lying on his back upon the earth, he who had been advancing more eagerly toward the attempt

uttered a prayer while his arrogant limbs lay stretched out.

The righteous man stood while the other fell, believing that he would stand by the righteous man’s fall.

In this reversal, the helpless man stood,

while the proud man fell.

[345] Again Martin completed his work and overturned the idols. And behold,

a certain man, who had been plotting Martin’s death, drew a knife;

but the booty destined to be seized was snatched from the predatory hand,

and the loosened flying iron fled without restraint,

taking a lighter path and never appearing again afterward.

[350] Thus, once the knife had been taken away, the robber was harmless in his hands.

He became gentle after being stripped of his weapons;

his rage did not depart from his spirit until the weapons had departed.

This was unwilling mercy, which removed the means by which he could harm.

**[Col. 0375C]** Often the blessed man likewise, even when the farmers themselves opposed him,

by the power of his faith, as he prayed, ordered

the savage shrines, badly tended by their own ministers, to fall.

Thus too, when the rebels customarily attacked the bishop,

[355] while they overturned the temples, they themselves became weapons for the blessed man,

and Martin’s battles were fought by a hostile hand.

He conquers through their factions and with another’s soldier.

[360] Then too, how great was the healing that flowed from the patron,

how great the grace that issued from the healer’s touch!

In the face of such praises, the eloquence of the world is speechless.

To have seen him was to have earned salvation;

[365] he himself is sufficient as his own noble witness and author.

Once, when he was entering the walls of Trier, the gentle man saw

a girl in whom a long-standing paralysis,

having dissolved through her limbs, flowed sluggishly,

**[Col. 0375D]** stiff with icy torpor,

[370] living as though already dead, with her final breaths.

Her eyes were the vigilant guardians of death,

her lights returning the funeral rites to her limbs.

Her spirit hastened to release the bonds of living flesh,

scarcely moving in a hidden breath,

[375] drawing through her nostrils a breath uncertain of its end.

Her foot, hand, face, and cheeks lay like the image of one buried,

**[Col. 0376A]** not even buried, but wholly a portion of the tomb.

Through tender affection for her, her father’s lifeless old age,

his cheeks torn and his white hair badly disordered,

was wasting away impatiently, while no healing care was available.

[380] When he learned that the holy man had been honorably brought into the city,

the old man flew toward him, taking up youthful strength in his limbs,

leaping eagerly and outstripping his years with his running.

With the chorus of bishops surrounding him and the people crowding around,

he burst into the midst with shameless cries;

[385] for exceptional grief pays no heed to the weapons of modesty.

The old man therefore collapsed, prone at the holy man’s feet,

licking his knees, hands, and soles with tender kisses.

At last, with a groan giving him release, the afflicted man began to speak:

**[Col. 0376B]** “Martin, man of God, born for the people’s salvation,

[390] man, a parent to all through goodness, I bring my grief before you.

May the tears of the wretched not perish, friend of piety.

You, whom my plight has drawn to come from such distant places,

may the labor of this journey provide a shortcut to life;

I have a daughter at home, lying stricken by the wound of disease,

[395] near her funeral rites, without any hope of healing.

Once she stood unharmed, my sole delight,

devoted to pious services, gentle in character;

in comforting my old age, this sweet life was mine.

Behold, she is dying and drags my vitals with her into death,

[400] leading her father’s gray hair, pitiably, into the underworld.

Indeed, I would wish to go first myself, if only it were permitted.

What life remains for an old man, or what prayers for me as a father,

when a father’s hope perishes with the loss of his child’s name?

Through her marriage and the future gifts of grandchildren,

[405] I might have become green again, though dry upon the branches of my offspring.

But the more I consider the losses of present salvation,

the more, while I look on, I see my daughter—the light of my eyes—snatched away from the light,

whose case would have been better pleased with the order reversed,

so that she might close the eyes of her aged father.

[410] Therefore, holy man, deign to hold back eager death,

and, minister of aid, come to meet the girl who is being snatched away.

If there is delay, my cause is lost; come to the aid of us both.

For anxiety kills me if healing ceases for her.”

At these words the holy priest, confused, blushed,

[415] **[Col. 0376D]** considering himself unworthy to be a minister of such power.

But the father persisted, urging him with the same words:

“Physician owed to frenzied veins, exert your care;

let the cleansing of the disease feel the physician’s arrival.”

Moved by these words, he went to where the exhausted girl lay,

while the crowd stood outside, as a shepherd would act in a sheepfold.

[420] From there, waging his own battles, the advocate returned to arms,

prostrating his body upon the ground, while his mind was raised beyond the stars.

**[Note: [Col. 0377D]**

*In this note, the numbers refer to lines.*

426. Vatican Codex: Penetravit olivi, “penetrated … of olive oil”; olivi, “of olive oil,” replaces olivae, “of the olive,” in the description of the liquid penetrating her limbs. Martin had poured blessed oil into the girl’s mouth, as Sulpicius relates, chapter 16.

431. Vatican Codex: Dentibus ut rabiens, “as, raging with his teeth—.”

446. Venetian edition: hic carnis erumnis, “this one from bodily troubles.” But the Vatican Codex reads erynnis, “Furies.”

470. Vatican Codex: sordidus egreditur, “filthy, he comes out”; this reading should be retained.

473. The report had evidently spread through Trier that the barbarians were invading with their forces.

**[Col. 0378D]** 474. Vatican Codex: “from the demonic flock.”

*Ibid.* Sulpicius relates that the demon, tortured by Saint Martin, confessed that the rumor had been fabricated and spread by sixteen evil spirits. When this became known, the city was restored to tranquility.

490. Venetian edition: “covered with a wound.”

494. Vatican Codex: “the saint to kisses.”

500. Vatican Codex and Venetian edition: rescribitur oris imago, “the image of the face is redrawn” (rescribitur rather than describitur); this should be followed.

506. Venetian edition: “gives form to the foul thing.”

**[Col. 0377A]**

Then, when he rose and looked upon the face of the girl,

immediately her voice returned, a guest in a foreign dwelling.

[425] And the organs of her restored tongue began to sing.

Gradually, as the fluid of the olive oil penetrated her limbs,

her body, brought back to life, stood upon the two pillars of her feet,

and her firmly founded limbs grew strong in their walking.

Afterward, the servant of Tetradius the proconsul, deprived of hope,

[430] became the property of another master when possessed by a demon,

and, raging with alien teeth, gnashed with hostile weapons.

His struggle was not his own but the enemy’s, as though he were the enemy’s soldier.

His master supplicates Martin and prays that he cleanse the servant,

but the savage guest and enemy forbade him to be led to the saint.

[435] **[Col. 0377B]** Tetradius again kissed the feet of the righteous man

and begged that they go where the savage robber lay concealed.

But the holy man himself refused to enter the pagan’s house.

Humble Tetradius promised, with his high official insignia,

that, if he rescued his servant from the enemy, he would believe in Christ.

[440] Therefore, when he laid his hand upon the boy, the savage ghost withdrew,

and the evil beast fled from the pleasing shepherd.

Tetradius likewise became worthy to be a catechumen

and was renewed in the stream of saving baptism.

Thus both boy and master were cleansed when their stains were removed:

[445] the former from the enemy’s snares, the latter from errors;

the former free from bodily Erinyes, the latter from the penalties of the soul.

Both remained free and shone with a double triumph:

the servant’s condition became the patron’s freedom;

**[Col. 0377C]** the latter received faith when the unbelieving demon departed from the former.

[450] Not long afterward, at about the same time, the saint happened to enter a house

and stopped right at the threshold,

claiming to see the terrible shadow of a demon.

A savage beast had seized a cook and tormented its prey,

tearing him or his companions with armed teeth.

[455] His companions turned their backs, and no one dared go to meet it;

they scarcely found safe places for flight in their swift leaps,

considering it enough either to withdraw themselves or to escape its bite.

But Martin was a martial sword, a warrior armed for battle:

he did not flee on foot, nor did he allow the fugitive to depart.

[460] He ordered the pest to stand still. The beast sharpened its molars in its throat,

and, when the holy man put his fingers into its mouth, he said:

**[Col. 0377D]** “If you can, behold, devour the prey offered to you, harmful wolf.

The food you would seek elsewhere is freely given to your teeth.”

At these words the two jaws were drawn back on either side.

[465] Lest it injure his fingers, the beast suspended its jaws,

and feared to be touched by the hands of the man whom it would have devoured with its teeth.

While it was being tormented within the possessed man by bitter punishments,

yet could not escape through the mouth because of the fingers,

it left behind foul traces of its foul service.

**[Col. 0378A]** It came out through the filth, by the path through which filth flows.

“Such a road as this, traveler, is fitting for you to take.”

Then, when the rumor of barbarians had spread throughout the city

and its savage outcome was bearing cruel seeds,

the shepherd ordered a certain member of the demon’s flock to appear before him.

[475] He commanded it to reveal whether the reports wandering about were true.

Tortured, guilty in its mouth, as though sent before a judge,

the ghost, carried along on human feet, confessed:

“This rumor was spread among the people by a sixteenfold demon,

so that Martin, driven by fear, might depart from the city.”

[480] The barbarian storm rests under a peaceful law.

There is no invasion of a people for you to fear,

nor should you dread the cause of war, lover of peace.

In Martin’s presence deceit loses its access;

**[Col. 0378B]** the liar reports the truth, and error announces what is certain.

The beast, insatiable for evil, roaring with its bloody mouth

and stirring up wars, restored the gifts of peace.

From there the holy man entered the gate of Paris in haste

and encountered face-to-face a leper coming toward him.

[485] He was unlike himself, no longer recognizable as his former self.

He went forward, a man mottled with marks, his skin bare and touched by sores,

flowing with corruption, weak in his gait, helpless in sight,

harsh in appearance, dull in mind, rotten in mouth,

lacerated in foot and rasping in voice.

Pallor had clothed him in the miserable covering of a stranger.

[490] Unexpectedly the holy man drew him to his kisses

and, clasping the man, healed him with poured-out medicine.

For as soon as his mouth touched the blessed saliva,

the burden of disease fled at the ointment-bearing touch.

The submerged form returned; a new skin clothed his face;

[495] the distinctive features returned, as to a mirror, upon his once-alien brow;

the image of his mouth, long since erased, was restored.

How exalted is the faith of the holy man,

when, through the holy man’s swift act of peace,

the battles of disease perished!

[500] In the embrace, the dreadful matter of the wicked disease,

with its plague falling away, brought forth a new battle through the kisses.

Renowned is Martin’s religion, whose honor

makes faithful bonds beautiful, and beautifies what is foul through faithfulness.

Blessed is the religion made illustrious by the saint’s foot, light, and touch,

**[Col. 0378D]** as the man purifies places, dens, and privet bushes,

cities, countryside, houses, temples, towns, walls, and estates.

[510] And you who merit such distinguished signs of so distinguished a man,

from whose sacred mouth—surpassing all other wonders—

the Jordan flowed forth in kisses for the leper’s healing,

and the water of flowing saliva washed the fountain of blemish.

# BOOK TWO

**[Col. 0379]**

**[Note: [Col. 0379C]**

*In this note, the numbers refer to lines.*

6. Vatican Codex: vela secundus, “favouring the sails.”

8. *Emptica*, a cargo ship or merchant vessel. A Greek-Latin manuscript glossary has ἀγόραστος (“purchased”), *empticus*, as Dufresne records in his *Glossary*. If metrical considerations permitted it, Browne adds, the poet might perhaps have written emporetica, “merchant vessel.” Fortunatus uses the same word shortly afterward in this verse:

**[Col. 0379D]** “To reach the harbor, the merchant ship jettisons goods.”

10. Venetian edition: erretur in ulnis, “let there be wandering in the arms” (an impersonal passive fragment).

11. Illo, “by that one.” The manuscript reads ullo, “by anyone.”

*Ibid.* Quodcunque, “whatever.” The manuscript reads quocunque, “wherever.”

17. Venetian edition: “very healthful.”

18. Venetian edition: “While the physician is unaware, he himself brings him vitality” (vivamen). Perhaps levamen, “relief.”

29. Venetian edition: “lest the vapor torment.”

31. Vatican Codex: “where he himself was not.”

33. Venetian edition: consideranda manu, “to be considered by the hand” (consideranda rather than consecranda, “to be consecrated”).

35. Vatican Codex: reddidit iste patri, “this man restored [her] to the father.”

38. This was Paulinus, a man of consular rank and later bishop of Nola, a very close friend of Saint Martin. Martin used to hold him up to his disciples as an outstanding example of piety, because he had left a great patrimony for Christ and devoted himself and all that he possessed to him.

59. This Maximus, after the emperor Gratian was killed, was proclaimed Augustus by the soldiers. He was later defeated by Theodosius and Valentinian and was beheaded at the third milestone from Aquileia in the year 388, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

60. Vatican Codex: “having obtained the empire.”

63. Venetian edition: “the circle of the clergy then went”; this reading should be retained.

69. Sulpicius lists in these words those who sat at the royal table: “The guests were present as though summoned for a festival: men of the highest rank and distinction, the prefect and consul Evodius, a man than whom no one was ever more just; two counts endowed with the highest authority; the king’s brother and his uncle.”

**[Col. 0379A]**

Long ago I loosened the hanging sails from the pine,

while the sea makes the voyage calm and the sailor recovers,

and the load, once secured, carries itself more lightly.

Now that the first part of my little book is finished,

[5] a light breeze calls me to my course; I prepare the sails for the winds.

Spirit flying high, fill my sails with favorable breath,

lest contrary blasts strike my trembling fleet.

Let my prow carry Martin, the holy merchant ship of the sailor,

the sweet summit, the faithful hope of the vessel, the light burden of the one who loves.

[10] The cargo of merchandise is sweet, whether he is held in the arms,

whatever he has touched with his hand, or has touched him:

from his fingers high salvation leaps; from nail to nail it flows.

Moreover, whatever the noble fringe ever touched,

**[Col. 0379B]** upon it the fringe scattered abundant healing from the scanty garment.

The stream of blood was dammed by the water of this spring,

and his flowing current dried up the streams.

The sick woman received help through the saving theft of a thread:

while the physician was unaware, the disease brought its crises to an end.

Arborius the magistrate, himself a man of prefectural rank,

[20] had a daughter severely tormented by a quartan fever.

Although he did many things, no treatment healed the girl.

The blessed letter of the man, sent to him, restrained the fever.

The sheet was placed beneath the girl as she lay upon it;

then, when the dry writing had wetted the waters of her sweat,

[25] the fever was drawn out, dried up, from within her limbs.

As the sky was cleared, clouds moistened without wool,

and the flame of the fever was extinguished by the dew of ink.

**[Col. 0379C]** Like another Moses of the Israelites,

the page extended a cloud so that the heat might not shake her.

[30] What a wondrous craftsman, giving health through writings!

Thus he worked while present, where he himself had knowledge.

Whom her wealthy father Arborius offers to Martin,

to be consecrated by the hand through which she herself was saved.

How well that heavenly Father himself returned the girl,

twice healthy together with her virginity, to her own father!

**[Col. 0380A]** Thus, through the one physician, he earned a double healing,

when he snatched his beloved child from both deaths.

And when Paulinus’ eye was submerged in dreadful darkness,

a sharp ray penetrated it through the laying on of hands,

[40] and serene daylight, with the cloud wiped away, shone again.

Light flashed forth, and the face, no longer one-eyed, gleamed with twin brightness,

through Martin’s fingers and the oil flowing from the lamp,

surpassing all eye medicines by its healing touch.

He himself, too, once slipped from the top of a staircase,

[45] counting the steps as he fell, his head and face scraped,

his limbs bruised as he descended in broad leaps,

a physician to many, bearing very many wounds.

While he lay heavily asleep at night in his cell,

**[Col. 0380B]** the Lord’s ever-watchful angel came, formed from the air.

[50] He treated each of the man’s wounds, touching each one in turn;

touching his limbs with his hand, he solidified his steps as he walked.

The wasting disease was shaken off in a fugitive leap,

and one skin returned across the limbs torn by the stakes.

The next day he went forth adorned with a healthy body,

[55] and the visible facts made witnesses of angelic aid.

Nor was it fitting that the pious man should endure prolonged scourges,

since he did not tolerate the scourging of anyone severely.

I must not pass over these greatest of events.

Maximus Augustus, greatest in arms after the king’s death,

[60] obtained the empire and grew proud through civil slaughter,

while he ruled the unfamiliar reins with unbridled power.

At that time the loose flattery of bishops favored him;

**[Col. 0380C]** at the prince’s nod the circle of the clergy moved about.

Yet when Martin came, the king himself begged

[65] to have the holy man at his table.

Often rejected, he at last earned the right to become the blessed man’s guest.

With the empire applauding and the city favoring him, he sat there together with him,

because the earthly court received a guest of heaven.

Nobles, the prefect, the consul, and dignitaries gathered,

[70] summoned in rivalry to honor the royal feast,

**[Note: [Col. 0381C]**

*In this note, the numbers refer to lines.*

74. Venetian edition: “the savage Geta.”

78. Venetian edition and Vatican Codex: “the Rhine, the Atax.”

81. *Sareptem.* Sidonius likewise presents Sarepta as rich in wine, writing to Ommatius, poem 17, in these verses:

“I have no Gazetic, Chian, or Falernian wines,

nor any wine you may drink sent from the Sareptan vine.”

On this passage Sirmondus says that Gazetic wine is called by Isidore according to the region from which it is brought—that is, from Gaza in Palestine—just as Sareptan wine comes from Sarepta of the Sidonians; Alexander of Tralles calls it Σερεφθῖνον οἶνον, “Sareptan wine.” Corippus in Book III and Fortunatus in Book IV (read Book II) of *The Life of Saint Martin* celebrate both. Gregory of Tours also mentions Gazetic wine in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 65, as does Cassiodorus in *Variarum* XII.12.

87. Venetian edition: “the Aragus balances”; corrupt.

109. Venetian edition: ordine presbyterali, “in the priestly order” (the printed note repeats the edition’s name).

118. Valentinian, on learning of Maximus’ arrival, had fled from Milan and withdrawn into Illyricum to seek Theodosius’ aid. Later, together with Theodosius’ forces, he defeated Maximus.

126. Vatican Codex and Venetian edition: “often advise.”

127. Quid, “what.” Perhaps qui, “who.”

129. Venetian edition: “seeking by voice, and joined in enduring love.”

138. Vatican Codex: Et quia a perfidis, “and because from the faithless—” (perfidis rather than perfidiis, “treacheries”). Venetian edition: cumque malignantis illusio, “and when the malicious one’s deception—.”

139. Venetian edition: probra beato, “insults at the blessed man,” with dative beato rather than accusative beatum; this reading should be retained.

141. Vatican Codex: ecce cruento, “behold, with the bloody—.” Venetian edition: ense cruento, “with a bloodied sword.”

142. Namely, an ox, driven on by a demon, had struck a herdsman with its horn. Paulinus expresses this in verse by making Martin speak as follows:

“Chance gave these weapons; the violent one drove in this weapon,

overcoming the obedience of the beast, but through our guilt.”

Fortunatus also expresses the same thing shortly afterward.

*Ibid.* Venetian edition: “to the blessed man’s house.”

**[Col. 0381A]**

With the emperor set aside, they marveled at the deeds of the holy man.

From everywhere the world, stirred up, resounded with service to Augustus,

bringing forth alike the riches and pleasures

possessed by the Indian, Arab, Getan, Thracian, Persian, African, and Iberian:

[75] what the south, north, west, and east produce,

what Boreas, Aquilo, Libs, Circius, Auster, and Eurus bring.

What the Gihon and Pishon, the Tigris and Euphrates pour forth,

the Rhine, Saône, Rhône, Tiber, Po, Danube, and Orontes;

what sea, land, and sky provide in fish, birds, and grain;

[80] **[Col. 0381B]** in worked vessels, gems, stones, engraved ornaments, incense, and Falernian wine;

what Gaza, Crete, Samos, Cyprus, Colophon, and Sarepta provide;

clear wines competing with shining stones,

crystal cups scarcely distinguishable from what they contain.

From there a snowy cup changes colors amid the wines;

[85] from here they drink deceptive Falernians from a painted bowl.

From there they decorate the buffet with silk embroidered in painted flowers,

worked by art, or with things such as a spider weighs out.

Silken fleeces are spread with purple threads,

smeared with scarlet on the couches, while gold glitters among the purple.

[90] All the coverings gleam with gems mingled throughout.

The attendants shine alike in equal splendor of age;

their dress is varied in every respect, but one brilliance belongs to all.

Whatever the mouth can utter could be borne beneath the emperor.

In imperial order this pageant is prepared for Martin,

[95] who was content with little and needed satisfaction in one thing.

Meanwhile the emperor reclines, together with the order and the senate.

The priest then leans his venerable arm upon the couch.

Beside the king the holy man sits upon a narrow seat.

From there the attendant first offers the cups to the king,

[100] who orders that they first be given to the holy man,

so that Augustus might receive the cup from him and drink second.

When Martin briefly drank from the offered bowl,

thirsting rather to be refreshed by the divine spring,

he set the emperor aside and gave the lowest portion of the libation

[105] **[Col. 0382A]** to the priest, knowing that he was more worthy.

The emperor, nobles, guests, and attendants marvel,

and by their own judgment recognized themselves as inferior.

Immediately the deed ran through the palace and filled it,

and one voice throughout the city sang that Martin, before the emperor’s face,

[110] had made Augustus a lesser guest—something no one could achieve

at even the table of the least judge.

The crowd and attendants did not dare say anything else.

For if Martin wished to pray for some suppliant,

he himself commanded the emperor.

Yet Martin foretold to Augustus what fate would bring:

[115] the prosperous things he would reap and what would soon oppose him.

When Valentinian fought amid the disturbances of Italy,

**[Col. 0382B]** after successful wars Maximus, the tyrant,

fell, and immediately met his heavy defeat at Aquileia.

Maximus’ fate hung in the balance according to Martin’s words and prophecy.

Often seen and conversing with angelic gatherings,

he mingled human ears with celestial throngs.

With a voice he was greeted by winged leaders,

or he himself greeted them with gestures as they slipped through the thinned air.

In gentle conversation he often discussed what moved them,

what they sought from the Father in heaven while he remained in his earthly dwelling;

and they sought him in speech and called him with enduring love,

as a kinsman and a citizen for long ages:

what was this soul, so free from faults, doing on earth,

to enter heaven as a stranger and guest from the countryside?

He also clearly perceived demonic forms and false appearances,

**[Col. 0382C]** however the deceiver transformed himself into different shapes,

through the penetrating acuteness of his inward sight.

[135] No false image deceived Martin’s eyes.

For although a changing mask covered the figure,

it was naked before the holy man, since the shadow could not hide itself.

And because no deception could prevail against him through treachery,

the fierce enemy, caught in his own device, hurled insults at the blessed man.

[140] When fraud failed, the enemy cast abuse at him.

For at one time, behold, he came with the bloody horn of an ox,

himself bloodied, and brought it into the holy man’s dwelling.

*In this note, the numbers refer to lines.*

160. Venetian edition: Explicitaque fide, “and when the truth had been explained” (explicita rather than explicata); this reading should be retained.

168. Varius, “varied” (nominative). Perhaps varium (accusative).

171. Venetian edition: “always among adversities.”

185. The Venetian edition reads: “the contagions defile.”

**[Col. 0384D]** 193. Venetian edition: Perfide despiciens, “faithlessly despising,” or “faithless one, despising.”

194. Venetian edition: Hostis inique tibi, [tibi noxie, te pereunte, “Unjust enemy, for you— [for you, harmful one, as you perish.” The printed bracket and phrase are incomplete.

206. Venetian edition: Fuitarca salutis (joined in the print), “was an ark of salvation.”

215. Reserari, “to be opened.” The manuscript reads reserantur, “they are opened.”

**[Col. 0383A]**

He rushed into the cell and explained the unjust cause:

“Where is your power, Martin? Do you see this?” he said.

[145] “For recently I killed one of your men in this slaughter,

and he lies there as prey, captured through an ox acting as agent.

The ox, armed for crime, has fulfilled the wicked deed imposed upon it.

I increase through your loss, rejoicing in your abundant grief.”

Immediately, after these words, the holy man summoned all the brothers

[150] and, speaking as a father, repeated everything the savage enemy had revealed,

anxious lest the wolf had carried someone away from the fold.

The monks searched among their companions and counted their number,

but not a single lamb was missing from the white flock.

**[Col. 0383B]** One hired rustic alone was absent:

[155] a herdsman who transported wood from the forests to be carried to the hearths.

The men sent to him hurried on their way and sought the reason.

They found him half dead, groaning in his final moments.

He revealed the manner of his death: the bull had torn his groin with its unleashed horn,

and, having disclosed this, he left life together with his voice.

Nor did what deceit had done cause the holy man to err.

From this point onward another marvelous order of events is added,

**[Col. 0383C]** while the treacherous enemy exercises a thousand arts of harming:

now falsely assuming the face of Jupiter, now that of Anubis,

[165] often wearing the appearance of Venus, most often the face of Minerva.

Assiduous in his snares, he interrupts the holy man’s serious pursuits.

In various forms, so that terror might grow, he presents himself;

and, changing his appearance, gives rise to varied fear,

so that, unable to prevail by force, he might rebel when overcome by craft.

[170] Yet Martin, undaunted, remains steadfast, scorning empty things,

the blessed man ever hurling the weapons of the cross against his enemies,

with this shield beating back hostile darts;

when its piercing edge passes through, the false contrivance falls apart.

Often also against the saint he sharpens empty disturbances,

[175] [Col. 0383D] slanderers, with a scourge falsely threatening.

But fragile uproar clatters through empty cymbals,

and, undismayed by threats set against him, he himself resists;

nor is it fitting that something firmly founded should be moved against what is emptied of substance.

Here too the deadly serpent, steeped in the gall of poisonous venom,

[180] treacherous, dreadful, savage, slippery, envious,

[Col. 0384A] bloodied about the mouth, challenges Martin with weapons:

Why should he have monks burdened with grievous guilt?

Why should a stained company inhabit the pious enclosures of the master?

Lest a guilty crowd violate the fellowship of the righteous through its wickedness,

[185] lest diseased contagions rub against the rest,

those who have wickedly polluted the water of the venerable bath,

and, sunk in sin, have forfeited their baptisms,

for whom, having fallen, there is no path of forgiveness,

since once someone is rushing into a pit it is scarcely possible to call him back,

[190] nor to restore the flower in a body laid waste;

nor does Christ’s indulgence return again to the wretched.

Then Martin spoke these words against the demon’s fury:

“Treacherous deceiver, because you do not perceive your own advantage—

[Col. 0384B] unjust enemy to yourself, since your own ruin is already destroying you—

[195] if now you should repent, if now you should wish to come to your senses,

so that you would no longer wish to cast souls headlong through your crimes,

and your weapons would no longer rage toward another’s destruction,

and you would condemn your errors, final judge that you are,

trusting in God’s mercy, I could promise

[200] that Christ would have mercy on you, so wretched,

and would quickly forgive the guilty expiations of your fault.

For this reason the Redeemer descended from heaven’s citadel to the fields:

to rescue what was lost, so that what was perishing might not itself perish;

for the immaculate one came to wipe away stains,

[205] and by his wounds to heal the sores of the world.

[Col. 0384C] The order of his burial was the pledge of our salvation:

spittle, scourges, the cloak, gall, vinegar, lance, nails,

the holy cross, death, tomb, stone, the underworld, shadow, and tyrant—

all overcome together, they held him for three days, and the author returned to the stars;

[210] his descent is my ascent on high,

nor does the avenger choose the sinner’s death more readily,

when by his own sufferings he gave us the weapons of salvation.

Thus the pious man attempts to tame the unconquered plague,

and promised the wolf that good pasture would be restored to him.

[215] How much more, then, should Christ’s rewards be opened to a human being,

[Col. 0384D] for whose sake God himself becomes human, lies down, and rises again?

O lofty mercy and profound faith, sweet presumption,

which promises help to the deceiver and the one doomed to perish!

He explained his wish: if he cannot go to give help,

[220] it is enough that he has shown his willingness to do what lies beyond his power.

For the one who does not conceal his love spends himself entirely.

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

222. Clarus is reported by Sulpicius to have been of the noblest lineage, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 25; afterward, having been ordained a priest, he distinguished himself in the monastery by every virtue.

225. Not far, evidently, from Martin’s monastery—as Sulpicius relates in the same place—Clarus had established his dwelling, or cell. This was generally the practice in ancient monasteries: they grew together from cells scattered here and there. Thus one reads in the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 10, no. 58: “There were monasteries on the mountain, like tents.” The same is read concerning other Egyptian monasteries in Jerome, letter 108, which serves as the preface to the translation of the rules of Saints Pachomius, Theodore, and Orsiesis.

236. Vatican Codex: “knowing God.”

242. Venetian edition: “he raises a varied tumult for him.”

260. Venetian edition, in the Venetian edition: “to be loosed by hand.”

264. Venetian edition: “and now he foams at the horses.”

272. Vatican Codex: “let him meet [him] at the sheepfold.”

280. Venetian edition: “And he attempts the lofty things in a degenerate manner.”

283. Sulpicius, chapter 26, relates that the devil showed himself to Martin in this form while Martin was praying in his cell. By the word *agger* is perhaps meant a mound of earth or straw on which he lay praying.

286. In printed books, *radiantius* is read instead of *radiatilis*. The latter expression is familiar to Fortunatus, as Browerus observes, as are also *lymphatilis*, *furiatilis*, and so forth.

290. Venetian edition: “flashing with memorial light.”

293. Venetian edition: “The holy man dull of speech, with restrained mouth.”

300. Vatican Codex: “battles with trophies.”]

[Col. 0385A] From there Clarus, a gentle young man in character and free from vice,

embracing Martin as his father and abandoning all that was his,

in a short time shone forth in virtue and faith.

[225] When he had established his dwelling near the bishop,

and several brothers sought his fellowship,

Anatolius then joined himself to him as a monk:

at first a humble companion in the common discipline,

but, inexperienced in judgment and deceived by the crafty enemy,

[230] afterward he claimed that an angel came to him from heaven,

to disclose to him the Thunderer’s hidden mysteries,

and that his messages would soon fly on starry wings,

while the man’s answer, once released, would touch the clouds,

and that the way between him and the Lord was near.

[235] [Col. 0385B] He boasted that heaven’s boundaries were close to him,

and that, by knowing God’s secrets, he was already a prophet.

But Clarus was not moved by this false opinion, so as to believe him.

Then the furious Anatolius boldly asserted, without restraint,

that the Lord was sending him a garment from heaven.

[240] “Let him put on the clothing brought during the silent night,

so that those who now mock his words may marvel at the signs.”

Thereupon the crowd of monks raises a varied tumult,

and the brothers hold a vain, suspended expectation.

Meanwhile, as though midnight had crossed the middle hours,

[245] and the turning wheel revolved around the goal on its even axle,

[Col. 0385C] suddenly there is a crash, the place is shaken, weapons are stirred,

and the hall roars with a confused murmur,

the hoarse-voiced uproar breaking the grace of speech.

You might think battling phalanxes were flying through the heavens,

[250] and see swift troops rushing about in a whirlwind.

When the leisure of peace returned among the shaken crowds,

and the storm, having been stirred up, resumed tranquil silence,

Anatolius immediately summons one of the monks,

and more proudly displays to him at close range a white tunic—

[255] one swollen with empty pride and shaded by false honor,

white in its outer covering but fashioned by the art of the black demon.

Then he summons the others; Clarus himself comes too,

[Col. 0385D] and touches the softness of the garment’s snowy whiteness.

They claim that silken threads have been woven from a fine-spun strand,

[260] [Col. 0386A] and that the fleeces cannot be distinguished by touch.

Meanwhile the monks pass the wakeful night in hymns,

and David’s reed resounds in ordered choirs,

so that the Most High enthroned might reveal the garment that had appeared.

Already dawn’s charioteer was foaming red,

[265] and the sun was guiding its light-bearing reins around,

while the reborn day was calling labor back to the fields.

Soon Clarus goes to show the monk to Martin,

knowing that no phantoms were hidden from the bishop.

When the saint’s eyes confronted the single figure in its varied appearance,

[270] the deceiver lost his snare upon him.

Thus the mad Anatolius began to resist,

for Martin had forbidden him to come to the sheepfold,

although he was dragged forward against his will, clinging with reluctant steps.

[Col. 0386B] The white coverings of the lying little black man vanish,

[275] and the wandering garments shamefully abandon the monk naked;

nor does the counterfeit shadow remain fixed in its illusory shapes.

Terrified by Martin’s name, the specter flees.

Then the idle enemy, daring greater things with his own powers,

treacherous and so often beaten down, yet not trusting himself,

[280] weakly wielding weapons and attempting lofty things in a degenerate fashion,

so that it might become his praise that he had at least troubled the powerful,

and that his titles might increase because he had attacked the strong with arrows—

finally, while the saint lay stretched out on a mound,

the priest insinuating prayers to the Lord for the people,

[285] the misshapen rebellious form stood before his eyes,

a radiant shadow glittering beneath sulphurous light,

[Col. 0386C] dark with feigned brightness and black as an abyss;

brilliant in its trappings, a royal-clad attendant,

covered with little plates and beautiful with an empty diadem;

[290] sparkling with the numerous light of an ordered array of gems,

powerful in false dress, with a shoe smeared with gold,

displaying itself in broader pomp and swelling triumph,

at whose appearance the saint held his mouth restrained,

and both kept silence for a long time in mutual pride—

[295] he marveling at the man, while the other despised the proud one.

The guilty and rash enemy addressed him first:

“What you have long desired, Martin, through penetrating prayer,

you now possess in pious vows: I am your glory, Christ.

[Col. 0386D] You demand forgiveness, to restore your hard-won labors,

and that I should make the battles you have endured into your triumphs?”

[Note: [Col. 0387D]

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

Manuscript books, Browerus says, ended the verse thus: “cruminating with the buttock.” For *crumina* is a kind of purse in Plautus; hence the ancients amusingly extended *cruminare* to that part of the body with which we perform nature’s work. Or does *cruminare* here perhaps mean “to fill,” just as coins are heaped into a purse or moneybag? The Venetian edition accordingly has: “he filled the cell with his buttock [perhaps *pedore*].”

358. *Pacificis*. Manuscript: *pacificus*.

364. Venetian edition: “he often washed the feet from the body.”]

[Col. 0387A] “A king must give the dues owed to military service;

for I am about to descend to earth, and direct my steps here,

so that your anxious hearts may rest from their cares.”

Here the holy man, undaunted and unwilling to give an answer,

[305] looks down and remains silent; he considers the matter and does not release a word.

His mind remains solid, examining what is high and profound,

not turning on a trembling hinge, nor being whirled about by a blowing wind.

Then the slippery serpent renews his biting hiss:

“Why do you doubt believing what you see with your own eyes?

[310] I too am Christ, speaking words with you,

and I utter these hidden things openly, graciously revealing the future.

[Col. 0387B] Do not tremble before me; radiant light bears witness to me.”

The truthful Spirit kindled Martin’s discernment,

and opened the way so that hidden poisons would not remain concealed,

[315] and so that he might distinguish the treachery of the serpentine enemy.

With the power of freedom, he said in holy speech:

“The Lord did not say that he would come into the world in this manner.

He did not reveal through the apostolic writings that he would be purple-clad

or supported by such a diadem,

[320] when his mortal form was carried up to the stars,

and the winds spread their wings beneath his holy feet,

when the air served the king beneath the pressure of his foot,

and he, borne upon angelic hands, swiftly trod the ether,

[Col. 0387C] entering the tender air without breaking it by his steps,

[325] flying with suspended foot as he entered and cleft the clouds,

where the wing of the winged oarsman leaves no mark,

when an angel, standing before the Galileans who watched,

said that the Most High enthroned would return in the manner

in which they had seen him go, and would bring the assembly above his footsteps.

[330] I approve what must be approved, and reject shameful things that must be rejected:

these are not the signs of my king, but the camp of a tyrant.

But unless I see the palms pierced by nails,

and unless I see him bearing on his blessed flesh the holy marks of the cross,

[Col. 0387D] and his side, his ribs dug out and pierced by the missile,

[335] [Col. 0388A] from which bloodied streams bring forth baptisms,

and the sacred water washes his cheeks with purple flow—

what the generous Redeemer gave as the price,

the balance of the cross weighing the coins of the price,

the author redeeming the whole world through the treasury of his body,

[340] since there was one jewel sufficient for all vessels—

unless I see you covered with that garment in which the author endured these things,

I shall deny, without this proof, that Christ has come.

For it is fitting that the victor teach his triumph through signs,

and that a fixed wound may add glory to the trophy.

Then the sluggish enemy, struck by the scourge of life,

[345] [Col. 0388B] the pest-bearing aerial being, thinned out and slipping through the air,

returning to his own form, dissolved into emptiness,

fled from his eyes into the clear air like smoke,

and, light, flew about as the image of a shadowy form,

[350] expelled from sight, fouling the cell with his buttock,

recognized by the evidence and soiling himself in his own tracks,

and fled with stench accompanying him like an attendant.

Neither was Martin’s faith deceived by the shining appearance,

nor did empty splendor deceive the ray of his mind,

[355] with the light spread over it beneath which the dreadful night concealed itself.

Could the humble man not overcome the proud?

Or would one so gentle in mind not cast down the unjust one?

With peaceful weapons, taught to tame rebels,

[Col. 0388C] whose favor was sweet and whose high honor was the love he inspired,

he not only washed another’s feet but licked them,

and with his tongue wiped the footsteps of a newly arrived guest.

He himself always offered water to those who came,

desiring, as a heavenly servant, to serve a human being,

and with his kindly hand washed a sinner’s feet,

[365] for even the touched fringe of his garment offered salvation.

He taught that the world’s allurements must be fled,

that one’s gains should be given to the age to come and nothing sought on earth,

so that anyone wishing to climb Olympus might flee wealth,

and possess no heavy burden of land or money,
