[Col. 0389A] nor retain possessions, being destined to meet heaven as an heir.

For a burden prevents ascent and makes descent easier;

weights pass downward, turned toward the bottom, and do not rise to the heights.

As a pillar climbs a mountain, it staggers beneath its load,

and its fragile foot gives way under the mighty weight.

[375] The heaped burden sinks the prow into the rolling waves,

and, seeking the harbor, casts its goods overboard like merchandise.

That illustrious father, who celebrated the deeds of Paulinus,

when Paulinus flourished in Italy as bishop of Nola,

where the Campanian region sits under its supreme ruler—

[380] rich in fields, prosperous in servants, wealthy in heaps,

[Col. 0389B] a man vast in resources, lofty in household and rounded in speech—

became richer in faith and made himself poor for Christ,

and gave countless coins that redeemed sins;

his wealth, scattered upon the ground, migrated to the stars.

[385] He caused sluggish earthly things to ascend to heaven,

standing in one place, and made brute things leap toward the stars.

Thus, with Paulinus fulfilling the evangelical teaching,

Martin admonishes everyone that such a path must be followed:

the rich man was able to travel along the difficult road,

[390] and, laying down his burden, the free man ascended to the citadel.

By his example he urges his followers to climb higher.

Now also let us tell what parable flowed from Martin’s mouth,

[Col. 0389C] what gravity he possessed, how keenly eloquent he was concerning the law.

No question escaped the man learned in heavenly law,

who was able to unlock whatever riddle one might deny;

a sweet prudence of intelligence overflowed abundantly,

drinking perpetually from the spring that little stream watered;

his speech was pious, ready, calm, skillful, suitable, and lovable.

The possessor of heaven among earthly minds,

[400] an ever-watchful advocate, entrusting affairs to Christ,

he laid before the Judge the complaints of the poor,

learned in sacred skill to plead the causes of the wretched,

[Col. 0389D] a powerful defender, overcoming courts, laws, and men in the toga,

a noble builder, an eloquent preacher,

[405] who by abundant prayer appeased the Lord’s guarantees,

as far as he was powerful in speech for widows and orphan-homes—

whose very silent silences strike the heavens?

[Col. 0390A] His mind was founded upon God, near to heaven without pretense,

spending no time in idleness and no time in bodily affairs.

[410] Whatever had to be done, he completed everything swiftly,

but Christ was his delay: he served him night and day.

For food and sleep, except insofar as nature requires them—

slow-eating, swift-waking, sleep and nourishment at the proper moment—

he would not undertake, except that without these the flesh cannot live.

[415] He devoted both periods of time to these two pursuits:

now reading resounded, now prayer flowed for him.

[Col. 0390B] His only rest was to change his labors.

If he went outside, he remained inwardly a man praying,

directing the eyes of his heart toward heaven, not toward the flesh.

[420] No hidden deceit escaped him, nor did anything false flow from his mouth.

A man free from worldly things, a pure possession of the Lord,

he condemned no one in judgment and repaid no evil with evil.

Perhaps this was his way: if an injury had been done to a brother,

when injured even by the lowliest person, revenge was never sweet to him.

[425] Nor did he drive away an attendant from his own rank.

Dear even to adversaries, pious toward the just, gentle toward the wicked,

anger, swelling pride, laughter, and grief stood banished from him.

He did not hold a cloud upon his brow or laughter in his mouth.

He was always the same in face, skin, heart, and complexion.

[430] His conduct did not vary; the man remained constant while still in the body,

bringing something immortal forth from a mortal image.

God held his face, devotion his mind, peace his heart.

Doing little for himself, he acted compassionately toward others,

setting aside the order of nature so that he might be angelic,

[435] rising above the heights, extending his mind beyond the clouds,

free from human cares, entering the stars,

bearing illustrious signs and prophesying many future things.

He still stood upon earth, an intimate heir of heavenly things,

knowing God’s secrets, like a confidant of a friend,

[440] when his flesh shared certain things with his dependent.

A man for whom Christ was love, Christ was honor, Christ was everything—

[Col. 0390D] flower, fragrance, food, flavor, fountain, light, glory, and Christ.

Planted, strengthened, and grown in affection for him,

and like a tree of the field beside the courses of waters,

[445] with flower-tressed leaves, rejoicing in an unceasing flow,

[Note: [Col. 0391B]

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

455. Vatican Codex: “from here the belt shines, from there.”

462. The same manuscript: “with whom the stream reddens for the martyrs.”

467. *Triumphi*. Manuscript: *triumphis*.

[Col. 0392B] 475. Venetian edition: “with a stammering throat and panting.”

476. Ibid.: “what I am certain of composing.”]

[Col. 0391A] it bears the everlasting fruits of eternal life,

among apostolic ranks and sacred prophets,

and choirs of martyrs and shining armies of heaven,

under the unconquered king, where that army flashes—

[450] through troops, nobles, legions, and cohorts,

growing in rank as soldier, companion, commander, and consul—

one shines in a milky robe, another gleams in a red-gold crown,

this one is adorned by a shining bordered robe, that one by a diadem.

Cloaks adorn some, while a topaz-studded armlet decorates others.

[455] A belt shines on one, a headband flashes in another’s hair.

One gleams in the honor of the palm-embroidered robe, another in the splendor of the military cloak.

Gem, gold, purple, and fine linen paint their adornment;

the senate above the stars possesses things no eye can see.

[Col. 0391B] You will enjoy these blessings, Martin, under heaven’s ruler,

[460] joined with angelic gatherings and equal to the patriarchs,

made comparable to the apostles and worthy, in merit, of the prophets,

added to the martyrs, for whom the stream reddens with blood.

Radiant confessor, surpassing the shining lilies,

crowned with purple light, resplendent in beauty,

[465] walking freely through the lofty palaces of the king.

A man translated into eternity, a powerful citizen for everlasting ages,

you carry the standard of the cross in the nobility of triumph.

Sweet, venerable, and to me to be honored in heart and voice,

your deeds Severus first sang in prose,

[470] [Col. 0392A] then blessed Paulinus thundered them forth in verse.

Each illustrious narrator was able to match the other,

but, defeated by their subject, even they yield in their poetry.

I, clouded, boldly insert myself among such great lights—

the least of the small, attempting the greatest of the great—

[475] stumbling in my step, stammering and gasping at the throat,

and, crude in speech, touching upon what I strive to compose.

Forgive me, because a guilty tongue has sung of you in narration.

Bring help through your mercy to a wretched man, compassionate as I am.

When the Most High Ruler comes as judge of the world,

[480] then, remembering me, obtain forgetfulness of my offense.

Kindly stand as mediator between me and the Lord,

that your intervention may release me, whom my own guilt binds.

May Fortunatus’ hope of salvation be secure, though he is needy,

[Col. 0392B] having humbly prostrated himself before you in supplication, patron,

[485] you who cleanse the stains of leprosy through healing kisses,

and recall the end of death at its very source.

Once constant beneath the appearance of fragile flesh,

I now ask that your gentleness lend favorable ears to my work.

For you can prevail with him through prayer, since you are held by him;

[490] what I ask, you can obtain, because he grants everything to his friends.

May the presence of the king grant you whatever you ask in this way.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0391]

[Note: [Col. 0391D]

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

4. Venetian edition: “and the shadow holds the night, with the green shore.”

12. In the two preceding books Fortunatus embraced in verse the matters that Sulpicius had related in the book *On the Life of Saint Martin*; in the two following books he expresses in verse what the same Sulpicius had explained in his *Dialogues* concerning the virtues of that same Saint Martin.

15. Venetian edition: “the ship proceeds on its journey, where now the shallows.”

17. This Gallus seems certainly to be none other than the man whom Sulpicius calls a disciple of Saint Martin and introduces in his *Dialogues* as recounting and praising Saint Martin’s virtues. I therefore do not know what came into the mind of the distinguished Joseph Liruti, who in his *Life of Fortunatus* asserts that the Gallus mentioned here was Paulinus of Pétrocorium, whom Fortunatus called Gallus so that he might be understood as distinct from Paulinus of Nola.

18. Venetian edition: “where the water reached the swelling.”]

[Col. 0391C] Until now the anchor stood fixed in the thirsty lands,

drawing out slow leisure and resting on its idle tooth,

gently playing about while the breeze hissed sleep,

and the shadow covered us, while the riverbank’s edge grew green.

[5] Behold, the serene day brings forth reddened dawn,

and the sailor seeks the open sea by ship; now I loosen the ropes.

Leaving the reedy shore, I raise the sails to the winds.

I seemed to be setting my sails before the Adriatic foam,

when, seized by a watery whirlwind amid the roar of crashing,

[10] under the leadership of Sulpicius, whose beautiful mouth

brought forth Martin’s holy deeds in a sweet style,

I run beneath a double set of books, with halting foot,

the least of men weaving together the deeds of an outstanding patron.

[Col. 0391D] Again I seem to be stretching toward the waves of Ocean,

[15] undertaking a greater journey, where the blue shallows break against one another,

and fear grows through the terror of ship, cloud, and deep.

Yet while I seek the heights, let Gallus resound in my ear,

with the blessed deeds of the man by which he calms the swelling waters,

and let a sweet tale lighten the journey with its eloquence.

[20] Behold, I am carried over the strait, and the shores flee from sight.

Let Gallus row here, let Martin steer the sails,

let Christ drive the winds by which the waves lead us back to port.

Now too, while I sail as a sailor, let the deeds of the holy man be told.

During the winter months, while the Bosphorus binds its waters

[25] [Col. 0392D] and rain prevents the liquid fields from being plowed by keels,

[Note: [Col. 0393C]

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

29. *Vestem*. Manuscript: *veste*.

33. Evidently this was the beggar whom Martin had ordered the archdeacon to clothe. He had entered the sacristy—or *parapetasma* (παραπέτασμα), the curtain or screen—where Martin, concealed from the people, had sat until he was summoned to perform the sacred rite; the beggar complained that he had received nothing from the archdeacon.

34. Vatican Codex: “covered the friend.”

36. That is, as Sulpicius has it: “The archdeacon entered and reminded him, according to custom, that the people were waiting in the church and that he ought to proceed to perform the solemn rites.” *Dialogue* II, chapter 1.

38. Vatican Codex: “when this had been told.”

Ibid. *Archidiaconus*. Vatican Codex: *arse diacon*.

39. Martin evidently ordered that the naked man should be covered and indicated that he himself was to be clothed, since, after removing his tunic in order to clothe the poor man, he had been left naked. But because no nakedness was visible in Martin—for he was seated—the archdeacon did not understand what he was saying.

41. *He did not see*. Vatican Codex: “he did not look at.”

42. *Amphibali*. Manuscript: *Amphibole*. An *amphibalus*—a word also used by Sulpicius, *Dialogue* II, chapter 1—was a garment woolly on both sides. Gregory of Tours also uses the word in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 59, relating of Saint Trajan: “If he had put on the new *amphibalus*, as was customary, in which he would go around the diocese to conduct his business, people of different kinds would tear away the fringe of this garment.” To this passage the distinguished Ruinart adds: “An *amphibalus*, or *birrus*, was a woolly garment with a hood sewn onto it.”

43. Venetian edition: “and troubles the uncertain man.”

44. Vatican Codex: “he gives it to the needy.”

45. Venetian edition: “Bring a covering, friend.” An *obolla* was a type of senatorial tunic, so called, as though from *bulla*, because it was covered on all sides with bosses. Prudentius, book I against Symmachus, writes:

[Col. 0394C] “Moreover, the heir of the Olybrian family and name,

added to the official lists, distinguished by the palm-adorned *obolla*,” etc.

Others prefer to understand it as a double garment. There was also an *obolla* that was a military garment and one worn by philosophers.

46. Vatican Codex: “nor is the poor man lacking.”

47. *Succensus*. Manuscript: *succensens*.

Ibid. *Tegmen*. Vatican Codex: *Tegimen fert*.

Ibid. “The humble servant brings a covering.” Sulpicius relates that the archdeacon, angry with Martin, rushed to the nearby shops and seized from there a short, rough, striped garment priced at five silver pieces, and brought it to Martin. A *bigerrica*, or *bigera*, as it appears in Isidore’s Glossary, was a rough or woolly garment. It was so called—as Dufresne adds—from the Bigerri, or Bigerrones, famous peoples of Gaul near the Pyrenees, whom Caesar and Pliny mention. Even today it is customary among them to wear short, woolly, rough cloaks made of coarse wool against bad weather, as Dufresne says. Browerus gives much the same account and also cites Paulinus in letter 4 to Ausonius, who writes:

“Deserving to inhabit the deserts of the fur-clad Bigerri.”

Paulinus of Pétrocorium, in book III of *The Life of Saint Martin*, renders this passage as follows:

“Then, irritated, he throws before the holy man’s feet

a garment bought for scarcely an eighth of a solidus,

woven from knotty threads of shaggy wool.”

51. Venetian edition: “thus the highest one proceeded.”

56. Venetian edition: “Licking his neck and hair, and . . .” Sulpicius relates that when Martin proceeded from there to the altar during the sacred rite, a globe of fire was seen to flash from his head, so that as it rose upward the flame extended his neck and hair farther.

67. Venetian edition: “Thinking that you would not refuse a small request.”

74. Vatican Codex: “he was lying on the ground.”

Ibid. *Evantius*. Sulpicius says that this Evantius was his maternal uncle, *Dialogue* II, chapter 3.]

[Col. 0393A] and Ocean refuses to carry traffic to the Britons,

when the seeds conceal their shoots beneath the hard frost,

and penetrating ice stiffens the water while the grass melts,

a sick, needy beggar stood before the doors, asking for clothing,

[30] his tongue bound by frost so that he could not release words from his mouth.

Therefore he orders the sacred servant to cover the destitute man.

He himself seeks privacy and avoids the commotion of the crowd.

When the holy man discovered that the trembling beggar had received nothing,

he removed his tunic and covered the freezing man with his cloak;

[35] he gave it secretly, with no witness, and compelled him to leave.

Behold, the servant arrives, asking the holy man to proceed.

But the holy man first tells him to clothe the naked man with a covering.

When the pious man said this, the archdeacon stood dull and stupefied:

what was he to do, when he saw no naked man there?

[40] [Col. 0393B] Nor, while the bishop sat, could he recognize a naked man,

since he could not see beneath the inner covering of the tunic,

while the limbs were hidden on the outside by the *amphibalus*.

He is troubled by the blessed man’s riddle, caught between alternatives;

such a great question binds him, and he cannot solve the beggar’s problem.

[45] Then the holy man said, “Bring me the covering of an *obolla*,

and let no poor man be lacking who needs those garments.”

Deeply angered, the servant brings the humble covering,

throwing it before his feet and saying: “Here is a garment without a poor man.”

The holy man puts on a shaggy *bigerrica* cloak,

[50] scarcely worthy of a wool-white and golden-yellow stole.

Then the highest honor proceeded, poor in clothing,

despised in his tunic, but a senator in the heavenly court.

Meanwhile, as he resumed the sacred ceremony before the people,

[Col. 0394A] and blessed the holocausts with his hands at the sacred altar,

[55] suddenly a globe of friendly fire flashed from his head,

licking his neck and hair, and the kindly flame flew,

soft to the touch, powerful in honor, sparkling in brilliance,

adorning his hair and revealing his merit, shining in place of a covering.

It rendered service in the place of the servant who had contributed too little,

[60] bringing hidden deeds into the light by its brightness.

O rich poor man, content with not even one tunic,

you who have no other and do not wish to retain even that one,

thinking that you have enough clothing for simple use,

for whom even a light cloak is burdensome while a beggar cries out—

[65] [Col. 0394B] desiring to proceed naked in place of the naked man’s covering;

you do not share your help but surrender everything to the needy.

Thinking that this was your only garment, if you had refused nothing when asked,

you would have become poorer by giving everything to the poor,

and you were not ashamed, reverent father, to sit without clothing.

[70] But the faithful devotion you gave felt no shame,

and, retaining nothing at all, became greater in honor.

I would like to speak of the beautiful deeds of the naked man,

but the splendors of the remaining events carry away my eager mind.

While Evantius, sick and wasting away, lay in bed,

[75] exhausted and at the point of death, when his breath was already departing,

he swiftly summoned the bishop with prayers, asking him to hurry,

so that the life of the sacred man restored might become his once begun journey.

[Note: [Col. 0395D]

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

78. Vatican Codex: “nor delaying the journey.”

80. Venetian edition: “he sent help while life remained.”

85. Venetian edition: “through the air they smoke.”

94. Vatican Codex: “safe, to the house.”

96. Venetian edition: “but then there was an opportunity for delay.”

98. *Percussi*. Manuscript: *percussor*.

121. Sulpicius, *Dialogue* II, chapter 3, narrates this event more clearly. When Martin was visiting the dioceses, he happened to encounter a government carriage in which soldiers were riding. The animals, terrified—as was believed—by Martin’s rough, black, hanging cloak, turned with all their force in the opposite direction and became entangled in the ropes, so that they remained stuck and caused the soldiers delay. Thereupon the soldiers jumped from the carriage and began to mistreat and beat Martin as the cause of their confusion and delay.

127. Vatican Codex: “vengeance is given to the beast.”

131. Vatican Codex: “the ignoble man who strikes.”

132. Vatican Codex: “the other counts”; against the meter.

136. “The public mound.” Sulpicius likewise relates that this journey took place along a public mound. Giselinus, in his notes on Severus Sulpicius, suspects that the mound mentioned is the one called the Long Bridge by Tacitus.

138. *Quadrigae*. Manuscript: *quadripae*.

145. Vatican Codex: “confused and weeping.”

148. Martin, having passed by, had told his men that the soldiers who had beaten him were being held back and were unable to proceed.

153. *Carnotus*. Vatican Codex: *Carnutis*. Venetian edition: “here too, while he came by passing.” Sulpicius says that the event related here by Fortunatus occurred when Martin was making for the town of Chartres and had stopped in a very crowded village.]

[Col. 0395A] Nor does Martin, the traveler, delay to undertake the journey.

Scarcely had he traversed half the distance with his advancing old age

[80] when he sent the aid of healing before he appeared,

and the remedy given to the sick man announced that the blessed man was coming.

The messenger also indicated that the cure was following:

while the hero was slow in foot, the healing had gone ahead in flight,

and the arrival of the holy man carried a healthy fragrance on the air.

[85] Thus ointments cross the air so that they may quickly bring help.

Just as the sun gives warmth farther away from its face through its rays,

so Martin provides aid even where he is not present, through his power.

The event is exceedingly wonderful: once the disease had been driven away,

before the physician could feel the pulse, the sick man leaped up.

[90] He went to meet the holy man and returned the service,

and himself led home the man who had restored him to the light,

[Col. 0395B] now lively in a leap, though a little earlier he had lain on a pallet.

Meanwhile Evantius, no stranger to wondrous deeds,

begs, now safe, that the Lord’s delay may postpone the next day,

[95] and holds the face of so great a guest for one little day.

But this delay was granted as an occasion for salvation.

Immediately a boy was struck by the dark tooth of a chelydrus,

and the fury of the poison stretched his stricken limbs.

When unwelcome death denied him any span of life,

[100] and mournful venom ruled throughout his body,

Evantius laid the boy before the feet of the kindly man,

trusting completely that Martin could earn this favor.

For the holy man soon passes over every limb by touch,

and with his healing hand feels the dying organs.

[105] [Col. 0395C] Then, when he placed his finger over the wound where the beast had fixed its bite,

a stream of venom flowed out everywhere,

and retraced the path by which the viper had given its poison.

Thereupon the holy man, observing the swelling gathered with corruption,

withdrawing his thumb, while the serpent’s poison poured into the wound,

[110] All the force of the venom escapes through the opening of the wound,

dripping with clotted blood like milk from a goat’s udder.

The swollen wound vomited death, spinning it out from the injury;

the vein, bursting forth, loosened the congealed pus.

It expelled the sluggish poison, the liquid flowing back through the channel,

[115] and the channel, once opened, drew the deadly stream back again.

When faith conquered, the serpent’s bite lost its force;

and because they did not kill, the weapons of the poison perished.

The boy stands unharmed, and no pallor remains on his face.

The master marvels at the servant, and the whole household is amazed.”

[120] [Col. 0396A] Whom he believed to be hastening in service toward the tomb.

Then the pious bishop, seeking each place according to his custom, met a shaggy man in the fiscal uniform. When the beasts saw the bishop’s sacred hanging garments, they fiercely pulled the wagon away from the road.

[125] The driver abandoned the wheels, and the soldier the reins; they assailed Martin with unjust whips and clubs. But a grim retribution was exacted by the beast for the assault upon the man. He himself, however, endured patiently, struck by a hailstorm of blows, while the Fury of the floggers raged.

[130] He returned no wounds with his hands, nor murmurs from his mouth.

[Col. 0396B] Then the base man’s anger, in striking him, inflicted an even harsher torture: because Martin endured it, the other thought that he was being mocked; and the more freely Martin endured, the more furiously the man raged.

Meanwhile they returned to the wagon amid the onslaught of their complaint.

[135] While the vindictive, frenzied anger satisfied its hunger, they urged the mules forward along the public road, pressing them with shouts, goading them with a stick, and tearing them with the whip. Yet the beasts, though driven, neither seized the yokes nor pulled the reins of the wagon team. They remained fixed and did not move, like bronze statues, as though the earth, liquefied by some new glue, had bound them—so that you would believe the animals were fastened to the rotting dust.

The men recognized that they were being held by the power of the god.

[Col. 0396C] They hurried forward and asked the name of the traveler. They found that Martin had been cruelly treated by them.

[145] Weeping in confusion, bowed down in reddening shame, they fell before the holy man’s feet and begged him to grant pardon for their error and allow the animals, which were bound, to proceed.

Yet the saint had already foretold that they would be detained. He proves the matter, welcomes the wound, grants pardon, and pleads that they may depart.

[150] Those whom his power had bound, softened compassion released. The road hung upon his lips: his words restrained it, his words relaxed it. And the driver recovered the yokes, reins, wheels, and mules.

Meanwhile, as he was passing through the territory of Carnutes, a pagan crowd streamed everywhere across the fields, coming toward him.

[155] [Note: [Col. 0397D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

156. Venetian edition: *undique visu* (“visible everywhere”).

163. Venetian edition: *saepius, atque iterans* (“more often, and repeating”).

166. Venetian edition: *semina surgunt* (“the seeds rise”).

173. Venetian edition and Vatican Codex: *cantica planctu* (“songs of mourning”), which should be followed.

190. Venetian edition: *pro plebe precatus* (“having prayed for the people”).

194. Venetian edition and Vatican Codex: *ordine disposito* (“the order having been arranged”).

211. *Sacrum ad comitatum* (“to the sacred imperial court”). In the Venetian edition: perhaps *ad se sacrum comitatum* (“the sacred court to himself”). That *comitatum* was customarily used for the emperor’s own court is testified by Ammianus, Book XXVIII, where he says, “Maximinus was summoned to the emperor’s court,” and by Sulpicius, *Dialogue* II, chapter 6, discussing this very event concerning Martin: “At almost the same time,” he says, “as he was made bishop, there also arose the necessity of going to the imperial court.” The *comites* were evidently called the intimate counselors of the emperor. But read Dufresne under this word in the *Glossary*.

215. *Uxor* (“wife”). This was the Arian wife of the elder Valentinian. She was Justina, the patron and supporter of the Arian party. Of her, as Socrates writes in Book V, chapter 11, and Sozomen in Book VII, chapter 13, she was *τὰ Ἀρειανῶν φρονοῦσα*—“of Arian beliefs.” Ecclesiastical writers say more about her.

218. “Namely,” as Sulpicius writes of him: “He wraps himself in sackcloth, sprinkles himself with ashes, abstains from food and drink, and continues in prayer day and night.”

223. Vatican Codex: *Quo angelus adsistens* (“where an angel stood by”).]

[Col. 0397A] Awakened by love of the sacred, though it did not itself believe this, the pagan crowd came running from every side to gaze upon the new spectacle; for as yet the mark of Christ’s honor did not shine upon these people, nor did the sacred word of the Word-bearing Thunderer flow over them.

But Martin, rejoicing while the Lord opened the depths, perceived that the place was at hand where a fertile field would arise.

He began by his speech to plow the savage breasts, the holy man clearing the weedy fallow with his shining mouth, breaking the soil, turning it again, and harrowing it twice, thrice, and four times. Gradually he had encouraged the astonished fields toward fruitfulness.

[165] Then he scattered the new seeds of Christ among the untutored peoples; tender shoots arose in human minds,

[Col. 0397B] and the grasses gently grew together in the rigid furrows.

What could the holy man do, when great crowds gathered? How could one laborer enter such an abundant harvest?

[170] He cultivated, enclosed, sowed, grafted, bound, and surrounded it.

Meanwhile a woman, hanging over her dead child, stretched out her arms and held the corpse before his face. In lamentation for the funeral she uttered savage songs of mourning; while grief drew tears from her, she scarcely managed to explain herself:

[175] “Strong friend of God, revered throughout the whole world, whom lamentation always moves through kindred compassion: let this cold body tell you what I ardently desire.

Look: my son has died, wretched that I am, torn from the breast—

[Col. 0397C] in him I was a mother; neither hope nor an heir remains. My child has fallen, my household has fallen, and my fruit has perished.

No comfort remains from my hard womb, nor is there anything left that I may sweetly call upon, on which I may rest when weary, or at which I may refresh myself with the breast. The whole order of parenthood is gone.

You who remain, I beg you, bring help by the medicine of your word. Restore my offspring, so that the name of mother may not be empty for me—unless my child returns and carries away my funeral with him.”

The people supported her, shouting: “Holy one, grant her prayers!” A single voice thundered throughout: “Have mercy on the suppliant!”

Then the pious bishop, stretched out upon his knees in the fields,

[190] [Col. 0397D] lay prostrate before the eyes of the Lord, laboring on behalf of the people, so that he might be found worthy of the sheep through whom the numerous flock would come into being.

[Col. 0398A] The Almighty assented, granting his servant the summit of honor. At once the good advocate sent prayers from his mouth into the divine ears.

After laying aside his posture, when his prayer was complete,

[195] the old man rose, and at the same moment the infant was restored to life. Before the people as witnesses, the child was returned to its mother’s breast.

A great cry arose, and the people rolled new vows through their hearts, marveling that a human being had joyfully changed his condition, and that one who had remained in death had taken away death’s rights from it.

[200] Then in crowds they confessed Christ, the Lord and God, and begged that they might be blessed under his law. Suddenly the entire population of the fields became catechumens.

[Col. 0398B] They did not wait for temples or the dedicated enclosures of a chapel; the open field more nobly fulfilled the form of a church,

[205] and what is usually provided by roofs was provided in the open meadows.

Thus one child’s death gave birth to a troop of life; while one person returned to the earth, the people received the stars. Under Martin as leader, this is a blessed army.

While the emperor Valentinian ruled proudly, with the world serving Roman power,

[210] a pious cause compelled Martin to go to the sacred imperial court. Since the emperor anticipated that Martin was coming to ask such things as he would be unwilling to grant him, he ordered him to be driven back from the fortress and forbade the righteous man to enter the palace through the doors.

[215] His wife, whose adviser at that time was Arrius, pressed this matter.

[Col. 0398C] But when the holy man saw that he was being repelled by such deception, excluded from the court, he returned and took up domestic weapons. He covered himself with haircloth, sprinkled himself with ashes, adopted the discipline of a soldier, and removed food and drink,

[220] devoting himself night and day to the continual practice of prayer.

The seventh day had therefore arrived, on which the saint, moved by love, stirred the strong camp and toiled in these weapons.

An angel standing beside him ordered the righteous man to go to the palace. Trusting in this aid, Martin proceeded to the fortress.

[225] No one barred the threshold; he entered directly to the emperor’s presence. When the emperor saw that the holy man had arrived, he growled in anger, and although the pious man stood before him, he did not rise from his lofty throne.

[Col. 0398D] Soon a blaze of fire encircled the royal seat. A wandering flame floated wherever the soft seat gleamed,

[230] poured out on every side, raging as the avenger of the emperor’s guilt.

245. Venetian edition: *tanta, majus* (“so great, greater”).

[Col. 0399D] 249. Vatican Codex: *palatia ducit* (“he leads him through the palaces”). Maximus’s piety is praised by Sulpicius, *Dialogue* II, chapter 3, excepting the civil dissensions in which he had involved himself.

251. Vatican Codex: *Quid sit honor justi* (“what is the honor of the righteous man”).

259. Venetian edition: *stetit illa immobilis, atque* (“she stood there motionless, and”).

262. Venetian edition: *regina sategit* (“the queen took pains”).

263. Evidently the wife of Maximus carefully preserved as precious the remnants of food that had been left over from Martin’s dinner.

265. Martin allowed himself to be received at the queen’s banquet for a good reason. Otherwise, both because of the holiness of his life and because of his age—for Sulpicius records that he was then seventy years old—he was far removed from every suspicion of wrongdoing. By this indulgence, the wretched people for whose salvation he had approached the emperor could more easily obtain pardon.

270. *Claudiomagum*. Sulpicius calls this village *Claudiomachum*, chapter 8.

272. In *Dialogue* II, chapter 1, Sulpicius plainly states that two *secretaria* were customarily built in churches, placed on either side of the apse. Paulinus shows us their use in Letter 32, where, writing to Severus, he sends verses inscribed in different places in the basilica of Saint Felix that he had built. “In the two *secretaria*,” he adds, “which I mentioned above as being near the apse, these verses indicate the duties of each”:

On the right side of the apse:

> This is the place of the revered storehouse, where the solemn procession  
> of the sacred ministry is stored and from which it is brought forth.

On the left side of the same apse:

> If anyone has the holy desire to meditate upon the law,  
> here, seated, he may attend to the sacred books.

273. Venetian edition: *Virgineique chori* (“and choirs of virgins”). Sulpicius relates, chapter 8, that there was “a church renowned for the holiness of its saints, and no less glorious for its multitude of sacred virgins.”

280. Vatican Codex: *quemdam ut rabies* (“someone, as madness”).

281. *Iret* (“might go”). Perhaps *ibat* (“was going”).

295. Venetian edition: *lupus egens* (“the hungry wolf”); an error.]

[Col. 0399A] The heat released the stiffness of his hard neck.

From one side the scourges boiled; from the other, flames battered the king. The imperial power was beaten by robbery and fire. Then the emperor quickly leaped away, tearing himself free and burning,

[235] and embraced Martin’s knees, rolling at his feet.

Thus punishment forced the proud man to recognize himself, proving the worthlessness of earthly kingdoms and bending lofty heights, bringing the imperial head beneath the saint’s feet.

Nor did the reverence due to the righteous man allow him to wait for prayers: before the suppliant had asked for what was to be given, the emperor, still swelling with pride, had already granted it.

[240] He regularly prepared royal banquets for the blessed man. Then, favoring his departure, the emperor offered him gifts:

[Col. 0399B] powerful through poverty, the saint rejected everything. By despising the gifts, he earned more from the emperor himself,

[245] possessing so much the more as the miser covets the less.

All things belong to the one who seeks to possess nothing.

When Maximus also ruled the Roman fortress, a man who had seized the summit through public triumphs,

[250] he often led the holy man through the lofty palaces. Throughout the entire conversation he spoke of the future light:

“What honor, praise, glory, victory, and crown belong to the righteous?”

Nor did the weeping queen cease to wet Martin’s feet with her tears,

[Col. 0399C] prostrating herself upon the ground and suspending her joys upon a vow.

Then she joyfully begged that she herself might prepare the banquet. Goodness obtains what lofty power cannot:

[255] she herself placed the seat with her own hands and prepared the table. Bringing water in her hands, the queen again served with joy; with her own hands she cooked the food.

When the holy man sat down, she stood there motionless,

[260] removing the dishes and presenting the cups herself. One servant was sufficient for the man in every task.

The little dinner ended, but the queen still took pains, gathering and storing the crumbs, leftovers, crusts, and fragments,

[Col. 0400A] valuing all these above imperial foods.

[265] Martin did this so that he might free those shut up in prison, bring back those driven into exile, and restore them to their ancestral homes.

But for you, holy father, what the empress accomplishes is a small thing; by carrying out this service, she grew greater.

There is a place at the edge of the territory of Tours and bordering that of Bourges,

[270] which the inhabitants call the village of Claudiomagus.

Perhaps it was a lodging for Martin as he passed by, where the church of the Lord possesses its *secretaria*.

When he departed, choirs of virgins sought the holy man’s place, asking where he had stood, sat, or bent his knees,

[275] [Col. 0400B] and all together licked those places or brought each one to their lips for kisses.

They divided among themselves the revered straw from his bed and weighed the light stalks against the burden of his virtue. No straw that the saint had touched went away useless.

At last, after the fragile stalk had crushed the strong one,

[280] for a savage frenzy had violently seized a certain man, and the savage spirit of error went about its work, whirling its prey around on the wheel of madness, this stalk hanging from the man’s neck drove the enemy away. A monstrous enemy was removed by a straw’s ear.

[285] The reed, fruitful with grain, shot at the phantom; the slender straw fixed it as though it were a hard spear.

Nor would the sharpness of any iron have terrified it so much, nor the arrows sent from a bow,

[Col. 0400C] slippery weapons coming through the air on feathered flight,

[290] whether a Parthian reed had pierced the frightened creature, or the wound had torn it more severely from a nearby blow.

Thus the adamantine enemy, trembling, feared the straw; and as though it were being burned by the flames of a straw-filled furnace, the man stood unharmed while the shadow fled swiftly.

[295] The enormous wolf and the growling lion abandoned their prey.

Then, as the blessed man returned from the city of Trier, a wild heifer happened to appear in the middle of the field.

A demon, sitting upon its back, drove it as it gasped, hanging there like a charioteer and shaking an aerial whip.

[300] The pestilential creature, by a new trick, drove the ox at a terrifying pace: a gloomy muleteer, urging the horned beast onward,

[Note: [Col. 0401D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

302. Venetian edition: *Exagitator iners* (“an idle driver”); this should be retained.

304. Venetian edition and Vatican Codex: *ibat ubique fero* (“it went everywhere in a savage manner”).

310. Venetian edition: *caede cruente* (“with bloody slaughter”); likewise the Vatican Codex.

317. Venetian edition: *Dedit meritis, quae* (“she gave what was due to his merits”).

319. Venetian edition: *Soluta reclivis* (“released, reclining”).

325. Sulpicius describes this fire, in which Martin did not burn, more fully in his letter to the presbyter Eusebius; I summarize it briefly. When Martin had gone, in winter, to visit a certain diocese, and the clergy had made his bed in the church’s *secretarium*, piling up a great quantity of straw and also placing a fire on the floor to temper the nighttime cold, Martin, sensing that he had bent down more softly than usual, began to throw out and scatter the straw beneath him. When it fell into the nearby fire, flames were kindled from it, and Martin would undoubtedly have been consumed had he not fled to prayer. At first he ran to the door to escape the fire, but after struggling for a long time with the latch, he felt the heat of the flames for so long that even his clothing was damaged. Then, coming to himself, he began to beseech God. At that point he sat down in the midst of the flames without being harmed by them even slightly.

In the same place: *Ignis* (“fire”). Manuscript: *ignem* (“the fire”).

327. Vatican Codex: *vicos circuit almus* (“the gracious man goes around the villages”).

341. *Bestola*. Manuscript: *bestiola* (“little beast”); Vatican Codex: *bistola*; Venetian edition: *biscola*.

350. That the hare fled to Martin and threw itself at his feet is met with complete silence in Sulpicius. Fortunatus should therefore be considered to have enlarged the matter in the manner of poets.

351. Vatican Codex: *pro luce precatur* (“it prays for light”).

377. Vatican Codex: *veteris potius carnalis* (“rather of the old carnal [man]”).

380. Venetian edition: *pars gramine florens* (“part flowering with grass”).

384. Venetian edition: *conjugii detinet* (“retains the form of marriage”).]

[Col. 0401A] The idle driver was driven onward, sitting across the beast’s back.

When he had aroused the animal’s countless rages, the furious heifer went everywhere under the harsh driver, rushing over bends and trackless places.

It came closer to the holy man with its raging horn, and he raised his hand and ordered the beast to stop.

The heifer stood fixed in its tracks, less wicked now in its movement.

When the holy man saw it pressing forward, he said at close range:

[310] “Go on, fierce one; flee, savage one; return, evil creature; withdraw, bloody one. Stop harassing the harmless beast, you destructive creature.”

Then the wild beast left the animal’s back, and the gentlest heifer recovered its proper senses.

It lay down before the saint’s feet, worshiping reverently.

[315] The creature, which has no understanding, itself bent its knee, discerning the blessed man’s deeds against nature.

[Col. 0401B] It offered obedience to his merit, though it did not know honor; and it was all the more humble because it carried a free neck.

Previously bound and swelling with pride, it now lay released from the plague.

[320] The creature that had stood roaring fell submissively after its bonds, and silently showed favor, having cast off its former burden from its shoulder.

Then the holy bishop ordered the beast to depart. Immediately it returned to the herd, recalled by the shepherd’s voice.

This happened at the time when the fire had not even touched the fringe of the blessed man’s garment amid the flames.

[325] Let the greatest of deeds also be related from the smallest events.

For once, while the gracious man was walking through the villages, a troop of horses came flying toward him, intent upon the hunt.

[Col. 0401C] Guided by the keen scent of the dogs, the quarry was found in the thickets.

[330] The riders leaped across the fields and pursued it with shouts. The mastiffs strained to chase the fleeing hare, springing forward with barking and threatening teeth.

They spread out and rushed swiftly in their love of plunder; each mingled its leaping tracks with those of the others.

[335] One silently followed; another sought the air with cries. One, deceived by the scent in an empty thicket, wheeled about; another was suspended in a leap among the movements of the trees.

The whole pack snarled with open mouths at the capture of the one animal, often deceived by an empty bite above the hare,

[340] while it slipped away beneath the claws that had been thrust out.

The crowd pressed upon it, but the slippery little animal escaped.

Meanwhile there was no path left for the little hare to take.

[Col. 0402A] Mountain, valley, rock, forest, and thicket had all failed it; across the open fields, without cover for its flight,

[345] with its knee failing, its foot weary, its nose bowed down, it hung entirely upon the dog’s mouth and every growl.

Yet it sensed that the signs of blessed Martin were near. Trembling, it turned its course through the shaggy grass by a cunning route, ears raised, wandering, harried, and breathless.

[350] Staggering, the hare fell before his feet, a suppliant stranger. If it could not pray with a voice, it prayed with its breath in place of a voice.

Thus the little wild creature lay there, safe beneath Martin’s protection, and rested defended under the sweet shade of a tree.

Then the holy man, as was his custom, moved by healing compassion,

[355] ordered the young hounds to stop and let the fugitive depart.

[Col. 0402B] At once that sacred command ran into the dogs’ ears.

The swift hounds grew numb, fixed in place by the word, unstable in their steps and hanging in the very leaps they had begun.

[360] The dogs returned as though following the tracks of a crab. The little hare escaped unharmed across the open fields; with the dog left behind, the traveler safely traverses the heights.

One flees, the other returns; no one perishes—behold salvation.

Thus the holy man brought peace even to the little beasts themselves. The dogs’ weakness became an image of compassion,

[365] for they learned rather to spare the forbidden bite.

And because human beings were absent where wondrous things occur, nothing is lost from the praise: the beast itself experienced the miracle.

How greatly, too, did the grace of the saint’s speech shine forth?

When he had recently seen a sheep shorn of its wool,

[370] he said that it had fulfilled these commands of the Gospel:

[Col. 0402C] “For, carrying two tunics, the innocent one offered one and clothed the needy woman who had been stripped of her covering.”

Likewise the saint looked across the countryside and saw a swineherd trembling, naked except for a garment of skins.

[375] “Behold Adam, once driven from the seat of paradise: exiled from Elysium, he feeds the mouths of a swineherd’s flock.

Having laid aside the garment of the old, carnal Adam, we must put on the likeness of the new Adam.”

Then again the blessed man saw verdant meadows:

[380] “One part was pasture, one part dug, and one part a flowering bank.

The pig had dug one part, the ox had fed upon another, and the flower adorned the third.”

The saint therefore compares three names with three things: the ditch among the sedges is the shameful image of adultery, and the shorn grass retains the figure of marriage.

[385] [Note: [Col. 0403D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

386. Venetian edition: *Feno apto* (“suited to hay”).

387. Venetian edition: *Et radiantior auro* (“and more radiant than gold”).

388. Venetian edition: *Miles item* (“the soldier likewise”).

The same passage: *Singula*. I do not doubt that the reading should be corrected, with the Vatican Codex, to *cingula linquens* (“leaving his military belt”). Thus Sulpicius tells the story: Martin “had cast away the belt, the soldier’s insignia.” When this soldier had professed the monastic life and wished to take back the wife he had dismissed, whom Martin had ordered to remain in the monastery of the girls, he was deterred from receiving her by this one speech of Martin: soldiers stationed in battle do not take their wives with them; rather, the women remain within enclosures and fortifications. Therefore he too ought not, in the training ground of monastic life, to think of reclaiming his wife.

391. Vatican Codex: *jus sacerdotii* (“the right of the priesthood”).

The same passage: Venetian edition: *hoc ordine dicens* (“saying in this order”), which should be retained.

415. *Nemausum*, the most celebrated city of Occitania.

418. Martin was evidently sailing: as Sulpicius relates in chapter 15, he sat alone far away from the others in a remote part of the ship.

422. Vatican Codex: *celebrarant ordine* (“they had celebrated in order”). Sulpicius relates that when Martin’s disciples afterward investigated the matter carefully, they discovered that a synod had indeed been held on that very day and that everything else had happened just as they had learned from Martin.

428. Vatican Codex: *rettulit ut prius* (“he reported it as before”).

433. Venetian edition: *ostia clausa die retinent geminante* (“with the doors closed, they remain during the doubled day”).

The same passage: *Mercurium* (“Mercury”). The demon evidently appeared to Martin under various forms of idols. For Severus Sulpicius writes of the same matter in chapter 20 of the *Life of Saint Martin*: “Frequently, while the devil attempted to deceive the holy man by a thousand arts of harm, he thrust his visible form upon him in very diverse shapes . . . For sometimes he presented himself in the guise of Jupiter, more often of Mercury, and frequently he offered himself with the features of Venus or Minerva transformed.”]

[Col. 0403A] It is an image fitting for virgins, blossoming with violets,

luxuriant in herbs, suited to hay, and beautiful with flowers.

Worthy of God, pleasing with gems, and more radiant than purple.

But the soldier, having professed himself a monk, leaving everything behind,

because he desired to spend his life with his own wife,

[390] changed his course and crossed the boundary by a better path. As a priest, he admonished him by this reasoning:

“Can a woman be joined to a warrior?

A man’s strength alone is better suited to forming the battle line;

let the weaker company hold the enclosures of the walls,

[395] and let the fragile sex conceal itself within the barriers.

This alone is enough to make a woman fear; the matter itself supplies the fear.

Let the soldier, powerful for war, go helmeted into battle,

gleaming with the shining scale armor of his triple cuirass,

[Col. 0403B] clothed in a breastplate over his shoulders and leaning upon his spear;

[400] accustomed to the shield and sending wounds from the bow.

Here he brandishes the sword-hilt; there he twists and hurls the missile.

Sweating beneath the weight, he sends streams through his iron tunic.”

By these words he soothed the young man and forced him to return to his senses. Leaving his wife behind, the hermit reclaimed his crown.

[405] Meanwhile, because he continually sang of false and holy things, neither can they be taken up in sequence nor can they be contained in writing.

What was the life of the holy man? Who could recount each deed?

How great was the faith of his soul, how lofty and pure his will,

that not only would people come to him from throughout the wide world,

[410] but heavenly honor also lovingly visited him, and an angelic choir frequently hastened to his presence,

[Col. 0403C] to refresh their weary friend with gentle conversations and, as it were, to restore a parent through an embrace expressed in words.

The following event proves this, recounting earlier deeds.

[415] A synodical council had been summoned at Nîmes, but the holy bishop refused to attend as mediator.

Therefore, boarding a swift vessel, he prepared to travel along the river, living apart as a hermit in the midst of the assemblies.

He himself sat in the stern; his prow kept him apart from all the others.

[420] But behold, a winged angel of the Lord came from the heights, on the very day when the council was being conducted,

[Col. 0404A] recounting in order everything that the bishops had done, fulfilling Martin’s role by being present at the synod, and crossing the distant air with concern for his friend.

[425] His wing did not grow weary in the air during the journey, but the swift wing floated onward until it brought the new report.

The Lord’s commands conceal nothing from his friend. As the holy man had previously reported, so this angel later confirmed everything.

The predictions do not break faith, nor do the things revealed prove false.

[430] It happened, then, when Severus sat at the door with his companion Gallus, ministers learned and beloved, that the blessed man’s cell was filled with a many-voiced murmur.

Holding the doors closed, at the hour when the day was doubled, they heard speech—but what it was, they confessed they did not know.

[435] [Col. 0404B] They sensed a disturbance but did not understand the articulate words. Perhaps this was part of the merit: to have sensed heavenly things in this way.

If they did not recognize what was said, it is enough that they deserved to hear it.

Afterward the holy man came out of his cell. When the elder Severus Sulpicius had long pressed him to explain what had happened,

[440] Martin, scarcely moved by the prayers, at last disclosed the matter in order.

He said that Agnes, Thecla, and Mary had spoken, explaining the appearance and dress of the holy women: their faces, eyes, cheeks, feet, hands, breasts, and form. With such pure sight he had often seen the faces of his sisters.

[445] What color and beauty, what form and grace they possessed—and how great it was—and how, in equal speech, they had offered a peaceful greeting.

[Col. 0404C] He asked after the brothers; they asked after the sisters.

But he returned by walking, while they returned by flight.

He had often been worthy to see Peter and Paul, the apostolic summit and lofty pillars of honor.

[450] He also endured demonic battles very frequently. Rebuking each demon by its own name, he forced them to depart.

Above all, he reported that the hostile Mercury was present; for he said that the brutish Jupiter was considered stupid.

[455] O sincere eyes, pressed by no darkness! O mind enlightened by wisdom, retaining clear vision without a cloud!

You see Thecla in the air with mortal sight,

and you behold Agnes, her forehead encircled with a crown,

[Note: [Col. 0405C]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

465. Edition: *dextrae adjacente hyacintho* (“with hyacinth placed beside the right hand”).

466. Edition: *Quanto zona die* (“how brightly the girdle shone”).

467. Edition: *cataclysis effora rasis*. Browerus, commenting on this passage of Fortunatus, says: “These are certain monstrosities of words.” An old book at Trier reads *cataclistis*. Browerus believes that the poet is here describing a *cyclas*, an outer garment ornamented with embroidery, from which *cataclisti*, visible at particular places, projected. He cites another passage of Fortunatus, Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, where he says:

> What artisan’s hand has twisted the cataclistic threads?

Dufresne, investigating what *cataclistus* or *cataclitus* may be, believes that *cataclistic* garments were clothing made with Phrygian workmanship, in which gems were inserted—as though “enclosed,” *κατακλεισθεῖσαι*. The same term was also used of cups in which gems were enclosed in this manner. Thus Gregory of Tours, in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 63, says: “Nevertheless, he did not break the cup, because *cataclyza* had been solidified in it.” This passage is clarified by what Arnobius the Younger says in his *Conflict with Serapion*, Book I: “I see one diadem, but in that diadem the gems have been constructed by the art of *cataclyzomata*.”

Dufresne also reports that the following verses of Fortunatus were copied from a codex written in Lombard letters—preserved, as he says, in the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris—and that they read as follows:

> You saw the bridegroom’s chamber, beautiful above all things,  
> adorned with gems, gold, and purple.  
> How brightly the girdle shone with the honor of its stones,  
> and what kind of *cyclades*, or what wild *cataclysis* upon the *rasis* [an uncertain textile term]?  
> What mantle fell from the shoulders, with *Chryso Phara* mingled with beryls?  
> What necklace gleamed with beauty around his neck?

Moreover, *rason* was a garment of monks who were still novices; for this reason the Greeks called them *ῥασοφόροι*—“wearers of the *rason*.”

470. Venetian edition: *aptissima vitta* (“a most suitable ribbon”).

471. *Alta*. Perhaps *alba* (“white”).

The same passage: Venetian edition: *et in auribus aura sigilli* (“and in the ears the golden glint of the seal”).

478. Venetian edition: *Nimis geminata* (“too much doubled”).

485. Vatican Codex: *pluviatilis imber* (“rainfall”).

501. Venetian edition: *prima tenent terris* (“they hold first place on earth”), which should be followed.

507. Venetian edition: *Lucifer, ut radiis* (“Lucifer, as to his rays”).

518. *Huic*. Manuscript: *hinc* (“from here”).]

[Col. 0405A] You see Mary, distinguished and radiant with precious light.

[460] You have seen the temple of the Lord supported by a diadem;

you have seen the bridegroom’s chamber, beautiful above all things,

adorned with gems, gold, and purple.

What kind of jasper was at the feet, what topaz at the side?

What rings adorned the fingers with green radiance?

[465] What bracelets, with the right hand glowing with hyacinth?

How brightly did the girdle shine with the honor of its stones?

What kind of *cyclas* or *cataclysis* appeared in the woven cloth?

What mantle from the shoulders, mingled with chrysoprase and beryls?

What beautiful necklace gleamed red around that neck?

[470] Perhaps an amethyst-colored ribbon lay upon her snow-white hair,

and a lofty ornament, impressed with carved images and gilded seals, hung from it;

[Col. 0405B] the diadem scattered both light and varied green hues.

What forehead, mouth, eyes, face, cheek, foot, hand, or arm

bloomed with reflected gems?

[475] Thus, good shepherd, what story of your sheep passed before you?

What, I ask, when you so often saw Peter and Paul,

the first shining vessels of the heavenly ministry,

golden, exceedingly beautiful, jeweled, lovely, and flashing—

with what serenity do you suppose those faces shone?

[480] They spread the teachings of Christ throughout the whole world.

They first declared: “You are Christ, the Son of the gracious God,

of the high-throned and all-powerful God;

and upon this rock the Church, founded, reigns.”

[Col. 0405C] Neither blasts move it, nor does the whirlwind of a storm overturn it,

[485] nor does rain drag sand through the wandering waves.

Because this living rock holds the foundations of salvation,

the gates of hell will never prevail against it.

What of that holy man Paul, the great trumpet for the nations?

Pouring forth the proclamations of Christ across sea and land,

[490] he filled Europe, Asia, and Libya with the salt and teaching;

[Col. 0406A] wherever the sun stretches with its rays, his stylus ran—

to the Bear, the south, the full west, and the rising east.

He crossed the Ocean too, wherever an island provides a harbor;

and wherever Britain possesses lands, even to farthest Thule,

[495] one trumpet resounded throughout every region.

He sets forth the gifts of Christ bestowed through the doctrine of such men:

Hebrew, Greek, Roman, barbarian, Indian—

Israel sings, and likewise the Greek and the Roman citizen.

Under the Prince of the faith, Rome has its two princely leaders,

[500] where there are the two lofty tombs of apostolic flesh.

They hold first place on earth and precedence in heaven;

equal in the utterance of doctrine and in the curule honor of their seats.

[Col. 0406B] Both triumphing, they scatter new gifts throughout the world.

A single sacred day blessed them through their martyrdom,

[505] and thus the twofold consul marked the sacred times.

How equally did splendor flash and glow from their faces?

Lucifer would be eclipsed by those countenances in his rays,

for even the shining disk of the sun itself does not gleam so greatly.

O sweet eyes, O faces capable of seeing blessed things,

[510] you saw Zion, whose beautiful gates stand in order;

you saw Zion, whose gates stand in four sets of three.

The Almighty loves them above all summits of Jacob:

gateways crowned with the varied light of gems,

carved with thin plates and inscribed with emerald workmanship,

[515] [Col. 0406C] glowing with chrysolites and white with glistening whites.

Whatever love could accomplish, grace poured forth in its entirety.

A topaz, beautiful in every color and one among all things,

through these gates that noble people of the kingdom enter

the starry city, advancing by the steps of their merits,

[520] and remain forever as citizens inscribed throughout the ages.

Among them are nobles and the lofty summits of the powerful,

mingled with patricians of noble birth and consuls,

and, seated nearest the king, Martin, a senator.

Faith gave him weapons, and the king himself is his confidence.

[525] A soldier who serves through love, he has become a fellow heir through honor.

[Col. 0407A] You who have power in speech, ask pardon for my sins;

and hear what my corrupted tongue murmurs to you,

[Col. 0408A] so that forgiveness may flow from the holy source to the one who has been wounded,

and, when you pray, the healed scar may be restored.

7. This passage corresponds to Sulpicius’s words in *Dialogue* III, chapter 1: “It is growing light, O Gallus; we must rise,” and so forth.

13. Vatican Codex: *in trifidis tribus nauta libellis* (“in three-forked [waters], the sailor in little books”); corrupt.

20. Vatican Codex: *Neque malleus* (“nor the hammer”).

31. Sulpicius relates that when the bishops Valentinian—or Valentinus—and Victricius were present, Martin himself withdrew from the place so that they might heal the girl instead, as though they were more worthy. But when they refused and begged him to heal the girl himself, he did not delay any longer—both actions being noble, since he showed humility without delaying compassion—and he accomplished what had been hoped for.

39. Vatican Codex: *tinnile plectrum* (“the tinkling plectrum”). Venetian edition: *inutile plectrum* (“the useless plectrum”). But Browerus says that what was incorrectly read as *inutile plectrum* was most aptly corrected by Sidonius’s interpreter to *lyra tinnula* (“the tinkling lyre”). Browerus also cites a passage of Alcimus Avitus, whom Fortunatus seems to have followed. It is this:

> Thus the flexible tongue is compressed against the hollow palate,  
> so that, pressed into the chamber by the stroke of the striking plectrum,  
> the speech, struck and modulated, resounds into the air.

Moreover, the same commentator adds, *frixillus* was a tower or box into which dice were put and cast onto a board. C. Sollius writes of these in *Narbonne*:

> Here one brings out smooth balls and hoops;  
> here dice rattle in their perforated boxes.

Hence John of Genoa, as quoted by Dufresne, says: “*Fritellum* is also used for a perforated vessel through which dice are customarily thrown, so that no fraud may occur there.” The likeness to human voices and the tongue is therefore drawn from the sound made by dice cast into this receptacle. In this sense Milo writes in the *Life of Saint Amandus, Bishop*:

> Who taught the boy—what sense, I ask, persuaded him  
> to utter unknown dice with Hebrew sound?

52. Avitianus’s savagery and cruelty will be discussed hereafter.

63. *Syrabracha*. Manuscript: *Syrabara*; Vatican Codex and Venetian edition: *nec syra bacca dedit merito virtutis adultum* (“nor did the Syrian berry give him maturity by the merit of virtue”), which is preferable. Browerus says that older books understand *Syrobara* as a kind of exotic, precious liquid ointment.]

[Col. 0407A] After crossing the wave-tossed sea and returning to the shores,

while I pluck white-haired lilies with my fingers,

I cut roses with my nail and run through beds of violets,

among the varied scents of a countryside rich in pleasantness,

[5] sleep then overtakes me. Weary, I also recline my neck,

and my limbs lie supported upon a grassy couch.

But behold, day returns; it is already growing light, and we must go,

while the swallow greets us with its morning voice,

and the swiftly hastening twilight breaks through the brief night.

[10] Although my eyes swim in heavy sleep, I shall rise;

[Col. 0407B] waking, I shall wipe sleep from my eyes with my thumb,

and I shall go, companions, where Gallus calls us to resume the journey.

As an inexperienced sailor among three-forked waters, ignorant of little books,

and like one amid the ambiguous waves of the Symplegades,

[15] amid the Ionian, Aegean, and pursuing storm of Malea,

lest the south wind drown me in its soaking sands,

the life of Martin, my patron, guided me from above.

I, unworthy, strive to carve it in rough words,

a rustic, unskilled in art, attempting to fashion a necklace,

[20] which neither file polishes nor hammer sharpens,

which is not rubbed upon an anvil, nor tested by fire in a furnace,

nor weighed by a biting pair of tongs with its double curved hook.

Rather, my tongue brings forth the unworked metal.

[Col. 0407C] Yet the work gives pleasure without any skill of its own,

because by itself its grace presents a beautiful gem.

Nevertheless, I shall discharge the remaining obligations of my task.

And to him, to whom I owe exceedingly great things, I repay small ones:

Meanwhile a father, anxious for his daughter, born at Chartres and sick from the womb, brings forth the mute girl to be healed by the holy mouth—

[30] For six full years she had been grievously dull, without a voice.

[Col. 0408A] Nor does Martin delay the merciful aid of compassion;

He lies prostrate upon the ground, silently striking the stars with prayer,

His body poured out upon the earth, while his mind flies above the heavens.

When he perceived that, through prayer, faith had obtained its desired effect,

[35] He asks that oil be brought to him to bless,

And pours the blessed liquid into the girl’s mouth.

Holding the wretched girl’s tongue with his finger,

He himself asks the girl for her father’s name.

At once the loosened lyre of her throat moves its tinkling plectrum.

[40] And the unaccustomed shell of her enclosed palate sings,

Producing words with a little rattle, rubbed out through the hollow of her tooth;

And the dutiful daughter sweetly answered with her father’s name.

Born mute from the womb, she now seemed to be reborn with a voice.

As an adult she restored the old whispers of nursing infants to her mouth,

Beginning to carve out words with a tender movement;

Her sluggish tongue moved gradually along its rough path,

With entangled sound, hoarse in its novelty, like a reed-pipe,

Until she sang a full symphony with her own breath.

Then the father, embracing the venerable knees of the blessed man,

[50] Crying aloud and weeping for joy now that speech had been granted,

Echoed forth praises to Christ in a vow of rejoicing.

Next the sick wife of the fierce judge Avitianus

Sends to the holy man, hoping for a remedy for her illness,

A glass vessel of oil, divided equally by measure,

[55] From which he might drive away the disease with life-giving ointment.

At once he himself made the sign of the cross over the flask.

[Col. 0408C] The liquid rises to its mouth and foams, boiling up to the brim,

Born in new abundance beneath the glass shell,

And generous moisture springs up within the dry vessel.

[60] It runs upward, although its nature is to flow downward,

And the container of liquid oil seeks the heights;

The juice was born neither from an olive root,

Nor did Syrabracha supply it, grown mature through the merit of virtue.

It rises to the very top, where the vessel is closed by its open mouth,

[65] [Note: [Col. 0409D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

100. *Dies.* Perhaps *diem*.

101. *Avitianus.* This Avitianus was perhaps the same man who is said to have been vicar of Africa under Julian, as is clear from the *Theodosian Code*, book 15, “On the Public Post,” book 1, “On the Remission of Debts,” and book 2, “On the Construction of Roads.” Ammianus Marcellinus also mentions him in book XXVII, under Valentinian and Valens, calling him “ex-vicar,” if indeed he is the same person whom Sulpicius Severus calls Count Avitianus.

106. *Confecta.* *Confectam* seems to be the reading required.

107. Vatican manuscript: *genus omne jubet*.

[Col. 0410D] 109. These things answer to what is related by Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 3, chapter 5: Avitianus, “on the following day, while the city was stunned, proceeded to undertake so grievous a task,” and so forth. I would rather read here: “And he ordered the wicked procession to advance,” and so forth.

111. Venetian edition: *jussa tyranni*—“the tyrant’s commands.”

124. Vatican manuscript: *reserent et claustra*—“that they should unlock the doors.”

139. Vatican manuscript: *poenas exsolvere*—“to pay the penalties.”

141. Vatican manuscript: *multantur tempora caedis*—“the times of slaughter are punished.”

154. Vatican manuscript: *Ipse recedit ab urbe*—“He himself withdraws from the city.”]

[Col. 0409A] Nor is the liquid content merely to fill the vessel,

For soon the overflowing wave of oil pours down from above,

And the urn cannot contain itself; such is the blessing of the right hand.

Overflowing, it drenched all the child’s garments.

Oil also ran from his fingers, watering them from the fountain.

[70] And after it had flowed in the manner of a flooding river,

The matron received the vessel, full through the merit of faith.

No less remarkable was what then happened:

The same blessed glass vessel, made noble by the miracle,

Had been placed by an unwary boy at the edge of a window,

[75] Covered, as it happened, with a linen cloth in veneration,

While another, unknowingly drawing back the flowing sheet,

The flask slipped and fell onto the hard marble pavement.

[Col. 0409B] Yet neither did the stones break the glass nor the vessel lose its liquid:

It remained whole, flying lightly as though suspended like a feather,

[80] Or as though, carried upward on two wings, it had descended gently.

No crack appeared, nor was there any scar in the vessel.

Thus the liquid within caused the exterior to remain unharmed,

And the one whom it was fitting to protect covered its own coverings.

Lest the glass perish, the oil’s guardianship preserved it;

[85] The enclosed moisture defended its own container,

And the strong blessing made the fragile fragment stand firm.

While his disciples were walking close together,

A terrifying dog assailed them with a great bark.

One of them, with devoted love, said in Martin’s name:

[90] “I command you: be silent, and do not weary us with your shouting.”

At once the mad dog’s voice was cut off and hung in its mouth;

It swallowed back the wandering cry from the middle of its throat.

That savage roar stuck beneath its eager jaws,

And the mastiff stood with its gaping mouth stunned, its voice restrained,

[95] Though fury pressed upon it, since it was not permitted to open its jaws.

Thus its trembling whisper returned, shut within and without a voice.

The holy man’s name also proved effective, though speech had failed the animal.

Therefore I shall continue toward the journey I have begun, walking slowly,

While I may travel the road and the healthful breeze calls me,

[100] And the hour draws on, moving the day’s slow footsteps.

While the proud companion Avitianus was conducting himself in this manner,

He approached Tours, supported by the terror of his office.

Crowds gathered, and a long chain of prisoners,

Their hair growing long, whose entire flesh was wasting away.

[105] [Col. 0409D] Their consumed bodies loosened the constricting iron,

Their emaciation scarcely allowing their shape to be discerned.

He himself ordered a kind of punishment to be prepared beyond the usual measure.

You would see the weeping people wandering through the city.

He ordered the abominable procession to proceed to the grim tribunal,

[110] From which fierce eyes would watch their bodies being burned.

[Col. 0410A] When the holy man learned that deadly commands were being carried out,

Under cover of night he hastened toward the savage praetorium,

And alone prepared to travel the road of compassion.

When the old man arrived, breathing heavily with pity,

[115] He lay down before the doors, kind even at those dreadful thresholds,

Where the judge lay buried in sluggish sleep.

Meanwhile a winged angel quickly entered the hall

And thundered in a threatening voice at the sleeping count:

“Sleep holds you here; Martin is standing outside,” he said.

[120] “You enjoy rest, while he endures hardships.

You lie softly on a couch; he lies upon cruel marble.”

Avitianus, trembling, was immediately shaken from sleep,

Crying out that Martin, the holy man, was lying at the doors.

He ordered his servants to unlock the barriers for the blessed man,

[125] [Col. 0410B] Lest injury should trouble the venerable servant of Christ.

The servants then mocked their master with ringing laughter,

Stupidly saying that he was seeing empty dreams:

There was no man sitting or standing before the doors.

Again Avitianus was overcome by precipitous sleep.

[130] Then the angel roused the man more forcefully, pressing him awake;

He shook him severely so that he would not yield to sleep.

Terrified now, the judge no longer trusting anyone,

He dismissed the servants and hurried to his own threshold.

There he found Martin, just as he had previously sensed.

[135] Then the fierce man addressed the holy one unprompted in these words:

“What are you doing to me, Martin, venerable priest?

You do not fight me in an equal contest, I confess.

You come to absolve the accused and scourge me with blows.

[Col. 0410C] Do you prefer that I pay the penalties for everyone,

Or do you choose that the crime be paid for through my torments?

Under a new torturer the seasons of slaughter have changed:

The daily punishment torments the prisoners, while at night you weary me.

Servant of God, it has become clear how lofty your power is,

When the judge is severely scourged while you sit in judgment.

[145] Yet now you yourself prove how I have been treated by you:

When I come through you, I neither ask for a friend nor beg a servant.

The one whom punishment restrains does not allow delays.

There is no need for words; though you are silent, I know what you desire.

[Col. 0410D] Yield, I beg you; depart from this place; grant what I ask,

[150] And let your avenging retribution not quickly punish me severely.”

He said this, and as the patron departed with hurried steps,

Avitianus, faint of heart, summoned the officials

And ordered them to unlock the instruments of torture, the prison cells, and the barriers.

When he had released them, he himself withdrew far from the city.

[155] [Note: [Col. 0411C]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

164. Vatican manuscript: *Adpropiante sacro*—“as the holy man approached”; this should be retained. Sulpicius reports that the clerics understood Martin to be approaching when they heard the groans of the demons with which the possessed were afflicted. They regarded this as a sign that Martin had left his house and was approaching the basilica.

165. Vatican manuscript: *actis versus in altum*—“carried upward.” The possessed, that is, were held suspended in the air by a demon, with their heads turned downward, while their garments stiffened so that, falling toward the head, they would not expose what modesty covers. Sulpicius, chapter 6.

167. *Nec.* Manuscript: *Ne*.

170. *Fateatur.* Manuscript: *fatebatur*.

The same place. Vatican manuscript: *Hic se testatur Anubem*—“Here he declares himself to be Anubis.”

171. Vatican manuscript: *Vasa ministeriis daemonis*—“vessels for the demon’s services.”

172. Martin drove demons out of the possessed neither by touching them with his hands nor by rebuking them, as others did, but by lying on the ground in ashes and sackcloth. The same place, Sulpicius.

197. Vatican manuscript: *horrificam facie*—“terrifying in face.”

[Col. 0412C] 209. This verse, *mitior atque*, and so forth, is absent from the Vatican manuscript.

210. *Ambaciensi.* This town, commonly called Amboise, lies at the confluence of the Loire and the Amasse. It is still famous, as the distinguished Ruinart reports in his notes on Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 35. Gregory of Tours mentions this town in the cited passage, saying: “And they joined together—Chlodovech and Alaric, king of the Goths—on an island of the Loire which was near the village of Amboise in the territory of the city of Tours,” and so forth.

212. Sulpicius describes this structure in chapter 9 as follows: “A towered mass had risen, built of highly polished stones; ascending aloft into a cone, it preserved the superstition of the place through the dignity of its workmanship.”

216. Venetian edition: *rite ruendum*—“properly to be demolished”; this is preferable to what follows. Sulpicius relates that Martin had ordered the priest of that place to demolish the structure, but the priest had done nothing, claiming that it could be accomplished only by force, armed soldiers, and a large public crowd.

225. Venetian edition: *Fremebunda tui, Martine, precatus*—“Roaring with prayers for you, Martin.”

229. Venetian edition: *Illico comminuit*—“Immediately it shattered.”]

[Col. 0411A] And the heavy anger fled; fear itself became his fear.

By a perverse reversal, the judge’s flight increased the peace,

And the shepherd drove away the wolf without slaughter, with the flock unharmed.

Whenever he hurried from the monastery toward the city,

Or set foot outside the cell when he came there,

[160] Crowds of apparitions trembled, their mouths and motions agitated.

And when the people did not know that the patron was approaching,

The groaning of the demons announced it.

As the holy man approached, you would see suspended bodies

Lifted high and carried far through the air.

[165] Others, with their feet raised above them, he turned upside down,

With their heads below, as though falling from a cloud.

Yet their garments did not fall away, covering their modesty.

Sent before the judge to declare their crimes or merits,

[Col. 0411B] They confessed their deeds while rushing headlong:

[170] One declared himself to be the foolish Jupiter, another Anubis,

And themselves to be vessels serving the wicked demon.

But under the compassionate torturer, the tormented savagery was driven away.

Now I shall also recount what he did in the district of Sens.

Whenever hail, compacted by frost, crushed the crops year after year,

[175] And the empty harvest defrauded the farmer,

Nor did the ripening ear invite the reaper’s work,

While the stolen threshing prevented the farmer’s hand,

The inhabitant, so often deceived by mature grain,

Saw his fields lie numb and barren in their furrows.

[180] The sick crop, pelted with stones, denied food to the people.

A faithful delegation was sent to the holy man in prayer,

Asking him to remove from the earth the raging storm as a scourge.

[Col. 0411C] The man’s lofty prayer soon accomplished this by itself.

For as soon as the good priest poured forth prayers from his mouth,

[185] The heavy storm clouds dried up their rain,

And the widowed fields married themselves to fertility once more.

For four times five years—the years during which he was prominent—

The undefiled gifts of the holy patron flourished.

But when the man of God himself, lifted to the stars, departed,

[190] The returning storm descended upon the forgotten fields,

And, with the bishop removed, savage disaster devastated the little farm.

The rain cruelly ravaged the captured ears of grain.
