[Col. 0412A] The defender died, and soon the hail sought its prey;

With Martin’s departure the elements resumed their scourge.

When the just man once again encountered Avitianus,

He saw the shadow of a savage demon threatening him,

A terrifying face, a plague of cruelty in bodily form.

Fixing his gaze on it from afar, the holy man drove it away with a breath from his mouth.

[200] The judge thought that the blessed man had blown upon him personally.

“Why, good shepherd,” he said, “does your insult trouble us

And make us unworthy through the contempt of a breath of air?”

The excellent father addressed him with a friendly reply:

“We do not do this to you because of the disgrace of guilt.

[205] We have blown upon the shadow that had settled wickedly upon your neck.”

At once the ghost, the attendant, fled from the tribunal,

And abandoned the seat it had occupied upon his neck.

Avitianus’s neck rose up in its new freedom.

The judge, relieved of his burden, was restored to honor,

[Col. 0412B] And he became gentler, though previously severe and implacable.

[210] Another marvel occurred in the village of Amboise.

Idols had been raised in towered metal,

A massive structure heavily loaded with exquisitely polished stones,

Rising aloft as a throne above a splendid temple—

False superstition, but the true deception of those who prayed—

[215] A great work devoted to crime, making its worshipers into nothing.

When the holy man, rejoicing, had properly ordered it to be demolished,

And no human resources could tear it down,

The holy bishop, returning to his accustomed weapon,

[Col. 0412C] Kept watch through the night hours, remaining constantly alert,

Breaking the silent stillness with conversations with the Lord.

But when fresh morning scattered dawn across the world,

And Phoebus stretched his golden covering through the clouds,

Behold, a sudden storm arose with varied roaring,

Shrill in its star-like flight and full of tumult,

[225] Raging with your aid, Martin, and striving,

And moving your host, armed with savage south winds.

When it touched the shrine, with a blow of swift whirling motion

It struck the structure, driven against it by furious rotation,

Shattered the idols, and dissolved the mass into dust.

[230] [Note: [Col. 0413D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

236. The idol, namely, stood set upon the top of the column.

346. Venetian edition: *lapsaque disperso*—“and, having fallen, scattered.”

The same place. Vatican manuscript: *pereunt simulacra metallo*—“the metal images perish.”

253. Vatican manuscript: *siccarant viscera*—“had dried the entrails”; this should be retained.

255. Venetian edition: *atque suae pluviae sub pondere fessa laborans*—“and laboring, exhausted beneath the weight of her own rain.”

264. Venetian edition: *damnatur fistula*—“the channel is condemned.” Vatican manuscript: *damnavit fistula*—“the channel condemned it.”

265. Vatican manuscript: *redit in fontem unda*—“the wave returns to its source.”

274. Venetian edition and Vatican manuscript: *vada remige*—“the waters with its oar”; this reading is preferable.

275. Vatican manuscript: *vaga caerula*—“the wandering blue waters”; corrupt.

[Col. 0414D] 286. Venetian edition: *edebatque bonus*—“and the good man ate”; this is preferable.

288. The monk, namely, whom Sulpicius says was skilled at fishing.

292. Venetian edition: *cui constanter ait*—“to whom he firmly says.”

298. Venetian edition: *Projicit in fluvio*—“he casts it into the river.”

304. Venetian edition: *vitae quam munere*—“rather as a gift of life.”

305. Above, Fortunatus calls this man Arborius the prefect, in book II of the *Life of Saint Martin*. Was he from the same family as Aemilius Magnus Arborius, the maternal uncle of Ausonius and son of Caecilius Argicius Arborius, about whom Ausonius wrote poems in books III and IV of the *Parentalia*?]

[Col. 0413A] And the lofty walls collapsed from their towered pride.

O holy bishop, sweet and memorable name—

Who would not submit to you, for whom even the clouds fight?

I shall also tell of these marvels, accomplished by equal power.

A tall, rigid, shapeless column stood there,

[235] Immense in appearance and unyielding in its broad extent.

It bore upon itself a hostile image.

When the devout man wished to bring it down but could not loosen the mass,

He again hastened to the victorious standards of prayer,

Calling upon the heavenly power to draw weapons to itself as in war.

[240] He lay stretched upon the ground, carried above the stars by his prayers.

After he had pleaded for a long time and poured out much dust,

[Col. 0413B] The column seemed, before his eyes, to descend from heaven,

Gently cleaving the clouds in an airy slide.

When it struck the opposing mass with a vibrating blow,

The column’s joint burst apart, its structure coming loose;

[245] And, scattering its fragments, it shattered the images of metal.

The false gods were struck by a new weapon,

False gods indeed, but receiving the true anger of divinity.

Overthrown, they produced gain from their own ruins,

And the temples, reduced to fierce ashes, were increased by their dissolution.

It is also fitting to reveal, in honor of the blessed man, what happened next.

A pale woman, with blood dripping from her,

[Col. 0413C] Whose entrails had been dried by the irrigating flow,

Dragging her shipwrecked limbs along on a wandering stream of blood,

Exhausted and suffering beneath the storm of her own rain,

Generating the showers of a hidden whirlwind within herself,

Was already falling beneath her own floods, about to be submerged.

She had no harbor left, no standard of safety.

When she touched the fringe of the blessed son’s garment,

[260] She felt the threads of the noble and exalted cloth.

From there health sprang forth, first filling her fingers with ointment.

Such great confidence in the hidden remedy passed through her.

At once the source of the irrigating flow was dried up.

The channels of the gushing stream were condemned,

[265] And the restrained flow returned harmlessly to its source of blood.

The continual flow fled its hollow, empty channels,

The streams were solidified by the binding power of the sacred garment,

And the liquids felt the restraints imposed by the man’s virtue.

[Col. 0413D] The fortunate woman returned safe from her loss,

[270] And, while the physician knew nothing, recovered the aid of healing.

O holy Martin, you do not know it, yet you bestow gifts.

[Col. 0414A] From there the bishop hastened away.

Behold, a serpent came swimming toward him through the river,

Cleaving the wandering water with the thrust of its breast and the oar of its tail,

[275] Moving its scaly back and splitting the blue waters with its coils.

The holy man, looking at it, said these words in Christ’s name:

“I command you, dreadful beast: turn back and retrace your course.”

The serpent bent its slow coils back into the river,

And soon turned around its great burden of venom.

[280] From there it sought the thirsty sands of the farther bank,

Swimming as it slipped through the current and crossed all the waters again.

Serving in obedience, the viper lost its rage;

The unjust venom did not resist the commands of the righteous man.

It happened that the days of the Paschal feast were at hand,

[285] [Col. 0414B] On which the bishop also ate a portion of fish.

The good man added a crawling creature as a dish to taste,

And asked whether there was an abundance of fish.

The minister entrusted with that duty replied

That he had spent the entire day fishing and had caught nothing:

[290] The hook cast with a line from a reed had accomplished nothing,

Nor had he been able to draw any prey into the nets.

To him the shepherd firmly said, with calm authority:

“Go now to the river; you will not be denied a catch.”

Certain hope moved the craftsman, and he hurried to the river.

[295] The banks were filled with a crowd of monks,

So that they might witness the holy words of Martin the prophet,

Whom they knew did not speak in vain, nor utter words that could be refuted.

When the master cast the net from the boat into the river,

The wet ropes glided gently through the glassy Loire.

[300] Soon he confined a huge pike beneath the modest net.

The fish, akin to the waters, was drawn to the shore,

Bound not by the fisherman’s net but by Martin’s word.

The swimming prey offered itself for the saint’s use,

Running toward such a death more as a gift of life.

[305] Arborius, formerly a prefect, also reports a noble sign—

A sign that he saw in the city, bearing witness himself.

When he was placing undefiled gifts upon God’s altar,

And the astonished father was performing the divine rite,

While the priest was blessing Christ’s gifts with his mouth,

[310] And the established offering of body and blood had been placed upon the altar,

A gracious hand suddenly flashed forth in splendid beauty,

[Col. 0414D] Sparkling with the varied brilliance of precious stones.

It appeared everywhere, scattering radiant light like a wheel,

Its arms shimmering with flashes from purple gems,

[315] And its light shining like the sun, its metals glowing golden.

[Note: [Col. 0415C]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

319. Venetian edition and Vatican manuscript: *justi pia dextera*—“the pious right hand of the righteous man”; this should be retained.

325. *Cataclistica.* The same source has *Cataclysa fila*. See what we said above in the notes on book III of the *Life of Saint Martin*, p. 405.

334. *Itachium.* Ithacius, a bishop in Spain, had persecuted the heretic Priscillian to the point of bloodshed and murder. For this reason some avoided him as bloodthirsty and did not join his communion, among them Martin; others defended and followed him, while the Church was divided into factions. The emperor Maximus especially supported Ithacius, who, either at his urging or through his agency, had Priscillian put to death.

The same place. *Tum.* Venetian edition: *cum*.

340. Sulpicius relates the following in chapter 15: “There is no doubt that this storm would also have destroyed a very large number of holy men, with little distinction among the classes of people. For at that time judgment was made merely by the eyes, when someone was judged a heretic more by pallor or clothing than by faith.” And in *History*, book II: “This Ithacius had advanced so far in folly that he summoned all holy men to accusation who either devoted themselves to reading or had resolved to contend in fasts, as though they were associates or disciples of Priscillian.”

341. Martin was also working to prevent the heretics from being condemned to the supreme penalty. As Baronius says under the year 386, no. 33: “It has become customary in the Catholic Church, when someone seeks assistance against heretics from secular magistrates, to preface the request deliberately with a protest, lest he seem to be a partner and follower of the Ithacian party; namely, to declare that he seeks the correction of incorrigible offenders, while nevertheless they are to be punished without the shedding of blood.”

342. Sulpicius reports that Martin labored especially on behalf of Count Narses and the governor Leucadius, both of whom had belonged to Gratian’s party with particularly stubborn zeal … the anger of the victorious veteran.

[Col. 0416C] 344. The bishops favoring Ithacius’s party had assembled at Trier. When they learned that Martin was approaching the city, they conferred with Maximus against him, so that officials would be sent to prevent him from coming nearer unless he first promised to make peace with the bishops who had gathered at Trier on Ithacius’s behalf. He deceived them by asserting that he would remain in the peace of Christ.

347. Venetian edition: *quo prius*—“which earlier.”

352. The emperor had evidently said to Martin that Theognistus had broken the separation out of hatred rather than for cause, and yet was the only one who had meanwhile separated himself from communion; nothing had been changed by the others. Sulpicius, chapter 16. This Theognistus had first absolved Ithacius and later condemned him. Sulpicius, same place.

356. That is, when the emperor had failed to persuade Martin to communicate with the Ithacians, he ordered executioners to be sent against those for whom Martin had requested pardon and release.

[Col. 0416D] 361. Venetian edition and Vatican manuscript: *pars fit*—“becomes a party.”

363. Vatican manuscript: *anxius, angens*—“anxious, distressed”; this should be retained. “On the following day,” says Sulpicius, “Martin, hurrying away from there—from Trier—while returning on the road and groaning sadly, lamented that he had even for an hour been mixed up in the guilty communion. Not far from a village called Andethanna, where the hidden depths of vast forest wildernesses lie, he sat down,” and so forth. Browerus labors to identify the location of this village; he is led to believe that Andethanna should be placed at Echternach, which, he says, is a famous monastery with a village on the Sauer in the territory of Trier, about thirteen miles from the city. “By an easy change,” he adds, “just as Antonnacum became Andernach, so Andethanna became Echterna, as it sounds in the local language.”

371. Vatican manuscript: *nec poteras exire*—“nor could you go out”; this should be retained.

The same place. Venetian edition: *nisi jussa facesses*—“unless you fulfilled the commands”; this should be retained.]

[Col. 0415A] So that the miracles of these things might become more credible.

Arborius himself, a powerful man, says that he then heard

The clatter of heavy gems.

Thus, with faith doubled, the righteous man’s right hand shone,

[320] And an emerald, transferred to the place of a sleeve, flashed there.

O graceful Martin, adorned with a covering of stones,

What a new mantle is yours, whose glittering texture—

Its woof was radiant topaz, its warp jasper,

And gems ran through your tunic in place of wool.

[325] What craftsman’s hand twisted these cataclystic threads?

Who was this artisan, where hyacinth-colored wool runs?

Who could bend rigid gems around the loom’s threads?

These things will be better reported through reverence than through speech.

[Col. 0415B] Why do you seek hidden things and fail to enter the concealed depths of light?

[330] There is something here, human being, to make you marvel, where grace weaves its webs.

A longer sequence of history arises here for us,

But I shall travel by a shorter road, running through an abridgment.

Maximus, directing the reins of empire like a ruler,

Ordered Ithacius to be protected by the authority of arms,

[335] So that no one might seek to condemn him by forensic law—

The inveterate accuser of Priscillian.

He sent armed tribunes by lot to Spain,

To search for the remnants of the heresy and seize their property,

And to condemn those discovered to capital punishment,

[340] Yet in such a way that the savage opportunity would strike everyone.

Therefore, driven by the many evils, the goodness of the blessed man,

As a ready intercessor for Governor Leucadius as well,

Went to Trier, moved by other complaints too.

The bishops approached the ears of the aforesaid prince,

[345] Asking that Martin not enter unless he were received in the peace of the synod.

But the holy man asserted that he remained in the peace of Christ,

while he had previously held aloof from those assemblies.

The bishops again came before the emperor’s court,

Asking that he compel the innocent man to participate with the guilty.

[350] The emperor gently addressed him, urging him

To join the communion of the righteous with the others,

For, he said, only Theognistus had withdrawn in complaint,

Because he did not approve the harmful communion of the brothers.

Since the holy man’s firmness could not be bent,

[355] The high authority of the prince removed him from his sight.

Soon he released executioners, with the sword threatening,

Who were to slaughter those once offended, with the spear striking them down.

When the holy man learned the guise of the treachery about to be unleashed,

He promised the king’s ministers that he would share their communion.

[360] Burning with compassion, he set aside his resistance out of love.

Where guilty intention is absent, communion is likewise free of fault.

Then Martin hurried away, escaping from there.

Meanwhile as he walked, he seethed, burdened, anxious, and increasingly distressed,

Asking why he had consented to the wicked even for the space of an hour.

[365] Having traversed the road through vast silences,

When his companions had gone ahead, he approached Andethanna.

Behold, a holy angel stood before the distinguished man.

Making his identity openly known by his present speech,

And with face revealed, he spoke to him at close range:

[370] “How rightly, Martin, you are pierced with remorse in this place,

And why you cannot depart otherwise unless you fulfill the commands.”

[Note: [Col. 0417C]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

376. Venetian edition: *te deinde redisce, magister*—“then recover yourself, master”; this is preferable.

380. *Diro ulcere.* Manuscript: *de vulnere*—“from the wound.”

385. From that time Martin lived scarcely sixteen years, and afterward attended no synod; he withdrew from all assemblies of bishops. Sulpicius, chapter 15.

388. *Pseudophorum*, or *pseudothyrum*. Ammianus, book XXIV, chapter 4, calls this a hidden door, that is, a doorway concealed at the rear of a building. Horace uses the word in this sense when writing to Torquatus, letter 5, book I:

“Keeping the client hidden by the back entrance.”

See Dufresne’s glossary under this word.

391. Venetian edition: *Ante monasterii, quam*—“before the monastery, than”; this should be retained.

404. Venetian edition and Vatican manuscript: *Denique cum quidam Tyrrhenum*—“Finally, when a certain man was sailing the Tyrrhenian Sea.”

405. *Quod.* Manuscript: *qui*.

408. *Ceruchi* are used for the sails’ yards, as Sirmondus notes in his notes on poem 7, book I, of M. Felix Ennodius. As he says, Lucan, Flaccus, and Apuleius take *ceruchi* for the yards, as though they were horned: for Greek *κεροῦχος* means “horned.” Hence yards are called *κεραῖαι*. Fortunatus explains this further in the following verse:

“Lightly the joined horns of the yard creak.”

Although Isidore, in his glossary, interprets *ceruchi*, or *cerachi*, as the ropes of ships. Is this because they hold or bind the yards—that is, *κεραίας ἔχωσι*? M. Ennodius, in the place cited above:

“For while the linen sails ripple, fastened to the highest ceruchi,” and so forth.

409. *Levis.* Manuscript: *Lenis*.

422. Venetian edition and Vatican manuscript: *data vela secundis*—“the sails given to favorable winds.”

426. *Lycontius.* This Lycontius, one of the former vicars—that is, one who had already served as vicar—is named by Sulpicius in chapter 18.

440. *Quid agant.* It seems that *quid agas* should be read, meaning: if you delay bringing aid, the contagions destroy what you are preserving.

The same place. *Perdunt.* Manuscript: *produnt*.

443. Martin had evidently been divinely warned that Lycontius’s house had been afflicted by that disaster through divine judgment and power—or, to use Sulpicius’s words, he perceived spiritually that the house was being scourged by divine will.]

[Col. 0417A] Between the two wicked deeds, he had purchased a bitter burden of sorrow.

“Now, stand firm and restore the honor of your virtue.

Call yourself back to yourself in your fear, lest guilty things shatter you;

[375] Lest glory perish, or prosperity, slippery as it is, destroy you.

Use your customary courage; then recover yourself, master.

The mishap of one blow does not overwhelm the spirit of a strong athlete.

A hand struck by pain pursues the enemy more fiercely;

A wound fixed in place usually arms courageous minds;

[380] And virtue, newly chastened, grows through a cruel wound,

While repeated wounds grant victory to the warrior.

Thus the angel explained his words in brotherly speech,

And, acting as a brother, encouraged his beloved with admonitions.

So great is God’s care to pull Martin away from his fall.”

[385] The innocent man no longer joined any synod,

And, through losses to his virtue, won new gains.

The event itself nonetheless proves this, in a holy and venerable deed.

For when a sick man, grievously afflicted by a savage demon’s rage,

was approaching the pseudophorum—the hidden rear entrance—of the cell,

[390] and a hostile shadow was torturing him with its grievous power,

before he touched the thresholds of the holy monastery,

the fierce enemy dwelling in the possessed man fled from Martin’s face.

The sight of the man’s blessed countenance was terror to it.

That most dark thing could not endure the light,

Nor could the faithless one evade the steadfast believer.

The savage fled from the good man, the furious from the devout,

The brutal from the kind.

Thus, too, the door of light restrains the blackness.

This medicine of the holy man alone was sufficient:

To see his excellent dwelling was to have merited healing.

[400] [Col. 0417C] The saint lies hidden within the church; outside, the source of healing emerges.

Care is bestowed before the physician’s form is seen.

Nor is it sufficiently marvelous what he gave while present in the body,

Since, under his name, gifts are scattered throughout the world.

When a certain sailor was sailing across the Tyrrhenian Sea,

[405] Making his way toward Rome with the sails flying,

Impatient of the whirlwind, the violence of the wind arose.

The waves leapt up and struck the hollow sails and ropes.

The sluggish pine vessel swayed; the rigging was torn from the yards.

[Col. 0418A] The light joined horns of the yard creaked.

[410] The master, stupefied and helpless in his skill, recoiled from the stern.

The waves stood up, the ship’s defenses fell, and the roar of the sea pressed on.

The prow drank water while the sailor vomited.

Skill perished, experience lay helpless,

Hope fled, anger pressed down, daylight was snatched away, and death threatened.

[415] As certain safety declined amid uncertain dangers,

While everyone trembled, one Egyptian said these words—

A man who had not yet experienced Christ’s gifts and stood outside them:

“God of Martin, rescue us!”

At once the dreadful storm collapsed,

And the sea’s towering swelling settled into the depths.

[420] The wave lay flat around the boat; the surface of the liquid field stood still.

The murmurs of the sea lay motionless.

[Col. 0418B] The vessel sped across the welcome expanse of the desired deep,

And they reached the shore’s edge, their vows borne by favorable winds.

Seeking the harbor, the sailor filled the shallows with his song.

Thus Christ rightly grants honors to his servant according to his merits,

[425] Whose faith, as it travels, fills the earth, the sea, and the stars.

I delight to set down the remaining deeds in venerable narration.

Lycontius, once descended from noble fathers,

Distinguished in honor and rich in faith, proceeding from an ancient line—

When deadly pestilence entered his household,

[430] And a wasting disease penetrated everything with its corrosive force,

So that among the miserable servants and dependents

There was one common slaughter, while each languished divided by sores—

You might have called them corpses prostrate beneath weapons.

[Col. 0418C] For utter extremity honors no distinction of nobility.

The only hope of protection remained: Martin in the world.

A letter was reverently sent to the holy man,

Begging for aid, pleading with this heart and this mouth:

“Unless he quickly comes to our aid, the bitter plague will seize everything,

[440] Dragging everyone through a deadly interval down to Tartarus.

After raging for a long time, what do the contagions accomplish?

They destroy what you are preserving.

You who can bring aid to a crowd suspended over death—

Despairing health requires faithful consolation.”

When the holy man first perceived that these things had been inflicted by a divine scourge,

[Note: [Col. 0419D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

448. Venetian edition: *per tempora mille precatus*—“having prayed for a thousand periods.”

458. Sulpicius reports that Lycontius offered one hundred pounds of silver.

491. Vatican manuscript: *carbone ingesto*—“with coal thrown in.”

504. Vatican manuscript: *se margine tendit*—“spreads itself to the edge.”

505. Venetian edition: *aut speculare*—“or a window.”

[Col. 0420D] 519. *Quod.* Manuscript: *quid*.

The same place. *Quod et obstet.* Venetian edition: *quod obstat*—“which obstructs.”

522. Vatican manuscript: *sedilia ligni*—“wooden seats.”

523. Vatican manuscript: *Prospicit hinc larvas*—“From here he looks out upon the ghosts”; this should be retained.]

[Col. 0419A] He did not fear that he could easily win it through prayer.

[445] Nevertheless, accepting the request of his compassionate friend,

For seven days and as many nights beneath the stars,

He kept watch constantly, relaxing none of his fasts,

Drawing out his continued prayers through a long period,

Nor did he stop until he granted that Lycontius’s prayerful vows

[450] Had been received and healing had returned to the household,

And renewed health had driven away the fleeing ulcer.

When Lycontius learned that the holy man’s labor had prevailed,

He hurried to him and returned thanks with devoted heart.

With his household restored, he repaid his joy with a gift of gratitude,

[455] A gift proportionate to his faith, like that of the centurion

Whom the Lord preferred to Israel with powerful speech,

And whose daughter received healing before he entered the house.

[Col. 0419B] Finally he offered the holy man a great weight of silver,

Thirty times three, with ten more added as the patron’s reward.

He also added these words, supplicating with a restored heart:

“What can I repay you, exalted father, for the gift of life?

[460] This light cannot be bought or sold for any price.

Can the life of a single soul be purchased?

When this one plague afflicted my household,

And no resource remained that could render any repayment,

Behold, through your protection, so many multitudes of my people live—

[465] A numerous throng of my household, of every sex and age.

I marvel that corpses have been restored to solid life,

And those whom I used to serve as they died now serve me.

For as soon as your innermost voice flew up to the stars,

[Col. 0419C] And seemed by its merits to bend the summits of heaven,

So that the oracles of Christ might be made near to you,

And prayers had been laid before the face of the Thunderer,

And the pious voice of the Lord had been recited into his ear,

[475] At once goodness, with aid present, granted healing.

The wasting plague left their bodies limb by limb.

Those who had been able to die suddenly returned to health,

And grew strong in hope, in step, in their vital organs, in sight, and in voice.

The sickness died, buried alive in living flesh,

[480] Therefore, father, take a small tribute from the living,

Enduring it as the least interest while I discharge what I owe:

[source boundary]

But he neither accepted nor rejected what was offered;

before he could properly approach the monastery’s threshold,

[Col. 0419D] he ordered a considerable sum to be given for the redemption of captives.

[485] Thus, blessed man, from a single event he brings forth twin gifts:

to these he gave freedom, to those the means of salvation,

so that now the harsh captives, released from their punishments,

sang out their joy with harmonious spirit and applause.

It is a wonder indeed, if these words shine when related.

[490] One of the brothers came shivering to the cell;

the holy man’s furnace was burning with a coal thrown into it.

So he sits down quickly, snatching, as it were, the profits of the heat,

with his groin uncovered, one foot extended, and his knee spread open.

The holy man, shut within his cell, immediately said:

[495] “Who, naked outside, is violating our dwelling,

with his body exposed, his bare knee and uncovered groin?

What was this? Tell us, learned sophists, I beg you:

did the wall before Martin’s eyes become like linen cloth in the light,

or did a spider weave its agile webs as though with thread,

[500] or nets through openings sparsely crossed by interlaced filaments?

Whence does this structure, so thin and gaping, become visible?

Do the stones rise up, or do they open a cleft into a window?

Or do the hard stones dissolve through a slow-bonding cement,

or does the hut of material open itself with a glassy edge?

[505] Or did it provide a window through which the holy man could pass in light?

Or did the lighter wall yield, folding back in an arch,

and remain unharmed, suspended in the swift stroke?

[Col. 0420B] Or was the nobility of his eyes able to pass through marble,

and did the clearer sight proceed through every obstacle?

[510] Or did a winged messenger fly to the mouth of the enclosed man,

open a passage through what was covered, and enter as a herald where no way existed?

Or, because he was light, did he possess the whole outside within?

While the flesh remained seated, did the spirit move swiftly through the place?

Open these closed things, eloquent teachers; comprehend them, learned men,

[515] you who can do so through numbers, atoms, reasoning, and speech.

Here art flees the eyes: unless you see Christ, you see nothing.

How great is God’s power, how great is Martin’s grace!

By this power the wondrous man accomplishes what man does not know;

by it, through the merit of faith, he explains what even origin obstructs.

[520] What remains should also be recalled in honor of our patron,

for the page hastens to complete its text under his protection.

Perhaps the holy man, seated on hard wooden benches,

was looking from here at two bright twin figures on a hanging rock,

clad in dark garments, stern with gloomy terror,

[525] laboring through deceit, hurling darts of gall,

craftsmen of wickedness, wielding heavy weapons for evil purposes.

With poisoned voice they rolled these serpent-like words:

“What does swelling anger accomplish? Come, Brictio, show yourself!”

They repeated this again and again, until Brictio, wickedly stirred,

[530] burst through the doors and poured insults upon the holy man;

he stirred up many quarrels, a henchman with disturbed mind,

exulting that he possessed greater merit than the saint.

Thus, raging in gesture, he did not recognize himself, bitter man,

a rash judge puffing himself up over the deeds of his own life,

[535] [Col. 0420D] boasting through empty, intolerable bombast,

an idle man moved by the wind, imitating the fluttering shadow of leaves,

stiff-necked and rebellious in his levity,

agitating his mind, flinging out his foot, swelling his chest,

irrational, with his inflated buskin growing larger,

[540] incapable of mastering himself in mind, wavering with wandering judgment,

and savagely pouring bitter abuse upon the priest.

But why does this storm rage against the despised Martin?

Why does it threaten the humble, peaceful man with such savage arrogance?

[Note: [Col. 0421D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

528. Brictio. This Brictio had been educated by Saint Martin in the monastery from childhood and later became a priest. When he began acquiring horses, boys, and more elegant girls, Saint Martin severely rebuked him for it. One day, therefore, he came to Martin full of fury and madness, attacking him with insults and curses; he came close to laying hands on him. He boasted that he was holier than the saint, since he had lived in the monastery from childhood and, unlike Martin, had not been worn out in youth by the squalor of military service, nor, in old age, occupied with visions and old wives’ tales. See Sulpicius, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 20.

535. Vatican Codex: *intolerabiliter*, “intolerably”; this reading is preferable.

536. *Vento*. Perhaps *ventos*, “winds.”

[Col. 0422D] 537. Venetian edition: *levitate rebellem*, “rebellious in levity.”

538. Venetian edition: *pede juncto*, “with foot joined.”

543. Venetian edition: *Quid humilem, placidum tam*, “Why such a humble, peaceful man?”

546. Vatican Codex: *dirus erat graviter qui*, “who was gravely savage.”

554. Vatican Codex and Venetian edition: *indulgentia fluxit*, “mercy flowed”; this reading should be followed.

555. Vatican Codex: *lacrymando rigari*, “to be bedewed with tears.”

577. Venetian edition: *vicem miseris*, etc., “to requite the wretched,” etc.

591. Vatican Codex: *pulcher quam si lucifer exis*, “more beautiful than if you rose as Lucifer”; this reading should be followed.

602. Vatican Codex: *pietas opulens miserando*, “abundant piety by showing mercy.”

611. Vatican Codex: *Tu, precor*, “You, I beg.”

613. Vatican Codex omits *nam*, “for.”

621. Vatican Codex: *trepido verecunde*, “timidly, modestly”; this reading should be followed.]

[Col. 0421A] Why does he serve so many bitter things to a soul excessively sweet?

It is not fitting for a pious or kindly man to hear or endure such things.

They are gravely mistaken who mix wormwood with honey.

Yet he, burning with compassion, inflicted nothing upon his enemy;

placated, he lovingly received the angry man’s bitterness,

soothing his fury and calming him with gentle words,

[550] and he knows how to be a father even without gall toward an enemy.

Nevertheless, when the man pleaded and the delusions had been driven away,

while the formerly furious Brictio returned to his senses,

he approached the bishop, submissive in vow, prayer, and body.

But the holy man’s goodness quickly bent toward mercy.

[555] With him there was no need to ask for a long time, weeping;

nor to hope for pardon for the offender through repeated prayer.

He was more eager to forgive guilt and release the guilty,

and regarded as a loss whatever he had not freely granted;

[Col. 0421B] he counted it as gain for himself to remit debts arising from wrongdoing,

meeting the seeker face to face with gifts of peace,

desiring to be angry with no one and to forgive everyone,

quickly binding only covenants and loosening offenses;

fleeing lest vengeance should ever bring him harm;

[565] practicing the work of compassion—for mercy is sufficient as an avenger—

which, gathering pious gifts, has no need to become vindictive,

increased by every good, whose dowry and glory is peace.

The holy man himself, a soldier in the army of compassion,

always loving covenants and triumphing in the arms of peace,

loosens his merciful heart at the voice of the suppliant,

[570] and, soothing the trembling man in the bosom of pardon,

brought him back and received the guilty man with his customary native compassion.

These were your holocausts, sweet one; these were your sanctuaries and temples;

[Col. 0421C] these were your riches, treasures, kingdoms, and talents,

your flower, fragrance, food, flavor, unmixed wine, cinnamon, balsam, and incense;

[575] all holiness was this, your whole and only concern:

to meditate on Christ with a pious heart and in action,

to refuse repayment, to pity and pardon guilt,

to forgive crimes, remember mercy, and be an altar for the guilty;

hope of the wretched, rout of phantoms, weapon against pursuers,

[580] prey of bands, path of wanderers, care of healers,

one salvation for all, love for all, the one lover—

who could speak words worthy of you, whom the world honors?

[Col. 0421D] What, pious man, is sufficient for you, when the world owes you praise?

Whatever one wishes to recount, the whole universe cannot express it.

[585] Always embracing and retaining Christ in heart and mouth,

not allowing the Lord to depart anywhere without you,

always keeping the Thunderer bound to you by devotion;

bound by prayers, the lover did not release himself,

whose friendly faith bestowed upon you such great citadels

[590] that you rival the sun in rays and the moon in its courses,

shining in splendor, beautiful like the rising star of the firmament;

through God’s radiance, the radiant man himself flashes,

white in his covering, golden with a marvelous diadem.

Therefore, mindful of the suppliant, generous hearer of your servant,

[595] of poor Fortunatus, trembling at the lot of his own guilt,

whose crimes bark all around him with diseased fury,

and whose savage wounds of sin gnaw deep within,

intercede, I beg you, for pardon, man who have attained the crown.

[Col. 0422B] Shepherd, rescue the sheep, lest it remain lame or outside;

stretch out your hand, exalted one; guide my step, direct my mind;

weigh my grave excesses on a lighter scale,

and rather let your rich compassion plead through mercy.

May the soothing applications of gentle medicine calm those excluded from comfort;

[605] stand as mediator between God and the guilty man,

with knees fixed to the ground and palms raised toward the stars,

with words enclosed and spirits penetrating the air.

May you prevail through your merits; when the Judge of the world comes,

you too will be ordered to sit on the right-hand seat,

an arbiter over peoples, a terror to tribes before the tribunal.

[610] How shall I escape the furnace with its roaring flame?

[Col. 0422C] Then, I beg you, conceal my frailty beneath your sacred covering,

and may your cloak defend my trembling self from the tearing fire.

For I know that any guilty man can yield Christ to you,

for Christ joins him to his own kingdom, which will endure through the ages.

[615] I beg you, gracious one, remember your servant in the Lord,

whose light you will behold without end.

Grant pardon, sweet, pious, gentle, kindly patron,

because, while I wished to compose, I injured the flowers with my poem.

But your abundant praise will not be shortened by any brief account,

[620] for God has extended it alike on earth and among the stars.

Set a limit, little book, to your warm but timid account,

[Col. 0422D] making many wrinkles in your spread-out thread,

and, not properly tying the threads, producing a rough fabric at the knot,

hairy, woven as though from the stiff fleece of a camel,

[Note: [Col. 0423B]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

632. Vatican Codex: *Facit hic sua rura*, “Here he makes his own fields.”

635. Venetian edition: *si tamen, urgeres*, “if nevertheless you should press on”; Vatican Codex: *si tamen urgueris*, “if nevertheless you are pressed.”

637. Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, died in the year 576; Fortunatus therefore wrote these books on the Life of Saint Martin before that time.

638. *Remedi*. That is, Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims.

639. Saint Medardus, bishop of Noyon, had been buried at Soissons. A basilica was begun there in his memory by Chlothar and completed by Sigibert. See Book II, chapter 20.

642. *Augustam*. Walser discusses Augsburg near the end of Book I of his *Augsburg History*. Among other things he says: “A place gently elevated on a very broad plain near the confluence of the Vindo and Lycus, close to the Danube for convenience yet not exposed through excessive proximity to the dangers of Germanic incursions, situated in the middle of Vindelicia, was given the name Augusta, with the additional designation of Vindelicorum, to distinguish it from other cities called by the same name,” etc. See Cluverius, *German Antiquities*, on Vindelicia and Noricum, chapter 4, where he discusses Augsburg at greater length and examines Walser’s testimony.

The same passage, *Vindo*. The Vatican Codex reads: “which the Virdo and Licca make flow.” Paulus Diaconus likewise calls it Virdo when describing Fortunatus’s journey into Gaul in Book II, chapter 13 of his *History of the Lombards*.

643. *Afrae*. Venetian edition: *virginis Afrae*, “of the virgin Afra.”

645. *Breonum*. The same edition: *Qua vicina sedent Breorum*, “where the lands of the Breonians sit nearby”; corrupt. See what we said in the notes to Book I, chapter 1 of Fortunatus’s works.

647. *Valentini*. Browerus interprets this as the man who, according to Aegippius, was a contemporary of Saint Severinus, apostle of Noricum, and who, chosen from the abbacy, became bishop of Raetia, perhaps at Passau. Driven out from there, he later lived a holy life in the Alps. He was buried at the fortress of Magiensis, or Maias, on 7 January. His Life appears in Surius, volume IV; see it under 4 August.

648. The river Birrus, says Cluverius in Book I, chapter 20 of *Italy Antiqua*, is now the Aicha, flowing into the Aisacum near the village of Pyrhach, etc. Paulus Diaconus mentions this river in Book II, chapter 13 of his *History of the Lombards*.

650. Venetian edition: *superbit Aminthus*, “Aminthus proudly rises.” Vatican Codex: *Avuntus*. Cluverius corrects this to *Aguntus*. Aguntus, Browerus adds, lies at the same bend where Lugdunum, Toletus, and Mediolanum are situated: a town in Noricum celebrated by Pliny, Ptolemy, and Antoninus, and also mentioned by Paulus Diaconus in his *History of the Lombards*. Cluverius says in *German Antiquities*, on Vindelicia and Noricum, chapter 4: “From the town of Lienz, which is Loncium in Antoninus, proceeding twenty-two miles westward toward the winter sunset, one sees the town of Doblach, which I interpret as Aguntum of Pliny, Ptolemy, and Antoninus.”

651. *Julia*. See what we noted at Book I, chapter 1.

653. *Foro Juli*. Forum Julii was a Roman colony, today commonly called Cividal, or Cividal del Friuli. This name corruptly means the “city of the forum of Julius.” Paulus Diaconus, giving the origin and reason for the name in Book II, chapter 14, says: “Aquileia was the chief city of this Venetia; in its place Forum Julii is now regarded, so called because Julius Caesar had established a marketplace of commerce there.”

The same passage. Vatican Codex: *Domine principis*, “of the lord prince”; corrupt. In the Venetian edition, some verses are thereafter missing and others are read in extremely corrupt form.

654. *Per rupes, Osope, tuas*. Commonly, and most corruptly: *per rupes, gelidisque tuas*, “through your crags and your icy [heights].” Osopum, or Osopium, is a fortress on the river Tagliamento, not far from the village of Venzone, in Venetia and on the borders of Austria and Carinthia.

The same passage. *Labitur*. Vatican Codex: *lambitur*, “is licked”; this reading should be retained.

655. *Reunia Tiliamenti*. We have corrected the extremely corrupt words *Reunatilia montis* from Cluverius. The Vatican Codex itself supports this correction, reading *Reunia Teliamentis*. The Venetian edition also comes close, reading *Renuta Teliamentis*. According to the same Cluverius, Reunia is a town or fortress commonly called Ragogna, on the left bank of the Tagliamento. Paulus mentions it in Book IV, chapter 38, and Book VI, chapter 3. Leander, in his *Description of Forum Julii*, speaks of Reunia as reported by Browerus: “It is the town of Rheuna, situated upon the Tagliamento where the overhanging mountain and the hill of Princianus constrict the river; and in the Celtic language this place-name meant ‘ford.’”

658. Vatican Codex: *si forte accesseris*, “if by chance you approach”; this reading should be retained.

659. *Cantianos*. Canitus, Cantianus, and Cantianilla were martyrs of the distinguished Anician family at Aquileia. Under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian they were beheaded, as Cardinal Caesar Baronius records under 21 May. Their acts are circulated under the name of Ambrose. On these martyrs see also the learned Ruinart in the preface to the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, no. 22.]

[Col. 0423A] when it was fitting for Martin’s silk robes to be drawn out,

or shining purple woven beneath a golden thread,

or hyacinth-colored cloth intermingled with white,

or a varied crown of roses, lilies, and gems to be painted—

let your withered tongue fall silent and ask your pardon, little book.

[630] Content with this alone, go humbly to the walls of Tours,

where Martin the priest possesses his venerable tomb;

may the honor of his grave cause him to protect his own fields,

and may he grant the help of compassion, for he is generous everywhere.

He knows that nothing is mine, but that his gifts return to him.

[635] Even so, you will press onward, entering rashly once more.

From there you will proceed quietly to the citadel of Paris,

which Germanus now governs, and Dionysius once governed.

If you go on foot, venerate the tombs of Remigius,

and embrace the temples of the pious brother Medardus.

[640] If you are permitted to travel along barbarian rivers,

[Col. 0424A] so that you can cross the Rhine and the Danube peacefully,

proceed to Augsburg, through which the Vindo and Lycus flow.

There you will venerate the bones of the sacred martyr Afra.

If you have time to travel, and the Bavarian does not obstruct you,

[645] where the lands of the Breonians sit nearby, proceed across the Alps,

entering where the Oenus rolls in a swift current.

From there seek the temples of blessed Valentinus;

making for the Noric fields, where the Birrus turns in its waters,

take the road along the Drava, where the fortresses rise upon the slopes.

[650] Here Aguntum, seated upon a hill in the mountains, proudly rises;

from here seek the steep roads where the Julian Alps extend,

rising higher, and the mountain proceeds into the clouds.

[Col. 0424B] From there go out to Forum Julii, named after its prince,

through your crags, Osope, where the river glides in its waters,

and above the waters stands Reunia of the Tilavemptus.

[655] From there proceed through the Venetian passes and across the level fields,

making your way beneath the mountain fortresses along the difficult heights.

Or, if by chance you approach the city of Aquileia,

venerate exceedingly the Cantian martyrs, friends of the Lord,

[660] [Note: [Col. 0425C]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

661. *Paulum*. See what we said about Paul, bishop of Aquileia, in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 15.

666. *Felicem*. Read what we said about Felix there, no. 24.

668. *Cenetam*. The manuscript has *Cenedam*; the Venetian edition, *per semitam gradiens* (“advancing along the path”), corruptly. See what we said in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 6.

675. *Joanni*. Nothing is found in Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra* about this John, if indeed, as seems likely, he was bishop of Padua. He appears to have sat between Peter Limianus and Virgilius, who in 579 attended the council of Aquileia celebrated by the patriarch Elias; see Ughelli on him.

677. *Retenone*. The manuscript has *Retinone*. Cluverius, book I of *Ancient Italy*, chapter 18, investigates the location of the river Reteno. From Aelian’s *History of Animals*, book XIV, chapter 8, he thinks it was the ancient Eretenus, which rises at equal distances between Vicenza and Rovereto and is commonly called the Lagno or Lagna. It passes Vicenza at a distance of no more than four miles, washes the town of Montagnana, crosses two lakes, and finally flows into the Athesis near the town of Anguillara. [Col. 0425D]

678. The same Cluverius wishes this passage of Fortunatus to be read as follows:

> *Si Patavina tibi pateat via, pergis ad urbem.*  
> *Hinc tibi Brinta fluens, iter est, Retenusque secundus,*  
> *Ingrediens Athesim; Padus excipit inde Phaselo:*  
> *Mobilis unde tibi rapitur ratis amne citato.* [Col. 0426C]

> “If the road to Padua lies open to you, you proceed to the city. From here your route is the flowing Brenta, with the Reteno second; entering the Athesis, the Po then receives you in a little boat, from which your moving vessel is swept along for you by the swift stream.”

“For who,” he says, “would believe that the Po enters the Athesis?” Cluverius also relates that those who wrote *Retenone secundo* thought Fortunatus’s river was the Reno, which within the city of Vicenza flows into the Lesser Meduacus, now commonly called the Bacchiglione. Yet this opinion does not seem unacceptable to me, since the Lesser Meduacus, into which the Reno flows, according to Cluverius’s testimony and as we ourselves know, joins the Brenta at Padua and with it empties into the Adriatic gulf; Fortunatus could therefore rightly say, “Here your route is the flowing Brenta,” and so forth. As for the words that follow, *ingrediens Athesim*, I would rather understand them as if they said *ingrederis Athesim* (“you enter the Athesis”): the subject is therefore not the river Po entering the Athesis, but the entire address is directed to the little book. Fortunatus is indeed sometimes found to have been freer in constructing a sentence than the rules not only of meter but even of grammar seem to permit. [Col. 0426D] Thus the same Fortunatus speaks in book IV, poem 14:

> *Nam quotiens monachus peccati est vulnere fixus,*  
> *Missus ad artificem, certa medela fuit.*

> “For whenever a monk was pierced by the wound of sin, once sent to the craftsman, the cure was certain.”

And in the poem *On Virginity*, p. 268, the sentence is constructed in the same way at the verse *Hanc Deus ingrediens* (“God entering her”), and so forth.

683. *Pauli sub*. The Vatican Codex has *parili sub* (“under an equal”).

686. *Et pete*. The manuscript has *expete* (“seek out”).

695. *Fenestris*. The manuscript has *fenestrae* (“windows,” nominative).

698. *Medicos*. Perhaps *medico* (“by a physician”). In the same place the Vatican Codex has *Et praesens medicis* (“and present among physicians”).

699. The Venetian edition has *munere sancti* (“by the gift of the saint”).]

[660] and the blessed martyr Fortunatus’s urn;

eagerly adore the pious bishop Paul,

who wished to convert me from my earliest years.

If you take that road, where Concordia girds itself,

Augustine and precious Basilius are there.

[665] Where my Treviso lies, if you enter gently,

please seek the illustrious companion Felix,

to whom Martin once restored the light together with me,

passing through Ceneda, and the friends of Duplavenum,

where my native soil is, through the blood and seat of my parents,

[670] the origin of my father’s offspring, my brother, sister, and line of nephews.

I honor them in heart and faith; briefly, I ask you, convey my greetings to them.

If the road to Padua is open to you, proceed to the city.

[Col. 0425B] There, I beg you, kiss the sacred tomb of blessed Justina,

whose wall contains in painted figures the deeds of Martin.

[675] Or where the work of salvation hangs from lofty John,

and, through songs, from his offspring joined to our companions.

Here your route is the flowing Brinta, with Retenus second;

enter the Athesis; then the Padus receives you in a little boat,

from which your moving vessel is swept along by the swift stream.

[680] From there seek Ravenna, the pleasing city, with greater delight,

passing through the pulpits of the saints in their holy places.

Adore the tomb of the outstanding martyr Vitalis,

and that of gentle Ursicinus, blessed under Paul’s lot;

again touch the threshold of precious Apollinaris,

[685] pouring yourself humbly upon the ground, and run through all the temples.

And seek Martin’s tomb, by whose right as guardian of the shrine

[Col. 0426A] the author restored to me the light already despaired of,

he who bestows gifts; at least, I beg you, return words in exchange.

Where the basilica of Paul and John has its roof,

there the wall preserves the holy man’s form beneath his image.

The sweet painting is worthy of embrace in its color.

Beneath the feet of the righteous man, the wall has an artistically made window;

[690] a lamp is there, whose fire floats in a glass vessel.

As I hasten to this place, while strong pain twists me,

my eyesight fading, I groaned at the windows;

but as soon as I touched the blessed light with the consecrated oil,

that fiery vapor withdrew from my languishing forehead,

[695] and, present there, he drove diseases away with soothing ointment.

The saint’s gifts did not forget my eyes,

for the faithful care of my eyes returned before my eyes,

[Col. 0426B] and I shall remember this as long as I remain in light and body.

With more eager affection, I beg you, seek the companions there.

If you speak to the companions, you will earn pardon through your compassion.

I offer them the material from which, with rounded speech,

[705] they may compose flourishing poems on Martin’s deeds,

and weave them with brilliant talent, to be scattered throughout the East.

Although that man shines through his merits and does not need these things,

his rejoicing grace and fame occupy the world’s roads,

filling the fields, entering the sea, flashing above the stars,

[710] distributing marvelous cures to the peoples as a largesse;

by serving his Lord he receives everything as a gift,

and wherever Christ has a name, Martin has honor.

[Col. 0427]

# INDIVIDUAL BOOKS ON THE DESTRUCTION OF THURINGIA, IN THE PERSON OF RADEGUNDIS. (C,S)

[Note: [Col. 0427] On the destruction of Thuringia. In the Trier manuscript this was the title: “Here begins another work by the same Fortunatus on the destruction of Thuringia,” according to Browerus. This book, as well as the two following ones, is missing from the Venetian edition and from the Vatican manuscripts. Gregory of Tours recounts the destruction of Thuringia and the reason why the Frankish kings Theuderic and Chlothar made war upon the Thuringians in Book III, chapter 7 of his *History of the Franks*.]

## BOOK ONE.

[Note: [Col. 0427] Fortunatus describes the destruction of Thuringia under the person and name of Radegundis. He represents her expressing longing and prayers for her absent cousin Hamalefredus. Radegundis is also introduced mourning her brother, who was unjustly killed, and lamenting bitterly that she herself had been unable to perform the final funeral rites for him. Finally, she addresses this book and asks it to bring greetings to her exiled relatives and to bring letters back to her from them.]

[Note: [Col. 0427C]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

15. *Curribus*. Manuscript: *crinibus*, “hair.”

16. *Amati*. Manuscript: *Ametys*.

55. *Vixerat in spatium* appears to mean the same as “an interval which would not have brought Hamalefredus back,” with Radegundis imagining that she is prolonged through a long period of time.]

[Col. 0427A] The condition of war is grievous, the fate of affairs envious—

how suddenly, in a single collapse, proud kingdoms fall!

The palace that formerly flourished with courtly splendor—

now mournful ash covers it instead of chambers.

[5] The lofty structures that had stood happily for a long stretch of time,

overcome by a massive disaster, lie burned.

The heights that gleamed adorned with radiant metal—

pale ash has overwhelmed the shining roofs.

Power, sent captive beneath a hostile master,

[10] has fallen; lofty glory lies in a low place.

Standing at the same age, the gleaming crowd of servants

is soiled by funeral dust, having fulfilled its day.

Surrounded by a bright circle of powerful attendants,

possessing no tombs, it lacks the honor of death.

[15] Glittering gold, surpassing flame-belching fire upon chariots,

lies strewn upon the ground, with the milk-white beloved.

Alas, the unburied corpses have covered the field,

and the whole people lies thus in a single tomb!

Let Troy no longer alone lament its ruins:

[20] the land of Thuringia too has suffered equal slaughter.

From here a matron is dragged away, bound with torn hair,

unable to bid a sad farewell to her household gods.

She was not permitted to press kisses upon the captive doorpost,

nor to turn her face toward places she would see no more.

[25] Barefoot she trod upon her husband’s blood,

and the loving sister passed by while her brother lay there.

A child torn from his mother’s embrace hung from his mouth,

and no one offered funeral water with a lament.

By grievous fate, it is less painful to lose a child in this way;

[30] the breathless mother also lost her pious tears.

I cannot equal in lament even the barbarian woman,

nor swim through the whole sad lake of tears.

Each person had his own tears; I alone, but the grief of all,

have that public sorrow as my private one.

[35] [Col. 0428A] Fortune took thought for the men whom the enemy struck,

so that I, the sole survivor, might mourn for everyone.

I am compelled to lament not only my dead relatives;

I also weep for those whom blessed life still retains,

often striking my eyes against my wet face.

[40] Murmurs lie hidden, enclosed, and my sorrow does not fall silent.

I gladly watch to see whether some breeze announces good news,

but no shadow of any kinsman appears.

The one whose tender presence comforted me with loving affection—

hostile fortune has released him from my embrace.

[45] Or does the fact that I am absent mean that my care does not torment you,

and that bitter disaster has carried away our sweet affection?

Or remember what I, Radegundis, was to you from your earliest years,

Hamalefredus.

How much you once loved me, sweet child,

[50] [Col. 0428B] and how, kindly son, you were parent to me as your father’s brother.

Whatever an extinguished father could be, whatever a mother,

whatever a sister or brother could be—you alone were all these to me.

Held by your pious hands—alas!—hanging upon your gentle kisses,

I, a little one, was soothed by your peaceful breath.

[55] The time had lasted only as long as the hour in which you might have returned;

now ages flee, and I do not hear your words.

I turned over the raging cares struck against my breast,

as though I might be summoned by them: when or from where, my kinsman?

If your father, your mother, or royal concern held you,

[60] while you hurried away, you were already slow for me.

It was an omen of fate, because I would soon be deprived of you, dear one;

importunate love does not know how to have a fixed day.

I was tormented with anxiety if one house did not shelter you.

When you went out, the very word “departure” made me afraid.

[65] Now the East shades you, and the West shades us;

the wave of the Red Sea holds you, while the ocean’s sea holds me.

[Note: [Col. 0429D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

71. *Parentum*. Fortunatus uses the word *parent*, “parent,” for a relative or kinsman, as above and in what follows.

124. Concerning Radegundis’s brother, killed by Chlothar, we said something in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 59.

[Col. 0430D] 134. *Percutitur*. Manuscript: *perculitur*, “is struck down.”

145. Radegundis attributes her brother’s death to her own fault because, when he wished to leave Gaul, she had retained him through her affection and love.

163. *Superis* is used for *superstitibus*, “survivors.”]

[Col. 0429A] Between lovers the whole world lies,

separating those whom no places had previously divided.

As much as the earth contains, so much has divided the lover;

[70] if there were more fields, the journey would have gone farther.

Yet may you be where the better prayers of your parents hold you,

more prosperous than the land of Thuringia gave you.

Here I am rather tortured, weighed down by powerful complaints:

why do you wish to send me no sign of yourself?

[75] The one whom I love but do not see—would that a letter had painted his face,

or an image brought back the man whom distant places hold.

With what virtue you restore your ancestors, with what praise your relatives,

as though the blush of a noble father played upon your face.

Believe me, my kinsman: if you gave words, you would not be wholly absent;

[80] a speaking page sent to me would be part of my brother.

Everyone has a gift; I have not even the consolation of tears—

what a crime! The more I love, the less I receive.

If others seek servants by the law of compassion,

why, then, am I passed over, though joined by blood, my kinsman?

[85] To redeem a servant, the master himself often crosses the Alps,

breaking through frozen waters compacted with snow.

He enters shadowy caves in cleft rocks;

no former obstacle restrains his ardent affection.

When the lover has no guide, he runs barefoot,

[90] and, though the enemy forbids it, carries off his own prizes.

He passes through opposing ranks and through his own wounds;

to seize what he desires, love spares not even itself.

But I, hanging upon every moment for your sake,

scarcely enjoy any space for care, peace of mind, or rest.

[95] [Col. 0429C] I ask what places hold you when the breeze whistles;

if you fly through the clouds, I demand the hanging place.

Does warlike Persia desire you, or Byzantium,

or the riches of the city of King Alexander?

Or do you reside near the citadel of Jerusalem,

[100] where Christ, God from a virgin mother, was born?

And since this letter has revealed none of these things,

it has taken up its weapons of sorrow all the more heavily.

But if neither land nor sea sends me any sign,

would that a bird, arriving, might bring favorable news!

[105] If the sacred cloisters of the monastery did not hold me,

I would appear unexpectedly in whatever region you inhabit.

Ready, I would cross stormy waters in a ship that breaks the waves;

through winter winds I would move joyfully over the waters.

Struggling more strongly, I would press upon the hanging waves,

[110] and the lover would not fear what the familiar person fears.

If hostile rains should loosen the vessel’s hull,

I would seek you, carried across the sea on a plank as an oarsman.

If ill fortune prevented me from seizing any timber,

I would come to you, exhausted, swimming with my hand.

[115] When I looked upon you, I would deny the dangers of exile,

and soon you would lighten the sweet burden of shipwreck.

[Col. 0430A] Or if my final fate should snatch away my lamenting life,

the sand would carry my tomb into your hands.

I would go as a lifeless corpse before your pious eyes,

[120] so that you might at least be moved to my funeral rites.

You who scorn the tears of the living would weep and be drenched in tears,

and would give lamentation, though now you deny me words.

Why do I flee from recalling it, my kinsman? Why do I postpone my grief?

Why are you silent about the deep sorrow over the death (a) of my brother?

[125] How the innocent man fell into unjust ambushes,

and was torn from the world despite the faith pledged to him—

and why should I bring back buried sorrow by a new lament,

and suffer it again while I speak in tears?

While he hurried, wishing to see your face,

[130] [Col. 0430B] and his own desire was not fulfilled because my love stood in the way,

while he refused to give me what was hard and inflicted wounds upon himself,

he who feared to injure me became the cause of grief.

The young man was struck down while his tender beard was still covered with down;

I, his absent sister, did not see the dreadful funeral.

[135] I not only lost him, but did not close his pious eyes,

nor, bending over him, offer the final words.

I did not warm your cold limbs with the warmth of my tears,

nor receive kisses from my dear one as he died.

In my misery I did not cling weeping to his neck in an embrace,

[140] nor warm his body, breathless, in my ill-fated breast.

Life was denied me, because the departing breath from my brother

should have been snatched from his mouth by his sister.

What did I do, that I did not go as a companion chosen for the bier?

Is even my love not permitted to adorn the dead?

[145] [Col. 0430C] Believe me, brother, I am impious and guilty of your death—

I alone was your death, and I gave you no tomb.

Once I left my homeland; twice I remained captive,

and again I endured enemies while my brother lay dead.

Then father, mother, uncle, and relatives,

[150] whom I was to mourn in the tomb, this grief restored to me.

No day is free of tears after my brother’s funeral,

for he carried our joys with him to the realm of the dead.

Thus, in my misery, our sweet parents came to their end;

royal blood, in this succession, was their origin.

[155] The evils I endured I could not recount face to face,

nor, wounded as I am, am I consoled by speaking with you.

I beg you, serene kinsman, let your page now run to me,

[Col. 0430D] so that a kindly tongue may soothe my powerful disease.

And I have this same concern for your sisters,

whom I cherish with the love of kindred hearts.

[160] I am not permitted to embrace the members of my family whom I love,

nor eagerly kiss both their eyes, sister that I am.

If, as I desire, they remain among the living, I beg you to convey them greetings,

and carry them dear kisses in place of my prayers.

[165] [Note: [Col. 0431A]

165. Radegundis seems to wish Hamalefredus to commend her to the Frankish kings, although otherwise their piety and goodness toward her were well known. It must therefore be said that some relationship or exchange of letters existed between the Frankish kings and Hamalefredus. Hamalefredus was serving as a soldier, and in the East, as we shall say below; hence Radegundis addresses him, already dead, in Book III:

“Do you send me this aid from your military service?”]

[Col. 0431A] “I beg you to commend me to the Frankish kings,

who honor me with such maternal affection.

May you enjoy life-giving breath for a long time,

and may my welfare bloom through the honor you receive.”

[Col. 0432A] Christ, favor my prayers: may this page behold lovers.

[170] And may the painted letter return with sweet marks,

so that the slow hope that torments him through long periods of time

may be relieved when prayers follow it at swift speed.

## BOOK TWO. TO JUSTIN THE YOUNGER EMPEROR AND SOPHIA, AUGUSTI.

[Note: [Col. 0431C] To Justin the Younger. Many attribute this poem under the name *Itinerary*, as we noted in the Preface. We explained in the *Life of Fortunatus*, no. 55, what occasion led to the writing of this poem. We also noted, under Book I, chapter 21, that a piece of the holy cross was sent as a gift by the same Justin and Sophia to Radegundis or to the city of Rome.]

[Col. 0431] [Note: [Col. 0431] In this poem Fortunatus begins with the glory of the most august and undivided Trinity. He then embraces the praises of the emperor Justin, especially commending his orthodox judgment and his pious care and diligence in defending religion. He next celebrates the praises of the Augusta Sophia, from whom he recalls that a portion of the Lord’s cross was sent as a gift to Radegundis, and therefore extols her beneficence toward the whole West. Finally, in Radegundis’s name, he offers prayers for the long duration and prosperity of their empire.]

[Note: [Col. 0431D]

[In this note, numbers refer to lines.]

16. Theophanes, under the first year of Justin, says: “Justin held sound views concerning the faith in all respects.” He succeeded Justinian in the year 566.

28. *Albis*. The Albis is a river of Alemannia. Sidonius Apollinaris mentions it in his *Panegyric*, recited before the emperor Avitus:

“and he binds the Chatti

with the marshy waters of the Albis . . .”

39. Justin had scarcely obtained the empire when he saw the Church being greatly troubled by dissensions over the three controversial Chapters. He imposed silence upon the parties, declaring: “Henceforth no one should quarrel under any pretext over persons or syllables.” By these words, Pagius adds under the year 566, he perhaps understood the person of Theodore, as well as the writings of Theodoret and Ibas, and also the question that had most recently arisen concerning whether Christ’s body was corruptible or incorruptible. A single syllable had carried the most distinguished bishops of the Roman Empire into exile, far from their sees. Fortunatus seems to indicate these exiles in this passage. See Cardinal Noris, *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, part II, chapter 9.]

[Col. 0431B] The highest glory belongs to the Father, the Son, and the life-giving Spirit;

one God, to be worshiped in this Trinity.

Majesty is threefold in persons, simple in substance,

equal, co-sharer, and coeternal with itself.

[5] One virtue remains, the same; one power belongs to the three:

whatever the Father can do, the Begotten and the Spirit themselves can do.

Distinct indeed in persons, but joined in power,

of one nature, equal in strength, light, and throne.

The Trinity was always with itself, reigning without time,

[10] needing no use of anything and incapable of receiving increase.

Highest glory to you, creator and redeemer of the world,

who, being just, grant Justin as a head in the world.

He rightly claims the citadel of dominion over kings,

pleasing the heavenly King by serving him.

[15] [Col. 0431C] How deservedly he rules Rome and the Roman world,

who follows what the chair of Peter teaches as doctrine!

What Paul proclaimed everywhere, one trumpet among thousands,

he poured from his mouth as salt upon the stupefied nations.

His tongue’s four-sided wheel circles its axis,

[20] and through the faith of his speech cold hearts grow warm.

Highest glory to you, creator and redeemer of the world,

who, being just, grant Justin as a head in the world.

The faith of the Church, troubled, now shines solidified,

and the revered law returns to its ancient place.

[25] [Col. 0432B] Render vows to God, because the new purple, whatever

the Council of Chalcedon decreed, upholds.

For this, Gaul also sings through your merits, Augustus;

for this the Rhône, Rhine, Danube, and Elbe act.

Under the western sky, Galicia heard what had happened,

[30]

Equal, coeternal, and consort with himself.

[5] One virtue, abiding the same; one power shared by the three:

Whatever the Father can do, the Begotten can do, and the Spirit likewise;

Distinct indeed in persons, but joined in power,

Of one nature, equal in strength, light, and throne.

The Trinity was always with itself, reigning without time,

[10] Needing nothing, nor capable of containing.

Highest glory to you, creator and redeemer of all things,

Who grant Justin, the just man, as head of the world.

He rightly claims the citadel as ruler over kings,

And by serving the heavenly King pleases him.

[15] [Col. 0431C] How deservedly he rules Rome and the Roman world,

He who follows the dogma proclaimed by the chair of Peter!

What Paul proclaimed everywhere, one trumpet among thousands,

He poured from his mouth as salt upon the senseless nations.

His tongue’s wheel circles the square axis,

[20] And by the faith of his eloquence cold hearts grow warm.

Highest glory to you, creator and redeemer of all things,

Who grant Justin, the just man, as head of the world.

The faith of the Church, once troubled, shines forth made firm,

And the venerable law returns to its ancient place.

[25] [Col. 0432B] Pay your vows to God, for the new purple, whatever

The Council of Chalcedon decreed, upholds.

For this, Augustus, Gaul sings in praise of your merits;

For this the Rhône, the Rhine, the Ister, and the Elbe resound.

Under the western sky Galicia heard of the deed,

[30] And nearby Cantabria reports it to the Basque.

The pious story of the faith runs to the world’s farthest peoples,

And across the Ocean the British land gives its support.

How well, as a lover, you share your care with the Lord!

He makes your causes his own; behold, you make his yours.

[35] Christ gives you aid, and you repay Christ with honor:

He gave you the summit of power, and you in turn give back faith.

There was nothing on earth that he could give more for ruling;

[Col. 0432C] Nor could you give anything more valuable than life-giving faith.

The Fathers, placed in exile for Christ’s name,

[40] Then returned to themselves when you received the diadem.

Released from prison and restored to their former seat,

They declare that you are the one universal good.

Healing the pains of so many confessors, Augustus,

You come as a single remedy to countless peoples.

[45] Thracian, Italian, Scythian, Phrygian, Daga, Dalmatian, Thessalian, African—

Whatever each deserved by his homeland, he now offers vows to you.

[Note: [Col. 0433C]

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

52. Cui. The manuscript has Hinc.

[Col. 0434C] 66. Subrigis. The manuscript has Surrigit.]

[Col. 0433A] Your praise, prince, has run around the world with the sun;

Wherever the human race exists, there your honor enters.

Highest glory to you, creator and redeemer of all things,

[50] Who grant Justin, the just man, as head of the world.

Sophia, lofty in her fortunate years, obtains

The august rank, equal in merit to his.

She cherishes and adorns the holy places with pious, steadfast love,

And by this vow brings herself nearer to heaven.

[55] Her first faith, flashing from the eastern sky,

Sent shining gifts to God in the west.

At the request of Queen Radegund, the Thuringian woman,

She offered the sacred gifts of the desired cross.

Upon which Christ, deigning to assume flesh, hung,

[60] And with his blood washed away our wounds.

[Col. 0433B] Highest glory to you, creator and redeemer of all things,

Because lofty Sophia holds the august rank.

O piety, whose love of Christ pours faith everywhere

From its gracious spring thus far!

[65] Behold, with equal devotion you two Augusti contend on either side:

You raise up your own sex; he raises up his.

You, a man, restore Constantine; you, a pious woman, restore Helena.

As the honor is alike, so too is the love of the cross.

She discovered the means of help; you scatter salvation everywhere;

[70] What was first the East fills the West as well.

Highest glory to you, creator and redeemer of all things,

Because lofty Sophia holds the august rank.

Through you the Lord’s cross claims the whole world for itself;

Where it was unknown, now seen, it will cover it.

[75] [Col. 0434A] Greater confidence in Christ came to the people,

When hope, seen with the eyes, beholds the aid of salvation.

O faith doubled in the senses, when through your gift

Souls believe more fully what they prove by the testimony of the cross.

By honoring this, Augusta, you cultivate what the Apostle urges to be ploughed in the wood;

[80] Here, by your word, you make the field glad.

This fame now finds favor wherever the north extends;

The east and west serve you with their voices.

From there the Roman, from here the Barbarian himself,

The German, Batavian, Basque, and Briton, proclaim your praises.

[85] May your portion, Augusta, flourish with the cross forever,

For which you cause vows to grow in the farthest lands.

Prostrate on the ground, suppliant Radegund worships this,

And asks your rule for long years.

[Col. 0434B] Watering it with tears, joined to her sisters,

[90] She prays that your faith may reap abundant joys from this.

May you remain happily the wife of Prince Justin,

Sophia, encircled with the sacred patrician rank.

Ruling the Roman realms, the Senate grants you its rights,

And the purple-clad people may honor you as their mistress.

[95] May God add heavenly vows to your fortunate vows,

And may what Radegund loves not perish for you.

She, who pours herself out in the dust and prays with unceasing song,

Asks that your crown may endure through generous ages.

Always doing good in vow, mind, understanding, and zeal:

[100] May she be your concern, and may she remember you.

## BOOK THREE. TO ARTACHIN

[Note: [Col. 0433D] To Artachis. The manuscript has Artachin. This poem is entitled *On the Destruction of Thuringia* in Trithemius. The Trier manuscript restores: “To Artarchis, Radegund’s nephew.” From Browerus.]

[Col. 0433] [Note: [Col. 0433] In this poem Radegund is introduced expressing her grief over the destruction of Thuringia and the ruin of her people. She then says that the hope she had placed in her full brother and her cousin Hamalefredus, the survivors of her family, was extinguished along with them; and she laments their fate most bitterly. Finally, she asks Artachis, whom she calls her nephew, to take the place of those relatives to whom she was bound by a closer relationship, through affection and the other duties of kinship.]

[Note: [Col. 0433D]

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

7. Hermenefridus was Radegund’s maternal uncle or paternal uncle; he was later thrown from the wall of the city of Tolbiacum and died, through the action and treachery—as was believed—of King Theodoric. See Gregory of Tours, Book III, chapters 7 and 8.

14. Here Radegund seems to be referring to her preceding letter, or poem, which she had written to Hamalefredus, not knowing where in the world he was; in reply to that letter, she received the bitterest news of Hamalefredus’s death.]

[Col. 0433D] After the ashes of my homeland and the fallen summits of my ancestors,

Which Thuringian soil suffered in the enemy’s battle-line—

If I speak of wars brought to an end by an ill-fated conflict,

To what tears must I, a captured woman, first be dragged?

[5] What leisure have I to mourn this people crushed by death?

Or that my beloved family has fallen in successive disasters?

[Col. 0434D] For first my father fell, and then my uncle followed,

And each parent fixed a grievous wound in me.

My brother’s branch still remained, but under an evil fate

[10] The sand of the grave likewise pressed me down with him.

With all extinguished—alas, how cruelly the heart of the mourner suffers!—

You alone who remained, Hamalefredus, do you lie dead?

[Note: [Col. 0435B]

[In this note, the numbers refer to the lines.]

16. In the book *On the Destruction of Thuringia*, Hamalefredus is said to have lived in the East; here he is now described as having followed military service. It therefore seems that he served under the Eastern emperors and perhaps fell in battle.

35. Should this Artachis, or Artarchis, be called the son of Hamalefredus’s sister? Radegund may perhaps be referring to her in the following verse:

“Together with your pious mother may this lasting care belong to you,” etc.

For she may have followed her brother to the East and married one of the Greeks; especially since the name Artarchis does not differ in sound from a Greek name. Certainly Radegund herself had neither brother nor sister surviving from whom she could have had a nephew. Therefore he was either Hamalefredus’s son or the son of his sister. And if in Book I Radegund does not hesitate, because of the bond of affection, to call herself the sister of Hamalefredus and his sisters, in these words:

“This care of yours is like my care for your sisters,

Whom I cherish with the blood-related love of my heart.

Nor may I embrace the limbs of the parents whom I love,

Or eagerly kiss both their lights, as a sister”—

why could she not likewise call the son of one of them her nephew?]

[Col. 0435A] Thus, Radegund, I am sought after through the long years,

And this page of mine has been forced to speak these sad words.

[15] For a long time I awaited such a gift from a loving man,

And you send me this aid from your military service.

You direct these silken fleeces to my spinning,

So that, while I draw out the threads, I may console myself with a sister’s love?

Was this how your care consulted my powerful grief,

[20] Giving me this as the first and last message?

We had pursued another course through abundant tears and prayers;

What came to the expectant woman was sweetness turned to bitterness.

Anxious, I was tormented in my troubled heart,

And so great a fever of the spirit is refreshed by these waters.
