[25] I was not granted the sight of you alive, nor attendance at your grave;

I am carried through your funeral rites to another loss.

[Col. 0435B] Why, dear Artarchis, fosterling, should I nevertheless recall these things to you,

[Col. 0436A] And add what must be mourned to your tears and mine?

I ought rather to have brought consolation to your parent,

[30] But grief for the dead compels me to speak bitterly.

He was not a close relative through a long line of blood,

But that parent was the nearest kin through my father’s brother.

For my father was Bertharius, and his was Ermenefredus;

Born of brothers, we are not of the same generation.

[35] Or you, dear nephew, restore to me the gentle relative,

And be to me in love what he once was.

And when I have been sent to the monastery, I ask that you often visit me,

And that this place may stand for God through your assistance.

So that, together with your pious mother, this lasting care

[40] May make you worthy of the starry throne,

While now he grants that abundant salvation be present

[Col. 0436B] For you who are fortunate, and hereafter glory.

[Col. 0435]

## TO THE BENEVOLENT READER

Since in the preceding volume we included those works which Browerus had previously published, together with other additions, as we indicated in the preface placed before this edition of ours, in this second volume we have collected the Lives of the saints, which are known to have been written by Venantius Fortunatus, as well as other short works that circulate under his name or that we have learned were attributed to him by some. Thus, friendly reader, you have in this volume all the short works of Fortunatus that were scattered through other works and writings. And so that you might not rightly complain that you had been defrauded in any respect, we have added even the most learned notes with which the distinguished editors have illustrated them, adding also something from our own judgment wherever it seemed appropriate. In this matter we do not doubt that we shall earn some gratitude from you.

Finally, we have added to this volume, as a supplement, the poem entitled *On the Phoenix* [Note: [Col. 0435] We published this poem among the works of Lactantius, *Patrologia*, volume VII. We shall therefore omit it here.]. Although at first we had decided to leave it out, not only because it is commonly attributed to Lactantius, but also because we found it assigned to our Fortunatus in no manuscript codices, and because, in our judgment, the difference of style from Fortunatus’s style argues against the attribution, as we shall note in its proper place, we later thought it appropriate to attach even this poem to the volume. Some, though few, ascribe it to Fortunatus himself as its author. We wished that nothing which is circulated under his name and has come to our knowledge should be missing from this edition, which we hope will emerge into public view more complete and more accurate than the others prepared previously.

Meanwhile, farewell, gracious reader.

# THE SECOND PART OF THE COMPLETE WORKS OF VENANTIUS HONORIUS CLEMENTIANUS FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF POITIERS, CONTAINING THE LIVES OF THE SAINTS

## [LIFE OF SAINT HILARY]

[Col. 0437]

## PREFATORY NOTICE ON THE LIFE OF SAINT HILARY, BISHOP OF POITIERS

The Life of Saint Hilary that we present here is divided into two books, each of which is found dedicated to Pascentius, bishop of Poitiers, and each of which bears the name of Fortunatus, its author. It remains highly uncertain, however, whether the Fortunatus who wrote both was one and the same, or whether the Pascentius to whom both are dedicated was one and the same. For, as the distinguished editors of Saint Hilary’s works, Paris edition of 1693, point out, several Fortunati are recorded to have lived after Hilary, and two Pascenti are likewise known from the Aquitanian Annals to have presided over the Church of Poitiers at different times. One was Hilary’s own disciple and successor in the see of Poitiers; the other presided over that Church in the time of Radegund and therefore in the time of our Fortunatus.

The author of the first book of Saint Hilary’s Life seems to belong to the first of these periods, since he says that he undertook its composition at the request of Pascentius, whom the most sacred Hilary had nourished familiarly from the very cradle, before his own feet, as a special household servant. Yet, as the most learned monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur, following Bollandus, observe, these words may mean that Pascentius had been raised from childhood among the clergy of Poitiers, as though under the guardianship and protection of Saint Hilary. Indeed, Venantius Fortunatus himself similarly calls Gregory of Tours the fosterling of the martyr Julian, because Gregory had adopted that patron as his own, as this verse indicates, *Carmen* 3, Book V:

> Julian sends his own fosterling to Martin.

A second point seems to indicate that the Pascentius discussed in this first book was the older man. The author of this book, declaring himself unequal to expressing Saint Hilary’s eloquence and virtues, says: “It would have been more fitting to entrust these matters concerning a brother to blessed Ambrose.” These words seem to indicate that Pascentius was a contemporary of Saint Ambrose. But who would not see that the author wished Saint Hilary’s Life to be entrusted rather to Ambrose—who had been his brother in episcopal dignity and his associate in defending the Church’s teaching against the Arians—than to himself, who was surpassed by Ambrose both in rank and eloquence? Moreover, what confirms the matter more strongly is that he speaks of Ambrose as someone who was no longer alive. For after the words just quoted he adds, “whose words blossomed.” Yet he calls Hilary “the most ancient shepherd,” which he certainly would not have done had Ambrose lived in Hilary’s time. Finally, as the aforementioned editors of Saint Hilary’s works observe, a man contemporary with Ambrose would not have been permitted, in a Life of Saint Hilary, to say nothing of the Council of Béziers, of Saturninus of Arles, or of Hilary’s encounter with Auxentius. Finally, the style itself does not suggest the fourth century. From these considerations it follows that the Pascentius to whom this book is dedicated was not the man who lived in Hilary’s time and succeeded him in the see of Poitiers.

There is likewise no universal agreement about which Fortunatus composed the first book of Saint Hilary’s Life. Some, since the book is dedicated to Pascentius, who governed the Church of Poitiers when Venantius Fortunatus came to Gaul, attribute it to him, especially because his well-known interest and labor lay in composing Lives of the saints. Bollandus believes that this first book of Saint Hilary’s Life may have been written by Justus, a presbyter and disciple of Saint Hilary, whom Buchetus mentions frequently in the Aquitanian Annals and Saussayus on November 25; he thinks that it was later recovered from the archives of the Church of Poitiers and polished by Venantius Fortunatus.

But the writers of the *History of French Literature*, volume I, page 301, Paris edition, prefer to attribute it to Fortunatus of Vercelli, a bishop of uncertain see who had withdrawn to Gaul and was living there before Venantius Fortunatus arrived in Gaul. They also contend that he composed the Life of Saint Marcellus, bishop of Paris, and they hold this view for reasons that are by no means negligible. First, the style of the first and second books does not appear to be one and the same, as is clear to anyone who compares them. Second, the same power of intellect, the same zeal, and the same character of writing shine forth in the prologue to this Life as in the prologue to the Life of Saint Marcellus—although what should be thought about the author of the Life of Saint Marcellus will be said in its proper place. Third, although both books were written about the same Saint Hilary, one does not in any way depend upon the other, nor is either mentioned in the other; this would not be the case if both had been composed by the same Venantius Fortunatus. Indeed, they are found separately in some manuscripts.

[Col. 0439] Nearly everyone, however, agrees that Book II of Saint Hilary’s Life should be attributed to Venantius Fortunatus, since it clearly bears the style of that Fortunatus himself. They therefore consider it to have been added, as a kind of supplement, to the preceding book, which was composed by Fortunatus of Vercelli. One thing alone seems to stand in the way: Gregory of Tours mentions this second book, from which he drew the Miracles of Saint Hilary, in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 12, in these words: “Many miracles performed at Saint Hilary’s tomb are reported, which his Life contains.” Yet he does not cite the name of Venantius as its author, although it was customary for Gregory, whenever he cited something composed by Venantius, also to record the name of his very dear friend. The writers of the aforementioned *History of French Literature* think this happened because another book about the Life of Saint Hilary was in circulation, and, so that Venantius would not also be thought its author, Gregory deliberately withheld his name even when speaking of the other book of Saint Hilary’s Life, which Venantius himself had composed.

But whatever the reason for the matter may have been, Gregory of Tours’ silence certainly is not important enough for us, on its strength, to deprive Venantius of the second book of Saint Hilary’s Life, which nearly all authorities attribute to him and which the similarity of style supports—especially since all the other circumstances agree with the period of Fortunatus. Add that the same Gregory of Tours, in Book II of the *History of the Franks*, section 31, mentions a book of the Life of Saint Remigius without naming its author; nevertheless, together with the Bollandists, we judge it to be Fortunatus’s, as will be shown in the notes to the Life of Saint Remigius.

Meanwhile, we present both books of Saint Hilary’s Life here as they appear before the works of that same Saint Hilary in the Paris edition of 1693, together with the notes of the distinguished editors. If we should occasionally think something ought to be added by us, we shall append it to the edition.

[Col. 0439]

# LIFE OF SAINT HILARY, BISHOP OF POITIERS

[Note: [Col. 0439B] In the Colbert manuscript: “The Life of Saint Hilary by his servant Fortunatus, presbyter, later bishop.” Monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur.]

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0439A]

[Note: [Col. 0439B] In place of this preface, the Compendian codex, written about eight hundred years ago, contains a shorter prologue, which, although faulty, may usefully be appended here:

“Prologue from the deeds of Saint Hilary, bishop and confessor of Poitiers, on the Ides of January. We have learned through the report of not one but many that the Life and works of the most blessed confessor Hilary were handed down in praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that the warrior of Christ was most brilliantly adorned by their little works against the treachery of Arius; and that through them his deeds were woven into many accounts for the confession of the true faith. In this matter blessed Jerome, the greatest advocate, shines forth. How and in what manner he fought as a soldier of Christ at the Council of Ariminum, in the time of the emperor Constantius and under the prefect Taurus, and how he endured exile and spent five years in exile in Phrygia, is known to all followers of the upright and pious faith.”

This prologue is followed by the Life, expressed in Fortunatus’s words, though with repeated alterations. The editors.]

## PREFACE

To the holy lord and most blessed father in merits, Pope Pascentius, Fortunatus.

[Note: [Col. 0440B] This Pascentius succeeded Pientius in the see of Poitiers after having been abbot of the basilica of Saint Hilary. Pientius died around the year 564, as Cointius reports; and Pascentius did so by order of King Charibert, as Gregory of Tours relates, Book IV of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 18. This Life was therefore written before the year 568, when Mauroveus, Pascentius’s successor, occupied the see of Poitiers.]

1. Most blessed pope, urged on and admonished by the zeal of a religious heart, you are continually occupied in divine works and intent upon the practice of your sacred calling, and you strive to remain intent upon being practiced in them, so that it may readily be evident that you were born and have advanced for the cultivation of ecclesiastical discipline. You faithfully guard the foundations of the Catholic teaching of the ancient dispensation, without possibility of contradiction, and, like a good instructor, hasten to continue the summit of the structure by adding something for the building up of the most loving people—not without fear of God.

[Col. 0439B] Moved beforehand by love for this work, you deigned to press me urgently to speak about the deeds of the most sacred man, the confessor Hilary, who from your very cradle nourished you familiarly before his feet, as a special household servant, so that I might return some words in payment for the service imposed upon me [Note: [Col. 0440C] Several manuscripts read *rependeres* or *rependeris*. Then: “Even if I might touch upon it not fully, but in part.” Monks of Saint Maur.], and, even if not fully, at least touch upon and embrace them in some measure. Thus the voice and life of that most ancient shepherd might in some way resound in the ears of the flock; he might approve the service, and you yourself might not conceal your affection.

2. But when I measure the smallness of my intellect, I recognize the greatness of blessed Hilary as so immense that it almost seems equally difficult for me to speak of this subject and to touch the sky with my finger—especially since, as I hear, even the torrent of blessed Jerome’s eloquence refused to attempt it. He judged himself so unequal to the subject that he remained silent.

But I, whom no flowing streams of knowledge assist, whom scarcely the thinned drop of a poor trickle moistens, breathing nothing from my own spring—by what audacity should I wish to extend my dry courses between mighty rivers, the Euphrates of blessed Hilary and the Nile of Jerome, when whatever the most learned men have been able to say about him falls short of what he deserves? Since it is wiser for me to admire the most holy man than to speak of him, it would have been more fitting to entrust these matters concerning a brother to blessed Ambrose, whose words blossomed together with his virtues.

Yet although, to my own embarrassment, I offer obedience to you and to him about whom I do not speak worthily, perhaps I am doing him an injustice; but we believe that what is done wrongly through devotion may be forgiven. And so that a prolonged page may produce weariness rather than summon the listener, let us now begin to speak of his Life.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

3. Therefore blessed Hilary, bishop of the city of the Pictavians, was born in the region of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0441D] In the old Colbert manuscript, “in the region of Aquitaine.” In the editions alone, “in the parts of the region of Aquitaine.” Here the author seems to have wished to avoid repeating the already stated city of Poitiers. The editors.], which is separated from the British Ocean by nearly ninety miles [Note: [Col. 0441D] The Gemetic manuscript, together with the Compendian, reads “eighty.” The editors.]. Among the Gallic families he was not obscure in the lamp of nobility; indeed, he advanced adorned more than others by the grace of high birth, with the brilliance of his heart added, shining like Lucifer among the stars.

From his cradle such wisdom nourished his earliest infancy that even then it could have been understood that Christ had decreed that a soldier should be raised up for his own cause, to secure victory. Finally, although he had a wife and a daughter, he entrusted their souls, venerable in the fullness of the Lord, to be formed by the rule of the Church. Although he still remained in the lay vocation, by divine prompting he possessed the favor of a bishop; so he disciplined himself by his own rule while still untonsured [Note: [Col. 0441D] The better manuscripts have this reading, by which is signified the time when Hilary had not yet been joined to the clergy through tonsure. Other books have *intentus*. The editors.], as though indicating his future state, so that an irreproachable priest might be prepared in the temple of Christ.

For although it still seems exceedingly difficult among mortals for anyone to be so cautious as to abstain from food with Jews or heretics, this most holy man so abhorred the enemies of the Catholic religion that, not to mention sharing a meal, he would not even exchange a greeting with one of them when passing by. He avoided them, supported by David’s example, lest by sharing a table with heretics he should become a stumbling block to himself.

O most perfect layman, whose imitators even priests themselves desire to be! For him, living meant nothing other than fearing Christ with love and loving him with fear. His followers run toward glory, while those who turn aside go toward punishment; rewards follow the believer, torments the one who refuses. Calling all to the pious work of religion, now instructing some in confession of the immeasurable Holy Trinity, now inviting others by the promise of the heavenly kingdom, he never ceased to sow among the people words of truth overflowing with the fruit of faith.

4. When this became known about Saint Hilary—for such a great light could not remain hidden even had he wished it, since he was destined to transfer the darkness of others into light—the people’s favor concurred, or rather the Spirit of God proclaimed him, and the man long assigned to the mysteries was at last elected priest for the sacred altars. Each day his reputation grew, serving his virtues. His fame was not content merely to illumine the surrounding regions of Gaul; it filled foreign nations and regions as well, as the grace of his merits spread everywhere. Thus it came about that throughout the whole world the glory of the blessed bishop swiftly prevailed.

5. Therefore, in the time of the emperor Constantius, when the Arian heresy was sprouting from a poisoned root [Note: [Col. 0441D] Some manuscripts have “of a poisonous flower.” The reading “when dreadful contagions were sprouting,” found with the Compendian manuscript, would be preferable if the other reading had additional support. The editors.], the most holy man, naked of fear but clothed in the fervor of faith, thrust himself fearlessly into the midst of the battle-lines, amid the hostile roar and the swords of the heretics, like a standard-bearer and warrior.

Secure in the love of Christ and fearing nothing for his own death [Note: [Col. 0441D] In the printed editions: “He feared only that, God forbid, the injury inflicted upon religion might prevail.” The reading we present, from the better manuscripts, is more elegant. In one of them *illatae* appears, not *in lato*. Soon after, from the same manuscripts, we restore *prava credulitate*, where the printed text had *crudelitate*. The editors.], he feared only this: lest, when injury had been inflicted upon religion—God forbid—he should continue to live. Hence the bishops Valens and Ursacius, who stubbornly persisted in disturbing the Church of God through perverse belief, persuaded the emperor to condemn the most learned man of whom we speak, together with Dionysius of Milan and Eusebius of Vercelli, to exile [Col. 0442D] [Note: This did not happen in one and the same year.].

For the heretic could obtain nothing against the invincible eloquence of Saint Hilary. The enemy of the faith hoped that he could cast some clouds before the Catholic brightness if such a man, shut away in exile, were absent from the contest. For if some perverse man wished to contend with him, he could neither produce words, as though mute and lame, nor run through replies; but, like a swimmer in the sea, he was submerged before the waves of Hilary’s eloquence.

And so, sent into the region of Phrygia in Asia for exile, he gave thanks to God for the increase of his virtue, because the farther he withdrew from his native soil for Christ’s name, the more worthy he became to draw near to heaven.

6. When he had reached the desired place, we must not remain silent about what was divinely granted to him. For at that time, with the Holy Spirit revealing it to him, he learned that a certain most noble young man, exceedingly rich and beautiful, was seeking to bind in marriage the most blessed Abra, his daughter, whom he had left at Poitiers with her mother [Note: [Col. 0442D] Several manuscripts consistently write *Apram*. The editors.]. But through the intervention of continual prayer he had provided her with a heavenly bridegroom without defilement.

As soon as an opportunity arose, he sent his daughter a letter signed in his own hand [Note: [Col. 0442D] These words were added here from below, after the second book; they entered the text from the margin. The editors.], seasoned with sufficient salt and infused, as it were, with aromatic ointments. It is preserved at Poitiers as a gift. In it he indicated that her anxious father had provided her with such a bridegroom: one whose nobility would rise to the heavens; whose beauty would surpass the comparison of roses and lilies; whose eyes would eclipse the light of jewels [Note: [Col. 0442D] The Gillot edition has “would shine with the light of lights.” The Compendian manuscripts have “would illuminate lights.” The editors.]; whose garment would overpower the whiteness of snow; whose ornaments would bloom with immeasurable brilliance; whose riches would enclose kingdoms within themselves; whose wisdom would be incomprehensible; whose sweetness would make honey seem inferior; whose chastity would remain undefiled; whose fragrance would breathe forth delight; and whose treasures would endure without exhaustion.

He therefore added a warning that his daughter, separated from her mother, should join herself to no one before she awaited the bridegroom promised by her father, who would come together with the promise. Abra received this sweetly and, embracing in her father’s letter the bridegroom who was to come as though he were already hers, followed the instruction and did not give herself in marriage to anyone. But how she reached that bridegroom is reserved for the following passage.

7. Meanwhile, when the perversity of the Arian heresy was sprouting throughout the whole world, the emperor issued a general edict that all the Eastern bishops should assemble at Seleucia, a town of Isauria, to debate what they believed concerning the truth of the faith. Then, among the others, Saint Hilary, already in the fourth year of his exile, was compelled to come from Phrygia to the aforesaid place, having been granted means of transport [Note: [Col. 0443D] Several manuscripts have *data vectione* or *evectione*. Sulpicius Severus has *data evectionis copia*. It is found in Book XII of the *Code*, under *On Public Transport*: “Our Serenity has granted the means of transport whenever the necessity of traveling to us has arisen.” The editors.].

When he had entered a certain fortress, he went into the church on the Lord’s Day. At once the pagan girl Florentia burst through the crowd and loudly declared that the servant of God had arrived there. Running to his feet, she did not cease asking until she had faithfully obtained from him the sign of the cross. Her father Florentius followed her, and the whole household together was judged worthy to be baptized in the name of the Lord.

Florentia, leaving her parents and clinging to his footsteps, was led all the way to Poitiers. She proclaimed that she had as her father not the man from whom she had been born, but the one through whom she had been reborn.

### 8

When he had reached Seleucia, he was received by everyone with great enthusiasm, because divine mercy had brought forth such a supremely wise man, distinguished by exceptional learning, as a spectacle for the world, at the place where judgment was to be given concerning the faith. Thus, after the examination had exposed and overthrown the enemies, and after decrees had been set down in writing, an embassy bearing the synod’s favorable decisions was sent to the emperor. Saint Hilary proceeded with it, although this had not been ordered of him, fearing that condemned perfidy might still be breathing against the doctrines of religion.

But it would take too long to relate how, at the Council of Ariminum, by means of a fabricated account—reporting one thing after another—heretical fraud crept in with a serpent’s winding movement, and how afterward the same slander was brought against the legates of Seleucia through the emperor’s injustice.

[Note: At [Col. 0443D], *mentitione* (“lying”) is undoubtedly to be read. This is said of the Arians’ lie, by which they shamelessly claimed falsely that the Easterners wholly rejected the term “substance.” The Compendium manuscripts read *compositum mendacium* (“a fabricated lie”). — Editors.] Yet the blessed Hilary, Christ’s athlete, recognized this and deeply grieved that the devil’s lie had prevailed at Ariminum, to such an extent that it likewise stained the Eastern party with the composed disguise of wickedness.

Having presented the emperor with three petitions, he begged that, once his adversaries had been assembled in the emperor’s presence, he might be granted permission to debate religion against the heretics, so that falsehood might not obscure the truth, injustice might not prevail over equity, the emperor might not resist God, and perfidy might not rebel against the faith.

[Note: In the printed editions: “lest the perfidy of iniquity should corrupt the faith of the Trinity through the interpolator’s work.” — Monks of Saint-Maur.]

Therefore Valens and Ursacius, terrified by the guilt of their consciences—for if an opportunity for debate were granted, they immediately recognized that they would be overthrown by Hilary’s contention—worked upon the emperor’s mind, making him captive to so malicious a party that he compelled the man of God to return to Gaul.

[Note: Thus in Sulpicius Severus, Book II.]

[Note: The better manuscripts read: “making him captive through so malicious a matter by means of a stratagem.” The other books read: “already largely captive.” — Editors.]

They said that, while Hilary was present, heretical schemes could not succeed. Under this pretext he was forced to return to Gaul, thinking that he was suffering exile once more, since he was leaving the disturbance of the Church there without having obtained the conclusion of the debate.

O blessed bishop, who, in the greatest danger, and with even his enemy sitting in judgment, approached the imperial tribunal without fear of torture! He truly loved Christ’s kingdom with all his heart, since he did not fear being in the presence of the emperor Constantius. By thrusting himself forward so openly into danger on the Lord’s behalf, he desired martyrdom, had an executioner not been lacking; yet his courage gained the glory, although the time did not bring the punishment.

I testify that he was preserved by divine providence for the correction of all. For many voices confess that, when nearly the whole world had been confused by grave error, Hilary brought it back to the way of truth by means of the councils repeatedly held in Gaul.

[Note: The printed editions read “or if”; most manuscripts read “or he”; the better manuscripts’ “or for himself” is preferable—that is, what would have benefited him alone. — Editors.]

What difference is there between his having been made a martyr for eternal life, or his having lived longer so that the rest might not perish? Thus, although the persecutor’s sword did not take away his most holy soul, he nevertheless did not lose the martyr’s palm.

### 9

And so, while he was returning to his homeland, blessed Martin—whose light of merit was likewise not hidden—

[Note: The older Colbertine manuscripts read “not obscure.” The Compendium reads: “who, having been defended by the holy exorcist Hilary,” omitting the word “afterward,” which Bollandus believes entered here as a gloss. Otherwise Fortunatus would clearly be in conflict with Sulpicius, who writes that Martin was ordained exorcist by Hilary before Hilary went into exile. — Editors.]

—having later been appointed exorcist by that same holy Hilary, learned of his arrival and hurried to meet him at Rome. When he discovered that Hilary had already passed by, he followed him as far as Gaul. For Martin, who, while still a catechumen, had deserved to see Christ clothed in his own cloak, would not have gone to meet Hilary with such devotion unless he had perceived beforehand that Hilary’s spirit was filled in every way with mysteries. Nor is it surprising that the man who had first seen God in a poor man should afterward recognize Him dwelling in a teacher.

### 10

It is also not fitting for us to pass over in silence so noble a miracle. For when Hilary was approaching the island of Gallinaria—

[Note: Several manuscripts read “near the island of Dives in Gaul”; Bouchet therefore reads it this way and thinks that the island lay near the Primaliensian rocks. Not far from La Rochelle, as Bollandus observed, the maps show the village of Yves and the bridge of Yves at Alnesio. Valesius, in his *Gallic Notes*, p. 390, n. 2, remarks that the island called Diva lies close both to the mouth of the Sèvre and to another island called in Latin Oia or Ogia, and commonly l’Île-Dieu. Although, on the authority of the older manuscripts, we retain “the island of Gallinaria,” we nevertheless believe that it was different from the island of the same name in the Tuscan Sea, which Martin inhabited. Otherwise Martin would have waited for Hilary there and would not have tried to meet him at Rome, had that been Hilary’s route. Nor would an island inhabited by Martin rightly be called uninhabitable. — Editors.]

—he learned from the report of the neighboring inhabitants that enormous coils of snakes wandered about there without number. Consequently, although the island seemed near to them, because of its inaccessible location it appeared farther away than Africa. When the man of God heard this, sensing that victory in the struggle against the beasts would come to him, he descended onto the island in the name of the Lord, with the aid of the cross going before him. At the sight of him the snakes turned and fled, unable to endure his presence.

Then, fixing his staff in the ground as a boundary, he marked by the power of his virtue how far they were to roam.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “the power.”]

They were no longer free to occupy what he had forbidden—as though the remaining part of the island were not land but the sea—for, since they were always afraid to touch that part, it was easier for them to cross the sea than to cross his word.

[Note: The older Colbertine manuscript reads “than to come here.” — Editors.]

O unalterable boundary, planted by a word! It is clear how much better the second Adam is than the ancient one. The first obeyed the serpent; the second has servants who can command serpents. The first was expelled from paradise by a beast; the second drove serpents from their lairs.

The serpent laid aside its ancient lie—

[Note: Thus the old Colbertine manuscript. Others read “its ancient falsehood.” A number of manuscripts immediately add “O sweetness of Hilary”; afterward, with the editions of Gillot, they read “medicine and merit.” — Editors.]

—the serpent that had learned to fulfill a command.

O sweetness of Hilary, medicine and purity, before whom the poisons were immediately driven away! He added land for human beings, because in place of the beast an inhabitant moved in.

But let us return to the order of our account.

### 11

When, after returning from exile, he entered Poitiers, everyone applauded together with the greatest enthusiasm, because the Church had received its bishop and the flock its shepherd. It was as though everyone had then returned to his homeland with him, so bitterly did they lament that they had been exiles without him.

### 12

And so, when blessed Martin had ordered that he be stationed in a village called Locogejac—

[Note: Sulpicius reports that this monastery was situated not far from the town, but he does not state its name, and the manuscripts do not agree in writing it. The old Colbertine manuscript reads *Locojaco*; another, no less ancient, *Casalis Bened., Locotejaco*; the Compendium, *Locodiaco*; several others, *Legudiaco*. Bollandus likewise gives the village variously as *Legudiacus*, *Tyacus*, and *Goteloicacus*, while the Sarum Breviary has *Lugduniacus*. He himself, together with Gillot’s edition, prefers *Tegiaco*. From the first two manuscripts we reconstruct *Locogejaco*, so that the first appears to have lost the letter *g*, which ancient writers, not expressing the sound in speech, more readily omitted in writing. From the other we supply the letter *e*, in agreement with the French name *Liguge*. *Legugejaco* would also be acceptable. — Editors.]

—blessed Martin merited, by divine power, to raise a dead man there.

Then, after a few days, a certain infant died without the regeneration of baptism. Condemned to a double death, he had lost the light of the present world and was not free from the punishment of the age to come. The mother of the dead child, who was no longer a mother because she no longer had a son, threw herself at the feet of Saint Hilary. With tears going before her, she laid out the body of her child and cried:

“Martin, still a catechumen at the outset, restored a dead catechumen. You, bishop, I beg you, restore my son either to me or to baptism.” You are recognized as the father of the people; obtain, I beg, that I may be called a mother.”

Since she asked more with tears than with words, the man of God was moved by compassion. In the sight of the people, he returned to his customary weapons and prostrated himself on the ground.

[Note: Gillot’s edition reads “turning to the weapons”; what follows concerning the dead man’s restoration to life has some affinity with what Venantius relates in the *Life of Saint Germanus* concerning a dying woman who was healed, saying that, after the pallor of death, her face changed to red. — Editors.]

[Note: It is pleasing here to cite the verses of Venantius Fortunatus, Book I of the *Life of Saint Martin*, which describe the catechumen restored to life by Saint Martin and are understood to have the greatest affinity and resemblance to this passage. They run as follows:

“Meanwhile, as an interval of two hours delayed,

behold, the complexion returns and warmth leaps through the limbs.

Then blush stands upon the cheeks, and the pupil restores the eyes;

and restored sight renews its windows.

The vein swells with streams, with the living spring of blood;

gradually the column rises, though the structure totters,

and both the fallen house and its own inhabitant rise together.” — Editors.]

Gradually the pallor of the dead man’s body was changed into redness; his cold limbs grew warm as breath returned; his eyes, with the gates of the eyelids opened, recognized the unfamiliar light; a voice, formed by the air drawn through the dwelling of the chest, issued forth; his restored step extended itself along its own tracks; and the whole structure of his body was renewed to the condition of its original foundation.

What more need be said? The bishop lay in the dust until both rose together: the old man from prayer, the child from death. Behold a praiseworthy life, which by its prayers drove death from another’s body, despoiled Tartarus, and placed its hope in Christ. Death held no rights there, where Hilary brought the power of prayer to bear.

Yet so great a deed cannot be adorned by our words more than by his merits. Now, however, we must recall what we passed over above.

[Note: One manuscript reads “we mentioned earlier.”]

We must relate how, through this miracle, he accumulated the rest of his miracles.

### 13

Finally, when he found his most blessed daughter Abra safe and well—the daughter to whom he had sent a letter from exile—he addressed her with all the tenderness of a father and the eloquence of an orator.

What shall I say? Hilary addressed her, and after him we scarcely dare compare anyone with his eloquence unless he too was filled with the divine Spirit as Hilary was. He tested her mind to see whether she wished to approach the bridegroom whom her father’s affection had provided for.

[Note: One manuscript reads “had cut off” instead of “had foreseen.”]

Then she gladly and eagerly desired to be joined to him as quickly as possible. Recognizing this desire, her devout father did not cease in prayer until, without pain and without defilement, in his presence, his daughter departed from the mockery of the world to Christ. With his own hands, as was fitting, he entrusted her to venerable burial.

O glory of burial, which is considered better than life, because what it has snatched from the earth it has transmitted to heaven! Truly, as I consider it, it was greater than resurrection to die in this way. For it is certain salvation not to be contaminated by sins. How many would wish, after surrendering their possessions together with their life, to obtain such a departure, if perhaps they could find a buyer?

What difference is there between the mystery of the infant who was brought to life and that of the daughter who was put to death? He raised the former to baptism; he predestined the latter for the kingdom—

[Note: The Colbertine manuscripts read “destined”; the Compendium reads “transmitted.” — Monks of Saint-Maur.]

—except that in the former there still remained the hope of sinning, while the latter had ended her life undefiled.

When Abra’s mother saw this, she asked the bishop that she too, if she were worthy, might be snatched from the guilt of the world and presented with her daughter to the kingdom. Considering her desire, he sent her also before him into glory through constant prayer.

Who could estimate how greatly such a man loved the Lord, setting aside the affection owed to wife and daughter? Yet it is recognized that he loved them all the more in this respect, since through him they were transferred to perpetual light.

### 14

Who could undertake to unfold the abundance of his flowing genius, or match his words with words?

[Note: The older Colbertine manuscript reads: “how he wove books in a swelling style upon divided [perhaps: diverse] matters.” The Compendium reads: “how he published books against the perfidy of Arius; how he opened the Book of Psalms, verse by verse, in elevated language; and how he was prepared also in the exposition of hymns” [where *discretione* was wrongly printed for *dissertione*]. It has *reservavit*, but *reseravit* (“opened”) should be read. — Editors.]

How he composed books on the undivided Trinity in a swelling style, or opened up the writings of David’s songs one by one in elevated language! How prudent he was in exposition, profound in treatment, eloquent through learning, marvelous through power, multifaceted in synthesis, subtle in analysis, crafty according to the prophet—or rather wise according to the Lord’s word—like a serpent, while not losing the grace of the simple dove.

He was the salt of a rich intellect, a fountain of speech, a treasury of knowledge, a light of teaching, a defender of the Church, and an assailant of its enemies. Whoever reads his words will not believe that he is speaking, but thundering.

[Note: The Compendium manuscript adds here: “The aforesaid bishop Hilary died on the Ides of January. His relics were buried at Poitiers; at that place divine benefits continue to be worked to this day, through the aid of him who lives,” and so forth. — Editors.]

This was wisdom surpassing the human, such was his prudence in judging concerning religion.

### 15

But whoever wishes to know him should recall his exiles, consider his merits, reread his volumes, weigh his words, and examine his daily signs.

[Note: Gillot’s edition reads “let him remember his aids.”]

While he lived in this world, he either wrote testimonies to the Church’s faith, or, by fighting, trampled down heretical crimes, or granted to those who asked him the assistance of miracles. By the Lord’s will, these miracles continue to the present day through his prayers.

But my tongue is not sufficient to set forth individually, as he deserves, all that the Holy Spirit both worked and spoke through him.

### 16

May he graciously pardon me, because I have passed over much, though I have written down scarcely a little.

[Note: In the Ottobonian, German, and Colbertine manuscripts, and in several others, this book is longer, as follows:

“Therefore, lest the page, extended at excessive length by the rusticity of my style and by an overabundance of speech, should become worthless, we must now set limits to our writing. Yet it is worthwhile, and will be helpful, to relate this one thing only: how the soul of this holy man departed, received in the splendor of divine light.

“For while so great a light of the Church had begun to grow dim through illness, he ordered the venerable man Leonius, a presbyter of the same city, to be summoned to him one day in secret. This priest was trusted and most dearly loved by him. After ordering him to go outside when the darkness of night was approaching, and to report to him anything he might hear outside, Leonius returned and explained that he had heard the voices of the city’s people, who were still in turmoil.

“Hilary therefore remained awake, awaiting the end appointed for the righteous and refreshing his spirit with the man’s final and most beloved exhortations. Then, deep into the night, the saint again asked him to go outside and report to him, as he lay on his bed, whatever he might hear.

“When Leonius reported that he had perceived no sound or murmur from anyone, suddenly an immeasurable brilliance of light entered through the window on the side of the altar of that same basilica in which the very healthy sick man lay. Leonius confessed that he could not endure it.

“For, according to the Apostle, though Hilary was weakened in the flesh, he was stronger in spirit. His soul—not merely blessed, but most blessed—was released from its bodily bonds and departed, received, as we believe, by that very light of divine brilliance. In its migration it entered the delight of perpetual splendor in paradise.

“There, now and forever crowned with the diadem of a precious stone, bathed in fortunate light in the everlasting citadel of heaven, he rejoices with the exultant saints.

“Thus blessed Bishop Hilary …” — Monks of Saint-Maur.]

Thus blessed Hilary departed from the life of the present age to Christ, while Valens and Valentinian were reigning, with earth mourning and heaven rejoicing, through the aid of the same Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK TWO

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript adds: “and here also; then priests, and afterward bishops of Poitiers.” — Editors.]

## PREFACE

To the holy Lord and Father Pascentius, most blessed in merits, pope, and to the inhabitants of the Church of Poitiers, who flourish everlastingly in Christ in flower-bearing charity: Fortunatus.

### 1

When the ancient authors of books belonging to unbelievers were provoked by the desire to display to everyone the pomp of their eloquence and to secure a reputation swollen with pride, and when, amid the vows or funerals of kings—that is, amid prosperity or adversity—they seemed, with a confused ordering of their voices, somehow to sing and weep at once, so that those who spoke or were spoken about might at least live on in books, even though they had failed emptily and uselessly in their deeds;

why, then, should I, stirred by the prompting of a better hope, suffer the living merits and victories of the supreme confessor to remain unspoken—unless, God forbid, heavenly vengeance should follow—when I would scarcely discharge what was owed if, with tireless voice, day joined to night, I were to sing of the splendor of blessed Hilary’s unfailing lamp?

By what ignorance ensnared, or by what offense driven, should I persist under heavy torpor in such a resolve that, while those deceived by lengthy argument compose something about the dissolved image of shadows and animate corpses reduced to dust with false praises, I would say nothing about the holy who remain and, what is more blessed, flourish daily in Christ’s kingdom?

This is especially true since the cause of the rewards belonging to the different parties appears to be different: the pagans wished the fruit of their labor to consist only in empty praise, whereas we ought to plant ours in the intercession of blessed men. If here we pay them words, there we obtain joys for ourselves.

### 2

Therefore let the mobile tongue proclaim him from whom hearts first conceived this affection. For his good deeds would plainly seem to be envied if what we have learned about him appeared to be hidden in silence.

Rightly, then, he compels me, along with others, to speak about him, since he even releases the mute so that they may speak. But although I could not, because the passage of many years had stolen the opportunity, reach all that he did while still living in the body, or all that he accomplished after he migrated victoriously from the world’s struggle to Christ, into eternal rest while the angels applauded him, nevertheless I desire not to deprive needy memory of even the miracles that his mercy has granted in the present time.

Thus whoever receives these things with faithful hearing, as is proper, may rejoice to learn what happened in the past and trust that similar things will be done in the future through the power of the confessor.

## THE BOOK BEGINS

### 3

Therefore, when Probianus was already hanging in the balance at the end of his life, and envious death was hastening to steal from his parents the hope of the child’s recovery, neither considering the bitter funeral of the little one nor looking upon the desires of the groaning old age, greedily enclosing everything it found outside its allotted portion, the sole opportunity of salvation that remained for the dying man was the intercession of blessed Hilary.

[Note: Bouchetus, chapter 15, and Claudius Robert say that this was Probianus, or Probatianus, the twenty-fourth bishop of Bourges, who in the second year of Pope Pelagius II, the forty-fourth year of Childebert, and the year 555 of Christ, signed the Second Council of Paris and, two years later, presided over the Third Council of Paris, thus reaching the period of Venantius Fortunatus. — Bollandus.]

His father, Franco, and his mother, Periculosa—whose name, by a more fitting reversal, showed her endangered through her son’s death—were already anticipating the funeral rites of one almost dead. With immense mourning and weeping, they carried him to the confessor’s sanctuary.

Then Saint Hilary, displaying the medicine of the secret art he had received from its author, accustomed as he was to exchange the losses of a funeral for the gains of health, suddenly raised the collapsing structure of his limbs through the working of a word and restored it to its former condition, as though nothing in it had come undone.

Immediately, when a mass of joy came upon them, he dried the parents’ tears and closed off their groans as their prayer was answered. There was no longer anything for them to bewail in grief, but only what they might weep for in joy.

What punishments and torments death itself then suffered, when it lost in this way what it believed it was about to seize! Clearly, when victorious death could not strike the other, it struck itself after being defeated.

Probianus later merited to attain the dignity of a bishop and, to the lamps of his healer, paid each year until the end of his life the tribute owed for his preservation.

[Note: The Ottobonian manuscript reads “the bishopric of Bourges”; immediately afterward, where the other manuscripts have “to the lamps,” it reads “to the thresholds.” A similar passage occurs in Venantius Fortunatus’s *Life of Saint Germanus*, no. 11, where, speaking of a woman healed from illness, he says: “She pays the tribute of life each year in return for the price.” — Monks of Saint-Maur.]

### 4

That singular miracle also must be recalled to the memory of the people, for the glory of the one who bestowed it.

Two men came from Cahors, disfigured by the marks of leprosy. Placing their hope of healing in the intercession of Saint Hilary, they persisted in washing their heads with water mixed with dust swept from his tomb and in anointing the rest of their limbs. They faithfully continued this treatment until the ulcerous variety of the disease departed from the body it had taken captive, itself becoming captive, so that, deceived by its own consolations, it left untouched the color it had invaded and no longer retained the hideous appearance it had brought with it.

[Note: Cahors, the metropolis of the Cadurci in Aquitania Prima, lies on the Lot River and is an episcopal city under the archbishopric of Bourges. — Bollandus.]

After innumerable wounds, one skin was restored over all their limbs. The faces that had long been erased by filth began to be repainted in their own image in both men, and no one could recognize what they had been like during their illness.

Through the most faithful bath of dust, a pure Jordan was found for them at Poitiers; they did not go to the river, but the river came to them. From this the confessor’s mercy proved itself so worthy of proclamation: it both removed from them the labor of a long journey and offered them the hopes of healing.

O how clearly the proofs of immeasurable powers shone forth, when the uncleanness of a tomb cleansed the marks of leprosy! What craftsman could have accomplished this, or brought the benefits of medicine from such dust?

Castorius, appointed deacon, and Crispus, appointed subdeacon, once healed, remained attached until their end to the service of him through whom they had been healed; and rightly they chose to bear the yoke of the Lord by whom they had been freed from punishment.

[Note: Bouchetus says that they were healed on the ninth day; Casterius says the same, as does Crispo. — Bollandus.]

### 5

A certain girl came into this life with a dead right hand, formed that way by nature. The contracted threads of the nerves had gathered the weak hand into the shape of a ball.

[Note: Thus the Ottobonian Codex. Others read “globe.” — Monks of Saint-Maur.]

The web of her fingers, loosened from its own thread, was withering.

[Note: Gillot reads “was decaying.” This recalls Fortunatus’s words in the *Life of Saint Germanus*, no. 14: “the web of the nerves is unwoven.” — Editors.]

Then she came to the burial place of blessed Hilary. Through his intercession, the functions of life were arranged in the hand: little by little strength entered the mobile joints and the stiff nails.

[Note: Others read “anointing.” Perhaps “stiffening”?]

After a long time, a hand was born for her when she experienced the gifts of the confessor. A dead hand came from the womb; it returned alive from the saint’s tomb.

Behold how abundant is the mercy of the generous giver, so that here he supplied limbs that nature had not produced.

### 6

Nor should we pass over what happened most happily to a blind man after his vows. For, while he was hastening with devotion to the threshold of blessed Martin in order to recover his sight, he passed by the church of Saint Hilary and entered it.

While the clergy were celebrating the vigils there according to their accustomed practice, morning came, and he opened his eyes and began to announce the day to others—the very thing he had always needed to hear.

For him there had always been one unbroken night; Saint Hilary dispelled his darkness during that night. He who had never seen the ornaments of day saw a new sun of wondrous brightness rise for him.

Then everything was fashioned for him, when he merited to see the making of all things; and, so to speak, the world was in a certain sense born for him afterward, when it became known to him.

[Note: Our manuscripts read: “He was hastening to the church of his brother, blessed Martin.” — Monks of Saint-Maur.]

The blind man was hastening to enter the church of blessed Martin; Hilary graciously chose to illuminate him in his own temple. How great is the grace that shines from the giver, who anticipates the desires of the suppliant!

### 7

What worthy account can I give of so royal a mystery, which was bestowed by him upon a king?

King Clovis had mobilized his armed ranks to fight against a heretical people. At midnight he merited to see a light coming from the basilica of blessed Hilary and shining over him. He was further admonished to descend quickly to battle against the enemy, but not without first praying at that venerable place.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way, while the printed editions have “when he had his battle lines armed.” Gregory of Tours should be consulted concerning this miracle, *History*, Book II, chapter 43. He relates that Clovis fought with Alaric, king of the Goths, five years before his death—that is, in the year 507—in the field of Vouillé, ten miles from the city of Poitiers, routed the army, and killed the king himself with his own hand. — Editors.]

Clovis carefully observed this instruction and went to prayer. With such success—with another fighting on his behalf—he proceeded to battle that before the third hour of the day he received from the Lord a victory beyond human hopes.

There the multitude of slain corpses seemed to have raised hills out of itself.

[Note: Gillot’s edition reads: “So many lay dead in the place that the hill itself seemed on that account to have raised itself upward”; this appears to be an interpolation. Bollandus and the Colbertine manuscript read: “the hills seemed to have raised mountains from themselves.” The reading of the Gemeticensis manuscript is more straightforward. — Editors.]

Behold terrifying wonders to be feared and miracles to be embraced with delight! It was not enough for him, as comfort for the king, to display the sign of the light unless he had also openly added words of warning.

A similar event occurred in the time of the Israelite people because of this power. There, a column of fire had gone before the people; here, the figure of a lamp gave warning.

### 8

I should like to know what secret mystery of such burning zeal was so clearly manifested. But as far as I seem to recognize it through his inspiration, I shall not keep silent.

For against the heretical ranks he did not cease to fight in spirit, just as once he had fought in the body.

[Note: Bollandus, together with the Ottobonian and Colbertine manuscripts, adds here: “Thus he believed that he had recovered his resolve to fight against Alaric the Arian once more.” The Gemeticensis manuscript reads: “At that time he believed that Constantius had returned to fight against Hilary the Arian once more.” — Editors.]

How great was his zeal always for the worship of the Catholic religion, since, even though he had been placed in rest, an abundance of solicitude was still not lacking in him! He who had then spoken words faithful to the faith in the synod to confound the enemy now wielded weapons of victory on the battlefield.

### 9

A woman in the village of Tonaciacum was carrying water for her work on Sunday—I do not know what sin had overtaken her—when her hand was drawn up, the course of her veins having dried up.

Then she was warned by a revelation that, if she wished to be healed, she should hasten to the saint’s threshold. Trusting this message, she ran joyfully, as though accompanied by the one who went before her as the guide of her healing.

While psalms were being sung in the church, she was likewise released on the Sunday on which punishment had preceded her; joy followed.

Behold the lovable custom of a singular patron, who, in order to find something to grant, even seeks out occasions for doing so. O blessed Hilary, to be sung in everyone’s heart, mouth, and voice! His kindness is so abundant that he not only does not hide himself from anyone, but voluntarily offers himself.

Let us come to the other fruits of this venerable miracle.

### 10

A certain paralytic girl, grown into adulthood, lived without the functions of life, though she had not deserved such a condition. Within the funeral of her extinguished body, only her soul remained fluttering; throughout the whole corpse her eyes alone seemed to be alive, and, as though she were dead, her watchful eyes guarded the limbs within her.

Her sluggish tongue did not move fluidly through the chamber of the palate—

[Note: Fortunatus commonly used such circumlocutions—Greek, *periphraseis*—as when, in Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, he describes a mute girl healed by Martin’s power and writes among other things:

“Soon released, she moves the ringing plectrum of her throat’s lyre,

and the shell of her vaulted palate sings unfamiliar things;

her tongue, rubbed against the hollow of her tooth, brings forth words like a rattle.”]

—nor could a voice drawn from the depths of her chest arrange articulated words. Her hands, while their relaxed nature languished, performed none of their appointed services; nor did her unsteady foot support the structure of her limbs.

[Note: The printed editions read “supported the ruins of her limbs”; this has been corrected from the Ottobonian and Colbertine manuscripts. — Monks of Saint-Maur.]

Moreover, the shapeless mass of her whole body still lay inert.

Placed within the basilica during the feast of blessed Hilary, she was raised up amid the immense enthusiasm of all who watched.

Thus, in the body of one weak person, the saint completed several miracles. He strengthened the attenuated joints of her knees; he adapted her stiff tongue to flexibility and ease of speech; he armed the once-weak palms of her hands for the work of spinning; and, through the grace of his kindly gift, he brought life to the lines and structures of her inward parts.

At one point the old infant burst into speech; and, what is especially striking, with her first voice she asked for nourishment of milk. Why else would she ask for such food before all else, unless it is understood that, when she was healed, she then first believed that she had been born?

### 11

Nor should that mystery, so faithful and true, be taken away through harmful forgetfulness.

Two merchants came to the basilica of the blessed man, carrying a piece of wax apparently joined together for common use. One of them addressed the other, saying that they should willingly offer it to so great a confessor, although it was such a small thing. But he spent his words in vain upon the mind of his unwilling companion.

Nevertheless, he prostrated himself in prayer with that same colleague and secretly placed the wax before the railings of the awesome tomb.

Immediately the wax divided itself into equal portions. The portion belonging to the faithful giver was accepted; the other part, before the eyes of many, rolled all the way to the other railings and, by divine command, was driven back with every mark of contempt, as though the saint were unwilling to take what the other, who was not devoted to him, had not offered.

And because he has always rejected whatever does not proceed from faith, he is as certain in judgment as he is merciful in granting requests.

O how incorruptible an arbiter he shines! He is more chaste [alternatively, more cautious] in examining judgment than she who chastely produces wax is in selecting flowers.

Then the man who had refused to offer it, exposed and confounded as a witness against himself of the crime he had committed, was struck by the burden of immense shame. Seeing that reproaches of such disgrace had sprung from the root of his own conscience and that the deeds of his hidden knowledge had been revealed before his face, he considered, groaned, and wept, so that at least, by watering them with the fountain of his tears, he might wash away what he had defiled with a sinful heart.

Afterward, when compelled to do so, he offered more, chastened by the judgment pronounced upon the wax.

12. Likewise, when one night, according to custom, a candle had been lit there, it happened to fall burning upon his tomb—he whose intercession gives life to the dead [Note: [Col. 0453C] Absent: “the dead” in the manuscripts]—so that it burned fiercely upon the mafort [Note: [Col. 0453C] Here Fortunatus uses *mafort* for the actual covering with which the tombs of saints were customarily covered. Otherwise, a *mafort* was a head-covering, especially a woman’s; see further Dufresne, *Glossarium*. It is also used for a monastic scapular, as is clear from Cassian, *Institutes of Monastic Life*, book I, chapter 7, where, discussing the clothing of monks, he says: “After this, covering themselves with a narrow cloak, pursuing both humility and cheapness and economy of price, they cover their necks and shoulders alike; this is called a *mafort* both in our language and in theirs.”] where it had fallen, without causing any damage. For as long as the candle was, so much wax was found lying there, the papyrus having been consumed—as though the wax itself had formed a boundary between the fire and the pallium, so that it was found to have been protected by that through which it could have been burned. Consider the benefit. So that the confessor’s command might be obeyed—he who always knows how to subdue [Note: [Col. 0454C] In Bollandus, *and consume* is added here. Gill has: “So that it might obey the command. Which it always knows how to consume in turn, here the wax,” etc. *Monastery of Saint Maur*]—here the fire feared the wax; and the very substance which it had taken to aid its burning seemed to resist it. But amid these events, the matter rather admonishes us to say that, by the confessor’s power, the wax extinguished the flames that it carried forth, and, in reversed order, smothered what could have devoured it. The different substances seemed to have changed their nature: so that the flames might harm nothing, the pallium became marble, and the wax became a river. Yet how great is it, in his presence, to extinguish the light of a candle, when he kindles light for the blind? Or, when at another’s burial he restores the fire of the eyes, how readily do we believe that he could drive flames away from his own tomb?

13. I should still like, being unsated, to sing the miracles of this most holy man as though they were my particular theme; but I fear that, while wishing to display my devotion, I may seem to block the listener’s mind by giving rise to weariness. Grant me, in your mercy, pardon for the brevity of this text; blame the accident, lest, while wishing to avoid the weariness of a human being, I seem to incur the displeasure of the confessor, about whom I would say little if I filled books. Yet I venture to say less about you in many respects, so that brevity may more greatly invite the people to read about you, with the help of the Lord our God, now and forever. Amen.

# [LIFE OF SAINT GERMANUS]

[Col. 0453]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING LIFE OF SAINT GERMANUS, BISHOP OF PARIS

[Col. 0453] We publish the following Life of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, as it appears in the first Benedictine century, together with the notes of the distinguished Mabillon. All readily agree that it was written by Venantius Fortunatus. Gregory of Tours, mentioning it in book V, chapter 8 of his *History of the Franks*, says: “If, however, some energetic man wishes carefully to investigate his [Saint Germanus’s] virtues, which he performed while in the body, he will find everything by reading the book of his Life, composed by Fortunatus the priest.” Saint Germanus died in the year 576, on 28 May; it is therefore likely that his Life was written around that time by his closest friend Fortunatus. It is also found in Surius and in Bollandus, under the same date, 28 May.

[Col. 0453]

## LIFE OF SAINT GERMANUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF PARIS (C, S)

[Col. 0453C] **1.** Blessed Germanus, therefore, bishop of the people of Paris [Note: [Col. 0453C] Bollandus omits *therefore*], a native of the territory of Augustodunum, was born to Eleutherius as his father and Eusebia as his mother, respectable and honored parents. His mother, because she had conceived him within a short interval after another child, was moved by feminine shame and wished to destroy the infant before birth. Having taken a potion so that she might cast him out as an abortive child, and finding that it could not harm him, she lay upon her belly so as to suffocate by weight the one whom the poisons could not injure. The mother struggled with the little child; the infant resisted from within the womb. There was therefore a battle between the woman and her entrails. The matron was injured, but the infant was not harmed; the unborn child fought back lest the mother become a murderess. This happened so that, preserved unharmed, he himself might emerge uninjured and restore his mother to innocence. Thus it was possible to foreknow future things from this: he had already worked a miracle before it happened that he was born [Note: [Col. 0455C] Bollandus adds these words: “Finally, as his virtues increased, he advanced daily toward better things and was entrusted by his most loving parents to the study of letters, so that thereafter he might be found worthy in the praises of God.”].

**2.** Then, while as a boy he attended school at the fortress of Avallon with his relative Stratidius [Note: [Col. 0455C] The manuscripts read: “His mother’s Stratidius”], the mother of his relative [Note: [Col. 0455C] Other copies have *of the relative*, but both words, *parent* and *relative*, are synonyms for Fortunatus. Hence below, section 3: “to his relative, Saint Scopilio,” etc.] plotted the youth’s murder in order to acquire his inheritance. She placed a prepared potion in one small flask and wine in another, instructing a girl that, when both men arrived, she should offer wine to the one and the poison to the other. But the servant, unaware, exchanged the flasks and the cups: she gave the wine to Saint Germanus and the poison to Stratidius. While death was being prepared for the innocent man, the author of the crime fell into the snare. When his mother learned of this, she rebuked the girl with tears, saying that she had killed her son. Through careful attention devoted to Stratidius, the very poison having made him variegated [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Varius*, that is, “spotted”], although death did not take away his life, it nevertheless stamped upon him the mark of death.

**3.** From there he went to his relative Saint Scopilio at Lausia [Col. 0455C] [Note: [Col. 0455D] Lausia, or Lausea, Luzy, a small town situated approximately midway between Augustodunum and the Loire. Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, in his *Chronicle*, p. 1, under the year 630, asserts that in the village of Lausia, on the estate of Saint Germanus’s birth, no dog or bird can seize prey without immediately dying; this has been established by experiment. The place still retains a church to this day, distinguished by the name and power of Saint Germanus], and there he was nourished and instructed in honorable conduct. When they were staying nearly a thousand paces from the village, they ran continually to matins, led by the warmth of faith, through storm and winter. During the period of three lustrums [Note: [Col. 0455D] It is uncertain whether this interval of fifteen years should be reckoned from Saint Germanus’s birth or from the time when he entered Scopilio’s discipline. The latter view is more appealing. For Agrippinus, bishop of Aedui, who ordained Germanus deacon, did not yet occupy the see in the year 517, when Pragmatius, Agrippinus’s predecessor, subscribed to the Council of Epaon. Yet Saint Germanus had already reached at least twenty years in that year, since he died nearly eighty years old—according to Fortunatus, section 67—in 576. The same author] he was instructed as a deacon by blessed Agrippinus, and in the following three years he was ordained priest. Thereafter, by Bishop Nectarius [Note: [Col. 0456C] Saint Nectarius, bishop of the Church of Augustodunum, subscribed to the Council of Orléans in 547. Bollandus. He presided over that Church as early as 542, as Cointius notes under that year, no. 29], he was deemed worthy to be assigned as abbot to Saint Symphorianus [Note: [Col. 0456C] Saint Symphorianus the martyr died at Augustodunum under Aurelian. His Acts may be found among the *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, under approximately the year 180].

How great his abstinence was there, how many vigils he maintained without interruption, and how lavish he was in almsgiving, one event alone bears witness. After he had distributed his remaining possessions to the poor, not even bread was left for the brothers’ refreshment. When the monks therefore rose up against him on this account, he withdrew into his cell and wept and grieved bitterly. Meanwhile, while he was praying, a certain matron named Anna sent two packhorses laden with bread [Note: [Col. 0456D] *Saumarii*, packhorses, called *sommiers* by the Gauls, from Greek σάγμα, “a burden”]. On the following day she also sent provisions in fully loaded wagons, so that the monks, when they were filled with food, were terrified by the miracle [Note: [Col. 0456D] After these words, Surius and some later copies insert the following verses: “The bishop, inflamed by his good works, threw the holy man, who still refused to reject these things, into custody; the demons even denounced him. I confess that by divine command the prison was opened for him, but he did not leave it until a supplication and an episcopal order had been given. Since these words are not found in the older and more reliable manuscripts, we have relegated them to an appendix. The same author]. Thus, devoted with celebrated zeal to these duties, he never ceased to reveal himself through miracles.

[Col. 0456B] **4.** Once, therefore, while he was tired and receiving food, the monk Amando entered the hayloft with a light. When a coal fell, the flame seized the hay, and the voracious fire began to lick up the dry fuel. The others ran together but did not come to the rescue. He himself, leaping out only after some delay, seized a cooking pot from the hearth, climbed upon the structure, sang the *Alleluia*, and poured a little water over the image of the cross. He extinguished the flames, and by the hand of the saint the wave of fire was calmed by a shower which rivers could scarcely have extinguished. The one whose plotting had caused this was himself forced to confess it on the following day.

**5.** A certain Frank named Chariulfus [Note: [Col. 0456D] Also called Warnulfus. Bollandus. Perhaps he is the same man whom Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book VII, chapter 38, reports as having entered into an agreement with Mummolus and Waddo to hand Gundovald over to his enemies?] had stubbornly seized part of the property belonging to the basilica of a village. When the man of God admonished him to return at least some of it, but without success, he turned to prayer, and faith did not delay vengeance [Col. 0456C]. Immediately a savage bear sprang out from nearby and killed three of his horses, but even then he did not turn back from his hardheartedness. On the following night the avenger doubled the disaster: it killed six beasts of burden, yet even this punishment was not enough. On the third night it knocked down nine wagons, with a threefold number of corpses; thus the destruction increased toward disaster. Thereafter he sent a boy, though belatedly, to the blessed man, restored the seized field, and the calamity was checked. This happened so that, while the beast administered punishment, the man might gain understanding, and the brute might give reason to one who did not understand.

**6.** Thereafter blessed Agricola [Note: [Col. 0457D] Saint Agricola lived as bishop of Cabillonum from 532 to 580. Bollandus. — *Cabillonensis*: today Chalon-sur-Saône]—bishop of Cabillonum, whose chamberlain was severely weakened by the violence of fever and, with his mind fixed on death, seemed wholly to be passing away—sent to the holy man for the assistance of his intercession. Then, having received the written request at the basilica portico, he proceeded to the tomb of Saint Symphorianus. Meanwhile the just man devoted himself to prayer, pressing the earth with his body and rising above the stars in his mind; and, as though he had the presence of the Lord before him, he approached as a suppliant pleading for the petitioner’s request. [Note: [Col. 0457D] The manuscript of Bonifontes reads: “And without delay he was heard by the ears of the Most High God.” Bollandus.] For he was immediately heard by the ears of the Redeemer, who was near; and while this man still lay in the dust, healing poured over the sick man. While the Just One lay prostrate on the pavement, the weakened man rose from his bed [Note: [Col. 0457D] “Before the healing that was already in progress”], before the suppliant had finished praying, so that the boy, for whom funeral rites were being prepared, went out to meet the returning messenger. It was therefore beyond doubt that the sick man was restored to health at the very hour when the most blessed man was found to have prostrated himself in prayer.

**7.** Nor should the event that occurred at Ebro’s house through the faith of the Just One be omitted. When he entered the house, the matron Anna exclaimed that she was witnessing a marvelous thing. Asked by her husband what she was looking at, she said: “Behold, blessed Germanus [Note: [Col. 0457D] Fortunatus seems to have referred to this apparition in poem 13 of book II, written to the clergy of Paris, where he compares Germanus to Moses in these words:

*Moses, stretch out your hands, and aid your camp*] seems to me to be walking with a horned face. I can scarcely endure either to look upon the holy man with my eyes or to describe him in speech, radiant with horns in a new form.” The woman, struck with astonishment, wondered that in our own time she could see a man in the likeness of Moses. We must believe that, after speaking with the Lord, this man too could be recognized by a woman as exalted with a horn. Out of fear at this event, Ebro did not dare to sit beside the saint that same day, for a twofold reason: grief and terror alike.

**8.** It happened that he went to meet King Theodebert at Cabillonum on behalf of the villages of the Church of Augustodunum. Remembering Saint Symphorianus as he entered the palace, he spoke with such an overflow of the Spirit of God that the king assented before the petitioner had explained his request. With prophetic speech he also announced the end of the king’s life. After a few days, while returning from Rheims [Note: [Col. 0457D] Yet Gregory of Tours, *History*, book III, chapter 36, writes that Theodebert was ill for a very long time and died in the thirty-seventh year after Clovis’s death, the fourteenth of his own reign—that is, in the year 548 of Christ. Mabillon. — Both accounts, what Fortunatus relates here and what Gregory of Tours reports, seem capable of reconciliation if Theodebert is said to have recovered somewhat from his prolonged illness, as often happens, so that he was able to undertake the journey, but shortly afterward died when the illness returned], the king died in the course of the journey by a final fate, as though the holy man’s words had been spoken by an angel.

[Col. 0458A] **9.** Since it was customary for the most blessed man to keep vigil alone in the basilica of Saint Symphorianus [Note: [Col. 0458D] Saint Symphorianus had suffered martyrdom at Augustodunum under Aurelian, as we said above], the monk Silvester accompanied him. When they entered together at about midnight and approached the tomb of the holy martyr, they heard from the altar a tumult and repeated noises, as though a crowd gathered for a robbery were rushing about. Believing that an attack by robbers was taking place, the man of God ordered the monk to sing psalms before the tomb. He himself approached the altar. Then that crowd hurried eagerly toward the monk who was singing. After beating him severely, throwing him to the ground, and leaving him half dead, they quickly fled. The monk, barely repeating his disaster in a faint voice, confessed that he had been beaten by demons in a violent encounter.

[Col. 0458B] **10.** It happened that a servant of Sabaricus, named Aesarius, having suffered an injury, fled to the man of whom we are speaking and begged him to free him, at any price, from the service of his insolent master. Enraged against Aesarius, Sabaricus demanded eighty solidi as the price for Aesarius, his wife, and their only son, so that he would release the servants from his servile power. Yet the mercy of the Just One did not hesitate either to seek out or to pay this price. After it had been paid, the aforementioned Sabaricus happened to pass before the basilica, yet did not even come upon the prayer service. When he entered his house, he was immediately afflicted and bound, and, fettered in chains, was led to the saint. Even then mercy was not withdrawn from him by the compassionate man; rather, a prayer was immediately sent up, and through the power of his faith Sabaricus was cleansed. Then Sabaricus added twenty gold pieces to the price he had received, and, from the hundred solidi, a cross was hung by him at the tomb of blessed Symphorianus; it remains there to this day as a testimony. On this occasion his sons and daughters conducted themselves so devoutly that they now govern communities of monks in monasteries. In a wondrous manner this event benefited both the father and his offspring, so that the small [Perhaps: “evil”] crime of the parent passed down to his descendants as gain.

**11.** The event occurred in the territory of Alise [Note: [Col. 0458D] Alexia, Alise, once a very powerful town situated on a hill among the Mandubii in Burgundy and well known to Caesar, *Gallic War*, book VII. It is now a village built upon a sloping hill. Mabillon]. Destasia, wife of the illustrious Vulfarius, deprived of every comfort that could sustain hope of life and bereft of the functions of her tongue, had lain mute for two days, breathing her last. Funeral rites had already been prepared, and she was twitching like a lifeless body. When blessings were sent to her through her priest and forcibly applied, her teeth—already dead—being pried open and the blessing passed into her mouth, as soon as the liquid entered the throat of the half-living woman, she immediately began to breathe the air of life. Her eyes, closed by death, sought the light of day, so that after the pallor of funerals her face changed to red, until, to the astonishment of everyone, she rose restored to life and those standing around proclaimed the author of the gift in gratitude.
