Each year thereafter she paid a tribute to life in return for this gift.

**12.** Moreover, let an investigator of his revelations enter here: had the very reason for his episcopate not been disclosed to him four years beforehand? Thus, while asleep, he saw an old man handing him the keys of the gate of Paris. He asked what this meant and received the answer that he should keep them safe. After the bishop of his city had died [Note: [Col. 0459D] It is disputed whether Libanius or Eusebius was Saint Germanus’s predecessor in the see of Paris. On this matter see Cointius under the year 551, no. 9, where he shows that what is related about Libanius should be attributed to Saint Germanus. He inclines toward the view that Eusebius the elder preceded Saint Germanus in the see of Paris, since this Eusebius is mentioned in the Acts of Saint Cloud. He was therefore made bishop of Paris in 551 and died around 555, as Cointius reports under that year, no. 18], when he went to meet the most distinguished King Childebert [Note: [Col. 0459D] Childebert, son of Clovis, held his court at Paris, as Fredegarius reports among others in the *Epitome* of the works of Saint Gregory of Tours, no. 30. He died in 558. Gregory of Tours repeatedly praises Childebert’s piety, and Fortunatus himself celebrates it in his poems; on this matter see what we said in the notes to book II, chapter 14], that utterance earned its fulfillment in his election. Once ordained bishop, what sort of man he was and how great his conduct was, mortal speech is not sufficient to explain, since everything he produced was above the human level. Finally, after attaining the office of pastoral care, he continued to live as a monk. On the one hand, he exercised himself through frequent vigils; on the other, he tormented himself with unbroken fasts. His aged body spent winter nights in the cold, enduring a double cold, that of age and of the season—something that even vigorous young men could not tolerate—almost forgetting himself for the victory of the body, as though dignity and necessity had arrived together. But the almsgiving that was made by the saint’s hands, whether from the Church’s possessions, the offerings of the people, or royal gifts, is known only to the One who knows, understands, and counts everything.

**13.** Finally, on one occasion the most distinguished King Childebert sent him six thousand solidi to distribute to the poor [Col. 0459C]. After spending three thousand, he returned to the palace. The king asked him whether anything still remained for him to give to the needy. He replied that half remained, and that he had not found poor people on whom he could spend it all. The king said to him: “My lord, give what remains. For, with Christ bestowing it, there will never be a lack of what may be given.” Breaking up golden serving-dishes [Note: [Col. 0459D] A *missorium* was a dish or bowl, so called because food was placed in it. Some think *missorium* derives from *mensorium*, because it was set upon the table. Gregory of Tours, book VI, chapter 2: “Then,” he says, “I had gone to Novigentum village to meet King Chilperic, and there the king showed us a great *missorium* that he had fashioned from gold and jewels, weighing fifty pounds,” etc.], and silver vessels, he gave to the priest whatever he first possessed, so that nothing might be lost. A contest between priest and ruler was therefore to be expected. Within themselves they waged a battle over mercy and a contest over piety, eager to scatter their treasures so that the poor might grow rich from their talents, hastening toward future profit, so that they might sow a golden [Note: [Col. 0460D] So the manuscript copies read, though *bracteum semen*, that is, “golden or silver seed,” seems to be the correct reading; for *bractea* is a thin sheet of gold or silver. The following reference to a golden harvest supports this interpretation. Mabillon] seed and afterward approach the reapers through a golden harvest, so that the priest might be enriched by royal treasures and the priest’s favor might flourish toward the king, who considered only what he had received while naked or needy to be his own.

**14.** But let us return to the sequence of events. A certain man named Gildomeris, one of the fiscal servants, had worked on the Lord’s Day in the village of Exona [Note: [Col. 0460D] Essonne, near Corbeil]. His fingers contracted so severely that the sharp points of his nails penetrated from one side to the other. He met the holy man at Paris in the oratory; after prayer had been offered and his hand anointed with oil, the nails were drawn back from the palm. The fingers recovered their function, and the fabric of the nerves was rewoven for its former service. After the miracle he made him a cleric, and, to preserve him whole and safe, freed him both from disease and from his offense.

**15.** Again, a certain woman named Favonia, in the city of Paris, had taken nothing for nine days except a little porridge. She was brought to the holy man with her mouth open and gasping. As though a piece of iron had been placed between them, she could not in any way bring her teeth or lips together. He anointed her with oil in the sacred oratory, touched her head on every side, and restored her to health without delay.

**16.** It happened that a girl of Medard’s household at Meglidunum [Note: [Col. 0460D] Melodunum, Melun on the Seine, ten leagues above Paris. Some manuscripts read “from the house of Medard, of the Meglidunian family.” Mabillon], while spinning on the Lord’s Day, had her hand contract and was condemned to punishment. When he touched it with oil, power infused a remedy. At this, her astonished fingers recovered their former strength; her restored joints resumed the work of the forgotten craft, her hand spread out like a branch, and her right hand, cleansed of its defect, was restored to health.

**17.** It is rightly believed that the following miracle should also be included. A certain Bobolinus, from the village of Noviomagus [Note: [Col. 0460D] Noyon in Picardy], grievously overcome by the enemy’s snares, was brought to the man of God bound in chains. Twisted and shaken by a rebellious spirit, he was thrown about and was not wearied [Perhaps: “was loosened”]. When the holy man prayed for him, on the seventh day he returned to himself and his own mind, as though from a long journey. Thus freed in two ways, when the shadow departed from his senses, the chain fell from his hands, and he was restored both sound and unbound.

**18.** This, too, must rightly be handed down to perpetual memory. A certain man from the family of Nantharicus [Note: [Col. 0460D] Perhaps Nemptodorus? Nanterre], with the joints of his jaws separated from one another and his mouth open, was brought to the holy man. After restoring him to health by the sign of the cross, the saint forbade him to take wine or eat meat [Note: [Col. 0460D] Something similar is related of Saint Benedict in Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 16. The same author]. But when he disregarded the command, he was immediately reduced to the condition of his illness. Yet, lest the negligent transgression deprive the Just One of glory, he was brought to him again at the estate of Spedotenus [Note: [Col. 0461D] Others have *Spedenotus*, *Espone*, a village near the fortress of Medunta, Mantes, ten leagues below Paris, not far from the confluence of the Mandra with the Seine. The same author]. The saint anointed the places of his jaws with oil, and with his blessed hands held his chin. After Christ’s name had been invoked, his lips, which had been shaken apart, returned to their proper joint through the saint’s fingers, and, by the merit of his faith, he was restored safely to his home.

**19.** Likewise, a smith named Ligerius, seized by the madness of a turbulent demon, had broken out with such bestial ferocity that, bound with chains around his neck and hands, he could scarcely be dragged into the blessed man’s presence. He was even more pitiable, since to the violence he endured from the enemy another punishment was added through the bonds. Nevertheless, the priest ordered him to be kept with him; and just as God rested from his work on the seventh day, so, when the week had passed, this work of God was rescued from the demon. Thus, freed from the enemy, he deserved to return safely to his own home.

**20.** Waddo, an illustrious man and participant in the king’s counsels [Note: [Col. 0461D] Perhaps this is the same man whom Gregory calls the queen Radegund’s mayor of the palace in book VII of the *History of the Franks*, no. 27, and who is there said to have gone over to Gundovald’s party. This Waddo was killed in 589], suffered a double attack of fever and chill and was brought before the holy man’s gaze to be cleansed. Meanwhile, at the customary hour, shaken by a very severe fever, he urgently begged for water so that he might be cooled. When it was denied him, he grew insolent against the holy bishop. Yet the man of God, intent on obtaining victory, completed his prayer and gave him a drink while it was warm. He restored the man to his former health and treated the impending danger with this antidote, curing the fever through warmth.

**21.** Nor should a miracle of a similar kind be passed over. Ulfus, a minister of Queen Chrodosinta [Note: [Col. 0461D] Gregory of Tours, book IV, chapter 3, calls her Chlothsinda, daughter of King Chlothar, who later married Alboin, king of the Lombards. From this passage one may see that the daughters of the Frankish kings, while still living in their father’s house, were called queens. Mabillon], was grievously afflicted by a recurring fever [Note: [Col. 0462D] That is, intermittent fever] [Note: [Col. 0462D] Is this the Wulfus who, according to the *Scholastic Chronicle of Fredegarius*, no. 29, was killed at Brunhild’s command?]. Seeking the assistance of healing, he went to the bishop. The man of God firmly led him to the baptistery. But when the saint prayed, he began to suffer more severely, being about to be freed. Burning and feverish, he begged for a little water, but it was denied. Stirred to the utmost fury by the bitterness of his bile, he threw his belt at the saint’s feet and cried: “You are killing me, my lord, when you ought to heal me. But know this: I am dying because of you. My life will be demanded from you by the king or by my parents.” Meanwhile [Bollandus: “while”] he rolled from the heat across the floor of the baptistery. While the blessed man prayed, he fell asleep; after being awakened from sleep a little later, the weakened man was restored by him to complete health. When the bishop asked why he had spoken so many insults against the priest, he replied that he had only been thanking him, and confessed that he remembered nothing of his own words.

**22.** When the most distinguished King Childebert had given the holy man a horse as a conveyance necessary for his saddle, the donor himself asked that he retain it for himself and give it to no one. Meanwhile, when a captive asked him, the blessed man gave the horse as payment, because in the bishop’s judgment the poor man’s voice counted for more than the king’s. He therefore ordered that it be sold for fifteen solidi. As the poor man was leading it away, a merchant met him and bought the aforesaid horse for twelve gold pieces. After purchasing it, the merchant brought it to the stable. But because he had paid less than the man of God had ordered, the horse died during the night, lest the saint’s word should come to nothing. On the following day the buyer dragged the dead saddle horse from the stable, joining oxen to the extinguished animal as to a vehicle. In a reversal of roles, it was led out with the halter tied not to its head but to its feet.

[Col. 0462B] **23.** It is worthwhile to commit to memory how the priest of Christ was accustomed to triumph even over kings themselves. Once, as usual, he had gone to meet the glorious King Chlothar. The king had not been informed that the holy man was standing before the palace, and, after waiting before the entrance without being admitted, he returned home. The following night was spent in vigils in the oratory, while the king was tormented by grief and the attack of a fever. At first light the nobles hurried to the church’s residence; they explained the king’s suffering and begged that, by his visit, he might lessen the force of the king’s pain. At once, in his compassion, he set aside the cause of injury; he who previously had not even been announced entered the palace, honored and entreated. The king barely rose from his bed and complained that he had been struck by a divine scourge. He licked the saint’s little cloak and drew the priest’s garment over the places of pain [Col. 0462C]. Having confessed the guilt of his offense, all pain immediately fled. This happened so that the man who had incurred danger through contempt might experience healing through touch.

**24.** An event took place in the Parisian territory at New Village [Note: [Col. 0462D] See below, section 40]. A certain man, torn apart by the attack of a rabid wolf and deprived of his senses, was mercifully brought to the blessed priest. He resorted to those remedies of his art: immediately he smeared the arm with the liquid of blessed oil and medicinally touched it with his sacred fingers. The disease that had invaded the entrails as pain spread through them fled the afflicted places; once they had been dissolved by putrefaction, their former strength was restored, and, as though the man had awakened from sleep, the pain withdrew without delay and his mind returned.

**25.** Likewise, in the village of Mantola [Note: [Col. 0462D] Is this the fortress elsewhere called Medunta? Certainly the vernacular name Mantes is quite close. See above, section 18. The same author. — Mantola, commonly Maule, is ten leagues from the city; but the nearby town of Mantes, called Medunta by others, lies in the French Vexin on the Seine. Bollandus], a maidservant of a certain Waldulfus, struck by severe blindness for a year and nine months, was warned in sleep that, if she touched the saint’s fringe, she would immediately recover her sight. One day she came upon the priest, but she was enveloped in deep night, with her eyes so tightly closed that they offered no opening through which he could apply blessed oil. Nevertheless, after anointing her eyelids from above and the other places of her head, he offered a prayer, blessed bread and salt, and ordered the woman to withdraw to her lodging. He himself remained awake in the oratory from his first sleep. Around midnight the woman cried out to her host that she was weeping profusely. Then, when a light was kindled, he saw blood flowing from the structure of her eyes. The next morning she returned to the saint with the same blood. He bathed and washed her eyelids with water, adding prayers, and one eye opened. Then, after anointing the other, he sent the woman home. Later that same night, after an excessive discharge of blood, as day approached, she presented herself to the priest. When he returned home from meeting the king and entered the oratory [Col. 0463B], the woman’s other eye immediately opened, and, by the Lord’s gift, she rejoiced to see with the twin light of both eyes.

**26.** A girl named Magnofledis [Alternatively: Rannoslidis], deceived and tormented by such snares that whenever she wished to approach the church she could not take a step, was brought to the servant of God at the estate of Savara [Note: [Col. 0463D] Savara, Seure, two leagues below Paris, near the fortress of Meudon. Mabillon]. As soon as the saint’s hands were placed upon the head of the stumbling girl, the hidden guest [Al.: enemy] was exposed through this investigation. He confessed with many groans that he had long been concealed and declared that in the presence of the blessed man he could not hide behind his own deception. Thus exposed, he complained bitterly that he would be forced to leave. Meanwhile the priest continued to trace the sign of the cross with his hand. As everyone watched, the enemy burst forth in the likeness of a fly, leaving through the woman’s nostrils together with blood [Col. 0463C]. He caused her, restored to health, clothed in a monastic habit, and dedicated to the service of God, to triumph twice over: once over the defeated enemy and once over the world.

**27.** What of the man who immediately cured a disabled right hand? When he had gone to Tours for the feast of Saint Martin, after he had left the monastery, a barbarian woman came forward. Her hand was contracted by the sinews, and she begged for a remedy. Taking her under his cassock, he smeared her with his saliva and kneaded it as though he were gathering scattered flour. Then, as the right hand began to sweat, she stretched and flexed her fingers, reviving long-standing numbness into vitality. Before she reached the door of blessed Martin, he had made her extended right hand sound again. As soon as he perceived that it had been straightened, he repelled the woman from him [Note: [Col. 0463D] For “sent her away”] and entered the basilica.

[Col. 0463D] **28.** Then, as he was leaving the aforementioned basilica and the servant of God was returning to his lodging, another woman presented herself, with one palm fixed in place. It had first been touched with saliva and then anointed with oil, and was immediately restored to its former health. For the holy man’s way of treating the causes of illness was to touch them.

**29.** It was indeed marvelous how often, whenever the servant of God wished to travel to Augustodunum, the demons immediately announced it at Saint Symphorianus. Meeting him through Murvinus, they cried out with weeping and groaning: “Holy man, if you thoughtlessly drive us from cultivated places, at least permit us to live in the solitude of the forests, so that we wretches may be allowed to wander safely through deserted regions. Before your eyes, neither bodies nor groves conceal us.” Weeping and unable to endure the saint’s presence, they were driven into flight in every direction from the possessed bodies when he laid on his right hand, and the demons lamented that they had been expelled for the people’s salvation.

30. Let that famous miracle be brought forward. When the bishop was returning from Saint Symphorianus and, traveling by way of the castle of Avallon [Note: [Col. 0463D] Above, no. 1.], entered it, he found a multitude of accused persons confined in the prison. From there Count Nicasius invited him to dinner. The man of God began a conversation about mercy, asking that guarantors be provided, that the prisoners be released from their bonds, and that, out of regard for compassion, some part of their guilt be remitted. But Nicasius, stubborn in spirit, delayed doing so. Therefore, before he had eaten, the saint slipped away from the table and, having gone down to the underground prison, prayed for a long time with tears that what the temporal judge had refused might be granted through divine assistance.

Thus that course of tears rose through the air to heaven, and his lamentation reached its goal. An angel was therefore assigned to accomplish the matter. Then the venerable man, promising hope, encouraged the prisoners. His speech did not fail of what it proclaimed: faith was fulfilled by deeds. When he departed, at once the links of the chains were broken [Note: [Col. 0463D] *Bacae* or *baccae* means the berries of the laurel or juniper; likewise gems and the head of a dead person; here, though unusually, it means the links of chains. THE SAME.

Saint Gregory of Tours likewise uses *baccae* in the same sense in which Fortunatus uses the same word here, [Col. 0464D] in these words, book I of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 23: “All the *baccae* of the chains, broken, fell.” Thus *baccae* is used in the same sense as *boja* or *baga*; see these terms in Dufr., *Glossary*.], the barred doors were opened, daylight was brought back into the prison, and the condemned came forth from darkness into [Col. 0464C] light. Punishment no longer held those whom it had tormented. Thus rescued, they hurried to Paris to meet the bishop while they were still in danger as prisoners. But, to confer something more upon the guilty, he obtained from the king whatever was owed to the treasury on their account.

31. Thereafter, when Nicasius wished to go to meet the holy man, he was immediately struck down upon the ground by a very severe seizure as soon as he had been presented to him. Almost entirely deprived of every support of health, he recovered strength and understanding through the intercession of the saint. At once he handed over to blessed Germanus, as a gift, the belt with which he was girded and his sword; but the count later bought them back by paying a price. This happened so that, having earlier delayed granting the prisoners their freedom, he might now repay his debt with doubled interest, and repair his losses by increasing the gift: previously postponing his mercy toward them, and afterward redeeming himself as well. Formerly not compassionate toward them, now fearful for himself, he learned through his own misfortune to assist the sufferings of others.

32. Let that utterly astonishing event be unfolded upon the page. As the holy man was going to meet blessed Symphorianus the martyr, while he was proceeding from the village of Cervedon [Note: [Col. 0464D] Cervedo, Cervon: a village near Corbiniacum, commonly Saint-Léonard de Corbigny, in the Morvan district, which separates Burgundy from the Nivernais. MAB.] in the Morvan, the inhabitants of the place came to him and suggested that he should visit the crop belonging to the widow Panitia [Note: [Col. 0465D] Or, “of the baker’s wife.”], who possessed nothing else and whose field was being ravaged by bears, so that the attack might be driven away by his holy arrival. He hastened there; although his attendants mocked him, he was led to the place, and after prayer he made the sign of the cross over it.

Then, by divine impulse, savage anger was kindled in the parent beasts; hatred arose in their hearts, and fighting broke out amid peace. The beasts were twice armed with fury: one bear was immediately strangled by the other, while the one that had remained, wishing to go outside, was pierced through by a fence-post. Thus both ravagers were killed in a single moment, and they themselves at once became the instruments of their own death. When he returned, the woman eagerly offered him the bears’ hides and presented the spoil to him as to her victor. He absolutely refused to accept it. Those who had previously laughed began to repent when they saw the miracle.

33. Since there ought to be no distaste for God’s gift, we shall briefly explain that event as well. [Note: [Col. 0465D] A certain Beretrudis is mentioned by Gregory of Tours, book IX, chapter 35, and is said to have deserved well of churches and monasteries. Yet she seems to have been the same woman whom Fortunatus praises in book II, chapter 12, for having built the basilica of Saint Saturninus at Toulouse; she is said to have been the wife of Launebodus. Either, therefore, she was another woman, distinct from the one mentioned here, or this woman must be considered to have previously been married to another man.] A certain woman, Beretrudis [Note: [Col. 0465D] Or, Munsuinth.], the matron of Munsunthus, was unable, during the time of the litanies, to go with the people because her eyes had been blinded. Hearing the choir singing, she implored the help of Lord Germanus with tears.

On the third night afterward, while asleep, she saw the most blessed man standing beside her bed and, as though for blind eyes, making the sign of the cross. When she awoke, the woman told her husband what had happened. Immediately, with blood trickling away, daylight was restored to her eyes, and after the long cloudiness her sight shone with a clear ray. When day had brightened, the woman proceeded with the people in procession to Mass, so that the image of the holy man seen in the dream became her remedy.

[Col. 0465C] 34. There is also an equally praiseworthy case: the life restored to a little girl. When, in the Touraine, the matron of the illustrious man Pientius was lamenting the final condition of her exposed daughter, and the infant lay with closed eyes and no moving breath, she entrusted all her hopes to the presence of the holy man. Invited by a messenger, he hurried, as far as he was able, to the girl who had been given up for dead [Note: [Col. 0465D] Ancient codex: “to the corpse.”]. Received amid the family’s abundant weeping and mourning, he approached the bench on which the infant already lay stiff.

By his pleas he assaulted heaven. After almost an hour had passed in this way, the girl’s breath was restored with a moving sob; the vital warmth of her inner organs spread through her limbs. Then, gradually revived, she asked for a drink, so that she might drink. The blessed man gave the infant bread marked with the sign [Col. 0465D] or a taste from the chalice; she who had been recalled from death [Col. 0466A] was wholly restored to health. Later she completed the course of her happier life in the monastery of blessed Radegund.

35. A certain cleric from near the monastery of blessed Silvester in Ternoderinse [Note: [Col. 0465D] The Ternoderensis district, whose center is Ternodorum or Tornodorum, Tonnerre, in the duchy of Burgundy, extends as far as the monastery of Réomay, commonly Moustier-Saint-Jean. At that time Saint Silvester was its abbot. Read the Life of Saint John of Réomay. MABIL.], when, on the Lord’s Day, as we customarily say, he had fashioned a pair of leggings, incurred weakness of his hands and feet. But, through blessed Silvester, he regained the use of his steps after being admonished in sleep; he came to Saint Germanus and asked for the remedy of health. When questioned by him, he confessed the cause of his fault. Then the saint ordered the cleric to proclaim publicly that no one should rashly work on the Lord’s Day. When the fifth day had passed, oil was poured over him; his weakened palm was straightened, and he was sent home free to walk.

[Col. 0466B] 36. Let what happened in the district of Amonia [Note: [Col. 0466D] Mosny, in Brie.] be related again. [Note: [Col. 0466D] Castellanus likewise seems to think that this place was in Burgundy, and therefore different from Rongy, only a league and a half from Paris; yet he does not believe it to be Rosoy, formerly Rosetum. BOLLAND.] Seven men, raving, were brought to him at the estate of Rotegiacum, belonging to the Church of Paris. After they had been cured, one who was more grievously afflicted by the spirit, when forced to leave, confessed to the man of God that, once expelled from him, he would cause great lamentation for the Parisians. Then, when the pest had been driven away by the passage of Saint Germanus, it spread his fame among the peoples and moved the shepherd’s flock to mourning over his death. Yet although that possessed man sowed a falsehood, once expelled he did not defend the one who had been possessed.

37. And because miracles compelled the works of the righteous to increase, a paralytic was likewise offered to him in the aforementioned place. His limbs were loosened; he was carried on a cart, deprived of walking and of movement. When he had been drenched with the liquid of sanctified oil, as soon as it touched the surface of his skin, strength entered his marrow. Then his restored hands returned to active use [Note: [Col. 0466D] Thus the manuscripts read; nevertheless, the passage seems to require: “The chest of the breast is strengthened by vital beating, the pillar-like weakness of the knees, etc.,” unless perhaps “knees” is being used adjectivally. MABIL.]; the chest’s vital beating grew stronger, the pillar-like weakness of his knees was strengthened, and the soles of his feet rose, their foundations made firm. In the midst of this, the whole structure of his limbs was repaired. Having recovered his health, when the holy man was returning, he met him on the road with a prepared gift, giving thanks to Christ for the body that had been restored.

38. Nor must it be passed over how, by a similar merit, power shone forth in another case. Accordingly, a very small boy named Emmegisilus from the village of Bucciacum [Note: [Col. 0466D] Bucciacus, Boissy, somewhat above Paris, between the Seine and the Marne. The same.] was brought to Saint Germanus in Paris, carried by bearers’ hands in a chair. Neither did his right hand possess active strength, nor did his foot rise firmly, nor did his tongue speak fluently; he was captive to the wasting weakness of his entire body, as though, contrary to nature’s order, he had been poured into the natural world without the proper organization of nature. The saint anointed him continuously for three days with holy oil and restored him to health; in a single moment he regained voice, hand, and step. Astonishment seized everyone, and a shout was raised to heaven, for all declared that Saint Germanus had surpassed every art of physicians.

[Note: [Col. 0466D] In several manuscripts the following words are inserted here: “For three days he is shaken in voice, hand, footstep, and modesty; the report is carried throughout the regions, and they give thanks to the Creator, acknowledging the man by whom diseases and morals are continually governed.” But they do not seem to fit the text. The same.]

39. Again, from the same village of Bucciacum, a certain woman came to Paris with her hand so contracted that the sharpness of her nails pierced her palm inward to the deepest part. He merely drew saliva from his mouth with his thumb, and the tension of the nerves relaxed; he restored the hand’s form.

40. The district of Bourges also preserves his triumphs. When the good shepherd had reached the village of Novigentum to visit his flock in his customary care [Note: [Col. 0467D] Fortunatus mentioned above, no. 26, a Vico Novo, which he places near Paris. This is certainly thought to be the same place, though a certain Gallic paraphraser wrongly sought it near Bourges, when the saint was visiting it in his usual manner. That woman, therefore, may have belonged to the diocese of Bourges, but the place was certainly not Novigentum, or the Vico Novo of Saint-Cloud, commonly Saint-Cloud, formerly called Novigentum. It is more plausible that this passage should be understood of Novigentum near the forest of Vincennes, from which Villa Nova of Saint-Georges, as it is commonly called, is not far.

Yet Germanus often used to visit the district of Bourges, as Gregory, bishop of Tours, testifies in On the Glory of the Confessors, chapters 80 and 92. He also visited the district of Angers, as is stated in the Life of Saint Albinus. MABIL.], an old woman appeared before him who had spent twice four decades of years in blindness. The priest placed the sign of our redemption over her eyes and ordered her to follow the route along which the bishop proceeded.

On the next day, when she unexpectedly met him again, her eyes wept her salvation: blood flowed from her sight in a generous stream. She was seen among the others while the holy man stood present. He withdrew from the assembly and, since she was blind, led the woman into the lodging where his room was. Washing her eyes with warm water in his own hands, he restored daylight to them. She immediately saw the light and, overcome with boundless joy, thrust the holy man’s fingers into her mouth. At the same time, while the attendants wept with emotion, she declared that she saw the man who, in his house, dispensed sight to the blind without payment. But these things happened in the room in my presence.

41. When the priest was approaching an ecclesiastical estate called Inethe [Note: [Col. 0467D] Another reading: “in Aethe.”], a certain man met him, complaining that in a certain village he alone remained healthy, while all the other inhabitants suffered from severe distress. When the priest’s blessed loaves were carried to the sick, every illness was immediately driven away, and at the first taste of the blessed bread the disease was consumed together with it. Thus health was eaten by that crowd along with the food.

42. Again, when the man of God was proceeding to Paris, to the basilica of the blessed Holy Cross [Note: [Col. 0467D] The basilica of Saint Cross, otherwise of Saint Vincent, now Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the Parisian suburb. Read the Life of Saint Droctoveus the abbot, no. 13. The phrase “situated in the suburb of the same city,” added in some manuscripts and printed books, is an interpretation by the copyists. MABIL. We shall discuss this basilica further at book II, chapter 14.], a woman placed before the holy man a little child dressed in white, trembling in his final breath and already about to depart, saying:

“Compassionate father, if you would look upon this mourner, I, the grieving mother, would not be bereaved; nor would you wish me to leave this place full of groaning, emptied of my fruit. Unless you hasten to help, you see this unhappy woman: death is tearing the child from my breast. Either restore my son, or obtain that I too may be buried with him. Have mercy, shepherd, on the wretched woman whom her grief makes bold.”

When she had made this mournful plea, as soon as the blessed man’s right hand impressed the sign of the cross upon the dying child, he sought his mother’s breast like one waking from sleep, although he had already grown cold in death. Thus in an instant the son was lifted from the jaws of death and the mother from grief. The surrounding people were shaken with astonishment; a great cry rose everywhere, and they gave thanks to the Creator for the reward, the timing, and the extraordinary priest, through whom diseases and deaths [Col. 0468B] are continually brought under command.

43. Then, when he reached the village of Bradeia [Note: [Col. 0468D] Bradeia, commonly Brie-Comte-Robert, in the province of Brie; but Castellanus doubts whether the reading should rather be Bundeias, meaning Bondis, two leagues from the city, formerly Vungeie. BOLLAND.], in the district of Paris, and Mass had been celebrated, a paralytic woman was carried to him in a chair in the sacristy. She was condemned to the uselessness of all her limbs and retained no strength in either her feet or her right hand. Immediately, trusting in him who bestowed generous gifts upon him, he anointed her with the blessing of life-giving oil. At once the disease was expelled and health-giving vigor flowed in. Her inner organs revived, and she was reborn to health more fully than a shoot to life, gaining from the gift more than she had received by birth. Thereafter she made a tunic for the saint with her own hands, as though she were a tributary of the medicine she had obtained.

44. [Note: [Col. 0468D] BOLL.: “it is handed down.”] Memory has handed down something useful for his praise. Accordingly, when Audegisilus, master of the royal household, was suffering severely from a quartan fever [Col. 0468C], he went to the blessed man, trusting in his beneficence. The man of God appointed him to remain confined in his cell with one deacon. Then the anxious and fasting attendant nervously considered what he should do and how the sick man might be cured.

Therefore he wrapped the feverish man completely in a *rachena* of the servant of God [Note: [Col. 0468D] Some write *rachana*, but both forms are rightly derived from the Greek word ῥάκη, “rags” or “torn pieces.” Hence Vossius thinks that *rachana* means a cheap and torn garment, in *On the Faults of Speech*. But the interpretation of our Menard is more suitable to this passage, in his *Concordance of the Rule*, p. 922, where he uses *rachanas* for coverings of beds. Elsewhere, however, Vossius’ explanation fits, as in book II of the *Life of Saint Radegund*, no. 4. MABIL.] and arranged him in his bed. That same day, at the touch of the noble garment, the entire fire of the quartan fever was extinguished as though by the force of a river. When the saint returned from dinner and the room had been opened, the man rose healthy from the bed. The attendant rejoiced at the reward of his health, since his fast had then been broken. Thus, though absent, the touch of the blessed man’s garment brought about his salvation.

45. Let us continue with the provisions for the journey undertaken. When the man of God was traveling from Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0469D] Poitiers.] to blessed Hilary the confessor, a certain Baudo-Feisa from the estate of Sene-Corbiacum [Note: [Col. 0469D] Secorby.] was brought before him, carried with difficulty by two people. She was mute, lame, and crippled. Her tongue was stiff and motionless, her breath fluttered, and her entire body was almost corpse-like, so that to those who saw her only the remainder of a corpse seemed to be left.

When, with compassion, he impressed upon her the sign of the holy cross, strength immediately spread through her limbs; the sluggish streams of her veins were stirred; the numb weakness of her nerves was shaken off; and the whole structure of her body was renewed for the living use of its natural movements. At once the tongue’s instrument was loosened, the knots of her fingers were stretched out, the bases of her feet were made firm, and for the holy man to give life to the whole mass of her inner organs was the same as to touch it. As the cure strengthened, on the third day she came into the city and met the saint’s footsteps, giving thanks to him.

46. It is thought worthwhile to insert this proclamation of healing as well. While the blessed man was passing through the district of Vendôme [Note: [Col. 0469D] The Vendômois.], he turned aside to Ransidon [Note: [Col. 0469D] Raucé.], intending to remain there. The power of his blessing became so great that whoever faithfully carried away a straw from the bed on which the holy man had rested carried with it the gift of healing; from the seed of straw he reaped the fruit of medicine.

47. Let the noble city of Nantes [Note: [Col. 0469D] Nantes, in Armorica.] bear witness here to the illustrious deed. When the man of God arrived there and was received with highly religious service, Thecla, the wife of Damian, a man energetic in business, came to him. She begged that either the shepherd himself or his messengers should visit her husband. Since access was difficult for the saint himself, he sent a deacon with his chrism-vessels [Note: [Col. 0469D] Chrismaria were vessels for receiving chrism. MABIL.]. The deacon hurried to the man and, as he had been ordered, touched the sick man’s inner organs.

The next day, after being entreated, the priest himself went to the weak man, who was being tormented by a double torturer: pressed on one side by illness and on the other afflicted by the wound of gout, a pitiable man treated harshly. Then the priest of the Most High anointed the sick man with blessed oil. At that moment the weak man’s hands were straightened, his long illness departed, and his step made firm; he leapt up.

48. But so that the mystery might be doubled in one household, and the cure that had preceded in the father might reach the child, they brought him a daughter named Mary, blind, deaf, and mute. They placed the living corpse [Note: [Col. 0469D] Another reading: “corpse.”] before the holy man’s feet, saying:

“Good shepherd, bestow upon this sick girl whatever remedy still remains. For we believe that this has been reserved for you, so that you might possess a proclamation of praise, and that, once the household has been restored, the priest might recover for it what it had lost from its offspring.”

Then his outstanding compassion was summoned to tears. At once he turned to the weapons of his spiritual warfare and, as a brave advocate, offered prayers to obtain victory. The blessed man then rose from prayer, anointed the places on her head with blessed oil, and, in the name of the Trinity, drove away the threefold disease. Immediately the passages of her ears and eyes were opened; while everyone applauded, the mute girl became eloquent. After this, the merchants of the city of Nantes, each according to his means, either offered money to the holy man for distribution to the poor or sent it to him devotedly as a remedy for themselves.

49. [Note: [Col. 0469D] Leudegisil the duke is frequently mentioned by Gregory of Tours, especially in book VII of the History of the Franks. He led the army of King Guntram, which is said to have besieged and captured the city of Comminges. He may also be the same man whom Fredegar the Scholastic calls the count of the stable in the appendix to Gregory of Tours’ History, no. 2. I believe him to be the same person whom Fortunatus mentions here; the addition of “illustrious” to his name also seems to indicate this.] Leudegisilus, an illustrious man, declared that whenever anyone from his household contracted a fever of any kind or suffered some chill, he washed the letters that the saint’s hand had traced in his signature, and by this remedy restored many of his people to health.

50. Having briefly touched upon these matters, let us proceed through the rest. A certain Chusinus, improperly tending a horse on the Lord’s Day [Col. 0470B], put his hand into a wound, and his finger swelled. Then, as the fever advanced, the whole part of his arm relaxed into putrefaction. When the saint was traveling through Belsa [Note: [Col. 0470D] La Beauce.], he obtained by pouring out prayers that the holy man would turn aside to his house. At once the man of God fomented his arm with warm water; then, anointing it with blessed oil, he placed cabbage leaves upon it and bound it like a marvelous physician. Thus the precious treatment extinguished whatever ulcer was present. Later, cured by such a poultice, he met the holy man and gave thanks.

51. Likewise, a servant of the Church named Libanius imprudently closed a hedge on the Lord’s Day, and his hands contracted as an immediate punishment. He hurried to the holy man in Paris, as the disease chastised him. The saint drenched him with the liquid of blessed oil, sprinkled him with the ointment of the mystery, and, adding prayer, restored him to health.

52. Let the miracles of individual events run briefly before us. Andulfus, a cleric of the Church of Paris, was shaking nuts from a tree in his little vineyard on the day of the Resurrection [Note: [Col. 0470D] That is, on the Lord’s Day.], because he had worked on the day of illumination; he was struck with blindness and remained with a darkened face for a year. Then he was brought to the bishop and anointed with holy ointment. He was restored once more to daylight, and the serene brightness of the priest dispelled the cleric’s cloudiness. Thus whatever the minister had lost, the healing bishop recovered.

53. And because kinds of miracles increase with time, when the blessed man came to be presented to the king at the estate of Rotegiacum, a cleric afflicted by a spirit of wickedness was brought to him. When the adversary had been expelled in the sight of those standing around, it emerged from the possessed man’s head like a little bird, its shadow driven away. As the others pursued it flying through the house, the saint himself crushed it beneath his feet. When it was pressed by his foot, the deceitful creature suddenly turned into blood, with a double display: it was not merely trampled underfoot, but, as a sign of its fall, the many-formed contriver became blood, guilty of bloodshed.

54. Let the district of Oximia [Note: [Col. 0471C] The district of Oximia, once distinguished by the title of a county, was so named from Oximus, a town of Neustria, commonly Hyesme. It lies between the sources of the rivers Dive and Orne and borders the district of Uche on the east. MABIL.] bring forward what belongs to it among our events, lest a deed of light remain hidden from posterity. When the most holy man had turned aside from his route to the estate of Tasiliacum [Note: [Col. 0471C] Ville-Taillac.], a woman was brought to him who suffered from a double illness: age on one side and blindness on the other. She began to implore health in trembling words. Moved by this supplication of the old and feeble woman, after prayer had preceded and oil had been poured over her, he restored rays of light to the lamps of her eyes; and when mirrors were provided, the darkness fled. Once she had been enlightened, those standing by Saint Germanus proclaimed his merits and gave glory to God, through whom Christ works.

[Col. 0471B] 55. The diseases must be counted, so that the physician’s fountain may be praised. Daningus, son of Ardulfus, was so swollen in his head, eyes, and entire inner body by dropsy that his whole belly seemed like a wineskin; the vital parts having been penetrated, the diseased skin shone through from within like glass. Despaired of by physicians, he fled as a last resort to the remedy of the blessed man. The saint immediately stripped him of his clothes and anointed him with his holy hands. The liquid enclosed by the dropsy was consumed by the liquid of the anointing, and the water was dried up by the infusion of oil. In a remarkable manner, no moisture flowed out of him and no illness remained within him: by an admirable art, moisture was dried by moisture.

56. Again, when he was going to keep vigil at the basilica of the most blessed Gervasius and Protasius, a certain blind man persisted in asking for mercy. The man of God ordered him to lie down between the altar and the relics of the saints. When this had been done, at first light he immediately brought the sign of the cross over his eyes, and light shone forth. The whole labor of the physician’s care was thus supplied by the power of the cross.

57. A woman from Oximia sought deliverance from the holy man but, by whatever fate, deserved to receive nothing. Thereafter she asked the priest Britannus for a blessing and for the relics of the aforesaid man on account of the illness of the ruler of her homeland. As he set out on his journey, he obtained lodging at the estate where the woman mentioned above lived. Her husband urged her to go with him, like the others, to meet the relics of Lord Germanus. She refused, because the holy man had not granted her deliverance.

But immediately, in the place where she stood, she could not move her foot, as though fixed in a stake; her hands contracted, and she was carried by her husband’s hand to the saint’s relics. Meanwhile, having repented of what had been said, she was restored to health through the compassion of the merciful man, confessing that the sudden danger had come upon her because she had despised him.

58. And since, by his merit, seeds of salvation were scattered everywhere, it happened that the venerable Flameris, abbot of Canonicum in the Touraine [Note: [Col. 0471C] Chinon above the Loire.], received a letter subscribed by the hand of blessed Germanus. When he visited his monk, who had been bedridden with fevers for two years, the sick man asked where the document had come from. The abbot replied that it had been sent to him by Lord Germanus. The monk asked that it be handed to him. As he touched with his tongue a letter of its subscription, health descended into his inner organs, and the writing of ink surpassed every ointment. Thus, when the sick man recovered, it was proved—as we may commonly say—that he had licked health from the saint’s signature.

59. Thereafter, when he was approaching the castle of Carnona [Note: [Col. 0471C] Charoy, in the district of Wastinensis.], a weak man with a contracted hand thrust himself before him because he had worked at something on the Lord’s Day. The saint ordered him to hurry after him to the estate of Cariacum [Note: [Col. 0471D] Cheury.]. When he arrived, the saint anointed his fingers with holy oil [Note: [Col. 0471D] Read the preface of the distinguished Mabillon and the Benedictine century I, no. 101, where he asks whether this oil was consecrated for the sacrament of anointing—the same oil that saints are said to have customarily used in treating illnesses.]. Suddenly the dry palm blossomed again from the other side. The skin, tightened over the bones, loosened the joints as moisture passed between them; the almost separated joints were extended into the fingers; long-standing dryness, drenched with fluid, flowed again through the veins. Immediately the right hand, closed by the wound, was restored sound and extended between the physician’s hands.

60. It happened that, as the holy man was returning from Nantes, he honored the house of the illustrious Nunnichus with his presence. A matron faithfully snatched a thread from his garment and stored it in an oratory. When illness attacked her [Note: [Col. 0471D] “Incurring” or “assailing.”], she solemnly celebrated vigils in honor of the saint, [Note: [Col. 0471D] This is an unusual expression, peculiar to Fortunatus, used by him again in book I of the Life of Saint Radegund, no. 14, but in both places it has been horribly corrupted in the printed books. Surius, following the authority of more recent copies, gives the passage as follows: “When vigils had been devoutly celebrated in the same oratory in honor of the saint, and Mass had been recalled, she was immediately cured.” The oldest copies, however, agree with our reading, which should therefore be retained. What, then, does “Mass recalled” mean? It means the annual return of the feast day. This is clear from the Council of Pîtres, chapter 3: “By common agreement we decree that, until the Mass of Saint Remigius”—that is, the Kalends of October—“those who during these times have committed such plunderings and other criminal and public misdeeds may have a period in which to make peace before the Lord and before those whom they have harmed.” In the Capitularies, book II, chapter 10, Charles the Great grants a period for correcting the coinage until the Mass of Saint Martin; and in chapter 20, for repairing bridges, until the Mass of Saint Andrew. If, therefore, the Mass of Saint Remigius, Saint Martin, or Saint Andrew is understood as the day dedicated to each saint, as is evident from the passages cited, Fortunatus may rightly and appropriately be interpreted here as referring to the annual return—as they say—of the feast of Saint Germanus; perhaps no other interpretation is possible. For when this author speaks of the most holy sacrifice of the Mass, he does not depart from the customary manner of speech, as above, no. 43. Yet Gregory, bishop of Tours, seems to use the same expression in another sense in On the Glory of the Martyrs, book I, chapter 51. Speaking of a mother, he says that she was admonished from heaven to keep vigil on the vigil of Saint Benignus and to “recall Masses” in order to avert the danger of bubonic plague: “Go and keep vigil throughout the night in honor of him, and recall Masses, and you will be freed from the plague.” Gregory also applies the celebration of Masses to laypeople in chapter 75 of the same book: “If those who now suffer from chills devoutly celebrate Masses in his honor,” and so forth. The same.] and when Mass had been recalled, she was immediately cured. Thus the most blessed man not only healed by his hand what he touched; even when named, he scattered cures.

61. Attila, an illustrious man and member of the royal household, fell in a bath. His arm was severely injured, and the whole hand had rotted from the shoulder. When a physician was summoned and wished to undertake treatment, a vein in his inner organs burst, and almost all the blood of his life poured out in an instant. The bishop was informed that the man was dying. Moved by compassion, the old man hurried to him and found him, with closed eyes, overcome and exposed as one whose death had been mourned, without any hope. He could barely open the man’s jaws with the handle of a knife. After first praying, he put a little cold water into his mouth once, twice, and a third time. Meanwhile he waited to see what the outcome would be and sat beside the bed.

After almost an hour had passed, the lifeless man was shaken by a restored sob, and breath, summoned by a gentle movement, returned. The passage of his throat was restored as his inner organs relaxed; breath passed through him, and as he gradually recovered, life returned from death. Then, as though waking from sleep, he asked who had been at his head. Those standing around told him that Lord Germanus was present. He requested that the saint’s hand be graciously extended to him and began to speak:

“My lord, you have recalled me as I was traveling a long journey.”

Immediately he offered a purse full of money and a heavy belt, so that they might be distributed to the poor as payment for his life or as an expression of gratitude.

62. As the holy man journeyed toward Augustodunum, he reached Rotagiacum and learned from Abbo that certain men had been shut up in prison. Accordingly, he humbly pleaded with the tribune for their release, but the man was hard-hearted and refused. Then, by a cautious plan, while saying that he was going around the field, the saint devotedly hurried to the prison. He threw himself down there in prayer and supplication. During the night, the chains were shaken apart, the strong severity of the instrument of torture was reduced to fragments, the heavy bolt was struck off, the doorpost was torn from its hinge, and the deadly prison was opened. The condemned returned to the vital air as though from the grave.

Thus it happened that, at dawn, they entered Rotagiacum and met him. The tribune, who had not granted the saint’s request for the condemned prisoners, himself became condemned.

63. Ever solicitous for the salvation of all, when he had come to Bourges [Note: [Col. 0473D] Bourges.] for the ordination of Bishop Felix [Note: [Col. 0473D] Felix succeeded Probainus in the see of Bourges in the year 568. See what we said about Felix in the notes to poem 25, book III, of Fortunatus’ works.], a certain Jew named Sigericus was converted after receiving the sacrament of faith, as the priest preached. He had a wife named Mammonah who remained in Judaism.

When she would not even hear mention of conversion and rejected the blessed man’s messengers when they admonished her, he held a vigil and went there himself. Since she would not even look at the holy man, after the office of the third hour had been sung, the bishop graciously brought his hand to the woman’s forehead as an act of compassion. Immediately those standing around saw smoke emerging from the woman’s nostrils with a sparkling flame, so that it became clear to everyone that, once the enemy had been expelled, the evil spirit had until then resisted the woman’s salvation by using her as a hostage.

Then, relieved of the enemy’s burden, she breathed freely and confessed that previously she had never been able to look upon the face of the blessed man. At her request and entreaty, she obtained the privilege of becoming a Christian together with her household; and, as though their head had submitted, many Jews were converted through her example.

64. It is fitting to insert here how the wandering light of an eye was restored. When he was going to Augustodunum for the ordination of Bishop Syagrius [Note: [Col. 0473D] See what we noted about Syagrius at chapter 6, book V.], Florentinus, an illustrious citizen, was brought there among the others to give his consent. He had a blemish in one eye, detracting somewhat from his appearance so that his face could not be considered flourishing.

Meanwhile, while acclamations of praise were being offered to the bishop, someone who did not know what he was doing suddenly struck him in that same eye. The eye was torn from its place and began to hang uncertainly above his cheek, together with his sight. Florentinus hurried with desperate speed toward blessed Germanus, crying out and uttering many complaints, as calamity makes people speak.

Then Saint Germanus restored the eye to its place with his hand and sent him from there to blessed Symphorianus [Note: [Col. 0473D] Namely, to the shrine of Saint Symphorianus, the martyr of Autun, whose Acts are found among the Acts of the Martyrs, around the year 180. [Col. 0474D]]. Symphorianus kept vigil for him until the lost eye, its former blemish cleansed and an additional benefit granted, was restored more complete than before; after the wound it returned better than it had been when he was born by nature. Florentinus was afterward ordained bishop at Mâcon [Note: [Col. 0474D] Mâcon.].

65. How great, moreover, was the power of his sign is shown by the following among the other testimonies. When he was returning from the basilica of Saint Martin to the estate of the holy church at Severiacum [Note: In the manuscripts of Boniface and Antwerp, “to a certain estate,” formerly Severiacum, commonly Sivray. BOLLAND.], he encountered on the road a certain young man named Amantius, whom he saw being led away by Jews, bound in iron chains. He asked what he had done. The boy truthfully replied that he was being led away in bonds because he had refused to submit himself to Jewish laws. Then the Jews pretended that they were unable to unlock the iron bonds with the key. When the holy man made the sign of the cross over them, the iron bolt was immediately torn away.

66. Likewise, when he was going to Paris to the basilica of Saints Gervasius and Protasius for prayer, entrance was denied him because the doors were barred. Then, when the keys had been sought and did not open them either, he unlocked the bolt by making the sign of the cross. Astonishment seized the minds of those present at the miracle: by the power of the sign, what could not be done with the key was opened. These events also took place in my presence and deserve veneration.

67. And because no metal resisted the blessed man, while wood, stones, and iron tools were loosened before him, one day it happened that, while he was offering prayer at the door of a prison in Paris, a light appeared in the prison to the prisoners during the following night. He seemed to admonish them to dig, so that they might get out. They said to one another that they had seen Lord Germanus, and each reported the signs he had perceived. Finding a rib of an animal, they dug and removed a stone, and at daybreak met the aforementioned friend of God at the church, when he was returning to rest. Thus the image of the bishop became for many the cause of salvation; and, in the place of blessed Peter, that likeness of our priest gave remedies.

68. After these men had been rescued, the city tribune began to rage against the soldiers, assigning to them as negligence what was reckoned to the most holy man as glory. Turning the judge’s anger against the guards who had been accustomed to keep them, he handed them over to be guarded in the prison; and, after taking away the keys, the judge became the guards’ guard. Meanwhile the blessed man invited the tribune to dinner. While they were sitting together at the same meal, those very men who had been put in fetters in place of the prisoners arrived at the holy man’s table. Holding the keys in his hands, the tribune could scarcely believe what he saw. Recognizing that he had guarded them in the same way as the soldiers had guarded the prison, he granted pardon in return, and the fault passed into favor.

69. Let Orléans [Note: Orléans.] offer a noble proclamation of the man. As the holy man was departing from that city, he heard the voices of condemned prisoners in a prison that was certainly an underground dungeon. Going up over it, he lay prostrate and offered prayer with tears, the friend of Christ. Clearly through the intercession of his prayer, the prison was opened during the following night, and they fled for refuge to the basilica of Saint Anianus. Thus the blessed bishop, although merely passing by, left assistance behind him.

70. Let it not be wearisome to hear what Christ grants to the faithful, while both the power and the number of miracles increase together. Thus a certain man met the most holy bishop in Paris whose eye had swollen out as though it were a fist, so that after the injuries it even hung forward, as if about to fall. At his request, the man of God smeared the eye with saliva from his mouth and restored healing and grace to the sight.

71. A certain Moverta [Note: Another reading: “stepmother.”] in Paris had a pustule on her arm and was tormented by pains. When she met the blessed man, she was cured by the same remedy, through the touch of saliva.

72. But if we were to relate one by one the miracles that flourished in his deeds during his earthly life, begun as they were without end, there would be no room on the page. For wherever the presence of the bishop turned, no kind of illness lacked a remedy; and as many wounds as the sick presented, so many seeds of healing he poured forth. Let us take up either the first or the last of the bishop’s deeds: many ulcers were cured by the saliva of his mouth, and possessed persons were cleansed.

Although the enemy’s wickedness had approached him secretly, its fraudulent deceit immediately revealed itself; and because they could neither hide from the holy man’s sight nor tolerate his presence, they bewailed their torments with terrible howling, displaying them as they flew about everywhere. Suspended in the air, they frequently confessed their crimes and their names without even being questioned. Often the demons, impelled of their own accord, ran to the holy man to be tormented. Wherever the servant of the saint held his staff, there the possessed person hung, bound by a bond of air, and was held fast to the spot as though fixed by a nail.

73. And because snares were often laid by the enemies against the holy man—so that either a horse might suffer a fall, or a tree branch strike him, or water in a valley or ice create danger—the possessed immediately confessed everything: who had done it, how many there were, in what manner it had all been contrived, and even the number. Whenever he stepped out of the house or church, one could see the demons strewn before the gaze of so great a bishop and victor. They fell in multitudes around the saint’s footsteps, scattered in various ways: some mute, others shouting; some fixed, others slippery. And, as before a judge, while they reported their own deeds, they did not escape their torments. What praise this is for the holy man, when so many ineffable and astonishing things were accomplished by him in an instant!

74. Nor can it be explained how lavish he was in almsgiving, even if the voice of the entire people were united into one. Often content with a single cloak or tunic, he used whatever remained to clothe a naked poor man, so that the needy might be warmed while the giver himself grew cold. Nor can the abundance of his redemptions be explained either by place or by number. Hence neighboring peoples bear witness—the Spaniard, Scot, Briton, Basque, Saxon, and Burgundian—when they came running at the name of the blessed man, from every direction, to be freed from the yoke of servitude.

But when he had nothing at all at hand, he would sit sorrowful and anxious, stern in appearance and austere in speech. Then, if someone happened to invite him to dinner, he compelled the guests or his own attendants to contribute together whatever would free at least one captive from service; and thus, by a little, the priest’s spirit would breathe again from its grief. If the Lord sent something from elsewhere to be distributed through the hands of the holy man, he would immediately foresee it in spirit and customarily say: “Let us give thanks to the divine mercy, for the means of redemption has drawn near.” At once the effect was proved to be present beyond doubt. When he received it in his hands, the wrinkle on his brow relaxed, the old man’s face blossomed, he went on his way with a livelier step, and his speech flowed more cheerfully, so that you would have thought that, in order to redeem others, the man himself had been freed from the bonds of servitude.

75. Who could worthily recount how great was the power of the words that rolled from his mouth when he preached to the people, so that all learning was astonished and a general compunction came upon the whole assembly? You would have thought that, as his words took shape, they came from an angel, while he spoke as more than human, transported in ecstasy of mind; for, wiping away stains, he compelled the hearts of the people, through the purity of his doctrine, to give forth the fragrance of divine spices.

76. While riding on a journey, he always contributed something concerning God, either by speaking or by singing, reciting the course of prayer with uncovered head, even when snow or rain pressed hard upon him. [Note: Ancient writers understood by the term “course,” or “procession,” the divine offices, or canonical hours, as they are called, because they are performed and run through daily. Rule of Saint Macarius, chapter 9: “Above all things you shall love the course of the monastery; but whoever wishes to pray more often will find a richer mercy of Christ.” In the manuscript Life of Saint Serenicus the abbot, which we shall publish in the coming century, the following is read: “He had been inflamed by such fervor in the practice of prayer that, without any special supplication, he would sing to the Lord at each hour the Roman or Gallican course, and that of the holy fathers Benedict or Columbanus.” Here the particle “or” is connective in both places, and the Roman course is not different from the Gallican. For we have observed in the preface to the Life of Saint Samson, bishop, p. 165, that the Gauls were formerly called Romans. The Gallican course is mentioned again in the Life of Saint Walaric the abbot, in Surius, April 1, no. 14. Nothing, moreover, is more common than this expression in Gregory of Tours, who mentions in Book X of his History one book on the ecclesiastical courses composed by himself. MABILLON.]

When he came to table, a minister immediately appeared, reciting divine discourses, so that amid the courses of food the guest might be even more fully satisfied by the nourishment of the soul. He left no interval of time in which he was not either benefiting others or making progress himself.

77. Who could describe how much care he always devoted to vigils, or praise, in the ardor of faith, the cold he endured, when frequently, while still on his little bed and before awakening the others from sleep, he would tirelessly sing fifty psalms or more to the Lord in the temple of his own breast?

But who ever heard or saw that happy theft [Note: Another reading: “blessed.”] when he frequently left his bed without stockings, so that no one would notice him, and went to the oratory, desiring that no witness to that theft should meet him except Christ? After completing the vigil, he would return to his bed and, as though he had done nothing, only then awaken the others.

How constant he was in psalm-singing, while his flesh endured as though clad in the hardness of iron, when frost peeled the stones and turned water into a crust! As he fought and conquered his own entrails, almost forgetting himself, he became a martyr and won a triumph over himself in peace through domestic torment and the subjugation of the body. Thus, while the clerics took turns, [Note: Fortunatus expresses in verse, Book II, chapter 13, the order and constancy of the Parisian clergy in psalm-singing under Germanus as master and leader.] he himself did not cease the melodies of psalm-singing without relief.

It is said almost incredibly, though it is known to be true: entering the church at the third hour of the night, he did not leave the order of the singers until, when day was growing bright, the entire course appointed by the canon had been solemnly completed in song.

When he returned home, weary from age or cold, or when the importunity of various people troubled him, or someone asked him where he might offer assistance, even when reclining for rest, the complaints of afflicted people or of the poor who came to him made his bed a cross. He postponed his own injuries, lest the necessity that prompted them oppress the petitioner. Ready for mercy, always running to grant pardon, father and shepherd of the people, he took upon himself the causes and complaints of others: either he soothed their pains by compassion, or, insofar as he could, he completely cured them by helping with all his heart.

78. He had also been so greatly advanced by sacred progress that he foretold the day of his blessed departure in the following manner. Several days beforehand, he summoned his notary and ordered him to write in the chamber, above his bed, only this: “The fifth day before the Kalends of June.” Since no one knew what this meant, after the holy man’s departure it made known that he had departed from the world. For the Lord did not permit him to conceal even this from a familiar soul. Finally, on that very day, after the battle had been completed, the blessed man departed to Christ.

Occupied and always intent upon these and similar pursuits, at nearly eighty years of age he flew forth from his bodily bonds, to be numbered among the martyrs through his wondrous deeds, joined to the apostles, glorified for his merits, and crowned among the peoples; he would live forever with an unstained spirit, endowed with the blessed gifts of faith. [Note: Concerning Saint Germanus’s death, Gregory of Tours writes in Book V, chapter 8: “In that year (namely, the first of Childebert the Younger [Col. 0478C], A.D. 576), blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, also died. At his funeral, this miracle confirmed the many powers which he had wrought in the body. For, while prisoners cried out, the body became heavy in the street; when they were released, it was again lifted without effort. Those who had been released likewise came freely, in attendance upon the funeral, as far as the basilica in which he was buried. At his tomb believers, by the Lord’s granting, experience many miracles, so that anyone who asks for rightful things quickly receives what he desires. Yet, if anyone wishes diligently to investigate his mighty miracles, which he performed in the body, let him read the book of his Life, composed by Fortunatus the priest, and he will find everything.” And in the Book on the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 90: “When King Chilperic entered the city of Paris, on the day after the king entered the city, a paralytic who sat in the portico of the basilica of Saint Vincent, in which blessed Germanus rests in body, was healed.” Aimoin adds, in Book III of the Deeds of the Franks, chapter 16: “When this had been reported to the king, he came there with great devotion; rejoicing greatly at so great a miracle, he composed his epitaph rhythmically in distichs,” etc. MABILLON.] Under the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are glory, honor, and power forever and ever. Amen.

# Life of Saint Albinus

[Col. 0477]

## Preliminary Notice on the Following Life of Saint Albinus, Bishop of Angers

[Col. 0477] That the Life of Saint Albinus was written by Fortunatus is attested by Gregory of Tours, in his Book on the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 96, in these words: “Albinus, moreover, the confessor, whose Life was recently written by Fortunatus the priest,” and so forth.

Likewise, in a letter circulated under the name of Gregory of Tours, written to Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, he relates that the Life of Saint Albinus, composed by Fortunatus, had been corrected by him, or purged of those errors that had crept into it through the incompetence of copyists. But that letter is rejected as inauthentic by the judgment of learned men, as Jean Launoy has shown in a dissertation written on the matter; we shall make further note of this elsewhere.

The authors of the *Literary History of France* think that this Life was elaborated by Fortunatus around the year 580, since Gregory of Tours, in his Book on the Glory of the Confessors [as we have related], mentions it as though it had recently been published. He completed that work of his, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, not long before the year 588, since in it he speaks of the funeral of Radegund, who died in 587.

Moreover, if Fortunatus is to be considered to have composed the Life of blessed Albinus no earlier than the year 576 or 577, the letter cited above, supposedly from Gregory of Tours to Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, is plainly fictitious and apocryphal, since Germanus died in that same year, 576, as we said in the notes to his Life. For how could Gregory have sent to him, while he was still alive, the Life of Saint Albinus, published by Fortunatus and corrected by Gregory himself? Therefore I am astonished that the distinguished Liruti, relying solely on this testimony drawn from the apocryphal letter of Gregory, should have decided that the Life of Saint Albinus was elaborated by Fortunatus, while passing over the earlier testimony of that same Gregory.

We publish this Life of Saint Albinus as it appears in the first Benedictine century, first published by Surius on March 1, then corrected and illustrated with notes by the distinguished Mabillon on the basis of two old manuscripts. The Bollandists likewise present it under March 1, augmented with notes, some of which we shall append where appropriate, in order to shed greater light on the Life of Saint Albinus.

[Col. 0479]

## Life of Saint Albinus, Bishop of Angers

[Note: Saint Albinus, formerly abbot of Tincillacum, or Cincillacum, was made bishop of Angers around the year 529 (as Cointius shows under that year, no. 1). He subscribed to the Third Council of Orléans in 538 and, through the abbot Sapaudus, to the Fifth Council of Orléans in 549. He died in that same year or the following one, as we shall say below.]

(C, S)

### Author’s Prologue

[Note: This prologue was absent from the Audomar manuscript. BOLLAND.]

1. I remember, apostolic man [Note: I readily believe that this was Domitianus, the second bishop of Angers after Saint Albinus. Fortunatus indicates in Book XI, chapter 27, that he had been invited by him to Angers to celebrate the festival of Saint Albinus, in these verses:

“From there I hasten forth and am carried from the palace of Cariacum;

From there I am borne to the place of Tincillacum.

From there the holy bishop Domitianus seized me,

Drawing me to the festival joys of Saint Albinus.”

Moreover, in the Escorial manuscript, as Rosweyde had noted, after the words “written by Fortunatus the priest,” the addition “to Pope Domitianus” was read, from Bolland. See our notes on poem 27 of Book XI of Fortunatus.], when I came to present myself before your gaze in the city that you govern under Christ as bishop, among the other mature counsels that you seemed to pour forth upon me, rich in understanding and like a torrent, you also made a brief mention of the most sacred man, Lord Bishop Albinus.

For, since his life is proved to flourish in heaven, stamped with unfading merits, you ordered that it be set down in writings for the instruction of the people and fixed in human records. In this way you would benefit the people by a double favor: in him they would retain admirable things to venerate, and in themselves they would see what each person should wisely correct; that is, while they learned so many things to praise in one man, they would not delay cutting away their own faults. Thus the single account of the blessed man might become a public remedy for its hearers.

2. Understanding how swiftly memories flee from the world and are snatched away, I fear that, through negligence, I might bind to writing certain things about the most holy man that are soon to perish, and that they would not easily be received again into the mind if, once beginning to be withdrawn, they were overtaken by the forgetfulness of time.

A certain instigator of this undertaking, carrying out the commands of your blessedness, asked me to agree to it, adding that whatever he himself had learned about the deeds of the holy man in accordance with the truth, I should, with him as informant, disclose without uncertainty. He thus increased the burden of his complaints, because although the aforesaid man had performed deeds secretly but worthy of being related, he had not been able to reach each one in his search for the truth, and he remembered having forgotten some of what he had learned.

Yet, in those things that he remembers without ambiguity, he brought us the people as consenting witnesses to his testimony, since surely one may not doubt the man’s past deeds when he daily performs clearer ones in each matter.

[Col. 0480A] 3. I rejoiced that such a man had grown under your nourishment, one who could so energetically plead the task entrusted to him and not inappropriately offer something of his own for the sake of elegance—or, if he wished, could himself explain what he had sought from elsewhere. For whatever is said about him is reckoned to your praise, since the merit belongs to the teacher, the pupil’s praise, and the bishop’s ornaments are found in the diligence of his servant.

Since I, conscious of my own smallness, trembled to undertake this, knowing that such a matter ought to be entrusted to men vigorous in talent, eloquent in speech, devoted in service, and proven in style—men rich in understanding, whose tongues pour forth like torrents, swift in service, and flashing in song—especially since even Cicero’s eloquence, as I suspect, would scarcely run securely before your skill, and the man who was freely permitted at Rome before Caesar to use an Aquitanian judge might perhaps fear to do so in Gaul,

4. what lofty task, then, is demanded from me, hiding beneath the footsteps of learned men, whom neither nature has made fluent in the sequence of writing, nor learning eloquent, nor long practice itself completely ready? Even if desire drew me onward, the greatness of the matter frightened me, because a radiant life is dimmed when an inadequate tongue of a sluggish narrator proclaims it, and what ought to illuminate is hidden beneath a cloud of speech. It would be more fitting for you to publish what you ask from others.

Therefore I understand with certainty that you do not need anything of this sort from me, but that you merely do not refuse to receive from a stranger some little provision [Note: On this word *sistarcia*, see Dufresne in the *Glossary*. It is also written *sitarchia* or *sitarcia*, and is understood sometimes as the food itself, sometimes as the pouch or basket in which food was carried; perhaps from Greek σίτῳ ἀρκούσα, “sufficient for food.” Hence Uguccio of Pisa: “Sitarcia,” he says, “a vessel and repository, like a sack and bag,” as it is read in the same Dufresne.] from me, and that, as among wheat crops, the barley of my sterility might be admitted.

Now, weighing the causes of uncertainty on the scales of judgment, I choose, as a rustic, to be recognized more for obedience than to become disobedient through learning, so that, although you may be displeased with my eloquence, you may at least approve my affection. In this work, however, I must take care above all that I present nothing insufficiently intelligible to the ears of the people. Therefore, content with complete modesty, although an inept narrator, I desire briefly to make known the deeds of so blessed a life.
