The One who knows how to heal [Note: Perhaps “ills.”] may himself provide the harbor of his right hand to my wavering page.

## The Life Begins

5. The life of religious men is the more frequently proclaimed by the voice of the peoples the more illustrious it is in merits, because, while they bestow benefits upon all, they stir the tongues of individuals to their praise. For this reason the life and deeds of the most blessed Albinus should be brought forward for the clearest proclamation.

Thus Albinus the bishop, a native of the Venetic region bordering the British Ocean [Note: Regarding the peoples of Venice in lower Brittany and their power among the Armoricans, one may consult Caesar, as well as the more recent Papirius Massonus in *The Antiquities of Gaul*. The chief city, renowned for its bishopric, is called Vannes in French. BOLLAND.], born of parents of no small standing [Note: Albertus le Grand, in the *Lives of the Armorican Saints*, writes that Albinus was descended from the family called “of the Strong Thorn.” BOLLAND.], indeed emerging as the most worthy offspring of a noble stock, increased through the merits of a blessed life the honor he had received from his lineage. In him Christ chose what he would glorify, and there shone forth what the whole world would venerate.

From the very beginnings of his early youth he burned with such fervor of faith that, for the love of Christ, he voluntarily abandoned his parents, to whose wishes childhood usually hastens to return, and fled carnal affections as enemies of the soul [Note: Two manuscripts read “fleeing.” BOLLAND.]. He believed it sufficient for him to plant all his love in the heavenly Father alone [Note: Surius reads “all delight,” instead of “love.”].

Soon he submitted himself in the monastery of Cincillacum [Note: The name of this monastery is expressed in various forms, as we observed from Browerus in his notes on chapter 27 of Book XI of Fortunatus’ poems.] to the Lord with such humility of spirit that, while preserving the integrity of his conduct, he claimed nothing for himself from the privilege of free birth. There, though birth had made him freeborn, his will made him a servant; he understood that it was more praiseworthy for nobility to humble what it was through love of Christ than, with arrogance, to seek to appear what it was not.

6. At length the progress of daily discipline advanced in him so that, always ascending beyond himself in merits, he did not conquer others but, after subduing his body, rather triumphed over himself. For who could adequately describe how distinguished he was in the austerity of fasting, how eager in the delight of vigils, how praiseworthy in the constancy of prayer, and how singular in the work of compassion? Thus he destroyed the enemy who opposed him and, by the very means through which he afflicted himself alone, came to the aid of all with the greatest hope.

He was ready to obey and mature in trampling down vices, so that even in the training of youthful age he was already an example to the old [Note: The manuscript of Saint Maximin has *juvenibus*, “to the young”; two others have *juvenili*, “in youthful [age].” BOLLAND.]. He shared with man only this, that he had been born; in every other respect he wished all that he lived to belong to Christ.

He did not accommodate his eye to pleasure, his ear to mockery, or his mind to frivolity, but always governed himself with the anchor of gravity. Within the enclosure of the monastery he conducted himself in such a way that, even when he went out into public, he remained shut within the prison of his own heart. He preferred to look upon nothing outside himself except Christ, whom he faithfully carried in his breast.

7. Occupied with these pursuits, he attained such distinction of life that the Lord testified to his devoted service to the world through miracles. While he was still a little boy and traveling through the countryside in the service of his abbot, they stopped at the house of a certain man. A storm thundered with such violence and so much rain poured down that even the house’s own roof could not protect it. Since, under the force of the rain, the hut was as exposed as a field, and everyone lodging there was drenched, the rain alone feared to touch blessed Albinus; for when it sensed the flame of faith, it turned aside drop by drop lest it do him harm.

When this was discovered, the holiness of his conscience, hidden by his years, became known through his merits, since in the flower of adolescence he exhaled the fragrance of virtue [Note: Surius reads “the holiness of conscience.”].

8. Thereafter, as his age grew together with his heavenly gifts, at about thirty-five years of age he was chosen rector of the monastery and devout father, since through his own brilliance he had drawn dignity to himself. Meanwhile, under the discipline of the master’s authority, order flourished in the community, where strict severity had destroyed the license to sin.

Thus the gaze of piety burned, the harmony of psalm-singing rejoiced, the ray of obedience flashed among the brothers, and the ornament of holy charity excelled, because just as he was vigilant in rooting out vices, so was he attentive in bringing heavenly gifts. In this office of abbot he ruled and successfully governed the community entrusted to him for five years [Note: Surius reads “twenty-five years,” but two manuscripts, which we have used, offer only five. MADII.].

9. And because the fame of so great a merit did not remain buried but, flying everywhere on blessed wings, occupied all places, it happened at that time that the city of Angers was deprived of the governance of a shepherd [Note: The manuscripts read *Andegavis*, “at Angers.” BOLLAND.]. Then, with the whole people in agreement, although he resisted out of a desire for humility, he was unanimously elected to the episcopal rank, with Christ as guide.

Having attained the honor proper to the priesthood, he displayed himself in the nourishment of the poor, the defense of citizens, the visitation of the sick, and the redemption of captives in such a way that the blessed action of one man became a universal salvation. Through these pursuits, heavenly virtues flourished in him.

10. Thus, in the city of Angers, when a certain woman named Grata—gracious in name but made ungracious by the weakness of her contracted hands—came before him with her nerves stiffened, he made the sign of the cross over her sick right hand. A living warmth first spread through the half-dead palm. The next day she again presented herself at the same place to be signed by him; when this had been done, the veins began to resume their courses. On the third day, when he impressed the seal of the cross upon her, the cords of her withered fingers immediately loosened, and, having recovered their service, the woman signed herself with her restored right hand in the name of Christ.

11. On one occasion, while passing near the village of Gegina [Note: This village seems to be the one designated by Gregory of Tours in Book IV of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, no. 14, where he relates that “a certain Baudegisilus from the territory of the city of Angers, son of Baudulfus, while he was wounded by a violent dart of illness, fell weakened in the village of Geina”—or, as the manuscripts of Beauvais and Clermont have it, *Geniensis*, as the distinguished Ruinart notes.], he came upon a young man named Alaubaudus [Note: Surius: Malabandus.] who had already lost the function of life. Hearing his parents lamenting the death of their son, he approached and, so that he might raise the dead to life, prostrated himself in prayer. He prayed for a long time, leaning over him.

While the priest grew pale in the dust, the vitality of the soul reddened in the body, until, heaven being struck and Tartarus opened, the young man was recalled from the funeral and the priest from prayer.

Afterward, when he visited the monastery of Asiacum with paternal concern [Note: Asiacum, commonly Assay, is a village in the territory of Tours. There are, however, several villages of this name in Touraine, as Valesius observes in his *Description of Gaul*. The following is drawn largely from Ruinart’s notes on Gregory of Tours, Book IV of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 15. The monastery of Asiacum mentioned here, however, seems to have been in the diocese of Angers.], a certain blind man, already enlightened by faith, cried out for him to come to his aid. Placing upon him the medicine of the holy cross, he made it as easy for him to recover his sight as it had been for him to ask for it.

Likewise, at Angers, when a certain Maurilius, his eyes closed, asked that light be restored to him, the bishop turned to his familiar weapon; and as soon as he extended the venerable sign of the cross over his eyelids, the cross, like a mighty ballista, pierced the darkness and brought light to the blind man behind it.

Again, when a certain Margellinus, who had spent about ten years in the cloudiness of blindness, had been brought to the blessed bishop, as soon as he extended the sign of the venerable cross over his eyes, blood burst forth, the darkness was driven away, and light entered.

12. We must also recount a memorable event that occurred to us. When an illustrious woman named Etheria was held under military guard and surrounded in the estate of Dullacum by order of a pursuing king, the holy shepherd came to the aid of the endangered sheep. Alone, so that no one would recognize him, he entered to see her. When she saw him, the grieving woman embraced his feet and clung to them.

Then the insane insolence of the unhappy guard tried, like a wolf, to tear her from the shepherd’s garment. The holy man suffered this insult. Then, breathing upon the guard’s face [Note: Surius reads “upon his face.”], the violator of the priest was punished by a swift death.

After this, compelled by fear, the others showed reverence to the bishop; and the punishment of one made the others free from guilt. He did not depart from the woman until, after a price had been paid to the king, he himself had freed her. Thus, in a single moment, salvation came to the suppliant and death to the presumptuous man.

13. Nor should we omit what is worthy of being handed down to memory. The holy Father came to a village called Albivia [Col. 0484A] in the pious zeal of devotion. There, when a certain blind man asked him for the help of mercy, the man began to be tormented by bodily affliction, because he had long been seized by the harassment of a demon.

Then the bishop prostrated his body in the prayer to which he always devoted himself with holy intention of spirit. He restored the man’s former light to his eyes and drove away the plague of the unclean spirit.

O ineffable grace of mercy! When only one thing is asked, a threefold remedy is obtained: he fed the needy with food, endowed the blind with sight, and restored the captive to freedom!

14. Likewise, when he encountered King Childebert in Paris, the bishop was informed that the king would leave the city on the following day for the sake of hunting. He sent word that he should be considered worthy of being awaited. But because bodily illness prevented blessed Albinus [Col. 0484B], the king hastened to meet him; and as long as he traveled along the road leading to the priest, he proceeded happily.

When he came to a certain crossroads and wished to turn elsewhere, his horse could not move a step, as though it were molten metal. Suspecting that the fault lay with the horse rather than with the cause, the king had another horse brought out. When he compelled it to proceed along the same road, it could not go on, as though obstructed by a wall, even when beaten.

Understanding that he had gained nothing by changing his mount unless he changed his encounter [Note: Surius: “and his course.”], he began to learn from the horse that the man was in the wrong, and that a beast had something by which to correct human understanding.

Turning onto the road that led to the priest [Note: The Audomar manuscripts read “turning aside on the road.” BOLLAND.], it began to run with such eagerness as though, rescued from a pit, it had regained the smooth level of the field.

15. It is worthwhile to bring forth a living event from a certain corpse. When the apostolic man himself had come to the city of Vannes [Note: Vannes, in Armorica. The manuscript of Saint Maximin has *Venetis*; the Audomar manuscript, *Venetus*. BOLLAND.], one of the attendants, a young man already converted and devoted to the service of Christ, whom he loved especially because of the quality of his conduct, died in that place and was buried.

After a year, he was bringing the deceased’s body back to its proper place with psalm-singing. While the bishop was delayed there on business, the servants wished to move the body before the priest arrived. But it became so heavy that they could sooner have grasped the limbs of a giant than lifted the body of the boy. Although the corpse was still believed to be unburied, it already seemed pressed down by marble; even the horses could not advance their steps, as though the dust of the dead man had generated bonds from itself.

This continued until the returning bishop released them by prayer—those whom, though his voice was silent, he had bound fast.

## 16

This miracle too deserves to be proclaimed no less than the others. When the monk Gennomerus in the monastery of Cincillacum had been deprived of the light of his eyes, and many years had passed in the darkness of a single night, he asked the holy man to make over him the sign of the cross. When this had been done, the splendor of living light entered him; the darkness was driven away, and the sun, long estranged, shone forth.

[Note: This miracle is absent from three manuscripts. Bolland.]

[Note: The name is also read Cenomerus and Gernomerus. From Bolland himself.]

This too is a venerable testimony among the other proofs. When, in the city of Angers, a tower adjoining the gate had been turned into a prison for condemned men, and blessed Albinus was passing by, the insolence of the prisoners’ voices broke out. Then the intercessor approached the judge and asked him, out of pity, to release them from custody. When the judge delayed, turning a deaf ear, the bishop immediately turned to God in faithful supplication and pleaded in so familiar a voice that, at the place where the holy man poured out his prayer, a stone block of astonishing size sprang outward and made an opening at the gate for the prisoners. For before his prayer the stone could not preserve its solidity. Coming out from there, alive as though from a tomb, they went to the basilica of Saint Maurilius, giving thanks to Lord Albinus, and prostrated themselves at his feet, because he had brought men suspected of death back to safety.

[Note: Saint Maurilius was bishop of Angers. See below the Life of this saint, which some believe was written by Fortunatus.]

## 17

Likewise, when a certain woman, seized by an evil spirit, had presented herself before the most blessed Albinus, crying out and lamenting, the adversary himself immediately gathered above her eye in the form of a bladder filled with blood. Then the bishop made the sign of the cross and rebuked him, saying: “Enemy, the eye which you did not give, you must not be able to take away.” At once, from that swelling, blood broke out delicately, like blood drawn by phlebotomy; as it flowed, without injury to the eye, the unclean enemy vanished, and the girl escaped unharmed under the authority of the sign of the cross.

## 18

[Note: See canon 10 of the Third Council of Orléans, held in 538, which Albinus subscribed. Mabillon. Consult Cointius under the year 538.]

This example of courage too ought appropriately to be explained: in God’s cause he showed no personal partiality toward kings or powerful men. Indeed, in seeking to increase heavenly grace, he rightly condemned the detestable unions of incestuous marriages and imitated the blameless Saint John. No one could adequately describe how much he endured as a result. For he desired to become a martyr; and, although the hand of the striker was lacking, he undoubtedly earned the martyr’s palm because he did not conceal forbidden desires.

Thus, in addition to his other labors, he repeatedly traveled to synods convened for this very cause. Finally, by the command of a great number of bishops, he was compelled by force of his brothers to absolve the persons whom he had excommunicated. When he was asked to sign the *eulogies*—the blessed offerings that the other bishops had blessed while sending them to the person suspended from communion—he himself said to the council of priests:

“Although I am compelled by your command to sign, while you refuse to defend God’s cause, he himself is powerful enough to take vengeance.”

After this had been done, before the excommunicated person could receive the *eulogies* into his mouth, that person expired. Before the bearer could arrive, the bishop’s pronouncement had taken effect. He also went to consult blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, concerning the same matter.

[Note: On the *eulogies*, see what we said in the notes to chapter 9 of book XI of Fortunatus’s works.]

[Note: “Expired” refers not to Saint Albinus, as Saussaius wrongly interprets it in the *Martyrology*—a mistake noted by Bollandus—but to the excommunicated person to whom the *eulogies* were being sent.]

[Note: In the Life of Saint Leobinus, bishop of Chartres, no. 13, Leobinus himself, then abbot of Brajacum, is said to have gone to Saint Caesarius with Saint Albinus to consult him. Mabillon.]

## 19

But since we cannot recount each of his deeds, it will suffice to have spoken of a few among the many. We also believe that, above all, this testimony concerning the most blessed man, necessary for the living after his death, ought to be explained: although his body was held enclosed in the tomb, nevertheless the reward of the just man’s soul overflowed into fruitful works.

Accordingly, when Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, together with his fellow bishops of the province, his successor in the episcopate, and the people, wished to transfer the relics of the saint to a new basilica, the narrowness of the little cell in which he had been buried prevented permission from being given to remove the sacred body. While everyone hesitated and was uncertain what to do, the power of the most blessed man, acting as mediator, intervened in the people’s distress.

For while everyone was waiting and no decision was being reached, suddenly, by divine will, the wall of the cell at his feet split open. On the eastern side three stones fell away, clearly giving a sign through which the saint wished it to be shown that he could be brought out.

[Note: In the notes of the venerable Baluze to Servatus Lupus, p. 378, there is a charter of Nefingus, bishop of Angers, in which it is recorded that the church of blessed Albinus was founded before the gate of the city of Angers by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, at the will and command of King Childebert. Mabillon.]

## 20

Meanwhile, after an opening had been made, as a procession of psalm-singers advanced toward the holy tomb, three paralytics, long given up as hopeless, were publicly restored to health at the place through which he was brought out; and their nearly lifeless nerves learned to live again through the merits of the buried saint. Immediately twelve blind persons were likewise given sight.

[Note: Surius reads: “two blind persons.”]

At last they received the light of day from the shadow of the dead man, plainly recognizing that through his aid they could obtain light, since by his power the wall had been opened like a window. Through these and the countless miracles that followed, although the limbs of the supreme bishop lie in a tomb, the merits of the confessor nevertheless live through the Creator’s grace for eternal ages.

Thus, adorned by heavenly grace with venerable flowers, having governed the episcopal office according to ecclesiastical discipline for twenty years and six months, and having fulfilled with blessed success, in the eightieth year of his life, that prophetic saying concerning the heights of blessedness among the mighty, he sent his soul, most dear to God, rescued from this world and destined to remain with Christ, amid the applause of the angels, to heaven on the Kalends of March.

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Maximinus have “twenty years and seven months.” Bolland.]

[Note: Saint Albinus died neither before the year 549, in which year he subscribed to the Fifth Council of Orléans through Abbot Sapaudus—perhaps being prevented by illness from attending personally—nor after 530, in which year Eutropius, his successor, dedicated the monastery of Glannafolium. See Cointius, under the year 550, no. 3.]

This was granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# [LIFE OF SAINT PATERNUS]

[Col. 0487]

## Preliminary Notice on the Life of Saint Paternus

Almost everyone agrees that the Life of Saint Paternus, which we place here, was written by Venantius Fortunatus. The manuscript codices also identify Fortunatus as its author. Among them, the manuscript codex that the distinguished Mabillon had before him bore this title: “Here begins the prologue of Lord Fortunatus, bishop, on the Life of Saint Paternus.” Fortunatus’s elevated style and character are evident throughout the work.

We publish the Life of Saint Paternus as it appears among the Bollandists under 16 April, examined and established on the evidence of several manuscript codices. It is also found in volume II of the *Benedictine Annals*, in the appendix to the first Benedictine century, extracted from papers communicated to Acher by the distinguished D. d’Herouval, and illustrated by Mabillon with various notes, which we shall place below at their appropriate locations. We shall also extract from the notes with which the Bollandists adorned the same text at great length those that seem more than the others likely to shed additional light upon it.

Indeed, since in several places we found that the reading differs substantially between the Life published in the Benedictine centuries and that published by the Bollandists, we thought it appropriate to record those differences in their proper places, so that both versions may consequently be said to have been published here by us.

A kind of abridgment of this Life had been published by Surius under 16 April; it was taken from there and inserted into volume I of the Benedictine centuries. But that abridgment, composed in a darker and more involved style, was, as Surius himself admits, given somewhat more Latinized phrasing for the reader’s benefit. It may originally have been prepared by some cleric or monk of Avranches—so the authors of the *History of French Literature* suppose—in order that it might be read in the Church during the celebration of that saint’s office.

This abridgment was regarded as the Life of Saint Paternus written by Fortunatus until the distinguished Mabillon extracted and published the present text from an ancient codex, which, he says, D. Antonius Vionius Herovallius had communicated to him. We therefore set aside that abridgment and place here the Life of Saint Paternus, which we believe to have been composed by Fortunatus.

[Col. 0487]

# Life of Saint Paternus, Bishop of Avranches (C)

[Note: Saint Paternus was born around the year 480 or 482. He lived in the monastery of Enixion in the diocese of Poitiers and later in the monastery of Scisciacum, in the district of Constantinus, which he himself had built. From there he was summoned to govern the Church of Avranches when he was seventy years old. His predecessor in that see was Aegidius, whom he succeeded around the year 552—or 550, as Cointius judges. He took part in the Third Council of Paris, held in 557, and died in 565, according to the Bollandists, or in 563, according to Cointius, under that year, no. 2.]

## Prologue

[Col. 0487A]

### 1

To the holy lord, venerable for his merits, Father Marcianus the abbot, whom I embrace in Christ with the whole depth of my heart: Fortunatus, humble [servant].

Great love gives proof of itself when care for a friend is not withdrawn even after the grave. For whoever strives to have the reputation of a lover cherishes the memory of the deceased with strength even after death; finally, he drinks in with his whole heart the affection of the living, whom oblivion, though buried, has not removed from his speech.

[Note: Acherius reads: “For he who strives for the renown of a lover after death.”]

Moved by this desire, most venerable father, you did not delay charging us to publish in written pages something concerning the celebrated reputation of blessed Paternus. That apostolic man is certainly neither forgotten among you nor absent from us in his power, since through his more sacred deeds he now possesses true life, in which death finds nothing to extinguish and has no further power to harm. Rather, it lies beneath the foot of the just man and is crushed under his heel—that death which was once feared—confidently entreating him, because it looks upon the glory of the man whom it attacked. Indeed, in a reversal of order, death has learned to fear the dead man.

[Note: Acherius reads: “nor [is he] in oblivion among you.”]

[Note: Marcianus seems to have been abbot of Sesciacum, or at least of the monastery of Ansion, which is mentioned shortly. Bolland. This cannot, however, be asserted with certainty, since it is clear that Paternus built and established several monasteries in various places, besides those two: at Bojacum, Le Mans, Avranches, and Rennes, among others. It is scarcely possible to conjecture which of these Marcianus governed; nevertheless, with the Bollandists, I believe that he presided over one of those founded by Saint Paternus.]

[Note: In the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, “in most blessed triumph” was added. Bolland.]

Although this work is inadequate for the task, since you have entrusted it to me, I shall nevertheless undertake it most willingly in obedience and transfer it into your domain. For, with a diligent person, willingness itself is enough if ability is lacking. Indeed, where love is devoted, willingness is greater than capacity; the person who wishes to please completely even exceeds his own strength for the sake of obedience. Therefore, because it reaches beyond itself and desires more than it can accomplish, love has no measure.

[Note: In the Dijon manuscript: “Although I am unequal to the task which you have entrusted to me”; elsewhere: “Although I am unequal to speak in this matter which you previously entrusted to me.” In order to make the sense clear, some conjectural emendation was necessary. Bolland.]

[Note: Acherius reads: “And so, through affection, I acknowledge myself a debtor even in those matters that are above me; and, as far as I am able, I shall endeavor to repay the loans of affection. Yet I owe even more in repayment,” and so forth.]

Thus, because of my affection, I acknowledge myself a debtor even in matters beyond my powers, and, as far as I am able, I shall endeavor to repay the loans of affection. Yet even when I have repaid them, I still owe more, because what is owed to charity is never fully returned.

The praiseworthy deeds of religious men, matured through the increasing progress of virtue and brought forth into a harvest of sacred blessing by venerable works, have already been made known through the testimony of faithful miracles handed down from the past. They remain fixed before the eyes of living minds even if they are not preserved in written pages, because an outsider does not need to serve as witness for one who excels through the proofs of his own household glory.

[Note: Here begins the prologue in the manuscripts of Trier and Bodec, as also in Surius. Acherius reads *deeds* instead of *men*. Bolland.]

[Note: Acherius reads: “And, brought forth into a culmination of sacred blessing through venerable works, declared by the testimony of faithful miracles handed down from the past, they always stand before the eyes of faith through their living merits, even if they are not fixed in pages, because they do not need an external newcomer as witness, since they excel through the proofs of their domestic glory.”]

Yet because the devoted flock is strengthened by the pastor’s assistance whenever it is refreshed by hearing of the virtues mentioned above, we have undertaken, for the benefit of those who hear, to lay bare as best we can what has been conveyed to our knowledge about the deeds and conduct of the blessed bishop Paternus.

[Note: The following lines are found in the Bodec manuscript. Bolland. Acherius, however, reads the preceding passage as follows: “Nevertheless, the devoted flock is strengthened by the pastor’s support whenever it is refreshed by hearing of the virtues mentioned above.”]

# The Life Begins

### 2

[Note: Acherius reads: “Therefore the most sacred bishop Paternus, a citizen of Poitiers, born of noble parents, brought forth for public administration and trained by his mother Julita in still nobler character, was most nobly raised by her, a widow of nearly sixty years,” and so forth. Surius instead has: “A widow for two years.” But in all the manuscripts, Bolland adds, it reads “a widow of nearly sixty years,” as though she had raised him as a widow for twelve or fifteen years, up to that age of her own.]

The most sacred Paternus of Poitiers, born, according to the worldly order, of noble parents of the Aquitanian region who had formerly been occupied in public administration, was trained in holy conduct. Raised by his mother Julita, a widow of nearly sixty years, he took up the reins of mature life under heavenly inspiration from the earliest years of childhood.

[Note: Acherius reads: “And he sought the monastery of Enixion, intending as a monk to bear the yoke of the Lord’s service.”]

He sought the monastery of Enixion to bear the monastic habit and the yoke of the Lord’s service.

[Note: The monastery of Ansion, or Enixion, or Hension—as Mabillon notes in his annotations to the Life of Saint Aicard—still exists, though of modest resources. It was cultivated by our people as Saint-Jouin de Marnes, in the diocese of Poitiers, toward Armorica, near the town of Thouars and the river Thouet.]

Soon afterward his abbot assigned him to administer the storeroom. In this first position he gave an indication that, by the Lord’s distribution of gifts, he would soon become a bishop capable of governing many things.

When his mother wished to make a tunic for him after the child had entered religious life, she placed the woven cloth by chance upon the roof.

[Note: The Rouen manuscripts read “the house”; Bolland. Acherius reads: “She placed it upon the roof; and shortly afterward, when it had been brought to its nest,” and so forth.]

A bird called a kite snatched it away and carried it to its nest. After the passage of a full year it was found unspoiled, so that neither the winter rain nor the heat of summer had loosened its warp by rotting the thread. It remained intact, as though it had just come from the hand of the spinner, hanging from the distaff as she twisted the thread.

[Note: Acherius reads: “Then, while he was extending himself toward greater virtue in the years of adolescence, leaping beyond the limit of dangerous youth,” and so forth.]

### 3

While he was still in his adolescent years extending himself toward greater virtue and leaping beyond the boundary of perilous youth, he made a plan with Scubilio, a monk of the same cell. For the love of Christ, they willingly chose to leave their parents and become pilgrims in the district of Constantinus, living together and carrying nothing but a Psalter.

[Note: The district of Constantinus was part of Normandy toward the west, on the British Ocean, commonly called the Cotentin. Bolland.]

Then Saint Scubilio, although he was older, seeing that Paternus was greatly worthy of honor for his merits, and wishing to make himself his equal as a brother, laid aside his own cloak.

[Note: Elsewhere, “he divided it.” Bolland. Why did the older Scubilio, rather than Paternus, wear the cloak? Did the monks of Ansion, or Enixion, imitate the custom of Greek monks, who, divided into three orders, use different garments? The tunic, belt, and cap belong to novices; the cloak to those perfected or bound by vows; and the cowl to the most perfect. See the notes of Jacobus Goar on the Greek *Euchologion*, p. 488. Mabillon.]

When they had decided to go to a certain island, out of love for solitude, so that there, far from the world, they might devote themselves to God, a certain holy, noble, and God-fearing man turned them from this intention. He asked them to go to Sesciacum, so that they might convert the people of the place from their superstition and idolatry and teach them the faith of Jesus Christ.

[Note: Other manuscripts and Surius read “Sisciacum.” Bolland.]

[Note: Some manuscripts call it “a cave refuge near the foot of the mountain.” Bolland. Acherius, however, reads the whole passage as follows: “Then, near the foot of the mountain, a hermit entered a cave refuge with his companion. When the people, according to custom, were raging through accursed rites at that shrine, the holy men warned them not to think they could be saved by worshiping vanities. They could be saved if they did not provoke the Creator by insulting him; rather, they should act more justly by serving their Creator as his living creature. But the common people, disrespectfully despising the reverend men, obstinately continued the rite they had wickedly begun. Then the saint and his companion, armed both with the fervor of faith and with the standard of the cross, approached the vessels in which they were cooking food and overturned each one with their staffs. They also wished to pull down—or pour out—the drink arranged in cups, setting aside concern for their own danger, provided that as strong soldiers they might fight for Christ, desiring martyrdom if a devoted executioner should not shrink from striking. But by divine will they themselves were held in fear, although they could have been slaughtered.”]

Then, going toward a cave, they found a great blinded populace celebrating their revels and festivals of the gods there. They zealously urged them to abandon their idols, worship the true God in order to be saved, and receive baptism for the sake of him who had made them.

But that accursed people maliciously closed their ears to such holy and salutary admonitions. They rejected the men’s speech and, with great defiance, carried out the dreadful sacrifices of their demons.

Nevertheless, Saint Paternus and Saint Scubilio, fortifying themselves with the sign of the cross and armed with steadfastness and the shield of faith, overturned with their staffs the pots and cauldrons in which those wretched worshipers of idols were cooking the meats they had dedicated to their images. The men of God did not fear for their lives; animated by zeal for the Christian faith and the glory of God, they desired to pour out their blood for Jesus Christ.

Yet although the barbarian multitude was numerous and could easily have killed them, God nevertheless cast such terror upon it that both men returned safely and unharmed to their cave.

### 4

[Note: Acherius reads this passage as follows: “Then, as they were returning, a certain woman stripped off her clothing to insult them. Immediately, in vengeance for the just men, she was struck by disease throughout all her limbs and contracted. For a year she was tormented, wasting away in strength; her sick nerves were afflicted as the ulcer struck her, until, after she had asked forgiveness and they had interceded for her, the medicine flowed from the place from which the vengeance had come.”]

It is nevertheless true that an immodest and shameless woman, wishing to put them to shame, lifted her garments from behind and showed them her buttocks. God did not allow her to escape punishment, for her buttocks immediately rotted with countless ulcers, which could not be healed until she had sought pardon from the servants of God.

### 5

[Note: Acherius likewise reads: “On one occasion, when only half a loaf of bread remained for their proper meal, blessed Paternus generously gave it as an act of kindness to a traveler who arrived. The man of God wished rather to store it as a reward than in his stomach. Then holy Scubilio, at the proper hour, asked that they should now eat. He replied: ‘Christ, who always abounds, prepares food for his servants.’ His brother was distressed by this, because after his labor he found nothing with which to refresh himself when tired. Yet the Lord’s care watched over the servant’s food and did not allow him to suffer hunger; he provided nourishment to the hungry. Nor did he fail to,” and so forth.]

Saint Paternus was especially merciful and charitable according to his means. Once, when he had nothing in his cell but half a loaf of bread for himself and his companion, he gave it to a poor man. Scubilio became angry and grieved for a while, because he was beginning to feel hungry and did not know where he would get food. Yet the Lord did not allow him to suffer hunger; he gave food to the hungry.

For without delay, Witherius, their first disciple, brought abundant gifts in the late hours of the fast.

[Note: Surius and two manuscripts read “Witheus”; the manuscripts of the Queen of Sweden read “Withenus”; another manuscript reads “Mattheus.” Bolland.]

[Note: Acherius reads “after the fast” and does not have “late.” He reads shortly afterward: “Thus, within the space of an hour, they received with great increase what they had given to the needy.”]

He multiplied their provisions after the meal had been delayed, and thus, within the space of an hour, they received with great rejoicing what they had needed.

[Note: Acherius reads: “They received with great increase what they had given to the needy.”]

When the meal was finished, however, they lacked water, for which they thirsted greatly, because the more the flesh is filled, the more ardently it desires drink after food.

Immediately, pouring themselves out in prayer, they asked Christ to give water in the wilderness to his servants, just as he had given the Israelite people abundant water from the hardest rock at Horeb. Their prayers were heard nearby by the ears of the Divinity; as soon as blessed Paternus touched the ground with his staff, a spring burst forth from the abyss. It sprang up so suddenly that it seemed another Moses had drawn water from the rock by piercing it with his rod.

[Note: Acherius reads: “The report of this event increasing, they bound themselves to a very arduous way of life”; and shortly afterward: “He took no food, but also withdrew himself from the presence of men, so that he was removed from everyone.” Later: “He never had a bed, never rested his head upon down, but was content at night with the same garment he had used during the day. Instead of soft wool he wore a rough hair shirt, so that between the hours of sleep and the time of rest,” and so forth.]

### 6

As news of this event spread, their venerable abbot, Generosus, went after three years to seek the monks who had fled so well to Christ.

[Note: The Rouen manuscript has the wording printed here, while three other manuscripts, together with Surius, transpose the words: “the venerable abbot Generosus.” In the Bodec manuscript the word “Generosus” is absent; in the others it is not called a name, so it may be understood as an adjective rather than a proper name. Bolland. On this Generosus, see Cointius under the year 508, no. 21.]

[Note: It is clear from this that Abbot Generosus belongs not to the seventh century, as we stated elsewhere, but to the sixth. The old Ansion lectionary must accordingly be corrected, for it says that Saint Generosus flourished when the Roman Empire was governed by Constantine Augustus, the third emperor after Heraclius, and when Childebert, son of King Theodoric and grandson of the first Dagobert, presided over the Frankish state. Generosus is said to have taken the monastic habit at the monastery of Ansion under Saint Launegisilus. In 1559 a weaver near the town of Thouars was punished with paralysis of his limbs for violating the feast day of Saint Generosus, but was healed after doing penance in the church of Saint Generosus. Likewise, a certain Aimericus, surnamed of Villia, seneschal of Thouars, is said to have suffered punishment for stealing the ornaments of the same church. Saint Generosus is celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of July in the monastery of Ansion, or Saint-Jouin de Marnes, and in the church of the priory of Saint Generosus, commonly Saint-Generoux, which lies one league from the monastery itself and preserves his relics. Mabillon.]

When he found them, he recognized that Saint Paternus had climbed to a very arduous way of life. Apart from bread and water, or vegetables seasoned with salt, he consumed no food.

He withdrew his gaze not only from the presence of women but also from that of friends, so that, removed from everyone, he might better await angelic visitations and that what was lacking in the human might increase in the divine.

He never used a bed, knew no bedding, and never reclined upon down. Content with one and the same garment by day and by night, he clothed himself in a rough hair shirt instead of soft wool, so that between the hours of sleep and rest his body might have no repose, and, in a reversal of order, night might follow the completed day still in labor.

When his abbot observed that this exceeded the purpose of the rule, he brought him back to moderate fasting, like a horse impatient of the bridle.

[Note: Two manuscripts add: “by imposing the weight of a bridle.” Acherius also has this reading. Surius reads: “by imposing a kind of bridle-rein.” Bolland.]

He ordered him not to shut himself away so severely that he deprived himself of the sight or conversation of men.

[Note: Acherius reads: “so that he would not be enclosed so harshly, nor deprived of the sight of men,” and so forth.]

Moreover, he ordered him to visit, in turn, the cells that he himself had built.

[Note: Bolland reports that two manuscripts read: “he visited them in a covered wagon by turns.” Acherius likewise reads this.]

Since he was of good parentage, this was attested both by Bishop Leontianus and by the citizens.

[Note: Acherius reads: “He was readily attested by Bishop Leontianus,” and so forth. Leontianus—Leontinianus in the Rouen manuscript—was bishop of Coutances. He subscribed to the First Council of Orléans in 509. In place of this, the notes of Sirmond, based on the Reims and Beauvais manuscripts, read: “Leontius, bishop from the city of Briovere.” According to Sirmond, Briovere was the ancient name of the city before the camp of Constantia was established there. Bolland.]

Commending him in that place, he recalled blessed Scubilio with him to the monastery and, after a short interval, allowed him to return to his brother.

[Note: In the Bodec manuscript this is expanded as follows: “After the abbot had commended Paternus sufficiently to all the brothers and to the princes of the world, and had established him in the place where he lived, he then ordered Scubilio to return to the monastery. After he had been corrected in certain matters, he allowed him after a short time to return to his brother Paternus.”]

### 7

Afterward the man of God Paternus was made deacon and priest by Saint Leontianus. As he grew in dignity, so he honored himself through his virtues.

[Note: Acherius reads: “He was appointed presbyter, and as his dignity increased,” and shortly afterward: “Through these twin cultivators, the fruit of grace grew so greatly at Tessiacum that,” and so forth.]

Through these two twin cultivators, the fruit of grace, born from the seed of the word, grew so greatly at Sesciacum that the shrine of profane worship was taken away from men and assigned to their hearts, and the senseless place became a cultivation of living beings.

[Note: Acherius reads: “a place enclosed for animals.” The cave, because it also received winged inhabitants, began to give off the fragrance of noble flowers; and from the mother’s hive, swarms of monks were founded. Finally, throughout the cities—namely Bayeux, Le Mans, Avranches, and Rennes in Brittany—and elsewhere, through various signs his faith was made clear and his life was sanctified by miracles.]

The cave, which had received such inhabitants, began to give off the fragrance of so noble a flower that, as though from the foundation of a father and the hive of a mother, many swarms of monks were born and nourished with the nectar of complete religious devotion.

Finally, throughout the cities of Coutances, Bayeux, Le Mans, Avranches, and Rennes, many monasteries were founded for the Lord through him. Through the signs of the Lord, his faith was made evident by works and his holy life by miracles.

[Note: These were five episcopal cities, whose dioceses are intended: three in modern Lower Normandy—Coutances, Avranches, and Bayeux—together with the neighboring district of Le Mans and Rennes in Upper Brittany. Bolland.]

### 8

[Note: Acherius reads this passage as follows: “Thus, one day at Sesciacum, touching her, he had been utterly unable to open the joint of her jaws; they made a sound as though fragments of chains had been struck together. When he placed in her mouth a liquid into which he had dipped something,” and shortly afterward: “the girl who had been silent because she was mute immediately answered in words.”]

On one occasion at Sesciacum, a certain Arastes offered him his female servant, who was mute in the use of her tongue.

[Note: The name is also written Arroastes and Oroastes; he is called both priest and pastor. Bolland.]

Then the holy man, touching the places around the girl’s lips with his hand, saw that she could in no way open the tight closure of her teeth. He immediately blessed oil and marked the joints of her jaws with it; at once they opened, as though fragments of chains had been struck together. Then he placed the aforementioned liquid in her mouth and asked what she had that made her remain silent. To this question she, who had been silent because she was mute, answered in words.

### 9

[Note: Acherius reads: “Likewise, when he had gone from Sesciacum to Avranches”; and shortly afterward: “he allowed them to be carried with him … let me keep the relics.”]

Likewise, when he departed from Sesciacum for Avranches, he asked Brother Scubilio to allow him to take with him two young pigeons that he himself had raised. Scubilio refused, saying: “For the sake of your presence, let me at least keep the relics of your pigeons.”

Paternus replied: “Let them remain with the one whom they love more.”

When he had traveled nearly eighteen miles, the two pigeons came swiftly to meet him there on the following day, so that they might follow the tracks of his journey, since they had not seen the signs of the road.

[Note: Acherius reads: “Having traveled nearly eighteen thousand paces”—with “paces” added in the margin—“the pigeons swiftly came to meet the venerable man there on the following day,” and so forth. Thus, after Saint Paternus, the birds themselves confessed their desire, since it was entirely fitting that pigeons should follow a spiritual man.]

Thus the birds followed blessed Paternus, fulfilling his desire; for it was entirely fitting that pigeons should follow a spiritual man.

### 10

At Avranches, the hands of a certain landowner Ursius’s female servant had contracted because of an illness and could not be unfolded; the threads of her fingers had become knotted together. But as soon as blessed Paternus had completed his prayer, the tissue of the contracted hands stretched out, health was restored, and the fingers began to move the cords of the nerves in proper order.

[Note: Acherius reads *licias*, “cords,” instead of *licia*.]

11. As rumor spread, and he was compelled by many petitions from King Childebert, he went to meet the glorious King Childebert at Paris, shut inside a covered cart [Note: Perhaps he traveled in a covered wagon to avoid the sight and crowds of people, who, stirred by the fame of his holiness and his arrival, would have flocked together from every direction; or so that he might preserve the solitude of his cell even while traveling.] [Note: Acher., “he was compelled to go and meet …”; ibid. omits “Milevo by name”; ibid., “and when he was already almost lifeless … he should withdraw … in the name of Christ, whose name … the spiritual arrival,” etc.] [Note: In the Rothomagensian manuscript, Autela; in other manuscripts the more confused name Mentelaricus is written. Surius has “a boy named Milevicus.” The town of Mante on the Seine seems to be intended. Bolland.] at the village of Mantela. A certain boy, named Milevo, had been bitten by a serpent; as he was already dying, the holy man approached so that the boy might not perish when death overtook him. Therefore, after making the sign of the cross and applying oil, he cured the venom that had penetrated him with such an antidote. At that very place, as a testimony to the event, they also built a basilica in his name and in the name of Christ. When unclean spirits recognized his spiritual arrival at Paris, they fled from the bodies they had possessed. Likewise, those who were tormented by chills were granted recovery. No illness prevailed there where such a physician applied his remedies.

12. Then, when the priest had made some request to the king for the relief of the poor [Note: The same author: he presented a petition to the king for the needs of the poor.], Childebert ordered Crescentianus [Note: Surius and some manuscripts have Crescentius; below, too, Crescentius. Bolland.], who was responsible for public administration, to carry out whatever Blessed Paternus should instruct him to do. Though he promised to fulfill this, he lied: and when he had set out toward Burgundy, without the knowledge of the holy man mentioned above, Crescentianus wandered blind for two days. Recalling his fault [Note: Acher., “when he remembered his guilt … when the guilt departed from his heart, light entered his eyes.”], and considering why such sudden darkness had overtaken him, he quickly returned. Having obtained pardon, as guilt departed from his heart, light entered his eyes; and, made wiser after his blindness, he fulfilled the commands of the servant of God, so that from this it might be believed that he had recovered the lights of his mind more than those of his body.

13. When, at the age of seventy [Note: The same: “while he was carrying out the duties of abbot” (in the margin, “duties” instead of “virtues”).], he was exercising the office of abbot with virtues, and was resting in his cell, which he had first built at Sesciacum, one night he saw that very place [Note: Ibid., “bathed in wondrous brightness.”] suffused with great radiance. In a vision, those who had departed to God came to him: Melanius [Note: Saint Melanius was bishop of Rennes; he attended the Council of Orléans with Leontianus in 509 (fol. 511) and lived until about 530. Bolland.], Leontianus [Note: Leontianus is also Leontius in the manuscripts, and Surius writes Lucianus. He is said above to have been bishop of Coutances. Bolland. He attended the First Council of Orléans in 511 and subscribed to it; from this date the ages of Saint Generosus and Blessed Paternus may be calculated. From Mabillon.], and Vigor, bishops [Note: “Saint Vigor was bishop of Bayeux; he is commemorated on the Kalends of November. He had certainly died before 537, since Leucadius, bishop of Bayeux, attended the Third Council of Orléans at that time. Surius incorrectly has Beor; the manuscripts also read Vehor and Victor. In the Rothomagensian and Queen of Sweden manuscripts, Vigor is correctly given.” So Bolland. Cointius notes under the year 550, no. 6, that these three bishops who ordained Paternus bishop had their sees in the regions where Paternus had built many monasteries.]. Through a revelation they ordained him bishop.

Then he himself was astonished. Although he kept these matters within himself and had not disclosed them at the time, he later made them known [Note: Acher., “but keeping it within himself, although he was then silent, he later proved it”; and shortly afterward: “when the pastor departed from Avranches … he immediately became bishop and so devoted himself to the restoration and new construction of churches … he arranged for the usefulness of cultivation … he poured out provision for the poor” (in the margin, “provided”).]. For not long afterward, at the request both of the people and of the prince, when the pastor of Avranches had died, he succeeded him. He could not refuse what had already been foretold by God’s hidden dispensation. Thus, once he had become bishop, he devoted himself to building new churches and restoring old ones, girded himself with the recovery of buildings, applied himself to the benefits of cultivation, and lavished care upon the poor, so that he was remarkable in each undertaking and singular in all.

This event, too, rightly deserves not to be deprived of remembrance [Note: Ibid., “This also is not undeserving of remembrance.”]. When on one occasion he had arrived at the estate of Tendenacum [Note: The Queen’s manuscripts have Teudecianum; the Bodecian manuscript, Theodeciacum; the Trier manuscript and Surius, Theodesiacum. Bolland.], in the company of Count Severus, a certain woman, a citizen of Rennes, was brought before him in prayer, mute [Note: Acher., “with the prayer offered, etc., she could no longer serve the enemy, for whom Christ was invoked as the author of her freedom.”]. Then, when the holy man had completed his prayer, the woman immediately broke her long silence and no longer served the enemy of muteness.

14. When the man of God had completed his thirteenth year in the episcopate, on the very day after Easter, as he desired to visit the brothers at Sesciacum, he fell ill. At the same time, Scubilion fell ill at the monastery of Mandana [Note: In several manuscripts, Maudanense, which we have suggested may perhaps be Saint Michael in the Mount. Arturus du Moustier, in *Neustria Pia*, p. 68, thinks it was otherwise called Maduinium, Maduinum, or Malduinium. Sammarthanus identifies it with the monastery of Saint-Maclou. It does not seem to have been so far away. Bolland.]. They therefore sent messages to one another so that, before they departed from this world, they might see each other. Then messengers, meeting them on the road, urged Blessed Scubilion to go to his brother, but he could not cross the arm of the sea that lay between them during the night [Note: Acher., “meeting one another, they warn Blessed Scubilion on the road”; and shortly afterward, “with his holy brother, his glorious and noble superior, in triumph.” Ibid. omits the words “and they met one another in glory.”]. Yet, although nearly three thousand paces separated the holy men, that same night Blessed Paternus, together with his aforesaid brother, glorious and noble in triumph, with a blessed provision for the journey, accompanied by an angelic choir and in the heavenly senate, sent their pious souls from earthly things to Christ, and met each other in glory.

Now, as Bishop Lauto [Note: Lauto, bishop of the Church of Coutances, or of Briovère, subscribed to the Fifth Council of Orléans in 547. He is entered in the Roman Martyrology on September 22. Bolland.]—who had come there eight days earlier to visit him, unaware of his illness—[Note: Acher. does not read these words, being unaware of his illness. “There, when he was escorting Blessed Paternus from Sesciacum to the basilica and preparing the funeral rites, while Lascivius likewise escorted Blessed Scubilion to the same basilica, the two bishops, each unaware of the other, came together with a single choir of psalm-singers.”] conducted Blessed Paternus to the basilica at Sesciacum and arranged his funeral, so Bishop Lascivius [Note: Bishop Lascivius subscribed to the Third Council of Paris in 556, but his see is not indicated. The manuscripts also write Laudus, and Surius has Lauscius. The Bodecian manuscript says: “two bishops from neighboring cities,” without giving either name. Bolland.] escorted Saint Scubilion to the same basilica, came to the funeral of the other, and the uninterrupted choirs came together without knowing it. [Note: The following is from the Trier and Queen of Sweden manuscripts. In the Rothomagensian manuscript there was only: “and they buried the bodies of the saints together with joy.” Bolland.] The most holy men likewise occupied, on the same day, the place of prayer that they had built together, in a blessed passing, [Note: Mabillon demonstrates in his notes on the Life of Saint Paternus, first Benedictine century, that Saint Paternus died in 565. Paternus died after the Council of Paris held in 557, which he himself attended and subscribed to, and he died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, a few days after Easter. For it is related that Paternus and Scubilion fell ill on the day after Easter and died on the same night. This must not be understood as though they died on the night following that on which they began to be ill, since Lauto, bishop of Coutances, is said to have remained eight days with Paternus at Sesciacum, whither Paternus had come on the day after Easter; it indicates only that Paternus and Scubilion, after an illness of several days, died on the same night. This being so, Saint Paternus’s death seems rightly placeable in 565, eleven days after Easter, which that year fell on April 5. So Mabillon. On these assumptions, Saint Paternus follows to have been made bishop of Avranches in 552 and born in 482, since he was made bishop at the age of seventy (as related in chapter 3 of his Life) and died thirteen years later. But Cointius thinks he was born in 480 and raised to the see of Avranches in 550, because he believes that Paternus died on Monday, April 16, the day on which his name is read in ecclesiastical calendars. He therefore assigns his death to 563, in which the dominical letter was G and April 16 consequently fell on a Monday. But this calculation, as Bollandus observes, rests on no certain basis, since the Life of Saint Paternus nowhere establishes that he died on a Monday; and in 563 Easter fell on March 25, from which it would follow that Saint Paternus lay sick for three whole weeks, which does not appear.] so that even death would not divide those whom one life had always united; and at the same moment one was buried together with the other [Note: To this day the cenotaphs of Saints Paternus and Scubilion are visible in the village of Saint-Pair, in the diocese of Coutances on the seacoast, not far from the town of Granville. There, without doubt, stood the abbey of Sesciacum, later called Saint-Pair, which Richard II, duke of Normandy, is said to have assigned to the monastery of Saint Michael in the Mount, as recorded in *Neustria Pia*. The place is now reduced to a village, though still distinguished by the name of a barony dependent to this day upon the aforesaid monastery of Saint Michael; there, recently—that is, in the year of Our Lord 1664, on September 1—the body of Saint Gaudus, bishop of Évreux, was discovered. Mabillon.], as in their pilgrimage one had followed the other. Thus the elect, with blessed merits, met our Redeemer, their one beloved, after leaving the world; they work miracles after death, and, living wholly through blessed deeds, remain alive beyond the tomb.

[Vita of Saint Radegund.]

[Col. 0497]

PRELIMINARY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING LIFE OF SAINT RADEGUND, QUEEN

That the Life of Saint Radegund was written by Fortunatus, her teacher, is established with complete certainty by Baudonivia, a nun of the monastery at Poitiers and a contemporary of Fortunatus. In the Life of Saint Radegund that she herself composed, she gives this testimony concerning him and herself:

“We do not repeat what the apostolic man Fortunatus, bishop, composed concerning the blessed woman’s life; rather, we give what he omitted because of the brevity of his work, just as he himself explained in his book when he said of the blessed woman’s virtues: ‘Let brevity suffice, lest abundance become tiresome; and let what is shortest not be considered insufficient, when greatness is recognized in what is small.’”

These words of Fortunatus are read in section 39 of the Life of Radegund herself, which we publish under Fortunatus’s name, as it appears in the first century of the Benedictine collection, p. 319, illustrated by the learned notes of the distinguished Mabillon; to these, wherever it seemed appropriate, we have added something of our own in the customary manner.

[Col. 0497]

LIFE OF SAINT RADEGUND, QUEEN (C, S)

PROLOGUE

[Col. 0497C]

1. So rich is the generosity of our Redeemer that he celebrates mighty victories in the female sex and makes women, weaker in body, glorious through the virtue of their renowned minds. Though they possess by birth the softness proper to their sex, Christ makes them strong through faith, so that those who appear weak, when crowned for their merits, may increase the praise of their Creator, by possessing treasures of heaven stored in earthen vessels. Within their very bodies Christ the King himself dwells with his riches. Mortifying themselves to the world, despising fellowship with the earth, purifying themselves from the world’s pollution [Al., “abandoning the world’s pollution”], not trusting in what is slippery, not standing upon what is prone to fall, seeking to live for God, they have been joined to paradise for the glory of the Redeemer [Col. 0497D]. Among their number is she whose course through this present life we have attempted to bring before the public, though in plain speech, so that the memory of one whose life is with Christ in glory might be celebrated in the world [Col. 0498C].

THE LIFE BEGINS

2. Therefore, the most blessed Radegund [Note: Saint Radegund, about whom we have written more fully in the Life of Fortunatus and concerning whom we have spoken frequently in the notes to his works, died in 587. Gregory of Tours says that he conducted her funeral in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 106. Her Life may therefore be thought to have been composed by Fortunatus approximately in that year.], barbarian by nationality and from the region of Thuringia, granddaughter of King Basin, niece of Hermenfrid, daughter of King Beretharius—insofar as worldly greatness is concerned, sprung from royal stock—was lofty in origin but far loftier in conduct.

After she had remained only a short time with her exalted parents, when a barbarian storm had devastated the region through the victory of the Franks [Note: Concerning this expedition of the Franks against the Thuringians, see Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book III, chapter 7, and Fortunatus in his separate book on the destruction of Thuringia.], she departed and migrated from her homeland in the manner of Israel. Then, among the victorious kings [Note: These were the kings Theodoric and Chlothar, brothers, as Gregory of Tours relates in the same passage.], a dispute arose over which of them should possess the royal girl among the captives. Had she not been surrendered, once the conflict had ended the kings would have taken up arms against one another.

Falling by lot to the exalted King Chlothar, she was taken to Attejas in the Vermandois [Note: Atteja, Athiés, in the Vermandois on the Somme River, was one of those villages commonly called public or royal estates because they belonged to the royal treasury, as Hadrian Valesius observed in *History*, book XXI. Mabillon.], where she was entrusted to guardians for rearing. Among the other tasks appropriate to her sex, the girl was instructed in letters. Frequently speaking with children, if circumstances had allowed it she desired to become a martyr. Even as a young girl she showed the merits of old age, obtaining in part what she had asked.

Finally, while the Church was flourishing in peace, she herself suffered persecution from her household. Even then, as a little girl, she undertook whatever remained for her from the table: after gathering the children, she washed each one’s head, arranged their seats, brought water in her hands, brought them food herself, and mixed it for the little ones herself.

She also practiced this devotion with the young cleric Samuel [Note: The passage reads as follows in Bollandus: “The most holy girl did this also with the little cleric Samuel: while a wooden cross went before them, the little children followed, singing psalms, and proceeded together to the oratory with mature solemnity; but she herself polished the pavement with her garment. Around the altar, with a towel, etc.”]. A wooden cross went before them, and the children followed, singing psalms, as they proceeded together to the oratory with mature solemnity. She herself, meanwhile, polished the pavement with her garment. Around the altar, gathering the dust that lay there with a cloth [Note: *Facitergium*, a cloth for wiping the dirt from the face. Mabillon.], she reverently stored it outside rather than sweeping it away [Note: Bollandus reads *verrebat* instead of *vergebat*.].

When the aforesaid king wished to receive her at Victuriacum [Note: Others have Victoriae, in the vernacular Vitry, in Belgium, two leagues from Douai; there King Sigibert was killed at Fredegund’s instigation. There is another town of the same name in Champagne, but it was not subject to Chlothar at that time. Mabillon.], with provisions prepared, she escaped by night from Attejas with a few companions through Beralcha [Note: Some think *barcam* or *barcham* should be read instead of *Beralcham*, as Bollandus notes in the annotations to this passage.]. Then, when he had sent her to Soissons so that he might raise her up as queen, she avoided royal pomp, lest she grow in worldly status; yet, although human glory was owed to her, she was not changed [Note: Bollandus: “but she avoided it.”].

3. She therefore married an earthly prince, yet was not separated from the heavenly one. And when secular power had been added to her, her will inclined itself more than dignity permitted. Always subject to God, following the instructions of priests, she shared more deeply in Christ than she was joined in marriage. In that period we shall attempt to disclose a few of the many things she did.

Because she had been joined to a prince, she feared that she might be degraded before God as she advanced in worldly rank, and so she devoted herself, together with her resources, to almsgiving. Whenever anything came to her from the taxes, from everything that reached her she gave the tithes before she received it. Then she distributed what remained among monasteries; and wherever she could not go on foot, she traveled around by sending gifts.

Even the hermit could not conceal himself from her generosity; and, just as he did not want to be weighed down by a burden, he distributed what he had received. Among her, the voice of the needy did not sound in vain, nor did she pass it by deafly. Often giving away clothing, she believed that she was covering the members of Christ beneath the garment of the poor, considering herself to have lost whatever she had not given to the needy.

4. Still directing her spirit toward works of mercy, she furnished a house at Attejas [Col. 0500A]. There, with beds carefully arranged and poor women gathered, she herself washed them in the baths and treated the rottenness of their illnesses. She washed the heads of the men, performed the necessary service, and personally mixed for those whom she had previously washed the drink that revived them when they were exhausted by sweat.

Thus, a devoted woman—born and married a queen, mistress of the palace—served the poor as a maidservant. At table, however, secretly, lest anyone recognize her, she placed before herself a dish of vegetables and, amid royal banquets, after the manner of the three youths, ate beans or lentils with delight.

As for chanting the office [Note: *Decursus*, or *cursus*, is used by Gregory of Tours and Fortunatus not infrequently for the divine offices, as was noted in the Life of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, no. 75. Here and elsewhere *decantare* means “to recite.” Mabillon.], even if she were seated at lunch, she would excuse herself to the king on some pretext and withdraw from the feast in order to render to God what was owed. Once outside, she sang psalms to the Lord and carefully inquired with what food the poor had been refreshed.

5. Likewise, at night, when she reclined with the prince, she would ask to rise for a human necessity. Then, leaving the bedroom, she would devote herself for a long time to prayer in a private place. Having thrown down a hair shirt, she would lie there, warmed only by the spirit but pierced by the frost, with all her flesh nearly dead. She cared nothing for the torments of the body; her mind was fixed on paradise, and she considered whatever she endured light, so long as she did not become worthless in Christ’s sight.

Returning from there to the bedroom, she could scarcely be warmed either by the fire or by the bed. People therefore said to the king that he had more a nun for a wife than a queen. For this reason he himself, irritated at her good works, was exceedingly harsh. But she, partly soothing him and partly enduring him, modestly tolerated the quarrels inflicted by her husband.

6. During the days of Lent, it is enough to know how she concealed herself beneath the royal garments as an exceptional penitent. As the season of fasting approached, she sent to a religious nun named Pia, who was devoted to the holy vocation. Pia reverently sent her a hair shirt sealed in linen. The saint put it on her body and carried it secretly beneath her royal clothing throughout Lent, bearing the pleasant burden.

When the days had passed, she likewise sent the hair shirt back, sealed. But whenever the king was absent, who could believe how fully she gave herself to prayer, how she bound herself to the feet of Christ as though he were present, and how, as though filled with delights, she satisfied herself through a long fast and was nourished by tears? For her, despising the food of the belly, Christ was complete nourishment, and in Christ complete hunger.

7. With what devotion and care did she carry out this practice: whenever the oratories or venerable places shone throughout the night, she continually supplied candles made by her own hands. Thus, when late in the evening she was informed that the king was asking for her at table, because she was occupied with matters belonging to God, she suffered quarrels from her husband, so that many times the prince had to make amends with gifts for what he had said against her with his tongue.

8. If, because of her reputation, any servant of God appeared, either coming on his own or summoned [Note: Surius adds “through another.”], you would have seen her possess heavenly joy. When the hour of night returned, she went with a few intimate companions through snow, mud, or dust, with hot water prepared. She herself washed and wiped the venerable man’s feet, and, without allowing the servant of God to refuse, offered him drink in a bowl.

On the following day, entrusting the care of the household to her confidential officers [Note: *Creditarii* were the same as counselors or chamberlains, to whom secrets were entrusted; in Greek, πιστικοί, “confidential persons.” See Du Cange, *Glossary*, under this word.], she occupied herself entirely with the words of the righteous man. For days she remained engaged with the principles of salvation and with the means of attaining heavenly life. If a bishop came, she rejoiced at his presence, and, after rewarding him, she herself—sad—sent him back to his own place.

9. How wisely and completely did she provide everything for her salvation! Whenever she put on, as though it were new, a *maforte*, a linen *sabanum* adorned with gold or gems [Note: A *maforte* was a woman’s head covering. The linen *sabanum*—from the Germanic word *saban*, meaning linen—seems here to mean a linen garment sewn with gold and gems. Mabillon.], and the girls around her praised it as exceedingly beautiful, she having put it on in barbarian fashion, she judged herself unworthy to be adorned with such a linen garment. Immediately removing it, she sent the garment to whatever holy place was nearest, and it was placed as a covering upon the divine altar.

10. Whenever someone, as commonly happened, was assigned by the king to be killed for a capital offense, how did the most holy queen die in anguish, lest the condemned culprit die by the sword! How she hurried among the household’s faithful servants and nobles, whose flattering words softened the prince’s mind, until, from the very anger of the king from which the sentence of death had proceeded, a word of salvation issued forth!

11. While she was occupied with these blessed acts, divine mercy advanced her so far that, although she was still a laywoman in the palace, miracles were nevertheless manifested through her by the Lord’s generosity.

Finally, at the estate of Perunna [Note: *Perunna* is used for *Peronna*, a fortified city of Gaul on the Somme in Picardy, about which more may be seen in Valesius, *Notitia Galliarum*, p. 442. This is approximately what Bollandus notes. There, drawing on Mabillon’s *De re diplomatica*, book IV, they observe that Radegund was held in celebrated veneration at Peronna, and that a suburban church had formerly been dedicated to her name.], while the most holy woman was walking through the garden after lunch, prisoners held for crimes cried out that they needed help, shouting from the prison. She asked what was happening. The servants lied, saying that a crowd of beggars was asking for alms. Believing them, she sent what the poverty required.

Meanwhile, those held in fetters were compelled by the judge to keep silent. But when night had come, while she was reciting the office [Note: In the Bodecian copy used by Bollandus, this passage is explained more freely by the copyist as follows: “When night had come, and she was reciting the office—that is, pouring out prayers to the Lord—the prisoners, released from their chains by divine power, came to Saint Radegund from the prison.”], those who had been bound appeared before the saint, freed from prison after their chains had been broken. When this became known, those who had lied to the blessed woman saw themselves as the guilty ones, while those who truly were guilty had been released from their chains.

12. And since, by divine providence, an event often turns toward salvation through some occasion, her brother was killed innocently [Al., “though innocent”] so that she might live more religiously [Note: Fortunatus, in his poem *On the Destruction of Thuringia*, Supplement, book I, depicts Radegund lamenting her brother’s death in an impassioned manner (παθητικῶς). Mabillon.—Concerning Radegund’s separation from King Chlothar, see more in Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, book V, chapter 22, and Bollandus in the preliminary notice to the Life of Saint Radegund (note of the first recension).—The distinguished Mabillon and the Bollandists worked very hard to resolve the difficulty concerning Blessed Radegund’s separation from her husband Chlothar without his knowledge and, as it seems, against his will. Mabillon proposes much but affirms nothing certain; the Bollandists incline to the view that the bishops of Gaul in that period were less knowledgeable about or less skilled in ecclesiastical law. Yet this cannot apparently be asserted of Blessed Medard, who, when Radegund asked him to impose the veil upon her, immediately rejected the request by citing the Apostle’s command that a woman bound to a husband should not seek dissolution. I would therefore prefer to say that Blessed Medard, who clearly understood the outstanding piety and holiness of Blessed Radegund, had no doubt that, by God’s will and command—for God is both the author and Lord of marriage—she should seek release from the bond of marriage so that she might please God more fully. For this reason he did not yield until Blessed Radegund said: “If you delay consecrating me, and fear a human being more than God, the Shepherd will demand the soul of a sheep from your hand.” Moved by these words, Saint Medard seems to have believed that he was not so much dissolving as that God was separating what He had joined. Nothing prejudicial to the permanence of marriage can nevertheless be inferred from such exceptional examples. (Note of the second recension.)].

Accordingly, coming from the king, she went to Blessed Medard at Noyon and earnestly begged him to consecrate her to the Lord after changing her clothing. But, remembering the Apostle’s saying (1 Corinthians 7), “If a woman is bound to a husband, let her not seek to be released,” he delayed covering the queen with the clothing of a nun.

The nobles still troubled the blessed man and dragged him violently from the altar through the basilica, lest he veil a woman joined to the king, lest he seem, as a priest, to presume to withdraw a queen from the prince—not privately but publicly married [Note: That is, publicly or solemnly married.]. When the most holy woman learned this, she entered the sacristy, put on the monastic habit, went forward to the altar, and addressed the most blessed Medard in these words:

“If you delay consecrating me, and fear a human being more than God, the Shepherd will demand the soul of a sheep from your hand.”

Shaken by this thunderous declaration, he laid his hand upon her and consecrated her as a deaconess [Note: Yet the Second Council of Orléans, held in the year of Christ 533, had shortly before decreed in canon 18: “It was also decided that henceforth no woman should be entrusted with the blessing of the diaconate, because of the weakness of this condition.” Although, according to the prescription of the ancient canons, this seems merely to revoke the required age of forty years, as John Morinus observes in *Exercitations on Holy Orders*, exercise 10, chapter 3, nevertheless the rule did not apply in Radegund’s case. That deaconesses had entirely disappeared before the tenth century is apparent from a letter of Atto, bishop of Vercelli, to the priest Ambrose, in volume VIII of the *Spicilegium of Ancient Writers*, p. 123. Mabillon. More on this matter in Cointius under the year 544, no. 96.].

13. Immediately removing the noble garment in which she customarily appeared as queen on famous days, accompanied by pomp, she placed upon the altar the purple garments [Al., “purple cloth”] and jeweled ornaments [Note: Bollandus reads this passage as follows: “and, when the gems had been removed, she reverently burdens the table of divine glory with ornaments”; another manuscript and Surius have “when the ornaments had been offered,” as Bollandus notes there.], loading the table of divine glory with so many gifts in honor. She broke up her gold-weighted belt and gave it for the work of the poor.
