Likewise, going to the cell of Saint Jumeris [Note: The name of this saint is read in various ways. Here, in Mabillon and in the manuscript of Vallis Lucens used by Bollandus, it is “the cell of Saint Jumeris.” Surius reads “the cell of Saint Nimeris,” or “Eumeris”; in a Dijon manuscript the name Vimerus occurs.], on the one day when the fortunate queen used to adorn herself, she presented to the holy altar, in carefully composed words—“to speak barbarously”—a *stapion* [Note: In the same manuscript of Saint-Germain it is written *stapione*, in the sixth case. It seems that *Scapionem* should be written, designating a royal diadem. For even today among the Germans *Scappel* means a ribbon or band for the head. If one wishes to retain *stapionem*, the word must be understood as referring to footwear, such as Isaiah mentions in chapter 3; for *stapia* is a stirrup. Mabillon.], shirts, sleeves, caps [Note: A *cofea*, or *cufia* or *coffia*, was a headband or covering that completely surrounded the head. More on this word may be found in Du Cange, *Chronological Glossary*. The Vosian manuscript, chapter 74, has the following: “Young men and women wore mitres on their heads, which they called bonnets, then linen caps, or *coffiae*, etc.”], brooches—everything ornamented with gold and some things with gems—whatever could be of benefit to her in the course of life.

From there she proceeded to the cell of the venerable Dadon [Note: Claudius Castellanus, as Bollandus reports, places the venerable Dadon among the saints without a fixed feast day in his Martyrology. He was the first abbot of the monastery of Conques, in the vernacular Conques, among the Ruthenians in Gaul. His date is uncertain.]. On the day when she ought to have been magnificently adorned in the world, she gave everything that a wealthy woman could wear, after rewarding the abbot, to the monastery.

Likewise, she proceeded to the *Synergium* [Al., “similarly”] of Saint Gundulf [Note: This is how the manuscript codices read. Yet no bishop of Metz named Gundulf is recorded until the time of Louis the Pious. Perhaps *Goscelinus* should be read instead of *Gundulfi*; he occupied the see of Metz in the sixth century. Mabillon.], after he had become bishop [Note: Or perhaps *from Metz to Noyon* should be read. In fact, after Blessed Medard and Faustinus, who succeeded him, Gundulf occupied that see; Radegund may have visited him while he was living in the monastery, before he became bishop of Noyon. Unless perhaps *Aigulfus* should be read instead of *Gundulfo*: Aigulf ascended the see of Metz in 578, according to Cointius under that year.], and, having proceeded from the lodging, ennobled the Synergium with no less effort [Note: *Synergium*, a place where several people work together, seems here to be used for a monastery, which for the same reason is sometimes called an *asceterium*. Mabillon.].

[Col. 0503B]

14. From there she reached Tours by a fortunate voyage. What eloquence could adequately describe how dutiful and how generous she showed herself? What did she do around the atria, temples, and basilica of Saint Martin? Weeping and never satisfied with tears, she lay at each threshold. Where the Mass had been recalled [Note: The ancient parchment manuscripts support this reading, not *missa revocato* or *missore vocato*, as in Surius. The codex of D. d’Herouval, interpreting the passage more freely, has “when the Mass had been celebrated,” but this seems incorrect, as is evident from the notes to the Life of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, no. 60. Mabillon. Bollandus, however, reads “when the Mass had been celebrated.”], she arranged the sacred altar with the clothing and adornment in which she customarily appeared at court in more splendid dress.

From there, when the servant of the Lord reached the village of Condat [Note: It is sometimes called Condat of Tours to distinguish it from another place of the same name. Bollandus.], where the glorious man Martin, a senator most intimate with Christ, departed from this world, she gave gifts no less worthy, increasing in the grace of the Lord.

[Col. 0504A] **15.** Then, when she was approaching suitably at the estate of Suaedas [Note: [Col. 0504C] Sais, between Tours and Poitiers.], in the territory of Poitiers, near the aforesaid village, with the journey proceeding favorably, who could enumerate how she conducted herself in every detail, since the details are countless?

[Note: [Col. 0504C] Fortunatus uses the same word again below, §21, where the Codex Conchensis writes *sub placentis* (“under cakes”), while other witnesses have *sub Fladone*. From this one may understand that *fladones* are cakes, which our people vernacularly call *flaons*. In Bollandus, vol. II for February, p. 105, in the writing of Henry, abbot of Centula: “There are thirteen ovens there, each of which yields annually ten solidi, three hundred loaves, and thirty *flatones* at the Litanies.” There the most learned man interprets *flatones* as cakes. Udalric, book II of the *Customs of Cluny*, ch. 4, says: “For the sign of *fladones*, having first made the general sign for bread and cheese with one hand, bend all the fingers, make the hand hollow, and place it upon the surface of the other.” Mabil.]

At table she ate secretly, beneath a *fladon* (cake), concealed rye bread [Another reading: wheat bread], and barley bread, so that no one noticed. For from the time when she was veiled by the consecration of blessed Medard until her illness, apart from legumes and vegetables, she ate neither fruit, fish, nor egg, nor anything else. As drink, apart from honeyed water and *piratium*, she drank nothing; [Note: [Col. 0504D] *Piratium*, or *pyraticum*, was juice pressed from pears, used in place of wine. St Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book II: “Paul advises Timothy, whose stomach was suffering, to drink wine, not *piratium*.”] and she did not touch pure wine, mead [Note: [Col. 0504D] A drink made from honey.], or the cloudy sediment of beer. [Note: [Col. 0504D] Fortunatus mentions this in book XI, poem 3, addressed to Radegund, where he urges her to drink wine. The same author, in book VIII, poems 7 and 11, congratulates the blessed queen on her contempt for the world and her seclusion. Mabil.]

**16.** Then, following the custom of Saint Germanus [of Auxerre], she ordered a millstone to be brought to her with the utmost secrecy; at it she labored throughout Lent as much as a four-day meal required. She also made the offerings with her own hands and distributed them continually among holy places. Thus, in the holy woman there was no less a practice of mercy than there was a throng of people: there was neither a petitioner lacking nor a gift that failed to be given. It was astonishing that she satisfied everyone. Where did such treasures come from for an exile, such wealth for a foreigner?

**17.** Only she knew how much the daily ransom cost, which she carried to those who asked. In addition to her daily table, by which she refreshed the poor [Note: [Col. 0504D] *Matricula* can mean either the little register in which the poor to be supported at the Church’s expense were enrolled, or the needy themselves, as here. See Gregory of Tours, *Miracles of Saint Martin*, book II, chapter 22. Mabill.], on two days each week, Thursday and Saturday, she had a bath prepared in turn. Girded for the task, she washed the heads of the poor with a *sabanum* [Another reading: linen cloth.] [Note: [Col. 0505D] For more on this word, *sabanum*, see Du Cange. The Greek manuscript lexicon, Royal MS 930, says: “περίψημα, τὸ σάβανον τοὺς ἱδρῶτας τοῦ κάμνοντος ἀποψῆχον,” that is, “a *sabanum* is that which wipes away the sweats of a sick person.”], scrubbing away whatever there was: scurf, scabies, tinea, and even pus, without disgust; sometimes she also extracted worms and cleansed the putrefaction of the skin. One by one she combed the heads she had washed. She soothed the ulcers of scars exposed by loose skin or aggravated by fingernails, following the evangelical manner, by pouring oil over them and relieving the contagion of the disease.

As for the women descending into the bath, she herself, with soap, washed each part of their bodies from head to foot. If, as they came out, she saw that anyone had old clothing, she took it away, had it stripped off, and gave back new clothing. She made those who had arrived in rags come to dinner well dressed. When they had gathered and the service had been prepared, she herself offered each one water or a napkin, and likewise wiped the mouths and hands of the weak.

Then, when three courses had been brought in, stuffed with delicacies, she stood before the diners fasting, present among the guests, and herself cut the bread, meat, or whatever was served. She never ceased offering food with a spoon to the sick and blind. Two women were present, but she alone served, so that, like a new Martha, she might be occupied until the brothers, filled with drink [Another reading: purulent], became joyful at the banquet. Then she withdrew to wash her hands, rejoicing wholly in the well-appointed feast. Yet if she heard any commotion, she ordered them to remain seated until they wished to rise. [Note: [Col. 0505D] Apparently, this refers to the disturbance made by those rising from the table, perhaps to escort her away as a mark of respect. Bollandists actually read: “But if any rose for the sake of honoring her, she ordered them,” and so forth.]

**18.** Every Sunday, summer and winter, she had this as a venerable custom: after the poor had been gathered, she first offered them unmixed wine with her own hand from the sweet drink, and afterward entrusted it to the girls to pour for everyone. She herself was hastening to attend prayer, so that she might complete the course of prayer and also attend upon the priests invited to table. Even then, in royal fashion, she would not let them return to their own homes without a gift.

**19.** With what sweetness she performed that other deed, which ought to make one tremble! When lepers came and announced themselves by a sign, she ordered her assistant to inquire with pious concern where they were and how many there were. When the assistant reported this, a table was prepared, with a shallow serving dish [Note: [Col. 0505D] *Missorium* sometimes denotes a gift sent by a prince, and sometimes a small bowl in which some liquid is placed. It seems to be used in the latter sense here. Mabill.], spoons, knives, wicker baskets [Note: [Col. 0506D] *Cannae* are little baskets or wicker vessels. Mabill.], drink, and cups. She alone, following behind, entered secretly, so that no one would notice her. [Note: [Col. 0506D] The Bollandists read: “When the table had been prepared, with spoons, bowls, stools, drink, and cups sent in, she alone, following behind, entered secretly, so that no one would notice her.”]

She then took the women covered with various marks of leprosy into her embrace, kissed their faces, and cherished them with all her heart. Next, after the table had been set, she brought warm water, washed their faces, hands, nails, and sores, and again served them, feeding each one herself. When they departed, she gave them gold or clothing, scarcely ever having a single witness to her generosity.

Her attendant, however, presumed to address her playfully: “Most holy lady, who could kiss you, since you embrace lepers in this way?” She replied kindly: “Truly, if you do not kiss me, I have no concern about it.”

**20.** Yet, by God’s favor, she shone with a different miracle. If someone was despairing over a pustule or wound, the attendant would offer the holy woman a vine leaf, pretending that this was what she needed. Once she had scarcely obtained the sign of the cross, she would carry it to the despairing person and place it upon the wound; immediately, a remedy followed.

Likewise, when someone suffering from a fever came, or a sick person said that in a dream he had seen that he should go to the holy woman for his recovery, he would offer a candle to one of the attendants. When it was lit, the illness would receive death during the night, and the sick person health.

Whenever she learned that someone was lying sick in bed, she carried foreign fruit, sweet and also warm, and restored the patient. And one who for ten days had been unable to take anything would, when she herself immediately administered food, receive both nourishment and health. Yet she ordered that no one should report this publicly. [Note: [Col. 0506D] That is, no one should spread the story. Fortunatus may be understood to use *fabula* for the speech itself or the matter narrated, as appears in book II of the *Life of Saint Martin*, where he says: “Now too, whatever story of Martin has flowed forth—” The Bollandists read *in fabulam*.]

**21.** How great was the popular gathering on the day when the holy woman decided to withdraw into seclusion, so that those whom the streets could not contain filled the rooftops as they climbed them! If anyone were to review everything she fervently undertook from that time onward—fasting, service, humility, charity, labor, and suffering—he would praise her as both confessor and martyr.

Thus, apart from Sunday, every day was a fast for the most holy woman. Her nearly fasting meal consisted of lentils or vegetables; she ate no bird, fish, fruit, or egg. Her bread of delicacies was rye bread or barley bread, which she ate concealed beneath a *fladon*, so that no one would notice. Her drink likewise was honeyed water and *piracium*, taken only in small sips when she was thirsty.

**22.** During the first Lent, when she withdrew into her cell, she took no bread or food until Lent had ended, except on Sunday. She ate only roots of plants or mallow greens, prepared without a drop of oil and without salt. Throughout the entire fast she did not drink even two sextarii of water. She suffered such thirst that, with her throat dried out, she could scarcely recite a psalm, her voice parched.

She continually wore a hair shirt against her body in place of linen. Reciting the canonical hours, she completed the vigils. Before her she spread ashes and covered them with the hair shirt; this served her as a bed. Even rest itself fatigued her, and she thought that this was scarcely enough for her little body to endure. [Note: [Col. 0506D] Surius adds the following: “Soft feathers never supported her, nor did the brightness of linen sheets furnish her bed. She had no sleeve with which to clothe her arm, except that she made two sleeves for herself from her stocking. Yet she treated herself in such a way that even the abbess did not notice these things.” These additions are absent from the manuscript codices and are taken from book II, section 8. Mabill.]

**23.** While all the nuns were still sleeping, she wiped and greased their footwear and returned it to each of them. During her other Lents [Note: [Col. 0507D] Those who revised Surius have explained “other Lents” as referring to the Lent of Advent and other fasts. But the sequence of the text shows that this passage should be understood of the other Lents she spent in the cloister after the first. Mabill.], she took somewhat more relaxed food [Another reading: she relaxed the fast] on Thursday and then on Sunday.

Indeed, throughout the rest of the year, except for the days of Easter and the greatest feasts, as long as her illness allowed, she always led an austere life in ashes and a hair shirt. She rose to sing psalms before the community had risen. Of the monastery’s duties, she was pleased with nothing unless she served first; and she disciplined herself if she performed a good deed after someone else.

Thus, at her appointed times, she swept the monastery’s streets and corners alike, cleansing whatever was filthy. She did not shrink from carrying out loads that others found horrible even to look at. She did not delay in cleaning the privy but undertook the task [Another reading: sweeping it]. Carrying the stench of dung, she believed that she would diminish herself if she did not ennoble herself through the lowliness of service.

Carrying wood in her arms, bringing it to the fire with her breath and tongs, growing hot and not withdrawing even when injured, she served the sick outside her assigned week. She herself cooked the food, washed the faces of the sick, and brought them hot fare; after visiting those whom she cared for, she returned fasting to her cell.

**24.** Who could explain with what fervor she rushed to the kitchen when her week came, taking it upon herself? In the end, no nun except her carried from the back entrance [Note: [Col. 0507D] Papias says in his *Vocabulary*: “A *posticium* is a hidden door, so called because it is removed from public view.” It was often located at the rear of a building. A *posticiaria* is the woman responsible for receiving what is brought into the monastery and sending out what is to be sent out, commonly called *la tourière*, as our Menard demonstrates in the *Concordance of the Rule*, chapter 61, section 14. Mabill.] nearly all the wood that was needed, alone bearing it in a bundle.

She drew water from the well and distributed it among the vessels. She cleaned vegetables, washed legumes, and revived the fire with her breath; she labored in the heat to cook the food. She herself lifted the vessels from the fire, washed and brought in the dishes.

After the meals were finished, she washed the vessels herself, thoroughly cleaned the kitchen, and carried whatever was muddy outside to the appointed place [Another reading: into the lowest refuse]. From there she brought what was necessary to the sick; she went without hesitation and, before she received the Rule of Arles [Note: [Col. 0507D] Learn what is meant by the Rule of Arles from what we said in the *Life of Fortunatus*, section 82.], after completing her week adequately, she provided warm water for everyone. [Note: [Col. 0508D] The Bollandists read: “She showed the utmost courtesy to everyone: she washed their feet,” and so forth.]

With most holy humility she washed and kissed their feet, and, still prostrate, begged everyone’s forgiveness for the negligence she had committed.

**25.** After all the labors and punishments she imposed upon herself—when she herself recounts them aloud, she shudders—who could endure them? [Note: [Col. 0508D] The Bollandists read: *intulerit ipsa, qui voce refert, perhorrescit* (“what she inflicted upon herself makes the one who reports it aloud shudder”). This seems to me to indicate a certain nun from whom Fortunatus heard these things related.] On one occasion, during the days of Lent, she fastened three broad iron rings around her neck or arms. Inserting three chains and binding them tightly around her body, she enclosed the hard iron within tender flesh, which grew over it.

When the fast had ended, she wished to remove the chains sealed beneath the skin but could not. The flesh had been cut in a circle over the iron chains across her back and breast, so that the blood poured out and finally emptied her little body.

**26.** On another occasion she ordered a brass plate bearing the sign of Christ to be made. Having heated it in the cell, she pressed it deeply into two places on her body, until all the flesh was cooked. Thus, with her spirit burning, she made her limbs burn.

Then, devising something even more severe against herself, during one Lent, in addition to the austerity of fasting and the torment of burning thirst, while the file of the hair shirt was tearing her tender limbs with its harsh bristles, she ordered an *aquamanile* filled with burning coals to be brought. [Note: [Col. 0508D] We learn what an *aquamanile* is from the Roman Order, where it describes how the office of the Mass is to be celebrated: “An aquamanile, that is, a hand-vessel, namely a basin suitable for receiving water from the washing of the hands.” Isidore, book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 10: “From the archdeacon we receive a bowl of water with an aquamanile and a hand towel.” Thus some people wrongly confuse an aquamanile with a pitcher. Mabill.]

When the others had departed, with her limbs trembling, her spirit armed itself for punishment, reflecting that since there were no times of persecution, she should make herself a martyr. Meanwhile, to cool such a burning spirit, she resolved to set her body on fire. She applied glowing bronze to herself; the burning limbs hissed, the skin was consumed, and wherever the heat reached the innermost flesh, it made a hollow. Silently she concealed the openings, but the blood, rotting within, revealed what her voice did not disclose amid the suffering.

Thus, for the sweetness of Christ, the woman willingly endured so many bitter things! And so what she had concealed was brought to light by miracles.

**27.** Accordingly, a noblewoman, Gislaadis, named Bella [Note: [Col. 0508D] Gregory of Tours, *Miracles of Saint Martin*, book I, chapter 19, also tells of a blind woman named Bella who was healed at the tomb of Saint Martin, and says that she was from the territory of Tours. This must be regarded as another woman, different from the one Fortunatus mentions here.], most miserable because of a long-lasting blindness, asked that she be brought devoutly from France to Poitiers, into the presence of the holy woman. Though entreated only with difficulty, the saint had her brought to her through the silence of the dark night.

Prostrate at the saint’s knees, Bella scarcely obtained permission for her eyes to be marked. As soon as the saint impressed the sign of the cross upon them in the name of Christ, the blindness fled and light returned. In the darkness of night, day shone upon the woman who had long been deprived of it, so that, although she had been brought there under escort, she departed without a guide.

**28.** Likewise, the girl Fraifledis, while being tortured so wickedly at the instigation of the enemy, deserved to be healed between the holy woman’s hands without any delay. Nor should the following deed of the blessed woman be passed over.

A certain woman named Leubilis, while she was being grievously tormented in the countryside by the adversary, was restored publicly to health the following day as the holy woman prayed: in her shoulder the skin split open and a new healing occurred, with a worm emerging. She trod upon the worm with her foot and reported that she had been freed.

**29.** What she had done in secret should be brought before the people. A certain nun, chilled by frost throughout the day and scorched by fire during the night, had not moved a step for six months. She lay as though lifeless, and another sister reported her illness to the holy woman.

Since she was exceedingly weak, the saint ordered that a warm bath be prepared, had the sick woman carried to her cell, and had her placed in it. Then she ordered everyone else to withdraw, leaving only the sick woman with the healer for nearly two hours. Supporting her sick limbs from head to foot, she bore her bodily weight. Thereafter, wherever her hands touched, the pain fled from the languishing woman; and she who had been carried in by two people came out of the warm water in good health.

She had never even smelled wine, but now she received it, drank it, and was restored. What more is there to say? The following day, when it had already been expected—or believed—that she would depart this world, she went out into public safe and sound.

**30.** Let us add to her praise a deed whose merit does not perish. A certain woman was suffering grievously from an attack by the enemy, and they could scarcely bring the rebellious demon to the holy woman. She ordered the adversary to throw himself onto the pavement in fear of her. At once, when he cast himself upon the ground at the blessed woman’s word, he feared the one who had been feared.

The holy woman, full of faith, then stepped upon his neck, and he came out through a discharge of the bowels. Even in small matters there is great glory for the Creator. Thus, by chance, when a ball of yarn that the holy woman had spun was hanging from the chamber, a mouse came to touch it. Before it could cut the thread, it died hanging from the bite.

**31.** Let a deed so worthy of a miracle be inserted into this work. A certain man named Florejus, one of the holy woman’s household, was laboring at sea to catch fish. A storm of winds arose and a mass of waves surged up. The sailor was scarcely able to keep the bilge clear before the wave poured over him [Note: [Col. 0509D] The Bollandists read: “not so much the sailor working at the bilge as the wave pouring over him.”]

As the ship filled and sank, he cried out at the top of his voice: “Saint Radegund, while we obey you, let us not perish in shipwreck. Obtain from God that we may be rescued from the sea.” At these words the cloud immediately dispersed, the sky became clear, the wave fell, and the prow rose up.

**32.** Goda, a secular girl who afterward served God as a nun, had long lain mournfully in bed and, despite extensive medical treatment, was becoming weaker. A candle was made to the measure of her height. Through the Lord’s mercy, in the name of the holy woman, at the hour when the fever was expected, the flame rose and continued burning. By its benefit the fever departed before the candle had been consumed.

**33.** If we omit many things because of brevity, we sin all the more. Therefore, after the remaining matters had been quickly cleared away and the remedy postponed, the wife of a certain carpenter, who had been tortured for many days by a demon [Note: [Col. 0509D] The Bollandists read: “while she was being tortured for several days by an evil spirit.” Surius uses the feminine *energumena* instead of *energumenus*, which follows.], was addressed jokingly by her venerable abbess [Note: [Col. 0509D] Thus it was not Radegund, as some claim, but Agnes who was abbess. This is also clearly apparent from Fortunatus, book VIII, poem 8, *On Virginity*, and from book II of the *Life*, below, section 5. See Fortunatus again in book VIII, poem 4; in poem 3 he congratulates Radegund on Agnes’s birthday. Mabill.]. She said to the saint: “Believe me, mother, I excommunicate you if this woman is not returned cleansed from the enemy within three days.”

She said this plainly, but secretly made the holy woman repent at the time when she was to be refreshed. To avoid delaying over what happened: the next day, while the saint prayed, the adversary, roaring as he came out through the woman’s ear, abandoned the vessel he had invaded, and the woman returned home safe with her husband.

Nor should a deed very similar to this be passed over. The most blessed woman asked that a strong laurel tree be uprooted from its place and transferred for her pleasure to her cell. When this had been done, the transplanted tree did not take root and became completely dry in its leaves. The abbess jokingly reproached her: unless she prayed that the tree might take hold in the earth, she would suspend herself from food. This was not said in vain: through the saint’s intercession, the laurel, dried up in its leaves, branches, and root, became green again.

**34.** One of the nuns, who was especially close to her, had blood from a bodily humor covered one eye. She took a sprig of wormwood, which the saint had kept near her breast to cool herself, and placed it over the eye. The pain and blood immediately fled, and from the greenness of the herb the clarity of sight shone forth.

Let us recall what has almost passed silently from memory. Anderedus [Note: [Col. 0510D] Surius incorrectly printed *anus* while speaking of a person handling the matter, as Bollandus notes. Bollandus himself reads *cliens*, “attendant,” instead of *agens*.], the agent of the most blessed woman, had children who were born only to die immediately, and, while the sorrowful mother was giving birth, she was thinking of burying the child. The weeping parents threw the lifeless infant upon the saint’s hair shirt. As soon as the infant touched the most health-giving garment, it returned from death to the work of life; and, reddened, it raised itself from the cloak, its pallor now resembling the pallor near a tomb.

**35.** Who could count the wonders that the merciful kindness of Christ performs? A nun named Animia was so swollen and distended by dropsy that her health was at its final extremity, and the sisters assigned to her were watching for the moment when she would breathe out her spirit.

In sleep she seemed to see the venerable abbess, blessed Radegund, order her to descend naked into a bath without liquid. Then she seemed to see the blessed woman pour oil over the sick woman’s head with her hand and cover her with a new garment.

When this symbolic action was complete, she awoke from sleep and no trace of the disease appeared, so that she had not even sweated, and the water within her had been consumed. By this new miracle, not even a trace of the illness remained in her abdomen. She who had been thought to be carried headlong to the tomb rose from her bed and walked, so that the oil testified by its odor on her head, while no harm remained in her belly.

**36.** Let this be brought into the midst, so that the region may rejoice. Once, when the twilight of night was already falling, secular people were singing around the monastery amid much noise, with *choraules* and citharas [Note: [Col. 0510D] *Choraules* means musicians; although Vossius, in *On the Faults of Speech*, proves that this word is used not for musicians but for those who blow the pipe and lead the chorus, in the proverb: “A bad choraules, a good symphoniacus.” Mabill.].

After the holy woman had prayed at length with two witnesses, a certain nun said jokingly: “Lady, I recognized one of my songs being celebrated by the dancers.” She replied: “It is a great thing if you enjoy hearing the scent of the world joined to religion.”

The sister continued: “Indeed, Lady, I have just heard two or three of my songs here, which I composed.” The saint replied: “With God as my witness [Another reading: I call God to witness], I have heard nothing worldly in the song.” Thus it was clear that, although in the flesh she was in the world, in mind she was in heaven.

**37.** Let an ancient form of miracle be proclaimed in Christ’s praise, after the manner of blessed Martin [Note: [Col. 0511C] “After the manner of blessed Martin” means that Radegund performed a miracle of the kind previously performed by blessed Martin, bishop of Tours, as Sulpicius relates in his *Life of Martin*, chapter 5.].

When the most blessed woman was shut up in her cell, she heard a nun weeping. At the sound of the signal, she asked the approaching woman what had happened. The woman reported that a young sister had died and was cold, and that the water prepared for washing her had already become warm.

The saint, grieving, then ordered that the body be brought to her cell. Once it had been carried to her, she received it with her own hands. She closed the door behind her and ordered the others to go far away, lest anyone discover what she was doing. But what she had done secretly could not long remain hidden.

While preparations were being made for the dead woman’s funeral, she handled the young woman’s little body for nearly seven hours. Yet Christ, who saw her faith, could not deny her: complete health was restored. The one rose from prayer; the other rose from death. The old woman raised herself when the young woman had revived. With another touch of the sign she joyfully returned alive the young woman whom she had received dead and weeping.

**38.** Let that noble deed performed through a dream also be commemorated. A treasury official named Domolenus, on the day when the most holy woman departed from this world, was wasting away completely from a severe illness of suffocation. He seemed to see the saint graciously approach his village. He ran to greet her and asked what the blessed woman desired.

She then said that she had come there to see him. Since the people wished an oratory of Saint Martin to be built, the most blessed woman took the official’s hand and said: “Let the venerable relics of the confessor be placed here; build on this site a temple that he will consider most worthy.” What a mystery of God! A foundation and pavement were found, and a basilica was built.

While he was still asleep, she drew her hand across his throat and, soothing his gullet for a long time, added: “I have come so that better health may be granted to you by God.” She also seemed to ask: “For the sake of my life, release, on my account, those whom you hold in prison.”

When he awoke, the official told his wife what he had seen, saying: “I truly believe that at this hour the holy woman departed from this world.” He sent someone to the city to discover whether this was true, and sent another to the prison with instructions to release the seven prisoners held there. When the messenger returned, he reported that the righteous woman had departed from this world at that very hour. Thus, through a threefold mystery—the prison released, the official restored to health, and the temple built—he proved the holy woman’s prophecy.

**39.** But let the smallness of this account of the blessed woman’s virtues suffice, lest abundance become wearisome. Nor should it be considered too brief, when from a few miracles the greatness of them can be recognized. How she lived in piety, moderation, affection, sweetness, humility, integrity, faith, and fervor, so that even after her death and glorious passage miracles continued to attend her—human eloquence, struck dumb with admiration, has no power to explain. Yet to him who gave her these things be glory, praise, and dominion, forever and ever. Amen.

# LIFE OF SAINT AMANTIUS

[Col. 0511]

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LIFE OF SAINT AMANTIUS, BISHOP OF RODEZ

Surius seems to have been the first to judge that the *Life of Saint Amantius, bishop of Rodez*, which we present here, was composed by Fortunatus, inferring this from the style and manner of writing familiar to Fortunatus. Others later followed Surius, including the distinguished Labbe, who says that some think, not implausibly together with Surius, that its author was Venantius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers.

Perhaps certain forms of expression may cause someone to doubt this attribution. They plainly savor of poetry, and the author of this *Life of Saint Amantius* is found to use them more frequently than seems generally to have been Fortunatus’s practice when he composed the Lives of saints.

Such are the expressions with which, describing the night, he says in section 6: “The setting of day is returned to the earth in the silence of night. Scarcely had deep repose relaxed mortal hearts in sweet sleep”; and, speaking of dawn: “Meanwhile the splendor of rosy light illuminates the world, and, when a face has been restored to things, light is restored to the earth,” and so forth.

Unless perhaps Fortunatus, not yet accustomed to composing Lives of saints, may be said, while laboring over this one, to have indulged rather freely in the poetic spirit and transferred into this prose work some of the colors of poetry, which he studied intensely.

Although the style itself is also more polished and cultivated than Fortunatus’s style usually tends to be, and the speech is grander and more rounded, these features may arouse suspicion in some that this is not genuinely his composition, contrary to the opinion of others. Yet it must not be denied that Fortunatus’s talent and care in arranging words often appear in the same work. For this reason, we have thought it should be published under his name.

Surius published the *Life of Saint Amantius* for 4 November, but his text was incomplete and corrupted by many errors and deformities. Later, the distinguished Philip Labbe of the Society of Jesus published the same work complete, copied from manuscript exemplars, in volume II of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, and so forth, p. 474 and following, Paris edition of 1657. From that edition we took the text which we append to the works of Venantius.

We compared it with the edition published by Surius and indicated the principal passages in which they appeared to differ. We have also added several notes to clarify it.

[Col. 0513]

# LIFE OF SAINT AMANTIUS, BISHOP OF RODEZ

[Note: [Col. 0513C] Saint Amantius is readily acknowledged by all to have been the first bishop of the people of Rodez; the French commonly call him Saint Chamant. A perpetual and constant tradition prevailed among the people of Rodez that Saint Amantius had been ordained bishop by Martial, apostle of Aquitaine, as Antonius Bonal reports. He is recorded on the day before the Nones of November in the ancient martyrology, volume IV of the *Spicilegium*. His feast is likewise celebrated on this day in the Roman Martyrology. These facts are taken from Sammarthanus, *Gallia Christiana*.]

*(S)*

## PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 0513D] This prologue is absent from Surius. From it, however, one may understand that Fortunatus had been urged by someone to compose the *Life of Saint Amantius*, just as he also composed several other Lives in order to satisfy the wishes of those who requested them, as we have noted in the appropriate place. If it is permissible to make a conjecture, since he says in section 14 that he had been in Rodez when, through the protection of Saint Amantius, a boy named Euphrasinus was freed from a demon, and since he himself was an eyewitness of this miracle, it is likely that the bishop of Rodez who then presided over that Church had urged him to write the Life of his predecessor Saint Amantius. In the same way he wrote the Life of Saint Albinus, bishop of Angers, at the request of Domitian, also bishop of Angers, when he had stopped at his residence during a journey. Certainly, the word “obedience,” which Fortunatus uses here, seems to indicate that someone superior to him in rank had imposed this burden upon him.]

[Col. 0513A]

A poor intellect succumbs beneath a splendid burden, and speech sterile and lacking all the fertility of learning is not sufficient for so immense a subject. Though I am therefore weak, I now take up upon my shoulders the burden of obedience. Forgive me, I ask, reader, when you take up a page discordant beneath my hands, and when unlearned muttering strikes your ears with chattering harshness; for it is no less blameworthy not to obey when one can than to presume to do what one does not know.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE WITH ITS MIRACLES

**1.** Thus, the most blessed [Note: [Col. 0514C] Surius has: *Beatissimus Amantius Ruthenae urbis quondam fuit civis ortu, vita pastor, nunc felici patronus est excessu* (“The most blessed Amantius was once a citizen of the city of Rodez by birth, a shepherd in life, and now its patron by his blessed departure”). [Col. 0514D]] Amantius was a native of the city of Rodez, a shepherd in life, and now, in his blessed departure, its patron. In the first flower of his youth, breaking the snares of the world, he undertook the service of Christ with a firm resolve to persevere. By the virtue of patience he trampled the vices by which human frailty is assailed [Note: [Col. 0514D] In the same edition, after the words *virtute calcavit* (“he trampled by virtue”), the intervening material is absent up to *qui beato fervens* (“burning with a blessed purpose”); and after *post honoris sui parem* (“matching the height of his honor”), the intervening material is omitted and the text is joined directly to *nunc brevi stylo* (“now, in brief style”).], drove empty cares far away, restrained impulses of boldness with the reins of constancy, and subjected to the rule of his mind the rebellious tumult of conflicting thoughts.

Burning with a blessed purpose and distinguished by the splendor of his happy merits, he earned the summit of the priesthood and a seat upon the lofty episcopal throne. His mind matched the height of his honor. There was nothing doubtful, nothing double, nothing changeable in him. In him there was perfect humility, ready mercy, tireless generosity, and holy simplicity.

He was praiseworthy in vigils, strong in fasting, gentle in forgiveness, diligent in conversation, mild in conflict, meek under insults, patient in tribulations, restrained in prosperity, steadfast in sorrow, stern amid flatteries, and gentle amid hardships. His freedom was not without modesty, nor his cheerfulness without gravity.

[Col. 0513C] Now, in brief style, I shall touch upon a few of the marks of his virtues. The Lord will grant me the power of speech through the prayer of the blessed bishop, for he knows how to pour out the riches of his goodness without any lack, [Note: [Col. 0514D] In the same place: “and does not know how to become empty when he has poured it out.”] and does not know how to change when he has poured it out.

## 2.

Accordingly, when the governor had taken his seat in the forum of the aforesaid city, raised above the others on a higher chair, and had condemned the defendant in that abominable crime to the final punishment of the cross and the extreme penalty of the gallows, the blessed bishop hastened to the forum. He asked the governor for the life of the man, who was already dying from fear, but did not obtain it.

> [Note: [Col. 0514D] In the same place: He repeats his pleas and wastes his prayer before the deaf governor. Thus the bishop returns to his cell . . . redoubles his sighs, etc. . . . Immediately the unrelenting governor is struck by a punishment worthy of him. For he is suddenly fastened, in wondrous ways, to the chair on which he had been seated higher . . .]

He repeated his pleas, but the mind of the proud man was not broken by its dreadful arrogance; rather, it grew hotter in anger. Therefore the bishop returned to his cell, prostrated himself upon the ground, poured forth his prayers, uttered repeated sighs, and beat his holy breast again and again. He asked from the Lord what he had been unable to obtain from the governor.

At once a punishment worthy of the unrelenting governor struck him. For he was suddenly afflicted in the chair on which he had been seated higher than the others, in a marvelous manner: vital warmth deserted his bones, and his limbs, loosened at their rigid sinews, lost the function by which they had served his soul.

People hurried to the cell of the most blessed man. The Father rose from prayer and proceeded to the forum. The governor perceived the man’s arrival, already half dead. His lost senses were therefore restored, and his limbs, which had served their functions, returned to their former strength.

Thus health was restored to the governor and life to the condemned man; and whatever the one had brought upon himself by committing the deed, or the other by refusing to forgive, was remitted through the mercy of the Lord. [Textual note: the parallel source reads *Pia Domini miseratione diluitur*, “it is washed away by the Lord’s merciful compassion.”]

In the end, the condemned man was granted life together with forgiveness of his crime, and the governor obtained pardon together with his health.

## 3.

Not long afterward a still more renowned miracle followed, equal in merit to the former. For not far from the city there stood, upon a high pedestal, an image, at which a great multitude of pagans used to gather.

> [Note: [Col. 0514D] The same author: Thus, while they sacrifice the flesh of animals—or rather their own deaths—to demons, and while they all, filled with food . . . [they make] long sighs over the impious crime of sacrilege, through pious exhortation, etc. . . . He prefers to preserve the harmful thing by another’s counsel rather than by his own; he tests the disadvantage in the manner of useful things against the measure of pleasure. The mob therefore burned with every goad of madness against the holy man; while he, taking up pious weapons against those raging . . . [offered] tears for his enemies . . . asking that, without his death—or at least by the fury of the raging men’s own cessation—their violence might stop. What he desired for himself as a crown, he prayed for from the merciful King on their behalf, so that the impious might not be punished. After long sighs, etc. . . . he asked the boy, who was standing nearby, to look . . . The servant denied seeing what he had seen before. When he had prostrated his holy limbs upon the ground for the third time, the one entrusted with the task said that a very thin and small cloud seemed visible from the east. Clearly he believed what he had foreseen would happen . . . lightning thundered with a terrible sound, etc.]

Accordingly, while they were sacrificing the flesh of animals to the demons according to their customs, and while they, stuffed with food and filled with wine, made a din with their singing, the most blessed priest arrived. Seeing the wretched people exulting in a joy more grievous than any mourning, he drew sighs from the depths of his breast and attempted, by pious exhortation, to call them back from the crime of sacrilege.

But remedies of salvation are always hated by slothfulness, which prefers to perish by its own choice rather than preserve another’s counsel, and strives to twist useful things into the measure of pleasure, regarding what is attractive and harmful as right and necessary.

The mob therefore blazed up under every goad of madness. But he, taking up weapons against those who raged, returned to his cell, prostrated himself upon the ground, poured out abundant prayers for his enemies, and redoubled deep sighs for those who hated him. He asked life for those who were certainly raging toward his death.

For what he desired as a crown—namely, that the impious should not be punished—he therefore offered pious prayers before the mercy of the Lord. For it is no lesser virtue of spirit to have entreated the Lord for an enemy than to have fallen prostrate for the Lord; to have poured out prayers for a persecutor than to have poured out an innocent life.

After these long sighs, he lifted his holy head and asked the boy, who was standing nearby, whether any cloud was rising from the east. The boy replied that he saw none. Again the blessed bishop prostrated himself upon the ground and groaned; then, raising his head from the earth once more, he asked the servant the same question as before. Clearly, he believed himself to see what he had foreseen would happen.

The man of God therefore rose from the earth and gazed upon the heaven, from which his mind had never been absent. Suddenly the day was covered with clouds, and soon a terrifying peal of thunder, bringing destruction to the devil, resounded. At the same time it struck the unhappy image, split it apart, and scattered it.

The stone idol of the sacrilegious people was hurled through the air. The whirlwind of the avenging storm cast its pieces in different directions, so that one part is now held by the stream of the Lauterna,

> [Note: [Col. 0515D–0516D] Lauterna is understood to be a flowing stream near the city of the Rutheni.]

while another is held by the bank of the river Avarion,

> [Note: [Col. 0516D] Segodunum of the Ruthenians—so say the Sammarthani in *Gallia Sacra*—was a city of Aquitania Prima, situated opposite the river Avarion. Formerly it was under the metropolitan see of Bourges; now it is under Albi and the parliament of Toulouse. It is called the city of the Ruthenians, etc.]

which will preserve it forever as a testimony to the miracle. Another part is retained by an open field far from the city,

> [Note: [Col. 0516D] Surius: “presenting the work of so great a miracle for human use”; after those words, “representing the memory,” he immediately adds: “A little time had passed after this when, behold, he commanded,” as is read below in section 4.]

and, by being useful to human beings, displays the work of so great a miracle and recalls its memory.

Thus divine providence scourges the impious in order to heal the sickness of the soul through the affliction of the body. Preparing remedies from adversities, it restores health through infirmity. Therefore he struck the sacrilegious people in order not to destroy them, [Textual reading: the printed text has *ut perderet eam*, “in order to destroy it/the people”; the editor conjectures *ne perderet eam*, “so as not to destroy it,” which the translation follows.] and with a merciful hand inflicted wounds so as not to punish them.

The punishment present there was therefore not vengeance for crime but a remedy for sin: it destroyed the sin and restrained the sinner. It extinguished the crime while preserving its perpetrator, and from pain health arose, while from anger forgiveness came to many.

When the image burst apart under the stroke of lightning, those who possessed the strength of youth and those who were passing from middle age into old age immediately lost their hearing, their ears blocked. The younger and less guilty generation remained unharmed; but those in whom the serpent’s poison had burned more deeply were struck.

Those whom holy preaching had not moved toward the faith were driven to it by the power of this remarkable miracle. For they hurried to the most blessed man, sought and obtained forgiveness for their crime, and recovered and received the senses they had lost. They perceived the streams of the healthy fountain and drank from them.

The wound inflicted therefore disappeared; what had been found was healed, and the blows brought them no further correction. Thus our Lord, through the faithful prayer of his servant, healed the ancient rottenness of their sores, cured their wounds, softened the scourges, and restrained anger through fear.

In this way, by divine gift, the outstanding warrior seized spoil from the enemy, carried it to heaven, took it away from the enemy and restored it to its author. He restored captives to freedom, though the plunderer himself was captive; he restored the dead to life, while the author of death lay prostrate.

Immediately, too, he drove the stains of sin from the inner chambers of the sacrilegious heart; love of Christ drew them away, water cleansed them, and a most powerful brightness clothed earthly people in the covering of spiritual faith. Thus the outstanding Father and faithful servant, remembering the evangelical command, returned to the Lord what had been entrusted to him, multiplied by a blessed increase.

## 4.

A little time had passed after this when he ordered two servants of the church to catch a few fish for those who were coming, in the river that flows past the city.

Without delay they obeyed the command, caught the fish, gathered up their nets, and returned to the city. Soldiers stationed in the city’s garrison encountered them on their return. Following the custom of enemies, the soldiers took possession of the fish, brutally beat the men with whips, and left them lifeless.

The servants returned to the priest, and the witness of their grief disclosed all that had been taken from them and inflicted upon them. Yet the blessed bishop did not grieve over what he had lost through contempt; rather, he groaned with compassion for the afflicted.

> [Note: [Col. 0516D] The same author: On one side rigor held Constancy firm; on the other he poured forth pious tears . . . the waters overflow. . . . Meanwhile the invading soldiers came to the priest, etc. . . . His mind, most ready in compassion, forgives . . . Soon what had remained undefiled after being seized outside is returned to the flames and subdued. Remarkable and glorious signs are followed by still more astonishing ones.]

On one side strength held him firm in constancy; on the other, compassion poured forth tears. He was blessed when he conquered through contempt, more blessed when he was overcome by feeling.

Meanwhile the soldiers returned home and attempted to subdue their booty with fire. When fire was placed beneath it, the waters leaped up, but suddenly, through a new miracle, the flame lost its power, bursting apart and raging uselessly. In a wondrous manner the fish became harder in the flames, nature’s law being changed, and their unyielding, hardened substance was softened by the novelty of so great a miracle.

Meanwhile the soldiers hurried to the priest, returned what they had taken, clung to his knees, and asked forgiveness for their crime. His mind, ready with the greatest compassion, forgave them and granted them forgiveness for their crime, together with the fish. Soon what had been seized outside, and had hardened when peace was violated, returned to the flames and was subdued.

Here the blessed bishop, through his most holy prayer, removed from the people the necessity of enduring injury and from the soldiers the habit of inflicting it. At the same time the violence of the avenging flames was extinguished, and the soldiers and the people were corrected.

Remarkable and glorious signs were followed by still more astonishing ones.

## 5.

> [Note: [Col. 0517D–0518D] The same author: There was in the forum . . . because now the eternal [nature] of present things, etc.; which must be retained . . . Accordingly, the people, having sent a messenger to the Ruthenian, reported to a certain man that at that time he was distinguished above others by the splendor of his birth, etc. . . . He gathered the assistance of servants, was carried in a wheeled seat, and immediately made for the city. Having already covered a day’s journey, he raged . . . the pair of horses stopped, and, as though insensible . . . then that distinguished man . . . asked that he graciously release him by pious prayer . . . the persecutor descended from the cart . . . asked for a remedy. Scarcely had he finished speaking when the animals . . . obeyed. After this the following is added immediately: “The criminal,” etc., with the intervening passages omitted.]

There was in the forum an image standing prominently upon a high pedestal. The most blessed man, inflamed by zeal for divine love, threw it down and shattered it.

Therefore the multitude of the sacrilegious people rose up in vengeance for their god, inflamed with the frenzied fury of warriors, and threatened the soldier of Christ with death. But the most blessed man did not fear death, because he loved life. For it was not fitting that the bravest warrior should fear present death when, by contempt for present things, he had earned eternal life.

Accordingly, the people sent a messenger to a certain man named Honoratus, who at that time was far superior to the others in nobility of birth, titles of honor, wealth, and influence. He gathered the assistance of servants and, carried in a wheeled seat, immediately set out for the city.

Having already covered the journey, he was near the city, raging fiercely and threatening dreadful and final things. Yet the blessed bishop had prostrated himself upon the ground at the middle of the gate the day before and had poured out a prayer to the Lord.

At that place the team of that man’s animals stopped in wondrous amazement, and stood rigid like lifeless statues. Neither goads nor savage blows achieved anything.

When that distinguished man, struck by the novelty of the miracle, sent one of his attendants to the most blessed man and asked him to release by pious prayer the one whom he had bound, as it were, with the chains of his merits, the priest arrived without delay.

The cart moved forward, and the persecutor clung to the saint’s knees, bathed his feet with tears, confessed his sin, and asked for help. Scarcely had he finished speaking when the animals, which had stiffened like hard rocks, received movement from heaven and obeyed the command.

While nature was now changed, now restored, by the holy prayers, the mind that had previously been savage and incapable of perceiving its master—like something born from hard rocks—was suddenly kindled by the fire of faith.

Immediately the saving water washed away the stains of sin, and, when the cloud of unbelief had been removed, a clear light was poured into his heart.

Meanwhile, one of the servants became, by swift running, the sad messenger to his mistress. Struck by sudden grief, she threw off her necklaces, tore her clothing, rent her hair, lacerated her cheeks, drenched her face with tears, and covered her beaten breast with anguished sighs. Now she mourned her master, crushed and mingled with dust; now she lamented him as a spouse lost.

The household was thrown into confusion. The tears of the servants were joined to the mistress’s lamentations. She soon hurried to the city and, with her face troubled and bruised, attacked the priest with all the fury—or mourning—of a woman.

When she looked upon the serenity of his venerable face, she suddenly trembled with fear. Immediately kindled by the glorious warmth of faith, she fell at the priest’s knees and condemned, with praiseworthy detestation, the demons whom she had previously worshiped with appropriate superstition.

He immediately cleansed her from the stain of her faults and bathed her in the waters of eternal life. Thus the most blessed bishop snatched his unhappy spoil from the jaws of the devil and made it happily his own.

At one time two men also came to the city, living an unhappy life in crime. They concealed their deadly hearts with lowered faces and forced tears, and, by drawing sighs from the depths of their breasts, pretended that they were poor through the wear of their wretched old clothing.

The necessities of life were given to them, and their feigned misery was relieved with the most compassionate pity. They lamented that they could not endure the force of the cold. At length they were admitted within the enclosure of the church.

Scarcely had the first quiet of mortal hearts, with a welcome forgetfulness of cares, loosened them, when they committed theft. With polluted hands—shame upon the deed!—they approached the sacred hangings, pulled down the veils, and, having opened the doors, quickly took flight, driven by their crime.

They were struck by a punishment worthy of their blindness, so that their wicked eyes, which had been witnesses to their crime, could not serve as guides in their flight. They wandered in uncertain circles here and there and spent the night in empty exertion.

Day was restored to the earth. Their crime was recognized, and people hurried to the priest. The blessed bishop revealed those whom he had held by prayer and declared that the perpetrators of the crime had been struck blind near the bridge closest to the city and were sitting there, exhausted by their fruitless journey.

They therefore went to the bridge and found the men guilty of the wicked crime. When asked where they were going and what business they had, they replied that they wished to go farther, but that, although it was almost the third hour of the day, they were prevented from continuing their journey by the darkness of an opaque night.

At last they were dragged before the priest. Although the most blessed man, as though placed on high, looked down upon the injury inflicted against him, he nevertheless remembered the divine command and did not wish another’s guilt to be punished without exercising his own virtue.

He removed his cloak and struck the sacrilegious men twice or three times across the back. The blows settled so deeply in their limbs that they thought nothing could be more severe than the beating they had received from him.

He also brought many who had transgressed the rule of a better life back to the health of correction through a light touch of the holy covering. Yet the remedy was always applied according to the measure of the sin, and punishment was imposed according to the nature of the fault.

Thus the hidden wound of the soul, inflicted through the prayer of the holy man, experienced a stronger remedy for its disease.

## 6.

Accordingly, a certain criminal saw the garden of the holy man, small indeed in extent but flourishing with beautiful greenery.

> [Note: [Col. 0519C] The same author: It shone with vegetables; for pleasant beauty enlarged the narrowness of the place . . . when he seized the convenient moment for his fraud, he sprang forward, full of boldness and crime, and, with a light push causing the things that obstructed him to yield, hastened to depart, but was held back by divine power. For no exit was open to him on his return, and thus the guilty man was held as though enclosed by a thin hedge like a wall. For small obstacles, etc. . . . The entire space of the night was the length of the garden’s path . . . [the dawn] illuminates the face of the world, and when it is restored to things, light returns to the earth. Accordingly the blessed old man went to the cell where, sleepless amid the heat of night, he drew [strength] through sweet meditation . . .]

Pleasant beauty enlarged the narrowness of the place. At once, with a savage mind, he conceived the crime of theft.

The day’s light therefore departed from the earth into the silence of night. Scarcely had the hearts of mortals relaxed in deep rest and sweet sleep when, seizing the moment convenient for his fraud, he sprang forth full of boldness toward crime. With a light push he passed through what obstructed him, entered the garden, tore up the vegetables, and hastened to depart.

Yet no exit was open for his return. Because he was guilty, he seemed to himself to be surrounded by a thin hedge like a wall; the small obstacles appeared to grow into a great mass, as though every kind of fortification had been constructed against the fugitive.

Thus the entire night’s journey was the length of the garden. Meanwhile the splendor of rosy light illuminated the world, and, when its face was restored to things, daylight was restored to the earth.

Accordingly, the blessed old man, who had spent the night in his cell, having rejected idle sleep and passed the hours in sweet meditation and holy labor, called one of the brothers. He sent him to the garden and ordered him to bring back the man whom he found there, wearied by his error and entangled in crime as though in certain bonds.

Without delay the brother went, found him,

> [Note: [Col. 0519C] The same author: “He drew him out.”]

and brought him back.

The criminal immediately appeared, threw down the stolen goods, and embraced the priest’s feet. The man, full of compassion, forgave the crime and granted him the stolen goods, while often warning him to ask for what was necessary for his needs rather than seize it, and to receive what he needed as a gift from those who gave it, not through the crime of robbery.

> [Note: [Col. 0519C] Thus he earned forgiveness from the holy man and departed.]

Thus, having received forgiveness from the holy man, he departed from him.

## 7.

Why should I mention that, in the same garden, honey taken by nocturnal theft from the beehives by a similar criminal and carried home was completely changed into the nature of pitch? The culprit was astonished at the miracle, although there was no lack of a cause for his crime and the awareness of his crime tormented its perpetrator.

> [Note: [Col. 0519C–D] The same author: “Although the cause of the crime was absent, the consciousness of the crime tormented its perpetrator; although loss remained after the theft, in which he sorrowfully persisted in his wickedness. At length, when the criminal had been shaken out of the deep stupor of his mind, [he came] to the bishop,” etc. . . . “And the nature of honey returned with no less a miracle than that by which it had been changed . . . he carried the gift home,” etc.]

At length, the criminal, shaken out of the deep stupor of his mind, hurried to the bishop, returned the stolen goods, prostrated himself at the holy man’s feet, and asked forgiveness for his crime. The bishop very readily forgave the suppliant.

Thus it was no lesser miracle for the nature of the honey to return than for it to have been changed. In this way the culprit carried home forgiveness instead of punishment, and a gift instead of a crime.

## 8.

While he himself was shining through these miracles of virtue, the time of his blessed and glorious completion arrived. His limbs, already broken by age, were failing, yet the labor of abstinence strengthened his afflicted and lifeless body.

> [Note: [Col. 0519D] The same author: “His lifeless body was strengthened by the burden of abstinence.”]

Yet merit supplied what nature had denied. Such was the fervor of faith in the holy man that, with insatiable ardor, the more discipline he had imposed upon his body, the more he desired to impose. Thus the increases of his merits were incentives to further progress.

For the love of God can refresh the spirit, but it cannot satisfy desire. Rather, the more it is drunk in,

> [Note: [Col. 0519D] “It inflames as it is drunk in, for by its sweetness it arouses,” etc.; “it entrusts earthly limbs to earthly things.”]

the more it inflames thirst. Through its sweetness it arouses appetite, but it does not produce disgust from satiety.

Accordingly, the most blessed Amantius, shining with this light of merits,

> [Note: [Col. 0519D–0520D] It cannot be determined with certainty in what year Saint Amantius died. Saint Quintianus, who sat after Saint Amantius, was in charge of the Ruthenian Church until the year 506, in which year he signed the Council of Agde; he also took part in the First Synod of Orléans in 511.

> Meanwhile, when Quintianus—as Gregory of Tours relates in his *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 4—had enlarged and expanded the basilica of Saint Amantius and moved the holy man’s body elsewhere, Saint Amantius appeared to him at night in a vision and gravely reproved him in these words: “Because you have presumed rashly to remove limbs resting in peace, behold, I shall remove you from this city, and you shall be an exile in another region; nevertheless, you shall not be deprived of the honor which you enjoy.” This happened not long afterward.

> Yet other bishops seem to have sat between Saint Amantius and Saint Quintianus. For Sidonius Apollinaris, writing to Basilius in Book VII, Letter 6, laments among other things the condition of the Ruthenian Church in these words: “Bordeaux, Périgueux, Rodez . . . deprived of their chief priests by their deaths, and with no bishops subsequently substituted in the offices of the deceased—for through them the ministries of lesser men were supplied—have drawn out a broad boundary of spiritual ruin.” These words seem to indicate that other bishops sat among the Ruthenians after Saint Amantius, and that they died by death’s blow.

> Certainly the Ruthenian Church was widowed and deprived of a shepherd when Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of Auvergne, was summoned by Elaphius to consecrate the baptistery which he himself had built in the Ruthenian territory, as can be gathered from Sidonius Apollinaris, Book IV, Letter 15. For why would Elaphius have summoned a bishop from another city and see—especially by difficult roads covered with winter snow—if the Ruthenian Church had not lacked its own shepherd?

> Nevertheless, those words of Fortunatus seem to indicate that not much time intervened between Saint Amantius and Quintianus. In section 11 he says: “Nor had the courses of many years yet completed their circuit and returned, when Bishop Saint Quintianus chose before the sacred altars a capacious place for a tomb, where he placed him with wondrous workmanship and commendable skill,” etc.

> Accordingly, Saint Amantius seems to have died not long before the Goths invaded Gaul under King Euric, at which time perhaps even the Ruthenian city was captured and afflicted. This occurred toward the end of the fifth century. If so, the opinion of the Ruthenian people must be considered false: namely, that Saint Amantius was ordained bishop by Saint Martial, the apostle of the Aquitanians.]

he commits his earthly limbs to earth, but his heavenly spirit ascends to the heights. There he now takes his place among choirs of angels; here he shines with the brightness of virtues. There he intercedes for servants with a suppliant voice; here he protects servants with sublime virtue. There he asks; here he grants. There he pours out prayers; here he answers prayers.

There he now shines, surrounded by eternity,

> [Note: [Col. 0521D] Surius: “He sparkles with light, or with the clear splendor of merits, or with the rosy and purple brilliance of the cross inflicted upon him. For in himself he also acted as a persecutor, extinguishing vices . . . and attained a new [thing], not death but the martyrdom of the flesh . . . . Amantius both persecutes and . . . the enemy in himself; and the death of the living is precious. Everything that follows is absent.]

either with the light of the clear splendor of his merits or with the rosy, purple radiance of the cross inflicted upon him.

For in himself he both extinguished vices by pursuing them as a persecutor and shone as a martyr by crucifying his body. He attained not death but martyrdom through the mortification of the flesh.

And since the death of a martyr is precious in the sight of the Lord, while the most blessed Amantius pursued and overthrew the enemy, the death of the living man was precious in the sight of the Lord.

## 9.

Thus far, by divine gift and as I was able, I have set forth in writing the life of the blessed confessor Amantius. Now, in a brief account, I shall compress a few things accomplished by the outstanding victor.

There was a certain woman named Juliana, a widow, an old woman, and poor. Old age’s weakness, solitude, and poverty pressed upon her all at once. Yet she possessed a strong spirit and contempt for hardships.

So that she might be nearer to divine service, she established a cell near the basilica of the holy bishop, in order that the nearness of the cell might restore the frequent attendance which advancing age had denied her.

Necessity, the teacher of various arts, had shown her how to buy and sell wine. She therefore bought and sold wine in such a way that whatever remained of the price became the substance of her labor; she did not increase her profit beyond what the necessities of life required.

A certain man then came to her, guilty of a savage crime and far more monstrous than other criminals, and said that he wished to buy wine. She received him into the cell as a purchaser and, so as not to detain the criminal longer—perhaps because he was in a hurry—reproved the delays of old age through her eagerness for speed.

He began to look around carefully, scanning everything with wandering eyes to see whether there was anything that the cruelest robber could take from the widow and the poor woman.

While she was thus disturbed with feminine carelessness, he soon saw a small box containing a little money, seized and carried it away, and, after buying the wine, fled. Three days later he returned, as though intending to display his innocence in person.

She, immediately certain that he was the wicked thief, began to fly into his face and seek help by shouting. The criminal, terrified by the crime of his own conscience, suddenly and swiftly broke away and mounted a horse.

The old woman came out of her cell, wishing to overtake by her cries the man whom she could not follow with her slow steps. Yet, raising her eyes toward the holy basilica, she cried out in faithful devotion and with the loudest voice:

“Do not allow him to depart, supreme bishop and strongest defender. Do not allow my robber to escape. Do not abandon a widow and a poor woman, whose wealth is my consolation and whose strength is my support.”

As she uttered this prayer, she suddenly saw, in a marvelous manner, the horse standing rigid in the middle of the courtyard like a stone.

For it happened that on that day the festival of his sacred deposition was being celebrated, the annual cycle having been completed, and the people were coming out of the basilica after the customary solemn rites. Struck by the novelty of the miracle, they stood amazed.

The criminal, too, stood there in astonishment, fixed in body, while the old woman remained leaning upon her staff. At last the criminal poured forth abundant tears, confessed his sin, returned the money, and was absolved; he returned home forgiven.

The people therefore raised such great virtue to heaven with marvelous exultation and ineffable praise. Thus the glorious bishop was strong in defending the poor, merciful in absolving the criminal, and displayed immense miracles both by hearing the innocent woman and by releasing the condemned man.

## 10.

Not long afterward, while he himself was present to protect his servants in danger, a clear and very great miracle followed.

> [Note: [Col. 0521D] Septimania is a province of Gaul which was formerly subject to the Visigothic kings dwelling in Spain; for this reason it was sometimes called Hither Spain. See Valesius, Book VII of *Rerum Francicarum*, where he confirms this latter point from ancient testimonies.]

A certain man was hastening to Septimania, wishing to buy wine. First, however, he entered the basilica of the glorious victor, sought his tomb, prostrated himself upon the ground, asked for a prosperous journey, and made vows.

Soon he set out. With little difficulty he completed the journey and came to Septimania, bought wine, and returned to the city. Already, rejoicing in his successful affairs, he had crossed half the distance.

From the summit of a lofty cliff he saw the river Tarn flowing below in a gentle stream.

> [Note: [Col. 0521D–0522D] Sidonius Apollinaris mentions the river Tarn in poem 24, addressing his little book:
>
> “When you have been received into their bosom,  
> You will go to Trevidon, and to the ridge—alas!—  
> too near to the litigious Ruthenians.  
> . . . . . . . . . . . .  
> From there Lesora, surpassing the Caucasus of the Scythians,  
> Will look upon you, and the swift Tarn,  
> Carrying in its clear water  
> A muddy fish pressed with solid flavor.”
>
> Furthermore, the Tarn—as the distinguished Sirmondus adds in his notes to Sidonius—is a gold-bearing river which rises in the Cevennes and flows through the borders of Aquitania and Narbonensis into the Garonne.]

Already close to the city, he looked upon it joyfully; already, summoned by his vows, he was fulfilling them. But while his whole hope was in the city and he had begun the roads along the ridge of the high mountain, joy was suddenly disturbed by dreadful grief.

For the vehicle, struck against a rock, was shaken; the vessel was thrown from the vehicle with a terrible crash and, plunging to the bottom of the valley, at last came to rest on level ground.

When the purchaser saw this, he tore his hair, lacerated his cheeks, and, turning toward the walls, lifted eyes flooded with tears and spoke briefly:

“Under your guidance, most blessed bishop, I entered these final places. Behold, now abandoned by you, already brought to the borders of my homeland, I am crushed beneath a great burden of hardships and suffer punishments worthy of my merits.”

As he recalled these things in profound grief, he hurried to the place where the vessel had fallen, increasing his tears by the cause of his tears and suffering even greater punishments from his present loss.

When he came to the place weeping, he suddenly saw, through an astonishing miracle, the vessel intact and full of wine. He understood that the patron whom he had lamented as absent was present there through his manifest power.

His tears therefore turned into joy, and sorrow was changed into gladness.

It was thus a greater miracle that the object entrusted to the patronage of the holy bishop had been saved in this way than that it had not fallen; that it had not felt the hard rocks when it struck them than that it had escaped dangers while being preserved; that it had encountered rough places without knowing peril than that it had been kept intact from precipices.

## 11.

Nor had many years yet run their course and completed their circuit when Saint Quintianus, bishop, chose before the sacred altars a spacious place for a tomb, where he placed him with wondrous workmanship and commendable art.

Previously, the tomb stretched out in the basilica of the holy man and, like a shining lamp, illuminated the minds of those awaiting it with the splendor of its own brightness.

The bishop therefore conceived this beautiful undertaking in his mind, pledged it in devotion, and, when the work was completed, appointed the day of the sacred translation.

The report of this spread swiftly. Not only did the enclosed places within the borders of the extended city send bishops or peoples to it, but so did other cities and neighboring provinces.

When the arrangements appropriate to faith had been completed, a certain Marturius, a commendable abbot distinguished by his life, also came from the city of Narbonne.

First, however, an artisan was chosen to remove what surrounded the tomb. As soon as he entered the place of sacred veneration, he boldly drove away what lay against the tomb. But immediately, struck by a blow from the rising right hand, he groaned, and his rashness, overcome by avenging punishment, fell prostrate.

The day dedicated to the sacred translation had now dawned. On that day the first teachers of the city of Rome, Peter and Paul—namely, the two greatest lights of the world—had been sent victorious to heaven through a triumphant punishment.

On this day, therefore, awaited by everyone’s prayers, the priests were present and the peoples gathered. Prayer was prescribed according to custom; the people prostrated themselves upon the ground, and the tomb was moved.

Then, through a sudden miracle, such a fragrance exhaled from the tomb and spread an ineffable sweetness that it filled not only all the people in the holy church but also the crowd situated in the porticoes and courtyards with extraordinary delight, refreshing them as though with a special draught, a gift of recompense.

Meanwhile the blessed burden was placed upon the vehicle by the hands of the faithful. The hand of Abbot Marturius was caught beneath the tomb.

He did not try to withdraw his hand, nor did he seek the assistance of those standing around to raise the sepulcher. Rather, he did not cease to implore the help of the most blessed Amantius with pious laments, recalling these words in a humble voice:

“Do not, once our priest and now the companion of angels, do not crush the hand of your servant, lest you exasperate your servant with any grief of affliction. Sweeter to me than honey is your sweetness. Do not allow our joys to be stained by a cloud of sadness. You are my joy and my exultation; you brought me as a guest to your solemnity. Return me unharmed to my cell!”

He had scarcely finished speaking when the tomb suddenly rose of its own accord, and the unharmed hand was withdrawn. Then, once withdrawn, it was again placed beneath the sacred burden.

## 12.

Meanwhile the vehicle struck a certain person who was in its path and knocked him down. Its wheel then ran across the fallen man, whose legs were splayed out, but at a command it checked its threatening force, so that it neither inflicted the sensation of pain upon him nor left marks of bruising.

It therefore ran on swiftly, crushed nothing beneath it, completed the services of its journey, and left behind signs of power.

Amid these distinguished miracles, without any hindering labor and to the supreme joy of all, the sacred relics were placed in the site carefully prepared for them.
