Some people, however, presumed in their mad boldness to heap one crime upon the earlier crime at the tomb of the holy man. Immediately seized by frenzied madness, they paid the penalty; afflicted by horrible groaning and consumed by hidden flames, they revealed their wickedness, returned what they had taken, prostrated themselves upon the ground, and asked forgiveness for their crimes.

Without delay, through the power of the most blessed bishop, they deserved to be cleansed from their obscene contagions.

Thus just vengeance struck them, while the mercy of compassion absolved them.

13. Again, when the savage Marcomani were advancing against the Rutheni and had covered the whole province far and wide with the cloud of war—for they had surrounded the city with a dreadful ring, bristling across the intervening distance before the walls with drawn swords—their enormous multitude, naturally fierce, also increased the enemy’s confidence. Their flight was everywhere strewn with dreadful pestilence, pitiless slaughter, and shameful famine. [Note: The Marcomani, a Germanic people, held the regions where the Moravians or Bohemians now live, as Cluverius believes; they were so called from horses, since they themselves called a horse *marc*, in the German tongue *Mark*, as is read in Richard Bartholinus’s notes on *De Bello Norico*, book VIII, in Justus Reuberus, p. 632. Hermannus de Lerbecke, however, reports that “Marcomani” was the name given to peoples collected from everywhere who inhabited *Marken*. There are, moreover, several *Marken* in Slavonia.]

At last our priest and most valiant champion rose up to avenge his servants, and struck the entire people with such a single terror that, as they departed, they took flight in fear, just as they had seized their weapons in furious rage. For when the leaders of that most powerful people entered the basilica according to custom, seeking favorable fortunes for their own people, they approached the tomb. Immediately the coverings placed around the sepulchre began to billow now to one side and now to the other, as though stirred by gusts—a new miracle of power—and a great sweat melted from the tomb. At the same time, by a marvelous sign, the sacred covering was shaken from the tomb. The leaders fell prostrate on the ground, asking that flight be granted them instead of glory and safety instead of success; and they themselves, who had previously surpassed savage ferocity in their cruel violence, returned, struck by this new fear, to human behavior.

Thus they rose from prayer, and at the terrible sound of the trumpet the whole people gathered together. Their pallor revealed their fear, the sign of terror; a trembling speech reported the miracle. Horror shook everyone’s limbs. In view of the extraordinary power, flight seemed the proper course, and in a dense mass they made their way back to their homeland. After three years had passed, they returned inflamed with the same fury with which they had come before, raging with the same savagery; but, warned by this miracle, they now returned from it, and, struck by this fear, fled from it. Thus the outstanding shepherd twice rescued his flock from the attack of wolves by a single act of power.

14. I shall relate another miracle, which I myself witnessed, with the city of Ruthena as my witness. A certain boy named Euphrasinus had been bound by that most savage enemy, skilled in many forms of harm, in the tight bonds of a dreadful illness. It had closed his mouth in savage fashion, taking away the movement of his tongue and the freedom of speech. He paid the penalty of prolonged grief in enduring silence, and no remedies of healing could be brought to the afflicted boy.

At last, inflamed by the ardor of bold faith, the sick boy sought the tomb of the holy Father. With force he placed the cloth touching the tomb against his mouth, and immediately, as the tongue struck the mouth like the plectrum of a lyre, a clear voice praised Christ the author. With his tongue released, he bore witness to the divine power and the merits of the ancient warrior. Thus that sick man left the basilica healed, giving thanks to Christ, and went rejoicing through the whole city as witness and messenger of so great a miracle.

15. Likewise, a most savage robber attacked an unwary traveler, killed and threw him down, and carried off his possessions; then, struck by the weapon of an accusing conscience, he fled. The clothing of the man killed by the robber was sold to someone who knew nothing of the matter. When the garments were publicly produced without delay, the innocent buyer was dragged to punishment and tortured for another’s crime. He was thrust into prison, brought out, beaten, returned to prison, and the penalty of a deadly gallows was postponed until the appointed day.

Meanwhile, in the silence of the dead of night, the prison shone with divine brilliance. The glorious Amantius appeared, conspicuous in snowy radiance. He visited the grieving man, declared his name, and urged him to escape the cruel torments. Immediately the tight iron bonds burst apart, the locks opened, and the prisoner came forth; the release of the innocent became the salvation of the guilty. The prison stood open. He took refuge in the basilica of the most glorious victor and struck upon the doors. At once the bolt sprang back unharmed to the ground by a new miracle. Thus the most blessed Amantius, by divine favor, rescued those condemned from the impending destruction, and received those whom he had saved into the sacred basilica’s gentle embrace, there to be preserved.

16. Likewise, a certain man was killed by a robber in the presence of a man of good conscience. But when the robber had concealed himself by fleeing at full speed, the innocent man feared that, while standing beside the dead body, he might suffer the penalty of another’s crime, and sought the basilica of the blessed victor. The dead man’s relatives bound him tightly with chains. With tears poured out [perhaps *effusis*], he cried out in a loud voice before the people:

“Most valiant champion, if you know me to be guilty and condemned to avenging punishment, strike me down; but if you see that I am innocent and unjustly bound, release me, defender of justice.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when, in the sight of his people, the iron burst apart and fell far away, displaying by the miracle-working power of the warrior both his merits and the innocence of the suffering man.

17. Therefore, amid the joys of so great a festival, let us ask our Lord with every form of supplication that, together with his most blessed Amantius, he may grant us what we rightly seek and mercifully forgive our sins—he who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[VITA OF ST. REMIGIUS]

## Preliminary Notice on the Following Life of St. Remigius, Bishop of Rheims

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, in his preface to the Life of Saint Remigius, bishop, relates that he had heard from his elders—who likewise said that they had received it from their own fathers—that Fortunatus had written a large volume on the Life of Saint Remigius. Later, at the request of Aegidius, also archbishop of Rheims, Fortunatus had condensed into a shorter form what he had treated at greater length in that volume, so that it might serve the Church of Rheims and so that the people could easily retain in memory what was narrated there.

This, moreover, was the reason why, when this second work of Fortunatus began to be read by many, and more frequently, because of its brevity, that great Codex began to be handled with less care and consequently perished entirely, except for one surviving copy, which at last was rotted by dripping water and gnawed by mice. It is preferable, however, to hear Hincmar himself recount the whole matter in the passage cited:

“As I have learned by faithful report from old men and religious men already advanced in age . . . they heard from their ancestors that they had seen a book of enormous size, written in ancient script, concerning the origin, life, virtues, and death of blessed Remigius, our most holy patron. It perished for this reason: Aegidius, the fourth bishop of this city after blessed Remigius, asked a certain religious man named Fortunatus, distinguished in metrical verse and at that time invited in many different places throughout these Gallic and Belgic regions by numerous powerful and honorable persons on account of the merit of his life and learning, to extract from that book certain miracles, composed in elevated Gallic diction but in plain speech, to be recited before the people, so that the people might hear them without weariness, store them in their minds, and through them be stirred to love, honor, and devotion toward God and his protector. The reader can observe this in the same excerpt, where it is written: ‘Let us endeavor to discuss a few things and pass over many.’ When this excerpt began to be frequently read aloud to the people and copied by many because of the ease afforded by its brevity, the great Codex began to be neglected, until, in the time of Prince Charles, and so forth. During that unhappy period, not only were all the precious things taken away from this Church of Rheims, but the churches and houses of religious people were destroyed, and property was divided from the episcopal estate. Even the few clerics who remained sought their livelihood through commerce, and sometimes bound the coins they acquired by trade in sheets of parchment and leaves of books. Thus the aforesaid book, partly rotted by dripping water, partly gnawed by mice, and partly broken up by the cutting away of its leaves, perished to such an extent that only a few scattered leaves were found.”

Fortunatus wrote a poem for this Aegidius, bishop of Rheims, whom Hincmar mentions; it survives in book III, chapter 20. See the notes we have added.

We therefore publish this abridgment of the Life of Saint Remigius as it appears among the Bollandists under the first day of October. It is also found under that day in Surius. We have likewise excerpted most of the notes with which the Bollandists elucidated it, and have added a few of our own.

# LIFE OF SAINT REMIGIUS, BISHOP OF RHEIMS (S)

### 1.

[Note: Saint Remigius—as Hincmar relates in his Life, chapter 1, nos. 10–11, and as Flodoard and others agree—succeeded Bennadius in the see of Rheims when he was twenty-two years old. He held it for seventy-four years and consequently died at the age of ninety-six, on the Ides of January. Cointius, under the year 486, no. 12, believes that Saint Remigius was made bishop of Rheims around the year 459 and died around 533; see his discussion. Gregory of Tours states that Clovis I, king of the Franks, was baptized by Saint Remigius, in book II, chapter 31, where he composed an excellent eulogy of the blessed Remigius’s learning and holiness and did not hesitate to compare him with Sylvester.

In our manuscript this abridgment of the Life, without any author’s name, has only the following title, written in illuminated letters: “The Kalends of October. Here begins the Life of Saint Remigius the Confessor.” Bollandists.

This first period is read somewhat differently elsewhere. In the Chifflet manuscript and that of Saint Benignus of Dijon it reads: “The holy deposition of the most blessed Remigius the bishop has today presented us with the festivals of a mystical solemnity, which every year, as the course of time rolls onward, is renewed for our desires.” The Surius edition is nearly the same and begins, “The blessed Remigius,” etc.; but in Mombritius it is shorter: “The deposition of Remigius the bishop has presently offered us a day mystically festive with solemnity.” It then immediately proceeds to the next period: “For, in the earliest beginnings of his birth,” etc. Bollandists.]

The holy deposition of the most blessed Remigius the bishop has today presented us with a day of mystical solemnity, which every year, as the course of time rolls onward, is renewed for our desires.

This man, therefore, distinguished by the nobility of his parents at the very beginning of his birth, [Note: The father of Saint Remigius was Emilius, or Aemilius; his brother was Principius, bishop of Soissons. On these men see letter 14 of book VIII of Sidonius Apollinaris, written to Saint Principius, bishop of Soissons. Hincmar writes of the parents of Saint Remigius in chapter 1, no. 4: “Both were noble by birth and renowned among their own people for their honor.” The Bollandists discuss them more fully in the preliminary notice to the Life of Saint Remigius.] was chosen by divine mercy not only before he was born but before he was conceived. So great was this that a certain monk named Montanus, while resting in the lightest sleep, was struck by a threefold warning to announce truthfully to his blessed mother Cylinia [Note: The Chifflet manuscript and the Surius edition have *Ciliniae*; the Dijon manuscript of Saint Benignus has *Chiliniae*; Mombritius has *Chilimae*. This mother of Saint Remigius is commemorated on October 21. Bollandists.] that she would conceive a male child, so that his name and merit might be signified. He immediately fulfilled the command and announced to the most fertile mother the joys of the offspring she was to conceive. [Note: Another reading: “and.”] Just as she showed no doubt in the credulity of faith, so she received in childbirth the one whom she had foreknown in the womb. [Note: Another reading: “whom she had foreknown.”]

[Note: The manuscripts vary somewhat here. The Chifflet manuscript, the Dijon manuscript of Saint Benignus, and the Surius edition read: “She was not slow, nor uncertain; secure, she immediately brought forth the happiest pledge, which she had first conceived in her heart.” Mombritius reads: “Not as one slow or uncertain, she immediately brought forth, secure, the happiest pledge, which she had first conceived in her heart.” Bollandists.]

She was not slow, as though uncertain; secure, she immediately brought forth the happiest pledge, which she had first conceived in her body.

### 2.

In him sweet infancy continually foreshadowed the merits of his future age, and what his mother had recognized before his conception he already displayed before his years had come. He strove to surpass his tender years by the maturity of his character and to season them with the honey of charity through the benevolence of his heart. Why say more? As a young man, when success followed success and he advanced in the pursuits of holy conduct, at the age of twenty-two, the just man [Note: The manuscripts again vary. The Chifflet manuscript and that of Saint Benignus of Dijon have *sumpsit* (“he took up”) instead of *sumpsisset* (“he had taken up”); Mombritius agrees, but adds the verb *polleret* (“he flourished”) after *adolescens*. Surius renders the same phrase: “As a young man he served the Lord amid the successive successes of holy conduct, and in his twenty-second year took the beginning of greater merit.” Bollandists.] was carried to the height of the episcopate by the unanimous votes of all the people of Rheims, as is recognized, rather than elected.

In this office he immediately appeared so suited and devoted to his duty that one would have thought that, if he had only recently ascended the position, he had nevertheless always presided over it. [Note: The Dijon manuscript of Saint Benignus reads, “who was newly ascending”; in the Chifflet manuscript one also finds *qui* (“who”) for *quo* (“to which”). Surius agrees with our text. Mombritius, however, certainly reads incorrectly: “As if something new had happened, he had always presided.” Bollandists.]

He was generous in almsgiving, diligent in vigils, devoted in prayer, perfect in charity, abundant in humility, [Note: The Dijon manuscript has “in kindness.”] outstanding in teaching, ready in speech, and most holy in his manner of life. Never did the adversary of the human race find in him either something by which to deceive through fraud or something to darken through pretense. [Note: I have restored the word *nec* (“nor”) here, as well as shortly below, from all the other copies, since our manuscript reads it corruptly. Bollandists.]

### 3.

He displayed the sincerity of his mind through the serenity of his face, and showed the piety of his most merciful heart through the gentleness of his speech. Whatever could contribute to eternal salvation, the most blessed man fulfilled no less by his actions than he taught by preaching. It would therefore be long to set everything out in words, lest we impose weariness on our hearers through excessive length—if I were to state how many ornaments of every virtue, whether precious or great, the privilege of heavenly reward had bestowed upon him [the transmitted syntax is defective]. [Note: The Bollandists assert that this defective sense could be restored if *contulerim* (“I have bestowed”) were read as *contulerit* (“it bestowed”), with the addition of *exponam* (“I shall explain”) or a similar verb. In the Chifflet and Dijon manuscripts, as they report, it reads: “It is a long task to weave in words”—in the Dijon manuscript, “to encompass”—“lest we impose on our hearers weariness through this excessive length. How much the ornament of all virtues, whether precious or great, conferred upon him by the privilege of heavenly reward.” The sense is complete in Surius in nearly the same words.]

Let us therefore endeavor to discuss a few things and pass over many. [Note: In the Chifflet manuscript and that of Saint Benignus of Dijon this reads: “For if either the barrenness of our speech could adorn, or memory retain, the signs of so many of his virtues, the present daylight would sooner reach its end than the page.” Mombritius agrees with our text except that it correctly has *prius* (“sooner”) rather than *plus* (“more”), and *poterit* (“will be able”) rather than *poterat* (“was able”). Surius is closer to the Chifflet manuscript. Bollandists.] For if we begin to relate such great signs of his virtues, either the barrenness of our speech could not adorn them, or memory could not retain them; the present daylight would more easily reach its end than the page could contain them.

The blessed Remigius sought to flee from boasting of his virtues, although in him lofty grace could not remain hidden. Whenever he happened to enjoy a more private meal among his household and took pleasure in the freedom of his friends, unafraid sparrows would come down to him and gather the remnants of the meal from his hand. Some departed satisfied; others approached to be fed. Thus the wildness of birds was tamed through the working of his virtues. [Note: In the Chifflet manuscript—and perhaps also in the Dijon manuscript—the reading is *trepidi* (“trembling”), and shortly afterward *saturati* (“having been filled”) instead of *saturi* (“satisfied”). Mombritius, Surius, and Hincmar himself in the Life below, no. 20, agree with our manuscript; there Hincmarus reported these words from his own copy of Fortunatus. Bollandists.]

### 4.

It happened at a certain time, [Note: The Chifflet manuscript has “him.”] while he was traveling through the parishes with pastoral diligence according to custom [Note: In the same manuscript, “to visit.”], so that the faithful servant of Christ might recognize whether anything was being done negligently in divine worship, that he came likewise to a village called Calmiciacum. [Note: This name, with some alteration of the letters, appears in the manuscripts as it is in the Bollandists.]

While he was there, a certain blind man asked him for the help of mercy; then the demonic assault by which he had long been possessed began to torment him through bodily affliction. Saint Remigius prostrated himself with devoted perseverance in prayer, to which his holy soul was always wholly given, [Note: The Chifflet manuscript adds “also.”] and immediately restored the former light to the man’s eyes and drove away the plague of the unclean spirit.

O ineffable grace of compassion! When only sustenance is requested from him, a threefold remedy is obtained. He fed the needy man, endowed the blind man with sight, and restored the captive to freedom. Thus, through this striking mystery, while one appeared in the poor man, the Trinity revealed itself for his salvation. [Note: In the same manuscript: “in salvation.”]

### 5.

[Note: In the Chifflet manuscript: “But just as the adversary of the human race never ceases to display his power to harm by damaging human beings”; in the Dijon manuscript, “the power of his forces.” Bollandists.]

Thus, just as the adversary of the human race never ceases to display his power to harm, at that same time he had set the city of Rheims ablaze through an immense devastation, when globes of flame suddenly arose. Nearly a third of the city had already been consumed by the conflagration, with embers still remaining, and victorious fire was licking what remained.

When news of this reached the hearing of the most blessed bishop Remigius, he immediately ran with swift speed toward the city’s destruction like an unconquered athlete, and, after completing his prayer, showed himself confronting the fire. [The words in parentheses are supplied from the Chifflet manuscript; in ours the passage is more corrupt: “Broken, or cut down, the people’s head brings devastation back upon itself; it burns the fire.” Surius has *rotatu* (“by rotation”) instead of *reatu* (“by guilt”). Bollandists.] At once, as though broken or cut apart by some guilt, the devastation of the fire drew itself back upon itself, as the people witnessed, and fled through the open gate, so that all might see that the man of God, [Note: The Chifflet manuscript reads: “He was hotter than the cruelty of so great an indignation, which he both conquered by his merits and extinguished.” Bollandists.] full of the fire of faith, was hotter than the cruelty of so great an anger, which he both conquered and extinguished by his merits.

### 6.

A certain girl from the city of Toulouse, born of illustrious parents, had been held captive from early childhood under the siege of a mad spirit. Since her most devoted parents loved her with tender affection, they led her with a very large multitude and great devotion to the tomb of Saint Peter in the city of Rome. [Note: The Chifflet manuscript has “in the Roman city.”]

There, a certain servant of God [Note: Only the Chifflet manuscript adds the name “Benedict”; but this is certainly incorrect, as will be explained below. Bollandists.] was performing many signs of power with the help of the sacred body. Yet no intercession could cleanse this girl, nor could the poison of the crafty demon be driven out of her. [Note: Another reading: “this.”] Then the ancient enemy, constrained by an invocation of the divine name, gave this answer: it could never be expelled from that dwelling by anyone else except through the cleansing of this most blessed bishop Remigius. [Note: The Chifflet manuscript reads “of the divine majesty.”] [Note: Another reading: “could be expelled.”]

Then her parents, supported by the assurances of that blessed man himself [Note: The word “Benedict,” which Fortunatus uses adjectivally of the servant of God just mentioned—as the learned Mabillon, cited below, demonstrates—was taken by Hincmar, in the Life of Saint Remigius, substantively, as they say. He perhaps therefore understood it to refer to Saint Benedict, the father of monks in the West, and others followed him in this opinion. Hence a letter has even been produced, apparently fictitious, which Saint Benedict supposedly wrote to Saint Remigius, commending to him for healing the girl whom he himself could not cure. The Bollandists, in the commentary prefixed to the Life of Saint Remigius, nos. 73 and following, refute this opinion chiefly on the ground that it has never been reported or heard that the holy patriarch Benedict performed many signs of power at Rome, at the tomb of Saint Peter, with the help of the sacred body. It is therefore more likely that the servant of God whom Fortunatus mentions here was Saint Abundius, also called Acontius, as the learned Mabillon believes in the *Annales Benedictini* under the year 530, followed by the Bollandists. Gregory the Great mentions him in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 25, and reports that he was the custodian of the church of Saint Peter, saying of him: “He served Almighty God faithfully, so that blessed Peter the apostle might show by signs what esteem he held for him.” The chronological circumstances also agree, as the Bollandists note in the same place.]

and by the assurances of Alaric, king of the Goths, came with their afflicted child to Bishop Remigius, praying that they might recognize his power in cleansing their child, just as they had previously recognized it in the confession of the robber. [Note: This is Alaric II, king of the Goths or Visigoths in Gaul. He held his seat at Toulouse and was defeated by Clovis I, king of the Franks, in the battle of Vouillé in 507. The Bollandists note this in no. 80 of their preliminary commentary, against those who think that Fortunatus meant Alaric I, whose dates do not agree with those of Saint Remigius. On this Alaric II see Gregory of Tours, book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapters 35 and following.]

### 7.

Then the most blessed Remigius, asserting that he was unworthy after his daily struggle and resisting with his customary patience, was overcome by the prayers of the beseeching people, so that he might pour out a prayer for the girl and sympathize with the parents’ tears. [Note: The Chifflet manuscript reads simply, “He, when,” omitting “Then the most blessed Remigius.” Bollandists.]

Saint Remigius, armed with the merits of holiness, commanded by the authority of his word that the wicked plunderer should depart by the route through which he had entered [Note: The Chifflet manuscript has “by which”; Surius, “the route by which he had entered.” Bollandists.] and release Christ’s servant. Accordingly, with an excessive vomit and foul stench, it departed through the mouth by which it had been introduced.

But shortly afterward, when the bishop had departed, within the space of that same hour, while she swayed, exhausted by excessive labor, she lost the hope of recovery. [Note: In the Chifflet manuscript: “While she was being sustained, exhausted by repeated labor, she lost the breath of life, deprived of vital warmth.” The Dijon manuscript adds “salvation.” Mombritius renders the end: “While she was being nourished, weary from great labor, and deprived of vital warmth, she lost the breath of salvation.” Surius also has a somewhat different wording: “While she was wavering, exhausted by excessive labor, her vital warmth having been taken away, she breathed out her spirit and deprived her family of the hope of recovery.” Bollandists.]

The crowd of petitioners therefore returned to the physician with repeated prayers. [Note: The Chifflet manuscript has “to him.”] But blessed Remigius accused himself, saying that he had committed a crime rather than granted the reward of healing, and had become guilty of homicide instead of bringing a remedy.

### 8.

At the basilica of Saint John, where the lifeless body lay, [Note: Another reading: “lifeless.”] he returned at the insistence of the people’s prayers. There Saint Remigius prostrated himself in prayer upon the pavement of the saints [Note: The words “in prayer” are absent from the Chifflet manuscript. Bollandists.] amid tears and urged the others to do likewise. Then Saint Remigius rose, pouring out a rain of tears, and raised the dead girl whom he had earlier healed when she was sick. [Note: Gregory of Tours also records this miracle of Saint Remigius in his *Book of the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 79, apparently taken from the longer Life of Saint Remigius written by Fortunatus. Gregory himself seems to indicate this work in book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 31, where he writes of Saint Remigius: “There is now a book of his life, which relates that he raised a dead person”—clearly referring to this girl, who is mentioned in the cited book on the Glory of the Confessors.]

She immediately took hold of the bishop’s hand, rose in perfect health, and happily returned to her home. We can judge how great the parents’ tears of joy must have been at this miracle, [Note: The Chifflet manuscript has *prae* (“for” or “from”) instead of *pro* (“for”).] and how great the people’s praise for the triumph. [Note: The same manuscript has *prae* instead of *pro*.] Do you suppose with what groaning and what devotion they sang, “Glory to God in the highest,” who had deserved, through the holy bishop, to behold divine mysteries? He was able to rescue his people from the fall of any impending danger who was able to restore life to the dead woman. [Note: The Chifflet manuscript adds “of the dead.”]

### 9.

Amid such signs of his virtues, blessed Remigius, Christ’s champion, chose—receiving the passage of death’s sleep—to leave the storms of the world when old age was already pressing upon him and to reach the harbor of the heavenly dwelling. After his death, such remedies are granted to the faithful through the protection of his body, and he is recognized to live by his merits alone, who shone with such examples (he is judged to have lacked the punishment of martyrdom, not the devotion of a confessor). [The sentence in parentheses was absent from the manuscript used by the Bollandists, but it was present in others and is not absent from Surius’s edition, although with some difference. There it reads: “But he is judged to have lacked the punishment of martyrdom, not the devotion of a confessor.”]

In those divine sanctuaries of the churches where we venerate his protection, [Note: Another reading: “where we venerated.”] whatever is asked in faith is found, and what is hoped for with earnest devotion is granted in fact. Therefore, with unanimous prayers poured forth, we beseech him to obtain for us, through the intercession of Saint Remigius the bishop and with the help of the Redeemer, the forgiveness of sins and a period of life-giving health.

May his prayer also obtain for all people in this world peaceful times from him who promised eternal things to the just. May he himself deign to grant this, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who is blessed forever. Amen.

[VITA OF ST. MEDARD]

# Preliminary Notice on the Life of Saint Medard, Bishop of Noyon and Tournai

An anonymous author from Soissons of the ninth century, in the preface to his supplement to the Acts of Saint Medard [which appears among the Bollandists under June 8], testifies that the following Life was written by Fortunatus, in these words:

“Fortunatus, an Italian by nationality and a Ravennate priest, most learned in his own time, setting out from Ravenna and proceeding toward the borders of Gaul, chose for himself a convenient residence in the territory of Poitiers . . . Finally, when asked by that venerable bishop”—Gregory of Tours—“he published many little works, chiefly playing in meter, on the lives and virtues of the saints. Among them he also treated the Life of the glorious lord Medard, who is to be named with every reverence, briefly indeed both in prose and in verse, but nevertheless in lucid language.”

Gregory of Tours seems to mention a book of this Life in his *Book on the Glory of the Confessors*, p. 95, in these words: “After he had written a book on his miracles”—that is, Saint Medard’s—“a woman, weak in her hand,” etc. Another author from Soissons, himself also a monk, whose sermons Boscius published in the *Floriacensis Library*, p. 150, mentions the Life written by Fortunatus, saying: “Fortunatus published the Life of the same Father in meter and in the most compressed prose.”

Since several Lives of Saint Medard circulate under the name of Fortunatus, we publish as genuine the one first edited by the distinguished D’Achery in the second volume of the *Spicilegium*, extracted from ancient manuscripts; the others, as falsely attributed to Fortunatus, we reject.

Indeed, there are strong reasons for rejecting the Life which Surius published under June 8, which for a long time was believed to be Fortunatus’s and which Valesius attributes to him. For the oldest manuscripts attribute it not to Fortunatus but to Radbodus, bishop of Noyon and Tournai. Thus the manuscript of the Thuane Library, as reported by the same D’Achery, bears this heading:

“Here begins the Life of the most blessed confessor Christianus, bishop of Noyon, which Lord Radbodus, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, dictated in this manner.”

The manuscript of Compiègne, also reported by D’Achery, has this title:

“Life of Saint Medard, which Lord Radbodus of Noyon dictated in this manner.”

The Bollandists, together with the Sammarthani, believe that this Radbodus was the second of that name, who died at Bruges in 1048 and was buried in the cathedral of Tournai. Nevertheless, it seems from the sermon of an anonymous author on the condition of the first church of Saint Medard, and so forth, which Joannes Boscius published in the *Floriacensis Library*, that he was rather the person who commissioned another to write that Life than its actual author, as the Bollandists observe.

A second and very serious reason for rejecting the Life published by Surius is that it names Drausius and Warimbertus as bishops of Soissons, although they are found to have lived approximately one hundred years after Fortunatus. Finally, the style itself differs from Fortunatus’s style; Surius himself does not deny this and therefore asserts that the work was interpolated by another hand and that much was added to it by someone else. Add also what Cointius observed under the year 456, no. 7, concerning this matter: the author of this Life calls Saint Remigius an “archbishop” and calls the people of Tournai “Flemings,” although in Fortunatus’s age neither the word “archbishop” was in use nor the name “Flanders” or “Flemings” was heard; moreover, three hundred years after the death of Saint Medard, Tournai did not belong to Flanders, which at that time embraced a very small territory, and so forth. From these considerations he concludes that the Life of Saint Medard read in Surius was composed by an author who lived after the year 1000.

The second Life of Saint Medard that presents Fortunatus as its author is the one which the aforementioned Boscius inserted into the *Floriacensis Library* edited by him. For serious reasons it too must be denied to Fortunatus. Its style is far different from Fortunatus’s, and it relates two miracles performed by Saint Medard while he was still a boy—miracles which the aforementioned anonymous author of the Acts of Saint Medard says Fortunatus omitted, as may be read in the Bollandists’ supplement to the Life of Saint Medard.

Add to this that the writer of this Life—as it survives in manuscripts among the Bollandists, compared with the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden—attributes the construction of the church of Saint Medard to King Clotaire alone, without mentioning Sigibert, although Fortunatus relates that Sigibert completed it and brought it to its full height in book II, chapter 20, where he discusses the virtues of Saint Medard.

The same writer also relates that confirmation of the privilege “granted by Saint Leo, bishop of the holy Roman city, and other venerable bishops” was obtained “by Clotaire from the supreme pontiff.” Whatever Clotaire or Leo may be intended, none of this can fit the chronology, as the Bollandists demonstrate in the same place. They therefore believe that the author of that Life was a monk of Saint-Medard, not earlier than the thirteenth century. The same Bollandists think that Boscius omitted such contradictory material in the Life of Saint Medard which he published “because of its absurdity.”

We therefore place here the Life of Saint Medard, edited by the distinguished Acherius in *Spicilegium*, volume II, and by the Bollandists under 8 June, believing it among the genuine works of Fortunatus. Some may think that he composed it at the end of his life, since at its conclusion he mentions King Theudebert and recalls his prosperous and extensive rule, which he prays may last long for him. For Theudebert began to reign at Soissons in the year 589, as may be read in Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IX, chapter 36. In 596 he was inaugurated king of Austrasia, after his father Childebert had already died. In 602 he defeated the Basques, subjected them to his rule, and thereby extended his kingdom farther. Fortunatus, moreover, prolonged his life almost to this time; elsewhere we have said that he died toward the end of the sixth century or at the beginning of the seventh. Nevertheless, I would rather believe that those final words, containing prayers for the kings, were added by someone to the Life written by Fortunatus than that they were added by Fortunatus himself—especially if this is the work of which Gregory of Tours speaks, Gregory of Tours himself having already died in 595. Certainly, as the Bollandists observe, those final words are absent from most manuscripts.

[Col. 0533]

# LIFE OF SAINT MEDARD, BISHOP OF NOYON AND TOURNAI

*(C, S)*

[Col. 0533]

## 1

The life of the most blessed bishop Medard, whose virtues are proclaimed throughout the world, we could not pass over in silence, although we are unable to touch upon all his deeds.

[Note: The manuscripts of Audomar and Velser add: “All his distinguished deeds.” Bolland.]

And since the annual celebration of his day, conspicuous for its veneration, invites crowds of all peoples to seek it, principally by commemorating his burial, may devotion grow in every heart through the fervor of faith,

[Note: The manuscripts of Belfort read: “through the love of faith.” Bolland.]

while the greatness of the saints is disclosed, so that, although in this life few may be found who imitate his deeds, his intercession may nevertheless make all more excellent.

Our discourse therefore first sets forth his origin, so that no one may perhaps offend more culpably through the obstacle of despair, since it is not a divided distinction among nations that prevents a person from loving God with an undivided love, but the united fullness of faith,

[Note: The manuscript of Noyon reads: “the fullness of unity.” The same editor.]

lest divine grace, which is shown to be universal for all who are willing, should mistakenly be believed to be particular.

[Note: Let the reader observe that Fortunatus is speaking here of the grace of holiness, which belongs properly and exclusively to no nation, family, or fortune, since no one is sanctified except in Christ Jesus, with whom there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, and so forth; rather, it is shown to be universal for all who are willing, though in such a way that the will itself is prepared by the Lord. For, as the Apostle says, it is he who works in us both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good pleasure. Read Fortunatus himself, in his exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, at the words: “Your will be done.” (A note belonging to the second recension.)]

[Note: That is, the grace is the particular possession of certain nations.]

## 2

The father of this man, named Nectardus,

[Note: The author of the Life of Saint Medard preserved by Surius says that Medard was born of Nectardus as father and Protagia as mother, at Salency, the hereditary possession of his ancestors, and was born and raised there. He adds that this estate of Salency lay within the bishopric of Vermandois, but in the region of Noyon.]

belonged to a distinguished Frankish family and was not of the lowest rank in freedom. His mother, a Roman named Protagia, was renowned for having been born free from servitude. She, fruitful in a precious birth within Christ’s tabernacles, as we believe, pleased him more than if, preserving her virginity, she had never surrendered herself to the bonds of marriage; their habitation and origin are known to have been in the territory of Vermandois.

When the boy went to school in that city, his mother sent a little *casula* which she had made for him, by his hand to a craftsman to be finished; but on the way he immediately gave it to a blind man whom he encountered.

[Note: Properly speaking, a *casula* is a priestly garment, so called as though “a little house,” because it covers and wraps the whole body. Yet it is clear from Procopius, book II of the *Vandalic War*, chapter 26, that this type of garment was also common among laymen. He says that it suited a slave or a private citizen, not an emperor, in these words:

“Arisbinda, caring nothing for the matter, followed him, wearing a garment wrapped around him which was suitable neither for any other soldier nor for a man on campaign, but entirely appropriate to a slave or a private citizen. The Romans call it *casula* in their Latin speech.”

]

Likewise, whatever he ought to have received as food, while he was tending his parents’ flock,

[Note: Three manuscripts add “of pigs”; Radbod more plausibly reads “of horses,” since this is more suitable for a free-born boy. Bolland. Indeed, what Radbod relates as having been done by Medard while still a boy clarifies the sense of Fortunatus’s words: when the servants happened to be away and there was no one to lead the tired horses out to pasture, his father assigned this duty to Medard. Moved by compassion for a passing man whose horse had died, Medard gave him one of his father’s horses.]

if he saw a poor person, he would offer food to the needy, himself enduring want and spending the day in fasting.

Nor should the mystery of the event be left unmentioned. While the holy man was still a small and innocent schoolboy, he said to a certain boy named Eleutherius that he would assume a public office,

[Note: Saint Eleutherius is celebrated on 20 February. On that day see his Acts among the Bollandists, where this prophecy of Saint Medard concerning him is also related.]

and declared that, when he reached thirty years of age, he would become the supreme priest of God. He was later given as shepherd to the Church in the city of Tournai.

[Note: Here *comitiva* means the dignity of a count. See what we said in the notes to poem 16 of book VII.]

Thus the saint, like a prophet, had already demonstrated by divine inspiration what he foretold.

## 3

Afterward, as he went more frequently to the shrines of the churches, proclaiming the admonitions of faith,

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “proclaiming the admonitions of faith.” Bolland.]

and moderated the years of youthful tenderness by habits disciplined through patience and by the judgment of his own will, despising the allurements of the world through avoidance of them, he undertook the priestly office, transformed alike in spirit and in dress.

Preeminent in the brightness of his character, he immediately became distinguished: among the city’s bishop he was foremost in his manner of life, and among all he was sincere in purity of mind.

[Note: The manuscript of Maximinus reads: “pure in sincerity.” Ibid.]

He never exalted himself more through an abundance of joy, nor was he ever more disturbed by the bitterness of sorrow. He was always patient in adversity, gentle in prosperity, preferring everyone to himself through devoted obedience, succoring the needy with generous compassion. Having trampled down the fuel of every vice, he climbed the narrow path by the advancing steps of holy conduct; he abhorred whatever was hostile and chose whatever was precious.

What more need be said? So that he might be seen as a guest in this world while already being its possessor in heaven, he proceeded through each priestly rank as his offices increased,

[Note: Acherius reads: “through each individual dignity of the priesthood,” that is, by passing through the lower grades which lead in due order to the priesthood.]

with intervals of time duly observed according to ecclesiastical custom. Chosen for the office of presbyter, he received it and, having been tested, obtained it. Thereafter he began to proclaim himself through holy virtues, so that he was thought to be Christ’s fosterling.

## 4

It happened, then, that in autumn, when the juice of the grape clusters was ripening and abundance revealed the variegated harvest,

[Note: Other manuscripts read: “when the softened clusters displayed the harvest with its varied juice.” Bolland.]

the audacity of a thief made his grace known.

In the dead of night, when rather, amid human bodies and with the variety of cares shut out, the burden of gentle sleep prevails in silence, a thief, driven by the desire for fraud, sought out his vineyard to seize it and burst in to be caught.

[Note: Boscius reads: “Driven by the urge to seize the fruit, the thief sought it and broke in.” Ibid.]

Then, taking up the prey as his sword cut it down, he himself was more truly taken as prey: he was confined within the open enclosure, and he did not escape what he had violently attempted to break through.

On the following day, held captive by his crime, he was not permitted to taste any of the fruit and, drunk, could find no way out. He could neither carry away what he had presumed to take nor lawfully remove what he coveted. When the master of the vineyard, aware of what had happened, came there at first light, he found the thief whom his own prey had already surrounded; and each guarded the other under an exchanged authority.

Then the saint’s vengeance upon the crime raged so fiercely that, tearing off the grapes with his own hand, he actually increased the thief’s gain by a lavish offering; and, rebuking his offense, he granted him a way to return.

## 5

By a similar punishment, therefore, he deserved to be struck and restrained by the continuing trap: a thief had approached his containers by night and stolen those filled with honey. He was able to deceive the guards by a cunning trick, but the reckless man did not escape with the animal he had taken.

The bees, deprived of their dwelling, left the camp with indignation. Everywhere they pursued the thief—not enriching him by their chaste labor, but attacking him with the fury of their stings—until the thief’s exposed confusion restored to the saint what he had stolen and, prostrate, found forgiveness. Nor without reason did the pious indulgence of the priest refuse to condemn the guilty man for his crime, since the very prey that avenged the offense was torturing him.

## 6

A similar mystery also occurred in connection with this treachery. As a certain traveler passed near his house with an opportunity to continue his journey, he cunningly seized a young ox and, by the crime of theft, tore the bell from its neck. Concealing the opening left in the trampled grass by his trick, he departed without being detected by anyone.

When he already thought that he had escaped either the danger of his crime or had obtained the gains he had secured through theft, the prey itself, with no obstacle preventing it,

[Note: Other manuscripts read: “with the prey preserved” or “with the prey preserved.” The same editor.]

gave forth a ringing sound, desiring to return to its master’s protection. Although it remained hidden in the most secret recesses, carefully placed or shut away behind the bolted barriers of the enclosure, its ringing circuit proclaimed the crime without any melody, and, pouring forth from its great opening, it confounded the author of the crime by a complaint repeated again and again.

Then the thief, remembering what had happened, was struck by confusion of mind and, terrified, brought back to its owner what he had taken,

[Note: Other manuscripts read: “By the zeal of mercy he did not go astray”; others: “By the zeal of mercy he did not beg for pardon.” Bolland. Compare this with the poem written by Fortunatus about the same Saint Medard, book II, chapter 20.]

which even through zeal for mercy he did not keep. Thus, once restored to the law of nature, the object began to conceal itself as an inanimate thing and revealed itself by sound only when struck.

The holy athlete of Christ, therefore, without personal guilt, was shamed for another’s offense; and for that reason he granted the guilty man a reward in place of punishment, lest he return more sorrowful through empty pride.

[Note: The Life related by Boscius in the Floriacensian Library ends here.]

## 7

[Note: This section, number 7, was lacking in the manuscripts of Maximinus. Bolland.]

On one occasion the lofty King Chlothar, preparing for war and moving the army of the Franks, had crossed a river named the Sumina,

[Note: Others read “Somme,” commonly *la Somme*, called *Somona* by the ancients. Bolland.]

and, plundering every place and all the livestock they encountered, arrived between the castle called Noyon

[Note: Perhaps Nigella, now the town of Nelle, situated midway between the two rivers? The third Life says: “between the river Oise and the city of Noyon,” as though the army had already crossed the latter; I find this less convincing. Radbod says that the event took place between Noyon and the Oise. Bolland.]

and the river Oise. Whatever vehicles there were—carts or those drawing loads, fixing their feet to the ground—they could not move them from the spot for three days.

[Note: “Vehicles,” that is, horses, in French *voitures*. Bolland.]

They came upon the most holy man at the estate of Saint Medard called Salency,

[Note: The manuscript of Noyon reads “Sacentiacum,” now Sallency, near Noyon. Bolland.]

and, after he had offered a prayer, they unloaded what they had brought

[Note: *Discaricare* means to remove a load from a cart or unload an animal. See Du Cange, *Glossary*.]

and, released, continued on their way.

## 8

Nor should the event performed by a miracle be omitted. When his swineherds were leading the pigs to feed on acorns, and the pigs had been stolen by wicked men, they were soon, through divine power, brought back alone from a distant region to the holy man, with no human being following them.

Nor should this other remarkable sign pass unnoticed. A certain man named Tosio, severely oppressed by demonic affliction, deserved to be cured by the manifest sign of the man of God.

[Col. 0538C]

## 9

But when he was already shining with many kinds of virtuous activity and his fame was spreading through various regions of the world as his grace increased, the bishop of the city of Vermandois died, and Medard was consecrated bishop in his place.

[Note: Cointius, under the year 530, section 14, says that Medard succeeded Alomerus that year in the see of Vermandois. He later transferred his see to Noyon, and shortly afterward, when Saint Eleutherius, bishop of Tournai, had died, he himself was made bishop of Tournai, with the complete agreement and acclamation of the clergy and the entire people, as well as the favor of the kings. Thus, by unanimous authority—both episcopal and royal—he made those two Churches one, as Radbod says in the Life of Saint Medard, section 19. Radbod also explains why he transferred the episcopal see from Vermandois to Noyon.

The city had been devastated by frequent barbarian raids, and a new invasion was feared. He therefore decided to transfer the see to Noyon, a safer place, sufficiently enclosed and defended both by human construction and by nature itself. That region, as Radbod describes it in section 16, is surrounded by forests and marshes and is well protected by its own configuration against hostile raids. Noyon itself lies between two streams: the Galliola flows around it on the east and the Margareta on the west; a third stream, called the Versa, receives both, and, thus joining together, they flow not far from those walls into the Oise, a river of great renown. The place itself is also so enclosed on the east and west by rocks and streams, and by mountains and the channels of valleys, that it can most conveniently be defended by a few against the greatest number of enemy attacks.]

There he was a precious priest in the holiness of his office, living a heavenly manner of life for fifteen years. Since he lacked only a bodily executioner, he fulfilled martyrdom as a confessor. He continually endured the devil’s accusations while the devil fought against him, but as a victor he reached the crown through his merits.

Then the most blessed bishop, exhausted by the long extension of his life and the structure of his limbs,

[Note: Cointius dates Saint Medard’s death to the year 545, arguing that he was neither made bishop of Vermandois after 530 nor died after 545. For, he says, the deeds performed by him before he became bishop of Tournai cannot be confined to a period shorter than two years. But Saint Eleutherius, whom Medard succeeded in the see of Tournai, died in 532. Medard therefore cannot be said to have been made bishop of Vermandois after 530. Nor can it be said that he ascended the see of Vermandois before 530, since Saint Radegund did not receive the veil from Saint Medard, bishop of Noyon, before 544, as her Life relates. Since he was bishop for fifteen years, it follows that he should be considered neither to have become bishop before 530 nor to have died after 545. This chronology seems to agree with Radbod’s account that Saint Medard was made bishop of Tournai under the most holy Remigius, archbishop of Reims, if, as Cointius holds, Remigius died in 533.]

sent forth his spirit while praying for rest, and the triumphant athlete ascended into the vaulted heavens.

Among the others, as the presbyter Willacarius also affirmed—for he had witnessed it—at the moment when Saint Medard underwent the passage from the body, the heavens were entirely opened, and for nearly three hours the divine lights stood before the saint’s little body, visible to everyone. Then a great flood flowed over the earth, so that much hot water rained from the cloud.

[Note: Other manuscripts read “Willicharius” and “Walcharius.”]

## 10

The city of Soissons deserved to receive the solemn relic of his body, through either the devotion or the timing of the most excellent Frankish prince Chlothar,

[Note: As Radbod relates in his Life, when Chlothar had come to visit him as he lay near death, and Medard had ordered that he be buried in his own church, the king earnestly asked and obtained permission from him to be buried at Soissons. He asserted that he would suitably build a basilica over his body and establish there a monastic community governed by the rule of God’s servants, for the praise and glory of the divine Majesty.]

and, enriched by the reward of so great a gift, it received him. When the faith of all peoples, in solemn eagerness, was carrying the body to burial in a most imposing bier, and their unanimity and love made the burden of bearing it seem light, a deaf man whose ears had long been closed came to meet the saint.

Kissing the cloth of precious covering, he immediately heard, in astonishment, the melody of the singers and, cleansed by faith, deserved to recover the use of his sense, which had been deprived of hearing.

## 11

After the urn of his tomb had been set up, adorned with the greatest splendor by the devotion of the faithful, it would be a lengthy task to recount by how many miracles and trophies it is exalted in answer to the cries of the afflicted, for their healing. Whatever is sought from it through poured-out prayers is obtained without delay in actual results.

A certain paralytic was laid down and cast aside before the doors of this church. The weakness of all his limbs, divided and crippled in different ways, had condemned him; yet he deserved to receive an increase of his former health and to obtain the glory of healing. Strength was immediately restored to each limb, and, with the remedy assisting, he stood unharmed. His tongue, previously attached to his palate and confusing his use of ordinary speech, now praised the power of the holy bishop with the loosened structure of his mouth.

[Note: In the third Life, chapter 24, his illness is described in these words: “With both feet bent backward, he was held as an image half-alive, so to speak, while his hands hung uselessly inactive and could neither be actively exercised for any task nor at least be made fit to be applied to his mouth.”

Here the manuscript of the island of Caesar ends. Chiffletius also possessed several manuscripts in which the prayers for the kings named shortly afterward were absent. Bolland.]

## 12

At once, as the mystery often openly triumphed, the supreme bishop granted access to the church’s shrine to those whom the unjust restraints of iron weights had bound by denying them the use of their feet. Surpassing the sturdy nature of metal, he shattered the immense chains of their fetters.

Thus the healing power indiscriminately released many persons of both sexes whom pitiable weakness of limb had crippled, restoring them to use. More frequently it also granted the protection of sight to those deprived of the light of their eyes, cleansing the darkness, and restored the benefits of renewed light to abandoned habitations.

Our account has passed over many other innumerable signs of his virtues, which grow day by day according to custom, so that the greatness of the work might not remain hidden in silence, yet such excessive length of speech might not consume the day.

## 13

[Let us therefore entreat his gracious Majesty with prayers poured forth without ceasing, that he may, in his piety, prolong the happiness of our most merciful king Theudebert, enlarged by repeated successes and extended far among foreign peoples by the just right of dominion, and that he may deign to grant eternal rest to the soul of the most merciful former king Sigibert. Sigibert, devoutly extending the spaces of the saint’s church, brought them through costly magnificence to the lofty coverings of the roof,

[Note: Concerning the basilica of Saint Medard and Sigibert’s zeal and work in completing it, see what we noted on chapter 20 of book II of Fortunatus’s works.]

so that, through the saint’s intercession, while the height of the royal diadem is preserved, the scepters of royal power may be extended, and likewise he may grant healing to the peoples and peace to all.]

[Note: In Acherius, this conclusion, taken from the Corbie and Resbac manuscripts, is somewhat longer and more suitable for annual use in churches. It reads as follows: “Let us therefore entreat his gracious Majesty with prayers poured forth without ceasing, that he may grant to all, for the forgiveness of sins, a universal protection, he who today has furnished the world with the special adornment of his solemnity. All these praises belong not merely to him who received the grace to stand before us as a worthy intercessor, but rather to the holy and inseparable Trinity, to whom belong honor and power, might and dominion, praise and rejoicing, in every nation, place, and time, throughout the infinite ages of ages.”]

May he also grant to all, for the forgiveness of sins, the universal protection that they ask, he who today has provided the world with the special ornament of his solemnity.

# LIFE OF SAINT MARCELLUS

[Col. 0541]

## Preliminary Notice on the Life of Saint Marcellus, Bishop of Paris

Whether Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, actually wrote the following Life of Saint Marcellus, bishop of Paris, learned men disagree among themselves.

The authors of the *History of French Literature* deny it to our Fortunatus and attribute it to another Fortunatus of Vercelli, about whom we have spoken in the preface to the Life of Saint Hilary. They are led to this view by the following indications or conjectures:

1. The Lives of the saints written by Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, call him only a presbyter, not a bishop; and whenever they call him a bishop, they add the name of the Church over which he presided.

2. The style in which the Life of Saint Marcellus was written seems simpler and more concise than Fortunatus’s style.

3. This Life was written many years before Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, died; and therefore not long after Fortunatus had come to Gaul, when he had not yet applied himself to writing the deeds of the saints. For he seems to have taken up the collection and recording of the saints’ deeds only later, after previously devoting himself more intensely to poetry.

Finally, when Gregory of Tours mentions this Life in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 89, he does not name its author, although it was customary for him to attribute the name of his intimate friend Fortunatus whenever he mentioned one of his works. Thus, when he mentions the Lives of Saint Severinus, bishop of Bordeaux; Saint Albinus of Angers; and Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, it is always found that he adds the name of Fortunatus to them.

Others, however, hold the opposite view: among them Adrian Valesius, in his dissertation against Launoy; Vossius, book II of *On Latin Historians*, chapter 22; Labbeus, volume II of *Ecclesiastical Writers*; Johann Albert Fabricius, in his *Latin Library of the Middle and Lower Ages*; Johann Molanus, in the *Martyrology of Usuard*; Caesar Baronius, in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology*; and others. They confirm that this is Fortunatus’s own genuine work.

For my part, I will state what I think. The reasons and conjectures that led the authors of the *History of French Literature* cited above to deny the Life of Saint Marcellus to our Fortunatus do not seem weighty enough for us to judge that the matter is as they maintain.

First, it makes little difference whether the person who prefixed the title to this Life called Fortunatus a presbyter or also a bishop. Otherwise, on the basis of a similar error and variation, several other works—genuine works of Fortunatus—could be called into question or even rejected, since they call Fortunatus at one time a presbyter and at another a bishop. It would be no more difficult for the title “bishop” to have been substituted for “presbyter,” especially since elsewhere it was known that he had been a bishop, while the name of the Church over which he presided had been omitted through the negligence or ignorance of copyists.

Certainly, the ancient Codex that Mabillon had in his possession gave the title of the Life of Saint Paternus—whose authorship by Fortunatus hardly anyone would deny—in this form: “Here begins the prologue of Fortunatus, bishop, on the Life of Saint Paternus,” and so forth.

Second, the style does not seem foreign to Fortunatus’s style, as anyone who reads the Prologue attentively will especially recognize. Although the different periods in which Fortunatus wrote the Lives of the saints could have produced some variation in style.

As for the claim that Fortunatus took up the task of committing the saints’ deeds to writing only late, did he not also write the Life of Saint Germanus, apparently not long after Germanus’s death, which Gregory of Tours mentions in book V of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 8? Why, then, could he not, while Germanus was still alive, compose at his request the Life of Saint Marcellus, bishop of Paris?

Finally, Gregory of Tours does not always add Fortunatus’s name whenever he mentions his works, as we have shown in its proper place concerning the Lives of Saint Hilary and Saint Remigius.

The close friendship and intimacy between Fortunatus and Germanus, together with the poems and letters that Fortunatus wrote to Germanus, scarcely leave room for doubt that, at Germanus’s urging, Fortunatus composed and published this Life of Saint Marcellus, his predecessor.

If you compare the Prologue of the Life with the letter customarily prefixed to Fortunatus’s works—considering the very title, the order of the sentences, the breadth and structure of the words, and that constant habit of Fortunatus in diminishing his own praises—you will understand how closely the two correspond.

Indeed, throughout the Life you will find expressions and figures of speech familiar to Fortunatus, as well as an almost uniquely characteristic sequence in the narration of miracles; this will become clear to anyone who compares it with the other Lives written by him.

Further support is supplied by what is read in ancient parchment manuscripts, according to Valesius. Where certain copies and Surius read in the Prologue:

“Why then, as has been said, should such bleary poverty presume to walk on a flat foot among the Gallic buskins?”

the manuscripts read:

“Why then, as has been said, should the Italian Patavinity [corrected: Italian Patavitality] presume to walk on a flat foot among the Gallic buskins?”

These words clearly indicate Fortunatus’s homeland, which was not far from Padua. I therefore incline strongly to the opinion that this Life should by no means be denied to our Fortunatus, and consequently should not be attributed to the other Fortunatus of Vercelli, about whom four manuscripts of the Martyrology of the Church of Paris speak under 18 June, as reported by Father Gerard Dubois in *History of the Church of Paris*, book I, chapter 8.

We publish it as it appears in Surius under 1 November.

[Col. 0541]

# LIFE OF SAINT MARCELLUS, BISHOP OF PARIS

## Preface of the Author to Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris

[Col. 0541A]

### 1

To the holy Lord, an apostolic man possessing the merits of that office, established in the love of Christ, to be placed before my own light, my lord and sweet father, Pope Germanus: Fortunatus sends greetings.

The most eloquent talents of distinguished orators, adorned with the varying flowers of speech and shaded by the flourishing tendrils of eloquence, customarily seek out humble subjects and barren material, so that, by saying great things about small matters, they may appear to display the abundance of their stream. Since they possess within themselves springs of eloquence, they have learned to draw forth waves even from a dry theme. Whatever is assigned to them is therefore explained with abundant, irrigating poetry.

By contrast, those who are scorched by the dryness of a narrow understanding and do not possess the overflowing abundance of eloquence with which they might refresh others or temper their own barrenness not only do not desire to say anything on their own, but even recoil if anything is assigned to them, since what it is useful for the learned to utter is equally useful for the unlearned to keep silent.

The former know how to speak at length about small matters; the latter do not know how to say even a little about great ones. Therefore what some seek, others fear.

So a warrior in arms considers it a loss if he cannot find an opponent whom he can defeat intact. But just as the strong man seeks the means by which he may carry off spoils, so the weak man fears being led away as prey; and what the bold man desires to discover, the sluggish man fears even to hear.

### 2

Since I must appropriately accuse myself of such barrenness of knowledge, and since there is nothing in me to commend the adornments of elegant speech, I am continually amazed, most blessed and loving Father, that you should entrust to my spark something worthy of that heavenly lamp, from the life of the most holy bishop Marcellus—a life that can be enclosed by no ending.

I am poor in talent, while he is rich in merit; I am humble in speech, while he is distinguished in reward. This is especially so since the famous abundance of many wise men supplies you with sufficient eloquence, Gallic speech following Gallic speech, and words weighed out in balanced constructions.

If they wish, they can paint in words whatever the mind has imagined. Among them, speaking itself is dictation, and what can scarcely be conceived in the heart is immediately formed into a written work on the page.

Why then, as has been said, should such bleary poverty presume to walk on a flat foot among the Gallic buskins, when, in comparison with them, our tongue’s poor wild hyacinth breathes as though among roses and lilies?

Another difficulty is added to the problem of an impeded talent: much about the deeds of blessed Marcellus has been lost and must be sought out, stolen away by the antiquity of time; nor does memory easily recall what the multitude of years has deprived us of. For whatever is not fixed in books is carried away by the wind of oblivion.

A few accounts of his blessed deeds have indeed survived to our times through living report, lest everything that his admirers might seek in the future should perish altogether. Although his holy limbs were buried long ago in the tomb, his miracles were not buried with them. They are all the more renowned because they have deserved to live in memory without being written down; for although they were not held on a page, they are fixed upon the membrane of the heart.

### 3

Amid these difficulties, therefore, I do not know where to turn, whether even to prepare my fingers for writing, when my tongue fears to dictate. Yet what the Father commands may not be postponed, since the person who resists you must fight more against himself; especially when, in order to teach me obedience, you willingly impose what I cannot bear.

Devotion is proved most fully in a difficult matter. Affection is complete precisely where, although strength cannot endure, the spirit does not refuse; and here I venerate all the more what charity does not lightly demand but boldly extorts.

Indeed, it is fitting for me to complete the work on this account, since the person who criticizes lesser things hastens to lead us toward greater ones.

After these considerations, I had wished this work to shine through another’s tongue rather than become sullied through mine. But let what the first put off be carried through by the last; what seems displeasing in eloquence appears pleasing through its intention.

# LIFE

### 4

The most blessed bishop Marcellus, therefore, was born at Paris but was a citizen of paradise; humble on earth, exalted in heaven; of modest parents, but lofty in merits.

[Note: Saint Marcellus, born at Lutetia of the Parisii, succeeded Prudentius in the see of Paris. Although nothing certain can be established about the time of his episcopate, Father Gerard Dubois conjectures, in the place cited above, that it fell during the reign of the elder Theodosius, so that Saint Marcellus was a contemporary of Saint Martin of Tours.]

The distinguishing light of his nobility was this: to serve Christ without fault. He did not swell with pride in his ancestry, but possessed the adornments of character. He did not derive boastfulness from his parents’ renown, but possessed grace as an example of virtue, retaining his treasures within himself and embracing God with a pure heart.

This poor man reigned with Christ. In humble conduct, in abundant charity, in the radiance of chastity, and in the richness of fasting, he surrendered himself entirely to heavenly discipline, so that he approached maturity from infancy and, though placed in a body, seemed to carry almost nothing of the flesh.

Thus girded with the noblest instruction and almost a priest before he was a cleric through his venerable works, he was already worthy to receive office and prepared beforehand for what he would soon become without delay. Having trampled underfoot the pomp and crimes of the world, and having been initiated into the divine arms and girded for the blessed hope of carrying away the palm from the public enemy, he became a reader through training in the service of Christ,

[Corr.: Perhaps *exercitanda*, “the service that was to be exercised.”]

and, first offering himself to Christ’s temple like Abel’s sacrifice, he was accepted as a victim of conquered flesh and a pure mind.

### 5

He who was more renowned for his reward than for his name, and greater in merit than in rank, carrying out his office without causing offense, began to grow in the military service he had received from the king. His virtues, long hidden, began to bear fruit like branches of a vine. Nor did he allow his gifts to remain concealed in him, since he so humbly embraced what he saw had come from above.

Finally, while he was concealed beneath the training of the clerical life, he was revealed by miracles and illumined by heavenly signs. Once he came to a blacksmith’s workshop. The craftsman, despising him, compelled him to lift with his own hand a glowing mass of iron drawn from the blazing furnace and to declare how much it weighed. Then the most blessed man, knowing that he must place his entire trust in Christ, and how great a cause of virtue it is to obey in matters that are not shameful, immediately placed his hand beneath the iron and lifted it higher, saying: “It is hot from the heat, but it weighs nine pounds.” Afterwards it was found on the scales to weigh exactly what his balanced utterance had foretold.

Thus, in one occurrence, he displayed a twofold miracle: the furnace’s heat did not burn him, and the weight of the iron did not deceive him. For, since the vapor of lust had no place in him after his vices had been purged, he freely escaped the fires of the furnace without being burned. In order to conquer the fire of the element, he had first extinguished the flames of the flesh; and, so that he might not err in the weighing itself, he proved the iron by its weight.

### 6

Next he was made a subdeacon in the religious order. While he was carrying out the ministry of a subdeacon, on the day of the Epiphany, he drew water from the river Seine and offered it to blessed Bishop Prudentius for washing his hands. The elements having been changed, the taste of wine was found in it.

When the bishop saw this, he was astonished and ordered that the contents of the very pitcher be poured into a sacred chalice. After Mass had been celebrated, the entire people received communion from it; and although the vessel had sufficed for the multitude of the congregation, it remained full, as though it had not been touched and were still intact. Through the mystical benefit of this wine, many sick people were afterwards healed.

[Note: The Seine is the best-known river of Gaul, flowing past Paris. Fortunatus mentions it elsewhere, writing to the deacon Dructo, Book III, chapter 33:

> The swelling sea of Ocean flows around us.
>
> You too, dear companion, are held by Paris:
>
> The Seine retains you, while the British wave encircles us, etc.]

Behold the most holy man: taking water from the river, he poured wine into the chalice. [Note: Perhaps read: “that while he carried water …”]

But whence such new miracles? Whence, while he carried water, did he somehow seem to press out grapes, so that a vine-shoot was born for him in his hand? Truly blessed Marcellus, worthy of the highest veneration! In whose hands, at one and the same moment, the vintage blossomed and wine was pressed.

We see that divine benefits are not confined to one place, since what the Lord did earlier in Galilee, this man accomplished afterwards in Gaul. There Christ changed water into wine at a wedding feast (John 2); here the altar received new wine sufficient for the table of Christ. The former preceded the latter in time, the latter followed it in honor. For then six jars supplied what was given; here one small vessel was filled. But then Christ brought about the sign so that the Lord might reveal himself, whereas here he did so that he might not conceal his servant. [The word “these” may perhaps be added.]

### 7

Let us come to that other miracle, second in order but not in honor. Once, while the most holy man was performing the service of his office and had offered water for the hands of the venerable bishop, balsams immediately began to give off their fragrance. As the water flowed, the chrism seemed to breathe forth its perfume, so that the bishop almost believed that he was anointing his hands rather than washing them, and sought other water with which to wash away the earlier water.

When he saw this, the venerable priest was astonished and returned thanks to God for the gift he had discovered. He also preserved reverence for blessed Marcellus in his religious devotion, recognizing that Marcellus was not merely one who served, but rather one whom others ought to serve.

Who, then, could sufficiently admire such a subdeacon, in whose right hand water became wine and balsam, and the pallor of the water was changed either into redness or into fragrance? Even then, by these signs, it was prefigured that he would become a bishop worthy to handle chrism. But since, while still a subdeacon, he had drawn chrism from the river, he was rightly worthy, once made a priest, to offer this sacrifice at the font.

### 8

That other mystery must not be passed over in silence which benefits the hearer, because, among the few things recalled by memory, whatever is not told is thought either to have been begrudged or to have been despised.

There was therefore a certain cleric named Mintucius, about ten years old. Because of the little bell of his exceptionally sweet voice and the musical sweetness issuing from his throat—since it happened that the repeated sound delighted the people and was accustomed to please their ears—the archdeacon ordered him to sing with honeyed tenderness.

When this had been done, the bishop ordered the boy to be flogged because he had himself ordered someone else to sing. Thus, while the cleric was beaten, the bishop was condemned in his tongue. For as soon as the cry of the one being beaten sounded in his ear, the bishop’s voice departed from his mouth, and the child’s voice, like a new robber, captured the bishop’s sound.

But if the reason for what happened is sought, it can be found. The man who had forbidden the boy to sing suffered the loss of his own voice because he begrudged the voices of others. Who, then, is not harmed by envy, if vengeance did not spare even a bishop?

[Note: The manuscript reads:

> Therefore whoever does not wish to see something in another will not have it; indeed, he loses for himself what he does not wish others to possess.]

Therefore, whoever does not wish to see something in another will not have it; indeed, he loses for himself what he does not wish others to possess. Everyone who prepares a fall for another has already fallen himself; before he leads someone into a snare, he is himself held captive and bound by the sin that captures him.

This is especially true if we wish to make progress: let us believe that the progress of others is our own. Thus for three days the priest, although he walked through the crossroads, nevertheless lay with his tongue buried. No sound could echo from the chamber of his struck palate, nor could a voice be arranged within the enclosure of his teeth by the revolving tongue; rather, with a mute mouth he expressed everything he had lost.

[Note: Fortunatus uses the same manner of speaking in the Life of Saint Hilary, book 2, no. 10, and in book 4 of the Life of Saint Martin. Consult the notes made on the Life of Saint Hilary at the cited place.]

Then blessed Marcellus addressed the bishop in these words:

“Although I understand, good shepherd, that such a misfortune has come upon you because of your fault, nevertheless, whatever you wish, burst forth in speech in the name of the Lord.”

After these words, while the speech of blessed Marcellus was still moving through his mouth, what he had commanded was already obeyed. Before Marcellus had finished speaking, the other replied:
