“You have done this to me, you whose command was that someone else should sing rather than the one I had ordered.”

As he spoke, the grace of the lost voice was restored. O merit of the subdeacon, who restored a voice to a priest and, in reverse, granted what he himself ought to have received; who armed a weakened throat with eloquence and poured words into another’s mouth through a word!

Why should I prolong the account? The bishop would always have remained silent if Marcellus had never questioned him. Truly worthy was the speech of blessed Marcellus to govern the Lord’s flock, since he gave salvation to the shepherd.

### 9

We believe it worthwhile also to weave into these pages that which is fixed deeply in the hearts of many. For although there is fear in recounting a terrible matter, there should be profit in its instruction.

When blessed Marcellus had been ordained bishop—a dignity that he had always regarded more as a burden than as an honor—one of the people wished to approach communion. His hands were bound behind him, and he could not reach the altar. Yet when he had passed through everyone, he began to stand still as though at a boundary-marker, so that he seemed to have come not to receive communion but to count the people.

When the bishop saw him, he asked what he had done. He replied that he had sinned.

[Note: Although the author of the Life says nothing here either about the power of the keys by which Saint Marcellus absolved the guilty man, or about the severe works of penance that he imposed in accordance with the Church’s perpetual discipline, he seems to have included all this generally in the words “Recognizing his confession.” Thus it should not be said that he released him beforehand and invited him to share in the Eucharistic table before learning what crimes bound him and what was the condition of his soul—whether he heard his confession publicly or privately.

Pauline, author of the Life of Ambrose, reports something similar:

> “Whenever someone who had fallen came to him to receive penance and confessed his sins, he wept in such a way that he compelled that person also to weep. The causes of the crimes confessed to him he spoke of to no one except the Lord alone, before whom he interceded—leaving a good example for priests who would come after him, that they should be intercessors before God rather than accusers before men. For, according to the Apostle, charity must be confirmed toward such a person, because he is his own accuser and does not await an accuser, but anticipates him; by confessing, he himself lightens his offense and leaves his adversary nothing to allege.

> “As he adds afterwards, confession alone is not enough for the penitent unless correction of conduct follows, so that the penitent does not do what must be repented of. He must also humble his soul, like holy David, who, after hearing from the prophet, ‘Your sin is forgiven,’ became more humble in correcting his sin, so that he ate ashes like bread and mingled his drink with weeping.”

Certainly, it can sufficiently be understood from this that the guilty man of whom Fortunatus speaks here recognized in blessed Marcellus the power of the keys as something necessary for himself: publicly declaring himself bound by his crime, he voluntarily presented himself to his bishop with his hands tied, so that he might be released.]

Recognizing his confession, Marcellus said to him:

“Come, draw near, and sin no more.”

Released by this command, he approached communion, endowed with a twofold benefit: he obtained forgiveness for his past fault and correction for his future life. How great was his confidence in the equality of the Holy Trinity, whose free mind uttered miracles through each word! Yet although it was enough to dissolve the chains of the bound man by speech, it is still more praiseworthy that he appeared to forgive sins in the love of Christ.

### 10

Let us also relate that triumphant mystery which, although last in order, is placed first in power.

A certain matron, noble by ancestry but vile in reputation, had stained with an evil crime the glory she possessed by birth. When she had brought to an end the days of her fleeting life, having been carried away with its light, she was taken to the tomb with a funeral procession that brought her no benefit.

When she had been buried there—I shudder to report what happened after the funeral—a twofold lamentation arose over the dead woman. A huge serpent began to frequent the place in order to consume her corpse; or, to speak more plainly, the dragon itself became the woman’s tomb, devouring her limbs. Thus the serpentine bearer inflicted a miserable funeral upon her, so that the corpse was not permitted to rest after death. She to whom the end of life had granted lying in one place was continually changed into punishment.

O accursed and greatly fearful misfortune! The woman who had not preserved the integrity of marriage in the world did not deserve to lie intact in the grave. The serpent that had drawn her living self into crime still raged against her corpse.

Then members of her family who remained in the city heard the noise and came running together. They saw an enormous beast emerging from the winding recesses of the tombs and gliding away, beating the corpse with its enormous bulk. Terrified beyond measure, the people moved away from their homes.

When blessed Marcellus learned of this, understanding that he could gain a triumph over the enemy, he gathered the people and went out from the city. Leaving the citizens behind, he alone, in full view of the people and with Christ as his guide, approached the place to fight.

When the serpent returned from the forest to the tomb, the two came face to face. As blessed Marcellus offered prayer, the serpent began with bowed head to beg pardon, coaxing him with its tail.

Then blessed Marcellus struck its head three times with his staff and, having cast an orarium—a cloth, or possibly a priestly stole—around the serpent’s neck—

[Note: Orarium is understood as a sudarium or small linen cloth with which the mouth is wiped. Saint Jerome uses the word in his letter to Nepotianus, as do Saint Ambrose and others, who may be consulted in Du Cange’s Glossary. Orarium also means a priest’s stole; see Du Cange there as well.]

—he led away his triumph before the eyes of the citizens. Thus, in the spiritual theater, while the people watched, he alone fought with the dragon.

The people, encouraged by this, ran to the bishop, wishing to see their enemy captive. Then, with the bishop leading, nearly three thousand people followed the beast, giving thanks to the Lord and performing the funeral rites of their enemy.

Afterwards blessed Marcellus rebuked it, saying:

“From this day forward, either keep to the wilderness or plunge yourself into the sea.”

The beast was immediately released, and no further trace of it was found.

Behold the defense of the homeland resting in a single priest! With a fragile staff he subdued the enemy more powerfully than if ballistae had passed over it. It could have turned back arrows, had not the divine power prevailed.

O most holy man, in whose light staff the weight of virtue was displayed, whose gentle fingers became a chain for the serpent! Thus private weapons overcame the public enemy; a general victory applauds the spoils of one man.

If the merits of holy men are compared by their deeds, let Gaul marvel at Marcellus as Rome does at Sylvester—unless there is this difference in their works: Sylvester sealed the dragon away, while Marcellus drove it out.

[Note: Concerning this dragon, which killed many by its poisonous breath and was shut up in a cavern by blessed Sylvester, see the Life of that same saint, composed by Symeon Metaphrastes, chapter 8. It appears in Surius under the last day of December.]

But who could encompass in words each of his miracles, or express in speech how many he performed and concealed, when only those deeds are written down which, witnessed by the people, became famous?

[Note: This Life of Saint Marcellus seems to have been composed by Fortunatus so that it might be recited in the Church of Paris during the sacred offices, just as we have said in its proper place concerning the abridged Life of Saint Remigius composed by the same author.]

Engaged continually in these works, the most holy Marcellus, illustrious in his manner of life, preeminent in his consummation, glorious in blessedness, enriched by his reward, and destined to reign perpetually with the Lord, overcame the world’s contagion and departed pure to Christ on the Kalends of November, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned. To him be honor and glory, might and power throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# Life of Saint Leobinus

## Preliminary Notice on the Life of Saint Leobinus, Bishop of Chartres

Launoy, Valesius, and others attribute the Life of Saint Leobinus, bishop of Chartres, to Fortunatus; the authors of the *History of French Literature* and others generally deny that he wrote it. Labbe asserts that it is by an unknown author.

The style in which this Life was composed does not seem entirely unlike the style of our Fortunatus, but no other argument is available by which we may attribute it to Fortunatus. If he arranged it, perhaps he composed it at the request of Pappolus, bishop of Chartres, who governed that church from the year 567 to the year 594. In the same way, he seems to have composed the Life of Saint Amantius, bishop of Rodez, at the request of the bishop of that church, as we observed in the notes to that work.

It also seems to have been composed so that it might be read annually in the church on the feast day of Saint Leobinus; this appears from the final chapter. We publish it as it appears in the first Benedictine century, page 123, adorned with notes by the distinguished Mabillon, to which we have added others that seemed capable of contributing something to its elucidation.

# Life of Saint Leobinus, Bishop of Chartres (C, S)

### 1

Therefore the most blessed Leobinus [Saint Lubin], a native of the city of Poitiers, was born of worthy parents.

[Note: Saint Leobinus succeeded Aetherius in the see of Chartres in 544 (as Cointius shows for that year, no. 91) and died in 555, according to the same Cointius.] He submitted himself to them with such devoted humility that, although placed in the earliest years of childhood, he was already said to have been approved by his merits.

As a youth he flourished in good character. The love of learning letters occupied his heart, and, surrounded as though by a heavenly cloud through the grace of the Holy Spirit, while he was tending cattle in the pastures he happened to meet the monk Noidgelinus and begged him to write out letters for him to learn.

Since the monk had no book or writing tablets available, he wrote letters on the boy’s belt as best he could. We believe that this was accomplished as a foreshadowing through the mystery of divine goodness: he who was destined to benefit many as an example of chastity would himself, surrounded by the belt of celibacy and fragrant like a lily of purity, wear around his loins a belt inscribed with the letters of truth.

Afterwards, when his father discovered this eagerness to learn in his son, he decided that lines of writing should be made on tablets. From then on Leobinus’ zeal advanced so greatly that he did both activities at once: he devoted himself to labor and applied himself to reading, carefully dividing his service between the demands of cultivation and study.

These two activities foreshadowed his future: through agricultural work he was shown to be a monk who would be energetic in obedience, and through his zeal for learning he was prepared to become a bishop, destined to sow the seeds of the divine word in the hearts of the faithful, furrowed by the plowshare of discipline.

### 2

Not long afterwards, having been somewhat illumined by the distinction of knowledge, he was piously received into a certain monastery. His head was tonsured and he was made a monk. Through the humility of obedience, the office of cellarer was entrusted to him, and he was charged with regulating the course of the hours and maintaining vigilance.

Occupied with this work, he discovered that he could not devote the daytime to reading. Therefore, when the monks withdrew to sleep, he stayed awake through the night with intense attention, so that he might learn the rule of justice.

When he realized that his constant reading was burdensome to the brothers, and did not wish their murmuring to turn into an uproar, he placed a curtain before the window that was open to the brothers’ eyes, making the light somewhat dim for them while allowing himself to advance in reading.

### 3

A certain distinguished deacon named Nileffus—

[Note: Labbe suspects that *Carilephus* should be read instead of *Nileffus*. But Cointius objects, saying that the Acts of Carilephus relate that he withdrew with Saint Avitus to the monastery of Micy, while Maximin was still governing that monastery as abbot—that is, many years before Leobinus went to Avitus at Segalo.]

—learning that Leobinus wished to visit blessed Avitus—

[Note: This seems to be the same Avitus of whom Gregory of Tours writes in Book on the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 99: “Avitus, abbot of the Chartres district called Pertensis, foretold, after the Holy Spirit had revealed it, that the dissolution of his body was often at hand,” and so forth.

Cointius, under the year 520, thinks that this Avitus was the man of whom Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book III, chapter 6, relates that he was still governing the monastery of Micy when Clodomir, king of the Franks, fought against Godomar, king of Burgundy, in an unsuccessful battle in the year 524; for he was killed by treachery.

Cointius admits, however, that this cannot readily be reconciled with what is related here about Avitus in the Life of Saint Leobinus, since at the very time when that war between the Franks and Burgundians was being waged, Avitus does not seem to have departed from the wilderness of Pertensis.

But the distinguished Mabillon, in the first Benedictine century, page 613, following Baronius, holds that two Avituses, monks of the monastery of Micy, must be distinguished: one a priest and hermit who later became abbot of Pertensis or Perticensis; the other the abbot of the monastery of Micy. What is mentioned here concerning Avitus, abbot of Pertensis, adds weight to Mabillon’s opinion. Consult Mabillon at the cited passage, where he confirms his view from the Martyrology of Ado.]

—who at that time lived as a hermit in the Perche, addressed him in gentle speech:

“I recognize, brother, that you wish to ascend from small things to greater ones. But, for your advancement, I shall instruct you in the purpose of learning that you have undertaken with three words.

“First, do not bind yourself to the services of any bishop, because, among the good, you will find many detractors.

“Second, I warn you not to govern the basilica of just anyone, whether you seek such an office or accept it when it is sought for you. Otherwise, amid differing customs, you will either lose the strictness of a monk, or, if you do not yield to flattering words, you will scarcely endure those who criticize you.

“Third, I warn you not to join yourself to a small cell, because, while individuals seek to place themselves over one another, obedience is rendered to no one.”

### 4

After he had lived the monastic life in that cell for eight years, he presented himself in his desire to seek the presence of the most blessed Avitus. Avitus replied that, after receiving the education he was to acquire in the community of monks, he should return to him.

Departing from there with a certain deacon who had spent some time in the monastery, Leobinus began to travel along the banks of the Loire. When he reached a certain cell that had been offered to him as a place of residence, he remembered the warnings mentioned above and refused to bind himself to that place.

Wishing to reach Lérins, he encountered a certain Lérins brother who said that he could not endure the hardship of the climate there. At these words Leobinus turned back from the journey he had begun.

Then, seeking the city of Gévaudan, he was received with priestly hospitality by blessed Hilary, bishop of that city—

[Note: Labbe calls him Hilarius rather than Hilarus. He was bishop of Gévaudan and subscribed to the First Council of Clermont, held in the year 535, according to Cointius under that year, no. 28.]

—and remained with him for some time. The brother began to complain that the place was not suitable for him to live in.

When blessed Hilary noticed these brothers arguing among themselves, he began to urge that restless and wandering brother not to leave the company of blessed Leobinus, lest by departing he lose the grace of obedience that he had gained by following him until then.

After they had departed from there and heard that the fame of blessed Lupus was spreading far and wide, they humbly went to him.

[Note: That is, Lupus, the anchorite of the Island of Barbe—so called because the monks of that monastery lived in separate cells in the manner of hermits—who later became archbishop of Lyon. The Island of Barbe, or L’Île-Barbe, is a very ancient Benedictine monastery in the territory of Lyon, situated in the middle of the Saône. In 1549 it was granted secular status. See Mabillon. Concerning this Lupus, see more in Cointius under the year 521, no. 2.

He governed the church of Lyon in 534, when Lyon, the Island of Barbe, and other Burgundian regions came under the power of the Franks.]

After they had stayed with him for a short time, the aforementioned brother, being unstable and wandering, urged blessed Leobinus to depart from there.

The holy man did not wish to yield to such persuasion. Resisting firmly, and refusing to keep so wandering a brother in his company, he remained in the same monastery for five continuous years.

### 5

Meanwhile, while the fierce violence of the Franks was stirring up wars against the Burgundians, and the monks of that cell were fleeing here and there out of fear of them—

[Note: At the passage cited above, Cointius assigns this flight of the monks from the Island of Barbe to the year 524, when Clodomir, king of the Franks, fought the Burgundians near Vienne.]

—the saint remained there fearlessly with another old man.

The barbarians questioned that other elder, demanding that he disclose all the monastery’s property. He replied that blessed Leobinus knew all those things, whereas he himself had no knowledge of them.

Thus, after that first elder had been released from interrogation by this excuse, the barbarians began to address the man of God gently, asking him to reveal immediately whatever he knew about those possessions.

When they could discover nothing of what they sought through their flattering words, they attempted to impose many kinds of punishment on him. They bound his forehead tightly with cords, fastened his feet in stocks, and repeatedly submerged him in deep water. Yet, just as they had been unable to extract anything from him by flattery, so they could not do so by torture.

Saint Leobinus, steadfastly enduring between the two forms of trial, preferred to bear the punishments of the wicked rather than reveal the secrets of the monks.

### 6

After he had been miserably afflicted by these punishments, although half dead, he was rescued by divine assistance. With two brothers, Eufronius and Rusticus, he again went to Saint Avitus, who was living in the vast wilderness of the Perche.

Avitus received them with fraternal charity and assigned the two brothers to suitable duties. When he perceived that the mind of the holy man shone more abundantly with heavenly goodness, he appointed him to the office of cellarer.

In administering this ministry, Leobinus proved so prudent that he gave nothing excessive to one who demanded more than was due, nor withheld suitable nourishment from one in need. Blessed Avitus had found his service so pleasing that, although his body was weakened by fasting and worn down by old age, he would accept no food to restore his strength except what blessed Leobinus had prepared through his own care.

### 7

It happened that, when the Lord rewarded the solitary labor of blessed Avitus with a heavenly recompense, removed him from earthly impediments, and enrolled him among the company of his saints, blessed Leobinus decided to settle with the two brothers mentioned above in a place called Carbonaria.

For some time the three competed in fulfilling the divine office in three cells they had built. When the two brothers departed, Leobinus remained there for five years, sustained by the labor of his hands, a cup of water, and meager food alone.

When summer came, the produce of the fields was ready and the ripe grain had to be threshed and stored in the granaries. Suddenly a storm arose in the air, breaking the tops of the trees and flattening the crops, so that everything seemed to have been reduced utterly to ruin.

Moved by the danger of so great a calamity, the man of God armed himself against the storm-cloud with heavenly weapons—that is, with prayers—and opposed to it the oil of sacred blessing. He caused not only the lightning and thunder that were stirring up the storm to fall silent and the shaken air to return to its former calm, but also caused everything owed for the cell’s support to be brought in full.

The spectacle of that miracle, performed by the holy man, must be preserved in memory for the praise of God.

### 8

While Bishop Aetherius—

[Note: Aetherius, bishop of Chartres, subscribed to the Second Council of Orléans in 533, the Third in 538, and the Fourth in 541.]

—was summoning blessed Leobinus to come to him at Brou—

[Note: Cointius states that Saint Leobinus was summoned to Brou by Saint Aetherius, bishop of Chartres, and was placed in charge of the monastery of Brou in the year 535.]

—it happened that a voracious fire found everything near his cell that lay in its path ready to be burned, sparing nothing and leaving nothing untouched.

The monks were entirely unable to restrain the heat of so great a fire by throwing water upon it; indeed, it seemed that they were only feeding the flames. But the man of God, Leobinus, through his prayers and tears—waters more powerful—caused the globes of flame, invoking the name of Christ, to be completely quieted.

### 9

The notable fame of that miracle also deserves to be entrusted to memory.

At the same time, the aforementioned Bishop Aetherius, observing the holiness of the holy man Leobinus, advanced him to the office of deacon and placed him over the brothers of the monastery of Brou. He considered it fitting that Leobinus should perform the office of prefect more effectively if he were duly elevated to the burden of the priesthood.

Later, when the flame of a raging fire had burned through forests and fields and reached the monastery, burning the crops, the monks rose from the table in fear. The holy man prostrated himself in prayer before the fire and merited from the God of heaven that all the fury of the blaze should be subdued and fall silent, and that the former calm of the air should return and bring relief.

### 10

That heavenly miracle should also be inserted into this work, which the Lord deigned to perform through blessed Leobinus.

At one time two possessed men, in whom the force of demons had grown so strong that they often shattered bonds and chains, encountered the most blessed man and humbly begged him to grant them the remedy of health.

The holy man, therefore, urged by the brothers to extend the grace of healing to those driven by demonic madness, was moved by compassion. Making the sign of the cross, he expelled the demons from them and effectively restored them to the safety of their former health.

Not long afterwards, while he was far from his cell and turned aside by a shorter road to a monastery where a few girls lived, he was kindly received by them.

After the service of hospitality had been most willingly shown to him, in the silence of the dead of night one of the girls, driven by the heat of a wicked lust, deceitfully brought her teeth against the feet of the sleeping saint beneath the bed covering.

When he felt himself touched by such a bite, he repelled her from his feet with a beating of his breast and a great groan. He escaped the woman’s snares like deadly poison, preserving the full integrity of his body and girded with the sash of chastity.

### 11

Thus, rescued from this temptation with God as his protector, it happened that he who had been a physician to the infirmities of others was himself struck by a cancerous wound in the nostrils.

When the monks begged him to heal himself by some human treatment, he trusted in the eternal Physician, who cures all things by a single word. For nearly twelve years he applied blessed wax to the discharge of the same disease, so that his virtue might increase through divine grace in the midst of infirmity.

Thus, remaining always in God’s service and giving thanks to God in all things, he later merited to recover the health of his nostrils without the help of any human aid.

### 12

That astonishing miracle of an accomplished deed must also be brought forward, since it can benefit all by strengthening faith.

One of the monks, named Tyrannus—a cruel name by contrast with his character, but illustrious in virtue—was keeping anxious and vigilant watch one night when a voice was directed to him announcing that the appointed signal had already sounded.

Warned by this voice, he rose at once and entered the basilica, which shone with the radiance of spreading light. There he saw two conspicuous men of splendid appearance, namely Saint Leobinus and another whose name he did not know.

Overcome with great fear at the sight, he fled and hid himself in his cell.

When, at the sound of the signal, he had gone to the aforesaid basilica for the hymns of Matins, and had completed the customary prayer, Tyrannus, now cautious and devout, went to Lord Leobinus and begged him to tell him who the person was whom he had seen in the basilica together with him.

The man of God recognized that the brother had been considered worthy of such a devotional miracle and said:

“Brother, when you entered the oratory and saw two men together, you recognized me, as I hear. But the other, whom you did not know, white with shining radiance, was blessed Avitus. He deigned to visit me in order to correct and warn me how I ought to correct a certain brother for his offenses.

“Rightly, then, did heavenly light shine upon the holy man, because, although he was bodily on earth, in mind he lived in heaven, according to the Apostle: ‘Our citizenship is in heaven’ (Philippians 3:20).

“Thus he deserved both a visitation and consolation; for in his heart and mouth, through the utterances of the divine commandments, the heavenly light of grace continually and ineffably shone.”

### 13

Not long afterwards, blessed Bishop Aetherius charged him that, for the purpose of advancing toward what was better, he should seek out and fearlessly visit Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

When Saint Leobinus reached him, together with blessed Albinus, who had been his companion on the journey, blessed Caesarius asked why he had undertaken the labor of so long a journey.

Blessed Albinus replied that he had come solely because of his own desire. But blessed Leobinus, having left the brothers over whom he had been placed—

[Note: The passage is corrupt.]

—was hastening to Lérins, where, having abandoned the brothers of that monastery, he was to be subjected to them, and, once he arrived there, desired to be subject to all the brothers.

Then Saint Caesarius rebuked him and ordered him to return quickly:

“See, brother, that in your absence the brothers do not break the force of the rule and, like sheep without a shepherd, fall prey to plunderers. For if this happens, it will be counted as your fault, and all their iniquity will rebound upon your head.”

Prostrated by this trembling warning, Leobinus returned as quickly as possible to his own cell to govern the brothers mentioned above.

When he discovered that those brothers possessed nothing envious in themselves and nothing liable to curse or slander, and when he loved them all equally and looked upon them all cheerfully, he returned immense thanks to almighty God, who had led them to such concord and unanimity.

14. Meanwhile, blessed Aetherius, bishop of the city of Chartres, having completed the course of his life, [Note: [Col. 0555D] Cointius assigns Aetherius’s death to the year 544, in which year Saint Leobinus succeeded him in the see of Chartres.] departed to the Lord. Since there was various inquiry concerning his successor, the Lord, the King of heaven, in whose hand is the heart of kings, [Note: [Col. 0555D] This was Childebert I, who began to reign after the death of his father, Chlodovech I, in the year 511, and died in 558. He had his seat at Paris.] so inclined the heart of King Childebert by his inspiration that he issued a royal decree for the election of the blessed monk Leobinus as bishop and successor. [Note: [Col. 0555D] No one who has any familiarity with the records of the Church can be unaware that at that time, when Fortunatus was writing, various practices prevailed in ecclesiastical discipline concerning the selection of bishops. They were usually elected by the clergy and people, who agreed among themselves in designating and choosing their shepherd; or, by concession of the Church, they were indicated and nominated by princes and kings, after which they were inaugurated by the metropolitan and provincial bishops; or they were declared and confirmed by the Roman pontiffs and conducted to their sees, especially when the clergy and people, divided into factions, disagreed in choosing a pastor for themselves. In this matter the discipline of the Church itself was often changed, as the ages passed, according to the varying circumstances of the times and the character of places and events: until our own age was reached, in which, according to agreements entered into, privileges granted, or ancient custom retained, bishops are designated by the Roman pontiff, by chapters, by cities, or finally by the kings themselves; they are then consecrated bishops by the legitimate authority and ought to feed the people of God in holiness, justice, and prudence, for the structure and unity of that building—or body—in which the Holy Spirit has placed bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.]

All who were present, rejoicing with eager hearts that the blessed Leobinus had been chosen not only by the king but by God, began with unanimous voice and united vote to proclaim him worthy to occupy the episcopal chair in succession. Since the entire people therefore assented to this election—which we believe was not carried out without the envy of jealousy—certain bishops began to resist and oppose his ordination, on the grounds that a small part of his nose appeared to have been mutilated when he had formerly suffered from a cancerous disease. But when the accusation of envy had been silenced and utterly frustrated by the unanimous outcry of all, the holy man was decreed worthy of ordination according to God’s dispensation and the people’s election.

15. Meanwhile, some of those men, knowing that the blessed Leobinus did not wish to rise to the dignity of the episcopate, reached an agreement and sent to him, asking that he send them one of his monks, worthy of the episcopal mitre, to be ordained. He readily obeyed their request and designated one of his disciples to be advanced to so great an ordination, instructing and teaching him how he ought to conduct himself in governing and how to display himself at the summit of holiness. But the brother, unwilling to hasten alone to that assembly without the presence of his abbot, earnestly begged him to go there together with him. The old man therefore arose, departed with him, and reached Chartres, as he had been requested.

While he was lodging at a certain residence, he saw in a dream during the night a pavement covered with nuts. By divine command, as we believe, he was instructed to remove the shells and keep the clean kernel for himself. When the night had passed, and on the following day he was about to present the monk, as he had been asked, for ordination as bishop, and the people’s consensus was determining that he should not be accepted, the king’s decree was immediately brought forward, and it was read that, by the king’s command and the vote of the entire people, Leobinus ought to be ordained bishop.

But he refused, judging himself unworthy to undertake the care of so great a government. He cast himself at the feet of the bishops, offering as his excuse that he could neither fulfill nor accomplish what they were imposing upon him. Since all resisted him and would not accept his excuse, the dream he had seen was interpreted appropriately: namely, that through the kernel cleansed from its shell the people were to be governed by him; that, after laying aside the severity of austerity, he would at some time correct them by his rule and nourish them with the nectar-like food of his teaching.

Thereafter, without delay, while the peoples applauded and offered the greatest hymns to the Lord on high, Leobinus, whom they all desired, was appointed bishop of the Church of the city of Chartres and established as an outstanding shepherd against the crafty devices of the ancient enemy. Later, constantly preserving the rigor of his purpose, he showed himself steadfast in his monastic calling, continuing to be a monk as he had been before, without any display of pomp.

16. Once he had assumed episcopal dignity, it would not easily be possible to describe in a profusion of words how and to what extent he conducted himself according to the law of God’s commandments. For he was an apostolic man, like a most splendid, burning lamp in the house of the Lord; radiant in speech, most eloquent in doctrine, outstanding in preaching, serene in mind, gentle in wondrous patience, always devoted to the practices of frugality, most zealous in works of mercy, and whiter than snow in the brightness of angelic chastity. Rich in an abundance of every virtue and adorned with a beautiful life, he was shown to be God’s friend, a faithful and prudent servant, by the miracles that follow. [Col. 0556D]

17. At a certain time, when that same blessed man Leobinus was customarily traveling through the parishes and visiting them in episcopal fashion, and had reached Avallotium, [Note: [Col. 0557D] Avallotium was a village in the diocese of Chartres, mentioned by Gregory of Tours in Book IV, chapter 50, of his History of the Franks. This village, as the learned Ruinart adds in his notes on the aforementioned passage of Gregory, lies on the River Loir; it was later called Allotium or Alogium, and in the vernacular Alluye.] a certain blind man, darkened by blindness for eight years, learned that the holy man was passing through that place and humbly asked him to restore his sight by the sign of the cross.

For some time the holy man refused, fearing that by performing a miracle he might seem to assume something arrogant from his episcopal office. But when he wished to pass by cautiously, he was at last compelled by his companions to offer merciful aid to the blind man in his distress. After he had immediately completed his devout prayers, he drove away the darkness of blindness with the sign of the cross and restored to its former light the face whose sight the blind man had lost.

18. To this honorable deed let us add the noble miracle by which the holy man healed a dropsical person. While the most glorious King Childebert was expecting the blessed Bishop Leobinus to come to him at Rotojalum, [Note: [Col. 0557D] Rotojalum is Rueil, three leagues below Paris; Gregory of Tours calls it Villa Rotojalensis in Book X, chapter 28. There is also a Rotojalum, Rueil, a village in the diocese of Rouen, notable for the exile of Queen Fredegund, mentioned by Gregory of Tours in Book VII, chapter 19, not far from the confluence of the Eure with the Seine. But this passage must be understood of the first place. MABILL.] and while he was approaching Avallovicum on that very journey [Al., “a Vallovico,” “from Vallovicum”], a certain dropsical man was brought forward to be restored to health, his entrails being excessively distended.

When the bishop refused to restore him to health because of the slanders of his detractors, he was pressed by the prayers of his companions. Having applied the sign of the cross, he caused all the dropsical swelling to subside; the pain of the entrails completely withdrew, and, the swelling having disappeared, the skin was brought back to a smooth surface, while the sick man was freed from the danger of death.

19. Let it be inserted in the narrative how fires vanished through the holy man. At a certain time, when the blessed Leobinus had been invited to Paris with his fellow bishop Medeveus by the aforementioned king, [Note: [Col. 0557D] This appears to have been Medoveus, bishop of Meaux, who attended the Fifth Council of Orléans with Leobinus in 549. [Col. 0558D]] and had celebrated Easter Day episcopally in place of the deceased bishop of that city, [Note: [Col. 0558D] The bishop of Paris who had died before Leobinus came to Paris is said by Cointius, under the year 547, no. 7, to have been Amelius. He had attended the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541.] a devouring fire suddenly leapt out at night from the side of the Basilica of Saint Laurence and began to burn the houses built over the bridge. Nor did the unceasing water poured upon it from the neighboring river cause it to stop; rather, it struck great fear into the citizens living nearby, as though it would consume everything.

When the king, awakened by the people’s outcry, [Note: [Col. 0558D] From this passage Hadrian Valesius, in his *Disceptation on the Basilicas*, chapter 3, concludes that this Basilica of Saint Laurence was located not in the northern suburbs of Paris, where it is now seen, but in the southern suburbs, where the royal palace of the Baths stood. MABILL.] broke off his peaceful sleep and learned the cause of the tumult, he immediately sent a messenger to the blessed Leobinus, asking him to come as quickly as possible and assist the city.

But when many urged him to go first to the place where the great fire was raging, he said: “Brothers, we must go there, where divine rather than human aid must be implored against the mass of flame.” When he proceeded to the church and, prostrate upon the ground, fervently sought divine assistance, he hastened boldly to the fire, relying upon prayer, together with the priest.

At once, restrained by his prayer, the fire failed within itself. It forgot the strength it had assumed in burning the buildings, and the flame was so utterly consumed through his intervention that, dead within itself, it fell completely asleep.

20. Nor must we pass over in silence the miracle that nobly flourishes among his virtues. A certain woman devoted to God, from a monastery of maidens, had received a tunic of the lord Leobinus to sew. After repairing and restoring it with new thread, she took the old thread from it and, in faith, tied it to her belt.

Her secular sister, who had fled to her in terror, rose at dawn and fastened around herself the belt of her sister, to which the thread tied to the bishop’s garment was attached. Then the demon by whom she had previously been seized, sensing that something great was near the girl and that he could not endure it for long, began to torment her more fiercely and cried out through the girl’s mouth that he could not bear the tunic of the lord Leobinus, as though it were fire.

With this outcry the demon departed, and the girl vomited forth his foul odors together with blood. This miracle does not appear inferior to that which is recorded as having been performed by the Lord in the case of the woman with the issue of blood: for just as that woman was healed of her hemorrhage by touching the fringe, so this girl was freed from demonic torment by touching the thread.

Once liberated both from the snares of the enemy and from worldly cares, she vowed to serve the Lord all her days, joining her sister in the same convent.

21. Among the remaining miracles of his virtues, it is marvelous to mention one that is particularly famous for driving away illnesses. If anyone had been seized by an attack of a daily, tertian, or quartan fever and had been girded with a little cloak of the holy man, he would return to his lodging healthy, restored to his former soundness.

Thus divine grace granted healing continued to flow [Note: [Col. 0558D] In Labbe this is read: “And thus the health granted by divine grace remained [perhaps, ‘flowed’] from the garment of the Redeemer.”] from the bishop’s garment, just as it had once flowed from the garment of the Redeemer.

22. Let it be added to the narrative what the holy man accomplished during his life. When the house of a certain citizen of Chartres, situated in the suburb of the city, was repeatedly battered by a demonic assault with a shower of stones, so that the neighbors, abandoning their prepared banquets because of the density of the clattering rocks, fled from their houses, they were urged by the servant of God to carry there water blessed by him, marked with the sign of the cross, and sprinkle it wherever the great mockery of demonic illusion was taking place.

When this had been done, the enemy fled in terror, and the owner of the house remained safe and fearless with his household.

23. We must also recall to memory that helpful miracle by which the holy and illustrious Bishop Leobinus shone among the people. A certain blessed man named Caletricus, [Note: [Col. 0559D] See what we said in chapter 7 of Book IV of Fortunatus’s works.] noble by birth but nobler by his merits, was appointed bishop at Chartres after the death of the blessed Leobinus. While, as a presbyter, he was making himself pleasing both in the sight of God and in the eyes of men by a holy way of life, he was seized by such a severe illness that he scarcely breathed his last breath.

His venerable sister, named Mallegundis, [Note: [Col. 0559D] Some scholars believe that this was Monegundis, whose Life is found in Gregory of Tours, in the *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 19.] quickly sent messengers to the holy bishop, asking him to send blessed oil for the relief of her brother’s illness.

He himself came in person with the oil and asked all to be silent, saying: “Lord, who know all things, if you judge this servant of yours necessary to your Church or to your people, restore him to health by your assisting power.”

As soon as the sick man had been anointed with the oil of sacred unction, he was restored by such a gift of health that no trouble of illness ever again touched his limbs. To prove the holy man’s virtue, the remaining portion of the oil is said to have been transformed into such radiant beauty that all who were present saw not the gleam of oil but the brilliance of crystal shining forth.

This clearly foreshadowed that the man who was to become bishop would, through his episcopal ministry, sanctify the oil of consecration and shine with divine virtues through heavenly grace.

24. It is also worthwhile to insert into this account the remarkable miracle that the holy man performed bodily, although unknowingly. At a certain time, when the aforementioned bishop was traveling with his companions to visit the parish of the region of Dunum, [Note: [Col. 0559D] Dunum Castrum, commonly Châteaudun, situated on the River Loir, belonged to the diocese of Chartres, as Gregory of Tours records in Book VII, chapter 17, of his *History of the Franks.] the only daughter of one of his parishioners, a man named Baudolenus, illustrious in birth and wealth, was so tightly held by the force of fever and prolonged illness that a burial and funeral procession were already being prepared.

When this man heard that Saint Leobinus was approaching from nearby, he hurried to present himself before him, asking him to bless his house and to give blessings both to himself and to all his household.

The holy Leobinus therefore rose promptly and, as he had promised, came to the aforementioned Baudolenus. As he entered the house, the man’s daughter, from the very illness with which she had been afflicted, became dead upon her bed.

No faithful person can doubt that the name of the holy bishop was glorified among the people through the girl’s resurrection from the dead. The aforesaid Baudolenus, wishing to maintain a cheerful appearance in the bishop’s presence, ordered his entire household under oath not to reveal the girl’s death to anyone. But since no one loses without grief what he possesses with love, he could not conceal it for long: the inward pain of his heart disclosed the outward sorrow of his body.

When the holy man of God saw the saddened household of that house, he too was overcome with grief. Holding himself back for a while from the preparations for the meal, he entered the church, prostrated his body upon the pavement, and with tears prayed to the Lord to deign to show him the cause of the sadness by which the grieving household was distressed.

When his prayer was completed, as the old man rose from the dust, the lifeless girl rose from death. Then the aforementioned Baudolenus, amazed at the excellence of so great a power, prostrated himself at the holy man’s feet with his entire household and humbly disclosed everything that had happened. For this reason, he gave him immense thanks, passing from mourning into joy.

25. Let us also relate the marvelous miracle that the holy man of God performed while already confined by illness. While he was being pressed by this illness, two little boys, driven by the torment of the enemy, prostrated themselves at his feet and were permitted to receive with his blessing the food that remained for him after eating.

Through this remedy, both returned unharmed to their own homes. When the blessed Leobinus had been afflicted by continuous illness for seven years, intent upon heaven through divine actions and honored with the distinction of miracles, he departed happily to the heavens, as though sleeping in a trance and destined to be rewarded with rich prizes, like a faithful servant who returns the talent entrusted to him doubled and is about to enter into the joy of his lord, while the angels applaud. [Note: [Col. 0559D]

Indeed, around the year of Christ 556. For he took part in the Fifth Council of Orléans in 549 and the Second Council of Paris in 551. Caletricus, his successor, confirmed by his subscription the Third Council of Paris, held in 557. Thus Mabillon. Mabillon himself demonstrates that Saint Leobinus died on the day before the Ides of March, in volume II of the Benedictine *Acts of the Saints*, p. 1104.

Moreover, the body of Saint Leobinus was reverently preserved in the suburban Basilica of Saint Martin, called “in the Valley,” until the year 1568, when the Calvinists reduced his sacred relics to ashes, except for his head, which is kept in the Major Church. In the manuscript codices of the Church of Chartres, it is read that he delimited the diocese of Chartres and occupied the see for approximately twelve years. MABILL.]

[lacuna]

[Col. 0560C] 26. Yet before he was committed to burial, the dead man revealed how great his virtue had been while alive. Finally, when he was being carried in a coffin to the Basilica of Saint Martin for burial, one of those standing nearby was using a carrying staff to hold back the crowd pressing forward. It happened that he knocked down to the ground a cross suspended with lamps full of oil.

Immediately the cross itself—marvelous to relate!—with the cord from which it had fallen, entwined itself again in its former place, with all the lamps intact and without any loss of oil, although no one raised it. It began to remain before the eyes of all as it had habitually done before. Although the lamps were thought to have been shattered into fragments, they remained solid and whole and did not allow a single drop of oil to spill.

Thus, at the funeral, the body of the most blessed man shone forth to the praise of his glory through the power of the cross.

27. O most glorious man, whose merits had such power with the Crucified One that the cross which had fallen to the ground, without anyone’s assistance, returned unharmed to the place from which it had fallen! O venerable bishop of Christ, continually protected by the guardianship of angels, by whose power neither the liquid oil suffered harm nor did any of those lamps sustain damage from being broken!

Truly, his joyful soul glories in eternal happiness, possessing a holy lamp with an unquenchable light, because without the pomp of human praise his hands never ceased from the work of mercy, which is signified by this kind of liquid.

These miracles were brought forth by the power of him who, through the trophy of the cross, redeemed the human race from everlasting death and, cleansed from sins, granted it the ascent to heaven.

And since we have recounted, for the sake of the reverent annual commemoration of the most glorious Bishop Leobinus, the celebrated praises of his miracles that deserve to be remembered—namely, a few from among innumerable ones—let us with humble prayers implore the holiness of so great a patron, asking that he who made him shine with miracles may cause us to abound in good works, grant us to pass through the course of this present life without offense, to obtain continual tranquility of peace, and in the age to come happily to reach the fellowship of him who lives and is glorified as God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Vita of Saint Maurilius]

[Col. 0561]

PRELIMINARY NOTICE ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MAURILIUS, BISHOP OF ANGERS

Some attribute the *Life of Saint Maurilius, Bishop of Angers*, to Fortunatus, among them Trithemius and Surius, under 26 September, and Vossius. They seem to have been led to this opinion chiefly by the authority and testimony of a certain Prologue, which we have mentioned elsewhere. That Prologue presents Gregory of Tours as its author and was written by him to Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris. In it Gregory affirms that, at Germanus’s request, he corrected the Lives and miracles that the Lord had deigned to perform through the blessed Maurilius and Albinus, bishops of Angers—Lives that the presbyter Fortunatus had described in polished language but that had by then been almost corrupted by scribal faults, and so forth. This Prologue is read in full appended to the works of Gregory of Tours edited by the learned Ruinart.

Most critics and learned men, however, regard this Prologue as spurious and falsely attributed to Gregory of Tours. Consequently, they do not hesitate to deny that this Life of Saint Maurilius was written by Fortunatus, since many and weighty considerations suggest both that the Life was not composed by Venantius Fortunatus and that it was not corrected by Gregory of Tours. John Launoy, doctor of sacred theology at Paris, sets forth and presses all these arguments in a dissertation in which he investigates the author of the *Life of Saint Maurilius*. It will not be out of place to report the principal ones here.

The first point, then, is that the heading of this Prologue, which Gregory supposedly sends to Saint Germanus—“To the most holy lord Germanus, bishop of the holy mother Church of Paris, from Gregory, humble bishop of the metropolis of Tours, greetings”—is foreign to the custom and usage of those times, when it had not yet become customary for every Church to be called “holy mother Church.” It was likewise foreign to Gregory’s practice to call himself “bishop of the metropolis of Tours.”

Second, it is not credible that a Life written by Fortunatus while he was still alive—and indeed by a man who lived for many years after Germanus—could have been so corrupted through the fault of copyists that it required a corrector.

Third, even if such a thing had occurred, why would Germanus have sent it for correction to Gregory of Tours rather than to Fortunatus himself, his closest friend, from whom he could have obtained complete and uncorrupted copies?

Fourth, in the aforementioned Prologue Gregory reports that he corrected the *Life of Saint Maurilius* by omitting or removing whatever might appear unbelievable. Yet he then appends the entirely extraordinary and beyond human belief resurrection of Saint Renatus, which took place seven years after Renatus had died and which, as Gregory himself admits, had been omitted by Fortunatus.

Fifth, contrary to his usual practice, he calls Fortunatus “blessed” in these words: “although blessed Fortunatus omitted this because of those who believe less readily,” and so forth.

Sixth, several features of that Life are plainly opposed to the style and practice of Gregory of Tours, which indicates that Gregory did not correct it with his own hand.

Finally, that Life praises Pope Gregory the Great, who says: “Faith has no merit when human reason provides proof.” Yet Gregory the Great is recorded as having ascended the Roman see only in the year 590, whereas Saint Germanus, to whom the corrected Life is supposedly sent, died in 579.

The Bollandists add to these arguments—something Launoy had also noticed earlier in the place cited above—that when Magnobodus, or Magbodus, bishop of Angers, admits that he wrote another *Life of Saint Maurilius* in the year 620, only twenty-five years after the death of Gregory of Tours, he could hardly have been unaware of a Life composed by Fortunatus and corrected by Gregory; nor would he have failed to use it, if he had known that it existed. Yet he himself records that, in composing a new *Life of Saint Maurilius*, he was assisted only by those documents left by the presbyter Justus, and for this reason he mentions only him.

The learned Ruinart, in the Preface to the works of Saint Gregory of Tours, no. 80, establishes the same point from two manuscript codices: one from the monastery of Vendôme, written approximately six hundred years ago, and the other from the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, five hundred years old. In these it is stated that the *Life of Saint Maurilius* was written at the command of Raino, who is counted as the thirty-fifth bishop of that church in the catalogue of the bishops of Angers, written under Bishop Eusebius. Here are the words of the manuscript codices:

“Raino, formerly a daily disciple of Saint Martin and always a canon, and shortly afterward humble bishop of the Holy Church of Angers, the thirty-third [Al., thirty-fifth] from the beginning of Christianity, for the honor of Almighty God and also of that same Saint Maurilius, and for the remission of the sins of his soul, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation still 905 and in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopal ordination, ordered this Life of blessed Maurilius to be written and sought out. Archanaldus, disciple and deacon of Saint Martin, wrote and sought it out at the command of the aforesaid lord Raino.”

For these reasons, almost all learned men agree on the view that the *Life of Saint Maurilius*—at least the one commonly circulated—is not a work of Fortunatus and was not corrected or reworked by Saint Gregory of Tours, but was written at the command of Raino, bishop of Angers. So the learned Ruinart in the place cited above, Launoy, Tillemont, the authors of the *History of French Literature*, the Bollandists, and others.

We append it here, although we judge it should be relegated among the apocryphal works of Fortunatus, as it appears in Surius under 18 September; and we have furnished it with notes where appropriate, adding also what the Bollandists have noted with great learning. Moreover, in the Life published by Surius there is no mention of Gregory the Great, nor is any testimony of his cited, contrary to what Launoy observed.

[Col. 0563]

LIFE OF SAINT [Note: [Col. 0563B] Another reading: *Maurilionis*. Surius gives the title of this Life as follows: *Life of Saint Maurilius, Bishop of Angers*. Its author was not identified in two manuscript codices; but since Trithemius states that Fortunatus wrote the Life of this holy man, and the style agrees, scarcely anyone will deny that Fortunatus was its author. [Col. 0563C]] MAURILIUS, BISHOP [Note: [Col. 0563C] Angers is a city of Gaul, the metropolis of the province of Anjou, bordering Tours and the duchy of Berry. It is near the ocean and is watered by the Loire, the best-known river of Gaul.] OF ANGERS (S)*

[Col. 0563A] 1. Maurilius was a native of the town of Milan. His parents were most distinguished, and from almost his very cradle he was instructed in the sacred writings by the blessed Martin, who in those days had established a monastery for himself at Milan. [Note: [Col. 0563C] Severus Sulpicius mentions this monastery of Saint Martin, which he built at Milan, in his *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 4.]

But after the blessed Martin had been expelled from that city by the perfidy of the Arians, [Note: [Col. 0563C] Saint Hilary was driven into exile through the agency of the Arians after the Council of Béziers in 356. After this had occurred, Saint Martin came to Milan in exile, but did not remain long in that city, being harassed and driven from his residence by Auxentius, the Arian bishop. He then followed Hilary when the latter returned from exile, although Martin himself had remained in exile in Phrygia for only four years, as Severus Sulpicius testifies in Book II of his *History*. If, therefore, Saint Maurilius, as a child and almost an infant, was taught letters by Saint Martin at Tours, as this passage relates, he was not born around the year 327, as the Bollandists maintain, but around 345 or later. As for the statement that, already ordained a lector by Saint Ambrose, he sought Martin under Julian and was initiated by him into the sacred orders, these matters cannot be reconciled in any way unless we say that the name Julian has entered the text in place of Valentinian. For the emperor Julian died before Ambrose was made bishop of Milan. Julian’s death is assigned to the year 363, whereas Ambrose did not obtain the see of the Milanese Church before 374. Magnobodus, indeed, writes in the *Life of Saint Maurilius* that Maurilius went to Gaul under Julian, already ordained a lector, but he says nothing of his having been advanced to that rank by Saint Ambrose. [Col. 0563D]] Saint Maurilius remained there until he received the office of lector from the blessed Ambrose, bishop of that city.

Meanwhile, after his father had died—his father, who governed almost the whole of Hesperia— [Note: [Col. 0564B] The author of the *Apology against Launoy, in Defense of Saint Renatus*, thinks that “Hesperia” here refers not to all Italy but to Cisalpine Gaul, according to Bolland. [Col. 0564C]] he abandoned his mother and every desire for possessing his property, in accordance with the evangelical commandment (Matthew 19). Under Julian, then Caesar, [Note: [Col. 0564C] This is a copyist’s error. Perhaps “Valentinian” should be read.] he sought Martin, who at that time governed the metropolitan see of Tours, and remained with him for a long time, occupied in divine duties, until, unwillingly and under Martin’s pressure, he received the remaining ecclesiastical orders and the grace of the priesthood. Having obtained the honor of the priesthood, and desiring to lead a stricter life than that of monks, so that he might follow the Lord alone more freely, he was thoroughly instructed by Martin’s teachings and strengthened equally by his blessings.

After they had kissed one another and wept greatly, Maurilius departed from Martin, although Martin did not wish it, and set out for the city of Angers. Hearing that not far from the city, beside the River Loire, there was an extremely ancient shrine in a certain village, dedicated to various idol-worships, [Note: [Col. 0564C] Magnobodus likewise reports that this shrine was in the territory of Angers, at a place called Calonna, on the bank of the Loire. That village, as the Bollandists note, lies in the county of Anjou, approximately four miles from Angers.] he went there.

Seeing that it could not be torn down by human power, he turned his mind toward the Lord and prayed that he himself would destroy the shrine in which human minds were being deceived by various errors, since Maurilius could not do so. Immediately, therefore, by divine action, fire sent down from heaven consumed within the space of an instant whatever images and impurity it found there.

After all the defilement had been removed, he founded an honorable church of Christ and subsequently established it as a village. [Note: [Col. 0564C] Launoy assigns Saint Maurilius forty years of residence in that village before he was made bishop, but we do not agree with him, as we shall attempt to show elsewhere. If what Launoy supposes is granted, almost the entire sequence and truth of the history of blessed Maurilius collapses. Magnobodus makes no mention of the length of time Saint Maurilius remained in that place; he merely asserts that he stayed there until he accepted the burden of the episcopate.] There he spent twelve years, devoting himself diligently to the Lord through many fasts and prayers; and there he also shone through many virtues.

2. For in an estate called Pontiacum, [Note: [Col. 0564C] In the Life written by Magnobodus it is called *Pociacense*. The Bollandists suspect that “Podium Andegavense” is meant here: “a little town in the province of Angers in Gaul, three miles south of Saumur and eight miles from Angers.” Gregory of Tours mentions Pontiacum in the territory of Berry in his *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 18, where he relates that a monastery had been built there by Saint Ursus, its abbot. It is certainly difficult to determine with certainty where this place called Pontiacum was situated.] there was a certain man named Saturnus, whom nature had brought into this life from his mother’s womb with both hands dried up.

When, living on alms, he had reached full age, he was warned one night in a vision and heard a voice saying to him: “Go to the man Maurilius and ask him to make the sign of the holy cross over your hands; and you will immediately be healed.”

When he awoke, he ran to the man of God. Throwing himself at his feet and wholly bathed in tears, he humbly begged him to lay his hand upon him, explaining the vision. Then blessed Maurilius fasted all day and all night, remained prostrate in prayer, and faithfully prayed for the sick man.

On the following morning he placed the sign of the cross upon the sick man’s hands and immediately made them sound.

3. Not long afterward, a certain woman from Nantes was being grievously tormented by a demon. It had made her weak in her entire body and also blind, deprived of sight. She was brought to the man of God by the faithful, bound in double chains.

On the next day, when the holy man directed his eyes toward her, the demon immediately left her. Then, by the sign of the cross, he restored her sight, and she who had been brought to the church of the blessed man bound in chains returned home free and unharmed.

4. At almost the same time, while certain shepherds were grazing and watching over their masters’ sheep in the same region, one of them, while guarding the flock at night, was bitten by a viper. Its venom suddenly spread through all the boy’s veins and turned his entire body into a swelling.

Since nothing other than death was expected for him—he was already lying stretched out, half alive—the other shepherds, prompted by faith, brought him into the presence of the confessor.

Then the holy man raised his eyes to heaven, marked all the boy’s limbs, and impressed the sign of the cross with his own saliva upon the little wound through which the viper’s venom had entered. [Note: [Col. 0565D] Magnobodus relates that Saint Maurilius poured saliva into the boy’s mouth, and that the boy thereby recovered his health. A nearly similar miracle performed by Saint Martin of Tours is read in his Life written by Fortunatus, Book III.]

Immediately the venom was drawn back from all parts of the body and ran toward the very place through which it had entered, and the boy was restored to complete health.

### 5

A certain matron of the territory of Angers, bound in marriage, had remained barren from the time of her union. Although she continually entreated the Lord to grant her offspring, she was entirely unable to obtain her desire; and, advancing into mature years, she was already approaching despair of attaining children. She turned wholly to the blessed man, so that what she herself did not deserve, he might obtain from the Lord through his merits. She promised with complete faith and devotion that, if by his prayers he could obtain a son for the aged woman, she would offer the child to the Lord and that he would serve Him perpetually.

When the blessed man saw the woman’s faith and tears, he approached to pray to the Lord for her. The Lord heard the holy man and granted the woman, who was making supplication, both conception and childbirth.

> **Note:** Magnobodus relates that this child later succeeded Maurilius himself in the see of Angers; therefore he was none other than Saint Renatus, of whom there will be discussion later.

She consecrated him to the Lord, as she had promised, to remain in His service.

### 6

Not far from the village of Calonna, where the blessed man lived, there was a certain hill called Praesciacus, adorned with various shrines of idols. Maurilius grieved that this superstition continued so long in a place where he believed destruction—perhaps, *of souls*—to be present. One day, therefore, he went to the place with a few faithful men.

When he arrived at the idol in order to destroy it, the demons hiding there began to cry out, saying:

> “Why do you persecute us here also, Maurilius? In these regions there is no place where we can escape you.”

Immediately, when he opposed them with the sign of the holy cross, the demons suddenly rose up with a great roar and fled, not without an immense stench. He then ordered all the images of the idols to be gathered together and, burning them in the fire, reduced them to ashes. Afterwards, carefully cleansing the place, he established there an honorable monastery, which remains to this day for the glory of Christ and the praise of His confessor.

### 7

A certain monk named Clemens was continually burned by quartan fevers for three full years. The heat together with the cold greatly wore him down, and he had an aversion to food, because the strength of his stomach had failed. As he weakened under such suffering and had already despaired of life, he ordered, at the urging of his friends, that he be carried to the blessed man.

When he was deemed worthy to see his presence, he earnestly asked to receive from him *eulogiae*—blessed tokens of health.

> **Note:** On the *eulogiae*, see what we noted at chapter 12 of book XI of Fortunatus’s works.

As the saint, having sanctified them according to custom, held them out, the illness vanished like smoke. Immediately strengthened with complete vigor, he returned home in good health.

### 8

A few days thereafter, while merchants, among various consignments of goods, had young men and women for sale—[the printed word is corrupt; Surius notes *Italos*, “Italians”; should one read *servos*, “slaves”?]—and were traveling with them toward Spain, they passed through the estate of Calonna.

As they went by the blessed man’s church, one of those being led away for sale suddenly sprang forward with great force, entered the church, and, throwing himself in tears at the confessor’s feet, begged him by his prayers or at a price to redeem him for the love of God and keep him with himself. He had been secretly captured in his native country and was being led away to be sold in a foreign land.

Recognizing from his words and tears that he was his fellow-countryman, the priest was moved by a compassionate spirit and immediately went out to plead with the captive’s master on his behalf. But when the master stubbornly denied that this could be done, he signaled to his men to drag the man quickly from the church.

As the servants beat him, used force, and carried out their master’s command, the captive began to cry out with immense volume:

> “Have mercy and help me, servant of God, whom I have devoutly sought in order to be freed.”

The priest, bending his knees briefly to the ground and raising his hands to heaven, said:

> “Lord God almighty, who help those placed in distress and those who truly trust in Your mercy, aid this captive, for whom I earnestly entreat You.”

At these words such a violent fever seized the captive’s master that, before repentance could come to his aid, he breathed out his spirit.

> **Note:** Magnobodus relates that the slave’s master was not dead, but became so ill that he was near death, and that through Saint Maurilius’s prayers he obtained life.

Then the others were struck with such terror, fearing that the earth might swallow them alive, that with one accord they tearfully sought the priest, pleading that he obtain both pardon for them and, through his merits, life for the dead man.

The blessed man, greatly fearing that he himself might be the occasion and cause of that man’s destruction, prostrated himself on the ground and, with immense sobs, called upon Christ to restore the dead man’s soul. He did not rise from the ground before he had obtained both life for the dead man and freedom for the captive.

Finally, so that their former presumption might be forgiven, the merchants honored the place with many gifts; the blessed man assigned nearly all of them to the needs of the poor.

### 9

Moreover, as human necessity required, a fairly large ship called Argo, loaded with merchandise, was being carried down the Loire.

> **Note:** Magnobodus expresses “ships” in the plural.

As it was ascending opposite Calonna, the sea suddenly became disturbed by the wind and the ship began to whirl about. The mast was broken; now the prow was lifted high into the waves, now the stern was forced down amid the clefts of the waters. The sailors, overcome and terrified by the violence of the storm, already despairing of their immediate safety, threw all the ship’s equipment onto the shore, awaiting only death.

Then suddenly they began to cry out with immense voices, saying:

> “Have mercy, man of Christ, Maurilius; help us in our shipwreck. For you can obtain this from Christ, since you obtained life for a dead man.”

At their cries Maurilius rose from prayer and hurried to the shore. Raising the sign of the cross against the storm, he commanded the tempest not to rage. At once the blasts ceased, their violence abating; the swelling waves turned back into the open sea, calm tranquillity followed, and the unharmed sailors happily reached the desired port.

### 10

It was customary for the blessed man, as a most faithful dispenser of the word of God, to travel sometimes around the churches and sometimes among the sick. So that he would not collapse from excessive fatigue, the humble rider had a little donkey, which he frequently used.

A thief did not fear to steal it during the night. But the wretched man, while stealing the donkey, was seized by a demon and, wandering astray, was tormented throughout the night as he roamed about.

In the morning he himself appeared with the donkey before the blessed man’s door, insane [*amens*, “out of his mind”], and unwillingly confessed the crime he had committed. Then, seized by the demon, he tried to flee so as not to be treated. But the blessed man first freed the madman from the demon through the grace of exorcism, and then freed him from his offense; after recovering the donkey, he absolved him. And because he had begun to steal out of necessity, not from vice, he also gave him three gold pieces and dismissed him.

### 11

A certain noble and extremely wealthy matron, descended from a senatorial family and named Amelia, had begun to be oppressed by a serious illness. After enduring it for twelve years and spending all her possessions on the arts of physicians, she could obtain no remedy for her recovery. Indeed, the more carefully they strove to apply all the ingenuity of their art to her, the more severely she was always burdened by the illness.

When her relatives, despairing of her health, were advising her to attend only to what was necessary for burial, she said to her friends:

> “Go; hurry as quickly as possible to the blessed man Maurilius. If you can obtain that I be deemed worthy to be visited by him, I trust that through him I shall be restored to health.”

Then her relatives and friends hastened without pause to the blessed man on behalf of the woman, asking him with devout prayers to visit the sick woman in his compassion. When he heard this, remembering the words of the Lord, “I was sick and you visited me” (Matthew 25), he immediately set out with them.

When he came into the house, he first prostrated himself in prayer, as was his custom. Then he anointed the woman’s limbs with blessed oil. She immediately rose completely restored.

### 12

Meanwhile, while the blessed man was flourishing at the village of Calonna in such merits and virtues, the city of Angers was deprived of its own shepherd.

> **Note:** It is established from the catalogues of the bishops of Angers that this man was Prosper.

Then the urban populace and the entire nobility, with priests gathered from every direction, came together in a single council, seeking to determine which of them ought to be substituted in the episcopal ministry. But some, whether through the windy favor of nobility or because they had been appointed by money to the dignity of so great a rank, preferred certain men to others; and therefore they could not reach a common decision, because it is written (Acts 5): “A decision that is not from God can never be established, but must be dissolved.”

While they were turning these matters over among themselves and could reach no conclusion, suddenly it was announced that the most holy archbishop Martin of the see of Tours was present. While nearly everyone awaited his judgment, he said:

> “Brothers, listen and attend to good counsel. Since God has chosen a bishop for you, receive him as your priest. Maurilius, priest of the Church of Calonna, shall be your bishop.”

When they heard this, they were astonished. But since they already knew Maurilius’s virtues and merits, setting aside their former ignorance, they immediately came to one judgment with equal mind and will. Having received the command of the lord archbishop, they hastened to the man of God. By episcopal authority—perhaps, *having seized him from his own church*—they brought him unwilling into Martin’s presence.

When he entered the church with Blessed Martin, a dove of snowy whiteness, released from heaven, descended and settled upon his head, thereby immediately revealing the merits of so great a priest. When many saw this, they all cried out with one voice that Maurilius was most worthy of the episcopate, chosen and manifested not merely by human beings but by the Almighty.

Then Maurilius, overcome by the miracle and by their prayers, fulfilled the command and accepted the priesthood. For, as many were privileged to see, whenever blessed Martin extended his hand over his head for the sacred blessing of the priest being consecrated, the aforementioned dove always gave way to him.

And when Blessed Maurilius had been established as bishop and Blessed Martin had returned to his own see, Saint Martin was accustomed to relate that, in blessing Saint Maurilius as bishop, not only the Holy Spirit but also a host of angels had been present in the form of the dove.

### 13

After Maurilius had been ordained bishop to guard Christ’s sheep, the grace of the Lord shone so brightly in him that through him signs and miracles were performed no fewer than formerly through the apostles. He drove out demons merely by his words, healed the sick by prayer alone, restored sight to the blind by the sign of the cross, and brought paralytics back to their former health through the efficacy of his merit.

He performed many other miracles as well. Although they are not found recorded in writing, nevertheless, because they are true, they cannot perish; they are celebrated by the mouths of many.

Thus clothed in apostolic simplicity and made radiant by purity of heart, the man of God continually devoted himself wholly to the Lord, through vigils, prayers, and fasts, on behalf of the flock of Christ entrusted to him, so that the ancient enemy, the devil, might not by temptation injure or carry off any of the sheep committed to him.

### 14

Soon after receiving the dignity of the episcopate, as he was leaving the basilica of Saint Peter, where he had spent the entire night awake in constant prayer, he encountered a certain blind man who had lacked the light of his eyes from his mother’s womb.

When the man earnestly asked that this be granted him by the Lord through the merits of the blessed Maurilius, the blessed bishop was briefly embarrassed. But when he impressed the sign of the holy cross upon the man’s eyes, blood immediately burst forth with pain, and he was deemed worthy to possess sight.

Thereafter, for love of the blessed Maurilius, the man was entrusted to the basilica of blessed Peter and served there faithfully for as long as he lived.

### 15

On the following day, while Bishop Maurilius was celebrating the holy solemnity in the same basilica of Saint Peter, a matron arrived with a dying child. This was the child whom, when she had once been barren, she had obtained from the Lord through Maurilius’s merits before his episcopate, asking that he give her son, whom she had offered to the Lord, the Holy Spirit through the laying on of his hands before the child died.

But while the bishop was delayed for a little while in the consecration of the holy body and blood of Christ, the boy died. After the holy solemnity had been completed, and after he had learned of the child’s death—he had died without the gift of chrism—he attributed the whole matter to his own negligence, mourning for a long time with unremitting tears the fault of his disobedience.

Since even this was not enough for him, and after struggling long and deeply within himself over what he should do, he finally realized that among his fellow citizens the sacrilege of such negligence could not be fully expiated unless, as one who had fled, he abandoned his homeland and fellow citizens.

Having found this course of action, he secretly withdrew, carrying with him keys from the relics of the saints with which the Church of Angers was adorned.

> **Note:** Magnobodus says not a word about this flight.

When he reached the sea, by divine providence, he who remained on the shore engraved on a stone the day of his crossing. Thus, having boarded the ship, he began to hasten the journey he had undertaken.
