As he proceeded out to sea and was considering why he had brought the keys of the relics with him, the enemy of the human race, wishing to add grief to the holy man’s grief, suddenly caused the keys to slip from his hands and sink into the sea.

> **Note:** Magnobodus omits the whole of this story: Saint Maurilius’s flight; the lost keys, later found after a long time in the entrails of a fish; the discovery of Saint Maurilius in the house of a king, where he served as a gardener; and the boy Renatus’s restoration to life seven years after his death. He says not a word about any of these events.

Then Maurilius is said to have cried out with tears, in words later confirmed by the outcome:

> “Unless I am once again deemed worthy to see these keys, I shall never return to the homeland and city from which I am fleeing.”

After crossing the sea, where he could conceal who he was, he changed his clothing and attached himself to one of the princes of the region, declaring that he was a gardener, so that he might discipline his body through his own labor.

As he advanced in this service, the Lord granted such an abundance of vegetables through his merits that he supplied enough to all who needed them, and yet the vegetables never ran out. For this reason he pleased many people and was well loved by everyone.

### 16

Meanwhile, the people of Angers, deprived of the shepherd once entrusted to them from heaven, were struck with no small fear. Through frequent visions they were threatened, and they were often warned to search everywhere for their own shepherd; unless Maurilius were found and restored to his Church, the city of Angers would swiftly be overthrown.

Therefore the entire nobility of that region, together with the immense common multitude, held a joint consultation and came to one decision. They chose from among their fellow citizens four men of outstanding virtue and faith. After providing, according to their vow, the funds needed for the affairs of so great a journey, they commanded the men never to return unless they had first found their own patron.

Having carried out their mission, they passed through all the cities, towns, and villages, and traveled through nearly all of Europe. At last, in the seventh year, they returned to the regions of Gaul. Since they had not found the man whom they sought, divine guidance brought them to a port of the Ocean Sea situated in Lesser Britain, so that they might try to seek across the sea the man whom they had been unable to find on this side of it.

As they waited for a ship with which they could complete the service they had undertaken, they were sitting on the shore when they found the inscription that we mentioned above, carved in the rock:

> “Here Maurilius, bishop of the people of Angers, passed.”

Rejoicing at such an unmistakable sign, they crossed the channel with confidence. When they were in the middle of the calm sea, behold, a huge fish suddenly emerged from the depths and leapt into the ship.

After they had given thanks to God and begun to gut the fish, they found in its liver the keys of the relics that Maurilius had lost in the sea. Recognizing them, they were greatly astonished and disturbed, fearing that Maurilius had suffered shipwreck with the keys and had perished.

They therefore lowered the anchors from the ship, intending to return by sea, while the sailors asserted that Maurilius was dead. But, by the Lord’s granting, each of them saw the same vision on the following night. In it they were told:

> “Do not be afraid, nor turn back from your journey. Hasten the task you have begun; without doubt you will find the desire you have sought for so long.”

When morning came, each related to the others what he had seen. Thus greatly strengthened, they pursued more eagerly the journey they had undertaken.

It came about that, under angelic guidance, they were led by a straight course to the house of the prince with whom Maurilius lived. When they entered, they immediately heard that Maurilius was to be summoned so that he might hurry forward with the vegetables customarily used by the king.

They directed their eyes toward the place from which they had heard him being called, and before long they saw Maurilius hurrying forward with the vegetables. As soon as they recognized him, they fell at his feet and, with much weeping, begged him to come to the aid of his own Church and city.

Unable to refuse their tears, he was overwhelmed and began earnestly to resist them with tears of his own, saying:

> “By a vow and an oath I have bound myself never to return to my homeland unless I am once more deemed worthy to see the keys that I lost.”

They immediately displayed the keys and recounted in order everything they had seen and suffered at sea. The news instantly spread and reached the king himself. Everyone was amazed, and the man whom they had regarded as a gardener they now venerated and worshiped as a most blessed bishop, competing to honor him with many gifts.

Then Maurilius, overcome by so many prayers that he return and by the miracles, hesitated in deep concern. As he planned to spend the following night sleepless in vigils and prayers, he at last, exhausted, fell briefly asleep and saw an angel saying to him:

> “Rise, Maurilius, and fulfill the desire of the peoples who seek you. For behold, through your prayers and merits the Lord has preserved the sheep entrusted to you, for whom you prayed; and, in addition, He has restored to you the boy whom you sought while weeping for so long.”

What more need be said? When morning came, as peoples gathered from every direction, he was led to the ship with great honor and, after crossing, was received by his own homeland with no less glory.

Thus, having returned to his own city, secure in the Lord’s promise and with the crowds awaiting him, he went to the boy’s tomb. After the tomb had been uncovered with mattocks, he called upon Christ for a very long time amid lamentation. At last, when his prayer had been completed with tears, both rose: Maurilius from prayer, and the boy from death.

Consecrated by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, the boy was called Renatus because of the event. Immediately devoted to divine worship and carefully instructed by the blessed Maurilius, he deserved to flourish in such great virtues that after Maurilius he inherited, as his posthumous heir, the episcopal chair of the Church of Angers.

If anyone should perhaps judge this story fictitious, let him return to the city of Angers. There he will find the most precious confessor of Christ, Maurilius, flourishing in immense virtues, and no less the bishop Renatus, his successor, shining with miracles.

### 17

After the most holy priest Maurilius had been restored to his own see, let us relate what happened in the days that followed.

A certain avaricious man, driven by greed, had taken up an axe and, on the Lord’s Day, become eager to work. Divine punishment immediately followed: the axe handle remained attached to his hands.

After five months, driven by his sufferings, he sought Maurilius and tearfully confessed the course of his offense. When the blessed man saw his repentance, he was moved in spirit and began to grieve.

But when Saint Maurilius touched the axe handle, the sinews immediately relaxed, the fingers straightened, all pain disappeared, and the hands were completely restored. The man returned home safe and joyful.

### 18

Another man, named Belgicus, had rashly ordered his own servants to clear his crops on the first day of Easter. When the slaves began to resist and to say that, contrary to authority, servile labor ought not to be performed on such a day, their master forced them to do it against their will.

But when they entered the fields and tried to hoe out the darnel and whatever else was useless, Belgicus was immediately struck blind. Unwillingly, he cried out in an immense voice that they should abandon the work they had begun.

After remaining in that blindness for three years, he heard that the blessed Maurilius, for the salvation of the people entrusted to him, had traveled through villages and estates as bishops customarily do. Compelled by continual suffering, he earnestly and devoutly sought permission at least to touch the priest’s garment, trusting that through this he could immediately be healed.

When, through the preparations made by his friends, he was deemed worthy to touch it, he immediately deserved through the priest’s merit to receive back the sight he had lost.

### 19

In the district called Commonia there was a certain lofty rock covered with various kinds of trees. Since the pagan rite had not yet been entirely dispelled, a crowd of fools gathered there to celebrate the solemnities of their religion each year.

For seven days they fulfilled their rites as though by an established right, feasting, leading dances, and reveling. But, as commonly happens amid wine and banquets, a sedition arose; many were wounded, and some were even slaughtered there according to custom. When this happened, they declared that it had occurred by unavoidable fate.

When Maurilius learned of this, he immediately went to the place with certain religious brothers. After spending one night there in vigil, fasting and praying, such a stench rose from the place at cockcrow that the blessed man could scarcely remain there with his companions.

When morning came, even those who had previously maintained the superstition of the place understood that they had been terrified by divine power. So that they would not oppose the bishop, they themselves hastened with him to cut down the entire grove and burn it in the fire.

After the place had thus been cleansed by fire, he immediately built there a basilica in honor of blessed Mary, the mother of Christ. The place, which had formerly been called the Rock or Grove of Mars, received the name “Castle of the Rock.”

### 20

In those same days it happened that the blessed Maurilius was summoned to the city of Le Mans to restore peace among certain people who were at odds.

> **Note:** Le Mans, a very large city of Gaul and capital of the province of the same name. It lies on the Sarthe, where that river receives the Huisne. —Bolland.

He came there without delay, restored peace among the disputants, and began to return. Before he reached the bridge of the Loir, the inhabitants of that place were devoutly awaiting his arrival, so that they might deserve to be strengthened by the bishop’s blessings.

Among them were the parents of a certain boy who had been burdened with an extremely severe illness from infancy. Knowing that the bishop would pass along the road, they placed their son beside it and said:

> “If he wishes, he will be able to obtain health for our little child—the man who obtained life for a dead boy even after the tomb.”

The child was indeed so tightly bound by the painful severity of his illness, with the sinews of all his limbs contracted, that he was curled up almost into a circle, so that he seemed more like a ball or wheel than to bear the form of a human being.

When the bishop arrived, everyone fell in a crowd at his feet while imploring his blessing, praying that in his compassion he would have pity on the sick boy. Compelled by their prayers, he immediately prostrated himself in prayer with tears. He did not rise from prayer before the child’s twisted legs began to straighten and each of his limbs began to stretch out.

Then he rose from prayer, took the boy by the hand, and immediately restored him unharmed to his parents. Thus the blessed Maurilius continued the journey he had begun.

When he reached the port of the river Loir, he found no ship there, but all the vessels were held on the opposite bank.

> **Note:** The Lédus is a river of Narbonese Gaul, now called *le Lez* in its own language. But there is no doubt that the Loir is meant here, in French *le Loir*. This river rises in the province of Perche, flows down through the district of Belsia in the territory of Chartres, then waters various places, and finally empties into the Sarthe a little above Angers. —Bolland.

Nor was there a sailor present who could bring a vessel. While he waited and there was no one to ferry him across, suddenly, by divine command, all the boats were moved away from the shore and brought to the opposite side for the bishop’s service.

After he had given thanks to almighty God, they boarded the ships and crossed with God alone as their pilot, without the assistance of human sailors. Nevertheless, when the sailors who had hurried up arrived, he ordered that they be given their fare, as though he had crossed through their labor.

### 21

The blessed man had purchased from the Church’s resources a certain estate called Geriacum, intended to provide food for captives, widows, and orphans, as well as assistance for clerics and the poor.

One day, as he was going around it with the brothers in order to carry out some work there, a horned heifer, driven by demonic impulse, came charging at him in a circle with tremendous force, bellowing loudly and raging with fierce eyes.

> **Note:** A similar event is recorded as having been performed by Martin of Tours in his Life, book III, by Fortunatus.

When the blessed bishop opposed it with the sign of the cross, the devil immediately emerged from its head in the form of a crow, flew away, and suddenly vanished like smoke. Many of the faithful who accompanied him were deemed worthy to see these things with their bodily eyes.

The heifer immediately became gentler and mingled with its herd like a sheep; thereafter it harmed no one.

### 22

One day, as Maurilius was safely traveling by boat down the river Maine into the bed of the Loire—

> **Note:** A river of Gaul called the Maine. It rises on the border of Normandy, flows through the territory of Le Mans, and waters the city of Mayenne and Laval. Above Angers, enlarged by the Sarthe and the Loir, it empties into the Loire. —Bolland.

—he had fallen briefly asleep in the stern of the ship, exhausted by fasting and prayer. Suddenly, while the enemy of the human race lay in wait, the waves of the deep began to swell, so that, with the waters falling from above, the ship seemed about to sink beneath the waves.

Then his disciples, terrified by fear, awakened him, saying:

> “Rise as quickly as possible and come to the aid of those placed in the shipwreck of supreme death.”

When he awoke, he said to them mildly:

> “Why do you seek me? You, brothers, could have dealt with it yourselves.”

Then he took a small vessel containing blessed liquid. As soon as he sprinkled the oil into the deep with prayer and the sign of the cross, the storm, which had been raging, immediately ceased, its winds becoming gentle.

Joyful and unharmed, they reached the port.

### 23

A certain young catechumen belonging to the Church entrusted to Maurilius had contracted such a violent fever, while Maurilius was absent, that he breathed out his spirit before he could be regenerated by baptism in the sacred font.

> **Note:** Magnobodus does not say that this man was dead, but that, already in imminent danger of death and scarcely still breathing his final breath, he was restored by Maurilius to his former health.

Without delay, his parents, with immense tears, carried him to the church while a place for the funeral was being prepared. Suddenly it was announced that the blessed Maurilius was present.

When he learned that the boy had died without the remedy of baptism, he groaned. Then, sensing through the Spirit that power was present to him, he ordered everyone to leave the small room in which the body lay.

Remaining alone with the boy, he prostrated himself in prayer with a groan, as was customary. Wetting the floor with his tears, after scarcely the space of an hour had passed, he saw the dead man gradually move all his limbs.

As soon as he rose from prayer, he returned him alive and unharmed to his parents, who were standing outside the door, and consecrated him with holy baptism.

Finally, two lepers who, at that same time, were covered and disfigured by various wounds asked the blessed man for a remedy of health. He healed them in an instant, curing them by his word alone.

> **Note:** Magnobodus adds that these lepers, who had asked Maurilius for alms, received health.

### 24

A certain pilgrim, wearing the garb of a penitent during the winter season and traveling through many villages and cities in search of medicine for his soul, eagerly sought the blessed Maurilius, whose reputation for goodness he had already heard, so that he might hear from him a word of salvation. He was a traveler, far exiled from his homeland, journeying with other pilgrims.

> **Note:** Magnobodus recounts this event somewhat differently and does not say that the pilgrim undertook that journey in order to see and meet Saint Maurilius.

But before he could reach him, he was overtaken by sudden death on the road and died.

When some pilgrims and many people from the neighboring regions had gathered at the pilgrim’s death, it happened that the chosen priest of God, who tirelessly labored to supply the needs of the flock entrusted to him, arrived at the corpse of the righteous and holy pilgrim as he was returning from the village of Saponaria.

> **Note:** The village of Saponaria is mentioned in the will of Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, where it is identified as lying on the river Cher.

After he had performed the customary funeral office for the absolution of the soul and had spoken to the people about religion, marvelous to relate, the dead man suddenly rose openly before everyone and, giving thanks to God with the others, clearly showed that the Lord had raised him through the blessed Maurilius.

When the crowds saw and heard this, they raised voices of praise to heaven.

### 25

To speak finally, the works of Maurilius are many and indescribable, and the human mind cannot comprehend what divine power accomplished through him.

Nevertheless, let us briefly relate something of his daily life for the edification of those who hear. From the beginning of his episcopate until the end of his life, in order to fulfill the canonical precept, he always had poor food, little water, and humble furnishings.

When the days of holy Lent arrived, throughout the entire season of affliction his food was, as has been said, dry and eaten in the evening on the third day; he had warm water, a little salt, and barley bread. During those days he did not set foot in public, always wearing sackcloth and ashes beneath his clothing.

Yet he was always robust in body, and his face was red like a rose. When he reached old age, he suffered neither in his head, nor his teeth, nor his sight, nor his stomach, nor any of his other limbs; he was not tormented by pains in his organs, nor had the dry earth lying upon him crushed his limbs. Rather, he always appeared wholly sound in body, sounder still in mind, and ever stronger in both.

For he held fast to the good that Maurilius had chosen; he did not abandon it but brought it to completion. Nothing was more pleasing than his severity, and nothing more severe than his pleasantness. He was silent in speech and speaking through silence. Cleanliness was neglected by him, and his clothing was unadorned.

26. Since he had flourished in such virtues from the very beginning of his childhood and perceived that the day of his departure was drawing near, he ordered a double crypt for his burial to be built not far from the city of Angers, on the northern side of that city. When it had been completed, one Sunday, after he had duly finished the service of the holy solemnity, being stricken with a slight illness, he summoned all the clergy and commended to them the final day of his departure, saying:

“I am entering the way of all flesh; but I admonish you: preserve charity, guard love, cherish chastity, be patient toward everyone, and always remember that you have all been redeemed at the price of Christ’s blood.”

Meanwhile, such crowds of people from every neighboring region came out of a desire to visit him as the city of Angers could contain, mourning and weeping greatly because they were about to be deprived of so great a patron. The most devout father, now standing at the very point of death, absolved them all with great devotion and strengthened them with blessings. On the seventh day of his illness, and in the ninetieth and final year of his whole life, Maurilius, the pious shepherd and teacher, returned his soul to almighty God on the thirtieth year of his episcopate, on the Ides of September, before many assembled crowds and choirs of singers, just as he had received it through the baptism of the sacred font.

[Note: Magnobodus says that Saint Maurilius governed the Church for forty years in the second rank of the priesthood, and presided over the episcopal see for thirty years in the dignity of the pontifical office. From this Launoy concludes that he could not have been ordained priest and bishop by Saint Martin of Tours, since, according to the testimony of Gregory of Tours—accepted by all learned authorities—Martin governed the Church of Tours for only twenty-six years. The Bollandists, however, maintain that the figure of forty years during which Saint Maurilius is said to have been a priest includes the years of his episcopate, which cannot be separated from his priesthood, so that he held the priesthood for ten years before being inaugurated as bishop. Indeed, Magnobodus says that he stayed in the village of Calonna after being ordained priest by Saint Martin and withdrawing from him, until the time when he was inaugurated bishop. Yet, according to the other Life written by Raino, he is said to have stayed there no more than twelve years. If he completed forty years as a priest of the second rank and thirty as bishop, he would already have been ordained priest at the age of twenty, which is not very plausible.]

27. When his holy little body was carried to the tomb on the following day, two men born blind from their mother’s womb, as soon as they were able to touch the coffin of the holy body, immediately merited to receive the light they had never possessed, thereby revealing the merits of the bishop. One of the townsmen was also afflicted by paralysis and had been confined to a little bed for thirty years.

[Note: Magnobodus relates that this paralytic had been held in bed by severe illness for twenty-eight years.]

When he heard the choir of singers carrying Maurilius, he immediately leapt from his bed like a stag and, with no one restraining him, reached the body of blessed Maurilius. After touching and kissing the bier of the blessed dead man, he immediately merited to recover his former health. Thus, when he had been buried in the glory of such great honor, the Lord showed everyone after his burial how great and of what kind his merit had been before God, adorning his tomb daily with his virtues and miracles. He is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

# The Passion of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius

[Col. 0575]

## Preliminary Notice on the Acts of the Passion of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius

The Acts of the passion of blessed Dionysius, bishop, and of Rusticus and Eleutherius were first published by Franciscus Bosquetus, bishop of Montpellier, in his work entitled *Ecclesiastical History of Gaul*, Part II. He believes that these Acts were written before the time of Dagobert I, king of Austrasia, who began to reign in 621 or 622 and died in 637 or 638, since they make no mention of the basilica of Saint Dionysius, built by Dagobert himself and furnished with great munificence. Hadrian Valesius agrees with him in the work entitled *Discussions on Basilicas, etc.*, against the *Defenses* of Launoy, theologian of Paris, chapter 4. He likewise believes that these Acts were written by Venantius Fortunatus, following Peter de Marca, archbishop of Toulouse, who judged that the same passion of Saint Dionysius had been composed by Fortunatus.

Launoy, however, devotes himself entirely to demonstrating that these Acts were in no way written by Venantius Fortunatus. He infers this:

1. The author makes no mention of Saint Dionysius’s miracle, which Gregory of Tours records in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 72—something he certainly would have done if he had been Fortunatus, Gregory’s closest friend, to whom Gregory’s writings could not therefore have been unknown.

2. The author makes no mention of the prefect Fescenninus, who pronounced sentence against Saint Dionysius, nor of the tower-like tomb in which the bones of Saint Dionysius himself were buried in the basilica. Nor does he mention the pious custom by which people cleared themselves by oath at the martyr’s tomb, although Gregory of Tours, Fortunatus’s contemporary, records all these things.

3. These Acts are filled with fables. They relate that the bodies of those martyrs were placed on ships by their executioners so that they might be thrown into the river Seine—as though they could not have been thrown into the Seine without a vessel, or as though several ships were needed for a task that one could have accomplished. The writer then adds that a certain matron invited the executioners to dinner, so that meanwhile her servants and household might carry away the saints’ bodies—as though the boatmen could not have prevented this, and as though they had not in fact been prevented from doing so. Nor is it plausible that the bodies of the martyrs, carried away by the matron’s servants, should have lain unburied for so long until they could be transported to the prepared place, without being torn apart by birds and wild beasts.

4. The author relates that Saint Dionysius was sent into Gaul by Clement, whereas Gregory of Tours writes that he came into Gaul under Decius.

5. The author writes that the city of the Parisians was distinguished both by an assembly of Germans and by nobility, and that it was crowded with inhabitants. None of this suits the age of Dionysius the Great, when Paris was a small town and did not extend its authority into Germany; that happened later under the Frankish kings Chlothar and Sigibert.

Replying point by point, Valesius says that it was not necessary for someone writing the passion of Saint Dionysius, rather than his Life, to compile all the miracles performed by him—especially, I would add, since these Acts of the passion seem to have been arranged for reading at the public assemblies of the Church. In such works, therefore, matters narrated at length in the *Acts* or *Lives* were indicated briefly and compressed into a concise style, as we noted in its proper place concerning the Life of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, written by Fortunatus.

Nor does it matter whether the author mentioned the prefect Fescenninus, or the tower-like tomb of Saint Dionysius, narrowing to a point like a pinnacle, or other matters of that kind. Such details belong to the writer of a Life, not of a Passion; here they are touched upon in briefer language, with only what is more necessary being included.

The bodies of Saints Dionysius, Eleutherius, and the others were placed on ships by the executioners so that they might not be scattered here and there and thrown onto the riverbank, but sunk into the depths of the Seine and concealed, lest Christians find and recover them. The matron invited the executioners to a banquet before the bodies had been placed on the ships and guarded by the boatmen; they were still lying at the place where they had been struck down. The matron or her servants afterward hid them—burying them in the lap of plowed earth—and did not expose them to birds and wild beasts until they could be carried away after the violence of the persecution had subsided.

Nor is there any difficulty in the fact that Gregory of Tours says that Dionysius came into Gaul under Decius, while the author of the Passion writes that he was sent into Gaul by Clement, the successor of Peter, or by the successors of the apostles. Two opinions and traditions circulated concerning the time when Saint Dionysius was sent into Gaul; nor does the author say that he was the Areopagite.

Finally, the author of the Passion wrote at a time when part of Germany was subject to the Frankish empire. Writers often adapt their whole style of expression to the period about which they are writing. Thus Zosimus, who flourished under the emperor Anastasius, when Clovis was reigning among the Franks, makes the same mistake and calls Paris a little town of Germany. In *History*, book 3, he writes:

> “While Julian was staying in Paris—this is a small town of Germany—…”

Nor, if he calls Paris an island crowded with inhabitants, does he thereby say that it was large; although in this respect too he may have adjusted his language to the period in which he was writing.

In this disagreement between distinguished men, then, when I state what should be thought, it seems that neither side has produced anything sufficient to show that these Acts of Saint Dionysius must either be taken away from Fortunatus or certainly attributed to him. The considerations Launoy brings forward are slight grounds for absolutely denying that the Acts belong to Fortunatus; and what Valesius adduces proves only that they were composed before the age of Dagobert and are compatible with the time of Fortunatus.

Some plausibility is nevertheless added to this opinion by the friendship between Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, and Fortunatus. Germanus may perhaps, by virtue of that friendship, have requested Fortunatus to write the Passion of his predecessor for reading at the public assemblies of the Church. It is also supported by Fortunatus’s constant interest in collecting and writing the Acts of the saints, and by a certain affinity with Fortunatus’s own style, apparent both in the use of sentences and in the structure of the words, as anyone who compares them can recognize.

We therefore publish these Acts here as they were published by the distinguished Boquetus in his work entitled *Ecclesiastical History of Gaul*, Part II, and we have illustrated them with such notes as we could provide. Valesius also read them in the Musciacensis Codex, but reports that it was full of errors.

[Col. 0577]

## Passion of the Holy Martyrs

[Note: Gregory of Tours, book 1 of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 28, relates that under Decius Saint Dionysius was sent into Gaul with six other bishops, who established sees for themselves in different cities there. He infers this from the Acts of Saint Saturninus, bishop and martyr of Toulouse, who was made bishop of Toulouse under the consuls Decius and Gratus, that is, in the year 250. Concerning this Dionysius he likewise reports that, after being installed as bishop of Paris, “he ended the present life by the sword after suffering various punishments for the name of Christ.”]

[Col. 0578A] In a diploma of Theodoric of Châlons—which is found after the works of Gregory of Tours in the Paris edition of 1699, column 1384—Dionysius is said to have come into the province of Gaul with his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, the first after the apostles, under the ordination of blessed Clement, successor of the apostle Peter. This is also how the Acts of the passion published here read. The reason for this discrepancy will be examined elsewhere.]

### Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius

Who suffered at Paris on the seventh day before the Ides of October. (C, S)*

[Col. 0577A] 1. Although the glorious passions of the martyrs and their precious struggles for the Lord deserve to be written down because of the greatness of their miracles, they nevertheless cannot be embraced without trembling fear. For when the undertaking of great events is considered, the magnitude of the work attempted is rightly feared, since a frail discourse cannot explain as much as the truth of the passion itself demands.

Yet, even if the presentation of so great a matter seems to have a difficult beginning, the mind breathes again amid its hesitation because the divine instructor always forms its servant by divine instruction, granting both a beginning to the one who starts and perfection to his intelligence.

With this consideration, therefore, taking up the boldness of excessive daring, we begin, with the help of the divinity itself, to disclose matters that had long been overshadowed by silence. For, as the testimony of truth declares, more has been learned through the report of the faithful than has been transmitted to us in writings for reading.

Thus it is inferred with some confidence that the recentness of the still-believing peoples, distressed by the cruelty of the pagans,

[Note: Perhaps “grieved” or “distressed.”]

feared to write what it nevertheless rejoiced that the servants of God had achieved, since writings are undoubtedly judged to have been fulfilled when the speech of the faithful bears witness to them.

One must believe these things and, once justified doubt has been wiped away,

[Note: Perhaps “once the darkness has been wiped away.”]

confess with all one’s strength that those who were deemed worthy to undergo martyrdom through confession of our Lord and God wished to endure even greater things than the report transmitted through succeeding generations seems able to recall.

Let common prayer therefore obtain this: that the devout writer may receive pardon if, through ignorance, he has omitted some virtues. For even if the whole community deserves to believe that not everything can be accounted for,

[Note: The passage is corrupt.]

let it believe that the servant of God experienced things even greater than the account of his passion can explain. For how did that place rejoice to possess the Lord’s worshiper and merit his protection, when we recognize that a fellowship of other saints was found to have been granted to it? Therefore, according to the report of the faithful, let us explain, with the help of the martyrs themselves, as much as they grant us to know about themselves.

[Col. 0579C] 2. After the saving passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, after the unique and singular mystery of his resurrection, and after his ascension, by which he showed human beings that he had never been absent from the place to which he returned, the preaching of the apostles, destined to benefit all nations, followed.

When they saw that their own passions were approaching, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, they taught what they had learned from our Lord Jesus Christ. As faith increased, not a few merited becoming confessors; thus the Catholic Church rejoices that she merited martyrs.

The election of the apostles judged these men, whose virtue the conflict with their persecutors could not overcome and whom the testing of flames rendered precious like gold, suitable to receive the Lord’s commands. The apostles entrusted to them the evangelical precepts, which were always to be observed, and prudently decreed by God’s arrangement that chosen men should be joined to them in episcopal honor, so that those won over by their preaching might more easily be advanced to the ministry of the sacred altar.

From this crowd of confessors the city of Toulouse rejoices that it received as bishop the holy man Saturninus, worthy of veneration. The impiety of the watching crowd gave him, bound with many cords to the feet of a bull, to be dashed against the steps of the Capitol. When the structure of his sacred head was broken apart, the violence of repeated blows scattered his brain; yet by such a descent he attained ascent to the Lord.

Happy was the man of such great merit and such dignity and virtue, to whom it was granted to be first a teacher and then a martyr, who fulfilled by evident examples what he had taught in words.

By a similar grace, the most blessed Paul, bishop and confessor, won the province of Narbonne through salutary speech. Domestic tribulation so exercised him that you would have recognized him as truly the Lord’s servant. But thanks be to you, Lord Jesus Christ, who allowed the weapons of the hostile enemy to become a test rather than wounds for your faithful, and who grant them such labor as a reward that none of your own may rejoice that the enemy found him unarmed.

Since the service undertaken turns toward the particular deeds of the patron, we do not pursue in full everything learned about the servant of God. It is enough that we not be forgetful of him. In such matters, it is more fitting for the faithful to believe than for human report to be able to display.

3. Saint Dionysius, then,

[Note: Alternatively: “who, according to blessed Clement, successor of the apostle Peter…”]

who, as they relate, had received from the successors of the apostles the task of distributing the seeds of the divine word among the nations, wherever he recognized the error of paganism to be raging more fiercely, went there fearlessly, inflamed by the ardor of faith, and, under the Lord’s guidance, reached Paris. He did not fear to confront the savagery of an unbelieving people, because the memory of punishments previously endured strengthened his courage; and he who had merited being a confessor did not hesitate to approach the peoples as a preacher.

[Note: It may reasonably seem strange that Saint Dionysius is here said to have been sent into Gaul with companions to spread the Gospel of Christ by the successors of the apostles, and, as it was read elsewhere, by Clement himself, the disciple of the apostles. Gregory of Tours and the authentic Acts of Saint Saturninus, bishop of Toulouse, published by the distinguished Ruinart among the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, page 109 of the Verona edition of 1731, report that Saturninus was installed as bishop of Toulouse only under the consuls Decius and Gratus, that is, in the year 250. Accordingly, Dionysius too—if he came into Gaul with Saturninus, as Gregory believed—would have been sent into Gaul only a few years earlier. It must therefore be said that the author of these Acts preferred to follow the popular opinion then current in Gaul. This is also indicated by his words, “who, as they relate, from the successors of the apostles,” and so forth. He may have feared that this opinion would be challenged when composing Acts intended to be recited annually among the common people or in the assembly of the Church. The same opinion appears in the diploma of Theodoric of Châlons, mentioned above, where blessed Dionysius and his companions are said to have come into Gaul sent by blessed Clement. They believed that this was Dionysius the Areopagite mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles. This opinion was later followed by Symeon Metaphrastes and Abbot Hilduin, as may be seen in Surius under 9 October.]

At that time the city in question was distinguished by an assembly of Germans and by nobility. It was healthy in climate, pleasant because of its river, fertile in its lands, exceedingly rich in vineyards, and wooded with trees. It was crowded with inhabitants, filled with commerce, and the space of the island—more like an island than a city—which the surrounding waters of the river provided for habitation was made small by the increasing crowds of settlers. The common people, drawn together by the attraction of pleasure, had nearly contracted their territory within the enclosure of the walls.

[Note: Valesius and others read *constipata populis*, “crowded with inhabitants.” See what we indicated about this passage in the preliminary remarks.]

The servant of God determined that this was a place worth seeking. When he first approached it fearlessly, armed with faith and strengthened by steadfast confession, he built a church for those peoples, where none had previously existed, and established the customary official service of the clergy. He advanced approved persons to the dignity of secular rank.

[Note: The same Valesius, arguing against Launoy, shows that it was fitting for Dionysius immediately to erect a basilica or temple at Paris, in which sacred worship might be conducted, and to furnish it with a number of clergy or, as it is called here, official service. He argues that this should not be considered false or implausible, as Launoy wishes. In the Life preserved by Surius under 9 October, written by Symeon Metaphrastes, it is related that when Dionysius found Paris a city indeed rich and fertile in soil and fields but disfigured by the treachery and savagery of its citizens, he went about searching to see whether he could find a suitable place for rest. When he found one, he immediately, as far as he could, established a temple … he raised an oratory and a temple, which was plainly the salvation of souls, and so forth.]

Thus girded with faith and already strengthened by the construction of the basilica, he did not cease to make known to the nations the God whom he knew. Setting both his judgment and his mercy before everyone, he gradually joined to God those whom he was taking away from the devil.

The Lord also deigned to perform such great miracles through him that he won the hearts of the rebellious pagans no less by miracles than by preaching. In wondrous fashion, an armed crowd could not resist an unarmed man. The stubbornness of Germany submitted to that contest, and, moved by compunction of heart, begged that the gentle yoke of Christ be placed upon it.

The idols that they themselves had made at their own expense and by their own efforts were also destroyed by them. Having found the harbor of salvation, they rejoiced that the shipwrecks of idols were perishing. The portion conquered by the devil mourned when the victorious army of the Church triumphed over it.

Then the ancient enemy, seeing that what had been established for the Lord’s benefit was perishing through the continual conversion of the peoples, turned the whole machinery of his craft against the works that had been built. He armed the leaders of his faction, who mourned the destruction of their gods, for a sudden persecution, so that they might hasten to destroy by various punishments those who had proclaimed that the one true God must be worshiped and feared, lest anyone survive who could acquire what was being lost.

When the sentence of persecution had been made public, the rejoicing crowd of the impious advanced and conspired to fight against the Lord’s people. They did not hesitate to attack with the sword those whom the Lord had shown to be marked as his own.

As they traveled through the western part of the world in search of Christians, they found Saint Dionysius fighting against unbelievers at Paris. With him, the fury of persecution found Rusticus, a priest, and Eleutherius, an archdeacon. These blessed men never endured absence from Saint Dionysius; the persecutor’s interrogation found them together and could not discover whom to separate from the fellowship of martyrdom.

When questioned, they confessed the one true God in the Trinity. Overcome by terror and afflicted with many insults and punishments, tortured by blows, they testified that they were Christians. Even as they saw the blow of the striker, they proclaimed in a loud voice of confession that they were servants of our Lord and God.

Persisting in this constancy of faith, they gave their bodies to the earth and brought their blessed souls to heaven. They merited to depart to the Lord with such a confession that, after their heads had been cut off, the still-trembling tongue was thought to be confessing the Lord.

A blessed and exceedingly pleasing fellowship to God: among them neither could one be first, another second, nor a third; but, confessing the Trinity, they merited to adorn a venerable place with a threefold martyrdom.

The executioners feared that the most faithful and proven devotion of the converted people would bury the bodies of the saints and their relics for their own benefit and protection. They therefore chose to entrust the bodies of the martyrs to the foul and deep currents of the Seine, so that they might be destroyed. They ordered them to be placed on ships and taken to the current they had selected.

[Note: This matron is called Catulla by Symeon Metaphrastes. He says that she appeased the anger of the lictors with money, after it had arisen because the bodies of Saint Dionysius and his companions had been carried away.]

Then a certain matron, although still entangled in the error of the pagans, showed by her intention that she desired conversion. Thinking of doing something pleasing to the Lord, she employed a subtle plan: she asked the executioners to come to a banquet. While extending to them the abundance of the hospitality they desired, she distracted them from remembering what they had undertaken to do and secretly entrusted to her faithful people the careful concealment of the saints’ bodies, which were to be stolen away.

[Note: Perhaps “those men.”]

When these men learned of the arrangement, they hastened to carry out what had been commanded them. They commendably stole and concealed the bodies at the sixth milestone from the city, in plowed earth prepared for seed.

Afterward, when the sowing had been done, the crop did not deny its service. Fertilized by such rich abundance, it poured forth its bounty so generously that both the cultivator obtained a hundredfold harvest and the homeland merited salvation.

As the crop grew, what would benefit the people of Paris remained hidden for a long time. The matron mentioned above, however, having forgotten these secrets, saw in a dream the place seething, which preserved the bones of such great men. She sought it with the diligence required and, when it was found, marked it by constructing a lofty mausoleum.

Thereafter the Christians built a basilica over the bodies of the martyrs at great expense and with splendid adornment. There, through the daily work of our Lord Jesus Christ, the frequency of their miracles proves their merits, and the sick learn how fitting it is to honor God’s servants: there blindness receives sight, weakness receives the power to walk, and the closed doors of the ears receive hearing.

Nor should this be omitted:

[Note: Perhaps “Nor should this be kept silent.”]

those tormented by the infestation of unclean spirits, when they are brought to the place mentioned above to be examined by divine power, are compelled by the authority of the saints themselves to indicate, assigning their names, where each of the martyrs has been placed.

The Lord willed that we rejoice in their passion on the seventh day before the Ides of October—he who promised that our fruit would be a hundredfold. To him belong honor and glory, power and dominion, forever and ever. Amen.

# Exposition of the Creed

[Col. 0583]

## On Fortunatus’s Exposition of the Creed

The distinguished Muratorius, in volume 2 of his *Anecdota*, page 212, published an exposition of the Creed commonly called the Athanasian Creed. He extracted this exposition from a parchment codex of the Ambrosian Library, copied, as he conjectures, about six hundred years before his own writing by the hand of a scribe. In the codex the exposition bore this title:

> “Exposition of the Catholic Faith by Fortunatus.”

He declares, however, that it is uncertain whether Fortunatus himself was the author of the Creed commonly called the Athanasian, or only of this exposition of the Creed.

Just as he says that others are free to investigate the author of the Athanasian Creed and follow their own conjectures, so he insists that he too may, relying on conjectures of equal weight, suspect Fortunatus to have been the author of that celebrated Creed.

The considerations that lead him to this opinion are these:

1. It is by no means implausible that Venantius Fortunatus, an Italian by birth and later bishop of Poitiers, composed that Creed, since most authorities agree that it should be attributed to a Gallic man, or to someone who lived in Gaul and for some time resided at Trier:

> “For it was celebrated before all others by Gallic writers, received and commended by the synods and bishops of Gaul from ancient times; and the opinion has also become widespread that it was worked out at Trier, the metropolis of Gaul.”

Fortunatus, having departed from Italy for Gaul, lived there until the end of his life. He was joined in friendship to Nicetius, bishop of Trier, and to Magnericus, who succeeded Nicetius in that see, as is clear from poems 11, 12, and 13 of book 3.

Muratorius’s conjecture may also be confirmed by the fact that Fortunatus openly relates that he himself came to Trier, saying in book 10, chapter 10:

> I am led to Trier, where the lofty walls lie open:
>
> A noble city, equally the head of nobles.

The distinguished Muratorius adds:

The chronology also agrees with the period in which the Creed seems to have been composed. Since it is generally believed that it was written after the condemnation of the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches, both of whom are mentioned so explicitly in it, it could certainly have been composed by Fortunatus, who did not die until the sixth century was drawing to a close. The faith of the Council of Chalcedon could also have been employed in proposing and confirming the Church’s doctrines.

The fact that the Creed mentions the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son likewise shows that it should be attributed to Fortunatus rather than to Vincent of Lérins. Vincent died under the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, that is, around the year 445, before this opinion concerning the Holy Spirit had generally begun to be counted among the dogmas of faith—or, rather, before what already belonged to the truth of faith had begun to be expressed against the new error that later arose. No trace of the doctrine appears in Vincent’s *Commonitorium*. By contrast, in the age of Fortunatus this formula began to be used more clearly by the most learned men and was approved by some councils of bishops.

One apparent obstacle is that the Creed bears the name of Athanasius, so that it might instead be attributed to Vigilius of Thapsus or to Vincent of Lérins. It was customary for them to title their short works not with their own names but with those of the ancient Fathers of the Church, especially Saint Athanasius, in order to lend them greater authority. Muratorius replies that the name of Athanasius attached itself to the Creed only many centuries later, since the oldest codices do not bear it.

When investigating why Fortunatus might have set forth this formula of faith, Muratorius proposes that questions concerning the doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches were being debated in Gaul during the sixth century, as may be understood from the formula of faith sent by Pope Pelagius to King Childebert. Fortunatus therefore, whether on this occasion or on another that presented itself, declared his judgment and faith by composing this distinguished Creed, just as everyone agrees that he composed and published an exposition of the Apostles’ Creed; he was therefore by no means alien to such a task.

Finally, Muratorius says, other works of Fortunatus contain what may be called seeds of words and ideas indicating that this Creed is genuinely Fortunatus’s offspring. He begins his exposition of the Apostles’ Creed in this way:

> At the beginning there is set forth the splendid foundation of heavenly testimony, because no one who has not rightly believed concerning salvation can be saved.

This corresponds to the words of the Athanasian Creed:

> This is the Catholic faith: unless each person believes it faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.

To these may be added the lines expressed by Fortunatus in book 8, chapter 5, which resemble the doctrine and structure of the words appearing in the Athanasian Creed:

> That God embraced flesh, and flesh was joined to him:
>
> God remains, and becomes man; Christ bears both.
>
> God did not pass into flesh; God assumes limbs,
>
> Not changing himself, but taking members to himself.
>
> One in both natures, true in each:
>
> Equal here to his mother, in divinity to the Father.
>
> He confounds nothing of his own, but joins all ours to himself,
>
> The man whom both parents beget without sin.
>
> Born from the Father, possessing what is divine, and from his mother what is human;
>
> Sublime from the Father, humble from his mother.
>
> When the incorporeal one mercifully puts on bodily limbs,
>
> He becomes equal to his mother, and thereby lesser than the Father, and so forth.

Muratorius adds to these arguments the authority of the Ambrosian Codex. Besides other material, it contains an exposition of the Apostles’ Creed “written by Fortunatus the priest.” This is the same exposition that is read attached to the works of Venantius Fortunatus in Brower’s edition. Later, after other material, there also appears the exposition of the Athanasian Creed under discussion, bearing the title:

> “Exposition of the Catholic Faith by Fortunatus.”

Nevertheless, the distinguished Muratorius candidly admits that he does not trust his conjectures so completely as to be able to assert with certainty whether the Athanasian Creed itself, or only its exposition, should be attributed to Fortunatus.

The authors of the *History of French Literature*, however, deny that this exposition is the work of our Fortunatus. To their judgment I add my own: the style of the exposition is more polished and refined than the style generally familiar from Fortunatus.

As for the Creed itself, I shall say nothing. So many opinions of the most learned men have been advanced concerning it that it is not appropriate here, in this place and work, to subject them to examination. Here, however, we append both the Creed commonly called the Athanasian and its exposition, transcribed from very ancient codices as they were published by the distinguished Muratorius.

[Col. 0585]

## Copy of the Athanasian Creed
[Col. 0585A] 1. Whoever wishes to be saved must above all hold the catholic faith; unless each person preserves it whole and inviolate, he will undoubtedly perish eternally. The catholic faith, moreover, is this: that we venerate one God in Trinity and the Trinity in unity, neither confusing the persons nor separating the substance. For one is the person of the Father, another that of the Son, and another that of the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0585] Another hand adds: “But of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”] There is one divinity, equal glory, and coeternal majesty. Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such also is the Holy Spirit. The Father is uncreated, the Son uncreated, and the Holy Spirit uncreated. The Father is immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, and the Holy Spirit immeasurable. The Father is eternal, the Son eternal, and the Holy Spirit eternal. Yet there are not three eternals, but one eternal. Just as there are not three uncreated beings, [Col. 0585B] nor three immeasurable beings, but one immeasurable and one uncreated.

Likewise, the Father is almighty, the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit almighty; yet there are not three almighty beings, but one almighty. Thus the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; yet there are not three gods, but one God. Thus the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord; yet there are not three Lords, but one Lord. For just as Christian truth compels us to confess each person individually as both God and Lord, so catholic religion forbids us to say that there are three gods or three lords.

The Father was made by no one, neither created nor begotten. The Son is from the Father alone, not made or created, but begotten. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, created, or begotten, but proceeding; he is coeternal with the Father and the Son. [Col. 0585C] Thus there is one Father, not three Fathers; one Son, not three Sons; one Holy Spirit, not three Holy Spirits.

And in this Trinity there is nothing prior or posterior, nothing greater or less, but [Col. 0586A] all three persons are coeternal with one another and coequal. Thus, in every respect, as has already been said, both the Trinity in unity and the unity in Trinity must be venerated. Therefore, whoever wishes to be saved must think thus concerning the Trinity.

But it is necessary for eternal salvation also to believe faithfully in the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. The right faith, therefore, is that we believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is equally God and man. He is God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages; and he is man, born in the age from the substance of his mother. Perfect God and perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh; equal to the Father according to his divinity, less than the Father according to his humanity.

Although he is God and man, he is nevertheless not two, but one Christ. [Col. 0586B] He is one, not by the conversion of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God; altogether one, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person. For just as rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.

He suffered for our salvation, descended to the underworld, rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sat at the right hand of the Father, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead. At his coming all human beings will give an account of their own deeds; those who have done good will go into eternal life, and those who have done evil into eternal fire. This is the catholic faith, and unless each person believes it faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.

2. On the same line of the Scripture the following occurs: “Nurse, mother, him who made you, because he made you such that he himself might become in you. Nurse him who, by being conceived, gave you the fruit of fertility and, by being born, did not take away the honor of virginity.”

[Col. 0585]

[Note: [Col. 0585D] The distinguished Francis Anthony Zacharia found this same exposition of the faith in a fourteenth-century paper manuscript in Florence, but with no author’s name explicitly given, as he himself reports in the book entitled *Literary Excursus through Italy*, p. 307, where he noted various readings, which we too shall indicate in their places.] EXPOSITION OF THE CATHOLIC FAITH BY FORTUNATUS. (C,S)*

[Col. 0585D] Whoever wishes to be saved must above all hold the catholic faith; unless each person preserves it whole and inviolate, he will undoubtedly perish eternally. Faith is therefore necessary before all else, as apostolic authority teaches when it says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6). [Col. 0586D] For it is certain that no one can attain true blessedness unless he pleases God, and that no one can please God except through faith. Faith is the foundation of all good things, the beginning of human salvation. Without it no one can attain fellowship with the children of God, because without it no one in this age receives the grace of justification, nor in the future will possess eternal life. And if anyone here does not walk by faith, he will not attain the blessed vision of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Catholic” means universal—that is, right—and it is what the whole Church must hold. The Church is called the gathering of Christians, or the assembly of peoples. It is not confined, like the assemblies of heretics, to certain parts of the regions, but is spread and extended throughout the whole world.

Let us venerate, believe in, worship, and confess one God in Trinity and the Trinity in unity: Trinity in persons, unity in substance. The prophet Isaiah did not conceal that this Trinity of persons and unity of nature had been revealed to him when he said that he saw seraphim [Col. 0587B] crying out: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isaiah 6:3). In the threefold repetition of “Holy” we plainly recognize the Trinity of persons; in the single expression “Lord God of Sabaoth” we recognize the unity of the divine nature.

Nor do we confuse the persons, as Sabellius errs, for he says that the same person is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We do not, therefore, confuse the persons, since there are altogether three persons. There is one who begets, one who is begotten, and one who proceeds. The Father is the one who begets, because he begot the Son; the Son is the one begotten, because the Father begot him; the Holy Spirit is the one who proceeds, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Father and the Son are coeternal and coequal with one another, and co-workers, as it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established”—that is, created by the Son of God—“and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6). [Note: [Col. 0587D] In the manuscript mentioned above it reads: “Where the Spirit is expressed in the singular, it shows the unity of the substance of the Godhead; where ‘all their power’ is expressed in the plural, it plainly demonstrates the Trinity of persons.”]

Where “his Spirit” is expressed in the singular, it plainly demonstrates the Trinity of persons, because the three are one, and the one is three. Nor do we separate the substance, as Arius chatters, because he says that there are three persons and falsely claims that there are also three substances. He says that the Son is less than the Father and is a creature, and that the Holy Spirit is still less than the Son, asserting that he is the administrator of the Father and the Son. We do not, therefore, separate the substance, because all three persons are one in the substance of the Godhead.

The person of the Father is one, because the Father is unbegotten, in that he was begotten by no one; the person of the Son is another, because the Son was begotten by the Father alone; the person of the Holy Spirit is another, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. But the divinity—that is, the deity—of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one; their glory—that is, their brightness—is equal; their majesty is coeternal. Majesty is glory, brightness, or power.

Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such also is the Holy Spirit—that is, in deity and omnipotence. The Father is uncreated, the Son uncreated, and the Holy Spirit also uncreated—that is, created by no one. [Col. 0588A] The Father is immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, and the Holy Spirit also immeasurable. He is not measurable in his nature, because he is without locality and without circumscription, wholly everywhere, present everywhere, powerful everywhere.

The Father is eternal, the Son eternal, and the Holy Spirit also eternal—that is, not three eternals, but one eternal God in three persons, who remains eternal without beginning and without end.

Likewise, the Father is almighty, the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit also almighty. He is called almighty because he can do all things and possesses power over all things. Therefore, if he can do all things, what is there that he cannot do? He cannot do what it is unfitting for the Almighty to be able to do. He cannot be deceived, because he is holy; he cannot die, because he is immortal life; he cannot come to an end, because he is infinite and everlasting.

Thus the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit also is God. [Note: [Col. 0587D] “God is power, not property” [perhaps: “of power, not of property”]; the proper name of the Father is “Father.”] “Father” is the proper name of the Father, “Son” the proper name of the Son, and “Holy Spirit” the proper name of the Holy Spirit.

Thus the Father is Lord, the Son is Lord, and the Holy Spirit is Lord. He is called Lord because he rules the whole creation, or because every creature serves his dominion. [Note: [Col. 0587D] In the same place: “He rules all things, and is Lord of all” [Col. 0588D: “ruler”].]

For just as Christian truth compels us to confess each person individually—that is, distinctly—as God and Lord, so, if you ask me, “What is the Father?” I shall answer, “God and Lord.” Likewise, if you ask me, “What is the Son?” I shall say, “God and Lord.” And if you say, “What is the Holy Spirit?” I shall say, “God and Lord.” Yet in these three persons I confess not three gods or three lords, but, as was said above, one God and one Lord.

Thus there is one Father, not three Fathers—that is, because the Father is always Father and never at any time Son. One Son, not three Sons—that is, because the Son is always Son and never at any time Father. One Holy Spirit, not three Holy Spirits—that is, because the Holy Spirit is always the Holy Spirit and never at any time Son or Father. This is the distinct property of the persons.

And in this Trinity there is nothing prior or posterior. For just as the Son never existed without the Father, so the Father never existed without the Son, and likewise the Father and Son never existed without the Holy Spirit. The Trinity is therefore coeternal, and the unity inseparable, without beginning and without end.

There is nothing greater or less. This expresses the equality of the persons, because the Trinity is equal and one deity, as the Apostle teaches and says: “Through the things that have been made, understood realities are seen, and through creation the Creator is understood,” according to these comparisons and many others.

The sun, its brightness, and its heat are three names, yet three are one. That which shines is what gives heat, and that which gives heat is what shines. [Note: [Col. 0588D] The examples brought forward at this point by the author of this exposition to show and explain the unity, in the same nature or essence, of the three divine persons, although in so unequal a matter they do not correspond in every respect to the proposed model, nevertheless tend toward this point: just as earthly and inanimate things, though one in nature, are related to one another in different ways and produce various effects, and are distinguished by different names, so nothing prevents the three persons, who are one by nature, from being distinguished in reality as they are related to one another, just as they are distinguished by their names. The author indicated this more explicitly above.] These three names are recognized to designate one reality.

[Col. 0589A] Thus the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, one in the substance of the Godhead, and are rightly believed to be an indivisible unity.

Likewise, in earthly things, vein, spring, and river are three names, yet three are one in their nature. Thus the substance and deity of the three persons—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are one.

The right faith, therefore, is that we believe and confess that the Lord Jesus Christ—Jesus is called “Savior” in Hebrew and in Latin, because he saves his people [Note: [Col. 0589D] The manuscript cited above adds “his own”—]; Christ is so called because he was divinely anointed with the Holy Spirit, as Isaiah says concerning his own person: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isaiah 61:1), etc. [Note: [Col. 0589D] In the same place: “in the person of Christ himself.”] Likewise, the Psalmist says of Christ the Lord: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

The Son of God is equally God and man. He is called “Son” from the happiness of his parents; “man” is derived from *humus*, earth, because he was made from the earth’s soil.

He is God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages—that is, God from God, light from light, radiance from radiance, strength from strength, power from power, life from life, eternity from eternity. In every respect, whatever the Father is in the divine substance, the Son also is.

For God the Father begot God the Son neither by will nor by necessity, but by nature. [Note: [Col. 0589D] The author of this exposition plainly takes “necessity” here to mean compulsion, indicating that God the Father begets the Son willingly, although, as he immediately adds, he begets him by nature and therefore necessarily.] Nor should one ask how he begot the Son—a matter unknown even to the angels and undisclosed to the prophets. Hence that outstanding prophet Isaiah says: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). As if he had said: No angel, no prophet.

The ineffable and immeasurable God is not to be scrutinized by his servants, but faithfully believed and loved in equal measure.

And he is man, born in the age from the substance of his mother. The Son of God, the Word made flesh—not that the Divinity had changed its deity, but that it assumed humanity. That is, the Word became flesh and took true human flesh from the Virgin’s womb. From the virginal womb a true man, as also true God, was born in the age, while the grace of virginity remained intact, [Note: [Col. 0589D] The cited manuscript reads: “Because the mother who gave birth remained a virgin before the birth and a virgin after the birth.”] because the mother gave birth and remained a virgin before and after the birth.

“In the age” means in this sixth millennium in which we now are. [Note: [Col. 0589D] The entire sentence from “for the ages” through “succeed” is absent in the manuscript. It adds instead: “God and man, Christ. One God, the Son of God, and himself the Son of the Virgin, because while the Godhead assumed humanity in the Virgin’s womb, and through the Virgin’s gate, whole and unharmed, entered the world by being born, he was the Virgin’s son and the man [perhaps: ‘human being’] whom he assumed.”] For the ages consist of generations, and they are called ages because they follow one another; as some pass away, others succeed them.

Perfect God, perfect man—that is, true God and true man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh, not, as the heretic Apollinaris first claimed, as though the Godhead had been in the flesh in place of a soul. Later, after he had been refuted by evangelical authority, he said: “He did indeed have a soul, which gave life to the body, but not a rational one.” On the contrary, the one who thinks catholicly says: “Subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh”—that is, a complete and perfect man.

He is equal to the Father according to his divinity, less than the Father according to his humanity—that is, according to the form of a servant, which he deigned to assume.

Although he is God and man, he is nevertheless not two, but one Christ. [Note: [Col. 0590D] The same manuscript reads: “The same Son of God, as we said above, so that divinity and humanity in Christ are equally the son of God the Father and the Virgin.”]

That is, there are two substances in Christ, divinity and humanity, but not two persons; there is one person. He is one, not by the conversion of divinity into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God. That is, not that the immutable Divinity was converted into flesh, but that he is one because, by assuming humanity, he began to be what he was not and did not lose what he was. He began to be man, which he had not previously been; he did not lose his deity, because [Col. 0590B] it remains immutable forever. [Note: [Col. 0590D] The same manuscript reads: “immutable”; and likewise below.]

He is altogether one, not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person. That is, the immutable divinity is with the man whom it deigned to assume, as it is written: “Your word, Lord, remains forever.” This means that divinity with humanity, as we have said, comprises two substances and one person in Christ. Thus, just as the Trinity was eternal before the assumption of flesh, so after the assumption [Note: [Col. 0590D] In the same place: “of human flesh.”] of human nature the true Trinity remains, lest, because of the assumption of human flesh, it be said to be a quaternity—which, far be it from the hearts or minds of the faithful to say or think—since, as was said above, both unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity must be venerated.

For just as rational soul and flesh are one man, so [Col. 0590C] God and man are one Christ.

Although the Son of God assumed our earthly and mortal flesh, [Note: [Col. 0590D] The same manuscript reads: “the condition of our redemption.”] he nevertheless in no way defiled himself, [Note: [Col. 0590D] The same manuscript adds: “nor the nature of the Godhead.”] nor changed the nature of the Godhead. For if the sun or fire touches something unclean, it purifies what it touches and is in no way defiled by it. [Note: [Col. 0590D] The same manuscript adds: “and in no way defiles itself by it.”] In the same way, the Godhead did not defile the burden it assumed from our humanity, but purified the flesh of our nature that it assumed and cleansed it from the stains and filth of sins and vices, as Isaiah says: “He himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses” (Isaiah 53:4).

For this reason he was born according to his humanity: to take our infirmities and bear our sicknesses—not that he himself possessed infirmities or sicknesses, since he is the salvation of the world, [Col. 0590D] but so that he might take them away from us, granting us, through the grace and mysteries of his holy Passion, redemption and likewise the salvation of our souls, with the bond of debt cancelled. [Note: [Col. 0590D] The same manuscript reads: “through the grace and sacrament, the bond of debt having been cancelled,” etc.]

He suffered for our salvation—that is, according to what could suffer, which is according to human nature; for according to his divinity the Son of God is impassible.

He descended [Note: [Col. 0591B] “to the lower regions.”] to the underworld in order to free the first-formed Adam, the patriarchs, the prophets, and all the righteous who were being held there because of original sin; and, released from the bond of that sin and redeemed by his blood from the same captivity and infernal place, to recall them to the heavenly homeland and the joys of everlasting life.

But the others, who in addition to original sin had committed capital crimes, remained, as Scripture asserts, in punitive Tartarus. As it was said through the prophet in the person of Christ: “I shall be your death, O death” [Col. 0591B] (Hosea 13:14)—that is, by his death Christ killed death, the enemy of the human race, and gave life. “I shall be your sting, O underworld.” He bit the underworld in part, on behalf of those whom he freed, and left part of it for those who remained in torments because of their capital crimes. [Note: [Col. 0591B] “The others, who were guilty beyond original sin.”]

He rose from the dead, the firstborn of the dead (Revelation 1:5). Elsewhere the Apostle says: “He himself is the firstborn among many brothers”—that is, he was the first to rise from the dead. And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose with him, as the Gospel authority says (Matthew 27:52); but he, who is the head, rose first, and afterward those who are the members, immediately.

Then he ascended into heaven, as the Psalmist says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ephesians 4:8)—that is, human nature, which had previously been sold under sin and held captive— [Note: [Col. 0592B] The same manuscript adds: “and, having redeemed it.”] and, having redeemed it, he led it captive into the heavenly heights and to the everlasting kingdom of the heavenly homeland, where it had not previously been, and placed it in everlasting glory.

He sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, in the Father’s prosperity and in the honor of being God. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. “The living” means those whom the Lord’s coming will then find alive in the body, [Col. 0592B] and “the dead” those already buried. Alternatively, he calls the righteous living and sinners dead.

At his coming all human beings will rise with their bodies and will give an account of their own deeds. Those who have done good will go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire. This is the catholic faith, and unless each person believes it faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.

# APPENDIX

[Col. 0591]

VERSES OF VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS UNKNOWN TO PREVIOUS EDITORS. (C,S)

I. [Note: [Col. 0591] These verses, absent from all earlier editions, were discovered a few years ago by D. Guerard in the manuscripts of the Royal Library at Saint-Germain and were first published by him in volume XII of *Notices of Manuscripts*.] TO RADEGUND AND AGNES.

[Col. 0591C]

What tale is borne into the ear with sweet words? [Note: [Col. 0591] Manuscript: *ore* (“mouth”).]

If a kindly table now holds peaceful minds for me,

mark your pleased spirits as the tablet returns,

so that a letter painted by hand may reveal affection.

Sweet mother and sister, alike in pious love,

celebrate your joys together with festive sound.

Thus may the honor of Caesarius adorn you throughout the world, [Note: [Col. 0591] Manuscript: *urnet*.]

and may Christ, dear with the Father, love you both. [Note: [Col. 0591] Manuscript: *anbas*.]

Thus may this Caesaria and lofty Caesaria arise,

so that through you this ancient honor may be restored.

Thus may such grace shine forth that it may increase through the ages, [Note: [Col. 0591] Manuscript: *tales*.]

through you, the Arelatan splendor of Poitiers.

[Col. 0591D] Thus may we deserve to live piously for the heavenly King,

and may my limbs be covered with a tomb together with you.

If some complaint is retained in an offended heart,

I beg that it be released in turn as a pardon.

May Christ, who loves peace and is full of wondrous sweetness,

bind your hearts in holiness, with himself as mediator.

[Col. 0592C] May the venerable Caesaria obtain this equally with me,

she who desires you both to be joined in a pious embrace.

May I first inscribe the mother, fixed in devotion,

in whom two mothers appear, yet one … [Note: [Col. 0591] Probably “sister.”]

Honor places first the one who is younger in years;

to these, age, more venerable, rightly granted senile favor.

But it is sweet for me to send greetings equally to all three,

since one and the same love is dear to you.

Happy is the table that holds three lights together

and makes the Paschal good multiply.

May you enjoy these things with the angelic company participating,

delights for you in the realm of God. [Note: [Col. 0591] Manuscript: *Diliciae*.]

May mother and sister remain through the saving night;

may the prosperous prayers of the son and [Note: [Col. 0591] Manuscript: “brother.”] brother bring this about!

The angelic assemblies revisit your hearts

and recall the dear conversations of your own heart. [Note: [Col. 0591] Manuscript: “their own.”]

The hours of night demand that, within this brevity, you bring greetings—only six little verses, or two, I beg.

[Col. 0593A] Although what I desired may flee me once evening has come,

this night nevertheless has not carried you wholly away from me.

Lovers are perceived not with the eyes but with the mind;

for where bodily form cannot reach, there our mind has been.

How holy is that place which never separates lovers,

where their vows allow them to behold those whom they seek,

with Christ, the source of goodness, placed in the midst,

whose sacred love keeps their hearts bound!

Here too, however, many verses have been bidden over the years; take from here with you that I may speak to you worthily.

Clap your hands, sisters, and return pious vows to God,

because such great joys sit with you.

With me excluded outside, you lovers retain this place;

what is pleasing to us both cannot be possessed together.
