May this long-lasting thing remain for us through every occasion,

and flourish for all to share in its blessings.

[Col. 0593B] Everyone today celebrates the festival; I alone in the world,

absent from my birthday, complain.

[Note: [Col. 0593] A recent editor notes at the foot of the page: *cunctae*: “I do not know why.”] Certainly, if I had perhaps been hidden in another region,

should I not all the more have had to hurry to you? [Note: [Col. 0593] Manuscript: *dubieram*.]

Now others give you gifts; I, your brother, give none,

although I was able to give little fruits by way of a joke. [Note: [Col. 0593] Manuscript: *mora joti*; reading uncertain.]

Although absent in appearance, I am present in heart,

and I ask you gladly to accept the gifts I have sent.

Thus may almighty God pardon mother and sister,

who did not act so as to keep me for themselves.

May you celebrate these pious festivals for many years— [Note: [Col. 0593] So in the manuscript]—

with your mother joyful, and with me also as your [Note: [Col. 0593] Manuscript: “brother.”] brother.

[Col. 0593C] Thus yesterday’s day carried away all my hours,

so that I complain that I did not deserve my mother’s voice. [Note: [Col. 0593] Manuscript: *sterna*.]

As a loving lamb, driven from its mother’s breast,

sad and anxious, wanders through grassy fields,

now it flees to the meadows, striking the air with its bleating,

now returns to the folds, yet is not content without its mother.

Thus I, absent from you, put myself forward through words;

one house scarcely contains me in its confined space.

[Note: [Col. 0593] This verse could be read: “But from here I give thanks to the peaceful and dear sister.”] But from here I give thanks to the peaceful and dear …

for what has consoled me through the aid of devotion.

You retain the middle, while she possesses me in the middle;

when I see you two, I am then wholly moved.

May Martinus and Hilary, I beg, stand beside you,

and may one hope in God protect you and your children.

[Col. 0593D] [Note: [Col. 0593] Manuscript: “If I cannot be present.”] If I cannot be present, absent I pay you my tribute,

so that my beloved mother may approve my affection.

If I were not absent, I would do whatever you commanded;

perhaps my sluggishness would please you through small services.

With devoted heart, though with rustic tongue,

I would give a sound through the shepherd’s reed into my mother’s ear,

serving your commands, [Note: [Col. 0593] Manuscript: “I would weary.”] I would wear out my limbs by day;

my submissive neck would serve its mistress.

My fingers would refuse nothing, nor would the hand that wrote this

hesitate to draw water from the deep well.

[Col. 0594A] It would stretch out vines and drive mattocks into the gardens;

it would plant and gladly cultivate the sweet vegetable.

It would be an honor to devote my limbs with you to the kitchen, [Note: [Col. 0593] Manuscript: *cocinae* (“kitchen/cooking”).]

and to wash blackened vessels in the pure lake.

Therefore, though absent, I have now sent you the gifts of Marcellus,

to whom blessed life has given an exalted place.

And if the words sound unworthy when reported,

may the heavenly signs please your heart.

May you live long for me with your daughter and the harvest of sisters,

while the sheepfold of God remains for the virginal choir!

If you gave me your words, they would be sweeter than if

bees had given none of their chosen flowers.

Anxious and afflicted, I bend beneath the weight of cares;

with troubled heart I cannot produce words.

[Col. 0594B] I am torn by uncertain murmuring and cannot release songs;

I do not know how to speak with certainty, my mind being empty.

Alas! If my prayers wished to hear me confessing my sadness,

the clouds sent to you would carry me away at once!

If I knew how to take wings in a Daedalian flight,

the lover would already have flown back to you as swiftly as possible.

For the Lord knows, he who touches hidden hearts,

what care, though silently, subdues my inward parts.

Return, since I cannot, the promises made to my kind mistress; [Note: [Col. 0593] An earlier editor: “Lord.”]

yet do not think that the fault here was mine.

Excuse me, if perhaps you can; I call the stars to witness

that I neither wish for delays nor carry word of delay to my mother’s ear.

Let her pray for her servant; I shall prepare to return more quickly,

and when I am present, let her voice silence the blows.

[Col. 0594C] Let the page sent forth speak commands of greeting

to mothers and mistresses through submissive prayers;

and while our journey refuses to restore our faces to you,

at least let solicitude prove our affection.

We are not absent if sweet prayer

always keeps us present through the love of the heart.

I, son to my mother and likewise brother to my sister,

bring small gifts with devoted heart.

The third, joined to the two, carries three gifts to the two;

such sweet souls deserve sweet fruits.

But now grant me pardon because in such a sanctuary

the letter will be the basket that carries the gifts.

[Col. 0594D] We continue to behold lands enclosed by the whirlpool,

where the wandering Ocean carries and brings back its tides,

when the sea rises to heaven in ceaseless waves;

here the shifting water barks with its wildness.

The shore flees its sand, now receives it in the tide;

now, while the sea swells, the shipwrecked land lies hidden.

Where heat occupies [the corrupt surviving reading: *gelidas se esse ren* … *dicus*]. [Note: [Col. 0593] So in the manuscript.]

And here three gifts of God are together in one place.

Although it is barren, that land bears blessed fruits,

while the sand feeds men worthy of heaven.

[Col. 0595A] But even if I were held in some city without you,

amid many thousands I would still be alone.

May I deserve to see you joyful, mother and sister,

when the blessed banquet of the Most High God comes.

If the simpler brother returns more quickly, I beg you,

bring him the help of greetings entrusted by me. [Note: [Col. 0595] Manuscript: “work.”]

And I beg you, commend me through your sisters;

thus may Christ make them his own through love. [Note: [Col. 0595] From Mai’s *Roman Spicilegium*, volume IX.]

II. EPIGRAM ON THEUDICHILDE.

[Col. 0596A]

Queen Theudichild built this place for monks from its foundations,

ennobling it with her own possessions.

Although her body is now enclosed in this cavern,

her spirit lives in the star-bearing sphere of God.

Imploring that the upright shepherds may say, “Well done, blessed one!”

may God give to this one things worthy of the wise—alas, evil things! [Reading and syntax materially uncertain.]

END OF VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS.

IN AN UNCERTAIN YEAR OF THE EIGHTH CENTURY. DEFENSOR, MONK OF LOCOCIAGUM (LIGUGÉ).

[Col. 0595]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON DEFENSOR.

(*Literary History of France*, volume III.)

[Col. 0595B]

Two periods lead us to place this writer here. [Note: [Col. 0595D] Mabillon, *Annales*, book XXI, no. 12.] The first is supplied by the work he left to posterity, in which, among the authors he used, he cites none later than Saint Isidore of Seville, who died around the year 636. [Note: [Col. 0595D] Volume II, p. 704, § 23.] The other period is likewise drawn from the same work, where Defensor states that he was raised and instructed by Ursinus, [Note: [Col. 0595D] Book XVII, no. 30.] who was none other than the prior or abbot of that name who wrote one of the Lives of Saint Leodegar, bishop of Autun, seventeen or eighteen years before the end of this century, as we have said in its proper place.

It is therefore on legitimate grounds that we assign our author to the indicated period; and although he may have lived into the following century, it seems to us that Dom Mabillon would place him too late if he dated him only around 732. [Note: [Col. 0595D] Book XXI, no. 12.]

[Col. 0595C] [Note: [Col. 0595D] Volume II, p. 704, § 23.] Having embraced the monastic life at Ligugé, near Poitiers, as he himself says, Defensor made study one of his principal occupations. He became so learned that he deserved to bear the title “Grammarian,” which in former times was given to those who possessed literary learning.

He devoted himself especially to reading the Fathers of the Church and, on the advice of Ursinus, who directed his studies, collected from them the passages that seemed most edifying to him. Arranging these under certain headings, he formed a book entitled *Scintillae, or Sentences of the Catholic Fathers*: a collection of sparks or sentences drawn from orthodox Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0596D] Ibid.] Explaining his purpose in a short [Col. 0596B] preface placed at the beginning of the work, he says that he undertook it to spare his readers the trouble of reading a great many volumes; that he took care to gather in his own book everything they might wish to find concerning the subjects he set out to treat; and that, to avoid being accused of imposture and to prevent his work from being regarded as apocryphal, he was careful to mark each sentence with the name of the Father from whom he had taken it. [Note: [Col. 0596D] Book XXI, no. 12.]

These sentences are generally very short. The Fathers he cites are Saint Clement, Origen, Saint Cyprian, Saint Basil, Saint Augustine, Eusebius—who seems to be Eusebius of Emesa, or rather the author to whom that name has been assigned—a certain Joseph, otherwise scarcely known, Saint Caesarius, Saint Gregory the pope, Saint Isidore of Seville, and the *Lives of the Fathers*.

The work is entirely moral and divided into eighty chapters, [Note: [Col. 0596D] *Spicilegium*, volume IV, p. 484.] or only seventy, according to other manuscripts. The author treats the principal Christian virtues, such as charity, patience, love of God and neighbor, and humility. From his preface it is clear that he was well instructed in the doctrine of Saint Augustine and possessed great modesty. His style is harsh, awkward, obscure, and sometimes barbarous.

[Note: [Col. 0596D] Six. Bib., book IV, p. 24, 2.] Sixtus of Siena, who had read this work, since he reports its opening words, nevertheless speaks of it with praise. As early as the beginning of the ninth century it was found, without an author’s name, in the library of Saint-Riquier in Ponthieu [Note: [Col. 0596D] Mab. *Mus. Ital.*, p. 128; *An.*, vol. II, p. 704, § 23.]. Dom Mabillon, having recovered a manuscript copy [Col. 0597A] in the library of Monte Cassino, had its preface printed in the appendix to the second volume of his *Annals*. He seems to suppose that the work was never printed [Note: [Col. 0597A] Poss. *App.*, vol. I, pp. 387, 680.]. Possevin, however, records three different editions: one produced at [Col. 0598A] Antwerp by Stelsius in 1550, another at Venice under the sign of Hope—that is, by Bartholomew de Albertis—in 1552, and the third at Cologne in 1554. These editions must be rare, for we find them mentioned nowhere else.

[Col. 0597]

## ANOTHER ACCOUNT OF DEFENSOR.

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis*.)

[Col. 0597A] Defensor, a grammarian and monk of Locociacum among the Pictones, author of the *Scintilla*, or collection of commonplaces and sayings [Note: [Col. 0597C] Others attribute the *Scintillae* to Alvarus of Córdoba, others to Bishop Caesarius, as does the codex of the Pauline Library of Leipzig in Feller’s catalogue of manuscripts, p. 122. Greek collections of a similar kind are discussed in book V, [Col. 0598C] chapter 30, of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*. In Latin, after Defensor, another work of this sort was composed around the year 1316 by Thomas of Ireland, of whom below in his proper place.] collected in eighty chapters from Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers—Ambrose, Anastasius, Augustine, Basil, Caesarius, [Col. 0597B] the books of Clement, Cassian’s *Conferences*, Cyprian, Ephraem, Isaiah, Eusebius, Gregory, Jerome, Hilary, Isidore, Josephus, Origen, and the *Lives of the Fathers*. John Mabillon reports that he copied this book from the library of Monte Cassino, p. 123 of the *Museum Italicum*, where he calls him an ancient author, since he cites none of the Fathers later than Isidore. Yet he wrongly regarded it as unpublished; for I have in my hands a Cologne edition of the year 1556, printed in a smaller format by Peter Horst. I also remember that Gesner mentions the Antwerp edition of 1550 and Simler the Venetian edition of 1552, not to mention the edition derived from the Roman edition of the Sicilian Antonius Gangutius, Rome, 1560, in quarto, which appears under Bede’s name in volume VII of his works; concerning it, as also concerning its Anglo-Saxon translation, see above, vol. I, [Col. 0597C] p. 191. But the author expressly stated the name of Defensor and of his spiritual father Ursinus in the preface, which I have placed below in full—for it is short:

> Reader, whoever you are, as you read this little book, I ask you, the writer, to read it with a willing mind and gratefully receive its honey-sweet words. Good will and labor—nothing else was mine—were involved in this work, which is an excerpt from the sayings of the Lord and of the saints and from which this *SCINTILLA* has been extracted. It is not the product of my own skill, but is wholly the grace of God. Wishing to obey the teaching of my spiritual father Ursinus, I searched every page, and, finding a shining saying—whether it were discovered as a pearl or a gem—I eagerly gathered it. Just as many drops collected together make a spring, so, gathering testimonies from various volumes, I attempted to compose this work. As sparks proceed from fire, so these brief sayings, written in many books, may be called the *SCINTILLA SCRIPTURARUM* [Spark of the Scriptures]. Whoever wishes to read it saves himself labor and need not grow weary by going through the pages again and again; here he has what has been culled from many sources. So that the work might not also be thought apocryphal, I wrote beside each saying, under the several chapters, the name of its author. I added my own name, which is DEFENSOR, not for empty glory, but so that whoever reads may remember me.

The chapter absent from the printed editions—the thirty-fifth, on Doctors—was published by our B. Nicholas Staphorst in volume III of the *Hamburg Ecclesiastical History*, pp. 359–361, from a manuscript in the library of the Hamburg church of Saints Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0597]

# THE BOOK OF SPARKS OF DEFENSOR, MONK OF LOCOCIACUM. (C, S)

[Note: [Col. 0597D] This reading, taken from Mabillon, vol. II of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 704, differs considerably from the one given above from Fabricius. The reader, having both, may judge between them. Before Mabillon’s prologue stand these words: “In the name of almighty God begins the book of Sparks, or Sayings of the Catholic Fathers, published by Defensor the grammarian.”]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0597D]

Reader, whoever you are, as you read this little book, I ask you, its writer, to read it with a willing mind and gratefully receive its honey-sweet words. Good will and labor—nothing else—were mine. This *Spark* has been excerpted from the sayings of the Lord and his saints; it was not produced by my own skill, but everything came from the grace of God, as I sought to carry out the instruction of my spiritual father Ursinus. Wishing to obey his command and teaching, I searched every page, and, finding a shining saying, immediately gathered it eagerly, as though it had been discovered as a pearl or a gem.

Just as many drops make a spring, so, gathering testimonies from various volumes, I attempted to compose this little book. As sparks proceed from fire, so brief sayings found shining in many books have been brought together here. Whoever wishes to read this volume of sparks thereby cuts short his labor and need not grow weary from having to go through the other pages. Here he has what he wishes to find. But lest the work be thought apocryphal, as though it had no author, I wrote beside each saying its proper author.

I dedicate it to the monastery of Saint Martin of Locutiacum, in which I had the hair of my head cut, and which may preserve it as a perpetual gift—having been generously endowed there from my youth by my lords who reside there. With Jesus’ favor I wrote it myself, and openly gave it so that it might grow in Christ, if he should make me obey their command and willingly render them abundant service in all things.

And if I have done anything less carefully than I should, I ask you, reader, not to reproach me as a rival, but to correct me as a friend. I have written my name, which is DEFENSOR, not for empty glory, but so that whoever reads may remember me. As a harbor is welcome to the sailor, so these verses were welcome to me. Finally, I solemnly entreat readers and implore hearers to pray for me: that, as long as I remain, I may abound in God’s wisdom, and, when I depart from the flesh, may deserve to enjoy blessed eternal life. Amen.

# CHAPTER ONE. On Charity

## CHRIST

“No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XIII).

## PETER

“Above all, maintain constant mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter IV; Romans XIII; Proverbs X).

## PAUL

“Charity is patient, charity is kind,” and so forth (1 Corinthians XIII).

“Love one another with brotherly affection” (Romans XII).

## JOHN

“By this we have come to know the charity of God: that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (1 John III).

“God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John IV).

## SOLOMON

“Hatred stirs up quarrels, but charity covers all offenses” (Proverbs X).

## AUGUSTINE

[Col. 0599D] If we wish to run along the way of true charity, we can happily reach our eternal homeland.

For without charity, whatever we do is of no benefit.

We expend empty and vain effort if we do not have charity, which is God.

Carnal desire reigns where the charity of God is absent.

A person is perfect when he is full of charity.

Without the love of charity, however correctly someone may believe, he can never reach blessedness.

So great is the power of charity that even prophecy and martyrdom are considered nothing without it.

So great is the power of charity that, if it is absent, the other virtues are possessed in vain; if it is present, everything is possessed rightly.

He truly holds what the Father holds, and nothing in divine conduct is hidden from him, who holds charity in his speech.

Pursue charity as a sweet and health-giving food: without it, the rich person is poor, and in it, the poor person is rich.

Those who close their eyes to charity fall asleep in lusts and the pleasures of the flesh.

Extend charity throughout the whole world if you wish to love Christ, because the members of Christ lie scattered throughout the world.

Just as your body, if it is without the spirit—that is, without the soul—is dead, so your soul will be reckoned dead without the Holy Spirit, that is, without charity.

For they do not dwell together unless perfect charity of Christ exists among them.

Where perfect charity is absent, people who are together are hateful, troublesome, and disorderly; by their anxiety they disturb the others.

## AMBROSE

Just as no one reaches the destination toward which he is heading without a road, so, without charity—which is called the way—people cannot walk, but wander.

Those whom the charity of God makes strong in enduring sins are not gently corrupted by any bodily delight or evil pleasure.

## GREGORY

The one and supreme proof of charity is this: that one loves even the person who opposes him, as well as the person who confers benefits.

Our neighbors are to be loved, and charity is to be shown to all, both relatives and strangers.

Yet for the sake of that same charity we must not be turned away from the love of God.

For just as many branches proceed from one root, so the other virtues arise from one charity.

A branch has no green growth of good works if it does not remain in the root of charity.

That person has charity who loves his friend in God and loves his enemy for God’s sake.

He asks nothing for his enemy who does not pray for him out of charity.

The law of Christ is the charity of unity. A person’s work is nothing if we do not have charity, which holds the highest place and authority among all God’s commandments.

[Col. 0600D] Charity is love of God and neighbor with the whole heart and the whole mind: whatever good we wish people to do for us, we should likewise do for them.

For this is the law and the prophets.

“To the one who has, more will be given, and he will abound,” because whoever has charity also receives other gifts.

Whoever does not have charity loses even the gifts he seemed to have received.

We must remain watchful regarding the bond of charity.

For the rust of sin is confounded all the more as the sinner’s heart is burned by a great fire.

Charity rises wonderfully to the heights when it mercifully bends down toward the lowliness of one’s neighbors; and when it kindly descends to the lowest things, it powerfully returns to the highest.

[Col. 0601A] The height of charity, therefore, is the virtue of true prayer.

Charity is broad, for it embraces love of enemies.

Charity bears the wrongs of brothers with long-suffering.

True charity is loving a friend in God and loving an enemy for God’s sake.

Whoever does not have charity loses every good thing he possesses.

Charity supplies the strength that ignorance denies.

Often charity, impeded by various occupations, burns undiminished in the heart and yet is not displayed in action.

For when the sun is covered by a cloud, it is not seen on earth, yet it still burns in heaven. So charity can be occupied: inwardly it consumes the power of its heat, while outwardly it does not display the flames of its works.

## JEROME

The length of the earth does not separate those whom love unites.

## ISIDORE

Although some appear to share in faith and holy works, because they are deprived of the charity of brotherly love they have no increase in virtue.

No reward is reckoned without charity.

For charity holds the chief place among all the virtues.

[Col. 0601C] Unity in charity with holy men must be maintained; and the more each person withdraws from the world, the more necessary it is for him to associate with the company of the good.

Charity consists in love of God and neighbor.

The person who is not separated from the charity of his neighbor preserves within himself love of God.

Whoever is separated from brotherly fellowship is deprived of participation in divine charity.

Those who separate themselves from charity separate themselves from the kingdom of God.

Perfect charity is love of God and neighbor.

All goodness proceeds from charity and humility.

## CYPRIAN

The person who knows and loves the bond of charity ought to restrain his tongue from the evil of discord.

## BASIL

The person who is full of charity proceeds with a calm spirit and a serene countenance.

But the man full of hatred walks in anger.

## CAESARIUS

While retaining true charity and true obedience, let us presume nothing from our own merits, but trust in God’s power.

Fasts without charity are like a lamp without oil.

It profits us nothing that we exhaust ourselves with continual vigils and labors if we do not have charity within us.

[Col. 0602A] For it profits nothing that you afflict your body when nothing advances in your heart.

If true charity and humility are absent, we must not presume or place our confidence merely in the religious habit.

## EPHRAEM

Charity is the pillar and foundation of the holy soul.

# CHAPTER TWO. On Patience

## CHRIST

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew V).

“By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI).

## PETER

[Col. 0602B] “For this is grace, if, because of conscience toward God, someone endures sorrows while suffering unjustly” (1 Peter II).

“For what credit is it if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it?” (Ibid.).

“But if, while doing good, you patiently endure, this is grace before God” (Ibid.).

## PAUL

“Tribulation produces patience, patience produces proven character, and proven character produces hope” (Romans V).

“Hope does not disappoint, because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Ibid.).

“If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Romans XII).

[Col. 0602C] “You need patience, so that, after doing the will of God, you may receive the promise” (Hebrews X).

“Pursue peace with all people and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews XII).

## JAMES

“Let patience have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing” (James I).

“Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him” (Ibid.).

## SOLOMON

“The patient person is governed by great wisdom, but the impatient person exalts his own folly” (Proverbs XIV).

[Col. 0602D] “The patient person is better than the mighty, and the one who rules his spirit is better than the conqueror of cities” (Proverbs X).

“A man’s learning is known by his patience” (Proverbs XIX).

“Patience will soften a ruler, and a gentle tongue will break hardness” (Proverbs XXV).

“The patient person is better than the arrogant” (Ecclesiastes VII).

## AUGUSTINE

Whoever is more patient under insult will be established as more powerful in the kingdom.

As patient as our Lord is in bearing our sins, so severe will he be in examining our deeds.

## JEROME

If Christ is the peace of believers, then whoever is without peace consequently does not have Christ either.

[Col. 0603A] Among Christians, it is not the person who suffers but the person who inflicts insult who is wretched.

It is harder to endure someone whom you do not wish for than to long for someone whom you love.

Just as we ought to be patient regarding personal injuries, so, if we see someone blaspheming God with sacrilegious speech, we must not be patient with him; rather, we should resist the sacrilegious person and condemn the blasphemous mouth with a reply of truth.

## AMBROSE

They feign patience in public, while hiding the poison of anger in their hearts.

They are ready to do harm when the time for doing harm arrives.

The virtue of patience is usually exercised in three ways.

[Col. 0603B] For sometimes we endure things from God, sometimes from the ancient adversary, and sometimes from our neighbor.

From our neighbor we endure persecutions, losses, and insults.

From the ancient adversary we endure temptations; from God, chastisements.

## GREGORY

The person who breaks the Lord’s peace in the fury of discord can never reach the gift of peace.

True patience is to endure the wrongs of others with one mind and not to be stung by any pain against the person who inflicts the wrongs.

We can be martyrs without the sword if we preserve patience for the truth in our hearts.

[Col. 0603C] The less patient someone is shown to be, the less learned he is proved to be.

Therefore, when patience is abandoned, the other good things already accomplished are also destroyed.

True patience is the kind that loves the very person whom it bears.

Not to tolerate someone but to hate him is not the virtue of gentleness but a covering for anger.

When we can resist the anger of the proud, let us humbly withdraw.

It is more glorious to escape an injury by remaining silent than to overcome it by replying.

Our heavenly judge, although he considers the weight of an act in granting recompense, nevertheless weighs strength against the burden.

As joyful the mind has been through love, so patient will it be through long-suffering.

Each person bears with his neighbor to the extent that he loves him: if you love, you bear with him; if you stop loving, you also stop tolerating.

The less we love someone, the less we tolerate him.

## BASIL

The peaceful person will deserve the fellowship of angels; the envious person will become a companion of demons.

Whoever patiently endures evils here will deserve glory in the future.

Peace drives away discords, but envy joins them together.

Just as secret peace illuminates the mind, so hidden envy blinds the heart. The peaceful person possesses a secure [Col. 0604A] mind; the envious person, however, is always in distress.

My son, if you wish to have patience, I first advise you to rouse your own mind to the divine commandments.

A peaceful person is recognized by the abundance of his joy, while the envious person is revealed by his withered and furious face.

A kind person, even if he suffers injury, regards it as nothing.

But the unjust person, even hearing a small word from his neighbor, considers it an insult.

Whoever welcomes peace into the lodging of his mind prepares a dwelling for Christ, because Christ is peace and is accustomed to rest in peace.

If someone has inflicted evils upon you, do not become angry; rather, grieve for him, because God is angry with him.

## ISIDORE

No one who places his hope in a human being can be at peace.

Whoever carefully considers the rewards of the future life bears all the evils of the present life with equanimity.

The wicked person is tormented more severely by imagining the world’s advantages than the righteous person is by enduring adversity.

Whoever loves the goods of the world, whether he wishes it or not, succumbs to the punishment of fear.

One must patiently bear from a single person what is tolerable when it happens to many.

The punishment of this world is brief; both the person who inflicts it and the person who suffers it are mortal.

The perversity of evils does not kill you but instructs you.

[Col. 0604C] Have patience in adversity, and be more ready to receive troublesome things than to bear them.

Patience overcomes the insults of slanderers.

The shield of patience breaks the arrows of insult.

Against the sword of the tongue, offer the shield of patience.

It is a great virtue not to injure the person by whom you have been injured.

It is a greater virtue, when injured, also to forgive.

But it is the greatest virtue of glory to spare the person whom you could have harmed.

## CYPRIAN

God has commanded peaceful and harmonious people to dwell in his house.

Since we have begun to be sons of God, let us remain in God’s peace; and since we have one spirit, let us have one mind and one understanding.

[Col. 0604D] A greater sacrifice to God is true peace and brotherly harmony.

Whoever breaks Christ’s peace and harmony acts against Christ, who said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you.”

The son of peace ought to seek peace.

No one can receive the crown of sorrows and sufferings unless patience in sorrow and suffering has preceded it.

No one can truly bestow good things by teaching if, by living, he does not know how to bear the evils of others with equanimity.

Whoever is gentle and mild is an imitator of God the Father.

## FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS

[Col. 0605A]

The patient person is a little stream that is a spring, offering everyone a delightful drink.

## JOSEPHUS

The patient person is one who does not fear present things, thinks about the future, and does not know how to tremble where there is fear.

# CHAPTER THREE. On Love of God and Neighbor

## CHRIST

“Whoever loves me will keep my commandment” (John XIV).

“If you love me, keep my commandments” (Ibid.).

“If you remain in me and my words remain in you, whatever you wish, you shall ask, and it will be done for you” (John XV).

[Col. 0605B] “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII).

“With sincere brotherly love, love one another attentively from the heart” (1 Peter I).

## PAUL

“Love of neighbor does no evil” (Romans III).

“Therefore the fullness of the law is love” (Ibid.).

“Walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians V).

“For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans VIII).

“What the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, and what has not entered the human heart, God has prepared for those [Col. 0605C] who love him” (1 Corinthians II).

## JOHN

“Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him” (1 John II).

“But whoever hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (Ibid.).

Let us therefore love God, because God first loved us (1 John IV).

“If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (Ibid.).

“We have this commandment from God: whoever loves God must also love his brother” (Ibid.).

“Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (Ibid.).

## JESUS SIRACH

“The friend loves at all times, and a brother is proved in adversity” (Proverbs XVII).

“Whoever loves God will pray for sins and restrain himself from them, and he will be heard in the prayer of his days” (Ecclesiasticus III).

“Love the one who made you, and do not abandon his ministers” (Ecclesiasticus VII).

“Love God and call upon him in your salvation” (Ecclesiasticus XIII).

“Every animal loves its own kind; so every person loves his neighbor” (Ibid.).

“All flesh joins itself to what resembles it, and every person associates with one like himself” (Ibid.).

[Col. 0606A] “Love your neighbor and join yourself to him in faith” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII).

“Like someone who releases a bird from his hand, so is one who abandons his neighbor” (Ibid.).

“The eyes of the Lord are upon those who love him” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV).

## AUGUSTINE

Our life is love; if our life is love, death is hatred.

You conquer a human being by human happiness; you conquer the devil by loving the enemy.

Let love be nourished in you, for it alone leads to life.

The love among you must not be carnal but spiritual.

Nothing is more precious to God than the virtue of love.

[Col. 0606B] Nothing is more desirable to the devil than the extinction of charity.

## JEROME

Holy love has no impatience; false rumor is quickly crushed.

Consider every person to be your brother; remember that one Maker created us.

Love knows no order.

Negligence can be corrected more easily than love can be born.

## AMBROSE

We love our neighbors as ourselves when we love them not because of benefits received or favors obtained, but solely because they share our nature.

[Col. 0606C] Whoever gains a brother through love gains a son.

## GREGORY

The proof of love is therefore the display of a work.

When someone loves God and keeps his commandments, the Lord comes into that person’s heart and makes his dwelling there.

No one could love God without possessing the person whom he loves.

By love of neighbor one can recognize how one must attain the love of God.

Those who expend their love not spiritually but carnally love their neighbor, yet do not attain those lofty rewards of love.

Just as the fire of love lifts up the mind, so the fire of malice envelops it.

By loving God, we pursue the evils within us.

By loving our neighbor, we hasten to help where we can be useful.

Just as death kills the body, so charity of eternal life kills love of bodily things.

The power of love usually acts in the mind so that it believes no one else is unaware of what it itself is always thinking.

Holy desires grow from love; if they weaken through delay, they are not desires.

Whatever is commanded is judged by charity alone.

Neither is God truly loved without one’s neighbor, nor is one’s neighbor truly loved without God.

But if someone loves anyone and does not love him for God’s sake, he does not have charity, although he thinks he has it.

[Col. 0607A] True charity exists when a friend is loved in God and an enemy is loved for God’s sake.

The person who loves those whom he loves for God’s sake is the one who also knows how to love those by whom he is not loved.

## BASIL

Every soul is as exalted in its knowledge of God as it is expansive in love of neighbor.

Whoever loves his brother has a tranquil heart.

But whoever hates his brother is surrounded by a storm.

Therefore love God with your whole mind, so that you may please him in all your actions.

For God wishes to be loved not only in words but with a pure heart [Col. 0607B] and righteous works.

Let us therefore love God more than all things: he fashioned both us and our parents with his own hands, and we should attribute all the good that happens to us each day to his benefits.

Christ is to be loved above our parents, because our parents do not give us what Christ gives.

Regard your neighbor as one of your own members.

When God bestows great benefits upon us, he asks nothing from us except that we love him and preserve our temples for him, so that he may always dwell in us and we may remain in him.

## ISIDORE

The person who hates a human being does not love Christ with all his heart.

The love of God is compared with death, as Solomon says: “Love is strong as death” (Song of Songs VIII).

Just as death violently separates the soul from the body, so the love of God violently separates a person from worldly and carnal love.

By loving your neighbor, you cleanse your eye for seeing God.

Whoever despises God’s commandments does not love God.

For we do not love a king if we hate his laws.

Nor can someone love God if he is known to err in love of his neighbor.

It is the mark of good judgment not to hate persons but [Col. 0607D] faults; not to reject what is right in favor of what is false, but to approve it.

Those who are imperfect in the love of God often resolve to separate themselves from vices; but, weighed down by the burden of vices, they return again to the vices they wish to abandon.

The love of God cannot be less than between two persons.

A person is greatly estranged from earthly things when he loves a mortal human being carnally more than he ought.

While we desire a temporal possession with love, we lose true love.

By loving God, we pursue the evils within us.

By loving our neighbor, we hasten to help where we can be useful.

## CYPRIAN

“God,” he says, “is love: whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him.”

Those who did not wish to be united in the Church of God cannot remain with God.

## FROM THE BOOK OF CLEMENT

It is foolish to love anything more than God.

The mind that the memory of God has filled leaves no room for the evil one.

## EPHRAEM

If someone loves God, his mind will not remain on earth; rather, it always desires the higher things that it has loved.

From there it is led out, from there it is enlightened, from there it is refreshed, as from a most sweet spring.

# CHAPTER FOUR. On Humility

[Col. 0608B]

## CHRIST

“Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew XI).

God said through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the poor and contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah LXVI).

“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV).

## PETER

“Clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter V).

[Col. 0608C] “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of his visitation” (Ibid.).

## JAMES

“Humble yourselves in the sight of God, and he will exalt you” (James IV).

## PAUL

“Be of one mind, thinking the same thing, doing nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility regarding one another as superior” (Philippians II).

“Do not be wise in lofty things, but associate with the humble” (Romans XII).

## SOLOMON

“Where there is pride, there will also be disgrace” (Proverbs XI).

[Col. 0608D] “But where there is humility, there is also wisdom.”

“Humility follows the proud, and glory will receive the humble in spirit” (Proverbs XXIX).

“Before he is crushed, the human heart is exalted; and before he is glorified, it is humbled” (Proverbs XVIII).

“It is better to be humbled with the gentle than to divide spoils with the proud” (Proverbs XVI).

## JESUS SIRACH

“The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus III).

“God is honored by the humble” (Ibid.).

“Do not be humble in your own wisdom, lest, having been humbled, you be led astray into folly” (Ecclesiasticus XIII).

“There is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inner parts are full of deceit” (Ecclesiasticus XXIX).

## ORIGEN

[Col. 0609A]

If you are not humble and quiet, you cannot have the grace of the Holy Spirit within you.

## AUGUSTINE

God became humble; let the human being be ashamed to become proud.

The conscience of God’s servant should always be humble and sorrowful: humble, so that it may not become proud, and usefully sorrowful, so that the heart may not dissolve into wantonness.

That conscience attends to God’s praise, and to the words of the mouth whose neck humility bends down and pride does not raise up.

## JEROME

The summit of the virtues is reached not by power but by humility.

## GREGORY

The carnal heart, while seeking the glory of this life, rejects humility.

The more humility bends down toward the lowest things, the more it advances toward the highest.

Each person must humble himself as much as he does not know whether he is among the elect.

Although each person displays his good qualities by recognizing them in his neighbor, they will not be right if they lack humility.

Whoever is humble will be exalted in glory.

Great is the virtue of the humble: holding the lowest places out of desire, even if they are not raised on high through humility, they preserve in their minds the purple of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0609C] The Lord’s way is directed toward the heart when the word of truth is heard humbly.

The person who professes himself humble in his own eyes despises himself in all things.

Whatever works may be present, they are nothing unless seasoned with humility.

Each person should be all the humbler because of the gift he has received, the more he sees himself obligated to give an account.

Truth flees the mind that it does not find humble.

There the judge separates from the lot of the humble those who here exalt themselves on the horns of pride.

The humble receive a gift by which they drive away from themselves the hearts of the proud.

## BASIL

[Col. 0609D]

Although the humble person may be most contemptible in outward appearance, he is nevertheless glorious in virtues.

But although the proud person may appear handsome to the eye, he is nevertheless contemptible in his works.

## ISIDORE

Whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust that has merely been found.

The thought of our heart is as low before God as it is high among human beings.

And the humility of our heart is as high before God as it is low among human beings.

Humble your spirit profoundly, because the life of sinful flesh is fire and a worm.

[Col. 0610A] Without humility and charity, every virtue will be counted as a vice.

The highest virtue of a monk is humility.

His greatest vice is pride.

Be grounded in humility; be the least and the last of all.

Humble yourself so that you may be exalted; make yourself least before everyone; put yourself before no one, and consider no one more proud than yourself.

Regard everyone as superior to you.

Although you may be the highest, hold fast to humility; for if you hold fast to humility, you will be glorious. The humbler you are, the greater the height of glory that will follow you.

Descend so that you may ascend; humble yourself so that you may be exalted, lest, having been exalted, you be humbled.

[Col. 0610B] Humility knows no fall.

Humility has never suffered a fall.

Whoever is lowly in his own eyes is great before God.

Whoever displeases himself pleases God.

Therefore be small in your own eyes, so that you may be great in the eyes of the Lord.

You will be all the more precious before God the more despised you are in your own eyes.

Always carry modesty on your face, in remembrance of your sin.

You are dust, and sit in dust.

You are ashes, and live in ashes.

In the highest honor, let your humility be highest.

Let honor not lift you up. You will be all the more distinguished by humility the more approved you are by dignity.

## CAESARIUS

True humility and true obedience will never exist, nor can they exist, without charity.

For just as fire does not exist without heat or brightness, so charity cannot exist without humility and true obedience.

## FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS

Bodily labor is the guide to humility.

All labor without humility is vanity.

Humility neither becomes angry itself nor permits others to become angry.

It is humility when, if your brother has sinned against you, you forgive him before he repents.

Just as John was the forerunner of Jesus, drawing everyone to him, so humility is the forerunner of charity.

Whoever does not have charity loses life.

# CHAPTER FIVE. On Forgiveness

## CHRIST.

If, therefore, you are presenting your offering at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your offering there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and present your offering (Matthew 5).

For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins (Matthew 6).

PAUL.

[Col. 0611A]

Supporting one another patiently and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another. Just as God forgave you, so also should you (Ephesians 4; Colossians 3).

PETER.

Not returning evil for evil or abuse for abuse, but, on the contrary, blessing; for to this you were called, that you might inherit a blessing (Proverbs 20; 1 Peter 3).

SOLOMON.

Do not say, “I will repay evil.” Wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you (Proverbs 20; Romans 12).

Forgive your neighbor who has injured you, and then, when you pray, your sins will be released (Sirach 28).

AUGUSTINE.

[Col. 0611B]

Each person will receive from God such forgiveness as he himself has granted to his neighbor.

JEROME.

Just as God in Christ forgave us our sins, so we too should forgive those who sin against us.

GREGORY.

He rightly asks forgiveness for his own offense who releases what was first committed against him.

For let us forgive what is owed to us, so that what is owed by us may be forgiven.

Each person then obtains rightly what he asks when, in making his petition, his mind is not darkened by hatred of his enemy.

[Col. 0611C] The mouth pours out a prayer for the adversary, but would that the heart might retain love.

When by loving we are able to gain our enemies, even those who persecute us become friends.

The ancient enemy does not care to take earthly things from us, but to strike charity within us.

ISIDORE.

Sins cannot be forgiven to one who does not forgive debts to the person who has sinned against him.

Whoever is slow to reconcile his brother to himself is slow to make God favorable to himself.

For in vain does one seek to appease God who neglects to be quickly reconciled to his neighbor.

Just as God in Christ forgave us our sins, [Col. 0611D] so we too should forgive those who sin against us.

Everyone should be forgiven when he asks for pardon.

CAESARIUS.

For whoever mercifully forgives one who has sinned against him leaves no trace of sin remaining in that person’s soul.

ANASTASIUS.

If you do not forgive the injury done to you, you do not pray for yourself; rather, you bring a curse upon yourself.

For this is what you say: “Forgive me as I also have forgiven.”

IN THE CONFERENCES.

For as much is forgiven to us as we have forgiven those who have harmed us by any kind of malice.

CYPRIAN.

[Col. 0612A]

Whoever forgives the one who has sinned against him by pardoning his sin undoubtedly gives alms.

CHAPTER VI. On Compunction.

CHRIST.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16).

PAUL.

“Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Romans 12).

[Col. 0612B] “Those who weep, as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice” (1 Corinthians 7).

JAMES.

“Be wretched, mourn, and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (James 4).

SOLOMON.

“Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Proverbs 14).

AUGUSTINE.

Whoever lacks compunction lacks pure prayer.

Good compunction is a treasure and an indescribable joy in the human soul.

The human soul that is pierced with compunction in prayer [Col. 0612C] greatly advances toward salvation.

JEROME.

A brave man is no less worthy of praise in mourning than in battle.

AMBROSE.

The voice of psalmody is produced with concentration of heart. Through it a path to the heart is prepared for almighty God, so that he may pour into the attentive mind either the mysteries of prophecy or the grace of compunction.

When compunction is poured in through prayer, a way is prepared for us in the heart by which we may finally reach Jesus.

The soul receives the upper irrigation when, out of desire for the heavenly kingdom, it afflicts itself with tears; [Col. 0612D] but the soul receives the lower irrigation when, by weeping, it fears the punishments of hell.

The Lord mercifully embraces us when we return, because a sinner’s life can no longer be unworthy of him when it has been washed by tears.

We should not doubt that, at the end, a person is justified through the compunction of repentance. But because this rarely happens, we must fear lest, while conversion is postponed until the end, unexpected death overtake us before repentance can help. Therefore let us trust not in tears, nor in deeds, but in the Lord.

Since, therefore, after baptism we defile our life, let us baptize our conscience in tears.

Defiled after the water of salvation, let us be reborn from tears.

BASIL.

[Col. 0613A]

Where there are tears, a spiritual fire is kindled that illuminates the mind’s hidden places.

ISIDORE.

First, the vices we have committed must be cleansed with tears; then, once the mind’s vision has been purified, let us contemplate what we seek. Thus, while the darkness of sin is first wiped away from us by weeping, the cleansed eyes of the heart may freely behold heavenly things.

Whoever continually pours forth true tears and yet does not cease sinning has lamentation, but not cleansing.

Compunction of heart is humility of mind, arising with tears from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment.

The more perfect form of compunction in converts is that which drives away from them every affection for carnal desires [Col. 0613B] and fixes their attention wholly upon contemplation of God.

We say that compunction is twofold, through which the soul of every chosen person is made fit for God: either when it considers the evils of its deeds, or when it sighs with longing for eternal life.

There are four qualities of emotion by which the mind of the righteous is healthfully pierced with sorrow: remembrance of past crimes; consideration of its pilgrimage during the long course of this life; remembrance of future punishments; and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that it may reach it as quickly as possible.

Some become accusers of themselves out of genuine compunction of heart; but they declare themselves sinners only to such an extent [Col. 0613C] that, through feigned humility, they may find a place for claiming holiness.

The tears of repentance are counted before God in place of baptism.

Therefore love tears, and let tears be sweet to you.

Let mourning and tears always delight you.

Be as ready to lament as you were ready to sin.

As intent as you were on sinning, so devoted should you be to repentance.

For serious sins require great lamentation.

EPHRAEM.

Blessed, indeed, and thrice blessed is whoever has [Col. 0613D] compunction according to God.

Compunction is the soul’s health.

Compunction is the soul’s illumination.

Compunction is the remission of sins.

Compunction brings the Holy Spirit into the soul.

Compunction makes Christ, the Only-Begotten, dwell within it.

Tears always give confidence before God.

Where tears abound, filthy thoughts do not approach.

CHAPTER VII. On Prayer.

CHRIST.

“Whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive” (Matthew 21).

[Col. 0614A] “Watch at all times, praying that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke 21).

“Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24).

PETER.

“Showing one another honor as fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Peter 3).

PAUL.

“Be devoted to prayer, praying at all times in the Spirit, watching in all righteousness” (Romans 12).

JAMES.

“Pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5).

For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful (ibid.).

SOLOMON.

[Col. 0614B]

“The Lord is far from the wicked, but he will hear the prayers of the righteous” (Proverbs 15).

“The end of prayer is better than its beginning” (Ecclesiastes 7).

“Before prayer, prepare your soul, and do not be like a person who tempts God” (Ecclesiasticus 18).

“Whoever keeps the word multiplies prayer” (Ecclesiasticus 35).

“God will hear the prayer of the injured” (Ecclesiasticus 34).

“The prayer of one who humbles himself will pierce the clouds” (ibid.).

“My son, in your weakness do not despise yourself, but pray to God, and he himself will heal you” (Ecclesiasticus 38).

“Turn away from sin, direct your hands, and cleanse your heart from every offense” (ibid.).

AUGUSTINE.

[Col. 0614C]

We are cleansed by prayers and instructed by readings. Both are good, if possible; but if it is not possible, it is better to pray than to read, because in reading we learn what we ought to do, while in prayer we receive the very things we ask for.

Do not be idle by day or by night; but when sleep has fallen from your eyes, let your understanding keep watch in prayer.

Pure prayer obtains salvation from sins.

Be ready in prayer; reveal the conscience of your heart, so that you may receive greater grace.

JEROME.

Just as it is not fitting for a soldier to go into battle without weapons, so it is not beneficial for a Christian to go anywhere without [Col. 0614D] prayers.

When people leave their lodging, prayer should arm them.

When they return from the street, prayer should meet them.

GREGORY.

The more heavily we are pressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more fervently we must devote ourselves to prayer.

To lift our hearts to God with our hands means to add the zeal of prayer to the merit of good works.

The judge is more quickly inclined to prayer if the petitioner is corrected from his own wickedness.

A person asks in the name of the Savior when he asks for what pertains to true salvation.

[Col. 0615A] For if someone asks for what is not beneficial, he does not ask in the name of Jesus.

When we have devoted ourselves intensely to prayer, Jesus stands ready to restore the light. When God is fixed in the heart, the lost light is restored.

Whoever has deserved to be free from earthly actions and to devote himself to God alone should pray for his delinquent neighbors.

What we strive more fully to investigate within ourselves, we often penetrate more truly by praying than by investigating.

ISIDORE.

Prayer belongs to the heart, not to the lips; for God does not attend to the words of the petitioner, but looks upon the heart of the one who prays.

It is better to pray silently in the heart than with words alone, without the mind’s attention.

[Col. 0615B] If the heart prays silently and the voice is quiet, although this is hidden from human beings, it cannot be hidden from God, who is present to the conscience.

Prayer is pure when worldly cares do not intrude upon it at its proper time.

The mind that is occupied with worldly thoughts in prayer is far from God.

We truly pray when we think of nothing else.

But very few possess prayers of this kind; and even if some do, it is difficult for them to remain so at all times.

Just as we are guided by prayers, so let us delight in the study of the psalms; for the usefulness of psalm-singing consoles sorrowful hearts.

[Col. 0615C] The devotion of one who prays toward God should be so great that he does not despair of the prayer’s effect.

We pray in vain if we do not have the confidence of hope.

Whoever turns away from God’s commandments will not deserve to receive what he asks for in prayer.

But if we do what God has commanded, without doubt we obtain what we ask.

Prayer is poured out in the present life alone as a remedy for sins; the chanting of the psalms, however, displays God’s perpetual praise and everlasting glory.

Whenever a servant of God is touched by any vice, he should devote himself to prayer.

For frequent prayer extinguishes the assault of vices.

[Col. 0615D] Nevertheless, we must persistently apply our mind to praying and singing psalms until, with the strongest concentration, we overcome the importunate suggestions of carnal desires that clamor against our senses.

When we pray, we bring our fault back to memory.

When we stand before God, we ought to groan and weep, remembering how grave are the crimes we have committed and how harsh are the punishments of hell that we fear.

Our mind is heavenly, and it contemplates God well in prayer when it is obstructed by no earthly cares or errors.

[Col. 0616A] The mind must therefore first be purified and separated from thoughts of temporal things, so that the clear vision of the heart may be directed truly and simply toward God.

We believe that divine mercy is obtained when we stand before God with a simple devotion as we pray.

The devil introduces thoughts of worldly cares into human minds especially when he sees them praying.

Whoever is injured should not cease praying for those who injure him; otherwise, according to God’s judgment, the person who does not pray for his enemies sins.

The prayer of one whose pain still remains in the mind or hatred in the breast accomplishes nothing.

One raises the heart with the hands who supports prayer with good works.

Whoever prays and does not act raises the heart but not the hands.

Whoever acts and does not pray raises the hands but not the heart.

Therefore it is necessary both to pray and to act.

A person raises his hand toward the Lord culpably when, in prayer, he boastfully discloses his deeds.

For whoever prays boastfully, seeking human praise, not only does his prayer fail to erase his sin, but the prayer itself is turned into sin.

Whenever we are not quickly heard while praying, let us set our deeds before our eyes, so that the delay itself may be attributed to divine justice and our guilt.

For God often does not grant many people what they desire, [Col. 0616C] so that he may hear them unto salvation.

It is not the many words of one who prays that win God’s favor, but the purest and most sincere devotion of prayer.

Frequent prayer drives away the devil’s darts.

Continual prayer overcomes the devil’s weapons.

Prayer’s persistence conquers unclean spirits, because demons are overcome through prayer.

FROM THE BOOK OF CLEMENT.

It is a discipline for us to pray for our killers and our persecutors.

BASIL.

Prayer is indeed a great admonition to the soul.

Through the purest prayers, the Lord grants us everything beneficial, and without doubt drives away everything harmful.

CYPRIAN.

[Col. 0616D]

Prayer is good together with fasting, and almsgiving together with righteousness.

Prayers quickly ascend to the Lord when the merits of our deeds raise them up to him.

CAESARIUS.

You ought to devote yourselves to reading and prayer in such a way that at times you are also able to work with your hands.

ISIDORE.

Prayer is hindered in two ways, so that a person cannot obtain what he asks: namely, if he is still committing evil, or if he does not forgive the debt owed by the person who has offended him.

FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS.

[Col. 0617A]

Just as stronger herbs or medicines drive away poisonous creatures, so prayer together with fasting repels filthy thoughts.

If we wish to discover prayers of a certain kind, we must prepare ourselves beforehand for prayer in that same way.

For a mind joined to Christ and especially attentive at the time of prayer receives nothing evil and nothing superfluous.

CHAPTER VIII. On Confession.

CHRIST.

“Everyone, therefore, who confesses me before human beings, I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10).

PAUL.

“With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

JAMES.

“Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5).

SOLOMON.

“Whoever hides his sins will not prosper” (Proverbs 28).

“But whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (ibid.).

JOHN.

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

[Col. 0617C] “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (ibid.).

JESUS SIRACH.

“Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not submit yourself to every person because of sin” (Ecclesiasticus 4).

“You shall confess while alive; alive and in health you shall confess, and you shall praise the Lord and glory in his mercies” (Ecclesiasticus 17).

ORIGEN.

If you confess your sins first, the Lord will hear you as his own people.

AUGUSTINE.

Confession of all evils is the beginning of all good works.

[Col. 0617D] Whoever confesses his sins and accuses his crimes makes a covenant with God.

Bear with a father who instructs, so that you may not experience a judge who punishes.

The time for confession is to confess what you have done: what you have done in word, what in deed, what by night, and what by day.

Confess at the appropriate time, and on the day of salvation you will receive the heavenly treasure.

JEROME.

It is ridiculous, when the whole body is weakened and broken, to display only a few wounds.

AMBROSE.

No remedy can be applied to a wound that is hidden.

GREGORY.

[Col. 0618A]

God does not wish to avenge wickedness; he urges people to confess their offenses.

God desires confessors to be released, lest he be forced to punish the obstinate.

A person will be weighed down with the burdens of sins to the extent that he has been alienated from good works.

The persistence that is usually disagreeable to human beings pleases the judge of truth.

Those who retain the wounds of their offenses closed within the breast nourish an ever more grievous pain within the more they suppress them in silence.

For when the corruption that is inside is expelled, the pain is opened for the sake of healing.

Every sinner, while hiding his guilt within his conscience, conceals it inwardly and hides it in his innermost chambers.

God sees sinners and tolerates them; God bears with those who resist and condemns them; and every day he mercifully calls them through the Gospel.

He desires our confession from a pure heart and releases all that we do wrong.

In confession, the poison of sin is healthfully exposed, though it had been festering pestilently in the mind.

In confessing sins, what else are we doing but exposing the evil that had been hidden within us?

For when a sinner turns from sins to tears, he begins to be just once he begins to accuse what he has done.

ISIDORE.

[Col. 0618C]

Those who hide their sins from human beings and do not confess them by themselves will have God, whom they have as witness, as their avenger.

Each person begins to be just from the moment when he becomes his own accuser.

Many confess themselves to be sinners against themselves, and yet do not withdraw themselves from sin.

A considerable part of justice already consists in a person recognizing that he is wicked, so that he may submit more humbly to divine power once he acknowledges his weakness.

The righteous person judges himself well in this life, so that he may not be judged by God with everlasting condemnation.

[Col. 0618D] A person passes judgment upon himself when, through worthy repentance, he condemns his evil deeds.

Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he failed to do good, or because through boldness he committed evil.

He did not do what he ought to have done, and he did what he ought not to have done.

It is already a portion of justice for a person not to hide his iniquity and to be ashamed within himself of his own sins.

Whoever calmly discloses the insults inflicted upon him opens the pain of his heart and easily resists the poison [the printed *virui* is uncertain] that he keeps in his mind.

For wounds of the mind, once opened, quickly heal; when closed, they fester excessively.

[Col. 0619A] Confession justifies a person; confession of sin grants forgiveness.

All hope rests in confession; in confession there is a place for mercy.

A disclosed sin is quickly healed.

But a crime is enlarged by silence.

If a vice is exposed, what was great becomes small.

If a vice is hidden, what was small becomes great.

By silence, guilt grows.

BASIL.

Pure confession concerning evil deeds is better than proud boasting about good works.

FROM THE BOOK OF CLEMENT.

When people remain silent, the timely and necessary remedy of speech cannot easily be applied.

Each person ought to bring forth the matter in which his soul languishes through ignorance.

CHAPTER IX. On Repentance.

CHRIST.

“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3).

PETER.

“Repent, and let each of you be baptized, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2).

PAUL.

“To those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption: eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, but believe iniquity: anger and indignation” (Romans 2).

SOLOMON.

“How good it is, when corrected, to show repentance; for in this way you will escape voluntary sin” (Ecclesiasticus 20).

“Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sorrowful thing has happened to me?’ For the Most High is patient in repaying” (Ecclesiasticus 5).

“Do not be without fear concerning a forgiven sin, and do not add sin upon sin” (ibid.).

“Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day.”

“Do not despise one who turns away from sin, and do not reproach him.”

“Remember that we are all in corruption” [Col. 0619D] (ibid.).

“The Most High hates sinners, but he has mercy on the repentant” (Ecclesiasticus 12).

“Turn to the Lord and abandon your sins” (Ecclesiasticus 17).

“My son, if you have sinned, do not do so again, but also pray concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Ecclesiasticus 21).

“Flee sins as though from the face of a serpent; if you approach them, they will seize you” (ibid.).

ORIGEN.

Repentance, even when slight, is not despised by God, the just judge.

AUGUSTINE.

Whoever considers his crimes and immediately turns back should believe that forgiveness is his.

[Col. 0620A] If you wish to repent only when you can no longer sin, your sins have abandoned you, not you them.

The impious soul is mourned in evils while it hopes for good things.

JEROME.

Would that the sinner might turn to repentance as quickly as the Lord is prepared to change the sentence he has determined.

For the Lord does not require a length of time, but weighs the sincerity of the repentant person’s devotion.

Whoever trusts in Christ with his whole mind, even if, having fallen as a human being, he has died in sin, will live forever through his faith.

A wound that is cured through pain must be guarded against.

Putrefaction of the flesh requires the knife and cautery.

[Col. 0620B] Sackcloth, filth, and uncut hair are not signs of a diadem, but of weeping and tears.

Sackcloth and fasting are the weapons of repentance and the remedy for sins, because an empty stomach and mournful clothing entreat God.

God is merciful by nature and ready, through clemency, to save what cannot be saved by justice.

But through our own vice we lose and abandon the mercy that is ready and offers itself willingly.

The Lord neither fulfills the good things he promised to the holy if they return to vices, nor inflicts the evils he threatens sinners if they have returned to salvation.

An unjust person who has gathered perishable riches through wickedness, if at some point he wishes to escape eternal punishments by turning back, must act so as to match the multitude [Col. 0620C] of his sins with an abundance of virtues.

HILARY.

Repentance changes one’s ways, and crimes of long duration perish in the blink of an eye if compunction has arisen from the heart.

GREGORY.

We do not make satisfaction for offenses if we do not cease from iniquity.

Whoever has committed what is forbidden must cut himself off from what is permitted; and he should rebuke himself in small matters who remembers having sinned in great ones.

A person is very far from faith if he waits for old age before undertaking repentance.

We must fear lest, while hoping for mercy, he fall into judgment.

To repent is to mourn the evils committed and not to commit again the evils that ought to be mourned.

For whoever mourns his sins but nevertheless commits others either does not know how to repent or pretends not to.

Almighty God declares that he labors when he bears the hard perversities of human beings.

If someone corrects you outwardly concerning a sin, confess inwardly what he does not know.

There can be no grace for offenses unless there is forgiveness of sins.

Therefore there is greater joy in heaven over a sinner who turns back than over a righteous person who stands firm.

It is necessary, then, for one who wishes to cleanse himself completely [Col. 0621A] from sin first to cut away the sins themselves.

The inner judge considers the mind rather than the words.

Sinners would never return to the lamentation of repentance if there were no examples of good people to draw their minds.

Every sin is serious, because it does not permit the soul to rise to lofty things.

For the person who now loses the fitting time for forgiveness will not find forgiveness then.

A person cannot earn from God there what he asks if here he refused to hear what God commanded.

Whoever loses the proper time for repentance comes in vain with prayers before the gate of the kingdom.

ISIDORE.

[Col. 0621B] Repentance must be practiced not in word but in deed.

A fault that is quickly disclosed is quickly corrected.

But a wound is healed more slowly when treatment is applied only after a long time, once the limbs have already begun to putrefy.

For whoever makes a habit of sinning is already buried.

A great crime necessarily requires great satisfaction.

Therefore whoever wishes to be certain of forgiveness at death should repent while healthy and, while healthy, mourn the crimes he has committed.

“Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1).

A person is washed and clean when he mourns past sins and does not commit again what must be mourned.

[Col. 0621C] A person is washed but not clean when he mourns what he has done but does not abandon it, and after his tears repeats what he had wept over.

There is danger for one who practices wickedness and repents at death; for just as condemnation is uncertain, so forgiveness is doubtful.

A person truly repents when he mourns his guilt with legitimate satisfaction—condemning and lamenting what he has done, and lamenting more abundantly in proportion to the greater readiness with which he fell into sin.

Although someone may be a sinner and impious, if he turns to repentance, he is believed capable of obtaining forgiveness.

Each person ought to hasten to God through repentance while he can, lest, if he wishes only when he cannot, he be unable to do so when he wishes too late.

God rejoices more over a soul that was lost and later converted than over one that was never lost.

There is greater joy before God and his angels over one who is rescued from danger than over one who never knew the danger of sin.

The more a lost thing causes sorrow, the more it brings joy when it is found.

Many, sprinkled with heavenly grace, return to God through repentance at the end of their lives.

Whatever evils they have committed, they cleanse with daily tears; and they exchange their evil deeds for good deeds, through which they are justly forgiven everything in which they sinned. [Col. 0622A] For through repentance they recognize what they did wrongly.

Repentance is the medicine of a wound and the hope of salvation, by which God is moved to mercy; it is measured not by time but by the depth of weeping and tears.

Repentance takes its name from punishment, because the soul is tormented and the flesh is mortified.

Those who practice repentance therefore grow their hair and beard, to demonstrate the abundance of crimes with which the sinner’s head is burdened.

Hair stands for vices, as it is written:

“Each person is bound by the hairs of his sins.”

[Col. 0622B] For this reason we practice repentance in sackcloth, so that through the prickling of the sackcloth we may recognize the vices we have committed through guilt.

The measure of time must not be considered as much as the measure of sorrow.

As great as the mind’s intention was in its rush toward evil, so great must its devotion be in love.

The groaning of repentance is twofold: either when we mourn what we have done wrongly, or when we failed to do what we ought to have done.

A person truly practices repentance when he neither neglects to repent of past deeds nor commits what will require repentance.

Although conversion at the end of life is good, conversion undertaken long before the end is better, so that one may pass from this life more securely [Col. 0622C].

In this world, God’s mercy helps those who practice repentance.

In the future, however, we will no longer be working, but giving an account of our works.

No one should despair of forgiveness, even if he turns to repentance near the end of life.

For if, by repenting, we perform deeds worthy of God, we will change his severity into clemency.

God tolerates us though we are evil; there is no doubt that he mercifully forgives those who turn back.

Just as one should not dwell affectionately upon the memory of sin, so each person must remember his own sin in mourning it.

[Col. 0622D] Every sin receives healing for its wound through repentance.

Nothing is worse than recognizing one’s guilt but not mourning it.

The freedom of repentance is available only in this life; after death there is no opportunity for correction.

Divine clemency helps the repentant, and forgiveness is granted through repentance.

A repeated wound is healed more slowly.

Medicine must be applied according to the illness.

Remedies must be applied in proportion to the wound.

CAESARIUS.

It is a very hard and deeply lamentable condition to devote all one’s effort and diligence to a task and, after the labor, receive no fruit.

[Col. 0623A] Someone says: “When I reach old age, then I will flee to the remedies of repentance.”

Why should human frailty presume this about itself, when it does not have even one day of its life in its own power?

If we acknowledge our iniquity, God forgives us.

Many believed that they would live for a long time, but sudden death took them away so completely that they could not even reach that momentary repentance.

We are ashamed to practice repentance for a short time, yet we do not fear enduring eternal punishments without end.

For God will quickly grant forgiveness to the person who does not spare himself for his sins.

CHAPTER X. On Abstinence.

[Col. 0623B]

CHRIST.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matthew 5).

PAUL.

“Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat” (Romans 14).

“And let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (ibid.).

Whoever eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God.

And whoever does not eat, does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God (ibid.).

“Every creature of God is good; nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (2 Timothy 4).

SOLOMON.

“The righteous eats and satisfies his soul, but the belly of the wicked is insatiable” (Proverbs 13).

“A satisfied soul tramples the honeycomb, but a hungry soul regards the bitter as sweet” (Proverbs 27).

“Whoever practices abstinence will add to his life” (Ecclesiasticus 37).

AUGUSTINE.

A mind wearied by lack of food will lose the vigor of prayer.

It is of no benefit to prolong a fast throughout the day if, after the satiety or excess of food, the soul is overwhelmed.

[Col. 0623D] Let food therefore be moderate; then the watered soil of our body will not produce the thorns of lust.

The flesh that receives food after many days is like the soul that is not continually nourished by the word of God.

He also says: Whoever cannot be cured by fasting can be redeemed by giving alms.

It is good to fast, but better to give alms.

Almsgiving suffices without fasting; fasting does not suffice without almsgiving.

Fasting together with almsgiving is a twofold good.

Fasting without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil.

Just as a lamp lit without oil can smoke [Col. 0624A] but cannot give light, so fasting without almsgiving torments the flesh but does not illumine the soul with the light of charity.

JEROME.

Fasts should be moderate, lest they weaken the stomach excessively, because moderate and temperate food is useful to flesh and soul.

A fat belly does not produce a refined mind.

A full belly readily disputes about fasts.

It is better for the stomach to suffer than the mind.

Impose upon yourself as much fasting as you can bear; and it is much better to take a little every day than to consume a sufficient amount rarely.

The best rain is that which does not descend upon the earth excessively.

[Col. 0624B] A sudden and excessive downpour overturns the fields headlong.

Even among legumes, all those that cause bloating and heaviness should be avoided.

Know that nothing contributes so much to Christian young men as eating vegetables.

The heat of the body should be moderated with cooler foods.

Some, desiring a chaste life, collapse halfway along the road because, while maintaining only abstinence from meat, they burden their stomach with legumes.

Nothing so inflames and excites the sexual organs as undigested food and violent belching.

Moderate food is always preferable to a hungry stomach’s three-day fast.

[Col. 0624C] Let the understanding, performing its service to God, always remain vigorous and be refined.

AMBROSE.

Fasts, vigils, almsgiving, and other practices of this kind should increase our goodness, not conceal our sin.
