That man should be considered abstinent who has become free from every vice.

For abstinence should not be credited where satiety of the belly has followed.

They mortify their members that are upon the earth when they chastise their insolent body through continual fasts.

Those who drink wine not in drunkenness but only for the health of the body do nothing contrary to abstinence; [Col. 0624D] pleasure does not offer it to them, but infirmity permits it.

Abstinence from food alone is not sufficient unless good works are joined to it.

GREGORY.

It is greater to nourish the mind for eternity with the food of the word than to satisfy the belly of dying flesh with earthly bread.

Food nourishes the body; the spirit is nourished by work.

Those who are abstinent and arrogant afflict the body through abstinence, but live through the desire for empty glory.

When the mind is stretched toward the commandment of charity, it unquestionably remains that the flesh be disciplined through abstinence.

A person fasts not for God but for himself if he does not give to the needy what [Col. 0625A] he temporarily withdraws from his stomach, but saves it to offer later to his stomach.

Those who practice abstinence must be admonished to understand that they offer abstinence pleasing to God when they distribute to the needy what they have taken away from themselves in food.

ISIDORE.

Those who abstain from food but act wickedly imitate demons.

Those, however, abstain well from foods who fast from evil deeds or from worldly ambition.

For lust grows through food, but through fasting sensuality is overcome.

This is perfect and rational fasting: when our outward person fasts, the inward person prays.

[Col. 0625B] Through fasting, moreover, hidden matters of the sacred ministries are revealed, and the mysteries of the divine sacrament are disclosed.

Fasts are strong weapons against the temptations of demons.

For through abstinence adversaries are quickly overcome.

Unclean spirits press in more insistently wherever they see more food and drink.

The flesh thirsts for God when it abstains through fasting and grows dry.

Moderate abstinence gives life, while excess kills: it gives life to the soul and kills the body.

Some practise incredibly strict abstinence in order to appear holy to curious people through devotion to prayer, rather than because of a vow of abstinence; they refrain from foods of flesh. These people [Col. 0625C] should rather be cursed, because they reject God’s creature, which has been granted for human use.

The fast that is renewed in the evening by filling oneself with food is despised.

The fast that is compensated for in the evening with delicacies is despised.

For anyone who prepares delicacies for himself in the evening to fill his appetite ruminates on banquets throughout the whole day.

Excessive bodily weakness breaks the soul’s strength and makes the mind’s intelligence wither; through feebleness one is unable to accomplish anything good.

Whatever is done with moderation and restraint is healthful.

[Col. 0625D] But whatever is excessive and beyond measure becomes harmful and turns one’s zeal in the opposite direction.

The body that abstinence weakens is not scorched by temptation.

Just as abstinence cuts away all carnal desires, so the vice of overeating destroys all the soul’s virtues.

No one can attain perfect virtue unless he has first subdued the belly’s gluttony.

BASIL.

We cannot keep watch properly when the stomach has been loaded with rich foods.

Strive to join fasts with vigils, so that you may flourish in every virtue.

[Col. 0626A] Just as bridles must be put on horses, so our hearts must be restrained by fasts.

For abundant food harms not only our hearts but also body and soul.

It is useless to cut off food from the belly while burying the soul beneath passions.

Make yourself such, my son, that when you wish to fast and abstain from food, you also abstain your tongue from unlawful thoughts.

Let us discipline the body with fasts and cleanse the mind of vices.

Fasting is also greatly beneficial for keeping vigil.

For just as a soldier is weighed down by a very heavy burden and hindered in battle, so a monk is hindered in vigils when he grows heated through an abundance of food.

[Col. 0626B] Often the strength of the stomach is broken by eagerness for food; likewise, through an abundance of food we suffer many illnesses from an excess of blood and bile.

CAESARIUS.

What good does it do if we afflict our flesh with fasts and vigils but do not amend our mind or care for what is inward?

FROM THE CONFERENCES.

Let each person eat as much food as sustenance of the body requires, not as much as the desire of the flesh demands.

Those who use food excessively dull their understanding all the more as they corrupt their stomach more deeply.

FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS.

[Col. 0626C] Just as flame consumes a forest, so hunger extinguishes evil visions.

Whoever restrains his belly will diminish his vices.

For whoever is conquered by food increases his vices.

As the increase of fire is wood, so the increase of the belly is abundant food.

Much wood raises a great flame; likewise, an abundance of food nourishes evil desires.

The flame is reduced when the forest fails, and the lack of food causes evil desires to grow mild.

Desire for food produced disobedience, and a sweet taste drove [humanity] from paradise.

Many foods delight the appetite, but they nourish the worm of fornication.

An empty stomach makes one watchful in prayers.

[Col. 0626D] For a stomach that is full brings on the deepest sleep.

Just as it is impossible to restrain a flame of fire running through straw, so it is impossible, once the belly is satisfied, to restrain the burning assault of lust.

The vapor of incense fills the air, and the prayer of the abstinent worships God. Proper measure fills a vessel, but a burst belly does not say, “Enough.”

When the passions and vices of our body are weakened by hunger, by fasting, and by the labor of vigils, then the power of our adversary demons is humbled.

## CHAPTER XI. On Abandoning the World

CHRIST.

Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, [Col. 0627A] or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life (Matt. XIX).

PAUL.

Do not conform yourselves to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern what is the good, acceptable, and perfect will of God (Rom. XII).

Those who use this world [should live] as though they did not use it (I Cor. VII).

JAMES.

Therefore, whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be constituted an enemy of God (James IV).

SOLOMON.

Turn to the Lord and abandon your sins [Col. 0627B] (Eccles. XII).

AUGUSTINE.

There are some who more readily give all their possessions to the poor than become themselves poor for God.

JEROME.

Many, after finding the way of truth, are captured by the pleasures of the world and turn back from the middle of the road.

The world is despised more easily than pleasure.

Many abandon riches but do not abandon vices.

It is evil that we serve the pursuit by which we seek again what we have sought.

Everyone is called the child of the one whose works he does.

If you desire to follow Christ and have the power to do so, sell what belongs to you; if you do not have it, you have been freed from a great burden.

He gave everything to God who offered himself.

The one who always thinks that he will die easily despises vices.

Whoever wishes to be perfect should flee crowds, titles, offices, greetings, and banquets as though they were chains of pleasure.

Would that what we renounce in the world were pleasure, not necessity.

Follow the naked Christ and the naked cross of Christ, naked yourself.

The Lord seeks the souls of believers more than their wealth.

AMBROSE.

[Col. 0627D] Whoever wishes to possess God must renounce the world, so that God may be his blessed possession.

The person whom the ambition for earthly possession delights has not renounced the world.

While each person does not abandon his own possessions, he serves the world whose goods he retains.

GREGORY.

Whoever has perfectly recognized, insofar as possibility allows, the sweetness of heavenly life willingly abandons everything on earth that he had loved.

Therefore, whoever has already recognized eternal life considers temporal benefits worthless.

Let the one who prepares a house of the mind for God wipe away the filth of evil works.

[Col. 0628A] The elect thus strive toward good that they do not fall back into committing evil.

Whoever does fully what he is fully able to do will receive what God has promised.

You abandon much if you renounce your desires.

For our outward possessions, however small, are enough for the Lord.

He weighs the heart, not the substance; he does not consider how much is in the sacrifice, but also when it is offered.

The kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess.

Those whom God tolerates for a long time so that they may convert, he condemns more harshly if they do not convert.

Those occupations that entangle one in sin must be abandoned so that, through conversion, the soul may turn back.

[Col. 0628B] It is not difficult for a person to abandon his possessions, but it is exceedingly difficult to abandon himself.

For it is a lesser thing to deny what one has; it is a very great thing to deny what one is.

Renunciation of the body is of no benefit to us without renunciation of the mind.

There are some who, having despised the desires of the flesh, plan to abandon everything; but when they see that others have fallen after beginning a good work, they fear doing what they had resolved to do.

BASIL.

Strive to please no one in your life except God alone.

For just as those who serve an earthly king obey all his commands, so those who serve the heavenly King must keep the heavenly commandments.

An earthly soldier goes to war against a visible enemy.

But an invisible enemy does not cease fighting against you every day.

ISIDORE.

It is necessary for every convert, after fear, to rise to the love of God like a son and not always lie under fear like a slave.

The beginnings of converts should be nurtured by gentle methods, lest, if they begin with harshness, they become terrified and rush back into their former falls.

Whoever instructs a convert without gentleness knows how to irritate rather than correct.

For that person is perfect who is perfect in heart and body with respect to this world.

Even after conversion, many unwillingly endure the movement of lust; yet they do not endure it as condemnation but as a test.

It is useful for God’s servant to be tested after conversion, so that, through the exercise of vices, the soul may be prepared for virtues and roused from the torpor of negligence by the vices that assail it.

The things dear to lovers of the world, the saints shun as though they were adversities; and they take more pleasure in the world’s adversities than they rejoice in its prosperities.

Everything in this world is opposed to God’s servants, so that, while they experience these adversities, they may be lifted more ardently toward heavenly desire.

[Col. 0629A] Great grace shines before God in the one who has become contemptible to this world.

For truly, the person whom the world hates must be loved by God.

For holy men there is no dwelling place in this world; their homeland and house are in heaven.

Those who love this world are troubled by its turbulent cares and anxieties.

Holy men who renounce the world die to this world in such a way that they delight in living for God alone.

To the extent that the saints withdraw from the way of life of this world, to that extent they contemplate, with the inward face of the mind, the presence of God and the fellowship and company of the angels.

If someone renounces what he possesses but does not renounce his former conduct in other respects, he is not Christ’s disciple.

For the one who renounces possessions denies what is his.

And the one who renounces evil conduct denies himself.

The mind to which this life is still sweet is far from God.

Many desire to fly toward God’s grace but fear being deprived of the world’s pleasures.

The love of Christ indeed summons them, but the desire for the world calls them back.

God terrifies people in many ways so that they may convert, even if late, and so that they may be more ashamed of having waited so long to return. Sometimes by threats, sometimes by blows, sometimes by revelations, he shakes certain people, so that those who disdain to convert willingly may be corrected when moved by terror.

We then show our love for conversion when we love the Lord as a father, though previously we truly feared him as God with a slave’s mind.

CAESARIUS.

It is useless for us to await a proper place if here we are the kind of people we were able to be in the world.

FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS.

Whoever loves the world will be exceedingly sorrowful; but whoever despises the things in it will always rejoice.

FROM THE BOOK OF CLEMENT.

Sudden change is difficult; but if people gradually become accustomed over a long period, there will be no difficulty in what comes through habit.

[Col. 0629D] God does not ask money of you, but a merciful soul and a devout mind.

## CHAPTER XI. On Fear

CHRIST.

Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matt. X).

Rather, fear him who can send both soul and body into Gehenna (ibid.).

PETER.

Conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourning; fear God and honor the king (I Pet. II).

Keeping your conduct pure in fear (I Pet. III).

PAUL.

[Col. 0630A]

You did not receive a spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons of God, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VI).

Always giving thanks for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ (Eph. V).

SOLOMON.

The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov. I).

Fear the Lord and turn away from evil (Prov. III).

The fear of the Lord will add days, but the years of the wicked will be shortened (Prov. X).

In the fear of the Lord there is confidence of strength, and his children will have hope.

The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life, so that they may turn away from the destruction of death [Col. 0630B] (Prov. XIV).

Whoever fears God neglects nothing (ibid.).

JESUS SIRACH.

The fear of the Lord is glory, boastfulness, joy, and a crown of exultation (Eccles. I).

The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and give gladness, joy, and length of days (ibid.).

It will go well with the one who fears God at the end, and he will be blessed on the day of his death (ibid.).

The fear of the Lord is the religious devotion of knowledge; the fullness of wisdom is to fear God (ibid.).

The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling one with peace and the fruit of salvation.

The root of wisdom is to fear God, for its branches are long-lived.

[Col. 0630C] The fear of the Lord drives out sin, for whoever is without fear cannot be justified (ibid.).

Wisdom and discipline are the fear of the Lord (ibid.).

Do not be unbelieving toward the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a divided heart (ibid.).

You who fear the Lord, wait for his mercy, and do not turn away from him, lest you fall (Eccles. II).

You who fear God, believe him, and your reward will not be lost.

You who fear God, praise him, and in gladness mercy will come to you (Ps. XXI).

You who fear God, love him, and your hearts will be enlightened (Eccles. II).

Those who fear God will not disbelieve his word; [Col. 0630D] and those who love the Lord will keep his way.

AUGUSTINE.

Those who fear the Lord seek what is pleasing to him, and those who love him will be filled with his law.

Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts and sanctify their souls in his presence.

Those who fear the Lord keep his commandments and will have patience until they behold him.

Keep the thought of God’s precepts, and be especially constant in his commandments.

Fear God with your whole soul; those who fear God will be in his sight.

[Col. 0631A] The fear of the Lord means not despising a beggar or a poor person.

The judge is great and powerful in honor; no one is greater than the one who fears God.

There is nothing better than the fear of God.

God hates every abomination of error, and it will not be pleasing to those who fear God.

The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and he himself knows all human works.

A wise person fears in all things and, in the days of the elect, guards against idleness.

Wisdom confirms the fear of God.

Whoever fears the Lord will receive his instruction and will kindle justice like a light.

Whoever fears the Lord will receive his instruction, and [Col. 0631B] whoever keeps watch for him will find his blessing.

Evil does not overtake the one who fears the Lord; in temptation he will preserve and deliver him from evil.

The spirit of those who fear God is sought, and in his answer he is blessed.

For there is hope for those who fear God, for their salvation.

Whoever fears God trembles at nothing and will not be afraid, because he himself is his hope.

The soul of those who fear God is blessed, and the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him.

The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing, and they covered him with every glory.

Blessed is the one to whom it has been granted to possess the fear of the Lord.

[Col. 0631C] The fear of the Lord is the beginning of his love.

Wealth and food elevate the heart, and above these stands the fear of the Lord.

JEROME.

Nothing keeps us so free from every sin as fear of punishment and love of God.

AMBROSE.

Whoever fears God turns away from error and directs his ways toward the path of virtue.

GREGORY.

A perverse mind, unless it is first overturned by fear, is not corrected of its habitual vices.

To fear God is to pass over none of the good things that ought to be done.

ISIDORE.

The fear of the Lord always corrects.

The fear of the Lord drives out sin.

And the fear of the Lord restrains vice.

Fear makes a person cautious and watchful.

But where there is no fear, there is disorder in life.

Where there is no fear, there is criminality.

Where there is no fear, there is an abundance of crimes.

If we do not wish to fear God in tranquility, let us at least fear his judgment when crushed by remorse.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Virginity

CHRIST.

The children of this age marry and are given in marriage; but those who are deemed worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead [Col. 0632A] neither marry nor take wives, for they cannot die any longer: they are equal to the angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection (Luke XX).

PAUL.

The unmarried virgin considers the things of the Lord, how she may please God (I Cor. VII).

He who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her does better (ibid.).

AUGUSTINE.

Virginity of the body is of no benefit where corruption of the mind is at work.

For just as a slain enemy does you no injury, so mortified flesh will not disturb your soul.

[Col. 0632B] Such ministers ought to belong to the Lord: they should not be corrupted by any defilement of the flesh, but rather should shine through the continence of chastity.

JEROME.

There is a great difference between the purity of a virginal soul polluted by no defilement and the filth of one that has been subject to the lust of many.

The number one hundred is perfect; it is assigned to virgins as the crown of virginity.

Sixty is the second rank, assigned to the continence of widows.

Thirty is the third place; it bears witness to the bonds of marriage by the very joining of the words, as though widows, having lost the first rank, reached the second through the third.

A woman’s reputation for modesty is a delicate thing, and, like [Col. 0632C] a most beautiful flower, it quickly withers at the slightest breeze.

A man’s age readily yields to the slightest breeze that is disturbed by the waves, if the authority of marriage is absent.

Strive to keep not only your eyes chaste but also your tongue.

It is useless to have a virgin body if one has married in mind.

ISIDORE.

Some who live luxuriously in youth take pleasure in becoming continent in old age; they choose to serve chastity only when lust has disdained to keep them as its slaves.

Such people will have no reward, because they endured no struggles of labor. Glory belongs to those in whom [Col. 0632D] there have been arduous struggles.

Those who dedicate their bodies to continence should not presume to live with women.

Virginity is a twofold good: in this age it loses the anxiety of the world, and in the future it receives the eternal reward of chastity.

Those who persevere as chaste and virginal become equal to God’s angels.

Chastity is the fruit of sweetness.

Chastity is security of mind and health of body.

If virginity falls, it cannot in any way be restored.

Although repentance receives the fruit of forgiveness, it in no way regains its former incorruption.

A virgin in body but not in mind has no reward in forgiveness.

[Col. 0633A] Continence brings a person near to God; wherever it remains, there God also remains. For death enters through the eyes.

Chastity joins a person to heaven.

Chastity draws a person up to heaven.

CAESARIUS.

It is useless to preserve virginity and bodily integrity if they do not wish to care for the desires of heaven.

Long chastity after sin is an imitation of virginity.

Bodily integrity is not preserved when the mind is corrupted by the swelling of pride.

Virginity in the body will be of no benefit if love or humility has departed from the heart. Humble [Col. 0633B] married life is better than proud virginity.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Justice

CHRIST.

Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. VI).

Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill (Luke V).

For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance (ibid.).

Just as through one person’s transgression death passed to all people, so through one person’s justice the justification of life came to all people (Rom. V).

Just as sin reigned in death, so grace might reign through justice unto eternal life (ibid.).

JAMES.

[Col. 0633C]

The fruit of justice is sown in peace by those who make peace (James III).

SOLOMON.

The Lord does not afflict the soul of the righteous with hunger, but he overthrows the plots of the wicked (Prov. X).

The memory of the righteous is with praises, but the name of the wicked rots (Prov. X).

The work of the righteous leads to life, but the fruit of the wicked leads to sin (ibid.).

Chosen silver is the tongue of the righteous; the heart of the wicked is worth nothing (ibid.).

What the wicked fears will come upon him, but what the righteous desire will be given to them (ibid.).

The tongue of the righteous considers what is peaceful, but the mouth of the wicked [Col. 0633D] speaks perversely.

The righteous is delivered from distress, and the wicked is handed over in his place (Prov. II).

The offspring of the righteous will be saved; every desire of the righteous is good (Prov. XII).

Overturn the wicked, and they will be no more, but the houses of the righteous will remain.

The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tents of the righteous will flourish (Prov. XIV).

Do not be excessively righteous (Eccles. VII).

The house of the righteous has abundant strength, but in the fruits of the wicked there is turmoil (Prov. XV).

The way of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord; whoever follows justice is loved by him.

[Col. 0634A] There are righteous people who are wise, and their works are in the hand of God; yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, for everything is reserved for the future in uncertainty (Eccles. IX).

There are righteous people to whom evil comes as though they had done the works of the wicked (Eccles. VIII). And there are wicked people who are so secure as though they possessed the deeds of the righteous (ibid.).

The wicked flee when no one pursues them (Prov. XXVIII).

But the righteous, confident like a lion, will be without error (ibid.).

JESUS SIRACH.

Strive for your soul in justice, even unto death (Eccles. IV).

Fight for justice, and God will fight down your enemies for you (ibid.).

[Col. 0634B] God’s gift remains with the righteous (Eccles. XI).

God’s blessing hastens as the reward of the righteous (ibid.).

Before a person are life and death, good and evil; whichever pleases him will be given to him (Eccles. XV).

Prepare justice for yourself before judgment (Eccles. XVIII).

Whoever keeps judgment will restrain his understanding (ibid.).

If you pursue justice, you will seize it and put it on as the modesty of honor (Eccles. XVII).

Whoever keeps justice will himself be exalted (Eccles. XX).

AUGUSTINE.

If I am righteous, I fear nothing; no one can terrify me.

“The righteous,” he says, “is confident like a lion.”

GREGORY.

[Col. 0634C]

Justice, if it has no measure, turns into cruelty.

The wickedness of those who remain merits that those who could have been of benefit should be swiftly removed; and when the end of the world approaches, the elect are taken away lest they see worse things.

God is angry with the unrighteous in such a way that their hearts are nevertheless consoled through the company of the righteous.

ISIDORE.

Many are thought elect among human beings, yet stand rejected before God.

And many are rejected among human beings, yet are elect before God.

Let no one consider himself elect, lest perhaps he is already rejected before God.

FROM THE BOOK OF CLEMENT.

[Col. 0634D]

The perfection of the law is peace.

Wars and struggles arise from sins.

But where sin is not committed, there is peace of soul.

Where there is peace, truth is found in disputes and justice in deeds.

## CHAPTER XV. On Envy

CHRIST.

Do not judge one another (Matt. VII).

Beware, however, of the leaven of the Pharisees (Matt. XVI).

PETER.

Therefore, laying aside all malice and all deceit, [Col. 0635A] hypocrisies, slanders, and envies (I Pet. I).

Love does not envy (I Cor. I).

Some indeed preach Christ because of envy, but others because of good will (Phil. I).

SOLOMON.

The life of the flesh is the health of the heart, but envy is the rottenness of the bones (Prov. XIV).

Do not eat with an envious person or desire his foods, for, like a diviner and soothsayer, he evaluates what he does not know (Prov. XXIII).

“Eat and drink,” he will say to you, but his heart is not with you (ibid.).

Whoever is envious of himself—nothing is worse than he is (Eccles. XIV).

AUGUSTINE.

[Col. 0635B]

Envy burns up all virtues; through envy Christ crucified is preached to you.

Envy and spite intoxicate the soul above all things.

Where there is envy, love of the brethren cannot exist.

Whoever envies does not love; the devil’s commandment is in him, because the devil fell through envy.

Thus it is recognized that envy cannot exist in love.

For through envy Christ was crucified.

Therefore, whoever envies his brother crucifies Christ.

JEROME.

Envy always follows virtues.

[Col. 0635C] Great is the man who overcomes envy through humility.

AMBROSE.

The person who makes his good consist in seeing another’s punishment is certainly envious.

GREGORY.

It is the death of sinners to envy in others the good of virtues that they themselves do not desire to possess.

Those who scarcely recognize the grace of gifts in themselves should not envy greater gifts in others.

ISIDORE.

From the very place where the good person advances, the envious person wastes away.

The envious person is a member of the devil, through whose envy death entered the world.

Many wish to imitate good people but waste away in the spite of envy at the progress of the good.

[Col. 0635D] Those who waste away in hatred of a brother are to be mourned and lamented.

Envy gnaws the understanding, afflicts the mind, and burns the breast.

Envy consumes the human heart like a kind of plague.

Let love be prepared against envy.

Do not grieve over another’s good; do not waste away over another’s progress.

Do not be made unhappy by anyone’s prosperity.

EUSEBIUS.

The error of envy penetrates not only religious souls but also base ones.

EPHRAEM.

For envy reveals that we do not possess the love of God at all.

JOSEPHUS.

[Col. 0636A]

It is difficult to be free from envy amid prosperity.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Silence

CHRIST.

A good person brings good things out of a good treasure, and an evil person brings evil things out of an evil treasure (Matt. XII).

Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory (John VII).

PAUL.

They are verbose, idle, and inquisitive, saying what they ought not to say (I Tim. V).

But speak what befits sound doctrine [Col. 0636B] (I Tim. II).

SOLOMON.

In much speaking sin will not be absent (Prov. X).

But whoever restrains his lips is most prudent (Prov. XVII).

Because of sins of the lips, ruin draws near to evil (Prov. XII).

Whoever guards his mouth guards his soul (Prov. XXI).

But whoever is thoughtless in speaking will experience evil; in every good work there will be abundance (Prov. XIII).

Where there are very many words, there is frequent poverty (ibid.).

A soothing tongue is a tree of life.

[Col. 0636C] But the undisciplined tongue crushes the spirit (Prov. I).

It belongs to a person to prepare the mind, but to the Lord to guide the tongue (Prov. XVI).

The lips of kings desire what is just; whoever speaks truth is loved (ibid.).

Whoever thinks perverse thoughts with staring eyes and bites his lips accomplishes evil (Prov. XVII).

Whoever exalts his heart seeks ruin (ibid.).

Whoever restrains his speech is learned and prudent, and an educated person is a man of precious spirit (ibid.).

Death and life are in the power of the tongue.

The poor person speaks with entreaties, but the rich person answers harshly.

Whoever neglects his ways will be put to death (Prov. X).

[Col. 0636D] He kisses the lips who gives a right answer (Prov. XXIV).

Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from distress (Prov. XXI).

JESUS SIRACH.

Do not be hasty with your tongue, or maimed and negligent in your works (Eccles. IV).

Before you hear, do not answer a word; and in the midst of elders do not add to your speech (Eccles. II).

Blessed is the person who has not stumbled in speech from his mouth and has not been pierced by the sorrow of wrongdoing (Eccles. I).

Before you speak, learn (Eccles. XII).

Whoever hates loquacity extinguishes malice (Eccles. IX).

[Col. 0637A] Do not repeat a wicked and harsh word, and you will not be diminished (Eccles. XVIII).

There is one who slips with his tongue but not from the heart (Eccles. XV).

For who is there who has not sinned with his tongue (ibid.)?

There is one who sends out his word while declaring the truth (Eccles. XIX).

A wicked word will change the heart (Eccles. XXXV).

There is one who keeps silent and is found wise; and there is one who is hateful because he is forward in speaking (Eccles. XX).

There is one who keeps silent because he lacks the ability to speak; and there is one who keeps silent because he knows the appropriate time (Eccles. XX).

A wise person will keep silent until the proper time, but the frivolous and imprudent person will not observe the proper time (Prov. II).

[Col. 0637B] Whoever uses many words injures his soul (Eccles. XXIX).

Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not as many as those who have perished through their tongue (Eccles. XX).

The yoke of his tongue is iron, and its bond is a bronze bond (Eccles. XXVIII).

Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue (ibid.).

Make doors for your mouth and bolts for your ears (ibid.).

Make a balance for your words and straight reins for your mouth (ibid.).

Take care lest you slip with your tongue, fall before your enemies lying in wait for you, and your fall become incurable unto death.

[Col. 0637C] Have you sat at a large table? Do not open your mouth over it first (Eccles. XXXI).

Young man, speak in your own cause only when necessary. If you are questioned twice, let your answer be concise (Eccles. XXXII).

Among many people be like one who does not know, and listen silently while also asking questions (ibid.).

Where there are old men, do not speak much.

Where there is no hearing, do not pour out speech, and do not inopportunely exalt yourself in wisdom.

JEROME.

Let the person who never learned to speak learn at some point to cease speaking properly.

AMBROSE.

There is a person who indeed cultivates silence, but his [Col. 0637D] heart condemns him greatly.

Such a person speaks much.

And there is another who speaks from morning until evening, yet preserves great silence with discretion.

GREGORY.

No one should presumptuously dare either to despise or to judge what he does not understand.

ISIDORE.

Know at what time you should speak; consider when you should speak.

Speak at the appropriate time; be silent at the appropriate time.

Do not speak unless you have been questioned; do not speak before you have heard; let a question open your mouth.

A talkative person is unlearned; a wise person uses few words.

[Col. 0638A] Knowledge makes speech brief.

To speak much is folly.

For the voice of a fool is found in an excess of speech.

Therefore let measure remain in the word, and let there be a balance in speech.

Let your words always be restrained; do not go beyond the proper limit of speaking.

Love listening more than speaking; listen more than you talk.

First listen, then speak.

The final outcome has more honor.

The final word is better than the beginning.

BASIL.

Do not bring forth a speech in an assembly; let appropriate words proceed from your mouth.

[Col. 0638B] When you find the appropriate time, speak so that you may offer grace to those who hear you.

CAESARIUS.

It is useless for there to be silence in a dwelling if in the dwellings of the vices there are tumult and the clash of passions.

FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS.

Carry out what you do in truth with silence and prayer.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Pride

CHRIST.

Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

What is exalted among human beings is an abomination before [Col. 0638C] God (Luke XIV, XVIII).

PAUL.

Do not be high-minded, but fear (Rom. XI).

Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up (I Cor. VIII).

Love is not puffed up.

SOLOMON.

Pride precedes ruin, and the heart is exalted before a fall (Prov. XVII).

JESUS SIRACH.

Pride is hateful before God and human beings (Eccles. X).

The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God (ibid.).

The beginning of every sin is pride (ibid.).

God has erased the memory of the proud (ibid.).

Pride was not created for human beings (Eccles. XIII).

[Col. 0638D] Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it, and whoever associates with the proud will put on pride (Eccles. V).

The tongue of the proud is a most evil devouring.

The shedding of blood in the quarrel of the proud consumes them with sorrow before they die (Eccles. XXVII).

Just as a goat is led into a snare, so is the body of the proud (Eccles. XI).

Do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull, lest your strength be shattered through folly (Eccles. VI).

AUGUSTINE.

We must avoid pride, which wished to deceive even angels—how much more would it destroy human beings?

JEROME.

[Col. 0639A]

A proud person will neither be honored nor bring his will to completion.

It is a grave fault when the crime of pride is added to inexperience and negligence.

Let no Christian strive more to avoid anything than a swollen and erect neck that provokes God’s hatred against him.

AMBROSE.

Pride turned angels into demons.

Humility, however, makes holy people like angels.

A proud will causes one to despise God’s commandments; humility causes one to keep them.

The proud desire to have proclaimed in themselves what they do not do; [Col. 0639B] the humble refuse to acknowledge whatever good they accomplish.

GREGORY.

By no means can a person learn the summit of humility who does not cease to be proud in the smallest matters.

ISIDORE.

Each person is that much nearer to the truth to the extent that he judges himself farther from pride.

The proud imitate the devil’s pride; against it is set the humility of Christ, by which the elect are humbled.

Pride is the queen of the principal vices, and every sinner is proud.

Every form of pride lies as low as it raises itself high; and the higher it is lifted, the more deeply it falls.

For whoever is lifted up through his own pride is bent down by God’s justice.

Those who are puffed up with pride feed on wind.

Pride, just as it is the origin of all crimes, is likewise the ruin of all virtues: it is first in sin and last in the struggle.

Those who become proud over their progress in virtue are humbled when they fall through the vice of the flesh, so that they may rise again.

FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS.

A rotten fruit is useless to the farmer, and the virtue of the proud is useless to God.

For just as the weight of fruit breaks a branch, so pride breaks the beauty of the soul.

The soul of the proud is abandoned by God and becomes the object of demons’ desire.

Pride cast the archangel down from heaven and made him fall upon the earth like a [Col. 0639D] flash of lightning.

Humility raises a human being to heaven and makes him rejoice with the angels.

Do not, through pride, deny your offspring, even though she is poor and you are wealthy; the one who fashioned both is himself the knower.

JOSEPHUS.

For whatever belongs to pride or ruin quickly falls; whatever belongs to grace endures for a long time.

CHRIST.

“Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matt. X).

“Wisdom is justified by her children” (Matt. XI).

“The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke XVI).

PAUL.

“Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety” (Rom. XII).

“Do not be wise in your own estimation” (ibid.).

“Since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.”

“For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (I Cor. III).

SOLOMON.

“Bend your heart toward understanding prudence” [Col. 0640B] (Prov. II).

“For if you call upon wisdom and incline your heart toward prudence; if you seek her as money and dig for her as for treasures, then you will understand the fear of God and find the knowledge of the Lord.

“Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not rely upon your own prudence, lest you be wise in your own eyes” (Prov. III).

“For her acquisition is better than the commerce of silver and gold; her first and purest fruits are more precious than all riches, and nothing that is desired [Col. 0640C] can be compared with her” (Prov. VIII).

“The wise shall possess glory, but the exaltation of fools is disgrace” (Prov. III).

“The beginning of wisdom: possess wisdom, and in all your possessions acquire prudence” (Prov. IV).

“Seize her, and she will exalt you.

“You will be glorified by her when you have embraced her” (ibid.).

“She will give increase of graces to your head, and an illustrious crown will protect you” (Prov. IV).

Wisdom is better than all precious things, and nothing desirable can be compared with her.

“The wise of heart accepts commandments, but the fool is beaten by his lips” (ibid.).

Wisdom is found on the lips of the wise.

The wise conceal wisdom.

But the mouth of the fool is near to confusion.

“The lips of the righteous instruct many, but those who are unlearned will die in poverty of heart” (ibid.).

“The tongue of the wise is health” (Prov. XII).

“The law of the wise is a fountain of life, so that he may turn aside from the ruin of death” (Prov. XIII).

“Whoever walks with the wise will be wise, but the friend of fools will become like them.

“The wise man fears and turns aside from evil” (Prov. XIV).

[Col. 0641A] “The crown of the wise is their riches, and the folly of fools is imprudence.

“Prudence rests in the heart of the prudent, and the unlearned will also be instructed.

“The lips of the wise disseminate knowledge, but the heart of fools will be unlike them.

“The heart of the wise seeks instruction, but the mouth of fools is fed with ignorance” (Prov. XVI).

“Possess wisdom, for it is better than gold; acquire prudence, for it is more precious than silver. Whoever is wise of heart will be called prudent, and whoever is gentle in speech will receive greater things.

“The heart of the wise instructs his mouth, and adds grace to his lips” (ibid.).

“Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth, and an overflowing torrent [Col. 0641B] is a fountain of wisdom” (Prov. XVIII).

“Wisdom shines on the face of the prudent” (Prov. XVII).

“The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth” (Prov. XIX).

“The guardian of prudence will find good things” (Prov. XX).

“For there is gold and an abundance of jewels, but the lips of knowledge are a precious vessel” (ibid.).

“Do not sell wisdom, or instruction, or understanding” (Prov. XXIII).

“A wise man is strong” (Prov. XXIV).

“A learned man is robust and vigorous; do not be wiser than necessary, lest you be stupefied” (ibid.).

“Wisdom will strengthen the wise man more than a ruler of ten cities” (Eccles. VII).

“The words of the wise are heard in silence more than the shouting of a prince among fools” (Eccles. IX).

“The words of the mouth of the wise are grace, but the lips of the fool will bring him down” (ibid.).

“All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Eccles. I).

“The love of God is honorable wisdom” (ibid.).

“In the treasures of wisdom are understanding and knowledge for the religious” (ibid.).

“But wisdom is a curse to sinners.”

“Desire wisdom, preserve justice, and God will provide it for you” (ibid.).

“For it is not necessary for you to see with your eyes the things that are hidden” (Eccles. III).

“The heart of the wise understands wisdom, and a good ear will hear wisdom with every desire” (ibid.).

“The wise and understanding heart restrains itself from sin” (ibid.).

“Wisdom inspires life in her children and receives those who seek her” (Eccles. IV).

“Whoever loves wisdom loves life; those who hold fast to wisdom will inherit life” (ibid.).

“For wisdom is recognized by the tongue” (ibid.).

“Sense, knowledge, and instruction are in the word of truth” (ibid.).

“For the beauty of life is in wisdom, and its bonds are a saving bond.

[Col. 0642A] “If you incline your ear, you will receive instruction; and if you love to hear, you will be wise” (ibid.).

“Wisdom will exalt the head of the humbled person and make him sit in the midst of nobles” (Eccles. XI).

“Blessed is the man who abides in his wisdom and meditates in his justice.

“Praise is not precious in the mouth of a sinner, since wisdom proceeds from God” (ibid.).

“For praise will stand beside wisdom, dwell in the mouth of the faithful, and the ruler will give it to him.”

“Every draught has acknowledged wisdom.” [The wording is uncertain.]

“All wisdom is the fear of God, and in it, fearing God is the ordering of the law in all wisdom” (Eccles. XIX).

[Col. 0642B] “A prudent man will please the great” (Eccles. XX).

“Better is the man who is diminished in wisdom and deficient in understanding but fears God, than he who abounds in understanding and transgresses the law of the Most High” (Eccles. XIX).

“A wise man makes himself lovable by his words” (Eccles. XX).

“But the favor of fools is poured out.”

“Hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what use are either of them?”

“Prudent instruction is a golden ornament, and like a bracelet on the right arm” (Eccles. XXI).

“But the words of the prudent will be weighed on a scale” (ibid.).

“Discipline and instruction are wisdom at all times” (Eccles. XXII).

[Col. 0642C] “Great is the one who finds wisdom and knowledge, but he is not above the one who fears God” (Eccles. XXIII).

“A holy man remains in wisdom like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” (Eccles. XXVII).

“The wise man does not hate commandments and ordinances” (Eccles. XXXIII).

“A wise man instructs his people” (ibid.).

“Wisdom will be planted in the mouth of the faithful” (Eccles. XXXVII).

“A skilled man instructs many, and is pleasing to his own soul” (ibid.).

“A wise man will be filled with blessing; the wise man among the people will inherit honor, and his name will live forever.

[Col. 0642D] “Write wisdom during a time of leisure, and whoever is reduced in activity will acquire wisdom” (Eccles. XXXVIII).

“The wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients” (Eccles. XXX).

“The wise man will test good and evil in all things” (Eccles. XXIX).

AUGUSTINE.

“The learned will shine like the stars in splendor.”

[Col. 0643A]

“It is much better to state the truth in rustic language than falsehood eloquently.”

“Wisdom is to fear God, but to deny oneself to evils.”

[Col. 0643B] “If the understanding of sacred Scripture were open in every respect, it would become cheap; and it refreshes with all the greater sweetness when discovered, the more greatly it tires the soul when sought.

“Wisdom is better than strength, and the prudent man better than the strong.

“But an abundance of wisdom is the health of the world.

“For the Lord loves no one except him who dwells with wisdom.”

“Every person who is wise according to God is blessed.”

“No one fully receives the wisdom of God unless he strives to withdraw himself from concern for every vice.”

“We know God rightly only when we deny that we know him perfectly.”

“No one is more deeply at fault than the one who does not know God” [Col. 0643D].

“Many seek the investigation of truth, but few find it.

“I have called simplicity combined with prudence wisdom.

“It is useful to know many things and to live rightly.

[Col. 0644A] “Nor is it blessed to know many things; rather, it is great to live blessedly.

“Many know God through knowledge, but do not honor him through action.

“Nothing is better than wisdom, nothing sweeter than prudence, nothing more pleasant than knowledge.

“We avoid harmful things only through wisdom.

“Wisdom becomes more abundant when given, and diminishes when withheld.

“Knowledge is a generous overflow, and the more it is imparted, the more abundantly it increases.”

CYPRIAN.

“For how can someone be wise or patient who possesses neither wisdom nor patience?

“That man is wise who is humble and gentle.”

## CHAPTER XIX. On Anger

[Col. 0644B]

CHRIST.

“Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. V).

PAUL.

“Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. IV).

“Be angry and do not sin.”

JAMES.

“For the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James I).

SOLOMON.

“A fool immediately displays his anger” (Prov. XII).

“But whoever conceals an injury is prudent” (Prov. XII).

“Among the proud there are always quarrels” (Prov. III).

“But those who do everything with counsel are governed by wisdom” (Prov. XIII).

“A gentle answer breaks anger” (Prov. XXV).

“A harsh word arouses fury” (ibid.).

“An angry man provokes quarrels” (ibid.).

“Whoever is wise calms what has been aroused” (Prov. XV).

“Do not be quick to anger, because anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccles. VIII).

“The wicked always seeks quarrels, and a cruel angel will be sent against him” (Prov. XVII).

“As the roaring of a lion is the king’s anger, and as dew upon the earth is his cheerfulness” (Prov. XIX).

“The spirit of a man sustains his weakness, but who can bear a spirit easily given to anger [Col. 0644D]?” (Prov. XVIII).

“Anger has no mercy, nor does bursting fury.

“Who can bear the violence of an agitated spirit?” (Prov. XXVII).

JESUS SIRACH.

“Do not quarrel with an angry man” (Eccles. IX).

“The heart of a man changes his face, either for good or for evil” (Eccles. XXXI).

“You will scarcely find, and only with difficulty, the mark of a good heart and a gracious face” (ibid.).

“There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and there is no anger worse than the anger of an enemy” (Eccles. XV).

“Remember the fear of God, and do not be angry with your neighbor” (Eccles. XXVIII).

[Col. 0645A] “As the wood of the forest is, so the fire blazes; and according to a man’s strength, so will his anger be” (ibid.).

“An angry man sets a quarrel ablaze.”

“Jealousy and anger shorten one’s days and bring on old age before its time.”

AUGUSTINE.

“Fury at its beginning is anger, and indignation boiling in the soul.

GREGORY.

“For the devil is accustomed to introduce the evil of quarrels into one person’s heart from the place where he sees another stirred to the work of piety” [Col. 0645B].

“In our good work we must sometimes avoid giving scandal to our neighbor, but at other times regard it as nothing.

“As far as we can without sin, we ought to avoid scandalizing our neighbors.

“But if scandal arises from the truth, it is more useful to allow scandal to arise than to abandon the truth.”

JEROME.

“If anger has overtaken you, calm it.”

FROM THE BOOK OF CLEMENT.

“That anger is evil which disturbs the mind so that it loses sound counsel.

“But that anger which punishes the wicked does not bring disturbance of mind.

FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS.

“Angry eyes, turbulent and bloodshot, are messengers of an angry heart.

“The prayer of the angry is hated incense, and angry psalmody is a dreadful sound.”

[Col. 0645D] “For sadness is an impediment to every good thing.

“A person made excessively sad does not direct his understanding toward contemplation of divine thought, nor will he ever utter a pure prayer.

“The strongest wind does not move a tower, and indignation does not move a soul without anger.

“Water is moved by the violence of winds, and the angry person is disturbed by angry thoughts.

“Whoever does not restrain his tongue in a time of anger will never be able to restrain the passion of his flesh.

“As the southwest wind is on the sea, so is a man’s fury in his heart.”

## CHAPTER XX. On Vainglory

[Col. 0646A]

CHRIST.

“Take heed that you do not practice your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. VI).

“Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father” (ibid.).

PAUL.

“Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I).

SOLOMON.

“Do not boast about tomorrow, not knowing what the coming day will bring” (Prov. XXVII).

“Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (ibid.).

JESUS SIRACH.

[Col. 0646B]

“Do not exalt yourself in doing your work” (Eccles. I).

“Do not seek leadership from a man, nor a seat of honor from a king” (Eccles. VII).

“Do not praise a man for his appearance, nor despise a person by his outward appearance” (Eccles. XI).

“Do not justify yourself before the Lord, for he himself is the knower of the heart” (Eccles. VII).

“Never boast in clothing, nor exalt yourself on the day of your honor” (ibid.).

“Do not praise anyone before death, for a man is known by his children” (Eccles. XI).

“The sinner and the proud man are caught in vanity” (Eccles. XXIII).

[Col. 0646C] “Do not praise a man before his speech” (Eccles. XXVII).

“For this is a test of human beings” (ibid.).

“Do not wish to appear wise in the presence of a king” (Eccles. VII).

“Take care of a good name, for this will profit you more than a thousand great and precious treasures” (Eccles. XLI).

“A good life has a number of days, but a good name will remain forever.”

JEROME.

“Do not seek glory, and you will not grieve when you are without glory.

“Whoever does not desire praise does not feel insult.

“Do not consider yourself good merely because you are called good.

“No one can know who you are better than you, who are conscious of yourself.

[Col. 0646D] “For what does it profit you, if you are wicked, to be called good?

“Beware lest you be lifted up by people’s rumors, lest, having offended God, you consume the praises of the peoples.”

GREGORY.

“The saints not only do not seek glory beyond what is fitting for them, but even avoid the very thing they know themselves to possess.

“What a person does is truly good when he desires to please the one from whom it comes.

“Whoever appears to do good but desires thereby to please not God but human beings labors in vain.

[Col. 0647A] “When human praise confronts a good work, it changes the minds of those who perform it.

“Through what we do, let us not seek external praise.

“Let the work be done publicly in such a way that it remains hidden in temptation.

“For those who, after receiving some grace, offer the splendor of glory to their own empty praises are selling oil, as it were.

“He anoints the head with the oil of the sinner when the favor of flattery soothes the mind.”

ISIDORE.

“Whoever gives alms for the sake of vainglory turns virtue into vice.

“Whoever turns some gift of God that he has merited toward his own praise undoubtedly transfers virtue into vice.”

[Col. 0647B] “He does not turn aside to the right who attributes the good he does not to himself but to God.

“Some people trust that they are righteous precisely where they are most severely condemned.

“The lover of vainglory never stops doing whatever may always bring him praise.

“But the person who should publicize the good he does is one grounded in perfect humility and untouched by any elation.

“For when a poor person is fed for the sake of ostentation, the work itself is turned into sin.

“We defraud God whenever we praise ourselves, not God, for our good work.”

[Col. 0647C] “But the most prudent person’s careful discernment watches lest he do good immoderately and pass from virtue into vice.”

FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS.

“Vainglory is a vice; without reason it inserts itself into every good thing.

“A stone thrown upward does not reach heaven, and the prayer of a person who pleases himself does not ascend to heaven.

“Do not undertake secret abstinence, nor display it as though in the light before many witnesses, so that the Father who sees in secret may repay you openly.

“Do not lose your labors for the sake of human glory, nor surrender future eternal glory for a small and temporal glory.

“For human glory is reduced to dust, and its honor [Col. 0647D] is extinguished upon the earth.

“But the glory of virtues glorifies throughout the ages.”

CHRIST.

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII).

PETER.

“Wicked men living in luxury, having eyes full of adultery and unceasing sin” (I Pet. II).

“Flee fornication, brothers: every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” (I Cor. VI).

[Col. 0648A] “For God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. XIII).

SOLOMON.

“For a prostitute is a deep pit, and a strange woman a narrow well. She lies in wait on the way like a robber, and kills those whom she sees to be unwary” (Prov. XXIII).

JESUS SIRACH.

“Do not give a woman power over your soul, nor let her enter into your strength, lest you be confounded” (Eccles. IX).

“Do not gaze upon a virgin, lest you perhaps be scandalized by her beauty” (ibid.).

“Many have perished because of hope placed in a woman, and from this desire a fire blazes” (ibid.).

“Whoever joins himself to fornicators will be wicked” (Eccles. XIX).

[Col. 0648B] “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your own will” (Eccles. XVIII).

“Whoever keeps a wicked woman is like one who grasps a scorpion” (Eccles. XXVI).

“As the rising sun is beautiful in the heights of God, so is the appearance of a good woman an ornament to her house” (ibid.).

“A woman’s wickedness changes her face and makes her countenance dark like a bear” (Eccles. XXV).

“A woman’s fornication is recognized in the excellence of her eyes and in her eyelids” (Eccles. XXVI).

AUGUSTINE.

“If what is true lives in you, fornication is dead in you.”

JEROME.

“Woe to those who had an end of lust only when they had an end of life” [Col. 0648C].

“Lust is hostile to God, the destruction of a father’s inheritance or property.

“Fornication stains not only the fornicator’s conscience but also the body amid banquets and the enticements of pleasure.

“Lust subdues even iron minds.

“For chastity is difficult to preserve amid delights.

“Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold.

“Whoever lives luxuriously is dead; therefore whoever becomes drunk is dead and buried.”

GREGORY.

“From the place where the belly is distended by satiety, the goads of lust are aroused.”

ISIDORE.

[Col. 0648D]

“Fornication of the flesh is adultery.

“Fornication of the soul is servitude to idols.

“But the luxury of the flesh is especially conspicuous to human beings because it is immediately shameful in itself.

“Just as through pride of mind one proceeds into the prostitution of corrupt lust, so through humility of mind the chastity of the flesh is saved.

“Chiefly through these two vices the devil rules the human race: pride of mind and luxury of the flesh.

“For through these two vices the devil possesses the human race, raising the mind into pride or corrupting the flesh through luxury.

“The first arrows of fornication are the eyes, the second [Col. 0649A] are words; but whoever is not captured by the eyes can resist through words.

“Whoever restrains the pleasure of a lustful suggestion does not pass to consent to lust.

“For a person quickly resists the act who does not yield consent to the pleasure that tickles him.

“If the pleasure of fornication delights the mind more than love of chastity, sin still reigns in that person.

“But if the beauty of inward chastity delights more, sin no longer reigns; righteousness reigns.

“Every unclean pollution is called fornication: for from the pleasure of fornication various acts of wickedness arise, by which the kingdom of God is closed and a person is separated from God.”

[Col. 0649B] “Fornication is the greatest of crimes, because through the uncleanness of the flesh it violates the temple of God and, taking away the members of Christ, makes them members of a prostitute.

“For a luxurious life quickly weakens the flesh and swiftly brings the broken body to old age.

“Fornication is greater than all sins, because fornication precedes other evils.

“For it is better to die than to fornicate or be stained by lust.

“Lust plunges a person into hell.

“Lust sends a person to Tartarus.

“Lust burns more grievously the one whom it finds slain.

“For a body wearied by labor takes less pleasure in wickedness.

“Luxury quickly creeps upon the person devoted to leisure.

[Col. 0649C] “The idle person is quickly overtaken by luxury.”

CAESARIUS.

“Against the remaining vices we ought to resist with every virtue; but against lust it is not expedient to fight—it is expedient to flee.”

FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS.

“Chastity produces abstinence, but gluttony is the mother of lack of self-control.

“Green grass growing near water, and the vice of lust in visits to women.

“Draw nearer to a blazing fire rather than to a young woman, when you yourself are also young.

“For it is of no value to be pure in body if one is polluted in mind.

“For a person will not avoid bodily heat unless he has first restrained the movements of the soul” [Col. 0649D].

## CHAPTER XXII. On Perseverance

CHRIST.

“But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV).

PAUL.

“But now, truly having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (Rom. VII).

SOLOMON.

“The end of prayer is better than its beginning” (Eccles. VII).

[Col. 0650A] “Stand by your covenant, converse in it, and grow old in the work of your commandments” (Eccles. XI).

JEROME.

“In Christians, beginnings are not sought but the end, because Paul began badly but finished well.

“Judas’s beginnings are praised, but the end of his perdition is condemned.

“Many begin, but few reach the summit.”

GREGORY.

“The virtue of a good work is perseverance.

“For good is done in vain if it is abandoned before the end of life.

“He sacrifices well who carries the sacrifice of a good work through to the end of the required action.”

ISIDORE.

[Col. 0650B]

“Our conduct pleases God when we complete with the greatest perseverance the good that we begin.

“The end of every person’s life must always be sought, because God does not consider what kind of people we were before, but what kind we were near the end of life.

“For God judges each person by his end, not by his past life.”

CYPRIAN.

“For by his end each person is either justified [Col. 0650C] or condemned.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Security

CHRIST.

“Therefore keep watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. XXIV).

“I say to all: keep watch” (Mark XIII).

PETER.

“Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers” (I Pet. IV).

PAUL.

“When people say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (I Thess. X).

JEROME.

[Col. 0650D] “Care must be taken lest what is best in us slip into vice.

“For this reason the Lord concealed from us the time of his coming: so that, hanging in uncertainty because of expectation, we might always believe that our judge is going to come, though we do not know when he will come.

“The whole life of the wise is a meditation on death.

“If there is any joy in the present time, it must be pursued in such a way that the bitterness of the coming judgment never departs from memory.

“For the cunning enemy often trips the mind together with sin; and when he sees it stricken by its downfall, he seduces it with the deadly flatteries of false security.

“Therefore whoever is secure in mind after committing iniquities is himself a witness to himself that he is not innocent.”

[Col. 0651A] “When the mind is made secure in the body, the spirit is relaxed.

“When you do good, brothers, always recall your evil deeds to memory.

“So that, when guilt is carefully recognized, the mind may never carelessly rejoice over a good work.

“Our God wished the final hour to be unknown to us for this reason: so that it might always be feared; and while we cannot see it, we may prepare ourselves for it without interruption.”

ISIDORE.

“Let the righteous neither trust in his own righteousness nor despair of God’s mercy; rather, let him hold hope and fear together in his heart. Let him hope for mercy in such a way that he fears justice; let him have hope of pardon in such a way that fear [Col. 0651B] afflicts him.

“However righteous someone may be, he must never be secure in this life.

“Although the conduct of the saints may be praiseworthy, it remains uncertain to human beings to what end they have been destined.

“Let nothing make a person secure concerning sin. Although repentance for sins is favorable, a person ought not to be without fear, because the satisfaction of repentance is weighed only by divine judgment, not by human judgment.

“Nor should a penitent ever have security concerning his sins.

“For security produces negligence; negligence often makes a person heedless and leads him back to former vices.”

ISIDORE.

[Col. 0651C] “The time of each person’s life is uncertain, and therefore one must hasten, lest sudden death unexpectedly overtake him.”

CAESARIUS.

“As secure as we are concerning the past, so concerned should we be about the future.

“For all crimes and sins quickly return upon us if they are not defeated daily by good works.”

CHRIST.

“Everyone who hears my words and does not do them is like a foolish [Col. 0651D] man” (Matt. VII).

PAUL.

“God chose the foolish things of the world in order to confound the wise” (I Cor. I).

SOLOMON.

“Fools desire the things that are harmful to them, and the imprudent have hated knowledge” (Prov. I).

“A fool is beaten by his lips; a fool is struck by his lips” (Prov. X).

“But the mouth of a fool is near to confusion” (ibid.).

“Whoever is foolish will serve the wise” (Prov. XI).

[Col. 0652A] “But whoever is a fool displays his folly” (Prov. XIII).

“The heart of fools will be unlike them” (Prov. XV).

“A fool is fed with ignorance” (ibid.).

“A foolish man claps his hands when he has pledged himself for his friend.

[Col. 0652B] “The mouth of a fool is his ruin, and his lips are the downfall of his soul” (Prov. XVIII).

“Foolish people do not grasp wisdom, and they will not see it” (Eccles. XV).

“A fool will reproach sharply” (Eccles. XVIII).

[Col. 0652D] “The gift of a fool will not be useful to you, for his eyes are sevenfold: he will give little and reproach much, and the opening of his mouth is defamation” (Eccles. XX).

“A fool will have no friend, and there will be no favor in his goods” (ibid.).

“For those who eat the bread of a fool are people of a false tongue” (ibid.).

“Instruction is fetters on the feet of a fool” (ibid.).

[Col. 0653A] “In the mouth of fools is their heart, and in the heart of the wise is their mouth” (ibid.).

“An undisciplined son is the shame of his father” (Eccles. XXII).

“Whoever teaches a fool is like one who glues pottery together.

“Do not speak much with a fool, and do not go with an insensate person” (ibid.).

“Sand, salt, and a mass of iron are easier to carry than an imprudent, foolish, and impious person.

“The innermost thoughts of a fool are like a wagon wheel; and as a turning axle, so is the thought of a fool” (Eccles. XXXIII).

“Better is the person who hides his folly than the one who hides his wisdom” (Eccles. XLI).

“The lips of the foolish will recount folly” (Eccles. XXI).

[Col. 0653B] “But the words of the prudent will be weighed on a scale” (ibid.).

“Do not associate with an unlearned man, lest he speak evil of your offspring” (Eccles. VIII).

JEROME.

“Foolish talk and buffoonery—or coarse joking—do not suit a Christian.

“The fool perceives according to his infirmities, and perceives according to the weakness of his nature.”

GREGORY.

[Col. 0653C] “Just as the ear does not recognize food, nor the throat words, so no fool understands the judgment of wisdom.

ISIDORE.

“Nothing is worse than folly, nothing more wretched than foolishness, nothing more shameful than laziness.

“Ignorance is the nurse of vices.
