“For the unlearned is easily deceived, and the fool quickly slips into vice.”

## CHAPTER XXV. On Avarice

[Col. 0653D]

CHRIST.

“Beware of all avarice, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses” (Luke XII).

PAUL.

“Let all fornication, uncleanness, and avarice not even be named among you” (Eph. V).

“Every fornicator, or unclean person, or avaricious person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (I Cor. V).

SOLOMON.

“He troubles his household who pursues avarice” (Prov. XV).

[Col. 0654A] “There is no trace of justice in that heart in which avarice makes its dwelling.

“But whoever hates gifts will live” (Eccles. V).

“The avaricious person is not filled with money, and whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them.

“Nothing is more criminal or more unjust in an avaricious person than to love money; for he has made his soul saleable.

“Gold and silver destroy many” (Eccles. VIII).

“Let your hand not be extended to take, nor closed when giving.”

AUGUSTINE.

Just as avarice consigns a person to hell, so the yoke of Christ is accustomed to raise him to heaven.

**JEROME**

[Col. 0654B] To the miser, what he has is as lacking as what he does not have.

Avarice knows no limit; although it devours everything, it does not know how to be satisfied at all.

He is always hungry and needy; though with savage teeth he tears apart all the kingdoms of the world, he still admits that he is fasting.

**GREGORY**

Whoever is ravaged in mind by avarice also has an impetigo in his body.

If we cannot abandon what belongs to us, at least let us not desire what belongs to others.

The fruitfulness of children draws a parent’s heart toward avarice; for the parent is thereby inflamed to accumulate an inheritance, because he is made fruitful with many heirs.

**CYPRIAN**

[Col. 0654C]

A miserly man is like hell.

**FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS**

Whoever loves silver will not see wisdom; and whoever gathers it will be darkened.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Virtues

**CHRIST**

No one who performs a mighty deed in my name can soon speak evil of me (Mark IX).

**PAUL**

For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power (I Corinthians IV).

To another is given the working of miracles through the Holy Spirit (I Corinthians XII).

[Col. 0654D] Let your faith not rest on human wisdom but on the power of God (I Corinthians II).

**SOLOMON**

Do not forbid one who can do good to do good, if you yourself are able to do good (Proverbs III).

Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds (Proverbs IV).

**JEROME**

There are many kinds of virtues, which bestow the kingdoms of heaven upon those who pursue them. There is indeed one road, but many shortcuts to reaching the destination. Whoever strives for perfection, even if he attains the degree of perfection, nevertheless always finds something in which he may grow, so that each day he may become better than himself.

[Col. 0655A] No one can possess both virtues and riches at the same time.

**AUGUSTINE**

Vice imitates virtue, and weeds confuse the grain.

**AMBROSE**

The mind cannot possess the kingdom of virtues unless it has first shaken off the yoke of vices.

**GREGORY**

Knowledge is indeed a virtue, while humility is the guardian of virtue.

Every holy person, even when sought with a perverse mind, does not turn away from the pursuit of his goodness.

Desire to have companions on the way of God.

Those minds behold the citizens above which, with the fragrances of virtues, proceed toward God through holy desires.

But when someone still does good out of fear, he has not completely withdrawn from evil.

By fear vice is frequently abandoned; by love, however, virtues arise: faith, hope, and charity.

Let each virtue rejoice in the good work it administers.

**ISIDORE**

We flee to virtues with difficulty, but without effort we slide into vices.

Hidden virtues are a safeguard against self-exaltation.

For we endure great exertions so that we may be able to ascend to heaven.

Just as a person gradually falls from the smallest vices into the greatest, so he rises step by step toward what is lofty.

Whoever attempts to grasp virtues without order is soon endangered.

This is the cause in the nature of things: whoever hastens rapidly toward perfection is without doubt quickly brought to an end.

First the vices must be uprooted in a person; then virtues must be planted.

For truth cannot be joined with falsehood.

Do you wish to increase your virtues? Do not publicize them.

**CYPRIAN**

It is of no benefit to proclaim virtue in words and destroy truth by one’s deeds.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Vices

[Col. 0655D]

**CHRIST**

For from within, from the human heart, evil thoughts proceed (Matthew XV).

Adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, avarice, wickedness, indecency, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and folly—all these evils proceed from within and defile a person (ibid.).

**PAUL**

Therefore let sin not reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires (Romans VI).

**SOLOMON**

His iniquities capture the wicked man, and he is bound by the cords of his sins (Proverbs V).

**AUGUSTINE**

[Col. 0656A]

No flesh that lives in vices rejoices in God.

**JEROME**

The evils of vices are not cleansed except by comparison with virtues.

For a bad knot in a tree, a bad peg or wedge must be driven in.

On the day of judgment, the virtues of some will not be able to lift up the vices of others.

For those surrounded by vices cannot see virtues.

Drive every vice from your soul, so that you may attain the virtues of the soul.

Let us overcome vices through love of virtues.

For all people favor our vices; and what we do by our own will, we attribute to the necessity of nature.

**ISIDORE**

When a person withdraws from God, he is immediately handed over to the power of vices,

so that, while suffering hostile vices, he may come to his senses by returning to the place from which he fell.

Those who wish to overcome vices without effort caress themselves quite delicately.

A person renounces vice completely when he avoids the opportunity to commit sin.

Reveal the vices of your heart.

Sometimes a person’s own vices pursue him, because the one who previously made them his companions by willing them later feels them—even against his will—as goads, and doubly so.

[Col. 0656C] He is guilty of a crime who both admits wicked deeds by his will and defends them through the swelling of obstinacy.

Vices grow upon one another, so that when one has departed, another takes its place.

Sometimes a person sins beneficially in lesser vices, so that greater sins may be avoided more usefully.

For vices are truly healed when vices are excluded by virtues, not by other vices.

**CAESARIUS**

Our vices are our enemies.

**IN THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS**

Just as rich soil brings forth what is hidden within it, so rich flesh produces vice.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Drunkenness

[Col. 0656D]

**CHRIST**

Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts perhaps become weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and with the cares of this life (Luke XXI).

**PAUL**

Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery (Ephesians V).

**SOLOMON**

Wine is wanton, and drunkenness tumultuous; whoever delights in these things will not be wise (Proverbs XX).

Do not look upon wine when it turns yellow, when its color gleams in the glass: it enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent and spread its venom like a basilisk (Proverbs XXIII).

[Col. 0657A] No secret remains where drunkenness reigns.

**JESUS SIRACH**

A drunken laborer will not become rich, and whoever despises small things will gradually fall (Ecclesiasticus XIX).

Wine and women make the wise apostatize and rebuke the sensible (ibid.).

For an educated person, a little wine is sufficient; when you sleep, it will not trouble you, nor will you feel pain from it (Ecclesiasticus XXXI).

Do not provoke those who love wine, for wine destroys many (ibid.).

Much wine drunk is bitterness of soul (ibid.).

Wine in moderation is an even life for human beings (ibid.).

If you drink it moderately, you will be sober.

Wine was created for enjoyment, not for drunkenness [Col. 0657B] (ibid.).

Wine drunk moderately is health of body and soul (ibid.).

Much wine drunk causes irritation and anger and many falls (ibid.).

As fire tests hard iron, so wine will test the heart (ibid.).

**JEROME**

Wherever there is gluttony and drunkenness, lust dominates.

Let the religious person never smell of wine, lest he hear the Philosopher say: “This is not offering a kiss, but offering a drink.”

Whatever intoxicates and overturns the state of the mind, let us avoid in the same way as wine.

[Col. 0657C] A belly distended with food and irrigated with wine and drink is followed by sexual pleasure.

Whatever consists of seminal pleasures is poison taken as drink.

**AMBROSE**

Moderate food and wine strengthen a weak stomach, but drunkenness weakens the body.

For gluttony and an abundance of wine shamefully lead many into debauchery.

Wine is not condemned as such in its proper use, but in excess.

**ISIDORE**

Drunkenness produces mental disturbance, madness of heart, and the flame of lust.

[Col. 0657D] Drunkenness so alienates the mind that a person does not know where he is; hence even the evil committed in drunkenness is not perceived.

For many, drinking much without becoming drunk is a matter of praise. Let them hear the prophet speaking against them: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness.”

People become drunk not only from wine but also from the other kinds of drink that are prepared in various ways.

**BASIL**

Just as a fish prepares itself to swallow the bait, so the drunkard receives the enemy in wine.

For the Lord gave us wine for gladness of heart, not for drunkenness.

[Col. 0658A] Many people have contracted the greatest weakness through wine and have been unable to regain their former strength, because they did not restrain the ardor of their appetite.

The drunkard thinks he possesses something excellent when he has rolled headlong into ruin.

In all things present yourself as sober in life; let sobriety be displayed to God in all things.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Tithes

**CHRIST**

Distribute all your tithes; bring the whole tithe into my storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me in this, says the Lord (Malachi [Col. 0658B] III).

**PAUL**

Those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law—that is, from their brothers (Hebrews VII).

God loves a cheerful giver (II Corinthians I).

**SOLOMON**

Some distribute their own possessions and become richer (Proverbs XI).

Others seize what is not theirs and are always in poverty (ibid.).

**JESUS SIRACH**

In every gift make your face cheerful, and sanctify your tithes with rejoicing (Ecclesiasticus XXV).

Give to the Most High according to his gift, and make your offering from the work of your hands with a good eye; for the Lord our God is one who repays, and he will return sevenfold to you (ibid.).

**AUGUSTINE**

Tithes are the taxes of needy souls. If you give tithes, you will receive not only an abundance of fruits but also attain bodily health.

The Lord God has no need; he does not seek a reward, but honor.

Our God, who has deigned to give everything, deigns to ask a tenth from us—not for himself, without doubt, but because it will benefit us. Hence the prophet says: “You shall not delay offering me the firstfruits of your threshing floor and of the winepress of your vineyard” (Exodus XXII; Ezekiel XLIV).

[Col. 0658D] If giving late is a sin, how much more is not giving at all?

From military service, from business, from craftsmanship, pay tithes.

Since by giving tithes you can gain heavenly things in exchange for earthly ones, why, through avarice, do you defraud yourself of a double blessing?

For this is the Lord’s most just custom: if you do not give him a tenth, you will be reduced to a tenth.

You will give to a wicked soldier what you are unwilling to give to a priest.

God is always ready to do good, but human wickedness prevents it.

For tithes are required as a debt, and whoever is unwilling to give them has invaded another’s property.

[Col. 0659A] And however many poor people in the places where he lives have died of hunger because he did not give a tenth, he will appear guilty of as many murders before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, because he reserved for his own uses what God had assigned to the poor.

Therefore whoever desires either to gain a reward for himself or to merit forgiveness of sins should return tithes to God.

Every Christian, and every order of Catholics, should strive to give alms even from the nine remaining parts.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Cupidity

**CHRIST**

How difficult it is for those who trust in money to enter the kingdom of God! It is difficult for one who has money to enter the kingdom of God (Mark X).

**PAUL**

The desire for money is the root of all evils. Some, longing for it, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows (I Timothy VI).

**SOLOMON**

The paths of every miser seize the souls of those who possess them (Proverbs I).

Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant (Proverbs IX).

A deceitful scale is an abomination before God, but an accurate weight is his will (Proverbs XI).

[Col. 0659C] Bread acquired by deceit is sweet to a person, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel (Proverbs XX).

**JESUS SIRACH**

For a greedy and grasping man, wealth is without reason (Ecclesiasticus XIV).

The insatiable eye of the greedy person is in a portion of iniquity; it will not be satisfied until it consumes and dries up his soul (ibid.).

Whoever builds a house at another’s expense is like one who gathers stones for himself in winter (Ecclesiasticus XXI).

Many have been brought to ruin through gold, and their destruction has come through its appearance.

**AMBROSE**

Cupidity and pride are so much one evil that neither can the proud be found without cupidity, nor the greedy without pride.

**ISIDORE**

What is possessed with great love is lost with great grief.

We grieve less in losing what we love less because we possess it less.

Those who pursue temporal glory, although outwardly bright with the splendor of power, are inwardly empty through the elation of pride.

Whoever persistently labors in seeking worldly honors or the prosperity of this world will also be found empty of rest in the future.

No one can undertake spiritual battles unless he has first subdued the desires of the flesh.

The mind cannot be free for contemplating God when it gapes after the desires and cupidities of this world.

Nor can an eye whose vision is blocked by dust behold lofty things.

Avarice and the love of money are worse than every sin.

Cupidity is the mother of all crimes. Therefore, if the mother of crimes is cut down, the other offspring of sins do not sprout.

Cupidity never learns to be satisfied; the miser is always needy. The more he acquires, the more he seeks.

Many powerful people are inflamed with such a frenzy of cupidity that they exclude the poor from their borders.

It is no wonder that those who are dying are carried into the fires of hell if, while alive, they did not extinguish the flame of their cupidity.

Those who burn with the desire for cupidity are consumed by the breath of demonic inspiration.

**EUSEBIUS**

The desire for money overcomes the hearts of mortal peoples and even violates brotherly necessity.

**FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS**

It is of no benefit not to possess money if there is a will to possess it.

Let us have as much as necessity demands, not as much as cupidity desires.

Nakedness is of no benefit to one who has cupidity within him.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Discipline

[Col. 0660C]

**JOHN**

Those whom I love, I chastise and reprove (Revelation III; Hebrews XII).

**PAUL**

All discipline at the present seems to be not a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those exercised by it (Hebrews XII).

**SOLOMON**

Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not abandon your mother’s law, so that grace may be added to your head and a necklace to your neck (Proverbs I).

Hold fast to discipline; do not abandon it. Guard it, because it is your life (Proverbs IV).

[Col. 0660D] Receive discipline, and do not cast it away.

Therefore do not reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you (Proverbs IX).

Reprove a wise person, and he will love you (ibid.).

Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge (Proverbs XII).

Whoever hates correction is a fool (ibid.).

The way of life belongs to the one who guards discipline (Proverbs X).

Whoever abandons reproof goes astray (ibid.).

Poverty and disgrace come to the one who abandons discipline (Proverbs XIII).

Whoever yields to the one who reproves him will be honored (ibid.).

A fool despises the discipline of his father, but whoever guards reproofs will become wiser (Proverbs XV).

Whoever hates reproof will die (Proverbs XVII).

[Col. 0661A] One correction benefits the prudent more than a hundred blows benefit a fool (Proverbs XVII).

**JESUS SIRACH**

A prudent and disciplined person will not murmur when corrected (Ecclesiasticus X).

Before you investigate, do not blame anyone; and when you have investigated, correct him justly (Ecclesiasticus XI).

Whoever hates correction will have his life shortened (Ecclesiasticus XIX).

Correct your friend, for a breach often occurs, and do not believe every word (ibid.).

There is deceptive correction in the anger of an abusive person (ibid.).

Correct your neighbor before you threaten him, and give place to fear of the Most High (ibid.).

A sinful person avoids correction (Ecclesiasticus XXXII).

Whoever hates correction is marked as a sinner [Col. 0661B] (Ecclesiasticus XXI).

For whoever fears God will return to his heart (ibid.).

**AMBROSE**

A person chastised gently shows reverence to the one chastising him; but one offended by harsh reproof accepts neither the correction nor salvation.

Bear patiently, as weak persons, those whom you have not been able to amend by chastising them.

Those who cannot be reproved because of their weakness must be carried with gentle compassion.

Because sinners differ, some must be carried and others chastised; for the measure of sins is different.

We correct the insolent more effectively when we show that the things they believe they have done well are evil.

**GREGORY**

[Col. 0661C]

There are some who hear words of reproof and strive to return to repentance, because punishments frighten those whom rewards otherwise do not attract.

Let each person hear about the kingdom, so that he may love it, and hear about punishment, so that he may fear it; so that if love does not draw him toward the kingdom, fear may invite him.

**ISIDORE**

The righteous accept reproof beneficially whenever they are corrected for their excesses.

The wicked often defend themselves, being alike to one another in evil.

Whoever is not corrected by gentle words must necessarily be reproved more sharply.

Things that cannot be healed gently must be cut away with pain.

[Col. 0661D] Since one who has been privately admonished neglects to be corrected from his sin, he must be reproved publicly, so that a wound which cannot be healed secretly may be amended openly.

Those who do harm openly must be reproved openly, so that, while they are healed by open rebuke, those who have sinned by imitating them may be corrected.

When one person is corrected, many are amended.

It is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered for the license of one.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Faith

**CHRIST**

All things are possible to one who believes (Mark IX).

[Col. 0662A] Have faith in God (Mark XI).

Whoever does not doubt in his heart but believes that whatever he says will happen, it will be done for him (ibid.).

Whoever believes in the Son of God has eternal life (John III).

Whoever is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him (ibid.).

**JAMES**

What good will it do, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works?

Can faith save him (ibid.)?

Faith without works is idle (ibid.).

For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead (ibid.).

**PAUL**

[Col. 0662B] The power of God is for salvation to everyone who believes (Romans IV).

Therefore those who are of faith will be blessed with faithful Abraham (Galatians III).

In all things take up the shield of faith, and receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians VI).

Without faith it is impossible to please God. For whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him (Hebrews XI).

**SOLOMON**

Maintain faith with your neighbor in his poverty, so that you may also rejoice in his prosperity (Ecclesiasticus XXII).

**AUGUSTINE**

If the righteous person is one who lives by faith, then the unrighteous person is one who does not have faith.

For the faithful person, the whole world is riches; but for the unfaithful person, there are not even modest riches.

For the faithful, night is changed into day; but for the unfaithful, even light becomes darkness. So powerful is faith that it makes people walk upon the sea with their feet.

Faith is great, but it is of no benefit if it does not have charity.

**JEROME**

What benefit is there if, while acting impiously, you invoke by voice the God whom you deny by your deeds?

In the good works of the faithful, God considers not so much the magnitude of the offering as the truth of faith.

**GREGORY**

[Col. 0662D]

That person truly believes who practices by his works what he believes; for through faith we are known by almighty God.

What benefit is there if we are joined to our Redeemer by faith but separated from him in conduct?

**ISIDORE**

Blessed is the person who both lives well by believing rightly and preserves right faith by living well.

For a bad Christian, by not living according to the teaching of the Gospel, easily loses under temptation even the faith that he honors in words.

If God is believed, he is rightly invoked and sought; and therefore he is perfectly praised when he is both believed and sought.

[Col. 0663A] Faith is by no means forced out by violence, but is commended to the heart through reason and examples.

God regards faith where people cannot excuse themselves; for faith retained in the heart is brought forth to salvation by confession of the mouth.

Many do not love the faith of Christ from the heart, but, out of human fear, pretend hypocritically to hold it. Those who cannot be openly evil are thus recognized as deceptively good through fear.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Hope

**PAUL**

We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, await redemption; for we have been saved in hope (Romans VIII).

But hope that is seen is not hope (ibid.).

[Col. 0663B] For who hopes for what he sees (ibid.)?

But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience (ibid.).

**JAMES**

For whoever doubts is like a wave of the sea, moved and carried about by the wind (James I).

**SOLOMON**

The expectation of the righteous is joy; the hope of the wicked will perish (Proverbs X).

Hope that is delayed afflicts the soul (Proverbs XIII).

**ORIGEN**

No one can have salvation unless he first makes the Lord favorable toward him.

**ISIDORE**

Those who do not cease from doing evil seek forgiveness from God’s compassion through vain hope; they would seek it rightly if they ceased from wicked action.

We must greatly fear both persisting in sin through hope of the forgiveness that God promises and, because he justly punishes sins, despairing of forgiveness. Having avoided both dangers, let us turn away from evil and hope for forgiveness from God’s compassion.

Every righteous person shines through hope and fear: at one moment hope lifts him toward joy, and at another the terror of Gehenna leads him to fear.

Whoever despairs of forgiveness for sin condemns himself more for despair than for the sin committed.

Despair increases sin.

Despair is worse than every sin.

[Col. 0663D] Therefore correct yourself and maintain hope of forgiveness.

No guilt is so serious that it cannot have forgiveness.

Let no false security deceive you and hold you back from the purpose of repentance.

Let hope and fear remain continually in your heart; let fear and confidence exist together in you.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Grace

**CHRIST**

You have received freely; give freely (Matthew X).

Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John I).

**PAUL**

Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more [Col. 0664A], so that, just as sin reigned through death, grace might also reign through righteousness unto eternal life (Romans V).

For the wages of sin are death, but the grace of God is eternal life (Romans VI).

To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Ephesians IV).

**SOLOMON**

Whoever is good will draw grace from the Lord (Proverbs XII).

Let your eyes guard the ways of the Lord, so that grace may be added to your head.

Grace is given in the sight of every living person.

There is a gift that is not useful to the one to whom it is given; and there is a gift whose recompense is double.

**GREGORY**

[Col. 0664B] The Lord who bestowed the talents returns to demand an account, because he who now mercifully grants spiritual gifts will strictly seek an accounting of merits at the judgment.

What is done in tranquility is revealed in tribulation.

For there are some who have received the gift of understanding but know only the things that belong to the flesh.

**ISIDORE**

Sometimes, when we sin, God withdraws his gifts so that the human mind may rise toward hope of divine favor.

For all good things are granted to us by him, with grace going before us.

A person’s progress is a gift of God; no one can be corrected by himself, but by the Lord. For a person has no good of his own whose way is not his own.

When someone receives a gift of God, let him not desire more than he has deserved, lest, while attempting to seize the office of another member, he lose what he has deserved.

For the person who is not content with his own office and steals another’s disrupts the entire order of the body.

That we are wise, rich, and powerful is not due to another but rather to a divine gift.

Let us therefore use divine benefits well, so that God will not regret giving them and our receiving them will be useful to us.

In the distribution of good things, different people receive different gifts of God; nevertheless, all are not granted to one person, so that what one admires in another may exist for the sake of usefulness. He also says: “The gifts of grace are given to this person in one form and to that person in another; nor are they given in such a way that one person has everything and does not need another.”

God is said to take away from a person a gift that the person did not possess—that is, one that he did not deserve to receive.

**EUSEBIUS**

Just as grace is received freely from God, so it should be freely administered.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Discord

**CHRIST**

Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated; and every city or house divided against itself will not stand (Matthew XII and Luke XI).

For it is necessary that scandals come (Matthew X).

Nevertheless, woe to that person through whom the scandal comes (ibid.).

**PAUL**

All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats through causing offense (Romans XIV).

God has called us to peace (I Corinthians VII).

For God is not of dissension but of peace (I Corinthians XIV).

Peace to the brothers, and charity with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans I and Revelation I).

**SOLOMON**

Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord, but those who act faithfully please God (Proverbs XII).

An angry person provokes quarrels, but one who is patient calms those that have been stirred up (Proverbs XV).

A perverse person stirs up disputes, and a talkative person separates rulers (Proverbs XVI).

The wicked person always seeks quarrels, but a cruel angel will be sent against him (Proverbs XVII).

**GREGORY**

God is in unity, and those deserve to have his grace who do not divide themselves from one another through the scandal of sects. For a gift is not received unless discord is first driven from the heart.

How serious is the guilt of discord, on account of which even a gift is not accepted.

Whatever an insolent or unworthy friend says is the fury of one who rebukes, not the affection of correction.

What kind of sacrifice of mercy is it when it is offered together with discord toward one’s neighbor?

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Oaths

**CHRIST**

You have heard that it was said to the ancients: “You shall not swear falsely” (Matthew V).

But you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord (ibid.).

But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven nor by earth (ibid.).

Let your speech be: “Yes, yes; No, no” (Matthew V).

Whatever is more than these is from evil (ibid.).

[Col. 0665D] Whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits upon it (Matthew XXIII).

**PAUL**

People swear by one greater than themselves, and every dispute among them ends with an oath for confirmation (Hebrews VI).

**SOLOMON**

Whoever tells lies is a deceitful witness (Proverbs XII).

Do not accustom your mouth to swearing oaths (Ecclesiasticus XXIII).

A person who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and plague will not depart from his house (ibid.).

If a person swears in vain, he will not be justified (ibid.).

Do not accustom your mouth to undisciplined speech, for there is a word of sin in it (ibid.).

**ISIDORE**

[Col. 0666A]

Just as one who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not desire to swear cannot swear falsely.

It is not against God’s commandment to swear, but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury.

Therefore let the person who fears perjury never swear.

Many swear falsely in order to deceive, so that by the faith of an oath they may establish the credibility of their word; and thus, while swearing falsely and lying, they deceive people.

Sometimes we are also led astray by false tears, and we believe those who weep even though they should not be believed.

Often we intend to speak without an oath, but the unbelief of those who do not believe what we say compels us to swear.

By such necessity we acquire the habit of swearing.

[Col. 0666B] There are many who are slow to believe and are not moved to trust a spoken word.

Those who compel people speaking to them to swear commit a grave offense.

Whatever artifice of words a person uses in swearing, God, who is witness to the conscience, receives it according to the understanding of the person to whom the oath is sworn.

A person becomes guilty in two ways: he both takes the name of God in vain and deceitfully catches his neighbor.

An oath must not be kept when evil has been rashly promised—for example, if someone pledges himself to remain perpetually with an adulterous woman. For it is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to remain in the disgrace of fornication.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Thoughts

[Col. 0666C]

**CHRIST**

Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew V).

For from within, from the human heart, evil thoughts proceed: adulteries, fornications, murders, thefts, avarice, wickedness, indecency, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, and folly (Mark VII).

All these evils proceed from within and defile a person.

**PETER**

Beloved, I urge you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul (I Peter II).

**PAUL**

[Col. 0666D]

Charity does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth (I Corinthians XIII).

Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God (I Corinthians XV).

Beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in fear of the spirit.

I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh (Galatians V).

**SOLOMON**

Whoever trusts in his thoughts acts impiously (Proverbs XII).

The thoughts of the righteous are judgments; the counsels of the wicked are deceitful (ibid.).

There is deceit in the heart of those who think evil (ibid.).

An evil thought is an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs XV).

Commit your works to the Lord, and your thoughts will be directed (Proverbs XVI).

Whoever thinks perversely with staring eyes and bites his lips accomplishes evil (Proverbs XVII).

No thought escapes the Lord, and no word is hidden from him (Ecclesiasticus XLII).

For there will be an inquiry into the thoughts of the wicked (Wisdom I).

The wicked will receive correction according to what they have thought (Wisdom III).

The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks of many things [Col. 0667B] (Wisdom IX).

The thoughts of the wicked are not wisdom.

The fainthearted person thinks vain things, and the imprudent and erring person thinks folly (Ecclesiasticus XVI).

Thought brings old age before its time.

**AUGUSTINE**

No one can be deceived by the devil unless he has wished to offer the assent of his will.

**JEROME**

The devil’s power lies not in his boldness and boasting but in your will.

Through what he sees to be exposed—or at least not firmly closed—the devil seeks to break in and reach the very citadel of the heart and soul.

The sole cause of piety exists where there is no knowledge of the flesh.

[Col. 0667C] Do not allow evil thoughts to grow in your heart.

**HILARY**

Not all our thoughts are aroused through the devil’s instigation; sometimes they also arise at our own prompting. Good thoughts, however, are always from God.

**GREGORY**

Just as the members are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind.

For when the will is not restrained in thought, it also rules in recognition.

The Lord searches all hearts and understands every thought of the mind.

For evil spirits hem the soul in from every side when they bring back to it not only the iniquities of its deeds but also those of its thoughts and, beyond these, of its speech.

We have eyes in our head when we contemplate the life of our Redeemer in silent thought.

What good does it do for an entire city to be guarded against the ambushes of enemies if one opening is left through which the enemies may enter?

For everything that we subtly think, we cook, as it were, in the mind.

Since we are unwilling to subdue the desires of the flesh in peace, how would we give that same flesh for God in war?

Our mind must be driven away from carnal pleasure, but must it not be cut off from the necessary care of the flesh?

**ISIDORE**

[Col. 0668A]

The cause of sinning is twofold: deed and thought. One is called iniquity, what is carried out in deed; the other is injustice, what is admitted in thought.

Action must be cut off first, and thought afterward.

First evil deeds, then desires.

For deeds proceed in turn from thought, and thought arises from deed.

Although someone may be free from an evil deed, he is nevertheless not innocent on account of the wickedness of his thought alone.

For we sin not only by deeds but also by thoughts if we take pleasure in them when they arise unlawfully.

There is no need to fear when good and evil enter one’s thoughts; rather, one should rejoice if the mind distinguishes evil from good by the understanding of reason.

It is of no benefit that we distinguish between good and evil with more prudent judgment unless by our deeds we avoid what we have thought to be evil or do what we have understood to be good.

Resist at the very beginning of a thought, and you will escape what follows.

If you separate thoughts from the heart, they will not burst forth into deeds.

If you do not consent to thoughts, you will quickly resist the deed.

For the body cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted.

The flesh can do nothing except what the mind has willed.

Cleanse the mind of thought, and the flesh will not sin; it is better to avoid vice than to correct it.

**FROM THE BOOK OF CLEMENT**

The devil will have no power against a person unless that person voluntarily subjects himself to the devil’s desires.

**FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS**

As fire warms wax, so good vigils warm the worst thoughts.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Lying

[Col. 0668D]

**CHRIST**

You shall not bear false witness (Matthew XIX and Exodus XX).

**PAUL**

Putting away all falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor (Ephesians IV).

Do not lie to one another, stripping off the old person with his deeds and putting on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his creator (Colossians III).

**SOLOMON**
Whoever speaks falsely is a deceitful witness (Prov. XII).

But a sudden witness fashions a lying tongue (ibid.).

Lying lips are an abomination to the Lord (ibid.).

But those who act faithfully are pleasing to him (Prov. XIV).

A faithful witness delivers a soul; the treacherous person utters lies (ibid.).

[Col. 0669A] A faithful witness will not lie, but a deceitful witness utters lies (ibid.).

## JESUS SIRACH

Do not accept a lie against your own soul (Eccles. II).

Do not love a lie against your brother, nor do likewise against a friend (Eccles. VII).

Do not desire to tell every kind of lie, for persistence in it is not good (ibid.).

An obscure answer will not go in vain, but the mouth that lies destroys the soul (Wis. I).

## JEROME

Liars bring it about that even those who speak the truth are not believed.

## ISIDORE

Often the person who is about to speak falsely puts forward truths first, so that, having [Col. 0669B] initially gained credibility, he may make his hearers credulous toward the remaining lies.

Many things that are false seem true to people, and therefore they speak not from God but from their own falsehood.

Usually the one who invents falsehoods begins with the truth.

Poisons often lie hidden, surrounded by the honey of words; and the deceiver pretends to be telling the truth until, by deceiving, he has deceived.

Every lie must be avoided with the utmost care; every kind of lying must also be shunned most diligently.

Everything that disagrees with the truth is iniquity.

Be truthful in speech; deceive no one with a lie.

Do not say one thing and do another.

Do not say one thing while holding another in your heart.

The constant practice of swearing creates a habit of perjury.

[Col. 0669C] Do not promise anything without careful consideration.

Do not promise what you cannot do.

You will be greatly liable if you do not fulfill what you know you have promised.

Truth has no hidden corners and does not seek interest.

What you have rashly vowed, do not do; a promise fulfilled through crime is impious.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Monks

### MOSES

When you make a vow to the Lord your God, do not delay fulfilling it, for the Lord your God will require it (Deut. XIII; Eccles. V).

### PAUL

Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything (I Cor. IX).

[Col. 0669D] They do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one (II Tim. II).

No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself (ibid.).

### SOLOMON

The path of the righteous turns away from evil, but whoever guards his soul preserves his way (Prov. XVI).

### JEROME

Let no shameful or wanton speech ever come from a monk’s mouth.

For by these signs a lustful mind is revealed, and through the outward person the vices of the inward person are displayed.

Let a monk not desire the crowds of cities, since he is understood in terms of solitude.

[Col. 0670A] Let a monk be watchful in mind, lest he be polluted by empty thoughts.

Let him love knowledge of the Scriptures, and he will not love the vices of the flesh.

Bishops imitate the apostles, and monks the perfect Fathers, so that they may strive to possess the merit of those whose honor they possess.

Let a monk have the simplicity of a dove, and let him plot deceit against no one.

Let him also have the cunning of a serpent, so that he may not be undermined by the snares of others.

Let a monk maintain true humility.

A monk who desires Christ seeks nothing else: his cell is a paradise to him. He gathers the varied gifts of the Scriptures, uses them as his delights, and enjoys their embrace.

[Col. 0670B] He is a true monk who despises gold and pursues the Scriptures; and when he falls into poverty, he persists more splendidly adorned.

Monks should especially seek solitude; their dwelling should be made away from the city.

Do not seek in a monk the splendor of glory, but the devotion of his spirit.

Whatever is said against monks rebounds upon the clergy.

Against us they are talkative; for themselves they are silent.

Though a monk hides with his body enclosed in a cell, let his tongue not run throughout the world.

### GREGORY

Let those serve earthly administrations whom [Col. 0670C] spiritual gifts do not adorn.

Those who cannot penetrate to inner matters should at least perform necessary tasks outwardly.

A monk who seeks possessions within is not a monk.

### ISIDORE

Let each person judge himself a monk when he has considered himself the least of all.

### BASIL

A monk receives a heavenly gift when he casts earthly activities away from himself and, serving God as a soldier, does not entangle himself in secular affairs.

## FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS

A person is not called a monk merely because he [Col. 0670D] has no wife, but because he has been devoted to the religion and service of God. His concern is how not to please the world, because he has chosen chastity, which is dear to God, and [to be] a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.

If a monk restrains his stomach and his tongue and does not give himself over to idleness, let him trust that he will not die eternally.

A monk who eats much and works much should not place his confidence in this.

But he who eats little, even if he works little, should trust and act manfully; he will not lose his reward.

Whoever wishes to build a house makes many preparations so that he can complete his work; likewise, a monk must take great care in order to complete the work of God.

[Col. 0671A] How many monks, while showing no compassion for father or mother, have lost their souls?

A gentle layman is better than an angry and irascible monk.

A weak layman who serves his brother is better than a monk who has no compassion for his neighbor.

A double-tongued monk disturbs the brothers.

But the faithful one brings rest.

Pallor together with humility, and emaciation, are a monk’s adornment.

If you are able to suffer insult and remain silent, to be subjected to abuse and endure it, this is a great thing, beyond the other commandments.

### EPHRAEM

As seed cultivated in good soil, so is the soul of a monk, bearing fruit through thoughts of the divine Scriptures.

[Col. 0671B] As a bright lamp shining in a dark place, so is a monk sober in mind and ever watchful in heart during his time of psalmody and prayer.

As a load of salt weighs down the weak, so sleep weighs down a monk during prayer.

As a worm corrupts wood, so envy corrupts a monk’s soul.

As a moth destroys clothing, so slander destroys a monk’s soul.

## CHAPTER XL. On Slander

### PAUL

Do everything without murmuring and hesitation, [Col. 0671C] so that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without reproach (Phil. II).

### JAMES

Do not slander one another, my brothers. Whoever slanders his brother, or judges his brother, slanders the law and judges the law (James IV).

### SOLOMON

Put away from yourself a perverse mouth, and let lips that slander be far from you (Prov. IV).

Whoever slanders anyone binds himself for the future (Prov. XIII).

But whoever fears the commandment dwells in peace (ibid.).

Do not associate with slanderers, for their destruction will suddenly arise; and [Col. 0671D] who knows the ruin of both? (Rom. XV).

The tumult of murmurings will not remain hidden (Wis. I).

### AUGUSTINE

Therefore do not slander, nor listen to one who slanders.

### JEROME

Never slander anyone. We often accuse what we ourselves do, and find our own vices in opposition to ourselves.

Do not slander, but speak the truth.

Beware lest you have itching tongues or ears—that is, neither slander others yourself nor listen to others who slander.

It is also a consolation to the wicked to seize upon the good, while they think that their sins are diminished by the multitude of sinners.

### GREGORY

[Col. 0672A] No one who murmurs receives the kingdom of heaven, and no one who receives it can murmur.

### ISIDORE

Do not slander the sinner, but suffer with him.

Whatever you slander in another, fear rather in yourself.

Slanderers criticize everyone and condemn everyone.

When you slander another, examine yourself.

When you bite another, rebuke your own sins.

See not another’s offenses, but your own.

You will never slander if you have examined yourself well.

Both commit a similar crime: the one who listens to the slanderer and the one who slanders.

## FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS

[Col. 0672B] It is better to eat flesh and drink wine than to despise one’s brother in condemnation.

As the whispering serpent expelled Eve from paradise, so whoever slanders his brother destroys not only his own soul but also the soul of the listener.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Will

### CHRIST

If anyone worships God and does his will, God hears him (John IX).

### PAUL

If the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have (II Cor. VIII).

[Col. 0672C] As the mind is ready in its willing, so let it be in carrying it out (Eph. V).

Do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.

### SOLOMON

A crooked heart is an abomination to the Lord, but his will is with those who walk simply (Prov. XI).

### AUGUSTINE

For everyone will have in his will what each person will have in his recompense.

Every work is preceded by our will, while we think about what we ought to do.

God seeks nothing else from us but a good will.

The evil of free choice is the offspring of the will.

### GREGORY

[Col. 0672D] Before God’s eyes the hand is never empty of a gift if the treasury of the heart has been filled with good will.

Therefore let a good work be ours in intention; through divine assistance it will be brought to perfection.

There the one who willingly endured the darkness of the will is compelled to suffer the darkness of punishment.

A good will is to fear another’s adversity as our own; to deny no one what you rightly desire to have bestowed upon you; to meet your neighbor’s need according to your strength; and to wish to help even beyond your strength.

Envy is always at variance with good will.

For God accomplishes many good things in some people through the many wills of others.

### CYPRIAN

[Col. 0673A] Necessity does not excuse one oppressed by guilt when the guilt lies in the will.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Clothing

### CHRIST

Your body is more than clothing (Matt. VI).

Whoever has two tunics should give to one who has none; and whoever has food should do likewise (Luke III).

### PAUL

Having food and coverings, let us be content with these (I Tim. VI).

### SOLOMON

[Col. 0673B] Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain (Prov. XXXI).

At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head (Eccles. IX).

### AUGUSTINE

Let a clean garment surround you, not for beauty but for necessary covering, lest, while you clothe yourself in elaborate garments, you fall into another kind of shame.

### JEROME

The softness of feathers should not warm youthful limbs.

For whatever can protect our bodies and assist human weakness should all be called one tunic.

### GREGORY

No one seeks costly clothing except for empty [Col. 0673C] glory—that is, so that he may appear more honorable than others.

No one wishes to be dressed in costly garments where he cannot be seen by others.

A costly garment is sought solely for empty glory.

### EPHRAEM

The adornment of clothing indicates how we understand eternal things; and by our zeal for a more splendid garment we are shown to be naked of eternal splendor.

To wash the face, hands, and feet with excessive care indicates that we are servants of vices.

### BASIL

When we gaze upon bodies excessively adorned, we offend the creator of body and soul.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Mercy

[Col. 0673D]

### CHRIST

Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy (Matt. V).

Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful (Luke VI).

### PAUL

Be kind and merciful to one another; clothe yourselves, as God’s chosen, holy and beloved, with a heart of mercy (I Tim. IV).

Train yourself in godliness.

For bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for everything (ibid.).

### MOSES

[Col. 0674A] You shall not deny your wage to the needy and the poor (Deut. XXIV).

### SOLOMON

Let mercy and truth not abandon you; the merciful man does good to his own soul (Prov. III).

But the cruel person rejects his relatives (Prov. VI).

Kindness prepares life; mercy and truth prepare good things (ibid.).

Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is strengthened by clemency (Prov. XX).

To practice mercy and judgment is more pleasing to God than sacrifices (Prov. XXI; and Matt. IX).

### JESUS SIRACH

In judging, be merciful to orphans as a father [Col. 0674B] (Eccles. IV).

Every act of mercy will make room for each person according to the merit of his works (Eccles. XVI).

How great is God’s mercy and his forgiveness toward those who turn to him (Eccles. XVII).

The compassion of a human being is directed toward his neighbor (Eccles. XVIII).

But God’s mercy is over all flesh (ibid.).

Whoever has mercy teaches and instructs; like a shepherd, he guards his flock (ibid.).

Whoever practices mercy offers sacrifice (Eccles. XXXV).

### AUGUSTINE

Even the one who seeks mercy [Col. 0674C] must labor in some way for his own salvation.

We can find mercy, but in a troubled soul and a spirit of humility.

At your departure, think of God, and in your testament leave something to the poor: you will go there, but your works remain here.

### GREGORY

Where mercy is sought without dispute, there is salvation.

Discipline without mercy is greatly deficient if either is maintained without the other.

### CYPRIAN

The person who is not himself merciful will not be able to earn God’s mercy.

Nor will the person who has not been humane toward a poor person’s [Col. 0674D] prayers obtain anything from divine compassion.

### ISIDORE

Mercy receives its name from compassion for another’s misery.

No one can be merciful toward another who, by living wickedly, is not merciful toward himself.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Compassion for One’s Neighbor

### CHRIST

Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them; for this is the law and the prophets (Matt. VII).

### PAUL

[Col. 0675A] Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep (Rom. XII).

Share in the needs of the saints; serve one another through love (ibid.).

If someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted (Gal. VI).

Support the weak; be patient with everyone.

### SOLOMON

Whoever despises his neighbor sins (Prov. XIV).

Share in your neighbor’s poverty, so that you may also rejoice in his prosperity (Eccles. XXII).

Remain faithful in the time of tribulation, so that you may be his heir in the inheritance [Col. 0675B] (ibid.).

Spend money for your brother and friend (Eccles. XXXI).

Do not turn your face away from your neighbor (Eccles. XLI).

Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor soon falls into it; and whoever sets a stone for his neighbor stumbles over it (Eccles. X).

Whoever lays a snare for another will perish in it (Prov. XXII; and Eccles. XXVII).

### ORIGEN

If anyone either does not report what he sees in his neighbor’s offense, or, when called to testify, does not speak what is true, the punishment for the offense returns upon the one who knew of it.

### GREGORY

[Col. 0675C] False piety often obstructs compassion for one’s neighbor.

Whoever receives another’s pain in his need carries the cross in his mind.

For we cannot otherwise become members of our Redeemer except by clinging to God and suffering with our neighbor.

The cross is so called from suffering, *cruciatus*; and the cross is taken up in two ways: either by carrying the Lord’s cross [Col. 0675D] through abstinence, or by compassion for one’s neighbor, when we regard his need as our own.

For if someone offers these things for a temporal reward, he carries the cross but refuses to follow the Lord.

The cross is taken up in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the spirit is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor.

We owe compassion to a human being, and we ought to desire that he be set right from his vices, so that in one and the same person we may love the good that has been done and pursue the evils he has committed. Otherwise, while carelessly forgiving faults, we may seem to have granted pardon not because we were pierced by love but because of negligence.

Therefore we ought to offer our neighbors what we see our Creator offering to us, though we are unworthy.

[Col. 0676A] We should refuse none of the good things we are able to bestow upon our brothers.

By this we draw near to the one who is above all: by lowering ourselves beneath ourselves through compassion for our neighbor.

The more deeply we are afflicted through compassion for our neighbor, the more closely we approach God.

Whoever cannot tolerate the wicked bears witness against himself through his intolerance that he is not good.

The person whom the wickedness of the wicked has not tested was not proved good.

The iron of our soul is never brought to the fineness of a sharp edge if the file of another’s wickedness has not scraped it.

The wicked must therefore be tolerated all the more in proportion as [Col. 0676B] they are more abundant.

We must so attend to our own care that we do not neglect the care of our neighbor.

Thus let us distribute to others what we rightly wish to have bestowed upon us, and let us ourselves avoid doing to others what we do not wish done to us.

Let us preserve the rights of charity unharmed.

### BASIL

What you do not wish to happen to you, do not desire to happen to your neighbor either.

Suffer with the calamities of others, and join your tears to the sorrows of others.

In another’s tribulation, be sad yourself; be toward others as you wish others to be toward you.

What you do not wish to suffer, do not do, and do not inflict upon another, [Col. 0676C] lest you suffer similar evils.

Be as merciful toward the offenses of others as toward your own, so that you do not think differently of yourself and of others; and judge others as you desire to be judged.

### EPHRAEM

When we bear one another’s burdens, we confound and overcome our adversary the devil, and we honor our Lord who is in heaven.

As a drink of water is to one who thirsts in the heat of the sun, so is a word of consolation to a brother placed in the tribulation of temptation.

## CHAPTER XLV. On Exaltation

### CHRIST

[Col. 0676D] Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke XVI and XVIII).

### PAUL

If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ (Gal. I).

Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another (Gal. V).

If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself (ibid.).

### SOLOMON

Everyone who is arrogant is an abomination to the Lord; even if hand joins hand, he will not be innocent (Prov. XVI).

Whoever boasts and enlarges himself provokes quarrels (Prov. XXVIII).

Whoever hopes in the Lord is lifted up (Prov. XXIX).

### GREGORY

[Col. 0677A] Let the mind abase itself in everything it knows, lest the wind of exaltation carry away what the virtue of knowledge gathers.

A remarkable deed performed with exaltation does not raise a person up but weighs him down.

When heavenly grace leads us to understand higher things, the more subtly we are lifted up, the more constantly we must press ourselves down in humility within our understanding.

A greatly exalted mind is blunted if it is subjected to the very one above whom it exalts itself.

Arrogant men within the holy Church, although they flee from God in horror, nevertheless confess him truthfully by believing.

### ISIDORE

[Col. 0677B] Do not pride yourself, in any self-exaltation, on the virtue of righteousness.

Do not exalt yourself over good deeds, and do not glory in a good work.

Exaltation casts down the high, and arrogance humbles the lofty.

Guard by silence what you could lose by revealing it.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Human Life

### CHRIST

Do not think in your heart about what you will eat or what you will wear (Matt. VI).

Is not the soul more than food? (ibid.).

It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but [Col. 0677C] what proceeds from the mouth defiles a person (Matt. XV).

### PAUL

The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. XIV).

For it is best to establish the heart by grace, not by foods, which have benefited none of those who have walked in them (Hebr. XIII).

### SOLOMON

The Lord does not afflict the soul of the righteous (Prov. X).

A dry morsel of bread with joy is better than a house full of sacrifices with strife (Prov. XVII).

### JESUS SIRACH

The beginning of human life is water and bread and clothing (Eccles. XXIX).

[Col. 0677D] A wretched life lodges from house to house (ibid.).

Death is better than a bitter life, and eternal rest better than lasting sickness (Eccles. XXX).

The stomach will eat every kind of food, and one food is better than another (Eccles. XXXVI).

The necessities of human life begin with water, fire, and iron, milk and bread of fine flour, honey and a cluster of grapes, wine, oil, and clothing (Eccles. XXXIX).

All these things will be turned to good for the holy, and likewise to evil for the ungodly and sinners (ibid.).

### AUGUSTINE

Every wicked person either lives in order to be corrected or lives so that the good may be exercised through him.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Gifts

### MOSES

[Col. 0678A] Gifts blind the eyes of the wise and pervert the words of the righteous (Deut. XVI; Eccles. XX; I Cor. II).

### SOLOMON

The wicked person accepts gifts from the bosom in order to pervert the paths of judgment (Prov. XVII).

Do not give your honor to a stranger (Prov. V).

### JESUS SIRACH

Until they receive, they kiss the hands of the giver, and in their promises they humble their voices; but at the time of repayment they demand time (Eccles. XXIX).

Where there are many hands, close yours. Whatever you hand over, count and weigh it (Eccles. XLII).

[Col. 0678B] Record everything given and received. When you give, do not reproach the recipient (Eccles. XLI).

### AUGUSTINE

They frequently flatter over what is not given willingly; for what is offered from one’s own will is given with complete willingness.

### GREGORY

Each person should be as much the humbler because of a gift as he sees himself more obligated to render an account.

Therefore the one who bestows sacred orders frees his hands from every gift only when, in divine matters, he seeks neither money nor human glory.

### JOSEPHUS

[Col. 0678C] We ought not to refuse the gift of this life, which God has given us.

If we reject what has been given to human beings, we are insulting; how much more ought we to preserve what we receive from our God?

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Almsgiving

### CHRIST

Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you (Luke XI).

Sell what you possess and give alms (Luke XII).

Make yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches [Col. 0678D] and no moth destroys (ibid.).

## FROM THE BOOK OF TOBIT

It is better to give alms than to store up treasures of gold (Tob. XII).

Those who give alms and practice righteousness will be filled with life.

### PAUL

It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts XX).

Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly (II Cor. IX).

Let us not grow weary of doing good; while we have time, let us do good to all, especially to those who belong to the household of faith (Gal. VI).

### SOLOMON

A man’s wealth is the redemption of his soul (Prov. XIII).

[Col. 0679A] But whoever has mercy on the poor will be blessed (Prov. XIV).

Whoever oppresses the poor insults their Maker, but whoever shows mercy to the poor honors him (ibid.).

### JESUS SIRACH

Enclose almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will pray for you against every evil (Eccles. XXIX).

As water extinguishes a burning fire, so almsgiving resists sin (Eccles. III).

It will not go well with those who are continually evil and do not give alms.

A man’s alms are like a purse carried with him (Eccles. XXIX).

For the sake of the commandment, receive the poor person, and because of his need do not send him away empty (ibid.).

[Col. 0679B] Store up treasure in the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold (ibid.).

Do not defraud the poor of alms, and do not turn your eyes away from the poor (Eccles. IV).

Do not despise a hungry soul, and do not embitter the poor in his poverty (ibid.).

Do not distress the heart of the needy, and do not delay giving to one in anguish (ibid.).

Do not reject the plea of the afflicted, and do not turn your face away from the needy (ibid.).

Do not turn your eyes away from the poor because of anger (ibid.).

The prayer of the poor person who curses you in bitterness will be heard.

He who made him will hear him (ibid.).

[Col. 0679C] Make yourself approachable to the assembly of the poor (ibid.).

Incline your ear to the poor without sadness, so that your propitiation and your blessing may be completed (ibid.).

Before death, do good to a friend, and according to your strength stretch out your hand and give to the poor (Eccles. XIV).

Give to the poor and you will receive; justify your soul. Before your death, practice your righteousness, for food cannot be found in the underworld (ibid.).

Whoever practices mercy lends to his neighbor (Eccles. XXIX).

Lend to your neighbor in the time of his need (ibid.).

### AUGUSTINE

In generosity toward the poor, not spoils but gifts are required.

[Col. 0679D] What sort of gift is it when one person receives it with joy and another loses it with tears?

One rejoices over it, while the other sighs.

Although you may give what is yours, you make a better almsgiving if you return what belongs to another.

What we possess is another’s if we do not use it suitably for salvation.

The almsgiving pleasing to God is that which is offered from one’s native property, not that which is given from fraudulent plunder.

They would rather lose what is theirs by giving it away than establish what belongs to others by arranging it.

### JEROME

At the table where devout poor people and strangers are present, [Col. 0680A] let it be recognized that Christ is their fellow guest.

The glory of bishops is to provide for the poor; the disgrace of all priests is to devote themselves to their own wealth.

When you have given alms to someone in need, do not be vain, nor consider yourself better than the person to whom you have lent.

### GREGORY

There are people who love great things and consider distributing much of what they possess to the needy, so that they may redeem their sins before God’s eyes through the compassion of mercy.

When we give whatever is necessary to those in need, we return what is theirs to them; we do not give them our own.

By preserving earthly things, we lose them; but by giving generously and well, we preserve them.

[Col. 0680B] Whoever now offers good works to the needy expends them especially for the one whose love moved him to provide them.

### ISIDORE

No crimes can be redeemed by alms if a person persists in sins.

There is no forgiveness of an offense when mercy precedes it in such a way that sins follow.

Whoever loves an enemy, gives compassion and consolation to one who mourns, or offers counsel in any kind of need unquestionably gives alms.

However needy a person may be, no one can plead poverty as an excuse for having nothing to give to the needy, [Col. 0680C] since by the Savior’s command we are required to offer even a cup of cold water to one in need.

There are two kinds of alms: one bodily, to give the needy whatever you can; the other spiritual, to forgive the one by whom you have been harmed.

To give alms from what has been stolen from others is not an act of mercy but the profit of crime.

Therefore whoever takes unjustly never gives justly; nor does he give another something beneficial when he extorts it wickedly from someone else’s property.

It is a great crime to give the property of the poor to the rich and to purchase delicacies for the powerful from the resources of the needy.

Do not choose whom you will pity, lest you pass over someone who deserves to receive.

[Col. 0680D] Goodwill is better than what is given.

Whoever extends his hand with sadness loses the fruit of his reward.

For there is no mercy where there is no goodwill.

Do not take from one person in order to give to others.

It accomplishes nothing if you feed one person from what you have made another destitute of.

### CYPRIAN

Whoever is wise according to God and gives alms believes in God; and whoever possesses the truth of faith preserves the fear of God.

But whoever preserves the fear of God in showing mercy to the poor thinks of and honors God.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On Tribulations

[Col. 0681A]

### CHRIST

Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise (Rev. III).

### PAUL

Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Hebr. XII).

In everything we suffer tribulation, but are not confined (Acts XIV).

We are perplexed, but not abandoned (II Cor. IV).

We suffer persecution, but are not forsaken (ibid.).

We are cast down, but do not perish.

For we always carry the dying of Jesus in our [Col. 0681B] body, so that the life of Jesus Christ may also be manifested in our bodies (ibid.).

### AUGUSTINE

Whoever does not deserve to be scourged in this world will be tormented in hell.

When we are scourged by the Lord, if we receive it patiently and give humble thanks, then, if we have been wicked, we will receive forgiveness of sins; but if we have been good, we will attain eternal blessedness.

### JEROME

Whoever receives evil once in this life will not suffer in death the same torments that he suffered in life.

It is much better for the stomach to hurt than the mind.

A wound that is healed with pain must be guarded against.

[Col. 0681C] Great is God’s mercy when he is angry with sinners.

If a physician ceases to treat, he despairs.

### GREGORY

It is brought about by divine administration when prolonged sickness burns away more prolonged vices.

### ISIDORE

When God returns to a person, he torments him; the one whom he had abandoned when sinning he visits again by scourging.

God’s mercy is ordered so that first, here, it corrects a person from sin through scourges, and afterward frees him from eternal punishment.

The chosen person of God is worn down by the pains of this life so that he may gain the perfection of the future life.

Temporal scourges advance the righteous toward eternal [Col. 0681D] joys; therefore the righteous ought to rejoice in punishments, and the wicked to mourn in prosperity.

God withdraws mercy from neither the righteous nor the reprobate.

Here he judges the good through affliction so that there he may reward them through mercy; and here he rewards the wicked through temporal clemency, while there he punishes them through eternal justice.

In this life God spares the wicked, yet does not spare the chosen.

In that life he will spare the chosen, but will not spare the wicked.

As much as a person endures scourges in body or mind, so much should he hope to be rewarded at the end.

[Col. 0682A] Although the reprobate may appear to have committed many damnable acts and to be despised by God, they are struck by no blow of correction.

Divine striking is twofold: one, for good, by which we are struck in the flesh so that we may be corrected; the other, by which we are wounded in conscience, through love, so that we may love God more ardently.

God scourges the righteous so that they may not fall by becoming proud of their righteousness.

For the scourge will then erase guilt when it changes the life.

Every divine blow is either a purification of the present life or the beginning of a punishment to come.

For in some people scourges begin in this life and continue into eternal punishment. Although [Col. 0682B] one guilt is not struck twice, there is understood to be one blow which begins here and is completed there: in those who are not corrected at all, the blow of the preceding scourges becomes the beginning of the subsequent torments.

By the secret judgment of God, some fare badly here and well there, namely, so that, while being chastised and corrected here, they may be freed from eternal damnation; others fare well here and badly there, as happened to that rich man in the Gospel.

Moreover, some fare badly both here and there, because, unwilling to be corrected, they begin to be scourged in this life and are condemned to eternal suffering.

[Col. 0682C] A sinful person ought not to murmur at God’s scourges, because he is corrected especially through the very thing by which he is rebuked.

Each person bears more lightly what he suffers now if he examines the evils for which just retribution is inflicted upon him.

Let the righteous recognize that they are being tested in adversity, not cast down.

Holy men fear prosperity more than adversity, because prosperity casts down God’s servants, while adversity instructs them.

God’s eyes are most upon the righteous when his higher providence permits them to be afflicted by the wicked.

Eternal joys are prepared for the righteous when they are tested by present tribulation.

The more we are broken in this world, the more firmly we are strengthened forever.

[Col. 0682D] The more we are afflicted in the present, the more we shall rejoice in the future.

If we are worn down here by scourges, we shall come purified to the judgment.

God always tolerates here those whom he prepares for everlasting salvation.

Therefore do not murmur, do not blaspheme, and do not say, “Why do I suffer evils?” For, in proportion to the offense, the retribution of punishment is lesser.

Whoever murmurs under scourges provokes God more.

But whoever patiently endures adversity appeases God more quickly.

If you wish to be purified through punishment, accuse yourself and praise God’s justice.

[Col. 0683A] Everything that happens to you occurs not without God’s will.

The power of the wicked over you is granted by God’s permission.

All who oppose you act by God’s counsel.

You will bear lighter things patiently if you remember heavier ones.

Sickness burns away vices; sickness breaks the strength of lust.

Severe illness makes the soul sober.

### CYPRIAN

He is not worthy to receive consolation in death who has not considered that he is going to die.

We overcome the sickness of the soul through sickness of the body.

Do you know that this is God’s judgment: that whoever is not corrected by benefits may at least come to his senses through blows?

## FROM THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS

[Col. 0683B] It is better to pay one’s penalties here than to be tormented afterward, once this life has ended, in eternal fire.

## CHAPTER L. On Firstfruits

### PAUL

Do not forget beneficence and fellowship (Hebr. XIII).

For God is pleased by such sacrifices (ibid.).

### SOLOMON

The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord, but the vows of the righteous are acceptable (Prov. XV).

My son, if you have the means, do good and offer offerings worthy of God. Remember that death will not delay [Col. 0683C] (Eccles. XIV).

### JESUS SIRACH

The sacrifice of one who offers from an unjust possession is polluted (Eccles. XXXIV).

The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked (ibid.).

In the offerings of the wicked, nor in the multitude of sacrifices, will God be reconciled concerning sins (ibid.).

Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of a poor man is like one who slaughters a son before his father (Ibid.).

You shall not appear before God empty-handed (Deut. XVII).

The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and is an odor of sweetness in the presence of the Most High (Eccles. XXXV).

The sacrifice of the righteous is acceptable, and the Lord will not forget its memorial (Ibid.).

[Col. 0683D] Do not offer wicked gifts, for God will not receive them (Ibid.).

With a good disposition give glory to God, and do not diminish the firstfruits of your hands (Ibid.).

**GREGORY.**

The guilt of reproaches must be washed away by a great cleansing of sacrifices.

## CHAPTER LI. On Sadness

**CHRIST.**

“Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice” (John XVI).

“But you will be sorrowful, yet your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

[Col. 0684A]

“Godly sorrow produces repentance leading to enduring salvation” (II Cor. VII).

“A joyful mind makes one’s age flourishing, but a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones.”

**JESUS SIRACH.**

“My son, do not complain in prosperity, and in every gift do not give sorrow through an evil word” (Eccles. XVIII).

“Every wound is a sorrow of the heart.”

“Do not give sorrow to your soul.”

[Col. 0684B] “Cheerfulness of heart—this is the life of a man” (Eccles. III).

“Drive sadness away from you, for sadness has killed many, and there is no benefit in it” (Eccles. XXX).

“A perverse heart will cause sadness, but a prudent man resists it” (Eccles. XXXVI).

“For death hastens toward sadness.”

“Sorrow of heart bends the neck” (Ibid.).

“Do not give your heart over to sorrow, but drive it away from you” (Eccles. XXVIII).

**ISIDORE.**

“Do you wish never to be sad? Live well.”

“A secret conscience bears sadness lightly.”

“A good life always possesses joy.”

“But the conscience of the guilty is always in punishment.”

“A guilty mind is never secure.”

[Col. 0684C] “Just as a moth consumes clothing and a worm devours wood, so sadness eats away the human heart.”

“A joyful heart makes for good health, but the sadness of men dries up the bones.”

“Son, the beauty that is accustomed to pour spiritual joy into us is to be loved.”

[Col. 0684D] “Let us avoid costly beauties, lest every kind of evil be inflicted upon us.”

“But a fool, desiring her, is overthrown.”

“A prudent man turns his eyes away from an imprudent woman.”

“But the lustful man, gazing upon her, is melted like wax before the face of fire.”

## CHAPTER LXII. On Association with the Good and the Wicked

**PAUL.**

“We beseech you, brothers, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly” (II Thess. III).

“Let everyone who calls upon the name of [Col. 0695B] the Lord depart from iniquity” (II Tim. II).

“It is therefore just, indeed entirely just, to separate the one who wishes to be saved from the one who does not.”
