“My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. I).

“Do not envy an unjust man, nor imitate his ways” (Prov. II).

**JESUS SIRACH.**

“Depart from the wicked, and evils will fail to trouble you” (Eccles. VII).

“Let righteous men be your companions at table, and let your glory be in the fear of God” (Eccles. IX).

“Whoever associates with one more honorable than himself takes a burden upon himself; and do not become a companion to one richer than you” (Eccles. XIII).

[Col. 0695C] “Whoever you know to observe the fear of God, remain constantly with him” (Eccles. XXXVII).

**AMBROSE.**

“The life of the saints is a standard of living for others.”

**GREGORY.**

“Whoever clings to a holy man receives from his continual presence and manner of speech an example of good works, so that he may be kindled to the love of charity.”

“Those who draw others toward iniquity by persuasion receive within themselves the ministry of demons on account of the iniquity, although by nature they are not demons.”

“For the holy Church is broad in carnal matters and narrow in spiritual matters.”

“It is not especially praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the wicked.”

[Col. 0695D] “For just as it is a more serious fault not to be good among the good, so it is a source of immense praise to have remained good even among the wicked.”

**ISIDORE.**

“Just as it is to be desired that the good be at peace with one another, so it is to be desired that the wicked be at odds with one another.”

“Those who desire the heavenly homeland should flee not only the ways of the wicked but also their companionship.”

“If you are the companion of the conduct of the good, you will also share their virtue.”

“For like is accustomed to be joined to like.”

“It is truly dangerous to lead one’s life with the wicked; it is harmful to associate with those who have a perverse will.”

[Col. 0696A] “It is better to hate the wicked than to share their company.”

“Just as the common life of the saints brings many good things, so the society of the wicked brings even more evils.”

## CHAPTER LXIII. On Friendship and Enmity

**CHRIST.**

“You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John VI).

**PAUL.**

“The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I).

**JAMES.**

“Friendship with this world is enmity with God” (James IV).

“Therefore, whoever wishes to be a friend of this age will be constituted an enemy of God” (Ibid.).

**SOLOMON.**

[Col. 0696B]

“Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come back, and tomorrow I will give you,’ when you can give immediately” (Prov. II).

“Do not devise evil against your friend when he trusts in you” (Prov. III).

“Whoever despises his friend is lacking in heart” (Prov. XI).

“The friends of the rich are many. Deal with your case with your friend, and do not reveal a secret to a stranger” (Prov. XIV).

“Just as one who hurls spears and arrows toward death, so is the man who deceitfully harms his friend” (Prov. XXVI).

“Do not become an enemy to your neighbor on account of your friend” (Ibid.).

**JESUS SIRACH.**

[Col. 0696C] “A sweet word multiplies friends and calms enemies” (Eccles. VI).

“If you acquire a friend, possess him in temptation, and do not readily trust him” (Ibid.).

“For there is a friend according to his own time, and he will not remain in the day of tribulation” (Ibid.).

“There is a friend who enters into friendship” (Ibid.).

“But there is a friend who is a companion at table, who will not remain in the day of need.”

“If a friend remains steadfast, he will be to you as an equal, and he will act faithfully among your household” (Eccles. VI).

“Be watchful concerning your friends, and separate yourself from your enemies.”

“A faithful friend is a strong protection” (Ibid.).

“But whoever finds him has found a treasure.”

“Nothing compares with a faithful friend” (Ibid.).

[Col. 0696D] “A faithful friend is a medicine of life and immortality” (Ibid.).

“Those who fear the Lord find a faithful friend” (Ibid.).

“Do not abandon an old friend, for a new one will not be like him” (Eccles. IX).

“New wine is a new friend; if it grows old, you will drink it with pleasure” (Eccles. XI).

“Do not bring every person into your house” (Eccles. XI).

“For the snares of the deceitful devil are many” (Ibid.).

“A friend is not recognized in prosperity, and an enemy is not concealed in adversity” (Eccles. XII).

“Do not tell your understanding to friend or enemy; and if you have a fault, do not expose it. For he will hear you and [Col. 0697A] keep it, and, as though defending your sin, he will hate you” (Eccles. XIX).

“If you have heard a word against your neighbor, let it die within you, trusting that it will not burst forth from you” (Ibid.).

“Reprove your friend, lest he fail to understand you and say, ‘I did not do it’; or, if he did it, lest he do it again.”

“Whoever insults his friend dissolves the friendship” (Eccles. XXII).

“Even if you draw a sword against your friend, do not despair; for there is a return to friendship” (Ibid.).

“If he humbles himself before you and hides himself from your face, you will have a good friendship united in harmony” (Eccles. V).

“If a friend appears with a sad face, do not be afraid” (Eccles. [Col. 0697B] XXII).

“Do not be ashamed to greet your friend; do not hide yourself from his face; and if evils come upon you through him, endure them” (Ibid.).

“Blessed is the one who finds a true friend” (Prov. XV).

“Whoever exposes his friend’s secrets loses trust and will not find a friend for his soul” (Eccles. XXVII).

“To expose the mysteries of a friend is despair for the soul” (Ibid.).

“Confirm your word with your friend, and act faithfully with him; at every time you will find what you need” (Eccles. XXIX).

“There is a friend who is a friend in name only” (Eccles. XXXVII).

“Do not forget your friend in your heart, and do not be forgetful of him in your deeds” (Ibid.).

[Col. 0697C] “Whoever fears the Lord will have a good friendship, for his friendship will be according to Him” (Eccles. VI).

“According to your ability, guard yourself from your neighbor, and associate with the wise” (Eccles. IX).

“Do not trust your enemy forever” (Eccles. XII).

“For his malice will rust like bronze” (Ibid.).

“An enemy speaks soothingly with his lips, but in his heart he lies in wait to cast you into a pit” (Ibid.).

“An enemy weeps in your sight, and, as though helping, will dig beneath your feet.”

“He will shake his head, and, whispering many things, will change his expression.”

[Col. 0697D] “An enemy weeps in your sight, and if he finds an opportunity, he will not be satisfied with blood” (Eccles. XII).

“If evils befall you, there you will find your former enemy” (Ibid.).

“The sinner will trouble a friend and introduce enmity among those who are at peace” (Eccles. XXVIII).

“Do not place your enemy beside you, nor let him sit at your right hand” (Eccles. XII).

**AUGUSTINE.**

“A malevolent mind is grieved if its enemy escapes after being corrected.”

**JEROME.**

“For in friends it is not possessions but the will that is sought.”

“Holy love has no impatience; false love is quickly crushed.”

[Col. 0698A] “Those whom charity joins are not separated by the distance of lands.”

**GREGORY.**

“Then we are truly faithful if we fulfill in deed what we promise in words.”

“For whoever cannot pursue his enemy with a sword should pursue him with prayer.”

**ISIDORE.**

“A friend is truly loved when he is loved not for himself but for God.”

“For whoever loves a friend immoderately loves him more for himself than for God.”

“Often friendship is gathered through pretense, so that one who could not deceive openly may deceive fraudulently.”

Then each person becomes all the more opposed to piety and divine justice [Col. 0698B] when he despises a friend struck by some adversity.

For when adversity arises, the fraudulent friend is exposed, and immediately despises the one whom he pretended to love.

True friendship is excluded by no force and abolished by no passage of time: wherever time may turn, it remains most steadfast.

Rare are the friends who remain dear to the end.

For those whom some people have held joined to themselves by affection, once they have risen to the summit of honor, cease to regard as worthy of having as friends.

That is true friendship which seeks nothing from a friend’s possessions except benevolence alone—that is, which loves the one who loves it freely.

[Col. 0698C] For the most part, friendship arises from necessity or need, so that there may be someone through whom each person obtains what he desires.

But the person truly seeks friendship who seeks it without doing anything [to obtain it].

For the former, born of poverty, is brief and counterfeit; the latter is pure and everlasting.

Do not be fickle in your friendship; always retain it in the bond of charity.

Whoever has lost a faithful friend recognizes what good he possessed only after he has ceased to have him.

It is better to endure the perpetual hostility of faithless men than to provoke God’s displeasure through harmful friendships.

If your enemy falls, do not rejoice.

[Col. 0698D] Do not exult over the death of your enemy, lest similar things overtake you.

For whoever rejoices at an enemy’s downfall soon falls into the same condition.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On Counsel

### From the Acts of the Apostles

If a plan or work is from human beings, it will be brought to nothing (Acts V).

But if it is from God, it cannot be brought to nothing (ibid.).

### Solomon

Counsel will guard you, and prudence will preserve you (Prov. II).

Keep the law and judgment, and they will be life to your soul and glory to your throat (Prov. III).

The way of a fool is right in his own eyes (Prov. XII).

But the wise person listens to counsel (ibid.).

Those who enter into counsels of peace will be followed by joy.

But those who do everything with counsel are guided by wisdom (Prov. XIII).

The prudent person does everything with counsel (ibid.).

Plans are scattered where there is no counsel (Prov. XV).

But where there are many counselors, they are confirmed (ibid.).

Plans are established by counsel, and wars must be conducted with steering-oars [that is, guidance] (Prov. XX).

There will be safety where there are many counsels (Prov. XXIV).

As deep water is counsel in a man’s heart, but the wise man will draw it out (ibid.).

### Jesus Sirach

[Col. 0699B]

Let many be your peacemakers, but let one out of a thousand be your counselor (Eccles. VI).

Do not take counsel with fools (Eccles. VIII).

For they cannot love anything except what pleases themselves (ibid.).

Do not take counsel in the presence of a stranger (ibid.).

Do not reveal your heart to everyone, lest he perhaps take away your favor and reproach you (ibid.).

The tongue of the wise will abound like a flood, and his counsel is like a fountain of life (Eccles. XXI).

A wooden tie fastened into the foundation of a building will not come apart; so too a heart established in the deliberation of counsel (Eccles. XXII).

Upon the one who devises the worst counsel, it will collapse upon him, and he will not recognize from where it has come upon him (Eccles. XXVII). [Col. 0699C]

Do nothing without counsel, and afterward you will not regret it (Eccles. XXXII).

Hide your counsel from those who are jealous of you (Eccles. XXXVII).

Treat of holiness with a religious man, and of justice with a just man.

A good heart will formulate counsels.

Before every undertaking, let your counsel be firm.

### Gregory

A mind that grieves over present things and hastens toward eternal ones harbors a counselor.

### Isidore

Before acting, think; before the time comes, deliberate for a long while; examine carefully what you wish to do, test it, and then act. When you have deliberated for a long time, do what you have approved. [Col. 0699D]

### Basil

In every work that you are considering doing, first think of God; and if what you are considering is according to God, examine it carefully. If it is right before God, complete it; but if it is perverse, do not even begin it.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Deceased

### Christ

“Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke XII).

### John

“Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. XIV).

### Paul

[Col. 0700A]

“For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself” (Rom. XIV).

“For whether we live, we live for the Lord; or whether we die, we die for the Lord” (Rom. VIII).

### Solomon

“The memory of the just is for praises, but the name of the wicked rots” (Prov. X).

“When the wicked man dies, there will be no hope thereafter” (Prov. I).

### Jesus Sirach

“Do not withhold kindness from the dead” (Eccles. VII).

“Walk with those who mourn; do not be reluctant to visit the sick” (ibid.).

“For among these you will be engaged in love” (ibid.).

“Do not rejoice over the death of your enemy, knowing that we shall all die” (Eccles. VIII). [Col. 0700B]

“All authority is brief-lived; the physician cuts short a brief illness” (Eccles. X).

“So too the king is king today and will die tomorrow” (ibid.).

“For when a man dies, he will inherit serpents, beasts, and worms” (ibid.).

“Weep briefly over the dead, for his light has come to rest. At the time of your departure, distribute your inheritance” (Eccles. XXII and XXXIII).

“Son, shed tears for the dead, and begin to mourn as though you had suffered terrible things” (Eccles. XXXVIII).

### Jerome

Whoever dies in this present time should not so much be mourned because he has been deprived of this light as congratulated because he has escaped from so many evils.

### Gregory

[Col. 0700C]

Just as blessedness gladdens the elect, so it must be believed that, on the day of their departure, fire consumes the reprobate.

Then, when the soul departs, the evil spirits seek their own works; then they recall the evils they suggested, so that they may drag the soul with them to punishments.

### Isidore

After death the wicked person is led away to be tortured, but the just person sleeps securely after his labor.

And although acts of piety toward the deceased are to be performed, faith nevertheless forbids mourning for them.

Those are to be mourned in death whom hell receives from this life in misery, not those whom the heavenly court, rejoicing, encloses within itself.

### Josephus

No one will be able to refuse the outcome which either chance has brought about or the will of God has decreed.

### Christ

“No one can receive anything for himself unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John III).

“It is not difficult for the Lord to save, whether by many or by few” (I Kings XIV).

### Paul

“For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III).

“If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. VIII).

[Col. 0701A] “Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX).

“Trust in the Lord your God” (Prov. III).

## CHAPTER LXVII. On the Old and the Young

### Christ

“Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX).

“Amen I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

### Paul

[Col. 0701C]

“Do not rebuke an older man, but entreat him as a father; younger men as brothers” (I Tim. V).

[Col. 0701D] “The turning away of the little ones will kill them” (Prov. I).

### Basil

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On Contention

### Paul

“When there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” (I Cor. III).

“Do not contend with words, for it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear” (II Tim. II).

“There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may also become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI).

[Col. 0702C] “Avoid a heretical person after one or two admonitions” (Titus III).

### Solomon

“Among the proud there are always quarrels; the wicked always seeks quarrels” (Prov. XVII).

“But a cruel angel will be sent against him” (ibid.).

### Jesus Sirach

“Do not quarrel with a powerful man, lest you fall into his hands; nor with a double-tongued man, lest you pile wood on his fire” (Eccles. VIII).

### From the Book of Clement

Let us seek that which ought to be done willingly.

For if, while this brief span of life continues, we occupy ourselves with useless questions, we shall undoubtedly proceed to God empty and void, where judgment will be passed on our works. [Col. 0702D]

### Gregory

All heretics, while striving to defend God, offend him.

The sacrifices of heretics cannot be acceptable to God.

### Isidore

Contention kindles the jaws of hatred.

Contention breaks concord.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On Curiosity

[Col. 0703A]

### Christ

“Do not shake anyone down, and do not make a false accusation” (Luke III).

“One witness shall not stand against anyone, whatever the sin or crime may be” (Deut. XIX).

“But by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. XVII).

### Solomon

“But the one who investigates evils will be crushed” (Prov. XI).

### Jesus Sirach

“Do not scrutinize your mind excessively in superfluous matters; it is not necessary for you to see with your eyes the things that are hidden. Do not quarrel over a matter that does not trouble you” (Eccles. III). [Col. 0703B]

### Augustine

Oh, how blameless we could be if we guarded our own vices as diligently as we investigate those of others.

But this is why we forget our own faults while investigating those of others.

### Jerome

Whoever strives to make progress should not consider what evil another person does, but what good he himself ought to do.

Therefore let the person who wishes to criticize take care not to commit the same fault.

It is enough for us to think about the present distresses of this age.

[Col. 0703C] Why is it necessary to extend our understanding toward uncertain and future things, which we either cannot attain or, having quickly found them, soon lose?

Therefore the one who forbade us to think about the future allowed us to concern ourselves with the present because of the fragility of human life.

It is enough for us to have our present struggle against the wickedness of this age.

### Ambrose

A person ought to weep over the sins he knows for as long as he carefully observes the sins of others.

But if, turning back to himself, he examines his own conduct, he does not seek what in particular he may criticize in others, but what he may mourn in himself.

### Gregory

[Col. 0703D] We ought to criticize the hearts of others boldly all the less, since we cannot illuminate with our own sight the darkness of another person’s thoughts.

Nor can the person whose own sins still devastate him wipe away the sins of others.

### Isidore

Do not defile your mouth with another person’s evil.

Attend to your own vices, not those of others.

Therefore be concerned with your own correction.

Therefore be attentive to your own salvation and amendment.

Do not inquire into what does not concern you.

Never desire to know what people say among themselves.

Do not ask what each person says or does. Avoid curiosity; abandon concern for what does not belong to your own affairs. [Col. 0704A]

Curiosity is a dangerous presumption.

Many discern the vices of others but do not look at their own; and although they themselves are held guilty of the greatest crimes, they do not forgive their brothers’ smallest sins.

Often we point out faults in others which we feel less keenly to be harmful in ourselves.

We pay attention more readily to each person’s vices than to his virtues.

We do not acknowledge what good someone has done, but investigate what evil he has done.

But that person will be condemned before God who either gives false testimony against the innocent or believes those who give it. Wicked judges put forward false witnesses. [Col. 0704B]

## CHAPTER LXX. On the Meek and the Fearful

### Christ

“Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. V).

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.”

### Paul

“Correct the restless, console the fainthearted, showing all meekness toward all people” (I Thess. V).

### Solomon

“The Lord derides mockers, but gives grace to the meek” (Prov. III).

[Col. 0704C] “The one who is lax and negligent in his work is a brother to the one who wastes his own work” (Prov. XVIII).

“Since wickedness is fearful, it gives testimony to condemnation” (Wis. XVII).

“For a troubled conscience always presumes savage things” (ibid.).

### Jesus Sirach

A talkative and reckless person is hateful in his speech.

### Augustine

When people are wicked, they consider themselves inferior to everyone.

Meekness does not arise from the will but from human nature.

Complete your works in meekness, and you will be loved above human glory. [Col. 0704D]

Be meek in understanding the word, so that you may understand; and with wisdom give a true answer.

Son, preserve your soul in meekness, and give it honor according to its merit.

### Jerome

“For as a city broken down and without walls, so is a man who does anything without counsel.”

### Gregory

Justice is represented in uprightness, and meekness in simplicity.

Often someone, devoting himself excessively to meekness, sees the vices of those subject to him yet neglects to correct them through the fervor of zeal. By failing to correct them harshly, he multiplies them; and so his gentleness becomes harmful to himself and hostile to those under him. [Col. 0705A]

### Isidore

Do nothing with excessive gentleness, lest you act rashly in some matter.

### Cyprian

The teachable person is one who is humble and meek in learning patience.

### Basil

Frivolity always wants to be praised, just as a ship is tossed about without a helmsman.

As it is tossed by the waves, so the frivolous and unstable person is carried about through all his actions.

### From the Lives of the Fathers

The Lord loves the meek, but drives the turbulent away from himself.

[Col. 0705B] As light is in heaven and happiness in paradise, so a pure mind is in a meek soul.

The more someone possesses gentleness and patience of heart, the more he will progress in purity of heart.

### Eusebius

The ferocity of beasts is tamed by God’s power.

But human rage is not softened even by examples drawn from wild animals.

### Josephus

Reckless rashness without counsel does not know how to await the leader’s advice.

“The just person knows the souls of his beasts” (Prov. XII).

“In the cheerfulness of the king’s face is life, and his clemency is like the latter rain” (Prov. XXVIII).

“Because of the sins of the land, its princes are many.”

“Remove the rust from silver, and a completely pure vessel will emerge” (Prov. XXV).

[Col. 0706A]

“A wise judge will judge his people, and cities will be inhabited through the understanding of the prudent” (Eccles. X).

“Excessive gifts blind the eyes of judges” (Eccles. II).

“The Lord says: I have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself” (Eccles. XXXII).

### Jerome

Let us not rejoice in human praise, nor fear their reproaches.

### Gregory

### Isidore

Whoever judges rightly and expects a reward of recompense for it commits fraud against the Lord, because he sells for money the justice which he ought to distribute freely.

First establish the facts, and then judge.

[Col. 0706C] For it is not the one who is accused, but the one who is convicted, who is guilty.

## CHAPTER LXXII. On Simplicity

### Christ

“Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X).

### Moses

“A delicate and luxurious man will greatly envy his brother” (Deut. XXVIII).

### Paul

“Let us not grow weary in doing good; in due time we shall reap without growing weary” (Gal. VI).

### Solomon

[Col. 0706D]

“The simplicity of the upright will guide them, but the treachery of the perverse will devastate them” (Prov. XI).

“The justice of the simple directs his way, but the wicked will fall in his wickedness” (ibid.).

“An innocent person believes every word.”

“Whoever deceives the upright into an evil way will fall in his destruction, and the simple will possess his goods” (Prov. VIII).

“Men of blood hate the simple, but the just seek his life.”

### Jerome

Holy rusticity benefits only itself; and insofar as it builds up the Church of Christ through the merit of life, it harms it if it does not resist those who destroy the truth.

In a servant of God, what is sought is not bodily adornment but vigor of soul, so that he may be stronger than the weakness of the flesh—not rustic, but simple. [Col. 0707A]

For us imperfect people, it is far better to possess holy rusticity than sinful eloquence.

For us imperfect people, it is far better to possess holy rusticity than sinful eloquence.

Holy rusticity, not loquaciousness, is to be held in veneration.

The spiritual structure is firm faith in the heart, the helmet of salvation on the head.

The sign of Christ on the forehead.

The word of truth in the mouth; a good will in the mind.

The love of God in the breast.

Chastity girded about amid ardor.

Honesty in action.

Sobriety in conduct.

Steadfastness in goodness.

[Col. 0707B] Patience in tribulation.

Hope in the Creator.

Love of eternal life.

Perseverance to the end.

### Gregory

If our intention is simple before God, our action will not be dark in his judgment.

Those who do not know how to be cautious through uprightness cannot remain innocent through simplicity.

The holy Church of the elect guards the ways of its simplicity and uprightness.

The zeal in which a person burns must also be tempered, lest, if he burns more than is proper, he lose the justice whose moderation he does not know how to preserve.

[Col. 0707C] For often, when someone overcome by the goads of anger is inflamed against offenders with zeal for avenging justice more than is necessary, he crosses the limit of justice in his vengeance and acts cruelly while believing that he is acting justly.

### Isidore

Let there be simplicity in your gait; let nothing of softness appear in your progress.

For the mind should appear in the body’s bearing.

The body’s gesture is a sign of the mind.

The mind is revealed through the body’s gesture.

Let your manner of walking offend no one.

### Basil

God is an observer not of words but of the heart, and he loves those who serve him in simplicity of heart.

### Eusebius

[Col. 0707D]

Those things that are despised and held in contempt by human beings are held in great glory before God.

The charity of God makes the things that are fragile by nature exceedingly firm through grace.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On Physicians

### Christ

“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke III).

“Physician, heal yourself first” (Luke IV).

### Jesus Sirach

“Honor the physician because of necessity, for the Most High created him” (Eccles. XXXVIII).

[Col. 0708A] All healing is from God.

“The physician’s discipline will exalt his head, and he will be highly praised in the presence of the great” (ibid.).

“An ointment-maker who prepares perfumes of sweetness and anointing contributes to health” (ibid.).

“Give the physician his place, for the Lord created him” (ibid.).

“And let him not depart from you, for his works are necessary” (ibid.).

“Whoever sins in the presence of the one who made him falls into the hands of the physician.”

### Cyprian

The wound must be opened and cut, and once the diseased matter has been removed, it must be treated with a stronger remedy.

Let the sick person cry out and shout, and even complain impatiently because of the pain; afterward he will give thanks when he feels himself healed. [Col. 0708B]

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On Binding

### Christ

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

“You shall not receive a false report, nor join your hand to the wicked by giving false testimony on behalf of the impious” (Exod. XXIII).

### Gregory

Those whom almighty God raises up through the grace of repentance, the pastor’s judgment will absolve.

We ought to absolve through pastoral authority those whom we recognize our Creator to bring to life through his life-giving grace. [Col. 0708C]

The pastors of the Church should strive either to absolve or to bind with great restraint.

Whether the pastor binds justly or unjustly, the pastor’s judgment must nevertheless be feared by the flock, lest the subordinate who is perhaps bound unjustly deserve, through another fault, the very sentence of his binding.

Therefore the pastor must fear either to absolve indiscriminately or to bind indiscriminately.

But the person who is under the pastor’s hand must fear being bound even unjustly, lest he rashly criticize his pastor’s judgment.

## CHAPTER LXXV. On Examples

### Christ

[Col. 0708D]

“The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat” (Matt. XXIII).

“Therefore do and observe everything they tell you; but do not act according to their works” (ibid.).

“For they say and do not do” (ibid.).

### Paul

“Always emulate what is good in doing good” (I Tim. IV).

“Be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, and in faith, so that your progress may be manifest to all.”

“In all things present yourself as an example of good works” (Titus II).

### Solomon

[Col. 0709A]

“God will give a good man, in his own sight, wisdom, knowledge, and joy” (Prov. I).

### Jerome

Just as constant association produces familiarity, so familiarity produces contempt.

It is better for one’s household possessions to diminish than to lose the salvation of one’s soul.

### Gregory

Those who refuse to let their life be known by others are inflamed for themselves, but are not lights of example to others.

For those who provide examples of virtues and demonstrate the light of good work through life and speech to those who walk after them are rightly called lamps. [Col. 0709B]

A fault is especially clearly displayed in an example when, out of respect for rank, a sinner is honored.

Therefore the person who, dying to all the passions of the flesh, already lives spiritually ought by every means to be brought forward as an example.

### Isidore

Let no one despair of pardon after a fall while repenting, when he sees that the saints were restored even after their ruin.

For this benefit, the falls and restorations of the saints are written down, so that they may inspire hope of human salvation.

If we have been capable of imitating the wicked in evil, why are we slow to imitate the just in good?

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On Disciples

[Col. 0709C]

### Christ

“A disciple is not above his teacher; but everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher” (Luke VI).

### Paul

“Let your speech always be seasoned with grace and salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. IV).

### Solomon

“A man rejoices in the answer of his mouth, and a word at the right time is best” (Prov. XV).

“Iron is sharpened by iron, and a man sharpens the face of his friend.”

### Jesus Sirach

“If you have understanding, answer your neighbor” [Col. 0709D] (Eccles. V).

“But if not, let your hand be upon your mouth, lest you be caught by an undisciplined word and be put to shame” (ibid.).

### Jerome

Beware of becoming a teacher before you are a disciple, or wishing to be a soldier before you are a recruit.

Beware of entering without a teacher upon a road you have never traveled; by turning aside in another direction, you may fall into error and walk farther than necessary; and by running you may grow weary, or by delaying you may fall asleep.

No art is learned without a teacher.

Learn for a long time before you teach.

Do not trust your flatterers; indeed, do not lend an ear to your mockers.

Do not seek things greater than your strength, for it is better to proceed in humble matters than to waver with an unsteady step on higher ground. [Col. 0710A]

A father does not teach a son unless he loves him; nor does a teacher correct a disciple unless he sees that he possesses an especially ardent intellect.

Whoever asks questions not from a desire to learn but from a zeal to refute approaches, in the manner of the Pharisees, not as a disciple but as a tempter.

An earnest and wise man, even when he wishes to learn something, teaches more by asking prudent questions.

There are some who, through excessive fluency of speech and audacity, explain to others what they themselves do not understand.

### Isidore

When questioned about good, I am silent; for it is better to remain silent before the wicked than to answer.

### Cyprian

[Col. 0710B]

The better teacher is the one who grows daily and progresses by learning better things.

For a soldier cannot be fit for service unless he has first been trained in the field.

Speech and sound reasoning are learned effectively only when what is being learned is heard patiently.

Discipline is the guardian of hope, the repository of faith, the guide of the way of salvation, the nourishment and activity of a good disposition, and the teacher of virtue. It makes one remain always in Christ and live continually for God, reaching the heavenly promises and divine rewards.

### Eusebius

It is not fitting to call someone a philosopher who publicly makes assertions about things he does not know.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On Temptation and Martyrdom

[Col. 0710C]

### Christ

“Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you” (Luke X).

“But rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (ibid.).

“Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.”

### Peter

“Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V).

### James

[Col. 0710D] “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James IV).

### Paul

“The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God” (II Cor. VI).

### Origen

Whoever comes out of temptation well, and whom temptation renders approved, comes to soundness of judgment.

Therefore, if you see your persecutor at some time raging excessively, know that he is being driven on by the demon who rides him.

### Augustine

Every person who persecutes another in the body is first understood to endure persecution in his own heart.

[Col. 0711A] For if he has also taken something from the possessions of the one he persecutes, he causes himself a greater loss.

For no one possesses unjust gain without just loss.

Where there is gain, there is also loss.

Gain in the chest; loss in the conscience.

He takes away a garment and loses faith.

He acquires money and loses justice.

### Jerome

Nothing is stronger than the one who conquers the devil; nothing is more intolerable than the one who overcomes the flesh.

If the stars of heaven are not pure in the Lord’s sight, how much less human beings, whose life is temptation?

The devil’s arrows must be restrained by the crash of fasts and vigils. [Col. 0711B]

It is therefore a great virtue and a matter of vigilant diligence to overcome the fact that you were born in the flesh and yet not live according to the flesh.

Not only the shedding of blood is counted as confession, but the undefiled service of a devoted mind is daily martyrdom.

The crafty enemy, seeking punishments that are slow to bring death, desires to slaughter souls, not bodies.

Let us not fear the savagery of wicked persecutors or the fury of blasphemers, because the day of judgment will come, on which our virtue will be crowned and their savagery punished.

### Gregory

When the perversity of the wicked increases, preaching must not merely remain unbroken; it must also increase.

[Col. 0711C] Divine mercy increases this, so that from the very thing by which it gives the carnal a scourge, it grants spiritual virtues an increase.

The devil scatters the faithful people like a wolf scatters a flock when he calls them through temptation.

Although the occasion for persecution is absent, our peace nevertheless has its own martyrdom: for even if we do not submit the necks of our flesh to the sword, we still slaughter carnal desires in the mind with a spiritual sword.

### Isidore

Although the devil always desires to bring temptation upon the just, if he does not receive power from God, he cannot in any way obtain what he seeks.

The devil kindles the fuel of desire nowhere except where he has first seen the delight of a wicked thought; and if we reject that delight, he undoubtedly departs from us in confusion.

The saints judge well concerning themselves when God enables them to understand the deceptive temptations of demons.

In the eyes of the carnal, the devil is terrifying.

In the eyes of the elect, his terror is contemptible.

For the devil is a slippery serpent; if its head—that is, the first suggestion—is not resisted, it slips wholly into the inner heart without being noticed.

The devil then rages more fiercely against the one he possesses when he recognizes that, through divine power, he is to be expelled from him.

When the devil wishes to deceive someone, he first examines that person’s nature, and from that point applies himself where he sees the person most suited to sin. [Col. 0712A]

For the devil never ceases to fight against a just person.

Either he agitates the person with tribulations of the heart or arouses bodily pain.

Whatever adversity the just person suffers, he suffers it by God’s permission.

But if he humbly refers this very thing to God’s glory, he is not separated from God but joined to him.

We sin where we bend desire toward the will.

For those whom unclean spirits tempt with vices while they are awake but do not overcome, they attack more fiercely while they sleep.

For often the things toward which we extend the sense of our thoughts are revealed, through a certain excess of mind, while we rest. [Col. 0712B]

Whoever is defiled by nocturnal illusion, although he feels himself polluted outside the memory of shameful thoughts, should nevertheless attribute the fact that he was tempted to his own fault and immediately wash away his uncleanness with tears.

We easily overcome an enemy whom we see; but one whom we do not see we drive away from us with difficulty.

Everyone ought to prepare his mind for temptation.

The just person ought to be tempted, but by the temptation of affliction, not by the temptation of lust.

Temptation tests you, but does not kill you.

What does one who has not been tempted know?

A man experienced in many things considers many things.

[Col. 0712C] Whoever has learned much will express understanding; whoever has not experienced things recognizes little.

### Cyprian

The greater the injury of persecution, the more just and severe will be the vengeance for persecution.

Those who have confidence in future goods feel no pain from the assault of present evils.

For the enemy cannot be permitted so much power that we, who love God with our whole heart, soul, and strength, do not always and everywhere proclaim his blessedness and praises with glory.

### From the Lives of the Fathers

As fire tests gold and silver, so temptation tests the monk’s heart.

Where the cross of Christ is brought upon someone, the devil’s wickedness will not prevail. [Col. 0712D]

### Eusebius

Nothing is frightening where Christ is loved; there is no pain where the faith of Christ is present.

The one who defends us is better than the one who persecutes us.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On Idle Words

### Christ

“I say to you that for every idle word which people have spoken, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII).

“For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (ibid.).

### Paul

[Col. 0713A]

“Let no one deceive you with empty words” (I Tim. IV).

“Avoid foolish and empty tales” (Prov. XII).

### Solomon

“Because of sins of the lips, ruin draws near to the wicked.”

### Jerome

A mind devoted to Christ guards against lesser things just as against greater ones, knowing that an account must also be given for an idle word.

**GREGORY.**

An idle word is one that lacks either the usefulness of uprightness or the reason of just necessity.

Just as heedless speech leads into error, so indiscreet silence leaves in error those whom it could have instructed.

**ISIDORE.**

Close your ears, lest they hear evil.

Flee heedless words.

Empty speech quickly pollutes the mind.

What is willingly heard is easily done.

Let nothing proceed from your mouth that could cause harm.

Let no sound of your voice burst forth that is not expedient; let that proceed from your lips which does not pollute the ears of the hearer.

Empty speech is an index of an empty conscience.

As the speech appears, so the mind is shown to be.

Keep silent about a word that does not edify. The ear that does not restrain idle words quickly turns to harmful ones.

Vices grow little by little, and while we do not guard against small things, we slide into great ones.

Be skilled both in speaking and in keeping silent.

Learn what you should say and what you should keep silent about: let not your tongue destroy you.

Set the barriers of silence against your tongue.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On the brevity of this life

**CHRIST.**

“Whoever eats me will also live because of me” (John VI).

**JAMES.**

“For what is our life? It is vapor that appears for a little while” (James IV).

**PAUL.**

[Col. 0713D] “That which exists in the present is momentary” [probably *momentaneum*].

**SOLOMON.**

“Do not boast about tomorrow, since you do not know what the coming day will bring forth” (Prov. XXVII).

“A man who is a leader will have a longer life” (Prov. XXVIII).

“A time to be born, and a time to die” (Eccles. III).

“There is no one who always lives and who has confidence in this matter” (Eccles. IX).

**AUGUSTINE.**

Every wicked person either lives in order to be corrected, or lives so that the good may be exercised through him.

**JEROME.**

The brevity of human life is the condemnation of sins.

Brief is the happiness of this life; slight is the glory of this age.

[Col. 0714A] Temporal power is fleeting and fragile.

Tell me, where are the kings? Where are the emperors? Where are the princes? Where are the wealthy? Where are the powerful of this age?

Certainly they have passed away like a shadow and vanished like a dream.

They are sought, and they are not.

Riches lead to danger.

Many are endangered because of wealth; for many, death comes because of wealth.

Therefore hate with all your soul, and count as loss, what the world loves.

Be dead to the world, and let the world be dead to you.

While alive, despise what you cannot possess after death.

**ISIDORE.**

For only in this life is it permitted to perform good works.

For there, no longer is action expected, but the recompense of merits.

Whoever considers the length of the present life not from its duration but from its end weighs very usefully how wretched and brief it is.

For the web is completed by its threads, and human life is lifted up day by day.

If you seek a long life, strive toward that life for which you are a Christian—that is, eternal life.

For this is the immortal life, whereas this present life is mortal.

A person must die in the flesh to the world, lest he die in soul to Christ.

[Col. 0714C] Each person is then believed to live if, dying according to the world, he delights in living in God alone.

The righteous suffer weariness from the delay of this life, because they reach their desired homeland late.

Everyone ought to live carefully and always consider the end of his life, so that he may beware of the allurements of this age.

Ignorance of the coming departure makes it uncertain; and while a person does not think he will die, he is taken away.

Therefore let everyone hasten, lest he be seized by his iniquities and his life end together with his guilt.

The devil, who inflames the living toward vices, tries to drag them, when they suddenly die, toward torments.

For however righteous a person may be in this life, [Col. 0714D] nevertheless, as he departs from this body, let him fear lest he be worthy of punishment.

For there is no human being without sin; nor can anyone be secure from God’s judgment, since an account must even be given for idle words.

The peaceful calling of the righteous to their excellent end commends that end, so that from this it may be understood that they have fellowship with the angels of the saints: they are taken from this body without harsh affliction.

Nothing lasts long; nothing is lengthy that does not end shortly.

It is impossible for you to be human and not taste distress.

There is no one in this world who does not suffer.

There is no one placed in this life who does not sigh.

[Col. 0715A] Everything is full of evils.

**CYPRIAN.**

Whoever hopes for eternity from God already counts these earthly times as nothing.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On reading

**CHRIST.**

“Let the one who reads understand” (Matt. XXIV).

“Everyone to whom much has been given, from him much will be demanded” (Luke XXII).

**PAUL.**

“Attend to reading and exhortation and teaching; do not neglect the grace that is in you” (I Tim. IV).

“Every Scripture inspired by God is useful” (II Tim. III).

[Col. 0715B] “Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly” (Col. III).

**JAMES.**

“Therefore, for the one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin” (James IV).

**SOLOMON.**

“Wisdom follows diligence” (Eccles. X).

**AUGUSTINE.**

Nourish your soul with divine readings, for the mind will prepare a spiritual table for you.

**JEROME.**

Whoever is constantly devoted to reading labors in the present, but afterward will rejoice when he has begun to understand.

From the bitter seeds of letters, gather sweet fruits.

[Col. 0715C] The prudent reader always guards against superstitious interpretation, so that he does not adapt the Scriptures to his own meaning, but joins his own meaning to the Scriptures, in order to understand what follows.

Let us strive on earth to learn those things whose knowledge will remain with us in heaven.

Blessed is the person who, reading the divine Scriptures, turns words into deeds; who naked follows the naked cross with pure hands and feet; and who, with a pure breast, takes glory in being poor in spirit and in works.

**GREGORY.**

For it is more a punishment than a virtue for anyone to know what he cannot do.

The more a person progresses in sacred Scripture, the more that same Scripture progresses in him.

[Col. 0715D] You will find as much progress in sacred discourse as you yourself have progressed in relation to it.

**ISIDORE.**

Whoever wishes always to be with God ought to pray frequently and read frequently.

For when we pray, we ourselves speak with God.

But when we read, God speaks with us.

All progress proceeds from reading and meditation.

For what we do not know, we learn through reading.

But what we learn, we preserve through meditation.

Reading the holy Scriptures confers a twofold gift: it trains the understanding of the mind, and, [Col. 0716A] drawing a person away from the vanities of the world, leads him to the love of God.

The more brightly eternal hope shines for us through reading, the more the single hope of this mortality grows worthless to us.

Let the diligent reader be readier to fulfill what he reads than to know it.

For it is a lesser punishment not to know what you should seek than not to fulfill what you have learned.

Just as by reading we desire to know, so by knowing we ought to fulfill the right things we have learned.

No one can know the meaning of sacred Scripture without familiarity with reading.

The more constant a person is in sacred writings, the richer an understanding he receives from them.

The higher a person ascends into any art, the more that art itself descends toward the person.

Some possess the gift of understanding but neglect the study of reading; and what they could know by reading, they despise through negligence.

Although the disposition for understanding may be strong, reading nevertheless supplies understanding.

Just as the person who is slow to grasp things nevertheless receives a reward because of the earnestness of his good study, so the person who neglects the gift of understanding granted to him by God is found guilty of condemnation, because he despises and abandons through laziness the gift he has received.

Some receive, by God’s judgment, the gift of knowledge that they neglect, so that they may be punished more severely for the things they believe.

Those who are slower, however, find with difficulty what they desire to know so that, through the greatest exercise of labor, they may receive the greatest reward of recompense.

A gift, although poured into the ears, never descends to the heart without God’s assisting grace.

Most people are lively at the summit of understanding, but are constrained by lack of ability to speak.

Some, however, are strong in both respects.

Most people, having received knowledge of the Scriptures, use it not for the glory of God but for their own praise, being lifted up by that knowledge; and they sin precisely where they ought to have cleansed their sins.

For the proud always read and never find.

The depths of divine law are open to the humble and to those who rightly direct themselves toward God; but they are closed to the perverse and [Col. 0716D] proud.

Although the divine utterances may be open in reading to the arrogant, they nevertheless remain closed and hidden in their mystery.

The word of God is light to the faithful, but it becomes, in a certain way, darkness to the rejected and proud: from the source by which the former are enlightened, the latter are blinded.

By no means does the person understand the law who runs through the words of the law in a carnal manner; rather, it is the person who grasps it through the sense of inner understanding.

Those who attend to the letter of the law cannot penetrate its hidden meaning.

For this reason Christians are forbidden to read the fictions of poets: through the pleasures of empty tales they arouse the mind toward incitements to lust.

[Col. 0717A] The holy books were written in simple speech so that people might be led to faith not by eloquence of language but by the manifestation of the Spirit.

In reading, it is not words but truth that must be loved.

Although reading is useful for instruction, when accompanied by discussion it provides greater understanding.

For discussion is better than reading.

What is obscure or doubtful is quickly made clear through discussion.

As discussion ordinarily instructs, so contention destroys.

[Col. 0718A] Devote yourself to reading when you are free from work, for reading teaches you what to avoid.

Reading will show you what to attend to.

You make much progress when you read, provided that you do what you read.

See to it that you do not despise in your life what you perceive.

**BASIL.**

Just as the flesh is nourished and fed by bodily foods, so the inner person is nourished and fed by divine readings.

## In an uncertain year of the eighth century. EVANTIUS, ABBOT

[Col. 0717]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON EVANTIUS THE ABBOT  
*(Hist. littér. de la France, vol. III.)*

[Col. 0717B] The writing that gives occasion for this article has already been discussed. It is a dogmatic letter under the name of Evance, an abbot, against certain people who maintained that one ought not to eat the blood of animals because it is impure, although they regarded their flesh otherwise and ate it without scruple. This error was particularly widespread in Spain, around Saragossa, as the letter relates. It has been seen that almost all our critics attribute it to Evance, bishop of Vienne, who died in 586. But this cannot be maintained, as has been incidentally observed. For it cites the *Pastoral* of St. Gregory, pope, whom it calls a saint and thereby implies that he was no longer in this world [Note: [Col. 0717C] Mab. *Act. B.*, vol. II, p. 540, n. 4.], circumstances that cannot fit the period of Evantius of Vienne.

Cardinal Aguirre, who rightly rejects this opinion, advances another, tending to attribute this letter to Evance, archdeacon of Toledo, a man of letters who flourished around the year 630 [Note: [Col. 0717D] *Conc. Hisp.*, vol. III, pp. 86–87]. It must be admitted that this circumstance, together with the one concerning the people for whom the letter was written, strongly supports the opinion of this learned cardinal. Yet it will always be opposed by the title of the letter itself, which, according to the manuscripts from which it was printed, attributes it not to an archdeacon but to an abbot.

This led Dom Mabillon to believe that [Col. 0718B] the author of this letter was none other than Evantius, abbot of Troclar in the diocese of Albi, celebrated in the *Life of Saint Sigolena*, abbess of the same place, where there was a double monastery, one for monks and the other for virgins [Note: [Col. 0717D] Mab. *ibid.*, p. 540, n. 4; p. 545, n. 16; *An.*, bk. [Col. 0718C] XVIII, n. 42.]. Everything combines to strengthen this opinion, already authorized by the title of the letter. Evantius, abbot of Troclar, lived at the end of the seventh century, the period to which it belongs; he was in a position to have connections in the direction of Saragossa, since the Albigensian region, where he resided, lay near the provinces of Gaul subject to the Visigoths of Spain until Charles Martel; finally, it appears that letters were cultivated in his monastery, since a monk of the house wrote the *Life of Saint Sigolena* shortly afterward.

[Col. 0718C] The writing in question was first published from a manuscript of Saint Gall, in the fifth volume of Canisius’s collection. From there it passed into the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and finally into the collection of the Councils of Spain by Cardinal Aguirre [Note: [Col. 0718D] Canis., vol. V, pp. 555, 557; *Bib. PP.*, vol. XI, pp. 1092–1093; *Conc. Hisp.*, ibid., pp. 87–88.]. The author shows himself to be thoroughly instructed in Holy Scripture and highly versed in the reading of the Fathers of the Church. He proves very well that one may eat the blood of animals without any scruple, just as one eats their flesh, and that to act otherwise would be to introduce a kind of Judaism into the Christian religion.

[Col. 0719]

## ANOTHER NOTICE ON EVANTIUS THE ABBOT

*(Galland, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XII.)*

[Col. 0719A] Basnage and Fabricius properly observe that our Evantius, or Evantus, must be distinguished from Evantius of Vienne, who died in 586. For he wrote a letter against those who in Saragossa said that the blood of animals was impure. In it, moreover, he praises the book of the *Pastoral Rule* of St. Gregory. Therefore he must be entirely distinguished from Evantius of Vienne, who had died before that book was published. [Col. 0720A] Cavaeus therefore erred in this matter (under the year 581). Cardinal Aguirre (*Conc. Hisp.*, vol. III) attempts to demonstrate that this Evantius was the archdeacon of Toledo. That he was certainly a Spaniard is clear from the letter itself. You will find no further information about him among writers. Nevertheless, it would not be unreasonable to affirm that he had Pirminius the abbot particularly before his eyes, as will be clear from what will be said about him below.

[Col. 0719]

## LETTER OF EVANTIUS THE ABBOT  
**Against those who judge the blood of animals to be impure and say that their flesh is pure.** (C)*

[Col. 0719B] Since a suitable opportunity has presented itself, my wretchedness has taken care to bring this little page of my insignificance before your eyes, by which I both more earnestly set forth the duties of salvation and entrust myself to be protected by your holy prayers. These matters [Note: [Col. 0719D] Perhaps “having been dismissed” or “having been refuted.”] having been put aside, it has come to our knowledge that you assert that in certain parts of Saragossa you have found Christians who, not yet instructed by the sacred pages, follow in Jewish fashion the letter that kills and set aside the life-giving Spirit. They say that a person becomes impure by eating the blood of any animal, not knowing or understanding that the ancient commands indicate human practices more than they preserve natural distinctions. For if these things are so, I do not know why they do not, with open face, hold carnally to the other commands of the ancient law that are forbidden together with the Jews.

Those who do not reject the flesh of swine or rabbits; who do not disapprove of the flesh of fish lacking fins; who do not offer the ancient sacrifices; who do not take the wife of a brother who has died without children in order to raise up his offspring; who do not reject from the priesthood those weak in body or afflicted by some bodily blemish [Note: [Col. 0719D] Manuscript: “bearing.”], although they seem worthy in spirit to approach; who do not carry pegs on their belts in order to cover excrement with earth—why do they seize, if they can, a bird found with its young, and do not, as commanded, let the mother go while keeping the young?

Why do they not observe the Sabbath rest with the Jews, and, having wiped away the blush of Christianity, reject the new grace of the Gospel? For in the name of Christ, marked upon the forehead and in Christian faith, we openly teach Christians to eat blood, and we exhort everyone to turn away from the work of bloodshed. We permit the eating of pork, and yet we desire by every means that everyone withdraw from the mire of vices. We allow fish lacking fins to be eaten; and yet we desire that all the faithful fly, as though possessing wings, [Col. 0720B] toward heavenly things.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] Manuscript: “priests who are physically weak.”—Perhaps read “concerning priests who are physically weak.” EDIT.] Let the *Pastoral Rule* of St. Gregory be read concerning priests who are physically weak or who have a bodily blemish, since it would take too long for us to explain many things.

To cover excrement with earth by means of a peg means that, by laboring in good works, we suppress the foulness of bodily pleasures produced by evil deeds, concerning which it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1).

We allow the mother found with her young to go away, while we keep the young, when we retain testimonies excerpted from the Law in order to refute Jews and heretics, but do not serve the Law carnally.

We neglect the Sabbath rest because, for the sake of that future rest which this Sabbath prefigures, we strive to reach it by understanding the law of the Lord spiritually. [Col. 0720C]

But if they should perhaps object that these things are contained in the canons, I do not deny that I know this; but these prescriptions are found in the ancient canons, from the time when the Church was being gathered from circumcision and uncircumcision, when it was still nourished not with solid food but with milk. Let them know that the apostles said something of this kind to the Corinthians, and they will find deeds of this kind in the Acts of the Apostles.

Now, however, the Church of God stands strengthened in faith by solid food, so that it may fight manfully against the assaults of heretics and not, weakened by the softness of infants, succumb.

But lest the epistolary custom, extended into lengthy periods, feed weariness among pleasant readers, let them come to what the Apostle says: “All things are clean to the clean. But to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Tit. I, 15). And in another place the same apostle says: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (I Tim. IV, 4).

And the Savior says in the Gospel: “Nothing entering into a person can defile him; because everything that enters into the mouth goes into the stomach [Col. 0721A] and is discharged into the latrine; these things do not defile a person, but the things that proceed from the heart. For from the heart proceed adulteries, murders, and things of this kind” (Matt. XV, 17–19).

For the reason why the apostles commanded the primitive Church to abstain from fornication, from what was strangled, and from blood (Acts XV, 19) was this: at that time believers were being gathered both from circumcision and from the nations, lest they be divided from one another because of distinctions concerning foods; therefore they were nourished with milk, not solid food.

To them he later wrote, saying: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able; indeed, even now you cannot, for you are still carnal” (I Cor. III, 1–2).

For if, wherever they read that blood is prohibited, they understand this literally and think that nothing spiritual is meant by it, what is the meaning of what the prophet says: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If you do not announce to the wicked that he should guard himself from his iniquity, the wicked person will die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. III, 17–18)?

What is this blood except the works of bloodshed? What is meant in the psalm, where he says, “Deliver me from men of blood” (Ps. LVIII, 3), except from works of iniquity? And what does the other prophet mean when he says, “Blood has touched blood; therefore the earth will mourn, and everyone who dwells in it will grow weak” (Hos. IV, 2–3)?

Since they boast that they observe these three commands from the Book of Acts—that is, abstaining from what is strangled, from blood, and from fornication—let them confess whether they fulfill the first and second together with the third: whether they do not fornicate; whether they do not use the services of bird-catchers; whether they heed the Apostle when he says, “Those who have wives should be as though they had none”; whether they obey his command where he says, “It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine”; whether they agree with what he commands them: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ”; whether they do what the same apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate”; whether they do what he proclaims: “Show yourselves as God’s ministers, in great patience, in chastity, in vigils, in fastings,” and similar things, so that they do not incur sin but may receive with thanksgiving the things God created good. For, as though obeying the apostles, they abstain from two things—from what is strangled and from blood—while concealing and casting aside the third command, which is the more serious sin, and they neglect [Note: [Col. 0721C] Manuscript: “and shrink weakly from carrying out the heavenly commands.”] the heavenly commands and recoil excessively from the ceremonies.

To such people the Savior says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, hypocrites, who tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and omit the weightier matters of the law” (Matt. XXIII, 23).

Why say more? Let them read the books of the Doctors, and especially Saint Augustine’s work *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, in which those things that these people nullify were both done and said, and let them blush, defeated together with those people. Let them also read the book of Saint Jerome *Against Donatianus*, and there they will find their salvation.

For it is ridiculous to devour pure meats, which God created, to the point of nausea, and to reject their blood as impure—as though God had created the flesh pure but had made the blood of the flesh, which is certainly the nourishment and health of the flesh, impure.

I ought to have written other things, but for one to whom small useful matters are not sufficient, not even many things will be of benefit. Far be it from the hearts of the faithful that, understanding these things carnally, they should depart from the bosom of Mother Church and hand themselves over to the fires of Gehenna together with those who believe in this manner.

## In an uncertain year of the eighth century. SAINT ARCULFUS AND SAINT ADAMNANUS

[Col. 0721]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT ARCULFUS

*(Cave, *Hist. litt.*, p. 392.)*

[Col. 0721D] Arculfus, bishop of a certain city in Gaul, flourished in 690. Having undertaken a journey to the East for religious reasons and visited the holy places, he also went to Damascus, Constantinople, Alexandria, and other places. Finally, while returning to Gaul, he was carried by a storm to the western shores of Britain, where he was kindly received as a guest by Adamnanus, abbot of Iona.

Adamnanus committed to writing the history of this pilgrimage and the description of the holy places, which he had received from Arculfus’s mouth, covering the material in three books. These books survive under the title *On the Situation of the Holy Land*. They were published by Serrarius at Ingolstadt in 1619, and afterward by Mabillon, *Benedictine Century* III, part II, p. 502.

[Col. 0723]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT ADAMNANUS

*(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis*.)*

[Col. 0723A] Adamanus, or Adamnanus, a Benedictine abbot on the island of Iona (Hu or Hey), near Scotland, died at nearly eighty years of age in A.D. 704, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. His three books on the life of Saint Columba, with notes by Francis Baertius, are found in the *Acta Sanctorum*, June 9, vol. II, p. 197 ff.; I omit the editions by Canisius, Surius, Mabillon, *Benedictine Century* I, Stephen of Vicenza in the *Triad of the Saints of Ireland*, Thomas Messingham in the *Florilegium of the Saints of Ireland*, Benedictus Gononus in the *Lives of the Fathers of the West* (Lyons, 1625, fol., p. 420), and others.

Usserius published the prologue and epilogue to the *Life of Columba* in his *Collection of Irish Letters*, p. 42, together with an adjuration to the copyists. Labbe published the prologue to the three books *On the Holy Places*, received from the dictation of Bishop Arculfus, a Gaul by nationality, returning from Palestine, in vol. I of his *Bibliotheca nova* [Col. 0723B] of manuscripts, [Col. 0724A] p. 667.

After Jacob Gretserus (Ingolstadt, 1619, quarto), John Mabillon published the books themselves in *Benedictine Century* III, part II, p. 502.

Bede praises him in V, 16 of the *Deeds of the English* and in the passage on Mark XV, 46, and at the end of the little book *On the Holy Places*, vol. III, p. 371, where he does not deny that he read the traces of Arculfus and Adamnanus. It cannot be inferred very firmly from Bede’s *Deeds of the English* V, 16 that he wrote about the legitimate date of Easter and committed the Canons to writing, nor from the passage of Matthew of Westminster under A.D. 701, which Vossius cited on p. 272 of his *Latin Historians*.

Alcuin shortens the third syllable in the name Adamnanus in these verses, which are found on p. 1756 of his works:

> Patrick, Ciaran, the glory of the Scottish people,  
> And Columbanus, Congallus, Adamnanus also,  
> Illustrious Fathers, teachers of conduct and life.  
>
> [Col. 0724B] Here may piety toward these men assist us all in our prayers.

[Col. 0723]

## OBSERVATION OF JACOB BASNAGE ON SAINT ADAMNANUS

[Col. 0723B] Although much is appended here concerning Adamnanus, some matters nevertheless remain to be observed.

First, his genuine name is Adamnanus. Adamnanus himself ought to have known his own name best; yet in this little work he frequently calls himself Adamnanus.

Second, he must be distinguished from another Adamnanus who lived as a monk in the monastery of Coludi. Bede speaks of the former in Book V, chapter 16, and of the latter in Book IV, chapter 19. The latter was the man who never took any food or drink except on Sunday and Thursday, and he was entirely different from the other, who left a written *Life of Columba*. Possevinus and Gesnerus therefore erred, whose fragments are appended here, and even Canisius himself, who wrongly joined two passages of Trithemius.

Third, Adamnanus presided over the monastery of Iona toward the end of the seventh century. For when Columba was dying, in 598, he had designated Battheneus as his successor. Abbot Battheneus died in 622 and left the administration of the monastery to Segienus. Segienus held it until 652, when Failbeus succeeded him; Adamnanus calls Failbeus his predecessor. Adamnanus himself did not return from England to his homeland until 665.

Fourth, Adamnanus was accustomed to celebrate Easter according to the custom of the Scots. At that time there was another very famous controversy concerning the tonsure, as is clear from the council held at Pharæ in 664. The Romans shaved the head in the form of a crown and pretended to have received this practice from Peter; others had a tonsure that, as was reported, came from Simon Magus.

Adamnanus initially stood on the side of the Scots against the Romans. But after being converted by Abbot Ceolfrid, both concerning the tonsure and concerning the celebration of Easter, he wished to change the former position of the monastery of Iona, but in vain; for the monks remained estranged from Roman practices.

Finally, the reader must be reminded that before Adamnanus a *Life of Columba* had already been written by Cumneneus Albus, which Adamnanus had seen and praised in his second book. This *Life* was published by the most learned Mabillon in the first *Benedictine Century*, but it is much shorter than the one we are bringing to light. Adamnanus, published by Canisius, included very many things omitted by Cumneneus; nevertheless, the entire *Life* is filled with miracles, which he had drawn from the sufficiently uncertain tradition of the elders. He frequently mentions the sign of the cross and holy water.

Intending to preach the word of God among the northern provinces of the Picts—that is, the Scots—Columba had crossed over into England. Returning to his homeland in 665, he remained there for thirty-four years, as Adamnanus asserts in his third book; therefore Columba died, as stated earlier, in 598.

He is said to have been buried with Patrick [Col. 0724C] and Brigid; hence the verses reported by Sylvester Giraldus of Wales in the *Topography of Ireland*:

> In one tomb,  
> In the town of Down,  
> Are buried Brigid,  
> Patrick, and pious Columba.

After writing the *Life of Columba*, Adamnanus, abbot of Iona, wrote three books *On the Holy Places*. But the tales found there are owed to Arculfus, bishop of Gaul, to whom our author, a zealous investigator of miracles, gave credence with excessive credulity.

> “I, Arculfus, a holy bishop, a Gaul by nationality, begin to compose a book on the Holy Places. I am a truthful and sufficiently suitable witness of many distant and far-removed places. Having stayed for nine months in the city of Jerusalem and traversed the places through daily visits, I dictated all these things, which are written below, to me, Adamnanus, who carefully investigated these experiences and first recorded them on tablets, with a faithful and undeniable account.”

I shall offer one example, so that judgment may be formed concerning the rest:

Between that basilica of Golgotha and a certain chapel of the Martyrs there is a chamber in which is the Lord’s Chalice. He himself, having blessed it with his own hand at the supper on the day before he suffered, gave it to the apostles as they reclined at table. This silver chalice held the measure of a Gallic sextarius and had two handles attached to it, one on either side. In this chalice there is also the sponge which, filled with vinegar and placed around hyssop, those who crucified the Lord offered to his mouth. From this same chalice the Lord drank while dining with the apostles after his resurrection. Saint Arculfus saw it, and so forth.

From this learned men conclude that silver chalices had been in use from the institution of the Sacrament. Those who used glass vessels, such as Exuperius, were therefore entirely mistaken.

Finally, Adamnanus was sent to King Aldfrid. He was king of the Northumbrians and died in A.D. 705.

[Col. 0725]

## VARIOUS OBSERVATIONS ON THE ROMAN MARTYROLOGY, JUNE 9  
**In Scotland, Saint Columbanus, priest and confessor.**

[Col. 0725A] Baronius notes the following concerning this:

> “Bede and other more recent writers speak of him on this day. Bede speaks of him at greater length in his *History of the Deeds of the English*, Book III, chapters 4 and 25, where he calls him Columbanus, while in the epitome of the years of the Lord he calls him Columba under the year 565. In that year he went from Ireland into Britain and lived there for thirty-two years, as the same author attests; thus he seems to have continued until A.D. 597. Sigebert also speaks of him under the years 596 and 598, where he always calls him Columbanus.

> “Adamandus, his contemporary, wrote his Life; Sigebert speaks of him in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 64. Let no one be troubled that Columba, contrary to the custom of the Church, celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon. Bede excuses him in his *History of the English*, Book III, chapter 4, at the end, and Walfridus in the same author, Book III, chapter 25. Saint Columbanus, abbot of Luxeuil, is a different person; he is treated below under the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.”  

> Thus Baronius.

Trithemius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Adamannus, priest and abbot of the monastery of Iona, which Saint Columbanus once built on an island of Scotland, was a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, cautious in intellect, sweet in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, and, not without a reputation for holiness, the father of many monks. Among other works, he wrote in sufficiently polished language one volume *On the Holy Places* and certain letters. He flourished under Justinian the Younger, the emperor, in the year of the Lord 690.”

Thus Trithemius. In Book III of *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 124, he says the following about the same Saint Adamannus—for this is how he gives the title:

> “Adamannus, monk and priest, superior of the monastery of nuns in England called the city of Coludi, a Scot by nationality, a man of austere conduct and holy life, so that he ate absolutely nothing during the week except on Sunday and Thursday, and often spent entire nights awake in prayer. He shone with great virtues. He flourished in the year of the Lord 670.”

This is Trithemius. In the same Book III, chapter 153, he says:

> “Adamannus, abbot of the monastery that Blessed Columbanus once founded on the island of Iona [Col. 0726A] in Ireland, a learned and holy man and father of many monks, by his most holy preaching brought a very large part of the Scots in Ireland, and also the Britons in Britain, back to the proper time of the Easter celebration. He flourished in the year 700.”

Thus Trithemius.

Antonius Possevinus, in the *Sacred Apparatus*:

> “Adamanus the Scot. Coludius, monk and abbot of the monastery of the island of Iona in Scotland, which Saint Columbanus built, belonging to the congregation of Bangor, flourished in the year 690. He wrote one book *On the Holy Places*; letters *On Easter*; and one book *On the Life of Saint Columba*—perhaps Columbanus—monk and confessor, beginning: ‘With Christ’s assistance, I am about to write the life of our blessed Father.’ It exists at Saint Gislenus. Arnoldus, and before him Trithemius, who had not known all his writings.”

The epitome of Gesner’s *Bibliotheca*:

> “Adamannus Coludius, a Scot, a monk of the Apostolic Order and superior of the monastery of Iona, wrote one book *On the Holy Places*, one book *On the Site of Jerusalem*, and one book *On the Legitimate Easter*. He also published letters. They say that Bede took much from him and inserted it into his own books. He flourished in the year 699.”

Thus Gesner.

Molanus, in the appendix to Usuard’s *Martyrology*:

> “Adamannus, abbot, by his preaching corrected a very large part of the Scots in Ireland, and also some of the Britons, bringing them to the Catholic observance of the Easter season. He likewise wrote a book *On the Holy Places*. Bede, Book V of the *History*, chapters 16 and 22.”

Thus Molanus. Since he includes Columba among the saints, it should be noted that the Rebdorf manuscript expressly calls him holy in the title of the book. Trithemius likewise calls him holy in Book III of *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapters 124 and 153.

Furthermore, concerning the name Adamannus, it should be observed that different people call him by different names. Some, including Baronius, call him Adamandus. Most others call him Adamannus. The Rebdorf manuscript everywhere calls him Adamnanus or [Col. 0726C] Adomnanus.

[Col. 0725]

# THREE BOOKS OF SAINT ADAMNANUS, BENEDICTINE ABBOT, ON THE LIFE OF SAINT COLUMBA (C)

# HERE BEGINS THE FIRST PREFACE AND APOLOGY OF ADOMNAN, ABBOT AND HOLY WRITER

[Col. 0725D] Since, with Christ’s assistance, I intend to write the life of our blessed patron, and wish to comply with the requests of the brethren, I shall first take care to admonish all who will read it to place confidence in what they find established and to weigh the facts more than the words, which, as I judge, may seem uncultivated and humble. Let them remember that the kingdom of God consists not in an abundance of eloquence but in the flowering of faith; and let them not, because of certain Scottish expressions—that is, of a humble language—or because of human names, or because the various languages of the nations are despised [Note: [Col. 0725D] Perhaps, “which are held in low esteem.”], disregard the recounting of useful deeds accomplished not without divine assistance.

[Col. 0727A] We have also thought it necessary to warn the reader that, for the sake of brevity, we have omitted many things concerning the man of blessed memory, including matters worthy of remembrance; and that, in order to avoid wearying readers, only a few things out of many have been set down.

And this, I think, anyone who reads these things will perhaps observe: that the widespread fame of the same blessed man, disseminated among peoples, has scattered the smallest details concerning the greatest matters in comparison with these few things that we now intend briefly to set down. Therefore, after this first little preface, I shall begin, with God’s help, by explaining at the beginning of the second the name of our bishop.

# HERE BEGINS THE SECOND PREFACE

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727B] He was a man of venerable life and blessed memory, father and founder of monasteries; he received a name homonymous with that of the prophet Jonah. For although the word has a different sound in the three different languages, it signifies one and the same thing: what Hebrew calls *Jona* (“dove”), Greek calls [Note: [Col. 0727D] I read *περιστεράν* (“dove”).] *Νηπιότητα* (*nēpiotēta*, “infancy”), *Peristera* (“dove”), and Latin calls *Columba* (“dove”).

We believe that such a great name was given to this man of God not without divine Providence. For, according to the testimony of the Gospels, the Holy Spirit is shown to have descended upon the only-begotten Son of the eternal Father in the form of that little bird called a dove.
