Hence, in the sacred books, the Holy Spirit is very often mystically signified by it. Accordingly, the Savior in the Gospel instructed his disciples to maintain in their hearts the simplicity implanted in doves. He was rightly called “Dove,” and “simple” and “innocent,” because in himself, through dove-like conduct, he provided hospitality to the Holy Spirit. To this name there aptly corresponds what is written in Proverbs: “A good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 22:1).

Therefore, from the days of infancy, this our bishop was not without reason adorned and enriched by God’s gift with this name as his own. Indeed, many cycles of years before the day of his birth, the Holy Spirit revealed him by wondrous prophecy to a certain soldier of Christ as though he were a son of promise.

For a certain British proselyte, a holy man and disciple of Saint Patrick the bishop, named Maveteus, prophesied about our patron, as we have learned from the trustworthy report handed down to us by the elders:

“In the last times of the world,” he said, “a son will be born whose name, Columba, will become known throughout all the provinces of the islands of the Ocean; and he will brightly illuminate the final ages of the world. The little plots of my two monasteries and his will be separated by the distance of a single hedge [Note: [Col. 0727D] In place of *sepiculae*.]; he will be a man greatly beloved by God and of great merit before him.”

In writing the life and character of this our Columba, I shall first, in a brief discourse and as far as I am able, summarize them concisely, and set his holy way of life before the reader’s eyes. I shall also offer, for readers to taste eagerly in advance, a concise account of some of his miracles [Col. 0728C], which will nevertheless be explained more fully below in three separate books. The first of these will contain prophetic revelations; the second, divine wonders performed through him; the third, angelic apparitions and certain manifestations of heavenly splendor shown above the level of human experience to the man of God.

Let no one therefore suppose that I have lied about this so highly praiseworthy man, or that I am going to write things doubtful or uncertain. Rather, let him know that I shall set down what I learned through the reports of trustworthy and faithful men who had received these traditions from their elders; and that I shall write it down without any ambiguity [Note: [Col. 0727D] That is, “I shall describe it.” Thus Aldhelm shortly below, *On Virginity*, chap. 10, says that letters were “traced with their strokes in squares upon the wall’s surface.” BASN.]. We learned this more carefully both from what we were able to find inserted in pages before our time and from what we heard from certain experienced and faithful elders, who recounted it without any doubt.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE, ON PROPHETIC REVELATIONS

[Col. 0727]

[Col. 0727D] **I.** Saint Columba was born of noble parents, having as his father Fedilinitus, son of Ferguso, and as his mother a woman named Aethnea. Her father’s name can be rendered in Latin as “Son of the Ship,” but in the Scottish language as *Magnave*. In the second year after the battle of Cule Drebene, and in the forty-second year of his own age, he sailed from Scotland to Britain, wishing to become a pilgrim for Christ.

From childhood he had devoted himself to Christian discipline and the study of wisdom, preserving, by God’s gift, bodily integrity and purity of soul. Although placed on earth, he showed himself suited to heavenly conduct. He was angelic in appearance, polished in speech, holy in deed, excellent in understanding, and great in counsel. For thirty-four years he served as an island soldier. Not even an interval of one hour could pass in which he was not occupied either with prayer, reading, writing, or some other work. He was also tireless in the labors of fasting and vigils, occupied without interruption day and night [Col. 0729A], so that the burden of each particular task seemed beyond human capacity. Yet amid all this he was beloved by everyone, always displaying a cheerful face; like the saints, he rejoiced in the innermost chambers of his heart with the joy of the Holy Spirit.

**II.** Saint Fintenus, who afterward became highly renowned throughout all the churches of the Scots, preserving from childhood, with God’s help, the integrity of body and soul, and devoting himself to the studies of dialectical wisdom, carried this intention in his heart throughout the years of his youth: to visit our holy Columba, leaving Ireland in order to become a pilgrim [Note: [Col. 0729D] He is called *Columbanus* by others. MABILL.].

Burning with this same desire, he went to an elderly friend of his, the wisest man in his people and a venerable cleric, who was called in Scottish [Col. 0729B] *Columbus* [Note: [Col. 0729D] Another Columba was wholly distinct from our Columba: the first teacher of the Christian faith to the northern Picts beyond the mountains, and the first founder of the monastery which, on the island of Hii, long remained venerable to many peoples of Scots and Picts. This Columba, moreover, is now called *Columcelli* by some, from a compound name formed from *cella* and *Columbarius*. Bede, IV, chap. 10. BASN.], in order to hear from him some counsel of wisdom. When he disclosed to him thoughts of this kind, he received this answer:

“Who, as I judge, could prevent so inspired and devoted a desire of yours, so that you should not sail across to Saint Columba?”

At that very hour two monks of Saint Columba happened to arrive. When questioned about their journey, they said: “Recently we came from Britain, rowing today from Roboreto.”

“Is your holy Father Columba safe?” Columbus asked.

They, weeping bitterly, replied with great sorrow: “Truly, our patron is safe—that is, he has recently departed to Christ.”

When Fintenus and Columbus, and all who were present there, heard this, they fell prostrate on the ground and wept bitterly. Fintenus then asked: “Whom did he leave as his successor?”

“Battheneum,” they replied, “his foster-son.”

While everyone was crying out, “He is worthy and fit,” Columbus said to Fintenus: “What will you do about this, Fintenus?”

He answered: “If the Lord permits, I shall sail to Battheneum, a holy and wise man; and if he receives me, I shall have him as my abbot.”

Then he kissed the Columbus mentioned above, bade him farewell, prepared for the voyage, and, crossing without any delay, reached the island of Jova. At that time his name was not yet known in those places. He was therefore received hospitably as a certain unknown guest. On the following day he sent a messenger to Battheneum, wishing to speak with him face to face. Since Battheneum was approachable and attractive to pilgrims, he ordered that Fintenus be brought to him.

When he was immediately brought in, he prostrated himself on the ground on bended knees, as he had come. The holy elder saw him and ordered him to rise. Sitting down, he was questioned by Battheneum, who was still unaware of his people, province, name, and manner of life, and of the reason for which he had undertaken the labor of the voyage. When questioned in this way, he recounted everything in order and humbly begged to be received.

When the holy elder had heard these things from his guest, and at the same time recognized that this was the man about whom Saint Columba had once prophesied, he said:

“I ought indeed to give thanks to my God for your arrival, my son. But know this also without doubt: you will not be our monk.”

Hearing this, Fintenus was greatly saddened and said: “Perhaps I am unworthy and do not deserve to become your monk.”

The elder continued: “I did not say this because you are unworthy, as you claim. Rather, although I would have preferred to retain you with me, I cannot violate the command of my patron Saint Columba, through whom the Holy Spirit prophesied about you. On another day, when we were alone, he spoke prophetically to me about this among other things:

“‘These words of mine, O Batthenee, you must hear attentively. Immediately after my expected and greatly desired departure from this world to Christ, a brother from Scotland, who is now spending the years of his youth honorably and is sufficiently instructed in the studies of sacred reading, will come to you. His name is Fintenus. He will humbly beg you to receive him and number him among the other monks. But it is not predestined for him in God’s foreknowledge that he should become anyone’s monk. Rather, he has been chosen by God to become an abbot of monks and a leader of souls to the heavenly kingdom. Therefore [Read: *Noli*, “do not.”], do not retain this man whom I have mentioned in these islands of ours with you, lest you appear to oppose God’s will. Instead, explain these words to him and send him back in peace to Scotland, so that he may build a monastery in the region of Laginen, near the borders of the sea; and there, feeding the flock of Christ’s sheep, may lead countless souls to their heavenly homeland.’”

When the holy young man heard this, he poured out tears to Christ and gave thanks, saying: “May it happen to me according to Saint Columba’s prophetic and wondrous foreknowledge.”

Finally, obeying the words of the saints and receiving Battheneum’s blessing, he sailed back to Scotland in peace.

**III.** At another time the blessed man, founding by divine inspiration a monastery in the central part of Ireland, called *Dairmag* in Scottish, stayed there for several months. He conceived the desire to visit the brothers who lived in the monastery of Cloene of Saint Ciaran.

When his arrival was heard of, everyone from the little plots surrounding the monastery, together with those who were found there, gathered from all directions. With great enthusiasm they followed their abbot Alitherus, going beyond the monastery’s enclosure as though to meet an angel of the Lord. With their faces bowed to the ground, they kissed him with every expression of reverence when they saw him, and, making the place resound with hymns and praises, led him honorably to the church. They also constructed a kind of wooden litter around the saint as he walked, and had it carried by four men walking at the same pace, so that the holy elder Columba would not be jostled by the crowd of brothers.

[Col. 0731A] At that same time a boy, very contemptible in appearance and dress, a household servant not yet pleasing to his superiors, approached while concealing himself as far as he could behind the others. He wished secretly to touch, if possible without the blessed man’s knowledge or awareness, the fringe of the cloak with which he was clothed. But this did not escape the saint. What he could not see happening behind him with bodily eyes, he perceived with spiritual ones.

Suddenly he stopped, stretched out his hand behind him, seized the boy by the neck, and, dragging him forward, set him before his face. Everyone standing nearby said: “Release him, release him! Why are you holding this wretched and insolent boy?”

But the saint, with a pure heart, uttered these prophetic words: “Let him be, brothers, let him be for now.”

Then he said to the boy, who was trembling greatly: “My son, open your mouth and extend your tongue.”

At the command, the boy opened his mouth with great trembling and extended his tongue. The saint stretched out his holy hand and carefully blessed it, then spoke prophetically:

“Although this boy now appears contemptible and exceedingly worthless, let no one despise him for that reason. From this hour onward he will not merely cease to displease you; he will greatly please you. He will gradually grow from day to day in good conduct and the virtues of the soul. Wisdom and prudence will also increase more and more in him from this day forward, and he will become greatly advanced in this congregation of ours. His tongue will also be endowed by God with wholesome teaching and eloquence.”

This was Ereneus, afterward famous and highly renowned throughout all the churches of Scotland [Col. 0731C]. He had recounted all these words written above—prophesied about himself—to Abbot Segeneus, while my predecessor Failbeus listened attentively; and he himself had been present with Segeneus. From his report I too learned these same things that I have recounted.

Many other things also were prophesied in those days while the saint was staying as a guest in the monastery of Cloene, revealed by the Holy Spirit: namely, concerning the disagreement that arose many days later among the churches of Scotland because of the difference in the celebration of Easter, and concerning certain more frequent angelic visitations revealed to him—places within the enclosure of that same monastery which at that time were regularly visited by angels.

[Col. 0731D] **IV.** At another time, when the saint was sitting in a house on the island of Jova [Note: [Col. 0731D] There is no single opinion among writers concerning the location in the Irish Sea of this island, which is called Hiona or Ihona. Mabillon, note on Cumneus, p. 362. BASN.], on a day of violent storm and intolerable waves, and was giving orders to the brothers, saying, “Prepare lodging quickly and draw water for washing the guests’ feet,” one of them replied: “Who can cross the strait safely on this very windy—indeed excessively windy [sic]—and extremely dangerous day, even though it is a short crossing?”

When he heard this, the saint said: “The Almighty will grant complete calm amid the storm to a certain holy and chosen man who will reach us before evening.”

And behold, on that same day, after the brothers had waited for some time, the boat arrived in which the holy Chamnechus was traveling, exactly as the saint had prophesied. The saint went with the brothers to meet him, and Chamnechus was received by him with honor and hospitality. The sailors who were with Chamnechus were questioned by the brothers about the conditions of the voyage. They reported everything just as Saint Columba had previously foretold: both the storm and the calm, granted by God in the same sea and at the same hours through a marvelous division. They declared that they had not felt the storm, although they had seen it from a distance.

**V.** On another day, while Saint Columba was staying in his principal church, he suddenly broke into a smile and exclaimed:

“Columbanus, beginning to sail across to us, is now in great danger amid the surging currents of Charybdis. The abbot, sitting in the prow and raising his hands toward heaven, is blessing the troubled and most fearful sea. The Lord terrifies him in this way, not so that the ship in which he is seated may be overwhelmed by the waves and wrecked, but rather so that he may be roused to pray more earnestly and, once the danger has been crossed, may reach us, with God’s favor.”

**VI.** At another time, concerning Cormac, a holy man who sought *Erenum* [perhaps *eremum*, “desert”] in the Ocean with great effort no fewer than three times but did not find it, Saint Columba spoke prophetically:

“Today again Cormac, desiring to find the desert, is beginning to sail from that region which lies beyond the river Moda and is called Cirros. Yet even on this occasion he will not find what he seeks, and for no other fault of his than this: that, without the permission of a certain religious abbot, he improperly took on his voyage as a companion a monk of that abbot who had departed.”

**VII.** At another time, many years later, when the holy man was on the island of Jova, he suddenly said to his attendant: “Strike the bell.”

At the sound of it the brothers, roused, quickly ran to the church, led by the holy bishop himself. There, with their knees bent, he said to them:

“Now let us pray earnestly to the Lord for this people and for King Aidan, for at this hour they are entering battle.”

After a short interval he left the oratory and, looking up to heaven, said: “Now the barbarians are being put to flight.”

Thus, though Aidan’s position was unfortunate, victory was granted to him. The blessed man also foretold the number of those killed from Aidan’s army: three hundred and three men.

**VIII.** At another time, before the battle mentioned above, the saint asked King Aidan about his successor to the kingdom. When Aidan replied that he did not know which of his three sons would reign, the saint then spoke as follows:

“None of these three will reign, for they will fall in battle, slaughtered by their enemies. But if you now have other, younger sons, let them come to me, and whichever of them the Lord chooses as king will suddenly rush into my lap.”

When they had been summoned, Euchodius arrived, in accordance with the saint’s word [Col. 0733A], and reclined in his lap. At once the saint kissed and blessed him, and said to his father:

“This one will survive and will reign as king after you, and his sons will reign after him.”

Everything was fulfilled in due time exactly as stated, and Euchodius succeeded his father in the kingdom.

**IX.** Domnallus, son of Aedus, still a boy, was brought to Saint Columba by his foster-fathers. When the saint looked at him, he asked:

“Whose son is this whom you have brought?”

They answered: “This is Domnallus, who has been brought to you so that he may return enriched by your blessing.”

When the saint had blessed him, he immediately said:

“He will survive all his brothers and will be a very famous king. He will never be delivered into the hands of his enemies, but will die a peaceful death in old age, within his own house, before a crowd of friends and retainers, upon his own bed.”

All these things were truly fulfilled concerning him according to the blessed man’s prophecy.

At the same time and in the same place, the saint went to visit Scandalanus, son of Colman, who was being held in chains by King Aedus. After blessing him, he encouraged him, saying:

“My son, do not grieve, but rather rejoice and take courage. King Aedus, by whom you are held in chains, will go before you from this world; and after some years of exile you will reign as king among your people for thirty years. Again you will be driven from the kingdom and will lament for some days [Perhaps: *you will live in exile*]; afterward, being proclaimed by the people [Perhaps read *reinvitatus*, “called back,” as below], you will reign for three brief periods.”

All these things were completely fulfilled according to the saint’s prophecy. After thirty years he was expelled from the kingdom and lived in exile for some time; afterward he was recalled by the people—not, as he thought, for three years, but for three periods of three months. Immediately after these he died.

**XI.** At another time two commoners came to the saint, who was staying on the island of Jova. One of them, Meldanus, asked the saint about his son, who was present, and questioned what would happen to him. The saint said:

“Is today not the Sabbath? Your son will die on Friday at the end of the week, and on the eighth day—that is, on Saturday—he will be buried.”

The other commoner likewise questioned him about his own son, whom he had there with him, and heard this answer from the saint:

“Your son will see his grandchildren and will be buried as an old man on this island.”

Everything was completely fulfilled in due time concerning both boys, according to the saint’s word.

**XII.** One day, while the venerable man was staying on the island of Jova, a certain brother named Berachus, intending to sail to the island of Ethica, approached the saint in the morning and asked to be blessed. The saint looked at him and said:

“My son, take special care today not to attempt to cross the sea directly toward the land of Ethica; instead, sail around by the smaller islands lying nearby, lest, terrified by some other monstrous marvel, you scarcely manage to escape from there.”

After receiving the saint’s blessing, Berachus departed. He boarded his ship and, treating the saint’s word as though it were of little importance, disregarded it. When he had crossed a considerable stretch of the sea around Ethica, he and the sailors who were there saw a whale of marvelous and immense size. It raised itself like a mountain, opened its broad and exceedingly tooth-filled mouth, and floated upon the surface.

The rowers, greatly terrified, lowered the sail. Turning back, they could scarcely escape the surge raised by the movement of the beast. Recognizing the saint’s prophetic word, they marveled.

On that same day the saint also told Baitheneus, who was going to sail to the island mentioned above, about the whale. He said:

“Last night at midnight a great whale rose from the depths of the sea, and today it will lift itself to the surface of the water between the islands of Jova and Ethica.”

Baitheneus answered: “I and that beast are under God’s power.”

“Go in peace,” said the saint. “Your faith in Christ will protect you from this danger.”

Baitheneus then received the saint’s blessing and sailed from the harbor. After he had crossed a considerable stretch of sea, he and his companions saw the whale. While everyone else was terrified, he alone fearlessly blessed the sea and the whale with both hands raised. At that very moment the great beast plunged beneath the waves and never again appeared to them.

**XIII.** At another time the saint woke the brothers in the middle of the night. When they had gathered in the church, he said:

“Let us now pray earnestly to the Lord, for at this hour an unheard-of crime has been committed, on account of which a fearful judicial vengeance is impending.”

On the following day, when a few people questioned him about this crime, he explained:

“After a few months that wretched little man will arrive on the island of Jova, without Lugaid’s knowledge.”

On another day, after several months had passed, the saint gave orders to Jormitius [Diormitius], saying:

“Rise quickly; Lugaid is approaching.”

He told him to drive the wretched man whom he had with him in the ship onto the island of Malea, so that he would not set foot on the soil of this island. Obeying the saint’s command, Diormitius went to the sea; and when Lugaid arrived, he reported to him all the saint’s words concerning the wretched man.

When the unfortunate man heard this, he swore that he would never again eat food with others unless he first saw Saint Columba and spoke with him. Diormitius returned to the saint and reported the man’s words. When he learned this, the saint went to the harbor. Baitheneus brought forward testimonies from sacred Scripture and urged that the wretched man’s repentance be accepted. The saint then said:

“O Baithenee, this man has committed fratricide in the manner of Cain and has committed adultery with his own mother.”

At last the wretched man, kneeling on the shore, promised that he would complete the prescribed penance according to the saint’s direction. The saint said to him:

“If you perform penance for twelve years among the Britons with weeping and tears, and do not return to Scotland until your death, perhaps God will forgive your sin.”

After saying this, the saint turned to his own people and said:

“This man is a son of perdition. He will not complete the penance he has promised; rather, he will soon return to Scotland and there will shortly perish, killed by enemies.”

Everything happened according to the saint’s prophecy. For the wretched man returned to Ireland in those same days, fell into the hands of his enemies in the region called Lea, and was slaughtered.

**XIV.** At another time Lugbeus, whom we mentioned above, came to the saint one day after the threshing of the grain. He was entirely unable to look upon the saint’s face, which was covered with a remarkable redness. Greatly frightened, he quickly fled. The saint clapped his hands and called him back after a little while.

When he returned, the saint immediately asked him why he had fled so quickly. He answered: “I fled because I was extremely frightened.”

After a short interval, gaining confidence, he dared to ask the saint:

“Was some vision shown to you at this hour that was frightening to you?”

The saint answered:

“So terrible a vengeance has now been carried out in a distant part of the world!”

“What sort of vengeance,” the young man asked, “and in what region was it carried out?”

The saint then said:

“At this hour a sulfurous flame from heaven has poured down upon a city under Roman jurisdiction situated within the borders of Italy, and nearly three thousand men have perished, apart from the number of women and children. Before the present year is completed [Addition: *absolvatur*, “is brought to an end”], Gallic sailors arriving from the provinces of Gaul will tell you these same things.”

After several months these words were proved to have been true. For Lugbeus, traveling with the holy man to the region of Capua [sic], carefully questioned a shipmaster and the sailors who arrived, and heard them recount all these things about the city and its inhabitants, exactly as they had been foretold by the praiseworthy man.

**XV.** On a certain winter day of intense cold, the saint was troubled by great sorrow and wept. His attendant Diormitius asked him the cause of his sadness and received this answer:

“Not without reason, my little son, am I grieved at this hour, seeing my monks, whom Laifranus is now tiring with heavy labor. He is troubling them by making them work on the construction of some large building, and this displeases me greatly.”

Wonderfully, at that very hour, Laifranus, living in the monastery of the field of Roboretum, was somehow compelled, as though kindled inwardly by a fire, to order the monks to stop working and to have some food prepared for their comfort. He ordered them not only to rest on that day but also to take their ease on the other days of severe weather.

Hearing in spirit the consoling words Laifranus had spoken to the brothers, the saint ceased weeping. He rejoiced wonderfully and, while remaining on the island of Jova, recounted everything to the brothers who were present at the time. He blessed the monk Laifranus as their consoler.

**XVI.** At another time, while the saint was sitting on the summit of the mountain that rises at a distance above this monastery, he turned to his attendant Diormitius and said:

“I wonder why a certain ship from Scotland is approaching so slowly. It is bringing a wise man who, having fallen into a certain crime and carrying a tearful repentance, will soon arrive.”

After a short interval, the attendant looked toward the south and saw the ship’s sail approaching the harbor. When he pointed out the arriving ship to the saint, the saint—[the text reads *inquiens*, “saying”; perhaps read *inquit*, “he said”]—said:

“Rise quickly; let us go to meet the proselyte whose true repentance Christ has accepted.”

Fechnaus came down from the ship and met the saint as he reached the harbor. Weeping and lamenting, he knelt at the saint’s feet and bitterly groaned. In the presence of everyone who was there, he confessed his sins.

The saint wept with him and said:

“Rise, my son, and be comforted. Your sins, which you committed, have been forgiven. For, as it is written: ‘A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.’”

Fechnaus rose and was joyfully received by the saint. After several days he was sent in peace to Baitheneus, who at that time was staying in charge at the field of Longus.

**XVII.** At another time the saint sent two monks to another of his monks, named Cailtanus, who at that time was superior of a cell. Through these messengers the saint sent him the following message:

“Go quickly to Cailtanus and tell him to come to me without any delay.”

The messengers obeyed the saint’s word, set out, and reached the cell. They informed Cailtanus of the nature of their errand. Without delaying at all, he followed the saint’s messengers and quickly reached the saint, who was staying on the island of Jova, accompanying them on their journey.

When he saw him, the saint addressed him as follows:

“O Cailtanus, you have done well to hasten obediently to me. Rest for a little while. I sent for you because I love my friend and wish you to complete the course of your life here with me in true obedience. Before the end of this week you will pass to God in peace.”

When Cailtanus heard this, he gave thanks to God, kissed the saint with tears, and, after receiving his blessing, went to his lodging. During the following night he fell ill and, according to the saint’s word, departed to Christ the Lord in that same week.

**XVIII.** On a certain Sunday, a cry was heard from across the frequently mentioned strait. Hearing the cry, the saint said to the brothers who were there:

“Go quickly and bring to us the pilgrims arriving from a distant region.”

They immediately obeyed and brought across the guests. The saint kissed them and then asked the reason for their journey. They answered:

“We have come so that this year too we may live as pilgrims with you.”

The saint gave them this reply:

“You will not, as you say, live as pilgrims with me for the space of one year unless you first promise the monastic vow.”

Those who were present were greatly astonished that this should be said to the guests arriving at that very hour. In response to the saint’s words, the elder of the brothers said:

“Although we have had no such intention at all until this moment, we shall nevertheless follow your counsel, which we believe has been divinely inspired.”

What more is there to say? At that very moment they entered the oratory with the saint, devoutly knelt, and vowed the monastic life.

The saint then turned to the brothers and said:

“These two proselytes, offering themselves to God as a living sacrifice and shortly completing the long years of Christian service, will soon, in this same month, pass to Christ the Lord in peace.”

When both heard this, they gave thanks to God and were led to their lodging. After seven days had passed, the elder brother began to fall ill; when that week had ended, he departed to the Lord. Likewise, after another seven days the other became ill and happily departed to the Lord at the end of the same week. Thus, according to the saint’s truthful prophecy, both ended their present life before the end of that same month.

**XIX.** While the blessed man was staying for several days on the island of Scotia, he struck with his staff a small plot of land belonging to some place near the sea and said to his companions:

“It is wondrous to say, my little sons, but today on this little piece of land a certain pagan old man, who has preserved natural goodness throughout his entire life, will be baptized, die, and be buried.”

And behold, after about an hour, a little boat came to the same harbor. An aged and feeble man named Geone, a captain of a cohort, was carried in its prow. Two young men lifted him from the boat and placed him before the blessed man.

Immediately, believing the word of God received from the saint through an interpreter, he was baptized by him. After the mysteries of baptism had been completed, he died there, just as the saint had prophesied. His companions buried him in the same place beneath a heap of stones. That heap can still be seen on this seacoast, and the river of that region, in which he had received baptism, has been named after him and is still called by that name by the local inhabitants.

**XX.** At another time, while the saint was staying in the region of the Scots mentioned somewhat earlier, he happened by chance on a Sunday to come to a nearby monastery called *Trioit* in Scottish. On that same day he heard a certain priest celebrating the mysteries of the sacred Eucharist. The brothers who lived there had chosen this priest to perform the solemnities of the Mass because they considered him very religious.

Suddenly the saint uttered this fearful statement:

“Clean and unclean are now seen to be mingled together: that is, the mysteries of the holy offering are being administered by an unclean man who is concealing some great crime in his conscience.”

Those who were present heard this and were struck with great trembling and amazement. The man about whom these words had been spoken was compelled to confess his sin before everyone. The soldiers of Christ who stood around the saint in the church, hearing him reveal the secrets of the heart, glorified the divine knowledge in him with great admiration.

At another time, while the Saint was living on the island of Iona, [Col. 0738A] he summoned two of the brethren, named Lugbeus and Silnanus, and ordered them, saying:

“Cross over from here to the island of Malea, and in the Fields near the sea seek Ert, the thief who, coming secretly alone from the island of Coloso last night, is trying by day to hide beneath his hay-covered little boat among the heaps of sand, so that at night he may cross to the small island where the sea-calves under our jurisdiction are born and reproduce. After secretly killing some of them and filling his boat, the very greedy thief intends to return to his dwelling.”

Hearing this, they obeyed and departed. They found the thief concealed in the places designated by the Saint and brought him to the Saint, as he had instructed them. When he saw him, the Saint said:

“Why do you so often steal other people’s property, transgressing the divine commandment? Whenever you are in need, come to us, and you will receive whatever necessities you ask for.”

After saying this, he ordered sheep to be killed and given to the wretched thief as compensation for his theft, so that he would not return home empty-handed. Some time afterward, foreseeing in the spirit that the thief’s death was near, the Saint sent to Baltheneus, who at that time was the superior residing in the field of Lunge, ordering him to send the same thief one fat animal and seven modii as final gifts. When Baltheneus had sent these things as the Saint had instructed, the poor thief was found that same day to have been overtaken by sudden death, and the gifts sent were expended at his funeral.

At another time, while the Saint was sitting with the brethren beside the Lake of God, near the mouth of the river that is called “ox” in Latin, a Scottish poet came to them. After he had withdrawn following some conversation, the brethren said to the Saint:

“Why, as Coronanus was departing from us, did you not ask him to sing tunefully some song in the customary manner of his art?”

The Saint replied:

“Why are you now uttering useless words? How could I have asked that wretched little man for a song of joy, when he has just been slaughtered by enemies and has reached the end of his life?”

No sooner had the Saint spoken these words than, behold, a man shouted from beyond the river:

“That poet who recently returned safely from you has at this very hour been killed by enemies on the road.”

All who were present were then greatly astonished; they looked at one another and stood stunned.

### XXIII

At another time likewise, while the Saint was living on the island of Iona, [Col. 0738D] he suddenly groaned with a very deep and mournful sigh while reading. When Lugbeus, who was present, saw this, he began to ask him the reason for his sudden grief. The Saint, deeply saddened, gave him this answer:

“Two men of royal stock have just perished in Scotland, pierced by one another’s wounds, not far from the monastery called Cellarois in the province of the Magdaeni. When the eighth week from now has passed, someone will shout from across the strait, coming from Ireland, and will recount that these things have happened in this way. But, my little son, tell no one of this as long as I live.”

Accordingly, on the eighth day, someone shouted from across the strait. [The printed narrative says “the eighth day,” although the prophecy immediately above says “after the eighth week.”]

The Saint then called the aforementioned Lugbeus to him and quietly said:

“He who is now shouting across the strait is the aged traveler of whom I told you earlier. Go and bring him to us.”

He was quickly brought in and, among other things, reported this:

“Two noblemen died after wounding one another—namely, Colmancanus and Romanus.”

After the narrator had spoken these words, Lugbeus, the soldier of Christ, began to question the Saint privately:

“Please tell me about these prophetic revelations: are they manifested to you by means of a vision, by hearing, or in some other way unknown to human beings?”

The Saint replied:

“You are now asking about a very subtle matter. I cannot disclose even the smallest part of it to you unless you first kneel and firmly promise me, by the name of the exalted God, that throughout all the days of my life you will never recount this most secret mystery to anyone.”

When he heard this, Lugbeus immediately bent his knees and, with his face prostrate on the ground, fully promised everything according to the Saint’s command. As soon as the promise had been completed, the Saint spoke to him as he rose:

“There are some—though very few—to whom divine grace has granted this: that, with the expanse of the ocean surrounding it and the heavens, they may at one and the same moment behold the entire circuit of the earth, clearly and most distinctly, as though the bosom of the mind had been wonderfully opened beneath a single ray of the sun.”

Although the Saint appears to be speaking here about other chosen persons, no one who reads how the Apostle Paul, the vessel of election, recounts visions revealed to him should doubt that he was speaking indirectly of himself, while avoiding vainglory. For Paul did not write, “I know myself,” but rather, “I know a man caught up to the third heaven.” Although he seemed to be speaking of another person, no one doubts that he was recounting something concerning his own person while preserving humility. Our Columba followed him in this account of spiritual visions, as did the man mentioned above, who, after offering many prayers, could scarcely draw from the Saint the revelation related earlier. He himself testified to this before other holy men after the holy Columba’s departure; from those men we unquestionably learned the things we have related above about the Saint.

### XXIV

At another time, a certain brother came to the Saint at the very hour when he was writing and said to him:

“Please bless this iron that I hold in my hand.”

The Saint extended his holy hand slightly and, making the sign with his pen, blessed it, turning his face toward the book on which he was writing. When the aforementioned brother departed with the blessed iron, the Saint asked:

“What sort of iron did I bless for the brother?”

Diormitius, his devout attendant, replied:

“You blessed a dagger for slaughtering bulls or oxen.”

But the Saint answered:

“I trust in my Lord that the iron I blessed will harm neither human being nor animal.”

The truth of the Saint’s firm declaration was demonstrated at that very hour. For the same brother, having gone outside the monastery enclosure and wishing to slaughter an ox, tried three times with a powerful thrust, yet could not even pierce its hide. When the monks learned of this and tested the matter, they melted the iron of that dagger [Add.: iron] in the heat of the fire and spread it over all the monastery’s iron tools; afterward they were unable to wound any flesh, while the power of the Saint’s blessing remained.

### XXV

At another time, Diormitius, the Saint’s devout attendant, fell gravely ill and remained so until death. The Saint visited him when he was at the point of death and, invoking the name of Christ, stood beside the sick man’s bed and prayed for him, saying:

“Lord, I beg you, be gracious to me, and do not take the soul of my devout attendant from this dwelling of the flesh while I survive.”

After saying this, he remained silent for a little while. Then he uttered this word from his sacred mouth:

“This boy of mine will not die now on this occasion; indeed, he will live for many years after my death.”

His prayer was heard. Immediately after the Saint’s prayer had been heard, Diormitius recovered full health. He also lived for many years after the Saint’s departure to the Lord.

### XXVI

At another time, a proselyte from the province of the Numinenses came to the Saint. He had humbly concealed, as far as he could, the fact that he was a bishop, so that no one would know it; nevertheless, this could not be hidden from the Saint. On another Sunday, when the Saint ordered him to prepare the body of Christ according to custom, he summoned the Saint so that they might break the Lord’s bread together, as though they were two priests.

The Saint accordingly approached the altar. Suddenly, after looking at the man’s face, he addressed him:

“May Christ bless you, brother. Let the bishop alone break this bread in the episcopal manner. Now we know that you are a bishop. Why have you tried until now to conceal yourself, so that the honor due to you would not be rendered by us?”

When he heard the Saint’s words, the humble pilgrim was greatly astonished and venerated Christ in the Saint. Those who were present, exceedingly amazed, glorified God.

### XXVII

At another time likewise, the venerable man sent his elderly uncle Ernanus, a priest, to govern the monastery that he had founded many years earlier on the island of Himba. When Ernanus kissed and blessed the Saint as he was departing, the Saint uttered this prophecy concerning him:

“I do not expect to see this friend of mine, who is now departing, again alive in this world.”

Accordingly, after not many days Ernanus was afflicted by an illness and wished to be carried back to the Saint. When he arrived, the Saint was greatly delighted and began to go out to meet him at the harbor. Ernanus himself, although ill, was nevertheless very eager and tried to meet the Saint on foot from the harbor. But when there was between them a distance of about twenty-four road paces, he was overtaken by sudden death. Before the Saint could see his living face, he breathed his last and fell to the ground, so that the Saint’s word would in no way prove false.

Therefore, at that very place, before the door of Canabe, a cross was planted; and another cross still stands to this day at the place where the Saint stopped when Ernanus likewise breathed his last.

### XXXIII [printed numbering; sequentially this is chapter XXVIII]

At another time, a certain commoner came to the Saint among others. When the Saint saw him coming to him in the evening, he said:

“Where do you live?”

The man replied:

“I live in a region bordering the shores of the lake.”

The Saint said:

“The little province you mention is now being ravaged by barbarian destroyers.”

When he heard this, the wretched commoner began to mourn his wife and children. Seeing him in deep grief, the Saint consoled him, saying:

“Go, little man, go. Your entire family escaped by fleeing to the mountain, but the invaders drove away all your little livestock with them, and the savage raiders likewise carried off all the household furnishings as booty.”

Hearing this, the commoner returned to his homeland and found everything exactly as the Saint had foretold.

### XXIX

At another time likewise, the strongest man among all the men of that generation asked the holy man by what death he was destined to die. The Saint replied:

“You will die neither in war nor at sea. Your traveling companion, the one from whom you do not suspect it, will be the cause of your death.”

Gorens said:

“Perhaps one of my accompanying friends is plotting to slaughter me, or perhaps my wife intends to kill me by magic because of her love for some younger man.”

The Saint replied:

“It will not happen in that way.”

“Why, then,” said Gorens, “do you not tell me now about my killer?”

The Saint answered:

“For this reason: I do not wish to disclose anything more explicitly to you now about that harmful companion of yours, lest frequent remembrance of him grieve you excessively, until the day comes when you will discover the truth of the matter.”

Why delay with words? After several years had passed, the aforementioned Gorens was one day sitting beneath a ship and scraping *christilia* from a *castile* with his own knife. [The two source terms are obscure, so their material is uncertain.] Then, hearing some others nearby fighting among themselves, he quickly rose to separate them. In the haste of the moment he carelessly left the knife in the ground; his knee struck it, and he was gravely wounded. Thus that companion became the cause of his death. Immediately, struck in spirit, he recognized this in accordance with the holy man’s prophecy. After some months, overcome by the same injury, he died.

### XXX

At another time, while the Saint was living on the island of Iona, he summoned one of the brethren and said:

“On the third day from this one now dawning, you must sit waiting on the western shore of this island, beside the sea. For from the northern region of Ireland a certain guest-crane, driven by the winds through long circuits of the air, will arrive after the ninth hour of the day, very weary and exhausted. With its strength almost spent, it will fall and lie on the shore before you. You must compassionately lift it up and carry it to a nearby house. There, received hospitably, you shall carefully feed it and attend to it for three days and nights. When the three days are complete and it has recovered, it will not wish to remain any longer as a stranger among us; it will return to its former sweet region of Scotland, whence it came, with its strength fully restored. I commend it to you so carefully because it comes from the region of our own fatherland.”

The brother obeyed. On the third day, after the ninth hour, he waited as instructed for the foretold guest. When it arrived, he lifted it from the shore where it had fallen, carried the sick creature to the guesthouse, and fed it in its hunger.

When he returned to the monastery in the evening, the Saint did not ask him about it but said:

“May God bless you, my son, because you have served a foreign guest well. It will not remain long in its exile but will return to its homeland after three days.”

Events proved this exactly as the Saint had foretold. After spending three days as a guest, the bird first rose from the ground before its host and attendant, flying upward. After surveying its route for a little while in the air, it crossed the expanse of the ocean and returned to Ireland by a straight course of flight on a calm day.

### XXXI

At another time, when the holy man was returning to the level fields, he and Abbot Congellus were sitting one secret summer day not far from the fortress mentioned above. Water from a nearby spring was then brought to the Saints in a bronze vessel for washing their hands. When Saint Columba had received it, he spoke to Abbot Congellus, sitting beside him:

“O Congellus, that little spring from which this water has been drawn and brought to us will one day be unfit for any human use.”

“For what reason,” said Congellus, “will its spring-water be corrupted?”

Saint Columba then said:

“Because it will be filled with human blood. For my kinsmen and friends, and your relatives according to the flesh, will join battle in this neighboring fortress. In that conflict some little man of my kin will be slaughtered; and the place of that same spring will be filled with his blood, together with that of the others who are killed.”

His truthful prophecy was fulfilled in its time many years afterward. In that battle, as many peoples know, Domnall son of Aed was raised to victory; and in the same battle, in accordance with the holy man’s prophecy, a man of the kindred was killed at the little spring.

Another man, Finanus by name, told me, Adomnán, soldier of Christ, about this same battle. For many years he had lived an irreproachable anchoritic life near the monastery of Campus Roboris. He declared that, while present at the battle, he had seen a headless corpse in the spring mentioned above. On that same day, after the battle had been fought, he returned to the monastery of Saint Congellus, called in the Scottish language Cambas, because he had come from there earlier. There he found two elderly monks of Saint Congellus. When he related to them something about the battle that had taken place before him and about the spring corrupted by human blood, they replied:

“Columbanus is a true prophet, for all these things that you report as having been fulfilled today concerning the battle and the spring he foretold many years ago to us who were listening, while sitting beside the fortress of Coethirni with Saint Congellus.”

[Col. 0743A] ### XXXII

At the same time Bishop Conall prepared lodging for the blessed man, with almost countless gifts, after the assembly of the aforementioned kings had followed him in great numbers as he returned. When the holy man arrived, many gifts from the people were laid out in the monastery courtyard to be blessed. As he blessed them, he noticed the gift of a certain wealthy man and, pointing him out, said:

“Whose is this gift for the mercies shown to the poor? By his generosity the mercy of God accompanies him.”

He also distinguished another gift among the many, saying:

“I can in no way taste this gift of a wise and greedy man unless he has first truly repented of the sin of avarice.”

When he heard this word quickly spread through the crowd, Columbus son of Aed, conscious of his fault, ran up and, kneeling, performed true repentance before the Saint. He promised that henceforth he would renounce avarice and acquire generosity together with a correction of his conduct. Ordered by the Saint to rise, he was from that hour healed of the vice of greed. For he was a wise man, as had been revealed to the Saint through his gift.

The wealthy and generous man, named Brendenus, whose gift was mentioned shortly above, also heard the Saint’s words spoken about him. Kneeling at the Saint’s feet, he begged the Saint to pour out a prayer for him to the Lord. The Saint first rebuked him for certain sins of his; he repented and promised that henceforth he would amend his ways. Thus both men were corrected and healed of their respective vices.

Here the first book comes to an end. Now follows the book concerning miracles of powers, which are often accompanied also by prophetic foreknowledge.

## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS: ON MIRACLES OF POWERS

[Col. 0743]

### I

At another time, when the venerable man was still young and was living in Scotland with Saint Findbarr, bishop, learning the wisdom of sacred Scripture, wine happened not to be available on a certain solemn day for the sacrificial mystery. When he heard the ministers of the altar discussing among themselves the lack of it, he took a pitcher and went to the spring, intending, as a deacon, to draw spring water for the ministry of the sacred Eucharist. In those days he was indeed serving in the grade of the diaconate.

The blessed man faithfully blessed the watery element that he had drawn from the spring, invoking the name of Jesus Christ, who at Cana of Galilee changed water into wine. Through the working of this miracle, the inferior substance—that is, the watery nature—was changed by the hands of the praiseworthy man into a more excellent form, namely, that of wine.

The holy man returned from the spring and, entering the church, set down beside the altar the pitcher containing the liquid. He said to the ministers:

“You have wine here, which the Lord Christ has sent for the performance of his mysteries.”

When this became known, the holy bishop and the ministers together gave exceptional thanks to God. The young Saint, however, attributed this not to himself but to Bishop Saint Vinnianus. Thus Christ the Lord revealed through his disciple the first proof of his power, for in the same matter he performed at Cana of Galilee the beginning of his signs through himself.

### II

There was a very fruitful tree near the monastery of Campus Roboris, on its southern side. Since the inhabitants of the place had once complained about the excessive bitterness of its fruit, the Saint approached it one day in the autumn. Seeing that the tree bore an abundance of fruit to no purpose, since those who tasted it were harmed rather than pleased, the Saint raised his hand in blessing and said:

“In the name of almighty God, let all your bitterness, O bitter tree, depart from you, and let your apples, hitherto most bitter, now be turned into the sweetest fruit.”

Wonderful to relate, no sooner had he spoken than, at that same moment, all the apples of the tree, their bitterness removed, were changed into extraordinary sweetness, in accordance with the Saint’s word.

### III

At another time, the Saint sent his monks to bring bundles of rods from the small field of a certain commoner for the construction of a guesthouse. When they returned to the Saint with a cargo vessel filled with the aforementioned material, they said that the commoner was greatly distressed because of the loss it had caused him. The Saint therefore ordered:

“So that we do not scandalize the man, let six modii of barley be brought to him from us, and let him himself sow them in the plowed earth during these days.”

When these were sent to the commoner, whose name was Frindehanus, and assigned to him in the Saint’s presence with this instruction, he received them gratefully and said:

“How will a crop sown after midsummer prosper against the nature of this soil?”

His wife, however, replied:

“Do as the Saint has commanded. The Lord will grant him whatever he asks.”

Those who had been sent added this as well:

“Saint Columba, who sent us to you with this gift, has commended this instruction concerning your crop through us. He says: ‘Let this man trust in the omnipotence of God, even though it was sown twelve days before the month of June has passed; it will be reaped at the beginning of August.’”

The commoner obeyed by plowing and sowing. The crop that he sowed at the stated time, contrary to expectation, ripened to the astonishment of all his neighbors, and he harvested it at the beginning of August, in accordance with the Saint’s word.

### IV

At another time likewise, while the Saint was staying on the island of Iona, he was sitting on a hill called in Latin “Great Fortress.” He saw a dense rain-cloud arise in the north, while the southern sky was clear. When he observed it rising, the Saint said to one of his monks sitting beside him, named Silvanus:

[Col. 0745A] “This cloud will be extremely harmful to human beings and cattle. Passing swiftly over part of Scotland today, it will release in the evening a disease-bearing rain. It will cause severe, purulent sores to grow on human bodies and on the udders of cattle; sick human beings and beasts will suffer from that poisonous affliction until death. But, taking pity on them, we must, with the Lord’s mercy, relieve their sufferings. Therefore, Silvanus, descend from the mountain with me now and prepare a voyage. Tomorrow, if life and God permit, accept from me bread blessed after the name of God has been invoked. Dip it in water, and sprinkle human beings and cattle with that water; they will quickly recover their health.”

Why delay? The next day, after the necessary preparations had quickly been made, Silvanus received the blessed bread from the Saint’s hand and sailed away in peace. As the Saint departed from him at that same hour, he added this consoling word:

“Have confidence, son. You will have favorable and prosperous winds day and night until you reach that region, so that you may quickly bring the health-giving bread to those who are suffering there.”

What more is needed? Silvanus obeyed the Saint’s word. With the Saint’s favorable and swift navigation, and with the Lord’s help, he reached the aforementioned region. He found its people, of whom the Saint had foretold, devastated by the overflowing disease-bearing rain of the aforesaid cloud, which had passed swiftly ahead of him. In particular, six men were found in a house near the sea, at the point of death as death approached. Sprinkled with the water of blessing by Silvanus, they were opportunely healed that very day.

The report of this sudden healing quickly spread throughout the region, which had been ravaged by the more pestilential disease, and summoned all the sick people to Saint Columba’s representative. In accordance with the Saint’s command, he sprinkled human beings and cattle with the blessed water into which the bread had been dipped. They immediately recovered full health. Human beings and beasts alike, saved in this way, praised Christ in Saint Columba with extraordinary thanksgiving.

In the account written above, as I think, two things plainly accompany one another: the grace of prophecy concerning the cloud and the power of a miracle in the healing of the sick. The aforementioned Silvanus, soldier of Christ and representative of Saint Columba, testified that all these things were entirely true before Segeneus the abbot and the other elders.

### V

At another time, while the Saint was staying on the island of Iona, he summoned a certain brother named Lugaid at the first hour of the day and addressed him:

“Prepare quickly for a swift voyage to Scotland, for I greatly need to send you as a messenger to Chiliocherus. Last night, by some accident, the holy virgin Maugina, returning home from the Oratory after Mass, stumbled, and her hip was broken into two pieces. She repeatedly calls upon my name, hoping to receive consolation from the Lord through me.”

What more is needed? When Lugaid obeyed and then departed, the Saint gave him a little pinewood box with a blessing, saying:

“When you reach Maugina to visit her, dip the blessing contained in this little box into a vessel of water, and pour that water of blessing over her hip. Immediately, at the invocation of God’s name, the bone of her hip will be joined and knit together, and the holy virgin will recover fully.”

The Saint added:

“Behold, I shall place on the lid of this box the number of twenty-three years, which is the number of years the holy virgin will live in this present life after receiving that healing.”

All these things were fulfilled exactly as the Saint foretold. As soon as Lugaid reached the holy virgin, her hip was sprinkled with the blessed water as the Saint had instructed, and she was completely healed without any delay, the bone being knit together. At the arrival of Saint Columba she rejoiced with immense thanksgiving, and, remaining in good works for twenty-three years after her healing, lived according to the Saint’s prophecy.

### VI

The man of praiseworthy life, as has been handed down to us by those who experienced it, healed various illnesses of the sick by invoking the name of Christ during the days when, traveling to an assembly of kings, he spent a short time at *Dorsum Cetae*. Many sick people, believing that they would recover full health, were healed either by the laying on of his holy hands, by water blessed by him and sprinkled upon them, by touching the fringe of his garment, or by receiving a blessing of some object—salt or bread, for example—and dipping it into water.

### VII

At another time, someone received from the Saint a blessed stone of salt [Col. 0746C] for the benefit of his sister, who was also his nurse, and who suffered from a very severe illness of the eyes, that is, ophthalmia or pain of the eyes. Receiving this eulogia from her brother’s hand, that sister and nurse hung it on the wall above her bed.

It happened some days later that the same village, including the woman’s little house, was entirely consumed by flames. Wonderful to relate, a fragment of that wall remained standing unharmed after the whole house had burned, so that the blessed object hanging upon it would not perish. Nor did the fire dare to touch the two stakes from which the stone of salt was hanging.

### VIII

I think another miracle should not be left unmentioned, which once occurred through the contrary element. Many cycles of years after the blessed man’s departure to the Lord, a young man fell from a horse into a river, sank, and died. He remained beneath the water for twenty days. When he fell, he had beneath his armpit a leather bag containing books; after the aforementioned number of days the sack was found between his arm and side, still containing the books.

When the corpse had been carried to dry land and the sack opened, a leaf written by Saint Columba with his holy little fingers was found among the other leaves of the books. The other leaves were not merely damaged but putrefied; this one, however, was in no way corrupted, as though it had been kept in a chest.

### IX

At another time, while the Saint was traveling on his pilgrimage, parents brought him an infant to baptize as he was journeying. Since [Col. 0747A] no water could be found in the neighboring places, the Saint turned aside to a nearby rock and prayed for a little while on bended knees. Rising after the prayer, he blessed a spring in that same rock, and water immediately boiled forth and flowed abundantly. In it he baptized the infant at once. Concerning the baptized child he then uttered this prophecy:

“This little boy will live to an extreme old age. In his youthful years he will serve carnal desires sufficiently; thereafter he will be devoted to Christian service until his end, and in good old age he will depart to the Lord.”

All these things happened to that man according to the holy man’s prophecy. The little spring, still flourishing there under the name of Saint Columba, may be seen today.

### X

At another time, while the blessed man was staying for several days in the province of the Picts, he heard a report spreading among the pagan people concerning a certain spring. Foolish men, their senses blinded by the devil, revered it as divine. Those who drank from that spring, or deliberately washed their hands or feet in it, returned—by a demonic art permitted by God—as lepers, one-eyed people, cripples, or afflicted with various other illnesses. Because of all this, the deceived pagans paid divine honor to the spring.

When he learned of these things, the Saint fearlessly approached the spring on another day. The Magi, whom he often drove away confused and defeated, saw this and rejoiced greatly, thinking that he too would suffer something similar through touching the harmful water.

First, however, the Saint raised his holy hand and invoked the name of Christ; then he washed his hands and feet. Afterward he drank with his companions from the spring, which he himself had blessed. From that day the demons withdrew from the spring. It was not merely prevented from harming anyone; after the Saint’s blessing and his washing in it, many illnesses among the people were also healed through that same spring.

### XI

At another time, the holy man began to be in peril at sea. The entire vessel was violently shaken and driven along by great heaps of waves, while a mighty storm of winds pressed upon it from every side. The sailors, who happened to be trying to bail with the Saint, said:

“What you are doing now helps us little in our peril; you should rather pray for those who are perishing.”

Hearing this, he stopped emptying the salt water and [Col. 0747D] began to pour forth a fervent and earnest prayer to the Lord. Wonderful to relate, at the very hour and moment when the Saint, standing in the prow with his hands extended toward heaven, prayed to the Almighty, the whole storm in the air and the violence of the sea were instantly calmed and ceased. Immediately the most serene tranquility followed.

Those who were in the vessel, struck with amazement, gave thanks with great wonder and glorified the Lord in the holy and praiseworthy man.

### XII

At another time likewise, when a very fierce and dangerous storm was pressing upon them, his companions cried out that the Saint should pray to the Lord for them. He gave them this answer:

[Col. 0748A] “Today it is not mine to pray for you who are placed in this danger; it belongs to Abbot Cahinnichus, the holy man. I shall tell you something wonderful. At this same fifth hour, Cahinnichus, staying in his monastery called in Latin Campus Bovis, heard through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, with the inner ear of his heart, the voice of Saint Columba mentioned above.

“When he happened to begin breaking the eulogia in the oratory after the ninth hour, he quickly left the table, with one shoe remaining on his foot and the other abandoned because of his excessive haste, and hurried toward the church, saying: ‘Now is no time for us to eat, when the ship of Saint Columba is in peril at sea.’”

Repeating the name of Cahinnichus, the Saint urged that he pray for him and his companions, who were in danger.

After speaking these words, he entered the oratory and prayed for a little while on bended knees. When the Lord heard his prayer, the storm immediately ceased and the sea became very calm. Then Saint Columba, seeing in the spirit Cahinnichus’s preparation to go to the church, although he was staying far away, wonderfully uttered this word from his pure heart:

“Now I know, O Cahinnichus, that God has heard your prayer. Your swift journey to the church with only one shoe is now of great benefit to us.”

In this miracle, therefore, as we believe, the prayers of both holy men cooperated.

### XIII

At another time, the holy men mentioned above came to the Saint and unanimously asked him to obtain from the Lord a favorable wind for their departure by different routes on the following day. The Saint answered them:

“Tomorrow morning Baitheneus, sailing from the harbor of the island of Iona, will have a favorable wind until he reaches the harbor of Campus Lunge.”

The Lord granted this exactly according to the Saint’s word. For that same day Baitheneus crossed the entire great sea under full sail and reached the land of Ethica.

At the third hour of that same day, the venerable man summoned the priest Columbanus and said:

“Baitheneus has now prosperously reached the harbor he desired. Prepare to sail today; soon the Lord will turn the wind toward the north.”

When the blessed man had spoken this word, the south wind obediently turned itself into a north wind at that very hour. Thus, on the same day, the two holy men, departing from one another in peace—[Col. 0748D] Baitheneus in the morning setting out for the land of Ethica, and Columbanus after midday beginning to make for Ireland—sailed with full sails and favorable winds.

By the power of the prayers of this illustrious man, through the Lord’s gift, this miracle was accomplished, for, as it is written: “All things are possible to the one who believes.”

After Saint Columbanus had departed that day, Saint Columba uttered this prophetic word concerning him:

“The holy man Columbanus, whom we blessed as he departed, will nowhere in this world see my face.”

This was fulfilled. For in that same year Saint Columba departed to the Lord.

## XIV.

[Note: [Col. 0747] A corrupt passage, like many others that we shall refrain from noting further. EDITOR.]

At another time also, a certain young man named Columbanus [Col. 0749A] suddenly arrived at the door of the little hut and stopped there, while the blessed man was writing. Afterward, returning from milking the cows, he carried on his back a small vessel newly filled with milk and asked the Saint, according to custom, to bless such a burden. The Saint, standing opposite at some distance, traced in the air with his raised hand the saving sign. Immediately the vessel was violently shaken, and the *gergenna*—the stopper of the vessel—was driven back through its two openings and thrown some distance away; the cover fell to the ground, and a greater quantity of milk was poured onto the floor. The young man set the vessel, with the little milk that remained, on its base upon the ground and humbly bent his knees.

“Rise,” said Columba to him. “Today you have acted negligently in your work. For, before pouring in the milk, you did not drive out the demon lurking at the bottom of the empty vessel by impressing upon it the Lord’s sign of the cross [Col. 0749B]. Now, unable to endure the power of that sign, it trembled and, with the whole vessel likewise thrown into disorder, fled away swiftly together with the spilling of the milk. Bring this little vessel closer to me, then, so that I may bless it.”

When this had been done, the Saint blessed the half-empty vessel, and at that very moment it was found miraculously filled; the small amount that had previously remained at the bottom of the vessel, under the blessing of the holy hand, quickly increased until it reached the brim.

## XV.

The following event took place in the house of a certain wealthy commoner, where the Saint was staying as a guest. There he judged, with correct judgment, a dispute between two rustics, whose arrival he had foreseen. One of them was a magician. At the Saint’s command, he extracted milk by diabolical art from a male ox [Col. 0749C] that was nearby.

The Saint did not order this to be done in order to confirm such sorcery—far from it—but so that he might destroy it before the assembled crowd. Thus the blessed man immediately asked that the vessel, apparently full of such milk, be brought to him, and blessed it with these words:

“Now it will be proved that what you thought was milk is not true milk, but blood made milk-colored by the fraud of demons in order to deceive human beings.”

At once that milk-like color changed into its proper nature, namely, into blood. The ox also, which for the space of one hour had been weakened and emaciated by a shameful wasting disease and was near death, was sprinkled with water blessed by the Saint and was miraculously healed with astonishing speed.

## XVI.

At another time, when the blessed man was staying one night as a guest with Columbanus, who was then poor [Col. 0749D], the Saint asked the commoner who was hosting him, early in the morning, about the amount and quality of his possessions.

When questioned, the man replied: “I have only five little cows; if you bless them, they will increase in number.”

Immediately, at the Saint’s command, he brought them. Blessing Columbanus’s five little cows equally, the Saint said: “By God’s gift you shall have one hundred and five cows; and there shall be a flourishing blessing among your sons and grandsons.”

All this was fulfilled most completely, according to the holy man’s prophecy, in his fields, his cattle, and his offspring. In a remarkable manner, the number prescribed by the Saint was fulfilled for the man in the precise number of one hundred and five cows, and it could not in any way be increased. For those that exceeded the prescribed number, carried off by various misfortunes, were nowhere to be found, except insofar as they might have been expended either for the household’s own uses or for works of charity [Col. 0750A].

Thus, in this account, as in the other miracles, miracle and prophecy are plainly shown together. For in the great multiplication of the cows the power of blessing and prayer alike appears, while in the determination of the number prophetic foreknowledge is revealed.

## XVII.

The venerable man greatly loved the aforementioned Columbanus, whom the power of his blessing had made rich from poverty, because Columbanus rendered him many services of piety.

At that time there was a certain evil-doer, a persecutor of good men, born of royal stock. He persecuted the aforementioned Columbanus, the friend of Saint Columba [Col. 0750B], and had devastated his house, carrying off everything found in it—not once, but twice, acting in hostility.

Therefore, perhaps not undeservedly, the following happened to that wicked man. On a third occasion, after the third plundering of the same house, as he was returning to his ship burdened with booty and accompanied by his associates, he encountered the blessed man, whom he had previously despised from afar, now approaching him nearby.

When the Saint reproved him for his evils and urged him to lay down the booty, the man, hard-hearted and obstinately unwilling to listen, despised the Saint. He boarded the ship with the booty and mocked and ridiculed the blessed man.

The Saint followed him as far as the sea. Entering the clear waters, he went in up to his knees and, raising both hands toward heaven, earnestly prayed to Christ, who glorifies his elect when they glorify him [Col. 0750C].

Then, having completed his prayer, the Saint returned to dry land and sat with his companions in a somewhat elevated place. At that moment he spoke these very fearful words to them:

“This miserable little man, who has despised Christ in his servants, will never return to the harbor from which he has just departed before your eyes. Nor will he reach the other lands he is seeking, for sudden death will overtake him together with his evil accomplices. Today, as you will soon see, a cruel storm sent from a cloud arising in the north will overwhelm him and his companions; nor will even one of them return to tell the tale.”

After a brief interval, on a perfectly clear day, behold: a cloud arose from the sea, and, as the Saint had said, a storm burst forth with a great roar of wind. It found the plunderer with his booty between the island of Malea [Col. 0750D] and the island of Colosus, suddenly overwhelmed him amid the disturbance, and drowned him in the middle of the sea. According to the Saint’s word, not one of those aboard the ship escaped. In a remarkable manner, while the sea remained calm everywhere around, that single storm struck down the plunderers and submerged them in hell—miserably indeed, but deservedly.

At another time, the holy man carefully entrusted a certain exile of noble Pictish birth to the custody of a wealthy man, so that he might live for several months in that man’s company as one of his friends. After receiving him from the holy man’s hand with this commendation, the wealthy man acted deceitfully and, by a cruel command, had him slaughtered a few days later.

When this monstrous crime was reported to the Saint by travelers [Col. 0751A], he replied and declared:

“That unhappy little man has lied not to me, but to God. His name shall be erased from the book of life. We speak these words now, in the middle of summer; but in autumn, before he tastes the flesh of a swine fattened on tree-grown fruit, sudden death will overtake him and he will be carried off to the infernal regions.”

## XVIII.

When this prophecy of the holy man was reported to the wretched little man, he despised and ridiculed the Saint. A few days later, during the autumn months, at his command a sow fattened on the kernels of nuts was slaughtered, before any of that man’s other pigs had been killed.

He ordered a portion of it to be quickly removed from the carcass and roasted on a spit, so that, impatient to taste it beforehand, he might disprove the blessed man’s prophecy. When it had been roasted, he asked that a small piece be given to him to taste. He stretched out his hand to take it, but before he could bring it to his mouth, he breathed his last, fell backward, and died.

Those who had seen and heard this were greatly shaken. In wonder, they glorified Christ, honoring him in his holy prophet.

## XIX.

At another time, while the blessed man was staying for several days in the province of the Picts, he had to cross the River Ness. When he approached its bank, he saw some of the inhabitants burying a miserable little man. As his buriers related, a water beast had recently seized him while he was swimming and had bitten him with a savage bite. Though late, some men in a boat had managed to recover the poor corpse by extending hooked poles.

When the man of God heard this, he ordered one of his companions to swim across and bring back to him the little boat that was standing on the opposite bank. On hearing the command of the holy and renowned man, Lugneus did not delay. Removing his clothing except for his tunic, he entered the water.

But the beast, which had been lurking in the depths of the river—not so much satisfied as inflamed by its prey—sensed the disturbance above the water caused by the swimmer. Suddenly emerging, it swam toward the man in the middle of the channel, rushing upon him with a tremendous roar and open mouth.

When the blessed man saw this, and everyone present—both the barbarians and the brothers—was struck with excessive fear, he traced the saving sign of the cross in the empty air with a devout hand. Invoking the name of God, he commanded the fierce beast:

“Do not go farther, and do not touch the man. Turn back at once.”

When the beast heard the Saint’s voice, it fled backward in terror with such speed that it seemed to be dragged back by ropes. It had approached the swimming Lugneus so closely that no more than the length of a short oar remained between the man and the beast.

When the brothers saw that the beast had retreated and that their fellow soldier Lugneus had returned to them untouched and unharmed in the little boat, they glorified God with great wonder in the blessed man. The pagan barbarians who were present at the time, compelled by the greatness of the miracle—which they too had witnessed—also magnified the God of the Christians.

## XX.

At the time when Saint Columba was staying for several days in the province of the Picts, a certain commoner, together with his entire household, heard the word of life through an interpreter as the holy man preached. He believed, and believing, was baptized—husband with wife, children, and servants [Col. 0752A].

After a short interval of several days, one of the sons of the head of the household was struck by a serious illness and brought to the boundary between death and life. When the magicians saw him dying, they began to mock his parents with great reproach, magnifying their own gods as though they were stronger and disparaging the God of the Christians as weaker.

When all this was reported to the blessed man, he was stirred by zeal for God and went with his companions to the commoner’s house, where the parents were performing the mournful funeral rites for their recently deceased child. Seeing them greatly saddened, the Saint strengthened them and addressed them with words of consolation, so that they would in no way doubt the divine omnipotence.

Then he asked: “In which little guest-room does the body of the dead boy lie?”

The bereaved father led the Saint, in sorrow, beneath the roof. Immediately the Saint left the entire crowd outside and entered the dwelling alone in grief. There, bending his knees and abundantly watering his face with tears, he prayed to Christ the Lord. After rising from prayer, he turned his eyes toward the dead man and said:

“In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, rise and stand upon your feet.”

At this honorable voice of the Saint, the soul returned to the body. The dead man revived, opening his eyes. The apostolic man took his hand, raised him, established him firmly on his feet, led him out of the house with him, and presented him alive to his parents [Col. 0752C].

Then the people raised a shout; mourning was changed into rejoicing; and the God of the Christians was glorified.
