In this miracle of power, our Columba shares something with the prophets Elijah and Elisha; and in the resurrection of the dead he shares a similar portion of honor with the apostles Peter, Paul, and John. Between both groups—that is, the prophets and the apostles—he possesses an honorable seat in the heavenly homeland: a prophetic and apostolic man, eternally with Christ, who reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages.

## XXI.

At the same time, the venerable man requested from the magician Broichan a Scottish slave woman, wishing to free her out of compassion for human suffering. When Broichan tried to retain her with a very harsh and foolish resolve, the Saint addressed him and declared:

“Know this now, Broichan—know it: if you are unwilling to free this foreign captive woman for me, you shall die before I return from this province.”

Having said this in the presence of King Brude, he left the royal house and came to the River Ness. There he lifted a white stone from the river and said to his companions:

“Mark this white stone, through which the Lord will bring healing to many sick people among this pagan people.”

After saying this, he continued:

“Broichan has now been violently shaken. For an angel sent from heaven, striking him severely, has broken into many fragments the glass he was drinking from in his hand, and has left him gasping with sick breaths, near death. Let us wait here a little while for two messengers of the king, sent quickly to us, so that we may come to the aid of the dying Broichan. Broichan has now been seized with fear and is ready to free the slave woman.”

While the Saint was still speaking these words, behold, as he had foretold, two horsemen sent by the king arrived. They recounted everything that had occurred concerning Broichan in the king’s agitation [perhaps *notione*, “knowledge”], in accordance with the Saint’s prophecy: the breaking of the cup, the condition of Broichan, the magician’s affliction, and the prepared liberation of the slave girl. They added:

“The king and his household have sent us to you, so that you may come to the aid of his foster-father Broichan, who is on the point of death.”

When the Saint heard the messengers’ words, he sent two men from among his companions to the king with the stone he had blessed [Col. 0753B], saying:

“If Broichan first promises that he will free the slave woman, then let this little stone be dipped in water. Let him drink from that water, and he will immediately recover his health. But if he refuses and resists freeing the slave, he will die at once.”

The two men obeyed the Saint’s word and arrived at the royal court. They respectfully recounted the holy man’s words to the king. When these words were reported to the king and to his foster-father Broichan, they were greatly terrified.

At that very hour the slave girl was freed and handed over to the holy man’s messengers. The stone was dipped in water. In a remarkable manner, contrary to the nature of stones, it floated upon the water like an apple or a nut; the Saint’s blessing could not be submerged. When Broichan drank while the stone was floating, he immediately returned from the brink of death and recovered complete bodily health.

That stone was afterward stored in the king’s treasury. Similarly, when dipped in water while floating, it brought healing to many illnesses among the people, through the Lord’s mercy [Col. 0753C].

Remarkably, when the same stone was requested by sick people whose end of life had arrived, it could not be found at all. Thus, on the day of King Brude’s death, it was sought, but it was not found in the place where it had previously been stored.

## XXII.

After the events mentioned above had taken place, Broichan addressed the holy man one day and said:

“Tell me, Columba, when do you wish to sail away?”

The Saint replied: “On the third day, God willing and if life accompanies us, we intend to begin our voyage.”

Broichan answered: “You will not be able to, for I can raise an opposing wind against you and bring over you a shadowy fog [Col. 0753D].”

The Saint replied: “The omnipotence of God rules over all things, and in his name all our movements are directed under his governance.”

Why say more? On that same day, as he had planned, the Saint came to the long lake of the River Ness, accompanied by a large crowd.

The magicians began to rejoice when they saw that a great fog had been brought over the place, together with an adverse wind and storm. Nor is it surprising that such things can sometimes be accomplished by demonic art, when God permits it, so that even winds and seas may be stirred into greater violence.

For at one time legions of demons had met the holy bishop Germanus in the middle of the sea as he sailed from the Gallic coast to Britain for the sake of human salvation. They raised storms by placing dangers in his way and covered the sky and daylight with the darkness of fog [Col. 0754A]. Yet when Saint Germanus prayed, all these things were calmed and ceased more quickly than words could tell, the fog being dispelled.

Thus our Columba, seeing the elements raging against him, invoked Christ the Lord. He boarded the little boat and, while the sailors hesitated, grew more resolute himself and ordered the sail to be raised against the wind.

When this had been done, while the whole crowd watched, the boat moved against the blasts with astonishing speed. After no great interval, the contrary winds returned, to everyone’s amazement, to serve the voyage. Thus throughout that entire day, with gentle and favorable breezes blowing, the blessed man’s boat was carried forward and driven into the desired harbor [Col. 0754B].

Let the reader therefore consider how great and distinguished this venerable man was, in whom almighty God displayed his illustrious name before a pagan people through such prescribed powers of miracles.

## XXIII.

At another time—namely, during the Saint’s first tiring journey to King Brude—it happened by chance that the same king, lifted up by royal pride and acting arrogantly in his royal stronghold, did not open the gates at the blessed man’s first arrival.

When the man of God learned this, he approached the gate with his companions. First he impressed upon it the sign of the Lord’s cross; then he placed his hand against the doors and knocked. Immediately the doors opened of their own accord, the strong bolts being forced back with great speed.

As soon as they had been opened, the Saint entered with his companions. When the king learned this, he was greatly afraid. He left the house with his senate and went respectfully to meet the blessed man. He addressed him very graciously with peaceful words. From that day forward, the ruler honored the holy and venerable man, throughout all the remaining days of his life, with very great honor, as was fitting.

## XXIV.

Likewise, at another time, while the blessed man was staying for some time in Scotland to visit the brothers who lived in a monastery of the divine countryside called Rivuli, he went there at their invitation.

By some chance, however, when he approached the church, the keys to the oratory could not be found. When the Saint heard the others searching among themselves for the keys, which had still not been found, and found the doors locked, he approached the entrance and said:

“The Lord is powerful enough to open his own house for his servants even without keys” [Col. 0754D].

At these words, the bolts were suddenly forced back with a strong movement, and the door opened of its own accord. To everyone’s amazement, the Saint entered the church before them all, and the brothers received him hospitably; everyone honored him reverently.

## XXV.

At another time, a very poor commoner came to the Saint. He lived in a region bordering the shores of the lake called Aporicus. This wretched man had nothing with which to feed his wife and little children. The blessed man took pity on him when he asked for help and, as he was able, gave him an alms. He then said:

“Poor little man, take a short pole from the nearby forest and bring it to me quickly.”

The miserable man obeyed the Saint’s command and brought the wood. The Saint received it and sharpened it into a spit [Col. 0755A]. Sharpening it with his own hand, blessing it, and handing it to the poor man, he said:

“Guard this spit carefully. As I believe, it will be able to harm neither a human being nor any domestic animal, except wild beasts and fish. And as long as you possess such a stake, your house will never lack an abundance of venison.”

When the wretched beggar heard this, he rejoiced greatly. He returned home, drove the spit into the ground in a remote place frequented by wild animals, and, after the intervening night, went early in the morning to visit it again. He found that a stag of remarkable size had been pierced and fallen upon it.

What more need be said? As it was handed down to us, no day passed on which he did not find either a stag, a hind, or some other animal fallen upon the spit in which it had been fixed. When his entire house had been filled with the meat of wild animals, he sold to his neighbors the surplus which his house could not contain [Col. 0755B].

Yet the devil’s envy found this miserable man through his companion, just as it had found Adam. She spoke to her husband in this way—not like a prudent woman, but like a foolish one:

“Take the spit from the ground. For if human beings or even domestic animals perish upon it, you yourself, and I together with our children, will either be killed or carried away captive.”

Her husband replied: “It will not happen so. The holy man blessed the stake for me and told me that it would never harm human beings or even domestic animals.”

After these words, the beggar agreed with his wife. He went and took the spit from the ground, brought it into the house, and, as though fond of it, set it beside the wall. Soon afterward his household dog ran into it and perished [Col. 0755C].

When it had perished, his wife said again: “One of your sons will run into the stake and perish.”

When he heard this, the husband removed the spit from the wall, carried it back to the forest, and fixed it in denser bushes, where, as he thought, no living creature could be harmed by it. But when he returned the next day, he found that a roe deer had fallen upon it and perished.

From there he removed it again and hid it beneath the waters of a river that can be called in Latin *Nigra Dea* (“Black Goddess”), fixing it beside the bank. When he revisited the spot the following day, he found an *esox*—a pike—of remarkable size pierced through and held upon it. Lifting it from the river, he could scarcely carry it home alone.

Taking the spit out of the water with him, he fixed it externally in a high place on the roof. There a crow, falling upon it in the force of its flight, perished, impaled and killed.

[Col. 0755D] After this, the wretched man, corrupted by his wife’s foolish counsel, took the spit down from the roof, seized an axe, cut it into several pieces, and threw it into the fire. Then, as though he had lost no small support in his poverty, he began, as he deserved, to beg again.

That relief from poverty had often depended upon the aforementioned spit, which, used in place of snares and nets, could have sufficed for every kind of hunting and fishing. It had been given through the blessing of the blessed man. Having lost it, the poor commoner, who had been enriched by it for a time, together with his entire little household, lamented it belatedly throughout all the remaining days of his life.

## XXVI.

At another time, a legate of the blessed man named Lugaidus, preparing at the Saint’s command to sail to Scotland, found among the ship’s equipment a milk-skin for which he had searched. He put it beneath the sea, heaping no small stones upon it so that it might soak, and then came to the Saint and reported what he had done with the milk-skin.

The Saint smiled and said:

“The milk-skin that, as you say, you placed beneath the waves will not, as I judge, accompany you to Ireland on this occasion. Why,” he said, “should I not be able to have it as a companion with me in the ship?”

The Saint added: “Tomorrow you will know, as the event itself will prove.”

Thus, early the next day, Lugaidus went to retrieve the milk-skin from the sea. But during the night a salt wave had carried it away. When he could not find it, he returned sadly to the Saint and, bending his knees to the ground, confessed his negligence.

The Saint consoled him, saying:

“Do not grieve, brother, over fragile things. The milk-skin that the salt wave carried away [Col. 0756B] will, after your departure, be restored to its own place [the transmitted *venalia* is uncertain].”

On the same day, after Lugaidus’s departure from the island of Iona, when the ninth hour had passed, the Saint said to those standing around him:

“Now let one of you go to the shore: the milk-skin about which Lugaidus was asking, and which the salt wave carried away, has now been restored to the place from which it was taken [the transmitted *venilia* is uncertain].”

When they heard the Saint’s words, a certain lively young man ran to the seashore. He found the milk-skin and, as the Saint had foretold, quickly returned at a run. Rejoicing greatly, he presented it to the Saint in the presence of everyone who was there, to the amazement of all.

In these two accounts described above, as has often been said, miracles of prophecy and power are seen together even in small matters—namely, a stake and a milk-skin. Let us now turn to other things.

## XXVII.

One day, while the Saint was staying on the island of Iona, he suddenly rose from his reading and, smiling, said:

“Now I must hasten to prayer, so that I may beseech God for a certain poor woman who is now in Ireland, calling upon and invoking the name of Columba while she is tormented by the great pains of an exceedingly difficult labor. She therefore hopes that through me the Lord will grant her release from her distress, since she is also my kinswoman, having a father descended from my mother’s family.”

Saying this, the Saint, moved by compassion for the woman, ran to the church. Bending his knees, he prayed to Christ, born of a human being, on her behalf.

After his prayer, he left the oratory and addressed the brothers who came to meet him:

“Now the merciful Lord Jesus, born of a woman, has timely come to the aid of the miserable woman and freed her from her distress; she has safely given birth to a child, and on this occasion she will not die.”

At that same hour, as the Saint had prophesied, the poor woman, invoking his name, was delivered and recovered her health. This was afterward reported by some people crossing over from Scotland and from the same region in which the woman lived.

## XXVIII.

At another time, while the holy man was staying on the island of Rechrea, a commoner came to him and complained about his wife. He said that, because she hated him, she would in no way admit him to marital intercourse.

When the Saint heard this, he summoned the woman and began, as far as he could, to reprove her for this conduct, saying:

“Why, woman, do you try to reject your own flesh from yourself? The Lord says: ‘The two shall be one flesh.’ Therefore your husband’s flesh is your flesh.”

She replied:

“I am prepared to fulfill whatever you command me, however difficult it may be, except for one thing: do not compel me in any way to sleep in one bed with Lugneus. I do not refuse to undertake all the work of the household, or, if you order it, even to cross the seas and remain in some monastery of women.”

Then the Saint said:

“What you say cannot rightly be done. For as long as your husband lives, you are bound by the law concerning a husband. What God has lawfully joined, it is impious to separate.”

After saying this, he continued:

“On this day, all three of us—that is, I, the husband, and the wife—shall fast and pray to the Lord.”

She then said: “I know that it will not be impossible for you to obtain from God the granting of things that appear difficult or even impossible.”

What more need be said? On that same day the wife consented to fast with the Saint, and the husband did likewise. During the following night, the Saint prayed for them without sleep.

The next day, in the presence of her husband, the Saint addressed the wife:

“O woman, if, as you said yesterday, you are prepared today to depart for a little monastery of women—”

She replied:

“Now I know that your prayer to God on my behalf has been heard. For the man whom I hated yesterday, I love today. My heart has been changed during the past night, though I do not know how, from hatred into love.”

Why delay? From that day until the day of her death, the soul of that wife remained inseparably joined to her husband in love, so that she no longer refused in any way the marital intercourse that she had previously declined to render.

## XXIX.

At another time, Cormacus, a soldier of Christ, of whom we briefly recalled certain matters in the first book of this little work, attempted on a second occasion to seek a desert in the ocean. After sailing with full sails from the lands across the boundless ocean, Saint Columba, who was at that time staying beyond the ridge of Britain, in the presence of King Brude commended them to the ruler of the Orkneys, saying:

“Some of our people have recently departed, wishing to discover a desert in the impassable sea. If, after long wanderings, they should perhaps come to the islands of the Orkneys, commend them carefully to this ruler, whose hostages are in your hands, so that no harm may be done to them within his territories” [Col. 0757D].

The Saint spoke this because he had foreknowledge in the spirit that the same Cormacus would come to the Orkneys after several months. This afterward happened, and, because of the holy man’s aforementioned commendation, Cormacus was rescued from imminent death in the Orkneys.

After a short interval of several months, while the Saint was staying on the island of Iona, someone suddenly mentioned Cormacus in his presence. Those speaking said:

“It is not yet known whether Cormacus’s voyage has turned out favorably.”

When he heard this, the Saint replied:

“You shall see Cormacus, of whom we are now speaking, arriving very soon today” [Col. 0758A].

After an interval of approximately one hour, astonishingly, behold: Cormacus unexpectedly arrived and entered the oratory amid everyone’s amazement and thanksgiving.

Since we have briefly introduced the blessed man’s prophecy concerning this second voyage of Cormacus, we must now also set down some words concerning his third prophetic knowledge.

## XXX.

While the same Cormacus was enduring hardship for the third time in the Ocean Sea, he began to be endangered even unto death. His ship had run from the lands for fourteen days and as many nights of summer, with full sails, a south wind blowing, on a course directed toward the northern quarter of the sky. Such a voyage seemed to exceed the limits of human travel and to be without return [Col. 0758B].

It happened, therefore, that after the tenth hour of that fourteenth day, terrors arose on every side, almost impossible to withstand and exceedingly fearful. For at that time certain unseen, exceedingly grim, and hostile little beasts had come forth, covering the sea. With horrifying force they struck the keel, the sides, the stern, and the prow so violently that they seemed capable of penetrating the ship’s leather covering.

As those who were there afterward related, they were nearly the size of frogs, extremely troublesome because of their spikes, yet not flying creatures but swimming ones. They also attacked the oar blades. When Cormacus and his sailor companions saw these among the other monsters—which it is not appropriate to relate at this time—they were greatly disturbed and terrified. Weeping, they prayed to God, who is compassionate and a timely helper in distress [Col. 0758C].

At that same hour, although our holy Columba was far away in body, he was nevertheless present in spirit with Cormacus on the ship. At that moment, therefore, he summoned the brothers to the oratory by the ringing of the signal and said:

“Brothers, pray with complete attention for Cormacus, who has now exceeded the limit of human voyaging by sailing beyond measure and is suffering terrifying disturbances from certain monstrous, previously unseen, and almost indescribable creatures.

“Therefore, since our fellow members, our brothers, are placed in intolerable danger, we must sympathize with them in mind and beseech the Lord together with them. For behold, Cormacus and his sailors are now abundantly wetting their faces with tears as they pray earnestly to Christ. Let us help him by praying, so that, in his mercy, the Lord may turn the south wind—which has blown until today for fourteen days—into a northern wind. That northern wind will draw Cormacus’s ship back from its dangers” [Col. 0758D].

Having said this, he bent his knees and, with a mournful voice, prayed before the altar to the omnipotence of the Lord, ruler of the winds and governor of all things.

After the prayer, he rose quickly, restrained his tears, and joyfully gave thanks to God, saying:

“Now, brothers, let us rejoice with our dear companions for whom we are praying, because the Lord has now turned the south wind into a northern breeze, drawing our fellow members back from their dangers. He will bring them back here to us.”

Immediately, as he spoke, the south wind ceased and the north wind began to blow [Col. 0759A].

After many days, Cormacus’s ship was brought back to land. Cormacus reached Saint Columba and, by God’s gift, presented himself face to face with him, to everyone’s great amazement and no small rejoicing.

Let the reader therefore consider how great and distinguished this blessed man was, who, possessing such prophetic knowledge, was able, by invoking the name of Christ, to command the winds and the ocean.

## XXXI.

At another time, while the Saint was staying for several days in Scotland, compelled by certain ecclesiastical duties, he mounted a chariot that had previously been blessed by him. At first, however, through some negligence—I do not know whose—the necessary pins had not been inserted through the holes at the ends of the axle [Col. 0759B].

That same day there was a holy man named Columbanus, son of Echudi, founder of the monastery called in the language of Scotland Snamluthir [Col. 0760A]. He served as driver of that same chariot together with Saint Columba.

The chariot was driven in this manner over long stretches of road without any separation or loosening of the wheels or their hubs. No retention or fastening by the pins, as mentioned above, held it in place; rather, through the daily grace granted by the venerable man, the chariot on which he sat proceeded safely along a straight track without any obstruction.

Up to this point, it is enough to have written about the miracles of power that almighty God worked through the renowned man while he was living in the present world. This second book concerning miracles of power must here be brought to an end. The reader should note that, even of the events established in this book, many have been omitted because of the tedium they might cause readers.

# HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK, ON ANGELIC APPARITIONS AND ON THE DEPARTURE OF SAINT COLUMBA

[Col. 0759]

[Col. 0759B] I. In the first of these three little books, as mentioned above, certain matters concerning prophetic revelations were briefly and concisely described, with the Lord’s help. In the second, the preceding book, the miracles of power manifested through the blessed man were described—miracles that, as has often been said, are very frequently accompanied by the grace of prophecy.

In this third book, however, the subject is angelic apparitions: those revealed either by angels concerning the blessed man or by the blessed man concerning others [Col. 0759C]. It also concerns those matters that were manifested by both parties, though in unequal ways—that is, to him directly and more fully, but to others indirectly and only in part, externally and through investigation.

Nevertheless, these things took place in the same settings of angelic or heavenly vision; and the locations of such visions, described below, will clearly be marked in their proper places.

But now let us begin to describe these angelic apparitions from the beginnings of the blessed man’s birth.

One night, between his conception and his birth, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to the mother of the venerable man. The angel brought before her, as it were, a cloak of extraordinary beauty, in which the various colors of all kinds of flowers appeared to be depicted. After a short interval, he took it back from her hands, lifted it up, spread it out in the air, and let it go.

Distressed that it had been taken away, she addressed the man of venerable appearance: “Why,” she said, “are you taking this joy-giving cloak away from me so quickly?” He replied: “Because this mantle is of such magnificent honor that you will not be able to keep it with you for long.” After he had spoken, the woman saw the aforementioned cloak gradually flying away from her, growing ever larger and exceeding the breadth of the fields, surpassing the mountains and forests by the greater extent of its size. Then she heard a voice saying:

“Woman, do not be saddened. For you will bear to the man to whom you are joined in marriage such a flourishing son that he will be counted among the prophets of God, and he has been predestined by God to be a leader of innumerable souls toward the heavenly homeland.”

When she heard this voice, the woman awoke.

## II

On another night, the foster-father of the same blessed boy—a notable man of holy life and a priest—was returning from the church to his little dwelling after Mass. He found the entire house illumined with brilliant light. For he saw a globe of fire standing above the face of the sleeping child. At this sight he immediately trembled; and, prostrating his face upon the ground, he understood with great amazement that the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured down from heaven upon his foster-son.

## III

After a long interval of time, when Columba had been excommunicated by a certain synod for some venial and excusable reasons—though wrongly, as became clear afterward—he came to the same assembly that had been gathered against him.

When Brendenus, the founder of that monastery, which in the Scottish language is called Birra, saw the saint approaching from a distance, he quickly rose, bowed his head in reverence, and kissed him. Some of the elders of that assembly then rebuked him privately, apart from the others, saying: “Why do you not hesitate to rise before an excommunicated man and kiss him?”

He answered them as follows: “If you saw what the Lord has not disdained to reveal to me today concerning this chosen one of his whom you dishonor, you would never have excommunicated him. The Lord not only does not in any way excommunicate him according to your erroneous judgment, but magnifies him more and more.”

They replied: “We wish to know how, as you say, God glorifies the very man whom we excommunicated for good reason.”

“I saw,” said Brendenus, “a fiery-haired, or exceedingly luminous, column going before this man of God whom you despise; I also saw holy angels accompanying him on his journey across the field. Therefore I dare not despise the one whom I see ordained by God as a leader of peoples toward life.”

After he had said this, they not only dared no longer to excommunicate the saint, but also honored him with great reverence.

## IV

At another time, the holy man visited the venerable bishop Finnio, his teacher when he was young. When the holy Finnio saw him approaching, he also saw an angel of the Lord accompanying him on his journey. And, as has been handed down to us by those who witnessed it, he informed certain brothers who were standing nearby, saying:

“Behold, you now see the holy Columba arriving, who has deserved to have a heavenly angel as the companion of his journey.”

In those same days the saint crossed the sea to Britain with twelve fellow disciples.

## V

At another time, while the renowned man was staying on the island of Himba, he saw in an ecstasy of mind an angel of the Lord sent to him. The angel held in his hand a glass-like book of the appointment of kings. When the venerable man had received it from the angel’s hand, he began to read at the angel’s command.

When, in accordance with what had been entrusted to him in the book, he refused to appoint Aidan king because he loved his brother Jogenan more, the angel suddenly stretched out his hand and struck the saint with a whip. The livid mark of the blow remained on his side throughout all the days of his life. The angel added these words:

“Know for certain that I have been sent to you by God with the glass-like book, so that, in accordance with the words that you have read in it, you may appoint Aidan to the kingship. If you refuse to obey this command, I shall strike you again.”

This angel of the Lord appeared to him for three successive nights, each time holding the same book in his hand and entrusting to him the same command concerning the appointment of the king. The saint therefore obeyed the Lord’s word, crossed the sea to the island of Jova, and, when Aidan arrived there in those same days, appointed him king as he had been commanded. During the words of the appointment he prophesied concerning the future of Aidan’s sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons; then he placed his hand upon Aidan’s head, appointed him, and blessed him.

Commeneus Albus, in the book that he wrote concerning the miracles of Saint Columba, said that Saint Columba began to prophesy concerning Aidan, his descendants, and his kingdom, saying:

“Without doubt I believe, O Aidan, that none of your adversaries will be able to resist you until you first act treacherously against me and my descendants. Therefore command your sons to pass this instruction on to their sons, grandsons, and descendants, lest through their evil counsels they lose the scepter of this kingdom from their hands.

“For whenever they do evil against me or against my kinsmen who are in Ireland, the scourge that I endured because of you from the angel will, by the hand of God, be turned against them into great disgrace; the hearts of men will be taken away from them, and their enemies will grow exceedingly strong against them.”

This prophecy was fulfilled in our own times in Belloroth, when Domnall Brecc, Aidan’s grandson, ravaged without cause the province of Domnall, the grandson of Amureg. From that day until now they have remained at the mercy of foreigners, a fact that brings sighs of grief to the heart.

## VI

At another time, while the holy man was staying on the island of Jova, one of his monks, a Briton devoted to good works, was seized by bodily illness and brought to the point of death. When the venerable man visited him at the hour of his departure, he sat for a short while beside his bed and blessed him; then he quickly left the house, unwilling to see him die. At that very moment, after the holy man had departed from the house, the monk ended his life.

The renowned man was then walking in the little street of his monastery. With his eyes raised toward heaven, he stood for a long time in great amazement. A certain brother named Aidan, a man of good character and religious, who alone of the brothers was present at that hour, began to plead on bended knees that the saint reveal to him the cause of such great wonder.

The saint said to him: “I have now seen the holy angels in the air waging war against hostile powers. I give thanks to Christ, the champion, because the victorious angels have carried the soul of this pilgrim—who was the first of us to die on this island—to the joys of the heavenly homeland. But, I ask you, reveal this mystery to no one during my lifetime.”

## VII

When the blessed man was still a young deacon, living in the territory of the Laigin while learning divine wisdom, it happened one day that a certain Bono—a savage and cruel persecutor of the harmless—pursued a little girl who was fleeing across an open field.

By chance she saw in the field an elderly kinsman of the aforementioned young deacon, his teacher, reading there. She fled toward him in a straight course with all the speed she could. Disturbed by this sudden event, the old man called Columba, whom he saw reading at a distance, so that both of them might defend the girl against her pursuer as best they could.

The persecutor immediately arrived. Without showing them any respect, he stabbed the girl beneath their garments with a spear, killing her. Leaving her dead at their feet, he turned away and began to depart.

The old man was then deeply saddened. Turning to Columba, he said: “How long, holy young Columba, will God the just Judge permit this crime, committed to our dishonor, to remain unpunished?”

The saint then pronounced this sentence against the criminal, saying:

“At the very hour when the soul of the girl whom he killed ascends to heaven, the soul of the murderer himself will descend to hell.”

No sooner had he spoken these words than, like Ananias before Peter, the slayer of the innocent fell dead before the eyes of the holy young man upon that same little patch of earth. The report of this sudden and terrifying vengeance was immediately spread through many provinces of Scotland, together with the remarkable fame of the holy deacon.

## VIII

At another time, while the blessed man was staying for several days on the island of Sicia, he withdrew alone from the brothers for the sake of prayer and entered a dense forest. There he encountered an immense boar, which hunting dogs happened to be pursuing.

When he saw it, the saint looked at it from a distance and stood still. Then, invoking the name of God and raising his holy hand, he addressed it in earnest prayer:

“Do not wish to come any farther. Die in the place to which you have now come.”

When the saint’s word rang out through the woods, the terrible beast was not only unable to advance farther, but, by the power of his word, was struck dead before his face and quickly collapsed.

## IX

At another time, when five vigorous Scottish fishermen of the renowned man had caught five fish in their net in the fish-filled River Sale, the saint said to them again:

“Cast the net into the river, and immediately you will find a large fish that the Lord has prepared for me.”

Obeying the saint’s word, they drew up in their little net a fish of extraordinary size, a chocem, which God had prepared for him.

## X

One day a young man of good character named Lugneus, who later became an elder in charge of the monastery on the island of Helena, came to the saint and complained of a stream of blood that frequently flowed excessively from his nostrils for many months.

When the saint had summoned him closer, he compressed both of his nostrils with two fingers of his right hand and blessed him. From the hour of that blessing, blood never again dripped from his nose until the final day of his life.

## XI

At another time an Irish pilgrim came to the saint and remained with him for several months on the island of Jova. One day the blessed man said to him:

“Now one of your countrymen, a cleric, is being carried to heaven by angels; I do not yet know his name.”

When the brother heard this, he began to search his memory concerning those from his province and the name of that blessed man. He then added:

“I know of another fellow soldier of Christ who built for himself a little monastery in the same territory in which I lived, named Diormitium.”

The saint said to him: “He is the one of whom you speak, who has now been led into paradise by the angels of God.”

It must also be carefully noted that this same venerable man never allowed the many mysteries of God revealed to him but concealed from others to become known among human beings. As he once explained to a few brothers, there were two reasons for this: namely, to avoid boasting and not to invite, through the fame of his revelations, unbearable crowds of people who wished to question him about various matters.

## XII

On another day, while the holy man was staying on the island of Jova, he sought in the woods a remote place, suitable for prayer and distant from human beings. When he had begun to pray there, he suddenly saw—as he later disclosed to a few brothers—an exceedingly grim and black army of demons battling against him with iron spits.

As had been revealed to the holy man in spirit, they wanted to attack his monastery and to stab many of the brothers themselves with those spits. He alone, armed with the armor of the apostle Paul, fought bravely against such enemies in a fierce struggle. The battle continued on both sides for most of the day. The countless demons could not overcome the one man, nor could the one man drive them from his island, until the angels of God, as the saint later reported to a few people, came to his aid. Terrified by them, the demons withdrew from the place.

On that same day, after returning to the monastery following the expulsion of the demons from his island, the saint spoke these words concerning the hostile troops:

“Those destructive enemies who today, by God’s favor and with the angels coming to our aid, have been driven from this little region into the land of Aethica [reading uncertain] will there invade the monasteries of the brothers as savage aggressors and inflict deadly illnesses. Many people, afflicted by their distress, will die.”

In those same days this happened exactly as the blessed man had foreknown. Two days later, when the Spirit had revealed something further to him, he said:

“Baitheneus, with God’s help, has made good provision, so that in the Church over which, by God’s authority, he presides at Campo Lunge, the community may be protected from the invasion of demons by fasting and prayers. No one there will die from this illness except one.”

This was fulfilled according to his prophecy. For while many people died of the same disease in the other monasteries of that island, no one died in Baitheneus’s community except the one of whom the saint had spoken.

## XIII

A blacksmith lived in the inland region of Scotland. He was deeply devoted to works of almsgiving and full of the other acts of justice. When he was brought to the end of his life in a good old age, the aforementioned Columbus—at the very hour when the man was taken from his body—spoke as follows to the elders who were with Saint Columba on the island of Jova:

“Columbus the blacksmith did not labor in vain. From the labor of his own hands he happily acquired eternal rewards. For behold, his soul is now being carried by holy angels to the joys of the heavenly homeland. Whatever he was able to acquire from the business of his craft, he spent in alms for the needy.”

## XIV

At another time, while the holy man was staying on the island of Jova, he suddenly directed his eyes toward heaven one day and spoke these words:

“Happy is the woman—happy, well conducted—whose soul the angels of God are now carrying into paradise.”

There was a religious brother named Genereus, a Saxon, who practiced the baker’s trade. He heard these words spoken by the saint. On the same day of the month, when the year had ended, Saint Columba said to this Genereus the Saxon:

“I see a wondrous thing. Behold, the soul of the woman of whom I spoke in your presence last year has now met in the air the soul of a certain religious commoner who was her husband. Together with the holy angels it is waging war against the hostile powers on her behalf. With the aid of those angels, and supported by the justice of that humble man, her soul has been rescued from the warfare of demons and brought to the place of eternal refreshment.”

## XV

On another day, while the venerable man was staying on the island of Jova, he summoned early in the morning his often-mentioned steward, named Diormitium, and ordered him, saying:

“Let the sacred Eucharistic ministry be prepared quickly, for today is the feast of the blessed Brendinus.”

“Why,” asked the steward, “do you order such solemn Masses to be prepared today? No messenger has reached us from Scotland announcing the death of that holy man.”

“Go,” said the saint. “You must obey my command. For last night I suddenly saw heaven opened, and choirs of angels descending to meet the soul of Saint Brendinus. At that moment the whole globe of the world was illumined by their radiant and incomparable splendor.”

On another day, when the brothers were putting on their shoes in the morning and preparing to go to various tasks of the monastery, the saint instead ordered them to rest that day, to prepare the services of the sacred offering, and to provide something like an addition to the Sunday meal.

“Although I am unworthy,” he said, “I must celebrate the sacred mysteries of the Eucharist today out of reverence for the soul that last night was carried among the choirs of the holy angels beyond the starry regions of heaven and ascended to paradise.”

After he had spoken, the brothers obeyed. According to the saint’s command, they rested that day; and, having prepared the sacred vessels and services for the church, they went with the saint in white garments, as on a solemn feast day.

While, among the other chants, the customary prayer was being sung in which the name of Saint Martin was commemorated, the saint suddenly addressed the singers when they reached that part of the chant:

“Today you must sing for Saint Columbanus the bishop.”

Then all the brothers who were present understood that Columbanus, bishop of the Laigin, Columba’s beloved friend, had departed to the Lord. After some time, certain travelers from the province of the Laigin announced that the bishop had died on the very night when this had been revealed to the saint.

## XVII

At another time, while the holy man was staying on the island of Jova, he was suddenly moved to action. When the signal had sounded and the brothers had assembled, he said:

“Now let us aid with prayer the monks of the abbot Congellus, who at this very hour have been submerged in the lake of the Calf. For behold, at this moment they are waging war in the air against hostile powers, attempting to rescue from them the soul of one of the guests who was submerged with them.”

Then, after a tearful and earnest prayer, he quickly rose before the altar while the brothers remained prostrate with him in prayer. With a joyful face he said:

“Give thanks to Christ, for now the holy angels have met the holy souls and have freed the guest himself, rescued from the warfare of demons, like victorious warriors released from battle.”

## XVIII

At another time, while the holy man was traveling beyond the ridge of Britain beside the lake of the River Nisa, he was suddenly inspired by the Holy Spirit. He said to the brothers traveling with him:

“Let us hurry to meet the holy angels who have been sent from the highest regions of heaven to carry away the soul of a certain pagan. They are waiting for us to reach that place, so that we may baptize him at the appropriate time, before he dies, since he has preserved the natural goodness of his character throughout his life and into extreme old age.”

As the holy old man spoke, he hastened ahead of his companions as far as he could, until he reached that field. There they found an old man named Enichatus. He heard the word of God preached by the saint, believed, and was baptized.

## XIX

At another time, while the holy man was sitting and writing in his little hut, his face suddenly changed, and he uttered this cry from the purity of his heart:

“Help! Help!”

Two brothers standing at the door, Colgus and Lugneus, asked the reason for this sudden cry. The venerable man gave them this answer:

“I ordered the angel of the Lord, who was now standing among you, to go immediately to the aid of one of the brothers who had fallen from the highest point of the great house being built these days in the field of Roboretum.”

The saint then added these words:

“Exceedingly marvelous and almost indescribable is the swiftness of angelic flight, equal, as I judge, to the speed of lightning. The heavenly being who flew from us here just now, when that man began to fall, came to his aid almost in the blink of an eye, before he touched the ground, and lifted him up. The man who fell was unable to feel any fracture or injury. How astonishing, I say, is this swift and timely aid, which could be accomplished so rapidly across such great intervening distances of sea and land!”

## XX

At another time, while the blessed man was staying on the island of Jova, he assembled the brothers and solemnly announced to them:

“Today I wish to go alone into the western field of our island. Therefore let none of you follow me.”

They obeyed him, and he went out alone as he had wished. But one brother, a clever spy, went by another route and secretly stationed himself on the summit of a small hill overlooking that same field, wishing to discover the reason for the blessed man’s solitary departure.

When this spy saw the saint standing on a hillock in the field, with his hands extended toward heaven and his eyes raised to heaven in prayer, something astonishing occurred. Behold, a wondrous sight suddenly appeared—something which, as I judge, that man saw with his bodily eyes from the place on the earlier hill, not without God’s permission, so that the name and honor of the saint, despite his reluctance, might afterward be spread more widely among the people through the vision that had been revealed.

For the holy angels, citizens of the heavenly homeland, came flying with marvelous suddenness and began to surround the holy man as he prayed, clothed in white garments. After they had conversed for some time with the blessed man, the heavenly company, as though sensing that it had been observed, quickly returned to the heights of heaven.

The blessed man himself, after the angelic conversation, returned to the monastery. He again assembled the brothers and, with no small rebuke, demanded to know which of them had been guilty of transgression.

When they all declared that they knew nothing of it, the brother who was conscious of his inexcusable transgression could no longer bear to conceal his offense. He fell on his knees in the midst of the circle of brothers and humbly asked the saint’s pardon.

The saint led him aside and, while he knelt, charged him under severe threat never during the blessed man’s lifetime to reveal anything, even something small or secret, to any human being concerning that angelic vision.

After the holy man’s departure from the body, the brother announced the appearance of that heavenly company to the other brothers, declaring it with great solemnity. Hence, even today, the place of that angelic conversation proclaims the event that occurred there by its own name. In Latin it may be called “the Hillock of the Angels,” while in Scottish it is called Cnogangei.

From this we must observe—or at least investigate with due care—how frequent and how gracious the angelic visitations must have been to the blessed man, often awake on winter nights and praying in remote places while others were resting. In no way could these visitations have become known among human beings. They were undoubtedly very numerous, since even those that human beings were able to discover in some manner, whether by day or by night, were certainly few in comparison with the angelic visitations that no one could know about.

The same should likewise be noted concerning certain luminous manifestations, a few of which, having been observed, will be described below.

## XXI

At another time, four holy founders of monasteries who had crossed over from Scotland to visit Saint Columba found him on the island of Hymba. Their distinguished names were Concellus, Cahinnechus, Brendenus, and Cormacus.

With one accord they chose that Saint Columba should consecrate the sacred Eucharistic mysteries in their presence in the church. Complying with their request, he entered the church with them on Sunday, according to custom, after the reading of the Gospel.

While the solemn rites of the Mass were being celebrated, Saint Brendenus saw—as he later related to Concellus and Cahinnechus—a certain fiery, flame-like globe, exceedingly luminous, burning for a long time above the head of Saint Columba, who was standing before the altar and consecrating the sacred offering. It rose upward like a column until the sacred mysteries had been completed.

## XXII

At another time, while the holy man was staying on the island of Hymba, the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured abundantly and incomparably upon him. He remained there in a marvelous state for three days, staying for three days and as many nights inside a locked house filled with heavenly radiance. He permitted no one to approach him, and he neither ate nor drank.

From that house rays of immense brightness could be seen at night bursting through the cracks of the doors and the openings of the locks. Certain spiritual and previously unheard songs were also heard being sung by him.

Moreover, as he himself later declared before a few people [perhaps: “very openly”], he saw many hidden mysteries, concealed from the beginning of the world, openly revealed. All the obscure and most difficult matters of the sacred Scriptures were disclosed to the eyes of his purest heart, made as clear as light. He complained that his foster-son Baitheneus was not present.

If Baitheneus had been there during those three days, he could have written down from the blessed man’s mouth many mysteries unknown to other human beings, concerning both past events and future ages, as well as a number of explanations of the sacred books. But Baitheneus was detained on the island of Egea by contrary winds and could not arrive until those three days and nights of the incomparable and glorious visitation had ended.

## XXIII

One winter night, the aforementioned Virgnous, fervent in the love of God, entered the church alone, while the others were resting, out of devotion to prayer. There he prayed devoutly in a certain small chamber attached to the wall of the oratory.

After an interval of about an hour, the venerable Columba entered the same sacred building. At the same time a golden light descended from the highest height of heaven and filled the entire space of the church. It also filled the separate little chamber where Virgnous was trying as best he could to hide himself. The radiance of that heavenly light burst through the inner door of the room, which was open only slightly, and filled him with no small terror.

Just as no one can look directly with unshielded eyes upon the summer sun at midday, so Virgnous, who saw it, was utterly unable to endure that heavenly brightness, because that luminous and incomparable effusion greatly dazzled his eyes.

When he saw this lightning-like and incomparable splendor, the aforementioned brother was so terrified that all strength left him. Saint Columba, however, left the church after a short prayer. On the following day he summoned Virgnous, who was very fearful, and addressed him with these brief words of consolation:

“Well done, my little son. By lowering your eyes toward the ground, you pleased God greatly last night, terrified as you were by fear of that radiance. For if you had not done so, your eyes, which saw it, would have been blinded by that immeasurable light. But you must carefully observe this command: never, during my lifetime, disclose this manifestation of light to anyone.”

This remarkable and astonishing event became known after the blessed man’s death, when Virgnous related it to many people. His sister’s son, Commanus, an honorable priest, had at some time narrated to me, Adomnán, the vision described above under oath. He had heard it from the mouth of Virgnous himself, his abbot and uncle, who had seen it as far as he was able.

## XXIV

On that same night, one of the brothers named Golgus, whom we mentioned at the beginning, happened to come to the church door while the others were sleeping. He stood there for some time and prayed. Then suddenly he saw the whole church filled with heavenly light. This lightning-like light quickly disappeared from his eyes.

He did not know that Saint Columba was praying inside the church at that hour. After the sudden appearance of the light, he returned to the house in great fear.

On the following day the saint summoned him and rebuked him rather severely, saying:

“Hereafter, my son, you must take care not to act like a spy by attempting to look upon the heavenly light that has not been granted to you to see, for it will flee from you. And do not tell anyone during my lifetime what you have seen.”

## XXV

At another time, the blessed man warned one of his pupils, named Berchan, who was studying wisdom under him, saying:

“Take care, my son, not to approach my little dwelling on the coming night, as you are always accustomed to do.”

When he heard this, the young man disobeyed the command. During the silence of the night, while the others were resting, he approached the house of the blessed man. Cunningly investigating the matter, he placed his eyes directly before the openings of the locks, evidently supposing—as the event proved—that some heavenly vision was being revealed inside to the saint.

For at that hour the blessed man’s little dwelling was filled with heavenly splendor and radiance. Unable to bear looking at it, the transgressing young man immediately fled.

On the following day the saint led him aside and rebuked him with great severity, addressing him in these words:

“This night, my son, you sinned before God, for you foolishly supposed that your stealthy inquiry [infitialis, uncertain] could be concealed or hidden from the Holy Spirit. Did I not see you approaching the door of my little dwelling at that hour and then returning from it? And unless I had prayed for you at that very moment, you would either have fallen dead there before the door or your eyes would have been torn from their sockets. But on this occasion the Lord spared you because of me.

“And know this: while living luxuriously in your Irish homeland, you will suffer reproach from everyone throughout all the days of your life. Nevertheless, by prayer I have obtained this from the Lord: because you are my pupil, you will undertake a tearful repentance before your death and will obtain mercy from God.”

All these things happened to him afterward according to the blessed man’s word, just as they had been prophesied concerning him.

## XXVI

At another time, while the blessed man was staying on the island of Jova, his holy face suddenly blossomed with wondrous and joyful cheerfulness. He raised his eyes toward heaven and, filled with incomparable joy, rejoiced greatly. After a brief interval, however, that pleasant and sweet joy was changed into sorrowful sadness.

Two men who were standing at the door of his little hut at that hour—which had been built in a prominent place—became deeply saddened along with him. One of them was named Lugneus; the other was called Pilu, a Saxon. They asked the cause of his sudden joy and of the sadness that followed it.

The saint said to them:

“Go in peace. Do not now ask me to reveal either the cause of that joy or the cause of the sadness.”

When they heard this, they began to weep and, falling on their knees with their faces prostrate upon the ground, they earnestly begged to know something about the matter that had been revealed to the saint at that very hour.

Seeing that they were deeply saddened, he said:

“Because I love you, I do not want you to remain sad. But first you must promise that during my lifetime you will reveal to no one the mystery about which you are asking.”

They immediately promised willingly to keep his holy charge. After this promise, the venerable man spoke to them as follows:

“Up to this present day, thirty years have been completed since I became a pilgrim in Britain. For many days I have devoutly asked my Lord that, at the end of this thirtieth year, he might release me from my present dwelling and immediately call me to the heavenly homeland, if I preferred to depart.

“This was the cause of my joy, about which you, in your sadness, are asking me. For I saw holy angels sent from the lofty throne to meet the soul that was to depart from my flesh.

“But behold, they have now suddenly been delayed. They are standing beyond the strait of our island upon a rock, wishing to approach in order to summon me from the body; yet they are not permitted to come closer. Soon they will return to the heights of heaven, because the Lord has changed, more quickly than words can say, what he had granted me when I prayed with all my strength: that on this day I should depart from the world to him.

“He has heard the prayers of many churches on my behalf. Because those churches have pleaded, the Lord has granted that four years be added to the time I remain in the flesh, even against my will.”

This sorrowful delay was therefore not without cause for my sadness today. When those four future years have ended, if God is favorable, I shall depart suddenly from this life, without any bodily illness preceding it. I shall joyfully depart to the Lord, with the holy angels who will meet me at that time.

According to these words of the venerable man—which, as has been handed down, he spoke with great sighing and grief, as well as abundant tears—he remained in the flesh for four more years.

## XXVII

As the end of the aforementioned four years was already approaching—after whose completion the truthful prophet long beforehand knew that the end of his present life would come—one day in the month of May, as we wrote in the preceding second book, the holy old man, weary with age, went by cart to visit the working brothers.

They were laboring in the western part of the island of Jova. On that day he began to speak to them as follows:

“During the Paschal solemnity recently completed in the month of April, I earnestly desired to depart to Christ the Lord, as he had granted me permission to do, if I had wished to emigrate. But, lest the joy of the festival be turned into sadness for you, I preferred to delay the day of my departure from the world for a little longer.”

When his familiar monks heard these words, they became very sad. He began to cheer them with consoling words as far as he could. When he had finished, while still seated in the vehicle, he turned his face toward the east and blessed the island and its inhabitants.

From that day, as it was recorded in the aforementioned little book, the poison of vipers with forked tongues has never been able to harm either human beings or cattle. After speaking the words of the blessing, the saint was carried back to his monastery.

Then, accordingly, after a few days had passed, while the solemn celebration of Mass was being performed, as usual, on the Lord’s Day, the venerable man suddenly lifted his eyes upward, and his face appeared suffused with a radiant flush; for, as it is written, “a face flourishes when the heart rejoices.” At that very hour he alone saw an angel of the Lord flying above within the walls of the oratory. Since the lovely and tranquil appearance of the holy angels pours joy and exultation into the hearts of the elect, this was the sudden cause of the joy infused into the blessed man. When those who were present there asked about the cause of this inspired rejoicing, the Saint, looking upward, gave them this answer:

“The subtlety of the angelic nature is marvelous and incomparable. Behold, an angel of the Lord, sent to reclaim a deposit dear to God, looked down upon us within the church and blessed us; then, returning through the side passage of the church, he left no trace of such an exit.”

These were the Saint’s words. Yet none of those standing around could discern the nature of that deposit for whose recovery the angel had been sent. Our patron, however, called the holy soul entrusted to him by God a deposit; and, as will be related below, it departed to the Lord on the Lord’s Day during the night, after several intervening days of the old man’s life.

## XXVIII

At the end of that same week, on the Sabbath—that is, Saturday—the venerable man and the pious minister Diormitius went to bless a nearby barn. When the Saint entered it, blessed it, and saw two separate heaps of grain stored there, he added these words with thanksgiving:

“I greatly rejoice with my familiar monks, because this year also, if indeed I must depart from you, you will have a sufficient supply of grain.”

When he heard this, the minister Diormitius began to grow sad and said:

“You have saddened us repeatedly during this year, because you often speak of your departure.”

The Saint replied:

“I have a certain secret little word which, if you firmly promise me not to reveal it to anyone before my death, will enable me to disclose something more clearly to you about my departure.”

When the minister had made this promise on bended knees, in accordance with the Saint’s wishes, the venerable man continued:

“This day is called the Sabbath in the sacred books, which is interpreted as ‘rest’; and truly this is my Sabbath today, because it is the last day of this present laborious life for me. After the hardships of my labors, I keep Sabbath on it. At the coming midnight, on the venerable Lord’s Day, according to the words of Scripture, I shall enter the path of my fathers. For my Lord Jesus Christ already deigns to invite me; at this midnight, I say, I shall depart to him, since he himself is inviting me. Thus has it been revealed to me by the Lord himself.”

Hearing these sorrowful words, the minister began to weep bitterly, while the Saint tried as best he could to console him.

## XXIX

After this the Saint left the barn and, returning to the monastery, sat down halfway along the road. At that spot a cross was later fixed into a millstone and can still be seen standing at the roadside.

While the Saint, as I have said, rested there for a short while, sitting down because he was weary with old age, behold, a white horse came toward him. It was an obedient servant, accustomed to carry milk-vessels into the monastery’s [*bocetum*—the word is uncertain]. When it approached the Saint, it placed its head in his lap. This is marvelous to relate: I believe that God inspired it—for every dumb animal has perception from him according to the sense which the Creator has assigned to it. Knowing that its own master was soon to depart and that it would not see him again, it began to mourn, pouring abundant tears like a human being into the Saint’s lap and weeping loudly, all covered with foam.

When the minister saw this, he began to drive away the weeping mourner. But the Saint forbade him, saying:

“Let him be, if he is a lover of us [Note: [Col. 0771] Perhaps: ‘Let him be, our lover.’ Or: ‘Let him be, if he is our lover.’], so that he may pour into this lap the tears of his most bitter mourning. Behold, although you are a human being and possess a rational soul, you could in no way know of my departure except that I myself recently revealed it to you. But to this dumb and irrational creature the Creator himself has clearly revealed, in whatever way he wished, that its master is departing from it [perhaps: ‘to reveal’].”

With these words he blessed the mournful horse, which turned back from him. Then he departed, climbed the little hill rising above the monastery, and stood for a short while at its summit. Standing there, he raised both hands and blessed his monastery, saying:

“To this place, however narrow and humble, rulers not only of the Scots with their peoples, but also of barbarian and foreign nations with the populations subject to them, will grant great and considerable honor. Saints too, and those of other Churches, will confer upon it no small veneration.”

After these words he descended from the little hill and returned to the monastery. He sat in a hut, writing the Psalter. When he reached the verse of Psalm 33 where it is written, “But those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing,” he said:

“At this point the page must end; what follows Baltheneus shall write.”

The final verse he had written fittingly suited the Saint who was about to depart, for he would never lack eternal good things. The verse that followed fittingly suited his successor, the spiritual father and teacher of his sons: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.” Just as the predecessor commended this successor, he succeeded him not only in teaching but also in writing.

After this verse, mentioned above, had been written to the end of the page, the Saint entered the church for the evening Mass of the Lord’s Day. When it had immediately been completed, he returned to the little guesthouse and sat through the night on his bed. For straw he had a bare rock, and for a pillow a stone, which still stands there beside his grave like a kind of memorial marker.

Sitting there, he entrusted his final instructions to the brothers, with only the minister listening, saying:

“These are the last words I commend to you, my little sons: that you maintain among yourselves mutual and sincere love, together with peace. If you observe this according to the examples of the saints, God, the helper of the good, will assist you. I, remaining with him, shall intercede for you; and not only will the necessities of the present life be supplied to you by him, but the rewards of eternal goods, prepared for those who observe the divine commandments, will also be granted to you.”

Thus far the final words of our venerable patron have been set forth in a brief account, as though he were passing from this wearisome pilgrimage to the heavenly homeland.

## XXXI

After the final hour of the blessed man’s approach had drawn near, the Saint remained silent for a short while. Then, when midnight had come and the bell rang aloud, he rose quickly and went to the church. Running faster than the others, he entered alone and knelt down in prayer beside the altar.

The minister Diormitius followed more slowly. At that moment, from a distance, he saw the entire interior of the church filled with angelic light around the Saint. As he approached the door, the same light quickly withdrew; a few other brothers, who were also standing at a distance, had seen it as well.

Diormitius entered the church and repeatedly cried out in a grieving voice:

“Where are you, Father?”

Before the brothers’ lamps had been brought, he felt his way through the darkness and found the Saint lying before the altar. Lifting him slightly, he sat beside him and placed the Saint’s head in his lap. Meanwhile the company of monks hurried in with lights, and, seeing the Father dying, began to mourn.

As we learned from some who were present, before the Saint’s soul had departed, he looked upward with open eyes and gazed from side to side with a living brightness and joy in his face, evidently seeing the holy angels coming to meet him.

The minister Diormitius then raised the Saint’s right hand to bless the monks. The venerable Father himself also moved his hand as much as he could, so that, since his soul could no longer bless the brothers with his voice as it departed, he might appear to bless them at least by the movement of his hand. Immediately after this blessing had been thus signified, he breathed out his spirit.

When the soul had departed from the body’s tabernacle, the face remained so flushed and wonderfully brightened by the angelic vision that he appeared not dead but like a living man asleep. Meanwhile the whole church resounded with mournful lamentations.

Nor should it be passed over that, at the same hour of the blessed soul’s departure, this was revealed to a holy man in Ebernia. In a certain monastery of the Scots there lived a holy old man, a soldier of Christ, named Lugudius, a just and wise man. At first light he related his vision to another Christian soldier with great groaning, saying:

“Last night at midnight Saint Columba, a pillar of many Churches, departed to the Lord. At the hour of his blessed departure I saw in spirit the island of Jova—which I have never reached bodily—illuminated throughout by the radiance of angels. The whole extent of the air up to the heavenly ether was likewise illuminated by the brightness of those same angels, for innumerable angels had descended from heaven to carry his holy soul away. At that very moment of its departure, amid the angelic choirs ascending with the holy soul, I also heard the high-sounding and exceedingly sweet songs of the angels.”

Virgnous learned of this angelic manifestation, as has been said, directly from the mouth of that holy old man to whom it had been revealed, and he learned it with complete certainty.

During those same days, a man returning by sea from Scotia to the island of Hymba, where he remained for the rest of his life, often related this to the monks of Saint Columba. This Virgnous, after completing many years irreproachably in obedience among the brothers, spent another twelve years in an anchorite settlement at Miurbulcmar, completing his life as an anchorite, a victorious soldier of Christ.

[Col. 0774B] We found this vision recorded not only in written pages but also learned it without any hesitation from certain experienced elders to whom Virgnous himself had related it.

At the same hour, another vision, revealed in a different manner, was related to me, the young Adomnán, with solemn testimony by one of those who had seen it. He was a very old soldier of Christ, whose name may be given as Ferreolus. He awaits the resurrection with the saints, buried at Dorsum Thomae among the remains of the other monks of Saint Columba, and he himself was a holy monk. He said:

“On that night when Saint Columba passed from earth to heaven by a blessed and fortunate end, I and other working men who were engaged with me in catching fish in the valley of the fish-filled river Fende suddenly saw the entire expanse of the sky illuminated. Moved by the suddenness of this miracle, we turned our raised eyes toward the east. Behold, there appeared what seemed to be a very great fiery column. Ascending upward at midnight, it appeared to us to illuminate the whole world as brightly as a summer day and the midday sun. After that penetrating column entered heaven, darkness followed, just as darkness comes after the setting of the sun.

“We saw the brightness of this luminous and remarkable column with immense amazement—not only we who were together in that same place, but also many other fishermen who were fishing at scattered points in the various pools of the same river. As they later told us, they too saw a similar apparition and were struck with great fear.”

These three miraculous visions, appearing at the same hour of the venerable patron’s departure, testify to the eternal honors bestowed upon him by God. Let us return to the subject.

## XXXIII

Meanwhile, after the hymns of the morning had been completed following the departure of the holy soul, the sacred body was carried from the church to the guesthouse from which he had come shortly before while still alive, accompanied by the brothers’ melodious psalmody. There, for three days and an equal number of nights, the honorable funeral rites were duly and reverently performed.

When these had been completed in praise of the wise God, the venerable body of the holy and blessed patron, wrapped in clean linen cloths and placed in a prepared tomb, was buried with due veneration, destined to rise again in luminous and eternal glory.

The customary ecclesiastical rites performed during those three days of funeral observance mentioned above, as they were handed down to us by experienced witnesses, will be related near the end of this book.

## XXXIV

On one occasion a certain brother, speaking simply before the venerable man, said to the Saint:

“After your death, as people suppose, the entire population of these provinces will cross over to this island of Jova to celebrate your funeral rites, and will fill the island.”

Hearing this, the Saint replied:

“My little son, matters will not turn out as you say. The common crowd of the people will in no way be able to come to my funeral. Only my familiar monks will fill my grave and honor the funeral offices.”

His prophetic word was immediately fulfilled after his departure by the omnipotence of God.

For during those three days and nights of the funeral there was a great windstorm without rain. Because it raged so fiercely, no one traveling by boat from either side could cross over. Immediately after the man’s burial had been completed, the storm subsided, the wind ceased, and the entire sea became calm.

[Col. 0776A] Let the reader therefore consider how great and how distinguished was the honor held by this renowned patron before God. At one time, while he was living in mortal flesh, storms were calmed and the seas made tranquil when, by God’s favor, he prayed. Again, when necessity required it on the occasion mentioned above, the seas were stirred up by the rising wind and became stormy at his will. Subsequently, when the rites of his burial had been completed, as was stated above, they were changed into great tranquility.

This, then, was the end of the life of our renowned patron and the beginning of his merits. According to the judgments of Scripture, he was added to the fathers as a companion in eternal triumphs, joined to the apostles and prophets, and gathered into the number of the white-robed thousands who washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. A spotless virgin, wholly free from every stain, he follows the Lamb as his guide. This was granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father, belong honor, might, praise, glory, and everlasting dominion, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0775]

# J. MABILLON’S PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK

*(Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum, third century.)*

[Col. 0775C] **1.** Damnanus, or Adomnanus, whom some call Adamnanus and, corruptly, Adamandus, flourished in the monastery of Iona, or of Saint Columba, toward the end of the seventh century. This monastery was situated on the island of Iona, adjacent to Ireland and to the province of the Picts, which in our age is commonly called Scotland.

After Columba, whom we discussed in the first century, the monastery was governed by Baitheneus, Segeneus—also called Segienus or Segenus by others—and Failbeus, whom Adamnanus succeeded. This appears to be established from the Acts of Saint Columba, which Adamnanus composed in three books. There he repeatedly calls himself Adomnanus, although he is called Adamnanus by Bede and in the books *On the Holy Places*.

Columba named Baitheneus as his successor at the end of his life, which occurred in the year 598. Segienus succeeded Baitheneus from 622 to 652, as Usserius proves from the Ulster Annals in his *Sylloge of Irish Letters*. He is the Segenus or Segeneus mentioned in the letter of the Roman clergy to the Irish. It is also said that the famous Erenaeus recounted throughout all the Churches of Scotland certain prophecies about himself made by Columba, in Book I of the *Life of Saint Columba*; in that passage Adomnanus mentions Failbeus, his predecessor.

**2.** This Adamnanus is praised by Bede in Book V, chapter 16, in the following words:

“At that time, through the Lord’s favor, the greater part of the Scots in Ireland, and some also from Britain, received the proper time of the ecclesiastical observance of Easter. For Adamnanus, a priest and abbot of the monks who were on the island of Iona, had come as an ambassador from his people to Aldfrid, king of the English. After remaining for some time in that province, he saw the canonical rites of the Church and was diligently admonished by many who were more learned not to presume to live, against the universal custom of the Church, either in the observance of Easter or in any other decrees, together with his very few companions placed at the end of the world.

“He was changed in mind, so that he gladly preferred to the custom of himself and his people what he had seen and heard in the Churches of the English. For he was a good and wise man, most nobly instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures. When he returned home, he took care to lead those who were on Iona, and those who were subject to the same monastery, to the path of truth which he had learned and embraced with all his heart, but he was unable to do so.

“He sailed to Ireland and, preaching to them and explaining the lawful time of Easter in a modest exhortation, corrected many of them, and almost all who were free from the authority of the Iona community, from their ancestral error and brought them back to Catholic unity. He thoroughly taught them to observe the lawful time of Easter.

“After celebrating the canonical Easter in Ireland, he returned to his island and earnestly preached the Catholic observance of the time of Easter to his own monastery. Yet he could not accomplish what he attempted. Before the completion of the annual cycle, it happened that he departed from this world. Divine grace evidently ordained that a man most devoted to unity and peace should be snatched away to eternal life before the return of Easter forced him to endure a more serious disagreement with those who were unwilling to follow him into the truth.”

**3.** Aldfrid, to whom Adamnanus was sent as ambassador, was king of the Northumbrians, son and successor of Egfrid; he was the king who ended his life in the year 705.

Adamnanus joined the Catholic party, chiefly at the urging of Ceolfrid, abbot of Wearmouth, as Ceolfrid himself testifies in his letter to King Naiton, preserved by Bede in Book V, chapter 22:

“Nor should you think that I have pursued these matters in such a way as to judge those who wear this tonsure worthy of condemnation, if they favor Catholic unity in faith and works. Rather, I confidently profess that many of them have proved themselves holy and worthy of God.

“Adamnanus, abbot and priest, an outstanding man among the Columban monks, had been sent as ambassador of his people to King Aldfrid. Since he also wished to see our monastery, and displayed remarkable prudence, humility, and devotion in his conduct and speech, I said to him, among other things, in conversation:

“‘I ask you, holy brother: since you believe that you are striving toward the crown of life which knows no end, why do you wear on your head the image of a crown bounded by a form contrary to your faith? If you seek the fellowship of blessed Peter, why do you imitate the appearance of the tonsure of the one whom he anathematized, rather than showing, as far as you can, that even now you love the appearance of him with whom you desire to live blessed forever?’

“He replied: ‘Know for certain, my beloved brother, that although I have Simon’s tonsure by the custom of my homeland, I detest and reject Simon’s perfidy with all my mind. As far as my insignificance permits, I desire to follow the footsteps of the most blessed prince of the apostles.’
