“But I said: ‘I truly believe that this is so; nevertheless, let it be evidence that you embrace in the hidden recesses of your heart the things that belong to the Apostle Peter if you also bear upon your face the things that you know to be his …’

“These were the things I then said to Adamnanus. How much he had advanced after seeing the regulations of our Churches he proved when, after returning to Scotland, he later corrected many groups of his people through his preaching and brought them to the Catholic observance of Easter. Yet he was still unable to lead back to the path of the better rule the monks who lived on the island of Iona and over whom he presided by the special authority of their ruler.”

**4.** From these two passages we understand, first, that Adamnanus was brought to the Roman rites at Ceolfrid’s urging, as I have already said. Second, we understand that he spent some time in the monastery of Wearmouth, where he learned and adopted the customs of the Benedictine rule observed there, together with the Roman rites.

Such was the custom among monks in those times: those who abandoned the tonsure of the Scots and adopted the Roman tonsure, together with the lawful observance of Easter, conformed themselves to the Benedictine institutions. Witnesses to this matter are the monks of Lindisfarne in Britain, those of Landevenec in Armorica, and those of Luxeuil in Gaul.

Furthermore, these same passages indicate that Adamnanus died shortly after his embassy to Aldfrid, who died in 705, as Bede testifies in Book V, chapter 19, before the twentieth year of his reign had been completed.

In addition, Ceolfrid calls Adamnanus himself the ruler and a saint of the Columban monks. He is called by the same title by Alcuin in a certain epigram:

> Patrick, Charanus, glory of the Scottish race,  
> And Columba, Congallus, and Adamnanus,  
> Illustrious Fathers, teachers of conduct and life.  
> May their piety assist us all through the prayers of these men.

This inscription appears to have belonged to some altar, as did several other epigrams.

Certainly Adamnanus is commemorated in our calendars on the ninth day before the Kalends of October—that is, September 23.

[Col. 0777D] **5.** Another Adamnanus is also commemorated on the sixth day before the Kalends of January—that is, December 27. He was a monk who lived in the monastery of Coludi, governed by the holy abbess Ebba, aunt of King Egfrid. According to Bede in Book IV, chapter 19, she had received the monastic habit from Bishop Wilfrid, that distinguished propagator of our rule.

That monastery, like the other convents of nuns generally, was double, containing both men and women. It was situated in a place called Coludi, which Bede says was a town in the region of the newer Scotland, now called Coldingham.

In that same monastery there was a man of Scottish origin named Adamnanus, leading a life greatly devoted to God in continence and prayer. He never took food or drink except on the Lord’s Day and the fifth day of the week, and he often spent entire nights awake in prayer.

This strictness of the more austere life first came upon him from necessity, as a means of correcting his wickedness; but in time he turned necessity into habit. Bede records the other details at length in Book IV, chapter 25, where Adamnanus is said to have foretold the burning of his monastery to the abbess Ebba.

Therefore take care not to confuse this Adamnanus, the monk of Coludi—as many have already done—with Adamnanus, the abbot of Iona, concerning whose writings certain observations must be made.

**6.** In addition to the *Life of Saint Columba the Abbot*, which he arranged in three books, Adamnanus wrote a book *On the Holy Places*, very useful to many readers, says Bede in Book V, chapter 16. Its authority was Arculfus, a bishop of Gaul, who came to Jerusalem for the sake of the holy places and communicated it by oral instruction and dictation.

Who Arculfus was, and who his companion and guide on the journey Peter was, is unknown. We know only that Arculfus was a Gallic bishop and that Peter was a hermit born in Burgundy.

I had long sought Adamnanus’s book—that is, his little work *On the Holy Places*—and at last found it in a manuscript of Corbie, though mutilated and incomplete. While turning over Volume I of Labbe’s *New Library*, I came upon the passage where Labbe indicates, from the papers of Sirmond, that those books existed in manuscript in the Vatican Library.

I wrote about this to our friend and fellow countryman Antonius Durbanus, who manages the affairs of our congregation at the Roman Curia. He searched the Vatican Library, found the long-desired copy, supplied the gaps and lacunae in the Corbie manuscript, and further informed me that Adamnanus’s little work *On the Holy Places* had been published at Ingolstadt in 1619 through the work and scholarship of Jacob Gretser, theologian and priest of the Society of Jesus.

At last I received a copy of that edition from the distinguished Raimundus Formentinus, a Sorbonne doctor, through the care and foresight of the distinguished Antonius Vion of Herovall, who never ceases to watch over the studies of learned men.

But because copies of that edition are so rare in these regions that scarcely anyone knew of its existence, learned men judged that it would serve the interests of scholarship if we reprinted these books of Adamnanus. The subject itself encouraged this, as did the memory of Adamnanus, which would become more illustrious through these books.

Gretser placed beside Adamnanus’s text the text of Bede, who had compiled his book *On the Holy Places* from Adamnanus’s writing. We thought it sufficient to reproduce Adamnanus alone, together with four figures. The fourth is absent from Gretser, while the others are incomplete.

The number of the books is certain in the copies, but not the sequence of the chapters, which differs in Gretser and in the Vatican and Corbie manuscripts.

**7.** It seemed appropriate to append to Adamnanus’s books the itinerary of a certain Frank to the holy places [Note: [Col. 0777] See Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, third century, part II, p. 523. EDITOR], composed toward the end of the ninth century, during the pontificate of Nicholas I.

In this itinerary mention is made of that fire which each year, on Holy Saturday, kindled the lamps of the Lord’s Sepulchre from heaven. Adamnanus’s books contain no mention of it, although the phenomenon is frequently reported by historians who later wrote about the war of Jerusalem. Nevertheless, I have read no author older than this Anonymous who remembers the matter.

The distinguished Carolus Fresnius, lord of Cange, mentioned it among the customary miracles in his notes on Anna Comnena, p. 389. He was supported especially by Rodulfus Glaber in Book IV, chapter 6; William of Malmesbury in Book IV *On the Kings of the English*, chapter 2, in two passages, sections 35 and 48; the Chronicle of Andres in Volume IX of the *Spicilegium*, p. 465; and the Chronicle of the Monastery of Fontaines, chapter 4, in Volume X of the *Spicilegium*. The same most courteous man pointed these passages out to me.

The first passage of William of Malmesbury should be quoted here, since it teaches us that the author of the later itinerary was Bernard, a Frankish monk, who traveled to the holy places in the year 870. William writes as follows about Jerusalem:

> There stands the spacious and suitably constructed Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built by Constantine the Great. It has never suffered any injury from the enemies of the faith, who are struck, as I suppose, with fear because of the heavenly fire that shines serenely each year on the vigil of Easter. When this miracle began, or whether it existed before the time of the Saracens, cannot be determined from the knowledge of any history. I have read in the writing of Bernard the monk that, two hundred and fifty years ago—that is, in the year 870 of the Incarnation—he himself traveled to Jerusalem, saw that fire, and lodged in the hospice that the glorious Charles the Great had ordered to be built, where he had also assembled a library at enormous expense.

And further:

> Nevertheless, because Bernard does not omit the name of Theodosius, who was then patriarch, the occasion itself prompts me to set forth all the names of the patriarchs.

All these details agree with the later itinerary. Therefore I do not hesitate to state with certainty that Bernard the monk was its author, although his name is absent from the Remigian manuscript that I used.

Who that Bernard was may perhaps be discovered at some future time. Let us now examine Adamnanus’s books.

[Col. 0779]

# THE THREE BOOKS OF SAINT ADAMNANUS, ABBOT OF IONA, ON THE HOLY PLACES, FROM THE ACCOUNT OF ARCULFUS, BISHOP OF GAUL

*(From the Vatican and Corbie manuscript copies and Gretser’s edition, in Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum, third century.)* (C)

## Prologue of the Author

[Col. 0779B] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I begin to weave a book concerning the holy places.

The holy bishop Arculfus, a Gaul by race, well acquainted with many distant and far-removed places, a truthful and sufficiently reliable witness, having lodged for nine months in the city of Jerusalem and having traversed its places by daily visits, dictated all the matters written below to me, Adamnanus, as I carefully investigated them and first set them down on tablets, in a faithful and certain account. They are now written on parchment in a brief text.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0779]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Situation of Jerusalem

[Col. 0779C] A few things must now be written about the situation of Jerusalem, drawn from what the holy Arculfus dictated to me. What we find in the books of others concerning the position of the same city must be omitted by us.

Within the great circuit of its walls, Arculfus counted eighty-four towers and six gates, arranged around the city in the following order:

1. The Gate of David is counted first, on the western side of Mount Zion.
2. The Gate of the Fuller’s Village.
3. The Gate of Saint Stephen.
4. The Gate of Benjamin.
5. The Little Gate—that is, the small gate from which one descends by steps (*gradus*; variant *grados*) into the Valley of Jehoshaphat.
6. The Gate of Tekoa.

This order, through the intervals between the gates and towers, proceeds from the aforementioned Gate of David around the circuit, turning northward and then toward the east.

Although six gates are counted in the walls, three entrances among them are more frequently used: one on the western side, another on the northern side, and a third on the eastern side.

That section of the walls, with the towers placed between them, which extends from the aforementioned Gate of David along the northern ridge of Mount Zion—rising above the city on the south—up to the face of the same mountain, which looks toward the eastern region over a precipitous cliff, is found to have no gates.

Nor should this be passed over: the holy Arculfus told us the following concerning the honor in Christ of this city:

“A nearly innumerable multitude of various nations from every direction customarily gathers at Jerusalem each year on the fifteenth day of September, in order to conduct commerce through mutual (*mutuis*; variant *motuis*) sales and purchases. It necessarily follows that, for several days, crowds of different peoples lodge in the same hospitable city. Their enormous number of camels, horses, asses, mules, and male oxen (*boum*; variant *bovum*), carrying various wares, spreads the abominations of their own dung everywhere through the paved streets. Its stench causes the citizens no small annoyance, and the dung also obstructs walking.

“Wonderful to relate! After the departure, on the day mentioned above, of the various groups with their beasts of burden, during the following night an immense quantity of rain pours down from the clouds upon that same city. Washing away all the abominable filth from the streets, it cleanses the city from its impurities.

“For the site of Jerusalem itself, beginning at the northern ridge of Mount Zion, is arranged by God the Creator on such a gentle slope down to the lower parts of the northern and eastern walls that the overflowing rainwater cannot remain in the streets like stagnant pools. Rather, like rivers, it runs from the higher places to the lower.

“This inundation of heavenly water flows through (*interfluens*; variant *influens*, ‘flows into’) the eastern gates, carrying away with it all the abominable filth, enters the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and swells the torrent of the Kidron. After this baptism of Jerusalem, the same overflowing stream immediately ceases.

“From this it should be carefully noted what great and distinguished honor this chosen and renowned city possesses in the sight of the eternal Father. He does not permit it to remain polluted for long, but quickly cleanses it for the honor of his Only-Begotten Son, since within the circuit of its walls it possesses the honored places of his holy cross and resurrection.”

Moreover, in that famous (*famoso*; variant *formoso*, ‘beautiful’) place where the Temple had once been magnificently built, situated near the eastern wall, the Saracens now frequently use a square house of prayer. They constructed it in a crude manner, with upright boards and large beams placed over certain remains of ruins. This building is said to be capable of holding three thousand people at one time.

When we asked Arculfus about the dwellings of the city, he replied:

“I remember both seeing and frequenting many buildings of that city, and I often observed throughout the great city, within its encircling walls, very many large stone houses constructed with marvelous skill. In my judgment all these must now be passed over, except for those buildings that have been magnificently constructed at the holy places, namely those of the cross and the resurrection.”

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Round Church Built over the Sepulchre
Of these matters we carefully questioned the holy Arculfus, especially about the Lord’s tomb and the church built over it, whose design he himself drew for me on a wax tablet. This church is exceedingly large, built entirely of stone, and arranged with remarkable circularity on every side. Rising from its foundations are three walls; between each wall and the next there is the width of a roadway. Three altars have also been artistically constructed in three places along the middle wall. This round and principal church, containing the altars mentioned above—one facing south, another north, and the third west—is supported by twelve columns of extraordinary size and made of stone.

It has twice four doors, that is, four entrances established through the three intervening spaces between the walls, each entrance standing opposite the others. Of these, four exits face toward the Vulturnus, also called the Calcias wind; the other four face toward the Eurus [Alternative: west].

In the middle of the interior space of this round building there is a round shrine [Alternative: shelter] cut from one and the same rock. Nine men standing can pray inside it, and from the crown of the head of a standing man of not short stature up to the roof of that little chamber there is a height of one and a half feet. The entrance to this shrine faces east. Its entire exterior is covered with choice marble; its upper outer summit, adorned with gold, supports a sizeable golden cross.

On the northern side of this shrine the Lord’s tomb is cut into the same rock inside it. The floor of the shrine, however, is lower than the place of the tomb. For from its floor up to the edge of the tomb’s side there is evidently a height of about three palms [Note: [Col. 0781] Alternative: a height of three palms, approximately the distance from the thumb to the little finger]. Thus Arculfus, who often visited the Lord’s tomb, confidently declared after measuring it himself.

Here one must note the proper distinction between the names “monument” and “tomb.” The round shrine mentioned repeatedly above is called by the evangelists by another name, “the monument.” They state that, when the Lord rose again, the stone was rolled toward its entrance and then rolled back from its entrance. The tomb, properly speaking, is that place within the shrine—that is, on the northern side of the monument—in which the Lord’s body, wrapped in linen cloths, was buried and rested. Arculfus personally measured its length as seven feet. This tomb is not, as some falsely suppose, double, with a rock cut from the same little structure separating two legs and thighs by an intervening partition; rather, it is entirely single from its crown to its foot, providing, in the manner of a cave, a bed capable of holding one person lying on his back [Alternative adds: “space”]. It has an entrance at its side facing directly toward the southern part of the monument, and above it rises a low, skillfully constructed roof.

In this tomb twelve lamps, corresponding to the number of the twelve holy apostles, burn and shine continually day and night. Four of them are placed below, at the lowest part of that funerary bed; the other eight are set above, along its upper edge on the right side, shining brightly with nourishing oil.

## CHAPTER III. On the form of the tomb itself and its shrine

It also seems necessary to note that the Savior’s mausoleum [Alternative: magisoleum], that is, the shrine mentioned so often above, may properly be called a cave or cavern. Concerning it, when the Lord Jesus Christ had been buried there, the prophet prophesies, saying: “He dwelt in a lofty cave of a very strong rock” (Isaiah 33). Shortly afterward, concerning the Lord’s resurrection, he adds for the joy of the apostles: “You will see the king in glory.”

The accompanying drawing explains the plan of the church mentioned above, with the round shrine placed in its center and the Lord’s tomb located on its northern side (p. following), as well as the figures of three other churches, which will be described below.

[Col. 0783]

[Col. 0783A]

A. The round shrine.  
B. The Lord’s tomb.  
C. Two altars.  
D. Altars.  
E. The church.  
F. The Golgotha church.  
G. The place of Abraham’s altar.  
[Col. 0784A]  
H. The place where the Lord’s cross, together with the two crosses of the robbers, was found beneath the earth.  
I. A wooden table.  
K. The little court in which lamps burn day and night.  
L. The church of Saint Mary.  
M. The Constantinian basilica, that is, the Martyrium.  
N. The apse containing the Lord’s chalice.

[Col. 0783B]

In the same church there is a cave cut into the rock beneath the place of the Lord’s cross, where a sacrifice is offered upon an altar for the souls of certain honored persons. Their bodies are meanwhile laid in the courtyard before the door of the same Golgotha church, until the holy mysteries offered for those dead have been completed.

We have therefore drawn the figures of these four churches according to the model that Arculfus, as stated above, sketched for me on a small wax tablet—not because their likeness could be adequately reproduced in a drawing, but so that the Lord’s monument, however poorly represented in this way, might be shown as situated in the middle of the round church, and so that it might be indicated which church is nearer to it and which lies farther away.

## CHAPTER IV. On the stone that was rolled to the entrance of the monument

Amid these matters, something brief should be said about the stone mentioned above, which, according to the testimony of many men, was rolled to the entrance of the Lord’s monument after the crucified Lord had been buried. Arculfus reports that it was cut through and divided into two parts. The smaller part was shaped with tools, and a square altar made from it can be seen standing in the round church described above, before the entrance of that often-mentioned shrine—that is, the Lord’s monument. The larger part of the stone was likewise worked all around, and in the eastern part of the same church there stands another square altar established beneath linen coverings.

When I questioned Arculfus about the colors of that rock—the rock in which the shrine repeatedly mentioned above was hollowed out within by the tools of stonecutters, and in which the Lord’s tomb was likewise cut on its northern side from the same single rock as the monument, that is, the shrine—he said:

“The shrine of the Lord’s monument, covered by no interior ornament, still displays throughout its entire hollow the traces of the tools with which the stonecutters or excavators worked on it. The color of that same rock of the monument and tomb appears not to be one color but two blended together, namely red and white; hence the rock itself appears two-colored.”

But let this suffice concerning these matters.

## CHAPTER V. On the church of Blessed Mary, ever-virgin, adjoining the round church

[Col. 0784C]

A few further details should be added concerning the structures of the holy places. To the right of the round church mentioned so often above—which is also called the Anastasis, that is, the Resurrection, because it was built at the place of the Lord’s resurrection—there adjoins a square church of Saint Mary, the mother of the Lord.

## CHAPTER VI. On the church constructed at the place of Calvary

Another very large church has been built facing east at the place called Golgotha in Hebrew. Above it hangs a large bronze wheel suspended by ropes, with lamps upon it. Beneath the wheel stands a great silver cross fixed in the very place where the wooden cross on which the Savior of the human race suffered was once fixed.

## CHAPTER VII. On the basilica of Constantine adjoining the church mentioned above

[Col. 0785A]

The square stone church built at the place of Calvary is joined on its eastern side by a neighboring stone basilica, constructed with great magnificence by King Constantine. It is called the Martyrium [Alternative: Monastery] and, according to report, was built at the place where the Lord’s cross, together with the two crosses of the robbers, had been hidden beneath the earth and was discovered, by the Lord’s gift, after a period of 233 years.

Between these two churches lies the famous place where the patriarch Abraham prepared an altar, placing upon it a pile of wood; and, in order to sacrifice his son Isaac, he drew and seized a sword. A sizeable wooden table now stands there, on which the people offer alms for the poor.

When I questioned him more carefully, the holy Arculfus added this:

“Between the Anastasis—that is, the round church mentioned so often above—and the basilica of Constantine, a small court extends as far as the Golgotha church. In that little court lamps burn continually, day and night.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On another apse within the church of Calvary

Between the Golgotha basilica and the Martyrium there is also an apse containing the Lord’s chalice. At the supper on the day before he suffered, the Lord himself, after blessing it with his own hand, gave it to the apostles as they reclined at table. It is a silver chalice holding the measure of a Gallic sextarius and furnished with two small handles, one on either side.

Within this chalice there is the sponge which, after filling it with vinegar and placing it on hyssop, those crucifying the Lord offered to his mouth. According to report, after the resurrection the Lord drank from this same chalice while dining with the apostles.

The holy Arculfus saw it and, through an opening in the cover of the little chest where it is kept, touched it with his own hand and kissed it [Alternative: “and kissed it”]. The entire population of the city visits this chalice with immense veneration.

## CHAPTER IX. On the soldier’s lance with which he pierced the Lord’s side

Arculfus likewise saw the soldier’s lance with which the soldier himself struck the Lord’s side while he hung upon the cross. This same lance is kept inserted into a wooden cross in the portico of Constantine’s basilica. Its shaft [Alternative: haft] has been cut into two pieces. The whole city of Jerusalem likewise visits it, kisses it, and venerates it.

## CHAPTER X. On the cloth with which the head of the buried Lord was covered

We also learned, from the account of the holy Arculfus, about the most sacred cloth that had been placed over the Lord’s head in the tomb. He saw it with his own eyes and gave the account that we now scratch out [Alternative: engrave; that is, write down]. The entire people of Jerusalem affirm that this account is true.

[Col. 0786A]

From the testimony of many faithful citizens of Jerusalem, the holy Arculfus learned the following account. They repeatedly declared it in his attentive hearing:

“About three years ago, the most sacred linen cloth—which a certain highly trustworthy and believing Jew had stolen from the Lord’s tomb immediately after his resurrection and hidden in his possession for many days—was discovered after the passage of many cycles of years, by the Lord’s gift, and came to the knowledge of the entire people.

“That fortunate and faithful thief, when he was at the point of death, summoned his two sons and, revealing the Lord’s cloth to them, brought it forth, saying: ‘My sons, an option is now given to you. Let either of you say what he would rather choose, so that I may certainly know which of you I ought, according to his own choice, to entrust with either all the property I possess or merely this sacred cloth of the Lord.’

“After hearing these words from their father, one son, who desired to receive all his father’s riches, accepted them from him, and, in accordance with his father’s promise, had them entrusted to him. Wonderful to relate! From that day all his riches and his entire patrimony, for which he had sold the Lord’s cloth, began to diminish; and everything he possessed, lost through various misfortunes, was reduced to nothing.

“But the other son of the aforesaid thief was blessed. He preferred the Lord’s cloth to every patrimony. From the day he received it from his dying father’s hand, he grew richer and richer, by God’s gift, even in earthly goods, and was not deprived of heavenly ones.

“Thus the fathers of that thrice-blessed man’s lineage entrusted the Lord’s cloth to their sons, as though by hereditary right, faithful men to faithful men, according to the succession of their ancestry, faithfully down to the fifth generation.

“But after the time of the fifth generation, when many years had passed and the hereditary faithful members of that family had died out, the sacred linen came into the hands of certain unfaithful Jews. Although unworthy of such a gift, they nevertheless embraced it honorably and, by God’s gracious generosity, became rich, enriched with exceedingly varied possessions.

“When the believing Jews heard that a definite report concerning the Lord’s cloth had arisen among the people, they began to contend vigorously with the unfaithful Jews over that sacred linen, seeking with all their strength to take it into their hands.

“This contention divided the people of Jerusalem into two parties: the faithful and believing on one side, and the unfaithful and unbelieving on the other.

“Therefore the king of the Saracens, named Navias [Alternative: Majuvias], was appealed to by both parties. He judged between them and said to the unbelieving Jews who stubbornly held on to the Lord’s cloth [Note: Grets. adds: “with Christian Jews present”]: ‘Give the sacred linen you possess into my hand.’

“Obeying the king’s command, they brought it out of the chest and placed it in the ruler’s lap. The king received it with great reverence and ordered a pyre to be made in the courtyard before the whole people.

“When the fire was burning with great intensity, he rose and approached the pyre. Raising his voice, he said to both disputing parties:

“‘Now let Christ, the Savior of the world, who suffered for the human race and who had this cloth—which I now hold in my lap—placed over his head in his tomb, judge between you who are contending over this same linen through the fire, so that we may know to which party of these two contending armies he may deign to grant such a gift.’

“Having said this, he threw the sacred cloth of the Lord into the flames. The fire could not touch it in any way. Rising from the pyre whole and unharmed, it began to fly upward like a bird with outspread wings. Looking down from above upon the two opposing parties of the people, seated in battle array against one another as though ready for war, it circled for a while through the empty air. Then, gradually descending, and guided by God, it turned toward the Christian party, who were meanwhile beseeching Christ the judge, and settled in their lap.

“Giving thanks to God with hands raised to heaven and kneeling with immense joy, they received with great honor the Lord’s cloth, a venerable gift sent down to them from heaven. They offered hymns of praise to Christ, its giver, and stored it in a chest of the church, wrapped in another linen cloth.”

Our brother Arculfus saw it on another day after it had been lifted from the chest. In the assembly of the church, amid the crowd of people kissing it, he too kissed it. It was approximately eight feet long. Let this suffice concerning these matters.

## CHAPTER XI. On the linen cloth which, as reported, the holy Virgin Mary wove

[Col. 0787C]

Arculfus also saw another, larger linen cloth in the same city of Jerusalem. It is said that the holy Mary wove it, and for this reason the entire people venerate it in the church with great reverence. Woven into this cloth are figures of the twelve apostles and an image of the Lord himself. One side of the cloth is red, while the opposite side, on the other edge, is green.

## CHAPTER XII. On another very tall column standing at the place where a dead youth came back to life after the Lord’s cross had been placed upon him

[Col. 0787D]

A brief account should be given of a very tall column standing in the holy places to the north, in the middle of the city, and visible to those proceeding along the road. This column was erected at the place where a dead youth came back to life after the Lord’s cross had been placed upon him.

In a remarkable manner, at the summer solstice, when the sun reaches the center of the sky at midday, it casts no shadow. After the solstice has passed—which is 24 June [VIII Kalends of July]—and after three days have intervened, it first casts a short shadow as the day gradually decreases, and then, as the days advance, a longer one.

This column, which at the summer solstice is illuminated from above on every side by the brightness of the sun, standing at midday in the center of the sky directly overhead, declares that Jerusalem lies in the middle of the world, at the center of the earth. Therefore the Psalmist, prophesying on account of the holy places of the Passion and resurrection contained within Aelia [that is, Jerusalem], sings:

“But God our King before the age  
has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 68),

that is, in Jerusalem, which is called a Mediterranean land and the navel of the earth.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the church of Saint Mary built in the valley of Jehoshaphat, in which her tomb is located

A diligent visitor to the holy places, the holy Arculfus, frequently visited the church of Saint Mary in the valley of Jehoshaphat. Its lower part, constructed in two levels, is built beneath a stone roof in a remarkable circular form. On its eastern side there is an altar; on its right side is the stone-hewn hollow tomb of Saint Mary, in which she once rested after being buried [Note: [Col. 0787D] Alternative: “rested,” as is sufficiently clear].

But no one, as is reported, can know with certainty how, at what time, or by what persons her holy body was removed from that same tomb, or in what place it awaits the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0788D] Alternative: “No one, as the aforesaid man testifies, can know with certainty”].

When people enter this lower round church of Saint Mary, they see on the right a stone inserted into the wall. Upon it the Lord prayed on bent knees in the garden of Gethsemane [Alternative: Gethsamani], on the night when he was handed over by Judas into the hands of sinful men, before the hour of his betrayal. On that stone the impressions of both his knees can be seen, deeply marked as though in the softest wax.

Thus our brother Arculfus, a visitor to the holy places, declared to us. He saw with his own eyes the things that we describe. In the upper, likewise round, church of Saint Mary, four altars are shown to be present.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the tower of Jehoshaphat built in the same valley; on the monuments of Simeon and Joseph

In the same valley mentioned above, not far from the church of Saint Mary, the tower of Jehoshaphat is shown, in which his tomb can be seen. A small stone building adjoins this little tower on the right. Cut out and separated from the rock of the Mount of Olives, it contains within it two tombs hollowed out with tools and without any ornament. One belongs to Simeon, the righteous man who embraced the infant Lord Jesus in the temple with both hands and prophesied about him. The other likewise belongs to the righteous Joseph, the husband of Saint Mary and the foster-father of the Lord Jesus.

## CHAPTER XV. On the cave in the rock of the Mount of Olives opposite the valley of Jehoshaphat, in which there are four tables and two wells

On the side of the Mount of Olives there is a cave not far from the church of Saint Mary, situated on higher ground opposite the valley of Jehoshaphat. It contains two very deep wells. One extends beneath the mountain to an immeasurable depth; the other is in the floor of the cave, whose enormous hollow, descending deeply—as is reported—runs straight downward. Both wells are always covered over.

In the same cave there are four stone tables. One is situated inside beside the entrance of the cave and belongs to the Lord Jesus; beyond doubt, his little seat adjoins it. There, when the twelve apostles were sitting together at the other tables located in that place, he himself was often accustomed to recline as a fellow guest.

The covered mouth of the well in the floor of the cave, which we described above as being there, is shown to be situated close to the apostles’ tables. According to Arculfus, who often visited this cave of the Lord, its small entrance is closed by a wooden door.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Gate of David

[Col. 0789C]

The Gate of David adjoins Mount Zion on its western side by a gentle slope [Alternative: incline]. For those leaving the city through that gate, with Mount Zion close at hand on their left, a stone bridge appears. It runs straight southward across the valley at a distance and is supported by arches.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the place where Judas Iscariot hanged himself with a noose

About halfway along it, toward the west, lies the neighboring place where Judas Iscariot, driven by despair, perished by hanging himself with a noose. There is still shown there a large fig tree, from whose top he is said to have hung after being strangled. The poetic priest Juvencus sang of Judas:

> “The fig tree’s top snatched an ugly death.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the form of the great basilica built on Mount Zion and on the situation of that mountain

[Col. 0790B]

Since Mount Zion was mentioned somewhat earlier, a few brief and concise remarks should be made about a very large basilica built upon it. Its plan is described as follows:

[Col. 0790]

[Col. 0789C]

A. The place of the Lord’s supper.  
B. Here the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles.  
C. Here stands the marble column to which the Lord clung when he was scourged.  
D. Here Saint Mary died.  
E. The gate.

Here is shown the stone upon which Stephen fell asleep after being stoned outside the city. Outside the great basilica described above—which encloses within it the holy places just mentioned—there stands another noteworthy stone on the western side. Upon it, as is reported, the Lord was scourged. This apostolic church, as stated above, is built of stone on the upper level ground of Mount Zion.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the little field called Acheldemach in Hebrew

Our Arculfus frequently visited this small field situated on the southern side of Mount Zion. It has a stone enclosure, and many pilgrims are carefully buried there. Others among them, covered only with cloths or skins, are more carelessly left unburied, lying rotting on the surface of the earth.

## CHAPTER XX. On the broad stretches of rough and rocky land extending from Jerusalem to the city of Samuel and onward westward to Caesarea of Palestine

[Col. 0790D]

From Aelia northward to the city of Samuel, which is called Ramathas [Alternative: Armathem], rocky and rugged land appears at intervals. Thorny valleys also extend as far as the region of Tamnitis. Another kind of landscape appears from the aforesaid Aelia and Mount Zion westward toward Caesarea of Palestine. Although some narrow and short stretches of rough ground are interspersed, broader level fields are especially evident, made more pleasant by the olive groves among them.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Mount of Olives

According to Arculfus, few kinds of trees other than vines and olive trees can be found on the Mount of Olives. Crops of wheat and barley, however, grow there very luxuriantly. The character of the land is not heathy (*brucosa*) but grassy and flower-filled.

Its height appears equal to that of Mount Zion, although, in comparison with the Mount of Olives, Mount Zion appears small and narrow in its geometrical dimensions, namely its breadth and length. Between these two mountains lies the valley of Jehoshaphat, mentioned above, extending from north to south.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the place of the Lord’s ascension and the church built there

[Col. 0791B]

On the entire Mount of Olives no other place appears higher than the one from which the Lord is said to have ascended into heaven. There stands a large round church, with three vaulted porticoes extending around it and covered above. The interior of this round church is open to the sky beneath the bare air, without roof or vault. On its eastern side there is an altar constructed beneath a narrow protective roof.

The interior building has no vault placed above it so that, from the place where the Lord’s divine footprints last stood when he was lifted into heaven in a cloud, a route always open and directed toward the heavenly heights might lie visibly before the eyes of those praying at that spot.

When this basilica, of which only a few details are now being mentioned, was built, the place of the Lord’s footprints could not, as has been found written elsewhere, be made continuous with the rest of the pavement. Whatever was applied there, the earth—unaccustomed to receiving human work—rejected, the marble stones being thrown back into the faces of those who laid them [Grets.: “immediately to the earlier ones”].

Moreover, there is such a lasting testimony of the dust trodden by God that footprints can be seen impressed there. Although the faith of those who flock there daily carries away dust trodden by the Lord, the surface nevertheless suffers no loss, and the earth still preserves the same appearance, as though marked with impressed footprints.

In that same place, as the holy Arculfus reports—he who visited it diligently—a large bronze wheel is laid out overhead all around. Its height is shown to have been measured up to the top. In the middle of it there is a sizeable opening, through which the clearly and distinctly impressed footprints of the Lord’s feet in the dust below can be seen from above.

In the western part of the wheel there is always open what may be called a doorway, so that those entering through it can easily approach the place of the sacred dust and, through the open aperture above in the same wheel, take particles of the sacred dust with outstretched hands.

Thus our Arculfus’s account of the place of the Lord’s footprints agrees correctly with the writings of others: the place could not in any way be protected either by the roof of the building or by any special lower and nearer covering, so that it might always be plainly visible to all who visit it and so that the Lord’s footprints might be clearly displayed in the dust of that place.

These same footprints of the Lord are illuminated by the great brightness of a lamp hanging above the wheel on pulleys and burning day and night. In the western part of the round church mentioned above there are eight upper windows, skillfully constructed and furnished with glass shutters. Inside, directly opposite these windows, lamps of the same number hang from ropes and burn. They have been arranged so that each lamp hangs neither above nor below but appears almost attached to the window opposite which it is seen nearby on the inside.

The brightness of these lamps shines so powerfully that their light, abundantly diffused through the glass as though flashing from the higher part of the Mount of Olives, brilliantly illuminates not only that part of the mountain which adjoins the round stone basilica toward the west, but also the ascent of the city of Jerusalem from the valley of Jehoshaphat, raised by certain steps [Alternative: grades] to a considerable height, even on similarly dark nights. The greater and nearer part of the city, situated directly opposite, is also illuminated by the same radiance.

This brilliant and celebrated flashing of the eight great lamps, shining at night from the holy mountain and the place of the Lord’s ascension, infuses, as Arculfus reports, greater eagerness of divine love into the hearts of believing observers and instills in their minds a certain fear, together with immense inward compunction.

Nor should we remain silent about what the often-mentioned Arculfus reported to me, when I questioned him carefully about this same round church:

“Every year, on the anniversary of the Lord’s Ascension, at midday, after the sacred solemnities of the Mass have been completed in that basilica, a violent storm of exceedingly powerful wind usually rushes in with such force that no human being can in any way stand or even sit in that church or in the neighboring places. All lie prostrate on the ground with their faces pressed down until that terrifying storm has passed.

“This cause of the dreadful blast prevents that part of the building above the place of the Lord’s impressed footprints—which are openly displayed within the central opening of the aforesaid wheel—from having a roof, so that it remains perpetually open and visible toward heaven. Whenever human hands attempted to build a roof above it with whatever materials, the force of the aforementioned divinely sent wind destroyed the construction.”

The holy Arculfus recounted this terrifying storm to us in such terms. At the very hour on the day of the Lord’s Ascension when that exceedingly powerful blast broke out, he himself was present in the same church on the Mount of Olives.

The form of this round church is shown in the accompanying drawing, although rendered in a crude picture; the design of the bronze wheel placed in its center is displayed in the following little description (p. following).

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793A]

From the account of the holy Arculfus we also learned that, in the same round church, in addition to the usual eight lamps mentioned above, which shine inside at night, almost innumerable other lamps are customarily added on the festive night of the Lord’s Ascension. Because of their terrifying and wondrous brilliance, abundantly poured through the glass shutters of the windows, the entire Mount of Olives appears not merely illuminated but actually aflame, and the whole city, situated in the lower and nearby place, appears lit up.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the tomb of Lazarus and the church built over it, and on the monastery adjoining it

[Col. 0793B]

Arculfus, the visitor to the holy places mentioned above, visited a certain small plain of Bethany surrounded by a great forest of olive trees. There is a large monastery there and a great basilica built over the cave from which the Lord raised Lazarus, who had been dead for four days.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the church built on the right side of Bethany

We think that a brief account should be written concerning another, more celebrated church founded south of Bethany, at the place on the Mount of Olives where the Lord is said to have addressed his disciples.

Here one must carefully inquire what discourse the Lord delivered, at what time, and to which particular disciples he spoke. If we open the Gospels of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—these three matters will become manifest to us. They speak harmoniously about the character of the discourse; no one will be able to doubt the place of the assembly or the form of the discourse who reads Matthew’s Gospel, where the evangelist himself records the Lord’s words:

“But as he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying: ‘Tell us, when will these things be? And what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age?’” (Matthew 24).

Here Matthew was silent about the persons who asked the question, but Mark does not remain silent. Writing thus, he says:

“Peter, James, John, and Andrew questioned him privately” (Mark 13).

When they asked him, he showed the character of the discourse delivered, in accordance with the three evangelists mentioned above, saying:

“See that no one deceives you. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ’” (ibid.),

and so forth concerning the last times and the consummation of the age. Matthew develops these matters at length until the passage in which the same evangelist clearly indicates, from the Lord’s words, the time of this extended discourse, saying:

“And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these words, he said to his disciples: ‘You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified’” (Matthew 26),

and so forth.

It is therefore clearly shown that on the fourth day of the week, with two days remaining until the first day of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover, the Lord spoke the discourse mentioned above at length to the four apostles who questioned him.

A church has consequently been founded at the place of that discourse mentioned above, in its memory, and is held in great honor.

Up to this point it is sufficient to have written about the holy places of the city of Jerusalem, Mount Zion, the Mount of Olives, and the intervening valley of Jehoshaphat, according to the reliable account of the holy Arculfus, who visited those places.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0795]

## CHAPTER I. On the situation of the city of Bethlehem

[Col. 0795A]

At the beginning of this second little book, a few things must briefly be set down concerning the location of the city of Bethlehem, in which our Savior deigned to be born of the holy Virgin. This city, not so much great in situation—as Arculfus, who visited it, reported to us—as renowned and celebrated by fame throughout the churches of all nations, is situated on a narrow ridge [Supply: of a mountain], surrounded on every side by valleys. This ridge of land extends for nearly a thousand paces from west to east. On the upper level of its open plain, a low wall without towers has been constructed all around along the crest of the extremity of the same hillock; it rises above the valleys lying around it on either side. Within the walls, at an intermediate distance, the dwellings of the citizens are spread out along the longer roadway.

## CHAPTER II. On the place of the Lord’s birth

In the easternmost corner of the same city there is, as it were, a kind of natural half-cave. Its innermost and furthest part is called the Lord’s manger, in which the Mother laid the newborn child. Another place, adjoining the manger mentioned above and nearer to those entering, is traditionally said to have been the actual place of the Lord’s birth. That Bethlehemite cave of the Lord’s manger has been entirely adorned within, for the honor of the Savior himself, with precious marble. Above this half-cave, on a stone upper chamber, a church of Saint Mary has been founded and built on a grand scale, directly over the place where the Lord is more particularly said to have been born.

## CHAPTER III. On the stone situated outside the walls, over which the water of his first washing after his birth was poured

I consider it worthwhile briefly to mention the stone placed outside the wall, over which the water of the Lord’s first washing after his birth was poured from a vessel tilted from the top of the wall, from which it was poured. This water of the sacred washing, poured from the wall onto the stone lying below, found there a hollow, as it were, naturally scooped out. The same little pool, filled at the Lord’s first birth, is shown from that very day to our own time, through many cycles of centuries, always full of the purest water, without any failure or diminution, while our Savior has continued to perform this miracle from the day of his birth. Concerning this the Prophet sings: “He brought water out of the rock” (Psalm LXXVII). And the Apostle Paul says: “Now the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians X), who from an exceedingly hard rock, contrary to nature, brought forth a consoling stream for the thirsty people in the desert. He himself is the power of God and the wisdom of God, who also brought water out of that Bethlehemite stone and preserves its hollow always full of water. Our Arculfus saw it with his own eyes and washed his face in it.

## CHAPTER IV. On the church in which that Davidic monument is seen

[Note: [Cols. 0795D, 0796D] That is, an honorary monument or cenotaph; for Adrichomius and Gretserus prove from 2 Esdras III, 8, and Acts II that David’s true tomb was in Jerusalem, although Jerome, in Letter 17 and in his book *On Hebrew Places*, agrees with Arculfus.]

When I asked Arculfus about the tomb of King David, he gave us this reply, saying:

“I myself diligently sought out and visited the tomb of King David, buried in the earth. It is situated in the central part of the pavement of the church, without any ornament placed above it; it has a low stone pyramid and a lamp always set upon it.”

This church, then, is founded outside the city walls, in the adjoining valley, which is connected on its northern side with the Bethlehemite hillock.

## CHAPTER V. On another church in whose interior the tomb of Saint Jerome is found

When we likewise inquired with similar concern about the tomb of Saint Jerome, Arculfus said:

“The tomb of Saint Jerome, about which you ask, I saw. It is located in another church, built outside the same little city in the valley; this church lies adjacent, on the southern side, to the ridge of the Bethlehemite hillock mentioned above. The tomb of Jerome, made in a similar manner to the Davidic monument, has no ornament.”

## CHAPTER VI. On the monuments of the three shepherds whom heavenly radiance surrounded when the Lord was born

Arculfus gave us a brief account of the monuments of those shepherds whom heavenly radiance surrounded on the night of the Lord’s birth, saying:

“I visited in a church the three monuments of those three shepherds, who were buried beside a great stone [Corbie: tower]. They are situated about a thousand paces east of Bethlehem. At the place where the Lord was born—that is, near the Tower of the Flock—the brightness of angelic light surrounded them. A church has been founded there containing the tombs of those same shepherds.”

## CHAPTER VII. On Rachel’s tomb

The Book of Genesis also relates that Rachel was buried at Ephrath, that is, in the region of Bethlehem; and the Book of Places likewise reports that Rachel was buried in the same region beside the road. When I questioned Arculfus about this road, he replied:

“There is a royal road that leads from Aelia southward toward Hebron. Bethlehem, situated six miles from Jerusalem, adjoins this road on the eastern side. Rachel’s tomb is located at the far end of the same road on the western side—that is, on the right-hand side for those traveling toward Hebron. It is constructed in a poor manner, without any adornment, and surrounded by a stone pyramid. There too, even today, her name’s inscription is displayed, which Jacob, her husband, erected over it.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On Hebron

Hebron, also called Mambre, was once the capital of the Philistines and the dwelling place of giants; David reigned there for seven years. Now, as the holy Arculfus reports, it has no circuit of walls and displays only certain surviving traces of the ruins of the city once destroyed. It does, however, have some lanes constructed in a poor manner and villages—some within and others outside the remaining ruins of those demolished walls—situated across the open plain. A multitude of people inhabits these lanes and villages.

## CHAPTER IX. On the valley of Mambre

On the eastern side of the same Hebron there lies a field facing Mambre and the double cave, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a possession for a double tomb.

## CHAPTER X. On the tombs of the four patriarchs

In this valley the holy Arculfus visited the place of the tombs of Arbec—that is, of the four patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam, the first man. Their feet are turned southward and their heads toward the north, rather than being turned eastward, as is customary for the buried in other regions of the world. The place of their tombs is enclosed by a low square wall.

[Note: [Col. 0797] On this matter, see the homily of Haimo, bishop of Halberstadt, for the vigil of Easter, and Baronius under the year 34.]

Adam, the first-created man, to whom God the Creator said immediately after he had sinned and committed the transgression, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” is separated from the other three not far away, at the northernmost edge of that square stone enclosure. He does not rest in a tomb cut into the rock above ground, as the others of his descendants, honored in this way, rest; rather, he was buried in the earth and covered with soil. He himself, turned from dust into dust, rests there awaiting the resurrection together with all his descendants. Thus, in the case of his tomb, the divine sentence spoken concerning him and about him is fulfilled.

Following the example of the tomb of the first parent, the other three patriarchs also lie sleeping and resting, covered with humble dust. Above their four tombs, small memorial structures have been built out of individual stones that have been cut and dressed, placed above them as if in the form of some basilica, each shaped according to the length and width of its respective tomb. The three tombs of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are protected by three nearby hard, carefully worked stones placed above them and formed according to the shape described above. Adam’s tomb, however, is protected by a stone placed above it that is darker in color and more poorly worked.

Arculfus also saw there the humbler and smaller memorials of three women, namely Sarah, Rebecca, and Leah, who were buried in the earth. The small burial field of those patriarchs is known to lie one stade eastward from the wall of ancient Hebron. This Hebron, it is said, was founded before all the cities not only of Palestine but also of Egypt; it now appears miserably destroyed.

Thus far, it is enough to have set down what concerns the tombs of the patriarchs.

## CHAPTER XI. On Mount Mambre and its oak

The hill of Mambre lies a thousand paces north of the monuments described above. It is exceedingly grassy and covered with flowers, facing Hebron, which lies opposite it toward the southwest. This little hill, called Mambre, has a level plain at its summit. On the northern side of that summit a large stone church has been founded. On its right-hand side, between two great walls of the same basilica—marvelous to relate!—there stands the oak of Mambre, rooted in the earth. It is also called Abraham’s oak because he once received angels as guests beneath it.

Saint Jerome relates elsewhere that it remained from the beginning of the world until the reign of King Constantine. Perhaps for this reason he did not say that it had wholly perished, since in that same age, although it was no longer as enormous as it had previously been, a very large oak was still visible. Nevertheless, part of it remained fixed in its place. As Arculfus, who saw it with his own eyes, reports, a certain truncated stump [Gretser: a certain trunk] still remains from it, rooted in the earth and protected by the covering of the church, with a length of about two men. From this stump, described as *conso* [Gretser: *corroso*, “corroded”], and cut around on every side with axes, small pieces of wood are carried away to various provinces of the world, out of reverence and remembrance for the same oak, beneath which, as was mentioned above, the famous and celebrated gathering of angels with the patriarch Abraham was once granted.

Around the same church, which is said to have been built there in honor of that place, a few dwellings of religious persons are visible. But enough has been said of these matters; let us proceed to others.

## CHAPTER XII. On the pine grove from which wood is carried on camels for the fires maintained in Jerusalem

As one leaves Hebron, in the broad plain situated to the north, a short distance from the edge of the road on the left, there appears a small pine-covered mountain, three miles from Hebron. From its pine grove, pinewood is carried on camels all the way to Jerusalem to feed the fires. On camels, I say, since throughout Judea, as Arculfus reports, wagons and even carts are rarely found.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Jericho

Our holy Arculfus saw the site of the city of Jericho, which Joshua overthrew after crossing the Jordan and killing its king. In its place, Oza of Bethel, of the tribe of Ephraim, built another city, which our Savior deigned to visit by his presence. At the time when the Romans were besieging Jerusalem, this city was captured and destroyed because of the treachery of its inhabitants. In its place a third city was founded, which itself was later overthrown after a long passage of time. Certain traces of its ruins are now visible, as Arculfus reports.

Marvelous to relate! Rahab’s house alone remained after three cities had been destroyed in the same place. She hid in the upper room of that house the two spies whom Joshua son of Nun [that is, Joshua son of Nun] had sent, concealing them beneath stalks of flax. Its stone walls remain without a roof.

The site of the entire city, deserted by human inhabitants and containing no house for dwelling, receives crops and vineyards. Between the site of the destroyed city and the Jordan River there are extensive palm groves. Among them lie small fields in which almost countless houses have been built for certain little people of the Canaanite stock who live there.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Gilgal

The often-mentioned Arculfus saw a large church founded at Gilgal. It was built at the place where the children of Israel, after crossing the Jordan, encamped and made their first settlement in the land of Canaan.

## CHAPTER XV. On the twelve stones that the children of Israel carried up after wading across the Jordan River and drying its depths

In that church the same holy Arculfus examined the twelve stones concerning which the Lord spoke to Joshua after the crossing of the Jordan, saying:

“Choose twelve men, one from each tribe, and command them to take from the middle of the Jordan’s channel, where the priests’ feet stood, twelve exceedingly hard stones. You shall place them at the site of the camp, where you will pitch your tents tonight” (Joshua IV).

Arculfus had seen these stones. Six of them lay on the right-hand side of the church pavement, and the other six on the northern side. All were unworked and humble. Each one, as Arculfus himself reports, can scarcely be lifted from the ground by two strong young men of the present day. One of them, no one knows by what accident, was broken into two pieces; it was again strengthened with iron and joined together by an artisan’s hand.

Gilgal, then, where the church mentioned above was founded, lies east of ancient Jericho, on this side of the Jordan, in the territory of the tribe of Judah, five miles from Jericho. The tabernacle also stood there for a long time, and the church mentioned above is said to have been built on its site. In that church the twelve stones mentioned above are preserved, honored with wondrous devotion and reverence by the inhabitants of that region.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the place where the Lord was baptized by John

That holy and venerable place where the Lord was baptized by John is always covered by the waters of the Jordan River. As Arculfus reports—for he reached that same place and swam across the river there and back—a wooden cross is fixed upright in the same holy place. Beside it, the water reaches up to the neck of a very tall standing man; at another time, when the waters have diminished because of extreme drought, it reaches only to the breasts. When a greater flood occurs, the entire cross is covered by the increased waters.

The place of the same cross, where, as was said above, the Lord was baptized, lies on this side of the riverbed. From there to the opposite bank, in the region of Arabia, a strong man could throw a stone with a sling.

From the place of the cross mentioned above, therefore, a stone bridge supported by arches extends as far as the dry land. Those who approach the cross itself descend by a slope and, after returning to the dry land, ascend again. At the river’s edge there is a small square church, founded, as tradition relates, at the place where the Lord’s garments were kept at the hour when he was baptized.

This church, supported by four stone piers (*cancri*), stands over the waters and is uninhabitable, because the waters enter beneath it from both sides. Above, it is protected by baked clay; below, as has been said, it is supported by piers and arches. This church stands in the lower parts of the valley through which the Jordan River flows.

In the higher parts there is a large monastery of monks, constructed opposite and above the church described above on the crest of the hillock. There too a church dedicated to Saint John the Baptist has been founded and is enclosed by the same monastery wall, built of squared stones.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the color of the Jordan

The color of the Jordan River, as Arculfus informed us, appears white on the surface, like milk. Its color can easily be distinguished from the color of the Dead Sea when it enters the salt sea and travels a long distance through its channel.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Dead Sea

The Dead Sea, when great storms cause its waves to collide, casts up abundant salt along the surrounding shores. This provides a very considerable benefit not only to the neighboring peoples everywhere but also to nations situated far away, since it is dried sufficiently by the heat of the sun.

Salt is obtained in another way from a certain mountain in Sicily. The stones of that mountain, torn from the earth, are shown by taste to be truly and naturally extremely salty salt; this is specifically called “salt of the earth.” Thus sea salt is called by one name and earth salt by another. Hence the Lord is also believed to have said metaphorically to the Apostles in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth,” and so forth (Matthew V).

Concerning this salt of the earth found on a mountain in Sicily, the holy Arculfus informed us, for he remained in Sicily several days and established by sight, taste, and touch that it was truly and extremely salty salt.

He also told us about the salt of the Dead Sea, which he likewise reported that he himself had tested by those same three senses. He also visited the shore of the lake mentioned above, whose length extends for five hundred and eighty stades to Zoara in Arabia, and whose width extends for one hundred and fifty stades to the vicinity of Sodom.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the sources of the Jordan

Our Arculfus also reached that place in the province of Phoenicia where the Jordan appears to emerge at the foot of Lebanon from two neighboring springs. One is called Jor and the other Dan; when combined, they receive the name Jordan.

It must be noted, however, that the Jordan does not begin at Panium, but in the land of Trachonitis, one hundred and twenty stades away, as far as Caesarea Philippi, which is now called Panias, taking its name from Mount Panium.

The name of the spring in Trachonitis is Fiala. It is always full of water, from which the Jordan is conveyed by underground channels and, divided at Panium, boils forth in streams of water. These waters, as was said above, are called Jor and Dan. Emerging from there and joining together into a single river after a certain interval, they form a river that then directs its course and proceeds for one hundred and twenty stades without interruption as far as the city called Julias.

Afterward it crosses through the middle of the lake called Genezar. From these places, after wandering through many deserts, it is received by the lake Asphalte and sinks into it. Thus, after victoriously leaving two lakes behind, it remains fixed in the third.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Sea of Galilee

Our often-mentioned holy Arculfus traveled around most of the Sea of Galilee, which is also called Lake Cinereth and the Sea of Tiberias. Large neighboring forests adjoin it. The lake itself [Corbie: its breadth] extends like a kind of sea for one hundred and forty stades in length and spreads for forty stades in width.

Its waters are fresh and suitable for drinking, since they contain nothing thick or muddy from marshy wetness. It is surrounded on every side by a sandy shore, and therefore its water is purer and better for use. No other place is said to have fish superior in kind, taste, or appearance.

We have reported these brief details about the origin of the Jordan and Lake Cinereth, drawn partly from the third book of the Jewish Captivity and partly from the experience of the holy Arculfus. He himself confidently reports that from the place where the Jordan emerges from the outlet of the Sea of Galilee to the place where it enters the Dead Sea, he traveled for eight days. The holy Arculfus also often viewed this exceedingly salty sea from the vantage point of the Mount of Olives, as he himself relates.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the well of Samaria

The holy priest Arculfus, traveling through the region of Samaria, reached the city of that province called in Hebrew Shechem and, in Greek and Latin usage, Sicima. Although incorrectly, it is commonly called Sychar.

Near this same city he saw a church built outside the wall. It extends in four divisions toward the four quarters of the world, as if in the likeness of a cross; its shape is described below.

At its center, the spring of Jacob, which is also commonly called a well, faces toward its four sides and is situated in the middle within it. Over this well the Savior, wearied by the labor of his journey, sat at the sixth hour of a certain day. At that same midday hour the Samaritan woman came to draw water from the well.

Concerning this well, the woman said to the Lord, among other things: “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep” (John IV).

Arculfus, who drank water from this well, also described its depth, saying:

“The well that I saw has a depth of twenty *oriae* twice over, that is, forty cubits. An *oria*, or cubit, is the extension of both hands stretched out from either side.”

Shechem, therefore, which is also Sicima, was once a priestly and refuge city. It is situated in the tribe of Manasseh and on Mount Ephraim, where the bones of Joseph are buried.

## CHAPTER XXII. On a certain little spring in the wilderness

The often-mentioned Arculfus saw a clear little spring in the wilderness. Saint John the Baptist is traditionally said to have drunk from it. It is protected by a stone roof coated with plaster.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On locusts and wild honey

Concerning the same John, the Evangelists write: “His food was locusts and wild honey.”

Our Arculfus saw in that wilderness where John lived a certain very small kind of locust. Their little bodies are slender and short, about the size of a finger. Since their flight is short, like the light leaps of frogs, they are easily caught in the grass; when cooked in oil, they provide a poor man’s food.

From Arculfus we learned the following through his experience concerning wild honey. He said:

“In the same wilderness I had seen certain trees whose leaves are broad and round, the color of milk and the taste of honey. These leaves are by nature exceedingly fragile. Those who wish to take them as food first rub them between their hands and then eat them. This is the wild honey found in the woods.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the place where the Lord blessed five loaves and two fish

Our often-mentioned Arculfus reached this place. Its grassy and level field has never been plowed from the day on which the Savior fed five thousand people there with five loaves and two fish.

No buildings are visible there. Arculfus saw only a few stone columns lying along the bank of the little spring from which, it is said, those people drank on the same day when the Lord refreshed them, hungry as they were, with such nourishment.

This place lies on this side of the Sea of Galilee, facing the city of Tiberias, which lies opposite it toward the south.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Capernaum

Those who descend from Jerusalem and wish to reach Capernaum, as Arculfus reports, travel by the direct road through Tiberias. Then, along Lake Cinereth—which is also the Sea of Tiberias and the Sea of Galilee—they have access to the place of the blessing mentioned above. From there, following the shore of the same lake mentioned above, they reach maritime Capernaum after a short circuit.

It lies in the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali. Arculfus, who viewed it from the neighboring mountain, reports that it has no wall and is confined within a narrow space between the mountain and the lake. It extends for a long distance along the shore, with the mountain to the north and the lake to the south, stretching from west to east.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Nazareth and its church

The city of Nazareth, as Arculfus reports—for he lodged there—also has no circuit of walls, like Capernaum, but is situated above a mountain. It nevertheless has large stone buildings, and two very large churches have been built there.

One stands in the middle of the city, founded upon two supports (*cancri*), at the place where the house in which our Savior was brought up once stood. This church, supported, as was said above, by two mounds with arches between them [Corbie: vaults], has a very clear spring situated below, between the same mounds. All the people of the city frequent it, drawing water from it. From this same spring, water in vessels is raised upward by pulleys into the church built above.

The other church is built at the place where the house once stood in which the archangel Gabriel entered to the blessed Mary and, at that very hour, spoke with her, whom he found alone.

We learned this account of Nazareth from the holy Arculfus, who lodged there for two nights and the same number of days. He could not stay there longer because a soldier of Christ, knowledgeable about the places, compelled him to hurry. This man, Peter by name, was born in Burgundy and led a solitary life. After the same circuit, he returned to the solitary place where he had previously lived.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Mount Tabor

Mount Tabor in Galilee lies three miles from Lake Cinereth. It rises in a remarkable rounded form, gathered together on every side, and faces the lake mentioned above on its northern side. It is exceedingly grassy and covered with flowers.

On its pleasant summit there is a broad plain surrounded by a very large forest. In the middle of this open field there is a large monastery of monks, together with many of their cells. For the level summit of that mountain is not narrowed into a confined peak but expands in breadth for twenty-four stades; its height rises to thirty stades.

On the same upper plateau, three celebrated churches of considerable size have been founded, corresponding to the number of those tents about which Peter, gladdened by a heavenly vision and greatly frightened on that holy mountain, spoke to the Lord, saying: “It is good for us to be here; let us make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew XVII).

The buildings of the monastery mentioned above, the three churches, and the monks’ cells are all enclosed by a stone wall. Saint Arculfus lodged there for one night on the height of that holy mountain. Peter of Burgundy, a worshiper of Christ and his guide along the paths in those lands, did not allow him to remain longer in one and the same lodging, out of consideration for the need to hurry.

In this connection it should also be noted that the name of that famous mountain ought to be written in Greek letters with theta and a long omega, Θαβὼρ (*Thabōr*); in Latin letters, with aspiration, *Thabor*, with the letter *o* lengthened. This spelling of the name is found in books written in Greek.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Damascus

Damascus is a great royal city. As Arculfus reports—he lodged there for several days—it lies in a broad plain and is enclosed by an extensive circuit of walls. It is also fortified with frequent towers and has many olive groves outside the walls. Four large rivers flowing through it make it flourish joyfully.

A king of the Saracens has obtained authority there and reigns. A large church has also been founded there in honor of Saint John the Baptist. A church of the Saracens, those unbelievers, has likewise been built in the same city and is frequented by them.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Tyre

Our Arculfus, who traveled through many regions, also entered Tyre, the capital of the province of Phoenicia. In Hebrew and Syriac it is called Soar. Greek, Latin, and barbarian histories report that it had no entrance from the mainland.

Some, however, assert that afterward embankments were thrown up by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans; that the place was prepared for attack by the besieger with projectiles and battering rams; and that it was then made into an island and a level plain.

This city was exceedingly beautiful and noble, and not without reason is its name interpreted in Latin as “narrowness,” for the island and city occupy the same narrow extent of land. It is situated in the land of Canaan, concerning which the Canaanite or Syrophoenician woman was mentioned in the Gospel.

It should therefore be noted that the holy Arculfus’s account of the location of Tyre agrees in every respect with what we earlier extracted from the commentaries of Saint Jerome. Similarly, what we described above concerning the location and shape of Mount Tabor according to the account of Saint Arculfus differs in no way from what Saint Jerome relates about the location and remarkable roundness of that same mountain. From this Mount Tabor to Damascus, Arculfus traveled for seven days [variant: eight].

## CHAPTER XXX. On Alexandria, the River Nile, and its crocodiles
That great city, which was once the metropolis of [Col. 0806A] Egypt, was formerly called in Hebrew No: a very populous city, which, from its famous founder, Alexander, king of the Macedonians, is known among all peoples by the name Alexandria, receiving both the city’s size and its name from that same restorer. Arculfus, too, in describing its location, differs in no respect from what we previously learned by reading. Coming down from Jerusalem and beginning to sail from Joppa, he made a journey of forty (thus) days to Alexandria, concerning which the prophet Nahum speaks briefly, saying:

> Water surrounds it.  
> Its wealth is the sea; its waters are its walls.

For on its southern side it is enclosed by the mouths of the Nile River, but on the northern side by Lake Mareotis. Thus its situation is clearly described: lying upon the Nile and the sea, it is surrounded on either side by waters; it lies like a barrier between Egypt and the Great Sea, a city without a harbor and difficult of access from outside.

Its harbor is more difficult than others: broad, as though shaped like the human body, at the head itself and at the anchorage, but narrower at the throat, where it receives the passage of the sea and ships, by which certain means of breathing are supplied to the harbor. Once one has escaped the narrows and mouth of the harbor, the sea spreads far and wide, like the remaining shape of the body. On the right side of the same harbor there is a small island, on which stands a very large tower. Greeks and Latins alike, following the use of the thing itself, have commonly called it the Pharos, because it is visible from far away to sailors, so that before they approach the harbor at night they may recognize from the blaze of its flames that the neighboring land is near them, and may not, deceived by darkness, strike the reefs or fail to find the entrance to the vestibule.

There are therefore attendants there who kindle a fire with torches and other piles of wood placed beneath it, as both herald and marker of the land, showing to those entering the harbor’s throat the narrows, the recesses of the waters, and the winding passages of the vestibule, so that a light keel may not graze the rocks and, at the very entrance, strike hidden reefs beneath the waves. The ship must therefore deflect its straight course slightly, lest, dashed against unseen rocks, it meet danger there. For the entrance to the harbor is narrower, being constricted on the right-hand side; on the left, however, the harbor is broad.

Around the island, therefore, [Col. 0806D] great masses of immense size are thrown down, lest the foundations of the island, struck by the constant assault of the rising sea, give way and be loosened by the violence of the winds. Hence, without doubt, it happens that the central channel between the opposing rough rocks and the shattered masses is always agitated and turbulent, and that the ship’s entry becomes dangerous throughout the entire passage.

The harbor extends for a length of thirty stadia. And although there may be a very great storm, inside the harbor it is entirely secure because of its configuration: by the narrows mentioned above and by the obstruction of the island it turns the waves of the sea away from itself. [Perhaps: because] through those same narrows of the harbor shore, the basin extending throughout the harbor is driven away from storms and calmed by the cold winds, through which the entrance is made rough.

Nor is it without reason that this harbor possesses such protection and such size, since it is necessary that goods useful to the whole world be conveyed into it. For innumerable peoples seek the commerce of those regions for the use of their entire city [Perhaps: world], and the land is rich in grain and abundant in other gifts of the earth and in merchandise; it feeds and supplies the entire world with grain and necessary commodities.
