To such a region—which is undoubtedly lacking in rain—the irrigating waters of the Nile provide spontaneous showers. There the fields are moderated by both things: the abundance of the sky and the fertility of the earth; and there the ground alone provides advantage and sustenance to sailors and farmers. These sail; those sow. The former transport goods by ships; the latter cultivate the earth, sowing without a plow and traveling without a wagon.

You can see the region marked out by streams, and, as though by lofty walls, the dwellings of ships extending across the whole land, which cling on both sides to the margins of the banks of the Nile River. For it is navigable as far as the city called Elephantine. Beyond that, the cataracts—that is, the riverine hills of water—do not allow a ship to proceed, not because of any lack of depth in the eddy, but because of the precipitous course of the entire river and the kind of waterfall formed by its rushing waters.

The account of the holy Arculfus concerning the situation of Alexandria and the Nile is therefore shown not to differ from what we have learned by reading in the books of others. From these works we have inserted into the present description, in a brief text, certain excerpts: namely, concerning the city’s lack of a harbor and the difficulty of its port; the island and tower constructed upon it; Alexandria’s position, bounded by the sea [Vatican manuscript: or] and the mouths of the Nile River; and other matters.

This undoubtedly causes the site of the same city, which is constricted and strangled in this way by two sides, to extend a very long distance, along a narrow route, from west to east. Arculfus’s account also demonstrates this, since, as he himself relates, he began to enter the city at the third hour of the day in the month of October, walking along the length of the city; and he could scarcely reach the end of its length before evening.

The city is enclosed by a long circuit of walls, further fortified with frequent towers, extending along the bank of the river and the shore of the curved sea. Likewise, for those arriving from the Egyptian side and entering the Alexandrian city, a large, solidly built church appears on the nearby northern side. There the evangelist Mark lies buried in the earth, and his tomb, constructed of marble stones and called a *Memoria*, is displayed before the altar in the eastern part of the same rectangular church.

[Note: [Col. 0807C] This section is absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

These things, then, have been said concerning Alexandria, which, before it was enlarged and built up by Alexander the Great, was called No [Col. 0808B], as stated above. Its adjoining mouth of the Nile River, called the Canopic mouth, separates Asia from Egypt and Libya.

Because of the overflowing of the Nile River, the Egyptians therefore construct high embankments around its banks. If these should be broken through the negligence of their keepers or by an excessive bursting of the waters, they do not water the fields lying beneath them at all, but overwhelm and devastate them. For this reason, as the holy Arculfus relates—he who often crossed that same river as it flows through Egypt—many of those who inhabit the flat lands of Egypt live in houses above the waters, supported by transverse beams.

Crocodiles, as the priest Arculfus relates, are aquatic four-footed beasts that dwell in the Nile River. They are not large, but extremely voracious, and so powerful that if one of them should happen to find a horse, donkey, or ox cropping grass beside the riverbank, it emerges in a sudden attack and assaults it; even biting one foot of the creature and dragging it beneath the waters, it devours the entire animal completely.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0807]

## CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the city of Constantinople

[Col. 0807C]

The often-mentioned Arculfus, returning from Alexandria, stayed for several days on the island of Crete. Sailing from there, he made for Constantinople, where he remained for several months. This is undoubtedly the metropolis of the Roman Empire. It is surrounded on every side by the sea, except on its northern side, where that sea, issuing from the Great Sea for sixty miles, extends as far as the city wall. From the wall of Constantinople, however, this same sea extends forty [Grets., sixty] miles to the mouths of the Danube River.

This imperial city, therefore, enclosed by a circuit of walls measuring twelve miles, has corners constructed according to the configuration of the sea along the maritime shore, as Alexandria or Carthage does, and walls fortified, after the manner of Tyre, with frequent towers. Within the city walls it has numerous houses, many of which rise in wondrously large stone structures resembling the dwellings of Rome.

## CHAPTER TWO. Concerning the foundation of the same city

[Col. 0808D]

Concerning its foundation, the citizens relate the following tradition, handed down by their ancestors. They say:

The emperor Constantine, having gathered an infinite multitude of people and having gathered from every side, at infinite expense and to the near-stripping of all the cities, began to build a city bearing a share of his own name in the Asian region—that is, in Cilicia—across the intervening sea which, in those lands, separates Asia from Europe.

One night, while innumerable armies of workers were sleeping in tents along the immense length of the camps, all the kinds of tools which craftsmen accustomed to various kinds of work had been using suddenly disappeared; no one knew how. When, early the next morning, many workers, distressed with grief at this sudden and unexpected disappearance, brought their complaint to the emperor Constantine, the king asked them in turn:

“Have you heard that any other things were taken from the camp?”

“None,” they replied, “except the tools belonging to every kind of work.”

Then the king ordered them, saying:

“Go quickly, and, moving back and forth, inspect the shores of the neighboring regions along the sea. If you should happen to find your tools in any field, guard them there for the time being, and do not bring them back here; but have some of your number return to me, so that I may know for certain that the tools have been found.”

Hearing this, the workers obeyed the king’s commands, and, going out as they had been ordered, inspected the sea and the neighboring boundaries of the fields on both sides. And behold, on the European side beyond the sea they found a heap of tools, gathered together between two seas.

After discovering the place, some of them returned to the king and reported that they had found the tools in such a place. When he learned this, the king immediately ordered the trumpeters to sound their trumpets throughout the camp and ordered the army to move, saying:

“Let us migrate from here to build a city in the place divinely designated for us.”

At the same time, having prepared ships with the whole army, he crossed over to the place where the tools had been found, recognizing from their transfer that this place had been prepared for him by God. There he immediately founded a city, which, by combining his own name with the Greek designation for a city, is called Constantinople, so that the founder’s name forms the first part of the compound.

This description of the location and foundation of that royal city may suffice.

## CHAPTER THREE. Concerning the church in which the Lord’s cross is kept

Moreover, we must not remain silent about the celebrated round stone church of that same city, of extraordinary size. As the holy Arculfus relates—he who attended it for no short time—it rises from the lowest foundations in three walls, is raised above them to a greater height in three tiers, and, perfectly round and exceedingly beautiful, is completed under a simple vaulted roof.

Supported by great arches, it has between each of the aforementioned walls a broad space suitable and convenient either for habitation or for praying to God. On the northern side of the interior building there is displayed a very large and beautiful cabinet. In it is kept a wooden chest, closed by a similarly wooden lid, in which is preserved the saving wood of the cross, on which our Savior was suspended and suffered for the salvation of the human race.

This celebrated chest, as the holy Arculfus relates, is raised with such a precious treasure above the golden altar on three consecutive days each year. That altar is located in the same round church; it is two cubits long and one cubit wide.

Only on three successive anniversary days, I say, is the Lord’s cross raised and placed upon the altar: namely, on the Lord’s Supper, when the emperor and the army of soldiers enter the church and approach that altar, open the holy chest, and kiss the saving cross.

First of all, the emperor of the world kisses it with bowed face. Then, in order of rank or age, each person approaches one after another and kisses the venerable gibbet.

On the following day, that is, Good Friday before Easter, the queens, matrons, and all the women of the people approach in the aforementioned order and kiss it with complete veneration.

On the third day, that is, Holy Saturday, the bishop, followed after him by the entire clergy, approaches in due order with fear and trembling and every mark of honor, kissing the victorious wood placed in its chest.

When these holy and joyful kisses of the most holy cross have been completed, the venerable chest is closed and carried back to its cabinet with so honorable a treasure.

This, too, must be observed carefully: there are not two but three short pieces of wood there, in the form of a cross—namely, one transverse piece and one long piece, cut and divided into two equal parts. When the chest is opened, from these three honored pieces of wood there rises an extraordinary fragrance, full of the sweetness of a wonderful scent, as though all the flowers gathered there had been combined. It fills, satisfies, and gladdens everyone who is openly present within the interior walls of that church and who enters and stands there during that same period.

For from the knots of those three pieces of wood some fragrant liquid, pressed out as though in the likeness of oil, causes all those who enter, gathered from different nations, to perceive the aforementioned fragrance of the sweetest odor. If even a small drop of this liquid is placed upon the sick, whatever illness or disease afflicts them, they recover full health.

But enough has been written concerning these matters.

## CHAPTER FOUR. Concerning the martyr Saint George

The holy man Arculfus, who related all these things to us concerning the Lord’s cross—which he himself saw with his own eyes and kissed—also brought us an account concerning another confessor named George. He learned it in the city of Constantinople from certain experienced citizens, who were accustomed to tell it to him in this manner.

In the city of Diospolis, in a certain house, a marble image of the confessor George is depicted on the column to which he was bound and scourged during the persecution. After the scourging, however, he was released from his bonds and lived for many years.

One day, when a certain hard-hearted and unbelieving little man entered that same house while seated on a horse, he saw the marble column and asked those who were present:

“Whose image is formed upon the marble column?”

They replied:

“This is the figure of the confessor George, who was bound to and chastised at this column.”

When the utterly foolish man heard this, he became very angry with the insensible object and, at the instigation of the devil, struck the image of the holy confessor with a spear.

The spear of that adversary, penetrating the stone column with wondrous ease as though through a soft ball of snow, pierced it on its outer side. Its iron point remained fixed within and could never be withdrawn by any means. The shaft, however, was broken off externally against the small marble image of the holy confessor.

At that same moment the horse on which the wretched little man was sitting fell dead beneath him onto the floor of the house. As the miserable man himself fell to the ground, he thrust his hands into the marble column, and his fingers, entering it as though into something soft [*palme*, corrupt; Note: [Col. 0811D] Gretser reads *politice*, corrected to *mollitie*, “softness”] or clay, became impressed and remained fastened in the same column.

When the wretch saw this—he could not draw the fingers of both hands back toward himself, for they were fixed and embedded in the marble image of the holy confessor—he invoked the name of the eternal God and of that same confessor, repenting, and prayed tearfully to be released by him from the bond.

The merciful Lord accepted his tearful repentance, he who does not desire the death of the sinner but that he should turn and live. He not only released him from that present visible marble bond but, by saving him through faith, mercifully freed him from the invisible bonds of sins as well.

From this it is clearly shown how great and what kind of honor George the confessor possessed with God amid his torments: God made his breastplate [Grets., *thoracida*, “breastplate”] naturally impenetrable penetrable by his power; by the same power he wonderfully made the adversary’s spear, naturally impenetrable, penetrable; and he made the fingers of that little man, weak and naturally unable to penetrate the same substance, powerfully able to penetrate it. At first the hard-hearted man himself could not withdraw them, once they had been bound and inserted in the marble; but at that same moment, greatly terrified and thereafter softened, he withdrew them in repentance by God’s gift.

Wonderful to relate! To this very day the same impressions of his ten fingers—five on each hand—are visible down to the roots, inserted into the marble column. In their place the holy Arculfus inserted his own ten fingers, which likewise entered as far as the roots.

The blood of that little man’s horse, whose thigh was broken into two parts when it fell dead upon the pavement, could in no way be washed away or erased. The same equine blood has remained indelible on the pavement of the house down to our own times.

The holy Arculfus also communicated to us another trustworthy account concerning the same confessor George. He learned it without doubt from certain experienced and sufficiently reliable narrators in the aforementioned city of Constantinople, who were accustomed to speak of that holy confessor in the following manner.

A certain secular little man entered the city of Diospolis on horseback at the time when many thousands of people were gathering from every side for an expedition. Approaching, he entered the house in which the aforementioned marble column stood, bearing upon it the painted image of the holy confessor George. He began to speak to it as though to George himself, saying:

“To you, George the confessor, I commend myself and my horse. May we both, through the power of your prayers, be delivered from every danger of wars, diseases, and waters, and may we return safely to this city after the expedition. If merciful God grants, according to the desire of my humble self, that our return prosper in this way, I shall offer you this horse of mine—which I love greatly—as a gift, presenting it before your image.”

When he had quickly finished these little words, he left the house. Moving among the multitude of the armies with his other companions, the man departed with the expedition. Although he first endured many and varied dangers of war, and many thousands of wretched little men were killed and lay scattered around him, he himself, seated upon his beloved horse, was preserved from every hostile circumstance according to the commendation he had made. By God’s gift, he returned safely to Diospolis.

Carrying gold with him as the price of his horse, he joyfully entered the house in which the image of the same holy confessor was kept. He addressed Saint George as though he were present, saying:

“Holy confessor, I give thanks to the eternal God, who has brought me back safely through the steadfastness of your exalted prayer. Therefore I bring you these twenty gold solidi, the price of my horse, which I first commended to you and which you have preserved for me until this day.”

As he said this, he placed the weight of gold described above before the feet of the image of the holy confessor, loving the horse more than the gold. Then he went outside, finished his genuflection, mounted the animal, and urged it to depart. But it could not be moved in any way.

Seeing this, the man dismounted, returned to the house, and brought ten more solidi, saying:

“Holy confessor, you were indeed a gentle protector to me, a horseman, amid the dangers of the expedition; but, as I see, you are hard and greedy in the sale of the horse.”

Having said this, he added ten to the twenty solidi and said to the holy confessor:

“I add these solidi to you, so that you may become favorably disposed toward me and release my horse to walk.”

After saying this, he went outside again, mounted the horse, and urged it to proceed. But it stood as though fixed in the same place and could not move even one foot.

Why say more? After mounting and dismounting four separate times, he entered the house, bringing ten solidi with him, and returned to the immobile horse. Again he went back into the house and ran back and forth. He could not move the horse by any urging until the number of the collected solidi reached sixty.

Then, repeating the speech mentioned above concerning the gentle kindness of the holy confessor and his safe protection during the expedition, and concerning his supposed harshness or even greed in business, and recalling such words, as is said, four times in succession, he returned to the house and finally addressed Saint George in this way:

“Holy confessor, now I know your will for certain. Therefore, in accordance with your desire, I offer you the entire weight of gold, namely sixty solidi, as a gift. I also give you my horse, which I had previously promised to donate to you after the expedition, although it is now bound by invisible bonds; but I believe that it will soon be released through your honor before God.”

When he had finished speaking, he left the house and found the horse released at that very hour. He led it with him into the house and assigned it as a gift to the holy confessor before the image. Then he departed joyfully, magnifying Christ.

From this it is clearly understood that whatever is consecrated to the Lord—whether a human being or an animal—cannot in any way be redeemed or exchanged, according to what is written in the Book of Leviticus (chapter XXVII):

> If anyone should exchange it, both the thing exchanged and that for which it was exchanged shall be sanctified to the Lord, and shall not be redeemed.

## CHAPTER FIVE. Concerning the image of Saint Mary

[Col. 0813C]

The often-mentioned Arculfus also related to us with certainty an account concerning the image of holy Mary, the Mother of the Lord, which he learned in the city of Constantinople from certain experienced witnesses. He said:

In that same metropolitan city, an image of blessed Mary was painted on a small wooden panel and hung upon the wall of a certain house. When a foolish and hard-hearted man asked whose image it was, he learned from someone who answered that it was the facial image of holy Mary, ever-virgin.

When that unbelieving Jew heard this, at the instigation of the devil he angrily took the image from the wall and ran to a neighboring house, where human excrement is customarily discharged through long openings in planks beneath the bodies of those seated there. There, to dishonor Christ born from Mary, he threw the image of his Mother through the opening onto the human excrement below. Then he himself sat over the same opening to relieve his bowels, and, acting with utter foolishness, discharged his own feces upon the image [Grets., *thoraciola*] of blessed Mary, which had just been placed there. After that most shameful evacuation, the utterly wretched man departed.

What he did afterward, how he lived, or what kind of end he met is unknown.

After that wicked man’s departure, another man from the Christian populace arrived—a fortunate man, zealous for the Lord’s things. Knowing what had happened, he sought the image of holy Mary. Finding it hidden among the human excrement, he lifted it up, carefully wiped and washed it, and cleansed it with the purest waters. He then placed it honorably in his own house.

Wonderful to relate! From that same panel of the image of blessed Mary, true oil continually boils forth and drips. Arculfus, as he is accustomed to relate, saw this with his own eyes.

This miraculous oil bears witness to the honor of Mary, the Mother of the Lord Jesus, concerning whom the Father says:

> With my holy oil I have anointed him. (Psalm LXXXVIII)

Likewise, the Psalmist speaks to the same Son of God, saying:

> God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. (Psalm XLIV)

These things, then, which we have diligently learned above from the mouth of the holy priest Arculfus concerning the situation and foundation of Constantinople, as well as the round church in which the saving wood is kept, and the other matters, are sufficient. He remained in that principal city of the Roman Empire from the solemnity of Easter until the Lord’s Nativity; afterward he sailed from there toward Rome.

## CHAPTER SIX. Concerning the volcanic mountain that always thunders

There is an island in the Great Sea, toward the east, twelve miles distant from Sicily. On it is Mount Vulcanus, which thunders like a storm throughout all days and nights, so greatly that the land of Sicily, although lying farther away, seems to be shaken by a terrifying trembling. It appears to thunder more loudly on Friday and Saturday; at night it is seen to blaze at all times, but by day to smoke.

Arculfus dictated this account of the same mountain to me as I wrote. He saw it with his own eyes, fiery at night and smoky by day. He also heard its thunderous sound with his own ears, having stayed for several days in Sicily [Note: [Col. 0813D] Thus far the Vatican manuscript.]

I therefore beseech all who read these brief books to pray for the divine mercy on behalf of the same holy priest Arculfus, who, as one who had most willingly visited those holy places, dictated these experiences to us. Although I have been occupied amid laborious and almost unbearable ecclesiastical concerns, gathered together from every side throughout the day, I have nevertheless described and made them known, however humbly, in writing.

I therefore admonish the reader of these experiences not to neglect praying to Christ, the Judge of the ages, for me, a wretched sinner and the recorder [scribe] of these matters.

[Col. 0815]

# THE CANONS OF ADAMNAN

*(Mansi, Councils, vol. XII, p. 154.) (C,S)*

[Col. 0815A]

## I

Sea animals cast upon the shores, whose deaths we do not know, may be eaten in good faith, unless they are putrid.

## II

Animals falling from a cliff are to be accepted if their blood has been shed. But if their bones are broken and the blood has not flowed out, they are to be rejected.

## III

As animals killed in water, whose blood remains hidden within, are carcasses, so animals caught by beasts and left half alive are to be eaten by *bestialibus hominibus* [“beastly men”; sense uncertain].

## IV

An animal rendered half-alive by a sudden death, with its ear or another part cut off, is a carcass.

[Col. 0815B]

## V

If pigs eat carrion, their flesh, when fat or greasy from the carrion by which pigs grow fat, is to be discarded. But when they have grown lean and returned to their former leanness—

[Col. 0816A]

## VI

But if they have eaten carrion once or three times, after it has passed from their bellies, their flesh may be eaten in good faith.

## VII

Pigs that taste human flesh or blood are always *incliti* [text uncertain]. For in the Law, an animal with horns that kills a human being is unlawful.

## VIII

If a horse or a head of cattle strikes a human being within the territory of its city, its owner shall pay half an ounce for the person whose blood has been shed. If a human being strikes an animal in his own field, nothing is paid for it.

# OF THE EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE WORLD, DATE UNCERTAIN. CRESCONIUS, AFRICAN BISHOP

[Col. 0815]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON CRESCONIUS

*(Fabricius, Library of the Middle and Later Ages.)*

[Col. 0815C]

Cresconius or Crisconius, an African bishop around the year 570, wrote a *Brief Summary of the Canons* for Bishop Liberinus, arranged under three hundred titles—three hundred and three in the Helmstedt manuscript [Note: [Col. 0815] See B. Gebhard’s historical account of Theodore Meier on the collections of canons, § XVII]—drawn from the canons of the Apostles and from those of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Chalcedon, Sardica, and Carthage, as well as from the decrees of the Roman bishops. He was the first to join these to the ecclesiastical canons, and the first to include among them the decrees of Siricius, then of Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, and Gelasius.

This *Brief Summary* was first published by Peter Pithaeus from a manuscript of the church of Troyes, or Tricassina, together with the *Brief Summary of the Canons* composed around the year 450 by Fulgentius Ferrandus, whom the aforementioned Cresconius commended, Paris, 1588, octavo. It was later published at the end of the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church*, Paris, 1609, octavo.

From there it was published together with the *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons* of Dionysius Exiguus—around the year 500—by Christopher Justellus, Paris, 1628, octavo. Then, after the edition of Antonius Dandinus Alteserra [Flavius Franciscus de Hauteserre of Salvaizon], together with notes and the *Brief Summary* of Fulgentius Ferrandus, Poitiers, 1630, quarto, in which an ancient index is appended with notes to the *Brief Summary*, and after the edition of Peter Francis Chiflet, S.J., Dijon, 1649, quarto, this *Brief Summary* of Cresconius was reprinted more accurately in volume I of the *Canonical Library* of William Voellus and Henry Justellus, p. 458, Paris, 1661, folio.

There are also there two concordant indexes to Ferrandus and Cresconius. In the appendix, moreover, pp. 34–112, there is the *Harmony of the Canons* of the same Cresconius, presenting the canons themselves and the decrees arranged under the same three hundred titles, from a manuscript of the library of the Jesuit College of Clermont.

The *Brief Summary* was subsequently reprinted in the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyon edition, volume IX, from Chiflet’s edition; and from Pithaeus’s edition, together with the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church* and the *Ecclesiastical Miscellanies* of Peter Pithaeus, p. 316, Paris, 1687, folio.

In the manuscript of the Fathers of the Roman Oratory, in the library of Vallicelliana, Mabillon, p. 69 of the *Italian Itinerary*, reports that he found the following note:

> This Cresconius described in hexameter verse the wars and victories which John Des., patrician, won against the Saracens in Africa, around the year 698, in books … These books exist nowhere today.

See Pagi on the year 696, no. 5, and on the year 527, no. 14.

Gesner, in the appendix to his *Library*, writes:

> Cresconius the African poet, whom others call Crescentius, described in verse the wars waged by the emperor Justinian in Africa, and also wrote a *Harmony of the Canons*.

Certainly this *Harmony* was not written in verse by Cresconius. Yet I scarcely doubt that this Cresconius is the same person as Flavius Cresconius Corippus. Concerning him, if desired, see what I shall say shortly.

[Note: [Col. 0817] It may perhaps not be useless to mention here that the writings which follow—namely, Ferrandus’s *Brief Summary*, as well as Crisconius’s *Brief Summary*, and also the *Harmony of the Canons* of both authors—are being reprinted by us from the edition of Voellus and Justellus. EDITOR.]

[Col. 0817]

# JUSTELLUS TO THE READER
[Col. 0817B] Ferrandus, a deacon whom Sigebert lists among ecclesiastical writers, mentions in his little book of Rules, addressed to Count Reginus, Bishop Fulgentius of Ruspe as having recently died; both of them therefore appear to have lived around the time of the Emperor Anastasius. And perhaps someone may reasonably think that the account of the Life of Fulgentius of Ruspe, published among the histories of the saints, belongs to this same Ferrandus. But this little index of canons too, which we now publish for the first time from the distinguished codex of our Church of Troyes, is, as far as we believe, the oldest of all works of this kind. Gratian, at least, will owe it the restoration of its proper place in Distinction 63, which had hitherto been seriously defective even in that Roman recension; from a single copy of Ferrandus we have finally learned how to restore it as follows:

“But, as is found in the Abbreviation of the Canons of Fulgentius, deacon of the Church of Carthage, it was established in the Council of Septimunicum and in that of Macrianum that, for the election of a bishop, the judgment of the mother church should suffice.”

We have also appended the Chapters from Crisconius’s Repetition of the Canonical Breviary to Liberinus—or, as certain of our copies have it, to Pope Liberius—being content to note here that Crisconius seems to have used that same collection down to the time of Gelasius. Indeed, it is that very collection which is called the Body of Canons, not only by Gratian (Distinctions 19–20), but also by the supreme pontiffs Nicholas I and Leo IV. Several ancient copies of it also exist among us; that it was sent by Pope Hadrian to the Emperor and King Charles is attested by the acrostics of political verses prefixed to it. [Col. 0818B]

This codex contains precisely the same canons of the councils as the Greek collection published here in 640 by Joannes Tilius, a man of illustrious rank, from a very ancient codex of the Church of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, which also includes the African synods; but the Latin codex has the added letters of the Roman pontiffs, from Siricius to the younger Gregory. The Nomocanons of Photius and Theodore Balsamon, patriarchs of Constantinople, show that the Greeks preserved this same place among their Decretals.

Moreover, the translation found in our Body of Canons is plainly different from that of Dionysius the Scythian monk—also called the Abbot and Exiguus—addressed to Stephen, bishop of Salona. At Stephen’s urging, Dionysius undertook a new translation because, as he says, he was offended by the confusion of the earlier translation. He retained, however, the fifty canons said to be those of the Apostles; for Anastasius testifies in his preface to the Second Council of Nicaea, addressed to Hadrian, that as many as that number had been received by the Roman Church through the synodal decree of Stephen. The ancient collections that we have been able to see, as well as the Gallican ones, likewise retain these canons, in this number, from Dionysius’s translation, so that this translation may reasonably be called the common one. The translation of the remaining Greek canons, however, appears in varied and differing forms, so that it is not easy to determine which one should be regarded as common to the Latin Churches, although it is more likely that the version found in that Body of Canons was the one more generally used among us. But these matters require fuller treatment; God will provide the occasion and time for that, when he wills. Meanwhile, enjoy this service of ours, and farewell.

[Col. 0817]

## ABBREVIATION OF THE CANONS OF FULGENTIUS FERRANDUS, DEACON OF THE CHURCH OF CARTHAGE (C)

[Col. 0817D] 1. That neophytes are not to be ordained. Council of Nicaea, title 2; Council of Sardica, title 14; Council of Laodicea, title 3.

2. That any layman chosen for the episcopate must first pass one year in ecclesiastical ministry through all the grades. Council of Suffetula.

3. That one who, after baptism, has enrolled in secular military service is to be barred from ordination. Council of Cella.

4. That a bishop is to be ordained by three bishops, with the consent of the others expressed in writing, and with the confirmation of the metropolitan or primate. Council of Nicaea, title 4; likewise, title 6; Council of Antioch, title 19; Council of Laodicea, title 12; Council of Carthage under Bishop Genethlius, title 10; Universal Council of Carthage, title 49; Council of Zella, from a letter of Pope Siricius.

[Col. 0818D] 5. That, when anyone objects, other bishops in addition to the three are also to be added in the ordination of a bishop. Council of Carthage, title 50.

6. That one bishop is not to ordain another bishop, except in the Roman Church. Council of Zella, from a letter of Pope Siricius.

7. That a bishop who, after receiving the laying-on of hands, refuses the ministry is to remain excommunicated until he consents. Council of Antioch, title 17. But if, though willing, he is not accepted by the people, he is to await a full synod without loss of his honor. Council of Antioch, title 18.

8. That a bishop who has been ordained but is not accepted is not to take possession of another Church, but is to sit as a presbyter in the Church where he had been a presbyter. Council of Ancyra, title 18.

9. That the decrees of the councils are first to be impressed upon an ordained bishop. Council of Carthage, title 10.

10. That an ordained bishop is to receive from his ordainer a signed letter containing both the date of his ordination and the name of the consul. Council of Milevis, title 4.

11. That, for the election of a bishop, the judgment of the mother church should suffice. Council of Septimunicum; Council of Macrianum.

12. That a bishop is not to be ordained in a village or hamlet. Council of Laodicea, title 55.

13. That a bishop is not to be ordained in a diocese that has never had a bishop, except with the consent of the bishop to whom that diocese belongs, and then only by a full council and with the authority of the primate. Council of Carthage, title 52; likewise, the fifty-fourth Council of Carthage, “In Basilica,” title 5.

14. That a bishop ordained for a diocese is to hold that diocese alone. Council of Carthage, title 54.

15. That bishops, presbyters, and deacons are not to be ordained unless they have made all those belonging to them Christians. Council of Carthage, title 3.

16. That bishops, presbyters, and deacons are to abstain from their wives. Council of Carthage, title 1; Council of Zella.

17. That no bishop is to establish a see in a diocese after abandoning the mother church. [Note: On the authority of old codices, “cathedram” should be added.] Council of Carthage, title 6.

18. That bishops or clerics are not to pass from city to city, nor from province to province. Council of Nicaea, title 11; Council of Sardica, titles 2 and 3; Council of Antioch, titles 3 and 21; Council of Constantinople, titles 2 and 3.

19. That bishops are to remain in a foreign city for only three weeks. Council of Sardica, title 15.

20. That those who wish to remain in a foreign city for fear of persecution are not to be prevented. Council of Sardica, title 22.

21. That no bishop, even if chosen by the people, is to take possession of a vacant church except by the authority of a full council. Council of Antioch, title 16.

22. That no bishop acting as administrator is to hold the see assigned to him for more than a year, but is to ask them for a bishop himself. Council of Carthage, title 9.

23. That episcopal administrators are to summon the peoples who have no bishop, so that they may receive one; but if they neglect to accept one, then, once the administrator has been removed, they are to remain as they are while they seek a bishop for themselves. Council of Macrianum.

24. That no bishop is to usurp another’s people. Council of Carthage under Saint Gratus, title 9; Council of Carthage under Bishop Genethlius, title 9; likewise, Council of Carthage, title 5.

25. That a bishop who, without the judgment of the bishops, has held a people whom he believes to belong to his see is to lose his case. Council of Carthage, title 12.

26. That no bishop is to dare assert a claim for himself in another’s congregation. Council of Junca.

27. That a bishop is not to receive or ordain another’s cleric. Council of Nicaea, title 12; Council of Sardica, titles 19 and 20; Council of Antioch, title 22; Council of Carthage under Saint Gratus, title 4; likewise, Council of Carthage, titles 28 and 53.

28. That no bishop is either to ordain another’s monk in the Church or make him superior in his monastery. Council of Carthage, title 14.

29. That a bishop is not to perform an ordination in the presence of catechumens. Council of Laodicea, title 4.

30. That if a bishop, compelled by necessity, has veiled a virgin before the age of twenty-five, the council’s decree concerning that number of years is not to harm him. Council of Carthage, title 18.

31. That a bishop’s property is not to be subject to ecclesiastical property, but that he himself may dispose of it as he wishes. Council of Antioch, title 24.

32. That no bishop is to appoint outsiders or heretics as heirs, even if they are relatives. Council of Carthage, title 15.

33. That bishops or presbyters are to grant nothing by gift to those who are not Catholics. Council of Carthage, title 23.

34. That bishops or presbyters are not to transfer to other places anything belonging to the places where they are ordained unless they have first rendered an account. Council of Hippo Regius, title 5.

35. That bishops are compelled to restore to the Church whatever they have acquired in their own name; but whatever is given to them, they may bestow upon whomever they wish. Council of Hippo Regius, title 8.

36. That a bishop is to have authority over the administration of ecclesiastical property. Council of Antioch, title 25.

37. That, without the bishop’s knowledge, no one is to dare either give or receive the offerings of produce owed to the Church. Council of Gangra, titles 7 and 8.

38. That the bishop of the mother church is not to usurp anything that has been given to Churches established in the diocese. Council of Hippo Regius, title 9.

39. That the children of bishops are not to be joined in marriage to pagans, heretics, or schismatics. Council of Carthage, title 21.

40. That the children of bishops or clerics are neither to stage spectacles nor attend them. Council of Carthage, title 20.

41. That bishops are not to emancipate their children unless they have already been tested. Council of Carthage, title 22.

42. That bishops are not to go indiscriminately to the imperial court. Council of Sardica, titles 9, 10, and 11; Council of Antioch, title 11.

43. That any bishop who has sought a public trial from the emperor is to be deprived of his proper honor. Council of Carthage, title 9.

[Col. 0821A] 44. That every bishop is permitted to draw up petitions when something must be requested from public courts against heretics. Council of Marazanum.

45. That a bishop is to do nothing without the metropolitan’s council except those things that concern the governance of his own Church. Council of Antioch, title 9.

46. That bishops are not to sail without a formal letter from the primate. Council of Carthage, title 36.

47. That bishops are not to sell Church property without the advice of the primate. Council of Carthage, title 5; Council of Hippo, title 9.

48. That, by the bishop’s foresight, a dwelling is to be selected for virgins who are orphans. Council of Carthage, title 40 [Troyes, title 11, incorrectly].

49. That the periods of penance are to be determined for penitents by the judgment of the bishops. Council of Carthage, title 39.

50. That, by the judgment of the bishop, the period of penance or reconciliation is to be determined for a Donatist who, after having performed penance among his own people, is converted. Council of Carthage, title 2.

51. That a bishop is to hear accused presbyters after summoning five bishops; cases involving deacons, with three; but he alone is to examine the cases of the rest. Council of Carthage, title 17.

52. That one bishop is not to claim jurisdiction for himself alone: this was dealt with in another Council of Carthage.

53. That no bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been excommunicated is to communicate. Council of Nicaea, title 5; Council of Sardica, title 17; Council of Carthage, title 8 [Codex Corbeiensis, title 9]; Council of Antioch, title 2.

54. That if a bishop has been excommunicated by a synod, he is not to dare to communicate; and if he does so, he is not to have hope of restoration. Council of Antioch, title 4; Council of Hippo Regius, title 3.

55. That, if a bishop has a case, he is to be heard by twelve bishops. Council of Carthage under Saint Genethlius, title 8.

56. That bishops appointed as judges in a case are to hear it within the fixed time. Council of Septimunicum.

57. That, if two bishops have a dispute in one province, they are not to summon bishops from another province for judgment. Council of Sardica, title 4.

58. That, if several episcopal judgments have been issued concerning an accused bishop, the metropolitan of another province is to be summoned. Council of Antioch, title 14. What is to be observed in accusations against bishops. Council of Carthage, title 15.

59. That a bishop who has been adjudged may appeal, if he wishes, to the apostolic see. Council of Sardica, title 5.

60. That, if he has appealed [perhaps something is missing], no one is to be ordained in his see. Council of Sardica, title 6.

61. That, if someone appeals from the judges appointed by the primate, other judges of greater number are to be appointed; and if he appeals from them as well, the matter is to be deferred to the judgment of the council. Council of Thenita.

62. That, if a bishop condemned by judging bishops has been acquitted by more eminent bishops, this is not to harm those judges if they judged with a good intention. Council of Carthage, title 19.

63. That a bishop condemned by all the bishops of the province is not to have the opportunity to reopen the judgment. Council of Antioch, title 15.

64. That a bishop condemned by the bishops whom he himself chose as judges is not to dare appeal elsewhere. Council of Carthage, title 3; likewise, Council of Carthage, title 15.

65. That bishops appointed as judges in any case are themselves to select the place of the hearing. Council of Zella.

66. That a deposed bishop is not to refer his case to the emperor. Council of Antioch, title 12.

67. That an accused bishop, or anyone from the clergy who has been accused before the Church, is not to proceed to the public courts. Council of Carthage, title 18.

[Col. 0829]

# The Canonical Summary of Crisconius, African Bishop

Here is presented the concordance of the canons of the councils written below and of the Roman pontiffs—that is, the canons of the Apostles, of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea [or: Novae Caesareae], Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Chalcedon, Sardica, and Carthage; likewise those of the pontiffs Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, and Gelasius. (C)*

[Note: [Col. 0829D] Another reading: “The Letter of Crisconius to Liberius.”]

## The Preface Begins

[Col. 0829C]

To the truly holy and ever-blessed pontiff Liberinus, Crisconius, the least of Christ’s servants.

The incomparable dignity of your priesthood, by which you shine exceedingly in purity of faith and uprightness of life, continually urges you to labor with greater concern and to exercise the greatest diligence for the benefit of the Lord’s flock, whose helm you have undertaken to guide. For the completion of this duty of yours, you also seek the industry of your subjects, whom you must so nourish with the spiritual food of the bread that you may abundantly feed that same flock of the Lord.

Accordingly, since I perceive that the ordering of human life rests upon both human and divine laws, and that the precepts of civil law restrain aberrant steps with stricter reins, while ecclesiastical sanctions set a limit of right living before devout and faithful minds, you command us, leaving those civil laws aside, to gather into one work all the canonical constitutions which, from the earliest beginnings of the Christian service, both the holy Apostles and apostolic men have brought forth through the succession of ages; and, arranging their agreement and inserting headings, to make them more clearly intelligible. [Col. 0829D]

You undoubtedly see that this undertaking exceeds my powers by reason of the magnitude of the matter. Although I had very often wished to excuse myself to you, you pressed me by paternal authority, confidently promising that divine assistance would be available to help us. With this refuge closed to me, I further proposed that this Summary of the Canons had already been compiled by the most reverend Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, and that it ought to suffice for our instruction, lest, by seeking something else, we should be found in any respect to detract from his prudence.

To remove this excuse of ours entirely, you likewise objected that you did not require this from us in order to criticize that most wise man, but rather to grasp and polish more industriously our own small store of knowledge. When this had been done, and now taking care not to offer any excuse to Christ speaking through you, fortified by heavenly aid, I preferred to obey your commands and, with God’s favor, most willingly serve your wishes.

I was especially moved by this consideration: the venerable man mentioned above is known to have made his Summary for those who had already acquired a sound knowledge of these matters, so that, whenever they wished, they might recall through it what they desired. But in that work he appears, so to speak, to have set aside the study of the unlearned, who are the great majority, since he sent them first in search of matters which not everyone can find and which, once found, are not read through without tedium. No one doubts how burdensome it is for a reader who eagerly awaits knowledge of a subject to be referred first to a book which he has perhaps not read or does not know where to find. [Col. 0830D]

Therefore, while giving due praise to the aforementioned man, I considered it necessary, in service to the advancement of the little ones and according to your command, to set down at the head of this work, under a series of headings, all the ecclesiastical constitutions that have come to our knowledge, as has been said, and to remove the maze of uncertainty for those able and willing to learn them, so that their complete instruction may depend not upon the difficulty of the writer but only upon the reader’s negligence. [Col. 0831A]

This work will also, with God’s aid, achieve the following useful result: whenever the most equitable judge sees that each canonical decree about which a question has arisen at a given time has been arranged in many ways, he may learn through a sound examination whether he ought to govern his judgment with severity or with leniency. This instruction will be supplied above all by the consideration that he has been forewarned of the constitutions of several authorities, especially the more authoritative ones.

Therefore, I ask that, in this repetition of the Canonical Summary, as our distinguished doctor declared, those who know may forgive, so that those who do not know may not be offended. For it is better to offer something to one who already has it than to delay giving it to one who does not.

I also beseech your holiness that, if you should perhaps see that in some respect your desire has not been fully satisfied, you would approve rather the devotion and grant pardon for genuine ignorance. Pray for me, and always remember me, pontiff worthy of God.

# The Book of Canons Begins

[Col. 0831]

[Col. 0831B]

[Note: [Col. 0831] Many considerations persuade us that this is not by Crisconius. Although it is read in a very corrupt form in the manuscript, we nevertheless set it down here, restored as best we can.]

The man who is to be ordained bishop must first be examined: whether he is prudent by nature; teachable; temperate in conduct; chaste in life; sober; always available for his duties; approachable to people; learned; instructed in the law of the Lord; cautious in interpreting the meanings of Scripture; trained in ecclesiastical doctrines; and, above all, whether he states the articles of faith in simple words.

He must likewise affirm that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God; proclaim that the whole Trinity in the Godhead is coessential, consubstantial, and almighty; affirm that each individual person in the Trinity is fully God and that all three persons are one God; and affirm that the divine Incarnation took place not in the Father nor in the Holy Spirit but in the Son alone, so that the one who was the Son of God the Father in divinity might himself become, in the human name, the son of a mother: true God from the Father and true man from his mother, possessing flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul.

Both natures are simultaneously in him: man and God, one Son, one Christ, one Lord, Creator and author of all that exists, and Lord and ruler with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He must affirm that he suffered a true passion of the flesh and died a true bodily death; likewise, the resurrection of his flesh and the true restoration of his soul, in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

He must also be asked whether he believes the New and Old Testaments, and likewise the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles, to have one and the same author and God; and whether the devil became evil not by his created nature but by his own choice.

He must further be asked whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh which we bear, and not of another; whether he believes that judgment will come and that each person will receive either punishment or glory for what he has done in this flesh; whether he does not disapprove of marriage; whether he does not condemn second marriages; whether he does not condemn the eating of meat; whether he communicates with penitents who have been reconciled; whether in baptism all sins are forgiven, both original sin and those committed voluntarily; and whether no one is saved outside the Catholic Church.

When, after examination on all these matters, he has been found fully instructed, he shall then be ordained bishop with the assembly of clergy and laity and the gathering of all the bishops of the province, especially with the authority or presence of the metropolitan. Having received the episcopate in the name of Christ, he must submit not to his own pleasure or impulses but to the definitions of the Fathers.

## I. On the Ordination of a Bishop

[Col. 0832D]

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 1. A bishop shall be ordained by two or three bishops.

Council of Nicaea, title 4, On those who are advanced to the episcopate in the provinces. A bishop ought above all to be ordained by all the bishops who are in the province. But if this is difficult, either because of pressing necessity or because of the great distance of the journey, the ordination shall nevertheless be celebrated by three bishops who meet for this purpose, while those who are absent likewise decide and give their consent in writing. The confirmation of what is done in each province shall be entrusted to the metropolitan bishop.

[Col. 0833A]

Council of Antioch, title 19, On episcopal ordinations in the provinces. A bishop shall in no way be ordained apart from a synod and the presence of the metropolitan. Since this has been established in every respect, it is better that all the priests of the same province be present together; the metropolitan bishop must summon them. If all appear, so much the better. But if this is difficult, it is in every way fitting that at least the majority be present, or at least that the same judgment be confirmed in writing; and thus the ordination shall be celebrated with the presence or decree of the majority.

If anything contrary to these definitions is done, the ordination shall have no force. But if it is carried out according to the established rule and some oppose it out of personal contention, the judgment of the majority shall prevail.

[Col. 0833B]

Council of Laodicea, title 12, On episcopal ordinations. Bishops are to be advanced to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and of the bishops who are situated around them—namely, those who have been tested over a long period both in the word of faith and by the example of upright conduct.

Council of Carthage, title 13. Bishop Aurelius said: “What does your holiness say to this?” All the bishops replied that the statutes of the ancients ought to be preserved. Just as, without consulting the primate of any province, many assembled bishops must not presume so readily to ordain a bishop, unless necessity should arise, so three bishops, wherever they may be, must ordain a bishop at his command. And if anyone should act contrary to his own declaration or subscription in any matter, he shall deprive himself of his office.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0833] This is from an African council in an ancient manuscript, ‘Canons of the Roman Church.’]

Council of Carthage, title 16. Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said: “We have also been commanded that, since recently two of our brothers in Numidia presumed to ordain a bishop, you should decree that episcopal ordinations be celebrated only by twelve bishops.”

Bishop Aurelius said: “The ancient form shall be preserved, so that no fewer than three who have been appointed to ordain a bishop shall suffice. For in Tripoli, perhaps, and in Arzug, barbarian peoples appear to lie between us. In Tripoli, as is reported, there are only five bishops, and perhaps two of that number may be occupied by some necessity; for it is difficult for all of any number to be able to attend.

“Should this itself be an obstacle to ecclesiastical usefulness? In this church also, to which your holiness has deigned to come, we frequently have men to be ordained, almost every Sunday. Shall I often be able to summon twelve, or ten, or not many fewer bishops? But it is easy for me to add two neighboring bishops to my insignificance. Therefore your charity sees that this cannot itself be observed.”

Likewise on the same matter: that bishops must be added if there has been opposition to his ordination.

[Col. 0834A]

Council of the same church, title 17. “It must also be established that, when we have assembled to elect a bishop, if any opposition should arise—for such matters have been dealt with among us—the three who are already present must not presume to clear the man who is to be ordained. Instead, one or two more of the number mentioned above should be requested, if they can be obtained; and in the very congregation for which he is to be ordained, the persons of those who oppose him must first be examined, and finally the accusations themselves must be investigated. Once he has been cleared, he shall then be ordained publicly.

“If this agrees with the mind of your holiness, let it be confirmed by the response of your dignity.” All the bishops said: “It is entirely agreeable.”

## II. On the Ordination of Priests, Deacons, and Others

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 2. A priest, a deacon, and the other clerics shall be ordained by one bishop.

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 8. We have learned that men of unexamined life, some of whom have had numerous marriages, freely and without restraint aspire to the aforementioned dignities, as each person pleases. We attribute this not so much to those who reach them through immoderate ambition as specifically to the metropolitan pontiffs, who, by conniving at prohibited ventures, to the extent that they can, despise the commands of our God.

To say nothing of what we suspect more seriously: where is that which our God established in the law given through Moses, saying, “My priests shall marry only once”? And elsewhere: “Let priests take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not a divorced woman, not a prostitute.” Following this, the Apostle, who changed from persecutor to preacher, commanded that a man of one wife should become both priest and deacon. All these provisions are disregarded by the bishops of your regions, as though they had rather been established to be violated.

Since we must not neglect such usurpations, lest the just voice of the indignant Lord rebuke us—he who says, “You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and you made your portion with adulterers”—we determine by a general pronouncement what all the churches must henceforth follow and what they must avoid.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 32. The periods of service established by our predecessors must certainly be observed, and no one should quickly become a lector, quickly an acolyte, quickly a deacon, or quickly a priest. If they remain for a long time in the lesser offices and their life and service are jointly approved, they may later come to the priesthood after their years of service have earned its merits; they must not be given what an approved life has not merited.

Since it has therefore been shown by a definite rule who ought to be admitted and who rejected, from among all those whom your dignity sees unable to be rejected you must choose those whom you will make clerics. For if we wish to bestow neither favor nor benefit upon anyone, we can find men whose promotion we can undertake without guilt or shame.

Likewise on the conduct of those who have devoted themselves to God from childhood.

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 9. Whoever devotes himself to the service of the Church must be baptized from infancy, before the years of puberty, and associated with the ministry of lectors. From the beginning of adolescence until his thirtieth year, if he has lived commendably, he must be content with one wife only, and with one whom he received as a virgin through the common priestly blessing; he must be an acolyte and subdeacon. Afterward he may approach the rank of deacon, if he first proves himself worthy by leading with continence. If he has served commendably in that office for five years, he shall properly receive the priesthood. Thereafter, after ten years, he may attain the episcopal chair, provided that during these periods the integrity of his life and his faith have been approved.

Likewise from the decrees of Pope Zosimus, title 3. The following periods must be observed for each rank.

If he has given his name to ecclesiastical ministries from childhood, he must remain among the lectors through his twentieth year by continuous observance. If he comes already older and advanced in years, but after baptism immediately desires to devote himself to divine service, he must serve for five years either among the lectors or among the exorcists. Thereafter he must be an acolyte or subdeacon for four years, and then, if he deserves it, proceed to the blessing of the diaconate. In that order he must remain for five years if he has conducted himself blamelessly. Thereafter, supported by the years of service spent through all these ranks and by the proofs of his own faith, he may earn the priesthood.

From that office, if a stricter life has led him to good morals, he ought to hope for the supreme pontificate, provided that this law is observed: neither a man with two wives nor [Note: [Col. 0835D] “A penitent,” according to Dionysius Exiguus and the Code of the Roman Church.] a man undergoing penance may be admitted to these ranks. The same observance must also bind the defenders of the Church who come from the laity, if they deserve to belong to the clerical order.

Likewise on those advanced in years.

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 10. Whoever, already advanced in age, hastens from the laity to the sacred service after proving himself through a life of better purpose shall obtain the fruit of his desire only if, at the time when he is baptized, he is immediately enrolled among the lectors or exorcists—provided that it is established that he has had or has only one wife and that he took her as a virgin.

After he has been initiated, once two years have been completed he shall for another five years be made acolyte and subdeacon; and then, if during these periods he has been judged worthy, he shall be advanced to the diaconate. Thereafter, as time advances, he will rightly receive the priesthood or episcopate if the election of the clergy and people calls him to it.

[Col. 0836A]

From the decree of Pope Celestine, title 16. We have learned, dearest brothers, that certain men have been ordained bishops who had not been trained in any ecclesiastical orders before being raised to such a height of dignity, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, through the usurpation of the man who acknowledges that he did this. Yet one must reach the episcopate through those ranks for which provision has most frequently been made, so that those initiated into lesser offices may be strengthened for greater ones. Whoever desires to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may teach what he has learned.

Every institution of life confirms by this principle the goal toward which it strives. Whoever has not devoted himself to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. Whoever has not grown through each period of service cannot reach the rank of one who has completed his service. Is the priesthood alone, I ask, cheaper among these offices because it is more easily bestowed, although it is more difficult to fulfill?

## III. On the Advancement of Monks

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 13. We both desire and command that monks, whom seriousness of character and the holy discipline of life and faith commend, be associated with the offices of the clergy. Those who are under thirty years of age are to be advanced through the lesser orders one rank at a time as time increases, and thus reach the insignia of the diaconate or priesthood through the consecration of mature age. They are not to ascend immediately by a leap to the summit of the episcopate unless the periods which we prescribed above for each dignity have been observed.

[Note: [Col. 0836D] “Immediately,” added by Dionysius Exiguus.]

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 17. Monks who have remained for a long time in monasteries and afterward entered the clerical order must not depart from their former purpose. Either he must remain as he was in the monastery and, when placed in a higher rank, must not lose what he observed for so long; or, if he had been sexually defiled and then baptized, and while residing in a monastery wished to enter the clerical order, he may not have a wife at all, since one who had already been sexually defiled cannot be blessed with a bride.

This rule is observed among clerics, especially since the ancient rule states that whoever, having been sexually defiled, was baptized and wished to become a cleric must promise that he would never take a wife.

From the decrees of Pope Zosimus, title 1. Zosimus, bishop of the city of Rome, to Hesychius, bishop of Salona.

Your affection has demanded a ruling from the Apostolic See, in which the decrees of the Fathers agree; and you report that some from the company of monks, whose solitude is greater than any crowd, and also some laymen, are hastening to the priesthood.

This has certainly been prohibited both under our predecessors and recently by us, in letters sent to Gaul and Spain, where this presumption is common. Africa, too, is not exempt from this warning of ours. No one who has not been instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines in due order and seasoned by the testing of time through divine service should presume to aspire to the highest priesthood of the Church, contrary to the commands of the Fathers.

Ambition is not only to be regarded as ineffective in such a person; the ordainers also are to be deprived of the rank which they presumed, contrary to the commands of the Fathers, to bestow without the proper order.

And a little later:

For if secular offices bestow the chief place not upon those who enter at the threshold of public service but upon those examined through many ranks and periods of service, who is so arrogant, so shameless, [Note: [Col. 0837D] “Impudent,” according to Dionysius Exiguus and the Code of the Canon of the Roman Church.] and so foolish as to desire immediately to become a leader in the heavenly service—which must be weighed with the greatest care and tested like gold in repeated fires—when he has not previously been a recruit, and wishes to teach before learning?

Let him first become accustomed in the camp of the Lord to the rudiments of divine service in the rank of lector. Let it not seem beneath him [Note: [Col. 0837D] “Let it not become contemptible,” according to Dionysius Exiguus and the Code of the Roman Church.] to become, in order, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon—not by a leap, but at the times of ordination established by the elders.

Let such a man then approach the dignity of the priesthood, so that both his age fulfills the name and his previous periods of service testify to the merit of his uprightness. From there he ought rightly to hope for the place of supreme pontiff.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, titles 2, 3, and 16. Since the ancient constitutions remain in place out of reverence for them, and since, whenever no urgency of circumstances or times presses, it is fitting for the churches to observe them according to the rule, we grant that the intervals for instituting and advancing clerical service may be distributed in the case of churches which are either entirely deprived of ministers or so stripped of sufficient service that they cannot supply the divine offices to the peoples belonging to them.

And if someone trained in a religious purpose and in monastic disciplines comes to clerical service, his life during the preceding periods must first be investigated:

1. Whether he is not shown to be stained by any serious crime;

2. Whether he perhaps has not had a second wife;

3. Whether he is not shown to have taken a woman abandoned by her husband;

4. Whether he has not perhaps performed public penance;

5. Whether he does not appear to be impaired in any part of his body;

6. Whether he is not subject to a servile or hereditary condition;

7. Whether he is shown already to be released from the bonds of the municipal council;

8. Whether he has acquired literacy, without which he can scarcely perhaps fulfill the ministry of doorkeeper. [Note: [Col. 0837D] “Without which he could scarcely fulfill the ministry of doorkeeper,” according to Dionysius Exiguus and the Code of the Roman Church.]

If he is supported by all the qualifications mentioned above, he shall immediately become a lector, notary, or at least defender, or after three months an acolyte. Especially if his age also supports him, in the sixth month he shall receive the name of subdeacon; and if he is of modest conduct and honorable intention, in the ninth month he shall be a deacon. When the year is completed, he shall be a priest. Nevertheless, he must be shown to have supplied by the devotion freely undertaken for his holy purpose what the intervals of years would otherwise have contributed.

From the decrees of the same pope, title 3. If someone from the laity is to be added to ecclesiastical offices, his person must be examined with all the greater care in each of the matters set out above, since it is clear that there is a distinction between worldly and religious life. Ecclesiastical ministries suited to the Church must be restored, not generated by unsuitable merits [Note: [Col. 0838D] “Introduced,” according to Dionysius Exiguus and the Code of the Roman Church.]; and the more suitable a person might be for sacred service, the more carefully this must be sought in his training.

The more time is taken away from the period in which these things should be attained, the more he must be shown to possess in moral character what a longer habit has not supplied. Otherwise, under the pretext of supplying a shortage of clergy, we may be judged to have introduced vices into divine worship rather than to have secured the advantages of a legitimate clergy. For their promotions we add six months beyond the yearly limits.

As has been said, there ought to be a distinction between a person devoted to divine worship and one who comes from a conversion of the laity. Nevertheless, we believe this concession may be made to the extent that churches whose ministries have been left either entirely absent or greatly reduced by the devastation of war may be restored.

Once these ministries have been restored, God being favorable, the ancient form of the fathers’ canons must be observed in appointing men to the ecclesiastical ranks. The provision made as a remedy for an existing deficiency must not in any way prevail against them; nor must a new rule be proposed against the statutes of the elders for other churches which have escaped a similar disaster. Such churches should retain the former rule in making ordinations.

For this reason, moved by this opportunity [Note: [Col. 0838D] “Admonished,” according to Dionysius Exiguus and the Code of the Roman Church.], we more earnestly commend observance of the venerable canons, warning the consciences of those in each rank not to attempt illicit excesses.

No pontiff should suppose it lawful to attach to divine service men with two wives, or men who have taken women abandoned by other husbands, or anyone after penance, or without literacy, or physically impaired, or bound by a servile condition, or entangled in the obligations of municipal councils and public affairs, or anyone examined casually without a suitable period of testing. Nor should they, at their own pleasure, attempt to invade the rights of others without a just disposition and command of the Apostolic See.

Likewise on this matter, title 16. We have learned that illiterate men and men impaired in some part of the body have also come to ecclesiastical service without any consideration. Neither ancient tradition nor the old rule of the Apostolic See accepted this, since one who lacks literacy cannot be fit for sacred offices, and the legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective may be offered wholly to God.

Therefore, from now on, these practices must be avoided in every way, and no such person may be received into the clergy. If any such men have previously been received, whether through their own rashness or through the negligence of those presiding, let them remain in the positions assigned to them, so that they never undertake any promotion; and let them consider it sufficient that, out of excessive compassion, this itself has been permitted to them.

## IV. That Neophytes Are Not to Be Ordained

Council of Nicaea, title 2. Since many things have been done contrary to ecclesiastical rule, either through necessity or because people were compelled by other persons—namely, that men newly converted from pagan life and instructed for only a short time were immediately brought to the spiritual washing, and that as soon as they were baptized they were promoted to the episcopate or priesthood—it has been very properly decided that nothing of this kind shall henceforth be done.

The person being catechized needs time, and after baptism a very extensive period of testing. For the apostolic Scripture is clear when it says: “Not a neophyte, lest, lifted up with pride, he fall into judgment and the snare of the devil.”

If, as time passes, some offense of the soul is discovered in such a person and he is accused by two or three witnesses, he must abstain from the clergy. But if anyone acts otherwise, setting himself against the great council, he will endanger his own clerical rank.

Council of Laodicea, title 3. Concerning those who have recently been illumined by baptism: they ought not to be promoted to the priestly order.

Council of Sardica, title 13. Bishop Hosius said: “I consider it necessary that you examine this with the greatest care. If perhaps a rich man, a scholar from the forum, or someone from public administration should be requested for the episcopate, he must not be ordained before he has served in the office of lector and in the office of deacon or priest.

“Let him ascend through each rank, if he is worthy, to the summit of the episcopate. Through these promotions, which will necessarily extend over a long period, it can be proved with what faith, modesty, seriousness, and reverence he acts; and, if he is found worthy, he may be honored with the divine priesthood.

“For it is neither appropriate nor permitted by reason or discipline that a neophyte be rashly and lightly ordained bishop, priest, or deacon, especially since the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, appears both to have declared that this must not be done and to have prohibited it. Rather, those should be appointed whose life has been examined over a long period and whose merits have been approved.”

From the decree of Pope Leo, title 33. In cities whose rulers have died, the following rule must be observed in appointing bishops in their place: the man who is to be ordained, even if supported by testimony of good life, must not be a layman, a neophyte, a husband of a second wife, or one who has or has had one wife whom he married as a widow.

For the election of priests is so excellent that matters which in other members of the Church are not considered grounds for blame are nevertheless regarded as unlawful in them.

## V. That Nothing Except What the Lord Established Is to Be Offered as a Sacrifice

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 3. If any bishop or priest, contrary to the Lord’s ordinance, offers something else upon the altar in the sacrifice—that is, honey, or milk, or strong drink [sicera] instead of wine, or prepared foods, or birds, or any animals, or vegetables—acting contrary to the Lord’s constitution, he shall be deposed at the appropriate time.

[Col. 0840A]

Council of Carthage, title 4. In the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing more is to be offered than the Lord himself handed down: namely, bread and wine mixed with water. Firstfruits, or honey and milk, which are customarily offered on one most solemn day in the mystery concerning infants, may indeed be offered on the altar, but they must have their own blessing so that they are distinguished from the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. Nor may anything more be offered among the firstfruits than what comes from grapes and grain.

## VI. Which Things Should Be Offered at the Altar Not for the Sacrifice but for a Simple Blessing

[Note: [Col. 0839D] Printed editions read “to be presented.”]

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 4. Nothing may be offered at the altar except new ears of grain, grapes, oil for the lamps, and incense [thymiama], that is, frankincense, at the time when the holy offering is celebrated.

## VII. That Things Which Cannot Be Offered in Churches Should Be Taken by the Faithful to the Priests’ Houses

Where above, title 5. All other fruits and firstfruits are to be sent to the house of the bishop and priests, and not offered on the altar. It is understood, however, that the bishop and priests distribute them to the deacons and the other clerics.

## VIII. That a Bishop or Priest Must Not Abandon His Wife, Whom He Ought to Govern Chastely

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 6. A bishop or priest must not under any pretext of religion cast away his own wife. If he does cast her away, let him be excommunicated; and if he persists, let him be deposed.

## IX. That Priests and Ministers of the Altar Must Abstain from Secular Concerns

[Col. 0840C]

Where above, title 7. A bishop, priest, or deacon must in no way take up secular concerns; otherwise, let him be deposed.

## X. When Easter Is to Be Celebrated

Where above, title 8. If any bishop, priest, or deacon celebrates the holy day of Easter with the Jews before the spring equinox, let him be deposed.

Council of Antioch, title 1. We decree that all who dare to dissolve the definition of the holy and great council assembled at Nicaea in the presence of the most devout and venerable emperor Constantine concerning the saving and most sacred solemnity of Easter are to be excommunicated and expelled from the Church.

If, however, they contend obstinately against what has been rightly decreed—and let this be understood as stated concerning laymen—then, if any of those known to preside over the Church, whether bishop, priest, or deacon, after this definition attempts, for the subversion of the peoples and the disturbance of the churches, to gather separately and celebrate Easter with the Jews, the holy synod has judged him henceforth alien from the Church. He would become a cause of corruption and disturbance not only to himself but to many others.

The synod removes such men not only from their ministry but also those who, after their condemnation, attempt to communicate with them. The condemned are likewise to be deprived of every external honor which the holy rule and the priesthood of God have earned.

## XI. That the Ministers of the Altar Must Communicate after the Offering Has Been Celebrated

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 9. If any bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone listed among the priests, after the offering has been made, does not communicate, he must either state a reason, so that, if it is reasonable, he may obtain pardon; or, if he gives no reason, he must be deprived of communion, as one who has caused injury to the people by giving rise to suspicion about the one who made the sacrifice—that he did not offer it correctly.

## XII. That Faithful Laypeople Who Enter the Church Must Communicate

[Col. 0841B]

Where above, title 10. All the faithful who enter the Church and hear the Scriptures, but do not persevere in prayer and do not receive holy communion, are rightly to be deprived of communion, as those who stir up disturbances in the Church.

## Council of Antioch, title 2

All who enter the Church of God and hear the sacred Scriptures, but do not join the people in prayer and, through some lack of self-control, turn themselves away from receiving Holy Communion: let such persons be removed from the Church until they show the fruits of repentance through confession and obtain pardon through prayers. It is not permitted to share in prayer with the excommunicated; nor should one pray together with those who gather in private houses while avoiding the prayers of the Church. Nor should anyone who does not assemble in one Church be received by another Church. But if any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone whatsoever from the clergy is discovered praying with excommunicated persons, let that person also be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rule of the Church.

## XIII. That one must not pray with the excommunicated
