In the Apostolic Canons, title 11. If anyone prays together with an excommunicated person, even in a house, let that person be deprived of communion.

Council of Nicaea, title 5. Concerning those who are deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the order of the laity: a regular judgment by the bishops of each province shall prevail, so that those who are rejected are not received by others. Let inquiry also be made, lest anyone appear to have been excluded from the congregation through faintheartedness, contentiousness, or any other fault of the bishop.

Council of Antioch, title 6. If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, let him not be received by others before he has been reconciled with his bishop; or, at least, let him come to the synod that is being assembled, give an account on his own behalf, and, persuading the council, receive another judgment. Let this decree also remain in force concerning the laity, presbyters, deacons, and all who are shown to be under the rule.

## XIV. That one must not pray with condemned clerics

In the Apostolic Canons, title 12. If anyone prays together with a condemned cleric as though with a cleric, let that person be condemned.

[Col. 0842A] Council of Antioch, title 4. If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, should dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry—whether a bishop, according to the preceding custom, or a presbyter or deacon—let it in no way be permitted for him to have either hope of restoration or a place for making satisfaction in another synod. Moreover, let all who communicate with him be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against the persons mentioned, they should have attempted to communicate with them.

Council of Carthage, title 9. Bishop Augustine, legate of the province of Numidia, said: “May you deem it right to establish that, if any persons have been expelled from the Church on account of the merit of their crimes, and have been received into communion by any bishop or presbyter, the one who received them shall also be held liable with them to an equal offense, while evading the regular judgment of their own bishop.” All the bishops said: “It pleases us all.”

## XV. That no member of the faithful be received without letters of recommendation

In the Apostolic Canons, title 13. If any cleric or layperson, whether suspended from communion or in communion, goes to another city and is received without letters of recommendation, both those who receive him and the one who has been received shall be deprived of communion. But in the case of an excommunicated person, the correction itself shall be prolonged, since he has deceived the Church of God by lying.

Council of Antioch, titles 7 and 8. No traveler shall be received without letters of peace—that is, letters of recommendation. Presbyters who are in the rural districts cannot issue canonical letters; they shall send letters only to neighboring bishops. But chorepiscopi who are irreproachable may issue letters of peace, that is, general letters.

## XVI. That bishops must not invade another’s parish

In the Apostolic Canons, title 14. A bishop may not invade another’s parish after abandoning his own, even if he is compelled by many people, unless someone should compel him for a reasonable cause—as one who might contribute greater profit to those established there and might in some way advance the cause of religion. Even then, he must not attempt this on his own authority, but must accomplish it by the judgment of many bishops and with the greatest supplication.

Council of Antioch, title 21. A bishop must by no means move from one parish to another, neither rushing there of his own will, nor compelled by force by the people, nor driven by necessity by the bishops. He must remain in the Church which he first received by lot from the Lord, and must not migrate from it, in accordance with the former rule established concerning this matter.

Council of Chalcedon, title 5. Concerning those who migrate from city to city, whether bishops or clerics: it was decreed that the canons established concerning this matter by the holy Fathers should retain their proper force.

## XVII. That clerics must not leave their own churches

In the Apostolic Canons, title 15. If any presbyter, deacon, or anyone whatsoever from the number of the clergy leaves his own parish and goes to another, and, having wholly migrated, remains in a foreign parish without the knowledge of his own bishop, we do not permit him to minister any longer—especially if, when summoned by his bishop, he refuses to return and persists in his disorder. Nevertheless, as a layperson, let him communicate everywhere.

Council of Nicaea, title 15. Because of the great disturbances and seditions that occur, it was decreed that a custom which appears to have been admitted contrary to the rule in certain places should be completely abolished. Thus no bishop, presbyter, or deacon may be transferred from one city to another. If anyone should attempt such an act after the decree of the holy and great council and should devote himself to such a matter, let the act be declared wholly invalid, and let him be restored to the church in which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

Council of Nicaea, title 16. Whoever rashly and dangerously departs from the Church, without keeping the fear of God before his eyes and without recognizing the ecclesiastical rule—whether bishops, presbyters, deacons, or anyone whatsoever who is entirely under the rule—must by no means be received into another Church. Rather, every necessity should be imposed upon them so that they return to their own Churches. If they do not do so, they ought to be deprived of communion. But if anyone should audaciously invade the territory belonging to another and attempt to ordain someone in his own Church without the consent of the bishop from whom the person subject to the rule departed, that ordination shall be declared invalid.

[Col. 0843C] Council of Chalcedon, title 20. Clerics ministering in one Church, as we have already decreed, ought not to be established in the Church of another city; instead, they should remain content with the places in which they were first found worthy to minister, except for those who, having lost their own provinces, have necessarily transferred to another Church. If any bishop, after this decree, receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, it was decreed that both the one received and the one receiving him be deprived of communion until the cleric who migrated has returned to his own Church.

Council of Antioch, title 3. If any presbyter, deacon, or anyone whatsoever from the clergy abandons his own parish and goes to another, then, having entirely migrated, strives to remain for a long time in the other parish, let him not minister there any longer—especially if he has refused to obey his own bishop when summoned and admonished to return to his own parish. If he persists in this indiscipline, let him be removed from the ministry in every way, so that he may in no way find a place of restoration. But if another bishop receives one condemned for this reason, let that bishop also be restrained by the common synod, as one who dissolves the ecclesiastical constitutions.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 38. If any bishop, despising the modesty of his own city, seeks the administration of a more distinguished place and transfers himself by any means to a greater people, let him indeed be expelled from the foreign see, but let him also lose his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he desired through avarice nor over those whom he despised through pride. Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries, and let no one seek to increase himself beyond the measure of his right.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 23. Whoever, abandoning his own Church without any existing cause, thinks that he should transfer to another and is rashly received and promoted shall not escape the provisions which the revered canons have prescribed to be reserved for such presumptuous persons—whether he himself, or the one who received and promoted him.

Council of Carthage, title 21. Bishop Epigonius said: It has been established in many councils, and must now also be confirmed by your prudence, most blessed brothers, that no bishop should seize for himself another’s cleric against the will of the one whose cleric he is. I speak of Julian, who is ungrateful for the benefits of God bestowed upon him through my smallness, and who has proved so rash and audacious that he has taken, without consulting me, the man whom I baptized and who, when he was a very needy boy, had been entrusted to me by that same man; although he was nourished and raised by me for many years, it is established that he was baptized in my church by the hand of my smallness. The same man began to be a reader in the diocese of Apala—or rather, he had read there for nearly two years—because of some contempt for my humility. This same Julian seized him, claiming that he was virtually a citizen of his own place, Vazapita, and usurped him without consulting me; for he also ordained him deacon. If this is permitted, most blessed brothers, let this permission be openly granted by you; but if not, let such shamelessness be restrained, lest he involve himself in anyone’s communion.

Bishop Numidius said: If Julian appears to have done this without requesting or consulting your dignity, everyone judges that it was done unjustly and unworthily. Therefore, unless Julian corrects his error and, with satisfaction, recalls to your people the same cleric whom he had dared to ordain, since he has acted contrary to the statutes of the council, he shall, separated from us because of his obstinacy, await judgment.

Bishop Epigonius said: Our brother and colleague Victor, a father by age and most senior by the very fact of his promotion, wishes this petition to be made general for all.

Council of Carthage, title 22. Bishop Aurelius said: Listen to my speech, brothers. It sometimes happens that Churches lacking overseers, whether presbyters or bishops, make requests; nevertheless, mindful of the statutes, I follow this practice: I approach that person’s bishop and impress upon him that his cleric is being requested by one Church or another. Perhaps today they have not resisted; but, lest it happen that they resist when they have been requested by me for this purpose—for you know that, by God’s favor, I bear the care of many Churches and of those to be ordained—it is just that we approach any fellow priest with two or three witnesses from our fellowship. But if he should prove unwilling, what does your charity judge should be done? For, as you know, brothers, by God’s favor I bear the concern of all the Churches.

[Col. 0845A] Bishop Numidius said: This see has always had the permission to ordain a bishop from wherever it wished, and concerning whomever a request had been made, according to the desire of each Church.

Bishop Epigonius said: Goodness separates you from the possibility of abuse; for you presume less, brother, when you make yourself good and merciful toward all. You have this within your authority. It is enough that each bishop’s person be satisfied at the first meeting alone. But if you should judge that what is permitted to this see ought to be claimed for itself, you must support all the Churches. We do not grant you a power, but assign your own power to you, so that you may always retain whoever you wish and appoint as overseers of peoples or Churches those who have been requested, and from wherever you wish.

Bishop Postumianus said: Then, if someone has only one, must that one presbyter be taken away from him?

Bishop Aurelius said: But there can be one bishop through whom, by divine favor, many presbyters may be appointed; whereas it is difficult to find one bishop who can be appointed. Therefore, if someone in need of a bishopric has a presbyter—and has only one, as you said, brother—he must give even that man for promotion.

Bishop Postumianus said: Then, if he has other clerics in abundance, another people ought to be assisted there.

Bishop Aurelius said: Certainly, when you have assisted another Church, the one who has more clerics will be persuaded to grant you one to be ordained.

## XVIII. That a bishop who receives another’s clerics is to be deprived of communion

[Col. 0845C]

In the Apostolic Canons, title 16. If it is established that clerics belonging to another bishop are staying with a bishop [Note: In the codex of Dionysius Exiguus, p. 113, “the aforesaid persons,” but incorrectly], and, treating as worthless the suspension decreed against them, he receives them as clerics, so to speak, as a teacher of disorder, let him be deprived of communion.

Council of Sardica, title 16. Bishop Hosius said: This too pleases everyone: if a deacon, presbyter, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his own bishop and goes to another bishop, and the bishop to whom he flees knows that he was rejected by his own bishop, he ought not to grant him communion. If he does so, let him know that, when the bishops have been summoned, he will have to give an account of the matter. Everyone said: This statute will preserve peace and safeguard harmony.

The aforesaid council, title 17. Bishop Hosius said: I must not withhold what still troubles me. If some bishop, perhaps being angry—which he ought not to be—and harshly aroused against his presbyter or deacon, should wish to expel him from the Church, care must be taken that an innocent person is not condemned or deprived of communion. Therefore, let the one who has been rejected have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, and let his case be heard and examined more carefully, because it is not right to deny a hearing to one who asks for it. Let that bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept the examination of the matter, so that his judgment may either be approved by many or corrected. Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully investigated, no one should presume to unite in communion the person who has been separated from communion before the case has been heard.

But if those who assemble to hear the case see that the clerics are acting from contentiousness and pride—for it is not fitting that a bishop should suffer insult or abuse—let them rebuke them in harsher words, so that they obey the bishop who gives honorable commands. For just as the bishop ought to show the clerics sincere love and charity, so also the ministers, in return, ought to show their bishop unfeigned obedience.

[Col. 0846B] From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 14. No one should presume to ordain a cleric from another Church unless, persuaded by the requests of that cleric’s bishop, he has been willing to grant permission. The Nicene synod also established this: one Church must not receive a cleric rejected by another.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 39. No one should receive or solicit another’s cleric against his bishop’s will, unless perhaps by an agreement founded on charity; the matter must be agreed between the giver and the receiver. For the person who dares either to expel or retain from a brother’s Church what is more useful or more precious is guilty of a grave injury. Therefore, if the matter occurs within the province, the metropolitan shall compel the fugitive cleric to return to his Church. But if he has withdrawn farther away, he shall be recalled by the authority of your command, so that no opportunity is left either to greed or ambition.

## XIX. That digamists are not to be admitted to the clergy

In the Apostolic Canons, title 17. If anyone has entered into a second marriage after baptism, or has had a concubine, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or one of the number of those who serve in the sacred ministry.

Council of Laodicea, title 1. Concerning those who, according to ecclesiastical rule, have freely and lawfully entered into a second marriage and have not contracted the marriage secretly: after a short period has passed, they ought to devote themselves to prayers and fasts; in accordance with mercy, we have also decreed that communion be restored to them.

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 11. Any cleric who has taken either a widow or, certainly, a second wife shall immediately be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical dignity, with only lay communion granted to him. He will be able to retain that only if afterward he commits nothing on account of which he may lose it.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, titles 11, 12, and 13. A cleric must not take a widow as his wife, because it is written: “Let priests take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been cast off.” Certainly, anyone who strives toward the priesthood through his labor and uprightness of life must take care that, obstructed by this disqualification, he cannot attain it.

A person who, although a layman, has married a widow—whether before baptism or after baptism—must not be admitted to the clergy, because he appears to be excluded by the same fault. In baptism, sins are forgiven; the union with a wife already taken is not annulled.

A man who has married a second wife must not become a cleric, because it is written: “The husband of one wife”; and elsewhere: “Let my priests marry once”; and again: “Let my priests not marry again.” Nor should anyone think that, if a man took a wife before baptism and, when she departed from this world, afterward married another, this was forgiven in baptism. He is greatly mistaken concerning the rule, because in baptism sins are forgiven, not the number of wives taken abolished. A wife is indeed taken according to the commandment of the law, so much so that even in paradise, when the parents of the human race were joined, they were blessed by God himself; and Solomon says: “A wife shall be prepared for a man by God.” Custom itself also shows that all priests observe this form in the Church.

For it is very absurd to believe that a wife taken before baptism is not counted after baptism, since the blessing imposed by priests upon those marrying is taught not to have provided material for sin but to have preserved the form of the law instituted by God from ancient times. If a wife taken before baptism is not considered to count, then neither should children born before baptism be regarded as children.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 29. There should have been no consultation concerning digamists, since the Apostle’s explicit reading says that the husband of one wife must be admitted to the priesthood or the clergy, and even then only if he took her as a virgin. For a woman who had had a husband before—even if that husband has died—if she afterward has been joined to a cleric, the cleric who took her cannot remain a cleric, because the law has stipulated that a priest may not have as a wife a widow or one who has been cast off.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 2. Since it is clear what kind of integrity of birth and conduct ought to characterize anyone who is to be joined to the ministry of the sacred altar, and since we have learned this both from the Apostle’s teaching and from divine instruction and the rules of the canons, we find that many of our brothers have deviated from these rules and entirely strayed from them. For it is evident that husbands of widows have attained the priesthood, and that some who had had numerous marriages, and whose lives were open to every license, had been freely admitted to sacred orders.

This was contrary to the blessed Apostle’s declaration, in which he exclaims concerning such men: “The husband of one wife”; and contrary to the command and safeguard of the ancient law, which says: “Let the priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not a repudiated woman.” Therefore, whoever of this kind has been admitted, we order by the authority of the Apostolic See to be excluded from ecclesiastical offices and the priestly name. They cannot claim for themselves what they were not capable of possessing, because the very impediment stood in their way.

We claim for ourselves especially the responsibility of examining this matter, so that, if any such offenses have perhaps been committed, they may be corrected, that it may no longer be permitted for them to be committed, and that no excuse may arise from ignorance—although it was never permissible for a priest not to know what had been defined by the rules of the canons.

## XX. That one who has taken a widow, a repudiated woman, or a prostitute is not admitted to the clergy

In the Apostolic Canons, title 18. If anyone has taken a widow, a repudiated woman, a prostitute, a slave woman, or any woman among those who are devoted to public spectacles, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or one of the number of those who serve in the sacred ministry.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 30. Your Religiousness consulted concerning laypeople whom the canons prohibit from being ordained. It is indeed certain that the ecclesiastical rules contain this provision, but it has not been defined in such a way that it applies to all laypeople. Clerics cannot be born; they must be made. Rather, categories have been designated from which persons cannot advance to the clergy: if a member of the faithful has served as a soldier; if a member of the faithful has pleaded legal cases—that is, has acted as a plaintiff;“ or if a member of the faithful has administered an office.

Concerning curiales, the reason is clear: even if men of this sort are found who ought to become clerics, nevertheless, because they are frequently summoned back to the curia, they must be avoided on account of the trouble that often comes upon the Church through them.

The same author, title 51. I have learned that those who are said to have taken widows as wives have not only become clerics but have even attained the insignia of the highest priesthood—something which no one is unaware is contrary to the commands of the law. For when Moses the lawgiver loudly declares, “Let the priest take a virgin as wife,” and, lest this command be thought ambiguous, adds, “Not a widow, nor one who has been cast off,” no defense based on another command can be brought against this command supported by divine authority, except your custom—which, as you yourselves admit, was established through ignorance, to put it more modestly, and not through apostolic tradition and sound reasoning. [Note: [Col. 0847D] In the printed editions: “established.”]

But let your affection know that we, and all the Churches throughout the East and the West, entirely reject this practice and do not admit such persons even to the lowest rank of the ecclesiastical order; and, if they are found, they are to be removed.

## XXI. That one who has married two sisters is not admitted to the clergy

In the Apostolic Canons, title 19. Whoever has taken two sisters in marriage, or his brother’s daughter, cannot be a cleric.

## XXII. That a cleric ought not to become a surety

[Col. 0848D] In the Apostolic Canons, title 20. Let a cleric who engages in suretyships be expelled.

## XXIII. That those who have not been voluntarily made eunuchs are to be received into the clergy

In the Apostolic Canons, title 21. If a eunuch was made so through the treachery of human beings, or if his male organs were cut off during persecution, or if he was born so, and is worthy, let him become a bishop.

Council of Nicaea, title 1. If anyone has been mutilated by physicians because of an illness, or castrated by barbarians, let him remain in the clergy. But if anyone has castrated himself while healthy, he ought to be excluded even if he has been established in the clergy; and thereafter no such person should be promoted. Just as it is clear that this statement concerns those who desire or dare to castrate themselves, so the rule receives into the clergy those who have been castrated either by barbarians or by their masters, provided that they are otherwise fully worthy.

## XXIV. That one who has castrated himself must not become a cleric

In the Apostolic Canons, title 22. If anyone has castrated himself—that is, if anyone has cut off his own male organs—he must not become a cleric, because he is his own murderer and an enemy of God’s creation.

## XXV. That a cleric who has castrated himself is to be expelled from the clergy

In the same collection, title 23. If anyone, while he is a cleric, has castrated himself, let him be utterly condemned, because he is his own murderer. [Note: The Theodosian Code: “He is his own murderer.”]

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 17. Concerning those who have castrated themselves, the canons of the Fathers have clearly laid down provisions that must be followed; it will be sufficient to insert their wording. For they say that those who have perpetrated such acts, as soon as they are recognized, must be excluded from the clerical office. We must guard this in every way, since no one is permitted to judge anything except what the memorable rule has decreed.

## XXVI. That a layperson who has castrated himself is to be deprived of communion for three years

In the Apostolic Canons, title 24. Let a layperson who castrates himself be deprived of communion for three years, because he has proved an ambusher of his own life.

## XXVII. That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, if condemned for crimes, is not to be deprived of communion; and likewise the other ministers of the Church

[Col. 0849C]

In the Apostolic Canons, title 25. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, or theft shall be deposed, but shall not be deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord will not exact vengeance twice for the same thing.”

The same collection, title 26. Let the other clerics likewise be subject to this condition.

From the decree of Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, title 7. We have learned that very many priests of Christ and Levites, after long periods of their consecration, have fathered children both by their own wives and through shameful intercourse, and have defended their crime by this pretext: that in the Old Testament priests and ministers are read to have been granted the power to beget children.

Let any follower of lust and teacher of vice now answer me: if he thinks that, in the law of Moses, the reins of wantonness were everywhere loosened by our God for the sacred orders, why does he warn those to whom the holy of holies was entrusted, saying: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy”? Why were priests also ordered to live far from their homes in the temple during the year of their turn of service? Clearly, this was so that they could not even have carnal relations with their wives, and could offer to God an acceptable gift while shining with purity of conscience.

After they had completed their period of service, the use of one wife alone was permitted for the sake of succession, because no one from any tribe other than Levi had been commanded to be admitted to God’s ministry. Hence, when the Lord Jesus enlightened us by his coming, he declares in the Gospel that he came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it. For this reason he wished the Church, whose bridegroom is the model of chastity, to shine with splendor, so that on the day of judgment, when he comes again, he may find her, as he established through his Apostle, without stain or wrinkle.

All priests and Levites are bound by an indissoluble law to these regulations, so that from the day of our ordination we dedicate both our hearts and our bodies to sobriety and chastity, provided that in all things we please our God through those sacrifices that we offer daily. For, as the chosen Vessel says, “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” “But you are no longer in the flesh, but in the Spirit”—if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. And where could the Spirit of God dwell, unless in holy bodies, as we read?

Since, as your Holiness has reported, some of those of whom we speak confess that they have fallen through ignorance, we declare that mercy must not be denied them on this condition: without any increase of honor, they must remain for as long as they live in the office in which they were detained, provided that afterward they strive to show themselves continent.

But those who rely on the excuse of an illicit privilege, asserting that this was granted to them by the ancient law, should know that, by the authority of the Apostolic See, they have been expelled from every ecclesiastical honor which they unworthily held. They will never be able to touch the venerable mysteries, from which they deprived themselves while they yearned after obscene desires.

And because present examples warn us to take precautions for the future, any bishop, presbyter, or deacon—something we do not wish—who is henceforth found to be such should understand that we have now closed every path of indulgence to him. For wounds that have not experienced the medicine of soothing remedies must necessarily be cut out with the sword.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, title 21. You have asked what ought to be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministry of the diaconate or in the office of the presbyterate, are or have been shown by the children they have begotten to be incontinent.

Concerning these matters, both the discipline of the divine laws and the clear admonitions of the blessed bishop Siricius of revered memory have stated that incontinent men placed in such offices must be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor and must not be admitted to such a mystery, which ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.

For there is a very ancient authority of the sacred law, preserved from the beginning: priests were ordered to live in the temple during the year of their turn of service, so that, serving the sacred offerings, they might claim the divine mysteries as pure and cleansed from every stain. It is not lawful to admit to the sacrifice those who practice carnal relations even with their wives, because it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.”

The use of a wife had been relaxed for them only for the sake of the succession of offspring, because no one from another tribe had been commanded to approach the priesthood. How much more ought those priests and Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, whose priesthood or ministry exists without succession and who have no day free either from the divine sacrifices or from the duty of baptism?

For if Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain for a time so that you may devote yourselves to prayer,” and certainly gave this command to laypeople, how much more must priests, whose continual duty is to pray and sacrifice, always abstain from such intercourse.

If anyone has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame will he presume to sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit does he believe that he will be heard, when it is said: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

Perhaps he thinks this is permitted because it is written, “The husband of one wife.” He did not say this of a man who remains in the desire to beget children, but with a view to future continence. For he did not exclude those sound in body when he said: “I wish that all were as I myself am”; and he declares more openly: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” He spoke of one who has children, not of one who is begetting them.

But the judgment is plainly distinct and separate. If that model of ecclesiastical life and discipline which came from Bishop Siricius to the provinces has not reached some people, pardon will be granted to those who were ignorant of it, on the condition that from now on they begin entirely to abstain and retain the ranks in which they are found, so that they are not permitted to advance to higher ones. It should count as a benefit to them that they do not lose even the position they retain.

But if anyone knows that he has learned of the way of life sent by Siricius and has nevertheless not immediately cast away the desires of lust, such persons must be removed in every way, because after receiving the admonition they judged pleasure preferable.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 33. One who, led by zeal for faith and discipline, does not tolerate the Church’s being polluted by unworthy persons, asserts that a presbyter has fathered children. I would explain that this is not permitted, if I did not know that your prudence has knowledge of the whole law.

Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the contents of the libellus submitted below, you will order those who are said to have perpetrated such acts to be placed in the midst of the assembly. After the charges brought against the presbyters themselves have been investigated, if they can be convicted, let them be removed from the priestly office, because those who are not holy cannot touch holy things; and let them be made strangers to the ministry which they polluted by living unlawfully.

We are astonished that their bishops conceal or overlook these matters, or are thought not to know that they are unlawful.

From the decree of Pope Leo, title 16. It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated in the rank of presbyter or deacon should receive, for some crime of theirs, the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands. This undoubtedly descends from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest has sinned, who will pray for him?” Therefore, for such fallen persons to obtain God’s mercy, withdrawal must be awaited, in which, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.

From the decree of Pope Gelasius, title 18. We have also discovered that persons entangled in certain horrifying crimes, with all discernment set aside, not only fail to undertake the necessary repentance for atrocious deeds, but, without any correction at all taking place afterward, strive for the honor of the divine ministry. Some who have been established in the very orders are not rejected even when they commit grave crimes, although the Apostle cries out that hands must not be laid quickly upon anyone and that one must not share in the sins of others. The venerable constitutions of our predecessors declare that, even if such persons have perhaps slipped in, those who previously sinned, once detected, must be expelled, and those who have forgotten their sacred profession and betrayed their holy purpose must without doubt be removed.

Council of Carthage, title 27. It was also confirmed that, whenever presbyters or deacons are convicted of some more serious fault, the manner in which they must be removed from the ministry is as follows: hands must not be laid upon them as upon penitents or faithful laypeople, nor may the rebaptized be permitted to advance to the rank of the clergy.

## XXVIII. Which clerics may be joined to wives

[Col. 0852C]

In the Apostolic Canons, title 27. Concerning unmarried men who have been advanced to the clergy, we decree that, if they wish, they may take wives—but only if they are readers or singers.

Concerning the Council of Carthage, title 16. It was likewise decreed that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should not be contractors or agents, nor become involved in any disgraceful business or seek a dishonest livelihood, since they ought to remember that it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.” It was decreed that, when lectors have reached the age of puberty, they must either marry wives or profess continence. It was likewise decreed that, if a cleric exchanges money, he must receive the same money; [Col. 0852D] if an object, he must receive the same kind and the same quantity as he gave; and that no one under twenty-five years of age be ordained a deacon; and that lectors not greet the people.

XXIX. That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon ought not to beat faithful persons who sin.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 28. We decree that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who strikes faithful persons who are delinquent, or unbelievers who act wickedly, and who wishes to make himself feared by such conduct, be removed from his office, because the Lord nowhere taught us this. On the contrary, when he himself was struck, he did not strike back; when he suffered, he did not threaten.

[Note: [Col. 0851] Dionysius Exiguus and Codex Theodosianus insert: “When he was reviled, he did not revile.”]

XXX. That those condemned for crimes ought not to usurp their former office.

[Col. 0853A]

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 29. If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, justly deposed for specified crimes, dares to take up again the ministry formerly entrusted to him, let him be completely cut off from the Church.

Likewise, that condemned clerics may not communicate.

From the universal Council of Carthage, title 29. It was likewise decreed by the whole council that whoever has been excommunicated for his negligence, whether bishop or any cleric, and during his excommunication presumes to receive communion before a hearing, shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.

[Col. 0853B] Likewise, from the universal Council of Carthage, title 29.

And this is to be requested: that they deign to establish that, if any cleric of whatever rank has been condemned by the judgment of the bishops for any crime, he may not be defended either by the churches over which he presided or by any person, under penalty involving loss of money and honor; and that they order that neither age nor sex is to serve as an excuse.

Likewise, that they conduct their case within a year.

Council of Carthage, title 46. It was again established that whenever clerics have been convicted and have confessed to some crime—or on account of those whose modesty is being spared, or because of the disgrace to the Church, or because of the insolent attacks of heretics and pagans—[Col. 0853C] if they should wish to appear in their own case and assert their innocence, they must do so within the year of their excommunication. But if they neglect to clear their case within a year, their voice is thereafter to be heard in no way whatsoever.

XXXI. That ecclesiastical offices ought not to be obtained with money.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 30. If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained his dignity through money [Note: [Col. 0854D] Dionysius Exiguus adds these words.], let both him and the person who ordained him be deposed and cut off from communion in every way, like Simon Magus by Peter.

Council of Chalcedon, title 2. If any bishop performs an ordination for money, reducing to a price the grace that cannot be sold, and ordains [Col. 0853D] for money a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any of those numbered among the clergy, or promotes for money a steward, defender, or anyone subject to the rule, for the sake of his own most disgraceful profit, whoever is proved to have attempted this shall be subject to the danger of losing his own rank. The person who has been ordained shall gain nothing from this ordination, or from the promotion made through commercial dealing, but shall be excluded from the dignity or responsibility that he acquired with money. If anyone has acted as intermediary in such disgraceful and abominable [Col. 0854A] gifts or payments, then, if he is a cleric, let him fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or a monk, let him be anathematized.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 24. Concerning monks and laymen, a fuller treatment of this injunction has been set out in the first part; it explains both the extent to which concessions have been made because of the needs of circumstances and times, and how, where no necessity of the situation is shown to exist, only the ancient institution ought to be maintained. Those who are clearly unworthy by their merits yet have purchased sacred dignity for a price must be excluded when convicted; and those who commit such a crime do so not without danger, because the condemnation of Simon, attested by sacred Scripture, envelops giver and receiver alike.

XXXII. That the Church not be invaded by secular power.

[Col. 0854B]

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 31. If any bishop obtains possession of a church by using secular powers, let him be deposed, and let all who communicate with him be separated.

XXXIII. Concerning presbyters who, despising their bishops, attempt to gather assemblies separately.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 32. If any presbyter, despising his bishop, gathers an assembly separately [Note: [Col. 0854D] Absent in Dionysius Exiguus.] and erects another altar, having no charge with which to reproach the bishop in matters of piety and justice, let him be deposed as one who loves preeminence; for he is a tyrant. Let all other [Col. 0854C] clerics who consent to such a person also be deposed, and let laymen be separated. This is to be done after the bishop has admonished him once, twice, and three times.

Council of Antioch, title 5. If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, withdraws from the Church, gathers separately, and establishes an altar, and does not heed the bishop when admonished, nor wish to consent or obey, let him, after being summoned once and again, be condemned in every way and obtain no further remedy, since he cannot recover his dignity. But if he persists in disturbing and troubling the Church, let him be suppressed by external powers as a seditious person.

Council of Carthage, titles 10 and 11. Bishop Alypius, legate of the province of Numidia, said: “Nor must this be omitted: if a presbyter, having been corrected by his bishop, should, swollen with resentment or pride, [Col. 0854D] suppose that sacrifices ought to be offered to God separately, or believe that another altar should be erected against ecclesiastical faith and discipline, he must not escape unpunished.”

Valentinus, bishop of the principal see of the province of Numidia, said: “What our brother Alypius has set forth is necessarily consistent with ecclesiastical discipline and faith. Therefore, say what seems right to your affection.”

All the bishops said: “If a presbyter has been corrected by his superior, he ought certainly to bring his complaint before neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his bishop. But if [Col. 0855A] he does not do this and, God forbid, inflated with pride, [text uncertain: “du erit”] separates himself from communion with his bishop and, making a schism with certain others, offers sacrifice to God separately, let him be regarded as anathema and lose his place. If, however, he has a just complaint against the bishop, it must be investigated.”

XXXIV. That condemned clerics ought not to be received by others.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 33. If any presbyter or deacon is separated by his bishop, he may not be received by another, but only by the one who separated him—unless, perhaps, that bishop himself, who is known to have separated him, has died.

Council of Sardica, title 18. Bishop Januarius said: “Let your holiness also establish that no bishop may solicit an ecclesiastical minister belonging to another bishop’s city and ordain him in his own parishes.”

All said: “It pleases us, because discord commonly arises from such disputes. Therefore, by the decision of all, let no one dare to do this.”

Council of Sardica, title 19. Bishop Hosius said: “We also unanimously establish that whoever wishes to ordain in another parish a minister belonging to someone else, without the consent and will of that bishop, shall have his ordination considered invalid. Whoever usurps this authority ought both to be admonished and corrected by our brothers and fellow bishops.”

XXXV. That no bishop, presbyter, or deacon be received without letters of commendation.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 34. No bishop, stranger, presbyter, or deacon is to be received without letters of commendation. When they bring written documents, they are to be examined carefully, and then received if they have proved to be preachers of piety; otherwise, what is necessary is not to be supplied to them, nor are they in any way to be admitted to communion, because many things arise through stealth.

Council of Laodicea, title 41. That a priest or cleric ought not to travel without canonical letters.

Council of Chalcedon, title 11. We have decreed that all poor persons and those in need of assistance, when they travel, are to be commended only through letters of proof or ecclesiastical letters of peace. Commendatory letters [Note: [Col. 0855D] Codex Theodosianus: “ecclesiastical.”] are therefore properly to be granted only to persons of rank.

XXXVI. Concerning the primacy of bishops.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 35. The bishops of each nation ought to know which one among them is first, and regard him as their head. They should do nothing beyond his knowledge except those matters alone that belong individually to their own parish and to the villages subject to it. Nor should he do anything without the knowledge of all. Thus there will be unanimity, and God will be glorified through Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0856A] Council of Antioch, title 9. It is fitting that the bishops of each region know that the metropolitan bishop has responsibility for the whole province. For this reason, all who appear to have business should come from every direction to the metropolis. It has therefore seemed right that he excel in honor, and that the other bishops do nothing beyond him according to the ancient rule established by our Fathers, except those things alone that pertain to their own diocese and to the possessions subject to them. For each bishop is to have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern according to the reverence due to each person and exercise care over every possession under his authority. Thus he is to ordain presbyters and deacons and settle each matter by his own judgment; but he must not attempt anything further [Col. 0856B] beyond the metropolitan bishop, nor may the metropolitan act without the counsel of the other priests.

Concerning the privileges belonging to certain cities.

Council of Nicaea, title 6. Let the ancient custom be preserved throughout Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these places, since a similar custom also belongs to the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in Antioch and the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their churches be preserved. It is generally clear, however, that if anyone is made bishop contrary to the decision of the metropolitan, the great synod has determined that he ought not to be considered a bishop. But if, by the reasonable common decree of all, approved according to ecclesiastical rule, [Col. 0856C] two or three oppose the decision on account of their own disputes, the opinion of the greater number shall prevail.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 9. First, no one should dare to ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop, for a judgment confirmed by the opinions of the majority is sound; nor should one bishop presume to ordain, lest the benefit conferred appear clandestine. This was established and defined by the Synod of Nicaea.

XXXVII. That a bishop may not ordain clerics in another province.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 36. A bishop must not dare to perform ordinations outside his own boundaries, in cities or villages that are subject to him by no [Col. 0856D] right. If he is convicted of having done this without the knowledge of those who possess authority over the cities and villages themselves, both he and those whom he ordained are to be deposed.

Council of Antioch, titles 13 and 22. No bishop from another province may dare to cross into another and ordain people for advancement to ministry in its churches, even if some appear to give their consent, unless he comes at the request of letters from both the metropolitan and the other bishops who are with him, and then proceeds to perform the ordination. But if, without anyone’s request [Note: [Col. 0856D] Dionysius Exiguus: “inviting him.”], he hastens in disorderly fashion to settle certain ordinations and ecclesiastical affairs that do not belong to him, let what he does be invalid, while he himself shall undergo punishment for his unrestrained impulse (*incompositi motus*, apparently corrupted in the source) and irrational audacity, having already been condemned for this by the holy council.

Likewise, from the aforesaid council, title 22. A bishop must not enter another city that is not subject to him, nor approach a possession that does not belong to him, for the purpose of ordaining anyone; nor may he appoint presbyters or deacons subject to another bishop, except perhaps with the counsel and consent of the bishop of the region. If anyone attempts to do such a thing, his ordination shall be invalid, and he himself shall be restrained by the synod; for if he cannot ordain, he certainly may not judge.

XXXVIII. Concerning those who have been ordained but not received.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 37. If any bishop does not accept the office and care of the people entrusted to him, let him be deprived of communion until he consents and offers obedience. The same applies to a presbyter and deacon. But if he proceeds and is not received, not because of his own decision but because of the wickedness of the people, he himself is to remain a bishop, while the clerics of the city are to be deprived of communion because they did not instruct the disobedient people.

Council of Ancyra, title 17. If bishops have been ordained but not received by the parish for which they were designated, and wish to seize other parishes and use force against their prelates by stirring up seditions against them, it has seemed right that they be rejected. But if they wish to remain in the rank of presbyters in which they previously [Col. 0857C] served as presbyters, they are not to be deprived of their proper dignity. If, however, they stir up seditions, then, once bishops have been established there, even the honor of the presbyterate is to be taken away from such persons, and they are to be marked by condemnation.

Council of Antioch, title 18. If an ordained bishop does not at all approach the parish to which he was elected, not through his own fault but because the people avoid him, or for some other reason not brought about by his fault, he is nevertheless to share in both honor and ministry, provided that he is not troublesome to the affairs of the Church where he is known to minister. He should also retain whatever the completed synod of the province, after judgment, has decreed as it saw fit.

XXXIX. That councils be held twice each year.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 38. Councils of bishops are to be held twice a year, so that they may examine among themselves the doctrines of piety and remove ecclesiastical disputes as they arise: once in the fourth week of Pentecost; and a second time on the twelfth day of the month Hyperberetaeus, that is, according to the Romans [Note: [Col. 0857D] Dionysius Exiguus: “the fourth day before the Ides.”], on the third day before the Ides of October.

Council of Nicaea, title 5. It was rightly decided that councils should be held twice each year in every province, so that, with all the bishops of the province gathered together, such questions might be examined communally, and those who had plainly sinned against their own bishop might reasonably be regarded by all as excommunicated [Col. 0858A] until either the community or the bishop should see fit to render a more humane judgment in such cases. One council is to be held before the forty days of Easter, so that, every dissension having been removed, the offering may be presented to God in complete purity [Note: [Col. 0857D] Dionysius Exiguus: “most pure.”]; the second is to be held around the time of autumn.

Council of Antioch, title 20. For ecclesiastical needs and for resolving matters that admit of doubt and controversy, it has seemed best that councils of bishops be held twice each year in every province: once after the third week of the feast of Easter, so that the synod may meet in the fourth week of Pentecost, with the metropolitan admonishing the bishops of the province; and a second synod on the Ides of October, [Col. 0858B] that is, on the fifteenth day of October, which the Greeks call Hyperberetaeus. Presbyters and deacons, as well as all who consider themselves wronged, are to be present at these councils and submit themselves to the synod’s examination [Note: [Col. 0858D] Dionysius Exiguus: “experience the examination of the synod.”]. No one may hold councils on his own authority except those to whom metropolitan rights appear to have been entrusted [Note: [Col. 0858D] Dionysius Exiguus: “to the metropolitans.”].

Council of Chalcedon, title 19. It has come to our ears that in the provinces the councils of bishops established by law are not being held, and as a result many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are being neglected. Therefore the holy synod decreed, according to the canon of the Fathers, that the bishops meet twice a year for this purpose in every province, wherever the metropolitan prelate approves, in order to examine and correct each matter [Col. 0858C] that may perhaps have arisen. Any bishops who do not attend, but remain in their own cities while in good health and demonstrably free from every necessary and unavoidable occupation, are to be rebuked in a spirit of brotherly affection.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 37. Concerning episcopal councils, we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers salutarily established: namely, that two assemblies be held every year, in which judgment is rendered concerning all the complaints that customarily arise among the various orders of the Church. If, perchance, a case should arise among those who preside concerning grave sins—which God forbid—and it cannot be decided by provincial examination, the metropolitan shall undertake to inform your fraternity concerning the whole matter, [Col. 0858D] so that, if the matter is not settled in the presence of the parties or by your judgment, whatever it may be may be transferred to our examination. Likewise elsewhere, title 41.

That bishops not remain more than fifteen days beyond the time appointed by the council.

And if a dispute concerning the matter has arisen among them, let everything be disclosed to the Roman pontiff through a report of the proceedings, so that he may arrange whatever pleases God.

XL. That the bishop alone have charge of ecclesiastical affairs.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 39. The bishop is to have charge of all [Col. 0859A] ecclesiastical affairs and administer them as under God’s scrutiny. He may not take anything at all from them for himself, or give what belongs to God to his own relatives. But if they are poor, he is to provide for them as for poor persons, and not, on their account, plunder the Church’s affairs.

Council of Antioch, title 24. Let the possessions of the Church be preserved with every care, with a good conscience and faith in God, who observes and judges all things. They are to be administered according to the judgment and authority of the bishop, to whom the people and the souls gathered within the Church have been entrusted. Let whatever appears to belong to the Church be made known, with the knowledge of the presbyters and deacons who are associated with it, so that they may recognize and not be ignorant of what belongs to the Church, and so that nothing may be hidden from them. If it should happen that the bishop departs from this life while the Church’s possessions are clearly identified, let them neither collapse and perish nor, under the pretext of such possessions, let what is properly the bishop’s be seized by the Church. For it is just and acceptable before God and human beings that the bishop leave his own property to whomever he wishes, while what belongs to the Church is preserved for the Church itself, so that neither the Church suffers loss nor the bishop is proscribed under the pretext of the Church, nor those belonging to him fall into legal troubles, nor he himself after death become burdened with curses.

XLI. Concerning the dignity of the bishop, and that he has authority over his own possessions.

[Col. 0859C] In the Canons of the Apostles, title 40. Presbyters and deacons must attempt nothing without the bishop, for the Lord’s people have been entrusted to him, and he will render an account for their souls. The bishop’s own possessions, if he has any, are to be clearly distinguished, as are the Lord’s possessions, so that when the bishop dies he may have authority to leave his own property as he wishes and to whomever he wishes, and so that what is proved to belong to the bishop may not perish under the pretext of ecclesiastical property. For perhaps he has a wife, children, relatives, or servants. This is just before God and human beings: neither should the Church suffer loss through ignorance of the bishop’s possessions, nor should the bishop or his relatives be proscribed under the pretext of the Church, nor those belonging to him fall into legal troubles, nor should his death be subjected to the injuries of a bad reputation.

XLII. That the bishop have authority over ecclesiastical possessions for the provision of the poor.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 41. We decree that the bishop have ecclesiastical possessions in his power. For if human souls have been entrusted to him as precious, it is much more necessary that he manage the funds. Thus everything is to be distributed by his authority to those in need through the presbyters and deacons, and administered with fear and every care. From these resources, he himself may receive what one who is in need requires for his necessities and for the use of visiting brothers, so that nothing at all may be lacking to them [Col. 0860A]. For the law of God commands that those who serve at the altar should be fed from the altar, since a soldier does not take up arms against his enemies at his own expense.

Council of Antioch, title 25. The bishop is to have authority over ecclesiastical possessions in order to distribute them, with the utmost reverence and fear of God, to all who are in need. He himself may also share in what he needs, if indeed he is in need, for necessary uses benefiting both his own household and the brothers received by him, so that they are defrauded in nothing on any pretext, according to the holy Apostle’s words: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content.” But if he is not at all content with these things, and converts Church possessions to his domestic uses, and manages its revenues or the produce of its fields without the knowledge of the presbyters [Col. 0860B] and deacons, but entrusts control of them to his household, relatives, brothers, or sons, so that through such persons the rest of the Church is secretly harmed, he shall pay the penalty to the synod of the province. If, moreover, a bishop or the presbyters who are with him are accused in another way—namely, of appropriating to themselves what belongs to the Church, whether from fields or from any other ecclesiastical resource, so that the poor are thereby afflicted and both the message of preaching and those who administer it are exposed to accusation and blasphemy—they too must be corrected, with the holy synod approving what is fitting.

That four portions be made, both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful: one for the bishop, another for the clerics, a third for the poor, and a fourth for the repair of the churches.

[Col. 0860C]

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 27. Four portions ought to be made, both from revenue and from the offering of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church permit, as was reasonably decreed long ago: one for the bishop, another for the clerics, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the fabric of the churches [Note: [Col. 0859D] Dionysius Exiguus adds “of the church.”]. Just as it is the priest’s responsibility to pay the whole of the stated amount to the ministers of the Church, so the clergy must know that they should demand nothing presumptuously beyond the sum assigned to them. As for what has been allotted to ecclesiastical buildings, the visible restoration of holy places should demonstrate that it has truly been expended for this work, since it is a sacrilege for the bishop, when sacred buildings have been left without resources, to convert the expenses designated for them to his own profit [Col. 0860D]. Nevertheless, even the portion assigned to the poor, although he may appear to show that he has distributed it according to divine accounts, ought, in accordance with what is written—“that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew IV)—also to be proclaimed by present testimony and not concealed from the praises of good reputation.

XLIII. That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon ought not to be a gambler or drunkard. Likewise, clerics and laymen, if they persist in gambling, are to be deprived of communion.

In the Canons of the Apostles, titles 42 and 43. A bishop, [Col. 0861A] presbyter, or deacon who devotes himself to gambling and drunkenness must either desist or certainly be condemned. A subdeacon, lector, or cantor who does similar things must either desist or be deprived of communion; and likewise a layman.

XLIV. That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon ought not to take interest.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 44. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who demands interest from debtors must either desist or certainly be condemned.

Council of Nicaea, title 17. Since many persons enrolled in the rule pursue avarice and disgraceful profits, and, forgetting the divine Scripture that says, “He who has not given his money at interest” (Psalm 14), lend money and demand hundredfold returns, the holy and great synod rightly judged that, if anyone is found after this [Col. 0861B] definition accepting interest, conducting business by any contrivance or in any manner, demanding *hemiolia*—that is, one and a half times the principal—or devising anything of this sort for the sake of disgraceful profit, he is to be deposed from the clergy and excluded from the rule.

Council of Laodicea, title 5. That priests and clerics ought not to lend at interest or receive what are called *sescupla*, that is, the principal sum and half the principal.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, titles 3 and 4. We have also judged that this must not be passed over: certain persons, seized by desire for disgraceful profit, practice usury and wish to grow rich through lending at interest. We grieve that this occurs not only among those established in clerical office, but also among laymen who wish to be called Christians [Col. 0861C]. We decree that it be punished more severely in those who have been exposed, so that every opportunity for sinning may be removed. We have also thought it necessary to warn that, just as no cleric may practice lending at interest in his own name, so no one should attempt to do so in another’s name; for it is indecent to devote one’s own crime to another’s advantage. The only interest we ought to regard and practice is this: that what we mercifully give here, we may receive from the Lord, who will repay it multiplied and abiding forever.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 15. It followed that we should not neglect what a report recently sent to us from the regions of Picenum announced: namely, that very many clerics were engaged in dishonest commerce and disgraceful profits, seeing without any shame [Col. 0861D] the Gospel reading, according to which the Lord himself is said to have driven the merchants from the temple after scourging them. Nor did they recall the words of the Apostle, who says: “No one serving as a soldier for God binds himself to secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2). They also turned a deaf ear to the Psalmist David, who sings: “For I have not known commercial dealings; I will enter into the powers of the Lord” (Psalm 70). Therefore, such persons must henceforth understand that they are to abstain from dishonorable gains and cease from every device and desire for commerce; or, whatever rank they hold, they must immediately be compelled to abstain from clerical offices, since the house of God both is and must be called a house of prayer, lest it instead be a workshop of commerce and a den of thieves.

XLV. That a bishop, presbyter, presbyter, or deacon ought not to pray with heretics.

[Col. 0862A]

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 45. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who prays with heretics is to be deprived of communion alone. But if he has encouraged them, as though they were clerics, to act or pray, let him be condemned.

XLVI. That Catholics may not approach the haunts of heretics for the sake of prayer.

Council of Laodicea, title 9. Ecclesiastical persons are not to be permitted to approach the cemeteries of heretics, or those places that they call martyria, for the sake of prayer or healing. If faithful persons do so, they are to be deprived of communion for a specified period; but penitents who confess that they have sinned ought to be received.

XLVII. That Catholics ought not to enter into marriage alliances with heretics.

[Col. 0862B]

Council of Laodicea, titles 10 and 31. Ecclesiastical persons ought not indiscriminately to join their sons or daughters to heretics in marriage.

Likewise, no one ought to celebrate marriage alliances with heretics generally, nor give sons or daughters to them, but rather receive them, provided that they promise to become Christians.

Council of Chalcedon, title 14. Since in certain provinces permission has been granted to lectors and psalmists to marry wives, the holy synod decreed that none of them may take a wife from another sect. If they have already had children from such a marriage, and, having been forestalled, have caused those born to them to be baptized among heretics, it is fitting that they offer them to communion with the Catholic Church; but those who have not been [Col. 0862C] baptized may no longer be baptized among heretics. Nor should a woman about to marry be joined to a heretic, Jew, or pagan, unless he promises that he will transfer himself to the orthodox faith and join himself to an orthodox person. If anyone transgresses this definition of the holy synod, he shall be subject to canonical correction.

Council of Carthage, title 21. It was likewise decreed that the children of clerics not be joined in marriage to pagans or heretics.

XLVIII. That eulogies ought not to be received from heretics.

Council of Laodicea, title 32. Eulogies ought not to be received from heretics, since they are curses rather than blessings.

XLIX. That the baptisms of heretics ought not to be approved.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 46. We decree that a bishop or presbyter who accepts the baptism of heretics be condemned. For what fellowship has Christ with Belial, or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever?

L. That one baptized with the Church’s baptism ought not to be baptized again, and that one not so baptized ought to be baptized.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 47. If a bishop or presbyter baptizes again someone who has truly received baptism, or does not baptize someone polluted by the impious [Col. 0863A] and not rightly baptized [Note: [Col. 0863D] These words are not found in Dionysius Exiguus], let him be deposed as one who mocks the cross and death of the Lord and does not rightly distinguish priests from false priests.

LI. That baptism ought to be administered in the name of the Trinity.

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 49. If any bishop or presbyter, in accordance with the Lord’s command, does not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but in three beginningless principles, or in three sons, or in three paracletes, let him be rejected.

LII. That a single immersion ought not to occur in baptism, as though in the Lord’s death.

[Col. 0863B]

In the Canons of the Apostles, title 50. If any bishop or presbyter does not celebrate the threefold immersion of the one mystery, but immerses a person once in baptism, which is said to be given in the Lord’s death, let him be deposed. For the Lord did not say to us, “Baptize in my death,” but, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

LIII. Concerning the Arians, who are not to be rebaptized.

And from the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 1. At the very beginning of your letter you indicated that many baptized by the impious Arians were hastening to the Catholic faith, and that certain of our brothers wished to baptize them again. This is not permitted, since the Apostle forbids it, the canons oppose it, and the general decrees sent to the provinces after the annulled Council of Rimini by my predecessor of venerable memory, Liberius, prohibit it [Col. 0863C]. We associate them with the Novatians and other heretics, as has been established in the synod, with the Catholic assembly solely through the invocation of the sevenfold Spirit and the imposition of the bishop’s hand. The whole East and West likewise observes this practice. You too must not hereafter deviate from this path, if you do not wish to be separated from our synodal fellowship by the judgment of the synod.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 47. Moreover, regarding Arians and the other plagues of the same kind: because we receive their laypeople who have been converted to the Lord under the appearance of penance and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands, it does not seem that we should receive their clerics with the dignity of the priesthood or of any ministry, since we allow only their baptism to be recognized as valid—baptism which is, of course, performed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. We do not judge that they possess the Holy Spirit from that baptism or from their other rites, because, when the founders of their sect departed from the Catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit that they had received, and they cannot bestow its fullness, which operates especially in ordinations. I should say that they lost it through the impiety of their treachery rather than through faith.

For how can we judge the profane priests of such people worthy of Christ’s honors, when we receive their laypeople, as I have said, as imperfect, so that they may receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, receiving them under the appearance of penance? Therefore let Your Gravity bring this to the knowledge of the co-bishops, either through a synod, if possible, or through the reading of this letter, so that what you yourself have so necessarily inquired about, and what we have answered with care, may be observed by the common agreement and zeal of all.

### LIV. Concerning those who are called Cathari, that is, the Pure

Council of Nicaea, title 8. Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, the Pure: if at any time they come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great council that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy.

Above all, they must make this profession in writing: that they accept and follow the doctrines of the Catholic and apostolic Church; that is, that they communicate with those who have married twice, and with those who have fallen during persecution, for whom periods and appointed times have been established, so that in everything they may follow the decisions of the Catholic and apostolic Church.

Wherever they alone are found in the cities, and those found among them are ordained, they shall remain in the same status. But wherever some of them come to a city in which a bishop or presbyter of the Catholic Church has been established, it is certain that the bishop of that church shall retain the dignity of bishop. The one who is called bishop among them shall possess the honor of the presbyterate, unless perhaps the bishop should wish him to retain the honor of the title. If the bishop does not wish this, he shall provide him with a place either as chorepiscopus or as presbyter, so that he may plainly be seen to belong to the clergy, and so that two bishops may not be found to exist in one city.

### LV. Concerning those who come to the Church from Paul of Samosata

Council of Nicaea, title 19. Regarding the Paulianists who flee to the Catholic Church, a decision has been issued that they must be baptized in every case.

If any of them formerly belonged to the clergy, then, provided that they appear blameless and irreproachable, they shall be baptized and ordained by the bishop of the Catholic Church. But if examination finds them unfit, such persons should be rejected. The same rule shall be observed concerning deaconesses and, generally, concerning all who live under a rule.

We recall regarding deaconesses who are found to have remained in the same status that they do not receive the laying on of hands, and therefore must in every respect be counted among the laity.

### LVI. Concerning other heretics who come to the Church

Council of Laodicea, title 7. Those who are converted from heretics—that is, from Novatians, Photinians, or Quartodecimans—whether they have been baptized or are catechumens, must not be received until they have anathematized all heresies, especially the one in which they were held.

Only then shall those who were called believers among them be taught the creed of our faith and, after being anointed with holy chrism, admitted to the holy mysteries.

### LVII. Concerning those who come from the heresy of the Cataphrygians

[Col. 0865A]

Council of Laodicea, title 8. Those who are converted from the heresy called that of the Cataphrygians—even if they are believed to have belonged to the clergy among them, and even if they are especially highly regarded—must be instructed with the utmost care by the bishops or presbyters of the Church and baptized.

### LVIII. Concerning those who come from the Novatians and Montanists

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 15. Those who come from the Novatians or Montanists are to be received through the laying on of hands alone, because although they were baptized by heretics, they were nevertheless baptized in the name of Christ—except those who, after passing from us to them, were rebaptized. If, having come to their senses and reflecting upon their ruin, they prefer to return, they are to be admitted after a lengthy penance and satisfaction.

### LIX. Concerning the heretical Bonosiacs, who are to be compared with the Jews, and concerning the reception of clerics whom Bonosus ordained before his condemnation

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 49. Innocent to Laurentius, bishop of Siena.

After reading the letter of Your Love, we were astonished to learn that in the territory of Your Love there are not only heretics who follow the poison of Photinus, but that they also publicly prepare meeting places for themselves on certain people’s estates, although almost nowhere in the entire world have so many of them chosen to live as among you.

Marcus, the author of their wicked doctrine, formerly expelled from the city, has been driven to such audacity that he first claims the leading place among them. But so that they may no longer have the opportunity to rage and drag with them into the hell to which they are destined the souls of the simple and the country people, action has been taken against them by the defenders of our Church, so that they may expel them. For those who deny that Christ God was begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages share the condemnation of the Jews, who denied and still deny his divinity.

It is your responsibility, dearest brother, to carry out the commands without slackness, lest you lose the people entrusted to you through dissimulation and begin to render an account to God for those who have been lost.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 50. Likewise, Innocent to Martianus, bishop of Narsitana.

In former times, if I remember correctly, I recall sending letters both to Your Love and to our brothers and fellow bishops Rufus, Eusebius, and the others of the same kind concerning the clerics of Narsus—namely, those who claimed that before Bonosus’s condemnation they had been ordained by him, both as presbyters and as deacons. The instruction was that, if they wished to abandon his condemned error and join the Church, they should gladly be received, lest those who might be worthy of recovering salvation should perish in it.

But now, while I am staying in the city of Ravenna because of the frequent necessities of the Roman people, Germanus, who claims to be a presbyter, and Lupentius, who says that he is a deacon, having undertaken what was almost an embassy on behalf of many such men, poured out their prayers and eagerly expressed their personal grievances. They asserted that they retained the churches situated in Your Love’s parishes but had been unable to obtain your communion, for the reason that a certain Rusticus had received the presbyterate through repeated ordination.

This creates no small difficulty: either they are distressed that such a man is retained in the Church, or he thinks that he ought to sin in this matter against others, [F., “just as”] one who recognizes that the sin exists in himself.

Although my letters on this same matter, which I mentioned above, contain a fuller discussion, we have nevertheless now thought it necessary to admonish Your Fraternity that, if it is truly established that certain men ordained by Bonosus before his condemnation later wished, or now wish, to return, we judge that they should be received—especially since the men mentioned assert that they were ordained so long ago that Cornelius, the bishop of the city of Sirmium, a man of holy memory, as well as our brother Nicetas and several others, were present when they were advanced to the honors that they recall possessing.

Therefore, dearest brother, if their assertion is found credible, you must not hesitate to receive those whom you have allowed for so long to retain the churches entrusted to them.

### LX. That those ordained by heretics are not to be admitted to the clergy

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 53. We have come to the third question, which because of its difficulty requires a longer discussion. We say that those ordained by heretics have their head wounded through that laying on of hands. Where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied so that health may be restored. But health following a wound cannot be without a scar. And where the remedy of penance is necessary, there the honor of ordination cannot have a place.
