For if, as we read, “Whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean,” how can that be bestowed upon him which purity and cleanliness ordinarily receive? Yet the opposing argument is made that one who has lost an honor cannot bestow honor, and that the recipient received nothing because there was nothing in the giver that he could receive. We accept this, and it is certainly true: one who did not possess something could not give it.

He certainly gave the condemnation that he possessed through a perverse laying on of hands; and how one who has become a participant in condemnation should receive honor, I cannot discover. But it is said that the true and just blessing of a legitimate priest removes every defect that had been inflicted by a corrupt man.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 54. If this is so, then let sacrilegious persons, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be brought to ordination, since they think that the crimes or defects are removed through the blessing of ordination. Let there be no place for penance, because ordination can provide what lengthy satisfaction ordinarily provides.

But the law of our Church is to grant merely lay communion, through the laying on of hands, to those coming from heretics who were nevertheless baptized there, and not to place any of them, even to the slightest degree, in the honor of the clergy.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 55. But as for those who have passed from the Catholic Church to heresy, whom it is proper to receive only through penance: among you they not only do not perform penance, but are even loaded with honors.

Nevertheless, the considered decision of our former brother Anysius and of the other priests was that those whom Bonosus had ordained, so that they would not remain with him and a serious scandal arise, should be received as ordained men. I think we have overcome the ambiguities.

It is therefore clear that what was established as a remedy under the necessity of the present time did not exist at first. There were ancient rules, handed down by the apostles or apostolic men, which the Roman Church observes and commands to be observed by those accustomed to listen to her. But the necessity of the time urgently demanded that this be done.

Therefore, what necessity discovered as a remedy must, when the necessity has ceased, likewise cease, because the legitimate order is one thing, and an irregular usurpation is another—an usurpation which present circumstances compel for the time being.

But the canons established at Nicaea permitted this to be done in the case of the Novatians. The canon first established by the Fathers must be set out, so that we may understand what they meant and how they understood or commanded it:

“Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, Pure, and who at some time come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should remain in the clergy.”

We may say, however, that this command concerns only the Novatians and does not apply to the clerics of other heresies. For if they had intended to make a general ruling about all of them, they would have added that those returning from the Novatians and from other heretics should be restored to their own order.

If that were the case, the statement made especially concerning the Paulianists could also confirm it, since those who come from them are commanded to be baptized. When they give this command concerning the Paulianists, are all who return from heretics to be baptized according to this example? Since no one dares to do this, reason shows that the command concerns only them.

Finally, Peter and John complete by the laying on of hands those who had been rightly baptized by the evangelist Philip. But those whom the apostle Paul found baptized with John’s baptism, and whom he asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit—when they confessed that they had not even heard the name—he ordered to be baptized.

You see, therefore, that those who have been rightly baptized cannot receive that gift a second time, while it is judged necessary that those who have been washed with water alone be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Thus it is plainly shown that this command applies only to the Novatians. The manifest reason why it was distinguished between these two heresies is that the Paulianists do not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Among them the question of the unity of divine power—that is, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—has never been raised. Therefore, among all the separated groups, this one alone was singled out as deserving this concession, because they committed no offense against the sacrament of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

If someone passes from the Catholic Church to heresy, or, having been faithful, returns to apostasy and then repents and wishes to return, can the clergy likewise be entrusted to him? Their offense can be erased only by lengthy penance; and the canons do not permit such a person to become a cleric after penance.

It is therefore clear that those who passed from the Catholic Church to the condemned Bonosus, and who allowed or desired themselves to be ordained by him, ought not to have received the dignity of ecclesiastical ordination. They had abandoned the common judgment of all the Churches and decided that the peculiar folly of Bonosus should be followed.

Yet it is established that many suffered violence and were forcibly dragged away and ordained by him against their will. Let whoever believes this tell me whether a man who, after Bonosus’s ordination, was not present when Bonosus celebrated the sacraments, did not take part in his communion, and returned to the Church immediately upon leaving his wicked assembly, may have some color of excuse.

But concerning those who returned to the Church after a year or a month, we understand that they knew that in the Catholic Church, because of their vices, they could not receive ordination. For this reason they went to him, because he indiscriminately performed illicit ordinations without any examination, believing that through this arrangement they could find in the Catholic Church a position of which they had previously despaired.

Now I ask about what remains: what do you judge concerning one who returned after a month or more, while confident that he had been ordained presbyter by Bonosus, if he did not perform the sacraments, did not distribute them to the people, and did not complete the Masses according to custom? I ask you to state your judgment more openly.

In short, those who received nothing from Bonosus are guilty of usurping a dignity: they claimed—or did not claim—the authority to perform the sacraments, and thought themselves to be what had not been granted to them by any lawful procedure.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 56. Your Love therefore clearly sees that such things have continued until now, and you should understand that what, as you say, necessity compelled cannot be presumed in churches now established in peace. But, as often happens, whenever a people or a crowd sins, because punishment cannot be imposed upon everyone on account of their number, the matter commonly passes without punishment.

I say, therefore, that the earlier cases should be left to God’s judgment; henceforth, however, the greatest care must be taken to prevent such things.

The same, title 57. I shall now come to what is almost a great theme: Photinus. Since this matter causes me anxiety and is exceedingly difficult, I shall review the decisions of my predecessors.

Something more severe had in some way been established concerning him, as you yourselves also recall. But since you demonstrate that it was obtained from this see through false rumor, as you assert, and extracted by deceit, and since the matter has returned to a concern for salvation, we now grant you this pardon after the condemnation, as you earnestly request it, in the apostolic manner. We judge it harsher than any hardship not to agree to such extensive assertions of yours and to men so good and dear as you are.

Therefore, dearest brothers, for the sake of your approval, decision, and request, consider it lawful to establish Bishop Photinus in such a way that you may plead his case, and, through your labor and testimony, receive as the fulfillment of your desire our decision, which has been turned toward what is better.

And do not expect Eustathius, whom I have very frequently approved, to be stripped of the grace of the diaconate. I gladly hear that you are concerned for his salvation, but I do not gladly accept anything directed against him, even if it must be done. To the one to whom you extend your hand, I extend mine with you; to the one to whom I extend mine, extend yours with mine. This is the apostolic kindness declared to the Corinthians, so that good men may always follow without distinction a decision guided and restored in one spirit.

For, I confess, this matter first moves me favorably toward the deacon Eustathius: he has neither said anything against the faith, nor admitted anyone who spoke against it, nor, as far as I have learned, committed any crime deserving death—whether one ever alleged against him or invented.

And if he is sound in these matters, but in some way lacks amiable conduct, he should for the time being be regarded as less loved, not as an enemy to be handed over forever to the devil.

I know that amid those rivalries and storms he held an opinion contrary to the efforts of many—I will not say what kind—and when the circumstances and misfortunes themselves have been corrected here, the correction concerning the subdeacons Dizonianus and Cyriacus has still not been able to revive among you.

I ask you to restrain the dispositions and unjust rivalries of all whom you see directed against him and the aforesaid men, so that he, whole among us and restored among you with his associates, may deserve to find peace, perceiving a charity that is not feigned.

Therefore, let charity meet all of you, individually and collectively, and rejoice in the Lord, joined with you forever by bonds which Christ in no way dissolves.

### LXI. That a cleric of any order who abandons the Catholic Church and joins a heretical communion, if he returns to the Church, shall remain in the rank he held, without advancement

[Col. 0869C]

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 14. Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia.

Having read the letter of Your Fraternity, we have recognized the strength of your faith, which we knew in former times. We congratulate you because you vigilantly carry out pastoral care for the protection of Christ’s flock, lest wolves who have entered under the appearance of sheep tear the simple apart with beastly savagery, and lest they not only fail to improve through correction themselves but also corrupt what is sound.

Lest viperine deception gain its end, we have thought it necessary to admonish Your Love, pointing out that it endangers the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics or schismatics and in some way defiled himself through contact with a heretical communion is, after repenting, retained in Catholic communion without a proper profession of satisfaction.

It is most salutary and fully beneficial as spiritual medicine that presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and clerics of every order who wish to appear corrected and desire to return to the Catholic faith, which they had long before abandoned, should first confess without ambiguity their errors and the condemned authors of those errors.

Thus, when their perverse opinions have also been destroyed, no opportunity for hope will remain, and no member can be polluted by association with such persons, since their own profession will in every respect begin to confront them.

Concerning such people, we also command that the canonical regulation be observed: they should regard it as a great benefit if, with every hope of advancement removed, they remain permanently in the order in which they are found—provided they have not been defiled by a second baptism.

He incurs no slight offense before the Lord who judges such persons fit for promotion to the sacred orders. If promotion is granted to the blameless only after a rigorous examination, it should much less be permitted to the suspect.

Therefore, let Your Love, whose devotion gives us joy, join its care to our instructions, and see that what has been laudably proposed and salutarily ordered for the safety of the whole Church is carried out carefully and promptly.

Your Love should not doubt that, if—which we do not believe—what we decree for the protection of the canons and the integrity of the faith is neglected, we shall be moved with even greater force. For the faults of inferiors are chargeable upon no one more than upon negligent and careless rulers, who often nourish great pestilence while neglecting to apply the necessary medicine.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Alipius and Ardabur.

### LXII. Concerning those about whom it is uncertain whether they have received baptism: they must be reborn

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 28. If no evidence exists among relatives or household members, and none among clerics or neighbors, by which those in question can be shown to have been baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn. Otherwise they would plainly perish, since reason does not permit us to regard as repeated what is not shown to have been done.

Those who can remember coming to church with their parents may be able to recall whether they received what was given to their parents. But if even this is absent from their memory, it seems that what is not known to have been conferred should be conferred upon them, because there is no rash presumption where careful piety is present.

Council of Carthage, title 39. It was likewise decided concerning infants that whenever no completely reliable witnesses are found who can testify without hesitation that they were baptized, and when, because of their age, they themselves are not capable of answering concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, they are to be baptized without any scruple, lest this hesitation deprive them of the cleansing of the sacraments. Our brothers, the delegates of the Moors, consulted us about this, because they ransom many such children from the barbarians.

### LXIII. That those who acknowledge that they have been baptized but do not know in what faith are to be received through the laying on of hands

[Col. 0870D]

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 29. Those about whom you have written—who do not know whether they themselves were baptized, but profess that they do not know of what faith those who baptized them were—are not to be baptized, since in some manner they received the form of baptism. Rather, through the laying on of hands, they are to be joined to the Catholics and receive the power of the Holy Spirit, which they could not receive from heretics.

### LXIV. Concerning those who were compelled to undergo baptism again, not voluntarily but against their will

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 47. Concerning those whom Your Love likewise believed should be referred to us for consultation—those who were compelled to repeat baptism either through fear or because they were led astray by error, and who now recognize that they acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith—the following moderation must be observed: they are to be received into our fellowship and restored to the unity of communion only through the remedy of penance and the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

The periods of penance are to be established according to your judgment and with due moderation, as you observe the devotion of the converts’ hearts. At the same time, you should take into consideration old age and the necessities arising from any dangers or illnesses.

If someone is so severely afflicted that, while he is still doing penance, his salvation is despaired of, priestly care must come to his aid by granting him the grace of communion.

### LXV. That those baptized by heretics are to be strengthened through the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone

[Col. 0871B]

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 48. Those who received baptism from heretics, having not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed through the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone, by the laying on of hands, because they received only the form of baptism without the power of sanctification.

As you know, we proclaim that this rule must be observed in all the Churches: a washing once begun must not be violated by repetition. The Apostle says: “One God, one faith, one baptism.” Its cleansing must not be profaned by repetition. Instead, as we have said, only the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is to be invoked, so that they may receive from Catholic priests what no one receives from heretics.

### LXVI. Concerning those who receive baptism during illness

[Col. 0871C]

Council of Neocaesarea, title 12. If someone has been baptized during illness, he cannot be promoted to the honor of the presbyterate, because his faith arose not from deliberate purpose but from necessity—unless, perhaps, his subsequent zeal, faith, and the scarcity of men should make it possible for such a person to be admitted.

Council of Laodicea, title 47. Those who receive baptism during illness must, after they have recovered, learn the faith thoroughly and understand what gift they have become participants in.

Council of Carthage, title 12. The sick are to be baptized if they cannot answer for themselves, provided that those who speak as witnesses to their will do so at their own risk. Reconciliation must not be denied to actors, stage performers, and other persons of this kind.

### LXVII. Concerning Christians who are known to keep the Sabbath or in some manner to practice Judaism

Council of Laodicea, title 29. Christians must not practice Judaism or rest on the Sabbath, but must work on that day. They should honor the Lord’s Day above all; if they wish to rest, they should do so on that day as Christians. If they are found practicing Judaism, let them be anathema from Christ.

### LXVIII. Concerning schismatics

Council of Laodicea, title 33. Christians must not pray together with heretics or schismatics.

### LXIX. Concerning the martyrs of heretics

[Col. 0872A]

Council of Laodicea, title 34. Christians must not abandon the martyrs of Christ and go to false martyrs, that is, to the martyrs of heretics—persons who are themselves known to have been heretics. For such people are alienated from God. Therefore, let those who approach them be anathema.

Council of Carthage, title 50. It was likewise decided that altars which are commonly set up throughout fields and along roads as memorials of martyrs, where no body or relics of martyrs are proved to have been buried, should, if possible, be overturned by the bishops who preside over those places.

If popular disturbances prevent this, the people must nevertheless be warned not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held bound there by any superstition. No memorial of martyrs should be accepted as credible unless there is a body or some relics, or unless the origin of a dwelling, possession, or martyrdom is transmitted with the utmost reliability.

Altars established anywhere through dreams and through the spirits of whatever persons, as though by revelations, must be rejected in every respect.

### LXX. Concerning those who receive the festival gifts of heretics or Jews

Council of Laodicea, title 37. Christians must not receive the festive gifts sent by Jews or heretics, nor celebrate festivals with them.

### LXXI. Concerning Christians who have eaten the unleavened bread of the Jews

[Col. 0872C]

Council of Laodicea, title 38. Christians must not accept unleavened bread from the Jews or share in their impieties.

### LXXII. Concerning Christians who celebrate pagan festivals

Council of Laodicea, title 39. Christians must not celebrate festivals with pagans or share in the perversities of those who are without God.

### LXXIII. Concerning heretics entering churches or basilicas of martyrs

Council of Laodicea, title 6. Heretics who remain in heresy must not be permitted to enter the house of God.

### LXXIV. Penance is to be granted to captives who, under necessity, eat sacrificial foods

[Col. 0872D]

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 46. Concerning those Christians who are said to have been defiled among their captors by sacrificial foods, we have thought that this also must be given in answer to the consultation of Your Love: they are to be cleansed through the satisfaction of penance, which should be measured not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart.

Whether terror extorted this food or hunger urged it, there should be no doubt that the offense is to be removed, since such food was consumed through fear or want, not in veneration of a religion.

### LXXV. How penitents are to be received in the Church

Council of Carthage, title 10. The bishops are to establish periods of penance according to the differences among sins and according to their own judgment. A presbyter must not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when the bishop’s absence makes necessity compelling.

If a penitent’s crime is public and notorious and has disturbed the entire Church, hands are to be laid upon him before the apse.

### LXXVI. Concerning those who have been advanced to the presbyterate without examination

Council of Nicaea, title 9. If any presbyters have been advanced without examination, or, when examined, have confessed their sins, and people, stirred up contrary to the canons, have attempted to lay hands upon those who confessed, the rule does not admit such men. For the Catholic Church defends what is irreproachable.

#### When it is appropriate to ordain a presbyter

Council of Neocaesarea, title 11. A presbyter must in no way be ordained before his thirtieth year, even if he is highly worthy. This period must be observed, for our Lord was baptized in the thirtieth year of his age and then began to teach.

### LXXVII. Concerning those who denied the faith during persecutions and were later promoted to the clergy

Council of Nicaea, title 10. Whoever among those who fell has been promoted to the clerical order through the ignorance or negligence of those who ordained him has not thereby prejudiced the ecclesiastical rule. Once discovered, such persons must be deposed.

### LXXVIII. Concerning laypeople who denied the faith, and concerning those who renounced it and then returned again to the world

Council of Nicaea, titles 11 and 12. Concerning those who transgressed apart from necessity, apart from the confiscation of their property, or apart from danger or something similar that occurred under the tyranny of Licinius: although the synod judges them unworthy of humaneness, it has nevertheless decided that kindness should be extended to them.

Therefore, all who truly repent shall spend three years among the hearers, and after that shall humble themselves with every form of contrition for six years. For two years they shall join the people in prayer without offering.

All who, having been called by grace, initially displayed zeal by laying aside the military belt but later returned to their own vomit, so that some even gave money and by means of benefits resumed military service, shall remain in affliction for ten years after the three-year period during which they will be among the hearers.

In all these cases, however, their purpose and the character of their penance must be examined. For all who demonstrate by their actual conduct—not by pretense—that their conversion is genuine through fear, tears, penance, or good works shall, after completing the prescribed period among the hearers, then join the faithful in prayer. Afterward it will be permissible for the bishop to consider showing them some greater humanity.

But those who bore their punishment indifferently and thought that merely gaining entrance into the church would suffice for their conversion must complete the prescribed period in every respect.

### LXXIX. Concerning those who request communion at the time of death

Council of Nicaea, title 13. Concerning those who are approaching death, the ancient and regular law shall still be observed, so that if anyone is departing from the body, he may not be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum.

If someone who was considered beyond hope, after receiving communion and becoming a participant in the offering, should recover, he shall be numbered among those who receive only communion in prayer.

In general, whenever anyone at the point of death asks that the grace of communion be granted to him, the bishop ought reasonably to give it from the offering.

### LXXX. Concerning fallen catechumens

Council of Nicaea, title 14. Concerning catechumens, the holy and great council has decided that they shall remain for three years among the hearers alone; after that, they shall pray with the catechumens.

### LXXXI. Concerning presbyters who sacrificed during persecution

[Col. 0874B]

Council of Ancyra, title 1. Concerning presbyters who sacrificed and afterward entered the struggle again: if they did this not through some deception but genuinely, and if they did not previously prepare, seek, or encourage the appearance that they were being subjected to torments, but merely submitted to the sight and outward appearance of them, it has pleased the council that they retain the honor of their own seat but may not offer, address the people, or perform any priestly functions at all.

### LXXXII. Concerning deacons who sacrificed

Council of Ancyra, title 2. Likewise, deacons who sacrificed may retain their honor, but must cease from every sacred ministry, whether offering the bread or the cup or preaching.

If some bishops are aware of their labor, humility, and gentleness, and wish to grant them something more, or to take something away, the authority shall rest with those bishops.

### LXXXIII. Concerning those who were captured after fleeing and sacrificed under compulsion
Council of Ancyra, canon 3. Those who were captured while fleeing, or betrayed by their household, or who, after their property had been confiscated, endured torture, or who, having been thrust into prison, proclaimed themselves Christians, and were constrained to such an extent that those who had seized their hands forcibly dragged them forward and brought them to impious sacrifices, or compelled them by necessity to consume some polluted food; and who continually confessed that they were Christians and unceasingly displayed grief over what had happened, with every sign of dejection, in their manner and the humility of their life—such persons, as being placed outside the offense, are not to be barred from the grace of communion. If, however, they have been prohibited by some on account of greater caution or through the ignorance of certain persons, they are to be received immediately. The same rule should likewise be observed concerning clerics and the other laity.

It was also investigated whether laymen who had fallen into such straits of necessity could be promoted to the clerical order. It was therefore decided that these too, as persons who had committed no sin, should be advanced to this office, provided that their preceding life had also been approved.

LXXXIV. Concerning those who, for various reasons, performed something according to the rite of the pagans.

Council of Ancyra, canon 4. Concerning those who were compelled to sacrifice and in addition dined in an idol-temple. Whoever among them, when they were being led there, appeared cheerful, wore more costly garments, and participated without distinction in the prepared banquet: it was decided that they should be placed among the hearers for one year, prostrate themselves for three years, share in prayer for two years, and then attain the grace of full restoration. But as many as went up to the temples in mournful clothing and, while reclining, wept throughout the entire meal, if they completed three years of penance, are to be received without the offering. If they did not eat, they are to undergo two years of penance and, in the third year, share in communion without the offering, so that they may attain full restoration after four years. The bishops shall have authority, after examining the manner of their life, either to treat them more humanely or to add further time. Above all, their former and subsequent life must be investigated, and mercy shown to them accordingly.

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, canon 3. It has also been reported that certain Christians, passing into apostasy—which it is impious even to mention—and profaned by the worship of idols and the pollution of sacrifices, are to be cut off, by our command, from the body and blood of Christ, by which they had formerly been redeemed and reborn. If at some time they should come to their senses and turn to lamentation, they are to perform penance for as long as they live, and at the very end of their life the grace of reconciliation is to be granted them, because, as the Lord teaches, we do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn and live.

LXXXV. Concerning those who performed the rites of the pagans out of fear.

[Col. 0875C]

Council of Ancyra, canon 5. Concerning those who sacrificed merely because of threats of punishment, or because they were terrified by the confiscation of their property, or because of exile, and who until now, neglecting repentance and failing to convert, have now presented themselves at the time of this council, forming resolutions for their conversion: it was decided that they should be received among the hearers until the great day; after the great day they should perform penance for three years; afterward they should share in communion without the offering for two years; and only then, when six years had been completed, should they attain the grace of full restoration. If some were admitted to penance before this synod, their six-year period is to be reckoned from that time. If, however, any danger, expectation of death—whether from illness or from another circumstance—should arise, communion is not to be denied them under the established rule.

LXXXVI. Concerning those who ate in places of idols.

Council of Ancyra, canon 6. Concerning those who on the feast days of the pagans held banquets in their remote shrines and, bringing their customary foods, ate there: it was decided that they should be received after two years of penance. Whether they are to be received with the offering, however, is to be determined by each bishop, who must examine their life and investigate their individual conduct.

LXXXVII. Concerning those who frequently sacrificed to idols.

Council of Ancyra, canon 7. Those who, under compulsion, sacrificed a second and third time are to undergo four years of penance; for two additional years they are to share in communion without the offering, and in the seventh year they are to be fully received.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, canon 30. If they merely attended a pagan banquet and consumed sacrificial foods, they can be cleansed by fasts and the laying on of hands, so that thereafter, abstaining from food sacrificed to idols, they may participate in the sacraments of Christ. But if they either worshiped idols or were polluted by murders or fornications, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.

LXXXVIII. Concerning those who also supplied others with reasons for sacrificing.

Council of Ancyra, canon 8. But all who not only went astray themselves, but also rose up against and compelled their brothers, and furnished the reasons why they were compelled: these are to receive a place among the hearers for three years; for another six years they are to undergo more severe penance; and for one further year they are to receive communion without the offering, so that, when ten years have been completed, they may attain full restoration. Meanwhile, their manner of life must also be weighed.

LXXXIX. Concerning those who sacrificed to idols while they were catechumens.

Council of Ancyra, canon 11. Those who sacrificed to idols before baptism and afterward received baptism may, it was decided, be advanced to the clerical order, since they have been proved to have been cleansed.

XC. Concerning those who seek divinations.

Council of Ancyra, canon 23. Those who seek divinations and follow the custom of the pagans, or who introduce into their homes persons of this kind to inquire into something by magical art or for the purpose of expiation, are to lie under the five-year rule, according to the defined stages of penance.

Concerning those who worship angels.

Council of Laodicea, canon 35. Christians ought not to abandon the Church of God, go away, invoke angels by name, or form assemblies which are known to be forbidden. Therefore, if anyone is found serving this hidden idolatry, let him be anathema, because he has abandoned our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and given himself over to idolatry.

That a cleric must not be a magician or enchanter, nor make amulets.

[Col. 0876D]

Council of Laodicea, canon 36. Those devoted to sacred offices, or clerics, ought not to be magicians or enchanters, nor make amulets, which are proved to be bonds of their souls. We command that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.

XCI. Concerning those who are promoted to the presbyterate or diaconate and are conscious of sins committed before ordination.

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 9. If a presbyter who has been overtaken by a bodily sin is promoted, and confesses that he committed the offense before ordination, he shall not consecrate the offerings; nevertheless, he shall retain the rest of his office on account of his good zeal, since many have said that other sins can be forgiven through the laying on of hands. If he has not confessed the matter himself and cannot be openly convicted, it is to be left to the judgment of his own authority.

Council of the same, canon 10. Likewise, if a deacon has fallen into the same sin, he is to be removed from the order of ministry.

XCII. Concerning deacons who, at the time of their ordination, made a declaration regarding marriage.

Council of Ancyra, canon 9. Any deacons who, at the very time of their ordination, protested and declared that they wished to marry because they could not remain otherwise: if afterward they take wives, they are to remain in the ministry, because the bishop had given them permission. Those who kept silent, however, accepted the laying on of hands, and professed continence, but afterward became bound by marriage, must cease from the ministry.

XCIII. That presbyters should observe the measure proper to them.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, canon 6. We also forbid presbyters to overstep their proper measure and boldly to assume for themselves what belongs to the episcopal dignity: they must not seize the authority to prepare the chrism or to administer episcopal confirmation; nor, in the presence of any bishop, unless perhaps ordered, presume to take upon themselves either a prayer or a sacred action; nor, in his presence, unless ordered, presume either to sit or to handle the venerable mysteries. Let them remember that in no way is it granted them, without the supreme pontiff, to have the right to appoint a subdeacon or acolyte. Nor should they doubt that, if they undertake on their own initiative anything specially belonging to episcopal ministry, they will immediately be deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate and of sacred communion. We judge that this must occur if such transgression is proved while their bishop delays to act; nor will their own bishop be free from the guilt of connivance and from punishment if he neglects to avenge such immoderate conduct.

Council of Carthage, canon 6. Bishop Fortunatus said: We remember that it was established in previous councils that the preparation of the chrism, the reconciliation of penitents, and also the consecration of virgins are not to be performed by presbyters. If anyone should be found doing this, what is to be decreed concerning him?

[Col. 0877D]

Bishop Aurelius said: Your Grace has heard the petition of our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus. What do you say concerning these matters? All the bishops said: The preparation of the chrism and the consecration of virgins are not to be performed by presbyters, nor is it permitted to a presbyter to reconcile anyone at a public Mass. This pleases us all.

Council of Carthage, canon 7. Bishop Aurelius said: If anyone is in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, and the bishop is absent, the presbyter must certainly consult the bishop and then, at his command, reconcile the person in danger. We ought to strengthen this practice by salutary counsel. All the bishops said: We approve what Your Holiness has deemed it necessary to instruct us in.

XCIV. Concerning the privileges of presbyters.

Council of Nicaea, canon 18. It has come to the attention of the holy and great council that in certain places and cities deacons give presbyters the grace of sacred communion—something handed down neither by rule nor by custom—so that those who have no power to offer give the body of Christ to those who do offer it. It has also become known that certain deacons touch the sacred offerings before the bishops. Let all these practices therefore be removed, and let the deacons remain within their proper measure, knowing that they are ministers of the bishops but are to be regarded as inferior to presbyters. Accordingly, after the presbyters, in due order, let them receive the grace of sacred communion, whether the bishop or the presbyter hands it to them. Nor is it permitted for deacons to sit among the presbyters, because if this is done, it is shown to be contrary to rule and order. If anyone, after these definitions, refuses to obey, he must cease from the ministry.

Council of Laodicea, canon 20. A deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a presbyter, but should sit at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, honor is to be shown to deacons by those who serve under them, that is, by subdeacons and all clerics.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, canon 8. A deacon ought not to sit in the presbyterium while divine services are being celebrated or any ecclesiastical business is being conducted; whoever he may be, he has no right to exercise the prerogative of distributing the sacred body in the presence of a bishop or presbyter, unless these are absent. Since we too strive with the greatest care to observe the decrees of venerable authorities, we say that even those matters which might perhaps appear relaxable for the sake of some practical advantage must not be relaxed at their expense.

XCV. That deacons should preserve their proper measure according to the statutes of the Fathers.

From the decree of Pope Gelasius, canon 7. We likewise establish that deacons must preserve their proper measure, and we do not permit them to attempt anything beyond the limit assigned by the canons of the Fathers. They must not appropriate to their ministry anything that antiquity decreed properly to belong to the higher orders. Without a bishop or presbyter they must not dare to baptize, unless extreme necessity should perhaps compel them to perform these offices when those persons are far away; this is also often permitted to Christian laymen.

XCVI. Concerning the chorepiscopus, that is, the bishop’s vicar; and what belongs to his office.

Council of Ancyra, canon 12. Chorepiscopi are not permitted to ordain presbyters or deacons; nor may presbyters of the city do so in any parish without the bishop’s command or letters.

Council of Antioch, canon 10. Those who are appointed chorepiscopi in villages or rural estates, although they have received the laying on of the hands of bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decided that they must recognize their proper measure and govern the churches subject to them, being content with their administration and care. They may also ordain readers, subdeacons, and exorcists; these promotions are sufficient for them. But they must not dare to ordain either a presbyter or a deacon without the city bishop, to whom both the chorepiscopus and the estate are subject. If anyone attempts to transgress these statutes, he is to be deposed and deprived of the honor he held. The chorepiscopus, however, is to be ordained by the city bishop to whom he is subject.

XCVII. Concerning ecclesiastical property alienated while the churches themselves were vacant through the death or absence of their bishops.

Council of Ancyra, canon 14. Concerning those things belonging to the Church which presbyters sold when there was no bishop: it was decided that, after the contract has been annulled, they are to be restored to ecclesiastical ownership. It will be for the bishop to judge whether the price should be accepted or not, because the return from the properties sold has often produced a larger sum than the price paid.

Council of Carthage, canon 26. It was likewise decided that no one may sell a possession of the Church. But if it produces no income and some extreme necessity compels the sale, the matter must be brought to the chief bishop of that province, so that, together with the prescribed number of bishops, he may determine whether it should be done. If such a great necessity presses upon the Church that its chief bishop cannot be consulted, the seller must at least summon neighboring bishops as witnesses and take care to report all the needs of his church to the council. If he does not do so, he is to be held liable before God and the council; having lost his honor, he is to be held accountable as the seller.

XCVIII. Concerning those in the clergy who abstain from eating meat.

[Col. 0879C]

Council of Ancyra, canon 13. Those who are presbyters and deacons in the clergy and abstain from meat: it was decided that they may indeed touch it and then abstain, if they wish. But if they abominate it to such an extent that they consider even vegetables cooked with meat unfit to eat, they must withdraw from the order as persons not consenting to the rule.

XCIX. Concerning those who commit unnatural fornication, that is, with animals or with males.

Council of Ancyra, canon 15. Concerning those who have acted, or are acting, unnaturally: all who committed such a crime before the age of twenty are, after completing fifteen years in penance, to merit communion in prayers; then, remaining in this communion for five years, they may finally touch the sacraments of the offering. Their life must also be examined, namely, what it was like during the time of their repentance, and they are to receive mercy accordingly. If they cling to these crimes without satisfaction, they must devote a longer period to performing penance. Those who, after reaching the age of twenty and having wives, have fallen into this sin are to be received into communion in prayers after performing twenty-five years of penance; remaining in that communion for five years, they may then receive the sacraments of the offering. But if any, while having wives and being over fifty years of age, have committed such an offense, they are to receive the grace of communion at the end of their life.

[Col. 0880A]

Council of Ancyra, canon 16. Those who have lived unnaturally and have infected others with the leprosy of this grievous crime: the holy synod has ordered that they pray among those who are afflicted by an unclean spirit.

C. Concerning monks and virgins who do not keep their profession.

Council of Ancyra, canon 18. All who promise virginity but make their pledge void are to be counted among those who have married a second time. We forbid virgins who come together with certain men to live with them as sisters.

Council of Chalcedon, canon 7. Those who have once been enrolled in the clergy or have chosen the life of monks: we decree that they may neither enter military service nor attain any worldly dignity. Those who attempt this and do not perform penance, refusing to return to what they originally chose for God’s sake, are to be anathematized.

Council of Chalcedon, canon 16. A virgin who has consecrated herself to the Lord, and likewise a monk, may not contract the rights of marriage. If they are found to have done so, let them be excommunicated. In the case of those who confess, however, we have decreed that the bishop of the place has authority to extend mercy and humane treatment.

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, canon 6. Furthermore, you report that certain monks and nuns, having abandoned their purpose of holiness, have sunk into such great wantonness that at first, secretly and under the pretext of monasteries, they entered into illicit and sacrilegious intercourse; afterward, driven by despair of conscience to the precipice, they openly begot children from their unlawful embraces—something condemned both by public laws and by ecclesiastical statutes. We therefore command that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the company of the monasteries and from the assemblies of the churches, so that, shut away in their prisons and lamenting such a great offense in continual mourning, they may purge it in the cleansing fire of repentance, and so that, even if only at death, the grace of communion may bring them forgiveness through the consideration of mercy.

CI. Likewise, concerning veiled virgins who have gone astray.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, canon 19. Those who spiritually marry Christ and are veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or secretly corrupt themselves, are not to be admitted to perform penance until the person to whom they joined themselves has departed from the world. For if this rule is observed among human beings, so that any woman who, while her husband is alive, marries another is regarded as an adulteress and is not granted permission to perform penance until one of the two has died, how much more must it be observed in the case of one who had first joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward passed over to human marriage?

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, canon 20. Those women, however, who have not yet been covered with the sacred veil but have always pretended to remain in the purpose of virginity, although they have not been veiled, if they should happen to marry, must perform penance for some period of time, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a good-faith contract ordinarily cannot be dissolved on any ground, how much more cannot this promise, which they made with God, be dissolved without punishment? For if the apostle Paul said that those who had departed from the purpose of widowhood had condemnation because they had made their first faith void, how much more so virgins who have attempted to break faith with their earlier promise?

From the decree of Pope Leo, canon 26. The monastic purpose, once undertaken by one’s own decision and will, cannot be abandoned without sin; for what one has vowed to God, one must also repay. Therefore, one who, having abandoned the profession of a solitary life, has turned to military service or marriage must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance, because, even if military service can be innocent and marriage honorable, abandoning the choice of better things is a transgression.

Canon 27. Girls who, not compelled by the authority of their parents but by their own free judgment, have adopted the purpose and habit of virginity, if afterward they choose marriage, are transgressors, even if the grace of consecration has not yet been conferred upon them. They would certainly not have been deprived of that gift if they had remained in their purpose.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, canon 20. We have learned that certain men rashly join themselves to sacred virgins and, after the purpose dedicated to God, enter into incestuous and sacrilegious unions. Such men should immediately be cast out from sacred communion and should not be received at all except through public and approved penance. Yet, if they have repented, the viaticum should not be denied them when they depart from this world.

CII. Concerning those who have adulterous wives or are proved to be adulterers.

Council of Ancyra, canon 19. If someone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he must attain full restoration through seven years of penance, according to the former stages.

CIII. Concerning those who in various ways kill their offspring conceived in fornication.

Council of Ancyra, canon 20. Concerning women who commit fornication and destroy their offspring, or who act upon themselves so as to expel what has been conceived in the womb: the ancient definition indeed removes them from the Church until the end of their life; but now we define more humanely that they be granted ten years, according to the prescribed stages of penance.

CIV. Concerning murderers and those who have committed homicide involuntarily.

Council of Ancyra, canons 21 and 22. Those who have committed voluntary homicide are to submit themselves continually to penance; they are to attain full restoration only near the end of their life. Concerning involuntary homicides, the earlier definition commands that they attain full restoration after seven years of penance; the second prescribes that they complete a period of five years.

CV. Concerning betrothed girls who are violated by others.

Council of Ancyra, canon 10. Betrothed girls who afterward are carried off by others are to be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence was inflicted upon them by their abductors.

From the decrees of Siricius, canon 4. You have inquired concerning violation of marriage, whether another man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to someone else. We absolutely forbid this, so that it may not occur, because among the faithful that blessing which the priest bestows upon those about to marry is like a sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

CVI. Concerning those who are accomplices in the violation of virgins.

Council of Ancyra, canon 24. A certain man, having a betrothed woman, violated her sister and made her pregnant; afterward he took his betrothed as his wife, while the woman who had been violated killed herself by hanging. Those who were accomplices were ordered to be received after ten years of satisfaction, according to the established stages of penance.

CVII. A layman who dismisses his wife is to be deprived of communion.

In the Canons of the Apostles, canon 48. If a layman dismisses his own wife and marries another, or one who has been dismissed by another, let him be deprived of communion.

CVIII. Concerning presbyters who have taken wives or committed fornication.

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 1. If a presbyter takes a wife, he is to be deposed from the order. But if he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled still more completely and reduced to penance.

CIX. That priests and Levites ought not to have intercourse with their wives.

[Col. 0882C]

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, canon 16. Furthermore, the Church must preserve in every way what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the daily necessities of the mystery [Note: [Col. 0881D] Dionysius Exiguus reads “of the ministry”]. For it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.” If in ancient times the priests of God did not leave the temple during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah, and did not touch their own house at all—although the use of a wife [Note: [Col. 0882D] Dionysius Exiguus reads “marital”] had been relaxed for them on account of the succession of offspring, since no one from another tribe, or from any lineage other than the seed of Aaron, was commanded to approach the priesthood—how much more ought these priests or Levites to preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry exists without succession, and no day passes in which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the office of baptism?

For if Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying, “Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer”—and he certainly gave this command to laymen—how much more must priests, whose continual duty is both to pray and to sacrifice, always abstain from such intercourse? If one of them has been polluted by carnal desire, with what shame will he perhaps presume to sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit will he believe that he is heard, when it is said: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

[Col. 0883A]

From the decrees of Pope Leo, canon 17. The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. While they were laymen or readers, they were lawfully able both to marry wives and to beget children; but when they reached the aforementioned grades, what had been permitted to them began to be forbidden. Therefore, so that a carnal marriage may become spiritual, they must not dismiss their wives, but have them as though they did not have them, so that the affection of marriage may be preserved while the activity of marriage ceases.

Council of Carthage, canon 25. Bishop Aurelius said: We add this, dearest brothers: since a report had been made concerning the lack of continence of certain clerics, even readers, toward their own wives, it was decided—and this has also been confirmed in various councils—that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, and deacons and presbyters, as well as bishops, are, according to the earlier statutes, to abstain even from their wives and appear as though they did not have them. If they do not do this, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. The other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this except at a more mature age.

CX. Which women may dwell with a bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

Council of Nicaea, canon 3. The great synod has entirely forbidden that a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy may have a woman introduced into his household, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, aunt, or only such persons as escape suspicion.

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, canon 12. We do not permit any other women to be in the houses of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely because of the necessity of family relationships.

CXI. Concerning presbyters who have had marriages.

Council of Gangra, canon 4. If anyone distinguishes himself from a presbyter who has had a wife, on the ground that one ought not, while that presbyter is ministering, receive from the offering, let him be anathema.

CXII. Concerning women who have married two brothers, or men who have taken two sisters as wives.

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 2. If a woman marries two brothers, she is to be cast out until death. Nevertheless, at the end of her life, out of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, she may obtain the fruit of penance. If the woman or the man dies in such a marriage, penance during the remainder of life will be difficult.

CXIII. Concerning those who marry repeatedly.

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 3. Concerning those who have entered into many marriages: the prescribed period is indeed clear, but their conduct and faith shorten the period.

CXIV. Concerning those whom God does not permit to fulfill their desire.

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 4. If someone, desiring a woman, plans to have intercourse with her, but his thought does not reach fulfillment, it is evident that he has been freed by the grace of God.

CXV. Concerning sinful catechumens.

[Col. 0884A]

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 5. If a catechumen enters the church and takes his place among those who are being instructed, but is then found committing sin: if he kneels, let him hear and not sin further; but if, while continuing to hear, he sins, let him be expelled.

CXVI. Concerning a pregnant catechumen.

Canon 6 of the same council. A pregnant woman ought to be baptized whenever she wishes. For the one who gives birth communicates nothing of this matter to the one being born, since each person’s own purpose is declared in confession.

CXVII. That a presbyter ought not to pray at the marriage of a man who has married a second time.

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 7. It is not fitting for a presbyter to dine at the marriage of a man who has married a second time, because, since such a man requires penance, who is the presbyter who could, on account of a banquet, give consent to such a marriage?

CXVIII. Concerning those who are joined to adulterous women.

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 8. If the wife of a layman has committed adultery and this is clearly proved, the man cannot afterward enter the ministry of the clergy. But if she commits adultery after his ordination, he ought to dismiss her; if he lives with her, he cannot retain the ministry entrusted to him.

CXIX. That rural presbyters in the city church ought neither to offer sacrifice nor administer what has been offered.

[Col. 0884C]

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 13. Rural presbyters cannot offer in the city church when the bishop or the city’s own presbyters are present; nor may they give the consecrated bread or offer the chalice. But if these are absent and the rural presbyters are summoned to give the prayer, they alone ought to give it. Chorepiscopi also appear to be modeled on the seventy in example and form; as fellow ministers, however, they are to be honored because of the zeal they display toward the poor.

CXX. That there should be only seven deacons in any large city, according to the apostles’ arrangement.

Council of Neocaesarea, canon 14. There ought to be seven deacons according to the rule, even if the city is very large; the same thing is also indicated by the Book of Acts of the Apostles.

CXXI. Concerning those who condemn marriage.

[Col. 0884D]

Council of Gangra, canon 1. If anyone condemns marriage and detests a faithful and religious woman sleeping with her husband, or considers such women blameworthy, as though they could not enter the kingdom of God, let him be anathema.

CXXII. Concerning those who abominate those who eat meat.

Council of Gangra, canon 2. If anyone condemns a person who eats meat—apart from blood, meat sacrificed to idols, and strangled meat—with religion and faith, as though such a person had no hope because of this consumption, let him be anathema.

CXXIII. Concerning slaves who cast off the yoke of servitude under the pretext of Christianity.

[Col. 0885A]

Council of Gangra, canon 3. If anyone, under the pretext of divine worship, teaches a slave to despise his own master, leave his service, and fail to serve him with goodwill and every honor, let him be anathema.

CXXIV. Concerning those who despise the assemblies of the Church.

Council of Gangra, canon 5. If anyone teaches that the house of God is contemptible, and the assemblies held there, let him be anathema.

CXXV. Concerning those who perform ecclesiastical ministries outside the church.

Council of Gangra, canon 6. If anyone holds separate assemblies outside the church and, despising the church, wishes to usurp the things belonging to the church, without a presbyter’s participation, in accordance with the bishop’s decree, let him be anathema.

CXXVI. Concerning offerings of fruits presented to the ministers of the Church.

Council of Gangra, canon 7. If anyone wishes to receive or give the Church’s offerings outside the church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and refuses to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.

CXXVII. Concerning things contributed for the use of the poor.

Council of Gangra, canon 8. Concerning things contributed for the use of the poor: if anyone gives or receives offerings apart from the bishop or the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, both the one who gives and the one who receives are to be anathema.

CXXVIII. Concerning those who do not remain legitimately in virginity.

Council of Gangra, canon 9. Whoever practices abstinence while guarding virginity as though he abhorred marriage, and assumes the name of virginity not because it is good and holy, let him be anathema.

CXXIX. Concerning those who take pride in virginity.

Council cited above, canon 10. If anyone among those who preserve virginity for the Lord exalts himself against married people, let him be anathema.

CXXX. Concerning those who ridicule agapae, that is, meals for the poor.

[Col. 0885D]

Council cited above, canon 11. If anyone despises those who faithfully provide agapae, that is, banquets, for the poor, and summon the brothers for the honor of the Lord, and refuses to share in such invitations, making light of what is being done, let him be anathema.

CXXXI. Concerning those who wear cloaks and thereby take pride.

Council of Gangra, canon 12. If any man, on account of the continence that is presumed of him, wears a cloak as though believing that by this he possesses righteousness, and despises those who reverently wear birri—woolen cloaks—and other ordinary and customary garments, let him be anathema.

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 14. For we have learned that the priests of the Lord serve superstitious worship rather than purity of mind or faith. [Note: [Col. 0885D] Dionysius Exiguus adds: “certain.”] But it is not surprising that they act contrary to ecclesiastical custom, since they did not grow up in the Church; rather, coming by another path, they brought into the Church with them practices that they had maintained in another way of life. Wrapped in a cloak and girded about the loins, they believe that they will fulfill the faith of Holy Scripture not through the spirit but through the letter. For if these commands were given so that they should be observed in this manner, why are the things that follow not likewise done—why are burning lamps not held together with a staff? [Col. 0886B]

These things have their own mystery, and to those who understand, they are so clear that they are observed in the more fitting sense intended. For the girding of the loins signifies chastity; the staff, pastoral rule; and the burning lamps, the radiance of good works, of which it is said, “So let your works shine.” Yet perhaps those who dwell in more remote places and live far from others maintain this form of dress, following custom rather than reason.

And shortly afterward:

We must be distinguished from the populace and from others by teaching, not by clothing; by conduct, not by dress; by purity of mind, not by outward observance. For if we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by the Fathers and make room for superstitions. Therefore we must not lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful into such things; they should rather be taught than praised, and the precepts should not be imposed upon their eyes but poured into their minds. [Col. 0886C]

### CXXXII. Concerning women who wear masculine clothing

Council of Gangra, title 13. If any woman, because of the continence that she imagines she possesses, changes her dress and, instead of the customary clothing of women, takes on masculine attire, let her be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0886D] Dionysius Exiguus adds: “which she imagines.”]

### CXXXIII. Concerning those who abandon marital intercourse as though it were a sin

Council of Gangra, title 14. If any woman wishes to leave and depart from her own husband, having condemned marriage, let her be anathema.

### CXXXIV. Concerning those who neglect their children under pretext of Christianity

[Col. 0886D]

Council of Gangra, title 15. If anyone abandons his children and does not nourish them, and, so far as he is concerned, does not train them in the piety of divine worship, but neglects them on the pretext of continence, let him be anathema.

### CXXXV. Concerning those who despise their parents under pretext of Christianity

Council of Gangra, title 16. Whoever leaves his parents under the pretext of divine worship and does not show due reverence to those who, undoubtedly, place divine worship before themselves, let him be anathema.

### CXXXVI. Concerning women who cut their hair under pretext of Christianity

[Col. 0887A]

Council of Gangra, title 17. If any woman cuts off her hair because of the divine worship, as she supposes, thereby abolishing the command of obedience represented by the hair that God gave her as a reminder of subjection, let her be anathema.

### CXXXVII. Concerning those who fast on the Lord’s Day as though it differed in no way from other days

Council of Gangra, title 18. If anyone fasts on the Lord’s Day because of supposed continence or out of defiance, let him be anathema.

### CXXXVIII. Concerning those who kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost

Council of Nicaea, title 20. Since there are certain people who kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, so that everything may be observed uniformly in all places, the holy council decreed that on the Lord’s Day prayers should be offered while standing. [Note: [Col. 0887D] Dionysius Exiguus adds: “to the Lord.”]

### CXXXIX. Concerning those who abolish the ecclesiastical fasts without necessity

Council of Gangra, title 19. If anyone among those who practice continence, without bodily necessity, proudly abolishes the fasts handed down in common and observed by the Church, driven by the impulse of his own thoughts, let him be anathema.

### CXL. Concerning those who condemn the gatherings held in commemoration of the martyrs

Council of Gangra, title 29. If anyone, moved by an attitude of pride, abominates the gatherings held at the memorials of the martyrs, and condemns the services performed there together with their commemorations, let him be anathema.

### CXLI. Concerning those who remain in another parish without the knowledge of their own bishops

Council of Antioch, title 3. If any presbyter or deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy, abandons his own parish and hastens to another, then, having entirely migrated, strives to remain for a long time in another parish, he shall no longer minister there—especially if he has contemptuously refused to obey his own bishop when summoned and admonished to return to his own parish. If he persists in this lack of discipline, he must be removed from the ministry in every way, so that he may never find an opportunity for restoration. [Col. 0887D] But if another bishop receives one condemned for this reason, that bishop too shall be restrained by the common synod, as one who dissolves ecclesiastical regulations.

### CXLII. Concerning bishops who approach the emperor

Council of Antioch, title 11. If any bishop, presbyter, or anyone subject to the rule of the Church approaches the emperor without the council and letters of the bishops of the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he must be rejected and expelled—not only from communion but also from the honor of which he appears to be a participant—because he has attempted to trouble the ears of the revered ruler contrary to the laws of the Church. If, therefore, necessity requires that anyone approach the ruler, it must be done with the deliberation and counsel of the metropolitan and of the other bishops residing in the same province; they should also accompany the traveler with their letters.

### CXLIII. Concerning condemned bishops or clerics who approach the emperor

Council of Antioch, title 12. If a presbyter or deacon has been condemned by his own bishop, or a bishop by a synod, and has troubled the ears of the emperor, he ought to appeal to a greater council of bishops and present to many bishops whatever they judge to be just, awaiting their investigations and judgments. But if, disregarding these provisions, they trouble the emperor, we judge them worthy of no pardon, entitled to no opportunity for satisfaction, and not to await any hope of future restoration.

Council of Carthage, title 71. It was decreed that whoever seeks from the emperor an examination of public judgments shall be deprived of his proper rank. But if he requests an episcopal judgment from the emperor, this shall not prejudice him.

### CXLIV. Concerning disputes arising over the judgment of bishops, and concerning a bishop consistently excluded by all the bishops of his province

Council of Antioch, title 14. If a bishop is judged concerning definite crimes [Note: [Col. 0887D] “is judged,” Dionysius Exiguus], and the provincial bishops happen to disagree about him—when some believe the one judged to be innocent and others consider him guilty—then, for the resolution of this uncertainty, the holy synod decreed that the metropolitan bishop summon other judges from a neighboring province, who shall remove the controversy, so that through them, together with the provincial bishops, whatever appears just may be approved. [Note: [Col. 0888D] Dionysius Exiguus reads “for the absolution of the whole uncertainty.”]

Council of Antioch, title 15. If a bishop, accused of definite crimes, is condemned by all the bishops of the same province, and all unanimously issue the same form of decree against him, he must in no way be judged by others; the decision of the bishops of the province who have agreed shall remain firm.

Council of Carthage, title 19. Bishop Aurelius said:

Whoever accuses a bishop shall bring the accusation before the primates of that bishop’s province. The person charged with the crime shall not be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned by letters to state his case on the appointed day before the chosen judges, he fails to appear—that is, within the period of one month from the day on which it is established that he received the letters. But if he proves that he was prevented from appearing by genuine causes of necessity, he shall have a full opportunity to state his case within the following month. Nevertheless, after the second month he shall not communicate until he has been cleared.

If he refuses to appear at the annual universal council so that his case may be resolved there, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation against himself. During the time in which he does not communicate, he shall not communicate either in his own church or parish.

But his accuser, if he has never failed to appear on the days appointed for stating the case, [Note: [Col. 0889D] This is absent from the Claromontanus manuscript.] [shall not be removed from communion. But if he has at any time failed to appear, withdrawing after the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser himself shall be removed from communion. Even so, he shall not be deprived of the opportunity to pursue the case if he proves that he did not wish, but was unable, to appear on the appointed day. It was further decreed that, once the matter has begun to be heard in the judgment of the bishops, if the accuser’s person is blameworthy, he shall not be admitted to bring the charge unless he wishes to assert his own causes, but not ecclesiastical ones.] [Note: [Col. 0889D] The bracketed material is absent from the Claromontanus manuscript.]

The procedure that must be observed in the accusation of a bishop, deacon, or other cleric.

[Col. 0889B]

Council of Carthage, title 20. But if presbyters or deacons are accused, their own bishop, joined by a lawful number of colleagues from neighboring places whom the accused themselves shall request—that is, six in the case of a presbyter and three in the case of a deacon—shall investigate their case, observing the same procedure concerning days, postponements, suspension from communion, and examination of the persons of the accusers and the accused. [Note: [Col. 0889D] Dionysius Exiguus reads: “with their own bishop.”] The cases of the remaining clerics shall be heard and concluded by the bishop of the place alone.

### CXLV. Concerning vacant bishops, who must not invade another vacant church

[Col. 0889C]

Council of Antioch, title 16. If any bishop who is without a see rushes into a vacant church and seizes its seat without a complete and perfected council, he must be expelled, even if the entire people whom he has seized choose to have him. A perfected council, however, is one at which the metropolitan bishop is present.

### CXLVI. That no one may appoint a successor to the episcopate for himself

Council of Antioch, title 23. A bishop may not appoint another as his successor, even if he has reached the end of his life. If anything of this kind has been done, such an appointment shall be invalid. Ecclesiastical law must be observed, which provides that this may occur only with the synod and judgment of the bishops, who, after the death of the bishop who has fallen asleep, have authority to promote whoever proves worthy.

### CXLVII. Concerning bishops who, having exchanged cities, are to be deprived even of lay communion

Council of Sardica, title 1. Bishop Hosius said:

A bad custom no less than a pernicious abuse must be eradicated completely, so that no bishop may be permitted to pass from his own city to another city. The reason why anyone attempts this is evident, since no bishop has been found in this matter who passed from a larger city to a smaller one. Hence it appears that they are inflamed by greed, serve ambition, and seek to exercise domination. If this pleases everyone, let such wickedness be punished more severely and strictly, so that one who acts in this manner may not even have lay communion.

All replied: It pleases us.

### CXLVIII. Also, if they change their see through ambition, they must not receive even lay communion at the end of life

Council cited above, title 2. Bishop Hosius said:

Even if some such rash person should arise and perhaps insist, by way of excuse, that he had received letters from the people, although it is clear that a few people without sincere faith could be corrupted by gifts and payment [Note: [Col. 0890D] “the many” should perhaps be read], so that they would shout in the church and appear to ask for him as bishop, I judge that such frauds must be condemned altogether, so that such a person may not receive even lay communion at the end of his life. If this pleases you all, decree it.

The synod replied: It pleases us.

### CXLIX. That, in disputes between bishops, the neighboring provincial bishops should hear the case; but if the condemned person appeals to the Roman pontiff, his decision must be observed

Council of Sardica, title 3. Bishop Hosius said:

This too must necessarily be added: bishops must not pass from their own province to another province where there are bishops, unless perhaps they have been invited by their brethren, lest we seem to close the door of charity. If in any province one bishop has a dispute with another bishop, let one of the two summon a bishop from another province as an examiner.

If any bishop has been judged in some case and thinks that he has a good case, so that the council should be renewed, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of Saint Peter. Let those who examined the case write to Julius, bishop of Rome; and if he judges that the judgment ought to be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges. But if he decides that the case is such that what has been done should not be reopened, whatever he decrees shall be confirmed. Does this please everyone?

The synod replied: It pleases us. [Note: [Col. 0890D] Dionysius Exiguus adds: “If a bishop.”]

### CL. That no one may usurp the see of an accused bishop

Council of Sardica, title 4. Bishop Gaudentius said:

If it pleases you, let this be added to the sentence you have issued, full of holiness [Note: [Col. 0890D] Dionysius Exiguus reads: “which you have pronounced”]: when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of the bishops residing in neighboring places and has declared that his case should be heard in the city of Rome, another bishop must absolutely not be ordained to his chair after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been decided in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

### CLI. When a bishop should be ordained by bishops of neighboring provinces

Council of Sardica, title 5. Bishop Hosius said:

If it happens that in one province, where there have been many bishops, only one bishop remains, and he, through negligence, refuses to ordain a bishop, while the people assemble, the bishops of the neighboring province ought first to approach the bishop who resides in that province and show him that the people are asking for a ruler, and that it is right for them also to come and ordain a bishop together with him. But if, when approached by letters, he remains silent and dissimulates, returning no answer, the people must be accommodated: bishops should come from the neighboring province and ordain a bishop.

### CLII. Concerning the non-ordination of bishops in villages and small cities

Council of Sardica, title 6. Permission must not be granted to ordain a bishop either in some village or in a small city for which one presbyter is sufficient, since it is unnecessary for a bishop to be appointed there, lest the name and authority of bishop be cheapened. Those invited from another province must not make someone a bishop except in cities that have had bishops, or in a city that is of such a kind or so populous that it deserves to have a bishop. If this pleases everyone?

The synod replied: It pleases us.

### CLIII. Concerning the revision of a provincial synod by vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome, if he so decrees

Council of Sardica, title 7. It was decreed that if a bishop has been accused, and the bishops assembled from his region have judged him and deposed him from his rank, and the one deposed appeals and flees to the bishop of the Roman Church, wishing to be heard, then, if the Roman bishop judges that a renewed examination is just, he shall deign to write to the bishops in the neighboring and adjoining province, so that they may investigate the matter diligently in every respect and decide according to the faith of truth.

But if the one who asks that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his petition to send a presbyter from his own side, it shall be in the power of the bishop to determine what he wishes and considers appropriate. If he decides that persons should be sent to judge in the presence of the bishops, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, that shall be at his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end, he shall do what he judges by the wisest counsel.

### CLIV. When and in what cases bishops ought to go to the imperial court

[Col. 0891D]

Council cited above, title 8. Bishop Hosius said:
