Insistent demands, excessive frequency, and just petitions [Note: [Col. 0891] Dionysius Exiguus reads: “unjust petitions”] have caused us not to possess so much favor or confidence, since certain bishops do not cease going to the imperial court, especially the Africans, who, as we have learned, disregard and scorn the salutary counsels of our most holy brother and fellow bishop Gratus. They bring to the imperial court not only many diverse cases that do not benefit the Church—as is customary and proper, so that the poor, widows, and orphans may be assisted—but also request secular honors and administrative offices for certain persons. This wickedness has long aroused not only murmuring but also scandals. It is honorable for bishops to offer intercession to those who are oppressed by unjust force, or when a widow is afflicted or an orphan despoiled, provided that all these matters involve just causes or petitions.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if it pleases you, decree that bishops must not approach the imperial court unless they have been invited or summoned by letters from the religious emperor. But since it often happens that those who suffer injury flee to the mercy of the Church, or that those who have sinned are condemned to exile or to islands, or receive some other sentence, assistance must be given to them and pardon must unquestionably be sought. Decree this, then, if it pleases you.

All said: It pleases us, and let it be established.

[Col. 0892B]

Council of Carthage, title 25. It was likewise decreed that bishops must not travel across the sea without consulting the bishop of the chief see of each province, so that they may receive from him especially a *formata*, or letter of recommendation.

Council cited above, title 28. It was likewise decreed that presbyters, deacons, and other lower clerics, when they have cases and complain about the judgments of their own bishops, should be heard by neighboring bishops with the consent of their own bishop, and that bishops appointed by them should decide between the parties. If they think that they ought to appeal even from these bishops, they must not appeal to courts across the sea but to the primates of their own provinces, as has often been established concerning bishops. But whoever thinks he should appeal across the sea must not be received into communion by anyone in Africa.

Also, universal Council of Carthage, title 73. It was decreed that whoever wishes to go to the imperial court with a *formata*—the letter sent to the Church of the city of Rome—must declare this, so that he may also receive from there a *formata* for the imperial court. If, after receiving only a *formata* for Rome, he conceals the necessity that requires him to go to the imperial court [Note: [Col. 0891] Dionysius Exiguus adds: “and wishes also to go to the imperial court”], he shall be removed from communion. But if, while he is there in Rome, a sudden necessity arises for him to go to the imperial court, he shall state that necessity to the bishop of the city of Rome and bring with him a written statement from that Roman bishop.

The *formatae* given by primates or by any bishops to their own clerics must bear the date of Easter. If the date of Easter for that same year is still uncertain, the date of the preceding Easter must be added, as is customarily written after the consulship in public records. [Col. 0892D]

### CLV. Concerning deacons to be sent to the imperial court

Council of Sardica, title 9. Bishop Hosius said:

Your Prudence must also consider this matter, since you have decreed that bishops’ misconduct must not strive toward going to the imperial court. Therefore, whoever has petitions of the kind mentioned above, or receives them, should send them through his deacon, because the person of a minister does not arouse envy, and he will be able to report more quickly what he has obtained. It also seems appropriate that, from every province, the bishops send petitions to that brother and fellow bishop of ours who resides in the metropolis, so that he may send both his deacon and the petitions, providing letters of recommendation in the same manner to our brothers and fellow bishops who at that time reside in the regions and cities in which the fortunate and joyful Augustus governs the commonwealth. But if a bishop has friends at court from whom he wishes to obtain something that is nevertheless honorable, he must not be forbidden to ask and to inform them through his deacon—those whom he knows can offer benevolent intercession on behalf of an absent person—provided that the occasion is suitable.

### CLVI. That one should go to the imperial court on behalf of orphans, widows, and those suffering necessity

Council of Sardica, title 10. Those who have come to Rome, as has been said, must hand over the petitions they possess to our most holy brother and fellow bishop of the Roman Church, so that he may first examine whether they are honorable and just and take care and concern that they be carried to the imperial court. All said that this pleased them and was an honorable counsel.

Bishop Alypius said:

If they have undertaken the hardships of travel for the sake of orphans, widows, or suffering persons whose cases are not unjust [Note: [Col. 0893D] This phrase is not lacking in Dionysius Exiguus], there would be some justification. But now, since they especially seek things that cannot be obtained without provoking people’s envy and criticism, it is unnecessary for them to go to the imperial court.

### CLVII. That bishops on the imperial route should carefully investigate those traveling to the imperial court

[Col. 0893C]

Council of Sardica, title 11. Bishop Gaudentius said:

The provisions you have wisely made, consistent with the judgment of all and pleasing to God, can remain firm only if fear is joined to this decision. For we ourselves know that, because of the imprudence of a few, the honorable name of the priesthood has very often been reproached. If, therefore, anyone, contrary to the judgment of all, wishes to please ambition more than God, let him know that, after due causes have been rendered, he will lose his honor and rank.

This can finally be fulfilled if each one of us, stationed along the route, when he sees a bishop traveling, investigates his passage, examines his reasons, and learns where he is going. If he finds that he is going to the imperial court [Note: [Col. 0894D] This is absent from the Codex manuscript], [let him inquire whether the provision stated above applies, lest perhaps he has been invited and thus has permission to go. But if, as your Holiness stated above, he is going to the imperial court] because of desires and ambitions, his letters must neither be countersigned nor may he be received into communion. If this pleases you, it must be confirmed by the judgment of all.

All said that this constitution was honorable and pleased them.

### CLVIII. Concerning those who do not know what has been established in the synod

Council of Sardica, title 12. Bishop Hosius said:

But moderation is also necessary, dearest brothers, lest some, still unaware of what has been decreed in the synod, suddenly come to the cities that lie along the route. The bishop of that city must therefore admonish and instruct him, so that from that place he may send his deacon, while he himself, once admonished, returns to his own parish. [Col. 0894A]

### CLIX. How long a bishop should remain in another city

Council of Sardica, title 14. Bishop Hosius said:

You must also establish this: when someone comes from one city to another, or from his own province to another province, and, serving ambition more than devotion, wishes to remain for a long time in a foreign city. For it may happen that the local bishop is not so well instructed or learned. The newcomer may then begin to despise him and frequently deliver sermons in order to dishonor and weaken his standing, so that on this pretext he does not hesitate to abandon the church assigned to him and move to another.

Therefore define a period, because it is inhuman not to receive a bishop, but it is harmful if he remains too long. Provision must be made to prevent this. I remember that at a previous council our brothers established that if a layman did not hold an assembly in the city where he resides for three Lord’s Days—that is, for three weeks—he would be deprived of communion. If this has been established concerning laymen, much less is it permitted or proper for a bishop, unless there is some very serious necessity that detains him, to be absent from his church for longer than the period stated above.

All said that this pleased them.

Those who wish to remain in another city during a time of persecution, however, must not be prohibited.

[Col. 0894C]

Council of Sardica, title 21. Bishop Hosius said:

At the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Olympius, this too was approved: if anyone has suffered violence and has been unjustly expelled for the sake of discipline and the Catholic confession, or for the defense of truth, and, fleeing danger, has come innocent and devout to another city, he must not be prohibited from remaining there for as long as he can either return or receive a remedy for his injury. For it is harsh not to receive one who is suffering persecution; rather, generous benevolence and humanity must be shown to him.

### CLX. That a bishop may not be absent from his church for more than three weeks

[Col. 0894D]

Council of Sardica, title 15. Bishop Hosius said:

Since nothing ought to be overlooked, there are certain brothers and fellow bishops of ours who do not actually reside in the city in which they appear to have been established as bishops, or who possess only a small property there; elsewhere, however, they are known to have suitable estates or relatives toward whom they may show indulgence. They should be permitted to go to their estates and arrange or manage the fruits of their labor, so that after three Lord’s Days—that is, after three weeks—if it is necessary to remain, they may stay on their own farms instead.

Or, if there is a nearby city in which there is a presbyter, so that he does not appear to spend the Lord’s Day without a church, he should go there, so that neither his domestic affairs suffer loss through his absence [Note: [Col. 0895D] Dionysius Exiguus reads: “through his absence”], nor does he, by frequently coming to the city in which the bishop resides, escape suspicion of ostentation and ambition.

All said that this pleased them.

### CLXI. Concerning those who practice penance more fervently for various offenses

Council of Laodicea, title 2. Concerning those who have sinned through various crimes and, persevering in the prayers of confession and repentance, have made a complete conversion from their evils: according to the nature of the offense, communion should be granted to such persons after a period of penance has been assigned, because of the clemency and goodness of God.

### CLXII. Concerning the time of ordination

[Col. 0895B]

Council of Laodicea, title 4. Ordinations ought not to be celebrated in the presence of those who are still hearers.

### CLXIII. That women called presbyterae should not be ordained

Council of Laodicea, title 11. Those called *presbyterae*, or women presiding, ought not to be ordained in the Church.

### CLXIV. That ordination must not be carried out by the decision of the crowd

Council of Laodicea, title 13. The crowds must not be permitted to make the elections of those who are to be promoted to the priesthood.

#### That the people should be taught, not followed

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 22. The people must be taught, not followed. If they do not know, we must admonish them concerning what is permitted and what is not permitted; we must not grant our assent to them. Whoever attempts to do what is forbidden will discover that the censure of the apostolic see will certainly not be lacking. For what we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone must necessarily be punished with the severity appropriate to the regulations. [Note: [Col. 0895D] Dionysius Exiguus reads: “must be avenged.”]

#### And that, once the clerics of the churches have been disregarded, a bishop must not be ordained from among the laity

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 21. We have heard that certain cities deprived of their proper rulers wish to request bishops from among the laity, and consider so lofty a dignity so cheap that they think we can bestow it upon those who have served not God but the world. In doing this they judge badly not only of their own clerics, whom they hold in contempt, but also of us, thinking most wrongly that we have the power to do this. They would never dare to do so if the opinion of certain people, consenting to what is unlawful, did not connive at it.

Thus nothing is accomplished by the decrees so frequently issued, since this matter is ignored as though nothing had ever been written about it. What benefit is there in clerics having served their terms one by one and spent their whole lives in the Lord’s camp, if those who are to preside over them are sought from among the laity—people occupied with worldly affairs, ignorant of the entire ecclesiastical order, and striving, with precipitous haste, to overstep into a foreign honor through immoderate desire [Col. 0896A] [uncertain reading: the manuscript appears to contain *immoderata moderata cupiditate*, “with immoderate/moderated desire”], passing into another way of life while trampling upon the reverence owed to ecclesiastical discipline?

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we guard the helm of our law—that is, of the canons—we must oppose such persons. By these letters we admonish your fraternity: let no one admit a layman to the clerical order or permit what would deceive that man and create for himself grounds on which he would become liable under the established decrees.

### CLXV. That the *eulogiae* offered at one parish must not be sent to other parishes

Council of Laodicea, title 14. Holy things must by no means be sent to other parishes during the Paschal feast under the pretext of *eulogiae*.

### CLXVI. Concerning those who should sing in the *ambon*, that is, in the pulpit

[Col. 0896B]

Council of Laodicea, title 15. Apart from those who are regularly cantors and sing from the book, no others should climb into the pulpit and sing in the church.

### CLXVII. Concerning the readings that should be recited on the Sabbath

Council of Laodicea, title 16. On the Sabbath it is appropriate for the Gospels to be read together with the other Scriptures.

### CLXVIII. That an interval should be made between the psalms in assemblies

Council of Laodicea, title 17. At the assembly of the faithful, the psalms should by no means be continued without interruption; rather, the readings should be recited at intervals—that is, between individual psalms. [Col. 0896C]

### CLXIX. Concerning prayers to be celebrated at the ninth hour and in the evening

Council of Laodicea, title 18. The same office of prayer must always be performed at the ninth hour and in the evening.

### CLXX. Concerning prayers to be made after sermons addressed to the people

Council of Laodicea, title 19. First, after the bishops’ addresses, a prayer should be offered separately over the catechumens. After the catechumens have gone out, a prayer should be offered over those who are doing penance. After these too have approached the priest’s hand and departed, three prayers for the faithful should be completed: the first in silence, and the second and third with the customary acclamations. Only then should they give one another the kiss of peace.

After the bishop has given the presbyters the kiss of peace, the laity should give peace to one another [Note: [Col. 0896D] Dionysius Exiguus reads: “the laity shall give peace to one another”], and then the holy offering shall be celebrated. For only those devoted to the sacred ministry may enter the altar area and communicate there.

### CLXXI. That subdeacons must be removed from the diaconium

Council of Laodicea, title 21. Subdeacons must not have a place in the *diaconium* [Note: [Col. 0896D] Dionysius Exiguus reads: “in the diaconium”] or touch the Lord’s vessels.

### CLXXII. That subdeacons may not assist wearing *oraria*

[Col. 0897A]

Council of Laodicea, title 22. A subdeacon must not use an *orarium* or leave the doors.

### CLXXIII. That readers and cantors may not perform their office wearing *oraria*

Council of Laodicea, title 23. Readers and cantors must not use *oraria* and thus read or sing.

### CLXXIV. That subdeacons must not bless or give a blessing

Council of Laodicea, title 25. Subdeacons must not distribute bread or bless the cup.

### CLXXV. Concerning exorcists who have not been ordained by a bishop

Council of Laodicea, title 26. Those who have not been ordained by bishops may not perform exorcisms either in churches or in houses. [Col. 0897B]

### CLXXVI. That portions must not be taken from meals held as *agapae*

Council of Laodicea, title 27. Clerics devoted to the sacred ministry, or laypeople invited to an *agape*, must not take portions of the food, because this also brings injury upon the ecclesiastical order.

### CLXXVII. That meals must not be held in churches except when required by travel

Council of Laodicea, title 28. In the houses of God—that is, in the Lord’s houses and churches—meals called *agapae* must not be held; nor may anyone eat inside the house of God or spread couches there.

[Col. 0897C]

Council of Carthage, title 9. No bishops or clerics shall feast in the church, unless, while passing through, they happen to refresh themselves there because necessity requires lodging. The people too should be prohibited from such banquets as far as possible.

### CLXXVIII. Concerning men bathing together with women

Council of Laodicea, title 30. Those devoted to the sacred offices, whether clerics, persons practicing continence, or any Christian layman, must not bathe together with women, because among the pagans this is the first ground of reproach.

### CLXXIX. That bishops must attend the synod without fail

[Col. 0897D]

Council of Laodicea, title 40. Bishops summoned to the synod must not disregard the summons in any way, but must go promptly and teach or learn those matters that pertain to the correction of the Church and to other affairs. Anyone who disregards the summons will accuse himself, unless illness prevents him from going.

The seventeenth canon of Antioch. If any bishop has received the laying on of hands for the episcopate, has been appointed to preside over the people, but neglects to undertake his ministry and refuses to go to the church entrusted to him, he ought to be deprived of communion until he has undertaken the office under compulsion, or until the synod of the priests of that province has otherwise decided concerning him. [Col. 0898A] [Note: [Col. 0897D] Dionysius Exiguus adds “in full.”]

### CLXXX. That a cleric should not depart without the bishop’s command

Council of Laodicea, canon 41. A priest or cleric should not depart without canonical letters.

Likewise, canon 42. A priest or cleric should not depart without the command of his own bishop.

And that subdeacons should remain at the doors.

Likewise, canon 43. Subdeacons should not leave the doors even briefly, but should devote themselves to prayer.

### CLXXXI. That women should not enter the sanctuary

[Col. 0898B]

Council of Laodicea, canon 44. Women should not enter the altar area.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, canon 26. We have nevertheless heard with indignation that contempt for divine things has reached such a point that women are asserted to minister at the sacred altars, and that everything assigned exclusively to the service of men is being handed over to a sex to which it does not belong. In fact, the guilt and crime of all the offenses we have separately touched upon falls upon those priests who either commit such acts or, by failing to make public those who commit them, show that they favor their wicked excesses—if indeed those who seek to overthrow the religious office entrusted to them should still be called priests.

They incline toward everything perverse and profane, and, without any regard for Christian rule, pursue ruinous and fatal precipices. Since it is written, “He who despises small things will gradually fall,” what ought we to think of such men, who, burdened by immense and manifold masses of depravity, have produced a great collapse through assaults of many kinds—a collapse that seems likely not only to overwhelm themselves but, unless they are healed, to bring deadly ruin upon all the churches?

Let those who have dared to practice these things, and also those who have hitherto remained silent despite knowing of them, not doubt that they lie under the loss of their own honor, unless they hasten with all possible speed so that these deadly wounds may be healed and saved by suitable medicine. [Note: [Col. 0897D] Dionysius Exiguus: “may be treated.”]

For by what manner do they uphold the rights of bishops who conceal, to this extent, what has been entrusted to episcopal vigilance, so that they do rather what is contrary to the house of God over which they preside? Let them consider how much they might be able to merit before God if they sought only what was appropriate, and how much they deserve when, with execrable zeal, they pursue what is contrary. [Note: [Col. 0897D] Dionysius Exiguus: “pursue.”]

As though this were rather the rule by which the churches ought to be governed, everything hostile to ecclesiastical regulations is thus perpetrated. For even if each bishop knows the canons, he ought to preserve them with unstained vigilance; and if perhaps he did not know them, it would have been proper for him, in his ignorance, confidently to seek advice. [Note: [Col. 0898D] Dionysius Exiguus: “by which the Church ought to be governed.”] [Note: [Col. 0898D] Dionysius Exiguus: “has.”]

Thus no excuse comes to the aid of those who err: the one who knew did not resolve to preserve what he knew, and the one who was ignorant did not take care to learn what he was doing.

### CLXXXII. Concerning those who come for baptism around the middle of the week

Council of Laodicea, canon 45. No one should be admitted to baptism after the second week of Lent.

### CLXXXIII. Concerning the reception of the faith and its recitation by those who are baptized

Council of Laodicea, canon 46. Those who come for baptism should learn the faith and recite it to the bishop or priests on the Thursday of Holy Week.

### CLXXXIV. That chrism should be given after baptism

Council of Laodicea, canon 48. Those who are baptized should receive heavenly chrism after the washing and be found to be participants in the kingdom of Christ.

### CLXXXV. That offerings should not be made during Lent

Likewise, canon 49. The bread of blessing should not be offered during Lent except on Saturday and Sunday.

### CLXXXVI. That the fast should not be broken on the Thursday of Holy Week

Council of Laodicea, canon 50. During Lent, the fast should not be broken on the Thursday of the final week, nor should the whole of Lent be passed without reverence; rather, it is more fitting to observe the entire Lent with a strict fast.

### CLXXXVII. That commemorations of martyrs should not be held on fast days

[Col. 0899C]

The aforementioned council, canon 51. The birthdays or feasts of martyrs should not be celebrated during Lent, but their holy commemoration should appropriately be observed on Saturdays and Sundays.

### CLXXXVIII. That birthdays or weddings should not take place during Lent

Council of Laodicea, canon 52. Weddings or birthday celebrations should not be held during Lent.

### CLXXXIX. That there should be no dancing at Christian weddings

Council of Laodicea, canon 53. Christians attending weddings should not applaud or dance, but should dine or take their meal reverently, as befits Christians. [Col. 0899D]

### CXC. That clerics may not attend theatrical entertainments

Council of Laodicea, canon 54. Priests or clerics should not attend any spectacles at banquets or weddings; rather, before the performers enter, they ought to rise and depart.

Likewise, the aforementioned council, canon 55. [Note: [Col. 0899D] This canon is not cited by Cresconius in his *Breviary* above, p. 463, col. 1, and appears to have been written by some copyist through confusion in place of canon 54 of the same council. It is absent from the Claromontanus manuscript, and we have restored it from the codex of Dionysius Exiguus.] Priests or clerics should not hold banquets from contributions or drinking-parties; nor can this properly be permitted to laypeople.

[Col. 0900A]

Council of Carthage, canon 15. The sons of priests should not put on secular spectacles, nor even attend them, although this has always been forbidden to all Christians; and they should not go where blasphemies are uttered.

### CXCI. That presbyters may not enter the altar area before the bishop enters

Council of Laodicea, canon 56. Presbyters should not enter the sanctuary or sit before the bishop’s procession; they should enter with the bishop or sit in the seats, unless perhaps he is detained by illness or the bishop is away.

### CXCII. Who should be ordained in rural districts or estates

Council of Laodicea, canon 57. Bishops should not be appointed in villages or rural districts, but visitors. [Col. 0900B] Nevertheless, those already appointed should do nothing without the knowledge of the bishop of the city; likewise, presbyters should do nothing without the bishop’s advice.

### CXCIII. That an offering should not be celebrated in private houses, and concerning what should be sung in the church

Council of Laodicea, canon 58. Bishops or presbyters should not celebrate the offering in private houses.

The aforementioned council, canon 59. The psalms of private individuals should not be sung in the church, nor books be used except those belonging to the canon of the Law, but only the sacred volumes of the New or Old Testament.

### CXCIV. That bishops, clerics, and monks should not lease other people’s estates

Council of Chalcedon, canon 3. It has come to the holy synod’s attention that certain men who appear to have been admitted into the clergy become lessees of other people’s possessions for the sake of shameful profit and undertake secular business under their care, making light of God’s ministry while going about the houses of secular people and, through greed, taking on the management of estates.

Therefore this holy and great council decrees that henceforth no one—neither bishop, cleric, nor monk—may lease possessions or involve himself in secular business, except in the case of minors, if the laws should impose an unavoidable responsibility; or if the bishop of the city should order him to manage ecclesiastical affairs; or in the case of orphans, widows, and persons lacking any provision, who especially require ecclesiastical assistance, when fear of the Lord demands it. If anyone thereafter attempts to violate these provisions, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical censures.

### CXCV. Concerning the honor due to monks; and that none of them should attempt to disturb ecclesiastical or secular business, or receive another’s slave without the knowledge of the slave’s master

Council of Chalcedon, canon 4. Those who truly and sincerely pursue the solitary life should be honored appropriately. But since certain men, using the monastic habit, disturb ecclesiastical and civil affairs by wandering indiscriminately through cities, and even attempt to establish monasteries for themselves, it has been decided that no one may build or establish a monastery or house of prayer anywhere without the knowledge of the bishop of the city.

Monks in each city or region are to remain subject to the bishop, love quiet, and devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer, remaining in the places where they have renounced the world. They are not to participate in ecclesiastical or secular affairs, nor to cause trouble in any way by abandoning their own monasteries, unless perhaps the bishop of the city orders them to do so for necessary work. No one is to receive a slave into a monastery under the pretext of monasticism without the knowledge of the slave’s master.

We decree that anyone who violates this definition of ours is excommunicated, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed. Nevertheless, it is fitting that the bishop of the city exercise appropriate oversight of the monasteries.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, canon 1. Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, and all the provinces. [Note: [Col. 0901D] Missing from the codex of Dionysius Exiguus.]

Just as the well-ordered condition of the churches, arranged in a healthy disposition, gives us cause for rejoicing, so we are distressed by no small sorrow whenever we learn that something has been attempted or committed contrary to the canonical provisions and ecclesiastical discipline. If we do not cut such things away with the vigilance we ought to exercise, we cannot excuse ourselves before the one who wished us to be watchmen, since we permit the sincere body of the Church—which we ought to guard pure from every stain—to be defiled by the wicked contagion of ambitious men, even though the joining of its members does not accord with itself through dissimulation.

Men are admitted indiscriminately to the sacred order who possess no dignity of birth and no dignity of character to support them. Those who have been entirely unable to obtain freedom from their masters are raised to the height of the priesthood, as though servile lowliness could obtain this honor; and it is believed that someone can be approved by the Lord God who has not yet been able to prove himself to his own master. [Note: [Col. 0902D] Absent from the codex of Dionysius Exiguus.]

There is therefore a double guilt in this matter: the sacred ministry is polluted by the dishonor of such association, and the rights of masters are violated insofar as this involves the rashness of unlawful usurpation.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let all the priests of your province abstain from these men, and not only from them: we wish them also to refrain from others who are bound by original status or by any other condition, unless perhaps the request or consent of those who claim some power over them has been obtained. Whoever is to be enrolled in divine service ought to be free from the claims of others, so that he may not be withdrawn by any bond of necessity from the Lord’s camp in which his name is enrolled.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, canon 14. The presumption giving rise to a general complaint must also be avoided: practically everyone complains that slaves and persons bound by hereditary status, fleeing the rights and estates of their masters, are indiscriminately admitted by bishops—under the pretext of religious conduct—to betake themselves to monasteries or to ecclesiastical service. This evil must be removed by every means, lest, under the institution of the Christian name, either another’s property appear to be invaded or public discipline to be overthrown.

This is especially so because it is not fitting that the dignity of the clerical ministry itself be darkened by such an obligation, forcing it to quarrel over the status and condition of those serving it, or—God forbid—causing it to appear subject to such claims.

After these persons have been prohibited by an appropriately careful injunction, any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or person known to preside over monasteries who keeps such individuals with him instead of restoring them to their patrons, or thereafter thinks of assigning them either to ecclesiastical service or to religious communities, unless they have first been released with the masters’ consent under written testimony or granted by a lawful settlement, should not doubt that he will incur danger to his own honor and communion, if anyone’s truthful complaint about this matter reaches us. For, according to the blessed Apostle, the greatest care must be taken lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed.

### CXCVI. That no one should be ordained without assignment

Council of Chalcedon, canon 6. No one should be ordained absolutely as a presbyter or deacon, or to any ecclesiastical rank, unless the church of the city, estate, martyr-shrine, or monastery to which he is to be ordained is specifically identified. Anyone ordained absolutely in this way—the holy synod decrees—has received an invalid laying on of hands and may nowhere minister, to the injury of the ordaining bishop.

### CXCVII. Concerning clerics who are in poorhouses, monasteries, and martyr-shrines under the authority of the bishops of each city

Council of Chalcedon, canon 8. Clerics placed in charge of poorhouses, or ordained in monasteries and basilicas of martyrs, are to remain under the authority of the bishops of the respective cities, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers, and are not to separate themselves defiantly from their own bishop.

Those who dare to overturn this arrangement in any way and do not submit to their own bishop shall, if clerics, be subject to canonical correction; if they are laymen or monks, they shall be deprived of communion.

### CXCVIII. That clerics who have disputes with one another should not abandon their own bishop and hasten to secular courts

Council of Chalcedon, canon 9. If one cleric has a dispute against another cleric, he should not abandon his own bishop and rush to secular courts. Rather, the case should first be examined before his own bishop, or, with that bishop’s advice, they may submit to judgment before those whom both parties choose. Anyone who acts otherwise shall be subject to canonical correction.

If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or against another bishop, it shall be judged before the synod of the province. If a bishop or cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan of that province, he should appeal to the primate of the diocese or to the see of the imperial city of Constantinople, and be judged before him.

### CXCIX. That a cleric may not minister in the churches of two cities

Council of Chalcedon, canon 10. A cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities: both in the church in which he was originally ordained and in one to which, out of a desire for empty glory, he has fled as though it were superior.

Those who do this must be recalled to their own church, in which they were first ordained, and minister there alone. If someone has already been transferred from one church to another, he is in no way to share in the resources of the former church, or of the martyr-shrines, poorhouses, or guesthouses belonging to it.

The holy synod decrees that those who, after the definition of this great and universal synod, dare to perpetrate any of these prohibited acts shall be removed from their own rank.

### CC. That a province should in no way be divided between two metropolitans

Council of Chalcedon, canon 12. It has come to our attention that certain men, acting contrary to ecclesiastical provisions, have resorted to secular powers and, through an imperial administrative arrangement, divided one province into two, so that as a result two metropolitans appear to exist in one province.

Therefore the holy synod decrees that henceforth no such thing is to be attempted by bishops. Otherwise, anyone who attempts it shall be subject to loss of his own rank. Whatever cities have been supported by imperial letters with the honor of the metropolitan title may enjoy the title alone, while the bishop who governs its church retains the privileges of the true metropolis.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, canon 46. You ask whether, when provinces have been divided by imperial judgment so that two metropolises are created, two metropolitan bishops ought likewise to be named. It has not truly seemed right that the Church of God should be altered according to the shifting needs of worldly affairs, or that it should undergo honors or divisions which the emperor has judged necessary for his own purposes. Therefore metropolitan bishops should be counted according to the former custom of the provinces. [Note: [Col. 0903D] Dionysius Exiguus: “therefore.”]

### CCI. That foreign clerics should not minister without letters of commendation

Council of Chalcedon, canon 13. Foreign clerics and readers must nowhere minister in another city without letters of commendation from their own bishop.

### CCII. Concerning women deacons

Council of Chalcedon, canon 15. A deaconess should not be ordained before the age of forty, and even then only with the greatest scrutiny. If, after receiving the laying on of hands and remaining for some time in the ministry, she gives herself in marriage, thereby insulting the grace of God, she and the man joined to her are to be anathematized. [Col. 0904A]

### CCIII. Concerning parishes

Council of Chalcedon, canon 17. The rural parishes or estates of each church are to remain undisturbed under those bishops known to retain them, especially if they have governed them under their administration for thirty years while holding them without force.

If a dispute concerning them has arisen or arises within the thirty-year period, those who claim to have been wronged may bring the matter before the holy synod of the province. If someone is wronged by a metropolitan, the case shall be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the see of Constantinople, as stated above.

If a city has been reorganized by imperial authority, or is immediately reorganized, the ecclesiastical arrangements and public ordering of its parishes must likewise follow the civil arrangements.

### CCIV. Concerning conspiracies and plots

Council of Chalcedon, canon 18. The crime of conspiracy or plotting is entirely prohibited even by secular laws; much more, therefore, should it be prohibited in the Church of God.

If any clerics or monks are found conspiring, plotting, or laying snares for bishops or clerics, they shall be completely stripped of their own rank.

### CCV. What must be observed concerning accusations against bishops or clerics

Council of Chalcedon, canon 21. Laymen or clerics who accuse bishops or clerics indiscriminately and without proof should not be admitted to bring an accusation until their reputation and standing have first been examined. [Col. 0904C]

Council of Carthage, canon 8. Numidius, bishop of Maxula, said: “Moreover, there are very many persons of bad conduct who think that elders or bishops may be summoned indiscriminately and at random for accusation. Should such people be admitted so easily or not?”

Aurelius, bishop, said: “Does your charity therefore agree that a person entangled in certain crimes should not have a voice to accuse an elder?” All the bishops said: “If he is a criminal, let him not be admitted. We agree.”

Likewise, the Council of Carthage, canon 95. It has pleased all that, since the earlier decrees of the councils have already established which persons are to be admitted to accuse clerics, but have not specified which persons are not to be admitted, we therefore define that no one is properly to be admitted as an accuser who, after being excommunicated, while still remaining under excommunication, wishes to bring an accusation, whether he is a cleric or a layman.

Canon 96. Likewise, it has pleased us that slaves or personal freedmen are not to be admitted as accusers, nor all those whom the public laws do not admit to accuse of public crimes, nor all who are stained by infamy—that is, actors and persons subject to disgraceful occupations—as well as heretics, pagans, and Jews. Nevertheless, all those to whom accusation is denied must not be denied the right to bring an accusation in their own cases.

And that someone who has failed to prove one crime should not be admitted to bring another accusation.

The aforementioned council, canon 97. Likewise, it has pleased us that whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by their accusers, and the accuser has been unable to prove one of those charges, which he brought forward first, he should no longer be admitted to bring the remaining charges.

Likewise on this matter, canon 98. Witnesses are not to be admitted to give testimony if they have been prohibited from admission even as accusers, nor are those whom the accuser himself has produced from his own household. Persons under fourteen years of age are not to be admitted as witnesses.

### CCVI. That clerics may not plunder property belonging to their bishop after his death

[Col. 0905B]

Council of Chalcedon, canon 22. Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, disperse or plunder property belonging to him, as the ancient canons also establish. If they attempt to do so, they shall place their ranks in jeopardy.

### CCVII. That clerics and monks may not go to the imperial city without the bishop’s consent

Council of Chalcedon, canon 23. It has reached the ears of the holy council that certain clerics and monks, to whom nothing has been entrusted by their own bishop—and sometimes they are even deprived of communion by him—arrive at the imperial city of Constantinople and remain there for a long time, stirring up disturbances, disrupting the ecclesiastical order, and even overthrowing the households of certain persons.

The holy synod decrees that such men should first be warned by the defensor of the holy Church of Constantinople to leave the imperial city. If they persist shamelessly in the same activities, the defensor is to expel them even against their will, so that they may return to their own places.

### CCVIII. That consecrated monasteries may not be turned into secular lodging places

Council of Chalcedon, canon 24. Monasteries once dedicated are to remain monasteries forever by decision of the bishops, and the property belonging to them is to be reserved for the monasteries. They may not thereafter be turned into secular dwellings. Those who permit this shall be subject to the judgments of the canons.

### CCIX. That episcopal ordinations should not be long delayed

[Col. 0905D]

Council of Chalcedon, canon 25. Since, as we have learned, certain metropolitans neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay carrying out the ordinations of bishops, it has pleased the holy synod that episcopal ordinations be celebrated within three months, unless perhaps an unavoidable necessity causes the period of delay to be extended.

If a metropolitan fails to do this, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction. Nevertheless, the revenues of the widowed church are to be preserved intact in the hands of its steward.

### CCX. Concerning the stewards of individual churches

[Col. 0906A]

Council of Chalcedon, canon 26. Since, as we have learned by report, in certain churches persons other than the steward manage the bishops’ resources, it has pleased us that every church possessing a bishop should also have a steward from its own clergy, who will administer the ecclesiastical property according to the judgment of his own bishop.

The administration of the church is thus not to occur without accountability, lest ecclesiastical resources be scattered and a derogation from the priesthood’s dignity be brought about. Anyone who fails to do this shall be subject to the divine constitutions.

### CCXI. Concerning those who commit abduction

Council of Chalcedon, canon 27. Those who abduct women under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or connive at the abductors—the holy synod decrees that, if they are clerics, they shall fall from their own rank; if laymen, they shall be anathematized. [Col. 0906B]

### CCXII. That baptism should not be celebrated except at Easter and Pentecost

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, canon 2. The unacceptable and uncorrected confusion concerning the various times for baptizing, according to each person’s whim, must be addressed. We say this with indignation: our priests presume to do this not on the basis of any authoritative reason but solely through rashness, so that, indiscriminately and freely, countless crowds—as you report—receive the mystery of baptism on the birthdays of Christ, at the feast of his manifestation, and also on the feasts of the apostles or martyrs.

For the privilege of celebrating baptism belongs especially to the Lord’s Easter, together with Pentecost, both among us and among all the churches. On these days alone throughout the year, when people flock to the faith, it is fitting that the general sacraments of baptism be administered.

Only those should be selected who have enrolled their names forty or more days beforehand and have been cleansed by exorcisms, daily prayers, and fasts, so that the apostolic command may be fulfilled: once the old leaven has been purged, the new dough may begin to be formed.

Just as we say that the reverence due to Easter must in no way be diminished, so we wish infants who, because of their age, cannot yet speak, and those for whom the water of sacred baptism is necessary in any emergency, to be assisted with all speed. [Col. 0906D] Otherwise it may lead to the destruction of our souls if, when the saving font is denied to those who desire it, someone departs from this world and loses both the kingdom and life.

Whoever encounters the danger of shipwreck, an enemy attack, the uncertainty of a siege, or despair arising from any bodily illness, and asks to be aided by the single resource of faith, should receive, at the very moment he asks, the reward of the regeneration he seeks.

Let enough error have occurred in this matter. From now on, let all priests observe the rule stated above, if they do not wish to be torn away from the solidity of the apostolic rock upon which Christ built the universal Church.

[Col. 0907A]

From the decrees of Leo, canon 7. Leo, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.

We are instructed by divine commands and apostolic admonitions [Note: [Col. 0907D] Dionysius Exiguus: “we are urged.”] to watch over the condition of all the churches with tireless concern and, wherever someone is found liable to reproach, to recall him promptly either from ignorant lack of understanding or from presumptuous usurpation.

The command of the Lord remains in force by which the most blessed Apostle Peter, through a threefold repetition of the mystical injunction, was instructed to feed Christ’s sheep, since he loves Christ. We are constrained by reverence for the very see over which, through the abundance of divine grace, we preside, so that we may avoid, as far as we can, the danger of negligence. Otherwise the profession of the chief Apostle, by which he testified that he loved the Lord, may not be found in us, because one who negligently feeds the Lord’s flock entrusted to him so many times is shown not to love the chief Shepherd.

Since, therefore, while I am concerned for the actions of your charity with brotherly affection, I have learned from reliable indications that in what is the principal matter among the Church’s sacraments you differ from the practice of apostolic institution—so that the sacrament of baptism is celebrated more frequently on the day of the Epiphany than during the Easter season—I am astonished that you or your predecessors could have adopted so irrational an innovation as to believe there was no difference between the day on which Christ was adored by the Magi and the day on which Christ rose from the dead, by confusing the times of the two mysteries. [Note: [Col. 0907D] Dionysius Exiguus: “with the times of the two mysteries confused.”]

You could never have fallen into this fault if you had taken the rule of all observance from the source from which you receive the consecration of your honor, and if the see of the blessed Apostle Peter—which is the priestly mother of your dignity—had been the teacher of ecclesiastical reasoning. Your departure from its rules could be tolerated with less forbearance if some rebuke in our admonition had preceded this.

But now, because correction is not despaired of, gentleness must be preserved. Although an excuse alleging ignorance is scarcely tolerable in priests, we have nevertheless preferred both to temper the necessary severity and to instruct you by the clearest reasoning of truth. [Note: [Col. 0907D] Dionysius Exiguus: “we preferred.”]

From the decree of Pope Leo, canon 8. The restoration of the human race was always present in the eternal counsel of God, preordained immutably. But the temporal order of events to be accomplished through Jesus Christ our Lord took its beginning in the incarnation of the Word.

Therefore one time is that when the blessed Virgin Mary, upon the angel’s announcement, believed that she would conceive through the Holy Spirit and conceived. [Note: [Col. 0908D] Dionysius Exiguus: “when the angel announced it.”] Another is that when, preserving her virginity intact, the child was born and announced to the shepherds amid the joyful exultation of the heavenly ministers. Another is when the infant was circumcised. Another is when the legal offering was presented for him.

Another is when the three Magi, stirred by the brightness of the new star, [Note: [Col. 0908D] Dionysius Exiguus: “prompted, they arrived in Bethlehem.”] arrived from the East at the city of Bethlehem and, having offered a mystical gift, [Note: [Col. 0908D] Dionysius Exiguus: “with the offering of mystical gifts.”] venerated the adored infant. [Col. 0908A]

Nor are the days the same on which he was withdrawn from the wicked Herod through his divinely ordered transfer to Egypt, and on which, after the persecutor’s death, he was recalled from Egypt to Galilee.

Among these various dispensations there are also bodily developments. The Lord grew, as the Evangelist testifies, in the advances of age and grace. During the days of Easter he came with his parents to the temple in Jerusalem. When he was absent from the company of those returning, he was found sitting among the elders and disputing with the teachers who marveled at him. Giving the reason for his remaining, he said: “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s affairs?” He thereby indicated that he was the son of the one whose temple it was.

But when, at a more mature age, he sought the baptism of his forerunner John, what uncertainty about his divinity remained, when, after the Lord Jesus had been baptized, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained, and the Father’s voice was heard from heaven saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased”?

We have briefly touched upon all these matters, as far as we could, so that it might be known to your affection that all the days of Christ were consecrated by countless acts of power and that the mysteries of the sacraments shone forth in all his actions. Yet what he announced by signs was fulfilled in another manner through events, and not everything counted among the Savior’s works can pertain to the time of baptism.

For if we also honor indiscriminately those things which we know were done by the Lord after the washing performed by blessed John, all times will have to be counted as continuous feasts, because all are full of miracles.

But because the spirit of wisdom and understanding so instructed the apostles and the teachers of the whole Church that, in Christian observance, it tolerated nothing disordered and nothing confused, the reasons for the solemnities must be distinguished, and rational discernment must be preserved in all the institutions of our Fathers and leaders.

For we are one flock and one shepherd only in the manner taught by the Apostle, when we all say the same thing: “Let us be perfect in the same understanding and in the same wisdom.”

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 9. Although, therefore, both those things that pertain to Christ’s humility and those that pertain to his glory converge in one and the same person, and all that in him belongs both to divine power and to human weakness tends toward the effect of our restoration, nevertheless, properly in the death of the crucified one and in the resurrection of the dead one, the power of baptism creates a new creature from the old, so that in those who are reborn both the death of Christ may work and his life. As the blessed Apostle says: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be together in the likeness of his resurrection,” and so forth—the things that the teacher of the nations discussed more extensively in order to commend the sacrament of baptism—so that it might be evident that, by the spirit of this teaching, that day and that time were chosen for the regeneration and adoption of the human race as children of God, when, through the likeness and form of the mystery, the things enacted in the members might correspond to those enacted in the head himself: since in the rule of baptism death intervenes through the slaying of sin, the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial, and the lifting up from the waters is like the resurrection from the tomb.

The very character of the act therefore teaches that the proper day for the universal celebration of grace is the day on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose. For confirmation of this, it is of the greatest importance that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, after he had risen from the dead, gave his disciples—in whom all the leaders of the churches were being instructed—both the form and the authority for baptizing, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” He could certainly have instructed them concerning this before his Passion, unless he had wished it to be understood specifically that the grace of regeneration began with his resurrection.

To this observance is rightly added the solemnity of Pentecost, consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit. It depends upon the celebration of Easter, and whereas other feasts belong to other days, this one always occurs on the day distinguished by the Lord’s resurrection, extending, as it were, the hand of assisting grace to those whom, from the day of Easter onward, the burden of illness, the length of a journey, or the difficulty of sea travel has prevented from attending, inviting them, though hindered by whatever necessities, to obtain the fulfillment of their desire through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

For the only-begotten Son of God did not wish there to be any separation between himself and the Holy Spirit in the faith of believers or in the power of works, because there is no difference in nature. He says: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth”; and again: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything I have said to you”; and again: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth.” Since, therefore, Christ is the truth and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth, and the name “Paraclete” is proper to both, the feast is not different where there is one sacrament.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 10. We prove by a sufficiently suitable example that we defend and preserve this practice not on the basis of our own persuasion but on apostolic authority, following the blessed Apostle Peter, who on the very day when the promised coming of the Holy Spirit filled the whole number of believers consecrated a crowd of three thousand converts through his preaching by the laver of baptism. Holy Scripture, which contains the Acts of the Apostles, teaches this in faithful history, saying: “When they heard this, they were pierced in heart and said to Peter and the other apostles, ‘What shall we do, men and brothers?’ But Peter said to them: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, whoever the Lord our God shall call.’” He testified also with many other words and exhorted them, saying: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” Therefore those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added on that day.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 11. Since it is therefore most clearly evident that these two times of which we have spoken are the proper ones for the chosen to be baptized in the Church, we admonish your Dilection not to introduce any other days into this observance. For there are other feasts to which much reverence in honor of God is owed; nevertheless, we must preserve the mystical and rational imitation of the principal and greatest sacrament. This does not prohibit the permission by which, at any time, assistance is given through the administration of baptism to those in danger.

Thus we defer the free requests of the healthy and those living in the security of peace to these two solemnities, joined and related to each other, so that in danger of death, in the crisis of a siege, in the distress of persecution, or in fear of shipwreck, we may at no time deny anyone this singular protection of true salvation. But if anyone thinks that the feast of Epiphany, which in its proper order is to be venerated with due honor, possesses the privilege of baptism because some believe that on that day the Lord approached the baptism of Saint John, let him know that the grace and purpose of that baptism were different, and that it did not possess the same power by which those who are reborn through the Holy Spirit are born, concerning whom it is said: “They were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.”

For the Lord, needing no remission of sin and seeking no remedy of rebirth, nevertheless wished to be baptized in the same way that he wished to be circumcised and to have a sacrifice of purification offered for himself, so that he who had been made from a woman, as the Apostle says, might also be made under the Law—which he had not come to abolish but to fulfill and, by fulfilling it, to bring to completion—and as the Apostle proclaims: “The end of the Law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

He established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding primacy in all things, he taught that he was the beginning. He then confirmed the power of regeneration when blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed from his side. Therefore, just as the Old Testament was a testimony to the New, and the Law was given through Moses but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, so various sacrifices prefigured one sacrifice, and the slaughter of many lambs ended in the immolation of him of whom it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away [Note: [Col. 0909D] “the sin”—Dionysius Exiguus.] the sins of the world.”

So also John was not Christ but Christ’s forerunner; he was not the bridegroom but the bridegroom’s most faithful friend, seeking not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ. He declared himself unworthy to loosen the sandals of Christ’s feet, because he baptized with water for repentance, whereas Christ would baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire—by a twofold power restoring life and consuming sins.

Since, then, dearest brothers, there are so many and such great proofs by which, once every ambiguity has been removed, you clearly recognize that only two times are to be observed for baptizing the chosen—those who, according to apostolic rule, are to be examined in exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preaching—that is, Easter and Pentecost, we declare this to your Charity, so that you may not thereafter depart in any excess from apostolic institutions. For after this, it cannot remain unpunished if anyone believes that apostolic rules may be neglected in any respect.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 10. Let no one believe that he may confidently be baptized indiscriminately at any time whatsoever, except at the Easter feast and the venerable sacrament of Pentecost, with the sole exception of an attack of the gravest illness, in which it is to be feared that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person—perhaps overtaken by exile—may depart without the saving remedy.

### CCXIII. Concerning those who have not kept penance

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 5. In the case of those who, after performing penance, return like dogs and swine to their vomit and wallowing [Note: [Col. 0911D] “Former things” is added by Dionysius Exiguus.], and again seek the military belt, theatrical [Note: [Col. 0911D] “Playful,” Dionysius Exiguus.] and slippery pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden intercourse, your Dilection has rightly thought that the apostolic see should be consulted. Their professed lack of restraint has been exposed by the children born after their absolution.

Since they now have no further refuge in penance, we have decided that they are to be joined to the faithful within the Church only in prayer and are to attend the celebration of the sacred mysteries, although they do not deserve to do so; but they are to be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table. Thus corrected at least by this severity, they may punish their own errors in themselves and provide examples to others, so that they may be withdrawn from obscene desires.

Nevertheless, because they fell through bodily weakness, we wish them to be assisted by the gift of viaticum through the grace of communion when they begin to depart to the Lord. We decree that the same rule be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves by such defilements [Note: [Col. 0911D] “We judge that it is to be observed,” Dionysius Exiguus.].

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 7. Concerning penitents who are doing penance either for more serious offenses or for lesser ones, Roman Church custom shows that, if no illness intervenes, they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter. As for assessing the weight of their offenses, it belongs to the priest to judge, attending to the penitent’s confession and to the tears and weeping of the one who is correcting himself, and then ordering him to be released when he sees suitable satisfaction.

Certainly, if anyone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before Easter, lest he depart from the world without communion.

### CCXIV. That clerics may not perform penance, and that after penance no one may be admitted to the clergy

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 14. It was equally necessary for us to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman may ever be permitted to attain clerical rank. For although they have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, those who were formerly vessels of vices ought not to receive the instruments for administering the sacraments.

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 34. Innocent to Agapitus, Macedonius, and [Note: [Col. 0911D] “Marianus,” Dionysius Exiguus.] Martianus, bishops in Apulia.

Many reports and highly trustworthy communications have informed us that, throughout your province, numerous persons usurp things contrary to the ecclesiastical canons and the decrees of our predecessors. These abuses could easily be cut away if bishops were not found to be their authors. While they strive to show favor either to friends or to those who obey them, they violate religion and corrupt the orders. Thus it happens that wholly unworthy men receive ecclesiastical honors and are admitted to the clergy, although they would not deserve to hold a worthy place even among the laity, as has now been shown to us in a petition: a certain Modestus, involved in many crimes and said on that account also to have performed penance, has not only been made a cleric—which is not permitted—but is even striving for the summit of the episcopate. Yet the canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest offices of the clergy.

Therefore, dearest brothers, after examining the tenor of the petition, you shall order him to be brought before you. If it is truly established that he is such as the petition asserts [Note: [Col. 0912D] “Such a man,” Dionysius Exiguus.], he is to be removed not only from his ambition for the episcopate but also from clerical office.

### CCXV. That if, through ignorance, a penitent, a bigamist, or the husband of a widow has been made a cleric, he is not to be promoted further

From the decrees of Pope Siricius, title 15. Since, in all these matters that incur reproach, the sole excuse offered is ignorance—which, for the time being and out of regard for mercy alone, we must pardon with clemency—let every penitent, every bigamist, and every husband of a widow who has improperly and incompetently entered the sacred service understand that our pardon is granted to him on this condition: he must count it a great benefit if, after every hope of promotion has been taken away, he remains permanently in the order in which he is found.

Let the bishops of all the provinces know henceforth [Note: [Col. 0912D] “So that all the bishops of the provinces may know henceforth,” Dionysius Exiguus.] that, after this definition, if they believe that anyone of such persons should be admitted to the sacred orders [Col. 0913A], a suitable judgment is to be issued by the apostolic see both concerning their own status and that of those whom they have promoted contrary to the canons and to our prohibitions.

### CCXVI. Concerning baptized persons possessed by demons

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 6. Your Dilection asked about baptized persons who afterward are seized by a demon, by some affliction, or through the intervention of sin, whether they can or ought to be signed by a presbyter or deacon. This is not permitted unless the bishop has ordered it; for hands must not be laid upon such a person at all unless the bishop has granted authority for this to be done. When it is to be done, it belongs to the bishop to command that hands be laid upon him either by a presbyter or by the other clergy. For how could this be accomplished without great difficulty, by bringing a person possessed by a demon from a distant place to the bishop, when, if such a case should occur during a journey, he could neither easily be carried to the bishop nor brought back home?

### CCXVII. That a priest ought to pray for the sick and anoint them with oil according to the command of Saint James

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 8. Since your Dilection wished to consult us about this matter, as about the others, my beloved son the deacon Caelestinus added in his letter that your Dilection had raised the passage written in the epistle of the blessed Apostle James: “If anyone among you is sick [Note: “If anyone among you is ill,” Dionysius Exiguus.], let him call the presbyters, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.”

There is no doubt that this should be understood of faithful sick persons, who may be anointed with the holy oil of chrism. This oil, prepared by the bishop, may be used not only by priests but by all Christians for anointing in their own need or that of their family.

However, we see that the added uncertainty concerning the bishop is superfluous, since it is beyond doubt that this is permitted to presbyters. The passage was therefore addressed to presbyters because bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot visit all the sick. But if a bishop can or considers someone worthy of being visited by him, he may without hesitation bless and touch him with chrism, since he is the one who prepares the chrism itself.

This, however, cannot be infused into penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For how can those to whom the other sacraments are denied be thought capable of receiving one kind of sacrament?

### CCXVIII. That a bishop is not to be ordained without the knowledge of the metropolitan

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 9. First, no one may presume to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan. A judgment is sound when it is confirmed by the opinions of many; nor may one bishop presume to ordain, lest the benefit appear to have been conferred secretly. This was established and defined by the Synod of Nicaea.

From the decrees of Pope Caelestine, title 17. First, according to the decrees of the canons, each province is to remain content with its own metropolitan, as the constitutions sent by our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne contain. No opportunity for usurpation is to be granted to any priest to the injury of another. Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him. No one is to presume anything in another’s province, nor are foreign and unknown clerics, who have previously been strangers there, to be placed over those who have earned the good testimony of their fellow citizens, lest some new college, from which bishops are to be made, appear to have been established.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 32. Therefore, according to the canons of the holy Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, whose oversight is entrusted to your Fraternity by our delegation, retain unimpaired the right of the dignity anciently assigned to them, so that they depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor through presumption.

### CCXIX. That a cleric is not to be made from the curial class

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 18. Moreover, some of our brothers frequently strive to make clerics of curials or of men occupied with various public functions. Later, when the emperor orders that something be done about recalling them, greater sadness arises than favor arose from their appointment. For it is clear that in those very public duties they also stage entertainments—plainly invented by the devil—and either preside over or perhaps participate in the arrangements for games or public shows [Col. 0914C].

Let the concern and sorrow of the brothers whom we have often endured in the presence of the emperor serve as an example. We frequently pleaded for these men, as you yourself know, when you were present with us, since not only inferior clerics from the curial class but also men already established in the priesthood were being pressed with great difficulty to return.

### CCXX. That final penance is not to be denied

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 22. It was also asked what should be observed concerning those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves throughout their lives to the pleasures of sexual excess and, at the end of their life, ask simultaneously for penance and reconciliation through communion.

The earlier practice was more severe; the later practice, after mercy intervened, is more lenient. The earlier custom held that penance was granted to them but communion denied. Since persecutions were frequent in those times, communion was rightly denied and penance granted, lest the ease of receiving communion make people secure about reconciliation and fail to recall them from falling. Thus, so that everything might not be entirely denied, the circumstances of the time made the remission more severe.

But after our Lord restored peace to his churches, once fear had been removed, it was decided that communion should be given to those departing, both because of the Lord’s mercy—as viaticum for those about to journey—and lest we appear to follow the harshness and severity of the Novatian heretics, who denied pardon. Therefore, final communion is to be granted together with penance, so that such persons, even at the end of their lives, may, with the permission of our Savior, be rescued from everlasting destruction.

From the decrees of Pope Caelestine, title 15. We have learned that penance is denied to the dying and that the wishes of those who desire these remedies for their souls at the time of death are not granted. I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such great impiety that he despairs of God’s mercy, as though God could not come to the aid of someone who at any time turns to him, and as though he would allow a person endangered beneath the burden of sins to perish when that person desires to free himself and be liberated.

What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and by one’s cruelty to kill his soul so that it cannot be absolved, when God is entirely ready to come to his aid and invites him to penance, promising the sinner: “On whatever day he turns, his sins shall not be counted against him”; and again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

Therefore, whoever denies penance to a person at the time of death takes salvation away from him and despairs of God’s clemency, not believing that God can suffice, even in a moment, to assist the dying. The thief on the cross, hanging at Christ’s right hand, would have lost his reward if the penance of a single hour had not helped him. He repented while undergoing punishment, and through the promise contained in a single utterance, with God promising it, he earned a dwelling in paradise.

True conversion to God in those placed at the end of life is therefore to be judged more by the mind than by the time, as the prophet asserts: “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved.” Since Christ is the examiner of the heart, penance is not to be denied at any time to one who requests it, since the person binds himself to that Judge to whom he knows all hidden things are revealed.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 21. Concerning those who delay performing penance. This delay may arise not from contempt for the remedy but from fear of committing a more serious offense. Therefore penance that has been delayed is not to be denied when it is sought with greater earnestness, so that the wounded soul may somehow reach the medicine of indulgence.

### CCXXI. Concerning the administration of secular judgments

[Col. 0915D]

From the decree of Pope Innocent, title 23. It was also asked concerning those who, after baptism, have administered public offices, exercised only tortures, or even pronounced a capital sentence. Concerning these matters we find nothing defined by our predecessors. They remembered that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that God’s minister had been appointed as an avenger in such matters. How, then, could they condemn an act that they saw had been granted by God as its author?

Therefore, concerning such persons, let us maintain what has been observed until now, lest we appear either to overturn discipline or to act against the authority of the Lord. Their actions, however, will all be taken into account when they render an account.

### CCXXII. That neither husband nor wife may turn to adultery against the marriage bond, since in this matter they are equally bound to each other

[Col. 0916A]

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 24. It was desired to know why men who remain in communion with adulterous wives are not themselves excluded, whereas wives appear to remain in the company of adulterous husbands. In this matter the Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins do not receive punishment; men, however, more freely customarily report adulterous wives to priests. Thus communion is denied to women when their crime is exposed, whereas, when the offense of men remains hidden, no one is readily excluded on the basis of suspicions. He is indeed removed if his disgrace is uncovered. Since the case is therefore equal, the process of punishment sometimes ceases when proof is lacking.

### CCXXIII. That those who dictate criminal petitions are to be without guilt

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 25. You also wished to inquire whether those who dictate petitions are granted freedom, after the regeneration of baptism, to request from princes the death or blood of someone accused of a crime. Princes never grant such a request without investigation; they always refer the matters or crimes to judges, so that punishment may follow an examination of the case. When the matter has been delegated to the investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the case. While the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the person who dictated the petition remains exempt.

### CCXXIV. That those who have been separated from each other by divorce may not enter another union

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 26. Your Dilection also inquired about those who, after a divorce had intervened, joined themselves in another marriage. It is clear that both parties are adulterers. Those who, while their wife is alive—even if the marriage appears to have been dissolved—hasten to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers, to such an extent that even the persons joined to them appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery”; similarly, “whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery.” Therefore all such persons are to be kept from the communion of the faithful. Nothing of this kind can be decreed concerning their parents or relatives, unless they are discovered to have encouraged the unlawful union.

### CCXXV. That if anyone deliberately cuts off part of his body, he cannot be a cleric

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 28. If anyone deliberately cuts off part of any finger, the canons do not admit him to the clergy. But if this has happened to someone by accident while he was attending to agricultural work, or if, while doing something, he struck himself unintentionally, the canons order that such a person be made a cleric; and if he is found among the clergy, he is not to be expelled. In the former case, the will that dared to apply iron to itself has been judged; clearly, it would not hesitate to do the same to others. In the latter cases, accident has deserved pardon.

### CCXXVI. If someone’s wife is carried away into captivity and her husband takes another, the second is to be excluded when the first returns. The same arrangement is to be observed concerning a woman if, after her first husband has left her, she took another man

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 37. Innocent to Probus.
