The turmoil of the barbarian storm brought an unforeseen complication into the operation of the laws. A well-established marriage between Fortunius and Ursa would have suffered a blemish through the incursion of captivity, unless the holy statutes of religion had provided for it. Since the woman Ursa was being held in captivity, the said Fortunius is known to have entered another marriage with Restituta. But by the Lord’s favor Ursa returned and approached us, and, with no one denying it, clearly proved that she was the wife of the said man. Therefore, illustrious lord and son, with the Catholic faith supporting us, we have rightly determined that the marriage originally founded by divine grace is the true marriage, and that the union with the second woman, while the first survived and had not been dismissed by divorce, could in no way be legitimate.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 42. Since, as you say, certain marriages have been so divided by the devastation of war and the gravest incursions of hostility that, when the men were carried into captivity, their wives were left abandoned—believing their husbands either to have been killed or never to be freed from the power of their captors—and, compelled by their loneliness, entered into the marriages of others; and since now, with circumstances changed for the better by the Lord’s help, some of those believed to have perished have returned, your Charity rightly appears uncertain what we ought to decree concerning the women who have been joined to other men.

But because we know that Scripture says that a woman is joined to a man by God, and because we recognize the command that what God has joined no human being may separate, we must believe that the bonds of legitimate marriages are to be restored. Once the evils brought by hostility have been removed, what each person legitimately possessed must be restored to him or her. Every effort must be made so that each person receives what is his or her own.

Likewise on this matter, title 43. Nevertheless, the man who assumed the place of her husband, who was thought no longer to exist, is not called guilty or regarded as an invader of another’s right. In this way, many things belonging to those who were led into captivity could pass into another’s ownership; yet it is entirely just that, when those persons return, their own property be restored to them. If this is rightly observed concerning slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be done in the restoration of marriages, so that what was disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored by the remedy of peace?

Likewise, title 44. Therefore, if husbands return after a long captivity and remain so devoted to their wives that they wish them to return to their marital partnership, what necessity brought about must be set aside and judged blameless, and what faith demands must be restored.

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 45. But if certain women have been so captivated by love for their later husbands that they prefer to remain with them rather than return to their legitimate marriage, they are rightly censured, so that they are deprived of ecclesiastical communion. They have chosen the pollution of crime over an excusable circumstance, showing that, through their lack of restraint, they preferred what a just release could have atoned for.

Let marriages therefore return voluntarily to their proper state of restoration, and let what the condition of necessity extorted not in any way be turned into a reproach for evil will. For just as those women who refused to return to their husbands are to be regarded as impious, so those who return to the affection begun by God are rightly to be praised.

### CCXXVII. Concerning a catechumen who loses his wife before baptism and afterward takes another, and who therefore cannot be a cleric

[Col. 0918B]

From the decrees of Pope Innocent, title 52. It is proposed that a man should not be called a bigamist if, while he was a catechumen, he had and lost a wife and, after baptism, obtained another, since the woman joined to the new man should be regarded as his first wife, because that former marriage, together with the other offenses, was removed by the sacrament of baptism. If this is said of one wife, then certainly, if he had three wives while he remained in the old man, the woman who is fourth after baptism will, by this interpretation, also receive the name of virgin, as the one married in the fourth place.

Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, which says that a priest must be the husband of one wife? But it is objected that in baptism everything done in the old man has been dissolved.

Tell me—I speak with your pardon—are only crimes forgiven in baptism, or also those things that are fulfilled according to the Lord’s commands and God’s ordinances? Is taking a wife a crime or is it not a crime? If it is a crime, then, with the aforementioned pardon, I would say that the one who blessed marriage in paradise, joining them himself so that they might commit crimes, would be the author of guilt. But if it is not a crime, because what God has joined cannot rightly be called a crime, and Solomon added: “For a wife is prepared for a man by God,” how can it be believed that what is read as having been accomplished by God’s authority was forgiven among crimes?

What is to be thought of the children of such persons? Are they not to be admitted to a share in the inheritance, although they were born from the woman who was a wife before baptism? Are they to be called either natural children or bastards because, as it seems to you, only the marriage entered after baptism is legitimate?

When the Jews asked the Lord whether it was lawful to dismiss one’s wife, and he explained that this must not be done, he added: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate.” And lest it be thought that he was speaking of unions entered after baptism, let them remember that he was questioned by Jews and answered Jews.

I ask, and I ask anxiously: if the wife of a man who was first a catechumen and afterward a believer is one and the same, and if he had children by her while he was a catechumen and afterward had others while he was a believer [Col. 0919A], are the children to be called brothers or not? After their father’s death, are they to have a share in the division of the inheritance, even though spiritual regeneration is believed to have taken away from them the name of children?

Since it is absurd to think and judge in this way, what reason—alas—is there for defending this and proclaiming it through empty opinion rather than strengthening it by some authority? What the Law commanded and God joined cannot be counted among sins.

If a catechumen devoted himself to virtues, followed humility, maintained patience, gave alms, rescued those condemned to death by whatever means, abhorred adulteries, and maintained chastity, I ask whether, when he became a believer, he would lose these things because baptism is thought to remove everything done by the old man.

Let us consider the gentile Cornelius, devoted to prayers and almsgiving, who saw an angel through a revelation, and Peter himself. Were these things taken away from him through baptism, on account of which baptism appears to have been granted to him? If this is believed, believe me, it is a considerable error, because whatever has been done well and preserved according to the precepts of the Law cannot be lost by those who did it.

The marital union, therefore, because it is completed by God’s command, cannot be called a sin. What is not a sin must absolutely not be believed to have been dissolved among sins. It will therefore remain proper to judge that the status of the former wife cannot be abolished, since it was not dismissed as a sin but was completed according to God’s will.

### CCXXVIII. That a bishop is not to be ordained against the will of the clergy or the people, and that unlawful ordinations are to be avoided

[Col. 0919C]

From the decrees of Pope Caelestine, title 18. Let no bishop be appointed against the will of those concerned. The agreement and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order must be sought. Only then may another be chosen from another church if no one worthy—which we do not believe can happen—can be found among the clergy of the very city for which the bishop is to be ordained. Those persons are to be rejected first, so that someone from another church may rightly be preferred.

Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the church in which he has passed his entire life through all the offices. Let no one improperly intrude upon another’s service, nor dare one person claim for himself the reward due to another. The clergy must have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being oppressed, and they must not fear to reject those whom they recognize as being thrust upon them from outside. If they are not to receive their due reward, they must at least have free judgment concerning the person who is to govern them.

From the decrees of the pope mentioned above, title 19. Let there also be abstention from illicit ordinations: no layman, no bigamist, no man who is or has been the husband of a widow shall be ordained; rather, let one be made irreproachable and of the kind the Apostle chose. Through Moses the Lord commanded: “Let the priest take a virgin as his wife.” The Apostle, speaking subsequently and in the same Spirit, confirms this: “The bishop must be consecrated as the husband of one wife.” Therefore priests are to be chosen according to this rule; and if any illicit ordinations have been carried out, let them be removed, since they cannot stand and will not be able to evade our investigation. Although they may think that it can remain hidden how they attained their positions, [Col. 0920A] this must be disclosed so that no reverence for religion may be darkened by obscurity.

Let there be no empty boasting by men covered with pretexts; let those who are bishops follow episcopal practice. Daniel, as we have said, who believed that he could evade accusation through pontifical honor and attained only to high office by concealing himself from his accusers, must know that for the present he is excluded from the assembly of your sanctity. He ought to cast himself away by our judgment if he knows that he possesses confidence in his own conscience. As for the priest of the church of Massilia, who is said—an unspeakable thing—to have rejoiced in this manner at the death of his own brother, so that he might meet the man who had come stained with the brother’s blood and was to have a portion with him, we delegate him to be heard by your college.

From the decree of Pope Leo, title 15. No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the bishops of the province with the judgment of the metropolitan. Since a dispute about improperly acquired honor often arises, who could doubt that nothing should be granted to those whose conferral is not shown to have taken place? If, however, any clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches that belonged to their own bishops, and their ordination was carried out with the consent and judgment of the presiding bishops, it may be considered valid, so that they may remain in those churches. Otherwise, the consecration must be regarded as void, since it was founded neither in the proper place nor secured by authority.

From the one mentioned above, title 35. When, therefore, the election of the chief priest is being considered, the one whom the consent of clergy and people have concordantly requested is to be preferred to all, so that, if the votes of the parties should happen to be divided among another person, by the judgment of the metropolitan the one who is supported by greater influence and merits may be preferred to the other—provided that no one is ordained against the will or without the request of the people. Otherwise the city might either despise or hate an unwanted bishop and become less religious than it ought to be, since it was not permitted to have the one it wanted.

CCXXIX. That no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons

From the decree of Pope Celestine, title 20. Celestine to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria. No priest may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy matter will be preserved by us if the standard of the established decretals is broken at the whim of certain persons, with permission granted to the people?

CCXXX. That a wife is one thing and a concubine another; and that no one who has given his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine should be in error

From the decree of Pope Leo, title 18. Not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. The agreements of marriage are legitimate among the freeborn and among equals; indeed, the Lord established this very principle long before the beginning of Roman law existed. Thus a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another.

For this reason the Apostle, in order to make clear the distinction between these persons, gives testimony from Genesis, where it is said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” Since, therefore, the fellowship of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it possessed the sacramental significance of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage when it is shown that the nuptial mystery was absent from her.

Accordingly, if a cleric of any place gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as giving her to a married man—unless perhaps that woman is seen to have been made free, legally endowed with a dowry, and honored by a public marriage. Women joined to men by paternal decision are free from blame if the women whom those men had were not wives: a married woman is one thing, a concubine another.

CCXXXI. That there is no duplication of marriage when, after the slave woman has been expelled, a wife is brought in

From the decree of Pope Leo, title 19. To cast away the slave woman [Note: [Col. 0921D] Dionysius Exiguus: “to cast her away from the marriage bed.”] upon taking a matron, and to take a wife of assured free birth, is not a duplication of marriage but an advance in honorable conduct. The negligence of such people is certainly blameworthy, but they are not to be entirely abandoned [Note: [Col. 0922D] Dionysius Exiguus: “despaired of completely”], so that, stirred by frequent exhortations, they may faithfully carry out what they necessarily sought. For no one is to be despaired of while he remains in this body, because sometimes what is postponed through distrust of one’s age is accomplished through more mature counsel.

CCXXXII. Concerning those deprived of communion and dying in that state

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 20. The case of such people must be reserved for God’s judgment, in whose hand it lay that the death of such persons should not be delayed until the remedy of communion. But we, who did not give communion to them while they were alive, cannot give communion to them after death.

CCXXXIII. That one who asks forgiveness for illicit acts must also abstain from licit ones

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 22. It is one thing to demand what is owed, and another to disregard one’s own possessions out of love of perfection. But one who asks forgiveness for illicit acts must also abstain from licit ones, since the Apostle says: “All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial.” Therefore, if penitents have a case which perhaps they ought not to neglect, it is better for someone to seek an ecclesiastical judgment than a civil one.

CCXXXIV. That it is not appropriate for a penitent to conduct any profit-making business

From the decree of Pope Leo, title 23. The character of profit either excuses or condemns the merchant, since there is honorable gain and there is shameful gain. Nevertheless, it is more beneficial for a penitent to suffer losses than to be bound by the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the transaction between buyer and seller.

CCXXXV. That after penance one ought not to return to secular military service

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 24. It is wholly contrary to ecclesiastical rules, after performing penance, to return to secular military service, since the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs.” Therefore, the person who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the snares of the devil.

CCXXXVI. That if a young man, under pressure from some danger of death, performs penance but does not remain continent, he ought to be supported by the remedy of a wife

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 25. If a man in adolescence, under pressure either from fear of death or from the danger of captivity, performed penance and afterward, fearing a lapse into venial incontinence, chose marital intercourse so as not to incur the crime of fornication, he appears to have done something venial, provided that he had no relations whatsoever with anyone except his wife. In this matter, however, we are not establishing a rule but judging what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more fitting for one who has performed penance than persevering chastity of both mind and body.

CCXXXVII. That carnal marriage is denied to subdeacons

From the decrees of Pope Leo, title 34. Although those outside the clerical order have free choice to pursue marriage and the begetting of children, nevertheless, in order to exhibit the purity of perfect continence, carnal marriage is not permitted even to subdeacons, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who do not have wives may remain solitary. If this is rightly observed in this order, which is the fourth order from the highest, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, and third, so that no one may be judged suitable for Levitical, presbyteral, or episcopal honor who is found not yet to have restrained himself from the desire for a wife.

CCXXXVIII. That no fees are to be demanded for baptizing and signing the faithful

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 5. Let them set no fees for baptizing and signing the faithful, nor seek to harass those who are being reborn by imposing any exactions, since we are commanded to give freely what we receive freely. Therefore let them make no attempt to demand anything at all from the persons mentioned above, lest, terrified by poverty or driven away by indignation, they disdain to approach the means of their redemption. They should be certain that those who are discovered to have committed what is forbidden, or who do not correct their offenses voluntarily, will incur the danger of losing their own honor.

CCXXXIX. That the ordinations of priests and deacons ought to be celebrated at fixed times

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 11. The ordinations of priests and deacons must not be performed except at fixed times and on fixed days: namely, during the fast of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and also at the beginning of Lent, and on the middle day of Lent, during the Saturday fast toward evening. Nor, for the sake of any advantage, should a priest or deacon be preferred to those who were ordained before them.

CCXL. That sacred virgins are to be veiled on appointed days

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 12. They should impose the sacred veil upon consecrated virgins only on Epiphany, during the Paschal white days, or on the feasts of the Apostles—unless perhaps, as was said concerning baptism, the veil should not be denied to those who, stricken by severe illness, ask for it lest they depart from the world without this gift.

CCXLI. That widows are not to be veiled

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 13. No bishop should presume to veil widows, since neither divine authority delegates this power nor the form of the canons prescribes it. It must therefore not be usurped at all; rather, ecclesiastical support should be provided to them in such a way that nothing illicit is committed.

From the one mentioned above, title 21. We have already discussed at length the veiling of widows under no blessing whatsoever. If, by their own will, they trample with changeable minds upon the chastity of their former marriage which they had professed, it will be their concern, at their own risk, with what satisfaction they ought to appease God. For just as, if they were perhaps unable to remain continent, they were in no way forbidden by the Apostle to marry, so, after deliberating with themselves, they ought to have guarded the pledge of chastity promised to God.

We, however, ought to impose no snare upon such women, but only set before them exhortations concerning eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may render an account to God for itself. One must indeed beware of what the blessed apostle Paul testifies concerning the morals and conduct of such women; we pass over explaining it more plainly, lest the unstable sex appear to be deterred rather than admonished.

CCXLII. That those ensnared by demons and other afflictions may not handle the sacred mysteries

From the decrees of the one mentioned above, title 19. We have discovered that illicit practices have advanced to such a degree that those ensnared by demons and similar afflictions are permitted to handle the sacred ministries. If, while engaged in this work, some personal necessity should befall them, who would have confidence concerning the salvation of the faithful when he saw the ministers themselves afflicted by so great a calamity requiring human healing? Therefore they must necessarily be removed, lest scandal be generated among the weak, for whom Christ died.

Finally, if divine law did not permit a person wounded in body or altogether infirm to touch holy things, how much less is it fitting for those struck in mind—what is worse—to be dispensers of the heavenly gift?

CCXLIII. That second marriages are not to be denied to secular persons, although those who have contracted them are wholly unsuited to aspire to the clergy on that account

From the decree of Pope Gelasius, title 22. Just as secular persons are permitted to enter into second marriages, so after them no one should be allowed to enter the clerical college. For one thing is the permission generally granted to human weakness, and another ought to be the life dedicated to the service of divine things.

CCXLIV. That new basilicas are to be dedicated by bishops upon papal instruction

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, title 4. They must not presume to dedicate newly established basilicas without the customary instructions having been requested. Let them not seek to claim for themselves clerics belonging to another’s authority.

And let no basilica be dedicated under the name of the dead.

From the one mentioned above, title 25. Although the consecration of holy places was briefly included above, it has also been revealed to us that some presume to consecrate churches or oratories that have been built without the instruction of the Apostolic See. We have nevertheless been moved by an even more detestable report: it is said that they boldly establish as sacred foundations buildings constructed under the name of various dead persons and, as is reported, not even of the faithful. Since these acts are so bitter and harsh that our hearing could scarcely bear them, if the Christian commitment in those regions is truly firm and established, these matters must be investigated with greater rigor, and those who carried them out must be disclosed.

For if, while the names of those hidden in this atrocity remain concealed, there is no one against whom the appropriate sentence can be pronounced, then, once the matter has been exposed by manifest evidence, the offender will in no way escape the vengeance demanded by the enormity of so great a crime [Note: [Col. 0923D] Dionysius Exiguus: “will not escape.”].

CCXLV. That if a bishop is detained under accusation outside the time of a synod, he is to be heard by twelve bishops; a priest by six; and a deacon by three

Council of Carthage, title 12. Bishop Felix said: “I propose, according to the statutes of the ancient councils, that if any bishop—which we do not desire—should fall under some accusation and there should be an extreme necessity preventing the gathering of many, so that he may not remain under accusation, he should be heard by twelve bishops; a priest by six bishops together with his own bishop; and a deacon by three.”

Council mentioned above, title 20. If priests or deacons are accused, their own bishop, joined by the lawful number of colleagues from neighboring places whom the accused persons themselves have requested, is to investigate their case: that is, six including himself in the case of a priest, and three in the case of a deacon. The same procedure concerning days, postponements, exclusion from communion, and examination of the persons is to be observed between the accusers and those accused. The cases of the remaining clerics may be heard and concluded by the bishop of the place alone.

CCXLVI. Concerning the various orders serving the Church, and that if anyone falls into a case and rejects ecclesiastical judgment, he must suffer the consequences

Council of Carthage, title 15. It was also agreed that any bishop, priest, deacon, or cleric, when a criminal charge has been brought against him in the Church or a civil case has been initiated, if he abandons ecclesiastical judgment and wishes to be cleared by public courts, shall lose his position, even if a judgment has been pronounced in his favor. This applies in a criminal case; in a civil case, if he prefers to retain his position, he shall lose what he won.

It was also agreed that, when an appeal has been made from some ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, this must not prejudice those whose judgment has been overturned, if they cannot be convicted either of having judged with an unjust disposition or of having been corrupted by some greed or favor. If, however, the judges were chosen by agreement of the parties, an appeal is not permitted even from a smaller number than the established number.

CCXLVII. That a cleric who is ordained must be admonished to preserve the decrees of the Fathers; especially that the Eucharist and baptism are not to be given to dead bodies

Council of Carthage, title 18. It was also agreed that, when bishops or clerics have been ordained, the ordinances of the councils must first be impressed upon their ears by those who ordained them, lest they regret having done anything contrary to the statutes of the council.

It was also agreed that the Eucharist must not be given to the bodies of the dead, for it is written: “Take and eat.” Corpses, however, can neither take nor eat. And let the negligence of priests not cause dead people to be baptized.

CCXLVIII. That bishops and clerics are to confer nothing upon those who are not Catholic

Council of Carthage, title 22. And it was agreed that bishops or clerics should confer nothing from their property upon those who are not Catholic Christians, even if they are relatives.

Also, from the council mentioned above, title 48. It was also decreed that if any bishop should prefer to the Church heirs unrelated to him, or heretics or pagans—even if they are his relatives—let anathema be pronounced against him at least after his death, and let his name in no way be recited among God’s priests. Nor can he be excused if he dies intestate [Note: [Col. 0925D] Dionysius Exiguus: “if he should die”], because, having become a bishop, he ought certainly not to have delayed arranging his property in a manner appropriate to his profession.

CCXLIX. Concerning the accused person or the accuser

Council of Carthage, title 30. It was also agreed that the accused person or the accuser should choose, in the place from which the accused comes, a nearby location—if he fears some violent act by a reckless crowd—where it would not be difficult to produce witnesses and where the case could be concluded.

CCL. That clerics who do not obey their bishops when they are to be promoted should not remain in the place from which they refused to depart

Council of Carthage, title 31. It was also agreed that any clerics or deacons who, for the needs of the Churches, do not obey their bishops when the bishops wish to promote them to greater honor in their own Church should not serve them in the rank from which they refused to depart.

CCLI. That if a poor cleric who has been promoted later acquires anything, it is subject to the authority of the Church

Council of Carthage, title 32. It was also agreed that bishops, priests, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained possessing nothing, and who during their episcopate or clerical office acquire lands or any estates in their own name, shall be held guilty of invading the Lord’s property, unless, after being admonished, they transfer those very things to the Church.

If, however, something comes to them personally through someone’s generosity or through inheritance from their kin, let them deal with it in a way consistent with their purpose. But if they deviate backward from their purpose, let them be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, like reprobates.

CCLII. That priests must not sell the property of the church in which they have been established, and that no bishop may usurp the property of the title of the mother Church

Council of Carthage, title 33. It was also agreed that priests must not sell the property of the church in which they have been established without the knowledge of the bishops, just as bishops may not sell the estates of the Church without the knowledge of the council or of their priests. Therefore, when there is no necessity, neither may a bishop usurp property belonging to the mother Church, nor a priest property belonging to his title.

CCLIII. That children baptized among the Donatists are not to be barred from ordination if they are converted

Council of Carthage, title 14. Concerning the Donatists, it was agreed that we should consult our brothers and fellow priests, Syricius and Simplicianus, concerning only the children baptized among them, lest, when they have been converted to the Church of God with a wholesome purpose, the error of their parents prevent them from being promoted as ministers of the sacred altar, since they did not commit the error by their own judgment.

Council mentioned above, titles [Note: [Col. 0925D] In the Code of the Canons of the African Church and in Dionysius Exiguus, these are canons 56 and 57. Nothing, however, needs to be corrected.] 23 and 24. Bishop Aurelius said:

“Our charity, most holy brothers, knows very well with me the needs of the Churches established throughout Africa. Since the Lord has granted that the presence of your holy assembly should be gathered here in part, it seems to me that we should bring forward those same needs which, in our concern, we have been able to investigate. When your sincerity has approved them, it follows that one of our number should be chosen as a fellow priest who, with the Lord’s help and your prayers, may undertake these very needs and diligently bring them to completion, traveling to the regions of Italy across the sea.

“He will be able to make known this need, grief, and poverty of ours both to our holy brothers and fellow priests, the venerable holy brother Anastasius, bishop of the Apostolic See, and also to the holy brother Venerius, priest of the Church of Milan. For it was from those sees that the matter had been forbidden; they know that provision must be made for it by common danger, especially because there is such a shortage of clerics and so many churches are deserted that they are found to have not even one deacon, however unlearned. I think we must remain silent about the other, higher ranks and offices, because, as I said, if the ministry of a deacon is not easily found, it is entirely certain that the higher honors can be found even less easily.

“Every day we can scarcely endure the lamentations of almost lifeless peoples of various kinds. Unless they are helped at some point, a grave and inexcusable responsibility for countless souls who are perishing will remain with us before God.

“Therefore, since your unanimity recognizes with me that it was established in the previous council that those who were baptized as children among the Donatists, not yet able to know the destruction caused by their error, and who, after reaching an age capable of reason, recognized the truth, rejected their falsehood, and were received into the Catholic Church of God, spread throughout the whole world, according to the ancient order through the laying on of hands, should not be prevented by the name of their former error from receiving the clerical office—since by approaching the faith they believed that Church to be the true Church, believed in Christ there, and received the sacraments of the Trinity.

“It is entirely certain that all these things are true, holy, and divine, and that in them all hope of the soul is established. Although the presumptuous audacity of heretics, cloaked under the name of truth, dares to transmit these things, nevertheless, since they are simple and, as the blessed Apostle teaches by saying, ‘one God, one faith, one baptism,’ and since what ought to be given once may not be repeated, let such persons, after the name of their error has been anathematized, be received through the laying on of hands into the one Church, the dove, as it is called, and the one mother of all Christians, where all the sacraments are received healthfully, eternally, and vitally.

“These same sacraments bring upon those who persevere in heresy a great punishment of condemnation, so that what would be more luminous for them in truth, for attaining eternal life, becomes darker and more destructive in error. Fleeing this, some have recognized the breasts of the Catholic mother Church and, through love of truth, believed and received all those holy mysteries. When upright conduct of life is added to their reception of the sacraments, no one can deny that such persons should be assigned to the clerical office, especially in so great a need.

“Although some clerics of the same sect desire to pass over to us together with their peoples and honors, and, through love of honor, either persuade them toward life or retain them for salvation, I think this should be left to the greater consideration of the brothers mentioned above. When they have weighed the words of our proposal with their wiser counsel, may they deign to inform us what they think about this matter.

“We are concerned only with those who were baptized as infants, so that, if it pleases you, they may agree with our will concerning their ordination. Let your honored brotherhood consider with me that everything we have set out above must be dealt with before the holy bishops.”

It was also agreed that clerics of the Donatists should be received in their honors.

Council of Carthage, title 35. It was then agreed that letters should be sent to our brothers and fellow bishops, and especially to the Apostolic See, where the aforementioned venerable brother and colleague Anastasius presides, so that he may know that Africa has a great need, for the peace and benefit of the Church, that any of the Donatists who, after correcting their judgment, wish to pass over to Catholic unity as clerics should be received in their honors, according to the will and counsel of each Catholic bishop who governs the Church in that place, if this is seen to benefit Christian peace.

This was done, as is evident, in the earlier periods of the same division, and the examples of many, indeed almost all, African Churches in which such an error arose bear witness to it. This is not intended to dissolve the council held across the sea concerning this matter, but so that its provision may remain applicable to those who wish to pass over to the Catholic Church in such a way that no compensation for unity is secured through them, while Catholic unity may, through others, either be fully achieved or aided by manifest gains of brotherly souls in the places where they live.

What was established in the council across the sea against their honors must not harm those through whom Catholic unity is being advanced, although salvation has been denied to no one—namely, that those ordained in the party of Donatus, if they wish to pass over to the Catholic Church after correcting their error, should not be received in their honors according to the transmarine council—except those through whom provision is made for Catholic unity.

CCLIV. That bishops and clerics should not easily emancipate their children

Council of Carthage, title 2. Bishops and clerics must not allow their children to leave their authority through emancipation unless they are secure concerning their character and age, so that their own offenses may by then properly belong to them.

CCLV. That clerics and continent men should not approach virgins and widows

Council of Carthage, title 5. Clerics and continent men must not approach widows or virgins except by order or permission of the bishops or priests. They must not do so alone, but with clerics or with those whom the bishop or priest has appointed. Nor should bishops or priests themselves have access to such women alone, but only where either clerics or some respected Christians are present.

CCLVI. That the chief priest must not be called a bishop

Council of Carthage, title 6. The bishop of the chief see must not be called “chief of the priests,” or “high priest,” or anything of that kind, but only “bishop of the chief see.”

CCLVII. That sacrifices to God are to be celebrated by fasting priests

Council of Carthage, title 8. The sacraments of the altar must be celebrated only by people who are fasting, except on the one annual day on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated. If, however, a commemoration of some persons who have died—whether bishops or others—must be made in the afternoon, it should be done only with prayers if those who are to perform it are found already to have eaten.

CCLVIII. Concerning care to be exercised for virgins

Council of Carthage, title 11. When sacred virgins have been deprived of the parents by whom they were being guarded, they are to be entrusted, through the care of the bishops—or, where the bishop is absent, of the priests—to more serious-minded women; or they should live together and guard one another, lest by wandering about indiscriminately they harm the reputation of the Church.

CCLIX. That a bishop must not be ordained in a diocese that has never had a bishop, except with the consent of the bishop to whom that diocese belongs

Council of Carthage, title 20. Bishop Epigonius said:

“It has been established by many councils and by the priestly assembly that peoples held by bishops in dioceses which have never had bishops may receive their own rulers—that is, bishops—only with the consent of the bishop by whom they are held.

“But because some, after acquiring a certain domination, reject communion with their brothers, or, once corrupted, claim domination for themselves as though in a tyrannical fortress, many proud and foolish priests raise their necks against their bishops, either by arranging banquets for their peoples or by malicious persuasion, so that they wish to place the same men over themselves as rulers through illicit favor.

“We hold as a notable expression of your mind, religious brother Aurelius, that you have often suppressed such things by taking no account of such petitioners. But because of their evil thoughts and their wickedly contrived plans, I say this: a people that has always been subject to a diocese and has never had its own bishop ought not to receive a ruler.

“Therefore, if it pleases the entire most holy assembly, let what I have stated be confirmed.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“I do not oppose the proposal of our brother and fellow priest, but I profess that I have done this and shall continue to do it, certainly toward those who have been in agreement not only with the Church of Carthage but with the entire priestly fellowship.

“For there are many who conspire with their own peoples, whom they deceive, as has been said, scratching their ears, pleasant in order to seduce them, men of vicious life, or certainly puffed up and separated from this fellowship. They think they should devote themselves to their own people and sometimes, when summoned, refuse to come to the council, perhaps fearing that their crimes might be exposed.

“I say, if it pleases you, that in the case of such men not only are their dioceses not to be preserved, but every effort must be made even against the church that has wrongly favored them, so that they may be rejected by public authority and removed from the principal sees themselves.

“For the one who has clung to all the brothers and to the whole council ought to possess not only his own see by full right but also the dioceses. But those who think their own peoples sufficient for them, despising brotherly love, should lose not only the dioceses but, as I have said, even their own churches through public authority, as rebels.”

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“The supreme prudence of your sanctity has united the minds of all, and I think that what you have seen fit to propose should be confirmed by the response of everyone.”

All the bishops said: “It pleases us; it pleases us.”

CCLX. That those who have been ordained as bishops in dioceses must not usurp any other diocese for themselves

Council of Carthage, title 23. Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

“We have heard it established that dioceses should not be permitted to receive bishops except with the consent of the one under whose authority they were constituted. But in our province, when some have perhaps been ordained as bishops in a diocese with the permission of the bishop under whose authority they had been constituted, they also claim the dioceses for themselves. This must be corrected by the judgment of your charity and prohibited henceforth.”

Bishop Epigonius said:

“The proper arrangement has been preserved for each bishop: no single diocese was to be taken from the body of dioceses in order to have its own bishop unless he himself had consented to the grant. It is enough, if he has granted permission, that the diocese thus permitted should have only its own bishop, and that they should not claim the other dioceses for themselves, since, taken out from the bundle of many, it alone deserved to receive the honor of the episcopate.”

Bishop Aurelius said:

“I do not doubt that it pleases all your charity that the man who was ordained in a diocese with the permission of the bishop who held the mother see should retain only that same people in which he was ordained. Since, therefore, I think everything has been discussed, if all this agrees with your minds, confirm everything with your statement.”

All the bishops said:

“All these things have pleased us, and we confirm them with our subscription.”

CCLXI. Concerning the remains of idols and the temples to be abolished by the emperors

Council of Carthage, title 25. Other needs also demand that requests be made to the religious emperors: that they order the remains of idols to be completely cut off throughout Africa. For in many maritime places and on various estates the wickedness of this error still flourishes. They should therefore order both the remains themselves to be destroyed and their temples, which have been established in fields or hidden places without any ornament, to be utterly demolished.

CCLXII. That clerics are not to be compelled to testify publicly concerning matters they have judged

Council of Carthage, title 26. It should also be requested that they deign to establish that, if they should wish to pursue some case in the Church under the apostolic law imposed upon the Churches, and if the clerics’ decision should perhaps displease one party, the cleric who was the investigator or was present may not be summoned before a court to give testimony, so that no ecclesiastical person may be pressed into giving testimony.

CCLXIII. Concerning the removal of pagan banquets

Council of Carthage, title 27. It should also be requested that the banquets held in many places against the divine commandments, which have been drawn from pagan error, be prohibited. Christians are now being compelled by pagans to celebrate them, so that, as a result, a second persecution seems secretly to be taking place in the times of Christian emperors.

Let them order such practices to be forbidden and, under penalty, prohibited both in the cities and on the estates. This is especially necessary because in some cities they do not hesitate to commit such acts even on the birthdays of the most blessed martyrs and in the sacred places themselves. On those days, too—shameful as it is to say—they practice most criminal dances through the streets and squares, so that the honor of married women and the modesty of countless women who come devoutly to the most sacred day may be attacked by wanton insults, and so that access even to the holy religion itself may almost be avoided.

## CCLXIV. On prohibiting spectacles on Sunday and other solemnities of the saints

[Col. 0931B]

Council of Carthage, title 28. It should also be requested that theatrical spectacles and other games be removed on Sunday and on the other most solemn days of the Christian religion, especially since, during the days of the octave of holy Easter, the people gather at the circus rather than at the church. Their days of devotion should be transferred whenever they coincide with such spectacles, and no Christian ought to be compelled to attend them—especially since, in carrying out activities contrary to the commandments of God, no necessity of persecution should be imposed by anyone [Note: [Col. 0931D] Dionysius Exiguus: “by anyone”]. Rather, a person ought to act by the free will with which he exists, granted to him by God [Col. 0931C]. For the danger to those subject to bodily compulsion must be considered above all: they are forced by great terror to attend the spectacles contrary to the commandments of God.

## CCLXV. On actors who have become Christians

Council of Carthage, title 30. It should also be requested concerning these matters that, if anyone wishes to come from any profession connected with public entertainments to the grace of Christianity and remain free from that stain, no one may compel him to return to the practice of the same activities.

## CCLXVI. On manumissions celebrated in the Church

[Col. 0931D]

Council of Carthage, title 31. Concerning manumissions, if our fellow bishops throughout Italy are found to perform them in the Church, it will also be our confidence to follow their procedure. Permission is plainly being granted to the envoy sent forth, so that whatever he may be able to undertake in good faith for the condition of the Church and the salvation of souls, we shall commendably accept in the sight of the Lord. If all these matters please Your Holiness, declare them, so that they may understand that you regard my proposal as ratified and that their sincerity may gladly receive the agreement of us all.

All the bishops said: “All that has been imposed for execution pleases us, and it has been prudently set forth by Your Holiness.”

## CCLXVII. That an intervening bishop should not occupy the episcopal seat where he is intervening

[Col. 0932A]

Council of Carthage, title 41. It was likewise decreed that no intervening bishop [Note: [Col. 0932D] Dionysius Exiguus and the Roman Ecclesiastical Code: “intercessor”] may retain the episcopal seat to which an intervening bishop has been assigned, regardless of the factions or seditions of the people. Rather, he must take care to provide them with a bishop within a year; and if he neglects this after the year has elapsed, another intervening bishop shall be appointed.

## CCLXVIII. On bishops who do not attend councils

From the aforementioned council, title 43. It was likewise agreed that whenever a council is to be convened, bishops who are prevented neither by age, illness, nor any more serious necessity should attend in due measure. The primates of each province are to be notified, so that from all the bishops either two or three companies may be formed and, from each company in turn, as many as have been chosen may attend the council’s appointed day with the greatest urgency. If they cannot attend, they must set down their excuses in the official dispatch; or, if some necessity should perhaps suddenly arise after the arrival of the dispatch, unless they render an account of the impediment to their own primate, they must be content with communion in their own Church.

## CCLXIX. That those received from another monastery may not be ordained either as superiors of monasteries or as clerics

Council of Carthage, title 47. It was likewise agreed that, if anyone wishes to promote to the clergy a person found in another’s monastery, or to appoint him as superior in his own monastery [Col. 0932C], the bishop who has done this shall be separated from communion with the other bishops and shall be content with communion with his own people; and that man shall continue neither as a cleric nor as superior.

## CCLXX. That bishops who are ordained should receive from their ordainers letters bearing the day and the consul

Council of Carthage, title 56. It was then agreed that all who thereafter are ordained throughout the African provinces should receive from their ordainers letters signed by their own hand and containing the name of the consul and the day, so that no dispute may arise concerning those ordained later or earlier.

## CCLXXI. That those who have once read in a Church may not be promoted by another

[Col. 0932D]

Council of Carthage, title 57. It was likewise agreed that whoever has read even once in a church may not be claimed by another church for the clerical order.

## CCLXXII. That a universal council should be held only from necessity

Council of Carthage, title 62. It was agreed that there should no longer be an annual necessity for wearying the brethren. Rather, whenever a common cause requires it—that is, a matter concerning all Africa—the synod is to be convened in that province where circumstances indicate it is most suitable, wherever letters concerning the matter have been sent to this see. Causes that are not common are to be judged in their own provinces.

## CCLXXIII. That no appeal may be made from judges chosen by agreement

[Col. 0933A]

From the aforementioned council, title 63. If an appeal has been made, the person who has appealed shall choose the judges, together with the person against whom he has appealed, so that thereafter neither party may appeal from those judges.

Likewise on this matter, title 89. No appeal may be made from judges whom common agreement has chosen. And if anyone who has been summoned is found, through contumacy, unwilling to obey the judges, once this has been proved to the bishop of the principal see, he shall issue letters so that none of the bishops may communicate with that person until he obeys.

## CCLXXIV. On communities that have never had bishops

Council of Carthage, title 65. It was also agreed that communities [Col. 0933B] which have never had their own bishops should receive none unless this has been decreed by a plenary council of the particular province, by its primate, and with the consent of the bishop to whose diocese that church belonged.

## CCLXXV. On communities or dioceses converted from the Donatists

From the aforementioned council, title 66. It was agreed that communities which have been converted from the Donatists and had bishops should certainly be permitted to retain them without consulting the council [Note: [Col. 0933D] Dionysius Exiguus and the Roman Ecclesiastical Code: “those communities”]. But communities that had a bishop and, after his death, wish not to have their own bishop but to belong to the diocese of some other bishop are not to be denied this.

It was also brought forward that, before the imperial law concerning unity was enacted, whichever bishops were converted to the Catholic Church ought themselves to retain the communities that had been converted. But from the law of unity onward, all churches must claim for themselves the Catholic bishops of those places to which the churches had belonged under the heretics, whether those places had been converted to Catholicism or had remained with heretical bishops, together with the dioceses and any church documents or property belonging to its right [Col. 0933C]. Those who have usurped anything are to restore to the converts whatever they usurped after the law [Note: [Col. 0933D] Dionysius Exiguus and the Roman Ecclesiastical Code: “when summoned”].

## CCLXXVI. On prayers to be said at the altar

Council of Carthage, title 70. It was also agreed that the prayers approved in the council—whether prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands—should be celebrated by all, and that no others at all should be pronounced contrary to the faith. Rather, whatever prayers have been collected by the more prudent should be said.

## CCLXXVII. On those who, not being in communion in Africa, attempt to slip across the sea

Council of Carthage, title 72. Whoever is not in communion in Africa, but slips across the sea in order to receive communion [Note: [Col. 0933D] Dionysius Exiguus: “not being in communion”; Roman Ecclesiastical Code, [Col. 0934D] “slip across in order to receive communion”], shall suffer the loss of his clerical office [Note: [Col. 0934D] Roman Ecclesiastical Code: “shall receive the penalty”].

## CCLXXVIII. On communities converted from the Donatists

Council of Carthage, title 84. It was likewise agreed that, since several years ago a plenary council was held in this church, establishing that all churches situated within a diocese which became Catholic before the laws concerning the Donatists were issued should belong to the episcopal seats through whose bishops they were brought into communion with Catholic unity; but that, after the laws, all those which entered into communion should belong to the episcopal seat to which they had belonged when they were in the Donatist faction.

Because many controversies have since arisen, and continue to arise, among bishops concerning dioceses—matters for which provision then seemed insufficient—this holy council now decrees that wherever the Catholic Church and the Donatist faction both existed and belonged to different episcopal seats, whenever unity was established there, whether before or after the laws, the church shall belong to the same episcopal seat to which the Catholic church already present there belonged [Col. 0934B].

## CCXLXIX. On how bishops are to divide dioceses among themselves, both Catholic bishops and those converted from the Donatist faction

Council of Carthage, title 85. The arrangement shall be as follows: if a bishop has been converted from the Donatists to Catholic unity, they shall divide equally among themselves those places in which both parties are found; that is, some places shall belong to one and some to the other. The one who has spent the longer time in the episcopate shall make the division, and the younger shall choose.

If there happens to be only one place, it shall belong to the bishop whose seat is found to be nearer. If it is equally near to both episcopal seats, it shall belong to the one whom the people choose. If the ancient Catholics wish to retain it for their bishop and those converted from the Donatist faction wish to retain it for theirs, the will of the greater number shall prevail over the fewer. But if the parties are equal, it shall be assigned to the bishop of longer standing.

If there are so many places in which both parties existed that they cannot be divided equally—for example, if their number is uneven—then, after the places have been distributed in equal numbers, whatever place remains shall be dealt with according to what was stated above concerning a single place.

## CCLXXX. That if a bishop has possessed a diocese for three years after freeing it from heresy, no one may reclaim it

Council of Carthage, title 86. It is likewise agreed that, if anyone has converted a place to Catholic unity after the laws and has retained it for three years without anyone reclaiming it, it may no longer be reclaimed from him. If, during those three years, there was a bishop who could have reclaimed it but remained silent, he shall suffer prejudice. But if there was no such bishop, the mother church shall not be prejudiced; rather, once the place has received a bishop where previously it had none, it may be reclaimed within three years from that very day.

Likewise, if a bishop has been converted from the Donatist faction to the Catholic Church, the prescribed period shall not prejudice him. From the day of his conversion, he shall have three years in which to reclaim the places that belonged to that episcopal seat.

## CCLXXXI. On those who invade communities they believe belong to them without summoning those who hold them

[Col. 0935A]

Council of Carthage, title 87. It was likewise agreed that, if any bishops reclaim communities which they judge to belong to their episcopal seat not by bringing their cases before bishops acting as judges, but by invading them while another person holds them—whether the communities wish it or not—they shall suffer damage to their case.

Those who have already done this, if the dispute among the bishops has not yet been settled but is still being contested, shall withdraw from the place if it is established that they invaded it while bypassing ecclesiastical judgments. No one should flatter himself that he has obtained letters from the primate authorizing him to retain the place. Whether he has such letters or not, he must summon the person who holds it and receive his letters, so that it may be evident that the latter has peacefully held the church belonging to him [Col. 0935B].

If he raises any question, the case shall be settled by episcopal judges—either those whom the primates assign to them or those whom the parties themselves, by agreement, choose from among the neighboring bishops.

## CCLXXXII. On those who neglect communities belonging to them

Council of Carthage, title 88. It was likewise agreed that those who neglect to win for Catholic unity places belonging to their episcopal seat should be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, so that they do not delay carrying out this task. If they have not done so within six months from the day of the summons, the places shall belong to whoever has been able to win them.

The provision shall be this, however: if the person to whom the places seemed to have belonged can prove that the heretics deliberately chose the other person's negligence, so that they might remain there with impunity, and that his own diligence was forestalled in order thereby to avoid his more vigilant care, then, once the episcopal judges have learned this, they shall restore the places to his episcopal seat.

If the bishops among whom the case is being disputed belong to different provinces, the primate of the province in which the disputed place lies shall appoint the judges. If, by common agreement, they choose neighboring judges, either one judge or three may be selected. If three are chosen, they must follow either the judgment of all three or that of two.

## CCLXXXIII. That if a bishop neglects his diocese, he is to be deprived of communion

Council of Carthage, title 90. If a bishop in a mother episcopal seat has been negligent toward the heretics, he shall be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, and his negligence shall be demonstrated to him, so that he cannot excuse himself. If, from the day on which he is summoned, within six months—provided that enforcement lies within his province—he has not taken care to convert them to Catholic unity, communion shall not be extended to him until he fulfills this duty. But if the executor has not come to the places, the matter shall not be charged against the bishop.

## CCLXXXIV. On bishops who falsely claimed that they had brought Donatists into communion

Council of Carthage, title 91. If it is proved that a bishop lied about having brought them into communion, saying that people had entered communion whom he knew had not done so, he shall also lose his episcopate.

## CCLXXXV. On presbyters and clerics, that they may appeal only to African councils

[Col. 0936A]

Council of Carthage, title 92. It was likewise agreed that, in cases involving presbyters, deacons, or other lower clerics, if they complain about the judgments of their own bishops, neighboring bishops should hear them and settle every matter between them, after calling in others with the consent of their own bishops.

If they think that an appeal should also be made from those judges, they may appeal only to African councils or to the primates of their provinces. Anyone who thinks that an appeal should be made overseas is not to be received into communion by anyone within Africa.

## CCLXXXVI. On veiling virgins, including those under age

Council of Carthage, title 93. It was likewise agreed that, when a bishop, because the chastity of a virgin is in danger—for example, when a powerful suitor or some abductor is feared—or when she has been troubled by some perilous fear of death lest she die unveiled, veils a virgin at the insistence of her parents or of those responsible for her care, even if he veils her before she is twenty-five years old, the council’s decree concerning that number of years shall not prejudice him.

## CCLXXXVII. On a bishop who excommunicates someone who he says confessed a crime to him alone

Council of Carthage, title 99. It was likewise agreed that, if a bishop says that someone confessed a particular crime to him alone, and that person denies it, the bishop should not regard it as an insult to himself that he alone is not believed, even if, under the scruple of his own conscience, he says that he is unwilling to communicate with the person who denies it.

### That a bishop should not rashly deprive anyone of communion

Council of Carthage, title 100. As long as a bishop has not communicated with the excommunicated person, the other bishops should not communicate with that bishop, so that the bishop may take greater care not to accuse anyone of what he cannot establish by other evidence.

## CCLXXXVIII. Against those who attack the grace of God and slander Saint Augustine

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 1. To our most beloved brothers Venerius, Marinus, Leontius, Auxonius, Arcadius, Filtanius, and the other bishops of Gaul, Celestine.

The words of the apostolic commandment are that we should give no offence to Jews or Gentiles; every Christian observes this with all the strength of his soul. Since this is so, a person who refuses to show this even to the faithful may not remain without considerable danger before God.

The Lord’s saying in the Gospel shows how these things should distress us—things which, when advanced by Christian authors, strike Christian minds. The Savior himself says that it is better for the one who causes one of the little ones to stumble to be plunged into the depths of the sea. Let us therefore consider what punishment awaits the person for whom we read that such a penalty is preferable.

Our sons Prosper and Hilary, whose concern for our God deserves praise, have reported to us that certain presbyters there are permitted to do—though I scarcely know by whom—so much that they devote themselves to dissensions among the churches. They bring undisciplined questions before the public and, as they say, persistently preach things opposed to the truth. But we more justly attribute the responsibility to your affection, since those men have opportunity to dispute above you.

We read that a disciple is not above his teacher; that is, no one ought to claim a teaching for himself as an affront to his teachers. We know that these very men have been appointed by our God to teach, since, as the Apostle says, the third place within the Church has been assigned to them. What hope is there where, while the teachers remain silent, those speak who, if the matter is as reported, were not their disciples? I fear that this silence is connivance; I fear that those who permit them to speak in this way are themselves speaking more through them.

In such matters silence is not free from suspicion, because truth would come forward if falsehood were displeasing. The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence. Therefore such men must be rebuked; they must not be free to speak as they please. If matters stand as reported, novelty must cease its assault upon antiquity, and unrest must cease disturbing the peace of the churches.

They often try to plunge into shipwreck those whom a secure station keeps safe while they stand within the harbor. For the station of all is secure whose footprints are not moved from their completed steps. The aforementioned men have appealed to the apostolic see, complaining to us of this very disturbance that assails them.

Regard this, most beloved brothers, as undertaken for the peace of the Catholic people. Let them know—if indeed they are counted worthy of the dignity of presbyters—that they are subject to you. Let them know that all who teach wrongly ought to learn more and more rather than teach. For what are you doing in the churches if they hold the chief authority to preach? Unless perhaps this objection is raised: that some recently admitted from the company of the laity into your college, without authority and without even now having established the matter by reason, do not know what they ought to claim for themselves.

Much has already been said about these matters at the time when we sent our written response to our brother Tuens. Now [Note: Col. 0937D, Dionysius Exiguus reads “nevertheless”], repeating our admonition again and again, we urge that such men be avoided—men who labor throughout the lands to sow something other than what that farmer of ours commanded. Nor can we marvel that they now dare to attempt such things against the living, since they also strive to scatter the memory of brothers who have died.

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 2. Augustine, a man of holy memory, was always held by us in our communion on account of his life and merits, and never did even a rumor of sinister suspicion touch him. We remember that he was once a man of such learning that he was counted among the best teachers even by all my predecessors.

All therefore judged well of him in common, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all. Consequently, resistance must be offered to such men, whom we see growing wrongly. It is impious for religious souls to endure these things. Since they are our members, their affliction ought to make us suffer as well, although blessedness remains promised to all who are proved to endure persecution for righteousness.

The following statement declares what the Lord promises them in the future. [Col. 0938A] This is not the concern of those alone who are acting; the universal Church is shaken by every novelty. Let us understand that the very things which displease us displease you also. We shall be able to prove this only if, once the wicked have been silenced, complaints about this matter cease hereafter.

May God preserve you unharmed, most beloved brothers.

## CCLXXXIX. That Adam injured all human beings and that no one can be saved except by the grace of Christ

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 4. All human beings lost natural ability and innocence through Adam’s transgression, and no one can rise from the depth of that ruin by free will unless the grace of the merciful God raises him up. Pope Innocent of blessed memory declared this, saying in his letter to the Council of Carthage:

“For free will, while falling through the transgression in which it used its own goods without due prudence, was plunged into profound ruin and found no way by which it could rise from there. Deceived forever concerning its freedom, it would have remained hidden beneath the oppression of this ruin unless the coming of Christ, in accordance with his grace, had afterward raised it up and, through the cleansing of new regeneration, purged every former fault by the washing of his baptism.”

## CCXC. That no one is good by his own powers except through participation in the One who alone is good

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 5. No one is good by himself unless the One who alone is good grants participation in himself. The judgment of that same pontiff bears witness to this in the same writings, saying [Col. 0938C]:

“After this, shall we consider the minds of those people sound who think that they ought to themselves the fact that they are good, and do not consider the One whose grace they receive daily, while confidently believing that they can attain so much without him?”

## CCXCI. That unless we are continually aided by the grace of God, we cannot overcome the devil’s snares

From the decrees of the aforementioned pope, title 6. No one renewed by the grace of baptism is capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he receives perseverance in a good way of life. The teaching of the same bishop confirms this in the same pages, saying:

“For although he redeemed the human being from former sins, nevertheless, knowing that he could sin again, he preserved many means by which he might restore him to himself and correct him even after those sins. He provides daily remedies; unless we rely upon and trust in them, we shall in no way be able to overcome human errors. For necessarily, by the aid of the one through whom we conquered, if he does not aid us again, we shall be conquered.”

## CCXCII. That through Christ we make good use of free will

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 7. No one makes good use of free will except through Christ. The same teacher proclaims this in a letter sent to the Council of Milevis, saying:

“Consider at last, O perverse doctrine of the most depraved minds, that freedom itself so deceived the first human being that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from this unless the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored to him the state of his former freedom.”

## CCXCIII. That all the merits of the saints are gifts of God

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 8. All the zeal, works, and merits of the saints are to be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him for any reason other than what he himself has granted.

The authoritative teaching of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us toward this judgment. Writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says [Col. 0939B]:

“But we have reported everything, through God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.”

The African bishops revered this statement, shining with the purest light of truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man as follows:

“But what you placed in the letter which you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Nevertheless, through God’s prompting,’ and so forth, we understand as meaning that you cut down, with the sharp sword of truth, as though passing swiftly by, those who exalt the freedom of human will against God’s help. For what did you do so freely as to refer everything to the awareness of our humility? Yet you saw faithfully and wisely, and you said truly and confidently, that this was done through God’s prompting.

“This is so because the will is prepared by the Lord, and, so that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with fatherly inspirations. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God. Thus we do not sense that our will is absent, yet we do not doubt that in each movement of human will toward good his assistance is more powerful.”

## CCXCIV. That every holy thought and movement of the will’s path is from God

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 9. God works in human hearts and in free will itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of good will are from God, because through him we can do something good, and without him we can do nothing [Col. 0939D].

The same teacher instructed us in this confession when, speaking to the bishops of the whole world about the assistance of divine grace, he said:

“What time, then, intervenes in which we do not need his help? In all actions, cases, thoughts, and movements, he must be entreated as helper and protector.”

For human nature is arrogant if it presumes anything for itself, while the Apostle cries out:

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this air, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”

And again, as he himself says:

“Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

And again:

“By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been empty; rather, I labored more than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me.”

## CCXCV. That the grace of God not only forgives sins but also helps us not to commit them and to fulfill the law—not as Pelagius says, easily, as though without God’s grace it could be fulfilled only with greater difficulty

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 10. We also embrace as belonging properly to the apostolic see what was established among the decrees of the Council of Carthage, namely, what was defined in its third chapter:

“If anyone says that the grace of God by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also for assistance so that they are not committed, let him be anathema” [Col. 0940B].

And again, in the fourth chapter:

“If anyone says that the grace of God through Jesus Christ helps us not to sin only because through it the understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to desire and what we ought to avoid, but does not grant that we may also love and be able to do what we have recognized must be done, let him be anathema.”

For since the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up,” it is exceedingly impious to believe that we have the grace of Christ for that knowledge which puffs up but not for that love which builds up, since both are gifts of God: both knowing what we ought to do and loving so that we may do it, so that, when love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up.

Just as it is written of God, “He who teaches human beings knowledge,” so it is also written, “Love is from God.”

Likewise, in the fifth chapter:

“If anyone says that the grace of justification is given to us for this reason only: so that we may more easily fulfill by grace what we are commanded to do by free will—as though, even if grace were not given, we could indeed fulfill the divine commandments without it, though not easily—let him be anathema.”

For the Lord was speaking of the fruits of the commandments when he did not say, “Without me you can do them with greater difficulty,” but said, “Without me you can do nothing.”

## CCXCVI. That all the prayers of the apostolic see resound with the grace of Christ, by which the human race is restored from eternal condemnation

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 11. Moreover, let us consider the inviolable decrees of the most blessed apostolic see. By them, after casting down the arrogance of a destructive novelty, our most devout fathers taught us to refer to the grace of Christ both the beginnings of good will, the growth of worthy endeavors, and perseverance in them to the end [Col. 0940D].

Let us also consider the sacramental prayers of the priests which, handed down by the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in the entire Catholic Church, so that the rule of prayer establishes the rule of belief.

When the leaders of the holy communities carry out an embassy entrusted to them, they plead the case of the human race before the divine mercy. Together with the whole Church groaning with them, they ask and pray that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, once the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may come to their senses through acceptance of the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be bestowed upon the fallen; and finally that, when catechumens have been brought to the sacraments of regeneration, the court of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.

The effect of these very things shows that they are not requested from the Lord superficially or vainly. For God deigns to draw many from every kind of error, transferring them, rescued from the power of darkness, into the kingdom of the Son of his love, and making vessels of mercy out of vessels of wrath.

The whole of this is so clearly understood to be the work of God that, for the illumination or correction of such people, thanksgiving and confession of praise are always offered to God who brings it about.

## CCXCVII. That the prescribed purification of those to be baptized also bears witness to the grace of God, since unclean spirits are driven from them through exorcisms and supplications

[Col. 0941B]

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 12. We do not contemplate casually what the holy Church uniformly does throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized.

Whether children or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not approach the font of life before the unclean spirit has been driven from them through the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy. Thus it may truly become evident how the ruler of this world is cast out, how the strong man is first bound, and how afterward his vessels are plundered and transferred into the possession of the victor, who leads captivity captive and gives gifts to human beings [Col. 0941C].

Accordingly, by these ecclesiastical rules and by the authoritative proofs drawn from divine sources, we have been conformed, with the Lord’s help, in such a way that we confess God to be the author of all good affections and works, of all endeavors and virtues by which one turns toward God from the beginning of faith.
