We do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

By this help and gift of God free will is not taken away; rather, it is liberated, so that what was dark may become bright, what was crooked straight, what was weak sound, and what was improvident may become provident [Note: [Col. 0941D] Dionysius Exiguus reads “from the imprudent”].

For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wills the merits which are his gifts to be ours, and, for what he has bestowed, he will grant eternal rewards. Indeed, he works in us so that we may both will and do what he wills. He does not permit the gifts he has granted for exercise—not neglect—to be idle in us, so that we may also be fellow workers with God’s grace.

If we see anything in ourselves growing weak through our own negligence, let us hasten anxiously back to him who heals all our weaknesses, redeems our life from destruction, and to whom we say daily:

“Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

## CCXCVIII. That deeper questions should neither be despised nor asserted absolutely

From the decrees of Pope Celestine, title 13. As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise, which those who resisted the heretics have treated at greater length, we do not dare to despise them, but neither do we consider it necessary to assert them absolutely.

For, in confessing the grace of God, from whose work and gracious favor nothing at all must be withdrawn, we believe that whatever the writings of the Apostolic See have taught us according to the rules mentioned above is sufficient [Col. 0942B]. We should in no way regard as Catholic anything that appears contrary to the judgments already established [Note: [Col. 0942D] Dionysius Exiguus: “we should not suppose”].

## CCXCIX. That nothing except the canonical Scriptures should be read in the Church

Council of Carthage, title 24. It was likewise agreed that, under the name of divine Scriptures, nothing should be read in the Church except the canonical Scriptures. The canonical Scriptures are these:

Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, the four books of Kings, the two books of Chronicles, Job, the Psalter, the five books of Solomon, the book of the Twelve Prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Tobit, Judith, Esther, and the two books of Ezra; of the New Testament, the four books of the Gospels, one book of the Acts of the Apostles, fourteen Epistles of Paul, two Epistles of the apostle Peter, three of the apostle John, one of the apostle James, one of the apostle Jude, and one book of the Apocalypse of John.

## CCC. That bishops and clerics should not be ordained unless they have made all their household Christian

Council of Carthage, title 3. Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are not to be ordained before they have made all those who are in their household Catholic Christians [Col. 0942D].

[Note: [Col. 0941] See, at the end of the volume, the two indexes: one to Ferrandus’s Abridgment of the Canons and one to Cresconius’s Abridgment of Canon Law.]

## In the uncertain seventh century. An uncertain author surnamed “Master”

[Col. 0943]

## Testimonies of the ancients concerning the Rule of the Master
[Col. 0943A] Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, transcribed the greater part of the *Rule of the Master* into his concordance of rules, and frequently reproduces entire chapters from it; he cites it more than sixty times.

[Col. 0944A] Smaragdus the monk also very often praises in his commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict a certain “Master of the Monks” as the author of this rule.

[Col. 0943]

## Critical Observation on the Following Rule

Among the other monastic rules, the present one is the most extensive, containing ninety-five chapters, besides the Prologue and a spiritual explanation of the Lord’s Prayer adapted for monks. Its author, however, is uncertain, and he obtained the title “Master” from no other source than the fact that at the beginning of each chapter the Disciple proposes a question, to which the Master immediately replies with the answer and supplies a teaching appropriate to the question.

Among more recent writers, Trithemius believed that the author of this rule was the deacon Vigilantius; but the often-mentioned Calmet rejects this opinion as supported by no authority. Whoever its author may have been, it is a plausible conjecture that he wrote it in Gaul, since he frequently uses expressions proper to that nation, such as “Major of the Household,” and so forth. Moreover, when speaking of the Gyrovagues, he derives them from neighboring Italy; this may in some measure indicate that he was a Gaul, and perhaps he lived in the seventh century, when the office of Major of the Household flourished especially among the Gauls.

For the rest, the author of this rule drew much from the Rule of Saint Benedict, which is why those who wrote commentaries on this rule cite it so frequently, even though he used a crude and barbarous style. Nor are those lacking who reproach this author with childishness: in chapters 23 and 25 he commands that after the meal crumbs be carefully gathered each day and cooked at the end of the week, so that all the monks present may eat from them; and he also orders that bread fall from above through a pulley into a basket, as though it had been sent down from heaven.

[Col. 0943]

# The Rule of the Master for Monks (C, S)

## The Prologue of the Rule Begins

[Col. 0943B] O man—first, you who are reading, and then you who are listening to me speak—set aside for now the other things you are thinking about; and recognize me speaking to you, and through my mouth God addressing you. We must go to this Lord according to our will, through good deeds and actions pleasing to justice, lest through negligence in sins we unwillingly be carried away when summoned by death.

Therefore, hearer, you who hear me speaking, receive what God—not my mouth—speaks to you through this writing: while you are still alive, he calls you to account for what you will have to render to him after death. For as long as we still live, we live on a reprieve, while God’s mercy waits for us each day, wishing us to be corrected and to be better today [Col. 0944B] than we were yesterday.

Therefore you who listen to me, pay attention in such a way that my words and your hearing, traveling through the consideration of the mind, may reach the crossroads of your heart. At that crossroads, leave behind you, after my words, the single road of ignorance of sins; and enter now before you the two roads of observance of the commandments.

As we seek to go to God, we stand in Christ at the crossroads of our heart, and let us consider these two roads of knowledge that we see before us. Let us consider by which of the two roads we can reach God. If we keep to the left, we fear it, because it is broad, lest it be the road that leads more surely to destruction. If we take the right, we go well, because it is narrow: [Col. 0945A] and it is the road that leads servants who love him to their own Lord.

Therefore let your unoccupied hearing follow my speech. Understand, you man whose attention we are urging, that through this writing God is urging you: while you are still alive and have time to correct yourself, run as far as you can! Otherwise, when you have been summoned by death, you will bring God no excuse on the day of judgment or in eternal punishment—that no one called you to correction while you lived—and when you can no longer help yourself, you will begin to repent eternally, without remedy.

Therefore observe now what you hear, before you depart from the light of this world; for if you leave here, you will not return here except in the resurrection. At the resurrection, if you have acted well here, you will be assigned to eternal glory with the saints. [Col. 0945B] But if you do not fulfill this writing that I am about to read to you, you will be assigned to the eternal fire of Gehenna [Col. 0946A] with the devil, whose will you followed more readily.

Therefore hear and do what is good and just, through which God is found to be merciful. Fulfill in deeds this rule that shows you the way. This rule received the name “rule” for bringing the right way to completion, as the Apostle says in his Letter: “According to the measure of the rule which the Lord has measured out for us, reaching even to you” (II Cor. X).

For the rule of truth has a beginning and justice as its end. As the Prophet says: “You shall rule them with a rod” (Psalm II)—that is, with the force of fear. As the Apostle likewise says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity?” (I Cor. IV.) The Prophet also says: “The rod of your kingdom is a rod of uprightness, with which you loved justice and hated iniquity” (Psalm XLIV). And again the Lord says: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Psalm LXXXVIII).

## The Theme Begins

[Col. 0945]

[Col. 0945B] The Prophet says: “I will open my mouth in parables” (Psalm LXXVII). And again he says: “I became a parable to them” (ibid., LXVIII).

Born from the earthen womb of our mother Eve, and begotten from our father Adam in the excesses of desire, we descended into the road of this world. Taking upon ourselves the temporary yoke of a life in exile, we traveled along the path of this road through ignorance of good deeds and the uncertain experience of death.

[Col. 0945C] For the pilgrimage of this world had loaded us heavily with the provisions of negligence and sins; and when our shoulders had been wearied by burdensome loads, the sweat of labor, having already fallen, had found death close at hand; and burning thirst panted toward destruction.

Suddenly, on the right, toward the rising sun, we saw an unexpected spring of living water. As we hurried toward it, a divine voice then came to meet us, crying out to us and saying: “You who thirst, come to the water” (Isaiah LV). And when it saw us coming burdened with heavy loads, it repeated: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI).

We, hearing this gracious voice, threw our burdens onto the ground and, driven eagerly by thirst, prostrated ourselves at the spring; and after drinking for a long time, we rose renewed.

[Col. 0945D] After our rising, we stood bewildered with overwhelming joy, looking in astonishment at the yoke of the road of such holy labor, and at our burdens, which through ignorance had wearied us with their weight all the way to death.

As we gazed at these things and considered them for a long time, we again heard a voice from the spring that had refreshed us, saying: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew XI).

Hearing these things, let us now say to one another: After being refreshed by so great a spring and by the voice of the Lord inviting us, let us not return to the burdens of sins that we threw down—that is, the burdens we renounced when we went to the fountain of baptism. These burdens of sins had earlier wearied us to death and, through ignorance of the sacred law or through a baptism not understood, had driven us to despair under their weight.

[Col. 0946B] But now, receiving the wisdom of God, we who had been weighed down by burdens of sins have been invited by the Lord’s voice to rest. Let us therefore renounce our former burdens of sins. Let the ways of the world belong to those negligent under the weight of their offenses.

We now recognize as our mother not Eve, formed for us from the clay of the earth, but the divine Christian law calling us to rest. Likewise, we no longer seek our father in Adam, in the power of sins, but in the voice of the Lord who invites us; and, though we do not dare by the merits of our desires, in our rebirth at your sacred font, where you are, we now find you.

### Our Father, who art in heaven

Behold, brothers, whether we have now found the Church as our mother and dared to call the Lord our Father from heaven. Therefore the earthly father and the carnal mother must now rightly be left behind by us, lest, obeying two sets of parents, we offend not only one at a time, but be judged adulterous, as though born from two parents, if we do not abandon our carnal parents.

Through the wood of offense our race had descended from paradise into the womb, from the womb into the world, and from [Col. 0946D] the world all the way into hell—unless, born again through baptism and restored again through the wood of the cross, the Lord’s Passion should cause it to rise, and that generation should return by grace to paradise, from which it had fallen through offense by free choice.

For the Lord crushed in us the sting of death that had reigned when Christ gave us the refuge of his cross. And after restoring us to the grace of his adoption, he does not cease to invite us also to the kingdoms of heaven. Hence the Lord’s voice says: “If you observe my commandments, I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons to me.”

Thus, although unworthy, because of our recognition of his baptism we dare to call him Father in prayer; and therefore we ought to share in his Passion, so that we may deserve to become fellow heirs of his glory.

Therefore, saying “Our Father, who art in heaven,” let us now show ourselves to be such brothers as God wishes to have as sons; and divinity will rightly implant in us the name of sons, though our will differs from his. For he is truly a son who not only wills what his father wills, but is also like his father in conduct.

When, therefore, we have deserved to say “Our Father, who art in heaven,” we continue in prayer, saying:

### Hallowed be thy name

Not that we now wish his name, which is most holy from eternity and unto eternity, to be made holy anew; rather, may he himself be hallowed more fully in the good deeds of his sons, so that as Father and Lord he may make his dwelling and the Holy Spirit an inhabitant in our minds; and so that God may help these hearts, that you may always guard them through his grace.

Then it is said:

### Thy kingdom come

See, brothers: behold, we desire the Lord’s kingdom to come, and we freely ask that his judgment be hastened, while we still have not prepared our accounts. Therefore we must act every hour in such a way that the Lord and Father may afterward receive us in this manner: daily pleasing him before him through good deeds, separating us from the goats, and bringing us from his right hand into the eternal kingdoms.

Let us recognize as a merciful judge in the future judgment the one whom in the present world we have dared to call Father.

Then we say:

### Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth

In this word, brothers, our state of free choice is involved; and whatever the ancient serpent’s harmful persuasion injects into us is cut off, if we wish it, when the Lord’s will is restored and accomplished in us, as the Apostle said: “so that you may not do whatever you wish” (Galatians V).

For the Spirit requires that the Lord’s will be done in us, so that the soul may no longer accomplish whatever it had desired for itself in lust along with rebellious flesh. We therefore pray that the Lord’s will may be done in us.

If his will is always accomplished by us, then it will not be our own will—the will which, examined at the judgment for its evils, will be condemned. For the Lord’s will is holy; it knows how to give, not to fear, judgment. Those in whom his will has been fulfilled are even promised that they will judge angels.

Our Savior also demonstrates this holy will in himself, by the pattern of doing it freely, so that he might cut off in us the choice of the flesh, saying: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI).

And again, in his holy Passion, he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew XXVI). This voice in the Lord was the voice of fear belonging to clothed flesh, showing us that the actions of life must always be carefully considered if the coming of death is to be feared.

And again, it was the Lord’s question to the Father whether what we wish in ourselves can be fulfilled by us, or whether what we do not wish can justly be imposed upon us against our desire. Hence there follows the pattern of faith by which the Lord entrusts himself to the Father’s will, saying: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.).

And again it follows: “If this cup cannot be taken from me unless I drink it, nevertheless let your will be done” (ibid.).

[Col. 0948A] See, therefore, that whatever we choose from our own will is recognized as unjust; and whatever is imposed upon us against our will from our youth contributes justly to our account. For just as a man cannot see his own face when his eyes are turned toward himself, so he cannot be his own judge, unless what is seen is justly judged by another.

If no one can see his own face, how can he prove his own will to be just, unless in all things what is seen is judged by another?

And behold, brothers, how great a mercy the Lord has brought to our restoration, and what a way of salvation he has shown to our error: he demonstrated in his only-begotten Son what he sought to accomplish in his servants.

“Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” What he said about heaven, brothers, we can understand well: just as it is accomplished in holiness by the angels in heaven, so on earth it is desired that the commandments of God be fulfilled through the prophets and apostles and among carnal human beings; so that, according to the holy Scripture, saying this of both elements—that is, heaven and earth—the Lord may reign in his good pleasure in both, and in us; and there may be one Shepherd and one flock.

Likewise, we can understand spiritually what he said: “Thy will be done, as in heaven”—that is, in the Lord, as in his Son. For when the heavenly will descended, the Father’s will was fulfilled, as the Lord himself said: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI).

You see, then, that the Lord and Savior himself showed that he came for this reason: not to do his own will, but to fulfill the Father’s commands. How then can the wicked servant neglect my commands and do his own will?

[Col. 0948C] Of him the Apostle also says: “Who is the one who ascended, except the one who also descended into the lower parts of the earth?” (Ephesians IV.)

Thus he also said “on earth,” that is, the structure of our body formed from the clay of the earth, to which God’s sentence was spoken: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Genesis III).

Likewise, the Lord’s will is demanded so that justice may be brought about in us. When the Lord’s will has been worked in us daily, our own will will not be found—the will that in the future judgment would be condemned to punishment—but the Lord’s will will be in us, crowned with glory.

Then we continue in prayer, saying:

### Give us this day our daily bread

Therefore, brothers, when the Lord’s will mentioned above has been fulfilled by us daily without blame, and all the commandments have been carried out in the fear of the Lord, the workers rightly ask him for their ration, since he does not deny a wage to a worthy laborer.

Then we say:

### And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors

Brothers, in praying this let us fear all the more lest the Lord answer these words of our prayers by saying to us: “By the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew VII).

And see, you who ask this, whether you have not done to another what you did not wish done to you. Therefore, before we hear these words of the Lord, brothers, let us first examine our hearts: whether we too justly ask from the Lord what has not been denied by us to those who ask us.

We ask: “Forgive us our debts.” God hears and desires to forgive, but only if we first release those who ask us. Or do I, wretched man, doubt that God will repay my good deeds? Look, recognize, and consider, O wretched man: are you perhaps more merciful than God? When, in order to instill some act of justice or mercy in you, he gives you his reward or gifts, what he himself does benefits you.

For the Lord lacks nothing in his power, nor does he need anything of yours in strength, nor is anything lacking in his glory. He needs only our salvation, which his grace provides for us—and through our negligence he possesses less of it from us.

Then we say:

### And lead us not into temptation

These words sufficiently warn us, brothers, to be vigilant. Therefore the Lord must be entreated, and our hearts and breasts must be struck with frequent groans, lest the Lord allow his servants to stand at any hour without his help; lest our adversary, the devil, who circles us daily like a lion, seeking someone to devour, have power or access by which to do so; for by his wicked persuasions he seeks to infect our hearts (I Peter V).

Therefore we must pray to the Lord without ceasing, that he may deign to surround us with the wall of his grace as a guard of his help, and close the entrances of temptations in us with his fortification; that he may not permit the work of his hands, his creature, to be taken captive and yield to the enemy’s servitudes.

This is so, provided that we do not voluntarily give our consent to the temptations of the enemy mentioned above, and, as though taking ourselves captive for him, begin to desire our enemy more than to flee from him.

[Col. 0949C] We continue and complete the prayer, saying:

### But deliver us from evil. Amen.

Most holy brothers, before he is asked, God desires to accomplish this in us, because he is powerful and nothing is difficult for him—but only if we deserve it. For he does not wish our structure, which he himself built with his hands, to fall.

He hastens to rescue us from the snare, provided that we do not voluntarily surrender our understanding to the enemy’s persuasions, but pray to the Lord without ceasing, so that, having been granted the help of his grace, we may rightly say: “Because the Lord is at our right hand, we shall not be moved” (Psalm XV); and, secure in the Lord, repeat again: “I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Psalm XXII).

May he who at the beginning of this prayer showed us through grace that we might dare to call the Lord “Father” also deign at the end of the prayer to deliver us from evil. Amen.

Therefore, brothers, when the prayer to the Lord has ended, with his help let us now proceed to the work of our service, so that he who has deigned to count us already among the number of sons may never have cause to grieve over our evil deeds.

At every hour we must obey him with the good things he has wrought in us, so that the Father, angered, may not at some time disinherit us as sons, and that the Lord, provoked by our evils, may not—he who is to be feared—hand us over as utterly wicked servants to eternal punishment, because we were unwilling to follow him to glory.

Let us finally rise, as sluggish people, with Scripture rousing us and saying: “For now it is the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans XIII). With our eyes opened to the divine light, and our ears astonished, let us hear what the divine voice cries out daily to admonish us, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation II).

It says: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm XXXIII). Run while you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you.

And when the Lord seeks among the multitude of the people the hearer who will be his worker, to whom he cries these things, he cries out again, saying: “Who is the man who desires life and wishes to see good days?” (ibid.)

You who hear, answer: “I.”

And the Lord says to you: “If you wish to have true and perpetual life, restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit; turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (ibid.).

“And when you have done these things, my eyes are upon you, the righteous, and my ears upon your prayers. And before you call upon me, I shall say to you: ‘Behold, here I am.’”

What is sweeter to us than this voice of the Lord inviting us, brothers? Behold, in his mercy the Lord shows us the way of life.

Therefore, with the loins of our faith and observance of good deeds girded, let us travel his roads under the guidance of the Gospel, so that we may deserve to see him who called us into his kingdom. If we wish to dwell in the tabernacle of that kingdom, we can by no means reach it unless we run there by good deeds.

But let us ask the Lord with the Prophet, saying to him: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm CXIV.)

After this question, brothers, let us hear the Lord answering us again and showing us the way to his tabernacle, saying: “He who enters without blemish, who speaks truth in his heart; who has not dealt deceitfully with his tongue; who has not done evil to his neighbor; who has not accepted reproach against his neighbor” (ibid.).

He is the one who, rejecting the wicked devil when he suggests something to him, together with the suggestion itself, from the sight of his heart, has reduced it to nothing; who has seized his nascent thoughts and dashed them against Christ, the rock.

Those who fear the Lord do not become proud of their good observance. Rather, recognizing that the good things within them cannot come from themselves but are brought about by the Lord, they magnify the Lord who works in them, saying with the Prophet: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm CXIII).

Nor did the Apostle Paul attribute anything to himself from his preaching, saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Corinthians XV). And again he says: “If I must boast, it is not expedient for me” (II Corinthians XII).

Therefore the Lord continues the way of blessed life through his admonitions, saying: “He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him; who has not lent his money at interest; who has not accepted gifts against the innocent” (Psalm XIV).

And the Lord continues in the Gospel, saying to us: “He who hears these words of mine and does them shall not be moved forever” (Matthew VII).

And we ask him, saying: “How, Lord, shall he not be moved forever?”

The Lord answers us again: “How? Because I shall compare him to a wise man who built his house upon a rock. The rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house; and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon a rock” (ibid.).

[Col. 0951A] Having completed these things, the Lord is silent, watching us and expecting us to answer his daily holy admonitions by our deeds. For this reason, for our correction, the days of this life are daily prolonged for us as a reprieve, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans II.)

For the merciful Lord says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel XXXIII).

When, therefore, brothers, we had asked the Lord about the inhabitant of his tabernacle, we heard the commandment concerning dwelling there—but only if we fulfill the duty of an inhabitant.

Therefore our hearts must be prepared, and our bodies enlisted in the holy obedience of the commandments. Whatever nature has made less possible in us, let us ask the Lord to command the help of his grace to be supplied to us.

And if, fleeing the punishment of Gehenna, we wish to reach perpetual life, while there is still time, while we are still in the body, and while there is time in this life of light to fulfill all these things, we must run and act now in the way that will benefit us forever.

Therefore we must establish the Lord’s school of service, so that, never departing from his instruction and persevering in the monastery in this teaching until death, we may deserve through patience to share in Christ’s sufferings, so that the Lord may make us fellow heirs of his kingdom.

# The Kinds—or Rather the Conduct and Life—of Monks in Cenobies Begin

[Col. 0951]

## Chapter One: On the Four Kinds of Monks

[Col. 0951B]

It is evident that there are four kinds of monks.

The first is that of the cenobites, that is, the monastic kind, serving under a rule or an abbot.

The second kind is that of the anchorites, that is, hermits. These are men who have learned, not through the novice’s fervor of conversion, but through long testing in the monastery, to fight against the devil, already trained with the support of many; and, well instructed, they are able to proceed from the brotherly ranks to the solitary combat of the desert, and there, without the consolation of another, to struggle with God and the spirit by their own hand or strength against the vices of the flesh and of thoughts.

The third and worst kind of monks is that of the Sarabaites. I would have called them more properly laymen, if the tonsure of the holy profession did not prevent me. Approved by no rule and tested by no experience, like gold in a furnace, but softened according to the nature of lead, they are known to continue in their deeds to serve the world while deceiving God through their tonsure.

They live in pairs, in threes, or certainly singly, without a shepherd, shut up not in the Lord’s sheepfolds but in their own. The pleasure of their desires is their law: whatever they think or choose, they call holy; and whatever they do not wish, they consider forbidden.

While they seek, according to their own judgment, to have cells, little cells, and retreat-cells, they do not know that they are losing their little souls.

The same applies to those who have recently converted and, in immoderate fervor, think that the desert is a place of rest. Not realizing that the devil lies in wait and does harm, they rashly and confidently undertake solitary combat with him, though untrained—without doubt advancing into the jaws of the wolf.

The fourth kind of monks is one that should not even be named; it is better to remain silent than to say anything about such people. This kind is called Gyrovagues.

They spend their entire lives traveling through different provinces, staying for three or four days in the cells and monasteries of different people. Because various hosts wish to receive them anew each day for the sake of their arrival, they arrange for choice dishes to be prepared for themselves as a joy to the newcomers, and they take care that living creatures—chickens—be killed daily with a knife by different hosts for their arrival.

They do not believe that they burden the various hosts in this way by changing hosts every day; for the sake of novelty, under the pretext of an unwelcome charity, they compel different people to prepare different things for them. And, as though demanding from unwilling hosts the Apostle’s command, in which he says, “Pursuing hospitality” (Romans XII), they use the pretext of the command to ask that their restless feet be refreshed after the road.

Under the pretext of the journey, they prefer their bowels, polluted by a more lavish dinner or meal, to be refreshed with countless cups rather than their feet.

After the table has been emptied by the hungry guest and even the crumbs of bread have been wiped away for the journey, they shamelessly impose their thirst upon the host; and if by chance a cup is lacking, the host is asked to mix the drink in the very dish.

[Col. 0952C] After they have stuffed themselves on both sides with an excess of food and drink, even to vomiting, they attribute everything to the hardships of life, though it was gluttony that profited.

Before a new bed receives the guest, wearied more by drinking or eating than by the road, they recount to their hosts the labors of their life as though they were of great importance, compelling the host to lavish upon them richer dishes and countless cups as the price of their rest. Concealing the account of their error through their wandering and captivity, they excuse themselves; and immediately they ask about the neighboring monks or the location of the monastery, so that, when they have left that place, they may settle or attach themselves there as though weary.

It is as though the whole world were closed to them, as though neither places nor forests nor even the breadth of the Egyptian desert could contain them, and as though all the monasteries could not receive them for the service of God. Since, as we have said, the whole world cannot contain them, they claim that they are rightly wandering and that nowhere can they find a place of rest, refreshment for the soul, or complete observance of discipline.

It is as though they were saying that they are so very wise that everything pleasing to God and to human beings displeases them alone.

Therefore they prefer to walk about, changing daily to different hosts and seeking new and varied meals; and, under the pretext of thirst, they drink cups offered again along the road. They do this so that each day their gluttony, rather than their soul, may appear to be traveling abroad.

When, after two days with one host, the provisions prepared for them have already been reduced in quantity, and on the following day, when they see that the host is occupied not with cooking a meal but with the work of his cell, they immediately decide to seek another host.

He has not yet arrived, and already they are leaving.

Then they hasten to say farewell to the now-grudging host; and when they are eager to leave such hospitality, they ask the host to pray for them after their departure. They hurry as though someone were driving them, as though the lunches of other hosts were already awaiting them.

Not far from that monastery, if they find a monk’s cell, while resting they say that they have come from far away, from the borders of Italy. Again, with bowed and seemingly humble head, they lie to that host, inventing something about their journey or captivity; and, under the pretext of compassion for the long journey, they compel the pious host to empty all his poverty into pots and onto the table.

Without doubt that host, stripped and emptied by the gluttons, will himself be abandoned after two days.

When, after three days, the host, his cell, his ways, and his discipline have also displeased them, and when after two days he has provided them with less food, they are immediately compelled to repack their double bags, which the toasted loaves of various hosts have already filled. At the hospices of different people, they take fresh loaves from the tables and, through their greed, compel those kept in reserve to become moldy.

Therefore, after their bags have been repacked, the poor donkey is immediately recalled from pasture. After the poor animal’s recent labors on the road, it had enjoyed the pasture, if only its master’s hospitality had not displeased them within two days.

The donkey is newly saddled and patched with various tunics and hoods—garments that either their importunity had demanded from different people or that an opportunity for fraud had stripped from various hosts. They pretend to clothe themselves in rags so that they may ask others for more.

And saying farewell to that host as well, they say that the others have not yet come, while they are already leaving, being invited in their minds to other hospices.

The poor little donkey is beaten, prodded, burned, and lashed with straps, but it does not go. Its ears are thrashed after its haunches have failed. Therefore the poor creature is beaten almost to death and, exhausted, is struck by their hands, because they hurry and strive to arrive at the lunch of another monastery.

When they reach the gates of another monastery or monk, they cry from outside in a cheerful and loud voice: “Bless!”—as though they had already taken in hand the cup that, once they entered the monastery, they would immediately request because of their thirst.

Entering the gates, before they have been announced and received, they unload their baggage. As though they had come there because of some debt or on someone’s assignment, their bags are handed inside before the host himself is received.

They do not hurry to the oratory until, under the pretext of a traveller's thirst, they seek wine from desire for it—so that you, out of charity, may offer wine to the guest, while in the morning he asks you for water.

Such men, who themselves know nothing of fasting as they travel, either compel those whom they visit, if they are fasting, to break their fast for the sake of the guest’s arrival, or are not ashamed to say to them openly that they are fasting more out of greed, as though they did not wish to refresh the guest after his journey.

Through the wandering gluttony of their custom, they compel the fasts of those who persevere to be violated, while they attribute whatever they presume to the hardship of the journey. They do not know that the reason they cannot fast, abstain, or remain anywhere for any length of time is not some necessity that compels them to travel, but the will of their gluttony.

Secure and arriving upon the labor of others, they seek to eat others’ bread and love to wipe away their sweat on the bedding and straw of different people.

When they lie on this straw, desiring sleep to compensate for food and drink undigested because of their excess, or when some of them, occupied with gluttonous wandering, have sometimes neglected to meditate on the Psalms, they answer with their own mouths that, exhausted after the road, their bones cannot rise from the bed, even though they were seen eating healthy food at the evening meal.

Soon, when the work of God at the morning office has been completed, they rise as though groaning and exhausted.

Thus, early in the morning, warmed by unmixed wine and asking for a piece of bread, they pretend to be sick and leave the monasteries or cells falsely, feigning illness and secretly confident that they are restoring their healthy steps from the very threshold.

For they do not wish an abbot, under the authority of the monastery, to think about all their necessities; nor do they wish, living anywhere according to their own judgment, to make a cell and remain there, where they themselves would have to think about the necessities of life.

And if our way of life displeases them, let them show us their own way. Thus, never remaining anywhere, they are driven each day to wander about, beg, sweat, and groan, rather than work and live by staying in one place.

Every day they enter the cells of different people as humble guests, bowing only their heads; then, proud and seemingly ungrateful, they depart after two days, as though the life and conduct of different people and the discipline of all monasteries displeased them. They prefer to walk about rather than remain.

Always wandering through different places, they do not know who will put up with their tedium; and, last of all, they do not know where to establish their burial.

Therefore, since we consider the first kind—the cenobites, whose service or probation is the will of God—to be great, let us return to their rule.

Fratres, clamat nobis quotidie Dominus dicens: “Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you” (Zech. I). Our turning back to God, therefore, brothers, is nothing other than turning away from evils, as Scripture says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXX). When we turn away from these evils, we look upon the Lord; [Col. 0954D] and he immediately enlightens us with his countenance, granting us his assistance. He soon gives his grace to those who ask, shows it to those who seek, and opens it to those who knock.

These three gifts of the Lord are granted to those who choose to do God’s will, not their own. For the Lord commands one thing in the spirit, while the flesh compels another in the soul; and whoever is overcome by the other is that one’s servant. For the Lord established three ranks of teaching for his Church according to the name of the Trinity: the first of the prophets, the second of the apostles, and the third of teachers. Under their authority and teaching, the Churches and schools of Christ are to be governed, so that, in the place of shepherds, they may both enclose and teach the divine sheep in the holy sheepfolds, as the Lord says through [Col. 0955A] the prophet Isaiah: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you, feeding you with discipline” (John XV); and the Lord himself says: “Simon, son of John, feed my sheep, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

Therefore, it is expedient that all who still have ignorance as their mother should be under the authority of one superior, so that, walking according to the teacher’s judgment, they may learn not to follow their own will. For through the teacher the Lord commands us; because, as he said above, he is always with those teachers themselves, with all of them, until the consummation of the age. Without doubt, this means nothing other than that he is building us up through them, as the Lord himself said to his disciples, our teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you [Col. 0955B] despises me” (Matt. X).

Therefore, if we do and put into practice what we have heard from the teachers, we no longer practice what we ourselves wish, so that on the day of judgment the devil may find nothing in us which he can claim for himself in hell; for the Lord has always brought about in us what he would judge worthy of glory.

## CHAPTER II

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

What ought the abbot to be like?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

The abbot who is worthy to preside over a monastery must always remember what is said, and must fulfill the name of “superior” by his deeds. He is believed to act in Christ’s place in the monastery when he is called by Christ’s name, as the Apostle says: “You have received the spirit of the adoption of sons, in which we cry out, ‘Abba, Father’” [Col. 0955C] (Rom. VIII).

Therefore this abbot must not, God forbid, teach, establish, or command anything outside the Lord’s precept, so that his command, admonition, or teaching may sprinkle the leaven of divine justice into the minds of the disciples. The abbot must always remember that, at the Lord’s fearful judgment, an examination will be made both of his teaching and of the disciples’ obedience. And let the abbot know that the shepherd is burdened with the guilt of whatever useful quality the master of the household is unable to find in the sheep.

At last he will again be acquitted if all diligence has been devoted to a restless or disobedient flock, and every care has been shown toward their diseased conduct. Then, at the Lord’s judgment, their shepherd may say with the Prophet to the Lord: “I have not hidden your truth in my heart; I have declared your salvation” [Col. 0955D] “but they, in their contempt, have rejected me” (Ps. XXXIX; Isa. I). And then, at last, let the punishment of disobedient sheep entrusted to his care be death itself, which prevails over them.

Therefore, when someone accepts the name of abbot, he must preside over his disciples with a twofold teaching: that is, he must show all good and holy things more by deeds than by words; and he must set forth the Lord’s commands to intelligent disciples, while showing the divine precepts by his own deeds to those who are hard-hearted and simple. Whatever he teaches the disciples to be contrary, he must indicate by his own deeds that it is not to be done: “Lest, after preaching to others, he himself should be found reprobate” (1 Cor. IX); and lest God should one day say to him in his sin: “Why do you recite my just deeds, and take my covenant upon your lips [Col. 0956A] while you hate discipline?” (Ps. XLIX; Matt. VII). And: “You saw the splinter in your brother’s eye, but did not see the beam in your own.”

No distinction of persons is to be made by him in the monastery; no one is to be loved more than another, except one whom he finds better in good works. A freeborn man is not to be preferred to a converted servant on account of his status. Why? Because whether servant or free, we are all one in Christ, and under one Lord we carry the equal service of military duty. For “with God there is no partiality” (1 Cor. XVII; Rom. II). We are distinguished before God only in this respect: if we are found better than others in our deeds.

Yet, to show that God extends the clemency of his mercy equally toward all, he commands the elements, or the earth, to serve the just and sinners alike. Therefore his love should be equal toward everyone [Col. 0956B], and one discipline should be provided for all.

In his teaching, the abbot must always preserve that apostolic form in which it says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” (1 Tim. IV). That is, blending seasons with seasons and gentleness with terrors, he should show both the sternness of a teacher and the affection of a devoted father. He should reprove the undisciplined and restless; entreat the obedient, the mild, and the most patient, so that they may progress toward what is better; and rebuke the negligent and contemptuous.

In himself, he must show them such a model of humility as the Lord demonstrated to the apostles who were disputing about rank: that is, when he had taken a child by the hand and brought him into their midst, he said: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be such a one” (Matt. XVIII).

Therefore, whatever the abbot enjoins the disciples to do for God, he must fulfill by his own deeds; and, when he has handed down all the arrangements of his rule, the members must follow wherever the head has led. He must have such love and favor toward all the brothers that, preferring no one to another, he may display in himself toward all his disciples or sons the name of both parents: offering them equally the affection of a mother and showing himself to them with the measured compassion of a father.

The abbot must always remember what is said: “To whom more has been entrusted, from him more will be required.” And let him know that he who has undertaken to govern souls prepares himself to render an account. And however many brothers he knows to be under his care, let him understand with certainty that on the day of judgment he will render to the Lord as many accounts for all those souls [Col. 0956D], without doubt with his own account added. For, so that the brothers in the monastery would not do their own will, they served under his commands with complete obedience.

When they are examined concerning all their actions, they will say in judgment before the Lord that all their deeds were accomplished through obedience to the command of the master. Therefore the master must always be careful that everything he commands, everything he teaches, and everything he corrects is shown, with justice dictating, to arise from God’s precepts—things that will not be condemned at the future judgment—always fearing the future examination of the shepherd concerning the sheep entrusted to him. For while he guards against accounts concerning others, he is made anxious about his own; and while he supplies corrections to others through his admonitions, he himself is corrected of his vices. [Col. 0957A]

Whatever the abbot wishes to undertake or accomplish for the benefit of the monastery, let him do it with the counsel of the brothers. When all the brothers have been summoned, let the monastery’s welfare be discussed jointly. Yet the brothers are to apply themselves to choosing counsel not by their own free initiative, nor against their will by the abbot’s gracious decision, but by the abbot’s command and authority.

For this reason the counsel of all is sought: because as many people as there are, so many opinions sometimes arise from their diversity. Perhaps a better counsel may suddenly be offered by one from whom it was not expected, and this may contribute more to the common good; and from many counsels it is easily found what should be chosen. But if no one among all of them is able to offer suitable advice, then the abbot, having explained the reasoning behind his counsel, shall establish what he wishes. And it is just that the members follow the head.

Therefore we said that all the brothers ought to be summoned for counsel [Col. 0957B], but into the judgment of the monastery; for the monastery’s property belongs to everyone and to no one. It belongs to everyone because, as they progress, the brothers expect that in time they will succeed one another in the monastery; it belongs to no one because nothing in the monastery is claimed by any brother as his personal possession. No one establishes anything for himself to do according to his own judgment; rather, all live under the authority of the abbot.

Therefore, let the abbot who is an artisan of this holy art assign the ministry not to himself but to the Lord, by whose grace whatever is accomplished by us in holiness is fashioned. This art must be taught and learned in the monastery’s workshop and practiced with spiritual tools.

## CHAPTER III

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION, CONTINUED

[Col. 0957C]

What is the holy art which the abbot ought to teach the disciples in the monastery?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

What is this holy art? First, to believe in, confess, and fear God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one God in Trinity, and three in unity; three in one divinity, alone and one in the threefold power of majesty.

Therefore, to love him with all one’s heart and with all one’s soul, and one’s neighbor as oneself. Then: not to kill; not to commit adultery; not to steal; not to covet; not to bear false witness; to honor father and mother; and not to do to another what one does not wish done to oneself.

To deny oneself in order to follow Christ; to chastise the body for the sake of the soul; to flee pleasures; to love fasting; to refresh the poor; to clothe the naked; to visit the sick; to bury the dead; to assist in tribulation; to console the grieving; to lend to the needy; to make oneself a stranger to worldly affairs; to prefer nothing to the love of Christ; not to carry anger through to action; not to reserve time for wrath; not to hold deceit in one’s heart; not to offer false peace from one’s conscience; to keep faith with one’s brother; not to love slander; to fulfill one’s promise and not deceive; not to abandon charity; not to love swearing, lest one perhaps commit perjury; to speak truth from heart and mouth; not to return evil for evil; not to inflict injuries, but patiently to endure those inflicted; to love enemies more than friends; not to curse back at those who curse, [Col. 0958A] but rather to bless them; to endure persecution for justice; not to be proud; not to be a lover of wine; not to be excessively gluttonous; not to be sleepy; not to be lazy; not to be a murmurer; to entrust one’s hope to God.

When one sees some good in oneself, to consider it accomplished by God rather than by oneself; to judge the evil as one’s own doing and attribute it both to oneself and to the devil; to desire that one’s desires be brought to completion by God; to hope for one’s sustenance not only from the labor of one’s hands but even more from God; to fear the day of judgment; to dread hell; to desire eternal life and holy Jerusalem; to keep death daily before one’s eyes as a matter of concern; to guard the actions of one’s life at every hour; to know with certainty that one is watched by God in every place; to strike at once against evil thoughts that come to one’s heart, bringing them to Christ; to guard one’s mouth from evil or corrupt speech; not to love speaking much; not to speak at length of empty words or matters suited to laughter; not to love excessive or uncontrolled laughter; willingly to hear holy readings; frequently to devote oneself to prayer; daily to confess to God in prayer one’s past evils with tears or groaning; thereafter to amend those very evils; not to fulfill the desires of the flesh; not to obey one’s own will; to obey the abbot’s admonition; not to desire to be called holy before one is holy, but first to be what one more truly should be called, and then to be called so.

Daily to fulfill God’s commands in deeds; to love chastity; to hate no one; not to be jealous; not to practice envy; not to love contention; before sunset to be reconciled with one’s enemy; to obey all good things with all one’s heart; and [Col. 0958C] never to despair of God.

Behold, this is the holy art which we must practice with spiritual tools. When this holy art has been fulfilled by you incessantly, day and night, and when each person has marked before the Lord God, in anticipation of the day of judgment, the works of his future and past deeds, then this art, which has descended from God’s will, when it has been perfected by us and returned to the Lord without blame on the day of judgment, will earn for us from the Lord that reward which the faithful Lord promises us, which is prepared for the saints, for those who fear God, and for those who fulfill these commands in their deeds: to dwell forever in a land seven times brighter than silver.

From its heavenly chamber there will shine not the radiance of this sun or moon, nor of the stars, but the perpetual majesty of God himself. In the splendor of that land, rivers of honey and milk, wine and oil are prepared to flow forever. Along their banks grow various fruits of different trees, born twelve times a year—not through human cultivation but through the abundance of the Godhead. They do not delight us in order to be eaten out of hunger, nor are they desired in order to be consumed from appetite; rather, after our eyes have been filled by the sight itself, each thing will taste in the mouth of each person as that person has delighted in it.

There, organs of hymns placed along the banks of those rivers sound continually. They are sung in praise of the King by angels who sing psalms together with the holy archangels. The sweetness of their voices so delights the hearing of the saints that, through the musical melody, the talkative mind, in its overwhelming delight, rejoices all the more gladly. Meanwhile, in the double radiance with which heaven and earth shine divinely, the city of Jerusalem, adorned with gold and gems in the very brightness of earthly light, gleams with the brilliance of various pearls.

Its walls and gates, its streets and lanes, resound with the sweet modulation of melodious voices: “Alleluia.” In this exultation, the saints, shining in a heavenly likeness, will rejoice that they have been freed from the world’s destruction and have merited these heavenly riches from God forever. Therefore, by what path such things are to be reached, let us recite from the text of the preceding page.

## CHAPTER IV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION, CONTINUED

What are the spiritual tools with which we can practice the divine art?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 0959B]

What are they? Faith, hope, charity, peace, joy, gentleness, humility, obedience, silence; above all, bodily chastity, a single-minded conscience, abstinence, purity, simplicity, kindness, goodness, mercy; above all, devotion, temperance, vigilance, sobriety, justice, equity, truth, love, measure, moderation, and perseverance to the end.

## CHAPTER V

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

What is the material or cause of evils which must be smelted away in the furnace of the fear of God? Or what is the rust or defilement of vices which it is fitting for the file of justice to cleanse from us?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 0959C]

These are the vices we must avoid: first, pride; then disobedience, excessive talk, falsehood, greed, covetousness, jealousy, envy, iniquity, hatred, enmity, anger, quarrelling, contention, fornication, drunkenness, gluttony, murmuring, impiety, injustice, laziness, theft, detraction, buffoonery, frivolity, uncleanness, empty talk, excessive or uncontrolled laughter, mockery, lust, deceit, ambition, and idleness.

All these things are not from God but are works of the devil. On the day of judgment they will earn from God their fitting reward: the hell of everlasting fire.

## CHAPTER VI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

What is the workshop of the divine art, or the operation of the spiritual tools?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 0959D]

The workshop is the monastery. In it, the tools of the heart, stored within the enclosure of the body, can persevere in carefully practicing the work of the divine art.

## CHAPTER VII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the disciple’s obedience: what ought it to be like?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

The first degree of humility is obedience without delay. But this form belongs to few, and to the perfect: to those who esteem nothing dearer to themselves than Christ, whether because of the holy service they have professed, or because of fear of hell, or because of the riches of eternal life [Col. 0960A]. As soon as they hear something commanded by the superior, they cannot endure delay in carrying it out.

Of such people the Lord says: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Ps. XVII). And again he says to the teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Matt. X). Therefore such men immediately abandon what belongs to them and renounce their own will. At once, withdrawing their hands from what they are occupied with and leaving unfinished what they were doing, they follow in deeds, with a foot swift to obedience, the voice of the one commanding. Thus, as if in a single moment, the master’s command and the disciple’s completed work are both accomplished more quickly through the fear of God.

But this model of the few and perfect must not leave the minds of the weak and lazy utterly stunned in despair; rather, it should urge them to imitate it, since we must consider that among us there are different kinds of fragile vessels, and that slow nature has contributed much to the laziness of different people. We know that the hearing of some grows dull with deaf stupor, and we see that the minds of others wander away through a sudden dispersal into wooded thoughts.

Therefore, we relax the strictness of obedience in teachers somewhat, so that, by combining commands, the master will not be reluctant to repeat his order to the disciples, according to the testimony of the Lord, who called, “Abraham, Abraham” (Gen. XXII). This repetition shows us that the Lord demonstrated that a single utterance may not be sufficient for the hearing. For in the very questions, the repeated voice of the master is presented to the disciples.

A second question is justly granted to those who do not respond, so that the disciple’s first silence may be assigned not to guilt but to the preservation of reverence reserved for the master [Col. 0960C]. In that reverence, a useful disciple is believed to break slowly the silence he maintains, so that he does not rush immediately to answer your question and occupy you with his replies first.

In commands, however, the master’s order is repeated for this reason: although the hearers may be slow or negligent, when what was first said is repeated to them a second time, it is so fitting that the delay should now be broken by obedient deeds. But if there should be a third delay in obedience among the disciples—which, God forbid, may not occur—the guilt is to be attributed to the offense of stubbornness.

For here, too, that saying about the two vices is appropriately and suitably applied (Matt. XVII): namely, the broad way that leads to death and the narrow way that leads to life. Along these two ways the obedience of different kinds of people proceeds [Col. 0960D]: along the broad way, that of worldly monks and of the Sarabaites and gyrovagues, who, whether singly, in pairs, or in groups of three, live for themselves as equals without a superior, moving about voluntarily and taking turns commanding one another according to whatever pleases them, while each personally defends whatever he wishes for himself.

Since none of them wants to be overcome in his own opinion, such men never lack occasions for scandal. Soon, after a deliberate but evil quarrel, they separate from one another; and, like a flock wandering without a shepherd, scattered in different directions, they will undoubtedly meet the jaws of wolves. Looking after themselves—not according to God but according to their own judgment—they again provide themselves with new cells and impose on themselves alone the names of abbots. You may see more monasteries than monks. [Col. 0961A]

This is believed to be the broad way walked by such people: while living together in the common manner under the name of monks, separated from laypeople only by the appearance of their tonsure, they offer their obedience more to their desires than to God. By their own judgment they think they are permitted to do what is evil; whatever they wish, they call holy, and whatever they do not wish, they consider forbidden.

They consider it acceptable for their bodies to be provided for according to their thoughts more than their souls—that is, they think they themselves can provide food, clothing, and footwear better than anyone else. For, by neglecting the future accounts of the soul, they make themselves so secure that, serving under their own judgment without the testing of superiors, they believe they are perfectly practicing every law and justice of God in their cell.

If, perhaps, some superiors arrive and offer them certain admonitions for correction, teaching them that such a solitary arrangement of living is useless, they immediately become displeased both with the advice and with the person of the teacher. They do not promise correction by consenting to or following him; instead, they reply that they ought to live simply, not knowing what the Prophet said: “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires” (Ps. XIII). Nor do they heed Solomon’s testimony, which says: “There are ways that seem right to people, but their end plunges down to the depths of hell” (Prov. IV).

The broad way is walked by such people because wherever the foot of their desires leads them, they immediately follow with their assent. Whatever they desire, the effect is instantly ready to serve their desires. They make new paths of license for themselves, acting as free people without a master, and delight in the way of their life through unlawful varieties of pleasure. Wherever their pleasures wish to advance, they provide themselves with open and unrestricted steps, always unwilling to know that, for a human being who has been created, death has been placed beside the entrance of pleasure (Ecclus. XVIII).

And when they are told, “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your wills” (ibid.), they pass by with deaf ears.

By contrast, those who are moved by a love of walking toward eternal life take hold of the narrow way so that they may not live according to their own judgment, obeying their own desires and wills. Instead, walking according to another’s judgment and authority, they are restrained not only in the desires and wills mentioned above [Col. 0961D] and refuse, when able, to do what they themselves decide, but also submit themselves to another’s authority. Living in coenobia, they desire to have an abbot preside over them.

Without doubt, such people imitate the Lord’s saying: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI). Not doing their own will, but denying themselves for Christ’s sake, they follow God wherever the abbot’s command leads them.

They are not compelled to think for themselves, under the abbot’s care, only about temporal necessities—food, clothing, and footwear—but, by offering their teacher obedience in everything concerning the future accounts of their souls, they are made secure concerning all their other needs, both of body [Col. 0962A] and of soul. For whether what is exercised in the sheep is good or bad, it rests upon the shepherd; and at the judgment of examination, the one who commands, not the one who carries out the commands, will be required to render an account, whether the commands are good or bad.

The narrow way is believed to be walked by such people because their own desires are not fulfilled in them. They do not accomplish what they wish; instead, bearing the yoke of another’s judgment, they are driven back from going wherever their pleasures wish to lead them, and the master denies them permission to act or do as they please.

Their will is embittered daily in the monastery for the Lord’s sake, and whatever is imposed upon them for testing they endure patiently as though in martyrdom. Without doubt, in the monastery they will say to the Lord with the Prophet: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are considered as sheep for slaughter” [Col. 0962B] (Ps. XLIII). And later, at judgment, they will say to the Lord: “You tested us, O God; you examined us by fire as silver is examined; you brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back; you set men over our heads” (ibid. LXV).

When they say, “You set men over our heads,” they are understood to have a superior appointed over them in God’s place, whom they fear in the monastery. And, appropriately following this testimony, they will also say to the Lord in that future age: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (ibid.). That is: we passed through the bitterness of our pleasures, and through the service of obedience we reached the refreshment of your mercy.

But this obedience will then be acceptable to God and pleasing to human beings if what is commanded is carried out neither lukewarmly nor slowly, neither with murmuring nor with a reply of unwillingness. For the obedience offered to superiors is given to God. As the Lord says to our teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Matt. X). And elsewhere he says: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Ps. XVII).

Therefore, let this very obedience be offered by the disciples with a good disposition, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. IX). For if a disciple obeys with an evil disposition, he reproaches not only us with his mouth but also God in his heart, because he does what he does with an evil disposition. Even if he fulfills what has been commanded, it will no longer be acceptable to God, who sees his murmuring heart. And even if he does what is commanded, if he does it with an evil disposition, the Lord will credit him with no reward for the deed [Col. 0962D], since God immediately searches his heart and finds in him the sad vow of one who acts unwillingly.

## CHAPTER VIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the disciples’ silence: what ought its character and extent to be?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

The mechanism of the human race is our little body. Though it is small in measure, and even in some unusually tall people rises scarcely five feet from the ground—O vanity of boasting!—every living human being, in this very smallness, thinks that by his wisdom he can measure the height of heaven and the breadth of the earth.

Therefore, knowing that we are fragile vessels made from the clay of the earth, like certain clods of earth raised from the ground for a short time and destined to fall again into their furrow, let us humble ourselves and, as dust from the earth, say what we are.

This flesh of our little body is therefore like a kind of house for souls, assigned to the service of life just as a sheath serves a sword. We believe that the dwelling place of the soul is founded in the root of the heart. That root possesses two upper branches in the body, and branches more fragile in sin.

One is the branch through which, as through certain windows and openings of the eyes, we believe the soul looks outward from within the body; and we understand that from inside it continually incites its desires. The other is the branch through which the heart’s conceived offspring sounds within us as it gives birth through the speech of the tongue, so that, going out through the gate of the mouth, it may occupy another person’s hearing. Whatever is stirred and moved within us is the soul’s action in the body. [Col. 0963B]

Conversely, when the soul departs from this dwelling, everything that was being done in the living person by the soul is absent from the dead person. Once the dead clod of earth has been returned to its earth, the human being—earth—returns to the nature of earth; when the human being is hidden in the grave and the pit covered over, the earth returns in its own form as pavement. Thus it is recognized that the human being was then like earth while alive, having been raised by the power of the soul and, as a stranger to life, changed for a time.

Therefore, when the soul departs from us, the earth of our body cannot stand firm; it falls into its own nature and hides in its bosom the earthly creation it brought forth.

If, then, this soul acts within us through the sight of the eyes, the speech of the mouth [Col. 0963C], and the hearing of the ears, and if, because of the future examination by its Maker, it desires to obey God’s will and serve his commands while it lives, let it close the windows of the eyes against its desires and lower its humbled gaze toward the earth, so that it may not see evil. And when our sight has been bent downward, let the soul not desire whatever it sees.

Our soul also has an established gate, the mouth, and a bolt, the teeth. Let it close this gate against corrupt speech, so that the soul may not accuse its generous Maker of having built for it insufficient protection. That is, when it has moved something from the root of the heart against a brother and senses that the enclosure of the outer wall—the mouth and teeth—denies it an exit, let it return again to the root of the heart and perish there in its abhorrence; and, like a little child, let it be dashed against the rock, lest, growing through the tongue, it increase toward punishment. [Col. 0963D]

The other branches of our body, which serve the command of the heart, are easily restrained from sin: namely, the touch of the hands and the steps of the feet. A chain’s enclosure restrains the thief; fear of judgment restrains the murderer; and a snare holds back the fugitive.

Therefore, those three highest faculties which we mentioned above must be guarded with particular care by the brothers: thought, speech, and sight.

Thought: as soon as an evil thought has taken the mind captive, the brother must immediately sign his forehead, or his breast itself, and at once turn his memory to Christ’s commands. Let the brother say to himself with the Prophet: “I remembered God, and I was comforted” (Ps. LXVII). And let him say likewise: “From you I shall be rescued from temptation, and in my God I shall leap over a wall” (Ps. XVII).

But if negligence has armed the mouth with angry, corrupt, or empty speech, let the brother immediately close his mouth and, marked with the seal of the cross in his heart, speak to himself, saying with the Prophet: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue. I placed a guard over my mouth; I was silent and was humbled exceedingly, and I kept silent even from good things.”

Through this the Prophet shows that if one must sometimes remain silent even from good speech, for the sake of silence, how much more must one refrain from evil words for fear of sin’s punishment?

Therefore, although perfect disciples are rarely granted permission to speak concerning good and holy matters and words of edification, because of the gravity of silence, nevertheless, unless questioned, the brothers must remain silent from all other speech until the abbot’s question loosens the reins of their mouths [Col. 0964B].

For this reason silence must be guarded with the greatest care by the brothers, because “sin is not avoided in much speaking” (Prov. X). And therefore, “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (ibid. X). It is fitting for the master to speak and teach, and for the disciple to be silent and listen.

## CHAPTER IX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

In what order should the silent brothers put certain questions to the abbot?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER
[Col. 0964C] When disciples are restrained by the bridle of silence from speaking about evil things as well as about good things, and the avenues of their speech are watched over by the custody of the master who is present, whenever some questions necessary for their usefulness arise, then, still with their mouths closed and sealed with the seal of silent gravity, they should stand before their superior, bowing their heads in humility, and open their mouths, closed in silence, with the key of blessing. But if, after the blessing has once been spoken in order to request permission to speak, the master’s permission still does not answer, then, bowing the head in renewed humility and repeating only the blessing once more, the monk should again request permission from the abbot. If he receives no answer even then, the disciple, bowing once more in humility, should at last withdraw; lest he appear either excessively importunate or shameless, and, having returned to his work, should still maintain the character of one who remains silent. He should judge himself, in that very humility of silence, to have been deemed unworthy by the abbot’s judgment to speak; [Col. 0964D] or perhaps the disciple should think that the enclosure of silence was not opened for him in order to test whether his humility could be discovered.

For this reason we have said that he should repeat the blessing alone: so that, although it is alone and without any other speech, the silence that has long been maintained may nevertheless be preserved; and when it is repeated, and he immediately withdraws from the unwilling superior, his humility may still be seen to have been preserved and tested. The disciple’s repetition is not offered again to the master merely so that, for the sake of the spiritual testing by which the disciple’s humility is discovered, the master may be said to remain silent; it is also so that the master [Col. 0965A], perhaps physically occupied by his thoughts, with his face benumbed by other reflections, may not fail to hear the disciple’s beseeching voice with deaf ears; and so that the disciple may not force the master, through excessive and importunate humility, to fall into the fault of anger, nor cause importunate humility to be counted as an occasion of scandal.

For this reason we said that, after the second blessing has been presented, the disciple should not repeat a third one to the unwilling superior, but should immediately withdraw from that place and, while maintaining the same silence, complete the labor he had been performing. This request for a blessing, which is scarcely released except by silence alone, should be made by the disciples with a humble inclination of the head; that is, in every place and at every hour: in the monastery, in the field, on the road, in the garden, or in any other place. Thus the remembrance of God, for whose sake all these things are done, may never be absent from our minds. [Col. 0965B] If someone ignorant of the matter should ask such a brother, saying, “Why are you silent and sad, and why do you walk with your face inclined?” he should answer him: “Because I flee sin and fear God; and in order to guard myself from everything that God hates, I am always watchful over myself.”

When they are sitting at table, however, if they wish to make their questions known to the abbot, before the blessing has been spoken, a blow of the knife, spoon, or bread should serve as a signal to the master that the disciple is requesting permission to speak. All these things are necessary for the soul for God’s sake. Therefore we have established that the substance of silence must be preserved within an enclosure, so that a person may not so easily be deceived by forgetfulness and may not always be headlong in speech. For when silence is contained by the enclosure of the mouth, what can be brought forth cleanly and without sin from the mouth may be long considered or purified in the heart, as the Apostle says: [Col. 0965C] “Let no idle word proceed from your mouth, but only whatever is for edification” (Ephesians IV). Scripture also says: “The wise man makes himself known by few words.”

For this reason above all we must fear and guard ourselves from loquacity at every hour, because it cannot happen that, among many words, some do not come out accompanied by sin, according to Scripture, which says: “In much speaking sin is not avoided” (Proverbs X). Hence the Prophet, giving us an example, shows that he was concerned about these matters and that he ought to remain silent about evil as well as good speech, saying: “He said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.’ I set a guard over my mouth; I became silent and was quiet even from good things” (Psalm XXXVIII). This shows the perfect disciple that he must remain silent about evil as well as good speech. For even if good things are to be spoken, instruction belongs not to disciples but to the master. Indeed, as Scripture says: “Life and death are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs XIV). Therefore the tongue itself must be restrained all the more carefully and properly.

[Col. 0965D] This strict custody of such profound silence is rightly enjoined upon those who are perfect and pure in heart, cleansed from sin, fearing the everlasting fires of Gehenna, and seeking the immortal riches of eternal life. Therefore, in the presence of the abbot, disciples should not speak unless questioned. In the abbot’s absence, however, if they speak about the word of God, they should do so to one another slowly and humbly, not in a loud voice, because every slow manner of speaking proceeds from humility. But if the disciples begin to speak about empty or worldly matters, or about any words that do not pertain to God, their superiors should immediately command them to be silent. [Col. 0966A] Psalms or Scriptures, outside those three hours in which they are appointed to be read daily without labor, may be recited from memory by the brothers who are engaged in work.

We have above prescribed such a great enclosure of silence, in the presence of the abbot, for those who are perfect before God: for those from whom forgetfulness of God never steals away, who carefully seek to avoid the vices of the mouth, and who, like angels, seek for the Lord to remain silent both from good and from evil speech. But because the diversity of grace granted may be diminished according to the measure of faith, especially among the negligent, we relax this rule for the lukewarm, imperfect, and less diligent, allowing them to speak about worldly matters under inquiry—provided that what they say is without sin and does not pertain to spiritual edification—only if permission to speak has been granted after the blessing has been requested [Col. 0966B]. When asking about some spiritual matter, however, the disciple should speak immediately after requesting the blessing.
