We condemn jests, idle words, and words that provoke laughter to an everlasting silence, and we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth for such speech.

## CHAPTER X

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning what the humility of the brothers ought to be, by what means it may be acquired, and how, once acquired, it may be preserved.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Divine Scripture cries out to us, brothers, saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV). In saying this [Col. 0966C], it shows us that every exaltation is a form of pride. The Prophet indicates that he guarded against this, saying: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Psalm CXXX). And again he repeats: “I have not walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me. But what if I was not humble in my thoughts, and exalted my soul? Like a child weaned from his mother, so is the recompense in my soul.”

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to reach the summit of the highest humility, and wish to arrive swiftly at that heavenly exaltation to which one ascends through the humility of the present life, we must erect, by our ascending deeds, that ladder which appeared in Jacob’s dream, set upright toward heaven, upon which angels were shown descending and ascending [Col. 0966D]. Without doubt, we understand that this descent and ascent signify nothing other than that exaltation must be descended from and humility ascended. The ladder itself, set upright, is our life in this world; with heart and head humbled in this present age, it raises toward heaven the exalted departure of death, granted by the Lord. The sides of that ladder, we most certainly believe, are our body. Upon these sides divine calling has inserted various steps of humility or discipline, to be ascended.

The disciple therefore ascends the first step of humility on the ladder of heaven if, always setting the fear of God before his eyes, he flees forgetfulness at every hour and continually remembers all that God has commanded; if he continually recalls in his mind both how Gehenna burns those who despise God because of their sins [Col. 0967A] and how eternal life, prepared for those who fear God, awaits them; and if he guards himself at every hour from sins and vices—that is, from the thoughts, tongue, hands, feet, and self-will, as well as from the desires of the flesh.

The disciple should consider himself always watched from heaven by God, and his deeds in every place to be seen by the sight of the divine presence, with everything reported daily by the angels. The Prophet demonstrates this to us when he shows that God is always present in our thoughts, saying: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Psalm VII). He also says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain” (ibid.). Again he says: “You have understood my thoughts from afar” (Psalm XCIII). Again: “For the thought of a human being will confess to you” (Psalm CXXXVIII). And: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God” [Col. 0967B] (Psalm LXXV).

Thus, in order to remain watchful against the perverse thoughts of his heart, the lowly brother should always say to himself in his heart: “Then I shall be without blemish before him, if I guard myself from my iniquity” (Proverbs XXI). With regard to the words of the tongue, we recognize God’s constant presence among us when the voice of the Lord says through the Prophet: “Whoever speaks wickedly shall not speak in the sight of my eyes” (Psalm XVII). The Apostle also says: “You will give an account for an idle word.” For “death and life are placed in the power of the tongue” (Psalm C; Proverbs XIV).

In the work of our hands we likewise recognize that God is present with us when the Prophet says: “Your eyes saw my unfinished work” (Psalm CXXXVIII). [Col. 0967C] In the movement of our feet we recognize God’s presence when the Prophet says: “I ran without iniquity, and I was directing my course; rise up to meet me” (Psalm LVIII). He also says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings before the dawn and dwell at the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm CXXXVIII).

We are forbidden to carry out our own will in the presence of the Lord when Scripture says to us: “Turn away from your own wills” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII; Matthew IV). We also ask the Lord in the Lord’s Prayer that his will be done in us. We are therefore rightly taught not to do our own will when we avoid what holy Scripture says: “There are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end [Col. 0967D] plunges down to the depths of hell” (Proverbs XVIII). We also avoid what is said concerning the negligent: “They have been corrupted and have become abominable in their own wills” (Psalm XIII).

With regard to the desires of the flesh, we should likewise believe that God is always present with us when the Prophet says: “Lord, all my desire is before you” (Psalm XXXVII). A wicked desire must therefore be avoided, because death lies beside the entrance of pleasure. Hence Scripture commands, saying: “Do not follow your desires” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII).

Therefore, if the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked, and the Lord always looks down from heaven upon the children of human beings to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God (Psalm XXXIII), and if the deeds of our actions are reported daily, by the angels assigned to us, to the Lord day and night [Col. 0968A], then we must be on our guard at every hour, brothers, as the Prophet says in the fourteenth psalm (Psalm XIII), lest the Lord at some hour see us turning toward evil and becoming useless. Though he spares us in this time because he is merciful and waits for us to turn toward what is better, he may say to us at the future judgment: “You did these things, and I was silent” (Psalm XLIII).

Next, the disciple ascends the second step of humility on the ladder of heaven if, not loving his own will, he takes no pleasure in fulfilling his desires, but imitates in his deeds the voice of the Lord, who says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI). Scripture also says: “Self-will has punishment, but necessity brings a crown.”

[Col. 0968B] Next, the disciple ascends the third step of humility on the ladder of heaven if, after presuming nothing on his own judgment, he chooses things that are not expedient, as Scripture says: “There are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end plunges down to the depths of hell” (Proverbs XIV). David likewise says: “They have been corrupted and have become abominable in their own wills” (Psalm XIII). The Apostle also says: “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything” (1 Corinthians VI).

Therefore the disciple must not only guard against these things but also submit himself in all obedience to his superior, imitating the Lord, of whom the Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death” (Philippians II). [Col. 0968C] Again, the voice of the Lord praises the gentile people for this obedience, saying: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Psalm VII). The Lord shows that we must obey under the abbot when he says to our teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke X).

Next, the disciple ascends the fourth step of humility on the ladder of heaven if, in that very obedience, he embraces silently the steadfastness of patience amid harsh and difficult things, or even amid whatever injuries are inflicted upon him, and, enduring, does not grow weary or depart, as Scripture says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew X). The Prophet also exhorts us concerning this, saying: “Let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm XXVI).

To show that the faithful person must endure every adversity for the Lord, the Prophet speaks through the persons of those who suffer: “For your sake we are put to death all day long [Col. 0968D]; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm XLIII). Secure in the hope of divine recompense, they then continue joyfully, saying: “But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us” (Romans VIII). Elsewhere Scripture speaks in their person: “You have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined by fire. You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back” (Psalm LXV).

And to show that we must be under a superior, it continues, saying: “You have set human beings over our heads” (Matthew V). We must also fulfill the Lord’s command in adversity and amid injuries through patience: when struck on one cheek, we offer the other; when our tunic is taken away, we surrender our cloak; when compelled to go one mile, we go two [Col. 0969A]; with the Apostle Paul, we endure false brothers and suffer persecution, and, when cursed, we bless all the more (2 Corinthians XI).

Next, the disciple ascends the fifth step of humility on the ladder of heaven if he does not conceal from his abbot, through humble confession of the tongue, any evil thoughts that come into his heart or any evil secretly committed by him. Scripture exhorts us concerning this, saying: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him” (Psalm XXXVI). It also says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever” (Psalm CV). The Prophet says to the Lord: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquities. I said, ‘I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord,’” and immediately: “You forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm XXXI).

[Col. 0969B] Next, the disciple ascends the sixth step of humility on the ladder of heaven if he is content with every lowly and inferior condition, and judges himself, with regard to everything provided for him, as a bad and unworthy laborer, saying to himself with the Prophet: “I have been reduced to nothing and did not know; I became like a beast before you, and yet I am always with you” (Psalm XCII).

Next, the disciple ascends the seventh step of humility on the ladder of heaven if he declares himself inferior and baser than everyone, not merely with his tongue, but also believes this with the deepest affection of his heart, humbling himself and saying: “But I am a worm and not a human being, a reproach of human beings and an outcast of the people” (Psalm XXI). “I was exalted, and I was humbled, and I was confounded” (Psalm LXXXVII). [Col. 0969C] Such a brother should also always say to the Lord with the Prophet: “It is good for me, Lord, that you humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments” (Psalm CXVIII).

Next, the disciple ascends the eighth step of humility on the ladder of heaven if he does nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of his superiors urge him to do, saying with Scripture: “For your law is my meditation” (Psalm CXVIII). “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you”: that is, the abbot through his teaching.

Next, the disciple ascends the ninth step of humility on the ladder of heaven if he restrains his tongue from speaking and, maintaining silence, does not speak until questioned, as Scripture shows: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs X). And: “The talkative man will not be established upon the earth” (Psalm CXXXIX).

Next, the disciple ascends the tenth step of humility on the ladder of heaven if he is not quick and ready to laugh [Col. 0969D], because it is written: “A fool raises his voice in laughter” (Ecclesiasticus XXI). And: “As the crackling of thorns beneath a pot, so is the laughter of a human being” (Ecclesiastes VII).

Next, the disciple ascends the eleventh step of humility on the ladder of heaven if, when he speaks, he speaks gently and without laughter, humbly and with gravity, using few and holy words, and is not loud in his voice. It is written: “The wise man makes himself known by few words.”

Next, the disciple ascends the twelfth step of humility on the ladder of heaven if he continually displays humility to those who see him, not only in his heart but also [Col. 0970A] in his body. This means that, in the work of God, in the oratory, in the monastery, in the garden, on the road, in the field, or wherever he may be sitting, walking, or standing, he should always have his head inclined and his eyes fixed upon the ground, considering himself at every hour guilty because of his sins and imagining that he is already being brought before the dreadful judgment. He should always say in his heart what the tax collector said while standing before the temple with his eyes fixed upon the ground: “Lord, I am not worthy—I am a sinner—to lift my eyes toward heaven” (Luke XVIII). Such a disciple should also say to himself with the Prophet: “I have been bowed down and humbled exceedingly” (Psalm CXVIII).

When all these steps of humility have been climbed by the disciple, the ladder of this life is duly traversed in the fear of God, and he will immediately arrive at that love [Col. 0970B] which, being perfect, casts out fear. Through it, he begins to observe without any labor, as though naturally and through habit, all the things he previously kept through fear—not now from fear of Gehenna, but from love of the good habit itself and delight in the virtues, which the Lord will deign to reveal through his laborer, cleansed by the Holy Spirit from vices and sins.

When these steps have therefore been climbed, such a soul will undoubtedly, after the departure from this life, enter into that recompense of the soul which the Apostle describes, saying: “The sufferings of this present age are not worthy of the glory to come that will be revealed in us” (Romans VIII). Such souls will receive that eternal life which remains in everlasting joy and exultation and knows no further end.

[Col. 0970C] There is the purple blossom of roses that never withers; there flowering groves remain green with perpetual verdure; there fresh meadows always overflow with honeyed streams; there the grasses breathe the fragrance of saffron flowers, and the fields, exhaling their aromas, abound in exceedingly pleasant breezes. There those who possess eternal life breathe through their nostrils. There is light without shadow, serenity without cloud, and the eyes enjoy perpetual day without the darkness of night.

No pleasure there is hindered by occupation; no security there is disturbed by any anxiety. The bellowing, howling, lamentation, and mourning are never heard or named there. Nothing foul, deformed, gloomy, black, dreadful, or filthy is ever seen there. Beauty is found in the loveliness of the groves; splendor in the pleasant air; and open eyes enjoy without interruption beauty and every elegance. Nothing at all that could trouble the mind is presented to the ears.

[Col. 0970D] For there the organs of hymns sound continually, sung by angels and archangels in praise of the King. Bitterness and the harshness of gall have no place there. Thunder is never heard there; lightning and flashes of light never appear. Those shrubs produce cinnamon, and the thickets bring forth balsam. The fragrance of the air spreads delight through every limb.

No food there produces excrement. For just as the ears are nourished by good news, the nostrils by a good scent, and the eyes by a beautiful sight, and as refreshment cannot break out into digestion, [Col. 0971A] because the nourishment of delight consists not in food and drink but in sight, smell, and hearing, so there the refreshment received by the mouth is honey-sweet in taste, and each person tastes in his mouth whatever has delighted him. Finally, whatever the soul desires, the effect is immediately prepared to serve its desire.

In that delight and joy, such pleasures fear neither age becoming old, nor life coming to an end, nor death being feared thereafter. Nor does the possessor cease in the enjoyment of these perpetual riches while an heir succeeds him, since those who have once purchased eternal life by the price of good deeds, dying once, no longer know death.

This is the heavenly homeland of the saints. Blessed are those who, in this everlasting region, having climbed through the steps of humility by the ladder of present observance, [Col. 0971B] are able to be raised up, so that they may rejoice in perpetual exultation with God—who has prepared it for those who love him, keep his commandments, and are pure in heart.

*[Here ends the practice of the warfare of the heart concerning the fear of God and how sins may be avoided. Here begins the organization of the monastery: its manner, observance, degrees, continence, custody, and measure; in these various matters this rule of the monastery is named, with the Lord dictating to us and examining what has been dictated.]*

## CHAPTER XI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the superiors of the monastery.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER
In the preceding pages of this Rule, brothers, the Lord has prescribed for us deeds of righteousness [Col. 0971C]; once these are perfected, eternal life is gained, and the heat and fires of Gehenna are escaped. But the devil, that enemy of good deeds, is hostile to humankind precisely because he does not allow a person to ascend there by doing good, whence he himself was cast down through his pride. Therefore, lest he infect the conduct of those who live well with his poisonous deeds, and perhaps seize our minds through forgetfulness by his various devices, in order to estrange them from God, it has been provided and ordained, with the Lord’s help, that two chosen brothers—whose seriousness, wisdom, moderation, vigilance, humility, and practice of perfect deeds have been proven—be appointed as superiors with charge of ten brothers.

For, as it is written, let earthly things teach you, and those things that are heavenly. Just as in a human household, so that he may be secure about all that must be prepared, the master of the property appoints heads of the household, whom those subordinate to the master fear—namely, the steward, the forester, and the head of the household, serving in the master’s place—so also in the divine households, that is, in churches and monasteries, God has placed superiors over those of lesser rank, experts over the ignorant, the shrewd over the simple, and teachers over the disciples of divine learning. In churches these are bishops, priests, deacons, and the clergy; in their place the people hear and fear God’s commands and learn from them the knowledge of the law that brings salvation. In monasteries, they are abbots and superiors, whom the brethren hear for the salvation of their souls, and whose authority, as representing God, the monastic soldiers fear.

For God said this either to priests in the church or to abbots [Col. 0972A] and superiors in the monastery: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10). And again the Lord says to us through the prophet Jeremiah: “I will give you shepherds and teachers according to my heart, and they will feed you while feeding you with discipline” (Jer. 13). Therefore, according to that model of a human household, how much more ought the ranks of instruction and fear to be maintained in the divine household for God’s cause? Thus, once superiors have been appointed to purge the vices and sins of the brethren, the abbot may be somewhat relieved of the accounting required for guarding the souls entrusted to him.

Let this, then, be the arrangement of their authority. After those same ten brethren have been summoned by the abbot, in the presence of the whole community, in the oratory, let two be placed over the ten by the abbot’s word, with the receiving of a staff, [Col. 0972B] in accordance with the testimony of Scripture: “You shall rule them with a rod” (Ps. 2)—that is, with the firmness of fear. The Apostle likewise says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love?” (1 Cor. 4).

Moses also, with the divine staff of power entrusted to him, showed the people committed to him the way of salvation through the depths of the sea (Exod. 14). By that judgment he is shown to have pleaded God’s cause before Pharaoh: the staff was thrown from his hands onto the ground and changed into a beast; then, taken up from the beast, it was restored to the sacred hands. Therefore, according to this ordinance, if the community is large, two superiors should be appointed over every ten brethren, possessing the qualification described above. For this reason we have ordained that no more than ten should be entrusted to the care of two superiors, so that, when the brethren are separated for different kinds of work, they may always have individual superiors with them to guard against their vices; and, where only a few are entrusted to him, the guardian’s diligence may be more effective. For among many, what is not noticed is negligently overlooked; whereas among a few brethren entrusted to them, the alternating care of two superiors is more diligent, and an exact account of a small number is easily rendered to the abbot.

The Lord indicates the suitable guardian of such a small number and enlarges what is entrusted to his diligent care when he says: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much” (Matt. 25). Therefore, when these superiors take charge of ten brethren, they must exercise this vigilance over them, by day or by night, and in every task they perform with them. They must first be present and work with them in every task; whether the brethren are sitting, walking, or standing, the superiors must restrain their actions from the devil by diligent observance and watchful inspection. If they are about to practice vices or sins of speech, the superiors must immediately correct them with admonitions and remove from them everything contrary to the divine command.

They must act as did Saint Eugenia, who presided over her subordinates in this way. According to the account written of her, she was so attentive to the speech of everyone that she allowed no one to burst into an oath or chatter about any idle matter. Rather, Saint Eugenia admonished those entrusted to her and said:

“With what reverence we ought to serve the Lord is shown by his commands, if we set before our eyes such a person as must not be despised in any command.”

We have therefore said that two superiors should be appointed over one group of ten, so that, if some brethren from the same group should be assigned by the abbot to another separate work, they may be entrusted to one superior, while the other remains with the brethren separated from him. If a brother must be sent on a journey, he should be sent on his way by his superior after being warned about the need for vigilant protection against various vices.

A brother should be sent from that group of ten only if his superior is confident that he can diligently guard against his vices, and that, in the absence of his superior, he will reckon the presence of God as especially present and will fear God’s presence more than man’s. A brother concerned for his soul ought to fear the presence of God, who will examine and judge us, more than the presence of a human being.

Therefore, because these superiors are present to the brethren at every hour, they must guard their mouths and conduct from sin and restrain various vices and wrongs in them.

If a superior hears a brother speaking without having been questioned, he should admonish him, saying:

“What are you doing, brother, when the Rule forbids it? Keep silence until you are questioned. Say to the Lord with the Prophet: ‘Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.’ Be quick to hear, but slow to speak” (Ps. 140; Jas. 1).

If an opportunity to speak has been given, the superior must guard him from speaking in an excessively loud voice, which does not befit the wise. The superior should immediately admonish him, saying:

“Stop, brother; humility does not know how to speak in this manner, for it is written: ‘The talkative man shall not be established upon the earth’” (Ps. 139).

If he should happen to speak quietly to another, the superior must nevertheless guard him lest he utter from his mouth any vain word, anything suited to laughter, or anything that does not contribute to edification and holiness. When he hears such a word, the superior should admonish him, saying:

“What are you saying, brother, when the Rule forbids it? For it is written: ‘You will give an account for every idle word’” (Matt. 12). And the Apostle likewise says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such speech as is good for edification, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. 4).

The abbot himself must provide that edification, so that the disciple’s silent hearing may answer the instruction supplied by the teacher through deeds. Therefore, let the superior admonish the disciple who speaks wrongly, saying:

“Close your mouth, brother, against evil speech. Let something good come forth from the place from which you bring forth evil, so that we who hear the good speech of your mouth may admire it rather than laugh with you at your evil speech. For the one who is laughed at is not useful. Let wisdom sit upon your mouth with the key of justice and fear of God, and let it itself close your lips with good speech.

“When an idle word, brother, has gone out from your mouth, even if through laughter, it is nevertheless lost to our hearing; for once it has gone out through the mouth, it cannot return. But its account is preserved until the presence of the examiner. Since it does not edify, it aggravates the case and wounds the soul, lest on the day of judgment it be said of our speech: ‘Each one spoke vain things to his neighbor’” (Ps. 11).

Origen, the wise man, also says: “It is better to throw a stone in vain than a word.”

If the superior hears a brother lying, he should admonish him to the truth, saying:

“Why are you lying, brother, when you know that it is written: ‘You will destroy all those who speak falsehood’?” (Ps. 5). And again, since you know that “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24).

If he hears a brother swearing excessively, the superior who is present should admonish him, saying:

“Hold back your tongue, brother. Why do you swear so much, when Scripture commands us not to swear at all?” (Matt. 5). Lest this give rise to perjury, let your speech be: “Yes, yes; no, no.” Say, “Believe me, believe me,” and we shall immediately believe what you have said.

If the superior sees a brother becoming angry with another brother, he should admonish him, saying:

“What are you doing, brother? Perform your works with gentleness, silence, and love, for it is written: ‘Cease from anger and forsake wrath’” (Ps. 36). And again: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” [Col. 0974B] (1 John 3). And again: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5). Moreover, “an angry man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1). Nor is anyone permitted to fail to be reconciled with his enemy before sunset, as the Lord says through the Apostle: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4).

But if he sees a brother excessively inclined to laughter, the superior who is present should admonish him, saying:

“What are you doing, brother? Do what you are doing with gravity, for the time of conversion is not a time for joyful laughter; it is a time of repentance for mourning sins, as it is written: ‘Let us fall down before the Lord; let us weep before God who made us’” (Ps. 94). And again: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 125). Scripture also says: “Blessed are you who weep for a time, for you shall laugh forever; but the fool raises his voice in laughter” (Eccles. 21).

If he sees another brother cursing, the superior who is present should admonish him, saying:

“Restrain your mouth, brother, from cursing. Remember God, who said to us through the Apostle: ‘Bless, and do not curse’” (Rom. 12).

Just as a spring cannot bring forth both bitter and sweet water from one opening, so, when we bless God with our tongue, how can we use that same tongue to curse human beings, who have been fashioned in the image and likeness of God?

Likewise, if he sees the brethren, with loose bodies or unrestrained senses, carrying themselves with some frivolity, the superior who is present should admonish them, saying:

“Sit, walk, and stand with gravity, brothers, because the eyes of the Lord look upon us from heaven at every hour and in every place, both good and evil, as David says: ‘The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there are any who understand and seek God’” (Ps. 13).

Therefore let us fear, brothers, lest he see us at some hour turning toward evil and becoming useless, so that there is no one who does good—not even one. For the Prophet says: “You have hated those who observe vanity to no purpose” (Ps. 30). Whatever is not from God is from sin, and whatever does not edify destroys.

While these superiors diligently search out such things in the brethren entrusted to them, day and night and at every hour, they themselves also make progress as they guard others. By emptying others of evil, they occupy themselves at every hour with good; for they make a blessed mouth by causing good things spoken through it to enter another’s hearing.

Therefore, while the superior diligently guards the brethren, he should be required less strictly by the abbot in whatever labor has been assigned to him. For what he performs less with his hands in bodily work, he performs more through his vigilant spiritual sense in correction for God’s cause; and what he does less with his hands, he works more deeply in minds.

For this reason we have said that the work of any labor should be required less strictly of superiors, lest the pressing demands of bodily tasks assigned to them produce negligence in the spiritual guardianship with which the superiors are occupied, and God’s cause perish beneath the force of growing vices, when more effort is devoted to the nourishment of the flesh than to the labor required by God’s cause.

Trusting in hope, then, let us believe that the Lord God will provide everything necessary for our needs that our hands have been less able to accomplish. The Scripture of the holy Gospel strengthens us in all this, saying:

“Do not be anxious about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear, for the nations think about all these things, who have not known God. But seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. For your Father who is in heaven knows that you need all these things. Consider the birds of heaven: they neither plow nor sow, and your heavenly Father feeds them. How much more will he feed you?” (Matt. 6.)

The superiors should keep the clothing of the brethren under their care. Their beds should be near the beds of the brethren, so that any fault arising from their vices may be corrected during the night. We command that they sleep one to a bed, not two.

If, when he rises, a brother has not properly covered his bed again, he should receive no unmixed wine at the next meal as a punishment.

When they sleep, they should sleep clothed and belted, that is, with belts, thongs, or a leather strap. We prohibit a brother from using a *bracile* at night, lest, while turning in sleep under its pressure, the point of the knife should come out through its sheath and pierce his flesh. During the day, however, they should wear knife sheaths, as Scripture teaches concerning Saint John: “He was girded around the loins with a leather belt” (Luke 5).

For this reason we have said that the brethren should sleep clothed and belted, so that when the hour of God’s work arrives and the signal of the oratory sounds at night, they may immediately rise ready. Scripture says concerning this signal: “And my signal in the mornings—if I said, I will declare thus” (Ps. 71). It is called a signal because by its sound it signals that the hour for psalmody has arrived. Therefore the Prophet says of it: “If I said, I will declare thus”—that is, when it signals that the hour of psalmody has arrived, “thus I will declare the praises of the Lord.”

Therefore the brethren should sleep clothed and belted, because a brother is not permitted to touch his naked limbs. From this, impurities of lust are introduced into the soul. When the nakedness of the limbs is touched, desires for women immediately tickle the heart, and thus the limbs are defiled by uncleanness during sleep.

Above all, the brethren should sleep clothed and belted so that, when they seek their belongings or belts in the darkness, they do not lose some prayers or psalms because the brethren who are entering the oratory, watchful and ready, are already there while they, through negligence, are still turning over and scattering their beds in the darkness.

The superiors should have their beds near the beds of the brethren, as we have said, so that any fault arising from their vices may be corrected in them, and so that they may sleep more reverently in the presence of their superior. They should be present at their tables, so that they may eat silently and moderately with them.

If, in any place, a brother goes outside without the command of either the abbot or his superior, the matter must be diligently investigated by them.

# CHAPTER XII

## QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

On the excommunication of faults

## THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

In all the matters mentioned above, if any brother repeatedly proves stubborn, proud, murmuring, or disobedient to his superiors, and, after being admonished and corrected once, twice, or three times—or for any other vice—according to the divine command, does not amend, the superiors must report this to the abbot. The one who presides must weigh the matter according to the nature and seriousness of the fault and condemn him to an excommunication appropriate to it, so that the one who despises God may know how he deserves to be judged for the contempt he has shown toward his superior. The Lord himself said to our teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

Let such be the penalty of excommunication.

# CHAPTER XIII

## QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

How an excommunicated brother should be treated

## THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 0976C] When the superiors have reported to the abbot the offense of the disobedient man, he must no longer be called a brother, but a heretic against the law; no longer a son of God, but a worker of the devil, who, by destroying the works of the saints, has been produced like a kind of scab in the flock.

The abbot should summon him in the presence of his superiors, with the rest of the community standing around. The abbot should ask his superiors what he has done wrong and how many times he was warned about that vice without correcting it; they should answer and state what they accuse him of.

When he has heard the fault, the abbot should address him with this voice:

“O wretched soul, what answer will you give to God, whom by your disobedience you provoke every day when you approach to worship him? Why, under God’s dominion, do you serve mammon instead? Why do you lie to Christ, another Judas?

“That Judas sold justice for the price of iniquity; you tear apart the Christian name by your evil deeds. That Judas produced a scandal for the Lord through a false peace; you, under the name of holy service, are all the more rebellious against God. That Judas, a false disciple, betrayed his teacher; you, a Christian under a holy name, follow the devil all the more by your deeds.

“Our admonition, or your own spirit—which, together with the flesh, you resist by your own will—will have you stand at the judgment, saying before God’s tribunal of dreadful judgment:

“‘Lord, he refused to understand so as to do good; he meditated iniquity and stood upon every path that was not good’ (Ps. 36). ‘He did not hate wickedness, but gloried in it; he was mighty in iniquity.’

“When you have been accused of these things at the judgment, after hearing both our voice and that of the dreadful Judge himself, you will hear him say to you:

“‘You are the one who hated discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit. Sitting, you slandered your brother and placed a stumbling block in his way. All day long your tongue devised injustice. Like a sharp razor you practiced deceit; you loved wickedness more than kindness, and iniquity more than speaking righteousness. You loved every word of precipitous speech with a deceitful tongue.

“‘You did these things, and I was silent. You thought that I was like you in wickedness. I will rebuke you and set it before your face, so that God may destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from your dwelling, and your root from the land of the living’ (Ps. 49, 51).

“Then all the righteous, in their glory at the judgment, will see you when you have been separated from them and placed on the left among the goats. They will laugh at you and say:

“‘Behold the man who did not set God as his helper, but prevailed in his vanity, and there was no fear of God before his eyes’ (Ps. 51). For he acted deceitfully in his presence and said in the folly of his heart: ‘God will not inquire; he has turned his face away so as not to see forever’ (Ps. 9).

“He did not know that the time of those who lie to the Lord will come, for eternal punishment.

“What will you say to God in response to these things? What excuses for your sins will you, wretched man, bring before him, when your own evil deeds will first attack you and gehenna will await you in order to set you ablaze?”

After this rebuking speech, before the congregation, the abbot should immediately order him to be expelled from the oratory and the common table, and he should be designated an outsider. Once he has been identified as an enemy of God, from that hour he must no longer be a friend to the brethren.

Therefore, from the hour of this excommunication, the superior should assign to him, alone and separated from the others, some labor to prevent idleness. He must not be joined in that labor by the assistance of any brother, nor be consoled by anyone’s speech; all must pass him by in silence and without looking at him. If he asks for a blessing, no one should answer him, “God bless you.” Whatever is handed to him, no one should make the sign over it. Whatever he performs voluntarily or in addition to the work assigned to him should be scattered or destroyed. Let him be alone everywhere, and let his only consolation be his fault.

If the abbot, because of the lightness of the fault, does not wish to double his fasts, then, if the brethren eat at the sixth hour, he should eat at the ninth hour from a single dish, and the superior should give him, as an act of mercy, a fragment of ordinary bread and water. If the blameless brethren eat at the ninth hour, the meal described above for him should be postponed until evening, so that he may feel what evils his fault has brought him and what good things he has lost through negligence.

But if any brother, openly or secretly, speaks or associates with him, he should immediately undergo with him the common penalty of excommunication and be held guilty by all. He should be separated by his superior for another work, and should himself be separated and alone both from that guilty man and from everyone else; immediately he too should be deprived of conversation with all.

Nor should he himself attain pardon from his superior unless an equivalent satisfaction of repentance has been performed by them both: the first because he was disobedient in the vice or sin, the second because he gave the evil-doer the reward of consolation.

A brother who has committed a light fault and has not corrected himself after the first, second, and third admonition concerning any vice should be excommunicated from the table, but not from the oratory. This excommunication should remain without violation for as long as the offender, with his head bowed to his knees in greater humility, promises that he will amend in the future.

But a brother who has committed a grave fault should be excommunicated from both places—that is, from the oratory and from the table. He should not obtain the superior’s forgiveness unless, prostrated before the threshold of the oratory, he has satisfied God and everyone by a tearful voice during the hours when the psalms cease, promising amendment.

Nevertheless, if the abbot wishes, because the weight of the fault is insignificant, to consent more quickly to forgiveness, the following page will show what the Lord dictates.

The brother who has been excommunicated from the table but not from the oratory must not impose an antiphon or reading until he has made satisfaction for that fault by promising amendment, either kneeling before the present abbot or before his own superior.

But if excommunicated brethren become so proud that, persisting in the pride of their hearts, they refuse on the third day at the ninth hour to make satisfaction to the abbot, they should be flogged under guard with rods until death. If the abbot wishes, they should be expelled from the monastery, because such a life has no need of bodily necessities or of the fellowship of brethren whom death possesses in a proud soul.

Such men rightly deserve to be slaughtered with blows and expelled, since they are not worthy to be with Christ, the Lord of humility. Instead, let them be separated from God’s eternal promises, together with their author, the devil, who was cast down from the kingdoms of heaven because of his pride.

Let us therefore continue, as we began, with the foregoing meaning of excommunications and satisfaction. We believe that God and the abbot accept the manner and satisfaction of this repentance.

# CHAPTER XIV

## QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

How an excommunicated brother should repent

## THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the hour of the office is being celebrated in the oratory—that is, when the psalm has been completed and everyone has devoted himself to prayer—the person guilty of excommunication should lie prostrate before the threshold of the oratory and cry out the following with tears:

“I have sinned, and I acknowledge my sin. I have gone astray; I promise to amend. From now on I will sin no more. Pray for me, holy community, from which I deserved to be separated through my negligence and the devil’s persuasion. Pray for me, my former superiors. Forgive me, good shepherd, pious shepherd and abbot. Leave the ninety-nine for the sake of the one. Come, gather me again, and carry me, the lost sheep, upon your shoulders, as our Lord showed you by the sign of his Passion; for he came and died not for the just but for sinners” (Matt. 18).

“And with him, through his justice, we shall rise again—we who had been struck down by our sins—for the Lord himself said: ‘I came only for the lost sheep of Israel’” (Matt. 15). And: “The physician is not needed by the healthy, but by those who are ill” (Matt. 9).

“Imitate the merciful teacher of the apostles, whose office you exercise in the monastery through instruction. For after the prophets and apostles he appointed you shepherds and teachers of discipline. Through the blessed Apostle Peter he also showed you that a brother’s sin must be forgiven not seven times but seventy times seven” (Matt. 18).

“Raise up, therefore, the one struck down by your saving counsel. Through your intercession before the Lord, release what negligence has bound in me. I acknowledge that I have sinned; I believe that I will amend, because through your admonition I find the way.”

After this speech has been poured out by the offender lying there, while everyone ceases from the psalms for prayer, and when the sacred office of the oratory has been completed, with the offender still lying before the threshold, the entire congregation leaving with the abbot should humble itself on its knees for him, together with his superiors.

When this has been done, if the abbot wishes in that same hour, because of the lightness of the fault, to consent to forgiveness, he should immediately order his superiors to raise him up. After his fault has been reproached to him and he has answered that he will amend in the future, the abbot should immediately say to the whole congregation:

“Come, brothers, with one accord and with tears, for this sheep of your flock, which, acknowledging its sin, promises to amend in the future. Let us reconcile him through prayer in the oratory before God, whom he provoked by his disobedience.”

Then the abbot, together with the brethren, should enter the oratory. Before they pray, his superiors should take him by the right and left hands outside and lead him into the oratory, both saying this verse:

“Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 117).

The rest of the congregation should follow, responding:

“For his mercy endures forever.”

Thus, while the superiors outside impose confession upon the penitent through this verse, the merciful God should immediately promise mercy inside the oratory through the mouths of the responding brethren.

When his superiors have led him into the oratory, they should prostrate him at the feet of the altar, and all, together with the abbot, should immediately prostrate themselves in prayer for him.

Then he who has been prostrated for his fault should pray to the Lord with tears in these words:

“I have sinned, Lord; I have sinned, and I myself acknowledge my iniquity. I ask and beg you: forgive me, Lord, forgive me. Do not drag me away together with my sins, and do not condemn me in the lower parts of the earth. Do not charge my evils against me forever, for you are the God of repentance. Show your goodness in me according to your great mercy, because you have said, Lord: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’” (Ezek. 33).

“Because of our evils, for the sake of amendment, you grant life to us all the more each day, as Scripture shows us when it speaks of your mercy: ‘Will he be angry throughout every day, unless you are converted?’” (Ps. 7).

“And your Apostle Paul says: ‘Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?’ The Lord has brandished his sword, bent his bow, and prepared it; and in it he has prepared vessels of death” (Rom. 1; Ps. 7).

“We fear those vessels, Lord; therefore we promise to amend swiftly.

“And because at the judgment you will say to the sinner: ‘You did these things, and I was silent. Will I be silent forever?’” (Ps. 49), you will set our iniquity before our face, so that, recognizing it in our guilt, we may justly condemn ourselves.

“For you, Lord, kill and make alive; you lead down to the underworld and bring back” (1 Sam. 2). You raise up those who are struck down; in heaven you release those bound on earth. By your grace you enlighten the eyes of our hearts for amendment, and by your help you direct the steps of the just, as Scripture says: ‘A man’s steps are directed by the Lord’” (Prov. 20).

“Unless you guard and build the house, those who build it labor in vain, and so do those who guard it” (Ps. 126). For willing is close to us, but accomplishing belongs to you. It belongs not to the one who wills or the one who runs, but to God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9).

“Nevertheless, you give us confidence to hope in you, saying: ‘Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For whoever asks receives, whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks it will be opened’” (Luke 11).

“And because you have said: ‘Turn to me, and I will turn to you’” (Zech. 1). “And when you cry out, I will say: ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isa. 58).

“And again, as the merciful and compassionate one toward your creation, you call us, unworthy servants though we are, to your grace, saying: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’” (Matt. 11).

“Therefore do not despise your servant, Lord, who acknowledges his sin, just as the Prophet promises concerning your mercy in relation to our guilt: ‘God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart’” (Ps. 50).

“For you are powerful enough to raise up children for Abraham from stones, since what our despair considers impossible in us, your grace declares possible.”

After these words have been completed with tears, the abbot should immediately raise him up with his own hand and say to him:

“See, brother, from now on; see that you do not sin, and undertake the proper repentance for this fault. If it is committed a second time, you will fall into the sect of the heretics.”

The former offender should immediately intone this verse, with everyone responding together:

“I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; gather your servant, Lord” (Ps. 118).

After this verse, the abbot should summon his superiors and restore him to their hands, saying:

“Receive your sheep, restore the number, restore him to the table. For he was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15).

On that same day, as a sign that his humility has been restored, he should himself minister water to the brethren as they enter for communion. As he gives it, he should first kiss the abbot’s hands and then the hands of each of the brethren, asking each one, as he ministers, to pray for him.

As soon as he has entered the oratory, he too should remind everyone in a loud voice that they must pray for him. Then, leaving with the brethren, he should proceed to the customary table.

We command that children up to fifteen years of age not be excommunicated, but be flogged for their faults. After fifteen years, however, it is appropriate that they no longer be flogged but excommunicated, since they already understand how they ought to repent and amend, at a mature age, what they do wrongly.

The one who sins should rightly repent in his heart, and the body should not be flogged on his account, because we use the body in service to the command of the mind. Therefore, when the soul commands and the body serves, the guilt of the one commanding is recognized as greater than that of the one serving.

For this reason, because amendment is understood, the root of the heart should be cleansed of the thorns of sins through excommunication. The branches of the body, upon which a sin has been unjustly imposed by the command of the heart against the will of the body, should not suffer punishment for another’s fault.

Those brethren beyond fifteen years of age should be flogged who have committed a very serious fault, whether theft, flight, or some other criminal offense.

# CHAPTER XV

## QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

[Col. 0981B]

On the disclosure of an evil thought to the superiors or the abbot by the junior brethren

## THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER
The brothers are then the branches of the tree of the world, if its wood is cleansed from the root. For it is not fitting that the royal chambers be cleansed outwardly while the room within is defiled by filth; rather, it is properly done when the filth has been expelled from within to the outside, and only then the exterior is rightly cleansed. Trenches cannot be secure when an enemy is within. Likewise, the gate is held captive within its own enclosure when the walls do not repel the enemy but contain him inside. For a wound knows how to swell when filled with corruption; and unless it is squeezed, and the pus expelled from it outwardly, and the suppuration itself cleansed by being pressed out, it can hollow out its evil more deeply.

Let us therefore understand this likewise of our soul: first we must cast out from the heart what we do not wish to carry in the body, saying to ourselves: “Why are you silent, soul, and do not burst forth in speech, displaying the ardor of your mind, and, once the very heat of evil has been cast out from within, providing relief to the suffering that has been wearied?” Therefore, when an evil thought has come into a brother’s heart and he feels himself troubled by it, let him immediately confess it to his superiors; and then, after prayer has been made, let them report the matter to the abbot.

The superiors themselves must always of their own accord inquire about this from those entrusted to them, lest perhaps, through the simplicity of some or, indeed, because shame itself causes evil things, a brother be ashamed to confess wicked or shameful matters. But when they have gained courage because the superior has taken the initiative, let them then confidently, without shame, disclose their sinful thoughts. The superiors themselves, if they too experience something of this kind, must report it concerning themselves to the abbot.

When the superior himself feels this in his own heart, let him ask in the oratory that the whole congregation pray for him. Therefore, when the superiors have reported concerning a brother to the abbot, let him immediately summon the whole congregation and say to everyone:

“Come, brothers; let us help one another through love before the Lord, as the Apostle says: ‘Brothers, if anyone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual, correct such a one in a spirit of gentleness; console the fainthearted’ (Galatians VI), ‘considering yourself, lest you also be tempted’; and, ‘You who stand, take heed lest you fall’ (I Corinthians X). Let us therefore pray with one accord to the Lord for this brother of ours, that he may deign, by the sign of his cross or by the command of his power, to restrain the devil’s temptations in him.”

When everyone had prayed for him at length, the abbot rose with them all and completed the prayer. Then, as they went out, let each return to the work he had been doing. Keeping only the brother who was suffering from the evil thought with him, let the abbot bring out books and, as a divine medicine suited to the necessity of his wound, let something be read against it. During the days when that brother is questioned by the abbot, if he should happen to answer that the thought has not passed during the hours at which reading normally takes place, whether in winter or in summer, let that decada to which the brother belongs read passages from the books relevant to the very need caused by the thought. [Col. 0982B]

For example, if it has suggested fornication to him, let passages be read from different books in which God loves chastity. If it frequently suggests falsehood, let passages be read from various books in which he commands truth. If it is some desire for the world, let passages be read in which the Lord commands that temporal things be despised and the eternal kingdoms of heaven sought.

For this reason the abbot ought to be very well instructed in the law, so that he may teach everything either through testimonies or by assigning passages relevant to the matter to be read. When a disciple who has been sick has therefore been refreshed with such nourishment, does he not recover not only his former strength but also acquire new strength against the enemy, while the adversary loses what he had thought he possessed?

Accordingly, on the following morning the abbot must question that disciple whether the hostile thought has ceased or not. If he answers that it has not ceased, a fast is to be imposed upon everyone. If, when questioned again on another day, he likewise answers that it has not passed, wine is to be withheld from everyone’s meal. For, God forbid, if on the third occasion we should already be judged to have little faith, as though we were slow to believe that God’s aid can come to us.

Moreover, we know that he is exceedingly merciful and compassionate and ready to fulfill his promise, because God does not forget to show mercy, “nor will he restrain his mercies in his anger” (Psalm LXXVI). Therefore, as we said above, if, when questioned again on the third day, he answers that it has not passed, oil is likewise to be withheld from the meal along with the wine, so that no one may perish through the labor of many or the affliction of abstinence, but all may escape; and so that amid the afflictions of all, the remedy of divine mercy may be hoped for, fulfilling the apostolic command, which says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians VI).

A brother who is being sent on a journey must also be warned by his superiors to be vigilant against the devil at every hour and in every place. The devil leads us away on the road and wishes to drag us with him into Gehenna, since he does not allow a human being to ascend to heaven by doing good, from which he himself was cast down because of pride. Therefore, the servant of Christ must remain watchful in every place, even without the presence of a superior, and carefully guard himself both against evil deeds and against wicked thoughts.

The brother must also be warned that whenever any thought comes to him, he should immediately fall to his knees, with his neck bowed toward the ground, or with the sign of the cross traced upon his forehead, and hasten to the Lord with prayers, so that he may deign to defend his soldiers from the devil. For vices, unless they are restrained while small, cannot be curbed when they become great; and when evil thoughts are fulfilled in deeds, perfect death is acquired from perfected sin. [Col. 0983A]

## CHAPTER XVI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the monastery’s cellarer: what sort of person he ought to be.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Brothers, every work has its reward, because wages are owed to a deserving laborer, and “you shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain” (Deuteronomy XXV). The labors of their own fruits also make the one who eats blessed (Psalm CXXVII), because the Lord subjected all things to the feet of the human being whom he created, for whose sake he created everything.

Therefore, if various created provisions serve the unjust and the enemies of God—that is, unbelieving pagans, heretics, and various sinners—and the whole world serves different purposes, how much more has the Lord justly and worthily entrusted to those who believe in God and serve him well the various creatures that he created for their life? Like a pledge of the future promise, by supplying in the present time everything necessary for life, “the Lord will not forsake those who seek him.” For “the rich have become poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing” (Psalm XXXIII). The Lord fills the hungry with good things and sends the rich away empty; thus, “as having nothing, yet possessing everything.”

The cellarer of the monastery is therefore nothing other than a steward of divine things—so truly divine that in the Gospel the Lord promises this to his faithful servants, saying: “Do not be concerned about what you shall eat, or what you shall drink, or what you shall wear” (Matthew VI). He likewise warns that no one should be anxious about tomorrow, saying: “Seek the kingdom and the righteousness of God, and all these things shall be added to you. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (ibid.).

Therefore, if the Lord supplies what is necessary for life to those who serve him, and our Lord, the heavenly Father, knows what we need and provides it, you see that our provisions, when they are prepared for us by him, are the Lord’s gifts. Just as a servant of an earthly master—though his master is another human being—is concerned only with rendering his service and is secure about the grain, clothing, and footwear supplied by his master, how much more does our heavenly Lord rightly command us not to worry about the necessities of our life? For if one human being, serving another human being, is believed capable of preparing what is needed for him, how much more can everything serve those who believe in or serve God, who created all these things and is powerful enough to bring everything to completion?

“For I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring begging bread” (Psalm XXXVI); rather, “all day long he is merciful and lends.” Therefore, when we are concerned only with our service in seeking his kingdom and righteousness, let us believe that the Lord supplies everything for us, since he freely promises to provide us with all necessities.

Therefore, if all the monastery’s provisions, which the Lord distributes as food for his workers, are badly or fraudulently distributed by the cellarer and are wasted, let the aforesaid cellarer know that on the day of divine judgment he will be examined before the tribunal through an accounting, when the Lord sees that the food of his servants has been squandered through negligence. For what the Lord justly gives to the deserving, he does not permit the destroyers to waste undeservedly.

Let the cellarer give, distribute, or expend nothing without the abbot’s command; nor, in the abbot’s presence, let him offer anything to a sick person without an order. Let the cellarer give alms with the abbot’s command and in his presence. In the abbot’s absence, however, let him be permitted to offer alms to a poor person who asks, because of the Lord’s command, which says: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke VI). And again: “Give, lest, by your not giving to someone, he himself should be Christ.” [Col. 0984B]

Every day the cellarer, together with the weekly servers, must receive Communion in the oratory before the abbot and the congregation. When the weekly kitchen servers enter upon their week, he himself shall hand over the kitchen vessels to them; when the week is completed, he shall receive them back clean from those who are leaving, to be handed over to those who enter.

If any monastery vessel is broken through someone’s negligence, the one who broke it must not approach the table before he has made satisfaction to the abbot in penitence, bending his knees in humility. After all the necessities have been brought out from the cellar, let the cellarer sit silently at table with the congregation and eat. If the cellarer rises to bring something, everyone at the table where he had been sitting and eating must wait for him until he returns.

The cellarer should undertake some task of labor during those hours when no care, diligence, or distribution pertaining to the cellarer’s office is being carried out, so that he is not idle during those hours.

If he is absent from the oratory because of his duties, the abbot should tell the brothers to remember him in prayer. Likewise, if the cellarer’s office is near the oratory, let the cellarer himself ask in his own voice that he be remembered in the prayers. Nevertheless, while so occupied with his work, let him quietly say the work of God to himself and follow the voice or verse of the oratory.

He rightly ought to be remembered by everyone within the oratory, since he is occupied with concern for all; and just as one person takes care of the common benefit of all, so the prayer of all should be shared with that one person.

The vices of his mouth and body must be guarded by the abbot himself, because the cellarer is not contained under a superior within the number of any decada. Otherwise, since the flesh loves what belongs to it, the work of God might be neglected because of some appetite or provision for gluttony, and a carnal indulgence might be devised for the sake of food or drink. [Col. 0984D]

He himself must receive all the monastery’s utensils according to number and hand them over to different persons. Of everything in the monastery apart from the abbot, no one may claim or defend anything as his own—whether what he brought, found, worked for, or acquired—as private property, because this is the judgment of the Rule: “The property of the monastery belongs to everyone and to no one.”

The cellarer should be a brother whom the abbot has tested and found faithful and temperate, whom the desire for food never overcomes, and who does not greatly love eating or drinking. Otherwise, greater opportunity may be given to the devil, as Scripture says: “Do not give an occasion to those who seek one”; and it may appear that provision is being made for the gluttony of voracious or greedy brothers rather than that it is being restrained. [Col. 0985A]

## CHAPTER XVII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the monastery’s tools and possessions.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

The monastery’s tools are to be kept in one room, and the abbot shall entrust responsibility for preserving them to one brother whose diligence he has recognized. That brother shall distribute them daily to the brothers for their work according to number, and shall likewise receive them back clean from those who have finished using them and put them away, while the abbot keeps a brief inventory of everything.

If a brother does not bring a clean tool back from the field, he shall be accused at table by the keeper of the tools and, as a penalty, receive one slice less from his portion of bread at the meal until he has made satisfaction or promised correction. For the tool rusts when it has not been put away clean.

The same brother shall also keep account of the whetstones, shoe sponges, towels, tablecloths, and sheets that have been assigned. He shall likewise keep the chest containing the abbot’s possessions; the chests of the various decadae containing the brothers’ possessions, together with the superiors’ locks; the chest containing the curtains, veils, and furnishings of the monastery; and the chest containing the monastery’s various books, parchments, and documents.

He shall also keep the chest containing the possessions of the brothers who have recently entered the monastery, which are ordered to be preserved, God forbid, because of a return to the world. He shall likewise keep all the products of the craftsmen which those laboring in the various crafts have handed in as completed for the day.

The brother shall receive completed items and put them away, while returning unfinished items individually to the workers on the following day. He shall likewise receive the tools of all the crafts from the various craftsmen in the evening and distribute them in the morning.

He shall also preserve in the room the chest containing the possessions recently brought into the monastery by donation, together with the abbot’s lock. He shall pay out all accounts of the monastery’s expenses in the monastery’s money at the abbot’s direction. Therefore that brother ought to be bound by divine faith, so that through fear and testimony of God he may faithfully fulfill what has been entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER XVIII [Col. 0985D]

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the weekly kitchen servers.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

We said above that each decada of brothers contains two superiors under its care. These two, in alternating pairs, shall have the ten brothers complete seven days each in kitchen service. When the service of one decada has been completed in these turns, after all the utensils have been handed over by the cellarer, another decada shall follow it in the exercise of service; when that has been completed, they shall succeed one another individually, week by week.

Each of the two superiors, however, shall cook with the assistance of whichever of his brothers he wishes. Thus, although we have said that each superior is to cook for a week with the assistance of any brother, we have said that each is to cook separately so that, when both are not occupied together in kitchen service, one may remain outside with the brothers of his decada and watch over their various faults and vices.

If other brothers are assigned to another work, let those be assigned who are better able to fear God’s presence, while one superior is occupied in the kitchen and the less diligent superior remains outside. Thus they may fulfill the honor of correcting in turn and practice the humility of serving in turn.

Therefore, as all complete their decadae, let them take turns again; for each decada shall complete seven days according to this arrangement. Two brothers are to be assigned by their superiors to kitchen service for a week, and the cellarer shall hand over all the kitchen vessels to them as they enter. The reason for having two brothers is that they may help one another through mutual assistance. The entrance into the week of this arrangement shall be as follows.

## CHAPTER XIX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How should the brothers enter upon the week of kitchen service?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

The brothers who are about to enter upon the week shall, after Prime has been recited in the oratory, be brought by their superiors before the abbot. The superior shall make a petition concerning them, saying:

“Command, lord abbot, that the whole congregation be summoned and pray for these brothers who are entering upon the week of kitchen service, so that, commended by your prayers, they may deserve not to fear the devil’s obstacles and may complete everything for God’s congregation without fault.”

After these words, the two brothers shall prostrate themselves in prayer before the abbot. The entire congregation, together with the abbot, must likewise do this behind them. When everyone has risen, the two brothers shall say this verse:

“Guard us, Lord, as the apple of the eye; protect us under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm XVI).

After everyone has prayed for them, the aforesaid two brothers shall rise, kiss the abbot’s knees, and give the peace to their superiors or to the whole congregation. After the peace has been given, their superiors shall say to them:

“Thus, brothers, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ: enter upon the week, and, having asked for a blessing, do everything, saying throughout all the tasks to be performed: ‘Bless.’ For once it has been blessed, whenever you carry it out, the accursed devil will have no power there to impede it.”

From that same day onward, every day, if the brothers are to eat at the sixth hour, the weekly servers, together with the cellarer, shall leave the oratory after Terce has been said, keeping their eyes upon the abbot and asking what he commands should be prepared for the congregation’s meal. Thus, as soon as they begin work in the kitchen at Terce and everything has been prepared, when Sext has been said they may go to the tables.

If the meal is to be at the ninth hour, the abbot shall be questioned by the weekly servers and the cellarer as he leaves after Sext, and immediately after Sext they shall begin cooking, so that when None has been said everyone may go to table.

If the weekly servers should fail to appear, they shall receive the penalty of excommunication, because through their laziness they have afflicted the congregation, wearied by both kinds of labor—that is, fasting and work. [Col. 0987A]

The sentence of excommunication shall be as follows: if the meal is at Sext, seven; if at None, ten. That is, if the weekly servers delay the meal at the sixth hour and fail to appear, they shall lose one slice of bread at each of the next seven meals. If they delay the meal at None, one slice shall likewise be taken from them at each of the next ten meals.

This sentence of excommunication shall remain as a loss of food for the excommunicated until the satisfaction promised on the following day has visibly brought correction.

If the congregation is large or many outsiders have arrived, the brothers assigned to assist them shall begin cooking after questioning the abbot about the meal from the time of Prime, so that they may be ready for the meal at the appointed hour.

During that same week, they alone shall perform all the service at the tables and exercise all the monastery’s duties. During that week all the brothers shall remove the shoes from their feet, with brothers from their decada assigned to assist them. They shall remove the shoes together and care for the footwear; in the morning, when the brothers are seated in order, they shall distribute it.

During the same week they shall also perform the monastery’s cleaning, wash the cooling vessels, chop wood, and provide water for washing the face. When the brothers enter for Communion, they shall themselves provide water for washing their hands. They shall wash the tablecloths, sheets, towels, and the brothers’ dirty garments during those hours when they are not cooking.

They shall light and tend every day the monastery’s candles made by the cellarer. As soon as they enter upon the week, as we have said, on the first day after Prime has been said, let the first task of their service be to clean the oratory and spread the mats across the floor of the oratory. Throughout all seven days of their week, after the Sunday Matins, they shall perform this as the first task of their service for the oratory.

While they are on their week of service, upon entering the kitchen they shall immediately ask the brothers who come to them to pray with them for their sake.

## CHAPTER XX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How should those who are absent be remembered in the oratory?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the weekly servers are occupied outside in kitchen service out of concern for the whole congregation, or the cellarer in the cellar, or the keeper of the tools or of the monastery’s possessions is occupied with the responsibility entrusted to him, their superiors shall say to the whole congregation inside the oratory:

“Keep the Lord in mind, and pray for those who are outside.”

If some are absent from the oratory and are occupied on the monastery’s business, or have gone on a journey, the abbot shall tell the whole congregation that the absent are to be remembered in prayer, just as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Pray for the absent” (Acts XII)—that is, when Peter was in prison, prayer was made for him in all the churches.

Therefore, if those occupied outside are not remembered in the oratory, they receive their full reward from God outside, while those inside depart empty. For the latter were free to pray inside because the former, outside, had made them secure by preparing the necessities of life.

It is right that the absent person be remembered in prayer inside, because he is occupied with concern for all; and just as one person is occupied with the common benefit of all, so the prayer of all should be shared with that one person.

The person who is occupied outside for the monastery’s benefit must also observe this: when those inside have completed the psalms in the oratory and devote themselves to prayer, he should ask in a clear voice that the oratory remember him in prayer, while he himself says the work of God in the same place where he is occupied.

The abbot must admonish everyone that the sick are to be remembered throughout every prayer. If a visiting brother from the monastery has gone on a journey, the abbot shall likewise tell the congregation at the next work of God that he is to be remembered. For when he departed, that brother himself asked everyone, saying: “You have the Lord; pray for me, and remember me through your angel.” [Col. 0988B]

## CHAPTER XXI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How should the weekly kitchen servers and the cellarer receive Communion?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When everyone stands in the oratory before the abbot for Communion, after all have received the peace, and the abbot has communicated, no one else should communicate immediately after him. Instead, the superiors of those weekly servers should immediately ask permission to go outside, so that they may bring the weekly servers to Communion in the oratory, taking their place outside.

As those superiors go out, one shall preside over the kitchen and the other shall set out the serving vessels. When they have gone outside, the weekly servers, after washing their hands, shall immediately enter and pray briefly. After the prayer they shall give the peace only to the abbot.

They shall do this only to him so that, by giving it to everyone, they do not delay the hour of the congregation’s meal, and, by leaving late, fail to prepare what is necessary, forcing the abbot, when the congregation leaves, to turn toward anger because the things needed have still not been prepared by them.

Therefore, after a brief prayer, let them rise, receive Communion, and be strengthened. Then, after again praying briefly, let them rise, receive Communion, and be strengthened; and, while the abbot slowly says the verse for them, let him conclude, so that when they leave they may bring their superiors back into the oratory.

As they leave, the abbot shall say to them:

“See, brothers, that before the common prayer at the table you do not, at the devil’s suggestion, presume to take anything of food or drink. Even if we who are placed here inside see you outside, God, who is present everywhere, sees everything, and nothing is hidden from him, observes you himself. Beware lest, when he sees your presumption, he hand your mind over to a reprobate sense and your thefts be consigned to you as punishment in judgment.”

After this warning, as they go out together with the cellarer, one shall return to the kitchen, and the other shall complete whatever his superior has not fully prepared: that is, they shall prepare the tables, arrange the sacred vessels, set out the serving vessels, and scour the cups, so that when the abbot leaves with the congregation he finds everything prepared. The bread rations for everyone shall likewise be placed in a basket hanging above the abbot’s table.

When the abbot finds everything prepared as he leaves, there will be no occasion for anger, heat, or shouting, but the monastery will be a place of silence and peace. [Col. 0989A]

## CHAPTER XXII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

After all the weekly servers have gone out, in what order should the others remaining in the oratory receive Communion from the abbot?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

After the abbot’s Communion, the superior whom he has appointed to stand beside him in his place shall communicate, and his decada shall follow him one by one. When they have completed this, another superior shall communicate, and his decada shall likewise follow him individually.

If, with the Lord’s help, the congregation is larger, let the succeeding groups do the same. They must stand in the oratory in the same way as they are ordered to receive Communion.

If a brother becomes puffed up at Communion and refuses to communicate, let him be dismissed and abstain. When he later wishes to communicate, he shall not be permitted to do so for as long as he remained puffed up without cause; for that same length of time the abbot or superior shall rightly be angry with him in this matter.
