Likewise, if someone becomes puffed up and refuses to come to table, let him be dismissed and not be permitted to eat at the next meal; rather, let him be raised from the table after he has sat down. For when the abbot wished it, he refused; and again, when he wished it, the abbot rightly refused.

The superiors or other brothers shall stand beside the abbot in turn each day in the oratory, so that the subordinate rank may always be kept unsettled. Thus no one, secure or elated because of his rank, may drive the others to despair; instead, let all eagerly strive to attain the hope of honor through the merits of good works, not through a title. We shall speak again of the character of this matter, with the Lord dictating it.

After the abbot, and at his command, the superiors shall always intone antiphons from one or the other choir. When these have been completed, at the abbot’s command the lesser brothers who have been called by name shall intone them individually from the other choirs, alternately from this choir and then from the other.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

After the abbot has left the oratory, how should the weekly servers serve the tables, and how should they share in the common meal?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the entire congregation has gone out of the oratory with its shepherd, after the verses and prayer the abbot shall sit in the chair at his table. Immediately the entire congregation shall respond: “Thanks be to God.”

While everyone is still standing at his table, the basket hanging above the abbot’s table shall descend by the rope of the pulley, so that it may appear that food is descending from heaven for God’s workers. As soon as the basket has descended, the abbot shall make the sign of the cross over all the bread, break it, first take his own portion to be blessed by the Lord, raise his hand, and place it before himself. While those who are to eat with him stand at his table, he shall distribute the portions to them. As soon as they have received them, they shall kiss the abbot’s hand and sit silently.

Then, having summoned the superiors of one table, he shall give them the provisions for their entire table. After dismissing them, he shall summon the others and give them theirs as well. If, with the Lord’s help, the congregation is large, let him do this for all the tables.

When the superiors receive both their own portions and those of their brothers, they shall kiss the abbot’s hands in honor of the superior. Likewise, when they themselves distribute the portions to their brothers at their tables, the brothers shall kiss their hands. After anyone has received his portion, he shall sit silently.

After everyone has sat down, the weekly reader at the tables shall rise. Receiving his own portion, he shall kiss the hand of the giver, entrust the portion to the cellarer, and sit again on his chair with the book until the weekly kitchen servers enter with the cellarer. They too, receiving their portions from their superiors, shall kiss their hands.

The cellarer, since he is not included under the number of any decada, shall receive his portion from the abbot’s hand. When he has received it, he too shall kiss the hand of the giver and place it at his table.

First they shall offer individual cups of unmixed wine to the abbot, then to everyone, including themselves and those at the end. Immediately the weekly servers shall go and serve first at the abbot’s table. Then the dishes for the various tables, brought by the lower-ranking brothers, shall be presented to the abbot for him to bless.

Everything placed on the tables, whether cooked or raw, shall likewise be signed. The one who makes the sign of the cross shall say aloud:

“Bless, Lord, whatever we are about to receive from this point onward.”

This is so that, if perhaps something is unnecessary, is cleaned away, falls, or does not contribute to nourishment, it may be thrown onto the ground without a blessing and trampled underfoot, lest a blessed thing appear to suffer injury.

The dishes that have been signed shall then be placed individually on the tables. When they have served them, the weekly servers shall sit with the cellarer at their superior’s table and eat together with the congregation.

When this has been completed, the weekly servers shall rise. One shall remove the dishes; the other shall first place a basin with water on the abbot’s table so that the brothers may wash the abbot’s hands. After it has been taken away, similar basins shall be placed individually on the tables. When everyone there has washed his hands, the basin shall be put aside.

Immediately, according to the number at the first table, measured portions of drink shall be mixed by them in a single jug. The one who has mixed it shall taste the drink from a cup after asking for a blessing, to see whether it has been mixed to an equal strength, and shall distribute it to everyone at the first table.

After these portions have been distributed, they shall go to the second table, remix a quantity according to its number, and, after again asking for a blessing and tasting it to ensure equal strength, distribute it to that table as well.

When they reach the table where the weekly servers and the cellarer are sitting, they shall add their portions to the number, and after everyone else they too shall drink, having asked for a blessing.

Whenever this vessel is mixed, before it is tasted or distributed it shall be offered to the abbot for his blessing. If the abbot is absent, the superiors shall sign, at their respective tables, the dishes brought to them and the vessels mixed with the drinks, taking turns at their own tables.

If any drink has been mixed in a cup, or hot liquid has been added to it, when someone wishes to drink he shall say again: “Bless,” so that what has been added may also be requested to be blessed by the Lord.

When the service of drinks has been completed, the weekly servers shall go outside to bring another dish. When they have brought it, they shall sit silently in their places and eat. After that dish has been finished, the weekly servers shall rise and remove it.

Again, according to the number at each table, they shall distribute a vessel signed by the abbot, mixed after it has been tasted with a blessing; and they too shall drink last in the same way.

After this has been completed, the cellarer shall rise and receive the cooked dishes brought by them, and shall bring in whatever raw food belongs to the cellarer’s service. After bringing out, signing, and placing these things in their proper places on the tables, they shall sit again silently and eat.

When these have been removed, the weekly servers shall first clean the bread crumbs from the abbot’s table, then those from the various tables, with reverence. As the crumbs are collected from each table, the weekly servers shall say with one voice: “Thanks be to God.”

As we have said, they shall gather them daily into one vessel and reverently hand them over to the cellarer for safekeeping. At the end of their week, little cakes shall be cooked from them, as the following title will show.

When the crumbs have been cleaned away, the customary measure of drink shall immediately be distributed by the weekly servers as prescribed; after asking for a blessing, they too shall drink last in the same way.

We have said that the weekly servers and the cellarer are to take part together at the tables so that no one at all may eat outside, apart from the others, secretly, or without restraint. Rather, the measure of temperance and sobriety must be common to all. For whatever is eaten secretly is done fraudulently; and to satisfy gluttony, one sins without measure.

When the duties at the tables have been completed and everyone has risen as the abbot rises, the entire congregation, together with the weekly servers and the cellarer, shall immediately say: “Thanks be to God.”

After this has been said, everyone shall attend at once to giving thanks to God through prayer. To ensure that no one is absent, the superiors shall count their decadae, so that just as all were present together at the tables, they may also be seen to be present at prayer. For prayer must open and close every food and drink with verses.

If a brother was not present to say the first verse at the table, he shall not sit at table with the brothers. Instead, he shall eat separately from an individual bowl, without a blessing having been given, unblessed and unsigned; and an unblessed drink shall be handed to him separately, mixed without the sign. Until he rises, no one shall speak with him. If he is spiritual, he should grieve that he has eaten without God.

If a brother was not present for the later verse at the end of the meal, at the next meal he too shall be separated from the table and eat and drink without the sign. These excommunications shall remain upon them for as long as, humbled in satisfaction with their heads bowed to their knees, they have promised correction to their superior.

If the weekly servers, while carrying out the service of the tables, should happen not to be able to serve everyone, they shall report this to their superiors. The superiors shall immediately assign one brother from the same decada to assist them.

Whenever the weekly servers have negligently served the tables, the next day at the meal hour the abbot shall rise and, together with one of the superiors—or two, if the congregation is large—shall himself perform the service at all the tables. Thus he may teach them how to do what they are unable to complete; and, recognizing this, all the brothers may be ashamed that, within the common human condition and in equal service of God, they have not been found worthy of an equal share in divine wisdom with their useful brothers. [Col. 0992A]

## CHAPTER XXIV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the weekly reader at the tables.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER
In both the summer and winter seasons, when the meal is taken at the sixth or ninth hour, [Col. 0992B] let the respective superiors from each group of ten take turns exercising the office of reading at the tables for one week at a time. But then let no superior read for the group of ten from which another superior is occupied in kitchen service, lest, while one reads and the other cooks, there be no one present at the tables to correct the faults of their brothers. When these superiors have each completed their successive weeks of reading at the tables, let them appoint literate brothers, one at a time for successive weeks, to read, so that all the literate brothers may in turn read from the various groups of ten. After all the brothers have completed their weeks of reading, let the superiors begin again in turn, so that divine food may never be lacking at the bodily meal, as Scripture says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. IV), so that they may refresh the brothers in two ways, when they eat with their mouths and are nourished through their ears.

This, then, should be the beginning of such a week. On Sunday, when the kitchen servers enter upon their week, this brother too, [Col. 0992C] at the meal of the sixth hour, after the verse and prayer of the table, when the abbot has taken his seat in his chair and before the basket containing the customary loaves descends by the pulley-rope, should announce himself in his own voice, saying: “Command, my lords, and pray for me, as I enter upon the week of reading at the tables.” At once the abbot, rising with the whole congregation, should pray with him, with their knees fixed to the ground. When they have risen, the new weekly reader should say this verse: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. L), with all responding together. After the verse has been said and the abbot has completed it, let him first offer peace to the abbot, then to all; afterward let him arrange a stool for himself in the middle of all the tables. After everyone has sat down at the tables, having asked for a blessing, let him also [Col. 0992D] sit on the stool with the book. When the abbot has first received pure wine with everyone at the table, let the reader likewise receive his own pure wine on account of the spitting involved in the sacrament, and then begin to read.

Let him read this Rule every day, placing a mark at the point to which he has read that day, so that thereafter everything may nevertheless be read daily in its entirety, and so that it may be completed and reread in successive weeks. When the weekly reader has completed his week of reading, let him show the following successor the mark from which the one beginning the week is to continue; and he too, on completing and rereading the text, should show the mark to his successor when his week has ended. Let him read in an orderly manner, without rushing, so that the listeners, occupied with their meal, may understand more clearly what they ought to fulfill by their actions. [Col. 0993A] If there are any ambiguous or obscure passages which the brothers do not understand clearly, let the abbot explain them either when questioned by the brothers or voluntarily.

But if laypeople should happen to arrive at the monastery tables, lest future detraction arise in the world when a worldly person has learned God’s secrets, the abbot, if he wishes, should have another reading from any book read, so that the monastery’s secret, or the established measures of holy life imposed as discipline, may not become known to mockers. Let him read another passage, nevertheless placing a mark in the Rule. But if such a layman is detained at the monastery table concerning whom the abbot is certain—not only that he is capable of admiring the divine ordinances, but also that he knows that the man may become a follower in this religious conversion and may be drawn toward divine customs—then, upon this layman’s arrival at the table, let the reader continue with the Rule. For those ought to hear the monastery’s Rule who are able worthily to observe it.

[Col. 0993B] Therefore the Rule ought to be read at the tables during the meal, because then the whole congregation, gathered together for eating, can properly observe the reading concerning observance or correction without excuse, since all the listeners will hear everything and nothing will pass anyone by: what all have heard, they ought to fulfill in their actions.

While this brother is occupied in this work during his week, the weekly servers should lift bowls from all the tables containing what has been brought to his table; the cellarer should preserve his measure of bread and the customary number of drinks. After everything has been removed, and after he has asked for a blessing, he too should refresh himself. [Col. 0993C] For this reason we have said that the monastery’s Rule should be read daily at the tables, so that no brother may excuse himself by claiming that ignorance caused him not to correct himself. When the Rule itself is put into daily use and its knowledge is better preserved, no brother can say that he did not know what he could fulfill through obedience.

During the meal itself, while the Rule is being read, so that the hearing of all the brothers may be awakened to attention, the abbot should question from each table whichever brothers he wishes about what has been read. When each brother has recited what he heard, it will be recognized that he attended more closely to the reading at that hour than to his belly. But when a deaf and negligent brother has not recounted what he heard, he should be judged to have loved the flesh more than the soul. He must immediately be justly reproved by the abbot, so that, while each brother fears being ashamed when questioned, he may not let his mind wander elsewhere but may attend to what is being read.

[Col. 0993D] The weekly reader should remain at the table with the brothers until the brothers rise. When they rise, he too should rise with the book, after placing a mark in the Rule. When the verse and prayer have been completed by all, he should respond with everyone: “Thanks be to God.” He should then immediately sit at his own table, where the weekly servers have preserved his meal and measures of drink, marked either by the abbot or by the superiors, and he too should receive everything.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0994A]

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the dish of crumbs to be cooked by the weekly servers on the seventh day.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

The bread crumbs which are gathered each day from the tables during cleaning and kept in one vessel should be cleaned by the weekly servers who are leaving their week, on the seventh day of their week, Saturday, toward evening. A dish should then be cooked from them, either bound with grain or with eggs, and placed on the abbot’s table before they drink the final hot drink of the evening.

Then, while the abbot is seated, let the weekly servers say before the whole congregation together: “Command, lords, and pray for us, who have completed our week in the ministry of humility.” [Col. 0994B] Immediately everyone should rise and pray with them together, with the abbot and with their knees fixed to the ground. When they have risen, let the weekly servers say this verse: “Let those who hate us see and be confounded, because you, Lord, have helped us and comforted us” (Ps. LXXXV).

Then, after the abbot has completed the response, let them together offer peace to the abbot and to their superiors, or to the whole congregation. When the abbot and the brothers have sat down again at the tables, let the abbot mark the dish, first taking a spoonful of the blessing himself, and then placing a spoonful in the mouths of the brothers who sit with him at his table. When he has served his own table-companions, let him call the weekly servers and place a spoonful in their mouths as well.

[Col. 0994C] Then, however many tables there are, let the weekly server bring that many bowls to the abbot. From each table, let them remove as many spoonfuls as there are brothers, and let them place these in the mouth of each brother through his superior, so that everyone may receive from that blessing. When this has been completed, let them rise as they take the final hot drink, saying: “Thanks be to God.”

But if the weekly servers fail through negligence to present this dish on the seventh day, let them lose from the abbot, during the following person’s week, one withdrawn quarter-loaf of bread on each day, until the promised amendment and satisfaction have been made.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the measure of food.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 0994D]

We believe that for the daily meal, both at the sixth and at the ninth hour, two cooked dishes and a third dish—whatever raw food there may be, together with fruit—are sufficient for everyone. Half a loaf weighing one pound should suffice for each brother per day, according to the pattern of divine provision, since a raven prepared for Paul, the servant of God, half of the heavenly bread for his daily food.

Therefore, when they eat at the sixth hour in summer or at other times, the cellarer should place a third quarter of that Lord’s bread on all the tables, withdrawing it from everyone’s daily allowance in the cellar beforehand, toward evening, before the raw dish is brought in. We said that these quarters should be withdrawn beforehand in the cellar from everyone’s allowances so that, if the full allowances had been placed on the tables, a newly arrived brother who did not yet know the measure of the Rule might think that his portion was to be set out again for supper and might consume it all at dinner, leaving himself nothing for the evening with the fruit; or so that a brother who loves to eat much, even though he knows the measure of the Rule, might, wishing to satisfy his appetite, choose to eat everything at that hour and then think that he would be content in the evening.

[Col. 0995A] When all these quarters have been reserved in the cellar, they should be brought out in the evening, placed on the abbot’s table, and marked by him, as custom indicates. He should first take some for himself or for his table, and the remainder, lifted by the cellarer into a basket, should be placed at the several tables for those who are to take it. These portions alone, together with whatever raw dish is mixed with fruit, or whatever may remain from the dishes of the midday meal, should suffice for the brothers’ supper.

[Col. 0995B] On Sunday, or on other feast days, and also on account of visiting outsiders, the abbot may add on any day whatever he wishes to the food, such as is permitted to a superior, or some sweeter food, according to the testimony read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, where on feast days they asked the Lord for delicate food, and an angel appeared to them with a honeycomb. The important thing is that he consider equality and avoid corruptible excess.

For those under twelve years of age, less than a pound of bread per day should suffice.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the measure of drink.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 0995C]

As soon as the brothers have sat down at the tables, before they eat, let them each receive a serving of pure wine. After receiving these servings, let them bring them individually to the abbot to be marked; at the other tables, let the superiors mark them for their brothers in turn. At all these tables, each brother should dip three pieces of his own bread into his serving, and no more. No more, so that a brother who spends much bread there, when he has none in the dishes, may not, because of his greediness, provoke the other brothers’ disparaging attention by exceeding his measure of bread.

After the first servings of pure wine, in summer, at the meal of both the sixth and the ninth hour, four hot drinks each should suffice for everyone, apart from that serving of pure wine. [Col. 0995D] In the same season, when the meal is taken at the sixth hour, three evening drinks should suffice for everyone. When these have been completed, both at the meal of the sixth hour and at that of the ninth hour or supper, the cellarer, standing in the middle of the tables, should say in a clear voice: “Let anyone who is thirsty indicate it confidently.” After this announcement, anyone who is thirsty should immediately answer from his table: “Bless.” Immediately, hot *pusca*—watered wine—or, if the brothers wish, *jutta*, mixed in one vessel, should be offered. More of this should always be prepared for the thirsty among the stronger dishes, or *galleta*, or cups, should be offered to the thirsty.

Also on these summer days, when the meal is taken at the ninth hour, two drinks each should suffice for everyone in the evening before they finish. They should nevertheless pray before drinking and pray again after drinking.

[Col. 0996A] Likewise, on these summer days, when the meal is taken at the sixth hour, after the ninth hour just mentioned, the abbot should leave the oratory each day, sit in his chair, and, with everyone standing in order around him, have the wine brought out by the cellarer. The weekly servers should mix, in the customary vessel, one drink for each group of ten at every table, according to the number of the congregation and of their own group. Immediately the abbot should rise and pray with everyone. After the prayer, before sitting down, he should mark the vessel of the mixture brought to him. Then he should order everyone to sit at their tables as usual. After drinking first himself, he should have the mixture served individually to everyone at the several tables. When this has been completed, they should rise again and pray; after the prayer, everyone should return to the work they had left.

[Col. 0996B] Therefore, anyone who is thirsty should drink immediately after the ninth hour. But once the tenth hour has arrived, no one should drink until after vespers. If a brother becomes thirstier during that ninth hour, before the tenth hour arrives as we have said, and wishes to drink, he should drink water not from a pitcher in one draught but in the measure of a cup, *galleta*, or *cancella*, because what is beyond the measure is excessive and unjust and will appear to fulfill desire in a corrupting manner.

For, according to that saying which declares, “Nothing in excess,” excessive water too can intoxicate the mind through dreamlike fantasies and burden the body with discomforts: that is, wind in the veins, cold in the marrow, heaviness in the eyebrows, dizziness in the head, sleep in the eyes, and continual sneezing in the nostrils.

[Col. 0996C] In winter, at the meals of the sixth and ninth hours, three hot drinks each should suffice for everyone, because there is no heat to provoke thirst. On those winter days when they eat at the sixth hour, nothing whatever should be eaten in the evening, except that one hot drink each should suffice for everyone. They should nevertheless pray before drinking and pray again after drinking.

After the ninth hour, the portion which was brought out daily from the cellar in summer for the thirsty should not be given in winter, because thirst does not arise and little time remains before the evening meal. On those days when the meal is taken at the ninth hour in winter, after vespers they should receive no more than one hot drink each; nevertheless, they should pray before drinking and pray again afterward.

[Col. 0996D] On those days from Easter to Pentecost when the meal is taken at the sixth hour, except Thursday and Sunday, they should receive nothing else in the evening on the other days apart from two hot drinks, on account of the days. Except during the eight days of the octave of Easter, when they should eat supper continuously. For this reason we have withdrawn suppers on the days mentioned above, except Thursday and Sunday, up to Pentecost: so that one meal may be maintained on those days and, although not at its customary hour, the appearance of the customary fast may nevertheless be preserved, since their suppers are changed into midday meals.

On Thursday and Sunday, however, they should eat in the evening what we prescribed above concerning food, with one dish added each day at midday; or, if provisions have remained from Easter, a drink of any kind. The cup or *galleta* through which the drink is to be served at different times should be such that, when filled, it holds one third of a mixed *hemina*. But either two or three cups or *galletae* of equal measure should serve the tables, so that the drink may be distributed to everyone more quickly through several vessels.

[Col. 0997A] Little children under twelve years of age should receive two hot drinks in winter, one in the evening; in summer they should receive three at the meal and two drinks in the evening, because of the conditions of their age. For just as we established above concerning food, so too we permit concerning drinks.

On Sunday, on feast days, or on account of visiting outsiders, the abbot may add whatever he considers suitable, as is permitted to a superior: that is, out of charity and joy for holy days or friends, let him add a drink of whatever provision he wishes. The important thing is that he remember sobriety and avoid drunkenness from wine. For unless the body is sober, it cannot keep vigil for the work of God, and the soul is not free from thoughts of lust.

[Col. 0997B] But if any of the disciples should wish to refuse a little of his established measure of drink or bread, while a fragment remains at the table, he is recognized as loving the spirit more than the flesh and as imposing the bridle of chastity upon lust. When an abstaining brother refuses this very thing, he should say quietly to the cellarer who is removing it: “Receive this, and let what has been denied to the flesh profit God.”

The cellarer should immediately set this aside in a single vessel, so that it may happily profit God, and should hand it over as an addition to the monastery’s alms for a poor beggar, as though it were some gift. This entire measure is from the monastery’s stores [the Latin *inthicis* is uncertain]. [Col. 0997C] But if the Lord causes something sent from outside to appear for his congregation, let the gift sent by the Lord be gratefully received; and, if it pleases the abbot, let it be added to the tables, since it is understood not to have come except through the Lord’s provision.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the days of fasting and the hours of meals.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 0997D] At all times during the week they ought to eat at the sixth hour on two days, namely Thursday and Sunday; on all the other days of the week they ought to eat at the ninth hour. For let us, who are spiritual, be ashamed to flee fasting until the ninth hour, since it is known that ancient custom formerly knew nothing of midday meals but always arranged the evening—namely, supper—as its meal. To such an extent was this so that the grain allowance which was distributed either to laborers or to soldiers is called *annona* to this day because it was distributed at the ninth hour of the day, when it was also consumed; and for this reason the name *annona* has remained to the present day.

I shall produce the holier testimony of the Lord himself, whom we know to have eaten supper but whom we do not read to have eaten a midday meal, when the Scripture of the holy Gospel says: “When evening had come, Jesus reclined with the twelve apostles, and while they were dining he said...” (Matt. XXVI).

Therefore fasts have been appointed to end at the ninth hour on all days, so that something more prolonged may be added on the days of Lent: namely, until evening, that is, after the lighting of the lamps. From the sixty-day period onward, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday they should always eat after the lighting of the lamps; on the other days until Lent they should eat at the ninth hour, so that what they subtract from the forty fasts of the Lord’s Lent may be restored by continuing the fasts until evening on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday from the period of Sexagesima, and so that the number of forty fasts may be completed. [Col. 0998A]

For the sick, definite fasts should be relaxed. When the brothers eat at the sixth hour, the sick should be restored at the third hour, except those who are gravely exhausted, for whom no hour is prescribed when the danger of death is feared. Therefore, according as necessity appears and has been certainly established, let those people be restored for whom this has been permitted.

If the healthy brothers eat at the ninth hour, the sick should eat at the sixth. But the abbot ought to test or recognize this with careful scrutiny through certain signs, lest anyone pretend to be sick because of his greed for food. For this reason we have said that fasts should be relaxed for the sick because of the weakness of the body, by which they cannot fulfill what they desire, as Scripture says: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI).

[Col. 0998B] Little children should fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, but on the shorter days, that is, during winter; on the other days they should eat at the sixth hour. In summer, however, the little children should eat at the sixth hour on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday; on the other days they should be restored at the third hour. For on the longer days the strength of their age is less, just as their capacity for endurance is distinct.

But we permit such children this relaxation as are under twelve years of age; those who are older should be held to the rule of adults. For by a just judgment, little children, the aged, and the sick ought to be granted relaxation according to the same principle governing meals.

[Col. 0998C] Brothers who are being sent on a journey should also receive this instruction from the abbot or their superiors: on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday during the longer days—that is, from Easter until 8 Kalends of October [September 24], which is the winter equinox—let them not fast while traveling, because of heat and thirst. Then, from the winter equinox until Easter, because the days are shorter for traveling brothers, let the fasts on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday continue until evening. Otherwise, if the brothers, occupied with travel, take a meal at the ninth hour, the shortened day may compel them to extend their lodging; or, since everything in the world is for sale, when their fast is ended at evening and the day is already declining, an inn might not wish to receive a brother who has already broken his fast, because lodging promises it neither a purchase nor any profit from trade. Since hospitality is denied to the brothers where there is no profit, they might be forced to spend again from their own resources and violate the fast through a second meal, which is not permitted.

[Col. 0998D] On the other days, outside Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday during the shorter days, let them rest for a meal at the sixth hour while traveling and eat supper in the evening, on account of the labor of the journey.

From Easter until Pentecost, except for those sent on a distant journey, let them always eat at the sixth hour in the monastery or wherever they may be, and let them change their suppers into midday meals, as holy Scripture says: “You cannot fast while the bridegroom is with you” (Mark II). Let them eat supper only on Thursday and Sunday.

[Col. 0999A] For this reason fasting is not permitted on Thursday at any time, because the Lord’s Ascension occurs every year on that day. Fasting is likewise not permitted on Sunday because the Lord’s resurrection is commemorated; holy Silvester prohibits this in his books.

Fasting is not permitted from Easter until Pentecost because Easter Saturday closes the fasts of sorrow and opens the alleluia of joy, while Pentecost Saturday closes the alleluia and opens the fasts. But in the churches the alleluia is closed; in the monastery, as in the special service of God, the alleluia established through the modes of the psalms remains open and is sung to the Lord by the servants of God until Epiphany.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

[Col. 0999B] Concerning the time of their sleeping, how the place should be arranged, and in what order they should sleep.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

In summer, after the sixth hour, whether during a fast or after a meal, let everyone rest, so that during those short nights the brothers, made sober by sleep, may rise lightly for divine work and prayer.

In one courtyard or dining hall, let beds be arranged in order around the circuit. In the middle of this circuit let the abbot have his bed, so that, observing all silence and reverence around him, he may watch over the whole flock of his sheep gathered within one sheepfold, like a diligent and watchful shepherd.

[Col. 0999C] In this courtyard let a lamp hang, which the cellarer prepares each day and which the weekly servers light in the evening before Compline, so that they may see how the various brothers arrange themselves. After everyone has settled in place, let the lamp be safeguarded by the aforementioned weekly servers if the monastery should happen to experience a shortage of oil.

## CHAPTER XXX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

No one should speak after Compline.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

After they have all drunk the hot drinks of the evening, when everyone has had his shoes removed by the weekly servers, let the abbot say to all the brothers: “Come, brothers, let everything be closed up in its place and everything be put away in its section. Weekly servers, wash the brothers’ feet.”

[Col. 0999D] When the weekly servers have washed everyone’s feet, or when they are washing the feet of visiting outsiders, let both of them say with one voice this verse, with everyone responding together: “You commanded, Lord, that your commandments be kept exceedingly; would that my ways were directed toward keeping your statutes” (Ps. CXVIII).

Then let the abbot say to everyone: “Come, brothers, stir yourselves, so that, when everything has been completed, there may be no occasion by which we are compelled to speak. It is now time for us to commend ourselves to the Lord; and, when all the offices of the day have ended and we enter the night together, let our mouths be closed from speaking for rest, and our eyes for sleep.”

When all these things have been completed, while permission still exists to speak and to give some command, let them say this verse at the end of Compline: “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. CXL). Immediately let them enter into silence and settle themselves in their beds, and let them be reduced to such silence that until the nocturns it may be thought that none of the brothers is there.

[Col. 1000A] For this reason we ought to be silent after Compline, so that at the nocturns we may rightly say first to the Lord: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. L). That is, let us ask the Lord to open at the nocturns the lips which his guardianship had closed at Compline. You see, therefore, that whatever is opened is recognized to have first been closed.

But lest, while silence is being kept, some necessary matter of practical concern should force a brother to speak, and one brother should wish to speak to another: if there is the light of the hanging lamp or a lantern, let him communicate by hand, by a nod of the head, or by a movement of the eyes. Or, if there is no light, let one brother go with another to the necessary place, and, whatever must be said, let him speak quietly into his ear, so that a third person may not hear him.

[Col. 1000B] Likewise, if some brother is compelled by necessity to say something after sleep and before the nocturns, let him first say quietly to himself the customary nocturnal verse, namely: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise”; then let him say what is necessary.

We grant no brother permission after Compline to eat anything, drink anything, or carry out any task. If any outsider should arrive at the monastery after Compline has been completed, let the resident brothers refresh him through silent service, and let an answer be given to him quietly, on account of the rule established. After their feet have been washed, let the brothers then quietly complete the office for themselves, and let the outsiders themselves be assigned to sleep in the travelers’ beds.

[Col. 1000C] Immediately, after the royal doors have been closed by the doorkeepers, let they too, lying on their beds, seek sleep through the hours of the night. But if any brother is found after Compline either eating or drinking anything, let him receive this penalty of excommunication: on the following day, after being accused, he is to eat on the third day after a continuous fast, because he presumed to do what was forbidden. Let this penalty of excommunication remain in force throughout the continuation of the fast until, through humble satisfaction concerning the promised amendment, pardon has been sought from the abbot present or from the superiors.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the weekly servers of the divine office during the nights.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 1000D] To awaken the divine office during the nights, let the superiors of each group of ten, whose brothers exercise the weeks of cooking, undertake the responsibility of awakening for as long as the ten brothers of their group, paired off—or, because of the size of the congregation, arranged in groups of three—complete their successive weeks of kitchen service.

When the turn of these superiors comes to cook, since they may be weighed down by sleep with limbs tired and exhausted from kitchen service, let two more watchful brothers chosen from their group of ten take over from them the responsibility of awakening during their week.

Likewise, when the brothers of another group of ten begin kitchen service, let their superiors also undertake responsibility for the entire flock under their care, to awaken it through their vigilance. Similarly, during their own week, when they are serving in the kitchen for their week, let their more watchful brothers assist them.

[Col. 1001A] If some are carrying out a week of awakening, let them be watchful night and day, consult the clock, and remind the abbot and the brothers of the hour for singing, lest they forget through the burden of their work and the appointed hour pass them by; let them announce that the hour for singing has arrived.

For this reason the awakening is entrusted in two ways: so that they may keep watch in turn, and so that, if one should be overcome by sleep according to the weakness of the flesh, another who happens to be awake may at the appointed hour perform the duty of awakening his negligent companion. Great indeed is the reward before the Lord of those who awaken people for the divine work, whom the Rule calls “watch-roosters” [*vigilgallos*].

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 1001B]

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How the awakening should be carried out by them.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the appointed hour for singing has already arrived in the night, let the one of these two who is found to be more watchful quietly awaken the more negligent companion of his week. Quietly, and rightly so, because all have not yet asked the Lord in the oratory that the lips closed at Compline be opened by him during the night.

We have appointed these two for this reason: so that they may anticipate one another in their watches. Therefore, when both have risen, let them go reverently to the abbot’s bed. [Col. 1001C] After praying there, let them quietly say to each other this verse: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.” After quietly completing it for each other, let them tap the abbot’s feet and awaken him.

When he has been roused, let them say together: “God.” When he hears this, let the abbot rise and enter the oratory. After striking the signal, let him pray for as long as it takes all the brothers to enter, including those who happen to be occupied by a necessary bodily matter.

But if anyone causes the abbot to prolong his prayer for a sufficiently long time—which is not permitted—because he has been brought late to the oratory, let the fault be attributed to his superiors.

For this reason we said that all should be awaited in the abbot’s first prayer and that they ought to hurry immediately: so that, after the abbot has begun, all may with one voice ask the Lord that their lips ought to be opened during the nocturns, just as, when all were asking together, they had been closed at Compline.

[Col. 1001D] Therefore, as they enter the oratory, let them say for the third time: “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.” We said that it should be said for the third time by all so that no brother who enters a little later may be deprived of this verse of petition.

After this verse has been said by everyone, let the shepherd invite and awaken his sheep to the praises of the Lord by a responsory, saying: “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us acclaim God our salvation.” At the sweetness of this voice, let every bee that has not hurried to arrive know that, emptied of the fruit of honey in the spirit, it is wearing out only the wax of its body in sleep, to be burned in the future fire of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 1002A]

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the divine offices during the nights.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

*[The supplied source ends here.]*
In the nocturnal office, during winter the nocturns are sung at one time before the crowing of the cock, as the Prophet says: “At midnight I rose to confess to you” (Psalm 118). Concerning summer he likewise says: “By night my spirit watches for you, O God” (Psalm 26); that is, during some part of the night, after the cock has already crowed, the signal for rising is to be given. But in winter those who keep watch must take care that the cock does not either precede or overtake the nocturns, because the nights are [lacuna] in the winter season. For the crowing of the cock is the boundary of the waning night, which immediately gives birth to the day: just as in the sun’s course the day is shown to begin declining from the sixth hour, and throughout the night the sun hastens downward as far as it advanced in its course, so that it might ascend to midday in the middle of its circuit. [Col. 1002B]

But in winter this must be done so that the crowing of the cock follows after the nocturns have already been completed, because the nights are long, so that the brothers, freed from sleep and alert in their clarified understanding, may recognize the work of God that they perform. Therefore an interval is placed between them, so that during the lengthy night the heaviness of sleep may come to an end.

In spring or summer, however—that is, from Easter until the eighth day before the Kalends of October, which is the winter equinox—because of the shortness of the nights, the nocturns are begun by the brothers at the crowing of the cock; and when the appointed number of psalms has been completed, they immediately add matins, and finish them according to the number of their psalms. Therefore, during these short nights we have ordained that the nocturns begin after the cockcrow and be joined to matins, so that the brothers may not grow drowsy by lying down again after the nocturns and, overcome by pleasant morning sleep, lose not only matins but also be embarrassed to say prime late. [Col. 1002C]

For this reason also we said that, after the cockcrow, the nocturns are to be joined to matins: so that the brothers, already freed from prolonged sleep, may soberly complete both offices; and, once the divine obligation of matins has been discharged, the brothers who wish may rest securely until prime. Thus, laying aside all heaviness during these hours of sleep, they may begin to work lightly after prime, fully refreshed. Scripture concerning Saint Helenus bears witness to this when it says: “For he was accustomed to rest after the morning offices.” [Col. 1002D]

Therefore, lest in the short nights the brothers be compelled to rise before the cockcrow, while still raw from sleep only just begun—when, in the very surge of the veins, blood and humor boil through the veins, and, shaken by the disharmony of heaviness, the limbs digest in sleep the food they had taken, still amid the fire of undigested food—when the brothers are compelled to rise, not awakened but rather slain, with a heavy head and indigested belching, they drive away the gifts of the Holy Spirit. And when what is sweet becomes bitter to their flesh—which, although it serves God, nevertheless meanwhile seeks what belongs to it in this life—it will seem bitter to some, though not to all, that what is sweet should be done for God. Thus a brother will not love God wholeheartedly in the psalms, when in sleep he desires to satisfy the flesh. [Col. 1003A]

Just as the moon, diminished in its circuit and assigned to the night, fulfills less of its office of light when it rises late at the coming of dawn and, moving late through its course, enters the day only to set, so the brevity of the nights, tempered by the day because of the frailty of human flesh, compels the divine offices in the psalms to be shortened and the offices of the day to be joined to the night.

Therefore, during the winter season—that is, from the winter equinox until the spring equinox, namely from the eighth day before the Kalends of October until the eighth day before the Kalends of April, or better, until Easter, because the nights are longer—thirteen antiphons are to be said, with the psalter always proceeding, and three responsories, so that there may be sixteen sets, according to the number of the prophets, apart from the lessons, the verse, and the prayer of God. Thus, both these sixteen nocturnal sets and the eight sets of matins together make twenty-four occasions on which, in imitation of the twenty-four elders, our knees are bent before God at night with praises. [Col. 1003B]

For this reason more should be sung during the longer nights: just as God has joined a lengthy period of rest to us during the night, so we should join the offering of our thanks to him in praise.

In summer, however—that is, from Easter until the eighth day before the Kalends of October—eight antiphons are to be said, with the psalter always proceeding, as we have said above, and three responsories, apart from the lessons, the verse, and the prayer of God. Thus these twelve nocturnal sets, together with the eight sets of matins, make twenty occasions on which the reason of the short night compels us to bend our knees before God. When sleep is brief, it seems sweet to the flesh, since the human body, wearied by the long labor of the day, rests for a shorter time during the night. [Col. 1003C]

Therefore in summer, as we have indicated above, because the nights are shorter, nine antiphons and three responsories are to be said, so that there may be twelve sets according to the names of the twelve apostles. These nocturns, as we said above, are begun and completed at the cockcrow during the summer season, and matins are immediately added to them because of the shortness of the nights.

But this must always be guarded against, both in winter and summer, by day and by night, and whenever psalmody is performed: psalms must never be combined, which is not permitted. Rather, each must be completed individually with its Gloria, so that the prayers which are to be made between them are not lost, and so that, through a convenient negligence, we do not appear to subtract their Glorias from the praise of God by inserting them into the psalms. For every psalm for which the Prophet established a beginning also has an appointed end. [Col. 1003D]

If some necessity presses upon all those who are singing psalms, they must not combine them, but may say three at a time; nevertheless, they must follow with their Glorias, so that they may complete the office more quickly without reducing the number of psalms. Therefore we said that they should be said either individually or three at a time: just as unity is recognized in the Trinity and the Trinity in unity, so, whether individually or, when necessity requires, three at a time, they must nevertheless be said with their Glorias.

Combining them in pairs is wholly forbidden, because whatever departs from unity and the Trinity, whether by addition or subtraction, is not fitting for a Christian. We possess perfect faith when we equally apprehend the perfect Trinity in unity and unity in the Trinity.

If some still greater necessity presses upon those singing psalms at any hour, let them complete the individual heads of all the psalms to be said with a single Gloria; and then let them leave the oratory, so that, despite whatever necessity, the work of God may not appear to have been omitted. [Col. 1004A]

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the divine offices during the day.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

In carrying out the divine office, above all things the order of the holy service must be established, and the sequence of proper observance must be arranged according to ancient custom and the ordinances of the fathers: namely, matins, prime, terce, sext, none, vespers, and compline. Thus the prophetic ordinance may be fulfilled, which says to the Lord: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118).

Prime should be said in the same manner as the twelfth hour, which is called vespers. Prime is to be said when the sun’s rays have already begun to pierce, and vespers while its rays are still declining. For just as the day begins with the work of God at its beginning, so it should be completed with it at the end, so that the Scripture may be fulfilled which says: “From the rising of the sun to its setting” (Psalm 112); it did not say, “after its setting, praise the name of the Lord.” [Col. 1004B]

For “the departure of morning and evening will delight the Lord” (Psalm 64). At these times the Lord will rejoice in the benefits of the righteous, announced by our daytime angels, just as Saint Paul says in his revelation: “Children of men, bless the Lord without ceasing, but especially when the sun has set.” For the sun rightly shows us the beginning and end of the day; by its departure it introduces the darkness of night. [Col. 1004C]

In summer, however, while the sun is still standing higher, the lighting of the lamps is to begin because of the short nights, so that, for the brothers wearied by the prolonged labor of the heat and by fasting, the sleep of exhausted rest may be added to the increase of the short nights while some daylight still remains.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the manner and number of the psalms during the day.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

At all times six psalms are to be said at matins, one responsory, the verse, a reading from the Apostle, and a reading from the Gospel, which the abbot always gives, together with the prayer of God.

At the hours of the day mentioned above—prime, terce, sext, and none—three psalms are to be said, with the psalter always proceeding, one responsory at each hour, a reading from the Apostle, and a reading from the Gospel, which the abbot is always to give; or, if he is absent, the superiors are to give them in turn. After this comes the prayer of God. [Col. 1004D]

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the psalms of the lighting of the lamps.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

In winter six psalms are to be said at the lighting of the lamps, with the psalter always proceeding, one responsory, the verse, a reading from the Apostle, and a reading from the Gospel, which the abbot is always to give; after this, the prayer of God. [Col. 1005A]

Thus these, together with the responsory and the Gospel, make nine psalmody-units, apart from the verse and reading; and the four sets belonging to the hours of that day—namely, at prime, terce, sext, and none, three antiphons at each hour and one responsory at each—make sixteen in all, apart from the verse and readings. Completing these, we should sing twenty-four times and bend our knees, in imitation of the twenty-four elders, who, ceaselessly worshiping God in heaven, cast down their crowns and, lying prostrate, give glory to God while praising the Lord day and night. [Col. 1005B]

Likewise, in summer five sets are to be made at the lighting of the lamps, together with the responsory and Gospel, apart from the verse and readings. Thus these five and the sixteen sets of the day make, as we said above, twenty-four sets each day. According to the number of the twenty-four elders in heaven, we too should bend our knees to God twenty-four times throughout the day.

During this season the lighting of the lamps should begin earlier because the nights of that period are short.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the psalms of compline.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

Three psalms are to be said at compline, a responsory, a reading from the Apostle, and a reading from the Gospels. After these, the abbot, if present, is always to say the prayer of God and the concluding verse. [Col. 1005C]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the psalm at meals.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

One psalm is to be said at the meal, together with a verse; likewise, when the table has been removed, another verse with a Gloria. This service at meals is a special act of thanksgiving, not one of the seven canonical praises of the day.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How psalmody should be performed at matins.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

The matins psalms are always to be sung with antiphons. Four are to be said without Alleluia; after these, two with Alleluia, a responsory, the verse, the readings, and the Gospel, which the abbot is to give, without Alleluia. On Sunday, however, they are to be said with Alleluia until Epiphany, so that, apart from the verse and readings, there may be eight sets with the Gospel. [Col. 1005D]

At matins, apart from the fiftieth psalm, the Lauds are to be taken from the canticles. On Sunday, on other feast days, or when there is a feast of a saint, the blessings are to be said. From the saying of these blessings on Sundays, the knees are not to be bent until the nocturns; and on that day all antiphons and responsories, after the blessings have been said, are to be sung with Alleluia until the nocturns of the following Monday. [Col. 1006A]

## CHAPTER XL

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How psalmody should be performed at the hours of the day.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

At prime, terce, sext, and none, when psalmody is performed, the third psalm is always to be imposed with Alleluia from Epiphany onward (the preceding printed word *absque* is textually uncertain); the psalter is always to proceed, with responsories, a reading from the Apostle, and a reading from the Gospels, which the abbot is always to give. If the abbot is absent, the superiors are to give it in turn, together with the verse and the prayer of God.

## CHAPTER XLI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How the lighting of the lamps should be performed.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

The psalms of the lighting of the lamps are to be sung with antiphons, of which the last two are to be sung with Alleluia. The psalter is always to proceed, with one responsory at each service, the verse, a reading from the Apostle, and the Gospel, which the abbot is always to give without Alleluia; on Sunday, however, with Alleluia. [Col. 1006B]

On that day, after the blessings have been said, all antiphons are to be sung with Alleluia, and the knees are not to be bent until the nocturns of the following Monday.

## CHAPTER XLII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How psalmody should be performed at compline.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

The psalms of compline are to be sung with antiphons at all times, because all seven occasions during the day on which, as the Prophet says, we ought to offer praises to God are sung with equal modulation, on account of the sevenfold Spirit, who is not divided in any part. [Col. 1006C]

## CHAPTER XLIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How psalmody should be performed at meals.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

The psalms at meals, both when the table is set and when it has been removed, do not belong to the seven canonical hours of the day. Rather, they are offered specially to God in thanksgiving for blessing or commending the food. They are to be said without an antiphon, as direct psalmody; but on Sunday or feast days, with an antiphon or Alleluia. [Col. 1006D]

## CHAPTER XLIV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How psalmody should be performed at night.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

At the nocturns the abbot must say the opening verse, followed by the responsory of prayer. Then, in winter, twelve antiphons without Alleluia; then a responsory without Alleluia, with the psalter alone always proceeding; then another responsory, now with Alleluia, so that there may be sixteen sets. This is followed by a reading from the Apostle and a reading from the Gospel, which the abbot is always to give. If the abbot is absent, the superiors are to give the verse in turn, together with the prayer of God. [Col. 1007A]

In summer, from Easter until the winter equinox, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of October, after the opening verse and the abbot’s responsory, six antiphons without Alleluia are to be said; then another responsory likewise without Alleluia; then three antiphons with Alleluia, with the psalter always proceeding, as we said above; then another responsory, now with Alleluia, so that there may be twelve sets. This is followed by a reading from the Apostle and a reading from the Gospels, which the abbot is always to give. If he is absent, the superiors are to give it in turn. Then come the verse and the prayer of God.

The person appointed to give a reading must recite it from memory, not read it from a book, except only at vigils. We have established this so that the brothers may meditate more frequently on the Scriptures and retain them in memory, so that, wherever there may be a lack of the text of a reading or of a page, if necessary it may be recited from memory. [Col. 1007B]

During the longer nights, if the abbot wishes, he may read by the light of a lamp or lantern in the brothers’ courtyard; or a brother who is pleased to do so of his own accord may have permission either to read, to meditate on something, or to perform some useful task for the monastery.

Those who wish to rest are likewise to have permission to sleep, because once the oratory has completed and discharged its obligation, the remaining hours of the night are owed to rest. If someone who is, as it were, spiritual wishes to rise from his sleep to hear someone reading, to read himself, or to perform some task, he is thereby particularly shown to love the spirit rather than the flesh through the good freedom of his will. [Col. 1007C]

Therefore the brothers ought to have their beds in one courtyard before the abbot, so that it may be recognized what each has chosen and what kind of soldier of his service each brother will become.

## CHAPTER XLV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How psalmody should be performed on feast days.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

From Easter until Pentecost all antiphons and responsories are to be sung day and night with Alleluia, and the knees are not to be bent.

At the Nativity of the Lord until Epiphany, all antiphons and responsories are likewise to be sung day and night with Alleluia. During those days the knees are not to be bent, nor are the brothers to fast or abstain. But during the eight days preceding the Nativity of the Lord, let the fasts or abstinence of Lent—or those prayers which are customarily performed purely during Lent—likewise be observed by the brothers. Thus, in the likeness of the sorrow of Lent, as placable servants performing more service beyond their daily obligation, we may rejoice that the Nativity of our Lord has immediately arrived with wages and gifts of joy. [Col. 1007D]

On the night of Epiphany, during the vigil itself and on that day alone, all antiphons and responsories are to be sung with Alleluia. From that day the Alleluia is to be closed, the office of the feast days is immediately withdrawn from the oratory, and on the day of Epiphany itself the knees of those praying are not to be bent.

We said that Alleluia is to be sung with its vigil on that day alone, and not until the octave, because from that day the Paschal hundred begins for those who fast and abstain. [Col. 1008A]

On all Sundays, after the blessings have been said, all antiphons and responsories are to be sung with Alleluia until the nocturns of the following Monday, and the knees are not to be bent, because Sunday is reckoned as the resurrection of Easter.

On every Sunday, after the blessings have been said and until the Masses of the Church have been completed, they are always to say in the work of God this verse: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their beds” (Psalm 149). This means that through the beds of all the saints—that is, through the churches where the Masses are celebrated—the exultation of the Mass is observed.

If the feast of a saint occurs on any day, after the blessings have been said the knees are not to be bent until prime has been said.

If it is the feast of the saint in whose oratory the psalmody is performed, then, after the blessings have been said, until the procession of the Mass to be celebrated there by the priest on that day, the knees are not to be bent. For the joy of the feast of that particular oratory, the entire day until the following nocturns is to be sung wholly with Alleluia, as on Sunday. [Col. 1008B]

## CHAPTER XLVI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the assignment of psalms in the oratory at any time.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

After the abbot, the superiors are to assign the antiphons in turn, at his command, with the psalter always proceeding, as we have said. After the superiors have completed their part, the individual brothers from each group of ten whom the superiors have ordered are to intone in turn.

The superiors are always to give the readings from the Apostle in turn. If the abbot is present, he is always to give the readings from the Gospel; if he is absent, the superiors are to give them in turn.

At matins and at the lighting of the lamps, after the reading from the Apostle has been recited, the abbot, if present, is always to follow with the Gospel; if he is absent, the superiors are to do so in turn. This is so that the order observed by the clergy in celebrating Masses may be maintained: namely, after the lesser cleric has read the Apostle, the senior deacon follows to read the holy Gospel. [Col. 1008C]

Thus also in monasteries the order of the Lord is maintained successively according to the rank of merit. At the nocturns, matins, and the lighting of the lamps, the psalms are to be completed in the responsories. At prime, terce, sext, and none, two heads are to be said in the responsories, and then they are to say the Gloria, so that the brothers may leave the oratory more quickly and be restored to the work they must perform. [Col. 1008D]

## CHAPTER XLVII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning discipline in psalmody.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

There must be such solemn gravity of reverence and such discipline in psalmody that the singing may be heard more lovingly by the Lord than by us, as Scripture says: “The going forth of morning and evening you will delight in” (Psalm 64). Again: “Sing well to him with jubilation, for the word of the Lord is upright” (Psalm 32). Again: “Exult in him with trembling” (Psalm 2). Again: “Sing psalms to the Lord wisely” (Psalm 46).

Therefore, since he commands that psalmody be performed wisely and with fear, the one singing must stand with an unmoving body, head bowed, and sing praises to the Lord in moderation. For he performs his ministry before the Divinity, as the Prophet teaches when he says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you” (Psalm 137). [Col. 1009A]

The one who sings must always take care that his mind does not wander elsewhere, lest, when our mind has turned to another thought, God say of us: “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15). Again he says of us: “With their mouth they blessed, but with their heart they cursed” (Psalm 61).

Nor, when we praise God only with the tongue, should we admit God only into the royal chamber of our mouth and place the devil within, having introduced him into the house of the heart. For the one who enters within, with one who leads him from within, is judged stronger than the one who waits outside.

Therefore, in singing and in such service, the heart must bodily correspond with the tongue, rendering its daily obligation to the Lord with fear. The one who sings should mark in his heart each and every testimony that he speaks. For individual verses, when marked, benefit the soul toward salvation, and in them is found everything that is sought. The psalm speaks all things for edification, as the Prophet says: “I will sing and understand in the blameless way, when you come to me” (Psalm 109). [Col. 1009B]

What sounds in the voice should also be present in the mind of the one singing. Let us therefore sing together with voice and mind, as the Apostle says: “I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14). It is fitting to cry out to God not only with our voices but also with our heart.

When psalmody is performed, care must be taken that frequent coughing, prolonged breathing, continual spitting, or filth drawn from the nostrils is not repeatedly thrown forward by the singer. Rather, the brother must throw it behind him, because the angels are taught to stand before those who sing, as the Prophet says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you” (Psalm 137). [Col. 1009C]

Therefore, when all these impediments have been supplied to those singing by the devil, the singer must immediately sign his mouth with the seal of the cross.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning reverence in prayer.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

If even carnal human beings are not addressed in prayer without humility when we ask them for some temporal benefits, how much more fitting is it that, for our sins and crimes, we should beseech Christ with every prayer of which we are capable! [Col. 1009D]

There must therefore be no duplicity in prayer. There must not be one thing in the mouth and another in the heart. Prayer must not be prolonged with many words, as the holy Gospel says that hypocrites become such.

There must be no frequent coughing, continual spitting, or excessive breathing, because all these things are supplied by the devil as impediments to prayers and psalms. What we said above must also be observed in prayers: if the one praying wishes to spit or throw out filth from the nostrils, he must cast it not forward but backward behind him, on account of the angels standing before him, as the Prophet shows and says: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you, and I will adore toward your holy temple” (Psalm 137). [Col. 1010A]

You see, therefore, that we have shown that one both prays and sings before the angels. We said that prayer should be brief so that no one might fall asleep under the pretext of prolonged prayer, or so that, if they lie there for a long time, the devil might perhaps present various things before their eyes or suggest something else in their hearts.

Therefore one must pray simply and with fear, so that the one who prays may seem to be holding the feet of Christ who is present. We ought to pray with such great fear that we recognize that we are speaking with God. We must therefore pray with the whole mind, as the Apostle says: “I will pray both with the mind and with the spirit” (2 Corinthians 14).

## CHAPTER XLIX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the monastery’s vigils.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

Every Saturday the vigils are to be held in the monastery, from evening until the cock has been heard crowing for the second time and matins have already begun. But because they are called vigils, the brothers must abstain from sleep; they must sing psalms and listen to readings being read. After matins they may rest in their beds. [Col. 1010B]

## CHAPTER L

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the performance of daily work at the various hours and at different times.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER

While the divine offices cease during the day, we do not wish the intervals of the hours that cease from psalmody to pass in idleness, judging that even a little idleness produces a diminished profit for those who are secure. For an idle person works death and is always in desires.

When a brother is doing something, while he fixes his eyes upon the work of his labor, he occupies his mind with what he is doing, and has no leisure to entertain other thoughts; he is not submerged in the waves of desire. For the eye of his thought does not grow dry through stupor when his hand, together with his mind, is occupied in completing something. Therefore the Apostle says: “When we were with you, we commanded you this: if anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat” (2 Thessalonians 3). [Col. 1010C]

Thus there must be both divine offices and bodily works, that is, works of the hands. And when there is something to give to the needy, they are to be laden with good acts and well-done deeds. Therefore different kinds of work should be assigned during the alternating intervals of the hours.

In winter, from the winter equinox—which is the eighth day before the Kalends of October—until Easter, because it is cold and the brothers cannot work in the morning, from prime until terce the groups of ten are to be separated from one another in different places, lest the whole congregation, gathered into one place, disturb one another with their voices. One of every ten is to devote himself to reading in different places, while the rest of his group listen.

During these three hours the little boys are to study letters in their groups of ten on their tablets under the guidance of one literate brother. In the alphabet, we encourage even the older brothers, up to fifty years of age, to study letters.

During these hours we likewise instruct those who do not know the psalms to study them under the direction of their superiors. In each group of ten, during these three hours, let them read and listen to letters in turn and show the psalms to those who do not know them. [Col. 1010D]

When they have completed these three hours in spiritual work, after putting away their tablets and sacred books, they are to rise at terce with praises, giving thanks to the Lord in the oratory that they have deserved to pass three hours of the day occupied in spiritual works without sin.

As soon as they have left terce, all the superiors are to keep their eyes upon the abbot and ask him what he commands their groups of ten to do. When he has assigned a different work of labor to each group, they are immediately, obediently and under the arrangement of their superiors, to perform the assigned work always in silence.

They must pray before beginning to work and pray again after completing the work. They must always work in the presence of their superiors. When they have completed these three hours with seriousness in such labor, they are to hasten to sext with divine praises, giving thanks in the oratory to the Lord, who has likewise granted them to pass another three hours of the day occupied in such work without sin. [Col. 1011A]

We say that the brothers must always preserve silence so that, when the mouth is guarded from all speech, the sins of the tongue may not be admitted. This silence is to be observed by the brothers at work by avoiding lawless chatter, worldly matters, and idle words that have no relevance.

They may meditate on psalms, review the Scriptures, or speak about something concerning God—only in the absence of the abbot, and nevertheless humbly and quietly—although during that hour the brothers have permission to do so.

As soon as they have left sext, they are to return to their places and complete their assigned work. Wherever the greater number of brothers are at work, a reading from some book is always to be read daily by one literate brother. We have ordered that a reading be given daily to those who work so that, when we are silent about evil and hear and speak about good, we may never sin. [Col. 1011B]

The brother who is unable to work because of some unavoidable necessity is himself to read. If the larger number of brothers to whom the reading is being given is near the monastery, and brothers working inside the monastery are engaged in some craft by which they can move over to those who are reading, they are immediately to join them and listen with their ears while continuing to work with their hands.

If the workshop is fixed in place, or the work is such that the brothers cannot move to those who are reading, the reading is to be given to them on another day.

When they have also spent these three hours in labor, they are to hasten to none with divine praises, giving thanks in the oratory to the Lord, who has likewise granted them to pass another three hours of the day without sin. [Col. 1011C]

After none, for whatever time remains until the lighting of the lamps, each is to work at whatever task presents itself, under the direction of the abbot or with their superiors overseeing them. The superiors are to attend the brothers at every hour for this reason: so that no brother may be wholly idle. When he is occupied in doing something, he has no leisure to think about anything else except what he is working on with attentive hands.

In summer, from Easter until the winter equinox, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of October, because the morning is cooler, they are to work more from prime until terce, so that they may forgo the fresh and pleasant—or heavy—sleep of the short nights.

Likewise, after terce has been said until sext, let them work, always in silence concerning worldly or idle matters and buffoonery, which do not contribute to edification. We relax permission for the disciples during that hour to review or meditate on psalms, to ask about divine instructions, or to speak about something concerning God for the sake of edification, but only in the absence of the abbot. In his presence, labor, humility, silence, and reverence are to be offered. [Col. 1011D]

In the absence of the abbot we permit them to speak about good and holy matters so that the guardianship of their mouths, which must be preserved for the service of God, may never be absent from their memory, and so that their speech may be occupied more readily with good than with evil.

When they begin the work of the earth or of any craft, they must begin with prayer preceding it, and always finish with the same prayer. They should begin with prayer preceding the work so that they may ask God that, helped by his merciful assistance and protected by his defense at every hour, no sin may steal upon them during the hours in which they labor, by which they might displease the Lord.

After they have withdrawn from their labor, they are to pray, giving thanks to God that they have been helped by God’s assistance.

When they have worked for three hours, they are to hasten to terce with divine praises, giving thanks in the oratory to the Lord, who has granted them to pass the time occupied in the labor of their hands without offense through sin.

As soon as they have left terce, each is to return to his work. When they have worked during the following hours, they are to hasten to sext with divine praises, giving thanks in the oratory to the Lord, who has likewise granted them to pass another three hours of the day occupied in labor without sin. [Col. 1012A]

Immediately after sext, or after the meal, whether they are fasting or not, all are to rest for a short time in their beds at midday, so that they may pass the midday hours and the burning heat in sleep. The brevity of the season’s nights is to be compensated by midday sleep in the bodies of the brothers wearied by fasting and labor, so that the brother may rise soberly at night when, in summer, he has begun to sleep by day.

After sext, when they have lain down in their beds, after a short rest all the brothers are to be awakened by their superiors, or the superiors themselves together by the watchman appointed for that week. For whatever portion of the day remains before none, they are to return to their crafts and their labor, again in silence concerning idle chatter. [Col. 1012B]
