Throughout the entire summer season, they may also take refreshment at the sixth or ninth hour. Nevertheless, after none, for whatever part of the day remains until the lighting of the lamps begins earlier, the groups of ten, separated from one another in different places under the arrangement of their superiors, are to engage in different activities: some are to read, others listen, others learn and teach letters, and others meditate on the psalms assigned to them.

When they have mastered these and retained them perfectly in memory, they are to be brought by their superiors and recite from memory to the abbot that psalm, canticle, or reading. When he has recited it, the brother is immediately to ask that prayer be made for him.

When those standing around have prayed for him, the brother who recited it is to kiss the knees of the abbot before whom he has completed the recitation. He is then immediately assigned another psalm either by the abbot himself or by the superiors. After whatever has been assigned has been given to him, before meditating on it by himself, he is again to ask those standing around to pray for him, and then he is to begin meditating. [Col. 1012C]

The lighting of the lamps is always to begin early, especially in summer, while the sun is still hanging in the sky, as the Prophet says: “Until sunset” (Psalm 122); he did not say, “after sunset.” For this reason especially we said that in summer the lighting of the lamps should begin early, because the nights of that season are short.

Those brothers are to be assigned to work in the earth or to journeys who do not know crafts, or do not wish to learn them, or cannot do so.

The craftspeople, on the appointed day and with the portion of work appropriate to their tested skill, are to sit daily at their crafts. Nevertheless, when some necessity of work in the earth or of journeys urgently arises for the benefit of the monastery, they are then to leave their crafts and devote themselves either to helping the brothers or to the necessities of travel. [Col. 1014A]

For delicate and sick brothers, work of such a kind is to be imposed that they may be nourished for the service of God, not killed. The hard-hearted and simple brothers, or those who neither wish nor are able to recite letters, are to be entangled in rough tasks, but with a measure of justice, lest they alone be continually oppressed by different labors.

Little boys, the very old, and the sick are likewise to be compelled according to an equal judgment.

# HERE BEGINS THE LENTEN RULE [Col. 1013]

## CHAPTER LI [Col. 1013B]

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the prayers of Lent during the day.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE TEACHER
Between Matins and Prime, all are to make a pure prayer; likewise between Prime and Terce; similarly between Terce and Sext; similarly between Sext and None; similarly between None and Vespers; similarly between Vespers and Compline. The same is to be done throughout all the days of Lent.

## CHAPTER LII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the prayers of Lent at night, or the Psalms.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 1013C]

After the first sleep, all ought to rise, pray before their beds, complete the office with the abbot, and all lie down again; likewise, after the night office, they are to lie down again. Then, when the cock has crowed, all are to rise, pray before their beds, complete the office with the abbot, and all lie down again. Therefore the cock-watchers ought to be very vigilant and attentive by night and by day during the nights and days of Lent, so that they may warn the brothers that the hours of prayer have arrived.

For this reason all ought to sleep in one atrium, so that these prayers may commonly be completed by all before their beds, and so that all may hear the abbot completing them. They must likewise rise and perform Matins, because before Easter Matins are still said separately from the night office. Likewise, between Matins and Prime a pure prayer is to be made.

## CHAPTER LIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning restraint in food and drink during Lent.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Let one cooked dish suffice for all; and as a second course, whatever raw food there may be, together with fruit: two pieces of barley bread. From the first day of Lent until the thirtieth day, because of the labor, the brothers are to receive two drinks per day, and no more—that is, one unmixed wine and one hot drink. From the thirtieth day until the twentieth, let each receive one unmixed wine; but from the twentieth day until Easter, wine is to be withdrawn from everyone, except the sick, children under twelve years of age, and those already weakened by old age.

With regard to the sick, however, the abbot must exercise judgment, lest anyone lie and pretend to be ill. For the healthy, or for those abstaining by their own vow, hot water mixed with salt and cumin, or with celery seed, is to be provided. Oil is to be served not in cooking pots but in dishes, for those who are abstaining.

Those who abstain are nevertheless to sit at their own tables, as many as are assigned to a table by the arrangement of the superior, so that those abstaining from one table may eat from one dish. We have said that those who abstain should sit together among the other brothers so that the gluttons may be ashamed that, though sharing the same human nature, they cannot equally restrain the desires of the appetite, nor, in choosing what is good, obtain divine grace together with those who abstain.

On the very day of Lent, when they receive Communion at the first fast, before they communicate, the abbot is to grant permission in the oratory as follows. Let the abbot say to all the brothers:

“Brothers, whoever wishes to labor spiritually for his soul and to abstain from something, to him we grant free choice for this good work. Whoever does not wish to do so shall accept what the Rule establishes under this heading and shall be content with the measure of Lent.”

Then those of the brothers who wish to abstain from something are to go there in the oratory and humble themselves at the abbot’s knees, giving thanks for the permission granted to undertake this good act. After making this act of humility, let them also tell the abbot with their own mouths what each wishes to abstain from.

We have said that those who abstain are to be designated in the oratory so that, while they maintain this discipline at table, lukewarm or gluttonous brothers will no longer persuade them to resume the same food or to eat with them what the body must lose during Lent, since no one wishes to see another better than himself. Let such men, therefore, be chosen before God through the testimony of the oratory concerning all things, and let those abstaining be publicly designated.

For such men rightly ought to rejoice with Christ at Easter in the Lord’s resurrection, since during Lent they have crucified their bodies with him through abstinence, as Scripture says concerning sorrow: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV). And: “Though they were disciplined in a few things, they shall be well ordered in many things” (Wis. III).

For Lent signifies this present brief age, while Easter signifies the eternal joy of the future life for the good, to such an extent that what is abstained from during the forty days may be eaten throughout the whole year. Thus, whoever in the present life withdraws something from his desires or from his flesh will, in that age, be permitted to feast abundantly and forever on the better delights of God. Since he wished to suffer sorrow for the Lord during this brief time, he will deserve to rejoice with him in the future.

The fasts of Lent are to continue until evening; that is, everyone is to be refreshed after the evening office throughout those forty days, because on Thursday there is a fast, except on Sunday. On those Sundays they are to eat nothing at all in the evening, so that there may be only one meal during the day. The fast during Lent is not to be broken by the resident brothers because of those who arrive.

If brothers wish to add a fast, on the day they have added they are not to be seen at labor with the brothers; they are only to read while the brothers are laboring, so that they may not be idle and may be refreshed by the word of God instead of by bread. For this reason they are to labor spiritually by reading, so that, just as it is written, “Whoever does not work, should not eat” (II Thess. III), so it is fitting that whoever does not eat should not work, except in that refreshment in which he is refreshed without bread—that is, in the word of God. Scripture says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Luke IV).

During those forty days, the weekly servers are not to wash the feet of the brothers in the monastery; they are only to remove their footwear. But when any outsiders arrive, their feet are to be washed, because of the testimony of that woman who washed and anointed the Savior’s feet with ointment from an alabaster jar while he was dining.

At the Lord’s Supper, let them present their hands for the blessing, so that the abbot’s feet may be washed, and afterward those of all the superiors, with the assistance of the brothers. The abbot, however, is to begin by washing at the same time; and he himself, as the superior, is to wash the feet of the doorkeepers, so that, by displaying humility toward them also in this service, he may rightly be judged more exalted in honor by all.

Then the superiors are to wash and dry the feet of all the brothers in their own groups.

At daybreak on Friday, which is before Holy Saturday, let them perform only the night office, because the night office said before cockcrow still belongs to Thursday. They are also to perform neither Matins nor the other hours nor the established offices of God until the Saturday Mass, when such a prolonged silence of psalmody in the mouths of those singing the Psalms is opened by the new “Alleluia” of the resurrection.

Therefore, after the night office said on Thursday, they are not to sing the Psalms any further until the Saturday Mass. Nevertheless, they are to complete those pure prayers of Lent, and on Friday itself they are to speak quietly among themselves about the sorrow of the Lord’s Passion; nor are they to greet one another.

Except for the sick, children, and those weighed down by old age, whoever among the healthy wishes to eat is to eat without receiving a blessing and without the meal being formally announced, so that, ashamed of being mastered by their appetite or by themselves, they may recognize that, while others undertake a day’s fast for the reward hoped for from God, they are unable voluntarily to pass through even one day of fasting, whereas necessity sometimes imposes three-day fasts upon others against their will.

And with what face can someone hope to feast on the future eighth day of Easter in the victory of the Lord’s Resurrection, if, in sorrow for the cause of that Passion, he has refused for one day to crucify his flesh with Christ?

The sacraments of the altar are to be completed on a larger glass paten, so that when the Jews seek Christ for his Passion on Friday, he may on that day be hidden from our minds, and on Saturday appear to us in the new sacrament through the resurrection.

Those who are going to eat on Friday are to eat without Communion, so that it may be recognized who unjustly eats on Friday without Christ.

The washing of objects and the preparation for Easter are to be undertaken on that very day. On Friday the altar covering and all the decoration of the oratory are to be removed; likewise, the sight of lamps and lanterns throughout the monastery is to be entirely denied, so that sorrow may be present in us on that day, when the true light of the Lord departs from the world through his Passion. At daybreak on the following Saturday, light is to be restored throughout the world for joy, when, through Christ’s resurrection, the light of joy returns to us.

At all times the monastery ought to be so adorned and clean that, throughout all the entrances and places of passage, it appears everywhere clean and decorated with hangings, like a single church, so that those who meet one another everywhere may fittingly, willingly, and joyfully pray.

*[The Lenten Rule ends.]*

## CHAPTER LIV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

When the hour of the divine office arrives, the brothers must immediately hurry to the oratory.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the struck signal in the oratory indicates that the divine hour has arrived, those who are laboring are immediately to abandon their work; the craftsmen are to put down their tools; the scribes are not to complete the letter they are writing; every brother’s hand is to leave whatever it was doing. At once, with a measured step, let the foot hurry to the oratory and the mind to God, so that they may immediately hasten to prayer. Like bees toward honey, let the swarm of the brothers entering the oratory boil forth, so that the place of the holy oratory, which had been silent, may immediately be filled with the cries of the Psalms, and the silence of the holy place may pass to the workshops and tasks left behind.

Whenever the signal in the oratory has been struck, all who hear it are immediately to make the sign of the cross on their foreheads before running, saying: “Thanks be to God.”

## CHAPTER LV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How many paces away must a brother be before he is to leave his work and hurry to the oratory?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the signal struck by the abbot has sounded, the laboring brother, whether alone or with many others, is immediately to judge more quickly by the assessment of his eyes, after leaving his tool, whether he ought to hurry to the oratory or not. He is to choose this rule: if he is fifty paces from the monastery gate, he ought to hurry to the oratory with measured dignity.

But if the distance is greater than this, they are no longer to go; instead, leaving the tool from their hands, they are to bow their heads and slowly say the Work of God themselves, kneeling as is done in the oratory. Or, if some work of the brothers urgently needs to be completed, they are nevertheless to recite the Psalms with their doxologies; for it is established that those doxologies said among them count as prayers.

The doxologies themselves are always to be said by the singer with bowed head. The Psalms, however, are to be said straight through, because of the urgent work, as we said above. When that work has been completed, he is immediately to complete the verse and prayer for himself and resume what he had been doing.

For this reason, if the place is more than fifty paces distant from the laboring brother, we have not commanded him to walk to the oratory, lest brothers running from a distance, stirred by excessive haste and competing in a race with one another, run not with dignity but with frivolity; and, exhausted by the long journey, enter the oratory late, with their stomachs still heaving from the road, unable to complete the Psalm’s voice.

If, although weary, he has arrived from a distance, he may find that the Work of God has already been completed by the brothers present. Then the spiritual brother would be placed in despair or suffer loss, deeply saddened because he had not deserved to perform the Work of God in the oratory; and the distance would cause him to lose the appointed hour.

Within the monastery, however, those occupied with urgent matters of common utility are to ask, in a clear voice, when the Psalm ceases and prayer is undertaken, that they should be considered as being in the oratory. In the very place where they are occupied, they are likewise to complete the Work of God quietly, following the voice of the oratory. When they have completed the Psalms in turn in that same place where they are standing or sitting, they are to kneel for the prayers.

## CHAPTER LVI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How the brothers are to complete the Work of God while on a journey.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When spiritual brothers travel together without a layman, singing as they go, they are to turn slightly aside from the road, kneel, and return to the road after the prayer. Immediately thereafter they are to remain silent, abstaining from every word unrelated to God, out of reverence for the Work of God.

Then, while walking, after first asking for a blessing, they are to break into the Psalm assigned to them. When they have completed it, they are to stand for a short time and, with bowed heads, pray briefly. When that prayer has been completed, they are immediately to begin walking along the road with a Psalm. When it has been completed, they are again to stand and pray. When that prayer has likewise been completed, they are to begin another Psalm while walking. When it has been completed, they are again to pray, bent over in humility.

When they have completed the whole customary office of that hour, they are to sit briefly, kneeling to one side, and pray. After completing the prayers in turn for one another, they are finally to return to the road, and then, if they wish, mingle with ordinary conversation.

Nevertheless, during those hours in which they are completing the Work of God while walking, they must take care not to introduce any other word among themselves while occupied with the divine work.

If they are traveling mixed with laymen, they are to separate themselves from them among the brush; or, if the place is open and provides no hiding place, they are to fall somewhat behind. Kneeling, they are to say the beginnings of three Psalms and immediately complete one doxology. Then, after saying the verse and making a brief prayer, they are to rise and follow their companions on the road.

We have not commanded the brothers to say more than the beginnings of three Psalms with one doxology, lest, while the lay companion proceeds—the one who has no concern for the cause of God—the spiritual brothers, perhaps abandoning the crossroads and not knowing the road, should be separated into many paths by error and afterward be overcome by bitter sadness, perhaps regretting that they had delayed their gains for the soul.

Brothers leaving the monastery are to be instructed by the abbot or by their superiors to complete the office in this way.

On a cloudy day, when the sun has hidden its rays from the world, whether in the monastery, on the road, or in the fields, the brothers are to estimate the passage of the hours. Whatever hour it may be, the customary office is nevertheless to be completed. Whether it is said before or after the appointed hour, the customary work of the hour is not to be omitted but performed, because the darkness of the clouds, with the sun quickly absent, excuses what religious observance does, where it finds no fault in the one performing it.

## CHAPTER LVII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

In what way are the brothers to observe some of the provisions of the Rule while on a journey?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

If a brother is sent out in the morning on the monastery’s business and, because of the demands of the journey, reads from Prime until Terce in winter, or from None until Vespers in summer, and is to return to the monastery on that same day, let him eat whatever hour he returns. Nevertheless, he is to read or meditate for a little while, so that he may appear to fulfill the Rule on that day.

If he is sent on a longer journey, let him carry with him from the monastery a small book containing some readings, so that whenever he stops on the road he may nevertheless read a little—provided that he has been trained in the Psalter. If he has not, let him carry with him tablets on which the superior has written Psalms, so that when he arrives at the midday meal or at his lodging, he may nevertheless meditate for a little while, as much as presents itself, and daily return to the Rule what belongs to it.

Likewise, a brother who is still learning letters is to carry with him from the monastery tablets supplied by the superior. If he travels with a literate man, then, when he arrives with him at a meal or lodging, he is to meditate for a little while with him or alone, as much as presents itself, as we said above—whether at midday meal or at the lodging—so that he may appear daily to fulfill the customary Rule.

Likewise, if a brother refuses to go on the monastery’s business, or, while walking, murmurs, or wishes to leave with some reluctance, then, if it pleases the abbot, he is no longer to be sent. He is immediately to receive the punishment of excommunication, and is to know that he has acquired the pride of resisting a divine command—divine because the Lord says to our teachers: “Whoever despises you, despises me” (Luke X).

When the brothers arrive at a lodging on the road, they are to choose a place that is secluded and clean in which to make their bed, so that there, lying quietly upon their bedding at night, they may worthily remember God.

Brothers going out on a journey are also to receive this command from the abbot or their superiors: whenever they visit any spiritual brothers who are settled somewhere, and enter their cells or oratories, they are to pray and say this verse:

“We entered his tabernacle; we worshiped in the place where his feet stood” (Ps. CXXXI).

When they leave, they are always likewise to pray and say this verse:

“Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Direct me in your truth” (Ps. XXIV).

Or, if they wish, they may say another verse in place of this:

“Make my steps firm in your paths, so that my footprints may not be moved” (Ps. CXVIII).

When our brothers begin to leave monasteries and the cells of spiritual men, they are first to bid farewell to the oratory. Then, specifically for their departure, they are to ask those whom they leave behind in the monasteries or cells to remember them in the subsequent Work of God, and so they are to proceed.

When our brothers enter churches, after the prayer in which they have humbly bowed before God, they are to rise and say this verse:

“The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their beds” (Ps. CXLIX).

Saying it slowly, and completing their prayer slightly bowed, they are then to go outside.

## CHAPTER LVIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Which Psalms should the brothers say at different times while traveling by night?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 1019C]

When a brother rises from his bed at night, whether alone or with another, to complete the night office, after the verse and silence, beginning at the start—or with a responsory [the reading is uncertain]—let them first say three Psalms, then another responsory, the readings, and the verse, and no more, because of the labor of the journey already undertaken and still to come.

At all times, however, once the night office has been completed on the road, they are immediately to join the following Matins to it, so that, when daylight overtakes them, Matins may not appear to be completed in squalid, unsuitable, or filthy places—a house or tavern—or before or after laymen who mock our way of life without reverence.

Therefore, once the brothers have completed Matins in the morning, they are to begin thinking only about continuing the journey, arranging the animals’ loads, or tightening the burden of their saddle-bags.

## CHAPTER LIX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

At what hour are the brothers to eat while on a journey?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

In winter, that is, from the autumnal equinox—which is the eighth day before the Kalends of October—until Easter, brothers traveling on a long journey are to eat on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday in the evening. They are not to break these fasts for any reason.

We have said “in the evening” because, if they wish to eat at None on the road, their occupation with the meal, prolonged through the short hours, causes their lodging to be lost when the day quickly closes.

Nevertheless, they are not to break these fasts in winter if they are not traveling with heavy loads on their backs. For then the abbot is to have the brothers traveling eat, after considering the time or the necessity, whether in winter or summer—if he judges that there are heavy frosts in the fields, burning heat on the roads, high mountains to be climbed, a heavy burden of baggage, or the weakness and incapacity of certain brothers. Then he is to have them eat and proceed from the monastery.

In severe winter cold he ought to send the brothers on their way warmed; in the burning heat of summer, cooled.

Children under twelve years of age are not only never to fast while traveling, but are not to leave the monastery on any fast day—unless they are being sent nearby, so that in summer they may be expected before Terce, or in winter before Sext, during which hours it has been established that they ought to eat.

## CHAPTER LX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the quantity of provisions to be received by brothers for a journey.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

The abbot is to consider the brothers’ due daily measure, the length of the journey, the time required to conduct the business, and also the quantity of the monastery’s resources, whether in money or in things that can be carried uncooked. In addition to provisions sufficient for the customary measure, he may add somewhat more for the labor of the journey, because of the charity owed to a companion or associate who may perhaps join them on the road—bread, wine, or other things or money—as much as the abbot wishes to add to the measure.

## CHAPTER LXI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

When a brother has been sent from the monastery and is expected back the same day, if someone persuades him to eat outside, ought he to share the meal, or, returning to the oratory, preserve the fast so that it may be observed before the abbot and Communion?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When a brother leaves the monastery, he is to ask the abbot, saying:

“What do you command, lord father? If, out of charity, I am detained at a meal by the person to whom I am being sent, or by someone else, and I am urged under oath to eat, what should I do? Must the fast be broken or not?”

Let the abbot reply:

“If a spiritual brother asks you to eat with him out of joy at your arrival and out of charity, then, if it is Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday, refuse his first request. But when he repeats his request a second time, consent out of charity. On other days, apart from these three, grant the spiritual man’s first request to eat.

“If it is a secular person who asks you to eat with him, we do not permit you to break your fast on Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday. Refuse no matter how many times he asks, until he swears an oath. But if he adjures you by something divine or holy, then consent on these three days, so that, when you consent after being adjured by him, you may be recognized as loving the Lord.

“What you grant to a spiritual brother’s second request out of charity, you rightly grant, though unwillingly, to a layman who adjures you in God’s name.

“If, on these three days, the persuasion to break the fast occurs without an adjuration in God’s name, we do not permit the brothers to eat among laymen; they are to wait until they return to the oratory for their meal.

“If the journey is so long that the brother will return late, and, as we said, a layman urges him on these three days, without an oath, to break his fast, he is nevertheless not to promise that he will eat.

“But if a brother is sent to a secular man who now appears wholly converted and resembles religious men in every respect, differing only in his tonsure, then, on the three days, after the first request to eat, the request is to be granted, because of the form of his conversion and out of charity.

“On other days, if the brother’s delay at the person urging him to eat is prolonged until None or Vespers, the brother is permitted to eat, so that the customary practice of the holy way of life may not be exceeded outside the appointed hours of meals.

“If there is no delay, and the brother must return by daylight, then, whatever hour the brothers are urged to eat while hurrying, he is immediately to consent. Otherwise the brother may have no provisions from the monastery, and the customary hour of the meal may encounter the long road; when the brother returns late and exhausted, the monastery’s table, having already been cleared, may be removed without a meal prepared for him, and the returning brother may be deceived on both sides.

“For this reason also, when a brother is hurrying, consent to a meal outside the customary hour is granted, so that the heart of the host, who has asked out of charity, may not be saddened.”

## CHAPTER LXII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Whether a brother may eat or drink on the road outside the appointed hour.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

No one is to presume upon his own provisions outside the appointed hour, since those provisions have themselves been given according to the privilege or measure of the Rule; for that reason they are owed at the appointed hours according to the measure of the norm.

If provisions belonging to someone else are given by an external companion for the labor of the journey, the brothers are to consent out of charity. Nevertheless, before consenting, they are to reply to the one offering them that they have received a command from the Rule or from the abbot not to touch the sacred provisions of the monastery outside the hour owed to them.

We have instructed holy or spiritual brothers who do not know this measure of discipline to make it known to their fellow travelers, lest, when they contribute nothing from their own provisions at the proper hour of the meal, they be thought to observe this more from greed than from discipline.

If those urging them respond to what the brothers have said, explaining that they seek only their favor or fellowship in eating out of charity, which the companionship of the journey has imposed, and that they wish to spend their own provisions for charity without touching the brothers’ provisions, then the brothers may finally agree, while the discipline of preserving their own hour and their own provisions remains in force.

When the appointed hour on the journey arrives, our brothers are first rightly to make their hours more fully according to the hour of justice. Then, placing their own provisions on the table—what the others had unjustly presumed upon out of charity—the brothers are now to serve twice over: both for reciprocal charity and according to the measure of justice. Thus, through them, the discipline may impart its knowledge to those who, though ignorant of the measure of justice, had persuaded them by charity.

If the hour of the meal arrives before the brothers reach the house appointed for them, then, wherever the appointed hour finds them on the road, the brothers are immediately to eat. Otherwise, when they reach the appointed place, they may be compelled by the farmer to eat, and the brother who was sent may appear to have lost the hour of the meal because he was not compelled by the master of the place to eat [the transmitted wording is internally difficult]. Later, compelled by hunger, he might be forced to eat outside the hour and violate the provisions of the appointed hour outside its proper time.

Before None, the brothers may drink anything on the road because of thirst.

## CHAPTER LXIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

What is the status of brothers who depart without greeting their brothers?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When spiritual brothers depart from one another on a journey, if they do not bid one another farewell, offer a common prayer to the Lord, or give one another the kiss of peace, they are to know that they depart excommunicated from charity, until they see one another again and bind the bond of charity between them.

This is recorded in the *Lives of the Fathers*: a brother departing from the regions of the East and coming to the regions of the West remembered that he had not bid one brother farewell. He retraced the roads of the journey he had already made so that he might complete in that brother what he had left incomplete.

Therefore the brothers ought to be attentive to this charity among brothers.

## CHAPTER LXIV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How often is a brother who leaves the monastery and returns again after straying to be received?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

If a brother frequently leaves the monastery, he is to be received when he returns up to the third time, but no more thereafter. For such a man’s faith in divine service before the Lord is recognized as being of the same quality as the instability of his feet before human beings.

And what use is such a man now in the monastery, whom God does not possess? Therefore, after the third correction, he is rightly to be treated by the monastery as a pagan and a publican.

## CHAPTER LXV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How are external brothers to be greeted by the resident brothers?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When outsiders arrive at the monastery and brothers of that monastery come to the common place where the outsiders are sitting, standing, lying down, or walking, the resident brother is first, immediately upon entering, to greet them in his own voice, saying, “Bless me.” Then he is to ask them to pray for him.

After the outsider has completed the prayer, the resident brother is immediately to go with his head bowed in humility to the outsider’s knees for his greeting. First, he is to be raised up for the kiss of peace, so that the apostolic sentence may be fulfilled: “Outdoing one another in showing honor” (Rom. XII).

When the external brothers enter, after the prayer and before it is completed, let the abbot say this verse with the resident brothers:

“We have received your mercies, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Ps. XLVII).

## CHAPTER LXVI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the brothers’ departure from the monastery on a journey.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When brothers leave on a journey, let them ask others to pray for them, saying the verse:

“Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths” (Ps. XXIV);

or, if they wish, another:

“Make my steps firm in your paths, so that my footprints may not be moved” (Ps. XVI).

Whenever they leave or enter, they are always to complete the verse with a doxology.

Likewise, when they return, let them ask others to pray for them, saying this verse:

“We entered his tabernacle; we worshiped in the place where his feet stood” (Ps. CXXXI),

with a doxology.

Whenever a brother enters or leaves the outer threshold of the monastery’s last enclosure, he is always to ask others to pray for him, though without a verse.

## CHAPTER XLVII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the return of brothers from a journey to the oratory.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 1023C]

Whenever brothers return from a journey to the monastery, at whatever hour, and find brothers singing Psalms in the oratory, they are immediately to sing with them. After the Psalm has been completed by those singing, they are all together, in their own voices, to ask that everyone pray for them, so that they may appear to fulfill the Rule by asking for prayer after entering through the outer gate of the monastery.

After the Masses of the holy Work in the oratory, they are first to receive the abbot, then their superiors, or all the brothers, for the kiss of peace after returning from the journey.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

That brothers must immediately keep silent when they leave the oratory.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 1023D]

When the brothers leave the oratory, they are immediately to keep silent; they are not even to leave while meditating on the Psalms, lest what was said reverently at its appointed time be sung outside that time through presumption.

Therefore, when they leave the oratory, they are to be silent at once, because the time of the Psalms has been completed and the beginning of silence has commenced, as Scripture says: “There is a time for every matter” (Eccl. III).

## CHAPTER LXIX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning sick brothers.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Brothers who say that they are sick, who do not rise for the Work of God, and who lie continuously are not to be summoned to punishment. They are to receive only broth, eggs, or hot water at the meal—something that true sufferers can scarcely accept—so that, if they are pretending, hunger may compel them to rise.

But if they rise after the appointed time of day, they are to be excommunicated and are not to approach the material table, because they were not present at the spiritual table of the oratory: they avoided the labor and despised the Work of God. For in such men the devil is recognized as supplying an excuse through weariness and the laziness of sleep; therefore let them receive such a penalty.

If a brother is weary without fever or pain in his limbs, and does not wish to undergo the punishment of excommunication for the weariness described above, let him nevertheless enter the oratory at the customary hour with the brothers. If he cannot stand, let him sing the Psalms lying on a mat as though in prayer. A standing brother nearby is nevertheless to watch over him, lest he sleep.

If afterward he has done no work at all, let him receive one piece of bread less in his ration and have two drinks withdrawn. This is only because he rose for the Work of God; nor is it just that an idle brother should be judged equal to a laboring brother, to whom the reward of worthy labor is due. For “you shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (I Cor. IX).

Likewise, one who does not work, if this is for a just cause, should, if the incapacity is complete, not eat at all; or eat only in proportion to the degree of weariness—“as much as a laboring or healthy man [does]” [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. The incapacitated man who declares that he cannot work ought likewise to be judged unable to eat, because it is consistent with justice that he be unable to do both, and this displays genuine necessity.

But if we cannot work, then we ought justly also to be unable to eat. For such an illness is recognized in the lazy, idle glutton: with his own mouth he declares that he cannot work, but concerning eating he is silent about his inability. If he wishes not to express his own inability, let him immediately begin to hear from another tongue that he is not willing, is unwilling, and cannot eat.

What justice shows this: that, just as soul, stomach, and limbs come together equally in one person, so one necessity must be felt commonly in all three, so that what these three things can commonly do in health may be recognized as impossible for them all together in necessity.

For why should necessity permit one thing to be unable while permitting another to be able, when, in one human body, soul, stomach, and limbs cannot separately feel and endure that same necessity? For the soul within us still feels all pains; when it departs, the dead body no longer knows how to feel what it has suffered.

O wickedness of injustice! The head is tortured by pains because of labor, while the stomach is not tortured because of love of food—as though the stomach itself were placed in another body.

## CHAPTER LXX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the brothers’ charity toward the sick.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Brothers who wish to show how full they are of charity are to visit sick brothers with earnest care. Let them console and serve them, so that brotherly charity may be proved in necessity and so that they may fulfill by their deeds the Lord’s words:

“I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. XXV).

## CHAPTER LXXI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Whether spiritual brothers who meet one another should first pray, give one another the kiss of peace, or offer a greeting.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER
When the brothers have entered the monastery, or have met spiritual brothers on the road, after greeting one another with a blessing, they should first pray and then give each other the peace. Thus we read of the meeting of the hermits Paul and Antony: when they had at once seen and encountered one another, after greeting each other by their own names, they immediately completed a prayer, and afterward joined one another in mutual embraces of charity, returning the peace to each other. [Col. 1025B] Therefore those who meet should pray first, before they offer each other the peace. For if prayer has not first been offered, how does a brother know that the encounter has not come in the form of a human apparition as a demonic temptation, so that, in place of the visible appearance of a body, a demonic phantom suddenly vanishes, and we deceive ourselves by our own sight if we believe our human eyes in something that we have not tested by divine prayers? Therefore those who meet should pray first, before they offer each other the peace. It is also fitting that, for the common occasion of their meeting, thanks should first be rendered to the Lord through prayer: he has deigned to make each known to the other, or to bring them together, through the sight they mutually desired. Then, after the Lord’s prayer has been completed, the grace of peace ought rightly to be returned to the human being. [Col. 1025C]

## CHAPTER LXXII

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Concerning a meal on account of charity toward visiting brothers.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When brothers from outside the monastery arrive, if it is Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday, they should be asked, by the voice of the abbot who is present—or of the cellarer, if the abbot is absent—to remain for the meal until None. But if, even after the third summons, they do not agree to remain until None and insist on continuing their journey, then, for the sake of the charity owed to their arrival, the fast having been broken, all the brothers of the monastery should eat with them at Sext. [Col. 1025D] If they insist on leaving before Sext, whatever hour their haste may dictate, they should eat by themselves without the household brothers, and should not be allowed to leave the monastery fasting because of the journey, because Christ’s charity is recognized in the breaking of bread. Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, it is read that after the Eucharist had been broken and taken, the apostles Andrew and John departed.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Concerning brothers who arrive late for the Work of God.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

If a brother has missed the first prayer or psalm at the night office, at Matins, or at Vespers, he should be expelled from the oratory, and the abbot should admonish him outside, with his head bowed in fear, privately concerning his amendment. [Col. 1026A] If he has missed the second prayer or psalm, he should be severely rebuked there in the oratory, in the presence of the congregation, after the psalm has been completed. But if he enters after the third prayer or psalm, he should immediately be cast out of the oratory as excommunicated, together with his superiors. He should not return for pardon until he has made an equally humble satisfaction before the threshold of the oratory; but this is to be done, as we said under the preceding heading, within a length of fifty paces.

At Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, whoever, after the signal has been struck, does not hurry to the first prayer and the first psalm should be severely rebuked in the oratory, with everyone present. [Col. 1026B] After the second prayer or psalm, whoever arrives should go outside in this excommunicated condition, together with his superiors.

Those who are not present for the antiphon or the preceding verse at table should eat and drink separately, without being marked, and without the appointed blessing being given or received, without anyone’s speech, until they rise. He rightly refreshes himself without any human speech who did not speak with God before the meal. Whoever is not present at the end of the meal to give thanks to God after the meal should receive, at the next meal, in seclusion, the same punishment as the one who did not speak with God before the meal.

These corrections or excommunications are established only for those who are late through deliberate negligence and are occupied by no necessity. [Col. 1026C] Even if they should proclaim with their own voice that, although absent, they ought to be remembered in the prayers in the oratory, the brothers should pass them over in silence, and they should know themselves to be excommunicated—those whom not the usefulness of the monastery but negligence has occupied. Those occupied for the usefulness of the monastery are rightly remembered as absent by those present in the oratory; yet, while occupied in that same place, they too should say the Work of God.

A brother who has been rebuked in the oratory, even if he is not ordered to leave the oratory, should not undertake the psalm, responsory, reading, or verse until he has made satisfaction in the oratory itself: he must bend his knees and humbly ask that prayer be offered for him.

A brother occupied for the usefulness of the monastery should be held in mind in the oratory while absent. [Col. 1026D] Those occupied by negligence or lateness should be silently passed over, because they would rather acquire sin by being unwilling to remember God in their prayers.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

That a brother’s free will must be restrained.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

A brother who has vowed, beyond the established measure, either to fast, to add further austerities, or to abstain, and who wishes to do anything without the abbot’s command, should not be permitted to act according to the judgment of his own will. For even through what is good the devil steals upon him, so that he compels the brother to do his own will, whereas in the monastery a brother is not permitted to do whatever he wishes according to his own will. [Col. 1027A]

## CHAPTER LXXV

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Concerning the Sunday cessation from work.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

From the ninth hour on Saturday, after the meal, they should read in summer. In winter, from the ninth hour on Saturday, as was established above, they should not work. On the following Sunday also they should cease from every laborious task, and, in both winter and summer, from their customary daily meditation for three hours of the day. [Col. 1027B] After the church services, however, each person may read whatever he wishes or enjoys, according to his own judgment; or they may have complete freedom for rest, so that they may rejoice in the Sunday established for their repose.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

How should blessings sent by a priest be received?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When blessings arrive at the monastery from the supreme Pontiff or from priests of the succeeding rank, the abbot should immediately kiss the gift of blessing that has been sent. Then, rising with all who are standing beside him, they should pray, saying this verse: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Psalm XLVII), with the Gloria; and, having completed it, he should sit. [Col. 1027C]

## CHAPTER LXXVII

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Concerning the blessing or sign of priests.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When priests are invited to the monastery for a meal, they themselves should make the sign over all food and mixed drinks. Or first, at their own table, they should themselves give the unmixed wine and the blessing, responding to those who request them. When those same priests ask others for a blessing while eating or drinking, it is not permitted for them to receive a response from their superiors, because those who have been consecrated can receive from the unconsecrated what they themselves give.

If clerics are present at the tables of the servants of God, they too should be given a place for making the sign; likewise, after the prayer, they should be given a place to complete it. [Col. 1027D]

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

That no one arriving, whether brother or layman, should be fed in idleness at the monastery for more than two days.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When a brother or guest arrives at the monastery, if, in the honor shown to a guest or because of the weariness of the journey, he wishes to remain idle, he may sit with the brothers at their common table at the customary hour for two days. On the third day, after Prime has been said, when the abbot leaves the oratory, the hebdomadaries and cellarers should keep the guest inside the oratory and say to him: “Help the brothers in their work, whatever the abbot orders, whether in the field or in a craft. If you will not help, depart, because the Rule has fulfilled its hospitality toward you for two days.” [Col. 1028A]

If he agrees to work, a task should immediately be assigned to him with the brothers. If he refuses to complete it, he should depart, and his bed should immediately be stripped, until another traveler arrives; when someone spiritual arrives, it should be newly made for him.

Therefore, if he does not wish to work, the hebdomadaries and cellarer should tell him to depart, lest the brothers laboring in the monastery be justly compelled to hate the hospitality shown to this idler, and, being turned to murmuring or slander, begin to hate such travelers—people who, through the inertia of their misery, fixed nowhere, consume in idleness the bread owed to those who labor, while visiting monasteries under the pretext of religion. [Col. 1028B] They neither openly present themselves as citizens of the monasteries by remaining permanently, nor openly declare themselves weak by begging.

For, as we said above, to such people an almsgiving extended beyond two days is a loss to the giver; whereas to a poor beggar whose weakness is manifest, it becomes a gain of reward for the beggar. Therefore, when such men refuse to work after two days, they should rightly understand that the Apostle’s command was given so that they might be received and fed in idleness for two days on account of the labor of their long journey: “Pursuing hospitality” (Romans XII).

Likewise, the command was given that they should be urged to labor with the brothers: “For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not idle among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without payment among you; but with labor and toil, working night and day, so as not to burden any of you—not as though we had no authority, but so that we might give you an example for imitation. For when we were with you, we commanded you this: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat. For we hear that some among you are walking disorderly, doing no work but meddling. Now we charge and exhort such people, in the Lord Jesus Christ, that by working quietly they eat their own bread” (2 Thessalonians III). [Col. 1028C]

But if spiritual guests cannot work on the very day they arrive because of the fatigue of the journey, nevertheless, on the following day they themselves voluntarily undertake whatever they see the brothers doing, lest they be judged by those who labor to be not only idle but also wretched.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

[Col. 1028D]

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Concerning the guest cell.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

A guest cell should be established apart from the monastery, with beds made up, where visiting brothers—especially strangers—may sleep and place their traveling bags. No property of the monastery, tools, or utensils should be stored there, lest those thought to be spiritual guests suddenly be found to be thieves causing loss.

For the sake of guarding them, two brothers should also be appointed from the group of ten whose others perform kitchen duty. In rotation, their superiors should assign brothers from that group in rotation to guard the visiting brothers unobtrusively for as long as all the members of the same group complete their weeks in turn. [Col. 1029A] When another group of ten begins to cook, and travelers arrive during the days of its weekly service, brothers appointed from that same group by their superiors should likewise guard the visitors unobtrusively until another group of ten succeeds them. Thus all the groups of ten, taking their turns and beginning again, should always guard every arriving traveler.

When travelers arrive, those two brothers whose turn it is to guard them should make beds for themselves together in the same cell. Thus, if one of the guests should wish to go to the oratory at night and the other should not wish to rise because of weariness, or if they should wish to go outside in turn, each of the two guests will have a separate, unobtrusive guardian. [Col. 1029B] In this way, the one who goes either to the oratory or outside is escorted by a household brother under guard through the monastery’s uncertain exits and entrances at night, while the other guardian remains with the guest who stays behind. Thus they appear both to fulfill the charity of companionship toward the guests and to guard the monastery’s property unexpectedly against uncertain threats.

During the day also, they should take care to watch them within the monastery, keeping an eye on them so that nothing is done. This care is entrusted to two men so that at night they may take turns being attentive to the guests, and during the day, if one of them happens to be occupied, the other may watch the guest from a distance.

The cell itself should have a lock of the same kind on the inside as on the outside. At night, when the guests are shut in with them, the key should be removed from the bolts fastened inside and hidden where they know it to be. [Col. 1029C] Thus, if a guest should wish to go outside, he must rouse his guardians by asking for the key; in the presence of the guardian, he may then begin to go outside into the unknown place of refreshment.

The brothers should receive the guests’ traveling bags and staffs and keep them in that same cell, faithfully securing them with the external key.

If guests of such a kind are found who, by remaining for a long time, faithfully and earnestly laboring, have judged that they should establish themselves firmly in the monastery, their guardians should report this to the abbot. The Rule should be read to them, and the number of days they have already spent in the monastery should be determined; the remaining days of their probation should be granted to them for consideration among themselves. When the appointed days of probation have been completed, and only then, if they are pleased with the tested way of life or with the discipline of the Rule, they should surrender themselves to the monastery, persevering there until death, as has been established under a later heading concerning brothers who are to be established in the monastery. [Col. 1029D]

But if they do not wish to establish themselves, yet wish to remain in the monastery while working daily with the brothers, then, if they are content to wear out their own clothing or garments in another’s work, they should be provided by the monastery only with the common table and the common measure of food. Preparation of their other necessities should be denied them. Everything should be prepared for those who are firmly established; but for those whose establishment is doubtful, the monastery’s table alone should suffice—only because they wish to remain by working with the brothers, being guarded by those brothers day and night.

## CHAPTER LXXX

[Col. 1030A]

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Whether brothers polluted in sleep should receive Communion or not.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Brothers who recognize that they have been defiled in sleep should secretly confess this very thing to the abbot, bent at his knees before the doors of the oratory, before they enter for the hour of psalmody at which they customarily receive Communion. The abbot should then ask them what shameful thing they may have thought about on the preceding day, so that consent to lust came upon them during the night.

If the brother is more spiritual, he should not be ashamed to confess that evil, as we said under the preceding heading, if he wishes to save his soul from death, so that the abbot may correct him through admonitions. [Col. 1030B] Nevertheless, they should abstain from receiving Communion for two days, so that on the third day they may communicate purified.

Brothers who frequently experience this should know that they bring excommunication upon themselves not by accident but by their own will. They themselves make themselves strangers to the Lord’s body, luring lust toward themselves through their thoughts and defiling their flesh with shameful desires. For just as a moth corrupts and consumes clothing, and worms corrupt and consume wood, so a shameful thought stains and prevents a pure soul from remaining pure. Therefore such men are believed to be in the spirit before God as they are found in guilt before human beings. For sacred Scripture says: “Perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wisdom I).

## CHAPTER LXXXI

[Col. 1030C]

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Concerning the clothing and footwear of the brothers.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

In winter the brothers should have a coarse, everyday woolen outfit and another night tunic, which they should take off after Matins, because during the day they are occupied with various labors. In winter they should also have a woolen cloak, woolen trousers, and bandages or foot-wrappings.

In summer they should have a linen outfit, not too coarse, on account of labor and sweat. They should have linen cloaks, fine but not excessively so, on account of the heat and sweat, and linen trousers. We prohibit linen bandages, so that there may be some distinction between a monk and a cleric.

They should also have individual finer linen outfits, which they should use only on feast days during processions. In summer they should have one linen hand-towel each on account of sweat, and one face-cloth for each group of ten.

All these things should be kept in separate chests for each group of ten, with the superiors holding the keys. [Col. 1030D] The chests should be placed in the wardrobe, where the monastery’s tools and all its possessions are kept; we have already specified above who is to guard that room.

We said that all the changes of clothing for one group of ten should be kept under the superiors’ keys in a single chest so that, when no brother has a chest under his own control, he has no place where he can hide anything privately. All the groups of ten should observe this arrangement.

If any brother seems, in his own appearance, to be conspicuously well dressed or overly pleased with himself, it should immediately be taken from him by his superiors, given to another, and another one given to him. This is so that his own will may not be exalted in the brother. Whatever his soul desires should not be given to him, because the spirit is opposed to the desires of the flesh; therefore the spiritual man belongs to God, not the fleshly man.

When the hebdomadaries enter the kitchen, they should have sackcloth tunics and rough hoods. Such garments should be able, without shame, to endure all dirt and damage within the monastery, including the filth of pots, kettles, or cauldrons, as well as heat from the oven and the various impurities of the kitchen. After the week has been completed, these things should be washed late on the final day and handed over to the other hebdomadaries who are entering service. [Col. 1031A]

As for footwear, the brothers ought to have iron-studded boots, triclinas—not for play but for use—which they should wear in winter. In summer they should be greased and stored away. All the boots ought to have nails, both those used in the monastery and those used on the road, so that boots kept for a long time may be preserved and the brother’s foot may remain cool within the boot.

For Matins in summer they should use wooden shoes with leather coverings, so that, returning to their beds with soiled feet, they do not dirty the bedclothes. In winter they should use leather foot-wrappings for Matins, because of the cold in their feet. [Col. 1031B]

In winter they should have on their beds one mat each, one padded bedcover each, and wool. In summer, instead of wool, they should use rushes because of the heat. Before each bed they should have a single hide on which to wipe the dirt from their feet, and then they should climb into their beds.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

[Col. 1031C]

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Whether a brother should have anything privately in the monastery.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Every person in the life of this world is stirred, labors, and strives for three things: the traveler on the road, the soldier in battle, the emperor in the palace, the farmer in the field, and the hired worker in his business—all are stirred and labor so that, while they live, they may have the means to clothe themselves, put on shoes, and live.

But to those to whom the Lord has entrusted the house of his service, he has shown that they should not think too much about the present world, because all these things pass away. Everything that we see and use is ours only for a few days, and these momentary things pass away with the time of our life. [Col. 1031D] Through the death of the body, when the light of this world has been extinguished in us and the eyes of life have been closed, everything we possess is left to the world.

Those things, however, are eternal which, when they come, do not know how to pass away any further. They endure either among the goods of eternal life for the righteous or in the punishments of Gehenna for sinners. Therefore, as though we already seemed to have been summoned there by desire for the good or fear of evil, let us occupy our minds in this life always with thoughts of things above.

For this reason the Lord commands his servants that no one should be anxious about the necessities of this life. He also warns those who believe in him not to think about tomorrow, but only to desire his kingdom and righteousness, saying in the holy Gospel: “Do not think about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear; but seek the kingdom and righteousness of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Luke XII). [Col. 1032A]

Since all these necessities are prepared for us by the Lord, and the abbot alone is concerned with God about administering everything, why should a disciple dare to make, possess, or claim anything privately for himself?

Anything private is therefore forbidden because no one who serves God entangles himself in worldly affairs, “so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy II). When he has subjected himself with all his possessions to another’s authority, there is no possession in which his own will—which is hostile to the will of God—can be exalted.

Ananias and Sapphira did not obtain acceptance from the apostles because of private property: although they placed all their possessions at the apostles’ feet, they were condemned to the judgment of sudden death for fraudulently withholding some of their property. [Col. 1032B] Fraud cannot be committed against God, since nothing is hidden that will not be revealed by him.

Since the abbot has already considered food and clothing for the body and footwear for the feet of every brother, why should anyone need or possess anything privately—any object, gold, coins, or whatever else is necessary—when God appears to provide everything to him through the abbot of the monastery?

If anything private is found in anyone, the abbot should condemn him to a severe and prolonged excommunication, so that, by the example of that punishment, no one else may dare imitate it. To prevent this from occurring frequently in anyone, let everyone be searched by his superiors. If a brother is seen to be especially delighted with or pleased by any object, it should be taken from him and given to another, and something belonging to the other should be given to him, whatever it may be, so that his own will may not be exalted in him. [Col. 1032C]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

How priests should be treated in the monastery.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Priests should be treated in the monastery as guests, especially those whose primacy and honor are contained and exercised in the Church. If they have chosen to live in monasteries for the love of God, for discipline, or for the measure of a holy life, they should be called fathers of the monastery in name alone. Nothing else should be permitted them in the monasteries except to gather, complete, and sign the prayers.

They should neither presume upon anything else nor be permitted anything else; nor should they claim any authority, domination, or administration. [Col. 1032D] The abbot, who has been appointed over the entire flock, should claim and defend every form of permission and every arrangement of the monastery’s governance together with the Rule.

We establish that they should be called fathers of the monastery in name only because of the consecration or ordination of the priesthood, and so that they themselves, under the pretext of honor, may not exclude the abbots, as though they were laymen, from the monastery’s accounts or governance.

If the priests themselves choose daily to use the monastery’s food, clothing, and footwear, they should work in common with the brothers according to the Apostle’s command. They should not be excessively compelled to do so by the abbot, but admonished with reverence. [Col. 1033A] For if they are spiritual, they should command themselves.

As a precaution, lest they be compelled by others, they should always remember the holy Apostle Paul, who showed an example in himself, saying: “We did not eat your bread without payment” (2 Thessalonians III). He also says: “We labored with our hands so that we would not burden any of you.” And again he says: “Whoever does not work, let him not eat” (ibid.).

Therefore, if they remain idle for a very long time and refuse to seek their food by the labor of their hands, the abbot should, with reverence and after confronting them before many religious witnesses, send them back to the churches.

If, God forbid, they do not wish to leave peacefully but rather to depart in scandal, they should be detained and stripped only of the monastery’s possessions, and expelled through the closed gate without serious insult. [Col. 1033B] For they themselves ought all the more to do what they preach generally to others as commanded by God: that the bread of those who labor should be denied to the idle.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Who should eat with the abbot.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

At the abbot’s table should sit the elders, visiting outsiders, and, in rotation, the brothers who recite the psalter, whom the abbot wishes to be there, apart from the superiors. The superiors are ordered to be present at their own tables in their groups of ten so that they may preserve among those entrusted to them the cause of God—that is, silence and gravity.

We have said that both superiors should preside at the table of their group of ten for this reason: so that, through their alternating care, they may guard the ten brothers entrusted to them from every vice. [Col. 1033C]

## CHAPTER LXXXV

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

How, and at what price, should completed crafts within the monastery be sold?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When any craft has produced something completed beyond the needs of the monastery or beyond what is required for sending blessings, the price should be determined by asking how much it can be sold for to secular people; but it should always be sold for a lower price, by a smaller number of coins. In this way it may be recognized that spiritual people are separated from secular practices and kept at a distance from them.

They should not seek profit above justice for the sake of business, which is hostile to the soul. Rather, they should agree, out of humaneness, to accept a lower price than justice would permit, so that they may not be thought to practice their crafts out of greed and avarice, but so that the hand, which must be maintained at fitting expense, may not lie idle, and the hours of an industrious day may not pass uselessly. [Col. 1033D]

The price received should be faithfully entrusted by the craftsmen themselves to the abbot. The reduction in price should be fixed for the craftsmen according to the abbot’s assessment, so that they may likewise know what sum should be charged to buyers and cannot commit fraud concerning the amount of the price already known to the abbot.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

Concerning the monastery’s farmhouses.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

The monastery’s farmhouses ought to be leased, so that a hired secular person may bear all the labor of the fields, the concerns of the farmhouses, the complaints of tenants, and the disputes of neighbors—one who does not know how to think about the soul alone, but expends all his concern on the love of the present life. [Col. 1034A]

Those who think only about this life love present things so greatly that they suppose they will remain in this light for a long time. Thus it happens that, loving present things, they never desire or recognize the future. While they delight in momentary uses, they do not desire perpetual life; and, making the impediments of the world objects of love, they become wretched each day, forced to leave this life unwillingly and without their possessions, carrying nothing with them except sins.

But spiritual converts do not entangle themselves in worldly affairs for this reason: so that they may please the one to whom they have proved themselves. Thinking not about possessions, which remain in the world at death, but about the soul, which alone passes beyond death together with the account of its deeds, they choose rather to think about what is beneficial. [Col. 1034B]

Since heirs remain in the world when we depart from this life and cannot follow our soul after death, we ought rightly not to occupy our thoughts with them while we live. Instead, always desiring things above and placing all our hope in the future, we should still hope for the delightful life which we already seem to be enjoying.

Therefore the monastery’s farmhouses ought to be leased, so that a worker of the world may be occupied with worldly affairs. But to us, to whom the priest cries, “Lift up your hearts,” and to whom we promise in response, “We have them with the Lord,” it is not fitting to be carried away by inward thoughts. The Lord also cries to us in the Gospel: “Unless someone leaves all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). [Col. 1034C]

But because the life of our body cannot be preserved without material sustenance, and especially because many things must be prepared for the congregation and for the needs of visiting travelers, and because we do not wish to be restrictive toward one who asks for alms, we do not seem to abandon the possessions of the world. Rather, we seem rightly to preserve the monastery’s property, which supports the servants of God.

Therefore, if these possessions are cultivated through our own concern or care, while they benefit the body they will become an impediment to the soul. It is better, then, to possess them under another’s responsibility and safely receive the annual rents, thinking about nothing except the soul. [Col. 1034D]

For if we wish to cultivate them through spiritual brothers, by imposing heavy labor upon them we make them lose the practice of fasting. Nor should a person work with fasting strength in such a way that he labors more for his stomach than for his soul or for God. Therefore, for labor in the monastery, the single craft together with the garden should suffice.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

### QUESTION OF THE DISCIPLE

How should a brother, whether already converted or still a layman, enter, offer himself, or be received into the monastery?

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER
On a new brother entering the monastery—whether already converted or still a layman—and requesting this, the abbot should first answer him that he may not be able to observe the rule that has been established. [Col. 1035A] When he has said that he can obey everything, then let this rule of the monastery be read to him. When the reading of the rule has been completed, and everything previously stated has been spoken by the abbot, if the new brother answers that he is ready in deed for everything, then the abbot should continue and say:

“What about your possessions, which you use according to your own judgment? For it is not expedient for you, having been placed here for God’s sake, to leave your possessions elsewhere; but, as Scripture says: ‘Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also’ (Matt. XVI). It is therefore not expedient lest, through the devil’s enticement, you should be summoned from the monastery by desire for your possessions left outside, and, abandoning the service of the holy school, return to serve your own will; and, like a dog that delights in returning to its vomit, return to your vomit and again swallow, with filth, the spittle you cast upon the ground.

“But since you love perseverance and desire to know no occasion for departing, we have therefore established this salutary counsel: hear the voice of the Lord saying to you, ‘Go, sell everything, give to the poor, and come, follow me’ (Matt. XIX). If, then, you wish to follow this voice, go, sell what you possess, and bring the entire price here before me, so that, while you are present, it may be distributed by me to the poor; so that no pledge of yours may remain in the world by which you could return to it.

“For this reason, since your entrance into the monastery has not yet been firmly established, you are still granted free choice concerning your possessions. After your entrance has been confirmed, however, the rule denies the disciple the possession of anything private, whether in the monastery or outside it, so that there may be no place for his own will to exalt itself.

“But if it seems burdensome for you to dispose of everything, and there are possessions that can serve the monastery together with you, nevertheless do not leave them in the world as a pledge for returning. Bring everything faithfully with you into the monastery, concealing nothing from God, whose service you enter together with all your possessions—God who sees everything everywhere and from whom nothing is hidden, who reveals what is concealed.

“Remember the fraud of Ananias and Sapphira. When they wished to conceal part of what they had offered to God, they incurred everlasting death for their deceit. As soon as the new brother has heard this, if, in accordance with the divine sentence, he has disposed of everything and it has been distributed through the abbot’s hands, and if he has determined that he will indeed dispose of everything and reserve nothing for the monastery, he is not to be compelled to do so unless he wishes it of his own accord.

“Therefore, when he wishes to bind himself to the monastery after everything has been distributed through the abbot’s hands, no written pledge of perseverance is to be demanded from him, because the pledge of his faith before God was contained in the almsgiving by which all his possessions were distributed. For by the expenditure of all his possessions it is known before God that he can remain faithfully—he who desires not to spare his possessions for God’s sake. Let him give only this assurance: that nothing at all has been secretly left for him outside.

“The abbot grants this choice to those entering, so that it may not be judged that he desires the possessions of men more than their souls.

“But if a brother chooses to surrender himself to the monastery together with his possessions and does not wish to dispose of them, lest at some time, changed or armed by the devil, he should desire to leave and cause the monastery trouble in order to reclaim his possessions, let him first, with his own hand, take precautions concerning his stability. Let him attach to it a brief concerning his possessions and offer himself, together with his soul, to God and to the monastery’s oratory by a deed of donation. Let the whole document be subscribed by religious witnesses: a bishop, presbyter, and deacon, or the clergy of that territory. In the deed itself let him stipulate that, if at any time he wishes to depart from the monastery, he shall depart from it without his possessions and without the forgiveness of sins from God. [Col. 1036A]

“Now, once the abbot has received those possessions into his authority, if he sees that anything unnecessary to the monastery’s essential needs remains in excess, he should, for the brother’s soul, in obedience to the command stated above concerning following the Lord, dispose of that surplus by almsgiving and give its price to the poor. Thus what that inexperienced brother did not know how to do, this learned master may fulfill on his behalf. [Col. 1036B]

“But if a brother declares that he possesses absolutely nothing, inquiries should first be made among the neighbors of the region where he lived. If it is discovered that his poverty truly is complete, then, provided he is already known, he should be received into the monastery after giving a guarantor for his perseverance under a stipulated penalty. This is necessary lest, having temporarily entrusted some possessions outside, he should pretend to be poor in the monastery and contribute nothing to God through almsgiving or to the monastery by donation, but, enticed by those who are awaiting him and having found a pretext, should depart.

“When he has provided reliable guarantors under penalty, then, without suspicion, possessions of the monastery, or the prices of things to be purchased, or provisions for transport, may safely be entrusted to him for the monastery’s business.

“But if such a brother comes to the monastery whose homeland does not know him, or whose face is unknown to everyone, and he wishes to bind himself to the fellowship of the monastery, only an oath of fidelity is to be required of him: that, if he ever wishes to leave the monastery, he will depart with the abbot’s or everyone’s knowledge.

“And when he wishes to leave, he must first swear that he has not committed theft involving the monastery’s possessions, nor previously entrusted anything outside, nor secretly carried anything away with him—unless perhaps the abbot should wish to give him something out of mercy. If he swears falsely, let him bear in his soul what he was unable to fulfill in his body.
