“Nevertheless, let him return to the abbot the things with which he had been clothed in the monastery, as well as the footwear, so that these may benefit the brother who remains in perseverance, since they are taken away from those who depart. Let the possessions of the monastery rightly belong to him who lives in the monastery, and let them rightly be taken back from him who unjustly separates his spirit from perseverance in the monastery; for let them not please the one who was displeased with the discipline governing those possessions.

“But if he has sworn in this way and does not bind himself firmly, but remains for a time, let him give only this assurance: that he will not leave without the abbot’s knowledge or farewell, nor with stolen property. Let him also be kept under unexpected watch, possess authority over nothing, and be driven to work together with the brothers, so that he may live by working. If he is naked, however, and the abbot wishes to clothe him, let him use the clothing temporarily, knowing that whatever he has will be returned when he wishes to leave.

“For if, upon entering, he has given no oath to the monastery, and, being unknown, has given the abbot no pledge of fidelity for security—whether because he has contributed nothing to God through almsgiving, or has left nothing to the monastery from his possessions as a pledge of surety through donation, or, being unknown, has found no guarantor, or is bound by no oath of fidelity—then, if this brother, whose steadfastness is uncertain, is sent out with pack animals and money for purchasing goods, as soon as, under the devil’s direction, he has found an opportunity through expenses or transport, he may begin to migrate in an orderly fashion into foreign lands belonging to others, secure in the expectation of receiving provisions daily, and, by delaying, either follow late or never follow at all.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the period of probation for brothers who are to be received, during which they should deliberate with themselves about establishing their stability.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the new brother has taken precautions regarding all the matters stated above for establishing his stability—whether through almsgiving from his possessions, donation to the monastery, a penal guarantor’s document, or, if he is unknown, through an oath of fidelity—then let him receive a period of two months for deliberation and self-examination.

Nevertheless, he must be content to work with the brothers, receiving only the common measure of food and submitting to the discipline of the rule and its excommunications. Thus he may test the customs of the monastery, and the monastery may test him, while he considers whether he should establish himself with God or return more readily to the devil.

During these two months, he should be under the care of the brothers who guard the pilgrims; he too should be kept under unexpected watch, sleep in the pilgrims’ cell, and have his entrance and departure within the monastery observed in the presence of the guards. Whenever he withdraws anywhere from the community of the brothers, the guards should diligently seek him out, lest he presume to depart without farewell and with stolen property.

If, when the two months have been completed, he does not find it pleasing to continue in acceptable discipline in that monastery, he may leave with the knowledge of the abbot or of everyone, after giving assurance that he has committed no theft and returning any possessions of the monastery that he may have received temporarily. Immediately after peace has been given to all, he should receive a staff in his hand and provisions for the journey, after prayer has been made, a verse recited, and peace returned to him—if indeed he wishes to depart as a guest. And let the devil reclaim his place, since Christ had unwillingly received him as a guest.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How the new brother should confirm his entrance into the monastery.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the two-month period granted for deliberation has been completed, and he has chosen stability in acceptable discipline, and desires to fulfill his perseverance after promising to observe firmly the rule that has been read to him, the abbot should ask the new brother again what he has decided during the time granted for deliberation. When he answers that he promises obedience in everything, the abbot should reply:

“Thanks be to God.”

On the following day, after the first Mass has been said, when he is leaving the threshold of the oratory with the community, the new brother should bend his neck at the abbot’s knees, asking him and his entire community to remain for a little while in the oratory and pray for him. They should immediately pray for him at length.

When everything has been completed and the abbot wishes to leave, the new disciple should humbly grasp his garment and detain him with his hand, indicating through his request:

“There is something I wish first to commend to God, to this holy oratory, and to you and the community.”

When the abbot replies, “What is it? Tell me,” the petitioner should continue:

“I wish to serve God through the discipline of the rule read to me in your monastery.”

When the abbot replies, “And does this also please you?” the future disciple should continue:

“This is first for God, and likewise for me.”

Then the abbot should say:

“See, brother: you promise nothing to me, but to God, and to this oratory or holy altar. If you obey all the divine commands and my admonitions, on the day of judgment you will receive the crown of good deeds, and I will earn some share of forgiveness for my sins, since I encouraged you to conquer the devil and the world.

“But if you refuse to obey me in anything, behold, I call upon the Lord as witness—and this community also will bear witness for me on the day of judgment—that, as I said above, if you do not obey me or the community in anything, I will be acquitted at God’s judgment, while you will render an account for your own soul and your contempt.”

After these words, if he has entered with his possessions, then the brief or deed of donation of his possessions made to God or to the monastery should be placed upon the altar, with the donor brother himself saying:

“Behold, Lord, together with my soul and my poverty, I return and offer to you whatever you have given me. I wish my possessions to be there where my heart and soul are, yet under the authority of the monastery and of the abbot whom, Lord, you set over me in your place, to be feared, when you say to them: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me’ (Luke X).

“Since through him you provide all that is necessary for us, we ought therefore to possess nothing privately; for you are sufficient for us in everything, and you alone suffice for all things. May Christ now be for us both life and hope, and may death be gain.”

After this the new brother himself should say the following responsory:

“Receive me, Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my hope” (Ps. CXVIII). [Col. 1038D]

After this responsory the abbot should say the following verse:

“Establish, O God, what you have wrought in us” (Ps. LXVII).

After the verse has been said, peace should immediately be given to him by everyone. The abbot should complete the rite, take the brief from the altar, and immediately place the new disciple under the authority of a superior. Entrusted to their hands, he should leave with the other brothers for discipline.

On that same day, as a sign of humility, he should himself bring water to the brothers entering for Communion; as he gives it, he should kiss everyone’s hands and ask each of them to pray for him.

The abbot should insert into his will the briefs of donation made by the brothers, restoring them at the time of his death for the expenses and needs of the monastery, together with the names of those whose possessions are known to have been contributed. Thus, after his death, no one who perhaps leaves the monastery will have the confidence to reclaim his possessions, break the stability of the monastery and the faith of the deceased, or say that anything of his remained in the monastery without a donation.

## CHAPTER XC

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

After a layman has entered the monastery, his clothing must not be changed within a year, nor may his head be tonsured according to his profession.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When someone newly come from the world has fled to the monastery for the service of God [Col. 1039B] and declares that he wishes to convert, he should not be believed so readily. Rather, the abbot should deny him residence in the monastery in words alone, not in practice; serious trials should be proposed to test him, things contrary and bitter to his will should be commanded in order to discover his obedience, and daily fasts should be promised to him.

From the reading of the rule and the abbot’s statement he should also learn that no one in the monastery is permitted to say, “This I want and this I do not want; this I love and this I hate,” so that his own will may not be chosen. He should know that whoever has been converted in the monastery is not permitted to do whatever he wants according to his own will. Why? Because “there are ways that seem right to a man, but their end descends into the depths of hell” (Prov. XIV).

What he does not want, therefore, he is compelled to do, so that his own will may be cut away from him, since it is hostile to God. Whoever desires to convert perfectly must be denied whatever he has loved and desired, and whatever he has hated must be imposed upon him, as the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to be my disciple must deny himself and follow me” (Matt. XVI)—that is, he must do not his own will but God’s.

He must endure everything for the Lord who desires to serve in his school. For what can we endure that is worthy of the Lord? The Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present age are not worthy of the glory that is to come” (Rom. VIII).

If a persecutor inflicts fire upon Christ’s servant, so that, when the temporal heat has ended, it is not felt as pain, nevertheless it is not like the unquenchable fire; nor does it burn in the way that eternal punishment is immortally reserved for the sinful soul. If he inflicts the punishments of claws, the rack, or words, then, in the endurance of that brief pain, the crown of eternal joy follows. If a dark prison shuts us in for God’s sake, eternal Jerusalem awaits us, built of pearls and adorned with gold and precious stones.

If the darkness of confinement blinds us for God’s sake, it can obscure us only for a moment; afterward that light will receive us into eternal life, shining not with the brightness of the sun or moon, nor with the stars of heaven, but with the perpetual majesty of God himself.

If, by dying for God, we deserve to depart from this earth that we tread in this life, then we are immediately destined to walk forever upon that earth which is seven times brighter than silver.

But if we despise for God’s sake what are thought to be the delights of this world—things that pollute our inward parts rather than refresh them—then we are immediately destined for those ever-flowing rivers that eternally abound in honey, milk, wine, and oil. We are also destined for the varied and diverse fruits of those trees, which grow twelve times a year, not through human cultivation but through the abundance of God. They do not delight us because of hunger or appeal to us because of appetite; rather, after the eyes of the saints have been filled by their very sight, each person finds in his mouth the taste of whatever has delighted him.

It is therefore fitting that for a short time we should be tormented by fasts and abstinence for the Lord, so that forever we may be satisfied with the things he has prepared for the good. We are darkened by the persecutor in prison for God’s sake, so that we may shine in that perpetual light like sparks running through a reed-bed. We willingly desire momentary death for God’s sake so that we may be freed forever from the perpetual death of Gehenna.

Finally, even without persecution, in the very peace of Christianity, we serve as soldiers in the monastery’s school under the abbot’s command, through trials and the embittering of our wills, so that after our pilgrimage through this worldly life, when our Lord summons us to his judgment, we may present him with worthy works. We offer him our patience, by which we gladly bore all the hard and varied things commanded to us by the abbot for his name’s sake, and the various embitterings of our wills, which for God’s name and the salvation of our souls we willingly endured, saying to the Lord:

“For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” [Col. 1040C] (Ps. XLIII).

“And when all these things have come upon us, we have not forgotten you, nor have we acted wickedly in violation of your covenant through observing obedience; our heart has not turned back from perseverance in good works or from the hope of future things. For our paths have not departed from your ways, in which ways you tested us, O God. You tested us by fire, as silver is tested by fire” (Ps. LXV).

“You brought us into the snare of testing; you placed the tribulations of embitterment upon the back of our humility, so that we would not be permitted to do our own will, but would be compelled to do yours. Therefore you placed men over our heads” (ibid.), because you showed that we must be tested under an abbot as teacher or under a superior of discipline.

Therefore, once these people have followed the Lord, let them say in that future world:

“We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment” (ibid.)—that is, we passed through the embitterments of our wills and the service of holy obedience; behold, we have reached the refreshment of your mercy.

And again we say to him:

“We have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evils” (Ps. LXXXIX),

so that the fire of Gehenna may have nothing in us to claim, since the devil has done nothing there that could be burned as his own.

Therefore he must endure everything for the Lord who desires to serve in his school, so that, like gold tested by the file, hammers, and furnace fire, he may be useful for God’s diadem and the Lord’s crown.

For when someone does not do his own will, he is compelled to do the will of him to whom we say daily in prayer:

“Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth” (Matt. VI).

For our body is earth, to which the Lord said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). Since every personal will is carnal and descends from the body, it entices us to commit injustices. For a short time in this life it is sweet to the flesh through its desires, but afterward and forever it will be more bitter than gall.

Therefore our tongue is rightly compelled to cry out daily to the Lord:

“Your will be done on the earth of our body.”

When this will has been taught to us by our superiors in the monastery’s school and fulfilled by us daily through obedience, we may rightly believe that the Lord will spare us in the future. We may also trust that by his grace we can be crowned, because we have always done his will, not our own; we have never preferred ourselves or the desires of the flesh to his love; and for his sake we are even now prepared to lose our lives, so that we may deserve to find them with him in the future.

Therefore, when someone approaches the fear of God in the monastery, desiring to convert and become a disciple, the future master should set this before him, as we have said above: whatever he once desired according to his own will may be denied him, and whatever he does not want may be imposed upon him.

His former private possessions should be denied him. The entire rule should be read to him, and he should promise to fulfill it in deeds. He should know that his parents’ house is henceforth foreign to him and believe that he may no longer approach its threshold. For “unless someone leaves father, mother, brothers, and house, he cannot be Christ’s disciple.”

He should know that he is not to leave the monastery without the command of his superior. After all these things have been stated by the abbot, when he promises that he will obey everything and is ready in deed for all the admonitions of the abbot and the rule, then he should be received into the monastery.

Nevertheless, the habit of the holy profession should not be imposed upon him too readily, lest he promise for the moment and deceive in the future, and a wolf enter under the name of a sheep.

When he was a secular, the devil did not tempt him, because he always openly accomplished the devil’s will as his servant. But from the day on which he has handed himself over from the devil’s persuasion and the world’s wickedness to the fear of God in the service of Christ, he should know with certainty that the devil has become his enemy—the devil whom he abandoned, together with his world, for fear of the Lord.

Therefore the one entering should not be believed so readily, until it is seen whether he fulfills in deeds what he promises in words, as Scripture says:

“Do not believe every spirit, but first test them” (John IV).

And again:

“Many come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII).

See, therefore, that Scripture commands us to conduct God’s business cautiously, so that what is holy may not be given to dogs, nor precious pearls cast before swine.

Rather, while admonishing him daily, the abbot says:

“Son, for the time being these things that you use in the monastery do not prejudice you in our judgment. But first cleanse the inward parts of your heart from secular deeds in divine matters; only then will you change your clothing, so that what you already possess in your mind from God may rightly be seen by everyone in your body. After the military service of your heart has been cut away, you will justly have your head tonsured. When you have perfectly fulfilled, while still wearing your own clothes, everything contained in the monastery’s rule, and have received our habit, you will remain more holy.”

When, therefore, from that day onward he has fulfilled everything blamelessly in the monastery with the other brothers for an entire year, only then should he be tonsured without any hesitation, or should the clothing of his holy profession be changed for him.

He should be tonsured in this manner: the brother himself should stand in the middle of the oratory with his knees bent, while the abbot tonsures him and everyone around him sings psalms.

During this year of probation, no psalm, antiphon, responsory, or verse should be assigned to him until he has deserved to receive the habit of the holy profession. Nor should he dare to eat with the abbot.

The secular clothes that he has removed should be carefully stored and preserved, both in the case of laymen and of one whose conversion has been confirmed. This is so that, if—something that should not happen among the converted—he wishes to return again to his former vomit, chooses once more to retrace the paths of the world, and cannot be held back by any bonds of Scripture or admonition, he may return to Christ what belongs to Christ.

That is, stripped of the holy clothing or sacred habit, and dressed again in the clothes in which he came, resembling the world, he may return to the devil who persuaded him; and the habit he had taken from Christ may not be polluted in the world by a fugitive. Let the world receive him as the kind of person it had sent; let him return what belongs to it, unworthy of what Christ had given, since the Lord could not find in him what he was seeking.

Whatever he acquired, worked for, or contributed in the monastery must not be returned to him at all when he departs, because every possession that has entered the monastery for God requires perseverance there. For this reason permission to depart is denied. Only the one who has free choice is not detained against his will: that is, the soul and body, which, in their wills and desires, claim to be established by free choice so that they may be captured by the devil, and think that what is evil is permitted to them.

The possessions of apostates, or possessions that have been contributed, are not ordered by the fathers to be returned from the monastery because, even if they have been removed and consumed for the use of the saints, they cannot be restored. Nevertheless, many possessions are certainly denied for this reason: so that, at least through the opportunity presented by their possessions, disciples who are persevering in God’s discipline in the monastery may be kept there. Therefore what has been offered to God must not be reclaimed by a person for return to the world.

For this is the threefold summary of this rule:

Labor in the monastery feeds the brothers; perseverance gives them shoes and clothing; departure restores to the monastery the possessions owed to it—and, if he wishes, let him depart.

## CHAPTER XCI

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

How a nobleman’s son should be received into the monastery.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

When the son of a nobleman wishes to flee to the monastery for the service of God, he should not be received before he has promised, as we said above, to fulfill complete obedience.

Then let his parents come, so that their attitude toward him may also be known. If they oppose him, let him meanwhile be claimed for the monastery’s enclosure, even to the point of force being inflicted upon them for the Lord’s sake. The Lord is able to defend him for his own sake, because his right hand is stronger for protecting than the devil’s wickedness is for harming.

But if his parents are more consenting to his vow, the abbot should summon them to the monastery and inquire of them concerning the vow of their converting son, so that he may be seen to be devoted or offered by those who gave him birth.

When the parents answer that they gladly wish to fulfill what he desires, the abbot should say to them:

“Indeed, one God is sufficient for all of us in everything. But because, for those approaching divine service or entering a monastery, hope in the world must first be cut away, and because one who has unloaded the burden of his possessions from himself must proceed safely and alone to the Lord, entangled no longer in the world’s snares—for ‘no one serving God involves himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself’ (II Tim. II).

“A man burdened with gold cannot follow Christ, since he cannot serve two masters. He serves God well who wishes to possess with him in heaven the treasure that moth does not eat and thieves do not break into and steal. The Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Unless someone renounces everything he possesses, he cannot follow me or be my disciple’ (Luke XIV).

“For, as we have said, a man burdened with gold cannot follow Christ. Indeed, the Lord warns someone who was following his footsteps, saying to him: ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, and come, follow me’ (Matt. XIX).

“Therefore, saddened because of his many riches, that man feared hearing this sentence of the Lord’s voice: ‘A camel can pass more easily through the eye of a needle than a rich man can enter the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. X).

“The Apostle also condemns such people in his own words, saying: ‘Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and snares, and into many desires that plunge people into destruction and ruin. The root of all evils is greed; by desiring it, some have fallen away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains’ (II Tim. VI).

“You see, therefore, that one who does not wish to leave behind the good things he possesses in the world cannot follow God; nor can one love God who wishes not to hate riches.

“The Lord knows how to repay those who make themselves poor for his sake—not merely with things as great or as valuable as those they despise, but, in addition, he grants them eternal life itself, for them to enjoy forever.

“God does not seek to strip you of your possessions so that he himself may gain something from them, nor does he rejoice in your poverty or take pleasure in your need. Rather, when you go to him or desire his eternal riches, he wishes the temporary obstacles of the world, which occupy your thoughts, never to make you think about your soul or be concerned about death.

“Thus, when your days have been brought by negligence to the final limits of life, and you have left behind in the world everything about which you were thinking, may the final reckoning of death meet you at judgment with your sins alone, so that you will possess nothing but everlasting punishments. Then you will begin to repent forever, when, because of the merit of repentance itself, you will be unable to find a remedy.

“Therefore Scripture rightly cries out to us: ‘Run while you have the light to provide for yourselves, lest the darkness of death overtake you to examine your negligence’ (John XII).

“What, then, if someone approaches the Lord without departing from greed for his riches? The Apostle said above that such people cannot remain in what they desired for God, and that they can easily fall away from the faith, since they retain from the world something that they love.

“Therefore, parents, considering these things, we give you this counsel according to God concerning your son: if you wish to offer your son worthily to God, first strip him of the world.

“If anything remains with you for him to preserve in the world, he will at some point feel the prick of demonic desire, like a dog delighted to return to its vomit. With his hand placed upon the plow, he will look backward and, no longer fit for the kingdom of heaven, eventually leave the monastery, secure in the portion kept for him, desiring to return to your worldly household.

“Wishing to be a coheir with his brothers, he will begin to return as husband and master of his possessions. Restored to his former pleasures and honors, he will desire nothing except marriage.

“Therefore, as we said above, if you wish to offer him worthily to God, think first about removing his obstacle, and only afterward about his soul.

“Listen, then, to the voice of that Lord whom your son says he is following, speaking to him: ‘Sell everything you possess, give to the poor, come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven’ (Matt. XIX). [Col. 1044C]

“But since his portion is still under your authority, and by your consent or permission he appears to offer it to God rather than to us, you are responsible for it according to the Lord’s command. If you wish to hear that command, let nothing remain for your son with you in the world except God.

“But if, because of the enormity of his wealth or your love for the household raised by you, this divine command seems burdensome and insufficiently pleasing to you, hear the salutary counsel established by the fathers of our rule.

“Let his portion be divided into three equal parts. Let one part be distributed through the abbot’s hands to the poor or needy. Let him leave another part to you or to his brothers as he proceeds to the company of the saints, as a gift under a formal title [the precise reading of *exagilario* is uncertain]. Let him carry the third part with him as travel provision, so that it may benefit the needs of the monastery of the saints.

“For just as your son contributes his portion to all the brothers in the monastery for the comfort of life, as the Apostle says concerning distribution, especially ‘to the members of the household of faith’ (Gal. VII), so all the brothers of the monastery, each in his turn and according to what he possesses, bring their contributions when they enter the monastery, following this pattern, so that it may benefit your son together with everyone.

“But if both commands seem burdensome to you—so that you will neither listen to God by distributing to the poor and redeeming your son’s soul, nor accept our counsel by dividing his portion and removing his secular substance—then give your son to God naked and alone.

“Promise him by oath on the holy Gospels that he will no longer possess anything from your patrimonial wealth, so that, now firmly persevering in the Lord, he may know that he has nothing to hope for from the world when he sees himself estranged from you and from it, desiring only heavenly things.

“For this benefits his soul: either, provided for by you, he may go to the Lord, or, disinherited by you for the Lord’s sake, he may go more happily to God, crying out to the God whom he follows naked: ‘You, Lord, will restore my inheritance to me’ (Ps. XV). [The supplied citation lacks the opening parenthesis.]

“The only requirement is that he possess nothing from the world for which, whether you are alive or dead, he may still hope from your possessions. For one to whom the world has once been crucified must not again take delight in it.

“But if you refuse to make any arrangement concerning him at all, I think that his case will be reserved for you before the divine judgment.

“Know with certainty that he will receive more from the Lord than he has despised, since he has made the Lord his debtor by following him naked.

“Your son will certainly receive much in heaven, since the Lord promises him in the Gospel: ‘Whoever has left gold, silver, possessions, or houses for my sake will receive a hundredfold in the kingdom of God, and, in addition, eternal life’ (Matt. XIX).

“When your son hears this, he is ready, if you wish to leave everything to yourselves, to find a hundredfold with the Lord, because our Lord is sufficient for us in everything. For what can be sufficient for one for whom the Lord himself is not sufficient?”

## CHAPTER XCII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning denying the other brothers honor or rank after the abbot.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

[Col. 1045C]

The abbot must take care never to appoint anyone as his second-in-command, or to assign anyone a third place. Why? So that, when he has not elevated anyone by conferring honor, but has promised the honor of succession to one who acts holily, he may make all compete eagerly in good works and humility. Thus the Lord instructed the apostles when they were contending over the higher rank: he brought a child into their midst and said, “Whoever wishes to be stronger among you, let him be such a one; and whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be your servant” (Matt. 10). Again the Lord said to his disciples: “Whoever first does my commandments and so teaches them will be called greatest in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

Therefore, following this pattern of humility, the abbot should always say to all the brothers:

“Brothers and sons, whoever among you strives to obey the divine commandments in every respect, to submit entirely to the Rule, or to be found like me in conduct; whoever rises to the point of completing my teaching by his deeds; whoever submits his conduct to correction through me—not according to his own will and judgment, but in obedience to God—that is, not in pride but in humility; not in loquacity but in silence; not in hatred but in grace; not in deceit but in charity; not in anger but in peace; not in drunkenness but in sobriety; not in satiety but in moderation; not in scandal but in self-restraint; not in murmuring but in obedience; not in sluggishness but in eagerness; not in contention but in agreement; not in frivolity but in seriousness; not in empty talk but in a few wise words; not in loud or excessive laughter but in tears of patience; not in luxury but in chastity—

whoever among you perfectly fulfills all these things shall, at the time of my death, be appointed master of God’s school, not merely by my judgment but by God’s, in order to show Christ’s disciples the Lord’s art, which he himself has already perfectly fulfilled. For how could anyone justly rise to greater honor if he has not been able to fulfill the merits of that honor in the divine commandments? Or how could he have learned greater admonitions who has not accomplished them by his deeds? How will he govern the school? How can he correct the faults of others who does not know how to correct his own conduct? Or how can he govern others under discipline who has not been able to correct in himself the offenses against discipline? Therefore, unless someone has first been a perfect disciple in all things, he cannot be worthy to be a master.”

When the abbot has often declared this to the community, and has designated no one for certain honor, he should continually obscure their ranks: at times he should have them sit beside him at table, at times he should command them all to stand beside him in the oratory, and at times he should have them all recite the psalms after him. Thus no one may become inflated because of a second honor, nor may anyone from the lowest rank fall into despair.

Therefore, since no one among the many is raised to a second rank, and since each person, through uncertain hope of receiving honor, may judge that—if he conducts himself holily—he might one day be chosen for the abbatial honor, let him confidently expect that he may be selected because of his good deeds. Thus, while no one is designated because of uncertain circumstances, but honor is promised to those who act well and holily, all, desiring to obtain the rank of honor, hasten to fulfill in themselves the commandments of God mentioned above. Even if not out of fear of the future judgment, then at least out of desire for the honor of the present life, they may all strive eagerly to perfect themselves.

Then, when the community is large, and no one has descended through different ranks of honor, the last person will not be able to despair because no one precedes him; nor will the second, with everyone placed after him, be able to rejoice in arrogance and, now secure in his single honor, neglect to fulfill God’s cause in himself. Nor will he begin to hope more for present things than future ones, since the human race is generally such that it loves more what it sees than what it hopes for without seeing.

Therefore, as we said above, when the abbot has established uncertain ranks among the different persons and sees all of them striving to reach this honor, let them hasten eagerly to fulfill their duties, so that they may be appointed because of their good deeds. Each one, displaying his holy works to the abbot and to God, should rightly suppose that God and the abbot may agree concerning him in this honor. When they have become increasingly zealous for one another because of their zeal for good honor and their desire for it, they are compelled to display in themselves every holy and good quality to God and the abbot, since they have begun to hope for the merits of the perfect. They must already demonstrate by their deeds what they later wish to teach the others by their words.

For this reason we have decided that all should have equal ranks, and that no one should be appointed to a second honor, lest perhaps, as Scripture says, “the last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. 19). It may happen that this brother should enter the monastery before the abbot’s death, because he may already have been approved by some Rule, or because—as is read in many accounts in the *Lives of the Fathers*—those who secretly leave their own monasteries or communities out of a desire for humility prefer to place themselves under another’s authority.

Since God does not deprive those who walk in innocence or humility of good things, and since a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, nor can a lamp that has been lit remain hidden when it is placed not under a bushel but upon a lampstand, what if the abbot, while still alive, should designate one of his more negligent brothers for the second rank, and this great man, whose school in a new monastery has been concealed through humility, should enter? What if his perfect deeds should daily shine forth of their own accord, and while the monastery’s new disciple is treated with contempt, he should be recognized by his deeds as an ancient soldier of Christ?

When the abbot suddenly recognizes such a man, will he not often regret that he had negligently appointed the other as his second, and, by his own judgment, become reprobate? Will he not consider undoing what he had done, since it is not fitting that the better should stand beneath the worse, or that one who cannot fulfill by deeds what has been commanded should command another by words?

Therefore, let the rank of honor be held in suspense for everyone. When good qualities have been displayed, and honor has at some time been promised, let the abbot often assure his brothers in these words:

“The Lord will give honor to the one who provokes him by holy deeds, and he will not defraud him of his desire—he by whom God himself has not been defrauded of his reward. Through him God provides what is necessary for other disciples, when the teacher himself has first ceased to need anything.”

Therefore, while the abbot sees all the brothers panting with this thirst for honor and eagerly displaying themselves in holy works and in the good desires of God’s commandments, let him always consider in his mind and scrutinize with his eyes who has proved superior or more perfect in the varied contest of observance. Then, at the time of his death, when all the brothers have been summoned before him, let him say to them:

“You have all acted well in holy observance; you have always presented your good deeds before God’s eyes.”

Then, suddenly calling that person by name or taking him by the hand whom he has secretly judged better than the others in every perfection, let him say to the whole community:

“Listen to me, sons. The holy Trinity knows by whose judgment this man is chosen: he has always proved better than all of you in every observance of God’s commandments—that is, in silence, obedience, faith, peace, grace, patience, goodness, simplicity, watchfulness, sobriety, self-restraint, and chastity.”

## CHAPTER XCIII

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the appointment of a new abbot chosen from among all by the prior.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Therefore, by God’s judgment and by my testimony, a shepherd is chosen for you, and an abbot is appointed for you by the Lord. May he always please the Lord by good deeds, and may he accept the Lord’s flock, which he will restore to the Lord’s judgment in the future.

Take care, brothers, that no one receives this appointment with an evil disposition and despises Christ, whose representative this man will be for you in the monastery.

After these acts have been completed and all have immediately offered prayer, the bishop of that territory’s Church is summoned. With his testimony, and through the office of the clergy, the bishop’s hand changes the man’s name to the honor of abbot; after the name of the prior, his name is recited by a cleric in the diptych during the Mass at the altar in the oratory, while he himself offers the brothers’ oblation.

If, however, the former abbot has not yet died and has not yet been removed from the living, the new name is placed after the name of the superior. Once the name of the deceased has passed among those who rest, the new name is written at the head.

When the Mass has immediately been celebrated in the oratory and completed in the presence—as we have said—of the bishop, or of the entire clerical order, and after the prior has given him the kiss of peace, followed by the community, the prior shall place this Rule in his hand, together with the keys requested from the cellarer to the monastery’s storerooms, and an inventory of all its possessions, tools, books, and movable property. Everything belonging to each person shall be assigned before the bishop according to its written record.

To the one to whom he gives this Rule, in the presence of the bishop, the entire clergy, and his community, he shall say:

“Receive, brother, the law of God, this Rule, in which you are to provide eternal life for those who observe it and proclaim everlasting judgment for those who neglect it. Here the soul conquers or perishes; here life is either lost or preserved. Here depends upon you the reckoning that God will demand for these souls whom you see. Concerning this inventory of this flock, you will render an account before the Lord’s judgment after me.

“Remember, brother, remember: from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more is demanded. Therefore be watchful now, and do not be secure against the devil’s future snares for your flock, which come through the devouring jaws of the wolf. Be watchful also over the wounds of souls and the ruins caused by sins, considering by what methods and admonitions you may restore souls to salvation.

“Be as vigilant and watchful as you can, since until today you have been secure.”

When he has completed this, he shall again say to the one holding the Rule in his hand:

“Abbot, enter the Lord’s oratory and stand in my place with your community, now your own. May the High Priest bind in the records of heaven what you have received on earth.”

After these words, he shall hand him his pallium. When he has received it, the recipient shall kiss the hand of the giver. Immediately afterward the new abbot shall enter the oratory with the priest and his community, and stand in the prior’s place. After the priest has offered prayer for him, the new abbot shall immediately go to the altar and place the Rule upon it. As he places it there, the entire community, together with him, shall sing this verse:

“Strengthen, O God, what you have wrought in us” (Ps. 67),

with glory and chant.

When they have finished, he shall immediately prostrate himself on the floor in prayer in a clear voice and ask the priest to pray again for him; the community likewise shall cling to the floor in prayer.

After the prayer has been completed and they have risen, he shall kiss the priest’s knees and be raised for the kiss of peace. He shall then give the kiss of peace to the entire clergy, next to the officials, and then to the whole community. Thus he shall leave the discipline, handing the keys to the cellarer with his own hand.

Then he shall go and complete prayer with everyone without the priest. Having received the requested blessing, he shall sit in the predecessor’s chair. The officials shall come first, followed by all the others, and kiss his knees.

Then he shall rise, go to the former prior who is lying down, and kiss his knees; he shall be raised to receive the kiss of peace. After receiving the peace, the former prior shall say to everyone:

“Brothers, pray for me, so that I may be able to present and faithfully deliver before the Lord, the Judge, on the day of judgment, the accounts of your souls, together with my own, complete and settled; and so that the Lord may establish you securely on earth and deem my good departure worthy of acceptance in heaven.”

If afterward the former abbot should perhaps recover and not die, he shall receive again all his former permission, authority, appointment, and honor in the discipline. And rightly so: God has restored his life for this very purpose. From that hour until the day of his true death, the newly appointed man shall claim nothing for himself from the honor that has been established.

When the former abbot’s appointed day of death arrives, the man who was previously appointed in the priest’s presence shall undoubtedly succeed him—provided that a circumstance of pride or arrogance has not destroyed his merits.

Therefore, since while the former abbot lives he has usurped nothing of the honor for himself, but has accepted this with the full intention of his heart and guarded it with careful observance, he must not become inflated because of the honor assigned to him. Rather, he must daily display before God, the brothers, and all people increasingly good conduct according to the commandments of God established in the Rule.

From that time onward he must humble himself in words and deeds, and even in his appearance, more than he had previously been bowed down for the sake of humility. Everyone should judge him to have become, after the designation of honor, humbler and more insignificant than all the others, rather than greater than before. Thus, as though he had advanced by merit, he may fulfill in himself the Lord’s saying:

“Whoever wishes to be stronger among you, let him be the last of you” (Matt. 20);

and whoever humbles himself shall rightly be exalted.

Nevertheless, because the priest had established this honor by his prayers and had written his name with his own hand in the monastery’s diptych after the former abbot became ill, and because the honorable prior and true abbot had chosen him by his judgment, what previously was not permitted by the Rule may, through the priest’s prayer, the abbot’s choice, and especially because of the greater and increased humility found in him, now be judged a second rank.

He did not presume this name by his own judgment; rather, the merits of his perfect observance chose him. For this reason the Rule forbids the appointment of seconds: because of arrogance and pride. God chose this man through his conduct of good observance and his extraordinary humility; the abbot granted it, and the priest appointed it. Yet the life granted to the prior did not permit the appointment to take effect fully.

Therefore, from that day he shall sit beside the abbot as though already designated as a spiritual Caesar. In the oratory he shall maintain another choir of those singing opposite the abbot; at table he shall receive the cup after him, and in prayers he shall be placed after him. Wherever the abbot walks, he shall have authority assigned to take his place, correct the brothers’ faults, or excommunicate.

If an excommunicated brother customarily refuses to make satisfaction to him, the brother’s offense shall be reserved to the abbot, while the offender himself shall remain under the guilt of excommunication until the abbot’s arrival.

He shall carry out all these things by delegation from the abbot when he is absent, and in every respect act as the absent abbot’s representative. Yet he must not claim this for himself by his own judgment, but by the command of the prior and true abbot. Only when permission has been granted to him by command may he have authority to arrange anything or believe that he can remain in this honor.

At every hour he must judge himself equal to everyone, and even more so: if he wishes to be perfect and wishes worthily to attain what has been assigned to him, he must humble himself before all his brothers, judge himself inferior and more insignificant than everyone, and believe in the deepest affection of his heart that he is last of all. For the Lord knows how to exalt such people, as Scripture says:

“Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 23).

That brother must always take care lest he ever assume inward pride because of the honor granted to him and, breaking out into some form of arrogance and falling in some respect either from humility or from the divine commandment, fulfill the Rule less completely than before, now secure because of the honor assigned to him.

Let him know with certainty that if the abbot frequently sees that the man he chose is not progressing toward greater things but has instead deteriorated through negligence, and if, after being admonished by the abbot, he does not correct himself, the priest, when asked by the abbot, shall erase his name from the diptych. He shall be judged to have returned to his former number and to be equal to the negligent; and he shall be subjected to the customary excommunication, since he does not avoid his faults. Through negligence he has lost what had intervened; he shall receive what he had incurred.

Once he has deservedly been restored to an inferior place, he shall immediately be separated from the abbot’s side. From that day the abbot shall seek another brother, superior to the negligent man, with all his attention and concern. He too shall be chosen secretly each day, so that at the time of his death the abbot may openly indicate him with his own hand as one who is justly and deservedly to be placed before all others by an appointment of primacy.

Let these reprobates, who through negligence fall from the highest summit of honor, hear the Apostle say to them:

“You were running well; who hindered you?” (Gal. 9).

It is Satan who brings down those who are elated.

Before the beloved man becomes reprobate and turns toward negligence, let him hear what Scripture daily urges him:

“Hold fast what you have, so that another may not receive your crown” (Rev. 3).

Whoever hears this and does not observe it must blame himself when he falls, because the proud, negligent, and unworthy are deposed by the Lord, so that those who worthily observe God’s commandment, or those who are humble, may be exalted.

With the just Judge, the Lord, there is no partiality. He does not wish to grant anything to the unworthy, since he knows how to love only the just, the good, and the holy, and to them alone he is debtor both for the honor of the present life and for the reward of the everlasting crown.

## CHAPTER XCIV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

If the abbot should suddenly die, by what procedure another abbot is to be appointed from among the brothers whose ranks are uncertain, since while alive he designated no one as better than the others and sudden death overtook him.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

Considering the sudden human condition and the arrival, as usually happens, of unexpected death, we have appropriately established that a solution is to be found from among those whose status is uncertain, so that a definite procedure may be discovered from uncertainty.

Since above we said that the ranks of different monasteries should be confused and that no one should be assigned a definite second honor, and since the living abbot has not judged whom he should appoint after him, whom he had found better than the others, if he should suddenly depart to the Lord, we answer as follows. Otherwise, with each person presuming succession according to his own judgment, everyone would be stirred to sedition, and an eager partisan struggle would turn a peaceful house into a scandalous contention.

Therefore we decree that, by the judgment of the bishop of that territory and his clergy, a most holy abbot shall be sought. After receiving this Rule, he shall reside over this community in place of the deceased prior for thirty days and shall himself consider, according to the provisions of this Rule, who among all can be found superior in observance.

On the thirtieth day, in the presence of that priest or clergy, this abbot shall swear on the holy Gospels and declare that he has not been bought by promises or flatteries from anyone, but will fully disclose the cause of God as he has found it.

Then, while the whole community stands before him, he shall suddenly take the hand of the one whom he has found better than all in the observance of God’s commandments and the provisions of the Rule. Only then shall the appointment to primacy be celebrated in him by that bishop or the clergy of the territory, according to the provisions of this Rule, as we said above.

## CHAPTER XCV

### THE DISCIPLE’S QUESTION

Concerning the gatekeepers of the monastery.

### THE LORD ANSWERS THROUGH THE MASTER

A cell shall be provided close to the monastery gates for two brothers of very advanced age. Assigned there, they shall at every hour close the monastery after those who leave, open it for those who enter, and announce arrivals to the abbot.

These two old men must also observe this daily: at the hours when it is proper for reading to take place in the monastery, they shall join the community at the barred gates so that they may hear the readers; and when the signal of the oratory sounds for the divine work, they shall likewise present themselves at the barred gates for the work of God in the oratory.

For work, they shall be assigned whatever they can fulfill according to the capacity of their age: either some craft, if they know one; or, if they do not, they shall help the weekly workers with whatever they can do each day. Yet they shall not be assigned other work if they are occupied every hour with opening and closing.

They shall receive the dogs’ grain from the cellarer and provide it to them with water or with the broth remaining from the kitchen. They shall care for the animals within the monastery, assisted by the weekly workers during their week of service, and they shall keep the gates clean. They shall also light each day the lamp hanging within the gate and made for that purpose, so that at night the arrival of anyone from outside may be recognized.

As we said above, these old men shall eat with the abbot in honor of their age, according to the pattern of perfect humility, as Saint Eugenia demonstrated when she said that she did not wish to show herself superior even to them. To such perfected persons Scripture says:

“The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find grace before God and human beings” (Eccl. 3).

All necessities should be located inside the gates: that is, an oven, mills, a cooling place, gardens, and everything necessary. Thus there will not be frequent occasions for a brother to go outside repeatedly, mingle with secular people, and perhaps be seen by the eyes of religious persons, so that, to our condemnation, they may worship us as angels and say undeservedly, “Bless us,” when they perhaps think we are holy although we are not. Or, through the mockery of certain unbelievers, the holy habit may become despised in public or in the streets as it is worn about.

When all these things have been established inside, the monastery gate shall always be closed, so that the brothers, shut inside with the Lord, may already be separated from the world for God’s sake in the heavenly places.

The monastery gate shall have outside an iron ring fixed in a small socket, so that, when it is struck by someone arriving, the arrival of anyone who comes may be announced inside.

## IN AN UNCERTAIN SEVENTH CENTURY. AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

### ANCIENT TESTIMONIES CONCERNING THE RULE OF A CERTAIN FATHER

Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, praises the Rule of a certain Father in nearly every chapter of his *Concordance of Rules*; see, for example, chapter 55, section 26, where he praises the Rule of a certain Father.

Abbot Smaragdus, in his exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapters 23, 28, and 29, cites testimonies from the same Rule of a certain Father.

John Trithemius, in *De propr. Mon.*, chapter 5, cites this Rule as follows:

“Likewise, in the Rule of the Servant of God for sisters, chapter 17, it is written: ‘Something of one’s own in the monastery,’ etc.”

## CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

We have observed that the Rule of this unknown author, composed for monks, was written for Scottish monks, because of the strict monastic discipline prescribed in it. For the same reason we believe that this present Rule was composed for religious women of the same nation, so that both Rules had one and the same author, namely Saint Columba, abbot of Iona and patriarch of the Scottish monks.

Nor do we depart greatly here from the opinion of the most reverend Calmet, who conjectures that Saint Comgall, once abbot of Saint Columbanus, was the author of the earlier Rule, because of the similarity of the discipline introduced among the monks of Luxeuil. For the same strict discipline was observed in all the monasteries of both sexes among the Scots.

Indeed, we do not read that Saint Comgall wrote a monastic Rule; but all historians recognize Saint Columba as the father and legislator of so many monasteries, especially the venerable Bede in his *Ecclesiastical History*.

In the Scottish monastic tradition there are many ancient convents of holy virgins where this strict and rigorous discipline was once observed, especially in the convent at Abernethy and at Tyninghame and Coldingham, as also among the Hebrides, or Western Islands, where Saint Columba founded convents for religious women. Accordingly, just as he prescribed a norm of life for monks, so he prescribed one for them.

Whatever the case may be, this much must be admitted: the foreign discipline contained in this Rule clearly reveals the obsolete rites and ceremonies of the Scots. Among these are especially the command given to virgins to confess their sins to the abbess or prioress, or to elders appointed for this purpose. If we also consider the many visitations of cells and beds, the severe punishments inflicted upon the disobedient and the murmurers, and the other rigorous admonitions, we must acknowledge that this Rule, containing twenty-four chapters, unmistakably reflects the severe Scottish monastic discipline, although the author appears to prescribe certain practices common to the Rules of Saint Benedict and Saint Columbanus.

Moreover, I wish to note that the author truly understood the confession made to the abbess to be sacramental. For it is forbidden there that lesser or greater crimes revealed in confession be disclosed:

“Let them reveal lesser or greater crimes to no one, except the just Judge alone, who washes away the crimes of all who confess.”

(Brockie, *Codex Regularum*, vol. 2.)

## HERE BEGINS THE RULE OF A CERTAIN FATHER FOR VIRGINS (C, S)*

### CHAPTER ONE. What kind of person should the abbess of a monastery be?

The abbess of a monastery should be noble not so much by birth as by wisdom and holiness, so that she who labors by sound instruction to teach souls may not contradict that instruction by her own deeds. For those subject to superiors imitate the form of their leaders’ actions more than they lend their ears to the doctrine delivered.

She must join sacred works to sacred speech, so that she who imitates her teaching from her voice may imitate her worship through her works. If her conduct should contradict her speech in any respect, the fruit of her speech will not be able to achieve its effect.

Thus she should be adorned both in voice and in conduct, so that deed may agree with word and word with deed. She should be decked with the flower of self-restraint and chastity, praised by everyone’s mouth and imitable by everyone’s desire as an example.

She should be adorned with the benevolence of charity, so that she may gladden the hearts of all the faithful. She should be ready to care for pilgrims and guests; attentive to the care of the sick; generous in assisting the poor and needy.

She should correct the sluggishness of offenders in such a way that she brings wanton and weary minds back to religious observance. She should distribute the gifts of goodness mercifully, yet in such a way that excessive goodness does not nourish the fuel of crimes.

Let her therefore be good to the good because of their merits, and severe toward the wicked through punishment—something that must be done with knowledge, according to the Psalmist’s prayer:

“Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, O Lord” (Ps. 118).

In both matters the abbess must take care that either excessive goodness does not nourish vices in the hearts of those subject to her, or excessive severity of discipline does not tear apart by harsh correction those things that should have been healed by gentle reproof.

She should assist the careless with gentle persuasion, so that, by healing them, she may somehow pour into their corruption the care of an antidote. To those of sound conduct she should offer encouragement, so that they may bring to completion by improvement what they have begun to do.

For it is of no benefit to have begun if they do not strive to persevere in the good work they began.

The mother must have as many dispositions as she has daughters under her governance, so that, in accordance with everyone’s character, she may know how to restrain everyone’s faults.

She should show such providence toward all that neither affection removes the place of discipline nor discipline removes the place of affection. She should care for everyone, so that she may receive the profit of her reward from everyone’s progress; so that, after rescuing them at some time from the corruption of the present life, she may receive as great a reward for her labor as the assistance she provided for overcoming the enemy was great.

### CHAPTER TWO. What kind of person should the prioress of a monastery be?

The prioress of a monastery should be appointed not because of advanced age but because of conduct. For the length of many years may elevate some people, but the disgrace of a sluggish life, through growing cold, brings them back to the immaturity of childhood.

The prioress should therefore be serious in conduct, skillful in speech, strong in understanding, watchful in judgment, tireless in activity, devout in correction, moderate in discipline, chaste in action, sober in conduct, fair in administration, adorned with humility, patient, gentle, not turbulent, not irascible, not stained by the vice of pride or arrogance, not lavish, not talkative, but adorned in every act of religion.

She must know how to assist those who are weak in conduct and to rouse the sluggishness of those growing cold. The abbess should rest her authority upon her, so that she deviates in nothing from the abbess’s commands. Rather, being subject in all things and restrained by the orders of her elders, she must neither do nor order anything contrary to the abbess’s will, but must act in everything through consultation with her, according to what is written:

“Ask your father, and he will announce it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32).

She must always be consulted, so that the souls subject to her may in no respect depart from the counsel of their elders, and so that the sheep may in no respect decline from the will of the shepherd.

Rehoboam despised the counsel of the elders and followed the advice of young men. Scripture’s truth bears witness to the kind of loss this caused: after abandoning his dominion over eleven tribes, he scarcely passed the remainder of his life with one tribe amid the losses of so many pressures and without cruel death.

She must be provident for every need, both of body and of soul, so that she may extend assistance for present necessity and, through constant admonition, rouse and lift the hearts of those subject to her to resound with praise of the Creator.

She should honor the humble and those subjected for Christ’s sake, raising them to a higher place; but she should draw back those who exalt themselves, by the scourge of correction, to the steps of humility.

She should be so attentive in caring for the monastery’s goods—whether vessels or furnishings—that she is found darkened by no shadow of negligence. While she devotes every care to sacred labor, she will receive from the Almighty the fruit of her labor.

Every Saturday, after the ninth hour of prayer, the prioresses—both the older and the younger—shall visit the beds of all the sisters. They shall make inquiry because of their negligence, or to see whether anything forbidden has been retained there without permission.

Likewise, after Compline, they shall visit all the beds with lights, so that they may recognize the alertness or sluggishness of everyone’s mind as they awaken, or their tepidity after prayer.

The same must be done at all the nocturnal offices, so that they may know which sisters rise for the office with fervor and which with tepidity. Those whom they find blameworthy because of tardiness or sluggishness shall be corrected according to their fault or age, either by reproof or by the scourge.

### CHAPTER THREE. Concerning the monastery’s gatekeeper.

Portresses, or doorkeepers, of the monastery should be such women as build up the reward of everyone together, advanced in old age, for whom the world is silent and who now desire nothing from its present spectacles; rather, clinging to the Creator with the whole affection of their hearts, let each of them say: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in God” (Ps. LXXII). For what should they desire from the ornaments of the present world, who, having despised its passing things, have begun to love Christ, in whom they have perceived through contemplation of the mind that the highest good abides?

Let them therefore be utterly firm in the disposition of their minds, so that in prayer they may say with the Prophet to the Lord: “Turn our eyes away, lest they see vanity; revive us in your way” (Ps. CX). Let them always display such an example to those who come, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified outside by strangers, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V); and so that inside they may prepare the gains of reward from their fellow sisters, while they undertake the care of all on behalf of the community outside.

Thus let them be careful in their conduct and possess the humility that is the teacher of the virtues, so that they may display every sweetness of patience through gracious conversation. Let no one of them ever speak alone or in pairs without a third witness. Let them never raise their eyes upward and stare intently at laypeople or clerics; but, with their faces modestly lowered and their eyes cast down, let them discuss necessary matters.

Above all, let them care for the poor, pilgrims, and guests, because Christ is received in them, as he himself says: “Whatever you did for one of these least ones, you did for me” (Matt. XXV). Let them presume to give anything outside, to provide anything to anyone, or to receive anything from outside only with the authorization of the abbess. Whatever they receive from outside as gifts or alms from others, let them not carry it to the storeroom beforehand; rather, bringing it first before the oratory, let the entire community pray for the person who supplied it.

Let them in no way pass on stories that they may have heard at the gate, whether from secular people or from anyone else; and if they have heard or understood such things unwillingly, let them in no way repeat them to their fellow sisters. If they transgress any of the matters we have mentioned, let them be corrected with the penitence prescribed by the Rule. If they disclose the matter with humble satisfaction, let the fault of the offender be judged according to the humility observed in the confession. But if the crime of obstinacy appears, it will increase the measure of the penance.

Let them never keep the keys of the doors or gate in their possession during the night; instead, let them bring and present them to the abbess at night, and receive them in the morning after the second hour. Let the storekeeper, the bakers, and the cooks likewise take care to fulfill this, so that from sunset—or from the completion of whatever necessary task is required—the abbess may retain the keys until the second hour, unless a necessity arises such that they must be kept overnight with the abbess’s authorization and returned again after the second hour.

From the evening signal until the second hour has been completed, let the doors of the gates in no way be opened, nor let any entrance from outside be made available. But if such a necessity arises that a decision must be made after vespers, let everything be discussed through the window that is in that same gate.

If such a necessity concerning guests or pilgrims arises that they cannot be present with the sisters at the hour of the meal, let them eat afterward with the cooks or servants, or whenever they have an opportunity to take food. Let them handle and guard the vessels and other utensils that they carry for the use of guests as though they were consecrated to God, lest through their negligence they fail to receive a reward from the one whose possessions they do not preserve from being plundered.

Within the enclosure or doors of the monastery, let them permit no man or woman whatsoever to eat or drink. Instead, let them serve all who arrive outside in the guesthouse, according to what honor requires and by order of the abbess. But inside, we decree that only those who have vowed the sacred religious life to God and are bound together in obedience under one Rule may eat or drink.

Thus let the portresses always act, so that, possessing zeal for God in all things, they may preserve the tenor of the Rule and receive an incorruptible reward for the labor of their diligence and care.

## CHAPTER IV. What the storekeeper of the monastery should be like

A wise and religious woman is to be chosen from the entire community as the monastery’s storekeeper. She should please neither herself nor her own preferences, but the whole community impartially and devoutly through her distribution. She should not strive to please in such a way that, by agreeing, she introduces both herself into the ruin of sin and others into the guilt of transgression; that is, she must distribute nothing beyond the proper measure on account of personal friendship or in favor of someone’s merit, knowing that “the just Lord has loved justice from the beginning; his face has seen equity” (Ps. XL).

Let her therefore be pleasing to everyone through just distribution; mature in conduct; sober; not gluttonous, arrogant, disorderly, abusive, slow, or lazy, but well composed in all her actions. She must serve the entire community—both the older and the younger—with affection and maternal order. Let her care for all the things entrusted to her, yet presume to do nothing without the abbess’s authorization.

Let her in no way disturb sisters who are older in age or younger; and if any sister asks something unreasonable of her, let her refuse the unreasonable request with a gentle reply and a humble voice. Let her serve sisters who are ill with diligent care and the readiest affection. Likewise, let her care for the poor, placing the fear of the Lord before everything and knowing that she will have to render an account to him if she does not do all these things to fulfill his commands, always remembering him who said: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John XII).

Therefore, let us join the fear of the Lord to every good work we do. Let her exercise such care in everything that she incurs no loss through negligence. Let her entirely avoid the plague of avarice and greed. Likewise, just as she must not be avaricious, so she must not be wasteful; that is, just as she must not hide and withhold what has been entrusted by the gift of almighty God under the vice of avarice, so she must not squander the common substance by excessive lending without just distribution. Rather, let her weigh and regulate everything with discretion.

And if she does not have what is requested to give, let her respond in gentle speech without any harshness, so that the sweetness of her heart may be revealed in her verbal reply, in accordance with what is written: “Good words are a honeycomb” (Prov. XVI); and again: “A good word is better than a good gift” (Ecclus. XVIII). Let her know that the work entrusted to her belongs to her reward if she strives to do everything with humility and devotion.

And although there may be nothing available to give, let her in no way answer that she does not have it; instead, let her say in a faithful voice: “The Lord will give” (Matt. XII). Whatever ought to be given, however, should be given without delay, lest an occasion of scandal or a cause of offense arise from the delay itself, always remembering the Lord’s commands, by which he does not permit any of his own to be scandalized.

## CHAPTER V. On loving and obeying one another

Through the Gospel of John, the Lord shows how carefully the nuns in the monastery ought to love one another when he says: “This is my commandment: that you love one another. No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). And again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (ibid. XIII).

We are therefore commanded to love one another so that we may be saved together; through mutual love, we are to imitate him who loved us, according to the Apocalypse, “and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I).

If, then, a sister loves another sister for Christ’s sake, she must not drive Christ away from herself through temporal affection. For true love, and love according to Christ, is not to do evil to one’s neighbor. Let one’s neighbor therefore be loved not with carnal affection but through the ministry of devotion; let her be loved with purity, with religious commitment, with gentleness, and with charity, so that Christ may always be found in every love, and love may remain according to God, not according to the world.

For the Lord commands this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII). If a sister loves another sister as herself, she will never incur the stain of sin, but, adorned with the practice of devotion and love, will receive eternal rewards.

Let love therefore always remain in the heart, so that it may extinguish the venom of the ancient enemy’s envy, through which, after deceiving the first-created human being, he opened the entrance of death, as it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II).

Let one’s neighbor be loved, lest she incur the crime of bloody murder through the stain of hatred, as the apostle John testifies, saying: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III). Let one’s neighbor be loved, lest, by retaining any fuel of discord, she remain bound by the chain of her own crime and not be released, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel, saying: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI).

Let us forgive our neighbors, so that the Almighty may forgive us. “Give,” he says, “and it will be given to you” (Luke III). O what a just exchange! O what a devout mercy—to receive by giving and to give by receiving!

Let no growth or nourishment of quarrels be retained. Thus the Apostle also exhorts us, saying: “Be kind and compassionate toward one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Col. III).

We are commanded to give nothing other than what we ask to be given to us. Thus, when we pray, we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). By forgiving our debtors, we are released from debt. Let us therefore release our neighbors through love and affection, so that God may release us from our own crimes through devotion and mercy. Amen.

## CHAPTER VI. On making confession continually

How frequently and carefully confession should be made is shown by the tradition of many Fathers in accordance with the sequence of the Scriptures. Confession must therefore always be made, so that it may continually preserve the condition of the mind—grown old and darkened by the daily enticements of sins—in its freshness, as Scripture teaches, saying: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV).

Thus blessed David said in prayer to the Lord: “I made known my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquities; I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. XXXI).

How powerful is a pure and prompt confession, when secure petition follows it! He confessed against himself in order to drive away the burden of his crimes; he groaned over himself by confessing, and glorified remission by receiving it. By grieving, he disclosed the crime; by making confession, he renewed hope.

For he did not lack the confidence of hope, because he remembered that he had once said, illuminated by the Lord through the Holy Spirit: “With you is propitiation, and because of your law I have waited for you, Lord” (Ps. CXXIX). And again: “With the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.” With the one beside whom he recognizes enduring mercy, he also recognizes abundant redemption. Let us therefore seek mercy there, where we already know that abundant redemption remains.

Let grief increase after the fall, so that a remedy for guilt may be found. “Confess your sins to one another,” so that the Almighty may forgive our sins. Scripture exhorts us in this way, saying: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another” (James V).

How great is the mercy of the compassionate Judge poured out upon us, that a crime contracted through grievous deeds may be dissolved by mutual prayer! Let the comfort of mutual prayer therefore be given, so that each may desire help through praying for the other. Indeed, the abundance of fruits is greater when salvation is acquired through the disclosure of sins.

“Reveal your way to the Lord,” says the Psalmist, “and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. XXXVI). If the soul is nourished by revealing sins, then let them be revealed daily through confession, so that daily wounds may be healed by daily medicine.

But at what suitable hours daily sins are to be washed away must be set forth by us. Whatever the mind or body commits through ease during the stretches of dark night after compline is to be cleansed through confession after the second hour. Whatever it commits during the day through action, sight, hearing, thought, or growing lukewarm is to be considered for purification after the course of the ninth hour has been completed. Whatever the mind draws to itself as a stain after the ninth hour must be confessed before compline.

The abbess, however, must take care that, after entering the school after the second hour and completing prayer, she permit no one to go outside unless confession has first been made. The same must be done after the ninth hour and before compline.

Those sisters who are being held in penance for serious faults must not stand in the church with the others who are receiving Communion. Instead, let them sing the office secretly in another church; and, when the office has been completed, they are to be ordered to go outside and stand before the doors of the church in which those receiving Communion complete the office. When the community comes out, let them prostrate themselves on the ground and ask that the Lord be entreated for them, so that grave offenses may be erased by contrition of heart, remembering: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. L); and, “In our humility the Lord remembered us” (Ps. CXXXV).

While at prayer, the penitent should always say: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. L), so that the anger of the accusing Judge, who is soon to render vengeance, may be appeased through the devotion of a pious mind and a humble prayer.

## CHAPTER VII. On not disclosing the confessions of the sisters

The abbess, the superior, or any senior sister whom the abbess has entrusted with receiving confessions must disclose neither lesser nor greater crimes, except to the just Judge, who washes away the crimes of all who confess.
