The woman who has confessed her wounds modestly did not confess in order to receive disgrace, but to have her salvation restored; she has God as her just witness, from whom she also expects healing. The senior woman who receives the confession must keep it most honorably hidden with gravity and moderation, lest, while applying medicine to another’s wound, she corrupt the brightness of her own mind.

No nun, however, should presume to receive a confession or impose a penance without the abbess’s authorization, lest the fault committed be concealed from the abbess; rather, everything must be done with her knowledge.

If one is found who attempts to violate this provision of the Rule, let her be corrected by the imposition of a severe penance, because she wished to conceal from the abbess the fuel of the offense.

## CHAPTER VIII. How one is to rise at the Lord’s signal

Whenever the signal sounds for the divine office at either the day or the night hours, one must rise immediately with the greatest haste, as though the king’s herald were sounding, setting aside whatever work was in one’s hands, so that nothing may be placed before the work of God.

With the mind attentive to the herald’s sound and relying upon the work of God, let her hasten with all gravity and gentleness to proclaim the glory of his majesty and give thanks to his goodness.

If she comes slowly and sluggishly after the end of the first psalm that is sung in the office, she should know that she is to be recalled from her place while the office is being completed and placed in the last position—that is, in the place assigned to such negligent persons—where she must stand and wait in fear of shame. After the office has been completed, she must make satisfaction before the assembly of the sisters who are going out by an extended request for pardon.

They must not be separated entirely outside, lest, overcome by sleep, they fall asleep or an opportunity be given in some way for the evil enemy to approach. For when she remains inside, she does not entirely lose what she had begun, and she is broken by shame and fear while she is seen by everyone.

When the others go out after the office has been completed, let the woman who has remained in the church because of her tardiness sing twelve psalms beyond the prescribed sequence of the office. But if she has entirely missed her office, especially during the night hours, when she has no other work to perform, let her be condemned to substitution.

The hours of the office are to be arranged, according to the abbess’s distribution, by whoever has been assigned this duty; that is, a woman who is found suitable for this work because she is attentive and diligent in mind, so that the work of God is not delayed. If, however, the proper order is departed from for any reason, so that the hours are not observed according to their order, let the offender be condemned to substitution.

## CHAPTER IX. How the rule of silence is to be kept in the monastery, during the daytime work and at table; and how reading is to be done at table

The sequence of the sacred Scriptures has made clear that the rule of silence must be observed at all times, when it says through the Prophet: “The work of justice is silence and peace.” One must be silent from idle, frivolous, clownish, wicked, and malicious stories, concerning which the Prophet prayed, saying: “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips. Do not incline my heart toward evil words” (Isa. XXXII; Ps. CXL).

One must cease from superfluous stories, lest through the sluggishness of an unrestrained mind the soul acquire the fruit of condemnation; for, according to the Lord’s command, we will have to render an account not only for clownish and abusive speech but also for idle speech.

What else should a nun strive for except to devote herself to God alone—to God in whom she once fixed her desire—both in speech of the mouth and in the desire of the soul?

During all the daytime hours, except at table, from the second hour until compline, one may speak whatever the usefulness of the sacred Rule requires, with the abbess’s authorization. From the hour of compline, when prayer is offered for taking sleep, no one should presume to speak at all unless a great necessity of the monastery requires it. Whoever has been authorized by the abbess should speak, or likewise by the superior who bears care for the others.

At table, no one at all should presume to speak except the abbess, or the person to whom the abbess has given an order to speak for the common necessity of the sisters. Instead, let all, giving thanks to the Creator in their hearts with attentive minds, enjoy food and drink in due measure.

The portress who seeks conversation with the abbess for necessary reasons may be permitted to speak, because perhaps a necessity has arisen that ought not to be delayed.

Before the meal, one or more chapters of the Rule should always be read, if the abbess wishes, so that, when food refreshes the body, reading may satisfy the soul. Let all these things be done with gravity of mind and gentle moderation, so that the Lord may take pleasure in everything.

On the Lord’s feast days—that is, the Nativity of the Lord, the solemnity of Easter, the Theophany, Pentecost, or any other especially sacred celebrations of the Lord or the holy martyrs—if permission has been granted by the abbess, we do not forbid speaking at table. Even then, however, let them speak in a restrained rather than an unrestrained voice, lest, bursting into loud chatter, they seem to be judged by laziness rather than joy. Let the conversation itself be of such a kind that it arises from discussion of the Scriptures and brings profit, not loss, to the soul.

Those receiving silence as a penance must strive to keep it in every respect, so that they may deserve to receive fruit from true mortification.

Wherever two women are placed, let them in no way presume to speak without a third witness; instead, three women should always speak together about necessary matters.

## CHAPTER X. How the administration and observance of the table are to be arranged

The abbess must weigh how the administration and observance of the table should proceed with what equality and sobriety, so that in everything, as befits ministers of God, the zeal of religious discipline may flourish.

Food and drink must be served to everyone in equal measure, according to what the season, solemnities, fasts, or daily usage require. On ordinary days we decree that two dishes are sufficient, apart from the gifts of fruit: dishes made from legumes or vegetables, or prepared with any kind of flour.

Everything is to be served in equal measure, except when a weaker age is unable to bear it, or bodily illness, or the inexperience of a newly begun way of life, cannot endure what is required; this is to be weighed by the judgment of the abbess.

As for drink, let the customary measure of the fermented liquor called *sicera*—that is, beer—be given. If the abbess wishes, or if labor, a feast day, or the pious entreaty occasioned by the arrival of a guest demands it, the portion of wine may be increased.

If there are to be two meals, the same rule is to be observed apart from the wine portion. On feast days, out of reverence for the sacred solemnity, the bodies are to be refreshed with more foods—that is, with three or four dishes—but in such a way that, if the number of foods is greater, the portions are smaller, so that the bodies may be refreshed with necessary food and not condemned by excessive satiety.

While sitting at table, no sister should look at another who is eating with raised eyes, nor should she scrutinize another’s measure of food or drink with improper attention.

When food is served at table, no one should eat before the signal sounds for the blessing. The abbess must take care to strike the signal immediately once the food has been served. When all hear the signal, let them ask for the blessing with one voice, followed by the abbess, who says: “May the Lord deign to bless.”

This is to be observed for every dish and for the serving of fruit and drink. We especially decree that no one should presume to give another anything from her portion or receive anything from another, except the abbess or the superior to whom the abbess has entrusted this duty.

If, through inexperience or presumption, anyone transgresses any of the matters stated above, let her be corrected by the discipline of the Rule, in proportion to the audacity of her presumption.

## CHAPTER XI. At what suitable hours food is to be taken in winter and in summer

From the arrival of the most sacred solemnity—that is, from the beginning of holy Easter, when the resurrection of the immaculate Lamb is celebrated—until the sacred solemnity of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the apostles, namely, for the space of fifty days, food is to be taken at the sixth hour. Likewise, supper is to be taken in the evening, because the order of the sacred season requires that no one, even while present in the church, display sadness.

From Pentecost, unless heavy labor requires it or the arrival of guests compels it, until the beginning of Lent, they are to take food at the ninth hour, that is, once a day, except on occasions of great solemnities or when great labor requires that they eat twice.

From the beginning of Lent until the most sacred solemnity of Easter, except on Sundays, they are to take food toward evening, so that the hour of refreshment may be completed before the beginning of night, while daylight remains.

When food is to be served, let the sisters rise one by one from each table, and come soberly to the kitchen window, so that they make no noise with their feet, vessels, or any other sound. First, let them all serve together at the table of the seniors; then let them carry the dishes to their own table where they are seated.

The superior of the table is to direct how the sisters at that table are to serve one another in turn, or how the younger ones are to serve if they are present.

## CHAPTER XII. How work with the hands is to be done on ordinary days

Work must be done at all times except on feast days, so that there may be provision either for one’s own needs or for giving assistance to the needy. The work of the hands must nevertheless be undertaken in such a way that the fruit of reading is not omitted; attention is to be given to work at the appointed time, and afterward one is to devote oneself to sacred reading.

Work with the hands is to begin at the second hour and end at the ninth hour. From the ninth hour, reading is to be practiced, unless some particular work must be done, such as making or washing clothing, or any other task, which may be carried out with the authorization of the abbess or superior.

If especially demanding work should arise, so that they must begin work earlier, or if this is necessary because of intense heat, the matter is to be considered according to the abbess’s judgment. As the season or the burden of harder labor requires, she may judge that work should cease at the sixth hour, and, after rest or a meal, work may continue until evening.

Above all, whether the abbess is present or the superior who has been left in her place, let her restrain this: she must not permit any nun to spend time in idle stories beyond necessary questioning. Rather, amid the work of the hands, remembrance of the work of God must be maintained; that is, while the hands are occupied externally with temporal tasks, the mind within should be sweetened by meditation on and remembrance of the psalms and Scriptures together with the tongue.

If a violator of this Rule takes pleasure in chatting, let her be punished with the penalty of silence.

If there are penitents in the school, they are to tend the hearths two by two for a week at a time. Likewise, on each Saturday they are to prepare for washing the heads of the sisters, or for the use of the baths on solemn feasts; or, if there are other arduous tasks to be done, the penitents are to perform them. Thus, while they perform these duties with humble minds and contrite hearts for fear of the Lord, they may be washed more quickly from their sins by the mercy of almighty God.

When they are going to work, this chapter is to be sung: “May the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us; direct the work of our hands for us; direct the work of our hands” (Ps. LXXXIX).

When the work is finished, this chapter is to be said: “May God, our God, bless us, and may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. LXVI).

The bakers are to perform the common work in turns, but there must not be fewer than three because of the need to speak. If it is necessary for them to remain there, there must not be fewer than four, and one of them must be an older superior whose religious character is trusted and who has permission to speak.

The senior among them is to present the bread they make in turn to the storekeeper, so that, protected by every precaution, they may be found blameworthy in nothing.

Likewise, among those who work in the brewery for making beer, one of them must be an older superior who guards everything according to the rule for the bakers.

The cooks are to cook by the week, so that three or more, if necessary, are assigned to cook in each week. This prevents imposed labor without discretion from producing, instead of the reward they ought to earn, the fruit of murmuring.

When entering upon their service, let them ask the whole assembly of sisters to pray for them, saying in prayer: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXXIII), and: “Help us, O God our Savior” (Ps. LXXVIII).

When they leave, let them wash the feet of all the sisters and present to the superior all the vessels they have used for necessary purposes, washed clean. Likewise, let them ask for prayers on their behalf and say this verse in prayer: “For you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me” (Ps. LXXXIII).

For each individual negligence, both the cooks and the storekeepers are to be corrected on ordinary days by twenty-five blows of the palm, lest, making light of the smallest faults, they be found more inclined toward greater ones.

## CHAPTER XIII. On utensils and household equipment

The monastery’s utensils and whatever is necessary for common work are to be arranged under the abbess’s care. Women are to be sought in the community whose concern of mind is active and whose firmness of conscience has been tested. The care is to be entrusted to them so that, when necessity requires, they may provide whatever is necessary to each person.

The utensils themselves, and whatever else has been entrusted to them by the abbess, are to be managed with vigilant fear, so that they may receive the reward of the care entrusted to them and not incur the judgment of condemnation, keeping this before the eyes of their minds: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. XLVIII).

## CHAPTER XIV. How they should sleep in the school

Although religious souls devoted to God always prepare a mind ready for God during both the daytime and nighttime hours, so that even when their limbs are numbed by sleep, the soul, intent through the Creator’s strength upon praises, may remain fully awake, according to the saying: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V), nevertheless careful vigilance must especially be exercised lest, through negligence in maternal care, the subject limbs suffer the harms of weakness.

Therefore we decree that, except for the sick and the older women, they sleep two by two in beds, but in such a way that they do not speak to one another or look at one another face to face. Instead, one should sleep resting behind the other, lest the ancient enemy, who eagerly desires to wound souls with his mouth, introduce some fraud by shooting it in, and arouse deadly desires through conversation.

Let this nevertheless be done so that one of them is always an older woman whose religious character is beyond doubt. We in no way approve that young women rest together, lest they be carried away by the heat of the flesh into some sinful adversity.

If possible, one house should accommodate everyone for sleeping, except when illness, old age, a fault, or untested inexperience requires that they be separated into a cell.

Let everyone sleep clothed and girded. In the school where they sleep, a lamp is to burn throughout the entire night.

When rising in haste for the office, let the sign of the cross be made upon the forehead, and let them say together in silence: “O God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me.”

## CHAPTER XV. What the care of the sick should be like

The nature of the care owed to those confined by illness is explained by the author himself when he says: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do likewise for them” (Matt. VII). Although this must be done in all circumstances, this command must especially be displayed in the care of the sick, because the Lord said: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. XXV).

Care must therefore be sought for the sick as though one were understood to be serving Christ who is present. Indeed, whoever provides care for the sick for Christ’s sake serves Christ in the sick.

The abbess must take care that the sick have a separate cell with every convenience, so that the woman who bears suffering in fragile flesh may feel no outside labor.

If the season requires it—for example, the season of Lent, when the others change their way of life—the sick must always be exempted, so that both drink and food may be provided more abundantly. The use of baths and care in providing treatment are to be supplied with the greatest diligence. They are to be granted more slowly to the healthy, especially the young.

The abbess must show such care toward the sick as she hopes to receive from the Lord, so that they feel no negligence either from the storekeeper or from the attendant.

For those exhausted by very old age, let such care be provided that there is no negligence in their case, but, according to the abbess’s judgment and as she sees necessary for each person, compassionate consideration may be granted to their weakness. For these women cannot be subjected to the tenor of the Rule; rather, an attitude of devotion must be shown toward them.

## CHAPTER XVI. On incidents that arise through negligence or by accident

The fault of negligence, through which many offenses occur in many circumstances, is to be weighed by the abbess’s judgment. Whether someone has broken, lost, or negligently left something in the refectory, kitchen, dormitory, or in any other useful place, everything must be weighed according to its measure and corrected in accordance with the person’s age—whether tender, old, or vigorous.

For if the vice of negligence is not corrected in small matters, a mind corrupted by lesser faults slips into greater offenses.

If a sister who has fallen into one of these circumstances immediately gives a pure confession to the abbess or superior, and it is established that what happened by accident was not her intention, this alone should suffice: she must not deny what she has done and committed, if it is possible, but must make amends with a satisfaction asking forgiveness.

If, however, the matter becomes known not through her own confession but through another’s betrayal, she will undergo penance according to the magnitude of the fault, because she did not disclose the fault through a pure confession.

But if she commits one of the greater faults, involving the greater condemnation of the soul, let her willingly disclose it more privately through a pure confession to her abbess, lest, while she is ashamed to uncover the fault of her mind in due time, she hide within herself, together with the guilt of the offense, the face of the devil.

## CHAPTER XVII. That no nun should claim anything as her own in the monastery
Nothing proprietary is to be possessed in the monastery; rather, everything is to be despised for the name of the Lord. For what proprietary possession of worldly things should a faithful soul claim, when the world has been crucified to it and it to the world? Since it has once died to the world, why should it begin again [Col. 1066D] to live for the world through some desire or painful longing for temporal things, when, having despised the world, it had already begun to live for God?

Therefore this vice must be cut out by the roots from every nun, so that she may claim no object as her own, whether among her clothing, footwear, or any other belongings, nor call it hers, except insofar as she is instructed by the abbess’s command to retain it in her possession—as though she were the guardian of another’s property, not the mistress of her own. Whatever the abbess entrusts to her—that is, for her present need, whether clothing or anything else—she must not presume to give or lend any of it to anyone, unless the abbess has specifically ordered her to do so. For what worldly goods could she confer upon another sister when, for Christ’s sake, she has handed over all her own wishes to the authority of the abbess?

[Col. 1067A] Everything, therefore, that is possessed in the monastery must be common to all, according to what we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “All things were common to them” (Acts 4). They are nevertheless to be held in common in such a way that no one presumes either to give or to receive anything except at the abbess’s direction, lest, by falling into the snare of the evil of greed or presumption, she be counted among the companions of Judas the traitor, who alone among the number of the apostles is reported to have had the money box, where the dealings of buyers and sellers were deposited. If any of the sisters is discovered to take pleasure in this vice and, after a first, second, or third correction, refuses to amend, she shall be subjected to regular discipline.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Excommunication of Offenses

[Col. 1067B] If any sister, instigated by the devil, appears obstinate, proud, disobedient, or murmuring; or if, having fallen in any circumstance, she attempts to violate the commands of the elders or the norm of the holy rule, she shall, according to the Lord’s command, be corrected privately by the elders once or twice (Matt. 18). If she refuses to amend, then she shall be rebuked by the whole congregation assembled together. And if she still refuses to amend, then she shall be judged according to the rule, as the magnitude of her offense requires: that is, she shall either undergo excommunication, if her understanding previously functioned properly; or, if obstinate persistence and hardness of mind continue in guilt and wrongdoing, she shall undergo bodily discipline.

## CHAPTER XIX. What Excommunication Should Be Like

[Col. 1067C]

The measure of excommunication is to be determined by the nature of the offense, as a just judgment shows to those who know how to weigh it. For lighter offenses, a lighter correction is to be applied; for more serious offenses, a more fervent condemnation is required. Accordingly, the abbess must carefully consider that if a sister is found liable for lesser offenses, she is to be deprived of the table until the hour appointed for her. For more serious offenses, however, the correction is to be brought to an end only after a period defined in days, weeks, or months has been extended as necessary. The rule is nevertheless this: if the period of excommunication lasts more than seven days, then, for as long as the order of penance is maintained under the appointed discipline, she is to be deprived of her place at the table and likewise segregated in the church; she is to remain in the place assigned to her, singing no psalm and holding no office, until, through humble satisfaction and contrition of heart, she merits pardon from the abbess or the elders.

[Col. 1067D] An excommunicated sister who, because of the seriousness of her offenses, is either confined to a cell or separated from the fellowship of the congregation is to receive from no one at all the benefit of conversation or visitation, except from one to whom the abbess has given permission. If anyone transgresses this rule, she shall undergo regular penance.

## CHAPTER XX. On Those Who, Though Frequently Corrected with Diligent Care, Refuse to Amend

If a sister, though frequently corrected, refuses to amend, she shall be corrected by excommunication according to the measure of her offense.

[Col. 1068A] If the correction of the one rebuking produces no improvement even then, she shall undergo the punishment of blows. If she still refuses to amend, but instead, lifted up by swelling pride, defends the works or actions for which she is being corrected, then she shall be corrected under the abbess’s wise governance, for it is written: “Whoever rejects discipline is unhappy” (Wisdom 3).

Accordingly, with wisdom moderating the care devoted to healing corruption, treatment is to be applied. If a deadly wound is not restored to health by the fomentations of chastisement and the ointments of compassion and gentleness, at least let it be cut away by incisions. And if, even after the corruption has been cut out, the swelling has not subsided, then she shall incur either the sentence of excommunication or the punishment of bodily discipline. If she is broken neither by fear of excommunication nor by the punishment of the lash, let the fire of compassion be increased still further,

[Col. 1068B] so that the whole congregation may pray to the Lord for her in the common service of prayer, that she who is held entangled in the devil’s snare may be healed by the Lord’s mercy and compassion.

But if she refuses to be corrected even then, she shall be segregated from everyone within the enclosure of the monastery under the terms of penance, except for the custodians, and shall be chastised with various corrections until her humility is clearly evident to all and truly believed. For salvation is often granted even to the unwilling. She is therefore to be separated from the congregation so that she may not stain the innocent by her vice.

Tender age, however, which does not understand the force of excommunication, is to be corrected not by excommunication but by the lash.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Reception of a Sister

[Col. 1068C]

If at any time—which may this never happen in the Christian religion—a sister should leave the monastery enclosure and, fleeing outside, later remember her former religious commitment and, struck by fear of eternal judgment, return, she must first promise to make every amendment to the monastery. Then, if her repentance is recognized as credible, she may finally be received within the monastery enclosure.

If she does this a second or third time, she is likewise to be treated with compassion, but only in such a way that, having been received in the last place among the penitents, she is examined for as long as necessary, until her life is found to be credible. If, however, after the third reception she is stained by the fault of flight, she must know that every avenue of return is thereafter to be denied her.

## CHAPTER XXII. How They Should Humble Themselves Toward One Another and Observe Their Ranks; and How the Precepts Are to Be Observed in Minor Actions

[Col. 1068D]

How great the affection and ministry of charity with which souls placed in a monastery ought to love one another has been established by the institutions of the holy Fathers; but in what actions or duties this should be demonstrated must be indicated by us, at least in part. The abundance of virtues, in fact, has a very broad sphere within which it easily overcomes the enemy who attacks it.

There are certain matters that appear insignificant in action and yet, whether observed or neglected, reveal whether the movement of the soul is lukewarm or fervent. Such matters include bowing the head and offering a gracious greeting in speech; these reveal either a rigid mind or concord,

[Col. 1069A] or, if the case is otherwise, a devout and pure affection.

The servants, both men and women, of Christ must therefore take care always to nourish within the state of their minds whatever does not depart from true humility and charity, in which the sum of the virtues consists. For just as true charity never remains without true humility, so true humility never remains without true charity.

Let us therefore undertake to lay the foundation, so that we may reach the summit of the virtues. First, humility must be displayed both in action and in affection, so that afterward the abundance of charity may be built upon it.

Whenever they meet one another on the way or in any place, they must ask each other’s blessing with all humility, bowing before one another. If one of them is senior, the younger must first ask for a blessing; only then should the senior proceed.

When they are in procession, according as the abbess has assigned them—whether to sing the psalm, recite the readings, or go to receive Communion—they must observe their own order,

[Col. 1069B] lest, by passing beyond the place assigned to them, they fall into the vice of ambition or arrogance.

The abbess must take care that, in the order in which they have entered religious life in the monastery, they are established in their proper rank, unless a more abundant religious life has deserved that one be promoted earlier, or serious guilt has required that she be moved backward.

If any of the sisters is known to seek a senior place, she is to be restrained with a shamefaced correction, because she has presumed upon a place of honor not owed to her and has attempted to seize an illegitimate honor—not through religious observance but through ambition.

In the assembly of the sisters, if another arrives, those who are younger in rank must rise and offer their place to the senior. The younger must in no way contradict the senior through pride, but must answer with all humility when questioned or corrected.

If a younger sister sees a senior falling into any offense, she must direct her to confess to the abbess or the superior, not by reproaching her but rather by grieving over her. The senior must do the same for the younger.

When coming to confession, she must first prostrate herself upon the ground and say that she is guilty; then, after she is ordered to rise, she shall make her confession known.

When permission is requested to undertake some task, permission must first be sought, and then permission to perform the work that is to be done must be requested.

When approaching the abbess, one must come with all humility, asking pardon; likewise, when departing, one must seek a blessing while asking pardon.

[Col. 1069C] No nun is to bring her personal need directly to the abbess herself; rather, all must endeavor to make known to the abbess, through the superior, whatever needs they may have.

If a priest or any religious person arrives, so that one is to go to meet him with the abbess’s permission, those standing at a distance must, with humility, bend the knee and ask for a blessing in a quiet voice.

If the abbess has ordered that one of the sisters speak with such a person, she must speak with all humility, restraint, and sobriety, so that in all these matters the virtue of humility and sobriety may be found.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Not Defending a Close Relation or Kinswoman in the Monastery

[Col. 1070A]

We consider it entirely impermissible to defend a close relation or kinswoman in the monastery. For why should one defend another when she no longer lives for herself but for Christ, whom she remains crucified in imitation of? She first lost her own life so that she might be joined more fully to salvation.

Since, then, she has lost her own wishes in order to fulfill Christ’s will in herself, why should she defend the offenses of others when she has crucified her own will? And if she has truly crucified it and now lives not for the world but for Christ, why should she defend those who fall into crimes in the world because of any personal familiarity?

Her love must therefore be impartial toward a kinswoman and toward any other sister who is not joined to her by blood relationship. Love must remain enclosed in the heart in all things, and she must not strive to protect anyone placed under the discipline’s governance, lest she extend the vice of defending one person to others.

Let it therefore be left to the discretion of the one who corrects, so that she may impose discipline upon those whom she corrects with loving care, not by fulfilling her own will but by correcting their vices.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Nurturing of Children

[Col. 1070B]

From many examples we have learned with how much care and discipline children are to be raised in a monastery. They must be nurtured with every expression of compassion and with the ministry of discipline, lest, stained in their tender age by the vice of idleness or wantonness, they later be corrected only with difficulty or not at all.

Such care must be exercised toward them that they are never permitted to wander here and there without a senior. Rather, always restrained by her discipline and imbued with instruction in the fear and love of God, they are to be trained for the practice of religious life.

They must have regular reading, so that during childhood they may learn what will benefit them when they have been brought to maturity.

In the refectory they are to have a table of their own, placed beside the table of the seniors. Two or more seniors, whose religious commitment is beyond doubt,

[Col. 1070C] must nevertheless sit with them, so that, with fear always placed before them, they may be raised under the reverence due to their seniors.

At what hours they are to eat and at what hours they are to sleep must be weighed according to the abbess’s judgment, so that discernment may be found in every safeguard of virtue.

[Col. 1069]

## TO THE READER

[Col. 1069] In an old codex containing the monastic enactments of the holy Fathers, the following two Constitutions were also read after the Rule of Saint Isidore: one, I do not know whose rule, concerning the devoted women; the other, of the Second Council of Seville. Since they likewise pertain to the ancient care and discipline of holy virgins, I have decided to present them here, so that I might reproduce all the relics of sacred antiquity as reverently as possible, even together with their fragments and dust.

[Col. 1071]

[Note: [Col. 1071D] Although we have already appended this fragment to the Critical Observation on the Rule of Saint Isidore of Seville, [Col. 1072D] it has nevertheless seemed appropriate, in accordance with the judgment of the illustrious Holstenius, to reprint it here because of its variant readings.]

## SENTENCE CONCERNING THE RULES OF THE DEVOTED WOMEN

[Col. 1071A] No one is to go to visit them except one who has there a mother, sister, daughter, close female relatives, or cousins, or the mother of his children. If, however, there should be a necessity for them to see such persons—for example, if before renouncing the world they entered the monastery and a paternal inheritance is owed to them, or if some other manifest reason exists—they are to send with them a man of approved age and conduct. They may see them, but are to return together.

No one is to go to them except those whom we have mentioned above. If they wish to see them,

[Col. 1072A] they must first have the matter reported to the father of the monastery; he will send to the elders who have been assigned to minister to the virgins. These elders, meeting them, will see with them those whom they need to see, with all discipline and fear of God.

When they have seen them, they must not speak with them about worldly matters. Whoever transgresses these commands shall, without any postponement, publicly perform penance for negligence and contempt, so that we may be able to possess the kingdoms of heaven.

[Col. 1071]

## COUNCIL OF SEVILLE, CHAPTER XI

[Col. 1071B] In the eleventh session, with common agreement, we decreed that the monasteries of virgins founded in the province of Baetica should be governed through the administration and protection of monks. For we provide salutary care for virgins dedicated to Christ when we select spiritual fathers for them, by whose governance they may not only be protected but also be built up through instruction.

This precaution must nevertheless be maintained concerning the monks: they are to be kept away from the women’s private affairs, and permission is not to be given them to approach even as far as the vestibule. Nor shall the abbot, or anyone appointed over the monastery apart from the woman who presides over it, be permitted to speak with Christ’s virgins about anything pertaining to the formation of morals.

They should not frequently converse even with the woman who presides, except in the presence of two or three sisters, so that the visits may be rare and the conversation brief.

[Col. 1071C] For far be it from us to wish monks to be familiar with Christ’s virgins—a thing which it is even impious to say. Rather, in accordance with what the rules and canons command and admonish, we assign them to the virgins’ governance while keeping them far removed and separated.

We decree that one monk of the highest proven character is to be chosen, whose responsibility will be to attend to the women’s rural or urban estates, construct buildings, or provide whatever else may be necessary for the monastery. Thus the servants of Christ, concerned solely for the benefit of their souls, may live for divine worship alone and devote themselves to their works.

Certainly, the one appointed by the abbot must be approved by the judgment of his bishop.

They are to make garments for the same monasteries from which they expect protection, and from those same monasteries, as stated above, they are again to receive the fruits of their labor and the assistance of administration.

## IN AN UNCERTAIN YEAR OF THE SEVENTH CENTURY. AUTHOR UNKNOWN

[Col. 1071]

## SERMON OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR ON THE TEN VIRGINS

[Col. 1071D] In the reading that was recited to us, dearly beloved brothers, we heard the Lord say: “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who, having taken their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride” (Matt. 25). If we understand this only according to the literal sense, it seems exceedingly harsh and severe. Far be it from our understanding that so small a number should come to eternal life even from the household of any poor Christian.

Therefore, since it must in no way be understood literally—for the Lord himself said that it is a likeness—let us inquire why five are called foolish and five wise. The five wise signify all the saints who will reign with Christ; conversely, the five foolish appear to represent Christians who, without good works, boast only in the name “Christian.”

They are called five foolish and five wise because all human beings are shown to possess five senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Through these senses, as through certain doors or windows, either life or death enters our soul. Concerning them the prophet also said: “Death entered through your windows” (Jer. 9:21).

Thus the five virgins who use these senses well are called wise, while the five foolish are those who through these five senses receive death rather than life.

Let us examine more carefully, then, how these five senses, like five virgins, either preserve virginity or fall subject to corruption.

If a man or woman sees a son, daughter, another person’s male servant, or female servant, and looks intently with desire, one virgin has been corrupted,

[Col. 1072D] because through the eyes—that is, through the body’s windows—the poison of death has entered the heart’s inner chamber.

If someone, whether religious or lay, willingly listens to people slandering, to idle talk, or to those uttering lustful or shameful songs, and receives these things with pleasure through a receptive ear, another virgin has been corrupted.

If someone is not content with moderate food but acquires expensive delicacies, or if he is always eager to speak wickedly, another virgin has been corrupted through perverse taste.

If someone carefully seeks exotic fragrances so that he may please people and incite lust, the fourth virgin has been violated.

If someone wishes with pleasure to touch another’s sons or daughters with his hands for the sake of lust, and seeks excessively soft clothing with a voluptuous mind, then the fifth virgin too has been corrupted.

In this order these five senses, like five virgins, are corrupted in human beings.

Conversely, when holy souls restrain these five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—from every illicit thing, and release their tongue soberly and chastely for what is permitted and lawful, they preserve the virginity of the five senses.

Thus the five virgins signify good people, while the other five prefigure those who are evil.

And truly, dearly beloved brothers, what does it profit a man or woman, cleric, monk, or nun if virginity is preserved in the body when the integrity of the heart is violated by evil desires? What does it profit to display chastity in one member while harboring corruption in all the others?

For those virgins who follow the Lamb, if you pay close attention, do not follow the Lamb merely because they preserved bodily virginity. After saying, “These are they who have not defiled themselves with women” (Rev. 14), he immediately added: “And no lie was found in their mouth; they are without blemish.”

[Col. 1073A] Therefore, those who boast of bodily virginity alone should pay close attention: if they love falsehood, they will not be able to follow Christ with those holy virgins.

Let no virgin, then, presume upon bodily virginity alone. For if she is disobedient or loose-tongued, she must know that she will be excluded from the bridal chamber of the heavenly bridegroom.

Although a virgin occupies the hundredth degree and a married woman the thirtieth, a chaste and humble married woman is nevertheless better than a proud virgin. By serving her husband chastely and humbly, she possesses the thirtieth degree; for the proud virgin not even one will remain. In both cases what the Psalmist said is fulfilled: “You will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. 17:28).

And because the blessed Apostle called the whole Catholic Church a virgin—not considering in her only those who are bodily virgins, but desiring the minds of all to remain incorrupt—he says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

The souls not only of nuns but also of all men and women, if they wish to preserve chastity in the body and, in the five senses mentioned above, the virginity of concord, may have no doubt that they are betrothed to Christ. For Christ is to be understood as the bridegroom not of bodies but of souls.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, men and women alike, boys and girls alike: if they preserve virginity until marriage and, by using these five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—well, do not corrupt their souls, they will happily merit entering through open doors into the eternal bridal chamber of the bridegroom on the day of judgment.

But those who corrupt their bodies before marriage through adulterous union and afterward, by living wickedly, hearing wickedly, and speaking wickedly throughout their lives, do not cease to violate their souls—unless fruits of repentance worthy of them come to their aid—will call out in vain behind closed doors: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. 25:11), and will merit hearing: “Truly I tell you, I do not know where you are from” (ibid.).

If we—clerics and laypeople, monks and nuns, and those living in marriage—faithfully and carefully attend to these matters, and, with the Lord’s help, preserve integrity of heart together with bodily chastity, then we will not be cast with the foolish into the outer darkness,

[Col. 1073B] but with the wise we will enter the spiritual wedding feast and merit hearing: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

May he himself deign to grant this.

## THE SAME AUTHOR’S WORK FOLLOWS

[Col. 1073]

[Col. 1073D] In the Gospel reading that has been recited to us concerning the ten virgins, dearest brothers, it was said that all the virgins trimmed their lamps, but the foolish ones did not have the oil necessary for their lamps. The wise, however, took oil in their vessels. When the bridegroom delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep.

[Col. 1074D] But at midnight a cry was made: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.” Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps (Matt. 25). When the lamps of the foolish virgins were going out, they asked the other virgins to give them some of their oil; and those replied: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; but go rather to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves.” While they went to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast, and the door was shut. Afterwards the other virgins came and said: “Lord, open to us.” They were answered: “I do not know where you are from.”

What these things signify, dearest brothers, according to what we have read in the exposition of the ancient Fathers, we briefly bring to your charity’s attention. The five virgins were not called five because so small a number will exist in eternal life, but because of the five senses through which either death or life enters our soul. We either use them badly and are corrupted, or, using them well, preserve the soul’s virginity.

When he says, “While the bridegroom delayed, they became drowsy and fell asleep, all of them” (ibid.), that sleep signified death. Thus the Apostle says: “Concerning those who sleep, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant” (2 Thess. 4:13, as cited).

[Col. 1075B] Midnight, when the great cry was made, signifies the day of judgment. It was called midnight because of ignorance, since no one knows when or at what hour the day of judgment will come.

The fact that all the virgins trimmed their lamps, and that the foolish ones had oil, but so little that it could not suffice for them—for they immediately began to go out—shows that we must labor as much as we can, with God’s help, dearest brothers, so that, since mercy or charity is understood by the oil, we may store in the vessels of our souls as much as will suffice for us eternally. A little is sufficient for no one, dearest brothers, unless perhaps poverty prevents someone from giving more.

[Col. 1075C] The lamp of the soul must be full, so that through the oil of charity our light may shine forever. Whoever has been given greater material means by God should open his hand as far as he can for almsgiving, and should not believe that a little can suffice him. Rather, let each person consider, from the time when he began to have understanding, how much he ought to give for the things he has thought wrongly, spoken wrongly, or done wrongly. Let him attend to the multitude of his sins and carefully weigh the price of each one; let him see how much he owes for lies, oaths, perjuries, curses, slanders, drunkenness, gluttony and lust, greed, envy, pride, filthy thoughts, and idle words.

[Col. 1075D] Let each person therefore consider all these things and the like, which cannot even be counted; then he will recognize how many alms he ought to perform. For even if we give everything, unless God’s mercy prevails, we cannot redeem all sins. Nevertheless, with a humbly contrite and repentant heart, let us labor as much as we can with God’s help, and let us do so not for human praise, but for the love of God and in contemplation of eternal life.

When the foolish virgins said to the wise, “Give us some of your oil” (Matt. 25), and those replied, “Perhaps there will not be enough for us” (ibid.), this was humbly said out of fear, because such terror and such an examination will occur on the day of judgment that even those who understand themselves to have prepared an abundance of the oil of mercy will fear

[Col. 1076A] that it may not suffice for the redemption of all their sins.

What was said—“Go rather to those who sell it, and buy some for yourselves” (ibid.)—can be understood of the poor. They are the merchants who sell the oil necessary for the lamps of souls. Through them Christ customarily conducts this commerce: through them he receives earthly things in order to return heavenly things; he receives perishable things in order to repay eternal things. Thus he himself said: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me” (Matt. 25:40).

The lamps are understood as souls. But what do those vessels signify, in which we are commanded to have oil, except storing good works within, in the conscience? And because some do good works for the love of God, while others do them out of a desire for human praise, those foolish virgins—although they were virgins in body, and although they exercised themselves in vigils, psalms, readings, and prayers—did all this for human praise, not for God or eternal blessedness. Therefore, when death intervened and human praise ceased for them, their oil failed at the same time.

What was said to them—“Go rather to those who sell it and buy some for yourselves” (Matt. 25)—can also be understood so that the sellers are flatterers, who with false praises exalt those who appear to perform good works for human glory. Indeed, whoever does something good for empty praise, if no one praises him, does not do it at all. Hence it is understood that all who desire to receive human praise sell to human flatteries what they appear to practice in God’s work, accepting empty praise and losing eternal rewards.

[Col. 1076C] But those virgins who had oil in their vessels placed every good work within, in their conscience, because they did this not for human praise but for divine mercy. Faithfully considering these things, dearest brothers, since this parable pertains to the whole Church, those who cannot preserve bodily virginity should preserve virginity of heart, so that, if they cannot attain the crown of martyrs or virgins, they may at least deserve to receive forgiveness for all their sins.

But virgins who, with God’s help, preserve bodily integrity should strive with all their strength and with God’s help to flee verbosity; reject slander as the poisons of the devil; fear the disease of envy or pride as the sword of the ancient enemy; retain obedience humbly; never despise the commands of their superior; devote themselves to reading and prayer; and, if illness does not prevent it, rise to the vigils with complete eagerness. Whether in church, at a banquet, or in any place whatsoever, they should always take care to utter from their mouths what pertains to obedience or humility. If they see someone sad, let them console him; if they recognize someone as disobedient, let them not cease to correct him.

[Col. 1076D] And because in every way of life both good and bad people are found, and because in Christ’s Church, which is now like a threshing floor, there is found not only wheat but also chaff, there are found there—what is worse—not only laypeople but also clerics, monks, and nuns so negligent and lukewarm that they do not, like spiritual bees, produce the sweet honey of souls, but, like the most savage wasps, strike the hearts of brothers or sisters with the poisonous stings of their tongues. Such people are proved to be not Christ’s helpers but the devil’s defenders.

[Col. 1077A] If they happen to see a brother or sister rising up proudly against a superior, they not only strive to calm the person, but by malicious words attempt to inflame him to even greater fury, saying that he cannot and ought not to endure this any longer. They also urge him to answer his superiors with such great bitterness or fury that the superiors regret having wished to admonish or correct them with paternal affection.

But because in every undertaking, as we have already said, there are not only helpers or ministers of the devil, but also helpers of God, vessels of Christ, and defenders of righteousness, Christ’s helpers strive to recall to obedience

[Col. 1077B] or humility all whom the devil’s helpers inflame to disobedience or pride by their crafty whispering, using gentle exhortation and holy, salutary counsel.

The former offer poison; the latter, an antidote. The former inflict wounds; the latter provide medicines. The former bring destruction; the latter, salvation. The former bring fury; the latter, gentleness. The former teach pride; the latter, humility. The former teach injury; the latter, patience. The former teach hatred; the latter, charity. However much evil the former may do, Christ’s medicines nevertheless prevail more than the devil’s wounds.

Those who, placed in the clergy or monastery, raise themselves and others up into pride are like quivers filled with the devil’s arrows: they strive to strike the hearts of the simple and extinguish all humility and gentleness within them. But because, by God’s favor, wheat and holy souls are also found amid the chaff—souls proved to be full of spiritual antidotes, as though in the [reading uncertain: *armaria*, perhaps “storehouses”] of Christ—whatever wounds the others inflict, these do not cease to heal with heavenly medicines.

[Col. 1077C] They say to every proud person: “Do not be proud, brother, because it is written: ‘God resists the proud’” (Jas. 4:6). “Do not be angry, because it is written: ‘Anger rests in the bosom of the fool’” (Eccl. 7:10). And again: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (Jas. 2:20).

If they happen to see someone disobedient, they say gently and humbly: “Do not be disobedient, brother, because it is written: ‘Obedience is better than sacrifice’” (1 Kings 11, as cited). And Paul cries out: “Obey your superiors and submit to them, because they keep watch as those who will give an account for your souls” (Heb. 13:17; the source citation reads “Gal. V, 17”).

[Col. 1077D] If these souls full of God see someone lukewarm or negligent, they strive to kindle him to repentance with medicines brought forth, as it were, from a spiritual storehouse—

[Col. 1078A] that is, from a good heart. If they see someone slandering or murmuring, they say to him the words of the blessed Apostle: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (1 Cor. 10:10). “Do not slander, because it is written: ‘Whoever slanders his brother will be uprooted.’” By this holy admonition they deter him from evil-speaking and begin to urge him to praise others.

If they recognize someone as talkative or contentious, they apply the medicine of silence, saying to him what is written: “Hear, Israel, and be silent” (Isa. 35:7). And what was prophesied concerning the Lord and Savior: “Like a lamb before its shearer, he did not open his mouth” (Matt. 12:36). And this also: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment.”

[Col. 1078B] With such medicines and others like them, whatever the vessels of the devil strive to wound, the vessels of Christ endeavor to restore to health.

Whether he is a cleric, monk, or nun, let each person examine his conscience. If, by speaking well, he recognizes himself to be Christ’s helper and a defender of righteousness, let him rejoice and give thanks to God, and, with God’s help, persevere to the end, because “it is not the one who begins, but the one who perseveres who will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

But whoever senses that through pride, disobedience, or envy he is a helper or vicar of the devil should grieve over the past, beware of the future, and, through humility, rebuild what he had destroyed by the tyranny of pride. Let gentleness calm what anger had inflamed; let the sweetness of charity repair what malice or disobedience had embittered. While that dark soul, accustomed to serving the devil, is still held in this mortal body, let it acquire a remedy for the day of necessity, so that, transferred from the left hand to the right, it may deserve to hear with Christ’s sheep: “Come, blessed ones; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

[Col. 1078C] And although these things are so, brothers, this nevertheless is necessary: the good must not be lifted up by their holy merits, nor should those who have been bad be broken by excessive despair. Rather, let the former persevere humbly in good works, and let the latter quickly correct their evil deeds, so that when the day of judgment comes, an upright life may be able to crown the good, and a corrected life may be able to excuse the bad. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns,

[Col. 1078D] God, forever and ever. Amen.

# SOME ECCLESIASTICAL MONUMENTS OF THE SEVENTH AND EIGHTH CENTURIES, AS A KIND OF INTERMEDIATE MATERIAL

[Col. 1079]

# THE LAST ECCLESIASTICAL AND PIOUS DONATIONS OF THE LAST KINGS OF THE FIRST FRANKISH DYNASTY

*(From Breq., Diplomas, Charters, Laws, etc., vol. II.) Years 691–748.*

## Diploma of Chlodoveus III, by which he confirms the immunity granted to the monastery of Sithiu

**Note:** [Col. 1079C] Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 607, from Folquin’s cartulary; reprinted in Miraeus’s *Supplementum operum diplomaticorum*, vol. II, p. 928; in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 667 [and in Folquin’s *Cartulary*, edited by the distinguished Guérard in 1841, p. 34]. We publish it again from a copy made from the same cartulary, written in his own hand by the lord De Wite, prefect of the archives of Saint Bertin, and brought into our archive. Mabillon’s edition occasionally differs from this copy; we have placed the various readings in brackets. The differences appear to have arisen

[Col. 1079D] from corrections adopted by Mabillon,

[Col. 1080C] indeed successfully, but without notifying the reader—something we consider improper. See the note that follows immediately. (Year 691.)

[Col. 1079A]

Chlodoveus, king of the Franks. If we confirm by our decrees those benefits which our ancestors bestowed or granted upon holy places, we both exercise royal custom and trust that this pertains, in God’s name, to our praise and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore the venerable man Bertinus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, which is in the district of Tarwan, built in honor of holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the other holy lords, came into our presence. He brought to the attention of the clemency of our kingdom that our grandfather Chlotarius

**Note:** [Col. 1080C] Here Mabillon reads *Chlodovius* instead of *Chlotarius*: correctly; for Chlodoveus II was the grandfather of Chlodoveus III, whereas Chlotarius and Childericus were his uncles. The correction emerges from the diploma itself, where below Chlodoveus—namely, the second Chlodoveus—is called the grandfather of Chlodoveus III, while Chlotarius and Childericus are called his uncles. Nevertheless, we ought to present the cartulary’s genuine, although corrupt, reading [which is also found in the edition of the distinguished Guérard]. [Mab., *Chlodovius*]

formerly king, had granted full immunity to his predecessor Mummolinus concerning all the little estates or villas of that monastery, whatever they possessed at the present time or might thereafter acquire through the gift of kings, through the contribution (*collato*; Mabillon: *collata*) of the people, by purchase, or by any other lawful acquisition (*quolibet recto*; Mabillon: *qualibet*), in whatever districts or territories the property had been added or granted there.

He had granted it so that no public judge might enter there at any time to hear cases, exact fines, take sureties, make lodging or requisition provisions, distrain the people of the monastery—both free persons and servants—who lived upon their lands, demand or exact any payments, or exercise judicial authority there. Instead, under the name of immunity, the monastery’s portion should possess all the granted fines and rights forever.

Accordingly, he showed us the decrees of the princes, as well as the confirmation of our uncles [Col. 1080B] Chlotharius and Childericus [text: *avunculi nostri*, “our uncles”; Mabillon: *avunculorum nostrorum*, “of our uncles”], and also of our father Theodericus, formerly king, explaining how these and those little estates, which afterwards the abbot Bertinus confirmed that he had received for the monastery’s portion by way of exchange or by written instruments, had been preserved from that time until now with the benefits granted. But the aforesaid abbot asked our highness, for the sake of firmness, that we should more fully confirm this concerning that place by our authority.

Know, therefore, that we have granted his request, both as a benefit for our merit and out of reverence for that holy place, and have confirmed everything.

For we command that whatever our aforesaid grandfather Chlodovius, formerly king,

**Note:** [Col. 1080C] Here four diplomas concerning the immunity of the monastery of Sithiu are enumerated: one from the grandfather Chlodoveus, two from the uncles Chlotarius and Childericus, and the fourth from the father Theodericus. We published the fourth above, under the year 682, October 23; we have not seen the other three [nor are they found in the new edition of the *Cartulary of Sithiu* brought to light by the distinguished Guérard]. For the diploma of Chlotarius concerning the monastery of Sithiu that we printed under the year 662 contains nothing about the immunities of this monastery.

[Col. 1080C] concerning that immunity, as it is set out above, justly and reasonably agreed to or confirmed for the aforesaid Mummolinus, and whatever afterwards [text: *ipsi*; Mabillon: *ipse*] our uncles Chlotharius and Childericus, as well as our father Theodericus, formerly king [text: *genitoris nostri Theodorici, quondam regis*; Mabillon: *genitor noster Theodoricus, quondam reges*], likewise agreed to or confirmed, and which has been preserved in a direct course from that time until now, shall also, by our decree, fully confirmed in God’s name, remain preserved in every respect for the abbot Bertinus, his successors, or the monastery of Sithiu, with all the benefits granted to it.

They shall never need fear any opposition or impediment from public judges on this account. Therefore, this confirmation (*confirmatio*; Mabillon: *congregatio*, “community”) must continually beseech the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and the safety of the country. And so that this authority may be firmer and preserved in every respect, we and our exalted mother, Queen Chrothechildis, have decreed that it be confirmed below by the marks of our hands.

The sign of the glorious King Chlodoveus.

The sign of our exalted mother, Queen Chrothechildis.

**Note:** [Col. 1081C] In Folquin’s cartulary [which D. De Wite had used], the monograms of Chlodoveus III and Chrothechildis are expressly displayed, but they appear to have been inaccurately fashioned by the cartulary’s scribe. The eye vainly attempts to detect in them abbreviations of either name. Mabillon mentions them in *De re diplomatica*, p. 378, where he does not doubt that they existed in the original, although he admits that monograms are rare in Merovingian diplomas. [I have not thought it necessary to have these monograms, which the reader will encounter in the new edition of the *Cartulary of Sithiu*, p. 36, engraved on copperplate.]

Done on the first day before the Kalends of June, in the first year of our reign.

**Note:** [Col. 1081D] Iperius, *Chronicle*, in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 472, says that this diploma was issued on the first day before the Kalends of May. Chlodoveus began his reign either in the year 690, after September had ended, or around the beginning of spring in 691, according to Longuerue, *Annales Francorum*, in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. III, p. 696.

## II. Judgment of Chlodoveus III, king of the Franks, concerning the dispute between Chaino, abbot of Saint-Denis, and the abbot Ermenoaldus, who had abandoned the appointed hearing

**Note:** [Col. 1081D] Published by Mabillon in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, section III, part II, p. 559, and more accurately in book VI of *De re diplomatica*, p. 473; reissued by Felibianus in *Proofs of the History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 12; both from the original [now preserved in the Royal Archives, K, chest 3, on the basis of which A. Teulet has prepared a new recension]. Felibianus nevertheless gives some variant readings, which we have marked in brackets. The document was reprinted by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 275, and in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 668. Cointius introduced many corrections and restorations, which may be seen in his edition. We follow the readings of Mabillon’s later edition.

The dispute here concerned the following matter: Chaino, abbot of Saint-Denis, had summoned a certain Abbot Ermenoaldus, who stood surety for one thousand five hundred pounds of oil and one hundred measures of wine delivered by Chaino to Anseberchtus. When the matter was brought to judgment before Bishop Sygofridus of Paris, Ermenoaldus promised that he would carry out the obligation within a fixed period; otherwise he would be brought before the king’s court. This was done, and when Ermenoaldus did not come to the appointed hearing, he was condemned by judgment. (Year 692.)

Chlodovius, king of the Franks, illustrious man. The agents of the basilica of the lord Dionysius, where that precious lord rests in the body and the venerable Chaino presides as abbot, came to us at Novientum, in our palace, and reported that some years earlier the venerable Abbot Ermenoaldus had given a pledge to him for one thousand five hundred pounds of oil [the text reads *milli quignentas* (sic)] and one hundred measures of good wine on behalf of Bishop Anseberchtus, which Chaino the abbot had entrusted to him; and that Ermenoaldus had promised that he ought to give and fulfill this for him, but had not done so.

Therefore, some days earlier, they had held hearings between themselves before Lord Bishop Sygofridus, as recorded in their matching written records (*noticias paricolas*; Felibianus spells *noctitias*), so that, in the middle of the preceding month of April, Ermenoaldus the abbot, together with three men, himself making the fourth, either had to swear before that bishop that he had never received or undertaken the pledge from the hand of the aforesaid Abbot Chaino, nor had promised to give and fulfill this for him, which he had failed to do; or else he would have to give him ten pounds of silver on that very day.

**Note:** [Col. 1082D] Here we read *adchramire*, whereas in the judgment of the year 691 we find *achranmire*; in other documents, *adhramire*, *adramire*, and *agramire*. For, as I have said, whoever promised to do or provide something handed over to his adversary a staff or some other token. See Du Cange, especially the new edition undertaken by the learned Henschel, under the word *Adramire*.

If he did not do this, after these Kalends of May had passed they would have to come before us, and, after their records had been examined [printed *eorum*, “their”; Mabillon and Felibianus: *coram*, “before”], they would have to present their case concerning this matter before us.

Accordingly, their aforesaid matching records established the hearing agreed between them concerning this matter. But those agents of the said abbot came to the hearing at Novientum, in our palace, and appeared to have observed their appointed hearing for three days or more, as the law required, and to have formally called Abbot Ermenoaldus to account (*abjectissent vel solsadissent*, two procedural terms in the irregular wording). They declared that he neither came to the hearing, nor sent a representative in his place, nor gave notice of any lawful impediment.

For this reason, together with our nobles, we have decreed as follows: if it is clearly shown by their matching records that they had agreed upon such a hearing between themselves concerning this matter, and since the illustrious man Vuarno, count of our palace, testified that the aforesaid agents had legally observed their hearing with the aforementioned Abbot Chaino, while the above-mentioned Abbot Ermenoaldus had neglected to observe his hearing, we command that, whatever the law of your place teaches concerning such a matter, the aforesaid Abbot Ermenoaldus, under your compulsion, shall not refuse to make payment and satisfaction in every way to those agents on behalf of the aforementioned Abbot Chaino and the basilica of his lord Dionysius.

Aghilus, recorder. [Felibianus: Agnilus.]

Given on the fifth day of the month of May, in the second year of our reign, at Novientum, prosperously, in God’s name.

**Note:** [Col. 1082D] In his earlier edition Mabillon noted that a wax seal had been attached to this charter. A fragment of it, impressed with a bearded face, still survives. [Col. 1083C] See N. de Wailly, *Elements of Palaeography*, vol. II, p. 377, and the table of seals, A, no. 3.

## III. Diploma of Chlodoveus III, king of the Franks, by which he grants and confirms exemption from tolls to the monastery of Saint-Denis

**Note:** [Col. 1083C] Mabillon published this diploma twice from the original [now preserved in the Royal Archives, K, chest 3]: first among the instruments illustrating the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. IV, p. 560; and again in book VI of *De re diplomatica*, p. 474. Felibianus copied it from the same original in *Proofs of the History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 12. Cointius reprinted it in his *Annals*, vol. V, p. 276, from Mabillon’s first edition; the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 669, from the later edition. We publish it after more carefully collating the original [on the authority of which A. Teulet has prepared a new recension]. The charter is full of solecisms and errors of every kind, which Cointius attempted to correct. (Year 692.)

[Col. 1083A]

Chlodoveus, king of the Franks, illustrious man. Whereas, a year ago, our great-grandfather Dagobertus, formerly king, granted one hundred solidi, exempted from the city of Massilia, just as they could have been exacted from the treasury’s storehouse, to the basilica

**Note:** [Col. 1083D] For the words *ad basileca*, Mabillon at first read *abbas Ileca* in the *Acts of the Saints* cited above, which misled Cointius. From this he concluded that an abbot of Saint-Denis named Ileca had to be admitted, although that name is absent from every catalogue of the abbots of this monastery. Later, however, Mabillon successfully established the true reading, *ad basileca*, in *De re diplomatica*, cited above; therefore the abbot Ileca must be dismissed entirely among fictitious persons. The later reading of Mabillon is confirmed by Felibianus’s edition based on the original.

of our special patron, the lord Dionysius, where that precious man rests in the body, and where the venerable man Chaino appears to preside as abbot, by his decree; and our kinsman Sigebertus, as well as our uncles Chlotharius and Childericus, and also our father Theudericus, formerly king, again granted or confirmed this there by their decrees.

The decrees appear to contain the following provision: both in that Massilia and throughout the other places in our kingdom, wherever tolls, transport duties, bridge tolls, road tolls, or other payments were exacted by public judges, from the cartloads that appeared to be brought in, nothing was to be demanded or exacted from the messengers of that basilica, unless this had been granted to them each and every year.

Therefore, by this present order, we command you absolutely and above all demand that, whenever the messengers of the basilica of the lord Dionysius or of the aforementioned Abbot Chaino come to you, you cause the one hundred exempted solidi to be given and fulfilled to them without any delay or postponement, according to custom in the treasury and according to the procedure of the *catabolus* [warehouse or customs depot; reading uncertain].

And concerning those cartloads that appear to be brought in, neither in that Massilia nor throughout the other places in our kingdom—by God’s favor, ours—must you, your subordinates, or anyone on behalf of our treasury presume to demand or exact from them any toll, transport duty, bridge toll, road toll, or any other payment.

See to it that you do nothing else on this account, if you wish to have our favor graciously bestowed upon you.

Aghilus, ordered to record.

**Note:** [Col. 1083D] Mabillon notes that the chancellor’s subscription existed here, but admits—and rightly so—that he was unable to read it.

(Place of the seal.)

Given on the fifth day of the month of June, in the second year of our reign, at Novientum, prosperously.

## IV. Diploma of Chlodoveus III, king of the Franks, by which he approves an exchange formerly arranged between King Childericus and the abbot of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy

**Note:** [Col. 1084C] Published by Henschenius in *The Three Dagoberts*, p. 148, and by Martène in the *Most Extensive Collection*, vol. II, col. 14, both from the archives of Stavelot; by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 286, from Henschenius; by Bertholetus, *Proofs of the History of Luxembourg*, p. 22; and by the collectors of the *Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 669, from Martène. We reprint it on the authority of Martène. [Some variant readings, which the learned De Reiffenberg most courteously communicated to me from a manuscript of the Royal Library of Brussels, although not very important, I have copied in brackets.]

The instrument of exchange between Childericus II and Remaclus,

[Col. 1084D] confirmed by this diploma, does not exist today, so far as we know. Papolinus or Pabolenus [or, as in the Brussels manuscript, Papolenus], who obtained the confirmation from Chlodoveus III, is called both bishop and custodian of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy. Thus Remaclus, one of his predecessors, was likewise called by both the names of abbot and bishop. Indeed, if we believe Martène, it was an ancient custom for the abbots of certain monasteries to be ordained bishops without any fixed or determined diocese. That this custom continued in the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy until the ninth century is proved by the *Most Extensive Collection*, vol. II, preface, p. 3. The reason is clear: the younger monks were to receive holy orders from their own abbots and were not to travel outside the monastery on the occasion of ordinations. (Year 692.)

Chlodoveus, king of the Franks, to the illustrious Duke Hericus [Charavius] and Count Chareieivus [Aericus]. Whenever an exchange concerning any matter has been made by written instruments between the majesty of earlier kings and a holy community of monks, it is proper for the sequence of the documents between the parties to be confirmed by our decree.

Therefore the apostolic man and our father Papolinus [Papolenus], bishop, brought to the clemency of our kingdom the information that our lord and uncle Childericus, formerly king, together with his predecessor, the lord Remaclus, formerly bishop, had exchanged certain little estates with his monks, where he appears to be custodian of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy [Stabulaus].

Accordingly, the portion of our lord and uncle Childericus, formerly king, received the little estate called Athetasis, with the people living there, and all their property or lands which they appear to cultivate, under these names: Radefridus with his nephews; Bertrannus [Bertramno, [Col. 1084C] Adelino]; Gisflobertus; Aganulfus; likewise Radefridus; Sigofridus; and Rigobertus.

In exchange for this property, the bishop himself received from our treasury the little estate called Maipa, with the people living there, under these names: Athelinus, Albode, and Vinegarius,

[Col. 1085A] together with the lands which they appear to cultivate and all their property, so that this portion should belong permanently to that bishop and his monks.

He then showed us for reading the exchange of that prince, confirmed by his own hands. For the sake of firmness, we have taken care that their petitions concerning those monasteries and the holy community should be more fully confirmed by decree.

Know, therefore, that we have granted, confirmed, and conceded in every respect this benefit: whatever, as is established by inspection of that exchange, was justly and reasonably exchanged or transferred between that prince and the glorious lord Remalgus, the aforesaid bishop—lands, garden-plots, houses, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, slaves, buildings, and all other property and possessions—our lord and father Pabolenus shall possess as confirmed and established [variant: “and granted”] for perpetual time, by our decree, for the aforesaid Stavelot and Malmedy [Stabelaco].

And so that this decree may possess firmer force in our time and in that of our successors, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by the marks of our hands.

The sign of Chlodoveus, most glorious [glorious] king, King of the Franks.

Given on the twenty-fifth day of the month of June, in the second year of our reign. Namucno, I have registered it.

**Note:** [Col. 1085D] The collectors of the *Writers on Frankish Affairs* deleted the word *recognovi* and accepted *Namucho* as the name of the place where the diploma was issued; elsewhere it appears as *Namuchum* and *Namurcum*. See Valesius, *Notes on Gaul*, under *Namucum*. They do not explain on what authority they corrected the received reading. Here *Namucho* appears to be the name of the referendary or notary subscribing for greater authenticity of the instrument, as is shown by the word *recognovi*, which could not be removed merely by conjecture.

## V. Diploma of Chlodoveus III, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunities and privileges of the monastery of Anisola granted by his predecessors

**Note:** [Col. 1085D] Published by Martène, *Most Extensive Collection*, vol. I, col. 8, from the cartulary of Anisola; reprinted by the collectors of the *Writers on Frankish Affairs* from Martène, vol. IV, p. 670. We published elsewhere, under the year 674, the diploma of Theodericus III mentioned here; the others referred to there, however, are now hidden. Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 544, says that he read in the small cartulary of Anisola a decree of Dagobert confirmed by Chlodoveus III; but it had not yet been made public. [This small cartulary was sought unsuccessfully in the archives of Le Mans.]

[Col. 1085C]

Chlodoveus, illustrious king of the Franks, to all present and future officials.
