If we willingly hear the petitions of priests whenever, for the needs of our churches or monasteries, they lay them open to our ears, we exercise the royal custom and trust that this pertains to our reward and to the stability of our kingdom. Therefore the venerable Ibbolenus, abbot of the monastery of Anisola, situated in the Cenomannian district and built in honor of our special patron, the pious confessor Carilephus, brought to our notice through envoys of our royal clemency that our cousin Guntramnus, formerly king, had granted that monastery, under complete immunity, by his authority; and that afterward our grandfather Chlotarius and Dagobertus, as well as Chlodoveus and likewise Chlotarius, formerly kings, and also our lord and father Theodericus, formerly king, had confirmed this for the monastery through their authorities, strengthened by their own signatures. Hence they assert that they possess these royal instruments. They maintain that this arrangement concerning the monastery has been preserved without anyone disturbing it; but, for the protection of the whole matter, they ask that our authority should more fully ensure its observance in that monastery. Your Magnificence should have no doubt that we have granted and generally confirmed this.

Therefore, by this present decree, we order that, just as is recorded in the authorities of the aforesaid princes [Col. 1086A] and has been observed until now, neither you, nor your subordinates, nor your successors shall presume in any way to enter the estates of that monastery, whether to hear cases, exact fines, or demand lodging. Rather, under complete immunity, having regard to the aforesaid decrees of the aforementioned princes, which they affirm they possess, the abbot himself and his successors shall be able to have, hold, and possess whatever those serving God there in the affairs of that monastery are reasonably seen to possess at present, or whatever may there be added or increased by God-fearing people; and, under this our authority, what has been confirmed shall perpetually advance the increase of that holy place, so that they may be more disposed to beseech the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom.

And, so that this petition of ours may obtain firmer force, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by the marks of our hand.

Chlodoveus, king.  
+ Given on the Kalends of September, in the second year of our reign, at Compendium.

## VI. Charter of Chlodoveus III, king of the Franks, by which he asserts in a judicial hearing the estate of Nocitum, granted by Angantrude to the monastery of Saint Dionysius

[Note: Mabillon published it in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, third century, part II, vol. IV, p. 558, from the original, and again in Book VI of *De re diplomatica*, p. 474, from the same original [now in the Royal Archives, K, chest 3], more accurately, as he himself explains. From this same original, Felibianus published it in *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, documents, p. 13. Cointius, *Annales*, vol. V, p. 274, and the Collectors of the Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 671, reprinted it from Mabillon. [The distinguished M. de Brequigny wished the reader to be informed that, in reprinting this judicial record, he had followed the readings of the original. Nevertheless, A. Teulet restored certain passages from the new recension.]] (a.d. 692).

Chlodovius, illustrious king of the Franks. While we, in God’s name, were seated at Lusarca, in our palace, together with the apostolic men, our fathers in Christ, the bishops Sygofridus, Constantinus, Gribo, and Ursinianus [Note: It is noteworthy that the names of the bishops are placed before those of the nobles. Of the bishops here listed, Sigofridus presided over the Church of Paris, and Constantinus over that of Beauvais, according to Mabillon, cited above, and Cointius. Mabillon conjectures that Ursinianus then occupied the see of Amiens, a view supported by *Gallia christiana nova*, vol. X, col. 1156. Cointius does not know the sees of this man or of Gribo.], and also the illustrious men Ragnoaldus, Nordebercthus, [Col. 1087A] Ermenfridus, nobles; Madelulfus and Erconaldus, counts; and Benedictus and Chardoinus, seneschals; and also Marso, our count of the palace, to hear everyone’s cases and settle them by a just judgment, the venerable man Chaino, abbot of the basilica of our special patron Saint Dionysius, where that precious saint rests bodily, came before us.

Against the illustrious woman Angantrude, consecrated to God, daughter of Ebrulfus and widow of the late Ingobercthus, he submitted that the estate called Nocito, situated in the Camiliacian district, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, and whatever Ingobercthus or the aforementioned Angantrude had held or possessed there, whether from their parents’ hereditary property, by purchase, or by any other acquisition, had been fully confirmed to him by her instrument. He therefore produced for reading in the present hearing that instrument itself and also the *precarium* by which Angantrude possessed property belonging to that abbot.

When the aforementioned Angantrude was present, she was asked whether she had confirmed the aforesaid estate of Nocito to the abbot Chaino or to the church of his Saint Dionysius, or whether she herself wished to stand as guarantor in the matter. Angantrude then publicly declared that she had confirmed the aforementioned estate of Nocito, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, and everything that she or her husband Ingobercthus had held or possessed there by any acquisition, to the aforementioned abbot Chaino or to the church of his Saint Dionysius, by the instrument itself; and that she had asked for that instrument or *precarium* to be drawn up for this purpose. She also declared that she stood as guarantor in the matter against anyone who might contest it and intended to remain so in the future.

Therefore we, together with our nobles, having examined the matter, decreed as follows: since the illustrious Marso, our count of the palace, testified that this case had been conducted in the manner described [Note: I have added this word from the original], we order that the aforementioned abbot Chaino, or the church of his Saint Dionysius, should hold the estate of Nocito, with all its appurtenances and entirety, after the instruments themselves had been examined, as they make clear, without any claim of restitution by the aforementioned Angantrude or her heirs, perpetually secured. And if the abbot Chaino, his successors, or the agents of the basilica should at any time have need of it, the aforementioned Angantrude or her heirs shall strive to defend them in possession against anyone.

Chlodoinus [Note: This is how Mabillon read it in his later work. At first he had mistakenly read Chlodoveus, taking it to be the name of the referendary Chlodoinus, as he admits in *De re diplomatica*, cited above. Felibianus, however, instead of *Chlodoinus recognovit*, read *Chlodovius rex subscripsi*—“I, King Chlodovius, have subscribed.”] recognized it. (Place of the seal.)

[Col. 1088A] Given on the Kalends of November, in the second year of our reign, at Lusarca, in God’s name, successfully.

## VII. Fragment of a charter of Chlodoveus III, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the privileges granted to the monastery of Grasellum by Aredius, bishop of Vaison

[Note: Mabillon appended this fragment to the charter of Aredius for the monastery of Grasellum, which Chlodoveus III confirmed by a charter; here we present the surviving portion, in *Annales*, vol. I, p. 700. Boyerus, *History of Vaison*, documents, p. 3, and the Collectors of the Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 673, reprinted it. Chlodoveus III began his reign in a.d. 690 or 691; therefore this charter, lacking chronological indications, may properly be placed around the year 692.] (a.d. 692).

Chlodoicus, king of the Franks. If we confirm by our royal pronouncements the acts of priests which they have performed for the repose of the servants of God at holy places, we trust that they will endure through our perpetual stability. Therefore the apostolic man, our lord Aredius, bishop of the city of Vaison, having sent a petition, made known to our royal clemency that he had built, on his own property, a monastery at the place called [Col. 1088B] Grasellum, in honor of Saint Victor the martyr and Saint Peter, out of love for Christ, and had assigned a very large portion of his possessions to that place by his instruments.

He had also established or granted there a privilege, together with several bishops, so that whatever was collected there by the said lord Aredius, or for God by any person, whether from the contributions of the people or from any legitimate acquisition, should be possessed perpetually and peacefully by the community residing there, without any interference by the bishops, archdeacons, or clergy of Vaison, or by anyone from any other church; and so that it should be governed and preserved there under the holy rule, according to the institutions of the Fathers.

If the abbot of that holy place should depart from this world, another abbot was to be elected not from elsewhere but, as propriety and order required, from the community residing in that monastery, without any payment or quarrel, by the whole community or by its better and more holy part. With the counsel, consent, and blessing of the bishop of Vaison, he was to undertake the dignity.

The bishop of that same city, if the need should ever arise, was to visit the monastery, together with priests and spiritually minded abbots, in order to remove sloth and negligence from the community; and, with paternal affection, he was to admonish and recall the brothers there to the accustomed path of the rule. The same bishop, without payment, [lacuna] and no pontiff himself, nor anyone of greater authority, whether from that city or another place, or any person of whatever rank, was to act or attempt or touch anything contrary to the tenor of that decree.

When his petition had therefore been heard and his request received, [lacuna] ...

## VIII. Charter of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he grants the estate of Napsiniacum to the monastery of Saint Dionysius

[Note: Mabillon had a specimen of this charter engraved in copper in *De re diplomatica*, p. 382, and published the entire charter from the original [now in the Royal Archives, K, chest 3] in Book VI of *De re diplomatica*, p. 476. Felibianus likewise published the complete charter from the original in *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, documents, p. 14. Germonius, *On the Ancient Charters of the Frankish Kings*, vol. I, p. 319, and the Collectors of the Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 673, reprinted it from Mabillon; we, however, follow the original [in the new recension prepared by A. Teulet].

Germonius attempts to diminish the charter’s authenticity—not because he detects anything in its text that would prove it false, but because, when he compared the subscription of the referendary Wlfolaecus attached to this charter with another subscription of his attached to the end of the charter of Theodericus III, which we placed under the year 688, the forms of the handwriting seemed so different to him that he judged them not to have been written by the same hand, supported in this view by highly experienced experts in distinguishing scripts. We ourselves, after carefully examining specimens of both charters engraved in copper under Mabillon’s direction, have recognized these discrepancies. Mabillon, however, in the supplement to *De re diplomatica*, p. 23, argues that this difference not only does not weaken the charter’s authority but rather removes every suspicion of forgery. For, he says, if either handwriting had been fabricated by a forger, he would have taken care to make the form appear the same in both places. We add that two signatures written by the same hand in extremely intricate strokes, when seven years have elapsed between them, may display some variation without giving rise to suspicion of forgery.

Accordingly, since the charter in question is attacked by no other argument [and is evidently genuine in appearance], we judge that it should by no means be counted among spurious documents. Its authenticity is supported by synchronisms. In the first year of Childebert III’s reign, Godinus presided over the Church of Lyon and Chaino over the monastery of Saint Dionysius, which agrees with the charter. Childebert III began his reign around March of the Christian year 695. The month of December in the first year of this reign therefore agrees with that same year.] (a.d. 695).

[Col. 1089A]

Childeberthus, illustrious king of the Franks. The Creator, God of all, delights in the offering of faithful people, although he is Lord over all; but he wills that what he has given, by his clemency, should be [lacuna] bestowed upon the especially distinguished people of the age, so that the more they seem to possess, the more they ought to expend.

Therefore let your Magnificence or Utility know that we have granted, with full and complete favor, for the increase of our reward, the estate called Napsiniacum, in the Biturician district, with all its appurtenances and dependencies. The apostolic man, our lord Godinus, bishop of the city of Lyon, had apparently given it from the property of his church, in exchange for another estate called [Col. 1089B] Orbana, during the time of our brother Chlodovius, of good memory, formerly king, as an exchange to the royal fisc; afterward it was granted from the fisc to the illustrious man Pannichius, and after the said Pannichius’s death it was recalled to the property of our fisc.

We have now granted it to the basilica of our special patron, our lord Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily and where the venerable man Chaino appears to preside, for the increase of our reward. The community residing there has relinquished the two hundred solidi which it had customarily received each year from the public treasury, from the palace, for the alms or lamps of that holy place; and likewise the one hundred solidi which the public judges of the city of Marseille had customarily given for the needs of that basilica, because that estate was to be possessed perpetually by the property of that lord Dionysius, and it has released those sums to our fisc.

Therefore, by this present decree, we order and determine what we wish to remain perpetual: that neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor anyone else, shall presume to raise any objection concerning the estate of Napsiniacum, with its appurtenances and whatever appears to belong to it; nor concerning anything which the church of the city of Lyon possesses there, or which was transferred to the fisc in exchange for the estate of Orbana and granted to the fisc, or which Pannichius received, or which, at his death, he left and which was recalled to our fisc. You shall presume neither to oppose anything concerning it, nor to diminish or remove anything from the property of our lord Dionysius, nor to generate any accusation on this account.

Rather, the aforesaid estate of Napsiniacum, with all its appurtenances and entirety—that is, lands, houses, buildings, resident tenants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, small enclosures, strongholds, waters and courses of waters, mills, and all other appurtenances, of both sexes, acquired property—whatever can be said or named—shall be granted and indulged perpetually, under the name of immunity, from our gift of generosity to the aforementioned abbot Chaino and his successors, or to the part of the aforesaid basilica of Saint Dionysius, or to the community residing there. [Col. 1090B]

Thus, when that community, according to its voluntary arrangement, receives the two hundred solidi which were customarily given from the public treasury, and also the one hundred solidi which came from Marseille and which it had been customary to distribute each year for lamps or alms, as the earlier kings had established there, our fisc shall receive those three hundred solidi perpetually in our treasury and shall distribute them wherever it is ordered.

No complaint from the side of that basilica of our lord Dionysius shall ever reach our fisc or our successors; and the aforesaid estate of Napsiniacum shall perpetually advance the increase of that holy place, so that the community may continually pray to the mercy of the Lord for the stability of the kingdom and the safety of the country.

We therefore order that, for the increase of our reward and for stability concerning the basilica of our lord Dionysius and what pertains to our palace, two decrees written in the same tenor be made concerning this matter: one shall remain in the fortress of the basilica of Saint Dionysius, and the other in our treasury.

And, so that this decree may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Childeberthus, king, subscribed.  
Vulfolaecus, having been ordered, presented it. (Place of the seal.)

Given on the thirteenth day of December, in the first year of our reign, at Compendium, our estate, in God’s name, successfully.

## IX. Judicial record of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he asserts the estate of Hordinium, with the churches built there in the Bellovacian district, for Haino, abbot of Saint Dionysius

[Note: Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 477, and Felibianus, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, documents, p. 15, both from the Sandionysian original [now preserved in the Royal Archives, K, chest 3]; it was reprinted from Mabillon in the Collection of the Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 674.

Haino, abbot of Saint Dionysius, is the same person more often called Chaino; see *Gallia christiana nova*, vol. VII, col. 341, when his name is pronounced with a harsher sound. Childebert, son of Theodericus, whose name heads the judicial record, is the king who was the third of that name.

The war mentioned, fought in the regions of Austrasia by Theodericus, must be understood as the war of Theodericus III against Dagobertus II. Its mention, as Pagius correctly observed in his notes on Baronius, vol. III, p. 77, no. 7, occurs in the Life of Saint Salaberga in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. II, p. 408, no. 13. It does not refer to the war between the same Theodericus and Pippinus. For Childebert’s nobles who attended the judicial hearing, being clients of Pippinus, would never have ratified the fine imposed in this document on Ibbo because Ibbo had not marched in a hostile manner against Pippinus.

This charter is still enclosed by a wax seal—we publish it from the original [on the authority of which A. Teulet prepared a new recension].] (a.d. 695).

[Col. 1093C]

Childeberthus, illustrious king of the Franks. While we, in God’s name, were seated at Compendium, in our palace, together with our faithful men, to hear everyone’s cases and settle them by a just judgment, the illustrious man Aigobertus, our household official, came in the case of the venerable man Haino, abbot of the basilica of our lord Dionysius, where that precious saint himself rests bodily.

He submitted that, some years before, when our father Theudericus, formerly king, had marched hostilely into the regions of Austrasia, a man named Ibbo, now deceased, had in no way marched there, and had therefore made a pledge of six hundred solidi; that, at Ibbo’s request, the abbot Haino had paid those six hundred solidi on his behalf; and that, in return for those six hundred solidi, Ibbo had assigned and confirmed to him by his instrument his entire share in the place called Hordinium, in the Bellovacian district, together with the churches built there and everything that he possessed there.

But when Ibbo’s son, the cleric Bottharius, was present, he was asked whether his father Ibbo had assigned or confirmed to the abbot Haino, by his instrument, that share in the aforesaid place of Hordinium. The cleric Bottharius publicly declared that his father Ibbo had assigned or confirmed that share in the aforesaid place of Hordinium to the said abbot Haino by his instrument, and that he acknowledged his authority in the matter; he produced the instruments for reading in the present hearing, and, on seeing them, acknowledged them to be such.

Therefore we, together with our nobles, decreed as follows: since the illustrious man Ermenricus, our noble, testified that this case had been conducted in the manner stated, we order that the aforementioned abbot Haino shall hold perpetually and vindicated against the cleric Bottharius that share in the aforesaid place of Hordinium, together with the churches, and everything that the aforesaid Ibbo, his father, held or left at his death in the said place. And should the abbot Haino or his heirs have need of it, the cleric Bottharius or his heirs shall strive to defend him in possession against anyone.

Syghinus recognized it. (Place of the seal.)

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the first year of our reign, at Compendium, in God’s name, successfully.

## X. Charter of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he grants immunity to the monastery of Tusonis-Vallis

[Note: Published by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 477, and Felibianus, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, documents, p. 15, both from the original (now in the Royal Archives, K, chest 3). It was reprinted in the Collection of the Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 675.

We have already encountered the monastery of Tusonis-Vallis in an instrument of exchange, where it is called Tucionis-Vallis; Magnoaldus, its abbot, is also mentioned there. Here, however, the monastery is said to have been founded by Chardericus, abbot of Saint Dionysius, and entrusted by him to the abbot Magnoaldus to govern. Mabillon therefore conjectures, *Annales*, vol. I, pp. 613 and 542, that it was subject to the abbey of Saint Dionysius, but admits that it has vanished so completely that its location is now unknown, unless it existed where the Cistercian abbey of Vallis Beatae Mariae now stands.

We publish it according to the original, sealed with wax, with which A. Teulet again compared the text.] (a.d. 696).

Childeberthus, illustrious king of the Franks. We have judged it right that we should make effective the petitions of priests which concern the interests of churches, and that whatever has been added or contributed there by them from any acquisition should be strengthened by our royal pronouncements, so that afterward the giver’s reward may endure and we may receive, for the benefit already bestowed, a good reputation and an everlasting recompense.

Therefore the venerable man Magnoaldus, abbot of the monastery of Tusonis-Vallis, situated in the Camiliacian district, which his maternal uncle Chardericus, formerly abbot, built on his own property in honor of Saint Dionysius and Saint Marcellus, established there under the holy rule as a monastery, and appointed the same venerable man Magnoaldus to be its abbot and governor.

The abbot Magnoaldus asked our Highness that whatever had been or should be added or contributed to that little monastery, whether by the abbot himself or by God-fearing men, in any properties or possessions, should be protected; and he affirmed that he had in his possession a decree of our lord and father Theodericus, formerly king, concerning this matter. No public judge, he requested, should have the right to enter there to hear cases or exact fines.

We recognize that we have granted, bestowed, and confirmed this for the increase of our reward. Therefore, by this present decree, we determine and order what we wish to remain perpetual: that neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor anyone at any time invested with judicial authority, shall presume to enter the estates or villages of that monastery to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, or claim any kind of payment which our fisc could obtain or hope to obtain from them, whether from what is presently established there or from what may afterward be added by the abbot Magnoaldus or by other God-fearing men in any properties or possessions.

Judicial authority, neither in our time nor under successor kings, shall presume to enter there; rather, whatever our fisc might have hoped to obtain therefrom shall, after the decree of our lord and father Theodericus, formerly king, and our decree, more fully confirmed in God’s name, have been examined, advance in increase for the lamps of that little monastery and for the monks who are frequently seen there performing the divine office, so that our reward before the Lord may prosper in everlasting ages and the community may delight in praying continually for the stability of our kingdom.

And, so that this decree may be firmer, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand. (Place of the seal.)

Childeberthus, king, subscribed.  
Nordeberthus presented it.

Given on the eighth day of April, in the second year of our reign, in God’s name, at Noviginto, successfully.

## XI. Judicial record of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which the estate of Nocitum is adjudicated to the monastery of Thunsonis-Vallis

[Note: It exists, according to the original (now preserved in the Royal Archives, K, chest 3, whose text A. Teulet again compared), in Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 479, and Felibianus, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, documents, p. 17; it was reprinted from Mabillon in the Collection of the Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 676.

Mabillon notes especially the following points in this judicial record:

1. Bercharius is called the husband of Adaltrude and the father-in-law of Drogo, which conflicts with the Fontanelles chronicle, chapter 7, and the Metz Annals under the year 693, where Adaltrude, Drogo’s wife, is said to be the daughter of Warathenus and Ansfledis.

2. Chardericus, who elsewhere—see the charter of Childeric concerning Tusonis-Vallis above, col. 1092—is distinguished only by the title of abbot, is here called a bishop. Mabillon says that he does not know which see he held; others conjecture that he occupied the see of Beauvais. But we stated above, p. 225, that the abbots of major monasteries were sometimes raised to episcopal dignity without being attached to any particular see.

3. Mabillon and the Collectors of the Frankish historical writings, cited above, observe that the formula “acting in the place of … ordered the recognition” is very rarely found in the recognition clauses of Merovingian charters.] (a.d. 697).

[Col. 1093C]

Childebercthus, illustrious king of the Franks. While we, in God’s name, were seated at Compendium, in our palace, together with the apostolic men, our fathers in Christ, the bishops Ansoaldus, Savaricus, Turnochaldus, Ebarcius, Grimo, Constantinus, and Ursinianus; and also the illustrious man Pippinus, our master of the palace; Agnericus, Antenerus, Magnecharius, and Grimoaldus, nobles; Ermentheus, Adalricus, and Jonathan, counts; Vulfolaecus, Arghilus, and Madlulfus, household officials; Benedictus and Ermedramnus, seneschals; and Hociobercthus, our count of the palace, together with all our faithful men, to hear everyone’s cases and settle them by a just judgment, the venerable man Magnoaldus, abbot of the monastery of Thunsonis-Vallis, came before us. His maternal uncle, our lord Chardericus, formerly bishop, had built that monastery by his own work.

Magnoaldus submitted to the clemency of our kingdom that the agents of the illustrious man Drogo, son of the likewise illustrious man Pippinus, our master of the palace, had taken or removed by wrongful action from the authority of Magnoaldus and his monastery the estate of the basilica called Nocito, situated in the Camiliacian district. It had formerly belonged to Gaerinus and had been granted from the fisc to that monastery by a decree of our lord and father Theudericus, formerly king. The aforesaid agents had also carried off or devastated slaves, money, and many other things there.

Drogo argued in reply that his father-in-law, the illustrious man Bercharius, formerly, had exchanged that estate with Magnoaldus, and that it ought most lawfully to be returned to his wife Adaltrude’s side according to the laws. Magnoaldus, in turn, argued that he had held a conversation and agreement concerning the matter with Bercharius, so that they might exchange the estates between themselves; but that they had never done so, and that Bercharius had never held possession of that estate, except that the agents of the aforementioned Drogo had removed it from his authority by wrongful action, force, and malicious design.

Drogo was asked whether he maintained that his father-in-law had made the exchange with Magnoaldus, whether they had made an exchange-document between themselves, or whether he could present the documents in our presence. He did not present any instrument concerning the matter, nor could he provide any evident reason by which Bercharius ought to have possessed it, or by which it ought to belong to Drogo on his wife’s side or on his own.

Thus the aforesaid bishops and nobles, our lords, rendered judgment and reached a decision—as the illustrious man Hociobercthus, our count of the palace, testified—as follows: the man Magnoaldus must have the estate of Nocito, to the extent that it had been granted from our lord and father to his monastery of Thunsonis-Vallis by his decree; and the said Drogo must restore it to him with sound title. Magnoaldus was to forgive him the produce, namely wine, grain, or hay, which his agents had destroyed. This was done.

Therefore we order that the property of Nocito, to the extent that Gaerinus possessed it there, or whatever came to him from elsewhere, and whatever was granted from that monastery to our father by his decree, be perpetually secured and defended against Drogo and his wife Adaltrude, their heirs, or anyone whatsoever on their side; and that no dispute concerning this matter arise between them thereafter.

Aigobercthus, acting in the place of Childebercthus, ordered the recognition. (Place of the seal.)

Given on the fourteenth day of March, in the third year of our reign, at Compendium, in God’s name, successfully.

[Note: It is not easy to determine whether the fourteenth day of March should be assigned to the third year of Childebert III’s reign, or to the year 697, since Childebert seems to have begun his reign in that month, but the precise day is uncertain.]

## XII. Charter of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he grants the forest of Cornioletum to the convent of Saint Mary at Argentolium

[Note: According to Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. VI, p. 174, with appendix, p. 656, this charter was discovered by the distinguished and learned Claude Fleury, commendatory prior of the monastery of Argentolium, in the tower of his priory house, where it had been carelessly thrown among discarded papers. It was written in Merovingian letters and enclosed by a wax seal.

Felibianus first published it in 1725 from the original, among the instruments relating to Parisian history, vol. III, p. 25. It was reprinted in the appendix to vol. VI of the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 656, and in the Collection of the Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 677. A. Teulet corrected certain errors in Felibianus’s reading in a new and very careful recension based on the original, now preserved in the Royal Library at Paris.

This instrument had nevertheless not completely disappeared until Felibianus’s time, for, as the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. VI, p. 174, report, it had been shown to Breulius, the author of the *Antiquities of Paris*, by Jacobus Fouin, commendatory prior of this monastery, while the sixteenth century was still drawing to a close.

The monastery in question was first inhabited by nuns, as may be read in *Gallia christiana nova*, vol. VII, col. 507 and following; it was then reduced to a priory of the abbey of Saint Dionysius and, around the beginning of the sixteenth century, was placed under commendatory priors.] (a.d. 697).

Childeberthus, illustrious king of the Franks. If we willingly grant suitable benefits to holy places, insofar as this pertains to the assistance of God’s servants or maidservants, we trust that this will pertain to our eternal recompense.

Therefore let your Magnificence or Utility know that we have granted, with full and complete favor, for the increase of our reward and for the consolation of the maidservants of God residing there, our forest called Cornioletum, above the River Seine, in the Parisian district, including everything that had long belonged to the fisc there, or that it had held around it, and everything that our foresters had defended until now, to the monastery of Saint Mary, Saint Peter and Saint Paul, and the other saints, which is built in the estate of Argentolium, where the illustrious woman Leudesinda, consecrated to God, presides as abbess.

Therefore, by this present decree, we determine and order what we wish to remain perpetual: that neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor anyone else shall presume to oppose the aforesaid Leudesinda, her successors, or her monastery of Argentolium concerning our forest of Cornioletum, nor diminish anything from it, nor generate any accusation on this account, except insofar as provided above.

The forest itself in its entirety, just as it belonged to our fisc or was defended by our foresters, shall be able to be held and possessed as perpetually granted and bestowed, under the name of immunity, by our indulgence to the said Leudesinda, to the part of her monastery of Argentolium, or to the community residing there, so that it may perpetually advance the increase of that holy place.

And, so that this decree may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Childeberthus, king, subscribed.  
Vulfolaecus [Note: We have restored from the original the name of the referendary, which Felibianus omitted], having been ordered, presented it.

Given on the third day of April, in the third year of our reign, at Compendium, in God’s name, successfully.

### XIII. Charter of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the gift made by Ephibius to the Church of Vienne

[Note: Dacherius published this in *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 103, from a copy by Louvet, and the editors of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 678, from Dacherius. This is certainly the charter that Ephibius stated in his testament, published above on p. 240, that he had requested: namely, that the legacies he had written for the Church of Vienne should be confirmed by royal authority. This charter suffers from the same defect as the testament itself; see the indications of forgery in the notes appended to the testament.] (year 697).

Childebert, king, to Father Caeoldus and to Ephibius, abbot.

Since your request and petition are worthy, we have entered above our edict concerning the estates of Genecium and whatever else belongs there, so that, because these have been handed over entire, together with all their appurtenances, to the Church of Vienne and granted to you, Ephibius, by your vow, they may always remain there by our authority. Whatever could have issued from them for our fisc, we wholly permit to belong to our God, to the holy apostles of God, and to their ministers, so that, under the immunity of the Church of Vienne, whatever the judges could have demanded—every due and jurisdiction, whether from slaves or free persons, in estates, lands, woods, or payments—may remain there forever without alteration.

Nor shall any public judge, or his official, dare to establish jurisdiction there or to exercise distraint. Rather, whatever could have come to our glory, or to our judges and officials, shall forever contribute to the sustenance and nourishment of the servants of God; and the Church of Vienne shall enjoy the right and authority granted to it by us through this charter.

I, Childebert, have confirmed this edict, established in the third year of my reign.

---

### XIV. Charter of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he declares that the estate of Ardun, with complete immunity, was granted to the Church of Le Mans

[Note: Published in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 284, and reprinted in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 679. By this charter Childebert confirms the immunities granted for the estate of Ardun to the Church of Le Mans by two charters of Childeric II. We have presented both elsewhere, taken from the same acts, and counted them among the spurious documents. We likewise consider this third instrument, drawn from the same source, which we have repeatedly found impure, to be of no better quality. Its falsity is shown especially by the fact that Childebert is represented as having issued the charter in question for Herlemund, bishop of Le Mans, who was not called to govern the Church of Le Mans until long after Childebert’s death, as we shall say in our notes to another charter of the same Childebert, likewise spurious, which follows immediately. See those notes.] (year 698).

Childebert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

If we preserve the acts of our parents, we trust that our own will remain permanently secure. Therefore the apostolic man, our father in Christ, Herlemund, bishop of the city of Le Mans, informed us that our uncle, the former king Childeric, by his charter, granted the following to his predecessor, the former lord Bishop Berarius, concerning the estate belonging to the Church of Le Mans called Ardun, in the county of Poitiers: whatever was expected for the fisc from that estate, no judge or anyone else was to exact; and in that estate no one was to presume to establish lodgings, exact fines, hear cases, demand provisions, or seek or exact any earthly profit, except that all this was granted for the lights of the Church of Le Mans, which has been built in honor of Saint Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, our patrons.

Afterward the same privilege was similarly granted to Bishop Aiglibert, after the former Berarius. The bishop therefore affirms that he has these charters in his possession and that this benefit has been preserved from that time until now. But for complete security he petitioned our Highness that we should once more confirm this by our authority to that man, Lord Bishop Herlemund, and to the basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. Know that we did not refuse his petition, but granted and confirmed it in every respect.

We therefore command that, just as our uncle Childeric, the former king, established complete immunities from that estate of Ardun for that church, so we likewise now grant and confirm by our authority that no judge shall ever presume in that estate to hear cases, demand provisions, fines, or any census or earthly profit that might be expected for our fisc, or to exact any such thing, unless, upon inspection of the charter issued by our uncle Childeric, the former king, it is to remain perpetually granted and conceded for the lights of the aforementioned basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

I, Childebert, king, have subscribed.

[Col. 1098A] Issued on the third day of March, in the fourth year of our reign, at Valenciennes, successfully.

---

### XV. Charter of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he grants Herlemund, bishop of Le Mans, that henceforth the king shall appoint no duke or count of Le Mans except one whom the bishop and the people of Le Mans have first chosen

[Note: Published by Corvaisier in the *History of the Bishops of Le Mans*, p. 255, from the pontifical of the Church of Le Mans; inserted, with variants, among the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 283; reprinted by Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 615, from Corvaisier, and by the editors of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 678, from the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*. We publish it according to Corvaisier, placing the principal variants in parentheses. The name Herlemund is an indication of forgery: he did not obtain the episcopal office at Le Mans until Childebert III had long since died. For, according to Cointius, cited above, p. 586, Aiglibertus, Herlemund’s predecessor, died in 716. To defend the authenticity of the charter, however, Cointius, p. 615, conjectures that Childeric should be restored in place of Childebert, and that the charter should be assigned to the year 719. Yet both in the pontifical copied by Corvaisier and in the substantially different copy followed by the compiler of the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, the name Childebert is read. We shall therefore count this document among the spurious ones until an authentic document emerges in support of Cointius’s conjecture. We have nowhere even seen mention of the charter of Chlotar granted at Berarius’s request, which Childebert praises. We are surprised that Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 616, and several other critics considered this instrument genuine.] (year 698).

Childebert, king of the Franks [addition: illustrious man], since it is fitting for the clemency of a prince to hear and bring to effect the just petitions of priests [variant: “it is fitting for princely clemency willingly to heed the just petitions of priests and to commit them to fulfillment in God’s name”], therefore the apostolic man, our father in Christ, Herlemund, bishop of the city of Le Mans, made known to the clemency of our kingdom that many years ago his predecessor, Lord Berarius, formerly bishop, had addressed such a petition to our illustrious uncle Chlotar, the former king, and to our grandmother Queen Balthild [addition: the former queen], and had received from them such a charter:

that in the county of Le Mans no one at any time should enter upon the administration of a dukedom or county, except by the election of the aforementioned bishop or his successors, or of the abbots and priests and the people of Le Mans who, by the will of God, reside there; and that no one should enter to exercise that office there except by the command of those princes and their succeeding kings.

He affirms that this was granted to him by his charter, confirmed by his own hand and by that of our aforementioned great-grandmother, together with the consent of her nobles, and that he has the charter in his possession.

But for complete security he petitioned our Highness that our authority should once more confirm this fully to the aforesaid bishop and to his successors in perpetuity, and to the people themselves [variant: “that we should confirm it”]. We wish all to know that we have granted and confirmed this in every respect [variant: “know that we have confirmed it”].

We therefore command and order—and ordering, we command [these three words are absent]—that, just as it is established that our aforementioned uncle Chlotar and our grandmother Balthild, by their charters, granted this to Berarius, the former bishop and predecessor, so we grant this privilege to Bishop Herlemund [variant: “granted this to the aforementioned predecessor, Bishop Herlemund”]: in that county of Le Mans they shall not receive a duke or count except by the election of the county, the bishop, and the people.

Thus we grant and confirm this authority, as before [variant: “and henceforth likewise”], so that no one at any time shall exercise the administration of the dukedom otherwise than as stated; nor shall anyone in that county of Le Mans, without the election of the bishop of the city of Le Mans or of those people [addition: “or of the abbots”], enter upon or exercise the office of count, except one whom the bishop has chosen, so that he may hold that county for administration by our command.

And so that this authority may be held firmly [variant: “more firmly”], we have decreed that this charter be strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand.

Childebert, king, after inspecting the earlier charters.

Issued in the month of March, on the third day, in the fortieth year of our reign [Note: To preserve the credibility of the charter, Cointius corrects the chronological note from the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*: he reads year four instead of year forty. But who could believe that Childeric issued a charter at Valenciennes at that time, if he had considered this king’s deeds and fortunes?], at Valenciennes. Vulfoletus wrote and subscribed [variant: “after inspecting the earlier charters; subscribed. Issued on the third day of March, in the fourth year of our reign, at Valenciennes. Vulfoecus”].

---

### XVI. Record in which Childebert III declares that the monastery of Lemaus belongs to the monastery of Saint Vincent or Saint Germanus

[Note: Mabillon published this three times: first among the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. IV, p. 561, from the Sangermanian original, now in the Royal Archives, K, chest 3; second in book VI of *De re diplomatica*, p. 480, more accurately copied from the same original; and finally, after further work, in the *Supplement to Diplomatic Studies*, p. 95. It was reprinted by Cointius, *Annales*, vol. V, p. 279, from Mabillon’s first edition; by Bulliardus from the original, *History of Saint-Germain*, proofs by Prat, p. 8; by the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. VII, documents, col. 42; and by the editors of the *Collection of Frankish Writers*, from Mabillon’s later editions, vol. IV, p. 680. We present it after carefully collating it with the original itself, with the most courteous assistance of Lord Poirier, highly experienced in Merovingian scripts. (In a new recension, A. Teulet omitted what I had enclosed in brackets and restored the text.) Mabillon had a specimen engraved, *Supplement to Diplomatic Studies*, p. 69. According to Germon, *On the Ancient Charters of the Kings of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 212 and elsewhere, this charter should be counted among the spurious documents because it calls the monastery of Saint Vincent by the name of Saint Germanus. Mabillon overturns this argument, *Supplement to Diplomatic Studies*, p. 25.] (year 703).

Childebert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

When we had taken our seat in the name of God at the estate of Carraciacum, together with Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, and our faithful men, the venerable man Chedelmarus, abbot, came there and, against Aigatheus, envoy of Adalgude, a woman consecrated to God, made this representation. He said that a little monastery in the county of Étampes, called Lemaus, together with its appurtenances, wherever they might lie in counties and territories, estates, houses, buildings, tenants, [Col. 1100A] slaves, freedmen, fields, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, herds with their shepherds, movable and immovable property—in short, everything that had belonged in full possession to the late Gammo and his aforementioned wife Adalgude—had been granted by their documents [to the monastery of Saint Vincent or Lord Germanus, where that precious lord rests bodily, built below the city of Paris, where Chedelmarus appears to preside as abbot; and the documents] [Note: The documents cited here should certainly be understood as follows: first, the charter of Gammo, published above, p. 243, concerning gifts made to the little monastery of Lemaus; second, another charter, now either lost or concealed, by which that little monastery of Saint Vincent or Saint Germanus was granted to the monastery. Mabillon notes, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 5, that nothing in the county of Étampes now belongs to Saint-Germain. He interprets Carraciacum, where the charter is said to have been issued, as Carisiacum on the Isère. The twenty-fifth day of February in the eighth year of Childebert III’s reign falls in the year of Christ 703.] he produced in the present assembly for reading.

After those documents had been read, Aigatheus was carefully questioned by us and by our nobles whether he wished to say or bring forward anything against those documents. He was to state it then and there. But he asserted that the instruments of gift presented by the venerable Abbot Chedelmarus were genuine; he acknowledged them and did not wish to say or bring forward anything against them [the earlier edition reads: “to propose”].

Aigatheus also declared at that time, by his own documents, both for himself and for Adalgude, that in every respect he had withdrawn from the little monastery of Lemaus, together with its appurtenances and dependencies mentioned above.

Therefore, after consultation with our nobles, we decreed the following. Since the illustrious man Ghyslemarus, count of our palace, testified to it, and judgment was rendered among them, and since he had nothing to say or bring forward against those documents, he declared by his staff that he had then and there withdrawn from the matter [Note: I have stated in another annotation that among the Franks promises and similar undertakings were made with the use of a staff; this was called *adhramire*, *adhramitio*. A staff was also employed when someone released himself from some matter in relation to another person. See the Salic Law, Eccard, XLII; Feuerbach, XLVI; Schilter, LXXX; Herold, XLIX; and also the formulas of Lindenbrog, LXIX, CLIII, CLV, CLVI, and Cange under *Exitus*, 2. From the rubric of title XLVIII of the revised Salic Law, and from the capitulary of the year 819, chapter X, it appears that this solemnity was called *affatomia*. See the new edition of Cange’s Glossary prepared by Henschenius and printed by the Didot brothers, who have long deserved so much from all lovers of the humanities through their many and careful editions.]

We therefore order that the aforementioned little monastery of Lemaus, with all its integrity and everything belonging or pertaining to it, which the late Gammo and his wife Adalgude granted by their documents to the monastery of Saint Vincent or Lord Germanus, together with whatever the dying Gammo left without recovery by the aforementioned Adalgude or by her heirs, shall at all times be vindicated and adjudicated to the part of that monastery of Saint Vincent or Lord Germanus, or to its rector; and that no dispute shall afterward arise between them concerning this matter.

Beffa [the earlier edition reads: Bessa] examined and subscribed.

Issued on the twenty-fifth day of February, in the eighth year of our reign, at Carraciacum, successfully.

---

### XVII. Charter of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he makes many gifts to the monastery of Fontenelle

[Note: We publish this from Mabillon’s memorandum, a copy of which was supplied to us by the authors of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*. They did not, however, admit this instrument among the charters of Childebert III, and there is no mention of it in the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*; hence its authenticity is highly suspect to us. Indeed, all credibility is removed from it by comparison with the notice of the charter inserted in the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, in Dacher, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 197. The instrument in question appears to have been fabricated from a copy of that notice and enlarged with extensive additions. The genuine charter mentions only these gifts: Adpiecum, Novitiacum, Curbaniam, Albacohan, Nidum, and Terrae Lidum with five dependent estates; the charter we publish has appended many others. Moreover, the forger copied the chronological notes from the Fontenelle chronicle so carelessly that he added even the indiction and the year of the Lord’s Incarnation as though they belonged to the charter itself, although the author of the chronicle says that he used them as an interpretation in order to connect the tenth year of Childebert III’s reign with the year of the Lord’s Incarnation. This year does indeed correspond correctly to the year 704, but the indiction then current was VIII or IX, not II; nor did the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November fall on a Monday that year, but on a Thursday. Mabillon mentions the grant of the estate of Adpiecus to the monastery of Fontenelle, but from the Fontenelle chronicle, not from the charter, which he certainly knew but had rightly rejected. Another indication of forgery in this instrument is that it says the body of Saint Wlfrannus had been transferred to the church of Saint Peter, although Wlfrannus was still alive in the tenth year of Childebert III’s reign, as Mabillon admits and as the authors of the *New Christian Gaul* demonstrate. Therefore, since so many errors prove the charter false, we do not hesitate to count it among the spurious documents.] (year 704).

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

I, Hildebertus, by the grace of God king of the Franks, give to God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul, and also to the most devout confessors Vandregisilus, Ansbertus, Wlfrannus, and Iterembertus, in honor and reverence of the translation of the aforesaid saints, recently made to that monastery by the lord and venerable bishop Bainus, abbot of the monastery of Fontenelle, and to the brothers who serve God day and night in that monastery of Fontenelle, as a pure and perpetual alms:

namely, in the bishopric of Beauvais, Revecuria and the church with its tithe and appurtenances; the chapel of Faiel; in Chivericeriis, six tenants and a share of the tithes; Rouvillare, with meadows and woods.

In the bishopric of Amiens, half of Buxeium, land for one plow, and half of the tithe; and a third part of the tithe of Dors; at Valiacum, a certain parcel of land.

Likewise, in the same diocese, in the county of Vimeu, Dareneyum and the church with the entire tithe; Waucort and the church with its tithe and tenants.

In the bishopric of Paris, Alpicum and the church with the entire tithe; Ursiniolum at De . . . . . vallem and a half; Viciniacas and the tithe of Villioliscortis; and at Marolium, the census and tithe of the vineyards; Marcouchies and the church with its tithe and tenants.

Moreover, free passage for the vessels of the aforesaid monastery, or for ships carrying wine or anything else for the use of the monks, along the Vienne, free from every customary due and exaction, both going and returning, insofar as our jurisdiction extends.

In the bishopric of Chartres, Raedonium and the church with the entire tithe, and the census; the vineyard-compascuum of Mount Nivelon; and three *gordos* there, with two mill-sites; and the estate of Saint Martin with some portion of the tithes.

The church of Rolleboise with its tithes; Callifurnum and the church with its tithes, and twelve and a half estates; Francavilla and the church of Viletta with the entire tithe, both from mills and from fields; and the entire fief of Hulo; land for two oxen; the land of Orthmari estate; the chapel beside the pillar called Fontana Bertholdi, with land and tenants; the land of Duco campo; half the land of Boscocortis; and the entire tithe of that estate.

And so that this gift or grant of ours may, with the Lord’s protection, remain unshaken in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and caused it to be strengthened by the impression of our ring.

Issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the tenth year of our reign, indiction II, on a Monday, in the year 704 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

---

### XVIII. Charter of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the privileges granted by his predecessors to the monastery of Saint Sergius at Angers

[Note: Sirmond mentions this charter in his note to Godefroy of Vendôme, *Works*, vol. III, col. 792, note b. Hiretus published a fragment of it in *Antiquities of Anjou*, p. 101, and Moricius among the proofs of the *History of Brittany*, from the cartulary of Saint Sergius, vol. I, proofs, col. 223. From this source the Sammarthani published the complete text, *New Christian Gaul*, vol. IV, p. 820, as did the editors of the *Collection of Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 681; Cointius reprinted it from the Sammarthani, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 441. We reprint it from a copy accurately transcribed from the same cartulary and once most courteously communicated to us by Dom Housseau of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, to whom the task of writing the history of Bourges and Angers had been entrusted, and who died long ago, in the flower of his youth, to the great loss of scholarship. The chronological notes are absent from the instrument. It was certainly issued by Childebert III, since his father is called Theodoric in the charter itself and his grandfather Chlodoveus; but the year is uncertain, nor can it be inferred from the period of Abbot Theodebert, about whom we know nothing from elsewhere. Cointius and Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 16, list this charter under the year 705 or 706. Various readings from the printed editions have been inserted in brackets.] (year 705).

[Col. 1102C] Childebert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all officials, present and future.

Whatever our predecessor princes and parents have granted to holy places for the love of heaven or for eternal reward, if we confirm it by our royal declarations, we trust that we shall thereby have the Lord as our rewarder.

Let your greatness and welfare therefore know that the venerable man Theodebertus, abbot of the monastery built in the suburb of the city of Angers in honor of our special patron Saint Sergius and Lord Medardus, bishop, came into our presence and informed the clemency of our kingdom that, from the estates of the aforesaid holy basilica called Marentius, Silviliacus, Taunucus, Noviliacus, Senona, and Genehonnus [printed editions: Genehtonnus], payments were annually rendered to the fisc: solidi, or [printed editions: six] payable solidi, and another [printed editions: six], from the gold payment of the *pugensis* [printed editions: *pagensis*], paid into the fisc.

Our grandfather Chlodoveus, of good memory, and our father Theodoricus, the former kings, granted this privilege to that monastery by their authority and by subscriptions of their hands, for the increase of their reward: no public judge was to enter those estates to exercise jurisdiction, demand fines, establish lodgings, hear cases, take sureties, or demand provisions or compulsory services; nor was he to seek any payment there by judicial authority, except that the same abbot himself or his envoys was to render that payment annually in the public treasury.

The abbot also affirms that he has in his possession other charters and confirmations, strengthened by the hands of our glorious predecessors, by which this benefit was granted by those princes and preserved until now.

Therefore, in the interest of security, he petitioned our Highness that our authority should once more confirm this generally for that monastery and its community. We could not refuse this petition, out of reverence for that holy place, as we could not refuse the petition of anyone who asks; rather, know that we have granted it gladly and confirmed it in every respect.

We command that, just as it is established, with reference to the earlier charter or confirmation, that this benefit has until now, over so long a period and without any opposition, been lawfully preserved there by those princes, so it shall henceforth be maintained. Neither you, nor your juniors or successors, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall dare to enter there to exercise jurisdiction, demand fines, establish lodgings, hear cases, take sureties, or exact any other payments whatsoever.

Whatever any part of our fisc might have been able to receive or exact from there, let none of you presume to demand at all, except that each year twelve solidi are to be paid by the abbot himself or by his envoy into our treasury, as stated, in our times and in those of our successors, with the Lord’s help.

Therefore, by the grace of God and our own, after inspecting the aforementioned charters, just as this benefit has always until now been preserved, we command that henceforth, for the sake of our reward, it be preserved in every respect.

And so that this authority may have fuller force, and so that we may more frequently implore the Lord’s mercy, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Childebert, king.

---

### XIX. Charter of Dagobert III, king of the Franks, by which he makes many gifts to the monastery of Petrimont [or Saint Peter at Erfurt]

[Note: “Trithemius had seen this charter in the monastery of Saint Peter at Erfurt. He copied and published the instrument in his historical works, p. 59, in order to expose its falsity, since the Erfurt monks claimed it as a genuine original. It was not furnished with a seal, but a hole was displayed as evidence of a missing seal, which they conjectured had been lost through the injuries of time. Trithemius, and after him Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 446, point out signs of forgery, which need only be touched upon briefly here. The charter is said to have been issued in the year of the Incarnation 706, indiction IX, but these chronological notes do not agree with one another. The monastery in question was founded long after 706, as Trithemius and Cointius, cited above, and the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. V, col. 627, demonstrate. This charter cannot be attributed to Dagobert, since no king of that name ruled in Francia in the year given. The forger seems to have had Dagobert III in mind when he calls Chlodoveus his grandfather, doubtless because Childebert III, Dagobert III’s father, had succeeded Chlodoveus III. But Chlodoveus III was Childebert’s brother, not his father: a delusion worthy of a foolish forger. We shall say nothing of the unusual formulas, nor shall we raise the question of Rigobert, bishop of Mainz, in an instrument deserving no credence.”—Thus the distinguished de Brequigny. It is useful to add a few points. Falckenstein published this charter in the *Chronicle of Thuringia*, book II, part II, p. 1101, considering it unpublished and indeed genuine. Erhard also printed it from the Erfurt archives in his German-language *Diplomatic Commentaries*, Hamburg, 1834, vol. I, p. 53, and extensively set out the arguments for its falsity, passing over in silence what Trithemius, Cointius, and de Brequigny had written. Placidius Matthaeus also published part of this charter in the *Proceedings of the Erfurt Academy*, 1799, vol. I, p. 198. Erhard testifies that the charter was written in letters closely resembling those used in imperial charters of the eleventh and twelfth centuries. It is further clear from the letters of Saint Boniface, which may be seen below under the year 720, that the Gospel was preached to the pagan Thuringians only at that time. Erhard asserts that the monastery of Saint Peter was founded in 1060 and that no mention of Dagobert’s charter can be found anywhere before 1290. He conjectures that, while numerous monasteries during the period of the interregnum claimed to belong immediately to the Empire, the monks of Saint Peter likewise contended, for the same purpose, that they had been endowed with royal estates by an ancient king. In the edition of de Brequigny the charter had been borrowed from Trithemius; I thought it more correct to publish it from Erhard, who used the Erfurt original, or a copy regarded as the original. I have nevertheless placed variant readings in brackets.] (year 706).

By the grace [variant: in the name] of the holy and undivided Trinity.

I, Tagebertus [Dagobertus], king of the Franks, make known to clergy and people, to Christians and pagans alike, that our city called Merwigesburc [Merouegesburg], which had come to us by hereditary right from our grandfather Merwigo [Meroveus] himself, the founder of that city in Thuringia, we have given by royal authority to Saint Peter and to his monks serving God there. The mountain itself, after the foundation of the monastery that I built in honor of the aforesaid apostle, took its name from him; its former pagan name having been erased, it was called Peter’s Mountain, and was to be possessed, with all its services, after the end of my life [variant: after my death].

We shall explain by what divine ordinance this was done.

In the aforesaid city, beside the church of the martyr Saint Blaise, there was a man of God named Adeodatus, enclosed at my request by Rigibertus, bishop of Mainz. While enclosed, fearing for his soul [the words “for his soul” are absent in the source], and unwilling to make use of communion with clerics who used wives and weapons [variant: “with clerics using wives and weapons”], he often asked me to summon for him from one of my monastic cloisters a monk from whom he could hear the divine office and the word of the true faith and receive communion in the sacred mystery [variant: “could receive it”].

Because of our intimate [variant: mutual] familiarity, I consented to his petition. I sent to the monastery of monks that I had likewise built at Wizenburc [Selsenburg], summoned from there the venerable [variant: “and venerable”] elder monk named Trutchindus [Truchintus], and sent him as teacher and director to the aforementioned enclosed Adeodatus.

When he arrived there, the number of believers gradually began to increase through the teaching and persuasion of the enclosed man, both through the conversion of pagans to baptism and through the conversion of clerics and laymen to the monastic habit.

Seeing this, and understanding the divine favor in it, I gave the city I have mentioned, with everything belonging to it, to Saint Peter and to his monks, so that monastic religion might be established there and an abbey founded with my assistance.

Furthermore, for various uses of Saint Peter and his monks, I gave the forest called Hirzbruil [Hirsbrulis] because of the abundance of its deer, extending from the southern side of the city eastward as far as the boundaries of the region of Orlaa [Orlavu], which region I gave as a benefice to Pippin, count of the palace [variant: to Count Pippin].

I likewise gave to the aforesaid monastery villages made by Slavs in that same forest, namely Tunecdorf [Tuneckdorff], Tagebrechtestete [Tugebrachtest], Tutelstete [Tuttelstet], Neuchenrod [Neukenrodt], Hochdorf [Hochdorff], and many others; and the river Gera for the monks’ catching of fish, from the southern side of the city as far as the boundary of the estate of my official Gisbodi [Gisboti].

I also gave from my estate, for the use of the brothers, one hundred measures of wheat [the numeral C is explained as “fifty” in the variant], one hundred of barley, and the same number of oats, together with all my other property in Thuringia.

For the protection [variant: maintenance] of this place dear to me, I gave my officials, with all their offspring [variant: descendants] and property. Their names are:

Gisbodus [Gisbotus], Elbertus [Gilbertus], Ekkehardus [Eckardus], Volfholdus [Vuolffoldus], Gisen [Hysen], Egenen [Egenhen], Woligisus [Vuolffgirus], Omarus [Omarus], Sigebertus [Sigebertus], Theodbertus [Theodobertus], Theodoricus [Theodoricus], Adelbotus [Adelbotus], Adelgozus [Adelgerus], Gelfratus [Gelferatus], Hyrfridus [Hingfridus], Gunzelinus [Huntzelinus], Guntram[n]us [Guntherinus], and all my other servants [variant: my servants], male and female, in Thuringia.

So that this transfer may remain eternally firm for my Lord Jesus Christ [variant: Jesus], we have caused it to be established by our charter, requested its confirmation by the ban of Rigibertus [Rigbertus], bishop of Mainz [bishop of Mainz], bound it with our ring, and completed it by attaching our seal.

Issued at Mainz, on the Kalends of March, in the presence of Bishop Rigibertus [Rigebertus].

Sign of the unconquered king Tagebertus of the Franks [Dagobertus of the Franks].

The witnesses to all these matters are the following: Pippin, mayor of the palace, and his son Charles; Rigibertus, bishop of Mainz [Moguntinus]; Guntamnus [Gunthernus], pagan count; Ecchabertus [Eckebi], count; and the entire Church in Thuringia and around the Rhine at Mainz [Moguntia].

These things were enacted in the year 706 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction IX.

## XX. Diploma of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he gives the estate of Solemnius to the basilica of Saint Dionysius

[Note: [Col. 1105D] Dublet first published this from the Dionysian archive, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, p. 688; afterward Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, p. 481, from a more accurate copy preserved in the same archive [which indeed was not transferred with the other Saint-Dionysian charters to the Royal Archive and has probably perished]. Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 447, and Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. I, p. 244, reprinted it from Dublet; it was reprinted from Mabillon in *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 682. A copy of this diploma, taken from a thirteenth-century parchment roll preserved in the archive of the Lille Chamber of Accounts, was kindly communicated to us by D. Godefroy, the diligent and discerning investigator of ancient instruments and archivist of that chamber. We follow Mabillon’s reading: he saw, not indeed the autograph, [Col. 1106D] but a very old copy, written, as he says, in *On Diplomatics*, pp. 627 and 278, in French letters, and in an interlaced form so difficult to read that Dublet, being entirely inexperienced in reading such scripts—as Mabillon himself explains—resorted to another copy written by an unskilled hand in the thirteenth century and disfigured by the most disgraceful errors. The Lille copy differs little from this one; we place its principal variant readings in parentheses. We have not thought it worthwhile to transcribe Dublet’s divergences.—A transcript of the same diploma, written in the thirteenth century with a French version, exists in the Royal Archive, Register XXII of the Treasury of Charters; Bonamy discussed it in the *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres*, vol. XXXVII, p. 444.] (year 706).

[Col. 1106C]

Childebert [Chilcedebert], king of the Franks, illustrious man. If we bestow or grant anything upon holy places or monasteries which pertains to the needs of holy places [of monasteries], we are confident that it will avail us for praise and eternal recompense in God’s name. Therefore let your greatness or utility know that our estate called Solemnius, situated in the district of Falmartina [Fanmartina], on the river Sale [Scalt], together with all its appurtenances and adjacent lands, and whatever our fiscus held there from Graraniga [from Graraniga] and from Remerteria [the text is corrupt], or possessed there by any acquisition [Col. 1107A], likewise the oratory at the Cross adjoining the boundary of that estate of Solemnius, which was built in honor of Saint Martin, together with all the property belonging to it, where Madalgisel, our servant, is seen to preside as custodian—that is, lands, houses, buildings, dependents, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, livestock, enclosures, herds with their shepherds, mills, movable and immovable property—in its entirety and without diminution [after a complete investigation, in its entirety], whatever is seen to belong to that estate, and whatever our fiscus has hitherto held there, we have seen fit to grant to the basilica of the lord martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily, and where the venerable man Chillard [Note: [Col. 1107C] In place of the name Chillard, Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, pp. 627 and 481 n., orders the name Chainan, or Delphinus, to be restored. For Chillardus was in charge of the monastery of Saint Dionysius after Delphinus, and Delphinus after Chainan. Delphinus was still in charge of this monastery in the sixteenth year of Childebert III’s reign, that is, four years after the diploma under discussion was issued, as is clear from the instruments that we shall present below. Mabillon considers that such an error could easily have crept into a very old transcript, cited above, p. 627, since the judgment of Pippin in the dispute over Solemnius and the charter of Charlemagne confirm Childebert’s diploma under consideration. These instruments may be seen below in their proper order. Germonius is less indulgent, *On the Ancient Charters of the Frankish Kings*, vol. II, p. 127, [Col. 1107D] for whom the name Chillard in this diploma appears to be a conspicuous defect.] [Col. 1107B] [Tayledus] is seen to preside as abbot—with all the property belonging or pertaining to that estate, with a full and complete grant, by proprietary right, under the name of immunity, together with all revenues granted to it, for the use of that lord Dionysius and of his community residing there.

Therefore, by this present charter we decree, ordering that we wish it to remain forever, that neither you nor your juniors or successors [our successors], nor anyone exercising judicial authority, presume to cause any resistance or impediment concerning the aforesaid estate of Solemnius, as our fiscus has hitherto held it, for the benefit of the aforesaid basilica of the lord Dionysius or its agents. Rather, as we have said, by the gift of our liberality, Solemnius, with all its integrity and substance [with all its lands made complete or consolidated], together with its appurtenances belonging or pertaining to it, and likewise the aforesaid oratory of Saint Martin at the Cross and whatever belongs to it, shall belong to the party of the basilica of the lord Dionysius and to its entire community forever, under the name of immunity, without any resistance or impediment by anyone [with proprietary right and without anyone’s resistance or impediment]. And, with God’s help, the basilica of the lord martyr Dionysius [our basilica] may increase in prosperity through present and future times. And, so that this charter may be more firmly established, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Childebert, king: I have subscribed.

Blatcharius, by command, subscribed.

Given at Mamaccas, in the month of March, on the twelfth day [at Corsartinca, on the twelfth day of March], in the twelfth year of our reign, happily in God’s name [Note: [Col. 1107D] These chronological indications are barbarously corrupted in Dublet’s copy and in the Lille transcript: in the former, *datum Corfintisce*; in the Lille copy, *datum Corfartinse, Martii die xij* [in Register XXII of the Treasury of Charters, Latin: *datum Corfartinche*; French: *données à Corfartinche*]. Thus the very common formula of this period, *quod ficit mensis*—“which was made in the month”—was not understood by the unskilled copyist and became the unheard-of name of a palace, *Corfintisce* or *Corfartince*, which Mabillon rightly rejects, cited above, p. 628; see also *Diplomatics*, book IV, p. 277. We find Mamaccas among the royal estates in the *Book of Royal Estates*, inserted in Mabillon’s *Diplomatics*, p. 295. It is not clear on which day of March the reign of Childebert III began; consequently it is uncertain whether the twelfth day of this month in the twelfth regnal year should be assigned to the year 705 or 706 of Christ.], the rest being absent after the word *Mamaccas*.

## XXI. Judgment of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which he adjudicates to Saint Dionysius the entire market toll of the fair transferred from the village of Saint Dionysius to Paris, between the basilicas of Saint Lawrence and Saint Martin

[Note: [Col. 1107D] Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, p. 482, and Felibianus, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, Documents, p. 18, published this from the autograph, now preserved in the Royal Archive [Col. 1108C], K, chest 3; it was reprinted from Mabillon in *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 684. We have reprinted it more accurately from the autograph. (Nevertheless, the latest editor, A. Teulet, made a new recension of almost every word, or rather of individual letters, and corrected many things.) From this document it is clear that the fair celebrated on the feast of Saint Dionysius, held in the village of Saint Dionysius, was transferred because of an intervening disaster to Paris, near the basilica of Saint Lawrence. According to Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 30, this circumstance later caused the fairs of Saint Lawrence to be retained, although the Saint-Dionysian fair was restored to its former place. Germonius, *Ancient Frankish Royal Charters*, vol. I, pp. 239 ff., accused this judgment of being false because Childebert there calls his brother, whom he had succeeded—namely Chlodoveus III—by the name Chlodocharius. Mabillon thinks this should be attributed either to the carelessness of the copyist, who wrote Chlodocharius for Chlodoveus, or he conjectures that Chlodoveus III had two names, after the example of his grandfather Chlodoveus II, who was also called Chlotarius, as is read in the chronicle of Dijon in Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 390, under the year 660; indeed, elsewhere we have noted that Childebert III’s own son was also called by both the names Dagobert and Chlodoveus. Germonius replies that no instrument can be convicted of falsity on historical grounds if one is allowed to attribute several names to the same king whenever it seems convenient. This certainly raises some suspicion regarding the authenticity of this judgment. But we testify that the autograph, which we inspected with our own eyes, displays every appearance of a genuine instrument.] (year 710).

Childebert, king of the Franks, illustrious man. When, in the presence of us and our nobles, the agents who had come to our palace at Mamaccas on behalf of the venerable man Dalfino, abbot of the basilica of our special patron Saint Dionysius, where the precious lord rests bodily, brought a claim against the agents of the illustrious man Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, they asserted that long ago Chlodoveus, once our grandfather, and afterward our uncle Childeric, and our lord and father Theuderic, and also our brother Chlodocharius, by their charters, had granted in full to that basilica, on the very holy feast of the lord Dionysius, whatever toll might be owed by all merchants, whether Saxons or people of any nation, who came to that holy feast and market to conduct their business at the basilica of Saint Dionysius. They had also granted that afterward, and even at that time, neither the fiscus nor anyone else should exact or collect any toll from those merchants at that market, nor within the district of Paris or in the city of Paris itself; rather, the whole toll should forever be granted and conceded to the party of the aforesaid basilica of the lord Dionysius.

Accordingly, they produced the charters of the aforesaid princes to be read publicly [Col. 1109B].
