After those charters had been read and examined, it was found that this had indeed been granted in full by those princes to the house of God. Then they said that the agents of that man Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, and also the count of the district of Paris, were taking half of that toll or withdrawing it from the share of the basilica. The agents of the illustrious man Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, replied that for a long time it had been customary for the house of Saint Dionysius to receive half of it and the count the other half for the benefit of our fiscus.

The agents of Saint Dionysius responded that Gairinus, formerly count of Paris, had forcibly introduced this custom there and had at some time taken half of that toll for himself; but they had reported this to the palace and had always renewed the charters of the princes in full. Again it was investigated through several persons and through the charters themselves whether the aforesaid princes had originally and thereafter granted or confirmed this in full [Note: [Col. 1109D] Earlier editors read: “whether the aforesaid princes had formerly granted it at the beginning.” The reading is nevertheless wrong, as the autograph testifies.].

Thus, with the consent of the man Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, and with several other of our faithful men, it was seen fit to decree and judge that the agents of the man Grimoald, for the benefit of our fiscus, should, by a formal pledge concerning that toll, restore them to the whole thereof; and so they did. Since this matter had thus been conducted, settled, investigated, and judged, as the illustrious man Sigofridus, count of our palace, testified, we henceforth order that at all times the party of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Dionysius, where the precious lord rests bodily, and Dalfino, the abbot, or his successors, shall have and retain as adjudicated and definitively assigned the entire toll from the feast of Saint Dionysius—both whatever is seen to be collected there on the lands of that basilica and, thereafter, at the market in Paris—according to their earlier charters [Col. 1110A].

And since at an earlier time, because of an intervening disaster, that market was transferred from the village of Saint Dionysius, and the market was held in the city of Paris between the basilicas of Saint Martin and Saint Lawrence, and they received from the charters of the aforesaid princes that wherever, at that feast, they held their market for conducting their business or commerce, the party of the aforesaid basilica of the lord Dionysius should receive the toll in full; if it should happen, whether because of a disaster or because of any other alteration [Note: [Col. 1109D] Earlier editors read *debecione*, a word that does not occur in the autograph and makes no sense.], that the market were transferred elsewhere, the aforesaid toll shall remain granted and conceded in full to the house of God, for the present and future times, in the lamps of Saint Dionysius, out of reverence for that holy place; and every dispute and contention between the party of our fiscus and the agents of Saint Dionysius shall thereby be ended.

Actalius, by command, examined and certified. (Place of the seal.)

Given at Mamaccas, in the month of December, on the thirteenth day, in the sixteenth year of our reign, happily.

## XXII. Judgment of Childebert III, king of the Franks, by which the mill of Cadolaicus is adjudicated to the monastery of Saint Dionysius

[Note: [Col. 1109D] It appears in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, p. 483, and Felibianus, *History of the Abbey of Saint Dionysius*, p. 19, copied from the autograph now preserved in the Royal Archive, K, chest 3; and in *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 685, from Mabillon. We have reprinted it after a more careful comparison with the autograph [Col. 1110D] (A. Teulet also undertook a new recension, not without reason). This judgment contains many noteworthy matters, which we have discussed more conveniently in our prolegomena. Although the document is horribly disfigured by faults of language, no one, so far as we know, has accused it of being false. For the place called Cadolaicus, see the little work of Dom Germain on royal estates, inserted in Mabillon’s *On Diplomatics*, pp. 296 and 336.] (year 710).

Childebert, king of the Franks, illustrious man. The agents of the basilica of our special patron, our lord Dionysius, where that precious one rests bodily, and the venerable man Dalf[inus], who is seen to preside as abbot and custodian, came to us at our palace at Mamaccas and reported that there was a mill in the place called Cadolaicus, within the boundary of Vernina, which for a long time their predecessor had always possessed at the estate of that basilica at Latiniacum. The agents of the illustrious man Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, contradicted them and said that it belonged to his estate at Verno.

Then the agents of Saint Dionysius said that for many years the mill had never belonged to Verno, but only to the estate of that basilica at Latiniacum; and that when Ebroinus was mayor of the palace and possessed that estate, he had assigned it there, and it was most justly owed to them and to the house of Saint Dionysius. But afterward the man Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, together with our faithful men, ordered the matter to be brought before him so that he might investigate it more carefully; and so he did.

Accordingly, it was judged by the man Grimoald that six men from Verno and six from Latiniacum, in good faith, should swear in his oratory or in the chapel of Saint Martin that for a long time the mill had always belonged to Latiniacum, the estate of the monastery of Saint Dionysius, and that it was most justly owed there. They fulfilled the oath imposed upon them, as the illustrious man Sigofridus testified on behalf of the man Grimoald. The agents received from him a judgment confirmed by the hand of Sigofridus and sealed with the ring [Note: [Col. 1111D] These two words were omitted by earlier editors because they escaped the eye.] of Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, that the mill should henceforth belong to and be possessed or held by Dalf[inus], abbot, and his monastery of Saint Dionysius, as adjudicated.

Therefore, together with our nobles, we have decreed this matter in such a way, as the illustrious man Bero, count of our palace, who was seen to act in place of the illustrious man Grimbercthus, count of our palace, testified: namely, that the aforesaid Sigofridus gave his testimony that this matter had been conducted and judged before the man Grimoald, our mayor of the palace. We therefore order that the aforesaid agents shall have the aforesaid mill, for the benefit of Dalfino, abbot, and the monastery of Saint Dionysius, without any reclamation by the aforesaid Grimoald, or by his agents, heirs, or successors, or by anyone else, in accordance with the judgment of the man Grimoald, our mayor of the palace, as it is declared by the same judgment; and let it remain forever adjudicated and definitively assigned to them. Henceforth let there be no litigation between them concerning this matter.

Dagobert, in place of Angilbald, examined and certified. (Place of the seal.)

Given at Mamaccas, in the month of December, on the fourteenth day, in the sixteenth year of our reign, happily.

## XXIII. Diploma of Dagobert III, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunities of the monastery of Anisola

[Note: [Col. 1111D] Martene extracted this from the Anisola manuscript codex, *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, vol. I, p. 6; the collectors of Frankish historical writers reprinted it in vol. IV, p. 686, from Martene. It is not found among the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, where we have seen so many spurious documents passed off as genuine. The year is lacking. That this diploma belongs to Dagobert III is clear because its author calls Childebert his father, Theuderic his grandfather, Chlodoveus his uncle, and so forth. If we assign this diploma to the beginning of Dagobert III’s reign, as Martene preferred, we shall date it to 712 [Col. 1112D], for Dagobert III began his reign in April of 711; consequently, January 18 in the first year of his reign belongs to the year 712 of Christ.] (year 712).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all present and future agents. If we willingly hear the petitions of God’s servants when they disclose to our ears what is useful for our churches or monasteries, we exercise the royal custom and trust that we thereby establish for ourselves a reward and the stability of our kingdom. Therefore the venerable Ibbolenus, abbot of the monastery of Anisola, situated in the district of Le Mans and built in honor of our special pious patron, namely the blessed confessor Carileffus, brought to the knowledge of our royal clemency through his messengers that our cousin, King Guntramnus, had granted that monastery complete immunity by his authority; and that afterward our grandfather Chlotarius, and likewise Dagobert, and also Chlodoveus, as well as Chlotarius, and moreover our lord and grandfather Theuderic, and also our uncle Chlodoveus, and our exalted lord and father Childebert, formerly kings, had confirmed this for that monastery by their authorities, strengthened by their own hands. They assert that they still have those charters in their possession and that this privilege has been preserved around that monastery without anyone disturbing it.

But for the complete security of the matter, he asks that our authority confirm it more fully for that monastery; and you should not doubt that we have granted this. Therefore by this present charter we order that, just as it is read in the authorities or writings of the princes and has been preserved until now, neither you, nor your predecessors, nor your successors, in the affairs of that monastery—whether to hear cases, exact fines, or demand lodging—presume to enter there at all. Rather, after examining the charters of the aforesaid princes, which they affirm that they have in their possession, the abbot and his successors, together with their community residing in that monastery by God’s help, shall be able to hold and possess under complete immunity whatever they are reasonably seen at present to have there, or whatever may thereafter be added or increased there by God-fearing men [Col. 1112C]. And, through this authority of ours, may what has been established for the holy place continue perpetually to increase, so that they may be more pleased to implore the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom.

And, so that this charter of ours may possess firm force, we have decreed that it be strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand and confirmed by our seal.

In Christ’s name, Dagobert, king. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

## XXIV. Diploma of Dagobert III, king of the Franks, by which, at the petition of Herlemundus, bishop of Le Mans, he confirms the immunities granted by the Frankish kings to the Church of Le Mans for the estates and monasteries subject to that Church, especially for the monastery of Anisola

[Note: [Col. 1112D] Labbe extracted a very incomplete fragment of this from the Anisola cartulary, *Miscellany*, vol. II, p. 412. The complete diploma was inserted among the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* in Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 282, and reprinted in *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 688. It appears to have been composed chiefly to assert the rights of the Church of Le Mans over the monastery of Anisola, and for that reason it was produced in the dispute, mentioned several times above, that arose over those rights, as is clear from the catalogue of instruments then brought forward [Col. 1113D]; see Baluze, *Miscellany*, vol. III, p. 128. But these instruments, as we have often noted elsewhere, were condemned as false by royal and apostolic authority, and afterward no one dared undertake the defense of the instrument under discussion. It must therefore be counted among the spurious documents, as though the matter had been judicially decided. The letters of Childebert III cited in this diploma appear nowhere, nor is it credible that they were of better quality, if they ever existed. [Nevertheless, although highly suspect, this diploma was confirmed by a charter of Charlemagne in 796, which may be seen in Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 258, and by another of Louis the Pious from the year 840, in Baluze, *Miscellany*, vol. III, p. 38. Furthermore, this diploma, together with the charters of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, was again confirmed by Louis XI in 1482, as is testified by the privilege inserted in vol. XIX of the *Ordinances of the Third Dynasty*, p. 53 [Col. 1114D].] For the dates of Herlemundus, which, according to Cointius, do not agree with the chronological indications attached to this diploma, see our notes on Herlemundus’s charter.] (year 713).

[Col. 1112D]

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man. Royal majesty strengthens the foundations of its exalted position when it listens to the petitions of priests or bishops concerning what is useful, and commits the matter to effect in God’s name [Col. 1113A]. Therefore the apostolic man, our father in Christ, Herlemundus, bishop of the city of Le Mans, reported to us that his predecessors had received immunities from an earlier king, our relative, against evil men; and that our lord and exalted father Hildebert, formerly king, had granted complete immunities for all the estates and courts of his church, and for the monastery of Anisola, in which Saint Karileffus, confessor of Christ, rests bodily—which belongs by right to his church of Saint Mary and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius—wherever they are seen to hold property in districts or territories, and also for his monasteries, which he governs, built within the city of Le Mans, and for their estates and cultivated lands in whatever districts and territories.

He had granted that no public judge should ever enter there to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, require food or any other payments, or collect them, unless they should quietly possess all the conceded rights. He asserts that he has those charters in his possession and that this privilege has been preserved from that time onward. He therefore asked our majesty to confirm the same arrangement for him. Know that we have not refused his petition but have granted it in every respect.

Therefore by this present charter we decree, and wish it to remain forever, that, after examination of the earlier charter, no public judge—neither you, nor your juniors or successors, nor anyone exercising judicial authority—shall ever presume to enter the estates or courts of that bishop or of his church of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, or his monasteries, or their courts or estates, whether to hear cases, exact fines, take sureties, make lodgings or provisions, provide food, or demand or collect any payments that appear to belong to our fiscus.

But the bishop himself or his agents shall, through their messengers, render and pay over the two hundred *inferendales* and the other two hundred solidi in gold payment (*auro pagins*) which were rendered to our fiscus from that estate, or from those courts, churches, and monasteries, and which it was customary to render at the public treasury [Col. 1114A]. Thus, by our indulgence, the aforesaid Herlemundus, bishop, or the party of his church and monasteries, shall possess and govern all their estates and courts, together with all the brothers granted to them, forever under the name of immunity. They shall not fear that they themselves or their successors will at any time suffer any requisition or impediment from public judges, unless this privilege may, with God’s help, be preserved through our present and future times and perpetually increase the prosperity of those holy places.

And, so that this charter may be held more firmly and better preserved through time, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

In Christ’s name, I, Dagobert, king, have subscribed. — Ingobaldus presented and subscribed. — Given at Mamaccas, in the month of March, on the second day, in the second year of our reign, happily.

## XXV. Diploma of Dagobert III, king of the Franks, by which, at the petition of Herlemundus, bishop of Le Mans, he confirms the immunities granted to the Church of Le Mans for the estate of Arduno

[Note: [Col. 1114D] Inserted in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* in Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 284; reprinted in *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 688. It was fabricated to confirm the instrument published above [Col. 1112], which we judged to be fictitious; nor does this diploma appear to deserve a better reputation. According to Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 598, Herlemundus, bishop of Le Mans, for whose benefit this diploma is supposed to have been issued, had not yet obtained the administration of the monastery of Anisola when Dagobert III was reigning.] (year 713).

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man. If we preserve the acts of our fathers, we trust that our own acts will remain stable forever. Therefore the apostolic man, our father in Christ, Herlemundus, bishop of the city of Le Mans, reported to us that Hilderic, once king and uncle of our father Hildebert, once king, had by his charter granted the following to his predecessor, the late bishop lord Berarius, and to Aichilbert, his episcopal successor: whatever was expected for the fiscus from the estate of his church of Le Mans called Arduno, in the district of Poitiers, no judge or anyone else should exact; and no one should presume to make lodgings there, exact fines, demand provisions, or require or collect any earthly profit or gain, unless this was granted for the lamps of that church of Le Mans, which was built in honor of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, our patrons.

Afterward he granted the same to Bishop Aibertus, who succeeded Berarius there. The bishop asserts that he has those charters in his possession and that this privilege has been preserved from that time until now. But, for complete security, he asked our majesty to confirm this anew by our authority for the same lord Herlemundus, bishop, and for the holy basilica of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. Know that we have not refused him but have granted and confirmed it in every respect.

We therefore command that, just as it is established that our uncle Hilderic, formerly king, granted complete immunity for that estate of Arduno to that church, so we too grant and confirm by our authority that no judge shall ever presume in that estate to hear cases, demand provisions, exact fines, or require any census or earthly profit that might be expected for the fiscus; nor shall anyone ever presume to demand or collect such things, unless, after examination of that charter of the uncle of our father Childebert, the late king, named King Childeric, it is to remain perpetually granted and conceded for the lamps of the aforesaid basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius.

And, so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved through time, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

In Christ’s name, I, Dagobert, king, have subscribed. — Ingobaldus wrote and subscribed. — Given at Mamaccas, in the month of March, on the tenth day, in the second year of our reign, happily.

## XXVI. Diploma of Dagobert III, king of the Franks, by which the right of the Church of Le Mans over the monastery of Anisola is asserted, according to the charter of Ibbolenus, abbot

[Note: [Col. 1115D] The *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* present this confirmation of the fictitious charter of the fictitious abbot Ibbolenus in Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 273, and in D. Bouquet, *Writers on the History of Gaul and France*, vol. IV, p. 687, note 1. The diploma is filled with the same false indications as the charter that it confirms. See our notes on the charter itself. This diploma, like the charter, is listed among the instruments condemned at the assembly of Vermeria and ordered to be abolished, as stated above.] (year 713).

[Col. 1115C]

Dagobert, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

If we grant assent to the petitions of the servants of God, we not only exercise royal custom but also trust that this will contribute to our receiving the reward of eternal blessedness. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, that the venerable Berarius, bishop of the city of Le Mans, came into our presence, bringing documents of charters showing how the lord Carileffus, priest and monk, built a certain little monastery in his parish and, with the consent of his predecessor, the lord Innocent, handed it over to King Childebert [Col. 1115D]; afterward he received it from him by census as a precarious grant [Col. 1116A]. The aforesaid King Childebert issued his precept, and afterward his predecessor Domnolus likewise made a precarious grant to Gallus the monk and to the lord Carileffus, his disciple; and, after Domnolus had become and been ordained abbot, King Chilperic ordered his precept concerning that precarious grant to be issued.

The aforesaid Bishop Berarius showed all these documents to us, asking that we likewise do for his abbot, named Gundolenus [Note: [Col. 1115D] The name Gundolenus was written through the copyist’s negligence in place of the name Ibbolenus, as is clear from the text of the diploma itself, in whose sequence the name Ibbolenus is more correctly assigned to the abbot of Anisola.], what our predecessors had done in their precepts for their predecessors. We received his petition with willing spirit and ordered it to be done as he had requested.

Accordingly, we ordered this precept of our authority to be issued, by which we firmly command that, just as the aforesaid little monastery was given by the aforementioned Bishop Berarius to the aforesaid abbot by right of benefice [Col. 1116B], so henceforth it shall remain in his benefice, possession, and precarious tenure throughout his lifetime, without any diminution; and that each year Abbot Ibbolenus shall pay the census, as it is contained in their precarious grants, to the aforesaid Bishop Berarius and his successors: namely, four pounds of wax for the lamp of the mother church and the city church; and, to the canonical brothers residing in the city and serving the aforesaid church, on Maundy Thursday, a full bushel of eggs and prepared full bottles of the finest wine; and to the bishop of that city one well-prepared crook and two shoes for carrying out his office.

After his departure, the aforesaid little monastery shall return to the power and lordship of the aforesaid mother church, without anyone’s withholding or taking possession of it, in its entirety and with all its improvements; and the bishops or rectors of the mother church shall have free power to do with it whatever they shall rightly and canonically determine.

And, so that this authority may be held more firmly, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand. [Note: [Col. 1115D] The chronological indications are lacking; we place this forged diploma shortly after the charter of Ibbolenus, which we judged should be assigned to 28 April 713.]

## XXVII. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunities granted to the monastery of Saint-Denis

[Note: [Col. 1116D] Frequently printed: by Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, vol. IV, p. 562, and *De re diplomatica*, p. 484, and by Félibien, *Histoire de l’abbaye de Saint-Denis, preuves*, p. 19, from the original, now preserved in the royal archives, K, no. 3; by Cointius, *Annales*, vol. V, p. 280, by the authors of *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VII, instruments, col. 5, and by the collectors of Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 690, from Mabillon. Dublet had earlier published a fragment of it, *Antiquités ecclésiastiques de Saint-Denis*, p. 684, and attributed it to Childeric II. Cointius, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 803, inserted it into his annals under the same name of Childeric, at the year 679, having been led into error by Dublet—a mistake which that keen-eyed man ought certainly to have exposed, since he reprinted the entire diploma from Mabillon under the true name of Chilperic, in the same work, vol. V, p. 280. For the king who issued this diploma calls Theuderic his uncle and Chlodoveus, Childebert, and Dagobert his cousins; [Col. 1117C] these facts sufficiently identify Chilperic, son of Chilperic [Col. 1117D] II, as Cointius himself observed, ibid. This Chilperic, commonly called the second of that name, is called the third by some, because they count as Chilperic II the child Chilperic, son of King Charibert, as may be seen in *Annales*, vol. II, p. 817. He died immediately after his father’s death, in 630, and is omitted by most writers from the catalogue of Frankish kings. We publish the diploma according to the original, with a more accurate reading, examined by the often-mentioned Dom Poirier and newly reviewed by A. Teulet. No one raised any suspicion concerning its authenticity except Germonius, and even he did so only slightly and did not dwell on the matter; hence one may infer that a man eager to exercise criticism was offended by a few blemishes in this document. A wax seal had been attached to this diploma, which Mabillon testified was almost obliterated in the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, cited above; now no trace of it remains except a hole in the parchment.]

Chilperic, king of the Franks, to the illustrious men.

It is fitting for princely clemency to hear among other petitions that which is presented for salvation and requested for the sake of the divine name, and without doubt to bring it to effect, so that eternal gain may be acquired from the perishable things of the present age, according to the Lord’s command: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.” Therefore, according to his saying, we ought to purchase eternal heavenly things with the mammon of iniquity; and, while we bestow suitable benefits upon priests, we deserve thereby to have the Lord as our recompense in the eternal tabernacles.

Accordingly, the venerable man Chillardus, abbot of the basilica of the special patron of our lord, the martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily, petitioned the clemency of our kingdom. He stated that, just as by the former kings, our parents, an immunity from the villa of the aforesaid holy basilica had long ago been granted, and he affirms that he still possesses the relevant precepts in his hands, so that this too should be granted and confirmed by our authority for the security of the holy place itself and of the people who entrust or donate themselves and their property to that basilica, in accordance with what our earlier parents, or our exalted uncle Theuderic, and also our cousins Chlodoveus, Childebert, and Dagobert, once kings, had granted or confirmed to that basilica by their authority. [Note: [Col. 1117D] We have published, in their proper order, several diplomas of Theuderic, Chlodoveus, and Childebert issued for the benefit of the monastery of Saint-Denis; we have none of Dagobert III.]

We therefore judged that this should be granted and confirmed anew to that abbot. Let your greatness or utility know that, out of reverence for that holy place and for the peace of those serving God there, we have again granted and confirmed everything by our most ready will; let your discernment know this in all respects.

Therefore, by this precept, which we specially decree and wish to remain perpetual, we order that neither you, nor your juniors or successors, nor anyone armed with judicial authority, presume ever to enter the courts of the aforesaid holy basilica of the lord Dionysius—wherever they may be, in whatever counties throughout our kingdom, with God’s favor, which at the present day the aforesaid monastery appears to possess or control, or which has been granted or assigned there by God-fearing men through lawful documents—or to hear cases, take sureties, exact fines, impose lodging, demand provisions, or seek any other dues; nor may anything be exacted, except whatever our treasury might have been entitled to receive from it.

All of this, in every respect, is granted and remitted for the benefit of our reward, with all fines wholly conceded to it, as stated above, after the precepts themselves of the former kings, our parents, have been inspected, and in accordance with what our present authority appears to contain. Whatever that holy place appears to possess at the present day, as we have said, and whatever may subsequently be added or donated there by God-fearing men or by us, or whoever may justly and reasonably hand himself over to that monastery with all his property and assign or confirm his possessions there through lawful documents, shall remain from the present day under complete immunity, quiet and secure.

And whatever our treasury might perhaps have expected from it shall perpetually be granted and remitted in full, in every respect, for the lamps, expenses, and alms of the poor of that monastery, for the sake of our prayers, so that they may pray the more earnestly for the stability of our kingdom and for the peace of all our people, through the mercy of the Lord.

And, so that this authority may remain perpetually firm and inviolate concerning that holy place in our times and in those to come, and may be preserved unharmed and secure throughout the ages, and may be more readily believed by all judges, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Chilperic, king, subscribed. Actulius, ordered, presented it.

Given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the first year of our reign, at Compiègne, prosperously in the name of God.

[Note: [Col. 1118D] After the death of Childeric II, in June 715, the eastern Franks chose a cleric named Daniel, whom they gave the name Chilperic. It is therefore clear that the month of February in the first year of his reign fell in the year of Christ 716.]

## XXVIII. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunity from tolls granted to the monastery of Saint-Denis

[Note: [Col. 1118D] Preserved from the original, now in the royal archives, K, no. 3, in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, vol. IV, p. 563, and *De re diplomatica*, p. 485, and in Félibien, *Histoire ecclésiastique de Saint-Denis*, p. 21; from Mabillon in the *Collection of Frankish Historical Writings*, vol. IV, p. 691. It is composed in the same words as the diploma by which Chlodoveus III granted this same immunity, which we have presented elsewhere. Dagobert’s grant has until now remained concealed. We publish Chilperic’s diploma according to the original, carefully collated by Dom Poirier with the printed editions and newly reviewed by A. Teulet. It is especially noteworthy that in this document Chilperic calls Childeric his father: “An illustrious monument,” says Cointius, *Annales*, vol. V, [Col. 1119D] p. 281, “by which Chilperic is proved to be Childeric’s son.” This had long been unknown, but it is also confirmed by other diplomas of Chilperic, which we shall soon report. Mabillon testifies that the document was fortified with a wax seal, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, cited above. A fragment of that seal, marked with a long-haired effigy and Chilperic’s name, still adheres to the parchment.]

Chilperic, king of the Franks, to all the illustrious men of the toll administration of Marseille.

Since, in former years, our great-grandfather Dagobert, once king, granted one hundred solidi exempt from the city of Marseille, just as they could have been exacted from the treasury’s storehouse, to the basilica of the special patron of our lord, the martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily and where the venerable man Chillardus appears to preside as abbot, by his precept strengthened by his own hand; and since our lord and father Childeric, as well as our uncles Chlodacharius and Theuderic, once kings, and afterward we ourselves, by our precept, are seen to have granted and confirmed the same thing there anew; and since the following appears to have been inserted in those precepts: that neither in Marseille nor in the other places throughout our kingdom, with God’s favor, wherever tolls, port duties, bridge duties, wheel duties, or other dues exacted by public judges are collected, shall any such charge be demanded or exacted from the carts of those who appear to transport these goods for the agents of that basilica, except that one hundred solidi have been granted to them each year—

therefore, by this present ordinance, we decree and altogether order that, whenever the agents of the basilica of the lord Dionysius or of the aforesaid abbot—that is [Note: [Col. 1119D] A space for one word is blank in the original.] … come to you with their companions, you shall in every respect give and fulfill for them those one hundred exempt solidi, just as they could be obtained from our storehouse according to custom, without any delay or postponement, in accordance with the order of the treasury.

And from the carts which appear to transport these goods, neither in Marseille nor in the other places throughout our kingdom, with God’s favor, you must never presume to seek or exact any toll, port duty, bridge duty, wheel duty, or other due, whether you, your juniors, or anyone acting on behalf of our treasury. See to it that you do nothing else concerning this, but strive to possess our favorable grace.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] Certain characters appear here in the original, in the form of a monogram; we think they should be read: “In the name of Christ.”]

Chrodebert reviewed it.

Given in the month of March, on an unspecified day, in the first year of our reign, at Compiègne, prosperously in the name of God. [Note: [Col. 1119D] Earlier editors wrote “the fifth day,” but no such chronological indication exists in the original, whether omitted by a careless copyist or perhaps because by the words “the day of March” the first day of March is to be understood.]

## XXIX. Judgment of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which land situated in Upper Bacivus is adjudged to the provost of the monastery of Saint-Denis

[Note: [Col. 1119D] Published twice by Mabillon, in *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum* [Col. 1120D] vol. IV, p. 563, and in *De re diplomatica*, p. 485, from the original, now preserved in the royal archives, K, box 3; again from the original by Félibien, *Histoire de l’abbaye de Saint-Denis, preuves*, p. 21; reprinted according to Mabillon in the *Collection of Frankish Historical Writings*, vol. IV, p. 691. A wax seal was attached to this document, as Mabillon testifies in *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, vol. IV, preface, p. IV; when he inspected it, more than one hundred and twenty years ago, it was already worn away by half. That fragment, marked with the king’s long-haired effigy, still exists. We present the original, which, as Mabillon himself admits, is extremely difficult to read because of the roughness of its style and letters, after it was examined by Dom Poirier and newly reviewed by A. Teulet. The formulae of this judgment agree with those of other judgments of this period.]

Chilperic, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

When, in our presence and that of our nobles, at Compiègne [Col. 1119D], in our palace, a certain man named Friulfus brought a complaint against the venerable Martin, provost of the basilica of the special patron of our lord, Saint Dionysius, saying that Martin had wrongfully opposed or retained from him the portion which ought to have come to him from the estate of his former father-in-law Edrone, at a place called Upper Bacivus, Martin himself gave this response: that he had a document which the son of the aforesaid Edrone, named Eodo, had sold to the venerable Chrodcharius, monk of Saint Dionysius; and he produced the sale for reading in the present hearing.

After the sale had been set aside, and while they were disputing among themselves, our nobles found as follows: that half of the portion at the aforesaid place, Upper Bacivus, ought to belong to the aforesaid Martin on behalf of Saint Dionysius. [Col. 1120B]

Accordingly, we, together with our nobles, decreed as follows. When the illustrious Warno, count of our palace, had given testimony, it was judged that, since this case had been conducted and investigated in this manner, it should be declared. We order, therefore, that the aforesaid Martin and the party of Saint Dionysius shall have and hold adjudged and legally established for all time, without any claim by the aforesaid Friulfus or his heirs, that half of the aforesaid portion in Upper Bacivus, with whatever appears to pertain to that half, together with lands, houses, buildings, dependents, slaves, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, adjoining lands, appurtenances belonging to it, livestock, stores, mills, and flocks with their shepherds—in every respect and in its entirety—the matter having been investigated and their documents having been inspected and established.

And between that Friulfus and his heirs or agents and the agents of Saint Dionysius there shall henceforth be no litigation.

Since Martin, in the case of the basilica of the lord Dionysius against that Friulfus, was seen in the present hearing to have transferred both the produce from the other half and the surety made by his pledge, we order that both Martin himself and the party of the lord Dionysius may at all times remain in possession, without any claim by Friulfus or his heirs, secure and undisturbed, concerning the surety given or the produce transferred.

Ermedramnus reviewed and subscribed.

Given on the seventh day of the month of March, in the first year of our reign, at Compiègne, prosperously in the name of God.

## XXX. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he grants one hundred cows annually to the monastery of Saint-Denis, just as they had formerly been granted by King Dagobert

[Note: [Col. 1121C] Mabillon published it from the original, now preserved in the royal archives, K, box 3, in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis [Col. 1121D] Benedicti*, vol. IV, p. 564, and again in *De re diplomatica*, p. 486; Félibien likewise published it from the same original, *Histoire de l’abbaye de Saint-Denis, preuves*, p. 21. Cointius, *Annales*, vol. V, p. 282, and the collectors of Frankish historical writings, vol. IV, p. 692, reprinted it from Mabillon. Henschenius had previously published a fragment of this diploma in his discussion of the genealogy of the Dagobertine kings, but inaccurately and in a very mutilated form. Cointius reproduced the same fragment in vol. IV of his *Annales*, p. 528, and again in vol. V, p. 282, alongside the complete diploma. In this document Chilperic II unfolds the entire sequence of his genealogy: he calls Dagobert his great-grandfather, Childeric his father, and Theuderic his uncle; he calls Chlodoveus, Childebert, and Dagobert—namely, Dagobert III—his cousins. We publish this diploma, as well as the other diplomas of the same king preceding it, from the careful examination by Dom Poirier and the new review by A. Teulet according to the archetype.]

[Col. 1121A]

Chilperic, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

We have preserved the deeds of our parents; we shall exercise royal custom and trust that our own deeds will afterward remain established. We willingly heed, and in the name of God commit to effect, especially the petitions of priests insofar as they concern the confirmation of their benefits; we trust that this contributes to the increase of our reward.

Therefore the venerable man Chillardus, abbot of the basilica of the special patron of our lord, the martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily [Col. 1121B], brought to the clemency of our kingdom the following request: our great-grandfather of blessed memory, Dagobert, once king, by his authority, strengthened by his own hand, had granted annually to that holy basilica one hundred solidary cows, which were expected as a levy from the fiscus districts of the county of Le Mans.

He further affirms that he has in his hands the grant of that prince, as well as the confirmations strengthened by the hands of our grandfather Chlodoveus, our father of blessed memory Childeric, our uncle Theuderic, and our cousins Chlodoveus, Childebert, and Dagobert, once kings; and he states that, just as this benefit had been granted and remitted to that basilica by those princes, it was annually delivered and fulfilled by the judicial authority of that place.

For the sake of securing its permanence, he therefore asked our highness to confirm this perpetually, by a fuller grant of our authority, for that abbot and the aforesaid holy basilica. Let your greatness know that we have granted and confirmed everything with joyful spirit, out of reverence for that holy place.

We therefore command by this precept that, just as the aforesaid prince Dagobert, once king, granted by his authority to that basilica the one hundred cows to be levied from the aforesaid county of Le Mans, which were expected each year from the fiscal districts [Col. 1122A], and which appear to be preserved and fulfilled each year by the judicial authority, so henceforth, after the aforesaid authorities and confirmations of those princes have been inspected, this shall be more fully confirmed and perpetually preserved and granted in every respect, in the name of God, concerning that holy place by our precept. With God’s help, may it also increase there in our times and in those to come, so that they may pray more fervently for the stability of our kingdom and for all our people, through the mercy of the Lord.

And, so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Chilperic, king, subscribed. Actulius, ordered, presented it.

[Col. 1122B] Given on the sixteenth day of the month of March, in the first year of our reign, at Compiègne, prosperously in the name of God.

## XXXI. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the forest of Jumièges and other gifts bestowed upon the monastery of Fontenelle by his predecessors

[Note: [Col. 1122C] We present it as it was inserted and confirmed in the original letters issued by Philip V, king of the Franks, in 1319 [Col. 1122D], a copy of which exists in our chartulary, taken from the Fontenelle archives. The collectors of Frankish historical writings published Chilperic’s diploma, vol. IV, p. 693, from papers in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 48, says that he included it in the appendix to this volume, but it is nowhere to be found there. Several passages are missing from the printed edition; we have taken care to reproduce them in the type called italic. In our copy the entire forest of Jumièges is granted to the monastery of Fontenelle, whereas in the commonly published text only the forest of Jumièges by name is said to have been granted, not the whole forest. We think this should be attributed not to interpolation in the example of the diploma confirmed by Philip V, but rather to an omission in the printed edition. At the foot of the copy preserved in our chartulary it is stated that several copies of Philip’s letters are kept in the Fontenelle archives, and that they can also be found in the Fontenelle cartulary, which appears to have been written in the fifteenth century.]

Chilperic, illustrious king of the Franks.

It is fitting for princely clemency to heed the petitions of priests concerning what belongs to the needs of holy places and to commit the matter to effect in the name of God. Therefore the venerable man Benignus, abbot of the monastery of Fontenelle, which is built within the diocese of Rouen on the river Seine in honor of Saints Peter and Paul, chief apostles, and Saint Lawrence the martyr, where that abbot with a very large company of monks appears to live under the holy Rule, reported to us that, by the precepts of our grandfather King Chlodoveus, and also of our uncles Clotarius and Theuderic, our father Childeric, and our kinsmen Childebert and Dagobert, as well as by whatever documents of charters concerning properties and persons had been granted or confirmed to that monastery, and concerning the forest of Jumièges, or whatever had been brought or donated there by God-fearing men and subsequently improved or bestowed, they had granted or confirmed all these things by their authorities [Col. 1123A].

He accordingly showed us for reading the precepts of the aforesaid princes, as well as other precepts of our uncle Theuderic and of our relatives, the former kings Chlodoveus and Childebert, showing how they had again granted or confirmed these things there, and how they had granted the entire forest of Jumièges to that holy place. He is also proved at the present time to possess and control these things in peaceful order.

But, for complete security, the aforesaid abbot asked our highness to confirm all this more fully by our authority concerning that holy place. We acknowledge that we have granted and confirmed his petition in the following manner.

We therefore decree that whatever, through the precepts of the aforesaid princes, or through confirmations, sales, donations, assignments, exchanges, agreements, or any document of charters from our treasury, and also the forest of Jumièges, or whatever has been added, donated, assigned, or granted to the monastery of Fontenelle by God-fearing men in any counties, places, or territories, and whatever at the present time appears to be justly and lawfully possessed there, shall henceforth likewise be fully confirmed in the name of God by our precept.

+ Having inspected the aforesaid precepts and documents which they possess concerning these matters, we confirm them; and, as they themselves declare, the aforesaid Abbot Benignus, his successors, or the congregation itself that shall live in the monastery of Fontenelle through the ages shall have, hold, and possess these things. With God’s help, they shall increase by right of ownership for that holy place in our times and in those to come.

And, so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have decreed that it be affirmed below by our hand.

King Chilperic subscribed.

Given on the twenty-fifth day of the month of March, in the first year of our reign, at Compiègne, in the name of God.

Fredebertus wrote it.

## XXXII. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he bestows numerous gifts upon the monastery of Corbie

[Note: [Col. 1123D] Published by Labbe, *Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 436, who received it from Sirmond, who had extracted it from a manuscript of the Vendôme library. Lalande reprinted it in his supplement to the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 72, and judged that it should be assigned to the year of Christ 715; incorrectly, since Chilperic II began his reign in June of that very year, and therefore April of the first year of his reign must be assigned to the year of Christ 716. The collectors of Frankish historical writings again published it from Labbe, vol. IV, p. 663. This diploma is especially worthy of notice [Col. 1124D] because, in addition to what the preceding diplomas of this king teach concerning his genealogy, it calls Queen Balthild his grandmother. This same document illuminates the succession of the abbots of Corbie and establishes the age of Abbot Sebastian; concerning him, see Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 580, and Mabillon, *Annales Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, vol. II, p. 48.]

Chilperic, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

To all officials, present and future.

Whatever we grant for the lamps of holy places or for the needs of the servants of Christ, and whatever our parents granted for their reward, we confirm for the sake of our prayers; we trust that this contributes to our reward and to the stability of the kingdom.

Accordingly, the religious and venerable abbot of the monastery called Corbie, situated in the county of Amiens [Col. 1124A], which our exalted uncle Chlodacharius, once king, and our lady grandmother Balthild, once queen, appear to have built, out of love for Christ, in honor of Saints Peter and Paul, chief of the apostles, and Saint Stephen the martyr, came into our presence. He reported to the clemency of our kingdom that the aforesaid uncle of ours, King Clotarius, and also our aforementioned lady grandmother, Queen Balthild, had granted each year to that monastery from the toll of Fos, for the lamps which the monks residing there ought to have:

ten thousand pounds of oil, thirty modii of garum, thirty pounds of pepper [Note: [Col. 1124D] From this one diploma we learn that certain commodities, commonly called spices, were in circulation.], one hundred and fifty pounds of cumin, two pounds of cloves, five pounds of cinnamon, two pounds of spikenard, thirty pounds of costus, fifty pounds of dates, one hundred pounds of dried figs (*caricae*), one hundred pounds of almonds, thirty pounds of raisins, one hundred pounds of olives, fifty pounds of hydrium, one hundred and fifty pounds of chickpeas, twenty pounds of rice (*oridia*), ten pounds of gold-colored pigment, ten skins of seoda, ten skins of cordelisae, and fifty reams of paper.

We therefore command that the toll officials who appear to administer the toll of Fos, in the year of collection, give and fulfill all these things to the agents of that monastery who shall be sent there. Moreover, for their transport, to the agents of the monastery who travel there to collect these things, they shall provide each year, without a renewed travel warrant:

ten riding horses or packhorses, ten fine loaves of bread, twenty *sequentes* [item uncertain], one modius of wine, one modius of beer, ten pounds of bacon, twenty pounds of meat, twelve pounds of cheese, twenty pounds of fish, one kid, eleven chickens, ten eggs, two pounds of oil, one pound of garum, one ounce of pepper, two ounces of cumin, salt, vinegar, vegetables, and sufficient firewood.

You ought to give and fulfill all the things mentioned above each year, at suitable places, to the same men both when going and when returning, without delay. You ought also to provide twelve carts for the return journey, from place to place, by the customary routes, until the cellarer himself reaches that monastery, in such a manner that this may accrue to their benefit without loss to the monastery.

Accordingly, the venerable Abbot Sebastian produced before us for reading the aforesaid precept subscribed by our uncle Clodacharius, as well as by our grandmother Queen Balthild, and also the confirmation by our lord and father, King Childeric; he affirms that he has these documents in his hands. But, for the sake of security, the lord Sebastian himself asked our highness that we should more fully confirm and grant this by our authority, in the name of God, for him, for the monastery of Corbie, for his successors, and for the congregation which appears to reside in that monastery.

Know that, with joyful spirit, for the benefit of our reward and out of reverence for that holy place, we have granted and confirmed his petition, and have also granted and confirmed it by our precept. We therefore command that, from the aforesaid toll of Fos, and according to the travel warrants themselves and the precepts of the aforesaid princes which have been inspected, as they declare, and by the full authority of this our precept, you procure that the toll official and the other judges give and fulfill these things to the agents of the aforesaid monastery in the name of Christ. Also, while they remain in the place, make every effort to give them the provision written above.

Moreover, you shall ensure that the other judges, at suitable places, provide and fulfill for them each year, without delay or postponement, from the prescribed transport allowance, whether by cart or by boat, and likewise the provision written above, in our times and in those to come, so that a complete and perpetual reward may reach us through this benefit.

And, so that this precept may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the first year of our reign, at Compiègne, prosperously in the name of God.

### XXXIII. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he donates the Roveritus forest to the monastery of Saint-Denis

[Note: Published by Dublet, *Antiquities of Saint-Denis*, p. 689, and by Félibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis: Proofs*, p. 22, from the original; by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 589, and by the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 694, from Dublet. Mabillon had a specimen of this document engraved in copper, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 385. We publish it collated with the original by D. Poirier, who often and most courteously assisted us in these matters [and, for greater accuracy, with the same original, now preserved in the royal archives, K, chest 4, after the recension made by A. Teulet]. Mabillon reproduces the seal and notes that the words *bene valete*, after the subscription, are written in abbreviated letters. In this diploma Cointius, in the same place, p. 590, seems to find nothing contrary to history or chronology; but he is greatly troubled by the frequent and barbarous interchange of vowels, which he says does not occur in the public documents of this period. Yet, with all respect to so distinguished a man, Merovingian originals teem with such faults; he appears to have known most of them only through corrected copies. Germonius suspected the document to be false on other grounds, *On the Ancient Diplomas of the Frankish Kings*, vol. II, pp. 129 ff.: first, because the major-domo Raganfrid seems in this diploma to perform the functions of referendary or notary, which he considers unusual and scarcely compatible with that dignity; and second, because Bishop Turnoaldus—that is, the bishop of Paris—is called abbot of Saint-Denis in the second year of Chilperic’s reign, which could not be the case unless there had been four abbots of Saint-Denis within a period of eight or nine years. To this we reply that Raganfrid may perhaps have presented this diploma in the capacity of referendary because it was issued at his petition, as the text of the diploma itself shows. On the chronology of the abbots of the monastery of Saint-Denis, and on Turnoaldus as simultaneously bishop and abbot or guardian of this monastery, see Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 49; Dubois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, vol. I, p. 215; Félibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 36; *New Christian Gaul*, vol. VII, cols. 312 ff. From these works it will be clear that there is nothing contradictory in what this document says about Turnoaldus.] (year 717).

**Chilperic, king of the Franks, illustrious man.** If we bestow or grant something from our gifts to holy places, we trust that this will redound to our reward and to the stability of our kingdom, in God’s name. [Col. 1125C] Therefore let your Dignity or Greatness know that we have granted, with full right and all its boundaries, our forest called Roveritus, situated in the Parisian district on the River Seine, together with the forester named Lobicinus, who resides on our estate at the Old Clippiacum, together with the mansus which appears to be held at that Clippiacum, and the lands belonging to that mansus in their entirety, to the basilica of our special patron, Saint Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily, and where Lord Turnoaldus, bishop, appears to preside as guardian, at the petition of the illustrious man Raganfrid, our major-domo, as a full and complete act of grace on the present day.

Therefore by this present special precept we determine and order that this shall remain permanently with that holy place: namely, that our forest Roveritus, with all its rights and boundaries in full, together with the aforesaid forester and his mansus, with the lands and meadows at that Clippiacum in their entirety, shall be held by Lord Turnoaldus, bishop, for that holy basilica of the Lord Dionysius the martyr, as a full and complete gift from our bounty, granted and bestowed under the name of immunity. [Col. 1126A] Thus they may always be more eager to pray earnestly to the Lord’s mercy for the stability of our kingdom and for the salvation of the fatherland; and no public judge, whether in our time or under succeeding kings, may permit them to suffer any requisition or hindrance on this account, except that it shall benefit the aforesaid holy basilica of the Lord Dionysius, in our time and in future times, through increase. And, so that this precept may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

**King Chilperic, subscribed. — Raganfrid presented it.** *(Place of the seal.)*

Given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the second year of our reign, at Compiegne, successfully, in God’s name.

---

### XXXIV. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the privileges granted to the monastery of Fosses

[Note: Published by Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 486, from his papers; reprinted by the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 695, and by the authors of *New Christian Gaul*, vol. VII, documents, col. 6, from Mabillon. Labbe had published a fragment, *Miscellanies*, vol. II, p. 438; but, as Mabillon noted, he mistakenly thought it had been issued for the monastery of Glanfeuil. Cointius, misled by Labbe, inserted the same fragment in his *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 593, as though it had been granted to the monks of Glanfeuil. The abbot of Fosses, who is called Waldemarus in this diploma, is called Waldorannus by others, according to *New Christian Gaul*, vol. VII, col. 284.] (year 717).

[Col. 1126C]

**Chilperic, king of the Franks, very illustrious.** If we lend our ears to the just petitions of God’s servants, we exercise royal custom, and we believe without doubt that this is beneficial to the condition of our souls and to the prosperity of our kingdom. [Col. 1127A] Therefore the venerable man Waldomarus, abbot, considering the weakness and frailty of his body and the frequent illnesses with which the Lord has deigned to chastise him, after deliberating with all the brothers who appear to serve almighty God in the monastery of Fosses, in the Parisian territory, brought before the clemency of our kingdom a request that, according to their privilege, which had been preserved by our predecessors and by the bishops, it should also remain confirmed and preserved by us for all time, out of reverence for holy Mary, Mother and Virgin of God, and for the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and out of regard for our soul and eternal recompense.

Therefore we order that such a precept and confirmation be made for the same abbot and his monks, with the consent of our major-domo Raganfrid, so that whatever is stated in their privilege, we desire and decree that it be preserved and kept inviolate through the ages by our authority and that of our successors. We command absolutely that no foreign or opposing person presume to enter that monastery to rule or contend there without the will of the abbot or his brothers. Rather, in accordance with the privilege which they presented to our presence, after the abbot’s death—or whenever the abbot himself wishes—they shall have permission, with his consent and the will of those subject to him, to appoint as abbot the person whom the abbot and the better part of the monks shall choose from that congregation, or, if necessity requires, from any monastery, as their privilege most clearly specifies. [Col. 1127C] He must, however, be one who is chaste in body, devoted in mind, learned in the sacred Scriptures, and instructed in regular observance, so that the monks, living in peaceful order and suffering no disturbance, may take increasing delight in praying for the stability of our kingdom and for the salvation of the whole people.

Moreover, he declares that he has in his hands the confirmation of our cousin, the former king Dagobert, concerning this matter; and the benefit granted at that time appears to have been preserved until now. Thus, after examining the aforesaid precepts of the princes, as they are explained by those same documents, may the benefit granted remain valid and preserved at all times hereafter. And, so that this precept may be firmer, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by the subscriptions of our hand.

**King Chilperic, subscribed. Ado, by order, presented it.**

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the second year of our reign, at the city of Paris, successfully.

---

### XXXV. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he donates the village of Marte to the basilica of Saint Arnulf at Metz

[Note: Preserved in Meurisse, *History of the Bishops of Metz*, p. 144, taken from the archive of Saint Arnulf. Reprinted by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 593, and Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, vol. II, p. 110, from Meurisse. Valladier published a French translation, *The Basilica of Saint Arnulf*, p. 177. We present it according to the copy of Dom Tabouillot, of the congregation of Saint-Vanne, who transcribed it from the archive of Saint Arnulf and brought it into our collection. Variant readings excerpted from Meurisse are placed within brackets.] (year 717).

[Col. 1128A]

**Chilperic** [Meurisse: *Chilpericus*], **king of the Franks, illustrious man.** If we bestow or grant anything to holy places, we trust that this will redound to our praise and to the stability of our kingdom, in God’s name, so that they may be more eager to pray continually to the Lord’s mercy for us [M.: for us or on our behalf] and for the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let your Dignity or Greatness know that we have granted, as of the present day, under the name of immunity, with full and complete grace [M.: *gratia*, “grace”], by proprietary right [M.: proprietorial right], our village called Marte, situated in the territory of Moselle [M.: Mollinse], together with all its entirety, whatever of our fiscus appears to be there, to the basilica of the holy lord Arnulf and of the holy apostles, where that precious man rests bodily [M.: rests in the body], beneath the fortress of the city of Metz, where the venerable man Leutbertus, abbot, appears to serve together with a very numerous body of clergy, for the increase of our reward [M.: as an increase of our reward] and out of reverence for that holy place.

Therefore by this precept we specially decree and order [M.: decree] that this shall remain forever with that place [M.: that location]. Thus the village named above, together with its lands, houses, buildings, slaves, holdings [M.: estates], vineyards, fields, [Col. 1128C] meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, appurtenances, dependencies, appendages, flocks [M.: herds] with shepherds of both sexes, everything and from everything, after investigation, in its entirety—whatever of our property is held there in that village of Marte [M.: in the village of Marte], together with every advantage or solidity belonging to it—shall be held by Leutbertus, abbot, for that holy lord Arnulf [M.: Arnulphus] or for the holy apostles [M.: the holy apostles], by right of proprietary gift from our bounty, under the name of immunity, with every fiscal right granted; and whatever he or his successors shall decide to do with it for the benefit of that holy place, they shall have full power in all matters, and he shall not fear any requisition or hindrance from the public judges, whether in our time or in the time of succeeding kings.

And [M.: and so that] this precept may be firmer, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

**King Chilperic, subscribed.**

The day which was made in the month of June, the eighth, in the second year of our reign, at Compiegne Palace [Note: The corrupt word *placatio* stands for *palatio*; Merovingian diplomas were frequently issued from the palace at Compiegne. Valladier did not recognize the true reading and ridiculously translated it into the vernacular as “instead of our placard.” He likewise incorrectly connects the second year of Dagobert’s reign with the year 724 of Christ. He asserts that the entire document was written in Chilperic’s own hand—a thing unheard of, and one no person who has even glanced at documents of this kind would believe.]—our own.

---

### XXXVI. Diploma of Chilperic II, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the gifts bestowed upon the monastery of Sithiu and the immunities granted to it

[Note: Published by Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 608, taken from Folquin’s chartulary. It was reprinted in the supplement to Miraeus’s *Diplomatic Works*, vol. II, p. 929, and in the *Collection of the Historians of Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 696, from Mabillon. In the supplement just mentioned it is attributed, through a typographical error, to King Childeric; the text of the diploma itself makes clear that it was issued by Chilperic II, whose father was Childeric and whose grandfather was Clovis. Mabillon notes concerning this document that Folquin omitted the subscriptions and the name of the place where the diploma was given, but fabricated the attached seal, making it entirely different from the authentic seals of the Merovingian kings and characteristic of the style and spirit of the tenth century. The authenticity of the diploma is supported, however, by its mention in the chronicle of Sithiu, written by Iperius, abbot of Sithiu, in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 482. We publish it on Mabillon’s authority. Compare the *Chartulary of Sithiu*, edited in 1841 by the learned Guérard, p. 42.] (year 718).

[Col. 1129A]

**Chilperic, king of the Franks** [*illustrious man*]. If we confirm by our royal pronouncements the deeds of our parents, by which they bestowed or granted things to holy places, we exercise royal custom, and we trust that this redounds to our praise and to the stability of our kingdom, in God’s name.

Accordingly, the venerable man Erkembodus, abbot of the monastery of Sitdiu, which is in the territory of Thérouanne and was founded in honor of holy Mary, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the other holy lords, came into our presence and brought before the clemency of our kingdom the following petition: our grandfather Clovis, formerly king, had granted to his predecessor, the lord Bertinus, formerly abbot of that monastery, and to the aforesaid monastery, complete immunity concerning all the estates and villages of that monastery—whatever they possessed at that time, or whatever thereafter had been or might be added or granted there from royal gifts, from offerings of the people, from purchases, or from anything acquired in any manner, in any territories or districts—so that no public judge should ever enter there under judicial authority to hear cases, exact *freda*, take sureties, make lodgings or requisitions, distrain the men of that monastery, whether free or servile, who reside upon their lands, or demand or exact any payments. Rather, under the name of immunity, with all *freda* granted, the monastery’s estate was to possess everything perpetually.

He further declares that he has in his hands the precepts of that prince, our grandfather Clovis, and the confirmations of our illustrious uncles Chlodochar and Theodoric, as well as of our father Childeric and our cousins Clovis and Childebert, formerly kings, and that the benefits granted have been preserved from that time until now. But, for complete security, the aforesaid abbot asked our Highness to confirm this more fully for that place by our authority. [Col. 1130A] Know, therefore, that, for the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that place, we have granted and confirmed his petition in every respect.

We therefore command and decree that whatever our aforesaid grandfather Clovis, formerly king, is known to have justly and reasonably granted and confirmed to the aforementioned Bertinus concerning that immunity, as set forth above, and afterward our uncles Chlodochar and Theodoric, our father Childeric, and our cousins Clovis and Childebert, formerly kings, and whatever has been preserved in a straight course from that time until now, shall likewise hereafter be more fully confirmed in God’s name by our precept. Having examined the precepts of the aforesaid princes, as their contents declare, may the benefits granted to Abbot Erkembodus and his successors, and to the monastery of Sitdiu, remain preserved in every respect at all times; and may they at no time suffer any opposition or hindrance from public judges. Thus the congregation may continually pray to the Lord’s mercy for the stability of our kingdom and the salvation of the fatherland.

And, so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Given in the third year of our reign. [Note: The third year of the reign of Chilperic II began in the year of Christ 717 and ended in 718.]

---

### XXXVII. Diploma of Theodoric IV, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the gifts bestowed upon the monastery of Sithiu by his ancestors and the immunities granted to it

[Note: Mabillon took this from Folquin’s autograph chartulary, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 609; it was reprinted by Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. I, p. 128; by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 649, from Miraeus; and by the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 657, from Mabillon, whom we follow. Iperius, in the Bertinian chronicle, in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 482, mentions this privilege of liberty and confirmation granted to the abbot of Sithiu. Compare the *Chartulary of Sithiu*, p. 44, published in 1841 by the frequently cited Guérard.] (year 721).

[Col. 1130C]

**Theodoric, king of the Franks, to the illustrious men, the counts, and all their agents and subordinates, both present and future, in whatever matters the monastery of Sitdiu appears to hold or possess.** If we confirm by our royal pronouncements the deeds of our parents, by which they bestowed or granted things to holy places, we exercise royal custom, doing so because we trust that this redounds to our praise and to the stability of our kingdom, in God’s name.

Accordingly, the venerable man Erkembodus, abbot of the monastery of Sitdiu, which is in the territory of Thérouanne and was founded in honor of holy Mary, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the other holy lords, came into our presence and brought before the clemency of our kingdom the following matter: our great-grandfather Clovis, formerly king, had granted complete immunity to his predecessor Bertinus, formerly abbot, and to the aforesaid monastery of Sitdiu, concerning all the estates and villages of that monastery—whatever they possessed at that time, or whatever thereafter had been or might be added or granted there from royal gifts, from offerings of the people, from purchases or prospective purchases, or from anything acquired in any manner in any territories or districts—so that no public judge should ever enter there under judicial authority to hear cases, exact *freda*, take sureties, make lodgings or requisitions, distrain the men of that monastery, whether free or servile, who reside upon their lands, or demand or exact any payments. Rather, under the name of immunity, with all *freda* granted, the monastery’s estate was always to possess everything perpetually.

He further declares that he has in his hands the precept of that prince, our great-grandfather Clovis, and the confirmations of our illustrious uncles Chlothar and Childeric, as well as of our grandfathers Theodoric and Childebert and our cousin Chilperic, formerly king, and that the benefits granted have been preserved from that time until now. But, for complete security, the aforesaid Abbot Erkembodus asked our Highness to confirm this more fully for that place by our authority in God’s name. Know, therefore, that, for the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that place, we have granted and confirmed his petition in every respect.

We therefore command and decree that whatever our aforesaid great-grandfather Clovis, formerly king, is known to have granted concerning that immunity to his predecessor Bertinus, as set forth above, and whatever afterward his uncles and our grandfathers Chlothar and Theodoric, Childebert and Childeric [Note: Several errors are found in the genealogical succession displayed by the diploma as it stands in Mabillon. The chief occurs in the words “his uncles, or our grandfather Chlothar and Theodoric, Childebert and Childeric,” where the order has been confused and the copyist’s carelessness has thrown everything into disorder. Miraeus’s reading, which is closer to the true text, is: “His uncles or our grandfathers Chlothar and Theodoric, Childebert and Chilperic.” But, so that the meaning may emerge more clearly and the preceding clauses may agree with what follows, the order of words must be restored, with Cointius, as follows: “His uncles Chlothar and Childeric, or our grandfathers Theodoric and Childebert.” There is nothing surprising in the words “uncles” being used here for great-uncles, or “grandfathers” for great-grandfather and great-great-grandfather; such usage may be observed elsewhere in documents of this period.], and the confirmations of our cousin Chilperic, formerly king, justly and reasonably granted or confirmed, and whatever has been preserved in a straight course from that time until now, shall likewise hereafter be more fully confirmed in God’s name by our precept. Having examined the precepts of the aforesaid princes, as their contents declare, may the benefits granted remain preserved in every respect at all times for Abbot Erkembodus and his successors and for the place of Sitdiu; and may they never have to fear any opposition or hindrance from public judges. Thus the congregation may continually pray to the Lord’s mercy for the stability of our kingdom and the salvation of the fatherland.

And, so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by the subscriptions of our hand.

**Sign of the glorious King Theodoric.**

[Col. 1132B] Given on the third day of March, in the first year of our reign, at the city of Soissons, successfully, in God’s name.

---

### XXXVIII. Diploma of Theodoric IV, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunities granted to the monastery of Sithiu

[Note: Published by Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 609, from Folquin’s chartulary. Reprinted by the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 993. Malbrancq published a fragment of it, *On the Morini*, book IV, chapter 58. Compare the aforementioned *Chartulary of Sithiu*, p. 47. Iperius mentions this diploma in the chronicle of Saint Bertinus, in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 482, where, among the chronological notes, he gives the eleventh of November instead of the tenth. In this document Theodoric IV calls his great-great-grandfather Theodoric—whom he ought to have called his great-grandfather—Theodoric III, whose privilege granted to the people of Sithiu he confirms. He uses “great-great-grandfather” in the sense that three degrees intervened between the two Theodorics. It is especially worth noting that the confirmation is broader than the grant. We have published the grant elsewhere; it establishes definite limits for the privilege below the fiscus of Attigny, whereas the confirmation establishes none. On Erkembodus, see Joan Iperius’s chronicle in Martène’s *Thesaurus*, and *New Christian Gaul*, vol. III, col. 487.] (year 721).

**Theodoric, king of the Franks, illustrious man.** Whoever divine piety raises to the kingship ought to preserve the deeds of his ancestors; especially those things which royal clemency is shown to have granted to the resources of churches or to holy places for eternal recompense ought to be preserved forever.

Therefore let your Greatness and Dignity know that the venerable man Erkembodus, abbot of the monastery of Sitdiu, through his agents brought before the clemency of our kingdom the following report: our great-great-grandfather Theodoric, formerly king, by a precept subscribed with his own hand, had granted to his predecessor Bertinus, formerly abbot, and to the aforesaid monastery of Sitdiu, the following benefit: whatever he possessed within our fiscus, wherever it might be, in any territories or districts, whether he had acquired it or might later find it available for acquisition, and whatever good men fearing God had given or might later give to the aforesaid monastery for the sake of their souls, was to be held by it. Whatever he had acquired from our fiscus or might later acquire, except the land from which carpentry work was produced, he had granted under this provision: no judicial authority should demand, exact, or seek from it any land revenues or public dues.

He therefore declares that he has in his hands the precept of our aforesaid great-great-grandfather, and he displayed it to us in our presence for reading; he also asserted that the benefits granted had been preserved from that time until now. But, for the sake of firm security, he asked our Highness to confirm this for the holy place by our royal pronouncements. Know that, for the Lord’s name and out of reverence for that holy place, we have gladly granted and confirmed his request in every respect.

We therefore command that whatever our aforesaid great-great-grandfather Theodoric, formerly king, is known to have granted to the aforesaid Bertinus or to the aforesaid holy place concerning that benefit, as set forth above, and whatever has been preserved in a straight course from that time until now, shall likewise hereafter be more fully confirmed in God’s name by our precept, after examination of the aforesaid prince’s precept, as its contents declare. Thus, concerning Abbot Erkembodus and his monastery of Sitdiu, may the benefits granted remain at all times and in every respect preserved, and may they never fear opposition or hindrance from public judges. Thus the congregation may take delight in continually praying to the Lord’s mercy for the stability of our kingdom and for the salvation of the fatherland.

And, so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved forever in every respect, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by the subscriptions of our hand.
