**Sign of the glorious Lord Theodoric.** Given on the tenth day of November, in the first year of our reign, at the fortress of Confelent. I, Conradus, by order, examined and subscribed.

---

### XXXIX. Diploma of Theodoric IV, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunities granted to the monastery of Anisola, subject to the Church of Le Mans

[Note: Published among the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, issued by Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 274; reprinted in the *Collection of the Historians of Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 700. This is one of the documents produced by the Church of Le Mans in court, condemned, and ordered to be abolished, of which we have spoken more than once. We therefore judge this document, like others of the same fabrication, to have been forged in order to assert the rights of the Church of Le Mans over the monastery of Anisola. Several features reveal its falsity. It says that Berarius was then presiding over the Church of Le Mans, which points to the time of Theodoric III, whose second year corresponds to the year of Christ 674; but the king who issued this diploma calls Dagobert his father, which suits Theodoric IV and not Theodoric III. The second year of Theodoric IV falls in the year of Christ 722, to which year the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum* assigned this document; but that cannot agree with the period of Berarius, whose successor as abbot was Aiglibertus. Since all these details contradict one another, we do not hesitate to number this diploma among the spurious documents, as well as several others inserted into the same acts of the bishops of Le Mans.] (year 722).

**Theodoric, king of the Franks, illustrious man.** Royal greatness then strengthens the foundations of its throne when it listens to the petitions of priests or bishops, when what concerns the welfare of churches is heard and, in God’s name, brought to fulfillment.

Therefore the apostolic man, Lord Berarius, bishop of the city of Le Mans, who appears to govern the mother church of Le Mans and the monastery of Anisola, in which Lord Carileffus rests bodily, which belongs by right to his see and mother church under the patronage of holy Mary, Saint Peter, and Saints Gervasius and Protasius the martyrs, brought before us the following report: his predecessors had obtained from an earlier king, our ancestor, immunities concerning all their property and the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius the martyrs, but afterward those immunities had been stolen by evil men.

Therefore our glorious and exalted predecessor Childebert, formerly king, as well as our father Dagobert, formerly king, and afterward our ancestor Chilperic, formerly king, had granted complete immunities concerning all the villages and estates of their Church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius the martyrs, in whatever districts and territories they might be, and also concerning their monasteries, which he himself governs and which have been built within that city of Le Mans, together with their estates and villages in whatever districts or territories, and whatever appears to be expected by that Church. They had granted that no public judge should ever enter there to hear cases, exact *freda*, make lodgings or requisitions, demand provisions, or require or exact any payments, except that the Church should possess all the *freda* granted and bestowed.

He therefore declares that he has that precept in his hands and that the benefit itself had been preserved from that time. He asked our Highness to confirm this in the same manner for that place. Know that we did not refuse his petition but granted and confirmed it in every respect.

Therefore we decree and command by this present precept, and desire it to remain forever, that, after examination of the earlier precept, no public judge—neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor anyone exercising judicial authority—shall ever presume to enter the villages or estates of that Church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius the martyrs, or its monasteries, estates, or villages, or whatever appears to be expected by that Church, to hear cases, exact *freda*, take sureties, cause any disturbance, make lodgings, provisions, or requisitions, or make any payments that are expected to be demanded from our fiscus, or exact them.

The only exception is that Berarius himself or his agents must render and transfer the promised payments: 200 *inferendales* solidi [Col. 1134D], and those other 200 *pagenses* in gold, which were rendered to our fiscus from those villages, those estates, his Church or monasteries, or whatever appears to be expected by that Church, and which it had been customary to render in the public treasury.

And, as we have said, by our indulgence the aforesaid Berarius, or the peers of his Church of Le Mans, or his monasteries, shall always possess and govern, under the name of immunity, all the fruits granted from all their villages and estates, and from whatever appears to be expected by that Church. Neither Berarius nor his successors shall ever fear any requisitions or hindrance from public judges. May this be preserved in our time and in future times, with God’s help, and may it perpetually benefit and increase those holy places.

And, so that this precept may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by our hands.

**Sign of the glorious Lord Theodoric, king. Ginantinus, by order, presented and subscribed.**

Given on the second day of March, in the second year of our reign, at Quierzy, successfully.

---

### XL. Diploma of Theodoric IV, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunities granted to the Church of Le Mans for the village of Arduno

[Note: Inserted into the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, in Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 285; reprinted in the *Collection of the Historians of Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 701. We have published elsewhere, in the same words, the diploma of Dagobert III, which Theodoric IV confirms in his own diploma. The document issued under the name of Dagobert III is revealed as fictitious by its chronological indications, as we noted in its proper place. It therefore appears that the diploma of Theodoric IV presented here was composed after the spurious diploma of Dagobert, whose wording it faithfully copies; consequently, it too must be numbered among the spurious documents. Charivius, to whom Theodoric appears to address this letter, as also to Herlemundus, was the son of Count Rotharius, who, if we believe the acts of the bishops of Le Mans, had seized the property of the bishopric of Le Mans by tyrannical power. See Mabillon, in the place cited above.] (year 722).

Theoderic, king of the Franks, illustrious man. If we preserve the deeds of our ancestors, we trust that our own will remain stable forever. Therefore our faithful servant, by God’s favor, our apostolic man and father in Christ, Herlemundus the bishop, and the illustrious man Charivius, who appears to govern the mother church of Le Mans, dedicated to the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, reported to us that his predecessors had obtained from earlier kings, our ancestors—namely, from our grandfather Childebert and our father Dagobert, as well as from our parent Chilperic, once king [Note: On Childebert’s charter, see above; no charter of Chilperic survives.]—by their commands, the following grant: whatever from the estate of that church of Le Mans called Arduno, in the district of Poitou, was expected for the treasury, no judge or anyone else was to exact; no one was to establish lodgings in that estate, exact fines, hear lawsuits, take sureties, cause any disturbances, demand provisions, or seek or exact any earthly revenue [Col. 1135D] expected for the treasury, except that this was to be granted and allowed for the lights of that church of Le Mans, which was built in honor of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, our patrons. Charivius further affirms that he has those commands in his possession and maintains that this benefit has been preserved from that time until now. But, for complete security, he asked our Highness that we should again confirm this, by our authority, to Charivius himself and to that church of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. Know, therefore, that we have not refused his request but have granted and confirmed everything accordingly.

We command that, just as our grandfather Childebert, or our father Dagobert, and afterward our kinsman Chilperic, the earlier kings, made complete grants of immunity for that estate of Arduno and for the church itself, so we too, by our authority, grant and confirm for the future that no judge at any time shall presume in that estate to hear lawsuits, take sureties, demand provisions or fines, or seek or exact any tax or earthly revenue whatever that might be expected for our treasury. Rather, after examination of the earlier commands of those ancient princes, our ancestors, all this must perpetually be granted and allowed for the lights of the aforementioned basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. And so that this authority may be held more securely and preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Sign of the glorious lord Theoderic, king. Confisius, ordered to do so, presented, wrote, and subscribed.

Given at Carisiacum, on the fifth day of March, in the second year of our reign. Prosperously.

### XLI. Charter of Theoderic IV, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the privileges granted to the monastery of Saint-Denis (Year 723)

[Note: Mabillon extracted this from the archive of Saint-Denis, *De re diplomatica*, p. 488. Ruinart reprinted it, following Mabillon, in the appendix to Gregory of Tours, col. 1383, as did the editors of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 702. [The original of this charter is not preserved in the royal archive among the other documents of the monastery of Saint-Denis; only two copies exist, one quite recent and the other apparently written on cotton paper in the fourteenth century. I have followed the reading of the latter, based on a collation made by A. Teulet; Mabillon also appears to have followed it, since he reproduces it verbatim and makes no mention of an original, which in fact had probably already perished many years earlier.]] (Year 723).

Theuderic, king of the Franks, illustrious man. It is fitting that princely clemency should receive with willing hearing, among other petitions, that which is offered for salvation or requested for the sake of the divine name, and bring it to fulfillment, so that it may become a reward when a petition is granted for the peace of God’s servants or in accordance with venerable places. Therefore, since the almighty Father, who caused light to shine from darkness, through the mystery of the Incarnation of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, has shone into the hearts of holy Christians, and since, for love of him and in desire for the glorious triumph among the other martyrs, the blessed Dionysius, together with his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, who were the first after the apostles to come into this province of Gaul under the direction of blessed Clement, successor of the apostle Peter, preached there the baptism of repentance and the remission of sins, and while striving in this manner earned the palm of martyrdom and received glorious crowns; there, in their basilica, where their precious bodies are seen to rest, Christ has deigned through them to perform no small number of miracles by his power for many ages and down to the present. In that same place our glorious ancestor—or rather our great-grandfather of blessed memory—Dagobert, once king, is also seen to rest. May we too, through the intercession of those saints, deserve to share in the heavenly kingdom with all the saints and receive eternal life.

Accordingly, our venerable and faithful servant, by God’s favor, Berthoaldus [Note: Berthoaldus, at whose request this document was issued, is otherwise unknown.], abbot of the basilica of our special patron, the lord Dionysius, sent a petition through the illustrious man Charles, our mayor of the palace, and they presented it to the clemency of our kingdom. They reported that from ancient times complete privileges had been granted by the bishops of the city of Paris to the basilica of the lord Dionysius, and that these had been confirmed from the time of the earlier kings, our ancestors, down to the present. They affirm that they have in their possession both that privilege and the commands and confirmations themselves. But, for complete security, the man Charles and the abbot requested our Highness that we too should confirm this anew by our command. Let your greatness know that we received their most religious petition with the greatest willingness and confirmed everything.

Since, moreover, this temple and holy place appear to have been enriched by the aforementioned princes, by other ancient kings, and also by all God-fearing Christians, for the love of God and eternal life, our complete devotion is directed toward granting or confirming a privilege for that holy place, for the abbot and the brothers living there, for their future peace, so that the congregation may more readily pray continually at the thresholds and tombs of those martyrs for the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore, by this statement of our authority, in accordance with the privilege made by the bishops and confirmed by the earlier kings, our ancestors, and for reverence for those martyrs and for the reward that we seek to confirm for ourselves, we grant and confirm anew to that holy place that whatever at the present time has been assigned or thereafter may be added to it—whether estates, dependents, or any other things and persons—by ancient princes or by our fathers, or by God-fearing people for the love of God, shall remain there. Since, as we have said, that holy place appears to have been enriched and established through the generosity of our ancestors, no bishop, whether present or future, nor any successor or ordainer of theirs, nor any other person, shall be permitted in any manner to remove anything from that place, or to usurp anything for himself in that monastery by any authority, or to take anything away under the pretext of an exchange, without the will of the abbot, the congregation, or our permission. They shall not remove or diminish chalices, crosses, altar vestments, sacred books, gold or silver, or anything whatever that has been contributed there or dedicated in the future; nor shall they be permitted or presume to carry such things to the city. Rather, the holy place and its congregation shall be permitted to possess forever whatever has been granted to them by a rightful conveyance.

It also pleased us to insert into this privilege of our serenity the following provision: when the abbot of that house of God has been summoned from this world by divine decree, the congregation of that holy place shall be permitted to choose from among themselves someone whom they find good and suitable, capable of governing and directing the office of abbot according to holy order. Once they have agreed unanimously, he shall be instituted as abbot in that house of God by authority granted by us or by our successors, so that they may be able to pray for the stability of our kingdom, for all our peoples, and for the salvation of the fatherland to the mercy of the Lord.

We appeared to have granted this through the gracious intention and complete devotion of our illustrious men and nobles [Note: In the other charters of Theoderic IV—and, so far as I know, in those of no other kings—there is no mention of the devotion of nobles and magnates.], with this order in particular: just as in the time of the earlier kings, our ancestors, singing in groups was established in that holy basilica, so, as holy order prescribes, it is to be celebrated perpetually in that holy place day and night.

We have decreed this authority of regulation, trusting that Christ assists us in all things: may he help those who preserve it and confound those who attempt to destroy it [Note: Here we have an example of a curse in a royal charter against violators of the charter. Mabillon teaches that such curses were used only very rarely under the Merovingian kings, *De re diplomatica*, p. 102. [The charters of Chilperic, Guntram, and Childeric already contain a more or less similar curse; another, composed with more elaborate wording, appears below in another charter of Theoderic IV (Col. 1146).]].

And so that it may possess firmer force and, with God’s help, remain unharmed and be preserved through time for us and for future generations, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Given on the Kalends of March, in the third year of our reign, at Valenciennes, prosperously in the name of God. Amen . . . . .

[Note: The dots added at the end of the document indicate missing subscriptions.]

### XLII. Charter of Theoderic IV, king of the Franks, by which he takes the monastery of Murbach under his protection and confirms whatever had been granted to it (Year 724)

[Note: Bruschius published this in *Chronicon monasterii Germanici*, fol. 84, and Coccius in *Dagobert*, p. 56; Cointius took it from Coccius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 733, and the editors of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs* from Bruschius, vol. IV, p. 703. Schoepflin, *Alsatian Charters*, vol. I, p. 29, and D. Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. I, documents, p. 56, reprinted it more accurately from an old parchment, as it actually exists—not genuine, as Eckard thought, *Origins of the Habsburgs*, p. 111, but forged, as all who have examined the matter carefully acknowledge. It is certain that all the documents preserved in the archive of this monastery were consumed by fire together with the monastery itself in 828, and that the monastery was subsequently restored by Abbot Celsus, insofar as this could be done from memory and traditions. This is attested by an old inscription carved on stone, which we shall reproduce in full in another volume of this collection. Its chronological evidence uses the completed year 828 from the Incarnation of the Lord. The words are as follows, according to *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. II, documents, p. 190: “Celsus, abbot of the monastery of Murbach, after its burning and the destruction of its charters, wished to write how the illustrious man Hildebert, once king, granted to that place the land of Saverne, from the Cisternata spring to the Gunzinus stream, and thence to Mount Cuoberg through the ash grove called Ascowa, and so by the River Sorne.” These same words, exactly, are read in the charter under examination. Hence one may infer that this document was fabricated to replace the lost genuine charter, but restored most unsuccessfully, since it abounds in indications of forgery. It is enough to point out the principal ones. 1. The initial formula does not appear in Merovingian charters. 2. Theoderic calls Childebert his father [Col. 1140C], although he should have called him Dagobert if he intended by that word to designate his father. 3. The year of the Incarnation and the indiction were not used as chronological markers in this period. 4. All the chronological markers conflict with one another: the year 724 of Christ does not agree with the fifth year of the reign of Theoderic IV, and indiction III agrees neither with the year of Christ nor with the regnal year. 5. The charter shows deliberate imitation of an authentic document, with a seal added; but the seal too reveals itself to be false. It is much larger than the seals, or rather rings, used by Merovingian kings. It displays the bust of a crowned king, holding a fleur-de-lis scepter in his right hand and a globe surmounted by a cross in his left, with the inscription “Theoderic, by the grace of God, king of the Franks,” a form inappropriate before the time of Charles the Bald. We pass over the rest; see D. Grandidier’s dissertation on this charter, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. I, p. 94 ff. We do not deny that several elements of this document are consistent with the truth, as Mabillon writes, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 74, but they cannot obtain any authority from the document itself. We have followed D. Grandidier’s text; it was not worth the effort to transcribe the various readings of the spurious charter. [For the manner in which lost monuments were restored, see what I discussed in *Library of the Diplomatic School*, vol. I, p. 217.]] (Year 724).

[Col. 1139A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Theoderic, by the favor of divine clemency king of the Franks, to the illustrious man Luthfrid.

If we willingly grant and bring to fulfillment the petitions of those who serve God, insofar as they concern their peace and tranquility, we exercise royal custom and trust that this contributes to the reward and stability of our kingdom. Therefore we wish it to be known to those now living and to those who will come after, how the venerable Maurus [Note: Here the document begins in Coccius.], abbot of the monastery of the lord Leobardus, formerly abbot, constructed in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Martin, our special patron, reported to the clemency of our kingdom that his predecessor, the lord Leobardus, formerly abbot, who is known to have built that monastery anew from its foundations through his own work, had received from our illustrious father Childebert, once king, for the needs of that monastery, the land which he himself had taken from the wilderness for cultivation and settlement, with the following boundaries: from the little bridge to Swenheim, as far as the public road to Saverne, and then to the road to Marlen; from there to the boundary at the Cisternata spring, with its adjacent lands, as far as the Gunzinus stream; thence to Mount Cuoberg, through the ash grove, to the place called Oschowa; and thus along the River Sorne as far as the stone cross; then finally to the Murbach stream. He granted it to that monastery for his future reward, so that no one should presume to make fields there, fatten pigs, cut timber, or violate its boundaries in any way. Rather, it was to remain granted to that monastery forever. Whatever, within or outside the prescribed boundaries, in any province or district, he himself or any of his predecessor kings, or his successors, had granted, or whatever any powerful or humble person might thereafter grant to the abbot of the aforesaid place and his successors for the salvation of his soul, was to be freely and lawfully possessed without anyone contradicting or resisting [Note: This is where Coccius ends, apparently escaping the learned man’s intention to transcribe only what seemed to him to belong to Childebert. So Cointius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 316.].

Maurus therefore showed us for confirmation the command of that prince, as well as those of blessed memory of Theodebert, Clothar, Dagobert, Sigebert, and again Dagobert, formerly kings, which were to be reread in the present document. But, for the sake of security, he requested that we confirm for him by this same document everything in that monastery and around its boundaries, and everything pertaining to it. Know, therefore, that, for the sake of God and the increase of our reward, we have graciously received his petition, confirmed it, and granted everything according to royal custom.

We command that whatever, upon examination of the commands of the aforesaid kings, is known to have been granted to that monastery, whether far or near, be preserved by this our authority, in God’s name, for that monastery and for the aforesaid Abbot Maurus and his successors, stable in all respects in our time and in that of future generations, with God’s help.

He likewise asked that we receive him, together with all the dependents and property of his monastery, whether situated near or far, under our protection and defense. Know that we have likewise granted and confirmed this for the increase of our reward. Therefore, by the present decree, we establish and command that neither you, nor your subordinates, nor your successors, nor any person whatsoever, regardless of rank or power, presume to injure or condemn that abbot, any monk, or his people, to do him any unreasonable act inside or outside the monastery, or to take away anything belonging to him. Rather, under the title of immunity and under our protection and defense, let him and his people remain peacefully and securely with all their property and that of their monastery, according to the rule of the fathers, the lord Benedict and the lord Columbanus. Thus the holy congregation may more readily delight in praying frequently, day and night, for the stability of our kingdom to the mercy of the Lord.

Given at Metz, in the monastery of Saint Arnulf, bishop of that place, which is situated in the suburb, on the Kalends of May, in the year 724 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction III, and in the fifth year of the reign of Theoderic. I, Grimaldus, chancellor, have reviewed this.

### XLIII. Charter of Theoderic IV, king of the Franks, by which the monastery of Honau is entrusted to Tubanus (Year 725)

[Note: This charter contains no mention of the monastery of Honau. But from several other documents concerning the monastery of Honau, published above or to be published below, it is clear that Benedict and Tubanus, who are discussed here, presided over that monastery: Tubanus, namely, when Benedict, advanced in years or for some other reason, had asked to have him associated with him. Those who supposed that the abbot of Honau was called by the two names Benedict and Tubanus had not examined this charter carefully enough. The two men are plainly distinguished: Benedict is called “father of fathers” and abbot, while Tubanus is called brother, to whom the monastery is entrusted in Benedict’s place. Coccius published this document in *Dagobert*, p. 132, without stating the source from which he drew it. Nor is it true, as certain writers—namely Mabillon in *Annals*, vol. II, p. 59, and the authors of *New Christian Gaul*, vol. V, col. 833—thought, that he said he had taken it from an old manuscript from which he had copied several others. Mabillon, in the place cited, although he admits that he detected unusual formulas in this document, did not consider it wholly suspect; D. Grandidier likewise supports it, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. I, p. 400 and documents, p. 59, having reprinted it from an eleventh-century manuscript. Yet everything in it appears fabricated and exposes it as false. 1. The name of King Theoderic is improperly placed at the beginning, as though this were a royal charter, although the document is addressed to Luitfrid, Eberhard, and Benedict. Nor would the king have said that he was appointing Tubanus in his own place to bear the burden of the abbacy. 2. It is truly strange that a charter composed in the form of a letter addressed to Benedict should be falsely represented as subscribed by Benedict himself. 3. The author of the charter says that he entrusts the burden of the abbacy to Tubanus in his own place; this implies that Benedict himself was the author of the charter as abbot, but that conflicts with the entire context of the document. Since this charter is burdened with so many defects, we do not believe it may be counted among genuine documents. We follow Coccius’s text and place within brackets the variants found in D. Grandidier’s edition.] (Year 725).

Theoderic, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to Luitfrid the duke, Eberhard the domesticus, the lord father of fathers [these two words are absent in Grandidier], and the venerable lord Benedict, abbot.

Since, according to our will and that of our bishop, as well as of the dukes, counts, domestici, officials, and myself, it is fitting that we should choose someone in our place to bear the burden of the abbacy, therefore, venerable brother Tubanus, we commend this venerable rule to your holiness. For just as the sun blazes and moves across the whole sky from the beginning of day, so the reputation of your outstanding benevolence shines brightly, widely spread throughout the entire world.

Therefore, as we have said above, from this day forward we entrust to your holiness this place, that congregation, the holy rule, and the stability of the monks. The Gospel of Matthew testifies to you [Note: Whether through ignorance or carelessness, these words are presented as though taken from the Gospel of Matthew, although they come from the First Letter of Paul to Timothy, chapter III, verse 13]: “For he who has served well will receive for himself a good work”; and you must consider, good Father, that you will stand to render an account for each person on the day of judgment, and that, by preserving this congregation, you will obtain a hundredfold reward for yourself on the day of judgment. Therefore, with Christ’s favor, we faithfully [Grandidier: firmly] commend this rule to you.

Sign of Luitfrid the duke. Sign of Eberhard the domesticus. Sign of the lord Benedict, abbot, who requested that this charter be made. [Here Grandidier has gaps between many names.] I, Haimo, unworthy sinner and priest, wrote and subscribed this little charter at the request of the lord Benedict.

[Note: The chronological markers are absent, but this document can appropriately be placed under the year 725. Benedict was still governing the monastery of Honau alone in 723, as stated in the preceding note; by 726, however, Tubanus is known to have been placed in charge of this monastery in Benedict’s place, although Benedict retained the title and dignity of abbot. Hence, when the abbot of this monastery is mentioned in certain charters, the names of both abbots are given: Benedict or Tubanus.]

### XLIV. Charter of Theoderic IV, king of the Franks, by which he declares, after a hearing, that the estate of Baudrino was sold to the monastery of Saint-Denis (Year 726)

[Note: Dublet published this in *Ecclesiastical Antiquities of Saint-Denis*, p. 686; Cointius reprinted it in *Annals*, vol. III, p. 802, as did the editors of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 704. Dublet, Cointius, in the places cited, and Labbé in his *Miscellanies*, vol. II, p. 432, attribute this document to Theoderic III, but wrongly. Mabillon proves that it belongs to Theoderic IV, *De re diplomatica*, p. 628, and *Annals*, vol. II, p. 75, since it was issued under Abbot Godobaldus, who governed the monastery of Saint-Denis from 723 to 748, as is attested by a parchment codex written more than eight hundred years ago [the Rheims Church codex entitled *On the Miracles of Saint-Denis*]. Felibianus supports Mabillon, *History of the Abbots of Saint-Denis*, p. 38, and even Germonius, a vigorous opponent of Mabillon, *On the Ancient Charters of the Frankish Kings*, vol. II, p. 126. Mabillon had initially assigned this charter to Theoderic III, in the place cited, p. 246, but acknowledged and corrected his error, *De re diplomatica*, p. 628. We publish it on the authority of Dublet.] (Year 726).

Theuderic, king of the Franks, illustrious man. When, in the name of God, we were seated at Pontegurre in our palace, together with our faithful men, to hear everyone’s cases and settle just judgments, there came the agents of the basilica of our special patron, the lord martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily, and where the venerable man Godobaldus appears to preside as abbot. They brought a complaint against the illustrious man Ermenteus, saying that his estate called Baudrino, situated on the River Hyssera in the district of Cameliacum, which had come to him by lawful inheritance from his father Nordebertus and his brother Gunthecharius, both formerly belonging to that lawful inheritance, he had transferred and confirmed to the venerable Abbot Godobaldus on behalf of the basilica of the lord Dionysius under the title of sale. The deed of sale was read aloud in the present hearing, and Ermenteus himself was present.

Our nobles asked him whether he had sold that estate of Baudrino to Godobaldus, abbot on behalf of the lord Dionysius; whether he had received the price for it; and whether he stood as guarantor for it. Ermenteus then publicly declared that he had sold the estate in the aforesaid place of Baudrino, in the aforementioned district of Cameliacum, to the Abbot Godobaldus on behalf of his basilica of the lord Dionysius; that, according to his own declaration, he had received the price for it; that he had requested the sale to be made and confirmed; and that he had stood as guarantor and wished to continue to do so.

Therefore, together with our nobles, we decreed as follows. Since the illustrious man Cumrodobaldus, count of our palace, testified that the case had been conducted and investigated in this manner, we order that the agents of the aforesaid party, on behalf of the venerable Abbot Godobaldus and his basilica of the lord Dionysius, should possess the aforesaid estate of Baudrino in the aforementioned district of Cameliacum, together with its lands, houses, buildings erected upon them, tenants, dependents, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, livestock, estates, mills, flocks with shepherds of either sex, and all additions and appurtenances belonging or pertaining to it, wholly and in every respect, as confirmed and adjudicated by examination of their documents, forever.

If necessity should later arise for the venerable Abbot Godobaldus, his basilica of the lord Dionysius, or his successors, the aforementioned Ermenteus and his heirs shall endeavor to defend them in the role of guarantor against anyone.

Gairebaldus reviewed this on behalf of Eonardus.

Judgment rendered on the third day of March, in the sixth year of our reign, at Pontegurre in our palace.

### XLV. Charter of Theoderic IV, king of the Franks, by which he confirms gifts made or to be made to the monastery of Murbach and the privileges granted to it (Year 727)

[Note: This document, full of defects, appears in Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, appendix, p. 700; Lünig, *Ecclesiastical Miscellany*, vol. IV, p. 173 and vol. V, p. 951; and in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, vol. I, October, p. 434. It is somewhat less inaccurately printed by La Guille, *History of Alsace*, documents, p. 13, and in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 706. Schoepflin published it on the authority of the original and made the original itself public by engraving it in copper. We reprint it according to Schoepflin’s reading. Perminus, otherwise Pirminius, expelled from his monastery on the island of Reichenau, came to Alsace, as Hermannus Contractus records in his *Chronicle* under the year 727 [in D. Bouquet, vol. III, p. 330], where he founded the monastery of Murbach, with expenses supplied by Count Eberhard, around the year 727. In that same year Theoderic issued the charter presented here for the benefit of the new monastery.] (Year 727).

[Col. 1143D]

Theoderic, king of the Franks, to the apostolic men, the fathers and bishops, and also to the illustrious men, patricians, counts, and all officials, both present and future.

If we grant with devoted mind the petitions of priests that concern the property of churches, we trust that through this we shall obtain the Lord Jesus Christ, the giver of all good things, as our recompense. Accordingly, since the venerable man Perminus, bishop by the grace of God [Note: Hermannus Contractus calls Perminus a chorepiscopus in his *Chronicle*; here he is called simply a bishop. Was he a regional bishop? Mabillon does not venture to decide, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 73. [The term *chorepiscopus* is not found in Hermannus at the place cited.]], in our time, together with his monks, inspired by God, undertook a pilgrimage for the Gospel of Christ and attempted, in the vast wilderness called the Vosges, in the district of Alsace, at the place called the Travelers’ Refuge, formerly called Murbach, on the estate of our faithful Count Eberhard, with his assistance and by God’s gift, to establish a monastery of men and institute a holy community there in honor of God and of Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, ever Virgin, and of Saint Michael the archangel, and of the blessed apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul, and of Saint Leodegar the martyr with his companions, where those servants of God might enjoy a solitary life under the holy rule, the man of God Perminus, bishop, together with our aforementioned faithful Count Eberhard, requested our serenity that we should issue this command concerning the entire body of property belonging to that monastery: whatever it appears to possess or have bestowed upon it at present, and whatever thereafter, by God’s inspiration, should rightly be contributed or assigned there, we should fully confirm in God’s name by our command.

Know that we have done this in all respects for our reward. We have issued the following decree for the aforesaid servants of God: no bishop, whether present or future, nor their successors or ordainers, nor anyone exercising judicial power, shall be able by any means or in any manner to take away or remove anything from that place. Thus the household of Christ assembled there in God’s name may more easily and peacefully possess through the ages whatever has been rightly assigned to them, and, preserving the holy rule by the privilege they showed us in their possession, may remain in tranquility by God’s command. Nothing granted to such a household of Christ so that it may sing God’s praise day and night is taken away from canonical authority.

Therefore, for the sake of heavenly regard, know that we have granted this benefit so that whatever the aforesaid men of God acquire or cultivate for that monastery, and whatever our aforementioned faithful Eberhard has confirmed there by his documents, or whatever has been or shall be contributed by others, may, under our immunity, benefit them in every way in their own times, without anyone causing them disturbance, with God’s help.

It is added, however, that if the abbot of that congregation requests bishops to ordain priests or deacons for the celebration of Masses, the bishop must institute them without accepting payment. If he is asked to consecrate the church, provide chrism, church tablets, or steps, he must do so without accepting payment. If he refuses, the abbot may ask any other bishop who will provide these things freely, and that bishop may do so. At no time shall the diocese of the bishop in whose diocese this monastery is situated have any power to disturb it. Neither that bishop, nor the archdeacon, nor the judges of the church shall dare to send a tax, demand food-supplies or service, or seek any honor or due from the monastery’s property.

If the abbot of that congregation is called from this life, no one from another monastery, from a city, through family connection, or appointed by a bishop, whether through authority, payment, or any other device, and no judge whatsoever, shall presume to appoint an abbot there. Nor, whenever necessity arises, shall anyone institute an abbot except the one whom the congregation and its better part have chosen. In accordance with what their rule and privilege contain, they themselves shall appoint a pastor worthy of them.

It also pleased us, for the integrity and stability of our kingdom, to add that this monastery, under the defense and protection of God and our royal lineage, may remain unshaken through succeeding ages. No public judicial authority, whether present or future, shall presume to enter the courts or territories of the monastery anywhere to hear cases or exact fines from any quarter, or to take sureties. Whatever, from free persons as well as from dependents residing throughout the monastery’s territories, the treasury might expect by way of fines or military levies, shall be assigned in full to the lights and provisions of the aforesaid servants of God and, through our indulgence, to their use. Whether during our reign or in the succeeding times of later kings, no one shall presume to overturn what we have granted for the love and fear of God. Rather, with God’s help, what we have decreed shall remain inviolate in complete and peaceful immunity.

And so that this command may be held more firmly with regard to that monastery, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Theoderic, king of the Franks. Issued in the month of July, on the twelfth day, in the seventh year of our reign; Gundulfi-villa [Note: Schoepflinus rightly numbers Gundulfi-villa among the royal estates, as above in the note. D. Germain, however, complains that it was omitted in the work on the royal estates; and we are surprised that Schoepflinus should have overlooked it, since Dom Germain discusses it at length in that very work, in Mabillon, *De Re Diplomatica*, p. 285 and following, where he says that no mention of this royal estate is found earlier than in the diploma under discussion.], in God’s name, prosperously. Amen. Gerbald presented it.

## XLVI. Diploma of Theoderic IV, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the gifts bestowed upon the church of Saint Vincent of Paris by Walter and his wife Goda

[Note: It appears in Bulliardus, *Historia Abbatiae S. Germani a Pratis*, documentary proofs, p. 8, who took it from the cartulary of that monastery. Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 542, attributes this diploma to Theoderic III and considers it dated around the year 678, because at that time Autharius was in charge of Saint Vincent of Paris [in later times, and down to our own, Saint-Germain-des-Prés and the Holy Cross], and, as he states on p. 614, Autharius lived no longer than 697. But Bulliardus correctly observes, in the work cited above, p. 17, that the diploma concerns another Autharius, who must be believed to have presided over the same monastery under Theoderic IV. The authors of the *Nouvelle Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 422, judge that this second Autharius succeeded Sigefrid as abbot of Saint-Germain [Col. 1146C], and that he governed the abbey from 730 [Col. 1146D] to 735. Certainly, the diploma presented here was issued by a king whose father is said to have been Dagobert and whose great-grandfather (*atavus*) was Childebert. This does not suit Theoderic III, whose father was Clovis and among whose ancestors there was no Childebert. Theoderic IV’s father, however, was Dagobert and his grandfather was Childebert; and *atavus* could easily have been written for *avus* through a copyist’s error. Indeed, no one will be troubled by the fact that in these times *atavus* may have been used for any ancestor. [The chronological notes of the diploma would have furnished grounds for doubt, had any existed in the cartulary from which Bulliardus copied it.] Since the chronological notes are lacking, we place this instrument, with Bulliardus, under the year 730. [By this diploma the king confirms to the church of Saint Vincent and the Holy Cross numerous properties granted to it by Walter, one of the nobles, and his wife Goda, under certain conditions. No record survives of what happened concerning these conditions.]] (A.D. 730).

Theoderic, by the grace of God king of the Franks. If we grant assent to the petitions of God’s servants or handmaids concerning places belonging to the saints and to people who fear God, we trust that this will benefit our future reward [Col. 1146B], as well as the stability and protection of our kingdom, in God’s name; so that, because of this, they may thereafter always be more eager to preserve their fidelity toward the royal authority and to pray daily to the Lord for the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore we make known to all our faithful that one of our nobles, named Walter, and his wife, named Goda, approached our clemency, requesting that we confirm by our authority the gift which they were making from their possessions situated in the pagus of Bourges to the church of the Holy Cross and Saint Vincent, situated in the suburb of Paris, where the precious confessor, Lord Germanus, rests bodily.

The following places are named: Fraxinum, with its churches; Caldunum, with the church of Lord Monialis the Confessor [Col. 1146C] on the river Chrosa; Graegilidum, with the church of Lord Germanus; Argentonem, with its church; and whatever they appeared to possess beyond the Loire, together with houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, tithes, flocks with their shepherds, male and female servants, waters and watercourses, and, in addition, everything belonging in full to the aforesaid possessions.

Namely, after Walter’s death, if his wife Goda should survive in the body, she was to be consecrated to God and serve God in the church of Lord Monialis the Confessor, together with many girls consecrated to God and associated with her. Walter and Goda, with equal and common consent, and with our authority confirming it, bequeathed that place together with the aforesaid possessions to the church of the Holy Cross and Saint Vincent the Levite and Martyr, where the precious confessor Germanus rests bodily, in the suburb of the city of Paris, under the rule and administration of Autharius, abbot of the aforesaid church and saints.

This was done on the condition that the aforesaid abbot, after the deposition of the aforesaid Goda, or the abbot who should succeed him after her death, or the rectors who should succeed him through future ages, should prudently elect and appoint an abbess there in the frequently mentioned church of the Holy Cross and the aforesaid saints.

We have confirmed this testamentary document, for the love of God and the aforesaid saints, and for the remedy of ourselves, our wife, and our sons, and for the salvation and repose of our father Dagobert II and our great-grandfather Childebert, kings of the Franks, by our hand and the authority of our seal.

Moreover, at the request of our faithful Walter and his wife Goda, we added this provision: if anyone—which God forbid, and which we in no way believe will happen—should attempt to challenge or violate this testamentary document, or should attempt to withdraw or remove anything from the rule of the church of the Holy Cross and Saint Vincent the Levite and Martyr, and of the lord, blessed Germanus, or of the rectors or monks of that church, let him first incur the wrath of God and, together with Judas the traitor and also Dathan and Abiron, suffer infernal punishments without end [Col. 1147C]; moreover, let him be compelled to pay three hundred pounds of gold to our treasury and fail entirely to obtain what he claims.

## XLVII. Diploma of Chilperic (Childeric III), by which, at the petition of Gauziolenus, bishop of Le Mans, he confirms the immunities granted to the estate of Arduno

[Note: We know this instrument from no other source than the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, in Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 287. The name Chilperic was incorrectly prefixed to it instead of Childeric, as Mabillon rightly observes, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 122. For under King Chilperic the church of Le Mans was not governed by Gauziolenus, who succeeded Herlemund, whose charter, dated 721, we published on p. 330.

We would attribute the error to a careless copyist if this charter could be considered genuine; but other indications reveal it as a spurious product. It may therefore be inferred that a forger, through ignorance, made the mistake while fabricating the false charter, in order to lend credibility to another charter which we presented elsewhere and demonstrated to be spurious.

These charters are by no means consistent with one another. The charter now under discussion confirms immunities which it says were granted by King Dagobert to Berarius, Achilbert, and Herlemund, bishops of Le Mans; whereas the other charter asserts that the same immunities had previously been granted to Berarius and Achilbert by Childeric.

We interpret the chronological note as follows. The Council of Soissons is known to have been convened on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the second year of Childeric’s reign—that is, on March 3, when the second regnal year was already in progress. Therefore March 2 of the first year of Childeric’s reign appears to fall in the year of Christ 743. See Longuer, *Annales*, in vol. III of the *Collection of the Historians of the Franks*, p. 704.] (A.D. 743).

Chilperic, king of the Franks, illustrious man. If we preserve the deeds of our ancestors, we trust that our own will remain stable forever. Therefore the apostolic man, our father in Christ, Gauziolenus, bishop of the city of Le Mans, represented to us that our cousin Dagobert, formerly king, had once granted by his precept to the late Lord Berarius, bishop, and to Bishop Achilbert, and also to Lord Herlemund [Col. 1147D], bishop, that whatever from the estate of that church called Arduno, in the pagus of Poitou, was expected by the treasury [Col. 1148A], no judge or anyone else should exact; that no one should establish lodgings in that estate, exact payments, hear lawsuits, demand provisions, or seek or presume to exact any earthly revenue, except that these things should be assigned to the lamps of that church of Le Mans, built in honor of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs and our patrons.

Afterward he granted the same to Bishop Herlemund, who held that place after Bishop Achilbert. The bishop therefore asserts that he has those precepts in his possession and that this benefit has been preserved from that time until now. But for complete security he petitioned our Highness to confirm this again by our authority to Bishop Gauziolenus and to the church of Saint Gervasius and Protasius the Martyr. Know that we did not refuse him, but granted and confirmed everything as requested.

We therefore command that, just as it is established that our cousin Dagobert, formerly king, and our other royal ancestors and predecessors made complete grants of immunity from that estate of Arduno to that church, so we too henceforth grant and confirm by our authority that at no time shall any judge presume in that estate to hear lawsuits, demand provisions, payments, any kind of tax, or any earthly revenue that might be expected by our treasury, or to seek or exact it; except that, after the precepts of our ancient ancestors and of our cousin King Dagobert have been examined, it shall perpetually be granted and assigned to the lamps of the aforesaid basilica of Saints Gervasius and Protasius the Martyr.

And so that this authority may be firmer and preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by our subscription. Chilperic the king subscribed. Issued on March 2, in the first year of our reign, at Compiègne, prosperously.

## XLVII. Diploma of Childeric III, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunities granted by King Theoderic to the monastery of Sithiu

[Note: Mabillon extracted it from the cartulary of Folquin, *De Re Diplomatica*, p. 610; Miraeus reprinted it from Mabillon, *Opera Diplomatica*, vol. II, p. 929.

Two things in particular deserve notice in this diploma. First, Childeric calls Theoderic his *parent*. Some understand this word to mean father, others kinsman. Mabillon defends the latter interpretation, *De Re Diplomatica*, cited above, and *Annales*, vol. II, p. 121, but on weaker arguments: namely, on the authority of three charters issued in favor of the bishops of Le Mans, in which Childeric calls Dagobert his cousin; whereas he would rather have called him grandfather if he acknowledged Theoderic, who was Dagobert’s son, as his father.

But the charters on which Mabillon relies have no authority. We have shown one of them elsewhere to be spurious, and we shall present the others in their proper places; they are of no better quality. Their testimony therefore does not overturn the opinion of Malbranc, *De Morinis*, book IV, chapter LXIII; Cointius, *Annales*, vol. V, p. 108; and many others, who infer from the diploma under discussion that Theoderic IV was the father of Childeric III.

This conclusion is made more doubtful by Mabillon’s observation, *De Re Diplomatica*, p. 610, note: in Childeric’s time, fathers were designated by the word *genitor*, while blood-relations were called *parentes*. Yet in this very diploma of Childeric, *parentes* is used in the broader sense of any predecessors.

Second, Childeric’s diploma is said to have been issued at the palace of Crisciacum. From this Cointius astutely argues, *Annales*, vol. V, p. 108, that Childeric lived in royal residences and did not hide at the estate of Mamaccas, as later writers invented. Iperius makes no mention of this diploma in his *Chronicle of Saint Bertin*, as can be seen in Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 482. We published in its proper place, p. 330, the diploma of Theoderic IV confirmed by Childeric.

It remains briefly to examine the chronological notes of Childeric’s diploma. It is established that the Council of Soissons was convened in the second year of his reign, on the fifth day before the Nones of March in the Christian year 744. Therefore April of the first year of the same reign appears to have fallen in the Christian year 743; hence chronographers correctly place this diploma under the year 743. See Longuer, *Annales*, in vol. III of the *Collection of the Historians of the Franks*, p. 704. Compare the *Sithiu Cartulary*, p. 51, edited by the distinguished Guérard in 1841.] (A.D. 743).

Childeric, king of the Franks, to the illustrious *graviones* (counts), and all their officials and subordinates, both present and future, in whatever jurisdictions the monastery of Sithiu appears to possess.

He whom divine goodness raises to kingship ought to preserve the deeds of his ancestors, especially those which royal clemency is known to have granted to churches or holy places as an eternal reward; these ought to be preserved forever.

Therefore let your greatness and usefulness know that the venerable man Waimarus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, brought to the notice of our royal clemency that our ancestor Theoderic, formerly king, had granted by a precept confirmed with his own hand, to his predecessor Erkembod, abbot, and to his aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, the following benefit.

Whatever he had acquired within our treasury—wherever it might be—in any pagus or territory, or whatever he might thereafter find available for acquisition, and whatever good men who feared God had given or would give to the aforesaid monastery for the sake of their souls, he had granted to it. Whatever he had acquired from our treasury or might thereafter acquire, except the land from which cartage services proceeded, he had also granted; and no judicial authority was to demand, exact, or seek from it any land revenues or public obligations on that account.

The abbot therefore affirms that he has the aforesaid precept of our ancestor Theoderic, formerly king, in his possession concerning this matter, and he has now shown it to us for rereading. He also asserts that the benefits granted by it have been preserved from that time until now [Col. 1149C]. But for the sake of security he petitioned our Highness to confirm this concerning the holy place by our pronouncement. Know that, for the Lord’s name and out of reverence for that holy place, we have granted and confirmed everything as requested.

We therefore command and order that whatever our aforesaid ancestor Theoderic, formerly king, granted to the aforesaid Abbot Erkembod and to the aforesaid holy place from that benefit, as set out above, for the increase of his reward, and which has been preserved in a straight course from that time until now, shall henceforth, after examination of the precepts of that prince, be more fully confirmed in God’s name by our precept, just as those precepts declare.

Accordingly, henceforth, under this arrangement, let the benefits granted to Waimarus, abbot, and to his monastery of Sithiu, always remain fully confirmed in every respect. Let them fear no opposition or impediment from public judges at any time, so that the community may continually beseech the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and the salvation of the fatherland.

And so that this authority may be firmer and preserved in every respect through the ages, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by our subscriptions.

The sign of the glorious King Childeric.

Issued on April 23, in the first year of our reign, at the palace of Crisciacum, in God’s name, prosperously. Amen.

## XLIX. Diploma of Childeric III, king of the Franks, by which he confirms, at the request of Gauziolenus, bishop of Le Mans, the immunities granted by his predecessors to the monastery of Anisola, together with the annual census which the abbot of that monastery paid to the bishops of Le Mans

[Note: This spurious confirmation among the spurious instruments appears in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, in Mabillon, *Annales*, p. 386; the collectors of the *Historians of the Franks* reprinted it, vol. IV, p. 709 [Col. 1150D]. We published in its proper place another equally spurious diploma, purportedly issued by Dagobert, and another in which the census to be paid by the abbot of Anisola to the bishop of Le Mans is asserted.

[The diploma of Childebert III now under discussion confirms these fictitious grants, especially mentioning the annual census to be paid to the church of Le Mans as a sign of subjection.]

All these instruments must be counted among the spurious documents, as is shown by the formal judgment by which, having been produced in litigation, they were condemned as false and ordered to be abolished in the ninth century. See Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. III, p. 128, article 18, and the *Collection of the Historians of the Franks*, vol. VII, p. 297. We have discussed these matters more than once.

The instrument presented here lacks chronological notes. We have tried to place it in an order compatible both with the reign of Childeric III and with the episcopate of Gauziolenus of Le Mans.] (A.D. 743).

[Col. 1150C]

Childeric, king of the Franks, illustrious man. If we preserve the deeds of our ancestors, we trust that our own will remain stable forever.

Therefore the apostolic man, our father in Christ, Gauziolenus, bishop of the city of Le Mans, represented to us that concerning the little monastery belonging to the church of his see, called Anisola, in which Lord Karilefus lies bodily, our cousin Dagobert, formerly king, and his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had made precepts for his predecessors, Lord Domnolus the bishop, Bishop Hadoindus, the late Bishop Bercharius, Bishop Aiglibert, and also the late Bishop Herlemund; and that they had confirmed by their own hands the immunities of his see and church, so that it might never be alienated or withdrawn from its title, church, or city, either then or in the future.

The bishop therefore affirms that he has those precepts in his possession and that from that time until now the little monastery has been preserved for his cathedral church [Col. 1151B]. But for complete security he petitioned our Highness to confirm this again by our authority to Lord Gauziolenus the bishop and to his city church. Know that we did not refuse him, but granted and confirmed everything.

We therefore command that, just as it is established that our cousin Dagobert, formerly king, and our other royal ancestors and predecessors granted complete immunity from that little monastery to the church, so we too henceforth grant and confirm by our authority that no judge shall ever presume in that little monastery or its dependencies to hear lawsuits, demand provisions, payments, any kind of tax, or any earthly revenue that might be expected by our treasury, or at any time seek or exact it; except that, after the precepts of the ancient princes, our ancestors, and of our cousin Dagobert, formerly king, have been examined, it shall perpetually be granted and assigned to the lamps of the aforesaid mother church and city basilica.

Moreover, the aforesaid Bishop Gauziolenus requested that we issue our precept concerning the lease (*precaria*) which he had made of the little monastery of Anisola to a certain abbot named Didonus [Note: Perhaps *Ibbolenus* should be read instead of *Didonus*. We possess, and reproduce elsewhere, the lease-charter of Ibbolenus, abbot of Anisola. It is indeed spurious, but it was inserted together with Childeric’s diploma among the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*. In it Ibbolenus declares that he holds the monastery of Anisola from the church of Le Mans subject to an annual census.], just as the aforesaid kings, his predecessors and ancestors, had done for their predecessors and for the abbots of the aforesaid little monastery.

The precepts of the aforesaid kings and the leases of the holy bishops of his city were therefore shown to us for rereading; we had all of them read aloud before us. In them we found it inserted that the abbots of the aforesaid little monastery of Anisola paid a census to the bishops of that city and to the senior church: six pounds of wax; for the use of the canonical brothers serving God in the aforesaid church, on the Lord’s Supper, a full modius of eggs and two prepared bottles filled with the best wine; and for the use of the bishops of that city, one excellent staff and two finely prepared shoes, together with many other gifts and services.

Having learned all this in detail, we ordered that this precept of our authority be made as he requested. By it we command that, for as long as the aforesaid bishop lives, the abbot shall hold the aforesaid monastery by the lease and benefice of the aforesaid Gauziolenus and his successors, and shall pay the aforesaid census every year without any delay, as it is contained in their leases, and shall always remain obedient to him in all things.

After his death, however, the little monastery shall return to the aforesaid mother church, and to its right and power and that of the bishops or rectors, in complete integrity and with all improvements made upon it, without anyone’s assignment or prohibition, so that thereafter the bishops and rectors of that holy church may freely enjoy in every respect the authority to do whatever they canonically and reasonably decide.

And so that this authority may endure with firm stability, by God’s help, in both the present and future times, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the seals made with our own hand.

## L. Diploma of Childeric III, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the immunities granted to the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy

[Note: Martène published it, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. II, col. 17, taking it from the archive of Stavelot; Bertholet reprinted it on the authority of Martène, *Histoire du Luxembourg*, vol. II, documentary proofs, p. 36.

The collectors of the *Historians of the Franks*, vol. IV, p. 711, tried to correct its atrocious corruption with the aid of one of the formulas of Marculf, book I, formula 2, which agrees fairly well with Martène’s readings. That formula, however, added certain things which they inserted into the instrument published by Martène, and omitted others which they deleted, so that they appear to have published the formula rather than Childeric’s actual diploma.

We have followed Martène’s exact readings, although we recognize that they are corrupt; for it is our practice to transcribe instruments faithfully, with their errors. [Col. 1152D] The year is lacking. We prefix the year 744 with Bertholet, although we admit that nothing prevents the diploma from having been issued at the beginning of Childeric’s reign.

This agrees at least with the opinion of Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, pp. 109 and 166, who is reluctant to admit that Anglinus was still in charge of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy when Childeric was called to the throne. Agilulf had succeeded Anglinus, and had already obtained the episcopal insignia of Cologne in 746.

But should Anglinus be considered identical with Agilulf elsewhere mentioned? Since the name Anglinus is found in the most corrupt instruments, and Anglinus is not known from any other source, this may perhaps be conjectured. [Although this is Cointius’s conjecture, the authors of the *Nouvelle Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, col. 941, assert that Cointius later abandoned his position.] We shall return to these matters when two other charters concerning the same Anglinus are discussed.] (A.D. 744).

Hildricus, king of the Franks, to the illustrious man Karloman, mayor of the palace and governor of our palace, who established us upon the throne of the kingdom; to our apostolic fathers, and also to the emperors [Note: More correctly, as in the formula of Marculf, “illustrious men.”], all counts and all officials, present and future.

It is fitting that the chief clemency should lend a kindly ear, among other petitions, to priests of every rank, and that what is requested for fear of God and for reverence of Christ’s name should unquestionably be brought to effect. Thus a bond of reward may be formed when an appropriate request is granted for the peace of God’s servants; and the faithful prophet does not doubt that through this he will attain the grace of the Most High. For according to sacred Scripture, devotion is especially offered by the household of faith, because it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Therefore, since Abbot Anglinus governs the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy, which are situated in our forest of the Ardennes and appear to have been built upon our treasury, and since he has been ordered by our promise to rule them, and since a great crowd of monks is known to be gathered there in unity where basilicas have been built in honor of the lords Saints Peter and Paul and Saint Martin, it has pleased our clemency to publish a grant of our authority for the peace of those servants of God.

Under this order of tranquillity, with the Lord’s protection, may those monks always remain according to the rule of religion. Let this document explain the matter more clearly: nothing is to be removed from canonical institution, and whatever is granted by the household of faith for the tranquillity of peace is not to be considered something that anyone may detract from us or that is newly decreed without reason, since, according to the institution of the bishops and by royal correction, the monasteries of the saints—Stavelot and Malmedy—are seen to stand by a privilege of liberty granted in ancient times.

Therefore, if anything has been assigned there to that abbot, or is thereafter added, according to what Abbot Anglinus or the other lord abbots have granted to the aforesaid monasteries or to the monks serving there, and according to the contents of the privileges which the aforesaid Abbot Anglinus produced for us to review, we recognize and know that it has been enacted.

No bishop, therefore, as we have said, neither one presently in office nor any successor, nor an archdeacon, nor their administrators, nor any other person, may thereafter introduce any arrangement into that place, or claim for himself any authority over the monasteries, or apply anything that is written, or diminish anything under the pretext of an exchange, or remove anything brought into the monasteries.

Nor may anything be taken away from the monasteries or their cells; rather, according to the grants and the terms of this authority, everything there should prosper and increase for the monasteries without disturbance.

We add further that, under this privilege, after an abbot has departed, the community of those places shall have the power to elect and install an abbot regularly from among themselves. They shall also have permission to acquire or exchange fiscal lands.

We further add that no judge or any other person shall have any license to defraud the aforesaid monasteries in any matter concerning their possessions without the consent of those servants of God, or to appropriate anything from the monastery for his own use. Whoever does so shall incur the wrath of God and our displeasure and shall suffer grievous loss to the treasury.

We have especially wished to add this full provision: whether a possession has devolved from our generosity, from the decision of the abbot himself or of others, or from anyone else, at no time shall any judicial authority—or any successor—presume to enter there to hear cases or to exact anything.

Rather, with complete immunity, you shall not presume to exact any toll for your own use from these monasteries, which appear to remain at the fortress of Dionant and at Hogio. Whatever our treasury might perhaps expect from their people, whether freeborn or servile, and whatever lawfully returns to those estates at the *mitium* [Note: The earlier editors, except D. Bouquet, wrote *initio*, following Martène and Bertholet. Bouquet has *mitio*, and I believe this word should be preferred. It is found in charters of the years 752 and 760 edited by Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, cols. 26 and 27, and in formulas XIII and XIV of book I of Marculf.

What *mitium* means is not entirely clear. Bignonius believed that the word signified a *missus*, and I myself initially adopted that view. On reconsideration, however, I suspect that in the charters and formulas cited, *mitium* should be understood as the immunity court at which the people residing within the territory of the immunity were required to assemble. Perhaps one might not implausibly derive the word from the Saxon verb *metan*, “to meet,” whence *mot* and *gemot*, “assembly,” and the word still used among the English, “meeting.”]—or whatever it might be possible to expect from our indulgence, and whatever appears to be cultivated in their fields, should nevertheless, in God’s name, benefit us who live in the present and those who succeed us in time, as a return for our reward, so that the monks may delight in imploring the immense mercy of the Lord for eternal salvation, the prosperity of the fatherland, and the stability of the kingdom.

Our decree approving this precept in every respect, and so that it may be firmer and preserved forever, we have endeavored to execute it with the subscription of our hand. Cadecissa’s hand recognized it. The sign of Childeric, the glorious lord king.

An immunity for the monastery of Stavelot or Malmedy, so that there should be no other abbot except those whom the monks themselves should choose, as God’s will may be. Issued in the month of July.

[Col. 1155]

# APPENDIX TO THE ROYAL DIPLOMAS. Pious Donations and Testaments, and Foundations of the Bishops, Abbots, Mayors of the Palace, Dukes, and More Illustrious Men of Francia and the Franks, down to the End of the Second Dynasty

*(Years 659–748.)*

*(From Breq., Diplomatic Charters, vol. II.)*

## I. Charter by which Adroaldus gives to Bertinus, Mommolinus, and Ebertramnus a portion of his inheritance for the construction of a monastery

[Note: This charter was published by Miraeus, *Opera Diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 7; Cointius, *Annales*, vol. II, p. 229; Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. I, p. 401; Malbrancq, *De Morinis*, book III, chapter XXVII; and the authors of the *Nouvelle Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, documentary section, p. 109; no one used the original.

We publish it from an authentic copy preserved in our archives, partly transcribed from a mutilated original and partly from the cartulary of Folquin; these matters are discussed at length in our preface. [Compare the *Chartularium of Saint Bertin*, edited by the distinguished Guérard in 1841, p. 18.]

In the lawsuit between the church of Thérouanne and the monastery of Saint Bertin, the authenticity of this charter was contested. It is neither our purpose to examine here the arguments advanced on both sides, nor do the limits assigned to our notes permit it. It is enough to say that the charter’s detractors have pointed to no diplomatic defect in it itself, and have drawn their objections from no source other than conjectures or testimonies whose authority does not diminish the charter’s credibility, which is supported by other testimony of no slight weight. On these matters see the *Dissertation on the Origin of the Monastery of Saint Bertin*, Paris, 1734, and the *Inquiry into the Historical Truth of the Church of Saint Audomarus*, likewise published there in 1754.] (A.D. 648).

[Col. 1155A]

To the holy lords and fathers Bertinus, Mommolinus, and Ebertramnus, I, Adroaldus, in God’s name, with sound mind and sound judgment and after mature deliberation, insofar as the Lord deigns to cleanse away my worldly sins and enticements, give to you the whole property of my hereditary share in the district of Ternois, which we had wished to give to the lord father Audomar, apostolic man, for the construction of his hospice. But he gave us sounder and better counsel: that I should transfer this property to you, so that you might build there a monastery in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, where monks should live, and where the blessed poor in spirit and members of the household of faith should be gathered, whose voices are known to resound daily in the ears of the Lord, whose petitions the Lord hears and fulfills.

Therefore, to you, fathers in Christ, by this deed of gift I give, in the district of Ternois, a villa of my property called Sithiu, above the river Agnion, with all its appurtenances, or dependencies and belongings. These are the villas of Magnigeleca, Vuiciacum, Tatinga, Amneium, Mastum, Fabricinium, Losantana, and Adfundenis or Malros, Alciacum, the villa of Launardiacum, and Franciliacum, with all their appurtenances, houses, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, homesteads with woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, or mills, slaves, female dependents, herds with shepherds, movable and immovable property, and every kind of benefit.

All these things I hand over and permanently transfer to you in their entirety, so that you may have, hold, and possess them, and leave them to whomever you wish for possession. If anyone, however—which I do not believe will happen—whether I or any of my heirs, or any opposing person, should at any time attempt to act against this donation, let him first incur the wrath of God and the offense of Saint Peter; moreover, under compulsion of the treasury, let him be forced to pay fifteen pounds of gold and thirty pounds of silver, and let him be unable to reclaim what he seeks.

And so that this donation may remain completely secure for all time, we have confirmed it with our own hand and have now asked those who were to mark or subscribe it to do so. This donation was made on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord King Chlodoveus. [Note: [Col. 1156C] The *Iperii Chronicle* reads: “Done at Sithiu.” Only the indications of place and year of this instrument are found there, as Martene testifies, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 463.]

Done at Ascio, a royal villa, publicly, before the distinguished persons whose names, with their subscriptions or marks, are inserted below.

I, Adroaldus, have made this donation in Christ’s name. The sinner Audomar, bishop in name but not in deed, as witness. I, Agolfus, though unworthy, priest. Ingobertus, though unworthy, priest. Mark of Chunebertus, the *graphio*. Mark of Landebertus. Of Babo. Of Maurilio, *sacebaro*. Of Adalbaldus. Of Chunericus. Of Babbinius. Mark of Bertolandus. Mark of Seoquinus. Mark of Tiodobaldus Casservus . . . . Mark of Chrodmarus, *sac*. Mark of Manasses. Mark of Osorovualdus. Leudolenus, abbot. Mark of Ermenbertus. Of Guobertus. Mark of . . . . Mark of Maurinus. Mark of Bainus. Mark of Adalcharius. Mark of Madalgisilus. Mark of Rigobertus. Mark of Burgastus. Mark of Chrodoboldus. Mark of Valdegisilus. Mark of Madalaulfus. Mark of Uninegerus. Mark of Aldebertus. Danoaldus, priest. Mark of Trasuvualdus . . . . Mark of Ermarus. Mark of Macrinus. Mark of Breulfus. Mark of Gislebertus. Mark of Baddo. Mark of Aldeb . . . . Ceberetus. Mark of Charricus. Mark of Radbaldus, *sacebaro*. Asilendus, *sac*.

[Col. 1156C] Mark of Isbertus, *sac*. Mark of Vualdemarus. Mark of Basinus. Mark of Amalgarius. Mark of Anschiddus, *sacebaro*.

In Christ’s name, I, Ragnulfus, at the command of the lord bishop Audomar and at the request of the illustrious man Adroaldus, wrote this donation.

[Note: In the printed editions some subscriptions are corrupt and many are omitted. In our copy, crosses are prefixed to each one, and some have handwritten marks added. The editors took the word *sacebaro* as the name of one witness. We discuss the *sacebarones* in our preface.]

## II. Charter by which Blidegisillus gives to the Fossatense monastery, which he himself founded, everything he had received from King Chlodoveus, for the construction of the monastery

[Note: First published by Breulius in his *Supplement to the Antiquities of Paris*, p. 142, from the *Life of Saint Babolene*, and from him reported by Cointius, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 117; later reprinted in the *History of the Church of Paris*, vol. I, p. 173; in Felibien’s *History of the City of Paris*, vol. II, p. 21; and finally in the *Nova Gallia christiana*, vol. VII, instruments, col. 3. We have followed the reading of Breulius’s supplement. Since we have judged the diploma of Chlodoveus reproduced there to be spurious, it follows that we cannot number the charter of Blidegisillus, which rests upon Chlodoveus’s instrument, among the legitimate documents. We have already stated, above, that Mabillon judged it not entirely genuine. The following features reveal it as spurious: namely, that the Fossatense monastery was founded according to the form and likeness of the monastery of Luxeuil, under the Rule of Saint Benedict. These statements do not agree. For, as we noted in Cointius’s discussion of Chlodoveus’s diploma, the monastery of Luxeuil was founded not under Saint Benedict’s Rule but under that of Saint Columbanus. We conjecture the forger’s reason for the error to have been this: since the Fossatense monastery existed for some time under Saint Columbanus’s Rule, it was later reformed and placed under Saint Benedict’s Rule. The maker of the charter, confusing all these facts, thought that it had been founded under Saint Benedict’s Rule. Hence it seems sufficiently probable that the charter was fabricated in the tenth century, perhaps by the very author of the *Life of Saint Babolene*, which is full of errors and fables, or at least derived from that Life.] (year 640).

[Col. 1157A]

In the name of the holy Trinity, I, Blidegisillus, deacon, servant of the servants of God. Whoever desires to possess the inheritance of eternal life with the saints in the age to come ought in the present age to make recompense by which he may obtain it from the most merciful Lord.
