Therefore, we wish it to be known to all orders, to clerics as well as laypeople, and to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, that a certain tract of land situated in the district of Paris, which the most glorious lord King Chlodoveus and his exalted mother, Queen Nandechildis, once granted to us by their charter, for their reward, for the building there of a church of God, namely that little fortress called Fossatus, which the vernacular calls the Fortress of the Bagaudae, situated on the river Maternus, having from its entrance to the bed of that same Maternus twelve *buinaria*—

[Note: Cointius, in the place cited, orders that *bunuaria* be read, which he interprets as a certain measure of land. Compare Cange, entry *Buinarium*.]

—together with the entire land called Varenna, which lies around that fortress and which the river Maternus encircles, while a water-filled ditch encloses it, we have decided to give to that holy place, constructed by us in honor of the Lord and of his holy mother Mary, as well as of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul. In it we have recently appointed an outstanding man named Babolene abbot, under the example of the holy father Benedict, for the washing away of the crimes of my sins and the obtaining of Christ’s grace.

Moreover, so that the aforesaid most holy man Babolene, whom, for the love of God, we have appointed abbot in that same place, as we have said, and his monks or their successors may hold and possess forever the aforesaid fortress together with the aforementioned Varenna, which the river Maternus surrounds and which the fortress’s ditch, as stated, encloses from water to water at its entrance, together with those inhabitants who depend upon it, with meadows and pastures, thickets and elms, with water and every kind of fishing, islands and mills, and also fisheries, with gates and all the crossings of that water, and with all its cultivated and uncultivated dependencies, from this day until the final hour of this age.

And just as we obtained this through a royal grant, so, from the right of our ownership, together with the charter and every instrument, or every donation, which the aforesaid lord King Chlodoveus and his illustrious mother Nandechildis made and, by God’s inspiration, graciously gave to us, we transfer and firmly convey it into their power, for the support of that place and, with God’s help, for the support there of their bodies in God’s service.

Thus may those servants of God and all their successors, as we have said, serve the Lord Christ there most devoutly under the Rule of Saint Benedict, according to the form and likeness of the monastery of Luxeuil, and follow that norm in everything, so that, having set aside all private possessions, they may, according to apostolic tradition, be able to possess everything in common; and so that they may gain salvation for themselves and may gladly beseech the Lord with their whole heart for the soul of the aforesaid lord King Clodoveus and his mother Nandechildis, who bestowed this upon me as stated above, and also for me, the unworthy and most wretched sinner Blidegisillus.

If anyone, however—which we never believe will happen—should rise against this transfer and decree of our conveyance, or presume to violate it, or remove it from that holy place or from the power of those serving God there, let him fear that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and dread losing forever the fellowship of the saints in heaven. Moreover, according to the penalty of this world, let him pay, under compulsion of the treasury, to that place and to the aforesaid servants of God five pounds of gold and weights of silver, and let him be unable by any means or device to reclaim what opposes this grant.

But so that this letter of our donation may retain its force and stability throughout all ages, we have subscribed it with our own hand, supported by a stipulation, and have asked the bishops, abbots, and other distinguished men present on this occasion to confirm it with their own ratifications. Many of them, with God’s help, gladly did so.

Done at Paris, on the day before the Nones of May, in the third year of the reign of Chlodoveus, most glorious king.

Mark of Blidegisillus the deacon, who requested that this deed of donation be made and subscribed it.

[Note: Concerning the subscriptions we note the following. The bishop of Paris, one of the subscribers, should not be called Audobertus but Angilbertus, as it is read in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter VII, in the copy we use, formerly carefully collated with nine manuscripts of the finest quality. Annobertus, bishop of Sens, is known from no other source except the *Life of Saint Babolene* and the charter under discussion. More plausibly introduced here are Marinus, bishop of Beauvais, who subscribed Dagobert’s diploma in 631, and Agomarus, bishop of Senlis, who had attended the Council of Reims in 625 and died, according to Cointius, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 183, in 649. But the name of Bishop Argundus appears to be entirely fictitious. Cointius indeed conjectures that he was bishop of Orléans, in the same place, p. 118, but he has no supporting argument. Nor is he recognized by the catalogue of the bishops of Orléans, *Nova Gallia christiana*, vol. VIII, col. 1416; nor is any bishop of Orléans of this name recorded, so far as we know, as having attended any council.]

Mark of Audobertus, bishop of the city of Paris, who subscribed this letter at the request of Blidegisillus. Mark of Annobertus, bishop of the church of Sens, who confirmed this, etc. Mark of Marinus, bishop of the Church of Beauvais, who also confirmed this document. Mark of Agomarus the bishop, who likewise marked it. Mark of Argundus the bishop, who likewise marked it. Mark of Audonus, who confirmed it. Mark of Waudebertus, who signed. Mark of Randegramnus, who wrote it together. Mark of Theodebertus. Mark of Charoaudus, abbot. Mark of Hildoaldus, abbot. Mark of Catherinus, abbot. Mark of the illustrious man Valdebertus, count.

## III. Charter by which Count Widericus declares that he gathered nuns in the church of Hasterium, expelled the clerics, and subjected it to the bishop of Metz

[Note: Published in Grammaius’s *Brabantine Antiquities*, vol. II, p. 67; from there in the supplement to Miraeus’s *Diplomatic Works*, vol. III, p. 2. It also exists, though not complete, in Wasseburg’s *Antiquities of Belgic Gaul*, vol. I, fol. CLVI verso. We reprint it from the supplement to Miraeus, adding variant readings in brackets from Wasseburg, who states that he copied this instrument from an original. The authors of the *Nova Gallia christiana*, vol. III, col. 575, note a, judged it to bear the mark of a forgery, although they nevertheless used its testimony elsewhere, vol. XIII, col. 720. Calmet praises the charter as nearly legitimate in his *History of Lorraine*, proofs, p. 227, note. We, however, consider it spurious, since the dukes of Lorraine do not seem to have existed in the seventh century, although Oharicus, Widericus’s father, is given that title. Add the chronological note taken from the Incarnation, which at this period had not yet been used in the diplomas of the Frankish kings. Nor does the year 656 from that era agree with the year in which Saint Gertrude died, which this charter adduces for synchronization. Gertrude died on 18 March in the year of Christ 658, as Mabillon teaches, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 466. If one may investigate the circumstances in which this spurious charter was produced, it seems to have been fabricated quite appropriately when, at the end of the sixth century, the church of Hasterium attempted to escape the authority of the church of Walciodorum and produced documents condemned as false, as Foppens relates, *Miraeus’s Diplomatic Works*, vol. III, p. 367 and following, in the notes to this charter.] (year 626).

[Col. 1159B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, etc. I, Count Widericus [Wasseburg: Wildericus], descended from a noble lineage, took care to leave to every future generation a record of how I conducted myself in my life.

After my father, namely Oharicus [Wasseburg: Oacrius], the most noble duke of Lorraine, who was descended from the stock of Hilpericus, king of the Franks, had died, I married a woman of great nobility named Berta, the paternal aunt of Sigibert, king of Metz. As her dowry I gave her the allodial estate of the villa of Hasterium, situated on the Meuse, with all its dependencies—namely Jetieres, Serevilla, Mareyna, Gedermo, Porvina, and that which is contained in Dionante, namely the church, Camba, and the land of Hermeatones and Goessenee; together with a manse in the villa of Vireux, Foscia, Samiracum in Famenne, Riennes in the Ardennes, with woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields and mills, and a large household of dependents contained within the boundary of these allodial estates.

[Note: The passages enclosed in brackets are absent from Wasseburg here and below.]

For a considerable time we lived our mortal life with great joy. But when, by God’s judgment, we were deprived of heirs of our flesh, we therefore, touched by divine counsel, resolved to make our allodial estates serve justice and truth, so that we might enjoy an everlasting inheritance.

The church of Hasterium had been consecrated in ancient times by Saint Maternus, a disciple of the apostle Peter. Many relics of the saints are placed there: some of Christ’s blood, some of his mother’s milk, a thorn from the crown, a piece of his garment, and straw from his manger. Saint Sirenus, the bishop who rests in the church of Hasterium, brought them from Jerusalem at the same time that Saint John, the bishop, discovered by divine revelation the relics of the protomartyr Stephen.

Since, therefore, Hasterium contained very important relics, and since my wife was a niece of Saint Arnulphus, bishop of Metz, we jointly resolved to transfer our allodial estates to the Church of Metz, which was considered preeminent above all the churches in the whole disrupted kingdom of our land (*confracto*; Wasseburg: *confinio*, “territory/border”).

Accordingly, I gave the villa called Stephano to the castle of Hasterium [Wasseburg: *legaliter tradidi*, “I legally gave”], and there I prepared a place for my burial and my wife’s in the monastery of Hasterium. After expelling the clerics who served God and me there in the capacity of chaplains, I established in that place a community of nuns and placed over them an abbess named Hametrudis. My wife swore that, after my death, she would serve God with them, if she survived me.

This was done publicly at Metz, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 656, in the fourteenth indiction [Wasseburg: twelfth indiction], while Sigibert, son of King Dagobert, was reigning, in the very year in which Saint Gertrude died.

## IV. Charter by which Aldegundis, on the day of the consecration of the church of Saint Mary at Maubeuge, assigns many gifts as its endowment to the church and to the sisters established there

[Note: Published in 1734 in the supplement to Miraeus’s *Diplomatic Works*, vol. III, p. 557, extracted from the archive of the chapter of Maubeuge; so far as we know, it has not otherwise been reprinted. When the authors of the *Nova Gallia christiana* published their third volume in 1725 and discussed the monastery of Maubeuge, they complained, col. 146, that the canonesses of Maubeuge had refused them access to their charters.

These are the words of those learned men: “For many years we have been concerned to compose a history of the abbesses who presided over the monastery of Maubeuge; and for this reason we repeatedly asked the noble canonesses to give us an opportunity to inspect their charters. But we were refused, with this reply added: that they had no concern to have matters relating to their community committed to writing; and that, if the contrary were done, they would take it badly.”

This was prudent if they suspected some of these documents of falsity; modest if they considered it preferable to neglect the task of spreading the reputation of their most noble monastery. In any event, the charter we present seems to teem with numerous indications of forgery and to have been compiled from the *Life of Aldegundis*—not the old Life published by Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, second century, vol. II, p. 773, but the more recent one published by Bollandus under 30 January, written in the ninth century, whose very words the charter in question reproduces. The falsehood is revealed by the chronological note drawn from the twentieth year of Dagobert, whose reign did not extend to a twentieth year. Moreover, according to Cointius, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 515, the monastery of Maubeuge was founded in 661, which agrees with the sixth year of the reign of Chlotar III. It follows that the charter should not have said that it was made with the consent of Chilperic, the illustrious emperor, and Dagobert. Furthermore, the title “emperor,” bestowed upon a king of the Franks, suggests the ninth century.

If we investigate the witnesses of the charter, we find Ursimarus, who should not be called abbot before 689, according to the *Nova Gallia christiana*, vol. III, col. 80. We say nothing of the scarcely credible gathering of four abbesses who are said to have been present at the drafting of the Maubeuge document. We say nothing of its unusual style. Nor is there any benefit in seeking the crime of forgery through conjectures when it is established by more certain arguments.] (year 661).

[Col. 1160C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

What wiser course is there than for an earthly person to prepare for himself eternal rewards from earthly things or from perishable substance? Therefore I, Aldegundis, warned by the divine calling and strengthened by the evangelical word that invites us thus to eternal rewards: “Whoever leaves father or mother, wife or children, or lands for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life”—desiring to attain this promise, utterly renouncing marital union, have transferred the possessions that I held by hereditary right from my father or mother, with the consent of Lord Hildricus—

[Note: Childeric II; but see the preceding annotation.]

—the illustrious emperor, and also of Dagobert and his princes, with the testimony and confirmation of the venerable bishops and abbots, religious and noble men, and holy women whose names are subscribed below, for the use of the servants of God, to that holy monastery called Maubeuge—

[Note: This monastery had been founded by Blessed Aldegundis for Benedictine sacred virgins. In 965 it was converted to the secular state by Bruno, archbishop of Cologne and papal legate.]

—where the venerable bishops Autbertus, Amandus, Audoinus, and Ursmarus dedicated the altar of the Lord in honor of holy Mary, God’s mother and ever-virgin, and of the holy apostles, on the fourth day before the Ides of June, for the use of the sisters who serve God there night and day.

I have publicly given my estates and substantial possessions for the use of those serving Christ there. First, this includes the very villa in which the monastery is situated, with everything belonging to it, called Maubeuge, situated in the district of Hainaut. I have also determined to provide certain villas, whose names are listed below, for the uses and support of the servants of God, so that they might serve Christ without any want or poverty and might suitably fulfill the life of the religious order.

[Note: In the copy published by Foppens, from which we make our transcription, the following is noted: “Much is missing here in the copy, by which the villas and other goods donated to this church were identified.”]

Therefore I, Aldegundis, give these things, and specifically for the use of the female and male servants living in the aforesaid monastery, and I wish them to remain donated forever, on this condition: that the sisters and brothers living in the aforesaid monastery should hold the aforementioned villas, with everything belonging to them, for their own particular uses, and should have complete power in every respect to do whatever they wish with them. Thus neither anyone nor any of the abbesses or administrators of that monastery should at any time presume to alter or tear away anything, or to alienate it from the present arrangement that I have made for the love of Christ; rather, it shall remain firm and inviolate at all times.

If anyone should attempt to act against this transfer or violate it with rash boldness, and should not correct himself afterward, let him first incur the wrath of the offended God and appear excommunicated before the tribunal of Christ. Let him wither in flower so that he never produces fruit, and moreover let him pay an unremitted penalty under strict judgment: namely, let him be compelled to pay one hundred pounds of gold and [two hundred] pounds of silver.

[Note: That is, two hundred pounds. We restore the lacuna with the help of the following charter.]

And let him be unable to reclaim what he seeks; but let this present donation remain firm and stable forever.

Done at the monastery of Maubeuge, before the altar of Saint Mary and the twelve holy apostles. Given in the twentieth year of the reign of Dagobert, illustrious king, in the presence of the men and servants of God whose names and marks are inserted below.

Mark of Autbertus, bishop. Mark of Amandus, bishop. Mark of Audoenus, bishop. Mark of Ursmarus, bishop. Mark of Vincentius, abbot. Mark of Humbertus, abbot. Mark of Eloquius, abbot. Mark of Ermenius, holy man and abbot. Mark of Etto, abbot. Mark of Gualdetrudis, abbess. Mark of Gertrudis, abbess. Mark of Aldetrudis, abbess. Mark of Maldeberta, abbess. Mark of Gervida, aunt of Blessed Aldegundis, who lifted her from the sacred font. Mark of Gunilandus. Mark of Landricus. Mark of Charibertus, count, etc.

[Note: See Foppens’s notes on these witnesses in the supplement to Miraeus’s *Diplomatic Works*, vol. III, p. 558.]

## V. Charter by which Aldegundis establishes twelve canons in the church of Saint Quintinus at Maubeuge and assigns them a substantial endowment, so that they may serve the church of Saint Mary at Maubeuge and the sisters established there

[Note: It exists in the supplement to Miraeus’s works, vol. III, p. 558, composed in the same words as the charter immediately preceding it concerning the same monastery and given on the same day. Both documents suffer from the same defects, which demonstrate their falsity. It was copied from an exemplar said to have been legally collated in 1569 with a transcript authenticated by formal instruments in 1518. Nevertheless, as the editor himself notes, this charter is highly suspect among scholars on grounds of falsity. See our notes, col. 1161, on the other charter concerning this monastery, where we have fully demonstrated the indications of forgery common to both charters.] (year 661).

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, amen.

[Col. 1163A] What wiser course is there than for an earthly person to prepare for himself eternal rewards from earthly things or from perishable substance? Therefore I, Aldegundis, warned by the divine calling, etc. The remainder is as in the preceding charter, up to the words “who serve God there night and day.”

[Note: So it appears in the published copy. The omitted portion contains chronological notes, namely, the fourth day before the Ides of June.]

But because the female sex could not itself perform the divine sacraments, with the aforesaid emperor confirming it, and with the counsel of the aforesaid bishops and other religious persons, I established twelve brothers in the church of Saint Quintinus the martyr, consecrated by the aforesaid bishops and situated in the villa of Maubeuge, on this condition: that those aforementioned brothers should serve the most holy church of Mary, God’s mother, named above, with reverence and honor, and that they should all be present together on the solemn days of the Nativity, Epiphany, Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, the dedication of that church, and all the solemnities of holy Mary, God’s mother, at the celebrations of Masses and Vespers, etc.

But so that those aforementioned brothers might serve Christ without any want or poverty and suitably fulfill the life of the order of holy canons, I gave by my own donation, for their support and use, on the same day on which the aforesaid venerable bishops Autbertus, Amandus, Audoinus, and Ursmarus dedicated the church in honor of Blessed Quintinus the martyr, a tenth part of what comes from the estate of Maubeuge, except for the demesne court, which I assigned for the use of guests and Christ’s poor; from the cultivated land, meadows, woods, mint, and bridge; five servants’ manses; thirty *fidelia*; two meadows; one wood called Faresbus; two mills on the river of Maubeuge; three *cambae*, one on the bank of the Sambre and two on the river of Maubeuge; and certain villas, Ittoiaen and Hanaen, with a church, dependencies, and slaves; another villa in the village of Ruvo, called Lamereias; another villa called Villeras; and another villa called Waldrecias, with a church, dependencies, and slaves.

And if there be anyone who, etc. (as in the preceding charter, up to the words “weights of silver”), let him be compelled to pay two hundred pounds, etc. (again as in the preceding charter, where the chronological note reads “in the twentieth year of the reign of Dagobert”).

## VI. Charter by which Annemundus, bishop of Lyon, recalls and confirms the gifts bestowed upon the Lyonese nunnery of Saint Peter and himself grants new gifts

[Note: Published by Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 690, from the archive of the nunnery of Saint Peter. He admits that it has been interpolated in some parts, but judges it nowhere else suspect, ibid., p. 425. The authors of the *Nova Gallia christiana*, vol. IV, col. 283, place very little trust in this instrument. Since it is not apparent which portions have been interpolated, and since the charter abounds in indications of forgery, it cannot be numbered among the legitimate documents.

The indications of forgery are these:

1. The title “archbishop,” unusual at this period, which Annemundus assumes and attributes to his predecessor. See, however, what is written above, vol. I, p. 147.

2. Since the entire charter seems to have been chiefly composed to list and confirm the gifts bestowed upon the monastery of Saint Peter, it ought to have mentioned the gifts bestowed in 587 by Girartus and his wife, concerning which we published an excellent instrument above, vol. I, p. 156.

3. The charter of Annemundus conflicts with Girartus’s own instrument. Girartus states that the monastery of Saint Peter was founded by King Gaudisellus and his betrothed Theudelinda at the beginning of the sixth century; see above, vol. I, p. 157. But Annemundus’s charter suggests that Albertus, a most noble man and one of the earliest converts, granted churches, villages, and estates to this already-founded monastery not long after the martyrdom of Saint Irenaeus—that is, three centuries earlier.

Whatever the truth may be, this appears to have been the Lyonese nunnery from which a certain Eulalius abducted a girl, as Gregory of Tours relates, *History*, book X, chapter 8. Annemundus, bishop of Lyon, restored that same monastery of Saint Peter, and after him Leidradus did so toward the end of the eighth century. At that time, according to a letter to Charlemagne, thirty-two nuns lived there according to the regular institution. See the *Nova Gallia christiana*, vol. IV, col. 284.] (year 653).

I, Annemundus, archbishop of the Church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr at Lyon, the first see of Gaul, make known to all the faithful, present and future, that, at the request of my predecessor, Viventiolus, of blessed memory, archbishop of that Church, who while still living ordained me archbishop of the aforesaid Church, and who had bestowed many benefits upon the monastery of Saint Peter, where nuns remain, I considered it best to give my assistance to that same monastery, on account of my two sisters, who there received the sacred veil through the continual prayers of my parents, namely Sigonius and Petronia. One of them was called Petronilla and the other Lucia.

When my parents saw that they had reached the end of their probation, they warned both me and my brother, named Dalfinus, to keep our eyes fixed upon that monastery, and they asked that God might deign to have mercy both upon them and upon their parents, whether living or dead. Mindful of this, while I remain in good health and desire to fulfill the petition of my father and mother, I make a perpetual gift to that monastery from my possessions and the property belonging to me.

I give, in the episcopate of the Church of Geneva, a church belonging to me, dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, with all its appurtenances and rights belonging to me in that region, together with the benefices, tithes, and burials that pertain to that church. In the county of Vienne, at the place called Turris-de-Pino, and all around it, I give all my rights belonging to me there.

For all the aforesaid rights, at the request of the abbess of that monastery, named Radagundis, and of the community of that place, we appointed stewards who would faithfully collect the rents and dues and faithfully render them to the aforesaid abbess, both for herself and for her successors.

Likewise, for Animonia, abbess of the aforesaid community of that place, we appointed stewards in the parish called Marines, as well as in the village called Loimipagus and in the estate of Bregovillicum, so that whoever was inducted should give one hundred solidi to the abbess, and the sub-steward sixty; and likewise upon a change of abbess. In the administration of the goods, they were to swear oaths of fidelity upon the altars to the abbess and the community of the monastery and faithfully observe them.

This arrangement was made so that the steward should go wherever the abbess ordered him; and the sub-steward, in his absence and at the command of the abbess and steward, should faithfully manage and administer the interests of the lands.

As for the lands to be plowed, those which they judged more suitable for plowing—except for those which the abbess should arrange for the benefit of the monastery—shall belong to the steward and sub-steward on the following terms: if those who receive them construct any building, the building shall revert to the monastery; but if they wish to sell them, they shall notify the abbess before anyone else and sell them more readily. [Mabillon: “and sell them to her more readily.”]

If the steward or sub-steward should begin, through haughtiness of spirit, to act against the abbess, or should violently commit any improper act, and, after the chapter of that monastery had been summoned three times, should refuse to do what is right toward the abbess, they shall be expelled from every office entrusted to them by their friends. [Mabillon: “we administer.”] The abbess shall seek out more useful men for herself.

Albertus, a most noble man, gave to the monastery of the blessed Peter of the nuns the parish of Marines with the church of Saint John the Evangelist, and the village of Dolomicuraticum with the church of Saint Peter, its lands, holdings, and woods, as well as the Bregon forest with its watercourses, together with the Trequafensian lands and the Bregonensian lands. He was one of the first converts, not long after the passion of Saint Irenaeus and his companions. He did this on account of his two daughters, whom he caused to be consecrated there: one was called Radagundis and the other Aldagundis. He likewise caused Perneta, the daughter of his brother Silvinus, whom her dying father had left in his guardianship, and another girl named Sibylla, to be consecrated.

Stephanus, a most illustrious man, likewise gave the estate of Carpezatum to the blessed apostle Peter, on account of his daughter named Armingardis, whom he caused to be consecrated.

Two noblemen gave the estate of Increrata, together with its church, to the blessed Peter. One was called Radulfus and the other Constantinus. This gift was made on account of their two daughters, one of whom was called Raimundia and the other Vandamodia. By God’s providence, they became abbesses of that same monastery, one after the other.

These aforesaid men gave the gifts mentioned above, which we confirm. In addition, we enlarge them from our own goods: namely, we give them the *paratae* (provisions) of the aforesaid churches, the tithes of all their vineyards, the offerings of the living, and the burials of the dead belonging to them.

All this, with God’s assent and providence, I arranged in the presence of the chapter of that monastery. If anyone should presume to violate these decrees established by me, in the name of almighty God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and of blessed Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all God’s saints, we excommunicate and anathematize him until he comes to the chapter of that monastery to make satisfaction to both the abbess and the community.

[Col. 1165D] Since chronological indications are lacking, this charter cannot be assigned beyond the episcopate of Annemundus. According to Mabillon, in the place cited above, he suffered martyrdom—so tradition says, by order of Brunhild—in 657; according to the *New Christian Gaul*, in the place cited above, in 655; according to Cointius, in 654.

## VII. Charter by which Adalsinda, abbess of Saint Martin at Dornatiacum, gives her monastery to the monastery of Besua

[Col. 1165D] Inserted in the Besua chronicle, Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, [Col. 1166D] p. 495; taken from there and reprinted at the end of the works of Abbot Guibertus, p. 612; also in Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. III, p. 442, and Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 442, and among Labbe’s *Curious Miscellanies*, vol. II, p. 428. It has been regarded by everyone as genuine, once certain matters interpolated by the author of the Chronicle have been removed. (657.)

[Col. 1166B]

To the holy lord and beloved brother in Christ, Waldalenus, Adalsinda, abbess.

Since I was being harassed by the injuries of evil men and by various adversities and could not remain there, I and my brother Adalricus asked you and your brothers that I should dwell at the monastery of Saint Peter under the rule and order of God; and, out of zeal for charity, you granted this.

Therefore, you ought to receive, in God’s name, the monastery of Dornatiacum, situated in honor of Saint Martin, which my father Amalgarius and my mother Aquilina constructed and to which they assigned the greater part of their possessions, together with the estates belonging to that place and all its appurtenances generally: namely, the estate of Assona, the estate of Parniacum, Potentiacum, and the half-share which our parents held at Balatonna.

As for the remaining property which our parents assigned to that monastery of Dornatiacum, receive it from this present day in God’s name. From the estate of Montaniacum, which our father Amalgarius and Amoloaldus jointly obtained from the royal fisc, take back our share from this present day under your authority, so that neither I, nor anyone from our side, nor any person brought in for the purpose, may presume to raise against you any claim or trouble concerning the aforesaid properties.

If anyone should do so, let him pay, together with *sacratissimo* [reading/recipient uncertain], twenty pounds of gold and fifty pounds of silver.

Done publicly at the monastery of Fonte-Besua.

In God’s name, I, Adalsinda, have subscribed this conveyance of ours.

Hermena, nun, at the command of my lady Adalsinda, subscribed.

Aga, nun, at the command of my lady Adalsinda, subscribed.

Daginus signed this gift.

S. Manaulfus, priest.

S. Victor.

S. Proculus.

S. Vualibertus.

S. Landebertus.

S. Trasgarius.

S. Rogitus.

I, Allo, [Col. 1167A] wrote and dictated this conveyance, in the year 652 from the Incarnation of the Lord, indiction 10, epact 6, [Col. 1167C] [Note: The indications derived from the year of the Incarnation, the indiction, and the epact do not agree; Cointius orders that they be deleted.] with King Chlotarius reigning in Francia, [Col. 1167D] in the first year of his reign. [Note: Chlotarius began his reign in September of the year 656. Therefore February of the first year of his reign was the year 657 of Christ.] With the venerable man Donatus holding the see of Besançon. [Note: Cointius, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 356, thinks that this synchronism should be deleted, since he places Donatus’s death under the year 652; but Chiffletius, *Besançon*, part II, p. 161, extends Donatus’s lifetime beyond the year 660.] On the Wednesday immediately preceding the middle of February.

## VIII. Charter by which Sichelmus and other faithful men inform the mayors of the palace of the plundering of the monastery of Besua and request that, by royal authority, they may peacefully retain the gifts whose documents had been taken away

[Col. 1167D] It survives in the Besua Chronicle, Dacherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 497; it was reprinted in the *Collection of Frankish Historical Texts*, vol. IV, p. 647. A formula of this kind is found in Marculfus, book I, form 34, and in several other forms of Marculfus and others; on this subject, see the dissertation inserted in the *Bibliotheca of Charters*, vol. I, [Col. 1168D] p. 217. Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 470, interprets “mayors of the palace” as the nobles of the royal court. According to the Besua Chronicle, cited above, Sichelmus held a duchy in Burgundy. When this charter—so it is called—was brought to King Chlotarius, a royal precept was issued. It was dated in August, in the eighth year of Chlotarius’s reign, that is, in 664; hence we think that Sichelmus’s charter, dated in October, should be assigned to the year 663. (663.)

To our own lords Reidebertus, Chrodebertus, Emerulfus, mayors of the sacred palace: Sichelmus, together with the other faithful men and servants of yours whose subscriptions or seals are inserted below in this petition.

We believe that our most glorious lord has heard how the illustrious man Amalgarius, during his duchy, constructed a monastery at the place called Fonte-Besua, in the county of Attoaria, in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, where he also gathered a community of monks to dwell, and assigned the greater part of his possessions to the aforesaid monastery.

We also believe that it has come to your knowledge how, some days ago, that monastery was broken into and devastated by evil men, and all the property which the monks possessed was carried away together with the documents, while their entire dwelling was given over to plunder and destruction. Therefore we humbly presume to submit to your piety that you make this known to our most glorious lord, so that by his clemency he may order such an authority to be written for that place that no one may presume to seize, violate, or disturb the aforesaid property which good men assigned there. Rather, whatever they presently appear to have or possess, may those monks, by your command, be able to have and hold it without disturbance, in your time and in that of your successors, so that they may be more diligently pleased to implore God’s mercy for your life, for the stability of your greatness, and for your kingdom.

Dominicus heard the petition.

Farulfus signed.

Abbo, signed.

Ermerbertus, signed.

Frodoaldus, signed.

Vuarato, signed.

Fulgoardus, signed.

Eurcharius, signed.

Given on the Kalends of October, while our lord Chlotarius reigns as king.

## IX. Precept of Emmo, bishop of Sens, concerning the subjection of the monks of Saint Columba to their abbot, the election of the abbot, and his authority over the monks and the monastery’s property

[Col. 1168D] Mabillon first made this document public in print in the *Annals*, vol. I, p. 448. Of the subscriptions of twenty-six bishops, he emends some and explains others by supplying the names of their episcopal sees; it is sufficient to place these in parentheses. A cross is prefixed to each subscription. [Reprinted by Mansi, *Great Collection of Councils*, vol. XI, cols. 119 ff.] (659.)

To our most beloved brother in the love of Christ and our honorable brother Agonus, abbot, and to the whole community of brothers living in the basilica where Saint Columba and the blessed bishop Lupus rest bodily beneath the town of Sens, over which you preside by heavenly dispensation: Emmo, by divine gift, though unworthy, bishop of the holy Church of Sens.

Since you, beloved brother in Christ, and your brothers appear to be inflamed with such great heavenly zeal that you intend to live according to the rule of the fathers, evangelical authority, and apostolic tradition—in such a way that, according to the pattern of the Acts of the Apostles, no monk at any time seeks or claims anything as private property, whether great or small, or presumes to call anything his own, but that everything among them be common—you therefore ask our extremity to grant you a privilege for the monastery already mentioned, confirmed by the subscription of our hand and strengthened by those of our brother bishops and fellow priests.

Let your holiness know, venerable brother, that I most gladly desire to grant this request, provided that whatever is expended for the sake of divine love does not prejudice ecclesiastical rule. For monks living regularly under the rule of an abbot have always been separated from and free of the obligations imposed upon clerics. If anyone desires to know this more clearly, let him read the Council of Carthage celebrated under Boniface of holy memory, bishop of that city’s Church, together with his fellow priests, as well as the letters of the aforesaid bishop to the old freedman; and he will quickly observe that all monasteries in which regular life is practiced have always been free from the obligations imposed upon clerics.

For the distinguished doctor of the Church, Augustine, also proves in his book *On the Conduct of the Clergy* that monasteries ought to be independent in their own right. Moreover, in these provinces many other royal monasteries, both those built in earlier times and those recently founded, have received privileges from the bishops in whose territories they were established, out of religious devotion and charity.

Finally, lest I prolong this discourse by counting everything, it will suffice to mention a few of the chief or nearby examples: the ancient monasteries of Lérins and Luxeuil, the basilica built at Chalon for the blessed Marcellus, and the monastery of Rebais, concerning which we have recently read that certain privileges were confirmed by bishops.

Therefore, let this privilege remain for you and your successors, on account of monastic discipline and for the removal of certain impediments, established with complete firmness, so that both the monks and everything belonging to the aforesaid monastery, as well as what is offered upon the altar, remain under the authority of the abbot of that monastery.

Let the abbot be subject to God and the rule with complete devotion; and let the monks, after God, submit to their abbot, for God’s sake, in true humility. Let him consider that he will have to render an account to God for himself and for them; let them believe that for their submission they will receive a reward from Christ.

An abbot shall never be appointed except from that same community or rule when another has completed the present life. Let the man be appointed whom the entire community of that monastery, knowing the rule well, shall choose with one mind. But if no one is found within that community capable of undertaking the care of the brothers, let the monks have permission to seek an abbot from another monastery that observes the same rule as they do.

Although that monastery is not within the jurisdiction of our possession, it is nevertheless within our authority and canonical administration, together with royal consent, to order this and to establish such privileges for monasteries, although monks, fortified everywhere by the privileges of bishops, may serve God alone and live in their own monastery in peace and tranquility.

It has also pleased us to attach this provision to the privilege: if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether any surviving bishop or one of our successors, should wish to declare invalid or in any way violate what has been decreed or set forth above, let him incur the most severe judgment of almighty God; let the leprosy of Naaman, which Gehazi earned through greed, descend upon him; let him be subjected to perpetual vengeance together with Judas; and, moreover, let him be deprived of communion with both the Church of the present and the Church of the future, and remain condemned forever under anathema.

Thus I desire that this privilege, made with the fullest devotion for the peace, tranquility, and defense of God’s servants, for present and future times alike, and framed for the monastery by our aforesaid religious brother Agonus, abbot, shall remain most firm, confirmed by the subscription of my hand; and I entrust it to my brothers and fellow priests—that is, the lord bishops—to strengthen it by their subscriptions.

Emmo, bishop of Sens, have subscribed.

Johannes, bishop of Arles, a sinner, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

Aunemundus, bishop of Lyon, a sinner, consenting, subscribed.

[Col. 1169D] Certain subscriptions raise doubts, especially that of Aunemundus, if he is believed to be the bishop of Lyon who was put to death under Chlodoveus II, according to Cointius, *Annals*, vol. III, pp. 393 ff., the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. IV, col. 46, and many others. Mabillon astutely understands that Canderis was not the bishop of Lyon but of Laon, for Laon was then called *Lugdunum Clavatum*. No bishop of Laon named Canderis, however, is found in the lists of Laon’s bishops.

In the name of Christ, Chaondius [read: Eoladius], bishop, humble servant of the Church of Vienne, consenting, subscribed.

Vulfoleudus (of Bourges), a sinner, subscribed.

Audoenus, a sinner, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

Chrodovertus (of Paris), a sinner, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

In the name of Christ, Gauciobertus, a sinner, bishop of the city of Chartres, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

Carlefredus, a sinner, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

Canderis, bishop of the Church of Lyon, consenting, subscribed.

Bertoaldus, though a sinner, bishop of Troyes, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

Bertarius, though a sinner, bishop of the Church of Saintes, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

In the name of Christ, Berecharius, though a sinner, bishop of Le Mans, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

Burgundofarus (of Meaux), in the name of Christ, though a sinner, bishop, subscribed to this privilege.

In the name of Christ, Eligius, bishop of Noyon, subscribed.

In the name of Christ, I, Adebertus (of Cambrai, the same as Autbertus), though a sinner, bishop, subscribed to this privilege.

[Col. 1170D] It is known from no testimony other than this charter that a bishop of Nevers named Leodebaudus existed; nor is Bertarius, bishop of Saintes, otherwise known.

Leodebaudus, a sinner, bishop of the Nevarensians—that is, of Nevers—subscribed to this privilege.

Amlecharius, in the name of Christ, though a sinner, bishop of Séez, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

Bertefredus, bishop of the city of Amiens, consenting, subscribed.

Drucfredus, in the name of Christ, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

Hincho, bishop of the city of Lisieux, subscribed.

In the name of Christ, [name omitted], though a sinner, bishop, subscribed to this privilege.

In the name of Christ, Concessus, bishop of Dorcey [Evreux], consenting, subscribed.

Deocarus, bishop of the Church of Antibes, consenting, subscribed.

In the name of Christ, Chariochaudus, though a sinner, bishop, consenting to this privilege, subscribed.

In the name of Christ, Ragnobertus, though unworthy, bishop of the Church of Autun, consenting, subscribed.

Boso, in God’s name, offered and subscribed.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, [Col. 1170D] [Note: If Chlodoveus II died around the beginning of September 656, as Dom Clement suggests in *The Art of Judging Individual Chronological Indications*, 26 August in the third year of Chlotarius III’s reign corresponds to the year 659 of Christ.] in the third year of the reign of our glorious lord King Chlotarius.

## X. Charter of Emmo, bishop of Sens, by which he grants privileges to the monastery of Saint Peter at Sens

[Col. 1171C] This charter is mentioned by Clarius, a monk of that monastery, in a twelfth-century chronicle of Saint Peter the Living; see Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 706. It lay hidden in the archives of that place until Mabillon published it after extracting it from them, among the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, third century, vol. II, p. 613. Cointius then had it reprinted, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. V, p. 285. [It was also published after the precept concerning the monastery of Saint Columba by Mansi, *Great Collection of Councils*, vol. XI, cols. 121 ff.]

Clarius says of it: “Emmo, together with the bishops of the neighboring province, synodically established a privilege of liberty for the monks of Saint Peter in the time of King Chlotarius and his mother Baltilde. At this assembly were the glorious bishops Saint Audoenus, bishop of Rouen; Saint Faro, bishop of Meaux; Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon; and Saint Amandus, bishop of Tongeren, together with thirty other bishops. At that time Agilenus was flourishing as abbot in the same monastery, and so forth.”

All this agrees with the charter we present. We are not moved, as Cointius is, by the fact that the number of subscriptions is smaller than the number of bishops whom Clarius reports as having attended the synod; perhaps all did not subscribe, or certain subscriptions were omitted by the copyists. Certainly this charter suffered serious damage at the hands of copyists, as is clear from the many barbarously corrupted words. Anyone wishing to emend these easily should compare Emmo’s charter with the very similar charter of Bertefridus for the monastery of Corbie, which follows below. Cointius acknowledges that Emmo’s charter agrees with the forms of Marculfus and regards it as genuine, apart from a few interpolations and supplied omissions; Mabillon offers nothing against the authenticity of this document. (659.)

[Col. 1171A]

To the holy lords who preside over the watchtower of the highest summit of the pontifical chair, our brothers in Christ, the bishops of the neighboring province of the city of Sens—Chrodobertus, Faro, Bertoaldus, Audoenus, Gauzbertus, and Eligius:

[Col. 1172C] Chrodobertus, bishop of Paris; Faro of Meaux; and Bertoaldus of Troyes were at that time bishops of the province of Sens, and Emmo rightly calls them his fellow provincials. So too was Gauzbertus, bishop of Chartres, whose see Cointius did not recognize. But what should be said of Audoenus and Eligius? If the former was bishop of Rouen and the latter bishop of Noyon, Emmo could not have called them fellow provincials. Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 450, suspects that “Audoeno” should be read “Audoni,” who at this time presided over the Church of Orléans. [Col. 1172D] Eligius causes greater difficulty if the bishop of Noyon is meant by that name. We, however, conjecture that Vigilius should be restored; he was then bishop of Auxerre and a fellow provincial of the bishop of Sens. Nor does this appear to concern Eligius, bishop of Noyon, since the name of Mummolenus, who succeeded him in the see of Noyon, appears among the subscribers. Clarius, misled by a false reading, attributed to the bishops of Rouen and Noyon what should be attributed to those of Orléans and Auxerre. The error was encouraged by the fact that the names of Eligius and Audoenus were better known than those of Audonius and Vigilius.

Emmo, a sinner, your suppliant in the Lord, presumes to send greetings.

Although it is fitting that we preserve with salutary observance what has been established by the ancient rule, nevertheless, after useful consideration, we shall establish that what does not detract from sacred deliberations be preserved with fearless observance.

Because the venerable abbot Agilenus, together with the brothers living with him in the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Paul—which Queen Theodechildis once built through her own efforts and where she herself appears to have her tomb—beneath the town of Sens, has brought to the innermost recesses of our ears the petition of a religious request, and because this petition has so moved our heart inwardly with a feeling of heartfelt compassion that they judged it irreligious for our soul either not to grant what was requested or at least not to fulfill it most willingly, therefore, inflamed with holy desire, they have resolved with devoted mind and complete dedication to live under the rule of blessed Benedict [Col. 1172D] [Note: Should the words “under the rule of Saint Benedict,” which may have been rashly interpolated, be deleted? Or should one read “the rule of Saint Columbanus,” which was the rule of the monks of Luxeuil, at a time when it had already been joined with the rule of Saint Benedict? Cointius discusses these matters at length, *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, vol. V, pp. 296 ff.; so does Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, pp. 214 and 328.] and according to the manner of the monastery of Luxeuil. They requested from the extremity of our office, by humble supplication, that we hasten to grant their petition, wherever we and our brothers of the Church of Sens assembled with us might most willingly provide it.

Although the holy synodal letter of the Carthaginian council of the lord Augustine commands that abbots and their monks possess the privilege of liberty, so that they may not be held by any bond of authority by bishops, but may remain in the places where the monks themselves have decided, according to the institution of their own deliberation, to live under the discipline of this rule; and since the place of the holy monks of Agaunum, as well as the monasteries of Lérins and Luxeuil and the basilica of the lord Marcellus, have been established as free from the inhabitants left there by any persons up to the present and are now preserved as such by their successors—by unanimous agreement, the aforesaid man’s petition for holy religion having been most willingly accepted by all—we decree that whatever has been given or shall hereafter be given to the aforesaid basilica or to the monks living religiously in that monastery under evangelical liberty, whether by that man, by royal gift, or by any Christians, in lands, slaves, service personnel, sacred books, or any other goods known to pertain to the adornment of divine worship, or in any other possessions, no one, whether of our own time or among our successors, whether cleric, bishop, or royal majesty, may presume to seize or diminish any part of it for his own use.

Only the altar and the altar-table in that monastery shall be blessed. If the bishop of Sens is absent, let them be blessed each year in God’s name with the holy chrism, out of reverence for the saints, and let no fee be exacted on that account. Whatever is offered upon the altar in God’s name, or sent to that monastery by divine inspiration for any purpose, no bishop may dare to claim for himself.

When that abbot has been called from this world, let the whole community of monks unanimously elect from among themselves a man known to possess the best observance of the rule. He shall be ordained by us or our successors, without any payment, according to the holy canons. We shall consecrate the remaining clerical orders without exception, in accordance with what the election indicates.

No other authority in the monastery, whether over its property or, as we have said, over its persons, shall the aforesaid bishop, archdeacon, or any other person presume to exercise, so long as that abbot, those monks, or their successors live under the holy rule. Nor shall anyone dare to give away or take anything from the monastery—such as parishes or other possessions—for the sake of a fee.

Unless requested by the community or the abbot, none of our people shall dare to enter the private places or women’s enclosed precincts, so that the monks, who are called solitaries, may, under God’s guidance, enjoy complete peace through the ages while living under the aforesaid rule and following the life of the holy fathers, and may pray for the condition of the Church and the safety of the king and the country.

If those monks should otherwise grow lukewarm in their religious observance, let them be corrected according to the rule of the lord Benedict and Saint Columbanus by their abbot, or, if he neglects this duty, by those abbots who live according to the rule. May this integrity, with God’s help, be preserved, and may the privilege mentioned above, together with the liberty by which the aforesaid monasteries have been established for their monks, remain for them and for future times.

Since nothing shall be taken away from canonical authority, whatever is granted by those within the household of faith for the tranquility of peace shall stand.

If anyone, overcome by cunning or greed, should be seen rashly to violate what is set forth above, let him know that he will be separated from the communion of all the brothers for a year; nevertheless, with Christ protecting it, let this privilege remain perpetually uncorrupted.

We have also sent this definition of our constitution, strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand, to be confirmed by our brothers and fellow servants, the abbots, so that it may remain stronger and endure for you and others for all time, with the attached stipulation.

Done at Mansolacum, the lord’s estate, in the third year of the reign of our lord King Chlotarius.

Emmo, bishop.

Johannes, a sinner, consented to this privilege.

Unemundus consented to this privilege.

Eodaldus, bishop, consenting to this privilege.

Bertaldus, a sinner, consenting to this privilege.

Leoboldus, bishop.

Amicharius, in the name of Christ, though a sinner, bishop, consented to this privilege.

In the name of Christ, Gautiobertus, bishop, consenting to this privilege.

Hughierius, a sinner, consenting to this privilege.

[Col. 1173D] Chrodobertus, a sinner, consented to this privilege.

Burgundofarus, [Col. 1174A] in the name of Christ, though unworthy, bishop, consented to this privilege.

Maurinus, a sinner, consented to this privilege.

Berthofridus, a sinful bishop of the city of Amiens, consented.

Bicgo, a sinner, bishop of the city of Lisieux.

In the name of Christ, Bercarius, though a sinner, bishop.

In the name of Christ, Concessus, a sinner, bishop of Evreux, consented.

Hecherius, a sinner, consented to this privilege.

In the name of Christ, Momolenus, though a sinner, bishop, consented to this privilege.

Rigwaldus, a sinner, consented to this privilege.

In the name of Christ, Lupus, bishop, consenting, consented to this privilege.

Gaudemundus, a sinner, consenting to this privilege.

Docharius, a serving sinner, consenting.

In the name of Christ, Gyroindus, though a sinner, consenting.

In the name of Christ, Drusio, [Col. 1174B] though a sinner, consented to this privilege.

In the name of Christ, I, Audebertus, though unworthy, bishop, consented to this privilege.

In the name of Christ, Ragnobertus, though unworthy, bishop, consented.

## XI. Charter by which Audomarus, bishop of Thérouanne, exempts from all episcopal subjection the basilica of Saint Mary established by him and to be governed under the patronage of Saint Bertinus

[Col. 1173D] We have published this according to the copy which D. Wite, keeper of the archives of Saint Bertinus, transcribed from the original and compared with Folquinus’s cartulary in 1782, depositing it in our archives. Malbrancq had already published this charter, *On the Morini*, vol. I, p. 669. Mabillon inserted a fragment of it in the *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 455. Cointius, however, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 516, rejected this document as of doubtful authenticity—not because it contained anything contrary to history, but because of certain subscriptions of bishops, which we shall discuss below. The charter was vigorously attacked and even more vigorously defended, especially in writings published in 1737 and 1754 concerning the origin and rights of the churches of Saint Audomarus and Saint Bertinus, or of the monastery of Sithiu. See *On the Origin of Saint Bertinus*, pp. 71 ff.; *On the Historical Truth of the Church of Saint Audomarus*, [Col. 1174D] pp. 100 ff.; and *New Diplomatic Collection*, vol. V, p. 5, note. The privilege of complete liberty granted by this charter was solemnly confirmed for the people of Sithiu by judgment of the Paris court on 3 February 1778. Liberties of this kind were not unusual in the seventh century, as is clear from the forms of Marculfus, who flourished in Audomarus’s own age. (662.)

To the holy and venerable lords in Christ attached to me, my brothers—both abbots and presbyters or deacons, and the entire clergy of the Church of Tarvanna, as well as illustrious men, nobles, persons of rank, and all the many others—Audomarus, by the grace of Christ bishop of the Church of Tarvanna.

Although it is fitting that we carefully observe the ordinances of the ancient rule [Col. 1174C], nevertheless, under divine inspiration and after useful deliberation, we have decreed that whatever does not detract from sacred deliberations shall be preserved through fearless observance. Since it pleased us, in accordance with fraternal agreement and heartfelt affection, and since this so softened our heart within us, we built, together with the monks themselves, for their consolation and assistance, a basilica on the island of Sitdiu, where previously a monastery appears to have been built in God’s name and where monks living according to the rule were present under a condition of liberty. We built it there, by common labor, as a place for their bodies and ours to rest, in honor of holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus, in the aforesaid basilica, [Col. 1174D] in accordance with the fullest charity of those brothers, my little body should, after my death, be deposited or buried in her small shrine [Note: The opponents of this charter object that the Council of Braga, in 563, forbade corpses to be buried in the basilicas of the saints. But here the word “basilica” is to be understood as referring, besides the church itself, to the cloisters adjoining the church. Certainly, in Audomarus’s time it was customary to bury the bodies of the dead in basilicas. For around the year 631 Eligius founded the basilica of Saint Paul for the burial of the bodies of the handmaids of God, as may be seen in the Life of Saint Eligius, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. V, [Col. 1175D] p. 173. Other examples could readily be produced; they are discussed at length in the dissertation on the origin of the monastery of Saint Bertin, published in 1737, pp. 82 ff.], after my death [Col. 1175A], among the little bodies of the monks themselves. These men, clothed in religious habit, gathered at the word of almighty God from diverse peoples and, out of the world’s squalor, were joined together in the bosom of the one holy Church through the love of Christ. They sought to shake the necks of their minds free from the world’s yoke, to abandon everything, lay down the burdens of earthly concerns, and open the breast of their spirit more widely toward heavenly desire. They chose a withdrawn life in expectation of the reward above, so that, devoted there to holy prayers, they might separate the oldness of their heart from the society and clamor of secular people, be fused in the fire of the Lord’s love, and renew themselves for the contemplation of heavenly joy.

Therefore, moved by this confidence, I humbly beseech my intercessors to deign, through their prayers, to provide me with assistance before the most merciful and almighty Lord [Col. 1175B]. I earnestly plead with that congregation that, wherever the place should be in which the Lord commands me to depart from this light, I may, with their shared charity and according to what we have disclosed in your hearing—for our will has decreed it thus—have permission to rest with those pilgrims in the very basilica that we built for their assistance, in accordance with the will of those monks and with God’s help. The brothers themselves shall be permitted to bring my body from whatever place in the aforesaid island and bury it there.

Accordingly, I decree, and in agreement with the brothers of the clergy of Tarvanna and with the illustrious men, I prohibit persons from presuming that the basilica, under the protection of the abbot of Bertin—who at the present time appears to preside over the aforesaid monastery—or under the governance of his successors, should be ruled otherwise. Rather, they shall possess it, together with the entire island of Sitdiu monastery, in the full strength of its own right, authority, freedom, and possessions belonging to it there, with divine worship, most devout affection, and the love that is fitting. Neither I, nor any bishop who succeeds me, nor anyone for the sake of a privilege or gift, under the pretext of assisting it or preserving intact the liberty of the servants of God and of the monks themselves, shall presume to make demands.

And just as monasteries of ancient times, or monasteries in the present age, have obtained their own privileges, and these are preserved by their successors, so whatever is offered in that basilica or its monastery there, the abbot or the monks serving there shall, with God’s help, possess freely, without opposition or claim by any bishop. And, in accordance with what has been decreed, whatever the aforesaid basilica or the monks living there regularly under evangelical liberty have received, or shall hereafter receive during this present life, in the form of royal gifts or from any Christians—lands, slaves, gold, silver, sacred books, or any kinds of things known to belong to the adornment of divine worship or to the work of those monks—or any other contributed possessions [Col. 1176A], neither I, nor any bishop who succeeds me, nor anyone ordained from the clergy of the Church of Tarvanna, shall presume to appropriate them for personal use, diminish them, or carry any such thing to the city.

And whatever has been offered at the altar itself in God’s name, or transmitted by anyone under divine inspiration, no bishop, out of reverence for holy Mary, in whose honor the basilica appears to have been constructed, along with those of the other saints, nor his archdeacon, nor any ordained official of the Church of Tarvanna, shall dare to claim anything from it. Neither I nor our successor bishops, nor the archdeacon, shall presume to prepare banquets at the aforesaid monastery or in its fields, unless we have been invited of his own free will by the aforesaid abbot of the monastery of Sitdiu. After the divine mystery has been completed, he shall take care to return to his own place without any advantage or profit.

Nor shall anyone exercise any other power in the monastery itself, as we have said, or over its possessions, service, or ornaments, or over its persons, whether by giving or exchanging them, out of reverence for holy Mary, or for Peter and Paul the apostles, or so that the monks serving that monastery may live in quiet under the holy rule. Thus, by God’s guidance, the congregation may rejoice through the ages along an unharmed path in perfect quiet and may happily reach the eternal harbor of rest.

And just as many monasteries live in liberty, so that they may pray more fully in that place or at the relics of its saints for the state of the Church and the salvation of kings, for the stability of the kingdom and the tranquility of the fatherland [Col. 1176C], and so that, in accordance with the decrees of the ancient fathers, they may persevere with the Lord’s help, it has pleased us that this letter, together with the privilege granted and the concession made under that liberty, should remain most firmly forever, just as the many monasteries and monks residing there are bound to remain. Thus the aforesaid monks of the aforesaid monastery and its cells [the surviving text is syntactically incomplete].

Since nothing of canonical authority is overturned, whatever is granted to the household of the faith for the tranquility of peace or out of reverence for the saints, it has also pleased us to add that, without the entry of a bishop, the monks themselves shall live under religion and the rule, as we stated above, with Christ protecting them, who may assist those preserving this letter [Col. 1176D].

We have strengthened this definition of our constitution with the subscription of our hand, so that it may remain valid for our times and for the future, and I have asked our brothers and the illustrious men to confirm it firmly.

Done at the basilica itself, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth year of the reign of our lord King Chlothar [Note: That is, the year of Christ 662, since Chlodoveus II, father of Chlothar III, died toward the end of the year 656, as Mabillon himself demonstrates in his *Analecta*, p. 517, in his discussion of the year of Chlodoveus’s death. It is therefore surprising that the same Mabillon placed this document under the year 660 in his *Annals*, vol. I, p. 455.].

In the name of Christ, although a sinner, I, Audomarus by name, an unworthy bishop, voluntarily dictated this letter and heard it read back, [Col. 1177A] and I asked those below to write it. I did this with my own eyes, and another, holding my hand, wrote and subscribed it [Note: The words “wrote and subscribed” here imply nothing other than that he wrote the subscription, with another hand directing his own. For he himself states that he dictated the entire text of the charter and heard it read back. Thus no suspicion of forgery arises, as one of the Bollandists, Stilting, himself admitted in the *Acta Sanctorum* for September, vol. II, p. 566. He nevertheless alleged other indications of forgery from the subscriptions of the witnesses, but without foundation, as may be seen in the following note.].

In the name of Christ, Mummolinus [Note: The subscriptions of Mummolenus, bishop of Noviomagus; Audebertus, bishop of Cambrai; Drauscio of Soissons; Berthefridus of Amiens; Audebertus of Senlis; and Amalcarius of Sées agree well with the chronological notes attached to this charter. See the *New Christian Gaul*, vols. III, IX, and X, under the respective churches. Gravangerus and Bainus, however, also subscribe; both succeeded Audomarus in the episcopate and therefore could not have taken part in the drafting of the charter. Hence Stilting, the author of the dissertation *On the Historical Truth of the Church of Saint Audomarus*, p. 123, and several others regarded it as spurious. It seems more probable, however, that the two successors of Audomarus added their names to a charter already prepared as a confirmation, since this was often customary in ancient times, as Mabillon teaches and demonstrates with examples in *De re diplomatica*, p. 154. See also the *Dissertation on the Origin of Saint Bertin*, pp. 134 ff. Nor does it matter that the subscriptions of both were placed among the names of the other bishops who had attended the drafting of the instrument. It is plausible that, in later times, the names of both successors of Audomarus were inserted in the spaces that happened to remain blank. [Col. 1177D] Here we think it worthwhile to transcribe what Dom Butler, then president of the Royal English College at Saint-Omer and a man highly versed in diplomatic matters, testified on 3 September 1772 concerning the authenticity of this charter and several others of the monastery of Saint Bertin:

“ I, the undersigned, attest that for three days, in the archive of the abbey of Saint Bertin and in the presence of venerable men, I handled and examined the original exemplars of the charter of Adroaldus, the charter of Saint Audomarus, the decree of Saint Folquinus, and the bull of Pope Victor II, issued for Bovo the abbot and the monastery of Sitdiu; and that I compared them with copies transcribed with the greatest diligence and fidelity. In every part and detail they correspond so exactly with the aforesaid originals, without even the slightest discrepancy in the smallest point that could properly be indicated, that these transcribed copies can and must be declared and regarded as authentic, word for word. I likewise testify that I examined the aforesaid originals with the utmost care and, after comparing them with diplomatic writings [Col. 1178B] and other documents from the same and neighboring centuries, and after weighing all the related circumstances impartially, I find it certain and established that each of these four exemplars preserved in the aforesaid archive is genuine, authentic, and autograph.”

Seven witnesses’ names follow; at that time they held the principal offices of the abbey of Saint Bertin. [The reader may readily compare the text with the *Chartulary of Saint Bertin*, published in 1841, p. 23.]], and, as though a sinful bishop, asked on behalf of the memorandum of Lord Audomarus, I subscribed.

In the name of Christ, Audebertus, an unworthy bishop, subscribed. In the name of Christ, Drausio, an unworthy bishop, subscribed. In the name of Christ, Cravangerus, an unworthy bishop, subscribed. Berthefridus the sinner subscribed this letter. In the name of Christ, Audobertus, a sinful bishop, subscribed. Amlacharius, in the name of Christ, although a sinful bishop, subscribed. Baginus, as though a sinful bishop, subscribed. In the name of Christ, I, Abel, as though an unworthy abbot, subscribed this privilege. I, Ramnebertus, a sinner, at the request of another, reread and subscribed this letter. I, Landobertus, as though an unworthy monk, at the request of another, wrote and subscribed this privilege.

## XII. Charter by which Berthefridus, bishop of Amiens, grants privileges to the monastery of Corbie

[Note: Published in Sirmond’s *Collection of Councils*, vol. I, p. 502; Labbe, vol. VI, col. 527; Hardouin, vol. III, col. 1010; and in Cointius’s *Annals*, vol. III, p. 537, and again vol. V, p. 285. Launoy attacked it in *Inquiry into the Charter of Saint-Germain of Paris*, part 4, chapter X, section I, §4; and after him Cointius, *Annals*, vol. V, pp. 285 ff. The arguments are exactly the same as those brought against Emmo’s charter for the monastery of Saint Peter, so much so that one appears to have been written after the model of the other. Cointius believes that both charters require corrections in their heading and subscription, and that the statements concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict should be removed. These objections, however, move us little. See our notes appended to Emmo’s charter.

For the rest, Cointius detected nothing in either charter that was contrary to common law; indeed, he admits that everything agrees with the formulas of Marculf. He develops this at length in vol. V, pp. 291 ff., comparing each chapter of the charter with Marculf’s formulas. Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. I, p. 639, and Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 470, transcribed a fragment of Berthefridus’s charter and noted nothing objectionable in it. Mabillon remarks that this charter is mentioned in a similar privilege granted to the Church of Metz in the eleventh century by the bishop of Terwaan. That document is found among Miraeus’s *Diplomatic Works*, vol. I, p. 64, and we shall have it reprinted in its proper place.

We publish Berthefridus’s charter according to Cointius’s reading. Although we have called Berthefridus’s and Emmo’s charters very similar, with the necessary changes, Berthefridus’s charter is nevertheless sometimes more expansive. The eye can grasp this at once in Cointius, who printed one charter alongside the other. We have enclosed in parentheses the principal passages that are more extensive in Berthefridus’s charter. We have placed the variant readings in brackets; D. Labbat of the Congregation of Saint Maur communicated them to us with the greatest kindness from a manuscript, prepared for an edition of the Councils of Gaul, whose publication he is soon to undertake diligently. [The edition was not completed; its first volume appeared in 1790. See what is written at the end of vol. I, p. 67.]] (year 662).

[Col. 1178A]

To the holy lords presiding at the watchtower of the highest summit of the pontifical see, brothers in Christ, Nivo, Genesius, Ethoaldus, Emmo, Audo, Audomarus, Audoenus, Audebertus, Burgondofaro, the other Audebertus, Drauscio, Berthefridus, bishop of the Church of Amiens by the office of the heavenly Giver.

Although it is fitting that we carefully observe the ordinances of the ancient rule, nevertheless, after useful deliberation, we have decreed that whatever does not detract from sacred deliberations shall be preserved through fearless observance.

Since the most glorious lord King Chlothar, and likewise the most exalted lady Queen Balthildis, enlightened by divine assistance, built a monastery through their own work, with Christ as its guide, at a place called Corbie, and disclosed a religious petition to our ears, this so softened our heart within us through heartfelt affection that our mind would have considered it irreligious not to grant what was requested, or at least not to fulfill it most willingly.

Therefore, inflamed by holy love, they asked the lowliness of our person that, with us and your fraternity consenting, we should grant a privilege to the aforesaid monastery, built in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, who, for their glorious and triumphant vow and for the love of Christ, obtained the crown of martyrdom.

Although the holy Council of Carthage, held by Boniface of blessed memory and his fellow bishops, and the letter of that priest addressed to Liberius do not forbid monks to reside under their own privilege [This word is absent from the manuscript], and although the books of Saint Augustine, the illustrious teacher, on the ecclesiastical orders teach that monks living quietly according to the rule may reside without disturbance from clerics or bishops—which we have taken into consideration, since canonical institution does not prejudice us in this matter, and since the aforesaid lord and lady have entrusted themselves, both in the present life and in the future, to the patronage of the aforesaid saints with fullest devotion, so that the saints’ intercession may deign everywhere to provide them assistance before the most merciful and almighty Lord, and also out of reverence for such great martyrs, and so that the monks dwelling there may live peacefully according to the rule—we have appeared to grant or concede this privilege with full willingness, together with the consent of my brothers [Col. 1179C].

Accordingly, I decree and, in testimony to the divine name, prohibit that either I or any bishop who succeeds me presume to violate it. Nor should posterity judge that we decreed this merely as an institution of our own private deliberation, since older monasteries, as well as monasteries of more recent times, have obtained their own privileges.

[The manuscript adds: “Among which, although it would be lengthy to list them all, let us name a few.”]

For the monastery of Agaunum, which, like this one, was endowed by a royal gift, and the monastery of Lérins, as well as the basilica of Lord Marcellus and also the monastery of Luxeuil, appear to have obtained this concession [the manuscript adds: “and to have obtained complete liberty”]. It is preserved by their successors in such a way that whatever is offered there, the abbots or monks serving there possess freely, with God’s assistance, without opposition or claim from the bishops.

Therefore, with one unanimous agreement, most willingly assenting to the aforesaid princes’ petition in common, we decreed that whatever has been or shall hereafter be contributed to the aforesaid monastery or to its monks during our lifetime or that of our successors, whether by royal gift or by any Christians—lands, slaves, vineyards, woods, gold, silver, clothing, or any other kinds of property—neither I, nor any bishop, nor any person from the order of the clergy of the Church of Amiens, shall presume to appropriate it for personal use or diminish it (or carry any such goods to the city; rather, the aforesaid monastery and the monks residing there shall possess them under complete liberty and immunity) [Col. 1180A].

The bishop of the Church of Amiens shall bless the altars of the aforesaid monastery, or the altar boards if they are lacking, in God’s name, and shall prepare the holy chrism without payment [these two words are absent from the manuscript], and each year, out of reverence for the saints, shall grant it without any reward or payment.

And whatever is offered to the monastery itself in God’s name, or transmitted by anyone under divine inspiration, no bishop, his archdeacon, or any ordained official of the Church shall dare to claim anything from it. (Nor shall I, or our successor bishops, or the archdeacon, or any ordained official of the Church of Amiens presume to approach the aforesaid monastery or prepare banquets in its fields, unless invited of his own free will by the abbot [Col. 1180B] of the aforesaid monastery.)

When the abbot has been called from this world, the congregation of that monastery shall unanimously choose from among themselves a good and worthy man, who shall be ordained, by authority granted by the aforesaid prince or his successors and by us or our successors, without any payment, in accordance with the holy canons.

Likewise, the other clerical grades, lower and higher, whom the abbot of the aforesaid monastery shall choose, whether within or outside the monastery [these five words are absent from the manuscript], we decree that they shall be ordained without acceptance of any reward, according to what the reading teaches.

(Nor shall anyone exercise any other power in the monastery itself, as we have said, nor in the monastery [these three words are absent from the manuscript], nor over its possessions or ornaments [Col. 1180C], nor over its persons, since the petition of so glorious a prince has intervened, because they themselves built and enriched the monastery, and out of reverence for the holy apostles and martyrs, and so that the monks serving that monastery may live peacefully under the holy rule.
