Neither the bishop, nor the archdeacon, nor any other ordained official of the Church of Amiens shall dare to appropriate or exchange anything belonging to that monastery as though it were one of the other parishes, or remove any possessions, or carry to the city any goods that have been contributed to the monastery. Thus the monks serving the aforesaid monastery may, under the Lord’s guidance, rejoice through the ages in perfect quiet, and, just as the aforesaid monasteries live in liberty, may pray more fully to the pious Lord for the state of the Church, the salvation of kings, the stability of the kingdom, and the tranquility of the fatherland.

And if any of those monks should be rebellious, he shall be corrected by the abbot of the aforesaid monastery according to canonical institution. Thus this privilege, under the liberty in which the aforesaid monasteries and monks live, shall remain most firmly forever, so that the monks serving the aforesaid monastery may remain under liberty in our times and in the future, since nothing of canonical authority is overturned by whatever is granted to the household of the faith for the tranquility of peace or out of reverence for the saints.

(It has also pleased us to add that the monks themselves shall conduct themselves and live under the rule of Saint Benedict or [Col. 1181A] Saint Columbanus.)

But if any bishop, overcome by cunning or greed, should presume in a reckless spirit to violate what has been set forth above, he shall perform the strictest penance for three years, separated from communion with the brothers. Nevertheless, this privilege, with Christ protecting it—he who also assists those preserving it and destroys those wishing to destroy it—shall remain forever uncorrupted.

We have strengthened this definition of our constitution with the subscriptions of our hand, so that it may remain valid for our times and for the future, and we ask the lord co-bishops and our brothers to confirm it in every respect.

Berthefridus the sinner, bishop of the city of Amiens, reread, approved, and subscribed this privilege made by me. Genesius, as though a sinful bishop, approved this privilege. Chaoaldus, bishop, approved and subscribed this privilege. Gautiobertus, as though a sinful bishop, subscribed this privilege. Boso, bishop in God’s name, approved and subscribed this privilege. Ragnobertus, as though an unworthy bishop, subscribed this privilege in agreement. Mummolenus, as though a sinful bishop, approved and subscribed this privilege. Audobertus, as though a sinful bishop, approved and subscribed this privilege. Audoenus [the name Audoenus is absent from the manuscript; almost all the others are preceded by the formula “In the name of Christ”], bishop, approved and subscribed this privilege. Dado the sinner approved and subscribed this privilege. Emmo, bishop, subscribed. Leodeboldus, sinful bishop, subscribed this privilege [Col. 1181C]. Chrodobertus the sinner subscribed this privilege. Paternus the sinner, as though an unworthy bishop of the Church of Églons, approved and subscribed this privilege. Drauscio, as though a sinner, approved and subscribed this privilege. I, Audebertus, as though a sinful bishop, approved and subscribed this privilege.

This privilege was made on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the seventh year of King Chlothar’s reign [Note: We calculate the years of Chlothar III’s reign from September of the year 656, after that month had elapsed or while it was in progress; so Mabillon, who places the charter in question under the year 662. The art of determining individual chronological notices teaches that Chlothar’s reign began after the fifth day of September.], at Captonnacum, in the public palace.

Sigo, deacon in God’s name, wrote and subscribed this privilege.

## XIII. Fragment of a charter by which Nivardus, bishop of Reims, grants a privilege to the monastery of Hautvillers

[Note: This fragment appears in Cointius’s *Annals*, vol. III, p. 527; Mabillon, vol. I, p. 467; in the first edition of the *Christian Gaul* by the Sammarthani, vol. IV, p. 32; and finally in the *New Christian Gaul*, with variants, vol. X, institutional column 1; and in Marlot’s *History of the Church of Reims*, vol. I, p. 277.

The Sammarthani were the first to recover it from the archive of Hautvillers. The authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. IX, col. 251, whose reading we follow, state that it survives there written on the final folio of a parchment Gospel codex, and that it has been interpolated several times in various ways. Marlot published a version obtained elsewhere; we place his variant readings in brackets. But nowhere do we possess the entire charter that Frodoard had seen [Col. 1182D]. He reports its substance, from which it is clear that, in the fragment we present, only the first of three sections has survived intact. The missing portions can be supplied from Frodoard’s account, which reads as follows, *History of the Church of Reims*, book II, chapter 7, p. 202:

“Blessed Nivardus, after establishing the monastery, transferred to that place whatever possessions he appeared to have had before becoming bishop. [lacuna] He also granted the monastery a privilege, at the request of the aforesaid abbot Beracarius, namely that the bishop should preserve that monastery under his own jurisdictional authority while he lived; and that, after his death, the bishop of Reims should govern the monastery and defend those same monks against all opponents. The monks themselves should have the power to choose for themselves a superior according to the rule, as is contained in the wording of the privilege itself.”

All critics, moreover, assign Nivardus’s charter to approximately the year 662. The variant readings taken from Marlot are marked with the letter M.] (year 662).

[Col. 1182A]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, amen.

I, Nivo, or Nivardus, although a sinful bishop, while all my brother bishops, and also Christian and good men, did not cease building monasteries according to the rule of the holy Fathers [Marlot: “and from Christian men [lacuna] we, the leading men, had assembled together”], Bercharius the abbot, together with his brothers [M.: “together with”], asked us that we should seek for them a suitable little place [“where” is absent in M.] in our own property, where they might live according to the rule of the holy Fathers Benedict and Columbanus, and might pray for us day and night for the Lord’s mercy, so that I might deserve to obtain forgiveness for my sins in the future [M.: “so that we might obtain”].

But since we could find no such little place in our property that would please those monks for the establishment of a monastery, a little place called Hautvillers was found for us, together with them, in the territory of Reims, on the River Marne, near the village of Disiacum. We exchanged it with Bavo and Theoderamus [M.: Theoderamnus] for estates belonging to our church; the documents concerning this are therefore retained in the archives of the church itself [M.: “we retain them”]. We also legally confirmed to the same monastery the village of Disiacum, with the church and altar of Saint Timothy the martyr, in whose parish the place of Hautvillers is situated [M.: “we confirm”].

But Bercharius himself, together with his brothers [the word “brothers” is absent in Marlot], considered it thus with a view to later times: while we live [M.: “while we assist”], the monastery called Hautvillers, which I built for eternal blessedness and for the remedy of our soul, to preserve the holy rule, in honor of the saints Peter and Paul, and also of Saint John and the other martyrs and confessors whose relics are known to be venerated there, should remain in our power, so that the monks themselves may more gladly live according to the order of discipline and the rule, or remain in quiet [M.: “quietly”].

And in this way they agreed with us, including my brother bishops [the words “my brother bishops also” are absent in M.], our counts, archdeacons, and abbots, and also our clergy of Reims [M.: “and abbots or members of the clergy of Reims”], as well as the illustrious men whose subscriptions [Col. 1183A] or seals are inserted below [M.: “holding the subscriptions”] [Note: Marlot adds the following: “So that, as has already been stated above, the monastery of Hautvillers itself [lacuna]” and the rest is absent. Hence it follows that, whenever this charter was written, it has not come down to us intact.].

## XIV. Charter by which Drauscius, bishop of Soissons, grants privileges to the convent of Saint Mary of Soissons

[Note: Fragments of this charter, by which Drauscius, bishop of Soissons, grants a privilege to the convent of Saint Mary at the request of Ebroin, mayor of the palace, and his wife Leutrude, by whom it had been built, have been published several times: by Reginald, *Summary of the History of Soissons*, proofs, p. 2; Dormeius, *History of Soissons*, vol. I, p. 271; Cointius, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 606; and Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 482.

Michael Germain had the complete charter, taken from the archive of the convent, printed at the end of the *History of that Monastery*, p. 421, without changing even a single syllable, and supplied it with notes. We reprint it according to his text; he also translated it into French there, pp. 14 ff., with additional annotations [Col. 1184D]. Dormeius, however, reports that the writing was difficult to read and admits that he was unable to understand its reading sufficiently.] (year 666).

## XIV. Charter by which Drauscius, bishop of Soissons, grants privileges to the convent of Saint Mary at Soissons

[Note: [Col. 1184D] These were the neighboring bishops of the ecclesiastical province of the metropolitan see of Rheims, to whom Drauscius addresses the charter in the form of a letter: namely, Nivo, bishop of that same Church of Rheims; Landebertus, bishop of Châlons; Mummolenus, bishop of Noyon; Audebertus, bishop of Cambrai; another Audebertus, bishop of Senlis; Clemens, bishop of Beauvais; Berthefredus, bishop of Amiens; and Audomarus, bishop of Thérouanne. Everyone knows that the Church of Cambrai was subject to the metropolitan see of Rheims until the time of Pope Paul IV, who raised the bishopric of Cambrai to metropolitan status. I have removed the earlier lines of this note, since in them the editor merely explained why he had inserted this charter in the Supplement. It is now published in its proper place.] [year 666].

To the holy lords and apostolic brothers, the bishops of the city of Soissons, fellow provincials of Bishop Nivo and of Landebertus, Mummolenus, Audebertus, likewise the other Audebertus, Clemens, Berthefredus, and Audomarus, Drauscius, though unworthy, a bishop, humbly sends greeting in the Lord.

Although the constitution of the ancient rule enjoins and obliges us to observe it in all things, nevertheless this too is added for preservation: that whatever does not stain orthodox definition should be maintained with resolute and perpetual observance for the quiet of religion [Col. 1183B] also throughout the passage of time. And because the illustrious man of good conduct, Ebroinus, master of the household, together with his illustrious wife Leutrudis and their only and most beloved son Bovo, by their religious petition, knocking at the doors of our ears and penetrating even the inner secrets of our hearts, so softened our heart inwardly through the heartfelt affection of their charity that they judged it irreligious for our soul not to grant what they asked, or at least not to fulfill with the greatest willingness what was requested, they therefore kindled us with the ardor of holy desire.

Within the enclosure of the monastery they built basilicas in honor of holy Mary, the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saint Peter and Saint Genevieve and the other saints, in the place called “within the walls” of the city of Soissons. There, virgins and women consecrated to God, under the abbess Etheria, having abandoned worldly pomp, have been placed under the rule of the most blessed fathers to sing Christ’s praises day and night and to seek eternal reward. They humbly begged, with a petition of supplication to our unworthiness, that we and our brothers—abbots, priests, deacons, and indeed all the clergy of the Church of Soissons, whose subscriptions appear below—should grant this.

After deliberating with charitable and faithful goodwill, we therefore graciously granted this privilege, in God’s name, to the aforesaid monastery built within the city of Soissons. Thus, since holy institution has fortified the aforesaid virgins consecrated to God according to their sex [Col. 1184A], the virgins, enclosed chastely within the monastery, are to serve the Lord according to the vow of those God-fearing persons who built it, following the rule and course of Saint Benedict. Once they have entered that monastery to serve the Lord, they are not to have permission to leave it; and, following the model of the monastery of Luxeuil, where blessed Columbanus presided, they are to strive to observe the rule in all things for the progress of their souls.

Nor should our present brotherhood of priests think that it has decreed or granted this privilege by its own deliberation or by some new invention, since in accordance with this constitution the status of the place of Agaunum, and likewise of the monasteries of Lérins and Luxeuil and the basilica of Saint Marcellus, has already been established both with respect to the freedom of their inhabitants and with respect to whatever has been entrusted there by anyone [Col. 1184B].

Therefore, by unanimous agreement, it has been decreed that whatever has been given or shall hereafter be given to the aforesaid monastery or to the virgins consecrated to God who live there under evangelical discipline—by the aforementioned illustrious man Ebroinus, master of the household, by his illustrious wife, by their son Bovo, by royal gift, by their parents, or by any Christians—whether lands, dependents, equipment, sacred books, or any objects known to belong to the adornment of divine worship, or any other goods; and whatever has been offered upon the altar or placed there by anyone under God’s inspiration, during the present lifetime of ourselves and of our successors [Col. 1184C], no cleric, bishop, or person of royal rank is to presume to appropriate or diminish any of it for personal use.

When the abbess of that monastery has been recalled from this world, the entire congregation of those servants of God is unanimously to choose from among themselves the person whom they find best versed in the rule, and appoint her as their superior, with Christ as their guide. If it should prove necessary to have altar tablets blessed, or a chrismal, or vestments consecrated in God’s name, they are to have permission to seek out and obtain this from whatever particular bishop they choose.

As stated above, no authority over their property, or over the appointment or veiling of persons, is to be exercised by us, by the archdeacon, by our successors, or by any other person, unless those servants of God themselves unanimously request it of their own accord [Col. 1185A]. No one is to dare to exact or take anything from that monastery as though it were a parish or another monastery, under pretext of a gift or service, unless the congregation or the abbess has made a vow or petition and it is for the salvation of the soul. Otherwise, none of us is permitted to approach the monastery’s private places or enter its enclosure.

No male is to be inside the gates of that monastery, nor is he to presume to eat or drink there, except for receiving holy communion. If a bishop, requested by them, comes solely to give or obtain the benefit of prayer, then, where the rule permits the place, he is to enter there individually with religious priests [Col. 1185B]. Once the divine mystery has been celebrated and completed, he is immediately to seek to depart without requesting any gift whatsoever. We permit no other clerics or secular persons to enter or dwell there, except when this is required for the good or usefulness of the monastery itself, or when a soul devoted to God has requested it, always with the rule as teacher and with religion observed in all things.

For it is clear to all that the monastery of women ought properly to be enclosed without the frequent presence of men, so that, enjoying a solitary life, they may, under the Lord’s guidance, rejoice through the ages in perfect quiet and preserved chastity; and, living according to the rule mentioned above and following the life of holy virgins, may more fully pray to the Lord for the condition of the Church [Col. 1185C] and the safety of the king and the country.

And if, perchance—which we do not believe—those holy nuns should allow themselves to become lukewarm in their religious observance and depart from the rule written above, they are to be corrected by their abbess concerning how they ought to live holily in all things. For nothing is torn away from canonical authority when anything is granted from the household of faith for the sake of quiet and tranquility.

But if anyone, overcome by cunning or greed, should be seen presumptuously violating what is set forth above, let him, struck down by divine vengeance, be subjected to the guilt of anathema; moreover, let him know that he is to be separated from the communion of bishops for three years, or incur the wrath of heaven, and recognize that he shares the lot of Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1185D], and that, as a denier of the poor, he will henceforth be held liable [Col. 1186A]. Nevertheless, he shall not be able to overturn this privilege in any respect; rather, with Christ our Lord protecting it, it shall remain inviolate in the present and future ages.

To ensure that this constitution of ours may endure with firm force, we have sent it to you and to the other bishops, strengthened by the subscriptions of our hands and destined to remain valid forever, and we have further asked that it be confirmed, with the stipulation appended.

Issued at Soissons. On the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the tenth year of our most glorious lord King Chlothar.

[Note: [Col. 1185D] Dom Germain states that he read the tenth year of Chlothar not only in the original instrument but also in four cartularies. Accordingly, we judge that this charter should be assigned to the year of Christ 666, whereas other editors assigned it to the third, fourth, eleventh, or fourteenth year of Chlothar (History of the Monastery of Blessed Mary of Soissons, p. 425). Drauscius died around the year 674, New Christian Gaul, vol. IX, cols. 338.]

Drauscius, though a sinner, have subscribed to this privilege.

Nivo, though a sinner and a bishop, have subscribed to this privilege.

In Christ’s name, Genesius, though a sinner, have subscribed to this privilege.

Audoenus, bishop by Christ’s mercy, have subscribed to this privilege with devotion, in accordance with canonical institution [Col. 1186B].

In Christ’s name, Leudtgarius, though a sinner and a bishop, have consented to and subscribed to this privilege.

Boso, in God’s name, have subscribed.

In Christ’s name, Gauciobertus, though a sinner and a bishop, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

Desideratus the sinner, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

Virgilius the sinner, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

In Christ’s name, Importunus, though a sinner and a bishop, have subscribed.

Emradius, bishop, have subscribed.

In Christ’s name, Burgundo, though an unworthy bishop, consenting, have subscribed.

In Christ’s name, Abbo, though an unworthy bishop, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

Clemens, though a sinner and a bishop, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

In Christ’s name, Raguobertus [Col. 1186C], though an unworthy bishop, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

In Christ’s name, Audo, though an unworthy bishop, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

Ragnomarus, though an unworthy bishop, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

Concessus, though an unworthy bishop, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

Leudeboldus the sinner, though an unworthy bishop, consenting to this privilege, have subscribed.

Sigoboldus the sinner have written and subscribed to this privilege.

## XV. Charter by which Leodebodus, abbot of Saint Aignan, bestows numerous gifts upon the monasteries of Saint Aignan and Saint Peter of Fleury

[Note: [Col. 1185D] Helgaudus, a monk of Fleury, was the first to copy this charter from the archives of Fleury, in Chesne, *History of France*, vol. IV, p. 59. It was reprinted by Saussey, *Ecclesiastical Annals of Orléans*, p. 154, and by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. III, p. 389. Hubertus inserted a fragment of it and the subscriptions in his *Antiquities of the Church of Saint Aignan of Orléans*, proofs, p. 72. The chronological indications seem to Cointius to have been corrupted; [Col. 1186D] for this reason Longueval accused the document of being false, *Ecclesiastical History of Gaul*, vol. III, p. 565. But Cointius himself, as above; Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 380; *New Christian Gaul*, vol. VIII, pp. 1518 and 1538; *New Diplomatics*, vol. V, p. 421 note, and others judge it to be cleared of all suspicion by the entire body of critics. Cointius, after correcting the chronological notes corrupted by an unskilled hand, regards it as genuine.

It already existed in the archives of Fleury in the ninth century, according to Adrevaldus, a monk of Fleury who wrote at that time, *Library of Fleury*, p. 2, and elsewhere. The chronological notes do indeed conflict with one another, so that they cannot be reconciled, and the invocation is unusual. But to infer from this that the document is false, when nothing else in it suggests falsity, is certainly too severe and harsh; for many other instruments accepted as genuine suffer from such defects, which are usually attributed to the carelessness of copyists.

Add the convenient method of emendation used by Cointius: in place of the name Clovis, he restores the name Chlothar; in place of the second year of the reign, the twelfth year. Both are easy slips by a copyist. He removes the years reckoned from the Incarnation, contrary to the practice of this period, in which they are often rashly inserted by modern editors even into documents of excellent quality.

Once these emendations are admitted, it is clear that Leodebodus’s charter was drawn up in the twelfth year of the reign of Chlothar III, that is, in the year of Christ 667. Certainly it does not concern the second year of the reign of Clovis II; for at that time Clovis, scarcely seven years old, could not have had Bathild as his wife, whom he did not marry until the tenth year of his reign, and yet she is mentioned in Leodebodus’s testament. ] (year 667).

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. In the second year of the reign of our lord, the most glorious King Chlodoveus [Col. 1186D–1187A], on the fifth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 1188D] We judge these indications should be corrected, following Cointius.].

By strength and firm power it is acquired that testimony should support both the rustic and the learned mind. And since this is so, with God’s right hand protecting me, I, Leodebodus, though unworthy and a sinner, an abbot, write these things down.

Since divine mercy raised me to the honor of abbot of the basilica of the lord Aignan, where that lord rests bodily, and appointed me guardian of that place, I rightly judged—and my will fully agreed in devotion—that I should give from the property belonging to me, both to that basilica and to the basilica of the lady Mary, which John of Fleury once built anew, where the venerable man Fulcaldus is known to preside as abbot and guardian, and also in the estate of Fleury, which I appear to have exchanged from my own possessions with the glorious and exalted lord King Chlodoveus and his glorious lady wife, Queen Baltilde [Col. 1187B]. There I intend to build a monastery in honor of Saint Peter, in which prayers may be offered for the king’s salvation and for the entire people [Note: [Col. 1188D] Cointius thinks *aedificavi*, “I built,” should be read instead of *aedificare delibero*, “I intend to build.” He rightly notes that the instrument repeatedly mentions the monastery of Saint Peter as already founded. But nothing prevents these words, “I intend to build,” from indicating a plan to renew a new construction. As for the statement here that Saint Aignan was already buried in the monastery of Saint Peter, Cointius makes the same assertion above, p. 396, explicitly testifying that the body of Saint Aignan was transferred to this monastery in the year 654. Therefore nothing here requires correction.].

There the aforesaid holy man of God, namely Bishop Aignan, lies honorably buried. In that monastery monks are to live according to the rule of the most holy Benedict and of Lord Columbanus. I intend, under Christ’s guidance, to bestow upon it individually from the property belonging to me.

Therefore I give to the aforesaid basilica of the lord Aignan, and to the monks serving there, who at present, by God’s favor, perform their office, and from my right I transfer into the right of the aforesaid basilica from this present day, portions of land situated within the estate of Nogromet in the territory of Berry, called Litmaro and Mariniaco, which I appear to have received from the women Aviana and Prosperiana by written instruments, together with houses, buildings, dependents whom I have not freed, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, with every right and benefit belonging to them, and with every kind of livestock residing there, exactly as I have possessed it.

Likewise, my portion situated within the estate of Littidum in Secalonia, which I appear to have bought from a woman named Agana for a stated price by a contract of sale, together with houses, buildings, dependents, except those whom I shall have released into freedom, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, and every benefit belonging to it, exactly as I have possessed it.

Likewise, my portion at Vetula Casa, which I bought from Abbo and his brother’s son for a stated price by a contract of sale, and which came to me through letters of donation, together with manses, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, every kind [Col. 1187D–1188A] of livestock, and its benefits, exactly as I have possessed it.

In the same way, my portion at the estate of Frieto in Secalonia, exactly as I have possessed it, with manses, resident dependents, woods, meadows, fields, and pastures in full, together with its boundaries and every kind of livestock residing there; and likewise the lands and meadows which I appear to have bought from Albuna in the district of Étampes, exactly as I have possessed them in full.

Likewise I give silver vessels: *anacleta* weighing eight pounds and two ounces, two sandals for the Mass, and table cloths, together with capes and all the equipment, and two embroidered veils. I establish all these things, with complete devotion, so that they may remain forever in the power and ownership of that monastery and of the monks serving God there.

Likewise, the portion of land in the district of Berry, called Monte, near the village of Cabrias, which I appear to have bought from Domolus and his wife Ingara, and from several other people, I give; and whatever has come to me there by letter of donation or by any contract; likewise what I possess in Bria, which lies above the river Flironte, which I appear to have bought from several people and which adjoins that Monte, together with houses, buildings, dependents whom I have not freed, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, with all their rights and boundaries, and every kind of livestock, exactly as I have possessed it, I give.

Likewise, I give to Saint Peter of Fleury the estate of Camberon, which lies near the boundary of Clariacum or the village of Ucellus, which I appear to have bought from the heirs of Nummolus for a stated price by a contract of sale, together with houses [Col. 1188C], buildings, dependents whom I have not freed, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, every kind of livestock, and every right, benefit, and boundary belonging to it, exactly as I have possessed it.

Likewise, in the estate of Rausedon, which is in the district of Meung, and which I appear to have bought from the heirs of Magnus for a stated price [Note: [Col. 1188D] This is how it appears in Saussey; something is missing here, for example, “which I appear to have bought.”] … I decree by full will that the portion of the aforesaid basilica of the lord Peter of Fleury shall possess the above-mentioned property forever by right and ownership.

Likewise, I assign forever for possession to the aforesaid basilica of the lady Mary my portion near the village of Columna, a fourth part of that estate of Colomna, with manses, resident dependents, cultivated and uncultivated fields, and every kind of livestock in full, exactly as I have possessed it.

Likewise, in Simpliciacum, which is in Secalonia, which I appear to have bought from a certain man named Aregisilus and from others, for a stated price by a contract of sale, I give that portion, with manses, woods, meadows, fields, pastures, every kind of livestock, and its benefits, to the basilica of the lady Mary; and I desire with complete willingness that it possess it forever.

In the same way, to the aforementioned monastery which, as stated above, I intend to build in honor of the lord Peter in the estate of Fleury, where monks are to live according to the rule, I give from the present day the estate of Fleury, with houses, buildings, dependents whom I have not released from the yoke of servitude, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, vineyards, waters and watercourses, with their appurtenances and adjacent properties, every kind of livestock, and all its rights and boundaries, exactly as the estate was possessed in former times or came to us [Col. 1189B].

Likewise, I grant the property at Melliacum, which I appear to have bought by a contract of sale, with houses, buildings, dependents whom I have not freed, cultivated and uncultivated fields, and the mill workshop which appears to be in Malua in that territory, in full, with its boundary and every kind of livestock, exactly as I have possessed it.

I also grant what I appear to have bought from the heirs of Paulonus, formerly a merchant: namely, plots in the town of the city of Orléans, with the houses built upon them and the resident dependents, and vineyards belonging to the town of that city; likewise the small estates called Curun, Canavarias, Simpliciacum, and Caliacum, beyond the river Loire, which I appear to have bought for a stated price in an earlier period.

Accordingly, before the apostolic man, Lord Bishop Audoenus, the illustrious man Chranulfus, a nobleman, and the other abbots, it was agreed in judgment that, of all these possessions—lands, dependents, and vineyards—the portion of the basilica of the lady Mary should retain one half, while I should receive the other half in full under my right. I appear to have received that half by their judgment. I assign it in full to the aforementioned monastery of Saint Peter built at Fleury, to be possessed forever.

Likewise, the estate of Asinaria, which is in the valley, and which came to me from the property of the illustrious man Trodoneus through letters of exchange, as their wording declares, while in return I appear to have given, in exchange for the aforesaid Trodoneus, that portion which is at Suncantum or Warentias, which I formerly bought from a woman named Machildis for a stated price by a contract of sale, I give in full, without anyone’s impediment, to the portion of the aforesaid monastery of the lord Peter built at Fleury, with every right and boundary, exactly as I have possessed it, and with every kind of livestock residing there, to receive and possess.

The plots within the walls of Orléans which I appear to have bought from the cleric Chonulfus for a stated price by a contract of sale, where Leobastus appears to reside, I decree with complete willingness to give to the aforesaid monastery of the lord Peter and to the monks dwelling there.

Likewise, thirty good horses, five herds of horses with their stallions, twenty herds of oxen, five cows, and ten head of cattle.

I have thought it proper to insert, through the force of this document, the silver which I give to that monastery of the lord Peter and to the monks serving there: namely, pure, sealed, overseas *bacchraicha*, weighing ten pounds, one of which has a golden cross in the middle.

I also give a dish bearing in its center the likeness of a man’s head, likewise made of gold. Likewise, two smaller gilded Massilian dishes, which have nielloed crosses in the middle [Col. 1190B]. I wish these silver objects to remain forever under the right and ownership of the aforementioned monastery of the lord Peter.

As for the garments which I appear to possess in my poverty, apart from what I assigned above to the basilica of the lord Aignan, the remainder that is left over shall be received for possession by the portion of the lord Peter of Fleury.

I hope—and do not believe that it could in any way happen—that any of my heirs, or any other person, will attempt to act against this present letter. But if anyone does so and attempts to invalidate my act, let him first incur the wrath of the heavenly Trinity; moreover, let him restore to the basilica of the lord Aignan, the basilica of the lady Mary, or the monastery of Saint Peter built at Fleury, double what I gave to those basilicas, according to the degree to which the properties themselves have been improved, and let him be held liable to the treasury for three pounds of gold and twenty pounds of silver [Col. 1190C].

To make this donation more secure, I have decided to attach it to the municipal records, and I have caused two letters of identical wording to be written concerning the property mentioned above: one is to remain in the archive of the lord Aignan, while the other copy is to be received for preservation by the monastery of the lord Peter for future ages, so that the monks serving God there may be able to defend what I have given them by this document, and so that this donation made by me may nevertheless remain firm and inviolate at all times, with a stipulation included in every respect.

Issued publicly at Orléans.

It is also appropriate to add what we ought to have stated above: whatever we have assigned to the aforesaid monastery of the lord Peter of Fleury, which we built anew, and whatever shall hereafter be assigned to it by God-fearing men, whatever the abbot presiding there wishes to do with it for the use or benefit of that monastery, or for the profit of his soul or the needs of the brothers, he shall have free authority to do, without detriment or impediment to the aforesaid monastery.

Leodebodus, sinful abbot: a letter made by me.

Audoenus [Note: [Col. 1189D] Among the bishops subscribing, Cointius, above, p. 592, proves that Audoenus and Leodegarius presided over the Churches of Rouen and Orléans in the year of Christ 667, when Leodebodus drew up the charter. There is no controversy concerning Audoenus. Regarding Leodegarius, Mabillon and the authors of *New Christian Gaul* disagree with Cointius; but Mabillon admits, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 380, that in such great obscurity it is difficult to determine the matter accurately, and he considers the authority of Leodebodus’s charter decisive in a doubtful case.]—a sinful bishop, at the request of the venerable man Leodebodus, abbot, have reread and subscribed to this letter.

Leodegarius, though an unworthy bishop, at the request of Abbot Leodebodus, have confirmed this letter of his devotion in Christ’s name.

Beccelenus, abbot.

Ado, abbot.

Salomon, abbot.

Leotsnidus, abbot.

Bulgulfus, priest.

Higecius, deacon and subdeacon.

Martinus, deacon.

Boso, deacon.

Agneramus.

Dagobertus.

Nummolenus.

Vapingus.

Sigirius.

Framesindus.

Antbertus.

Salomon, or Boso.

Pappolus.

Sirobaldus, or Saxo.

Amnegisillus, witness.

Manasses.

Authacarius.

Nonno.

Hildulfus.
