## XVI. Charter by which Numerianus, archbishop, grants privileges to the monastery within the place called Galilee, at the request of Bishop Deodatus

[Note: [Col. 1191D] Mabillon published this in his *Annals*, vol. I, p. 696, from an old copy which he says he possessed, ibid., p. 508. Honteimius, *Diplomatic History of Trier*, vol. I, p. 82; Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, vol. II, proofs, p. 79; and the editors of *New Christian Gaul*, vol. XIII, instruments, col. 291, reprinted it, all from Mabillon. It appears at the end of Sommier’s *History of the Church of Saint Adeodatus*, p. 237, from an old transcript preserved in that church’s archives; and among the proofs appended to the defense of the Church of Toul, p. 1, published at Toul in 1727, according to a transcript said to have been collated with the original.

We follow Mabillon’s edition, adding in brackets various readings drawn from the defense of the Church of Toul. Since chronological indications are lacking, it was possible to derive them from synchronisms; we discuss them in the final part of the prolegomena. We shall demonstrate that this charter, which, according to Calmet above, several learned men had declared of doubtful authenticity, must altogether be counted among spurious instruments.] [year 667].

[Col. 1191B]

To the holy lords and those presiding at the summit of the highest dignity and over the watchtower of the episcopal chair, our brothers in Christ, the neighboring bishops Childulfus, Gisloaldus, and Ebroinus [Clodoaldus, Eboricus], Numerianus, archbishop, your humble and faithful servant, presumes to send greeting.

Although it is fitting that we too should preserve the rule established in ancient times with salutary observance, nevertheless, so that it may be carried out through your provision [through deliberation over your provision], we have decreed that whatever does not detract from sacred deliberations [does not detract] shall be observed with fearless observance.

And because the venerable Bishop Deodatus, through his religious petition, penetrated the innermost parts of our ears and, by the heartfelt affection of piety, so softened our heart inwardly [softened us within] that we considered it irreligious for us not to grant his requests, or at least not to fulfill them most willingly, he therefore kindled us with the ardor of holy desire.

The aforesaid Bishop Deodatus built within the enclosure of a monastery basilicas in honor of holy Mary, God’s mother, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and their companions [addition: and of Saints Eucharius, Maternus, Maximinus, and all their companions], and of Saints Maurice, Exsuperius, and Candidus and their companions. He built them within the secluded wilderness at the place called Galilee, formerly called Juncturas, above the rivers Murtas and Raurobacius [the little rivers Murta and Raurobacius], on property which he had obtained through the generosity of the royal fisc. There he established monks and pilgrims under the rule of blessed Benedict [Col. 1191D] and of Saint Columbanus the abbot.

He humbly begged our unworthiness, with a supplication of prayer, that we and our brothers should grant a privilege to that church there [to his church there]. And lest posterity of priests judge that we had decreed this through an improper impulse of deliberation, since under such a norm the matter had already been arranged both regarding habitations and regarding whatever had been entrusted there by anyone [Col. 1192A], we and our brothers—abbots, priests, and clerics—therefore, in one accord and agreement, assenting to the petition of the aforesaid man, decreed unanimously as follows:

Whatever has been given to the aforesaid monasteries [monastery] and to the monks living there under evangelical discipline by that venerable father, Bishop Deodatus, by other Christian men and women, by royal gift, or by any persons—whether equipment, sacred books, or whatever they may be able to add and increase by their own labors, or whatever is known to belong to the adornment of the place—during the present lifetime of ourselves and of our successors, no bishop, abbot, priest, cleric, or archdeacon, nor any royal authority, is to dare to appropriate or diminish any of it for personal use [Col. 1192B].

When the aforementioned Bishop Deodatus, who is the father of that monastery, has been called away from this world [called], the entire congregation is unanimously to choose from among themselves the person best versed in the rule and appoint him as their superior and abbot.

And if it should be necessary for them to have a church blessed and to receive the sacred orders, they shall have permission to seek this from whatever bishop they choose [to approach a church for blessing and to receive sacred orders]. No one from that monastery, or from parishes or other monasteries living without any rule or privileges, shall dare, for the sake of a gift, to seek or take anything [Col. 1192C]. Nor shall anyone be permitted to wear down the enclosure of that monastery unless he has been invited by the abbot and by the entire unanimous congregation.

If a bishop, jointly requested by them for their benefit, comes, whatever the abbot himself or his holy congregation chooses shall be done. Once the divine mysteries have been celebrated and completed, he is immediately to strive to depart without requesting any gift whatsoever, so that the monks called solitary may, with the Lord’s help, rejoice through the ages in the quiet they have received; and, living under this holy rule and following the life of the blessed fathers, may more fully pray to the Lord for the condition of the Catholic Church and for the desirable salvation of Childeric, the glorious ruler.

And if those monks should do anything at all improperly against religion [or exact anything, however little], they are to be rebuked by their own abbot according to the aforesaid rule of the lord Benedict and of Saint Columbanus the abbot [Col. 1192D].

And if—God forbid—some disagreement or murmuring should arise between the abbot and the monks, such that it cannot at all be settled there by that abbot, then a bishop sent by them, together with other abbots who observe this kind of rule, is to convene at the monastery [Col. 1193A] and suppress the scandal by a ruling according to the rule. For nothing is torn away from canonical authority when anything is granted from the household of faith for the sake of quiet and tranquility.

But if anyone is found daring to violate with a presumptuous spirit what is set forth above, let him, struck down by divine vengeance [judgment], be subjected to the guilt of anathema, and moreover incur the wrath of almighty God and of all the saints.

Therefore, so that this privilege may not be overturned in any respect, but may remain incorrupt in the present and future ages, with Christ our Lord protecting it, and may endure with the firmest force, it is strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand and of those of our brother bishops, abbots, priests, and archdeacons. We have also sent it to our venerable brothers, the priests Blidoaldus [Blisaldus] and Archivo [Ahino], to be confirmed, so that it may remain inviolate forever [Col. 1193B].

Sign of Numerianus, archbishop, who ordered this to be done.

Sign of Dragobodus [Dragobondus], bishop.

Sign of Grotcharius.

Sign of Baldonus, bishop.

Sign of Dodo, bishop.

Sign of Chroabaldus, bishop.

Sign of Garibertus, archdeacon.

Sign of Prodagi us, bishop.

I, Filbertus [Filibertus], wrote this at the request of others.

## XVII. Charter by which Vigilius, bishop of Auxerre, grants numerous possessions to the monastery of Blessed Mary founded outside the walls of Auxerre

[Note: [Col. 1193D] Mabillon alone published this, in his *Annals*, vol. I, p. 694, partly mutilated; nor does he indicate where he obtained it. Its authenticity is supported by the *Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre*, edited by Labbe, *Manuscript Library*, vol. I, p. 427, and by the *Chronicle of Auxerre*, fol. 67 verso, which Camusat made publicly available.

The *Deeds* state that the monastery was built by Vigilius in the suburb of the city of Auxerre and enriched with numerous gifts, as the sequence of his testament demonstrates; these words sufficiently indicate the charter under discussion. Since Mabillon copied it from a specimen that is truncated at the end [Col. 1194D], the chronological indications are missing, nor do they appear capable of being derived with certainty.

Vigilius occupied the see of Auxerre from the year 660 to the year 686. We may properly place Vigilius’s charter around the year 670, following Mabillon, who mentions it under that year in the body of his *Annals*. Abbot Lebeuf discussed this document extensively in his *History of Auxerre*, vol. I, p. 141, especially regarding the ancient names of places, in interpreting which he differs greatly from Mabillon.] (year 670).

The holy and venerable basilica of Our Lady Mary, mother of the Lord, [lacuna], which by my work we were seen to have built in the suburb [Col. 1193C] of the city walls of Auxerre [lacuna], and for the monks serving there, I, Vigilius, a sinner, by divine inspiration [lacuna], have judged it proper and fitting to foresee, in pontifical order, that this consent be given, so that the name of religion may increase for the better and the holy places may become worthy of veneration, with Christ the Lord inspiring it.

Therefore I give to that basilica of Saint Mary, for the sustenance of the poor residing there, and I wish that it be regarded as given forever after the day of my death, namely, those vineyards where the basilica itself has been built. On one side they adjoin the public road that runs from the Parisian gate to Sens; on another side, the public road that runs from the Parisian gate to Broile; and above they adjoin the Midranian vineyards from the upper spring. From there, along the vineyards, to the heirs of the late Atto, as far as the vineyards of Lord Germanus; and from there to the road named above, which leads to Saint Simeon: whatever has come to me there from every side, or appears at present to be held by me, together with the dependants whom I have established there, all of it in its entirety. [Col. 1194A]

Therefore I give to that basilica the plots of land within the walls of the city which I exchanged with the illustrious man Helchilenus; and likewise other plots outside the walls of that city, beside the gate mentioned above, adjoining the wall itself, which I bought from Abbot Luponus for a price paid.

In like manner, my portion [lacuna] at Bercuiacum, which is known to have come to me there from the estate or from whatever source, or which I appear presently to hold, together with the meadows along the river Belcha, from that Bercuiacan estate which my parents held, adjoining on one side and at both ends the boundaries of Patriniacum, by the spring called Dianna, in the manner in which I appear presently to hold it from the basilica itself, together with the farmstead which the late Quentilla held beside the little river [Col. 1194B] Belcha: all of it and every part of it in its entirety.

Likewise I give to that basilica the land of my portion in the estate of Cauliacum, beside the river Yonne, as much as my parents held there, or as is known to have come to me in addition, together with homesteads, buildings, farmsteads, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, and livestock of both sexes.

In the same way, the estate of Pauliacum, situated in the district of Auxerre, my property, beside the river Loire, with buildings, vineyards, woods, meadows, fields, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, and livestock of both sexes.

Likewise, the land of that basilica which lies in the estate called Flivenasa: four *cingae*.

In the same way I leave to that basilica a small tract of my portion which lies at Jarricas, beside the river Belcha: one homestead. [Col. 1194C]

Again I give to that basilica my property, the estate called Busciacum, beside the river Belcha, with homesteads, woods, meadows, farmsteads, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and dependants of both sexes.

Also, in the district of Sens, in the estate of Bonertum, situated beside the river Yonne, which I received as my property by giving a large sum of money, seven homesteads, with their adjuncts, appurtenances, benefits, vineyards, pastures, woods, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, male and female slaves: all of it and every part of it in its entirety I give as alms for the poor serving God there.

Likewise, in the district of Tonnerre, my portions in the estate of Flauniacum, which I appear to have received from the illustrious man Helchilenus and my sister Frautilde, [Col. 1194D] together with male and female slaves, buildings, farmsteads, vineyards, dependants, woods, meadows, fields, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, and livestock of both sexes, with their adjuncts, appurtenances, benefits, or appurtenances of whatever kind: all of it and every part of it [Col. 1195A] in its entirety.

Likewise my portion in the same district, in the estate of Cassiacum, which the woman Dolena and her son Ado sold to me, with homesteads, male and female slaves, dependants, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses: all of it and every part of it in its entirety [lacuna].

Also I give to that basilica of Our Lady Mary, in the districts of Sens and Tonnerre, in the estates named Treviciacum, Melarion, Cadugium, and Imantia, an undivided half of the property formerly held there by Asper, which I acquired there by agreement from his brother, the late Abbot Gregory, namely, as much of that agreement and of that property, in whatever things and possessions, as came to me in the places written above; also male and female slaves, with homesteads, buildings, farmsteads, vineyards, dependants who have not obtained freedom from me, [Col. 1195B] woods, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, livestock of both sexes, with their adjuncts, appurtenances, benefits, or appurtenances of whatever kind: all of it and every part of it in its entirety.

In the same way, I willingly give to the aforesaid basilica of Saint Mary the small tract of my portion in the estate of Tresoginum and before Maiacum, situated in the district of Auxerre, together with my portions in the estates of Matiriacum and Solemniacum, situated in the district of Tonnerre, which the late Bishop Diddo, or his sons Claudius and his brother Warnferius, were seen to have held within those places, with resident male slaves and female slaves, dependants, buildings, farmsteads, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, with their adjuncts, [Col. 1195C] appurtenances, benefits, or appurtenances of whatever kind, granted as a gift—whatever I appear to hold in the places written above, all of it and every part of it, in whatever things, in its entirety.

Likewise the farmstead of Potiolus, which I appear to have received from the heirs of the late Helegius, together with the farmstead of Ferrarias, with homesteads, buildings, farmsteads, male and female slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses: as much as is possessed at the present time, all of it and every part of it in its entirety.

Likewise the small estate belonging to my property, the estate of Donatus, together with my portion in the estate of Tresovium, which I appear to have there.

In the same way the estate of Dulcium, which lies beside the boundaries of Intranimium and remains between the aforesaid estates—that is, between Intranimium, the estate of Dulcia, the estate of Donata, and Tresovium—and eight and a half [homesteads?], which my aunt Flotildis appears to have given me after her departure, together with male and female slaves, farmsteads, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, and all appurtenances, with animals of both sexes, in the manner in which my aunt Flotildis appears to possess it by right of usufruct, or as she may have left it on the day of her death: after her departure, it must pass in its entirety to that basilica.

Likewise my portions in the estate of Patriciniacum [lacuna], Hispatium, and Britaniola, together with my portions in the estate of Domitiacum, in the estate of Mirisela, and the dwelling of Arigisillus, as much as I appear to hold there lawfully or at present, I leave by my will to the aforesaid basilica, all of it and every part of it in its entirety. [Col. 1196A]

Likewise my portion in the estate of Scubiliacum, which Ranesindus and his wife Arthemia appear to possess and gave to me, and which they appear to possess by right of usufruct: all of it and every part of it, in whatever things and possessions they leave behind at their death, in its entirety.

Likewise my portions in the estates of Saciegum and Casidum, as much as my parents appear to have held, together with my portion in the farmstead of Quaciaria, which I exchanged with my sister Avolana and which came to her through the testament of my mother, with [Col. 1196B] homesteads, buildings, male and female slaves, farmsteads, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, animals of both sexes, all of it and every part of it, in whatever things and possessions. With her consent, that basilica must receive this in its entirety.

Moreover, I give a certain rustic named Wulbertanus, and his children Wasco and Magnetrude, together with a great multitude of their relatives.

In the same way my portion in the estate of Compesciacum, which I appear to have there from Hebercaptus, with all its appurtenances, with animals of both sexes, all of it and every part of it, in whatever things and possessions, in its entirety.

Furthermore, my small estate called Lanovilla, which I formerly received from Abbot Ebroaldus or his heirs; and Longus Campus, which I formerly received from Leotbertus or his heirs; likewise my portion in Lanosicum, which I formerly received from Nestorius or his heirs; and that portion on a certain mountain at Compesciacum, which I exchanged with Odgisilus, with homesteads, buildings, inhabitants, male and female slaves, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, with animals of both sexes: all of it and every part of it in its entirety. [Col. 1196C]

Likewise I give for one *cappa* the estate of Leodebarum, my portions which I appear to have from Sperius and the priest Domnolenus, and that land which I bought there from Ebolena, and the estate of Escalittas, which my parents held, and Cardonareta, which lies before Saint Ferreolus, with [Col. 1196D] homesteads, buildings, farmsteads, male and female slaves, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, and livestock of both sexes: all of it and every part of it in its entirety.

Then I leave the estate of Leuga, which is beside the river Lupa, with inhabitants, homesteads, buildings, and everything appropriate, except vineyards, in its entirety.

Likewise, in the estate of Odo, the homesteads which I appear presently to have; and in Catella, one homestead; and the entire estate of Osellum, with homesteads, buildings, male and female slaves, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, and waters: all of it and every part of it in its entirety.

---

### XVIII. Charter by which Huntbertus, abbot, grants gifts to the monastery of Maroilles

[Note: [Col. 1197C] This charter has been published several times: first, in Balderic’s *Chronicle of Cambrai*, p. 52, by Colomerius, where it is said to have been taken from the archive of the church of Saint Humbert; second, by Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. I, p. 9, who appears to have corrected it from the autograph preserved by the people of Maroilles; [Col. 1197D] third, reprinted by Cointius, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 629, from Balderic and Miraeus; fourth, by the continuators of the Bollandists, March, vol. III, from what they believe to be the autograph itself. We follow the editions of Miraeus and Colomerius, which differ only in that Colomerius reads the name Humbertus where the other reads Chronebertus, and vice versa. The restoration is supported by the copies seen by Miraeus and the Bollandists, and the context itself indicates that it should be corrected in this way. The error is readily explained in writing the names Humbertus, Huntbertus, or Chunebertus, since among the ancients the letter *c* was often prefixed to a vowel beginning with aspiration, as Mabillon notes, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 421, while asserting this very correction.]

(Ann. 671)

[Col. 1197A]

In the twelfth year of the reign of our lord Childeric, glorious king [Note: [Col. 1197D] The twelfth year of Childeric II’s reign corresponds to the year of Christ 671. Bollandus, under 1 February, in the preliminary commentary on the *Life of Saint Sigibert*, and Henschenius, *On the Three Dagoberts*, book II, chapter 4, deny that the date indication exists in the autograph; according to them, it was interpolated by Balderic and Miraeus.]—on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

I, Huntbertus, in the name of God, although an unworthy sinner, reflecting upon the fear of God and the recompense of eternal good, or upon the cleansing of my sins, since Scripture says, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may lead you into the eternal dwellings of the saints”; and again it says, “Make for yourselves bags of alms that do not grow old”—for this reason I give, and wish it to be given forever, to the holy monastery called Maroilles, which the illustrious man Chronebertus [Note: [Col. 1198C] The *Chronicle of Cambrai* reads Huntbertus. In one of the three manuscript codices seen by Colomerius, it read, as he states on p. 417, Rudobertus; but after erasure it was restored on a second examination [Col. 1198D].] formerly built by his own work, where I myself, an unworthy sinner, appear to preside as abbot, consecrated in honor of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saints Peter and Paul the apostles, and of the other lords who are venerated in that basilica, situated in the district of Famarus beside the stream called the Helpre:

namely, the greater part of our possession in the estate called Maceria, situated in the district of Laon beside the river Oise, which I bought from my grandmother Audeliana, consecrated to God, by paying a price and under a deed of sale. This consists of the lordly homesteads where Audeliana herself lived, or which we later built, together with lands, male slaves, and female slaves, those men and women.

These homesteads, with their lands, meadows, and pastures, in their entirety, by this document of our donation, which we asked the notary Ulsinus to write, we hand over from the present day for possession to the basilica of Saint Mary constructed at Maroilles. [Col. 1197C]

All the things named above we have assigned to that monastery, so that the monks themselves or our successors may from the present day receive them for possession under their own right and dominion, both the lands and houses, buildings, dependants, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, without interference by any judge; and so that they may have in their power to hold, give, sell, exchange, or do whatever they wish with them. [Col. 1198A]

Therefore in this document we decree that no claim may thereafter arise by any other means between those servants of God and our heirs. But if anyone after us—which we do not believe will happen—if any of our heirs, or any opposing person, should wish to come against or violate this donation which we have ordered to be made, let him first incur the anger of the Triune Majesty and be anathema; let his name be erased from the heavenly book of the living, and let him not be written among the just, but let him be a companion of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the Lord. If he refuses to amend, may God change his mind, and at that judgment may he receive what Ananias and Sapphira received in the present life. Moreover, let him be compelled to pay to the demanding treasury ten pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver; and if he makes any claim, let him have no power to vindicate anything; while our reward may henceforth advance toward salvation.

And if any document, earlier or later, in our name, concerning our relatives or outsiders, should be produced or should ever appear at any time by any device or argument, let it be recognized as forged and remain void. But this present donation made by me shall remain firm and inviolate forever, supported by the stipulation of suitable witnesses, namely Lord Bishop Vindicianus and my brother Fulbertus, and [such-and-such persons] [Note: [Col. 1198D] The abbreviated words “of that one and of that one” do not at all appear to preserve the reading of the autograph; rather, they seem to reflect the negligence of the copyist, who did not take care to add the other subscriptions.]

Executed at Maroilles. I, Huntbertus himself (*Chronicle of Cambrai*: Chonebertus), although a sinful abbot, confirm this with my own hand.

---

### XIX. Charter by which Hunaldus and his wife Deodata give to Berarius, bishop of Le Mans, retaining the usufruct, whatever they possess in the estate of Gaviriacum, which had been granted to them for usufruct by Berarius

[Note: [Col. 1198D] We publish here a charter which we mentioned in our notes, p. 169, on the diploma issued in the third year of the reign of Theuderic III. It is inserted in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 274, and appears nowhere else, which naturally raises some suspicion regarding its authenticity. Since, however, it exhibits no manifest signs of forgery, it cannot properly be counted among spurious charters. Certainly it conflicts with several documents found among the same acts, but we have clearly shown those to be fictitious, and therefore they do nothing to diminish the credibility of this charter. The fourth year of the reign of Theuderic III, in the month of July, corresponds to the year of Christ 677 according to our method of calculating the years of this reign.]

(Ann. 677)

[Col. 1198C]

To the holy lord and most worthy of the apostolic see, our lord and Father Berarius, bishop, and likewise to the whole congregation of the holy Church of Le Mans, Hunaldus and his wife Deodata.

Since you granted us, for the duration of our lives, the benefit of usufruct from the estate of your aforesaid Church called Gaviriacum, situated in the territory of Bordeaux, it therefore pleased us, for the sake of God, that we should grant to you and to your Church, for the remedy of our souls and in return for that usufruct, our request concerning whatever we are known to possess or hold as property in that estate. It is therefore established that we have done this by the present document, on the following condition: as long as we live, we are to possess in its entirety both the portion belonging to your Church and our own portion, together with their adjoining properties, so that neither you nor your successors, whoever they may be on behalf of your aforesaid Church, may during the days of our lives have any claim or inquiry against us concerning them.

Accordingly, as written above, I or my wife Deodata are to possess this in its entirety; and likewise you, or your Church, after our departure, shall recover our own portion under your dominion. You shall not fear that we, or our heirs or heirs’ heirs, at any time make any contrary claim or demand; rather, in the name of God and for the remedy of our souls, after our departure it shall perpetually benefit the Church in your charge as an increase.

And [which we do not believe will happen] if anyone—whether you and your successors, or we ourselves or our heirs—should attempt to oppose, resist, or claim anything contrary to this document, whoever presumes to do so shall pay to the opposing party, together with the most sacred treasury, five pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver. [Col. 1199C] May this present document remain firm and enduring forever in the name of God, supported and secured by a firm stipulation.

This document was made on the second day of the month of July, in the fourth year of the reign of our lord King Theuderic.

Hunualdus, I have subscribed.  
Deodata, I have subscribed.  
In the name of Christ, Leodebertus, I have subscribed.  
In the name of Christ, Bosolenus, as though a sinful bishop, I have subscribed.  
Jesus Christi, the humble, I have subscribed.  
Neonus Christi, the humble, I have subscribed.  
Probatus Christi, the humble, I have subscribed.  
In the name of Christ, Bertranus, abbot, I have subscribed.  
In the name of Christ, Iggonardus, I have subscribed.  
Eodinus, I have subscribed.  
Audobertus, ordered by my lord Hunaldus, wrote and subscribed this document.

---

### XX. Letter of Bishop Vindicianus to Pope John, containing his reply confirming the privileges granted by Vindicianus to the church of Saint Mary of Arras

[Note: [Col. 1199D] Inserted in Balderic’s *Chronicle of Cambrai*, p. 46; reprinted in the supplement to Miraeus’s diplomatic works, vol. IV, p. 10. The chronological indications reveal it to be false: they associate Pope John’s pontificate with the seventh year of the reign of Theuderic III and with the period when Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, was deposed by Ebroin. Leodegarius was removed from the episcopate in 674; the seventh year of Theuderic III’s reign was the year of Christ 680. Chantereau Lefebvre, in the manuscript *On Salic Law* preserved among the manuscripts of the Royal Library, states concerning this letter of Vindicianus—wrongly, in my judgment—that Childebert was killed in the year 667, in the tenth indiction, so that Theuderic’s seventh year would correspond with 674. Even if this were true, it would not alter the opinion of Brequigny. The pontificate of Pope John V began around the year of Christ 685 or 686, while John IV died in 642; [Col. 1200D] all these facts conflict so completely that they cannot possibly be reconciled. In truth, neither in 674—which according to Chantereau Lefebvre’s view would have been Theuderic’s seventh year—nor in 680, which the distinguished Brequigny accepts, was there any pope named John. We omit the points inferred by Cointius from the formulas and subscriptions, *Annales*, vol. III, p. 820, which provide certain signs of disgusting falsity.]

(Ann. 680)

[Col. 1200A]

To the holy and universal Church’s guardian, the most blessed John, Roman pope and bishop of bishops, Vindicianus, the least of the servants of God: whatever may be most prosperous in Christ the Lord.

Let it be known to your fatherhood, and to all the children of the holy Church of God, that if we contribute anything from our possessions to holy places or to the substance of the poor, we confidently believe that this will undoubtedly be repaid to us in eternal blessedness.

Trusting in the Lord’s great mercy and piety, we confirmed this letter in the assembly of our venerable bishops, in the presence of the most pious King Theuderic, at a general public court, and we wish it, once confirmed, to remain so forever. The law of the ancients likewise demands authority, so that whoever wishes to sell, cede, or donate anything from his own property may have permission, according to Salic law, to bind his written instrument [Note: [Col. 1200D] Under Salic law—Eccard XLII; Feuerbach XLVI; Schilter LXXX; Herold XLX; Emend. XLVIII—formalities in the count’s public court, or before the king, were required when someone intended to make a donation of his property to another. In practice, however, this requirement had been abandoned, for several donations exist that were made by simple letters, as the formulas of Marculfus and others prove; it would be unnecessary to indicate them individually.]

Therefore let all the faithful, present and future, know that by pontifical authority this episcopal privilege was established by the aforesaid King Theuderic, so that it may be preserved inviolate. From this day onward, by pontifical authority, we exclude all secular and judicial powers, and every claim and every invasion, from the church of Saint Mary in the city of Arras. But so that the canons serving God there may be permitted to live peacefully from now and for all time, we separate it from every worldly disturbance. [Col. 1200C]

If, however, a case should arise in which our successors prefer to create precaria or benefits from property belonging to the use of the clerics, we forbid this under the prohibition of anathema also, and by pontifical authority we establish that the monastery, together with these estates—Belrenium, Medonivilla, with sixty homesteads between the two estates, eleven cultivated holdings, and two churches, with every endowment and all their appurtenances; Aquis in the district of Arras, with its church, endowment, and all its appurtenances; Friscini court with all its appurtenances; Batsala with its church and all its appurtenances; Berleta with all its appurtenances; Squavia with its church, endowment, and all its appurtenances; [Col. 1201A] Ors with all its appurtenances; Sautscidum with its appurtenances; Radonivilla with one mill on the stream of Crientonus; another mill in the lordly court; Maraculum in its entirety, with its church and endowment; a small tithe in Rodulfus’s court, and likewise in Unziacum—from this day onward and for all time shall be in the power of the canons serving God in that monastery.

Let no one presume to inflict any trouble upon the things we have named, which the illustrious king mentioned above assigned to that place by royal decree from his own property and from other sources for the use of the clerics. Rather, let them be permitted to possess everything peacefully, so that they may pray more freely for the peace of the holy Church of God, for the life of the king, his wife and children, and for the condition of the kingdom, entreating the Lord’s mercy.

But if anyone proves obedient to this privilege issued by us, let him receive a reward from the Lord and a blessing from you and from all of us, both in the present life and, in the future, eternal life. Amen.

But those who have thought little of our authority and have wished to violate this pontifical authority confirmed by our hand, we refer to your clemency, so that what has been confirmed by us may be permitted to remain stable not only by you but by all our bishops who are associated with you.

Almighty God, who placed the teaching of truth upon the chair of unity, may he make you mindful of him and understanding of him, and may it please you, for his sake, to remember me also in your prayers [Note: [Col. 1201D] Here the *Chronicle* reads “but he,” words that make no sense.]

From Vindicianus, together with the fellow bishops dwelling within the boundaries of Gaul: fraternal visitation and paternal blessing.

Hear the judgment that I pronounce. If anyone among your successors, or any count, or the greed of judges, or any opposing person, should wish to diminish or withdraw from the place this donation or confirmation which you have resolved to make or confirm for the sake of God and divine love, we condemn him by apostolic judgment; by pontifical authority we separate him from the thresholds of the holy Church of God, exclude him from the assembly of the heavenly powers, and cast him out of the kingdom of God. By the prohibition of Saint Peter, Christ’s doorkeeper and holder of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, we forbid him; and together with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, we consign him by lot to suffer, on the day of judgment, with the devil and his ministers, amid the trembling lamentation of hell, without joy. Amen.

I, John, pope, have confirmed and strengthened this privilege issued by my humble self.  
I, Marinus, vicar of the apostolic see, have confirmed and strengthened it.  
I, Andreas, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Bonibertus, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Laurentius, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Pedelbrandus, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Nautor, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Hilarius, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Constantius, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Martinus, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Christophorus, bishop, [Col. 1202A] have subscribed.  
I, Thomas, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Felix, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Audoinus, archbishop, have subscribed.  
I, Austregisilus, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Ravengarius, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Silvinus, bishop, have subscribed.  
I, Leodegarius, deposed from the see of Autun by the impious judge Ebroin, have written and subscribed.

Issued on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the seventh year of the reign of our lord King Theuderic, in the second indiction.

I, Vindicianus, bishop, at the command of Lord King Theuderic and at the request of John, supreme pontiff, wrote and subscribed.

---

### XXI. Charter by which Nizezius and his wife Ermintrudis transfer many possessions to the monastery of Moissac by right of sale

[Note: [Col. 1201D] Mabillon published this charter, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 686, recovered from the archive of the monastery of Moissac. There appears to be no reason to doubt its authenticity. Leotadius, who is called abbot of Moissac, in the month of May of the seventh year of the reign of Theuderic III—that is, in the year of Christ 680—lived at this time, according to the catalogue of the abbots of Moissac, *New Gaul of Christ*, vol. I, col. 159; he was certainly distinct from Leotadius, who was bishop of Auch at the beginning of the eighth century. On this matter see Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 358, and Cointius, *Annales*, vol. IV, p. 252. The same charter exists in the Royal Manuscript numbered 4491, written in the fifteenth century, but so inaccurately that it is not worthwhile extracting variant readings from it. I determined this for myself after inspecting the codex.]

(Ann. 680)

[Col. 1202B]

To the venerable Father in Christ and apostolic lord, Leotadius, abbot, and to the whole congregation of the monastery of Moissac, which is situated in the district of Quercy and appears to have been founded in honor of Saint Peter.

I, Nizezius, and my wife Ermintrudis, having recognized the guilt of our conscience, ought, while God has placed it within our will, to carry out the administration of our possessions according to the evangelical reading, so that the Lord may deal with us as he deigned to say in his Gospel: “Go, sell everything that you have, give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”

Therefore, by this true declaration, I give to you, the aforesaid servants of God, and to the whole congregation which appears to be established in the monastery named above, in the district of Toulouse, the estates called Calmeabilidem, Barolingus, Vivaderemus, and Sambilianus, in their entirety, within the boundaries and places designated by us.

In another place, within the same district, our other estates: Aufinianus; our lordly courts, with churches or solar houses, fishponds, orchards, fisheries, mills, together with their appurtenances; Besingus; the estate of Scoternum; Orfollingus; the estate or village of Gannicolas, with the church of Saint Medard, which lies within that boundary, in its entirety and completeness, with male slaves, tenants, and the substance of freedmen, together with the boundaries and places designated by us:

that is, from the river Garonne through the whirlpool of Mamare; [Col. 1202D] from there through the boundaries of the estate of Salis, with the church of Saint Saturninus, which, after paying our price, we appear to have bought from the late Guirardus; from there through the former stream-bed of Perucia, by the spring in the *conasticis*, which is in the middle of the fields; and from there it reaches as far as Navaliense, or to the mountain of the late Beretonius, as far as Stirpiniacum, and the rampart of Envaldus as far as the middle of Saldimia; from there through Livigonus as far as the aforesaid river [Col. 1203A] Garonne.

And in another place, within the same district of Toulouse, our other estates named as follows: Lampidiacum, with the church of Saint Martin; Vulpiliacum; Speutingus; Prareti; the church’s exchanges with the village of Saint Gemma; the estate of Sarpana, with the church of Saint Germanus; the estate of Gainagum; the estate of Novolium, with the church of Saint Medard.

These estates named above, with their churches, all their villages, and their adjoining properties, within the boundaries designated by us, which are: through the middle of the Garonne, then through the middle of the fields, then as far as the Larona, and from there through the Novolian marsh as far as the Garonne written above.

And in another place, in the district of Agen, our estate of Viriacaria, in its entirety, within the boundaries below: by the ford and boundary of Vasalonus; on the other side, the boundary of the estate of Bordouse; [Col. 1203B] from there by the stream of Oppinio as far as the middle of the Garonne.

And in the district of Eauze, our other estates, Giuvigus and Sauviacum, in their entirety, as they appear to be possessed by us within the ancient boundaries.

We likewise leave to our own heirs, in Faldidium, our estates: in the district of Toulouse, Modorciacum, Altomons, and Basilla; in the district of Agen, Pompeiacum; and in the district of Eauze, Malarouta.

These estates also named above, except those which we leave in Faldidium, and all the others which we have inserted here, with their courts, churches, buildings, houses, dependants, tenants residing there, and the rights of freedmen and tenants of both sexes, with cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, with all their rights and adjoining properties, whether acquired or to be acquired: by this deed of sale I hand over, transfer, and convey all these things to you for possession. [Col. 1203C]

We have received the price from you, and it has fully satisfied us, namely, seven hundred solidi of the purest gold and four cloaks worth two hundred solidi.

We have expended these prices, received by us, for the remedy of our souls, in the sustenance of the poor serving God there.

All the things named above we hand over into your hands and those of your successors, so that you may possess them and freely enjoy, at your own discretion, whatever you wish to do with them, under a supporting stipulation.

This deed of sale was made in the month of May, in the seventh year of the reign of our lord King Theuderic.

Nizezius, a sinner, and Ermintrudis: we have acknowledged and signed this deed of sale.

Mark of Gundobertus.  
Mark of Sicandus.  
Mark of Almarius.  
Mark of Sicarubis.  
Mark of Autricus.  
Mark of Dacolenus.  
Mark of Bertinarus.  
Mark of Froticus.  
Mark of Guntarius.  
Mark of Bertallus.  
Mark of Belbonus.

Executed publicly at the monastery of Moissac.

### XXII. Donation made by Aloinus to the monastery of Saint Gall

[Note: [Col. 1203D] I reprint this document from the *Traditions of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, p. 2. It had already been published by Vadianus in Goldast, *Writers on German Affairs*, vol. III, p. 37; by Lunig, *Ecclesiastical Spicilegium*, part III, p. 190; and also by Neugart, *Alemannic Diplomatic Codex*, vol. I, p. 6, though not in full.]

(Ann. 680)

In the name of God and of good peace. It pleased me, and was agreed upon, and my will increased, that I should make a donation of land belonging to my right, for the honor of Saint Gallus and Saint Desiderius, in the place called by the name of the estate of Athorinswanic: three *hubae*, and in Gundlihespuria, four *hubae*.

And I did so. Thus I, Aloinus, made the donation of the land, and by this deed of donation, which is to remain firm from the present day, [Col. 1204B] I confirm it.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs, should attempt to come against or act against this donation, let him first incur the anger of God, be excluded from the common body and from the priesthood, and pay as a composition to the treasury two pounds of gold and three of silver. Let him have no power to claim what he seeks; but let this present donation remain firm forever, supported by the attached stipulation.

Executed in the monastery of Saint Gall.

Mark of Aloinus, who requested that this donation be made.  
Mark of Stephanus.  
Mark of Jactatus.  
Mark of Petrus.  
Mark of Whalao.  
Mark of Landelhelm.  
Mark of Valotus.

I recorded what I did in the month of July, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

I, Petrus, wrote and subscribed, under King Theuderic. [Note: [Col. 1203D] I have supplied the year 680 conjecturally; the codex of Saint Gall indicates approximately 690 in the margin.]

### XXIII. Charter by which Aredius, or Petruinus, bishop of Vaison, confirms gifts made by himself or others to the monastery of Grasello and grants privileges

[Note: Mabillon published this charter in *Annales*, vol. I, p. 698, on the authority of a copy he had received from Ludovicus Antonius Rufus. Boyer published it again in his *History of the Church of Vaison*, documentary evidence, p. 7, collated with the original by the prior of Saint-André. We follow Mabillon’s reading, placing within parentheses the differences drawn from Boyer’s edition. Aredius, or Petruinus, appears to be the same man who, under Clovis II, signed the Council of Chalon under the name Petronius, about the year 650, according to *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. I, col. 923, and the *Ecclesiastical History of Vaison*, p. 67. The authors of *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. I, p. 920, assert that no traces of this monastery survive. Boyer, however, p. 66, reports that in his own time, in 1731, part of the old church still stood intact; on Sundays, a gathering of young people devoted themselves there to pious exercises in a beautifully decorated space. The remaining buildings, destroyed by barbarians or heretics, showed nothing but ruins. Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 572, notes that this monastery was subjected by Peter, bishop of Marseille, in 1059, to the abbey of Saint-Victor of Marseille, of which it was a cell and under whose title of Saint Peter and Saint Victor of Grasello it still remains.] (Year 683.)

[Col. 1204C]

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. To our venerable, most beloved, and holy brothers, our fellow provincials, who by the Lord’s dispensation are rulers of the holy churches: Aredius, also called Petruinus, of the see of the church of the city of Vaison, though unworthy, by the Lord’s dispensation bishop.

We are confident that we begin some good spiritual work when, for the needs of God’s servants, together with the counsel of our people, we apply spiritual resources, considering how, by mutual agreement, the reward of both parties may increase according to their needs: so that they may receive assistance from us, and we, through their intercession, may deserve the Lord’s support. For in this way the lofty summits of the monastic order of God’s servants are raised to a high stature, when the faithful lay their foundations upon solid rock.

Therefore, since it has pleased us that a monastery in the suburb of the city, at a place called Grasello [Boyer: Grassello], which we appear to have built in honor of Saint Victor and Saint Peter and the other holy lords, should be established according to the institutions of the holy Fathers, the venerable man Fredeghisolus, abbot, and the congregation of monks, with the Lord’s favor, are to serve in the aforesaid monastery. They are to live and dwell according to the rule of the venerable holy Father Benedict, abbot, and of Saint Macarius and Saint Columbanus, so that, holding to the path of the holy Fathers and to the institutions of the primitive Church—as the Acts of the Apostles testify, whose members had one heart and one soul in the Lord and did not claim anything as their own, but held everything in common, and whatever they could possess, after selling and disposing of everything, they placed the proceeds at the apostles’ feet—everything might be common to them, as we have already said.

Elsewhere the Lord promised the kingdom of heaven and eternal life to those whom he calls blessed poor people in the Gospel, to whom the hymn is appropriately sung: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

And since the small monastery of Saint Victor and Saint Peter, as we have said, is situated in the suburb of the city, and is known to lie beneath that city, we have therefore decided to attach to its support whatever, by letters—whether by transfers or by any sort of written instruments—the lord Aredius, also called Petruinus, bishop of the city of Vaison [Boyer: Vasiensium], or his grandmother, the lady Gregoria, a bishopess [Note: *Episcopiae*, also called *episcopae* or *episcopissae*, were women who had been the wives of bishops before their husbands had attained the episcopal insignia and who, once their husbands had been elevated to the episcopate, lived in monasteries. This was not the arrangement prescribed by the Council of Tours of 567, whose canon 12 ordered only that a bishop who had married before entering the priesthood should treat his wife as a sister. The councils contain no mention of a bishopess withdrawing to a monastery unless voluntarily. The only requirement was that a married man should not be promoted to holy orders without his wife’s consent, as the Council of Agde of 506 confirms.] may have granted to that place or to the monks named above, whom God shall command to be called there, according to his will. Thus they may obtain fuller forgiveness before God through preserving the rule and transmitting the tradition of the orthodox Fathers; and we, as we have said, may deserve through their intercessions to be released from the bonds of our sins.

Nor do we believe that, by this benefit granted by us to them, we are acting contrary to the wishes of certain fellow bishops of the churches of Gaul [Boyer: “to be contrary”], since we are already supported in large measure by their authority, given that similar benefits have been granted to many monasteries, and there are countless privileges, whose enumeration in order would be lengthy. Nevertheless, the passage concerning our predecessors and the monasteries of Lérins, Agaune, Saint Marcellus the Martyr at Chalon, Lyon, Vienne, and all Gaul is textually corrupt; it adds that many are known to have obtained this favor of devotion from the apostolic see.

Therefore we too have not considered it contrary to establish comparable arrangements in our city, trusting in the Lord’s governance, so that, in accordance with the apostle’s words, we may be God’s [Boyer: “are”] fellow workers, approved cultivators. We become fellow workers if, with the apostle Peter, we prepare pasture for the holy sheep, so that those servants of God may gladly pray more earnestly for our sins, for the whole city, and for the stability of this kingdom of the Franks.

Therefore I, Aredius, also called Petruinus, appointed bishop of the cathedral church of the city of Vaison, devoted—with your, as is fitting, agreement [Boyer: “concurrence”] and holy brotherhood—by our indulgence, now grant them this privilege of liberty. With the Lord’s help, the congregation itself and their successors who remain in this holy community, or who hasten to contemplate the heavenly homeland, shall observe inviolably for all time what is now granted by us with the consent of your brotherhood and confirmed by your holy hands. Our successors shall preserve what we have decreed, just as other monasteries, as we said above, receiving this benefit of privilege, may enjoy it in complete quiet, without disturbance or harassment from bishops or the officers of the church, or from the assaults of secular persons, while the holy congregation remains undisturbed.

The present provision is to stand likewise, since our indulgence is understood to begin with them and with us. Accordingly, with devotion and for the sake of the congregation, we humbly instruct our successors that, if the bishop whose pastoral care involves the keeping of sheep should come to the monastery, as befits a shepherd, for the purpose of visiting or comforting it, then, having observed the congregation’s devout disposition and zeal for edification, he should proceed directly to the monastery as is fitting; and, after celebrating the holy mysteries and giving his blessing, he should depart cheerfully.

He shall impose there no exaction sought as a due, nor any of the former payments which ancient custom had required to be offered, except what they may voluntarily decide to offer for fear of God. No obligatory provisions are to be demanded from them by bishops, archdeacons, or any other collectors of this church, nor is any payment that might have been judged due on account of ancient custom to be exacted.

And I expect that everything will be devoted entirely to their reward and increase, just as it is known to be released by us with every expression of piety; so also our successors, for the increase of their reward [Boyer: “of the rulers’ reward”], shall grant it with a generous spirit in hope of eternal recompense.

When necessity requires it, if the abbot departs from this world, no one from elsewhere shall be appointed. Rather, as is fitting and as their dignity and order require, the abbot shall be chosen from that fellowship within the monastery, so that the congregation itself may be maintained as one thoroughly and perfectly instructed in the rule and founded in the fear of God.

The abbot shall be elected in that monastery without any payment. The election shall nevertheless be conducted by the entire congregation, so that it is not some inferior party, but the one whom the order of the perfect has chosen, who, by the Lord’s dispensation, is instituted without strife by the bishop of this city. Far be it that, through payment being offered, or through intrigue within the congregation, or through the opposition of any other party, someone arriving from outside should be irregularly installed. Rather, as we have said, the person chosen from the congregation shall be the elder whom the entire congregation, perfect in its devotion to divine service, has selected for itself.

Yet, with the counsel and will of the bishop of this city—not out of fear, but after being requested with all humility—the monks shall take up the dignity of whomever they have chosen, with his blessing.

Likewise, as is accustomed to happen over succeeding generations, if the monks who ought to be subject to the sacred order of the congregation should stand negligent, glorying in their liberty, then the bishop of this city shall associate with himself priests or abbots who appear to follow the path of the same rule. With fatherly affection, and with spiritual persons accompanying him, according to the Gospel—two or three, or more if necessary—he shall summon them to a conference in the monastery itself and, in accordance with their rule and custom, graciously correct them or restore them to their proper order. May it never be permitted that, through fear or negligence, what the holy Fathers established should be changed over the course of time.

When it is necessary to bless the church’s tablets, or perhaps to request chrism or holy baptism, they shall receive these from the bishop of this church without payment. Nor shall that bishop, arrogating to himself any prerogative of power, dare rashly to take anything from the affairs of the monastery or from its holy altars, ornaments, vessels, sacred books, or anything else, great or small.

When the abbot wishes to permit someone to enter an ecclesiastical order, he shall approach the bishop of this city with all humility; and the bishop, as is proper for a shepherd, shall grant it freely and without payment. Before the tribunal of Christ we adjure and beseech that bishop, before God and his angels, where the order of dignity prevails and where their petition appears meritorious according to their way of life, not to be opposed to them.

Therefore we ask, testify, and, by the indulgence of charity, strictly forbid all bishops—both our successors and those established near or far from the aforesaid monastery—to attempt anything contrary to the tenor of this present decree, induced by any petition of whatever congregation, or to touch anything that has been prohibited. This applies to the matters named above, to the ordination of persons, to the possessions of the monastery itself, to whatever is known to be under its jurisdiction, and to anything that, as we said above, we have granted to that monastery by our letters.

No bishop, archdeacon, vicedominus, or any officer of this church shall demand from it any compulsory provisions, lodging, other payments, or possessions which, as we have already said, have been granted to this monastery from the property of this church by us, or which in the future, with God’s help, may be bestowed by pious and religious men. No one shall demand or exact them, or, at the instigation of an evil bishop, dare to take or withdraw anything from them by force and presumption. Rather, under complete protection, let those servants of God be permitted to live and dwell under the authority [Boyer: “strictness”] of their rule.

This privilege granted to them, which we have said above was modeled on that of many monasteries of Gaul, we command to remain wholly undisturbed, and by almighty God we dare to adjure our posterity that it remain so, provided that our brothers look upon it as granted with complete agreement. By their consenting counsel, what has now been established is seen to have been confirmed by their hands and assent; what we have issued and written with the fullest will of our heart shall be confirmed below in due order.

Yet we do not believe that any successor of yours will arise in the course of time who ought to overturn this present institution. But if anyone, through some cunning or imposed desire, should presume to attempt anything prohibited, or in any way, in succeeding times, to act against the decrees stated above, let him first be struck by the vengeance of almighty God, separated in this matter and portion from communion with the holy Church and from the fellowship of all Christians, and let him appear excommunicated both here and in the future. By the aid of him who received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, let him be cast down and alienated. Let the portion of the traitor Judas Iscariot [Boyer: Iscariot], who betrayed the Lord, be assigned to him as a punishment; let him descend alive into hell with Dathan and Abiron; and, separated from the fellowship of all the saints, let him never be able to do anything from his possessions or property for the remedy of his soul, since he wished to overturn or violate the benefit granted by us to God’s servants.

Rather, in everything that, with God’s help, has been arranged or bestowed by us for the advantage of those servants of God, let this present document, with adversaries deterred, remain firm forever and in every respect complete and inviolable [Boyer: “this present document,” “the document”]. To strengthen this privilege still further, and so that it may not, through the deed of evil men, be broken into and transferred to another [Boyer: “another thing”], we have resolved to affirm it by the subscriptions of our hands. We ask that it be strengthened by the hands of all our provincial brothers [Note: The provincial bishops seem to be meant here: namely, the bishops of the province of Arles. The church of Vaison, which is now subject to the church of Avignon, was subject in the seventh century to the metropolitan of Arles. Wolbertus, who subscribes first to the charter under consideration, was himself bishop of Arles. It would be difficult to determine which sees each of the other subscribers governed, as the authors of *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. I, col. 543, acknowledge, because the lists of bishops of the province of Arles in the seventh century are incomplete. Boyer, in the work cited above, assigns the sees to them individually on the basis of conjecture: Aghiacus governed the church of Avignon, Ambrosius that of Carpentras, Fredicus that of Orange, Godebertus that of Tricastin, Leodegarius that of Venasque, Pascasius that of Cavaillon, and finally Rusticus that of Viviers.] with the stipulation appended for complete validity.

This privilege was made on the Kalends of February, in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Theodoric [Boyer: Theodoricus], the glorious king.

In the name of Christ, Petruinus, also called Aredius, though a sinner, bishop, reread this privilege made and reconfirmed by me, and subscribed it with the readiest will.

In the name of Christ, Wolbertus, though a sinner, who, at the request of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege, subject to canonical institution.

In the name of Christ, Aghiacus, bishop, at the request of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege of institution.

In the name of God, Ambrosius, bishop, at the request of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege, subject to canonical institution.

By the grace of God, Fredicus, though a sinner, bishop, subscribed this privilege of institution.

In the name of Christ, Godebertus [Boyer: Godelbertus], though a sinner, bishop, at the request of lord Bishop Aredius, according to what seemed most proper to the lord bishops, subscribed.

In the name of Christ, Leodegarius, though a sinner, bishop, at the request of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege of institution.

In the name of God, Pascasius [Boyer: Paschasius], bishop, at the request of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege, subject to canonical institution.

Rusticus, by the grace of God, though an unworthy sinner, bishop, at the request of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege, subject to canonical institution.

In the name of Christ, Ago, abbot, at the request of my lord Aredius, bishop, subscribed this privilege.

In the name of God, Pascasius [Boyer: Paschasius], priest, at the request of my lord Aredius, bishop, subscribed this privilege.

In the name of Christ, Delphinus, abbot, at the command of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege.

In the name of God, Maurontus, archdeacon, at the command of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege.

In the name of God, Genno, deacon, at the request of lord Bishop Aredius, subscribed this privilege.

### XXIV. Charter by which Amalfridus grants the monastery of Hunulfocurtis to the monastery of Sithiu

[Note: Mabillon had published fragments of this charter in *De re diplomatica*, p. 607, from Folquin’s cartulary. On Mabillon’s authority it was reprinted in the *Supplement to the Diplomatic Works of Miraeus*, vol. II, p. 927, and in the *Collection of Writings Concerning the Affairs of the Franks*, vol. IV, p. 665, in the notes. The authors of *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. III, documentary section, col. 26, published the complete charter from the papers of Hunulfocurtis. We present the same charter, which lord de Witte, keeper of the archives of Saint-Bertin, extracted from Folquin’s cartulary and deposited in our archive. We add variant readings in parentheses, copied from *Gallia Christiana*. Theodoric III confirmed this charter by a diploma that we shall publish below, p. 202; J. Iperius mentions both the charter and the diploma in his *Chronicle*, in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 471. Compare the edition of the cartulary published by the distinguished Guerard in 1841, p. 29.] (Year 685.)

As far as human understanding can weigh with the mind’s discernment and consider through diligent inquiry, no greater gain can be secured in the fleeting light of this world from transitory joy than to take care that one’s possessions be spent in places deserving reverence for the support of the poor, so that all may endure the frailty of nature before sudden change overtakes them.

It is necessary to keep watch for the salvation of the soul, lest that day find anyone unprepared, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever gives little acquires for himself a kingdom and glory that will endure without end.”

Therefore I, Amalfridus, an illustrious man, in the name of God, inspired by divine power and for the remedy of my soul, have designated, granted, and transferred by this deed of donation to the monastery of Sithiu [*Gallia Christiana*: Sithiu], which was built in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, Saint Martin, and the other saints [*Gallia Christiana*: “which was built”], and where the venerable man Bertinus appears to preside as abbot, with the consent and agreement [*Gallia Christiana*: “of the consenting”] of my daughter Auriana [Note: It is clear from this charter that Auriana was the first abbess of the monastery of Hunulfocurtis; Baldwin also attests this in his *Chronicle of Cambrai*, book II, chapter 10. Malbrancq, *De Morinis*, book III, chapter 44, and Carpentier, *History of Cambrai*, vol. I, p. 506, place Austreberta before her; but Mabillon refutes this in the *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict*, third age, p. 22, in his observations on the Life of Saint Austreberta.] who appears to be its superior:

Namely, our monastery called Hunulfocurtis, in the district of Cambrai, on the River Scheldt [*Gallia Christiana*: Scale], which I possess as our property, in honor of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, Saint Martin, and Saint Polline [*Gallia Christiana*: Polaena], where that precious gem rests in bodily form. I have arranged this as seemed good to me, on the following condition: that we should transfer to the monastery of Sithiu [*Gallia Christiana*: Sithiu], for the use of Saint Peter, the aforesaid monastery in its entirety and with all its substance, together with everything belonging or pertaining to it.

This we have done, both from the hereditary property of my parents and from what was purchased or acquired in any manner from elsewhere, by which the monastery appears to have been endowed—both from our share and from goods bestowed by other good men, and from whatever we have held in our possession and which was our rightful property—together with the lands, manses, fortified places belonging to it, houses and buildings erected upon them, residents, slaves, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, mills, waters and their courses, livestock, provisions, movable and immovable property, appurtenances, dependencies—in short, everything, without exception [*Gallia Christiana*: “everything fully”].

For as long as I live in this world, we are to use, govern, or improve this monastery for the benefit of Saint Peter or of you by way of a precarious tenure. After my death and departure from this light, my aforesaid daughter Auriana shall dwell in and govern that monastery [*Gallia Christiana*: “the monastery itself”]. After her death, the monastery named above, Hunulfocurtis, in its entirety, with all that belongs or is subject to it, shall always remain subject to the monastery of Sithiu [*Gallia Christiana*: Sithiu].

The abbot who is then present, or the brothers of the monastery of Sithiu who reside there, shall have full authority to appoint as provost of our monastery whomever they wish. We beseech those brothers and rulers of that monastery, for God’s sake [*Gallia Christiana*: “the Lord’s sake”] and for the gaining of our reward, to take care of the monastery that we have transferred there [*Gallia Christiana*: “transformed”], its masses, its course [Note: *Gallia Christiana* reads *cursu*. The *cursus* was called the ecclesiastical office, or the series of ecclesiastical prayers. See Du Cange, under *Cursus*, sense 2, and the authors cited there], and its lights; and to show charity toward guests and pilgrims, so that they may obtain a reward from this and record our name in the book of life [*Gallia Christiana*: “make our name live again”].

Let them hold, retain, and possess the monastery under their authority in perpetuity—that is, under the authority of the monastery of Sithiu—and let them have free discretion in everything concerning it, whatever they may wish to do.

If anyone, however—which we absolutely do not believe will happen—God forbid, whether I myself, or any of my heirs or successors, or any other outsider or foreign person [*Gallia Christiana*: “any woman”], should wish to act against this testament or presume to violate it, let him first incur the wrath of almighty God, and before the tribunal of Christ, together with Saint Peter himself, render an account on the day of judgment. Moreover, together with the associate treasury enforcing the penalty, let him be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold and twenty weights of silver.

Furthermore, let him be compelled to pay double the value at which the monastery may then have been improved [*Gallia Christiana*: “to the community”], and let him not prevail in the claim he brings. Rather, this testament shall remain firm now and forever, with the stipulation appended.

Executed at Vermandis [Note: Mabillon notes, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 572, that this place should be distinguished from Augusta Viromanduorum, or Saint-Quentin], on the eighth day of February, in the twelfth year of the reign of our lord Theodoric [*Gallia Christiana*: Frederic], the most glorious king.

Amalfridus reread this testament made by me and [Note: Here, and below, after the word “consenting,” there appears a sign which, like other such signs prefixed to certain subscriptions, was used in place of a written subscription.]

I, Auriana, abbess, consenting.

+ Sign of Adalfridus. Wulfahaldus. Niuacio. Anganbertus. Hildramnus. Erchanfridus. Siginus. Waraulfus, deacon. Blitmarus. Crasmarus. Dudan. Bruno. Ermenfridus. Constantinus. Gislefridus, centenarius. [Col. 1212B] Gerfridus. Baldethramnus. Bladardus, having been asked, wrote this testament and [Note: *Gallia Christiana*: Unulfasiale, Nivalio the deacon, Blitmarus, Crasmarus, Dudan, Bruno, Ermenfridus, Constantinus, Gislefridus, the *centenarius*, Gerfridus, Baldechramnus, Bladurdus.] [Note: After this word there are signs which it did not seem important to reproduce in type. At the end of the copy whose reading we follow, the copyist added the following statement for greater reliability: “Collated with Folquin’s cartulary, p. 28, in the year 1782. Signed: D. Ch. de Witte, keeper of the archives of Saint-Bertin.”]

### XXV. Charter by which Reolus, bishop of Reims, grants the village of Gaugiacum to the abbot Beracharius for the construction of a monastery for women

[Note: Until now Mabillon alone had published this charter, in *Annales*, vol. I, appendix, p. 701, from the cartulary of the monastery of Dervensis. We copied it from the same cartulary, folio 128, which D. Laurentius Dumay, keeper of the archives of this monastery, most courteously shared with us. There we found several other instruments that we published above, before that cartulary had come into our hands, having been written at the beginning of the thirteenth century. We collated these with the old Codex and extracted from it, in later work, various readings, which we shall present at the end of this volume among the additions. They are now inserted in their proper places; but the cartulary which the distinguished man testifies that he saw in the Royal Library is no longer found there.] (Year 686.)

In the name of Christ. Reolus, though unworthy and a sinner, bishop. Since all ought to think about the salvation of their soul and offer small things for great ones, perishable things for heavenly ones, upon the altar of almighty God, so that I may deserve to be lifted up by him, as the Truth said: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into eternal dwellings”; and since pastoral order teaches that, wherever they are able, they ought to build sheepfolds of the flocks according to the cenobitic order, whether for men or for women, therefore Abbot Beracharius asked us [Note: If Beracharius, or Bercharius, had been killed shortly after the charter we are examining was issued, as is commonly believed, he would not have had sufficient time to construct the convent on the site granted to him; and it would not be surprising that no mention of this monastery is made in the Life of Bercharius that we possess, written by Adso, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedictini*, vol. II, p. 311. Most writers, indeed—Mabillon, in the place cited above, and Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 130—say that Bercharius died in 685, on 15 September. But, as Cointius admits, the year in which Bercharius died may be disputed, and this is clear from the chronological notice of this charter. Indeed, it must be said that Bercharius lived much longer, according to Cointius, ibid., on the basis of the old catalogue of the abbots of Der, published by Chesnius in the notes to Peter the Venerable’s *Epistle*, at the end of the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 114; this is also proved by the charter of Bishop Bertoend, dated in the second year of Chlodovech III.] to grant him a suitable place, from our property, whether from the ancestral estate or from something acquired in another way, for the construction of a monastery for women.

But, for the remedy of our soul, we did not at all refuse the opportunity to do so. Together with him, however, we considered that we could find no nearby place in our possession that possessed every convenience required for building a monastery. While such was our intention, we found a place belonging to the property of our Church of Reims, within the city of Châlons, in the pagus of Perthois, above the river Marne: a villa called Gaugiacus, also known by another name as Bishop’s Villa. A religious woman named Ama, who ended her life under the title of religion, had donated it to the Church of Reims by her charters.

Since that place pleased the abbot for the construction of a monastery, we, with the consent of my brothers and fellow citizens of Reims—that is, the archdeacons, abbots, priests, [Col. 1213B] deacons, and all the clergy of the churches, as well as the illustrious men who appear to reside within the city, whose names and signatures are inserted below—have determined that, by our letter, from the present day and without opposition from anyone, for the salvation of our soul and for eternal reward, we should transfer the villa Gaugiacus, also called Bishop’s Villa, to the aforesaid Abbot Beracharius for the construction of a monastery for women.

This is done, however, with the counsel, consent, and agreement of the brothers of Reims, in such a way that we have given to our Church of Reims, in exchange for this villa Gaugiacus, our villa Tinnoverus, which we purchased in the pagus of Limousin from the deacon Vetranio for a price, together with the house built at Novum Castrum. We have transferred it to the Church of Reims to possess, with its lands, houses, buildings, the slaves residing there, the tenant farmers belonging to it, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses—in its entirety, as much as appears to belong to the villa Tinnoverus, with everything pertaining to it—together with the house built at Novum Castrum, in the city of Limoges, as compensation in exchange for the villa Gaugiacus.

We have done this so that, both during our lifetime and after our departure from this world, the monastery for women may possess a firmer stability and suffer no disturbance from our episcopal successors or from any opposing persons. Instead, by this present letter of ours, the abbot himself and those handmaids of God who are known to dwell in that appointed place, or their successors, may always possess and rule it in perpetuity, so that they may be more inclined to pray to the Lord’s mercy on our behalf; so that we may deserve to be freed from the bonds of hell; so that, after our departure from this world, our name may be placed or recorded there in the Book of Life; and so that their priests may always be able to offer sacrifices for us.

And if, as commonly happens, they should wish to move those servants of God from that place to another for the construction of a monastery, whether for convenience, improvement, or the sake of stability, they shall retain the villa Gaugiacus [Note: According to the law prescribed here, Gaugiacus, or Bishop’s Villa, now belongs to the monastery of Hautvillers (before 1789), since the nuns have died out in the monastery founded through Reolus’s grant.] called Bishop’s Villa, and it shall revert to the monastery of Hautvillers, which our predecessor and father, Lord Nivardus, formerly bishop, built through his own work. Together with the present letter, which we have requested be drawn up of our own free will, the monks who are known to live there under the holy rule shall, by these instruments, possess and rule it for the whole duration of their lives, without any claim being made against the nuns or their abbess, and shall pray to the Lord’s mercy for the salvation of our soul, so that they, or their priests, may be more inclined to offer sacrifices after our departure from this world.

This is provided, however, on the condition that they wish to remove the nuns from that place. For as long as they are seen to live and dwell there regularly under the holy rule, we, from the present day, by this letter of ours—which is also our testament, made with complete and deliberate counsel and ready will—have transferred the place to them to possess, so that they may have, hold, and possess it.

If anyone, God forbid—whether after us, a successor bishop, any opposing person, or any of my heirs—should wish either to remove them from that place or to disturb them, or should attempt to violate this letter of ours, let him first lose his own life, be enslaved together with his stock, and incur the wrath of the Godhead; let his dominion be scattered, just as the power of Holofernes was scattered; and just as the terrifying dominion of the great Alexander was divided, so may his power henceforth be scattered. Just as Sodom and Gomorrah were struck in the present age, so may his power or dwelling be struck. Let him be struck with the anathema *maranatha*, that is, destruction, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let him appear excommunicated from the thresholds of the Church and from participation in the communion of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. With Judas the traitor, who betrayed the Lord with a false kiss, let him become a partaker. Let the leprosy of Naaman come upon him, which Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, acquired through greed. Let their entire race and offspring wither in the flower, so that it may never bear fruit or ripen into grain; and let him not deserve forgiveness from the Lord.
