And so that this present letter of ours may remain firm for all time, and for the complete security of the matter, we have subscribed this letter below with our own hand. We have personally asked those who have subscribed or signed below to do so in our presence. Moreover, together with the associated treasury, let the violator be compelled to pay to the monastery twenty pounds of gold and nine pounds of silver; let him be unable to establish the claim he is making, and nevertheless let this present letter remain firm and inviolate forever.

Done at the villa of Compiègne, on the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth year of the reign of our lord King Theuderic.

In the name of Christ, Reolus, though a sinner, bishop, have reread and subscribed this letter made by me.

I, Bishop Ansoaldus, at the command of Lord Bishop Reolus, have subscribed this decision.

I, Abbot Peter, have subscribed.

I, Abbot Harmarus, have subscribed.

I, Abbot Hilduinus, have subscribed.

I, Abbot Leocadius, at the command of Lord Bishop Reolus, have reread and subscribed this letter.

I, Amalgisilus, have subscribed.

I, Bertohindus, have subscribed.

I, Gando the priest, have subscribed.

I, Caldemarus the notary, wrote and subscribed this letter of donation at the command of Lord Bishop Reolus.

## XXVI. Charter by which Pippin and Plectrudis, his wife, grant the fortress of Ambra in the Ardennes to Beregisus, so that a monastic cell and church may be founded there

[Note: This charter exists nowhere else except in the supplement to Miraeus’s *Diplomatic Works*, vol. II, p. 1125. It was taken from the archive of the abbey of Saint-Hubert in the Ardennes; it is regarded as the foundation document of the monastery of Andage, which was later given the name Saint-Hubert. The charter is spurious, since the beginnings of the monastery of Andage seem to belong, with Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 436, to the year 702, or even, with Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, p. 16, to 706; nor was Beregisus known to Pippin and Plectrudis before 696, as is clear from the same Cointius. The *Nouvelle Gallia Christiana* notes that the manuscript codex of the abbey of Saint-Hubert, entitled *Cantatorium*, traces the origin of this monastery to 687, perhaps on the basis of this charter, which we declare false and which has been inserted into that manuscript. Yet the authors of the *Nouvelle Gallia Christiana* themselves admit that the monastery of Andage was not founded until the eighth century.] (ann. 687)

[Col. 1215B]

In the name of the Holy Trinity. Every earthly eminence must in every way be subject to divine ordinance. Therefore, since the supreme Lord of heaven and earth, who has no need of our goods, has nevertheless, in his wondrous goodness toward me, deigned to choose the fortress of Ambra, the administrative center of the Amberlactian fisc, by means of a little document miraculously fallen from heaven, as a patrimony for his servants, I, Pippin, son of the illustrious Anchisius, together with my illustrious lady Plectrudis, make known to all present and future that I have surrendered the aforesaid fortress of my dominion, severed from the principality of the Ardennes, with the boundaries and confines designated below, to almighty God, just as I now transfer it in the person of the venerable Beregisus [Col. 1215C] and his successors. I reserve to myself or my successors no right of ownership, dominion, or any authority there, so that it may be the true possession of God alone and subject to him alone.

This is done so that a church and monastic cells may promptly be built there, where his servants may sing the praises of the Most High day and night.

But so that this donation of mine may not be violated by any sophistry, curtailed by any spirit of avarice, or disturbed by any force or malice, let everyone know that this charter of donation contains the whole stretch of land enclosed between the stones, boundary markers, and ditches designated in the presence of my sons and nobles: between the divisions to the south and east; between Mollem Campellum, Campilon, Haletum, and the Iron Mountain; to the north, between Nasania and Awanna, and the Fountain Table; to the west, the river Lumna and the Sulmonian Rock.

This includes the ban, every jurisdiction, the praetoria and their appurtenances; every right and census, both in denarii and in oats; the toll, market, and their appurtenances; the right of mortmain; and the advocacy of all the inhabitants for the works of the royal fisc, as a sign of the freedom received; the tithes belonging to me; and all possessions, lands, meadows, pastures, waters; flour mills; woods, villages, and hamlets; manses and dwellings; households, freedmen, and slaves; [Col. 1216B] flocks and herds.

I have accepted this donation, thus made to God and confirmed in the presence of the illustrious Plectrudis, my sons, and my officials, into my own protection, and I commend it to my descendants so that it may remain stable.

This, however, is the wording of the heavenly document:

> “This place has been chosen by God for the salvation of many souls. The holy land is greatly to be honored, and the patrimony of God’s servants will increase and be protected by the powers, though it will also suffer various tribulations. Whoever harasses this place shall wither at the root, so that he does not flower in the branches, or shall endure the avenging punishments of eternal vengeance.”

Publicly enacted in the palace of Joppille, on the Ides of November, in the year 687 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

Those whose names are subscribed below were present:

The illustrious Pippin; the illustrious Plectrudis; Drogo, son; Grimoaldus, son; Hubertus, count; Sisibertus, count; Godefridus, count; Chudbertus; Caribaldus; Cosmarus; Winetharius, who subscribed.

## XXVII. Charter by which Vandemiris and Ercamberta, his wife, bestow numerous gifts upon churches

[Note: Mabillon printed this charter in *De re diplomatica*, p. 472, from the original document, now preserved in the Royal Archive, K, no. XI; he also had a specimen engraved there, p. 381, plate 20, in Merovingian characters. It is, as he says, an outstanding monument of antiquity. It is unfortunate that it is torn in places. [Col. 1216C] We have indicated the missing portions with dots, and A. Teulet established the recension. Germonius, *De veteribus regibus Francorum diplomata*, vol. I, p. 310, and Bulliardus, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*, proofs, p. 5, reprinted it; Marini also reprinted it, *Diplomatic Papers*, no. XCVI. A major dispute arose over its authenticity. Mabillon defended the charter, which he had published. Germonius attacked it in three separate efforts. Fontaninus, *Diplomatic Vindications*, p. 193, and Ruinart, *Vindication of the Church of Paris against Germonius*, assisted Mabillon. Germonius, alone against everyone, accused the document of being false, chiefly on the following grounds.

1. He argued that of the two churches called in the charter the basilicas of Saint Germanus, the first, to which Vandemiris donates the villa Fraxinetum, was dedicated, according to Mabillon, to Saint Germanus of Auxerre and had not yet been founded in the time of Theuderic III; and that the other, over which Abbot Audacharius presided according to the same Mabillon, and which is today called Saint-Germain-des-Prés, was not called by this name at that time. I would be interminable if I were to gather here everything that was said on either side in this controversy; I shall select a few points from many.

1. Germonius says that the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre near Paris was founded by King Robert, as Helgaud testifies. But the defenders of the charter reply that this church already seems to have existed in Abbo’s time, as Abbo himself testifies, and therefore before King Robert’s time; Helgaud’s words should be understood of its restoration. It must nevertheless be admitted that here Helgaud is speaking of several churches that were founded, not restored, among which he mentions the basilica of Saint Germanus.

2. Mabillon and his followers assert from the Lives of Saint Balthildis and Saint Eligius that the basilica now bearing the name Saint-Germain-des-Prés was already called by this name under Theuderic III. The opponents of the charter reply that it is not sufficiently clear whether these writings concern the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés or some other church dedicated to Saint Germanus, since several churches in Paris existed under this designation.

We say nothing of the rest and refer the reader to Mabillon, *De re diplomatica* and *Supplement*, p. 24; to the *Annals*, vol. I, p. 594; and to Germonius, Ruinart, and Fontaninus. The venerable antiquity of the document itself, which entirely bears the character of the Merovingian period, chiefly supports its authenticity. Besides the authors cited above, it was accepted as genuine by the *Nouvelle Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 419; Dubois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, vol. I, pp. 212–213; Félibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, proofs, p. 30; and many others.] (ann. 690)

[lacuna] we ought to bestow, so that in the future we may obtain the forgiveness of mercy for our souls. We donate, and wish it to remain donated forever, to the basilica of the lady Stefana in Paris, where Lord Bishop Sigofridus is seen to preside, a villa called [lacuna] in the pagus of Miliacum, with all its rights, appurtenances, and dependencies, just as it is possessed by us at the present time.

In like manner we donate to the monastery of the lady [lacuna], where the abbess [lacuna] is seen to preside, a villa called Ingolinocourt, in the pagus of Camiliacum, with all its integrity and appurtenances, just as we [lacuna] possess it.

In the same way we donate to the basilica of the lady Germana, where the venerable man Landebertus is seen to preside as abbot, a villa called Fraxineto, in the pagus of [lacuna], and whatever we presently possess there in quiet order.

In like manner we donate to the basilica of the lady Vincentia and of Lord Germanus, where the venerable man Audacharius is seen to preside as abbot, the villas called Oxma in the pagus of Dorcas, and Noviolium in the pagus of Anjou, with their entire integrity and [lacuna], wholly and completely, just as they are presently possessed by us.

In the same way we donate Vuabuniacus in the pagus of Beauvais, to the basilica of the lady [lacuna], where Abbot Noaldus is seen to preside, wholly and completely, with its appurtenances and dependencies, just as it is presently possessed by us.

We donate [lacuna], where the venerable Vandremarus is seen to preside as abbot, a villa called Gomario-Villa in the pagus of Étampes, with all its integrity and appurtenances [lacuna], just as it is presently possessed by us.

In like manner we donate to Lord Christivolus, the monastery of women in Paris, where the abbess Landetrudis is seen to preside, [lacuna] Noviliacum in the pagus of Camiliacum.

In the name of God we donate Gundulfocourt in the pagus of Camiliacum and Premiaco in the pagus of Orléans to the basilica of the precious lady [of Saint Dionysius the martyr, where he rests bodily] and where the venerable Abbot Chaeno is seen to preside, with all their integrity and dependencies, just as they are presently [lacuna].

To the monastery of Aolino-Villa, where the venerable man Vigur is seen to preside as abbot, we donate a villa called Villare, in the pagus of Oximus, with all its rights and integrity [lacuna].

We donate in the name of God [lacuna] to the monastery of Port-Maur, where the venerable man Amalcarius is seen to preside as abbot, a small estate called Alticiacus, in the pagus of Maceracum, with all its integrity [lacuna], whatever is presently possessed there by us.

In like manner we donate Badenacus [Col. 1218A] at Fontenelle to Lord Peter, where Lord Vande [Note: Marini, p. 150, writes “Landoinus”; Mabillon had already judged this reading erroneous in the place cited.] rests bodily [lacuna], with its appurtenances and dependencies, wholly and completely, just as it is possessed by us.

We donate to the basilica of Lord Peter [lacuna], where the venerable man [lacuna] presides, the villas called Ispaldus in the pagus of Vexin, Brinnacus in the pagus of Évreux, Ararnius in the pagus of Oximus, Ociciacus in the pagus of Oximus, and Cormiliacum [lacuna], whatever we appear to possess there at the present time.

In the name of God we donate to Lord Desiderius, where the venerable man Adroaldus is seen to preside as abbot, [lacuna] where the venerable man Caro is seen to preside as abbot in the pagus of Évreux, with all its rights, just as it is presently possessed by us.

We donate to [lacuna] a villa called [lacuna] in the pagus of Lexovium, with all its integrity and rights [lacuna], just as it is presently possessed by us.

We donate in the name of God [lacuna] Prisciacum in the pagus of Camiliacum, to Lord Martin at Prisciacum itself, where the venerable man Farulfus is seen to preside as abbot, where we have our tombs deposited [lacuna].

[lacuna] I shall give, and [lacuna] human frailty has [lacuna] here in this life [lacuna], which God avert from us. [lacuna] my sweetest wife Ercamberta, while all the things mentioned above remain in this condition, if she should survive us and, God willing, [lacuna] the villas called Lubariacus in the pagus of Oximus, [lacuna] a village by the sea in the pagus of Lexovium, Colzo in the pagus of Lexovium, Cambrimaro in the pagus of Lexovium, Caedracum in the pagus of Cilimanum, and Abaciacum in the pagus of Cilimanum.

As I have already said, if my sweetest wife Ercamberta survives me, she shall cause the aforementioned villas, both those belonging to her and those belonging to us, to be restored to her dominion, and [lacuna] to the monastery which she chooses [lacuna]. In future times, the aforementioned villas ought to contribute to that monastery as an increase.

And so that this decision of ours, which we have resolved to make for the sake of our souls, [lacuna] may be preserved through the ages, just as [lacuna] has been reserved for our heirs: the villas called Edoniacum and Miscellum in the pagus of Cadurcum, Ocella and Buciacum [lacuna].

Since all the matters stated above have been arranged by common agreement, it has been agreed that whichever of us survives the other shall possess the property of the deceased, so that [lacuna] he ought to assign the joint estate to the holy places. Therefore, it has been agreed that two letters, written in one form, should be made and confirmed between us. [lacuna] at Paris, where our apostolic lord and father Sigofridus is seen to preside, shall be deposited; [Col. 1219A] and the other, written in the same manner, [shall be retained] by whichever of us survives the other, for as long as [lacuna] lives. We have reserved a fourth part [lacuna].

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—or if we ourselves or any of our heirs [lacuna] should attempt to come against this present decision of ours, or should wish, in opposition to God, to violate it [lacuna], let him first incur the anger of the Trinity in its majesty [lacuna], and of the holy lords whose relics are known to be placed in the aforementioned basilicas; let him appear excommunicated from all churches, and let him be unable to obtain forgiveness either here or in the future [lacuna]. Together with the associated treasury, let him be compelled to pay one hundred pounds of gold and two hundred pounds of silver, and let the claimant be entirely unable to establish his claim.

May this decision of ours, with God’s help, remain firm and inviolate for all time, with a stipulation appended for complete security.

Enacted at Camiliacum, in the public village, which [lacuna] made [lacuna], in the seventeenth year of the reign of our most glorious lord King Theuderic.

I, Vandemiris, in the name of God, have reread and subscribed this letter made by me [Note: In place of the subscription of the name, there appears here, in the engraved specimen, a sort of monogram formed by many lines, intricately intertwined. Other such monograms are attached to the names of Ghrannus and Aurelius, or Acerelius; these names seem to have been written by the subscribers’ own hands, while the notary added others in a different hand, with crosses prefixed to them, which we have reproduced.]

Ercamberta, subscribed.

Ghrannus, subscribed.

Sign of the illustrious man Acerelius + [Note: In this subscription Mabillon directs that the name be read “Aurelius,” although it appears to be written “Acerelius.”]

Sign of Boso +.

Auronius, requested by those subscribed above, subscribed this letter.

Sign of Bositto +.

Sign of Chlodoaldus +.

Sign of Ingobertus +.

Sign of Gamardus +.

Sign of Gandulfus [lacuna], subscribed.

Ch [lacuna], subscribed.

[Note: I shall publish below, under the year 729, another charter bearing the same names, Vandemiris and Ercamberta, his wife, which was unknown to the distinguished scholar de Brequigny.]

## XXVIII. Charter by which Pippin and his wife Plectrudis transfer the villa Nugaretum to the basilica of the holy apostles near the borders

[Note: Meurissius published this charter, *History of the Bishops of Metz*, p. 109, from the archive of the monastery of Saint Arnulphus of Metz; Cointius used Meurissius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 262, omitting the preface, which may have seemed to him to have been rashly inserted by copyists; the *Collectors of the Writings on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 646, published it in full from the same source; Valladier translated it into French, *History of the Basilica of Saint Arnulphus*, p. 184. We reprint it from a copy deposited in our archive by Father Tabouillot of the congregation of Saint Vanne, transcribed from the old cartulary of the monastery of Saint Arnulphus. We place variants from Meurissius within brackets. The basilica designated here by the name of the Holy Apostles later acquired the name of Saint Arnulphus, which it still retains; see *Nouvelle Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, col. 893, and elsewhere.

Not everyone agrees about the year in which the charter was issued. Some believe that the twelfth year of Theuderic III’s reign should be counted from the beginning of his Neustrian reign; others, from the beginning of his Austrasian reign. If, with Meurissius, the years are counted from the beginning of the reign in Neustria, Theuderic’s twelfth regnal year, in February, must be referred to the year 685 of Christ. If they are counted from the beginning of his Austrasian reign, as Cointius prefers, the charter under examination must be referred to the year 691. For Theuderic III began to reign among the Austrasians after the death of Dagobert II, who, according to the better chronographers, died in December of the year 679, nearly at its end. Mabillon supports this opinion, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 597, and we defend it likewise.

In the charter in question Pippin assumes the title of mayor of the palace. Now Pippin was not appointed mayor of the palace until 687, according to Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 188; Longuer, *Frankish Annals*, vol. III, in the *Collection of Writings on Frankish Affairs*, p. 693. Therefore he had not yet issued this charter under that title in 685.

Someone might object that Pippin’s wife Plectrudis was present when the charter was drawn up; but this could not have happened in 691, since Pippin had long before repudiated Plectrudis and taken Alpais as his secondary wife. Yet in this year Pippin had already been reconciled with Plectrudis and had dismissed Alpais, as Cointius argues in the place cited above, and Mabillon supports him. For these reasons we have assigned the year 691 to this charter.] (ann. 691)

[Col. 1219C]

Pippin [M. Pipinus, here and below], duke, son of King Anchisius, illustrious offspring of Saint Chlodulfus his brother, administered the royal principality of the Franks under the title of mayor of the palace. For, since the knowledge and strength of kings were declining, it was the splendid arrangement of the Most High to give the insignia of the Frankish kingdom to this distinguished lineage, which had sprung from the same root. Nor was this undeserved: for, through their generosity [M. liberality], with the grace of God preceding and following them, the more distinguished churches throughout Gaul still stand founded today.

Indeed, if the noble founders of monasteries are sought, they are found to have sprung from this illustrious stock. Hence it is that I, Pippin the duke, and my wife gave to almighty God a certain villa of ours called Nugaretum.

Therefore I, Pippin, again, and my wife named Plectrudis, thinking of our salvation, so that we might receive from the Lord great things for small ones and heavenly things for earthly ones, donated, for the remedy of our soul and to acquire eternal rest, and firmly transferred, to the basilica of the Holy Apostles constructed near the city of Metz, where our lord and grandfather Arnulphus rests bodily, a villa held as property and called, as stated above, Nugaretum, situated in the pagus of Wabrensis: namely, a demesne mansus, with all its appurtenances, both buildings and fields, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, slaves of both sexes residing there, and whatever I have so far appeared to possess in the aforesaid villa, wholly and completely.

Thus, from the present day and thereafter, everything is to pass to the aforementioned holy place, under the authority of the servants of God who are there now or will be there in the future, where at present the venerable man Romulus is seen to preside as abbot; and from our right it is to pass perpetually into their inheritance. In this way, with those same servants of God interceding more earnestly for us and our offspring, may we, with the Lord directing us, pass more successfully through the course of the present life and afterward be able to become participants in eternal glory.

But if any of our heirs, or any other person or power, should come against this dominion [Col. 1221A] of ours [Note: I think “donation” should be read. The matter concerns pure generosity. I admit that in some documents the word *dominium* has the same meaning as property; see Du Cange, s.v. Nevertheless, if *dominium* is used here in that sense, the charter becomes, in my opinion, difficult to understand. Pippin and Plectrudis are adding a penal clause to their donation, and the penalty is established to strengthen the donation.] or attempt in any way to violate it, let him first incur the anger [the word “anger” is absent in Meurissius] and vengeance of God and his saints, and let him be unable to establish the claim he is making.

Enacted publicly at the villa of Nielsum [M. Hielsum], on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twelfth year of the reign of our lord [this word is absent in Meurissius] King Theuderic.

## XXIX. Charter by which Drogo, duke of Burgundy and Aquitaine, donates to the church of Saint Arnulphus whatever he possesses in the villa of Mariolas

[Note: Meurissius published this, p. 110, in the *Lives of the Bishops of Metz*; Valladier translated it into French in the *History of the Basilica of Saint Arnulphus*, p. 186. We reprint it from the old cartulary of this church, on the authority of a transcript deposited in our archive by Lord Tabouillot of the congregation of Saint Vanne. We have placed Meurissius’s variants in brackets.

The charter is spurious. Drogo should not have been called “son of Pippin, duke of Aquitaine” (*filius Pipini, dux Aquitaniae*), but rather “son of Pippin, duke of Aquitaine” (*filius Pipini Aquitaniae ducis*), according to Meurissius’s reading; the Latin distinction makes Pippin, rather than Drogo, duke of Aquitaine. This correction can defend the charter’s authenticity. But Drogo is called duke of Burgundy there, which admits no excuse: Drogo was by no means duke of Burgundy, but duke of Champagne. Cointius adduces other indications of forgery, *Annals*, vol. IV, pp. 298, 454, 459 and following, and the authorities cited there, when examining a charter of Godefridus very similar to this one.] (ann. 691)

I, Drogo, duke of the Burgundians, son of Pippin the duke, duke [this word is absent in Meurissius] of Aquitaine, make known that, for love of blessed Arnulphus of Metz, whatever I possessed in the villa of Mariolas I gave in its entirety to the church of Saint Arnulphus: in pastures, woods, ploughlands, manses, buildings, vineyards, lands and cultivated areas, and with all slaves of both sexes; with fields, cultivated and uncultivated land, meadows, pastures, woods, waters, watercourses, mills, and whatever can be named there [M. whatever can be named there].

And in all these things, whatever came to me by law in that villa, whether from my father or mother, whether acquired by purchase or obtained by any other means, and whatever I appear to have possessed or to be able to donate, I give, transfer, and convey in its entirety, in the name of God, to that holy church of Saint Arnulphus, or of the holy apostles John and James, or to the portion of those brothers who serve there, to possess perpetually; and whatever the party of that church chooses to do with it, let it enjoy freely in all things [M. “to do”].

If anyone, which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, any of my heirs, or any outsider—should attempt to come against this donation made by me or wish to violate it, let him first incur the anger of God, the holy apostles, and Saint Arnulphus; and, moreover, let him incur a penalty against that church, together with the associated treasury: one pound of gold; and let him pay a fine of two pounds of silver [M. a weight of two]; and let him be unable to establish the claim he is making. Instead, let this present donation remain firm and stable forever, secured by stipulation.

Enacted at Metz, in public, on the day and at the time stated above [Note: The day and year are absent from the copy we follow.

Meurissius supplies them: the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twelfth year of the reign of King Theuderic. For this is how he has it: “on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twelfth year of the reign of our lord King Theuderic.” If, with Cointius, this is counted from the beginning of Theuderic’s reign among the Austrasians, we obtain the year 691 of Christ.]

## XXX. Charter by which Duke Godefridus donates to the church of blessed Arnulphus whatever he possesses in the villa of Flavigneiacum

[Note: Published by Meurissius, *Lives of the Bishops of Metz*, p. 110, [Col. 1222D] and by Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 459; translated into French by Valladier, *History of the Basilica of Saint Arnulphus*, p. 197. We reprint it from a transcript of the cartulary of the church of Saint Arnulphus, brought into our archive by D. Tabouillot, whom we have already praised more than once. This charter is composed in exactly the same words as the charter of Drogo immediately preceding it and is not to be regarded as of better quality. As Cointius correctly observes, several expressions undermine its credibility, especially since the church of Saint Arnulphus is so called there, although it had not yet acquired this name; indeed, in Pippin’s charter, issued in the same year and on the same day, it is called the basilica of the Holy Apostles. Grave suspicion arises from the fact alone that three charters are represented as having been issued on the same day by grandfather, father, and son—Pippin, Drogo, and Godefridus—enriching the same church of Saint Arnulphus; and two of them appear to have been copied from the same model, so that one egg is not more like another.] (ann. 691)

I, Godefrid, duke, son of Drogo, make known that, for love of blessed Arnulf of Metz, I have given everything I possessed in the village of Flavigneiacum entirely to the church of Saint Arnulf [Col. 1222B]: pastures, woods, plowlands, manses, and buildings, together with vineyards, lands and cultivated holdings, and all slaves of both sexes, together with fields, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, mills, and everything that can be named there.

And in all these things, whatever legally came to me in that village, whether from my father or my mother, whether acquired by purchase or known to have come to me by any other means, and whatever I appear to possess or to give, I give, hand over, and transfer in its entirety to that already holy church of Saint Arnulf, or of the holy apostles John and James, or to the community of the brothers who serve there, in God’s name, to possess perpetually [Col. 1222C]. Whatever the portion of that church chooses to do with it, let them enjoy in every respect by free judgment.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs, or any outside person, should attempt to oppose this donation made by me or wish to violate it, let him first incur the wrath of God, the holy apostles, and Saint Arnulf; and, in addition, let him be required to pay to that church, together with the associate of the treasury, one pound of gold and two pounds of silver as a penalty [Col. 1223A]. Let him not be able to vindicate what he claims, but let this present donation remain firm and stable for all time, supported by formal stipulation.

Done at Metz, in public, on the day and at the time stated above.

[Note: [Col. 1223C] In the chartulary there are no chronological indications. They appear in Meurissius, and also in Bouchet, *De vera origine domus Franciae*, p. 69: namely, in the twelfth year of King Theodoric, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March. Bouchet, however, interprets this as Theodoric IV, or Theodoric of Chelles, which would make the charter belong to the year 732; that cannot stand, since Godefrid had already died by then. Valladier supplies entirely different chronological indications, namely, the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth year of King Dagobert (A.D. 715); it is unclear on what authority he relies.]

### XXXI. Charter by which Pippin the Elder grants gifts to the monastery of Lobbes

[Note: [Col. 1223D] Published in the supplement to Miraeus’s *Opera diplomatica*, vol. II, p. 1126. The Pippin whose name this charter bears is the man called of Herstal. In the middle of June 687 he was elected by the Austrasians as supreme prince and duke, according to Longuerue, *Annales Francici*, in *Collectio scriptorum rerum Francicarum*, vol. III, p. 693. Thus he was entering the fifth year of his rule in November 691, when he defeated Theodoric III in the battle of Tertry; and the fourth indiction was then in progress. All this agrees perfectly with the chronological indications attached to the charter. Yet elsewhere the signs of forgery are clear. First, the charter confirms a diploma of King Dagobert, which we have counted among the spurious charters; this creates some suspicion concerning the authenticity of the confirmation. Second, we have found this instrument cited nowhere except in the supplement to Miraeus’s *Opera*. Third, the chancellor Asdolgus and the archchaplain Ruothpertus are entirely unknown. Moreover, the opening formula is unusual for Merovingian times; the year is reckoned from the Incarnation of the Lord; and the style differs from that of Pippin of Herstal’s other charters. Pippin neither assumed the title “prince” nor the title “elder,” which later writers imposed upon him. All these features reveal the document as false. We do indeed find Hidulf among the nobles in the *Life of Ursimarius*, but never under the title “duke.” Finally—and this admits no excuse—the same Hidulf subscribed here with the title “duke of Lorraine,” although the name Lorraine originated with Lothair, grandson of Louis the Pious, under the Carolingian dynasty. These considerations are more than sufficient.] (A.D. 691).

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, amen.

The universal mother and singular virgin, the bride of Christ, the Catholic Church, has merited by the privilege of fruitful chastity that we incline our devoted consent to her interests, especially by watchful care for the tranquility and peace of sacred religion. Thus she may devote herself more freely to divine contemplation and prayer for our salvation and the stability of the kingdom, so that, once the enemies of the Christian faith have been driven out, the kingdom may flourish and grow in the complete well-being of its whole body under our exertions, and hostile arrogance may everywhere recognize itself as subjected [Col. 1223B].

I, Pippin the Elder, moved by this favor and desire, especially because by the grace of God I have been delivered victorious from the proud king Theodoric, grant and give to the monastery of the most religious man and outstanding preacher, Bishop Ursmar, which is at Lobbes on the River Sambre, as a permanent endowment for that church, the land and forest situated between the stream of Grunghart and the stream of Hergnaut, which flow [Col. 1223C] into the Sambre; this forest has long been called Forestella.

I receive under my protection and defense the site of the monastery of Lobbes, its villages, lands, woods, meadows, waters and watercourses, and all the possessions that my faithful man Hidulf, duke and co-founder in that monastery of the aforesaid bishop, gave to the same place; and I restore them to perpetual freedom and peace, reserving no right or authority for myself or my successors in those places.

Whatever the man of God Landelin, who first labored in that place, acquired and subjected to it, I likewise assign in its entirety to the same monastery, namely the church of Alna with all its dependencies and possessions. Likewise, I assign the monastery of Wallers with all its dependencies and possessions, just as the most pious King Dagobert, at the request of Aubert of blessed memory, bishop of Cambrai, gave them to the aforesaid Landelin within specified boundaries and assigned them to the monastery of Wallers for its foundation. Let them be the true and secure possession of the church of Lobbes, without the advocacy or oppression of any count, centenarius, or *vice-dominus*; and let no one presume to erect or construct a building within the territory of the aforesaid churches without their will or permission, or to inflict any violence.

I receive all the aforesaid places, faithfully described and bounded both in our document and in that of the aforesaid King Dagobert, under my protection, and completely release them from every exaction and authority of the ruler. I decree that they are to suffer no harm from violation or invasion, nor any prejudice through occupation [Col. 1224B]. But if anyone presumes to act against this and violate our edict, let him be stripped of every freedom and honor and punished by capital sentence.

That this donation of mine may remain undefiled through succeeding ages, I have confirmed it with my own hand and ordered it to be marked by the affixing of my seal.

The sign of Lord Pippin the Elder.

The sign of Hidulf, duke of Lorraine.

The sign of Philippicus, duke of Metz.

I, Asdolgus, chancellor, acting in place of Ruothpertus, archchaplain, have examined and subscribed.

Given at Leptines [Col. 1224C], on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year 691 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth indiction, in the fifth year of our principate, after the proud King Theodoric had been crushed, successfully, in that same year of this grant.

### XXXII. Charter by which Pippin the Elder grants gifts to the church of Saint Peter of Cambrai

[Note: [Col. 1224D] We reprint it as Carpenter published it, *Historia Cameracensis*, vol. II, proofs, p. 4, from the archives of the church of Cambrai. It is mutilated, but we did not think it worthwhile to extract a complete version from the archives themselves, since the fragment presented here is everywhere marked by signs of forgery. They are precisely the same as those we detected in another charter fabricated under the name of the same Pippin and presented above. The two charters are so similar that everyone would judge them to have come from the same workshop. Both bear the date 691, with this sole discrepancy: the first is said to have been issued in the fourth indiction, the second, less plausibly, in the second. The formulas, style, chronological indications, the names of the subscribers, and especially Hidulf, duke of Lorraine, reveal the forgery. We have discussed all these matters at length in the notes to the other charter mentioned above.] (A.D. 691).

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

The universal mother and singular virgin, the bride of Christ, the Catholic Church [Col. 1225A], and so forth.

I, Pippin the Elder, moved by this favor and intention, especially because by the grace of the Almighty I have been delivered victorious from the proud king Theodoric, grant as a perpetual alms to the church of Saint Peter of Cambrai my land between Elimont and Salicourt, in the pagus of Arras, and so forth.

Likewise, to the church of the brethren’s oratory at Cambrai I give two small estates, the villages of Maniliacum, Kuneias, and Demicourt, and so forth.

The sign of Lord Pippin the Elder.

The sign of Hidulf, duke of Lorraine.

The sign of Philippicus, duke of Metz.

I, Asdolgus, chancellor, have examined it.

Given at Cambrai in the year 691, in the second indiction, in the fifth year of our principate.

### XXXIII. Charter by which Bertoendus, bishop of Châlons, grants privileges to the monastery of Dervy and the neighboring monastery of virgins

[Note: [Col. 1225D] Published by D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. X, p. 627, according to a copy taken from the chartulary of Dervy; we transcribed it from the chartulary itself and reprinted within brackets the variant readings found in D’Achery.] (A.D. 692).

[Col. 1225B]

To the holy lords presiding at the summit of the highest [Dach., apostolic] pontifical chair, our brothers and fellow bishops in Christ—Ingobert [Dach., Rigobert], metropolitan; Basinus; Stephanus; Adalbertus; Alonus; and Madalgarius—presiding in episcopal sees: Bertoendus [Note: [Col. 1225D] From *episcopal* to *Bertoendus* is absent in D’Achery.], although unworthy, yet bishop in the order of the church of Châlons, sends humble greetings in the Lord.

Although the decrees of the ancient rule teach us what must be observed perpetually and what the custom of the fathers requires us to maintain without diminution, nevertheless, while also making regular decisions on these matters, we wish with the greatest willingness to devote our favor to the petitions of those who ask, especially of those who shine with orthodox faith, by considering their requests with provident care.

Since, therefore, the glorious lord King Clovis and the illustrious man Pippin, mayor of the palace, are known to have earnestly requested us, out of religious concern [Dach., on behalf of religion], to grant a privilege to the monastery of Puelle, in the wilderness of Dervy, built by the most religious man, Saint Bercharius [Note: [Col. 1226D] See what we have said concerning Bercharius in the notes to the charter of Reolus. We have printed the diploma of Childeric II for the monastery of Dervy.], in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, Saint John the Baptist, Saint John the Evangelist, and all the saints, through the munificence of the former King Childeric, where Bercharius himself appears to preside as abbot; and also to another monastery of virgins [Note: [Col. 1226D] Concerning this monastery of virgins, the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. IX, col. 997, write: “Besides the monastery of men, Bercharius also built another monastery for women, not far from Dervy, likewise on the Vige, under the patronage of Blessed Mary, the foundation being supplied by a noble and wealthy matron named Waltilde … It was destroyed about seven hundred years ago, but the place where it stood still retains the name ‘the monastery of virgins,’ only one league distant from the monastery of Dervy.”], likewise on the River Vige and the Drea [Dach., Dria], at Dervy, in the territory [Dach., boundary] of Flaciniacum, which Wuatmerus [Dach., Waimerus], his wife Wualtildis [Dach., Waltidis here [Col. 1225D] and below], and Lord Bercharius the abbot built together; and in which place Wualtildis, consecrated to God [Dach. omits “to God”], appears to be the mother of many virgins [Col. 1226A], who have joined themselves with her in many bands and companies, united in equal devotion and pious endeavors, moved by heavenly inspiration with one spirit of rule, to sing praises to Almighty God [Dach., to compose them], and render devoted service—we ought to confer this privilege.

Giving our wholesome assent to this, know that we have willingly granted the privilege which they requested with complete devotion, to be preserved with perpetual authority. For the authority to grant privileges is not new among those who ask or those who show indulgence, since all the pontiffs of the apostolic see from ancient times—from that see whence sacred authority is propagated—have decreed that petitions should always be granted, not only in neighboring provinces but also in other distant regions.

Therefore I beseech the lords, the bishops who will succeed the church named above—I dare even to entreat and solemnly adjure them, sufficiently and more than sufficiently, by the omnipotence of the immense Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that they order the aforesaid monastery to be loved, cherished, maintained, and preserved by devout minds. And lest the succeeding fraternity of priests should think that we have established these provisions in these regions through some impulse of private judgment or by a new invention, let them know that under the rule of this constitution the place of the holy men of Agaunum, as well as the monastery of Lérins, the monastery of Luxeuil, and many other monasteries, together with the basilica of Lord Marcellus and countless monasteries in the eastern regions, are maintained under their own privileges by decree of the bishops [Col. 1226C].

Therefore, by one unanimous agreement and by the will of God, weighing the religion of the aforesaid fathers, it has been decreed by all that neither we nor our successors shall exercise any domination over the aforesaid monasteries of men or virgins, where the communities are gathered whom Bercharius, Wuaimerus, and his wife Wualtildis are known to have built together for the salvation of their souls. Thus they may live a contemplative life more freely, with God’s help, without hindrance from anything.

When the father of the monastery has been called from this world, let the entire congregation of those servants of God unanimously choose from wherever they may find someone who knows the rule best, and appoint him as their elder and abbot [Col. 1226D]. Likewise, when the mother of the virgins has been called from this world, let the entire congregation of those handmaids of Christ unanimously choose from wherever they may find someone who knows the rule best, and appoint her as their elder mother and abbess, together with the counsel of the monks, the brothers of Dervy. If it should be necessary for them to have an abbot blessed, chrism consecrated, or sacred orders conferred, we reserve this solely for ourselves, for the sake of canonical institution and without prejudice to our church, without any disturbance.

For the rest, as stated above, neither we nor the archdeacon, nor our successors, nor any person whatsoever, ought to have any authority or domination; nor should anyone presume to bring forward or remove any matter concerning that monastery, its cells, and parishes or other monasteries [Dach. omits from “but” onward]. And if that congregation should conduct itself negligently in matters of religion, let its members be corrected according to the rule of Saint Benedict or Lord Columbanus by the abbot or abbess who, at the time, serves as their spiritual father or mother [Col. 1227A].

Let no bishop, whether we or our successors, hold authority in the same monastery for the sake of greed or, God forbid, avarice; rather, let them enjoy their privilege in God’s name.

As for the food and clothing supplied from the property of the aforesaid founders of this holy monastery for the support of the aforesaid holy monks and virgins, or supplied in future by other God-fearing persons, or granted by royal power, no authority whatsoever—whether of bishops or of any other persons—shall exist to alienate or diminish it [Col. 1227B], except that its mothers or fathers and their superiors (*propositi*; Dach., *prepositi*) shall have discretion in governing, directing, and administering it.

We have granted this privilege to God [Dach., “therefore”], because nothing is taken away from canonical authority when anything is granted for the peace and tranquility of those who are members of the household of faith, especially those leading a contemplative life.

If anyone, overcome by cunning or greed, should dare with a rash spirit to violate what is set forth above, let him be struck down by divine vengeance and subjected to the guilt of anathema. Let the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian come upon him; let him be excommunicated from the holy Catholic Church; and nevertheless let this privilege remain incorrupt for all time.

That this constitution of ours may stand with firm force, it has been strengthened by the subscriptions of our hands. And, so that it may be more fully confirmed, we have also sent it to the other brothers and fellow bishops who were not present, for their further ratification.

Done publicly at Reims.

Given in the month of February [Dach., “of the month”], on the fifteenth day, in the second year of our glorious lord King Clovis.

[Note: [Col. 1227C] If Theodoric III died before the end of the year 690, the month of February in the second year of Clovis III must be assigned to the year 692. But if Theodoric’s life extended into the spring of 691, February in the second year of Clovis III corresponds to the year 693.]

### XXXIV. Charter by which Aiglibertus, bishop of Le Mans, grants the tithes of certain villages to the monastery of Saint Mary

[Note: [Col. 1227D] It is found nowhere else except in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, published by Mabillon in the *Analecta*, p. 278. Ada, who is said to preside over the convent of Saint Mary, appears to Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 560, to be the same person as Alrechildis, who was brought from the monastery of Saint Mary at Soissons to govern the monastery of Saint Mary at Le Mans. The authenticity of this charter rests solely on the testimony of the acts, in which it was inserted so that it might be known from them that this monastery stood under the jurisdiction of the mother church of Le Mans, as the acts themselves indicate. Several other instruments are also included in those acts for the same purpose, and these have been condemned as false; we have likewise published a diploma concerning this same monastery of Saint Mary, which we have counted among the spurious documents. Yet in the charter now presented we confess that we have detected no defect that would allow us to pronounce it supposititious, although the granting of tithes to monasteries at this period may perhaps arouse some suspicion.] (A.D. 692).

In God’s name, Aiglibertus, bishop, to all the sons of the holy church who act or travel as messengers from the villages of the holy church of Mediaquinta, Trition, Alnetum, Betas, Longa Aqua, Lucdunum, Geneda, half of Tredente, Vithlena, and Tauriniacum.

Know that we have granted to the monastery of Saint Mary, where Ada, consecrated to God, appears to preside as abbess, all the tithes from the aforesaid villages, both from grain and from the agricultural produce, wine, hay, all livestock, cheese, and whatever else is subject to tithe. We decree and order that the whole and entire amount be assigned to that monastery, and that without delay you cause it to be delivered to its messengers. As we have said, let that tithe remain granted to the monastery for all time.

And that you may believe this more certainly, we have confirmed it below with our own hand.

Given on the ninth day of the month of July, in the second year of the reign of Lord King Clovis.

In Christ’s name, Aiglibertus, although a sinful bishop, have subscribed.

### XXXV. Privilege granted by Ageradus, bishop of Chartres, to a monastery dedicated to Saint Mary on the River Loire

[Note: [Col. 1228C] This very mutilated instrument was taken from the Saint-Denis original, now in the Royal Archives, K, box 3, by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 478, and Félibien, *Histoire de l’abbaye de Saint-Denis*, proofs, p. 16. We reprint it according to Mabillon’s example, with a new examination by A. Teulet. The words enclosed in brackets appear to have been added by Mabillon to fill certain lacunae. Ageradus declares himself the author of the privilege in his subscription and the successor of Deodatus, who was bishop of Chartres. Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, pp. 605–606, unsuccessfully investigates which monastery received the privilege. At least it may be conjectured that it was subject to the monastery of Saint-Denis. Since many bishops subscribe to this privilege, while only one abbot subscribes—Chaino, who at that time presided over the monastery of Saint-Denis—it seems that this was so. Chrotcharius the deacon appears to have led a colony of monks from there to the monastery adorned by Ageradus’s privilege, as Mabillon conjectures, *De re diplomatica*, p. 479. Mabillon had a specimen of the charter engraved there, p. 382.] (A.D. 696).

[lacuna] with the consent of his son Lord Deodatus, formerly our predecessor and bishop of this city, and of many bishops [Col. 1229A] and priests, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, built a sacred monastery on his own property at a place called [lacuna] within the same wall, on the River Loire, in honor of Saint Mary ever-virgin and the other saints, by his own labor, endowed it from his possessions, and confirmed it to the venerable man Chrotcharius the deacon by his [letter] [lacuna], so that monks living there under the holy order, leading a theoretical life under the cenobitic rule, might dwell there; and he was to admit them there, and to place the same monastery under the charge of an abbot [lacuna], whom he might appoint during his lifetime or after his departure.

And when we saw this most devoted man serving the Lord in this work, we therefore, with complete willingness, granted this holy privilege, together with the consent of our brothers and the counsel of the elders, in such a manner that it should be lawful for the holy congregation of God’s servants established in that monastery to live in peaceful order, without oppression by any bishop, or by the bishop of the city of Chartres, or by clerics, and without insolence from secular youths. Let no one presume to impose banquets, lodging, provisions, or gifts upon them [Col. 1229B].

And if the bishop of Chartres is invited by the abbot for their benefit, let him come without any motive of ambition or deceit, to consecrate churches, bless the abbot, consecrate altars, or ordain priests, deacons, and the remaining orders, and let him confer the blessing without any demand arising from perverse greed.

And, as human frailty dictates, if Abbot Chrotcharius himself, or whoever he may appoint there as abbot, should depart from this light [lacuna], let the holy congregation of God’s servants established in the aforesaid monastery be permitted to choose from among themselves, for the governance of the monastery and the direction of souls, such a governor as is of honorable conduct—not one distinguished by noble birth, but one more fully awakened and prudent in the love of God—and to appoint him as a father under the holy rule of obedience [lacuna]. We decree and grant to them that this sacred privilege may in no way be violated by our successors, but may be preserved entirely and in every respect [Note: [Col. 1229D] Earlier editors read *conservitus consistat* (“let it remain preserved”). But they read badly: in the first hand the word *conservitus*, with its final letter retouched, was changed into *conservitur*, while the following word *consistat* was cancelled by dots placed beneath it.]

And if scandals—which we do not believe will happen, with God’s help—should arise in the aforesaid monastery, and the abbot with his congregation should be unable to correct them, let them invite a spiritual father who appears to live under the holy rule in the parish of Chartres, or whom they may choose from anywhere, to calm the scandal [Col. 1229D].

But if even they—which we by no means believe—should be unable to correct it, then, for peace and harmony and without any crime of greed, the bishop of Chartres is to be invited by the abbot or his congregation, so that, in the manner of a father, he may recall those who are in disagreement to peace [Col. 1230A], while preserving their privilege.

Our pontifical authority has granted them this provision [lacuna], that none of our successors—neither the archdeacon, nor the *vice-dominus*, nor the clerical or lay messengers traveling through [lacuna] of the same monastery—may presume to enter, hold, or exercise authority over the endowment (*conlacione*) of the aforesaid Adrebertana [Note: [Col. 1229D] Adrebertana appears to have been the mother of Bishop Deodatus, who, with her son’s consent, founded the monastery in question.], or over what has been bestowed by God-fearing persons in the past or may be bestowed in the future; nor may anyone enter to hear cases, exact payments, demand lodging, food, or provisions, seek any kind of return, constrain the monastery’s people, or diminish anything from their possessions. Rather, let all things remain in God’s name under the governance of that abbot and his successors.

We have established through this privilege that these things shall be preserved in God’s name perpetually, for the present and future ages [Col. 1230B].

And, as is often the case, if the adversary, through some rashness or cunning, should stir up one of our successors—as malice commonly obstructs good works—and by wicked counsels should induce him to endeavor to have this privilege, which we established out of regard for God in order to share in the common reward of our successor-brethren, violated, perverted, or corrupted, religion being set aside and unto a mass of impiety, let him not only be struck here, according to the statutes of the canons, by sentence for the alleged crime of inhumanity, but also in the future, before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, the angels, and all the saints, let him be condemned by divine vengeance to destruction [Col. 1230C].

And since we have observed our own lowliness (*extremitas nostra*) in the oft-named monastery, greatly devoted to Christ’s worship, [the syntax is corrupt] to live a holy life, meditating regularly upon the knowledge of truth in God’s praises [lacuna], and since we desire this with the greatest longing, we implore the mercy of Christ that, from now on, while all support is supplied by us, they may advance ever more and more in the love of God, enjoying eternal life with lamps brightly burning. Thus, for the labor with which they toil in the contest of contemplation, they may bring to Almighty God the benefit of their reward; and may we be able to reap and attain eternal rewards from the multiplied harvest, made fruitful in the gathered laps of the peoples, with the filth of the rags removed and the wheat stored in the granaries [Col. 1230D].

Therefore we ask the lords, the metropolitans of the lofty sees, for the divine assistance, so that your blessedness may deign to associate itself with this holy privilege in the reward to be granted, and to confirm it together with us.

In the second year of the reign of our lord Childebert, the most glorious king. At Captonacum, publicly.

[Given on the day which was] the sixth of the month of March [Note: [Col. 1230D] Childebert III began his reign around March 695, but the precise day of that month is unknown. It is therefore uncertain whether this privilege should be assigned to the year 696 or 697. Mabillon and Félibien identify the sees of most of the subscribing bishops; see their works.]

In God’s name, Ageradus, although a sinful bishop, have read and subscribed this privilege made by me.

[lacuna]ericus, bishop, have consented to and subscribed this privilege.

In Christ’s name, Gripho, although a sinful bishop, have consented to and subscribed this privilege.

Anseberchthus, servant of Jesus Christ, subscribed this privilege at their request.

In God’s name, Ebarcis, although a sinful bishop, [have subscribed] this privilege [lacuna].

In Christ’s name, Ayglibercthus, although a sinful bishop, have subscribed this privilege with my consent.

In Christ’s name, Beracharius, bishop, have subscribed this privilege with my consent.

Tretecor, bishop by the mercy of God, have subscribed this privilege.

In God’s name, Ansoaldus, although a sinner, have subscribed this privilege.

In God’s name, Attur, bishop by the grace of God, subscribed this privilege at their request.

In Christ’s name, Ermeno, sinful bishop, have subscribed.

Soabericus, sinful bishop, have subscribed this privilege with my consent [Col. 1231B].

Turnochaldus, although a sinful bishop, have subscribed this privilege.

Constantinus, sinful bishop, have subscribed this privilege.

Chaino, abbot by the grace of God, subscribed this privilege at their request.

### XXXVI. Charter by which Ansebertus grants gifts to the church of Saint Nazarius of Autun, the basilica of Saint Symphorian, the oratory of Saint Leodegarius, his sister Segolina, and his brother Autarius

[Note: [Col. 1231D] Published by Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, appendix, p. 702, from a chartulary supplied by Bouhier, president of the senate of Burgundy; and by the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. IV, instruments, col. 43. Since they did not indicate where they obtained the charter, and consequently failed to report the few and minor variants they display, we have not included them. We follow Mabillon’s reading. Although this instrument is not composed in the formulas of a will, it nevertheless appears to be regarded in place of a will, and the editors prefixed that title to it. Ansebertus, bishop of Autun, is mentioned several times in the charters published above; he is also called Anseberchthus, and even Autbertus [Col. 1232D] and, according to the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. IV, col. 356, Amalbertus. Segolena, Ansebertus’s sister, was a nun in the monastery of Saint Mary at Autun, now Saint John’s. Mabillon notes, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 636, that this instrument establishes that at this time nuns entered into the inheritances of their parents and devoted them to pious uses; our collection contains many examples of this. He also observes that the clerics of Saint Symphorian, although they were then organized as a monastery, are nowhere in this charter called monks.] (A.D. 696).

To the administrators of the church of Saint Nazarius the martyr of Augustodunum and of Saint Symphorianus the martyr, where his precious body rests, Ansebertus, a sinner and bishop.

Divine teaching admonishes us to offer, for the washing away of the burden of sins, from the abundance of what Christ’s mercy bestows in earthly possessions, whatever we use in this age from his goodness among his poor. Therefore I give to the aforementioned church of Saint Nazarius the martyr, where I, although unworthy, serve in pastoral care, from the estate inherited from my parents, the estate called Hauxiacum, in the pagus of Belna, together with its full holdings and appurtenances: houses, farmsteads, fields, meadows, woods, vineyards, pastures, waters, slaves, freedmen, and tenant farmers, together with all the other things, and whatever we are able to possess at the present time in that pagus, or may hereafter acquire there in God’s name, and whatever else can be said or named. I wish the aforementioned church of Saint Nazarius to have it with full title.

And for that share which my brother Autarius has there among us, I wish our share in the estate of Binago to be held by the church. And perhaps—though we do not believe it—if he should oppose this, I wish and decree that, in the aforementioned estates of Hauxiacum and Binago, whatever belongs to us by reason of my share of the inheritance of my parents, both the paternal and the maternal inheritance due to us, be held by the church of Saint Nazarius.

As for the estate of Pagetis, which we acquired in part, I wish the church of Saint Nazarius to have it. As for the estate of Solempriacum, which Wlbertus gave us by his charter and which Leodebertus holds in usufruct, I wish and decree that the church of Saint Nazarius have it.

The basilica of Saint Symphorianus the martyr has protected my substance in every way since my youth; and because we trust that his future intercession will also stand as an intercessor before eternal mercy for the forgiveness of my sins, I wish the estate of Tres-valles, in the pagus of Maginontum, together with its appurtenances—houses, farmsteads, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, and all other things—which Wlbertus delegated in our name by his charters, to be held by the church of Saint Symphorianus for feeding its clerics, as our alms.

Likewise, to the oratory of Saint Leodegarius, which appears to have been built below Saint Symphorianus, where—if it pleases God—my little body will also come to rest, I wish the tenant holdings in the pagus of Maginontum, at Taviniacum, which Wlbertus gave us by his charter, and those tenant holdings which Bertoaldus gave at Eulnicius by his charter, to be held by the oratory of Saint Leodegarius.

As for the estate of Corvillo in the pagus of Autissiodorum, which we acquired together with all its appurtenances, I wish and decree that the same oratory of Saint Leodegarius have it. Likewise, in the pagus of Augustodunum, I wish the tenant holdings which Beroaldus gave us by sale to be held by the same oratory of Saint Leodegarius. As for the estate of Buxidum, whatever my brother holds there in usufruct, I wish the same oratory of Saint Leodegarius to have it.

As for the estate of Muidum, which is near Mount Wavina, in the pagus of Vertudum, together with everything belonging to it, I wish the oratory of Saint Leodegarius to have it; but on the condition that from it he establish a light and the sacrifice for that oratory, and that everything must remain in all respects under the authority of the brothers of the church of Saint Symphorianus.

We also establish there four matricularii who serve that oratory of Saint Leodegarius, so that they may have all their food and clothing from the aforementioned properties, just as those other matricularii who appear to serve the basilica of Saint Symphorianus receive their share of food and clothing.

And concerning everything that we have assigned in this document, we have granted the usufruct to our sister Sicolina: she shall retain and administer the matricularii and the light for the oratory of Saint Leodegarius. After her departure, both the aforementioned bishop and the church of Saint Nazarius, as well as the clerics of the said church of Saint Symphorianus, shall, in God’s name, administer whatever we have established in this charter.

As for the remainder of our property, whatever we acquired during our lifetime and which has remained unmentioned in this document, wherever we wish it to increase, I wish the church of Saint Symphorianus to have it.

From the inheritance of my parents, whatever share of ours in any places or territories is due to us—our share both of the paternal and of the maternal inheritance—together with every possession, whatever can be said or named, my most beloved sister Sigolina, if she survives us, shall receive in full; and wherever she wishes to assign it for the faithful of Christ and for the Church of God, she shall have complete authority.

As for the slaves whom we purchased or acquired at a price, I wish them all to be free, and, as free persons, to remain in the service of my aforementioned sister as long as she lives. After her departure, if they wish to choose a defender or king of the Christians, this shall be in their power.

With regard to the property assigned to the aforementioned churches of Saint Nazarius and Saint Symphorianus, while my sister Sigolina has renounced the world and while we have learned that she has continually offered herself to Christ and given herself as a handmaid to Saint Mary, she shall retain it under usufruct and benefit. After her departure, it shall pass by this document, in full title, to the aforementioned churches, and it shall reach those churches with the property improved.

If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether one of our heirs or any opposing person, should wish to resist the provisions written above, which we have decreed with completely free will, he shall not be able to vindicate what he claims, but shall become like Judas the betrayer. In addition, he shall pay to the administrators of the church, or to whomever we have assigned anything by this document, together with the fisc, six pounds of gold and sixty pounds of silver. This document, which our simplicity has decreed with completely free will, shall retain perpetual validity.

In the name of Christ, I, Ansebertus, a sinner and bishop, have reread and subscribed this document made by me.  
Adoneus, bishop, subscribed at the request.  
Agnericus, bishop, subscribed at the request.  
Aglius, bishop, subscribed at the request.  
Winebertus, at the command of Lord Bishop Ansebertus, wrote and subscribed this document.

I noted the act made on the fifth day of August, in the second year of the reign of Lord King Childebert.

### XXXVII. The testament of Ephibius the abbot, concerning gifts bestowed upon the church of Vienne (the testament of his sister Rufina is inserted)

**Note:** Published by Dacherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 101, from a copy which Louvet had transcribed; he does not state where it had been found. It was reprinted by the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 678, with the testament of Rufina omitted, although Ephibius, her brother, inserted it in his own testament. Mabillon mentions this document, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 386. It would be difficult to guess which monastery Ephibius had been abbot of. The authenticity of the testament, however, seems capable of being overthrown chiefly by the following argument. Caeoldus is there called bishop of Vienne, a name which critics—especially Mabillon, in the passage cited above—wish to understand as either Caldoldus or Edaldus. Both were indeed bishops of Vienne, but Caldoldus was so during the final years of Dagobert I, around 687; Edaldus died during the reign of Theuderic III. Neither, therefore, lived under Childebert III. Consequently, Ephibius’s testament offers an obvious indication of forgery, since it is said to have been issued in the second year of the reign of Childebert III, in the time of Caeoldus, bishop of Vienne, whether Caldoldus or Edaldus is intended by that name. *(Year 696.)*

In the name of Christ, I, Ephibius, for the love of God and of the blessed apostles and of the lord Desiderius, bishop and martyr, make a testament concerning my property and inheritance, which came to me by legitimate authority from my parents Leobius and Teodigna, and from my sister Rufina, who died without children and, while I was alive, left me her inheritance according to legal procedure.

These, then, are the things which by this testament I hand over to God and his saints, to serve in the church of Vienne through our lord Caeoldus, bishop: the entire estate of Geneciacum, with everything belonging to it, without any share belonging to any of my relatives, together with slaves of both sexes, lands, woods, waters, ports and jurisdictions, and whatever belongs to the aforementioned estate, without any participation by any of my relatives.

Likewise, the third part which came to me by lawful succession from my aforementioned sister, namely of the estate of Parthenis, with slaves of both sexes, lands, woods, waters, and the other things belonging to the tax or service of that third part, so that it may never at any time be alienated from the power of the Church.

We also hand over other properties in the surrounding area which we acquired from our glorious lord Childebert in return for our service: three estates in the Angoulême region, concerning which we have already drawn up a testament.

We have inserted the testament of our sister into this testament of ours, with the senate sitting in judgment in the city of Vienne.

To my lord and beloved brother Euphibius the abbot, Rufina, your sister, who remain bereft of children: since you are handing over your property to God and his saints at Vienne, I have thought nothing better than to give you, from the gift of our father and mother, namely the third part of Parthenis, which adjoins the estate of Geneciacum, so that, just as you have brought the other property under your control, you may also join this to your inheritance and associate it with the holy place, so that I may have a share in your vow and gift, together with God’s saints, for whose love you do these things.

I, your sister Rufina, subscribe this testament of mine. Without another sister or other relatives, I have legally possessed all of it in full until now, and I have asked the sacred senate to strengthen by their hands all these things contained above, so that they may remain firm. Concerning these matters I have also requested that a royal edict be made. I hand over and transfer for possession to the holy Church of God at Vienne all things in their entirety, with my reverend father Caeoldus presiding, so that from this day forward they may remain to it: 1,400 slaves of both sexes, as well as 500 free persons who perform service there.

Whoever comes against this testament in order to disturb my vow, so that the servants of God may not be provided with food, services, and necessities, shall be compelled by senatorial judgment to pay publicly 400 pounds of gold, apart from many estates, which shall be compensated to the Church of Vienne and restored to the servants of God.

**Note:** These words would be of the greatest importance for proving that the senates of the cities retained judicial authority under the barbarian kings after the overthrow of Roman rule. But what can be inferred from a document that is manifestly false?

I, Ephibius the abbot, have personally confirmed this testament from the estate of Geneciacum and concerning the other third portion of my sister, and I have properly asked and requested all the senators to confirm the same.

Senator Eulogius, kinsman.  
Rufina, sister.  
Deuphibus, senator.  
Contumacus, senator.  
Pelagius, senator.  
Leubinus, senator.  
Caracteius, senator.  
Arginus, senator.  
Silvanus, senator.  
Gregorius, senator.  
Artemius, senator.  
Eulogius, senator.  
Deophilus, senator.  
Siagrius, senator.  
Rufus, senator.  
Ergerius, senator.  
Spectabilis, senator.  
Macrinus, senator.  
And so the others.  
Simplicius, quaestor and senator.  
The public notarial clerk.

**Note:** The designation *notarius libellarius* occurs nowhere in the documents of this period, nor have we found this expression elsewhere; Mabillon, Cange, and the other writers on diplomatics evidently derived it from no other source.

I dictated and subscribed this, in the second year of the glorious King Childebert.

### XXXVIII. Charter by which Gammo and his wife Adalgudis declare the gifts bestowed upon the monastery of Lemausum, founded by them, and arrange for their confirmation at an assembly of nobles

**Note:** Published by Mabillon, *Annales*, vol. I, p. 704, from the chartulary of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; Bulliardus published it from Mabillon in the proofs to his *History of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*, p. 4. It is there said that Autharius presided over the monastery of Saint-Germain, which raises some suspicion concerning the falsity of this charter. For Waldromerus had already succeeded Autharius in the third year of the reign of Childebert III, as Mabillon himself testifies in the passage cited above, from a document which he says he possessed. Gammo’s charter, however, derives its chronological date from this same third year. This is not an obvious contradiction: Autharius could have died during that same year, and Gammo’s charter could have been made then. But we resolve the difficulty in another way. We suppose that the monastery in question was founded and endowed before Autharius’s death; after Autharius had died, Gammo and his wife wished to have their gifts to this monastery confirmed at an assembly of nobles held at Bourges, before the king, according to Frankish custom, in the third year of Childebert. Thus the charter is freed from suspicion. *(Year 697.)*

In the name of the holy Trinity. It is recognized as a prosperous, wholesome, and indeed most joyful purpose when someone bestows upon God the perishable wealth of this world, by which he may redeem and wash away his sin. And what purpose could be wiser than for a human being to purchase paradise with worldly goods and transfer something from earthly substance to heavenly things?

Therefore I, Gammo, and my wife Adalgudis, considering how we might wipe away the burden of our sins and attain everlasting joys, began to build, on a place belonging to us called Lemausum, a small monastery in honor of Saint John and the holy Cross and the other saints, so that we might establish girls there in honor of Saint Mary, where they should live under the holy standard of the rule.

And so we did. We established our daughter Berta in that place, so that throughout the days of her life, both she and those who appear to live with her in that monastery should live and conduct themselves under the monastic order and the rule of Saint Benedict. We also established our daughter Berta as abbess there, and assigned the place of Lemausum to her, together with everything that appears to belong to it, with all its integrity and appurtenances, in whatever pagi or territories they may be situated, whether beyond or this side of the Loire.

The places are called as follows: Nova-Villa, Vintoris, Britinniacum, Quintiacum, Bragogilum, Grimoaldo-Villare, Prulliace, Rovere, Mauro-Villa, Barbarione-Villa, Villa Milies, Galdono-Maso, Ferrarias, and another Ferrarias, Culmellas-Montis, Alnaum, Tricafines, Felcariolae, Noiolium, Mundone-Villa, Childeno Villa, Potiosus, Hadone-Villa, Flaviacum, Alvernis, Posthimiacum, Caceriae, and Busxeriae.

Likewise, beyond the Loire, Balbiacum, Cervatiacum, and Valle; as we have said, both beyond and this side of the Loire, whatever appears to be our possession at the present time or, with God’s help, may become so hereafter.

We have assigned and confirmed the places listed above to the small monastery called Lemausum, on this condition: that while we both live, I, Gammo, and my wife Adalgudis, as well as our daughters Berta and Maria, shall cause both this monastery of Lemausum and the said estates to be possessed and governed, together with their lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, freedmen, fields, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, livestock, properties movable and immovable, cultivated and uncultivated—in every respect and altogether—so that everything may contribute to the support of the nuns and to that monastery which we have built, for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, in honor of Saint John, the holy Cross, and the other saints, for its increase.

Moreover, everything from my property which, on the day of my death, is found or discovered in my possession—namely gold, silver, clothing, or estates—the abbess who at that time is seen to preside over the small monastery of Lemausum shall receive, against my heirs, one-third of everything. The condition shall be that they must perpetually give it as alms to the poor, strangers, and those who fear God, for the remedy of our souls.

And since the female sex by itself is scarcely able to carry out anything, whether for increasing our reward or for administering their necessities, they are in no way permitted to go outside. Therefore we wish all the things already mentioned, and the monastery itself called Lemausum, together with its estates and all its appurtenances, as we have said, in whatever pagi or territories they may be situated, both beyond and this side of the Loire, to be given in perpetuity to the monastery of Saint Vincent and the holy Cross in the city of Paris, where Saint Germanus rests in body, and where Abbot Autharius appears, in God’s name, to preside together with a numerous community of monks under a rule.

We wish these things to remain there forever, and by this document we transfer them. So that no one may dare to contradict or rashly violate the property inserted here, neither we nor our heirs nor anyone else shall have the right to sell, give away, alienate, or diminish it by any charter or document.

And if it should happen, by divine dispensation, that Berta, to whom we have assigned the nuns and the monastery of Lemausum, departs from this life, the rulers of Saint Vincent or Saint Germanus shall establish an abbess in that place as they decide. That abbess shall not dare to send other nuns to the aforesaid place, nor shall they dare to admit another shepherd within it, except from the monastery of Saint Vincent and Saint Germanus, or those who appear to be its rulers there.

We, Gammo and my wife Adalgudis, and our aforementioned daughters Berta and Maria, for as long as we live, must hold and govern the monastery of Lemausum and the aforesaid property. After our departure, according to what we have said above, Autharius the abbot, or his successors who at that time are in the monastery of Saint Vincent, the holy Cross, and Saint Germanus, shall possess the monastery itself and the aforementioned estates with their appurtenances forever, so that they may have them under their authority.

If anyone—as commonly happens and as human frailty allows—whether we ourselves, or any of our heirs or successors, or any opposing person, should presume to come against this present charter of donation, which we ordered to be made for the salvation of our souls, or to violate it by any claim through any persons, may he first incur the wrath of God, be condemned with Judas the betrayer to everlasting fire, be excommunicated by all churches and by all bishops and priests, and, before the presence of Saint Vincent and Saint Germanus, to whom we have assigned these properties, be counted among the portion of the condemned, if he wishes to make a claim from property assigned to churches or to the poor.

May his reward in no way prosper, nor may he deserve to have eternal life, if he wishes to tear apart our alms. In addition, he shall be compelled to pay to the king’s fisc thirty pounds of gold and sixty pounds of silver, and even then shall not be able to obtain what he claims.
