And so that this charter of donation may remain firm, it was reread at Bourges at an assembly of nobles, in the presence of our lord King Childebert, and in the city of Paris, in the monastery of Saint Vincent, it was placed upon the altar of the holy Cross on the sixth day of April, in the third year of that same lord, our King Childebert.

Turnoaldus, although a sinner and bishop, subscribed.  
Guntharius, likewise an unworthy deacon, subscribed.  
Madolandus, an unworthy abbot, subscribed.  
In the name of Christ, Andeboldus the abbot subscribed.  
Durandomarus, abbot by the grace of God, subscribed.  
Desiderandus, abbot in the name of Christ, subscribed.  
I, Gammo, rereading this charter of my donation, subscribed.  
Adalgudis subscribed.  
Bertinus, a soldier, subscribed.

**Note:** Mabillon doubts whether the title *miles*—“soldier” or “knight”—was already in use at that time, or whether the word was instead misread in the old codex by the chartulary’s copyist.

Berdandus, a soldier, subscribed.

### XXXIX bis

**Note:** Charter of an exchange made between Adalricus and Wualdromerus, abbot of Saint-Germain (697). This charter, dated 25 April in the third year of the reign of King Childebert III and still unpublished, is preserved in the royal archives, K, chest 3. For many years it lay concealed, glued to the cover of an old register of Saint-Germain; quite recently it was discovered by A. Teulet, but too late for it to be inserted here in full and in its proper order.

### XL. Charter by which Pippin the Elder bestows new gifts upon the monastery of Laubium

**Note:** Published in the supplement to Miraeus’s works, vol. III, p. 283, after an example of a spurious charter in the name of the same Pippin, which we presented above. In addition to the indications of forgery which we noted in that earlier charter, we have detected others in this later one.

First, this charter calls Pippin’s wife Brunihelda, although she should have been called Plectrude. Second, Hydulphus is again introduced, bearing the title duke of Lorraine. Third, the Forestella wood, which is donated to the monastery of Laubium in this later charter, had already been granted to it six years earlier by the preceding document. Fourth, the maker of the later charter copied the earlier charter so literally that he used the very same chronological notation, namely the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, thereby betraying the model which he had taken for his original. It would be embarrassing to linger longer in examining such a document. *(Year 697.)*

In the name of the holy undivided Trinity. Amen.

The universal Mother and singular Virgin, the Bride of Christ, the Catholic Church, has earned by the excellence of her fruitful chastity that we should incline our devoted assent to her interests. We especially provide, with vigilant care, for the tranquillity and repose of sacred religion, so that she may more freely devote herself to divine contemplation and prayer for our stability and that of our kingdom, and may approach God, so that, once the enemies of the Christian faith have been driven out, with the whole of her body unharmed, the kingdom may flourish and grow under our labor, and hostile arrogance may everywhere feel itself subjected.

I, Pippin the Elder, moved by this favor and desire, together with my wife Brunihelda, give to the monastery of that most religious man and outstanding preacher and bishop Ursmarus, which is at Laubium on the Sambre River, as an endowment to be possessed by that church forever, the land and wood situated between the stream of Grunghart and the stream of Hergnaut, which flow into the Sambre; that wood has long been called Forestella.

But since, through preceding grace, the illustrious man Dodo, drawn by the preaching of the aforesaid man to the orthodox faith, was baptized and devoted himself to monastic discipline and conversion, he, prompted by the counsel of our faithful Hydulphus, duke of Lorraine, became a monk and gave to the monastery of Laubium, which is in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, as perpetual alms, his entire estate and patrimony—namely, the estates of Moustiers and Bavis, with the whole integrity of their lordship, and all lands, estates, meadows, waters and watercourses, ban, and jurisdiction, male and female slaves, as he lawfully possessed them—to be possessed by resigning them into our hand, subscribing them to the said church, enclosing them within definite boundaries, and securing them by our authority.

These, then, are the places within the boundary of that property. The water boundary begins at the place called Ralhiers, and extends beneath Moustiers, ending at the wood of Saint Monegundis. The forest boundary includes the entire wood called Eumont, as far as the water coming from Walhiers, together with the whole territory, pasturage-right (*pannage*), and jurisdiction in every respect; and from the water of Walliers, the entire wood called Bruelh and Fangias, as far as Levoion, as far as Willemier; and another wood beside Wilhies, from the mountain called Gomont and the ford of Merdosum, as far as the estate of Wilhies; and the wood situated at the boundary of Duchon.

We place these places under the protection of our immunity and grant them to the aforesaid monastery for the use of the brothers serving God there, so that they may possess them freely and peacefully, without the advocacy or oppression of any count, centenarius, or deputy-lord. No one may presume to build a house above the territory of the church without its will and permission.

We receive all the aforementioned places, and whatever they possess or may later lawfully and reasonably possess, under royal protection, and decree that they shall suffer no molestation from any attempted interference. If anyone should become a violator of this immunity and privilege of ours, stripped of all liberty and honor, let him be struck with capital punishment.

But so that this concession of ours may remain undisturbed through successive times, we confirm it with our hand and have ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Pippin, the unconquered king.

**Note:** Did Pippin the Elder arrogate the title of king to himself? But these things bear the character of a charter fabricated in the eighth century.

I, Adelgus the chancellor, acting in the place of Ruothpertus the archchaplain, examined and subscribed.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, at Lestines, in the year 697 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

### XLI. Charter by which Aiglibertus, bishop of Le Mans, grants immunities to the monastery of Saint Mary beside the Sarta

**Note:** We possess two charters of the same wording, both inserted in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, pp. 276 and 278. We consider them one and the same charter, composed in exactly the same words except for the subscriptions and the chronological notes, which are entirely different.

We conjecture that this discrepancy arose because, when the subscriptions and chronological notes were lacking in some old exemplar, the copyist supplied them on his own initiative—a thing which those who have examined old documents know happened frequently.

The first charter is said to have been issued in the eleventh year of King Theuderic III—for Aiglibertus did not live under Theuderic IV—and the second in the sixth year of Childebert III. Mabillon, who was aware of both, since he published both in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, mentioned only one in his *Annales*, vol. I, p. 560, namely the first. He was silent about the second, evidently because he considered the two to be identical, with only the subscriptions and chronological notes changed, and judged those in the first to be more authentic.

We, however, if we may say so with due respect to so great a man, conjecture that these were rashly added to the first charter, and that those attached to the second are genuine. Why was this repeated concession made fifteen years after the immunity had already been granted? To confirm it? But in that case the second charter would have contained some mention of the first. And what sort of confirmation would the second charter have provided, being supported only by the subscriptions of a few abbots, compared with the earlier privilege, fortified by the subscriptions of more than thirty bishops?

Moreover, the accumulated names of so many bishops raise substantial suspicion of interpolation. Add to this that most of those bishops are unknown, as Mabillon admits; and that some, although known, did not exist at that time. Thus: Berarius, Aiglibertus’s predecessor; Vindicianus, bishop of Cambrai; Adalbertus, bishop of Soissons; Blideramnus, bishop of Vienne; Protasius, bishop of Aix; Clemens, bishop of Beauvais; and Abbo, whether one wishes to identify him as bishop of Metz or of Verdun.

Finally, the subscription of Aiglibertus himself, who composed the charter, is inserted indiscriminately among the witnesses. We therefore have not thought it appropriate to insert the first charter in full into this collection. We shall nevertheless provide in the notes the subscriptions and chronological notes by which it alone differs from the second, and shall place in brackets the very few variant readings, even if they may not appear to be of great importance. *(Year 700.)*
[Col. 1240B] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. To our most beloved kinswoman Adrehild, abbess, Aiglibertus, bishop—though unworthy—of the city of Le Mans.

Because, out of fear, divine love, and reverence for holy Mary, Mother of God, with the clerical brothers and fellow priests, and with our sisters and nuns giving their consent, it has seemed good to us that in the basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God, where we have established the aforesaid kinswoman of ours, Abbess Adrehild, through our benevolence, divine generosity, and virginal or abbatial blessing, and with the consent, as we have said, of the fellow priests and canons of our church of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and [Col. 1240C] Protasius, whose church receives the cell of Saint Mary, built between the Sarthe River and the city wall, they ought to observe the institutions established there: namely, that, so long as it is the will of holy Mary, Mother of God, humble and devout nuns living there under a rule should first direct their own consciences and make that place a pleasant habitation, so that our common reward may increase there and the praise of the Lord may devoutly proceed.

Therefore, by this present charter, we grant for the use of spiritual nuns, of pilgrims and of the poor who, for God’s sake, have abandoned their places or possessions, that in the aforesaid monastery of holy Mary, Mother of God—which belongs justly and legally to the mother church of the city of Le Mans, over which I ought to preside and for which I ought to provide—and under the authority of its bishops and their ministers, the payments and burdensome dues owed from that monastery to the aforesaid mother church, as long ago established by the founders, endowers, and founders of that monastery and by the former bishops of this city, and hitherto paid, shall henceforth be lighter and easier.

In that same cell we appoint our aforesaid kinswoman, the venerable Abbess Adrehild, with the consent of [Col. 1241B] our priests, so that there, in the name of Christ, our aforesaid kinswoman the abbess and the other nuns, both within the city and outside it, beside the aforesaid church of holy Mary, Mother of God, may live according to the rule and, for the present, whenever [or: “when indeed”] they ought to live.

Whenever the aforesaid abbess, or another appointed in her place, dies, they shall choose another with the consent and appointment of the bishop of the aforesaid city, selecting from among themselves the woman whom they find most useful for preserving and governing their souls and, with God’s help, saving them.

Accordingly, we now admonish both her and the others who may appear to preside, as well as the nuns themselves who live there under the rule, that, just as the other regular monasteries [Col. 1241C] which live more correctly under the order of the rule, so also the aforesaid convent of nuns should live under the authority and governance of the bishop of the aforesaid city and preserve the rule in it at all times.

And we earnestly admonish you, or whoever among your successors may be exactors of that church, not to demand burdensome or difficult impositions from the appointed little place. Rather, they should diligently perform the work of garments and whatever pertains to the nuns’ duties, and should wash or repair ecclesiastical or episcopal vestments, so that the rule of the nuns may not be neglected there because of the burdensome dues or exactions of the bishops or their ministers, but, as it has been established by us, may be preserved for all time.

We humbly ask our successors who will occupy the episcopal office in this see not to violate what has been established by us. Just as they will wish their own institutions to be preserved, so let them preserve ours, so that the nuns established there may be permitted to maintain the holy order and [Col. 1242B] the rule, and to pray for us and for all the people of the Lord for mercy.

And, so that this writing may hereafter be held in place of a privilege, we admonish them to keep the holy order, and at all times to reside there holily and regularly in the name of God, and to devote themselves continually to readings, holy meditations, and prayers.

We therefore ask and solemnly adjure before God and his angels all kings, princes, powers, dominions, consuls, nobles, whether counts or others, and all the powerful and noble, or procurators, not to break or corrupt this privilege made by us with the consent of our fellow bishops and priests, nor to violate or tear it apart in any way, [Col. 1242C] nor to corrupt it in any respect; but to permit the nuns in the aforesaid place or convent to live peacefully and regularly, in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and of holy Mary, Mother of God, securely and holily, without any harassment or disturbance.

[Note: [Col. 1241C] The following is missing; in its place, the following material was inserted in the charter that we consider interpolated, as may be seen in Mabillon’s Annals, p. 279:

### XLII. Fragment of the testament of Erminethrudis, in which she records many bequests to churches and persons

[Note: [Col. 1243C] Mabillon published this at the end of the *Gallican Liturgy*, p. 463, and again in the appendix to the supplement to *De re diplomatica*, pp. 92 ff., from the authentic document of Saint-Denis (now preserved in the Royal Archives, K, tab. XV; Marini also published it, *Papiri diplomatici*, no. LXXVI). The testament was drawn up by Eminethrude, an illustrious matron, as may be inferred from the rank of Count Mummolus and of certain others who reinforced the instrument with their subscriptions. Mabillon considers it to belong to the beginning of the eighth century, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 623. Chronological notes had been placed at the beginning, as is clear from the final clause of the testament itself; but they were destroyed by the injury of time and by the fragility of the material, which was Egyptian papyrus, as Mabillon likewise explains.

Erminethrudis records bequests to many basilicas, among them the basilica of the Holy Cross, or of Saint Vincent, in Paris; this confirms that this same basilica was already then called by the two names. She also mentions the basilica of Saint Sinsurianus, which some have thought to be the little church of Saint Symphorianus joined by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, to the basilica of Saint Vincent; see Mabillon, cited above, p. 624. But the name basilica was by no means assigned to such little churches. [Col. 1244C] [Yet, with all respect to the distinguished scholar, this cannot be considered doubtful, since the name Saint Sinfurianus, not Sinsurianus, is read everywhere with complete clarity in the original document.]

Among other things, Erminethrudis bequeaths the carriage in which she rode and oxen, according to the custom of matrons under the Merovingian kings; see Gregory of Tours, *History*, book III, chapter 26. She also bequeaths the estate of Latiniacum in the district of Meaux, which at first sight seems to conflict with the charter of Theuderic III (see above), by which the same estate had been granted to Saint-Denis in the year 688. But both grants must be understood as concerning some part of the estate, not the whole of Latiniacum. When this conjecture occurred to Mabillon, he later learned from the monks of Saint-Denis, who were thoroughly familiar with the property of their monastery, that this was indeed the case, *Supplement to De re diplomatica*, p. 22. They testified that Saint-Denis had never possessed anything in the estate of Latiniacum except a peasant holding together with a share of the rights.] (ann. 700).

. . . . . . . . the most sacred treasury shall receive. But if you preserve intact everything that I have inserted in this testament, whatever I have bequeathed to you above shall remain permanently in your possession. [If there is anything] in this testament that I have not assigned to anyone else, I wish you, my dearest son, to have it. Likewise, . . . . . At the request of the good-memory Deorovaldus, I give you a silver vessel worth approximately twenty-five solidi, and on my own account I give you a silver cup worth thirty solidi; and half of the sheep watched over by Vigilius, together with the shepherd named Gaugiulfus.

In the same way, from Latiniacum and Balbiniacum, both clothing and bronze vessels or utensils, and half of all the oxen, I order you, my dearest son, to have. Likewise, at the request of the good-memory Deorovaldus, I give you, my dearest son, from his portion and from my property, the following slaves: Unnegiselo, Aunemundus, and the daughters of Patricius, namely Fedana, Ausegunda, Agnechildis, and Baccio, together with a herd of pigs; two vine-yards’ measure situated on Mount Maurilio, which Theodaharius and Garimundus cultivate; a third vine-yard’s measure situated on Mount Metobaurus, with the vine-dresser Guntracharius; a fourth vine-yard’s measure situated at Tauriniacum, cultivated by Imneredus, with the vine-dresser Munegisilus; and a fifth vine-yard’s measure situated on Mount Vultorisinus, cultivated by Sevila, together with that vine-dresser.

[Col. 1244A] All the things written above I have determined that you, my dearest son, should have, both from my own will and at the request of the blessed-memory Deorovaldus.

A vineyard situated on Mount Me. . . ., cultivated by Habundantius: I order half of it to be given to the holy church of . . . elia; the other half of that vineyard I order my dearest nephew Bertigisilus to have.

The vineyard held by the woman Agila, and the vineyard cultivated by Imnacharius, I order my dearest niece Deorovara to have, together with Imnacharius himself.

The vines that are beside Sevila’s vineyard I order my dearest nephew Bertericus to have.

The vineyard cultivated by Vincimalus on Mount Vultorisinus, and the girl named Sunnechildis, and the female slave named Iveria with her son Leudinus, I order my dearest daughter-in-law Bertovara [Col. 1244B] to have.

Likewise, to my dearest nephew Bertegisilus I assign a silver *ichriarius* [the term is uncertain], and the following slaves: Sunniulfus, his sister Gibethrudis, the daughters of Anthimius, and the son of The. . . . , the younger [name incomplete].

To my niece Deorovara I assign a silver cross-marked [or cruciform] bowl, and the following slaves: Tanechildis, Imnegunthe, and Imnegisilus; also bedding for one bed, whichever is better, a boy named Gundofredus, a female slave named Thaigundis, and also a girl named Audechildis.

To my dearest nephew Bertericus I order the boy named Medigisilus to belong.

To the basilicas established in Paris: to the basilica of Saint Peter, a silver pitcher worth twelve solidi, and a gemmed gold brooch. . . . I determine that a cloak be given.

To the basilica of Our Lady I order a silver bowl [Col. 1244C] worth twelve solidi and a gold cross worth seven solidi to be given.

To the basilica of Saint Stephen I wish a blackened gold ring worth four solidi to be given.

To the basilica of Saint Gervasius I order a gold ring to be given, bearing my name written upon it.

To the basilica of Saint Sinfurianus, in which my son Deorovaldus of good memory rests, I order a bridle worth twelve solidi, a saddled horse, and the cart in which I was accustomed to sit, together with oxen, and bedding with all its equipment [Note: [Col. 1244D] These words correspond to the heading added to chapter 6 of the Salic Law, where *lectum stratum*—“a made-up bed”—is mentioned; compare Marini, note 5, p. 261], to be given for my devotion and for the repose of Deorovaldus.

I order another cart with oxen and all its equipment to be given to the church of the village of Bonisiacum. Likewise, I order the farm called Volonno, with its dependencies, to belong to the aforesaid church of Bonisiacum, for the remedy of my soul.

To the Holy Church of the city of Paris I order a silver *missorium* worth fifty solidi to be given.

To the basilica of the Holy Cross, or of Saint Vincent, I order ten silver spoons to be given.

I order one set of bedding and one set of my clothing to be given to the brothers at the table of the basilica of Saint-Denis.

I determine that another set of clothing be given to the brothers at the village of Bonisiacum.

I order a third set of clothing to be given at the village of Emilia.

Likewise, for the remedy of my soul and at the request of my son Deorovaldus of good memory, I order the estate called Latiniacum, situated in the territory of Meaux, with its fields, tenant holdings belonging to it, meadows, pastures, woods, and all its rights and boundaries—for it came to the share of my aforementioned son Deorovaldus—to be given in its entirety to the basilica of Saint Sinfurianus, where he is known to have his burial, for his repose.

Likewise, I order the swineherd named Gundilanus, together with his herd of pigs, and Baudomeres, together with his herd of sheep and a troop of pack animals, which are at the aforesaid estate of Latiniacum, to belong to the aforesaid basilica of Saint Sinfurianus.

I order Godericus and Gundericus, at the aforesaid estate which I have bequeathed to the basilica of Saint Sinfurianus, to work so that offerings may be supplied daily to that basilica.

I wish Leudulfus, together with the vineyard cultivated by Sabucitus, to be given to the oratory situated in the estate of Latiniacum, so that an offering may be presented there.

I order Baudulfus and Sumthaharius likewise, together with the oxen, to work so that an offering may continually be supplied to the basilica of Saint Sinfurianus for the repose of Deorovaldus.

In the same way, I order one vine-yard’s measure situated at Tauriniacum, cultivated by Pinpo, to be given to the basilica of Saint George at Cab. . . . .

I determine that one vine-yard’s measure situated on Mount Buxata, cultivated by Juvius, be given to the church of Bonisiacum.

The vineyard cultivated by Uvassio, together with Uvassio himself. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . by the name of Theudericus, whom . . . . . ought to cultivate, I determine that it be given to the basilica of Saint Sinfurianus . . . . . for an offering.

I order one vine-yard’s measure situated on Mount Blixata, cultivated by Leudefredus, to be given to the basilica of Saint Martin as a *ciperent* [term uncertain].

I determine that the names of my freedmen be appended to this testament: Medibergana, Honorius, Gunddeubana, Piana, Sumthulfus, Ciuccirana, Hicchicio, Maxa his wife, Chioberga, Sinderedus, Angilo, Leudefredus with his wife Vuandilona, Chaideruna, Childeruna, Thrasteberga, Theodacharius, Vigilius with his wife Sunnina, Agio with his son Garilulfus, Vincimalus with his wife Maurella, Mellita with her younger son, Coccionius with his son Daigisilus, Mudilana with her children Munegisilus and Monechrudis, Acchio, Bonana, Leubosuinthus, Gibulfus son of Vigilius, Dommoruna, Childerimanus, Baso, Childegisilus, Childegunthe, [Col. 1246A] Chrodulfus, Asindebergana, Monechildis, Aeternus, Bauderuna.

I order all these people, together with all their personal property—small plots, little dwellings, gardens, or vineyards, and everything they appear to possess in any kind of property—to be free, both men and women; and whatever they wish to do with it thereafter, let them have free power.

Likewise, I order Mumolana to be free, with all her personal property; she is only to take care to provide lamps in the church of Bonisiacum.

I order Vualacharius to be free, with all his personal property and with the oxen he tends, on the condition that he provide wood only for making offerings.

I order Gundefredus to work with two oxen, so that wax may be purchased for the basilica of Saint Sinfurianus.

I order Martinianus and Theoderuna, together with their elder son and their personal property, to be free, just like those written above who have deserved well.

Likewise, for the remedy of my soul and at the request of my son Deorovaldus, I determine that the following people be free, together with all their personal property—small plots, little dwellings, vineyards, or gardens—and with everything they appear at present to possess: Gygone, Septereda with his wife Goderuna, Theodonivia, Baudonivia, Carana, Patricius with his wife Eusebia, Dagaricus with his wife Aurovefa, Ciunciolenus, Blidemundus with his daughter Blidechildis, Manileubus, Trasilana, Eumundus, Imneredus with his wife Torigia, Chadulfus, Aridia, Rocculana, Babicco, Gunthivera.

I order Baudulfus and Sumthaharius, with the oxen they tend, to work so that offerings may continually be supplied from them to the basilica of Saint Sinfurianus. [Col. 1246C]

Thus I give, thus I bind, thus I testify. You, Quirites, bear witness to me as I testify; all other male and female relatives, be disinherited by me and keep far away.

If there are any erasures or corrections in this my testament, I made them and ordered them to be made, since I often wished it to be reread to me.

I have also determined that, if anyone should wish to act against this testament or attempt in any respect to corrupt my will, he shall be made an outsider from the communion of all the saints and from the thresholds of the churches, and moreover shall remain accursed before the tribunal of Christ.

Executed at Paris on the day and at the time written above.

The mark + of Erminethrudis the testatrix.  
+ Mummolus, count, at the request and in the presence of Erminethrudis, subscribed this testament.  
Scupilio, sword-bearer, at the request [Col. 1246D] of Erminethrudis, appended a subscription to this testament, on the day and in the year stated above.  
Munegiselus, at the request and in the presence of Erminethrudis, witnessed and appended a subscription to this testament, on the day and in the year stated above.  
Baudacharius the defender subscribed.  
Eusebius, requested by Erminethrudis, wrote, reread, and subscribed this testament.

### XLIII. Charter by which Pipin and Plectrudis, his wife, exchange certain property with Armonius, bishop of Verdun, and Anglebertus the archdeacon, who presided over the church of Saint Videnus (Saint Vitonus); and by which Pipin, Armonius, and Anglebertus give gifts to that church

[Note: [Col. 1246D] This charter has been published several times. Wasseburg first printed it, *Antiquitates Belgicae*, p. 110 recto, extracted from the archive of Saint Vitonus, but with gaps, since he had been unable to make out the reading of certain words in the old document. Labbe later printed it from the same archive, *Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 434, omitting many passages. Cointius reprinted it, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 384, from Wasseburg; and the *Collection of Writings on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 680, from Labbe. Calmet published it more accurately, *History of Lorraine*, vol. II, documentary proofs, p. 83, from the old chartulary of Saint Vitonus.

We publish it on the authority of a copy preserved in our archive, transcribed with the greatest care from the same chartulary. Mabillon, who had seen this instrument in Labbe, made an error in reporting the chronological notes, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 164: namely, he wrote “seventeenth” for “thirteenth day before the Kalends of February.” He himself, together with Cointius, Calmet, and others cited above, *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. XIII, col. 1170, etc., assigns this charter to the year of Christ 701. But since the beginning of Childebert’s reign must be reckoned from March of the year 695, the seventh year of his reign, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February—that is, on January 20—fell in the year of Christ 702.] (ann. 702).

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen. [Col. 1247A] Since between the illustrious man Pipin and his illustrious matron Plectrudis, on the one hand, and the apostolic man Armonius, bishop of the city of Verdun, and the venerable man Anglebertus, archdeacon who presides in the church of Saint Videnus, where that saint’s precious body rests, on the other, there had been a discussion concerning certain small estates which they ought to exchange with one another and concerning what was appropriate and advantageous for them to do—and this they did—therefore, by this present exchange, the illustrious man Pipin and his illustrious matron Plectrudis give, at the place called Pararitus, whatever they appear to possess or control there at the present day, with buildings, meadows, and woods.

The boundaries of the woods are: from Luponis Fountain to Domus Fountain; the second boundary runs along the Perfunt River to Biunna; the third and fourth boundaries are common, namely Filealina [Col. 1247B] from the estate of Herberica, and Saint Mauritius.

And within these boundaries they give the pastures, waters, and watercourses, with every right and the entire boundary or status belonging in the name of God to the aforesaid place, together with the slaves, both rural and urban—whatever they appear to control there from the present day—to the church of Saint Videnus, or to whoever may preside there, or to the clerics serving there, as a complete and permanent gift and confirmation, so that, concerning these things, the will of the aforesaid church may have free power to do whatever it decrees.

Likewise, the apostolic man Armonius, bishop, and the venerable man Anglebertus, archdeacon, give and confirm to that church the place called Commenarias, which Pipin himself and his illustrious matron Plectrudis [Col. 1247C] transferred to the church of Saint Videnus by their charter of grant, with buildings, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, with its entire boundary and status, as it is possessed at the present time by that church, without any claim or demand by anyone.

And if any party, or any disturbance or harassment, should arise, and we ourselves, our heirs, or our successors should presume to cause it contrary to this agreement, the party maintaining this charter shall receive three pounds of gold and fifty weights of silver.

This exchange was made on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventh year of the reign of our lord Childebert, king.

I, Hardricus, at the command of my lord Pipin and his illustrious matron Plectrudis, wrote and subscribed this charter.

The sign of Count Ansigisubus.  
The sign of Count Ansbertus.  
The sign of Count Hardricus.  
The sign of Count Bovo.  
The sign of Count Erimardus.  
The sign of Count Bathisus.  
The sign of Count Gonduinus.  
The sign of Count Ramfridus.

### XLIV. Charter by which Eodebertus sells all his property at Rumeliacum to Rigobertus, abbot of Sithiu

[Note: [Col. 1248D] We publish this previously unpublished charter from a copy made by Dom de Witte, superintendent of the archives of Sithiu. He extracted it from the chartulary of Folquinus and deposited it in our archive. [Compare the *Chartulary of Sithiu* published by the distinguished Guérard, p. 38.]] (ann. 704).

[Col. 1248A]

To the holy lord and venerable man in Christ, Rigobertus, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, Eodebertus, seller.

It is established that I have sold to you, not by a merely pretended right but by my fullest will, and thus have sold and delivered, and thus have delivered at the present time, namely, all the property of my portion at the place called Rumliacum, in the district of Tarvanna, which came to me from the share of my son Chardebertus, now deceased, by a mournful inheritance; that is, with lands, houses, buildings, slaves, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, mills, herds together with shepherds, and property not yet inventoried, in its entirety—whatever my wife held there and left behind at her death, or whatever came from her share to our son named above.

All this, in its complete order, let the abbot himself or the part of his monastery receive or possess from the present day in their right and dominion. For this we have received from you, as the agreed price, according to what was satisfactory and acceptable to us, in gold and silver, one thousand five hundred solidi only.

Thus, from this day forward, let the abbot himself or the part of his monastery have complete and firm power in every respect to possess, hold, give, sell, exchange, or do whatever they wish with it.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, or any of our heirs or heirs’ heirs, or any opposing party, should presume to act against or break this sale, which I asked to be made and written down with my fullest will, and it should not be defended by me or by my heirs, then we or our heirs shall pay as much again, and an additional equal amount, as we received from you, or as much as the property itself may then be worth after improvement; a double sum shall be paid, with the stipulation remaining in force, and the claimant shall not be able to vindicate what he claims. Rather, this present sale shall remain firm and inviolate for all time, supported by formal stipulation.

Executed at the monastery of Sithiu, on the sixteenth day of the month of May, in the tenth year of the reign of our glorious lord King Childebert.

The sign of Eodebertus, who requested that this sale be made.  
The sign of Fladebertus.  
The sign of Madalcharus.  
The sign of Erlebertus.  
The sign of Childolfus.  
The sign of Mauriana.  
The sign of Sigebertus.

Erchembodus the lector wrote and subscribed this sale.

### XLV. Charter by which Arnulphus, duke of the Burgundians, gives the estate of Floriacum and many other possessions to the monastery of the Holy Apostles near Metz

[Note: [Col. 1249C] This charter, extracted from the archive of the monastery of the Holy Apostles, now Saint Arnulphus, appears in Meurissius, *Lives of the Bishops of Metz*, p. 111; in Bouchetus, *On the Origin of the Royal House of France*, documentary proofs, p. 69; in Cointius, *Annals*, and from the charter of Saint Arnulphus, vol. IV, p. 456; and in *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. XIII, instruments, col. 369.

Walladerus published the same charter in French translation, *Basilica of Saint Arnulphus*, p. 188, from an original document which he says he saw with his own eyes, written in very ancient characters on bark.

We publish it from a copy deposited in our archive by Dom Tabouillot of the congregation of Saint Vitonus, carefully collated by him with the original. In the printed editions the following is prefixed to this instrument:

“I, Arnulphus, duke after my father Drogo, grant my estate of Creanto after the death of my father Drogo; and let it be done according to this writing which follows.”

Then follows the charter as we present it, with a few discrepancies of lesser importance which we have not thought worth recording.

Those who published this charter regarded it as genuine, except Cointius, who demonstrates by strong arguments that it is spurious:

1. Drogo, whom Arnulphus is said in this charter to have succeeded in the dukedom of Burgundy, was by no means duke of Burgundy but of Champagne.

2. The same Drogo, according to the unanimous agreement of the ancient annalists, did not die until the year 708. Therefore the charter said to have been issued after Drogo’s death, in the tenth year of the reign of Childebert III, in the month of June—that is, in the year of Christ 704—is fabricated.

We omit the chronological note reckoned from the Incarnation, contrary to the custom of this period. We omit the discrepancy between the tenth regnal year and the year 706 of the Incarnation. These matters might perhaps appear to be interpolated; but the other points we have noted reveal the falsity sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

In support of the authenticity of this instrument, three sons are assigned to Drogo: Arnulphus, Hugo the priest, and Godefridus. A fourth, Pipin, is added in a charter of no better standing, that of Hugo the priest, which we shall present and examine elsewhere.

[Nevertheless, the charter could be defended:

1. Nothing prevents Drogo from having been duke of Burgundy and of Champagne at the same time. Even if he held only the dukedom of Champagne, nothing prevents Pippin, after Drogo’s death, from having placed his son over Burgundy, lest it appear that he had acquired the dukedom of Champagne by hereditary right.

2. There is no controversy that the tenth year of Childebert III is incorrectly given; it ought to have been the fourteenth or fifteenth. But this can easily be attributed to the carelessness of a copyist or notary; and the distinguished scholar de Brequigny has employed numerous excuses of this kind. Certainly, it would be an unjust law of criticism if, because of errors—such as occur not infrequently even among our more careful printers—faith were denied to ancient instruments which contain nothing inherently incredible. [Col. 1250D] De Brequigny himself supplies an example of such carelessness: three times, once in a note and twice in his prolegomena, he assigns the death of Drogo to the year 608; I have taken care to correct this error.]] (ann. 706).

[Col. 1249A]

The prudent foresight of the ancients once provided, with sufficient usefulness, that it should be committed to writing for the memory of posterity if anyone, taking thought for himself and his soul, should transfer something from his own possessions to the Church of God, either before death or at the moment of death. Therefore let the future age know that I, Arnulphus, duke of the Burgundians by the grace of God, after my father Drogo, through the gift of my grandfather, the glorious prince Pippin, considering the instability of this life, and that the glory of the world withers like hay, and thinking about a remedy for my soul so that I may find life after death, asked the venerable man Luitbertus, abbot of the monastery situated near the city of Metz, which is called [the monastery] of the Holy Apostles, where my great-grandfather, the glorious confessor of Christ, Saint Arnulphus, from whom I derive both my name and my lineage, rests in the body, that a place of burial might also be granted to me in that same monastery, beside my aforesaid father Drogo and my brother Hugo the priest, since almost all my family, led by love for our pious predecessor and kinsman Saint Arnulphus, chose burial there. The same venerable abbot Luitbertus kindly granted this to me.

Therefore I too, in return for such benevolence, and so that my soul may deserve to have an inheritance in heaven with our pious father, the often-mentioned Saint Arnulphus, give, and wish to be given forever to that place, my estate called Floriacum, situated in the district of Wabrinse and in the county of Scarponne: namely, a lordly estate, with the buildings erected upon it and the slaves of both sexes belonging to that estate, and whatever I or my predecessors appear to have possessed in that allod, both in cultivated and uncultivated fields, in woods, meadows, vineyards, pastures, waters and watercourses, roads and trackless places, outgoings and revenues, mills, four-footed animals, movable and immovable property, or whatever can in any way be said or named.

I also give in the estate of Liedes a lordly estate with the building situated upon it, and beside this estate another settlement with arable lands amounting to approximately twenty-two days’ work, two quarter-measures, and a meadow amounting to three scythe-cuts.

Likewise, in the estate of Beruldi, three demesne *cuminæ*, situated as follows: one in the estate of Beruldi itself, another in the place called Marconis Meadow, and the third in the place called Amolbert’s Field, with seven quarter-measures; and a small wood amounting to twenty days’ work in the place called Bouerex Wood; also a meadow in the same estate amounting to three scythe-cuts; and, in another place called Intriberis, and in Marchei Meadow, sixty scythe-cuts.

Moreover, in the estate of Mariolas I give whatever came to me by inheritance after my brother Godefridus, of blessed memory: namely, more than two hundred jugera of lordly arable land, also a meadow amounting to thirty scythe-cuts, and a small wood amounting to ninety days’ work.

These things, and everything pertaining to them, I give and transfer to that place, and from my right completely place them under the power of the servants of God dwelling there, on the terms on which I have hitherto possessed them: that is, with complete integrity and without any participation by another lordship. Thus I transfer them so that those servants of God may firmly hold and possess them from the present day onward and may have free power to do with them whatever they judge beneficial to themselves and to that basilica.

But if anyone—which God forbid, and which I do not believe will happen—from among our descendants, or any other person or power, should wish to employ violence against this our donation, and should attempt to take away the estate itself or anything belonging to it from that holy place, or should try to usurp for himself any unjust dominion over the things that we give outright, let him know that on the day of judgment he will render an account of these matters before the just Judge, and will share the portion of eternal malediction with Dathan and Abiron and Judas the traitor.

Nevertheless, so that this our donation may remain firm forever, we confirm this testament in writing and strengthen it with our own hand.

Executed publicly in the estate of Oppilla, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 706, in the fourth indiction, while Childebert was reigning as king, in the tenth year of his reign.

I, Arnulphus, have signed and confirmed this donation committed to writing with my own hand.

Sign of Count Adilo.

Sign of Count Wido.

Sign of Count Trembertus.

Sign of Count Lambertus.

Sign of Count Warnarius.

Sign of Tmuson the *scabinus*.

[Note: This word, which, as the eminent de Savigny notes, is found nowhere before the second dynasty of the Frankish kings, would seem to weigh heavily against the authority of the document. Nevertheless, nothing is known with such certainty about the institutions of Austrasia that it can be asserted that the name scabinus was never given to certain men living under the authority of princes or nobles.]

Sign of Rozelo.

Sign of Tietuinus.

Sign of Tuleradus.

Sign of Amelius.

Sign of Urso.

Sign of Remigius.

I, Adelardus, in place of Bernardus, chief of the record office, wrote this at request.

## XLVI. Charter by which Darmundus sells estates in the districts of Vermandois and Noyon to Erlifridus, abbot of Sithiu

[Note: This charter is drawn up in the same words as the charter of Eodebertus, which we published above. It was taken from the same cartulary of Folquinus and deposited in our chartulary by the often-mentioned D. de Witte. Malbrancus had published a fragment of this charter in *De Morinis*, book IV, chapter 48; Cointius reprinted it from him, *Annals*, volume IV, page 492. [Cf. the edition of the cartulary of Sithiu, published by the learned Guérard, page 40.] Neither author was led to suspect the charter’s authenticity because the chronological notes mention the “years of the empire” of Childebert. Certainly, nowhere are the years of Merovingian reigns called “years of the empire”; see Mabillon, *Diplomata*, page 195, and *Diplomata nova*, volume IV, page 539. Nor was this expression used in documents of good quality before the Carolingian reigns. We would indeed regard this as evidence of forgery if it were certain that the autograph had been written in this way. But since the document was extracted from a cartulary, we attribute the error to the copyist’s carelessness, since otherwise there is nothing throughout the charter that smacks of forgery. Moreover, Iperius, in the chronicle of Sithiu, in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, volume III, column 476, mentions the charter itself and gives its chronological notes as follows: “on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the thirteenth year of our lord Hildebert, the glorious king,” with no mention of either reign or empire. There is another discrepancy there, namely the thirteenth year instead of the fourteenth. We would be endless if we undertook to transcribe discrepancies of this sort, with which the ancient books abound. Thus the writers do not agree even about the name of Erlifridus: Mabillon calls him Erlebertus, *Annals*, volume I, page 620, and the authors of *Nova Gallia Christiana*, in the passage cited above, acknowledge both names. But we cannot dwell longer on the examination of these matters.] (ann. 708).

To the lord and venerable man Erlifridus,

[Note: Erlifredus, who in Guérard’s recent learned edition of the cartulary is called Erlefredus, had been placed in charge of the monastery of Sithiu after Rigobertus, as Saint Bertinus [the source’s wording] had been, of whom see page 264, note 3. During Erlifridus’s time Bertinus died—not in 698, as we read in the cartulary, page 41, but, as the learned editor correctly notes, in 709, which was the fifteenth year of Childebert’s reign.]

abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, Darmundus, seller.

It is established that I have sold to you, not by an imaginary right but with fullest willingness, and thus I have sold: namely, two parts of my share of the property in the place called Saroaldsclusa, on the river Sumna, in the district of Vermandois; likewise, at Appiliacum, on the river Isara, two parts situated in the district of Noyon, namely, in Diva and Corbunacum, two complete parts—that is, in lands, houses, buildings, slaves, vineyards, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, livestock, cultivated and uncultivated lands. These aforesaid portions I hand over and request that they be transferred to you from the present day, for perpetual possession.

Accordingly, I received as the price agreed between us, namely, in gold and silver—

[Note: Here, as in the charter of the year 704 above, page 265, the words *inter aurum et argentum* (“between gold and silver”) should be noted. Learned men who composed the prolegomena to this collection, part II, section X, chapter 3, § 1, no. 18, did not find it easy to determine how the phrase should be understood. If I may touch upon the matter they left uncertain, I would conjecture that *inter* here has the same force as *tam quam*, “both … and,” as Cangius seems to have thought, and that the clause means that payment was to be made both in gold and in silver. Let the learned decide.]

—one thousand five hundred solidi, so that from the present day you may have, with Christ’s favor, wholly free and most secure power over these portions in every respect: to have, hold, give, sell, exchange, or do with them whatever you wish.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, any of my heirs, or any opposing or extraneous person, should act against this sale, let him be compelled, under pressure from the treasury acting jointly, to pay you as much, and another amount as much, as we received from you, together with double the money; and let him be unable to establish the claim he makes. Rather, let this sale remain firm at all times, supported by stipulation.

Executed at the monastery of Sithiu, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the fourteenth year of the empire of our lord Hildebertus, the glorious king.

I, Darmundus, the seller, at whose request this sale was made.

Ravangerus, an unworthy bishop, subscribed.

+ Of Fulbertus.

+ Of Madalharius.

+ Of Humbertus, vicar.

Chrodbertus wrote and subscribed this sale.

## XLVII. Charter by which Sigibaudus, bishop of Metz, and Count Wolfaudus exchange estates between themselves

[Note: Published by Baluzius, *Miscellanea*, volume IV, page 409, from the cartulary of Saint Michael on the Meuse; reprinted by Calmetus, *History of Lorraine*, volume I, proofs, page 267. Wasseburgus mentioned this charter in *Antiquities of Belgian Gaul*, folio 115 verso, and assigned it to the fourteenth year of the reign of Childebert III. Cointius thought that Theoderic should be substituted for Childebert, *Annals*, volume IV, page 829. But Wasseburgus is supported by the reading of the cartulary presented by Baluzius, and Mabillon agrees, *Benedictine Annals*, volume I, page 21. Cointius objects in vain that Sigibaudus, bishop of Metz, who exchanges estates with Count Wolfaudus, did not obtain the episcopal office at Metz before the year 716. This does not prove the point; indeed, the authors of *Nova Gallia Christiana*, volume XIII, column 703, warn that Cointius was mistaken here, and show that his conjecture is overturned by this very charter. We shall publish another charter of the same Wolfaudus below, page 280; see it, together with the notes attached to it.] (ann. 708).

In the name of God.

The good of peace was pleasing, in accordance with the agreement between the apostolic man Sigibaudus, bishop of the Church of Metz, and Count Wolfaudus, that they should exchange their little estates with one another; and so they did.

Bishop Sigibaudus gave Count Wolfaudus the little estate called Marsupia, in the district of Verdun, which Godo and Haerevius had assigned to the church of Saint Stephen for the salvation of their souls. It included lands, houses, buildings, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and slaves named Leubigisus, Feroinus, Adoinus, Fante, and Gaerelinde—everything, completely and in full, that Godo and Haerevius had possessed there or that Saint Stephen appeared to have there. He gave it all to Wolfaudus for possession.

Conversely, in like manner, Wolfaudus gave Bishop Sigibaudus, for the portion of Saint Stephen, the little estate called Vineiacum, at the boundary of the estate of Ausiniaca, in the district of Fugentum, on the river Moselle. It included lands, houses, buildings, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, and slaves named Autaldus, Balsimius, Macionus, Eusebius, Haervinus, Bertridus, and Madalhundus; also whatever he had purchased there, for a price paid, from a man named Aegino, or whatever he appeared presently to possess there. He donated everything, completely and in full, to the portion of Saint Stephen. And whatever they should wish to do with these properties, on either side, they had free and entirely secure power to do in every respect.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, the heirs of Wolfaudus or of Adalsinda, or of Lord Sigibaudus, should wish to bring any action against these exchanges, let him lose the portion he received and, in addition, be compelled to pay two pounds of gold and five weights of silver; and let him be entirely unable to reclaim what he seeks. Rather, let this present exchange remain firm and stable, supported by stipulation.

Executed at Novo-exsartum, the estate of Saint Stephen. Given on the twentieth day of December, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our lord Childebert, the king.

## XLVIII. Fragment of a transfer made by Godefridus, duke of Alemannia, to the monastery of Saint Gall

[Note: This fragment, unknown to the learned de Brequigny, survives in the book of transfers of the monastery of Saint Gall, page 2, under the title: “Godefridus, duke of Alemannia, transfers the village of Aiberburg on the Neckar.” Neugart published it from there, *Alemannic Diplomatic Codex*, volume I, page 9. Nothing more survives from several charters of the same Godefridus, twenty of which Goldastus had examined, as he himself attests, *Writings on Alemannic Affairs*, volume I, page 176.] (circa 708).

Godafridus, duke, illustrious man.

Magulfus, priest and pastor of Saint Gall, coming into our presence, proposed and requested our support, that we should grant something for the lamps of the church of Saint Gall, and so forth.

Executed at Canstat on the Neckar.

[Note: The chronological notes do not survive. But since Godefridus died in 709, as Baluzius asserts, *Miscellanea*, volume I, page 496, I have assigned the charter to the year 708.]

## XLIX. Charter by which Wolfoaldus and Adalsinda, his wife, confer many gifts on the monastery of Saint Michael in the district of Verdun

[Note: Wasseburgus published a fragment of this charter, *Antiquities of Belgian Gaul*, folio 114 verso, and Cointius reprinted it on his authority, *Annals*, volume IV, page 495. Baluzius published it in full from the cartulary of Saint Michael, *Miscellanea*, volume IV, page 403; Mabillon from the original, more accurately, *Annals*, volume II, page 691; Calmetus, *History of Lorraine*, proofs, column 85, from Mabillon. We follow Mabillon’s reading.

In the chronicle of the monastery of Saint Michael, written around the eleventh century, this charter is assigned to the times of Childebert, Brunhild, and Sigibert, incorrectly, as Mabillon demonstrates, *Analecta*, pages 351 and 356. Others confused Wolfoaldus, the author of this charter, with Wulfoadus, royal mayor of the palace under Childeric II, as may be seen in Mabillon, *Annals*, volume II, page 21. Nor can this be maintained, since Wolfoaldus, the person concerned here, lived into the time of King Pippin, as Mabillon notes. Cointius had already mentioned this error in the passage cited above, page 496. We published another charter of the same Wolfoaldus or Wolfaudus above (column 1252); see it, together with the note appended to it.

Since the month is not indicated, we cannot determine whether this document should be assigned to the year 709 or to the following year.] (ann. 709).

Since Christians ought to choose the way of truth, by which they may offer to their Creator a fitting gift of mercy, so that the offering may lead to salvation and devotion may obtain its reward, I therefore, Wolfoaldus, son of the late Gislaramnus, and likewise our wife Adalsinda, daughter of the late Adalbertus, donors, although, since there are many kinds of property, a person might wish, by the wording of documents, in whatever ways for his own lost crimes or to redeem the punishment of sins, to transfer from his own possessions places belonging to the holy God, or to His servants and those who have served them well—for the ancient decrees of wealthy princes and the laws have also established that only the hand of the donor should be clearly displayed in the subscription, and that they did not wish such property to be assigned with complete firmness without citation of the acts, so that what each person should give according to the inclination of his mind might be confirmed by a formal document—

yet while we too, as we believe, are inspired by the Lord, in accordance with the custom of all the faithful of the Catholic Church of Christ, whose benevolence demands that, for the salvation of souls and out of regard for God, with the Lord’s help, we should establish with the most devoted mind a monastery and community of servants of God from a new foundation on our own property, in the district of Verdun, in the place called Castillionis, at the boundary of Vindiniaca, where a little stream called Masupia rises at the very foot of the mountain, in honor of the holy archangel Michael and of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, of Saint Martin, and of Saints Peter and Paul the apostles, as well as of the holy martyrs and confessors and the others, we appear also to have built it after the example of the most blessed.

And counsel was added to us that we should record, from our common substance, for that monastery and for the servants of God dwelling there in God’s service, whatever we ought to record according to God’s will. And so we did.

First, therefore, we give our portion called Widinovilla, situated in the district of Verdun, with houses, dwellings, buildings, slaves, estates, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, with every appurtenance and appendage belonging to it.

Likewise, we give our estate on the river Masupia, in that same district of Verdun, which the people call Godonecurtis, with houses, dwellings, buildings, slaves, resident tenants, estates, fields, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, whether of our own property, purchased, or acquired in any other manner that came to us, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, on that same little river Masupia, we give the portion that we purchased from Crudelbertus for a price paid, with estates, meadows, fields, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, on that same little river Masupia, we give the portion called Tavanorum-Vallis, which we purchased from Gennulfus for a price paid, with estates, fields, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, we give those portions in the estate called Byscriblata, in that same district of Verdun, on the river Meuse, which we purchased for a price paid from Valdradana, Godana, and Chrodlinda, with slaves, estates, houses, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, we donate that portion in the place called Monnone-Villa, on the river Meuse, in the district of Verdun, which we purchased for a price paid from Gundoinus—the preceding words “the late Adalbertus” are syntactically uncertain in the transmitted text—with slaves, houses, estates, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, we give those portions in the place called Calvonecurtis, in that same district of Verdun, on the river Meuse, which we purchased for a price paid from Adalfus or his heirs, and from Erlinus or Fulgoinus, with lands, slaves, estates, fields, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, in that same district of Verdun, on the little river called Cruia, we give one portion at Castellio, which we purchased for a price paid from Felicius or his heir, with slaves, houses, estates, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, on that same little river Quala, we donate that portion which we purchased for a price paid from a woman named Brantruda, with slaves, houses, estates, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, on the same river Cruia, we give that portion which we purchased for a price paid from the late Chaldebertus, son of Champertus, with slaves, houses, estates, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, at Baudemetrovilla, we give that portion which we purchased for a price paid from Chaico or from his wife Ganna, with estates, houses, slaves, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

In like manner, we give our estate situated in the district of Verdun, called Buxarias, which we purchased for a price paid from the late abbess Austruda, with houses, estates, slaves, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, in that same district of Verdun, in Teudegisilo-Villa, we give the portion which we purchased for a price paid from Rodebertus and Ratfredus, with estates, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, at Vigo-Marsallus, a *juno*—

[Note: Calmetus, in the passage cited above, column 87, note z, directs that *inno* be read, which is elsewhere called *inna*: that is, a bronze vessel, specifically a bronze pan used in making salt. [Cf. Carpenterius, *New Glossary*, s.v. *Inno*.]]

—for making salt, with an estate, a house, a *sersus*, and every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, we give one estate called Tronio, situated in the district of Verdun, with houses, dwellings, buildings, slaves, fields, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, whether our own, purchased, or acquired in any other manner belonging to us, with its appendages and every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, we give one portion in the estate called Bedernaca, situated in the district of Verdun, which we purchased for a price paid from a woman named Alsinda, with houses, buildings, slaves, estates, fields, woods, meadows, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, in Epponecurtis, we give one portion which we purchased for a price paid from that same woman Adalsinda, with slaves, estates, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

Likewise, we give our portion in the estate called Ulmo, which the people call Coria, situated in the district of Verdun, on the river Meuse, whether our own or purchased, which we purchased for a price paid from Gailanus, Gennulfus, Godelinda, and Felicius, our heirs, with houses, estates, dwellings, buildings, slaves, resident tenants, meadows, fields, vineyards, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with all appendages and appurtenances belonging to it.

Likewise, we give one estate at Cussiliacum, situated in the district of Bar, with houses, slaves, estates, fields, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, with every appurtenance belonging to it.

All the things named or recorded above, together with movable and immovable property of both sexes, livestock of every kind, and every furnishing—whatever can be said or named in the places written above and belonging to them—both examined and unexamined property, we transfer and convey completely, with fullest willingness, from the present day for all time, so that from this day forward they may possess them under the firmest right, without the participation of our co-heirs; and that they themselves may have the power to have, hold, and possess them, so that in the name of God they may enjoy them forever.

And so that this our intention may obtain fuller force and be preserved through the ages, we have confirmed the aforesaid named properties with our own seal, so that everything written above may remain in perpetual prosperity.

We have been pleased to have this written into our intention: that no judge or bishop of the city, or from the district of Verdun itself, should have any authority in that monastery to demand any exactions or requisitions—

[lacuna] have the power to enter—

[Note: Several documents in this collection attest that kings granted bishops, abbots, and churches the right of immunity from all judicial authority. As Bignonius puts it, in note 4 on formula III of book I of Marculfus, this resulted in the appearance that jurisdiction over subjects was granted to them in that capacity, which they exercised through advocates and vice-lords. Kings also granted the same rights to their faithful in diplomas that have perished through the injuries of time. This is evident not only from the Marculfian formulas XIV and XVII of book I, but also from chapter 12 of Childebert’s Edict of 595, above, volume I, page 173, and no less from chapter 19 of Chlothar’s Edict of 615, volume I, page 196.

Wolfoaldus and his wife Adalsinda were probably endowed with such a grant, and they transfer the right belonging to them to the monastery of Saint Michael. The clause in which they establish that no judge should have authority to enter the monastery must, in my view, be interpreted in this way. Private persons did not have the right to establish such immunity on their own authority. A formula of Marculfus, II, book II, presents words almost identical with those of this diploma.]

—because we built the estate there at our own expense and by our own labor.

We have agreed to add this: that if at any time—which we do not believe will happen—any charter, whether earlier or later, should be produced to undermine or diminish this our intention and should bear our name, let such documents appear void and empty and have no effect thereafter.

But if anyone, as commonly happens, from among our heirs or descendants—which we do not believe will happen—or any opposing person or judicial authority, should at any time wish to violate or in any way break or oppose this our donation and decision, which we requested should be made with spontaneous will and fullest devotion, let him first incur the offense of God and appear excommunicated and excluded from every place of the holy coenobites and from the fellowship of Christians. Moreover, let him be judged by a similar sentence as Judas, the traitor of our Lord, and as Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, who deceitfully accepted gifts; and let him be anathema-maranatha, that is, destruction at the Lord’s coming. Even so, let no one be able to overturn my intention.

Furthermore, together with the associated treasury, let him be compelled to pay to our party five hundred pounds of gold and eighty weights of silver, and let him be wholly unable to recover what he claims. Rather, let this charter of our donation remain inviolable at all times, supported by confirmation.

This donation was made in the monastery itself, in the presence of many good men, in the fifteenth year of the reign of our lord Childebert the king.

… Sign of the illustrious Wlfoaldus, who requested that this testament of donation be made.

Sign of Adalsinda, his wife, who, consenting, requested that the testament of donation be made.

I, Wlfuidis, abbot, subscribed.

Gairebaldus, bishop, subscribed.

Pepp[inus], abbot, requested by the aforesaid Wlfoaldus, subscribed.

Sign of Dodinus.

Sign of Sequeno, witness.

Sign of Chrodelbertus, witness.

Sign of Wlfredus, witness.

Sign of Disoenus, witness.

Sign of Ercambertus.

Sign of Desastus, witness.

Sign of Anglibertus, witness.

Sign of Chugo, witness.

Sign of Flodoenus, witness.

Sign of Attolane, witness.

I, Robertus, priest, subscribed.

Ermoaldus, requested.

Sign of Gislaranus, subscribed.

Heteraenus, subscribed.

Sign of Gundoenus.

I, Richramnus, having been requested, wrote this testament of donation.

## L. Charter by which Ingoara, consecrated to God, makes gifts to the monastery of Saint Peter at Sens

[Note: Published by Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume IV, page 557, from the cartulary of Saint Peter of Sens; reprinted by Cointius, *Annals*, volume IV, page 234, from Mabillon. Ingoara was the sister of Leotheria, whose charter concerning gifts made to the same monastery of Saint Peter we published elsewhere. Leotheria’s charter contains much that arouses suspicion of forgery; Ingoara’s charter, however, does not appear liable to the same objections. Its authenticity is supported by the chronicle of Clarius, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume II, page 708, whose words are: “Lady Ingoara, consecrated to God, sister of Ebbo, made a testament concerning her inheritance for blessed Peter, which lies in the district of Tonnerre, while Chrodolinus was abbot.”] (ann. 711).

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Since every gift descending from above can be light from the Father, and since it is necessary for each person to consider eternal salvation and to prepare for himself eternity from the perishable wealth of this age, so that when the final day arrives it may not find each person unprepared but carefully girded with good works—for the Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer of all, cries out in a clear voice through the holy Gospel, saying: “Store up for yourselves treasure in heaven, where thieves neither come nor steal”; “Make for yourselves a purse from the mammon of iniquity, which does not grow old”; and elsewhere: “You give a little and purchase the kingdom; you bestow a small amount of money and receive what will endure without end”—

therefore, since every human being is guided by God’s counsel, it seems right that His command should be fulfilled by them in every respect.

Thus I, Ingoara, illustrious and consecrated to God, considering with a sound mind a wholesome counsel and eternal recompense, whether for the lessening of my sins or for the remedy of my soul, was moved by the apostolic and evangelical exhortation to give something of my own possessions to the monastery of Saint Peter, which is built below the city of Sens, where the venerable abbot Chrodolinus and the monks dwelling there appear to preside, so that I ought to donate it there for the service of those ministering in that place.

And so, by this charter of donation, from the present day I give and decree that it be given forever: namely, my portion in the estate called Fontanas, situated in the district of Tonnerre, whatever came to me both from my father and from my mother, together with the adjacent lands and appendages belonging to Fontanas; also, in the district of Ladscense, at Pauliacum and Bagnolum, and the other little estates that appear to pertain to the estate of Fontanas, including lands, houses, buildings, freedoms, the labor of resident tenants, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, every resource and every kind of household property of either sex that can be said or named, and whatever I may subsequently be able to increase or improve. Let it profit that monastery there in perpetual increase.

But if anyone—whether I myself, any of my heirs, or any opposing person of whatever kind—should attempt by any device to act against or violate this present donation, which I requested should be made and confirmed with my fullest will, let him first incur the anger of the eternal Trinity and remain excommunicated and excluded from the thresholds of the saints, from good Christian men, and from that holy place itself. Moreover, let him be fined and pay to the parties of that monastery, together with the treasury, two pounds of gold and five weights of silver.

Let this present donation remain firm and stable for all time, enduring with stipulation attached.

Executed at Sens. Know that Ingoara made this donation.

In the name of God, Ebbo, sinful bishop, subscribed.

Gaudegengus, archdeacon, subscribed.

Filex, lector.

Leodechinus.

Boso, unworthy sinner and abbot.

Austrapius, lector.

Leotarius, sinful abbot.

Agobaldus.

Ermenaldus.

I, Ermbubertus, at the request of Ingoara, consecrated to God, wrote and recorded this donation.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the first year of the reign of our lord Dagobertus the king.

## LI. Charter by which Ermenoara, consecrated to God, gives to the monastery of Saint Benignus of Dijon whatever she possesses in the village of Ruffiacus

[Note: Perardus published it in *Instruments for the History of Burgundy*, p. 9; Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 561, reprinted it from Perardus. The Chronicle of Saint Benignus, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 393, recalls the gift conveyed by this charter in these words: “In the year 714 Pippin died in December, and likewise Grimoald, his son, died, and Charles succeeded in his father’s place. At that time Astoricus was bishop of Langres, and Bobolenus governed this monastery [Saint Benignus]. Then Ermenoara, consecrated to the Lord, gave to Saint Benignus whatever she possessed in the village of Ruffiacus.” The charter we present, however, is said to have been issued after the death of Lord Theoderic and the election of Charles as mayor of the palace. Hence Perardus, in the place cited above, assigns it to the year 735; Mabillon, in the second volume of his *Annals*, p. 104, more correctly assigns it to the year 737, when Theoderic IV died and Charles, the mayor of the palace, succeeded him, although he did not assume the title of king. Cointius, following the authority of the chronicle of Saint Benignus, assigns the charter to the year 715 and orders Theobald to be substituted for Theoderic in the charter, so as to reconcile it with the chronicle. Yet another difficulty remains in the charter. For there Assoricus appears to be called abbot of Saint Benignus; but at that time Bobolenus governed the monastery, while Astoricus, or Assoricus, presided over the Church of Langres, as the chronicle of Saint Benignus testifies. It may be replied that Assoricus, who is here called an apostolic man, was plainly a bishop; and that, when he is likewise said to have exercised authority in the town of Dijon, this must be understood not of governance of the church of Saint Benignus but of governance of the town of Dijon itself. For the lordship of the Dijon fortress formerly belonged to the bishop of Langres, as the authors of *The New Christian Gaul*, vol. IV, p. 508, testify—a fact that agrees perfectly with the words of the charter.] (year 715).

To the lord of the most holy basilica of Saint Benignus the martyr, built below the town of Dijon, where the apostolic man Assoricus exercises authority:

I, Ermenoara, consecrated to God, for the remedy of my soul, now transfer to the aforesaid basilica, and to the monks and matricularii who are known to live there, or who may be there at any time, whatever I appear to possess in the village of Ruffiacus, which is in the county of the Atuarian people, or within its boundaries, whether from hereditary property, purchase, or acquisition: namely, homesteads, with the buildings erected upon them, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, and whatever can be said or named—in every respect and in its entirety—to the aforesaid basilica of the lord Benignus and to its monks and matricularii. By my present letter I have assigned all this to them by a completely voluntary decision, [Note: Cointius deletes the word *penes* here as corrupt and indicates its absence by a blank space.] so that from the present day they may reclaim it as their rightful possession.

If anyone from the basilica of the lord Benignus, or from among those monks and matricularii, wishing to turn what I have bestowed over to his own uses, should refuse in this matter to obey the bishop of Langres, his attempt shall have no effect. But if they should do this—which God forbid—the property itself shall in every respect lawfully return to my heirs, and to the other persons named Ermonarius and Ermenricus and their children; likewise to those named Bliderannus and Ermenbaldus, who were formerly released by letter to my brother Bobolenus. Otherwise, I wish that, as is right, and with respect to everything that I have freely given to the place of Dijon in the aforesaid village of Ruffiacus, whether on account of opportunity, protection, patronage, or service, according to what their letter states, from the present day the aforesaid ministers of Saint Benignus shall have free power over those properties to do whatever they wish.

But if—which I do not believe will happen—I should myself wish to take anything away, or any opposing person should wish to act against this letter of donation or attempt anything contrary to it, let that person pay to the basilica of the lord Benignus and its agents twice the value to which the properties themselves have been improved, and to the public treasury one pound of gold. Nevertheless, let this present letter of donation remain firm and inviolate for all time, secured by the accompanying stipulation.

Executed publicly at Ruffiacus. The sign of Ermenoara, consecrated to God, who requested that this letter of donation be made. The sign of Farlago, her nephew, who consents. The sign of Arembertus, Trasacofia, Cassinus, Landradus, and Godulfus.

I, Artaldus, acting in the place of the chancellor, wrote and completed this document, at the request of Ermenoara, consecrated to God, on the day before the Kalends of May [Note: We interpret this as the day immediately preceding the Kalends], after the death of Lord Theoderic and the election of Charles as mayor of the palace.

## LII. Charter by which Ado, abbot, confers gifts upon the basilica of Saint Remigius (year 715)

[Note: Mabillon published this from a very mutilated authentic document written in Franco-Gallic letters, in *Annals*, vol. II, appendix, p. 694. He conjectures there, pp. 43 and 52, that Ado, the author of this charter, was abbot of Saint Remigius of Reims; *The New Christian Gaul*, vol. IX, col. 225, supports the conjecture. Frodoard, however, strongly opposes it in his *Ecclesiastical History of Reims*, p. 219, written in the tenth century. For when listing Ado’s benefactions to the basilica of Saint Mary at Reims, he calls him “a certain abbot,” which is scarcely likely if he meant the abbot of the most celebrated monastery of the city of Reims. Moreover, the gifts remembered by Frodoard are entirely different from those contained in the charter we reprint. It is therefore possible to infer that the Ado mentioned by Frodoard was different from the author of this charter. It was issued in the fourth year of Dagobert III’s reign; in the year of Christ 715, the fourth regnal year had ended, having begun in 714. To whom this document should be attributed is not clear.]

[The opening and much of the text are mutilated.]

…I transfer and assign to Saint Remigius… namely, my portion at Altro, on the little river Altro, situated in the county of Vongensis, with its appurtenance… Bairo, and another appurtenance, Crisciacus, on the little river Bebropricus, which other half is in… Mauriliana; and afterward, by their document, I transferred that property to the basilica of Saint Remigius…

…with usufruct for our lifetime, for the use of the aforesaid portion of ours, with manses, houses, lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated land, both the portion which belonged to… and our portion in its entirety, with all its appurtenances.
