After our death, the party… [lacuna] shall receive them into its power from the present day, to have, hold, alter, sell… for the basilica of Saint Remigius and whichever of its agents they shall choose, with free and most secure power to do everything… and all… of the brothers or clerics residing in that holy basilica…

…to beseech the Lord’s mercy, and… after our departure, our name may be… [lacuna] be chanted.

If anyone—which we wish may never happen—whether… or any opposing person, should wish to violate this deed made by me… first, let him incur the wrath… and be excommunicated from every threshold of the saints, and never deserve to obtain forgiveness from the Lord. If he should refuse… and moreover pay to the basilica, together with the associate of the treasury, five pounds of gold and twenty pounds of silver… and should not be able to recover it; and may this donation remain firm and inviolable for all time… [lacuna]

Executed at Reims, in the month of April, in the fourth year of the reign of our lord Dagobert, king. Ado, abbot: “this donation…” Rodfridus: “ter…” Allinus, abbot, subscribed. I, Abblicus, subscribed… Chaireber… Adolulfus [prot.], subscribed. The sign + of Gundoinus. The sign + of Vandrebertus. The sign + of Winon. The sign + of Silvester, count. The sign + of Bertelmus. The sign + of Marcius.

[Note: Mabillon notes that in the authentic document autograph signs were attached to the names of most of the subscribers; because these are lacking, cross-signs are inserted here.]

## LIII. Charter by which Hugo the priest, son of Drogo, confers gifts upon the basilica of the Holy Apostles at Metz

[Note: Mabillon published this in *Annals*, vol. II, appendix, p. 695, from a very old copy. It is also found in Meurissius, *Lives of the Bishops of Metz*, p. 112; Bouchet, *Proofs of the Origin of the Frankish House*, p. 71; Cointius, *Annals*, vol. IV, pp. 457 onward; and the authors of *The New Christian Gaul*, vol. XIII, instruments, col. 470. Valladier printed the same document in the vernacular in *The Basilica of Saint Arnulf*, p. 494. Some copied it from what they call the original, others from the cartulary of Saint Arnulf. We reprint it from two copies, one carefully collated with the archetype and the other with the cartulary, and brought into our archives by the often-mentioned Lord Tabouillot. The readings of the archetype are given in our text; the cartulary’s divergences are supplied in brackets. The following words precede this charter in the cartulary: “I, Hugo, first cleric of Metz, a humble priest, and my brother, the illustrious man Arnulf, duke, together with Pippin and Godefrid, displayed this in the following manner and according to the tenor of this letter.” This document causes learned men no small difficulty, as Mabillon notes in *Annals*, vol. II, pp. 43 onward, although he regarded it as genuine, chiefly because of the antiquity of the parchment. Cointius, however, in the place cited above, p. 458, considers it no more authoritative than the other charters of Hugo’s father and brothers, which he declares false. See what we noted at columns 1221 and 1249 concerning these same charters, which we present in their proper places. “Take care,” says Cointius, “lest, influenced by their reading, you follow the opinion of modern writers who attribute four sons to Drogo.” [Note: I acknowledge that this charter does not establish the number of Drogo’s sons, but it does prove that Drogo had several sons.] Among other indications of falsity, one may cite the Chronicle of Fontenelle, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 207, written in the ninth century by a monk of the monastery of Fontenelle, over which Hugo had presided. It says that Hugo was still a layman in the first year of Chlothar’s fourth reign, that is, in the year of Christ 718 [Note: These words are corrected in the Prolegomena of the earlier editors, section XI, chapter 2, §2, no. 3. The place in the chronicle where Hugo is called a priest belongs to the year 713, not 718], whereas in the charter under examination, issued in the fifth year of Dagobert III, that is, in the year of Christ 715, he is called a priest. Add that the most learned modern historians of Metz deny that Hugo was ever first cleric of the Church of Metz, although that title appears at the beginning of this charter in the cartulary of Saint Arnulf. We therefore judge that these circumstances deprive the document of all credibility.] (year 715).

In the name of Christ. On the seventh day according to the cartulary, the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth year of the reign of our lord Dagobert, king.

Whenever, as human frailty commonly requires, certain persons depart from this age, it is proper that their heirs should assign some portion of their property, for the remedy of their souls, to the holy places, so that for this act their reward may increase in eternal blessedness. Therefore we, in God’s name, Hugo the priest [Cartulary: “Hugo, a humble priest”], and my brother, the illustrious man Arnulf, duke, together with Pippin and Godefrid, when it happened that our father, the illustrious man Drogo, formerly departed from this life, petitioned the venerable man Leutbertus, abbot of the basilica of the Holy Apostles, built outside the walls of the city of Metz, where our grandfather, Lord Arnulf, rests bodily, that we might bury our aforesaid father Drogo there. Leutbertus appeared to grant this with a kindly disposition [Cartulary: “was seen to have granted it”].

Therefore, both for the place of burial itself and for the remedy of the soul of our aforesaid father, we appear by this charter of donation to have granted, from the present day, to the clerics of the basilica of the Holy Apostles, or to the poor receiving sustenance there, or to the readers serving there, a village called Vidiacus [Cartulary: Judiacus], situated in the county of Metz, which his father, our grandfather Pippin, had granted to him as a gift.

This includes both our house within the walls, in the place called Roman Hall [the cartulary lacks the words from “our house” through “called”], and outside the walls of the city of Metz: lands, houses, basilicas, buildings, tenants, slaves, freedmen, vineyards, thirteen small farms in the village with their tithes, and seven little farms [the cartulary lacks the words from “thirteen” through “little farms”], woods, meadows [Cartulary: fields and meadows], pastures, mills, appurtenances, cultivated and uncultivated land, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, with the whole of its integrity and with whatever adjoins or belongs to it, and every kind of four-footed animal—whatever Pippin and our aforesaid father were seen to hold or possess in that village, within and outside the city [the cartulary lacks “within and outside the city.”]

Let the abbot himself or his successors hold, retain, and possess all this on behalf of the aforesaid basilica; and whatever they decide to do with it for the benefit of that basilica, let them enjoy free authority in every respect.

And if—which we do not believe will happen—we ourselves, or any of our heirs or successors, or any opposing person, should presume to act against this deed of assignment or testament, or attempt to remove any claim arising from it, let that person first incur the anger of almighty God and become an outsider to the thresholds of the saints; and let him wither at the root so that he may never blossom in the branches. Moreover, let him pay within the basilica itself and to the most sacred treasury five pounds of gold and ten pounds of silver; and let him be unable to recover what he claims. But let this assignment or testament, secured by stipulation, possess complete firmness for all time.

Executed publicly at Metz, on the day and at the time stated above. The sign of Hugo, although a sinful priest, by which I confirmed this assignment or testament made by me. The sign of Arnulf, duke, consenting to this testament. The sign of Milo. The sign of Wido, count. The sign of Rembertus, count. The sign of Lambertus, count. The sign of Warnarius, count. [The subscriptions are lacking in the cartulary.]

## LIV. Charter by which Ibbo, bishop of Tours, grants extensive privileges to the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours

[Note: Mabillon published this charter three times: first among the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. V, p. 745, from an old manuscript; second in book VI of *On Diplomatics*, p. 487, from the *pancharta*, as it is called, preserved in the archives of Saint Martin of Tours; and third in the *Annals*, vol. II, appendix, p. 693, from an authentic document written in Franco-Gallic letters, which Martene, as he states there, p. 30, had inspected with his own eyes and of which he sent Mabillon an exact copy. That same authentic document was produced in a lawsuit that arose at the beginning of this century between the archbishop of Tours and the church of Saint Martin of Tours, and was printed in the chapter’s legal memorials in 1708; see *Defense and Proof of the Privileges of the Church of Saint Martin of Tours*, p. 2. We reprint the charter according to this last edition. It was attacked especially by Launoy, who had argued for the archbishop in this case. The defenders of the church of Saint Martin refuted the charge of forgery, in the second appendix to the work cited above, pp. 69 onward. There is no time to examine all these matters individually. This charter contains no chronological indications. In assigning a date, we have considered the periods of Ibbo, bishop of Tours, and Guntramnus, abbot of Saint Martin of Tours. So too did the defender of the rights of the church of Saint Martin, in his *Compendium of the Defense*, p. 2, who assigns the charter to the year 720 and says that Ibbo assumed the episcopate of Tours in 719. The charter’s genuineness is principally supported by the fact that it was reduced to the form of a privilege more than nine hundred years ago, as Mabillon acutely notes in *Annals*, vol. II, p. 30; and that the privilege was not fabricated from the formula, but the formula derived from the privilege, is shown by the words of the formula itself, in the second appendix, p. 69, against Launoy, defender of the church of Saint Martin. [From the judgment of 13 April 1709 it may be inferred that the charter was regarded as genuine, since the privileges it expressly granted were confirmed.] (circa 720).

The invisible God, creator of all things, instructed the human race through the tongues of the prophets. Through the prophet Isaiah he gives us the distinguished command that, if we seek God and wish to know his ways, we should not demand back what our debtors owe us; that we should loosen every oppressive bundle, break apart every burden that weighed heavily upon us, and observe the other things that follow. Then, once the weight of all our crimes has been cast off, the bonds of our offenses undone, and the darkness of sins driven away, he promised that our light would burst forth like the dawn, so that we might behold the Creator with spiritual eyes as he is; that our healing would quickly arise; that righteousness would go before our face; and that the imperishable glory of the Lord would gather us to itself.

Then we shall call, and the Lord will answer; we shall cry out, and he will say with a heavenly voice: “Behold, I am here.” To this depth of the Old Testament there resounds an invocation and confirmation, in the voice of our cataracts, through the voice of the Redeemer himself: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven”; and again: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them”; and: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”

This command is therefore entirely sufficient for us, in which Scripture has affirmed that the whole law, both old and new, and all the prophets, depend and are fulfilled. And concerning the contemplative life, that better portion which the Lord praised Mary for choosing, we believe his own testimony is sufficient. Although the active life also receives its reward from the giver of good works, he nevertheless preferred Mary, who contemplated him, to Martha, who was occupied with many things.

Exercised in spirit by such great and weighty testimonies, I, Ibbo, in God’s name—although a sinner, I am called by God’s grace bishop of the city of Tours—resolved to grant a privilege and bestow liberty upon the congregation of the monastery of the basilica of the most blessed confessor Martin, renowned throughout Gaul after the Apostles, where he rests bodily. The venerable man Guntramnus appears to preside over it. This privilege had long ago been granted to that holy basilica and to the congregation residing there, with most Christian devotion, by our predecessor Chrotpercthus, formerly bishop of the city of Tours; and by the authority of the apostolic see, the pope of the city of Rome, with Chrotpercthus’s consent, this privilege was confirmed according to the model of the apostolic declaration itself.

Nor do I think it undeserved that this privilege should come upon men who live in such a manner, piously and catholicly, and who, serving our patron continually day and night, strive to please Christ in his great compassion, restraining and subjecting their bodies to servitude through every form of honesty and moderation of conduct. They give liberty to the monks, whose honor the treasury has entirely assigned to the city together with the census, and whose name it established as that of an heir, allowing them to live freely. Since our entire city has earned from kings an exemption radiant with miracles, by the gracious favor of the most merciful former king Dagobert, I judge it a worthy gift to present, with trembling arms, to him who lives under that patronage, the complete exemption obtained from the same king.

Therefore, while the aforesaid brothers and abbot preserve the rights of their fathers, we relinquish to them, and declare relinquished, the church dues, services, labor, lodgings, provisions, gifts, fines, and payments owed to the treasury, the bishop, judges, royal agents, and the archdeacon; and we cut off and remove all secular customs. Whatever they were accustomed to serve or give to us or to those same authorities, and whatever they possess or may hereafter receive from Christian people by the Lord’s generosity, let them always claim for themselves, hold, and defend in perpetual right during our time and that of our successors; let it benefit them with everlasting firmness.

Let them give nothing else either to us or to any successor of ours, except, according to the petition of the brothers or the statutes of the holy fathers, the honors associated with the laying on of hands, the blessings of the succeeding ranks, and those pertaining to the altar, chrism, and holy oil; and let them receive these very things without any payment, according to the holy Scriptures.

If the abbot should depart from this life, let his successor be established by the election of the aforesaid monastery’s congregation, whose life is believed to be perfect, as the Rule of Saint Benedict teaches, with their consent. The authority of Pope Adeodatus of the city of Rome likewise states, through the text of his privilege, that the religious abbot or the monks living there should suffer no burdens from any bishop under the pretext of investigation; nor should bishops, claiming the right to lodge with them, impose expenses or insolent obligations of forced service upon them; nor should they inflict any injuries under the pretext of examining and enforcing regular discipline.

We shall likewise decree that the religious abbot who for the time being presides over the aforesaid venerable monastery, under the care of that venerable place, shall have free permission in all matters, while the observance of the monastic rules is preserved. Thus he shall strive to preserve what the article of ancient tradition contains, remind each person governed by his administration to guard it diligently, and strictly compel them to do so.

The most reverend bishop in whose diocese the aforesaid venerable monastery, or its property and possessions, may be situated shall have authority only to ordain and promote priests and deacons, and to prepare chrism, insofar as such permission has been granted. But the administration of the venerable place and the supervision of monastic life we assign to its religious abbot and prior, or to whichever persons are most approved in that monastery. The aforesaid bishops also established this by a concordant judgment.

Whoever, therefore, at any time—which we in no way believe will happen—should attempt to violate, wholly or in part, this decree of privilege, which we have confirmed by consenting to it and supporting it with apostolic authority, and should not correct the audacity of his presumption by suitable amendment, let him know that he is to be struck down forever, not only by the judgment of so many priests but also by the most just sting of apostolic condemnation, because he has stubbornly attempted to violate what he ought to have preserved for salvation.

Thus may the sanction of this privilege also remain firm and ratified, without diminution, and endure. We have learned from written records that the most excellent kings of all Gaul likewise deigned, by royal piety, to protect this venerable monastery by edict against the attacks of laymen. Therefore, inspired by the Lord, we too wish henceforth fully to confirm the venerable Guntramnus, its abbot, and his congregation, as well as the aforesaid monastery of Saint Martin the confessor, so that, once the privileges themselves have been inspected—those of our predecessors Crotperthus [Note: Cointius argues that Crotperthus must be distinguished from Bertho and wrongly conjectures that the name Bertho was inserted into Ibbo’s charter, since no other bishop of Tours is known by the name Bertho. But the authentic charter, carefully inspected by Mabillon, distinctly gives both names, which overturns Cointius’s conjecture], Bertho, and Adeodatus, pope of the city of Rome, together with the confirmations of glorious kings—we may ensure that they are preserved in every respect inviolate in our time and that of our successors, and that they be corrupted in no part, just as we have decreed.

We ask and adjure our successors, following the example of Saint Paul, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all may feel as we do and preserve the Lord’s command with us, as it is said: “You received without payment; give without payment.” And likewise the prophetic testimony: “Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift”—that is, so that neither by an improper service, nor by praising with the tongue, nor by a hand full of gifts, they may corrupt the gift of the Holy Spirit. Rather, let them contemplate those immortal gifts stored up in heaven, concerning which it is said: “Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him and keep his law.”

The abbot who is to be elected should not be preferred because of birth, wealth, or noble status; rather, let them prefer one whom holiness, conduct, seriousness, and piety adorn.

In none of the ways we have mentioned should you, our aforesaid successors, depart from us, under the adjuration we have made—unless Martin excludes you from his fellowship, unless Christ excludes you from his kingdom.

You also, my venerable bishops of Gaul, metropolitans of Belgica and Aquitania, and all brothers and fellow bishops, I humbly beg that you grant your assent to this little document for the sake of your fellow bishop and our patron Saint Martin. By subscribing within it with your own hands, give it perpetual strength, so that through prayer this privilege may reach you as an eternal reward, and may reach us also.

In the name of Christ, I, Ibbo, although a sinful bishop, have subscribed this privilege with complete willingness and devotion to the monastery of Saint Martin, where the monks are seen to preserve the Rule of Saint Benedict. I, Dido, a sinner, consenting, have subscribed. I, Bertacharus, abbot, consenting, have subscribed. I, Dodo, although an unworthy deacon, consenting, have subscribed. I, Mummolenus, abbot, consenting, have subscribed. I, Berthcramnus, consenting, have subscribed.

[Note: Mabillon understands Dido to have been a bishop of Tours who succeeded Guntramnus. “Nor should you wonder,” he says, “that two bishops of Tours subscribed the same document. For it was then customary for successors to subscribe the privileges of earlier bishops in the blank space deliberately left for that purpose in the authentic document.” We have observed the same practice elsewhere.]

## LV. Transfer of property at Oppenwiller and Eberingen by Erfoinus for the benefit of the church of Saint Gall

[Note: It is found in the *Traditions of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, p. 2. Goldastus published it in *Writers on Alemannic Affairs*, vol. III, part II, no. 41. Neugart, in the *Alemannic Diplomatic Code*, vol. I, p. 9, printed only fragments.] (year 720).

In the name of Christ. I, Erfoinus, and my sons Teotarius and Rotarius, have considered God’s regard, divine recompense, and the means of earning forgiveness for our sins. Therefore, on my own hereditary land in the place called Oppenwilare [Note: Neugart conjectures that the first letter was omitted and that the reading should be Popenwillare, today Pfaffenweiler, a village in Breisgau above Freiburg], we transfer to Saint Gall twenty *juchi*; and at Eberingen, one *juchus* of vineyard [Note: Neugart notes that this is the first mention of vineyards in the charters of Saint Gall. For it is established that at this time the neighboring Rheingau and the adjoining Thurgau, which lay near Saint Gall, had no vineyards].

Of my tenants, we transfer Erfoinus with his wife and all his appurtenance, with a house, land, and all that belongs to him; and another slave named Waldolfus, with a house, land, and everything belonging to him. So long as I and my sons are still alive, let them remain under our authority, and each year let us pay a wagonload of wine, a wagonload of rye, a wagonload of hay, and a *friskinga* [Note: Neugart criticizes Du Cange for understanding this word to mean a certain kind of vehicle. Correctly so; but in a special case, the capitulary of Louis the Pious from the year 821, Du Cange expressly writes that *friskinga* means a young sow or another kind of pig, as Neugart also maintains. See Scherz’s *German Glossary*, edited by Oberlin, under *Frischling*].

And if children should be born to my sons, let them pay the census and have the authority in the manner stated above. If they do not wish to pay the census from it, let everything we have mentioned above be transferred to the church of Saint Gall. And if anyone—which we do not believe—of our heirs should wish to act against or violate this deed of ours, let him first incur God’s judgment and pay two pounds of gold. Let this deed of ours remain unharmed, secured by stipulation.

This charter was made in the place called Anninchova, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, under the reign of our lord King Elperic [Note: Certainly Chilperic II, called Daniel before he ascended the throne. The charter does not state the year of his reign, so it must be placed between 715 and 720. Chilperic II was called to the kingship by the Franks in 715, preferring him to Theoderic IV, the son of Dagobert III, and died in 720].

The sign of Teotarius and Rotarius, who requested that this charter be made. The sign of Siguinus, witness. The sign of Regandozus, witness. The sign of Vulpertus, witness.

## LVI. Testament of Wideradus, abbot, by which he bequeaths many things to the basilicas of Saint Andochius, Saint Regina, and Saint Ferreolus, and appoints the church of Saint Praejectus of Flavigny heir to all his remaining possessions

[Note: We have two testaments of Wideradus. Mabillon published this earlier one among the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. III, p. 632, accurately transcribed from two manuscript codices, one of which had been written eight hundred years earlier. Cointius reprinted it in *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 680, and D. Plancher, historiographer of Burgundy, reprinted it from the cartulary in vol. I of his *History of Burgundy*, proofs, p. 1. It is said to have been drawn up in the first year of King Theoderic, which Hugo, in the eleventh-century chronicle of Verdun, understood as Theoderic II, grandson of Sigebert and Brunhild, in Labbé’s *Manuscript Library*, vol. I, p. 113. We are certainly surprised that he should have made this mistake, since Wideradus himself presided over the monastery of Flavigny for whose benefit he composed his testament. But since Wideradus was still alive in the year of Christ 744, as is clear from his second testament, which we shall present in its proper place, the chronological notes of the first testament concerning King Theoderic must be understood of Theoderic IV. Mabillon demonstrated this more fully in the place cited above and in *Annals*, vol. II, p. 64, and Cointius supports him in *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 680. The historiographer of Burgundy likewise holds this view in vol. I, p. 107, in the narrative of his history; nevertheless, in the same document, reproduced among the proofs of his history on p. 1, he assigns the year 606, which must certainly be attributed to a copyist’s carelessness. Mabillon investigates in *Annals*, vol. II, p. 65, whether Wideradus was abbot of Flavigny. He proves that this cannot be said unless Magoaldus is also said to have presided over the monastery at the same time. He considers it highly probable that both were in fact abbots of Flavigny, but that Wideradus, whom the author of the Chronicle of Verdun, cited above, attests to have been ordained abbot, was only an honorary abbot who had founded several monasteries and taken them under his care. Cointius, in the place cited above, and the authors of *The New Christian Gaul*, vol. IV, col. 55, adopt this view. Since the beginning of Theoderic IV’s reign is reckoned from December of the year of Christ 720, the February of his first year agrees with the year of Christ 721. Others use a different method for calculating Theoderic’s regnal years. We follow the author of the excellent work *An Investigation of the Authenticity of Chronological Notes in Ancient Documents*, vol. I, p. 549. [For interpreting this testament and correcting certain words of its text, the Lindenbrogian formula LXXII, or Baluzian XXVIII, is of great assistance; it appears to have been drawn from this document almost word for word.]] (year 721).

In the first year of King Theoderic’s reign, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, I, Wideradus, abbot, son of the late illustrious man Corbo, being of sound mind and possessing unimpaired judgment, fearing the hazards of human frailty, drew up my testament and entrusted it to the notary Aldofred for writing. Thus, when the lawful day after my death shall have arrived, after the seals have been examined and the wood cut through [Note: I would rather read here, as in the aforesaid formula, “the linen cut through.” For after the testator’s death the testament was opened after the seals had been examined and the linen with which the bound testament was fastened shut had been cut; the words “the wood cut through” make no sense.], as the authority of the law has decreed, through the illustrious man Amalsindus, whom I have appointed legatee in this testament, it is to be registered in the municipal records, so that it may be secured by their official enforcement, and I decreed that it be preserved in the chartary [Note: It should certainly be read “in the chartary,” or, as the formula teaches, “in the archia” or “in the archiae.”] of the basilica of Saint Praejectus, which I built.

As for the remainder, whatever letters, testaments, or written instruments [Note: “Written instruments” should preferably be plural, as in the formula.] of any kind [Note: An error appears to have entered the text; as in the formula, *aut quaecumque* (“or whatever [instruments]”) should be read.], from anyone, bearing my name or authenticated by my hand, shall be produced and recorded before this testament—those which I shall not mention here—shall remain void, except for the manumissions which we have made, or may yet wish to make, for the remedy of our souls.

And whatever I have given or ordered to be given to each person through this testament, so that it may be done, given, delivered, and fulfilled, I appoint you, Almighty God, as witness.

Therefore, since it is not unknown how, by God’s dispensation, I undertook the care of the holy places, namely Saint Andochius of Saulieu, Saint Regina of Alise, and Saint Ferreolus, where their precious bodies rest, and since moreover at the place called Flavigny, in the territory of Beaune, in the county of Alise, I built with my own labor and property a monastery and regularly entrusted it in perpetuity to Abbot Magoaldus and his monks for possession, I therefore give to the aforesaid basilica of Saint Andochius the portions and properties belonging to me that are named here.

These are: in the county of Alise and in the county of Pauliacum, Meseriacum, Cecesiacum, and Vallis; in the county of Avallon, Passariniacum; in the county of the Commiavi, Stolingus and Macereas; in the county of Portus, Criffonville and Vagomundi-curtis; in the county of Nevers, Senseriacum and Ariacum, except for those vineyards along the course of the stream which runs from Aldebert’s vineyards to the meadow: the entire enclosure which we ordered to be planted, in its entirety, with its access [Note: Cangius, under the word *exsus*, conjectures that *exio* should be read. In the Lindenbrogian formula: “with access and return”; in the Baluzian formula: “with access and return.” A charter of Eligius from the year 631 has “with comings and goings.”] and return, together with the farmstead and tenant holding which belonged to Ansebert and is now held by Sicbert, and Sicbert himself, with his wife and their children, who are to care for the vineyard that we gave to Saint Praejectus.

As for the remainder, just as everything has been held, possessed, dominated, and owned by me, whether as my parents’ allodial property or through any acquisition whatsoever: everything, in its entirety, with houses, buildings, lands, fields, cultivated and uncultivated ground, slaves, resident dependants, freedmen, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, every kind of livestock, large and small, movable and immovable property, every unenumerated possession—whatever I appear to possess in the places named above—let it all, in its entirety, accrue to the basilica of Saint Andochius as an increase to its property.

Likewise, we give to the basilica of Saint Regina, where her precious body rests: in the county of Ternodrum, Vibelum, Cicunias, Anciacum, and Rabarias; in the county of Leotincum, the estate of Mauriana, Altam-ripam, and Baniolum; in the county of Duismum, Stafiacum, Colubarium, and Vilnovetum; in the county of the Ammavi, Cariniacum and Casellae; in the county of Portus, Aviciacum and Puscio; in the county of the Atthoarii, Pussessio.

All these properties specified above, just as we gave the other properties to Saint Andochius, we have likewise entrusted these to Saint Regina’s authority, with all their appurtenances in their entirety.

Likewise, we give to the basilica of Saint Ferreolus, where that holy lord rests in body and which we hold in governance: in the county of Pauliacum, Aciacum with all its appurtenances in its entirety. Just as we gave the other properties to Saint Andochius and Saint Regina, so we have given this to the basilica of Saint Ferreolus.

The arrangement is that, for as long as we live, we shall peacefully cause the aforesaid abbeys of Saint Andochius, Saint Ferreolus, and Saint Regina, together with all the property owed or belonging to them, and also the properties of ours that we have entrusted to them, to hold and possess everything in its entirety. After our departure, however, let the aforesaid churches, each estate through its own administrators and without anyone’s opposition, recover the aforesaid churches and properties into their own dominion, on condition that they diligently preserve in every respect our little monastery of Flavigny and the instruments that we have made for that place in honor of Saint Praejectus.

If they should presume to violate those instruments, disturb that little monastery, or diminish its property, and should be unable to vindicate their action, let them lose the property of ours that we have entrusted to the aforesaid basilicas of Saint Andochius, Saint Ferreolus, and Saint Regina; and, under royal protection, let the house of Saint Praejectus of Flavigny receive those properties perpetually for possession, in their entirety.

But if, while we are alive, any bishop or anyone else should wish to dispossess us of those abbeys or their property, or should presume to diminish anything, or if I should abandon those abbeys while still living, let us have the right to recall into our dominion the property that we entrusted there, and let us have complete freedom in every respect to do whatever we wish with it.

Moreover, we give, and wish it to belong in perpetuity, to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Praejectus of Flavigny, which we built through our own labor in the territory of Beaune, in the county of Alise: Bornadum itself, together with the fortress of Flavigny itself and all its appurtenances and dependencies, in its entirety; and small holdings or tenant farms at Cadonatum, Darciacum, Ceresium, Aguniacum, Gessiacum, Luveriacum, Luviniacum, Pruviniacum, Auderatum, and Monticelli; and, in the county of Ternodrum, Blavacum and Marcomania; in the counties of Avallon and Nevers, the estate called Corbiniacum, and Antonum with all their appurtenances and dependencies in their entirety; and tenant holdings at Lisconium, Dumsatium, Viriacum, Valentingos, Vallecrovaria, Juliacum, Pagatiacum, Cassaniola, Wldonacum, Careacum, Cappas, Degantiacum, Casseacum, Rioscella, Palatiola, Govilices, Sipiciacum, and Sapiliacum; and also the tenant holding at Ariacum which belonged to Ansebert, together with the man who currently resides there, named Sigbert, and his wife [Col. 1271C] Leda, our dependent, and their children, in its entirety, whatever appears to belong to that holding, together with everything situated upon it; and the enclosure at Ariacum, where the stream descends from Aldebert’s vineyard to the meadow: the entire enclosure that we ordered to be planted, with its access and return, in its entirety; and, in the county of Bar, Falciolum and Ulmodum; in the county of Pauliacum, Balma and Corniciacum; in the county of the Atthoarii, Hicio, Blandoniacum, and a tenant holding; in the county of the Amavi, Fraxinum, and plots in the saltworks at Crosone and Vigris.

Likewise, plots within the city of Augustodunum: all these properties that we have named above, with all their appurtenances and dependencies, as much as we appear to hold and possess there, whether they have come to us through any acquisition or ought to come to us by law, in their entirety and with everything situated upon them, from this day forward we have delivered, in honor of Jesus Christ our Lord and Saint Praejectus the martyr, to Abbot Magoaldus and his monks for possession.

This includes houses, buildings, slaves, resident dependants, and freedmen, both those born there and those transferred from elsewhere or residing there; vineyards, woods, fields, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, every kind of livestock, large and small, movable and immovable property, every enumerated and unenumerated possession, and whatever can be said or named. Let all of it, in its entirety, accrue as an increase to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Praejectus of Flavigny or to its administrators.

Likewise, the transfers that we made to our freedmen Ghisbertus and Gimbertus, clerics, to confirm their manumissions—Daoloneca at Bornadum and at Ceresium—when we released them as free persons for the remedy of our souls, are to be held by them while they live; after their departure, let them cause these properties, with everything situated upon them, to return to the aforesaid house of Saint Praejectus, where we established their patronage and protection.

We also wish that those whom we have made free, or may hereafter make free, however many remain in the very places that we have entrusted to Saint Andochius, Saint Regina, Saint Ferreolus, or Saint Praejectus, after their freedoms have been examined, should remain as free persons upon those lands [Note: “Those whom” seems to be the proper reading, as in the formula.], and should have no power to reside elsewhere, but must belong to those holy places [Note: The formula has *spectare*; but sometimes, as Cangius testifies, *sperare* has the same meaning as *pertinere*, “to belong.”]. Let none of them pay our heirs the *lidimonium*; and concerning what we have given them by charter, let them have no right to sell or alienate it elsewhere.

Besides all these properties, we have reserved in falcidia [Note: This is how it appears in Mabillon; D. Plancher instead has *infancidia*. [Col. 1272D] But it should be read “in falcidia,” as in the formula, or “in faucidia,” a corrupt form used to designate the share reserved for the heirs. A charter of the year 680 has *in faldidio*.] for our heirs: Pagatiacum; in the county of Nevers, the estate called Mount of Porcio. Likewise, in the county of the Atthoarii, Vedis-vineyards, Voguntiae, Luco, and Sagonecum; in the county of Portus, Solvillare, Monricovilla, Ebrouvillare, and Saegalaria, on condition that they diligently preserve and defend all my arrangements.

If they neglect to do this, let them lose whatever we have assigned to them, and let them be excluded from the whole body of my property. If I acquire or obtain anything, or if anything comes to us on behalf of any freedman, or shall hereafter come to us, which we have not mentioned above in this testament, after our departure the house of Saint Praejectus shall receive it perpetually for possession through its administrators.

Therefore, through this testament I appoint as my heir the basilica of Saint Praejectus, which I built at Flavigny through my own labor, and I entrust this present codicil to it. Through it I establish that no bishop of any city, no archdeacon, no member of the clergy, and no ecclesiastical administrator shall in any way presume to exercise authority over the aforesaid monastery of Saint Praejectus—not by demanding lodging dues or provisions, nor by requisitioning services, nor by sending an abbot—except when it is necessary to request chrism, consecrate tablets or altars, or confer holy orders.

As with the monks of Laon, Lérins, or Agaune, they may freely request these services from whichever of the holy bishops they choose to perform them, and that bishop may bless them. If, however, prompted by charity, any bishop is invited there by the abbot or monks, let him simply accept what the brothers offer him, and let him demand no additional hospitality-gifts or presents.

If he does so, let the glorious lord whom God shall then permit to govern the kingdom of Burgundy immediately correct the matter.

When the abbot of that place has died, whichever of the monks residing there the community chooses, according to God’s will—or, if by common agreement they wish to choose someone from elsewhere—let the matter remain in their power.

But, God forbid that the holy order there should grow lukewarm: let the monks residing there have the power to send for someone from one of the holy monasteries and, with their salutary counsel, reform their rule.

Therefore, you, my lady and holy mother, the church of Saint Praejectus, I appoint as my heir; whatever I have assigned to each person I entrust to your fidelity. You also, my heir, I commend to God and the king’s authority, so that, after God, his strength may defend you against every disturbance.

For I would rather have you possess what I have assigned to you than possess it myself; I prefer you to have it rather than any of my other heirs or heirs apparent.

I therefore entreat the glorious king, both the one reigning at the present time and whoever shall succeed him in the future, and I dare to adjure him by God’s dreadful judgment, to order this present codicil and my aforesaid little monastery to be defended by his strength and kept secure in every respect, so that it may in no way be violated by the attacks of wicked men.

Let it rather please the monks living there, and the priests residing in the holy places mentioned by this present codicil, to pray earnestly to the Lord for me and for the life of the king and his sons.

If anyone—and I do not believe this will happen—whether one of my heirs or heirs apparent, or any opposing person, should attempt to violate this present testament of mine or presume to challenge it, until he is corrected and brought to true satisfaction for the offense, let him first have God and his saints against him and be expelled from the thresholds of the churches as an outsider; moreover, let him be compelled to pay to the person whom he has wronged, together with the royal treasury, thirty pounds of gold and five hundred weights of silver. Nevertheless, let this present document remain firm, supported by stipulation.

I have confirmed it below with my own hand and decreed that it be strengthened by the signs and bonds of good men.

And whatever we ought to have mentioned above—whether gold, silver, other manufactured objects, ecclesiastical vessels or equipment, written instruments, books, ecclesiastical garments, or every possession that, while alive, I appear by law to possess and that is owed to me—after our departure, upon examination of the instrument that we previously made for Saint Praejectus or for Abbot Magoaldus and his monks, let it return to the monastery of Saint Praejectus of Flavigny.

Let Abbot Magoaldus himself, with his monks, receive these things for the salvation of our souls, and let them perpetually accrue to their increase; or, whatever they wish to do with them, let them have complete freedom in every respect.

—Wideradus, abbot. Gerefredus, defender. Amalsindus. Haldofredus.—

Executed at the fortress of Sinemurum, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, and written by the hand of Haldofredus the notary, at the urging and request of the same venerable abbot Wideradus—indeed, with the royal seal affixed by the illustrious man Amalsindus. In the first year of the reign of our lord King Theoderic, with the attendance and confirmation of the noble common people, together with the defender Gerefredus, a most distinguished man.

## LVII. Charter by which Bertrada bestows many gifts upon the monastery of Prüm, founded by her

[Note: Martenius published this from the chartary of Prüm, *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 23; Calmet reprinted it, *History of Lorraine*, vol. II, documents, col. 91; Bertholet, *History of Luxembourg*, documents, vol. II, p. 29; Hontheim, *History of Trier*, diplomatic volume I, p. 112; and the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. XIII, instruments, col. 295.

This is the first foundation of the monastery of Prüm. It stood in the meadow where there still exists, says Martenius, a church called Saint Benedict’s chapel, the burial place of deceased monks. Later King Pippin built another and more splendid basilica nearby, at the urging of his wife Bertha.

Take care not to confuse this Bertha with the earlier Berta, who issued the charter presented here and who is called here by three names: Berta, Bertrada, and Bertradana. This woman had a son named Charibert, whereas Pippin’s wife had Heribert as her father; Hontheim considers Heribert to be the same person as Charibert, in his notes on Bertrada’s charter cited above, and therefore supposes that the earlier Berta was the grandmother of the later one.

Some suspicion concerning the authenticity of this charter had been raised by its wholly unusual invocation formula. For among the many instruments that we have so far reviewed, beginning with an invocation of the Holy Trinity, there is none that we have not counted among the spurious—apart from one or two papal bulls and a single charter of Gammo dated to the year 697, printed above at col. 1235. Since this charter, however, can be cleared of the other indications of forgery and was taken from a chartary, one may conjecture that the unusual formula was rashly prefixed by the chartary’s scribe.

We judge the same concerning Bertrada’s charter, likewise extracted from a chartary, which has appeared suspect to no one known to us. We have already discussed above our method of calculating the regnal years of Theoderic IV (col. 1268, note g).] (A.D. 721.)

In the name of the holy divinity of the Trinity. I, Bertrada, or Berta, and my son Charibert, reflecting upon the burdens of our sins, so that we may deserve to offer small things in exchange for great, earthly things in exchange for heavenly, perishable things in exchange for future things upon the altar of the supreme almighty God, and so that we may obtain deliverance from them through the continual mercies of God’s dwelling, therefore we ardently desire to build a monastery beside the river Prüm.

And so we did: in honor of Saint Mary, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Saint John, and Saint Martin; and the monks there are to live under a monastic and regular order and pray more attentively day and night for the Lord’s mercy concerning our sins, so that we may deserve to be cleansed of our harmful crimes and—though the Latin is syntactically defective—for my deceased sons.

Therefore, we give to the monastery called Prüm, from our forest, from the monastery downstream along the water as far as the ford in the Prüm [the intervening reading *desuetus illo exarte* is uncertain], and from that ford directly as far as the river Melina, then along the flowing water of the Melina as far as what lawfully falls to us, as far as Winard’s estate, and as far as the boundary that falls to us.

For the support of those servants of God we also give from our estates: from the estate of Romair, half of our share, and likewise half of Prüm; at Saaingas in Moslisi, on the river Moselle, everything at Bursis that belongs to our share, and at Blancium everything that falls to us.

We give all our share of Bertelingas, and wish it to belong perpetually to the monastery of Prüm, in honor of our special patrons Saint Mary, Saint Peter and Saint Paul, and Saint Martin, as well as the other saints whose relics are known to be venerated there, where Angloaldus is known to preside with Christ’s favor.

These are the estates named above, with all their possessions in their entirety: Sessi with its *widriscapi*, houses, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, woods, slaves, resident dependants, clothing, utensils, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated land, dwellings, movable and immovable property, and whatever our ancestors held there in those estates and we appear to hold from this day forward.

All of it, in its entirety, as I have said above, we give and transfer from our right into the right and dominion of those servants of God, for the remedy of our souls and of my deceased sons and for eternal recompense, so that it may perpetually accrue to their increase there.

From this day forward, let those servants of God who appear to contemplate the holy order in those places have, hold, and possess the aforesaid estates, and leave them to their spiritual successors for possession; or, whatever they wish to do with them, let them have complete and most secure freedom in every respect to do so.

If anyone—whether we ourselves, or any of our heirs [Note: The word *testamentum* is not to be understood in its ordinary sense here. Bertrada is transferring property from the present day and later writes a charter of donation. There are several instruments of this kind in this collection in which gifts made between living persons are called *testaments*, that is, attestations or declarations of will. Thus, in the law of the Ripuarian Franks, titles LIX and LXVII are entitled “testament of sale” and “testament of transfer.” See Cangius, under *Testamentum*.], heirs apparent, or any opposing person—should attempt to come against this testament made by us or wish to alter it, which we do not believe will happen, let him first incur the anger of almighty God, and of Saint Peter who holds the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and of Saint Paul together with the Lord’s apostles and the other saints.

Let him wither at the root so that he does not flower in the branches; and if branches grow upon him, let them come to nothing, like one anathematized in the rays of the sun. Let him never at any time be able to recover what he claims, but remain empty and void with those curses.

And further, for the complete security of the matter, so that our small gifts, which we have offered to God, may remain unharmed; and moreover, according to the law of the legislator and what the princes have decreed [Note: The charter incidentally alludes here to constitution 8, title IX, book II of the Theodosian Code, which imposes penalties upon those who refuse to fulfill agreements. See Gothofredus’s commentary on that constitution.], let him pay us ten pounds of gold and twenty weights of silver.

And so that no one may at any time violate our act, let this present testament made by us remain firm forever.

Accordingly, we have ordered this charter of donation to be made from the present day, have decreed that we confirm it below with our hands, and have asked distinguished men to confirm it.

The charter of donation was publicly executed at the estate of Prüm, on the day which made the twenty-third day of the month of June, in the first year of the reign of our lord King Theoderic.

Sign of Bertradana, who requested that this charter be made, made with her own hand. I, Charibert, have subscribed. I, Bernarius, have subscribed.—Sign of Chrodolanda. I, Theoderic, have subscribed.

## LVIII. Charter acknowledging the rents owed from the county of Ardennes and payable to Herlemundus, bishop of Le Mans

[Note: There is nothing in this instrument that gives the impression of being false. Nevertheless, it is known from no other source than the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, among Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 284, which contains many instruments of doubtful reliability. From that work we published above, p. 156, one document granting fiscal revenues in the estate of Ardennes to the Church of Le Mans, and counted it among the spurious documents.

Was the document presented here fabricated as a confirmation of that one? We would be reluctant to raise such a suspicion, since there are no indications of a forged product. Herlemundus had already governed the Church of Le Mans for several years when Theoderic IV began his reign.] (A.D. 721.)

To our lord and senior, the apostolic man Herlemundus, who appears to have the house of Saint Gervasius in his governance: we, in the name of God, Domnolenus, Bodoardus, Rogobertus, Bosolenus, Gembertus, Audobertus, Gundoaldus, and Adobertus, junior members acting under Audrannus, from your estate of Saint Gervasius called Ardennes.

Since it is known that, with the permission of Audrannus himself, we receive or are to receive through our hands from our countrymen the levies and all the exactions that are owed from that estate to the portion of Saint Gervasius, and since we made arrangements concerning them with the *vicedominus* at Hadingan, he required from us, in full, on the basis of the announced charter dating from the reign of King Chilperic, concerning that levy, that we make it clear that our countrymen paid this, either we together with them or the countrymen themselves, and that they be convicted concerning it.

Therefore, through this letter of security we make our promise to you, and confirm it with our hands.

I, Domnolenus, owe seventy-two solidi from that grain levy.

I, Bodoardus, seventy-three solidi.

I, Rigobertus, thirty-four solidi.

I, Bosolenus, forty-three solidi.

I, Audobertus, thirty-eight solidi.

Likewise, I, Gembertus, eighty-two solidi and two denarii.

I, Gundoaldus, thirty-six and a half solidi.

And I, Adobertus, twenty-one solidi and a tremissis, as we have stated.

We, the younger men under Audrannus, promise you through this letter of security that, in the middle of July, we shall fully pay you the levy mentioned above, which each person is bound to pay from his own share, as has been inserted above and is known among us. We promise that, as we have said, we shall pay you the whole amount in the middle of July, so that we may fulfill your favor in this matter.

Likewise, concerning those who have given security—our countrymen who have refused this—and concerning whom we have made this promise to you from those villages, we promise you that, for each person, we shall make full satisfaction among ourselves on the day appointed, according to his service, as they have indeed done for you and as your written memorandum states. [Note: This charter deserves especially careful consideration because no similar document is found in which debtors of revenues acknowledge what each owes for his share and, making themselves liable for the promise, individually undertake to pay the entire revenue on behalf of all. Here we detect the first traces of the practices of a later age concerning the payment of feudal rent.]

If we do not do this and do not fulfill your wish in the matter, we promise you through this letter of security that afterward, following that settlement, we shall pay you the whole amount twofold. We have therefore confirmed this letter of security, supported by stipulation, below with our hands and have requested its confirmation.

Executed at the city of Le Mans, in the month of June, in the first year of the reign of our lord King Theoderic.

Sign of Domnolenus. Sign of Rigobertus. Sign of Haudeharius. Sign of Bauslenus. Sign of Audobertus. Sign of Gembertus. Sign of Gundoaldus, who knowingly confirmed this letter of security. Bertrannus, asked to do so, have subscribed. Theobaldus have subscribed. Adebertus have subscribed. Odilus wrote and subscribed.

## LIX. Charter by which Count Ebroinus bestows many gifts upon the basilica of Saint Peter at Rinharim

[Note: Miraeus published this, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. III, p. 560, from a very old charter [and notes that among the other charters of the counts of Holland it is one of the oldest]. The same document, with many discrepancies, was communicated to us by Dom Turpin of the Congregation of Saint Maur, taken by D. Michael Colloz, subprior of Saint Agericus of Verdun, from the chartary of Echternach, which they call the Golden Book and which was written toward the end of the twelfth century.

Take care not to confuse Count Ebroinus with Ebroinus the mayor of the palace, or Theoderic, under whose reign this charter was issued, with Theoderic III. Ebroinus the mayor of the palace had died in A.D. 682, as can be seen in the *Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 47, and Fredegar’s Continuation, chapter 98; Theoderic III died around A.D. 691, as Longuer testifies in the *Annals of the Franks* under the year 690, in the collection of the writings of the history of the Franks, vol. III, p. 694. Willibrord, who is called bishop here, did not receive the episcopal insignia until A.D. 695, according to Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 610. Therefore the Count Ebroinus under discussion is someone other than Ebroinus the mayor of the palace [as Miraeus correctly proves in the work cited above; Heda speaks of our Ebroinus in his *History of Utrecht*, p. 28].

The Theoderic here must be understood as the fourth king of that name, who appears to have begun his reign after the death of Chilperic II, in December of the year 720. Willibrord, however, lived until A.D. 738, or perhaps even until A.D. 740, as the *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 63, testifies.

Who that Count Ebroinus was is not clearly established. We know of a Count Ebroinus who subscribed the earliest charters of the foundation of the monastery of Corbie in A.D. 685, Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 271. Is he the same man who was responsible for the charter under examination? It would be difficult to determine this.

We publish the charter according to the copy communicated by Dom Turpin; we place Miraeus’s readings within brackets.]

(A.D. 721.)

In the name of God. I, Count Ebroinus, son of the late Oda [M., Odo], donor, have decided to give some of my property to the holy places for the remedy of my soul and of my most beloved wife Theodelinda’s soul.

That is, to the basilica of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of John the Baptist and the other saints, which has been built at the place called Rinharim [M., Reynaren], in the county of Dublum, beside the river Rhine, where the lord father and bishop Willibrordus [M., Willebortius] now appears to be guardian:

I give at Nitro, our estate, three households with their wives and children, lands with my hall and farmyard [M., courtyard], together with the adjoining property and whatever belongs to the same place; and I give in its entirety my portion at the place called Haemmi, the woodland belonging to me.

I also give what has legally come to me at Dangaesbroch [M., Doensbrug]: half the woodland belonging to the same place according to my right; and at our estate of Meri, one household with its wife and children and its share [M., with lands, their personal property, and a share] of the woodland; and at our estate of Rinhari, four households with their wives and children, with their lands and personal property and shares of the woodland; and at our estate of Millingi, the basilica of our lady Mary, with all its property in its entirety, which we established there and have decided and ordered to be transferred to the same Saint Peter; and our servant Folcharius who serves there, with his wife and children; Eodfrid [M., Godefridus], with his wife and children and lands [“and lands” is absent in M.].

And at the place called Meginun, Walamunt [M., Megrim, Walamnum], with his wife and children, with two *hobinnae* of land [M., two *soburinae*]; and at the estate of Dagaerburge, Oda, with his wife and children and his personal property.

All these possessions, in their entirety—that is, houses, farmyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, enumerated and unenumerated property, and every other appurtenance belonging there—I give to the aforesaid holy place, and wish them to be given in perpetuity [“to be” is absent in M.], for the benefit of prayers and for the solemn celebration of Masses perpetually for me and mine.

Let the holy place itself and its custodians have, hold, possess, and defend these things, and let them have complete and most secure power in every respect to do whatever they wish with them. [“And defend” is absent in M.]

If anyone—and I do not believe this will happen—whether we ourselves, or any of our heirs [M., heirs or heirs apparent], or any opposing person [these four words are absent in M.], should attempt to come against this testament [M., this charter of donation] or wish to alter it, let him first be excommunicated by Saint Peter and Saint Paul.

Moreover, let him pay to the treasury ten pounds of gold and twenty weights of silver, together with the most sacred treasury.

[Note: Thus Miraeus has the passage: “And if he should wish to violate it, and should attempt to take away any part of the aforesaid property as though by hereditary right, let him utterly incur the anger of almighty God and of the holy angels, and be expelled from the thresholds of the Church of God and from the company of the saints; let him suffer the leprosy of Gehazi or the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, and share the lot of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed the Lord, after the curse and excommunication.”]

Executed publicly at Rinharos, in the first year of the reign of our most glorious lord King Theoderic [Miraeus adds: “in the seventh indiction”].

I, Ebroinus, reread [M., *reliqui*, “I left”] this testament made by me [M. adds: “in the presence of”] and confirmed it with my own hand.

I, Ugilius, an unworthy priest, at the request of Count Ebroinus, wrote and subscribed this in the name of God.

Guntbrechtus. Folchbrectus. Godobrectus. Raedbrectus. Redualdus. Herifusus.

[Note: Miraeus reads the subscriptions as follows: “I, Vigilius, an unworthy priest, at the request of Count Ebroinus, wrote and subscribed in the name of God. Cunebrechtus. Polikbertus. Godebrectus. Raedbeisus. Redualdo, son of Herifus.”]

## LX. Charter by which Rigobertus sells to Erkenbodo, [bishop of Taruanne], estates in the counties of Taruanne and Pontieu

[Note: Malbrancq published this, *On the Morini*, vol. I, p. 570, and Cointius reprinted it on his authority, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 699.

In the same year in which this charter was issued, Erkenbodo, also called Erkembodus or Erkenbodus—for his name is written both ways—had been promoted to the bishopric of Taruanne. He had been abbot of Sithiu; concerning him, see John Iperius in the chronicle of Sithiu, in Martène, *Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. III, col. 482.

There the sale whose charter we present here is mentioned, and the beginning and chronological notes of this instrument are transcribed in precisely the same words. But Iperius incorrectly associates the third year of the reign of Theoderic IV with A.D. 716.] (A.D. 723.)

To the lord and apostolic father Erkenbodus, bishop and purchaser, and to his congregation residing there, I, Rigobertus, sold and presently delivered all my villas called Sethiaco, on the river Agniona, with their appurtenances Kelmias and Strato, and, below Mempiscus, the estates of Leodedringa, or Bebrinio, situated on the river Quantia, in the pagus of Taruanne, with their appurtenances, which are in the pagus of Pontivus, at a place called Mentek, on the river Aeteya.

Executed publicly at the monastery of Sithiu, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the third year of the reign of our lord Theodoricus, the glorious king.

I, Rigobertus, reread and subscribed this sale made by me.

Sign of Doddo. Sign of Leudegesilus. Sign of Chimbaldus, centenarius. Sign of Cherebaldus. Sign of Ellemberthus. Sign of Ingomar. Winidmarus, deacon, wrote and subscribed this sale.

### LXI. Charter by which Haicho gives to the monastery of Honau the share belonging to him in the island of Honau

[Note: [Column 1279D] Mabillon published this from an old exemplar, *Annales*, volume II, appendix, page 696; Eccard reprinted it, *Origin. Habsburg.*, page 99, and Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*, volume I, page 6, from a fifteenth-century manuscript of the senior College of Saint Peter at Strasbourg. D. Grandidier produced a more accurate text in *Histoire ecclésiastique de Strasbourg*, volume I, documents, page 55, from the same manuscript and from a chartulary preserved in the archives at Saverne. We follow this last edition.] (year 723).

[Note: [Column 1279D] Haicho was the brother of Boronus, whose charter we shall publish below, page 346. [Adalricus begot Duke Adalbertus, Heticho, and Baticho. Adalbertus was the father of Luitfridus and Ebrohardus, whose charter may be seen above, page 338. Heticho was the grandfather of Haicho, whose charter is now under discussion; Baticho, Adalricus’s third son, begot Boronus, whose donation is to be cited at page 346: see Grandidier, volume I, documents, page 78.]] (year 723).

[Column 1279C]

To the most holy monastery called Honau, constructed in honor of Saint Michael above the river Rhine, where at the present time Benedictus appears to be abbot, I, Haicho, thinking upon God and upon the benefit of my soul [Column 1280A] and eternal recompense, have resolved that I ought to give to that monastery my share of the island called Honau, which the Rhine surrounds; and so I have done.

Therefore, from this day forward, I deliver all the aforesaid property to the said monastery and to its agents under your dominion, to possess it, so that, whatever you may wish to do with it, you may have full and most secure power in every respect, with Christ’s favor.

But if anyone—whether I myself, or any of my heirs, or any opposing person—should wish to contravene or act against this present document, or to bring any claim, let him pay to the agents of the aforesaid monastery one pound of gold; nevertheless, let this present document remain firm and stable there, supported by formal stipulation.

[Column 1280B] Executed publicly at the villa of Sunthusis.

[Note: [Column 1280C] Mabillon read *Sunthuris*. Schoepflin, *Alsatia illustrata*, volume I, page 785, and *Alsatia diplomatica*, volume I, page 6, understands it as the village of Sunthausen near Sélestat.]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the third year of the reign of our lord Theodoricus, king.

Sign of Haicho, who requested that this donation be made. Sign of Hugo, his son, who consented. Sign of Albricus, his son, witness.

I, Guntramnus, though an unworthy priest, wrote and subscribed this document at the request of the parties.

### LXII. Charter by which Boronus gives to the monastery of Honau his share in the island of Honau and one mansus at a place called Gwillesteti

[Note: [Column 1280C] Mabillon published this from an old manuscript, *Annales*, volume II, appendix, page 695; Eccard reprinted it, *Origin. Habsburg.*, documents, page 90; Laguille, *Histoire d’Alsace*, volume I, documents, page 5; and Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*, volume I, page 6. A more accurate text was produced from the chartulary of the archives at Saverne by D. Grandidier in *Histoire ecclésiastique de Strasbourg*, volume I, documents, page 60, which we follow. We have spoken elsewhere of Benedictus and Tubanus, abbots of the monastery of Honau, among the notes to the diploma of Theodoricus IV under the year 725. All editors, in the chronological notes, read “the third year of the reign of Theodoricus,” except D. Grandidier alone, who reads “the sixth year,” following the Saverne chartulary. This reading is supported by the diploma stating that the monastery of Honau was entrusted to Tubanus in the fourth year of this reign; hence it is clear that the document under consideration, issued in the time of Abbot Tubanus, could not have been produced before the third year of this reign. But the instrument by which this monastery is entrusted to Tubanus is of doubtful authenticity.] (year 726).

To the most holy monastery called Honau, constructed in honor of Saint Michael the archangel above the river Rhine, where at the present time Benedictus or Tubanus appears to be abbot, I, Boronus, thinking upon God and upon the affection for my soul and eternal recompense, have resolved that I ought to give and transfer entirely to that monastery my share of the island called Honau, which my father left to me and which came into my possession; and likewise, at another place called Gwillesteti, one lawful mansus which Bobo held.

I deliver all the aforesaid property to the said monastery and to its agents, from this day forward, under your dominion, to possess it, so that, whatever you may wish to do with it, you may have full and most secure power in every respect, with Christ’s favor.

But if anyone—whether I myself, or any of my heirs, or any opposing person—should wish to contravene or act against this present document, or to bring any claim, let him pay to the agents of the aforesaid monastery six ounces of gold; nevertheless, let this present document remain firm and stable, supported by stipulation.

Executed publicly at the villa of Ebrotheim. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the sixth year of the reign of our lord Theodoricus, king.

Sign of Boronus, who requested that this donation be made. Sign of Ratberthus, witness. Sign of Albericus. Sign of Hanubaldus. [Column 1281B] Sign of Gozbertus. Sign of Ballunus, witness.

I, Guntramnus, though an unworthy priest, wrote and subscribed this deed of donation at the request of the parties.

### LXIII. Charter by which Widegern, bishop of Strasbourg, confirms the foundation of the monastery of Morbach, founded by Count Eberhardus, and adorns it with privileges

[Note: [Column 1281D] We publish this according to D. Grandidier, *Histoire ecclésiastique de Strasbourg*, volume I, documents, page 63, who drew the instrument from the chartulary of Morbach and compared it with another authentic charter of Heddon, bishop of Strasbourg, issued in the year 748; he conjectures that Heddon’s charter was copied from Widegern’s. We shall discuss Heddon’s charter in its proper place.

Widegern’s charter had previously been published by Eccard, *Origin. Habsburg.*, page 116; Laguille, *Histoire d’Alsace*, documents, page 9; Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, volume IV, page 174, and volume V, page 953; Mabillon, *Annales*, volume II, page 702; and finally Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*, volume I, page 9—but all of them corruptly.

Mabillon considered the chronological notes defective, denying that during the entire reign of Theodoricus IV the Ascension of the Lord ever fell on 13 May [Column 1282D]; but he is mistaken. In the eighth year of his reign, the year in which the charter under consideration is said to have been issued and which corresponds to the year of Christ 728, Easter fell on 4 April, and consequently the day of the Ascension necessarily fell on 13 May. Thus all the chronological notes of this charter agree correctly.

The chartulary records, as *Histoire ecclésiastique de Strasbourg*, documents, page 67 note, attests, that a seal was affixed to this instrument, bearing the image of a standing bishop, holding a pastoral staff in his right hand and a book in his left, surrounded by the inscription: “Widegern, by the grace of God bishop of Strasbourg.”] (year 728).

To my holy lords, most worthy of honor, apostolic fathers and fathers in Christ, Widegern, by the grace of God and of the holy Church of Mary, called bishop in the city of Strasbourg.

Let your holy diligence know how carefully and earnestly the shepherds of the Church ought to labor so that the Church of God may advance through the gain of souls and, through our salutary admonitions, insofar as we are able, may obtain increase, so that those who, leaving all things willingly, desire to follow the eternal Shepherd, denying themselves and walking along the narrow path and confined way, may hear the voice of our eternal King and Redeemer:

“Go out from your land and from your kindred, and go into the land that I shall show you”;

and also:

“Whoever has left father, or mother, or sons, or fields, and so forth, for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life”;

and:

“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

We ought to hear him who said:

“I was a stranger and you welcomed me”;

and:

“Whoever receives you receives me”;

and:

“As often as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me.”

Thus, what was instituted by the prince of the apostles at the beginning of the Church—that the whole multitude of believers was united as one, and no one called anything his own, but everything was common to them, and they were of one heart and one soul—was subsequently developed by the holy fathers. From this holy institution, from East to West and throughout the regions of Gaul, religion brought forth many monasteries under a holy rule, especially the monasteries of Lérins, Agaune, and Luxeuil, and throughout the world, under the rules of the holy fathers, especially of the blessed Benedict and Saint Columbanus, the common life was admirably ordered under abbots and firmly strengthened by the authority and clemency of kings and by the privileges of holy and catholic pontiffs. The holy canons do not diminish this institution, but rather commend it with great brilliance.

Therefore, having learned that the illustrious man Eberhardus, count, has attempted, in the wilderness called the Vosges, in the pagus of Alsace, within our parish, at the place formerly called Morbach and now Vivarium of the Pilgrims, to build anew, with God’s help and our counsel, a monastery on his own property, in honor of the holy apostles, holy Mary the Mother of God, and the other saints; and that, after inviting Bishop Perminius with his pilgrim monks who are there in a cenobium, he should complete it, with God’s grace and our assistance, under the holy rule of the blessed Benedict—

Therefore, rejoicing in this man’s holy devotion and glorious purpose, moved by visceral charity and piety, with the most ready devotion, together with the consent of our brother abbots, priests, and archdeacon, and of all the clergy of the church in which I serve, as well as of the duke, judges, and the God-fearing catholic people of this province, we have determined that a privilege should be written and confirmed by our authority and yours for that monastery, cenobium, and congregation of pilgrim monks. And so we have done.

Accordingly, we confirm by this privilege to that monastery everything belonging to its jurisdiction: buildings, basilicas, furnishings and ornaments of every kind, sacred books, instruments and documents, gold, silver, bronze, and any other goods of the monastery, as well as its cells and dependencies; also villas with fields, houses, slaves of both sexes, servants, and whatever the aforesaid illustrious Eberhardus or others have donated or assigned in any way for the salvation of their souls, and whatever hereafter he himself, or the munificence of kings, princes, pontiffs, clergy, or any human being, inspired by Christ, may bestow.

All this, in its entirety, we confirm, so that from the present day the monastery itself, the aforesaid pilgrim monks, and their successors, gathered cenobitically under the rule of Saint Benedict according to their holy purpose, may hold and exercise it as their right, without anyone’s claim or demand.

Neither we ourselves, nor the bishops of this city who succeed us, nor archdeacons, collectors, nor anyone acting on behalf of the Church, nor any other person, shall ever presume to exercise authority over anything, issue commands, demand a tax, gift, or offering, or require any contribution whatsoever.

When it is necessary to request chrism, consecrate altars, ordain sacred orders, seek any blessing, or build oratories in their places, the rector of that monastery or the pilgrim monks residing there, or, if they have a bishop of their own, or whichever holy bishop they may choose, shall have permission to request that he perform these acts, and he shall be permitted to deliver, bless, or consecrate them.

No one shall presume to enter that monastery in an unlawful manner against the will or decision of its monks, or secretly to enter its enclosure.

If at any time, for whatever reason, the rector or the pilgrim monks should deem it appropriate and an invited bishop should come to the monastery, then, after celebrating the service, he shall return immediately to his own place without demanding any gift.

When the abbot of that place has died, the pilgrim monks living there shall choose as abbot whichever among themselves they find, according to God and the rule, to be the best, and shall appoint him.

If they do not find such a man among themselves, they shall obtain and appoint as their regular abbot someone from another monastery of the aforesaid Bishop Perminius, from those congregations of pilgrim monks whom he united under one manner of observance and one holy institution of the blessed Benedict, with their own consent.

If, God forbid, the holy order should grow cold there, or any discord should arise among the monks, and they should be unable or unwilling to correct it, then whichever of them wishes to live according to the rule and its ordered discipline shall have the power to seek another monastery wherever the aforesaid bishop’s pilgrim monks are found residing and where he finds stricter regular observance. With their salutary counsel, by God’s gift, they shall cause that holy order and those monks to be restrained, corrected, amended, and reconciled according to the rule.

No opportunity shall be given for another abbot to be imposed there by any device against their holy order, nor for anything to be diminished from the property of the aforesaid monastery.

Therefore, my holy and apostolic fathers and brothers, with your catholic authority and our twofold support, we establish this privilege so that it may possess the strongest force for all time, and so that no one may ever presume to act against it. Let it remain inviolate for future generations.

Now I exhort, beseech, and presume to adjure, in charity, all bishops and all people who fear God, that when this privilege is shown to them, they may deign to subscribe and confirm it with their hands, so that, supported by your authority, it may remain unshaken, and so that the pilgrim monks residing in that monastery may more freely pray to divine mercy for the condition of the Church and the integrity of priests, for the safety of kings and the peace of Christians, for the remission of the sins of penitents, and for the rest of the faithful departed.

Therefore I exhort and charge, before God and his blessed angels and all the saints, all successors and all Christians, not to presume in any way to violate this privilege, which we have decreed and established with the consent of the clergy, the God-fearing laity, the people, and our church.

Rather, by the ineffable Trinity we adjure all that, insofar as they are able, they strive to preserve it in every respect. If, however, with obstinate mind, or at the devil’s instigation, deceived by envy or greed, or in any other way—which God forbid—we ourselves, or our successors, or anyone from any quarter should attempt to act against this privilege, or should presume to harass the aforesaid pilgrim monks or their successors, or to diminish anything belonging to them, and should refuse to amend his conduct or quickly correct his evil intention, let him expect, before the sight of the eternal King, Christ our Lord, together with the Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, the blessed apostles, and all the saints, in whose love we have granted this privilege to the aforesaid pilgrims and cenobium, to be burned in eternal fires for his wicked sins and most evil malice.

Let him experience the sentence with which the Lord threatens false priests:

“Woe to you, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of God, because you yourselves do not enter, nor permit another to enter”;

and:

“Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be thrown into the depths of the sea.”
