And, because he has neglected the fear of God who judges human beings, let him pay to the parties of the monastery itself and to the pilgrim monks living there, together with the associated treasury, a fine of thirty pounds of gold and fifty pounds of silver, and let him bear and discharge the penalty. Let him not prevail in recovering what he seeks; nevertheless, let this present privilege remain firm for all time.

And, so that it may obtain firmer strength, we have subscribed with our hands and have requested those who subscribed or signed it to do likewise, with stipulation attached.

Executed publicly in the city of Strasbourg, on the thirteenth day, in the month of May, on the Ascension of the Lord, in the eighth year of the reign of our lord Theodoricus, king.

I, Widegern, though an unworthy bishop, subscribed.

I, Wuolfradus, archdeacon, consented and subscribed.

I, Libulfus, priest, subscribed.

I, Haimulfus, deacon, subscribed.

I, Altmannus, deacon, subscribed.

Sign of Fulcherius, tribune, in the name of God.

I, Hariboldus, abbot, consented and subscribed.

I, Hadalricus, consented and subscribed.

I, Ardolinus, called bishop in the name of God, consented and subscribed.

Sign of Wuolfoaldus, count.

Magobardus, archdeacon, subscribed.

I, Ghrbuinus, bishop, consented and subscribed.

I, Willibertus, bishop, subscribed.

[Column 1285A] I, Hagoaldus, abbot, subscribed.

Sign of Leodofredus, duke.

I, Ebrobardus, count, subscribed.

Sign of Audachro.

Sign of Nordoldus.

Sign of Gundoberthus.

Sign of Witharius.

Sign of Wigrao.

I, Hagino, abbot, subscribed.

Sign of Leodobertus.

I, Willibrordus, in the name of God, subscribed.

Romanus, a cleric, wrote this privilege at the command of the person named above.

### LXIV. Charter by which Theodo sells to the monastery of Morbach his share in the estate of Hamarisstad

[Note: [Column 1285C] Until now Schoepflin alone has published this charter, *Alsatia diplomatica*, volume I, page 13, and we reprint it on his authority. He states that he drew the charter from the chartulary of Morbach. He notes above, page 723, that the place called Hamarisstad in this instrument, with its name slightly altered, is today called Hammerstater-Hof, a village situated four miles from Neuf-Brisach.] (year 730).

To the venerable lord and father in Christ, Romanus, abbot, together with your holy congregation of the monastery called Morbach:

I, Theodo, in the name of God, acknowledge that I have sold to you—and so I have sold—all my portion in the estate of Hamarisstad, namely a fifth, together with whatever possession of land and woodland appears to be mine there, as we have stated above, insofar as it lies within that boundary.

For this I received from you, as was agreed and arranged between us, payment in grain or another price worth thirty solidi, on the condition that from this day you shall have and possess these lands and woods, and whatever you may wish to do with them, you shall have full and most secure power in every respect.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, or my heirs, or any other person who attempts to act against this sale, which I willingly requested to be made, or wishes to invalidate it, and if my heirs do not defend it, let him first tremble lest he incur the offense of almighty God and his angels.

Moreover, let him be compelled to pay twice as much as I received from you; and let him know that he is liable to the treasury for one pound of gold and five [the manuscript is lacunose here] of silver. Let him not be able to recover what he seeks, but let this sale remain firm for all time, supported by stipulation.

Executed publicly at the monastery of Marbach, in the tenth year of the reign of King Theodoricus, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.

Sign of Theodo, who requested that this sale be made.

Sign of Sigrannus. Sign of Odihardus. Sign of Wiglulfus. Sign of Adalindus. Sign of Feumillus. Sign of Luntbertus. Sign of Trodolaigus.

I, Johannes, reader, in the name of God: this sale, at the dictation of Lord Abbot Romanus.

### LXV. Testament of Adela, abbess of Palatiolum near Trier

[Note: [Column 1285D] Browerus drew this from ancient records of the Church of Trier, *Annales Trevirenses*, volume I, page 357. Henschenius reprinted it, *De tribus Dagobertis*, book II, page 127; Cointius, *Annales*, volume IV, page 790; Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti*, volume IV, page 499; Calmet, *Histoire de Lorraine*, volume II, documents, column 94; Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, volume I, page 88; and Bertholet, *Histoire du Luxembourg*, volume II, documents, page 35. All followed Browerus, removing from the instrument every kind of error with which documents of this period abound—for Browerus was accustomed to cleanse documents extracted from originals of such defects.

The writers of *Gallia Christiana nova*, volume XIII, instruments, column 294, published this same testament, apparently taken from Browerus. There Adela declares herself the daughter of King Dagobert, whom Browerus, in the place cited, considers Dagobert I; Masenius, in his extensive defense of Browerus, *Annales*, volume I, page 610, supports this view. Cointius overturns it with stronger arguments, *Annales*, volume IV, pages 380 and following, and asserts that Adela’s father was Dagobert II, son of Sigebert.

It follows that the twelfth year of King Theodoricus, in which Adela composed her testament, must be understood as the reign of Theodoricus IV, as Cointius proves with several arguments that the limits of our notes do not permit us to reproduce here.

It is enough to say that, according to Cointius and Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, volume IV, page 698, Adela received the use of light—that is, was born—around the year 668; built the monastery of Palatiolum around the year 700, when she was already a mother and widow; composed her testament in the year of Christ 732, at the age of sixty-four; and, according to the authors of *Gallia Christiana nova*, in the place cited, died in the year of Christ 735.

We are surprised, however, that these same writers, and Hontheim as well, in the place cited, considered Adela’s testament to have been composed under Theodoricus III, in the year of Christ 690, when Adela would scarcely have been twenty-two and had not yet built the convent of Palatiolum.] (year 732).

Adela, consecrated abbess in the Lord Christ, formerly daughter of King Dagobert.

Since it is widely known and recognized by all good people how we established the monastery in the villa called Palatiolum [Note: [Column 1286D] Palatiolum was so called from an ancient palace, according to Mabillon, *Annales*, volume II, pages 3 and 96; around the middle of the eleventh century, however, canons were substituted there for the virgins.], situated on the bank of the river Moselle, which we acquired from Pippin, mayor of the palace, at Trier by exchange, and which we long ago built for the use of our own monastery in honor of Saint Mary, Virgin and Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the blessed Peter and Paul and the other saints, and in which we gathered a community of nuns living under the discipline and rule of Saint Benedict, we have finally judged it necessary to confirm by this present testamentary document the resources necessary for conducting this life, which until now we have bestowed from our own property.

Therefore, we bequeath and donate to this monastery, of which we have spoken, our villa called Palatiolum, in which the cenobium appears to have been built, in its entirety, with its houses, buildings, additions, cottages, courtyards, manses, slaves, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, appurtenances, mills, waters and watercourses, and everything that is known to belong to that villa.

We also wish to add our estate of Scripnasium, situated in the pagus of the Moselle on the bank of the river Moselle, together with all the possessions of that villa, except for one field of forty jugera called Insula, which we previously donated to our most beloved son Albericus.

Likewise, I wish this monastery of the Mother of God to possess all the estates situated at Bietberg and Beslancius, which I purchased from my most beloved sister Regentrude for a stipulated price.

Again, I add my portions of the villas of Enchiariacum, Ursiacum, and Caimetae, all of which are situated on the Moselle.

To these I am also pleased to add the property and resources which formerly came to me in the estate of Regimoset from Feronius, son of Tullonus, by a valid contract of sale.

To these are also added the possessions of Baldelingis, situated in the pagus of Benta, which I purchased from Ganciofridus and Wigericus and brought into my ownership and private property.

Likewise, everything that was given to me by Bertonius in the estate of Machariacum: all this I grant and donate.

Finally, we have determined, with the agreement of the aforesaid congregation, that whatever wealth and possessions we have transferred to this monastery shall always remain under the authority and protection of the archbishops of the Church of Trier.

Given on the Kalends of April, in the twelfth year of King Theodoricus.

### LXVI. Charter by which Goyla grants property to the basilica of Saint Benignus, to be possessed after her death and that of her husband

[Note: [Column 1287D] Perard published this among the documents relating to the history of Burgundy, page 8; Cointius reprinted it, *Annales*, volume IV, page 826, from Perard. The donor, called Goyla in the text, subscribes under the name Goylana.

Perard conjectures that the charter was issued during the reign of Theodoricus III; but Cointius and Mabillon, *Annales*, volume II, page 95, consider it more likely to have been issued under Theodoricus IV. The fourteenth year of Theodoricus IV fell in the year of Christ 734; the Saturday before the middle of April designates the tenth day of that month, according to the chronological tables inserted in *The Art of Judging Individual Dates in Ancient Documents*. Cointius, in the place cited, understands the twelfth day. The cause of the error is that Cointius believed the year of Christ 734 to have been marked by the Sunday letter E, whereas, according to the same tables, that year was marked by the letter C.

This charter is mentioned in the chronicle of Saint Benignus, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume I, page 376, and is said to have been issued in the fourteenth year of the reign of Theodoricus I, grandson of Brunhild; hence this instrument would appear to belong to the year 609 or 610. Mabillon, however, prefers Cointius’s opinion, which assigns the charter to the reign of Theodoricus IV, and supports it especially by the argument that at that time the Benignian documents used chronological formulas of the same kind as those employed in the charter under consideration.

Thus, in charters published by Perard under Kings Pippin and Charles, the following chronological formulas occur: “On the Saturday immediately after the middle of July …”; “on the Sunday immediately after the Kalends of March …”; and “on the Saturday before the Kalends of February.” Cointius and Mabillon are supported by the authors of *Gallia Christiana nova*, volume IV, column 670.

The abbot of Saint Benignus who subscribes Goyla’s charter under the name Goinus is called Gudinus in the chronicle of Saint Benignus.] (year 734).

To the most holy basilica of the lord martyr Benignus, which is constructed beneath the town of Dijon, where that precious saint rests bodily in great honor:

I, therefore, Goyla, a sinful woman, reflecting on human frailty, have considered that, while the soul is in the body and possesses all its powers, it ought to think in such a way that, from the goods rightfully belonging to it, it may acquire paradise for itself.

Therefore, to that basilica and to its agents, after the day of my death or that of my most beloved husband, Bonuaso by name, I cede and have permanently ceded, and I wish the cession to remain in force:

Whatever I appear to have, possess, or control in the pagus of the Atoarii, in the villa or territory of Longouiana—namely, lands, lordly houses, and all their appurtenances, together with every property mentioned above: courtyards, farmsteads, fields, meadows, woods, vineyards, orchards, pastures, and all accessions; waters and watercourses, with every right and all their appurtenances and dependencies, namely Fedenniacum, Postenniacum, Monasteriolum, half of Ataenae, Glonnocum, the Bunciana court, Fisciacum, Cheneuas, and Marcenniacum.

Whatever I appear to have or possess there, entirely and in every respect, together with slaves, freedmen, their property and all their possessions, servants, and every unexplored or unspecified asset; everything that, as I have said, I have in those aforesaid territories, villas, or fields, whether from my own inheritance or from that of my parents, through written instruments, or by any method or acquisition; whatever has come to me there from any source, or may hereafter come to me, with Christ presiding; whatever I have now justly and reasonably possessed there, or whatever may hereafter accrue, be acquired, or improved there—all this entirely, with complete integrity and firmness—the agents or administrators of the aforesaid basilica of the lord Benignus shall, after the day of my death or that of my aforesaid husband Bonuaso, from the present day, without any opposition or anyone’s objection, take into their possession in the name of God and hold under their authority.

Thus, whatever they may wish to do with it for the benefit of that place, they may freely enjoy it according to their own judgment, in the name of God, without anyone’s opposition.

And if—which I do not believe will happen—I myself, or any of my heirs, or any other opposing party or person, should at any time attempt to act against this present deed of cession, which I have requested to be written and confirmed with the fullest willingness for the redemption of my soul, or should seek to reclaim or challenge it, let that person pay to the parties of the aforesaid basilica of Saint Benignus and its agents, together with the associated treasury, three pounds of gold and three pounds of silver. Nevertheless, let this present cession and my will remain firm and inviolate for all time, supported by stipulation.

Executed publicly at Bagnavilla.

Sign of Goylana, who requested that this cession be made and confirmed.

Sign of Boneuaffus, her husband, who consented.

In the name of God, I, Goinus, abbot, signed.

Sign of Gotofredus. Sign of Landonus. Sign of Teuderamnus. Sign of Elmoaldus. Sign of Graffio. Sign of Richselinus.

I, Brandalenus, priest, in the name of God, having been requested, wrote and recorded this properly confirmed cession, on the Saturday immediately before the middle of April, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our lord Theodoricus, king.

### LXVII. Charter by which Bilehilt establishes and endows a convent for girls beside the walls of Mainz

[Note: [Column 1289C] Serrarius published this from a tablet hanging before the altar of Saint Bilehildis, *Rerum Moguntinarum*, book II, page 284. Eccard reprinted it, *Francia orientalis*, volume I, page 221, and Cointius, *Annales*, volume IV, page 827.

Mabillon, *Annales*, volume II, page 97, declares these letters extremely corrupt and unworthy of credence. More is related of Bilehildis, widow and abbess, in the Mainz breviary, and material is included in her Life published by Serrarius and Surius, *Acta Sanctorum*, under 27 November; but Mabillon considers these no more worthy of confidence than the very document under examination.

Saint Bilchildis is commemorated in a very ancient sacramentary under the fifth day before the Kalends of December, as may be seen in *Gallia Christiana nova*, volume V, page 589. The convent said to have been founded by her appears to be the Alto-Monastery, or old monastery of Saint Mary, in Mainz.

The chronological notes reveal the instrument to be spurious, since they employ formulas unusual for this period. Moreover, Bilehildis had not yet been born in the year of Christ 635; she withdrew to Mainz around the year 712, deprived of her husband and pregnant. At that time her uncle Sigebertus occupied the episcopal see of Mainz; he is incorrectly called archbishop here, since the bishops of Mainz did not yet bear that title. This is another indication of falsity.

Furthermore, in the year 635 neither Chlodoveus was reigning, nor was the tenth indiction current, nor did the Kalends of May fall on a Thursday. Bilehildis was born during the reign of Chlodoveus III, if we trust the ancient writers of her Life; and none of Chlodoveus’s successors reached the fourteenth year of his reign, except Theodoricus IV. The fourteenth year of that Theodoricus corresponds to the year of Christ 734.

Hence Cointius assigns the charter under consideration to that year, when Geroldus occupied the episcopal see of Mainz, having succeeded Sigebertus, and subscribes the charter. It follows that Asmundus, at the end of the instrument, ought to have stated that he wrote Bilehildis’s charter at the command not of Sigebertus, as he says, but of Geroldus.

Thus this instrument is riddled with defects on every side, and for that reason we judge it should be classified as spurious. Since a place must nevertheless be assigned to it, it is permissible to place it, with Cointius, under the year 734.] (year 734).

[Column 1289A]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. I, Bilehild, wish it to be known to those living now and to those to come how, for the love of God and for the hope of future recompense, I acquired certain property—that is, one plot of land near the wall of the city of Mainz, on the southern side—from my uncle Sigebert the archbishop, together with twelve red shields furnished with gold and an equal number of black horses; and on it I built a house of the Lord and of the holy Virgin Mary. There I gathered a holy community of women and gave to them as my alms and that of my parents whatever property or inheritance I appeared to possess: plots of land and buildings, meadows, pastures, woods, lands, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and slaves, so that they might have and possess them until the end of this age.

The possessors of the same little plot within the aforesaid city shall not concern themselves with watches, nor add anything to the collections of money given sometimes to the bishop and sometimes for repairing the walls, nor observe other civic customs; they shall recognize that they are subject only to the use, service, and authority of the abbess and the community. If any of them commits homicide, theft, robbery, or any other offense, or if some outsider and wrongdoer who has done such things flees to that plot and takes refuge there, he shall be judged and dealt with not by the judgment of the urban judges or princes, but by that of the rulers of the same place.

Let them have the mundeburdium and protection of the archbishop of the Church of Mainz forever; but let them themselves have the election of the abbess. Let them receive no widow or any other outsider, unless she has been raised among them. And if any bishop, through his rashness, should wish to violate this charter of conditions, may he experience the anger of almighty God and of all the saints, and nevertheless may he in no way accomplish what he wishes; rather, let this present charter of the transfer remain firm and stable at all times, supported by a formal stipulation.

Moreover, if any widow or outsider is placed over these holy women without their consent, may she fall into the worst kind of leprosy, and afterward, condemned to a most shameful death, perish; and may she not have a place here in which to putrefy.

Done in the aforesaid city, while the most serene King Chlodoveus was reigning, in the fourteenth year, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 635, in the tenth indiction, on the Kalends of May [Eckardus: the tenth day before the Kalends of May], on Thursday, in the presence of the undersigned witnesses.

The sign of Bilehild, who carried out this transfer.  
The sign of Bishop Gerold.  
The sign of the deacon Ruodbert.  
The sign of Recholff.  
The sign of Count Adelhelm.  
The sign of Grimolff.  
The sign of Hagan.  
The sign of Hildimin.  
The sign of Mimihilt.  
The sign of Reginhilt.  
The sign of Hobolff.  
The sign of Gumolff.

I therefore, Asmund, at the command of my lord Archbishop Sigebert, wrote this and recorded the day and time as above.

LXVIII–LXIX. The Testament of Abbo, by which he grants very extensive gifts to the Monastery of Saint Peter at Novalesa

[Note: Cointius was the first to publish this, long remaining unpublished, in his *Annals*, volume VI, page 422, from a manuscript written, as he says, about six hundred years earlier, after its errors of ancient writing had been corrected. Mabillon published it again, preserving its barbarous style, in *De re diplomatica*, page 507; it was inserted into the diploma of Charlemagne by which Abbo’s testament was confirmed about the year 805. Herouvallius had given Mabillon a copy of this document, which Herouvallius himself had transcribed from the cartulary of Grenoble [now in the Royal Library, F. Sang. Harl. 487], written about five hundred years earlier. This testament is mentioned in the chronicle of Novalesa, a fragment of which may be seen in Chesnius, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, volume II; but the Novalesa chronicler is mistaken when he thinks that Abbo, whom he calls a patrician, made his testament in the time of Theodoric, king of the Goths, who reigned in the sixth century. Abbo made his testament in the twenty-first year while the most illustrious Charles was governing the kingdoms of the Franks, in the seventh indiction, as is read in the document itself. [I have admitted the chartulary’s text, collated through the efforts of the distinguished Claude; I shall nevertheless indicate certain of Mabillon’s readings in brackets.]] (year 739).

[Column 1290C] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. On the third day before the Nones of May, in the twenty-first year while our most illustrious Charles was governing the kingdoms of the Franks,

[Note: These words must plainly be understood not of Charles the king or emperor, but of Charles whom they call Martel, who, after King Theodoric IV had died—or rather, while he was still reigning—governed the kingdoms of the Franks and had exercised supreme authority for twenty-one years in the year of Christ 739. That year coincides with the seventh indiction, which is used here as a chronological synchronism. [It is established that, after the death of Theodoric IV in the year 737, an interregnum existed in Frankish Gaul for seven years, if credence is given to certain chronicles, some of which D. Bouquet published in *Rerum Gallicarum et Francicarum Scriptores*, volume III, page 691; but, as the better critics infer and as appears from the document of the year 741 below (Column 1302), it lasted only five years. Eccard must not be passed over in silence: in the chronicle of this kind which he published at the end of the Salic Law from a Wolfenbüttel manuscript, he wrote *reigned* instead of *did not reign*, which would have contradicted the other documents. But, after inspecting the manuscript, which the most learned keeper of the Wolfenbüttel Library courteously showed me, I became certain that the word is not written there, and that Eccard fell into error.]] [Column 1291A] in the seventh indiction, happily.

[Note: Nor should you think, with Cointius, *Annals*, volume IV, page 422, marginal note, that the indication of the indiction must be removed as though it were unusual in this period; for Mabillon observes, *Annals*, volume II, page 109, that although this chronological notation was then unusual in royal diplomas, it was by no means unusual in private documents. Indeed, what is said in the same testament about the Saracen invasion agrees extremely well with it: the places donated by Abbo to the Novalesans had shortly before been devastated, namely around the year 737. See the *Annals of Nazarius*, Tillani, Petavius, and others, and Longuerius in volume III of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, page 702. We therefore judge, with Mabillon, whose view is supported by the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, volume I, column 457, that Abbo’s testament can be assigned to the year 739. All regard this document as of the highest quality. Lancelot interpreted most of the place-names mentioned in it; his explanations were published at the end of Mabillon’s *De re diplomatica*, page 647.]

I, Abbo, in the name of God, son of Felix and of the woman formerly named Rustica, being of sound mind and deliberating prudently upon the circumstances of human frailty, have drawn up this testament. I asked the venerable cleric Hytbert to write it, so that, if my testament should in any way fail, whether under praetorian law or under whatever law or legal form by which it might not be able to stand, it should nevertheless have the force of a codicil, as though I had died intestate; and those whom I have determined to be free, whether male or female [M.: free men and free women], shall be free in every respect. Whatever I have given, bequeathed, or ordered to be given through this testament, I entrust to the good faith of my heir, so that it may be done, given, and furnished.

I, Abbo, in the name of God, when divine providence commands me to depart from this light, or when I have fulfilled the debt of nature, then you, holy Church in honor of the blessed apostle Peter and of the other saints, namely the monastery at Novalesa in the valley of Susa, which we built from our resources upon our property, where, with the Lord’s help, we have established a community of monks under a religious order and the rule of Saint Benedict, and where the present Abbo appears to preside—you are my heir [M.: be my heir]. I wish and command that you be my heir; let all others, men and women, be disinherited.

You, holy Church of the aforesaid blessed apostle Peter, of the monastery in the valley of Susa, shall have whatever has come to me most justly under the laws, both within the walls of that city and in the same district, from the estate of my parents or from any other source: whatever at the present time appears to belong or pertain to that holy place in the valley of Novalesa, and also at Barro, at Albanato, beyond Cinisca [Column 1291C] below Cravasca, at Faido, and in the other places, together with woods, meadows, Alpine pastures, waters and watercourses; whatever at the present time appears to pertain to that holy place, whether from my own property, from acquisitions, or from an exchange—in Promaciano, in the valley of Maurienne, which we received—together with slaves, lands, vineyards, and woods, in complete possession. I wish and command that you have it all.

Likewise, whatever we appear to possess at Balmas, where an oratory has been built in honor of Saint Veranus, and at Lastadio, Gallionis, Grummo, Camundis, Luxomone, Corvallico, Petracava, Trebocis, and throughout the territory around the city, whatever from the property of our parents or from acquisitions we appear to possess in those places [Column 1292A], I wish and command that you, my heir, have. Whatever we appear to possess around the city of Susa or in that valley—that is, at Orbano, Cicimiano, Voroxio, and Raudenoviliano—I wish and command that you, my heir, have.

At Valaucis, the portion which we gave to our freedman Theudald: I wish that he and his children have it, and I wish and command that they are to pertain to my heir. Likewise, Upper Cammite and Lower Cammite, Brosiolis, together with the free people of Rogation and Tannoborgo, together with our steward John and his children, Libertatus with his children, Crivotis, Orbana, Bicorasco, together with the descendants of Vualane—namely Hariold and his sister, whom Dunimius possesses—Galisiaca, and the Alpine pastures in Cinisio, which we exchanged with the church of Saint Peter built there in the territory of Lyon: all these things listed above, together with slaves, freedmen, lands, houses, buildings, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, Alpine pastures, and every appurtenance belonging to them, I wish and command that you, my heir, have.

And the cell within the kingdom of the Lombards called Tollatecus: whatever came to me there from the estate of our parents, together with the slaves residing there and every right belonging to it, I wish and command that you have. Also the tenant-estate in the valley of Diubiasca, within the boundaries of the Lombards, at the place called Bicciatis, which our parents and we possessed there, I wish and command that you have.

In like manner, whatever in the valley of Maurienne came to us from the estate of our parents or by any lawful and reasonable title, and whatever is legally owed to us, namely in Maurienne itself the house which we exchanged with the church of Maurienne, together with buildings, courtyards, outbuildings, gardens, vineyards, fields, and mills, together with the church of Saint Peter which our parents built there, in complete possession and with all its appurtenances; likewise the church of Saint Pancras belonging to our property, together with the tenant-estate at Birisco and all its appurtenances: I wish that you, my heir, have these.

In the same valley of Maurienne, at the place called Fontana, whatever we presently appear to possess there from our parents, and also at Nanosces, together with the free people of Ambert, and our freedman at Alsede, named Orbano [Column 1293A], and our free woman named Rigovera of Bonnosco,

[Note: From these and similar words in the testament of Widerard above (Column 1268), it becomes clear that there was a distinction between slaves granted freedom and slaves given simple liberty: the latter were called *liberti*, the former *ingenui*.]

and whatever in Bregis belongs to the estate of our parents and is held by Austruald as a benefice, I wish and command that you, the aforesaid Church of Saint Peter, my heir, have.

Likewise, whatever we acquired from Lady Siagria in the valley of Maurienne—at Misiottano, Obliciacis, Mago, the tenant-estate at Albiadis, at Bausetis, and the tenant-estate above Bricoscis; at Amalicione, where Blancollus the *verbicarius* lives; and at Gratavinnia, together with the other named places and their appurtenances—I wish and command that you, holy Church, have.

Moreover, whatever in the valley of Durance came to us from the estate of our parents or from Siagria, together with slaves, freedmen, tenants, dependants, and serfs, I wish and command that you have as heir.

[Column 1293B] Of the district of Grenoble [omitted in M.]. Likewise, in the district of Grenoble, at Olonna, which I gave to my freedwoman named Sendebert, I wish that she have it. At Missoriano, which I acquired from Siagria, and at Piniaco and Corennum, which I gave to my freedwoman named Auriliana, I wish and command that you have those freedwomen with those properties. Likewise at Aravardo, together with our freedmen, Magnebert and his brother Columbo, Misicasiana, Mesatico, Cambe, Quintiaco, and Viennatico: all these things listed above, together with their freedmen, tenants, slaves, and all their appurtenances belonging to those places in the aforesaid district of Grenoble, I wish and decree that you, my heir, have.

Likewise, in the district of Vienne, Maconiano, which came to us from the estate of my parents and which we acquired from Siagria, and the tenant-estate in the same district of Vienne, at Baccoriaco on the river Carusium, where our smith Majorian lived, and his son Ramnulf of Blaciaco, whom we successfully claimed against Ardulf through the judgment of the patrician Agnaric.

Likewise, in the districts of Vienne and Leudun, at Bornaco, Basciasco, Amblariaco, Blaciaco, and the tenant-estate at Sevorio: all these things listed above, together with lands, houses, vineyards, fields, meadows, all their rights, and the tenants, slaves, and freedmen pertaining to those places, I wish and command that you, my heir, have.

Likewise, in the district of Mâcon, at Carnaco and Aebasciaco, which we acquired from Siagria, together with the free people, freedmen, tenants, and slaves, and all the appurtenances belonging to those places, I wish and command that you have.

Likewise, in the district of Briançon, at Aquisiana and Annevasca, in the places called the valley of Briancione, together with freedmen, tenants, and slaves; at Anneda, together with free people, freedmen, and slaves; at Agracianis, Exoratiana, and Aquislevas, together with freedmen and slaves and all their appurtenances: I wish and command that you, holy Church, have these. And the tenant-estates within that valley of Briançon and Aquisiana, which we acquired from Vuidegunda, from which Bardinus is the *capitolarius*.

Likewise at Gerentonnis, the tenant-estates belonging to Vuidegunda’s share that came to us, which our freedman Siguald holds as a benefice. The tenant-estate which we received in a third share from the woman Gismund, named Pannutia, in that valley, where our *verbicarius* Marius lives in the same tenant-estate.

Likewise my estate at Salliaris, the Alpine pastures, meadows, free woman, Vendanum, Mullinaricus, Vuilla, and Jutole: all these things listed above, together with freedmen, tenants, slaves, and all their appurtenances belonging to those places, I wish and command that you, my heir, have. And the tenant-estates in the valley of Gerenton and at Ralis, which I gave to my freedmen Theudald and Honorius, so that they and their children may have them and pertain to my heir, the holy Church: all these things listed above, with their additions and appurtenances [Column 1294B], fields, meadows, pastures, woods, Alpine pastures, mountains, streams and watercourses, and all their contents, together with every right and boundary belonging to them, I wish and command that you, holy Church, my heir, have.

Likewise, our freedmen in the valley of Aquisiana, who belonged to our parents, and those who appear to live in the district of Briançon, from which Vitalis is *capitolarius*, I wish and command that they pertain to the aforesaid church, my heir, and render service.

Moreover, at Bruitico in the district of Embrun and in the valley of Oca, our portions which we acquired from the priest Vualdelbert and from Rigaberga, together with my own property and what came to me from my kinswoman Godana, and in the same valley of Oca what we acquired from Siagria, together with the Alpine pastures and what came to us from Dodon and Godana, and what we acquired there from Lord Bishop Waldebert and from Riguberga; and the tenant-estate at the place called Albariosco, held by our slave Marcian, which came to me from my kinsman Dodon in the same district of Embrun; also our tenant-estates in the district of Riez, which our freedman Baronta holds as a benefice; and my freedman Baronta himself, together with the property at Solia which we gave him, I wish and command that Baronta himself pertain to you, my heir.

Likewise, in the same district of Embrun, the tenant-estates at Boresio, which Sauma holds as a benefice; Rodis, where our *verbicarius* named Laurence lives; and the tenant-estates at Velentio, which came to us by a lord’s order from the estate of Riculfus and his brother Rodbald: everything, absolutely everything, that came to us in the district of Embrun, in the valley of Oca, and in the district of Riez, whether through acquisition or from the estate of our parents, in full, together with the Alpine pastures, I wish and command that you, the aforesaid holy Church, my heir, have.

In like manner, in the district of Gap, my estate at Talarno, together with our freedman Sicuald, his sisters and their children; Maximus with his wife and their children; Calaicus, together with our freedmen; and Allionicos, which we acquired from Vuidegunda, where our freedmen appear to live; Marius with his brothers; and our freedmen at Venavella; Hidebert with his wife and their children, who came to us from Vuidegunda; Kalares, which we acquired from Vuidegunda, where our freedman Matarellus lives; in the lord’s tenant-estate, both within it and outside it, there are lands and lordly vineyards: all these things listed above, together with freedmen, tenants, and slaves, and their additions and appurtenances belonging to those places, I wish and command that you, holy Church, have.

And I give to the church my freedman named Amalbert, who has as wife the daughter of that Matarellus whom I emancipated; and I gave him two slaves for the household at Gap, named Rusticius and Lupolina. Likewise, in the same district of Gap, Altana, which I possess from the estate of my parents; Curenno; and the female slave Galisca, whom my father acquired from Persa; and the lands there in Campania, with the Alpine pasture called Cassauda, which we possess there from Lavarnosco; and those lands up to the chief slaves whom we acquired from Siagria: all these things listed above, together with the fields, meadows, woods, pastures, Alpine pastures, and their appurtenances belonging to those places, I wish and command that you, holy Church, have.

In like manner, in the same district of Gap, my estate at Opaga with all its appurtenances belonging to it, which I possess from the estate of my parents at the tenant-estate which I acquired from Venator through my uncle, Lord Bishop Semforianus,

[Note: Semforianus, otherwise unknown, here calls him his maternal uncle; below Abbo calls him his paternal uncle. From this it is clear that in this period both words were used as synonyms. He calls him bishop of Gap; and, lacking any other authority, the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, volume II, column 457, included him among the bishops of Gap under the name Symphorianus, around the year 730.]

I wish and command that you, my heir, have. The tenant-estate below the banks, which we gave to my freedman named Bertarius, I wish and command that his children have, and that they themselves pertain to my heir. At Bonis and Graviosco, I wish and command that you, my heir, the holy Church of the Monastery of Saint Peter at Novalesa, have them.

Likewise my estate at Valerignaca, together with my freedman Savinus, his sons, and the sons of my freedwoman Siseberga; Magnibert with his brothers and sons; and the other freedmen of ours who pertain to that estate, I wish and command that you have. Roma, together with its appurtenances and Alpine pastures, except what we gave at Roma to the children of my freedmen Aldefred and Godobert, I wish that they have, and that they themselves pertain to my heir.

At Laquatico, together with its appurtenances belonging to those places, and what I gave at Laquatico to my freedwoman Dumnulina, which I received in exchange, I wish that she have it, and that she pertain to my heir, the holy Church. The lands at Esturbatina, which I acquired from Boneval and gave to my aforesaid freedwoman named Sendebert, I wish that she have, and that she pertain to my heir. The tenant-estates at Taraone, which we acquired from Riguberga; and the lands at Crariis; and our freedman Moroald with his wife and children, whom my mother Rustica had brought from the district of Geneva and settled upon that land.

The land and slaves at Sevelis, which my uncle, Lord Semforianus, acquired from the priest Avolo and the woman Freberga; and our freedmen at Artonosco—Victor’s son Vere, John’s son Justebert, Paul, Verissimus, Justina, and Bertildes—who hold that land and the slaves at Sevelis as a benefice: I wish and command that you, my heir, the holy Church of the Monastery of Saint Peter at Novalesa, have them.

The tenant-estates which I gave to my freedwoman named Bertoldis, I wish that she have and pertain to my heir. Vobridium, which I acquired from Maurus and gave to my aforesaid freedwoman named Justina, which Dadinus holds, I wish that she have and pertain to my heir. The tenant-estate at Utronno from the estate of my parents; Glasia, Pentus, Bullonne, Muccunava, and Bladonis: I wish and command that you, my heir, have them.

Likewise, the properties at Maurovila and Rodanone, together with their appurtenances, and whatever came to us there from our parents Dodon and Godan; the properties which we acquired from Gondobert, which Marabert holds as a benefice; and the properties which we acquired from Escussarius, together with the slaves, lands, and all the appurtenances belonging to those places: all these things listed above, I wish and command that you, holy Church of Lord Peter, my heir, have.

At Cronno Luciano, from the estate of my parents, and at Latiomaus, where our female slave Mora lives, what came to me from our mother Rustica; the tenant-estates at Gradosa, which our steward Baio held as a benefice: I wish and command that you, my heir, have them.

At Quonaone in the district of Vaison, together with the free people whom we acquired from Vuidegunda; at Doliana in the district of Vendascino, which came to us from Vuidegunda herself, and which we gave to my aforesaid freedmen Justina and Dadinus, I wish that they have them and pertain to my holy Church as heir.

In the district of Sisteron, the vineyards and lands at Planciano, which we acquired from our kinsman Abbot Wandalbert; and in Marseille our own properties, houses and gardens, which came to me from my uncle Dodon and from our grandmother Dodina. Likewise at Pero, the houses and gardens which came to me from my kinswoman Godana; and fields and vineyards within the city; and our portion at Centron and at the fountain of Lisola, lands and pastures; in the district of Arles, Anglarias and Vivarium, our portion, and the other property which came to me from my uncle Dodon: I wish and command that you, my heir, have these.

At Cronia in the district of Toulon, together with freedmen, tenants, and slaves, lands, vineyards, olive groves, and the appurtenances belonging to it, I wish and decree that you, my heir, the holy Church of the Monastery of Saint Peter at Novalesa, have them.

In the district of Riez, at Vuardacelis, our own property and the portion which we acquired from Godana, together with the tenant-estate at Cumbolis and Pratalioni, which pertains to Vuardacelis, where our *siricarius* Peter lived: I wish and command that you, my heir, have them.

The saltworks at Vieu, in the district of Arles, which came to us from our kinswoman Godana, and the portion of Siagria which we acquired from her, together with threshing-floors, fields, vineyards, olive groves, slaves, and pastures, both there and in the field; and the saltworks at Alternet, Cattorosco, and Leonio, both our portion and what we acquired there from our uncle Dodon.

In the district of Die, Cassies with its holdings, and our portion at Bosedone, which we acquired from Siagria, together with its freedmen, slaves, and appurtenances, and our freedman Unebert with his sons, whom I possess from my father’s estate: I wish and command that you have them.

At Ambillis, where our slave Gavioald lives, together with the cultivated land which came to us from Lady Siagria, which Unebert himself holds as a benefice; and the tenant-estate belonging to my kinswoman Godana above Deraus, in the district of Die, where the slave Orbician lives, at the place called Riaciosco: I wish and command that you, my heir, the holy Church, have them.

The tenant-estates in the district of Apt at Variates, and the tenant-estates in the district of Cavaillon at Attanisco, Quossis, Pecciano, and Torrido, which came to me from the estate of my mother Rustica and my uncle Dodon: all these things listed above, together with their additions and appurtenances belonging to those places, I wish and command that you, holy Church of the blessed apostle Peter’s Monastery at Novalesa, have as my heir.

[Column 1297C] The tenant-estates in the district of Die, at the place called Macitha, together with the saltworks at Verdone, which belonged to our estate at Lavariosco and which we acquired from Lady Siagria: I wish and command that you have them as my heir. The farmstead at Tenegaudia, together with the lands and pastures on the same mountain, which my father Valerian acquired: I wish and command that you, my heir, holy Church of the Monastery of Lord Peter, have it.

And it pleased me to add to this page of my testament what is known concerning the estate of my parents and my grandparents Maurinus and Dodina, which we divided among ourselves with my cousin Honorata, daughter of my paternal aunt Eptolena, under the title of an agreement: namely, that she has now received her entire share of that property; and from our property whatever, by reason of the Falcidian portion, she herself or her surviving heirs could have retained or claimed by law, we have now left to them from the portion of our property in the places governed by us, as is contained in our agreement and written down as reckoned against the Falcidian portion.

This is so that neither she nor her heirs at any time hereafter may proceed against or oppose this testament of mine or our agreement. If they do so, let them incur the penalty contained in our agreement by common consent, and let them be unable to reclaim what they attempt to claim.

And I wish that all our freedmen, both male and female, whom our parents made free and whom we afterward made free, pertain to that church, my heir, Saint Peter, and render service and payment to it, just as they are bound by legal order to render them to our parents and to us; likewise, they must perform their obligations toward that heir of mine, the Monastery of Saint Peter at Novalesa.

But if they remain obstinate or ungrateful toward the aforesaid church, my heir, and wish to rebel, then let the agents of my heir restrain them with due clemency, so that they render the service which they rendered to our parents and to us. If they persist in ingratitude and rebellion, then let them pay to my heir, after judicial summons and distraint, what the law provides concerning ungrateful and contumacious freedmen, and I wish and command that they return to it.

And in the aforesaid district of Grenoble I give my freedwoman Sanctitild, who lives at Pino, together with her sons Sicufred and Sigiric; Sicumara and their siblings Helena and Sigilina. And in the same district of Grenoble we give our eunuch freedman named Gondobert, together with his sisters, and all the property which Vuidegunda gave by cession to their parents in Pagnanum; I wish that they have it and pertain to my heir.

We give our freedwoman Droctesenda together with her sons; and that freedwoman of ours has a freeborn man named Radbert as husband. We gave Celsebert the tenant-estate at Glisione, near Arcia; I wish that he have it and pertain to my heir.

The tenant-estate lands and lordly vineyards which our *lerator* Jocos held by cession and which Opilonicus has until now held as a benefice, which we acquired from Siguberga: I wish that he himself become a freedman through our testament and have those tenant-estates under the status of a freedman; and just as our freedmen pertain to my heir, so he too must act. If he wishes to withdraw himself from the monastery as a freedman, let him return to his former servitude; and let the monks themselves receive those tenant-estates for my heir, the Monastery of Saint Peter.

And I also thought it appropriate to add this to my testament: while my paternal uncle, Lord Semforianus, formerly held the bishopric of Gap under his administration and by his devotion, he wished to assign half of the deductions from his portion in the valley of Susa to that church by his own instruments; and during his lifetime he held my guardianship under his authority and rendered no account of it to us. Since by law he could not assign anything from it, and our properties remained undivided, he wrote a deed of gift of half of our common small estate in the valley of Susa to the aforesaid Church of Saint Mary at Gap, although the law prohibited this; and afterward he was driven from that episcopal office by wicked men, and that portion of the deduction was never transferred or received by the Church of Gap.

Therefore, both for the remedy of our soul and on account of our common settlement with our aforesaid uncle Lord Semforianus, we give to that Church of Saint Mary at Gap our small estates in the district of Riez, called Braccio, together with Vocontius, which came to us from our kinswoman Godana, together with freedmen, tenants, slaves, houses, buildings, lands, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, and woods—in short, everything that appears to pertain within that district of Riez to Braccio and Vocontius, except what is written above, which I gave to my heir, the Church of Saint Peter.

I wish and command that this gift, as we have said, both for the remedy of our soul and out of devotion to our uncle Lord Semforianus, may for all time increase the lights of that church and benefit the substance of the poor.

Moreover, we give to that Church of Saint Mary at Gap our small estates in the same district of Gap, called Ruarmo; Ambillis at Taraone, together with the freedmen pertaining to those places; and, in the district of Cavaillon, Memiana, which our lord and grandfather Marro formerly acquired from Lord Bishop Crammelinus.

Of all these things listed above, while I still live I reserve the use and enjoyment for myself. After my death, whenever God wills it, I wish and command that the agents of the Church of Saint Mary at Gap receive and possess those places.

In like manner we give to the Church of Saint John the Baptist at Maurienne, for the lights of that holy place and for the remedy of our soul, the places called, in the district of Grenoble, Crispiaco, which we acquired from Siagria; Abrici, a tenant-estate in the district of Vienne, which came to us from Siagria herself; Macciano, which I possess from the estate of my parents and which, in an exchange, we gave to that house at Maurienne in place of tenant-estates at Venavis in the valley of Susa; and Vircarias in Malenciano, which we gave to Bertelin’s son, a slave of Saint John, in return for freedom.

These places, together with the tenants, resident dependants, slaves, and freedmen living in them, with all their appurtenances belonging to them, I wish to be held for the lights of that Church of Saint John at Maurienne and for the support of the poor, so that it may have them and prosper through their increase.

We have donated to our sweetest Virgilia [Note: [Col. 1299D] Pingonius was astonishingly careless when, in the *Chronicle of Augusta Taurinorum*, in Chesne’s *Collection of Frankish Histories*, vol. II, he abridged Abbo’s testament. On the authority, as he says, of this document, he attributes to Abbo three daughters: the first named Virgilia, the second unnamed, and the third Honoria; he adds one son, Riculfus. The text of the testament overturns all of this. There Abbo calls Riculfus not his own son but the son of Rodulfus; he calls Virgilia “his sweetest,” but by no means his daughter; and finally he calls Honoria his freedwoman and says that Tersia was her daughter. Pingonius took the word *Tersiae* for the numerical word “third,” and carelessly wrote that the third daughter was named Honoria, although Abbo expressly calls Honoria his freedwoman. Cointius correctly refuted this, as well as other errors of the same Pingonius, about which we shall say nothing.] properties called Laciomaus and Licentiacus, Cassaniola, and Ciconiola, in the district of Vuapencium, which we acquired in those places from Lord Bishop Waldebert, Lady Siagria and Vuidegunda, and Ricuberta, a woman consecrated to God. Likewise, in the district of Segistericum, Lavarioscum, together with all its appurtenances, insofar as they appear to belong below in that district of Segistericum to that estate, which came to us from Lady Siagria; and also in the district of Regense, Cinicinus, which came to us from Lord Waldebert. In those properties, together with freeborn persons, freedmen, resident dependants and slaves, lands, houses, buildings, bondservants, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, vineyards, and all their appurtenances belonging to them, I wish you to have them. For this reason, in the districts of Segistericum, Regense, and Vuapencium, we have given them to my heir, the church of Saint Peter of the monastery of Novalesa, so that it may have them; this I wish and command.

And it pleased me to have my fullest will written in this testament, since Lord Walchunus, our father in Christ and bishop, from the beginning of the undertaking laid the foundation of the church of Saint Peter of the monastery of Novalesa, my heir, and brought the building to the completion of its summit, and stood as helper and governor in all the work of construction, so that, while he lives, that monastery of Saint Peter, my heir, with all the possessions to be assigned to it, may continue under his name and governance and our common authority. And, as is humanly ordained, when the abbot of that monastery has departed from this light, then let him appoint there the abbot whom that lord Bishop Walchunus may wish to choose for that monastery; and let that abbot, or his monks, act there, while that lord Walchunus lives, in such a way as he may wish spiritually to admonish them. They shall have no permission to do anything else with those possessions except what that aforesaid lord Bishop Walchunus shall order them for the common benefit of that monastery.

And thus it pleased me, adding that all my property which, by this testament or by letters, I have assigned to that monastery shall, while both I and that lord Walchunus live, as has already been said, remain under his name and ours throughout his lifetime for the advancement of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1300C]. And, if he should survive me for the days of his life, it shall remain for the advancement of the aforesaid monastery; and, if he should survive me for the days of his life, it shall remain in his power. [The wording is corrupt or repetitive in the transmitted text.]

And if anyone—which God forbid—among the monks of that monastery should be contumacious or, through tales of intrigue, a corrupter against the aforesaid lord Bishop Walchunus, or should wish to rebel, he shall have permission to restrain them according to the character of their conduct and to judge them according to the sentence prescribed by the canonical rule of the institution of Saint Benedict. And if he refuses to correct himself under his discipline and remains rebellious, he shall have permission to expel him from that monastery in his contumacy.

I give to the aforesaid heir of mine, the holy church of Saint Peter of the monastery of Novalesa, lands [Col. 1300D] and vineyards, together with dependants, at Matanatis, which I possess from the inheritance of my parents and which Beroleus held as a benefice; I wish and command that it have them. I give to my faithful Protadius those properties in the district of Vuapencium where Semprugnanum is said to be, together with their appurtenances, which we acquired from Agloald; and that portion which we acquired from Maurengo the cleric because of his treachery, since he lied to us and we acquired it by the lord’s word [Col. 1301A], when he himself had lied to us; Palatius ceded those properties to us, and I wish Protadius to have them.

We give to Tersia, daughter of Honoria, our freedwoman, whom Teudaldus of Segucium had as his wife, those properties which belonged to Riculfus, formerly the son of Rodulfus, which, by the order of Lord King Theoderic [Note: [Col. 1301D] It is evident from this that Abbo lived under King Theoderic IV and Charles Martel. For Charles was himself that illustrious man called Martel, who, while Theoderic was still reigning, administered the affairs of the whole of Francia. See above, col. 1290, note b.] and of the illustrious lord Charles, we acquired in the districts of Diene, Vuapacium, and Gratianopolis, except for the estates in the district of Ebrodunum, at Velencium, which we assigned to the monastery of Saint Peter, my heir, since Riculfus joined himself to the Saracen people in betrayal of the kingdom of the Franks and committed many evils with that pagan people. I wish that Tersia should have those aforesaid possessions. And I wish that our freedmen, the sons of Vualane, together with those properties of that Vualane which we gave to my heir, the church of Saint Peter, should belong to it. I give to my heir, the church of Saint Peter, my freedwoman named Fredberga, the wife of Tasculfus, together with the grandchildren of that Fredberga, wherever they appear to dwell, at Etone or at Parelianum, so that their freedmen’s property may belong to that church; this I wish and command.

And it pleased me that an addition should be made to this page of my testament, since the proper provinces have been laid waste and destroyed by the attacks of the Saracens, and both our freedmen and the slaves and female slaves of both sexes have been scattered through many neighboring places out of necessity. I wish that, wherever the agents of my heir, the monastery of Saint Peter of Novalesa [Col. 1301C], are able to find them, they may have permission to recall them into their lordship without anyone’s opposition; and just as they belonged to our parents and to us, so I wish and command that they should belong to my heir, the church of Saint Peter of the monastery of Novalesa.

And I wish that our freedman Gislarannus and his wife, who came to us from Lady Siagria, together with those estates which we gave them at Comarius in the district of Gratianopolis, should have them and should belong to my heir, the monastery of Saint Peter of Novalesa. And those things which have not been named, which belong to our right and which we have assigned nowhere, I wish to come to my heir. And if any character-mark or writing is found on this page of my testament, we asked that it be made, since we requested him not once but repeatedly [Col. 1302A].

And I humbly beseech the lord princes, or all those in authority and the bishops, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who possess the power to rule and govern, that you permit in no way to be overturned or violated this disposition of our will which, by this testament, I have assigned to my heir, the church of Saint Peter of the monastery, for the support of the monks and the poor, so that it may contribute to the increase of your common reward.

And if anyone should hope rashly to act against this will of mine, which I asked to be written as the fullest expression of my devotion, and should become an assailant and refuse …, may he incur heavenly wrath, appear excommunicated from the communion of all the churches, and moreover pay to that holy place, my heir, together with the treasury, fifty pounds of gold [Col. 1302B]. What he claims, moreover, he shall not be able to recover or vindicate, this stipulation being added for complete security.

I, Abbo, subscribed to this testament made by me. Rusticius, most illustrious man, subscribed [Note: [Col. 1301D] In place of the word *subscribed*, here and below the chartulary contains lines in the form of monograms.] Magnabertus, most illustrious man, subscribed. Widbertus, most illustrious man, subscribed. Semphorianus, most illustrious man, subscribed. Vitalis, most illustrious man, subscribed.

### LXX. Charter by which Charles, mayor of the palace, gives the villa of Clippiacum to the basilica of Saint Denis

[Note: [Col. 1301D] It appears in Dublet, *History of the Abbey of Saint Denis*, p. 690, and in Félibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint Denis*, documentary section, p. 32, from the original; in Cointius, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 46, and in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 707, from Dublet. Besides these, Labbe, *Miscellany*, vol. II, p. 73; Michael Germain, in his treatise *On Royal Villas*, inserted in Mabillon’s *Diplomatic Art*, p. 275; the authors of the *New Diplomatic Art*, vol. V, p. 679; and Mabillon, who states that he inspected the autograph, *On Diplomatic Art*, p. 189, regarded this document as genuine. Nevertheless, Germon, *On the Ancient Royal Charters of France*, vol. II, p. 132, found it no less suspect, being repeatedly and excessively hostile to the documents of Saint Denis. It would be lengthy to examine arguments of lesser weight. It is enough to say that no indication of forgery follows from the fact that, in the charter of Charles the mayor of the palace, the formulas differ from those ordinarily used in the diplomas of the Merovingian kings. Germon himself admits that the unusual chronological notice displayed by Charles’s charter seems to him to have been taken from some genuine document—namely, one reckoned from the death of King Theoderic. [The autograph seen by Mabillon is not present in the royal archive.]] (year 741).

If we give something of our possessions to holy places, we undoubtedly trust that it will be repaid to us by the eternal Lord in eternal blessedness. Therefore I, in the name of God, Charles, illustrious man and mayor of the palace, formerly son of Pippin, for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and for the remission of my sins, so that I may thereafter deserve to obtain pardon for my offenses, give and wish to be forever given to the basilica of Saint Denis, where that precious lord rests bodily, a villa called Clippiacum [Note: [Col. 1302D] Michael Germain discusses at length the villa of Clippiacum, granted by this document to the basilica of Saint Denis, in the treatise cited above], situated in the district of Paris; with lands, houses, buildings, resident dependants, bondservants, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters [Note: [Col. 1302D] The word *waters* appears in Dublet and is omitted by Félibien], or watercourses, with livestock of both sexes, everything and from everything whatsoever seems to belong or pertain to that villa of Clippiacum. We give and cede all this in its entirety to the basilica of Saint Denis [Col. 1303A], so that from this day the aforesaid villa of Clippiacum may be in the free and most secure power of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Denis or of its agent, to possess, hold, or do whatever they may wish for the convenience of that monastery.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, or any of our heirs, or any opposing or foreign person, should wish to come or act against this charter of our gift, which we have decreed should be made and confirmed for the name of the Lord, or should wish thereby to raise any complaint against the people of Saint Denis, first let him incur the wrath of the heavenly God; and moreover let him be compelled to pay to the people of that monastery, the treasury enforcing it, ten pounds of gold and twenty pounds of silver [Col. 1303B], and let him be unable to recover or vindicate what he claims. But let this present charter of our gift remain firm and stable for all time, supported by stipulation.

Executed at the villa of Careciacum, in the palace, on the seventeenth day of September, in the fifth year after the death of King Theoderic [Note: [Col. 1303D] This charter is of considerable importance, for it shows that an interregnum of five years existed after the death of Theoderic IV, during which Charles alone ruled; hence, in public documents, it was necessary to count the years from the death of the last king, since no successor had followed him. Theoderic died in 737, around April; therefore the fifth year after his death, in September, coincided with the year of Christ 741.]. Sign of Charles, illustrious man and mayor of the palace, who caused this charter of gift to be made. + Sign of Radbertus, count. Sign of Raygaubaldus, count. Sign of Salaco, count. Sign of Sonechildis, illustrious matron, consenting. Sign of Grifo, her son, consenting. Sign of Hrodericus. Sign of Adabaldus. Sign of Deodatus. Sign of Helinebertus. Audoenus, chaplain, subscribed. I, Theoderic, subscribed. Crothgangus, ordered to do so, examined this charter of gift.

### LXXI. Charter by which Pippin, mayor of the palace, renews the charter of immunity granted to the church of Saint Vincent of Mâcon after it had been burned

[Note: [Col. 1303D] The authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. IV, documents, col. 263, published it from the Mâcon chartulary of Boherius. Labbe had published a fragment, *Miscellany*, vol. II, p. 443, and Severtius had made the complete charter public in his *Bishops of Mâcon*, under Bishop Domnolus. It was corrupt in several places, which Cointius restored; he reprinted it in *Annals*, vol. V, p. 77. We follow his text. This charter also appears in the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 703, taken from Cointius. [Col. 1304D] The year of Christ, approximately 743, was correctly placed in parentheses. For when Pippin, after the death of his father Charles the mayor of the palace, assumed administration of the Frankish kingdom in 741, the second year of his administration or principate, at the beginning of January, coincided with the year of Christ 743. The year marked in this charter must be understood as belonging to Pippin while he was still mayor of the palace, as is clear from Pippin’s subscription. Severtius, however, interprets it as referring to Pippin after he had already obtained the kingship, and therefore assigns the charter to the year 752. In this he is mistaken, as Cointius rightly argues, and we entirely agree with him.] (year 743).

[Col. 1303C]

In the name of God, Pippin, mayor of the palace. We believe that the memorial of our rule is increased if, after benevolent deliberation, we grant suitable benefits to ecclesiastical places, and, with the Lord protecting us, we trust that we shall securely advance it. Therefore let your prudence know that our faithful Domnolus, holding the episcopate of the holy see in the city of Mâcon, petitioned us on behalf of the clergy, in honor of Saint Vincent, saying that the immunity formerly made for that house of God [Col. 1304A] had been burned by fire in the preceding year through the negligence of its keeper. He asked us to renew or confirm that immunity, in our name, for that house of God. We did so with willing spirit out of reverence for that holy place. Moreover, we appeared to grant the following benefit for eternal recompense: in the villas of that church, which at the present time appear to be held by our grant or by anyone’s gift, or which divine piety may thereafter enlarge in the right of that place, no public judge shall ever presume to enter to hear cases or exact fines of any kind; and Domnolus, or his successors, shall be able to exercise full authority over that place under the complete title of immunity, for the name of God.

Therefore we decree that neither you, nor your subordinates, nor your successors, nor any public judicial authority, at any time, shall presume to enter the villas of that church—whether conveyed by the king’s generosity, by private generosity, or held previously—or to enter demesne houses to hear disputes, nor to take lodgings, provisions, or sureties [Col. 1304B]. But whatever the treasury may be able to expect from everywhere in the fields or boundaries or upon the lands occupied by the aforesaid church, by our indulgence and for future salvation, shall forever advance to the lights of that church through the hands of its agents. And what we have granted with full devotion for the name of the Lord and the remedy of our soul, and likewise for our descendants who shall follow us, neither royal majesty nor any judicial authority [Col. 1304C] shall attempt to oppose. But, so that this present authority may remain inviolable, with the Lord’s help, both for the present and future times, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscription of our hand.

Sign of Pippin, mayor of the palace. I, Rodolgus, ordered to do so, wrote it. Executed on the Kalends of January, in the second year of the principate of that same Pippin, in the city of Metz, in the royal palace.

### LXXII. Charter by which Felix the priest grants to the monastery of Sithiu a cell of Saint Michael in the district of Flanders

[Note: [Col. 1304D] Malbrancq took it from Folquin’s chartulary, *On the Morini*, vol. I, p. 580; Cointius reprinted it in *Annals*, vol. V, p. 168. This charter is mentioned in Iperius’s chronicle of Saint Bertin, in Martène, *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, vol. III, col. 484. From this it is clear that the preamble was omitted in the copy from which we published the charter. According to Iperius, the document began as follows: [Col. 1305D] “As the Lord says in the Gospel,” etc. Everyone knows that it was customary in this period to place such preambles at the beginning. Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 121, should also be consulted. He testifies that the gift conveyed by this charter was made on the condition that the donor’s name be inscribed in the book of life, which was likewise omitted here. Iperius copied exactly the chronological notes displayed by the copy we follow. These indicate the year of Christ 746, since the second year of the reign of Childeric III, reckoned from the beginning of March, coincides with the year of Christ 744, when the council of Soissons was convened, as we noted above (col. 1148). [See the complete text below.]] (year 745).

I, Felix, in the name of God, priest, by divine clemency’s inspiration and for the remedy of my soul, have assigned, granted, and transferred by this charter of gift to the monastery of Sithiu my cell at the place called Rochashem or Therealdus’s Grove, in the district of Flanders. I built it in honor of Saint Michael the archangel, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the other saints, after purchasing it from outside persons for a given price. We therefore ask the brothers and rectors of that monastery of Sithiu, for the Lord’s sake and in order to gain our reward, to take care of that cell which we have transferred there, with Masses, the liturgy, and lights; and they should show charity to guests and pilgrims and thereby obtain reward. Yet on this condition: as long as I live in this world, with Christ propitious, [Col. 1305B] I may lawfully possess that cell for the benefit of the monastery.

Executed publicly at the monastery of Sithiu, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the third year of the reign of our lord Childeric, glorious king. I, Felix, reread and subscribed this testament made by me. Sign of Chrodgarius, illustrious man. Sign of Rimbertus. Sign of Odbertus. Sign of Godobertus Guniuvinus. Sign of Waningus. Sign of Gontbertus. Sign of Chramnus. Sign of Erlarius. Sign of Clodbaldus. Sign of Clidebaldus. Sign of Guntharius, priest. Sign of Chereuvinus. Sign of Austroaldus, centenarius. Sign of Theodbertus. I, Vioradus, deacon, wrote and subscribed at his request.

### LXXIII. Charter by which Felix the priest grants to the monastery of Sithiu a cell of Saint Michael in the district of Flanders (complete text)

[Note: [Col. 1305D] A copy of this complete charter exists in the Royal Library, sent by D. de Witte, archivist of Saint Bertin, in 1782, and annotated in the hand of the distinguished de Brequigny so that it might be inserted among the additions. [Col. 1306D] Today a parchment copy is preserved at Ghent in the archive of East Flanders. It is reputed to have belonged to D. de Witte, and the learned Professor Warnkönig appended a specimen of it, in what we call lithography, to vol. I of the French edition of his *History of Flanders*. I believe it certain that the Royal Library copy was transcribed from the Ghent parchment, which in 1782 existed in the Saint-Bertin chartulary. I have placed within brackets certain variations of reading that can easily be attributed to the scribe’s carelessness. The same does not apply to the text found on p. 53 of the chartulary of Saint Bertin, published by the distinguished Guérard in 1841, which I shall reprint among the additions.] (year 745).

[Col. 1305C] As the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who gives little acquires the kingdom for himself, and he who gives a little money will receive a reward of glory that remains without end” [“a little money, he receives without end a measure”].

I [“Therefore I”], in the name of God, Felix the priest, by divine clemency’s inspiration and for the remedy of my soul, devoutly granted [“assigned and granted”] and transferred by this charter of gift to the monastery of Sithiu, which is in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Paul the apostles, and Saint Martin, and Saint [or Saint] Bertin the confessor, where that lord rests bodily and where the venerable man Nantharius appears to preside as abbot, my cell at the place called Hrochashem or Herualdus’s Grove, in the district of Flanders [Col. 1305D]. I built it in honor of Saint Michael [*Michahel*; variant *Michaelis*] [Col. 1306A] the archangel, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ (*Ihu Xpi*), and the other saints, with poor workmanship, after purchasing it from outside persons for a given price. Thus it pleased me [*mihi*; variant spelling *michi*], on such a condition [*tale ratione*; variant *tali ratione*] that we should transfer to that monastery of Sithiu, for the work of Saint Peter, the aforesaid cell, with its entire integrity and solidity, together with everything belonging or pertaining to it. And so we did: completely and perpetually, for possession, so that it may belong to and be subject to that monastery at all times, together with lands, manses, houses, buildings, bondservants, both freeborn and slaves, and the remaining fullness of its possessions, namely fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, livestock, defenses, movable and immovable goods—everything and from everything, the unexamined property, whatever can be said or named. From this day I give, deliver, and transfer all this perpetually to the brothers, or for the use of the monastery of Sithiu, for possession. After my death, let he who then exercises the office of abbot, or the brothers of the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu, do with it whatever they wish and deem suitable, and let them have secure power in all matters to place over it whatever provost they wish.

And, so that our reward may become more glorious with God in the future age, I earnestly implore, with most humble petition, the piety of the rectors and brothers, that they strive with every effort to maintain honorably the cell which I have subjected to our authority [*nostro jure*; variant *vestro jure*, “your authority”] by a bond of perpetual firmness [*conexione perpetuae firmitatis*; variant *conexione perpetua firmitatis*], with Mass, liturgy, and lights [Col. 1306C], and above all to provide for guests and pilgrims, so that they may thereby deserve to obtain a reward of eternal blessedness. But, as long as I live in this world, with Christ propitious, let me be permitted to possess that cell in ordinary use for the benefit of that monastery, on this condition: I shall have no power to give, sell, exchange, alienate, or cause to be wrecked (*naufragare*) elsewhere either that cell [*ipsam cellam*; variants *ipsa cella*] which I have transferred to that monastery or the properties belonging to that place. I therefore ask that the priests who dwell in that monastery deign to keep my name in the book of life [Note: [Col. 1306D] Consult Du Cange’s *Glossary* under the entries “Diptychs of the Living” and “Book of Life.”].

After my death and departure from this light, let the aforesaid cell, with all its improved and added possessions [Col. 1306D], be received in its entirety by the brothers of the aforesaid monastery of Sithiu [Col. 1307A], without opposition through anyone’s intimidation, into their right and dominion, for possession from the present day onward; and let them do with it whatever useful thing they choose.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or successors, or any foreign person of noble status, should attempt to act against this testament of gift or violate it, let him incur the wrath and judgment and offense of almighty God; and, with those holy apostles Peter and Paul and Saint Martin and Saint Bertin, to whom we have transferred this cell, let him render an account before the tribunal of Christ, and let him become excommunicated and estranged from their churches, unless he makes satisfaction thereafter through the severity of penance. Moreover, let him be compelled by the treasury to pay double the substance, whatever the improved cell shall then have been worth, or whatever I shall leave at my death [Col. 1307B], and let him be unable to recover or vindicate what he claims. But let this gift of my reward remain firm forever, supported by stipulation.

Executed publicly at the monastery of Sithiu, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the third year of the reign of our lord Childeric, most glorious king.

I, Felix, reread this testament made by me. + Sign of Chrodgarius, illustrious man. + Sign of Rimbertus. Sign + of Odbertus. + Sign of Godobertus. Sign + of Gumbertus. + Dramnius. + Erlulfus. + Clodbaldus. + Childebaldus. + Gumbarius, judge. + Cheriuunus. + Austroaldus, centenarius. + Gumardus. + Berdbertus. + Nordbertus. + Sign of Waningus. [Col. 1307C] + Sign of Gummuuvinus. + Sign of Widgrimus. (In the copy in the Royal Library the order of the names has been changed, but none is missing.)

I, Vioradus, wrote and subscribed this testament at the request of Felix the priest.

### LXXIV. Charter by which Carloman, mayor of the palace, grants gifts to the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy

[Note: [Col. 1307D] We publish this according to Martène, *Most Ample Collection*, vol. II, col. 20, who took the charter from the archive of Stavelot. The authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. IV, p. 713, reprinted it from Martène, as did Bertholet, *History of Luxembourg*, vol. II, documentary section, p. 36, who, in the absence of a year-date, thought that the year of Christ 746 should be prefixed. The name of Abbot Anglinus, however, fits this year poorly. In 746 it was not Anglinus but Agilulfus who presided over the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy, as Cointius demonstrated, *Annals*, vol. V, pp. 109 and 167. Perhaps Agilulfus’s name should be read in place of Anglinus’s, as we have noted elsewhere. See what we shall discuss more fully below concerning another charter of the same Carloman, to be assigned to the year 747. The document we now present appears to lack its preamble and the initial formula found, according to the custom of this period, in another charter of the same Carloman published below (col. 1310).] (year 746).
