Therefore I, Carloman, mayor of the palace, formerly son of Charles, give and wish to be forever given, as our alms, to our abbot Anglinus, for the monastery of Stavelot or Malmedy, built in honor of our patron Saint Peter and Saint Paul, and also Saint Martin and the other martyrs whose relics are known to be venerated there, where Anglinus is known, with Christ propitious, to preside as abbot: these are the villas whose names are Lenione, with all its appurtenances, in the district of Condruse; Caldina, Mosania, Warsipio and Barsina, and also Rudis, Pronote, Halma, and Haist in Gnoldo’s mansus, Solania.

Likewise, we have given and transferred from the present day to those houses of God the villa called Wadalino, with all its appurtenances—Rudis, Olisna, Serario, Palatiolo, and Brabant [Col. 1308A]—I, Carloman, for the sake of our soul and of Anglinus, so that it may please them better, for us and for the stability of our kingdom [Note: [Col. 1308D] This expression must not be understood as Carloman proclaiming himself king; it signifies only the administration of the kingdom], to pray more earnestly for the Lord’s mercy. This is on the condition that, as long as Anglinus lives, he shall cultivate those properties for his ordinary use; and if his nephew, named Gotbaldus, survives him, he shall, without prejudice and by the permission or consent of the said Unadelinus, hold or cultivate them for the monks; the subsequent reference to Unadelinus is corrupt or uncertain, without any diminution [Col. 1308B].

Thus, entirely and in full, I transfer and give all the foregoing to those monasteries, for the sake of our soul and of our abbot Anglinus: lands, buildings, resident dependants, bondservants, meadows, fields, pastures, waters and watercourses, appurtenances, dependencies, livestock of both sexes, movable and immovable goods, and also, in the aforesaid small places and manses, at Mosali and Barsena, whatever our men of Condruse origin—Adalinus, Agibertus, Bertegis, and Astremundus by name—held, together with those very men named above. Whatever Anglinus appears at the present time to hold there, and whatever he may thereafter cultivate, increase, or acquire there, shall belong to the aforesaid monasteries as our alms and his; after his departure, it shall return there without opposition [Col. 1308C].

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—should presume to act against this establishment of our transfer, we have left him to the judgment of our successors, the kings.

Done with stipulation attached, at the villa of Wasidio, publicly, on the sixth day of June, while King Childeric was reigning. Sign of Carloman, illustrious man and mayor of the palace. Sign of Drogo, illustrious man, his son, consenting. I, Hildradus, chancellor, wrote and subscribed this testament at his request.

### LXXV. Judgment by which Pippin, mayor of the palace, confirms a mansus at Marolium to the monastery of Saint Denis

[Note: [Col. 1308D] Mabillon took it from the Dionysian archive, *On Diplomatic Art*, p. 489; the compilers of the *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. IV, p. 713, reprinted it on Mabillon’s authority. [The autograph of this judgment is not present in the royal archive among the other documents of Saint Denis; and in the indexes of documents concerning that abbey it is recorded only from Mabillon.] Amalbertus, abbot of Saint Denis, is known solely from this testimony, as the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. VII, col. 343, admit. They, together with Mabillon, declare that this judgment was held in the year of Christ 748, as do Cointius, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 203, and Félibien, *History of the Abbey of Saint Denis*, p. 41. But the eleventh day of February, in the fifth year of the reign of Childeric III, as it appears in the chronological notes, seems rather to belong to the year of Christ 747, since we noted elsewhere that the second year of this reign, on the third day of March, coincided with the year of Christ 744. The old royal palace of Verno or Vernolium is discussed at length in D. Germain’s treatise *On Royal Villas*, *On Diplomatic Art*, book IV, p. 335 and following. Dublet mentions this judgment, *Antiquities of the Abbey of Saint Denis*, p. 691, but errs in copying the chronological notes and in the name of the palace, which he interprets as Vernon. [The distinguished Lebeuf, in a dissertation published among the *Miscellaneous Works* of 1768, vol. I, pp. 88 and following, demonstrates with strong arguments that the royal villa called Vernum in this judgment was not Vernolium on the Oise, as D. Germain had thought, but rather Ver or Vern, between Paris and Compiègne. In light of the same dissertation, an annotation should apparently be corrected in which the distinguished de Brequigny agrees with D. Germain that Cadolaicum and Latiniacum, places named in another judgment, were situated near Vernolium on the Oise. Abbot Lebeuf proves that these places are the same as those now called Chailly and Lagny-le-Sec. D. Bouquet agrees with him, in the notes on pp. 685 and [Col. 1310C] 686 of vol. IV of the *Writers of the Affairs of Gaul and France.]] (year 747).

[Col. 1308D]

When Pippin, illustrious man and mayor of the palace, had taken his seat at Verno, in the public palace, to hear everyone’s cases [Col. 1309A] and settle them by just judgment, a woman named Christiana came there and brought a complaint against a certain man named Hrodgarius, advocate of Saint Denis, and against Amalbertus the abbot. She demanded from him the return of what the house of Saint Denis or Abbot Amalbertus held wrongfully: at the place called Marolium, a house, a mansus, vineyards, and bondservants.

But Hrodgarius himself was present and gave this answer: he had documents showing that Witgaudius had donated those properties to the house of Saint Denis with full authority. Accordingly, he presented the document before us for rereading, and we found the documents truthful. Afterward Christiana appeared to have acknowledged that document and then declared herself to have withdrawn from those properties [Col. 1309B], so that she should thereafter make no counterclaim against the house of Saint Denis.

Therefore, together with our faithful men—namely Haginus, Theudebertus, Remedius, Garehardus, Fulgarius, Bovilo, Walcherius, Rauchingus, and Ermenaldus, our count of the palace, together with many others—we appeared to have judged as follows: because the aforesaid Christiana had appeared to acknowledge that document, because we found it truthful, and because Christiana declared herself withdrawn from those properties, we therefore order that, since this case had been conducted and concluded in this manner, Hrodgarius shall forever hold and vindicate against Christiana, in the case of Saint Denis, the mansus named above at Marolium—the mansus and house, vineyards, lands, and bondservants—having inspected his testament; and thereafter let the litigation between them concerning this matter be ended [Col. 1309C].

Issued in the month of February, on the eleventh day, in the fifth year of King Childeric. Wilecharius, ordered to do so, examined it.

### LXXVI. Record in which Carloman, mayor of the palace, restores to the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy the estate of Lethernau, with its appurtenances, which had been donated by his grandfather and then unjustly taken away  
*[Note: [Col. 1310C] Published by Martenius, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. II, col. 19, from the archive of Stavelot; Bertholetus, *History of Luxembourg*, vol. II, p. 39, and the collectors of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 712, reprinted it from Martenius. The date indicates the year 747 of Christ; Cointius, however, *Annals*, vol. V, p. 109, therefore calls the charter’s authenticity into question. For there Anglinus is called abbot of Stavelot and Malmedy; but at this time, says Cointius, ibid., p. 166, Agilulf was in charge of both monasteries, and from there he was called to the bishopric of Cologne [Col. 1310D] in that very year. The authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. III, col. 941, seem to support Cointius. It is difficult to escape these difficulties unless one says that the name Anglinus, otherwise unknown, was corrupted, and that the name Agilulf was altered into Anglinus, as we conjectured elsewhere. It remains to make it probable that, through a persistently repeated error, the name Anglinus was substituted for Agilulf’s name in three documents. These three documents may, moreover, be considered to have been taken from some cartulary, and in the originals the name Agilulf may have been written in such a way that it appeared to the cartulary scribe to have the form of the name Anglinus; once he had erred in a doubtful reading, he readily erred repeatedly in the same way. Certainly it is clear either that the originals were extremely difficult to read, or that the person who copied these three documents was entirely inexperienced in reading old charters, since the copies in question are disgracefully filled with innumerable errors of writing.]* (year 747).

[Col. 1310A]

The illustrious Carloman, mayor of the palace, son of the late Charles, to whom the Lord has entrusted the care of governing. It is necessary to examine carefully the disputes of all, so that a salutary judgment may not be granted to either party unless justice has approved it.

Therefore, when we, in the name of God, together with our nobles and bishops and illustrious men, were seated at Dunavilla to hear all cases and investigate just judgments, Anglinus, abbot and rector of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy, came before us and asserted, saying [Col. 1310B] that our lord and grandfather, the late Pippin, by his testament had donated or assigned to the house of Saints Peter and Paul, Stavelot and Malmedy, a certain estate called Lethernau, together with its appurtenances and adjacent lands, whose names are Brastis, Feronio, Unalia, and Aldanias, and that we were now retaining that estate after his death in an improper and unjust manner. He also affirmed that he had the testament in his possession; and when he had handed it over to us for rereading, we found it genuine.

We, considering with justice the condition of human frailty, for the salvation of our soul and the stability of our kingdom, appeared to have restored the estate of Lethernau, together with its appurtenances and adjacent lands, to Abbot Anglinus by our pledge, and by our staff [Col. 1310C] to have delivered everything to him.

Accordingly, together with our faithful men—namely Fenaldus, Hildeboldus, Hrodericus, the bishops Christianus, Abbot Ermenerus, and Hugbert, our count of the palace, along with very many others—we appeared to have judged as follows: since we have recognized that this case was thus conducted and completed, and since we have found the testament itself to be genuine, we therefore order that the said lord Abbot Anglinus, or his successors or the rectors of those monasteries, shall possess the estate of Lethernau, together with its appurtenances, in complete integrity and in perpetual right, for those monasteries. If, however, any one of our heirs or successors should arise who wishes to act against this donation of ours, we leave him to be judged by the kings who succeed us.

Given on the fifteenth day of August, in the fifth year of the reign of King Childeric.

Sign of Carloman, mayor of the palace.

I, Childradus, have subscribed.

---

### LXXVII. Charter by which Bodalus donates to the monastery of Saint Gregory whatever he possesses in the estate of Hodulseshaim  
*[Note: [Col. 1311C] It appears in Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum continuatum*, vol. I, p. 1096, and in Martenius, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 8, taken from the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Gregory in Alsace, but mutilated in its opening wording, where the words enclosed in brackets are missing. Schoepflinus restored them, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 16, and reprinted this charter [Col. 1311D] from the same cartulary, more accurately copied. We follow his reading, placing in brackets the alternative readings that he himself transcribed. Martenius places Bodalus’s charter under the year 746 of Christ, incorrectly: for when, in the second year of the reign of Childeric III, the year 744 of Christ was running in March, as we said above (Col. 1148), the year 746 of Christ had already been completed in December of the sixth year of that reign. Schoepflinus therefore more correctly assigns this document to the year 747 of Christ. This Bodalus seems to be the same person who is called Bodolus in another charter to be published below (Col. 1818).]* (year 747).

[Col. 1311B]

It is fitting that everyone, while living in this life in this [mortal body, should strive to think, as long as it is permitted, about the future life, where he hopes to live immortally and forever]. Therefore I, Bodalus, son of the late Hugo, for eternal blessedness and the forgiveness of my sins, make this donation for the remedy of my soul and for the soul of my son Gherhanus [or Egerhandus], to the monastery of Saint Gregory and of the other saints, which is built in the Vosges between the two rivers called the Pachina, where, in the name of God, Abbot Agoaldus, together with the monks dwelling there, appears to serve according to the rule. I wish what has been donated to remain there forever [Col. 1311C]: namely, in the estate or territory of Hodulseshaim, whatever I appear to possess there—that is, houses, house-sites, granaries, buildings, structures, vineyards, slaves, lands, fields, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, and whatever Balduinus and his wife have rendered to us—all of it completely and in its entirety. From the present day I hand over and transfer it to that holy place, so that from this day the aforesaid property may be held, retained, and possessed by that house of God or its community, and, with Christ’s favor, left to their successors [Col. 1312A], with free power in every respect to do whatever they wish.

If I [or: therefore], or my heirs, or any opposing person should attempt to act against this donation made by me or wish to violate it, then I [or: they] shall pay to you and your successors double the amount claimed, with the royal treasury receiving two ounces of gold; and nevertheless this present donation shall always remain firm, supported by stipulation.

Executed in the monastery of Confluentis, publicly issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth year of the reign of our lord King Childeric. (The numerical date is missing in another copy.)

Sign of Bodalus, who requested that this donation be made. [Col. 1312B] Sign of Hucbertus [or Excambertus]. Sign of Excombertus. Sign of Starculfus [or Strarculfus]. Sign of Ghisalmondus. Sign of Libulfus. Sign of Haimbertus. Sign of Warinulfus. Sign of Herchambertus. Sign of Sighertamnus [or Sigertmannus]. Sign of Bebo [or Belo]. I, Rodaccius, wrote and subscribed at his request.

---

### LXXVIII. Charter by which Boronus makes a donation to the monastery of Honau  
*[Note: [Col. 1311D] Published by Mabillonius, *Annals*, vol. II, appendix, p. 696, from an eleventh-century manuscript. Eccardus, *Origins of the Habsburgs*, proofs, p. 101, and Schaepflinus, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 20, reprinted it from a fifteenth-century manuscript of the collegiate church of Saint Peter the Elder; finally Abbot Grandidier, *Ecclesiastical History of Strasbourg*, vol. I, proofs, p. 70, reproduced it more accurately from the same manuscript and from a sixteenth-century cartulary preserved in the archive at Saverne. We follow this most diligent copyist’s readings [Col. 1312C]. Boronus’s other charter, issued for the benefit of the same monastery, was published above (Col. 1280). Dubanus, who is here said to preside over the monastery of Honau, seems to some authorities—namely, the authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. V, col. 833, Mabillonius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 59, and others—to be different from Tubanus, [Col. 1312D] the abbot of the same monastery, whom we discussed above. The author of the *History of Alsace*, cited above, considers Tubanus and Dubanus to be one and the same person, and we willingly agree with him. We are led to this by the similarity of the names; nor do the intervals of time stand in the way. Dubanus is indeed called a bishop, whereas Tubanus is said to have lacked this title; but abbots were sometimes called bishops, not because they occupied an episcopal see, but because they performed an episcopal function in their monastery. This was not unusual in that period. The year 748 of Christ was running in April, according to our method of reckoning the years of Childeric III’s reign, which we have discussed several times.]* (year 748).

To the most holy monastery of the archangel Saint Michael, and of the other saints, Peter and Paul, which is built within the island of Honau, where, in the name of God, Bishop Dubanus appears to preside.

I, Boronus, an illustrious man, considering the condition of my frailty and for eternal reward, donate to the aforesaid monastery and wish this donation to remain forever. Namely, within the district called Gamhbapine, one hide which Wolvinus held, with its house-sites, fields, meadows, woods, all its appurtenances, buildings, and pastures.

Likewise I donate to the aforesaid holy place my portion, which is Niuzwern—that is, lands, woods, meadows, and pastures. Likewise I donate to the same holy place my portion of the aforementioned island of Honau [Note: [Col. 1312D] It was stated above under what title Baronus held a portion in the island of Honau. In the charter of 726, above (Col. 1280), he had already donated certain parts of this portion, though not the whole, to the monastery of Saint Michael. He now donates the remainder in the charter under discussion.]. I hand over and transfer all of this, completely and in its entirety, from the present day to that most holy monastery, so that from this day the agents of the aforesaid monastery and their descendants may have in the name of God free and most secure power to do whatever they wish with the property.

If I, or my heirs, or any claimant should arise, let him pay to the aforesaid monastery and its custodians, together with the associated royal treasury, three ounces of gold; and nevertheless this present donation shall remain firm, supported by stipulation.

Executed publicly at the castle of Mandouro. Sign of Boronus, who requested that this donation be made and confirmed. Sign of Cantsoaldus. Sign of Milo, witness. Sign of Wolferahus. Sign of Audebertus, witness. I, Wachyndus the deacon, in the name of God, wrote and subscribed at his request.

This donation was given on the Tuesday immediately following the middle of April, in the sixth year of the reign of our lord King Childeric.

---

### LXXIX. Charter by which Hugo makes donations to the monastery of Honau  
*[Note: [Col. 1313D] Mabillonius, *Annals*, vol. II, appendix, p. 696, took this from an eleventh-century manuscript; Eccardus, *Origins of the Habsburgs*, p. 101, reprinted it from Mabillonius; Schoepflinus, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 21, from a fifteenth-century manuscript; and Abbot Grandidier, *Ecclesiastical History of Strasbourg*, vol. I, proofs, p. 71, more accurately from the same manuscript and from a sixteenth-century cartulary preserved in the archive at Saverne. Mabillonius, Eccardus, and Schoepflinus omit the clause by which Hugo donates his portion in the district of Odradesheim to the monastery of Honau. Was it rashly inserted by more recent editors? We discussed Bishop Dubanus in our notes to the immediately preceding charter.]* (year 748).

To the most holy church of Saint Michael, which is built on the island called Honau, where Bishop Dubanus appears at present to preside.

I, Hugo, in the name of God, considering that, with God’s favor, I ought to give something of my possessions to that holy place—and I have indeed done so—namely, within the island called Honau, whatever my father Bleonus, when dying, left me there, that is, within the island itself: lands, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, plots of ground, and trees. This is given on the condition that from the present day these possessions remain forever established and secure for that holy place.

Likewise I donate to that holy place my entire portion in the district of Odradesheim, with lands, meadows, and pastures.

If I, or my heirs, or any opposing person should attempt to act or proceed against this testament of donation, or should presume to raise any claim—which I do not believe will happen—then I, or my heirs, promise that we shall restore to you or your successors double the amount written in this charter, within the island itself [Col. 1313D], and five gold solidi to the most sacred treasury [Col. 1314A]. And this donation shall remain established and secure forever, supported by stipulation.

Executed publicly on the island of Honau. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the sixth year of our lord King Childeric.

Sign of Hugo, who requested that this testament of donation be made. Sign of Gaozbertus. Sign of Agynus. Sign of Theodoaldus. Sign of Theothelmus. Sign of Amaloinus. Sign of Otho. I, Amalgerus, wrote this testament of donation.

### LXXX. Charter by which Heddo, bishop of Strasbourg, confirms the donations granted to the monastery of Arnulfsau by Rothardus and others, and grants privileges  
*[Note: [Col. 1313D] The authors of the *New Christian Gaul*, vol. V, documents, col. 458, had published this in a very fragmentary form. Schoepflinus published it without gaps, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 17, from an original preserved in the archive of the bishop of Strasbourg and written in Merovingian cursive script [Col. 1314D]; he also had a specimen of the original engraved on copper. Abbot Grandidier likewise transcribed it from the original, *Ecclesiastical History of Strasbourg*, vol. I, proofs, p. 72. Both present this document complete, from a torn parchment, but successfully restored with the aid of Widegern’s charter, which we published above (Col. 1281) and which is composed in the same formulas. The name Heddo was corrupted in many ways, as Schoepflinus showed in the work cited above. He thinks Heddo was the brother of Odilia, whose testament may be seen above; he believes that Count Rothardus held the county of Lower Alsace. The monastery of Arnulfsau, originally founded in Lower Alsace, as Heddo’s charter makes clear, was transferred by Louis the Pious in 826 to Ortenau, on the river Schwarzach, from which it received its new name.]* (year 748).

To the holy lords and those most worthy of honor [thus in the copper-engraved plate; Schoepflinus reads *dignissima*, “most worthy”; *dignissimis*, “most worthy ones,” is better], my apostolic and spiritual fathers in Christ: Heddo, by the grace of God called bishop of the church and mother church in the city of Strasbourg.

Let your holy diligence know how carefully and with what supreme effort the shepherds of the Church ought to labor so that the Church of God may advance through the gain of souls and, through our salutary admonitions, receive strength insofar as we are able to provide it. This is for those who, having voluntarily abandoned everything for the sake of the eternal Shepherd, desire to follow him, denying themselves and walking along the narrow path and constricted way, hearing the voice of our eternal King and Redeemer: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and go into the land that I shall show you”; and also: “Whoever leaves father or mother or children or fields and the rest for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life”; and: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”

We ought to heed him who said: “I was a stranger and you welcomed me”; and: “Whoever receives you receives me”; and: “As long as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me.” Thus, what was instituted by the prince of the apostles at the beginning of the Church was that the whole multitude of believers was one, and no one claimed anything to be his own, but everything was held in common by them, and they had one heart and one soul.

From this holy institution the holy Fathers later promulgated, from East to West and throughout the regions of Gaul, a celebrated religious life, establishing many monasteries under a holy rule in accordance with this example—especially the monasteries of Lérins, Agaunum, and Luxeuil—and throughout the world arranging communal life excellently under the rule of the holy Fathers, especially the blessed Benedict and Saint Columbanus, abbots; this was firmly strengthened by the authority and clemency of kings and by the privileges of holy and catholic bishops. The sacred canons do not detract from this but rather strongly encourage it.

Therefore, we have learned that the illustrious man Rothardus, count, has attempted, with God’s help and our counsel, to build anew, on his own property, a monastery in honor of the holy apostles, Saint Mary the Mother of God, and the other saints, on an island called Arnulfsau, beside the river Rhine, within our diocese. He has summoned Abbot Saroardus with his foreign monks so that there, in a coenobium and holy order [Col. 1315B] under the rule of blessed Benedict, they might complete it with God’s grace and our assistance.

Therefore, rejoicing in this man’s holy devotion and glorious purpose, moved by heartfelt charity and piety, and with the most ready devotion, together with the consent of our brother abbots, priests, the archdeacon, and all the clergy of the church in which I serve, as well as the dukes, judges, and the God-fearing Catholic people of this province, we ought to draw up and confirm by our authority and yours a privilege for that monastery, coenobium, and community of foreign monks. This we have indeed done, so that to that monastery everything belonging to its jurisdiction—buildings, basilicas, furnishings and ornaments, sacred books, instruments and charters, gold, silver, bronze, and every other possession of that monastery, its cells, or its appurtenances, including estates with fields, houses, male and female slaves, inhabitants, and whatever the aforesaid illustrious Rothardus or others have donated or assigned in any manner for the salvation of their souls, as well as whatever he himself or the munificence of kings, princes, bishops, clergy, or any person inspired by Christ may hereafter bestow—we confirm in its entirety through this privilege.

From the present day, therefore, we deliver and entrust all these possessions to the said monastery, the foreign monks, and their successors, gathered together in community under the rule of Saint Benedict according to their holy purpose, to be held by their right, without any claim from anyone. Neither we ourselves, nor the bishops who succeed us in this city, nor archdeacons, nor officials, nor anyone on behalf of the church, nor any other person, shall ever presume to exercise lordship over anything, issue orders, demand dues or gifts, or exact any kind of offering.

Whenever it is necessary to request chrism, confirm altars, confer holy orders, seek any blessings, or build oratories in their places, the rector of that monastery or the foreign monks residing there may request whichever bishop they have among themselves, or whichever holy bishop they choose for themselves, to perform these acts. He shall be permitted to deliver, bless, or consecrate them, and no one shall presume to enter that monastery unlawfully against their will or decision, nor secretly enter its enclosures.

If at any time, for whatever reason, the rector or foreign monks should desire it and the bishop, having been invited, should come to the monastery, then, after the service has been celebrated, the abbot shall give that bishop, in his honor, a *camputta* and *subtelaria* [Note: [Col. 1315D] Schoepflinus, *Alsatian Diplomas*, cited above, read *seu telariis*. Abbot Grandidier correctly emends this to *subtelaria*, *Ecclesiastical History of Strasbourg*, vol. I, proofs, p. 74 n.; namely, footwear worn by bishops performing sacred rites [Col. 1316D]. We follow this reading conjecturally; for Widegern’s charter, although similar in other respects, offers no support for it, since it lacks this clause.].

When the abbot of that place has died, the foreign monks living there shall choose from among themselves, according to God and their rule, whichever person they find, and appoint him abbot for themselves. If they do not find among themselves such a person, they shall obtain and appoint as their regular abbot someone from another monastery of that congregation of foreign monks whom one manner of petition and the one holy institution of blessed Benedict have united, with their own consent. If the holy order should grow lukewarm there—which God forbid—or if any discord should arise among the monks and they should be unable or unwilling to correct it, then whichever of them, according to the rule, wishes to live in the rector’s order may have the power to seek another monastery wherever the aforesaid foreign monks are dwelling and where they find a more correct and regular life. Those monks, through their salutary counsel and with God’s help, shall cause the holy order and those monks to be restrained, amended, corrected, and pacified according to the rule.

No occasion shall exist for another abbot to be placed there by any device against their holy order, or for anything to be diminished from the possessions of the aforesaid monastery.

Therefore, holy and apostolic fathers and my fellow brothers, we join your catholic authority with ours in a twofold bond, so that this privilege may possess the strongest force forever, and so that no one may ever presume to act against it, but that it may remain inviolate for future times. I now urge, implore, and dare to adjure, through charity, all bishops and God-fearing men that, when this privilege is shown to them, they may deign to subscribe and confirm it with their hands, so that, supported by your authority, it may remain unshaken, and so that the foreign monks residing in that monastery may more freely pray to divine mercy for the welfare of the Church and the integrity of priests, for the safety of kings and the peace of Christians, for the remission of penitents’ sins, and for the repose of the faithful departed.

Therefore I urge and testify before God and his blessed angels and all the saints, and before successors and all Christians, that they not presume in any way to violate this privilege, which we have decreed and granted with the consent of the clergy, the laity, the God-fearing people, and our church. Rather, we adjure all through the ineffable Trinity to preserve it in every respect insofar as they are able.

If, however, with stubborn mind, or at the devil’s instigation, deceived by envy or greed, or in any manner—which God avert—we ourselves or our successors, or anyone from any side, should attempt to act against this privilege, or should presume to disturb the aforesaid foreign monks or their successors, or diminish anything belonging to them; if he should refuse to amend his conduct and refuse to correct himself promptly from his evil will, then, with the Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, and the blessed apostles and all the saints, before the sight of the eternal King, Christ our Lord, in whose love we have granted this privilege to the aforesaid foreign monks and coenobium, let him expect to be burned in eternal fires for his most wicked sins and most iniquitous malice, and to suffer the sentence with which the Lord threatens false priests:

“Woe to you, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of God, because you yourselves do not enter, nor permit others to enter”; and: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone were tied around his neck and he were thrown into the depths of the sea.”

And whoever has neglected the fear of God shall, when judged by men, pay to the monastery and the foreign monks dwelling there, together with the royal treasury, thirty pounds of gold and fifty pounds of silver as a penalty, and shall bear and discharge it; and he shall not recover what he has claimed. Nevertheless, this present privilege shall remain firm forever. And, so that it may possess still greater force, we have subscribed with our hands and requested those who would subscribe or sign to do so, with stipulation attached.

Executed publicly in the city of Strasbourg, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the seventh year of the reign of our lord King Childeric.

*[Note: [Col. 1317C] We have the subscriptions engraved on copper from the original in Schoepflinus, plate opposite p. 17. Abbot Grandidier transcribed them in another order [Col. 1317D]; this is not surprising, since in the original they are mixed together, so that no order governed by a definite rule can be established in copying them. They all seem to have been written by the subscribers’ own hands, as may be inferred from the different script of each person: some are in minuscule script, others in capitals, and most in cursive. The names of abbots and bishops are mixed together, and no one adds the name of his church; Schoepflinus, however, derived the names of almost all the churches from other records, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 19 n., which should be consulted. He notes that Lullo subscribed under the name of a bishop; he was indeed bishop of Mainz, but had not yet obtained the episcopal insignia when the charter under consideration was drawn up. [Col. 1318C] We have noted elsewhere that this was customary in that period, so that bishops would add their names to documents composed long before, either as a mark of honor or for confirmation [Col. 1318D].]*

I, Heddo, a sinner in the name of God, called bishop by God’s mercy, have read and subscribed this privilege made by me.

+ In the name of God, I, Baldobertus, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Dubanus, bishop, subscribed at the request of others.

Chrodegangus, sinner and bishop, have subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Hiddo, a sinful bishop called to the episcopate, have subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Lullo, a sinful bishop, have subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Magingaoz, an unworthy bishop, have confirmed it by subscribing.

In the name of God, I, Gutfridus, a sinful bishop, have subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Remedius, a sinner and bishop, God’s gift, have subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Gayroinus, abbot, have subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Yppolitus, a sinful abbot, have subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Nitho, at the request of the aforesaid bishop, wrote and subscribed.

I, Hysamnus, a sinful bishop, have subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Jacob, a called abbot, have subscribed.

### LXXXI. Charter by which Bodolus makes donations to the monastery of Honau on the island of Honau  
*[Note: [Col. 1318D] Published from an old manuscript by Mabillonius, *Annals*, vol. II, appendix, p. 697; from Mabillonius by Eccardus, *Origins of the Habsburgs*, p. 102; by Schoepflinus, *Alsatian Diplomas*, vol. I, p. 21, from a fourteenth-century manuscript preserved in the collegiate church of Saint Peter the Elder; and finally by Abbot Grandidier, *Ecclesiastical History of Strasbourg*, vol. I, proofs, p. 77, from the same manuscript and from a sixteenth-century cartulary kept in the archive at Saverne. We reprint it on the authority of the latter. Bodolus, son of Hugo, who is discussed here, seems to Mabillonius, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 146, to be the same person who is called Bodalus in the charter presented above (Col. 1311).]* (year 748).

To the most holy church of Saint Michael, which is built on the island called Honau, where, in the name of God, Abbot Dubanus appears to preside.

Therefore I, Bodolus, make this donation for the remedy of my soul to that holy place, and wish what has been donated to remain there forever. Namely, on the river Rhine, in the aforesaid island of Honau, whatever my father, the late Hugo, left me there when he died, together with land, woodland, and marshland, in my entire share: from the present day I hand over and transfer it to that holy place, so that from this day that church or its agents may hold, retain, and possess the property, and, with Christ’s favor, leave it to their successors.

If I, or my heirs, or any opposing person should attempt to act against this donation made by me [Col. 1318C] or wish to violate it, then we shall pay to you and your successors double the amount contained and written in this donation, together with the royal treasury, three ounces of gold; and nevertheless this present donation shall remain firm forever, supported by stipulation.

Executed publicly at the monastery of Suraburg.

Given in the month of October, on the twelfth day, in the seventh year of the reign of our lord King Childeric.

Sign of Bodolus, who requested that this donation be made. Sign of Hugo. Sign of Gauzbertus. Sign of Theodoradus. Sign of Graodobardus. Sign of Theodichonus. Sign of Wolfebertus. Sign of Burgoaldus. Wanulfus wrote at the request of others.

TABLE OF THE CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME.

Dedicatory Letter. 9  
Preface. Ibid.  
Life of Venantius Fortunatus. 19

FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS.

## Prologue (to Saint Gregory of Tours)

Fortunatus excuses himself in this letter to Gregory, who had strongly urged and adjured him to publish his poems, collected into a single volume, pleading his own inexperience and the affairs that had occupied him and prevented him from polishing them sufficiently. At last he yields to Gregory’s request, declaring that Gregory’s benevolence and goodwill toward him had proved stronger than his own fear and modesty. Taking the opportunity, he describes the journey he had undertaken from Italy to Gaul. 59

## Book One of Miscellanies

Ibid.

### Chapter One (to Vitalis, bishop of Ravenna)

In this poem he relates that the basilica of Saint Andrew had been built and dedicated by Vitalis. He commemorates the solemnity of the dedication itself and the people’s exceptional devotion and affection toward Vitalis. 63

### Chapter Two

He recounts that the same basilica of Saint Andrew was built and completed within a short time through Vitalis’s great zeal and generosity. He lists the sacred relics by which it was distinguished. 65

### Chapter Three

He describes the triumph and glory of Saint Stephen, the protomartyr, in undergoing death for Christ; Palladius had dedicated a basilica in his memory. 67

### Chapter Four

In this poem he celebrates the basilica erected in honor of Saint Martin by Bishop Faustus and made renowned by religious devotion. Ibid.

### Chapter Five

In this poem he celebrates the generosity of Saint Martin of Tours in removing his own tunic and then clothing a needy man with it; at the same time he commends the sanctity of the place where this occurred. Ibid.

### Chapter Six

He commends the generosity and religious devotion of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, in constructing the basilica of Saint Martin, and of Placidina, formerly his wife, in adorning it. He then describes the pleasant setting in which it had been built. 68

### Chapter Seven

He commemorates the temple in honor of Saint Martin restored by Basil and his wife, after the waters that covered the site of the building had been diverted elsewhere. 69

### Chapter Eight

The martyrdom and glory of Saint Vincent of Agen. Leontius’s generosity toward his basilica. Ibid.

### Chapter Nine

The aforementioned basilica is celebrated. The healing of a possessed person is attributed to the dedication of the same basilica. 71

### Chapter Ten

He celebrates the basilica erected by Leontius in memory of the martyr Saint Nazarius, as well as the martyr’s own triumph. 72

### Chapter Eleven

The praises of Saint Dionysius of Paris, and of his basilica enlarged by Leontius. Ibid.

### Chapter Twelve

The basilica of Saint Bibianus, bishop of Saintes, had been begun by Eusebius and completed by Leontius, with Placidina, formerly Leontius’s wife, contributing no small amount to the undertaking. Their piety and munificence are commended. 74

### Chapter Thirteen

He relates that the basilica of Saint Eutropius was restored and adorned by Leontius, not without divine admonition and guidance. 76

### Chapter Fourteen

He commemorates the chalice offered to the sacred church by Leontius and Placidina. 77

### Chapter Fifteen

He celebrates Leontius’s nobility, episcopal rank, and pious generosity, adding praises of Placidina. Ibid.

### Chapter Sixteen

When a certain man, aspiring to Leontius’s see, falsely spread the report that Leontius, who was absent, had died, and Leontius unexpectedly returned, Fortunatus celebrated his return in this poem. 80

### Chapter Seventeen

From the island where he was living, Fortunatus sends little gifts to Placidina, relating that, while sailing against the north wind, he had landed at Placidina’s own home. 83

### Chapter Eighteen

He describes the pleasantness of Bissonum, an estate situated in the territory of Bordeaux, and mentions the buildings restored and adorned by Leontius. Ibid.

### Chapter Nineteen

He celebrates the location and appearance of Vereginum, as well as the buildings restored by Leontius. 84

### Chapter Twenty

Passing through Praemiacum, Leontius’s estate, Fortunatus celebrates it as enlarged by Leontius with new buildings. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-One

He describes the character and changing features of the river Egircius. 85

[Col. 1344]

## Book Two of Miscellanies

87

### Chapter One

On the power and dignity of the Lord’s cross. Ibid.

### Chapter Two

A hymn in honor of the holy cross. 88

### Chapter Three

He celebrates the power and worth of the cross, as well as Gregory of Tours’s devotion toward it, commending Gregory’s generosity in adorning an oratory at Tours. 89

### Chapter Four

On the sign of the holy cross. 91

### Chapter Five

On the holy cross. 93

### Chapter Six

Also on the holy cross. 95

### Chapter Seven

A hymn in honor of the holy cross. Ibid.

### Chapter Eight

On holy baptism. 96

### Chapter Nine

In praise of chrism. 97

### Chapter Ten

A hymn to Saint Dionysius. 98

### Chapter Eleven

On the lord Saturninus. 99

### Chapter Twelve

He declares his zeal in celebrating the deeds of the martyrs. He describes the martyrdom of Saint Saturninus. He praises Duke Launebodus and his wife because, through their generosity, a basilica had been built in memory of that saint. 100

### Chapter Thirteen

He declares that he had long since grown unaccustomed to writing poems. Nevertheless, when challenged, he celebrates the various qualities of the Parisian clergy, especially those of Saint Germanus, the bishop. 102

### Chapter Fourteen

He raises the praise of the Parisian basilica dedicated in honor of the holy cross above Solomon’s Temple. He commends Childebert for his generosity toward it. 104

### Chapter Fifteen

On the baptistery at Mainz. 105

### Chapter Sixteen

He commemorates the basilica of Saint George built by Bishop Sidonius and commends the glory of that martyr, renowned in the West. 107

### Chapter Seventeen

He treats in verse the oratory built by Trasaric in honor of Saints Peter and Paul, Saint Martin of Tours, and Saint Remedius. Ibid.

### Chapter Eighteen

He sings of the triumph of Saint Maurice and his companions. 108

### Chapter Nineteen

The steadfastness of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, against the Arians is celebrated. 109

### Chapter Twenty

On the holiness and miracles of Saint Medard, bishop of Noyon; also on the basilica in his honor begun by Chlothar and completed by Sigebert. 110

### Chapter Twenty-One

The praises of Saint Martial, the first bishop of Limoges. 115

## Book Three of Miscellanies

Ibid.

### Chapter One

Having received a letter from Euphronius, he tells him how much joy he had felt on that account. He extols Euphronius’s remarkable humility and commends himself to his prayers. Ibid.

### Chapter Two

Again he expresses his gratitude to Euphronius, praising the benefits he had conferred upon him. He develops various virtues of Euphronius and asks him to intercede with God for his sins. 117

### Chapter Three

He congratulates Euphronius on his virtues, especially his pastoral concern and diligence. 118

### Chapter Four

He tells Felix, bishop of Nantes, that he had been struck by the eloquence and grandiloquence of Felix’s letter. He exalts him, attempting to repay the praises he had received from him, and expresses his most ardent longing for Felix’s presence. 119

### Chapter Five

He writes to the same man and relates that through Felix’s efforts and faith the Breton forces had been put to flight. 124

### Chapter Six

He writes to the same man, praising his zeal in constructing and consecrating a basilica in honor of Saints Peter and Paul. He describes the dedication itself. Ibid.

### Chapter Seven

The praises of the saints whose relics had been deposited in the basilica at Nantes. A description of the same basilica. 126

### Chapter Eight

Writing to Felix, he praises him for the antiquity and nobility of his family, as well as for his virtue and pastoral concern. 128

### Chapter Nine

Writing to the same man, he celebrates the Easter festivals and consecrates in verse Felix’s diligence in winning the Saxon people. 130

### Chapter Ten

He celebrates Felix’s most costly work in diverting the course of a river and describes the resources that would thereby come to the neighboring peoples. 134

### Chapter Eleven

He praises Nicetius, bishop of Trier, for his innocence, mercy, generosity, and pastoral concern. Ibid.

### Chapter Twelve

He celebrates Nicetius’s fortress situated above the Moselle, [Col. 1345] as well as Nicetius’s zeal and elegance in adorning and fortifying it. 135

### Chapter Thirteen

He praises Magneric, bishop of Trier, for his virtue and diligence in governing his church, for his courtesy toward everyone, and for his generosity toward the needy and guests. 137

### Chapter Fourteen

A description of the city of Metz. The manifold virtues of its bishop, Villicus, to whom he writes, are celebrated. 138

### Chapter Fifteen

A quatrain addressed to the same man. 139

### Chapter Sixteen

A couplet addressed to the same man. Ibid.

### Chapter Seventeen

Taking occasion from a painting in which a bird was plucking grapes with its beak, he extols Villicus’s generosity toward his guests. Ibid.

### Chapter Eighteen

Taking occasion from the fish that had been abundantly served at Villicus’s table, he commends his heavenly calling. 140

### Chapter Nineteen

He praises Charentinus, bishop of Cologne, for his charity and gentle manners, as well as for his generosity toward churches. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty

The pastoral diligence, eloquence, and beneficence of Aegidius, bishop of Rheims. 141

### Chapter Twenty-One

He sends a greeting to Hilary, the bishop, and declares his remembrance and affection for him in his absence. 142

### Chapter Twenty-Two

Writing to Bishop Bertichramnus, he praises his benevolence toward everyone, especially toward himself, since Bertichramnus had received him into his carriage. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Three

He tells Bertichramnus that he had received the poems he had composed by night-work, praising part of the work and criticizing part of it. 143

### Chapter Twenty-Four

Writing to Bishop Agricola, he commemorates the benefits Agricola’s father had conferred upon him, asking that the son nourish and complete what his father’s diligence had sown in him. 144

### Chapter Twenty-Five

Writing to Felix, bishop of Bourges, he celebrates in verse the tower that Felix had arranged to be built for preserving the body of Christ. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Six

He celebrates the hospitality and pastoral diligence of Bishop Avitus, to whom he writes, and commemorates the gifts sent both to himself and to Agnes and Radegund. 145

### Chapter Twenty-Seven

To Avitus, who had strongly urged him to write some verses, he relates that he had satisfied him, saying that his own poverty of language was compensated by his good intentions. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Eight

Writing again to the same man, he celebrates his remarkable talent for winning hearts through affection, especially his generosity toward everyone and his goodwill toward Fortunatus himself. 146

### Chapter Twenty-Nine

He praises the beneficence, pastoral virtues, and generosity toward churches of Agericus, bishop of Verdun. 147

### Chapter Thirty

The same Agericus’s remarkable learning, contempt for the world, innocence, and generosity. Ibid.

### Chapter Thirty-One

He writes to the priest Amphio, praising his pious and gentle manners, prudence, firmness of spirit, and hospitality. 148

### Chapter Thirty-Two

He praises the holiness of Pater, the abbot to whom he writes. He then asks pardon if some error has slipped into the manuscript that he had undertaken to correct at Pater’s command. 149

### Chapter Thirty-Three

From the coastal region where he lived, Fortunatus sends greetings to the deacon Draco and declares his goodwill toward him. Ibid.

### Chapter Thirty-Four

He thanks the archdeacon of Meaux, who, although not yet known to him by sight, had sent him new wine. 150

### Chapter Thirty-Five

About to undertake a journey, he sends this poem to the deacon John, through whom he sends greetings to their common friends. Ibid.

### Chapter Thirty-Six

Fortunatus excuses himself to Anthemius because, so as not to disturb his sleep, he had departed without greeting him. Ibid.

### Chapter Thirty-Seven

He urges the deacon Sindulf to patience, affirming that nothing is difficult for one who loves. 151

## Book Four of Miscellanies

Ibid.

### Chapter One

He praises the already deceased Evemerius, bishop of Nantes, for his nobility, gentleness, and universal charity. Ibid.

### Chapter Two

He praises Gregory, bishop of Langres, although deceased, for his lineage, pastoral virtues, and miracles. 153

### Chapter Three

Likewise, an epitaph for Tetricus, bishop of Langres. After praising his pastoral virtues, he commemorates the goodwill of kings and people toward him. 154

### Chapter Four

Likewise, an epitaph for Gallus, bishop of Clermont: his contempt for the world from childhood, Theodoric’s goodwill toward him, and his pastoral virtues. Ibid.

### Chapter Five

He warmly praises Ruricius the elder and Ruricius the younger, both bishops of Limoges and both deceased, affirming their holiness. 156

### Chapter Six

Likewise, an epitaph for Exotius, bishop of Limoges: [Col. 1346] his chastity, patience, and charity, and the pious affection of the people toward him. 157

### Chapter Seven

He mourns the premature death of his friend Calactericus, bishop of Chartres, and celebrates his virtues. 159

### Chapter Eight

He praises Chronopius, deceased in the see of Périgueux, for his lineage, character, eloquence, charity, and pastoral care. 160

### Chapter Nine

He praises Leontius, deceased in the see of Bordeaux, celebrating the people’s love and longing for him. 161

### Chapter Ten

Likewise, an epitaph for Leontius the younger, bishop of Bordeaux. 162

### Chapter Eleven

The diligence of Victorinus, the deceased abbot, in multiplying monks, his constancy in prayer, and his miracles are praised. 163

### Chapter Twelve

He praises Hilary, the deceased priest, for his lineage and describes his priestly virtues; he commemorates the services performed by his mother-in-law Evantia in memory of the dead man. 164

### Chapter Thirteen

An epitaph for Servilio, who had once been a court official and had properly administered the royal resources; later, having become a priest, he proved generous toward widows and orphans. Ibid.

### Chapter Fourteen

He commends Praesidius, the deceased abbot, for the sanctity of his teaching and his pastoral diligence. 165

### Chapter Fifteen

He mourns the deacon Bobolenus, who, while indulging in sleep, was killed by an assassin’s axe-blow. Ibid.

### Chapter Sixteen

He accompanies the funeral of Atticus, who had died worn out by old age, in this poem, and exalts his qualities, renowned throughout Gaul. 166

### Chapter Seventeen

He honors in a funeral poem Arcadius, still a young man, carried off by premature death. Ibid.

### Chapter Eighteen

He praises the deceased Basil for his eloquence, learning, and generosity; he commemorates the embassies he undertook to Spain and his innocence in the administration of public offices, and shows how dear he had been to kings and peoples. 167

### Chapter Nineteen

He mourns Aracharius, who had been distinguished at the royal court and dear and pleasing to the king, carried off by death while still in the flower of his age. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty

He follows with a mournful poem Brumachius, a powerful man overcome by death on the journey as he returned to Gaul from the embassy he had completed. He praises him for eloquence and prudence and at the same time commends the diligence of his wife, Phrygia, in caring for her husband’s funeral. 168

### Chapter Twenty-One

He praises Avolus for his piety and religious devotion toward sacred buildings, his generosity toward the poor, and his munificence toward fellow citizens. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Two

He honors in a funeral poem the tomb of the children who, as it seems, had been born in a single birth: one died earlier, the other at five years of age, and both had been placed in the same tomb as their mother. 169

### Chapter Twenty-Three

He praises Julianus, who had once practiced commerce and afterward had spent his accumulated wealth on guests and the needy, now deceased. He commends the affection and care of his son John toward his dead father. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Four

He praises Orientius, who had held a leading position of dignity and favor at the king’s court, after his death, for prudence, justice, and moderation. He then displays the concern of his wife Nicatia in caring for her husband’s funeral and honoring his memory. 170

### Chapter Twenty-Five

He splendidly praises Queen Theodechild, now deceased, for her royal descent and connections, her generosity toward the poor, and her munificence toward churches. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Six

He laments Vilithuta, a noble woman, though descended from a barbarian people and family, who died in childbirth together with her child. He briefly discusses the final judgment and then attempts to console her surviving husband with the happiness Vilithuta now enjoys. 172

### Chapter Twenty-Seven

He rejoices that Euphrasia, a woman of the highest nobility and rich in good works, had exchanged this mortal life for immortality. He celebrates her charity and nobility. 176

### Chapter Twenty-Eight

He laments in this mournful poem the death of Eusebia, who had died prematurely at the age of ten, already betrothed to a husband. 177

## Book Five of Miscellanies

Ibid.

### Chapter One

He compares the virtues of Martin, bishop of Galicia, to the delights of paradise. Having received a letter from him, he declares how much joy he had felt, and incidentally praises his eloquence and learning. He commends himself, as well as Agnes and Radegund, to Martin’s prayers. Ibid.

### Chapter Two

Writing to the same man, he says that, just as various regions of the world had been assigned to the apostles, so Galicia had been divinely given to Martin, in order that he might sow there the truth of Catholic [Col. 1347] doctrine. He commends himself, as well as Agnes and Radegund, to his prayers. 181

### Chapter Three

Writing to the people of Tours, he treats in this poem Gregory, bishop of Tours, as he arrives in his church, and from Gregory’s presence, teaching, and vigilance he predicts every blessing for the people of Tours. 184

### Chapter Four

On the birthday of Bishop Gregory. 185

### Chapter Five

He replies to Gregory of Tours, who had strongly urged him to celebrate in verse the remarkable deed of Avitus, bishop of Clermont, in converting more than five hundred Jews to Christ Jesus. He writes that he has satisfied Gregory by sending the poem appended to this letter. 186

### Chapter Six

Writing to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, Fortunatus relates that, after he himself had long since grown unused to composing poems, a father suddenly appeared before him, suffering grievously on behalf of his captive son, and that this father had shaken him out of his sluggishness and idleness. He therefore commends the case of this father and wretched son to Syagrius. He sends an acrostic poem about the Redeemer. 191

### Chapter Seven

The poem mentioned in the preceding letter. 195

### Chapter Eight

He replies to Felix, bishop of Nantes, who had invited him to the countryside. He describes the location and pleasantness of Felix’s estate; nevertheless, he prefers Felix’s own presence and appearance to it. 197

### Chapter Nine

He congratulates Gregory on his return to Tours from a journey and commends himself and the bearer of the letter to him. 198

### Chapter Ten

He greets Gregory by sending a poem and praises his virtue and learning. He excuses the brevity of the letter and affirms that it is compensated by the greatness of his affection. Ibid.

### Chapter Eleven

He thanks Gregory for certain poems, apparently written by Gregory and lent to him, and commends the bearer of the letter. Ibid.

### Chapter Twelve

To Gregory, who had invited him to Tours, he offers the excuse that another bishop was preventing him from going. He then asks Gregory, out of his concern for peace, to forgive him for not coming. 199

### Chapter Thirteen

He writes to Gregory, praising his virtue, and likewise commends to him a woman whom Gregory had recommended and who was returning to him. Ibid.

### Chapter Fourteen

He declares his affection for Gregory and announces that he had arrived safely at Poitiers, although, after departing from the city of Tours, he had made a difficult and dangerous journey over roads covered with ice. Ibid.

### Chapter Fifteen

Writing to the same man, he praises his virtue and learning and also attests his own goodwill toward him. 200

### Chapter Sixteen

He thanks Gregory for sending him apples with their shoots. Ibid.

### Chapter Seventeen

When Fortunatus had come to the place where stood the tree that had once been uprooted and, through the prayers and power of Saint Martin, had blossomed again, and from which the sick sought healing, he stopped, moved by the tears of certain parents who were lamenting miserably that their daughter had been taken from them. He therefore relates the matter to Gregory and implores his help and authority so that the abducted daughter may be restored to her parents. Ibid.

### Chapter Eighteen

He praises Gregory’s piety and commends both himself and a traveling stranger to him. 201

### Chapter Nineteen

He celebrates Gregory’s qualities and again commends himself to him. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty

Having received Gregory’s letter announcing that he was enjoying good health, he shows how greatly he had rejoiced and asks Gregory to be more expansive in writing. 202

### Chapter Twenty-One

He commends to the bishops a traveler of Italian nationality who was returning to Italy, so that they might supply him with the necessary provisions and other assistance for completing his journey. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Two

He says that he communicates by letter with Aredius, the abbot, whom he could not meet in person, and earnestly commends himself to his prayers. Ibid.

## Book Six of Miscellanies

203

### Chapter One

He celebrates the marriage of King Sigebert and Brunhild, daughter of Athanagild. He declares the joy that arose throughout the kingdom from this marriage and the royal generosity displayed in celebrating it. 203

### Chapter Two

He sings an epithalamium on the marriage of Sigebert and Brunhild. First praising Sigebert’s chastity, he then introduces Cupid and Venus, representing them as competing with each other in proclaiming the praises of Sigebert and Brunhild respectively. Finally, he predicts good fortune for both. 204

### Chapter Three

He sets forth at length Sigebert’s virtues and military praises and rejoices that his wife Brunhild had been converted from Arian error to the truth of Catholic doctrine. 208

[Col. 1348]

### Chapter Four

He lists and extols Charibert’s manifold qualities. 210

### Chapter Five

He splendidly praises Queen Theodechild for the nobility of her royal family, her courtesy and generosity toward the needy, and her munificence toward sacred buildings. 213

### Chapter Six

He commends Bertechild, or Berthild, a religious woman, for her chastity, generosity toward the needy and captives, and disdain for transient things. 214

### Chapter Seven

In this poem he mourns the bitter death of Celeswintha, daughter of Athanagild and wife of Chilperic. He also describes the tears of her mother, Goiswintha, and the grief and most bitter lamentations of others at Celeswintha’s funeral. 215

### Chapter Eight

He describes the pleasantness of the gardens once planted by King Childebert and then held by his wife Ultrogotha; from this he takes occasion to celebrate Childebert’s praises. 226

### Chapter Nine

When Fortunatus had come to the estate called Canto, he wittily describes his greediness in eating apples. Ibid.

### Chapter Ten

When Fortunatus had come to Mettin, he relates that the royal cook had unjustly taken from him the small boat in which he was traveling. He humorously describes the cook’s appearance and office. He then commemorates the kindness and generosity shown toward him by Sigebert and his ministers, Gogo and Papulus. 227

### Chapter Eleven

He declares his goodwill and longing for Dynamium in his absence and demands from him, in the name and by the right of friendship, a similar remembrance of himself. Finally, he urges him to return to him. 229

### Chapter Twelve

In midsummer Fortunatus had arranged to have a vein opened. He therefore complains to Dynamium that his hand was hindered from writing poems. He testifies at length to his goodwill toward him. Ibid.

## Book Seven of Miscellanies

231

### Chapter One

He praises Gogo for his eloquence, generosity, prudence, evenness of temper, piety, and physical beauty. He commends King Sigebert’s judgment in selecting him as one of his ministers. Ibid.

### Chapter Two

He commemorates Gogo’s benefits toward him and excuses himself to him for not coming when invited to dinner. 234

### Chapter Three

Fortunatus clears himself before Gogo, shifting onto Gogo the blame that Gogo had assigned to him; nevertheless, he shows that the grace of their friendship remains unharmed and complete. Ibid.

### Chapter Four

The poet asks the clouds and winds what Gogo is doing and where he is staying. He then sends greetings to Gogo through them. 235

### Chapter Five

He praises Duke Bodegisil for the sweetness and grace of his speech, the courtesy of his character and disposition, and the provinces he administered with loyalty, justice, and innocence; he then commends his other virtues. 237

### Chapter Six

In this poem Fortunatus praises Paliatina, daughter of Gallomagnus and wife of Godegisil, commending her outstanding beauty, joined with equal intelligence and sweetness of speech. 239

### Chapter Seven

He praises Duke Lupus, listing his manifold virtues and qualities; he declares Lupus’s services to Sigebert and Sigebert’s goodwill toward him. 240

### Chapter Eight

In this poem Fortunatus declares the joy he had felt on receiving news that Lupus was safe and well; he then gathers together Lupus’s virtues and excellent praises. 243

### Chapter Nine

He thanks Lupus for the letters and gifts sent to him. He commemorates his departure from Italy and complains that in the meantime no letters had reached him from his relatives; he says that Lupus had taken their place in affection toward him. 245

### Chapter Ten

He praises Magnulfus, Lupus’s brother, for his knowledge of law and fairness in governing peoples. He then excuses the brevity of his letter. 246

### Chapter Eleven

He reproaches Jovinus, governor of a province, for his prolonged silence and delay in replying. He asks him, since he is less able to enjoy Jovinus’s presence and appearance, at least to relieve and console his longing by sending letters. 247

### Chapter Twelve

He describes the brevity and emptiness of human life, affirming that only piety survives all mortal things and is far superior to them. From this he reproaches and gently rebukes Jovinus for sending him no letters during so brief a life, although he indicates that he eagerly awaits them. Ibid.

### Chapter Thirteen

He says that he approaches Felix, distinguished in poetic praise, timidly and reluctantly. Nevertheless, relying on the bond of the companionship they had shared and on their common homeland, he addresses him in the following poem. 250

### Chapter Fourteen

He relates that Mummulenus had received him as a guest [Col. 1349] during his journey. He wittily describes the harshness of his stomach, which he had contracted from an abundance of food, especially from eating peaches. He warmly commends Mummulenus himself. 251

### Chapter Fifteen

While waiting to be invited to lunch by Berulfus, Fortunatus relates that he had meanwhile suffered from a double hunger. Finally, he offers favorable and joyful omens for Berulfus. 252

### Chapter Sixteen

He praises Condon, a household official, for the honors he had earned through virtue and had attained step by step under various kings of Austrasia. 253

### Chapter Seventeen

Fortunatus excuses the brevity of his letter and affirms that scarcely any page could match the extent of his goodwill toward Gundoarius. He then praises Gundoarius. 254

### Chapter Eighteen

He commemorates his own attentiveness toward Flavus and his diligence in sending letters to him. He then amicably reproaches Flavus for sending him no letters and asks him to write back. 255

### Chapter Nineteen

He commends the affection and harmony of Flavus and Evodius, brothers of the same parents, joined by the same bodily likeness. He declares that he had been added as a third to them and asks that conversations by letter also be added to bind this affection more closely. 256

### Chapter Twenty

He declares his concern for Sigismund and asks him to inform him about the affairs of Italy and Germany as they then stood. 257

### Chapter Twenty-One

Having received a letter from the brothers Sigismund and Aregisilus, he declares what joy he had felt and predicts every good fortune for himself from their arrival in Gaul. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Two

He prays to the divine power for the safety and prosperity of the king and his ministers, among whom was Boso, auguring this from the flourishing condition of the kingdom and its king; he also predicts that Boso himself will long remain happy and safe. 258

### Chapter Twenty-Three

He praises Paternalus on the basis of the etymology of his name and commemorates his generosity toward him. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Four

Taking occasion from certain silver serving dishes and the words inscribed on them, Fortunatus commends to the reader integrity and purity of mind prompted by that work and material. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Five

He shows that a guest invited to a household’s ordinary and familiar meal had been lavishly received. 259

### Chapter Twenty-Six

He invites a certain poet away from serious cares to the festivity of a banquet. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Seven

From the brevity and frailty of life he commends the virtues of the spirit and heavenly delights. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Eight

He invites a certain person away from the noise and business of the law courts to the pleasure and security of a banquet. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Nine

He asks a guest, having laid aside his devotion to lawsuits and quarrels, to bring a free and tranquil mind to the banquet. Ibid.

### Chapter Thirty

He invites someone and demands that the courage he possesses in warfare be brought equally to the cups. He commends his banquet not so much for its food as for its goodwill. 260

### Chapter Thirty-One

He relates to Count Galactorius that he had often wished to become a sailor so that he might reach Bordeaux more quickly and visit him. He then prays for every good fortune for Lord Galactorius and asks him to commend Fortunatus to the bishop of Bordeaux. Ibid.

## Book Eight of Miscellanies

261

### Chapter One

Fortunatus writes generally to poets and orators, and specifically to Christians, about his circumstances and condition. Taking the opportunity, he splendidly praises Radegund, whose wishes and prayers, he says, had caused him to remain in Gaul. Finally, he invites each of them to send pious poems and letters to Radegund. Ibid.

### Chapter Two

As the day approached when he was to depart for Germanus, bishop of Paris, he says that his love for Radegund caused him in some way to hesitate. Although he would therefore be physically absent from Radegund, he affirms that he would always be present to her in spirit. 263

### Chapter Three

A hymn on the nativity of the Lord. 264

### Chapter Four

On Saint Mary. 265

### Chapter Five

Again on Saint Mary. 266

### Chapter Six

In this poem addressed to Agnes, the abbess, the choirs of heavenly spirits, the gatherings and festivals of other saints, are described. Radegund is praised. Christ is introduced among the saints proclaiming virginity, and its superiority to marriage is declared. 266

### Chapter Seven

He reviews the prophecies uttered concerning the Virgin’s childbirth and likewise reports other oracles concerning Christ, the fruit of her womb. He then pursues at greater length the praises of that Virgin, the Mother of God, and describes the obedience of the heavenly host and of all nature toward her. 276

### Chapter Eight

He praises virginity and describes the happiness and glory of virgins in heaven. From this he urges virgins to preserve chastity both of soul and of body. 284

### Chapter Nine

He commemorates the glory of the saints in heaven and [Col. 1350] asks their intercession, especially that of the most holy Mother of God, against the snares of the common enemy. Finally, he commends the majesty of the divine power. 285

### Chapter Ten

He praises Radegund for despising the world and kingdom and predicts that a reward equal to her piety and labors will await her in heaven. 286

### Chapter Eleven

He excuses himself to Radegund because he is sending her violets rather than lilies and roses as a gift. He commends the violets for the excellence of their color and fragrance and from this urges her, as well as Agnes, to cultivate virtue. Ibid.

### Chapter Twelve

He says that flower-bearing spring had arrived after winter and from this commends Radegund’s and Agnes’s zeal in adorning the altars, whose appearance and manifold variety he describes cheerfully and elegantly. 287

### Chapter Thirteen

He sends flowers to Radegund, excusing the smallness of the gift. Taking occasion from them, he raises her mind toward hope and contemplation of heavenly things. Ibid.

### Chapter Fourteen

As Radegund was about to withdraw into seclusion, he declares his longing for her. 288

### Chapter Fifteen

In this poem he congratulates Radegund, who had already returned from her withdrawal. With her return, he professes that everything had blossomed again for him and that the abundance of the whole year had been restored to him in her return. Ibid.

### Chapter Sixteen

When Fortunatus was suffering from a fever in the countryside, he relates that Leo the priest had been sent to him by Gregory of Tours to invite him to celebrate the sacred festivals of Saint Martin. He describes his illness and reports that it subsided once perspiration appeared. Ibid.

### Chapter Seventeen

In this poem Fortunatus implores Gregory’s help against a serious difficulty that, it seems, had intruded into the monastery at Poitiers. 289

### Chapter Eighteen

Fortunatus commends the same matter to Gregory as in the preceding poem, sending his fellow priest to him, and asks, by the vows and memory of blessed Radegund, that Gregory come to the aid of the monastery’s afflicted circumstances. Ibid.

### Chapter Nineteen

Fortunatus writes this poem in the person and under the name of Justina. Through her he asks Gregory to commend her to her father and to thank her grandmother because she had come to visit her. 290

### Chapter Twenty

Having received a letter from Gregory and learned of his good health, Fortunatus declares that he had rejoiced especially on that account and commends himself to him. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-One

He praises Gregory’s virtue, renown, and pastoral concern. 291

### Chapter Twenty-Two

He declares his own attentiveness and devotion toward Gregory and commends himself to his prayers. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Three

To the same man. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Four

He says that no eloquence is so great that it could adequately thank Gregory for his generosity toward him. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Five

He thanks Gregory for assigning him a field to cover his personal expenses. He then describes the field itself. 292

### Chapter Twenty-Six

He likewise gives thanks for the gift of part of a small field and extols Gregory’s generosity. Ibid.

### Chapter Twenty-Seven

He declares his joy at receiving Gregory’s letters. He gratefully mentions the snow-white hides sent to him for use as footwear. Ibid.

## Book Nine of Miscellanies

293

### Chapter One

He addresses the fathers of the council of Brinnacium and asks their permission to speak of Chilperic’s praises, whom he celebrates with lavish eulogies of every kind. Ibid.

### Chapter Two

A consolatory poem to Chilperic and Fredegund on the death of their children. 298

### Chapter Three

From the appearance of approaching spring and the joys of the Easter festivals, he urges Chilperic and Fredegund, having laid aside all grief, to return to cheerfulness. 303

### Chapter Four

On the death of Chlodobert, whom he praises, denying that his death ought to be mourned because he died young and innocent. Ibid.

### Chapter Five

An epitaph for Dagobert, another son of Chilperic and Fredegund, whom he calls fortunate because he died scarcely baptized. 304

### Chapter Six

He sends poems to Gregory, asking for time to prepare the Sapphic verses that had been demanded of him. 305

### Chapter Seven

He sends Sapphic verses to Gregory. He commemorates a little book sent to him by Gregory, which he professes barely to have understood. Finally, he addresses his own little book and orders it to go to Gregory. Ibid.

### Chapter Eight

He greets Bishop Baudowald, distinguished by his rank of dignity, cultivation of studies, and learning, and flourishing in piety; he commends himself to his prayers. 307

### Chapter Nine

He congratulates Sidonius, appointed to the church of Mainz, which had already been deprived of its shepherd, and his
mentioning dowries. 308

CHAPTER X.—He thanks Ragnemundus, in the name of Radegund and Agnes, for the serving dish of Parian marble that he had sent, and for the gems that he had sent as a gift to adorn the holy cross of the monastery at Poitiers. 308

CHAPTER XI.—He praises the abbot Droctoveus, disciple and imitator of Saint Germanus of Paris. 310

CHAPTER XII.—Writing to Faramundus, he says that he meets him through his letters, since he could not do so in person; he asks him to commend him to the kings and to write back to him. Ibid.

CHAPTER XIII.—He greets the deacons Lupus and Waldo with the greatest affection, praying that they commend him to the kings and to others. Ibid.

CHAPTER XIV.—He relates that the martyr Laurence, who while alive had become renowned for miracles and virtues, continued to assist the people even after his death. He says that, in the basilica being constructed in his honor, a beam that had already been cut grew again, and that pieces removed from it restored sight to the eyes of the blind. 311

CHAPTER XV.—He declares that, because of the excellence of its workmanship, a certain wooden building is far superior in his estimation to bronze and stone buildings. A description of the building follows. 312

CHAPTER XVI.—The praises of Duke Chrodinus. Ibid.

THE FOUR BOOKS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MARTIN. 363

ON THE DESTRUCTION OF THURINGIA. 427

BOOK ONE.—Fortunatus describes the destruction of Thuringia under the persona and in the name of Radegund. Radegund is introduced mourning her brother, who was unjustly killed. Finally, she addresses this work and asks it to carry greetings to her exiled relatives. Ibid.

BOOK TWO.—Fortunatus begins this poem of his with the glory of the Holy Trinity; then he continues with the praises of the Emperor Justin. Next he praises the Empress Sophia, recalling that Radegund had received from her, as a gift, a portion of the Lord’s cross. 431

BOOK THREE.—Radegund expresses her grief over the destruction of Thuringia and the ruin of her people. Then she says that the hope she had placed in her brother and her cousin Hamelfred had perished together with them; she mourns their fate most bitterly. 433
